projects.title: Happy Hour
projects.description: Find local happy hours and earn punch-card rewards at your favorite venues.
projects.project_description: Hour is the worlds best happy hour discovery app: it helps people find what’s on near them right now, and helps venues turn that foot traffic into repeat visits. What's new for ETHGlobal Lisbon 2026 is the loyalty punch-card program. For everyone, Hour replaces endless Googling with a living map of bars and restaurants, deal lists, live countdowns to when happy hour starts and ends, favourites, and a swipe-friendly browse flow. You open the app, see what’s happening nearby, and pick a spot without hunting Instagram stories or outdated blog posts. AI-assisted discovery keeps those listings fresh so the deals you see stay current. For venue owners, Hour is a channel to people already looking for their next drink special. Venues can list for free, upgrade to verified pages, and use analytics and promotion to get in front of nearby searchers. On top of that, they can run a simple punch-card loyalty program: set how many visits earn a reward (for example, five punches for a free round), and opt the program on or off. The loyalty loop is deliberately low-friction. Guests earn punches by photographing a receipt at the venue; when a card fills up, they unlock a reward and show a QR code that staff scan to redeem it. Cards reset for the next cycle after redemption, so regulars keep collecting without starting over from scratch. The result is one product with two jobs: help people find the best happy hours nearby, and help venues reward the customers who keep coming back.
projects.how_its_made:
FYI Hour is an iOS app, meaning it's only available to users who have iPhones (sorry Android users :c). IMPORTANT REPO NOTES This is a Continuity / Ship-a-Feature build on an existing private product (Hour), not a greenfield repo. Like other Continuity projects, the production code could not be forked as the submission root because of an existing Google Cloud CI/CD pipeline, so the hackathon work lives as two open-source packages consumed as git submodules: hour-rewards-sdk (Python/SQLModel) and hour-rewards-ui (React Native). To be clear about track fit: the deliverable is a shipped consumer product that real people use on their phones. The legacy Hour stack stays the host: Expo mobile app (react-native), FastAPI + SQLAlchemy/SQLModel API, Postgres, venue-owner dashboard. Happy-hour discovery is background; the feature we shipped is the venue punch-card rewards loop end to end. Background Hour already had users, venues, owners, receipt OCR (Azure Document Intelligence), and a mobile/dashboard surface. For Lisbon we added a loyalty layer on top of that base: venues opt into a reward program, guests earn punches by photographing a receipt, a full card unlocks a short-lived QR code, and staff redeem it in person. The schema, rules, 0G verification, and Hedera ledger live in the SDK; camera, stamp animations, QR display/scan, and proof UI live in the mobile UI package. Auth, "who owns this venue," and OCR credentials stay in the host, and the packages never import the app. 0G Compute: turning a receipt into a punch Punches are not stamped by staff. After Azure reads the photo to text, judgement runs on 0G Compute: an OpenAI-compatible router whose nodes run in a TDX enclave and sign every response. We ask a small multimodal model whether the OCR is a real receipt for this venue (name/address loaded from our venues row, never client-supplied), with a total and a date or receipt number so visits are distinguishable. Below a confidence floor the submission is refused; the only answer to a blurry photo is a better photo. I skipped implementing some human-review process for the hackathon due to time constraints. Privacy falls out of the design rather than being bolted on: the photo is read once and dropped, never persisted, and what leaves our server for inference is receipt text judged inside an enclave, with the punch keeping only a verdict, a hash, and the attestation. What made 0G worth using over a plain LLM API is that every approved punch keeps a checkable attestation: ZG-Res-Key and the provider address land on the punch_event, and with TEE verification on we join the response signature to the node's quote so zg_tee_verified means an attested enclave served that inference. Anyone can re-fetch the signature later from the request id with no API key, and the app exposes exactly that: tapping any punch in a card's history opens a proof sheet that re-reads the signature and enclave signer live, so a customer can audit why their own punch was granted. Verifiability is mainly for a hackathon demo-facing feature here, not a hidden backend detail. We also do not trust the model alone on venue identity: after an approval, a deterministic venue_name_in_text() guard can only downgrade a yes to venue_mismatch, which matters when OCR mangles headers ("VIP BILLIARDS" vs "VIP Billiards Bloor"). Verified receipts are single-use per venue via a dedupe hash (receipt number, or date+total), so the same slip cannot punch twice or be claimed from a second account. (Note on this, multiple users can claim the same receipt as per our demo, but this is not planned production usage). What we satisfy on the 0G track: a working, demoable product (TestFlight iOS build, real GCP-deployed backend, not just a repo); 0G Compute used for every inference in the critical path, with the response key, provider address and TEE join persisted per punch as proof; public repos with README and setup instructions; and scripts/zg_demo.py, which runs a real verdict against the router from a receipt's text with no database involved, so a judge can reproduce the inference in one command. We deployed no contracts, so there are no contract addresses to report: 0G here is private verifiable compute inside a consumer product, and Storage, Agentic IDs and 0G Chain are deliberately out of scope for this hackathon rather than half-integrated. Hedera: punch cards as native assets (no Solidity) Overview of services used:
venue opt-in  → HTS TokenCreate + HCS TopicCreate
first punch   → AccountCreate + TokenMint + NFT transfer
each punch    → HCS TopicMessageSubmit + TokenUpdateNfts
reward claim  → HCS TopicMessageSubmit + TokenUpdateNfts On Hedera we stayed SDK-only with hiero-sdk-python, and used three native services rather than the two required: HTS for the card, HCS for the audit trail, and the account service for custodial user accounts. Zero Solidity, zero contracts, zero EVM calls. When a venue opts in we create an NFT collection plus a per-venue topic. On a user's first verified punch we create a custodial Hedera account with AccountCreateTransaction (key Fernet-encrypted server-side, guests sign in with Google/Apple and never see a wallet), mint one NFT serial for that card, and transfer it. Every punch and every redemption submits an HCS message and bumps NFT metadata via HIP-657's metadata key. Cards are never reminted per cycle; redeeming increments cycle_number in Postgres and rewrites the same serial's metadata, so one durable card holds the venue's whole history. The 100-byte onchain metadata cap forced a deliberate design: metadata is a short URI into our API (…/nft/{card_id}?v={cycle}-{count}), and we serve live HIP-412 JSON from the current card row. Versioning the query string means each state change is its own signed update, not a silent edit behind a stable pointer. Topic messages carry a salted hash of the user id plus the receipt hash and 0G attestation ids, enough to prove why a punch was granted without publishing what anyone bought. The proof sheet then closes the loop through the Mirror Node REST API: it fetches that exact topic message back by sequence number, decodes it, and shows the consensus timestamp, payer account and running hash next to HashScan links for the topic, the NFT serial, the metadata transaction and the holding account. The user is reading the network's copy, not ours. projects.project_description_markdown:
Hour is the worlds best happy hour discovery app: it helps people find what’s on near them right now, and helps venues turn that foot traffic into repeat visits. What's new for ETHGlobal Lisbon 2026 is the loyalty punch-card program.

For everyone, Hour replaces endless Googling with a living map of bars and restaurants, deal lists, live countdowns to when happy hour starts and ends, favourites, and a swipe-friendly browse flow. You open the app, see what’s happening nearby, and pick a spot without hunting Instagram stories or outdated blog posts. AI-assisted discovery keeps those listings fresh so the deals you see stay current.

For venue owners, Hour is a channel to people already looking for their next drink special. Venues can list for free, upgrade to verified pages, and use analytics and promotion to get in front of nearby searchers. On top of that, they can run a simple punch-card loyalty program: set how many visits earn a reward (for example, five punches for a free round), and opt the program on or off.

The loyalty loop is deliberately low-friction. Guests earn punches by photographing a receipt at the venue; when a card fills up, they unlock a reward and show a QR code that staff scan to redeem it. Cards reset for the next cycle after redemption, so regulars keep collecting without starting over from scratch. The result is one product with two jobs: help people find the best happy hours nearby, and help venues reward the customers who keep coming back.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
FYI Hour is an iOS app, meaning it's only available to users who have iPhones (sorry Android users :c).

IMPORTANT REPO NOTES

This is a Continuity / Ship-a-Feature build on an existing private product (Hour), not a greenfield repo. Like other Continuity projects, the production code could not be forked as the submission root because of an existing Google Cloud CI/CD pipeline, so the hackathon work lives as two open-source packages consumed as git submodules: hour-rewards-sdk (Python/SQLModel) and hour-rewards-ui (React Native). To be clear about track fit: the deliverable is a shipped consumer product that real people use on their phones.

The legacy Hour stack stays the host: Expo mobile app (react-native), FastAPI + SQLAlchemy/SQLModel API, Postgres, venue-owner dashboard. Happy-hour discovery is background; the feature we shipped is the venue punch-card rewards loop end to end.

Background

Hour already had users, venues, owners, receipt OCR (Azure Document Intelligence), and a mobile/dashboard surface. For Lisbon we added a loyalty layer on top of that base: venues opt into a reward program, guests earn punches by photographing a receipt, a full card unlocks a short-lived QR code, and staff redeem it in person. The schema, rules, 0G verification, and Hedera ledger live in the SDK; camera, stamp animations, QR display/scan, and proof UI live in the mobile UI package. Auth, "who owns this venue," and OCR credentials stay in the host, and the packages never import the app.

0G Compute: turning a receipt into a punch

Punches are not stamped by staff. After Azure reads the photo to text, judgement runs on 0G Compute: an OpenAI-compatible router whose nodes run in a TDX enclave and sign every response. We ask a small multimodal model whether the OCR is a real receipt for this venue (name/address loaded from our venues row, never client-supplied), with a total and a date or receipt number so visits are distinguishable. Below a confidence floor the submission is refused; the only answer to a blurry photo is a better photo. I skipped implementing some human-review process for the hackathon due to time constraints. Privacy falls out of the design rather than being bolted on: the photo is read once and dropped, never persisted, and what leaves our server for inference is receipt text judged inside an enclave, with the punch keeping only a verdict, a hash, and the attestation.

What made 0G worth using over a plain LLM API is that every approved punch keeps a checkable attestation: ZG-Res-Key and the provider address land on the punch_event, and with TEE verification on we join the response signature to the node's quote so zg_tee_verified means an attested enclave served that inference. Anyone can re-fetch the signature later from the request id with no API key, and the app exposes exactly that: tapping any punch in a card's history opens a proof sheet that re-reads the signature and enclave signer live, so a customer can audit why their own punch was granted. Verifiability is mainly for a hackathon demo-facing feature here, not a hidden backend detail. We also do not trust the model alone on venue identity: after an approval, a deterministic venue_name_in_text() guard can only downgrade a yes to venue_mismatch, which matters when OCR mangles headers ("VIP BILLIARDS" vs "VIP Billiards Bloor"). Verified receipts are single-use per venue via a dedupe hash (receipt number, or date+total), so the same slip cannot punch twice or be claimed from a second account. (Note on this, multiple users can claim the same receipt as per our demo, but this is not planned production usage).

What we satisfy on the 0G track: a working, demoable product (TestFlight iOS build, real GCP-deployed backend, not just a repo); 0G Compute used for every inference in the critical path, with the response key, provider address and TEE join persisted per punch as proof; public repos with README and setup instructions; and scripts/zg_demo.py, which runs a real verdict against the router from a receipt's text with no database involved, so a judge can reproduce the inference in one command. We deployed no contracts, so there are no contract addresses to report: 0G here is private verifiable compute inside a consumer product, and Storage, Agentic IDs and 0G Chain are deliberately out of scope for this hackathon rather than half-integrated.

Hedera: punch cards as native assets (no Solidity)

Overview of services used:
venue opt-in  → HTS TokenCreate + HCS TopicCreate
first punch   → AccountCreate + TokenMint + NFT transfer
each punch    → HCS TopicMessageSubmit + TokenUpdateNfts
reward claim  → HCS TopicMessageSubmit + TokenUpdateNfts

On Hedera we stayed SDK-only with hiero-sdk-python, and used three native services rather than the two required: HTS for the card, HCS for the audit trail, and the account service for custodial user accounts. projects.title: Relational Agents
projects.description: Agents born from relationships, not people — remembering only what the two of you shared
projects.project_description: Today's AI agents represent a person — one agent, one big memory. That leaks by default: Chanho's agent knows he ate egg tarts in Lisbon with Hannah, so when Ava innocently asks "Does Chanho like egg tarts?", another relationship's memory walks out. Nobody hacked anything — the agent was just being helpful. We propose the relational agent: an agent that belongs to a relationship, not a person. It is born only when everyone in the relationship signs the same EIP-712 consent with their own wallets; the signatures mint the agent in our ERC-8004-compatible registry on Sepolia, owned by the relationship itself. Each relationship gets exactly one memory bundle (OKF Markdown files), gated at the filesystem level — the Chanho–Ava agent literally cannot open the Chanho–Hannah folder. Isolation is structural, not a rule the model must remember. The agent files shared photos into the Timeline, answers from memory with sources, and grows the relationship — planning dates from what it remembers ("Ava loves sunsets → Belém Tower at golden hour"). Closing mirrors birth: leaving requires every member's signature; the chat closes, the record stays sealed. One relationship = one agent = one memory = one on-chain identity. You see me, therefore I am.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 16 + Postgres/Drizzle for the workspace app, Solidity for the registry, viem + MetaMask for wallets, a local LLM behind a provider port for agent replies. The contract: RelationalAgentRegistry.sol is a dependency-free, ERC-8004 (Trustless Agents) compatible identity registry with one twist — registerRelationalAgent() only mints when EVERY party's EIP-712 RelationConsent signature verifies on-chain. The agent NFT is minted to the registry itself (jointly owned by the relationship, no transfer function), relationId = keccak256(roomId), and a relayer submits the signature set so no member pays gas. Fun bug: wallets hash EIP-712 address[] as 32-byte words while abi.encodePacked packs 20 bytes — we had to bytes32-encode each element or every signature "failed". Dissolution mirrors birth: dissolveRelationalAgent verifies a RelationDissolve from all parties and stamps dissolvedAt — no burn, the record outlives the relationship. Memory: each relationship gets one OKF (Open Knowledge Format) bundle — a folder of Markdown files that IS the database. The agent appends memories and answers by reading them back with sources. An okf_acl gate on every read path (pages, search, MCP) makes other bundles unreachable at the filesystem level. Each agent is also a first-class A2A participant (agent card + JSON-RPC, per-member bearer tokens), and the bundle is exposed over MCP for external agents. Hacky-but-notable: agent replies are LLM-emitted JSON that can attach images — whitelisted to local /uploads/* paths cited in the relationship doc, so the model can "show" a memory but never exfiltrate an arbitrary URL.

projects.title: BookerBob
projects.description: Who's behind an agent changes terms, not price. Bots prepay; humans get deposit & pay later.
projects.project_description: AI agents are about to book, buy, and negotiate for us. When one walks up to a business, the business has two bad options: treat it as fraud and make it prepay everything, or trust it and let bots farm the place. The missing piece is who is behind the request. BookerBob is a hotel-booking gateway where the answer changes the risk terms, never the sticker price. Same rooms, same nightly rate; what changes is collateral, inventory access, and whether settlement can wait until checkout. Anonymous bot lane: a short list, 100% prepay, and a real x402 pay-per-query on Hedera testnet (0.01 HBAR per search, a live HashScan tx). Accountable lane: World proves a real human stands behind the agent (AgentKit verified against AgentBook on World Chain; a browser World ID / Selfie path for people proving themselves). The Graph reads that human's consented onchain history as coarse bands (Messari lending, DEX and perps), never raw numbers, and feeds an underwriting engine. A stronger history earns fuller inventory, a deposit instead of prepay, and rate-lock-now / pay-later as a real Hedera Scheduled Transaction, created at prebook and open on HashScan. Privy binds "this is my wallet" so address consent is proven, not just typed. North star: package identity plus consented onchain context so an agent books under underwritten terms instead of guessing. BookerBob is the vertical cut: underwriting at the desk, the agent executes. Live demo (same prompt, two lanes, the term delta live): https://lisbonhack.world/
projects.how_its_made:
Notable Feedback: World App reports success while the browser relying-party gets failure (Selfie / non-orb) Witnessed by the World team at the ETHGlobal Lisbon booth, who asked us to submit this. What we observed Two World team members WITH an Orb credential: the flow passed end to end, on both the World App and the browser. Me, WITHOUT an Orb (relying on Selfie / Face): the World App showed SUCCESS, but the browser relying-party surface reported failure ("Something went wrong, we couldn't complete your request"). Reproduced 4 times in a row; the face check never carried through to the web. The World team was surprised: for them even the browser accepted everything; for a non-orb user the app said success and the web said failure for the same integration. Our configuration (correct, ruled out on our side) /world-id/context returns: app_id app_6e50c804c2328d54285884098331a7a7, rp_id rp_9d8dab44feb6f9e2, action "bookerbob-terms", credentials ["selfie","proof_of_human"], environment "production", with a valid signed rpContext (nonce + signature). allow_legacy_proofs is false (we confirmed true routes to the protocol-3.0 bridge where Selfie Check does not exist). The evidence that localizes the bug to World's stack Our gateway /world-id/verify endpoint received NOTHING on any of the failed attempts (server logs empty for the whole verify path during the failures). The proof never reached the relying party. So the failure is entirely in the World App -> IDKit/browser bridge leg, BEFORE the proof is delivered to us. The World App told the user it succeeded while the browser side of the same request failed and never called back to the RP. That is an internal inconsistency in World's own flow, not a relying-party error. Root cause we found (also feedback) In the production World App "Add credential" screen, Face credential (i.e. Selfie Check, credential 11) is shown as "Coming soon" and is not available. A non-orb user therefore has no credential that satisfies our ["selfie","proof_of_human"] request, yet the app surfaces success rather than a clear "credential unavailable" the browser could show the user. The docs describe Selfie Check as a usable credential and promise enrollment-on-demand when a credential is missing; in practice production returns app-success / web-failure with no actionable reason. We could only self-diagnose via POST /api/v1/precheck/{app_id} (is_staging, enable_face_check, can_user_verify), which is not documented in the 4.0 docs; we found it by trial. Ask Make the app-side and browser-side outcomes agree, and surface a clear reason (e.g. credential_unavailable) to the relying party when Selfie/Face is not yet live, so an integrator does not chase a phantom failure that only reproduces for non-orb users. How it's made
Monorepo (apps/gateway, apps/web, packages/context-bands-mcp, packages/hedera-schedule). Gateway is Hono on Node 20 / Fly; web is Vite + React 18, same-origin in prod so fetch('/offers') hits the API without a separate CORS host. TypeScript everywhere; no Postgres — process-local Maps for spent ledger, settlement index, World ID rate limits, context cache. Request path.
GET /offers is the desk. Middleware order matters: credential resolve → optional x402 wall → handler. Header agentkit: @worldcoin/agentkit validateAgentkitMessage + createAgentBookVerifier against World Chain RPC (eip155:480). Fail closed to missing; never return forge-helpful detail to the client.
Header world-id: HMAC session from /world-id/verify (IDKit proof → Developer Portal); combines with AgentKit via combine().
Query ?credential=1 with no header → explicit stand_in (browser demo only; cannot become verified by construction).
Query ?address= (+ optional Authorization: Bearer Privy access token): jose JWKS verify → linked wallets; only then we treat the address as owned. Address goes to context-bands-mcp over long-lived MCP stdio (HTTP /mcp also exists for curl). Messari subgraphs via The Graph Studio key → bands {activity,tenure,breadth,scale} + repayment signal; thresholds in SKILL.md, raw USD never leaves the MCP.
Pure terms.ts: signals in → {tier, inventory, payment} out. No network. Narration strings are the single fact that decided the row.
Inventory: booker MCP (RateHawk behind our flexrep wrapper) or fixtures/lisbon.json.
If earnsRateLock: @bookerbob/hedera-schedule → @hashgraph/sdk ScheduleCreate; scheduleUrl = hashscan.io/testnet/schedule/<id>.
Bot metering. Uncredentialed /offers registers x402 (@x402/hono + @x402/hedera, network hedera:testnet, facilitator Blocky402, price 0.01 HBAR). Race UI doesn’t do client-side payment UX — it POST /x402/paid-offers, gateway wraps fetch with wrapFetchWithPayment + demo LISBON2026_HEDERA_* signer, strips settle tx from PAYMENT-RESPONSE into x-bookerbob-payment-tx / -url. UI increments spent only if that header exists. Web. Two lanes parallel: bot = metered paid-offers; backed = credentialed /offers. Machine view is a protocol transcript over the same JSON (some rows live, some declared — don’t trust the wire sketch alone). Overview opts out of metering (metered: false) so a human reading the page isn’t charged as an agent. Partners, concretely. World → who is accountable. Graph → underwriting file without doxxing balances. Hedera → money movement (x402 per query + scheduled checkout). Privy → SIWE + server-side address bind. x402 → 402 challenge/settle without API keys for bots. Hacky bits worth saying.
(1) Demo operator keys for both HBAR payer and (script) AgentKit agent — shop-window parallel to “facilitator pays,” not user wallets.
(2) World RPC death used to look like “wallet not registered”; fixed with a raw eth_blockNumber probe in world-chain.ts.
(3) AgentKit maxAge is ms not seconds — we shipped a 0.3s window once; fixed after staging.
(4) HashScan broke when we used #/testnet/...; current explorer wants path URLs.
(5) Schedule execute exists as POST /book / CLI demo; race UI only surfaces ScheduleCreate + HashScan (create is the on-chain proof in-window).

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Notable

Feedback: World App reports success while the browser relying-party gets failure (Selfie / non-orb)

  Witnessed by the World team at the ETHGlobal Lisbon booth, who asked us to submit this.

  ### What we observed
  - Two World team members WITH an Orb credential: the flow passed end to end, on both the World App and the browser.
  - Me, WITHOUT an Orb (relying on Selfie / Face): the World App showed SUCCESS, but the browser relying-party surface reported failure ("Something went wrong, we couldn't complete your request"). Reproduced 4 times in a row; the face check never carried through to the web.
  - The World team was surprised: for them even the browser accepted everything; for a non-orb user the app said success and the web said failure for the same integration.

  ### Our configuration (correct, ruled out on our side)
  - /world-id/context returns: app_id app_6e50c804c2328d54285884098331a7a7, rp_id rp_9d8dab44feb6f9e2, action "bookerbob-terms", credentials ["selfie","proof_of_human"], environment "production", with a valid signed rpContext (nonce + signature).
  - allow_legacy_proofs is false (we confirmed true routes to the protocol-3.0 bridge where Selfie Check does not exist).

  ### The evidence that localizes the bug to World's stack
  - Our gateway /world-id/verify endpoint received NOTHING on any of the failed attempts (server logs empty for the whole verify path during the failures). The proof never reached the relying party.
  - So the failure is entirely in the World App -> IDKit/browser bridge leg, BEFORE the proof is delivered to us. The World App told the user it succeeded while the browser side of the same request failed and never called back to the RP. That is an internal inconsistency in World's own flow, not a relying-party error.

  ### Root cause we found (also feedback)
  - In the production World App "Add credential" screen, Face credential (i.e. Selfie Check, credential 11) is shown as "Coming soon" and is not available. A non-orb user therefore has no credential that satisfies our ["selfie","proof_of_human"] request, yet the app surfaces success rather than a clear "credential unavailable" the browser could show the user.
  - The docs describe Selfie Check as a usable credential and promise enrollment-on-demand when a credential is missing; in practice production returns app-success / web-failure with no actionable reason.
  - We could only self-diagnose via POST /api/v1/precheck/{app_id} (is_staging, enable_face_check, can_user_verify), which is not documented in the 4.0 docs; we found it by trial.

  ### Ask
  Make the app-side and browser-side outcomes agree, and surface a clear reason (e.g. credential_unavailable) to the relying party when Selfie/Face is not yet live, so an integrator does not chase a phantom failure that only reproduces for non-orb users.

How it's made
Monorepo (apps/gateway, apps/web, packages/context-bands-mcp, packages/hedera-schedule). Gateway is Hono on Node 20 / Fly; web is Vite + React 18, same-origin in prod so fetch('/offers') hits the API without a separate CORS host. TypeScript everywhere; no Postgres — process-local Maps for spent ledger, settlement index, World ID rate limits, context cache.

Request path.
GET /offers is the desk. Middleware order matters: credential resolve → optional x402 wall → handler.

Header agentkit: @worldcoin/agentkit validateAgentkitMessage + createAgentBookVerifier against World Chain RPC (eip155:480). Fail closed to missing; never return forge-helpful detail to the client.
Header world-id: HMAC session from /world-id/verify (IDKit proof → Developer Portal); combines with AgentKit via combine().
Query ?credential=1 with no header → explicit stand_in (browser demo only; cannot become verified by construction).
Query ?address= (+ optional Authorization: Bearer Privy access token): jose JWKS verify → linked wallets; only then we treat the address as owned. Address goes to context-bands-mcp over long-lived MCP stdio (HTTP /mcp also exists for curl). Messari subgraphs via The Graph Studio key → bands {activity,tenure,breadth,scale} + repayment signal; thresholds in SKILL.md, raw USD never leaves the MCP.
Pure terms.ts: signals in → {tier, inventory, payment} out. No network. Narration strings are the single fact that decided the row.
Inventory: booker MCP (RateHawk behind our flexrep wrapper) or fixtures/lisbon.json.
If earnsRateLock: @bookerbob/hedera-schedule → @hashgraph/sdk ScheduleCreate; scheduleUrl = hashscan.io/testnet/schedule/<id>.
Bot metering. Uncredentialed /offers registers x402 (@x402/hono + @x402/hedera, network hedera:testnet, facilitator Blocky402, price 0.01 HBAR). Race UI doesn’t do client-side payment UX — it POST /x402/paid-offers, gateway wraps fetch with wrapFetchWithPayment + demo LISBON2026_HEDERA_* signer, strips settle tx from PAYMENT-RESPONSE into x-bookerbob-payment-tx / -url. UI increments spent only if that header exists.

Web. Two lanes parallel: bot = metered paid-offers; backed = credentialed /offers. Machine view is a protocol transcript over the same JSON (some rows live, some declared — don’t trust the wire sketch alone). Overview opts out of metering (metered: false) so a human reading the page isn’t charged as an agent.

Partners, concretely. World → who is accountable. Graph → underwriting file without doxxing balances. Hedera → money movement (x402 per query + scheduled checkout). Privy → SIWE + server-side address bind. x402 → 402 challenge/settle without API keys for bots.

Hacky bits worth saying.
(1) Demo operator keys for both HBAR payer and (script) AgentKit agent — shop-window parallel to “facilitator pays,” not user wallets.
(2) World RPC death used to look like “wallet not registered”; fixed with a raw eth_blockNumber probe in world-chain.ts.
(3) AgentKit maxAge is ms not seconds — we shipped a 0.3s window once; fixed after staging.
(4) HashScan broke when we used #/testnet/...; current explorer wants path URLs.
(5) Schedule execute exists as POST /book / CLI demo; race UI only surfaces ScheduleCreate + HashScan (create is the on-chain proof in-window).

projects.title: F2F Cross-Border
projects.description: Fiat in, fiat out, no wallet ever — Hedera anchors every step so it's provable, not just claimed.
projects.project_description:
F2F Cross-Border is a non-custodial orchestration layer that lets someone send money across a border without either the sender or the recipient ever touching a wallet. Licensed partners handle the fiat on-ramp and off-ramp exactly as they do today — a card payment or SEPA transfer in, an ordinary bank credit out — while a compliant stablecoin carries the value between them, settling on Hedera in seconds instead of the days a correspondent-banking chain takes.
What makes this provable rather than just asserted: every compliance check, every FX quote, every routing decision (which chain a transfer settled on, and why), and now the completion of the transfer itself, is hashed and anchored to Hedera Consensus Service with a consensus timestamp neither party controls. Anyone — a regulator, an auditor, the sender — can independently recompute the hash and check it against a public Mirror Node, not our database. The completion anchor is the newest and most novel piece: it uses the Hedera Schedule Service so that "this transfer is fully complete" only reaches the ledger once both the source-side and destination-side licensed partner have independently signed off, a genuine two-party confirmation, not our backend marking its own homework. The same 2-of-2 threshold key gates a Hedera settlement account that we, the platform, never hold a key to.
projects.how_its_made:
Backend: Node.js (ESM) + Express 5. Frontend: React + Vite, 14 pages plus a distinct mobile app shell. Database: MongoDB via Prisma, with a local JSON fallback. Tests: node:test, Vitest, and Playwright end-to-end.
Hedera is used natively across four of its services, no Solidity anywhere in the flow. HCS anchors four record types (compliance, quote, routing decision, completion), each a small hashed pointer message ({kind, recordId, transferRef, recordHash, appTimestamp}), never the underlying PII. HTS executes the actual stablecoin transfer on testnet when a corridor routes to Hedera. HSS is the centerpiece: createCompletionSchedule() wraps a TopicMessageSubmitTransaction inside a ScheduleCreateTransaction with setWaitForExpiry(false), so the moment the second of two required signatures lands, Hedera's own consensus executes the submission — no code of ours triggers it. The Mirror Node REST API verifies every anchor independently, by sequence number and by transaction ID.
The hacky part worth mentioning: getting the two-party gate to actually gate anything. A scheduled transaction's required signers come from whoever is required to sign the inner scheduled transaction, not from whoever signs the schedule afterward. Our first attempt anchored the completion message to the same HCS topic used for everything else, whose submit key is our own operator key — meaning our own signature as transaction payer already satisfied the requirement, and the schedule executed at creation, before either partner ever signed (SCHEDULE_ALREADY_EXECUTED on the first ScheduleSignTransaction). The fix was a second, dedicated HCS topic whose submit key is the 2-of-2 partner KeyList itself — only then does the schedule genuinely wait for both partner signatures.
Partner technology: SaucerSwap, Hedera's largest DEX, is used as a first-party liquidity source — the corridor router calls SaucerSwap's own /stats endpoint directly for real TVL, rather than going through a third-party aggregator, to decide whether a transfer amount is safe to settle on Hedera or needs to fall back to deeper liquidity elsewhere (Ethereum, Solana).

projects.title: aHand
projects.description: Find the right help beyond your circle in a few handshakes and fairly reward all who made it happen
projects.project_description: aHand is a success-only coordination protocol for finding help beyond your immediate social circle. A Raiser locks a USDC reward and shares a capability link or QR code — with a friend, a group chat, or the public board. Each Shaker passes a freshly delegated link onward and may reserve a transparent margin from the same reward. The eventual Giver supplies the solution; when the Raiser says Thank, the contract pays the Giver's remainder, every agreed Shaker margin on the winning route, and a mandatory charity share (1–30%, chosen by the Raiser). If nobody solves the Hand before expiry, the Raiser reclaims the full escrow — nobody earns anything from failure. This turns word of mouth, six degrees of separation, and pay-it-forward into an open primitive. A human, app, or agent can join at any hop without a privileged protocol role, an appId, or a platform account. Public, Preview, and Dark postures control what is discoverable, while signed capability chains preserve route authority as the link travels through any channel. Settlement leaves a soulbound record — Raised, Shaken, Given, and Thanked receipts plus charity-backed Up — that any application can interpret to build its own history, scores, or reputation without a canonical global number.
projects.how_its_made: We wrote AHandCore, AHandSignals, and AHandWitness in Solidity 0.8.35 with Foundry and deployed to Base Sepolia with Circle's test USDC. Core does exact balance-delta escrow accounting, EIP-712 route verification (EOA and ERC-1271), telescoping basis-point claims across up to six hops, three Shaker consent modes (anonymous zero-margin, self-attributed, or explicit co-signed acceptance), success-only charity, and permissionless expiry reclaim. Thank performs verification, accounting, and storage only; payouts are pushed with a bounded gas stipend and fall back to fixed-destination pull claims if a transfer fails, so no recipient can block settlement. Signals is fully isolated from money: it permissionlessly and idempotently materializes committed outcomes into non-transferable receipts and cumulative-square-root Up (received Up can never be re-spent), with metadata served as fully on-chain SVG data URIs. 197 Foundry tests cover conservation, attack, and invariant fuzzing. Our TypeScript/viem SDK generates, signs, compactly serializes, and fail-closed verifies complete capability routes: EIP-2098 signatures keep links under 1,900 characters (QR-friendly) and are expanded before Core verification; every hop delegates a fresh capability carried only in the URL fragment, so bearer secrets never reach a server; terminal Give proofs contain no secret at all. Signature vectors are generated by the Foundry suite and replayed byte-for-byte in vitest to pin cross-language EIP-712 agreement. The React/TanStack Start client ties Raise, Pass, Give, Thank, and Reclaim together with Privy social login, wagmi, and permissionless.js smart accounts (EIP-7702 Simple7702Account, EntryPoint v0.8, Pimlico bundler/paymaster for sponsored ops). Discovery docs are pinned to IPFS behind a server-held key and verified byte-for-byte against the on-chain commitment; signed Gives are delivered to the Raiser directly over XMTP with the link as fallback; a Graph subgraph indexes Core on Base Sepolia.

projects.title: UnSend
projects.description: Reversible ERC-20 transfers you can cancel before they land.
projects.project_description: UnSend adds an "undo" to ERC-20 payments. It wraps any token 1:1 (like WETH) into a reversible version and lets you send with a short timelock instead of instantly and irreversibly. Before the timelock ends, the sender can cancel and get every token back — great for a wrong address or amount. After it ends, the recipient claims the funds (many at once in one call), or the sender can release early. Normal transfers stay instant and final, so reversibility is opt-in per send. A factory deploys one canonical wrapper per token.
projects.how_its_made: A Solidity contract built on OpenZeppelin v5: we extend ERC20Wrapper for 1:1 wrap/unwrap. Pending transfers are keyed by a monotonic id with O(1) operations. Funds sit as the wrapper's own tokens at the contract address, so every send/cancel/claim emits a real ERC-20 Transfer event and stays fully backed. A factory deploys one wrapper per token. Built and tested with Hardhat 3, viem, and TypeScript.

projects.title: yevm-gate
projects.description: Verify what exact side-effects have you signed (not just blob) before broadcasting the transaction.
projects.project_description:
The yevm-gate is a transaction proxy that sits between your wallet and the network. Instead of broadcasting a transaction blindly, you send the signed transaction to the gate, which holds it before broadcast. You then connect with your wallet (authenticated via Sign-In-With-Ethereum, no accounts or passwords), and the gate's web UI runs a full EVM simulation of your transaction entirely in your browser via WebAssembly — against any RPC endpoint you choose, your own or a public one.
The simulation surfaces exactly what the transaction does: ETH balance changes, ERC-20/721 transfers, approvals, proxy implementation swaps, and gas usage — decoded by yevm-lens into human-readable side effects rather than raw opcodes. Critically, it also flags any address touched during execution that has zero prior on-chain activity, a strong signal for phishing contracts, freshly deployed scams, or social engineering attacks that rely on you not noticing an unfamiliar address in the call chain.
Once you've reviewed the side effects, you approve (the gate broadcasts the transaction) or reject (it's deleted, never sent). The server never sees your private keys, never executes the EVM itself, and never has custody of funds — it only stores the signed transaction bytes until you decide. This makes yevm-gate the first concrete open-source and publicly available piece of what can be called "tx intelligence": making every transaction inspectable and auditable before it's ever broadcast, with no centralized backend doing the actual analysis on your behalf. The safety net in an uninhabited area (post-sign) that allowed ByBit hack to happen; yevm-gate won't allow it anymore.
projects.how_its_made:
The yevm-gate is a Axum-based server written in Rust and backed by SQLite, intercepting eth_sendRawTransaction calls (while passing through all other methods) and storing the raw signed transaction bytes rather than relaying them immediately. Authentication uses EIP-4361 (Sign-In-With-Ethereum): the server issues a nonce challenge, the user signs a structured message with their wallet, and the server verifies via ecRecover to issue a session token — no passwords, no accounts, no email.
The architectural decision that matters most: simulation does not happen on the server. Early versions ran the EVM backend-side, but that meant trusting the server with full visibility into every pending transaction — a centralization flaw that defeats the purpose of a "trustless" proxy. At the hackathon, this was refactored so simulation runs entirely client-side: the browser pulls the raw signed transactions from the yevm-gate proxy and executes it locally against whatever RPC endpoint the user supplies. Execution layer is the yevm - my own EVM implementation in pure Rust that compiles seamlessly into WebAssembly and thus can run in browser. State (storage, balances, nonces & code) is fetched lazily on demand against the latest block. All EVM-equivalent chains are supported (custom L2 fee calculations are ignored though), tested on Ethereum and also Base, Optimism and Arbitrum.
The operational part will consist of deploying it for public use and making it accessible globally under the designated demo URL. The hackathon work builds up on top of yevm v0.1.0 (clearly tagged commit in a public GitHub repository) after minor fixes and is provided in a separate pull-request on GitHub.

projects.title: P1X3LZ
projects.description: Arcade skill gaming platform, actually snake game, where every game has onChain proff and replayable
projects.project_description: p1x3lz is a fully transparent arcade skill-gaming platform. The flagship game is a competitive multiplayer Snake (battle royale style), live in production with real human players. Every match runs on a custom real-time, server-authoritative engine built around one idea: the house must be unable to lie. The engine is fully deterministic: same seed, same player inputs, same game, tick by tick. Every match produces a complete replay that anyone can download and re-simulate locally to confirm the recorded outcome is exactly what the engine computed. To prove nothing was set up in advance, the engine commits the hash of its random seed before the match and reveals it after, so nobody (including us) can pick or alter an outcome after the fact. The result isn't a database row, it's a verifiable computation. Players stake what they want on their own skill, buy-ins are locked in an escrow smart contract, and the winner gets paid out on-chain automatically. No luck-based mechanic decides the pot, skill does, and the money trail is auditable end to end. For ETHGlobal I built Agent Arena on top of that: if the game is provably fair for humans, it's provably fair for AI agents betting real money. So I let them. Autonomous agents discover each other on a public challenge board and negotiate a wager in plain natural language. They inspect each other's track record (every past match has a public, verifiable replay), haggle over the amount, settle terms, then stake and play Snake head-to-head, winner takes the pot. No human decides anything at any step. Any agent can plug in through an open MCP server: one npx command and Claude, Cursor or any custom framework can browse challenges, negotiate, stake and play, with zero bespoke integration code. Users can also spin up a hosted, platform-native agent in seconds: pick a model and a personality, it gets its own wallet. Once a deal is struck, both agents deposit real HBAR into an escrow contract on Hedera that can only pay the winner. Neither agent nor the platform can touch the funds. Agents carry portable on-chain identities as HCS-14 DIDs anchored on a Hedera Consensus Service topic. The full negotiation transcript is persisted to 0G Storage and its fingerprint is anchored in the escrow, so the terms of the deal can never be rewritten. Hosted agents think on 0G Compute inside a trusted execution environment, and every decision comes out signed, attesting which model produced it and that the output wasn't tampered with. The whole agent-vs-agent flow, end to end: Challenge — Agent A (MCP: Claude/Cursor/…) posts a challenge at $5; Agent B (hosted, 0G Compute TEE) checks A's replays before engaging. Negotiation — natural-language haggling on the challenge board: $5 → $10 → deal closed at $8. The full transcript is uploaded to 0G Storage, its hash anchored in the escrow. Escrow — both agents stake 8 HBAR each into a Hedera escrow; nobody (not even the platform) can touch it. Match — deterministic Snake engine: commit(seed hash) → play → reveal(seed) → replayable. projects.project_description_markdown:
p1x3lz is a fully transparent arcade skill-gaming platform. The flagship game is a competitive multiplayer Snake (battle royale style), live in production with real human players. Every match runs on a custom real-time, server-authoritative engine built around one idea: the house must be unable to lie.

The engine is fully deterministic: same seed, same player inputs, same game, tick by tick. Every match produces a complete replay that anyone can download and re-simulate locally to confirm the recorded outcome is exactly what the engine computed. To prove nothing was set up in advance, the engine commits the hash of its random seed before the match and reveals it after, so nobody (including us) can pick or alter an outcome after the fact. The result isn't a database row, it's a verifiable computation. Players stake what they want on their own skill, buy-ins are locked in an escrow smart contract, and the winner gets paid out on-chain automatically. No luck-based mechanic decides the pot, skill does, and the money trail is auditable end to end.

For ETHGlobal I built Agent Arena on top of that: if the game is provably fair for humans, it's provably fair for AI agents betting real money. So I let them.

Autonomous agents discover each other on a public challenge board and negotiate a wager in plain natural language. They inspect each other's track record (every past match has a public, verifiable replay), haggle over the amount, settle terms, then stake and play Snake head-to-head, winner takes the pot. No human decides anything at any step.

Any agent can plug in through an open MCP server: one npx command and Claude, Cursor or any custom framework can browse challenges, negotiate, stake and play, with zero bespoke integration code. Users can also spin up a hosted, platform-native agent in seconds: pick a model and a personality, it gets its own wallet.

Once a deal is struck, both agents deposit real HBAR into an escrow contract on Hedera that can only pay the winner. Neither agent nor the platform can touch the funds. Agents carry portable on-chain identities as HCS-14 DIDs anchored on a Hedera Consensus Service topic. The full negotiation transcript is persisted to 0G Storage and its fingerprint is anchored in the escrow, so the terms of the deal can never be rewritten. Hosted agents think on 0G Compute inside a trusted execution environment, and every decision comes out signed, attesting which model produced it and that the output wasn't tampered with.

The whole agent-vs-agent flow, end to end:

1. Challenge — Agent A (MCP: Claude/Cursor/…) posts a challenge at $5; Agent B (hosted, 0G Compute TEE) checks A's replays before engaging.

2. Negotiation — natural-language haggling on the challenge board: $5 → $10 → deal closed at $8. The full transcript is uploaded to 0G Storage, its hash anchored in the escrow.

3. Escrow — both agents stake 8 HBAR each into a Hedera escrow; nobody (not even the platform) can touch it.

4. Match — deterministic Snake engine: commit(seed hash) → play → reveal(seed) → replayable. Same engine and anti-cheat as human lobbies.

5. Settlement — the verified result pays the winner automatically from escrow. All on-chain, all auditable.


The match itself runs on the exact same engine and anti-cheat as human lobbies, and when it ends the Hedera escrow pays the winner automatically. Verifiable game, verifiable payment, verifiable deal, verifiable mind. In traditional skill gaming the truth is whatever the house's database says. Here the truth is what the chain proves. Don't trust, check. Open source and live now.

projects.title: Pact
projects.description: Pact: Mutual B2B escrow on ENS — both parties fund USDC, terms are on-chain.
projects.project_description:
Pact is a mutual B2B engagement layer, not a one-sided clientflow tool. Two businesses — e.g. a dev studio and a design agency co-pitching a client — propose work using one of six templates (Fixed, Milestone 2-5 phases, Retainer, Time & Materials, Recurring, Split Delivery + a guided custom builder), countersign, and fund USDC escrow before work starts. Both have skin in the game.
Terms don't live in a PDF. They are written as ENSIP-5 text records (pact:type, pact:scope, pact:amount, pact:terms-hash, per-milestone records) under eng-<hex>.pact-hack.eth and *.pact-hack.eth business subnames. Either party can click "Verify on ENS" to resolve the name live in the browser — no backend call — and compare the on-chain hash to what was shown. Scope ambiguity, the #1 cause of B2B payment disputes, becomes impossible.
Completion is backend-optional: PactEscrow.releaseMilestone() and autoRelease() are callable directly by the accepting party's wallet. If Pact's server disappears, the other party still gets paid. The final release emits PactCompleted — both ENS subnames, template, total value, on-time and disputed flags — a permanent, portable reputation event. Anyone can reproduce a profile from Etherscan. World Selfie Check proves a live human behind each business at signup and again for high-value (> $5k) accepts. Privy provides email-only login, embedded wallets, and gas sponsorship — no seed phrase, no chain selector.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Foundry, Solidity ^0.8.24, Sepolia): PactRegistry.sol handles business registration, createEngagement/signEngagement (2-of-2 -> ACTIVE), and setEscrow (one-time wiring). PactEscrow.sol holds MilestoneTerms per milestone (deadline, grace, evidenceHash, acceptanceWindow) and enforces lateness on-chain, high-value World attestation via attestWorldVerification, N-way releaseSplit with pull-payment claimShare fallback, and optimistic disputes (proposeResolution -> challenge window -> executeResolution or pre-agreed default). PactScore.sol attests score tiers [200,550,800]. MockUSDC (6 dec) is the test USDC. Custom errors only; PactCompleted is guarded by completedEmitted. We hit the 24kb limit at 32kb — enabled optimizer=true, runs=200 in contracts/foundry.toml to ship at 19.6kb.
Backend (Node/Express/TS, ESM, Pact/backend): Supabase Postgres is a mirror only — on-chain is authoritative. 9 migrations (0001 core + 0007 M4 obligations + 0008 bonds + 0009 optimistic proposals, etc., all pgcrypto). Routes: POST /businesses/register, POST /proposals + GET /:token (410 after 14d) + POST /:token/accept, POST /engagements + submit/release/world-check, dispute/resolve + resolve-propose/resolve-challenge, GET /businesses/:subname/reputation (now returns score/tier), POST /scheduler/sweep (supports Authorization: Bearer <CRON_SECRET> for external cron, otherwise Privy). Auth is PrivyClient ( @privy-io/node ) verifyAccessToken -> resolveIdentity (prefers embedded wallet), dev fallback via x-wallet-address only when ALLOW_DEV_AUTH=true. New Supabase sb_secret_... is aliased to SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY in config/env.ts.
Frontend (Next.js 16 App Router, Tailwind v4, Pact/frontend): Warp-inspired dark canvas #2b2622 + turquoise #2DD4BF, Inter 400 tight tracking, DM Mono/Instrument Serif. Privy PrivyProvider (@privy-io/react-auth + @stripe/stripe-js peer) wraps AuthProvider (lib/auth.tsx) which fetches a fresh getAccessToken() per request (not cached) and derives the embedded wallet from linkedAccounts. lib/api.ts is a typed client for all 18 endpoints with async getAuth. Canvas-UI effects are vendored (components/canvas/DecryptReveal + GlyphRain + ParticleReveal + rect-cache) — all html-in-canvas WebGL with plain-HTML fallback and prefers-reduced-motion crisp path.
Partner benefit: ENSv2 makes terms verifiable without trusting our DB; Privy removes seed-phrase friction and lets auto-release work via session signers; World ID gives sybil resistance without KYC. The hack is that every critical fund movement has a direct on-chain path and the UI just offers a one-click wrapper for it.

projects.title: sidereal.hedera
projects.description: Split yield-bearing assets into principal and yield, then trade each side separately on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Sidereal is a yield-tokenization protocol for stablecoins and real-world assets. A user deposits a yield-bearing asset into Sidereal, and the position is split into two separate tokens: one representing the principal and the other representing the future yield generated by that asset. This creates two very different products from the same underlying position. A user who wants predictability can sell the future yield and effectively lock in a fixed return, while another user can buy the yield token to get leveraged exposure to changes in the underlying yield. Our goal is to bring this market structure to assets on Hedera, especially tokenized treasuries, stablecoins, and other yield-generating RWAs. Instead of yield being something that is passively attached to an asset, Sidereal makes it a separate, tradable financial primitive that can be priced, exchanged, and composed with other DeFi applications.
projects.how_its_made:
Sidereal is built with Solidity smart contracts deployed on Hedera. Users deposit a yield-bearing stablecoin or RWA position into a vault, which splits it into two tokenized claims: a Principal Token representing the underlying principal at maturity, and a Yield Token representing all yield earned until that date. The contracts handle deposits, PT/YT minting, maturity accounting, and redemption. We use Hedera’s EVM compatibility for the core contract logic and Hedera Token Service for issuing and transferring the resulting positions. The frontend connects directly to the contracts through an EVM wallet, while Hedera Mirror Node data is used to track transactions and positions.
The interesting part was turning a continuously accruing asset into two independently transferable claims while making sure PT + YT always reconcile back to the original underlying position at maturity.

projects.title: DeFa By InvoiceMate
projects.description: Undercollateralised revolving credit for payment companies, settled in USDC on Arc
projects.project_description: Payment service providers pay merchants out today and get paid by the corridor three to seven days later. Someone has to fund that gap on every transaction, and working capital — not demand — is what caps how much volume they can process. Today that gap is filled by bank credit: weeks to underwrite, priced against a balance sheet rather than the receivables actually securing it. DeFa is that facility rebuilt so the credit process is enforced by the contract instead of reported after the fact. A credit committee still underwrites — relationship manager, credit analysis, then risk — and the terms they approve become the pool's on-chain parameters. After that the borrower draws and repays on their own, inside a line that cannot be exceeded, at a finance charge the contract computes per second rather than per statement. Repaid principal revolves back into the available line until the facility matures. This is undercollateralised institutional credit, which is the part DeFi normally cannot do. The collateral is the receivable and the underwriting, not 150% of the loan in volatile tokens. What makes it safe is that every constraint the committee agreed to is checked on-chain at the moment money moves: the borrower wallet is fixed at facility creation and immutable, the payout receiver must be pre-authorised, the draw must fit inside the committed line, and a repayment waterfall pays principal before protocol fees before lender yield. Lenders deposit USDC into risk-tiered facilities, earn yield accrued on dollar-seconds held rather than on a balance snapshot, and claim principal and yield separately. Everything is live on Arc testnet today: contracts, subgraph, risk agent and both portals.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Foundry/Solidity on Arc testnet (chain 5042002). A PoolFactory deploys one EIP-1167 clone per facility, so each credit line is its own contract with its own terms, borrower and balance. Settlement is in native USDC — on Arc, USDC is the gas token, so a facility is funded, drawn, repaid and priced in the same unit the borrower already settles in, with no bridge and no second token to hold. The backend is Node/Express/Mongoose. It never custodies funds and never signs a user transaction: the API returns calldata and the browser wallet signs it. The one privileged action the server performs is executing drawdowns under AGENT2_ROLE, and even there the contract constrains it — the receiver must already be authorised and the amount must fit availableToDd. The Graph is the read layer. A Subgraph indexes both factories and, by template, every pool clone they deploy — deposits and withdrawals in the ERC-4626 event shape, drawdowns, repayments with their finance charge, and lender claims. The schema is built on the ERC-4626 standard rather than a bespoke shape, so a credit facility is legible to any tool that already reads vaults. On top of it sits a risk agent that reasons over live facility state and flags what a human should look at: drawdowns past grace accruing uncapped penalties, facilities approaching finality with debt outstanding, single-borrower concentration. It has no RPC client and no database — if the Subgraph is down it has nothing to reason about. Cross-facility questions cost one RPC call per pool per field, enough to trip the node's rate limiter, which is exactly what pushed us to make The Graph load-bearing rather than decorative. Privy holds the agent signing key. It was a private key in an environment variable — anything that could read the environment could move lender capital. It is now a Privy server wallet whose key lives in their enclave, governed by a policy that denies any transaction carrying native value. On Arc that is precise rather than cosmetic: USDC is the native token, so value is money leaving the wallet, while every legitimate agent action is a zero-value contract call. Arc is not in Privy's supported-chain list, so we sign with eth_signTransaction (which accepts an arbitrary chain id) and broadcast through our own Arc RPC. Notably hacky: we run a second, byte-identical factory built with SECONDS_PER_DAY = 60, so a 30-day facility completes in half an hour. It made a lifecycle that takes a month testable in a sitting — and the Subgraph indexes both, because indexing only the production factory produced an index that was correct and completely empty.

projects.title: Otterpot
projects.description: Telegram-native challenge pool with shared prize vaults on ARC.
projects.project_description: OtterPot is a Telegram-native platform for friend challenges with a shared prize pool on ARC. Users can create or join challenges directly from Telegram, while funds are held in an onchain ChallengePool smart contract. The contract coordinates deposits, withdrawals, and payouts through a separate TreasuryVault, enabling a simple, transparent, and social way to manage pooled funds without leaving Telegram.
projects.how_its_made: OtterPot is built as a monorepo with TypeScript, Rust, Shell, Solidity, CSS, and JavaScript. The core onchain logic is implemented in Rust, while the app experience is delivered through a Next.js frontend and a Telegram Mini App interface. A backend worker/service handles Telegram integration and automation, and the smart contracts manage challenge state plus vault operations on ARC. The project was assembled to keep the user flow lightweight and conversational, while still relying on onchain contracts for fund custody and execution.

projects.title: Quorly
projects.description: Your face approves it. A quorum releases it. The contractor gets paid in a minute.
projects.project_description: Quorly is invoice approvals and stablecoin payouts, run from Slack, where the approval is proven to come from a live human and the payout is released by a key quorum rather than by our application. The problem. Today "approve" is a button click authenticated by a session cookie. A stolen laptop, a hijacked cookie or an over-eager automation can click it, and the audit trail records only that a click happened. Meanwhile the invoice itself waits days in a tool nobody opens, and the contractor chases payment. How it works. A contractor DMs an invoice PDF to the Slack bot, or files it from the dashboard. Claude reads the document and extracts the amount, invoice number and description. Quorly routes it against the company's spend policy and notifies only the people who actually hold authority to approve it. Above a dollar threshold the approver must pass a live World ID Selfie Check before their approval counts. Once the quorum is satisfied, a Privy server wallet releases the payment in stablecoin on Base Sepolia, and the transaction hash lands on the invoice. Approvals scale with risk. Under $500, one approval and no biometric check. $500 to $5,000, one approval with a live selfie. Above $5,000, two approvers each with a check under three minutes old. Nobody can approve their own invoice. What makes the guarantees real. Each Selfie Check proof is bound to one invoice and one approver, expires in minutes, and is burned before verification, so a stale or replayed proof records nothing. The treasury is owned by a 2-of-3 Privy key quorum with its spend policy enforced inside a secure enclave: "two approvals required" is not a flag in our database that we could flip, it is the wallet's owner. The payout is an eth_sendTransaction carrying a threshold of quorum signatures, so Privy's enclave checks the signatures and the policy in one pass and either broadcasts or refuses. Engineering. A Go backend owns all state. Approvals and their payout jobs are written in the same transaction, a transactional outbox, so an approval can never exist without its payout being scheduled. The job queue lives in Postgres using SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with leases, jittered exponential backoff and dead-lettering, because a message broker would reintroduce the dual-write problem the outbox exists to solve. Everyone on the roster gets their own Privy wallet, so being paid means holding the money rather than waiting on a bank. Also in Slack. Mention the bot and it answers from your real invoices — what is waiting on you, where a payment got to, why you cannot approve something — and hands you the link into approving it. It has no tools and no database access; every fact is assembled server-side first, so it cannot invent an amount or an invoice. Live at quorly.xyz
projects.how_its_made: The stack. A Go backend owns everything — policy, Privy, World ID, Slack, and the worker pool — and is the only thing that touches Postgres. Next.js 15 on the front is a client: it forwards the viewer's Privy token and renders what comes back, so authorisation is decided in exactly one place. Foundry for QUSD, the test settlement token on Base Sepolia. Deployed with Docker and Caddy on a single box, Postgres on Neon. The queue is the interesting part. Approvals and their payout jobs are written in the same transaction — a transactional outbox — so an approval can never exist without its payout being scheduled, and vice versa. That's why the queue lives in Postgres rather than a broker: a broker reintroduces the dual-write problem the outbox exists to solve. Workers claim with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, hold leases so a crashed worker's job becomes claimable again, retry with exponential backoff jittered across [d/4, d] to desynchronise a fleet, and dead-letter rather than silently dropping. A RetryLater return reschedules without consuming an attempt. Privy gives the guarantee the product is built on. The treasury is a server wallet owned by a 2-of-3 key quorum with an enclave-enforced spend policy: settlement token only, allowlisted payees, per-transfer ceiling. "Two approvals required" isn't application state we could flip; it's the wallet's owner. Every member also gets their own Privy wallet, so being paid means holding the money. World ID Selfie Check is used as a risk signal, never as identity. It's medium-assurance — liveness and facial similarity, no one-person-one-account guarantee — so authority still comes from the quorum. Selfie Check answers one narrower question: was a live human behind this click? We mint a signed rp_context per approval and record its nonce as a single-use challenge bound to one invoice and one approver, burned before verification so a slow verify can't be raced. Claude reads the invoice PDF and extracts amount, number and description. A second model on OpenRouter powers the Slack assistant, which gets no tools and no database access — every fact is assembled server-side and passed in as context, because retrieval the model controls is retrieval nobody can audit, and this system moves money.

projects.title: Vector52
projects.description: Evidence-first onchain forensics for humans and AI agents, powered by x402.
projects.project_description: Vector52 is an evidence-first onchain investigation platform for humans and AI agents. It transforms a wallet, transaction, or claim into a reproducible investigation where every graph connection can be traced back to observable blockchain evidence. Most blockchain explorers show transfers but do not explain what each connection actually proves. They often turn interactions with routers, pools, and smart contracts into misleading wallet attributions. AI-generated reports can amplify this problem by producing confident conclusions without preserving the original query, raw data, methodology, or limitations. Vector52 separates evidence from interpretation. Its forensic Core acquires and normalizes onchain activity, preserves source data with SHA-256 integrity, reconstructs wallet flows, and classifies every result as evidence, claim, hypothesis, assertion, or unknown. When the available information is insufficient, the system returns UNKNOWN instead of inventing an explanation. The Graph provides indexed protocol and event data for efficient investigation and reproducible queries. Uniswap activity is analyzed with protocol-aware rules that distinguish total pool or router volume from the value that can actually be attributed to the investigated address. This prevents a wallet interaction from being incorrectly presented as responsibility for an entire protocol transaction. AI agents access Vector52 through structured tools and ARC-oriented agent workflows. Using x402, an agent can discover a forensic capability, receive its price, pay for a single request, and obtain structured evidence without requiring a subscription or privileged API account. The agent may explain the findings, but deterministic services perform the calculations and preserved evidence supports the final result. Investigations can be explored through an interactive web application and exported as portable .v52 evidence files containing transfers, provenance, query limits, warnings, the generated report, and a SHA-256 integrity digest. This allows another researcher, application, or agent to independently inspect and verify the investigation.
projects.how_its_made: Vector52 is built as five modular layers: a React investigation interface, a FastAPI evidence Core, blockchain data adapters, an MCP server for AI agents, and an x402 payment boundary. The frontend is an installable PWA built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Reown AppKit, Wagmi, and viem. Investigators can enter a public address, define a date range, add optional context, and explore the resulting flow through an interactive graph. Every edge retains its transaction hash, block, timestamp, asset, value, direction, counterparty, and data source. The FastAPI backend performs validation, evidence acquisition, normalization, reconciliation, and report generation. Provider responses are preserved and hashed with SHA-256 before analysis. Token values remain integer strings with their decimals instead of being converted to floating-point numbers, preventing silent precision errors. The Graph supplies indexed protocol events and Uniswap activity. We reconcile indexed data with RPC receipts and logs, then apply protocol-aware normalization so interacting with a Uniswap router or pool is not automatically interpreted as ownership of, or responsibility for, the entire transaction volume. Provider disagreements and indexer delays produce explicit states such as PARTIAL , DEGRADED , or UNKNOWN . Our MCP server is built with Node.js, TypeScript, the Model Context Protocol SDK, and viem. It exposes the same forensic Core to ARC-oriented AI agent workflows, ensuring that agents and human investigators receive the same evidence and limitations. x402 provides machine-to-machine, pay-per-request access. A protected endpoint first returns an HTTP 402 challenge containing the price and payment requirements. The client validates those conditions, authorizes the exact payment, and retries the original request with proof. Only after verification does the backend execute the investigation. No private key is sent to the API or included in an agent prompt. One notable design choice is that the AI layer never calculates token amounts or creates forensic verdicts. Deterministic services compute the result; the agent only requests tools and explains structured evidence. Investigations can be exported as .v52 files containing the evidence, provenance, limits, warnings, report, and SHA-256 integrity digest, allowing another application or agent to verify the result independently.

projects.title: Provenance
projects.description: Sepolia fund that allocates capital to trading agents by verifiable process, not just PnL.
projects.project_description: Provenance is a research-stage application on Ethereum Sepolia that runs a fund whose capital allocation rewards deterministic, recomputable trading process rather than raw profit and loss. It links four concerns into one pipeline. Identity and authority. ENSv2 names identify each trading agent and control who is authorized to trade. Execution flows through Aqua and a custom SwapVM opcode that check authority and trade limits at fill time. Revoking an agent's authority blocks its next fill, so permissioning is enforced on-chain rather than in application logic. Evidence and scoring. A Substreams oracle indexes public execution events and converts them into reward vectors. Bounded Rust predicates score hedge efficacy, slippage, mandate respect, and price freshness from that indexed evidence, so a third party can recompute an agent's score from public chain data rather than trusting a reported number. Allocation. An allocator reallocates capital toward agents with strong verified process using structured LLM intents, a relative-ranking judge, discounted EXP3-style bandit allocation, drift-based retirement, and drawdown controls. Presentation and reproducibility. A Next.js frontend shows fund equity, verified process scores, agent allocations, reward history, and hire/promote/retire activity, with a cursor-revealed frosted hero, Framer Motion transitions, and static fallbacks for reduced motion and missing WebGL. A replay panel compares two runs over the same block range and shows payload previews and hashes when live replay evidence exists. Structure and status. The repo is a pnpm workspace on Node 22 with packages for backend, frontend, ENS, execution, oracle, config, shared code, and a subgraph, plus a Foundry Solidity contracts package including AuthoritySwapVMRouter. A demo mode runs the full dashboard with synthetic, clearly labeled rewards and no blockchain transactions, requiring no RPC credentials, funded wallet, LLM key, Postgres, Foundry, or Rust. Live Sepolia deployment, hosted-provider verification, package publication, and recorded reproducibility evidence still require external setup and remain the main gaps between the demo and a fully live system.
projects.how_its_made: Provenance is a pnpm workspace on Node 22 split into packages for contracts, backend, frontend, oracle, ENS, execution, config, shared code, and a subgraph. The smart contracts are Solidity 0.8.30 built and tested with Foundry, and include an ENSv2Authority that reads agent authorization from ENS names, an AgentAuthorityManager and adapter, a FundIdentityRegistry, an AgentDesk, PriceMarks, a ProgramFactory, and an AuthoritySwapVMRouter that wraps a custom SwapVM opcode so authority and trade limits are checked at fill time. Execution builds on 1inch tooling — the Aqua SDK, SwapVM SDK, and solidity-utils — with OpenZeppelin contracts underneath. The reward oracle is a Rust crate compiled to a wasm32 Substreams module using the substreams and substreams-ethereum crates, prost for protobuf, and sha3 for hashing, so it indexes public execution events into deterministic reward vectors that anyone can recompute. A companion subgraph (schema plus manifest, built with the Graph CLI) exposes indexed data for the dashboard. The backend is plain TypeScript run through tsx on a raw node:http server, with modules for the agent registry, the EXP3-style allocator, the LLM policy, runtime, a store, and a stream module that pushes updates over Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream). The policy layer calls any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint through configurable LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, and LLM_MODEL env vars rather than hardcoding a provider, and demo mode substitutes synthetic labeled rewards so nothing hits the chain or an LLM. The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion, and wallet connectivity through wagmi, viem, and RainbowKit, with TanStack Query for data. Deployment config is present for both Vercel and Render (render.yaml), and Postgres was dropped in favor of a local file-based SQLite database to keep the demo dependency-free. The whole thing runs end to end locally without RPC credentials, a funded wallet, an LLM key, Foundry, or Rust — those are only needed to go live on Sepolia.

projects.title: Agentry
projects.description: A Ledger-secured, Graph-powered autonomous purchase agent on Hedera Network
projects.project_description:
A Ledger-secured, Graph-powered autonomous purchase agent. It pays for goods and services over Hedera's x402 rails, gates every payment behind a physical Ledger Nano approval, and reasons over its own on-chain purchase history — indexed by a subgraph — to suggest restocks and compare prices across vendors.
The commerce-agent architecture draws on established patterns from prior Zepto402/Maid402-lineage builds, but Vault402 itself — the Ledger payment gate, the Hedera/Blocky402 settlement path, the purchase-log contract, and the subgraph — is built fresh for this event.
projects.how_its_made:
Ledger's role is scoped entirely to protecting the key behind the Hedera payment. It is not involved in the Ethereum Sepolia write at all — that's a separate, ordinary-key transaction, since Ethereum Sepolia's only job here is being a chain The Graph can index. Decides — the agent identifies a purchase to make (restock or new order).
Unlocks the key — the Hedera operator's ECDSA key is encrypted at rest via the Ledger Key Ring (ring encrypt). The agent never holds it in plaintext; right before settlement it calls ring decrypt, which requires the physical Nano to be connected and confirm before releasing the key into memory. Note this is a gate on the key, not a hardware-produced signature — Hedera isn't a wallet-cli-supported currency, so the actual ECDSA signing happens in software once the key is released, not inside the device's secure element.
Settles — the agent uses that briefly-decrypted key to build and submit the payment through the Blocky402 facilitator, settling on Hedera testnet in HBAR.
Logs — the agent calls PurchaseLog.recordPurchase(...) on Ethereum Sepolia, using a standard key from .env — no Ledger involvement on this leg.
Indexes — a subgraph deployed to Ethereum Sepolia picks up the PurchaseLog event live.
Reasons — the agent queries its own purchase history through the Subgraph MCP in natural language, computes consumption patterns, and surfaces restock suggestions and cross-vendor price comparisons.

projects.title: Zentis
projects.description: One market-making position across three chains that rebalances by pricing instead of   bridging.
projects.project_description:
Zentis is one market-making position whose inventory lives on three chains at once. Every leg quotes off the same mid, published at the same instant by a Chainlink Confidential Workflow, and the book is managed as a single book — without bridging. Nothing crosses a chain boundary but a signed number. The problem
A market maker running the same pair on three chains is running three businesses that cannot see each other. When one leg gets bought out, the textbook fix is a round trip: sell the asset here, bridge the stablecoin, buy it back there. That costs three ways — you wait for the transfer, you pay fees on both sides, and while the value is in flight it sits on neither leg. The bridge fee is not really the problem. The problem is that a market maker exists to earn the spread, and the bridge route makes it cross the spread as a taker, twice, to fix its own inventory. Zentis does not move the money.
