One mid, one book. A confidential workflow reads one real WETH/USDC mid from Ethereum mainnet and writes it to all three registries under one sequence number, at one instant. Each leg then anchors its own constant-product curve back onto that shared mid. This matters more than it sounds: before it existed, three unarbitraged testnet pools quoted the same pair at 30,187, 4,156 and 2,583 USDC per WETH, and a book weight measured against one of those is not comparable with a weight measured against another. The cross-chain term — the entire claim of the project — was being computed from incommensurable inputs until this was fixed. A correction and a concession. Each leg's quote shifts off the mid by two terms with different justifications. The correction reprices the leg's own curve back onto the mid; it is a correction, not a cost the maker chooses to pay. The concession is what a leg pays to shed what it holds too much of — and it is capped by what bridging would actually have cost, priced from a real 1inch Fusion+ quote. Pricing therefore never costs more than the bridge it replaces. This is Avellaneda–Stoikov's reservation price expressed as a SwapVM instruction, with Guéant's multi-position term on top. The reference cannot drain the position. The tilt is applied to balanceIn only, never balanceOut. Since amountOut = amountIn·balanceOut/(balanceIn′+amountIn) < balanceOut for any balanceIn′ > 0, a quote can never exceed the maker's real Aqua balance regardless of what the reference says. There is no clamp, no post-check and no revert at settlement — the failure is unreachable rather than guarded. A published boundary can only ever narrow the cap the maker signed, never widen it. Funds never leave the maker's wallet. Aqua records a balance and pulls from the maker at settlement; its own token balance is zero. We verified this by reading the chain rather than assuming it. ship() and dock() move no tokens at all, and push() tops a live position up with no dock and no re-ship. The three sponsor integrations, and why each is load-bearing
Each layer consumes the one above it. Removing any of them breaks the product, not just a prize claim. 1inch — three custom SwapVM instructions on official, unmodified Aqua contracts. ZentisSkew (0x9e) reads the reference and scales balanceIn. ZentisSpread (0x9f) applies the dynamic half-spread as a fee, mirroring FeeFlatIn including its partial-fill correction. ZentisBand (0xb3) bounds the realised, taker-facing price against the reference. Dropping the nine stock instructions a Zentis program can never reach leaves the router at 17,437 bytes, 7,139 under EIP-170 and smaller than the stock 16-entry router carrying none of our code. Chainlink — two Confidential Workflows computing the reference in a TEE. The fast workflow is strictly deterministic over block-pinned data and owns the mid, the tilt and the slope. The slow workflow is hourly, bucketed to the nearest basis point, and owns the spread, the adverse-selection markout and the bridge-priced budget — a live quote endpoint would return a different answer every call, which is why the Fusion+ read sits there and not on the deterministic path. The TEE constraint is pinned to AWS Nitro in us-west-2 rather than left permissive, and there is zero runtime.log() inside either enclave, enforced by test rather than promised. What stays secret is the maker's aggression — the gains that turn inventory into a concession — plus the API keys and the Fusion+ payload, whose size and direction are exactly what a front-runner would want. The market price, the Aqua balances and the published reference are deliberately not secret: they are public data, and claiming otherwise would be theatre. The Graph — an authored standard, not a dashboard. Every Aqua event (Shipped, Docked, Pulled, Pushed, and SwapVM.Swapped) carries zero indexed parameters, so nobody can filter Aqua activity by maker, app or token through eth_getLogs topics — every consumer must ingest and decode the whole venue. aqua-standard does it once, for every app, keyed by the triple (maker, app, strategyHash) because that is how Aqua actually keys balances. It is deployed on Ethereum mainnet and Arbitrum One, where it spans multiple apps; zentis-fills runs on all three testnets, where one identical GraphQL document returns one position with each chain's own leg — and nothing configures that join, because the subgraph decodes the shipped program, finds ZentisSkew, and reads the positionId out of its arguments. The decoder never guesses: an app's program is read against an opcode table only when that table is known from verified source, and every other app is marked UNKNOWN with its opcodes reported as custom and the raw blob retained. That rule earned its keep. The deployed Aqua router uses completely different opcode numbering from the repository we compile against — the constant-product swap is 0x50 in source and 17 on chain, and the fee denominator is 1e9 rather than 1e7 — so decoding live positions against the source table produces confident nonsense rather than an error. projects.how_its_made: The stack, and why each piece is there Contracts. Solidity 0.8.30 exactly, because swap-vm and aqua both pin an exact pragma and anything else fails to compile. Foundry, with via_ir, optimizer_runs = 700, fuzzing pinned at 2,000 runs and seed 0x1 so every number regenerates identically. Fixed point is plain int256 at 1e18 scale with no PRBMath — the arithmetic needs multiplication only, and one less dependency buys real headroom against EIP-170. Five unmodified pinned submodules: 1inch/swap-vm@f09a41e, 1inch/aqua@9c5c42e, forge-std, openzeppelin-contracts, 1inch/solidity-utils. Off-chain. TypeScript strict on bun 1.4.2 with viem 2.34.0, everywhere — the workflows, the quote service, the console readers, the console itself. @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.20.0 with the cre CLI 1.32.0. The subgraphs are AssemblyScript on graph-cli 0.98 with matchstick 0.6.0. The reference model is Python 3.12 with nothing outside the standard library, deliberately, so it can be run by anyone with a Python and no install step. The site is Next 16 / React 19 / Tailwind v4 with GSAP 3.15 (ScrollSmoother), three.js and xterm.js. The console is Ink 7 on React 19, compiled to a single binary with bun build --compile. Infrastructure. The publisher runs as one Cloud Run job on one Cloud Scheduler entry, with the CRE session on a GCS volume and secrets in Secret Manager; systemd user timers are the local equivalent. There is no root workspace manifest — every package installs its own dependencies — and two install orderings are load-bearing, which CI comments on so nobody has to rediscover them. How the layers are pieced together The seam between layers is deliberately narrow: the instruction receives one signed scalar and does not care where it came from. That is why three separate extensions to this design — portfolio covariance tilt, a chain-graph routing solver, and adding a third chain — each needed zero contract changes. The tilt could come from a pairwise difference, from a reservation price, or from the dual of a twelve-node flow problem; on chain it is the same int16 in the same struct field. Concretely, one ZentisRef struct (two storage slots) is the entire interface between the enclave and the curve. The fast workflow owns the mid, tilt, slope, reference balance and sequence; the slow workflow owns the spread, markout and boundary through a read-modify-write. When they race, the loser is rejected by the registry's sequence guard — which, because rejections emit and return rather than revert, makes two writers on one slot safe by accident of a fix made for a different reason. The same policy exists in three languages — Solidity (ZentisTiltLib), TypeScript (@zentis/strategy-sdk), and Python (reference_model) — held together by committed fixture vectors rather than by discipline. That caught a real bug: Python floored where TypeScript and Solidity truncate toward zero, so the implementations disagreed whenever the first leg was the lighter one and the difference was odd. The "three implementations agree bit for bit" claim had only ever been checked with a positive imbalance. What the partner technologies actually bought us 1inch / Aqua + SwapVM made the product possible rather than merely hosting it. _dispatch / _runOpcode as a virtual hook means extending the VM is one contract and nine lines with no fork. Aqua's non-custodial model — a recorded balance plus an approval, with settlement pulling from the maker's wallet — is what makes "funds never leave your wallet" literally true and re-shipping cheap. And Shipped emitting the full strategy blob for data availability is what lets a cross-chain position be verified from chain data alone: our positionId lives inside the program bytes, so anyone can prove two legs are one position with no messaging layer, no attestation and no registry. Chainlink CRE is the only reason the maker's aggression can be secret while the number it produces is public. But the specific thing that made it buildable in a hackathon window was learning — from Chainlink Labs in Discord, not from the docs — that cre workflow simulate runs a confidential workflow with no deploy access. And LAST_FINALIZED_BLOCK_NUMBER plus blockNumber(n) turned out to be exactly the right primitive for determinism: resolve the finalized block once, then name that number in every subsequent read. The Graph gave us a signal that did not previously exist. Because Aqua's events carry no indexed parameters, the only way to ask "how is this venue positioned" is to ingest and decode everything — which nobody had done. Building the standard produced a venue-level positioning dataset that the slow workflow now reads to allocate each leg's rebalancing budget away from chains the venue already leans into.

projects.title: Vigil
projects.description: Autonomous working capital & solvency surveillance OS for AI agents on Hedera.
projects.project_description: AI agents can now pay for compute, data, and APIs on a per-request basis using protocols like x402. But there is a glaring blind spot in the agent economy: an agent that knows how to make a single payment does NOT know how to maintain ongoing financial solvency. When an autonomous agent is assigned a multi-step task and its token balance runs dry mid-flight, the entire workflow crashes with no recovery mechanism. Vigil is an Autonomous Working Capital and Solvency Surveillance Operating System for AI agents, built natively on Hedera. Operating like an automated corporate treasury desk, Vigil continuously forecasts an agent's upcoming payment obligations, calculates a real-time Payment Coverage Ratio (PCR), and identifies liquidity deficits before failures happen. When a shortfall is detected, Vigil evaluates competing liquidity routes, autonomously executes two-leg swaps via liquidity providers (converting reserve HBAR into service tokens like FUSDC), and restores the agent’s solvency ratio back above 100%. Once funded, the agent executes metered x402 micropayments with cryptographic proof of payment, while automatically queuing future recurring renewals via native on-chain schedules. Every single forecast, shortfall alert, route decision, and payment receipt is immutably anchored to the Hedera Consensus Service, giving humans and auditors a verifiable flight recorder of machine financial behavior.
projects.how_its_made: Vigil is built as a modular TypeScript monorepo powered by Turborepo, Next.js 14, Node.js, Express microservices, and the native @hashgraph/sdk. We deeply leveraged three native Hedera network primitives to eliminate third-party smart contract risk: Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): We created an immutable audit trail topic (0.0.10524552) where every financial transition—shortfall alerts, liquidity quotes, LP swaps, and HTTP 402 payment receipts—is sequenced with decentralized consensus timestamps. We also implemented an HCS-14-inspired identity registry (0.0.10524553) anchoring agent capabilities, public keys, and spending policy bounds. Hedera Token Service (HTS) & HIP-18 Custom Fees: We minted a fungible token (FUSDC, 0.0.10510032) configured with an on-chain Custom Fixed Fee. Instead of handling protocol fees in application code, Hedera's ledger automatically intercepts transfers and routes a 0.01 FUSDC surcharge directly to a dedicated Fee Collector account (0.0.10510030). Hedera Schedule Service (HSS): For recurring workflow continuity, Vigil uses ScheduleCreateTransaction to schedule forward payments (0.0.10524570) that execute autonomously at expiration without requiring human signatures. x402 Metering & Replay Protection: Our market intelligence service gates data behind HTTP 402 Payment Required. When the agent pays on Hedera, it passes a base64-encoded payment proof in the X-PAYMENT header. The merchant verifies the transaction ID directly against the Hedera Mirror Node REST API and validates freshness (<120s) with an in-memory nonce store to prevent double-spend replay attacks. Treasury Desk & VigilRouter LP: When PCR drops below 100%, the agent queries liquidity routes. If a DEX pool is absent on testnet, it falls back to VigilRouter LP (0.0.10510029) via a two-leg atomic flow: the agent transfers HBAR, the router verifies settlement on the mirror node, dispatches FUSDC, and flips PCR from 0% to 110%. Frontend & Telemetry: The UI is crafted in Next.js 14 with a warm Swiss-editorial aesthetic, polling the Hedera Mirror Node to stream live consensus events, and includes an interactive mission configurator allowing judges to dynamically test custom call volumes and reserve buffers.

projects.title: Held
projects.description: x402 payments that land in escrow, not the seller, until the buyer has read what they bought.
projects.project_description: x402 pays the seller the moment a request is served. For a weather API that is fine. For agent work it is backwards: you find out whether you got anything useful only after the money has gone, and your only recourse is a support email. Held keeps the x402 flow exactly as it is and changes one field. payTo points at an escrow account instead of the seller. You pay, you get the deliverable immediately, and then you decide. Approve and the seller is paid. Reject and you are refunded. Say nothing and a Hedera scheduled transaction pays the seller when the review window expires, so silence is not a veto and a seller cannot have their money trapped by a buyer who never looks. That last ending is the one people do not expect. A card authorisation that nobody captures expires backwards, and the payer keeps the money. This expires forwards. Everything that happened is appended to a Hedera Consensus Service topic: what was asked, which build of the agent answered, the hash of what it produced, and what the buyer decided. Anyone can read it from the mirror node without trusting either party. Three real paid requests settled on Hedera testnet, one for each ending. The transaction ids are in the repo and on HashScan.
projects.how_its_made: The service is an ordinary x402 resource server built on @x402/core, @x402/fetch and @x402/hedera at v2.25.0, with Blocky402 as the facilitator on testnet. A client that already speaks x402 needs no changes to buy from it. The escrow is a plain Hedera account rather than a contract. Settlement happens immediately and irreversibly, so the seller knows the money is real, but it lands somewhere neither party can unilaterally take it from. Release is a separate, later transfer. The deadline is a Hedera scheduled transaction armed at payment time, with the review deadline as its expiry and waitForExpiry set true. When nobody decides, Hedera executes it and the service only observes the result. The sweeper watches rather than transfers, which is what stops a job being paid out twice. I tried the deferred x402 flow first. The Hedera scheme declares authorization as its default, so on paper settlement can be deferred past the request. It cannot be deferred far enough: the payload is a partially signed Hedera transaction and those expire in minutes, while a review window runs for hours. So Held holds money in an account rather than holding a signature. The agent's version id is a hash of its prompt template, its model and its own source, because that is what a buyer is really approving. Not some agent, a specific identifiable build. The proof page reads Hedera's mirror node from the visitor's own browser, with no server of ours in the path, so it keeps working whether or not the service is running.

The service is an ordinary x402 resource server built on @x402/core, @x402/fetch and @x402/hedera at v2.25.0, with Blocky402 as the facilitator on testnet. A client that already speaks x402 needs no changes to buy from it.

The escrow is a plain Hedera account rather than a contract. Settlement happens immediately and irreversibly, so the seller knows the money is real, but it lands somewhere neither party can unilaterally take it from. Release is a separate, later transfer.

The deadline is a Hedera scheduled transaction armed at payment time, with the review deadline as its expiry and waitForExpiry set true. When nobody decides, Hedera executes it and the service only observes the result. The sweeper watches rather than transfers, which is what stops a job being paid out twice.

I tried the deferred x402 flow first. The Hedera scheme declares authorization as its default, so on paper settlement can be deferred past the request. It cannot be deferred far enough: the payload is a partially signed Hedera transaction and those expire in minutes, while a review window runs for hours. So Held holds money in an account rather than holding a signature.

The agent's version id is a hash of its prompt template, its model and its own source, because that is what a buyer is really approving. Not some agent, a specific identifiable build.

The proof page reads Hedera's mirror node from the visitor's own browser, with no server of ours in the path, so it keeps working whether or not the service is running.

projects.title: AUETH
projects.description: Modern SIWE-style auth for systems older than Ethereum using PAM
projects.project_description:
The core product of aueth is the SIWE-style authentication correlating a Unix system user to an Ethereum address (1:1) with PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules). A system administrator of a corporation or similar can configure aueth with
[directory]
provider = "ens"
[directory.ens]
root = "acmecorp.eth"
chain = "sepolia"
rpc_url = "https://your-sepolia-rpc.example" then give their employees subnames under acmecorp.eth (if they don't already), and then simply set a few text records (such as uid and gid, and Unix username if it shouldn't be the ens name). Then the system administrator hooks up the aueth PAM module. Now any user can instead of using their passwords for sudo or ssh or whatever simply connect their wallet to their terminal and sign a payload.
projects.how_its_made: I wrote a Rust daemon and user program that uses the openlv sdk to do terminal wallet connection, then I used ENSv2 as the directory with simple RPC calls. The business logic is just hooking up two primitives. Reason I chose to not use SIWE was because I didn't want the UX of the PAM module directing you to a webpage in order to sign (like prior art). Instead I simply show the openlv connection url and have the terminal act as the dApp itself.

projects.title: Late Gate
projects.description: Decentralized insurance for flight delays with automatic payout
projects.project_description: Late Gate is a travel utility for people who fly a lot and are tired of eating delays. Before you fly, you pick a real flight, choose a Takeoff delay or Arrival delay stub, set how late counts (30, 45, or 60 minutes), and pay a fixed USDC premium. If the flight crosses that line, the stub pays out automatically. No airline claim form. No waiting weeks for a voucher. We refuse flights that are already a mess or past the buy window, because a random average book would lose money at these prices. Selective underwriting (and one stub per verified human per flight) keeps the shared liquidity pool solvent. Anyone can deposit USDC into the house pool that backs payouts. Same stub shape later extends to timed events like concerts. Built as a World Mini App so verified humans can buy cover without a crypto-cosplay UI.
projects.how_its_made: Late Gate is a Next.js travel UI wrapped as a World Mini App with MiniKit for wallet auth and World Chain USDC payments. Traveler flow: airline and route pick → buyable flights → Takeoff or Arrival stub → fixed premium with payout scaled by 30/45/60 → World ID verification in checkout → pay USDC → OPEN stub → worker settles PAID or EXPIRED from flight observation. World is the partner prize path. We use IDKit for uniqueness (one human bound to one flightKey) as abuse prevention for the pool, with an honest Sandbox / orbLegacy path when Selfie Check Beta is still access-gated, plus FEEDBACK.md. Money lives on World Chain: travelers pay and get paid in USDC; LPs deposit into a USDC vault that backs max payout exposure. Pricing uses delay probabilities with a load factor and p_max gates so we only sell when expected value stays positive. Hacky but useful: consumer surface hides rails (no wallet chrome theater), while settlement and pool accounting stay on-chain where it matters. Demo fixture centers ETHGlobal Tokyo (SFO→NRT).

projects.title: Solvent Aqua
projects.description: Solvent: the sum 1inch Aqua never computes and never over commits.
projects.project_description: 1inch Aqua lets makers quote directly from their wallets without deposits, with one wallet supporting multiple strategies. Aqua stores each commitment independently as balances[maker][app][strategyHash][token] and never aggregates them. ship() does not verify solvency. A maker can commit 15,000 USDC across three strategies while holding 10,000, leaving all quotes active until a taker triggers pull() and pays gas for the revert. On Base, Aqua has 191 real makers and roughly 2,500 fills, with material books repeatedly under backed. Solvent provides the missing aggregate. A view contract reads Aqua's registry, aggregates each maker's commitments by token, and compares them with effective wallet capacity, min(balance, allowance). It exposes PROMISED / BACKED / SHORT. Uniswap v4 pool state converts multi token shortfalls into one value. The Graph adds external exposure across 22 live lending and DEX deployments using Messari standard schema data. A Uniswap v4 hook enforces solvency and rejects insolvent fills with a decoded reason. Ballast removes the revert. It runs on SolventVM, our custom SwapVM Aqua app, with a new AggregateClamp instruction. At quote time it aggregates live commitments, checks wallet capacity, and clamps each fill to the amount actually available after sibling claims. No oracle or keeper. Quotes remain byte identical to 1inch's router. Where the second 1inch fill reverts, SolventVM settles the 4,000 USDC actually available. When the wallet is drained, the position quotes zero and resumes automatically when refilled. The Graph also reconciles Aqua commitments with external app positions so solvers can see the maker's wider book. Validation: Aqua's registry and SwapVM router are deployed and bytecode verified on Ethereum mainnet and Base forks. Demo makers use real addresses and positions, and the shipped strategies are ours. 54 contract tests and 20 engine tests run through one command and fail if the UI disagrees with a direct cast call.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts use Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, with 1inch/aqua and 1inch/swap-vm vendored as untouched submodules. Our app extends AquaApp and our router extends SwapVM. SolventReader computes the aggregate Aqua lacks. SolventSwap is a fixed rate Aqua app for exact demo fills. SolventVM adds AggregateClamp at opcode 0x93 using the documented _dispatch extension pattern. Every router instruction requires strategy enlistment, making the maker's router book enumerable without an oracle. The clamp limits size, not price. Exact out is capped before the curve. Exact in probes the curve once, then reruns as exact out if output exceeds deliverable balance, preserving the curve's native price and SwapVM invariants. SolventVM is 24,259 bytes, 317 bytes below EIP 170, with optimizer runs fixed at 700. Mainnet and Base router v1.0.2 uses a positional opcode table and ABI that differs from swap vm HEAD, so the demo hand encodes v1.0.2 bytes and fork tests include a translator. Details are in FEEDBACK.md. SolventPriceV4 reads slot0 directly from PoolManager via extsload and selects the deepest of four ETH/USDC tiers by live liquidity. It is the only pricing path. SolventHook is a mined beforeSwap hook with only BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG set and rejects fills from insolvent makers. The Graph uses three query documents for the versioned Messari lending schemas, covering 22 live deployments with no protocol specific code and six concurrent requests. Our subgraph indexes SolventVM Enlisted, Clamped, and Swapped events, with refused phantom liquidity as the impact metric. Hidden book reconciliation combines our on chain aggregate with the Naumachy Aqua index. Live data also showed that DEX TVL can contain corrupted rows, so depth uses only liquid reference assets. The engine is TypeScript, viem, and React with two phase reads. Chain state renders in about 140 ms, then Graph data arrives seconds later and re ranks results. Demos use pinned Anvil forks with real Base makers impersonated without holding their keys, and ERC20 balances written directly to storage. verify.sh compares the UI against cast call and fails on any single digit difference. Puppeteer runs the end to end test against the real UI.

projects.title: Sentinelio
projects.description: Sentinel: AI smart contract security scanner that matches bugs to real historical hacks.
projects.project_description: Sentinel is an AI-powered smart contract security scanner built for anyone — not just developers — who wants to know if a smart contract is safe before interacting with it. Users simply paste an Ethereum contract address into the app. Sentinel fetches the contract's publicly verified source code via the Etherscan API, then sends it to Google's Gemini AI with a specialized security-auditing prompt designed to detect common vulnerability classes: reentrancy, integer overflow/underflow, unchecked external calls, access control flaws, front-running risk, and denial-of-service vectors. What makes Sentinel different from existing tools like Slither or Mythril is accessibility and context. Instead of returning dense, developer-only technical output, Sentinel translates every finding into plain-English explanations that a non-technical investor can actually understand — using analogies where helpful. Critically, Sentinel also cross-references each detected vulnerability against a set of well-documented historical exploits (such as The DAO hack of 2016 or the Parity multisig freeze), flagging when a contract's code pattern resembles a real-world incident that cost users millions of dollars. This turns an abstract security score into a concrete, memorable warning. The app requires zero setup — no installing security tooling, no command-line tools, no wallet connection. Users get a color-coded overall risk score, a list of specific issues with severity ratings, and a one-click "Copy Report" feature to share findings. No user data or scan history is stored, keeping the experience private by design. Sentinel was built to make Web3 security literacy accessible to everyday users navigating an ecosystem where scams and exploits remain a major barrier to trust and adoption.
projects.how_its_made: Sentinel is built with Next.js 14 using the App Router and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind CSS for a clean, dark themed UI. The entire app is stateless with no database, which keeps the architecture simple and means no user data is ever stored. The core flow works like this: when a user submits a contract address, our Next.js API route first validates the address format, then calls the Etherscan API to fetch that contract's publicly verified Solidity source code. If the contract isn't verified, we return a friendly error rather than a technical one. Once we have the source code, we send it to Google's Gemini API (using the fast, free tier Gemini Flash model) with a carefully engineered system prompt instructing it to act as a smart contract security auditor. The prompt asks Gemini to identify vulnerabilities across categories like reentrancy, integer overflow, unchecked external calls, and access control issues, and to return the findings strictly as structured JSON. A key technical decision was designing the prompt to also cross reference each finding against a list of well known historical exploits, such as The DAO hack and the Parity multisig freeze, so the AI can tell users when a pattern resembles a real world incident, not just abstract terminology. We parse Gemini's JSON response, strip any accidental markdown formatting Gemini sometimes adds despite instructions, and render it into risk score badges, severity coded issue cards, and collapsible technical detail sections on the frontend. One genuinely hacky but practical choice was building this entirely through an AI assisted development workflow using Cursor, since our team had no prior professional coding experience. We wrote detailed, structured prompts describing exact API behavior, UI components, and error states, and let Cursor's AI agent scaffold, implement, debug, and commit the code step by step. We also had to adapt on the fly when a model name for Gemini changed between versions, which the agent caught and corrected automatically after hitting an API error during testing. For deployment, the app is hosted on Vercel, with both the Etherscan and Gemini API keys stored securely as environment variables rather than in code, and explicitly excluded from git via .gitignore to avoid ever exposing credentials publicly.

projects.title: hackpass
projects.description: Real, unique human check-ins for events using World ID Selfie Check — no fakes, no duplicates.
projects.project_description: HackPass proves that a real, unique human attended a hackathon event — without relying on shareable QR codes or self-reported names that anyone can duplicate. Participants verify with World ID's Selfie Check, a live facial liveness scan completed through World App. This produces a cryptographic proof containing a unique identifier tied to that person and that specific event, without ever revealing who they are — no name, no email, no photo is stored by HackPass. If the same verified human tries to check in twice, HackPass recognizes it immediately and blocks the duplicate, since the protection is tied to their real, verified identity rather than something they type in. This stops the common hackathon problem of the same person claiming swag, prizes, or workshop credit multiple times through shared links or fake sign-ups — while keeping every participant's actual identity completely private.
projects.how_its_made: HackPass is built with a plain Node.js/Express backend and a vanilla HTML/JS frontend — no framework overhead. The core integration uses World ID's IDKit v4 SDK (@worldcoin/idkit-core) with the selfieCheckLegacy preset, requesting a real-time facial liveness scan through World App rather than a mocked or simulated flow. The backend signs each verification request server-side with an RP signing key, then independently verifies the returned proof against World's v4 verify endpoint before creating a check-in record — ensuring the proof can't be forged or replayed client-side. Each event's attendance is keyed by the proof's nullifier, giving deterministic, privacy-preserving duplicate detection with zero personal data stored. Getting the real Selfie Check flow working involved genuinely deep debugging — tracing SDK-level request/response cycles, fixing an internal double-fetch bug that was silently sending duplicate signed requests, and correcting the verification API integration to match World's actual response shape once the proof succeeded.

projects.title: AutoAMM
projects.description: An autonomous research lab that tests and refines programmable market-making strategies.
projects.project_description: AutoAMM brings the autoresearch loop to market making: propose a strategy change, run an experiment, evaluate it against the incumbent, and keep or reject the result. The prototype searches fee levels and active capital allocations for a WETH/USDC constant-product strategy. Candidates must pass drawdown and inventory limits and improve on both training and validation scenarios. A separate holdout is unlocked at the end of a 24-experiment run. The Next.js dashboard exposes the experiment journal, rejection reasons, performance comparisons, strategy code, and downloadable evidence. Accepted parameters compile into real 1inch Aqua/SwapVM program bytecode and unsigned transaction plans. The public demo uses a deterministic heuristic optimizer and synthetic order flow; it does not sign transactions or claim simulated results are live trading profits. A server-side Graph adapter supports indexed market prices when credentials are configured.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Recharts, Zod, viem, and the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM SDKs. The deterministic constant-product simulator models fee-sensitive order flow, arbitrage, retained fees, and estimated execution costs. An autonomous search loop explores fee levels and capital allocations while a fixed evaluator checks net equity relative to HODL on training and validation paths. The dashboard streams the resulting experiment history and unlocks a separate holdout after 24 candidates. The Aqua compiler combines flatFeeAmountInXD with xycSwapXD and prepares token approvals and ship calldata using the official SDKs. A server-side Graph adapter queries and validates hourly WETH/USDC pool prices. The Vercel deployment intentionally contains no market-data, model, or wallet keys. Simulation and bytecode compilation work without credentials; live-data access and transaction signing are separate. Drawdown and inventory-percentage gates are offchain evaluator checks, not guarantees encoded in the compiled program. Codex provided substantial coding and design assistance.

projects.title: FieldProof402
projects.description: AI agents pay people to verify real-world facts via x402, with auditable Hedera receipts.
projects.project_description: FieldProof402 is a marketplace where software agents can pay people to check real-world facts. For example, an agent creates a task to inspect a bicycle and offers a reward in HBAR. A person accepts the task, scans a QR code, takes two photos, answers a question, and submits the evidence from an iPhone. The Apple Watch helps the user receive and accept tasks quickly. Before verification begins, the agent pays a small fee through x402 and Blocky402 on Hedera Testnet. The backend checks the evidence, prevents photo reuse, and publishes hashes and results through Hedera Consensus Service. If the task is approved, the contributor receives the reward directly in their Hedera account. The demo uses real x402 payments, real HBAR rewards, and real HCS records. The visual analysis is currently a clearly labelled rule-based simulation, so the project does not claim to prove that a physical object is genuine or in good condition.
projects.how_its_made: I built FieldProof402 with a TypeScript backend using Node.js, Fastify, PostgreSQL, Zod, Drizzle, and an S3-compatible MinIO store. The iPhone prototype is written in SwiftUI and uses AVFoundation for QR scanning, the camera for evidence capture, and CryptoKit for SHA-256 hashes. The Apple Watch companion is part of the planned complete flow but is not finished yet. Hedera is the main trust and payment layer. I use the Hedera JavaScript SDK to publish task, evidence, verification, and reward events through Hedera Consensus Service. Approved tasks trigger real HBAR rewards on Hedera Testnet. Mirror Node is used to check accounts, transactions, transfers, and HCS messages, while HashScan links make every public transaction easy to inspect. The verification endpoint uses x402 v2 with Blocky402. The requesting agent checks the price against its task budget, signs an HBAR transfer locally, and sends the signed payment authorisation to the API. Blocky402 verifies and settles it, so the backend never stores the agent’s private key. This gave the project a proper pay-per-use verification flow instead of a normal subscription or API key. One notable hack is the recovery system. Signed transaction bytes are stored before submission, and the agent keeps a private local payment journal. If the network fails after settlement, the worker checks Mirror Node and reuses the same transaction instead of signing another one. A unique purchase memo links the x402 payment to the task, while database locks and unique constraints prevent duplicate charges and rewards. Photos stay private and off-chain. Only hashes, decisions, and payment references are published. The current visual decision is still a clearly labelled rule-based mock, but the x402 payment, HBAR reward, HCS events, and receipt verification are real.
projects.project_description_markdown:
FieldProof402 is a marketplace where software agents can pay people to check real-world facts. For example, an agent creates a task to inspect a bicycle and offers a reward in HBAR. A person accepts the task, scans a QR code, takes two photos, answers a question, and submits the evidence from an iPhone. The Apple Watch helps the user receive and accept tasks quickly.

Before verification begins, the agent pays a small fee through x402 and Blocky402 on Hedera Testnet. The backend checks the evidence, prevents photo reuse, and publishes hashes and results through Hedera Consensus Service. If the task is approved, the contributor receives the reward directly in their Hedera account.

The demo uses real x402 payments, real HBAR rewards, and real HCS records. The visual analysis is currently a clearly labelled rule-based simulation, so the project does not claim to prove that a physical object is genuine or in good condition.

projects.title: Playces.fun
projects.description: Show up. Play. Earn. Set up an event page, invite friends, and play head-to-head.
projects.project_description: Playces is a venue arena: check in, play head-to-head, earn onchain. Integrations are the product. Privy: email/Google login creates an embedded wallet. Fund Base USDC with useFundWallet, then play. Blink: both players stake USDC into StakeEscrow on Base; winner takes the pot. Lichess: hosts pick friendly/rated, time control, and $0.25–$100 stake; Playces opens the challenge and reads the result. ENSv2 on Sepolia: pick a custom label and get {name}-{event}.playce.eth under playce.eth, registered on the Permissioned Registry with resolver records. Chainlink CRE reports the chess winner on-chain; CCIP mints the Ethereum-rep win badge Sepolia-to-Sepolia. Loop: Privy wallet → fund USDC → Blink stake → Lichess or 67 → ENS ticket → CRE/CCIP payout.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js plus a Node WebSocket server. Partners sit on one path: identity, money, match, settlement. Privy (@privy-io/react-auth) creates the embedded wallet and signs API calls. useFundWallet onramps USDC onto Base; we EIP-6963-announce that wallet so Blink can deposit without a second login. Blink deposits to StakeEscrow on Base. Chess rooms store a custom stakeAmount; the Blink signer and /api/stake/confirm require that exact amount. Lichess is the chess VM (/api/challenge/open). Redis + WS poll game/export until the game ends. ENSv2 on Sepolia: register on the Permissioned Registry with EAC roles (renew, resolver, subregistry; not transferable), then resolver multicall for addr + text. Gas is sponsored. Missing config returns 503, not a fake name. Chainlink CRE reads Lichess and calls ChessArbiter to settle the pot. CCIP (ProofSender on Arbitrum Sepolia → ProofReceiverPass on Ethereum Sepolia) mints the Ethereum-rep badge. Notable: Blink was a fixed $0.25 rail; we made it per-room without changing the escrow contract. ENS writes use the parent-owner minter so users never pay Sepolia gas. Lichess “rated” only counts if both players are logged into Lichess.

projects.title: Battles
projects.description: Oracle-less prediction market: back memecoins in 1v1 battles powered by custom Uniswap v4 hooks.
projects.project_description: Battles is a decentralized prediction market for coin vs. coin performance with zero external oracle dependence. Two tokens face off in a fixed-duration battle, and whichever coin achieves a higher percentage price growth takes the pot.  Traditional prediction markets rely on off-chain reporters, feeds, or dispute windows. MemeMarket eliminates third-party reliance by measuring performance directly inside each coin's native pool using a custom Uniswap v4 hook. Relative performance is calculated in log-space via tick accumulators, making it mathematically impossible for single-block flash loans or last-minute price spikes to alter the outcome.  Participants take positions in an in-contract constant-product odds market. Buying a side shifts odds based on crowd sentiment without altering token prices or touching the underlying assets. Once the timer expires, any user can execute settlement to claim a keeper bounty, and winning predictions redeem their share of the pool. Fully trustless, admin-free, and automated.
projects.how_its_made: Smart Contracts (OracleHook.sol & Arena.sol): We developed a cardinality-1 accumulator hook in Uniswap v4 to track running sums of tick-times-seconds during afterInitialize and afterSwap events. Since ticks are log-space, the relative performance between two tokens simplifies to basic subtraction, eliminating precision loss or overflow concerns. The Arena contract oversees battle creation, operates an in-contract FPMM odds market for low-overhead trading, and facilitates trustless bounty-rewarded settlements with automated refund paths for scenarios like dead heats, dead oracle pools, and empty corners. The entire suite has undergone thorough verification, successfully passing 11/11 end-to-end tests against a live PoolManager. Indexing (The Graph): We implemented a custom Subgraph to map events such as BattleCreated, Staked, Sold, and Settled. For every trade, the mapping retrieves exact odds() and performance() views directly from the contract within the same block, enabling the generation of real-time performance line charts and live stake reports. Frontend & App Engine: The frontend is built with Next.js, SCSS Modules (BEM), and Wagmi/Viem. It employs a hybrid architecture where state and balances are queried directly from the blockchain, while historical charts and activity reports are seamlessly integrated from the indexer.

projects.title: Klaxon
projects.description: CI secrets a stolen credential can't use: split in two, released only against an on-chain payment.
projects.project_description: KLAXON makes CI/CD secrets useless to steal. Today a deploy key sits in plaintext in every step of a workflow, so one compromised dependency can read it and reuse it anywhere, forever, and nothing records that it happened. KLAXON splits each secret into two shares. Share A is encrypted under your Ledger Key Ring and committed to your repository in public — worthless on its own. Share B never leaves a witness service that only releases it when the workflow pays a tiny payment on Hedera whose transaction memo is a commitment naming the exact secret, environment and run, and proves, with GitHub's own OIDC token, that it really is the job you authorized. A job the policy doesn't name gets nothing, even holding every credential. And because the witness publishes every release and every refusal to a Hedera consensus topic before it answers, no secret can be opened quietly: each attempt leaves a permanent, timestamped receipt the owner sees the instant it happens. Stolen, but never quietly.
projects.how_its_made: KLAXON is a TypeScript/Node monorepo (pnpm, vitest). A GitHub Action runs on the hosted runner: it builds a signed commitment, then pays the witness through Hedera's x402 flow via the Blocky402 facilitator — the transaction memo IS the commitment hash — and presents GitHub's OIDC token bound to that commitment plus an ephemeral proof-of-possession key. The witness (Fastify) runs a pipeline of checks — JWT signature, commitment binding, policy match, and an atomic budget/replay guard — and only then returns share B. Share A is encrypted under Ledger's Key Ring Protocol (LKRP): the trustchain is enrolled on a physical Nano, and the hosted runner restores it headlessly to decrypt inside that one step. Policy is anchored on a Sepolia registry contract the owner's Ledger controls, with ERC-7730 descriptors so the device can review each call. Every decision is chunked and written to a Hedera consensus topic (HCS); a Next.js audit site re-reads the Hedera mirror node directly in the browser and re-verifies each payment memo against its commitment, so it trusts nobody and would show the gap if the witness ever lied. Alarms go out over ntfy. Partner tech: Ledger (Key Ring), Hedera (x402 payments + HCS via Blocky402), and Bazantic (Track 2 recipe over the Mirror Node).

projects.how_its_made:
STACK
pnpm workspace. TypeScript for the app, SDK, CLI, MCP server and the CRE
workflow; Solidity + Foundry for contracts; Next.js 16 (App Router) for the
interface; viem for all chain access; zod for the typed domain model. THE EVALUATOR IS THE SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH packages/domain holds one pure function, evaluateSettlement , that turns a
private policy plus a live ERP delivery record into a payable amount and a
reason code. It never signs, never authorises a transfer, and has no partial-pay
branch — every invariant violation returns eligible=false with payableAmount=0.
The real Chainlink CRE handlerInTee path and the local adapter both reach it
through the identical runEvaluation orchestration, so evaluation is
bit-for-bit the same in simulation and in the confidential runtime. The
confidentiality boundary is purely a property of which dependencies were
injected, not a branch inside the logic. CONTRACTS AND THE KEY DESIGN DECISION
PolicyEpochRegistry (EIP-712 approvals, monotonic epochs), AmendmentEscrow
(prefunded, capped, atomic settle-and-transfer, reentrancy-guarded) and
ReceiptConsumer (the only path into the escrow). The decision that makes the whole thing work is what economicEventId is
derived from: keccak256 over (source tenant, PO id, delivery line id) and
nothing else. It carries no epoch. That is what makes "a new amendment cannot
re-pay an old delivery" an identity property rather than a bookkeeping rule.
The escrow also re-derives beneficiary, cap and revocation live from the
registry rather than trusting the report for anything but amount and event
identity, so a tampered report cannot redirect funds. CHAINLINK CRE (primary)
The workflow is written against the real @chainlink/cre-sdk : cre.handlerInTee for the confidential handler, runtime.getSecret for policy material the Vault
DON releases only into an attested enclave, and the confidential-HTTP capability
for the ERP read (the CRE WASM sandbox has no fetch/fs/crypto, so policy secrecy
is CRE's provisioning guarantee, not something we re-implement). The confidential
verdict is a necessary input to settlement, not decoration on top of it. Honestly: Confidential Workflows is invite-only private beta, so we have NOT run
a live TEE execution. Local simulation is labelled "local adapter" everywhere it
appears — in the UI's runtime panel, in the logs, in the docs. Simulation is
evidence of simulation; we never call it attestation. PRIVY (secondary)
Research surfaced that @privy-io/server-auth is deprecated, so the server
adapter is built against @privy-io/node instead. We build real Privy Policy
documents that allowlist exactly two destinations on one chain — the settlement
token and the escrow — and nothing else. The notable piece: we also wrote a local evaluator implementing Privy's
documented default-deny semantics ("a request satisfying no rule is DENIED"), and
it consumes the exact same policy object that gets registered with Privy when
credentials are present. So the credential-free path enforces the identical
document rather than mocking it away. The app shows a real ALLOW (fund escrow)
and a real DENY (pay the supplier directly, bypassing escrow) with the
per-condition check that decided each — and the denied action never reaches a
signing key. FRAPPE / ERPNEXT
One fetch -based REST client against the documented /api/resource/:doctype contract with token auth. It runs unmodified against a live tenant or the
bundled fixture. The settlement report commits to the document's modified stamp, so an ERP rollback to an older revision cannot be silently replayed as a
fresh confirmation. THE HACKY BIT WORTH MENTIONING
The web app is not a wireframe over a documented flow. On first request the
server spawns a real anvil devnet, deploys PolicyEpochRegistry, AmendmentEscrow,
ReceiptConsumer and a test token from the project's OWN compiled Foundry
artifacts, and binds a Frappe-shaped fixture server. Every button then drives
that for real: real EIP-712 signatures, real ERC-20 transfers, real reverts. If
Foundry is missing the app says so instead of pretending to work. Consequence: a revert raised inside the escrow surfaces through the consumer as
a bare 4-byte selector, because the consumer's ABI doesn't declare the escrow's
errors. So we walk the viem error chain for revert data and decode it against
all four contract ABIs — a duplicate settlement reads as EventAlreadyConsumed(0xfb38…) in the UI rather than 0x12bd301a . CONFIDENTIALITY ENFORCED AT THE SERVER
Two endpoints serve two projections of the same deal. /api/deal (buyer and
supplier) carries the amendment terms those counterparties already hold. /api/deal/public (auditor) is built from named public fields only — the
private keys are not hidden by the client, they are never serialised. A test
asserts this with high-entropy sentinel values (a naive substring check gave a
false positive against a millisecond timestamp, which is why the sentinels are
12 digits), and separately asserts the party view DOES carry them. The auditor
component adds defence in depth by destructuring only named fields — never a
spread, never JSON.stringify. PROVING THE REPLAY DEFENCE PROPERLY
Re-running the evaluator on an already-settled delivery just returns
ALREADY_CONSUMED, which proves the evaluator works but not the contract. So the
demo also does a forged replay: it resubmits the exact report that already paid,
with a fresh nonce, so the consumer's nonce check cannot catch it. The escrow
reverts. That is the proof that the guarantee lives in the contract, not in
bookkeeping. MONEY IS NEVER A FLOAT
Every amount is an integer count of minor units carried as a decimal string
across JSON and parsed to bigint at the evaluator boundary. The UI divides by
100 for display only. BEYOND THE UI
The same capabilities ship as a typed SDK, an npx CLI and an MCP server, all
wrapping one client so there is no second implementation to drift. Payment
arithmetic, signatures and authorisation stay entirely outside model control. TESTING AND DEPLOYMENT
71 tests: 33 Foundry (unit, integration, 128k-call stateful fuzz invariants),
plus deterministic evaluator vectors, ERP contract tests, a real-anvil SDK
end-to-end settlement + replay rejection, and the full browser flow driven
against a devnet. GitHub Actions runs all of them with Foundry installed. A hosted path exists: a second runtime mode connects to Sepolia instead of
spawning anvil, with off-chain state in Supabase (RLS enabled with zero
policies, so only the service-role key reaches the tables) and the ERP fixture
re-served at Frappe's real path so the client stays unmodified. Mode is derived
from configuration rather than a flag, so a half-configured deployment lists
each missing variable by name instead of looking like it works. WHAT WE DROPPED
ENSv2 was a candidate third integration. ENS's own docs state the Enhanced
Access Control interfaces are "not yet final", and we could not independently
verify the role methods are live against the published Sepolia addresses. Rather
than ship a cosmetic integration for a logo, we documented the exclusion and
shipped two sponsors properly.

and a real DENY (pay the supplier directly, bypassing escrow) with the
per-condition check that decided each — and the denied action never reaches a
signing key.

FRAPPE / ERPNEXT
One `fetch`-based REST client against the documented `/api/resource/:doctype`
contract with token auth. It runs unmodified against a live tenant or the
bundled fixture. The settlement report commits to the document's `modified`
stamp, so an ERP rollback to an older revision cannot be silently replayed as a
fresh confirmation.

THE HACKY BIT WORTH MENTIONING
The web app is not a wireframe over a documented flow. On first request the
server spawns a real anvil devnet, deploys PolicyEpochRegistry, AmendmentEscrow,
ReceiptConsumer and a test token from the project's OWN compiled Foundry
artifacts, and binds a Frappe-shaped fixture server. Every button then drives
that for real: real EIP-712 signatures, real ERC-20 transfers, real reverts. If
Foundry is missing the app says so instead of pretending to work.

Consequence: a revert raised inside the escrow surfaces through the consumer as
a bare 4-byte selector, because the consumer's ABI doesn't declare the escrow's
errors. So we walk the viem error chain for revert data and decode it against
all four contract ABIs — a duplicate settlement reads as
`EventAlreadyConsumed(0xfb38…)` in the UI rather than `0x12bd301a`.

CONFIDENTIALITY ENFORCED AT THE SERVER
Two endpoints serve two projections of the same deal. `/api/deal` (buyer and
supplier) carries the amendment terms those counterparties already hold.
`/api/deal/public` (auditor) is built from named public fields only — the
private keys are not hidden by the client, they are never serialised. A test
asserts this with high-entropy sentinel values (a naive substring check gave a
false positive against a millisecond timestamp, which is why the sentinels are
12 digits), and separately asserts the party view DOES carry them. The auditor
component adds defence in depth by destructuring only named fields — never a
spread, never JSON.stringify.

PROVING THE REPLAY DEFENCE PROPERLY
Re-running the evaluator on an already-settled delivery just returns
ALREADY_CONSUMED, which proves the evaluator works but not the contract. So the
demo also does a forged replay: it resubmits the exact report that already paid,
with a fresh nonce, so the consumer's nonce check cannot catch it. The escrow
reverts. That is the proof that the guarantee lives in the contract, not in
bookkeeping.

MONEY IS NEVER A FLOAT
Every amount is an integer count of minor units carried as a decimal string
across JSON and parsed to bigint at the evaluator boundary. The UI divides by
100 for display only.

BEYOND THE UI
The same capabilities ship as a typed SDK, an `npx` CLI and an MCP server, all
wrapping one client so there is no second implementation to drift. Payment
arithmetic, signatures and authorisation stay entirely outside model control.

TESTING AND DEPLOYMENT
71 tests: 33 Foundry (unit, integration, 128k-call stateful fuzz invariants),
plus deterministic evaluator vectors, ERP contract tests, a real-anvil SDK
end-to-end settlement + replay rejection, and the full browser flow driven
against a devnet. GitHub Actions runs all of them with Foundry installed.

A hosted path exists: a second runtime mode connects to Sepolia instead of
spawning anvil, with off-chain state in Supabase (RLS enabled with zero
policies, so only the service-role key reaches the tables) and the ERP fixture
re-served at Frappe's real path so the client stays unmodified. Mode is derived
from configuration rather than a flag, so a half-configured deployment lists
each missing variable by name instead of looking like it works.

WHAT WE DROPPED
ENSv2 was a candidate third integration. ENS's own docs state the Enhanced
Access Control interfaces are "not yet final", and we could not independently
verify the role methods are live against the published Sepolia addresses. Rather
than ship a cosmetic integration for a logo, we documented the exclusion and
shipped two sponsors properly.

projects.title: Turing Swap
projects.description: An identity-aware DEX where humans trade cheaper, bots pay dynamically, and LPs earn smarter.
projects.project_description:
Turing Autopilot Turing Autopilot lets a verified human describe a trading goal in plain English. A human-backed agent executes it as a limited, multi-step position on World Chain while the user keeps custody of their funds. It builds on TuringSwap, which won ETHGlobal Lisbon 2026’s World AgentKit “New Use Cases” prize. What I built at Lisbon TuringSwap gives verified humans a lower-fee trading lane. I added opcode 34, _humanGate , to 1inch SwapVM. It checks World’s canonical AgentBook to verify that a unique World ID human backs the wallet. Verified users get lower fees, while everyone else trades in a wider risk-priced lane. The cheap lane has a daily quota tied to the human, not the wallet, so creating more wallets doesn't help. LPs still target a 30 bps blended fee. What’s new: Autopilot At Lisbon, TuringSwap handled a single swap. Autopilot turns that into a strategy that runs over time. Describe the goal — for example, “Buy tETH with 500 tUSD in 5 slices while searcher flow is low.” Compile it safely — the text maps to a fixed DCA schema with hard limits. It cannot generate arbitrary code or calldata. Verify the human — AgentBook must show a verified human before anything can execute. Check live conditions — Nuthatch provides searcher flow, fees and execution-price spread. If the data isn't trustworthy or up to date, execution fails closed. Keep the human in control — the user activates and can pause the strategy at any time. Execute each slice — every transaction goes through the user's wallet, opcode 34 and 1inch Aqua. The user signs every slice; there are no server trading keys. Verify the result — after each transaction, the system checks the actual receipt, events, calldata, amounts, fees and timing before updating the position. Where it runs Everything runs on World Chain mainnet: identity, execution, liquidity, test tokens, faucet and indexing. The stack is World ID + AgentBook, 1inch Aqua + SwapVM, The Graph Nuthatch, Solidity/Foundry, Hono/TypeScript and React/Vite. Why it matters Trading agents need two things most demos skip: Proof that a real human is behind the agent.
Hard limits the agent cannot talk its way around. Autopilot combines World ID for human accountability, a fixed strategy schema for safety, Nuthatch for live evidence, and TuringSwap's verified-human fee lane for execution.
projects.how_its_made:
STACK AT A GLANCE Contracts: Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry (via-IR), built on 1inch's SwapVM and Aqua libraries. API: TypeScript on Hono and viem, using the official @worldcoin/agentkit SDK. Frontend: React 19 and Vite, with raw EIP-1193 wallet calls (no wagmi) and IDKit for World ID. Indexing: a self-hosted Nuthatch nest from The Graph, with custom SQL views, a semantic layer and MCP. Workspace: a pnpm monorepo with contracts, server, web, agent, nuthatch, economics and scripts. Chain: everything runs on World Chain mainnet (480). Continuity: the ETHOnline work is the diff from the Lisbon baseline 6acd9b5 to 1dc5c02, which covers 84 files, +7,215 and −1,273 lines. ON-CHAIN LAYER We redeployed a 1inch SwapVM router (1inch explicitly allows this) with the standard Aqua opcode table and one new instruction appended at the end: opcode 34, _humanGate. It takes 48 bytes of packed arguments: AgentBook address, quota controller address, and fallback wide and tight fees. It makes one staticcall to AgentBook.lookupHuman(taker) and checks that human's remaining daily quota in the token whose amount the taker fixed. The fee is applied continuation-style: it adjusts amountIn, runs the rest of the SwapVM program through ctx.runLoop(), then restores the amount. This mirrors 1inch's own flat-fee instruction. The same code runs for quotes (static context) and for swaps. It only writes quota usage and emits HumanGated during a real swap, so a quote always matches what the swap will execute. HumanQuota.sol stores used[humanId][token][day] and runs the fee controller on-chain. After every fill it re-solves the two fees so that tightVolume × tightFee + wideVolume × wideFee = totalVolume × 30 bps. The tight fee is rounded first and the wide fee absorbs the integer remainder, so the blended fee stays exactly on target. There are separate cases for when all volume is in one lane. LP vaults. Aqua strategies are immutable, so every deposit or withdrawal does the following in one transaction: dock the current order, revoke its quota authorization, move the tokens, build a new opcode-34 program with a fresh salt, authorize the new order hash, and ship the full inventory back to Aqua. Many vaults share one router, so we added version 2 of HumanGate. It binds each quota write to the executing orderHash, and without that, someone else's order on the shared router could corrupt a vault's fee state. A permissionless factory creates vaults, each with its own quota controller. An on-chain faucet hands out test tETH and tUSD every 24 hours. Risk policy. A strategist agent can only nudge two parameters, the desired tight fee and the risk spread, through applyRiskPolicy. The contract requires the indexed block to be newer than the last one applied and within a maximum lag of the chain tip, limits each step to a maximum size, and requires a non-zero decisionHash. The agent computes that hash with keccak over the exact Nuthatch window it used, including the nest's registry hash. The result is then passed back through the same on-chain fee solver. INDEXING (The Graph Nuthatch)
The nest follows three contracts on World Chain: the vault router (HumanGated, Swapped), the vault quota controller (UsageRecorded, FeeScheduleUpdated, RiskPolicyApplied) and the active vault (LiquidityAdded, LiquidityRemoved). The lane and the fill arrive as separate events, so a SQL view joins Swapped and HumanGated on tx_hash and orderHash. On top of that sit views for fee history, activity mix and a 50-fill risk window with tight/wide volume share, average fees per lane and average execution price per lane. The server and the strategist query these over Nuthatch's SQL endpoint, and the same data is exposed over MCP. TURING AUTOPILOT (the new ETHOnline layer) Compiler: a deliberately deterministic parser, not an LLM. Regexes pull out amount, direction, slice count, searcher-share limit, fee limit and price-spread limit. Every value is clamped to a fixed conditional-DCA schema, and invalid directions, slice counts or zero-size slices throw errors. Each plan carries a sha256 decision hash over its parameters and the evidence it was evaluated against. Evidence client: before trusting any row, the server validates Nuthatch's /ready response: ready, not stalled, lag within bounds, and the nest's registry hash. Then every SQL response's provenance must not be ahead of the final readiness snapshot and must match the nest's registry hash. Any failure sets evidence to unavailable, and the plan's decision becomes "wait". On World Chain there is deliberately no fallback to raw events. Service: plans move through draft, active, paused and completed. All changes, including checking whether a receipt was already used by another plan, are serialized through a promise-chain mutex. Plans are persisted by writing a temp file and atomically renaming it. For each slice, the server reads the chain again, looks up the owner in AgentBook, requires every check to pass, simulates the SwapVM call, checks that the quote is in the right lane (tight for verified humans, wide otherwise) and within the fee limit, and records a preparation that expires after five minutes. Receipt reconciliation: after the user's wallet broadcasts, the server checks the mined receipt's SwapVM, Aqua and HumanGated events for wallet, direction, exact amount, lane and fee. It also requires a block after the preparation block, calldata byte-for-byte equal to what was prepared, the same from and to addresses, and a timestamp inside the window. Replaying a hash in the same plan does nothing; replaying it in another plan is rejected. Frontend: the Autopilot workspace shows the Agent Passport, each check's measured vs. allowed value with its Nuthatch block, a progress ring for slices and explorer links for every confirmed slice. The user approves each slice in their own wallet. HOW PARTNER TECH HELPED World: AgentBook is a plain public mapping, so a smart contract can use it directly. That turns "is a unique human behind this wallet?" into one staticcall inside the swap, with no oracle and no per-trade ZK verification. The humanId nullifier is the same for every wallet a person registers, so a per-person quota takes about 20 lines of Solidity. AgentKit's 402, SIWE and verify flow protects the quote API. 1inch: SwapVM made pricing by personhood an instruction instead of a new AMM. Aqua let LP inventory stay in vaults the owners control while trades settle directly between wallets. The Graph: Nuthatch gave us correlated per-lane fills as SQL with provenance and registry hashes. That let both agents refuse to act on stale or mismatched data rather than trusting whatever an RPC returned. HACKY BITS WORTH MENTIONING Adding one 48-byte-argument instruction pushed the forked router past EIP-170's 24,576-byte limit. We fixed it by dropping the Simulator mixin and re-tuning the optimizer. The project started on a Base fork. For fork tests we worked out that AgentBook's lookupHuman mapping sits in storage slot 4 and checked it against the deployed bytecode. We later moved everything to World Chain so opcode 34 could read AgentBook in the same transaction, with no cross-chain relay. AgentKit's validateAgentkitMessage expects the SIWE domain to be the hostname without the port, so "localhost:4021" fails. We also built the x402-style 402 challenge by hand, because we weren't running a full x402 server. Public World Chain RPCs cap eth_getLogs ranges and rate-limit hard. We wrote a small JSON-RPC proxy that splits log queries into chunks, rotates across several upstreams, spaces out requests, backs off on 429s, and removes duplicate logs and re-sorts them. The price of a quote depends on who the taker is, so RPC batching must never lose msg.sender. We have regression tests that prove sender-bound quotes survive viem's multicall batching. pnpm demo:market starts a local-only Anvil market where two actors keep trading, with guards on loopback origin and chain ID. This lets us rehearse the full browser flow without spending mainnet gas. TESTING
The suites cover 40 Foundry tests plus 57 server, 18 frontend, 8 agent and 9 economics tests. An isolated Anvil end-to-end run passes 16/16 assertions, including a mined multi-slice strategy, exact receipt matching, fake-hash rejection and idempotent replays. A read-only live check simulates quotes, approvals, liquidity and the faucet against the deployed mainnet contracts and live Nuthatch.

At Lisbon, TuringSwap handled a single swap. Autopilot turns that into a strategy that runs over time.

7. Verify the result — after each transaction, the system checks the actual receipt, events, calldata, amounts, fees and timing before updating the position.

Everything runs on World Chain mainnet: identity, execution, liquidity, test tokens, faucet and indexing.

The stack is World ID + AgentBook, 1inch Aqua + SwapVM, The Graph Nuthatch, Solidity/Foundry, Hono/TypeScript and React/Vite.

Proof that a real human is behind the agent.

projects.title: Recibo
projects.description: Escrow and proof-of-delivery for x402 agent payments, with an on-chain audit trail on Hedera.
projects.project_description: x402 gives AI agents a clean rail for machine-to-machine micropayments. What it does not give them is a receipt. Once an x402 payment settles, it settles. If the service took the money and never responded, the paying agent has no reversal path, no on-chain record of what was actually delivered, and no audit trail of what it spent. At one payment per API call, an agent making thousands of calls a day is running blind. The ecosystem is building the payment rail. Nobody is building the receipt. Recibo puts escrow between the agent and the provider. The x402 payment settles into an escrow account rather than going straight to the provider. The provider then has to prove delivery: Recibo computes a sha256 hash of the response body and anchors it on Hedera Consensus Service. Only then are the funds released. If the provider fails to deliver, the escrow reverses itself and the payer is refunded automatically, with the failure reason recorded on-chain. Every state transition — HELD, DELIVERED, RELEASED, REFUNDED — is anchored as an immutable message on a public HCS topic before the response is returned. The audit trail can be independently verified at hashscan.io without trusting our server. The refund path is not an edge case here. It is the product. A payment protocol without a reversal path is incomplete, and Recibo is the layer that completes it.
projects.how_its_made: Node/Express server using @x402/express with the ExactHederaScheme, settling through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Client side uses @x402/fetch. Ledger interaction is via @hiero-ledger/sdk (the Hiero rebrand of the Hedera SDK — worth noting, since most tutorials still reference @hashgraph/sdk and the import silently fails). Three Hedera testnet accounts: payer, provider, and an escrow account that holds funds between payment and delivery. The x402 payment requirement's payTo points at the escrow account rather than the provider, which is the single change that makes reversal possible. The escrow core exposes four operations — hold, proveDelivery, release, refund — with enforced one-way state transitions. Any invalid transition throws. "Verifiable delivery" is deliberately narrow: sha256 of the response body and nothing else. No arbitration, no voting, no LLM judgment. That constraint kept the design honest and shippable in a weekend. Every transition anchors a message on HCS via TopicMessageSubmitTransaction. consensusTimestamp comes from getRecord() rather than getReceipt() — a non-obvious detail that costs an hour if you get it wrong. The HCS sequence number, not the local clock, is the canonical ordering of events. Read-only dashboard in Next.js 15 with 3-second polling, showing live escrow state, event timelines, and HashScan links per transaction. Two Hedera-specific things made this viable. First, gas is sponsored by the Blocky402 facilitator, so the paying agent never needs HBAR for fees. Second, a refund costs roughly $0.0001 — on an expensive L1, reversing a micropayment would cost more than the payment itself, and the product simply would not exist. Known scope limits, documented rather than hidden: escrow state is in-memory and resets on restart, there is no automatic timeout sweep, and allowedAssets restricts which asset can be paid but not the amount.
