projects.title: DeComp
projects.description: A GPU compute market where AI agents rent Macs and pay per 5s of GPU time
projects.project_description: DeComp is a GPU compute market for AI agents. Providers sell time on their Apple-silicon Macs; agents rent it and pay per five seconds of measured GPU time, using x402 over HTTP and settling every payment on Hedera through the Blocky402 facilitator. The problem. An AI agent that needs a GPU today has to sign up for a cloud account, hold a credit card, and rent by the hour. Meanwhile there are a lot of idle Apple-silicon Macs with capable GPUs and no way to sell five seconds of that time to a machine that only needs five seconds. Neither side can transact without a human in the loop. How a job works. The agent reads an HCS topic where providers have published their prices, and picks the cheapest one that offers the job type. It calls POST /jobs and gets back HTTP 402 with an x402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED challenge: the exact scheme on hedera:testnet, one tick's price, the provider's payTo account, and the facilitator's fee-payer account. The agent builds a Hedera TransferTransaction, signs it, and retries. The provider verifies the payment, starts the job on its GPU, settles through Blocky402, and answers 202 with the job id and the settlement transaction id. While the job runs, each new 5-second tick is a fresh 402 challenge — payment streams alongside the compute, and the provider kills any job whose measured runtime passes its paid time plus a 5-second grace. Stop paying, and compute stops. When the job ends, the agent confirms every settlement on the mirror node and publishes an audit record to a second HCS topic. No private keys exist in this system. Every account — agent, providers, operator, and every connector user — is a Privy wallet plus the Hedera account it keys. Privy has no Hedera chain type, so these are secp256k1 wallets used as raw signers: a Hedera ECDSA signature is plain secp256k1 over the keccak256 digest of a transaction body, which Privy's raw_sign produces directly (normalized to low-s, which Hedera requires). .env holds no Hedera key material at all. Every component consumes one HederaIdentity interface — an account plus a signer — so the same agent, provider, and payment-gate code runs unchanged whether the identity comes from a fixed role, an OAuth-authenticated person, or a self-custodial wallet in a desktop app. What's in the repo: Agent (apps/agent) — CLI and library: HCS discovery, cheapest-first routing with fallback, tick payments, mirror-node confirmation, audit publishing. Provider (apps/provider) — Bun server: the x402 gate, per-GPU-second pricing, a metered job queue, HCS self-registration on boot. Job runner (services/job-runner) — FastAPI sidecar running a fixed job menu (a matmul benchmark, a Mandelbrot render) on MLX or PyTorch MPS as killable subprocesses, metered by wall clock. It refuses to run on CPU. Claude connector (apps/connector) — a remote MCP server behind its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server. Add DeComp as a custom connector in Claude, sign in once with Privy, and run paid GPU jobs by chatting — no terminal, no key. Provider bridge (apps/bridge) — a WebSocket relay so a provider behind NAT is reachable with no public IP, domain, or tunnel. It holds no keys and trusts nothing but a connect-time signature checked against the mirror node. Decomp Node (apps/provider-node) — a macOS desktop app (Electron + React, ships as a .dmg). Log in, and it provisions your Hedera account, starts the GPU runner and provider, publishes your listing, and shows earnings and job history. Hedera is used for four distinct things: HBAR and HTS transfers for settlement; an HCS registry topic for provider discovery and pricing; an HCS audit topic for per-job records; and the mirror node for confirmation and for verifying payer keys. Jobs can be paid in HBAR or in DCC, an HTS compute-credit token. A standalone script (bun run audit:reconstruct) rebuilds every provider's earnings from HCS and the mirror node alone, with no agent code involved — so the audit trail is checkable by anyone against the chain. Status. Live on Hedera testnet with four validation gates that run against the real network: paid jobs end to end, discovery and fallback, metered ticks with billing matching measured time, and a job paid entirely in DCC with its audit record reconstructed from chain data.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. TypeScript on Bun throughout (workspaces monorepo, Bun.serve, bun:sqlite, bun test), Python 3.12 + FastAPI for the GPU sidecar, React + Electron for the desktop app, and Hedera testnet for everything on-chain. The x402 layer is built on the official @x402/core and @x402/hedera packages; Hedera access is the @hiero-ledger/sdk plus the public mirror-node REST API. How it fits together. The monorepo splits into four shared packages and five apps. @decomp/privy-hedera turns a Privy wallet into a Hedera signer and exposes one HederaIdentity type — an account id, an x402 payment signer, and a client factory. @decomp/hedera-x402 is the x402 layer: a Bun.serve payment gate, a step-by-step paying client, facilitator wiring, and mirror/token helpers. @decomp/hcs-registry holds the HCS message schemas and chunk-aware mirror readers. Every app consumes HederaIdentity and nothing else, which is why the same agent and provider code runs unchanged behind a CLI role, an OAuth-authenticated connector user, and a self-custodial wallet in a desktop app — the identity seam was the single most useful design decision in the project. Partner tech and what it actually bought us: Hedera does four separate jobs here, not one. HBAR/HTS transfers settle payments; an HCS topic is the provider registry, so discovery needs no server we run; a second HCS topic is the job audit log; and the mirror node confirms settlements and supplies payer public keys. Because HCS is a durable public log, bun run audit:reconstruct rebuilds every provider's earnings from the chain alone, with no agent code in the loop — the audit trail is verifiable by a third party, which is a property we got essentially for free by putting it on HCS instead of in a database. Sub-cent, seconds-to-finality fees are also what make a 5-second billing tick economically sane at all; per-tick settlement on a chain with dollar fees would be absurd. x402 gave us metering for free. We didn't build a billing system: the 402-challenge/retry cycle is the meter. Each tick is just another 402, so payment streams alongside compute, and "stop paying" and "stop computing" are the same event. Blocky402 as facilitator means the agent never holds HBAR for gas or submits anything itself — it signs a transfer whose transaction id sits under the facilitator's fee-payer account, and the facilitator adds its signature and submits. Privy is why there are no private keys in this repo at all. The genuinely hacky parts: Privy has no Hedera chain type. We use secp256k1 "ethereum" wallets as raw signers, which works because a Hedera ECDSA signature is plain secp256k1 over the keccak256 digest of a transaction body — exactly what Privy's raw_sign produces. Two gotchas: Hedera rejects high-s signatures, so every signature is normalized to low-s; and signatures are verified locally against the account's on-chain key before anything is sent, so a mismatched wallet fails immediately instead of as an opaque INVALID_SIGNATURE twenty seconds later. One signature per consensus node. A Hedera transaction carries a separate body per node, and the SDK asks the signer for each — a default freeze meant seven Privy round-trips per payment. We pin payments to two nodes: two signatures, with a spare node left for the facilitator. Subtlety that cost real debugging time: the client's network map is keyed by address, and one node answers on several, so naively taking two entries can yield the same account twice — two bodies for one node, and the signed payload fails to parse. The node list is deduplicated by account first. We don't trust the facilitator's /verify. On 2026-09-12 Blocky402's hosted testnet /verify returned isValid: true for transfers signed with the wrong key; they only failed at settlement — meaning a provider that trusted it would burn GPU time on payments that could never settle. The provider now checks every debited account's signature against its on-chain key itself, before starting any paid work. HCS registrations outlive the processes that publish them. A provider that went offline hours ago is still in the registry, so list_providers was routing agents to dead nodes. Discovery now probes each candidate's /health with a 3s timeout and drops anyone that doesn't answer. (Deliberately not added to the routing path — that already falls back on connection failure, so a probe there would only add latency to the happy case.) The provider bridge. A relay so anyone with a Mac can be a provider without a public IP, domain, or tunnel. The provider opens one persistent WebSocket outward and proves control of its Hedera account by signing a connect-time challenge, which the bridge verifies against the mirror node. Requests to <bridge>/p/<accountId>/... are relayed over that socket. The bridge holds no keys and trusts nothing but that signature. Sandboxing by subprocess, not Docker — containers can't reach the Metal GPU on macOS. Jobs run as killable subprocesses from a fixed menu with validated parameters and hard runtime limits. The runner refuses to start on CPU, so "GPU job" is enforced, not assumed.

projects.title: Enscribe
projects.description: ENS invoices for freelancers. Clients pay USDC; settlement stays private on Solana.
projects.project_description:
Enscribe turns freelancer invoices into ENS names. Each invoice mints a subdomain under commons3nse.eth on Sepolia (for example inv-abc123.commons3nse.eth). That name is the public pay link: who it’s for, what the work was, how much is owed, and where the client should send USDC with MetaMask. The important part is what stays off ENS. The freelancer’s Solana receive address never goes on-chain in the name records. Settlement uses Aurora confidential Intents, so the client pays USDC on an EVM chain and funds route privately to Solana. Public metadata stays useful for the client; settlement stays private for the freelancer. How it works Freelancer connects MetaMask, sets a Solana wallet (Phantom or MetaMask Solana), and creates an invoice.
Enscribe requests an Intents quote, mints the ENS subdomain, and generates a PDF with the pay URL.
Optionally, the PDF and an encrypted profile/ledger are stored on EthSwarm (Bee). Postage batch IDs and Swarm refs stay server-side.
The client opens /pay/[ens], Enscribe resolves the Sepolia name, and they pay USDC from MetaMask.
Status moves pending → sent → paid. There’s a simple invoice list plus monthly accounting with CSV export.
What we built ENS subdomain minting for invoices (ENSv2 Sepolia)
Confidential Intents quotes and deposit addresses
MetaMask client pay flow
Freelancer wallet setup (EVM identity + Solana settlement)
Invoice PDFs and optional encrypted Swarm storage
Per-wallet encrypted Swarm feed for profile + ledger sync
Payment status checks and bookkeeping export
Privacy model On ENS: invoice name, client, description, amount, deposit address
Off ENS: Solana settlement address, Intents route, Swarm secrets, freelancer ledger
projects.how_its_made: Enscribe is a Next.js App Router app (TypeScript on Vercel). Server routes hold the secrets; the browser is mostly MetaMask / Phantom for wallets and the pay UI. Create flow: POST /api/invoice asks Aurora Intents for a confidential quote (USDC on an EVM chain → Solana), mints inv-*.commons3nse.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia with our controller key (UserRegistry proxy + text records for amount, client, deposit address), builds a PDF with pdf-lib, optionally encrypt-uploads it to EthSwarm Bee, and returns /pay/[ens]. The Solana receive address never lands on ENS. Clients resolve the Sepolia name in-app and send USDC with MetaMask via viem. Payment status mixes Intents status with on-chain ERC-20 Transfer checks. Freelancer profile + invoice ledger sync as AES-GCM blobs on Swarm feeds, keyed by MetaMask address and gated with personal_sign. Partner stack: ENS for human-readable invoice identity, Aurora Intents so settlement stays private without putting Solana on the name, EthSwarm so PDFs and ledgers don’t need a normal app database (postage batch stays server-only). Notable hacks: talking to ENSv2 Sepolia (factory proxy, role bitmaps, PermissionedResolver multicall) instead of classic ENS registrars; dealing with Intents bridge minimums (~0.3 USDC); hard-capping Swarm upload time so a slow Bee gateway can’t take down a 30–60s ENS mint on Vercel.

projects.title: Floatt
projects.description: The ENS wallet for agent-paid businesses: sweeps idle stablecoins into yield an agent can't misuse.
projects.project_description: Float is a non-custodial, ENS-named treasury wallet for businesses that get paid in stablecoins — increasingly by AI agents, not people. The problem: real institutional-grade yield exists on-chain today (tokenized Treasuries, a market headed toward the trillions), but almost none of it reaches ordinary businesses, and under the GENIUS Act, payment stablecoins like USDC are legally barred from paying yield directly. Meanwhile, businesses are increasingly paid by autonomous agents rather than humans — and an agent has no legal identity, so it can't complete KYC, and handing it a wallet with broad permissions is exactly how recent AI-agent wallet drains have happened. Float solves both problems with one mechanism. A business completes KYC once and gets a wallet named after itself — mybiz.float.eth — which it fully owns and can recover independently of Float. It sets one number: a working-capital buffer. From then on, a narrowly-scoped agent automatically sweeps any balance above that buffer into a real yield-bearing tokenized-Treasury position through a Uniswap v4 Permissioned Pool, and sweeps it back out before bills come due — with zero manual intervention. The safety guarantee is the actual product: the agent's session key is scoped at the protocol level (an ERC-4337 permission validator) to call exactly one thing — a fixed sweep-in/sweep-out contract, capped at a per-transaction limit the agent itself can never raise. It cannot approve a different spender, target a different contract, remove the cap, or move funds anywhere else — no matter what instruction it's given. We proved this live: nine different adversarial attempts to break out of policy were all cryptographically rejected against a real bundler and a real Sepolia smart account, with zero state change. ENS v2 is more than a name here — the same mybiz.float.eth carries the compliance attestation the pool checks before allowing a swap, so the AMM's allowlist and the business's KYC status are literally the same on-chain fact. And the underlying "should this business sweep right now" decision is exposed as a metered, agent-callable API via Bazantic, so any other agent-commerce builder can use Float's treasury logic without building their own. Float is live on Sepolia today: a real business is fully provisioned end to end, real sweeps route through a real permissioned pool, and the admin key has already been rotated off a single EOA onto a 2-of-2 Safe multisig.
projects.how_its_made: Float is a full-stack, multi-tenant TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) built around one idea: a business's wallet should be safe to hand to an autonomous agent because it's cryptographically incapable of doing anything unauthorized — not because the agent is trustworthy. Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, deployed live on Sepolia): six contracts — FloatComplianceRegistry, FloatAllowlistChecker, FloatPolicyView, FloatSweepExecutor, FloatUSTB (ERC-4626), FloatYieldReserve. The centerpiece is FloatSweepExecutor — a minimal, immutable contract that is the ONLY thing the agent's ERC-4337 session key (ZeroDev Kernel v3 + @zerodev/permissions toCallPolicy) is allowed to call. Partner tech, load-bearing, not decorative: Uniswap v4 Permissioned Pools — we deployed a real PermissionsAdapter through Uniswap's own factory, wrote FloatAllowlistChecker as a genuine IAllowlistChecker bridging our on-chain compliance registry into the pool's protocol-level allowlist, and hand-built the Universal Router's execute() calldata (SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE → SETTLE_ALL → TAKE) inside the executor. This is why the executor exists at all: a permissioned pool's router call is opaque ABI-encoded bytes a call-policy can't bound by amount — so we built a thin, unprivileged shim with two typed uint256 functions (sweepIn/sweepOut) that can be bounded, and let it build the router complexity internally, off the agent's signable surface. ENS v2 (Sepolia beta) — mybiz.float.eth resolves directly to the smart account and carries two record groups on its own Permissioned Resolver: owner-writable policy records and oracle-only compliance records, split via Enhanced Access Control's authorizeTextRoles. One name carries payment, compliance, and delegation. Bazantic/x402 — the sweep-decision logic is exposed as a metered gateway (checkSweep, getPolicy) and published as a Recipe, tested live against real on-chain data. Backend: a Node.js agent-service running BullMQ workers over Redis (balance watcher, evaluate, execute, oracle-sync, policy-sync, provisioning), Postgres via Drizzle, a Hono gateway for x402, and a Next.js 16 dashboard with SIWE auth via wagmi/viem. Hacky/notable, all found running against real infrastructure, not mocks: BullMQ silently rejects ":" in both queue names and job IDs; worker failures were completely silent until we added explicit failed/error listeners (an unfunded oracle key stalled for minutes with zero trace before that); Turbopack choked because our wallet package's root export barrel transitively pulled node:fs into the browser bundle, fixed with a dedicated browser-safe subpath export; and — the best one — our own SIWE sign-in kept failing mid-demo with "account not authorized," root-caused to multiple installed wallet extensions racing to inject window.ethereum, so the page read one wallet's address while the signature request never reached the extension that actually held permission. We validated the core security claim live, not with a fork test: an out-of-policy attack script fires nine adversarial UserOperations (over-cap sweeps, unlimited approvals, wrong targets/selectors, non-zero value, mixed batches) at a real ZeroDev bundler against a real provisioned Sepolia business. All nine were cryptographically rejected at validation with zero state change — proof a fully compromised agent still can't move funds anywhere except in/out of the approved position, within a cap it can't raise. Two pieces are deliberately stubbed behind real interfaces because no live counterparty exists yet: FloatYieldReserve pays FloatUSTB's yield from a Float-funded reserve instead of real T-bill coupons, and KYC runs through an admin-review queue instead of a live issuer webhook.

Float solves both problems with one mechanism. A business completes KYC once and gets a wallet named after itself — mybiz.float.eth — which it fully owns and can recover independently of Float. It sets one number: a working-capital buffer. From then on, a narrowly-scoped agent automatically sweeps any balance above that buffer into a real yield-bearing tokenized-Treasury position through a Uniswap v4 Permissioned Pool, and sweeps it back out before bills come due — with zero manual intervention.

The safety guarantee is the actual product: the agent's session key is scoped at the protocol level (an ERC-4337 permission validator) to call exactly one thing — a fixed sweep-in/sweep-out contract, capped at a per-transaction limit the agent itself can never raise. It cannot approve a different spender, target a different contract, remove the cap, or move funds anywhere else — no matter what instruction it's given. We proved this live: nine different adversarial attempts to break out of policy were all cryptographically rejected against a real bundler and a real Sepolia smart account, with zero state change.

ENS v2 is more than a name here — the same mybiz.float.eth carries the compliance attestation the pool checks before allowing a swap, so the AMM's allowlist and the business's KYC status are literally the same on-chain fact. And the underlying "should this business sweep right now" decision is exposed as a metered, agent-callable API via Bazantic, so any other agent-commerce builder can use Float's treasury logic without building their own.

Float is live on Sepolia today: a real business is fully provisioned end to end, real sweeps route through a real permissioned pool, and the admin key has already been rotated off a single EOA onto a 2-of-2 Safe multisig.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Float is a full-stack, multi-tenant TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) built around one idea: a business's wallet should be safe to hand to an autonomous agent because it's cryptographically incapable of doing anything unauthorized — not because the agent is trustworthy.

Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, deployed live on Sepolia): six contracts — FloatComplianceRegistry, FloatAllowlistChecker, FloatPolicyView, FloatSweepExecutor, FloatUSTB (ERC-4626), FloatYieldReserve. The centerpiece is FloatSweepExecutor — a minimal, immutable contract that is the ONLY thing the agent's ERC-4337 session key (ZeroDev Kernel v3 + @zerodev/permissions toCallPolicy) is allowed to call.

Partner tech, load-bearing, not decorative:
- Uniswap v4 Permissioned Pools — we deployed a real PermissionsAdapter through Uniswap's own factory, wrote FloatAllowlistChecker as a genuine IAllowlistChecker bridging our on-chain compliance registry into the pool's protocol-level allowlist, and hand-built the Universal Router's execute() calldata (SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE → SETTLE_ALL → TAKE) inside the executor. This is why the executor exists at all: a permissioned pool's router call is opaque ABI-encoded bytes a call-policy can't bound by amount — so we built a thin, unprivileged shim with two typed uint256 functions (sweepIn/sweepOut) that can be bounded, and let it build the router complexity internally, off the agent's signable surface.
- ENS v2 (Sepolia beta) — mybiz.float.eth resolves directly to the smart account and carries two record groups on its own Permissioned Resolver: owner-writable policy records and oracle-only compliance records, split via Enhanced Access Control's authorizeTextRoles. One name carries payment, compliance, and delegation.
- Bazantic/x402 — the sweep-decision logic is exposed as a metered gateway (checkSweep, getPolicy) and published as a Recipe, tested live against real on-chain data.

Backend: a Node.js agent-service running BullMQ workers over Redis (balance watcher, evaluate, execute, oracle-sync, policy-sync, provisioning), Postgres via Drizzle, a Hono gateway for x402, and a Next.js 16 dashboard with SIWE auth via wagmi/viem.

Hacky/notable, all found running against real infrastructure, not mocks: BullMQ silently rejects ":" in both queue names and job IDs; worker failures were completely silent until we added explicit failed/error listeners (an unfunded oracle key stalled for minutes with zero trace before that); Turbopack choked because our wallet package's root export barrel transitively pulled node:fs into the browser bundle, fixed with a dedicated browser-safe subpath export; and — the best one — our own SIWE sign-in kept failing mid-demo with "account not authorized," root-caused to multiple installed wallet extensions racing to inject window.ethereum, so the page read one wallet's address while the signature request never reached the extension that actually held permission.

We validated the core security claim live, not with a fork test: an out-of-policy attack script fires nine adversarial UserOperations (over-cap sweeps, unlimited approvals, wrong targets/selectors, non-zero value, mixed batches) at a real ZeroDev bundler against a real provisioned Sepolia business. All nine were cryptographically rejected at validation with zero state change — proof a fully compromised agent still can't move funds anywhere except in/out of the approved position, within a cap it can't raise.

Two pieces are deliberately stubbed behind real interfaces because no live counterparty exists yet: FloatYieldReserve pays FloatUSTB's yield from a Float-funded reserve instead of real T-bill coupons, and KYC runs through an admin-review queue instead of a live issuer webhook.

projects.title: Freeride
projects.description: Free AI inference until it runs out — then the agent pays for itself on Hedera via x402
projects.project_description:
Coding agents run on free inference tiers, and free tiers run out mid-task. The usual
answers are a paid gateway you have to adopt, or a bare x402 meter you have to wire up
yourself. FreeRide is neither. FreeRide is a local gateway that keeps the free tier working: it fans every request
across OpenRouter, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, HuggingFace, Cerebras and your own Ollama, with
automatic failover when one rate-limits or retires a model mid-session. When free
genuinely cannot serve, the agent buys the inference it needs — itself, on Hedera, in
the same terminal, with no subscription, no top-up and no human in the loop. Free stays
free; paying is the escape hatch. Three parts share one wallet. The gateway runs as a local daemon. A native terminal
coding agent (a fork of vercel-labs/fx) reads files, writes code and runs commands with
every model call served through it — and a paid turn says what it cost right in its
footer: "37s (↑22 ↓120) · 0.001 HBAR". And a set of always-on AI teammates ("Bots"),
each with its own computer and browser, can buy paywalled resources mid-job: under the
job's budget they pay and keep working, over it the run parks on an approval card and
waits for a human. That last part is the argument. A bot that wakes you for every cent is not autonomous;
one that can spend without limit is not safe. A budget with a human backstop is what
makes an unattended agent trustworthy with money. The payer key never leaves the daemon,
so a prompt-injected agent can ask for a payment but cannot take the wallet. A funded testnet payer ships in the package, so the whole thing works with no setup.
projects.how_its_made:
The gateway is Python and FastAPI, serving five wire protocols (OpenAI, Anthropic,
OpenAI Responses, Gemini, and Vercel's fx/AI-Gateway dialect) so existing tools work
unmodified. The agent is Zig — a fork of vercel-labs/fx with FreeRide as its default
provider. The Bots are Next.js on the eve framework. Hedera is the settlement layer. When free inference is exhausted, the daemon builds an
x402 v2 PAYMENT-REQUIRED challenge, signs it with the Hedera SDK (@x402/hedera, ECDSA
secp256k1) in a Node helper, and posts it to the Blocky402 facilitator's /verify then
/settle. That puts a CRYPTOTRANSFER on Hedera testnet — agent wallet debited, merchant
credited, facilitator covering the network fee — and only then does the paid request
run. The response carries PAYMENT-RESPONSE and the transaction id. Two things worth calling out. First, the payer key is deliberately trapped in the
daemon: agents POST payment requirements to a localhost endpoint and get back a
ready-to-send PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, so they need no Hedera dependencies and never see the
key. That endpoint enforces its own ceiling, a network check and an optional payee
allowlist, because unlike the inference lane the caller now chooses both amount and
payee. Second, the Bot spending policy is not bolted on — eve's approval hook is an
async function with access to the tool input, so the budget check is the approval
gate, and spend is summed from the durable activity feed rather than a counter, so the
number enforced is the number you audit. Hackiest bit: free-first means the cash lane is invisible whenever free works, which
made it impossible to demo without deleting your own provider keys. So there's a
runtime switch — /paid on inside the agent, flipped in the daemon's memory, deliberately
not persisted so an abandoned demo can't leave the wallet spending.

projects.title: Galvanic
projects.description: A margin account where a crypto crash can liquidate your crypto, but never your tokenized bond.
projects.project_description: Galvanic is a cross-margin lending account that lets you post a tokenized real-world bond and volatile crypto as one pool of collateral, without accepting that a crash in the crypto can force a sale of the bond. Normally cross-margin collateral is fungible: when the volatile leg crashes, the protocol sells whatever pays off the debt fastest, often the asset that did nothing wrong. Galvanic's vault computes two outcomes side by side from the same debt: under pooled margin, a shortfall reaches into the bond; under the firewall, it can't. Borrowing power on the bond is withdrawn and new borrowing restricted instead, and the protocol absorbs the loss. On our live demo account, a bond issued through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio is genuinely load-bearing — the crypto alone can't support the loan — and a 92% crash in the crypto mark liquidates the crypto leg while leaving the bond's KYC-gated holder register untouched. Every step settles on Sepolia and Hedera testnet, with transaction hashes to check.
projects.how_its_made: Galvanic is three systems: contracts-sepolia (Solidity + Hardhat) holds CryptoMarginVault (crypto and attested-RWA valuation, health factor, and previewLiquidation for the counterfactual), ProtectedCollateralRegistry (records a claim on the Hedera note, never moves it), and FirewallMarginExecutor, the only address allowed to write a verdict. contracts-hedera issues the bond through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio (Factory + Business Logic Resolver): KYC-gated issuance, a real 2.5% coupon corporate action read back from an on-chain record-date snapshot, and a KYC revoke/restore we prove by making a transfer actually revert mid-demo. The decision itself runs in cre-workflow, a Chainlink CRE workflow registered with cre.handlerInTee on AWS Nitro. The health floor, close factor and exposure cap load as CRE secrets inside the enclave, never in config or logs. The Hedera mirror node is read directly for the bond's balance, so there is no bridge and no wrapped token. subgraph/ sends one query, written once against Messari's standardized Lending schema v3.1.0, unmodified, to live Aave v3, Compound v3 and Spark Lend, which sets the collateral mark, raises the required health factor under market stress, and caps borrowing against external exposure. The frontend is Next.js and Tailwind, calling the real cre workflow simulate CLI server-side and settling the enclave's own report bytes on Sepolia. The one honest gap: Chainlink Confidential Workflow deployment access is a permission we don't have yet, so the executor currently accepts the report from an operator key instead of the CRE Forwarder. One owner-only call switches that, and the decision logic itself is unchanged either way.

projects.title: Honest Harness
projects.description: Six fixes so the Hedera harness judges its AI coding agent's work correctly, plus Codex support.
projects.project_description: The Hedera harness is Hedera's command-line tool for building apps with AI. A coding agent (Claude Code or Cursor) builds a feature into a Hedera app, then the harness checks the work and decides if it passed. If it failed, the agent gets a repair prompt and tries again. I ran the harness on real projects and found it often judged the agent's work wrongly. Honest Harness is six pull requests that fix that: #66: When a build failed, the agent was shown a harmless warning instead of the real error, so its repair attempts were blind. Now it sees the error. #63: A run that passed every check still crashed on its own git commit, because the project's pre-commit hook failed. The harness's own commits now skip project hooks. #65: The same crash twice was reported as "1 fixed, 1 new". That looked like progress and stopped the harness from switching to a stronger model. It now says "2 still open". #64: Apps that already log errors in the browser console failed every attempt, even though the agent did not cause those errors. The harness now records them before the agent starts and only fails on new ones. #57: Adds Codex as a third agent. It also fixes the activity log, which recorded only 2 lines for a whole Claude Code run and now logs every tool call, and stops the harness from killing an agent in the middle of a long command. scaffold-hbar #78: In a fresh scaffold-hbar app, every git commit failed because the pre-commit hook had no lint-staged config. This adds the config. Every harness PR comes with a test that fails without its fix. With all five harness PRs combined, the full test suite passes (226 tests).
projects.how_its_made: All the changes are TypeScript inside the existing hedera-harness CLI, plus one config fix in scaffold-hbar, Hedera's starter template for dApps. I kept each fix in its own pull request with its own test, so maintainers can review and merge them one at a time. How I found the bugs: I ran the harness end to end, on a fresh scaffold-hbar app and on small test projects built to trigger each problem, using Claude Code and the Codex CLI as agents. Every bug in the list showed up in a real run. How I proved the fixes: every harness PR has a "How to run it" section. You undo the fix, run its test, and watch it fail. I also wrote a demo script that runs the harness twice for each PR, once on the current code and once with the fix, and shows both results. That is what the video shows. A few notable parts: The Codex settings came from trial runs with codex-cli 0.147.0, not from the docs. Without them Codex loaded the user's personal config, cancelled every browser tool call, and had no network inside its sandbox. The browser console check had a timing bug. Chrome can deliver a console error just after the page loads, so a broken page could pass. The fix waits for messages already on their way before it stops listening. The logging tests replay real output captured from the Claude Code and Codex CLIs, so they run without any paid model calls. AI use: I used Claude Code as a coding assistant to investigate bugs, write code and tests, and draft text. I reviewed every change and verified it by running it.

projects.title: Orbital Swap
projects.description: Multi-token concentrated liquidity on Aqua, with atomic USDC payments on Arc.
projects.project_description:
Orbital is a multi-asset stablecoin exchange and payments application built on Arc Testnet. It combines concentrated liquidity, 1inch Aqua, custom SwapVM instructions, and Privy wallet onboarding into one experience: providers create wallet-backed liquidity strategies, traders swap against them, and merchants receive USDC through direct or swap-funded payments.
The project adapts the Orbital automated market maker research into an executable Aqua application. Its mathematical model represents liquidity across multiple assets using spherical geometry and concentration boundaries. A single strategy can support trading between multiple token pairs, with liquidity concentrated around the price relationships the provider chooses. The implementation handles movement between concentration regions, token decimal differences, conservative output rounding, and separate accounting for liquidity principal and earned fees.
For liquidity providers, the workflow starts with selecting two or three supported assets, allocating amounts, and choosing a Wide, Balanced, or Focused concentration profile and trading fee. Providers then review and sign the approval, Aqua allocation, and strategy activation steps. Tokens remain in the provider’s wallet until used in settlement. Available liquidity reflects the strategy’s allocation, wallet balances, and allowances, so quotes account for whether the strategy is actually backed. Providers can inspect their strategies and manage their lifecycle through the application.
For traders, Orbital offers live quotes, slippage settings, approval reviews, gas estimates, and transaction receipts. The application discovers available strategies and checks their current onchain state before preparing execution. Custom SwapVM instructions apply the provider’s fee and execute the Orbital curve, while Aqua supplies the allocation and token-transfer mechanism. Each transaction remains explicitly reviewed and signed by the user.
Payments extend that same liquidity into a practical merchant workflow. A merchant creates a USDC invoice with an amount, expiry, and optional recipient splits, then shares its payment page. The payer can settle directly in USDC or select another supported token. For swap-funded payments, Orbital calculates the required input and combines conversion with invoice settlement in one atomic transaction. Recipients receive the requested USDC, excess output is refunded to the payer, and a failed settlement reverts the operation.
Privy provides existing-wallet connection and the configured email and embedded-wallet onboarding flow. Both wallet types use shared transaction controllers for approvals, swaps, liquidity management, and payments. The frontend keeps financial reviews explicit while placing advanced protocol details behind optional disclosures.
Underneath the interface, a shared TypeScript SDK validates configurations and constructs transaction plans. An API and event indexer provide strategy discovery, invoice history, quotes, and receipt-backed observations. The repository also includes an independent high-precision mathematical reference, contract tests, paper-to-code documentation, and retained execution evidence.
The current demonstration uses Arc Testnet USDC and two clearly identified demo tokens, including assets with different decimal precision. Its Arc deployment uses a project-deployed copy of the pinned upstream AquaRouter alongside the custom SwapVM implementation. Strategy publication, swaps, and swap-funded invoices have recorded onchain receipts. Orbital remains an experimental testnet implementation, with broader mathematical and security release validation tracked separately.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Orbital as a pnpm monorepo connecting a Solidity execution engine, an independent Python mathematical reference, a shared TypeScript SDK, and a full-stack web application. The main engineering challenge was translating a multi-asset concentrated-liquidity mechanism into wallet-backed Aqua strategies while keeping quoting, execution, accounting, and the user interface consistent.
The contracts use Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, with a pinned, minimal fork of 1inch SwapVM. We implemented two custom instructions: 0x72 applies the maker’s fee, and 0x52 executes the Orbital curve. The curve engine handles interior liquidity, concentration boundaries, and inward and outward tick crossings. It uses fixed-point arithmetic, wide integer operations, directed bounds, and conservative token-unit rounding. Principal and earned fees are tracked separately so fee accumulation does not silently change the geometric reserves.
One particularly interesting modification was extending SwapVM’s token selection. The pinned upstream implementation binds an order to two tokens, while Orbital needs multiple trading pairs to share one strategy and one evolving reserve state. We extracted a token-resolution hook used by both quoting and swapping, then implemented an Orbital resolver that validates input/output indices against the strategy’s immutable token list. This allows the three-token demonstration to support all six directed trading pairs within a shared strategy.
Aqua provides the wallet-held liquidity and settlement layer. Makers publish allocations using Aqua’s lifecycle, with the strategy keyed to the encoded SwapVM order. Tokens remain in the maker’s wallet, and execution uses Aqua’s push/pull mechanics to settle trades. Orbital checks the allocation, current balances, allowances, and actual transfer deltas. This made wallet-backed liquidity a core protocol behavior. On Arc Testnet, we deployed a copy of the pinned upstream AquaRouter alongside our custom router; that deployment is documented separately from canonical 1inch deployments.
For the mathematics, we built a Python reference using mpmath and exact arithmetic. It explicitly evaluates individual ticks and produces high-precision fixtures for comparison with Solidity. The reference and production engine use different computational approaches, helping expose mistakes that two copies of the same solver could share. We retained counterexamples, rounding regressions, and paper-to-code notes as the implementation evolved. Another practical challenge was contract size: initialization, numerical, storage, and settlement functionality had to be organized into linked libraries to fit EVM deployment limits.
Arc supplies the USDC settlement environment. Its use of USDC for both payments and gas introduced an important accounting detail: the ERC-20 interface uses six decimals, while native gas accounting uses eighteen. Our SDK handles these representations separately and reserves gas when calculating spendable amounts. The payment adapter combines a supported swap with USDC invoice settlement, optional recipient splits, and excess-output refunds. If a required payout fails, the transaction reverts atomically.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, CSS Modules, and Radix UI. Privy supplies wallet connection and configured email/embedded-wallet onboarding, while wagmi and viem handle the shared wallet actions and chain interactions. Financial logic lives in the SDK and feature controllers; presentation components receive typed state and callbacks. That separation let us redesign the interface without rewriting calldata construction or payment accounting. Approvals and execution have separate reviews, and submitted transaction hashes are retained for receipt recovery after interruptions.
The backend uses Fastify, PostgreSQL, and Drizzle, with a dedicated event indexer. It reconstructs strategy and invoice history, tracks chain reorganizations, and serves quotes and receipt-backed observations. A notable integration fix was batching authenticated block and event ingestion so the indexer could keep up with Arc. We also introduced a bounded, same-origin read-only RPC route after browser extensions blocked direct RPC requests; signing still goes through the selected wallet.
The frontend is deployed through Vercel, with Railway hosting the API, indexer, and PostgreSQL. Local development uses Docker Compose and Anvil. The repository retains contract, reference, browser, and onchain execution evidence, while broader mathematical and security release obligations remain explicitly tracked.

The implementation handles movement between concentration regions, token decimal differences, conservative output rounding, and separate accounting for liquidity principal and earned fees.
For liquidity providers, the workflow starts with selecting two or three supported assets, allocating amounts, and choosing a Wide, Balanced, or Focused concentration profile and trading fee. Providers then review and sign the approval, Aqua allocation, and strategy activation steps. Tokens remain in the provider’s wallet until used in settlement. Available liquidity reflects the strategy’s allocation, wallet balances, and allowances, so quotes account for whether the strategy is actually backed. Providers can inspect their strategies and manage their lifecycle through the application.
For traders, Orbital offers live quotes, slippage settings, approval reviews, gas estimates, and transaction receipts. The application discovers available strategies and checks their current onchain state before preparing execution. Custom SwapVM instructions apply the provider’s fee and execute the Orbital curve, while Aqua supplies the allocation and token-transfer mechanism. Each transaction remains explicitly reviewed and signed by the user.
Payments extend that same liquidity into a practical merchant workflow. A merchant creates a USDC invoice with an amount, expiry, and optional recipient splits, then shares its payment page. The payer can settle directly in USDC or select another supported token. For swap-funded payments, Orbital calculates the required input and combines conversion with invoice settlement in one atomic transaction. Recipients receive the requested USDC, excess output is refunded to the payer, and a failed settlement reverts the operation.
Privy provides existing-wallet connection and the configured email and embedded-wallet onboarding flow. Both wallet types use shared transaction controllers for approvals, swaps, liquidity management, and payments. The frontend keeps financial reviews explicit while placing advanced protocol details behind optional disclosures.
Underneath the interface, a shared TypeScript SDK validates configurations and constructs transaction plans. An API and event indexer provide strategy discovery, invoice history, quotes, and receipt-backed observations. The repository also includes an independent high-precision mathematical reference, contract tests, paper-to-code documentation, and retained execution evidence.
The current demonstration uses Arc Testnet USDC and two clearly identified demo tokens, including assets with different decimal precision. Its Arc deployment uses a project-deployed copy of the pinned upstream AquaRouter alongside the custom SwapVM implementation. Strategy publication, swaps, and swap-funded invoices have recorded onchain receipts. Orbital remains an experimental testnet implementation, with broader mathematical and security release validation tracked separately.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built Orbital as a pnpm monorepo connecting a Solidity execution engine, an independent Python mathematical reference, a shared TypeScript SDK, and a full-stack web application. The main engineering challenge was translating a multi-asset concentrated-liquidity mechanism into wallet-backed Aqua strategies while keeping quoting, execution, accounting, and the user interface consistent.
The contracts use Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, with a pinned, minimal fork of 1inch SwapVM. We implemented two custom instructions: 0x72 applies the maker’s fee, and 0x52 executes the Orbital curve. The curve engine handles interior liquidity, concentration boundaries, and inward and outward tick crossings. It uses fixed-point arithmetic, wide integer operations, directed bounds, and conservative token-unit rounding. Principal and earned fees are tracked separately so fee accumulation does not silently change the geometric reserves.
One particularly interesting modification was extending SwapVM’s token selection. The pinned upstream implementation binds an order to two tokens, while Orbital needs multiple trading pairs to share one strategy and one evolving reserve state. We extracted a token-resolution hook used by both quoting and swapping, then implemented an Orbital resolver that validates input/output indices against the strategy’s immutable token list. This allows the three-token demonstration to support all six directed trading pairs within a shared strategy.
Aqua provides the wallet-held liquidity and settlement layer. Makers publish allocations using Aqua’s lifecycle, with the strategy keyed to the encoded SwapVM order. Tokens remain in the maker’s wallet, and execution uses Aqua’s push/pull mechanics to settle trades. Orbital checks the allocation, current balances, allowances, and actual transfer deltas. This made wallet-backed liquidity a core protocol behavior. On Arc Testnet, we deployed a copy of the pinned upstream AquaRouter alongside our custom router; that deployment is documented separately from canonical 1inch deployments.
For the mathematics, we built a Python reference using mpmath and exact arithmetic. It explicitly evaluates individual ticks and produces high-precision fixtures for comparison with Solidity. The reference and production engine use different computational approaches, helping expose mistakes that two copies of the same solver could share. We retained counterexamples, rounding regressions, and paper-to-code notes as the implementation evolved. Another practical challenge was contract size: initialization, numerical, storage, and settlement functionality had to be organized into linked libraries to fit EVM deployment limits.
Arc supplies the USDC settlement environment. Its use of USDC for both payments and gas introduced an important accounting detail: the ERC-20 interface uses six decimals, while native gas accounting uses eighteen. Our SDK handles these representations separately and reserves gas when calculating spendable amounts. The payment adapter combines a supported swap with USDC invoice settlement, optional recipient splits, and excess-output refunds. If a required payout fails, the transaction reverts atomically.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, CSS Modules, and Radix UI. Privy supplies wallet connection and configured email/embedded-wallet onboarding, while wagmi and viem handle the shared wallet actions and chain interactions. Financial logic lives in the SDK and feature controllers; presentation components receive typed state and callbacks. That separation let us redesign the interface without rewriting calldata construction or payment accounting. Approvals and execution have separate reviews, and submitted transaction hashes are retained for receipt recovery after interruptions.
The backend uses Fastify, PostgreSQL, and Drizzle, with a dedicated event indexer. It reconstructs strategy and invoice history, tracks chain reorganizations, and serves quotes and receipt-backed observations. A notable integration fix was batching authenticated block and event ingestion so the indexer could keep up with Arc. We also introduced a bounded, same-origin read-only RPC route after browser extensions blocked direct RPC requests; signing still goes through the selected wallet.
The frontend is deployed through Vercel, with Railway hosting the API, indexer, and PostgreSQL. Local development uses Docker Compose and Anvil. The repository retains contract, reference, browser, and onchain execution evidence, while broader mathematical and security release obligations remain explicitly tracked.

projects.title: Clearing House
projects.description: Tokenised bonds where delivery and payment settle atomically, compliance checked inside.
projects.project_description:
CLEARING HOUSE is a settlement venue for tokenised bonds, running live on Hedera's testnet. Anyone can connect a wallet, get verified and funded in a few seconds, and actually clear a trade against the real chain. It fills a specific gap. Platforms like Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio can issue a compliant bond, but they don't ship a market to trade it. And in any bond trade, the real danger is the two sides settling separately: one party can hand over the bond while the other fails to pay.
CLEARING HOUSE removes that risk by settling the bond and the cash in a single transaction- both move, or neither does. There is no in-between state where only one leg completed. Compliance is enforced inside that same settlement, not as a separate step afterward. Before anyone signs, the venue asks the chain itself whether each side of the trade is even allowed to move, so a buyer who has lost their verification simply cannot be filled, and a rejection comes back with a real, named reason instead of a generic failure. The part that sets it apart is that the venue cannot lie about what it cleared. A separate, independent checker rebuilds every trade's compliance from public chain data alone — sharing no code with the venue and compares that against what the venue reports. If the venue ever fabricated a trade or misreported who it settled for, the checker flags it immediately. Users don't have to trust the operator; they can verify it themselves. It's built on Hedera for issuance and settlement, uses The Graph to reconstruct that compliance history independently, and can settle the cash side over Circle's Arc as an alternate payment rail. Every part of it is real: real tokens, a real on-chain escrow backing every resting order, and real atomic settlement recorded on a public chain.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a set of Foundry-built Solidity contracts. A matching engine talks to trades through one interface, so the two legs, bond and cash, are handled identically regardless of chain or token. Settlement executes both legs in a single transaction or reverts entirely; there's no path that leaves one leg settled and the other not. It enforces two rules: a preflight that never reverts (so it names a reason before anyone signs) and an execute that must revert on failure, unwinding the whole trade. Hedera is the backbone. Bond and cash are issued via Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio as ERC-1400/3643 compliant tokens. The key mechanism is the ATS Hold: seller and buyer each escrow their leg in a hold naming the venue's settlement contract as escrow. Because the token only checks that the caller equals that escrow, the venue needs no role, whitelist, or issuer trust to move held tokens, enough to run a permissionless market on a compliant token. Compliance is checked inside settlement, so a party who lost verification can't be filled. Contracts are source-verified on HashScan. The Graph keeps the venue honest. A subgraph ingests two independent streams — settlement receipts and token identity events — and reconstructs each trade's compliance in the mapping, sharing no code with the venue, so it catches a fabricated or misreported trade. The same check is exposed as an MCP server, so an agent can independently ask whether the venue lied. Arc (Circle) is the swappable cash rail: the engine can settle payment over Arc's Memo contract, emitting a USDC transfer from the payer plus an indexed memo with the trade id, so anyone can reconcile the payment to its trade from logs. Arc's CallFrom precompile means the payer submits the memo call directly. The venue is a Next.js/TypeScript app using viem. The order book and matching are off-chain, but every resting order is backed by a real on-chain hold. Users sign their own holds with an injected wallet; the operator signs onboarding and settlement server-side. Onboarding is open  the operator verifies and faucet-funds any address in seconds. Hacky bits: the contracts target the "paris" EVM so one artifact deploys on both Hedera and Arc; the mirror node rejects topic filtering without a time bound, so we pull all logs and filter client-side; the hold preflight treats "insufficient funds" as passing, since the balance is short only because it's in the hold; and onboarding awaits four sequential receipts (~35s), so we raised the serverless timeout.

projects.title: Ripcord
projects.description: Parametric wallet insurance: submit a tx hash, an automated adjuster verifies and pays in seconds.
projects.project_description: Ripcord is parametric insurance for retail wallets. Add any address, get a live risk score computed from real on-chain data (wallet age, unlimited approvals, prior contact with flagged addresses, contract verification), get a risk-priced USDC quote, and bind a policy on Arc testnet. It's self-custodial the whole way; the backend never touches your premium. If your wallet gets drained, paste the transaction hash into a claim. An automated adjuster independently re-reads that exact transaction from the chain instead of trusting your word for what happened. It confirms the sender is a covered address and the destination is a known-malicious one, and if both hold, pays your full coverage cap in USDC within seconds. No claims committee, no DAO vote, no days-long wait. Every other wallet-cover product (Fairside, MetaMask Protection, Nexus Mutual) routes a claim to a human or a vote. Ripcord covers one narrow, provable trigger: an outgoing transfer to an address already known to be malicious. In exchange, the payout is instant and deterministic instead of discretionary.
projects.how_its_made: Five independently-deployable pieces share one backend brain (Fastify + TypeScript) that owns all the real logic: risk scoring, quoting, and the claims adjuster. The Next.js web app and the Manifest V3 browser extension are both thin clients hitting the same API, so nothing is duplicated or able to disagree. PolicyVault.sol (Foundry, 11/11 tests) is deployed live on Arc testnet, Circle's stablecoin-native L1 where USDC is the actual gas token. Premiums and payouts move exclusively in USDC, including the gas itself. payClaim() is a real on-chain gate: only the claims-agent address can call it, and only against a policy that's active, unexpired, and unclaimed. The claims process is deliberately not an LLM call. When a policyholder submits a tx hash, claimsAdjuster.ts independently re-fetches that transaction from Arc via viem and decodes its Transfer logs. It confirms the sender is a covered address and the destination is on a known-malicious registry (ScamSniffer, plus a demo flagged-address list), then triggers the payout. The check is identical whether a user submits manually or the background monitor (polling The Graph's Token API per insured address) catches it live, so the same transaction always produces the same verdict. The Graph does two distinct jobs. The Token API (via Pinax) supplies wallet age and activity for risk scoring and doubles as the live-monitoring feed, since a custom Subgraph can't watch arbitrary EOAs (data sources are bound to fixed contract addresses). A purpose-built subgraph separately indexes Approval events across major mainnet tokens as a faster, independent signal for the same "unlimited approval" risk factor. For the demo, MockDrainer.sol reproduces the actual mechanics of a phishing drain (approve a spending cap, get pulled via transferFrom) instead of faking it, and forwards whatever it pulls straight into PolicyVault's own reserve so repeat demo runs self-fund instead of stranding testnet USDC in a dead contract. A few hacky, real bugs worth mentioning. Arc emits a second, Transfer-shaped log from a sentinel address for every USDC movement, since USDC doubles as native gas, so the adjuster has to filter logs by contract address first or it records the wrong token and amount. An "unlimited" approval is a permission ceiling, not a balance, so MockDrainer pulls min(allowance, balance) the same way a real drainer bot has to. Policy IDs are SHA-256 hashes truncated to 0x plus 32 hex characters, not a sequential counter, so nothing leaks how many policies exist. Postgres via Supabase backs everything, because Railway's filesystem is ephemeral and neither an in-memory store nor a JSON file survives a redeploy.

projects.title: Warrant
projects.description: An agent buys what it needs and pays for it itself. The chain says no when the budget runs out.
projects.project_description: Warrant is a pay-per-call resource marketplace where an AI agent buys the things it normally cannot get without borrowing a human's credentials — a permanent on-chain name, an email inbox it owns and receives replies at, sealed agent-to-agent mail, a real phone number and SMS, language model inference, and memory written to a Hedera file nobody can edit. Each one is bought per call in USDC over plain HTTP using x402. There is no API key and no signup: the account that pays is the identity. The interesting part is not that an agent can pay. It is that it can be stopped. An owner funds an AgentTreasury contract on Hedera with a lifetime cap, a rolling window ("five dollars a day"), and an allowlist of resource kinds. The agent draws from it and spends without asking anyone — no approval step, no queue, no human in the loop. When it reaches past its limit, the contract refuses the draw before any money moves. That refusal comes from the chain, not from this service's database, and it would still hold if this service were shut down tonight. An agent cannot inflate a draw either: it names a listing, and the price comes from the on-chain market rather than from the agent. Everything is public and verifiable without credentials. The catalogue is the same table the server charges against, so it cannot advertise a price it will not honour. The ledger shows every purchase and every refusal. Every settled purchase carries a signed receipt binding the account, the resource, the amount and the settlement transaction, checkable against Hedera's mirror node without trusting us. The agent signs with a key it does not hold a copy of. Its spending key is a Privy server wallet under a key quorum, and the signing policy refuses to move HBAR or touch the stablecoin contract directly. It is live: the API, the console, a public ledger, an npm client, a skill file for coding agents, and an MCP gateway plus two published Recipes on Bazantic.
projects.how_its_made: The service is Node 22 and TypeScript on Express, with x402 v2 (@x402/core, @x402/express, @x402/fetch, @x402/hedera) doing the payment handshake: a paid route answers 402 with terms, the client signs an x402 payment and retries, and the middleware settles through the Blocky402 facilitator on hedera:testnet in USDC 0.0.429274. The facilitator sponsors the network fee, so a paying agent carries stablecoin and no HBAR at all. Three Solidity 0.8.24 contracts on Hedera's EVM, built and tested with Foundry (28 tests passing). AgentIdentity is a soulbound ERC-721, one per address, carrying the public key other agents seal mail to. ResourceMarket is a permissionless listing registry — anyone may list, and draws are priced from it so an agent cannot name its own number. AgentTreasury holds the money and the ceilings: a lifetime cap, a rolling window, and an allowlist of kinds, reverting with WindowCapExceeded before anything moves. Registration and listing are both open on purpose; a registry behind an admin key is a customer list, not a registry. The piece I am most pleased with is the Privy integration, because it required an insight rather than an import. AgentTreasury.draw pays msg.sender on the EVM, while the x402 payment is a native Hedera transfer — so the account that draws and the account that pays must be the same one. They can be: a Hedera signature is secp256k1 over keccak256(bodyBytes), returned as a compact r‖s, which is exactly Privy's secp256k1_sign primitive. So one Privy server wallet, owned by a key quorum whose private half was generated locally and never sent to Privy, covers both worlds. It even co-signed the AccountCreateTransaction that attached its own EVM alias. The signing policy is written as what Privy's engine can actually enforce rather than what would read best — a matching DENY beats any ALLOW, there is no neq operator, and starts_with is unsupported on the destination, so "only ever call the treasury" is inexpressible and I shipped the enforceable complement instead, documented as such in the code. One deliberate split: sealed mail is decrypted with a separate messaging key the agent holds itself, because an agent that signs with a custodial key still needs a key nobody else can read its post with. Sealed mail is ECIES over secp256k1, with the recipient's key read from the contract and never from the request, so a sender cannot be talked into sealing to an attacker's key. For discovery: the OpenAPI document is generated from the same catalogue constant the server charges against, and Bazantic turns it into 20 MCP tools with x402-mpp auth, plus two published Recipes — one that stands up a new agent end to end, one that audits what an agent spent using only free reads. There is also warrant-client on npm, where warrant create generates a key locally, warrant fund walks both faucet steps with a QR code, and warrant buy wraps the 402, the payment and the retry into one call. Frontend is Vite, React and Tailwind 4, with an ogl shader field in the hero.

projects.title: Under
projects.description: Under: resell unused AWS/GCP/Azure cloud commitments, priced by a Uniswap v4 time-decay hook.
projects.project_description: Under — a secondary market for unused cloud commitments Enterprises pay for years of AWS, Google Cloud and Azure up front to unlock discounts, then leave a large share of that capacity unused. Today it's almost impossible to resell: deals are slow, bilateral and opaque, and whatever isn't consumed by the deadline is simply written off. Under turns that wasting asset into a liquid, on-chain market. A verified seller tokenizes their commitment into an ERC-20 (ccAWS / ccGCP / ccAzure). It trades against USDC on a Uniswap v4 pool whose price is set by a custom time-decay hook: the value of a commitment falls toward zero as it nears expiry, because a buyer has less time left to actually spend the credit. The hook prices this mechanically — factor = timeLeft / horizon — so the discount widens automatically as the deadline approaches. Under — a secondary market for unused cloud commitments

Enterprises pay for years of AWS, Google Cloud and Azure up front to unlock discounts, then leave a large share of that capacity unused. Today it's almost impossible to resell: deals are slow, bilateral and opaque, and whatever isn't consumed by the deadline is simply written off. Under turns that wasting asset into a liquid, on-chain market.

projects.title: Captable
projects.description: Compliance-aware venue for Hedera ATS securities - bids    breaching the investor cap get refused.
projects.project_description:
Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio lets issuers create and
administer compliant securities (ERC-3643/ERC-1400) with
KYC, freezes, and transfer restrictions — but it provides
no venue to trade them. Cap Table is that venue: a
compliance-aware secondary market for ATS securities
running on Hedera testnet (chain id 296). Price discovery runs on Uniswap's Continuous Clearing
Auction, deployed and used unmodified. The novel part is a
validation hook attached to submitBid() that asks a
question no gated auction asks today: not just "is this
bidder permitted to hold the token?", but "if this bid
fills to its worst case, does the resulting shareholder
register still satisfy the issuer's compliance rules?"
Because compliance for a security is a property of the
whole register rather than a per-address flag, a
permissionless auction with pro-rata fills can turn one
large bid into dozens of small holders and silently build
a cap table the issuer cannot legally own. Cap Table
refuses to build that register: every bid is projected
against the live investor-count and
ownership-concentration limits read from the token's own
compliance module, and bids that would breach them are
rejected on-chain with legible, typed errors — visible in
the UI before submission via a live chain-state preview. Cleared allocations settle the way a compliant security
should: through ATS's own hold and clearing facets via a
settlement router (the auction discovers the price, ATS
settles the trade — delivery-versus-payment with a
secret-reveal leg, no raw transfers). A compliance-aware
claim path refunds any bidder whose eligibility lapsed
between bidding and claiming, at the clearing price from a
funded settlement reserve, so funds are never stranded. A
Chainlink AggregatorV3-compatible NAV feed sets the
auction floor price and a deviation band rejects
out-of-band bids — failing open when stale so an oracle
outage can never halt the auction. Everything is live on Hedera testnet: seven
Sourcify-verified contracts (auction, hook, settlement
router, compliance module, NAV oracle, bond), a TypeScript
indexer serving a REST API on Railway, and an SSR web app
on Cloudflare Workers where you can get KYC from a
self-serve faucet, place bids, and watch them be refused
or accepted — with every refusal recorded in a public
ledger along with the exact compliance rule it would have
broken.
projects.how_its_made:
The stack is Foundry/Solidity on-chain, TypeScript off-chain, and three partner technologies stitched together through
extension points rather than forks. Price discovery is Uniswap's Continuous Clearing Auction — deployed and used
completely unmodified. The whole contribution hangs off the validationHook parameter CCA passes into submitBid(): a hook
that projects the post-fill shareholder register against the issuer's compliance rules and reverts with typed errors.
The two genuinely tricky parts there: five simultaneous bids each individually project currentHolders + 1 and all pass,
so the settlement router keeps pending-beneficiary accounting written before submitBid (and rolled back on revert) and
the hook is router-only — that indirection is what makes the projection sound. And it turned out ATS's balanceOf returns
available balance while getTotalSecurityHolders counts total, so a fully-held holder reads as zero and the projection
fails open; we closed it with a total-of helper (available + held + locked) proven by a fork test against the deployed
bond. Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio is driven through raw ABIs against its diamond facets (the published docs describe a
newer version than the deployed v4, so every selector was resolved through DiamondLoupe first). The nastiest integration
detail: CCA's constructor reverts unless the full token supply already sits at its address, and ATS only transfers to
compliant addresses — so the auction's CREATE2 address had to be KYC-granted before the contract existed (getAddress →
grantKyc → transfer → create). Settlement uses ATS's own hold/clearing facets for DvP: a secret-hashed hold, then a
reveal leg — with the hash stashed in the hold's data field because the documented lockHash field doesn't exist in the
deployed version. The Chainlink integration is an AggregatorV3 NAV feed powering the floor price and a ±10% deviation
band that fails open on staleness, wrapped in a bounded-gas staticcall so a reverting oracle can't brick bidding. Off-chain: a viem indexer backfills 200k blocks of auction/ATS events into Postgres (chunked, checkpointed, idempotent
schema) and serves a REST API on Railway; the SSR frontend on Cloudflare Workers calls the hook's previewValidate
staticcall on every keystroke so refusals render before you sign — and "Submit anyway" broadcasts refused bids with a
fixed gas limit so the rejection is a real reverted transaction on HashScan, recorded in a public refusal ledger. 30
Foundry tests cover the four adversarial cases; fork tests replay the live testnet deployment end-to-end, including the
DvP hold settlement and the frozen-bidder refund path.

projects.title: PotLuck
projects.description: On-chain ROSCA savings circles: collateral-backed, with portable reputation resolved via ENS.
projects.project_description: PotLuck is an on-chain ROSCA (Rotating Savings and Credit Association) — the oldest savings product in the world, the way billions of unbanked people already save today (chit funds, tandas, susus, hui). N people each contribute a fixed amount every round, and each round the whole pot rotates to one member; after N rounds everyone has paid in N times and received the pot once. It runs entirely on trust, which is exactly where it breaks: someone wins an early round and disappears, the organizer absconds, and there's no recourse and no record. PotLuck keeps the social product people understand and replaces the fragile trust layer with code. To join a pool you lock 50% of the pot as collateral; miss a payment and the contract slashes your collateral so the round still completes and honest members are never short-changed. The payout order is drawn randomly when the pool fills, so nobody can buy the coveted early slots. Completing a cycle cleanly raises your on-chain reputation (New → Bronze → Silver → Gold), unlocking larger pools; defaulting sets a permanent flag. Crucially, that reputation is served as a LIVE ENS text record — resolved on-chain at read time through the UniversalResolver on Sepolia — so it's a portable credit history any ENS-speaking app can read. It's a credit score for the unbanked, built from savings behavior instead of debt.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity + Foundry on Ethereum Sepolia. ROSCAFactory deploys pools and enforces a 3-member floor plus per-tier caps at creation. ROSCAPool runs one cycle: join-with-collateral (collateral = pot/2), a Fisher–Yates payout shuffle seeded from keccak256(prevrandao, timestamp, address), and a per-round contribute → slash-on-miss → pay-winner → advance loop, with final settlement writing reputation and taking a 2% protocol fee (+5% creator bonus on invite-only pools). ReputationRegistry is the one piece of shared cross-pool state: cleanCycles plus a permanent hasDefaulted flag. Tiers.sol holds the tier ladder and caps as the anti-sybil ceiling. The headline integration is ENS v2. We registered potluck.eth on Sepolia and attached a custom ReputationResolver as a wildcard resolver (ENSIP-10) with NO CCIP-Read and no off-chain gateway — every answer is computed at read time from on-chain state. When the factory creates pool N, our PotluckENS adapter auto-mints poolN.potluck.eth; on join, members get 0x<address-hex>.poolN.potluck.eth. The resolver answers the text key potluck.reputation by reading cleanCycles + hasDefaulted from the registry live, returning e.g. cleanCycles=3;defaulted=false;tier=Silver. The frontend (Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi 3 + viem 2, Privy for wallet onboarding, TanStack Query) resolves this through UniversalResolverV2 and displays reputation ONLY when it genuinely resolves live — never a client-fabricated value. Everything shared (identity, naming) sits behind an interface, so partner integrations are upgrades not dependencies: World ID drops in behind IIdentityGate (we shipped a NoOpGate — Selfie Check integration was attempted but we couldn't land it end-to-end in time), and ROSCAPoolVRF is a real Chainlink VRF v2.5 drop-in subclass swappable via a single setter, though the demo runs the synchronous on-chain shuffle so it needs no funded subscription. Deployed link : https://pot-luck-iota.vercel.app/

projects.title: Boscon Space
projects.description: A trustless satellite oracle that turns real RF signals into verifiable evidence.
projects.project_description: Boscon Space turns signals from satellites into evidence you can actually trust. Using an RTL-SDR, we capture the radio signals satellites send to Earth and measure how their frequency changes as the satellite moves across the sky. We compare that real signal against the satellite’s predicted orbit and Doppler curve using SGP4 to check whether the observation physically matches the claimed satellite. The resulting PASS/FAIL evidence is recorded on-chain on Arbitrum, while The Graph makes the observations and satellite-agent relationships easy to query. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) adds a tamper-evident chain of custody: hashes of the recorded RF evidence are continuously streamed to a Hedera topic, creating a public timestamped trail that can later be used to detect if a recording was altered or replayed. AI agents can then discover verified observations, evaluate their reliability, and pay for evidence programmatically through x402.
projects.how_its_made: Boscon Space starts with something simple: a satellite sends a radio signal, and an RTL-SDR records it. The hard part is proving that the signal actually came from the satellite someone claims it came from. A satellite moving across the sky constantly changes the frequency we receive because of the Doppler effect. But the signal also contains errors from the receiver, oscillator, timing, noise, the satellite's changing position, and the accuracy of the orbital data. We therefore can't just look for a frequency and say “that's the satellite.” Our Python pipeline uses NumPy, Skyfield and SGP4 to reconstruct the satellite's expected motion and Doppler curve, then fits only the receiver-related error. What remains is the part that should be explained by the satellite's orbit. We measure the fit with RMSE and correlation, and then make the problem harder by testing the claimed satellite against other possible satellites. For our METEOR-M2 3 observation, the system searched 643 candidates and ranked the correct satellite #1, without being given its identity. That physics result is then sent to our smart contract on Arbitrum Sepolia. We don't submit “PASS” or “FAIL”; we submit the measurements and let the contract apply the rules itself. This makes the verification reproducible instead of trusting whoever uploaded the observation. The Graph makes those on-chain results easy for applications and AI agents to query. An agent can look at an observation, inspect a station's previous history, and make a decision without understanding blockchain internals. Hedera provides the second layer of trust. We continuously hash the RF recording and stream those hashes to Hedera Consensus Service, creating a public timestamped trail. The recording itself doesn't need to be stored on-chain, but anyone can later check whether the evidence was modified or replayed. Hedera's x402 integration also lets agents pay for evidence automatically using HBAR. Finally, AI agents can discover observations, evaluate the reliability of the station, purchase evidence, and verify what they received. So the core idea is: we don't trust the radio signal, we don't trust the seller, and we don't trust the submitted verdict. We make the physics, blockchain, provenance, and payment layers check each other.
