projects.title: NOMEN
projects.description: Find AI agents with live registry evidence, ENSv2 identities and transparent complaint records.
projects.project_description: NOMEN helps people answer a practical question: which AI agent should I try for this job? A user describes a task in plain English. NOMEN retrieves relevant ERC-8004 agent records and uses DeepSeek to produce a short list with grounded reasons and explicit unknowns. On Sepolia and Arc, live data from The Graph checks current ownership and metadata-URI continuity before candidates reach the model. The AI also cites supplied registry facts in its recommendations. Users can inspect an agent, check its published service endpoints and prepare a small trial to run with the provider. Eligible agent owners can claim expiring, non-transferable ENSv2 subnames under nomen-demo.eth on Sepolia. These identities connect a readable name to an eligible registry record and its current owner. Orders lets users publish a structured complaint for a one-time 5 test USDC fee. Payment commits the original statement; signed edits, registered-owner responses and author-controlled resolution remain visible in the record history. A fee is evidence of publication payment, not proof that someone bought a service or that a complaint is true. Synthetic demonstrations are labeled and excluded from complaint counts. The application runs on testnets. It does not execute agent tasks or guarantee agent performance.
projects.how_its_made:
A Python scanner creates scoped ERC-8004 snapshots, deterministic eligibility results and Merkle proofs. Next.js, React, wagmi and viem provide the application and wallet interactions. DeepSeek extracts task requirements and ranks retrieved records; strict validation rejects fabricated IDs and unsupported source quotes. Custom The Graph subgraphs index identity and reputation events on Sepolia and Arc. The discovery backend pins a fresh indexed block and checks owner/URI continuity against each record's snapshot baseline. Changed or unavailable evidence withholds candidates. Surviving registry facts are passed to the model and cited in its output. Arbitrum Sepolia discovery separately uses published capabilities and live historical trial receipts. Solidity contracts integrate with the ENSv2 Sepolia registry hierarchy. A policy-controlled registrar verifies current ERC-8004 ownership and Merkle eligibility. Subnames expire, cannot be transferred and can be revoked under the documented administrator policy. Resolver records are scoped to the current registration generation and endorsement state. Complaint publication verifies a canonical successful payment and its original-draft commitment. Arc uses 5 native test USDC. New Sepolia and Arbitrum Sepolia drafts use Circle ERC-20 test USDC, with exact transfer calldata and Transfer-log verification. Legacy drafts preserve their original Arc policy. Neon Postgres stores statements and versioned signed updates. Payments cannot be reused for another complaint, and only the author can resolve or reopen it. AI assistance and solo contribution:
I built NOMEN as a solo participant with AI-assisted development. I defined and iterated the product requirements, including task-first agent discovery, a dedicated landing page, testnet-only use, trial preparation, ENS naming access and the complaint-and-resolution model. I reviewed the user flows and tested wallet interactions, including Arc publication payment. Claude and Codex assisted code implementation, debugging, tests, UI changes, documentation and review. Assistance spans tarayici/, kontratlar/, subgraph/, site/ and inceleme/. DeepSeek is also an application dependency for request interpretation and ranking. Open-source dependencies include Next.js, React, wagmi, viem, Foundry, ENSv2, The Graph tooling and Neon. Relevant source, tests, architecture and sanitized product specifications are public in this repository. No claim is made that the source was written entirely by hand.

projects.title: Preflight-Agents
projects.description: Before your AI agent pays a stranger's API, Preflight checks it's alive, honest, and pays out.
projects.project_description:
AI agents are starting to pay other agents for things, using a payment system called x402 - no
login, no API key, just money. But an agent has no way to check first: is this API even online?
Is its price real? Will it actually deliver what it promised, or just take the money and vanish? We scanned every single agent registered on Ethereum's ERC-8004 identity registry - all 10,249 of them to find out how many are actually ready to be paid safely. The answer is 5. Five in ten
thousand. And even those 5 don't all speak the same version of the payment protocol, so many of
them can't pay each other. Preflight is the check an agent runs before it pays. It asks: is the endpoint alive? Is its price
quote valid? Does it deliver what it promised? Then it gives a plain answer - SAFE, CAUTION,
UNSAFE, DEAD, or UNKNOWN ,never a made-up trust score. And the check itself is sold the same way, over x402, on Hedera, for a fraction of a cent. We even built a small buyer agent that finds Preflight on the blockchain by itself, pays for a check in HBAR, and uses the answer to decide whether to pay the real target. Every risky test we could have run only ever runs against our own practice server, never against
a stranger's real API. That's not just a policy, it's written into the code so it can't be
switched off by mistake.
projects.how_its_made:
Preflight is a Node.js and TypeScript project split into a few pieces that talk to each other. The scanner reads Ethereum Sepolia directly through an RPC node, using ERC-8004's registry
contract to pull every registered agent, resolve its metadata (including files stored on IPFS),
and find any payment API it declares. The checker is a small set of pure functions - is it alive, is the price quote valid, does it
actually deliver each one unit tested so a published number can always be re-checked from the
raw data. The paid API is an Express server on Hedera testnet, using the x402 payment protocol through the Blocky402 facilitator. Pricing is metered: you pay per endpoint and per depth of check, not one flat fee, and a payment signed for one endpoint can't be reused for ten we tested that attack on real testnet and it's refused. Every paid check writes a receipt to Hedera Consensus Service,
after the payment settles, so nobody can fake one after the fact. Preflight is also registered as its own ERC-8004 agent on Hedera, so another agent can discover it purely onchain no hardcoded URL. We built a buyer agent that does exactly that: reads the
registry, pays in HBAR, and decides. For Bazantic, we turned Preflight into an agent tool and paired it with a Hedera mirror node
gateway, in one recipe. On its own, Preflight can say a payment quote is well-formed. It can't say
whether the account behind it actually exists. The mirror node can answer that but only once
Preflight has pulled the account out of the quote. Neither service can answer alone, the recipe
needs both. We caught a real bug while testing it, the same account ID exists on both Hedera
testnet and mainnet as two different accounts, and the AI model once looked up the wrong one. We fixed it by only ever connecting the recipe to the testnet mirror node, so that mistake can't
happen again. The one hacky bit is this project also contributes a fix to the Hedera Harness's own documentation, which had the payment header name wrong for the newer version of x402 - a bug that would silently break any agent built by following it.

projects.title: recoverly
projects.description: Recoverly turns overdue export invoices into approved calls, collections, and USDC settlement.
projects.project_description:
Recoverly is an AI-powered recovery workspace for Kenyan coffee and tea exporters managing overdue cross-border invoices. A user uploads a contract and invoice in Slack, and Recoverly reads the documents, pairs them into a case, checks payment terms, drafts a professional collection email, and asks for approval before any outreach happens.
The workflow is coordinated through Slack and a local Recoverly console. Users can approve, reject, or revise collection emails and voice-call scripts. If a buyer raises a legal threat or asks not to be contacted, Recoverly pauses outbound activity and opens an arbitration review with an AAA strategy and demand-letter approval flow.
When a buyer pays through the secure portal using USDC, Recoverly matches the Hedera transaction to the case, updates the balance, posts a receipt in Slack and the console, emails the operator, and closes the case with an audit trail.
projects.how_its_made:
Recoverly is built as a Python and Flask application with a local multi-agent console and Slack as the operator workspace. Slack Events receives uploaded contracts and invoices; a PDF extraction and intake-pairing layer identifies the buyer, invoice number, balance, due date, and contract terms before creating a case.
The agent workflow includes Preflight, Investigator, Diplomat, Tone Coach, Concierge, Payment, Voice Agent, Escalator, and AAA Specialist roles. Slack Block Kit cards provide human approval controls for emails, voice calls, arbitration escalation, demand letters, and settlement decisions. Revision buttons open Slack modals so the user can give direct instructions to the relevant agent.
Twilio powers approved voice calls, with conversational callbacks, hostile-language detection, and automatic pause-and-escalate behavior. Resend delivers approved collection and settlement emails. Hedera USDC payments are monitored through the Mirror Node; Recoverly matches the transaction memo to the case, reconciles the balance, and posts payment confirmation back into Slack and the local console. HashPack is used for the buyer-side USDC payment flow.

projects.title: Studio
projects.description: ENS-approved pricing code, Aqua and Uniswap trades, and author fees in one transaction.
projects.project_description:
Studio lets a trader turn custom pricing code into a complete, signed trading route across Aqua and Uniswap. The trader chooses the tokens, amount, pricing strategy, author fee and minimum final return. After preparation, one Ethereum transaction checks the strategy’s live ENSv2 approval, deploys its pricing contract if needed, buys the intermediate token through SwapVM/Aqua, sells it through Uniswap v4, pays the code author and returns the proceeds to the trader. The entire route succeeds or reverts together. If the final return falls below the signed minimum, both trades, the new contract deployment, author payment and nonce consumption roll back. A relayer cannot strip away the Uniswap leg and reuse the authorization for just the Aqua trade. Revoking the ENS release blocks execution before
trading. The interface makes this inspectable: users can customize route parameters, edit and test pricing code, inspect the predicted deployment address, review setup transactions and preview the signed outcome. A transaction viewer groups the ENS check, deployment, swaps and author payment under one transaction hash. We demonstrated successful execution, intentional late rollback and rejection after ENS revocation on Sepolia. The successful transaction spent 100 demo sUSD and returned approximately 102.630526 sUSD, with the author paid in demo rUTH. Liquidity and prices were seeded; this demonstrates execution, not discovered arbitrage. Approvals, liquidity setup, release publication and Aqua position registration happen separately. The final trade is atomic on one chain. https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0xa18c378e881f3abe9074e746ade151df89cce0e10e471b649eaaccd00906dd07
projects.how_its_made:
Studio is built with Solidity, Foundry, Node.js, viem and a plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend. It integrates 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, Uniswap v4 and an ENSv2 Permissioned
Resolver on Sepolia. Our StudioRouter inherits SwapVM and supplies a restricted custom pricing opcode. The instruction calls a pricing module through a gas-bounded STATICCALL, validates the returned amounts and writes them into SwapVM’s registers. Aqua handles the maker’s allocation accounting and token settlement. The module’s init-code and runtime-code hashes are committed in the authorization, and CREATE2 determines its deployment address before execution. AtomicExecutor combines that Aqua fill with a swap through the official Sepolia Uniswap v4 PoolManager. An authenticated unlock callback performs the swap, settles the input and takes the output. The executor then enforces the signed minimum final return and pays the module author. ENS is an execution dependency: the swapvm.release data record pins the approved pricing release and verification-report digest. The executor reads this live record before deployment or trading. Revocation invalidates execution without changing the signed transaction. The hardest part was preventing the signed route from being fragmented. We bind the trade and hedge parameters, final minimum, ENS resolver/node and report digest into one EIP- 712 authorization. The signing domain also binds the chain and executor. Regression tests attempt to remove the hedge, substitute ENS configuration, replay authorizations, invoke unsolicited callbacks and exploit partial settlement.

projects.title: Dungeon Divers
projects.description: A turn-based dungeon RPG with dragon summons, verifiable NFT loot, and player-to-player trading.
projects.project_description: Dungeon Divers is a browser RPG that connects turn-based dungeon combat with usable, tradable NFT weapons. Players begin with Iron Guard and explore the three-room Mossroot Hollow without connecting a wallet. Completing a dungeon unlocks Ember Mage, who uses her own mana pool for magic and a frame-animated dragon summon. Characters act in speed order, with individual health and resource bars, potions, and saved progress. The five-room Emberdeep Vault adds testnet-paid entry and NFT weapon rewards. MetaMask users play on Base Sepolia; HashPack users have a separate native Hedera testnet payment and reward flow. Chainlink VRF supplies randomness for weapon selection. Players can verify ownership, equip supported NFT weapons, and use purchased Base weapons in subsequent dungeon runs. The Base Sepolia marketplace supports fixed-price listings, purchases, and cancellations. Listing deposits the NFT into escrow. A successful purchase atomically delivers it to the buyer and splits payment: 97.5% to the seller and 2.5% to the platform. Item-level confirmation progress and toast notifications keep trading understandable. The demo is deployed on Vercel with cloud Supabase persistence. Payments and NFT assets use testnets. Combat is server-authoritative rather than fully on-chain, and browser guest saves are separate from wallet ownership. Artwork provenance: selected character, weapon, enemy and environment assets were reused from the creator's earlier BraveLets work, alongside new summon and casting artwork. Sources are recorded in docs/assets.json. Reused assets are not claimed as new hackathon work.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses React for menus and PixiJS for battlefield rendering, modular characters and authored animation frames. Shared TypeScript combat rules and Zod schemas define the command/state boundary. A Fastify backend validates turns, revisions, payment admission, wallet proofs and equipment ownership. PostgreSQL through Supabase and Drizzle persists runs, inventory, payment attempts and reward records in a private RLS-protected schema; the browser cannot write game state directly. Solidity contracts handle Base Sepolia paid admission, Chainlink VRF-backed NFT rewards and marketplace escrow. The marketplace applies a 250-basis-point platform fee. Chainlink price data supplies the USD reference for EVM entry pricing. Historical Ethereum Sepolia rewards remain separate. Native Hedera payments use HashPack/WalletConnect and Blocky402 verification and settlement; native NFT delivery uses the Hedera SDK and a trusted backend applying a pinned Chainlink randomness result. This is not a trustless cross-chain bridge. Vercel serves the frontend and same-origin API. Cloud Supabase uses verified TLS through its session pooler. Authenticated scheduled requests run bounded payment/reward reconciliation jobs, with durable transaction records and advisory locks for recovery across serverless invocations. Secrets and issuer/operator keys stay server-side. NFT artwork and metadata are hosted on IPFS. One challenge was reconciling relayed wallet transactions: confirmation checks use trusted contract events and exact operation details. Purchased weapon discovery combines saved mint records with current on-chain ownership, so buyers do not need to have earned the original reward. ENS integration performs Ethereum mainnet primary-name lookup; dungeondivers.eth resolves to the platform address. This is not an ENSv2 implementation. AI assistance was used extensively through Codex for implementation, tests, debugging, deployment preparation and documentation, and for generated visual assets. Human contributions included product and game-design direction, feature scope, visual and animation review, approval of reused art, and live wallet/payment testing. Existing art sources and hashes are recorded in docs/assets.json. No BraveLets game code was copied.

projects.title: Flow-fi
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that detects MEV and redistributes it to loyal, long-term LPs.
projects.project_description: Flow-Fi is a DeFi protocol that flips the economics of MEV extraction on Uniswap v4. Today, liquidity providers routinely lose value to sandwich attacks and JIT (just-in-time) liquidity — where sophisticated actors insert liquidity right before a large trade to capture fees, then withdraw immediately after, without bearing any of the real risk long-term LPs take on. Flow-Fi is built as a Uniswap v4 hook that detects these patterns in real time and imposes dynamic fee surcharges on the actors causing them, rather than letting that value simply disappear from the pool. The captured surcharge revenue isn't just refunded generically — it's redistributed through Flow-Fi, a tenure-weighted rewards system inspired by vote-escrow tokenomics. LPs who commit their liquidity for longer periods earn a proportionally larger share of the redistributed MEV, which directly disincentivizes the flash-in, flash-out behavior that JIT liquidity depends on. In effect, Flow-Fi realigns incentives so that patient, genuine liquidity providers are rewarded at the expense of extractive short-term actors. projects.title: Leash Protocol
projects.description: A spending firewall for AI agents: pay freely within policy, escalate anything over the line.
projects.project_description: Leash Protocol is a spending firewall for autonomous AI agents. When an AI agent holds its own crypto wallet to pay for APIs, data, or compute, a bad prompt or a runaway loop can drain that wallet with no human involved. Leash solves this with an on-chain policy contract that enforces a daily spending cap, a per-transaction cap, and a vendor allowlist. Payments inside policy settle automatically over the x402 payment protocol. Payments that break policy are held, not rejected, and require a human to review and release them before funds move. Every payment is logged on-chain, building a reputation trail for both agents and vendors over time.
projects.how_its_made: Leash Protocol's core is a Solidity contract, PolicyVault, deployed live on Hedera Testnet. It enforces spending policy on-chain and emits events for every approved, escalated, rejected, or released payment. In-policy payments settle through the x402 payment protocol via the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera, producing real, verifiable transactions. Over-policy payments are held in an Escalated state; a human releases them through the dashboard, with the flow designed around Ledger's Device Management Kit as the intended hardware signing layer. USD-denominated caps are converted using an AggregatorV3Interface price feed — currently a MockV3Aggregator, since Hedera testnet has no live HBAR/USD Chainlink Data Feed. A subgraph is written to index agent and vendor reputation from PolicyVault's events via The Graph, and the agent layer is built on the Hedera Agent Kit. The most notable technical decision: policy enforcement, payment settlement, and human escalation all live on-chain in one contract, rather than being faked in a frontend.

projects.title: x402Router
projects.description: OpenRouter-compatible AI inference gateway where humans and agents pay per call using x402.
projects.project_description: x402Router is an OpenRouter-compatible AI inference gateway for agents and humans who do not want accounts, API keys, or monthly plans. You connect a Hedera wallet, authorize a session once, and inference calls are paid directly from that wallet. The wallet address becomes the identity, while models and sessions are represented as ENSv2 names inside the gateway. The gateway routes Claude and Gemini through one OpenAI-compatible API, so OpenCode, Cursor, and existing SDKs can work without changes. The model catalogue is not hardcoded in the source. Every model is an ENSv2 name. For example, claude-opus-5.router402.eth stores its price, context window, upstream model ID, settlement terms, and endpoint as text records in a Permissioned Resolver. The gateway resolves these records at runtime. Changing a price therefore becomes an on-chain transaction instead of a deployment, and registering an agent becomes a registry operation instead of a pull request. Every inference request is priced before it runs. The gateway token-counts the prompt and calculates a quote for the prompt plus a bounded completion using the published model rate and a small margin. The upstream request is then capped at exactly the budget that was authorized. This means callers are never charged for tokens they did not authorize and do not get unexpected overages. Reasoning models are handled separately because thinking and output cannot always share the same limit. In one test, a 256-token budget resulted in 245 tokens being spent on reasoning and only 7 tokens reaching the final answer. x402Router therefore quotes the thinking allowance separately and accounts for it explicitly. The quoted price comes directly from the ENS record, and the HTTP 402 response identifies the record used for the quote, allowing the caller to verify the price against the registry instead of blindly trusting the gateway. Payments are handled through x402. An unpaid request returns HTTP 402 with the payment requirements and a complete quote breakdown. The client signs a Hedera transfer using its session key and retries the request. Blocky402 verifies and settles the payment on Hedera before the gateway returns the inference result. A session is also a name. Opening a session registers a name such as s7fj2k.keys.router402.eth in our hierarchical ENSv2 registry. The registry stores the owner and expiry and provides on-chain revocation through unregister() . Revocation is therefore a public, ordered fact that can be checked independently of the gateway database. Session names are deliberately non-transferable. The session owner receives ROLE_UNREGISTER , but not ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN or ROLE_RENEW . A session key therefore cannot transfer the session to another party or extend its own lifetime. For ECDSA-backed Hedera accounts, the ENS name is registered to the account's EVM alias, allowing the caller to revoke the session on Sepolia without connecting a separate Ethereum wallet. Every request checks the registry rather than relying only on a database row. Each settlement is published to a public Hedera Consensus Service topic, creating a tamper-evident payment history that can be independently verified. The demo supports settlement in HBAR and HTS tokens with a custom fee schedule. The service is also exposed through an x402 Bazaar listing, /.well-known/agent.json , and /v1/discovery , with each agent's ENS name included so other agents can discover and call the service programmatically. For harnesses that cannot sign x402 payments themselves, x402Router provides an encrypted and revocable access URL that allows an agent to pay automatically within the limits of its session. This is intentionally restricted to testnet. The core design is simple: ENS provides the naming, discovery, identity, and policy layer, while Hedera provides the payment and settlement layer.

The gateway routes Claude and Gemini through one OpenAI-compatible API, so OpenCode, Cursor, and existing SDKs can work without changes. The model catalogue is not hardcoded in the source. Every model is an ENSv2 name. For example, `claude-opus-5.router402.eth` stores its price, context window, upstream model ID, settlement terms, and endpoint as text records in a Permissioned Resolver. The gateway resolves these records at runtime. Changing a price therefore becomes an on-chain transaction instead of a deployment, and registering an agent becomes a registry operation instead of a pull request.

Every inference request is priced before it runs. The gateway token-counts the prompt and calculates a quote for the prompt plus a bounded completion using the published model rate and a small margin. The upstream request is then capped at exactly the budget that was authorized. This means callers are never charged for tokens they did not authorize and do not get unexpected overages.

Reasoning models are handled separately because thinking and output cannot always share the same limit. In one test, a 256-token budget resulted in 245 tokens being spent on reasoning and only 7 tokens reaching the final answer. x402Router therefore quotes the thinking allowance separately and accounts for it explicitly. The quoted price comes directly from the ENS record, and the HTTP 402 response identifies the record used for the quote, allowing the caller to verify the price against the registry instead of blindly trusting the gateway.

Payments are handled through x402. An unpaid request returns HTTP 402 with the payment requirements and a complete quote breakdown. The client signs a Hedera transfer using its session key and retries the request. Blocky402 verifies and settles the payment on Hedera before the gateway returns the inference result.

A session is also a name. Opening a session registers a name such as `s7fj2k.keys.router402.eth` in our hierarchical ENSv2 registry. The registry stores the owner and expiry and provides on-chain revocation through `unregister()`. Revocation is therefore a public, ordered fact that can be checked independently of the gateway database.

Session names are deliberately non-transferable. The session owner receives `ROLE_UNREGISTER`, but not `ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN` or `ROLE_RENEW`. A session key therefore cannot transfer the session to another party or extend its own lifetime. For ECDSA-backed Hedera accounts, the ENS name is registered to the account's EVM alias, allowing the caller to revoke the session on Sepolia without connecting a separate Ethereum wallet. Every request checks the registry rather than relying only on a database row.

Each settlement is published to a public Hedera Consensus Service topic, creating a tamper-evident payment history that can be independently verified. The demo supports settlement in HBAR and HTS tokens with a custom fee schedule. The service is also exposed through an x402 Bazaar listing, `/.well-known/agent.json`, and `/v1/discovery`, with each agent's ENS name included so other agents can discover and call the service programmatically.

For harnesses that cannot sign x402 payments themselves, x402Router provides an encrypted and revocable access URL that allows an agent to pay automatically within the limits of its session. This is intentionally restricted to testnet.

The core design is simple: ENS provides the naming, discovery, identity, and policy layer, while Hedera provides the payment and settlement layer.

projects.title: Kazuo
projects.description: Sell your idle AI subscription one job at a time, paid in USDC on Arc via x402.
projects.project_description: Kazuo turns AI subscriptions people already pay for (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, OpenCode) into a marketplace that sells compute one job at a time. Most of the day a paid AI plan sits idle, while someone else who needs one job done has to buy a whole plan. Kazuo connects the two. A provider runs one command, kazuo start , and their machine joins the network as a node. A buyer can be a person on the web job board, a terminal user, or an AI agent over MCP. They describe a task, get a quote naming the node, the price and the address that gets paid, then pay per request. The job runs on the provider's machine inside an OS sandbox and the answer streams back. Every job settles as a real USDC transfer on Arc, straight from buyer to provider. There is no escrow and no platform float, and the protocol fee is 0%. The buyer signs an EIP-3009 authorization over x402 and spends zero gas: a facilitator relays it and pays the fee in USDC, Arc's gas token. Every registration, heartbeat and job receipt (including a SHA-256 of the answer) is written to our KazuoLog contract on Arc, so anyone can audit the network on ArcScan. A reputation-based market is easy to farm with bots, so Kazuo uses World to mark human-backed nodes. Nodes sign a World AgentKit challenge with their payout key, and the broker looks the address up in AgentBook on World Chain. World ID Selfie Check is a second route to the human label. Human-backed nodes win price ties, one human can back at most three nodes, and buyers can require human-backed providers only. Privy signs people in with an email (embedded wallet on Arc) or an existing wallet. The same wallet pays for jobs with a typed-data signature, so no gas and no network setup are needed. It is live on Arc testnet: landing at kazuo-arc.vercel.app, job board at kazuo-arc-app.vercel.app, with real settlements and receipts on testnet.arcscan.app. Kazuo began as Xorv on Hedera and was ported to Arc, World and Privy for ETHOnline.
projects.how_its_made: A TypeScript pnpm monorepo with five parts: Broker (Hono + WebSockets + SQLite via node:sqlite). It matches quotes to live providers, serves HTTP 402 with x402 v2 "exact" payment requirements, and runs a self-hosted facilitator that relays EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization on Arc and pays the gas. Jobs, earnings and the audit-log index persist across restarts. If a provider disconnects mid-job, the job fails over to another node at no extra charge after a 60 s grace; a cancelled job publishes a failed receipt. KazuoLog contract on Arc. Registrations, sampled heartbeats and receipts are indexed events. The broker keeps a forward index so pages never scan the chain, and the indexer yields whenever a settlement is in flight so it can't starve payments of the public RPC's rate budget. Provider CLI ( kazuo ). Nodes dial out over WebSocket, so they work behind NAT. It drives agent CLIs as adapters (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, OpenCode, OpenAI-compatible) inside an OS sandbox (macOS seatbelt, bubblewrap, or a container) with an allowlisted environment, so a hostile prompt can't read the payout key or SSH/cloud credentials. kazuo doctor and kazuo test check auth, sandbox and pricing before a node sells anything. MCP server with a hard per-call spending ceiling, plus a /kazuo skill so Claude Code can buy a job from someone else's machine and pay for it. Next.js 16 job board and landing on Vercel. Partner tech: Arc: USDC is the gas token, so a buyer needs nothing but the USDC they spend. We assert the buyer's gas is 0 wei in a script against live testnet. World AgentKit: broker-minted SIWE challenges verified with @worldcoin/agentkit, with AgentBook read on World Chain. World ID Selfie Check: IDKit 4 with RP-signed single-use requests. The broker checks nonce, expiry, action and signal hash before calling World's verify API. Privy: email with embedded wallets, and external wallets through the same modal. Both pay with the same x402 signing path. Notably hacky: x402's EVM scheme only fills in the EIP-712 domain for networks in its stablecoin registry, and Arc isn't one. So each quote freezes the USDC domain and exact amount, keeping both 402 round-trips byte-identical. Arc's native USDC shows two faces (18-decimal gas balance vs 6-decimal ERC-20). The CLI shows both views of one balance. The no-wallet demo relays payment to the broker, so the demo key never leaves our machine. Paid quotes stay refused (409 with the job id) even after they expire or the broker restarts, so a retry can't pay twice. We recorded the demo by driving real Chrome with an injected testnet wallet. That surfaced and fixed two real bugs: BigInt typed data breaking eth_signTypedData_v4, and on-chain receipts not appearing without a reload. 360+ tests, GitHub Actions CI, and an end-to-end test plan verified live in the browser and on chain.

A TypeScript pnpm monorepo with five parts:

- Broker (Hono + WebSockets + SQLite via node:sqlite). It matches quotes to live providers, serves HTTP 402 with x402 v2 "exact" payment requirements, and runs a self-hosted facilitator that relays EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization on Arc and pays the gas. Jobs, earnings and the audit-log index persist across restarts. If a provider disconnects mid-job, the job fails over to another node at no extra charge after a 60 s grace; a cancelled job publishes a failed receipt.
- KazuoLog contract on Arc. Registrations, sampled heartbeats and receipts are indexed events. The broker keeps a forward index so pages never scan the chain, and the indexer yields whenever a settlement is in flight so it can't starve payments of the public RPC's rate budget.
- Provider CLI (`kazuo`). Nodes dial out over WebSocket, so they work behind NAT. It drives agent CLIs as adapters (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, OpenCode, OpenAI-compatible) inside an OS sandbox (macOS seatbelt, bubblewrap, or a container) with an allowlisted environment, so a hostile prompt can't read the payout key or SSH/cloud credentials. `kazuo doctor` and `kazuo test` check auth, sandbox and pricing before a node sells anything.
- MCP server with a hard per-call spending ceiling, plus a /kazuo skill so Claude Code can buy a job from someone else's machine and pay for it.
- Next.js 16 job board and landing on Vercel.

Partner tech:
- Arc: USDC is the gas token, so a buyer needs nothing but the USDC they spend. We assert the buyer's gas is 0 wei in a script against live testnet.
- World AgentKit: broker-minted SIWE challenges verified with @worldcoin/agentkit, with AgentBook read on World Chain.
- World ID Selfie Check: IDKit 4 with RP-signed single-use requests. The broker checks nonce, expiry, action and signal hash before calling World's verify API.
- Privy: email with embedded wallets, and external wallets through the same modal. Both pay with the same x402 signing path.

Notably hacky:
- x402's EVM scheme only fills in the EIP-712 domain for networks in its stablecoin registry, and Arc isn't one. So each quote freezes the USDC domain and exact amount, keeping both 402 round-trips byte-identical.
- Arc's native USDC shows two faces (18-decimal gas balance vs 6-decimal ERC-20). The CLI shows both views of one balance.
- The no-wallet demo relays payment to the broker, so the demo key never leaves our machine.
- Paid quotes stay refused (409 with the job id) even after they expire or the broker restarts, so a retry can't pay twice.
- We recorded the demo by driving real Chrome with an injected testnet wallet. That surfaced and fixed two real bugs: BigInt typed data breaking eth_signTypedData_v4, and on-chain receipts not appearing without a reload.

360+ tests, GitHub Actions CI, and an end-to-end test plan verified live in the browser and on chain.

projects.title: Reserva AI
projects.description: USDC-backed loyalty on Arc, run from chat. Points can't go underwater.
projects.project_description: Reserva is a loyalty system where every point a merchant issues is backed by real USDC held in an on-chain vault. A café, salon, gym, or small retailer funds a program once. From that moment, the vault is the ceiling: the contract will not issue more points than it holds. When a customer redeems, settlement releases from escrow on Arc in the same transaction — not as a favour the merchant later chooses to honour. The problem it targets is simple and almost never audited. Small-business loyalty lives in spreadsheets. Airlines reserve against their miles because regulators force them to; a shop with 400 members reserves against nothing. Customers have learned not to trust those balances — punch cards from shops that closed, points that quietly expired — so they do not redeem, behaviour never changes, and the merchant concludes loyalty does not work. Meanwhile the owner has no live number for what they already owe. projects.title: Tashan
projects.description: The trusted directory for your AI's toolbox — and what agents actually pay for.
projects.project_description:
tashan scores the MCP servers and agent skills you can install into an AI agent, using public
evidence only. 95,574 tracked, 12,662 with a published measurement: upkeep, freshness, adoption, and OSV advisories checked against the version you'd install today. Every number links to its source. Nobody can buy a rank. A test reads the scorer's source and fails the build if it touches anything that isn't public evidence. It also measures what agents actually pay for. Downloads and stars can be faked by the author, a payment can't. x402 makes those payments public, so we read the chain for every payment address in Coinbase's x402 directory — $247,356 settled across 10.4M payments, 998 of 1,079 services paid at least once. That directory publishes no evidence about any of them. A capability page shows whether a tool has ever been paid for, alongside whether it's maintained. npx tashan-cli doctor reads the agent configs on your machine — Claude Code, Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf — and flags what's deprecated, archived, abandoned, or running an install script. Nothing uploaded.
projects.how_its_made:
Python 3 stdlib, no dependencies. SQLite as the source of truth. Static site, no build step, strict
CSP, on Cloudflare Pages — Functions for the paid endpoints, R2 for the DB cache, KV for licences. The Graph, two products: an x402 settlement subgraph on the Network, read through The Graph's Subgraph MCP server. The query is printed on the page so anyone can re-run it. Their documented client is an npx bridge, so we wrote an MCP client over HTTP+SSE in stdlib urllib — ~120 lines, no Node. We also shipped our own subgraph over the same economy: USDC Transfers on Base filtered on the indexed recipient, so graph-node matches at the log level and sync is bounded by the economy, not the chain. One query decision: we ask about every listed address in batches instead of ordering by volume and taking the top 1,000. A top-N query drops every service that earned almost nothing, and those rows matter. An address the chain doesn't know is reported as never paid, not omitted. Bazantic: published an OpenAPI spec for our endpoints, registered it as an x402/MPP gateway, and published a Recipe that returns install / caution / do-not-install for anything an agent is about to install. Security findings are not inputs to the score — "maintained" and "nothing known is wrong" are
different claims, and merging them hides the package that scores 86 and runs an install script.

projects.title: MACH402
projects.description: MACH402 — rent GPUs by the second on Hedera via x402. No API keys. Built for agents too.
projects.project_description:
MACH402 is a peer-to-peer GPU rental marketplace where payment itself is the only credential anyone ever needs.
A provider with an idle GPU runs a lightweight daemon that turns their machine into an x402 resource server; a renter — a person at a terminal, or an autonomous AI agent — pays that node directly, by the second, for a live container on it, and gets back whatever credit they didn't use. There are no accounts to create, no API keys to issue, and no subscription to manage. The HTTP 402 Payment Required status code, largely unused since the early web, becomes the actual authentication and authorization mechanism: a renter's signed payment transaction is their access grant. Every session is metered rather than prepaid in a lump sum. A renter buys a small chunk of credit up front; the provider node burns that credit continuously while the container runs and automatically refunds whatever's unused the moment the session stops — paid back from the node's own operator account, with no separate escrow contract holding funds in between. What makes that trustworthy rather than a blind promise is that every provider publishes a running "what I currently owe this renter" figure to its own Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) audit topic every fifteen seconds while a session is live — a continuously signed, publicly verifiable trail that exists before any dispute ever could. The marketplace has four cleanly separated parties. The renter holds a Hedera key and pays. The provider node runs the x402 resource server, verifies and settles payments through the Blocky402 facilitator, and runs the rented container — but it never holds a Hedera private key or links a Hedera SDK itself; all cryptographic signing lives in TypeScript using @x402/hedera, the reference implementation of Hedera's exact payment scheme. A discovery registry tracks which nodes are online via 30-second heartbeats but never touches money — it's pure metadata. And the shared Blocky402 facilitator co-signs as fee payer and submits transactions to Hedera testnet.
Security is treated as load-bearing, not incidental. A rented container gets a real root shell (so pip install works) but sits on an internal-only Docker network with no route off the host except through a purpose-built egress proxy that denies every destination by default and allowlists only package and model registries. Access is granted by a short-lived SSH certificate signed by the node's own certificate authority — never a shared key — so revocation is simply letting the certificate expire.
Renters can connect two ways. A website lets a person browse listed nodes, pick one, and pay directly from their own connected wallet. For autonomous use, we built and published mach402-mcp-server on npm — a standalone Model Context Protocol server that exposes the identical rent flow (search nodes, get a price quote, open a session, top up credit, stop and collect a refund) as tools any MCP-capable AI agent can call on its own, complete with configurable daily spending caps and a confirmation gate for payments above a threshold.
Providers also get an on-chain ERC-8004 identity and a live terminal dashboard showing real-time earnings, GPU utilization, and session state.
projects.how_its_made: The stack splits cleanly along one rule: whichever side needs to sign a Hedera transaction is written in TypeScript, and nothing else is. The provider daemon (agent/) is a single static Go binary — deliberately, since a provider should be able to drop one file onto a stranger's GPU box and run it. It's the x402 resource server: it builds price challenges, calls the Blocky402 facilitator's /verify and /settle endpoints, runs and meters Docker containers, and serves the whole /v1/ HTTP API. It talks to Docker over its raw HTTP API on the unix socket rather than linking the Docker SDK, to keep the binary small and dependency-light. The interesting constraint: Go has no mature Hedera SDK, and hand-rolling frozen TransferTransaction bytes was out of scope. So the Go daemon never holds a private key and never imports a Hedera SDK at all — every signed transaction it needs (HCS topic submissions, ERC-8004 registration, session refunds) is produced by shelling out to a small TypeScript sidecar (hederakit/, invoked as the cleargate-hedera binary) that reads a node-local operator key, signs one transaction, and prints JSON back over stdout. This is the same pattern used for ssh-keygen (the node's own SSH certificate authority) and cloudflared (NAT traversal via Cloudflare quick tunnels) — trusted external binaries doing one job, invoked as child processes, rather than reimplemented or linked in. All renter-side payment signing lives in TypeScript using @x402/hedera, the reference implementation of Hedera's exact payment scheme — there's no second implementation to drift out of sync with the spec. That same signing logic is vendored into a fully standalone MCP server package (packages/mcp-server, published on npm as mach402-mcp-server) with zero dependency on the rest of the monorepo, so an AI agent host can npx it with nothing but Node.js. packages/types re-exports the x402 SDK's own wire types rather than redeclaring them, so a facilitator update surfaces as a compile error instead of a silent runtime mismatch. Money is handled as strings and BigInt end to end — tinybars, never floats — because floating-point arithmetic on currency is a bug waiting to happen. A golden-fixture test pins the Go challenge builder's output byte-for-byte against a captured response from the official @x402/express reference server, so any accidental protocol drift fails CI immediately rather than surfacing as a mysterious client-side rejection weeks later. The sandbox is the most deliberately over-engineered part: a rented container needs a real root shell (so pip install works), which rules out --network=none. Instead it sits on a Docker network with Internal: true and no route off the host at all, except through cleargate-egress — a deny-by-default proxy we built from source specifically for this project, matched on domain boundaries so notgithub.com can't pass as github.com. The discovery registry (Fastify + Postgres) and website (Next.js) are conventional on purpose — discovery isn't where the interesting engineering need to happen. The genuinely hacky bit, in the good sense: settlement only ever happens after the container is proven reachable through its tunnel, not after payment verification — so a session that never actually comes up costs the renter nothing, at the cost of doing container startup, cert signing, and a tunnel health check all inside the payment payload's 300-second expiry window.

projects.title: Gabhru
projects.description: Pay AI agents privately by ENS name — stealth addresses, any wallet, no setup.
projects.project_description: Every payment to an AI agent today is public and permanent. ERC-8004 gives agents an on-chain identity, but that makes their revenue, customer list, and payment schedule readable by any competitor with a block explorer. Gabhru gives each agent a free ENS subname (alice.gabhru.eth). When anyone resolves that name, they get a fresh, single-use stealth address — never the same one twice. The sender pays exactly like they'd pay any ENS name, from any wallet, with no plugin and no special flow. The agent sees the USDC land in its dashboard about two seconds later. No observer can link two payments to the same agent, count its customers, or total its revenue. Agents get privacy without asking their users to do anything differently.

projects.title: TARE
projects.description: Measures what a Uniswap v4 hook really takes from your swap. 125,072 measurements, each replayable.
projects.project_description:
When you swap on Uniswap v4, a small program called a hook runs during your trade, and it can
take a cut. Nobody publishes how much. Uniswap asks hooks to declare it through the HookSwap and HookFee events its own guide
recommends. Across 1,559 hooks seen in 200,000 Base blocks, nine emit either one. The official
registry describes 978 entries with 27 fields each, 19 of them booleans — and not one of the 27
is a quantity. Its schema does not merely omit a number, it forbids adding one. So TARE measures it. The obvious comparison is impossible: a v4 pool's identity — its PoolKey —
contains the hook's address, so "the same pool without its hook" does not exist. TARE does not
change the pool: it changes the hook. On a fork pinned to a block, anvil_setCode replaces the
hook's bytecode with an inert 89-byte stub. The poolId, the liquidity, slot0 and the reserves
stay byte-identical; the only thing that changed is the code that runs during the swap. Quote
the same swap twice and the gap IS what the hook took. 125,072 measurements, 7,817 pools, 112 hooks, 8 sizes, both directions. Every row carries its
block, its size, its direction, its label and a command that reproduces it. What could not be
measured keeps its reason instead of a zero: 61,916 of those rows are not values, and we
publish that too.
projects.how_its_made:
The engine is Python. It pins an anvil fork of Base at block 50,614,000, quotes a swap through
V4Quoter, rewrites the hook's bytecode with anvil_setCode to an inert 89-byte stub that
satisfies Hooks.sol's return-data validation (96 bytes from beforeSwap, 64 otherwise, selector
echoed), quotes the same swap again, and restores the bytecode. The gap is the take. A gate
re-executes real swaps and checks the quote against the execution: 96.74 bps quoted, 96.74 bps
executed, to the wei. The agent exposes fourteen named tools in three families — collection, analysis, action — and
the rule it cannot get around is written into the tool descriptions themselves: it never states
a number a tool did not return. Four of them are served over MCP to Claude Desktop, offline,
reading the committed corpus from disk. Hedera carries the paid path: a fresh measurement costs 0.001 USDC over x402, settled through
the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet and read back on the mirror node — a settlement is
only counted if the mirror node returns it, never on our own word. The agent's identity is
HCS-14, derived from six canonical fields so a caller recomputes it instead of trusting us, and
the usage log is anchored on an HCS topic. Ledger secures what is irreversible. The signing key lives in the Key Ring (wallet-cli ring),
and the guard's verdict is encoded as EIP-712 and rendered field by field on the device — you
do not sign an opaque digest. Cancelling returns 4001 and no call goes out. The front end is React with no runtime backend: the whole corpus is column-encoded into 8.3 MB
and shipped inside the page, so the site answers with zero network requests. A browser
extension does the same offline, 12 kB of content script, and reads the Universal Router
calldata three seconds before you sign. When a cheaper door exists it builds the replacement
transaction and signs it through Permit2 (command list 0x0a10, PERMIT2_PERMIT then V4_SWAP) —
and never broadcasts it. On 99.71% of corpus rows there is no cheaper door, and it says so
rather than inventing one. 1,230 tests green across engine, API, MCP, guard, keyring and front end.

projects.title: UXORA
projects.description: AI-native Web3 wireframe studio with Hedera EVM, Subgraph Studio, and Arc.
projects.project_description:
Uxora is an AI-native wireframe studio designed for Web3 product teams. Traditional design workflows rely on isolated tools like Figma, which creates friction when bridging visual vector states with on-chain registries, decentralized metadata, and real-time indexing.
Uxora unifies the vector design workspace with decentralized protocol infrastructure. Built on a flexible canvas powered by Tldraw, Uxora allows designers to visually draft UI components, hash and pin design payloads deterministically to IPFS, register state provenance to a verified Hedera EVM smart contract, index and query canvas logs in real-time using The Graph Subgraph Studio, and synthesize UI components autonomously using natural language prompts via the Arc Agent Stack with micro-settlements.
projects.how_its_made: Uxora is engineered as an end-to-end decentralized application leveraging React, TypeScript, and Vite: Canvas Engine & IPFS: Built on top of Tldraw for fluid visual composition. Layout data is serialized and deterministically hashed with client-side SHA-256 to generate authentic IPFS CIDs before any contract execution. Hedera EVM Registry: We deployed and verified UxoraRegistry.sol on the Hedera Testnet at contract 0.0.10518047. The contract binds metadata and IPFS content identifiers into immutable ownership state records and emits WireframeSaved consensus events. The Graph Subgraph Studio: We deployed a dedicated indexing subgraph called uxora-registry to Subgraph Studio. It indexes all WireframeSaved events from our Hedera contract. The Uxora Copilot executes GraphQL POST queries directly to our Subgraph Studio endpoint, retrieving and verifying indexed wireframe entities in milliseconds. Arc Agent Stack: An autonomous AI agent stack inside the workspace parses natural language design prompts (e.g. 'design auth modal'), synthesizes responsive layout schemas, and executes autonomous simulated USDC micro-settlements for each generative compute execution.

projects.title: Insight-AI
projects.description: Autonomous Telegram bot predicting whale moves via x402, Chainlink, Uniswap v4, ENS & LI.FI
projects.project_description: Insight AI is an autonomous crypto intelligence agent delivered through Telegram. When a whale moves large amounts of ETH, the bot: Detects the transaction and resolves the wallet's ENS identity (name, avatar, social profiles) Queries Chainlink oracles on-chain for verified, tamper-proof ETH/USD pricing Analyzes Uniswap v4 pools for whale swap patterns and Hook behavior (TWAMM, LimitOrder, Dynamic Fee) Scans cross-chain activity across 6 EVM chains via LI.FI bridge intelligence Uses Google Gemini AI to autonomously decide which premium APIs to purchase Pays for data via x402 micropayments (USDC on Ethereum) — no subscriptions, pay-per-insight Synthesizes everything into a single actionable report delivered to Telegram The AI agent operates with full autonomy — it evaluates oracle confidence, calculates cost-benefit ratios, and only spends when the data is worth purchasing.
projects.how_its_made: Insight AI is a Bun/TypeScript monorepo running a Telegraf Telegram bot in front of an Express server that exposes x402-gated endpoints; when a whale-monitoring service flags a large ETH transfer, a Google Gemini agent weighs the transaction's size and volatility and decides which premium data sources are worth paying for in USDC via x402 — no subscriptions, no API keys, just per-call micropayments. It then pulls Chainlink oracle prices (with on-chain confidence/staleness checks, cached and snapshotted via Prisma/Postgres), resolves the whale's identity through ENS ( lookupAddress / getText , backed by a curated whale mapping for addresses without public ENS records), checks Uniswap v4 pools for Hook activity (TWAMM, LimitOrder, Dynamic Fee) to catch swap patterns, and layers in LI.FI cross-chain data across six EVM chains to read bridge behavior — synthesizing all of it into one Telegram report. The hackiest bit is letting the LLM make real (if tiny) autonomous spending decisions, which meant building confidence-threshold and cost-ceiling guardrails so Gemini couldn't just buy every data source for every alert.

projects.title: Best before
projects.description: On-chain price data with a freshness SLA. Stale data is refused, refunded, and logged on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Best Before is a paid price data service for agents. The provider is responsible for meeting the freshness guarantee before delivering the data. When an agent queries a subgraph, it can get a valid response without knowing how stale the data is. The response has the right format, no errors, and HTTP 200, but the underlying data may still be far behind the chain. If an agent makes a bad decision using that data, the buyer has no way to tell whether the strategy was wrong or the input was stale. We saw this happen during development. The same subgraph deployment returned data that was 1 block behind the chain head, then about 20 million blocks behind, then 3 blocks behind, all within the same day. The deployment ID stayed the same, and every response reported hasIndexingErrors as false. This means freshness cannot be checked once and assumed to stay the same. It needs to be measured for every request. Best Before currently sells WETH/USDC price data from Aerodrome on Base. There are three pricing tiers, each with a different maximum data age. Before payment, a request returns HTTP 402 with the current measured age, block lag, and the tiers that the data currently satisfies. This gives the buyer a preview of the current state, but it is not the freshness guarantee. After payment is settled, Best Before measures freshness again. It compares the subgraph's _meta block with the current chain head to calculate the age and block lag. Both values come from sources that the buyer can query independently. The price is delivered only if the new measurement satisfies the tier the buyer paid for. If the data no longer meets the tier, Best Before does not deliver it and refunds the payment in full. The outcome is also recorded on a Hedera Consensus Service topic created without an admin key. The receipt includes the values used to make the decision, including the delivered block, chain head, deployment ID, measured age, and purchased SLA. This lets anyone reproduce the freshness calculation instead of simply trusting a result reported by Best Before. Freshness can also be checked on the buyer side, and several projects already do this. The difference is that a buyer side check happens after the buyer has paid. Best Before puts the check on the provider side. If the provider cannot meet the freshness requirement after payment, the data is not delivered and the buyer gets the payment back. That way, stale data costs the provider instead of the buyer.
projects.how_its_made: Best Before runs as a Hono server on Node 20 and is deployed on Railway, with a /health endpoint for health checks. The Graph is the main data source. Pool price and _meta are fetched in a single GraphQL request so the price and its freshness measurement always refer to the same indexed block. Fetching them separately could mean checking one block while returning a price from another. Block lag is calculated as chain_head - delivered_block. The chain head comes from the RPC of the chain indexed by the subgraph. A caller can retrieve these values independently and reproduce the calculation. Payments use x402 with the exact scheme on Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. We use the upfront payment flow because settlement needs to complete before the route handler runs, and it gives us a settled payer address for refunds. Prices are denominated in HBAR (asset 0.0.0) and represented in tinybar, so neither party needs HTS token association. Best Before has three freshness tiers: strict (<0s), realtime (<5s), and delayed (<60s). Strict is deliberately impossible to satisfy, giving us a reliable way to demonstrate the refusal and refund path without modifying the data source or adding a debug mode. Receipts are written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created without an admin key. Delivered receipts are submitted asynchronously so they do not delay data delivery. For refusals and upstream failures, we wait for consensus before returning the response, so the refund has a public record before the request finishes. We also use Messari's standardized Lending Protocol schema. One query retrieves comparable TVL and freshness information across five protocols without a custom adapter for each one. That query also surfaced problems in the deployments themselves. Two Base deployments were unreachable: one had no indexer allocations, while all available indexers for the other returned HTTP 400. Another deployment had its manifest declare BASE while Protocol.network returned MAINNET. We caught the mismatch through the standardized schema itself. Receipts are validated when they are built. A paid request that was not delivered cannot have refund_status = NOT_APPLICABLE, and refund_tinybar must equal paid_tinybar. An UNAVAILABLE snapshot uses null for derived fields rather than zero, so a missing measurement cannot look like a real zero. We also ran into two Hedera SDK issues. new Hbar(2000000) means two million HBAR, not 0.02 HBAR. Tinybar amounts need Hbar.fromTinybars(); otherwise the mistake only shows up later as an insufficient balance error. Using @hiero-ledger/sdk alongside @x402/hedera can also load two separate SDK instances, causing internal instanceof checks to fail with "t.startsWith is not a function". Best Before avoids this by importing all Hedera primitives from @x402/hedera. Receipts store the inputs used to make a freshness decision, not just the result: delivered block, chain head, deployment ID, measured age, and purchased SLA. Anyone can use those values to reconstruct why a request was delivered or refused, without trusting what Best Before reported.

projects.title: Arova
projects.description: Proactive AI risk radar for DeFi — one standardized Graph query, every protocol.
projects.project_description: AROVA is a proactive AI agent that continuously monitors DeFi lending and DEX protocols — Aave, Compound, Uniswap, and Balancer — for early warning risk signals like sudden TVL drops or unsustainable yield spikes. Instead of manually checking separate dashboards for each protocol, AROVA runs live audits using one reusable query pattern across every protocol it tracks, flags anomalies in plain English, and lets you ask natural-language follow-up questions through a built-in AI Copilot to understand exactly why something was flagged. It also includes a protocol comparison view and a yield calculator, all powered by live on-chain data.
projects.how_its_made: AROVA is built with Next.js on the frontend and deployed on Vercel. Its core data layer uses The Graph's Messari Standardized Subgraphs — because lending protocols (Aave, Compound) and DEX protocols (Uniswap, Balancer) share the same schema, AROVA runs a single query per category, unmodified, against every protocol in it, rather than writing protocol-specific query logic for each one. The Subgraph MCP powers the natural-language layer, translating a user's plain-English question into the right live query. Google's Gemini model handles reasoning — turning raw TVL, revenue, and yield deltas into clear, explained risk flags, and answering AI Copilot follow-up questions grounded in the same live data. The trickiest part was designing the signal-detection thresholds to generalize across both lending and DEX categories despite their different underlying metrics, without needing category-specific tuning for every new protocol added.
projects.project_description_markdown: AROVA is a proactive AI agent that continuously monitors DeFi lending and DEX protocols — Aave, Compound, Uniswap, and Balancer — for early warning risk signals like sudden TVL drops or unsustainable yield spikes. Instead of manually checking separate dashboards for each protocol, AROVA runs live audits using one reusable query pattern across every protocol it tracks, flags anomalies in plain English, and lets you ask natural-language follow-up questions through a built-in AI Copilot to understand exactly why something was flagged. It also includes a protocol comparison view and a yield calculator, all powered by live on-chain data.
projects.how_its_made_markdown: AROVA is built with Next.js on the frontend and deployed on Vercel. Its core data layer uses The Graph's Messari Standardized Subgraphs — because lending protocols (Aave, Compound) and DEX protocols (Uniswap, Balancer) share the same schema, AROVA runs a single query per category, unmodified, against every protocol in it, rather than writing protocol-specific query logic for each one. The Subgraph MCP powers the natural-language layer, translating a user's plain-English question into the right live query. Google's Gemini model handles reasoning — turning raw TVL, revenue, and yield deltas into clear, explained risk flags, and answering AI Copilot follow-up questions grounded in the same live data. The trickiest part was designing the signal-detection thresholds to generalize across both lending and DEX categories despite their different underlying metrics, without needing category-specific tuning for every new protocol added.

projects.title: MarginMM
projects.description: Risk-bounded market making for leveraged Aave positions, enforced inside 1inch SwapVM.
projects.project_description: MarginMM is a collateral-aware market-making system for leveraged Aave V3 positions. A maker can use WETH and USDC collateral as liquidity through 1inch Aqua, while MarginMM continuously protects the lending position from unsafe execution. For each trade, MarginMM calculates qMax — the maximum safe executable amount — using the maker’s live Aave state, an active stressed-risk policy, and the maker’s minimum StressHF floor. Safe trades execute fully, oversized trades are reduced to a risk-capped partial fill, and trades with no safe capacity fail closed. Live market evidence from The Graph calibrates the stress policy, while a Risk Agent pays for fresh calibration through x402 using HBAR on Hedera Testnet. The Maker retains final control by approving the signed policy from their own browser wallet.
projects.how_its_made: MarginMM is built with Solidity and Foundry on a pinned Ethereum mainnet fork, using Aave V3 for the maker’s collateral and debt state and the official 1inch Aqua/SwapVM stack for market-making execution. We extended SwapVM with a custom MarginMM risk instruction that checks the active policy and computes qMax directly in the execution path. The Risk Agent uses the OpenAI Agents SDK for orchestration, while risk-critical calculations remain deterministic. It fetches live Uniswap and Aave evidence through The Graph, which is converted into a WETH downside shock and an EIP-712 signed MarketPolicy. Fresh calibration is exposed as a live x402-gated service: the Agent pays real HBAR on Hedera Testnet through Blocky402, validates the settlement receipt, then receives the signed policy. The policy can only be activated by the Maker through their browser wallet. The frontend is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, and shows Current HF, StressHF, qMax, full fills, liquidity-capped fills, risk-capped partial fills, and confirmed onchain execution evidence.

projects.title: Coram
projects.description: A soon formally-verified modern multisig implementation with clear signing
projects.project_description: Coram is a new multisignature wallet written in "Core Solidity" (the work in progress Solidity 2.0 from Argot), which enables it to: use novel features (most notably algebraic datatypes (ADTs)) previously unavailable in the language, making it less error prone, be subject to "automatic" formal verification (the entire compiler is not yet covered, but it is work in progress). Furthermore, certain technical decisions were made to reduce the security surface area and better end-user readability during signing. The best example is since ADTs are used, batching can be easily implemented, which removes the need for "multicall" wrappers, which ruin signing clarity quite a bit.
projects.how_its_made: This is a highly technical project.  It is continuity from EthGlobal Lisbon this year. Since Lisbon all the work needed in the compiler has been finished and merged upstream. An initial version of formal verification was reviewed, but work is to be continued on that. During this week most of the focus was on improving the UX. All the basic features are working as planned.

projects.title: Mofu
projects.description: Launch and trade Arc tokens and RWA markets with curves, orders, and locked pools.
projects.project_description:
Mofu is an Arc-native DeFi marketplace for launching and trading community tokens and RWA-linked markets from one wallet-connected app. Creators can launch fixed-supply ERC-20 tokens using
USDC, EURC, another Mofu token, or an available RWA or stock token as the quote asset. Users can discover markets, buy and sell through reserve-backed bonding curves, and place fully
collateralized bids and asks in an onchain spot orderbook. Mofu V2 graduates a sold-out curve into a constant-product pool with permanently locked liquidity. The dashboard also includes
portfolio holdings, token discovery, stablecoin swaps, and CCTP bridging. Mofu provides the market infrastructure while the underlying RWA issuer remains responsible for the asset itself.
projects.how_its_made:
Mofu is built with a Next.js and React dashboard in TypeScript, using wagmi, viem, RainbowKit, Radix UI, Circle App Kit, Solidity, Foundry, and OpenZeppelin. Mofu V2 accepts any ERC-20
quote asset, allowing launches to be denominated in USDC, EURC, another Mofu token, or a deployed RWA or stock token on Arc. The protocol uses bonding curves for price discovery, fully
collateralized onchain orders for secondary trading, and a permanently locked liquidity pool after a curve sells out. The frontend reads live contract state, simulates transactions,
refreshes quotes, enforces slippage protection, and marks unsupported assets as having no verified route. This keeps RWA support modular while allowing issuers to provide their own
compliant tokenized assets.

projects.title: CredibleExec
projects.description: CredibleExec puts agent collateral behind financial promises with deterministic onchain slashing.
projects.project_description:
CredibleExec is an economic accountability protocol that puts real skin in the game for autonomous AI financial execution. Today, financial AI agents operate under a fundamental trust gap: users grant execution permissions, but absorb 100% of the financial risk while the AI agent risks zero. Loose natural language promises (such as "receive at least 0.48 ETH") dissolve the moment raw transaction calldata is submitted. CredibleExec solves this by enforcing strict economic accountability onchain: Separation of Funds: User principal ($1,000 USDC) and Agent collateral ($100 USDC) are strictly separated. The user's money is never used to satisfy the agent's bond.
Collateral Locking: Before execution begins, the AI agent must deposit $100 USDC of its own collateral into our OpenZeppelin-backed CredibleExecBond.sol smart contract.
Immutable Mandate Hash: The user's intent is compiled into four immutable financial conditions (Max Spend, Min Output, Recipient, Deadline) and hashed onchain (keccak256).
Authorization & Orchestration: Bazantic Recipes orchestrate the multi-phase workflow (Compile → Fund → Settle), while Privy Embedded Wallets handle user transaction authorization. 1inch supplies decoded DEX swap routes.
Deterministic Verification: Post-execution, our deterministic verifier evaluates block receipts, ERC-20 log transfers, and native ETH call traces.
The Key Innovation — Transaction Success ≠ Commitment Success: A transaction can execute successfully on a DEX, but if it fails to satisfy the user's approved financial conditions, CredibleExec evaluates MIN_OUTPUT_NOT_MET and triggers automated onchain slashing. The agent's $100 USDC collateral is seized and transferred directly to the user's wallet as compensation. CredibleExec bridges the gap between natural language user intent and onchain economic guarantees, scaling from single-token DEX swaps to automated corporate treasury management and open agent marketplaces.
projects.how_its_made:
CredibleExec was built as a monorepo workspace using pnpm, TypeScript, Next.js App Router, Viem, Solidity, and OpenZeppelin v5. Smart Contract Architecture (contracts/src/CredibleExecBond.sol)
The collateral custody layer is written in Solidity 0.8.24 utilizing OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20, ReentrancyGuard, and Ownable2Step. It strictly enforces the separation of User Principal from Agent Collateral. The contract locks agent-deposited ERC-20 collateral (depositBond), activates commitments (activateCommitment), and executes one-way deterministic settlement: settleSuccess releases collateral to the agent, while settleFailure slashes collateral to the user. Domain & Mandate Packages (packages/)
@credibleexec/domain: Defines wire types, Zod schemas, and keccak256 canonical JSON hashing (hashMandate) ensuring mandate conditions cannot be mutated after activation.
@credibleexec/mandate: Handles exact decimal arithmetic (6-decimal USDC and 18-decimal ETH) avoiding floating-point precision loss.
@credibleexec/verifier: A pure, deterministic verification engine evaluating actualSpend <= maxSpend, actualOutput >= minOutput, recipient, and deadline. Sponsor Integrations & Execution Pipeline
Privy (@privy-io/react-auth): Handles embedded wallet creation, JWT token verification, and presents Privy's transaction confirmation UI for bounded USDC allowances and swaps.
Bazantic (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk & @bazantic/cli): Orchestrates the multi-phase agent workflow (Compile → Fund → Settle) via custom Bazantic MCP tools.
1inch Classic Swap v6.1: Provides DEX routing. We built a custom calldata decoder that inspects raw V6 swap calldata to verify routers, assets, amounts, and recipients before Privy authorization. Backend & Evidence Engine (app/lib/server/)
The backend is built on Next.js with SQLite WAL for durable transaction journaling and nonce locks. Evidence collection uses Viem RPC clients to inspect transaction receipts, ERC-20 transfer logs, and native ETH call traces (debug_traceTransaction with callTracer). Notable Technical Feats
Native ETH Trace Parsing: Because native ETH transfers do not emit ERC-20 events, we built an RPC call-tracer parser that extracts net internal ETH transfers while ignoring reverted subtrees.
Dual Execution Architecture: Created a loopback EVM development chain (pnpm local:chain & pnpm local:demo) allowing complete end-to-end HTTP-to-blockchain testing with automated success & slashing proofs without requiring mainnet funds.

projects.title: SettleOne
projects.description: Prepare contractor payments, approve the exact list, settle once on Arc
projects.project_description: SettleOne is a contractor payment app. You build a USDC batch off-chain, check every recipient and amount, then send one on-chain settlement. Connect a wallet on Arc Testnet. Sign a short message so the API knows the draft is yours. That signature does not spend money. Add payees and amounts under a budget. Optional Sepolia ENS names get pinned to an address before they go in the list. When the list is ready, Prepare builds the exact settleBatch call: each recipient, each amount, Arc chain 5042002, official USDC 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000, expiry, and total. If you change anyone or any amount, you prepare again. You tick that the preview is right, approve that USDC total, and sign one transaction. The contract enforces replay protection, expiry, a total cap, and atomic transfers. The API will not mark the draft confirmed unless the Arc receipt matches the payer, the settlement contract, the calldata, a USDC Transfer, DraftPayment, and DraftSettled. A random hash cannot lock the draft as submitted. A second tab cannot sign the same draft while a send may still land. Identity writes stay on Sepolia. Vendor evidence from The Graph can only exclude or send a wallet to the form. It never types an amount. The wallet is the only spender.
projects.how_its_made: The app is three pieces that stay separate on purpose. The Next.js frontend talks to Arc Testnet and Sepolia through wagmi and viem. RainbowKit connects the wallet. Prepare is a backend job. The browser then rebuilds settleBatch with encodeFunctionData and refuses to send if that calldata does not match the preview byte for byte. USDC on Arc is 6 decimals on the ERC-20 at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 and 18 decimals as native gas, so the client checks both the token balance and a native reserve before approve and settle. The Rust Axum API owns drafts in SQLite. Sign-in is a one-time personal_sign challenge, recovered address, hashed bearer token. Amounts are canonical integers. After Prepare the calldata is immutable. Finalize asks Arc for the transaction and receipt, then checks chain id 5042002, payer, to, input, USDC Transfer, DraftPayment, and DraftSettled. A null getTransactionByHash is not treated as pending. That was a real bug. An unknown hash used to pin submitted and trap the session. The Solidity contract is SessionSettlement. settleBatch takes a draftId, the recipient/amount list, a totalLimit, and expiresAt. Replay is payer-scoped. Transfers are atomic. The backend will not register a contract unless the signer matches on-chain owner() and the runtime bytecode keccak matches the live Arc deploy. Arc is the settlement network. ENSv2 is Sepolia only. We resolve the current resolver before a write, grant authorizeTextRoles for service.metadata, and keep a tab-local secondary key for the allowed text update and the forbidden setAddr check. The Graph Agent0 subgraph is queried server-side. If _meta is older than seven days the agent is exclude. Graph never types an amount. We hit this. The live index is still 4 March 2026, so inclusion is blocked. Hacky bits worth saying. The payer deployed the contract from MetaMask because this Linux box had no PRIVATE_KEY. A signing state is written before the wallet popup so a second tab cannot send a second batch. Replacement hashes are accepted only after a successful receipt. Demo hosting is Tailscale Serve onto 127.0.0.1, not a public port. Native USDC gas and ERC-20 USDC share the same pool, so spending the whole token balance leaves nothing for the settle tx. The old Yellow and LI.FI path is still in the tree. It is not wired into this payment flow.
