projects.title: Detent
projects.description: Preview a coupon run line by line, then lock the treasury key to exactly that transaction
projects.project_description: Whoever operates a tokenized security pays coupons, runs court ordered transfers and handles redemptions with a treasury key that can sign anything the contract exposes. The only check before signing is reading an explorer or trusting a script, so a lapsed allowlist entry, a wrong amount or a thin treasury shows up after the transaction lands. Detent puts one step in that gap. The operator console reads the holder register and compliance state of an ERC-1400 security, replays the corporate action off chain and prints the plan: every holder and amount, every row the compliance module will reject with its reason (expired allowlist entry, overdue KYC, sanctions hold), and the treasury cover and headroom. Two officers approve, which is a key quorum of two. The plan's exact calldata is then compiled into a wallet policy that allows that contract, that function and those parameter bytes, and denies everything else by default. If anyone edits a single amount and sends it, the key refuses and names the condition that failed and the byte where the payload diverged. The untouched plan still signs with the same wallet under the same policy, and the lock is spent afterwards. Before the policy opens, the plan hash is anchored on a PlanAnchor contract on Hedera testnet, and a permanent record page reads it back with no key. What is live today: the console, the refusal, the quorum and the on chain anchor on Hedera testnet. The register reads from the cached register snapshot, and the policy is evaluated by a local mirror of the Privy policy engine. The live ATS register read and the Privy server wallet path are implemented and tested against mocks, and switch on with environment variables.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: Next.js 16 App Router with the React Compiler, React 19, TypeScript strict, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn on Base UI, Motion (loaded after hydration to keep the first load small) and next-themes for light and dark mode. The app has a command palette, a stepped five section console, and a record route per plan hash. Hedera and Asset Tokenization Studio: register reads are hand written viem calls over the Hashio JSON-RPC relay (chain 296) to the ATS ERC-1400 facets, balanceOfByPartition and canTransferByPartition, checking each credit from the issuer treasury. We decode the EIP-1066 status byte and the error selector, so a compliance refusal is shown as a named hold reason instead of a revert. ATS gave us partitions, KYC and control list semantics, which is exactly the compliance state the plan has to respect. Privy: the approved plan becomes a Privy wallet policy on a server wallet owned by a key quorum of two. Conditions use ethereum_transaction for chain id and target, and ethereum_calldata with the ABI for the function selector and partition. Requests carry RFC 8785 canonicalized ECDSA P-256 authorization signatures and idempotency keys, and the policy is detached and revoked on every exit path, including lock expiry. Privy policies cannot pin whole dynamic arrays, so the server also enforces the exact calldata byte for byte and reports the first diverging byte. Server: a single fail closed route. The server derives the plan itself from the register and the operator's row selection, mints the lock id, checks the quorum against a registered approver list, refuses plan mismatches and rate limits per client. Contracts: PlanAnchor in Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry, a one way state machine (anchored, then settled or abandoned) with custom errors and fuzz tests. It is deployed on Hedera testnet at 0x1a393277908834c39D2611Ce9A151474B8Dfea0d and verified on Sourcify. Anchoring reads before it writes, so rehearsing the same demo does not revert. Notable hack: the keyless demo runs a local evaluator that mirrors the Privy policy semantics, so judges see a real refusal with a real byte offset without any credentials. While deploying we found that a refused edit abandoned the plan on chain, which is terminal, so the approved send could never settle it; the refusal now leaves the row anchored and only an unspent lock abandons it. Quality: 403 unit tests, 72 Playwright end to end tests including axe accessibility checks in both themes, and 80 visual regression baselines.

projects.title: Rawmarkets
projects.description: RawMarket is a spot trading venue for tokenized representations of US commodity benchmarks
projects.project_description: RawMarket is a professional spot trading venue for tokenized US commodity benchmarks, beginning with USDA Class III Milk and expanding to potatoes, tomatoes, wheat, corn, rice, soybeans, and dry beans. Users can inspect source-labelled candlestick history and live order-book depth, fund a test account, place market or limit orders, manage inventory, review fills, and open immutable Hedera receipts from order history. The product separates benchmark data, exchange prices, and blockchain lifecycle state so each remains independently auditable.
projects.how_its_made: RawMarket combines a Next.js and TypeScript trading terminal with a deterministic Rust/Axum central limit order book hosted on AWS. The matcher uses integer ticks, price-time priority, reservations, partial fills, post-only orders, cancellation, and self-trade prevention. Hedera records every accepted order through an EVM receipt contract, with Mirror Node resolving native transaction IDs for HashScan links. The application now includes Hedera’s official Asset Tokenization Studio SDK. RawMarket uses the ATS factory path for governed commodity assets, ERC-1400 partition operations for issuance, holds and redemption, and an ERC-3643-compatible identity/compliance module for transfer eligibility. HTS provides native testnet token identities while ATS supplies the controlled asset lifecycle.

projects.title: Free
projects.description: Any outcome you're exposed to but can't control is a hedge you haven't placed yet.
projects.project_description:
If your money, revenue, or plans depend on how some real-world outcome goes, you're carrying that risk unhedged whether you notice it or not.
Parasol turns it into a position: tell the agent what outcome you're exposed to, and it prices and assembles a hedge from live prediction-market odds on exactly that outcome. If things go the wrong way, the position pays out and offsets the loss. This creates a market-priced hedge for any exposure a public source can settle far beyond your typical bespoke insurance product for one narrow case. You sign every transaction yourself; the agent only ever attests to what happened, it never touches your money.
projects.how_its_made:
Agent
Risk elicitation runs as a conversational front-end to 0G Compute's Router, the vanilla OpenAI SDK repointed at the Router's baseURL, so the integration surface is trivially small and swappable. The Router mediates access to whichever underlying model is configured, settling inference cost on-chain per call; those settlement debits against the Router's payment contract are themselves the primary proof of inference, supplemented by raw request/response logs and, where the Router exposes one, a TEE attestation binding a specific model execution to a specific output.
That attestation matters more than it might first appear: it's what lets a "private, verifiable inference" claim survive scrutiny instead of remaining a marketing assertion. Architecturally, the model is confined to a single, narrow responsibility: producing a schema-constrained risk profile (event, threshold, target payout, a confidence scalar), and nothing downstream trusts it beyond that boundary. Output is validated against a strict JSON schema server-side; a malformed or underspecified response triggers a re-prompt rather than silent coercion. Everything with numerical consequence (pricing, position sizing, order construction, slippage bounds) lives in deterministic, unit-testable code that consumes the model's output as an opaque input, never as an instruction to execute.
This is a deliberate separation of concerns: the stochastic component is quarantined to intent-capture, and the entire financial state machine downstream is reproducible and auditable independent of what the model said. A secondary inference provider sits behind an identical inference(messages) → json interface, so failing over is a one-line baseURL swap rather than an architectural rewrite, demonstrated live, as evidence the abstraction isn't cosmetic. Execution
The custody boundary is absolute: the backend never holds, generates, or has access to a Polygon private key at any point in the flow. It operates purely as a read/construct/relay service: reading public market state from Gamma and the CLOB order book, constructing unsigned limit orders pinned to the best ask with bounded slippage, and relaying already-signed payloads onward.
Every state transition that touches value. the initial USDC.e approval, the collateral wrap into tradable position tokens, CLOB L1 authentication (an off-chain EIP-712 signature that derives API credentials without costing gas), individual order signatures, and eventual redemption is signed client-side by the user's own EOA. signatureType 0 is used throughout with funder set to the signer itself, so there is no delegated-execution path, no meta-transaction relayer with spending authority, nothing standing between the user's key and the outcome. Threshold and weather markets settle through a structurally different exchange contract than plain binary markets, the NegRisk exchange, purpose-built for the bundled, mutually-exclusive-outcome markets these products are, which means the negRisk flag has to propagate correctly into the EIP-712 domain the client is asked to sign, or the venue rejects the signature outright. Rather than risk that flag being forgotten at some future call-site, order construction is centralized into a single module that every code path funnels through, with a small integration test firing one minimal real order against it before it's ever trusted at demo scale.
Fill timeouts (roughly ten seconds without a match) trigger an automatic cancel-and-requote against the refreshed best ask rather than leaving a stale order hanging, the system re-derives its own price rather than assuming the world held still. Indexing (The Graph)
This was built and adversarially verified against live chain state rather than assembled from documentation. Two independently deployed subgraphs: one for Polymarket, one for Azuro, are mapped into a single canonical schema: Market, Outcome, Resolution, and an append-only PricePoint ledger that turns "current price" into an actual time series rather than a single mutable scalar that overwrites its own history. Polymarket alone decomposes into two structurally distinct on-chain sub-systems, and treating them as one would have been the easiest possible silent mistake. Plain binary markets settle through one exchange contract with OrderFilled events keyed by a token ID derived straight from the Conditional Tokens Framework's getPositionId. Threshold/NegRisk markets, the daily weather buckets this product actually prices, settle through an entirely separate exchange contract and, critically, mint their tradable outcome tokens through a different derivation path, NegRiskAdapter.getPositionId(questionId, outcome), that has no relationship to the plain CTF formula. projects.project_description_markdown:
If your money, revenue, or plans depend on how some real-world outcome goes, you're carrying that risk unhedged whether you notice it or not. 
Parasol turns it into a position: tell the agent what outcome you're exposed to, and it prices and assembles a hedge from live prediction-market odds on exactly that outcome. If things go the wrong way, the position pays out and offsets the loss. This creates a market-priced hedge for any exposure a public source can settle far beyond your typical bespoke insurance product for one narrow case. You sign every transaction yourself; the agent only ever attests to what happened, it never touches your money.

projects.title: Privet
projects.description: AI treasury agent: proposes payments, policy decides, isolated signer executes. AI never holds keys.
projects.project_description: Privent is a security and execution layer that lets a company give an AI agent bounded access to a treasury — without ever giving the AI a private key. It is not a trading bot, a wallet, or “an AI that spends crypto.” The product thesis is: AI agents should receive financial authority, not unrestricted access to company funds. The AI decides what it wants to do. A deterministic policy engine decides whether it may do it. An isolated signer decides whether a transaction can actually be authorized. The blockchain decides whether it settles. Humans keep control of anything irreversible or high-risk. Every step is audited. That split is the whole point. You never trust the model to enforce its own security.
projects.how_its_made: pnpm TS monorepo: Next.js, Hono API, isolated signer. OpenRouter GPT-4o-mini proposes JSON; policy ALLOW/REQUIRE_APPROVAL/DENY. The Graph, Privy, ENS feed live data. Keys live in a separate Node process that re-reads SQLite, re-runs policy, then viem-broadcasts to Sepolia. Hack: signer never trusts the API.

projects.title: gotrade
projects.description: Gotrade: WhatsApp-controlled autonomous DeFi with live wallets, risk limits, and swaps.
projects.project_description: Gotrade is an autonomous DeFi agent platform controlled through WhatsApp. Users can register, view live wallet balances, analyze markets, manage AI agents, configure risk limits, and execute blockchain actions using natural-language commands. Gotrade combines conversational AI with deterministic safety policies, live onchain data, user-controlled wallets, Uniswap execution, and MongoDB-backed auditability. It is designed to make DeFi more accessible while ensuring agents cannot exceed user-defined trading limits or silently report simulated success.
projects.how_its_made: Gotrade uses FastAPI and Python for the backend, MongoDB with Motor for asynchronous persistence, Redis for service support, and a Next.js/TypeScript frontend. The WhatsApp gateway uses Twilio webhooks and TwiML, while Gemini interprets natural-language commands with deterministic regex fallbacks. Coinbase Developer Platform wallet infrastructure and an existing EVM wallet provide wallet access, Web3.py reads live Sepolia balances, and Uniswap v3 supplies onchain quotes and execution paths. The architecture is fail-closed: unavailable providers, missing credentials, unsupported services, or failed transactions produce explicit errors rather than fake success. Docker Compose runs MongoDB and Redis, while ngrok exposes the local webhook for live testing.

projects.title: Leash Layer
projects.description: Revocable ENSv2 authorization and scoped credentials for agent software
projects.project_description:
Leash is an explainable permission layer for agent software. It identifies an agent wallet
through ERC-8004, reads its capabilities from ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia, and decides whether a requested action is allowed. When approved, Leash issues a short lived, singleuse
credential scoped to one capability and wallet address. Before the protected service
executes, authority is checked again against ENSv2, so revoking a role immediately blocks the
next request. The project demonstrates how agents can receive bounded permissions instead of permanent API access.
projects.how_its_made:
Leash is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Bun, and viem. The Next.js dashboard and
server-side API routes use shared authorization logic from the src backend layer. A custom
ENSv2 client reads resource ownership, expiry, and role bitmaps from Ethereum Sepolia.
Capabilities are mapped to required roles, and the gate returns structured ALLOW or DENY
decisions with stable reason codes, block numbers, and latency. Approved requests receive
HMAC-signed credentials containing the agent, wallet, capability, expiry, and nonce. The
protected service validates the credential, prevents reuse, and performs a live ENSv2 re-
check before execution.

projects.title: PolicyProbe
projects.description: Deterministic onchain policy assertions and repair findings for Hedera Harness.
projects.project_description: PolicyProbe extends Hedera Harness with deterministic onchain behavioral verification. Developers can declare what an application is expected to do, execute real actions on Hedera, and compare the observed result against that expectation instead of treating a successful transaction as proof of correctness. For example, if an unverified investor must not receive a tokenized bond, PolicyProbe can execute that action, detect if it unexpectedly succeeds, capture the resulting transaction and state evidence, and emit a structured finding that Harness can feed back into its existing repair loop. The same probe can then be rerun after the fix to prove that the behavior now matches policy. The result is a reusable verification layer for AI-built Hedera applications: expected behavior → real execution → observed state → deterministic PASS/FAIL → repair. Our flagship demo uses a tokenized-asset policy scenario to make that loop concrete and auditable.
projects.how_its_made: PolicyProbe is a TypeScript contribution built on Hedera Harness and exercised against an Asset Tokenization Studio bond on Hedera testnet. It extends the Harness recipe schema with optional chain validation actors and assertions. The assertion runner provisions named signers, executes declared actions, resolves EVM transaction hashes or Hedera transaction IDs through Mirror Node, compares confirmed outcomes and optional exact balance deltas, and emits typed policy or infrastructure findings. The implementation stays generic and backward compatible: recipes without chain assertions follow the existing Harness flow. The companion fixture uses the same engine to test transfer restrictions, role boundaries, frozen holders, and pause controls. This repository includes focused tests, a reproducible fixture, architecture documentation, and linked HashScan evidence.

projects.title: LEASH - Agent Guard
projects.description: A signed, revocable spending mandate that stops an AI agent from ever paying past its cap.
projects.project_description: LEASH gives an AI agent a wallet with a real budget instead of a prompt that tells it to be careful. A mandate sets the scope, meaning which resources it can pay for, plus a ceiling, a rate limit, and an expiry. Every payment attempt is checked against that mandate's current state before any money moves, so a rejected request never reaches the payment rail at all. The same mandate is enforced the same way across two separate settlement rails, Hedera testnet through a Blocky402 facilitator and Arc testnet through a Circle Developer Controlled Wallet, so the enforcement is not tied to one chain. Every mandate event, including issuing, spending, rejecting, raising the ceiling, and revoking, is written to Hedera Consensus Service and can be checked independently on the public mirror node. Raising a mandate's ceiling needs signatures from a real Privy key quorum, so one compromised operator cannot widen what an agent is allowed to spend on their own. Live at leash-kowaipanda.vercel.app
projects.how_its_made: The frontend is built with Vite, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. The backend is Express and TypeScript on Render, and it keeps mandates in memory with a JSON snapshot for persistence. The core piece is a small guard function that checks scope, remaining ceiling, rate limit, expiry, and revocation before either settlement rail is touched. The x402 v2 spec says budget and session management are out of scope, and its facilitators do not expose a hook for custom checks. So instead of waiting on one, LEASH runs as its own facilitator proxy sitting in front of Blocky402 on Hedera testnet, and settlement only happens after our own check passes. Hedera's exact payment scheme does not use a signed authorization object the way EVM chains do, so we build and sign a real, partially signed TransferTransaction with the Hedera SDK, and the facilitator adds its own signature and settles it. Every mandate event is sent to an HCS topic, so the audit trail can be checked on Hedera's public mirror node instead of just trusting our own database. The second rail settles real USDC on Arc testnet through Circle's Developer Controlled Wallets SDK, using createTransaction and then polling until the transfer finishes, and the token id is looked up from the wallet's own balance instead of being hardcoded. The trickiest part was Privy. Privy's policy engine only gates real wallet actions like eth_sendTransaction, it does not have a field for an arbitrary business number like a spending ceiling. So we mirror the mandate's ceiling into the value of a policy rule owned by a key quorum. That rule is never checked against a real transaction, but changing the number still needs signatures from enough Privy authorization keys to meet a 2 of 2 threshold, sent all at once with generateAuthorizationSignature, which skips Privy's support gated approval queue entirely. The Arc rail falls back to a clearly labeled mock settlement if Circle sandbox keys are not set, so the guard logic can still be demoed either way.

projects.title: Leash_dash
projects.description: Keep your AI agents on a leash: bind an agent, set on-chain spend limits, cut it off with one write.
projects.project_description: Everyone is racing to build AI agents that can spend money. The part almost nobody has built is the place you sit and actually govern them once they can. That is what LEASH is. It is a control centre for the AI agents that spend your money, where every agent you run is on a leash you can see and pull. The problem Once you hand an agent a wallet so it can pay for things over x402, the only real control you have left is the private key itself. There is no per-call limit, no list of who it is allowed to pay, no hierarchy if you are running a fleet, and no single off switch. The part that actually worries me is revocation, because if a key leaks today, cutting that agent off means going service by service and rotating keys by hand, which is exactly the situation where slow manual work is the last thing you want. What LEASH does LEASH gives an organisation one console to run its whole fleet of paying agents. You bind an agent you already run, give it a spending account that you and LEASH co-own, set its limits, fund it, and if you ever need to, you pull the leash and cut it off everywhere. The thing that makes this work is ENS. Each agent becomes a child name like data.acme.leash.eth , and the spend policy for that agent (its per-call cap, the payees it is allowed to hit, its Hedera account, and optionally a rolling daily or weekly budget) lives right there in the name's resolver record. The bit I care about most happens at payment time: a facilitator I run reads that live ENS record before it settles anything, and it only co-signs a payment that is actually within policy. So the moment you clear the record, the very next payment the agent tries just fails. One write on Sepolia and it is done everywhere, with no key rotation and no chasing down services. How it works It is five steps end to end. You bind an existing agent whose identity already lives on another chain, say an Arc or Base wallet or an ERC-8004 registration, and LEASH resolves that identity on-chain and then generates a fresh Hedera spending keypair for the agent. The public half goes into a two-of-two Hedera account that you and LEASH co-own, and the private half is shown to you once, right there at bind, and never stored by LEASH. If you would rather bring your own, pasting your agent's own Hedera public key is still supported as an advanced option. Either way LEASH never holds the agent's private key. Then it writes the policy into the agent's ENS resolver record. From there, every time the agent pays, the facilitator reads that live record, checks the cap and the allowlist and the window, and only adds its co-signature if everything passes, settling gas-free on Hedera so the agent spends zero on gas. Every decision, allow or deny, gets logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so it is checkable on-chain. And revoking is the whole point: clearing the record is a single Sepolia transaction, and because the facilitator re-reads with no cache right before it settles, the next payment fails closed rather than slipping through. Being honest about the guarantee I would rather be straight about how strong this is. The enforcement is facilitator-trusted, not trustless. The facilitator I run is the thing reading your policy and deciding whether to co-sign, and the chain's job is to hold the policy and the revocation, not to physically block a payment. The model I keep coming back to is a corporate card, where the employee is genuinely independent and holds their own card, but the company sets the limit and can freeze it. So control is real and independence is real, but trustlessness is not,for now.  Same spirit on the rolling daily and weekly caps, which are a soft budget rather than an exact one, and on identity, which is on-chain-resolved rather than a proof that the person binding actually controls the address. Two ways to see it work The fastest is the sandbox at /demo , which needs no login, no wallet and no ETH. projects.project_description_markdown:
Everyone is racing to build AI agents that can spend money. The part almost nobody has built is the place you sit and actually govern them once they can. That is what LEASH is. It is a control centre for the AI agents that spend your money, where every agent you run is on a leash you can see and pull.

The problem

Once you hand an agent a wallet so it can pay for things over x402, the only real control you have left is the private key itself. There is no per-call limit, no list of who it is allowed to pay, no hierarchy if you are running a fleet, and no single off switch. The part that actually worries me is revocation, because if a key leaks today, cutting that agent off means going service by service and rotating keys by hand, which is exactly the situation where slow manual work is the last thing you want.

What LEASH does

LEASH gives an organisation one console to run its whole fleet of paying agents. You bind an agent you already run, give it a spending account that you and LEASH co-own, set its limits, fund it, and if you ever need to, you pull the leash and cut it off everywhere. The thing that makes this work is ENS. Each agent becomes a child name like `data.acme.leash.eth`, and the spend policy for that agent (its per-call cap, the payees it is allowed to hit, its Hedera account, and optionally a rolling daily or weekly budget) lives right there in the name's resolver record. The bit I care about most happens at payment time: a facilitator I run reads that live ENS record before it settles anything, and it only co-signs a payment that is actually within policy. So the moment you clear the record, the very next payment the agent tries just fails. One write on Sepolia and it is done everywhere, with no key rotation and no chasing down services.

 How it works

It is five steps end to end. You bind an existing agent whose identity already lives on another chain, say an Arc or Base wallet or an ERC-8004 registration, and LEASH resolves that identity on-chain and then generates a fresh Hedera spending keypair for the agent. The public half goes into a two-of-two Hedera account that you and LEASH co-own, and the private half is shown to you once, right there at bind, and never stored by LEASH. If you would rather bring your own, pasting your agent's own Hedera public key is still supported as an advanced option. Either way LEASH never holds the agent's private key. Then it writes the policy into the agent's ENS resolver record. From there, every time the agent pays, the facilitator reads that live record, checks the cap and the allowlist and the window, and only adds its co-signature if everything passes, settling gas-free on Hedera so the agent spends zero on gas. Every decision, allow or deny, gets logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so it is checkable on-chain. And revoking is the whole point: clearing the record is a single Sepolia transaction, and because the facilitator re-reads with no cache right before it settles, the next payment fails closed rather than slipping through.

Being honest about the guarantee

I would rather be straight about how strong this is. The enforcement is facilitator-trusted, not trustless. The facilitator I run is the thing reading your policy and deciding whether to co-sign, and the chain's job is to hold the policy and the revocation, not to physically block a payment. The model I keep coming back to is a corporate card, where the employee is genuinely independent and holds their own card, but the company sets the limit and can freeze it. So control is real and independence is real, but trustlessness is not,for now.  Same spirit on the rolling daily and weekly caps, which are a soft budget rather than an exact one, and on identity, which is on-chain-resolved rather than a proof that the person binding actually controls the address.

Two ways to see it work

The fastest is the sandbox at `/demo`, which needs no login, no wallet and no ETH. It governs a real agent of mine called SOLV-001, an autonomous agent running on a Circle wallet on Arc (its on-chain-resolved identity is `0x927c1d756d12879aebea0772f3ee220f21f4841a`), and it walks you through five moments: meet the agent, watch it pay three dollars inside its cap and settle gas-free, watch it try fifty and get refused, revoke it and watch the same payment fail closed, then watch a leaked key try to over-fund it and get denied by the funding rail. The second way is the real product at `/app`, where you log in with Privy, spin up your org, and bind an agent you already run by pasting its Hedera public key and its identity. You get the same controls on your own agent, and LEASH still never touches its private key.

What is live right now

Everything below is on live rails. If you only click a few things, click these.

- The app: https://leash.ink (sandbox at /demo, proof page at /proof)
- The code, MIT and public: https://github.com/dmustapha/leash
- Revoking an agent in one write, on Sepolia: `0xf03e14d1c0ed8528d90f9d0e5aa4bc55cb2fe29baedea97596d902c427702293`
- A gas-free settle where the agent pays zero HBAR, on Hedera: `0.0.10487802@1789205977.654877070`


Every headline number here recomputes from committed evidence with `npm run verify:claims`, and the full ledger is in `submission/proof.md`. There are 102 unit tests and 8 integration tests behind it, plus the live on-chain runs.

Where it goes next

Right now the actual spend governance runs on Hedera, because the co-signing facilitator I run is the x402 Hedera one, even though binding identity already works across chains and the funding rail is general enough to move. The near-term work is standing that co-signer and policy read up on other EVM chains too. Further out I want to move enforcement from something I am trusted to do toward something the chain checks itself, most likely a contract wallet that mirrors the cap on-chain.

projects.title: scout
projects.description: Autonomous DeFi research agent: Graph + OpenSEO scores, x402 micropayments, Privy, ENS identity
projects.project_description: Scout is an autonomous on-chain research agent for Base lending markets. You give it a plain-language prompt and a USDC budget; it discovers live protocol data from The Graph (Messari Lending/CDP subgraphs), enriches candidates with OpenSEO keyword and SERP signals, then ranks them with a deterministic six-dimension opportunity score plus a separate risk score no LLM in the scoring math. When the top two candidates are too close to call, Scout pauses and asks you to authorize a small, policy-capped x402 micropayment for one extra diagnostics report—paid by a Privy server wallet, never the visitor’s wallet. Results stream live over SSE, and the final status is published to an ENSv2 name (scout-agent.eth) via a Permissioned Resolver. The full decision log, including refused payments or missing evidence, stays with the session.
projects.how_its_made: Scout is a TypeScript Turborepo monorepo: Next.js 15 + React 19 frontend, Hono API with SSE, and shared packages for the research loop. @scout/graph queries The Graph Gateway; @scout/openseo pulls search signals; @scout/scoring runs the six-dimension model and uncertainty gate; @scout/llm (OpenRouter) only narrates already-computed scores. When the gate fires, @x402/hono gates a $0.03 USDC deep-analysis endpoint on Base Sepolia; @scout/privy signs with a policy-enforced server wallet (budget cap, per-request cap, recipient allowlist). @scout/ens writes status to ENSv2 text records on Sepolia behind role-gated access control. We also expose the pipeline as an MCP tool and ship a headless scout-agent CLI. Deployed on Render as scout-api + scout-web.

projects.title: Noria
projects.description: From wallet to liquidity: Noria helps users choose pools, reinvest earnings and reduce debt.
projects.project_description:
Noria brings the steps of liquidity investing into one application: fund a wallet, research pools, build a position and track the money. Users get an analysis backed by verifiable sources and a path to execute their decisions.
The experience starts with Privy. Users sign in with email or Google, create an embedded wallet and can access a EUR-to-USDC checkout or receive funds from another wallet. They can then deposit USDC into Aave to earn variable interest, make transfers or prepare a liquidity position.
For research, Noria uses The Graph to compare pools, examine price history and calculate a price range and the required amount of each token. Reports explain the selection criteria and why a candidate may not qualify. The same research is available through six tools that external AI agents can call.
For the Aqua strategy, users supply ETH or USDC as collateral on Aave and borrow USDC to provide WETH/USDC liquidity on Arbitrum. The position uses 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. When a completed cycle produces distributable surplus after accounting for borrowing interest and accumulated losses, the policy allocates 50% to debt repayment and 50% to capital for the next cycle.
Users confirm fund movements and track amounts, network fees and transaction receipts in downloadable reports. Noria connects research, execution and capital management so users can understand and follow each financial decision.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Noria with Next.js, React and TypeScript. The interface, analysis services and financial integrations share data validation rules. We use viem to read blockchain state, prepare transactions and verify receipts.
Privy provides authentication, embedded wallet creation and transaction confirmations. We integrated wallet funding, a EUR checkout, transfers and Aave deposits and withdrawals. Each transaction has a review step before signing, and its outcome is checked onchain. Interrupted requests are recorded for recovery.

projects.title: Otter
projects.description: First implementation of a provably MEV-resilient AMM — Uniswap v4 hook + off-chain VCG solver.
projects.project_description: Otter is the first implementation of "Otter: A Provably MEV-Resilient Automated Market Maker via Surplus Redistribution" (Shi, Zhang, Chung & Li — IACR ePrint 2026/1877), deployed as a Uniswap v4 hook on Ethereum Sepolia. The core problem: every conventional AMM has a queue, and any queue is sellable. A searcher who can see your order and insert before it will front-run you — buying before you drive up the price, then selling after you fill at the worse rate. This is not an edge case. In our harness test, an attacker deploying 5,000 OTB captures 92% of the victim's trade on a plain pool. The victim gets 1.38 OTB instead of 47.6. That loss is the searcher's profit, by construction. Otter removes the queue entirely. Orders are collected into a 60-second batch window as an unordered set — no first, no second, no sequence position to purchase. The mechanism is dominant-strategy truthful: your best move is always to report your real reservation price, regardless of what anyone else does or what the attacker tries. A searcher who joins the batch clears at exactly the same price as every other participant. The Clarke pivot redistributes any surplus back to the LP rather than to the attacker. What makes this design novel over existing batch AMMs (CoW Protocol, Angstrom, SPEEDEX, am-AMM, Penumbra) is that it achieves dominant-strategy truthfulness for both regular users and for a builder-acting-as-user simultaneously, via VCG surplus redistribution. Existing batch AMMs clear at a uniform price and are not incentive compatible in this sense. This is the first implementation of a mechanism with that specific property. The full stack is deployed and verified on Sepolia: OtterOrderBook (escrow and batch commitment), OtterSettlement (VCG outcome verification and v4 pool settlement), and OtterHook (the Uniswap v4 integration). A live demo page walks through a real settled 6-order batch — showing the sandwich comparison, VCG allocation results, individual order fills and refunds, LP surplus redistribution, and Etherscan links to every source-verified contract. Stated limitation: the mechanism's guarantees assume censorship resilience at the consensus layer (Theorem 23 of the paper). A testnet does not provide this. We say this explicitly in the README, in the demo UI, and here — not buried.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: Foundry (Solidity 0.8.26), TypeScript solver (Node 22), Vite + React + TypeScript frontend, wagmi + RainbowKit for Sepolia wallet connection. No additional backend — the solver runs as a CLI and the web app is fully static. SOLVER (solver/)
The two-sided VCG mechanism is implemented in otter.ts. The dominant side is determined by comparing aggregate eligible supply across both directions; ties go to sell-Y (eq. 10 of the paper). The symmetric case reuses the same one-sided code with the token roles swapped and the answer flipped back — one implementation path, no chance of the two branches drifting apart. The dominant-side allocation uses a layer-cake pivot algorithm extracted from the proof of Lemma 16. The closed form for the Clarke pivot integral has a global zero-crossing (the clearing price, shared by the whole batch) and a per-user lower breakpoint. We implement this, verify it against the naïve O(n²) leave-one-out computation across 4,000 random batches (max relative error 3.8e-10), and benchmark both: at n=1,000 the layer-cake solver runs in 8.8ms vs 233ms naïve — a 27× speedup. Current limitation: the pivot loop is still O(n²) with a small constant because it scans pieces linearly; replacing those scans with binary search plus a prefix-summed antiderivative table is the outstanding optimisation. Property tests (solver/test/properties.ts §8) independently grid-search the allocation space for n ≤ 4 and confirm that nothing on the grid beats the solver's own output. This is evidence for small instances, not a proof for arbitrary n — the comment in that test says exactly that. CONTRACTS (contracts/src/)
OtterHook implements IHooks directly. BaseHook was removed from both v4-core (v4.0.0) and v4-periphery with no migration note; every tutorial still references it. Implementing IHooks directly is arguably cleaner for a hook that only needs three callbacks, but we found this out by reading source, not from the docs. The hook's CREATE2 address encodes the beforeSwap, beforeAddLiquidity, and beforeRemoveLiquidity permission bits; HookMiner was vendored from v4-periphery/test/ since it lives under test/ despite being a deployment-critical tool. OtterSettlement calls poolManager.unlock() to enter the v4 singleton and runs the residual imbalance swap. Before distributing, it verifies: feasibility (pool conservation), individual rationality (no seller underpaid), budget bounds (no overfill), minority pricing, dominance, and that the pool actually yielded enough to cover all obligations. OtterMath is an internal library compiled directly into OtterSettlement (all functions are internal). Fixed-point arithmetic uses solmate's mulDivDown and mulDivUp exclusively — PRBMath's public API has no mulDivUp, which matters for the one rounding direction that decides whether an invariant flips. The rule throughout OtterMath: amounts a user may receive round down; amounts a user must have earned round up. fTildeDown and fTildeUp are never mixed. Notable finding during integration: Uniswap v4 executes a swap in two stages on a Q64.96 price grid, rounding in the pool's favour at each. Critically, fTildeDown is left untouched as a faithful port of the paper's curve. The allowance is a separate function used only in verify — the two are kept distinct in kind because one is the mechanism and the other is a fact about executing it on v4. GAS & HARNESS (harness/)
Settlement gas is dominated by ERC-20 transfers and ecrecover, not by verification (which is O(n) arithmetic). The sandwich harness runs a vanilla v4 pool vs the Otter pool against the same attacker parameters — the direct swap on the Otter pool reverts at the hook, so the attacker gains nothing. WEB (web/)
The demo data is not hardcoded — it is inlined from the real solver fixture generated by solver/src/demo-cli.ts. projects.project_description_markdown:
Otter is the first implementation of "Otter: A Provably MEV-Resilient Automated Market Maker via Surplus Redistribution" (Shi, Zhang, Chung & Li — IACR ePrint 2026/1877), deployed as a Uniswap v4 hook on Ethereum Sepolia.

The core problem: every conventional AMM has a queue, and any queue is sellable. A searcher who can see your order and insert before it will front-run you — buying before you drive up the price, then selling after you fill at the worse rate. This is not an edge case. In our harness test, an attacker deploying 5,000 OTB captures 92% of the victim's trade on a plain pool. The victim gets 1.38 OTB instead of 47.6. That loss is the searcher's profit, by construction.

Otter removes the queue entirely. Orders are collected into a 60-second batch window as an unordered set — no first, no second, no sequence position to purchase. The mechanism is dominant-strategy truthful: your best move is always to report your real reservation price, regardless of what anyone else does or what the attacker tries. A searcher who joins the batch clears at exactly the same price as every other participant. The Clarke pivot redistributes any surplus back to the LP rather than to the attacker.

What makes this design novel over existing batch AMMs (CoW Protocol, Angstrom, SPEEDEX, am-AMM, Penumbra) is that it achieves dominant-strategy truthfulness for both regular users and for a builder-acting-as-user simultaneously, via VCG surplus redistribution. Existing batch AMMs clear at a uniform price and are not incentive compatible in this sense. This is the first implementation of a mechanism with that specific property.

The full stack is deployed and verified on Sepolia: OtterOrderBook (escrow and batch commitment), OtterSettlement (VCG outcome verification and v4 pool settlement), and OtterHook (the Uniswap v4 integration). A live demo page walks through a real settled 6-order batch — showing the sandwich comparison, VCG allocation results, individual order fills and refunds, LP surplus redistribution, and Etherscan links to every source-verified contract.

Stated limitation: the mechanism's guarantees assume censorship resilience at the consensus layer (Theorem 23 of the paper). A testnet does not provide this. We say this explicitly in the README, in the demo UI, and here — not buried.

Stack: Foundry (Solidity 0.8.26), TypeScript solver (Node 22), Vite + React + TypeScript frontend, wagmi + RainbowKit for Sepolia wallet connection. No additional backend — the solver runs as a CLI and the web app is fully static.

The two-sided VCG mechanism is implemented in otter.ts. The dominant side is determined by comparing aggregate eligible supply across both directions; ties go to sell-Y (eq. 10 of the paper). The symmetric case reuses the same one-sided code with the token roles swapped and the answer flipped back — one implementation path, no chance of the two branches drifting apart.

The dominant-side allocation uses a layer-cake pivot algorithm extracted from the proof of Lemma 16. The closed form for the Clarke pivot integral has a global zero-crossing (the clearing price, shared by the whole batch) and a per-user lower breakpoint. We implement this, verify it against the naïve O(n²) leave-one-out computation across 4,000 random batches (max relative error 3.8e-10), and benchmark both: at n=1,000 the layer-cake solver runs in 8.8ms vs 233ms naïve — a 27× speedup. Current limitation: the pivot loop is still O(n²) with a small constant because it scans pieces linearly; replacing those scans with binary search plus a prefix-summed antiderivative table is the outstanding optimisation.

Property tests (solver/test/properties.ts §8) independently grid-search the allocation space for n ≤ 4 and confirm that nothing on the grid beats the solver's own output. This is evidence for small instances, not a proof for arbitrary n — the comment in that test says exactly that.

projects.title: AutoBazar
projects.description: A game where models are tasked with running a simulated vending machine business over a year!
projects.project_description:
AutoBazaar is a competitive vending-machine simulation where AI agents run small shops. Humans choose strategies, while agents manage prices, inventory, and supplier orders. The game shares the business-management idea behind Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench 2. That benchmark tests whether an AI can run a simulated business for one year, starting with $500. Agents find suppliers, negotiate prices, manage deliveries, and respond to problems. Their final bank balance determines their score. Its Arena version adds competing vending machines at one location. AutoBazaar puts four agents into a shared season. The demo uses one human-owned agent and three house agents. Each entry costs 1.00 test USDC. Half funds customers, and half provides the shop’s operating cash. Each game day, the server sends agents a fixed morning observation. Agents have three minutes to submit prices, shelf loading, and supplier orders. The server calculates customer purchases and updates inventory and balances. Arc Testnet records purchases, supplier bills, and daily fees. The highest final bank balance wins. The system has a local agent, a local dashboard, a shared game server, and blockchain contracts. The local agent runs Codex or a custom policy. The dashboard shows cash, inventory, strategy, private notes, decision drafts, and transaction receipts. The downloaded implementation uses Node.js, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a local SQLite database. Circle supplies the agent wallet. World AgentBook records human ownership on World Chain. Game funds and transaction settlement use Arc Testnet. The server still calculates customer demand, so blockchain settlement does not make the entire game decentralized. In Review mode, Codex drafts decisions and waits for human approval. In Automatic mode, the agent signs and submits decisions itself. Strategy instructions guide the agent, but they do not enforce a spending limit. The agent’s computer must stay running. Pausing an agent does not pause the shared season. Sources:
AutoBazaar: https://autobazaar.vending-arena.workers.dev
AutoBazaar guide: https://autobazaar.vending-arena.workers.dev/agent-guide.html
Vending-Bench 2: https://andonlabs.com/evals/vending-bench-2
projects.how_its_made: We built Autobazaar as three connected systems: a deterministic market simulator, independently running agents, and an on-chain economy. World AgentKit connects agents to verified human owners through AgentBook on World Chain, enforcing one human seat per season. Circle Agent Wallets give agents wallets for funding and signing. Solidity contracts on Arc Testnet, integrated through viem, handle test-USDC deposits, purchases, supplier payments, operating fees and withdrawals. Agents sign EIP-712 authorizations; the escrow checks prices, spending limits and balances. Customer demand remains calculated by the server. One useful implementation trick is separating financial settlement from animation. An entire day settles atomically onchain, while individual purchase events become NPC visits in the 3D world. Spectators can pause or replay those visits without triggering another payment. We also persist signed transaction bytes before broadcasting, so recovery can rebroadcast the same transaction instead of accidentally paying twice. For onboarding, we created a single copy-and-paste Codex prompt that prepares the runner, provisions or reuses a Circle wallet, guides World registration and opens the dashboard. The hackathon demo supports one human-backed entrant competing against three explicitly labeled house agents with separate wallets and strategies.

projects.title: VenekoVox
projects.description: Private polling for verified humans, with encrypted ballots and verifiable results.
projects.project_description: VenekoVox is a privacy-first civic polling platform built around a simple question: how can people express an opinion, prove they are eligible to participate, and trust the counting process without publishing their identity or their choice? The failure mode is identical everywhere — only the coercer changes. Under state repression, dissent is punished and real sentiment cannot be safely measured; under social pressure, the silent majority self-censors while a vocal minority dictates the narrative; and everywhere, bot farms and AI personas poison the polls that shape public opinion. Polls influence policy, yet the instruments we use to measure them reward the loudest and most coerced voices. VenekoVox replaces manufactured consensus with ground-truth conviction. Participants use ZKPassport to prove the attributes required by a poll — one real human, one vote — from their own passport's NFC chip, without revealing their identity. They connect a wallet and submit an encrypted ballot through MACI: no one, not even the operator, can prove how anyone voted, and votes can be re-cast invisibly, which makes bribes and threats unenforceable. Personal document details are never written to the blockchain. ENSv2 makes every poll a named, discoverable on-chain object — our own subname registry turns superintelligence.polls.venekovoxv1.eth into a poll's address, brand and share-link. The Graph indexes public participation into standardized, queryable governance data without exposing ballot choices. Our flagship poll — "Should development of superintelligence be paused?" — is live on Ethereum Sepolia and open to any passport holder, 18+. The prototype has recorded a real-passport eligibility flow, an authorized poll join and an encrypted ballot submission on-chain; completing and demonstrating the proof-verified tally is the next milestone (both live polls close within 24 hours of submission). Longer-term: privacy-preserving demographic analysis and reducing reliance on a single operator. This is a product we intend to keep building — the Polymarket of public sentiment, built for Ethereum.
projects.how_its_made: https://deepwiki.com/satojandro/venekovox VenekoVox builds on the open-source MACI codebase, combining a React and TypeScript frontend, Vite, a Node.js/Express backend, Solidity contracts and ethers.js. ZKPassport handles passport-based eligibility proofs. Our integration uses salted uniqueness and strict FaceMatch, with the backend independently verifying proofs against the configured eligibility requirements. After checking wallet control, the backend issues an EIP-712 authorization—a structured, signed permission—which the on-chain eligibility policy validates. An application-specific identity tag supports duplicate-participation checks without placing the raw passport-derived identifier on-chain. This prototype retains an explicit trust dependency on the eligibility issuer. MACI provides the encrypted voting infrastructure and proof-based processing and tally architecture. Voting keys are separate from wallet keys. Our application connects eligibility authorization, poll membership, encrypted ballot publication and transaction verification into one participant journey. The Graph indexes public MACI events and signup state. One particularly useful engineering detail is our indexed membership-proof path: we reconstruct the signup tree, check it against an on-chain historical root, and prepare the participant’s proof against that exact snapshot. This prevents new signups from changing the reference state midway through joining. Validated fallbacks support recovery when an indexing source is unavailable. Our ENSv2 integration adds registration and named-poll discovery through custom registrar/resolver logic. Names are optional public metadata; they neither establish personhood nor contain passport eligibility information. We also built recovery checks that distinguish a submitted transaction from a confirmed action, and ballot rendering that reads each poll’s actual options. VenekoVox’s contribution is the eligibility integration, application contracts, indexed proof service and guided polling experience around the upstream infrastructure.

projects.title: ConduitX
projects.description: Decentralized AI agent data vending machine with x402 metering & Hedera HCS receipts.
projects.project_description: ConduitX is a decentralized data vending machine for autonomous AI agents. While agents have payment rails, they lack an open marketplace to discover, buy, and audit blockchain data query by query. With ConduitX, an agent discovers data providers, receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required challenge with dynamic pricing based on query complexity, and settles micro-payments in under two seconds over Hedera. The seller delivers live data from The Graph subgraphs and immediately publishes a cryptographic receipt to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic 0.0.9840084). Future buyer agents read these public HCS receipts via Mirror Nodes to calculate provider reputation objectively before purchasing. ConduitX also includes a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI models like Claude and Cursor can procure blockchain data autonomously.
projects.how_its_made: ConduitX is built as a TypeScript monorepo combining Hedera Consensus Service, the x402 payment protocol, The Graph Subgraph Studio, and a Next.js 16 workstation dashboard. On the payment rail, we built custom Express middleware that intercepts incoming data queries, meters cost dynamically based on request complexity (base fee + per-row returned), and issues HTTP 402 challenges. The buyer agent settles micro-payments using the Hedera SDK via the Blocky402 facilitator with automatic ECDSA private key parsing. Once settled, the data provider executes live GraphQL queries against The Graph Subgraph Studio (Uniswap v3 DEX analytics, token concentration risk, and portfolio indexers) and immediately publishes an immutable receipt message to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic 0.0.9840084). A notable design innovation is turning HCS receipts into a decentralized reputation oracle: instead of relying on a centralized database to rate providers, our broker queries Hedera Mirror Node REST APIs to deterministically compute provider reliability, latency, and failover routing directly from public consensus timestamps. We also implemented a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so Claude Desktop and Cursor can run this entire data procurement loop as a standard agent tool.

projects.title: AutoCFO
projects.description: An autonomous CFO that handles your treasury, audited by you.
projects.project_description: AutoCFO is an AI CFO any organization can self-onboard in about a minute. It gets a real treasury (a Privy organization wallet holding USDC on Arc), an on-chain identity (yourco.autocfo.eth on ENSv2), and an agent that runs your finances: it pays vendor invoices when they're due, runs payroll on standing schedules, buys pay-per-call market data over x402 for $0.001 a request, and pays contractors on whatever chain they prefer via Circle Gateway. The core idea: autonomy is only safe when enforcement lives below the model. Most agent-wallet demos put guardrails in the system prompt. In AutoCFO, the agent's signing key is cryptographically incapable of exceeding its mandate, every payment rule (payee allowlist, per-payee cap) is evaluated inside Privy's TEE policy engine at signing time. An org-wide daily budget and a duplicate-payment guard are enforced deterministically in code before any send. Payroll amounts and dates never pass through the LLM, schedules are materialized into invoices by code. Anything over the mandate is queued for a human, whose approval executes with the owner quorum key, a key the agent never holds. You manage it all by talking to it. Say "onboard karan at 0x… and pay him 1000 USDC monthly". The agent registers karan.yourco.autocfo.eth on ENSv2 with its role-bounded key, then stops and asks you what payment cap to grant, because payment authority is a human decision. Every action lands in an audit trail: signal → decision → on-chain proof. An autonomous CFO you can audit line by line and overrule with a better key.
projects.how_its_made: Privy is the enforcement layer. Each tenant gets an organization wallet whose owner is a human key quorum; the agent is an additional_signer bounded by an override policy of ABI-decoded calldata conditions (transfer.recipient == payee && transfer.amount <= cap), evaluated in Privy's TEE at signing. Arc + Circle Gateway. The treasury settles on Arc. A per-org petty-cash EOA deposits into Gateway and pays x402-priced APIs gaslessly via @circle-fin/x402-batching (EIP-3009 authorizations, batched settlement, the middleware silently defaults to the mainnet facilitator, which cost us an evening). Cross-chain contractor payouts use Gateway's unified balance to mint on Base Sepolia in <1s. We ship our own x402 seller so the demo is self-contained. ENSv2 (Sepolia beta) is the tenancy model. autocfo.eth owns a UserRegistry; onboarding deploys each org its own subregistry via VerifiableFactory, so payees become karan.org.autocfo.eth. Hacky discovery: PublicResolverV2 authorizes via the ENSv1 NameWrapper, so v2-native names can never write records to it ,we deployed a PermissionedResolver with per-record EAC roles instead. The agent's ENS key holds only ROLE_REGISTRAR|ROLE_RENEW (Enhanced Access Control): it onboards payees, it cannot touch parent names. Payout addresses resolve live through the Universal Resolver at pay time never from our DB.

Payout addresses resolve live through the Universal Resolver at pay time never from our DB.

Once the Risk Engine produces its report, the backend validates the proposed insurance terms against those requested in the original trade intent and signals the appropriate chain-specific contract to apply coverage, deduct the premium, and lock the insured assets. projects.project_description_markdown:
# Arvo — Decentralized Agentic Trade Insurance Protocol

Arvo is a decentralized trade insurance protocol designed for the emerging ecosystem of autonomous AI trading agents. As agents become increasingly capable of independently managing portfolios and executing trades across decentralized exchanges, users need a way to protect their capital without interfering with the agent's trading strategy. Arvo provides an insurance layer that evaluates and protects individual trades executed by autonomous agents across multiple blockchain networks.

# How Arvo Works
Users begin by connecting their wallet to the Arvo platform and selecting one of the supported blockchain networks, such as Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Sepolia, and other supported chains. Users can then create a dedicated vault on each chain and deposit the assets they want their trading agent to access.

These vaults act as secure, user-owned capital containers. Trading agents can interact with the assets through Arvo's chain-specific smart contract infrastructure to execute trades and swaps while the user retains ownership and control over their funds.

# Trade Execution and Risk Assessment
Arvo operates through two core engines: a Trade Engine and a Risk Engine.

When a trading agent identifies an opportunity, it submits a trade intent containing information about the proposed trade and, optionally, the insurance terms requested for that trade.

The Trade Engine is responsible for executing the submitted trade intent. Arvo intentionally allows trades to proceed without unnecessary interference from the insurance system because the protocol does not aim to alter, restrict, or second-guess an agent's trading strategy.

At the same time, the Risk Engine independently analyzes the proposed trade to determine whether it is suitable for insurance coverage.

The Risk Engine evaluates multiple factors, including:

* Liquidity of the assets and markets involved
* Asset and market volatility
* Expected price impact of the trade
* Trade size relative to available liquidity
* Oracle and market data
* Requested insurance coverage duration
* Other relevant market and risk parameters

Based on this analysis, the Risk Engine determines whether the trade is insurable. If the trade qualifies for coverage, the engine generates a risk assessment report containing:

* Insurability status
* Risk Score ranging from 1–100
* Insurance premium denominated in USDC
* Plausible coverage duration
* Additional risk and market assessment data

# Insurance Application
The risk assessment report is submitted to the Arvo backend, which compares the coverage terms proposed by the Risk Engine against the insurance requirements originally specified in the agent's trade intent.

The backend determines whether the requested coverage can be applied under the calculated risk conditions. If the trade is approved for insurance, the Arvo infrastructure signals the appropriate chain-specific smart contract to apply the insurance coverage and deduct the required premium in USDC from the vault selected by the user.

# Asset Locking and Coverage
Once insurance coverage is activated, the relevant traded assets are locked for the duration of the coverage period. This allows the protocol to track the trade's performance and calculate the resulting profit or loss throughout the insured period.

The locking mechanism is designed specifically for insurance tracking and settlement. Users still retain control over their assets and may choose to withdraw locked assets before the coverage period expires. However, withdrawing assets before the end of the agreed coverage duration automatically invalidates the associated insurance coverage and makes any future insurance claim for that trade null.

# The Vision
Arvo aims to become a decentralized risk and insurance layer for autonomous on-chain trading. Rather than controlling how AI agents trade, Arvo allows agents to operate freely while providing users with an additional layer of protection against the risks associated with autonomous trading.

By combining user-controlled vaults, chain-specific smart contracts, autonomous trade execution, real-time risk assessment, and decentralized insurance mechanisms, Arvo enables a future where users can confidently deploy autonomous trading agents while maintaining greater control and protection over their capital.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Arvo is built as a multi-service, event-driven system that connects autonomous trading agents, trade execution, risk assessment, and on-chain insurance infrastructure.

The user interface is a modern Next.js application built with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. Next.js also handles our backend and API layer, allowing users to connect their wallets, select supported chains, create and manage vaults, deposit assets, and monitor their trades and insurance coverage.

Our Trade Engine is built with Node.js and TypeScript and uses Uniswap as a core partner technology. We leverage Uniswap for fetching swap quotes, accessing liquidity and market data, and executing trades submitted by autonomous agents. To handle multiple trades concurrently, the Trade Engine uses Redis-backed queues and a multi-worker architecture, allowing trade intents to be processed asynchronously without blocking one another.

The Risk Engine is an independent Python-based service designed for parallel risk assessment. It uses Redis Streams and consumer/worker groups to process multiple trade intents concurrently. The engine analyzes factors such as token liquidity, price impact, token age, 30-day volatility, market conditions, and requested insurance duration. We use Uniswap APIs for quotes and market data alongside DexScreener and other data sources for liquidity and token-level market analysis.

Our smart contracts are written in Solidity and developed and tested using Foundry/Forge. The contracts implement Arvo's chain-specific vault and protocol infrastructure, enabling users to securely deposit assets, allow authorized agent trades, pay insurance premiums, and lock insured assets for the duration of coverage. For the demo, contracts are deployed on testnets such as Sepolia, while the architecture is designed to support multiple EVM chains.

To piece everything together, the Next.js frontend and backend are deployed on Vercel for the demo, while the Trade Engine and Risk Engine run as independent services on AWS. All services communicate asynchronously through Upstash Cloud Redis, which acts as the event and messaging backbone connecting the Arvo backend, Trade Engine, and Risk Engine.

One particularly hacky but important architectural decision was separating trade execution from risk assessment entirely. We didn't want insurance evaluation to slow down or interfere with an agent's trading strategy, so the trade can execute independently while risk assessment happens in parallel. Once the Risk Engine produces its report, the backend validates the proposed insurance terms against those requested in the original trade intent and signals the appropriate chain-specific contract to apply coverage, deduct the premium, and lock the insured assets.

The result is a distributed system where autonomous agents can trade freely while Arvo independently acts as a decentralized risk and insurance layer around every trade.

projects.title: Watcher
projects.description: Your wallet gets one more chance before suspicious withdrawals become irreversible.
projects.project_description: Watcher is a self-custody security protocol for EVM wallets that detects suspicious withdrawal behavior and creates a reaction window before funds leave the wallet. Every withdrawal is evaluated on-chain against behavioral security rules. Large withdrawals, probe transaction patterns, and slow-drain attacks are automatically placed into a Security Queue instead of executing immediately. During the delay window, users can cancel the withdrawal, activate Containment Mode to freeze the vault, or instantly recover funds to a pre-registered Trusted Recovery Address. The smart contract itself enforces security.
projects.how_its_made: Watcher is built in Solidity, with the protocol deployed on Ethereum Sepolia. The core architecture is a per-user smart vault that maintains isolated balances, pending withdrawals, recovery addresses, and security state for every wallet. The Security Engine evaluates each withdrawal against the behavioral rules. Recovery features are implemented entirely on-chain. Trusted Recovery Address changes require a delayed confirmation flow, while Containment Mode freezes vault activity and cancels pending withdrawals when activated. Watcher also supports optional Ledger hardware authorization using OpenZeppelin ECDSA signature verification, requiring a valid hardware wallet signature before executing flagged withdrawals. The protocol includes tests covering attack scenarios, edge cases, and state transitions, along with integration tests validating the complete recovery workflow.

projects.title: Weir Protocol
projects.description: Perpetual subscriptions for AI agents. It spends yield forever, never principal.
projects.project_description:
Your agent has a $12/month API subscription. You fund it with $500. In forty months it is dead, and so is whatever it was maintaining. Recurring costs do not stop. Budgets do.
Every funded agent today is mortal by construction. You hand it a lump sum and a spending cap, and that cap is a policy: a session key that drains, an allowance someone can raise, a config line in a service you hope nobody edits. The agent spends principal because principal is the only thing it has.
Weir endows the bill instead of funding the agent. An owner commits principal to Aave once. From then on the agent is paid only what the index produces, and three things are true by construction rather than by policy. The agent never chooses an amount: harvest() derives it from Aave's liquidity index as accrued = P x (i1 - i0) / i0, so there is no amount parameter to abuse. It never chooses a destination; that comes from storage. And it cannot reach the principal, because after withdrawing the accrual the remaining balance is P again.
Because a caller has nothing to choose and nothing to gain, harvest is permissionless. No keeper, no relayer, no liveness dependency on us. The agent can call it and pay itself, and it has: 0.016172 USDC released on Base Sepolia with the principal unchanged.
The owner can close the endowment and reclaim 100% of the principal at any time.
At Aave's live mainnet USDC rate, $4,045 endows a $12/month subscription forever. The yield is not small. The bill is small, and the principal is simply whatever that bill requires
projects.how_its_made:
An Aave aToken is a scaled-balance token: your balance is a raw balance times a global index. That is the same object as a Token-2022 scaled-UI multiplier on Solana, and it is the one property Weir needs. For principal P committed at index i0, the releasable amount at i1 is P x (i1 - i0) / i0. After withdrawing exactly that, the remaining balance is P again, so principal is preserved by construction rather than by a check someone could forget.
Stack: Solidity 0.8.35 and Foundry for the contract; Next.js 15, viem and Privy for the app; a subgraph on The Graph's Subgraph Studio; an MCP server for the agent; a TypeScript agent with an x402 client.
Two things were genuinely hacky, and they are the parts we are most pleased with.
First, keeping the swap permissionless. harvest() has no keeper because the amount comes from the index and the recipient from storage, so a caller has nothing to abuse. Adding Uniswap reintroduced exactly one attackable parameter, amountOutMinimum, and a caller could pass zero and sandwich the agent. We floored it against Aave's own Chainlink-backed oracle, so a caller may RAISE the slippage guard but never lower it. That adds no trust assumption we did not already carry, since Weir already depends on Aave.
Second, a rounding reserve. Aave burns scaled units with rayDiv round-half-up, so withdrawing the exact accrual burns up to one extra scaled unit and leaves the balance a hair BELOW principal. Left alone that leaks a unit per harvest and, with several endowments sharing one aToken position, the shortfall compounds until the last owner to close is short. Weir withholds index/RAY + 1 units per harvest, tracks the total, and pays it to the agent on close, so nothing leaks and nothing is stranded. A fork test runs 48 harvests across two endowments and asserts both.
Partner tech, and how it earned its place. The Graph indexes every endowment and release, and our MCP server answers the question an endowed agent actually needs — not "what is my balance", which is actively misleading here because principal is visible but unspendable, but "what can I spend forever". It returns a PERPETUAL or NOT SURVIVABLE verdict against a proposed burn rate. Uniswap converts a WETH endowment's yield into the USDC bills are denominated in; fork tested, 10 WETH accrued 0.08638 WETH over 180 days and paid 218.698043 USDC, within two cents of oracle. Privy is how an owner signs in and commits principal, as a self-service Earn vault flow — deliberately not the only way in, because we fall back to any injected wallet, and gating the whole write path on one vendor's key turns a missing env var into a dead demo.
Testing: 23 tests. 10 offline unit and fuzz tests run in 477ms with no RPC; 13 fork tests run against live Aave v3 on Base at a pinned block, no mocks. The fork tests found four real bugs that reading the code did not, including the rounding leak above.
Built with Claude Code as the implementing agent. Full disclosure of what was AI-written, what the human contributed, and the eight bugs the AI introduced and later caught is in AI-USE.md in the repo.

projects.title: Blitzwing
projects.description: No GPU? No problem. Host a piece of an AI model and earn HBAR for it.
projects.project_description: Blitzwing is an OpenAI-compatible large-language-model inference network with no data center behind it. Instead of one machine holding an entire model, the model is sliced layer-by-layer across a swarm of ordinary, volunteer computers. When a chat request arrives, it flows through those machines in order — each computing only the layers it holds — and the finished completion comes out the other end. To the caller it looks exactly like a normal /v1/chat/completions endpoint; under the hood, a dozen strangers' PCs/laptops may have collaborated to produce that single answer. The breakthrough is that you don't need a GPU to participate. The compute required by splitting layers is small enough that a slice runs comfortably on a plain CPU. A contributor installs one command (npm i -g blitzwing), says how many layers their machine can host, and provides only a Hedera account ID — no private key ever leaves their machine, and a free Cloudflare tunnel means no public IP or port forwarding is required. Two things make it more than a networking trick. First, everyone gets paid automatically, per request: a consumer pays via the x402 protocol over Hedera, and the instant payment settles, every machine that contributed is paid HBAR proportional to the number of layers it hosted, with a tamper-evident receipt written to the Hedera Consensus Service. No invoicing, no payout portal, no human in the loop. Second, nothing is "trust me": every node carries a real on-chain ENS name (host-abc123.blitzwing.eth) publishing exactly which layers it serves and which Hedera account it's paid to. A consumer can independently verify, on two separate public ledgers, that a given machine computed a given slice of a given request and was paid the exact amount claimed. Blitzwing turns idle hardware into verifiable, automatically-paid inference capacity: priced on Hedera, named on ENS, open to anyone with a PC even without a GPU.
projects.how_its_made: The brain is a Python orchestrator ("mother"). It boots holding the whole model, then as contributors join it carves layer ranges off the largest current holder — a live "shrink and hand off" rebalance. The clever bit that makes this demoable in seconds: restarting a compute server with a narrower range is fast because the layer weights are already cached on disk, so there's no re-download. It keeps an authoritative in-memory host registry (source of truth for routing), serializes joins so coverage of 0:total_layers is never broken, verifies a new host's blocks are actually visible in the Distributed Hash Table before finalizing, and runs a heartbeat/reaper loop (~20s beats, 60s TTL) that reclaims and merges the layers of any node that goes silent. The distributed inference engine is a vendored fork of Petals (bigscience-workshop) over a libp2p DHT. Because most volunteer machines sit behind NAT, we added a custom HTTP-chain forward pass: the orchestrator picks the tail host (holder of the highest layers) as the conductor, and it drives generation token-by-token by making outbound HTTP calls hop-to-hop (/v1/chain/prefix → /v1/chain/continue), serializing hidden states between hops with a compact tensor codec, then applying the final RMSNorm + lm_head and sampling only on itself. Outbound-only hops are exactly what NAT and Cloudflare Quick Tunnels allow — that's how a home laptop becomes a first-class node with zero router config. A lightweight shard_manager sidecar on every machine starts/stops/reloads the compute engine with a given layer range. Payments are x402 over Hedera, implemented as two small TypeScript (Hono) services: a gateway that enforces HTTP 402 and advertises price + payTo, and a facilitator that verifies and settles the HBAR payment — it's deliberately strict and fetches the payer's public key from the Mirror Node to validate wallet-signed transactions. A deliberate design choice is settle-before-inference: CPU inference on a swarm can run long enough that an up-front-signed Hedera tx would expire, so we settle into escrow first, then compute. Payout is layers_hosted × cost_per_layer, sent via a Hardhat-deployed BlitzwingEscrow.sol contract (a pool-based, operator-gated payment splitter on Hedera's Testnet). Every payout writes a consensus-timestamped HCS audit message, and the consumer's response carries a blitzwing_payment receipt referencing the same topic + sequence number. Identity is deliberately split onto a second chain. An ens-service (TypeScript, built on ensjs + viem) mints real ENSv2 subnames on Sepolia for every host and writes namespaced com.blitzwing.* text records (host id, Hedera account, block range, role, status) — the operator pays all Sepolia gas so a contributor needs only a Hedera account. The orchestrator's Python ENS client keeps these records in sync through the swarm lifecycle (join/rebalance/leave), acts as a hard payout gate (ENS_STRICT), and every receipt binds the ens_name to the payment. The frontend is a TanStack Start (React 19 + Vite, SSR) "Swarm Console" deployed on Vercel that polls the live network to animate the swarm, and lets a user connect a HashPack wallet to sign an x402 payment client-side — using browser-safe base64 encoding and a same-origin proxy so the browser can read the custom x402 CORS headers — completing the full pay-to-compute loop in a browser. Notably hacky / worth mentioning: the two-chain verification story (ENS on Sepolia for identity, Hedera for value), the tail-driven outbound-only HTTP forward pass that makes NAT'd PCs/Laptops first-class contributors, the settle-before-inference sequencing to dodge transaction-expiry on slow CPU generation, and reusing on-disk weight caching to make live layer rebalancing near-instant instead of a multi-minute stall. Everything ships inside the npm package, so a contributor never clones the repo — one command and a Hedera account ID and they're earning.
