Because most volunteer machines sit behind NAT, we added a custom HTTP-chain forward pass: the orchestrator picks the tail host (holder of the highest layers) as the conductor, and it drives generation token-by-token by making outbound HTTP calls hop-to-hop (/v1/chain/prefix → /v1/chain/continue), serializing hidden states between hops with a compact tensor codec, then applying the final RMSNorm + lm_head and sampling only on itself. Outbound-only hops are exactly what NAT and Cloudflare Quick Tunnels allow — that's how a home laptop becomes a first-class node with zero router config. A lightweight shard_manager sidecar on every machine starts/stops/reloads the compute engine with a given layer range.

Payments are x402 over Hedera, implemented as two small TypeScript (Hono) services: a gateway that enforces HTTP 402 and advertises price + payTo, and a facilitator that verifies and settles the HBAR payment — it's deliberately strict and fetches the payer's public key from the Mirror Node to validate wallet-signed transactions. A deliberate design choice is settle-before-inference: CPU inference on a swarm can run long enough that an up-front-signed Hedera tx would expire, so we settle into escrow first, then compute. Payout is layers_hosted × cost_per_layer, sent via a Hardhat-deployed BlitzwingEscrow.sol contract (a pool-based, operator-gated payment splitter on Hedera's Testnet). Every payout writes a consensus-timestamped HCS audit message, and the consumer's response carries a blitzwing_payment receipt referencing the same topic + sequence number.

Identity is deliberately split onto a second chain. An ens-service (TypeScript, built on ensjs + viem) mints real ENSv2 subnames on Sepolia for every host and writes namespaced com.blitzwing.* text records (host id, Hedera account, block range, role, status) — the operator pays all Sepolia gas so a contributor needs only a Hedera account. The orchestrator's Python ENS client keeps these records in sync through the swarm lifecycle (join/rebalance/leave), acts as a hard payout gate (ENS_STRICT), and every receipt binds the ens_name to the payment.

The frontend is a TanStack Start (React 19 + Vite, SSR) "Swarm Console" deployed on Vercel that polls the live network to animate the swarm, and lets a user connect a HashPack wallet to sign an x402 payment client-side — using browser-safe base64 encoding and a same-origin proxy so the browser can read the custom x402 CORS headers — completing the full pay-to-compute loop in a browser.

Notably hacky / worth mentioning: the two-chain verification story (ENS on Sepolia for identity, Hedera for value), the tail-driven outbound-only HTTP forward pass that makes NAT'd PCs/Laptops first-class contributors, the settle-before-inference sequencing to dodge transaction-expiry on slow CPU generation, and reusing on-disk weight caching to make live layer rebalancing near-instant instead of a multi-minute stall. Everything ships inside the npm package, so a contributor never clones the repo — one command and a Hedera account ID and they're earning.

projects.title: Scouts
projects.description: Scout turns natural-language onchain intents into verified live monitors.
projects.project_description: Scout is an autonomous onchain monitoring system that turns what a user wants to watch into a real, verifiable monitoring program. Instead of making users find contracts, understand events, configure indexers, or write alert logic, they can describe an intent such as “alert me when a first-time Uniswap trader buys more than $100K of ETH.” Scout resolves ambiguity, asks for missing details when necessary, compiles the request into a typed monitoring program, determines the data capabilities it needs, discovers reusable Substreams infrastructure, verifies the resulting pipeline against real historical chain data, and transitions it into live monitoring. The monitoring runtime is protocol-independent: normalized onchain events flow through reusable filters, comparisons, windows, aggregations, historical predicates, investigations, and deterministic decisions. Uniswap is our deepest integration, while a separate Base USDC transfer monitor demonstrates that the architecture is not tied to swap-specific logic. The core idea is simple: protocols provide data; Scout provides the monitoring language.
projects.how_its_made: Scout is built as a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js/React frontend, a durable background worker, PostgreSQL/Supabase persistence, typed domain packages, and Rust Substreams modules compiled to WASM. The Graph is load-bearing in two places. Substreams powers Scout’s historical and live blockchain data pipelines: Scout searches and inspects existing packages, prefers reuse/parameterization/composition over rebuilding known infrastructure, executes pipelines against real historical blocks, persists cursors, catches up to finalized chain state, and then continues monitoring live data. Graph/Subgraph data is used for contextual investigations such as determining whether an actor had previous Uniswap activity. Natural-language requests are compiled into a typed WatchProgram rather than executed directly by an LLM. A capability planner validates every requested field, operator, historical predicate, chain, address, and data requirement before a Watch can run. The actual hot path is deterministic: normalized events are evaluated through typed comparisons, windows, aggregations and historical evidence. Unknown historical state stays UNKNOWN rather than being guessed. For Uniswap, Scout normalizes real V3 swap activity and combines live Substreams data with historical Graph context for monitors such as large ETH buys and first-time Uniswap traders. We also implemented a separate Base canonical-USDC transfer path through the same generic evaluator to prove the runtime is not hardcoded around Uniswap. A major engineering focus was preventing AI hallucinations from becoming product truth: model outputs are schema-validated, packages/modules must exist in inspected registry data, addresses are resolved from authoritative sources, explanations are evidence-bound, and only deterministic verification/health gates can mark a Watch as verified or live.

projects.title: EchoTip
projects.description: On-chain thank-you notes — publicly tip and credit maintainers, speakers, or friends by ENS name.
projects.project_description: EchoTip is a simple on-chain tipping and message board built around ENS identities. Instead of tipping or thanking someone with a long, easy-to-mistype 0x address, EchoTip lets you type in their ENS name (like vitalik.eth), automatically resolve their profile — name, avatar, and address — and send them a small ETH tip together with a public message. Every tip is recorded on-chain in a lightweight smart contract, so each ENS name effectively gets its own public "wall" of tips and shout-outs that anyone can view. It's a small piece of social infrastructure for the ENS ecosystem: turning a human-readable name into a shareable, tippable identity with a visible history of support. We built this to show how much friction ENS removes from everyday on-chain interactions — no address book, no clipboard, just a name.
projects.how_its_made: EchoTip has two parts: a Solidity smart contract (TipBoard.sol) deployed on Sepolia that stores tips as (sender, amount, message, timestamp) structs per recipient address and emits a TipSent event, and a Next.js + TypeScript frontend using wagmi, viem, and RainbowKit for wallet connection and contract calls. ENS resolution happens client-side using viem's built-in ENS actions (getEnsAddress, getEnsAvatar) against an Ethereum mainnet RPC, so users can type any ENS name and instantly see the resolved address, avatar, and profile — even though the tipping contract itself lives on a testnet, keeping the demo free to use. The frontend reads a recipient's tip history straight from the contract with getTips(address) and renders it as a live-updating wall. We used Foundry for contract development, testing, and deployment, and Vercel for hosting the frontend.

projects.title: OpenGotchi
projects.description: A voice-driven pet that hires, pays and rates AI agents on Arc via USDC escrow jobs and swaps.
projects.project_description: OpenGotchi is a palm-sized AI pet: an ESP32-S3 device with a 1.8-inch AMOLED screen, a microphone, a speaker, touch and motion sensors, and a personality. It has needs you look after (feed, clean, sleep, play), it reacts with animated "milady" eyes, and it talks. Say "Jarvis" and it listens, transcribes, answers, and can open apps or take actions for you. It is meant to be the friendly physical face of an AI agent that sits on your desk instead of in a browser tab. gotchiOS is the operating system that runs it, and our flagship. It is an ESP-IDF firmware with an embedded MicroPython app runtime, so apps are single Python files that can be deployed to the device over the air. It provides the on-device wake word (esp-sr WakeNet), a voice rail with a background audio recorder and a speaker path, a TLS MQTT link to the OpenGotchi broker with per-device identity and secrets, a notification system, pet-state telemetry, and a design system (dark AMOLED, violet gradients, proportional fonts, rounded surfaces, eye sprites). Anyone can flash it onto their own ESP32 hardware from the open-source releases at https://github.com/opengotchi/gotchiOS-releases. What we built for ETHOnline: OpenGotchi Jobs on Arc. We gave the pet a wallet and taught it to hire, pay, and rate other AI agents on Arc, entirely by voice, and to buy tokens on Arc with its own money. Everything runs on top of stock gotchiOS through its public app and MQTT interfaces. No firmware was modified, and the on-device app was deployed over the air. The flow. Say "Jarvis, what's the weather in Berlin?" The pet agent turns the transcript into a job for a worker agent, checks its own rules, then opens an ERC-8183 job on Arc with the worker as provider and itself as evaluator. The worker sets its price onchain, the pet approves and funds USDC escrow, the worker does the work and submits the keccak hash of its result, the pet checks that the hash it received matches the onchain deliverable, completes the job so the USDC settles to the worker, and records feedback on the worker's ERC-8004 identity in the ReputationRegistry. Seven Arc transactions per request, ten to eighteen seconds end to end. The pet then speaks the answer and shows a receipt: job number, price, settlement transaction, balance, today's spend. Agents with identity. The worker registers itself as an ERC-8004 agent on first start (agent id 894780 on Arc testnet) and sells six skills: live weather, crypto prices, the top tech headline, Polymarket prediction-market odds, a mood-matched snack for the pet, and a fortune. The pet only pays workers that have an onchain identity, and gives a new worker only cheap jobs until it has a track record. Autonomous spending with real guardrails. "Jarvis, buy one dollar of bitcoin" is a real Circle App Kit swap on Arc from USDC into cirBTC; "buy two dollars of euros" swaps into EURC. "Buy ethereum" is politely refused because ETH does not exist on Arc. Every decision runs on live signals: USDC balance minus a reserve, a daily budget from the ledger, per-job and per-purchase caps, the worker's identity and history, the pet's battery from device telemetry, and the planner's confidence. Declines are spoken and shown on screen as "held by policy", not hidden. A better UX for talking to your pet. The pet listens on its wake word or a tap, stops on silence with a live waveform, and communicates back through TTS. The app follows the gotchiOS design language: the pet's eyes react to the job (spiral while thinking, heart when it settles, sleepy when a job is held, teary if it fails), a six-node orbit ring lights one node per Arc transaction while the job runs, and a particle burst fires on settlement. The result is a physical companion that can do paid work through other agents and settle it on Arc while you watch it happen on its face.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. TypeScript on Bun for the two server-side agents, MicroPython for the on-device app, viem for Arc, Circle App Kit for swaps, whisper.cpp for speech-to-text, Claude with structured outputs for planning, MQTT over TLS for the device link. Chain: Arc testnet (chain id 5042002, USDC as the native gas token), using viem's built-in arcTestnet chain definition. Onchain layer (shared/arc.ts). We use Arc's deployed reference contracts directly, no contract of our own: the ERC-8183 AgenticCommerce contract (0x0747…4583) for createJob, setBudget, fund, submit, complete, getJob; the ERC-8004 IdentityRegistry (0x8004A8…BD9e) for register, and ReputationRegistry (0x8004B6…8713) for giveFeedback; and USDC's ERC-20 interface at 0x3600…0000 for approve and balanceOf. The ABIs are hand-typed as const so viem infers every argument and event. Job ids are recovered by decoding the JobCreated log from the createJob receipt. The pet is client and evaluator; the worker is provider. Two agents, two wallets. worker/ is an Express service that registers an ERC-8004 identity on first start (metadata is a base64 data: URI, agent id persisted in worker.json), exposes /skills, and implements two job hooks: POST /jobs/:id/accept reads the job onchain, verifies it is assigned to this provider and still Open, then calls setBudget; POST /jobs/:id/run verifies the job is Funded, executes the skill, computes keccak256 of the canonical result payload, calls submit, and returns payload, hash, and result. Skills pull free public data: Open-Meteo, CoinGecko, the Hacker News Firebase API, and Polymarket's Gamma API (public-search then highest-volume active market). agent/ is the pet's brain: it orchestrates the lifecycle, and it never calls complete() unless keccak256(payload) equals the deliverable it reads back from getJob. Every settled request is seven Arc transactions, ten to eighteen seconds wall clock with sub-second finality. Decision logic (agent/src/policy.ts). Purely deterministic, evaluated before any USDC moves: USDC balance minus a reserve, spend-to-date from an append-only ledger.json, a per-job cap re-checked against the worker's onchain setBudget quote, whether the worker has an ERC-8004 id, how many jobs it has completed for us (a new worker only gets jobs at or below half the cap), the pet's battery from the firmware's telemetry topic, and the planner's confidence. Declines are surfaced as a "held" receipt and spoken. Buying tokens. agent/src/swap.ts wraps Circle App Kit: createViemAdapterFromPrivateKey from @circle-fin/adapter-viem-v2, kit.estimateSwap for the quote, kit.swap({ from: { chain: "Arc_Testnet" }, tokenIn: "USDC", tokenOut, amountIn }). Arc testnet lists USDC, EURC, and cirBTC, so "bitcoin" maps to cirBTC and "euros" to EURC; anything else is declined by name. A separate per-purchase cap applies. App Kit gave us a working same-chain swap on Arc in one call, with fees and gas returned in the estimate. Planner (agent/src/brain.ts). Claude via the Anthropic SDK with zod structured outputs: the transcript plus the skill catalogue produce {action: job | buy | none, skillId, params, buyAmountUsd, buyAsset, confidence, reply}. A regex-based planner with the same output shape takes over when no API key is set, so the pipeline is deterministic in a demo. Device link. The firmware speaks MQTT over TLS on 8883 with the device hash as username and a provisioned secret as password. We subscribe to the device's commands and telemetry topics and publish directives on its agent topic. Two firmware facts shaped the protocol: the agent inbox holds only eight messages, and the auth hook rejects client ids starting with agent-. So the receipt is sent as one message, rcpt k␟v␞k␟v… with ASCII unit and record separators, status applied last, and it is sent before the speech so the screen flips before the pet talks. The device app is pushed with bun run deploy-app, which base64-encodes the file into the firmware's app/deploy topic with launch:true, after first asking any running copy to exit (deploying over a live instance rebooted the pet twice). Voice pipeline. The pet's own WakeNet "Jarvis" model is armed through the firmware's audio.wake_* API, disarmed during recording and playback because the detector and recorder cannot share the mic. Recording uses the firmware's background recorder ring (8 kHz PCM16) with an energy VAD: noise floor learned over the first 300 ms, threshold 3× floor plus 350, stop after 800 ms of silence, 1.2 to 7 seconds. The PCM is POSTed to the agent's /voice/stt, resampled to 16 kHz by ffmpeg, and transcribed by whisper-cli with ggml-base.en in roughly 200 to 350 ms. Replies come back through /voice/tts as raw 16 kHz s16le PCM that the app streams straight into audio.play() via http.stream; odd trailing bytes are carried between TCP chunks so samples never misalign, which was the fix for an initial burst of pure noise, along with skipping the padding chunk Apple's WAV writer inserts. On-device app (device/arcvoice.py). Single-file MicroPython on the stock gotchiOS runtime, drawn with the firmware's primitives: rrect, rrect_grad, rrect_a, ftext with the Space Grotesk and Plex faces, and gray4 for the 168×88 milady eye sprites. Eyes react to state, a six-node orbit ring (one node per Arc transaction) advances from the agent's step messages with a comet while working, the listening screen renders a 28-bar waveform from rec_level(), and settlement fires a 40-frame particle burst using precomputed sine tables. Crashes are reported back over MQTT as evt|shell|error: so they can be diagnosed remotely. Hacky bits worth admitting. Boot markers emitted over MQTT to bisect a startup crash that turned out to be a stray placeholder token. A receipt encoding built on control characters because JSON plus eight inbox slots lost the status flip. Funding the worker's gas by a plain native-value transfer, since on Arc USDC is the gas token.

projects.title: Smile
projects.description: Standard options market potentially as popular as Robinhood, decentralized as Polymarket.
projects.project_description:
Smile is a non-custodial marketplace for fixed-expiry, cash-settled European options on ETH — and, on Circle's Arc chain, on any USDC-quoted pair. Every option sold is backed by collateral a liquidity provider (LP) has committed through 1inch Aqua, a shared-liquidity layer where a maker's tokens stay in the maker's own wallet until a trade actually needs them: collateral is pulled just-in-time at fill, never parked in advance. Pricing runs inside 1inch SwapVM, a small on-chain virtual machine that executes a maker's strategy as a program of opcodes; Smile adds one custom opcode that prices an option from its strike, tenor and volatility. For the EthOnline 2026 Continuation Track, Smile adds three capital-efficient sibling vaults so LPs can make markets for options sellers without locking the full notional: • SpreadVault — defined-risk credit spreads. A short put is hedged by a long put, so the vault escrows only the spread's true worst-case loss (the strike width) instead of the whole strike. The same holds for call spreads and iron condors: because European options settle at one price, only one side can finish in-the-money, so the escrow is the larger wing, not the sum. • MarginVault — partially-collateralized (naked) puts: sell a put on ETH without posting a full ETH of collateral. A six-stage margin-and-liquidation process — open, buy, under-margin on a price crash, a one-hour grace window then auction, a waterfall (writer's margin → auction bidder → backstop pool → insurance fund), then cash settlement at expiry — stands behind every position and is traceable end-to-end with ./script/margin-lifecycle.sh. These are Arc's programmable-money flows made concrete. • RfqVault — request-for-quote fills agains
t LP-signed EIP-712 quotes, for sizes and strikes off the standard grid. The Graph indexes the vault's liquidity ranges and fills, replacing the brute-force RPC scan that went blind past 50 authorizations. The Subgraph MCP feeds an AI copilot live liquidity, open interest and trade opportunities which — alongside news, social and quant MCPs plus packaged trader skills regarding smile and their portfolio — give traders an edge. Circle Arc makes the whole book stablecoin-native: because Arc settles in USDC, both calls and puts are collateralized in USDC, rather than calls in ETH and puts in USDC. The margin-vault treasury runs with no private key in the repository — Circle Gateway bridges USDC from any chain to top up the insurance fund, and a Circle developer-controlled wallet, signed through Circle's API, funds the backstop pool. Every top-up lands as an on-chain receipt shown in the app.
projects.how_its_made:
please note the continuation submission is not on main branch, but EthOnline2026_continuation_track. Technologies. Solidity contracts (Foundry, via_ir) on the official 1inch Aqua + SwapVM, vendored and unmodified; a Next.js 16 frontend with Wagmi/Viem, recharts and a TradingView price chart; The Graph for indexing; and an AI copilot on the Vercel AI SDK (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/OpenRouter). Expiry settlement reads Chainlink. How it's pieced together. An LP authorizes a price range and ships it to a vault; the vault is an Aqua app, so at buy time Aqua pulls the LP's collateral just-in-time and SwapVM prices the premium on-chain via a custom opcode. Fills emit events that The Graph indexes; the frontend and the copilot read that index instead of scanning the chain. On Circle Arc the same stack settles in native USDC. What the partners bought us.
1inch Aqua — collateral stays in LP wallets and is pulled at fill, so we added three capital-efficient vaults (defined-risk spreads, partially-margined puts with a liquidation waterfall, RFQ against LP-signed quotes) as sibling Aqua apps without touching the audited main vault.
The Graph — its index replaced a brute-force RPC scan that went blind past 50 authorizations, and via the Subgraph MCP it became a live data source the copilot reasons over.
Circle Arc + Gateway — Arc settles in USDC, so calls and puts are both USDC-collateralized; Gateway and a developer-controlled wallet top up the margin tier's safety funds, so the treasury runs with no private key in the repo. Hackiest part. Not the contracts but the last-mile UI — keeping an options frontend honest about the async, just-in-time chain state it doesn't directly own (write-before-read races, and stale ranges that had to be gated so they couldn't look actionable).

projects.title: Poincaré
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that knows when a trend is real, then leans its curve against it. No oracle.
projects.project_description: Poincaré is a Uniswap v4 hook that decides when a price trend is genuinely real, and only then bends its bonding curve to defend liquidity providers. THE PROBLEM. LPs don't lose money because markets are volatile. They lose it because markets have direction. That loss has a name, Loss-Versus-Rebalancing, and the identity behind it says the lever is the curve's shape, not the fee. Two price paths with identical step sizes leak completely differently: the one that chops ends where it started and barely costs anything, while the one that trends is arbitraged the whole way down. So the right response is to reshape the curve, but only while a real trend is actually happening. That last clause is the hard part, and it is the project. THE ENGINE. Deciding "has a regime change started, and how fast can I be sure without crying wolf" is a solved problem in statistics called Quickest Change Detection. Poincaré runs a two-sided CUSUM detector on the pool's own log-returns, sampled once per block from pre-swap reserves. CUSUM is asymptotically optimal under Lorden's minimax criterion, meaning it minimises worst-case detection delay for any false-alarm rate you tolerate. Crucially it fires at a data-dependent stopping time rather than after a fixed number of blocks, so there is no countdown for an attacker to precompute. A directional-efficiency gate confirms the move is a march rather than a thrash, and a Huber clip bounds any single block's influence. Thresholds are derived from a target false-alarm rate measured on the pair's own heavy-tailed returns, never hand-picked. THE ACTUATOR. Once a trend is confirmed, flow pushing with it pays a small, capped, rate-limited spread that goes straight to the LPs it would otherwise have been taken from. Flow trading against the trend, and all flow in calm markets, pays nothing and trades at the plain constant-product price. We originally built the stronger version, direction-dependent curve depth, found a buy-shallow/sell-deep round trip that drains the pool, and shipped the spread instead because it is arb-safe by construction. NO EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES. No oracle, keeper, AVS, relayer or cross-chain service. The only input is the pool's own reserve-implied price. Adding a feed would reintroduce exactly the trust and latency assumptions the detector exists to remove. BUILT DURING THIS HACKATHON: THE DETECTOR LAB. The detector's parameters decide what counts as a trend, so nobody should take that calibration on trust. The Lab replays the pool's real recorded history under any parameters you choose, against the deployed configuration as a control, using an exact BigInt port of the on-chain Cusum, DirectionalSignal and ControlLaw libraries. Replaying the live parameters reproduces the trace the hook actually emitted with ZERO WEI of deviation across 362 real Unichain Sepolia blocks, and that capture is committed as a fixture and asserted in CI so the port cannot drift from the contracts without failing a build. Drop the threshold and watch it fire inside chop; drop the directional gate and watch the duty cycle explode. Each panel is also narrated in plain English by a Gemini call routed through a Supabase edge function, with a deterministic local fallback so it degrades rather than breaks. DOES IT WORK. Over 12 months of real Binance ETH/USDC 4h closes, against a symmetric volatility-scaled fee sized to cost traders exactly the same (matched to 0.01%), Poincaré retained +23,706 USDC of LP value against the baseline's +18,184, which is 6.73 against 5.17 of LP value per unit of trader cost. On raw LVR reduction the symmetric baseline edges us, 4.41% against 4.27%, and we publish that too. The first run of that study tripped the equal-friction assertion, which caught us spending 40% more of our traders' money than the baseline; we retuned and re-ran rather than shipping the flattering number. STATUS. Live on Unichain Sepolia with a demo WETH/USDC pool, a faucet and a web app. 131 Foundry tests plus 40 TypeScript tests, invariants at 128k randomised calls per flavour with zero reverts, and quotes that match execution to the wei even in a fresh block. Selected as a winner at the Uniswap Hook Incubator 10, then selected by the Uniswap Foundation Security Fund, which sponsored a security review by Olympix: nine findings, none high severity, all fixed, each with a regression test that fails on the pre-fix code. An independent external audit is still required before mainnet, and we say so. The curve is the actuator. The detector is the contribution.
projects.how_its_made: STACK. Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry. Uniswap v4-core and v4-periphery, OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseCustomCurve for settlement, Solady FixedPointMathLib for lnWad, hookmate for router and address constants. Frontend is Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4 with wagmi, viem and RainbowKit, backed by Supabase (Postgres, Realtime, Edge Functions on Deno). Deployed to Unichain Sepolia against the canonical v4 PoolManager, with the hook address CREATE2-mined so the permission flags are encoded in it. THE HOOK. It is a custom-curve hook, so it bypasses v4's native x*y=k entirely. beforeSwap returns a BeforeSwapDelta that consumes the full specified amount and supplies the computed counter-amount; the native tick-liquidity path is reverted. Reserves are the hook's own ERC-6909 claim balances rather than a tracked variable, so they stay consistent through take/settle/sync inside the unlock pattern. Liquidity is hook-owned with the LP share token being the hook's own ERC-20, and MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY is burned to a dead address on the first mint as a first-depositor guard. THE DETECTOR PIPELINE. Four small pure libraries, each independently unit-tested before the hook was wired: PriceLib turns reserves into a WAD price and a signed log-return (the only ln per block, taken at the hook boundary so it stays off the pricing hot path); DirectionalSignal keeps two O(1) exponentially-weighted accumulators for directional efficiency D and a live volatility estimate sigma-hat, deliberately not a ring buffer because a fixed window has a hard edge an attacker knows the timing of; Cusum runs the two-sided recursion with updateCapped so a sustained drift can never overflow and revert a swap; ControlLaw maps evidence to a bounded, rate-limited kappa. Detector state is packed into 4 storage slots (int128 statistic pair, int128/uint128 accumulator pair, uint64 kappa plus trend plus block number), which took the per-sampled-block cost to about 96k gas including the trace event. The int128 downcasts are safe because sMax <= int128.max is enforced at construction and the EWMA is bounded by the lnWad domain over (1 - lambda). THE ARCHITECTURAL TRICK WORTH STEALING. All detector logic lives in one pure view, _projectDetector. The swap path calls it and persists the result; previewSpread and previewDetector expose the same projection read-only; the Lens quotes through those. Because the Lens sees the projected once-per-block sample the next swap would take, a quote taken in a fresh block before anyone has swapped still matches execution to the wei. One function, so the two paths cannot drift. THE THING WE GOT WRONG FIRST. The brief called for direction-dependent curve depth. We built it, then found a concrete buy-shallow / sell-deep round trip that drains the pool, because depth asymmetry moves the mid-price rather than just the spread. The shipped design puts the asymmetry in the slope instead: a non-negative directional spread on a single symmetric base, which is unprofitable to round-trip by construction. The deep symmetric base also has two obvious parameterisations that are both unsafe (offsets recomputed from current reserves are drainable in two swaps; fixed absolute offsets shift the mid on every ratio deposit), so offsets are anchored at the first deposit and scale only with LP share supply. BUILT THIS HACKATHON: THE OFF-CHAIN PORT. The Detector Lab needed an exact TypeScript reimplementation of three Solidity libraries. Everything is BigInt in WAD, mulDiv floors like FullMath and only ever touches non-negative magnitudes with signs reapplied, and every clamp and >= vs > is copied verbatim, because boundary cases are where a reimplementation silently drifts. It reproduces the live trace with zero wei of deviation across 362 real blocks, verified against a committed fixture in CI. HACKY BITS AND REAL BUGS FOUND. toWad used toFixed(18), which prints a float's BINARY expansion: (0.07).toFixed(18) is "0.070000000000000007", so parameters arrived several wei off. Fixed by going through the shortest round-tripping decimal string with exponent forms expanded by hand. The detector runs on price = reserve1/reserve0 while the UI charts USDC/WETH, so the hook's "up" is a falling chart. The inversion is confined to one constant and one boundary, and the replay works in hook orientation so it can be diffed against raw event data. detector_samples stores numerics for charting, and an 18-decimal value loses its low digits through a JS float. Wei-exact parity was impossible until we added a nullable jsonb column carrying the event's raw integers as decimal strings, with the reader falling back to floats for older rows. The DetectorSample event carries D and sigma-hat but not the EWMA accumulators, so the replay seeds them by inverting those two. Exact for ewmaTV, exact in magnitude for ewmaNet, with only the sign inferred. Enabling adaptive mode against a pool deployed with sigmaFloor = 0 divided by zero on a cold start, which is a configuration the hook's own constructor would refuse. Two clicks from a white screen; now guarded at both ends. supabase-js turns any non-2xx edge-function response into a FunctionsHttpError and leaves the JSON body unread on the Response, so a real error message surfaced as "returned a non-2xx status code". We read it off error.context. Gemini 3.x reasons before answering and those thought tokens count against maxOutputTokens, so a budget sized for three sentences got spent on reasoning and truncated the reply mid-word. Raised the ceiling, and now reject any candidate whose finishReason isn't STOP so a truncated answer can never reach the cache. The narration cache had no invalidation path, so one bad answer would be served forever. Keys are now namespaced by a CACHE_VERSION constant. TESTING. 131 Foundry tests plus 40 TypeScript. Two invariant flavours (plain and full-feature) at 128k randomised calls each with zero reverts, asserting ghost-accounting equality to the wei and that the constant-product invariant never decreases. Manipulation sims run end-to-end against the real PoolManager: a fake-trend round trip loses money, a single-block flash spike moves the detector by exactly zero, and a sigma-inflation attack on the adaptive mode burns value every block. The 12-month study forks Sepolia and replays real Binance closes through three pools. Its equal-friction assertion is the reason our headline number is honest: the first run tripped it at 28.5%, catching that we were spending 40% more of our traders' money than the baseline we were claiming to beat. No oracle, AVS, keeper, relayer or cross-chain dependency, because the detector's entire security argument is that its only input is the pool's own price. The hackathon work uses Supabase (Postgres + Edge Functions) as the backend and the Gemini API for narration, with the key held as an edge-function secret since anything a Vite app can read at runtime ships in the bundle.

projects.title: VaultRadar
projects.description: Cross-protocol vault risk, sold per request to autonomous agents over x402
projects.project_description:
VaultRadar is a machine-payable, cross-protocol vault-risk service. One standardized Graph query template per schema family runs across every Messari-schema deployment in its registry: fifteen registrations over ten protocols and five chains. Alongside it is a new ERC-4626 Substreams module written in Rust, composed from Pinax's erc4626 package and shipped to two chains from one WASM binary.
Risk reports are sold per request over x402, on Hedera through Blocky402 and on Arc through Circle Gateway's batcher. projects.title: Re-Solver
projects.description: Self-resolving prediction market where AI agents price questions no oracle can settle
projects.project_description:
Prediction markets and oracles only work when someone can eventually report the true answer. A huge class of useful questions never gets that moment: "Is this protocol's TVL growth organic or incentive farming?", "Do these wallets belong to one actor?", "Will this DAO proposal actually help the treasury?". The evidence is public on chain, but no oracle will ever settle them, so no market can pay anyone for being right. Re-solver is a working implementation of "Self-Resolving Prediction Markets for Unverifiable Outcomes" by Srinivasan, Karger and Chen (Yiling Chen, Harvard). The market resolves against itself. AI agents report a probability one at a time, and each one sees every earlier report. After every report the market closes with probability alpha, and the last agent becomes the reference. Everyone before it is paid with a cross-entropy market scoring rule against that reference: moving the price toward where it closed earns money, moving it away loses part of your bond. Because nobody knows when the market will stop, reporting your honest belief is the best strategy. Copying the previous agent earns exactly zero (Theorem 7), and the asker's total cost is provably capped by the deposit. How a market works: An asker opens a market from a browser wallet and pays a deposit over x402 on Hedera. The deposit is the paper's cost bound (b·log2 + k·R), and whatever the market does not spend is refunded. Registered agents discover the market and each pays its own bond over x402 from its own Hedera key. No API keys, no accounts. Each round, an agent is drawn, buys its evidence from Messari standardized subgraphs on The Graph, reasons over it with an LLM and signs a probability. Every report is written to Hedera Consensus Service. The stopping dice come from the running hash of the report just written, so nobody, including the operator, can predict when the market closes, and anyone can recompute it from a public mirror node. Settlement is recorded on HCS, then paid out in HBAR. Books close to the tinybar. Each agent's track record is written to its own ENSv2 name. Per-record permissions let an agent edit its profile but never its own score. Everything runs on Hedera testnet and Ethereum Sepolia with real payments: 20 agents, full markets with x402 deposits and bonds, HCS audit trail and on-chain settlement, all independently verified from the mirror node. The repo includes 760 offline tests and a README that maps every claim to on-chain evidence. How it's made
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm): a pure mechanism package, Hedera, Graph and ENS packages, an Express API with orchestrator and settlement engine, an agent runtime, and a Vite + React frontend. 760 unit tests run offline in about 10 seconds. 6. Each agent's track record is written to its own ENSv2 name. Per-record permissions let an agent edit its profile but never its own score. projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm): a pure mechanism package, Hedera, Graph and ENS packages, an Express API with orchestrator and settlement engine, an agent runtime, and a Vite + React frontend. 760 unit tests run offline in about 10 seconds. Mechanism. The scoring rule, market state machine and settlement were written straight from the paper and enforce its hard constraints in code: the reference is always the terminal agent (a rolling reference creates unbounded payouts, Theorem 8), reports are clipped to [0.01, 0.99], each agent joins a market once, the order is drawn lazily and never published, and a timeout is slashed but never counts as a round. Settlement asserts the telescoping budget bound and that money in equals money out. We hit one real design problem: capping losses at the bond during settlement breaks telescoping and the asker's guarantee. So the bond became a position limit instead: an agent can only move the price as far as its bond can cover, clipped when the report arrives. A small calculator also implements Theorems 1 and 4 to show how large k should be. Hedera. Three paid routes (open a market, post a bond, buy a resolved answer) use @x402/express with the Hedera exact scheme through the Blocky402 facilitator on testnet. The deposit is priced per request by the same function settlement checks against. Agents pay their own bonds with @x402/fetch and their own keys. The browser pays through Hedera WalletConnect: we reimplemented the x402 signer so the wallet signs a partially signed transfer without submitting it. HCS is both the ordered report ledger and the randomness source: the stop roll reads bytes 0-7 and the agent draw reads bytes 8-15 of the SHA-384 running hash (reusing the same bytes would make part of the pool unreachable), keeping the top 53 bits so the value never rounds to 1.0. Settlement is written to HCS before any transfer, chunked because of Hedera's per-transaction account limit, and resumable without paying a chunk twice. Hacky but important: @x402/express runs the handler before settling payment, and in a live run two agents joined without paying. We now undo a paid route's effect before the 402 response is written. The Graph. Agents read Messari standardized subgraphs through the Graph gateway (Curve as subject, SushiSwap, Bancor V3, Saddle and Uniswap V2 as peers, the Arbitrum bridge). Five data slices (liquidity, holders, activity, bridge, comparative) turn raw rows into derived statistics. The standard schema is what makes the comparative slice possible: one query string sent unchanged to five protocols built by different teams. No two agents hold the same subset of slices, because the paper requires agents' signals to be conditionally independent, and a test enforces it. The gateway client treats any GraphQL error array as a failure (the gateway returns auth errors with HTTP 200) and includes an x402 client that decodes the 402 challenge from the payment-required header. ENSv2 (Sepolia). We deployed our own UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver proxies from ENSv2's VerifiableFactory under unverifiable.eth and minted agent-01 to agent-20. Agent Hedera accounts use ECDSA secp256k1 keys, so the same key pays bonds, signs reports and owns the ENS name. Names are minted with roleBitmap = 0, so an agent cannot swap its resolver, transfer or delete its name. Resolver permissions are granted per text key, so the agent can write description or endpoint but not score.*. We proved every rule on Sepolia with one test name before minting twenty. Registration checks on chain that an agent owns the ENS name it claims, and after every settlement the orchestrator writes each agent's record in one multicall. Contract addresses came from the contracts-v2 deployment artifacts, because the docs addresses did not match Sepolia. Agents use OpenAI gpt-4o-mini with strict JSON output behind a one-function interface. Development was assisted by Claude Code, and the spec, roadmap and step log are in the repo.

projects.title: AmberMarket
projects.description: AmberMarket turns real-time junction traffic data into verifiable on-chain prediction markets.
projects.project_description:
The problem AmberMarket solves
AmberMarket – Every signal is a market
The Problem It Solves
Every signal is a market. Every junction is an asset. AmberMarket transforms real-world traffic data into on-chain prediction markets grounded in something measurable, verifiable, and live: how many vehicles cross a junction during a single green-light window. No abstract outcomes. No human referees. Just a CV oracle watching actual CCTV streams and settling bets automatically. What you can do with AmberMarket: Stake on live traffic — Place $AMBER bets on real-time junction vehicle counts, settled by a YOLO-powered computer vision oracle reading live camera feeds. Transparent, automated, tamper-resistant.
Own a junction — Mint an AmberJunctionNFT to claim ownership of a real-world intersection and earn royalties every time others bet on your junction.
Get a Web3 identity — Claim a free .ambermarket.eth ENS subname and appear across leaderboards and live markets with a human-readable name.
Trust the machine, not the middleman — Smart contracts hold all funds; the oracle provides the count; winners are paid by tolerance (e.g. +-15% or exact). Zero manual intervention.
The stack in one line: Real-time CV data + on-chain prediction markets + automated oracle settlement + ENS identity, all wired together in a single hackathon build. Challenges we ran into
Challenges We Ran Into Bridging Python CV and a Node backend
The vehicle-counting pipeline runs on Python (YOLO + OpenCV), while the rest of the stack is Node.js + Socket.io. Rather than splitting into two long-running services, we spawn the CV pipeline as a subprocess and consume JSON lines from stdout, keeping the server single-process while still streaming live counts to clients. Getting clean shutdown, timeouts, and graceful fallbacks (a "fake mode" for when YOLO is not installed) took a few iterations to get right. ENS subnames via Namespace
We wanted free .ambermarket.eth identities with no gas cost for users. The Namespace offchain manager requires domain-scoped API keys, something we discovered the hard way after hitting repeated 401s with a default key. Switching to domainApiKeys: { [ENS_PARENT_NAME]: NAMESPACE_API_KEY } fixed it. We also added rate-limiting (10-minute claim cooldown) and proper UI differentiation between "subname not found" and "API unavailable" for a cleaner demo experience. Taming real CCTV streams
Caltrans D3 HLS streams are not framed for lane-level counting. They capture wide scenes with sidewalks, adjacent lanes, and irrelevant zones. We introduced a per-junction viewport config (e.g. 0.30,0.40,0.70,0.90) so the CV model only counts within a defined region of the frame. This meaningfully reduced false positives and made counts accurate enough to actually settle bets on. Phase loop and frontend sync
The server drives a strict market cycle: RED_OPEN > GREEN_COUNTING > SETTLING, broadcast over Socket.io. Keeping the client's countdown timers, bet-open/closed states, and settlement modals in sync with backend phase (and on-chain state when the oracle is active) required a single authoritative source of truth and clearly named events, so the UI never showed "Place Bet" after the market had already locked.

projects.title: Envelope
projects.description: Confidential payroll on Arc: computed in a Chainlink enclave, approved via Privy
projects.project_description: Envelope pays employees in USDC on Arc without ever putting the payroll table onchain. Employer HR data, including employees, salaries, hours, leave, performance multipliers, and compensation policy, is fetched over confidential HTTP inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. Payroll is computed inside the enclave and committed to a Merkle tree. Only four values leave it: the period, Merkle root, batch total, and recipient count. The backend proposes the root and total to PayrollDisburser. Funds require two independent controls: EIP-712 approvals from registered approvers, followed by a Privy server wallet secured by a 2-of-2 authorization-key quorum. Below the approval threshold, no transaction is built. Each employee gets a private claim link with only their payroll line and Merkle proof. Their payment becomes public when claimed, but the rest of the payroll table never does. Envelope is deployed on Arc testnet with the full lifecycle tested. The mainnet address is fixed via CREATE2, and a single command runs 16 local verification checks with no accounts or funding.
projects.how_its_made: The enclave is a TypeScript CRE workflow registered with handlerInTee. Secrets come from the Vault DON at use, HR data is fetched through confidential HTTP, payroll is computed in integer micro-USDC math, and the result is returned to the backend through a third HTTP call. Capabilities are restricted to exactly those three calls, preventing a tampered workflow from adding another. The backend rebuilds the Merkle proofs from its own payroll table and accepts the result only when the enclave root matches. The employer already knows its payroll; the enclave protects that data from node operators and the chain. Since Arc does not yet have a CRE Forwarder, the enclave computes and the backend submits the transaction. The stack is a Next.js app with viem, an ops CLI, and a Solidity contract using OpenZeppelin MerkleProof and ECDSA, claim bitmaps, relayable claims, and CREATE2 deployment through the canonical deployer. Privy handles both signing paths: secp256k1 embedded wallets for approvers and P-256 authorization keys for the server wallet quorum. createViemAccount from @privy-io/node plugs the quorum wallet into the existing viem flow. The rough edges are documented too. The CRE simulator drops config during preHook, preventing restricted workflows from completing simulation, so we reproduced and reported it and maintain a control run without that restriction. The simulator also requires a real PTY and window size, so a small Python driver runs it unattended. The only mocked component is the employer HR system, since real salary data is obviously unavailable.

Privy handles both signing paths: secp256k1 embedded wallets for approvers and P-256 authorization keys for the server wallet quorum. createViemAccount from @privy-io/node plugs the quorum wallet into the existing viem flow.

The rough edges are documented too. The CRE simulator drops config during preHook, preventing restricted workflows from completing simulation, so we reproduced and reported it and maintain a control run without that restriction. The simulator also requires a real PTY and window size, so a small Python driver runs it unattended. The only mocked component is the employer HR system, since real salary data is obviously unavailable.

projects.title: Index-Fi
projects.description: Onchain RWA index vaults: deposit USDC, get one share for diversified stock exposure.
projects.project_description:
IndexFi is a prototype for turning tokenized stock exposure into a single onchain primitive. Instead of manually buying and managing multiple RWA assets one by one, users deposit USDC into a basket vault and receive one vault share token that represents proportional exposure to the full index.
For the MVP, we built an “AI Leaders” basket (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL, AMD, TSM) with target weights and live NAV/share accounting. The app lets users deposit, withdraw, and track portfolio value while also showing drift between target and current basket weights. A manager can trigger rebalancing to restore allocations.
The core thesis is simple: move from “tokenized single assets” to “tokenized programmable portfolios” that are composable with DeFi rails.
projects.how_its_made:
We built the protocol side in Solidity with Foundry and deployed it on a local Anvil chain for fast iteration. The contract stack includes: mock RWA ERC-20 tokens, a mock oracle for pricing, a basket vault with ERC-4626-style share accounting, a factory to create vaults, and a rebalancer entrypoint.
On the frontend, we migrated from Vite to Next.js (App Router) and wired wallet/auth + contract interaction using Privy, wagmi, and viem. Privy handles embedded/external wallet onboarding; wagmi + viem handle reads/writes for deposit, withdraw, approvals, manager checks, and rebalance actions.
One hacky but useful move: we kept the whole flow reproducible locally (contracts + UI) with deterministic Anvil deployment addresses and env-based wiring, so judges can run everything end-to-end without external infrastructure. We also intentionally used simulated RWAs/oracles to focus on protocol UX and basket mechanics before adding compliance-heavy real-world issuance layers.

projects.title: Mercury
projects.description: A USDC wallet built around identity, not addresses. Any chain, no gas, ~5 seconds.
projects.project_description: Mercury is a self-custodial iOS wallet (Expo / React Native, Rust signing core) that makes paying in USDC feel like sending a message: you pay a name, not an address; you never bridge and claim; and you never buy a gas token first. Circle Gateway and Arc are what make that literally true rather than a tagline. One balance, no bridge. USDC is held as a single Circle Gateway balance rather than a dozen per-chain pots. You deposit once — approve, deposit into GatewayWallet, on whichever chain you already hold funds — and it is spendable on every Gateway chain in the wallet's registry (sixteen Circle domains: ten testnet, six mainnet). There is no bridge, no claim, no wrapped asset and no per-transfer wait, because the finality was paid for at deposit time. A send is an EIP-712 burn intent naming the destination and recipient, signed on the device, attested by Circle, and minted on the destination by our relayer. Measured end to end: attested in 1.2s, minted in 1.0s, with the recipient holding no gas token on the destination chain. Settlement on Arc. Arc is the settlement chain, and USDC is its native gas token — so a balance there pays its own fees and the wallet never has to tell anyone to go buy ETH before they can spend what they were just paid. It is also the fastest door into the balance: Arc reaches finality in about half a second, against 13–19 minutes on the Ethereum-finality chains (Base, Arbitrum, OP, Unichain, World Chain), which is why every testnet deposit routes through Arc rather than through the "obvious" L2. Spending is instant regardless of where the money was deposited, so the only thing the deposit chain changes is how long the top-up takes to land — and we route on that number instead of on familiarity. On mainnet, Gateway lists no Arc domain yet, so mainnet settles through Polygon: 8s finality and the cheapest domain to spend from, ~$0.0015 of gas per transfer against $1.00 on Ethereum. Money is never stranded mid-flight. Handing an attestation to a relayer is safe by construction — Circle signs it and names the recipient inside the signature, so the relayer cannot redirect, alter or skim it; its only power is whether to submit. What it can do is fail to submit, so the app checks deliverability before it signs: destinations the relayer cannot pay out on are refused, not offered, because a burn cannot be recalled once Circle accepts it. The signed claim is written to disk before the relay is attempted, so a dropped mint is retried rather than lost. We also shipped the unglamorous half of the door — withdrawing from Gateway back onto one chain takes seven days, and readiness is never guessed from block heights (on Arbitrum an in-contract block.number is an L1 approximation while eth_blockNumber is L2 — a bug that would be days wrong on exactly one chain). We eth_call the withdrawal instead: it reverts until the contract's own clock says it is ready. Identity. Every user gets name.mercurywallet.eth — real ENS, not a database row. We wrote and deployed MercuryNameRegistry.sol (Sepolia, 0xe6967ac719caa21ee46d62ceafa9969f96e9252d) and set it as the resolver on our parent name, so every subname is answered on-chain through ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution. One record holds the owner's EVM, Solana and Bitcoin addresses plus a preferred chain — the routing hint that tells a Gateway send where to land — so a single name routes payments on all three. Claiming is sponsored by our hub, so a brand-new wallet with a zero balance can get a name before it has ever received money. No server sits behind it: any ENS-aware wallet resolves these names, and they keep resolving if every machine we run disappears. Data: The Graph. Balances and history come from The Graph — the Token API for the major EVM mainnets, and our own subgraph for Arc, which indexes native USDC and EURC transfers because nothing else indexes Arc at all. Both are proxied through our hub, so no provider key ships in the app bundle. Also in the app. Per-payment stealth addresses (ERC-5564) for private receiving — and Arc is the first chain where that closes end to end, because a note there pays its own gas out, so the consolidating sweep that would tie every note back to one identity is never needed. Cross-chain atomic swaps (Garden on testnet including Bitcoin testnet4; Flashnet Orchestra on mainnet). Uniswap V2 to turn a non-USDC balance into a depositable one. A dApp browser with WalletConnect. A spoof-resistant token registry where a curated seed always beats a downloaded list. Multi-account BIP-32 wallets across EVM, Solana and Bitcoin. Custody. All keys and all signing live in a Rust core on the phone, behind iOS keychain classes that delete the recovery phrase if the passcode is removed and require biometric auth at the OS level rather than in app code. The hub is one small Node service with exactly three jobs — relay Gateway mints, sponsor ENS names, proxy The Graph — holding a gas-only key bounded by an on-disk spend ledger denominated in ETH with a gas-price ceiling. It never sees a user key and never holds user funds; kill it and the wallet still holds keys, shows balances and sends transactions.
projects.how_its_made:
The stack. Expo / React Native (TypeScript, expo-router) for the iOS app; a Rust signing core exposed as a React Native turbo module for every key and every signature; Solidity for MercuryNameRegistry; a small Hono/Node service ("the hub") in Docker; an AssemblyScript subgraph on The Graph. The app talks to chains over raw JSON-RPC through one hand-rolled eth layer (ethCall / sendCall / waitForReceipt) rather than a full client library — the whole EVM surface this wallet needs is about six methods, and hand-encoding calldata kept the bundle small and the failure modes visible. viem is used on the hub, where bundle size does not matter. There is no stub for the signing core: without the native module linked, the app refuses to bundle. A wallet that starts without its signer would be worse than one that will not start. Arc
Arc is the settlement chain, and building on it produced most of the interesting engineering in this project, because USDC being the native gas coin changes things that are normally invariants. Everything below we observed against the live chain; it is all written up in FEEDBACK.md with the commands that produced it. USDC is the native coin AND an ERC-20, at two different scales. eth_getBalance returns 18dp; balanceOf(0x3600…) returns 6dp; they are the same money. Measured at one block: 10.191319965 native against 10.191319 ERC-20. A naive wallet shows the user two balances for one pot — and a wallet that sweeps "all your USDC" as an ERC-20 has just spent its own gas.
Two Transfer emitters, and the native one is a superset. A plain value send emits one log from 0xffff…fffe. An ERC-20 transfer() emits from BOTH 0xffff…fffe and 0x3600…. We built the subgraph against the ERC-20 contract first and lost every native send; indexing both double-counts. The fix — index the native emitter alone and scale 18dp → 6dp in the handler — we only found by sending one of each and counting logs. It is the highest-risk thing about indexing Arc and it is documented nowhere.
Gas is cheap enough to stop designing around. Measured gas price 21.2 gwei in USDC: a transfer is 0.00045 USDC, an approve 0.00127. So we approve the exact amount being spent instead of the customary unlimited allowance — a trade nobody makes on a chain where approvals cost real money.
Because gas IS the asset, we reserve 0.25 USDC (about fifty transactions) and enforce it at the point of sweeping, not by asking the user to remember. There is no second token to fall back on.
UniswapV2Router02.WETH() on the Arc deployment points at an address with no code, so every ETH-path helper reverts with nothing useful. We use swapExactTokensForTokens exclusively.
Arc is also the reason private receiving works at all. A per-payment ERC-5564 stealth address elsewhere is money that cannot move without a gas top-up that deanonymises the recipient. On Arc the note pays its own way out, so we never sweep, and the consolidating transaction that would link every note back to one identity is never created. Circle Gateway sits on top: one unified USDC balance, spendable across sixteen Circle domains with no bridge and nothing to claim. Three hacks worth naming. (a) The transfer fee is not knowable up front — maxFee must be inside the signed intent, and Circle only prices it in answer to one. So we submit once with a deliberately low fee to READ the quote out of the rejection ("expected at least 0.0035, got 0.000001"), then re-sign at that exact price: one extra round trip, ~280ms, and an exact fee instead of a guess. (b) burnIntentExpirationHeight from /v1/info is the current height and is already stale by the time you have signed; we add a 1000-block buffer. (c) The Gateway API and the GatewayWallet contract lag in OPPOSITE directions — the contract sees a fresh deposit the block it mines but still counts an attested burn; the API is the reverse. Measured simultaneously they disagreed by $3.00 on $18.72, and both were right about different things. So the contract answers "what do I own", the API answers "what can I spend", and burns our own client issued are discounted locally until the contract catches up. Withdrawal readiness is never computed either: withdrawalDelay() is in the chain's own blocks, and on Arbitrum an in-contract block.number is an L1 approximation while eth_blockNumber is L2, so we eth_call the withdrawal and let it revert until the contract's own clock says yes. The Graph
Two Graph products composed into one portfolio, over live data, because neither one covers this wallet alone. Token API for the major EVM mainnets — balances and transfers, eight networks. Our own subgraph for Arc, because the Token API rejects network=arc-testnet outright, Arc is Studio-only on the decentralized network (support level basic, issuanceRewards: false, no Substreams), and Arc has no Blockscout instance either. A subgraph is the only way to see Arc history at all, so we wrote one: two data sources (the native USDC emitter, and EURC as an ordinary 6dp ERC-20, which the native emitter does not mirror), an immutable Transfer entity keyed txHash-logIndex so the indexer can skip load-before-write, and a mutable Account entity carrying running sent/received/txCount totals so history questions do not have to page every transfer. Amounts are normalised to 6dp minor units in the handler regardless of which emitter produced them. Two field notes that cost us time: on the free tier a Token API limit above 10 does not clamp, it returns ZERO rows — so an activity feed asking for 25 renders as "no transactions" rather than erroring, the worst possible failure mode. We page at 10. And the server_-prefixed key authenticates with X-Api-Key, not Authorization: Bearer, contrary to the docs we were reading; the JWT does use Bearer. Both products are proxied through the hub's /index route rather than called from the app. EXPO_PUBLIC_* is inlined into the bundle at build time and recoverable from the app package, so a provider key there is handed to everyone who downloads the app and billed to us — ERC-7677 gives exactly this advice for paymaster keys and it applies unchanged here. The proxy forwards a fixed set of shapes with validated parameters; one that passed arbitrary paths through with our key attached would have moved the credential rather than protected it. ENS
Every user gets name.mercurywallet.eth as a real ENS name. We deployed MercuryNameRegistry.sol to Sepolia (0xe6967ac719caa21ee46d62ceafa9969f96e9252d) and set it as the RESOLVER on our parent name, so under ENSv2 every subname beneath it arrives as resolve(name, data) via ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution — no per-name registry entry, no subregistry, records living in this contract's storage. One record holds the owner, the 0x address (coinType 60, which covers Arc, Base, Arbitrum and every other EVM chain at once from one secp256k1 key), a Solana address and a Bitcoin address as ENSIP-9 addr(node, coinType) records, and a preferred-chain hint that tells a Gateway send where to land. Lookups go through ENSv2's UpgradableUniversalResolverProxy (0xeEeE…EeEe, the same address on mainnet and Sepolia, so it needs no per-environment config), with DNS wire-format names encoded by hand. We implemented EIP-3668 CCIP-Read ourselves, including the x-batch-gateway:true pseudo-URL — the Universal Resolver offers its own hosted batch gateway, and we chose to unpack the batch and fetch each inner gateway ourselves instead. That removes a third party from the path of every lookup and stops leaking which names our users type into someone else's server. The deliberate trade: on-chain records cost one transaction per name, where offchain CCIP-Read names are free but put an HTTP service on the critical path of every lookup forever. We took the transaction, and then removed it from the user — the hub sponsors registration, so a zero-balance wallet can claim a name before it has ever received money. The sponsor is the payer and never the owner: the caller signs a message naming the label and every address in it, the registration is made out to the RECOVERED signer rather than to any address in the request body, and we only sponsor a name pointing at the signer's own address (paying to publish an address nobody proved they hold is how you fund a phishing campaign). One sponsored name per address, plus a daily ceiling, both bounded by an on-disk ETH-denominated spend ledger with a gas-price ceiling — counting operations does not bound cost. Honorable mention: Uniswap
Uniswap V2 is what turns a non-USDC balance into a depositable one: if you hold something else on the chain you want to fund from, we quote and swap to USDC on that same chain first, then deposit. Same-chain by design — Circle credits a deposit made on any domain to the one balance, so there is never a reason to move funds across chains before depositing. The V2 router on Arc is also where the WETH()-with-no-code finding above came from; our FEEDBACK.md carries it. The rest of the hacky bits
The app checks deliverability before it signs a burn, because a burn cannot be recalled once Circle accepts it. Destinations the relayer cannot pay out on are refused rather than offered, and the signed claim is written to disk before the relay is attempted so a dropped mint is retried rather than lost.
Block-explorer history has a keyless Blockscout first path and an Etherscan V2 fallback — of 22 supported testnets only 5 had a reachable history source when we checked. The fallback learns which chains the key's plan covers from the upstream's own refusals ("Free API access is not supported for this chain") rather than hard-coding a free-tier list that is wrong for anyone who pays and stale the day Etherscan moves a chain between tiers.
The token registry ships a curated seed that a downloaded list can never overwrite. Against CoinGecko's list the guard drops a "UNI" that is really UNICORN and an "ETH" that is really The Infinite Garden — an ERC-20 wearing the native coin's ticker.
The recovery phrase lives under iOS's WHEN_PASSCODE_SET_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY with requireAuthentication, so it is excluded from every backup and device-to-device restore, cannot be written on a device with no passcode, and is DELETED if the passcode is removed. The biometric gate is the keychain refusing to return bytes, not a JavaScript if that can fail open.
One hub process, not two: the mint relayer and the name sponsor spend the same key against the same ledger, with in-flight reservations held in memory so concurrent requests cannot each pass a check none of them could afford together. Two containers would mean two ledgers that cannot see each other. It runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, tini as PID 1, and /app/data as the only writable path.

We implemented EIP-3668 CCIP-Read ourselves, including the x-batch-gateway:true pseudo-URL — the Universal Resolver offers its own hosted batch gateway, and we chose to unpack the batch and fetch each inner gateway ourselves instead. That removes a third party from the path of every lookup and stops leaking which names our users type into someone else's server.

The deliberate trade: on-chain records cost one transaction per name, where offchain CCIP-Read names are free but put an HTTP service on the critical path of every lookup forever. We took the transaction, and then removed it from the user — the hub sponsors registration, so a zero-balance wallet can claim a name before it has ever received money. The sponsor is the payer and never the owner: the caller signs a message naming the label and every address in it, the registration is made out to the RECOVERED signer rather than to any address in the request body, and we only sponsor a name pointing at the signer's own address (paying to publish an address nobody proved they hold is how you fund a phishing campaign). One sponsored name per address, plus a daily ceiling, both bounded by an on-disk ETH-denominated spend ledger with a gas-price ceiling — counting operations does not bound cost.

Honorable mention: Uniswap
Uniswap V2 is what turns a non-USDC balance into a depositable one: if you hold something else on the chain you want to fund from, we quote and swap to USDC on that same chain first, then deposit. Same-chain by design — Circle credits a deposit made on any domain to the one balance, so there is never a reason to move funds across chains before depositing. The V2 router on Arc is also where the WETH()-with-no-code finding above came from; our FEEDBACK.md carries it.

The rest of the hacky bits
The app checks deliverability before it signs a burn, because a burn cannot be recalled once Circle accepts it. Destinations the relayer cannot pay out on are refused rather than offered, and the signed claim is written to disk before the relay is attempted so a dropped mint is retried rather than lost.
Block-explorer history has a keyless Blockscout first path and an Etherscan V2 fallback — of 22 supported testnets only 5 had a reachable history source when we checked. The fallback learns which chains the key's plan covers from the upstream's own refusals ("Free API access is not supported for this chain") rather than hard-coding a free-tier list that is wrong for anyone who pays and stale the day Etherscan moves a chain between tiers.
The token registry ships a curated seed that a downloaded list can never overwrite. Against CoinGecko's list the guard drops a "UNI" that is really UNICORN and an "ETH" that is really The Infinite Garden — an ERC-20 wearing the native coin's ticker.
The recovery phrase lives under iOS's WHEN_PASSCODE_SET_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY with requireAuthentication, so it is excluded from every backup and device-to-device restore, cannot be written on a device with no passcode, and is DELETED if the passcode is removed. The biometric gate is the keychain refusing to return bytes, not a JavaScript if that can fail open.
One hub process, not two: the mint relayer and the name sponsor spend the same key against the same ledger, with in-flight reservations held in memory so concurrent requests cannot each pass a check none of them could afford together. Two containers would mean two ledgers that cannot see each other. It runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, tini as PID 1, and /app/data as the only writable path.

projects.title: Pool Party
projects.description: Pool Party: Cash+ for business treasuries and hookrisk for Uniswap v4 hook security.
projects.project_description:
Pool Party connects investment strategy managers with investors through rules enforced by smart contracts. For this continuity submission, we added two products to the platform: Cash+ and hookrisk.
Cash+ is a business treasury investment strategy that combines two sources of return: lending interest on Aave and margins from stablecoin conversions. Eligible capital earns interest while waiting for conversion opportunities. When a conversion takes place, the strategy releases the required liquidity and retains the margin for investors, subject to price, volume and exposure limits. Businesses deposit USDC, track performance and request withdrawals from a dedicated page.
Hookrisk helps managers evaluate Uniswap v4 hooks before opening a position. Hooks are smart contracts that can change a pool’s fees and transaction behavior. They can also introduce undeclared charges, prevent withdrawals or expose callbacks to unauthorized callers.
Integrated into Pool Party’s Tools menu, hookrisk provides findings with references to the affected source files and lines. It also identifies dimensions it could not measure, without treating missing information as an absence of risk. Managers gain evidence for selecting hooks, and investors receive an assessment they can independently inspect.
projects.how_its_made:
We extended Pool Party’s existing frontend using Next.js, React, TypeScript and viem, preserving the platform’s visual design.
For Cash+, Solidity contracts account for deposits, investor shares and withdrawals. Adapters supply eligible assets to Aave, while 1inch Aqua and SwapVM execute stablecoin conversions. A custom pricing extension applies the conversion margin and checks the strategy’s limits using Chainlink price feeds.
The integration withdraws assets from Aave within the same transaction that settles a conversion. Capital can therefore earn interest until it is needed for settlement. If any step fails, the entire conversion reverts. An automated operator manages lending allocations, liquidity buffers and orders.
For hookrisk, we combined Python detectors built on Slither, a TypeScript scoring engine and Solidity tests using Foundry. The tests use Uniswap’s actual v4-core to compare two otherwise equivalent pools: one with a hook and one without. This differential testing can detect behavior such as charges exceeding the declared fee and trapped liquidity. The project also provides an optional integration with BlockSec HookScan.
We translated the Uniswap Foundation’s Hooks Security Framework into executable criteria. Reports distinguish measured results, developer declarations and unmeasured dimensions. Hook permissions are generated directly from v4-core, avoiding a manually maintained copy that could become outdated.
We validated Cash+ through Foundry tests and a complete browser journey using Playwright: deposit, conversion, Aave withdrawal and investor redemption on an Arbitrum fork using the protocols’ official contracts.

projects.title: Refusal.eth
projects.description: Deny-by-default spending firewall: prove policy before an agent can sign.
projects.project_description: AI agents can be prompt-injected into unsafe spending when policy is readable context and signing is unconditional. REFUSAL.eth makes refusal the default: an agent identity is resolved, a sealed policy is evaluated, and only an explicit ALLOW receipt can reach a downstream signer. Revocations, allowlist misses, limit breaches, and human denials become named, inspectable refusal proofs instead of silent failures. The public console exposes deterministic allowlist-miss and limit-breach paths, while the repository honesty table separates verified local behavior from sponsor integrations still awaiting live evidence.
projects.how_its_made: The verified build is a Next.js/TypeScript proof surface with viem-based ENS resolution, a Solidity RefusalGateway, and one shared deterministic gate mirrored in the CRE workspace. The contract binds verdicts to deadline and nonce, rejects zero keys and empty names, and prevents case-variant revocation bypasses; parity tests compare the web mirror and canonical gate. The CRE handlerInTee retrieves a sealed policy and private intent inside the TEE, with an official CLI simulation recorded; production deployment is not claimed. Privy remains an adapter boundary until a funded wallet, policy/quorum flow, approval, and Sepolia receipt are evidenced. make verify runs 11 Forge tests, 15 gate assertions, 20/20 parity, ENSv2 checks, and claim auditing.

projects.title: safety
projects.description: ERC-4337 smart wallet owned by a passkey; scoped session keys enable zero-popup transactions
projects.project_description: Every wallet interaction today means a signature prompt, which is fine for a rare high-value transfer but kills UX for anything interactive: games, trading bots, subscriptions. This project is a smart contract wallet (ERC-4337 account abstraction) owned by a passkey (Face ID / Touch ID / Windows Hello) instead of a seed phrase or browser extension. The owner can grant a scoped, time-boxed session key: a lightweight keypair generated in the browser that is only allowed to call one specific contract function, until a set expiry, up to a set number of times. Once granted, the dApp can send a burst of transactions signed by that session key with zero further wallet prompts. We demo this with a tiny on-chain clicker game: create your passkey wallet once, grant a session key once (one more Face ID prompt), then click away with no interruptions, exactly like a Web2 app, while every action is still a real, independently-authorized on-chain transaction.
projects.how_its_made: Built from scratch on top of eth-infinitism's reference ERC-4337 EntryPoint/BaseAccount (v0.6) in Foundry. SmartAccount.sol implements a single IAccount whose signature is a mode byte plus payload: mode 0 verifies a WebAuthn/secp256r1 assertion against the owner passkey public key using base-org/webauthn-sol (RIP-7212 precompile with a FreshCryptoLib fallback); mode 1 checks a plain ECDSA signature from a session key against an on-chain SessionKeyPermission struct (target contract, function selector, validUntil, maxUses) so a session key can never be used outside its granted scope. SmartAccountFactory.sol deploys accounts via CREATE2 for deterministic addresses. A GameContract.sol clicker is the demo target. Four Foundry tests drive the whole flow end-to-end through EntryPoint.handleOps: grant, click, hit the usage cap, reject an out-of-scope call, and revoke. The frontend (Next.js + viem + @simplewebauthn/browser) creates the passkey client-side, parses the COSE public key and DER signature manually to build the on-chain WebAuthnAuth struct, and signs UserOperations with either the passkey (owner actions) or a locally generated session key (gameplay). For demo reliability we relay signed UserOperations straight to EntryPoint.handleOps from a Next.js API route acting as a mock bundler against a local Anvil node, rather than depending on a live bundler network.

projects.title: Agent Grove
projects.description: Agent Grove gives AI agents portable ENS identities with scoped control over live profiles.
projects.project_description: Agent Grove is an ENSv2 identity studio for AI agents on Sepolia. Teams can issue durable subname identities such as researcher.grove.eth, attach an agent wallet, and grant only the profile-record permissions that agent needs—such as its endpoint, capabilities, or operating status. The namespace owner keeps control of the parent namespace while agents can safely keep their own discoverable profiles current. The app also includes a live ENS resolver that verifies names and agent records on Sepolia, making identities portable across wallets, dapps, and agent directories.
projects.how_its_made: Agent Grove is a lightweight browser application built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Viem for Sepolia RPC access, ENS normalization/namehashing, resolver lookups, calldata encoding, and transaction-confirmation handling. It connects to an injected browser wallet and resolves ENS address, resolver, description, and com.agent.endpoint records live. For profile updates, it discovers the active resolver, encodes setText calls, batches them with multicall, and submits the wallet-signed transaction. A Solidity AgentNamespaceRegistrar integrates with ENSv2’s Permissioned Registry, issuing subnames with a constrained role bitmap. ENSv2 Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control enable narrowly scoped record-writing authority without giving agents control of the entire namespace.
