projects.title: attesta
projects.description: Marketplace for trading strategies whose returns are attested inside a TEE, not self-reported
projects.project_description: attesta is a marketplace for automated trading strategies where the track record is attested rather than claimed. The problem it attacks is simple. Anyone can publish a 40% APY. The number is produced by whoever profits from it, and a strategy with a real edge will not reveal the code behind it — so an investor is asked to trust a screenshot. attesta removes the need to trust either side. HOW IT WORKS A creator writes a strategy in TypeScript against a fixed six-function contract (describe, onTick, balanceOf, totalAssets, onDeposit, onWithdraw) and submits it in the browser. The platform compiles it and deploys it as a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, so the strategy's identity becomes its binary hash: binary hash + config hash -> workflow hash, registered on-chain in a StrategyRegistry. Swap the script after building a track record and the hash changes, in public. Creators need no CRE account of their own; the platform deploys under its owner identity, and anyone can recompile the published source and check the hash matches what is registered. When a tick fires, the strategy does not run on a node — it runs inside a TEE (AWS Nitro Enclaves, us-west-2). It fetches prices over HTTP from inside the enclave, reads its creator's parameters as Vault DON secrets that are released only into an attested enclave, and returns a target allocation in basis points. Risk guardrails are evaluated in the enclave too, so the rules stay private while remaining verifiably applied. Strategy parameters never reach the platform in the clear. They are encrypted in the creator's own browser before they leave the machine; the backend relays ciphertext, stores it in a table with no plaintext column, and holds no key that opens it. There is no read-back API at all. So a creator can publish a verifiable track record without revealing the thresholds and signals that produce it — which is the thing that makes a real quant willing to list at all. Investors sign in with a wallet, browse the marketplace, and allocate USDC. Each strategy has its own on-chain vault with ERC-4626 share math. Deposits and withdrawals are signed in the browser and settled on-chain into that vault; the backend records what the transaction receipt says happened, not what the client claims, so a forged or replayed hash records nothing. The strategy page shows NAV per share, the investor's own position series, every trade, every execution log line, total return, max drawdown and — once the history is long enough to state it honestly — APY. WHY THE NUMBERS HOLD Nothing about performance is hardcoded; that is the point of the whole build. Each tick runs the real strategy against a live price series, prices the decision it returned (target weights x price delta since the last tick, minus venue cost in bps), and applies the resulting profit or loss on-chain with vault.applyPnl(int256), which emits PnlApplied. Performance is then read back from the vault's own settlement log — PnlApplied, Deposited, Withdrawn — rather than from a table the backend wrote. The number on the screen is the chain's account of what happened, not the server's, and one getLogs call covers a whole listing. Total return, max drawdown and APY are derived from that series and stored nowhere as inputs. APY is deliberately withheld until the series is long enough to annualise honestly. Annualising twenty minutes of history turns a 1.4% move into a meaningless exponent and turns every loss into exactly -100%, so below that threshold the metric returns null and the card leads with since-inception total return instead. That is a real figure at any span, and it still separates a strategy down 1.4% from one down 13.4%, which saturated annualisation does not. A strategy that picks badly shows a negative return because its weights lost money, not because a field says so. Three seeded strategies — momentum, mean-reversion, and a deliberately bad overtrader that churns itself into fees — demonstrate exactly that, side by side in the same marketplace. The verifiable chain runs end to end: TypeScript workflow -> registered workflow identity -> TEE attestation -> signed reports -> on-chain settlement record -> reported returns. Break any link — a different workflow, a different enclave, an unsigned record — and the performance claim stops verifying. WHAT IS HONEST ABOUT THE LIMITS This build integrates two partner technologies: Chainlink CRE for confidential compute, and Privy for investor onboarding. Settlement is USDC vaults on a local chain, and a strategy's operator — the only account allowed to settle a tick — is a local EOA. Circle Agent Wallets on Arc are the intended production form for that operator, and the design is written against them: one policy-capped wallet per strategy, its control credential held as a Vault secret so only the attested workflow could direct it. That integration is out of scope here and nothing in the demo depends on it. Saying so plainly matters more than the extra logo would. Two further limits. CRE Vault secrets are scoped to the owner rather than to a single workflow, so isolation between creators rests on every workflow under the owner being enumerable and hash-verifiable rather than on the Vault itself. And phase 1 does not audit strategy code — "verified" means "this exact code produced these results", not "this code is safe". All of these are stated in the docs and in the UI rather than glossed over, because a product whose entire claim is verifiability cannot be vague about what is not verified. Everything runs locally against an anvil chain, which is why the demo link points at the repository: ./scripts/dev.sh brings up anvil, deploys the contracts, seeds the marketplace and serves the backend on :4000 and the frontend on :3000.
projects.how_its_made: Five packages in one repo: contracts/ (Foundry), backend/ (Fastify + Drizzle + better-sqlite3 + viem), frontend/ (Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4), chainlink/ (the CRE workflow), and shared/ — two files, types.ts and strategy-contract.ts, that every other layer builds against so the DTOs and the strategy interface can never drift between frontend, backend and enclave. CHAINLINK CRE CONFIDENTIAL WORKFLOWS — the compute layer The workflow is TypeScript against @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18.0, compiled through bun to WASM and driven by the CRE CLI v1.32.0. The cron callback takes a TeeRuntime rather than a Runtime, and that type is what moves execution off the node and into the enclave. Inside it, runtime.getSecret({ id, namespace }) pulls a Vault DON secret that is decrypted at the moment the call runs and only inside an attested enclave, and cre.capabilities.HTTPClient().sendRequest() has a TeeRuntime overload, so the outbound price fetch keeps its request and response payloads confidential from node operators. (ConfidentialHTTPClient is the wrong tool here — it has no TeeRuntime overload and is not meant to be called from a TEE handler; that cost us an afternoon.) Simulation prints "Trigger requested TEE Execution ... AWS Nitro in us-west-2", and that is the only attestation claim this project makes anywhere — no SGX, no MRENCLAVE, no zero-knowledge proofs, in code, copy or docs. Two CRE gotchas worth passing on. @chainlink/cre-sdk declares engines: { bun: ">=1.2.21" }, and on an older bun the workflow still compiles, then dies at engine start with "wasm trap: wasm unreachable instruction executed" rather than a version complaint — the toolchain goes TypeScript -> JavaScript -> WASM through bun, so an old bun silently emits a broken binary. And the CLI does not read .env on its own: without -e .env, simulation fails with a missing-secret error and silently falls back to a default private key. CONTRACTS — Foundry, with unit and invariant tests StrategyVault holds one strategy's capital with ERC-4626 share math, plus applyPnl(int256) and recordTrade(), both restricted to the strategy's operator account, and a reserve prefunded at publish time so a gain is actually payable. The invariant is usdc.balanceOf(vault) >= totalManagedAssets. Four revert cases shaped the whole scheduler, and none of them are visible in the ABI: a gain with no depositors (NoSharesOutstanding — otherwise the next depositor mints 1:1 against zero supply and redeems the stranded amount), a gain larger than the reserve (ReserveExhausted — the vault refuses to promise value it cannot pay), a loss larger than the book (LossExceedsManagedAssets), and settling from the wrong account (NotOperator). So a tick caps its delta at the reserve, caps a loss at totalManagedAssets, and skips settlement rather than losing the tick — the strategy still decides, still records trades and still snapshots NAV, so an unfunded strategy is visibly running rather than silently absent. navPerShare() returns par when totalShares == 0 instead of dividing by zero, so the UI reads NAV as a claim per share and totalShares as the evidence of capital. StrategyRegistry anchors keccak256(strategyId) -> vault + binary hash on-chain; the platform id is a uuid, and the hashing lives in exactly one file with the chain layer taking the bytes32 pre-hashed, so nothing can ever anchor a strategy under keccak(keccak(id)) — a key nothing looks up, with nothing anywhere to report it. THE SUBMISSION PIPELINE — nine stages, in order, first failure stops the rest parses -> required-exports (all six) -> forbidden-imports (and no dynamic import()) -> no-side-effects (no forbidden globals, no top-level statements beyond imports, declarations and exports) -> tsc --noEmit against the shared strategy contract -> describe-valid (metadata and declared assets) -> deterministic (onTick twice on an identical context must return identical output) -> cre workflow build, capturing the binary hash -> cre workflow simulate, yielding a parseable decision. Only after stage nine can a submission publish, which deploys its vault, funds the reserve and registers the measurement. Results stream into the create screen as each stage lands. THE SCHEDULER — where returns actually come from cre workflow simulate fires a cron trigger once and exits; the CLI has no scheduled mode and rejects --listen for cron, so the scheduler owns the interval (60s default, bounded concurrency). Each tick refreshes a seeded, deterministic price oracle, runs the workflow for that strategy, parses the decision, prices the target weights against the price delta since the last tick, charges venue cost in bps on turnover, sends applyPnl and recordTrade from the strategy's operator account, and writes an execution row. The composition root builds one ChainPort and one OraclePort and is called after listen() — because the enclave fetches prices over HTTP from this same process, so the oracle route has to be answering before the first tick can complete. The whole loop (publish, deposit, four ticks, metrics) is proved end to end by a single npm run verify:loop. METRICS — read from the chain, not from our own table Performance is quoted from the vault's own settlement log rather than from a table the backend wrote: lib/chain-metrics.ts reconstructs the NAV series from PnlApplied, Deposited and Withdrawn events and the strategies routes serve that, falling back to the stored snapshots only if a chain read fails. One getLogs covers a whole listing — 63ms cold, 5ms warm. It matters for the product's claim, not just for correctness: the figure on the card is the chain's account of what happened, which is exactly the thing a sceptical investor can independently recompute. lib/metrics.ts is pure — same series in, same value out, no clock, no database — and returns null rather than zero when history is too short, because zero reads as "flat" when the truth is "unknown". APY is the case that bites: annualising wall-clock over a twenty-minute demo turns a +1.4% move into an astronomic exponent and saturates every loss at exactly -100%. So the annualisation window is passed in through the MetricsOptions parameter the module already exposes rather than by editing the module, APY comes back null below it, and StrategyCard falls back to since-inception total return (headline = apy ?? totalReturn, label flipping to SINCE INCEPTION). A real figure at any span beats a saturated one. AUTH AND MONEY — the backend never holds a user key POST /auth/challenge issues a nonce inside a multi-line SIWE-style message whose domain line is derived from CORS_ORIGIN; the browser signs that string verbatim with viem and POST /auth/verify recovers the signer with recoverMessageAddress and compares. Nonces are single-use with a 5-minute TTL. Investing has the same shape: the browser sends approve + deposit itself, waits for receipts, then posts the tx hash, and the backend fetches the receipt, parses the Deposited event and verifies it came from the caller's address and targets this strategy's vault before recording a position. GET /api/chain/config is authoritative for chain id, RPC URL and every contract address — addresses must never live in env, because anvil redeploys move them and a stale .env pointing at a dead address fails in a way that looks exactly like a bug in the contract. CREATOR SECRETS — the part that took the most research The production path is TDH2 threshold encryption performed in the creator's browser against the Vault DON's P256 key, fetched from vault.publicKey.get on the CRE gateway, using Chainlink's own pure-JS TDH2 (src/tdh2.js in @chainlink/functions-toolkit) with the envelope matching the Go implementation field for field. Two things make it non-trivial: the toolkit's exported encrypt() hardcodes an empty label, while CRE requires the label to be the owner address left-padded to 32 bytes, so tdh2.js has to be vendored and the internal tdh2Encrypt called directly; and the gateway returns no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header and fails the OPTIONS preflight, so the browser cannot post to it and the backend has to relay. projects.project_description_markdown:
attesta is a marketplace for automated trading strategies where the track record is attested rather than claimed.

The problem it attacks is simple. Anyone can publish a 40% APY. The number is produced by whoever profits from it, and a strategy with a real edge will not reveal the code behind it — so an investor is asked to trust a screenshot. attesta removes the need to trust either side.

HOW IT WORKS

A creator writes a strategy in TypeScript against a fixed six-function contract (describe, onTick, balanceOf, totalAssets, onDeposit, onWithdraw) and submits it in the browser. The platform compiles it and deploys it as a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, so the strategy's identity becomes its binary hash: binary hash + config hash -> workflow hash, registered on-chain in a StrategyRegistry. Swap the script after building a track record and the hash changes, in public. Creators need no CRE account of their own; the platform deploys under its owner identity, and anyone can recompile the published source and check the hash matches what is registered.

When a tick fires, the strategy does not run on a node — it runs inside a TEE (AWS Nitro Enclaves, us-west-2). It fetches prices over HTTP from inside the enclave, reads its creator's parameters as Vault DON secrets that are released only into an attested enclave, and returns a target allocation in basis points. Risk guardrails are evaluated in the enclave too, so the rules stay private while remaining verifiably applied.

Strategy parameters never reach the platform in the clear. They are encrypted in the creator's own browser before they leave the machine; the backend relays ciphertext, stores it in a table with no plaintext column, and holds no key that opens it. There is no read-back API at all. So a creator can publish a verifiable track record without revealing the thresholds and signals that produce it — which is the thing that makes a real quant willing to list at all.

Investors sign in with a wallet, browse the marketplace, and allocate USDC. Each strategy has its own on-chain vault with ERC-4626 share math. Deposits and withdrawals are signed in the browser and settled on-chain into that vault; the backend records what the transaction receipt says happened, not what the client claims, so a forged or replayed hash records nothing. The strategy page shows NAV per share, the investor's own position series, every trade, every execution log line, total return, max drawdown and — once the history is long enough to state it honestly — APY.

WHY THE NUMBERS HOLD

Nothing about performance is hardcoded; that is the point of the whole build. Each tick runs the real strategy against a live price series, prices the decision it returned (target weights x price delta since the last tick, minus venue cost in bps), and applies the resulting profit or loss on-chain with vault.applyPnl(int256), which emits PnlApplied.

Performance is then read back from the vault's own settlement log — PnlApplied, Deposited, Withdrawn — rather than from a table the backend wrote. The number on the screen is the chain's account of what happened, not the server's, and one getLogs call covers a whole listing. Total return, max drawdown and APY are derived from that series and stored nowhere as inputs.

APY is deliberately withheld until the series is long enough to annualise honestly. Annualising twenty minutes of history turns a 1.4% move into a meaningless exponent and turns every loss into exactly -100%, so below that threshold the metric returns null and the card leads with since-inception total return instead. That is a real figure at any span, and it still separates a strategy down 1.4% from one down 13.4%, which saturated annualisation does not. A strategy that picks badly shows a negative return because its weights lost money, not because a field says so. Three seeded strategies — momentum, mean-reversion, and a deliberately bad overtrader that churns itself into fees — demonstrate exactly that, side by side in the same marketplace.

The verifiable chain runs end to end: TypeScript workflow -> registered workflow identity -> TEE attestation -> signed reports -> on-chain settlement record -> reported returns. Break any link — a different workflow, a different enclave, an unsigned record — and the performance claim stops verifying.

WHAT IS HONEST ABOUT THE LIMITS

This build integrates two partner technologies: Chainlink CRE for confidential compute, and Privy for investor onboarding. Settlement is USDC vaults on a local chain, and a strategy's operator — the only account allowed to settle a tick — is a local EOA. Circle Agent Wallets on Arc are the intended production form for that operator, and the design is written against them: one policy-capped wallet per strategy, its control credential held as a Vault secret so only the attested workflow could direct it. That integration is out of scope here and nothing in the demo depends on it. Saying so plainly matters more than the extra logo would.

Two further limits. CRE Vault secrets are scoped to the owner rather than to a single workflow, so isolation between creators rests on every workflow under the owner being enumerable and hash-verifiable rather than on the Vault itself. And phase 1 does not audit strategy code — "verified" means "this exact code produced these results", not "this code is safe".

All of these are stated in the docs and in the UI rather than glossed over, because a product whose entire claim is verifiability cannot be vague about what is not verified.

Everything runs locally against an anvil chain, which is why the demo link points at the repository: ./scripts/dev.sh brings up anvil, deploys the contracts, seeds the marketplace and serves the backend on :4000 and the frontend on :3000.

Five packages in one repo: contracts/ (Foundry), backend/ (Fastify + Drizzle + better-sqlite3 + viem), frontend/ (Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4), chainlink/ (the CRE workflow), and shared/ — two files, types.ts and strategy-contract.ts, that every other layer builds against so the DTOs and the strategy interface can never drift between frontend, backend and enclave.

CHAINLINK CRE CONFIDENTIAL WORKFLOWS — the compute layer

The workflow is TypeScript against @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18.0, compiled through bun to WASM and driven by the CRE CLI v1.32.0. The cron callback takes a TeeRuntime rather than a Runtime, and that type is what moves execution off the node and into the enclave. Inside it, runtime.getSecret({ id, namespace }) pulls a Vault DON secret that is decrypted at the moment the call runs and only inside an attested enclave, and cre.capabilities.HTTPClient().sendRequest() has a TeeRuntime overload, so the outbound price fetch keeps its request and response payloads confidential from node operators. (ConfidentialHTTPClient is the wrong tool here — it has no TeeRuntime overload and is not meant to be called from a TEE handler; that cost us an afternoon.) Simulation prints "Trigger requested TEE Execution ... AWS Nitro in us-west-2", and that is the only attestation claim this project makes anywhere — no SGX, no MRENCLAVE, no zero-knowledge proofs, in code, copy or docs.

Two CRE gotchas worth passing on. @chainlink/cre-sdk declares engines: { bun: ">=1.2.21" }, and on an older bun the workflow still compiles, then dies at engine start with "wasm trap: wasm unreachable instruction executed" rather than a version complaint — the toolchain goes TypeScript -> JavaScript -> WASM through bun, so an old bun silently emits a broken binary. And the CLI does not read .env on its own: without -e .env, simulation fails with a missing-secret error and silently falls back to a default private key.

CONTRACTS — Foundry, with unit and invariant tests

StrategyVault holds one strategy's capital with ERC-4626 share math, plus applyPnl(int256) and recordTrade(), both restricted to the strategy's operator account, and a reserve prefunded at publish time so a gain is actually payable. The invariant is usdc.balanceOf(vault) >= totalManagedAssets. Four revert cases shaped the whole scheduler, and none of them are visible in the ABI: a gain with no depositors (NoSharesOutstanding — otherwise the next depositor mints 1:1 against zero supply and redeems the stranded amount), a gain larger than the reserve (ReserveExhausted — the vault refuses to promise value it cannot pay), a loss larger than the book (LossExceedsManagedAssets), and settling from the wrong account (NotOperator). So a tick caps its delta at the reserve, caps a loss at totalManagedAssets, and skips settlement rather than losing the tick — the strategy still decides, still records trades and still snapshots NAV, so an unfunded strategy is visibly running rather than silently absent. navPerShare() returns par when totalShares == 0 instead of dividing by zero, so the UI reads NAV as a claim per share and totalShares as the evidence of capital. StrategyRegistry anchors keccak256(strategyId) -> vault + binary hash on-chain; the platform id is a uuid, and the hashing lives in exactly one file with the chain layer taking the bytes32 pre-hashed, so nothing can ever anchor a strategy under keccak(keccak(id)) — a key nothing looks up, with nothing anywhere to report it.

THE SUBMISSION PIPELINE — nine stages, in order, first failure stops the rest

parses -> required-exports (all six) -> forbidden-imports (and no dynamic import()) -> no-side-effects (no forbidden globals, no top-level statements beyond imports, declarations and exports) -> tsc --noEmit against the shared strategy contract -> describe-valid (metadata and declared assets) -> deterministic (onTick twice on an identical context must return identical output) -> cre workflow build, capturing the binary hash -> cre workflow simulate, yielding a parseable decision. Only after stage nine can a submission publish, which deploys its vault, funds the reserve and registers the measurement. Results stream into the create screen as each stage lands.

THE SCHEDULER — where returns actually come from

cre workflow simulate fires a cron trigger once and exits; the CLI has no scheduled mode and rejects --listen for cron, so the scheduler owns the interval (60s default, bounded concurrency). Each tick refreshes a seeded, deterministic price oracle, runs the workflow for that strategy, parses the decision, prices the target weights against the price delta since the last tick, charges venue cost in bps on turnover, sends applyPnl and recordTrade from the strategy's operator account, and writes an execution row. The composition root builds one ChainPort and one OraclePort and is called after listen() — because the enclave fetches prices over HTTP from this same process, so the oracle route has to be answering before the first tick can complete. The whole loop (publish, deposit, four ticks, metrics) is proved end to end by a single npm run verify:loop.

It matters for the product's claim, not just for correctness: the figure on the card is the chain's account of what happened, which is exactly the thing a sceptical investor can independently recompute.

lib/metrics.ts is pure — same series in, same value out, no clock, no database — and returns null rather than zero when history is too short, because zero reads as "flat" when the truth is "unknown". APY is the case that bites: annualising wall-clock over a twenty-minute demo turns a +1.4% move into an astronomic exponent and saturates every loss at exactly -100%. projects.title: POP
projects.description: A Uniswap-like prediction market on Arc, using native USDC and powered by Chainlink CRE.
projects.project_description: POP is an AMM-based prediction market built on Arc. Instead of matching buyers and sellers through an order book, every market has its own liquidity pool where users can trade outcome tokens continuously and prices move with the market. POP uses Arc-native USDC as the base asset, making markets simple to fund, trade, and settle without introducing another collateral token. Chainlink powers the connection between onchain markets and real-world information, allowing POP to automate market resolution and settlement while also exploring privacy-preserving prediction market flows. The goal is to make prediction markets feel more like open onchain markets: permissionless to create, continuously liquid, composable, and programmable.
projects.how_its_made: POP is built on Arc with smart contracts handling market creation, outcome-token accounting, AMM liquidity, trading, resolution, and redemption. Native USDC is used as the collateral and settlement asset across the entire market lifecycle. When a market is created, liquidity is deposited into an AMM pool and users trade directly against that liquidity. The relative reserves and trading activity determine the market price of each outcome, giving POP continuous onchain price discovery without requiring a traditional order book. Chainlink CRE is used to connect POP's onchain contracts with external data and computation. A CRE workflow can retrieve the information required by a market, apply its resolution logic, and trigger settlement on Arc once the outcome is determined. We also experiment with Chainlink-powered privacy workflows for cases where some market inputs, positions, or data should not be publicly exposed before settlement. The final result can still be brought back onchain for transparent settlement. The frontend connects directly to the Arc contracts, allowing users to create markets, provide liquidity, trade outcomes with USDC, follow changing probabilities, and redeem their positions after resolution.

projects.title: Handshake
projects.description: Deals become verifiable on-chain objects with their own ENS identity and history.
projects.project_description: Handshake lets two people make a deal and put real money behind it. Both sides stake USDC collateral, funds lock in an on-chain escrow, and the agreement's full lifecycle — created, funded, active, completed or disputed — becomes a permanent, verifiable object rather than a private off-chain promise. Each deal gets its own ENS identity: <dealId>.handshakedeal.eth resolves live to that deal's current status, straight from the contract, with nothing cached or hardcoded. Instead of a reputation score built on stars and reviews, anyone can inspect a deal's real factual history — a Deal Passport reconstructed entirely from on-chain events. Login uses Privy's embedded wallets, so funding a deal is as simple as signing in with Google and confirming a transaction — no MetaMask install, no seed phrase.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity contracts written and tested with Foundry: a single Handshake.sol contract holds the escrow state machine (no factory/registry split), enforces terms-locking by simply never exposing an edit function once a deal is accepted, and resolves disputes winner-takes-the-full-pot via a fixed per-deal reviewer address. Reentrancy is guarded manually and proven against a malicious ERC20 in the test suite — 18 tests total, all passing. HandshakeResolver.sol is a custom ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver that stores zero deal data: it decodes the DNS-encoded subdomain label into a dealId and calls Handshake.getDeal() live on every query, which is what makes "not hardcoded" a structural fact rather than a claim — verified directly with a raw cast call against the deployed contract on Sepolia, before and after a real state change. The name handshakedeal.eth is registered on ENS's actual ENSv2 beta deployment on Sepolia. The frontend is Next.js with Privy for auth and embedded wallet creation, and wagmi/viem for all contract reads and writes.

projects.title: Glide
projects.description: Self custodial glide path liquidity on 1inch Aqua, reachable through a Uniswap v4 hook.
projects.project_description:
Glide lets a wallet rebalance itself without ever depositing into a pool. The maker keeps tokens in their own wallet and publishes a glide path: the value split now, the split they want, and a time window. Glide prices the wallet like a weighted AMM whose weights slide along that path. Whenever the market moves, an arbitrageur can profit by trading against the position, and every such trade walks the wallet toward the target while paying the maker a fee. Instead of paying slippage to sell at once or fees to a bot, the maker collects fees. It is a liquidity bootstrapping pool for a single wallet, with no pool contract holding the money. Positions live on 1inch Aqua, so tokens are pulled only when a trade executes.
A Uniswap v4 pool with a custom hook forwards any Uniswap swap into the position, so routers and aggregators reach it while the pool itself holds no liquidity. Paths can be linear or any piecewise schedule: ease-in, S-curve, hold-then-move. The demo ships a USDC/WETH position on a Unichain fork, an arbitrage loop keeps the pool at the reference price, and the maker's value share tracks the path while fees accrue in their wallet.
projects.how_its_made: Glide is two new SwapVM instructions in a redeployed router, settling through the official 1inch Aqua registry on Unichain. GlideSwap moves the token A weight in a straight line between two endpoints; GlideSwapPiecewise follows a schedule of up to 20 segments. Both apply a weighted constant-mean curve modelled on Balancer V2 math, using solady's powWad with an upward error bump so every rounding step favours the maker. Schedule and curve had to live in one instruction, because SwapVM instructions can only talk to each other through the four swap registers. In Aqua mode the program is stateless: balances come from Aqua on every quote, and fees land as tokenIn in the maker's own wallet. The Uniswap side is a v4 hook using beforeSwap custom accounting. It takes the swapper's input from the PoolManager, fills against the Aqua order through the router, settles the output back, and returns a delta that consumes the whole specified amount. Liquidity adds are refused, so the pool never holds tokens. Tests: fuzz against an unrounded reference, 1inch's CoreInvariants suite at fixed, extreme and mid-glide weights, hook tests on a fresh PoolManager, and a fork test against the real Aqua and PoolManager. 47 green.

In Aqua mode the program is stateless: balances come from Aqua on every quote, and fees land as tokenIn in the maker's own wallet.

The Uniswap side is a v4 hook using beforeSwap custom accounting. It takes the swapper's input from the PoolManager, fills against the Aqua order through the router, settles the output back, and returns a delta that consumes the whole specified amount. Liquidity adds are refused, so the pool never holds tokens.

Tests: fuzz against an unrounded reference, 1inch's CoreInvariants suite at fixed, extreme and mid-glide weights, hook tests on a fresh PoolManager, and a fork test against the real Aqua and PoolManager. 47 green.

projects.title: deCAPTCHA
projects.description: A CAPTCHA that lets real AI agents through with human pre-approval built on World's Selfie Check.
projects.project_description: Your AI agent just got blocked by a CAPTCHA. Again. Every bot gate on the internet asks one question: are you a human? For an agent booking your flight or grabbing your ticket, there's no good answer. (Because let's be real, it's all going to be automated now.) So it gets treated like a scraper, and you go do it yourself. deCAPTCHA asks a better question: Not "are you human" but "is a real human accountable for this?" Here's how it works. You pass World's Selfie Check once - takes a second. That mints a vouch: an ENS subname on Sepolia that says a verified human is standing behind this agent, it can do exactly this much, until exactly this time, and that human can pull the plug whenever they want. Your agent carries that name around like a badge. No vouch? CAPTCHA. Blocked. Nothing changes for the bots. With a vouch? Straight through. Instantly. Logged as acting for you. One claim past what you allowed? Blocked, exactly like a bot. Agent decides it wants more? It tries to raise its own limit and ENS slaps it down.The agent has zero permission over its own credential. Then you hit revoke. The transaction lands on Sepolia, you watch it confirm, and the agent's very next request bounces. No waiting for a cache to clear, because there is no cache. When a vouch is minted, we hand the human write access and then throw away our own. Read the resolver yourself. The agent can't touch it and either can we. Bots still walk away with nothing, exactly as they should. But an agent working for a real person finally gets treated like one, with access that reaches precisely as far as that person allowed and lasts precisely as long as they're comfortable with it. The second they aren't, it's gone.
projects.how_its_made: Node and Express backend, ENSv2 on Sepolia, a vanilla-JS embeddable widget, and a Chrome extension as the human's vouch wallet. The widget is the product. One script tag and one div, and the server-side check is POST /api/siteverify with a secret - deliberately the same shape as reCAPTCHA, because adopting this should be a swap and not a re-architecture. The response carries two fields reCAPTCHA never had: whether a human or an accountable agent passed, and which human is on the hook. It renders in a shadow root so a host page's CSS can't break it and it can't leak styles outward. ENSv2 does the heavy lifting, and the primitive that makes it work is PermissionedResolver scoping Enhanced Access Control resources to keccak256(node, part) - a name AND a record type. Permission is granted on one specific field of one specific vouch. The human holds ROLE_SET_TEXT on the revocation record. The agent holds nothing, anywhere. When it tries to bump its own scope the chain throws EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles naming the agent's address and the exact role it lacks. That refusal is ENS talking, not us. Every vouch gets its own resolver, cloned through VerifiableFactory, so its records and permissions belong to it alone instead of a shared table. Minting is three transactions: deploy the resolver with records already baked in, register the subname, then grant the human and renounce ourselves in one multicall. That first one works because PermissionedResolver skips permission checks during init, so records exist before anyone has rights over them. Authorisation needs no identity provider. The human signs readable terms naming the agent, scope and expiry, and that signature is published on the record. Anyone can recover the signer from chain data alone. Ten tests prove it binds rather than merely exists: change the scope, the expiry, the agent or the name and verification fails. Expiry is layered. The subname outlives its vouch by a week on purpose. We tried setting them equal and it broke the story - the name stopped resolving before the gate could read the record, so an expired vouch looked identical to one that never existed.

GlobalCare is the Kayak for medical tourism — but it goes far beyond finding a hospital. It uses AI to analyze medical reports, compare treatment options, hospitals, and costs across countries, connect patients with doctors for second opinions, and plan flights and stays. projects.how_its_made: built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Supabase, Gemini, Privy, Arc, viem, Mapbox, SerpAPI, and Calendly. Gemini powers the medical-travel AI and report analysis, while Supabase handles journeys, consultations, medical documents, and persistent chat state. Privy provides the embedded patient wallet and a familiar login-to-payment experience. The key technical piece is a custom Arc escrow smart contract using USDC. When a patient pays, funds move from their Privy wallet into escrow and are released through programmable 20/60/20 treatment milestones, with trustee-controlled release/refund logic and on-chain verification. Live flight and hotel data comes through SerpAPI, Mapbox handles location experiences, and Calendly connects patients to real doctors. The result is a full-stack application where AI, real-world healthcare workflows, travel infrastructure, and programmable money work as one system.

projects.title: The Pit
projects.description: The Pit: a public proving ground where AI trading agents can't fake their results.
projects.project_description: The Pit is a public, adversarial proving ground for AI trading agents. AI trading bots are everywhere now: copy-trading bots, autonomous DeFi agents, Claude-powered trading assistants, but there is no trustworthy way to prove one is actually good before anyone hands it real capital. Backtests get cherry-picked, screenshots get faked, and a claim like "my agent returns 12% a week" is unverifiable because nothing about it is public or tamper-proof. The Pit fixes that by giving any registered agent a fixed stake, a fixed clock, and on-chain rules it structurally cannot get around, then writing every result into a permanent public record. Any agent can register through the same generic pipeline: fund a backend-managed wallet with a small amount of USDC, register with our contracts, and commit a hashed strategy config before the match starts. Each match runs six fixed-length rounds on a house-seeded Uniswap v3 pool. Agents trade through PitRouter, a custom contract we built that wraps the pool's swap function and enforces on-chain, per round, which wallet can trade, how many trades it gets, and tracks swap fees so they get rebated back into the agents' stakes instead of quietly punishing active trading. Balances are read directly on-chain at each round lock, no oracle needed since USDC is already a dollar. After the match, strategies are revealed and the contract settles: it picks the winner by final balance and pays out the fee rebate. Every round lock, every revealed trade, and every result gets written into a custom subgraph on The Graph, a permanent, publicly queryable proof layer that outlives the demo. Agents can even query their own subgraph-indexed match history through The Graph's Subgraph MCP before deciding their next move, so their reasoning is genuinely informed by their own track record, not just the current tick. This is not a mockup: the contracts are deployed for real on Base Sepolia, backed by 51 automated tests including a live fork test against the real Uniswap v3 Factory and PositionManager, and we ran a full real rehearsal end to end (register, six real on-chain rounds of trading, lock, reveal, settle) with three separate agent wallets, confirmed indexed correctly in the live subgraph. At least three agents run through the identical registration pipeline in the demo, two of our own strategies plus one deliberately different one, to prove the proving-ground claim is real infrastructure and not two names hardcoded into a frontend.
projects.how_its_made: The Pit is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces) with a Foundry project for the contracts, glued together by a shared match-state model so the loop, the board, and both subgraphs never disagree about what a match looks like. Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, Base Sepolia). PitRouter wraps a single Uniswap v3 pool's swap function and is the entire "structurally cannot cheat" layer: it checks the caller is a registered participant, that match's round is currently live, and the agent is under its per-round trade cap, then forwards to the real pool and tracks swap fee volume per agent. MatchController handles generic commit-and-fund registration, on-chain-enforced round timing (not just a runner promise), reveal, and settlement, and deploys its own CommitReveal contract internally for the hashed strategy configs. We originally scoped this against Uniswap v4 hooks, then pivoted to v3 mid-build since v3 has no hook slot at all, so all enforcement had to move into a router contract we fully own instead, which actually made the fairness logic easier to reason about and test in isolation. The Graph. A custom subgraph indexes every MatchController and PitRouter event (registrations, round locks, reveals, settlement, trades) into a permanent record, composed alongside a Messari Standardized DEX AMM subgraph over the same pool for the composability track. The agent itself queries its own subgraph-indexed match history through The Graph's Subgraph MCP before each decision, so its reasoning is genuinely grounded in its own track record rather than just displaying a query result. Agents, runner, board. Each agent runs a tick loop on the Claude Agent SDK across three distinct strategies (momentum, mean reversion, and a passive baseline), submitting swaps through PitRouter with a viem wallet client. A runner package orchestrates the full match lifecycle on-chain (register, start, lock each round, reveal, settle) and pushes live state to Supabase, which a Next.js board subscribes to for a coarse, delayed leader indicator so a live position cannot be reverse engineered mid-round. The genuinely hacky part. We caught two critical bugs by running an adversarial security review against our own contracts before touching a demo: registration originally pulled each agent's stake into the contract with nothing to ever pay it back out, and settlement could brick itself forever on a misconfigured house liquidity position. Both were fixed and are now covered by tests. To actually prove the integration rather than assume it, we forked live Base Sepolia in Foundry and ran a full register-to-settle match against the real, canonically deployed Uniswap v3 Factory and NonfungiblePositionManager, not mocks, which is how we discovered that a zero sqrtPriceLimitX96 silently reverts on real pools even though our own mock happily accepted it. We then deployed for real, dropped the stake to $1 and shortened rounds to 50 seconds to fit what we could actually faucet and rehearse in the time we had, and ran a genuine end-to-end rehearsal on-chain with three separate funded wallets, confirmed correctly indexed in the live subgraph.

projects.title: LeashGuard
projects.description: Approve what your agent buys. Allow bounded credit top-ups with ENSv2 and Privy.
projects.project_description: Leash separates permission to buy a new service from permission to keep using one. A coding agent's first purchase waits for owner approval, even when it fits the agent's ETH transaction limit. After that purchase settles, the owner can separately authorize credit top-ups for the same merchant, product, account, and agent wallet. Each authorization has a per-top-up limit, cumulative budget, and expiry. A new product, exhausted budget, or expired permission brings the agent back for review. The working demonstration sells prepaid dependency-report credits. A matching successful Sepolia receipt delivers three credits; a report consumes one. Repeating the same request does not pay or consume credits twice. A ten-tool MCP server exposes the workflow to coding agents without giving them permission to approve themselves. Owners can revoke top-ups or the whole agent. ENSv2 provides agent identity, lifecycle, and standing transaction limits. Privy provides wallets and synchronized transaction policies. The trusted Leash service enforces product approval and cumulative budgets. This is a native-ETH Sepolia prototype, with one owner per workspace and a single-host SQLite ledger. Leash operates the demonstration merchant; npm advisory data is public. Budgets exclude gas and separately approved purchases. There is no external SaaS billing, subscription, USD trial budget, x402 support, or production custody claim. The demonstration link points to verification evidence, including real Sepolia first-purchase and automatic-top-up receipts. Supplementary UI clips and the first-approval and budget screenshots use mocked login, chain, and npm. They are simulated UI evidence, not an authenticated owner/coding-host recording. There is no public hosted application.
projects.how_its_made: A Solidity registrar creates ENSv2 workspace and agent registries on Sepolia, with per-key resolver roles and lifecycle controls. The service checks the exact live agent token and workspace ownership before reading its payment cap and recipient records at a single block. This prevents stale wildcard resolver records from reviving expired or revoked agents. Privy supplies owner authentication, agent wallets, and transaction policies. Scoped agent credentials are hashed at rest and cannot approve purchases or authorize top-ups. For an exact owner-approved exception, the service synchronizes a temporary recipient/amount policy, submits once, and restores the current ENS-derived policy, falling back to deny-all on read failure. Service revocation disables credentials and top-up permissions and sets the wallet policy to deny-all. The Next.js/React owner dashboard and TypeScript APIs share a durable node:sqlite ledger for invoices, approvals, budget reservations, payment IDs, credit accounts, and report replay. Mutations serialize per agent. Automatic top-up budget is reserved before submission; ambiguous outcomes retain their reservation and freeze further spending for operator reconciliation. Credits are delivered only after matching the successful receipt and transaction. Reports retrieve public npm advisory data and consume one credit atomically. The MCP stdio server exposes ten tools shared by Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. Validation: 35 application/MCP tests and 16 Foundry contract tests pass, along with typecheck, lint, production build, dependency audit, and deployment preflight. Live integration tests exercised actual ENS/Privy wallets, policy restoration, first approval, automatic top-up, budget exhaustion, product isolation, and revocation. Their owner actions used an operator ownership check, not a Privy browser login. Product/account approval and cumulative budgets are trusted-service controls, not independently enforced on-chain. Deployment: leash-tools-2026.eth; registrar 0xaa1b19B741fF876F95eE83054c561750af1CdE8f. Public deployment details and receipts are in the repository. Attribution and timeline: the first project commit is September 4, 2026 at 19:33:20 +03:00. September 4-5 built the initial prototype; September 10-11 hardened lifecycle/payment behavior and implemented purchase-versus-top-up rules; September 13 packaged and published it. Original history is preserved, including the larger final implementation commit. Development was AI-assisted. ENS Namechain, OpenZeppelin, Solady, and other third-party dependencies retain their original licenses; project-specific code is MIT licensed.

projects.description: Stake 1 USDC and challenge an on-chain agent to guess your job in 10 questions
projects.project_description: Legilimens is an on-chain fortune booth. You stake 1 USDC, secretly pick your job, and answer 10 yes/no style questions. The Seer, an autonomous agent with its own wallet, then guesses your job. If it names your exact job, it keeps your stake. If it misses, you win your stake back plus half the pot. How it stays fair: Your job is locked on-chain as a hash before the first question, so you cannot change it later and the Seer cannot see it. The Seer commits to its question seed before you play, so it cannot change its strategy after seeing your answers. The smart contract decides the result and pays out in the same transaction. If you lie to trick the Seer, the contract checks whether your answers fit your sealed job. Answers that clearly do not fit forfeit your stake. Anyone can replay any game with one command and check whether the Seer played fair. The Seer is not an LLM. It uses Bayesian inference (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference) over a published table of 66 jobs and 24 traits, similar to a naive Bayes classifier (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier). It picks each question by information gain (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_gain_(decision_tree)), the classic twenty questions strategy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty_questions). Built with: Arc: USDC stakes, payouts and the Seer's wallet, which earns a 5% cut and pays its own gas. The Graph: a subgraph of past games that the Seer learns from before each game. ENS: the Seer's identity and settings live on seer.legilimens.eth. Each player gets a name like abc123.players.legilimens.eth with their game record, written only by the Seer. Players caught lying twice are refused.
projects.how_its_made:
Legilimens has four parts: a smart contract on Arc, a Next.js app that also runs the Seer, a subgraph on The Graph, and ENS names on Sepolia. Smart contract (Solidity, Foundry)
The LegilimensVault contract holds stakes and runs a commit-reveal game. The player locks their job as a hash with a secret salt. The Seer locks a hash of its random seed. When the Seer guesses, it publishes the seed plus the full transcript (which question it asked and each answer, packed into two bytes10 values). When the player reveals, the contract checks the hash, compares job codes, and pays out in one transaction. Winners take a share of the pot, never a fixed amount, so the pot can never pay out more than it holds. 27 Foundry tests cover every outcome, timeouts, bad signatures and a solvency check. The Seer (not an LLM)
The Seer is a Bayesian solver written in TypeScript. It uses a table of 66 jobs and 24 traits, updates a probability for every job after each answer, and picks the next question by information gain. The pick uses a seeded softmax, so there is no fixed question tree to exploit, but any game can be replayed exactly. We tuned the question count and randomness with Monte Carlo simulations so the Seer wins about half the time. Hacky bits worth mentioning Catching liars on-chain: a script turns the job table into Solidity constants. At reveal, the contract scores how well the answers fit the sealed job compared with every other job, using integer math. A Foundry test proves the contract and the TypeScript solver produce the exact same scores. Blatant liars forfeit their stake. In simulation this turned lying from a big profit into a loss. No database: the server re-derives each game's secret seed from on-chain data, so it is completely stateless. Deterministic learning: the Seer only learns from games settled before the current game started, so replays always rebuild the same starting beliefs. A replay script rebuilds any game from public chain data and checks every question, the guess and the verdict. Partner technologies Arc: USDC is the gas token, so stakes, payouts and the Seer's running costs are all in USDC with no conversion. The Seer has its own wallet, earns a 5% cut when it wins, pays its own gas, and records its costs on-chain. The Graph: a subgraph indexes every game. The Seer reads it before each game to learn which jobs people pick, which changes the questions it asks. It also powers the live ledger of recent games. ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): seer.legilimens.eth stores the Seer's wallet, agent records and the app's settings (vault address, subgraph URL, matrix hash). The app reads these at runtime instead of hard-coding them. The owner gave the Seer's wallet only two permissions: creating names under players.legilimens.eth, and writing specific record keys. After each game the Seer writes the player's record to their own name, like abc123.players.legilimens.eth. Players caught lying twice are refused. Frontend
Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, Motion for animations, and wagmi and viem for the wallet. The whole game is designed as a candlelit fortune booth with a wax seal, scrying orb and a pot that fills up. Deployed on Vercel.

projects.title: theworldiscollapsing
projects.description: A world that grows forever. Bet on anything in it. Nobody knows the outcome, not even us.
projects.project_description: theworldiscollapsing is a world that never stops. An AI grows it event after event, forever. Matches get played, elections get called, awards get handed out, bills pass or fail, and every result becomes history that the next event builds on. Because something is always happening, there is always something to bet on, and every possible outcome of every event is its own market. Normal prediction markets can be gamed. Someone learns the result first, someone can move it, or someone decides how it settles. Here nobody can do any of that: not the players, not the house, and not us. Every outcome comes from a drand randomness round that is committed on chain before the first bet and does not exist until betting has closed. When it publishes, the contract verifies its signature on chain and derives the result from it. No person, model or operator picks the result, and anyone can re-check it from their own browser. The AI builds the world but cannot choose how anything in it ends. Every possible ending is rendered before betting closes and kept sealed. A Chainlink CRE confidential workflow running inside a TEE releases the key for the one ending the chain settled on. The losing endings are never released. That is a prediction market nobody in the world can control, not even the house. You watch the world live and bet with play USDC on Base Sepolia: https://theworldiscollapsing.vercel.app
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm monorepo: Solidity contracts, a Node engine that grows the world, a Next.js site, a subgraph and a Chainlink CRE workflow. Why it cannot be gamed. Two locks. The first decides: every event commits a drand evmnet round on chain when it is created, and that round must publish at least 10 seconds after betting locks. At resolve, the contract verifies the round's BLS signature on chain and sets outcome = keccak256(signature ‖ eventId) mod n. Nobody can know the result while money is on the table, and nobody can choose it. The second seals: every possible ending is rendered before the lock and stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext, and only a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow inside a TEE derives the key for the ending the chain settled on. What we still hold is liveness, not outcomes: one resolver key can delay a result but not change it, and after three days anyone can bail an event for a full refund. Engine. One Node 24 process in TypeScript with viem and zod runs the world as one state machine per part of it (sports, politics, culture, region): author, render, createEvent, bet, lock, resolve, reveal, then the result is written into the world's history. It is restart-safe against chain state, presence-gated so an empty site costs nothing, and metered against a hard spend cap. All AI goes through OpenRouter. GPT-6 Astra grows the world: it writes each next event as strict JSON from everything that has already happened, which lives in Postgres and is injected into every prompt. GPT-5 mini is the cheap fallback for long soak runs. Gemini 3.1 Flash Image draws a key frame and MiniMax Hailuo 3 Max turns it into footage with image-to-video, under house-style prompts that make it look like real life filmed live: real time, never cinematic, never slow motion. Rendering every future. Generated video cannot stream, so every ending exists before anyone bets. The first half is shared and ends level. While it plays and people bet, one second half per outcome renders in the background, seeded from the first half's last frame. Only the winning branch is ever released, so the reveal has zero latency and nobody can skip ahead. Measured cost is $3.27 per event for 45 seconds of video. Contracts. Foundry, on Base Sepolia, verified on Basescan. Arena runs a YES/NO parimutuel pool on every outcome with a 2% fee, voids markets captured with dust, and has the three-day bail. DrandVerifier checks BN254 BLS signatures with the EVM pairing precompiles. The hacky bit: hash-to-curve needs field inverses and square roots, which we compute through the modexp precompile, so a verify costs about 153k gas with no external library. We chose drand over Chainlink VRF because a VRF result is public the moment it is fulfilled and costs LINK per request, and on OP-stack chains prevrandao can be set by the sequencer. Sponsors. Chainlink CRE: the confidential workflow in TypeScript listens for Arena's Resolved log, reads the outcome from chain on the Workflow DON, and inside the TEE pulls the seal root from the Vault DON and derives the key for the winning ending only. Keys are derived with keccak256 because the workflow runtime has no crypto library. It compiles to WASM and passes its handler tests, deployment is waiting on Confidential Workflows access, and until the engine drops its fallback copy of the root the engine can still decrypt a late key itself. The Graph: a subgraph on Studio indexes every Arena event and powers the markets and positions pages, and the engine can feed the last event's pools back into the next event. Privy: email login with an embedded wallet on Base Sepolia. World: Selfie Check through IDKit 4 with a server-side verify, then Gate.setVerified on chain gates the faucet and every bet; the hosted demo runs a checkbox fallback while the Selfie Check beta is pending. Web. Next.js 16 on Vercel, Prisma 7 on Neon Postgres, Vercel Blob for media. Every event page has a verify badge that fetches the round from api.drand.sh and re-derives the outcome in the browser. Testing without burning money. A fake OpenRouter server replays real MiniMax clips we already paid for, and perpetual bettor bots fund, verify and bet both sides of every market from six wallets. A 10-minute soak across four parts of the world placed 776 bets on 68 events with zero voids and survived restarts of the engine and the bettors mid-window. One framing note. Nowhere does the text say the AI or the TEE decides outcomes, because they don't. drand decides every ending and the chain verifies it. The AI only grows the world, and the TEE keeps the endings sealed. That split is what makes "not even the house can control it" true, and a judge who reads the code will see it matches. Three honest status lines are kept inside "How it's made": The CRE workflow isn't deployed yet, and the engine still holds a fallback copy of the seal root. The hosted demo uses a checkbox instead of World Selfie Check. GPT-5 mini is the fallback author, so set the engine to Astra before any live demo.

projects.title: Plumb
projects.description: Lets you or your agent analyze live DeFi data from one GraphQL query across many protocols.
projects.project_description: Plumb is a cross-protocol DeFi copilot for agents (Claude, Cursor, or a small web chat). It answers questions like “where is this wallet’s lending risk?” and “how do comparable markets look ?” by running one GraphQL document against many pinned subgraphs on The Graph, not by hard-coding a single protocol API. Today that means Messari lending markets: Aave v3 (Ethereum), Spark (Ethereum), and Moonwell (Base). The same MARKETS_QUERY and POSITIONS_QUERY are POSTed to every deployment. Adding another lending protocol is a registry.json row (display name, chain, pinned deployment ID) not a new mapper. The same registry-and-shared-query shape is how Plumb can later grow into other DeFi families (for example DEX) without becoming a pile of one-off integrations. Honesty is the product. Each protocol is pinned to a subgraph deployment ID. Queries go to The Graph gateway by that ID. If _meta.deployment does not match the pin, _meta.block is more than six hours behind, the call times out, or GraphQL/HTTP fails, the payload is discarded. Tools return structured failures[] and the UI/agent must say unavailable. They must not fill a cell with 0, a cache, or an LLM guess. The demo can break a pin on purpose so judges see that path. Agents do not just dump JSON. Four reusable MCP tools (list_lending_markets, query_market, compare_markets, wallet_lending) return the same columns across protocols: APYs, deposits/borrows, derived available liquidity, LTV/liquidation fields, and _meta provenance. The model is instructed (tool descriptions + SKILL.md) to reason on those rows: compare borrow APY and liquidity, talk about liquidation risk from schema fields only (Messari has no healthFactor), and always surface failures. A CLI and a local web UI call the same tools. The Graph API key never leaves the server. There is no swap execution, no fake health factor, and no mocked market numbers in the product path.
projects.how_its_made: We built Plumb as a TypeScript (Node 22+, ESM) service with pnpm, Zod, and Vitest. There is no Next.js app and no GraphQL client that could cache answers. The product path is: MCP or UI → tools → honest Graph fetch → structured rows and failures. The Graph is the only partner in the loop. A Subgraph Studio / Network API key lives only in the server process. Every query is an HTTP POST of a shared document to gateway.thegraph.com/api/<KEY>/deployments/id/<PIN> never /subgraphs/id/..., so we do not silently follow “latest.” registry.json maps protocol slug → chain → pinned deployment ID. Enabled protocols are queried in parallel (Promise.allSettled); one dead subgraph does not abort the others. Two GraphQL templates cover everyone: Messari lending MARKETS_QUERY and POSITIONS_QUERY, both requesting _meta. After a 15s timeout, HTTP/GraphQL errors become QueryFailure. Success still goes through honesty: normalize _meta.deployment against the pin; stale if _meta.block.timestamp lags more than six hours (or is in the future). Failed bodies are dropped—callers never see numbers from a bad pin. Mapping is schema-faithful, not protocol-specific. Supply/borrow APY come from rates (LENDER / BORROWER, prefer VARIABLE). availableLiquidityUSD is derived as max(0, deposits − borrows) because Messari has no such field. Positions use the intersection of Aave/Spark 3.1.0 and Moonwell 2.0.1 so one document still runs; we do not invent healthFactor. Asset match is inputToken.symbol with case variants; USDC.e is a separate row. MCP (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk, stdio) exposes list_lending_markets, query_market, compare_markets, wallet_lending. Handlers call the real tools and return JSON text. Logs go to stderr so stdout stays JSON-RPC. A small node:http API and Vite + React UI (and a CLI pnpm compare) use those same tools. Optional in-app chat is Anthropic tool-calling on the server; with no key, the UI is forms only. Notable hack: --break / a UI checkbox still hits the live gateway with a wrong CID or a mismatched pin. Unavailable is a real HTTP_ERROR or DEPLOYMENT_MISMATCH, not if (demo) return 0.

projects.title: Limit order book
projects.description: fully on chain limit order book built on arbitrum stylus using a novel bitmap algorithm
projects.project_description: We are solving an open problem in DeFi- bringing limit order books on chain. This was impossible on EVM given its limitations on computation and memory-till now. Arbitrum stylus allows you to write smart contracts in rust unlocking 10x more memory and throughput. We paired it with a novel bitmap based algorithm to make limit orders possible with EVM's 256 bit K-V storage trie structure.
projects.how_its_made: Tech stack Smart contract: rust Chain: arbitrum stylus Indexing: subtraphs (wip) The smart contract builds up on a large number of innovations Bitmap tree: instead of a traditional tree structure to store orderbook nodes, we use EVM's 256 bit key value trie as the store. projects.title: Margit
projects.description: Margit is a marketplace for private Github repositories for AI agents to trade.
projects.project_description: Pronounced almost like MARKET (Mar-Git) Margit is a marketplace for private GitHub repositories, built for humans and AI agents. Sellers connect GitHub, choose a repository, set a price and access terms, and receive payments in USDC or EURC on Arc testnet. Buyers pay to unlock authenticated Git clone or ZIP access. GitHub does not provide a native checkout for selling private repository access. Margit connects discovery, payment, and code delivery in one workflow, helping developers monetize templates, plugins, starter kits, and complete applications directly from their repositories. The same workflow is available to agents. Imagine asking your coding agent to build something useful, then authorizing it to list the repository for sale. Another agent can discover it, evaluate whether it fits a project, and purchase access within its user’s budget. Margit makes repository commerce accessible through both a visual interface and agent tools. Users can browse listings, explore sales activity, and use our Bazantic-powered Repository Advisor to compare options against their requirements and budget. Think about it this way: You have your agent creating code, next logical step - just Margit! Let it be a verb like just google it, but for putting your code for sale - just marg-it!
projects.how_its_made: We built Margit with React, TypeScript, and Vite , backed by a Hono API on Vercel . GitHub OAuth connects sellers’ repositories, while Upstash Redis stores listings, sessions, purchase records, and encrypted credentials. After payment verification, our backend issues scoped Git clone or ZIP access without exposing the seller’s GitHub token. Arc and Circle power payments. Our contract ↗ (0x72c54ecd669acb19d6e6d5b5160f67d03b4d5b7b) handles buyer-bound signed orders, publisher payments, and platform fees. Circle Gateway provides a separate x402 payment path for agents: request access, receive an HTTP 402 challenge, sign payment authorization, and retry to unlock the repository. We support demo and personal agent wallets, Circle-managed wallets, and a 1Claw remote-signing integration. Our payment evidence ↗ documents a successful 0.05 USDC Gateway purchase and authenticated Git delivery. The Graph makes marketplace activity queryable. Our Subgraph ↗ indexes contract purchase and fee events for catalog statistics, bestseller rankings, and buyer/seller leaderboards. These statistics cover contract checkout activity; Gateway x402 purchases follow a separate payment path. Our OpenRouter-powered assistant connects discovery and actions. It combines indexed activity with current catalog data, manages authorized seller listings, and executes requested purchases through backend tools. External agents can use our MCP or API ↗ and published SKILLS ↗ to interact with the marketplace. Bazantic powers our Repository Advisor. We connected Margit’s catalog API and GitHub’s public API through two Bazantic gateways, then published a reusable Recipe that evaluates project requirements against a USD repository budget. For explicitly supplied comparison repositories, it checks GitHub metadata, languages, and releases. The same Recipe serves the Catalog’s advisor form and an optional tool in the agent sidebar. Our guide ↗ includes gateway URLs, tool bindings, the Recipe prompt, and test evidence. One particularly hands-on part was implementing the Git delivery proxy , which enforces purchased access terms while keeping seller credentials private. Another was handling uncertain payment outcomes: we validate payment requirements before signing, retain purchase records, and block automatic payment retries when the result is unclear. This helps prevent duplicate charges while allowing buyers to recover access after a completed purchase.

**Our OpenRouter-powered assistant connects discovery and actions.** It combines indexed activity with current catalog data, manages authorized seller listings, and executes requested purchases through backend tools. External agents can use our MCP or API [↗](https://api.margit.sh/) and published SKILLS [↗](https://margit.sh/skills/margit/SKILL.md) to interact with the marketplace.

**Bazantic powers our Repository Advisor.** We connected Margit’s catalog API and GitHub’s public API through two Bazantic gateways, then published a reusable Recipe that evaluates project requirements against a USD repository budget. For explicitly supplied comparison repositories, it checks GitHub metadata, languages, and releases. The same Recipe serves the Catalog’s advisor form and an optional tool in the agent sidebar. Our guide [↗](https://github.com/vm06007/margit/blob/master/bazantic-track/README.md) includes gateway URLs, tool bindings, the Recipe prompt, and test evidence.

![Published Margit Repository Advisor Recipe in Bazantic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vm06007/margit/master/docs/images/bazantic-published-recipe.jpg)

One particularly hands-on part was implementing the **Git delivery proxy**, which enforces purchased access terms while keeping seller credentials private. This helps prevent duplicate charges while allowing buyers to recover access after a completed purchase.

projects.title: Ratip
projects.description: Ratib is a SvelteKit, Convex, and Privy operations workspace for crypto-native businesses.
projects.project_description: Ratib is a governed finance-operations platform for businesses working with digital assets. It brings wallets, payments, approvals, invoices, automation, reconciliation, reporting, and audit evidence into one shared workspace. Instead of forcing finance teams to coordinate transactions across wallet interfaces, spreadsheets, messaging apps, and accounting tools, Ratib turns each financial action into a structured, traceable workflow. A team can organize wallets by company, review payment requests, apply internal approval rules, execute deterministic batch operations, monitor transaction status, and reconcile onchain activity with its business context. Every action is scoped to the organization and recorded as append-only evidence, giving operators and reviewers a clear history of what was requested, who approved it, which policy applied, and what eventually settled. Ratib deliberately separates business permissions from cryptographic authority. Ratib manages roles, workflow approvals, policy previews, and operational records, but those roles never grant signing power. Privy remains the final authority through embedded wallets, owners, signers, quorum rules, MFA-backed approvals, and provider-enforced policies. Transactions currently settle in USDC on Base Sepolia, so the prototype is clearly testnet-only. The long-term vision is to become the operational layer between programmable money and modern finance teams—expanding into invoice checkout, transaction simulation, recovery and gas management, developer APIs, accounting connectors, forecasting, fiat accounts, global payouts, cards, and qualified custody partnerships.
projects.how_its_made: Ratib is built with SvelteKit and TypeScript on the frontend, with Convex providing the real-time database, server functions, scheduled automation, and append-only audit history. Privy supplies embedded wallets, verified user identity, owner/signer configuration, policy enforcement, MFA-backed approvals, and secure transaction execution. Transactions settle using USDC on Base Sepolia. The key architectural decision was separating finance workflow from wallet authority: Ratib coordinates requests, roles, approvals, policy previews, and reconciliation, while Privy remains the final signing authority. Every operation is organization-scoped and follows a strict state machine. Deterministic run keys and idempotent actions prevent duplicate payments, while verified webhooks reconcile onchain results back into Convex.

projects.title: Obscura protocol
projects.description: Shielded prediction markets with zkVM-proven solvency bet privately, prove you were right.
projects.project_description: Obscura is a prediction market where your position is shielded end to end, yet every market's payouts are provably correct and solvent no operator is trusted for the numbers. Today's markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) make every bet public, leaking strategy and inviting front-running on correlated markets. In Obscura your side and stake never touch the chain in the clear only a Poseidon commitment does. When a market resolves (via a Chainlink feed, a Graph metric, or a Chainlink CRE workflow), an SP1 zkVM proof establishes the per-outcome totals and the commitments-tree root and proves they reconcile with the escrowed USDC so payouts are correct and solvent by proof, not by trust. Winners then prove in-browser (Noir) that they hold an unspent winning note and withdraw to a fresh address, unlinkable to the deposit. On top of shielded positions it adds Private Parlays, Proof of Foresight (an anonymous, verifiable "I called it" track record), a ZK accuracy reputation badge, and a live AI solvency/risk oracle. Most "private" markets stop at hiding individual bets; the hard, largely unsolved part is proving the aggregate settlement is correct and solvent while revealing nothing about individuals which is exactly what Obscura demonstrates.
projects.how_its_made: Privacy layer: Noir zk circuits for shielded deposit commitments, private claims, Proof of Foresight, parlays, and reputation; claim + foresight proofs are generated in the browser with @noir-lang/noir_js + @aztec/bb.js (UltraHonk) against on-chain verifiers. Solvency proof: an SP1 zkVM program (guest/host/aggregation in Rust) recomputes each market's per-outcome totals + Poseidon commitments root and asserts solvency; PredictionMarket.settleWithProof verifies it via the SP1 gateway before payouts unlock. Poseidon is byte-compatible across Noir / Rust light-poseidon / JS poseidon-lite (pinned test vectors) so every layer agrees on roots. Chainlink CRE: three TypeScript CRE workflows confidential settlement (TEE aggregation reconciled on-chain vs SP1 totals), Graph-metric resolution, and cron auto-resolution (the successor to classic Automation, sunset in 2026) driving an on-chain AutoResolver keeper. Resolution is source-agnostic: Chainlink feeds, The Graph, or CRE. The Graph: a subgraph indexes only public aggregates; an AI risk oracle (MCP server + in-browser port) computes solvency coverage + HHI concentration with a pinned deployment id + freshness gate, benchmarked against a Messari-standardized mainnet subgraph. Circle/Arc: USDC-denominated escrow (ERC-20 + EIP-2612 permit), deployed on Circle Arc testnet (USDC-native gas), with a CCTP entry that bridges USDC Base -> Arc into a shielded position. Client: Next.js 16, Wagmi, Viem, lightweight-charts. Everything is deployed + verified on Ethereum Sepolia and Arc testnet (addresses in the README). Hacky-but-notable: the SP1 EVM/Groth16 settlement proof is memory-heavy, so it runs on prover infrastructure and is verified on-chain by the SP1 gateway the standard production path.
