projects.title: Bombus
projects.description: Agents vote in secret. A TEE tallies them. Only the verdict comes out. Paid per query via x402.
projects.project_description: Hear the swarm, never the bee. DAOs, protocols, and agent networks need collective private signals — votes, risk assessments, price estimates — but today they must either publish every input on-chain (killing the signal's value, inviting front-running and copying) or hand everything to a centralized aggregator (defeating the point of a decentralized swarm). Bombus is a confidential aggregation substrate for agent swarms. Independent agents each hold a private value; that value is encrypted to a Trusted Execution Environment, combined inside it, and only the aggregate ever becomes public. No individual input is exposed — not to other agents, not to the chain, not to the coordinator operator. The first use case is DAO deliberation : each agent deliberates with its own persona and an LLM, encrypts its ballot, and submits it to a blind coordinator. When quorum is reached, a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow decrypts the batch inside the enclave, computes a confidence-weighted tally, and emits a signed verdict (pass / fail / contested). The verdict is served per query behind an x402 payment on Hedera — consumers (agents or humans) pay to read it, and anyone can verify the TEE's signature in the browser against a key published on ENS. The demo runs live: three agents with distinct stances (Growth Hawk, Risk Auditor, Community Steward) deliberate on a real proposal, the quorum fills, the verdict reveals only after its signature verifies, and the paid-access receipt links to a settled Hedera transaction. The absence is the product: the UI shows that agents voted, never how . Privacy guarantees, stated honestly: individual ballots are visible to no one — coordinator included (it routes ciphertext); participation metadata is public by design; the workflow deployer is a trusted party; and external LLM providers see only public proposal text, never ballots or private strategy.
projects.how_its_made: Swarm (off-chain): N independent Node.js agent processes, each with an ed25519 keypair and an ENSv2 identity ( agent1.bombus.eth ) on the hackathon deployment. Each agent deliberates via a hosted LLM (OpenAI-compatible endpoint — NVIDIA Nemotron) with a distinct persona, producing a confidence-weighted ballot, then seals it to the TEE's X25519 key (X25519 + XChaCha20-Poly1305) and signs the envelope. Agents are fully independent — no shared state, no coordination among themselves. Blind coordinator (Node.js/Express): verifies envelope signatures against the agent keymap, deduplicates and quorums per round, and hands the batch onward. It never sees a plaintext ballot — validation is signature + schema only. Round metadata (who submitted, ciphertext hash) is public; content is not. Tombstones persist closed rounds so replays are rejected across restarts. Confidential aggregation (Chainlink CRE): a confidential workflow runs inside an AWS Nitro TEE. The handler decrypts each envelope with a Vault-stored key, validates against the use-case schema, computes the confidence-weighted tally ( net = (W_support − W_oppose) / total , pass at ±0.5), suppresses detail below N=5 for small-cohort privacy, and signs the result with a TEE-held ed25519 key. Only the signed verdict leaves the enclave. The same handler code runs in cre workflow simulate (both confidential and plain targets) and in the coordinator's local seam, so the demo is resilient while the deployed path fires real DON executions as attestation. Delivery (x402 + Hedera): the resource server verifies the TEE signature at intake and refuses anything unverifiable, then serves the verdict behind an x402 payment on Hedera testnet via the Blocky402 facilitator ( @x402/express + @x402/hedera , x402 v2). A paid request settles a real test-USDC transfer on-chain — receipt visible on HashScan. Trust layer (ENSv2): agent identities, the enclave encryption key, and the TEE signing key are published as text records on the hackathon ENSv2 deployment ( bombus.eth ), giving the whole system a tamper-evident, human-readable root of trust. The web UI resolves the TEE key from ENS and verifies every verdict signature in the browser before revealing it. UI: a Vite + React observatory that polls the coordinator for live round state (dynamic quorum slots, sealed envelopes as hashed cells), reveals verdicts only after in-browser signature verification, and shows the Hedera receipt — never any ballot content.

projects.title: Preflight MCP
projects.description: The check an AI agent clears before it signs. High risk needs a press on your Ledger.
projects.project_description: An AI agent can read a contract, decide it looks fine, and sign against it with no human in the loop. The text it reads to make that decision was written by whoever deployed the contract, for the price of gas. Here is a real token on Ethereum mainnet. It reports 1.1 trillion dollars of liquidity. Four transactions have touched it in four years. The source is verified and the name is friendly, so an agent reading the contract finds nothing wrong. Preflight scores it HIGH 94, because it asks a different question: not what the contract says, but what it has done. An agent crosses five boundaries. What it installs, what it reads, what it trusts, what it submits, and what it is allowed to do. Four of those have somebody defending them. The one nobody defends is what the agent reads, and it is the cheapest of the five to attack. Preflight sits at that boundary. It ships as an MCP server, so the check happens inside the agent that was about to sign. Eleven weighted signals, four of which read Uniswap V3 pool state through The Graph across Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Source code tells you what a contract may do. Indexed pool history tells you what it has done, and only one of those predicts a rug. The score is arithmetic, not a judgement call. The same address in the same on-chain state gives the same answer every time, and the language model in the pipeline writes one advisory paragraph that structurally cannot move the number. Every on-chain string is treated as hostile. It gets sealed before a model reads it and wrapped in an unpredictable nonce before an agent does. When the verdict is high, the approval leaves software entirely and goes to a Ledger for a physical button press. Unplug the device and the flow breaks. That is the point: the device is the only part of the loop an attacker cannot reach over the network. This extends Inspector AI, which I built at ETHGlobal Singapore in 2024. Everything after the ethonline-2026-start tag is new. Twenty one hand verified addresses in the repo, zero false positives.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript throughout, pnpm workspaces, eight packages. The MCP server speaks stdio and exposes three tools, so an agent in Claude Code or Cursor calls preflight_check before it approves anything. The Graph is where the project earns its answers. Four of the eleven signals query the official Uniswap V3 subgraphs through the decentralised gateway with a Subgraph Studio key, on Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Uniswap ships identical subgraph code per chain, so one query string covers all three and only the deployment id changes. That is the reason this supports three chains instead of one. Pool queries run on both sides of the pair because a Uniswap pair is directional and a token on the wrong side would be invisible. Etherscan V2 supplies source, ABI, proxy resolution and transfer history. Scoring is noisy-OR over independent evidence rather than a weighted average. Averaging assumes findings dilute each other, and they do not: a pool holding 1.1 trillion dollars that four transactions have touched is damning on its own. Under averaging that address scored 18 and read LOW. It now reads HIGH 94. An AI agent can read a contract, decide it looks fine, and sign against it with no human in the loop. The text it reads to make that decision was written by whoever deployed the contract, for the price of gas.

Here is a real token on Ethereum mainnet. It reports 1.1 trillion dollars of liquidity. Four transactions have touched it in four years. The source is verified and the name is friendly, so an agent reading the contract finds nothing wrong. Preflight scores it HIGH 94, because it asks a different question: not what the contract says, but what it has done.

An agent crosses five boundaries. What it installs, what it reads, what it trusts, what it submits, and what it is allowed to do. Four of those have somebody defending them. The one nobody defends is what the agent reads, and it is the cheapest of the five to attack.

Preflight sits at that boundary. It ships as an MCP server, so the check happens inside the agent that was about to sign. Eleven weighted signals, four of which read Uniswap V3 pool state through The Graph across Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Source code tells you what a contract may do. Indexed pool history tells you what it has done, and only one of those predicts a rug.

The score is arithmetic, not a judgement call. The same address in the same on-chain state gives the same answer every time, and the language model in the pipeline writes one advisory paragraph that structurally cannot move the number.

Every on-chain string is treated as hostile. It gets sealed before a model reads it and wrapped in an unpredictable nonce before an agent does. When the verdict is high, the approval leaves software entirely and goes to a Ledger for a physical button press. Unplug the device and the flow breaks. That is the point: the device is the only part of the loop an attacker cannot reach over the network.

This extends Inspector AI, which I built at ETHGlobal Singapore in 2024. Everything after the ethonline-2026-start tag is new. Twenty one hand verified addresses in the repo, zero false positives.

projects.title: Clearing Bell
projects.description: Batch auctions for tokenized bonds on Hedera, with one clearing price and eligibility checks.
projects.project_description: Putting a bond on-chain is only half the job. The harder question is what happens when its holder wants to sell. Clearing Bell is a secondary-market prototype for tokenized bonds on Hedera. It brings buyers and sellers together in timed batch auctions: participants submit public limit orders, and the clearing engine determines a single price for matched trades. Eligible orders can fill partially, and an auction with no matching demand closes without forcing a trade. We chose this approach for assets that may not trade every second. Gathering orders into a shared window gives buyers and sellers a common moment for price discovery, without requiring a continuously funded liquidity pool. Eligibility is part of the trading process. The contracts check the bond’s configured identity registry when an order is submitted and recheck eligibility before settlement. Matched bond and payment-token transfers execute together in one transaction. The architecture also supports a curated multi-issuer model. A platform administrator registers bond issuers, while bond-specific permissions govern their auction operations. The frontend brings markets, auction depth, wallet balances, settlement records and issuer controls into one workspace. Our focus is the gap between issuing a digital asset and giving its holders a usable market. Clearing Bell is currently a hackathon prototype; multi-issuer workflow validation and security hardening remain in progress.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Clearing Bell with Solidity contracts, a React and TypeScript frontend, and Hedera’s EVM-compatible testnet. The frontend uses Vite and viem to read contract state and prepare wallet transactions directly, without a separate application server. The auction logic is split between AuctionEngine and a pure ClearingLib library. The library evaluates executable demand and supply across submitted price levels, selects a uniform clearing price, and allocates fills using price priority and submission order. Keeping the calculation separate from token transfers makes the matching logic easier to inspect and test. Settlement uses a collect-and-distribute flow inside one transaction. We also handle token amounts using integer base units, with explicit decimal conversion between bond quantities and payment tokens. This matters because small rounding errors can otherwise leave settlement underfunded or create leftover balances. Our Hedera integration includes bond-deployment scripts targeting the Asset Tokenization Studio factory and a compliance gate that queries the configured identity registry. One particularly tricky integration detail was matching the deployed ATS factory’s ABI: the scripts explicitly encode its v7 bond-creation structure, whose field order differs from newer versions.
For the interface, we built reusable auction charts from actual order-book data, wallet-session restoration, and separate investor and issuer views. Three.js provides optional spatial visuals, with still-image fallbacks and reduced-motion support. We use Foundry and Anvil for contract development, alongside frontend tests, TypeScript and ESLint. The repository also includes a Uniswap v4 hook integration, but the current frontend routes directly to the auction engine; real PoolManager integration is not presented as a completed production flow.

projects.title: Sight
projects.description: Sight — selfie-proofed human agents on ENSv2, with on-chain reputations you can graph and trust
projects.project_description: Sight, what we originally called Agent Passport, is an abuse-prevention primitive for the agentic-web era. The problem we’re trying to solve looks a bit like this: anyone with an automated script and some compute can spin up 50 sock-puppet agents, Sybil an application, and farm reputation or rewards. As autonomous agents increasingly interact with applications, marketplaces, and each other, there is currently very little tying an agent’s identity back to a real, unique participant. Sight operators on a very simple principle: one verified human ⇒ one wallet ⇒ a set of trusted agents. Every agent is registered on ENSv2’s Sepolia deployment under the root agentpassport.eth . It is impossible to register one without first passing a live World Selfie Check. There is no CAPTCHA and no KYC involved—only a ZK-backed proof that the wallet belongs to a unique human. Once verified, a human can register individual agent subnames beneath agentpassport.eth . Each agent identity carries three independent records: who owns the name, whether that owner has been verified as a unique human, and the agent’s reputation score. This separates human provenance from agent reputation: verification establishes that an agent ultimately originates from a scarce human identity, while reputation captures how that particular agent has behaved over time. All of this state can be indexed through a The Graph subgraph, allowing applications to efficiently query verified humans, registered agents, ownership relationships, and reputation without repeatedly reading raw contract state. On top of this, an MCP server exposes the same trust layer directly to AI systems. An agent can therefore ask questions such as “Is agent-x backed by a verified human?”, “Who controls this agent?”, or “What reputation has this agent accumulated?” before deciding whether to interact with it. The goal is to give the agentic web something it currently lacks: a lightweight, privacy-preserving way for agents and applications to distinguish persistent, human-backed identities from an unlimited swarm of disposable ones.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are written in Solidity, with Foundry, against ENSv2's Sepolia registry. The app itself is a just React + Vite + ethers v6. The backend is an Express verifier uses World's Developer Portal /verify API and calls HumanVerification. the frontends IDKit widget mints a Selfie Check Proof which the backend validates against World. So now a verified human can register an Agent. This mints a "agent passpot" and configures the EAC role bitmaps and sets the initial records. Reputation writes go through onlyScorer. Everything that emits state is indexed by Graph Node and queried via GraphQL from both the dashboard and the MCP server. Some of the things we'd love to improve on: the nullifier claim is held in an in-memory set. We'd like to swap that to a store. Right now, since we're based of in India, World selfie checks dont really work. So for the purposes of the video we've set it to testing.

projects.title: ArcSet
projects.description: ArcSet turns a DeFi thesis into a self-custodial portfolio you can review and execute on Arc.
projects.project_description: ArcSet is a self-custodial portfolio app for Arc Testnet. It turns an investment thesis, such as stablecoin yield, Bitcoin income, currency diversification, or cross-chain liquidity, into a basket with clear target weights. Users create a Circle modular wallet secured by a device passkey, fund it with USDC, inspect the assets, protocols, risks, fees, and exit paths, then request a fresh execution plan. Every swap, vault deposit, minimum output, and estimated fee is shown before signing. ArcSet uses Circle App Kit to swap USDC into EURC or cirBTC and EarnKit to deposit USDC into a screened Morpho ERC-4626 vault. Its experimental cross-chain basket deposits part of the investment on Arc, bridges canonical USDC to Base Sepolia through CCTP, swaps half for WETH, and creates a Uniswap V3 liquidity position. Confirmed steps are recorded, allowing an interrupted route to resume without repeating an earlier transaction or bridge burn. Assets and positions remain in the user's wallet. ArcSet reads live balances, values holdings, links receipts to each basket, calculates allocation drift, and provides reviewed exit and rebalance flows. Since Arc uses USDC for gas, the same balance can fund investments and network fees. The project also includes a Messari-compatible Graph subgraph for Morpho deposits, withdrawals, TVL, and vault activity.
projects.how_its_made: We built ArcSet with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, viem, and Circle's Arc stack. The frontend talks to Arc Testnet through viem, with fallback RPC endpoints for balance reads, contract checks, and transaction receipts. Circle Modular Wallets provide the wallet layer. A device passkey controls a Circle smart account, so users never handle a private key. We wrote a custom EIP-1193 provider that translates standard wallet calls into sponsored ERC-4337 user operations through Circle's bundler and paymaster. It supports wallet_sendCalls , transaction status polling, and regular transaction requests, which lets Circle App Kit work with the passkey wallet on both Arc Testnet and Base Sepolia. Circle App Kit supplies fresh swap quotes for USDC, EURC, and cirBTC. Each quote includes fees and a 1% minimum output before execution. EarnKit discovers the active Morpho USDC vault on Arc. We then verify the vault ourselves by checking its deployed bytecode and ERC-4626 asset() , decimals() , and totalAssets() responses. ArcSet rejects mock or inactive vaults, non-USDC assets, and vaults with red risk warnings. Each basket is a versioned set of execution adapters. An adapter must support entry, exit, position reads, and valuation before its strategy appears in the catalog. Composite baskets quote every leg together, then execute the swaps and Morpho deposit in sequence. We record each confirmed transaction separately. If a later step fails, ArcSet keeps the completed receipts and retries only the unfinished steps with fresh quotes. The cross-chain basket uses Circle CCTP to bridge canonical USDC from Arc to Base Sepolia. It deposits one part into Morpho on Arc, bridges another part, swaps half of the received USDC for WETH, and mints a wide-range Uniswap V3 LP NFT. Exact approvals, minimum outputs, and a Testnet pool-price sanity check protect the Uniswap steps. We persist progress after each stage so resuming the route cannot repeat a completed CCTP burn. One surprisingly tricky Arc detail is USDC accounting. Arc exposes the same underlying USDC balance through an 18-decimal native interface for gas and a 6-decimal ERC-20 interface for transfers and approvals. ArcSet treats these as one asset, uses the ERC-20 view for portfolio accounting, and reserves the native view for gas and msg.value . This avoids displaying or counting the same money twice. We also wrote a Messari Yield Aggregator compatible subgraph for The Graph. It indexes Morpho ERC-4626 deposits and withdrawals on Arc and calculates vault activity, TVL, share supply, and user metrics. The portfolio view combines live onchain balances with locally recorded execution attribution, then calculates allocation drift and prepares user-reviewed exit or rebalance actions.

projects.title: Cope Market
projects.description: A social feed where every take is backed by a real USDC position.
projects.project_description: Cope Market is a social feed where every opinion costs something. You post a thesis — an asset, a direction, and your reasoning — and back it with real USDC. Other people can copy your position with one tap, and if their copy closes in profit, you get paid automatically, on-chain, by the contract. The problem it solves is that financial opinions are free to give and impossible to score. Crypto Twitter is full of calls nobody tracks, from people with no position. Here a thesis without a position is visibly marked as such, every track record is derived from settled trades rather than self-reported, and the incentive to share a good call is paid by the protocol instead of by a sponsorship deal. Positions are synthetic and oracle-priced. A shared USDC pool is the counterparty to every trade — LPs deposit into an ERC-4626 vault, traders' losses and fees become LP yield, traders' wins come out of the pool. Each position is an ERC-721 you actually hold and can sell; the credit for the call stays with whoever opened it, so buying someone's position doesn't buy their leaderboard rank. The copy mechanic is where the money flow gets interesting. A copy records which position it followed and the author's fee rate at that moment, so changing the protocol's fee later never rewrites a deal someone already took. On a profitable close the contract pays the original author a share of the profit only — never the notional, and capped at the payout so it can't be funded out of anyone else's collateral. The author never signs that transaction and may not know it happened. There's no invoice and nothing to reconcile. It runs on Arc, where USDC is the collateral, the quote asset and the gas, so no leg of that settlement touches a second token. Everything described is deployed and verified on Arc testnet: three contracts, three subgraphs across two chains, an MCP server, and two always-on services. The numbers in our demo were read from the chain, not typed into a slide — the indexed open interest reconciles to openInterest() on the contract to the wei.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.36, Foundry). SyntheticVault mints ERC-721 positions and does all settlement; LiquidityVault is an ERC-4626 pool whose totalAssets nets out what it owes open positions, so an LP can't deposit just before traders lose and withdraw just before they win. Entry prices are skewed against the trader by the oracle's confidence interval — a long enters at mid + conf, a short at mid − conf — so the pool never takes the oracle's uncertainty onto its own balance sheet. 166 Foundry tests including fuzz and invariant runs. Arc / Circle. USDC being native is not a detail here. Collateral, the pool's balance sheet, the author fee, the payout and the gas are one asset, so the conditional settlement has no swap, no wrapped representation and no price risk between the leg that pays and the leg that settles. One thing that catches people: Arc's native currency is USDC at 18 decimals and the ERC-20 at 0x3600…0000 is the same balance at 6. Gas therefore moves your USDC balance, and we had to account for that when reconciling — our liquidation test came out 3,920 units short until we realised the gap was gas. The Graph. Three subgraphs. One indexes any ERC-4626 vault — nothing about Cope Market appears in its schema, its mappings, or even its ABI, which is hand-written from the standard rather than exported from our vault. We proved that by pointing the same unmodified code at two MetaMorpho vaults on Base from a config file: a 6-decimal-asset vault and an 18-decimal one, priced correctly by the same expression. Then an MCP server on top, seven tools that compute drawdown, windowed rankings and whether copying a given author has actually paid — deliberately no raw GraphQL passthrough, and a test that fails if a tool name ever looks like one. Privy. X login creates an embedded wallet, and Arc is registered as a custom chain via defineChain so that wallet signs Arc transactions directly — no extension, no seed phrase. The backend holds no key at all: it validates, quotes, simulates the call as you with eth_call, and hands back an unsigned transaction. A compromised API server can lie to a user but cannot move their money. Backend. Next.js with Postgres holding only social content — theses, follows, comments. Wipe it and every position, balance and copy relationship survives on-chain. Routes are declared once as zod schemas, folded into an OpenAPI 3.1 document, and compiled into a typed client that's vendored into the frontend with a CI check that fails on drift. Pyth's pull oracle does not work on Arc. We proved it with a cross-chain control: the identical Hermes blob is accepted on Base mainnet and rejected on Arc testnet with InvalidWormholeVaa. Root cause is that Arc's Wormhole receiver holds Wormhole's guardian set (19 guardians) instead of Pythnet's (5) — not our bug, and not fixable from our side. Because the vault only ever knew an IPriceOracle, swapping to a push oracle was a constructor argument plus a service, not a rewrite. So we wrote a price pusher that fetches from Hermes, rescales to 18 decimals in exact BigInt arithmetic, drops feeds whose timestamps haven't moved, and — crucially — judges its own success by reading the oracle back and comparing each feed's age to that asset's maxAgeSec, because a mined transaction is not a usable price.

Collateral, the pool's balance sheet, the author fee, the payout and the gas are one asset, so the conditional settlement has no swap, no wrapped representation and no price risk between the leg that pays and the leg that settles. One thing that catches people: Arc's native currency is USDC at 18 decimals and the ERC-20 at 0x3600…0000 is the same balance at 6. Gas therefore moves your USDC balance, and we had to account for that when reconciling — our liquidation test came out 3,920 units short until we realised the gap was gas.

The Graph. Three subgraphs. One indexes any ERC-4626 vault — nothing about Cope Market appears in its schema, its mappings, or even its ABI, which is hand-written from the standard rather than exported from our vault. We proved that by pointing the same unmodified code at two MetaMorpho vaults on Base from a config file: a 6-decimal-asset vault and an 18-decimal one, priced correctly by the same expression. Then an MCP server on top, seven tools that compute drawdown, windowed rankings and whether copying a given author has actually paid — deliberately no raw GraphQL passthrough, and a test that fails if a tool name ever looks like one.

Privy. X login creates an embedded wallet, and Arc is registered as a custom chain via defineChain so that wallet signs Arc transactions directly — no extension, no seed phrase. The backend holds no key at all: it validates, quotes, simulates the call as you with eth_call, and hands back an unsigned transaction. A compromised API server can lie to a user but cannot move their money.

Backend. Next.js with Postgres holding only social content — theses, follows, comments. Wipe it and every position, balance and copy relationship survives on-chain. Routes are declared once as zod schemas, folded into an OpenAPI 3.1 document, and compiled into a typed client that's vendored into the frontend with a CI check that fails on drift.

Pyth's pull oracle does not work on Arc. We proved it with a cross-chain control: the identical Hermes blob is accepted on Base mainnet and rejected on Arc testnet with InvalidWormholeVaa. Root cause is that Arc's Wormhole receiver holds Wormhole's guardian set (19 guardians) instead of Pythnet's (5) — not our bug, and not fixable from our side. Because the vault only ever knew an IPriceOracle, swapping to a push oracle was a constructor argument plus a service, not a rewrite. So we wrote a price pusher that fetches from Hermes, rescales to 18 decimals in exact BigInt arithmetic, drops feeds whose timestamps haven't moved, and — crucially — judges its own success by reading the oracle back and comparing each feed's age to that asset's maxAgeSec, because a mined transaction is not a usable price.

projects.title: alpha402
projects.description: An on-chain market where AI agents pay for live signals on Hedera and act on Uniswap.
projects.project_description:
AI trading agents can't participate in markets on their own. Every API key,
card, and subscription assumes a human is present to buy the data, and placing
a trade still needs a person to click "swap" — so an agent that should run
autonomously ends up needing someone at both ends. The rails for
machine-to-machine commerce, where software pays for a read and then acts on
it, simply don't exist yet. alpha402 builds those rails. It's a market made for machines: instead of a raw
API, it sells synthesized market alpha — whale flows and volume momentum pulled
live from Uniswap through The Graph, fused with macro news by AI into a single
market read. An agent queries the signals, reads them, and pays for exactly
what it uses, per query, with x402 on Hedera; or it holds an on-chain HTS
subscription pass for the recurring AI brief. Then it acts on the answer: the
agent recommends a Uniswap pool and executes a real swap, with no human in the
loop. Every payment is a genuine on-chain transaction that settles on Hedera
and leaves a verifiable receipt on HashScan, and the whole payment engine ships
as a reusable npm package so any agent can plug in. The economics are part of the design. Raw signals are metered per query, while
the AI brief runs on a schedule and is cached and gated by a subscription pass
rather than charged on every request — which is the reason the pass exists at
all. You can watch the entire loop end to end: ask a question, subscribe on
Hedera, and the autonomous agent reads the market and pays for the data it
needs on its own, out loud, before recommending a pool and swapping on Uniswap.
Every "paid" line is a real settled transaction you can open on HashScan.
projects.how_its_made:
alpha402 is one pnpm monorepo, and data flows through it Uniswap to The Graph
to AI to Hedera to pay, then back to Uniswap to invest. The reusable payment
engine lives in packages/hedera-x402 and is published to npm as alpha402 ; it
handles both sides of x402, mints and verifies HTS passes, writes HCS receipts,
and schedules renewals, so any agent can run npm i alpha402 and plug straight
in. On top of it, apps/api is a single Hono server that serves the feed
catalog, gates each feed, runs the signal scheduler and the autonomous agent
loop, and settles payments, while apps/web is a React (Vite) dashboard the same
server serves in production. The whole thing deploys as one Docker image on
Fly.io, with the API and the dashboard on a single port behind an SPA fallback,
so the entire product is one deploy. Hedera is the settlement core and roughly eighty percent of the build.
Per-query payments run through x402 via the blocky402 facilitator, priced
dynamically rather than flat. Subscriptions mint an NFT pass on the Hedera Token
Service to the agent's wallet, and entitlement is checked against the mirror
node — hold a valid, unexpired pass and the AI brief is served with no payment.
Every payment and subscription writes an audit record to a Hedera Consensus
Service topic, all verifiable on HashScan, and recurring renewals are queued
on-chain with Scheduled Transactions. An autonomous buying agent completes real
paid requests end to end. The market signals come from live Uniswap v3 subgraph queries on The Graph,
using a real Studio key rather than mocked data: whale swaps above a USD
threshold, and volume and liquidity momentum measured today against the prior
day. A watchlist and a watcher loop turn watched-wallet activity into a
near-real-time smart-money feed, and the AI reasons over all of it, with each
query paid per request through x402. The AI itself is OpenAI, behind a
provider-agnostic llm() function so it swaps to Claude or a local model with one
line, running on a scheduler and cached between requests. When the agent acts, it executes a real swap on Unichain Sepolia through the
Uniswap Trading API, running the full Permit2 flow: quote, approve to Permit2,
sign a PermitSingle, submit to the swap endpoint with the signature, simulate
with eth_call, then broadcast — verified with live testnet swaps of USDC into
WETH. Two things fought back along the way. The published hak-uniswap-plugin
never signed the Permit2 permit, so swaps reverted with no logs until we rewrote
the swap path to sign the PermitSingle ourselves; and the public Unichain
Sepolia RPCs accepted transactions but never mined them, so tx.wait hung until
we moved to an RPC that actually confirms. Across the three sponsors it is one product. For Hedera, it is x402 plus HTS
passes plus HCS receipts and real HashScan transactions, with an agent
completing paid requests end to end. For The Graph, it is live subgraph queries
with AI reasoning over them, each one paid per query with x402. And for Uniswap,
it is pool intelligence the agent acts on with a real swap through the Trading
API and Permit2, with our developer notes written up in FEEDBACK.md.

projects.title: zBase
projects.description: zBase enables private x402 agentic payments onchain, using ZK Privacy Pools and sanctions screening.
projects.project_description:
zBase is a private payment rail for AI agents on Base. It lets an agent fund a Privacy Pool with USDC, withdraw to a fresh address using a zero-knowledge proof, and pay an x402 API seller without exposing the direct on-chain link between the agent’s original funding wallet and the seller. zBase is proud to be a Base Batches 003 finalist, selected as one of 12 teams in Base’s Spring 2026 program. The cohort focuses on companies building across AI, DeFi, prediction markets, stablecoins, and agentic payments, with Demo Day held in San Francisco.
base
+1 For ETHOnline, we focused on two things: helping agents make honest privacy decisions and making paid API trials harder to farm.
projects.how_its_made: Technical implementation The Graph subgraph We built the zbase-pool-base subgraph with @graphprotocol/graph-cli 0.98 and AssemblyScript mappings. It uses minimal contract ABIs taken from the vendored 0xbow Privacy Pool contracts, with Base configured as the default network in networks.json . We identified the correct Base mainnet deployment start block by binary-searching eth_getCode , rather than assuming a block number and risking missed historical events. The subgraph is deployed on The Graph Subgraph Studio and synced to the current chain head: https://api.studio.thegraph.com/query/1760283/zbase-pool-base/version/latest We verified that the roots indexed by the subgraph match the values returned on-chain by currentRoot() and latestRoot() . pool-state decision tool We built pool-state as both an MCP tool and a CLI command in run.ts . It queries the subgraph directly using plain fetch and GraphQL, then passes the result into a pure decidePoolState() function with unit tests. Keeping the decision logic pure and tested makes the payment decision predictable, reviewable, and easy to reuse across agent environments. Before a payment, pool-state checks for subgraph indexing errors through _meta , reads the current ASP root and leaf count, converts 256-bit root values safely using BigInt , and cross-checks the result with the facilitator. If the subgraph is unavailable, missing, or returning indexing errors, the tool fails closed. The agent does not attempt a privacy payment when it cannot verify the pool state. The tool is registered in our MCP server through @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and exposed through the run.ts CLI. SKILL.md documents when an AI agent should call it before making a payment. World AgentKit integration We integrated @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1 into the x402 seller built with @x402/express 2.11. The integration uses registerExtension , onProtectedRequest , and createAgentBookVerifier to verify AgentBook-backed identities and enforce human-level free-call limits. We added a file-persisted AgentKitStorage implementation that stores per-human trial counters and a capped nonce replay-protection window. The cap is important because an unbounded nonce store could be abused to exhaust storage or memory over time. The stock AgentKit hook does not include a request ID, so we use AsyncLocalStorage to safely associate hook events with the correct incoming request. The entire World integration is behind an AGENTKIT_ENABLED feature flag. When the flag is disabled, the seller remains byte-identical to the original payment-only implementation. We added 15 node:test cases covering the key trial, verification, replay-protection, and payment paths. We also built a demo client with a fetch shim to handle the x402 interoperability issue where the payment challenge may be delivered in a response header rather than the response body. Mainnet safeguards and RPC compatibility The demo registry stub intentionally throws during startup on Base mainnet. This prevents development-only identity behavior from accidentally being enabled in production. We also fixed the seller’s eth_getLogs behavior. The original implementation queried a 50,000-block range, but public Base RPC endpoints enforce a 2,000-block cap. The seller now scans logs in ranges compatible with public Base RPC limits.

For ETHOnline, we focused on two things: helping agents make honest privacy decisions and making paid API trials harder to farm.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
## Technical implementation

### The Graph subgraph

We built the `zbase-pool-base` subgraph with `@graphprotocol/graph-cli` 0.98 and AssemblyScript mappings. It uses minimal contract ABIs taken from the vendored 0xbow Privacy Pool contracts, with Base configured as the default network in `networks.json`.

We identified the correct Base mainnet deployment start block by binary-searching `eth_getCode`, rather than assuming a block number and risking missed historical events.

The subgraph is deployed on The Graph Subgraph Studio and synced to the current chain head:

[https://api.studio.thegraph.com/query/1760283/zbase-pool-base/version/latest](https://api.studio.thegraph.com/query/1760283/zbase-pool-base/version/latest)

We verified that the roots indexed by the subgraph match the values returned on-chain by `currentRoot()` and `latestRoot()`.

### pool-state decision tool

We built `pool-state` as both an MCP tool and a CLI command in `run.ts`.

It queries the subgraph directly using plain `fetch` and GraphQL, then passes the result into a pure `decidePoolState()` function with unit tests. Keeping the decision logic pure and tested makes the payment decision predictable, reviewable, and easy to reuse across agent environments.

Before a payment, `pool-state` checks for subgraph indexing errors through `_meta`, reads the current ASP root and leaf count, converts 256-bit root values safely using `BigInt`, and cross-checks the result with the facilitator.

If the subgraph is unavailable, missing, or returning indexing errors, the tool fails closed. The agent does not attempt a privacy payment when it cannot verify the pool state.

The tool is registered in our MCP server through `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and exposed through the `run.ts` CLI. `SKILL.md` documents when an AI agent should call it before making a payment.

### World AgentKit integration

We integrated `@worldcoin/agentkit` 0.2.1 into the x402 seller built with `@x402/express` 2.11.

The integration uses `registerExtension`, `onProtectedRequest`, and `createAgentBookVerifier` to verify AgentBook-backed identities and enforce human-level free-call limits.

We added a file-persisted `AgentKitStorage` implementation that stores per-human trial counters and a capped nonce replay-protection window. The cap is important because an unbounded nonce store could be abused to exhaust storage or memory over time.

The stock AgentKit hook does not include a request ID, so we use `AsyncLocalStorage` to safely associate hook events with the correct incoming request.

The entire World integration is behind an `AGENTKIT_ENABLED` feature flag. When the flag is disabled, the seller remains byte-identical to the original payment-only implementation.

We added 15 `node:test` cases covering the key trial, verification, replay-protection, and payment paths. We also built a demo client with a fetch shim to handle the x402 interoperability issue where the payment challenge may be delivered in a response header rather than the response body.

### Mainnet safeguards and RPC compatibility

The demo registry stub intentionally throws during startup on Base mainnet. This prevents development-only identity behavior from accidentally being enabled in production.

We also fixed the seller’s `eth_getLogs` behavior. The original implementation queried a 50,000-block range, but public Base RPC endpoints enforce a 2,000-block cap. The seller now scans logs in ranges compatible with public Base RPC limits.

projects.title: Star Wallet
projects.description: Kids earn USDC-backed Stars while parents save through 1inch Aqua, SwapVM and The Graph.
projects.project_description: Star Wallet helps families turn kids' completed tasks into onchain savings: parents award Stars backed by matching USDC deposits, then manage those savings through 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. The child sees Stars, quests and goals. A device passkey can sign only those actions; it cannot transfer tokens, withdraw savings, trade assets or call arbitrary contracts. The parent uses a normal Ethereum wallet and retains control over USDC, WETH, savings positions and financial approvals. When a parent awards five Stars, the same transaction contributes five USDC to the family vault and issues five STAR to the child. If the USDC transfer fails, the STAR issuance also fails. STAR is a zero-decimal, non-transferable reward token. It is not a stablecoin, a claim on one USDC or a share of the vault. After issuance, the reward and savings ledgers are independent. A child can spend Stars while the original savings remain invested, change in value or are withdrawn by the parent. Parents can keep the contributed USDC in the family vault or combine it with WETH in a programmable savings position powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua tracks the position's balances, SwapVM handles exchanges between USDC and WETH, and the vault applies Chainlink-based price and safety checks before any position is opened or changed. The Graph turns the protocol's Sepolia events into the family data shown throughout Star Wallet, including children, Star balances, quests, goals, requests, savings positions and activity history. Live blockchain reads are still used whenever current balances, permissions or transaction status must be confirmed.
projects.how_its_made: Star Wallet runs on Ethereum Sepolia. Its Solidity contracts separate the system into family registration, child accounts, quests, goals, STAR accounting and one isolated savings vault per family. STAR is a zero-decimal, non-transferable ERC-20. Issuing a reward atomically deposits one USDC of principal into the family vault, so the deposit and reward either both succeed or both fail. Parents sign financial actions with their Ethereum wallets and always retain custody. Children use WebAuthn P-256 passkeys through deterministic ERC-4337 smart accounts. Each child operation travels through Alchemy’s Bundler and Paymaster to EntryPoint v0.8. Gas sponsorship gives children a wallet-free experience, while the smart account’s onchain allowlist prevents transfers, withdrawals, arbitrary contract calls and other actions outside Star Wallet. The savings system integrates 1inch Aqua’s virtual-balance accounting with SwapVM’s programmable execution. The family vault remains the maker and allocates its available USDC and WETH to a concentrated-liquidity strategy. We built an SDK-free viem encoder that reproduces canonical token ordering, maker traits, strategy hashes and SwapVM instruction bytes. Before accepting a position, the vault independently decodes and verifies the maker, token pair, fee, salt, deadline and program structure. Chainlink feeds enforce fresh prices, bounded ranges and maximum USDC/WETH exposure. Positions can be opened, topped up, replaced, safely closed, paused and recovered during emergencies. The Graph is the system’s read layer. Custom AssemblyScript mappings index Star Registry, STAR, Goals, Quests, family-vault, Aqua and SwapVM events. Dynamic data-source templates start indexing each new family vault and quest contract as it is deployed. Aqua events can occur before the corresponding vault position event within the same transaction, so we queue and replay those events in log order using the maker and strategy hash as the position identity. Subgraph responses are pinned to the expected deployment and verified against Sepolia RPC block state. ENSv2 provides commit-reveal family namespaces and permissioned child subdomains that resolve to each child’s deterministic smart account. The application is built with Next.js, TypeScript, wagmi and viem, with a Fastify service that verifies deployments, prepares transaction intents and Aqua strategies, validates live protocol state and constrains sponsored RPC requests. Together, these components keep parents in control of funds, limit children to safe family actions and provide responsive indexed data without replacing live onchain verification.

projects.title: Strikeline
projects.description: Name a price to sell your ETH at and get paid to wait. Covered calls on 1inch Aqua.
projects.project_description: Strikeline lets anyone holding ETH name a price they'd sell at, pick an expiry, and earn while they wait, without the ETH ever leaving their wallet. Each offer is a covered call written as a pricing curve on 1inch Aqua. With nothing locked, one wallet can back many offers: in the demo, a wallet holding 10.4 ETH backs offers for 15.4 ETH at once, and every trade checks the real balance so it can never owe more than it holds. Example: ETH trades at $2,440 and you hold 10 ETH. You'd happily sell 5 of them at $2,600. In Strikeline you pick that price, an expiry one week out and a volatility, then publish the offer in one click. All 10 ETH stay in your wallet. The offer is a quote registered on 1inch Aqua that traders can fill. Volatility (IV) is how much you expect ETH to move, as a yearly percentage, and it sets the shape of the curve. A higher IV prices each trade further from the market, so trades are rarer but earn more. A lower IV gives tighter pricing and more frequent, smaller trades. The app pre-fills it from how much ETH has actually moved recently. While the offer is live, nobody pays more than the market price. If ETH moves on other exchanges by more than your offer's spread, 1inch resolvers trade with it. When ETH rises, the offer sells a little ETH. When it falls, the offer buys some back. The spread widens in both directions every day, so small wiggles don't trigger trades. Your result is the P&L of a covered call. It works like selling insurance: you come out ahead if ETH moves less than the volatility you chose, and behind if it moves more. At expiry, if ETH is above $2,600, whatever remains of the 5 ETH sells at exactly $2,600. If ETH is below, nothing more sells and you keep your ETH. One wallet, many offers: every trade checks your real wallet balance and your approval to Aqua. A fill on one offer immediately shrinks what the others can deliver, with no keeper, so you can post more offers than you could fill at once and never owe a trade you can't pay. There is no vault, no option token, no oracle and no settlement transaction. There is also a buy side: an offer to buy ETH below today's price with USDC. Every fill pays a 0.10% protocol fee. The app shows each offer's fill progress and average sale price, how its spread widens over time, and its payoff at expiry compared with just holding. It also notifies you when an offer is filled or withdrawn. Withdrawing takes one click and moves no tokens. Limits: you earn only when someone trades, and you end up behind holding when ETH moves more than you priced. I replayed a week of real Base ETH prices on a four-offer book of about $50k. It beat holding by $201. When the offers were written far below realised volatility (15% vs 46.6%), a plain 5 bp liquidity pool beat it. What's next: a mainnet launch on Base with a real audit; more pairs beyond ETH/USDC (cbBTC, LSTs); ladders, where one click writes a spread of strikes and expiries from a single wallet; automatic rolling into the next expiry when an offer ends; and routing so Strikeline offers show up directly inside 1inch swaps for regular traders.
projects.how_its_made: Strikeline is built on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Every offer is a SwapVM program shipped to the official, unmodified Aqua registry (0x1111113CCf1426A8E30e2bfF5E005d929bF6a90a): Deadline, FeeProtocol, Coverage, RmmSwap, Salt. projects.project_description_markdown:
Strikeline lets anyone holding ETH name a price they'd sell at, pick an expiry, and earn while they wait, without the ETH ever leaving their wallet. Each offer is a covered call written as a pricing curve on 1inch Aqua. With nothing locked, one wallet can back many offers: in the demo, a wallet holding 10.4 ETH backs offers for 15.4 ETH at once, and every trade checks the real balance so it can never owe more than it holds.

Example: ETH trades at $2,440 and you hold 10 ETH. You'd happily sell 5 of them at $2,600. In Strikeline you pick that price, an expiry one week out and a volatility, then publish the offer in one click. All 10 ETH stay in your wallet. The offer is a quote registered on 1inch Aqua that traders can fill.

Volatility (IV) is how much you expect ETH to move, as a yearly percentage, and it sets the shape of the curve. A higher IV prices each trade further from the market, so trades are rarer but earn more. A lower IV gives tighter pricing and more frequent, smaller trades. The app pre-fills it from how much ETH has actually moved recently.

While the offer is live, nobody pays more than the market price. If ETH moves on other exchanges by more than your offer's spread, 1inch resolvers trade with it. When ETH rises, the offer sells a little ETH. When it falls, the offer buys some back. The spread widens in both directions every day, so small wiggles don't trigger trades. Your result is the P&L of a covered call. It works like selling insurance: you come out ahead if ETH moves less than the volatility you chose, and behind if it moves more.

At expiry, if ETH is above $2,600, whatever remains of the 5 ETH sells at exactly $2,600. If ETH is below, nothing more sells and you keep your ETH.

One wallet, many offers: every trade checks your real wallet balance and your approval to Aqua. A fill on one offer immediately shrinks what the others can deliver, with no keeper, so you can post more offers than you could fill at once and never owe a trade you can't pay. There is no vault, no option token, no oracle and no settlement transaction. There is also a buy side: an offer to buy ETH below today's price with USDC. Every fill pays a 0.10% protocol fee.

The app shows each offer's fill progress and average sale price, how its spread widens over time, and its payoff at expiry compared with just holding. It also notifies you when an offer is filled or withdrawn. Withdrawing takes one click and moves no tokens.

Limits: you earn only when someone trades, and you end up behind holding when ETH moves more than you priced. I replayed a week of real Base ETH prices on a four-offer book of about $50k. It beat holding by $201. When the offers were written far below realised volatility (15% vs 46.6%), a plain 5 bp liquidity pool beat it.

What's next: a mainnet launch on Base with a real audit; more pairs beyond ETH/USDC (cbBTC, LSTs); ladders, where one click writes a spread of strikes and expiries from a single wallet; automatic rolling into the next expiry when an offer ends; and routing so Strikeline offers show up directly inside 1inch swaps for regular traders.

projects.title: Transvia
projects.description: Cross-border payments for humans and AI agents — USDC in, local currency out, onchain in seconds.
projects.project_description: Transvia is a cross-border payments platform on Arc, Circle’s stablecoin L1 where USDC is the gas token. Anyone holding USDC can send value to 11 destination currencies — EUR, GBP, MXN, BRL, PHP, NGN, AED, SGD, CAD, AUD, and INR — at a flat 0.50% fee shown upfront, with no hidden spread. Funds are locked in TransviaEscrow, an open-source, zero-dependency Solidity contract. Settlement executes three atomic onchain legs — FX, payout, and fee split — while recipients claim funds using a gasless EIP-712 signature from an embedded wallet created through email login with Privy. This removes seed phrases and gas-token friction from the receive flow. The same payment rail is machine-native. Transvia exposes a REST API, TypeScript SDK, MCP server at /api/mcp with six tools for AI assistants such as Claude, and an x402 HTTP payment layer where software pays 0.01 USDC per quote using EIP-3009 signatures. Automation agents monitor every transfer and record every decision. They purchase FX feeds through x402, apply compliance rules including holds above 5,000 USDC, and can trigger timeout refunds through the escrow contract’s agentFallback. The live system runs on Arc Testnet with real USDC, Neon Postgres persistence, and Vercel hosting. Every transfer has a complete, auditable trail including state transitions, agent decisions, and Arc explorer transaction hashes.
projects.how_its_made: Transvia uses hexagonal architecture: a framework-free core built from pure TypeScript domain logic, ports, and adapters, wired through a single composition root. The Next.js 16 application, REST routes, MCP server, and TypeScript SDK all call the same underlying services rather than maintaining separate implementations. Arc’s USDC-as-gas model eliminates the need for users and agents to acquire a separate gas token. Privy handles identity and embedded wallets: email login creates the recipient wallet, which signs the EIP-712 claim. Sessions are automatically restored on page load, with a browser-local demo wallet fallback when Privy is unavailable so the receive flow remains usable. Settlement is enforced by TransviaEscrow, an MIT-licensed, zero-dependency Solidity contract built without OpenZeppelin. We hand-rolled EIP-712 verification and a 20 Gwei gas floor. We also added AlreadySettled reconciliation after identifying and fixing a double-settlement race between concurrent state-machine advancers. For x402, we implemented the verification layer ourselves: EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization signatures are recovered with viem, checked against the payer, and recorded in a payments ledger. We validated the implementation with an independent client and confirmed that tampered signatures are rejected. A few deliberately hacky reliability features make the rail resilient: it self-heals the escrow’s maximum USDC allowance when approval drifts, while polling endpoints also advance in-flight transfers, effectively making GET requests part of the settlement state machine. This allows transfers to continue progressing without requiring a separate worker process.

projects.title: Exit Drill
projects.description: Turn treasury liquidity risk into bounded exits and independently verified settlement.
projects.project_description: A treasury balance is not a cash guarantee. A team holding WETH needs to know whether an exit can cover its cash commitments, control how that trade is executed, and prove what actually arrived. Exit Drill connects those decisions in one product. Users sign in, open a managed Sepolia treasury, fund its displayed address, and choose WETH from their actual balance. Optional risk analysis uses fresh Ethereum liquidity evidence to compare exit routes under a user-selected price shock. A portable risk brief preserves the source block, inputs, cash coverage, route comparison and modeling assumptions. When the user decides to trade, Exit Drill obtains a fresh Sepolia quote. The user reviews a bounded approval, minimum received and expiry before confirming. Proceeds return to the same treasury. After confirmation, a receipt reconciles settlement against token movements; anyone can independently verify the transaction, plan hash and output without signing in. The same evidence and analysis engine is available through a reusable, read-only MCP server for external AI hosts. It compares scenarios against a single Graph snapshot and produces structured cash-coverage assessments, while leaving trade authorization to the human. This release executes actual Sepolia transactions with custom test WETH/USDC and independent Uniswap v3 pools. The assets have no monetary value. Ethereum risk estimates and Sepolia execution quotes are clearly separated. The liquidity model infers full-range pools from live TVL and price.
projects.how_its_made: Exit Drill uses Next.js, React, TypeScript and viem, with Solidity execution guards and a responsive treasury interface. The Graph adapter queries Ethereum Uniswap v3 WETH/USDC pools at 0.05% and 0.30% fees, reads liquidity and recent history, and rejects stale data or indexing errors. When a subgraph omits a timestamp, the adapter verifies the exact Ethereum block through RPC. The analysis engine deploys official Uniswap v3 bytecode to ephemeral Ganache chains, calibrates full-range liquidity from that evidence, applies the selected shock, and compares both routes using snapshots and reverts. This is a model, not a mainnet fork. A standalone MCP server exposes fresh evidence, treasury exit assessments and same-snapshot shock comparisons. It reuses the engine directly rather than calling the website, needs no Privy account, and exposes no signing tools. An external AI host supplies the language model. Privy verifies access tokens and maps each authenticated account to a managed treasury. Attached signing policies restrict Sepolia, contract addresses and methods. Each backend action verifies treasury ownership. The Solidity executor fixes the router and tokens and enforces the recipient, amount cap, fee allowlist, minimum output, expiry, nonce and reentrancy protection. Router approval is cleared after settlement. Wallets are app-managed rather than self-custodial. The public verifier reconstructs the plan hash from calldata, checks the executor and treasury, and reconciles USDC transfer logs against the settlement event. A recorded browser exit of 0.01 test WETH settled for 24.984094 test USDC on Sepolia. Unit tests, actual-EVM rejection tests, MCP protocol and stdio checks, and the production build pass in CI.

projects.title: TrustLine
projects.description: TrustLine lets AI agents privately verify solvency and automatically settle deals onchain.
projects.project_description: TrustLine is a trust and payment layer for autonomous AI agents. Before an agent pays for a deal, TrustLine privately verifies whether the agent can cover the required amount without revealing its wallet balance. Chainlink CRE handles the confidential solvency logic, while Privy provides a policy-controlled wallet for automated settlement. Bazantic makes the capability discoverable and callable by other agents through an x402-enabled service. If the private check returns SETTLE, the approved wallet can release the exact deal amount to the counterparty; if it returns INSUFFICIENT, payment is blocked. Our MVP demonstrates the complete orchestration on Base Sepolia, with the confidential CRE computation currently simulated locally due to CRE access constraints.
projects.how_its_made: TrustLine combines Bazantic, Chainlink CRE, Privy, and Base Sepolia into one agent-to-agent payment flow. An AI agent calls TrustLine through the Bazantic/x402 interface with a deal amount and reference ID. The backend passes the request to our solvency-check workflow, which determines whether the wallet can cover the deal without exposing its actual balance. A SETTLE result triggers the Privy policy-controlled wallet to authorize the payment, while INSUFFICIENT stops the flow. We use BigInt-based amount handling and reference IDs to prevent rounding errors and duplicate payments. The MVP uses a local simulation of the Chainlink confidential execution environment, while the wallet settlement path is designed for real Base Sepolia transactions.

projects.title: x402-validate
projects.description: Add validation layer to x402, so ai agent don't pay for low effort response
projects.project_description:
What this project is x402_validate is a Chainlink CRE (https://docs.chain.link/cre) (Chainlink Runtime Environment) workflow that acts as a confidential, trust-minimized validation oracle for API responses. A caller asks: "call this API and check whether its response satisfies my private criteria" — and the workflow executes that check inside a hardware enclave so that neither Chainlink's node operators, nor network observers, nor other callers can see what's being validated or how. The core flow (main.ts) Trigger: anyone can fire the public HTTP trigger with a payload of { api: { url, requestType, body }, validationFunction } — an API to call plus an arbitrary JavaScript snippet that must return a boolean verdict on the response. TEE execution: the handler is registered with handlerInTee, so all logic runs inside an AWS Nitro enclave (Confidential Workflows, private beta), not on regular DON nodes. Authenticated API call: before calling the target API, the workflow fetches an ed25519 private key (API_SIGNING_KEY) from the Vault DON — released only into attested enclaves — and signs {timestamp, body}. The API verifies this signature against the workflow's published public key, which proves the request genuinely came from this workflow, inside a TEE (the Vault DON's release policy stands in for raw attestation, since CRE doesn't expose enclave attestation documents to workflow code). Validation: the caller's validationFunction is eval'd against the response (delivered base64-encoded, since the runtime lacks atob and text() mangles binary) and must return a boolean. Result: the verdict is returned as the workflow result — note HTTP triggers are fire-and-forget, so callers get results via callback, not the trigger response. The demo application: color-gated image API mock-api.js is a stand-in protected API that serves one of two paint images at random (paint_high_small.png / paint_low_small.png), only to requests bearing a valid, fresh enclave signature (401/400 otherwise). The showcase validationFunction (in payload-color-validation.json) is a self-contained ~35KB PNG decoder: it base64-decodes the response, inflates IDAT chunks with an embedded copy of fflate, reverses PNG scanline filters, computes mean HSV saturation, and accepts only if it's above 0.44 — the high-color image (0.484) passes, the low-color one (0.402) is rejected. The point: a proprietary, non-trivial algorithm can run as caller-supplied data, invisible to everyone but the enclave. What the experiments established • Payloads can be encrypted client-side to a workflow x25519 public key (ECIES: ephemeral ECDH → HKDF → AES-GCM), decrypted only in-enclave via a Vault-DON-held private key (main-tee.ts) — including the validation function itself, keeping it private even from other
callers. • CRE limitations found empirically: no CSPRNG in the WASM sandbox, no workflow-writable secrets (so no ZK-ceremony-style TEE-born persistent keys), no attestation API, 250KB HTTP response cap, and eval scope leaks that required AsyncFunction isolation.

Before calling the API, the enclave fetches an ed25519 private key from the Chainlink Vault DON, which threshold-encrypts secrets and releases them only to attested enclaves, then signs the request body and timestamp so the receiving API can verify against the workflow's published public key that the call genuinely originated from this workflow inside a TEE. Because CRE never returns trigger responses synchronously, the workflow calls the API itself and the verdict flows back through the workflow result. The demo API is a small Node server that serves one of two paint images at random only to validly signed requests, and the showcase validation function is a self-contained 35KB string that base64-decodes the image response, inflates PNG

projects.title: BasePetition
projects.description: Create and sign transparent, on-chain petitions on Base with IPFS-powered metadata.
projects.project_description: BasePetition is an on-chain petition platform built on Base that helps communities turn public concerns into transparent, verifiable action. Anyone can create a petition with a title, description, image, signature goal, and deadline. Petition metadata and images are stored through IPFS, while petition creation and every signature are recorded on Base through a smart contract. Visitors can browse petitions, review their progress, connect a wallet, and sign without relying on a centralized database. Creators can manage their petitions and track activity from a personal dashboard, while anyone can inspect petition details and signer addresses directly on-chain. The platform also includes petition lifecycle management, deadlines, creator controls, and basic moderation visibility for safer public participation.
projects.how_its_made: BasePetition is built with Next.js 16 App Router, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The frontend uses Wagmi and Viem for wallet connection, contract reads, transaction submission, chain selection, and receipt tracking, with TanStack Query handling caching and reactive updates. The application runs on Base and interacts with a Solidity 0.8.20 smart contract that manages petition creation, deadlines, lifecycle status, signature uniqueness, signer records, creator dashboards, pagination, and owner moderation controls. Petition text and images are uploaded through a Next.js API route to Pinata/IPFS, with the resulting metadata URL stored alongside the petition on-chain. The blockchain remains the source of truth, while the UI reconstructs progress and status from contract reads and events. We also use ERC-8021 transaction attribution through ox so submitted transactions can be identified as coming from the application. This combination keeps the interface responsive while preserving publicly verifiable petition data.

projects.title: IntentGraph
projects.description: From a question to on-chain data, pay-per-query for The Graph, priced natively in HBAR via x402
projects.project_description:
IntentGraph gives AI agents paid access to The Graph’s subgraphs through a verifiable Hedera payment flow. Describe the data you need, let your agent unlock the toolkit, and follow the evidence from discovery to the final query result. What you can do
Ask for blockchain data in natural language. Your agent translates the request into discovery, schema inspection, and GraphQL calls.
Access The Graph without managing a Graph key. The service operator supplies the upstream credentials. Pay for a bounded access session. One confirmed payment unlocks the toolkit for the advertised duration and usage allowance.
Inspect how an answer was produced. The playground shows tool arguments, returned data, and a settlement receipt alongside the answer.
Use your preferred agent. Connect an MCP-compatible client, or try the hosted Gemini demonstration in your browser. IntentGraph is useful for developers exploring protocols, analysts inspecting indexed activity, and agent builders who need a clear path from a data request to paid tool access. Available data depends on the subgraphs discoverable through the upstream service, their schemas, and their indexing status.
projects.how_its_made:
We built IntentGraph as a TypeScript application with a React/Vite frontend and an Express backend. It turns a natural-language request into a payment-gated workflow for discovering and querying blockchain data.
The core integration is The Graph’s Subgraphs MCP. Our server authenticates with an operator-owned Graph API key, discovers the upstream tools and their JSON schemas, and registers those tools using the MCP TypeScript SDK. Users never need their own Graph key. Initially, only unlock_data_access is available; the actual data-tool handles remain disabled.
Calling the unlock tool returns an x402 v2 quote denominated in native HBAR on Hedera testnet. The payer signs the exact requirements locally, and our backend uses Blocky402 to verify and settle the payment. Only after confirmed settlement do we call .enable() on the tools and notify the agent that its toolkit has changed. SQLite stores payment receipts, canonical transaction IDs for replay protection, and usage statistics.
The interactive playground uses Gemini’s function calling through a real MCP client connection. Gemini requests access, then the server signs the payment using a shared, faucet-funded Hedera testnet wallet. Each visitor gets a separate MCP session. After unlocking, Gemini searches subgraphs, checks deployment activity, inspects the selected schema, and builds a bounded GraphQL query. Streamed events power the frontend console, showing tool calls, responses, payment receipts, and the final answer.
The most interesting implementation detail is that payment changes the agent’s available tools mid-conversation. We gate the real tool handles rather than merely telling the model not to use them. We also preserve Gemini’s function-call metadata across turns while keeping payment proofs and private keys out of model context and browser responses.

projects.title: Chakra
projects.description: Chakra is a liquidity aggregator for Arc that deliver hyper-optimized executable swap.
projects.project_description: Problem: Arc stablecoin liquidity is split across isolated DEX venues with different pool mathematics, factories, and swap interfaces. Single-pool routes often suffer avoidable slippage; wallets and payments apps otherwise maintain separate venue adapters and routing logic. Users see one venue's price instead of an executable comparison. Solution & impact: Chakra provides a production routing layer (web + API) for route discovery, split optimization, and wallet-ready transaction building (quote + build_tx) on Arc Testnet — improving execution quality, increasing venue utilization, and giving wallets and dApps a single USDC/EURC integration entry point. The user authorizes in their own wallet. Chakra never holds keys and never submits.
projects.how_its_made:
Components
The implementation is these pieces.
Aggregator contract. The public swap entrypoint. splitSwap pulls tokenIn from the user through Permit2, executes one or more SubRoutes (a one-path swap is one entry; a split is several), checks minAmountOut, transfers tokenOut to msg.sender, and sweeps leftover catalog tokens to the sender. Factory allowlist gates every hop. An empty Permit2 signature skips permit(). Splits cannot share a pool. The contract does not retain funds after the call. chakra-market-data-worker. The single writer of market state. Discovers pools, watches Arc logs, and publishes the routing graph and per-pool reserves or ticks under the chakra: Redis prefix. chakra-api-server. Stateless HTTP API. Quotes, encodes unsigned splitSwap calldata, and serves tokens, balances, stats, health, and readiness. Horizontal replicas read the same Redis. The API does not submit transactions. router-engine. In-process PathFinder (BFS), QuoteEngine (local pool math), and SplitOptimizer (Brent on two paths, pairwise merge on more). dex-adapters. Per-venue discovery, log matching, and quote math for Xylo, Presto, UnitFlow V2.5 (30 bps xy=k), and generic xy=k / stable / CLMM factories on the seed list. Redis. Routing topology (chakra:snapshot: ), live pool state (chakra:pool:xyk|stable|clmm: ), factory allowlist (chakra:factories), and additive swap analytics (chakra:analytics:*). Swap UI and @chakra-ag/sdk. Browser UI and TypeScript client for quote, build, sign, and submit. A public dashboard is at https://chakra-ag.vercel.app/stats.

projects.title: pm amm
projects.description: Prediction markets resolved by Chainlink, monitored by a Graph agent, yield-backed via 1inch Aqua
projects.project_description: PM-AMM is a decentralized prediction market protocol using a Gaussian-CDF pricing curve from Paradigm's research. Anyone can create a YES/NO market, trade shares priced by the AMM in real time, and redeem winnings once it resolves. Originally built May-June 2026 with a full indexing, charting, and telemetry stack, this event added three integrations that each close a real gap rather than bolt on for eligibility: Chainlink Price Feeds now auto-resolve objective markets with zero admin involvement, and Chainlink VRF fixes what used to be a genuine dead end - disputing a market previously had no resolution path at all, and now a fair, unpredictable resolver gets picked from a registered panel instead. A subgraph on The Graph indexes the whole protocol and feeds a natural-language risk-monitoring agent that flags when the crowd's price disagrees with the real-world price, gated to only fire near a market's deadline so it's not just noise. A 1inch Aqua strategy lets idle, already-resolved collateral earn swap fees while sitting unclaimed, without ever leaving the protocol's own custody.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity/Foundry: Router.sol is a factory routing trades to per-market LvrMarket.sol instances implementing the PM-AMM curve (Gaussian CDF math, using Solady's FixedPointMathLib for precision). For Chainlink, resolveWithChainlink() pulls AggregatorV3Interface.latestRoundData() directly on-chain to auto-resolve price-target markets, and a new DisputeResolverVRF contract requests Chainlink VRF v2.5 randomness on dispute, handing the final call to one address from a registered pool - the original dispute() function had literally no resolution mechanism before this. For The Graph, LvrMarket is a dynamically-instantiated data source template off Router's factory pattern, with ABIs exported straight from the Foundry build so they can't drift from the real contracts; a backend agent cross-references the subgraph's live AMM price against the Chainlink feed and calls Gemini for a natural-language risk briefing, gated to only fire within 6 hours of a market's deadline (an always-on version would falsely flag almost every market, since a rational AMM price correctly differs from the current spot price when there's still time left for it to move). 1inch Aqua has no testnet, so CollateralYieldStrategy.sol - a real AquaApp - is fork-tested against the actual deployed mainnet Aqua registry with real numbers (1,000 USDC in, ~0.4936 WETH out). It's deliberately not wired into the live redemption path: Aqua's non-custodial design means a market's collateral composition can shift the moment a taker swaps against it, and risking that in the same path a user might be redeeming from, under a hackathon deadline, wasn't a trade worth making. Frontend is React/wagmi/viem; backend is Express/Prisma/BullMQ on Neon Postgres with Redis pub/sub and Prometheus/Grafana telemetry.
