projects.title: Enclave Portfolio
projects.description: Private strategy, public trades: portfolio rebalancing and liquidation protection in a Chainlink TEE
projects.project_description: Enclave Portfolio is two Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows built on one idea: an automated trading strategy has to live somewhere, and wherever it lives, someone can read it. In a bot, the host can. In a smart contract, everyone can. In an oracle node's config, every operator can. Once a strategy is readable, every future move is predictable — and predictable moves get front-run. Confidential Workflows put the strategy inside an AWS Nitro enclave: hardware-isolated memory the node operator physically cannot inspect, with secrets released only to an attested binary. Delete the enclave from either workflow and there is no decision left to make. Workflow 1 — Confidential Rebalancer (Best Confidential Workflow). Most "private rebalancers" hide a set of target weights. That doesn't work: a rebalance moves the book toward the target, so anyone reading balances before and after recovers it in one observation. We fixed this at the design level. The user's entire portfolio construction is one secret spec — which assets, the strategic base allocation, which market signals tilt it (risk parity, momentum, equal-weight, composable by strength), per-asset weight bounds, and the rebalancing policy. Each cycle the enclave composes target weights from that spec and live prices, sizes trades under a per-trade cap, checks price impact against a secret ceiling, and emits only the orders. The targets are never stored and never the same twice, so the trades don't converge on anything an observer can solve for. Two users on the same deployed workflow can run entirely different portfolios; the public code reveals only that "a spec is evaluated." Workflow 2 — Automated Liquidation Protection (the Challenge). Protects a vETH-collateral / vUSD-debt position on the challenge's ChallengeLending contract. Two facts from the contract shape the strategy: deposits don't reduce debt (so they cost nothing in the loan-continuity score), and liquidation only fires when the admin separately calls checkAllHF(). So: on ChallengeStarted, deposit exactly enough collateral to survive down to a secret floor price — one transaction, before any price moves, no race. On every PriceUpdate, recompute the health factor with the contract's exact integer math; if it falls under a secret trigger, top up to a secret target, then repay within a secret cap, then repay whatever it takes. The transaction is signed inside the enclave with a Vault-held key. Logs carry only held or acted and a tx hash — never a threshold, an amount, or a price. Engineering. No float ever touches money: token amounts are bigint base units, USD is fixed-point 1e8, health factors are computed bit-for-bit as the contract does. Every parser refuses rather than guesses. 102 tests, including a bit-exact offline model of ChallengeLending that replays all five published scenarios and harsher ones. A private copy of the challenge contracts on Sepolia, with our wallet as admin, serves as a live test harness — we've watched the enclave sign a deposit() between a price drop to $1,500 and the liquidation check, and survive.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. TypeScript on the Chainlink CRE SDK (@chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18), compiled to WASM by the CRE CLI and run in a Javy/QuickJS sandbox. viem for ABI encoding and for signing transactions with @noble/curves — pure JS, so it works inside the enclave. Bun for tests and tooling. Foundry for the Solidity side. No framework, no floats. How the enclave is wired. Every handler is registered with handlerInTee(trigger, fn, [{ tee: "nitro", regions: ["us-west-2"] }]) — the third argument is the TEE constraint, which is what pins execution to an enclave (Chainlink's own template has it commented out in the wrong argument slot). The callback receives TeeRuntime, a different type from Runtime: chain reads and writes won't accept it, so every crossing of the enclave boundary is a deliberate line of code. Secrets come from runtime.getSecrets(), released by the Vault DON only to the attested binary. Data enters over confidential HTTP (JSON-RPC eth_call to Sepolia with TLS terminating inside); the decision runs; a transaction is signed inside and leaves via eth_sendRawTransaction. The only other exits are return and runtime.log, and the logs carry one word plus a tx hash. Rebalancer. The strategy is a single JSON secret — a PortfolioSpec — parsed by a refuse-don't-guess validator (weights must sum to exactly 10,000 bps; bounds must be satisfiable; unknown signal types rejected with the list of known ones). Signals are pluggable blocks (signals/), composed as a convex combination with the base view, then water-filled into per-asset bounds and forced to an exact sum by largest-remainder assignment with ties broken on token id so two nodes agree bit for bit. Momentum, inverse-volatility and equal-weight ship; adding one is write-and-register. Liquidation protection. The policy is pure integer math (policy.ts) with the contract's calcHF reproduced exactly, including its floor division. The test file is a bit-exact model of ChallengeLending — partial liquidation, the 5% penalty, time-weighted debt — so scenarios replay offline in milliseconds. The live harness is a private copy of the three challenge contracts deployed to Sepolia with our wallet as admin, plus a runner that plays Chainlink: updatevETHPrice → wait → checkAllHF. What Chainlink gave us. CRE turned "put the strategy in a TEE" from an infrastructure project into a type signature. Attestation-gated secrets mean a modified binary can't get the policy; the log trigger on PriceUpdate fires inside the window between the price update and the liquidation check. Hacky bits worth admitting. All money math is bigint. Volatility needs a square root, so there's a Newton's-method integer sqrt; log returns need a logarithm, so we use simple returns and say so. The first version stored fixed target weights. Then we noticed one uncapped rebalance lands the book exactly on target — anyone reading balances before and after recovers the whole strategy. The fix became the design: derive targets from a signal so they move for reasons an observer can't see. The price-impact check runs inside the enclave on purpose; emitting the cap with each trade would publish it. runtime.log is public. Validation errors were stripped of values so a bad secret fails as policy.floor_price is invalid, never with the number. The private key in .env lacked a 0x; cast didn't care, viem did. There is now a normaliser that never echoes the value. The scenario runner parses cast's tuple output with a regex that first strips its [7e5] annotations. It works.

Signals are pluggable blocks (signals/), composed as a convex combination with the base view, then water-filled into per-asset bounds and forced to an exact sum by largest-remainder assignment with ties broken on token id so two nodes agree bit for bit. Momentum, inverse-volatility and equal-weight ship; adding one is write-and-register.

Liquidation protection. The policy is pure integer math (policy.ts) with the contract's calcHF reproduced exactly, including its floor division. The test file is a bit-exact model of ChallengeLending — partial liquidation, the 5% penalty, time-weighted debt — so scenarios replay offline in milliseconds. The live harness is a private copy of the three challenge contracts deployed to Sepolia with our wallet as admin, plus a runner that plays Chainlink: updatevETHPrice → wait → checkAllHF.

What Chainlink gave us. CRE turned "put the strategy in a TEE" from an infrastructure project into a type signature. Attestation-gated secrets mean a modified binary can't get the policy; the log trigger on PriceUpdate fires inside the window between the price update and the liquidation check.

Hacky bits worth admitting.
- All money math is bigint. Volatility needs a square root, so there's a Newton's-method integer sqrt; log returns need a logarithm, so we use simple returns and say so.
- The first version stored fixed target weights. Then we noticed one uncapped rebalance lands the book exactly on target — anyone reading balances before and after recovers the whole strategy. The fix became the design: derive targets from a signal so they move for reasons an observer can't see.
- The price-impact check runs inside the enclave on purpose; emitting the cap with each trade would publish it.
- runtime.log is public. Validation errors were stripped of values so a bad secret fails as policy.floor_price is invalid, never with the number.
- The private key in .env lacked a 0x; cast didn't care, viem did. There is now a normaliser that never echoes the value.
- The scenario runner parses cast's tuple output with a regex that first strips its [7e5] annotations. It works.

projects.title: OpenBook
projects.description: The data marketplace for AI agents. Fresh data or your money back.
projects.project_description: The people driving the next trillion-dollar economy have a blind spot that is going to hemmorage as high as $7 billion by the end of this year The people driving this are infact not people. They are AI agents, and entire economies will be built around how they make decisions as well as the data they use for those decisions. Every day, agents spend real money on data at machine speed. On Polymarket's fastest markets, bots already move 55 to 62% of the volume (Dune). A prediction-market agent buys odds before it takes a position, and for it, current data is edge worth paying for. Every day, some of that data arrives stale, and the agent acts on it anyway. There is no refund, no dispute, no half dead discord, nobody to call at tech support. Bad data of every kind already costs the average organization $12.9 million a year (Gartner, via IBM). Today 54% of organizations are deploying agents (KPMG, Q1 2026). Gartner's own forecast is that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027, and it names the reason: inadequate risk controls. These problems are only going to get more expensive as the agentic ecconomy approaches $1.5 Trillion dollars by 2030 (Juniper). Recourse is the missing primitive of the agentic economy. Agents will not be trusted with real budgets until spending can be undone. Not by a court or a support ticket, but by the contract that holds the money. Recourse is the missing primitive of the agentic economy. A refund that the contract executes itself bounds an agent's loss per query to the gas it spent, which is what makes an agent's budget underwritable. It is also what turns freshness into something people can profit from: a seller can charge more for a tighter freshness window and forfeits the fee when it misses, so the incentive runs toward faster indexers and better feeds, and the freshness premium becomes an open, observable price instead of a private contract. Refundable spend lets agents hold real budgets, real budgets create demand for fresher data, and that demand pays the people who make data fresher. An economy where agents decide every block needs data priced every block. OpenBook is that market: the data marketplace for AI agents, with a freshness guarantee that enforces itself. Sellers list a dataset under their own onchain name (an ENS name) with a price per query and a freshness promise. A buyer agent asks in plain English, its payment locks into an escrow on Arc with the promise written in, and the data arrives from The Graph stamped with the block it was recorded at. Fresh: 98% to the seller, 2% to the protocol. Stale: the contract refuses to pay and the money goes back. Every settlement, refund and fee is written into public books anyone can audit. Prediction markets, lending rates, pool prices, NFT trades and name registrations are on the market today; any active ubgraph (15k+ as of today) can be transformed into it's own monetized market with one config line, and an MCP server lets agents discover, compare and buy. Tomorrow, anything an agent acts on is sold this way, and the $7 billion blind spot is not litigated. It is refunded.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Solidity contracts with Foundry; a TypeScript seller service, buyer CLI and MCP server on Bun; a Vite and React web app served from one bundle on Cloudflare Pages and Vercel, with its server routes as Cloudflare Workers and Vercel functions; a Graph subgraph in AssemblyScript; a server-side language model on Fireworks (DeepSeek) for the console; Circle developer-controlled wallets for the page and a Circle Agent Wallet for the x402 lane; 409 unit tests, 20 Foundry tests and a 20-check browser audit in CI. Settlement runs on an ERC-8183 hook on Arc. Every purchase is a job on my own instance of Circle's ERC-8183 escrow on Arc testnet, paid and gassed in USDC. I wrote SlaHook.sol, the hook the escrow calls on every action: on submit it records the hash of the delivered bytes, and before complete it requires a signed attestation over that hash and checks that the delivery's block clears the freshness floor set at payment. If either check fails it reverts with SlaNotMet and the job can only be refunded. The 2% platform fee goes to a PolicyWallet treasury I wrote with onchain per-transaction and daily caps, since Circle's policy engine is not available on testnet. The data comes from The Graph, stamped with its block. Every dataset is a live subgraph on The Graph gateway (three on Messari standardized schemas, plus ENS and Overtime). I append _meta { block { number } } to each query, hash the payload and sign the observation; that block number is what the hook compares against the floor, which is the only reason a freshness guarantee can be enforced onchain. One route settles a job: verify the hash, post the attestation, simulate complete(), then send complete() or reject() in the same request. My own open-book subgraph indexes every payment, settlement, refund and fee into public books. Every ENS name is a market. openbook.eth is registered in the ENSv2 registry on Sepolia and runs its own UserRegistry subregistry, so the name is a namespace of markets: each dataset is a subname with its own price, freshness window and payee in text records (svc.price, svc.sla, svc.payee), and aave-v3-arbitrum-lending.openbook.eth already quotes 0.15 while the parent quotes 0.10 and pays a different wallet. A new subname needs no setup: without a resolver it inherits the parent's, so a market exists the moment the name does. The identity is the storefront and the ledger at once: svc.pnl points at the name's public books, and agent-registration, agent-context and agent-endpoint records (ENSIP-25/26, tied to ERC-8004 agent 894065) let an agent find the market, its terms and its history from the name alone. Onboarding a seller is an Enhanced Access Control grant: I gave alpha.openbook.eth's key write access to svc.price only, on its own node, and it repriced itself onchain while every other write reverts, so a seller runs its own market under a parent it does not control. Anyone can register a name and set three records to sell; the server re-resolves price and payee before every job and there is no default anywhere in the code. No ENS, no market. The interface is a console that takes English, plus an MCP server for agents. Anything typed that is not a command goes to a server-side LLM that maps it to a validated command; the model never touches data or produces a number, and a purchase asks for its freshness window before spending. sla-subgraph-mcp is my open-source MCP server (seven tools, keyless quickstart): discover_datasets searches The Graph's Subgraph MCP and returns config entries, choose_seller reads live ENS terms and current index lag and picks a seller with a written rationale, and the buy tools return a signed, block-stamped payload. Wallets are Circle's. On the web app the buyer and seller are Circle developer-controlled wallets with gas from Circle Gas Station, so a judge can buy with nothing installed; with a browser wallet connected, the wallet creates and funds the job and the seller quotes it from its Circle wallet. The treasury funds the buyer across chains with App Kit's CCTP bridge and a Gateway unified balance, and an x402 lane sells the same delivery per call, paid from a Circle Agent Wallet.

projects.title: NEAP
projects.description: Instant cross-border payments need pre-funded cash. NEAP cuts that cash by 84.6%.
projects.project_description: NEAP is an intraday treasury engine for institutions that promise instant cross-border payments. To settle a payment in seconds, a bank has to be holding the destination currency before the customer's money arrives. It cannot wait for the transfer to clear. So it pre-funds every corridor and every currency, all day. That capital earns nothing, and it carries an exchange rate position nobody chose. The usual way to size it is to look at the worst day of the last quarter and provision that much. It is robust, and it is far more cash than an ordinary day needs. NEAP replaces that heuristic with stochastic control. It forecasts net flow per corridor and solves the rebalancing bands that minimise a single cost function: the carry on the balance, the fixed cost of a rebalance, execution cost under square root market impact, foreign exchange risk priced as expected shortfall, and the cost of a payment failing for lack of funds. The band is not a setting. It is the minimum of that function, and it is recomputed whenever the parameters change. This only becomes possible now because band width grows as the cube root of the fixed cost of a rebalance. On correspondent banking rails that cost is tens of dollars and settlement takes two days, so rebalancing during the day is uneconomic. On Arc it is about two cents in USDC, final in 350 milliseconds. Divide the fixed cost by ten thousand and the optimal band divides by twenty one. Three integrations, none of them decorative. The decision runs inside a Chainlink CRE confidential handler, because live balances, upcoming commitments and internal limits map a liquidity position precisely enough for a counterparty to trade against it. They never leave the enclave. What leaves is a signed report carrying a commitment to the orders and metrics in basis points, never amounts. Privy holds the role wallets, whose policies allow three function selectors and nothing else, so a stolen key passes authentication but does not pass the policy. Arc settles payment versus payment, both legs or neither, with gas denominated in USDC, which is what turns the fixed cost into a known number inside the objective. The contract never trusts the report. A cap per order, a cap per epoch, a rolling twenty four hour window and a price deviation check against an oracle are all applied independently, because a broken model produces a perfectly signed and perfectly absurd plan. Measured over twenty random seeds and six walk forward windows, with every parameter estimated only from data predating the decision it informs, idle capital falls 84.6 percent and tail risk 89.4 percent. The mechanism is not the one you would expect. Carry is almost negligible at a six percent cost of capital. What actually happens is that execution cost falls 19.7 percent while the engine places thirty times more orders, because many small orders cost less than a few large ones once the fixed cost collapses. What is honest about it: the payment flows are synthetic, since no institution publishes its own by corridor. They come from a compound Poisson process calibrated on public aggregates, with five validity tests and a fixed seed. The market impact coefficient is not calibrated, so its sensitivity is published next to every number that depends on it, and the cost reduction moves between 13 and 38 percent across that range. 241 tests, no JavaScript dependencies outside the CRE workflow, and one command that runs the whole chain: deploy, decide, sign, approve, execute.
projects.how_its_made: The system is built around one constraint: the decision is a pure function. No I/O, no clock, no randomness. That rule is what lets the same code run inside a Chainlink CRE confidential handler and in a local runner, and it is what makes the backtest binding, because the policy tested is literally the policy executed. Stack: TypeScript run natively by Node 24, Solidity with Foundry, a dashboard served by node:http with hand written SVG. No npm install, no build step, zero JavaScript dependencies outside the CRE workflow. Vercel serves it as a static site plus one serverless function, since exactly one endpoint computes anything. The engine: compound Poisson flows with seasonal intensity, EWMA volatility at the RiskMetrics lambda of 0.94, Ledoit Wolf shrinkage on the correlation of standardised residuals, and expected shortfall at 97.5 percent by filtered historical simulation. Math.random is banned repository wide, and the Poisson sampler is exact in both regimes rather than normal approximated, because that approximation biases the lower tail and the quiet hours are what cause a breach. Bands come from a pattern search warm started by the Miller Orr closed form, evaluated on common random numbers so the optimiser is not chasing simulation noise. Miller Orr doubles as the regression test: on the driftless case the numerical solver must recover the closed form. Three places where the obvious implementation is silently wrong. Pricing a rare event. Counting breaches in simulation leaves the solver completely insensitive to their cost: from 20k to 5M per breach, the optimum does not move by a dollar. That is a resolution limit, not a bug. The breach probability at the optimum is about ten to the minus five, and 300 paths of 400 periods is 120,000 draws, so the term is zero everywhere and its gradient with it. It is now charged in expectation against an exponential tail fitted by peaks over threshold. The test guarding it checks a relation rather than a value: at the optimum the breach probability must scale as one over the breach cost. Measured across four decades: 1.29e-5, 1.34e-6, 1.35e-7, 1.32e-8. Hashing like Ethereum. Node exposes sha3-256, which is not Keccak: standardisation moved the padding byte from 0x01 to 0x06 after Keccak was published, and Ethereum kept the original. Keccak256 is implemented here in 64 bit bigints with a minimal ABI encoder and EIP-712 struct hashing, validated against cast at the 135, 136 and 137 byte block boundaries where padding bugs hide. A committed fixture is then checked in both directions: Solidity recomputes it, and a TypeScript test asserts it is still what the engine produces. Without that second direction, regenerating the fixture would make both suites pass while silently changing the contract. Proving the absence of lookahead. A canary injects an extreme shock into the future and asserts no earlier band moves. Its counter test matters as much: the same shock in the past must move them, otherwise a canary that detects nothing could simply be dead. The contracts assume the model will one day be wrong. Separation of duties is a revert, not a UI rule. The EIP-712 quorum requires strictly increasing signer addresses, so one signature cannot be replayed to reach it, and the EIP-2 low s bound stops a single report having two identifiers. The attestation is bound to the payload hash, otherwise a valid attestation could be recycled onto another report: it would prove an enclave exists, not that this content came out of one. The vault reveals a salted commitment, then applies caps the report cannot influence. What each partner unlocks. Arc denominates gas in USDC, turning the fixed cost of a rebalance from an estimate into a known number inside the objective, and its atomic PvP let a compensation state be deleted from the vault state machine rather than defended. Chainlink CRE is what makes the product commercially plausible, since no institution will publish its liquidity position, and its synchronous handler is exactly the shape of a pure function. Privy catches what the contract structurally cannot see: a compromised key signing a transaction the contract never receives. All of it is checkable: 241 tests, a committed end to end trace, and one command that deploys, decides, signs, approves and executes in five seconds.

projects.title: Godaam
projects.description: Farmers borrow above collateral value using a private TEE risk score on tokenized crop receipts.
projects.project_description:
A smallholder farmer with a crop in a licensed warehouse holds a receipt worth 400 gUSDC and can borrow maybe 300 against it. The things that would justify lending more years of consistent yields, a clean repayment record, secure land tenure are exactly the things that cannot go onchain, because they are commercially sensitive and personally identifying.
Godaam is a confidential agricultural lending vault built on India's e-NWR warehouse receipt system. A warehouse operator issues the receipt as a real ERC-1400 security token on Hedera using the Asset Tokenization Studio, with an allowlist and controller powers rather than a token with a name on it. The farmer pledges it, and a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow underwrites them inside a hardware-isolated TEE. Yield history, repayment history and land tenure are fetched into the enclave and never leave it. Only a score, an LTV band, a principal and a keccak commitment of the inputs reach the chain.
That private score is what makes undercollateralized lending possible. Our demo lends 880 gUSDC against 400 of grain a 220% LTV the collateral alone would never justify. Loans repay in installments; default triggers a forced transfer of the receipt to the treasury, enforced by the token's own controller powers.
Identity is gated by World ID: one verified human, one collateral claim, with the nullifier written onchain so a second address presenting the same identity is refused. Every number in the interface carries its provenance beside it, and a figure with no enclave behind it renders in red.
Six contracts are deployed and Sourcify-verified on Hedera testnet, including a NAV oracle reading a live Chainlink price feed.
projects.how_its_made:

A smallholder farmer with a crop in a licensed warehouse holds a receipt worth 400 gUSDC and can borrow maybe 300 against it. The things that would justify lending more years of consistent yields, a clean repayment record, secure land tenure are exactly the things that cannot go onchain, because they are commercially sensitive and personally identifying.
Godaam is a confidential agricultural lending vault built on India's e-NWR warehouse receipt system. A warehouse operator issues the receipt as a real ERC-1400 security token on Hedera using the Asset Tokenization Studio, with an allowlist and controller powers rather than a token with a name on it. That private score is what makes undercollateralized lending possible. Our demo lends 880 gUSDC against 400 of grain a 220% LTV the collateral alone would never justify. Loans repay in installments; default triggers a forced transfer of the receipt to the treasury, enforced by the token's own controller powers.
Identity is gated by World ID: one verified human, one collateral claim, with the nullifier written onchain so a second address presenting the same identity is refused. Every number in the interface carries its provenance beside it, and a figure with no enclave behind it renders in red.

projects.title: ExitLane
projects.description: ExitLane lets treasuries pre-authorize secure exits before market emergencies.
projects.project_description: ExitLane is a pre-authorized emergency exit system for onchain treasuries. Crypto markets operate continuously, but treasury teams and multisig signers may not be available when prices move sharply. Giving an autonomous agent unrestricted wallet access solves the speed problem by creating an even larger security risk. With ExitLane, an operator defines and signs a narrowly constrained EIP-712 Exit Mandate in advance—for example: “If ETH falls below $2,000, sell no more than 5 WETH into USDC with maximum 1% slippage.” An AI copilot can translate the operator’s natural-language request into an untrusted draft, but the operator must review and sign the final mandate. ExitLane monitors live market evidence from The Graph. A deterministic policy engine verifies the trigger, signature, amount, assets, recipient, approved Uniswap route, slippage, expiry, chain, evidence freshness, and one-time nonce. If every condition matches, a restricted Privy signer can execute the validated Uniswap transaction. Any changed field, expired mandate, stale evidence, incorrect signer, or replay attempt is blocked. AI provides an evidence-grounded explanation of what happened and why, but it can never authorize execution or override the policy engine. ExitLane’s Attack Lab makes these security guarantees visible by demonstrating that mutations to transaction amounts, recipients, routers, calldata, chains, and nonces are rejected. ExitLane gives organizations the speed of automation without handing an agent unrestricted control of treasury funds: pre-authorize the emergency plan, not the wallet.
projects.how_its_made: The architecture deliberately separates market observation, mandate signing, policy evaluation, AI assistance, transaction construction, and execution so that no single external service—or language model—can move funds on its own. Treasury operators authenticate through Privy and use a Privy wallet. They create an EIP-712 Exit Mandate that binds the signer, treasury, input and output tokens, maximum amount, trigger price, slippage limit, approved execution target, recipient, chain, validity period, and one-time nonce. The Graph is ExitLane’s live market-evidence layer. We used the Subgraph MCP in Cursor to discover and inspect suitable Subgraphs, then query live Base mainnet WETH/USDC data through The Graph Gateway. A pure, deterministic policy engine compares that evidence against the signed mandate using integer or fixed-point values. When triggered, the backend requests a real quote and execution payload from the Uniswap Trading API. It independently validates the tokens, amount, recipient, router, chain, slippage, deadline, and calldata-derived execution hash before allowing the restricted Privy signer to execute on Base Sepolia. Anthropic is used only as a constrained operator copilot. It converts natural-language instructions into an untrusted mandate draft and produces an evidence-grounded explanation of the final policy result. Its structured output is validated with Zod, and it cannot approve execution, generate trusted calldata, alter policy, or access signing credentials. A notable part of the demo is Attack Lab, which deliberately mutates the amount, recipient, router, token, calldata, chain, expiry, and nonce. Each mutation is evaluated against the same authorization path to visibly prove that the mandate cannot be reused for a different transaction. Live Base mainnet evidence and Base Sepolia execution are clearly labeled so the demo remains real without risking mainnet treasury funds.

projects.title: Tenor-market
projects.description: A compliance-native secondary market for Hedera ATS security tokens, settling atomically in USDC.
projects.project_description: Compliant bonds can already be issued on Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS). They cannot easily be traded, because every transfer has to keep obeying the issuer's rules: KYC on both sides, control lists, freezes, a global pause. Tenor is the missing venue: a peer-to-peer secondary market where listings settle atomically against USDC and the security token itself enforces compliance on every fill. No custody. A listing does not move the seller's tokens into an escrow contract. It places an ATS hold over part of their balance with the Tenor diamond as the hold's escrow. The tokens stay in the seller's wallet, visibly reserved, until a buyer fills. The market never holds a security token, so it needs no KYC status of its own, and the seller's own ERC-20 approval to the diamond is their self-imposed selling cap. Compliance by construction, not by copy. Tenor contains no compliance logic. A fill calls executeHoldByPartition on the token, and the token checks KYC on both parties, the control list and the pause state. An unverified buyer's fill reverts, and because the USDC leg is in the same transaction, their money is untouched. Tenor cannot get compliance wrong because Tenor does not implement it. One transaction per action. Enable selling once with a single approve, then each listing is one transaction that creates the hold and records the listing together. A listing can never exist without its hold, and vice versa. Coupons. The issuer funds a coupon and books it with the Hedera Schedule Service (HIP-1215), and the network fires it at the pay date. Settlement itself is a permissionless, idempotent payCoupon, so correctness never depends on who triggers it, and a holder who never associated with USDC is recorded as skipped rather than stranding everyone else's coupon. Investors sign in with a passkey. Privy creates an embedded wallet silently, the app drips test HBAR and demo USDC, and every transaction is simulated as the connected wallet before it is offered, so no user is ever asked to sign something that will fail. The primary button's label is the blocking condition: Enter an amount, Insufficient USDC balance, Approve USDC, Buy, or Verification required. Everything runs on Hedera testnet and every deployed contract is verified on Sourcify as an exact match. On-chain evidence, linked from the README: an atomic delivery-versus-payment fill of 25 TGN27 against 2,450 USDC between two different wallets; the same transfer to an unverified holder refused by the token with InvalidKycStatus(); a 1,462.50 USDC coupon paid across two holders, triggered by a non-issuer; and a freshly generated passkey wallet funded and buying.
projects.how_its_made:
On-chain, Tenor is a single EIP-2535 diamond composed from Lattice, my pre-existing MIT module library, consumed as a pinned Forge submodule. Lattice supplies DiamondCut, Loupe, ERC-165, AccessControl and Pausable. Two facets were written for this event: TenorMarket (listings, fills and cancels built on ATS holds) and TenorCoupon (funding, scheduling and permissionless idempotent settlement). Solidity 0.8.36 on Foundry, with the deploy recipe shared between production and the test suite. Hedera. The bond (Tenor Green Note 2027) is issued through Asset Tokenization Studio, an ERC-1400 / ERC-3643 diamond, and configured for third-party holds. A fill calls executeHoldByPartition, so the token enforces KYC, control list, freeze and pause on every trade. USDC settlement goes through the Hedera Token Service system contract at 0x167 on the HIP-906 allowance path (transferFrom), plus associateToken for new wallets. Coupons are booked with the Hedera Schedule Service at 0x16b using HIP-1215 scheduleCall / scheduleSelfCall. Privy. Passkey sign-in with silently created embedded wallets. The Next.js client drips test HBAR and demo USDC to brand-new users so they reach a first trade without leaving the page, and it simulates the exact fill as the connected wallet before offering it. The financial flow the embedded wallet signs is a single transaction moving USDC from buyer to seller and the bond from seller to buyer under the issuer's rules. The notable and hacky parts: Lattice's HTS and HSS modules were authored during the event. Every mutating helper in them is access-controlled on msg.sender, and a facet's delegatecall frame preserves msg.sender as the original caller. Routing the permissionless fill() through them would have required the buyer to hold an operator role, so TenorHTS.sol makes the two 0x167 calls the permissionless paths need directly. The original spec's account of the Lattice and ATS surface was written from memory and was wrong in ways that did not compile: wrong function names, wrong argument order, and no mention of the access control above. docs/GROUND-TRUTH.md records every external API as read from source, plus the seven deviations that followed. The whole deploy chain (ATS system, USDC, bond issuance, KYC, market) was rehearsed against a local Hedera node before it was run on testnet. That found six real breaks.
The scheduled coupon call fires within 25 ms of its pay date but fails with INVALID_PAYER_SIGNATURE, so settlement is completed by the permissionless payCoupon. The app copy says exactly that and no more; the evidence is in GROUND-TRUTH.md section 10. Every deployed contract, including the ATS system contracts, is verified on Sourcify as an exact match, checked by a script that discovers nested deployments from the broadcast record.
Compliance failures are asserted by selector (InvalidKycStatus, 0xfc855b1b), not just "it reverted". Built with Claude Code, which produced the contracts, tests, scripts and client under direction and, more usefully, was used to verify assumptions against actual Solidity source and runtime npm exports rather than trust the spec. Design explored in Claude Design. The spec, ground-truth notes and planning documents are committed under docs/.

projects.title: Cascade
projects.description: Dated dollars: money that pays bills before it becomes cash.
projects.project_description:
A dated dollar is USDC with a maturity date. Cascade turns a dollar into a dated dollar: one dollar of principal, redeemable on a calendar date, fully backed by value held in a vault on Arc. Every dated dollar with the same date is interchangeable. A dollar dated earlier settles any bill due later, at face value — no pricing, no negotiation, no credit check. That single property lets a supplier network run on one committed dollar instead of a chain of loans. Apple commits principal once; the supplier it pays settles its own bill with the same dated dollars, same day; that supplier's supplier does the same. Nobody borrows and nobody waits on a bank. Four operations carry the system: issue a dated dollar against an invoice, pay a bill with dated dollars, extend a dollar's date to earn the vault's yield for the days you commit it, or withdraw once it matures. Every operation is atomic and checked against the protocol's invariants immediately. The vault is live and verified on Arc testnet. The public app plays a year of an illustrative global supply chain — Apple's folding-display buildout — as ten thousand of these settlements move across a live globe. A buyer issues it against an obligation, and the receiving supplier can use those dated dollars to pay its own suppliers before maturity. That is the cascade. At maturity every dated dollar redeems 1:1 for USDC. Our vault runs on Arc and mints ERC-1155 tokens, one token id per UTC maturity day. Tokens with the same maturity day are interchangeable. We ran a year of the Apple display supply chain through the reference implementation: 12,028 invoices registered, 6,923 settled, $1.399B gross settled on $458.2M of committed principal. In our branched run, one $100M issue moves through 9 pay hops to 8 payees and settles $450M, with no new principal created at any split. Our app replays that year on a globe alongside a ledger sidebar and a year timeline, and director mode controls the shots. Its Verify on Arc panel reads balances and date tokens directly from the testnet vault instead of a bundled copy. Live app: https://cascade.vellum.network
Repo: https://github.com/mcorrig4/cascade-money
Video: https://shared.claude.do/public/cascade-money-demo-v4a.mp4
projects.how_its_made: We wrote the vault in Solidity, built and tested it with Foundry, and deployed and verified it on Arc testnet (chain id 5042002) at 0x4E7D5b438d38b93b811F7f847613100023d7DafE. Dated dollars are ERC-1155 tokens: the token ID is a calendar date, so every dollar dated the same day is fungible with every other by construction. Because ERC-1155 balances alone are awkward for wallets and integrators, the vault deploys a deterministic CREATE2 clone of a per-date ERC-20 view ( DatedDollarERC20 ) the first time each date is touched — six decimals, a computed USD+N / USD spot symbol, ISO maturity metadata — reading balances and supply straight from the ERC-1155 ledger rather than holding a second copy of state. uri() returns base64 JSON with a rendered SVG coin per date for wallet display. Dated dollars are ERC-1155 ids derived from the UTC maturity day, and a DateMetadata library names each id USD spot or USD+N so a wallet shows the maturity instead of a raw number. The on-chain demo run is 16 transactions: 10 USDC of principal settles 40 USDC across four invoices, and balanceSheet() returns deficit 0 at the end. The protocol itself — the yield index, entitlement accrual, reserve, deficit mode, and every hard invariant in the Tier One specification — is implemented twice: once in the Solidity vault, and once in a Python 3.11+ reference simulator that models settlement, exact yield accrual under the funded index, and discount-window trades without touching a chain. The simulator is what generates the year-long event stream the app plays, and it is also the correctness harness: property-based tests written with Hypothesis exercise the protocol's invariants — principal identity, yield conservation, index monotonicity, date-only-moves-later — across randomized operation sequences and a dedicated ten-thousand-operation stress run, asserting every invariant after every single operation rather than only at test boundaries. The front end is a Vite + React + TypeScript app rendering the simulated year on a 3D globe with globe.gl (built on three.js): animated arcs per payment, a live ledger, a year-long timeline scrubber, a daily volume chart, and a director mode that reproduces every shot in the demo video on demand from one baked NDJSON data file, no backend required. We use Arc's native USDC for gas and for settlement. Arc gives us fast finality and a public explorer for every step, so our settlement path carries no bridge and no wrapped asset. Director mode replays every shot in the film from the same NDJSON file the app plays, so the video cannot drift from the product. A checksum gate refuses to render when narration timestamps are stale. ERC-1155 date ids make every maturity fungible inside its own day, so a dated dollar settles a bill with no pricing step.

The protocol itself — the yield index, entitlement accrual, reserve, deficit mode, and every hard invariant in the Tier One specification — is implemented twice: once in the Solidity vault, and once in a Python 3.11+ reference simulator that models settlement, exact yield accrual under the funded index, and discount-window trades without touching a chain. The simulator is what generates the year-long event stream the app plays, and it is also the correctness harness: property-based tests written with Hypothesis exercise the protocol's invariants — principal identity, yield conservation, index monotonicity, date-only-moves-later — across randomized operation sequences and a dedicated ten-thousand-operation stress run, asserting every invariant after every single operation rather than only at test boundaries.

The front end is a Vite + React + TypeScript app rendering the simulated year on a 3D globe with globe.gl (built on three.js): animated arcs per payment, a live ledger, a year-long timeline scrubber, a daily volume chart, and a director mode that reproduces every shot in the demo video on demand from one baked NDJSON data file, no backend required.

We use Arc's native USDC for gas and for settlement. Arc gives us fast finality and a public explorer for every step, so our settlement path carries no bridge and no wrapped asset.

Director mode replays every shot in the film from the same NDJSON file the app plays, so the video cannot drift from the product. A checksum gate refuses to render when narration timestamps are stale. ERC-1155 date ids make every maturity fungible inside its own day, so a dated dollar settles a bill with no pricing step.

projects.title: Try Mandate
projects.description: ERC-8004 identity + ENS naming for AI agents, gated by a hardware-signed second approval.
projects.project_description:
Mandate gives on-chain AI agents a real identity, an ERC-8004 registration paired with a
human-readable ENS name, instead of just a bare wallet address. From there, any change to
that agent's ownership or permissions has to go through a PermissionGate contract: the
request sits blocked as Pending until a separate approver signs it with a physically
connected Ledger. Nothing executes until that second, hardware-held signature happens, and
it can be rejected outright instead. The whole flow is self-serve and non-custodial: connect your own wallet, register your own
agent's identity, and deploy your own PermissionGate naming your own approver. No backend
ever holds a user's keys. Every agent also carries public reputation feedback left by other
users, and its full action history is queryable live from a subgraph, so trust in an agent
isn't just assumed, it's inspectable. Everything is live on Sepolia today against real
deployed contracts, not a mock or a testnet simulation layered on fake data.
projects.how_its_made:
Identity is ERC-8004 (an Adapter8004 contract binding an ENS-registered ERC-1155 token to a
persistent agent identity) plus ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry for the human-readable name.
Gating is a custom PermissionGate.sol (Solidity, Foundry-tested): requestOwnershipTransfer
and requestPermissionEscalation queue an action, and it only executes once the approver
signs an EIP-712 typed-data payload, verified on-chain and relayed by anyone. A
PermissionGateFactory deploys one gate per user for the self-serve path, checking
Adapter8004.isController so only the real identity owner can deploy a gate for it. A
subgraph (The Graph) indexes every GatedAction and reputation-feedback event so the
frontend never has to trust a centralized read path. Frontend is React + Vite, wagmi/viem
for chain calls, RainbowKit for wallet connect. Backend is a small Express service whose
only remaining trusted job is issuing the ENS subname label; everything that touches
custody or approval is a direct call from the user's own connected wallet. Backend
persistence is MongoDB (swapped in from a local JSON file specifically to survive
serverless cold starts on Vercel, where both frontend and backend are deployed).

projects.title: Mesh402
projects.description: 3D for AI agents: one HTTP request, one x402 payment, one production-ready GLB.
projects.project_description: Mesh402 gives AI agents instant access to 3D generation without accounts, subscriptions, provider API keys, or SDK integrations. An agent makes a single HTTP request describing the asset it needs, receives an HTTP 402 payment requirement, pays with its own wallet on Hedera, and gets back a production-ready GLB. Behind that simple interface, Mesh402 turns 3D generation into a machine-purchasable capability. It handles payment verification and settlement through x402 and Blocky402, invokes Tripo, waits for generation to complete, persists the asset, and returns a stable URL the agent can immediately consume. We also built an autonomous demo using Qwen through Nebius: the agent decides when it needs a real 3D asset, selects the Mesh402 tool, pays, waits for generation, receives the GLB, and continues its task—all without a human manually operating the 3D provider. Mesh402 turns “I need a 3D asset” into one programmable transaction: request → 402 → pay → GLB. Agents shouldn't subscribe to tools. They should buy capabilities.
projects.how_its_made: Mesh402 is a TypeScript/Node.js service that turns Tripo's 3D generation API into an agent-purchasable capability using x402 payments on Hedera. A request without payment receives an HTTP 402 with x402 v2 requirements for hedera:testnet. Blocky402 verifies and settles the caller's HBAR payment, and only after successful settlement does Mesh402 invoke Tripo v3, poll the generation task, persist the resulting GLB, and return a stable asset URL. We built two ways to consume the capability. In the autonomous demo, Qwen3-235B through Nebius Token Factory receives generate_3d_asset as a function-calling tool and decides when a user's request requires purchasing a real 3D asset. Separately, POST /api/v1/generate exposes the same x402 capability to external agents, which receive the 402 response and sign with their own Hedera wallet rather than giving Mesh402 custody of their key. The frontend is built with Vite and Three.js and visualizes the real execution path: intent → tool call → 402 → Hedera settlement → Tripo → 200 → GLB. We deployed the full application as a persistent Node service on Render, with server-side credentials, persistent asset storage, execution locks, and protection against duplicate paid generations. We also preserve a verified replay of a real autonomous run so judges can inspect the exact transaction and generated asset without spending credits. The key engineering idea is that Mesh402 doesn't expose another subscription-based AI interface: it puts a machine-readable payment boundary directly in front of a capability, allowing agents to discover a price, pay, and consume the result programmatically.

projects.title: Denominator
projects.description: An AI-assisted onchain claim checker that returns inspectable evidence from The Graph.
projects.project_description: Denominator checks numerical claims about selected Ethereum Uniswap v3 pools. Gemini converts a natural-language claim into a structured comparison, which the user reviews. The Graph supplies daily observations pinned to a block hash, and deterministic decimal arithmetic calculates the verdict. Results include the baseline, target value, chart, corrected claim, source query and downloadable evidence receipt.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Gemini, Zod and Decimal.js, and hosted on Vercel. The Graph provides live pool metadata and daily observations from an existing public Uniswap v3 subgraph. The app validates the interpretation, dates and source metadata before calculating a verdict. Project-specific application code was built during the hackathon; frameworks and the public subgraph are existing dependencies.

projects.title: RankedShares
projects.description: Ranked-ballot budgeting in stablecoins, sealed votes. Each group funds its share, not the majority.
projects.project_description: RankedShares is on-chain participatory budgeting with a proportionality guarantee. In ordinary token voting a bare majority wins every proposal, so 51% of the voters can direct 100% of the treasury while the other 49% pay in and get nothing out. RankedShares replaces that rule with the Expanding Approvals Rule for participatory budgeting (Aziz and Lee, AAAI 2021). Voters rank the projects they want, ties allowed, and the tally funds projects step by step so that each group of voters ends up funding a share of the budget proportional to its share of the weight. The majority cannot spend the minority's money. Money is weight. Stablecoins deposited into a pool are both the budget and the voting power, and the pool keeps one invariant: total voting weight equals the money in the pool. Every proposal carries a concrete cost in USDC or EURC, and a project is funded the moment its supporters' unspent weight reaches that cost. That is why the pool lives on Arc: gas is paid in USDC, so an entire round runs in a single stable asset from the first proposal to the last claim. Funded projects claim directly from the contract, with no treasurer in between. Weight can also come from Uniswap v4 liquidity. Liquidity providers who pair a DAO token against a stablecoin carry the ecosystem's risk first, since bad spending shows up as impermanent loss on their position, so they get a vote on what the DAO does. Positions never leave the LP's wallet: the pool subscribes to the v4 PositionManager and tracks modify, transfer and burn events. Each position is valued in the sponsorship's stablecoin at a reference price, and weight accrues as value multiplied by time, so LPs who carried the risk longer receive a larger share of the sponsored budget. Two Chainlink CRE workflows run in confidential compute. The first refreshes the reference price every two minutes from a finalized block and the v4 pool state, so LP weight stays honest for the whole voting period rather than being frozen on day one. The receiver settles accrued credit at the old rate before applying the new one and rejects stale or out-of-order reports. The second workflow tallies sealed ballots. Voters encrypt their ranking in the browser to the round's public key. Inside the enclave the workflow derives the round's secret, decrypts the ballots, runs the full tally, and reports the inputs root, the funded set and the transcript. The pool verifies the forwarder, the workflow identity and its own commitment before finalizing, so nobody, including the organiser, ever sees an individual ballot. The same pool also accepts Noir proofs and a ZisK zkVM proof, making the confidential workflow one of three interchangeable verifiers. The product includes round, project, proposal, voting and liquidity pages on top of a read API, contracts deployed on Arc testnet with a self-deployed Uniswap v4 stack, a differential fuzz against a Python reference implementation, and a FEEDBACK.md on building with the Uniswap stack.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts. Everything on-chain is Solidity built with Foundry. The core pool keeps the invariant that total voting weight equals the stablecoin balance, and the tally is a Solidity implementation of the PB-EAR rule. A ballot is a byte string with one byte per project holding the project's competition rank, so ties are natural and the contract rejects rankings with gaps. Each step() call either funds one project or expands every ballot by one rank tier, and the cost deduction uses cumulative rounding so it is integer-exact across supporters. The algorithm is checked by an ffi differential fuzz against a Python reference implementation, plus a brute-force checker for the proportionality guarantee from the paper. Arc. The pool runs on Arc testnet with USDC as both gas and pool token, and an EURC pool alongside. Because costs, weight and gas are the same unit, there is no conversion anywhere in a round. Uniswap v4. Arc testnet has no official v4, so we deploy the pinned v4-core and v4-periphery ourselves with forge scripts that also seed DAO/USDC and DAO/EURC pools with a wide and a narrow range. The LP voting module is a PositionManager subscriber, not a hook and not a vault: subscribe, modify-liquidity, transfer and burn callbacks drive the accounting while the NFT stays in the LP's wallet. Position value is computed from the principal implied by the liquidity at a reference price, both legs converted into the sponsorship's stablecoin, fees excluded. Weight is the integral of that value over time. The notifier can swallow a failing unsubscribe, so the module caches rates, settles eagerly on every update and keeps unsubscribe to constant storage work, with a test that fills all 64 position slots and asserts the callback fits under 200k gas. Chainlink CRE. Both workflows are TypeScript on the CRE SDK, run with bun, and use confidential execution on AWS Nitro. The price workflow fires on a two-minute cron, reads a finalized block header and the v4 StateView slot0 for each sponsored pool, and writes a signed report through the Keystone forwarder. The receiver checks the forwarder address, the workflow owner and name, a strictly increasing source block, observation age under five minutes and at least sixty seconds between updates, then settles at the old rate before switching. The tally workflow pulls a master secret with getSecret , derives the round's tallier key from it and the pool's public salt, decrypts the ballots, replays the PB-EAR transcript and reports the inputs root, funded set and transcript. The pool refuses the report unless that inputs root matches its own commitment. One hacky detail: the forwarder prepends the workflow name as ten bytes of the SHA-256 of the name, so the pool stores and compares that truncated form. Sealed ballots. Ballots are encrypted in the browser with noble curves and a Poseidon2 port. The same encrypted ballot format feeds three verifiers on one pool interface: the CRE attestation above, chained Noir Honk proofs of every tally batch, and a single ZisK zkVM proof of the whole tally. Frontend. A React Router 7 single-page app with React 19, Tailwind 4, wagmi and viem, served with a small Deno read API. It covers rounds, projects, proposals, voting and a liquidity page for registering positions and watching accrued weight.

projects.title: Mev Tax Hook
projects.description: Taxing Arb bot so that LPs can get the extra income for dealing with the Loss.
projects.project_description:
Passive LPs bleed to arbitrage. Every time the real price moves on a faster venue, the first
bot to trade against the stale pool price keeps the difference (loss versus rebalancing).
Since UNIfication, LPs also hand part of their fee income to a UNI burn. Paradigm's
"Priority Is All You Need" showed that on a chain with strict priority ordering, a bot racing
to be first must bid roughly the value of the opportunity as its priority fee, so the bid is an
honest signal of extracted MEV. Unichain's Flashblocks made that ordering provable in
2025. I built the hook that reads that bid and hands the money back to the LPs it was
taken from.
projects.how_its_made:
It moves the arbitrage value from the sequencer to the LPs without shrinking it or
touching retail. On 33 hours of real ETH/USDC minute prices replayed through the actual
hook and PoolManager, the same $162 of arbitrage value left the pool either way; without
the hook 95% of it was priority fees to the sequencer, with the hook 86% was donated to
LPs, LP income rose 11.8%, and 0 of 399 retail swaps were taxed. Unique execution: the
tax is charged through a beforeSwapReturnDelta and donated through PoolManager.donate in the same call, so the credit and debit cancel inside the flash-
accounting lock and the contract has no ERC20 code at all. It cannot hold funds, so it cannot lose them, and donations sit outside the protocol fee switch so all of it reaches
LPs. No oracle, no AVS, no FHE, no second chain. Six additions harden it: a clamped
rolling-average exemption, absolute caps, an immutable hard ceiling, a price-impact
surcharge, a backrun rebate and a PFDA coexistence discount. Live on Unichain Sepolia
with a frontend where anyone can send the same swap as four bidders and watch the tax
land with the LPs.

projects.title: TrustedSwarm
projects.description: Pool laptops you already own into a WebGPU room. Split an LLM. Hedera pays the work.
projects.project_description: Trusted Swarm puts blockchain at the edges of browser GPU inference: ENS identifies who may earn, Hedera collects and splits payment, HCS records whether the job actually finished. Devices still run the model in-tab over WebGPU/WebRTC. A *.trustedswarm.eth name carries a hedera text record that must match the pay-to account or the paid path is 403 and no HBAR moves. POST /v1/chat/completions returns x402 HTTP 402 until Blocky402 settles on Hedera testnet; no host tab means 503, not a silent charge. Success receipts and worker HBAR splits (by pledged GPU, 10% host cut) land on HashScan; failed generations write a receipt and pay nothing. Agents use Bazantic: quote → Hedera pay → swarm completion → HashScan.
projects.how_its_made: The inference engine is WebGPU + WebRTC in the browser (Vite/React PWA + a SwarmLLM-derived runtime). Blockchain sits only at the identity, payment, and audit boundary — not on every token. node runtime/serve.mjs is an OpenAI-compatible localhost bridge (127.0.0.1:11435). It does not run the model. The host tab on /market connects out over WebSocket; curl, agents, and Bazantic POST /v1/chat/completions into that same queue. Marketplace posting stays free. Paid mode is env-gated: set HEDERA_ACCOUNT_ID and the bridge returns HTTP 402 until the client retries with an x402 v2 X-PAYMENT. Hedera is the settlement layer. Blocky402 on testnet verifies and settles a flat HBAR price per completion. On success we split credits by pledged GPU memory (host cut default 10%, observers get nothing); on failure we still write a receipt and pay zero. @hiero-ledger/sdk submits that receipt to HCS, and /market shows the HashScan link. Solo host already received the x402 payment, so we do not send them a second transfer. Worker credits ≤ 0.10 ℏ auto-transfer; larger amounts are recorded, not sent. ENSv2 is admission, not decoration. Hedera-on implies ENS-on. Devices paste a *.trustedswarm.eth name on /onboard. viem resolves the Sepolia hedera text record; it must equal payTo before settle. Bad or missing host name → 403, no HBAR taken. Paid retry with no host tab → 503, no settle. Skip ENS and you can still compute, but you earn nothing. Bazantic gets a public OpenAPI spec and GET /v1/price on Vercel. The Recipe is quote → Hedera pay → localhost completion → HashScan. Vercel cannot run WebGPU, so it never infers.

Success receipts and worker HBAR splits (by pledged GPU, 10% host cut) land on HashScan; failed generations write a receipt and pay nothing. Agents use Bazantic: quote → Hedera pay → swarm completion → HashScan.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The inference engine is WebGPU + WebRTC in the browser (Vite/React PWA + a SwarmLLM-derived runtime). Blockchain sits only at the identity, payment, and audit boundary — not on every token.

node runtime/serve.mjs is an OpenAI-compatible localhost bridge (127.0.0.1:11435). It does not run the model. The host tab on /market connects out over WebSocket; curl, agents, and Bazantic POST /v1/chat/completions into that same queue. Marketplace posting stays free. Paid mode is env-gated: set HEDERA_ACCOUNT_ID and the bridge returns HTTP 402 until the client retries with an x402 v2 X-PAYMENT.

Hedera is the settlement layer. Blocky402 on testnet verifies and settles a flat HBAR price per completion. On success we split credits by pledged GPU memory (host cut default 10%, observers get nothing); on failure we still write a receipt and pay zero. @hiero-ledger/sdk submits that receipt to HCS, and /market shows the HashScan link. Solo host already received the x402 payment, so we do not send them a second transfer. Worker credits ≤ 0.10 ℏ auto-transfer; larger amounts are recorded, not sent.

ENSv2 is admission, not decoration. Hedera-on implies ENS-on. Devices paste a *.trustedswarm.eth name on /onboard. viem resolves the Sepolia hedera text record; it must equal payTo before settle. Bad or missing host name → 403, no HBAR taken. Paid retry with no host tab → 503, no settle. Skip ENS and you can still compute, but you earn nothing.

Bazantic gets a public OpenAPI spec and GET /v1/price on Vercel. The Recipe is quote → Hedera pay → localhost completion → HashScan. Vercel cannot run WebGPU, so it never infers.

projects.title: Usance
projects.description: Policy-controlled capital operations for tokenized assets, including live collateral replacement.
projects.project_description: Usance is a capital operations layer for organizations holding tokenized real-world assets. It lets them finance, move, govern and settle those assets from one policy-controlled capital account. For ETHOnline, we built an institutional collateral-replacement workflow around one hard problem: how can an organization replace tokenized collateral without closing an active financing facility? The live testnet flow secures the replacement asset first, verifies organizational authority and lender policy, checks current valuation and facility safety, and only then releases the previous collateral. We completed a real Series A → Series B replacement with 150,000 replacement units secured while the facility remained ACTIVE and financing remained OPEN. The workflow combines Hedera ATS for tokenized-security lifecycle, ENS for delegated organizational authority, Privy for organization approval, and Chainlink CRE for confidential lender-policy evaluation. Every step is preserved as evidence and recoverable through durable orchestration. Usance also includes Ask Usance, a live read-only explanation layer powered by 0G Compute Router. It can explain facility state and safety events, but it has no wallet, signer, or financial write authority. Usance existed before ETHOnline. This submission is continuity work: the institutional facility, collateral-substitution lifecycle, sponsor integrations, durable recovery flow, live proof, receipt UI, and related product surfaces were developed during ETHOnline 2026.
projects.how_its_made: Usance is a TypeScript/Solidity monorepo with a Next.js 15 frontend deployed on Cloudflare Workers, Postgres-backed durable orchestration, and smart-contract infrastructure for institutional secured credit. The ETHOnline flow centers on a separate InstitutionalFacility. Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio represents and controls the tokenized securities: replacement collateral is committed through ATS before the old collateral can be released. ENSv2 on Sepolia provides delegated organization-role evidence. Privy provides organization approval using a 2-of-2 quorum-backed signing flow. Chainlink CRE evaluates lender policy and returns a bounded ALLOW/ELIGIBLE verdict; the facility still performs the final financial-safety checks itself. The orchestration layer persists every operation before external effects, reconciles uncertain outcomes instead of treating timeouts as failures, and blocks release when authority, policy, settlement pricing, collateral pricing, or coverage is stale or invalid. This was exercised against real testnet state, including stale-price blocks and a gas-execution recovery, before the final successful collateral release. The product also uses 0G Compute Router for Ask Usance, a live read-only explanation surface. The server sends a bounded context packet containing only already-visible facility state. Obvious financial-action requests are refused before inference, and the feature has no signer or state-changing code path. The frontend, institutional receipt, evidence timeline, status surfaces, and responsive product UI are all deployed at usance.xyz.

projects.title: LedgerMind
projects.description: Payment intents for AI agents: hard caps, instant revocation, and a subgraph that proves it
projects.project_description:
Giving an AI agent a wallet key gives it unlimited authority over your funds.
Revoking that authority means rotating the key, and auditing what it did means
trusting logs the agent wrote about itself. LedgerMind replaces the key with a payment intent: a smart contract that holds
funds and enforces four things on every payment — a total cap, a
per-transaction cap, a time window, and an optional merchant allowlist. The
agent holds a key that can only call execute() within those bounds. It never
holds your funds, it cannot exceed the caps, and you can revoke it at any time.
Every payment emits a receipt hash committing to the off-chain context that
justified it, so spending is auditable after the fact rather than on trust. This project existed before ETHOnline 2026 and is frozen at the git tag
pre-ethonline-2026, so everything new can be diffed against it. Two things in
that baseline were broken, and both are what we fixed during the event. First, the indexer could silently lose data. It only ever looked back 1000
blocks; Sei produces a block every ~400ms, so any downtime beyond ~6.7 minutes
skipped events permanently with no backfill, no reorg handling, and an RPC
fan-out that grew with every intent. We replaced it with a subgraph. Second, the "assistant" queried nothing. It was ~210 lines of hardcoded strings
including invented market data — a fabricated 24h volume and APY typed into the
source. It now reads live subgraph data and returns ranked findings and typed
actions: revoke this intent, withdraw the remainder from that one, restrict the
merchants on a third — each naming a specific contract, how urgent it is, and
how much capital it recovers. It also returns the facts it reasoned from, so
every claim is checkable. We also made the whole thing legible to other agents: an OpenAPI 3.1 document,
an MCP server exposing five tools, and a Bazantic Recipe whose effect we
measured in a controlled A/B rather than asserted. Deployed on Sei Atlantic testnet. All data in the demo is live.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts are Solidity on Sei Atlantic testnet (eip155:1328). A
PaymentIntentFactory deploys each PaymentIntent as a full CREATE2 contract —
not a minimal proxy — which matters downstream: the subgraph needs a dynamic
data source template spawned per intent rather than a single shared source.
The intent enforces totalCap, perTxCap, a start/end window, and an optional
merchant allowlist, and emits Executed / ToppedUp / Revoked / Withdrawn /
MerchantUpdated. THE GRAPH (Continuity pool). We built a subgraph in packages/subgraph that
indexes the factory and every intent it deploys. The factory handler spawns a
PaymentIntent template per IntentCreated event; the template indexes all five
intent events. The schema adds things the old indexer never computed:
IntentDailySnapshot rollups, denormalised remainingCap, and capUtilizationBps
(what share of the per-transaction cap each payment consumed — repeated values
near 10000 mean an agent is being throttled by a mis-sized cap). Deployed to
Subgraph Studio on sei-atlantic. The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative. The dashboard, the HTTP API, the MCP
server's list_intents tool and the assistant all read from it and nothing else.
There is deliberately no RPC or cached fallback anywhere in that path: pull the
subgraph and the API returns 503 and the assistant says it has no data rather
than guessing. The dashboard hook previously made 1 + 5N eth_calls per page
load; it is now a single request whose cost does not grow with the number of
intents. The assistant (/api/v1/analyze) does the unit normalisation and every ratio in
TypeScript before the model sees anything, so the model's job is judgement, not
arithmetic. That let us run it on Claude Haiku 4.5 — roughly 5x cheaper and 2x
faster than Opus on the same payload — with a strict JSON schema for the output. BAZANTIC. The same data is described as an OpenAPI 3.1 document served at
/api/v1/openapi and registered as an x402/MPP Gateway, plus a Recipe explaining
when an agent should reach for a payment intent and how to read the fields.
We then tested whether the Recipe actually changes anything, rather than
claiming it does. scripts/bazantic-ab.mjs runs six tasks twice against the same
live API; both arms are built from the same TASKS, TOOLS and model constants in
one file, and ARMS is literally {A: BASE_SYSTEM, B: BASE_SYSTEM + RECIPE}. Each
run logs both system prompts verbatim so "the Recipe was the only variable" is
checkable rather than asserted. The harness probes the API first and exits
non-zero if it is not live, so no run directory can contain fixture-derived
results. The result, honestly: on Haiku the Recipe is the difference between a usable
answer and a wrong one — asked how much its agents can still spend, the
un-recipe'd agent answers "60,920,000" in raw base units, which a human reads
as sixty million dollars; the true figure is 60.92 USDC. It also leaves units
unconverted elsewhere and hallucinates dates. On Opus 5 the gap nearly vanishes
— neither arm fails, and the Recipe only saves a round trip. We wrote up the
three tasks where it made no measurable difference too. MCP. packages/mcp exposes create_intent, execute_payment, revoke_intent,
list_intents and top_up_intent over JSON-RPC on stdio — the protocol Claude
Code and Claude Desktop speak. The agent never sees a private key; it calls
tools, the server holds the key, and the caps are enforced on-chain regardless.
list_intents was rewired from a 1 + 6N RPC fan-out to the subgraph during the
event. Notably hacky bit: to record the demo against the real UI we inject a genuine
EIP-1193 provider into Playwright, backed by the actual payer key, with signing
done in Node and broadcast as a raw transaction. The wallet connects for real
and the intent created on camera is a real CREATE2 deployment — not a stub. Stack: Solidity + Foundry, The Graph (AssemblyScript mappings), Next.js 14 with
wagmi/viem, TypeScript MCP server, Claude Haiku 4.5 for the analysis, Sei
Atlantic testnet.
