projects.title: ContextLock
projects.description: An agentic IDE to design, simulate, deploy and operate DeFi agents with on-chain spending limits.
projects.project_description: ContextLock Studio is an agentic IDE for building confidential financial agents that can be trusted with money. Detailed Video at : https://youtu.be/MM4qlYC4SGU?si=O3XhylvHud5XgqLt THE PROBLEM Every agent that can move funds today is given a key and told to behave. The limits live in a system prompt, and a prompt is a suggestion, not a boundary. It takes one of: an injected instruction from untrusted content a stale oracle round that still parses and still looks reasonable a confused tool call and the transaction is already signed. The model isn't malicious; it's obedient, and obedience is the vulnerability. Anything that can be talked out of enforcing a rule was never enforcing it. Guardrails that live inside the model's own context window are reachable by anything that can write into that context. WHAT WE BUILT A workspace where the thing being authored is not source code but an agent and its authority model. You describe an agent in natural language and the IDE compiles that into a versioned Blueprint: identity, data requirements with trust classes and freshness windows, permitted actions, and an explicit authority envelope. Every other surface is a projection of that artifact. The architecture graph, the generated code, the simulation runs and the deployed policy all carry a revision, and anything built against an older one is marked stale rather than shown as current. Authority itself is enforced by a deterministic policy layer sitting outside the model and outside the runtime. Every proposed action is evaluated against stated limits (amount, recipient allowlist, data trust class and age, rolling window budget) and resolves to one of three outcomes: ALLOW, under the per-action limit, where the agent acts alone ESCALATE, between that and the escalation band, where a human approves DENY, above the hard ceiling, refused outright whatever the model believes When an action is permitted the agent receives a capability that is scoped to that single action, single-use, nonce-bound and already expiring. It never holds a standing key, so a compromised runtime inherits no authority beyond the capability currently in its hand. The one number we refuse to generate is the financial ceiling. The built-in assistant interviews you through every gap in your requirements: protocol, triggers, recipients, data sources, forbidden actions. But when it reaches the limits that bound your money it asks and then refuses to answer. A figure it suggested would become the figure you accepted. HOW YOU USE IT Describe the agent, generate a Blueprint, and inspect the permission matrix it produces, which is computed from the policy rather than described by the model. From there: Run 24 deterministic simulation scenarios and 16 attack scenarios (prompt injection, recipient mutation, amount mutation, target mutation, stale oracle data, runtime compromise, mainnet write attempts) and see the exact layer that stopped each one, and whether a capability was ever issued Test against real market conditions with mainnet as a read-only source or an isolated local fork, where fork transactions are labelled as such and never given a public explorer link Deploy to a testnet with the policy starting disabled, and enable financial authority only once every precondition passes After deployment you operate it from the same workspace: observed on-chain state with per-source freshness, a correlated event log that traces any transaction back through capability issuance to its original trigger, drift detection between expected and observed configuration, and an Emergency Lock that attempts the financial policy first. INTEGRATIONS Chainlink Data Feeds supply verified oracle rounds carrying a trust class and a freshness window, so a decision that depends on a source past its TTL is refused with an explicit reason code rather than taken on old numbers Chainlink CRE runs the agent workflow, and the product tracks the provenance of every run, so a simulated result can never be presented as production execution ENS gives every agent its own name, and with it its own policy hash, budget and keys: separate principals rather than one super-agent, each revocable independently, with revocation invalidating previously issued capabilities without touching what the policy permits Ledger provides hardware signing over WebHID, with real device detection that walks connect, PIN, review, signed as the hardware changes state, the address derived on the device, and a rejection surfaced as a legitimate outcome rather than swallowed as an error
projects.how_its_made: THE SHAPE OF IT Next.js 15 App Router on React 19 and TypeScript. React Flow draws the architecture graph, Monaco backs the code surface, TanStack Query holds server state with a deliberately short stale time because observed chain state should never be served from cache as if it were current. The design system is hand-written CSS, no Tailwind and no component library, scoped under one root with container queries so a card responds to the pane it sits in rather than the viewport. Every page reads from a typed layer that mirrors the exact shapes the chain and the policy engine return: Blueprint revisions, policy matrices with reason codes, simulation runs with deterministic inputs and stopping layers, runtime events with correlation IDs. The domain types live in one file that every surface imports, so changing an artifact shape fails the typecheck everywhere it is wrong. CHAINLINK DATA FEEDS: WHERE FRESHNESS BECAME A TYPE A policy layer can enforce an amount on its own. What it cannot invent is whether the price it is deciding on is still true. Data Feeds return a round, not a number, and the round carries provenance: aggregator address, decimals, heartbeat, deviation threshold, and the timestamp of the last update. That shape is why freshness is a first-class field everywhere in this product rather than a nice-to-have. Every data requirement in a Blueprint declares a trust class and a maximum age, for example VERIFIED_ORACLE with a TTL of 60 seconds Before an action is evaluated, the round's age is checked against that TTL. Past it, the action is refused with ORACLE_STALE and no capability is issued at all Trust class is a property of the source and cannot be promoted by prose. An indexed query cannot satisfy a verified-price requirement, and the built-in assistant is explicitly forbidden from claiming otherwise Where a required source is unavailable it is reported UNAVAILABLE rather than silently substituted with a weaker one The attack suite exercises this directly: a stale price round and a source-unavailable scenario both stop at the policy layer, and the run records which layer stopped them. CHAINLINK CRE: A RUNTIME WITH A PROVENANCE TRAIL CRE gave us something to compile the agent's workflow to, and a boundary we would not have designed on our own. The workflow compiles to WASM and its hash is recorded in the deployment receipt alongside the runtime image digest, so the artifact that ran can be checked against the artifact that was approved. Runs execute through the official CRE CLI simulator, and every run carries its mode with it. That last part shaped the product. Because a simulated run and a production run are distinguishable in the data, we could make them distinguishable in the UI and refuse to let one be displayed as the other. The CRE surface states execution mode, DON status, consensus and hardware attestation as separate evidence flags rather than one green "connected" badge, and those flags travel into the exported safety report. A report cannot claim more than the run it was built from. ENS: IDENTITY AS A STRUCTURAL CONSTRAINT ENS changed the architecture more than any other integration. Agents live under an organisation namespace, each holding its own subname, node hash, owner and manager. Because identity is per-agent rather than per-deployment, "separate principals, not one super-agent" stopped being a convention and became something the product can check: Each agent has its own ENS name, policy hash, budget and keys Two agents resolving to the same policy hash is surfaced as a blocking critical issue, because one agent's authority would then be indistinguishable from another's Resolver records carry agent context, an endpoint and resolver metadata Revocation invalidates capabilities already issued under that identity, and leaves untouched what the policy permits That last line is the separation we think is correct and that ENS forced us to be explicit about: ENS identifies and revokes, the policy governs money. The UI refuses to let either stand in for the other, and no spending limit is ever stored as a text record, because a name record is not an authority boundary and nothing enforces it at execution time. LEDGER: THE ONE PART RUNNING ON REAL HARDWARE Signing goes over WebHID using @ledgerhq/hw-transport-webhid and @ledgerhq/hw-app-eth. viem serialises the unsigned EIP-1559 transaction, the device derives the address on the standard path, and the signature comes back as r, s and v from the hardware. Nothing about the flow is staged. The hacky part is that there is no API which reports "the Ledger is locked". The entire connection state machine is derived from a single getAddress() call and the status code it throws: 0x5515: powered but locked, waiting on a PIN any other status: answering, but the Ethereum app is not frontmost an address returned: unlocked, correct app, ready to sign 0x6985 during signing: the user pressed reject The signing promise stays pending for exactly as long as the user is reviewing on the device, which is what makes the "Review on your Ledger" panel literally true rather than a timed guess. A rejection is treated as an answer and surfaced plainly, not swallowed as an error, because for this product a refused signature is a legitimate outcome. Two details that cost real time. A 1.2 second poll runs alongside WebHID connect and disconnect events, because unplugging the cable fires an event but entering a PIN on the device fires nothing at all. And a guard stops the poll interleaving with a signature, since both share one HID pipe and two conversations over it corrupt each other. The device artwork is Ledger's own. Ledger open-sources Ledger Live, and the Nano S Plus animations ship as Lottie JSON under MIT, so we render the exact animation a Ledger owner already recognises, licence carried alongside the files. THE ASSISTANT, AND WHY IT CANNOT ACT The page-aware assistant sends a typed context envelope rather than a hand-built mega prompt: route, page kind, current revisions, selected entity, explicit attachments. Mentions resolve to real entity IDs in the frontend before the turn is sent, so the model never guesses what @guardian refers to. Responses render as structured cards bound to an authority tier. A proposed patch cannot mutate anything; accepting it hands the proposal to the page that owns the artifact, which shows it as a pending draft change. A control suggestion can only open the product's own typed confirmation dialog. There is no code path from the assistant to a privileged action, which is the same argument the policy layer makes, applied to our own UI. OTHER THINGS WORTH MENTIONING Keeping the wallet stack out of the bundle. RainbowKit pulls roughly 7,000 modules transitively and one connector reaches a package that does not resolve here at all. The wallet session is a tiny context that imports nothing heavy, the real runtime mounts behind a dynamic import only once someone connects, and unused connector subpaths are aliased to an empty module in both the Turbopack and webpack configs. Turbopack matches alias keys as exact specifiers with no prefix matching, so all 22 subpaths had to be listed individually. Every route now ships 135 to 144 kB, including the deploy page, instead of 353 kB. A circular layout bug worth the warning. The signing sheet resizes between steps by measuring the active panel and setting the container height from it. The panels were absolutely positioned with inset: 0, which makes a panel's height equal to its container's, so the measurement returned the value it was about to set and the card could never grow to fit its content. Dropping bottom from the positioning fixed it.

Every other surface is a projection of that artifact. The architecture graph, the generated code, the simulation runs and the deployed policy all carry a revision, and anything built against an older one is marked stale rather than shown as current.

Authority itself is enforced by a deterministic policy layer sitting outside the model and outside the runtime. Every proposed action is evaluated against stated limits (amount, recipient allowlist, data trust class and age, rolling window budget) and resolves to one of three outcomes:

- ALLOW, under the per-action limit, where the agent acts alone
- ESCALATE, between that and the escalation band, where a human approves
- DENY, above the hard ceiling, refused outright whatever the model believes

When an action is permitted the agent receives a capability that is scoped to that single action, single-use, nonce-bound and already expiring. It never holds a standing key, so a compromised runtime inherits no authority beyond the capability currently in its hand.

The one number we refuse to generate is the financial ceiling. The built-in assistant interviews you through every gap in your requirements: protocol, triggers, recipients, data sources, forbidden actions. But when it reaches the limits that bound your money it asks and then refuses to answer. A figure it suggested would become the figure you accepted.


HOW YOU USE IT

Describe the agent, generate a Blueprint, and inspect the permission matrix it produces, which is computed from the policy rather than described by the model. From there:

- Run 24 deterministic simulation scenarios and 16 attack scenarios (prompt injection, recipient mutation, amount mutation, target mutation, stale oracle data, runtime compromise, mainnet write attempts) and see the exact layer that stopped each one, and whether a capability was ever issued
- Test against real market conditions with mainnet as a read-only source or an isolated local fork, where fork transactions are labelled as such and never given a public explorer link
- Deploy to a testnet with the policy starting disabled, and enable financial authority only once every precondition passes

After deployment you operate it from the same workspace: observed on-chain state with per-source freshness, a correlated event log that traces any transaction back through capability issuance to its original trigger, drift detection between expected and observed configuration, and an Emergency Lock that attempts the financial policy first.


INTEGRATIONS

- Chainlink Data Feeds supply verified oracle rounds carrying a trust class and a freshness window, so a decision that depends on a source past its TTL is refused with an explicit reason code rather than taken on old numbers
- Chainlink CRE runs the agent workflow, and the product tracks the provenance of every run, so a simulated result can never be presented as production execution
- ENS gives every agent its own name, and with it its own policy hash, budget and keys: separate principals rather than one super-agent, each revocable independently, with revocation invalidating previously issued capabilities without touching what the policy permits
- Ledger provides hardware signing over WebHID, with real device detection that walks connect, PIN, review, signed as the hardware changes state, the address derived on the device, and a rejection surfaced as a legitimate outcome rather than swallowed as an error
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
THE SHAPE OF IT

Next.js 15 App Router on React 19 and TypeScript. React Flow draws the architecture graph, Monaco backs the code surface, TanStack Query holds server state with a deliberately short stale time because observed chain state should never be served from cache as if it were current. The design system is hand-written CSS, no Tailwind and no component library, scoped under one root with container queries so a card responds to the pane it sits in rather than the viewport.

Every page reads from a typed layer that mirrors the exact shapes the chain and the policy engine return: Blueprint revisions, policy matrices with reason codes, simulation runs with deterministic inputs and stopping layers, runtime events with correlation IDs. The domain types live in one file that every surface imports, so changing an artifact shape fails the typecheck everywhere it is wrong.


CHAINLINK DATA FEEDS: WHERE FRESHNESS BECAME A TYPE

A policy layer can enforce an amount on its own. What it cannot invent is whether the price it is deciding on is still true.

Data Feeds return a round, not a number, and the round carries provenance: aggregator address, decimals, heartbeat, deviation threshold, and the timestamp of the last update. That shape is why freshness is a first-class field everywhere in this product rather than a nice-to-have.

- Every data requirement in a Blueprint declares a trust class and a maximum age, for example VERIFIED_ORACLE with a TTL of 60 seconds
- Before an action is evaluated, the round's age is checked against that TTL. Past it, the action is refused with ORACLE_STALE and no capability is issued at all
- Trust class is a property of the source and cannot be promoted by prose. An indexed query cannot satisfy a verified-price requirement, and the built-in assistant is explicitly forbidden from claiming otherwise
- Where a required source is unavailable it is reported UNAVAILABLE rather than silently substituted with a weaker one

The attack suite exercises this directly: a stale price round and a source-unavailable scenario both stop at the policy layer, and the run records which layer stopped them.


CHAINLINK CRE: A RUNTIME WITH A PROVENANCE TRAIL

CRE gave us something to compile the agent's workflow to, and a boundary we would not have designed on our own.

The workflow compiles to WASM and its hash is recorded in the deployment receipt alongside the runtime image digest, so the artifact that ran can be checked against the artifact that was approved. Runs execute through the official CRE CLI simulator, and every run carries its mode with it.

That last part shaped the product. Because a simulated run and a production run are distinguishable in the data, we could make them distinguishable in the UI and refuse to let one be displayed as the other. The CRE surface states execution mode, DON status, consensus and hardware attestation as separate evidence flags rather than one green "connected" badge, and those flags travel into the exported safety report. A report cannot claim more than the run it was built from.


ENS: IDENTITY AS A STRUCTURAL CONSTRAINT

ENS changed the architecture more than any other integration.

Agents live under an organisation namespace, each holding its own subname, node hash, owner and manager. Because identity is per-agent rather than per-deployment, "separate principals, not one super-agent" stopped being a convention and became something the product can check:

- Each agent has its own ENS name, policy hash, budget and keys
- Two agents resolving to the same policy hash is surfaced as a blocking critical issue, because one agent's authority would then be indistinguishable from another's
- Resolver records carry agent context, an endpoint and resolver metadata
- Revocation invalidates capabilities already issued under that identity, and leaves untouched what the policy permits

That last line is the separation we think is correct and that ENS forced us to be explicit about: ENS identifies and revokes, the policy governs money. The UI refuses to let either stand in for the other, and no spending limit is ever stored as a text record, because a name record is not an authority boundary and nothing enforces it at execution time.


LEDGER: THE ONE PART RUNNING ON REAL HARDWARE

Signing goes over WebHID using @ledgerhq/hw-transport-webhid and @ledgerhq/hw-app-eth. viem serialises the unsigned EIP-1559 transaction, the device derives the address on the standard path, and the signature comes back as r, s and v from the hardware. Nothing about the flow is staged.

The hacky part is that there is no API which reports "the Ledger is locked". The entire connection state machine is derived from a single getAddress() call and the status code it throws:

- 0x5515: powered but locked, waiting on a PIN
- any other status: answering, but the Ethereum app is not frontmost
- an address returned: unlocked, correct app, ready to sign
- 0x6985 during signing: the user pressed reject

The signing promise stays pending for exactly as long as the user is reviewing on the device, which is what makes the "Review on your Ledger" panel literally true rather than a timed guess. A rejection is treated as an answer and surfaced plainly, not swallowed as an error, because for this product a refused signature is a legitimate outcome.

Two details that cost real time. A 1.2 second poll runs alongside WebHID connect and disconnect events, because unplugging the cable fires an event but entering a PIN on the device fires nothing at all. And a guard stops the poll interleaving with a signature, since both share one HID pipe and two conversations over it corrupt each other.

The device artwork is Ledger's own. Ledger open-sources Ledger Live, and the Nano S Plus animations ship as Lottie JSON under MIT, so we render the exact animation a Ledger owner already recognises, licence carried alongside the files.


THE ASSISTANT, AND WHY IT CANNOT ACT

The page-aware assistant sends a typed context envelope rather than a hand-built mega prompt: route, page kind, current revisions, selected entity, explicit attachments. Mentions resolve to real entity IDs in the frontend before the turn is sent, so the model never guesses what @guardian refers to.

Responses render as structured cards bound to an authority tier. A proposed patch cannot mutate anything; accepting it hands the proposal to the page that owns the artifact, which shows it as a pending draft change. A control suggestion can only open the product's own typed confirmation dialog. There is no code path from the assistant to a privileged action, which is the same argument the policy layer makes, applied to our own UI.


OTHER THINGS WORTH MENTIONING

Keeping the wallet stack out of the bundle. RainbowKit pulls roughly 7,000 modules transitively and one connector reaches a package that does not resolve here at all. The wallet session is a tiny context that imports nothing heavy, the real runtime mounts behind a dynamic import only once someone connects, and unused connector subpaths are aliased to an empty module in both the Turbopack and webpack configs. Turbopack matches alias keys as exact specifiers with no prefix matching, so all 22 subpaths had to be listed individually. Every route now ships 135 to 144 kB, including the deploy page, instead of 353 kB.

A circular layout bug worth the warning. The signing sheet resizes between steps by measuring the active panel and setting the container height from it. The panels were absolutely positioned with inset: 0, which makes a panel's height equal to its container's, so the measurement returned the value it was about to set and the card could never grow to fit its content. Dropping bottom from the positioning fixed it.

projects.title: Touchstone Assay
projects.description: A benchmark price of AI Inference work,real agents can compare offers before paying in USDC.
projects.project_description: AI work has no common price. Every model prices in its own tokens, but tokens aren't comparable — different tokenizers count the same text differently, verbosity varies several-fold, and reasoning tokens are billed as output while never appearing in your prompt. The same task can cost far more on one model than another at similar headline prices. So an AI agent choosing between providers has no basis for comparison, and the finance team funding it can't tell whether it's buying more work or paying more for the same work. Touchstone Assay publishes Dated SIU: the price of one Standard Inference Unit, defined as a fixed basket of inference tasks completed at a defined quality threshold. Output that fails the gate counts as zero regardless of compute burned — a cheap model that doesn't finish the work isn't cheap. We measure the price by actually buying inference across ten models daily, reconciling against provider invoices, and publishing a signed print hash-anchored on chain. For this hackathon we brought that onto Arc. Quotes travel as an extension of x402: a seller's HTTP 402 response carries the SIU amount, its own rate, and a signed quote hash alongside the USDC ask. A buyer agent fetches two quotes, compares them in SIU, funds a non-custodial escrow, settles after the work completes, and verifies the receipt against the on-chain settlement. The live demo runs two seller agents on genuinely different model tiers. Quote-side the spread is 14.9×; the settled spread came out at roughly 23×, because the frontier model's real output ran longer relative to its own estimate. That divergence is the whole argument — headline token prices underpredicted the real cost of identical work by around 50%. Escrow stays on Arc testnet deliberately. It holds funds, it's immutable once deployed, and external review is outstanding. Arc mainnet opens on 16 September, three days after this deadline; the attestation deploy script is written and waiting.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo. Solidity with Foundry for contracts. Cloudflare Workers for the agents and the MCP server. Everything settles in USDC. Two contracts on Arc testnet: TouchstoneAttestation stores signed price-print hashes so anyone can verify a published number was issued under a stated methodology version, and TouchstoneEscrow handles quote-then-settle payments — buyer funds against a quoted maximum, seller settles the actual amount, remainder refunds automatically, no admin path to user funds in any code path. Both are byte-identical to our Base Sepolia deployment with zero contract changes, because every chain-specific value was already a constructor parameter. The touchstone-quote extension rides inside the 402 response. An MCP server, listed on the official registry, exposes four tools — get_index free, get_quote, convert and verify_receipt paywalled through Circle's Gateway nanopayments over x402. Three real platform gotchas, each worth knowing. Cloudflare blocks a Worker's own fetch() to another Worker's bare *.workers.dev URL — fixed with custom domains. Arc's real gas price is far above typical Base Sepolia defaults, so the funding helper needed an override. And the primary Arc RPC rate-limited under our own sustained traffic, so we moved to the documented dRPC mirror. The hackiest thing worth admitting: the demo task was resized four times, each iteration verified against a real settlement, because the original prompt settled below the escrow's MIN_SETTLEMENT floor and reverted. We learned along the way that soft word counts barely move a smaller model's output — a "≥2800 words" instruction produced only 23% more tokens — while explicit section structure nearly doubled it. That's a real finding about prompt-to-cost sensitivity, and it shaped the basket design.

projects.title: Procure
projects.description: Procure-to-pay for onchain companies. Unmatched invoices can't be paid — the contract refuses.
projects.project_description:
Procure is a multi-tenant B2B procure-to-pay system for companies whose treasury is onchain. Purchase requests, approvals, purchase orders, goods receipt, vendor invoicing, three-way match, double-entry accounting, and settlement in USDC on Arc. The problem. A company with an onchain treasury has no way to run procurement without trusting a person or a server. A multisig approves transfers, not purchases — the signer has no idea whether the goods arrived or whether the invoice matches what was ordered. ERPs know all of that and enforce none of it cryptographically: "approved" is a database field, and invoice fraud is a multi-billion-dollar problem because of it. Every control sits in software beside the money rather than in it. What we built. The claim is simple: an invoice that doesn't match its purchase order cannot be paid — not by policy, by construction. The cycle: a requester raises a request against their department's budget → approvers sign it with their own Privy wallet (EIP-712, free, instant, no gas, no transaction) → a purchaser issues the order and its terms are fixed onchain before anyone can act on them → the requesting side confirms delivery, never whoever pays → the vendor submits their own invoice from a separate vendor portal, typing their own figure → the three-way match compares all three, and ProcureRegistry.executePayment on Arc recovers every approver signature, checks it against an onchain approver set and threshold, checks the vendor allowlist, the budget and replay — then transfers the USDC, or reverts. Why signatures rather than transactions. Arc charges gas in USDC, so one transaction per approval would mean funding every approver's wallet before they could act. Instead approvers sign off-chain for free and one transaction carries every signature to the chain, which counts them before the money moves. It's a cheque: you sign at your desk, the bank verifies at the counter. Compromise our server and you still cannot pay an unapproved vendor an unapproved amount. Vendor risk screening — where The Graph does real work. Before a vendor's payout address can receive anything, it is screened through The Graph's Token API across Ethereum mainnet, Base and Arbitrum. Seven weighted signals are computed from raw transfer history: Address age — binary-searched on existence rather than trusting returned timestamps, which are unreliable under rate limiting
Forwarding behaviour — does money arrive and immediately leave? A pass-through address is not a business
Counterparty diversity — how many distinct parties has it genuinely traded with
Activity level — sustained commercial movement, not a single spike
Account type — EOA, contract, or EIP-7702 delegated EOA
Dust activity — explicitly detected and reported, not silently dropped
Stablecoin holdings — current balances across all three chains These produce a 0–100 score and a band: CLEAR, REVIEW or BLOCKED (thresholds configurable per deployment). An LLM writes the narrative assessment from the computed signals, never from raw data, so it explains a decision rather than making one — with a rule-based fallback when no key is present. Results render as a weighted breakdown plus an interactive 3D counterparty graph, where dust nodes are hidden by default except when there are fewer than three commercial counterparties — because then the dust is the finding. Crucially this is not advisory. A vendor's status drives setVendorAllowed on the contract, so a blocked address leaves the onchain allowlist and executePayment refuses it regardless of what our database later says. Making it spam-resistant took two rounds, both found by testing against real addresses. An unused vanity address scored 100/100 — worthless airdropped tokens looked like counterparty diversity and holdings. We switched to screening stablecoins only; it scored 100 again, because address-poisoning attacks send genuine sub-dollar USDC to lookalike addresses. A $10 dust floor fixed it. Final spread: Circle treasury 88, Vitalik 100, a poisoned vanity address 60, a never-used address 47. Privy — org and department wallets, policies, and the approver signatures the contract verifies. Arc rejects eth_sendTransaction, so Privy signs and we broadcast; the policy engine still fires at the signer.
Arc — USDC as both gas and settlement. A full cycle costs under a cent. Also built: configurable approval workflows (levels, quorum, amount thresholds, per org per module, snapshotted onto each request so later edits can't move the bar), auto-settlement of matched bills, a double-entry ledger where GR/IR clearing nets to zero only when receipt and invoice agree — making the exception report a number that won't go away — trial balance with CSV export, PDFs for all five documents, and transactional email at every step. Live: ProcureRegistry at 0xa033ac540710763422618453C80AA026c0FE11f0 on Arc testnet, 14 contract tests (mostly revert paths), and a completed cycle settling real USDC in tx 0x6a698c9213bc3b489ccbec8e4c707132f9c1d77193503ae4de815c3fd4180039.
projects.how_its_made: Stack App: Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, server actions — no separate API layer), TypeScript, Tailwind. Data: Postgres on Supabase, Prisma 7 with the @prisma/adapter-pg driver adapter. Contracts: Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry, deployed to Arc testnet. Chain access: viem. Auth & wallets: Privy — @privy-io/react-auth on the client, REST for server wallets. Indexing: The Graph's Token API via Pinax. Email: Resend behind a Mailer interface. AI: GPT-4o for risk narratives. 3D: react-force-graph-3d. How it fits together Postgres holds documents and workflow state. The contract holds spend authority . The two stay in step through explicit sync points: saving an approval level writes setApprovers to Arc, issuing a purchase order writes commitOrder , activating or blocking a vendor writes setVendorAllowed . Every chain write is signed by the organisation's Privy treasury wallet and broadcast by us. ProcureRegistry stores, per organisation: the approver set and threshold for each level, the vendor allowlist, the budget ceiling, and each order's committed terms. executePayment recovers every approver signature, checks each against the on-chain set, counts them against the threshold, verifies the payee is allowlisted and the amount is within budget and unpaid — then moves USDC, or reverts. Privy Privy gives every actor a wallet without anyone touching a seed phrase: email OTP sign-in, an embedded wallet per user, and server wallets for the org treasury and each department. The critical use is approvals as signatures . An approver signs an EIP-712 struct naming the order hash, level and amount with their own embedded wallet — free, instant, no gas, no transaction. We sign through the wallet's EIP-1193 provider ( eth_signTypedData_v4 ) so approval is a single click with no dialog, which matches what the action actually is. On the treasury side, an integration detail worth knowing: Arc doesn't accept eth_sendTransaction through Privy , but eth_signTransaction with chain_id inside the transaction returns signed RLP — and Privy's policy engine still evaluates on that path (a disallowed recipient is rejected before signing). So the split is deliberate: Privy holds the key and enforces policy; we own the RPC and broadcast to Arc. Both control layers stay intact, and the vendor allowlist is enforced twice — once at the signer, once in the contract. Before writing any Solidity we validated the premise the whole design rests on, by calling Arc's ecrecover precompile directly via eth_call : a Privy signature recovers to the approver's address on-chain, exactly as ECDSA.recover will inside the contract. The Graph Every vendor payout address is screened through the Token API across Ethereum mainnet, Base and Arbitrum before it can receive anything. We pull raw transfer history and balances and compute seven weighted signals ourselves — address age, forwarding behaviour, counterparty diversity, activity level, account type (including EIP-7702 delegated EOAs), dust activity and stablecoin holdings — producing a 0–100 score and a CLEAR / REVIEW / BLOCKED band. Two design decisions made it robust: Stablecoin-only screening with a $10 dust floor. Raw token history is full of airdropped junk and address-poisoning dust, both of which imitate legitimate trading. Filtering to stablecoins above a commercial threshold means the score reflects real payments. Address age is binary-searched on existence , not on returned timestamps, and the search is skipped entirely when the oldest sampled transfer already proves the address is over a year old — keeping a full screen inside the free tier's rate limits. GPT-4o writes the narrative from the computed signals , never from raw data, so it explains a decision rather than making one. Results render as a weighted breakdown plus an interactive 3D counterparty graph. The Graph turns screening from advice into enforcement: a vendor's band drives setVendorAllowed , so a blocked address leaves the on-chain allowlist and the contract refuses it. Arc Arc is the settlement layer and the reason the economics work. USDC is both the gas token and the money , so a vendor is paid in the same asset that pays for the transaction, and a complete cycle — register approvers, commit an order, allowlist a vendor, execute payment — costs under a cent . That also shaped the architecture. Because gas is USDC, one transaction per approval would mean funding every approver's wallet before they could act. Signing off-chain and verifying on-chain means approvers need zero balance and only the treasury ever holds funds. One Arc-specific detail we handled carefully: native gas accounting uses 18 decimals while the USDC ERC-20 uses 6. Same asset, two scales, a factor of 10¹² apart. We branded them as distinct TypeScript types ( Usdc6 , Native18 ) so mixing them is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. Every amount in the system is a BigInt count of base units — never a float. Other implementation notes Signatures must arrive sorted by recovered address, strictly ascending — that makes counting one approval twice structurally impossible rather than something to check for, and it's cheaper than a seen-set on-chain. Approvals are keyed by the request, not the order , because approvers sign before an order exists; commitOrder then writes under that same key so signature and commitment refer to the same thing. Approval flows are snapshotted onto each request at submit , so editing org policy later can't retroactively move the bar a live request has to clear. The double-entry ledger posts automatically on receipt, bill and payment. GR/IR clearing nets to zero only when what arrived and what was invoiced agree — the exception report is a balance, not a screen. PDFs are generated without a library — the base-14 fonts are guaranteed present in every reader, so nothing is embedded and each document is 3–4KB, with no font or bundler configuration inside a serverless route. Prisma 7 moved connection URLs out of the schema and requires a driver adapter; the client is built lazily so a build needs no database, and cached so warm serverless instances reuse one pool.

## Stack

**App:** Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, server actions — no separate API layer), TypeScript, Tailwind.
**Data:** Postgres on Supabase, Prisma 7 with the `@prisma/adapter-pg` driver adapter.
**Contracts:** Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry, deployed to Arc testnet.
**Chain access:** viem.
**Auth & wallets:** Privy — `@privy-io/react-auth` on the client, REST for server wallets.
**Indexing:** The Graph's Token API via Pinax.
**Email:** Resend behind a `Mailer` interface. **AI:** GPT-4o for risk narratives. **3D:** react-force-graph-3d.

## How it fits together

Postgres holds documents and workflow state. The contract holds **spend authority**. The two stay in step through explicit sync points: saving an approval level writes `setApprovers` to Arc, issuing a purchase order writes `commitOrder`, activating or blocking a vendor writes `setVendorAllowed`. Every chain write is signed by the organisation's Privy treasury wallet and broadcast by us.

`ProcureRegistry` stores, per organisation: the approver set and threshold for each level, the vendor allowlist, the budget ceiling, and each order's committed terms. `executePayment` recovers every approver signature, checks each against the on-chain set, counts them against the threshold, verifies the payee is allowlisted and the amount is within budget and unpaid — then moves USDC, or reverts.

## Privy

Privy gives every actor a wallet without anyone touching a seed phrase: email OTP sign-in, an embedded wallet per user, and server wallets for the org treasury and each department.

The critical use is **approvals as signatures**. An approver signs an EIP-712 struct naming the order hash, level and amount with their own embedded wallet — free, instant, no gas, no transaction. We sign through the wallet's EIP-1193 provider (`eth_signTypedData_v4`) so approval is a single click with no dialog, which matches what the action actually is.

On the treasury side, an integration detail worth knowing: **Arc doesn't accept `eth_sendTransaction` through Privy**, but `eth_signTransaction` with `chain_id` inside the transaction returns signed RLP — and Privy's **policy engine still evaluates on that path** (a disallowed recipient is rejected before signing). So the split is deliberate: **Privy holds the key and enforces policy; we own the RPC and broadcast to Arc.** Both control layers stay intact, and the vendor allowlist is enforced twice — once at the signer, once in the contract.

Before writing any Solidity we validated the premise the whole design rests on, by calling Arc's `ecrecover` precompile directly via `eth_call`: a Privy signature recovers to the approver's address on-chain, exactly as `ECDSA.recover` will inside the contract.

## The Graph

Every vendor payout address is screened through the Token API across **Ethereum mainnet, Base and Arbitrum** before it can receive anything. We pull raw transfer history and balances and compute seven weighted signals ourselves — address age, forwarding behaviour, counterparty diversity, activity level, account type (including EIP-7702 delegated EOAs), dust activity and stablecoin holdings — producing a 0–100 score and a CLEAR / REVIEW / BLOCKED band.

Two design decisions made it robust:

- **Stablecoin-only screening with a $10 dust floor.** Raw token history is full of airdropped junk and address-poisoning dust, both of which imitate legitimate trading. Filtering to stablecoins above a commercial threshold means the score reflects real payments.
- **Address age is binary-searched on existence**, not on returned timestamps, and the search is skipped entirely when the oldest sampled transfer already proves the address is over a year old — keeping a full screen inside the free tier's rate limits.

GPT-4o writes the narrative **from the computed signals**, never from raw data, so it explains a decision rather than making one. Results render as a weighted breakdown plus an interactive 3D counterparty graph.

The Graph turns screening from advice into enforcement: a vendor's band drives `setVendorAllowed`, so a blocked address leaves the on-chain allowlist and the contract refuses it.

## Arc

Arc is the settlement layer and the reason the economics work. **USDC is both the gas token and the money**, so a vendor is paid in the same asset that pays for the transaction, and a complete cycle — register approvers, commit an order, allowlist a vendor, execute payment — costs **under a cent**.

That also shaped the architecture. Because gas is USDC, one transaction per approval would mean funding every approver's wallet before they could act. Signing off-chain and verifying on-chain means approvers need **zero balance** and only the treasury ever holds funds.

One Arc-specific detail we handled carefully: **native gas accounting uses 18 decimals while the USDC ERC-20 uses 6.** Same asset, two scales, a factor of 10¹² apart. We branded them as distinct TypeScript types (`Usdc6`, `Native18`) so mixing them is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. Every amount in the system is a `BigInt` count of base units — never a float.

## Other implementation notes

- **Signatures must arrive sorted by recovered address, strictly ascending** — that makes counting one approval twice structurally impossible rather than something to check for, and it's cheaper than a seen-set on-chain.
- **Approvals are keyed by the request, not the order**, because approvers sign before an order exists; `commitOrder` then writes under that same key so signature and commitment refer to the same thing.
- **Approval flows are snapshotted onto each request at submit**, so editing org policy later can't retroactively move the bar a live request has to clear.
- **The double-entry ledger posts automatically** on receipt, bill and payment. GR/IR clearing nets to zero only when what arrived and what was invoiced agree — the exception report is a balance, not a screen.
- **PDFs are generated without a library** — the base-14 fonts are guaranteed present in every reader, so nothing is embedded and each document is 3–4KB, with no font or bundler configuration inside a serverless route.
- **Prisma 7** moved connection URLs out of the schema and requires a driver adapter; the client is built lazily so a build needs no database, and cached so warm serverless instances reuse one pool.

projects.title: MDCP - MCP for DeFi
projects.description: A faster MCP standard for DeFi agents — far more token-efficient, and far faster in execution
projects.project_description: Agentic finance today is agentic in name only. Almost everything that ships is a script — a strategy hard-coded in advance, with no model anywhere near the decision. Not because nobody wants autonomous agents, but because the standard way to give a model access to a chain, MCP, costs too many tokens and too much time per action to survive a loop. And an agent that trades is a loop that never ends. It runs 24/7, so every cost inside it compounds: an inefficiency that looks trivial on a single call is your entire AI bill by the end of the month, and the strategy stops paying for itself long before it stops working. Time is the harder wall. With today's official trading skills, getting from "make this trade" to a signed transaction averages around 5 seconds, and it is the good case. Worse, it degrades with complexity: the moment a strategy is more than a couple of calls, every intermediate result stays in the context window, the window grows, and each next step — including the trivial ones — takes longer than the last. We measured exactly that on Uniswap. Use skills from more than one vendor together and it compounds again. Each brings its own tens of kilobytes of instructions and its own payloads into the same context, so running two protocols together costs more than running each apart. For agents to actually operate in DeFi, a complex strategy has to execute in under a second and stay flat as it grows. That is the target mdcp is built against. Measured against the protocols' own official agent tooling, it cuts what reaches the model by 10x to 100x and wall-clock time by 1.5x to 11x — and, more importantly, the cost stops scaling with the strategy: triple the work and our side stays roughly flat. The mechanism is code mode. Instead of calling tools one at a time, the agent writes one small program, and it runs in a sandbox sitting next to the chain with Uniswap, The Graph and Hedera already mounted. The loop happens there. Only the answer comes back. And because it is code, the safety is code too: keys never enter the sandbox, and the whole strategy is planned and approved once before anything is signed. DeFi needs its own standard for how agents touch it. This is a proposal for what it should be.
projects.how_its_made: A TypeScript MCP server over stdio (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk). It exposes three tools — execute, resume, skills — and every chain capability lives behind them. Programs run in QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly. The runtime itself is an off-the-shelf npm dependency (@executor-js/runtime-quickjs, MIT) used as published; everything that turns it into a chain gateway is ours. Inside it a program gets no network, no filesystem, no environment and no reach into our process. Its only exit is a host-controlled bridge, so every call leaving the sandbox is a checkpoint we own. What we built on top is the part a general code runner does not have: A policy gate keyed on a declared side-effect class — view / local / chain. It is data on the tool rather than an instruction in a prompt, so it holds regardless of what the model decides to do. Only chain is gated. Plan, then approve once. The first execute runs the whole strategy to completion without broadcasting anything and returns a single transaction plan. The operator approves the plan rather than each leg, so approval cost does not grow with the number of legs. On resume the program re-runs against live state, so a quote taken before the human answered is recomputed instead of replayed stale. Transaction-intent idempotency. Each chain write is hashed over its economic fields only — token, direction, amount — plus an occurrence index, so re-quoting does not change an intent's identity and a transaction that already landed replays from a ledger instead of being sent again. Chain access is viem, against anvil mainnet forks and live Sepolia. Uniswap runs through the production Trading API (check_approval to quote to swap, with x-agent-info attribution), signed host-side: the key never enters the sandbox and only ever signs an intent from an approved plan. Hedera uses the Hiero SDK for HTS and HCS on testnet, with recipient keys in a host keystore so a token association can be signed without key material reaching the program. Two integrations are generic MCP-upstream adapters. mdcp connects to another MCP server as a client, discovers its tools at runtime, converts their JSON Schema into compact TypeScript signatures and re-exposes them inside the sandbox. The Graph's subgraph-mcp and Hedera's 43-tool mirrornode-mcp-server are both mounted that way, unmodified. Upstream failures come back as values rather than thrown exceptions, so a program sweeping ten subgraphs still returns for the ones that answer. Measurement is built in rather than bolted on: both interaction shapes are served from one capability registry by two thin servers, so the only thing that differs between arms is the shape, never the implementation, and every invocation logs argument bytes, result bytes, duration and whether it crossed the model boundary. That instrumentation caught two bugs in our own idempotency design that would have re-sent a transaction. A reviewer can mount one protocol at a time with MDCP_PROFILE=uniswap|graph|hedera|all. All together it is 76 capabilities behind 3 MCP tools and 13KB of always-loaded description.

projects.title: Ledger-of-Work
projects.description: Agents buy multi-step web work over x402 on Hedera, metered, with a receipt anyone can verify.
projects.project_description:
When software pays software, the buyer gets bytes and no way to check them. No invoice,
nothing tying the data to a real retrieval, and the money has already moved. A person would
notice a number that looks wrong. An agent has no such instinct — which is how a $7M
prediction-market resolution came down to a screenshot in a Discord channel that nobody
could verify. Ledger of Work sells completed web work to agents over x402 on Hedera — logging in,
searching, paginating, extracting — and hands back a receipt anyone can check without
trusting us. PRICED BY THE WORK, NOT THE REQUEST
Ten records cost the same as three, because they sit on one page. A hundred costs five times
more, because it is ten pages. The meter charges for pages traversed and steps taken, against
a price book published before you buy. THE RECEIPT IS THE PRODUCT
Every job commits the answer, the rendered page, a screenshot, and — where the source allows
it — a zkTLS proof from an independent attestor who watched the TLS session and signed what
the site actually returned. That proof is the one thing on the receipt we could not forge,
because we do not hold the attestor's key. CHECK IT YOURSELF IN A MINUTE
Open the verifier, enter topic 0.0.10413059, sequence 18, seller 0.0.10410493, and drop in
the four files from samples/ in the repo. Fourteen checks, all green. Now swap
result-proof.json for result-proof.tampered.json — one character different. Thirteen checks
still pass: the payment settled, the price follows the book, the page, screenshot and proof
are all intact. One goes red. VOID. That page never contacts our servers. It reads the public Hedera mirror node from your
browser, so it works if you assume we are lying. WHAT IS ON CHAIN RIGHT NOW
57 receipts. 53 paid jobs across five capabilities, from three separate accounts, four
settled in an HTS token, seven carrying attestor proofs. Four charged nothing, because a job
that delivers nothing is not billed. AN AGENT NEEDS NOTHING FROM US TO START
It reads an open HCS directory with no submit key, resolves an HCS-14 identity and an A2A
agent card, and negotiates over A2A message/send: state a budget and the seller offers a
smaller job at the same published rate — never a discount, because the verifier re-checks the
price against the book and a discount would fail its own audit. Then it pays and verifies.
One command, starting from nothing but a topic id.
projects.how_its_made:
A pnpm TypeScript monorepo: six packages, eight apps, 501 tests, none of which touch the
network. Partner technologies, and what each actually bought us. Hedera Consensus Service is the
receipt log — ordered, timestamped, append-only, and cheap enough that a fifth-of-a-cent job
can afford to write to it, which is the property that makes per-job receipts viable at all.
The mirror node REST API is what makes verification trustless: the verifier reads it directly
from a browser, so a sceptic never has to ask us for anything. Blocky402 settles the x402
payments. HTS carries settlement in a token so an agent holding a stablecoin need not hold
HBAR. Scheduled Transactions (HIP-423) give recurring payment, and setWaitForExpiry(true) is
the difference between a standing order and every transfer firing at once. HCS-14 gives the
service a name derived from what it is rather than where it is hosted. The genuinely hacky parts. Hedera only has x402's exact scheme — there is no upto — so
work-based pricing is built from it: a pure plan() prices the job before any work, the buyer
signs that one number, and the seller absorbs every overrun. The verifier therefore checks the
quote against the published price book rather than the bill. Receipts must fit 1024 bytes
because the mirror REST API does not reassemble chunked messages, which is why the receipt
stores hashes rather than payloads and fails at build time naming the field to drop.
transactionId.accountId must be the facilitator's feePayer, not the buyer's, or settlement
returns InvalidSignature with no explanation — that one cost a day. Reclaim's attestor-core
needs setCryptoImplementation because @reclaimprotocol/tls ships an empty crypto object in
Node. Playwright drives the browser behind a policy we wrote after realising an allowlist was doing
security by accident: robots.txt is now fetched and obeyed per request to RFC 9309 (a bare
"Disallow:" means no restrictions, which whitehouse.gov serves), and an SSRF guard checks
every address a hostname resolves to, judges IPv4-in-IPv6 by IPv4 rules, refuses zero-padded
octets, and re-checks the URL after redirects. The proof tests run against a real captured attestor signature, because a hand-built fixture
cannot tell a valid signature from a forged one and every test would pass.

projects.title: Event Seal
projects.description: Fail-closed verification for onchain events before relayers, agents, or backends act.
projects.project_description:
Solana programs can emit convincing logs even when the surrounding transaction fails. A backend that trusts a webhook or decoded log too early can release a reward, grant access, or update a ledger for state that never committed.
EventSeal gives relayers, indexers, agents, and application backends a fail-closed checkpoint before they act. A developer submits a transaction signature and network, then separately supplies the expected program ID and Anchor event discriminator from a trusted source. EventSeal fetches finalized transaction evidence, confirms execution succeeded, reconstructs the active program invocation frames, and checks that the event came from the intended program. Missing or ambiguous evidence is never presented as success.
The live demo makes the failure visible using two Solana devnet transactions that emit the same event shape. The successful transaction verifies and receives a deterministic public receipt. The failed transaction returns TX_FAILED and receives no receipt. Duplicate deliveries of the same verified event resolve to the same receipt identity, giving downstream systems a stable basis for idempotent processing.
Continuity disclosure: EventSeal’s core SDK, hosted verifier, and Anchor devnet demonstration existed before ETHOnline 2026. Work completed during the event window includes stronger receipt-identity integrity, public receipt pages, an authenticated saved-receipt dashboard, hardened browser-to-function authentication, automated release tests, a public product homepage, developer documentation, and a redesigned verification workflow. The public Git history separates this work from the pre-event foundation.
projects.how_its_made:
EventSeal is a TypeScript monorepo containing a verification SDK, Next.js web application, InsForge edge functions, PostgreSQL receipt storage, and an Anchor program written in Rust for adversarial testing.
The core @eventseal/sdk reads Solana JSON-RPC using finalized commitment. It requires complete transaction metadata and meta.err === null, reconstructs nested program invocation frames, matches the expected eight-byte Anchor discriminator, and attributes the event to the expected active program. It returns an explicit verified, rejected, or indeterminate result. Missing, malformed, truncated, or unavailable evidence fails closed.
The browser first calls POST /api/inspect using only the signature and network. Inspection reports transaction facts and untrusted event candidates, but cannot authorize an event or create a receipt. Verification begins only after the caller independently provides the trusted program ID and discriminator through POST /api/verify. The Next.js server attaches the internal function credential, keeping backend credentials out of the browser.
Verified results are stored as immutable v2 receipts in PostgreSQL. Each receipt ID binds the network, finalized commitment, signature, trusted program, discriminator, event position, emitter, and event-data hash. Row-level security keeps writes server-only while permitting public evidence lookup.
The Anchor devnet program exposes emit_success and emit_then_fail. Both emit the same event bytes, but the second deliberately aborts. This matched pair proves EventSeal’s central claim: observing the expected log is insufficient; the complete transaction must have succeeded.

projects.title: Erebuz
projects.description: Privacy router for payments. Best pool, compliance, and bridge in one SDK call. No custom crypto.
projects.project_description: Erebuz is a privacy router for payments. Any app or wallet plugs in with about 10 lines of code and gets private, compliant transactions without building any crypto themselves. One SDK call finds the best privacy pool, runs a compliance check, and bridges funds to any chain. Right now the router supports two privacy options: our own pool, deployed natively on Arc, and Railgun's pool, which has stronger anonymity today simply because it has more volume. The router isn't locked into one tool, it picks whichever fits the transaction based on fees, speed, and privacy strength. projects.title: GRAPE AI
projects.description: You pay for AI. Now make your attention pay you back every time. ⚡
projects.project_description:
GRAPE AI is an AI Extension that creates a new economic loop between advertisers, developers, and AI compute. Today, developers spend money to access AI, while brands spend money to capture developer attention. GRAPE connects these two economies: advertisers fund campaigns, developers earn credits by engaging with relevant ads, and those credits pay for the AI compute developers already use. GRAPE uses The Graph Protocol to understand a user’s onchain activity and build detailed personas, allowing advertisers to target highly relevant audiences based on roles, regions, protocols, and real-time blockchain behavior. Campaign budgets are secured through smart contracts, with transparent spending and performance analytics. For developers, GRAPE integrates contextual ads directly into the AI workflow rather than interrupting it. When developers use GRAPE’s AI models, relevant ads generate regenerative credits, with developers earning up to 70%+ of ad spend toward future AI queries. The platform runs AI inference on its own compute infrastructure, turning developer attention into a mechanism for continuously funding AI usage. GRAPE also extends beyond human users. AI agents can interact with GRAPE programmatically through an extension and use the x402 protocol for pay-per-request micropayments on Hedera, receiving structured, onchain data without traditional API integrations. Extension link:
https://open-vsx.org/extension/GrapeTools/grape-ai https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=GrapeTools.grape-ai&ssr=false#review-details
projects.how_its_made: GRAPE AI is a developer AI assistant with a credit-based economy, combining AI inference, onchain intelligence, and blockchain-based payments. The extension is already live for VS Code and Cursor, so developers can install it and experience the full loop themselves. The client integrates with developer workflows, while our backend handles AI inference, campaign management, ad selection, credit accounting, and analytics. AI inference runs on our AWS EC2 infrastructure, where developer credits are consumed based on AI usage. Developers receive an initial credit grant and earn additional credits when qualified sponsored ads are served alongside their AI responses. Advertiser spend funds these rewards, creating a regenerative loop where developer attention helps pay for future AI compute. For onchain intelligence, we use The Graph Protocol (https://thegraph.com/) to analyze wallet activity and generate developer personas from live blockchain data. GRAPE uses Subgraphs, Token API, and Substreams across Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Base to identify activities such as DeFi usage, trading, NFT ownership, and smart-contract development. The same infrastructure allows the AI to query live onchain data and generate responses from current blockchain activity. Hedera provides the financial settlement layer. Advertisers fund campaigns using HTS USDC, with smart contracts managing campaign budgets, settlement, and developer withdrawals. CampaignVault handles campaign funds and settlement, while RewardPool enables controlled and replay-protected reward withdrawals. The deployed contracts can be verified here: https://hashscan.io/testnet/contract/0.0.10502346 For autonomous AI agents, GRAPE implements the x402 payment protocol on Hedera. Agents can discover pricing, receive a 402 Payment Required, pay per inference request in native HBAR through the Blocky402 facilitator (https://blocky402.com/), and receive the AI response without an API key or subscription. Together, Grape provide AI models, The Graph provides onchain intelligence, and Hedera provides transparent payments and settlement—connecting AI usage, developer attention, and blockchain economics into one regenerative loop.

projects.title: Kairos
projects.description: Kairos auctions temporary Uniswap v4 app-fee rights through sealed bids.
projects.project_description: Kairos turns a temporary trading privilege into an open, accountable market. Bidders first commit a domain-bound hash, then reveal a funded MockUSDC bid. The highest valid reveal wins a fixed-time right to route one KRA/KRB pool through an authenticated Uniswap v4 executor without paying Kairos's 5 bp application surcharge. The pool's 25 bp LP fee remains unchanged. The workstation makes the full lifecycle legible: fixed scheduling, encrypted local secret recovery, allowance and balance preflight, wallet-confirmed commit/reveal/refund/proceeds actions, live countdowns and event evidence, and a value calculator for comparing expected surcharge savings with bid and gas cost. A one-click local rehearsal proves the full interaction even if a public RPC or wallet is unavailable during judging. The auction, executor, fee hook, MockUSDC, KRA/KRB tokens, and hook-enabled pool are deployed on Unichain Sepolia. Kairos clearly separates verified deployment receipts, local simulation receipts, and the still-pending public two-bidder auction rehearsal.
projects.how_its_made: Kairos is a Solidity and React implementation built around unmodified Uniswap v4 core. PFDAAuction implements fixed-window sealed first-price commit/reveal allocation. Commitments bind chain ID, auction address, auction ID, bidder, bid amount, and salt; equal bids favor the earlier commitment. Successful revealers recover their fixed bond, non-revealers forfeit it, and pull-based settlement keeps operations bounded. PFDAExecutor authenticates the active winning caller and scopes eligibility to the current pool swap. PFDAFeeHook uses v4 hook accounting to collect a separate 5 bp application surcharge from ordinary callers and waive only that component for the eligible executor path. It does not modify the configured LP fee or claim to waive a native Uniswap protocol fee. PFDAHookDeployer mines the CREATE2 address bits required by v4 hook permissions. The Vite/React/TypeScript workstation uses viem for Unichain Sepolia reads and explicit wallet writes. It validates immutable wiring, encrypts bid recovery records locally with AES-GCM, checks commitment recovery before reveal, surfaces event receipts, and models fee-right value without presenting a quote or forecast. Foundry unit, integration, fuzz, invariant, and real-v4 tests cover the contracts; Vitest covers domain binding, the vault, dashboard, wallet runtime, and value arithmetic.

projects.title: Nyaya
projects.description: AI jurors stake real money judging real-world events; accuracy becomes a tradeable share token.
projects.project_description: Nyaya is a prediction market with a twist: instead of betting on outcomes, you invest in the judges. Three AI juror agents independently research and rule on objectively resolvable real-world questions (will a rocket launch scrub, will a flight land late, will a GitHub repo cross a star count), each staking real money on its own verdict via commit-reveal so no juror can copy another's answer. Call it right and split the reward pool (the case bounty plus the stakes clawed back from wrong jurors) proportional to your stake; call it wrong and the stake is gone. The real product isn't the cases, though. Every juror has a tokenized share, minted via Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, whose value tracks that juror's live accuracy over time. For the first time, a third party can hold a position in a specific AI agent's judgment quality, not just its output on one question.
projects.how_its_made: Built as a pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout. Contracts are in Foundry, deployed to Hedera testnet (jurors, staking/slashing, the reward pool, and ATS share token registration and mass payouts) and Sepolia (ENSv2 subnames with Enhanced Access Control gating case size, plus a results-anchoring contract indexed by a subgraph on The Graph so anyone can query a juror's track record). The frontend is React/Vite/Tailwind/shadcn, wired to MetaMask/wagmi/ethers over Hedera's EVM JSON-RPC relay rather than native Hedera wallet tooling. Off-chain, jurors pay per-investigation through an Evidence Gateway via x402 (Blocky402), and an operator-run resolution checker reports real outcomes from public APIs. Hedera produced some real surprises: forge's estimateGas fails on contract-deploying calls over Hashio, Hedera entities have both a long-zero and an EVM-alias address that aren't equal as Solidity values, the relay refuses to broadcast anything it predicts will revert, senders must front gasLimit × gasPrice + value regardless of gas actually burned, and balances read back in weibars (18 decimals) while the contracts think in tinybars (8 decimals), each one cost real debugging time.
