projects.title: Xander
projects.description: Graph-native risk engine that escalates to World ID Selfie Check only when real evidence earns it.
projects.project_description: THE PROBLEM Every large token claim or airdrop has fought the same battle after the fact, with no reasoning a flagged user can inspect: LayerZero flagged over 800,000 addresses as sybils in one sweep; Linea's 2025 airdrop initially flagged 50.45% of eligible wallets before walking the number back; Arbitrum's shared-funding-source heuristic restricted real users who'd withdrawn from the same exchange hot wallet as an actual sybil ring. Detection happened once, inside a backend nobody could see into, with no appeal beyond a forum thread. The same failure mode reappears the moment an AI agent, not a human, is the one holding the wallet. An agent that can move funds is usually handed a key and a system prompt telling it what not to do — and a prompt is a suggestion, reachable by anything that can write into the model's context. The limit was never actually enforced; it was described. WHAT WE BUILT Xander is two things built as one system. The foundation is a Graph-native risk engine: every fact behind a decision — a transfer, a deposit, a borrow — is pulled live from The Graph and stored with its source, deployment, and block number attached, then scored by five named, auditable features (funding correlation, timing, wallet-age similarity, shared counterparties, protocol-behavior similarity) combined by weights stored in a database table, never a hardcoded number. On top of that foundation sits a general-purpose agent trust and authorization runtime: every actor — wallet, human, or AI agent — gets a 7-dimension trust context built from real evidence, where every dimension is either a known value or explicitly UNKNOWN, never a silently-assumed zero. Trust resolves to a scoped, expiring capability, never a standing key, and that capability is enforced at a real execution boundary — including a live on-chain role check, not just a database flag. Nothing here is a simulation: the risk score gates a real World ID Selfie Check when a wallet needs it, agents mint real ENS identities and real on-chain reputation, and they can pay each other over a real, working x402 machine-payment flow. HOW YOU USE IT A wallet submits a claim; evidence is fetched live from The Graph; the risk engine clusters and scores it; only a claim that actually lands in the escalation band ever sees a Selfie Check, bound to that exact wallet and claim so a proof can't be replayed onto a different one. In parallel, an operator can register an agent, watch it move through a verification lifecycle (DRAFT → VERIFYING → HUMAN_BACKED → ACTIVE), and see the exact capability it holds and why. Every proposed action resolves to ALLOW, LIMIT (an attenuated grant, not a refusal), CHALLENGE, REVIEW, or BLOCK — computed by policy, never asserted by the agent. If something goes wrong, an incident opens automatically, containment (revoke or restrict) happens before an AI investigator is even asked to look at it, and the investigator's own recommendation can only tighten that decision, never loosen it — enforced in code, not just policy. A human operator carries the final authority on a phone: approve, deny, limit, freeze, or revoke, over a channel that's bound to that operator's device and can't be replayed. INTEGRATIONS The Graph is the evidence layer for the entire product — Token API for wallet history, Standardized Subgraphs (one Messari schema query reused across every lending/DEX/yield protocol tagged into it, zero protocol-specific code), Substreams for a live, reorg-safe, cursor-resumable stream off Base Sepolia, and Subgraph MCP powering an investigation agent whose every claim is checked against its own tool-call trace before it's trusted. World ID Selfie Check is the escalation step, fired only once risk crosses a real threshold. ENS (ENSv2) gives every agent its own on-chain identity and revocable role, deployed and live on Sepolia. ERC-8004 supplies real, cross-verified on-chain reputation instead of a hardcoded "unknown." x402 lets agents transact machine-to-machine in real Base Sepolia USDC, policy-gated at every step.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript throughout. The backend is Express + Prisma/Postgres + Redis/BullMQ, with a real Rust/WASM Substreams module bridged into Node over @connectrpc/connect-node, Temporal (@temporalio/*) running the durable workflows behind authorization, capability mutation, and incident response, and Mastra (@mastra/core, @mastra/mcp) driving the investigation agent over Subgraph MCP. The frontend is Next.js 15 (App Router) with a console for operators and a separate mobile-first "Remote Authority" app, sharing typed API clients that deliberately do not share an auth model — more on that below. Roughly 33 Prisma models span the two halves: the original evidence/risk schema (wallets, clusters, evidence events, risk weights) and the newer actor/trust/capability/agent/incident/operator schema, wired together at one locked interface (getOrComputeClusterRisk / refreshWalletEvidence) so the newer layer is provably additive rather than a rewrite. THE GRAPH: WHERE EVIDENCE BECOME PROVENANCE, NOT ASSUMPTION A risk score is only as trustworthy as the evidence under it, so nothing is inferred. The DeploymentRegistryEntry table is the single place "which protocols we support" lives — adding a lending market is an INSERT, never a code change, because the same lending-cdp query module runs unmodified against every deployment tagged into that Messari schema family. Substreams delivery is cursor-resumable and reorg-safe; a chain reorg triggers handleUndo, and cursor state is checked and resumed correctly, verified against a real 1,521-event Base Sepolia stream. The investigation agent doesn't get to assert anything for free either — every sentence in its report is checked against its own recorded tool-call trace, and an uncited claim is rejected before the caller ever sees it. WORLD ID: A BIOMETRIC STEP THAT ONLY FIRES WHEN IT'S EARNED The RP-signature is signed server-side with a secret signing key that never reaches the client, so a request can't be forged into looking pre-approved. The proof's signal is bound to a hash of the wallet and the specific claim (or agent context) it's for, so a completed proof can't be lifted onto a different wallet or a different claim by the same wallet. Every nullifier is stored and checked for reuse before a claim resolves. A timed-out or invalid verification never falls through to an approval — it holds exactly like a failed Graph query does. This was run for real: a phone running the real World App completed a real Selfie Check that this backend's verification logic accepted end to end. ENS: IDENTITY THAT CANNOT GRANT ITSELF AUTHORITY Every agent mints a real subname under a deployed Sepolia registry (0x8993Df8b8f5C10d9B3d157B7191431429c51F039), and freezing or revoking an agent performs a real on-chain role revocation, not just a database flag. But identity and authority are kept structurally separate: minting a name grants zero capabilities on its own — trust and capability come from a completely different evaluation path. The database stays authoritative for security decisions; the chain is a public, checkable mirror of them, and a reconciliation pass (built in the hardening phase) treats any case where the chain shows more authority than the database as an urgent, revoke-only drift to repair. ERC-8004: REPUTATION THAT REFUSES TO BE INVENTED Three live Sepolia registries — Identity, Reputation, Validation — are read directly over RPC, cross-checked against each other (getIdentityRegistry() on both the Reputation and Validation contracts must return the same Identity address, or the deployment isn't trusted as one coherent system). The deployed contracts turned out to diverge from the EIP draft in shape (bytes32 tags instead of string, a 2-value not 3-value getSummary), so the client was written against what's actually on-chain. An agent with no feedback and no validations returns null for its reputation dimension, never a synthetic 0 or 1 — and where both exist, validations are weighted over feedback (0.6/0.4), because a validation is a check a contract actually ran and feedback is just an opinion anyone can post. X402: MACHINE-PAYABLE, STILL POLICY-GATED The live x402.org facilitator speaks protocol v2, which is wire-incompatible with v1, so the client had to be built against the real deployed version rather than the spec's first draft. Payment moves as a real Base Sepolia USDC EIP-3009 authorization to a receive-only address Xander never holds the key for. Every outcome — including a refusal — is written to a payment ledger. An agent whose capability doesn't cover the requested spend gets a 403 (refused by policy), never a 402 (payment required) — the two failure modes look similar but mean opposite things, and conflating them would let a denied agent think it just needed to pay more. THE CAPABILITY MODEL, AND WHY NOTHING HOLDS A STANDING KEY An agent never receives blanket authority. It receives a Capability, scoped, expiring, and re-evaluated continuously — a live piece of on-chain evidence can attenuate or suspend it mid-flight (mutateTrustForWallets), and a first-time evaluation or an improvement in trust is never allowed to silently expand authority on its own. Enforcement at the actual execution boundary returns one of three outcomes — CONFIRMED, FAILED, or UNKNOWN — and an unreachable boundary resolves UNKNOWN, which blocks exactly like a FAILED does. A dependency-policy table enumerates every external dependency the system relies on and states, for each one, explicitly, whether losing it blocks authorization or degrades safely — there is no IGNORE value permitted anywhere in that table. OTHER THINGS WORTH MENTIONING The test suite (749 tests, zero vi.mock() module mocks anywhere) runs its files serialized rather than parallel — not for coverage reasons, but because 30+ files sharing one real Postgres and one real Redis produced a steady drip of failures that had nothing to do with the code under test, and serializing removed the cause instead of chasing each symptom individually. One of those symptoms was a genuine bug, not a flake: an "unknown wallet" test screened a literal 0xdead...beef-style address, which turned out to have 82 real evidence rows from a live Token API fetch and silently inverted the assertion to a pass. It now generates a random address per run. Fixture rows are deduplicated forever on re-seed but originally kept their original createdAt, so every fixture wallet quietly resolved to PENDING_REVIEW from wall-clock time alone six hours after seeding — fixed with a --refresh-only seed mode that re-stamps freshness without touching the relative timing every fixture scenario is encoded in. The upstream Subgraph MCP server doesn't compile on Windows as-is (tokio::signal::unix is called unconditionally despite being #[cfg(unix)]-gated) and needed a ctrl_c() fallback patched in locally. And a known-funder registry — labelled exchange/bridge addresses scored separately from unlabelled ones, max(unlabelled, labelled × 0.15) — exists specifically to stop the Arbitrum false-positive pattern from reproducing here: a benign shared funder is heavily down-weighted, but a ring still scores full risk even if it routes one decoy transfer through an exchange first.

A wallet submits a claim; evidence is fetched live from The Graph; the risk engine clusters and scores it; only a claim that actually lands in the escalation band ever sees a Selfie Check, bound to that exact wallet and claim so a proof can't be replayed onto a different one. In parallel, an operator can register an agent, watch it move through a verification lifecycle (DRAFT → VERIFYING → HUMAN_BACKED → ACTIVE), and see the exact capability it holds and why. Every proposed action resolves to ALLOW, LIMIT (an attenuated grant, not a refusal), CHALLENGE, REVIEW, or BLOCK — computed by policy, never asserted by the agent. If something goes wrong, an incident opens automatically, containment (revoke or restrict) happens before an AI investigator is even asked to look at it, and the investigator's own recommendation can only tighten that decision, never loosen it — enforced in code, not just policy. A human operator carries the final authority on a phone: approve, deny, limit, freeze, or revoke, over a channel that's bound to that operator's device and can't be replayed.

INTEGRATIONS

The Graph is the evidence layer for the entire product — Token API for wallet history, Standardized Subgraphs (one Messari schema query reused across every lending/DEX/yield protocol tagged into it, zero protocol-specific code), Substreams for a live, reorg-safe, cursor-resumable stream off Base Sepolia, and Subgraph MCP powering an investigation agent whose every claim is checked against its own tool-call trace before it's trusted. World ID Selfie Check is the escalation step, fired only once risk crosses a real threshold. ENS (ENSv2) gives every agent its own on-chain identity and revocable role, deployed and live on Sepolia. ERC-8004 supplies real, cross-verified on-chain reputation instead of a hardcoded "unknown." x402 lets agents transact machine-to-machine in real Base Sepolia USDC, policy-gated at every step.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
TypeScript throughout. The backend is Express + Prisma/Postgres + Redis/BullMQ, with a real Rust/WASM Substreams module bridged into Node over @connectrpc/connect-node, Temporal (@temporalio/*) running the durable workflows behind authorization, capability mutation, and incident response, and Mastra (@mastra/core, @mastra/mcp) driving the investigation agent over Subgraph MCP. The frontend is Next.js 15 (App Router) with a console for operators and a separate mobile-first "Remote Authority" app, sharing typed API clients that deliberately do not share an auth model — more on that below. Roughly 33 Prisma models span the two halves: the original evidence/risk schema (wallets, clusters, evidence events, risk weights) and the newer actor/trust/capability/agent/incident/operator schema, wired together at one locked interface (getOrComputeClusterRisk / refreshWalletEvidence) so the newer layer is provably additive rather than a rewrite.

THE GRAPH: WHERE EVIDENCE BECOME PROVENANCE, NOT ASSUMPTION

A risk score is only as trustworthy as the evidence under it, so nothing is inferred. The DeploymentRegistryEntry table is the single place "which protocols we support" lives — adding a lending market is an INSERT, never a code change, because the same lending-cdp query module runs unmodified against every deployment tagged into that Messari schema family. Substreams delivery is cursor-resumable and reorg-safe; a chain reorg triggers handleUndo, and cursor state is checked and resumed correctly, verified against a real 1,521-event Base Sepolia stream. The investigation agent doesn't get to assert anything for free either — every sentence in its report is checked against its own recorded tool-call trace, and an uncited claim is rejected before the caller ever sees it.

WORLD ID: A BIOMETRIC STEP THAT ONLY FIRES WHEN IT'S EARNED

The RP-signature is signed server-side with a secret signing key that never reaches the client, so a request can't be forged into looking pre-approved. The proof's signal is bound to a hash of the wallet and the specific claim (or agent context) it's for, so a completed proof can't be lifted onto a different wallet or a different claim by the same wallet. Every nullifier is stored and checked for reuse before a claim resolves. A timed-out or invalid verification never falls through to an approval — it holds exactly like a failed Graph query does. This was run for real: a phone running the real World App completed a real Selfie Check that this backend's verification logic accepted end to end.

ENS: IDENTITY THAT CANNOT GRANT ITSELF AUTHORITY

Every agent mints a real subname under a deployed Sepolia registry (0x8993Df8b8f5C10d9B3d157B7191431429c51F039), and freezing or revoking an agent performs a real on-chain role revocation, not just a database flag. But identity and authority are kept structurally separate: minting a name grants zero capabilities on its own — trust and capability come from a completely different evaluation path. The database stays authoritative for security decisions; the chain is a public, checkable mirror of them, and a reconciliation pass (built in the hardening phase) treats any case where the chain shows more authority than the database as an urgent, revoke-only drift to repair.

ERC-8004: REPUTATION THAT REFUSES TO BE INVENTED

Three live Sepolia registries — Identity, Reputation, Validation — are read directly over RPC, cross-checked against each other (getIdentityRegistry() on both the Reputation and Validation contracts must return the same Identity address, or the deployment isn't trusted as one coherent system). The deployed contracts turned out to diverge from the EIP draft in shape (bytes32 tags instead of string, a 2-value not 3-value getSummary), so the client was written against what's actually on-chain. An agent with no feedback and no validations returns null for its reputation dimension, never a synthetic 0 or 1 — and where both exist, validations are weighted over feedback (0.6/0.4), because a validation is a check a contract actually ran and feedback is just an opinion anyone can post.

X402: MACHINE-PAYABLE, STILL POLICY-GATED

The live x402.org facilitator speaks protocol v2, which is wire-incompatible with v1, so the client had to be built against the real deployed version rather than the spec's first draft. Payment moves as a real Base Sepolia USDC EIP-3009 authorization to a receive-only address Xander never holds the key for. Every outcome — including a refusal — is written to a payment ledger. An agent whose capability doesn't cover the requested spend gets a 403 (refused by policy), never a 402 (payment required) — the two failure modes look similar but mean opposite things, and conflating them would let a denied agent think it just needed to pay more.

THE CAPABILITY MODEL, AND WHY NOTHING HOLDS A STANDING KEY

An agent never receives blanket authority. It receives a Capability, scoped, expiring, and re-evaluated continuously — a live piece of on-chain evidence can attenuate or suspend it mid-flight (mutateTrustForWallets), and a first-time evaluation or an improvement in trust is never allowed to silently expand authority on its own. Enforcement at the actual execution boundary returns one of three outcomes — CONFIRMED, FAILED, or UNKNOWN — and an unreachable boundary resolves UNKNOWN, which blocks exactly like a FAILED does. A dependency-policy table enumerates every external dependency the system relies on and states, for each one, explicitly, whether losing it blocks authorization or degrades safely — there is no IGNORE value permitted anywhere in that table.

OTHER THINGS WORTH MENTIONING

The test suite (749 tests, zero vi.mock() module mocks anywhere) runs its files serialized rather than parallel — not for coverage reasons, but because 30+ files sharing one real Postgres and one real Redis produced a steady drip of failures that had nothing to do with the code under test, and serializing removed the cause instead of chasing each symptom individually. One of those symptoms was a genuine bug, not a flake: an "unknown wallet" test screened a literal 0xdead...beef-style address, which turned out to have 82 real evidence rows from a live Token API fetch and silently inverted the assertion to a pass. It now generates a random address per run. Fixture rows are deduplicated forever on re-seed but originally kept their original createdAt, so every fixture wallet quietly resolved to PENDING_REVIEW from wall-clock time alone six hours after seeding — fixed with a --refresh-only seed mode that re-stamps freshness without touching the relative timing every fixture scenario is encoded in. The upstream Subgraph MCP server doesn't compile on Windows as-is (tokio::signal::unix is called unconditionally despite being #[cfg(unix)]-gated) and needed a ctrl_c() fallback patched in locally. And a known-funder registry — labelled exchange/bridge addresses scored separately from unlabelled ones, max(unlabelled, labelled × 0.15) — exists specifically to stop the Arbitrum false-positive pattern from reproducing here: a benign shared funder is heavily down-weighted, but a ring still scores full risk even if it routes one decoy transfer through an exchange first.

projects.title: Thenar
projects.description: Robot training data by verified humans, paid per run, tokenized & sold to AI agents on Hedera
projects.project_description: Physical AI is short of data, not compute. Thenar pays people to record robot arm demonstrations, and sells what they record to AI agents as training data. Anyone can drive a six-axis robot arm from a browser. Each task (put the spoon and the mug into the crate, stack the blocks) runs in a 3D station with a MuJoCo physics check. When the object settles, the run is scored on placement (55%), smoothness (25%) and efficiency (20%), and an accepted run is paid on the spot in USDC from a bounty held in escrow. The easy attack on a bounty market is one person with a hundred wallets. Thenar signs a run only for a wallet that has passed a World ID Selfie Check: one face scan per human for this action, bound to one wallet. A wallet with no proof is refused (HTTP 403) before anything is paid. Robotics labs fund the bounties. A lab's budget sits in a Privy server wallet whose policy only lets it fund Thenar tasks, up to 1 USDC. Ask that wallet to send money anywhere else and Privy refuses to sign. Operators sign in with just an email, and Privy creates their wallet. The recordings are sold over HTTP 402 on Hedera. An agent asks for a task's data, pays 0.5 HBAR with x402 (settled by the Blocky402 facilitator, which pays the network fee) and receives the file. Every sale is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10519262) with the SHA-256 of the exact file served, so the buyer can check its copy against the mirror node. World AgentKit checks AgentBook on World Chain first: an agent with a verified human behind it downloads for free. The corpus itself is a security issued through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio: Thenar Robot Corpus (THNRC, ISIN USTHNRCRP019, 0.0.10520394). Holders must be on its whitelist, and the token itself refuses an address that isn't (AccountIsBlocked). Shares are issued into a treasury reserve and a dividend has been declared, so the dataset people build can be owned in shares. Everything in the demo is a real testnet transaction, captured from the running app: a bounty funded and paid on Arc, a data sale settled on Hedera and logged to HCS, ten new shares issued through the Tokenization Studio, and a real Selfie Check.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 (App Router) and React 19, with wagmi and viem on the client, SQLite for off-chain state and Foundry for the contracts. The station is React Three Fiber: inverse kinematics on a six-axis arm, with MuJoCo compiled to WebAssembly checking the physics in the browser. The recorded trajectory goes to the server, whose verifier signs an EIP-712 verdict; the Thenar protocol contract on Arc Testnet checks that signature and pays USDC in the same transaction that records the run. Ten contracts are deployed and source-verified on Sourcify and Arcscan, and a CorpusManifest contract commits a Merkle root of each task's recordings. Hedera sells and tokenizes the data. The data endpoint uses @x402/next with @x402/hedera (exact scheme, 0.5 HBAR), and Blocky402 is the facilitator, so the buying agent needs only a funded account. After settlement the server submits the served file's SHA-256 to an HCS topic with @hashgraph/sdk, and the buyer reads it back from the mirror node. The corpus is an Asset Tokenization Studio security with a whitelist control list, reserve issuance and a dividend, and its proxy is source-verified on Sourcify (exact match). When a run is paid on Arc, the server issues that contributor's corpus shares on Hedera, but only if they hold a World ID proof, so the chains meet at one verified human. World: IDKit 4 with the Selfie Check credential, on an action capped at one verification per human. The server verifies the proof, binds the nullifier to the wallet through a signature over a server nonce, and will not sign a run without it. World AgentKit checks AgentBook on World Chain for a human behind the buying agent. Privy: email login with embedded wallets, and a server wallet under a policy (only the Thenar protocol contract, only chain 5042002, up to 1 USDC) for lab budgets. Notable hacks: AgentKit's client reads the payment offer from the response body, while x402 v2 sends it in a header, so the server copies the decoded offer into the body. AgentKit's challenge failed with extension_echo_mismatch until its nonce and timestamps were declared dynamic. One secp256k1 key signs the AgentKit challenge and is also the Hedera account's ECDSA alias, so the agent has a single identity on World Chain and Hedera. Privy signs but will not broadcast on Arc Testnet, so the app broadcasts the transaction Privy signed. The ATS SDK only signs through MetaMask, HashPack or a custodian, so Thenar calls the ATS contracts directly with viem through Hashio JSON-RPC. Sourcify verification of the ATS proxy rebuilds the compiler input, because the npm package ships without build-info. The demo video was recorded by a Playwright script driving a Chrome DevTools screenshot loop at 1920x1080, narrated with Kokoro TTS.

projects.title: Sentinel
projects.description: A confidential DeFi oracle that detects hidden cross-protocol leverage before cascades.
projects.project_description: Sentinel is a confidential systemic-risk oracle for DeFi lending. It measures something that is difficult to see from any single protocol: how much debt belongs to borrowers who are simultaneously leveraged across multiple lending markets, often against the same collateral. That matters because DeFi protocols normally evaluate risk in isolation. A position may look manageable on Aave or Compound by itself, while the same borrower is using correlated collateral and carrying debt elsewhere. When that collateral falls, those positions can become liquidatable together, turning an individual liquidation into a system-wide cascade. Sentinel joins live lending positions across Aave V3, Compound V2, Compound V3, Morpho Aave V2 and other standardized lending deployments, then combines that exposure with real DEX liquidity to understand not only which debt becomes stressed, but whether liquidations can actually exit through available market depth. The challenge is that calculating this signal requires constructing a per-address map of who borrowed where, what collateral they hold and how close they are to liquidation. Publishing that dataset would create a target list for liquidation bots and expose sensitive wallet behavior. Sentinel therefore computes the cross-protocol map inside a Trusted Execution Environment and publishes only privacy-safe aggregate statistics. The resulting signal includes cross-protocol debt concentration, leverage, shock-response estimates, protocol coupling and a composite systemic-risk score. Thin groups are suppressed with k-anonymity so the aggregate cannot accidentally identify individual borrowers. Sentinel then makes the signal useful in three ways: an interactive risk dashboard for humans, an MCP server that lets AI agents query the signal with block-level provenance, and an on-chain GuardedVault that can automatically increase collateral requirements or pause new borrowing when systemic risk rises. On the live mainnet run used for our demo, Sentinel scanned 37,862 accounts and identified roughly $35.9 million of evaluable debt held by borrowers leveraged across multiple protocols on the same collateral. The goal is to turn a risk pattern that is currently hidden between protocols into a privacy-preserving piece of public infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made: Sentinel is built around two partner technologies: The Graph for standardized live blockchain data and Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows for private computation. For data ingestion, we use The Graph's Messari standardized schemas instead of writing a custom adapter for every protocol. Five lending deployments including Aave V3, Compound V2, Compound V3 and Morpho Aave V2 can all answer essentially the same GraphQL query because they expose the same Lending/CDP schema. The key trick is that Account.id represents the wallet address consistently across those subgraphs, so our cross-protocol exposure calculation becomes a primary-key join instead of fuzzy address matching. Adding another compatible lending protocol is largely just adding another deployment to our registry. We also compose that lending data with the Messari DEX AMM schema across Uniswap V3, SushiSwap V2/V3 and Curve. Lending data tells us what can become liquidatable, while DEX liquidity tells us whether that collateral could actually be sold without severe market impact. The cascade pipeline makes hundreds of live depth queries across asset pairs and deduplicates pools before calculating available exit liquidity. The sensitive part runs as a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. We register the workflow with handlerInTee and run it inside a Nitro TEE. The Graph API key and Sentinel's risk policy are fetched as secrets directly inside the enclave, and the Graph requests themselves are made from inside the TEE. That means the raw per-address position rows, API responses, risk thresholds and resulting cross-protocol leverage map never need to leave the enclave. CRE's HTTP limits forced us into a pretty interesting three-pass query design. First we bootstrap each protocol's market state and reported totals. Next each protocol independently nominates its largest borrowers so one giant protocol cannot dominate the sample. Finally we fetch complete lending books only for the selected population. We then normalize the positions, join them by wallet, calculate health and shock exposure, suppress protocol-pair buckets that do not meet our k-anonymity threshold, and release only the aggregate Sentinel signal. We also built consistency checks rather than blindly trusting standardized data. Aave V2 is intentionally kept in the deployment registry even though its current subgraph position mappings can dramatically overstate outstanding debt. Sentinel detects that a sampled subset cannot legitimately contain more debt than the protocol reports in total and automatically excludes the deployment, without any Aave-specific exception in the aggregation logic. The enclave output is ABI-encoded and reported with ECDSA/keccak256 signing. A Next.js 16 + React 19 frontend consumes the verified aggregate and visualizes cross-protocol coupling, shock scenarios and cascade risk. We use TypeScript throughout the data and risk pipeline, Viem for Ethereum-facing code, Vitest for testing and Playwright for UI verification. For an on-chain consumer, we built GuardedVault.sol with Solidity and Foundry. It verifies Sentinel reports and reacts to changes in systemic risk rather than blindly using the absolute score. As risk rises it can increase collateral requirements and, at the highest alert state, pause new borrowing. It also fails closed if the risk signal becomes stale. Finally, Sentinel exposes an MCP server using the Model Context Protocol SDK. It provides eight tools for querying the signal, protocol coupling, shock ladders, coverage and alert calibration. The agent never receives the private wallet-level exposure map. Those refusals are implemented in the tools themselves rather than relying on a prompt, and every numerical answer is tied back to a specific subgraph and block. One command, npm run verify , runs the project's full verification pipeline against live data. There is deliberately no mock-data mode. We also successfully run the CRE workflow through Chainlink's confidential-workflow simulator, while being explicit that the hackathon version is simulated rather than deployed to the live CRE network.

projects.title: agent-snapshot
projects.description: Archive and verify off-chain files belonging to ERC-8004 trustless agents.
projects.project_description: ERC-8004 agents publish an off-chain agent-card.json file that on-chain records only reference by URI — so its contents can be silently swapped without leaving any on-chain trace. This site lets anyone browse the crawl history of any registered agent and verify, entirely in-browser, that a given snapshot is authentic and untampered. For each agent, it shows a timeline of past crawls with drift flagged whenever content changed, and a "no change" state proven whenever it didn't. Clicking any entry runs a full independent verification: it fetches the record's Merkle path and reads the on-chain transaction log directly by RPC (so the indexing subgraph itself is never trusted), reconstructs the Merkle root to confirm the record's inclusion in that batch, checks the TLSNotary proof against its on-chain hash, and finally verifies the proof against the notary's public key to confirm the server genuinely returned that content. All of this runs client-side in WebAssembly — the only party trusted is the TLSNotary notary. The site also surfaces a direct comparison against Agent0, the standard ERC-8004 subgraph: an agent can look completely normal there while its actual off-chain content has already been swapped, making the blind spot this system closes immediately visible. Where a snapshot is available, the site fetches the real agent-card.json from IPFS/Arweave to show exactly which fields changed and how — the indexing layer itself only ever compares hashes, never raw content.
projects.how_its_made: This project uses TLSN (ZKTLS library in rust), IPFS, and The Graph fousing on verifiability and decentralized infrastructure. This project also uses Cloudflare and AWS S3 for high availability. https://agent-snapshot.kryor.studio are static, and built using snapshots and hosted on cloudflare. It updates when crawl happens. The most difficult thing I encounter is the choice of primitives. It actually uses Incremental Merkle Tree (IMT) for storing snapshots (tree of hases) and keccak256, but the existing library in rust uses poseidon as a hash. So I implemented minimal IMT from scratch in rust. The second problem is discovery and verifiability at scale - The Graph solved both. ERC-8004 has ~500k agents across five chains. Finding which ones have a registration file would have meant scanning the Identity Registry from its deployment block per chain and resolving tokenURI per token. The Agent0 Subgraph already indexes all five against one shared schema, so it collapsed into one GraphQL query — zero lines of discovery logic, multi-chain for free. Verification was the harder half. projects.project_description_markdown:
ERC-8004 agents publish an off-chain agent-card.json file that on-chain records only reference by URI — so its contents can be silently swapped without leaving any on-chain trace. This site lets anyone browse the crawl history of any registered agent and verify, entirely in-browser, that a given snapshot is authentic and untampered.

For each agent, it shows a timeline of past crawls with drift flagged whenever content changed, and a "no change" state proven whenever it didn't. Clicking any entry runs a full independent verification: it fetches the record's Merkle path and reads the on-chain transaction log directly by RPC (so the indexing subgraph itself is never trusted), reconstructs the Merkle root to confirm the record's inclusion in that batch, checks the TLSNotary proof against its on-chain hash, and finally verifies the proof against the notary's public key to confirm the server genuinely returned that content. All of this runs client-side in WebAssembly — the only party trusted is the TLSNotary notary.

The site also surfaces a direct comparison against Agent0, the standard ERC-8004 subgraph: an agent can look completely normal there while its actual off-chain content has already been swapped, making the blind spot this system closes immediately visible. Where a snapshot is available, the site fetches the real agent-card.json from IPFS/Arweave to show exactly which fields changed and how — the indexing layer itself only ever compares hashes, never raw content.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
This project uses TLSN (ZKTLS library in rust), IPFS, and The Graph fousing on verifiability and decentralized infrastructure. This project also uses Cloudflare and AWS S3 for high availability. https://agent-snapshot.kryor.studio are static, and built using snapshots and hosted on cloudflare. It updates when crawl happens. 

The most difficult thing I encounter is the choice of primitives. It actually uses Incremental Merkle Tree (IMT) for storing snapshots (tree of hases) and keccak256, but the existing library in rust uses poseidon as a hash. So I implemented minimal IMT from scratch in rust. 

The second problem is discovery and verifiability at scale - The Graph solved both. ERC-8004 has ~500k agents across five chains. Finding which ones have a registration file would have meant scanning the Identity Registry from its deployment block per chain and resolving tokenURI per token. The Agent0 Subgraph already indexes all five against one shared schema, so it collapsed into one GraphQL query — zero lines of discovery logic, multi-chain for free.

Verification was the harder half. Serving Merkle paths from my own API would have made the trust argument circular. With a subgraph, anyone can pull the path, reconstruct the root, and compare it to the on-chain batchRoot read straight from RPC.

projects.title: AgentPermit Delta
projects.description: AI proposes, you approve: delta-neutral Uniswap V3 LP hedged on Hyperliquid, with ENSv2 identity.
projects.project_description: AgentPermit Delta turns a natural-language goal into a bounded, human-approved WETH/USDC strategy. Nothing is ever signed by a model. You describe what you want. The server then makes three real reads before it will answer. The Uniswap V3 Ethereum subgraph on The Graph returns the 0.05% and 0.3% USDC/WETH pools with exactly seven complete UTC days of TVL, volume, fees and prices, plus the indexed block. Hyperliquid mainnet returns ETH mark price, funding, open interest and order-book depth at plus or minus half a percent. OpenAI then compares the two fee tiers under a strict JSON schema and returns a pick-a-tier, open-or-wait recommendation where every stated reason must cite a metric ID that was actually supplied, with both pools represented. Missing, incomplete or stale data fails the proposal. There is no fabricated fallback. The full GraphQL query, raw inputs, model request and model response are written atomically to a local evidence file with no API keys in it. The model advises. It never sizes or sends anything. Deterministic code fixes the test limits: 500 USDC total, 300 for the LP, up to 200 of perp reserve, a range of plus or minus twenty percent, isolated 1x leverage. A proposal older than five minutes cannot be approved, so historical evidence cannot be replayed as a current decision. On approval the executor mints a real Uniswap V3 position against the official Ethereum contracts on a pinned Anvil mainnet fork, resolving the pool through the factory and rechecking both tokens and the fee before minting. It reads the confirmed on-chain LP amounts, then opens a matching ETH short on Hyperliquid testnet with deterministic client order IDs. A ten-second monitor recomputes LP WETH plus free WETH plus pending fees plus perp ETH, and only re-hedges when residual exposure passes twelve dollars. It closes after sixty seconds outside range or when liquidation sits within ten percent of mark. The interesting part is what happens when things go wrong. Every external intent is persisted before it is sent. A timeout leaves that intent "unknown", and on restart the process looks the order up by its deterministic client order ID and requires a fresh account read before it touches anything. Unknown outcomes block replacement orders instead of double-sending. If initial coverage fails three times, it unwinds both legs. Closing demands the perp position reach exactly zero; residual exposure is not written off as dust. ENSv2 on Sepolia gives the service a discoverable identity. The owner delegates only the endpoint record to an operator key and keeps payout and protected records, and a wallet-free client resolves the endpoint independently. This is test funds on a fork, a testnet and Sepolia. Delta neutrality is not a profit promise: funding, basis, range, liquidation and execution risk all remain.
projects.how_its_made: The whole thing is one TypeScript repo with no build-time framework beyond Vite: a Node 24 server that runs .ts files natively via type stripping, a React 19 client, and viem instead of ethers for every chain call. 33 deterministic Node tests, strict TypeScript and a production build all run under one command. The Graph leg queries the documented Uniswap V3 Ethereum subgraph on The Graph Network with a server-side API key, pulling two pools plus their poolDayDatas and validating that seven consecutive complete UTC days came back, that the token identities match the real USDC and WETH addresses, and that the subgraph's indexed block is recent. That validation is the point: the AI never sees data the code has not already vouched for, so the model's citations can be checked against the supplied metric IDs after the fact. OpenAI Responses with gpt-5-nano runs under a strict structured-output schema. The schema forces the model to reference metric IDs from the payload and to cover both fee tiers, and the server rejects the response if a citation does not resolve. The model returns a fee tier and an open/wait call, and that is all it is allowed to influence. Uniswap execution uses the official V3 SDK for tick math and mint calldata, driving the real NonfungiblePositionManager, SwapRouter and factory on an Anvil fork pinned to mainnet block 25965916. Funding happens by impersonating a USDC whale inside Anvil only. A separate disposable-fork script proves the full lifecycle end to end for both fee tiers: mint, read, remove, collect, burn the NFT, sell the WETH, and assert zero WETH residue. Hyperliquid uses the nktkas client. Sizes and price precision are discovered from exchange metadata rather than hardcoded, orders go out IOC with deterministic client order IDs, and mainnet is used read-only for analysis while only testnet ever receives an order. The client order ID is the whole recovery story: it is what lets a restarted process ask "did my order land?" without ever guessing. ENSv2 on Sepolia uses the permissioned resolver so an operator key can write exactly one record, agentpermit.endpoint, and nothing else. The client resolves that endpoint with no wallet at all. Two hacky bits worth naming. First, persistence is temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync, so a kill -9 mid-mint cannot produce a half-written ledger. Second, there is a deliberate chaos mode: two env vars make the first hedge order request only 80 percent of the needed size and then throw away a known-good response to simulate a network timeout, which is how the recovery path gets demonstrated live instead of merely claimed. Keys never reach the browser bundle; the client gets an ephemeral session token minted at server startup and writes additionally require a loopback Host and an allowed Origin.

projects.title: Bank Rock
projects.description: A NFC Connected Physical rocks that contains a self-custodial DEFI liquidity
projects.project_description: Bank Rock is a rock with an NFC chip in it. It is the physical interface for a fun, rule-breaking, self-custodial and very giftable DeFi liquidity account. We built it with normal people in mind: someone who has never touched crypto can be onboarded for the first time through this rock. The MCP server helps a lot here. A newcomer can chat with their rock through their favourite AI agent and just ask it stuff (what do I own, what has it earned, who had it before me) and get answers from live chain state, in plain language. Tap the rock with a phone and its page opens. Anyone can see what the rock holds, which liquidity streams it runs, what it has earned in fees and who has owned it. Sign in with an email code or a passkey through Privy and you get an embedded wallet with no seed phrase. If you are the owner you can fund the rock, start it earning, stop it, or give it away. Each rock has its own onchain account: a Safe smart account controlled by the owner's Privy wallet. The rock's tokens stay in that account the whole time. Through 1inch Aqua the rock acts as a market maker. It "ships" virtual USDC/WETH balances to one or more constant-product strategies without depositing anything into a pool. Visitors can trade against the rock, and the trading fee stays inside the rock's own reserve. Several streams with different fee levels (Wide 30 bps, Tight 5 bps, Patient 100 bps) can share one reserve, and the UI shows actual, virtual and executable balances separately and never adds them up. The gift is the core flow. A giver names a recipient and signs once. The recipient taps the rock, signs in on a brand-new account with zero ETH, and claims it. The registry moves ownership and the rock's smart account changes hands with everything in it: balances, live strategies and history. Every operation is gas-sponsored, so nobody ever needs to hold ETH. A rock can be retired and the same chip can awaken a fresh rock into the same funded account. The NFC tag is an NTAG 424 DNA chip that signs a fresh URL on every tap (this is the magic rock hardware at work!). The server verifies that signature and a strictly increasing read counter before it will attest to a physical tap, so a copied URL proves nothing: paste it into a second browser and the badge reads "unverified". The tag identifies the object. It never holds a key and never authorises a payment. Financial ownership is always the Privy-controlled smart account. Bank Rock also exposes a read-only MCP server, so an AI agent such as Claude can be asked "what does this rock hold, who owns it and what has it earned?" and answer from live chain state. It never invents a number, and it never moves money: it reads, the owner signs. Super friendly for a newcomer, and safe by construction. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia with Circle USDC and WETH, and the whole story (awaken, ship, visitor swap, gift and claim, archive and re-awaken) has been executed end to end on chain. We show no APY and promise no yield.
projects.how_its_made: FRONTEND. Next.js 16 (Turbopack) on React 19, Tailwind 4, shadcn/base-ui, framer-motion, and react-three-fiber for the 3D rock on the landing page. Wallets through Privy (@privy-io/react-auth) with wagmi and viem. It is an installable PWA. Deployed as a Cloudflare Worker through OpenNext, with Cloudflare D1 (Drizzle) holding the tap counter store, telemetry and presentation data. GitHub Actions deploys on push to main and applies D1 migrations before publishing the Worker. CONTRACTS. Hardhat 3, Solidity 0.8, OpenZeppelin 5, unit and fuzz tests, verified on Sepolia Etherscan. BankRockRegistry (Ownable2Step, Pausable, EIP-712) is identity and lifecycle only: it holds no tokens, takes no approvals and has no function that can move money. awakenRock and claimHandover are authorised by an EIP-712 attestation signed by the server that verified the tap, not by msg.sender, so both can be relayed for a user with no ETH. Replay protection is on chain: the tag's read counter must strictly exceed the last one the registry accepted. 1INCH AQUA. We deployed the reference XYCSwap constant-product AquaApp, vendored unmodified, against the canonical Aqua on Sepolia. The Rock Account is the maker: it approves Aqua once and ships virtual balances, and tokens never leave its wallet. The strategy salt is keccak256(domain, rockId, streamIndex), so a rock's streams are addressable from public data alone: recompute the hash for streamIndex 0, 1, 2 and call safeBalances. A revert means "not shipped". No indexer, no database. XYCSwap settles by calling back into its caller, which must answer with Aqua.push, so an EOA or a plain Safe cannot swap against it at all. We wrote XYCSwapTaker, a stateless periphery that pulls the input, calls the app and fulfils the callback, and the visitor's swap is one sponsored approve + swapExactIn batch from their own Safe. Aqua has no fee accumulator, so realised fees are summed from Pushed events, none of which are indexed, so it is a log scan and decode. PRIVY + ACCOUNT ABSTRACTION. Each Rock Account is a counterfactual Safe 1.4.1 on EntryPoint 0.7 built with permissionless.js, owned by the user's Privy embedded wallet, with saltNonce = keccak256(tag UID). The account follows the tag and the owner, not the rock id, so retiring a rock and tapping again awakens a new id into the same funded account. Pimlico's verifying paymaster sponsors every UserOperation. Approvals and ship go into one atomic executeBatch, and embedded-wallet signing is silent (showWalletUIs: false): the app's own button, which states the exact on-chain effect, is the confirmation. Only receipt.success counts as landed, because ERC-4337 hands back a perfectly good tx hash for an included-but-reverted operation. GIFTING. The giver's single signature both opens the handover on the registry and pre-signs a Safe.swapOwner UserOperation that the recipient could never produce themselves. On claim our relayer lands the owner swap first (carrying initCode, so the Safe deploys as a side effect), then the registry asks the account isOwner before rebinding it, so a gift never leaves the giver's Safe recorded against a rock they no longer own. Relayer spend is capped per UTC day in D1 and unset means off. NFC. NTAG 424 DNA with Secure Dynamic Messaging. The verifier is our own implementation from NXP's application notes AN12196 and AN10922: AES-CBC PICCData decryption, SV2 session-key derivation, RFC 4493 AES-CMAC and a 3-byte little-endian counter, tested against NXP's published worked example. The counter is monotonic in D1, so a copied URL reads "unverified" in a second browser and no client code path can paint the "Verified Physical" badge. MCP. A TypeScript server on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk that reads the registry and Aqua over RPC with viem, plus the same fee route the rock page uses. Every tool returns live data or {status: "unavailable", reason}. It never invents a value. HACKY BITS. (1) "Balance and ship": most people fund a rock with USDC only and a constant-product stream needs two tokens, so Bank Rock ships its own house USDC/WETH stream on the same app, and the ship UserOperation swaps half of the deposit against it through our own taker periphery before shipping. Five calls, one tap, atomic. (2) A demo-only "magic tap" route forges a genuine SDM pair for a synthetic tag with the real master key, so the whole production verify path could be rehearsed on the live site before physical chips were programmed. (3) A rehearsal script ran the entire demo on Sepolia (awaken, ship, visitor swap, named gift and relayed claim, archive and re-awaken) and committed every hash. (4) Honesty is enforced by CI: a grep fails the build if "APY" appears in any component, and a drift check compares the committed contract addresses against the deploy records. Every value on screen is REAL, UNAVAILABLE or badged SIMULATED, and no catch block invents a number.

projects.title: Alt Agent
projects.description: Pay-per-inference AI on Hedera. x402 micropayments auto-routed to the cheapest capable model.
projects.project_description: An agentic AI gateway on Hedera where every inference call is paid per request via the x402 protocol — no subscriptions, no prepaid balances. A prompt classifier automatically routes each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it, and every paid call is settled through Blocky402 and logged to Hedera Consensus Service for a verifiable on-chain audit trail. One endpoint replaces a stack of separate AI subscriptions, and the agent proves what it paid for.
projects.how_its_made: The project is built on top of Hedera's x402-inference-pay-per-request-poc starter, extended with a custom broker overlay that adds intelligent model routing and on-chain auditing. The core is split into two packages. packages/router holds a prompt classifier, an offering catalogue (each model tagged with capability and cost-per-call), and selection logic that picks the cheapest model capable of handling a given prompt — so a trivial query never gets billed at frontier-model prices. This is what turns a plain gateway into an actual router. It ships with unit tests, including a word-boundary regex fix that was killing us early on: the classifier was matching substrings inside unrelated words and misrouting requests, so we tightened the matching to whole-word boundaries. Payments run through the x402 protocol on Hedera testnet, with Blocky402 as the facilitator (X402_TESTNET_FACILITATOR_URL=https://api.testnet.blocky402.com). The flow is genuinely pay-per-request: a call only settles once the request completes, and the gateway won't forward the inference until payment confirms. The model itself is served locally through LM Studio sitting behind the x402 gate, which let us test the full paid loop against a real open model without external API keys. Every settled call is logged to Hedera Consensus Service via packages/audit — an HCS logger plus a topic-creation script — giving each transaction a tamper-evident, verifiable on-chain receipt rather than a claim in a database. On the hacky side: because the starter repo wasn't designed to be extended, we kept our overlay as isolated packages and wired them into the agent with three surgical edits documented in INTEGRATION.md, which kept the reused-vs-new boundary clean for attribution and let us iterate on the router without touching the upstream PoC.
projects.project_description_markdown: An agentic AI gateway on Hedera where every inference call is paid per request via the x402 protocol — no subscriptions, no prepaid balances. A prompt classifier automatically routes each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it, and every paid call is settled through Blocky402 and logged to Hedera Consensus Service for a verifiable on-chain audit trail. One endpoint replaces a stack of separate AI subscriptions, and the agent proves what it paid for.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The project is built on top of Hedera's x402-inference-pay-per-request-poc starter, extended with a custom broker overlay that adds intelligent model routing and on-chain auditing.

The core is split into two packages. packages/router holds a prompt classifier, an offering catalogue (each model tagged with capability and cost-per-call), and selection logic that picks the cheapest model capable of handling a given prompt — so a trivial query never gets billed at frontier-model prices. This is what turns a plain gateway into an actual router. It ships with unit tests, including a word-boundary regex fix that was killing us early on: the classifier was matching substrings inside unrelated words and misrouting requests, so we tightened the matching to whole-word boundaries.

On the hacky side: because the starter repo wasn't designed to be extended, we kept our overlay as isolated packages and wired them into the agent with three surgical edits documented in INTEGRATION.md, which kept the reused-vs-new boundary clean for attribution and let us iterate on the router without touching the upstream PoC.

projects.title: Mandi
projects.description: Humans set the rules. Agents spend the money — ENS discovery, policy checks, x402 on Hedera.
projects.project_description:
Mandi is a procurement layer for autonomous agents. A human signs a spending policy with their own wallet. An agent discovers competing suppliers by name, but it cannot pay. A separate executor — the only module that holds the payment key — re-derives every fact from chain state and either signs an x402 payment on Hedera or refuses with reasons. Both outcomes are public. Sellers connect their wallet, sign a registration, and get <label>.mandi.eth minted to their wallet on the ENSv2 Sepolia. Price, capability and the x402 endpoint live in the resolver. A Selfie Check in World App, bound to that same wallet, is the only accreditation a policy will accept. Buyers sign the policy, deposit HBAR from their wallet over Hedera’s JSON-RPC relay, and run a task like “Assess risk of Aave.” The agent ranks suppliers on attestation, then reliability from settled receipts, then price. The executor resolves the name again, checks price, remaining budget, the deposit ledger, success rate, and the verifier-signed attestation, then pays per call through Blocky402. Failures cancel (x402 v2 authorization flow) and the agent falls back. Nothing eligible means nothing paid. Live console: https://mandi.up.railway.app/
Seller + Selfie Check: https://mandi.up.railway.app/seller
HCS audit trail: https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10454931
ENS Names: https://app.ens.dev/mandi.eth
projects.how_its_made: One Hono process (server/) and one Vite + React app (web/). No database, no queue. ENS. server/src/ens.ts talks to the live ENSv2 Sepolia contracts with viem. A UserRegistry subregistry under mandi.eth, a PermissionedResolver, and seller-owned names. Records: ENSIP-26 agent-context and agent-endpoint[x402], plus custom mandi:capability, mandi:price, mandi:chain, mandi:verified, mandi:upstream. The executor re-resolves at decision time. Prices are never hard-coded. Hedera / x402. @x402/hono gates every supplier route with a per-route HBAR price. @x402/fetch + @x402/hedera sign the transfer only after policy checks, settled through Blocky402 (exact, HBAR 0.0.0). Buyers fund the executor from MetaMask on chain 296. server/src/buyer/funding.ts nets mirror-node deposits against anchored spend. POLICY_ACTIVATED, DECISION, and RECEIPT go on one HCS topic via @hiero-ledger/sdk and join on the transaction id. Reliability is computed from those receipts only. Agent identity is the ENS name, not HCS-14. executor.ts is the only file that reads BUYER_KEY. World App, selfieCheckLegacy, signal = seller wallet. The server signs RP context, verifies on the v4 endpoint, binds a 90-day attestation to the ENS name, and enforces one accreditation per human via a hashed nullifier. requireVerifiedFor reads the attestation, not the ENS flag. The Graph. Messari subgraphs (aave-v3-ethereum, compound-v3-ethereum, morpho-aave-v3-ethereum, lido-ethereum) feed the paid risk endpoints. risk-pro does more queries per call than risk-basic — extra work, not a claim of being more correct.

projects.title: usufruct
projects.description: Sell a fixed window of your Uniswap fees upfront. Keep the position, get the same NFT back.
projects.project_description: Three things are deliberately decoupled, and that's the core of the design. Capture happens after the end block, so it collects more than the sold period; the contract reserves the actual USDC received rather than trusting any projection. The residual owner can retrieve the NFT before allocation is resolved at all — that withdrawal cannot touch the protected fee reserve. And settlement is authenticated against historical chain state, with allocation bounded by what was captured. Holders then redeem independently, so one recipient failing cannot block anyone else. Payouts use the immutable original claim count, never the remaining token supply, so somebody else redeeming never changes your fraction. This ran end to end in public. Series 1 on Sepolia: position NFT 39216 activated at block 11696226, end block N at 11696317, 10,000 claims issued against a 0.25 USDC upfront payment for 2,500 of them. A teammate bought 1,000 claims across three real Aqua trades. Capture collected 1.499999 USDC. The NFT returned at 11696393 while allocation was still unresolved. Allocation at 11696450 separated 0.999999 USDC earned by N from 0.500000 USDC earned after it. 9,010 claims have since been redeemed for 0.900996 USDC across four independent holders. Every figure shown before allocation is an estimate. Estimates never authorise a payout.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity built with Foundry 1.5.1 (Cancun) and run through Slither. Four first-party contracts: FeeStrip.sol escrows the canonical Uniswap v4 NFT for a fixed window, FeeClaim.sol issues the transferable claims against that window's unpaid native USDC fee income, and market/FeeStripMarket.sol with market/FeeStripRouter.sol provide the claim/USDC market. Coverage is 20 protocol tests plus two invariant campaigns totalling 16,384 calls with zero unexpected reverts, with separate proof and market suites on top. Uniswap v4 is the substrate rather than a dependency. We work against canonical position NFTs with a native v4 lifecycle, freezing the fixed range for the window. Series 1 ran the complete lifecycle in public on Sepolia against NFT 39216: activation at 11696226, end block N at 11696317, capture, NFT return at 11696393 before allocation resolved, then allocation at 11696450 costing 4,396,570 gas. Settlement authenticates the historical block header, position manager account and pool storage, and an independent native-endpoint oracle on an isolated fork produces 999999 USDC micros matching the authenticated witness. The claim market runs on official source-pinned Aqua and SwapVM sources from 1inch, extended with a custom two-instruction dispatcher so a fee claim is a first-class position inside Aqua rather than a token bolted on beside it. That's the hackiest and most useful thing we did. In series 1 a teammate bought 1,000 claims across three real public trades of 189, 63 and 748 — genuine FeeClaim and USDC transfers on Sepolia, not a fork. Tests cover both directions, unavailable and shared maker capital, stale lifecycle state, and adversarial callback ordering. That teammate's redemption of 1,000 claims for 0.099999 USDC cost 122,011 gas. Buyer analytics compose two Graph products. Hosted Substreams joins Subgraph Studio series 1 instrument state at finalized block 11696247, with 22 of 22 observed blocks covered and in range, at zero indexing lag relative to finalized history. packages/data/src/compose.mjs does the join with identity, common-block and hash checks, packages/data/src/store.mjs handles cursor persistence and reorg recovery, and packages/core/src/economics.mjs computes range occupancy and break-even. The snapshot is partial-period and carries no exact-fee or forecast authority. Analytics inform buyers; they never authorise settlement. The repo is a pnpm 12 workspace on Node 24. The web app in apps/web deploys to Vercel; an operations service runs from Dockerfile.operations on Railway with an api/ surface. The complete browser lifecycle — sale, trade, capture, return, settlement, redemption — runs end to end against a real local chain and reproduces in hosted CI via pnpm test:browser:chain . Endpoint durability is handled by a dedicated keeper that saved N at N+2. Exact proof was then restored from two remote GETs into a fresh local database and two authenticated copies, with zero remote writes, no RPC witness fallback and no hosted failover. An operations service runs from Dockerfile.operations on Railway; the web app deploys to Vercel; the repo is a pnpm 12 workspace on Node 24.

projects.title: Cadence
projects.description: Cadence makes liquidity scarce, time-bound, and tradable through ERC-1155 slots.
projects.project_description: Cadence makes market depth a scarce, priced, time-boxed resource — sold as ERC-1155 slots. A Uniswap v4 hook splits reserves each epoch: 25% active, 75% locked. beforeSwap gates every trade — hold a slot, burn your notional, fill active-only. No slot, no fill; unused slots expire worthless. Includes commit-reveal private intents (size hidden until fill), a slot CLOB, a multi-pool router, a live The Graph index, and a paid Hedera x402 intel call that writes the ask on-chain. LPs earn 90% of slot sales. Live on Sepolia, end-to-end verified.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity v4 hook + ERC-1155 slots, Foundry-tested, deployed via CREATE2 with versioned salts. Next.js + TypeScript frontend with viem and a custom EIP-1193 wallet layer — one reducer mirrors live chain truth, with simulate-first writes that surface decoded reverts before the wallet opens. The v4 hook is the product: beforeSwap enforces slot ≥ size, burns notional, fills active-only. The Graph Studio indexes every event (commit→reveal included); one real Hedera x402 micropayment buys the capacity/toxicity quote that writes the slot price. Notable hackiness: hook address mined to fit v4 permission flags, and a full-audit pass that caught a reducer never receiving the wallet address — silently no-op'ing every UI write.

projects.title: Squash
projects.description: One QR splits any bill. Everyone confirms, then one Hedera transaction settles it all.
projects.project_description: Squash is a bill-splitting app where nobody pays until everyone says yes. One person pays the tab, creates a bill in pesos or dollars, and shares a QR code. Guests scan it, join with just their name, and see their exact share update live. Each person signs in with their email through Privy, which creates a real Hedera wallet in the background — no seed phrase, no crypto knowledge required. When the organizer asks for confirmation, every share is frozen and converted to dollars at that day's exact exchange rate, so everyone agrees on the same number. Each guest then taps "Yes, I pay," sending the amount from their own wallet. Nothing moves until the very last person confirms — then every transfer executes together, in one shot, and everyone lands at zero at the same time. The same engine that computes a single bill also solves a whole shared trip: given 15 crossed debts between 6 people built up over several days, it finds the provably minimum number of transfers to settle everyone — 3 transfers, an 80% reduction — instead of naively running every individual debt one by one.
projects.how_its_made: Squash is a Next.js app on Hedera testnet. The settlement engine is a greedy net-settlement algorithm (net each participant's balance, then repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor) that finds the minimum number of transfers to zero out a group's debts — for our 6-person, 15-debt sample trip, that's 15 crossed debts collapsed to 3 transfers, an 80% reduction, computed live rather than hardcoded. The engine isn't free to call: every settlement plan, including a single bill at the table, is bought over x402. The app receives a 402 Payment Required, pays the facilitator (Blocky402) in HBAR based on the size of the debt graph, and only then gets the plan. Every run's inputs and outputs are hashed and published to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), so anyone can recompute the plan and verify we didn't fudge the numbers — that HashScan link ships right in the product, not just in a slide. For money movement, we use a Hedera fungible token (tUSD, 1 unit = 1 cent) as the settlement currency; the same code path settles in USDC on mainnet. Privy handles identity and custody: signing in with an email creates a real Hedera account with a real balance, so every participant pays from their own wallet, not a shared pool the app controls — that was the trickiest part, since most bill-splitting demos fake this with a single custodial account. We also built World ID verification for "no fake guests, no double seats" — it's fully implemented against World's SDK, but it's gated behind partner approval that hadn't come through by submission time, so it's present in the code and disabled in the live demo rather than pretending it works on camera. The genuinely hacky bit: freezing the FX rate at the moment confirmation is requested (not at bill creation, and not at settlement) so that every participant is cryptographically agreeing to the same dollar figure, without needing an oracle contract on-chain — we treat the rate as an off-chain input that gets hashed into the plan alongside the debts.

projects.title: PayeeLock
projects.description: Recover unpaid invoice balances without rewriting completed onchain payments.
projects.project_description: PayeeLock is a recovery protocol for approved supplier payments. If a supplier's payout wallet becomes unsafe, a constrained guardian can pause the unpaid invoices, but it cannot move funds or choose a new recipient. The supplier proposes a replacement wallet and the buyer accepts the exact same invoice set onchain. Previously paid value stays final, only the unpaid balance moves, and every authorization signed before recovery becomes stale. Anyone can use it today. Connect a wallet at payeelock-sentinel.vercel.app and the app deploys your own vault where your wallet is the buyer: register a supplier, prefund an invoice, pay it with a signed authorization, pause the supplier, and complete recovery. A separate review mode walks through a completed Sepolia case between Meridian Labs and Harbor Systems, where 2,400 MockUSDC was paid before the incident, 11,600 was settled after recovery, and an old queued payment reverted with zero tokens moved.
projects.how_its_made: I built the PayeeLock vault in Solidity and tested it with Foundry, including replay, expiry, wrong-beneficiary, freeze, exact-invoice-set recovery, fee-on-transfer, partial-payment fuzz cases, and factory ownership isolation. EIP-712 payment signatures bind the beneficiary, supplier epoch, invoice nonce, amount, expiry, chain ID, and contract. A permissionless factory deployed on Sepolia creates a vault and its payout resolver in one transaction with the caller as buyer, so anyone can run their own workspace. ENSv2 on Sepolia is the supplier identity and authority layer: a Permissioned Resolver lets an invoice publisher edit invoice text but not the payout address. A Privy server wallet is the freeze-only guardian under a default-deny policy scoped to one chain, one PayeeLock deployment, and freeze(bytes32). The recovery monitor reads indexed history from a deployed Graph Subgraph, confirms current state through Sepolia RPC, and may request only that freeze call. The Graph also indexes payment, recovery, and ENS events for the case review. The frontend uses Next.js and viem, signs typed data in the browser, and is hosted on Vercel. The repository is a Turborepo with separate web, Foundry, and Subgraph workspaces plus isolated Anvil lifecycle tests.

projects.title: LiquidPay
projects.description: Liquid Pay keeps your positions working until the instant you need to pay.
projects.project_description:
Liquid Pay provides just-in-time liquidity for everyday payments. Instead of keeping capital idle in stablecoins, users can remain exposed to assets they want to hold and liquidate only the amount required when a payment is made. Before paying, Liquid analyzes the connected wallet, considers the user’s liquidation preferences, identifies eligible positions, compares available exit routes, accounts for gas and slippage, and presents a controlled liquidation plan. Once approved, the required positions are converted into USDC and the recipient is paid.
This makes capital more efficient: users can preserve market exposure until liquidity is actually needed, while retaining control over which assets may be sold, how much may be liquidated, and where the payment goes.
projects.how_its_made:
Liquid Pay is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, Convex, The Graph, Privy, OpenAI and viem. The Graph is the intelligence layer. Subgraphs provide indexed pool prices, liquidity, volume and historical market evidence; the Token API helps discover supported assets held by the wallet; and Substreams supplies recent onchain activity. Liquid composes this information into wallet exposure, sector analysis, exit evidence and route selection context.
Users authenticate and connect embedded or external wallets through Privy. Natural language instructions such as protecting an asset or limiting how much may be liquidated are converted by OpenAI into a structured policy. The AI interprets intent, but deterministic application logic validates and enforces the resulting constraints. A payment is always previewed before execution, and Privy provides explicit wallet approval and narrowly scoped, time limited permissions for supported reviewed transactions.
The liquidation planner checks existing USDC first, then evaluates eligible positions and compares executable exit routes using live Base contract reads. It includes gas reserves, slippage protection, token approvals and minimum-output constraints. viem is used for contract calls, transaction encoding, simulation and receipt verification. Convex privately stores wallet snapshots, signed preferences, payment plans and execution checkpoints so an interrupted multi-step payment can be recovered without blindly sending the same transaction twice.
The result is a controlled just-in-time liquidation workflow: keep capital deployed, liquidate only what the payment needs, and verify that the recipient received the expected USDC.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Liquid Pay provides just-in-time liquidity for everyday payments. Once approved, the required positions are converted into USDC and the recipient is paid.
This makes capital more efficient: users can preserve market exposure until liquidity is actually needed, while retaining control over which assets may be sold, how much may be liquidated, and where the payment goes.

projects.description: Autonomous AI trading protocol with EVM escrow caps, Backpack L2 & Hedera audit logs.

Currently, most autonomous AI crypto trading bots have two drawbacks: they are either perilous black boxes or they require the use of TypeScript or Solidity programming languages to modify a trading rule. Atlas was created to address this trust and accessibility concern in trading. Atlas enables traders to easily create automated trading logic like Dip Buying, Momentum breakout, and customized price triggers at a visual no-code level. One of their most remarkable features is that every trading event is conducted through smart, agent vault non-custodial contracts (AgentVault.sol). Users impose a number of restrictions on their spending, going from dictating the upper limit on each trade to establishing the maximum amount of money to spend throughout the trading process and involving traders in multiple steps of trading activity. When using the service, users are able to see the execution of the trading strategy on the shocking depth interest order book from Backpack Exchange and TradingView candlestick charts simultaneously. Moreover, every trading signal and emergency kill switch are being recorded immutably on Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) along with links to HashScan, thus guaranteeing the complete audit trail.
