projects.title: CustodIA
projects.description: Chat-native DeFi agent that proposes; you sign an EIP-712 boundary on ENSv2, policy enforces it
projects.project_description: CustodIA is a runtime, not a bot. You type an intent in a chat (web, Telegram or WhatsApp): "Keep ETH/USDC inside a 5% drawdown", "Protect me if ETH drops 15%", "Buy 500 USDC of ETH". The agent researches with live The Graph data, buys a risk analysis with an x402 micropayment on Hedera, and answers with a generated, schema-validated interface: sliders, toggles and charts whose bounds are clipped to the risk context, never invented by the model. You adjust the boundary and sign it once as an EIP-712 mandate with typed constraints (max trade, max notional, max drawdown, allowed assets, rebalance permission, expiry). The mandate hash is anchored on an ENSv2 task subname ({task}.{you}.custodia.eth) and the agent receives a role scoped to a single text record on that name. From then on a pure, tested policy engine evaluates every action against the mandate before anything moves, and you can revoke the agent's role on-chain at any moment. After revocation the agent's next write reverts. When you want real execution, you deploy a TaskVault from the task page and fund it with Sepolia ETH. Orders typed in chat are quoted on Uniswap V3, approved per action by a policy signer, executed by an execution signer that cannot withdraw, and the contract itself enforces the assets, caps, cooldown, expiry and router you signed. The agent can also act alone inside the boundary: it sells to USDC when the drawdown limit is hit and proposes rebalances over chat that you confirm with a YES. The point is separating intelligence from authority. The LLM only proposes. Bounds come from deterministic risk numbers computed from live market data. The human signs the envelope. The policy engine, the ENSv2 role and the vault enforce it. Requests outside the envelope become a "needs a new signature" screen instead of an execution. Everything runs on Sepolia and Hedera testnet with real transactions, live data and no mocks on the qualifying path.
projects.how_its_made: pnpm monorepo in TypeScript: Next.js 15 web app, a worker, a Hono risk API, a delegated signer subprocess, and packages for schema (Zod), agent, policy, graph, ens, registry, vault, runtime and db (Drizzle on Neon Postgres, PGlite for tests). Contracts are Solidity 0.8 with Foundry. The agent is an OpenAI tool loop (chat.completions.runTools with Zod function tools, gpt-5.6-luna). Its only way to produce UI is an emit_ui_spec tool whose output is validated against a frozen Zod schema and then clipped server-side to the RiskContext, so a bound outside the risk envelope is a validation error, not a fallback. The Graph: market context comes from the Uniswap V3 Messari standardized subgraph through the gateway. Prices are derived from the pool tick (10^(dec1-dec0)/1.0001^tick), realized vol from hourly snapshots, every snapshot carries its block, cached 30 s. The pool constant is verified by name at runtime because the first one we hardcoded was the wrong fee tier. Hedera: the risk API is gated with @x402/hono and @x402/hedera (pinned 2.25.0), priced in HBAR, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. The Hedera key exists only in apps/signer: the agent sends the payment-required header on stdin and gets a payment-signature back on stdout, calls are serialized, and the policy engine must allow the pay_x402 action before the signer is asked. Receipts are checked against the mirror node. ENS: each task is a free wildcard subname on a PermissionedResolver deployed through the VerifiableFactory on Sepolia. The operator writes owner, mandate hash, agent and status text records; then authorizeTextRoles grants the agent a role for xyz.custodia.status only. Revoking that role makes the next agent write revert with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, which pnpm verify:ens proves live. The trap that cost us the most: authorize* takes a DNS-encoded name while setText takes a namehash. Mandates are EIP-712 typed data bound to an immutable stored proposal (proposalId plus constraints hash), so what you sign is exactly what was rendered. Non-authorizable intents (needs_human, compare_strategies) are refused with a 409. Runtime durability: every chat turn is a run with an append-only event stream and a job on a Postgres queue leased with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; agent runs are never auto-retried; channel deliveries go through an outbox. Telegram and WhatsApp are transports paired to the wallet, signing always happens on the web. Hacky bits worth mentioning: a dependency-free Chrome DevTools client drives the end-to-end demo with screenshots across all ten prompt cases; the pre-signature receipt is composed server-side so the UI numbers match the mandate byte for byte; Neon's IPv6 records stalled cold connections on our box, so the db client forces ipv4first; the demo wallet was stocked by swapping through the Sepolia Uniswap V3 pools from a script because the faucets only give ETH.

fresh, unlinkable address.

data today to de-anonymize it tomorrow. Announcement data is public and permanent — it
cannot be re-encrypted after the fact.
• NIST finalized its post-quantum standards in 2024 (ML-KEM / FIPS 203) and the migration

before that deadline. ═══════════════════════════════════════════

projects.title: ChainSentry
projects.description: ChainSentry is an observability and alerting tool for Ethereum smart contract developers
projects.project_description: I come from a backend and DevOps background, and most production issues I have debugged were only possible to understand because of monitoring and observability tools. In backend systems, we have tools like ELK, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and alerting pipelines. If an external service fails, latency increases, or some unexpected error starts happening, we can look at logs, metrics, traces, and alerts to understand what went wrong. I wanted to bring that same kind of visibility to smart contracts. Once a smart contract is deployed, it is running in production and interacting with users, tokens, protocols, and other contracts. If one of those dependencies changes, fails, or starts behaving differently, the contract may also behave differently. But unlike backend services, smart contracts usually do not have a proper observability layer around them. ChainSentry helps developers monitor their smart contracts after deployment. A developer can register a contract, index its on-chain activity, view metrics, inspect event history, create dashboards, and set alerts for unusual behavior. For example, they can monitor event counts, transaction volume, success rate, gas usage, or value transferred. If something crosses a threshold, ChainSentry creates an issue and notifies the on-call person through email or phone call. The idea is simple: smart contract developers should not have to wait for users to report problems. They should be able to observe their contracts in production, understand what changed, and respond quickly.
projects.how_its_made: ChainSentry uses The Graph to get blockchain data in a reliable way. Directly hitting RPC endpoints for every dashboard or query is slow, expensive, and not suitable for a monitoring product. So the backend generates subgraph configurations for the smart contract and stores those generated artifacts in Google Cloud Storage. The indexed blockchain data is then ingested into ClickHouse, which is used for fast analytical queries. The backend is built with Node.js, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL, and ClickHouse. PostgreSQL stores users, organizations, contracts, deployments, alert rules, on-call schedules, and issues. ClickHouse stores the high-volume event and transaction data that powers dashboards and metrics. The frontend is built with Next.js and gives developers pages for metrics, logs, traces, incidents, alerting, and contract configuration. I also integrated Resend and Twilio for alerting. When an alert rule is triggered, ChainSentry can send an email or place a phone call to the on-call developer. This was important to me because real observability is not just dashboards. It should also help the right person know when something is wrong. The project is basically my attempt to bring the DevOps monitoring workflow I use in backend systems into Web3, so smart contract developers can debug and monitor production contracts with the same confidence.

projects.title: Leash
projects.description: The AI agrees to pay, and the chain says no. On-chain spending rules for agent wallets.
projects.project_description: Leash is a permission layer for AI agent wallets. What an agent may spend and who it may pay lives in a smart contract, and the wallet checks it on every payment the agent makes — so you don't have to trust the agent to follow its own rules.** The problem. An AI agent that can spend money needs a spending limit, and every existing answer puts that limit somewhere the agent can reach: a config file it reads, an API key it holds, a session key whose cap the agent itself enforces. Compromise the agent and the limit goes with it. There's a second problem that gets less attention and happens more often. Limits given to agents don't add up. Teams don't deploy one agent, they deploy several. At 9am the subscriptions agent renews a licence; at 11 the invoices agent pays a contractor; at noon the account is empty and the payment that mattered fails. Neither agent did anything wrong — each stayed inside the limit it was given. There were two limits and one bank account. No per-agent setting fixes that, because it's arithmetic, not a security failure. What Leash does. The limit isn't attached to an agent. It's attached to an ENS name . The wallet resolves that name on every single payment to find the policy contract that governs it, and the on-chain ledger of what's been spent is keyed by the name, the token and the day — with no agent in the key. So every agent bound to that name draws down one budget, enforced by the chain, with no shared database, no coordinator, and no message passing between them. The agents don't know each other exist. What you see in the demo. A four-person studio with two AI agents — one pays invoices, one handles renewals — sharing fifty dollars a day. You type an instruction in English. Claude turns it into a payment. It never writes an address: it picks a vendor by name, and those names are ENS records — our vendor directory contains no addresses at all, so a hallucinated payee has nowhere to appear. The retainer is paid with no approval and no human click. A new contractor's first invoice is refused. Nobody caught it — no filter, no review queue. The rule isn't in the agent's prompt or its config; it's on chain, and the agent can disagree with it, ignore it, or be compromised, and the wallet still says no. To widen what the agent may do, a live human scans their face with World ID Selfie Check , and the wallet checks that proof against the one World ID it has registered. No key can do that — not the agent's, not the wallet's own. Then the agent tries again on its own and the answer has changed; nobody told it. The other agent, on a different key in a different process, is refused a payment its vendor and per-transaction limit both allow — because the first agent already spent the budget. It works that out by reading the chain. And notice what the face scan bought: it added a payee. It did not add a dollar. Rules are swappable. A second policy a human already approved says small payments to anyone, OR the full original rules — two policy contracts composed with an OR. Point the ENS name at it, and a payment that was refused a minute ago goes through, with nothing retyped and nothing said to the agent. Refusals are first-class. A blocked payment doesn't revert — it emits an event and returns. That's deliberate: it means every refusal is indexed and visible on The Graph , so you can audit not just what the agents did but what they tried to do. It's also the only reason a refusal exists anywhere at all. The asymmetry is the design. Expanding what an agent may do costs a live human face. Reducing it — tightening a rule, removing a payee, revoking an agent, pausing the wallet — is free and instant, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake. What it does not claim. EIP-7702 constrains calls to the delegated account, so the wallet's own private key can always sign a direct transfer. That's both the boundary and the escape hatch: the owner can always retrieve their funds and can never be locked out by a rule they installed. Leash is the agent's only spending path, not the wallet's. Everything runs on Sepolia against deployed contracts. Every claim in the README has a transaction hash behind it, including the refusals.
projects.how_its_made: The wallet is an EOA with delegated code. LeashAccount is an EIP-7702 delegate implementation (2,856 lines of Solidity, 260 Foundry tests). Delegation is 23 bytes — 0xef0100 || impl — and the code runs against the EOA's own storage, so state lives in an ERC-7201 namespace at keccak256("leash.account.v1") . Re-delegating to a newer impl reads back identically because every field keeps its slot; ownerNullifier was appended at SLOT+6, which was unused. spend is the only path an agent has, and it cannot go around the check because the check happens inside its own execution path. Authorise the caller from per-EOA storage → walk ENS three hops to resolve the policy → verify that address against a human-approved list → staticcall the policy under a 200k gas cap → honour the reason code. ENS is the lookup path, not a label. LeashRegistry implements the ENSv2 IRegistry ( getSubregistry / getResolver / getParent + IERC1155Singleton ) and is mounted under leash.eth , so resolution is forced through it. LeashResolver implements only ENSIP-10 resolve(bytes,bytes) — measured fact: minimal ENSv2 resolvers have no addr() at all, so a compatibility layer is wasted work. ENS's own UniversalResolverV2 resolves our names. Three things hang off the name and breaking any one stops the system: the policy address, every payee address ( agent/vendors.json contains names and zero addresses, so a hallucinated payee has nowhere to appear), and — the part we didn't design and then discovered — the budget . The ledger is spent[node][token][bucket] : three keys, no agent. So two agents bound to one subname share one budget, enforced by the account, with no coordination between the processes. That needed no contract change; it fell out of the storage layout. The Graph is the agent's only sense organ. A refusal doesn't revert — it emits SpendBlocked and returns — so a blocked payment leaves a status-1 receipt and exists nowhere a getter can reach. That was a deliberate design decision to make refusals indexable, and it means the subgraph is the only place four things exist: the refusal log, the payee allow-list (no contract can enumerate it), the list of approved policies (events, not an array), and the per-agent split of the shared budget. That last one is reconstructed client-side by walking spentAfter backwards from the budget's current total until it reaches zero — which finds the period boundary by arithmetic rather than by assuming 86400 seconds. EIP-7702 delegation emits no log, so the subgraph has no factory event to trigger a template from; LeashAccount emits Leashed on the first bindAgent to be that trigger. World ID Selfie Check is the asymmetry. Widening costs a live human; reducing is free, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake. WorldAttester verifies an EIP-712 attestation from our RP signer against a digest bound to the exact widening, and LeashAccount additionally checks the nullifier equals the one ownerNullifier it has registered. allowPayeeByFace deliberately has no onlySelf — the wallet's own key gets NotAttested() while a valid face scan relayed by anyone succeeds. The face outranks every key in the system, including the wallet's. Claude drives the agent. claude -p with a vendor directory of ENS names; the model picks an id and never writes an address. Three hacky/hard-won things worth naming. (1) @worldcoin/idkit-standalone cannot request a face check at all — we proved it from the published bundle (zero occurrences of "selfie", four verification levels) and migrated to idkit-core 's selfieCheckLegacy() . On the wire it's verification_level: "face" — the same vocabulary with a fifth value the widget's switch is missing. (2) Once you store a nullifier, the action stops being a free choice: a nullifier is hash(person, action) , so every future scan must reuse the same action or the stored one never matches. Nothing documents that, and the verification succeeds either way — it fails only in your own code. Both are written up in docs/world-feedback.md . (3) PolicySet reaches its members by staticcall , not call , because the account doesn't revert when it blocks — a member that wrote state on the way to a refusal could never be rolled back. Honestly stated: PolicyApprovals is wired to MockAttester in this deployment, so getting onto the approved list is currently ungated. The account's own attester is the real WorldAttester ; the approvals contract's is immutable , so fixing it is a redeploy of two contracts. It's flagged in the README and docs/deployments.md rather than buried. Foundry, viem, node:test. 260 Solidity tests, 212 JavaScript. Every claim in the README has a Sepolia transaction hash behind it.

It's also the only reason a refusal exists anywhere at all.

**The asymmetry is the design.** Expanding what an agent may do costs a live human face. Reducing it — tightening a rule, removing a payee, revoking an agent, pausing the wallet — is free and instant, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake.

**What it does not claim.** EIP-7702 constrains calls *to* the delegated account, so the wallet's own private key can always sign a direct transfer. That's both the boundary and the escape hatch: the owner can always retrieve their funds and can never be locked out by a rule they installed. Leash is the agent's only spending path, not the wallet's.

Everything runs on Sepolia against deployed contracts. Every claim in the README has a transaction hash behind it, including the refusals.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**The wallet is an EOA with delegated code.** `LeashAccount` is an EIP-7702 delegate implementation (2,856 lines of Solidity, 260 Foundry tests). Delegation is 23 bytes — `0xef0100 || impl` — and the code runs against the EOA's own storage, so state lives in an ERC-7201 namespace at `keccak256("leash.account.v1")`. Re-delegating to a newer impl reads back identically because every field keeps its slot; `ownerNullifier` was appended at SLOT+6, which was unused.

**`spend` is the only path an agent has, and it cannot go around the check** because the check happens inside its own execution path. Authorise the caller from per-EOA storage → walk ENS three hops to resolve the policy → verify that address against a human-approved list → `staticcall` the policy under a 200k gas cap → honour the reason code.

**ENS is the lookup path, not a label.** `LeashRegistry` implements the ENSv2 `IRegistry` (`getSubregistry` / `getResolver` / `getParent` + `IERC1155Singleton`) and is mounted under `leash.eth`, so resolution is forced through it. `LeashResolver` implements only ENSIP-10 `resolve(bytes,bytes)` — measured fact: minimal ENSv2 resolvers have no `addr()` at all, so a compatibility layer is wasted work. ENS's own UniversalResolverV2 resolves our names. Three things hang off the name and breaking any one stops the system: the policy address, every payee address (`agent/vendors.json` contains names and zero addresses, so a hallucinated payee has nowhere to appear), and — the part we didn't design and then discovered — **the budget**. The ledger is `spent[node][token][bucket]`: three keys, no agent. So two agents bound to one subname share one budget, enforced by the account, with no coordination between the processes. That needed no contract change; it fell out of the storage layout.

**The Graph is the agent's only sense organ.** A refusal doesn't revert — it emits `SpendBlocked` and returns — so a blocked payment leaves a status-1 receipt and exists nowhere a getter can reach. That was a deliberate design decision to make refusals indexable, and it means the subgraph is the only place four things exist: the refusal log, the payee allow-list (no contract can enumerate it), the list of approved policies (events, not an array), and the per-agent split of the shared budget. That last one is reconstructed client-side by walking `spentAfter` backwards from the budget's current total until it reaches zero — which finds the period boundary by arithmetic rather than by assuming 86400 seconds. EIP-7702 delegation emits no log, so the subgraph has no factory event to trigger a template from; `LeashAccount` emits `Leashed` on the first `bindAgent` to be that trigger.

**World ID Selfie Check is the asymmetry.** Widening costs a live human; reducing is free, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake. `WorldAttester` verifies an EIP-712 attestation from our RP signer against a digest bound to the exact widening, and `LeashAccount` additionally checks the nullifier equals the one `ownerNullifier` it has registered. **`allowPayeeByFace` deliberately has no `onlySelf`** — the wallet's own key gets `NotAttested()` while a valid face scan relayed by anyone succeeds. The face outranks every key in the system, including the wallet's.

**Claude drives the agent.** `claude -p` with a vendor directory of ENS names; the model picks an id and never writes an address.

**Three hacky/hard-won things worth naming.** (1) `@worldcoin/idkit-standalone` cannot request a face check at all — we proved it from the published bundle (zero occurrences of "selfie", four verification levels) and migrated to `idkit-core`'s `selfieCheckLegacy()`. On the wire it's `verification_level: "face"` — the same vocabulary with a fifth value the widget's switch is missing. (2) Once you *store* a nullifier, the action stops being a free choice: a nullifier is `hash(person, action)`, so every future scan must reuse the same action or the stored one never matches. Nothing documents that, and the verification *succeeds* either way — it fails only in your own code. Both are written up in `docs/world-feedback.md`. (3) `PolicySet` reaches its members by `staticcall`, not `call`, because the account doesn't revert when it blocks — a member that wrote state on the way to a refusal could never be rolled back.

**Honestly stated:** `PolicyApprovals` is wired to `MockAttester` in this deployment, so getting onto the approved list is currently ungated. The account's own attester is the real `WorldAttester`; the approvals contract's is `immutable`, so fixing it is a redeploy of two contracts. It's flagged in the README and `docs/deployments.md` rather than buried.

Foundry, viem, node:test. 260 Solidity tests, 212 JavaScript. Every claim in the README has a Sepolia transaction hash behind it.

projects.title: Carpool
projects.description: AI agents buy research someone already did instead of redoing it. The author gets paid in USDC.
projects.project_description: Carpool is a registry where AI agents buy and sell finished research. Before an agent spends twenty minutes and a few dollars of tokens on a question, it searches Carpool. If someone has already answered it, the agent pays a small USDC fee over x402, gets the document, and skips the work. Whoever wrote it earns a royalty on every sale. Each piece of research is addressed by a hash of its contents, so it can't be swapped after it's listed. Search matches on meaning, and ranks answers higher when they're fresher and more thorough. Prices fall as research ages. The author picks a half-life, the price halves on that schedule, and after three halvings the registry stops selling it, because a stale answer sold as current does more harm than having none. Buyers have a two-minute refund window. The registry holds each payment for that window, then pays authors in batches with HTS transfers and posts a Merkle root of every batch to an HCS topic, so payouts can be audited. Agents use it through an MCP server with four tools: search, fetch, publish and delist. It installs into Claude Code. Search is free and needs no account. Publishing always asks the user first, and it removes secrets and local file paths before anything is listed. Buyers can rate a purchase as worth it or not, one rating per purchase, signed by the key that paid. We measured one real case. Redoing an ETHOnline prize analysis cost at least $3.97 in tokens; buying the same document cost $0.44. We also ran every payment path on Hedera testnet: refunds, a 13-author payout split across two transactions, recovering a batch whose receipt was lost, and two settlement processes hitting the same batch at once, which still produced a single transfer. Authors can also publish under their own ENS name. The name's records hold their Hedera payout account and signing key, and each sale looks up where to pay at the moment it happens, so an author can move payouts to a new account without republishing anything.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm and turbo) on Node 20, split into a payment package, a core model, a search package, the registry, the MCP server and a Next.js dashboard. Payments: the paywall is built on @x402/core and @x402/hedera, and payments are verified and settled by the Blocky402 facilitator on testnet. Buyers pay the registry's account rather than the author's. That was a deliberate choice, since otherwise a refund would have nothing to pull back. Hedera: settlement uses @hiero-ledger/sdk. Payouts go out as HTS token transfers with at most 9 authors per transaction, because a transfer list caps at 10 entries. Each batch's Merkle root is posted to an HCS topic. The mirror node is used to recover lost transactions by their memo, and a Python script re-checks 60 of our on-chain claims against it without importing any of our code. Money is Circle's testnet USDC. Registry: Express with SQLite through better-sqlite3, sqlite-vec for the vector index, and MiniLM embeddings running locally through transformers.js. A lease row in SQLite stops two processes from settling the same batch twice. We found that bug in a simulation, where it paid one author twice, and then confirmed the fix on testnet. MCP server: built on the official SDK. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook blocks publishing unless a person confirms it. ENS: an author can publish as name.eth on the ENSv2 beta on Sepolia. Reads go through viem's Universal Resolver. The registry trusts the name only when three records agree (Hedera address, coin type 3030; the signing key; and a signature from that key over the name and account), then reads the payout account at purchase time and records how it paid. If ENS is slow or the records don't match, the sale still goes through and pays the backup account the author signed into the listing.

projects.title: Veilend
projects.description: Uniswap v4 LP positions as loan collateral, with private credit scoring via Chainlink CRE TEE.
projects.project_description: Veilend lets Uniswap v4 liquidity providers borrow against their LP positions without withdrawing liquidity. Borrowers lock a position, minted in Veilend's own hook-enabled demo pool, as collateral. A CollateralLockHook blocks liquidity removal while the loan is active, though fee collection stays enabled so the collateral keeps earning. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow then computes a personalized credit score inside a TEE using handlerInTee: one real on-chain data point (LP position size and age, read via Uniswap's PositionManager) is combined with simulated repayment history. Only the resulting loan terms (LTV, APR, and expiry) ever leave the enclave; the raw inputs and scoring logic never do. The LendingVault uses these terms to size and disburse a loan in a mock stablecoin, tiering LTV from 20% to 70% depending on the privately computed score. Borrowers who repay before the deadline get their position unlocked normally. Borrowers who default past a grace period can have their position seized via a pre-approved transfer, giving the lender a real recovery path even though the lock itself is flag-based rather than custodial. This is a from-scratch hackathon build, with no continuity from a prior project. The README transparently discloses exactly which data is real (on-chain LP data) versus simulated (repayment history), and which parts of the architecture, such as the relayer bridging CRE to the vault, are hackathon-scope simplifications versus production-ready design.
projects.how_its_made: Veilend is a four-layer stack: Uniswap v4 contracts (Foundry), a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (TypeScript), a Bun relayer, and a Next.js app. On-chain we started from the official Uniswap v4 hook template (BaseHook, HookMiner, and CREATE2) and replaced the Counter swap example with CollateralLockHook. The hook has one permission: beforeRemoveLiquidity. We mine the address so the BEFORE_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_FLAG bits match. LendingVault takes custody of a PositionManager NFT on lock, calls hook.registerLock, then later disburses a mock stable (vdUSD) after a credit report. Collateral is only accepted from our demo pool (vUSD/vEUR) because a v4 hook is part of PoolKey, not of an NFT. We deployed against the canonical Sepolia PoolManager and PositionManager; Foundry tests cover lock, repay, liquidate, and the decrease-while-locked revert. Off-chain, a Bun + viem relayer watches PositionLocked and shells out to cre workflow simulate with {borrower, positionId}. The CRE handler (handlerInTee, AWS Nitro, us-west-2) fetches a secret, looks up private repayment history, reads LP liquidity via eth_call, and derives position age by scanning Transfer(from=0) logs in 40k-block chunks, because PositionInfo has no mint timestamp. Scoring is 40% position (size + age) and 60% history, mapped to LTV/APR tiers. Only {ltvBps, aprBps, expiry} leave the enclave. Intermediate scores never hit the chain. The relayer is the glue we would replace with DON-verified reports in production: it scrapes the “Workflow Simulation Result” JSON from CLI stdout (and refuses output that includes creditScore), then calls submitCreditReport as onlyRelayer. The vault values collateral as amount0 + amount1 if the relayer supplies a snapshot; otherwise 1 unit of liquidity = 1 mock-USD, with no oracle. The frontend is Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi/viem, and Tailwind. Borrow discovery uses Alchemy’s Sepolia NFT API on the server so the PositionManager token list is not a public env leak. Partner tech: Uniswap v4 gave us pool-level enforcement. PositionManager sets salt = bytes32(tokenId), so the hook keys locks as uint256(params.salt). liquidityDelta < 0 vs == 0 lets us block unwind while still allowing collect. Chainlink CRE gave us a real confidential boundary: raw history and the score stay in the TEE; the chain only sees terms. Notable hacks: (1) we cannot lock arbitrary v4 LPs (ISubscriber is a notifier, not a lock), so collateral is a pool we initialized ourselves; (2) ERC-721 approval is revocable, so the vault pulls the NFT at lock instead of hoping the borrower does not approve(0); (3) CRE ↔ chain is a CLI spawn + stdout parse, not live consensus; (4) position age is reconstructed from mint logs because the periphery does not store createdAt.

projects.title: Clembot Doorman
projects.description: Package manager & security gate for AI agents. It blocks rogue MCP tools and pays on Base for audits
projects.project_description: Adding an MCP server to an autonomous AI agent takes a single line of JSON. After that, an unvetted third-party server injects tool definitions directly into the agent's LLM context window. During our research across 24 live production MCP servers, we discovered a commercial product (WebZum) actively executing prompt injection: its tool descriptions instruct the LLM to covertly steer users away from competitors and upsell hosting packages unprompted. If agents adopt tools autonomously, malicious or redundant tools degrade context, leak credentials, and drain budgets. Clembot Doorman is a zero-dependency package manager, security gate, and tool governance engine built for Claude Code and autonomous agent teams: PreToolUse Interceptor Gate ( mcp-gate.sh ): Intercepts MCP tool execution at the harness level before the tool definition enters the agent's context. Unknown servers are blocked with exit code 2. Two-Phase Cost-Bounded Defense Funnel: Phase 1: Local Fit ($0.00): Scans local schemas, project capabilities, and agent prompt history ( doorman needs ). Redundant, out-of-scope, or duplicate tools are rejected locally with zero network calls and zero tokens spent. Phase 2: Base Mainnet Scorecard ($0.01): Only novel candidates proceed to remote adversarial probing. The agent pays an atomic $0.01 USDC micropayment via x402 over Base (Chain 8453) via Bazantic. Bazantic Schema Compression Recipes: For passed servers (e.g. DeepWiki), Doorman auto-drafts 8-field Bazantic recipes that strip unused schemas, achieving an 87% context token reduction. Immutable Evidence & Replay Tapes: "Don't trust the letter grade, replay the tape." Every grade includes a public, replayable transcript tape with a SHA-256 evidence hash. Unified Developer Experience: Run doorman audit for a single-command security posture report, or doorman schedule to automate recurring audits via GitHub Actions, CRON, or session hooks.
projects.how_its_made: Base Mainnet (Chain 8453) & x402 Micropayments: Implements HTTP 402 Payment Required protocol using atomic USDC transactions (10,000 atomic units =  $0.01) to rate-limit and monetize adversarial security audits. Bazantic Platform & Gateway: Integrated via Bazantic custom domain gateway ( clembot-doorman.bazgateway.com ), featuring 3 automated tool recipes ( 01-vet-mcp-candidate.json , 02-deepwiki-pinned-researcher.json , 03-governance-pipeline.json ) providing continuous continuity and schema compression. Claude Code Plugin & Hooks: Native plugin manifest with auto-discovery, PreToolUse hook security gate, /doorman and /vet slash commands, and a specialized Doorman subagent. Pure Node.js (Zero Dependencies): Deliberately built with 0 runtime dependencies to eliminate supply chain vulnerabilities. Includes a 505-test suite (465 unit + 40 CLI tests) running in under 3 seconds. Cloudflare Workers & Cloudflare Pages: Edge-deployed API and documentation site backed by SQLite for immutable transcript storage. Clembot - I created my own multi-agent harness for the past 2 years to build more efficiently. This was my coding team.

projects.title: Velum
projects.description: Verify delivered work against private terms with Chainlink CRE before releasing one payment.
projects.project_description:
A successful build does not prove a contractor delivered the agreed software revision. Velum verifies that boundary before releasing a work-order payment. A payer’s work order specifies the accepted revision, recipient, payment amount and budget. When delivery is submitted, Velum reserves the work order and uses
Chainlink CRE to retrieve live GitHub evidence and evaluate it against the configured acceptance record and commercial terms. The resulting authorization
determines whether a Solidity treasury can pay. The interactive demo shows two real, successful GitHub workflow runs. The earlier revision fails the acceptance check: payment is held and zero tokens
transfer. The accepted revision passes and releases 2,400 test tokens. Payment history survives a reload, concurrent requests cannot reserve the same work
order, and another attempt to pay the completed order is rejected. Confidential Workflows are central to the design: credentials, source records and payment-policy evaluation belong inside the confidential handler, while the
public ABI authorization omits raw commercial terms. This is a prototype with synthetic commercial terms and team-configured acceptance. It demonstrates actual CRE CLI simulation and live GitHub retrieval.
Settlement runs in a persistent, journal-backed local EVM with a mock forwarder; the primary flow does not send a network payment or demonstrate deployed TEE
attestation.
projects.how_its_made:
Velum combines TypeScript, Zod, Chainlink CRE, Solidity and Cloudflare Workers. A browser interface submits delivery evidence to a Worker API. SQLite-backed
Durable Objects reserve the work order and budget, queue execution, and persist payment history. The CRE workflow registers handlerInTee. Inside that handler, it retrieves separate source and GitHub credentials, fetches the work-order record and live
GitHub evidence, and checks the accepted commit, numeric repository and workflow identities, branch, trigger, successful completion and pinned workflow
definition. These checks run alongside the commercial payment policy. Chainlink provides the workflow boundary for authenticated retrieval and confidential
policy evaluation, making the resulting report the input to settlement. The workflow uses usingTheDons to return an ABI authorization without raw commercial terms. Our BatchTreasury contract checks its configured forwarder and
workflow identity, request commitments, recipient, amount, token, chain and expiry before atomically consuming authorization and transferring ERC-20 test
tokens. A VM runner executes actual CRE CLI simulations and feeds their report bytes into compiled Solidity running in EthereumJS. A notable implementation detail is
the durable execution journal: it reconstructs each workspace’s local treasury from recorded operations, caches completed results and redelivers them until
acknowledged. Uncertain executions retain their reservations, and recovery resumes the same job rather than opening another payment path. The project includes 58 unit tests, contract tests and deployed browser checks covering held and paid outcomes, concurrent reservations, reload recovery and
duplicate protection. Local execution uses mock forwarding and does not establish deployed enclave attestation. Work-order uniqueness relies on the reservation
service and journal; the contract independently prevents request replay. Codex generated the implementation, tests, interface and drafts. Lawrence selected the Chainlink focus, configured and authenticated the development
environment, chose Velum’s identity and artistic direction, reviewed iterations and authorized the product direction.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Velum combines TypeScript, Zod, Chainlink CRE, Solidity and Cloudflare Workers. A browser interface submits delivery evidence to a Worker API. SQLite-backed
  Durable Objects reserve the work order and budget, queue execution, and persist payment history.

  The CRE workflow registers handlerInTee. Inside that handler, it retrieves separate source and GitHub credentials, fetches the work-order record and live
  GitHub evidence, and checks the accepted commit, numeric repository and workflow identities, branch, trigger, successful completion and pinned workflow
  definition. These checks run alongside the commercial payment policy. Chainlink provides the workflow boundary for authenticated retrieval and confidential
  policy evaluation, making the resulting report the input to settlement.

  The workflow uses usingTheDons to return an ABI authorization without raw commercial terms. Our BatchTreasury contract checks its configured forwarder and
  workflow identity, request commitments, recipient, amount, token, chain and expiry before atomically consuming authorization and transferring ERC-20 test
  tokens.

  A VM runner executes actual CRE CLI simulations and feeds their report bytes into compiled Solidity running in EthereumJS. A notable implementation detail is
  the durable execution journal: it reconstructs each workspace’s local treasury from recorded operations, caches completed results and redelivers them until
  acknowledged. Uncertain executions retain their reservations, and recovery resumes the same job rather than opening another payment path.

  The project includes 58 unit tests, contract tests and deployed browser checks covering held and paid outcomes, concurrent reservations, reload recovery and
  duplicate protection. Local execution uses mock forwarding and does not establish deployed enclave attestation. Work-order uniqueness relies on the reservation
  service and journal; the contract independently prevents request replay.

  Codex generated the implementation, tests, interface and drafts. Lawrence selected the Chainlink focus, configured and authenticated the development
  environment, chose Velum’s identity and artistic direction, reviewed iterations and authorized the product direction.

projects.title: Sweem
projects.description: A yield router on Base that moves your money to the best venue without ever taking custody.
projects.project_description: The same dollar of USDC on Base earns a completely different rate depending on which contract happens to hold it, and the spread is neither small nor stable. A snapshot from our own mainnet subgraph, live as of writing, shows three Aave V3 markets on one chain paying 1.78 percent, 0.0002 percent and 0 percent. Nobody watches that. The two things you can do about it today are both bad: hand your money to a vault that takes custody and issues you a share token, or read a dashboard that tells you to go move the funds yourself. sweem is the third option. The money stays in your own wallet, and something else does the watching. A basket in sweem is a published weight configuration, not a pool. There is no vault, no share token, no NAV, and no redemption queue. When you subscribe to a basket, your own Privy embedded wallet starts following those weights. Each slice of your deposit is routed to the highest yielding venue for that asset, and it is moved again when the rates move. What you own is whatever your wallet holds, which is why our portfolio endpoint reconciles our database against on chain balances rather than treating the database as the truth. Two consequences follow from refusing custody, and they shape the entire system. First, the component that signs can only move funds, never hold them. Every destination in every transaction it builds is either a venue on a committed allowlist or the user's own address. The executor process has no wallet of its own. A withdrawal pays out to the owner and nowhere else. An approval targets the asset contract while a deposit targets the venue, so the two can never be confused. Second, there is no accounting to get wrong, which means the only way to be wrong is to be wrong about a number we read. So the system refuses to guess. A missing price feed, a stale Chainlink round or an unreachable node produces a null value and a stated reason, and the leg is skipped rather than routed. A supply APY of zero means "no trustworthy rate yet", never "this pays nothing, route here". A fabricated one dollar price misroutes money exactly as badly as a fabricated APY, and it does it silently. Roughly fifteen tests in this repo exist solely to enforce that distinction between unknown and zero. The user experience is four steps. Log in with an email, which creates a Privy embedded wallet. Grant a delegated signer with one click. Pick assets, either concrete instruments like USDC and wstETH or a family like ETH that sweem resolves to the best routable instrument at deposit time. Deposit USDC. From there the router does the work, and every allocation is shown before anything is signed. Revocation is one button and it is the feature we are proudest of. Removing the signer strips the app's ability to act, and the backend immediately reports the wallet as undelegated and returns a 412 naming the missing precondition on any attempt to execute. Granting delegation is a promise; being able to take it back in one click without asking us is the proof. What is actually proven on chain today: a full round trip on Base Sepolia, a five dollar USDC deposit routed into Aave V3 and then withdrawn back out, both transactions sent from the user's own embedded wallet at 0x0e5cC5C5c14e89a4DaFf87ea314C25EF37c8C08f and not from any wallet this service controls. A product you can enter and cannot leave is not a product, so closing that loop came before anything else. We are equally clear about what is not proven. The keeper that decides when to rebalance is built and unit tested, and it has never executed against a live position. Base mainnet is read only so far: 28 venues allowlisted, rates indexed, prices read, swap quotes taken against real pools, and zero transactions sent. That list lives in the README under a heading called "What is not done", and nothing in it is hidden elsewhere in the repo.
projects.how_its_made: The Sweem client talks to a Go wallet service, which is the only client of a Rust executor, which is the only thing that signs. A Go market data service answers "where is the best yield for asset X" from Redis. A Go keeper watches for drift and decides when to move, and it never signs anything, so it can be crashed, restarted or duplicated without putting funds at risk. Its decision is a trigger, not an authorization: the wallet service rechecks delegation, drift and every guard before it calls the executor. Postgres holds users, baskets, weights, subscriptions, positions and executions. Everything is fail closed at boot. The wallet service refuses to start if it cannot fetch its Privy verification key. The executor refuses to start on a missing, unparseable or empty allowlist. The keeper forces dry run without a shared secret. On The Graph, we wrote and deployed one subgraph that indexes Aave V3, Compound III and MetaMorpho from a single manifest on both Base mainnet and Base Sepolia, and normalizes all three into one Venue entity. The leverage claim is concrete: three protocols publish yield in three incompatible units and none of them is an APY. Aave publishes liquidityRate, a ray scaled 1e27 annual simple rate. Compound III publishes getSupplyRate(getUtilization()), a per second factor scaled 1e18 and not a per block one, which a careless reading would make roughly two times wrong on Base's two second blocks. MetaMorpho publishes nothing at all, so the rate has to be derived from ERC 4626 share price growth between two snapshots. All three land on the same compounding step, written as expm1(n times log1p(r)) rather than (1+r)^n, because at a per second r of about 1e-9 the addition in 1 + r discards most of r's significant digits in float64. The share price is scaled 1e36 rather than 1e18 because MetaMorpho shares carry a DECIMALS_OFFSET of 12 on USDC vaults, and 1e18 leaves about six significant digits and rounds an hour of yield away. mwETH has an offset of 0, which is how we learned the scale is not optional. We deliberately did this inside the subgraph mappings rather than in Go. In Go, comparability would be a property of our service, useful to us and to nobody else. In the mapping, the normalized schema is the artifact: anyone can query venues and get Aave, Compound and Morpho side by side, already compounded identically, without running a line of our code. A script pins the subgraph's rate math against the Go implementation so a divergence is a failing check rather than a wrong route. Two more Graph products are load bearing. The Token API answers what the wallet actually holds on Base, and the portfolio endpoint reconciles that against our own position rows; a position that disagrees reports reconciled false with a reason rather than being quietly trusted, and a position we cannot price reports a null value rather than a number. The decentralized network gateway serves third party subgraphs for protocols we do not index ourselves, such as Moonwell, and acts as a mainnet fallback while ours syncs. Deployed and live, not mocked: Base mainnet: https://api.studio.thegraph.com/query/1759980/sweem-base/v0.0.5 Base Sepolia: https://api.studio.thegraph.com/query/1759980/sweem-base-sepolia/v0.0.1 One deliberate and slightly hacky decision worth naming: mainnet data sources start at a recent block rather than at their deployment blocks, because we never query history. Aave's and Comet's rates are spot reads. Only two paths derive a rate from a series, and the start block is sized to about two and a half times the wider of them. Indexing from deployment meant scanning 49 million blocks to serve numbers that are identical either way. Making that safe required removing two discovery dependencies first, so we seed every Aave reserve from getReservesList in a once block handler and adopt the nine large pre existing MetaMorpho vaults by verified address rather than waiting for a factory event that fired ten million blocks ago. A fast sync that indexes nothing is worse than a slow one. Privy is the wallet layer, the auth layer and the signing layer, and there is no other key material in this system. The embedded wallet is created on login, every transaction is sent from it, and access tokens are verified as ES256 with the issuer and audience pinned. Privy has no JWKS endpoint, so the verification key is fetched once at boot over HTTP Basic and the service refuses to start without it. That key arrives as a single line SPKI PEM that Go's pem package will not parse, so we rewrap it at 64 characters. Delegation is the product. The user calls addSigners with a key quorum that wraps the executor's authorization public key, plus a policy id. From then on the executor can sign for that wallet, and only by producing a valid ECDSA P-256 signature over an RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization of the exact request. We implemented that from scratch in Rust, because the executor is not a Node process and no Rust SDK exists. Two details cost real time and are now pinned in tests: an empty object body canonicalizes to the empty string rather than to an empty object literal, and the signature is DER encoded standard base64 rather than raw r concatenated with s in base64url. We checked the implementation byte identical against the official Node SDK's own signature generator and committed those golden vectors, so a serialization regression fails cargo test instead of failing in production. The Privy policy is generated, not hand written. A Go command reads the same two allowlist files the executor reads and emits a policy that pins the callable addresses, the methods allowed per venue kind, the chain ids, and the rule that actually matters, which constrains approve.spender to allowlisted targets. An unconstrained approve is how funds genuinely leave a wallet. Native value transfers are denied outright. We measured enforcement rather than assuming it, using nine probes against a throwaway wallet with eth_signTransaction, which signs without broadcasting so nothing was spent: allowed calls signed, while an approve to an unlisted spender, a transfer to an unlisted address, a wrong chain id, a non zero value and personal_sign all came back as policy_violation. On Uniswap, a deposit into a non USDC asset becomes approve router, swap, approve venue, supply, with the user's own wallet as the swap recipient so the output never lands in a contract we control. We use SwapRouter02 and QuoterV2 on Base through alloy's sol macro. The contribution is two rules. First, a swap is never submitted without a live quote. amountOutMinimum is always the quoted amount times (10000 minus slippage bps) divided by 10000, never zero, and the caller's requested slippage is clamped server side to between 10 and 300 bps with a 50 bps default, so a caller cannot widen its own loss bound. An unreachable quoter fails the leg rather than submitting an unbounded trade. Second, the direct pools are a trap and nothing warns you. We measured price impact at two sizes before trusting any path. USDC to wstETH direct at the 500 tier fills at minus 3.23 percent on 100 dollars and minus 78.4 percent on 1000 dollars. USDC to cbETH direct at 3000 fills at minus 1.79 and minus 15.5 percent. Routed through WETH, the same trades cost minus 0.0003 and minus 0.0033 percent. Nothing in the contract interface distinguishes a deep pool from a nearly dead one at the same fee tier. The obvious, well typed, fully tested single hop function loses most of the user's money. So we shipped a static measured path allowlist rather than integrating a routing API: 40 paths covering 20 pairs, every one chosen by measurement, with no external dependency and no way to use a path we did not measure. Tokens that failed the bound on the exit leg, such as tBTC at minus 91 percent, stay unreachable rather than reachable at a loss, and a test asserts that every entry path has a matching exit with the tokens and fees exactly reversed. A hold venue you can enter and cannot leave is worse than no venue. That finding and three others, including the exactInput calldata offset, the QuoterV2 non view warning reading worse than it is, and sqrtPriceLimitX96 silently partial filling, are written up in FEEDBACK.md, written from the integration rather than after it. The executor is the security boundary. It is written in Rust, roughly 3,200 lines, with 77 tests that need no network to run. The single most important design decision in the codebase is that the destination address never comes from the request. The request names a venue id; the address is resolved from a committed local file. That makes the set of contracts a delegated signer can call independent of the request path, so a compromised caller, or a compromised indexer, cannot make the executor call an arbitrary contract. It is also why the allowlist is generated at build time and committed rather than fetched at runtime. That allowlist is generated by a Go command from the same indexed data the market data service serves, plus on chain verification. A venue is emitted only if it is encodable, meaning it maps to a venue kind the executor implements; priceable, meaning a verified Chainlink feed exists for the underlying on that chain; liquid, meaning it clears a TVL floor and a measured withdrawable liquidity floor; verified on chain via symbol, decimals and a protocol identity check such as getReservesList, baseToken, asset or isMToken; and exitable, meaning an allowlisted swap path back to USDC exists. Everything else is skipped with a printed reason. The result is 32 venues, 28 on Base mainnet and 4 on Base Sepolia, across five venue kinds. We deploy no contracts of our own; every address the system touches already existed. In the market data service, two sources feed one reconciler, split by what each protocol can actually publish. Spot rates come from direct eth_call, because getReserveData and getSupplyRate are the rate right now and need no indexing at all. Derived rates come from the subgraph, because a MetaMorpho vault's yield exists only as share price drift between two indexed snapshots. Each APY component is taken from whichever source can measure it: the base rate from RPC, rewards from the subgraph since COMP emissions need a price feed that does not exist on Base, and intrinsic staking yield from whichever has it. Where the two sources disagree on the base rate by more than 0.25 percentage points, the gap is logged with both numbers, which is how a repeat of the per block versus per second mistake would surface in one cycle rather than after a rebalance. The reason this matters is that a reverting call, a rate limited node, a frozen Aave reserve or a Comet whose symbol does not match our table must never become a rate of zero. Every one of them omits the venue with a logged reason. Zero would read as "this market pays nothing" and route money in exactly the wrong direction. One subtlety we got wrong first and then fixed: liquid staking tokens earn without any protocol interaction, because the exchange rate against the underlying simply rises. Aave pays about 0.1 percent on wstETH because nobody borrows it, so a real 3.1 percent position reads as 0.1 percent, and a naive keeper would helpfully improve the user out of it. We now read those intrinsic rates from the Chainlink exchange rate feeds that publish them on Base, since a feed keeps its past rounds on chain and the drift is therefore readable without indexing anything, and stack the intrinsic component onto every lending venue in that asset. Each provider is identified by calling description before its answer is used, because a market price also drifts and annualizing a market dip would invent yield outright, which is exactly why ezETH is excluded on Base. The keeper decides when to move. It is a pure decision function, fully unit tested, that runs guards cheapest first and then prices the actual economics. Already in the best venue, position below a floor, rate limited, inside a hysteresis window, drift below an absolute floor, and finally breakeven: the extra yield over an assumed holding period must beat the gas cost times a safety margin. Venues are ranked on reward discounted APY rather than the headline rate, because emissions are less durable than borrower paid interest. Nothing in the cost calculation is a configured guess. The gas price comes from eth_feeHistory over five blocks, taking the next base fee plus the median priority tip, because one outlier block should not reprice every user's decision. The ETH price comes from the Chainlink aggregator on Base, read on chain with no API key and no rate limit, with the decimals read rather than assumed and a stale round rejected outright. Gas units are measured from real Base transactions and pinned at the top of the observed range, since over pricing makes the keeper too cautious while under pricing makes it churn. If any input is missing or stale the pass is skipped and counted, never downgraded to a default, because a rebalance decided on fabricated cost data is worse than no rebalance. The keeper also owns the one thing nothing else resolves. When the executor's receipt poll times out, the transaction is probably in the mempool but we do not yet know whether the money moved, so the wallet service records the row as pending and deliberately withholds the position. The keeper sweeps those rows, fetches the receipt, and writes the position the wallet service withheld. It claims each row with a conditional update so only one instance can win, and writes the position with an upsert keyed exactly as the wallet service keys it, so running two keepers cannot double count. The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19 and the React compiler, Tailwind v4, hand rolled primitives rather than a component library, and Framer Motion with every animation guarded by a reduced motion check. The allocation view is a React Flow diagram showing wallet to asset to venue with live APYs. Settlement is the interesting part of the UI, because partial failure is a first class outcome rather than an error: a deposit of a three asset basket is three independent legs, so the API returns 207 Multi Status with a per leg result, and the toast reports "two of three legs settled" with the step by step trace and a Basescan link per leg. A pending leg says so explicitly and warns that retrying can send the same money twice. The amount field only clears on a clean settle. Numbers are rendered with tabular figures and four decimal places below one dollar, and anything unpriceable renders the words "value unknown" rather than a zero. None of this is demoable if it is wrong, so it is tested accordingly. The 77 Rust tests cover canonicalization against the vendor SDK's golden vectors, every ABI selector, the allowlist load invariants, and the property that every allowlisted non USDC venue must have a swap path back to USDC or it must not be allowlisted. The Go suites cover the APY conversions against hand computed values, the largest remainder allocator proving no cent leaks across awkward weight and amount combinations, the reconciler never fabricating a value under six distinct failure modes, the keeper's breakeven and hysteresis boundaries including the case where a clock skewed future timestamp must stay locked, and the sweeper's idempotency under a double run. A script pins the subgraph's rate math against the Go implementation, and a browser free assertion script pins the client's formatters and its split arithmetic. None of them need a network. What we would call the actual engineering here is not the feature list. It is that the system consistently refuses to convert "we could not measure this" into a number, and that the refusal is enforced by tests rather than by discipline. Every place a default would have been easier, there is a null and a reason instead.

A venue is emitted only if it is encodable, meaning it maps to a venue kind the executor implements; priceable, meaning a verified Chainlink feed exists for the underlying on that chain; liquid, meaning it clears a TVL floor and a measured withdrawable liquidity floor; verified on chain via symbol, decimals and a protocol identity check such as getReservesList, baseToken, asset or isMToken; and exitable, meaning an allowlisted swap path back to USDC exists. Everything else is skipped with a printed reason. The result is 32 venues, 28 on Base mainnet and 4 on Base Sepolia, across five venue kinds. We deploy no contracts of our own; every address the system touches already existed.

In the market data service, two sources feed one reconciler, split by what each protocol can actually publish. Spot rates come from direct eth_call, because getReserveData and getSupplyRate are the rate right now and need no indexing at all. Derived rates come from the subgraph, because a MetaMorpho vault's yield exists only as share price drift between two indexed snapshots. Each APY component is taken from whichever source can measure it: the base rate from RPC, rewards from the subgraph since COMP emissions need a price feed that does not exist on Base, and intrinsic staking yield from whichever has it. Where the two sources disagree on the base rate by more than 0.25 percentage points, the gap is logged with both numbers, which is how a repeat of the per block versus per second mistake would surface in one cycle rather than after a rebalance.

The reason this matters is that a reverting call, a rate limited node, a frozen Aave reserve or a Comet whose symbol does not match our table must never become a rate of zero. Every one of them omits the venue with a logged reason. Zero would read as "this market pays nothing" and route money in exactly the wrong direction.

One subtlety we got wrong first and then fixed: liquid staking tokens earn without any protocol interaction, because the exchange rate against the underlying simply rises. Aave pays about 0.1 percent on wstETH because nobody borrows it, so a real 3.1 percent position reads as 0.1 percent, and a naive keeper would helpfully improve the user out of it. We now read those intrinsic rates from the Chainlink exchange rate feeds that publish them on Base, since a feed keeps its past rounds on chain and the drift is therefore readable without indexing anything, and stack the intrinsic component onto every lending venue in that asset. Each provider is identified by calling description before its answer is used, because a market price also drifts and annualizing a market dip would invent yield outright, which is exactly why ezETH is excluded on Base.

The keeper decides when to move. It is a pure decision function, fully unit tested, that runs guards cheapest first and then prices the actual economics. Already in the best venue, position below a floor, rate limited, inside a hysteresis window, drift below an absolute floor, and finally breakeven: the extra yield over an assumed holding period must beat the gas cost times a safety margin. Venues are ranked on reward discounted APY rather than the headline rate, because emissions are less durable than borrower paid interest. Nothing in the cost calculation is a configured guess. The gas price comes from eth_feeHistory over five blocks, taking the next base fee plus the median priority tip, because one outlier block should not reprice every user's decision. The ETH price comes from the Chainlink aggregator on Base, read on chain with no API key and no rate limit, with the decimals read rather than assumed and a stale round rejected outright. Gas units are measured from real Base transactions and pinned at the top of the observed range, since over pricing makes the keeper too cautious while under pricing makes it churn. If any input is missing or stale the pass is skipped and counted, never downgraded to a default, because a rebalance decided on fabricated cost data is worse than no rebalance.

The keeper also owns the one thing nothing else resolves. When the executor's receipt poll times out, the transaction is probably in the mempool but we do not yet know whether the money moved, so the wallet service records the row as pending and deliberately withholds the position. The keeper sweeps those rows, fetches the receipt, and writes the position the wallet service withheld. It claims each row with a conditional update so only one instance can win, and writes the position with an upsert keyed exactly as the wallet service keys it, so running two keepers cannot double count.

The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19 and the React compiler, Tailwind v4, hand rolled primitives rather than a component library, and Framer Motion with every animation guarded by a reduced motion check. The allocation view is a React Flow diagram showing wallet to asset to venue with live APYs. Settlement is the interesting part of the UI, because partial failure is a first class outcome rather than an error: a deposit of a three asset basket is three independent legs, so the API returns 207 Multi Status with a per leg result, and the toast reports "two of three legs settled" with the step by step trace and a Basescan link per leg. A pending leg says so explicitly and warns that retrying can send the same money twice. The amount field only clears on a clean settle. Numbers are rendered with tabular figures and four decimal places below one dollar, and anything unpriceable renders the words "value unknown" rather than a zero.

None of this is demoable if it is wrong, so it is tested accordingly. The 77 Rust tests cover canonicalization against the vendor SDK's golden vectors, every ABI selector, the allowlist load invariants, and the property that every allowlisted non USDC venue must have a swap path back to USDC or it must not be allowlisted. The Go suites cover the APY conversions against hand computed values, the largest remainder allocator proving no cent leaks across awkward weight and amount combinations, the reconciler never fabricating a value under six distinct failure modes, the keeper's breakeven and hysteresis boundaries including the case where a clock skewed future timestamp must stay locked, and the sweeper's idempotency under a double run. A script pins the subgraph's rate math against the Go implementation, and a browser free assertion script pins the client's formatters and its split arithmetic. None of them need a network.

What we would call the actual engineering here is not the feature list. It is that the system consistently refuses to convert "we could not measure this" into a number, and that the refusal is enforced by tests rather than by discipline. Every place a default would have been easier, there is a null and a reason instead.

projects.title: Arbiter402
projects.description: Sub-second conditional micro-escrow & zero-hallucination adjudication for machine commerce.
projects.project_description:
Arbiter402 is an autonomous, sub-second conditional micro-escrow and deterministic ground-truth adjudication protocol built for the machine economy. While demonstrated on high-stakes DeFi indexing as its reference implementation, the protocol is fundamentally modular and generalizable to any verifiable machine-to-machine compute task. Why Human-in-the-Loop Fails for AI Agents:
Traditional escrow and human arbitration (e.g., Kleros, multi-sig signers) are completely infeasible for machine-to-machine commerce:
• Cost Inversion: AI agents execute micro-transactions ($0.05 - $1.00). Paying human jurors $10+ to review a $0.20 dispute is an immediate economic failure.
• Latency Destruction: Human dispute cycles take days or weeks. An autonomous agent making automated market actions needs settlement in seconds, not days.
• The LLM Trap: Using an LLM to judge another LLM introduces stochastic drift, hallucinations, and prompt injection. Machine commerce demands deterministic mathematical ground truth. How Arbiter402 Solves It:
• Sub-Second Micro-Escrow: Buyer agents lock micro-escrows into ArbiterEscrow.sol on Hedera EVM (~0.84s finality, ~$0.007 gas fee) via HTTP 402 and MCP tool-calling.
• Zero-Hallucination Adjudication: When deliverables are contested, our referee queries The Graph's decentralized indexing network to evaluate mathematical invariants (e.g., Uniswap v3 VWAP over verified block ranges) directly from raw onchain swap logs.
• ERC-8004 Machine Reputation: Lost disputes trigger atomic refunds and slash rogue agents by -50 points onchain, while honest completions award +5 points.
• Immutable HCS Audit Trail: Signed ECDSA audit proofs are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service for public verifiability on HashScan.
projects.how_its_made: Arbiter402 brings together Hedera EVM, Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), The Graph, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into a unified, hardened machine-commerce pipeline: • Hedera EVM Smart Contracts: We developed and deployed ArbiterEscrow.sol (0.0.10520281) and ERC8004ReputationRegistry.sol (0.0.10520278) on Hedera Testnet (Chain ID 296), both 100% verified on Sourcify with Exact Match. Hedera's ~0.84s finality and fixed sub-cent fees enable high-frequency micro-escrow transactions that are cost-prohibitive on L1. • Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Every dispute adjudication generates a tamper-proof audit payload containing the job specification hash, deliverable hash, ground-truth value, error delta, and the referee's ECDSA signature, permanently anchored to HCS Topic 0.0.10520952 with nanosecond consensus timestamps and stored in the contract's auditLogUri. • The Graph Decentralized Oracle: To eliminate subjective LLM arbitration, our referee queries The Graph’s decentralized network for raw Uniswap v3 swap events (amount0, amount1, sqrtPriceX96). It deterministically computes the true Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) across the requested block window to evaluate deviations against basis-point contract tolerances. • Bazantic MCP Recipe & HTTP 402: Built with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, our recipe server exposes standardized tools (adjudicate_escrow_dispute, verify_agent_reputation) allowing autonomous agents in Claude, Cursor, and LangChain to negotiate escrows and trigger dispute settlements natively over standardized HTTP 402 headers. • Security Hardening: We engineered a cryptographic deliverable substitution defense (pre-flight checks ensure payloads match onchain keccak256 hashes), push-to-pull fallback queues (pendingWithdrawals) that immunize against denial-of-service reverts, and liveness safety valves for uncontested claims and expired deadlines.

projects.title: Intentra
projects.description: Intentra finds the right human. USDC escrow makes sure they get paid.
projects.project_description:
Intentra is a decentralized service marketplace , framed as an "AI Commerce Protocol." Here's how it works: AI-driven matching – you describe what you need and your budget, and an AI parses your intent to find a matching service provider, with the arrangement secured by EIP-712 cryptographic mandates (structured, signed data commitments).
Human verification – providers must prove they're real humans (not bots) using World ID's "World Selfie Check," aiming to eliminate scams and fake accounts.
Escrowed payments
funds are held in USDC via a smart contract escrow on the Arc testnet, only releasing to the provider once the job is completed and approved by the client. In short, it's a trust layer for hiring freelancers/service providers where an AI agent handles the negotiation/matching, identity is verified cryptographically, and payment is escrowed on-chain until work is confirmed done.
projects.how_its_made:
The backend is a FastAPI modular monolith, organised domain-per-package rather than
by layer: intents, providers, transactions, authorization, payments, fulfillment,
evidence, disputes, identity and audit each own their router, models, schemas and
service. Boundaries are not a convention here, they are CI — 14 import-linter
contracts fail the build if a domain touches another domain's tables, if the shared
kernel imports a domain, if an adapter reaches back inward, or if pure rule code
(money, hashing, state machine, policy) imports FastAPI, SQLAlchemy or web3. The one
deliberate exception is the Transaction aggregate root, and a test walks the source
tree to prove the state machine is its only writer. SQLModel/SQLAlchemy async over asyncpg, Alembic migrations, 20 tables. Three worker
loops (chain watcher, transaction outbox, reconciliation) run in-process, guarded by
a Postgres advisory lock so only one instance is leader and the same code scales to
several replicas untouched. 572 tests. ON-CHAIN IntentraEscrow is Solidity on Arc testnet (chain 5042002), built with Foundry. Two
rules drive the whole design: money states commit only on confirmed chain events,
never on an optimistic write, and settlement needs two distinct signatures from
{customer, provider, AI arbitrator}. The watcher reads eth_getLogs from the escrow's
deploy block, advances a cursor only after every log in a range is handled, and keys
events on (tx_hash, log_index) so a replay after a crash is a no-op. Outbound calls
go through an outbox: rows are claimed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, the
transaction hash is committed to the database before we wait for a receipt, and one
lock serialises the resolver's nonce. PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES Arc — escrow and settlement in USDC, with gas paid in USDC too, which removes the
"buy the native token first" step that kills onboarding for the Nigerian users this
targets. Deterministic finality let us run the watcher at 1 confirmation. Privy — email login to an embedded wallet, so a customer signs an EIP-712 mandate
without ever seeing a seed phrase; also signTypedData and sendTransaction for the
escrow calls. Access tokens are ES256-verified server-side against the app's
verification key. World — Selfie Check proof-of-human gates authorisation and complaint, the two
places fraud pays. One nullifier per action per transaction, so a proof cannot be
replayed onto another job. The Graph — a subgraph over the escrow's own events turns completed, disputed and
refunded jobs into provider trust scores, so reputation comes from chain history
rather than rows we could edit.
