For auditability, every decision — allowed, rejected, or dry-run — is serialized to JSON and submitted to a dedicated HCS topic. If no topic ID is configured, the app auto-creates one on first run, making deployment frictionless. I used dotenvx for encrypted secret management and built the entire flow as a single-file demo (demo.js) that runs three scenarios end-to-end in under 10 seconds.
The hacky part: I treated the compliance policy as a pre-flight middleware rather than a post-transfer filter. This means non-compliant transactions cost exactly zero HBAR — they never touch the network — while still producing an immutable HCS audit trail of the attempt. This pattern could plug directly into custodian wallets or payment rails that need provable compliance without wasting gas on rejected transactions.

projects.title: AgenIPO
projects.description: Startup fundraising where the investor is an AI agent bound by a human mandate
projects.project_description:
AgentIPO is a fundraising platform where the investor is an AI agent, not a person. We are trying to solve two problems at the same time: Founders get funding from verified investors Investors can run their own AI agent that analyzes and verifies data (onchain & offchain), with the ability to close deals autonomously. How does this work: A founder lists a startup with links, contracts, token, and all data they think is important, such as MRR, DAU, growth, etc. They can gate it and send it upon request from an agent Investor run their own AI agent, based on their investing rules - thesis, sectors, minimum
diligence score, max ticket, per-round share, daily budget, risk tolerance. Agent working in the background and does the research for every new startup on the platform, then shows investors good matches. It has two modes: fully autonomous, where the agent tries to send money ASAP, and human-in-the-loop, where investors can review data themselves and proceed with investing.
projects.how_its_made:
pnpm monorepo: NestJS 11 API, Next.js 16 dashboard, a zod contract package shared by
both, and Foundry contracts. Every module is ports & adapters, every source file is
capped at 100 lines by ESLint and a CI script, and the domain layer — evaluators,
mandate gate, spending policy, approval policy, growth math is framework-free pure
functions with Vitest specs. The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative: agents cannot decide without it. Three Graph
products compose in one pipeline — the Token API for holders, top-10 concentration,
30-day transfers and treasury stables; a Messari standardized DEX subgraph so one query
works against any DEX by swapping the subgraph id; and the Agent0 / ERC-8004 subgraph,
whose reputation for the agent's own identity is fed back into its decision prompt.
Every signal carries a provenance badge in the UI, and fixtures are labelled as
fixtures rather than passed off as live. Arc is where money moves. RoundEscrow.sol (Solidity 0.8.24, 52 Foundry tests) is a
milestone escrow settled in USDC — which on Arc is the native gas token, so the same
asset pays fees and fills the round. createRound sells equityBps; invest is
target-or-refund; releaseMilestone pays tranches; settleExit(kind, valuation,
proceeds, evidenceUri) pays a liquidity event into the claim pool, callable only by the
platform or the round's founder. Claims are floored per investor so the sum can never
exceed the pool. Agents hold their own wallets — HD-derived from one mnemonic, or
Circle developer-controlled wallets on ARC-TESTNET behind the same SettlementRail port. Hedera carries the audit trail: data access requested and granted, decision made,
approval, settlement, exit, claim — each written to an HCS topic with sequence numbers.
Agents also get their own Hedera accounts and ERC-8004 identities. Two decisions worth naming. First, we removed our own x402 paywall on the diligence
report. Charging agents to read public on-chain evidence is the wrong product, and it
broke every run without Hedera keys; x402 survives as an opt-in flag
(X402_GATE_REPORTS), with the real scarcity moved where it belongs — the founder's
private numbers, gated by the founder and opened per agent. Second, missing data is
never zero: a withheld metric, an unreadable index and a single reading with no
trajectory all land as "unknown", which lowers the report's data coverage instead of
inventing a score. The mandate gate then refuses low-coverage rounds before any LLM
call or any signature. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Prisma's engine binaries were blocked by our network, so
the whole app runs on Prisma 7 with the Rust-free @prisma/adapter-pg and hand-written,
transaction-safe migrations. For offline development and for the hosted demo we run a
local Arc stand-in — anvil on Arc's chain id with MockUSDC injected at Arc's native
USDC address — so the entire escrow lifecycle, including exits and claims, executes as
real EVM transactions with no testnet funds. Sign-in is Privy, and when no Privy app is
configured the same screens run on a local session that is labelled "demo" in the nav,
on the sign-in step and in the stored account record, so a screenshot can never imply a
verified login.

projects.title: ETH Arcade
projects.description: Trading was boring. So we built a handheld arcade where ETH price becomes the game, plus an SDK.
projects.project_description: ETH Arcade is an open-source handheld console and SDK for games powered by live financial markets. It turns the ETH price chart into something you can physically interact with: a screen, a rotary knob, two buttons, and a speaker, all housed in a custom enclosure powered by a Raspberry Pi. Our first game is Box Run . The player turns the knob to position a box on the price chart and presses a button to commit a stake. Each round lasts ten seconds. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, the player scores a hit and receives the corresponding payout; otherwise, the stake is lost. The market supplies the movement, making every round different. We built ETH Arcade to explore what happens when interacting with crypto becomes tactile, playful, and social. Instead of watching charts across multiple monitors, players can pick up a handheld, learn the controls, and pass it to a friend. Three integrations power the experience: The Graph supplies the live market data. We compose Uniswap v3 and v4 Substreams packages into a reusable price pipeline that runs across Arbitrum and Base. Standardized subgraph queries discover supported liquidity pools, while the price consumer filters outliers and calculates a liquidity-weighted ETH price. This connects actual onchain trading activity to gameplay. Circle’s Arc provides USDC session settlement. On Arc testnet, players fund a session with USDC. An escrow contract locks the player’s funds alongside a house reserve, and cashing out settles the final session balance back to the player. Gameplay rounds run offchain, keeping the controls responsive, while session funding and settlement happen onchain. Gas is also paid in USDC. The designated device reports the final balance; the contract enforces authorization, payout limits, and refund conditions. ENSv2 provides player identity and the leaderboard. On Sepolia, players receive wallet-owned subnames under tick.eth . ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control separates profile permissions from score permissions: players can update their profiles, while a scorekeeper updates designated statistics after observing settled sessions on Arc. The handheld reads names and statistics from ENS records to construct the leaderboard, without a separate leaderboard database. ETH Arcade also includes a Python SDK that packages reusable components for price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can scaffold a game and build their own market-driven experiences using these building blocks. Box Run demonstrates the concept; the SDK makes it extensible. The website brings everything together with an interactive 3D hardware walkthrough, a playable browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, integration explanations, source links, and our launch video. The browser demo uses simulated prices and paper balances; the integrated onchain flow currently uses testnets. ETH Arcade combines hardware, live blockchain data, stablecoin settlement, and programmable identity into a working arcade experience—and opens the tools for others to build what comes next.
projects.how_its_made: We built ETH Arcade from the hardware up. We wanted to take a live ETH chart off a trading dashboard and put it into something you could hold, play, and pass to a friend. That meant building a physical console alongside the game, contracts, data pipeline, and SDK. Building the handheld We borrowed a friend’s 3D printer to make the enclosure. That was a very hands-on part of the project: translating a digital design into a shell that had to fit the electronics, expose the controls, and feel comfortable to use. Inside is a Raspberry Pi Zero W connected to a 3.5-inch 480×320 display, a rotary encoder, two buttons, and a rear speaker. The hardware design also includes a lithium-ion battery and charging circuit. We had to account for mounting points, component clearances, display connections, and space for wiring—not just how the outside looked. The controls shaped the game itself. Turning the knob positions a box on the price chart; pressing a button commits the stake. We wanted the interaction to be understandable through your hands, with sound and immediate visual feedback making each action feel like an arcade input. Firmware and game software The Python firmware brings together rendering, physical inputs, sound, networking, and the different screens: funding, gameplay, cash-out, receipts, and the leaderboard. Our first game, Box Run, uses ten-second rounds. Players position a price interval and commit a stake. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, they receive the corresponding payout; otherwise, they lose the stake. A key architectural decision was keeping the game loop local. Individual rounds do not wait for blockchain transactions. Funding and settlement happen at session boundaries, so the controls stay responsive while the money flow remains connected to onchain contracts. The Graph: making the market move the game We compose Pinax’s Uniswap v3 and Uniswap v4 Substreams packages into a custom map_pool_prices module. This reuses existing event decoding and produces a common representation of pool price, liquidity, and block time. The same compiled module runs on Arbitrum and Base with different pool configurations. We also use a shared Messari standardized DEX subgraph query to discover pool metadata for supported Uniswap v3 and SushiSwap v3 deployments. A relay sends live updates to the price consumer, which rejects outliers more than 0.5% from the weighted median and calculates a liquidity-weighted aggregate. This helps keep one thin or stale pool from dominating a round. The Graph is effectively the connection between onchain trading activity and what moves across the handheld’s screen. Circle and Arc: replacing arcade coins with USDC We wrote a Solidity escrow contract, TickEscrow , and deployed it to Arc testnet. The player funds the device with USDC, and the device opens an escrow session in the player’s name after retaining a configured gas allowance. The contract locks the session funds alongside a house reserve. Rounds execute offchain. At cash-out, the device submits the final balance and the contract settles to the recorded player address. The contract enforces authorization, payout limits, reserve constraints, and a timeout-based reclaim path. Arc lets us use USDC for both session balances and gas. The device is trusted to report the final session balance; the contract does not independently verify every gameplay round. ENSv2: an arcade identity that holds your score On Sepolia, we deployed an ENSv2 UserRegistry under tick.eth and a shared PermissionedResolver through ENS’s VerifiableFactory . Players receive wallet-owned subnames. Enhanced Access Control separates permissions: players can edit their profile records, while the scorekeeper can update seven designated tick.* statistics records. A deterministic Python scorekeeper watches settled sessions on Arc and writes the resulting statistics to ENS. The handheld discovers registered names and resolves their records through the Universal Resolver to construct the standings. One particularly unusual choice is that the leaderboard has no separate application database. ENS stores the player statistics, including a reference to the latest Arc settlement, connecting the payment flow to the player’s arcade identity. Making the hardware reusable through an SDK We packaged reusable game infrastructure into a Python SDK: price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can start with tick new mygame and build their own market-driven games. The goal is for someone else to spend their time designing a game rather than rebuilding the connection between a knob, a price feed, a wallet, and a leaderboard. The website uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber to show the hardware through an interactive 3D walkthrough. It also includes a simulated browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, and our launch video. Firebase Hosting serves the website, and Firestore stores email signups. The most memorable part of building ETH Arcade was bringing all those layers into one physical object: borrowing a friend’s printer, fitting electronics into a custom shell, wiring real controls, and making a live market respond on a tiny screen.
projects.project_description_markdown:
ETH Arcade is an open-source handheld console and SDK for games powered by live financial markets. It turns the ETH price chart into something you can physically interact with: a screen, a rotary knob, two buttons, and a speaker, all housed in a custom enclosure powered by a Raspberry Pi.

Our first game is **Box Run**. The player turns the knob to position a box on the price chart and presses a button to commit a stake. Each round lasts ten seconds. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, the player scores a hit and receives the corresponding payout; otherwise, the stake is lost. The market supplies the movement, making every round different.

We built ETH Arcade to explore what happens when interacting with crypto becomes tactile, playful, and social. Instead of watching charts across multiple monitors, players can pick up a handheld, learn the controls, and pass it to a friend.

Three integrations power the experience:

**The Graph supplies the live market data.** We compose Uniswap v3 and v4 Substreams packages into a reusable price pipeline that runs across Arbitrum and Base. Standardized subgraph queries discover supported liquidity pools, while the price consumer filters outliers and calculates a liquidity-weighted ETH price. This connects actual onchain trading activity to gameplay.

**Circle’s Arc provides USDC session settlement.** On Arc testnet, players fund a session with USDC. An escrow contract locks the player’s funds alongside a house reserve, and cashing out settles the final session balance back to the player. Gameplay rounds run offchain, keeping the controls responsive, while session funding and settlement happen onchain. Gas is also paid in USDC. The designated device reports the final balance; the contract enforces authorization, payout limits, and refund conditions.

**ENSv2 provides player identity and the leaderboard.** On Sepolia, players receive wallet-owned subnames under `tick.eth`. ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control separates profile permissions from score permissions: players can update their profiles, while a scorekeeper updates designated statistics after observing settled sessions on Arc. The handheld reads names and statistics from ENS records to construct the leaderboard, without a separate leaderboard database.

ETH Arcade also includes a **Python SDK** that packages reusable components for price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can scaffold a game and build their own market-driven experiences using these building blocks. Box Run demonstrates the concept; the SDK makes it extensible.

The website brings everything together with an interactive 3D hardware walkthrough, a playable browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, integration explanations, source links, and our launch video. The browser demo uses simulated prices and paper balances; the integrated onchain flow currently uses testnets.

ETH Arcade combines hardware, live blockchain data, stablecoin settlement, and programmable identity into a working arcade experience—and opens the tools for others to build what comes next.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built ETH Arcade from the hardware up. We wanted to take a live ETH chart off a trading dashboard and put it into something you could hold, play, and pass to a friend. That meant building a physical console alongside the game, contracts, data pipeline, and SDK.

**Building the handheld**

We borrowed a friend’s 3D printer to make the enclosure. That was a very hands-on part of the project: translating a digital design into a shell that had to fit the electronics, expose the controls, and feel comfortable to use.

Inside is a Raspberry Pi Zero W connected to a 3.5-inch 480×320 display, a rotary encoder, two buttons, and a rear speaker. The hardware design also includes a lithium-ion battery and charging circuit. We had to account for mounting points, component clearances, display connections, and space for wiring—not just how the outside looked.

The controls shaped the game itself. Turning the knob positions a box on the price chart; pressing a button commits the stake. We wanted the interaction to be understandable through your hands, with sound and immediate visual feedback making each action feel like an arcade input.

**Firmware and game software**

The Python firmware brings together rendering, physical inputs, sound, networking, and the different screens: funding, gameplay, cash-out, receipts, and the leaderboard.

Our first game, Box Run, uses ten-second rounds. Players position a price interval and commit a stake. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, they receive the corresponding payout; otherwise, they lose the stake.

A key architectural decision was keeping the game loop local. Individual rounds do not wait for blockchain transactions. Funding and settlement happen at session boundaries, so the controls stay responsive while the money flow remains connected to onchain contracts.

**The Graph: making the market move the game**

We compose Pinax’s Uniswap v3 and Uniswap v4 Substreams packages into a custom `map_pool_prices` module. This reuses existing event decoding and produces a common representation of pool price, liquidity, and block time.

The same compiled module runs on Arbitrum and Base with different pool configurations. We also use a shared Messari standardized DEX subgraph query to discover pool metadata for supported Uniswap v3 and SushiSwap v3 deployments.

A relay sends live updates to the price consumer, which rejects outliers more than 0.5% from the weighted median and calculates a liquidity-weighted aggregate. This helps keep one thin or stale pool from dominating a round. The Graph is effectively the connection between onchain trading activity and what moves across the handheld’s screen.

**Circle and Arc: replacing arcade coins with USDC**

We wrote a Solidity escrow contract, `TickEscrow`, and deployed it to Arc testnet. The player funds the device with USDC, and the device opens an escrow session in the player’s name after retaining a configured gas allowance. The contract locks the session funds alongside a house reserve.

Rounds execute offchain. At cash-out, the device submits the final balance and the contract settles to the recorded player address. The contract enforces authorization, payout limits, reserve constraints, and a timeout-based reclaim path.

Arc lets us use USDC for both session balances and gas. The device is trusted to report the final session balance; the contract does not independently verify every gameplay round.

**ENSv2: an arcade identity that holds your score**

On Sepolia, we deployed an ENSv2 `UserRegistry` under `tick.eth` and a shared `PermissionedResolver` through ENS’s `VerifiableFactory`.

Players receive wallet-owned subnames. Enhanced Access Control separates permissions: players can edit their profile records, while the scorekeeper can update seven designated `tick.*` statistics records.

A deterministic Python scorekeeper watches settled sessions on Arc and writes the resulting statistics to ENS. The handheld discovers registered names and resolves their records through the Universal Resolver to construct the standings.

One particularly unusual choice is that the leaderboard has no separate application database. ENS stores the player statistics, including a reference to the latest Arc settlement, connecting the payment flow to the player’s arcade identity.

**Making the hardware reusable through an SDK**

We packaged reusable game infrastructure into a Python SDK: price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can start with `tick new mygame` and build their own market-driven games.

The goal is for someone else to spend their time designing a game rather than rebuilding the connection between a knob, a price feed, a wallet, and a leaderboard.

The website uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber to show the hardware through an interactive 3D walkthrough. It also includes a simulated browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, and our launch video. Firebase Hosting serves the website, and Firestore stores email signups.

The most memorable part of building ETH Arcade was bringing all those layers into one physical object: borrowing a friend’s printer, fitting electronics into a custom shell, wiring real controls, and making a live market respond on a tiny screen.

projects.title: Alive402
projects.description: One selfie-verified AI trial. Then agents pay per call on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Alive402 makes AI free trials fair and turns the moment after a trial into a native agent-payment flow. AI APIs commonly offer free credits, but email addresses, browser cookies, and wallet addresses are easy to rotate. Alive402 gives a person one promotional API call after they complete World Selfie Check. The backend verifies the World proof, uses its scoped nullifier as a privacy-preserving continuity signal, and atomically records the entitlement for that provider campaign. The next request reaches the same protected inference endpoint and receives a real HTTP 402 Payment Required response. A budgeted agent reads the x402 payment requirements, pays 0.001 test USDC on Hedera through Blocky402, retries the original request, and unlocks the AI response. The app then shows the execution receipt and Hedera transaction. The result is a reusable access pattern for AI inference, data APIs, developer tools, and other metered HTTP services: let a real person try once, then let humans or agents pay per request without subscriptions or API keys.
projects.how_its_made: Alive402 is built with TanStack Start, React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind. The application uses Supabase Postgres for persistent provider campaigns, World enrollment records, one-time proof-signal hashes, opaque server sessions, access decisions, and sanitized payment receipts. For World, we use the IDKit Selfie Check legacy preset. The browser never receives the RP signing key. Instead, the server creates a short-lived random signal, stores only its hash, signs the RP context server-side, and sends the completed IDKit result unchanged to World’s backend verification API. After verification, Alive402 normalizes the scoped nullifier and grants one promotional entitlement per provider campaign. Selfie images are never stored. For paid access, the protected OpenRouter inference endpoint uses x402 v2 with canonical PAYMENT-REQUIRED, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, and PAYMENT-RESPONSE headers. We use @x402/core, @x402/hedera, @x402/fetch, and the Blocky402 facilitator to build, verify, and settle an exact payment in test USDC on Hedera Testnet. The demo agent is server-side and constrained to one network, one USDC asset, one merchant account, a maximum payment amount, and a daily spend limit. A HashScan-linked receipt proves the settlement. Vercel hosts the application and Vercel Analytics measures real product traffic.

projects.title: Xenia
projects.description: Slashable-stake trust for AI agents: ENS identity, Graph standing, Hedera x402 pay-per-check.
projects.project_description: Xenia is slashable-stake infrastructure for AI agents, named after Greek guest-friendship. Agents register as *.xenia.eth (ENS namehash on Sepolia). A host locks ETH behind an agent and sets a premium; the agent pays that trust fee to keep coverage live. If the agent defaults, stake can be slashed to the victim after a dispute window. The Graph indexes registry events into standing scores (premiums up, defaults/slashes down). Hedera is not the stake ledger — it meters API access: POST /xenia/check returns HTTP 402 until ~0.001 HBAR settles via x402/Blocky402, then returns standing. Live demo theater runs mint → stake → premium → default → slash → Pay HBAR → decide (transact vs refuse).
projects.how_its_made: Xenia is a pnpm monorepo: Foundry Solidity for XeniaRegistry on Sepolia; Next.js + wagmi/viem/RainbowKit for apps/web and the CRT-style apps/demo theater; Fastify for apps/api; AssemblyScript subgraph; optional MCP standing tool. ENS gives each agent a *.xenia.eth handle. Registration stores the namehash on-chain; scripts set backing text records (xenia.host, stake, premium) and demo host-only EAC so non-hosts can’t rewrite trust metadata. The Graph indexes registry events into standing: clamp(50 + 10×premiums − 25×defaults − 40×slashes). Product UI and the demo Decide step read Studio GraphQL — not raw RPC — so scores stay queryable after slash. Hedera is only for API metering. Stake never leaves Sepolia. POST /xenia/check returns HTTP 402; the client signs an exact HBAR transfer with @x402/hedera, Blocky402 settles ~0.001 HBAR, then standing is returned. Demo Run requires pnpm dev:api after the slash path. The demo orchestrator mints fresh agent wallets each Run, funds them from a host key, and streams NDJSON over SSE into the theater. Notable hack: payer ≠ payTo (self-transfer nets to 0 under x402), so we auto-provision a distinct testnet payer and cache it; Decide also polls the subgraph so A’s ~60 isn’t race-zeroed like B’s post-slash 0.

Xenia is a pnpm monorepo: Foundry Solidity for XeniaRegistry on Sepolia; Next.js + wagmi/viem/RainbowKit for apps/web and the CRT-style apps/demo theater; Fastify for apps/api; AssemblyScript subgraph; optional MCP standing tool.

ENS gives each agent a *.xenia.eth handle. Registration stores the namehash on-chain; scripts set backing text records (xenia.host, stake, premium) and demo host-only EAC so non-hosts can’t rewrite trust metadata.

The Graph indexes registry events into standing: clamp(50 + 10×premiums − 25×defaults − 40×slashes). Product UI and the demo Decide step read Studio GraphQL — not raw RPC — so scores stay queryable after slash.

Hedera is only for API metering. Stake never leaves Sepolia. POST /xenia/check returns HTTP 402; the client signs an exact HBAR transfer with @x402/hedera, Blocky402 settles ~0.001 HBAR, then standing is returned. Demo Run requires pnpm dev:api after the slash path.

The demo orchestrator mints fresh agent wallets each Run, funds them from a host key, and streams NDJSON over SSE into the theater. Notable hack: payer ≠ payTo (self-transfer nets to 0 under x402), so we auto-provision a distinct testnet payer and cache it; Decide also polls the subgraph so A’s ~60 isn’t race-zeroed like B’s post-slash 0.

projects.title: DeFi-Risk-Sentinel
projects.description: AI-powered DeFi liquidation risk monitor for Aave V3 on Ethereum
projects.project_description:
Detailed Description
What It Does
The Sentinel continuously monitors DeFi lending positions on the Aave V3 protocol (Ethereum mainnet) and answers one critical question: "How close is this wallet to liquidation?" It fetches real user reserve data — collateral balances (aTokens), stable/variable debt, per-asset liquidation thresholds, and oracle prices — directly from a live The Graph subgraph via GraphQL. No mocks, no hardcoded data. Every number originates from on-chain state. How It Works Data Layer (src/data/)
graphClient.js
— A GraphQL transport client that queries The Graph's decentralized gateway (gateway.thegraph.com), with built-in retries and rate limiting.
aaveQueries.js
— Aave V3-specific GraphQL queries to fetch user reserves, price oracles, and active users. Parses raw subgraph responses into a normalized position format. Risk Engine (src/engine/)
riskEngine.js
— Core computation module. Calculates the health factor using the formula: Health Factor = Σ(collateral_i × price_i × liquidationThreshold_i) / Σ(debt_j × price_j)
Classifies positions into three risk tiers: Level	Health Factor	Meaning
🔴 DANGER	< 1.05	Imminent liquidation
🟡 WATCH	< 1.20	Elevated risk
🟢 SAFE	≥ 1.20	Healthy
Also identifies the weakest collateral (the asset whose price drop has the largest marginal impact on health factor) and the largest debt position. scenarios.js
— Scenario simulation engine. Can: Simulate arbitrary price changes and recompute health factors
Analytically solve the exact liquidation price for any collateral asset (not just brute-force search)
Run multi-drop stress tests (e.g. 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50% simultaneous crashes)
Handle correlated assets via aliases (WETH/stETH/cbETH all track ETH; USDC/USDT/DAI all track USD)
3. AI Reasoning Layer (src/reasoning/)
nlGenerator.js
— Generates rich, natural-language risk reports from computed data. Not template-filling — produces context-aware narratives explaining why a position is risky, what the weakest link is, and what actions to take. Supports an optional OpenAI GPT-4 integration for even deeper analysis and a conversational Q&A interface.
4. Alerting System (src/alerts/)
poller.js
— Configurable polling loop (default 60s) that re-fetches positions and detects when a wallet transitions from SAFE/WATCH into DANGER.
webhook.js
— Sends alerts to Discord, Slack, or any generic webhook endpoint.
5. Interfaces
REST API (
api.js
) — 12 endpoints covering health checks, watchlist CRUD, risk assessments, simulation, stress testing, and natural-language queries.
Web Dashboard (
public/
) — Premium dark-themed glassmorphic UI with animated backgrounds, real-time risk tables, an AI chat panel, per-wallet stress test controls, and auto-refresh.
CLI (
cli.js
) — Interactive terminal interface for all features.
Tech Stack
Component	Technology
Runtime	Node.js 18+ (ES Modules)
Data Source	The Graph (Aave V3 Ethereum Subgraph, decentralized network)
Server	Express.js
HTTP Client	node-fetch
AI (optional)	OpenAI GPT-4 for enhanced NL reasoning
Frontend	Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS (glassmorphic dark theme)
Agent Integration	MCP config + SKILL.md for AI agent compatibility
Key Design Decisions
Protocol-agnostic engine: Only src/data/aaveQueries.js is Aave-specific. The risk engine, simulation, reasoning, and alerting layers operate on a normalized position format — swapping to Compound, Morpho, or any lending protocol only requires a new data adapter.
No mocks: Every data point is fetched live from Ethereum mainnet via The Graph. The app works against real positions with real risk.
Analytical liquidation solving: Instead of binary search, the scenarios module solves the liquidation price algebraically for O(1) precision.
Graceful AI degradation: Works fully without an OpenAI key (rule-based NL generation), but produces richer output when one is configured.
projects.how_its_made: We built the Sentinel as a from-scratch Node.js (ES Modules) application with a clean five-layer architecture: Data → Engine → Reasoning → Alerts → Interface. Each layer only depends on the one below it, making the whole system protocol-swappable — only one file knows anything about Aave. The Graph (Partner Technology) is the backbone. Every number in the app — collateral balances, debt amounts, liquidation thresholds, oracle prices — comes from live GraphQL queries to the Aave V3 Ethereum subgraph (GQFbb95cE6d8mV989mL5figjaGaKCQB3xqYrr1bRyXqF) on The Graph's decentralized gateway. No RPC calls, no mocked data, no indexing infrastructure of our own. We fire two parallel GraphQL queries per wallet: one for userReserves (positions, collateral flags, reserve config) and one for priceOracles (live USD pricing). The Graph handles the heavy lifting of indexing Ethereum's state into a queryable schema — without it, we'd need our own indexer, archive node, and weeks of setup. We also ship an mcp_config.json for @thegraph/subgraph-mcp, so AI agents can query the same subgraph through the Model Context Protocol. The trickiest engineering problems: Parsing Aave V3's on-chain encoding. Balances come as raw BigInt strings scaled by token decimals (6 for USDC, 18 for WETH, 8 for WBTC). Liquidation thresholds are basis points (8250 = 82.5%). Rates use ray precision (1e27). Prices use a double-indirection: a priceInEth field scaled by 1e18, plus a separate usdPriceEth oracle value you invert and multiply. We wrote a parseTokenAmount() function using JavaScript BigInt to split integer and fractional parts without floating-point loss, and a multi-fallback pricing pipeline that tries the USD oracle first, then falls back to priceInEth × ethPrice. Analytical liquidation price solving. Instead of binary-searching for the price drop that pushes health factor to 1.0 (which is what most tools do), we derived a closed-form solution: dropFraction = 1 - (totalDebt - effectiveOther) / (balance × price × LT). This gives O(1) exact answers and lets us compute liquidation prices for every asset in every wallet on every poll cycle without blowing up compute. Correlated asset aliasing in simulations. When a user asks "what if ETH drops 20%", we need WETH, stETH, wstETH, cbETH, and rETH to all move together — they're the same underlying exposure. We built an alias map that groups synthetic/wrapped variants under their base asset (ETH, BTC, USD), so one simulation input cascades correctly through the whole portfolio. Graceful AI degradation. The NL reasoning layer works in two modes. Without an OpenAI key, it uses a rule-based engine that pattern-matches user questions with regex (price drop queries, stress test requests, wallet lookups, portfolio summaries) and generates reports by computing real numbers — collateral shares, repayment amounts to reach target HF, margin-to-liquidation percentages. With an OpenAI key, it injects the full position dataset into GPT-4o-mini's context as a system prompt and lets the LLM reason over actual numbers. If the LLM call fails, it silently falls back to rule-based. Zero-config, always works. Tech stack: Node.js 18+, Express for the REST API (12 endpoints), vanilla HTML/CSS/JS for the frontend (glassmorphic dark theme, animated gradient background, custom markdown-to-HTML renderer for the chat panel), node-fetch for HTTP, dotenv for config. Four total dependencies. The frontend auto-refreshes every 60 seconds, the backend polls The Graph on a configurable interval, and the alerting layer detects risk-level transitions (SAFE→WATCH, WATCH→DANGER) and fires Discord/Slack/generic webhooks with auto-detected payload formatting.

projects.title: MeteredSignal
projects.description: Arc agent pays Hedera x402 for live Graph DeFi signal, then spends USDC on GO.
projects.project_description: MeteredSignal is a pay-per-call intelligence market for agents that move capital in DeFi. You do not buy a monthly Graph API seat or dump a single subgraph into a prompt. You buy a metered signal. Before the agent spends, the product only exposes a catalog of priced routes: lending compare or wallet risk, HBAR price, and a freshness contract so you know the data is live. The capital move stays locked until the verdict is GO. That gating is the product. Raw subgraph access is free but hard for agents to budget, and blind USDC transfers treat every call like a green light. MeteredSignal flips both sides at once. Merchants sell standardized Messari lending intelligence as an HTTP 402 service instead of a subscription. Agents get live multi-protocol risk they can afford per call, with a policy so Arc USDC only moves when the signal is fresh and actionable. The agent journey is built around that meter. An Arc-side wallet discovers the free catalog, hits a paywalled merchant route, settles Hedera x402 through Blocky402 without an API key, then receives a paid JSON signal built from Messari Standardized Subgraphs on The Graph — Aave v3, Compound v3, and Spark under one query shape. The merchant runs a freshness gate on _meta.block; fewer than two fresh sources means UNAVAILABLE, not a soft maybe. The agent reasons to GO, NO_GO, or UNAVAILABLE, ranks venues by TVL and utilization on lending-compare, and scores cross-protocol borrow exposure on wallet-risk. Only on GO does Circle Agent Stack settle a nanopayment on Arc to the GO-action seller. Identity of the human operator never has to sit in the payment path; the economic actor is the agent wallet. Settlements can append to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so payment is auditable on HashScan, not just logged in memory. Merchants get the other half of the loop. An Express service lists metered routes, challenges unpaid GETs with an exact-scheme Hedera 402, queries live GraphQL after settle, and sells a separate Arc USDC GO-action behind Circle Gateway batching. Treasury agents, lending desks, and autonomous spenders all hit the same inventory: one Messari template, two prices (compare cheaper than risk), one freshness policy. Demand can arrive through the demo console or a headless agent, while supply still publishes once. Agent loop: discover → 402 → settle → Graph → freshness → decide → USDC or refuse. Merchant loop: catalog → challenge → query → signal → HCS audit. Arc loop: GO-only nanopay with a spend cap. The whole point is one market that meters truth for buyers and liquidates intelligence as a payable service without spoiling either side. Less noise. More signal.
projects.how_its_made: MeteredSignal was built from scratch during ETHOnline as an npm workspaces monorepo. The demo console is a Vite React app with a live SSE pipeline rail. Express owns the merchant and agent surfaces; on Vercel they mount together as one serverless app so /, /demo, /api, and /v1 ship from a single deployment. A shared packages/graph registry pins Messari Standardized Lending deployments and runs the freshness-gated queries. Partner tech is not bolted on for a checklist: each one sits on a critical path in the decision loop. The UX is intentional about failure modes, not just happy paths. The console streams Discover → 402 → Settle → Paid → Graph → Fresh → Decide → USDC → Receipts so judges can watch the meter in real time. A labeled Simulate indexer lag toggle still pays for a live Messari query, then injects tip ahead of _meta.block so sources go stale, the verdict becomes UNAVAILABLE, and Arc policy refuses spend — the demo beat that proves the gate is real. Wallet presets drive high-borrow NO_GO versus clean GO without mocking Graph. ArcScan, HashScan, and HCS topic links land next to decoded PAYMENT-RESPONSE payloads so receipts are evidence, not decoration. Money runs through Hedera x402 and Arc Circle rails, not a custom auth stack. On the intelligence leg, @x402/express plus Blocky402 as facilitator challenges unpaid routes; the agent signs with ExactHederaScheme and settles HBAR — about 0.001 for lending-compare and 0.0025 for wallet-risk. On the capital leg, @circle-fin/x402-batching GatewayClient pays the merchant’s Gateway-batched GO-action on Arc Testnet (eip155:5042002), capped by ARC_SPEND_AMOUNT_USDC. Missing Arc keys yield an explicit dry_run instead of a panic spend; an optional native USDC fallback stays behind a flag if Gateway fails. The UI and receipts treat HBAR meter cost and Arc USDC spend as separate ledgers on purpose, because agent demos often die when one rail is funded and the other is not. The signal layer is The Graph. One Messari query template covers Aave v3 (Ethereum and Arbitrum), Compound v3, and Spark; the agent ranks and decides rather than dumping raw JSON as the product. Freshness requires _meta block number and timestamp against GRAPH_MAX_BLOCK_LAG. Without Graph there is no evidence and no verdict. Without Hedera and Blocky402 the merchant is not a payable agent service. Without Arc and Circle nanopayments the loop never closes from intelligence to capital under Agent Stack rails. The audit trail is Hedera Consensus Service. After a paid settle, the merchant can append settlement metadata to an HCS topic so HashScan shows more than a transfer — a verifiable payment history for the metered route. HCS is best-effort: if topic or creds are missing the response still returns, and that is disclosed. The hacky but useful glue is shipping merchant and agent in one Vercel function with a long maxDuration, plus demo tip-lag and wallet presets that keep the video cinematic while every Graph query and 402 settle stay live. Mainnet for Arc is an env flip when Circle publishes RPC and chain ID — same GO-only policy, documented in ARC_MAINNET.md for the Launch track unlock. Put together, The Graph supplies the evidence, Hedera meters and audits the call, Arc moves USDC only on GO, and the product in the middle stays what it claims to be: less noise, more signal.

projects.title: Pocket
projects.description: Spending limits for AI agents. Each agent gets its own wallet and a cap it cannot raise.
projects.project_description: Everyone who has handed a task to an AI agent has had the same small moment of hesitation. You are about to let it run on its own, and somewhere in the back of your mind is the question: what if it doesn't stop? We are comfortable letting agents write code, book things, and read half the internet. We are not comfortable handing one a credit card. And that is the thing standing between where agents are now and where they are obviously going, because almost everything useful an agent needs is sold per call. Search results, market data, compute, other agents' output. Someone has to pay for it, and right now the only options are to do it yourself in advance or to give the agent your card and hope. Pocket is the third option. Give the agent its own wallet and a limit it cannot raise. WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE → You create an agent in a dashboard and you set the rules in plain terms. How much it can spend a day. How much on any one purchase. How much on a particular job. Who it is allowed to pay. And the amount above which you want to approve things yourself. → Then you let it go. Every time it tries to buy something, Pocket checks the purchase against those rules before any money moves. If it passes, the payment goes through in about a second and nobody is interrupted. If it fails, the purchase is refused and written down along with the exact rule that stopped it, so you are never left guessing why your agent did not do something. → The agent cannot change any of this. It does not hold the key to its own wallet, and it cannot raise its own limit. Those are set by you, and the agent only ever spends against them. The limit is not a suggestion it agrees to follow. It is a wall. And everything is written down. Every purchase, every refusal, every change you make, in a record that cannot be edited after the fact. If you want to know what your agents spent last week and why, the answer is one page. HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER → Agents pay sellers using x402, an open payment standard that lets a website charge for a single request without the buyer ever opening an account or holding an API key. It is what makes an agent buying one search result for one cent actually practical. We built Pocket to sit inside that exchange: the seller names its price, Pocket decides whether that money may be spent, and only then is anything signed. → The wallets are held by Privy, so no private key ever touches our servers. We also set a second, independent limit inside Privy itself, which means even if Pocket were compromised, the wallet would still refuse to overspend. → Payments settle on Hedera, which is fast and cheap enough that buying something for one cent is not absurd, and every settled payment links out to a public block explorer so any number on the screen can be checked against the chain. → The Graph prices the limits you set in dollars. We deliberately ask two independent Graph sources for every price and require them to agree. If they disagree, Pocket refuses the purchase rather than guessing, because a limit enforced with a wrong price is not a limit. → Agents connect through MCP, the standard Claude and other assistants already use for tools. There are eight of them (tools), and only one can actually spend money. projects.project_description_markdown:
Everyone who has handed a task to an AI agent has had the same small moment of hesitation. You are about to let it run on its own, and somewhere in the back of your mind is the question: what if it doesn't stop?

We are comfortable letting agents write code, book things, and read half the internet. We are not comfortable handing one a credit card. And that is the thing standing between where agents are now and where they are obviously going, because almost everything useful an agent needs is sold per call. Search results, market data, compute, other agents' output. Someone has to pay for it, and right now the only options are to do it yourself in advance or to give the agent your card and hope.

Pocket is the third option. Give the agent its own wallet and a limit it cannot raise.

WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE

→ You create an agent in a dashboard and you set the rules in plain terms. How much it can spend a day. How much on any one purchase. How much on a particular job. Who it is allowed to pay. And the amount above which you want to approve things yourself.

→ Then you let it go. Every time it tries to buy something, Pocket checks the purchase against those rules before any money moves. If it passes, the payment goes through in about a second and nobody is interrupted. If it fails, the purchase is refused and written down along with the exact rule that stopped it, so you are never left guessing why your agent did not do something.

→ The agent cannot change any of this. It does not hold the key to its own wallet, and it cannot raise its own limit. Those are set by you, and the agent only ever spends against them. The limit is not a suggestion it agrees to follow. It is a wall.

And everything is written down. Every purchase, every refusal, every change you make, in a record that cannot be edited after the fact. If you want to know what your agents spent last week and why, the answer is one page.

HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER

→ Agents pay sellers using x402, an open payment standard that lets a website charge for a single request without the buyer ever opening an account or holding an API key. It is what makes an agent buying one search result for one cent actually practical. We built Pocket to sit inside that exchange: the seller names its price, Pocket decides whether that money may be spent, and only then is anything signed.

→ The wallets are held by Privy, so no private key ever touches our servers. We also set a second, independent limit inside Privy itself, which means even if Pocket were compromised, the wallet would still refuse to overspend.

→ Payments settle on Hedera, which is fast and cheap enough that buying something for one cent is not absurd, and every settled payment links out to a public block explorer so any number on the screen can be checked against the chain.

→ The Graph prices the limits you set in dollars. We deliberately ask two independent Graph sources for every price and require them to agree. If they disagree, Pocket refuses the purchase rather than guessing, because a limit enforced with a wrong price is not a limit.

→ Agents connect through MCP, the standard Claude and other assistants already use for tools. There are eight of them (tools), and only one can actually spend money. The other seven let an agent check what it is allowed to do before it tries, so it can ask "would this be approved?" without moving anything.

TRY IT

1. Dashboard: https://www.pocket-app.xyz
2. Documentation: https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs
3. API: https://api.pocket-app.xyz
4. MCP server: https://mcp.pocket-app.xyz

5. An example seller, with six live data feeds priced from one cent to seventy-five: https://pay.pocket-app.xyz

That last one is worth a click. It is a genuinely separate business that knows nothing about Pocket and has no account with the buyer. It states a price, gets paid, and serves the data. We built it so the demo is a real purchase from a real counterparty rather than Pocket paying itself.

How the whole exchange works: https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/how-it-works

projects.title: Tempo
projects.description: A SwapVM instruction that gives a 1inch Aqua strategy memory of its own fill history
projects.project_description: Tempo is a custom instruction for 1inch's SwapVM. A maker ships a bytecode program that prices their swaps; Tempo hooks in through the Extruction opcode as a separately deployed contract, tracking per-strategy fill velocity in persistent storage and widening the spread as velocity rises, saturating at a bound. It runs against the already-deployed Aqua registry and AquaSwapVMRouter on Base with no changes to 1inch's contracts. The question was whether a strategy that remembers its recent fill history prices better than one that doesn't. To answer it I built a replay harness: real hourly ETH/USD price tapes, an arbitrageur sized endogenously from the pool's own quotes rather than a scripted trade list, and price-sensitive organic flow that walks away from bad execution. The control is Tempo against itself configured with a constant spread — same contract, same placement, same rounding, same gas shape — bracketed around Tempo's own realised average spread. The result is negative. Adaptiveness does not beat a matched constant spread in any of nine tape and flow-mix combinations. An earlier version of this measurement reported the opposite; that finding came from a control with structural disadvantages and did not survive a fair one. The diagnosis is in ANALYSIS.md: in every configuration tested the decay window was shorter than the interval between trades, so the velocity ramp only ever activated on fills sharing a timestamp and was never exercised across ticks. Also shipped: an HTTP API that encodes SwapVM programs and replays Tempo's pricing offline, live at https://tempo-ysu3.onrender.com with an OpenAPI spec at /openapi.json, exposed through a Bazantic x402 gateway.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, tested against pinned Base mainnet forks using the live deployed Aqua registry (0x1111113ccf1426a8e30e2bff5e005d929bf6a90a) and SwapVM router (0x111111338c5091e8440b67b168bae16a668ac0de), verified byte-identical to swap-vm v1.0.1 and aqua v1.0.0 via Sourcify before building against them. Only my own contracts are deployed; 1inch's are consumed as pinned git submodules, never vendored. Tempo is an Extruction target implementing IExtruction and IStaticExtruction, placed after XYCSwap in the program. It keys velocity state on orderHash, packs volume and timestamp into one slot, and takes a genuinely read-only path under isStaticContext — the router issues a STATICCALL to the target whenever quoting, so a write there reverts at the EVM level. The replay harness runs both arms over identical tapes and seeds, with paired per-seed differences and a measured noise floor established against a pass-through stub before the real logic existed. Four bugs worth naming. The deployed router's opcode dispatch has an off-by-one: _opcodes() reuses the fixed array's memory as the returned dynamic array's length word, shifting every opcode index down by one, so XYCSwap is 17 and Extruction 32 rather than 18 and 33. That only surfaced by executing against the real contract. The gas measurement was biased by EIP-2929 warm/cold leaking between sequential swaps in one test function. The harness never advanced block.timestamp, making the decay window inert. And the first control arm used swap-vm's own Fee instruction, whose pre-curve placement was itself a confound — replacing it with constant-spread Tempo reversed the headline result. The API is Python stdlib only, Dockerised, with the program encoding byte-matched against fixtures captured from real Foundry output.

projects.title: Stylus Hook
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hooks written entirely in Rust on Arbitrum Stylus
projects.project_description:
This continues a project from ETHGlobal Scaling Ethereum 2024, built when Stylus was still
testnet-only and Uniswap v4 was still in development. Back then the contract v4 actually called was
a Solidity proxy, forwarding every callback to the Rust code behind it. It was never Stylus end to
end, because a hook must sit at an address whose low 14 bits encode its callbacks, and Stylus could
not deploy to a mined one. Both have shipped since. Stylus is on mainnet and CREATE2s through StylusDeployer, so we finished
it: the contract the PoolManager calls is now the Stylus contract itself, with no Solidity in it. The other half is finding out whether that is worth doing. Entering a Stylus contract costs ~7,900
gas more, storage is identical, and arithmetic is 3-640x cheaper. So most hooks should stay in
Solidity, and we publish that: a counter hook costs 2.8x more in Rust. Where it pays, it pays widely. Against the TWAMM live on Base and Unichain, at 32 concurrent order
streams, Solidity spends 2,849,561 gas per swap and Rust spends 1,891,213. Replaying v4's swap math
is 7.1x cheaper per tick. And a post-quantum signature check is 11.3M gas in Solidity against 33k
in Rust, because SHAKE is not reachable through the EVM's keccak opcode. Porting v4-core also found a failing input in Uniswap's own TickMath fuzz test. The fix is one
character.
projects.how_its_made:
Rust on stylus-sdk 0.10.9, compiled to wasm32 and run on Arbitrum Stylus. stylus/base-hook is
BaseHook.sol's counterpart: the v4 types, the permission flags, all ten IHooks callbacks, and the
calls back into the singleton. A test pins all ten selectors against the compiled IHooks.sol. Solidity's onlyPoolManager can't be forgotten because BaseHook is abstract; Rust has no abstract
types, so a proc macro inserts the guards instead. And hook-miner reimplements StylusDeployer's
salt derivation, keccak(salt || initData), to find an address carrying the declared flags. Two things worth stealing. The SDK has no immutable, so build.rs bakes the pool manager in as a
Rust const rather than paying a cold SLOAD per callback: 2,568 gas a swap. And rustc at opt-level 2
or 3 emits a DataCount section ArbOS refuses to activate, so Stylus looks capped at size-optimised;
--llvm-memory-copy-fill-lowering fixes it. Both builds pass cargo stylus check and only fail at
deploy. Every ratio here doubled when we found it. Forge can't run WASM, so the Solidity twins are tested through a real local v4 stack and the Rust
side against TestVM, cross-pinned to the same values. Every gas figure is a receipt from an
Arbitrum Nitro dev node, not an estimate. Hackiest bit: the TWAMM is 41 KB, so it needs ArbOS 61 code fragments, but cargo stylus
get-initcode refuses fragmented contracts. We deploy once with --wasm-file, read the root back off
chain, re-wrap it in the EVM prelude, mine against that, and hand it to StylusDeployer ourselves.

projects.title: Recourse
projects.description: x402 pays before delivery. Recourse escrows it and refunds you when the API breaks its SLA.
projects.project_description: When an agent pays for an API call with x402, the money moves before the response exists. If what comes back is empty, stale, or quietly wrong, it's already gone. A person notices and stops buying from that seller. An agent making a thousand calls an hour doesn't notice, and has no refund path to reach for. Recourse changes one thing. The payment goes into an escrow contract on Hedera instead of straight to the seller. Before any money moves, the seller publishes an SLA: a short list of checks a machine can run on the response, like "bid must be greater than zero" or "the spread must be within 50 basis points". The 402 response carries the hash of that document, and the buyer refuses to pay if the terms don't hash to what was advertised. The seller returns the data along with a signature over what it sent. If the response breaks one of the published checks, the buyer disputes and posts a bond worth 10% of the payment. A Chainlink CRE workflow running inside an AWS Nitro enclave then reads the response, checks it against the SLA, and rules on it. The payload never goes on-chain and no node operator sees it. That matters, because the thing being argued over is usually the exact thing the buyer paid to keep private. The verdict arrives back on Hedera carrying a reason code that names the clause that failed. Reason 102 means clause 2 broke. So a refund points at a specific promise the seller made and didn't keep, rather than at somebody's opinion about data quality. If nobody disputes, none of that happens. The window closes, the seller withdraws, and the whole exchange costs one extra contract call with no oracle involved. Disputes are the exception, and only the exception pays for the machinery. It runs end to end on testnet today. In one run the seller returned a negative bid, and the buyer got 0.11 HBAR back: the payment plus the bond. In another the seller behaved and was paid 0.1 HBAR with no adjudication at all.
projects.how_its_made: The escrow is Solidity on the Hedera testnet EVM, built with Foundry, with 40 tests including a fuzz test on the accounting. The SLA checker is a small TypeScript package with canonical JSON hashing so the buyer, the seller and the enclave all agree on what a document hashes to. The adjudicator is a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow. The site is Next.js, and it reads the chain directly rather than from a database, so nothing on it can drift from what actually happened. Payments settle through Blocky402 on Hedera. Three things forced the design into a shape we didn't expect. First, Hedera doesn't run contract code on a plain transfer. A native TransferTransaction credits a contract's balance without ever calling receive() or fallback(), and the x402 facilitator settles that way. So the escrow can't be told about its own funding. We split it into two steps: the facilitator settles, then anyone calls bind() to attach terms, and the contract only commits money it can prove it already holds by checking its balance against what it has already promised out. One deposit can never back two payments. That invariant is the thing the fuzz test protects. Second, CRE can't write to Hedera. It isn't in the 57 chains a tenant can target, so there's no forwarder for writeReport to reach. The enclave writes its verdict to a relay contract on Ethereum Sepolia instead, where the KeystoneForwarder checks the DON signatures, and CCIP carries it the rest of the way to Hedera. The escrow only accepts a message from the CCIP router with that relay as the sender. projects.project_description_markdown:
When an agent pays for an API call with x402, the money moves before the response exists. If what comes back is empty, stale, or quietly wrong, it's already gone. A person notices and stops buying from that seller. An agent making a thousand calls an hour doesn't notice, and has no refund path to reach for.

Recourse changes one thing. The payment goes into an escrow contract on Hedera instead of straight to the seller. Before any money moves, the seller publishes an SLA: a short list of checks a machine can run on the response, like "bid must be greater than zero" or "the spread must be within 50 basis points". The 402 response carries the hash of that document, and the buyer refuses to pay if the terms don't hash to what was advertised.

The seller returns the data along with a signature over what it sent. If the response breaks one of the published checks, the buyer disputes and posts a bond worth 10% of the payment. A Chainlink CRE workflow running inside an AWS Nitro enclave then reads the response, checks it against the SLA, and rules on it. The payload never goes on-chain and no node operator sees it. That matters, because the thing being argued over is usually the exact thing the buyer paid to keep private.

The verdict arrives back on Hedera carrying a reason code that names the clause that failed. Reason 102 means clause 2 broke. So a refund points at a specific promise the seller made and didn't keep, rather than at somebody's opinion about data quality.

If nobody disputes, none of that happens. The window closes, the seller withdraws, and the whole exchange costs one extra contract call with no oracle involved. Disputes are the exception, and only the exception pays for the machinery.

It runs end to end on testnet today. In one run the seller returned a negative bid, and the buyer got 0.11 HBAR back: the payment plus the bond. In another the seller behaved and was paid 0.1 HBAR with no adjudication at all.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The escrow is Solidity on the Hedera testnet EVM, built with Foundry, with 40 tests including a fuzz test on the accounting. The SLA checker is a small TypeScript package with canonical JSON hashing so the buyer, the seller and the enclave all agree on what a document hashes to. The adjudicator is a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow. The site is Next.js, and it reads the chain directly rather than from a database, so nothing on it can drift from what actually happened. Payments settle through Blocky402 on Hedera.

Three things forced the design into a shape we didn't expect.

First, Hedera doesn't run contract code on a plain transfer. A native TransferTransaction credits a contract's balance without ever calling receive() or fallback(), and the x402 facilitator settles that way. So the escrow can't be told about its own funding. We split it into two steps: the facilitator settles, then anyone calls bind() to attach terms, and the contract only commits money it can prove it already holds by checking its balance against what it has already promised out. One deposit can never back two payments. That invariant is the thing the fuzz test protects.

Second, CRE can't write to Hedera. It isn't in the 57 chains a tenant can target, so there's no forwarder for writeReport to reach. The enclave writes its verdict to a relay contract on Ethereum Sepolia instead, where the KeystoneForwarder checks the DON signatures, and CCIP carries it the rest of the way to Hedera. The escrow only accepts a message from the CCIP router with that relay as the sender. We confirmed the lane by calling isChainSupported on the live Sepolia router, which was necessary because Chainlink's own docs leave Hedera off the destination list.

Third, we wanted an LLM to judge disputes and couldn't. The enclave result is attested and verified by DON consensus, which needs the same input to produce the same output every time, and a model doesn't. So the model moved upstream to help sellers write the SLA, and the enclave enforces a contract both sides already agreed to. There isn't even a clock read in the handler, because Date.now() would break consensus. Freshness is judged against a deadline that's already on-chain.

The most expensive bug: our first live verdict reached Hedera and did nothing. CCIP said the message was delivered, the OffRamp transaction succeeded, and the escrow never moved. Our trimmed CCIP receiver was missing supportsInterface. The router staticcalls it before delivering, and an address that reverts gets treated as a normal account, so the router skips the receiver and still records the message as executed. Nothing reports a failure anywhere. The verdict just disappears. Two tests now pin that, including the literal interface id the router looks for.

Two smaller ones worth passing on. Blocky402 answers HTTP 200 for a payment that failed, with the real result in the body, so our gateway gated on the status code and briefly gave away paid work for free. And cre workflow simulate --broadcast submits real transactions without needing deployment access, which is how we produced genuine on-chain state while our CRE org was still gated.

projects.title: Matoi
projects.description: A working economy where AI agents price information, buy what they need, and prove every payment.
projects.project_description:
Matoi is an agent-to-agent market for paid intelligence. Provider agents collect and evaluate information from sources such as Telegram, RSS feeds, market APIs, protocol data and other live streams. They decide what is useful, price their output, and publish it for other agents to buy. A BuyerAgent searches the market for information relevant to its task, compares available providers, evaluates quotes against its budget and risk policy, and pays for the sources it chooses. Circle Developer Controlled Wallets and testnet USDC handle agent spending, while paid requests are settled through a Hedera x402 flow using a Blocky402-compatible facilitator. Each completed call produces a receipt and an audit trail. Payment records are kept in the app ledger, and proof is anchored to Hedera Consensus Service so the full mission can be reviewed afterwards. One of the working providers reads a live Telegram news stream, evaluates incoming messages and sells the resulting signal per request. The same model can be extended to video analysis, policy speeches, market data, security events, onchain activity, or any other source an agent can evaluate and price.
The product is a Next.js control room, an in-process BuyerAgent, a provider marketplace, a Hedera payment signer, an Arc spend ledger and an HCS audit topic — all wired into one A2A transcript.
projects.how_its_made: I built Matoi as one Next.js app that talks to two rails. Frontend is plain Next.js with TypeScript. A control room page lets you pick a buyer scenario and click RUN. There's a Blocky402 toggle that decides which payment rail gets used. Backend lives in the same repo. /api/mission/run is the single entry point. It runs a BuyerAgent in-process, asks provider agents for quotes, picks the ones that fit the budget, and writes the whole interaction as an A2A transcript. Providers are small modules. TelegramPulse uses a local Telethon bridge that reads a public Telegram channel and turns the messages into a paid signal. The other providers hit CoinGecko, DefiLlama, RSS feeds and GitHub directly through their public APIs. No keys needed for the demo. When Blocky402 is ON, the mission endpoint calls /api/x402/blocky402/pay. That route uses @hashgraph/sdk to build and sign a Hedera USDC TransferTransaction off-chain, encodes it as an x402 payment header, and posts it to my self-hosted /settle route. The route acts as a Blocky402-compatible facilitator, opens a challenge, settles the receipt and returns an HMAC-signed envelope with a receiptId. Arc/Circle side: the BuyerAgent authorizes spend through Circle Developer Controlled Wallets. There are three role wallets on ARC-TESTNET — Trader, ArcResearch, Risk. Authorization goes through an Arc spend ledger on disk with idempotency keys so nothing double-pays. Real ARC-TESTNET transfers are gated behind two env flags that have to both be true. Nanopayments: every accepted call appends a meter entry (base price + costPerCall × calls). HCS: receipt hashes and the mission summary land on topic 0.0.10426202 on Hedera testnet. Allowlisted payloads only. Partner tools that actually matter: Circle Developer Controlled Wallets — the agent's identity and treasury Hedera x402 + Blocky402-compatible facilitator — the pay-per-call rail HCS — the public proof layer

projects.title: Receivables Flow
projects.description: The capital flywheel for invoice receivables: source, fund, resell, repay, and reprice capital cost
projects.project_description:
Business App:  https://business-production-0df2.up.railway.app
Investor App:   https://investor-production-d938.up.railway.app A business is owed $50,000 on an invoice and has to wait 60 days for it. Payroll does not wait. Invoice factoring/financing exists to bridge that cashflow gap, but it has two problems: the investor's money is locked until the customer pays, and nobody outside one lender can see whether the business pays on time. Receivables Flow fixes both. Two of three business directors approve the invoice sale through a Privy key quorum, and the invoice is minted on Hedera as a token that only KYC-approved investors can hold. For example: Day 0: an investment fund buys it for $47,990, a 4.02% fee priced off the business's public repayment record. Day 20: the fund sells half of the invoice to another investor for $24,330 on the secondary market, so the fund gets liquidity before the invoice is due. Day 60: the business repays $50,000 on-time and each holder is paid $25,000. The first fund made $1,340, the second $670, and the whole $2,010 of return is the fee the business paid. Then the loop closes. The on-time repayment is written to the business's ENS name (ironline.business.receivablesflow.eth) and its credit score rises from 83 to 86 — so in the next round of financing, the business gets a lower cost of capital because of its own timely repayment behavior.
projects.how_its_made: This project has two Next.js apps: a business portal for Ironline Freight and an investor portal for Woodgrove Capital. They share three workspace libraries: the Privy layer, the Hedera contracts, and the ENS registry code. Hedera settles the full lifecycle of the receivable. The invoice is issued with Asset Tokenization Studio as a whitelist-only security: $50,000 face value, 60-day maturity, one unit per dollar. Payment is in mUSDC, a mock dollar deployed for the demo because Circle's testnet faucet caps at $20. A delivery-versus-payment contract settles each sale by moving the mUSDC and the token in one atomic transaction. The same transaction also books the day-60 repayment on Hedera's schedule service. KYC is enforced by the invoice token itself. Only wallets on its approved list can hold the security. Every step of the lifecycle runs on Hedera: issuing the token, the sale to the fund, the day-20 resale on the secondary market, and the day-60 repayment to each holder. ENS holds a business's creditworthiness in public, under its own name. On the ENSv2 hackathon deployment on Sepolia, receivablesflow.eth issues ironline.business and woodgrove.investor, so both portals show a readable name instead of a wallet address. A Permissioned Resolver lets only the platform key write the fields that matter. The investor's KYC pass is a wallet record plus the name's expiry. The business's repayment history is five counts on its name: financed, paid on time, paid late, defaulted, and outstanding. The fee on every invoice is computed live from those counts by a published formula, so each on-time repayment raises the score and lowers the cost of the next invoice. In the demo the score rises from 83 to 86 and the fee falls from 4.02% to 3.84%. Privy provides the controls a B2B financial product needs. Both portals sign in with email OTP, with no extension or seed phrase. On the business side, tokenizing an invoice requires two of the company's three directors to sign, enforced by a Privy key quorum on the company wallet. For the demo, the first signature is made automatically by the app backend, and whoever signs in as demo user is seated as a director so their approval is the second.  On the investor side, the fund's wallet is governed by a Privy policy that enforces its mandate: no payment above $100,000, and no payment to a business that is not on the approved list. Anything outside the mandate is refused by Privy, not by application code. Both wallets transact on Hedera through Privy's EVM RPC.

projects.title: Orbit
projects.description: A DeFi collectible economy where trading fees fund rewards and liquidity stays permanently locked.
projects.project_description: Orbit is a DeFi collectible economy on Base that connects liquid tokens, permanent collectibles, and rewards funded by trading activity. FUEL is the tradable side of a 4,444-identity collection. Gaining a whole FUEL unit triggers a random Discovery that reveals a Grounded Craft, including its rarity and reward track. Collectors can keep trading or choose to Launch a favorite: permanently burn one FUEL to turn that craft into an Orbiter. The Orbiter keeps its identity, becomes reward-eligible, and no longer depends on a FUEL balance. Unclaimed rewards belong to the collectible and transfer with it to its next owner. The economy runs through a canonical Uniswap v4 FUEL/WETH market. A custom hook charges 3% on WETH-side trading volume: 2% funds stock-reward conversion, 0.85% builds permanently locked protocol liquidity, and 0.15% goes to the creator. Reward cycles split the available budget across AAPLc, GOOGLc, METAc, and NVDAc tracks. Ordinary Orbiters share their track's allocation by rarity weight; three Stations and an Observatory receive allocations across all four tracks. Rewards depend on actual activity and successful conversions. Uniswap's Continuous Clearing Auction distributes 4,000 FUEL, discovers the opening price, and combines auction proceeds with 444 reserved FUEL to seed permanently locked market liquidity. Privy lets a collector start with email or an existing wallet and use the same account for funding, trading, Launch, and claims. The Graph integration makes pooled fee allocations and completed reward conversions inspectable. The working demo is deployed on Base Sepolia. Settlement and stock-reward tokens are valueless test assets, demonstrating the mechanics rather than live stock ownership or guaranteed returns.
projects.how_its_made: Orbit combines Solidity contracts tested with Foundry, a Next.js/React/TypeScript frontend, and Effect-based TypeScript services with SQLite persistence. The protocol pairs ERC-20 FUEL with ERC-721 collectible identities. Whole-unit acquisitions create pending Discoveries. Chainlink VRF supplies a verifiable seed; separate, retryable finalization applies identity draws in acquisition order. Launch burns exactly one FUEL and activates permanent collectible reward accounting. The reward ledger accrues rewards to identities and checks current ownership when a wallet claims. Uniswap is the market and launch infrastructure. CanonicalRouter settles swaps through the official v4 PoolManager, while CanonicalFeeHook enforces the registered FUEL/WETH market and collects the WETH-side fee using hook deltas. The initial distribution integrates the official Continuous Clearing Auction and Liquidity Launcher with wallet-bound bidder escrows. A launch coordinator verifies pool initialization and permanent liquidity custody before enabling trading. EpochConverter processes four fixed WETH-to-USDC-to-reward-token routes independently; failed tracks keep their reserved budgets for retry. Privy's React SDK and wagmi adapter support email-created embedded wallets and external wallets on Base Sepolia. The same connected account signs the faucet proof, approvals, trades, Launch, and claims. A bounded testnet faucet supplies gas and test WETH. Saved transaction evidence and receipt reconciliation recover interrupted wallet responses without automatically replaying a trade. The Graph subgraph preserves the Messari DEX AMM 1.3.2 schema and adds v4 hook-fee, reward-funding, and auction lifecycle entities. Standard pool/token/swap fields support reusable market queries; custom entities expose exact fee allocations and successful conversion spending. Live Studio integration evidence and reproducible queries are included in the repository. The frontend requests funding analytics through a cached, budgeted API. Direct contract reads serve current balances and ownership; a separate SQLite index serves protocol history. Two subtle integration challenges were separating PoolManager swap deltas from the user's total payment after hook fees, and checking actual auction-to-pool readiness because a successful migration transaction can still contain an internal migration failure. Both are covered by contract checks and lifecycle tests.

projects.title: VendingAgent
projects.description: Autonomous pay-per-call API proxy using Hedera x402 and Chainlink CRE for agentic workflows.
projects.project_description: This project is an autonomous pay-per-call API proxy (VendingAgent) designed for the emerging Agentic Economy. It solves the problem of AI agents needing rigid subscriptions or hardcoded API keys to access premium Web2 data. Using Hedera's x402 standard, it gates a premium data endpoint, requiring autonomous agents to stream sub-cent micro-transactions in HBAR to unlock the payload. Furthermore, to protect the upstream Web2 API key from being exposed on-chain or leaked in the logs, the project utilizes Chainlink's CRE Confidential Workflows (running inside a hardware TEE enclave) to securely fetch and return the data. We also integrated Bazantic MCP Recipes so other autonomous agents can easily discover, understand, and autonomously interact with the service.
projects.how_its_made: We built the backend API proxy using Node.js and TypeScript, integrating the @hashgraph/sdk to verify x402 micropayments on the Hedera testnet via the Blocky402 facilitator. The core data fetching logic is handled by a Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) handlerInTee script. This script securely decrypts the upstream Web2 API key exclusively inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) enclave, ensuring the secret never leaks to the public while executing the confidential workflow. To make the service discoverable, we created a Bazantic Model Context Protocol (MCP) server alongside a recipe.json file that instructs any consumer LLM on exactly how to construct the HBAR transaction and request the data. Finally, a separate autonomous client agent script was written to simulate the end-to-end HTTP 402 payment negotiation and successful data retrieval loop.
