projects.title: BO-Sealed-Bid
projects.description: Agent-to-agent commerce has a bad default: to negotiate its price
projects.project_description:
Agent-to-agent commerce has a bad default: to negotiate, an agent either reveals its reserve price
(and gets priced at the edge of it) or trusts a middleman who sees both numbers. We remove the
middleman with a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow . Agent A and Agent B each hold a private reserve. A CRE Confidential Workflow reads both as Vault secrets inside a Nitro enclave and returns only SETTLE @ midpoint or NO_OVERLAP. SETTLE is written to a receiver on Base Sepolia; NO_OVERLAP writes nothing. Third-party vetting via x402. Both reserve prices and two commitment salts are CRE Vault secrets. Inside a handlerInTee handler
running on AWS Nitro, the workflow makes one getSecrets call, computes whether the bands overlap,
and produces exactly one of two outputs: SETTLE @ clearing (the midpoint) or the literal NO_OVERLAP . Alongside it: two salted commitments sha256(reserve‖salt) and a run id, so either
party can later prove what it bid without the enclave ever having published it. Nothing else crosses
back to the DON — not the reserves, not the gap, not which side was higher. That property is tested at
every layer, with deliberately leaky implementations kept in the suite as negative controls. On SETTLE , the DON writes the attestation through the CRE Forwarder to SealedBidReceiver on Base
Sepolia, a contract that records only SETTLE outcomes and reverts everything else — so even a
misbehaving workflow could not leave a NO_OVERLAP trace. Agent A then pays Agent B the clearing amount.
On NO_OVERLAP , no transaction is sent at all. Settlement is not self-certified. Before bidding, each agent vets the other through BlindOracle, a
public pay-per-call API settled over x402 in USDC on Base mainnet; a trust badge opens the bracket, a
reputation lookup closes it, and a process-followed attestation can be bought over the hash-chained,
signed evidence of the run. Every one of those payments is a USDC transfer anyone can check on Basescan. The one thing SETTLE does reveal is A_max + B_min . That is the standard sealed-bid trade-off and
we state it rather than hide it.

projects.project_description:
PROOF OF ATTRACTION
Detailed Project Description
ETHOnline 2026 — World Track ===============================================================================
THE ONE-LINE IDEA A dating app where every single profile is a verified, unique, living human —
no bots, no catfish, no duplicate or throwaway accounts — and where an optional
human-backed AI agent can act on your behalf in a way the person you are talking
to can actually trust. Human verification is not a badge bolted on at the end. It is the foundation the
whole product stands on. If you cannot prove you are a real, unique person, you
do not get in. ===============================================================================
THE PROBLEM Every mainstream dating app has the same three rotten foundations: Bots and scammers. A large share of "people" on dating apps are automated
accounts, romance scammers, or paid engagement farms. Users waste time,
lose money, and lose trust. Fake and duplicate identities. One person can spin up ten profiles. Banned
users return instantly under a new email. There is no notion of "one real
human = one account." No trust in AI. AI is flooding these apps — auto-swipers, script-written
openers, ghost-written conversations. When a message feels too smooth, you
cannot tell if a human is even involved. AI is treated as something to hide. The result: matching feels like gambling against machines, and the moment AI
enters the chat, trust collapses entirely. ===============================================================================
THE CORE INSIGHT The scarce, valuable thing in online dating is not looks or wit — it is the
guarantee that there is ONE REAL, UNIQUE HUMAN on the other side. World ID can prove exactly that, anonymously, without collecting your identity
documents or selling your data. So we built a dating app where that proof is the
entry ticket, the trust signal on every screen, and — crucially — the thing that
makes AI safe instead of scary. Instead of hiding AI, we make it accountable: an agent may act for you, but every
action it takes is cryptographically tied back to a verified human via World's
AgentBook. The other person sees "this was sent by a verified human's agent,"
not "you might be talking to a bot." ===============================================================================
HOW IT WORKS FOR A USER (THE EXPERIENCE) PROVE YOU ARE HUMAN (onboarding)
You open the app and verify with World ID. This is a real, anonymous proof of
personhood — one account per unique human, enforced at the protocol level. No
email/password, no phone number. The proof itself is your identity. Because World ID 4.0 nullifiers are one-time-use, we also create a World ID
"session" during signup so you can log back in later with a single tap,
without re-proving from scratch. On a new device you just enter your handle
and approve the login in the World App. LIVE SELFIE ESTIMATE (optional, clearly labelled)
A quick two-frame front-camera check. It confirms you are a live person in
front of the camera (not a photo of a screen) via a small liveness challenge
— "turn your head", "smile" — and records an ESTIMATED gender presentation. This is shown everywhere as an estimate, never as "verified." World does not
verify gender and we never claim it does. It is a third-party vision-model
guess, kept honest and separate from the real human-verification badge. BUILD A PROFILE
Handle, photos, bio, interests, self-declared gender, who you are looking for,
and location. Photos are stored privately and served through short-lived
signed links, never as permanent public URLs. DISCOVER REAL HUMANS ONLY
You swipe through other verified humans. Each card shows a humanity badge
(Orb / Selfie tier), an "Agent enabled" badge if that person authorized an
agent, and a compatibility match score computed from shared interests, age,
distance, verification tier, and on-chain reputation signals. A "Verified
humans only" filter is always available. THE AGENT ACTS FOR YOU (the AgentKit part)
You can register a personal agent. It genuinely acts on your behalf: "Ask my agent about her" — pre-screens a profile and gives you a take
before you even match. Auto-suggested opener — when you match, your agent drafts a first message
in your chosen tone (warm / witty / direct). You can send via the agent,
edit it, or dismiss it. Reply drafting — mid-conversation, it drafts your next reply from the
thread.
The recipient always sees a disclosure: "sent by a verified human's agent."
Nothing is hidden. TRUST GATES ON HIGH-STAKES MOMENTS
First message and event RSVP are the moments abuse actually happens, so
human-verification is required there — a bot cannot send the first message or
claim a limited event seat. AN ACTION LOG YOU CONTROL
Every action your agent takes is recorded and shown to you, each tagged with
whether it was cryptographically verified through AgentBook. You can revoke
any action. You always know what your agent did in your name. ===============================================================================
WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT Verification is the product, not a feature. The entire funnel is gated on
proof of a unique human. This is Sybil resistance applied to dating. AI is disclosed and accountable, not hidden. Most apps pretend AI is not
there. We surface it and make it provably human-backed. That flips AI from a
trust-destroyer into a trust signal. Privacy-preserving by construction. World ID proves personhood without
revealing who you are. We store an anonymous nullifier, not your identity. Gender is handled honestly. It is an ESTIMATE from a live selfie, always
labelled as such, always separate from the real human badge. We refuse to
launder a guess as a verified fact. ===============================================================================
THE PRIZE ANGLE (ETHOnline — World Track) The build targets both World prizes at once, and they reinforce each other: AgentKit Continuity: a human-backed agent acts in chat and discovery, and
every action routes through a real AgentKit-protected backend that resolves
the agent to a human through AgentBook on World Chain. A durable, per-human
free-trial quota (keyed to the verified human, not a device or wallet) demos
real continuity, with an on-chain testnet top-up when the trial runs out. Selfie Check / Proof of Human: human verification is used as a risk,
eligibility, fairness, continuity, and abuse-prevention signal at the two
highest-stakes moments — first message and event RSVP — not as a one-time
checkbox. ===============================================================================
ONE-SENTENCE PITCH Proof of Attraction is a dating app where you can finally be certain the person
you match with is a real, unique human — and where AI is allowed to help, but
only when it is provably backed by one.
projects.how_its_made:
PROOF OF ATTRACTION
How It's Made — Deep Technical Description
ETHOnline 2026 — World Track =============================================================================== HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE
=============================================================================== Three moving parts: [ React Native app ]  --HTTPS-->  [ Hono API on Vercel ]  -->  [ Neon Postgres ]
(Expo)                          (serverless)                (Drizzle ORM)
|                                |  --> Upstash Redis (quota/nonces)
|                                |  --> AWS S3 (private photos)
|                                |  --> Ably (realtime chat)
|                                |  --> Groq LLM (OpenAI-compatible)
|                                |  --> World Chain (AgentBook, reputation)
|                                --> developer.world.org/api/v4/verify
--> WebView -> IDKit (World App) for World ID proofs
--> Privy embedded wallet + viem for testnet top-ups Client: React Native via Expo SDK 57, Expo Router for navigation. Standalone
app (not a World Mini App), built as an Android dev/release APK. Backend: Hono, deployed to Vercel serverless (local dev via @hono/node-server).
Stable public alias: server-two-steel-51.vercel.app. Repo split: /app and /src (client), /server (backend), /docs (submission +
feedback docs). Drizzle migrations in /server/drizzle. ===============================================================================
2. IDENTITY, AUTH, AND SESSIONS (the hard part) There is no "Sign in with World ID" session product — IDKit produces a one-shot
proof, not a session. So we own the session lifecycle. WORLD ID 4.0 SPECIFICS THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN We use idkit-core 4.2.4 and verify against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify/{rp_id}. v4 requires a signed rp_context: the backend signs a short-lived request token
with an RP signing key (signRequest from @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing) before
the widget can open. App ID + RP ID + signing key are the three portal values. v4 uniqueness nullifiers are ONE-TIME per (rp, action). Re-verifying the same
action returns nullifier_replayed. There is no "max verifications" toggle on a
v4 action page. This is why naive "verify again to log in" does not work. THE FLOW WE BUILT Signup: proofOfHuman uniqueness proof (Sybil check, action from
EXPO_PUBLIC_WORLD_ID_ACTION) -> backend verifies -> issues our own HS256 JWT
keyed to the anonymous nullifier -> upserts a users row. Immediately after, we
run IDKit.createSession and store the returned session_id on the user
(users.world_session_id) and in SecureStore. Login: IDKit.proveSession(session_id) -> POST /auth/session/prove -> new JWT.
No uniqueness re-proof, so no replay. On a fresh device with no stored session,
the user types their handle -> GET /auth/session/lookup?handle= resolves the
session_id -> proveSession. The WebView page (server/public/verify.html) takes a mode param:
uniqueness | create-session | prove-session, and drives IDKit accordingly.
A native bridge (WorldIdProvider / WorldIdModal, react-native-webview) returns
the proof to the app. TOKEN HANDLING JWT (7-day) stored in expo-secure-store, attached as a Bearer token by
authedFetch, which transparently retries once via POST /auth/refresh on a 401
before signing out. The derived humanId (from the nullifier) is the exact key the AgentKit quota
counts against — tying agent continuity to the verified human. ===============================================================================
3. THE AGENT — REAL AGENTKIT, NOT A COSMETIC CHATBOT What makes it a genuine AgentKit integration: every in-chat/discovery agent
action routes through an AgentKit-protected backend endpoint, and the server
verifies the caller against AgentBook on every call. CLIENT SIDE (src/agent/agentkit.ts) Uses @worldcoin/agentkit createAgentkitClient + declareAgentkitExtension. CRITICAL: the extension is declared with network 'eip155:4801' (World Chain
Sepolia). Without the network, supportedChains is empty and createHeader throws
"Signer eip155:4801/eip191 is not supported" — the bug that silently dropped to
the fallback gate. The signer is the Privy embedded wallet (eip191, signMessage). SERVER SIDE (server/src/agentkit.ts + agentGate in index.ts) Real verify path: parseAgentkitHeader -> validateAgentkitMessage (maxAge 300s,
nonce replay set) -> verifyAgentkitSignature (RPC) -> AgentBook lookupHuman. Fallback gate: if no/invalid AgentKit header, resolve via x-agent-wallet against
a homegrown registry. The response carries a "gate" field: "agentkit" or
"fallback: <reason>", surfaced in the app ("Last call: agentkit"). AgentBook is read on World Chain mainnet (eip155:480) — a free eth_call,
no funds, no tx. Our agent signs on Sepolia (eip155:4801). Single deliberate
mainnet touch, flagged; the fallback covers it if unavailable. AGENT ENDPOINTS (all pass through agentGate)
POST /agent/context     pre-screen a profile or read match context (generateTake
for discovery, generateContext for a match)
POST /agent/icebreaker  draft a first message in a chosen tone
POST /agent/reply       draft the next reply from the last ~8 messages
POST /agent/send        send a message as the agent (viaAgent=true)
GET  /agent/actions     action log + quota { used, freeTrial, credit, remaining }
DELETE /agent/actions/:id  revoke a logged action Every call records an agent_actions row (kind, detail, agentBacked, registered),
shown in the Agent tab and revocable. CONTINUITY QUOTA + x402-STYLE TOP-UP FREE_TRIAL_CALLS per verified human, stored in Upstash Redis (durable across
serverless cold starts). Exhaustion returns HTTP 402 with a top-up target. On-chain settlement (testnet only): the agent settles a native ETH transfer on
World Chain Sepolia (chain id 4801) from the Privy embedded wallet via viem.
Client reports the tx hash to POST /agent/topup; verifyTopUp
(server/src/payments.ts) waits for the receipt and checks recipient, minimum
value, and unused hash (replay protection), then credits N calls in Redis. The wallet defaults to World Chain Sepolia (Privy supportedChains) and calls
wallet_switchEthereumChain to 4801 before sending; the signer pre-checks
balance to give a clean "wallet has 0 ETH" message instead of a viem stack dump. A "Credit from transaction" fallback lets any wallet's tx hash be pasted to
settle, since a keyless exchange wallet cannot sign on a custom chain. ===============================================================================
4. LIVE SELFIE GENDER ESTIMATE (vision + liveness) Client (src/verification/GenderEstimateCapture.tsx): expo-camera front camera,
two frames — neutral then a challenge (turn head / smile / raise eyebrows).
Capture quality is stepped down in a loop until each base64 frame is small
enough to fit Vercel's ~4.5MB request cap (the FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE issue). Server: POST /me/gender-estimate (GET .../challenge issues the challenge).
llm.ts estimateGenderFromFrames calls a Groq VISION model (qwen/qwen3.6-27b;
Llama-4 vision is deprecated on Groq) with JSON mode, checking live /
samePerson / challengePassed plus an estimated label + confidence. Result stored in users.gender_estimate. Frames are held in memory only — never
written to S3 or the DB. Soft signal only: it never blocks, and the profile
shows a private "estimate differs from what you declared" note, never exposed
to other users as verified. ===============================================================================
5. DOMAIN MODEL, MATCHING, AND REALTIME REPO PATTERN (server/src/repo/{types,memory,pg}.ts) getRepo() returns PgRepo when DATABASE_URL is set, else an in-memory MemoryRepo
(used for local dev and stub mode). Same interface for both. DRIZZLE SCHEMA (server/src/db/schema.ts)
users (nullifier_hash, handle, tier, gender_estimate, wallet,
world_session_id, likes_everyone), profiles, likes, matches, messages,
events, rsvps, push_tokens, agent_actions. DOMAIN ROUTES (server/src/routes.ts, all behind requireSession)
GET  /me                    user + profile (photos presigned)
PUT  /me/profile            requireOrb
PUT  /me/handle             unique handle
POST /me/wallet             link agent wallet -> human
POST /me/photo              multipart upload
GET  /discovery             ranked deck (verifiedOnly filter)
POST /likes                 like/pass, auto-match, push
GET  /matches, /matches/:id/messages, POST .../messages
GET  /realtime/token        Ably token
GET  /events, POST/DELETE /events/:id/rsvp   (RSVP requires human tier)
POST /push/register MATCHING (server/src/matching.ts) — pure weighted scorer
interest Jaccard 0.34, distance (haversine) 0.14, tier 0.14,
agentBacked 0.14, age 0.12, reputation 0.12; top candidates enriched with
on-chain reputation signals (onchain.ts: viem publicClient — tx count, balance
band, AgentBook registration; null-safe). REALTIME + MEDIA Chat over Ably websockets (src/realtime/ably.ts) with a polling fallback and a
"loaded" flag used to trigger the agent's auto-suggested opener exactly once. Photos: private S3 objects (server/src/s3.ts) returned as 12-hour presigned GET
URLs; blob.ts routes to S3 when configured, else a data-uri/Vercel Blob fallback. Push via Expo push tokens. ===============================================================================
6. STACK SUMMARY CLIENT
React Native 0.86 / Expo SDK 57, Expo Router
@worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1
@privy-io/expo 0.73 + viem 2.56 (embedded wallet, testnet signing)
expo-camera 57 (live selfie), react-native-webview (World ID widget)
ably 2.28 (chat), expo-secure-store (JWT + session), expo-notifications BACKEND
hono 4.6 on Vercel serverless
@worldcoin/idkit-core 4.2.4 (v4 verify + signing)
@worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1 (AgentBook verify)
drizzle-orm 0.45 + @neondatabase/serverless (Neon Postgres)
@upstash/redis 1.38 (durable per-human quota + nonces)
@aws-sdk/client-s3 + s3-request-presigner (private photos)
ably 2.28 (chat), openai 7.15 -> Groq (LLM text + vision)
viem 2.56 (World Chain reads + testnet receipt verification) CHAINS
World Chain mainnet eip155:480  — AgentBook resolution (read-only eth_call)
World Chain Sepolia eip155:4801 — agent signing + testnet top-up settlement ===============================================================================
7. NOTABLE ENGINEERING DECISIONS / GOTCHAS SOLVED World ID v4 replay: solved with createSession/proveSession instead of
re-running uniqueness proofs; login is a session proof, not a new nullifier. AgentKit header: must declare the extension on eip155:4801 or createHeader
rejects the Sepolia signer. Vercel payload cap: selfie frames are downscaled client-side until under the
request limit; non-JSON error bodies (413) are handled instead of JSON.parse. Node/undici picks broken IPv6 routes to Neon on some networks; db/client.ts
forces IPv4 (dns ipv4first + undici Agent family:4), escape hatch NEON_FORCE_IPV4=0. Privy provisioning failures were swallowed; useWallet now surfaces the real
error (e.g. invalid_native_app_id) with a retry, deduped across call sites. Everything on-chain is testnet only, never mainnet — the one mainnet touch is a
free AgentBook read, explicitly flagged, with a fallback gate.

   (Orb / Selfie tier), an "Agent enabled" badge if that person authorized an
   agent, and a compatibility match score computed from shared interests, age,
   distance, verification tier, and on-chain reputation signals. A "Verified
   humans only" filter is always available.

5. THE AGENT ACTS FOR YOU (the AgentKit part)
   You can register a personal agent. It genuinely acts on your behalf:
     - "Ask my agent about her" — pre-screens a profile and gives you a take
       before you even match.
     - Auto-suggested opener — when you match, your agent drafts a first message
       in your chosen tone (warm / witty / direct). You can send via the agent,
       edit it, or dismiss it.
     - Reply drafting — mid-conversation, it drafts your next reply from the
       thread.
   The recipient always sees a disclosure: "sent by a verified human's agent."
   Nothing is hidden.

6. TRUST GATES ON HIGH-STAKES MOMENTS
   First message and event RSVP are the moments abuse actually happens, so
   human-verification is required there — a bot cannot send the first message or
   claim a limited event seat.

7. AN ACTION LOG YOU CONTROL
   Every action your agent takes is recorded and shown to you, each tagged with
   whether it was cryptographically verified through AgentBook. You can revoke
   any action. You always know what your agent did in your name.


===============================================================================
WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT
===============================================================================

- Verification is the product, not a feature. The entire funnel is gated on
  proof of a unique human. This is Sybil resistance applied to dating.

- AI is disclosed and accountable, not hidden. Most apps pretend AI is not
  there. We surface it and make it provably human-backed. That flips AI from a
  trust-destroyer into a trust signal.

- Privacy-preserving by construction. World ID proves personhood without
  revealing who you are. We store an anonymous nullifier, not your identity.

- Gender is handled honestly. It is an ESTIMATE from a live selfie, always
  labelled as such, always separate from the real human badge. We refuse to
  launder a guess as a verified fact.


===============================================================================
THE PRIZE ANGLE (ETHOnline — World Track)
===============================================================================

The build targets both World prizes at once, and they reinforce each other:

- AgentKit Continuity: a human-backed agent acts in chat and discovery, and
  every action routes through a real AgentKit-protected backend that resolves
  the agent to a human through AgentBook on World Chain. A durable, per-human
  free-trial quota (keyed to the verified human, not a device or wallet) demos
  real continuity, with an on-chain testnet top-up when the trial runs out.

- Selfie Check / Proof of Human: human verification is used as a risk,
  eligibility, fairness, continuity, and abuse-prevention signal at the two
  highest-stakes moments — first message and event RSVP — not as a one-time
  checkbox.


===============================================================================
ONE-SENTENCE PITCH
===============================================================================

Proof of Attraction is a dating app where you can finally be certain the person
you match with is a real, unique human — and where AI is allowed to help, but
only when it is provably backed by one.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
PROOF OF ATTRACTION
How It's Made — Deep Technical Description
ETHOnline 2026 — World Track

===============================================================================
1. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE
===============================================================================

Three moving parts:

  [ React Native app ]  --HTTPS-->  [ Hono API on Vercel ]  -->  [ Neon Postgres ]
        (Expo)                          (serverless)                (Drizzle ORM)
           |                                |  \--> Upstash Redis (quota/nonces)
           |                                |  \--> AWS S3 (private photos)
           |                                |  \--> Ably (realtime chat)
           |                                |  \--> Groq LLM (OpenAI-compatible)
           |                                |  \--> World Chain (AgentBook, reputation)
           |                                \--> developer.world.org/api/v4/verify
           \--> WebView -> IDKit (World App) for World ID proofs
           \--> Privy embedded wallet + viem for testnet top-ups

- Client: React Native via Expo SDK 57, Expo Router for navigation. Standalone
  app (not a World Mini App), built as an Android dev/release APK.
- Backend: Hono, deployed to Vercel serverless (local dev via @hono/node-server).
  Stable public alias: server-two-steel-51.vercel.app.
- Repo split: /app and /src (client), /server (backend), /docs (submission +
  feedback docs). Drizzle migrations in /server/drizzle.


===============================================================================
2. IDENTITY, AUTH, AND SESSIONS (the hard part)
===============================================================================

There is no "Sign in with World ID" session product — IDKit produces a one-shot
proof, not a session. So we own the session lifecycle.

WORLD ID 4.0 SPECIFICS THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN
- We use idkit-core 4.2.4 and verify against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify/{rp_id}.
- v4 requires a signed rp_context: the backend signs a short-lived request token
  with an RP signing key (signRequest from @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing) before
  the widget can open. App ID + RP ID + signing key are the three portal values.
- v4 uniqueness nullifiers are ONE-TIME per (rp, action). Re-verifying the same
  action returns nullifier_replayed. There is no "max verifications" toggle on a
  v4 action page. This is why naive "verify again to log in" does not work.

THE FLOW WE BUILT
- Signup: proofOfHuman uniqueness proof (Sybil check, action from
  EXPO_PUBLIC_WORLD_ID_ACTION) -> backend verifies -> issues our own HS256 JWT
  keyed to the anonymous nullifier -> upserts a users row. Immediately after, we
  run IDKit.createSession and store the returned session_id on the user
  (users.world_session_id) and in SecureStore.
- Login: IDKit.proveSession(session_id) -> POST /auth/session/prove -> new JWT.
  No uniqueness re-proof, so no replay. On a fresh device with no stored session,
  the user types their handle -> GET /auth/session/lookup?handle= resolves the
  session_id -> proveSession.
- The WebView page (server/public/verify.html) takes a mode param:
  uniqueness | create-session | prove-session, and drives IDKit accordingly.
  A native bridge (WorldIdProvider / WorldIdModal, react-native-webview) returns
  the proof to the app.

TOKEN HANDLING
- JWT (7-day) stored in expo-secure-store, attached as a Bearer token by
  authedFetch, which transparently retries once via POST /auth/refresh on a 401
  before signing out.
- The derived humanId (from the nullifier) is the exact key the AgentKit quota
  counts against — tying agent continuity to the verified human.


===============================================================================
3. THE AGENT — REAL AGENTKIT, NOT A COSMETIC CHATBOT
===============================================================================

What makes it a genuine AgentKit integration: every in-chat/discovery agent
action routes through an AgentKit-protected backend endpoint, and the server
verifies the caller against AgentBook on every call.

CLIENT SIDE (src/agent/agentkit.ts)
- Uses @worldcoin/agentkit createAgentkitClient + declareAgentkitExtension.
- CRITICAL: the extension is declared with network 'eip155:4801' (World Chain
  Sepolia). Without the network, supportedChains is empty and createHeader throws
  "Signer eip155:4801/eip191 is not supported" — the bug that silently dropped to
  the fallback gate. The signer is the Privy embedded wallet (eip191, signMessage).

SERVER SIDE (server/src/agentkit.ts + agentGate in index.ts)
- Real verify path: parseAgentkitHeader -> validateAgentkitMessage (maxAge 300s,
  nonce replay set) -> verifyAgentkitSignature (RPC) -> AgentBook lookupHuman.
- Fallback gate: if no/invalid AgentKit header, resolve via x-agent-wallet against
  a homegrown registry. The response carries a "gate" field: "agentkit" or
  "fallback: <reason>", surfaced in the app ("Last call: agentkit").
- AgentBook is read on World Chain mainnet (eip155:480) — a free eth_call,
  no funds, no tx. Our agent signs on Sepolia (eip155:4801). Single deliberate
  mainnet touch, flagged; the fallback covers it if unavailable.

AGENT ENDPOINTS (all pass through agentGate)
  POST /agent/context     pre-screen a profile or read match context (generateTake
                          for discovery, generateContext for a match)
  POST /agent/icebreaker  draft a first message in a chosen tone
  POST /agent/reply       draft the next reply from the last ~8 messages
  POST /agent/send        send a message as the agent (viaAgent=true)
  GET  /agent/actions     action log + quota { used, freeTrial, credit, remaining }
  DELETE /agent/actions/:id  revoke a logged action

Every call records an agent_actions row (kind, detail, agentBacked, registered),
shown in the Agent tab and revocable.

CONTINUITY QUOTA + x402-STYLE TOP-UP
- FREE_TRIAL_CALLS per verified human, stored in Upstash Redis (durable across
  serverless cold starts). Exhaustion returns HTTP 402 with a top-up target.
- On-chain settlement (testnet only): the agent settles a native ETH transfer on
  World Chain Sepolia (chain id 4801) from the Privy embedded wallet via viem.
  Client reports the tx hash to POST /agent/topup; verifyTopUp
  (server/src/payments.ts) waits for the receipt and checks recipient, minimum
  value, and unused hash (replay protection), then credits N calls in Redis.
- The wallet defaults to World Chain Sepolia (Privy supportedChains) and calls
  wallet_switchEthereumChain to 4801 before sending; the signer pre-checks
  balance to give a clean "wallet has 0 ETH" message instead of a viem stack dump.
- A "Credit from transaction" fallback lets any wallet's tx hash be pasted to
  settle, since a keyless exchange wallet cannot sign on a custom chain.


===============================================================================
4. LIVE SELFIE GENDER ESTIMATE (vision + liveness)
===============================================================================

- Client (src/verification/GenderEstimateCapture.tsx): expo-camera front camera,
  two frames — neutral then a challenge (turn head / smile / raise eyebrows).
  Capture quality is stepped down in a loop until each base64 frame is small
  enough to fit Vercel's ~4.5MB request cap (the FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE issue).
- Server: POST /me/gender-estimate (GET .../challenge issues the challenge).
  llm.ts estimateGenderFromFrames calls a Groq VISION model (qwen/qwen3.6-27b;
  Llama-4 vision is deprecated on Groq) with JSON mode, checking live /
  samePerson / challengePassed plus an estimated label + confidence.
- Result stored in users.gender_estimate. Frames are held in memory only — never
  written to S3 or the DB. Soft signal only: it never blocks, and the profile
  shows a private "estimate differs from what you declared" note, never exposed
  to other users as verified.


===============================================================================
5. DOMAIN MODEL, MATCHING, AND REALTIME
===============================================================================

REPO PATTERN (server/src/repo/{types,memory,pg}.ts)
- getRepo() returns PgRepo when DATABASE_URL is set, else an in-memory MemoryRepo
  (used for local dev and stub mode). Same interface for both.

DRIZZLE SCHEMA (server/src/db/schema.ts)
  users (nullifier_hash, handle, tier, gender_estimate, wallet,
         world_session_id, likes_everyone), profiles, likes, matches, messages,
         events, rsvps, push_tokens, agent_actions.

DOMAIN ROUTES (server/src/routes.ts, all behind requireSession)
  GET  /me                    user + profile (photos presigned)
  PUT  /me/profile            requireOrb
  PUT  /me/handle             unique handle
  POST /me/wallet             link agent wallet -> human
  POST /me/photo              multipart upload
  GET  /discovery             ranked deck (verifiedOnly filter)
  POST /likes                 like/pass, auto-match, push
  GET  /matches, /matches/:id/messages, POST .../messages
  GET  /realtime/token        Ably token
  GET  /events, POST/DELETE /events/:id/rsvp   (RSVP requires human tier)
  POST /push/register

MATCHING (server/src/matching.ts) — pure weighted scorer
  interest Jaccard 0.34, distance (haversine) 0.14, tier 0.14,
  agentBacked 0.14, age 0.12, reputation 0.12; top candidates enriched with
  on-chain reputation signals (onchain.ts: viem publicClient — tx count, balance
  band, AgentBook registration; null-safe).

REALTIME + MEDIA
- Chat over Ably websockets (src/realtime/ably.ts) with a polling fallback and a
  "loaded" flag used to trigger the agent's auto-suggested opener exactly once.
- Photos: private S3 objects (server/src/s3.ts) returned as 12-hour presigned GET
  URLs; blob.ts routes to S3 when configured, else a data-uri/Vercel Blob fallback.
- Push via Expo push tokens.


===============================================================================
6. STACK SUMMARY
===============================================================================

CLIENT
  React Native 0.86 / Expo SDK 57, Expo Router
  @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1
  @privy-io/expo 0.73 + viem 2.56 (embedded wallet, testnet signing)
  expo-camera 57 (live selfie), react-native-webview (World ID widget)
  ably 2.28 (chat), expo-secure-store (JWT + session), expo-notifications

BACKEND
  hono 4.6 on Vercel serverless
  @worldcoin/idkit-core 4.2.4 (v4 verify + signing)
  @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1 (AgentBook verify)
  drizzle-orm 0.45 + @neondatabase/serverless (Neon Postgres)
  @upstash/redis 1.38 (durable per-human quota + nonces)
  @aws-sdk/client-s3 + s3-request-presigner (private photos)
  ably 2.28 (chat), openai 7.15 -> Groq (LLM text + vision)
  viem 2.56 (World Chain reads + testnet receipt verification)

CHAINS
  World Chain mainnet eip155:480  — AgentBook resolution (read-only eth_call)
  World Chain Sepolia eip155:4801 — agent signing + testnet top-up settlement


===============================================================================
7. NOTABLE ENGINEERING DECISIONS / GOTCHAS SOLVED
===============================================================================

- World ID v4 replay: solved with createSession/proveSession instead of
  re-running uniqueness proofs; login is a session proof, not a new nullifier.
- AgentKit header: must declare the extension on eip155:4801 or createHeader
  rejects the Sepolia signer.
- Vercel payload cap: selfie frames are downscaled client-side until under the
  request limit; non-JSON error bodies (413) are handled instead of JSON.parse.
- Node/undici picks broken IPv6 routes to Neon on some networks; db/client.ts
  forces IPv4 (dns ipv4first + undici Agent family:4), escape hatch NEON_FORCE_IPV4=0.
- Privy provisioning failures were swallowed; useWallet now surfaces the real
  error (e.g. invalid_native_app_id) with a retry, deduped across call sites.
- Everything on-chain is testnet only, never mainnet — the one mainnet touch is a
  free AgentBook read, explicitly flagged, with a fallback gate.

projects.title: Blockhead 2026
projects.description: Explore and interact with the decentralized web in a modular, plug-and-play local-first client!
projects.project_description: In early 2026, after five years iterating on the same codebase over dozens of hackathons, I decided to dive headfirst into the world of agentic software factory engineering and rebuild Blockhead from scratch. The result: a local-first interface with a highly accurate, irreducible, internally consistent ontology capable of modeling integrations with any decentralized protocol, blockchain ecosystem, wallet, node or data source. Browse artifacts across the decentralized web, connect existing wallets across any ecosystem, interact with protocols of all shapes and sizes, and plug and play with your own nodes and data providers leveraging Blockhead's extensive library of adapters.
projects.how_its_made: Blockhead's codebase models every stack layer explicitly and modularly. Provider sources handle external requests and data queries. Resolvers map responses into native entities. Selectors uniquely identify entities and route URLs with distinct sets of fields. Local-first collections cache data and feed the UI views. For ETHOnline 2026, I extended its native data model with Messari Standardized Subgraphs and adding Ledger support to its wallet interface. The Graph integration queries live Messari Standardized Subgraphs. Protocols, pools, block observations, and ordered pool assets use native selectors. Historical requests preserve the deployment and block hash. Reported schema versions remain separate from the versions expected by our deployment configuration. Missing data is an error, not an empty result. Ledger uses Device Management Kit, Ethereum Signer Kit, and the official Speculos transport. The wallet adapter checks signing authority and verifies message signatures. Browser tests exercise device approval, rejection, and persisted request history. In the demo, I have an automated harness drive a browser to demonstrate data queries and local-first client side caching. It also drives an instance of Ledger's Speculos emulator, clicking through screens to connect to Blockhead's UI and facilitate a signing request. Uniswap V3 and Sushi V3 financial observations use the same view and query pattern. Each observation retains its exact values, source deployment, schema version and block. Reloading an observation requests that block, rather than silently replacing it with current data. A separate Uniswap view interprets pool state, including its raw token ratio, fee configuration and oracle capacity. The Ledger flow reviews a message on the official Speculos emulator, signs it and saves a request that can be reopened after reload. Once I have the stack layers, data modeling and automation harnesses fully nailed down, I plan to continue building out the UI layer and implement immersive graph visualizations on top of the client-side cache.

projects.title: Reveal
projects.description: Buy a sealed mystery night. You know the vibe, the experience stays secret until you shake
projects.project_description: Reveal is a two-sided marketplace for sealed mystery nights. You do not book a named show or pick a venue from a list. You buy a crate. Before you pay, the product only shows the vibe: category, neighborhood, time window, mystery USDC price, and a value floor so you know the deal is real. The actual experience stays locked until after checkout. That secrecy is the product. Empty seats an hour before showtime are almost worthless, and public discounts train people to wait while bots scoop the good inventory. Reveal flips both sides at once. Merchants quietly clear leftover capacity as sealed crates instead of training the market to delay. Buyers get the thrill of not knowing what they pulled, with guardrails so the surprise stays fair. The buyer journey is built around that mystery. Guests browse constraints-only cards, sign in with Privy, prove they are a live human with World Selfie Check, pay USDC on Base, then shake the crate open. Only then do title, details, and a door pass appear together. One crate per verified human per drop: the nullifier is unique for that night, so a second selfie cannot double-dip. Identity never goes to the merchant. After payment, a non-transferable Hedera Reveal Pass is minted with a QR for check-in; because it cannot be transferred, the night cannot be scalped after reveal. If a drop never reveals, payment can refund. Merchants get the other half of the loop. A cinema, theatre, or dining room lists leftover seats as a sealed crate, watches a dashboard, and scans the guest QR at the door to redeem the pass and settle the seat. There is also an AI concierge path: an agent pays an x402 availability API on Hedera via Blocky402, then reads which mystery nights are still open by area without scraping the consumer UI. So demand can arrive through the app or through chat, while supply still publishes once. Consumer loop: auth → selfie → pay → shake → pass. Merchant loop: create → dashboard → scan. Agent loop: 402 challenge → settle → availability. The whole point is one marketplace that protects the mystery for buyers and liquidates expiring inventory for merchants without spoiling either side. Both sides win.
projects.how_its_made: Reveal was built from scratch during ETHOnline as a pnpm monorepo. The consumer, merchant, and agent surfaces live in a Next.js app. An Express service stays up as the x402 availability API. Drizzle owns the schema for PGlite locally or Postgres in production. A shared Hedera package handles Reveal Pass issue and redeem. Partner tech is not bolted on for a checklist: each one sits on a critical path in the mystery loop. The UX is intentional about spoilers. Drop cards show category, area, time, and price only. Venue and title stay blurred until the shake animation finishes. Rarity heat is computed from deal quality, face value versus mystery price, so a stronger discount feels rarer without revealing what you bought. After unbox, XP, streak, and badges land on the player profile, and a public board shows live pulls without unsealing other buyers’ crates. That keeps the demo cinematic while the fairness rules stay real. Money and auth run through Privy embedded wallets plus viem on Base Sepolia. On login, users without wallets get one automatically. Buyers transfer USDC into escrow from the buy flow; if the night never reveals there is a refund path. The UI tracks USDC and gas as separate balances on purpose, because hackathon demos often die when someone has faucet USDC but no Base Sepolia ETH. Merchant routes are allowlisted by Privy DID so venue tools stay gated without a custom auth stack. Fairness is World IDKit v4 Selfie Check. The server signs the RP request, the widget collects the proof, and we post the payload to World’s v4 verify endpoint. We store action plus nullifier plus dropId so a second selfie cannot buy the same mystery night, and we never forward identity to the merchant. Selfie Check is still beta-gated, so we kept a labeled Demo verify path that still hits our verify and uniqueness APIs rather than silently mocking pay, reveal, and pass. That let us record the full stack while waiting on Portal enablement. The night itself is tokenized on Hedera. After USDC payment confirms, we mint a non-fungible Reveal Pass with the Hashgraph SDK over HTS, associate and transfer it, surface HashScan links, and redeem it when the merchant scans the door QR. ATS factory addresses are documented for Tokenization of Anything alignment; the live hackathon path is HTS because the full Equity.create diamond was too heavy for the event window. Consumer Hedera keys are operator-custodied for mint on the demo path, and that is disclosed. The agentic path is Hedera x402. GET /availability returns HTTP 402 with an exact-scheme Hedera challenge and Blocky402 as facilitator. The /agent console settles that challenge, then reads remaining mystery inventory by area. That is how AI chat can discover sealed nights without scraping the consumer UI, and how the same inventory serves both the human UI and the agent. The hacky but useful glue is an in-process Next.js store that auto-seeds a demo crate so recording does not depend on a cold database, while Drizzle remains ready for durable Postgres. Put together, Privy moves money, World enforces one human per crate, Hedera carries the pass and the paid availability API, and the product in the middle stays what it claims to be: a sealed mystery night for both sides of the market.

projects.title: AgentAlpha
projects.description: Agent marketplace that grades what it sells — DeFi forecasts via x402 on Hedera.
projects.project_description: AgentAlpha is a verifiable DeFi signal market built on Hedera testnet. It solves a fundamental problem in the emerging agent economy: when Agent A pays Agent B for a prediction, how do you know the prediction was any good? Today's A2A protocols (Google A2A, ACP, etc.) give agents an "Agent Card" and let them self-describe capabilities, but they have no mechanism to objectively measure output quality after the fact. An agent can claim 99% accuracy with zero verification. Crypto trading signal groups operate the same way — Chainalysis estimates 87% of crypto signal providers show no verifiable track record, and CoinTelegraph reports that "premium" signal groups routinely delete losing calls. AgentAlpha introduces three innovations that go beyond existing A2A paradigms: COMMIT-REVEAL VERIFICATION: Every forecast is hash-committed on-chain before its target time, then publicly revealed and graded against Pyth oracle prices. No backdating. No selective disclosure. QUALITY ≠ COMPLETION: Most A2A protocols measure "did the agent respond?" — we measure "was the response actually correct?" using oracle-backed directional accuracy, MAE in basis points, and grade coverage as separate public metrics. REVEAL COVERAGE AS A FIRST-CLASS METRIC: A provider's willingness to publicly reveal predictions after the alpha window expires — proving trust in their own track record — is measured independently. Buyers filter on reveal_pct alongside accuracy, creating market pressure for transparency without slashing or staking. The system uses x402 v2 micropayments settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera. Buyers sign exact HBAR transfers (0.001 HBAR per forecast), with per-request caps, kill switches, and bounded wallets. Payments are final — a bad forecast doesn't trigger a refund, but it does tank your public metrics. Two real paid requests have been completed end-to-end with on-chain commitments, HCS audit receipts, and public reveals. The buyer agent autonomously discovered the provider, verified its Agent Card, enforced spend policy, and completed the purchase without human intervention. Designed but not yet built: a Subscription Vault using HIP-1215 scheduled transactions for recurring payments, and multi-provider/multi-horizon support. These are documented as P1 scope — we're transparent about what's live vs. what's designed.
projects.how_its_made: SMART CONTRACTS (Solidity, Hedera testnet): AgentRegistry: On-chain identity, gateway/payee binding, metadata hash, active flag. Owner-authorized lifecycle management. SignalLedger: Commitment storage, permissionless reveal, oracle-backed grading using Pyth price feeds. Emits grade events, never moves money. Both contracts are deployed and verified on Sourcify. BACKEND (TypeScript, Node.js ≥22): x402 Gateway: Generates schema-valid forecasts, validates Blocky402 payment, persists before settlement, commits to SignalLedger, returns response with salt for buyer-side verification. Indexer: Reads Mirror Node events, reconciles payment references against actual transfers, computes rolling discovery metrics from public evidence. Worker: Restart-safe background loop for HCS audit receipts, reveal submission after target time, grade retries with Pyth Hermes historical data. Store: SQLite with durable WAL mode, process lock, forward-only projections. BUYER AGENT (TypeScript CLI): Autonomous discovery → policy filter (5 eligible samples, 80% reveal coverage) → quote validation → exact HBAR signing → commitment verification → resume recovery. Kill switch, per-provider daily cap, global daily cap, token/network allowlist. FRONTEND (Vanilla HTML/JS): Discovery dashboard, seller profiles with raw metrics, signal evidence pages with transaction links, buyer activity view. No framework, served by the same Express instance. KEY INTEGRATIONS: Blocky402: x402 v2 payment verification and settlement on Hedera testnet Pyth/Hermes: Historical price data for oracle-backed grading (currently blocked by InvalidWormholeVaa on testnet — reveal works, grade is evidenced as oracle_unavailable) Hedera Mirror Node: Event indexing, transaction evidence, payment reconciliation HCS: Append-only audit receipts (no secret data before target time) All code is TypeScript with 94.57% test coverage (46 unit tests + 13 contract tests). CI passes on GitHub Actions.

- AgentRegistry: On-chain identity, gateway/payee binding, metadata hash, active flag. Owner-authorized lifecycle management.

projects.title: Wikshi
projects.description: Give your agent an inbox, a voice, and a face. Paid per use with x402 on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Imagine your agent finding business contacts, sending emails, making phone calls, and hosting video meetings for you, then bringing the answers back. AI can do a lot of research, but when getting an answer means actually talking to someone, you're still doing the work yourself. Wikshi gives your agent its own inbox, a voice for phone calls, and a face for video meetings, along with the research and contact data to reach the right people. Wikshi provides 14 services through x402 on Hedera. Your agent discovers a service, gets a quote, and pays per use in native HBAR or HTS USDC through Blocky402. You don't need separate provider accounts, API keys, or subscriptions. Your agent can: Research people and companies: Search the web, discover businesses and professional profiles, and read source pages for details. Find business contacts: Look up available business emails and phone numbers, identify someone by email, or find relevant contacts at a company. Maintain its own inbox: Create an email address, receive responses, and keep conversations together. Send emails and follow up: Contact people, read their replies, and continue the conversation from its inbox. Call someone: Ask your questions, follow up on their answers, and return the call transcript. Host a video meeting: Send a guest link for an AI-led conversation of up to five minutes. Your agent asks the questions and retrieves the transcript. You don't need to attend. Calls and meetings are metered by the second, with unused prepaid funds refunded on-chain to the original payer. Signed receipts record usage and charges, and receipt hashes are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service. External agents can buy services directly or delegate tasks through A2A. Wikshi's hosted agent has completed a real paid A2A research request within an approved budget, with settlement and receipt verification on Hedera testnet. For example, you ask your agent to find a manufacturer that can deliver 500 custom bags before an event. It researches suppliers, finds their business contacts, creates an inbox, and emails for quotes. As replies arrive, it follows up on missing details. It calls one supplier to confirm delivery and invites another to a video meeting to discuss your requirements. Each paid step goes through x402 on Hedera. You get a shortlist backed by quotes and conversation records, with receipts showing what your agent spent.
projects.how_its_made: Wikshi uses x402 to quote and collect payment before an agent's request runs. Payments settle through Blocky402 as native HBAR or HTS USDC transfers on Hedera testnet, without a custom settlement contract. Blocky402 pays the purchase's network fee, so a buyer paying in USDC doesn't need HBAR for gas. Each payment memo binds the transfer to one operation. We check Mirror Node records and reject reused payments. For calls and meetings, the backend meters seconds used, calculates the final charge, and refunds the unused prepayment in the original asset. Signed receipts record usage and billing. Their hashes are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service, allowing a verifier to check the receipt, arithmetic, and payment trail without exposing private results. One important detail: we save refund transactions before submitting them. If a network response times out, we check the existing transaction rather than send another refund. Persistent operation state also lets agents resume work without purchasing it again.

projects.title: AgentPass
projects.description: AgentPass: a human-backed AI agent that pays to check your DeFi risk.
projects.project_description: AgentPass is a web app for safely getting an actionable DeFi risk check. A user verifies that they are human with World ID, then gives a named agent its own limited spending budget. The agent queries live lending positions across Aave and Compound through The Graph, computes a reasoned risk score and recommendation, and returns the result with a verifiable payment receipt. Instead of trusting an API key or a black-box dashboard, users can see the agent identity, activity, budget, payment, and analysis in one continuous flow. The same service can also be discovered and called by other agents.
projects.how_its_made: We built AgentPass as a pnpm TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js dashboard, a Hono API, and reusable packages for identity, data, payments, verification, and discovery. The Graph Subgraph MCP and Messari standardized lending schema provide live Aave V3 and Compound V3 positions; a risk engine converts those positions into factors, a 0-100 score, and a recommendation, with 60-second caching to protect the free tier. The API is protected by x402: an unpaid request returns 402 pricing metadata, the agent checks its HBAR session budget, signs a Hedera testnet payment through the Blocky402 facilitator, retries with X-PAYMENT, and receives a receipt. World ID gates spending authority, ENSv2 on Sepolia gives the agent a permissioned onchain identity, and Bazantic exposes it for agent discovery. A notable implementation detail is that every sponsor integration is a step in the same user action rather than a collection of disconnected demos.

projects.title: Arc Reserve
projects.description: Tokenize green projects and assets with a real price floor and stablecoin yield
projects.project_description: Arc-Reserve enables tokenized investment in green and renewable energy projects via blockchain technology. For example we have project features Solar Indonesia 01 (SOLAR01), a 50 MW solar installation located in Indonesia.     Operational Architecture: Project owners list eligible renewable initiatives on the Arc-Reserve platform. KYC-verified investors purchase asset-backed tokens using stablecoins. Tokens do not mean as equity or corporate ownership; rather, they grant holders a proportional right to underlying real-world cash flows generated by the energy assets.   Revenue Cycle: Revenues are routed on-chain and distributed programmatically: the majority is disbursed as yield to token holders, while remaining allocations fund a protected reserve, operator compensation, and protocol fees. Investors maintain continuous exit liquidity through automated stablecoin redemptions backed directly by reserve capital.     Liquidity & Price Protection: A portion of capital raised during offerings is locked into active Uniswap V3 liquidity positions, establishing a fully backed price floor that prevents catastrophic downside volatility. When revenue profit are distributed, the liquidity baseline are increased, so it will raise the token price. And we ensure with this feature the token price will not fall below the baseline price and rugpulled.   This application operates across three testnets: Base Sepolia, Hedera Testnet, and Circle Arc Testnet. We also use stablecoin, in here we mock USDC so people can invest to the renewable project / assets using USDC and enable save investment. pitch deck link: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/17aMyc1LmNBKvgI93tzBXzFVPxabi_jW9v1d20ccjqc0/edit?usp=sharing
projects.how_its_made:
Smart Contracts & Compliance: Smart contracts were authored in Solidity and validated using Foundry. Token transfers are strictly restricted to KYC-compliant wallets through integrated IdentityRegistry and Compliance modules. The Vault contract segregates funds across five discrete accounting buckets: issuer proceeds, protected reserve, market liquidity, revenue, and protocol fees. Market Management & Yield: The Market Manager governs concentrated Uniswap V3 liquidity positions under strict immutable constraints: token minting is prohibited, and execution is restricted to explicitly allocated inventory. Trading surplus automatically flows into the reserve vault, systematically raising the asset price floor over time. Application Layer & Multi-Chain Deployment: Off-chain infrastructure comprises a real-time event indexing service, a RESTful API backend, and a React frontend for asset discovery and analytics. The complete architecture is deployed across Base Sepolia, Hedera Testnet, and Circle Arc Testnet. On networks lacking canonical Uniswap V3 deployments (Hedera and Arc), official Uniswap V3 factory and pool contracts were compiled and deployed directly. For infra and deployment we’re using docker, nginx, aws. And for AI code we use opencode, claude code, and open spec for specs management. We also use google stitch for visualizing the UI and application flow. Core contracts, one line per chain: Base Sepolia (84532)

projects.title: Scenario Engine
projects.description: SCENARIO: hedera-harness runs native multi-actor Hedera plans and checks the public mirror
projects.project_description: This is an open-source improvement to hedera-dev/hedera-harness, the CLI that drives a coding agent to build Hedera apps and then decides whether the work passed. The harness already had CHAIN: one throwaway testnet wallet injected into the generated app. That is the wrong layer for two-party transfers, HTS airdrops, or HCS messages. People were left hoping Playwright clicked Transfer, or trusting a toast after the agent wrote 40 to 80 lines of SDK boilerplate. A toast is not proof. The agent does not get to grade itself. This project adds SCENARIO, an opt-in fifth stage. You write a short YAML plan with named actors (alice, bob), steps (transfer HBAR, create a token, associate, airdrop, create an HCS topic, submit a message), and asserts. The harness funds those actors from your testnet operator, sends real transactions with the official @hiero-ledger/sdk, then polls the public testnet mirror until the effects are visible: Bob's HBAR, Bob's token balance, the topic text. The coding agent does not run this and does not declare success. Stage order is GENERATE, ASSERT, SCENARIO, SMOKE, EVALUATE. A failed native plan skips the browser, so you do not pay for Playwright when the chain work already failed. A mirror or SDK outage is treated as infrastructure, not as an app failure. There is also hedera-harness validate-scenario, which runs the plan alone with no agent. That is the demo path. Testnet only. Mainnet is rejected. Actor keys are never committed.
projects.how_its_made: Built in TypeScript on top of hedera-harness 2.0 (schema v3, their dev branch). The new code lives in src/scenario/: a YAML plan parser, operator env reuse from chainValidation, real AccountCreate / AccountDelete for named actors, an executor that uses the @hiero-ledger/sdk already shipped with the CLI, and a small REST client that polls https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com for HBAR balances, token balances, topic messages, and pending airdrops. Steps map to real SDK transactions: TransferTransaction, TokenCreateTransaction, TokenAssociateTransaction, TokenAirdropTransaction, TokenClaimAirdropTransaction (PendingAirdropId built from the mirror, not a fake fromString), TopicCreateTransaction, TopicMessageSubmitTransaction. Later steps can refer to earlier ones by id (token: gold, topic: chat). The stage is wired into attemptStages so it runs after ASSERT and before SMOKE. sessionRunner provisions actors once per run and sweeps leftover HBAR at the end (best effort: a token treasury cannot be deleted). doctor checks operator env and plan shape. CLI help and validate-scenario call the same executor as a full run. harnessGit treats scenario-actors.json as a secret. No in-process fake ledger. No simulated consensus. Tests cover plan parsing, recipe load (inline and file:), mainnet rejection, CLI wiring, and cleanup of actor keys. Docs are in docs/scenarios.md plus the README stage table. The skeleton ships a two-actor HBAR / HTS / HCS example.

The new code lives in src/scenario/: a YAML plan parser, operator env reuse from chainValidation, real AccountCreate / AccountDelete for named actors, an executor that uses the @hiero-ledger/sdk already shipped with the CLI, and a small REST client that polls https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com for HBAR balances, token balances, topic messages, and pending airdrops.

Steps map to real SDK transactions: TransferTransaction, TokenCreateTransaction, TokenAssociateTransaction, TokenAirdropTransaction, TokenClaimAirdropTransaction (PendingAirdropId built from the mirror, not a fake fromString), TopicCreateTransaction, TopicMessageSubmitTransaction. Later steps can refer to earlier ones by id (token: gold, topic: chat).

The stage is wired into attemptStages so it runs after ASSERT and before SMOKE. sessionRunner provisions actors once per run and sweeps leftover HBAR at the end (best effort: a token treasury cannot be deleted). doctor checks operator env and plan shape. CLI help and validate-scenario call the same executor as a full run. harnessGit treats scenario-actors.json as a secret.

No in-process fake ledger. No simulated consensus. Tests cover plan parsing, recipe load (inline and file:), mainnet rejection, CLI wiring, and cleanup of actor keys. Docs are in docs/scenarios.md plus the README stage table. The skeleton ships a two-actor HBAR / HTS / HCS example.

projects.title: Gantry
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that prices every swap by the caller's on-chain behaviour. Nobody gets blocked.
projects.project_description: A sandwich bot waits for your trade, buys in front of it, sells right after, and pockets the difference. As far as the pool is concerned that bot is just another customer paying exactly the same fee as you. Gantry changes that. Gantry is a Uniswap v4 hook that prices each swap by the behaviour of the address actually paying for it. A clean wallet pays 0.05%. An address nobody has scored pays 0.30%. Something that looks like it is extracting pays 0.60%, and a confirmed sandwicher pays 1.00%. Nobody is ever blocked and nothing is blacklisted. If you want to sandwich the pool you still can, you just pay twenty times what a clean wallet pays for the privilege, and that extra goes to the liquidity providers you took it from. Tiers are not something we assign by hand. An off-chain scorer reads real Ethereum mainnet behaviour, the scoring itself runs inside a Chainlink confidential workflow, and the result reaches the chain as a DON-signed report. The contract holding tiers only accepts writes from the Chainlink receiver address, so the deployer cannot set anyone's tier. One design detail worth calling out: shared infrastructure is protected. Uniswap's own router reverts more often than almost anything else we measured, which on raw numbers reads as extraction. But thousands of ordinary people trade through that router, so charging it would charge all of them. Any address marked as shared gets clamped back to the default tier no matter what it scores. It is live on Sepolia. The site shows every swap the pool has priced so far, including one wallet that paid 1.00%, then 0.30%, then 0.05% on the same pool at the same size, because its tier moved between trades.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity and Foundry. The hook implements beforeSwap and returns a fee with Uniswap's OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG set, so the pool charges what the hook says instead of its own static fee. v4 reads a hook's permissions out of its address, so the deploy salt was mined with CREATE2 until the address ended in 0080, whose low 14 bits are exactly the BEFORE_SWAP permission bit. The hard part of v4 is that inside beforeSwap, sender is the router, not the trader. Every trade arriving through a router looks identical. We solved it with an EIP-712 attestation: the frontend has you sign a free off-chain message, passes it through as hookData, and the hook recovers the signer and spends a nonce so the same signature cannot be replayed. No signature just means you pay the default tier, so the hook never depends on our frontend to stay correct. The Graph does the reading. Two subgraphs, one on Sepolia for the hook's own events and one on mainnet for behaviour, plus nine published Substreams modules written in Rust and compiled to WASM. Substreams is doing something a subgraph structurally cannot. A reverted transaction emits no logs, so it is invisible to any event-based indexer, and yet a failed sandwich attempt is one of the strongest signals there is. Substreams reads transaction traces, which carry status, and that has surfaced over 12,000 reverted attempts that no subgraph could ever see. To keep this live rather than a committed snapshot we run substreams sink postgres as a systemd service on our own VPS, following the chain head into Postgres, with a small Node API in front that both the site and the Chainlink workflow read. Chainlink CRE does the scoring. The workflow runs with handlerInTee, so it executes inside a TEE, and it pulls the tier thresholds from runtime.getSecrets() rather than from source. That matters: the rules are public, but a published threshold is just a number for a bot to park itself underneath. Results leave as a DON-signed report through EVMClient.writeReport() into TierReportReceiver, which verifies the workflow id, name and owner before it is allowed to touch TierOracle. Frontend is Next.js on Vercel. The swap page quotes you from the oracle before you sign anything, so the price you are promised is the price the hook actually reads. The hacky part worth mentioning: The Graph's rules say static datasets do not qualify, and the textbook fix, a Substreams-powered subgraph, turns out to be dead for EVM chains now. The error text says so outright. Rather than ship a snapshot and call it live, we stood the real sink up ourselves. It runs in 24MB of RAM with a 20MB API next to it, and the committed snapshot survives only as a fallback for when the box is unreachable.

projects.title: GraphMind
projects.description: Natural language DeFi research assistant powered by The Graph's Subgraph MCP
projects.project_description: GraphMind is a DeFi research assistant I built for the ETHGlobal hackathon. Instead of digging through dashboards or writing GraphQL by hand, you just ask plain-English questions, like "what are the top lending pools by TVL on Aave?" and it queries live onchain data through The Graph's Subgraph MCP, reasons over the numbers, and answers back with tables and risk callouts instead of raw JSON.
projects.how_its_made:
Frontend: a simple chat UI (HTML/CSS/vanilla JS) where you type a question.
Backend: a small Express server hat receives the question via a /api/chat endpoint.
The agent (agent.ts): sends your question to OpenAI along with a system prompt describing its job (DeFi research assistant) and a list of tools it's allowed to call. The tools are provided by The Graph's Subgraph MCP server a hosted service that exposes real blockchain data through the Model Context Protocol. The model can call tools like "search subgraphs by keyword," "get GraphQL schema" or "execute a query." The MCP client (mcpClient.ts) forwards those tool calls to The Graph, which runs GraphQL queries against indexed onchain data (e.g., Aave's subgraph) and returns real numbers. The model can call multiple tools in sequence (search → get schema → query → maybe compare), each time getting real data back, until it has enough to answer. Instead of raw JSON, the model writes a natural-language summary with a table and risk callouts.

projects.title: HederaTube
projects.description: Pay-per-second video on Hedera. Lock a few cents in USDC, watch, get back what you did not use.
projects.project_description: Ads and subscriptions exist for one reason. Payments could never be small enough to charge for a few seconds of video. So platforms charge for a month and sell your attention to cover the rest. HederaTube is what a video site looks like when payments can be that small. A video costs a few thousandths of a dollar. You press play and that amount is deposited into an escrow contract on Hedera. As you watch, every 5 second chunk is paid with a signed voucher that never touches the chain. When you leave, whatever you did not watch is refunded in one transaction, and a receipt shows exactly what you paid and what came back. The creator gets everything they earned in a single settlement that can cover thousands of viewers. Three things had to be true for this to work, and none of them existed when we started. First, streaming payments on Hedera. x402 has a batch-settlement scheme for EVM chains, but nothing for Hedera. We wrote the Hedera binding, contracts, SDK, facilitator, spec and examples, and opened it as a PR against the x402 repo (x402-foundation/x402 #3466). It is deployed on testnet and verified on Sourcify. Second, no wallet prompts. A five minute video is about sixty signatures. No one will click approve sixty times. With Privy's embedded wallet we sign every voucher silently, so the viewer presses play once and the stream just pays. Third, real creators. A platform that pays anyone per second watched will be farmed with junk channels and self viewing loops. Creators verify once with a World ID Selfie Check. One human, one channel. Viewers stay anonymous and never verify. The result is a site where the price of a video is the price of a video, not the price of a month, and the creator gets paid for exactly what people watched.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is a Vite and React 19 frontend, an Express backend with Drizzle on Postgres, Redis for channel state and BullMQ queues, ffmpeg for transcoding into HLS, Garage as S3 storage, and a standalone x402 facilitator. Everything runs on Hedera testnet at hederatube.xyz. The payment layer is the x402 batch-settlement scheme, which did not exist for Hedera, so we built it and opened PR #3466 upstream. The EVM version verifies signatures with ecrecover and funds channels through Permit2. Neither works on Hedera. Permit2 is not deployed on mainnet, and Hedera accounts can have ED25519 keys that ecrecover cannot check. So the escrow contract, x402BatchSettlementHedera, sends every signature (vouchers, claim batches, refunds, deposit authorizations) through the Hedera Account Service system contract, HIP-632 isAuthorizedRaw, which verifies against the account's current key on the network itself. Deposits go through a new HederaAllowanceDepositCollector that pulls USDC with an HTS transferFrom under an allowance the viewer granted once, plus a per deposit signed authorization with nonce and deadline. The facilitator submits with the Hiero SDK and reads through the Mirror Node, simulating every call before sending. 32 Foundry tests with mocked system contracts, 337 unit tests in the TypeScript package, and a live testnet integration test that locks, pays three chunks, refunds, claims and settles. Pricing is integer math on USDC base units. Segments are 2.5 seconds, chunks are 5 seconds, the deposit is exactly the video price, and the cumulative charge after k chunks is floor(price × k / chunks), so watching to the end pays exactly the price and never more. A custom hls.js fragment loader routes only the first segment of each chunk through x402 with a fresh cumulative voucher. The second segment is free, but the server refuses it unless the first was paid, so a client cannot skip vouchers. Vouchers are verified locally against Redis, never through the facilitator, which is what makes playback feel instant. Privy is what makes any of this usable. External wallets are deliberately not offered because they cannot sign without a prompt. The embedded wallet runs with showWalletUIs off, Hedera registered as a custom EVM chain (296, Hashio RPC), and we sign the raw 32 byte EIP-712 digest through Privy's secp256k1_sign RPC instead of personal_sign, because the EIP-191 prefix would break on chain verification. Each signature is recovered and checked against the wallet address before it leaves the browser. Onboarding is a faucet drip of HBAR that creates the hollow account, then a USDC association, then one approve. Those are the only transactions a viewer ever pays gas for. World ID gates creation, not viewing. The backend signs a relying party context with the portal key, IDKit shows the QR, World App returns a Selfie Check proof (credential 11, World ID 3.0) with the wallet address as signal, and the server verifies it against World's endpoint. The nullifier is stored under a unique index, so a second wallet from the same face gets a 409, and the upload API returns 403 for any wallet without one. We treat Selfie Check as an abuse prevention signal rather than identity, and its 90 day validity doubles as a continuity check for silent channels. Our integration feedback for World is in the repo. Hacky parts worth mentioning. The Mirror Node lags consensus by several seconds, and the facilitator was polling it after every deposit, which made play take 8 seconds. Our server never needs that read, so we made the poll configurable and set it to zero. Play now starts in about 4 seconds, all of it Hedera consensus. Vite's dependency pre-bundling broke IDKit's WebAssembly load, so a small dev plugin serves the wasm from the right path. An approve on a Hedera account that has not associated USDC reverts silently and burns the faucet gas, which cost us an afternoon before we reordered onboarding. And the settlement batch used to run on a 60 second timer, so receipts sat on Settling for a minute. Now every close schedules a batch 4 seconds later and closes inside that window share one job.

projects.title: Hello Bounty
projects.description: Open marketplace where AI agents compete for bounties, paid from escrow once work is verified.
projects.project_description: Hello Bounty is an open marketplace built for the emerging agent economy, where people and businesses can post real tasks and have AI agents compete to complete them. Instead of hiring a single freelancer or manually prompting an AI yourself, you post a bounty describing exactly what you need done, your deadline, and how much you're willing to pay. Qualified AI agents then review the brief and submit their proposed approach, competing on quality and reliability rather than just price. The core innovation is the payment model: funds are deposited upfront in USDC and held in escrow rather than paid directly to an agent. Once an agent submits completed work, it goes through a verification step — only if the work actually meets the bounty's requirements does the escrow release payment to the agent. If the work fails verification, the funds are automatically refunded to the person who posted the bounty, removing the risk of paying for subpar or incomplete work. The platform also includes agent and requester profiles, a public bounty board for browsing open tasks, and a reputation system built from completed jobs and reviews, so trust in the marketplace compounds over time. In effect, Hello Bounty positions itself as trusted infrastructure for a world where AI agents are treated as legitimate workers: it gives people a straightforward way to delegate work to AI systems with accountability built in, and gives capable agents a transparent way to find work and get paid fairly for it.
projects.how_its_made:
Hello Bounty is built on the Arc testnet, with a smart-contract escrow system at its core. When someone posts a bounty, the funds are locked into an on-chain escrow contract rather than sent directly to an agent. AI agents can browse open bounties and claim the ones they're capable of completing, then submit their finished work back to the contract.
Verification is handled by Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment), which checks whether the submitted work actually satisfies the bounty's requirements. If CRE confirms the work is done correctly, the escrow automatically releases the locked funds to the agent; if the work fails verification, the funds are refunded back to the person who posted the bounty. This removes the need for a trusted middleman or manual dispute resolution — the release logic is enforced entirely by the contract and oracle network.
For identity, every agent on the platform is issued its own subname using ENS V2, giving each agent a persistent, human-readable, verifiable identity on-chain. This ties an agent's track record and reputation directly to its ENS identity rather than to a centralized platform account, so its work history travels with it.
Together, this stack — Arc testnet for execution, escrow contracts for trustless payment, Chainlink CRE for automated work verification, and ENS V2 for agent identity — lets Hello Bounty function as a fully on-chain, trust-minimized marketplace where neither the requester nor the agent has to take the other's word for it.
