projects.title: Revoke.eth
projects.description: Grant, limit, or revoke an AI agent's spending through ENS — instantly, no key rotation.
projects.project_description: Revoke turns an AI agent's ENS name into its authorization. A parent grants an agent a narrow, expiring, revocable capability recorded on ENSv2 - a delegated right, not a handed-over key - and services check that capability before honoring a paid request. A subgraph indexes the full delegation tree and verifies freshness on every read, refusing to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Payments settle over x402 on Hedera, and every HCS receipt is bound back to the ENS name that permitted it, so the full chain - who allowed this, when, and what happened - is publicly auditable. The result is a kill switch for agent access: revoke the name, and the agent's spending stops everywhere at once, with no key rotation and no service-by-service cleanup.
projects.how_its_made:
ENSv2 on Sepolia is the source of truth. Each agent gets a Permissioned Resolver with Enhanced Access Control, defining exactly which records it can modify. A registrar built around ETHRegistry handles subname issuance. The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry, deployed and verified on Sepolia.
The Graph indexes every grant, revocation, and expiry through a subgraph with AssemblyScript mappings. Every query returns a provenance envelope containing the deployment ID, indexed block, live chain head, indexing lag, and authorization verdict. The service refuses to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Freshness is a security control, not a UX feature.
Hedera handles payments. An x402-gated service checks the agent's live capability before accepting a request, settles payment through a real ContractExecuteTransaction using EIP-712 transferWithAuthorization, and writes an HCS receipt bound to the ENS name that authorized it. The receipt can be independently verified through the Hedera mirror node.
One of the key security challenges was establishing a trustworthy chain head. An initial high-water-mark approach could silently report data as fresh after a cold start. This was replaced with a real eth_blockNumber RPC call on every authorization check, ensuring freshness is independently verified before a payment is allowed.
The system was built with contracts and shared types defined first, followed by parallel ENS, Graph, Hedera, and UI implementation against those interfaces, then integrated and re-verified against live Sepolia and Hedera testnet data. Planning documents, implementation specs, and fix history are included in the repository.
projects.project_description_markdown: Revoke turns an AI agent's ENS name into its authorization. A parent grants an agent a narrow, expiring, revocable capability recorded on ENSv2 - a delegated right, not a handed-over key - and services check that capability before honoring a paid request. A subgraph indexes the full delegation tree and verifies freshness on every read, refusing to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Payments settle over x402 on Hedera, and every HCS receipt is bound back to the ENS name that permitted it, so the full chain - who allowed this, when, and what happened - is publicly auditable. The result is a kill switch for agent access: revoke the name, and the agent's spending stops everywhere at once, with no key rotation and no service-by-service cleanup.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ENSv2 on Sepolia is the source of truth. Each agent gets a Permissioned Resolver with Enhanced Access Control, defining exactly which records it can modify. A registrar built around ETHRegistry handles subname issuance. The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry, deployed and verified on Sepolia.
The Graph indexes every grant, revocation, and expiry through a subgraph with AssemblyScript mappings. Every query returns a provenance envelope containing the deployment ID, indexed block, live chain head, indexing lag, and authorization verdict. The service refuses to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Freshness is a security control, not a UX feature.
Hedera handles payments. An x402-gated service checks the agent's live capability before accepting a request, settles payment through a real ContractExecuteTransaction using EIP-712 transferWithAuthorization, and writes an HCS receipt bound to the ENS name that authorized it. The receipt can be independently verified through the Hedera mirror node.
One of the key security challenges was establishing a trustworthy chain head. An initial high-water-mark approach could silently report data as fresh after a cold start. This was replaced with a real eth_blockNumber RPC call on every authorization check, ensuring freshness is independently verified before a payment is allowed.
The system was built with contracts and shared types defined first, followed by parallel ENS, Graph, Hedera, and UI implementation against those interfaces, then integrated and re-verified against live Sepolia and Hedera testnet data. Planning documents, implementation specs, and fix history are included in the repository.

projects.title: Countersign
projects.description: An agent's Hedera treasury cannot move until an independent guard, paid per decision, countersigns.
projects.project_description: Autonomous agents are being handed treasuries. The usual protection is a policy check inside the agent's own code — which a compromised agent simply skips. Countersign removes that assumption. The treasury account holds a native Hedera key tree: 1-of[ownerKey, 2-of[agentKey, guardKey]]. The owner can always recover funds alone. The agent alone satisfies neither branch — when it signs a transfer by itself, the Hedera network rejects it with INVALID_SIGNATURE. Nothing inside the agent's process can talk its way past that. So the agent proposes instead. It publishes the transfer it wants as a Hedera Scheduled Transaction — public, and unexecuted, carrying only its own signature. It then pays an independent guard to review it. That guard is a live service at https://countersign.gudman.xyz. It answers HTTP 402 Payment Required, quotes its price in HBAR, and settlement goes through the Blocky402 x402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Only after payment does the guard do any work. It resolves the ScheduleID from consensus — it never trusts a summary the caller sent it — and checks 48 decoded fields against a mandate the treasury owner signed: recipient allowlist, amount cap, asset, fee, expiry, who created the schedule, who pays for it, and that its own key is not already on it. If every check passes it adds its signature and Hedera executes the transfer. If one fails it refuses, and the schedule simply never executes. The caller pays either way. A refusal is a delivered service, not a failed request. Refusal has no state of its own on Hedera, so it is proved by absence: the schedule exists, its executed_timestamp is null, only the agent's key prefix appears in signatures[], and the treasury balance is unchanged. Every verdict is also written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic. All of it is readable from the public mirror node without running any of my code. You can pay the guard yourself. curl https://countersign.gudman.xyz/guard returns its public key and HCS-14 identifier for free, and npm run hosted-review in the repository sends a real paid review request to it from your own machine. The approved and refused runs linked in the README were made exactly that way, from a separate machine, against that endpoint. Honest limits, also stated in the README: these are my own operator runs, not external users, and testnet payments are paid protocol trials, not revenue. One guard process authorizes exactly one treasury, so this is a deployed service and not a marketplace — a second treasury needs a second guard. HTS token approval is deliberately disabled, and every token proposal is refused.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript on Node 24, and no Solidity anywhere — Hedera native services only, through @hiero-ledger/sdk. The treasury is a nested KeyList, 1-of[ownerKey, 2-of[agentKey, guardKey]]. Hedera evaluates it at consensus, which is what makes the guarantee structural instead of procedural. Scheduled Transactions are the product mechanism rather than decoration: they are how a second signature arrives asynchronously. The agent's ScheduleCreate publishes the exact transfer; the guard's ScheduleSign completes the threshold. Payment is x402 through @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled by the hosted Blocky402 facilitator on hedera:testnet. Hedera's x402 is exact-scheme only, so the price is one known check-unit quoted up front in the 402 challenge — not post-usage metering, and the README says so. The fee is paid from a separately keyed operational account, so no treasury authorization key ever enters a payment payload; startup asserts that separation and refuses to run otherwise. The validator is a pure function, and the subtle part is what it is allowed to trust. ScheduleInfo returns an already-decoded body, and a protobuf decoder silently drops fields it does not know. So the guard pins the exact HAPI protobuf and services versions, reads them from the same consensus node both before and after resolving the schedule, and refuses on any mismatch — a schema change makes it fail closed rather than approve something it cannot see. It also rejects any body carrying a field outside the audited schema. Mandates are RFC 8785 JCS-canonicalized, domain-separated and Ed25519-signed by the owner, so the agent cannot rewrite its own policy. They are single-use: the nonce is atomically reserved in SQLite before approval, and only the request that wins the reservation may submit ScheduleSign. Participant identity is HCS-14 for both agent and guard, and verdicts go to immutable, submit-key-protected HCS topics with custom fees rejected at startup. 360 tests across 15 files, all offline. One defect the offline suite could not have caught surfaced on the first live run: the mirror node returns signatures[].public_key_prefix as base64 and three code paths expected hex. The fixtures used "a".repeat(16), which is itself valid base64, so they passed while asserting nothing about the real encoding. The regression tests now run against verbatim mirror-node responses captured from that run. The build briefs each task was run from, and a full AI usage disclosure, are published in the repository.

projects.title: WorldMod
projects.description: Anyone with a phone records short real-world tasks for robot training and gets paid in USDC.
projects.project_description: Go in as much detail as you can about what this project is. Please be as clear as possible! (min 280 characters) World Mod is a permissionless network for physical-world data. Anyone with a phone opens a web page, does a short physical task while the camera watches, and gets paid in USDC once the recording is accepted. A buyer posts what they need and escrows what it pays. Nothing to install, no hardware to buy, no gas to hold. Why this exists. Robots cannot learn from the internet the way language models did. They need first-person video of humans handling objects, and the datasets that exist today were collected by expensive, centralised research programs with recruited participants and custom hardware. The scarce resource is not storage or compute. It is someone doing a physical thing while a sensor is pointed at it. World Mod makes that contribution nearly frictionless and pays the person who made it. How an episode earns A buyer posts a bounty ("15 seconds of keyboard typing, hands in frame") and escrows the full budget in real USDC. A bounty is only listed once it is funded. A contributor opens the app inside World App. Their World wallet is their identity, and a one-time Selfie Check keeps one person from farming payouts across many devices. They record a 15-second task on their phone. A head strap gives the best first-person footage but is optional; holding the phone works too. The app shows a live hand skeleton so they can see they are in frame. The recording is sealed on the device before a single byte leaves it: hashed, signed with the contributor's key, and queued so going offline mid-task loses nothing. The server scores every frame. Are the hands in frame? Does the camera motion agree with the gyroscope (a screen replay fails this)? Is it a near-duplicate of something already submitted? We measured the replay check against real recordings: genuine takes correlate at 59% on average, replays at 24%. The buyer's acceptance threshold is checked inside a TEE by a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow, so the bar a buyer sets is never visible on-chain or to the operator. A pass is written on-chain as a DON-signed report. A rejection makes no on-chain call at all. The contributor is paid from escrow in real USDC, into a balance only they can withdraw. They never need gas. What accepted episodes become. Episodes are bundled into a licensed dataset with a real IPFS content address and an on-chain registry entry. A buyer can tokenise that dataset as a KYC-gated Bond on Hedera, mint licence seats to the dataset's creator, and pay licence-fee coupons in USDC. Meanwhile a world model trains over the episodes and runs live during the next take, showing the wearer what it thinks happens next. A second Confidential Workflow settles each contributor's share of model improvement on-chain. What is real today. All six registry and escrow contracts are deployed on both Ethereum Sepolia and Hedera testnet, using Circle's testnet USDC on both, not a mock token. Real episodes from three contributors have been captured, scored, anchored, paid and tokenised. A real Selfie Check has completed end to end against World's sandbox. What we say plainly. A browser has no secure enclave, so every episode carries a "heuristic" trust level in the UI: the checks measure whether a capture is plausible, not that pixels came from a real camera. With five episodes the world model does not yet beat a "predict no change" baseline, and the buyer dashboard shows that curve rather than hiding it. We would rather ship a real pipeline that improves with every episode than a mock that looks finished.
projects.how_its_made: The phone. A Next.js PWA, installable on iOS and Android. Capture is getUserMedia plus MediaRecorder with per-browser codec negotiation recorded into the manifest, DeviceMotionEvent for 60Hz IMU, and TensorFlow.js hand-pose detection with self-hosted 4MB lite models for the live skeleton. The manifest is canonicalised with RFC 8785 and the IMU is hashed as a binary stream, because float formatting across two runtimes is where byte-exactness dies. Scoring used to run on the phone too. We measured it dropping capture to 26.9fps with 818ms gaps during movement, so it moved to the server; a client-computed score was never authoritative anyway. The server. ffmpeg decodes every frame. Optical flow is correlated against the gyroscope with lag estimation, because the frame and IMU clocks are offset and a zero-lag correlation scored a genuine capture below a spoof. Fixing that took one episode from 5.2% to 59.6%. Perceptual hashing catches duplicates. Episode bytes and dataset metadata are pinned to IPFS through a local kubo node. Contracts. Foundry. EntityRegistry, AssetRegistry, EpisodeRegistry, BountyEscrow, DatasetRegistry and FederatedRound, plus a native WMOD token whose one shipped function is a ValidatorBond that stakes and slashes validators. Contributors sign EIP-712 payloads that a relayer submits, so nobody needs gas. Escrow credits a pull-based balance so nobody else can redirect a payout. The same contracts are deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and Hedera testnet, switched by one environment variable. Chainlink CRE. Two Confidential Workflows, both registered with cre.handlerInTee. The episode validator fetches the buyer's minimum framing and plausibility thresholds with runtime.getSecrets so they are only ever decrypted inside the enclave, pulls scored episodes over HTTPClient, compares in-enclave, and on a pass calls donRuntime.report then evmClient.writeReport into a consumer contract registered as an EpisodeRegistry validator. The utility oracle holds the utility weighting exponent as a secret, computes normalised basis-point shares in-enclave, and the DON co-signs them into a second consumer that is now BountyEscrow's registered oracle. Both consumers follow Chainlink's ReceiverTemplate and accept the production Sepolia KeystoneForwarder. This replaced the product's biggest trust assumption: one EOA acting as validator and oracle. Hedera. The core contracts call the HTS precompile in their constructors to self-associate with Circle's HTS USDC. Forge's local EVM has no HTS precompile, so those three had to be deployed via raw viem over Hashio instead of forge script. On top, a licensed dataset becomes an Asset Tokenization Studio Bond: the app reads the DatasetRegistry live, maps it through a tested dataset-to-bond mapping with a valid ISIN, issues via Bond.create, grants KYC with a real Terminal3 Verifiable Credential, mints licence seats to the dataset creator, sets a 5% coupon, and distributes it in real USDC. Four Bonds are source-verified on Sourcify for chain 296. World. The app is a MiniKit mini app. MiniKit.walletAuth gives contributors a recoverable identity, and MiniKit.signTypedData signs the same EIP-712 payloads the previous Privy signer did, a transport swap rather than a redesign. Selfie Check uses IDKitRequestWidget with the selfieCheckLegacy preset and a server-signed RP context. The verify route calls World's production v4 verify API and only records a verification when World says success. World model. A PyTorch encoder plus GRU dynamics head, exported to ONNX and checked against the PyTorch graph over an eight-step recurrent sequence (worst-case difference 2.5e-5). During capture the phone streams a cropped frame and motion sample twice a second, the server keeps the GRU hidden state per session, and returns the nearest-neighbour frame from the same take. Hacky things worth mentioning. The Hedera ATS SDK has no raw-key signing path; its public wallet list is MetaMask, WalletConnect and enterprise custody only. We wired an ethers.Wallet directly onto its transaction adapter and stubbed the hard global.window gate. That stub then broke Next.js server rendering across the whole app, because React checks typeof window in its own internals, so ATS issuance now runs in a short-lived child process that starts, issues one Bond, prints one line of JSON, and exits. Granting KYC and setting coupons both revert on a fresh Bond because the diamond owner does not receive _KYC_ROLE or _CORPORATEACTIONS_ROLE automatically; we found that by decoding reverts on the mirror node, and in the process discovered our own account-id and private-key pair had been mismatched from day one. Nobody had verified the ATS ResolverProxy on Hedera testnet before, so we recovered the compiler version from the on-chain metadata CBOR and rebuilt 153 source files to a byte-exact match.

projects.title: Nametoll
projects.description: Agents pay a desk they found by name. TEE gates spend. Hedera bills on HCS.
projects.project_description: If an agent needs live lending data today, somebody hands it a URL, an API key, and a monthly bill. There is no name you can pass to another agent. The spend limit sits in a config the buyer can read. And when the payment goes through, there is no receipt a stranger can check. Nametoll is a desk for that job. You find it by a name. A spend rule the desk itself cannot see decides whether the buyer may pay. If they may, they pay only for what came back, in HBAR, and the bill is written where anyone can recompute it. The public origin is https://nametoll.run.place. You paste a parent such as nametoll.eth on /desks, or a child such as desk.nametoll.eth on /app. The happy path does not ship a name. The name resolves to an HTTP origin, who to pay, what it costs, and where the receipt will be written. Two protocols cost two hundred thousand tinybars against a secret cap of one hundred fifty thousand, so the desk refuses and Pay stays locked. One protocol is one hundred thousand, which is allowed. Unpaid traffic is still HTTP 402. After settle you get live rows, and the same numbers show up on HashScan and on HCS topic 0.0.10464309. What you buy is two things on the same meter. A snapshot is priced by how many protocols you asked for: Aave v3 and Compound III, one Messari-shaped query, fail-soft if an indexer is down. A risk score is one unit. You pass a wallet; the desk computes a health factor, distance to liquidation, and the worst market from those same markets. If the indexer has positions it uses them. If not, it builds a deterministic book from live TVL ratios. The wallet never goes into the spend check. Positions on a public chain are not private, and we do not sell them as if they were. The Graph is the data you pay for. We used it. We did not apply for its prize. The name lives on ENS, version two, on Sepolia. nametoll.eth is the parent. desk.nametoll.eth and agent-02.nametoll.eth are children under that UserRegistry, each with its own Permissioned Resolver. Three documented text keys (url, agent-context, agent-endpoint[web]) carry the origin, the Hedera pay-to, the price rule, the HCS topic, and HBAR asset 0.0.0. The operator can edit those keys and cannot transfer the name. /register issues a new child that resells this desk: the label and endpoint vary, price and pay-to stay this origin. Optional expiresIn writes a bounded expiry. gone.nametoll.eth was registered for ninety seconds; on-chain state is now AVAILABLE and /desks marks it unresolved. npm run agent -- nametoll.eth discovers a live child and pays it. The spend rule is a Chainlink confidential workflow, handlerInTee from their official scaffold. Before Blocky402 settles, the desk asks nametoll-brain. getSecret loads SPEND_CAP and, if set, BUYER_ALLOWLIST and RATE_LIMIT inside the enclave. The public reasons are under cap, over cap, buyer not allowlisted, or rate limited. Deny, or a skipped TEE, is HTTP 403: no settle, no snapshot, no bill. Four cre workflow simulate logs in the repo show AWS Nitro in us-west-2 for allow, over-cap deny, allowlist deny, and rate deny. The same handler can emit unsigned join() calldata for the official ChallengeLending contract on Sepolia; that join is already on-chain. Functions and Automation are not used. If an agent needs live lending data today, somebody hands it a URL, an API key, and a monthly bill. There is no name you can pass to another agent. The spend limit sits in a config the buyer can read. And when the payment goes through, there is no receipt a stranger can check.

projects.title: Mycelium
projects.description: Connect devices to run verifiable distributed inference of open source models, get paid with x402
projects.project_description: Mycelium connects multiple devices into cooperative networks that run open-source AI models through distributed inference. Instead of relying on a single centralised AI provider, people can pool their hardware to jointly host models, users can discover and pay per request whilst the system stochastically ensures that the advertised model is the model they requested inference from. While one user may be unable to wrong the open source model they want to use, in a swarm each individual needs to have less compute power. Together, more powerful models can be run. The long term goal being that people can function both as users and providers, with the system either handling or integrating routing through services like open router, compared to the current provider self-selection. The application brings that infrastructure into a practical flow: choose a model and provider, receive a request-bound quote, authorize an x402 payment, stream the response, and keep a signed receipt. Hedera provides the payment rail, ENS gives providers human-readable identities, and The Graph makes published receipt history queryable to inform future provider selection. Our verification design separates the machines doing inference from the checker. We utilise model-specific statistical screening and private reference spot-checks, with the checker being run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) so users can ensure the checker is behaving honestly. The aim is to detect model substitution and forgerys without requiring every inference device to have confidential-computing hardware, or needing to trust in any centralised service or even a quorum of verifiers. Dishonest providers have their staked bond slashed, and the system is designed to ensure that it is economically unfeasible to run inference that is not the model the user requested. In the future we aim to have a system that allows users to also serve as verifiers for inference. Mycelium is designed for both people and software agents, with browser, SDK, CLI, and MCP access. The goal is an open decentralised inference marketplace where users can choose who serves their models, hardware owners can offer underutilised edge compute(phones, laptops, desktop PC's, small Racks), and provider history helps give both humans and agents the information they need to make informed decisions based on the inference providers past history. A system that benefits humanity as a whole and not just people owning data centers.
projects.how_its_made: We built the hackathon application around the existing Mycelium distributed-inference project. We built model integrations for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and a 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B model. The demonstrated 0.5B and 27b routes splits one model across two physical Apple Silicon Macs: MLX executes most transformer layers, while a NumPy worker executes the final layer and output head. The architecture of Mycelium is designed for heterogeneous hardware, although these demonstrated execution paths are Mac-based for simplicity purposes. The application uses Node.js, JavaScript modules, versioned JSON contracts, SQLite-backed state, and a shared HTTP API for browser, SDK, CLI, and MCP clients. Execution, payments, discovery, indexing, and assessment are separate components. Ed25519-signed receipts bind the provider, requested model profile, request, and output. For payments, we integrated native Hedera x402 through Blocky402. The service returns an HTTP 402 challenge containing the payment requirements; the client authorizes the quoted payment, and the application verifies and settles it before admitting the job. Persisted payment-attempt state allows interrupted requests to be reconciled without blindly paying again. ENSv2 records on Sepolia provide human-readable provider identities and discovery. To provide inference, providers must put up a stake. Payments are settled only after verification has occured, and if inference providers are found to be dishonest they are slashed to a mathematically determined degree (based on stake amount, inference price, chance of being audited etc.) to ensure it is not economically viable to serve a different model than the one the user requested. The Graph provides the application’s queryable provider history. Solidity registries on Sepolia emit receipt and assessment events, which custom AssemblyScript subgraph mappings turn into immutable claims, daily activity records, and provider metrics. A reputation formula combines a smoothed assessment pass rate, capped receipt volume, and recent activity. The application uses indexed history to compare providers, while preserving separate counts for mismatches, inconclusive results, and unavailable checks. This makes The Graph part of provider selection rather than just a transaction dashboard, as it allows humans and agents to make informed decisions on where they wish to get their inference from. Our verifier uses two complementary mechanisms. First we have model-specific binary classifier screening ordinary response text: a TF-IDF/LinearSVC model captures lexical patterns, while a trained RoBERTa detector captures learned text features. They are combined in an ensemble and return a likelihood that the respective model was served. Separate trained bundles exist for 0.5B and 27B. Screening runs asynchronously, outside response delivery, and is a monitoring signal as well as a requirement for inference providers to be paid for their inference (withdrawal of attached x402 payment can only be made after verification has occurred). Second, the checker conducts private reference audits. An independent random policy selects observations for auditing (utilising some information from TheGraph to analyse all inference provider swarms and ensure they are roughly all selected at the same rate, 10% uniform per request, given their current uptime, with higher likelihood assignment to new providers, overdue checks and mismatched histories, with the aforementioned classifier triggering audits for three consecutive negatives. The checker sends a new challenge containing exact input token IDs and pinned generation parameters to the provider. It then compares the native output token sequence, output length, and EOS-versus-length termination against a private, profile-bound reference bank. Expected answers remain checker-side. The TEE design places the classifiers, private reference bank, audit scheduler, and comparison logic inside confidential computing on a GCS, while the large generative models remain on providers’ ordinary hardware. With this architectural split, the verification is quite lightweight compared to the actual inference, and even with the auditing it still makes it far easier to do verification than inference. The fees for upkeeping the verification TEE are paid for by a 5% fee on all inference payments, with the remaining 95% going back to the inference providers.

They are combined in an ensemble and return a likelihood that the respective model was served. Separate trained bundles exist for 0.5B and 27B. Screening runs asynchronously, outside response delivery, and is a monitoring signal as well as a requirement for inference providers to be paid for their inference (withdrawal of attached x402 payment can only be made after verification has occurred).

Second, the checker conducts private reference audits. An independent random policy selects observations for auditing (utilising some information from TheGraph to analyse all inference provider swarms and ensure they are roughly all selected at the same rate, 10% uniform per request, given their current uptime, with higher likelihood assignment to new providers, overdue checks and mismatched histories, with the aforementioned classifier triggering audits for three consecutive negatives. The checker sends a new challenge containing exact input token IDs and pinned generation parameters to the provider. It then compares the native output token sequence, output length, and EOS-versus-length termination against a private, profile-bound reference bank. Expected answers remain checker-side.

The TEE design places the classifiers, private reference bank, audit scheduler, and comparison logic inside confidential computing on a GCS, while the large generative models remain on providers’ ordinary hardware. With this architectural split, the verification is quite lightweight compared to the actual inference, and even with the auditing it still makes it far easier to do verification than inference. The fees for upkeeping the verification TEE are paid for by a 5% fee on all inference payments, with the remaining 95% going back to the inference providers.

projects.title: Warrant Protocol
projects.description: Warrant Protocol - My bot acted. I fired every agent under me. Nobody learned who I was.
projects.project_description: Warrant is a permission slip for AI agents. You keep your wallet key. Your bot gets a time-limited warrant instead of your identity. It can call services, leave a public note, even hire a helper. Whoever it called still cannot tell who authorized the request. When you are done, you Fire in the tab and every agent under that warrant stops. The problem is simple. Today, if you want a bot to act, you hand it a key or an account. Then whoever the bot called can name you. If it hires helpers, you often lose the ability to shut the whole chain down. Warrant splits those jobs. MetaMask authorizes. The bot carries only a bearer. Hedera pays when a shop requires x402. Fire takes the warrant back. On the hosted product at warrant-beta.vercel.app you authorize a guest warrant (about 30 minutes). Install the skill once into Hermes or another HTTP agent. Paste the warrant. The bot POSTs to Warrant’s agent API. Warrant’s prove worker builds a Groth16 hop proof over Baby Jubjub mandates in a LeanIMT on Base Sepolia (MandateRegistry). The bot never sees the witness or the zkey. The shop verifies the proof and learns a context-scoped nullifier, not you. For the memo demo, Hermes posts to /api/agent/memo. The memo shop on Railway returns 402 until ExactHedera payment settles via Blocky402. A local warrant ready purse on your machine shows /fund so you can send testnet HBAR. After pay, the shop submits the note to Hedera Consensus Service topic 0.0.10416077. The text is public on HashScan. Who asked is not. Fire this warrant (or Fire every) tombstones the hop or bumps the identity so the next call dies with a stale root. The north star: my bot acted, I fired every agent under me, nobody learned who I was.
projects.how_its_made: I built Warrant as a pnpm monorepo with hard process boundaries, not one app that does everything. Stack. Circom WarrantHop(20) plus a Groth16 ceremony (artifacts-groth16-v3, pot16). Foundry contracts on Base Sepolia: MandateRegistry (LeanIMT + epoch, no Groth16 in Solidity), generated WarrantVerifier, optional WarrantGate. TypeScript domain in @ronnakamoto/warrant-core (Poseidon, Baby Jubjub / Semaphore identity, witness, snarkjs prove/verify, exactly eight public inputs). Shop middleware in @ronnakamoto/warrant-x402 (policy pipeline, challenge nonce, nullifier seal, ExactHedera pay fallthrough, createWarrantShop + warrantHono). Agent CLI @ronnakamoto/warrant for ready / act and a local fund page. Next.js dashboard (Astryx + Carbon language) on Vercel. Isolated prove worker, translate shop, and memo shop on Railway. The Graph Studio subgraph indexes registry events for the console, not as a second mandate model. How it pieces together. Authorize on the dashboard mints a guest session on prove: 2-hop mandate tree, operator bind into MandateRegistry, bearer = random session id. Hermes installs /skill.md and POSTs to /api/agent/memo with that bearer. The BFF calls prove with the live x402 challenge; prove returns a warrant header. The memo shop verifies Groth16, checks merkleRoot == currentRoot, seals (nullifier, requestHash), then Blocky402 settles HBAR and the service submits the note to Hedera Consensus Service. Fire is an on-chain revoke from the MetaMask that bound the leaf; the next prove fails as root revoked. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs enforces the split: dashboard never imports snarkjs, shops never call prove, prove never imports Hedera or x402. Partner tech. Base Sepolia holds the public revocation and membership root so Fire is real, not a cookie delete. Hedera gives us live x402 settlement (Blocky402 ExactHedera) and a public HCS scar for the demo note, which is the honesty punchline: words public, person private. Semaphore-style LeanIMT / identity primitives let us reuse a known anonymity-set pattern instead of inventing a tree. x402 is the payment extension slot so warrant verify and pay compose in one shop request. Hacky but deliberate. Hosted Copy means Warrant sees the witness so cloud bots never touch a 28MB zkey. Guest tier=0 with a random session tag (no World ID on the land) so strangers can try on real rails. Free calls = 0 forces a real 402. Chat must never invent a Hedera key, so payment is a local purse + /fund on 127.0.0.1. Hire returns a helper skill paste instead of spawning a subagent on camera. The bearer is intentionally not the proof: it is an opaque capability handle into prove’s session store.

projects.title: gUSD: GPU Exposures
projects.description: Trade onchain exposure to real-world GPU compute prices across H100, H200, L40S and RTX 4090.
projects.project_description: gUSD is the GPU Assets Protocol, enabling onchain markets for trading exposure to GPU compute prices. The protocol tracks live GPU-hour pricing across providers, aggregates this data into a benchmark oracle, and uses those prices to power markets for assets such as H100, H200, L40S, and RTX 4090. Trading is executed through Uniswap v4 with custom hooks, while gUSD acts as the settlement asset and sgUSD as the protocol’s savings and revenue-sharing layer. The system also includes primary GPU asset issuance, protocol-owned liquidity, an Envio-powered indexer, and a web application with Privy-based embedded wallets for simplified onboarding.
projects.how_its_made: gUSD is built as a TypeScript + Solidity monorepo using pnpm and Turborepo. The protocol contracts are written with Foundry and deployed on Robinhood Chain, with GPU markets settling through Uniswap v4. We built a custom v4 hook for GPU-specific market execution, primary GPU asset issuance, protocol-owned liquidity, gUSD settlement, sgUSD savings, and oracle-aware market logic. Offchain, a Fastify-based oracle pipeline collects GPU rental prices from multiple providers, normalizes them into GPU-hour benchmarks, and publishes price updates onchain through a dedicated oracle publisher. Envio HyperIndex + HyperSync index protocol activity into Postgres for portfolio, market, and historical views. The frontend is built with Next.js and Privy, allowing users to sign in with familiar Web2 methods while receiving a self-custodial embedded wallet, or connect an existing wallet directly. The result is a full-stack onchain market where users can trade exposure to real-world GPU compute prices such as H100, H200, L40S, and RTX 4090.

projects.title: Facture
projects.description: An invoice is a zero-coupon bond nobody ever priced. Facture is the market that prices it.
projects.project_description: Invoice factoring is bond pricing done over the phone. A business owed $40,000 in sixty days calls a factoring house, waits, and takes whatever single price comes back. There is no screen, no curve, and no second buyer. A market never formed here because invoices are not fungible. Every receivable has a different debtor, a different amount and a different number of days to maturity, so no two are the same asset and an order book has nothing to book. Facture stops trying to standardise the paper and standardises the bid instead. A funder writes a standing mandate (any A-rated paper, 90 days or less, 12.5% annualised, up to $200,000 of exposure), funds it, and walks away. Any invoice that arrives is priced immediately by reading the curve at its own rating and tenor. The assets stay unique and the buyers become fungible. The instrument was always a bond. A discounted invoice is a zero-coupon bond: bought below par, redeeming at face on a fixed date, with the discount being the yield. Each receivable is issued as its own zero-coupon bond on Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, maturity set to the invoice due date and principal to the face value. Five moves, each of which has now run on testnet more than once. List. The invoice becomes a bond. A uniqueness registry keyed on hash(debtor, invoice number, amount) means one receivable mints exactly one token, ever, which answers the specific fraud factoring has always had. Quote. A confirmed invoice carries a live price already. Not a button that requests one: the number is simply there, and it moves as the curve moves and as the due date approaches. Match. Eligibility is checked against the security's own control list and KYC facets before matching, not at settlement. An AMM matches first and discovers the transfer was illegal afterwards. Here an ineligible counterparty is never matched, and the refusal comes back as a sentence a funder can read rather than a reverted transaction. Settle. Delivery versus payment across two chains with no bridge. The bond stays on Hedera, the USDC stays on Arc, and neither side moves first. Buyer capital already lives where stablecoins live, so the second chain is not a flourish. Mature. The debtor pays and settlement routes to whoever holds the paper now, not whoever bought it first. Without that the paper cannot legitimately change hands, because a second buyer would have no way to be paid. Nobody using Facture needs to know it is on a blockchain. A seller sees invoices with prices beside them. A buyer sees mandates, exposure and yield. The chain surfaces in one place: a proof view, one click from any trade, showing the on-chain receipts, the compliance decision and both settlement legs.
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm workspace of five packages: a Next.js 15 and React 19 frontend, a Hono backend over SQLite and drizzle holding the quote engine, settlement and issuance, a market-maker agent, a shared package holding the curve, the state machines and one refusal vocabulary, and a Hardhat workspace that no other package imports. The paper is Hedera. Every receivable is its own ATS zero-coupon bond via deployBond, about 7 million gas and 7 to 9 HBAR an issuance, measured on chain rather than estimated. Eight contracts are deployed and verified on Sourcify: a uniqueness registry, an invoice registry whose isConfirmed is a public view, a mandate book that reads rating and confirmation out of that registry instead of from whoever wants the match to succeed, a compliance gate, and a party registry where a business signs an EIP-712 profile and the venue only relays it, so it can never write a profile on somebody's behalf. Refusal and match digests go to an HCS topic as SHA-256 commitments, never the reason itself, because a topic is public and a refusal names a customer and an amount. The money is Arc. A funded mandate escrows USDC in MandateVault and settles out of it in one call, with no challenge and no signature, because a funded standing bid already said yes to anything meeting its terms. An unfunded one settles pay-as-you-go over x402 on Hedera through the Blocky402 facilitator. That reads x402 as a settlement protocol instead of an API paywall: the challenge holds the asset leg, the payment signature is the cash leg, and the facilitator is what makes the two simultaneous. One of those payments was made by an agent rather than a person, signing a native Hedera TransferTransaction with the buyer's own key. Privy signs a seller in by email, and the wallet it makes carries a policy with exactly two rules, so that key gained two permissions rather than becoming general purpose. Circle developer-controlled wallets fund the vault. Three things worth flagging. Backend issuance had never once succeeded: the deployBond tuple was a plausible flattening of the real one that compiled, typechecked and encoded cleanly to a selector the deployed diamond does not have. A wrong selector is not a wrong type, so nothing in the toolchain could see it. Three ATS compliance selectors that the docs imply exist do not, and the gate probing them failed closed, so it refused every buyer on every instrument while looking correct. And the asset leg is an ATS hold rather than an escrow transfer, because createHoldByPartition acts on the caller's own tokens. That is also what made the secondary market buildable, after authorising the venue as an ERC-1400 operator turned out to succeed and confer nothing.

projects.title: Kurabase
projects.description: Supabase-like database DX for EVM apps: SQL, RLS, delegated gateways, and account-owned writes.
projects.project_description: Kurabase is a local-first relational data layer for EVM applications. It starts from a simple premise: distributed ledgers are databases, so application developers should be able to work with familiar database concepts instead of starting with Solidity. Run kura start to launch an Anvil chain, delegated gateway, and database workspace together. Use the Dashboard to create tables, define schemas, inspect rows, and run SQL. In an application, the JavaScript SDK provides a SQL-shaped client for querying data, inserting rows, and applying row-level security. Kurabase keeps authority explicit. Developers delegate gateways; users grant scoped, revocable sessions; and account-abstraction writes remain account-owned. ENS schema resolution also lets an instance query a named relation from another instance.
projects.how_its_made: Kurabase is an open-source monorepo built around Solidity contracts and Foundry tests for the authority layer, a Rust gateway for chain-backed query and write handling, and TypeScript packages for the JavaScript SDK and CLI. kura start uses Docker Compose and Anvil to create a complete local stack. The Dashboard provides a Supabase-like workflow for tables, SQL, migrations, policies, gateway authority, and authentication configuration. The SDK exposes familiar relational operations while the gateway enforces delegated authority and scoped user sessions. ENS resolution maps named instances to schemas for cross-instance SQL. The documentation site covers the local workflow, production configuration, SDK, SQL, and architecture.

projects.title: AutoVoyage
projects.description: AI agent plans and books full travel itineraries, paying per-query in HBAR via x402 on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Our AI travel agent plans and books full trip itineraries end-to-end, autonomously paying for real flight data over Hedera's x402 payment protocol. Instead of API keys or subscriptions, the agent pays per-query in native HBAR through a self-hosted x402 facilitator that verifies and settles each payment on Hedera testnet in real time. The user authorizes once — setting a spending budget and approving a HIP-336 HBAR allowance in their HashPack wallet. From there, the agent searches and pays for flight (and stay/activity) data autonomously from the user's own account, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before it settles — non-custodial and revocable at any time. Before booking, the agent requires an explicit human confirmation bound to the exact itinerary hash, preventing any bait-and-switch between what was quoted and what gets booked. Every payment, approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext event to a public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic, giving a fully auditable trail anyone can verify on HashScan — no black box, no trust required. The paid flight-data supplier is a real, live x402 service (not a mock) with metered per-result pricing, and it also self-registers on an HCS-based agent registry with a signed identity claim, so other agents can discover it and verify who they're paying without a hardcoded endpoint.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is a monorepo: a Next.js frontend (the planner/agent), an Express-based supplier service (the paid flight-data API), and a self-hosted x402 facilitator, all wired for Hedera testnet. Payments (x402 + HBAR): The supplier gates its search routes with HTTP 402 — each request returns a price, the agent signs an HBAR transfer, and the facilitator verifies + settles on-chain before the real data is returned. Pricing is metered per result (not a flat fee), using a quote cache keyed by a canonical hash of the query so the unpaid 402 price and the paid response always agree. Autonomous, non-custodial payment: Rather than the agent holding user funds, we use Hedera's HIP-336 HBAR allowance. The user signs once in HashPack to grant a spending allowance; the agent then pays the supplier directly from the user's account using its own server-held key, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before settling. This took real HAPI-level probing to get right — Hedera requires the spender (our agent), not the fee-payer or facilitator, to own the transaction ID for an allowance-debited transfer, a rule that's undocumented for HBAR (only stated for NFTs in the protobufs) and had to be discovered empirically with test transactions. Auditability (HCS): Every payment, human approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext JSON event to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, readable live via Mirror Node — a public, tamper-evident audit trail with no local cache. The supplier also self-registers on a second HCS topic with a signed identity claim (Ed25519), so other agents can discover and verify it without a hardcoded URL or trusted middleman. Booking safety: Before any booking executes, the agent re-derives a SHA-256 hash of the exact itinerary (flights, prices, passenger count) server-side and requires it to match a human-confirmed session — preventing a stale or swapped itinerary from being booked without consent. The honest hack — flight data: Real flight-search APIs (Amadeus, Duffel, etc.) are paid and gated behind commercial contracts we couldn't get for a hackathon timeline, and scraping live fares isn't something we were willing to do. So the "supplier" is a real, live x402-gated service — the payment, pricing, and settlement are 100% real on-chain — but the flight inventory it serves is a curated dummy dataset rather than a live GDS feed. Every dollar (well, tinybar) spent buying that data is a genuine Hedera testnet transaction; the data itself is fixtures. We were explicit about this boundary throughout the build rather than dressing it up as real.

Before booking, the agent requires an explicit human confirmation bound to the exact itinerary hash, preventing any bait-and-switch between what was quoted and what gets booked. Every payment, approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext event to a public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic, giving a fully auditable trail anyone can verify on HashScan — no black box, no trust required.

The paid flight-data supplier is a real, live x402 service (not a mock) with metered per-result pricing, and it also self-registers on an HCS-based agent registry with a signed identity claim, so other agents can discover it and verify who they're paying without a hardcoded endpoint.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The stack is a monorepo: a Next.js frontend (the planner/agent), an Express-based supplier service (the paid flight-data API), and a self-hosted x402 facilitator, all wired for Hedera testnet.

Payments (x402 + HBAR): The supplier gates its search routes with HTTP 402 — each request returns a price, the agent signs an HBAR transfer, and the facilitator verifies + settles on-chain before the real data is returned. Pricing is metered per result (not a flat fee), using a quote cache keyed by a canonical hash of the query so the unpaid 402 price and the paid response always agree.

Autonomous, non-custodial payment: Rather than the agent holding user funds, we use Hedera's HIP-336 HBAR allowance. The user signs once in HashPack to grant a spending allowance; the agent then pays the supplier directly from the user's account using its own server-held key, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before settling. This took real HAPI-level probing to get right — Hedera requires the spender (our agent), not the fee-payer or facilitator, to own the transaction ID for an allowance-debited transfer, a rule that's undocumented for HBAR (only stated for NFTs in the protobufs) and had to be discovered empirically with test transactions.

Auditability (HCS): Every payment, human approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext JSON event to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, readable live via Mirror Node — a public, tamper-evident audit trail with no local cache. The supplier also self-registers on a second HCS topic with a signed identity claim (Ed25519), so other agents can discover and verify it without a hardcoded URL or trusted middleman.

Booking safety: Before any booking executes, the agent re-derives a SHA-256 hash of the exact itinerary (flights, prices, passenger count) server-side and requires it to match a human-confirmed session — preventing a stale or swapped itinerary from being booked without consent.

The honest hack — flight data: Real flight-search APIs (Amadeus, Duffel, etc.) are paid and gated behind commercial contracts we couldn't get for a hackathon timeline, and scraping live fares isn't something we were willing to do. So the "supplier" is a real, live x402-gated service — the payment, pricing, and settlement are 100% real on-chain — but the flight inventory it serves is a curated dummy dataset rather than a live GDS feed. Every dollar (well, tinybar) spent buying that data is a genuine Hedera testnet transaction; the data itself is fixtures. We were explicit about this boundary throughout the build rather than dressing it up as real.

projects.title: Aquastack
projects.description: One balance, two yields: Aave lending + 1inch Aqua liquidity, with automated depeg exit
projects.project_description: In normal DeFi, a dollar can only do one job at a time: it's either lent out on a money market like Aave, or it's paired into a liquidity pool on a DEX. You have to choose, and whichever you don't choose sits there earning nothing. AquaStack removes that choice by making a single stablecoin deposit do both jobs simultaneously, without ever splitting or moving the underlying funds. The mechanism relies on a property of 1inch Aqua, a shared-liquidity layer where a liquidity provider registers a "virtual balance" with the protocol instead of transferring tokens into a pool. Aqua only ever touches the real tokens at the exact instant a swap settles, pulling from the maker's wallet and pushing the counter-asset back. Because the tokens sit in the wallet the entire time rather than being locked in a pool contract, they are free to simultaneously be something else: a rebasing Aave v3 aToken, quietly accruing lending interest every block. Nothing is double-spent, since Aqua can never pull more than the registered virtual balance allows. The full flow: you deposit two stablecoins (USDC and USDT on our Base Sepolia deployment). Both are supplied to Aave v3, minting rebasing aUSDC and aUSDT directly into your wallet. Those aTokens are then registered with Aqua as a pegged, narrow-band automated market maker strategy. From that point on, the aTokens keep rebasing with Aave yield in the background, while real swaps route through the pegged pool and pay the position a small spread on top — two independent income streams from one balance. Because pegged pools carry depeg risk, every position carries a protective rule you configure at deposit time: a peg-deviation limit, a take-profit target, a stop-loss, and a max-drawdown limit, any combination of which can be active. An automated keeper runs a pass over every open position on a schedule, reads its live on-chain state, evaluates the rule, and either holds, raises an alert, or executes a full unwind: docking the Aqua position, repaying any variable debt left by an asymmetric swap, and withdrawing both legs from Aave back to your wallet as plain stablecoins plus yield. This happens automatically, even if you are offline, without ever taking custody of your funds. The keeper only ever holds a Privy session signer scoped to exactly two functions, dock() and withdraw(), on the one position it was delegated for.
projects.how_its_made: AquaStack is a Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) app with the entire chain-facing layer built as Server Actions, so none of the 1inch SDK code or RPC logic ever ships to the browser. The client only ever receives pre-built, ready-to-sign transaction plans and read-only position state. The stack: wagmi + viem for chain reads and transaction sending, Privy for wallet auth (both a plain browser-wallet fallback and Privy's embedded wallets with delegated session signers), Tailwind for styling, and Upstash Redis for the position/rule store in production — it falls back to a local JSON file in dev, since a serverless deployment's filesystem doesn't persist between invocations but a long-running dev server's does. The core partner technology is 1inch Aqua, via the official @1inch/aqua-sdk and @1inch/swap-vm-sdk. Aqua's key property a maker registers a virtual balance and the underlying tokens only move at the instant a swap settles  is what makes the whole product possible: it lets the same aToken be Aave-earning and Aqua-liquidity at once, since Aqua never actually takes custody. Aave v3 supplies the lending side for real, live yield rather than a simulated APY. The most notable hacky bit: neither 1inch Aqua nor SwapVM has an official Base Sepolia testnet deployment, so we redeployed both ourselves  opcode-identical to the official SDK builds — and verified the whole flow end-to-end against our own deployment, which the 1inch bounty rules explicitly allow. Close behind that: the 1inch SDKs ship a broken ESM build (extensionless relative imports that Node can't resolve), so we had to add the packages to Next.js's serverExternalPackages config to force it to fall back to native require() and pick up the working CJS build instead  without that, the build silently fails at import time. Another deliberate design choice: a deposit ships min(suppliedLegA, suppliedLegB) to Aqua so the pegged curve always starts exactly at 1:1, leaving any small remainder from an unbalanced deposit sitting in the wallet, still earning Aave yield, just outside the Aqua position. And the keeper itself only ever holds a Privy session signer scoped to exactly dock() and withdraw() for one position at a time a deliberately narrow blast radius instead of a general-purpose delegated signer.

projects.title: Maqam Protocol
projects.description: Discover agents with The Graph. Authorize one exact USDC payment on Arc.
projects.project_description: Maqam Protocol connects live agent discovery to exact, single-use payment authorization. The Graph supplies ERC-8004 registrations on Base Sepolia. The app screens declared capabilities, active status, indexed agent wallets and distinct non-owner feedback reviewers, explaining which candidates can proceed to human review and which are held. A real recorded model analysis uses a fresh Graph snapshot to recommend a candidate, with its complete input and output preserved. For a selected agent, the wallet review refreshes Graph data and binds the agent ID and snapshot hash into the exact payment evidence. The owner independently verifies the invoice and recipient, then signs the token, amount, recipient, executor, expiry, nonce and revocation epoch. A Solidity executor on Arc Testnet enforces those terms and transfers USDC once. Changed recipients or amounts, replay and revoked approvals fail. The demo shows live Graph screening, recorded model reasoning, and a separate mined Arc payment fixture with controlled owner, executor and recipient accounts. The receipt viewer verifies that real payment against live Arc RPC. We do not claim the Graph-discovered third-party agent was hired or paid. Registry claims and feedback do not prove trust or an Arc payment agreement. This is a new ETHOnline application using the existing public MIT maqam@0.3.3 npm library as a disclosed dependency. Its contracts, UI, APIs, Graph integration, assets and tests were created during the event. The initial Continuity classification was corrected to Building from Scratch based on the public-library exception; see BUILD-PROVENANCE.md. This is an unaudited testnet prototype.
projects.how_its_made: The Graph is the live data backend for agent selection. A server-side GraphQL request reads the Agent0 ERC-8004 Subgraph on Base Sepolia. Deterministic screening checks active registration, an explicit agent wallet, task keyword matches and a configurable distinct-reviewer threshold. Index errors or data more than 15 minutes behind halt discovery. We retain exact snapshots and hash them; a selected candidate is queried again during payment review, and the snapshot commitment is included in the signed evidence. Packet import checks the snapshot and recipient linkage. A separate real model adapter uses live Graph results for a candidate recommendation; the hosted model panel clearly labels that preserved call as recorded. The Solidity executor uses OpenZeppelin EIP712, SignatureChecker (including ERC-1271), SafeERC20 and ReentrancyGuard. Owner nonces are consumed atomically with transferFrom. Cancellation and epoch invalidation revoke pending approvals. An ethers 6 browser client verifies runtime bytecode, manages exact token allowances and requests typed signatures. The public Cloudflare Worker serves Vite assets and bounded policy/discovery APIs. maqam@0.3.3 is an existing MIT public library used for proposal policy, not claimed as newly authored code. Graph credentials remain server-side. The initial demo uses documented public read-only gateway access distributed by Agent0's SDK; a dedicated Graph Studio key is configurable. Thirty-two automated tests cover contracts, policy, Graph screening and evidence integrity, plus the real UI handlers against a local EVM: exact allowance/signing, settlement, replay, revocation, wallet changes and separate-executor packet import. Clean Linux CI and the production build pass. Pending wallet or input changes invalidate stale reviews; imported packets undergo onchain signature, nonce and epoch validation. Public Chrome checks verify live Graph results, the Arc receipt and a narrow-screen layout. Arc USDC is the settlement asset and gas currency: ERC20 amounts use six decimals, native gas uses eighteen. The fully verified contract and retained 1 USDC fixture prove exact authorization and replay protection. That fixture is separate from Graph-discovered third-party agents. A second Chrome test connected the participant’s MetaMask wallet and settled a 0.10 test-USDC self-payment on Arc (block 61761093). The participant confirmed wallet prompts while Codex operated the app; recipient/amount tampering and replay were rejected through eth_call simulations. Public receipt and consumed-nonce verification are retained in evidence/participant-wallet-test.json. This second test is not a separate-executor or third-party agent payment. AI assistance: OpenAI Codex assisted research, implementation, tests, UI and documentation. Specifications, model prompts, live-query evidence and incremental commits are retained. Participant direction, automated tests, scripted signing, human wallet testing and narration are distinguished honestly in AI-ASSISTANCE.md.

projects.title: product tracker
projects.description: Transparent USDC grants on Arc — one-sig contribute + ERC-8004 agent IDs.
projects.project_description: Open Treasury is a transparent public-funding vault on Arc Testnet. It is built for NGOs, DAOs, grant programs, and anyone who needs to collect USDC and later pay it out as grants — with every contribution and allocation visible on-chain. The problem. Typical treasuries are opaque: money goes into a wallet or multisig, and the public cannot easily see who funded it, how much is still free to grant, or what has already been promised to recipients. Open Treasury separates who paid from what the vault holds, and it keeps grant state on-chain. How funding works. A contributor connects a wallet (MetaMask, Rabby, Coinbase Wallet, Trust, or Phantom) on Arc Testnet, gets test USDC from Circle’s faucet, and submits an amount plus a short reference (for example a campaign or grant name). That reference is hashed with keccak256 and stored in a ContributionRecorded event. Approve and contribute happen in one signature using Arc’s Multicall3From, so the recorded contributor is the user’s wallet, not a helper contract. The same Arc USDC balance pays both the donation and gas. How the vault works. Funds sit in TreasuryVault. Operators (role holders) can create grants, approve them, and recipients can claim (including partial claims). The UI today focuses on connect, inspect balances, register an agent, and contribute. Grant create/approve/claim is already in the contracts and is planned for the UI next. Agents. On Arc, actors can have a portable ERC-8004 identity (an NFT ID on Arc’s shared Identity Registry — we did not deploy our own). Users can register an agent, then optionally tag a contribution as agent:{id}|their-reference. That does not move money by itself; it lets funding be attributed to an on-chain agent, not only a bare address. Reputation and ERC-8183 jobs (for example agent-assisted grant review) are the next step. What you can see. The app shows wallet USDC, vault total, available (unallocated) and allocated balances, transaction finality with Arcscan links, recent contribution history, and in-app docs from the project README.
projects.how_its_made: Open Treasury is a transparent USDC grants vault on Arc Testnet. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.20, built and tested with Foundry (unit + invariant tests) and OpenZeppelin (AccessControl, Pausable, SafeERC20). The protocol is split on purpose: TreasuryVault holds tokens and grant state (Pending → Approved → Claimed); a thin TreasuryFundingRouter pulls USDC and emits ContributionRecorded so the vault never stores who paid. Contributors get one wallet signature by batching USDC.approve + router.contribute through Arc’s Multicall3From (aggregate3 + CallFrom). That preserves the original EOA as msg.sender — a normal multicall would record the batcher as the contributor. We always use Arc USDC’s ERC-20 6-decimal interface for amounts; the same USDC balance also pays gas (native 18-decimal). The frontend is Vite + React + TypeScript, wagmi / viem, and TanStack Query. Wallet connect uses explicit injected targets (MetaMask, Rabby, Coinbase Wallet, Trust, Phantom) so providers don’t race on window.ethereum. History prefers Arcscan’s logs API because Arc RPC caps eth_getLogs at 10k blocks. A known router ABI typo (refrenceHash) is kept so event topics still decode. For Arc’s agentic stack we did not deploy a private registry: we call register(string) on the shared ERC-8004 Identity Registry. Contributions can optionally hash agent:{id}|reference so funding is attributable to a portable agent ID. Docs in the app are the root README parsed into sections at build time. Hacky-but-necessary bits: Multicall3From sender preservation, USDC 6 vs 18 decimals, chunked/Arcscan log fallbacks, and collapsing huge wallet-reject hex dumps behind Details. Hosted on Vercel from the frontend/ app. That’s about 1,600 characters. projects.title: Mandate Run
projects.description: Give your agent a mandate, not a credit card. It refuses what it can't justify.
projects.project_description: An agent handed a wallet will spend it. Mandate is the layer that decides whether a purchase is worth making at all. Give it a purpose, a budget, and hard constraints. It sends each x402 seller the real request to collect a live 402 quote, then competes three plans over the remaining work: staged evidence, a hybrid, or one bundle. It picks the lowest expected cost among plans whose worst case still fits the budget at full coverage, reserves the final step so it can always finish, and pays one signed Hedera transfer per purchase. When no plan can guarantee coverage, it refuses before spending a cent and says what completion would have cost. That refusal is the product, not a failure mode. The worked example investigates Uniswap v3 liquidity. It screens five pools, finds the one that moved, buys transaction-level evidence for that pool alone, and writes an explanation in which every number is checked back against purchased facts. A model only writes prose; the runtime computes every claim itself. Settlement is proven from the Hedera mirror node's records for the runtime's own transaction id, never from an HTTP response. A lost response is recovered with the original signed payment rather than a second one. A crash costs at most one attempt. Every decision writes a receipt to Hedera Consensus Service. Payment behavior is verified by Proctor, a harness in the same repo. Its task contracts have two halves: one reads the buyer's own report, the other reads what Proctor measured independently from the seller's journal and the buyer's ledger. A check passes only when both agree, because an application is never its own oracle. Proctor caught a real double-payment bug during development from the journal, not from anything the buyer said about itself.
projects.how_its_made: The buyer runtime is Rust, edition 2024 on 1.98.1, with its own x402 types and an exact-scheme Hedera signer built on the Hedera Rust SDK. State lives in SQLite as a recovery ledger: signed payment bytes are persisted before anything leaves the process, so a crash or a dropped response never costs a second payment. A single ledger invariant (settled + outstanding + held <= budget) is enforced on every transition and tested across 200 randomly interleaved operations. The sellers are TypeScript on Node 24: four x402-gated endpoints with published tariffs, priced per pool, per pool-window, and per input KB rather than a flat rate. They serve evidence from the Uniswap v3 subgraph on The Graph Network (5zvR82QoaXYFyDEKLZ9t6v9adgnptxYpKpSbxtgVENFV) through the gateway with a Subgraph Studio key, reading token-denominated TVL at the window's two observation blocks, hourly volume, and the largest events above a materiality threshold. Every response states its block range, coverage, truncation, and indexing status, so the buyer can tell thin data from no data. Payments settle on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator, which acts as fee payer and co-signs. The asset is a field of the mandate, so one code path settles HBAR and any fee-free fungible HTS token. Circle's testnet faucet never delivered USDC to us after four attempts, so rather than fake it we made the runtime mint its own HTS token and proved settlement in that instead. projects.project_description_markdown:
An agent handed a wallet will spend it. Mandate is the layer that decides whether a purchase is worth making at all.

Give it a purpose, a budget, and hard constraints. It sends each x402 seller the real request to collect a live 402 quote, then competes three plans over the remaining work: staged evidence, a hybrid, or one bundle. It picks the lowest expected cost among plans whose worst case still fits the budget at full coverage, reserves the final step so it can always finish, and pays one signed Hedera transfer per purchase.

When no plan can guarantee coverage, it refuses before spending a cent and says what completion would have cost. That refusal is the product, not a failure mode.

The worked example investigates Uniswap v3 liquidity. It screens five pools, finds the one that moved, buys transaction-level evidence for that pool alone, and writes an explanation in which every number is checked back against purchased facts. A model only writes prose; the runtime computes every claim itself.

Settlement is proven from the Hedera mirror node's records for the runtime's own transaction id, never from an HTTP response. A lost response is recovered with the original signed payment rather than a second one. A crash costs at most one attempt. Every decision writes a receipt to Hedera Consensus Service.

Payment behavior is verified by Proctor, a harness in the same repo. Its task contracts have two halves: one reads the buyer's own report, the other reads what Proctor measured independently from the seller's journal and the buyer's ledger. A check passes only when both agree, because an application is never its own oracle. Proctor caught a real double-payment bug during development from the journal, not from anything the buyer said about itself.

projects.title: Aether Credit
projects.description: Evidence-aware AI treasury for policy-constrained USDC payments on Arc.
projects.project_description: Aether Credit is an agent-native treasury platform that helps organizations manage USDC spending without surrendering control to an AI model. Employees submit expenses, managers approve an exact immutable version, and an evidence-aware analyst compares lending markets using The Graph. The agent can recommend, abstain, or require review, but it can never authorize a transfer. Every payment must independently pass deterministic rules covering recipients, per-payment limits, cumulative budgets, reserves, expiry, pause state, approvals, and replay protection. Eligible payments are executed through Circle Agent Stack against a customer-owned vault on Arc and reconciled into an inspectable audit trail. Privy provides organization authentication, wallets, role-bound approvals, and constrained funding controls.
projects.how_its_made:
Aether Credit is a TypeScript monorepo with separate Next.js consumer and admin applications, a Fastify API, PostgreSQL and Drizzle ORM, and durable analysis and payment workers backed by pg-boss. Shared Zod contracts keep validation consistent across the browser, API, and workers. The analyst is a typed Vercel AI SDK harness that queries standardized lending data through The Graph, records deployment IDs, query parameters, freshness, block height, response hashes, citations, calculations, model metadata, and failure states, and fails closed when its evidence is stale or incompatible.
Privy authenticates three organization roles, binds users to wallets, captures exact EIP-712 approvals, and constrains treasury funding with a deposit-only signer policy. Payments are submitted by Circle Agent Stack on Arc Testnet to a non-upgradeable Solidity vault whose customer wallet is the immutable owner. The vault rechecks allowlists, caps, budgets, reserves, expiry, pause state, signatures, and replay protection onchain. The payment worker uses idempotency keys and independently reconciles transaction receipts and decoded events, treating timeouts as unknown outcomes instead of blindly retrying.
One particularly hacky integration detail came from Circle Agent Stack CLI 1.0.0 rejecting the vault’s original nested-tuple ABI before broadcast. We added scalar contract entry points while preserving the same policy checks, then covered the adapter with regression tests. The result is deliberately split between probabilistic advice and deterministic authority: AI explains what should happen, while application and contract policy decide what is permitted to happen.

projects.title: GaussVM
projects.description: Gaussian prediction-market liquidity, powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
projects.project_description:
GaussVM brings Gaussian prediction-market liquidity to 1inch Aqua, using SwapVM to turn a research pricing curve into executable onchain trades. It builds on the pm-AMM research by Ciamac Moallemi and Dan Robinson and connects it to a working application where users can trade YES/NO outcome tokens, create liquidity positions, and inspect transaction receipts.
Aqua’s approach to liquidity is central to the project. Makers authorize trading strategies while keeping their outcome tokens in their wallets until a trade executes. A single wallet can support both GaussVM’s static and experimental time-scaled strategies without making separate token deposits for each position. Actual execution still depends on the wallet’s balances and allowances.
SwapVM provides the other essential piece: programmable execution. GaussVM implements Gaussian pricing as a custom SwapVM instruction, while the surrounding engine handles order validation and settlement through Aqua. Together, these 1inch technologies provide a practical foundation for taking a specialized market-making idea from a paper to a usable trading experience.
The live Sepolia demo asks a simple, slightly self-referential question: “Will this project win ETHOnline 2026?” Users can obtain free test tokens, swap between YES and NO, and follow confirmed transactions on an explorer. Liquidity controls support creating and removing positions, while the market contracts handle merging complete sets and redeeming outcomes after resolution.
GaussVM demonstrates how Aqua and SwapVM can support a pricing model tailored to binary outcomes. It is currently an unaudited testnet prototype with worthless test assets and manual resolution. Its time-scaled mode is an experiment, rather than a claim to reproduce the research paper’s complete economic result.
projects.how_its_made:
The project is built around two complementary pieces of 1inch infrastructure: Aqua for liquidity accounting and token transfers, and SwapVM for programmable trade execution. GaussVM extends the official SwapVM base with a custom Gaussian instruction, opcode 0x80, and uses an unmodified deployment of official Aqua source.
When a maker creates a position, the application encodes the market, liquidity scale, timestamps, and strategy mode into a SwapVM order and authorizes it through Aqua. During a swap, the custom instruction reads that strategy’s current allocations and calculates how many outcome tokens the trader receives. SwapVM then applies its execution checks and settles the transfer through Aqua. This division lets GaussVM focus its custom logic on prediction-market pricing while using 1inch’s infrastructure for the surrounding execution flow.
The mathematical implementation uses signed 18-decimal fixed-point arithmetic, bounded Gaussian cumulative-distribution and density calculations, and a bisection solver with conservative output rounding. One useful optimization computes the density once and shares it between the calculations that need it. Regression tests compare the optimized and earlier implementations, including returned values, rejected inputs, and complete swaps.
Separate Solidity contracts provide test collateral, ERC-20 YES/NO tokens, collateral-backed splitting and merging, manual resolution, and timeout cancellation. Positions support either a static liquidity scale or an experimental scale based on the square root of the remaining market lifetime.
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and viem. It reads balances and allocations, obtains quotes through contract simulation, requests limited token approvals, and links confirmed transactions to Sepolia receipts. Submitted hashes are preserved when confirmation is unavailable so users can recheck the same transaction. The public interface is hosted on GitHub Pages without a hosted backend or database.
The repository includes numerical tests, contract integration tests, Playwright browser tests, and a standalone Hardhat lifecycle demo. That demo exercises two Aqua strategies sharing one maker wallet, executes trades, checks actual balance changes and Aqua events, removes the positions, and completes merging and redemption. A separate fork demo runs the same lifecycle against 1inch’s canonical Aqua deployment, with all writes confined to a local Ethereum fork.
