projects.title: LockENS
projects.description: ENSv2-powered NFC access passes with wallet proofs and resource-level authorization.
projects.project_description: LockENS turns wallet-held ENSv2 identities into access credentials that can be presented over NFC. The final demo uses one Android holder and three Android gate stands representing a Front Door, Lab and Server Room. A user selects a pass in the LockENS Android app and presents it through Android HCE/NFC. The holder signs a fresh proof with a Privy embedded wallet. A local verifier checks holder control offchain and reads the current credential state and resource permissions from ENSv2 on Sepolia before returning ALLOW or DENY. This means the same credential can remain owned by the same wallet while its global access, validity or permissions for individual resources change independently. The demo shows real NFC grant and denial flows, wallet switching, suspended credentials and resource-specific authorization. The gates are virtual interfaces rather than physical lock actuators.
projects.how_its_made: LockENS is built as an Android + NFC + Node.js authorization stack backed by ENSv2 on Sepolia. The holder app is written in Kotlin and uses Android Host Card Emulation to present the selected credential over NFC. Privy provides embedded wallets and signs a fresh resource-bound EIP-712 holder proof. On the gate side, Android devices act as persistent NFC Gate Stands for the Front Door, Lab and Server Room. A local Node.js verifier uses viem to validate the holder proof offchain and then reads the current ENSv2 state on Sepolia. ENSv2 UserRegistry establishes registration and ownership, while PermissionedResolver data provides global access and resource-level policy. The verifier only returns ALLOW when holder control and the current ENSv2 policy both pass; errors and denials fail closed. For the final four-device demo, each Android gate reaches the same local verifier through ADB reverse. We also built and validated an experimental ESP32-S3 + PN532 route during development, but the final submission uses the more reliable Android gate architecture. The notable part is that NFC presentation, wallet control and ENSv2 authorization are separate layers: possession of the phone or credential alone is not enough to open a gate. The verifier evaluates fresh holder proof plus current onchain policy for the specific resource being requested.

projects.title: Bloom
projects.description: The Bloomberg terminal for trading with AI agents — chat to buy, sell, and track assets live
projects.project_description: A smart helper answers you and at the same time builds clear, live pictures on the screen for you price charts, market lists, your money balances, and simple trade boxes with a Confirm button. You can watch live prices move second by second, pause or switch what you are watching, and see a full history of all your past trades in one small floating box. For safety, there is a practice mode where you start with play money. In short, it turns confusing trading work into a calm conversation with live pictures, a practice playground, and one-click real actions.
projects.how_its_made: This project used privy wallet for auth, sub-graph for sub second real time data and uniswap api for trading and executing trades. And open ai, openUi for agents and real time UI generation for interaction and agents trade. Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS frontend.   Substreams for live prices. PostgreSQL + Redis for state and caching.

projects.title: Plimsoll
projects.description: Tokenised notes the network refuses to settle once their real backing falls below the line.
projects.project_description: Every tokenised asset today prices itself with a number its issuer typed in, and a market that trusts that number has no way to stop trading when it stops being true. Plimsoll is a market for tokenised notes backed by real ERC-4626 vault positions, where coverage is computed continuously from the vault flows themselves and never taken from the issuer. Nothing in the calculation is typed in: the note's obligations are read from its own supply and nominal value on Hedera, the holder is the note's own on-chain issuer, and we value what that address actually holds in the nominated vaults on Base, so a claim of backing larger than the real balance has nowhere to go. When coverage falls below the note's load line, the network refuses: transfers revert with a typed reason, coupons stop settling because the cash leg is frozen at consensus, and a paid request for a coverage attestation returns a signed refusal that is never charged. Moving the load line or halting a market requires a human to approve it on a Ledger device, and a refusal on the device produces no signature at all. The name comes from the Plimsoll line, the mark on a ship's hull made law in 1876 after ships were deliberately overloaded and sunk for the insurance: a visible limit past which the authorities will not let a vessel sail.
projects.how_its_made: Plimsoll is five pieces that each own one job. The truth layer is a Rust Substreams package ( packages/substreams ) that imports Pinax's ERC-4626 extractor by pinned URL, so its module hash and server-side cache are unchanged, and adds what they deliberately left out: a vault registry resolved by an asset() probe instead of topic0 matching, entry and exit rates kept apart so a fee spread cannot hide in one blended number, a consistent() check that refuses a zero or out-of-band share price, per-holder positions read with batched eth_call s inside the stream ( map_positions ), and Messari Yield Aggregator v1.3.1 entities, all from one spkg that runs on Ethereum and Base and is published to substreams.dev as v0.2.0; a cross-check script compares the stream against independent archive nodes wei for wei, and check_package.py refuses to release a package whose embedded README names a module the package does not contain, a check that exists because we shipped exactly that mistake once. An MCP server ( packages/mcp , Streamable HTTP plus an A2A card) serves that feed with the package hash, module hash and block on every answer and refuses rather than serve a stale figure. The attestation service ( packages/attestor , TypeScript with viem and the Hedera SDK) values the issuer's positions on Base with eth_call pinned to a block hash and corroborated by a second RPC, reads the note's supply, par, issuer and load line from Hedera so no number in the ratio is configured, and signs EIP-712 over CoverageOracle 's own domain and types, with a test that hashes the same payload in TypeScript and in Solidity; it is sold per call over x402 through Blocky402, where the exact scheme settles only after the handler succeeds, so any refusal returns a 4xx and settlement is never called, which makes a refusal free by construction rather than by refund, and every verdict is anchored to an immutable HCS topic so verify-charge can check from public data that a charge exists if and only if an attestation was warranted. The contracts ( packages/contracts , Foundry, 201 tests, Sourcify-verified on Hedera testnet) put a coverage gate in front of an order book built on ATS's non-reverting canTransferByPartition pre-flight and holdByPartition escrow, pay coupons in an HTS cash token whose freeze key is a contract key with no admin key, and re-arm coupons with HIP-1215 scheduleCall ; moving a load line or halting a market needs a mandate approved on a Ledger device through the Device Management Kit, the contract rebuilds the displayed text from typed arguments rather than parsing it, and the verifier answers only to its adapter while the adapter answers only to LoadLine, so a signed mandate cannot be spent through a side door. One command ( packages/verify ) checks all of it from public endpoints with no keys. The hackiest part: the Ledger Ethereum app reflows newlines into spaces and wraps at about nineteen characters, so a market code containing NONCE: 9 could make a human approve what reads as a mandate with two nonces; we found it on the emulator and closed it with a charset rule enforced identically in TypeScript and Solidity. The most humbling part: our own checks caught an attestation we had submitted from test fixtures while the real backing was zero, and the deployment record now says so beside the stored number instead of letting it read as a measurement.

projects.title: Private Hire
projects.description: Hire agents for private work, verify their deliveries, and settle payments onchain
projects.project_description: PrivateHire is a platform for hiring agents to perform private work with verifiable delivery and onchain payments. A buyer chooses an agent, defines a task, and funds an escrowed request. The agent receives the inputs needed to complete the work, while the buyer’s evaluation policy remains separate. An evaluator checks the committed delivery against that policy and produces a decision used to resolve payment. The goal is to verify work without publishing its underlying inputs, full results, or evaluation policy onchain. Public records contain participants, payment amounts, lifecycle events, and cryptographic commitments. Inputs and results are stored encrypted and exposed through authenticated routes. The current backend operator remains trusted and can access the stored data. Our first integrated agent is Portfolio Calculator. It processes a synthetic portfolio and returns deterministic position values, portfolio weights, and concentration. It provides a concrete example of the hiring flow: request an analysis, agree on its price, fund it, receive a report, and evaluate the delivery. PrivateHire brings together ERC-8004 agent identity, A2A communication, Chainlink CRE evaluation, and ERC-8183 contracting on Arc Testnet. The prototype integrates one agent; onboarding additional agents is the next step.
projects.how_its_made: PrivateHire is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces and Turborepo. The frontend uses Next.js App Router, deployed to Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. Browser wallets connect through wagmi and RainbowKit, with viem for contract interactions and Sign-In with Ethereum for authenticated sessions. Cloudflare D1 stores request correlations, task states, and processed events. Private payloads are encrypted with AES-GCM and stored in a private R2 bucket. Conditional writes and task reservations prevent concurrent requests from replacing an existing delivery. Recovery retrieves the same persisted artifact and commitment rather than silently generating a new result. Portfolio Calculator communicates through A2A. Its calculations use BigInt, explicit decimal representations, and deterministic rounding. The buyer’s evaluation policy is not included in the agent request. A separate provider service is implemented to confirm budgets and submit deliveries, with restricted transaction construction and a durable journal that preserves signed transaction bytes across retries. Chainlink CRE connects private evaluation to onchain settlement. The workflow checks request funding and commitments, retrieves the A2A delivery, evaluates it against the private policy, and constructs a public report for an evaluator receiver. The confidential path uses handlerInTee and Vault secret references. Our demonstration uses CRE simulation; deployed enclave execution is not claimed. On Arc Testnet, we reuse an existing ERC-8183 deployment for the request lifecycle and USDC payment escrow. ERC-8004 supplies the agent’s registered identity. The evaluator receiver is configured specifically for simulation reports and validates report context, state, expiry, and replay before resolving a request. A key engineering challenge was coordinating browser transactions, encrypted offchain artifacts, agent delivery, and evaluation without treating client-side assertions as truth. Receipts and RPC reads establish onchain state, while transport or integrity failures leave evaluation pending instead of turning technical failures into business rejection.

projects.title: Priime
projects.description: The vault structuring platform to compose, test & distribute vaults; in one verifiable venue.
projects.project_description:
The vault structuring platform to create, test & distribute vaults; in one verifiable venue. Problem
The chain can hold a vault. It cannot run one.
A vault has an infrastructure problem: a smart contract cannot react to markets, and it cannot compute the math a strategy needs, so the work that actually operates a vault sits on private servers, and that breaks composability, growth and trust. That server is a legal entity to structure, a breach waiting to be disclosed, and a centralized dependency no other protocol can build on. Solution
Priime is where a strategy becomes a verifiable, automated onchain vault.
So we built the infrastructure and the killer app on top of it. A strategy is composed on a canvas, backtested and launched as a vault, and the off-chain work it needs runs as decentralized compute on our own Trustless Execution Network. Sophistication, efficiency, security and reach all go up without giving up decentralization. That is what lets DeFi products get better now, and what will let TradFi products be built onchain tomorrow. Discover what we built during ETH Online hackathon here: https://priime.finance/ETHOnline-Priime-Hackathon
projects.how_its_made: The chain can hold a vault. It cannot run one. A contract cannot react to a market or compute what a strategy needs, so the work that operates 7.5 billion dollars of curator-run vaults runs on someone's private server. Nobody outside can check it. The Priime canvas replaces the company with modules. A Liquidity source pins the venue and the market; Dynamic leverage holds the position inside a published health band; Auto-compound puts the earnings back to work. Every number is modeled from live market data before publish. Corrupt one operator and the chain still takes the honest number. Publishing hands the composition to the Trustless Execution Network, where operators each re-execute the same deterministic WASM component against the same pinned input block, and only a quorum of identical signed results settles. In our sabotage strike the honest operators reported 500.000000 USDC and the corrupted one reported 750.000000. The lie never settled. A quorum-signed plan cannot drain the vault. Settlement is an ERC-4626 vault on Base with an ERC-7540 redemption queue, one per strategy. Operators sign a plan and the vault executes it against a whitelist of target and selector pairs in which every address argument is decoded and pinned to the vault itself, so no foreign receiver and no rogue approval spender can be named. The operators never touch funds. Every dependency a strategy touches gets a watcher. A vault does not have to be exploited to lose money, it only has to hold something that was: of this year's 165 DeFi exploits, 44 ran through a bridge, a cross-chain message or a price feed, and cost 405.3 million dollars. They are watched as one stack, every block. The Graph gives one schema across protocols, so a single query spans many of them and a strategy becomes backtestable before it ships. Wallets, policies and quorum approvals run through Privy, and the depositor keeps ownership of the position. Uniswap is the trading engine on every entry and exit, with v4 hooks at the edges. Discover what we built during ETH Online hackathon here: https://priime.finance/ETHOnline-Priime-Hackathon

projects.title: Levee
projects.description: An on-chain wallet that turns planned spending into time-locked funds
projects.project_description: Freelancers and gig workers rarely experience income as a steady stream. Three weeks can pass with nothing, followed by two invoices at once. Yet rent, subscriptions, and bills arrive on fixed dates regardless. The real problem is knowing what is genuinely safe to spend today without spending tomorrow's rent. Most financial tools are advisory. They warn you, and you dismiss the warning and spend anyway. The failure is not the maths. It is that nothing stands in the way at the moment the decision is made. An actual levee, the embankment kind, does not persuade water to stay back. It simply does not let it through. This one works the same way with money. People with irregular income already do a version of this by hand, with separate accounts, cash set aside, or fixed deposits. Those work right up until the moment you decide to override them. And no bank budgeting tool reaches on-chain income at all. Define an obligation, such as rent, 0.006 ETH, due on the 25th, and those funds move into a contract that will not release them early. Not to the app, not to an agent, not to you. Your home screen shows one number: what is actually free to spend right now. Try to spend past it and Levee declines, names the obligation protecting the money, and tells you when it unlocks. No transaction is sent. An in-app assistant answers questions about your position in plain language. It reads live contract state for what is spendable right now and indexed history for what has happened over time. It answers only from data it has, and never invents a figure. The same guarantee extends to software. Subscription bots and payment agents do not know what you have set aside, so Levee publishes a spend-check service they can call before spending. They get back a verdict and the specific obligation standing in the way. Every budgeting tool asks you to be disciplined. Levee makes discipline a property of the system instead.
projects.how_its_made: Levee is built around a Solidity smart contract deployed on Ethereum Sepolia through Remix. The contract implements four core operations: "deposit", "commit", "spendFree", and "release". "commit" earmarks a portion of the user's balance against a Unix timestamp and label. "release" reverts before the unlock date, making early release impossible regardless of caller, while "spendFree" can access only uncommitted funds. A read-only "canSpend" check runs before spending and returns whether an amount is allowed, along with the earliest-unlocking commitment blocking it. This enables deterministic refusal without submitting a transaction that would revert. Everything else hangs off that one function. "canSpend" drives three separate surfaces: the refusal screen in the app, the assistant's answer when a user asks why they are blocked, and the public endpoint an autonomous agent calls. All three read the same verdict from the same source, so a bot and a human are never told different things about the same wallet. The frontend uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind, and viem. Privy handles email and social authentication while creating embedded wallets automatically, so users never need to manage seed phrases or connect external wallets. External wallet connection is deliberately disabled. Without embedded wallets this would be a dapp for people who already own MetaMask, which is the opposite of the intended user. Subgraph Studio indexes the "Deposited", "Committed", "Released", and "Spent" events. Live contract reads answer what can be spent right now; the Subgraph answers what has been committed over time. Without that indexed history the assistant could only read a balance back to you, rather than reason over commitments made and released. The in-app natural-language assistant combines both feeds to answer real-time and historical questions. It operates strictly on supplied data and never fabricates figures. The same pairing powers a public agent endpoint, whose responses include a "sources" field identifying the origin of each result. The endpoint is documented through OpenAPI and published through a Bazantic gateway with a Recipe explaining when and why an autonomous agent should call it, which turned a plain endpoint into a discoverable service rather than something only I knew existed. Two things were genuinely painful to get working. Privy's RPC rejects "wallet_sendTransaction", which is exactly what viem defaults to when the wallet client is created without an explicit account and chain, so every write failed with an opaque "unsupported method" error until both were passed into "createWalletClient" directly. And the Gemini model catalog is inconsistent with its own serving endpoint: "gemini-2.5-flash" is listed as healthy with "generateContent" supported, but calling it 404s, and the error body redirects to a different model. Trusting the error over the catalog was the only way through.

projects.title: Plimsol
projects.description: Proof of enough, not proof of how much: a confidential credit check for autonomous agents.
projects.project_description: Two agents want to do a deal on credit. The buyer wants the goods now and will pay later. The seller has to decide whether the buyer is good for it. Right now the buyer has two ways to answer, and both are bad. It can show its whole balance sheet, in which case the seller knows exactly how hard to squeeze it. Or it can say "trust me", which is worth nothing. Plimsoll is a third option. The seller pays a few cents to ask one question, "is this agent above the line?", and gets back one signed bit on chain. We call that a Mark. It says ABOVE, BELOW, or INDETERMINATE, plus a timestamp and an expiry. That's it. No balance, no amounts, no price. Not even the reason if it failed. The reading happens inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow running in an AWS Nitro enclave. The enclave fetches the buyer's private holdings with a key only it can see, prices them at Chainlink, applies a haircut, and compares to the threshold. Only the verdict comes back out. The privacy comes from the structure, not from asking nicely. The buyer decides in advance which thresholds it's willing to be asked about (we call that the ladder). Nobody can ask anything finer, so the most you can ever learn is "somewhere between two rungs", and the buyer picked the rungs. Requests are rate-limited per counterparty so you can't just ask every rung. And because a "no" leaks more than a "yes", publishing a no is opt in per rung. One good answer can be faked with a flash loan, so lenders look for Standing: three yeses spread over a day. Bazantic is how an agent actually uses this. Two live gateways and a published Recipe that an agent calls as one tool: price the deal at Chainlink, pick the rung, ask, read the Mark, decide. The Recipe also carries the rule that matters most: if the answer is no, don't ask again at a lower rung. Everything is live on Sepolia. Real Marks have been posted by the workflow, and the dashboard lets anyone request one and watch it land.
projects.how_its_made: We started with the contracts. PlimsollRegistry (Foundry, Sepolia) holds subjects, their ladders, survey requests and Marks. It's a CRE receiver, so the Forwarder calls onReport and the contract decodes the six fields and checks them the same way it would a hand posted Mark. Lines are stored as structs rather than hashes so one Mark can serve any counterparty whose exposure it covers. CreditDesk is the reference lender and won't pay out without Standing. 42 tests. The Survey is a CRE workflow in TypeScript. An EVM log trigger fires on SurveyRequested and the handler is registered with handlerInTee, so it runs inside AWS Nitro. In there it pulls the Hold credential from the Vault DON, makes three HTTP calls (the ladder, the Chainlink price, and the buyer's holdings), does the valuation in plain integer math, and crosses back to the DON with only the verdict and its provenance. Debug logging is off in every shipped config because logs leave the enclave too. We simulated it with the CRE CLI against real Sepolia transactions, then left it running in listen mode so new requests get answered on their own. The transcripts are in the repo. The API is a Next.js app on Vercel with route handlers for price, line derivation, ladder, requests, Marks and Standing, all reading the chain with viem. The Hold adapter lives there too, behind a shared key that only the enclave presents, and it's deliberately missing from every public spec. For Bazantic we served two OpenAPI specs, registered two gateways with x402 settlement (sandbox, test USDC on Base Sepolia), and published two Recipes from JSON definitions with Claude Sonnet as the model. We ran the composed Recipe end to end with paid calls.

projects.title: Heirloom
projects.description: Non-custodial HBAR inheritance: an allowance, not a deposit, released by the chain itself.
projects.project_description: Every crypto inheritance product today is a vault: you hand your savings to a contract and hope it gives them back later. Heirloom does the opposite. The owner grants our contract a native HBAR allowance (HIP-906) from their own wallet. No money moves. They keep spending normally. The allowance lies dormant until the switch fires, and then a single HTS cryptoTransfer with isApproval=true moves the HBAR directly from the owner's account to the beneficiary's. Our contract's balance never changes. This is only possible on Hedera: Ethereum has no allowance mechanism for its native asset. There is also no server, keeper, or cron job. The vault schedules calls to itself with HIP-1215 scheduled contract calls. It wakes up, checks whether the owner is alive, and reschedules. The interval tightens as the deadline approaches (30 days, then 7, then 1), so the system watches harder the closer it gets to acting. Liveness is detected passively. Every transaction the owner signs costs a fee, so any activity lowers their balance, and only the key holder can cause a decrease. The heartbeat sees that and resets the timer. The owner never has to open our app. A one-tap "I am alive" covers the rest. Before releasing, the vault re-checks liveness one last time and reads the allowance live from the ledger; if the owner has been active, it resets instead of releasing. It fails toward not releasing. The beneficiary needs no setup and need not know the vault exists. The factory indexes vaults by beneficiary, so connecting a wallet is enough to find one. The owner can revoke at the ledger level at any time by setting the allowance to zero, with no cooperation from our contract. This is running on Hedera Testnet. We watched a scheduled self-call release 100 HBAR from the owner's account to the beneficiary's, three times, with nobody clicking anything. The vault's balance only ever moved by its own heartbeat fees.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry, tested against mocked Hedera system contracts etched at 0x167 (HTS), 0x16a (HAS) and 0x16b (HSS), 63 unit tests plus fuzzing on the timer maths. Three Hedera primitives do the real work: HIP-906 HBAR allowances (the owner calls hbarApprove on the Hedera Account Service; the vault reads hbarAllowance live, never cached), HIP-206 atomic cryptoTransfer with isApproval=true to spend that allowance, and HIP-1215 generalized scheduled contract calls for the vault to schedule its own heartbeat(). The scheduler never reverts: failures are emitted, and a permissionless poke() restarts a dead chain. The frontend is Next.js 16, Tailwind 4, wagmi and viem, with MetaMask over the Hedera JSON-RPC relay. The activity log is built entirely from mirror-node event queries; no subgraph. Deploy and lifecycle scripts are TypeScript with viem and the Hedera SDK. We spent the first hours on verification spikes before writing production code, and they earned their keep. Two findings overturned our plan. First, inside the Hedera EVM every value (msg.value, address.balance, call{value}) is already tinybars; the relay presents weibars. Our spec assumed weibars in the contract and would have released 10^10 times too little. The contract now does zero unit conversion. Second, a scheduleCall costs about 1.5M gas, so our planned 400k heartbeat budget would have killed the chain on its first link, and each heartbeat costs about 1.75 HBAR, which we surface as runway in the dashboard. Calling release() from the owner's own wallet aborted the release, because paying the fee proved the owner alive. Only a non-owner can trigger a release now. We also drained the fee reserve exactly at the finish line in one test run (INSUFFICIENT_PAYER_BALANCE on the final scheduled call), which is why the reserve is refundable, runway is shown, and anyone can restart the chain. And MetaMask refuses to send calldata to one of its own accounts, so the allowance grant goes through the Account Service system contract instead of the HIP-906 own-address redirect. Nothing is faked: the demo runs on testnet with compressed timings (3-minute timeout, 15/10/5-second heartbeats) using the same code path as production. projects.project_description_markdown:
Every crypto inheritance product today is a vault: you hand your savings to a contract and hope it gives them back later. Heirloom does the opposite. The owner grants our contract a native HBAR allowance (HIP-906) from their own wallet. No money moves. They keep spending normally. The allowance lies dormant until the switch fires, and then a single HTS cryptoTransfer with isApproval=true moves the HBAR directly from the owner's account to the beneficiary's. Our contract's balance never changes. This is only possible on Hedera: Ethereum has no allowance mechanism for its native asset.

There is also no server, keeper, or cron job. The vault schedules calls to itself with HIP-1215 scheduled contract calls. It wakes up, checks whether the owner is alive, and reschedules. The interval tightens as the deadline approaches (30 days, then 7, then 1), so the system watches harder the closer it gets to acting.

Liveness is detected passively. Every transaction the owner signs costs a fee, so any activity lowers their balance, and only the key holder can cause a decrease. The heartbeat sees that and resets the timer. The owner never has to open our app. A one-tap "I am alive" covers the rest. Before releasing, the vault re-checks liveness one last time and reads the allowance live from the ledger; if the owner has been active, it resets instead of releasing. It fails toward not releasing.

The beneficiary needs no setup and need not know the vault exists. The factory indexes vaults by beneficiary, so connecting a wallet is enough to find one. The owner can revoke at the ledger level at any time by setting the allowance to zero, with no cooperation from our contract.

This is running on Hedera Testnet. We watched a scheduled self-call release 100 HBAR from the owner's account to the beneficiary's, three times, with nobody clicking anything. The vault's balance only ever moved by its own heartbeat fees.

projects.title: Signa Covenant
projects.description: An FX coverage gate on Arc: USDC drawdowns are refused onchain when the hedge stops covering them.
projects.project_description: A credit originator owes investors USDC while its loans repay in euros. The loan book lives in a servicing system, the hedge lives at a bank, and the capital sits in a vault that cannot see whether that hedge is current, sufficient, or even matched to this facility. The covenant meant to govern all of this is checked by operations on a calendar, while capital moves on demand. Signa Covenant puts the covenant in the money path. The servicer and the hedge provider each sign an EIP-712 credential: one states what is owed, the other what is hedged. A coverage engine on Arc computes how much of the outstanding USDC obligation the hedge actually covers, after a haircut. Every drawdown asks the gate first, and when coverage falls below the facility's minimum, the vault refuses the draw onchain. It is live on Arc Testnet and proven with receipts. The same draw, with byte-identical calldata, was sent three times to the same vault: accepted at 100% coverage, refused at 68.4% with DrawNotAllowed(CURE), and accepted again once a fresh hedge credential restored coverage. Nothing changed between the three calls except the evidence underneath them. Overriding the covenant is governed too. The facility admin is a Privy 2-of-2 key quorum, fixed at creation, so a waiver needs two named approvers, and the wallet's policy only lets it call createWaiver on this vault on Arc. Boundary: signatures authenticate who asserted what. They do not prove a hedge legally exists. The hedge feed in the demo is a labelled mock, and no bank has signed anything.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity, built and tested with Foundry: FacilityRegistry, CredentialRegistry, CoverageEngine and CovenantVault, deployed to Arc Testnet (chain 5042002) and verified on Arcscan. The product is one small interface, ICoverageGate.assess(facilityId, amount). CoverageEngine implements it. CovenantVault is the reference host: every draw is ruled by assess and reverts with a typed reason when coverage is short. The offchain side is TypeScript and viem, using arcTestnet from viem/chains. A credentials package builds and verifies the EIP-712 exposure and hedge credentials, and the registry only accepts a sequence number higher than the last one for that trade, so a stale credential cannot be replayed. A scenario runner drives the acceptance sequence against Arc and writes every hash, receipt and block reference to a JSON evidence file. A Vite dashboard reads the deployment manifest, simulates before any write, and explains a refusal in plain language. Arc made us careful about money. USDC is the gas token with 18 decimals, while its ERC-20 view has 6: one balance, two views, 10^12 apart. Every amount crossing into a credential goes through a single decimals module. And cast send exits 0 even when the transaction reverts, so every step asserts its receipt status in the direction it expects: the refusal has to be a failed receipt carrying the DrawNotAllowed selector, not just any error. Privy governs the override. A server wallet owned by a 2-of-2 key quorum is the facility admin, and each approver holds a non-extractable P-256 key in their browser. The hacky part: authorizing a Privy intent needed two fields the docs don't mention, intent_id and timestamp, signed over Privy's normalized request body (RFC 8785 canonical JSON, ECDSA P-256). Privy's managed broadcast isn't enabled for Arc on our app yet, so Privy signs the transaction and we broadcast it ourselves. The wallet policy restricts the key to createWaiver on this vault on Arc. It can't cap the waiver's uint32 duration, so the contract enforces that cap. 64 TypeScript and 31 Solidity tests run in CI. A local Anvil replay covers the states the testnet run doesn't reach: breach, cure expiry, and repayment during breach.

projects.title: Riptide
projects.description: An AMM that charges a volatility-indexed fee and auctions stale-price arb back to LPs.
projects.project_description: RIPTIDE — an AMM on 1inch Aqua + SwapVM that prices and reclaims the money LPs lose to arbitrage The problem A normal AMM quotes a price from its reserves and collects a swap fee. That quote lags the rest of the market. When ETH moves on a CEX, the pool still quotes the old price until someone trades against it. The trader who does that is usually an arbitrageur, and the profit comes from the LP. This is called Loss-Versus-Rebalancing (LVR) . Since 2022 there has been a closed-form expression for it. For a constant-product pool it is σ²/8 of pool value per unit time. At 100% annualised volatility that is one eighth of the pool per year, paid to arbitrageurs, before fees. Two consequences: A fixed fee does not match the cost. LVR scales with σ² . A flat 30 bps overcharges on quiet days and undercharges on volatile ones. The arb profit can be auctioned instead of left to the mempool. When the pool is stale, the size of that profit is known. Today it goes to whoever pays the highest priority fee. It can instead go to whoever pays the LP the most for the right to take the trade. What RIPTIDE is A RIPTIDE strategy is a constant-product pool ( x · y = k ) with two extra layers: a fee that moves with volatility, and an auction for the right to reprice the pool when it is stale. The curve itself is unchanged. Mechanism 1 — a fee that tracks volatility. An on-chain controller reads a live volatility estimate and moves the fee toward the break-even point where expected fee revenue covers expected LVR: φ* = (σ̂²/8)/λ , clamped into the maker's [feeMin, feeMax] band, approached by a clamped PI controller with anti-windup. Higher volatility, higher fee; lower volatility, lower fee. To a trader this is an ordinary protocol fee. It is delivered through 1inch's existing fee instruction — no new fee opcode . SwapVM already staticcalls an IProtocolFeeProvider ; RIPTIDE answers that call with a contract that reads an on-chain EWMA volatility estimate. Because it is a staticcall, the fee a quote shows and the fee a swap charges are the same number. Mechanism 2 — a Dutch auction for the rebalance. When the external price moves, the strategy opens a declining-price auction for the right to rebalance the pool. Resolvers compete on time priority. On settlement the contract measures surplus S on-chain, pays the resolver ⌊(1−β)·S⌋ , and leaves at least β·S with the LP. With β = 0.95 , at most about 5% of the arb value leaves. A reverse swap immediately afterwards is penalised, so the rebalance cannot be sandwiched. If S is not positive the trade reverts, which also stops a resolver from filling at a loss. The loop between them. A resolver only settles when the rebalance is profitable, so the price they pay is a traded price, not just an oracle print. That price is written into the volatility oracle and moves the next fee target. This is a design property, not a theorem. The research this is built on Nothing in the economics is invented. Three papers, all included in the GitHub Repo arXiv:2208.06046 (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden, Zhang) — the definition and closed form of LVR, and the identity that decides everything: LP value − rebalancing value = fees − accumulated LVR . arXiv:2210.10601 ("Diamond", McMenamin, Daza, Mazorra) — the recapture result: auction the rebalancing right and retain β , and the LVR escaping to arbitrageurs is bounded by E[LVR] ≤ (1−β)·L . Their simulations use β = 0.95 . arXiv:2305.14604 (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden) — the fee is the instrument that offsets LVR, with an interior optimum. We take the principle, not a closed-form constant. EWMA/Garman–Klass volatility estimation and the PI controller come from outside that set and are labelled as engineering mechanics, not economic claims. Papers we deliberately did not use are listed with a written reason for each. How it uses 1inch This is built on Aqua and SwapVM, not merely alongside them. Aqua is the custody layer. Makers keep tokens in their own wallets. Aqua holds an allowance record, not the money — so there is no vault to trust and no LP share token. RIPTIDE's routers are registered as Aqua apps that pull / push against a maker's ledger entry. No RIPTIDE contract ever holds inventory. All five Aqua primitives ( ship / dock / pull / push / safeBalances ) are load-bearing. SwapVM is the execution layer. A strategy is a bytecode program. RIPTIDE emits two: a 41-byte swap program built entirely from upstream opcodes ( Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt ), and a 66-byte rebalance program that adds two RIPTIDE instructions — the declining-price schedule and the β-split. A 226-byte policy payload (fee band, auction policy, oracle config, salt) rides in the same order via the MakerTraits program slice, which is what lets a strategy's full policy be committed in Aqua's immutable strategy hash. Everything compiles against swap-vm@v1.0.2 and aqua@v1.0.0 — the releases 1inch has actually deployed to mainnet, never main — and @1inch/aqua-sdk builds all Aqua calldata in production . We deploy two slimmed routers rather than the all-opcodes SwapVMRouter (which does not fit EIP-170) because RIPTIDE needs a custom instruction; the resulting swap program is still a plain Aqua-AMM program, and a fork test ships it to a stock, unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and asserts it prices identically to ours, to the wei. Integration against the real 1inch mainnet Aqua registry is proven by a separate mainnet fork test. Who gets what Liquidity providers — tokens stay in your wallet; no vault, no LP token. Your fee rises when volatility rises, so you charge more precisely when you are losing more, and when the price gaps, most of the re-pricing profit comes back to you instead of going to a searcher. The dashboard shows the number that matters: cumulative value recaptured. Traders — a quote that shows the applied fee and the σ that produced it , before you sign. Orders are split across makers by a solver and settle atomically: if any fill fails the whole route reverts and you keep your funds. Resolvers / searchers — a legible source of flow instead of a mempool race. See open auctions with their live declining price, preview your exact take ⌊(1−β)·S⌋ before committing, and settle through a permissionless entry point from any wallet. Analysts — every headline number links to the on-chain event that produced it, with the indexed block stated and an honesty panel marking which claims are verified on-chain versus validated by simulation. What is actually deployed Fourteen contracts live on Base Sepolia with three seeded strategies running different fee bands and β values (0.90 / 0.95 / 0.97), a six-page web app (one per persona: explainer, maker studio, swap terminal, resolver board, positions, analytics), a subgraph on Graph Studio indexing six contracts into thirteen entities, and four off-chain services (solver API, resolver bot, volatility indexer, and an MCP server exposing executable-liquidity tools). The off-chain layer is untrusted and replaceable — none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute everything. How we verified it 120 Solidity test functions across 45 files. Five named protocol invariants, each shipping a negative control — a deliberately broken variant that must make the test fail, so a green suite is evidence the tests can fail. Plus 10 fuzz tests at 10,000 runs, 12 differential tests against a committed Python oracle, atomic-rollback and reentrancy tests, and fork tests against the canonical 1inch mainnet Aqua deployment. On top of that, a scripted end-to-end run against the live deployed app — it generates two wallets, funds them from the faucet, and walks every persona (ship → swap exact-in → swap exact-out → skew the oracle → preview → settle → dock → read analytics) through the same HTTP endpoints the browser uses. Nothing pre-approved, no fixtures. The most recent run: 20 transactions, 41/41 assertions , every hash linked to BaseScan in docs/E2E_RUN.md . in our Github repo. It observed σ move from 0 to 0.1124 after a settlement, with the fee target shifting to 15954 against a reported 10892 — the loop closing, measured rather than asserted.
projects.how_its_made: RIPTIDE is a constant-product AMM that runs as SwapVM programs over 1inch Aqua. The curve is ordinary x · y = k . Around it sit two control layers: a fee that tracks realized volatility, and an auction that sells the right to reprice a stale pool and keeps most of the surplus with the maker. The repo is a pnpm monorepo. Contracts are Foundry (Solidity 0.8.30, via_ir , 700 optimizer runs, Cancun — the same settings as pinned SwapVM, because opcode-table layout is build-dependent). Everything else is all-ESM TypeScript. The subgraph is AssemblyScript. The app is Next.js 15. Python is used only as an independent math oracle. Aqua holds allowance records. Maker tokens stay in maker wallets until a trade pulls them. Two slim SwapVM routers execute the programs — one for taker swaps, one for rebalances. Behind them sit a volatility oracle, a fee provider the VM staticcalls mid-swap, and a stateless kernel that does the surplus and β split. Periphery is a quoter that prices through the real VM, a lens, a permissionless auction settler, and a batch executor for atomic multi-maker routes. Off-chain (solver, resolver bot, vol indexer, MCP server, subgraph, web app) is untrusted: none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute from live state. We compile against SwapVM v1.0.2 and Aqua v1.0.0 — the releases 1inch has actually deployed, never main . GitHub main has a different fee-provider signature that does not exist in any published release; we implement the v1.0.2 one, getFeeBpsAndRecipient → (uint32, address) , which Fee.sol decodes as exactly 64 bytes. @1inch/aqua-sdk 0.3.4 builds all ship/dock calldata in production. @1inch/swap-vm-sdk is installed and unused. OpenZeppelin 5.4.0 and Solady 0.1.26 (ln/exp/pow/sqrt, wrapped with explicit domains) fill the rest. 1inch has no Aqua on Base Sepolia, so the demo deploys an unmodified official Aqua v1.0.0 instance; integration against the real registry is a mainnet fork test that ships WETH/USDC into the canonical Aqua address. Aqua Aqua is a shared-liquidity registry. A maker approves it once and distributes virtual balances across strategies. RIPTIDE's routers register as Aqua apps, which is what lets them pull and push against a maker's ledger. ship is called from the maker's own wallet — no RIPTIDE contract ever calls it — and commits strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order)) . safeBalances is read on every quote and every swap; SwapVM seeds balanceIn / balanceOut from it before running the program, never from a cache or an indexer. pull sends swap output to the taker, the β rebate to whoever is settling a rebalance, and the protocol fee (that last one pulled by SwapVM itself). push credits taker input into the maker's strategy. dock cancels and releases balances. There is no RIPTIDE vault and no LP share token. The same tokens can back several strategies at once because Aqua distributes allowance, not capital. A docked strategy cannot execute even if router runtime is stale. Fee collection on the swap path is best-effort by upstream design: SwapVM wraps the fee pull and emits a skip rather than reverting, so a one-sided maker position stays tradable. SwapVM A strategy is a bytecode program: [opcode:1][argsLength:1][args:N] . RIPTIDE emits two. Mechanism 1 uses only upstream opcodes. Mechanism 2 adds two RIPTIDE instructions. Reserves are not loaded by a balance opcode — the Aqua trait makes the router seed registers from safeBalances before runLoop . Emitting DynamicBalances would overwrite those Aqua-seeded registers, so it is absent. Aqua stores no policy, and neither does either router. The full policy has to be immutable at ship time, so it goes in the order: order.data = [226-byte payload][program bytes] , order.traits = (1 << 254) | (226 << 208) . Bit 254 tells SwapVM to authorise via Aqua and seed from safeBalances . 226 << 208 writes the program start into MakerTraits slice index 3 (bits 208–223), so the VM sees data[226:] and never the payload. On-chain resolution honours this packing; the SwapVM SDK normalises it away. Re-encoding a live order through that SDK returns 224 bytes instead of 448, drops the payload, and orphans the Aqua position — which is why order construction stays with our codec. The Aqua SDK produced byte-identical calldata to what we had hand-rolled, so it replaced that code. The SDK's ESM build is also broken (a deep import with no exports map), so it cannot be imported from this workspace anyway. Because the Aqua trait is set, SwapVM's order hash is the same value Aqua computes as strategyHash . Any change to payload, program, or auction start is a different Aqua position. The payload is packed big-endian, magic RPT1 : tokens, salt, reserve snapshots, fee band, PI gains, auction parameters, oracle config, fee-provider address. maker is deliberately not in it. Decoding is never authorisation — every runtime path re-reads live Aqua balances. The codec exists in Solidity, TypeScript, and Python, held identical by committed vectors. Four identifiers are never interchangeable: policyHash = keccak256(payload) , strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order)) , strategyKey = keccak256(abi.encode(maker, salt)) , and marketId of the ordered pair. Aqua events speak in hashes; router and fee-provider events speak in keys. The subgraph is what reconciles them. SwapVM dispatches on an index into a function-pointer array. Aqua's opcode set builds a fixed array and converts it to a dynamic one by writing the length into slot 0 with assembly, which overwrites element 0. Every runtime index is therefore one less than its source position — XYCSwap dispatches at 17, not 18. A test resolves the indices from the live table so a silent upstream renumber fails the build instead of swapping in the wrong instruction. We do not repeat that assembly write when extending the table; we allocate a new array and append at 34–37. Opcode 37 ( OraclePriceAdjuster ) is reserved and unused: it rewrites swap amounts toward a Chainlink price, which would fight Mechanism 1 rather than observe volatility. 1inch's all-opcodes router does not fit EIP-170, and the stock Aqua AMM router has no slot for a custom instruction. We deploy two slimmed routers on the same SwapVM base, each with a reduced opcode table at the canonical Aqua indices. Mechanism 2 is further split into a router and a module. The swap router is 24,548 bytes against the 24,576-byte cap — 28 bytes of headroom, asserted in CI. To check it is still a real Aqua AMM program, the Mechanism 1 program is shipped to a stock unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and asserted to price identically, to the wei. Mechanism 1 The swap program is 41 bytes: Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt . Every opcode is upstream. The dynamic fee needed no new opcode — SwapVM already staticcalls a provider; we answer with a contract that returns a committed, volatility-indexed rate. The fee instruction wraps the rest: save amountIn , subtract the fee, run the swap and salt on the net input, restore, then try to pull the fee. Volatility is estimated on-chain (EWMA of log returns, optional Garman–Klass range term, clamped, stale-frozen). Only the rebalance router and a governed indexer key may observe ; quoting is static and writes nothing. The controller targets φ* = (σ²/8)/λ , clamps into the maker's [feeMin, feeMax] , and steps with a PI loop and anti-windup. The maker sets the band and the gains, not the fee. The provider is view and returns the already committed feeReported . The controller advances only after a swap or a rebalance, so within a block the quoted fee and the charged fee are the same number. RIPTIDE denominates fees at 1e7 = 100% ; SwapVM v1.0.2 uses 1e9 . We initially returned the wrong scale, so the VM charged 100× too little, silently, with every test still green because they shared the bug. The conversion now lives at the one provider return ( ×100 ). Setting the scale back to 1 breaks five tests. Mechanism 2 The rebalance program is 66 bytes: Deadline, then a declining-price instruction that scales balanceIn by decay^(now − start) , then wrapping Decay (anti-sandwich), XYCSwap , the custom rebalance instruction, and Salt. Deadline is first so an expired auction reverts before any balance is touched. SwapVM's DutchAuction lives in the limit-order opcode group, not the AMM group. Rather than borrow across that boundary, the schedule is a RIPTIDE instruction that only scales a reserve register. XYCSwap still prices from the constant-product curve. Shrinking balanceIn reduces what the resolver must pay over time, so surplus decays toward zero and they race to be first at a still-profitable price. On settlement the module decodes (beta, staleInWad) from 24 bytes of args, takes the rebate recipient from the VM taker (not from the args), measures S = executedIn − staleIn , reverts if negative, and pays ⌊(1−β)·S⌋ via Aqua pull . projects.project_description_markdown:
## RIPTIDE — an AMM on 1inch Aqua + SwapVM that prices and reclaims the money LPs lose to arbitrage

### The problem

A normal AMM quotes a price from its reserves and collects a swap fee. That quote lags the rest of the market. When ETH moves on a CEX, the pool still quotes the old price until someone trades against it. The trader who does that is usually an arbitrageur, and the profit comes from the LP.

This is called **Loss-Versus-Rebalancing (LVR)**. Since 2022 there has been a closed-form expression for it. For a constant-product pool it is `σ²/8` of pool value per unit time. At 100% annualised volatility that is one eighth of the pool per year, paid to arbitrageurs, before fees.

Two consequences:

1. **A fixed fee does not match the cost.** LVR scales with `σ²`. A flat 30 bps overcharges on quiet days and undercharges on volatile ones.
2. **The arb profit can be auctioned instead of left to the mempool.** When the pool is stale, the size of that profit is known. Today it goes to whoever pays the highest priority fee. It can instead go to whoever pays the LP the most for the right to take the trade.

### What RIPTIDE is

A RIPTIDE strategy is a constant-product pool (`x · y = k`) with two extra layers: a fee that moves with volatility, and an auction for the right to reprice the pool when it is stale. The curve itself is unchanged.

**Mechanism 1 — a fee that tracks volatility.** An on-chain controller reads a live volatility estimate and moves the fee toward the break-even point where expected fee revenue covers expected LVR: `φ* = (σ̂²/8)/λ`, clamped into the maker's `[feeMin, feeMax]` band, approached by a clamped PI controller with anti-windup. Higher volatility, higher fee; lower volatility, lower fee. To a trader this is an ordinary protocol fee. It is delivered through 1inch's existing fee instruction — **no new fee opcode**. SwapVM already staticcalls an `IProtocolFeeProvider`; RIPTIDE answers that call with a contract that reads an on-chain EWMA volatility estimate. Because it is a staticcall, the fee a quote shows and the fee a swap charges are the same number.

**Mechanism 2 — a Dutch auction for the rebalance.** When the external price moves, the strategy opens a declining-price auction for the right to rebalance the pool. Resolvers compete on time priority. On settlement the contract measures surplus `S` on-chain, pays the resolver `⌊(1−β)·S⌋`, and leaves at least `β·S` with the LP. With `β = 0.95`, at most about 5% of the arb value leaves. A reverse swap immediately afterwards is penalised, so the rebalance cannot be sandwiched. If `S` is not positive the trade reverts, which also stops a resolver from filling at a loss.

**The loop between them.** A resolver only settles when the rebalance is profitable, so the price they pay is a traded price, not just an oracle print. That price is written into the volatility oracle and moves the next fee target. This is a design property, not a theorem.

### The research this is built on

Nothing in the economics is invented. Three papers, all included in the GitHub Repo

- **arXiv:2208.06046** (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden, Zhang) — the definition and closed form of LVR, and the identity that decides everything: *LP value − rebalancing value = fees − accumulated LVR*.
- **arXiv:2210.10601** ("Diamond", McMenamin, Daza, Mazorra) — the recapture result: auction the rebalancing right and retain `β`, and the LVR escaping to arbitrageurs is bounded by `E[LVR] ≤ (1−β)·L`. Their simulations use `β = 0.95`.
- **arXiv:2305.14604** (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden) — the fee is the instrument that offsets LVR, with an interior optimum. We take the principle, not a closed-form constant.

EWMA/Garman–Klass volatility estimation and the PI controller come from outside that set and are labelled as engineering mechanics, not economic claims. Papers we deliberately did *not* use are listed with a written reason for each.

### How it uses 1inch

This is built *on* Aqua and SwapVM, not merely alongside them.

**Aqua is the custody layer.** Makers keep tokens in their own wallets. Aqua holds an allowance record, not the money — so there is no vault to trust and no LP share token. RIPTIDE's routers are registered as Aqua **apps** that `pull`/`push` against a maker's ledger entry. **No RIPTIDE contract ever holds inventory.** All five Aqua primitives (`ship`/`dock`/`pull`/`push`/`safeBalances`) are load-bearing.

**SwapVM is the execution layer.** A strategy *is* a bytecode program. RIPTIDE emits two: a **41-byte swap program built entirely from upstream opcodes** (`Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt`), and a **66-byte rebalance program** that adds two RIPTIDE instructions — the declining-price schedule and the β-split. A 226-byte policy payload (fee band, auction policy, oracle config, salt) rides in the same order via the MakerTraits program slice, which is what lets a strategy's full policy be committed in Aqua's immutable strategy hash.

Everything compiles against **`swap-vm@v1.0.2` and `aqua@v1.0.0`** — the releases 1inch has actually deployed to mainnet, never `main` — and **`@1inch/aqua-sdk` builds all Aqua calldata in production**. We deploy two slimmed routers rather than the all-opcodes `SwapVMRouter` (which does not fit EIP-170) because RIPTIDE needs a custom instruction; the resulting swap program is still a plain Aqua-AMM program, and a fork test ships it to a **stock, unmodified `AquaSwapVMRouter`** and asserts it prices identically to ours, to the wei. Integration against the *real* 1inch mainnet Aqua registry is proven by a separate mainnet fork test.

### Who gets what

- **Liquidity providers** — tokens stay in your wallet; no vault, no LP token. Your fee rises when volatility rises, so you charge more precisely when you are losing more, and when the price gaps, most of the re-pricing profit comes back to you instead of going to a searcher. The dashboard shows the number that matters: cumulative value recaptured.
- **Traders** — a quote that shows the applied fee **and the σ that produced it**, before you sign. Orders are split across makers by a solver and settle atomically: if any fill fails the whole route reverts and you keep your funds.
- **Resolvers / searchers** — a legible source of flow instead of a mempool race. See open auctions with their live declining price, preview your exact take `⌊(1−β)·S⌋` before committing, and settle through a permissionless entry point from any wallet.
- **Analysts** — every headline number links to the on-chain event that produced it, with the indexed block stated and an honesty panel marking which claims are verified on-chain versus validated by simulation.

### What is actually deployed

Fourteen contracts live on Base Sepolia with three seeded strategies running different fee bands and β values (0.90 / 0.95 / 0.97), a six-page web app (one per persona: explainer, maker studio, swap terminal, resolver board, positions, analytics), a subgraph on Graph Studio indexing six contracts into thirteen entities, and four off-chain services (solver API, resolver bot, volatility indexer, and an MCP server exposing executable-liquidity tools).

The off-chain layer is **untrusted and replaceable** — none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute everything.

### How we verified it

120 Solidity test functions across 45 files. Five named protocol invariants, each shipping a **negative control** — a deliberately broken variant that must make the test fail, so a green suite is evidence the tests *can* fail. Plus 10 fuzz tests at 10,000 runs, 12 differential tests against a committed Python oracle, atomic-rollback and reentrancy tests, and fork tests against the canonical 1inch mainnet Aqua deployment.

On top of that, a scripted end-to-end run against the **live deployed app** — it generates two wallets, funds them from the faucet, and walks every persona (ship → swap exact-in → swap exact-out → skew the oracle → preview → settle → dock → read analytics) through the same HTTP endpoints the browser uses. Nothing pre-approved, no fixtures. The most recent run: **20 transactions, 41/41 assertions**, every hash linked to BaseScan in `docs/E2E_RUN.md`. in our Github repo. It observed σ move from 0 to 0.1124 after a settlement, with the fee target shifting to 15954 against a reported 10892 — the loop closing, measured rather than asserted.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
RIPTIDE is a constant-product AMM that runs as SwapVM programs over 1inch Aqua. The curve is ordinary `x · y = k`. Around it sit two control layers: a fee that tracks realized volatility, and an auction that sells the right to reprice a stale pool and keeps most of the surplus with the maker.

The repo is a pnpm monorepo. Contracts are Foundry (Solidity 0.8.30, `via_ir`, 700 optimizer runs, Cancun — the same settings as pinned SwapVM, because opcode-table layout is build-dependent). Everything else is all-ESM TypeScript. The subgraph is AssemblyScript. The app is Next.js 15. Python is used only as an independent math oracle.

Aqua holds allowance records. Maker tokens stay in maker wallets until a trade pulls them. Two slim SwapVM routers execute the programs — one for taker swaps, one for rebalances. Behind them sit a volatility oracle, a fee provider the VM staticcalls mid-swap, and a stateless kernel that does the surplus and β split. Periphery is a quoter that prices through the real VM, a lens, a permissionless auction settler, and a batch executor for atomic multi-maker routes. Off-chain (solver, resolver bot, vol indexer, MCP server, subgraph, web app) is untrusted: none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute from live state.

We compile against SwapVM v1.0.2 and Aqua v1.0.0 — the releases 1inch has actually deployed, never `main`. GitHub `main` has a different fee-provider signature that does not exist in any published release; we implement the v1.0.2 one, `getFeeBpsAndRecipient → (uint32, address)`, which `Fee.sol` decodes as exactly 64 bytes. `@1inch/aqua-sdk` 0.3.4 builds all ship/dock calldata in production. `@1inch/swap-vm-sdk` is installed and unused. OpenZeppelin 5.4.0 and Solady 0.1.26 (ln/exp/pow/sqrt, wrapped with explicit domains) fill the rest. 1inch has no Aqua on Base Sepolia, so the demo deploys an unmodified official Aqua v1.0.0 instance; integration against the real registry is a mainnet fork test that ships WETH/USDC into the canonical Aqua address.

### Aqua

Aqua is a shared-liquidity registry. A maker approves it once and distributes virtual balances across strategies. RIPTIDE's routers register as Aqua apps, which is what lets them pull and push against a maker's ledger.

`ship` is called from the maker's own wallet — no RIPTIDE contract ever calls it — and commits `strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order))`. `safeBalances` is read on every quote and every swap; SwapVM seeds `balanceIn`/`balanceOut` from it before running the program, never from a cache or an indexer. `pull` sends swap output to the taker, the β rebate to whoever is settling a rebalance, and the protocol fee (that last one pulled by SwapVM itself). `push` credits taker input into the maker's strategy. `dock` cancels and releases balances.

There is no RIPTIDE vault and no LP share token. The same tokens can back several strategies at once because Aqua distributes allowance, not capital. A docked strategy cannot execute even if router runtime is stale. Fee collection on the swap path is best-effort by upstream design: SwapVM wraps the fee pull and emits a skip rather than reverting, so a one-sided maker position stays tradable.

### SwapVM

A strategy is a bytecode program: `[opcode:1][argsLength:1][args:N]`. RIPTIDE emits two. Mechanism 1 uses only upstream opcodes. Mechanism 2 adds two RIPTIDE instructions. Reserves are not loaded by a balance opcode — the Aqua trait makes the router seed registers from `safeBalances` before `runLoop`. Emitting `DynamicBalances` would overwrite those Aqua-seeded registers, so it is absent.

Aqua stores no policy, and neither does either router. The full policy has to be immutable at ship time, so it goes in the order: `order.data = [226-byte payload][program bytes]`, `order.traits = (1 << 254) | (226 << 208)`. Bit 254 tells SwapVM to authorise via Aqua and seed from `safeBalances`. `226 << 208` writes the program start into MakerTraits slice index 3 (bits 208–223), so the VM sees `data[226:]` and never the payload. On-chain resolution honours this packing; the SwapVM SDK normalises it away. Re-encoding a live order through that SDK returns 224 bytes instead of 448, drops the payload, and orphans the Aqua position — which is why order construction stays with our codec. The Aqua SDK produced byte-identical calldata to what we had hand-rolled, so it replaced that code. The SDK's ESM build is also broken (a deep import with no `exports` map), so it cannot be imported from this workspace anyway.

Because the Aqua trait is set, SwapVM's order hash is the same value Aqua computes as `strategyHash`. Any change to payload, program, or auction start is a different Aqua position. The payload is packed big-endian, magic `RPT1`: tokens, salt, reserve snapshots, fee band, PI gains, auction parameters, oracle config, fee-provider address. `maker` is deliberately not in it. Decoding is never authorisation — every runtime path re-reads live Aqua balances. The codec exists in Solidity, TypeScript, and Python, held identical by committed vectors.

Four identifiers are never interchangeable: `policyHash = keccak256(payload)`, `strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order))`, `strategyKey = keccak256(abi.encode(maker, salt))`, and `marketId` of the ordered pair. Aqua events speak in hashes; router and fee-provider events speak in keys. The subgraph is what reconciles them.

SwapVM dispatches on an index into a function-pointer array. Aqua's opcode set builds a fixed array and converts it to a dynamic one by writing the length into slot 0 with assembly, which overwrites element 0. Every runtime index is therefore one less than its source position — `XYCSwap` dispatches at 17, not 18. A test resolves the indices from the live table so a silent upstream renumber fails the build instead of swapping in the wrong instruction. We do not repeat that assembly write when extending the table; we allocate a new array and append at 34–37. Opcode 37 (`OraclePriceAdjuster`) is reserved and unused: it rewrites swap amounts toward a Chainlink price, which would fight Mechanism 1 rather than observe volatility.

1inch's all-opcodes router does not fit EIP-170, and the stock Aqua AMM router has no slot for a custom instruction. We deploy two slimmed routers on the same SwapVM base, each with a reduced opcode table at the canonical Aqua indices. Mechanism 2 is further split into a router and a module. The swap router is 24,548 bytes against the 24,576-byte cap — 28 bytes of headroom, asserted in CI. To check it is still a real Aqua AMM program, the Mechanism 1 program is shipped to a stock unmodified `AquaSwapVMRouter` and asserted to price identically, to the wei.

### Mechanism 1

The swap program is 41 bytes: `Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt`. Every opcode is upstream. The dynamic fee needed no new opcode — SwapVM already staticcalls a provider; we answer with a contract that returns a committed, volatility-indexed rate.

The fee instruction wraps the rest: save `amountIn`, subtract the fee, run the swap and salt on the net input, restore, then try to pull the fee. Volatility is estimated on-chain (EWMA of log returns, optional Garman–Klass range term, clamped, stale-frozen). Only the rebalance router and a governed indexer key may `observe`; quoting is static and writes nothing. The controller targets `φ* = (σ²/8)/λ`, clamps into the maker's `[feeMin, feeMax]`, and steps with a PI loop and anti-windup. The maker sets the band and the gains, not the fee.

The provider is `view` and returns the already committed `feeReported`. The controller advances only after a swap or a rebalance, so within a block the quoted fee and the charged fee are the same number. RIPTIDE denominates fees at `1e7 = 100%`; SwapVM v1.0.2 uses `1e9`. We initially returned the wrong scale, so the VM charged 100× too little, silently, with every test still green because they shared the bug. The conversion now lives at the one provider return (`×100`). Setting the scale back to 1 breaks five tests.

### Mechanism 2

The rebalance program is 66 bytes: Deadline, then a declining-price instruction that scales `balanceIn` by `decay^(now − start)`, then wrapping `Decay` (anti-sandwich), `XYCSwap`, the custom rebalance instruction, and Salt. Deadline is first so an expired auction reverts before any balance is touched.

SwapVM's `DutchAuction` lives in the limit-order opcode group, not the AMM group. Rather than borrow across that boundary, the schedule is a RIPTIDE instruction that only scales a reserve register. `XYCSwap` still prices from the constant-product curve. Shrinking `balanceIn` reduces what the resolver must pay over time, so surplus decays toward zero and they race to be first at a still-profitable price.

On settlement the module decodes `(beta, staleInWad)` from 24 bytes of args, takes the rebate recipient from the VM taker (not from the args), measures `S = executedIn − staleIn`, reverts if negative, and pays `⌊(1−β)·S⌋` via Aqua `pull`. The retained remainder stays in the maker's Aqua balance. The split also runs in static context, so a quote of a loss-making rebalance reverts the same way settlement would. The price written back to the oracle is the auction-clearing price, which moves σ and therefore the next fee target. That loop is a design property, not a theorem.

The rebate recipient used to be encoded in the program args. The program is part of `order.data`, which is part of the strategy hash, so an address in the args pinned the order to one resolver. On a live deployment only the pre-designated wallet could settle, which also breaks the auction: a monopolist waits until the price decays to wherever their margin is fattest. Args are now `beta ‖ staleInWad`, and the recipient is `ctx.query.taker`. That immediately showed a second bug: the settler is the VM taker, so the bought base landed on the settler and was never forwarded. It now sweeps both legs — unspent quote plus rebate, and the base — back to `msg.sender`. Anyone can call it; protection is the surplus check, not an allow-list.

`RebalanceSettled` names the VM taker, which on this path is the settler contract. `AuctionSettled` names `msg.sender`. The subgraph joins them in the same transaction so attribution is per wallet rather than one contract address forever.

### Math

WAD fixed point, explicit rounding, revert on zero denominator or overflow. `amountIn` ceils, `amountOut` floors, the β rebate floors — all three favour the maker. SwapVM registers are output-per-input; the UI shows quote-per-base; conversion happens only at the market boundary.

### The Graph

RIPTIDE is single-maker micro-pools: each maker ships their own strategy, and there is no on-chain registry to enumerate them. Aqua is keyed by hash and exposes balance getters only. So the taker path is discover off-chain, verify on-chain. The subgraph answers what exists; the contracts re-derive every number that matters. A stale snapshot can make a route revert. It cannot authorise a bad fill. It also gives the time series (fees vs σ, recapture vs payout) that an RPC node does not.

Six datasources, including 1inch Aqua. Lifecycle and inventory are Aqua's `Shipped`/`Docked`/`Pushed`/`Pulled`, filtered to the RIPTIDE app. The rest are our router, fee provider, batch executor, rebalance router, and settler. A fill on our router resolving to a strategy created by an Aqua `Shipped` is a cross-contract join, which is why this is one subgraph.

The load-bearing field is `orderBytes`. Policy lives only in the 226-byte payload inside the Aqua order. Aqua has no getter for it; neither router stores it. projects.title: Zuno.fun
projects.description: A community-governed launchpad that recycles liquidity from inactive tokens into active projects.
projects.project_description: ZUNO is a liquidity-recycling token launchpad on Arc Testnet. Creators launch tokens on a bonding curve; traders buy and sell until the graduation target is hit. Instead of burning LP forever, ZUNO locks LP in a vault when the token lists on Uniswap V2 so liquidity stays recoverable. If a graduated pool goes quiet, ActivityMonitor flags it as inactive. The community can then propose healthier listed tokens, stake USDC to vote, and execute a recycle: dead LP is removed and redeployed into the winning pool, then locked again. The app covers the full loop Explore, Launch, Trade, Lifecycle (list / vote / recycle), charts, and recent trades with native USDC gas on Arc.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity + Hardhat): Core bonding curve (Core, BondingCurveFactory), local Uniswap V2 stack, DexRouter, LPRecyclingVault, ActivityMonitor, and RecyclingGovernor. Deployed stepwise on Arc (chain id 5042002) after a one-shot deployer hit Arc’s initcode size limit a practical hack we worked around with scripted multi-step deploys and wiring. Indexing: A The Graph Studio subgraph on arc-testnet indexes Create / Buy / Sell / Listing / Swap into tokens, trades, and 1m candles for Explore, charts, and trade feeds. Frontend: Next.js + wagmi / ethers / Privy for wallet + Arc network. Token lists prefer subgraph → Mongo → short RPC lookback so the UI stays snappy. Mongo stores lifecycle state (phase, progress, vault, proposals); post-trade soft-refresh updates mcap, progress, chart, and trades.

The app covers the full loop Explore, Launch, Trade, Lifecycle (list / vote / recycle), charts, and recent trades with native USDC gas on Arc.

Contracts (Solidity + Hardhat): Core bonding curve (Core, BondingCurveFactory), local Uniswap V2 stack, DexRouter, LPRecyclingVault, ActivityMonitor, and RecyclingGovernor. Deployed stepwise on Arc (chain id 5042002) after a one-shot deployer hit Arc’s initcode size limit a practical hack we worked around with scripted multi-step deploys and wiring.

Indexing: A The Graph Studio subgraph on arc-testnet indexes Create / Buy / Sell / Listing / Swap into tokens, trades, and 1m candles for Explore, charts, and trade feeds.

Frontend: Next.js + wagmi / ethers / Privy for wallet + Arc network. Token lists prefer subgraph → Mongo → short RPC lookback so the UI stays snappy. Mongo stores lifecycle state (phase, progress, vault, proposals); post-trade soft-refresh updates mcap, progress, chart, and trades.

projects.title: PrivyShild
projects.description: AI-powered DeFi agent with Privy-secured wallets and policy guardrails
projects.project_description: PrivyShield AI is an autonomous DeFi agent designed to let users perform on-chain actions while keeping wallet operations within strict security boundaries. The project combines Privy Server Wallets and the Privy Policy Engine with an AI agent, allowing the agent to execute approved DeFi actions while enforcing transaction limits, destination restrictions, and chain restrictions. It also includes a Red-Team simulator that demonstrates how a malicious transaction can be rejected by the policy layer
projects.how_its_made: PrivyShield AI was built with Next.js 14, React, TypeScript, Solidity, and Base Sepolia. Privy is the core of the wallet and security layer: we use Privy Server Wallets for programmatic transaction signing, Privy Policy Engine to enforce spending and destination rules, and Privy Embedded Auth for user authentication. The AI agent uses a tool-based execution flow to understand user intents and prepare blockchain actions. Viem and ethers.js handle EVM interactions, while our AgentVault smart contract manages the on-chain DeFi logic. We also built a Red-Team simulator to demonstrate how the policy layer blocks unauthorized transactions

projects.title: Gifty
projects.description: Give a friend ETH and an ENS name with one link. Privy signup faster than fintechs, 0 crypto jargon.
projects.project_description: Gifty is a social wallet for sending ETH to people who do not have a wallet yet. You lock some ETH into a gift, get a link, and send that link the way you already talk to them. They open it, sign in with Privy (email or Google), pick a free username, and claim the money. After that, friends send to eg. "vitalik" (vitalik.gifty.eth), not a hex address. The gift is ETH behind a secret. Signup always includes a free ENS subname on gifty.eth (vitalik resolves to vitalik.gifty.eth). Full names like vitalik.eth still resolve through ENS. Raw 0x addresses still work. Money lives on Base. Usernames live on Sepolia, because ENS v2 beta is Sepolia-only. The app never asks the user to switch networks. We sponsor Sepolia gas for every username so a new account can get a name before it holds any ETH. Once you are in: live Privy onramp from fiat into Base USDC, live Privy swaps, balances, contacts after someone claims your gift, and more gift links. The spend card is in the dashboard; the full issuing flow is mocked because we do not have KYB and Bridge fully set up on Privy yet. Claims are on-chain. The contract stores a hash - Poseidon(code), not the code, and a browser PLONK proof authorizes release. If the claimant has no Base ETH, the operator pays gas and takes a small fee from the gift. If they already have gas, they claim with no fee and pay the tx themselves, seamless, easy. Login, a real ENS name, money in, money out, and a way to pull the next person in, without teaching anyone a seed phrase.
projects.how_its_made: Production Next.js app (Bun) with Privy for auth and embedded self-custodial wallets, including Google OAuth. Privy wallets stay on Base. Fiat top-ups use Privy’s live useAddFunds onramp. Swaps are live Privy swaps into Base ETH or USDC. Card UI talks to Privy cards and stops at a demo path; live issuing needs KYB we do not have. ENS v2 on Sepolia: parent gifty.eth, plus GiftyRegistrar on the ENSv2 UserRegistry and Permissioned Resolver. Register is free and one username per wallet. An operator key always submits the Sepolia tx (/api/operator/register) so the user’s Base wallet never needs Sepolia ETH. No-dot labels resolve as label.gifty.eth. Dotted names go through the Sepolia Universal Resolver. Gifts on Base: GiftyClaimer stores Poseidon(code) and the locked ETH. The secret is packed into two BN254 limbs. Circom circuit gifty_claim Poseidon-hashes those limbs, range-checks the claimant to 160 bits, and exposes codeHash and claimant as public signals so a proof for address A cannot be replayed for address B. Prove in the browser with snarkjs PLONK. Verify on-chain with the snarkjs EVM verifier (GiftyVerifier). Sender always pays createGift. Claim is either claim() (user pays gas, fee 0) or operator claimFor() (sponsored gas, small operatorFee capped at 0.00075 ETH). The app picks based on whether the wallet can cover the tx. The awkward bit we leaned into: two chains, one session. Alchemy RPCs are proxied server-side. Operator routes exist only for register and sponsored claim. code → amount is not trusted to our database.
