projects.title: Ladder
projects.description: CEX-style WETH/USDC grid on 1inch Aqua + SwapVM. Custom opcodes; rungs re-arm in-wallet.
projects.project_description: Ladder is a CEX-style grid we shipped as maker liquidity on official 1inch Aqua. The pair is WETH/USDC on Base. You approve Aqua once; the tokens never leave the wallet. We did not redeploy Aqua - that registry is 1inch's. What we built is LadderRouter (SwapVM pointed at that Aqua), GridManager to ship discrete rungs, and LadderLens so the UI can tell which rungs would actually quote. A rung is a price, not a curve. When a bid fills, Aqua push() flips inventory and the ask on that same rung is live with no extra maker transaction. WalletGuard caps each quote to a live share of the real wallet at quote time. CoverageGuard stops the quote if coverage is below the maker's floor. Both sides have already filled on Base through LadderRouter.swap. Here is the contract - https://basescan.org/address/0xD810CD7E5Aa03848596a86277fffc6a50DA1121b
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts are Foundry, Solidity 0.8.30. We left official 1inch Aqua in place and subclassed 1inch SwapVM as LadderRouter.
LadderOpcodes extends AquaOpcodes so 1inch's stock instructions still run; we added five of our own, then fall through to theirs.
OracleEnvelope reads Chainlink ETH/USD. WalletGuard, CoverageGuard, RungQuote, and ProtocolFee sit in the same table.
GridManager builds every rung as one program - envelope, WalletGuard WETH, WalletGuard USDC, CoverageGuard, fee, RungQuote, salt and ships it through Aqua.
Takers call LadderRouter.swap.
The UI is Next.js, viem, wagmi, and RainbowKit. A small TypeScript resolver quotes those rungs and hedges leftovers through the 1inch Swap API. https://basescan.org/address/0xD810CD7E5Aa03848596a86277fffc6a50DA1121b

projects.title: Vaultara
projects.description: Private file storage with onchain, revocable ENS sharing and live access logs.
projects.project_description: Vaultara is a privacy-first decentralized drive: each file is encrypted in the browser before its ciphertext is stored on IPFS. File ownership and every sharing decision live in a Base Sepolia smart contract, giving users a verifiable audit trail rather than trusting a storage provider. Owners share files to an ENS name or address through a revocable onchain grant. Recipients see the file in Shared with me and can decrypt it; owners can revoke future access and both sides see the change in a live access log indexed by The Graph. Privy provides email/social onboarding with an embedded self-custodial wallet. Vaultara is a testnet hackathon reference implementation. Revocation prevents future access but cannot revoke a file someone has already downloaded; device-to-device owner key sync and key-layer revocation are future work.
projects.how_its_made: Vaultara is a monorepo with a Next.js frontend, a Foundry Solidity contract, and a The Graph subgraph. The DriveRegistry contract on Base Sepolia records file ownership plus grant and revoke events; it never stores plaintext or holds funds. The Graph indexes those events for the UI's live, two-sided access log. In the browser, WebCrypto encrypts each file with AES-GCM before upload. Only ciphertext is pinned to IPFS through Pinata. File keys are wrapped for recipients with a secp256k1 ECIES envelope using @noble tooling; an owner derives their deterministic key from a wallet signature. ENS resolves human-readable recipients and reverse-resolves them in the interface. Privy supplies embedded wallets with an injected-wallet fallback. The project includes Foundry tests for the contract and Vitest coverage for crypto and sharing helpers. The deployed Base Sepolia contract is verified, and the hosted Vercel app uses security headers plus server-side upload controls.

projects.title: AgentDock
projects.description: Policy controlled AI agents that buy risk data without exposing keys or private policy.
projects.project_description:
AgentDock is a policy-controlled workflow platform for organizations that want AI agents to purchase specialist services and produce recommendations without receiving unrestricted credentials, treasury access, or private policy data.
Its first workflow is a private treasury-risk assessment: a delegated agent discovers and pays for an independent risk report, evaluates it against an organization’s confidential risk policy, and produces a minimal verifiable receipt. The project combines scoped, expiring agent identity, metered service payments, confidential policy evaluation, and auditable workflow events. The goal is to make AI agents useful in high-trust financial workflows while preserving human control, revocation, spending bounds, and privacy.
projects.how_its_made: AgentDock is built as a TypeScript pnpm/Turborepo monorepo with a Next.js/React dashboard, a Fastify workflow orchestrator, and a separate Fastify x402-gated Risk API. ENSv2 on Sepolia provides organization, agent, and service identities with scoped capabilities, expiry, and revocation. The agent uses Hedera x402 to obtain a paid risk report without receiving unrestricted treasury authority. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow evaluates the paid report against private organizational thresholds inside handlerInTee, returning only a decision and decision hash. The orchestrator persists immutable, idempotent workflow events and writes a minimal Sepolia receipt containing hashes, ENS references, payment reference, CRE decision, status, and timestamp. The dashboard supports onboarding, workflow creation, live event inspection, evidence links, approval/rejection, and agent revocation. Private keys, policy inputs, and service credentials remain outside the agent context and source repository

projects.title: Harness
projects.description: Every AI agent gets a container with limits your Ledger sets and ssh to it by its ENS name.
projects.project_description: Harness gives every AI agent its own machine, its own name, and a spending limit it cannot go past. Right now, giving an agent money means giving it a key. Once it has the key, it can spend everything, and the only thing stopping it is the agent's own judgement. We think that is backwards. With Harness you tap your Ledger once. That creates a container for the agent, mints it an ENS name like runner.acme.harness.eth, and writes a daily spending limit on chain. The agent gets a shell, tools, and whatever credentials you sealed for it. Inside its limit the agent acts on its own, with no approvals and no waiting. Past that, a human has to sign. There is no server deciding any of this. The contract enforces it. The name is real ENS, so you just ssh to it. No wallet, no plugin, no copied IP address. The same name that resolves for DNS is the one sshd checks your key against. Revoking is one transaction. The name stops resolving, the shell stops opening, and the money stops moving, all at once, because all three were reading the same record the whole time.
projects.how_its_made: Ledger Key Ring, on a machine with no USB port The host is a VPS. There is no device attached to it and there never will be, so the ring has to be joined over the network without a key ever crossing it. The host generates its own member keypair and keeps it. The browser opens a relay session and does nothing but forward bytes between the Ledger over WebHID and the ring flow running on the host. It never holds a key and never sees one. One confirmation on the device admits the host as a member of the tenant's ring. Once that is done we write the trustchain and the member credentials into wallet-cli's state directory, so wallet-cli ring encrypt and ring decrypt work on the VM from then on with no device present. That is how the ring ends up usable directly inside the machine. We use it to hold the agent's credentials. Model keys and service tokens are sealed under the tenant's ring and sit on disk as ciphertext. They are opened at container start, in memory, and only if the chain still says the agent is live. A revoked agent does not get them back the next time it starts. The agent never sees a private key at any point. The fiddly part was the transport. LKRP's SDK speaks hw-transport-webhid and the Device Management Kit speaks its own, and only one of them can hold the HID handle at a time. So a session is something we open, use, and explicitly release, and the device is passed back and forth between the two as the flow moves from Ledger Sync to the Ethereum app. WebHID permission is per origin and per device and it persists, so the handover is invisible to the person holding the Ledger. The Ledger signs a grant that says what the agent may spend and over what period. Inside that permission the agent acts on its own, whether that is an x402 call or any other transaction. Anything outside it is pushed back to the Ledger for the person to sign, so they stay in the loop for what they did not already allow. The registry enforces it by measuring the tenant's balance before and after the batch and reverting if the difference is over the allowance. Payments use EIP-3009 out of the tenant's account, the one the Ledger controls. We use @x402/express and @x402/core, so none of the payment code is ours and it works with any x402 seller. EIP-7702 Setting up a machine needs four transactions. We batch them with 7702 so it is one confirmation on the device instead of four. ENS We deployed our own registry on the ENSv2 Sepolia contracts, using PermissionedRegistry and EnhancedAccessControl. Each tenant's registry roots its own subtree. harness.eth holds acme.harness.eth, and acme's registry holds runner.acme.harness.eth. EAC is what stops one tenant writing into another's subtree, and it is also why the agent cannot rewrite its own records, so it cannot change the key or the fingerprint it is admitted by. None of that is us checking it in application code. AgentResolver answers for those names. It resolves the machine's address, the agent's key, and the ssh host key fingerprint, computed from the grant when you ask rather than written in as separate records. Both are fine to have in public. An ssh host key fingerprint is meant to be published, which is what GitHub does with theirs. The address is a Tailscale mesh address, so it only means anything to a device already in the tailnet. We run a nameserver in front of it that answers .eth over DNS. That is what makes ssh runner.acme.harness.eth work with no wallet and no plugin. On the machine, sshd's AuthorizedKeysCommand asks ENS whether the key being offered is allowed in, and known_hosts comes from the same name. Revoking is one transaction. It unregisters the name, so resolution, ssh access and spending all stop together.

projects.title: Carrentic
projects.description: Own a share of a real car as an ERC-3643 token on Hedera, and earn its rent on-chain.
projects.project_description:
A car is one of the most expensive things a person ever buys, and it sits
parked most of the time. Ownership is all-or-nothing: you can't buy a slice of
a car you like, and you can't earn from a car you don't fully own. The rent a
vehicle could generate goes entirely to whoever holds the title, and there's no
simple, compliant way to split that asset — and its income — across several
people. Carrentic turns a real car into shares. The car becomes an ERC-3643 security
token on Hedera: people buy a share, the car is rented out, and the rent flows
back to every owner on-chain, pro-rata to what they hold. An AI fleet manager
watches the car, explains how it's performing, and drafts the on-chain actions —
paying out this month's rent, marking the car's value — while the car's worth
and the rent owners receive are priced against a live market through the Uniswap
stack rather than a hard-coded number. Tokenizing a car is a single click: no

projects.title: PayPilot
projects.description: PayPilot — B2B treasury: invoice emails in, quorum-approved payouts onchain, bank-grade controls.
projects.project_description: PayPilot is a B2B treasury and payout platform built on Base, where companies run payroll, vendor and bounty payments from multi-signature organization wallets. Anyone can sign in with Privy and self-serve create their own organization with named wallets (Treasury, Payroll, Bug Bounty Rewards, Ops) — each wallet carries its own onchain policy: a vendor address allowlist plus a per-transaction spending cap that Privy enforces inside the signing enclave, not in our app code. The core workflow is a real dual-control loop: a vendor simply emails an invoice (e.g. "Please pay 0xAbC… 0.02 USDC") to our receiving address — a Resend webhook parses the recipient and amount, checks the vendor against the allowlist, and creates a payout request backed by a Privy intent on the org wallet. The request needs quorum approval: an authorized team member clicks Approve, and the app's quorum signing key submits a real ECDSA authorization signature to Privy — when the threshold is met, Privy broadcasts the transfer onchain and the payout flips to Executed with the transaction hash. On top of that, PayPilot ships: role-based access (Owner, Treasurer, Finance Officer, Viewer), amount-tiered approvals (small payouts route to a single-approver Ops wallet, larger ones require the full quorum threshold), pre-generated employee wallets by email, scheduled recurring payments, and balance-condition automations. It's a finance team's controls — allowlist, caps, quorum, roles — running onchain instead of in a bank's database. Stack: Next.js, MongoDB, Privy (auth, organizations, wallets, key quorums, policies, intents, authorization signatures), Resend for the email pipeline, deployed on Vercel and live on Base Sepolia testnet.
projects.how_its_made: PayPilot is a Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind) app deployed on Vercel, with MongoDB Atlas as a pure UI-state mirror — deliberately. Every money-critical operation runs through Privy: @privy-io/node drives organizations, wallets, key quorums, policies, condition sets and intents server-side, while @privy-io/react-auth handles embedded email auth in the browser. The architecture's core principle: authority lives in Privy, never in our database. Even a fully compromised app server can't move funds — quorum thresholds, policy gates and intent execution all live in Privy's enclave. The genuinely hacky/notable bits: Amount-tiered approvals done wallet-level. A quorum has exactly one threshold, so instead of bolting logic on top, each org runs two quorums: a main quorum (owner-settable 1-of-N…N-of-N) governing Treasury etc., and a single-signer ops quorum governing an Ops wallet whose Privy policy cap equals the org's amount tier. Payouts ≤ $300 auto-route to Ops; bigger ones need the full quorum. The tier is enforced at signature time by the policy, not just by routing logic. Governance that can't change itself solo. Once the main threshold is ≥2, adding a signer or changing the threshold is itself an async Privy intent that the quorum must approve — the same signing pipeline as payouts. Vendors as condition sets. Onboarding a vendor adds their address to a Privy condition set that every wallet policy references — allowlists enforced in the enclave. (We store both checksummed and lowercase forms after discovering calldata comparisons are case-sensitive.) Pregenerated employee wallets. Inviting by email creates the employee's Privy user + embedded wallet up front, so it's waiting the moment they first log in. Email-triggered payouts with policy replies. Resend webhooks carry metadata only, so we fetch the full email body via resend.emails.receiving.get, regex-parse the invoice, create the payout, and reply to the vendor — "received, pending approval" or "blocked by policy" for a spoofed address. The fraud-beat plays out in email, fully automated. Automation with human rules. Scheduled sends (daily/weekly/monthly) and balance-condition rules (sweep excess, notify on thresholds) fire through the same pipeline as manual requests — policy gates apply to automation exactly as they apply to humans, and a policy failure pauses the automation with an audit trail. Sponsored gas everywhere — org wallets never hold ETH, every transfer is Privy-sponsored. Partner technologies: Privy (the entire security story), Resend (inbound invoice inbox + outbound approval emails), Vercel (deploy + cron), MongoDB Atlas (org-scoped app state), viem (calldata encoding, balance reads). The build also taught us the hard way: Privy's env vars are newline-sensitive, its intent members report user IDs without the did:privy: prefix, and its webhook secrets are base64 — all three are now documented in the repo and handled.

projects.title: rehold
projects.description: REHOLD is a repoplatform which lets institutions post bonds as collateral for short-term cash loans
projects.project_description:
REHOLD is a repo-financing platform built on Hedera, on top of the Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS). It lets institutions post tokenised treasury bonds as collateral for short-term cash loans — with pricing, margin monitoring, and liquidation all running as smart contract logic instead of manual back-office reconciliation.
The name comes from the core technical insight the platform is built around: collateral is never moved into a separate custody wallet, it is placed on Hold — locked in place under ATS's own native escrow primitive, in the investor's own compliant identity, until it's released or executed. The Problem Institutional finance runs on repo. Every day, trillions of dollars change hands in short-term loans secured by high-quality collateral — mostly government treasuries — because it's one of the safest, most liquid ways for cash-rich institutions to earn a return and for asset-rich institutions to access cash without selling what they own. But the mechanics behind that trade haven't caught up with what's possible today.
A repo trade has two "legs": the cash leg (money moving from lender to borrower) and the collateral leg (the bond moving from borrower to lender, as security). The cash leg is often fast — but the collateral leg still runs on a parallel paper-and-legal process: custody agreements, manual valuation checks, phone calls and faxes to confirm a margin call, and overnight batch reconciliation to make sure both sides agree on who holds what. It's slow, it's manual, and it's opaque outside of the two counterparties involved.
Tokenising the collateral changes what's possible. If the treasury itself is a compliant, programmable token, the collateral leg can become a provable, automatic, on-chain state change — the same trade, but the slow half disappears. What REHOLD Does REHOLD is a full repo desk for tokenised treasuries: Issuers create tokenised, KYC-gated treasury bonds through ATS, with real lifecycle features — coupons, maturity, redemption.
Investors buy those bonds, then pledge them into REHOLD as collateral to raise cash without selling — the token gets locked in place, not moved to some separate custody wallet, so their compliance status and ownership record never leave their own identity.
Lenders supply the actual cash liquidity that funds these trades, earning a return for taking on well-collateralized credit risk — the same economic role played by money-market funds and cash desks in the real $4-trillion-a-day repo market. A live price oracle continuously values the pledged collateral. If its value falls too far relative to the loan, the system automatically issues a margin call, and — if unaddressed — force-liquidates just enough collateral through REHOLD's own secondary market to restore safety, without anyone needing to notice, call, or intervene manually. At the end of the trade, either the borrower repays and gets their bond back, or — if they don't — a Hedera Scheduled Transaction fires automatically at maturity to settle the position, redeeming the bond at face value from the issuer rather than dumping it into a possibly depressed market. Every transfer anywhere in this flow — issuance, trading, pledging, liquidation, redemption — passes through ATS's own compliance machinery: KYC verification, freeze/blacklist enforcement, and pausability. None of it is bypassed or reimplemented;
REHOLD is built to work with ATS's compliance layer, not around it.
projects.how_its_made: REHOLD is a repo desk that sits next to a live Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio bond. This repo is the cash/risk layer: Solidity on Hedera testnet (chain 296) plus a Vite desk.. Stack. Solidity 0.8.28 (Hardhat, OpenZeppelin, Hedera HTS precompiles). Four contracts: BondPriceOracle, RepoVault, SecondaryMarket, MarginEngine. Cash is Circle testnet USDC (HTS). UI is Vite + React + wagmi/viem against Hashio; MetaMask. Event tape comes from the Hedera Mirror Node. A Node keeper heartbeats NAV. Market view uses lightweight-charts. Architecture. Two layers, one chain. ATS owns the bond: KYC, allowlist, coupons, Hold, maturity redeem. ReHold never copies that. The vault is bond-agnostic: it takes a diamond address, looks up a per-bond NAV oracle, and lends from one USDC pool. The trade is a Hold, not a transfer. The investor authorizeOperators the vault. originateRepo locks units in place under their identity (createHoldFromByPartition), then sends USDC. Title never leaves them, so coupons still accrue. Repay pulls principal + fee, releaseHoldByPartition, done. Term is on the vault (termEnd), not hold expiry. Risk is a separate contract. MarginEngine.evaluate is permissionless: mark collateral with the 8-decimal NAV, then healthy (≥110%), issueMarginCall (102–110%), or liquidatePartial (<102%). Liquidation executes the hold, ships bonds to SecondaryMarket.sellOnBehalf, and sells only enough to restore 110%. Peer trades use the same book; ATS compliance still reverts ineligible transfers. ow it is pieced together. The investor stays the bond holder. RepoVault.originateRepo calls ATS createHoldFromByPartition as an operator, then wires USDC from the lender pool. Repay calls releaseHoldByPartition. If NAV falls under 102%, MarginEngine.evaluate (permissionless) executes the hold and SecondaryMarket.sellOnBehalf sells just enough to restore 110%. ATS still owns KYC, control list, freeze, coupons, and fullRedeemAtMaturity. We only vendor ABI shims that match the diamond’s selectors. Partners that actually matter. Hedera gives HTS (bond + USDC), HIP-719 association, and cheap marks. ATS Hold is the whole product: collateral locks in the investor’s identity instead of moving to a vault. Circle USDC is the cash leg. HashScan is the explorer we verify against. The hacky bits, all real: ATS rejects hold expiry 0 (WrongExpirationTimestamp), so we set expirationTimestamp = type(uint256).max and enforce term on the vault, not the hold — otherwise borrowers could reclaim via reclaimHoldByPartition. Creating a hold also burns ERC-20 allowance to the vault, so the desk has a separate Approve Vault step. HTS needs HIP-719 associate() on every EOA before approve/transferFrom; contracts associate in the constructor. Hashio wraps ATS AccountIsBlocked as RPC 0x128, so the UI pattern-matches both. Liquidation has no bid book — we scan asks and treat the seller as the cash-paying counterparty (demo-scale, O(n)). The NAV oracle is a single updater with a 30% circuit breaker; the keeper re-pushes the same price every 5 minutes just to refresh updatedAt. After every vault/market redeploy we must allowlist and KYC those contract addresses on the bond, same as people.

projects.description: A prediction market humans and AI agents pay to ask: curve orders, shared USDC liquidity, no fees.
projects.project_description: Every AI model is trained on the past; the data that matters most is about the future, and nobody has it yet. Prediction markets are where people put real money on what happens next. Horizon is a binary prediction market on Ethereum Sepolia built so that a person or an AI agent can ask the world any question and pay for the answer. Creation is a paid service over Hedera x402; a verified World credential tells humans and agents apart, at half price; 1inch Aqua puts real USDC behind every quote, with one balance shared across markets; executable pricing curves let people and agents rest orders that reprice themselves; The Graph and Substreams keep the page true to the chain; and Hedera Consensus Service records the whole creation flow. The rest of this description is how each of those works. Makers publish executable pricing curves instead of resting single-price orders. A curve is a start price, an end price and a size; the chain evaluates it on every fill, so a BUY curve declines as the maker accumulates and a SELL curve rises as inventory leaves. Equal endpoints are just a fixed-price limit order. Fills are partial, exactly accounted, and cancellable at any time. One USDC balance backs quotes in every market at once. Maker funds sit in the wallet and are drawn through 1inch Aqua only at fill time, so a small maker can express views across several markets without pre-funding each one. Within a market, an on-chain per-market budget stops a maker's resting orders from ever committing more than the wallet can currently spend. Markets bootstrap themselves: a YES buyer paying 0.60 USDC and a NO buyer paying 0.40 USDC mint a fully backed pair in one transaction. Nobody has to seed inventory. An off-chain allocator picks up to four fills across direct and complementary legs, and RouteExecutor settles the whole route atomically or reverts it. Stale state, drained balances and slippage produce a clean rejection, never a partial trade. Trading carries no fee of any kind: no maker, taker, routing or protocol fee. The only charge is market creation, offered as a paid service to people and agents alike. A drafting step grounded on live indexed markets from The Graph proposes the question, outcomes, close time and resolution rules and warns about duplicates by market id; the requester approves a hash of the draft before anything is charged. Payment runs over Hedera x402, settled through Blocky402, and is resumable: a retried request never charges twice and never creates two markets. A verified World credential halves the price, at most once per credential per day. Every approved draft, settled payment and deployed market is then stated on a Hedera Consensus Service topic, in order, with a consensus timestamp anyone can read back from a mirror node. Markets, curves, fills, routes, collateral and resolutions are indexed by a Subgraph, mirrored into PostgreSQL for fast reads, and overlaid by a Substreams-fed live layer so a fill or a new market shows up in the open browser tab seconds after its block, before the indexer has it. Several binary markets can be grouped as an event under one review and one payment, optionally importing definitions (question, outcomes, criteria, dates; never prices or liquidity) from a Polymarket page. After close, a disclosed resolver submits YES, NO or INVALID once, with an on-chain evidence reference. Winning tokens redeem 1 USDC; INVALID pays 0.50 per token. Resolution and creation authority are deliberately centralized and stated in the UI; neither role can spend from a user wallet, withdraw collateral or mint unbacked outcomes. Demonstrated live: an atomic two-curve route on Sepolia and its indexed result, an agent completing a paid creation end to end (1 HBAR on Hedera testnet, then a market on Sepolia, then indexed by The Graph), a human verified through World Selfie Check paying the discounted 0.5 HBAR, and the creation audit trail on HCS topic 0.0.10473191 (62 statements at submission) verified byte for byte against the mirror node.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, Cancun). Horizon extends the pinned, unmodified official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM sources; all 329 vendored files are hashed in vendor-lock.json and re-verified in CI. HorizonSwapVM overrides SwapVM's _runOpcode hook to add two application-local instructions in the reserved opcode range, 0xf0 (fixed-price BUY) and 0xf1 (curve). Each reconstructs and hashes the maker's canonical Aqua order against the MarketRegistry, refuses any order the router has not admitted, prices it (the curve through CurveMath: an exact rational integral of p(x) = start + (end - start) * x^alpha, alpha in {1,2,3}, BUY rounds down, SELL rounds up) and tracks filled shares. RouteExecutor performs up to four fills per transaction with a spend limit, a deadline and full rollback; for complementary legs it escrows 1 USDC per pair into BinaryMarket inside SwapVM's pre-transfer-in callback and mints YES to one side and NO to the other. OrderBudget is a ledger the router deploys and owns. The Foundry suite is 54 tests including three fuzz properties, and an Anvil test cross-checks 44 contract vs. TypeScript curve results. Backend (Node 24, TypeScript, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL 18, pg-boss). The API returns prepared unsigned transactions only; the worker is the sole process holding a key, for createMarket and resolve. Every quote re-reads balances, allowances, fill counters and market status over RPC at a single block, rejects an indexed snapshot more than 64 blocks behind or on a reorged hash, and simulates the full route before returning calldata. AdminJS sits on top for record inspection. Drafting goes through a MarketDraftProvider interface with an Anthropic-backed provider and a deterministic development provider; both read the same live Graph data. The Graph. A Subgraph in Studio (horizon/0.3.2) indexes markets, curves, fills, routes, collateral and resolution, and validates Aqua Shipped bytes against the deployed router rather than trusting them. On top of that a Substreams package (horizon_events, Rust compiled to WASM) extracts the same events per block for a stream consumer that writes a live overlay into Postgres, one block per transaction with the cursor included, and wakes the API through pg_notify. The API exposes a POST /api/live SSE endpoint with Last-Event-ID replay, and reads apply only live changes whose block is newer than the snapshot's, so a lagging sweep can neither hide a market nor duplicate a fill. BlockUndoSignal handling marks trades reverted rather than deleting them. Hedera. Creation is an x402 v2 resource: the server answers 402 with scheme exact, network hedera:testnet, a per-request nonce and the facilitator's advertised fee payer (read from Blocky402's /supported endpoint, never assumed); the signed payload is checked field by field against what was issued before the facilitator is contacted. Browser payers sign over Hedera WalletConnect, agents with their own key. Audit statements (horizon.audit.v1) are written to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the workflow transition, then published to an HCS topic by the worker in sequence, so Hedera being unreachable can never cause a second payment or deployment. Unknown outcomes are reconciled against the mirror node by event id before any resubmission. World. IDKit Selfie Check verifies server-side and lowers the 402 amount from 1 to 0.5 HBAR, once per credential per UTC day; the server re-checks action, environment and signal_hash against the request id before contacting World, and stores only the nullifier. Sandbox access arrived late in the hackathon; a credential has since been verified in Sandbox against the production deployment and a creation was then paid at the discounted price over Hedera x402. Frontend. React 19, Vite, viem, @x402/hedera, served by the API process. Deploys on Railway as three processes (API, worker, stream consumer) and one database. Hacky bits worth mentioning. Aqua's ship has no application callback, so publication is two transactions, Aqua.ship then HorizonSwapVM.admitCurve, and the router refuses to fill anything it has not admitted; a strategy shipped straight to Aqua is inert and filtered from discovery. Aqua's default dispatcher does not enable LimitSwap, so the probe harness overrides _runOpcode to permit it. Idempotency on the paid path comes from deriving creationId = keccak256("horizon-creation:" + requestId) and checking marketByCreationId before every broadcast. INVALID payouts of half a base unit are carried per holder in invalidRemainder so combining or splitting claims never changes total payout.

projects.title: ArcFlow
projects.description: Cross-chain intent protocol — interact with Arc DeFi from any EVM chain, no bridging needed.
projects.project_description: ArcFlow is a cross-chain intent forwarding protocol that lets users interact with Arc-native DeFi applications directly from any supported EVM chain — Somnia, Base Sepolia, Monad Testnet — without bridging or switching networks. Users sign a single transaction on their preferred source chain. ArcGateway emits an intent event, a permissioned relayer picks it up and executes it on Arc Testnet via ArcExecutor, which maps each external wallet to a Universal Arc Account. The result is seamless cross-chain DeFi: one wallet, any chain, instant execution. The primary feature is an Arc-native Stablecoin Vault — users can deposit, withdraw, and harvest yield on Arc USDC through intents submitted from any supported source chain. Counter and Todo demos are included as live testable examples of the intent pipeline in action.
projects.how_its_made: ArcFlow is built on a three-layer architecture: source chain contracts, an off-chain relayer, and Arc Testnet execution contracts. On the source side, ArcGateway.sol (deployed on Somnia, Base Sepolia, and Monad Testnet) accepts user-signed intent transactions and emits IntentForwarded events with nonce-based replay protection. No state is stored — it's a pure event emitter. The relayer is a TypeScript/Node.js service that polls source chains for events, validates intent targets against an allowlist, and submits execution transactions to Arc Testnet via ArcExecutor.sol. It handles retries, duplicate protection, health reporting, and writes intent history to a JSON endpoint consumed by the frontend. On Arc, ArcExecutor.sol verifies relayer authorization, maps each external wallet address to a deterministic Universal Arc Account, and calls the target contract — Vault, Counter, or Todo — with a try/catch wrapper so failures are handled gracefully. The frontend is built with Next.js 15, wagmi v2, RainbowKit, and TailwindCSS v4. Multi-source chain selection, intent submission, real-time status polling, and history are all handled through custom React hooks (useIntent, useVaultIntent, IntentFlowContext). The dark/lime RemitStar visual system is applied throughout.

projects.title: flowfi.finance
projects.description: FlowFi: an AI-powered DEX aggregator on Arc  swap, bridge, launch tokens in native USDC
projects.project_description: FlowFi is a stablecoin interface on Circle's Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), with an AI Copilot reading live on-chain data across Portfolio, Dashboard, and Analytics views. Gas and balances are both USDC: native units are 18 decimals, the ERC-20 contract (0x3600...) is 6 decimals — one asset, two interfaces, handled explicitly in code. What works today: browser wallet or Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet (no seed phrase); USDC/EURC swap; USDC bridging Sepolia↔Arc via Circle's CCTP V2 (burn, attestation, mint); curated liquidity pools; an ERC-20 launch tool with permanent-liquidity locking. FlowFi does not custody funds or market-make: on testnet, thin pools are flagged rather than quoted as live prices. After Arc mainnet, the same UI is meant to route swaps through real external liquidity (Uniswap, LI.FI) and earn an interface fee, not hold reserves itself.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, viem. Wallets are EIP-1193 in the browser, or Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets through a backend so the seed never sits in the client. Same-origin proxies sit in front of Arc RPC and Arcscan because public eth_getLogs and explorer rate limits fail under load. Contracts: Solidity 0.8.19 factory + constant-product pool, shipped in several testnet revisions as bugs showed up. One revision called addLiquidity with a deadline on a v2 pool that had no deadline and the tx reverted. Later pools pull both tokens with SafeERC20, record reserve deltas from balanceOf, and (in the newest code) match Uniswap-style amountAMin / amountBMin so a skewed deposit is not silently donated. Pause, where it exists, is queued for two days; unpause is immediate. None of this is audited; it stays testnet infrastructure Integrations that actually move value: Circle CCTP V2 (burn on Sepolia, attest, mint on Arc) and Circle wallets. USDC on Arc is one balance, two interfaces — eth_getBalance / gas at 18 decimals, ERC-20 0x3600… transfer / approve at 6. We hardcode 6 on the ERC-20 path instead of trusting decimals() on that precompile. What we refused to ship as product: quoting a residual pool (cents of USDC/EURC) as a live FX price. A constant-product pool only knows its reserve ratio. FlowFi is an interface; after Arc public mainnet the same screen is meant to route to an external venue and take a fee, not to market-make.

projects.title: Proctor
projects.description: An AI agent stops mid-payment and pays a live, verified human for permission to continue
projects.project_description: Proctor is a human-oversight gate for AI agents, built on x402. When an autonomous agent is about to take a consequential action (releasing funds, executing a trade, anything past a policy threshold) it stops on an HTTP 402 instead of proceeding. The agent then pays a small fee to ask a real, live human for permission to continue. That human is a witness, deliberately distinct from the agent's operator. The witness answers on their own phone through a single-use link, proves liveness with World ID's Selfie Check (bound to that one decision via a signed nonce, so the proof can't be replayed elsewhere), and approves or refuses within a short deadline. No answer before the deadline is a hard refusal, not a default approval, the system fails closed. Every decision produces an attestation written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic with no admin key, so the record can't be edited or deleted after the fact, by us or anyone else. The attestation states exactly how the human was authenticated and whether their independence from the operator is cryptographically provable or only policy-asserted, so a third party auditing the log doesn't have to take our word for it. Anyone can verify the evidence directly on HashScan. The gate itself is x402-native: agents pay per-interrupt to escalate, then pay again per-second of actual human review time on release, settled over Hedera and Circle Gateway rails. Proctor ships as an installable MCP server ( proctor-mcp on npm and in the official MCP Registry), so any MCP-capable agent, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a custom client, can add real human-in-the-loop oversight with one command, without building the escalation, identity-proofing, or evidence-logging infrastructure itself.
projects.how_its_made:
Backend
Bun and Fastify, with Prisma 7's new driver-adapter mode ( @prisma/adapter-pg , no native query-engine binary, so the Docker image stays small and boots fast on Railway). The gate speaks x402 v2 ( @x402/core , @x402/fastify , @x402/hedera ) against the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, with Circle Gateway ( GatewayEvmScheme ) as a second settlement rail and its own capability cache with retry/fallback so a facilitator outage degrades gracefully instead of failing every request. Every decision is a state machine (OPEN -> DISPATCHED -> APPROVED/REFUSED/EXPIRED) persisted in Postgres (Supabase), with a TTL sweeper that fails a decision closed the instant its deadline passes, evaluated inside the same SQL statement that performs the write so there's no check-then-act race window. Identity and liveness
The witness proves they're a live, present human via World ID 4.0's Selfie Check, requested through IDKit and verified server-side with a signed RP (Relying Party) nonce minted fresh per decision and bound into the World signal, so a proof from one decision can never be replayed against another. Getting this genuinely working end-to-end meant independently re-implementing World's RP signature algorithm (secp256k1 + EIP-191, not ES256 as commonly assumed) to diagnose a stale signing key after a Portal key rotation, and excluding just @worldcoin/idkit-core (not its React wrapper) from Vite's dependency optimizer, since the wrapper's WASM binary was 404ing under default pre-bundling. Evidence
Every resolved decision is attested to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created with no admin key, so nobody, including us, can alter or delete the log after the fact. The attestation body states plainly how the human was authenticated and whether their independence from the operator is cryptographic (a separate World ID nullifier scope) or only policy-asserted, so a skeptical third party can verify the actual guarantee on HashScan rather than trust the UI. Frontend
TanStack Start (React 19, SSR), Tailwind 4, GSAP and Lenis for the landing page and floating glass-effect nav, and a live operator console that drives an on-camera countdown/meter over Server-Sent Events. That stream now has a polling fallback for resilience: a long-lived SSE connection is powerful for a live "on-camera" feel, but a production demo can't depend on one persistent connection behaving perfectly for its entire lifetime, so the same evidence record is also polled every two seconds as a safety net. Distribution
proctor-mcp is published to npm and registered in the official MCP Registry ( io.github.louissarvin/proctor ), so any MCP-capable agent gets real human-in-the-loop oversight with one claude mcp add` command instead of building escalation, identity-proofing, and evidence-logging from scratch. Notable hacky bits, honestly stated
The SSE stream writes straight to Fastify's raw response to control chunk timing precisely, which turned out to silently bypass @fastify/cors 's header injection, fixed by reflecting Origin manually before the raw writeHead . And more than once during deployment, Railway's GitHub webhook went stale after a force-push and needed an empty commit to re-trigger a deploy; Supabase's free-tier pooler needed a project-level restart (paired with a Railway app restart, since a stale Prisma pool otherwise reuses dead sockets) after connection-heavy testing exhausted its pool. Neither is glamorous, but both are the kind of infrastructure reality a real deployment surfaces that a purely local demo never would.

Proctor ships as an installable MCP server (`proctor-mcp` on npm and in the official MCP Registry), so any MCP-capable agent, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a custom client, can add real human-in-the-loop oversight with one command, without building the escalation, identity-proofing, or evidence-logging infrastructure itself.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Backend
Bun and Fastify, with Prisma 7's new driver-adapter mode (`@prisma/adapter-pg`, no native query-engine binary, so the Docker image stays small and boots fast on Railway). The gate speaks x402 v2 (`@x402/core`, `@x402/fastify`, `@x402/hedera`) against the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, with Circle Gateway (`GatewayEvmScheme`) as a second settlement rail and its own capability cache with retry/fallback so a facilitator outage degrades gracefully instead of failing every request. Every decision is a state machine (OPEN -> DISPATCHED -> APPROVED/REFUSED/EXPIRED) persisted in Postgres (Supabase), with a TTL sweeper that fails a decision closed the instant its deadline passes, evaluated inside the same SQL statement that performs the write so there's no check-then-act race window.

Identity and liveness
The witness proves they're a live, present human via World ID 4.0's Selfie Check, requested through IDKit and verified server-side with a signed RP (Relying Party) nonce minted fresh per decision and bound into the World signal, so a proof from one decision can never be replayed against another. Getting this genuinely working end-to-end meant independently re-implementing World's RP signature algorithm (secp256k1 + EIP-191, not ES256 as commonly assumed) to diagnose a stale signing key after a Portal key rotation, and excluding just `@worldcoin/idkit-core` (not its React wrapper) from Vite's dependency optimizer, since the wrapper's WASM binary was 404ing under default pre-bundling.

Evidence
Every resolved decision is attested to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created with no admin key, so nobody, including us, can alter or delete the log after the fact. The attestation body states plainly how the human was authenticated and whether their independence from the operator is cryptographic (a separate World ID nullifier scope) or only policy-asserted, so a skeptical third party can verify the actual guarantee on HashScan rather than trust the UI.

Frontend
TanStack Start (React 19, SSR), Tailwind 4, GSAP and Lenis for the landing page and floating glass-effect nav, and a live operator console that drives an on-camera countdown/meter over Server-Sent Events. That stream now has a polling fallback for resilience: a long-lived SSE connection is powerful for a live "on-camera" feel, but a production demo can't depend on one persistent connection behaving perfectly for its entire lifetime, so the same evidence record is also polled every two seconds as a safety net.

Distribution
proctor-mcp` is published to npm and registered in the official MCP Registry (`io.github.louissarvin/proctor`), so any MCP-capable agent gets real human-in-the-loop oversight with one `claude mcp add` command instead of building escalation, identity-proofing, and evidence-logging from scratch.

Notable hacky bits, honestly stated
The SSE stream writes straight to Fastify's raw response to control chunk timing precisely, which turned out to silently bypass `@fastify/cors`'s header injection, fixed by reflecting `Origin` manually before the raw `writeHead`. And more than once during deployment, Railway's GitHub webhook went stale after a force-push and needed an empty commit to re-trigger a deploy; Supabase's free-tier pooler needed a project-level restart (paired with a Railway app restart, since a stale Prisma pool otherwise reuses dead sockets) after connection-heavy testing exhausted its pool. Neither is glamorous, but both are the kind of infrastructure reality a real deployment surfaces that a purely local demo never would.

projects.title: proofads
projects.description: Ad inventory as revocable ENSv2 rights. Pay only for delivery proven in a Chainlink enclave.
projects.project_description: ProofAds turns advertising inventory into a revocable ENSv2 rights hierarchy, and settles payment against delivery verified privately inside a Chainlink Confidential Workflow. Two pieces of the ad supply chain are assertions nobody can enforce: who may sell a placement, and what was actually delivered. Today the first is ads.txt — a plaintext file, domain-wide, never checked at transaction time. The second is a number produced by the party who benefits from it being large, computed over data the buyer never sees. Publishing that data on-chain doesn't fix it; it publishes a viewing log. Delivery has to be verifiable without being public. The ENS layer. Each ad slot is a name the publisher owns: hero.ads.proofads-pub.eth. AdInventoryRegistry extends ENSv2's real PermissionedRegistry, and the right to sell a slot is ROLE_SELL_SLOT — an application-defined Enhanced Access Control role in an unassigned nybble (1 << 40), living alongside ENS's own roles. The marketplace calls hasRoles() at listing and again at auction finalization, never a cached copy, so revocation takes effect on the next block. The payout address is registry.getOwner(labelhash), read live from ENS — a delegated agency can sell a slot but can never redirect the money. The Chainlink layer. A browser SDK measures a view: ten seconds at ≥50% of the viewport, foregrounded, with the creative's bytes hashed against the creativeHash committed on-chain at bid time. Raw events are frozen into an immutable batch, then read inside an AWS Nitro enclave by a CRE Confidential Workflow (cre.handlerInTee). The enclave holds the collector's token, released by the Vault DON, and recomputes the batch digest to catch tampering. Five scalars leave — campaignId, cumulativeVerifiedUnits, batchDigest, windowStart, windowEnd — signed by the DON and delivered through the Keystone Forwarder. Session ids, visibility traces and per-view timestamps never cross the boundary. Settlement is cumulative and idempotent: the workflow reads what the chain says is already paid rather than trusting the collector's arithmetic, and each batch digest applies once, so retries can never double-pay. Escrow is unitPrice × targetUnits USDC, released as delivery is verified, with the undelivered remainder refunded at close. Live on Sepolia. Contracts deployed and verified; proofads-pub.eth registered on the ENSv2 beta with ads, hero and sidebar beneath it; an auction listed by a delegated agency, bid with escrowed USDC, measured in a real browser, and settled by the confidential workflow in tx 0x320ea411…36e29b — 20 raw events in, 1 verified unit out, 0.11 USDC paid to the publisher. The agency sold it; the publisher got paid.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts in Foundry/Solidity 0.8.30, built against ensdomains/contracts-v2 compiled from source — ENS is real here, not mocked, and the local test chain stands up the actual ENSv2 hierarchy. AdInventoryRegistry extends PermissionedRegistry, so authorization and the payout address both come from a registry we don't control: revocation is protocol-level, and we never had to build a permission system. ROLE_SELL_SLOT squats an unassigned Enhanced Access Control nybble (1<<40) beside ENS's own roles, and the marketplace re-reads hasRoles() at listing and again at finalization. Chainlink CRE is what makes private verified delivery possible at all — without a TEE the raw measurement data would have to be either public or trusted. The workflow is TypeScript on bun, running under cre.handlerInTee in an AWS Nitro enclave: the Vault DON releases the collector's API token inside, DON consensus signs the aggregate, and the Keystone Forwarder delivers it on-chain. Rest of the stack: Next.js 15 + wagmi/viem, a Fastify + Postgres measurement collector, browser SDK in TypeScript. Hackiest bit: ENSv2 re-mints an ERC-1155 token id on every role change, so slot identity had to become keccak256(registry, labelhash) rather than the token id. Runner-up: our first real settlement was a transaction with status: success that paid nobody — the receiver ran out of gas inside Circle's USDC and the Forwarder swallowed the revert. Every local test was green; they all settle against a mock token.

projects.title: Hark Protocol
projects.description: An open intent layer for ads. Platforms publish intent. Agents pay to reach it on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Hark Protocol is an open intent advertising protocol with on-chain machine payments on Hedera. Platforms such as search apps, social feeds, shopping apps, or AI assistants detect that a user has a temporary commercial interest, for example wanting a laptop, and publish that intent to Hark as a normalized, anonymous, short lived signal, without exposing the user's identity. Autonomous advertiser agents discover these anonymous opportunities, use an LLM to decide for themselves whether the opportunity is relevant to their campaign and budget, and if it is, pay Hark programmatically through the x402 protocol on Hedera testnet, settled via the Blocky402 facilitator, to earn the right to reach that user. The human never pays, and their identity, wallet address, and browsing history never leave the publisher. Hark's core paid endpoint, POST /v1/reach, is protected by x402. An unpaid request returns HTTP 402, the agent signs a real HBAR payment, and Blocky402 settles it on Hedera testnet, after which Hark queues the ad delivery for the publisher to show. Advertiser agents can see the publisher's identity, the placement, the topic, a sanitized summary, and the price, but never the user's name, email, IP address, or any stable cross platform identifier. Beyond the mandatory paid flow, the project also implements a publisher revenue share so publishers earn a portion of every payment, an HCS based audit trail for every settled payment, and HCS 14 based advertiser agent identity. Everything described here is live and deployed, not simulated. There is a published npm SDK and protocol package, a working web demo covering the publisher experience, an agent dashboard, and a system explorer, plus real, independently verifiable Hedera testnet transactions backing every claim.
projects.how_its_made: Stack TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces and ESM. apps/api: Express, Zod, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL, deployed on Railway, database hosted on Neon. apps/web: Next.js, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, deployed on Vercel. Covers the Demo Publisher screen, an Agent Dashboard, and a Hark Explorer. agents/runner: a CLI advertiser agent (discover, score relevance, decide, pay). Two published npm packages: @hark-protocol/protocol (shared Zod schemas and topic taxonomy) and @hark-protocol/sdk (publisher and advertiser clients). Payments (the core of the project) x402 protocol v2, using @x402/core, @x402/express, @x402/fetch, and @x402/hedera. POST /v1/reach is protected by x402 on the API side. An unpaid request returns a real HTTP 402. The agent side signs and retries automatically, paying in native HBAR. Settlement runs through the Blocky402 facilitator against Hedera testnet. Every settled transaction shown in the app and pitch deck is independently confirmed against the public Hedera testnet mirror node, not just Hark's own API response. Why Blocky402 and Hedera mattered here Blocky402 is the actual value add of the project. It lets an autonomous agent sign and settle a real payment inline in a single HTTP request response cycle, with no manual invoicing or offchain reconciliation. Hedera testnet gives fast, cheap settlement, which fits a per-request micropayment model like this far better than a slower or more expensive chain would. Relevance reasoning Uses the Vercel AI SDK with an OpenAI model. Wrapped behind a RelevanceScorer interface, with a deterministic fallback scorer, so the demo never silently breaks if a key is missing or a network call fails. The LLM only recommends relevance. Budget and price limits are enforced entirely in code, never by the model.

projects.title: Jenny Builds
projects.description: AI agents pay only when answers pass a public deterministic check.
projects.project_description: Verity is a pay-per-correct-answer protocol for AI agents on Hedera. Existing x402 services settle as soon as a provider delivers a response, even when that response is wrong. Verity reverses the flow: the buyer receives the real response first, checks it against a versioned deterministic , and only then settles the signed payment through Blocky402. The live reference market uses FX rates and entity resolution, where correctness has objective ground truth. When a buyer rejects an answer, Verity requires a bond and a verified human root. Independent checkers compare competing provider responses under a strict-majority rule. The result, content hashes, votes, bond resolution, and reputation evidence are anchored to Hedera through HCS and can be independently replayed. Providers earn reliability standing, buyers earn honesty standing, and reputation follows durable human identity rather than disposable wallet addresses. The public demo is live on Hedera testnet.
projects.how_its_made: Verity was built from scratch as a TypeScript monorepo with independent HTTP provider processes, a deterministic buying agent, a Solidity bond escrow contract, and a two-entry-point SDK. Providers use the SDK to protect existing x402 handlers with a price and published verifier rule. The FX provider supports a real DEGRADE_MODE that returns an incorrect rate without using a mock, while the entity-resolution provider charges according to observed cached or fresh usage. The payment path uses the Hedera SDK, Blocky402 x402 v2, runtime capability discovery, HCS settlement and dispute topics, Mirror Node verification, and Hedera testnet consensus. HCS receipts are compact and content-addressed so replay never stores response bodies on-chain. A separate Go checker provides an independently implemented adjudication vote. World ID verifies the human-root input, while ERC-8004 and Agent0 provide the portable identity and reputation model. The public explorer reads live hosted Graph data and exposes the real Hedera purchase flow.

projects.title: Lute
projects.description: Build, independently verify, and deploy AI-generated Graph infrastructure.
projects.project_description:
Lute is an AI-native build, verification, and deployment layer for The Graph. It lets AI coding agents build Graph infrastructure, but it does not let those agents approve their own work.
AI can now generate Subgraphs, schemas, mappings, tests, and other indexing infrastructure in minutes. The problem is that code can compile, sync successfully, and answer GraphQL queries while still indexing the blockchain incorrectly. A mapping can silently miss an event, duplicate one, store the wrong value, or produce data that no longer matches what actually happened onchain.
Lute adds an independent verification step before deployment.
A developer can ask an agent to build a Subgraph, but before that candidate is allowed to ship, Lute independently reconstructs the blockchain facts it should represent from canonical chain data and compares those facts against the indexed output. The verifier is deliberately separated from the generated mapping logic, so a mistake in the code being tested cannot automatically reproduce itself inside the system judging it.
When Lute detects a disagreement, it does more than return a failed test. It identifies the first divergent block, transaction, log, event, field, and expected-versus-observed value. Deployment is immediately blocked.
That evidence can then be passed to a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex to repair the candidate. The repaired candidate receives a new cryptographic hash and must pass the same independent verifier again before Lute allows it to deploy.
This creates a simple trust boundary:
The AI can build it. The AI cannot approve its own work.
Lute's first verification standard is an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack, which verifies observable vault activity such as Deposit and Withdraw events, assets, shares, ownership fields, event presence, duplicate records, and blockchain provenance. Integrity Packs are designed as reusable verification specifications so the same system can later support additional standards and protocols.
Lute also supports auditing compatible existing Graph deployments, not just projects originally generated through Lute. A supported Subgraph can be checked against historical blockchain evidence to determine whether its indexed representation agrees with the underlying chain.
The core lifecycle is:
BUILD → VERIFY → DEPLOY
If verification fails:
VERIFY → DIAGNOSE → REPAIR → REVERIFY → DEPLOY
And for deployed infrastructure, the same verification model can be reused to detect integrity drift over time.
Lute is ultimately building a trust layer between autonomous software and blockchain data infrastructure: AI remains responsible for generation and repair, while deterministic evidence decides what is safe to ship
projects.how_its_made:
Lute is built around a deliberately separated verification architecture.
At the center is a deterministic verifier written in TypeScript. For EVM-based Subgraphs, Lute independently reads canonical blockchain events from the source chain using standard JSON-RPC calls such as eth_getLogs. Events are decoded from the contract ABI and normalized into canonical records containing information such as block number, transaction hash, log index, contract address, event type, and event parameters.
Separately, Lute queries the corresponding indexed data from The Graph through GraphQL. That data is normalized into a second representation.
These two paths are intentionally kept independent:
Blockchain → independent decoder → canonical facts
and
Subgraph mappings → indexed entities → GraphQL
A reconciliation engine then compares them.
For supported Integrity Packs, Lute can check whether expected events exist, whether records are missing or duplicated, whether indexed values match their onchain values, and whether transaction, block, contract, and log provenance agree.
When a mismatch appears, Lute searches for the earliest deterministic divergence instead of simply reporting that two totals differ. A failure can therefore be reduced to evidence such as:
block → transaction → log → decoded event → expected entity → indexed entity → failed check
That structured evidence is also what Lute provides to a coding agent during repair.
The first implementation uses an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack. The pack defines which Deposit and Withdraw properties can be independently reconstructed and verified. Lute explicitly distinguishes between claims it can verify, claims that are only conditionally verifiable, and properties it cannot independently prove. Unsupported properties are never silently converted into a successful result.
Every candidate also receives a deterministic cryptographic hash derived from its execution-relevant source. A Verification Run is bound to that hash. If the candidate changes after verification, the previous result becomes stale and the deployment gate rejects it. This prevents a dangerous workflow where one version is verified and a different version is deployed.
The deployment gate therefore checks both the verification result and candidate identity before permitting deployment to The Graph.
Lute also exposes its capabilities programmatically so coding agents can request actions such as auditing, verification, evidence retrieval, repair context, and deployment checks without gaining control over the actual verdict.
The Graph is the core infrastructure behind the project: Lute works around Subgraphs, GraphQL data, Graph deployment tooling, and reusable Graph data products. Where included, Substreams provide another independently implemented data-processing path that can be compared against both raw blockchain events and Subgraph output.
Hedera extends Lute into an agent-to-agent verification service: an external agent can pay for a verification job through an x402 flow, after which Lute performs the actual audit and returns the resulting evidence and verdict. Compact verification attestations can also be anchored through Hedera Consensus Service. Bazantic exposes Lute's API as reusable agent tooling and allows the verification step to participate in a Verify Before Trust Recipe, where another autonomous workflow can continue only if Lute's policy requirements are satisfied.
The result is not another AI-generated testing dashboard. Lute deliberately separates generation from approval: agents can write and repair infrastructure, but only independently reconstructed evidence can unlock deployment.

Lute's first verification standard is an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack, which verifies observable vault activity such as Deposit and Withdraw events, assets, shares, ownership fields, event presence, duplicate records, and blockchain provenance. Integrity Packs are designed as reusable verification specifications so the same system can later support additional standards and protocols.
Lute also supports auditing compatible existing Graph deployments, not just projects originally generated through Lute. A supported Subgraph can be checked against historical blockchain evidence to determine whether its indexed representation agrees with the underlying chain.
The core lifecycle is:
BUILD → VERIFY → DEPLOY
If verification fails:
VERIFY → DIAGNOSE → REPAIR → REVERIFY → DEPLOY
And for deployed infrastructure, the same verification model can be reused to detect integrity drift over time.
Lute is ultimately building a trust layer between autonomous software and blockchain data infrastructure: AI remains responsible for generation and repair, while deterministic evidence decides what is safe to ship
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Lute is built around a deliberately separated verification architecture.
At the center is a deterministic verifier written in TypeScript. For EVM-based Subgraphs, Lute independently reads canonical blockchain events from the source chain using standard JSON-RPC calls such as eth_getLogs. Events are decoded from the contract ABI and normalized into canonical records containing information such as block number, transaction hash, log index, contract address, event type, and event parameters.
Separately, Lute queries the corresponding indexed data from The Graph through GraphQL. That data is normalized into a second representation.
These two paths are intentionally kept independent:
Blockchain → independent decoder → canonical facts
and
Subgraph mappings → indexed entities → GraphQL
A reconciliation engine then compares them.
For supported Integrity Packs, Lute can check whether expected events exist, whether records are missing or duplicated, whether indexed values match their onchain values, and whether transaction, block, contract, and log provenance agree.
When a mismatch appears, Lute searches for the earliest deterministic divergence instead of simply reporting that two totals differ. A failure can therefore be reduced to evidence such as:
block → transaction → log → decoded event → expected entity → indexed entity → failed check
That structured evidence is also what Lute provides to a coding agent during repair.
The first implementation uses an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack. The pack defines which Deposit and Withdraw properties can be independently reconstructed and verified. Lute explicitly distinguishes between claims it can verify, claims that are only conditionally verifiable, and properties it cannot independently prove. Unsupported properties are never silently converted into a successful result.
Every candidate also receives a deterministic cryptographic hash derived from its execution-relevant source. A Verification Run is bound to that hash. If the candidate changes after verification, the previous result becomes stale and the deployment gate rejects it. This prevents a dangerous workflow where one version is verified and a different version is deployed.
The deployment gate therefore checks both the verification result and candidate identity before permitting deployment to The Graph.
Lute also exposes its capabilities programmatically so coding agents can request actions such as auditing, verification, evidence retrieval, repair context, and deployment checks without gaining control over the actual verdict.
The Graph is the core infrastructure behind the project: Lute works around Subgraphs, GraphQL data, Graph deployment tooling, and reusable Graph data products. Where included, Substreams provide another independently implemented data-processing path that can be compared against both raw blockchain events and Subgraph output.
Hedera extends Lute into an agent-to-agent verification service: an external agent can pay for a verification job through an x402 flow, after which Lute performs the actual audit and returns the resulting evidence and verdict. Compact verification attestations can also be anchored through Hedera Consensus Service. Bazantic exposes Lute's API as reusable agent tooling and allows the verification step to participate in a Verify Before Trust Recipe, where another autonomous workflow can continue only if Lute's policy requirements are satisfied.
The result is not another AI-generated testing dashboard. Lute deliberately separates generation from approval: agents can write and repair infrastructure, but only independently reconstructed evidence can unlock deployment.

projects.title: Reality Bridge
projects.description: Privacy-preserving citizen data layer bridging recorded stats & lived reality using EAS & World ID.
projects.project_description: Socioeconomic circumstances can shift rapidly due to economic shocks, employment changes, or health events, but official welfare and statistical databases ("Recorded Reality") often take years to update. This creates a critical gap between recorded data and citizens' actual circumstances ("Lived Reality"). Reality Bridge is a privacy-preserving citizen data-quality layer that empowers citizens to report changes in their socioeconomic status and generate verifiable on-chain proof without exposing sensitive personal information. Key Features & Workflow: Unique Human Verification: Integrates World ID to prevent duplicate submissions while preserving participant anonymity. Cryptographic Commitments: Sensitive household data remains strictly off-chain. A salted SHA-256 cryptographic commitment binds the submission on the client side, producing a downloadable JSON receipt. On-Chain Attestation: Uses Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS) to log lightweight attestations containing only the commitment hash, schema version, region code, and a privacy-preserving "Reality Signal" (classified as LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH severity based on directional indicators). Public Observatory: Displays aggregated, real-time insights, category trends, and regional distributions without revealing individual household data. By adhering to the principle: "We don't put citizens' data on-chain; we put proof that their voice was counted," Reality Bridge provides a verifiable, citizen-controlled bridge to improve public data quality and social safety net responsiveness.
projects.how_its_made:
Reality Bridge was built using Next.js (App Router, React 19), Tailwind CSS, Wagmi/Viem, and Recharts, combined with privacy and Web3 primitives to create a secure citizen data layer. Technologies & Partner Integration: World ID Integration (@worldcoin/idkit):
Used for Sybil resistance and Proof of Personhood. World ID ensures each unique human can submit socioeconomic data signals without linking their on-chain wallet address to their real-world identity. Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS):
On-chain attestations are generated using @ethereum-attestation-service/eas-sdk. The schema records non-sensitive metadata: the salted commitment hash, signal level (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH), schema version, region code, and timestamp. Client-Side Zero-Knowledge Privacy & Canonical Cryptography:
All sensitive responses remain strictly on the user's browser. We use the Web Crypto API (crypto.subtle) to canonicalize JSON payloads with sorted keys, append a 32-byte cryptographically secure random nonce, and generate a SHA-256 commitment hash. The raw data is saved directly to the user's device as a downloadable JSON receipt. Viem-to-Ethers Adapter:
Because the EAS SDK expects an Ethers.js signer while Wagmi v3 uses Viem WalletClients, we built a lightweight client-side bridge (walletClientToSigner) that maps Viem transports directly to Ethers JsonRpcSigner interfaces without requiring a heavy full Ethers setup. AI Agent Engineering with Matt Pocock Skills:
Development and codebase architecture were designed and refined using Matt Pocock's Agent Skills framework (mattpocock/skills). We leveraged TDD (Test-Driven Development with Vitest), domain-driven modeling, deep-module architecture, and strict TypeScript patterns to ensure rapid, clean, and verifiable implementation. Dynamic Observatory & Heuristic Engine:
We designed an illustrative Weighted Severity Scoring algorithm across six weighted domains (employment=3, housing=2, health=1, etc.). The Observatory operates on a pre-seeded synthetic dataset of 2,500 records and dynamically injects new user attestations in real time using client-side immutable state reducers.

projects.title: LATCH
projects.description: Authorization and access control for AI workers inside organizations.
projects.project_description: LATCH is an authorization and access control system for AI workers inside organizations. It helps companies give AI agents specific jobs without giving them unlimited access to company tools and services. Each AI worker gets its own verifiable identity and specific capabilities through ENSv2. For example, a Procurement Agent can handle purchase requests, while a Research Agent can search for information. One agent cannot simply use another agent’s permissions. Before an AI worker can perform an action, LATCH checks who the agent is, whether it has the right capability, and whether the exact action follows the organization’s policy. Companies can use normal server side policies or Chainlink Confidential Workflows when sensitive rules, such as spending limits or approved vendors, need to remain private. LATCH can also be used by other AI workflows. Through Bazantic, I created a reusable procurement Recipe that combines Exa for product sourcing with LATCH for authorization. LATCH also uses Tavily for authorized research tasks. The main idea is simple: AI agents should be able to work for organizations, but only within the authority they have been given. Give AI workers a job, not the keys to everything.
projects.how_its_made: LATCH is built as an authorization layer that sits between an AI worker and the tools it wants to use. When a user gives an agent a task, Gemini first turns the request into one structured action. It can only choose from capabilities that LATCH supports, such as procurement.purchase or research.search. Gemini only understands and proposes the action; it never decides whether the action is allowed. Each worker has an ENSv2 identity under its organization’s namespace. LATCH reads fresh ENS records to verify the worker’s wallet, role, status and capabilities before every protected action. This means permissions are tied to an onchain identity instead of only being stored in a normal application database, and an organization can revoke a worker’s authority. After ENS verification, LATCH checks the exact proposed action against the organization’s policy. Organizations can use normal server side policies or Chainlink Confidential Workflows. With Chainlink, sensitive rules can be loaded and evaluated inside a TEE, while the agent only receives a simple approved or denied result instead of learning the private policy itself. For execution, the Procurement Agent handles authorized product sourcing, while the Research Agent uses Tavily only after receiving the research.search authorization. I also exposed LATCH through a Bazantic Gateway and built a reusable procurement Recipe that combines Exa for real product sourcing with LATCH for authorization. A key security detail is that LATCH binds authorization to the exact proposal. An agent cannot get one product, quantity or capability approved and then execute a different action with that approval. The application is built with Next.js and TypeScript on the frontend, with a NestJS API and MongoDB for application data and audit records. Overall, ENSv2 handles worker identity and capabilities, Chainlink handles private policy evaluation, and LATCH connects those checks to external tools so an AI worker only gets the authority needed for its specific job.
