projects.title: fly402
projects.description: An autonomous travel agent that watches flight fares and holds your seat while you sleep
projects.project_description:
Web3 doesn't meet in one place. ETHGlobal, Devconnect, Token2049, EthCC — a different country every time, and if you build here you're on a plane six times a year. Every trip goes the same way: you know weeks ahead, you book days ahead. Not because you forgot — watching a fare is a job, and you already have one. By the time you open that tab the good flights are gone: the direct one, the sane hour, the price you saw first. You book when you're free, which is never when it's best. What Fly402 does Describe the trip once — where, when, your budget, and how much the agent may commit for you. Then close the tab. The agent watches real fares. When one fits, it doesn't just tell you the good option exists — it takes the seat off the market, then emails you. You open the link whenever you get to it.
The price is still there. The seat is still there. Confirm, or walk away. What we actually built A price hold today is free and therefore worthless, or it doesn't exist at all. Fly402 makes it a
real product: an option on a seat , with a price and a lifecycle. One payment, two kinds of money. A small fee buys the time and is gone — that's what the seller
earns for pulling inventory. The ticket money goes into an escrow contract instead of the seller's
pocket, and leaves by exactly one of three doors: you book and it pays for the seat, you pass and
it comes back, you forget and it comes back anyway. "We'll refund you" is a promise; a contract isn't. Once the hold expires, anyone can trigger the refund — the seller doesn't have to cooperate, or even be online. No owner, no pause button, nobody who can change the rules once your money is in. That's why a traveller will pay for a hold, and why a seller can finally charge for one. Fly402 is an agent with its own wallet and a spending limit you set once. It pays for each search as it goes, and your money sits in a contract — the seller can't take it, and neither can the agent. The same pattern fits anything that sells out before you're ready to decide: hotels, conference tickets, limited drops.
projects.how_its_made:
Fly402 is a React frontend, an Express 5 TypeScript seller, and a Solidity escrow on Hedera
testnet. Two endpoints are x402-gated: POST /holds and POST /booking , priced in HBAR and quoted in tinybars under the exact scheme on hedera:testnet . The seller registers ExactHederaScheme on an x402ResourceServer pointed at the Blocky402 facilitator, so calling either endpoint without paying gets you a real 402 back. The buyer is an agent running in the browser. It holds an ECDSA Hedera key, and wrapFetchWithPayment does the rest — 402 → sign → retry, all inside one ordinary fetch . Booking a flight is a single function call. The payment is the transport. The fun part is what a seat hold actually is. It's an option on a seat, so one atomic x402 payment
has to become two different kinds of money: a fee the seller keeps, and a deposit it is only
holding. The seller splits them on arrival and forwards the deposit into HoldEscrow.sol with a ContractExecuteTransaction , keyed by a SHA-256 of the hold id so off-chain ids stay opaque
on-chain. The escrow has no owner. No pause, no upgrade, no admin key. settle() works only for the payer, and only before expiry. After expiry, refund() is open to anyone — a seller that
disappears can't strand a traveller's deposit. TVL is a chain read. The dashboard calls the contract's stats() instead of counting
locally, and every settlement and escrow call resolves to a real HashScan link. The agent can't overspend. Auto-hold, max fee and max deposit are checked before a 402 is ever answered, so it runs unattended inside limits the traveller set once. Real fares, not fixtures. Live Google Flights data via server-side SerpApi, cached 12h and
served stale if the upstream dies. Match emails go out through Resend and deep-link straight back into the booking page.
projects.project_description_markdown:
**Web3 doesn't meet in one place.** ETHGlobal, Devconnect, Token2049, EthCC — a different country every time, and if you build here you're on a plane six times a year. Every trip goes the same way: you know weeks ahead, you book days ahead. Not because you forgot — watching a fare is a job, and you already have one. By the time you open that tab the good flights are gone: the direct one, the sane hour, the price you saw first. **You book when you're free, which is never when it's best.**

## What Fly402 does

Describe the trip once — where, when, your budget, and how much the agent may commit for you. Then close the tab.

The agent watches real fares. When one fits, it doesn't just tell you the good option exists —
**it takes the seat off the market, then emails you.** You open the link whenever you get to it.
The price is still there. The seat is still there. Confirm, or walk away.

## What we actually built

A price hold today is free and therefore worthless, or it doesn't exist at all. Fly402 makes it a
real product: **an option on a seat**, with a price and a lifecycle.

One payment, two kinds of money. A small fee buys the time and is gone — that's what the seller
earns for pulling inventory. The ticket money goes into an escrow contract instead of the seller's
pocket, and leaves by exactly one of three doors: you book and it pays for the seat, you pass and
it comes back, you forget and it comes back anyway.

"We'll refund you" is a promise; a contract isn't. Once the hold expires, anyone can trigger the refund — the seller doesn't have to cooperate, or even be online. No owner, no pause button, nobody who can change the rules once your money is in. That's why a traveller will pay for a hold, and why a seller can finally charge for one.

Fly402 is **an agent with its own wallet and a spending limit you set once.** It pays for each search as it goes, and your money sits in a contract — the seller can't take it, and neither can the agent. The same pattern fits anything that sells out before you're ready to decide: hotels, conference tickets, limited drops.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Fly402 is a React frontend, an Express 5 TypeScript seller, and a Solidity escrow on Hedera
testnet. Two endpoints are x402-gated: `POST /holds` and `POST /booking`, priced in HBAR and quoted in tinybars under the `exact` scheme on `hedera:testnet`. The seller registers `ExactHederaScheme`on an `x402ResourceServer` pointed at the Blocky402 facilitator, so calling either endpoint without paying gets you a real `402` back.

The buyer is an agent running in the browser. It holds an ECDSA Hedera key, and
`wrapFetchWithPayment` does the rest — 402 → sign → retry, all inside one ordinary `fetch`. Booking a flight is a single function call. The payment is the transport.

The fun part is what a seat hold actually is. It's an option on a seat, so one atomic x402 payment
has to become two different kinds of money: a fee the seller keeps, and a deposit it is only
holding. The seller splits them on arrival and forwards the deposit into `HoldEscrow.sol` with a
`ContractExecuteTransaction`, keyed by a SHA-256 of the hold id so off-chain ids stay opaque
on-chain.

- **The escrow has no owner.** No pause, no upgrade, no admin key. `settle()` works only for the payer, and only before expiry. After expiry, `refund()` is open to anyone — a seller that
disappears can't strand a traveller's deposit.
- **TVL is a chain read.** The dashboard calls the contract's `stats()` instead of counting
locally, and every settlement and escrow call resolves to a real HashScan link.
- **The agent can't overspend.** Auto-hold, max fee and max deposit are checked before a 402 is ever answered, so it runs unattended inside limits the traveller set once.
- **Real fares, not fixtures.** Live Google Flights data via server-side SerpApi, cached 12h and
served stale if the upstream dies. Match emails go out through Resend and deep-link straight back into the booking page.

projects.title: PayGate
projects.description: Team payments with built-in approval rules, settled instantly in stablecoins.
projects.project_description: PayGate is a treasury and spend-management tool for companies that pay  contractors, vendors and staff in stablecoins. Today most teams route every  payout through one person with wallet access — a bottleneck, a single point of  failure, and an approval trail that lives in email. PayGate replaces that  with a shared company treasury where every payment carries an enforced rule:  who can approve it, how many of them, and up to what amount.  A company signs up with an email and gets a Privy organization wallet as its  treasury — no seed phrase, no key for anyone to lose. Admins then define  approval groups, each backed by its own Privy key quorum and spending policy:  "Payroll — HR, one approval, up to 10,000 USDC", "Grants — the four-person  committee, two approvals, up to 50,000", "Vendors — finance, two approvals, no  ceiling". Groups attach to the treasury as scoped additional signers with  override_policy_ids, so Privy evaluates only the policy of whoever actually  signs. That's what lets one wallet enforce genuinely different limits per team  instead of needing a wallet per budget.  Any team member raises a payment — payee (an external address or a teammate by  name, resolved to their Privy embedded wallet), amount, asset and an attached  invoice. Before submitting they see exactly which rule will govern it and who  must approve. Payments under a group's threshold clear on the requester's own  signature; larger ones wait for a second approver. Approvals are signed in  each approver's browser with their own Privy key via  useAuthorizationSignature() — PayGate only relays the signature and never  holds signing material, so even a fully compromised backend cannot manufacture  an approval. Once enough signatures exist they're submitted together and  Privy verifies them against the treasury's key quorum before anything moves.  The treasury holds multiple assets — USDC, EURC, WETH and native ETH — with  per-asset balances and per-asset limits, handling both native value transfers  and ERC-20 calldata. Changing the rules is itself an approved action:  attaching a group is owner-level at Privy, so it requires the same sign-off as  a large payment. Everything lands in an audit trail recording who acted,  when, and the on-chain transaction, exportable to CSV with approvers included.  Settles in USDC on Base Sepolia. Live at usepaygate.xyz.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19 and TypeScript, Tailwind 4,  Prisma 7 against Postgres (Neon, provisioned through Vercel), and viem 2 for  chain reads and calldata encoding. Privy via @privy-io/react-auth 3 in the  browser and @privy-io/node 0.34 on the server. Deployed on Vercel at  usepaygate.xyz, settling on Base Sepolia.  How the pieces fit. Org setup runs a fixed sequence against Privy: create  users → create key quorums → create a spending policy → create the  organization → create the treasury wallet with entity: {type: 'organization'}  and the member quorum as an additional_signer carrying override_policy_ids.  Approval groups are the same shape — each one is a quorum plus a policy,  attached as another scoped signer, which is what lets a single wallet enforce  different limits depending on who signs. Payments store the exact transaction  at submit time so every approver signs identical bytes; signatures are  collected and submitted together, comma-delimited in the  privy-authorization-signature header. Prisma holds what Privy doesn't know  about: invoices, memos, roles, group membership and the audit trail.  The notable hacky parts:  @privy-io/node@0.34's public client is missing methods the docs show —  users.create, keyQuorums.create, and the entire organizations service exist  only on a private underlying client. I reach it through one narrow cast that  names exactly the surface used, typed with the SDK's own param types, so an  SDK change surfaces as a type error rather than at runtime.  I built the whole approval flow on Privy intents first, then had to tear it  out. intents.authorize() doesn't exist on either client — only the  IntentAuthorizeInput type ships — and the REST endpoint rejected signatures  built to the documented payload spec across eleven variants, including the  intent_id and timestamp fields that appear in the browser SDK's types but not  the server's. Separately, POST /v1/wallets/authenticate rejects valid Privy  access tokens on this app, so no server-side user signing key can be issued at  all. The way through was to sign in the browser with  useAuthorizationSignature() and have the server merely relay — which turned  out to be the better architecture, since PayGate then never touches signing  material.  additional_signers is replaced wholesale on a wallet update. Attaching a new  group by sending just that group would have silently detached every other one,  including the original member quorum and its capped policy — it would have  demoed perfectly and quietly broken every other rule. desiredSigners()  rebuilds the complete list every time.  Smaller things that mattered: invoice types are sniffed from magic bytes  rather than trusting Content-Type or the extension, and stored as Bytes in  Postgres because Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral. Money is integer base units  as BigInt everywhere with per-asset decimals — which caught a real bug where  the dashboard was adding micro-USDC to wei. Balances are cached server-side  for 10s after the public RPC started throttling under polling. Privy caps  display_name at 50 characters, which silently broke org creation for longer  names until I truncated.

Once enough signatures exist they're submitted together and  Privy verifies them against the treasury's key quorum before anything moves.  The treasury holds multiple assets — USDC, EURC, WETH and native ETH — with  per-asset balances and per-asset limits, handling both native value transfers  and ERC-20 calldata. Changing the rules is itself an approved action:  attaching a group is owner-level at Privy, so it requires the same sign-off as  a large payment. Everything lands in an audit trail recording who acted,  when, and the on-chain transaction, exportable to CSV with approvers included.  Settles in USDC on Base Sepolia. Live at usepaygate.xyz.
projects.how_its_made_markdown: Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19 and TypeScript, Tailwind 4,  Prisma 7 against Postgres (Neon, provisioned through Vercel), and viem 2 for  chain reads and calldata encoding. Privy via @privy-io/react-auth 3 in the  browser and @privy-io/node 0.34 on the server. Deployed on Vercel at  usepaygate.xyz, settling on Base Sepolia.  How the pieces fit. Org setup runs a fixed sequence against Privy: create  users → create key quorums → create a spending policy → create the  organization → create the treasury wallet with entity: {type: 'organization'}  and the member quorum as an additional_signer carrying override_policy_ids.  Approval groups are the same shape — each one is a quorum plus a policy,  attached as another scoped signer, which is what lets a single wallet enforce  different limits depending on who signs. Payments store the exact transaction  at submit time so every approver signs identical bytes; signatures are  collected and submitted together, comma-delimited in the  privy-authorization-signature header. Prisma holds what Privy doesn't know  about: invoices, memos, roles, group membership and the audit trail.  The notable hacky parts:  @privy-io/node@0.34's public client is missing methods the docs show —  users.create, keyQuorums.create, and the entire organizations service exist  only on a private underlying client. I reach it through one narrow cast that  names exactly the surface used, typed with the SDK's own param types, so an  SDK change surfaces as a type error rather than at runtime.  I built the whole approval flow on Privy intents first, then had to tear it  out. intents.authorize() doesn't exist on either client — only the  IntentAuthorizeInput type ships — and the REST endpoint rejected signatures  built to the documented payload spec across eleven variants, including the  intent_id and timestamp fields that appear in the browser SDK's types but not  the server's. Separately, POST /v1/wallets/authenticate rejects valid Privy  access tokens on this app, so no server-side user signing key can be issued at  all. The way through was to sign in the browser with  useAuthorizationSignature() and have the server merely relay — which turned  out to be the better architecture, since PayGate then never touches signing  material.  additional_signers is replaced wholesale on a wallet update. Attaching a new  group by sending just that group would have silently detached every other one,  including the original member quorum and its capped policy — it would have  demoed perfectly and quietly broken every other rule. desiredSigners()  rebuilds the complete list every time.  Smaller things that mattered: invoice types are sniffed from magic bytes  rather than trusting Content-Type or the extension, and stored as Bytes in  Postgres because Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral. Money is integer base units  as BigInt everywhere with per-asset decimals — which caught a real bug where  the dashboard was adding micro-USDC to wei. Balances are cached server-side  for 10s after the public RPC started throttling under polling. Privy caps  display_name at 50 characters, which silently broke org creation for longer  names until I truncated.

projects.title: BalamOS
projects.description: BalamOS is the grok bot of crypto, give your agents an asolated environment for executions.
projects.project_description: BalamOS is "the Grok bot of crypto" — a chat-first agent operating system. You talk to an AI agent that has its own sandboxed Linux desktop, a real crypto wallet, and a toolbox for on-chain work, and you watch it operate live: researching data, paying for services, and driving a browser. Its signature feature is a manual-control handoff — when the agent gets stuck, or hits something only a human should do, it hands you its desktop; you take over, act, and hand control back. Under the hood it enforces financial guardrails (governance spend caps) so the agent can transact autonomously within limits you set. It ships with live integrations: querying on-chain data through The Graph, and discovering and paying for x402-gated services on Hedera with real, verifiable on-chain settlement — no API keys, and no human tapping "confirm" on every step.
projects.how_its_made:
BalamOS is a Tauri + React desktop app over a Rust daemon (orbit-daemon) that manages sandboxed Linux "webtop" Docker containers — each agent gets its own isolated XFCE desktop the AI drives via screenshots (scrot) and input (xdotool). The agent runs on opencode with GPT-5.6-Luna; the desktop streams into the app so you can watch and take manual control (a toggle pauses the agent, unlocks the live desktop, then hands back).
Crypto capabilities are packaged as zero-dependency Node CLIs baked into the container image, so any coding agent can invoke them:
The Graph — a balamos-graph CLI plus an MCP server exposing a query_subgraph tool, auto-wired into the agent's opencode config; verified live returning real Ethereum data.
▎ - Hedera x402 — balamos-x402 pay <url> inspects an x402 paywall, gates the amount against a governance spend cap, signs and submits a real HBAR transfer via the Hiero SDK, then re-requests with an X-PAYMENT proof; the service verifies the transfer against the public Hedera mirror node (no API key). Verified live on testnet with real settlement txns on HashScan. Governance + Secrets — hard spend caps plus a credential store that injects the agent's wallet key as env vars: the key never enters prompts, logs, or the repo; the daemon signs. A live treasury dashboard shows balances moving as the agent transacts. Partner tech: Hedera (Hiero SDK + mirror node) gives near-instant, cheap, verifiable settlement that makes autonomous agentic payments practical; The Graph's MCP lets the agent pull on-chain context natively. We also preinstall Foundry (cast/anvil) and MetaMask/HashPack in Chromium so the agent can operate any EVM/Arc chain and dApp.

projects.title: Aquifer
projects.description: Quote ERC-4626 vault shares at the live rate on 1inch Aqua — no AMM deposit needed.
projects.project_description:
What it does Aquifer prices a swap between an ERC-4626 vault share and its underlying asset at the vault’s live convertToAssets rate. The maker never deposits into an AMM. Aqua already lets tokens stay in the maker’s wallet as virtual liquidity. What it does not ship is a way to price vault shares. A vault share is not a curve and not a peg. Its fair price is the vault’s conversion rate, and that rate moves when the vault earns yield or takes a donation. Maker points Aquifer at a vault and sets a spread plus min/max bounds. Aquifer reads the vault on every quote and every fill. Taker asks for a price. SwapVM hits the Extruction, applies the spread, and refuses anything outside the band. Fill happens from the maker’s wallet. The shares were never locked in a pool. They kept earning vault yield until the swap. No new pool. No redeem-then-dump. No invented peg. If someone donates into the vault and the rate jumps outside ±1%, the quote dies. That is the point. Demo, not audited production software. Testing Started with a handful of golden vectors for exact-in and exact-out. Ended with 100+ unit, property, and mainnet-fork tests. Every failure path got a name: wrong config length, dirty padding, spread ≥ 10000, zero min rate, band wider than ±1%, unsupported pair, self-referential vault, zero vault rate, dust that rounds to zero, recompute on a populated register, insufficient balances, unauthorized allowlist, stranger mint on the mock token. Fuzz tests: quote equals swap on both layouts, zero spread matches convertToAssets / convertToShares, spread applied once, output falls as spread rises, a round-trip never mints value, a quoted amount never exceeds the maker’s balances. Fork tests hit the real Aqua router. A donation that pushes sDAI’s rate out of band blocks every leg and every mode. If it can go wrong on a vault rate, there is a test for it. Challenges I ran into Two opcodes, one mental model. The first encoding used the opcode in the SDK table. The router never called the contract. Live Aqua is 0x20. Current main is 0x04. The SDK’s 0x21 is a fossil. The library now has buildDeployed and buildCurrent. They differ by one byte. That byte is the whole integration. Quote and swap must be the same function. Aqua requires identical amounts from quote() and swap(), and a non-upgradeable target. A view quote plus a state-changing swap was a footgun. Both ABIs are view. The swap path is side-effect free. Tests assert that. Vault rates are not oracles. convertToAssets is live and attackable. The first version let bounds sit at 0 and uint256.max. That made the Extruction a very expensive wrapper. Now the band cannot exceed ±1%, and a failed share/asset round-trip reverts. Still not an oracle. A refusal to pretend it is one. Explaining Aqua to a human. “Virtual liquidity” sounds like a slogan. The sentence that works: “The tokens stay in your wallet. The strategy can still sell them. The vault keeps paying you yield until someone takes the trade.” Accomplishments that I'm proud of One price path — quote and swap cannot disagree because they cannot branch.
The opcode that actually hits the router — proven on a fork, not a mock VM.
Bounds that mean something — ±1%, donation out of band reverts, inconsistent 4626 math reverts.
The UI does not pretend to be a solver. Shipping stays in the CLI. Less demo-sizzle. More honesty. What I learned An Extruction that is “almost deterministic” is not deterministic.
Opcode tables rot. The deployed router is the spec.
ERC-4626 convertToAssets is a price, not a promise. Donations, empty vaults, and decimal offsets all lie in different ways.
mulDiv rounding is a market-making decision. Both legs lean toward the maker.
Aqua’s story is capital efficiency. The moment the demo deposits into a pool, you have built a zap and lost the plot.
A confused judge picks the project that pasted a vault and showed a number. What's next Tighten UI errors when a vault is not 4626. Cached quote path so a public RPC timeout does not kill the demo. Backup recording of the sDAI fork quote. Short list of allowlisted real vaults. Optional Sepolia fill only with a real resolver credential — the flag in the CLI does not grant one. Longer term: a small solver, multi-chain once the opcode table stops being a special case, and an audit. Until then this stays a demo.
projects.how_its_made: he contract is the product. Everything else is a way to point at it. Vault4626Extruction — Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, OpenZeppelin. It implements both SwapVM Extruction ABIs: current-main (IExtruction / IStaticExtruction) and the deployed Aqua router v1.0.2 (IExtructionV102 / IStaticExtructionV102). Quote is STATICCALL. Swap is CALL. Both hit the same view function. If those paths can diverge, Aqua’s invariant is dead, so they cannot diverge. OpenZeppelin’s IERC4626, IERC20Metadata, and Math.mulDiv are the pricing primitives — we did not roll our own fixed-point. Strategy args are four words: vault, spreadBps, minRate, maxRate. The decoder rejects dirty ABI padding so a packed address cannot silently become someone else’s vault. Spread is applied once. Exact-in rounds down in the maker’s favour. Exact-out rounds up. Dust that would round to zero reverts. Liquidity is checked on both balanceIn and balanceOut. A recompute guard refuses any quote where the opposite register is already populated. Rate bounds cannot be wider than ±100 bps around the live rate. A vault that fails a convertToAssets → convertToShares round-trip inside 10 bps is treated as inconsistent and rejected. AquiferStrategy packs the instruction as opcode || 0x94 || target || abi.encode(...). Opcode 0x20 is what the live Aqua router actually calls. Opcode 0x04 is current SwapVM main. They are not interchangeable. The SDK’s stale table still says 0x21. We never use that value. Fork tests against the real router prove 0x20 reaches the target and 0x04 / 0x21 do not. CLI — TypeScript, @1inch/aqua-sdk, @1inch/swap-vm-sdk, viem. prepare / ship / quote / fill. Aqua-sdk encodes ship and strategy hashes. Swap-vm-sdk builds orders, traits, quote calldata, and fill calldata. Those two packages pin adjacent versions of @1inch/sdk-core. Casts across that boundary compile and are wrong, so the CLI rebuilds Aqua’s Address and HexString from canonical hex. That is the hacky part worth mentioning: the official SDKs do not share a core, and reconstructing from hex is the only honest crossing. Private keys stay in the shell. Frontend — Next.js + viem, not a solver. Paste a vault. It reads asset(), decimals, and convertToAssets over RPC. It previews rate, spread, and bounds. It copies a CLI ship command. Wallet connect only identifies the account and network. The browser never submits strategy calldata. Local Anvil traffic goes through a same-origin /api/rpc/local relay so the client cannot pick its own upstream URL. Live quotes go through /api/aqua-quote to the SwapVM router. Partner tech. 1inch Aqua is the liquidity layer: the maker’s wallet balance is the inventory — no pool deposit. SwapVM Extruction is the reason this exists; built-in opcodes price curves and pegs, not vault conversion rates. Path C (external pricing) is the whole architecture. OpenZeppelin gives us the 4626 and decimal surface we refuse to reimplement. Foundry gives us unit, fuzz, and mainnet-fork tests against real sDAI. Three deploy scripts: local mocks, a mainnet-fork Extruction against live vault state, optional Sepolia mocks. Aqua and SwapVM are already on Sepolia. We did not redeploy them.
projects.project_description_markdown:
What it does

Aquifer prices a swap between an ERC-4626 vault share and its underlying asset at the vault’s live convertToAssets rate. The maker never deposits into an AMM. Aqua already lets tokens stay in the maker’s wallet as virtual liquidity. What it does not ship is a way to price vault shares. A vault share is not a curve and not a peg. Its fair price is the vault’s conversion rate, and that rate moves when the vault earns yield or takes a donation.

Maker points Aquifer at a vault and sets a spread plus min/max bounds. Aquifer reads the vault on every quote and every fill. Taker asks for a price. SwapVM hits the Extruction, applies the spread, and refuses anything outside the band. Fill happens from the maker’s wallet. The shares were never locked in a pool. They kept earning vault yield until the swap.

No new pool. No redeem-then-dump. No invented peg. If someone donates into the vault and the rate jumps outside ±1%, the quote dies. That is the point. Demo, not audited production software.

Testing

Started with a handful of golden vectors for exact-in and exact-out. Ended with 100+ unit, property, and mainnet-fork tests.

Every failure path got a name: wrong config length, dirty padding, spread ≥ 10000, zero min rate, band wider than ±1%, unsupported pair, self-referential vault, zero vault rate, dust that rounds to zero, recompute on a populated register, insufficient balances, unauthorized allowlist, stranger mint on the mock token.

Fuzz tests: quote equals swap on both layouts, zero spread matches convertToAssets / convertToShares, spread applied once, output falls as spread rises, a round-trip never mints value, a quoted amount never exceeds the maker’s balances.

Fork tests hit the real Aqua router. A donation that pushes sDAI’s rate out of band blocks every leg and every mode. If it can go wrong on a vault rate, there is a test for it.

Challenges I ran into

Two opcodes, one mental model. The first encoding used the opcode in the SDK table. The router never called the contract. Live Aqua is 0x20. Current main is 0x04. The SDK’s 0x21 is a fossil. The library now has buildDeployed and buildCurrent. They differ by one byte. That byte is the whole integration.

Quote and swap must be the same function. Aqua requires identical amounts from quote() and swap(), and a non-upgradeable target. A view quote plus a state-changing swap was a footgun. Both ABIs are view. The swap path is side-effect free. Tests assert that.

Vault rates are not oracles. convertToAssets is live and attackable. The first version let bounds sit at 0 and uint256.max. That made the Extruction a very expensive wrapper. Now the band cannot exceed ±1%, and a failed share/asset round-trip reverts. Still not an oracle. A refusal to pretend it is one.

Explaining Aqua to a human. “Virtual liquidity” sounds like a slogan. The sentence that works: “The tokens stay in your wallet. The strategy can still sell them. The vault keeps paying you yield until someone takes the trade.”

Accomplishments that I'm proud of

One price path — quote and swap cannot disagree because they cannot branch.
The opcode that actually hits the router — proven on a fork, not a mock VM.
Bounds that mean something — ±1%, donation out of band reverts, inconsistent 4626 math reverts.
The UI does not pretend to be a solver. Shipping stays in the CLI. Less demo-sizzle. More honesty.

What I learned

An Extruction that is “almost deterministic” is not deterministic.
Opcode tables rot. The deployed router is the spec.
ERC-4626 convertToAssets is a price, not a promise. Donations, empty vaults, and decimal offsets all lie in different ways.
mulDiv rounding is a market-making decision. Both legs lean toward the maker.
Aqua’s story is capital efficiency. The moment the demo deposits into a pool, you have built a zap and lost the plot.
A confused judge picks the project that pasted a vault and showed a number.

What's next

Tighten UI errors when a vault is not 4626. Cached quote path so a public RPC timeout does not kill the demo. Backup recording of the sDAI fork quote. Short list of allowlisted real vaults. Optional Sepolia fill only with a real resolver credential — the flag in the CLI does not grant one. Longer term: a small solver, multi-chain once the opcode table stops being a special case, and an audit. Until then this stays a demo.

projects.title: Decentralized Value
projects.description: Decentralize how progress is defined—not just value transfer—so multiple values can coexist.
projects.project_description: Most funding systems turn many dimensions of value into one weighted score. That looks objective, but the weights already encode one definition of what “better” means. A solution can create an important new tradeoff and still receive no support simply because it does not maximize the organizer’s chosen score. Value Decentralization replaces one ranking with multiple independent funding decisions. Every submission is tested under the same published rules. Solutions that fail required conditions are rejected first. For valid solutions, each result stays separate instead of being averaged into one number. Different funders can then create Value Pools that support the kind of progress they care about—such as efficiency, resilience, fairness, or a genuinely new tradeoff. The same solution can be valuable to several pools, and the system does not need to declare one universal winner. The product makes this visible through interactive Arenas. Participants submit code, strategies, or decision rules; the system runs reproducible evaluations, shows what each solution improves and what it sacrifices, identifies non-dominated alternatives, and calculates rewards separately for each Value Pool. One Arena executes compiled Solidity bytecode and measures the tradeoff between calldata gas and decoder execution gas. Other Arenas apply the same protocol to multi-objective strategies, zero-knowledge proofs, and AI decision policies. The individual problems change, but the funding model stays the same. Ethereum is the settlement layer, not a magic judge. Evaluation can remain domain-specific and offchain, while final allocations and payments become publicly auditable and difficult to rewrite. We completed a real Sepolia demonstration that committed an allocation and executed a reward payment. Our ambition is much larger than building a better competition platform. We want any community to be able to define a value, make it measurable and verifiable, attach independent capital to it, and create sustained demand around improving it. If that demand persists, new builders, evaluators, standards, companies, and eventually entirely new industries can form around values that markets previously ignored. Ethereum decentralized who can own and transact. Value Decentralization asks the next question: can we decentralize what gets funded?
projects.how_its_made: We built Value Decentralization as a verifiable evaluation layer for problems where “better” cannot honestly be reduced to one number. The core is our own deterministic multi-objective evaluation engine. Each metric remains independent and can be either minimized or maximized. Invalid solutions are removed by Hard Constraints before comparison. Valid results are normalized against published bounds, placed on a Pareto Frontier, and measured by exact hypervolume and exclusive frontier contribution across up to six dimensions. Reward calculations use deterministic integer arithmetic and stable tie-breaking, so changing submission order cannot change the result. What makes the system Web3-native is not simply that rewards are sent through a smart contract. We built an evidence chain around the evaluation itself. Every evaluation environment is versioned. Dataset, constraints, metrics, evaluator settings, submitted artifact, and measured outcomes are canonicalized and connected through Keccak-256 hashes. If the benchmark changes, the Context Hash changes. If a submission or measurement changes, the Result Hash changes. This makes an offchain evaluation reproducible and tamper-evident before Ethereum is used to finalize the outcome. For our Ethereum-native benchmark, we do not use mocked gas numbers. Ethereum Calldata Compression compiles real Solidity codecs and executes their runtime bytecode inside an EthereumJS Cancun EVM. The evaluator checks output correctness, verifies malformed-input rejection, measures calldata gas and decoder execution gas independently, and then calculates the resulting Pareto contribution. This lets us evaluate competing Ethereum implementations from executable evidence rather than self-reported benchmark numbers. We also built a real privacy primitive with Semaphore V4. Secret Gate creates a disposable identity locally and generates a zero-knowledge membership proof inside a browser Web Worker. The private identity never needs to leave the device. The server verifies the proof and atomically rejects reuse of the same nullifier. This demonstrates how future competitions can prove eligibility or one-use participation without turning identity data into public onchain state. A second unusual problem appears when AI Agents become participants: LLM execution is non-deterministic, but evaluation must be reproducible. In Rescue Room, an OpenAI Agents SDK Commander sees only the current public state and returns structured Actions. We do not treat hidden model reasoning as evidence. Instead, every Action is recorded against the exact Public View Hash that produced it. The recorded Action sequence is then replayed through a deterministic state machine. The model may make a different decision on another run, but the submitted behavior always reproduces the same outcome and Result Hash. These components share the same evidence model. A Solidity optimization, a zero-knowledge interaction, a deterministic strategy, or an AI policy can all become an Artifact evaluated under a fixed Context and compared without inventing one universal score. Ethereum is used at the boundary where trust should stop. Our Solidity settlement contract commits a final allocation, prevents duplicate allocation and payment, checks available reward reserves, and exposes the final transfer publicly. We demonstrated the complete commitment and reward path on Sepolia. The blockchain does not pretend to prove that an offchain metric is socially correct; it proves what result was committed and what was actually paid. The sponsor technologies extend this architecture rather than define it. ENSv2 adds fine-grained identity and permission management for evaluators and protocol actors. Bazantic makes the evaluation API discoverable and usable by autonomous Agents. Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows are being explored as the Hidden Final boundary, so committed private scenarios can evaluate frozen submissions before those scenarios are revealed for public reproduction. The application layer uses Next.js, TypeScript, React and Vercel, with Upstash Redis for durable competition state and Privy for account and wallet UX. Solidity contracts are tested with Foundry and accessed through viem. The result is not just another leaderboard or optimization dashboard. It is reusable infrastructure for open competitions, protocol engineering, AI Agent evaluation, grants, procurement, and other systems where several legitimate definitions of progress must remain visible at the same time. The technical idea is simple to state but difficult to implement: measure different values independently, make the evidence reproducible, preserve real tradeoffs, and use Web3 to make the rules, identities, results, and final commitments harder for any single operator to rewrite.

One Arena executes compiled Solidity bytecode and measures the tradeoff between calldata gas and decoder execution gas. Other Arenas apply the same protocol to multi-objective strategies, zero-knowledge proofs, and AI decision policies. The individual problems change, but the funding model stays the same.

Ethereum is the settlement layer, not a magic judge. Evaluation can remain domain-specific and offchain, while final allocations and payments become publicly auditable and difficult to rewrite. We completed a real Sepolia demonstration that committed an allocation and executed a reward payment.

Our ambition is much larger than building a better competition platform. We want any community to be able to define a value, make it measurable and verifiable, attach independent capital to it, and create sustained demand around improving it. If that demand persists, new builders, evaluators, standards, companies, and eventually entirely new industries can form around values that markets previously ignored.

Ethereum decentralized who can own and transact. Value Decentralization asks the next question: can we decentralize what gets funded?
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built Value Decentralization as a verifiable evaluation layer for problems where “better” cannot honestly be reduced to one number.

The core is our own deterministic multi-objective evaluation engine. Each metric remains independent and can be either minimized or maximized. Invalid solutions are removed by Hard Constraints before comparison. Valid results are normalized against published bounds, placed on a Pareto Frontier, and measured by exact hypervolume and exclusive frontier contribution across up to six dimensions. Reward calculations use deterministic integer arithmetic and stable tie-breaking, so changing submission order cannot change the result.

What makes the system Web3-native is not simply that rewards are sent through a smart contract. We built an evidence chain around the evaluation itself.

Every evaluation environment is versioned. Dataset, constraints, metrics, evaluator settings, submitted artifact, and measured outcomes are canonicalized and connected through Keccak-256 hashes. If the benchmark changes, the Context Hash changes. If a submission or measurement changes, the Result Hash changes. This makes an offchain evaluation reproducible and tamper-evident before Ethereum is used to finalize the outcome.

For our Ethereum-native benchmark, we do not use mocked gas numbers. Ethereum Calldata Compression compiles real Solidity codecs and executes their runtime bytecode inside an EthereumJS Cancun EVM. The evaluator checks output correctness, verifies malformed-input rejection, measures calldata gas and decoder execution gas independently, and then calculates the resulting Pareto contribution. This lets us evaluate competing Ethereum implementations from executable evidence rather than self-reported benchmark numbers.

We also built a real privacy primitive with Semaphore V4. Secret Gate creates a disposable identity locally and generates a zero-knowledge membership proof inside a browser Web Worker. The private identity never needs to leave the device. The server verifies the proof and atomically rejects reuse of the same nullifier. This demonstrates how future competitions can prove eligibility or one-use participation without turning identity data into public onchain state.

A second unusual problem appears when AI Agents become participants: LLM execution is non-deterministic, but evaluation must be reproducible. In Rescue Room, an OpenAI Agents SDK Commander sees only the current public state and returns structured Actions. We do not treat hidden model reasoning as evidence. Instead, every Action is recorded against the exact Public View Hash that produced it. The recorded Action sequence is then replayed through a deterministic state machine. The model may make a different decision on another run, but the submitted behavior always reproduces the same outcome and Result Hash.

These components share the same evidence model. A Solidity optimization, a zero-knowledge interaction, a deterministic strategy, or an AI policy can all become an Artifact evaluated under a fixed Context and compared without inventing one universal score.

Ethereum is used at the boundary where trust should stop. Our Solidity settlement contract commits a final allocation, prevents duplicate allocation and payment, checks available reward reserves, and exposes the final transfer publicly. We demonstrated the complete commitment and reward path on Sepolia. The blockchain does not pretend to prove that an offchain metric is socially correct; it proves what result was committed and what was actually paid.

The sponsor technologies extend this architecture rather than define it. ENSv2 adds fine-grained identity and permission management for evaluators and protocol actors. Bazantic makes the evaluation API discoverable and usable by autonomous Agents. Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows are being explored as the Hidden Final boundary, so committed private scenarios can evaluate frozen submissions before those scenarios are revealed for public reproduction.

The application layer uses Next.js, TypeScript, React and Vercel, with Upstash Redis for durable competition state and Privy for account and wallet UX. Solidity contracts are tested with Foundry and accessed through viem.

The result is not just another leaderboard or optimization dashboard. It is reusable infrastructure for open competitions, protocol engineering, AI Agent evaluation, grants, procurement, and other systems where several legitimate definitions of progress must remain visible at the same time.

The technical idea is simple to state but difficult to implement:

measure different values independently, make the evidence reproducible, preserve real tradeoffs, and use Web3 to make the rules, identities, results, and final commitments harder for any single operator to rewrite.

projects.title: Aivy Quorum
projects.description: Earthquake cover with precommitted Hedera payouts, paid oracle checks and access to Uniswap.
projects.project_description: After an earthquake, a family or small business may need cash immediately, even when the damage is too small to justify a traditional claim. Aivy Quorum explores a simpler promise: agree on the place, measurable trigger and fixed payout before the event, then make that commitment verifiable. Choose a city, set a premium budget and create cover. Quorum issues a geographic NFT receipt, publishes the policy terms and prepares a Hedera Scheduled Transaction. The agent's signature plus two of three oracle keys authorize the transfer. A qualifying recorded earthquake triggers the agreed amount; damage alone does not. Judges can try the complete product without installing a wallet: buy testnet cover, inspect its NFT and receipts, pay for policy-bound earthquake checks through Blocky402, fund the shared insurance pool, and test a broker referral commission. The map's interactive history shows how modeled premiums change for a fixed $800 payout. A separate Hedera → Axelar → Uniswap journey connects the product to EVM liquidity. Funded demo wallets support real Sepolia swaps and Uniswap V3 positions, including fee collection and withdrawals. Insurance-pool shares (ARPS) remain distinct from Uniswap liquidity positions. At https://aivylabs.xyz/quorum, a user can authorize a bounded monthly-cover agent for Medellín or another city. It checks fresh terms before each purchase. Read-only companions explain policy and network status with evidence links. The contribution goes beyond the interface: I extracted a new reusable HAK settlement plugin, and the product also integrates my previously published Uniswap and Axelar plugins. My Mirror Node developer skill informed the verification layer, and an account-key limitation led to an upstream HAK improvement proposal. The README links each contribution and distinguishes new work, reuse and open PRs. This is a Continuity submission. Public interactive transactions use test tokens with no cash value. The mainnet settlement is a labeled, controlled 4 HBAR experiment, not a real earthquake claim. Oracle keys currently share an operator; checks are user-triggered. ARPS earnings and redemption are not implemented. Commercial deployment would require insurance partners, risk calibration and legal review.
projects.how_its_made:
The app uses a React/Vite frontend and a Node.js backend with the Hedera SDK. Hedera provides the settlement mechanism directly: an account key requires agent AND 2-of-3 oracle authorization; a pre-signed Scheduled Transaction fixes the transfer; HCS records policy terms; HTS supplies the cover NFT, demo asset and pool shares. Premium and broker allocations settle atomically. Mirror Node reads expose balances, ownership, signatures and transaction evidence. I extracted the conditional-settlement helpers into hak-scheduled-settlement during this event. Quorum imports its key builders and expiry limit, then constructs schedules with the SDK. The work also produced hedera-agent-kit-js issue #1087 and open PR #1088 for flat threshold/key-list account creation. The proposed core change is not merged and does not implement Quorum's nested keys. The oracle services expose policy-bound x402 endpoints. The consuming agent validates published terms and exact payment requirements; hosted Blocky402 verifies and settles the testnet payment and sponsors network fees. Recorded payments to USGS, EMSC and GEOFON checks returned no match: a paid request is not a payout approval. My existing hak-uniswap-plugin, published on npm, gives other Hedera Agent Kit developers reusable access to Uniswap's EVM swap tooling. During this event I added the quote-only uniswap_quote tool (GitHub 0.2.0, September 5), which Quorum consumes for Base/Unichain without an EVM signing key, token approvals or broadcast. The npm swap release remains 0.1.0 and is prior work. New project-specific Sepolia adapters use the Uniswap Trading API for executable swaps and V3 position operations. My existing hak-axelar-plugin builds Hedera ITS transfers; Quorum adds validation, journaling and matched delivery evidence. Axelar moves the asset; Uniswap supplies liquidity. No custom Solidity swap contract was added. Sponsored starter tokens were bridged previously; a new pending bridge is shown separately. Signing is deterministic and constrained by network, token, recipient, amount, allowance, slippage, expiry and budget checks. Transactions are journaled before broadcast; uncertain outcomes are reconciled rather than blindly retried. AI companions only select from a strict read-only topic set; trusted code fetches and renders facts. They cannot spend, sign or alter a mandate. My pre-existing Mirror Node skill proposal (hedera-skills PR #16) informed concrete read-path fixes. The separate Accounts & Keys skill and wider plugin portfolio are linked as related contributions, not claimed as runtime dependencies. New event work includes the earthquake product, guarded cross-chain execution, paid oracles, settlement package, monthly-cover worker, companions and evidence-focused UI. Earlier Aivy projects, plugins and art are disclosed in docs/PRIOR-WORK.md; docs/CONTRIBUTIONS.md maps their exact use. Codex and Claude assisted implementation, tests, design and documentation; docs/AI-ASSISTANCE.md attributes the work and assets. The public repo includes setup, security boundaries, integration code links, onchain receipts and Uniswap FEEDBACK.md. projects.title: Bursar
projects.description: Manage AI agents like employees: roles, budgets, and hard spending limits enforced on-chain.
projects.project_description: Bursar is where you manage a team of AI agents and the money they spend. AI agents increasingly pay their own way in stablecoins — search queries, model calls, data pulls, even hiring a person for a one-off job. Around 160 million payments have settled over the x402 payment protocol so far, now running at roughly 16 million a month, and nearly all of it is USDC. One agent is easy to keep an eye on. A team of them isn't — once you're running five, there is no single answer to what the team is allowed to spend, what it has already spent, or how to stop one agent without disturbing the rest. Each agent is a separate wallet you keep funded by hand, their spending is spread across wallets and vendor invoices, and the limits you set live in a dashboard that can't actually stop a payment. So you either approve every payment yourself, which defeats the point of hiring them, or you find out what happened when the bill arrives. Bursar puts the whole team on one shared balance and gives each agent two limits: how much it can spend on a single purchase, and how much it can spend in a month. Inside those limits it just pays — no approval, no interruption, and you never handle a wallet or a key. Go over either limit and the payment doesn't go through; it waits on your screen until you approve or reject it. And you can cut off any one agent instantly, while the rest carry on working. What makes it hold is where the limits live. They aren't settings in our app — they're in the smart contract that holds the money, so they're checked at the moment a payment is made rather than reported after it.
projects.how_its_made: At the centre is the Roster contract — one per team, deployed from a RosterFactory. It is the team's account and its rulebook in one: it holds the team's USDC and, for each agent, two limits (per purchase and per month), what that agent has spent this period, and whether it is still employed. Every payment goes through it, and nothing else checks a limit — an agent can always talk to the chain directly, so the only check worth having is the one between the money and the door. Hiring is a name, a role and two limits in the UI. Bursar provisions a Claude managed agent carrying a version-pinned skill for paying through the Roster; on startup that agent generates its own keypair inside its own sandbox and reports back nothing but an address, which Bursar registers with those limits. We never see the agent's key, and the owner never sees an address. From then on it spends on its own. It calls a paid service, gets a 402, and signs an intent — it holds no gas, because gas on Arc is USDC and a float would be spendable outside its limits — which a relayer submits and pays for. The Roster contract verifies the signature, rolls the monthly counter if the period has turned, and checks both limits. Inside them it releases the USDC to the agent's wallet and the agent pays the service; the owner is never asked. The contract never pays the service itself, so the payee on a request is the agent's stated intent rather than a guarantee. Every payment lands as an event on the Roster, so the dashboard reads live limits and month-to-date spend from the contract and history from the chain's explorer API. There is no indexer. Over either limit, nothing moves: the payment is held for the owner, who approves or rejects it. Approving overrides the per-purchase limit but still counts against the month, and firing an agent beats a request already waiting. Firing writes one field on one agent's record, in a function with no loop over agents, so one agent can be cut off mid-loop while the others keep spending in the same block.

projects.title: AgentKey
projects.description: Give your AI agent a spending key it can't misuse — limits set and enforced from your Ledger.
projects.project_description: AgentKey is a hardware-backed permission system for AI agents. Any AI — running on EC2, inside Claude, inside GPT — can take onchain USDC actions, bounded by hard limits that only the owner's Ledger hardware device can configure and reinstate. The kill switch is not a software flag. It is enforced inside a Chainlink CRE Nitro TEE, attested by hardware, with policy stored live on ENS and reinstatement gated to a physical button press on the Ledger device. Every agent is a real ENS subname. Its spend policy — daily cap, weekly cap, whitelist, velocity limit, and live status — lives as ENS text records on a per-agent resolver. The Chainlink CRE workflow runs inside an AWS Nitro TEE, reads that policy from ENS on every request, enforces a three-tier kill switch (GREEN / YELLOW / RED), and either writes a DON-attested report to AgentVault.onReport() to execute the transfer, or writes status="suspended" back to ENS to block the agent immediately. No single operator can bypass this — the policy is onchain, the enforcement is in hardware, and the only reinstatement path is an EIP-712 signature from the physical Ledger that created the agent, displayed as clear-signed human-readable text on the device screen. AgentVault.onReport() verifies the Chainlink DON threshold signature via KeystoneForwarder.verify() before executing any USDC transfer, and double-checks ENS status at settlement — so a suspension that fires between CRE report generation and on-chain settlement still blocks the transfer. The result is an AI agent permission system where the safety guarantee is architectural, not a policy promise.
projects.how_its_made: AgentKey is a Next.js frontend, a set of Solidity contracts, and a Chainlink CRE TypeScript workflow running inside an AWS Nitro TEE. Contracts (contracts/src/): AgentRegistrar creates each agent as a real ENS subname via ENSRegistry.setSubnodeRecord(), deploying a per-agent AgentTextResolver and AgentVault atomically. The vault becomes the ENS node owner — this is the vault-as-owner pattern that authorizes the vault to write its own policy text records without any separate role grant. AgentVault.onReport() verifies the Chainlink DON threshold signature via KeystoneForwarder.verify() before executing any USDC transfer, then double-checks ENS status at settlement. Reinstatement requires an EIP-712 signature verified against agentLedgerWallet[node] — the stored Ledger wallet address — not ENSRegistry.owner() which returns the vault. CRE Workflow (cre/agentkey-workflow.ts): Registered via cre.handlerInTee with { tee: 'nitro' } on an HTTP trigger. On every agent request it pulls all secrets (RPC URLs, contract addresses) from the CRE Vault DON via runtime.getSecrets() — nothing in source or env. It reads the agent's live policy from ENS, evaluates the three-tier kill switch, and either calls evmClient.writeReport() to settle the transfer or routes a suspension report through AgentVault.onReport() which triggers AgentRegistrar.suspend(). ENS as live policy layer: Every agent's spend limits, whitelist, velocity cap, and status are ENS text records (daily_cap, weekly_cap, whitelist, velocity_max, status, spent_today, agentkey.endpoint) on a per-agent AgentTextResolver. The CRE relayer can only ever call AgentRegistrar.suspend() — hardcoded to write status and suspension_reason only. There is no function surface for CRE to touch caps or whitelist. Ledger integration (app/lib/ledger.ts, components/ledger/): EIP-712 domain and type definitions for CreateAgent and Reinstate match AgentRegistrar._domainSeparator() byte-for-byte. LedgerSign renders each field as a named clear-signing screen. For the demo, a Speculos Ledger emulator runs in Docker; LiveSpeculosScreen.tsx polls the real emulator screenshot at 300ms so judges see the actual device frame during signing. Encrypted credential keyring (app/lib/keyring.ts): Agent JWTs are AES-256-GCM encrypted client-side before being stored as an ENS text record via AgentRegistrar.setEncryptedCredential(). The AES key is derived by signing a fixed EIP-712 KeyringDerivation message with the owner's wallet. The chain only ever sees ciphertext. Write access is gated by the same EIP-712 pattern as reinstatement, with a per-agent nonce for replay protection. The notably interesting design point: ENSRegistry.owner(node) returns the vault address, not the human owner. Reinstatement verification uses agentLedgerWallet[node] — the address stored at agent creation time — so the Ledger wallet check is always against the human, even though the ENS token is held by the contract.

*Ledger integration (app/lib/ledger.ts, components/ledger/):* EIP-712 domain and type definitions for CreateAgent and Reinstate match AgentRegistrar._domainSeparator() byte-for-byte. LedgerSign renders each field as a named clear-signing screen. For the demo, a Speculos Ledger emulator runs in Docker; LiveSpeculosScreen.tsx polls the real emulator screenshot at 300ms so judges see the actual device frame during signing.

*Encrypted credential keyring (app/lib/keyring.ts):* Agent JWTs are AES-256-GCM encrypted client-side before being stored as an ENS text record via AgentRegistrar.setEncryptedCredential(). The AES key is derived by signing a fixed EIP-712 KeyringDerivation message with the owner's wallet. The chain only ever sees ciphertext. Write access is gated by the same EIP-712 pattern as reinstatement, with a per-agent nonce for replay protection.

The notably interesting design point: ENSRegistry.owner(node) returns the vault address, not the human owner. Reinstatement verification uses agentLedgerWallet[node] — the address stored at agent creation time — so the Ledger wallet check is always against the human, even though the ENS token is held by the contract.

projects.title: buildergame
projects.description: A living 3D home for GitHub builders to showcase projects, share progress, and grow together.
projects.project_description: Buildergame gives builders and their projects a place to belong. It transforms public GitHub repositories into a cozy, explorable 3D town, making a portfolio or hackathon community feel like a neighborhood people want to visit again. The idea begins with a simple problem: after demo day, promising projects are easily buried in repository lists. What if following their progress felt like returning to a familiar little town? Every repository has a permanent plot. Five building appearances grow from green land into a furnished garden home, while recorded snapshots let visitors travel through the town's history and see what has changed. Town owners choose the growth values that matter to their community: cumulative commits, stars, a weighted combination of commits/stars/forks, or their own score table. Builders keep the progress they have already earned. Individual developers can create a home for their public projects; hackathon organizers and communities can bring many builders together. Visitors explore flat streets, a valley or cloud neighborhoods, open wooden signs to meet creators, discover projects through the directory and minimap, and follow links to the work itself. Personal and community planning, GitHub data capture, snapshot playback, portable JSON backups, static deployment, and English/Chinese interfaces form the working demo. The broader vision is to turn discovery into lasting participation. We have implemented an optional Privy-powered support extension, starting with native test ETH on Ethereum Sepolia. A personal town can nominate its builder's receiving address; a community can configure a separate recipient for each participating project. In a wallet-enabled deployment, visitors can sign in by email or connect a wallet, review the recipient, network and amount, and explicitly confirm a transfer directly to the builder. The mailbox celebrates only a verified successful chain receipt. Concise notices, acknowledgment, repeat-send guards and pending-transaction recovery support this flow. The sample town demonstrates the playful coin animation; configured towns connect that interaction to builder support. Each creator decides whether to enable wallets for their community. The deployed town, live Privy login, insufficient-funds guard, a human-approved Sepolia transfer with a matching successful receipt, and cancellation before submission are verified. Interrupted session/reload recovery remains unverified and is deferred to the next version. Wallet/ENS identity, community membership and town-management permissions remain future directions. On-chain milestone records could also preserve the relationship between an event, its projects and their continuing progress. Buildergame starts by making creation visible and inviting. It aims to grow into a place where attention, encouragement and community support help builders keep building long after a hackathon ends.
projects.how_its_made: Buildergame uses TypeScript, Three.js 0.180.0, Vite 7.3.6 and Node.js. HTML, CSS and original SVG components create a shared interface of wooden controls, kraft-paper planning sheets, cream project cards and translucent teal panels. The five accepted building appearances were authored with reproducible Blender Python scripts and exported as GLB files. Each has a full-detail and a distant model. The renderer combines instanced distant assets with a bounded number of detailed nearby buildings. Deterministic layout code generates terrain, roads, water and cloud districts from the town's initial roster. All ten building files are protected by SHA-256 checks. Six scoring labels remain for schema compatibility, with the last two sharing the final visual appearance. Repository capture is separate from rendering. Shared GitHub REST transport gathers public repository and builder data, handles pagination, cancellation, timeouts, rate limits and unavailable observations, then stores deliberate snapshots in validated JSON. Personal-access-token connection runs directly in the browser; the token stays in page memory and is excluded from URLs, backups and persistent storage. An optional Node service supports OAuth and owner-checked publication. Town snapshot JSON committed to public/data/towns/ produces physical /towns/<name-and-timestamp>/ pages during the build, supporting static hosting such as Vercel. This keeps project history portable and lets organizers manage it through their own repository. Complete backups can also be imported locally on the deployed site, letting us test recipient-configured towns without publishing test-wallet data in GitHub. Browser storage remembers exploration progress, and an all-land founding snapshot makes the first measured version replayable. Native Web Audio plays six locally hosted Kenney CC0 interface effects. A single lazy HTMLAudioElement loops a supplied Suno track quietly on the planner only and shares the mute control. The submission recording excludes background music. The mailbox prototype combines a Three.js raycast target, contextual coin cursor, animated delivery and a demo receipt to make builder support tangible within the town. The optional support layer uses Privy's React SDK in an on-demand React island, preserving the main TypeScript/Three.js application. Privy's standard Email/Wallet login offers embedded or connected wallets, making wallet onboarding accessible to builders and visitors. The implemented transfer path sends native Sepolia test ETH directly to the configured builder recipient, with no custody contract or platform transaction fee. Personal towns use one recipient; community towns map recipients to repositories. Creator/login notices and a fresh per-transfer acknowledgment precede explicit approval. Recipient addresses are shortened by default with full review and copy available. Critical signing and pending states lock unrelated controls; Web Locks and public localStorage checkpoints coordinate participating tabs on the same origin. Recovery checks the original transaction instead of automatically resending. Receipt sender, destination, value and success checks gate the existing coin animation. Controller and real-React/mock-SDK browser fixtures have passed. Hosted verification covered real login, the low-balance guard, funded review and a human-approved 0.001 test-ETH transfer. The app and Sepolia Etherscan agreed on success, sender, recipient and value. A separate Privy final-preview cancellation submitted no transfer and released the interaction lock; interrupted session/reload recovery remains unverified and is deferred to the next version. ENS identity and community permissions remain on the roadmap. Codex assisted with specifications, research, implementation, Blender authoring scripts, tests and documentation. The human supplied the concept, growth policy, visual references, acceptance of the five building stages and successive interaction revisions.

projects.title: RiskSearcher
projects.description: AI-powered smart contract risk analysis with live onchain data and USDC-gated access.
projects.project_description: RiskSearcher helps users understand whether a smart contract may be dangerous before they interact with it or put funds at risk. A user simply connects with a passkey, pastes an EVM contract address, selects the chain, and starts a scan. RiskSearcher then investigates the contract and presents an easy-to-understand SAFE, UNSAFE, or THREAT verdict, a risk score, and a clear explanation of what it found. Behind that simple workflow, RiskSearcher checks verified source code or bytecode, suspicious contract permissions and functions, transaction behavior, known scam patterns, and live liquidity activity. It also uses an AI specialist and judge to reason across those signals, helping catch risks that a basic rules engine can miss while still showing the evidence behind the final decision. Users can review their previous scans, inspect individual risk findings, view live Uniswap V3 liquidity evidence powered by The Graph, and re-run analyses when needed. New users can claim a Sybil-resistant 3-scan free trial through World Selfie Check, while additional scan credits can be purchased with USDC on Arc Testnet. Passkey authentication makes access passwordless, and scan credits, payment history, and usage are enforced and recorded by the backend. Before this hackathon, RiskSearcher existed as a local CLI-based analysis engine. During ETHOnline, I turned it into a deployed full-stack product with a real web interface, streamed five-stage analysis, user accounts and scan history, The Graph live-data integration, Circle-powered passkey and wallet infrastructure, Arc USDC payments, World ID-based free-trial protection, and server-enforced access control.
projects.how_its_made: RiskSearcher uses a React + Vite frontend deployed on Vercel and a FastAPI backend on Render, with Server-Sent Events streaming analysis progress to the UI. The analysis engine combines Etherscan-verified source code, Alchemy RPC bytecode and transaction data, deterministic Solidity/EVM rules, behavioral transaction analysis, FAISS scam-pattern similarity, and an LLM specialist + judge layer. For live market evidence, The Graph Gateway queries Uniswap V3 liquidity, pool, age, and volume data and feeds that evidence into the AI reasoning pipeline rather than simply displaying it. For user access, Circle Modular Wallets provides WebAuthn/passkey-based ERC-4337 identity, while Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets on Arc Testnet handle real USDC balances and payments. A $5 USDC payment grants 10 scans only after backend confirmation. World Selfie Check is verified server-side and its nullifier is stored in Firestore to enforce one 3-scan free trial per verified human. Firestore also persists entitlements, ledger activity, and scan history, so access control is enforced by the backend rather than trusted frontend state.

projects.title: Nugget
projects.description: Private Period Tracker | Be rewarded for anon participation in decentralised science
projects.project_description:
Video with subtitles for those hard of hearing or non-native english speakers here: https://www.veed.io/view/947cca44-19f4-496c-a5c3-eee37642c23b?source=editor&panel=share Another period cycle tracker, how boring, there's a million of them. But actually they are all terrible (I've tested ALOT! And most sell your data without you even knowing about which is at best annoying and at worst can actually be life threatening.
I never opt in yet somehow my ads just know when I'm ovulating, when i'm pms-ing, which make me even more mad and sad, but at least crying for a reason. Women have only been legally mandated to be included in clinical research testing since 1993! That's younger than Taylor Swift, she was 4 when we officially started trying to understand womens bodies. Complex bodies that create life but we still barely know anything about, so there is a lot of catching up to do! De-sci gives us a unique opportunity now to open source womens data, whilst still protecting women and their data and that is what I set out to build here. The premise of this app to be a privacy preserving period tracker that pays women for their data anonymously and can opensource research on women. Web3(decentralisation) is a good fit, but also I wanted this to be for everyone, and did not want the user to ever have to see transaction, a gas fee, or a seed phrase, except  maybe when they choose to cash out.
Decentralisation is one of the most important parts of this app. Merkle trees and a smart-contract escrow let a contributor's data be used and paid for without that payment ever being traceable back to them. I wanted to take all the good about crypto but abstract it out. So making the UI extremely simple and easy whilst the backend does all the heavy lifting. A user puts in their period cycle information and can choose to either leave it at that, or to allow their data to contribute to research. You must have logged 2 or more cycles to contribute but then you can create a wallet at a push of a button and start waiting for the rewards to come in. Meanwhile a lot is happening on the backend. That period data gets encrypted and sits on supabase in a batch with other contributers data until a buyer requests a report.
At that moment, when the buyer buys the report to show all the aggregated period data, it triggers a sequence  designed so that the user who submitted their period data can get paid without their identity ever being linked to their data The buyer pays into the contract, the contract triggers the
CRE to fetch the encrypted data from supabase,
CRE fetches the current encrypted pool from supabase
CRE decrypts and aggregates it.
CRE identifies the eligible contributors for the relevant payout window.
CRE creates a Merkle root for those wallets.
That root is attached to the buyer’s unique purchase escrow batch.
Each eligible contributor can claim once from that purchase. The buyer gets their data. Contributors get paid. Nobody in between ever sees both halves of that equation at once
projects.how_its_made:
Tech stack: Started with a blank Next.js typescript project and built out from there, using onRender to host and supabase to store the encrypted data (as its way to expensive to store all that onchain). The solidity contract was deployed on Remix. On the frontend, contributors log cycle data locally and can choose to contribute only an encrypted summary to the shared pool. The buyer side report purchases are funded on Sepolia.
Privy embedded wallets, which lets the app handle wallet creation and transaction signing without requiring a traditional crypto-native onboarding flow are used for the full financial flow. Chainlink has a lot to do. The core privacy boundary is implemented in Chainlink CRE: the buyer report runs as a confidential workflow inside a TEE, where it retrieves an enclave-only secret, decrypts the encrypted contribution batch, validates records, enforces k-anonymity thresholds, computes only public aggregate statistics, and derives the eligible reward wallet set plus a Merkle root for payout claims. That Merkle root is then settled into the escrow flow so contributors can claim rewards onchain with a wallet address and proof, while the raw period data never needs to leave the confidential execution path.
Privy wallets remove the wallet friction from the flow. I wanted to abstract the crypto/web3 completely out, the backend  tech can speak for itself it what its allowing people to do with it. For the contributor who gives their data, I wanted that they wouldnt even know it was crypto until they were ready to offramp, however as I couldnt find out if Privy support gas sponsorship payments on testnet I couldnt put that in the demo, however if ever live that is what we would do, with the cost being covered by the buyer money from the pool. Contract address: 0xf0344b5768BB2796D32E16523EF2d47D11F71a68
