projects.title: MelodyPay
projects.description: Air-gapped hardware wallet for sending EVM payments securely over sound.
projects.project_description: MelodyPay : Air-Gapped Acoustic Hardware Wallet MelodyPay is an air-gapped payment system that replaces QR codes, NFC, and Bluetooth with sound. A merchant's phone plays an audio invoice. A custom offline hardware wallet hears it, shows the payment details on screen, and waits for a physical button press before signing anything. The signed authorization plays back as audio, the receiver's web terminal picks it up, and transaction settles on-chain seconds later. No gas token needed on the customer's end, no internet connection required on the wallet's end. The problem: every existing in-person crypto payment method has a hole in it. QR codes can be overlaid or spoofed and need good lighting and a clean camera. NFC needs special reader hardware and is vulnerable to relay attacks. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi bring a whole software stack's worth of remote exploits along with them. And most flows still assume the customer is holding gas tokens and has a live data connection at checkout, which is where a lot of transactions quietly fail. Here's how MelodyPay avoids all of that: Acoustic transport: Payloads move as FSK-modulated audio via ggwave , no radios involved. Reed-Solomon error correction handles noisy environments, and a simple framed protocol (64-byte frames, 300ms silence between bursts) keeps the two sides in sync. The hardware wallet: A custom ESP32-S3 board with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth stripped out at compile time, so there's no radio stack to exploit even in theory. Signing requires a physical button on a GPIO interrupt, not a software command, so nothing can trigger a signature remotely. Every transaction is shown in full on a small OLED screen before signing: amount, recipient, nonce, no hidden fields. Gasless settlement. The wallet signs EIP-712 authorizations under EIP-3009 (ReceiveWithAuthorization) for USDC on Arc Testnet. The merchant's terminal submits the transaction and covers gas, so the customer never needs a gas token or a live connection. Merchant identity. Merchants register a subname like cafe.melodypay.eth through a custom registrar contract on Sepolia. The web terminal resolves it to a checksummed address via Viem and shows both before generating an invoice, and pulls routing config from ENS text records instead of a centralized API. The terminal. A browser-based PWA using the Web Audio API, so any phone or laptop becomes a POS terminal with no app install and no private key on the merchant's side. A companion CLI (built with terminui) gives real-time balance monitoring across chains and diagnostics for connected wallets.
projects.how_its_made: MelodyPay sends payments as sound instead of over a network. ggwave handles FSK modulation across carrier tones between 1875 Hz and 2187 Hz, with both the ESP32-S3 firmware and the browser's Web Audio API locked so the two sides stay in sync. Every packet carries Reed-Solomon error correction, so demodulation holds up even in a noisy room. Packets are framed as fixed 64-byte blocks, sent in chunks with 300ms of silence between bursts so transmitting and listening never overlap. A full transaction is four messages: the wallet announces its address, the receiver terminal broadcasts the invoice (chain ID, recipient, amount, expiry, nonce), the wallet broadcasts the signed authorization once the button is pressed, and the terminal confirms the on-chain settlement back to the wallet. On the hardware side, the ESP32-S3's two cores split by function : Core 0 handles I2S DMA audio and FSK synthesis in real time, Core 1 handles crypto, the keystore, button debouncing, and the OLED. The mic, amp, and display run on I2S and I2C, and the confirmation button sits on a dedicated GPIO interrupt. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are disabled in sdkconfig , so the drivers never make it into the compiled binary : there's no radio stack on the device to attack. For settlement, we implemented EIP-3009's ReceiveWithAuthorization against Arc Testnet's USDC contract. Since there's no Web3 library for a microcontroller, we wrote our own EIP-712 signer in C: it encodes the authorization struct, hashes it with an embedded Keccak-256, and signs it using Trezor-crypto's secp256k1. The wallet signs entirely offline; the merchant's terminal submits the transaction and covers the gas. For merchant identity, we deployed a custom ENSv2 subname registrar on Sepolia, so merchants register names like cafe.melodypay.eth instead of showing a raw address. The terminal resolves the name via Viem, reads routing config from ENS text records, and shows both the name and the checksummed address before generating an invoice. On security: payloads never carry keys or credentials, and each authorization has a random nonce with a 60-second expiry, so a recorded chime is useless once it lapses. Replay is blocked three ways : the contract marks each nonce used on-chain, the receiver keeps its own dedup table, and expired authorizations are rejected before either check runs. There's no radio stack in the firmware, so there's no wireless attack surface at all. The firmware only parses native transfers or EIP-3009 structs, so blind signing of arbitrary calldata isn't possible, and the full amount and recipient always render on the OLED from RAM. Signing only runs after a real hardware interrupt from the button, so no software or serial command can trigger it. And the serial protocol only exposes capability status and chain config , nothing in the firmware can read or export a key. A few build details worth mentioning: the mic and speaker sit close together on the same board, so we added a squelch routine that mutes the mic's DMA channel during transmission and unmutes it with a short decay buffer after, keeping the speaker's own output out of the mic. The operator CLI talks to the hardware over raw USB serial at 115200 baud, built with terminui instead of a heavier framework, with private keys never touching the serial line.

projects.title: RedFlag_Trail
projects.description: See what AI agents spend on x402 — and block risky payments in the wallet before they're signed.
projects.project_description: RedFlag_Trail is built as a live pipeline across three partner integrations. The Graph: a Substreams package ("papertrail") composes the official x402 module with erc20-tokens, streaming live Base mainnet payments into a Postgres ledger via substreams-sink-sql. Token decimals are sourced by batched eth_call since no prebuilt package carries them. Vendors are enriched against the live ERC-8004/Agent0 subgraph on Base to check registry status. Privy: wallet policies are default-deny, with an explicit ALLOW scoped to Base (chainId 8453) plus a DENY rule per flagged vendor, keyed on the EIP-3009 to field inside eth_signTypedData_v4's typed-data message — never on tx.from or eth_sendTransaction, since the agent never calls the latter. Human approval is a real 2-of-2 Privy key quorum: we implemented the full authorization-signature spec by hand (RFC 8785 canonical JSON → SHA-256 → ECDSA P-256 → DER → base64), since Privy's docs don't give a worked example. Privy itself refuses unsigned and 1-of-2-signed policy changes — the quorum is enforced server-side, not by our app. Bazantic: we published a Recipe ("agent-spend-audit") on a gateway serving live x402 402-challenges, and ran a controlled A/B test — same model, same tools, the Recipe as the only variable — showing it drives the agent to cite 13 verifiable transaction hashes versus zero, and add honesty guardrails (nothing-enforced disclosure, human-quorum requirement, unpriced≠zero, heuristic confidence) that the raw API spec alone doesn't produce. A backtest engine (lib/backtest.mjs) replays any proposed rule over indexed history before it can be approved, flagging vendors with many independent payers as false positives. An MCP server exposes 5 tools (spend_summary, vendor_risk, list_findings, backtest_rule, propose_enforcement) so any agent framework can call the same audit. A review console and REST API sit on top for human operators. Everything is reproducible end-to-end with one command: node scripts/e2e-demo.mjs .

Bazantic: we published a Recipe ("agent-spend-audit") on a gateway serving live x402 402-challenges, and ran a controlled A/B test — same model, same tools, the Recipe as the only variable — showing it drives the agent to cite 13 verifiable transaction hashes versus zero, and add honesty guardrails (nothing-enforced disclosure, human-quorum requirement, unpriced≠zero, heuristic confidence) that the raw API spec alone doesn't produce.

A backtest engine (lib/backtest.mjs) replays any proposed rule over indexed history before it can be approved, flagging vendors with many independent payers as false positives. An MCP server exposes 5 tools (spend_summary, vendor_risk, list_findings, backtest_rule, propose_enforcement) so any agent framework can call the same audit. A review console and REST API sit on top for human operators. Everything is reproducible end-to-end with one command: `node scripts/e2e-demo.mjs`.

projects.title: Stavlos
projects.description: Simulation-only DeFi yield analytics for cross-chain stablecoin lending, with risk-adjusted yields.
projects.project_description: Stavlos is an institutional-grade, simulation-only DeFi yield analytics platform designed to analyze and optimize cross-chain stablecoin lending opportunities. It tracks stablecoins such as USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS, and USDe across major DeFi protocols including Aave, Compound, Morpho, and Spark. The platform ingests yield and protocol data from DeFiLlama, validates and normalizes the data, filters pools based on liquidity and stability criteria, and stores historical yield observations in an idempotent SQLite time-series database. The core of Stavlos is a quantitative risk-scoring engine that risk-adjusts nominal APYs using multiple factors, including TVL/liquidity depth, protocol age, APY volatility, blockchain security tiers, and bridge friction. It provides deterministic risk grades and plain-English explanations so users can understand why a particular lending pool receives its score. A historical backtesting engine then simulates capital rotation between opportunities while accounting for gas costs, bridge fees, minimum holding periods, slippage, and churn penalties, allowing strategies to be compared against a static benchmark. The project also includes a FastAPI analytical backend and a Next.js dashboard with sortable pool rankings, historical APY charts, quantitative audit information, and interactive 180-day backtest visualizations. An advisory alerting system monitors sudden TVL contractions, abnormal APY increases, and risk-grade changes and can dispatch alerts through console, database, or webhook channels. Stavlos is deliberately non-custodial and simulation-only: it does not contain private keys, request transaction signatures, or broadcast transactions. Its Web3 integration is read-only, using standard JSON-RPC calls to inspect stablecoin balances across multiple chains and compare idle wallet assets with risk-adjusted lending opportunities. Overall, the project combines data engineering, quantitative finance, DeFi analytics, backtesting, Web3 infrastructure, and full-stack development into a single production-oriented research platform.
projects.how_its_made: Stavlos was built as a modular Python + Next.js system, with a strong focus on quantitative analysis, data reliability, and non-custodial Web3 architecture. The backend is written in Python using FastAPI, Pydantic, Pandas, NumPy, and SQLite. The frontend uses Next.js 14 with the App Router and Recharts to provide an interactive analytics dashboard. The data pipeline starts with DeFiLlama’s yields API, accessed through an HTTPX-based ingestion client with Tenacity-powered retries and jittered exponential backoff. Incoming pool data is validated and normalized with Pydantic, filtered for supported stablecoins and sufficient TVL, deduplicated, and persisted into a WAL-enabled SQLite time-series database through an idempotent repository layer. On top of this data layer, I built a deterministic risk-scoring engine that applies penalties for TVL, protocol age, APY volatility, chain security, and bridge friction. A historical backtesting engine then replays multi-month yield data and simulates portfolio rotation while accounting for gas costs, bridge fees, slippage, minimum holding periods, and churn penalties. The results are exposed through FastAPI and visualized in the Next.js dashboard. The Web3 layer uses Viem and standard EIP-1193/JSON-RPC eth_call requests to inspect stablecoin balances across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, and Sepolia. The integration deliberately has no private keys, signing, or transaction broadcasting, making the system fully read-only and non-custodial. A particularly notable engineering choice was keeping the entire strategy simulation deterministic and auditable rather than simply ranking APYs. The platform can explain why a yield is considered attractive, replay historical decisions, calculate net performance after realistic friction, and generate advisory alerts for TVL contractions, APY spikes, and risk-grade changes. This turns raw DeFi yield data into an end-to-end research, risk, simulation, and monitoring pipeline.

projects.title: TradeLayer
projects.description: TradeLayer: confidential institutional stock trading, unifying TradFi and on-chain liquidity.
projects.project_description:
Gitbook Link: https://helix-5.gitbook.io/tradelayer
PPT Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B3c3GfzceXX_N0WlIDR1r_Dim4UsEvAJ/view?usp=drive_link
vimeo Link for hedera video: https://vimeo.com/1226332274?share=copy&fl=sv&fe=ci Institutional money doesn't trade in the open — and on-chain, right now, it has no choice. Every tokenized-stock platform that exists today writes a firm's entire position, order size, and identity onto a public ledger the moment they touch it. Front-running bots watch every mempool. Competitors reconstruct a strategy that took months to build within seconds of the first transaction. The only fix the industry has offered so far is a centralized middleman: hand your order to a company's server, let them execute it off-chain, and take their word that nobody looked. That's not privacy — it's a company asking to be trusted, with no way to check. TradeLayer is the confidential trading desk that lets institutions buy and sell real-world stocks with crypto without any of that exposure. An order is sealed the instant it's created and is only ever opened inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow — logic that runs inside a hardware-isolated enclave, not on a company server. This is the piece that makes the whole product possible: the enclave is the only place, anywhere in the system, where an order is ever readable, and Chainlink's network releases the keys to unlock it only after proving that enclave hasn't been tampered with. Nobody — not a bot, not a competitor, not even TradeLayer — ever sees the order in the clear. The stocks themselves are issued as real, compliant tokens through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio — which is what makes the privacy safe rather than reckless. KYC, wallet freezing, and transfer restrictions are enforced by the token itself, not by a policy someone has to trust. An institution can instantly lock a compromised wallet, guarantee that only verified accounts ever hold its shares, and prove every token is fully backed by a real share at a real broker — all without a single order, quantity, or trade ever being visible on-chain. Compliance and confidentiality aren't in tension here; ATS is what lets us give institutions both at once. That solves the other half of the problem too: institutions sitting on crypto-native capital are today locked out of markets that don't touch crypto at all. TradeLayer is the execution layer that bridges both worlds — real, regulated markets and on-chain liquidity — at blockchain speed, without asking institutions to give up the privacy or compliance they've always required to trade at size. As tokenized real-world assets move from experiment to infrastructure, privacy and enforceable compliance stop being separate asks — an institution needs both to actually show up on-chain. TradeLayer, built on Hedera's tokenization and compliance primitives, is designed to be that missing piece.
projects.how_its_made: TradeLayer is a full-stack confidential trading system spanning a Hedera settlement layer, a Chainlink CRE confidential compute layer, and a real brokerage for genuine market execution — wired together so that no single component ever sees a complete, plaintext trade. An order starts life sealed client-side, encrypted before it ever leaves the browser. It's picked up by our backend intake API and dispatched into a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow — TypeScript logic running inside an AWS Nitro hardware enclave. Three handlers do the real work there: one opens and validates a sealed order against an institution's encrypted trading rules, one reconciles fills as they come back from the broker, and one runs on a timer to net every institution's fills per stock symbol into a single batched settlement — the mechanism that keeps individual trades from being reconstructable on-chain. Chainlink's Vault DON releases the enclave's decryption keys only after remote attestation, so the keys that matter never exist outside a verified enclave. On the Hedera side, we issue tokenized equities through the Asset Tokenization Studio, so KYC, freezing, and transfer restrictions are enforced by the token itself rather than by our own policy layer. Our custom contracts — OrgWalletRegistry, ComplianceRouter, OrderEscrow, OmnibusVault, and ConfidentialLedger — handle mutual-consent onboarding, per-institution compliance isolation, and an encrypted balance/positions ledger that only the enclave can ever decrypt. Buy-side escrow uses Hedera's native HIP-1215 scheduled transactions so an abandoned order refunds itself automatically, with no off-chain keeper needed. The genuinely hacky part: the enclave never submits directly to Hedera. Instead it signs an EIP-712 struct, and a separate relayer submits that struct on-chain, where the contract recovers the signature. That split means the relayer can censor a transaction but can never read an order or forge a settlement — a small architectural trick that buys a meaningful trust boundary for free. We also built our order-sealing crypto so the exact same routines run in the browser and inside the enclave, letting us test both sides against a shared vector suite instead of trusting two independent implementations to agree.

projects.title: incepSON
projects.description: IncepSON which is an autonomous LLM agent can *request* payments. It can never *authorize* them.
projects.project_description:
Every payment an agent asks for passes through a deterministic policy engine
plain TypeScript, no language model, no I/O - that resolves the request to
exactly one of three outcomes: ALLOW- small, in-budget, allowlisted. Settles over x402 on Hedera testnet, autonomously.
ESCALATE - legal but worth a human's attention. Suspended until a physical button is pressed on an ESP32.
DENY- breaches a hard limit. Refused unconditionally. No appeal.
projects.how_its_made:
AgentPay/IncepSON is built on three honest boundaries. The agent (OpenAI tool-calling loop) has one tool: request_payment(service, amount, reason). Module structure, a grep check, and a unit test together ensure it has no import path to payments/x402.ts  the only file allowed to touch the x402 client. That boundary isn't convention; it's enforced.
Every request hits a pure TypeScript policy engine  no I/O, no network, no LLM, clock injected so it's testable with a frozen timestamp. Evaluation order is itself a security property: hard denials (allowlist → per-transaction limit → rolling 24h aggregate budget) before escalation signals. A request that's both anomalous and over-budget is denied, never escalated  a human can't be socially-engineered into approving something the policy already forbids.
Payments settle over x402 on Hedera testnet through the public x402.org facilitator (no API key). The client registers Hedera's exact scheme via @x402/hedera, and the merchant process returns a genuine HTTP 402  faking it in-process would make the demo a lie.
The ESP32 escalation path was the trickiest piece. The device polls GET /device/pending every 2s (outbound, no port forwarding on venue WiFi), recomputes the HMAC locally before rendering anything, and refuses to arm the button on a mismatch. A pinned cross-language HMAC test vector guards the wire format between the Node backend and the Arduino firmware. One notable gotcha: HEDERA_KEY_TYPE must match the account's actual on-chain key type — a mismatch signs silently but fails facilitator verification with no client-side error.

projects.title: Copywrite
projects.description: Prove you made it first, backed by a verified human and ENSv2.
projects.project_description: Copywrite is a creator authenticity registry: prove you made a piece of content first, as a real unique human. Social platforms have no portable way to attribute who created media first. Copies are easy — AI tools can recompress or lightly edit files to dodge naive duplicate filters — and any registry without identity gating is sybil-gamed by bots racing to claim content. Copywrite combines two sponsor primitives: World ID Selfie Check :- registration stays locked until the creator verifies as a real, unique human, so disposable wallets cannot mass-claim media. ENSv2-style naming :- creators get a portable identity like alice.copywrite.eth; each registered file gets a content subname (post-<hash>.alice.copywrite.eth) with perceptual hash, timestamp, origin URL, and license. Claims are non-transferable and owner-revocable. Anyone can use the public Authenticity Checker to upload an image or paste a URL and see whether it is already claimed, by whom, and when. Near-duplicates are blocked via perceptual hashing (Hamming distance), so lightly edited copies cannot sneak in as “new” content.
projects.how_its_made: Copywrite is a Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind app with a Foundry/Solidity claims layer. Identity / World: We integrate @worldcoin/idkit Selfie Check on the creator dashboard. The client prepares a signed RP request via POST /api/worldid/sign, the user completes Selfie Check in IDKit, and POST /api/worldid/verify forwards the proof to World’s verify API. A server-side HMAC cookie gates registration so unverified wallets cannot claim. Optionally POST /api/operator/sync-verified marks the wallet verified on-chain. ENS / claims: ContentProofClaims.sol (Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry tests) models creator labels and content claims mirroring ENSv2 hierarchy (alice.copywrite.eth / post-<hash>.alice.copywrite.eth): unique labels, non-transferable claims, owner-only revoke, and a verified-human gate. The frontend uses wagmi/viem + RainbowKit on Sepolia; @ensdomains/ensjs is in the stack for ENS naming. Naming and access-control semantics are designed for ENSv2 Permissioned Registry / Resolver wiring. Detection: Uploads are fingerprinted with sharp + blockhash-core (perceptual hash). POST /api/check finds near-matches (Hamming ≤ 10). POST /api/register rejects duplicates after the World gate, then upserts Prisma/Postgres; POST /api/revoke is owner-only. The checker UI is public; the dashboard lists claims and supports revoke.

projects.title: Agent Bazaar
projects.description: An AI agent that discovers, pays for, and rates APIs on its own across Hedera and Arc testnets.
projects.project_description:
Agent Bazaar is a working two-sided marketplace where AI agents buy and sell services
from each other with no human in the loop. Two seller agents each run a real API behind an HTTP 402 paywall. "Bazaar Market Intel"
sells DEX pool risk briefs and settles in USDC on Hedera testnet. "Bazaar Task Runner"
sells summarisation and risk classification and settles in USDC on Arc testnet via
Circle Gateway nanopayments. Both hold real ERC-8004 identities on Base Sepolia (agents
#9179 and #9180) and publish their priced route catalogs in their registration files. A buyer agent, powered by Claude, is given a task and a hard USD budget. It queries The
Graph's Agent0 subgraphs to discover who is selling what — there is no central
directory, so discovery genuinely has no other path. It finds our two sellers alongside
14 other unrelated public agents, ranks them on price, reputation and validations, pays
the winner over x402 on whichever rail that seller uses, then posts a signed review back
to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry. Those reviews are real on-chain transactions, and
they change how the next run ranks the same seller. The reputation loop closes. Nothing is mocked or seeded. Roughly $44 USDC has settled across both rails in live
testnet transactions, with individual purchases of $0.50 to $2.00. Current seller
reputation — 71/100 and 86/100 — was earned entirely from the buyer agent's own
feedback calls. The public dashboard shows the marketplace, the agent's live decision log as it reasons,
every settled payment with explorer links, and a seller view with real withdrawable
balances.
projects.how_its_made:
A pnpm monorepo: two seller services, one buyer agent, a Next.js dashboard, and shared
packages for Graph access, ERC-8004 identity, and chain config. The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative. Discovery is a single query across the Agent0
(ERC-8004) subgraphs on Base Sepolia and Ethereum Sepolia — one query, both chains — and
there is no fallback directory, so without it the buyer agent cannot find anyone. The
sellers' pool briefs are built on the Messari Standardized DEX-AMM schema
(liquidityPools, inputTokens, fees, liquidityPoolDailySnapshots), so the same query runs
unchanged against any Messari DEX subgraph. The buyer also has a graph_query tool that
pays The Graph's x402 gateway per query with no API key. Payments use the x402 standard on both rails. Hedera settles through @x402/hedera and
the Blocky402 facilitator; Arc settles through @circle-fin/x402-batching against Circle
Gateway. One notable gotcha: Circle's Gateway deposit balance is a separate pool from
the native wallet balance, so payments fail with a full wallet until you explicitly
deposit. Arc also uses USDC as its native gas token, which means a small withdrawal can
cost more in gas than the amount withdrawn. The buyer agent is a Vercel AI SDK tool loop with seven hand-built tools. Budget safety
is enforced in code, never by the model: BudgetLedger.reserve() throws before any tool
touches the network, so an over-budget purchase is refused rather than trusted not to
happen. I also integrated the official @hashgraph/hedera-agent-kit so the agent verifies
its real on-chain HBAR balance before committing — the ledger is a policy cap, not proof
the wallet can settle. I deliberately registered only the read-only account query plugin:
the kit's transfer and mint tools would call the Hedera SDK directly and bypass that cap
entirely, and there is a test asserting no fund-moving tool is ever registered. Three bugs worth mentioning. Feedback kept reverting with ERC721NonexistentToken because
the agent passed the payment rail as the identity registry chain — a Hedera-rail seller
still registers identity on Base Sepolia; I decoded the selector via 4byte to find it.
Each Railway service has its own ephemeral disk, so the buyer's JSONL decision log was
invisible to the dashboard; both now share a Postgres table, which is what makes the live
agent view work. And mid-build, the sole indexer serving the base-sepolia Agent0 subgraph
went offline and returned "bad indexers: Unavailable" for every query, blanking all
reputation. Since the subgraph only indexes the ERC-8004 contracts, I added a fallback
that reads the ReputationRegistry directly over RPC — discovering that getSummary reverts
on an empty client list, that public RPCs cap eth_getLogs at 10,000 blocks, and that too
narrow a scan window silently under-counts (a 60k-block scan found 3 of 6 reviews and
reported the wrong average).
projects.project_description_markdown:
Agent Bazaar is a working two-sided marketplace where AI agents buy and sell services
from each other with no human in the loop.

Two seller agents each run a real API behind an HTTP 402 paywall. "Bazaar Market Intel"
sells DEX pool risk briefs and settles in USDC on Hedera testnet. "Bazaar Task Runner"
sells summarisation and risk classification and settles in USDC on Arc testnet via
Circle Gateway nanopayments. Both hold real ERC-8004 identities on Base Sepolia (agents
#9179 and #9180) and publish their priced route catalogs in their registration files.

A buyer agent, powered by Claude, is given a task and a hard USD budget. It queries The
Graph's Agent0 subgraphs to discover who is selling what — there is no central
directory, so discovery genuinely has no other path. It finds our two sellers alongside
14 other unrelated public agents, ranks them on price, reputation and validations, pays
the winner over x402 on whichever rail that seller uses, then posts a signed review back
to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry. Those reviews are real on-chain transactions, and
they change how the next run ranks the same seller. The reputation loop closes.

Nothing is mocked or seeded. Roughly $44 USDC has settled across both rails in live
testnet transactions, with individual purchases of $0.50 to $2.00. Current seller
reputation — 71/100 and 86/100 — was earned entirely from the buyer agent's own
feedback calls.

The public dashboard shows the marketplace, the agent's live decision log as it reasons,
every settled payment with explorer links, and a seller view with real withdrawable
balances.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
A pnpm monorepo: two seller services, one buyer agent, a Next.js dashboard, and shared
packages for Graph access, ERC-8004 identity, and chain config.

The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative. Discovery is a single query across the Agent0
(ERC-8004) subgraphs on Base Sepolia and Ethereum Sepolia — one query, both chains — and
there is no fallback directory, so without it the buyer agent cannot find anyone. The
sellers' pool briefs are built on the Messari Standardized DEX-AMM schema
(liquidityPools, inputTokens, fees, liquidityPoolDailySnapshots), so the same query runs
unchanged against any Messari DEX subgraph. The buyer also has a graph_query tool that
pays The Graph's x402 gateway per query with no API key.

Payments use the x402 standard on both rails. Hedera settles through @x402/hedera and
the Blocky402 facilitator; Arc settles through @circle-fin/x402-batching against Circle
Gateway. One notable gotcha: Circle's Gateway deposit balance is a separate pool from
the native wallet balance, so payments fail with a full wallet until you explicitly
deposit. Arc also uses USDC as its native gas token, which means a small withdrawal can
cost more in gas than the amount withdrawn.

The buyer agent is a Vercel AI SDK tool loop with seven hand-built tools. Budget safety
is enforced in code, never by the model: BudgetLedger.reserve() throws before any tool
touches the network, so an over-budget purchase is refused rather than trusted not to
happen. I also integrated the official @hashgraph/hedera-agent-kit so the agent verifies
its real on-chain HBAR balance before committing — the ledger is a policy cap, not proof
the wallet can settle. I deliberately registered only the read-only account query plugin:
the kit's transfer and mint tools would call the Hedera SDK directly and bypass that cap
entirely, and there is a test asserting no fund-moving tool is ever registered.

Three bugs worth mentioning. Feedback kept reverting with ERC721NonexistentToken because
the agent passed the payment rail as the identity registry chain — a Hedera-rail seller
still registers identity on Base Sepolia; I decoded the selector via 4byte to find it.
Each Railway service has its own ephemeral disk, so the buyer's JSONL decision log was
invisible to the dashboard; both now share a Postgres table, which is what makes the live
agent view work. And mid-build, the sole indexer serving the base-sepolia Agent0 subgraph
went offline and returned "bad indexers: Unavailable" for every query, blanking all
reputation. Since the subgraph only indexes the ERC-8004 contracts, I added a fallback
that reads the ReputationRegistry directly over RPC — discovering that getSummary reverts
on an empty client list, that public RPCs cap eth_getLogs at 10,000 blocks, and that too
narrow a scan window silently under-counts (a 60k-block scan found 3 of 6 reviews and
reported the wrong average).

projects.title: Nymspace
projects.description: ENS-backed architecture for AI swarms enforcing financial guardrails and dynamic access control.
projects.project_description:
Nymspace is an identity and permission console for organizations running AI agents. As teams delegate more work to agents, they need clear answers to three questions: Who does this agent belong to? What is it allowed to change? How much authority should it have over funds?
Nymspace starts with an ENS name. An organization manages agents as subnames such as research.nymspace.eth, trader.nymspace.eth, and deploy.nymspace.eth. Each name provides a discoverable identity with records describing the agent and its endpoints. Organizations can delegate permission to update a specific record while retaining control over sensitive identity information and the ability to revoke access.
The console brings together ENS identity management, ERC-8004 agent discovery through The Graph, AI-assisted candidate ranking, and Privy wallets with transaction amount policies. Operators can inspect agents, discover external candidates, manage delegated permissions, and see whether a payment is allowed or denied.
Our testnet implementation demonstrates these boundaries with real integrations: an agent controller can update its MCP endpoint but cannot rewrite its organization-controlled identity binding, and a wallet can execute a payment within its policy while rejecting an over-limit request. Nymspace makes agent authority visible, narrowly scoped, and revocable.
projects.how_its_made:
We started with the smallest permission we wanted to demonstrate: let an agent change one record on its own name. That led us to ENSv2’s PermissionedResolver on Sepolia. Using viem, we grant SET_TEXT against a resource derived from the agent’s namehash and a specific record key. The controller can update agent-endpoint[mcp], but the same controller is refused when it tries to change agent-context or the ENSIP-25 registration binding. The boundary is enforced by the resolver contract. The organization keeps the parent authority needed to revoke the grant or reclaim the subname.
We then connected the naming layer to ERC-8004 registrations on Base Sepolia, with runtime verification of the ENSIP-25 binding. This gives discovery a connection back to an organization-controlled ENS identity. For discovery, The Graph’s Agent0 subgraph supplies the candidate data. Our server applies hard filters, then Gemini 2.5 Flash orders the remaining candidates and returns reasons with field citations. A validator checks that each ranked agent came from the candidate set and that its cited fields exist. Missing reputation data stays missing. This separation gives the model a useful but bounded job and makes part of its output mechanically checkable.
Privy handles server wallets and enforces the transaction amount policy. We exercise an allowed payment and an over-limit request against the same policy, so the demo shows both execution and refusal. The application is a TypeScript monorepo built with pnpm and Turborepo: Next.js, React, and Astryx for the console; Hono for the API; and PostgreSQL with Drizzle for coordination data and activity records. It runs on Railway. One unusual detail is how we collect proof. Successful onchain actions produce transaction hashes. A payment rejected before broadcast should produce none. Our live acceptance gates check both kinds of outcome, including unauthorized record writes and revoked permissions. Building those checks forced us to make “the agent cannot do this” as concrete as “the agent can do this.

projects.title: Aegis
projects.description: The safe execution layer for agentic payments: MEV free batch settlement, run by an agent
projects.project_description: Agents can move money now. The problem is that every payment an agent makes onchain is mempool-visible before it lands, which means bots can front-run it. Aegis is the payment infrastructure that fixes this. Users and agents submit payment intents. Aegis pools them into a batch and settles at a single uniform clearing price. There is nothing to front-run because no individual order is visible until the whole batch settles. The price is computed from three independent oracle networks (Chainlink, Pyth, API3) with dynamic weighting, so there is nothing to manipulate either. The Solver Agent drives the entire lifecycle autonomously. It reads live batch state from a The Graph subgraph, collects oracle prices from Chainlink Data Feeds, matches orders internally, routes uncrossed liquidity to 1inch Aqua, and settles onchain in native USDC via the Circle Agent Stack. No human turns any crank. Remove the agent and nothing settles. This is a Continuity submission. Aegis V3, a live verified batch settlement engine on Sepolia with multi-oracle dynamic weighting, existed before ETHOnline. At the hackathon we replaced mock oracles with live Chainlink, Pyth and API3 feeds, upgraded to real two-asset WETH/USDC swap execution in AegisV4, built the Graph subgraph the agent depends on, and shipped the Solver Agent on the Circle Agent Stack with USDC settlement verified on both Sepolia and Arc testnet. AegisV4 is live and verified on Sepolia at 0x0a16364229EeFDA44332cB6D194E20937C51CE5b. Native USDC settlement is proven on Arc testnet (chain 5042002). Evidence is in agent/settlement-evidence.sepolia.json and agent/settlement-evidence.arc.json.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is Scaffold-ETH 2 with Hardhat, ethers v6, Next.js, Wagmi and Viem. The core contract is AegisV4.sol, a permissionless 4-phase batch settlement engine forked from the pre-existing AegisV3 and extended with real two-asset swap economics (WETH base, USDC quote) and provably-solvent fill accounting. The Solver Agent is TypeScript with Vitest and 20 unit tests green. Chainlink powers the price layer. The existing contract already used the Chainlink latestRoundData() interface, so replacing five MockOracle contracts with the live ETH/USD Data Feed (0x694AA1769357215DE4FAC081bf1f309aDC325306, stack 1), a PythOracleAdapter (stack 2) and an API3OracleAdapter (stack 3) was close to a drop-in. Each adapter exposes the same latestRoundData() surface at 8-decimal scale. Dynamic confidence weighting picks the most reliable reading per batch. The API3 proxy is verified live at roughly $2,460 on Sepolia. The Graph is the agent's data source. A subgraph in subgraph/ indexes all seven AegisV4 events including BatchCreated, Deposited, OraclePriceCollected, OracleWeightUpdated and BatchSettled into five entities. The Solver Agent queries it for live batch phase and oracle state on every tick. A direct contract read fallback activates when the subgraph is unavailable, so the agent never stalls. Circle and Arc handle settlement. The Solver Agent routes all write transactions through a Circle developer-controlled wallet using createContractExecutionTransaction. It drives every permissionless phase transition automatically. 5 USDC settled agent to counterparty on Sepolia and again on Arc testnet (chain 5042002, native USDC gas). The Circle wallet (0xd503dd91837dde9fb7d96628acfdae45058c57fd, state LIVE) is verified via yarn circle:verify. 1inch Aqua is integrated but not submitted due to the 3-track limit. AquaRouter.sol forwards uncrossed batch remainder to the official 1inch SwapVM entrypoint at 0x111111338c5091E8440b67B168bAe16a668AC0De. It is fork-tested against a MockAqua with the money path deterministically covered. The part worth highlighting: the Solver Agent's decideAction() core is a pure function. Given batch state and block number it returns the next action with zero side effects. This made it possible to exhaustively unit test all phase-transition edge cases before touching any onchain code, and then plug the same function into the live executor unchanged.

projects.title: Hush Protocol
projects.description: Send USDC to a @username on Arc. A ZK proof breaks the on-chain link between deposit and withdraw.
projects.project_description: The repo is a monorepo built in strict dependency order: contracts, then the ZK circuit, then a shared proof SDK, then the indexer, backend and frontend. Contracts. Solidity 0.8.28 on Hardhat with OpenZeppelin. BulletPool holds funds, verifies proofs, tracks spent nullifiers permanently, and carries an embedded token registry, plus Ownable2Step, ReentrancyGuard and pause. MerkleRootManager keeps a rolling window of 64 accepted roots so a withdraw must prove against a root the chain has seen. The verifier is swappable, so we ship a mock during development and drop in the snarkjs-exported WithdrawVerifier after the ceremony. ZK. One circuit, written in Circom with circomlib Poseidon, Groth16 over BN254. Deposit needs no circuit. The statement is that the prover knows a secret where nullifier = Poseidon1([secret]) and commitment = Poseidon4([secret, recipientDigest, amount, tokenHash]) is a leaf under the public root, with depth-20 Poseidon2 membership. Public input order is locked to [root, nullifier, recipientDigest, amount, tokenHash]. Because the digest, amount and token are bound inside the commitment, a watcher cannot front-run a withdraw and redirect or inflate it without the secret. SDK. A TypeScript package (circomlibjs, snarkjs) owns secrets, commitments, nullifiers, Merkle math and proof encoding, including the G2 limb endian swap snarkjs needs for the Solidity verifier. The indexer and frontend both link it via pnpm, so the tree built server-side and the proof built client-side cannot drift apart. No ad-hoc crypto in the UI.
projects.how_its_made: Public chains leave a visible trail. Every transfer writes a permanent sender to recipient edge that anyone can follow, which makes salaries, donations, remittances and contractor payments uncomfortable when the relationship itself should stay private. Hush is a ZK-private payment rail on Arc Testnet. It works as a shielded note pool: The sender picks a recipient by @username or X handle, and the app resolves it to a wallet and an encryption key. The SDK generates a secret and a Poseidon commitment, the sender approves the ERC-20 and calls deposit on BulletPool. The note details are sealed to the recipient's public key and stored as ciphertext. An off-chain indexer watches Deposit events, inserts each commitment into a depth-20 Poseidon Merkle tree, and posts the root on-chain to MerkleRootManager. The recipient opens their inbox, decrypts the note locally, fetches a Merkle witness from the indexer, and generates a Groth16 proof in the browser. BulletPool verifies the proof, checks the nullifier has not been spent, and transfers the tokens out. Nothing on-chain connects the deposit transaction to the withdraw transaction. The withdraw event carries the nullifier and the recipient, never the commitment.

projects.title: Aegis Governance
projects.description: Uniswapv4 pool governance and ENSv2 permissions enforced on-chain
projects.project_description: Aegis is an ENSv2-powered governance and identity layer for Uniswap v4 pools. It demonstrates how human-readable ENS namespaces can be used to represent real organizational roles, while smart contracts remain the final source of truth for permissions and enforcement. The project is built around a live Uniswap v4 pool on Sepolia, a custom HookGovernance contract, an OperatorRoleManager authorization contract, ENSv2 identities, and a Next.js/ethers frontend. Instead of managing a DeFi protocol using anonymous wallet addresses alone, Aegis gives participants readable identities such as aegis.eth , operator.aegis.eth , alice.operator.aegis.eth , bob.operator.aegis.eth , and charlie.contributor.aegis.eth . The key idea is that identity and authority are deliberately separated. Owning or resolving an ENS name does not automatically give a wallet administrative permissions. ENSv2 provides the identity and namespace structure, while OperatorRoleManager determines which wallets are currently authorized to perform specific governance actions. At the top of the hierarchy is aegis.eth , which represents the ultimate governance owner. The parent owner retains final control over the governance system and can add, remove, replace, or reactivate delegated operators. A separate delegated account, operator.aegis.eth , acts as an operator administrator and can manage pool operators without needing to be the ultimate owner. Below that are active pool operators such as alice.operator.aegis.eth and bob.operator.aegis.eth . These wallets are authorized through OperatorRoleManager and can pause or unpause the governed Uniswap v4 pool. The HookGovernance contract checks their current authorization on-chain before allowing those actions. This means revocation takes effect immediately. For example, the aegis.eth owner can remove Alice as an operator. Alice still owns and resolves to alice.operator.aegis.eth , but her authorization state becomes inactive. If she then attempts to pause the pool, the transaction reaches HookGovernance and reverts with Unauthorized() . If she is later reactivated, her governance authority is restored without needing to create a new ENS identity. Aegis also includes charlie.contributor.aegis.eth to demonstrate that having a valid identity inside the wider Aegis namespace does not imply governance privileges. Charlie can connect to the application, resolve his ENSv2 identity, and use the pool normally, including executing swaps, but he cannot pause or unpause the pool. A governance attempt from Charlie is rejected on-chain by HookGovernance with Unauthorized() . This creates a clear permission model: aegis.eth → ultimate governance owner operator.aegis.eth → delegated operator administrator alice.operator.aegis.eth / bob.operator.aegis.eth → active pool operators charlie.contributor.aegis.eth → identified participant with no governance authority The Uniswap v4 integration is fully functional rather than simulated. The deployed pool uses ETH and a Sepolia MockUSDC token. Users can execute a real ETH-to-MockUSDC swap through the Aegis swap router. When the pool is active, the swap succeeds. When an authorized operator pauses the pool, HookGovernance's Uniswap v4 beforeSwap() callback detects the paused state and reverts the swap. Once another authorized operator unpauses the pool, swaps immediately work again. This creates a simple but powerful live demo flow: swap succeeds → Alice pauses the pool → the same swap is rejected → Bob unpauses the pool → the swap succeeds again. The frontend also reconstructs the operator directory from on-chain OperatorAdded and OperatorRemoved events rather than hardcoding Alice and Bob into the interface. It then checks the current OperatorRoleManager state for each discovered wallet and resolves their ENSv2 primary names. This means the interface reflects current blockchain state rather than maintaining a separate off-chain permission database. Aegis uses ENSv2 not simply as a naming system, but as a composable organizational identity layer. A project could create a namespace such as project.eth and organize wallets under roles such as security.project.eth , trader.project.eth , liquidity.project.eth , or agent.project.eth , while separate authorization contracts determine what each identity is actually allowed to do. The same model can extend beyond human operators. Autonomous agents could receive readable ENS identities while being granted tightly scoped permissions such as swap-only access, liquidity management, emergency pause authority, treasury actions, or monitoring roles. Those permissions can then be revoked without destroying the agent's underlying identity. Aegis therefore demonstrates a broader design for on-chain organizations: ENS provides readable, hierarchical identity; application contracts provide revocable authorization; and Uniswap v4 hooks enforce those permissions directly at the protocol execution layer. The result is a governance system where users can understand who an account represents, what role it belongs to, and what authority it currently has, while every important permission remains verifiable and enforceable on-chain.
projects.how_its_made: Aegis is built with Solidity, Foundry, ENSv2, Uniswap v4, Next.js, TypeScript, ethers.js and MetaMask, with the frontend deployed on Vercel and the contracts running on Sepolia. The core architecture is: ENSv2 identity → OperatorRoleManager authorization → HookGovernance → Uniswap v4 execution. On the smart-contract side, OperatorRoleManager is the authorization layer. Each governance resource has a parent owner, a delegated operator admin and a set of operators. Every operator is linked to an ENSv2 identity registry and identity resource, but identity and authorization are deliberately kept separate. This means a wallet can keep its ENS identity while its application permissions are revoked or restored independently. HookGovernance is a custom Uniswap v4 hook. Each pool is mapped to a governance resource, and operators can pause or unpause that pool. The hook enforces the state directly inside Uniswap v4: its beforeSwap() callback checks the pool configuration and reverts with PoolIsPaused() when governance has paused the pool. The hook also checks OperatorRoleManager before allowing governance actions, so an inactive or unauthorized wallet gets an on-chain Unauthorized() revert rather than relying on frontend access control. I built a real ETH/MockUSDC Uniswap v4 pool on Sepolia and added liquidity to it. For the demo I also wrote an AegisSwapRouter that talks directly to the v4 PoolManager using the unlock flow and performs an exact ETH-to-token swap. This gave me a real end-to-end test: swap succeeds, Alice pauses the pool, the same swap is blocked by the hook, Bob unpauses it, and the swap succeeds again. ENSv2 is used for the human-readable identity hierarchy. Aegis is an ENSv2-powered governance and identity layer for Uniswap v4 pools. It demonstrates how human-readable ENS namespaces can be used to represent real organizational roles, while smart contracts remain the final source of truth for permissions and enforcement.

The project is built around a live Uniswap v4 pool on Sepolia, a custom HookGovernance contract, an OperatorRoleManager authorization contract, ENSv2 identities, and a Next.js/ethers frontend. Instead of managing a DeFi protocol using anonymous wallet addresses alone, Aegis gives participants readable identities such as `aegis.eth`, `operator.aegis.eth`, `alice.operator.aegis.eth`, `bob.operator.aegis.eth`, and `charlie.contributor.aegis.eth`.

The key idea is that identity and authority are deliberately separated. Owning or resolving an ENS name does not automatically give a wallet administrative permissions. ENSv2 provides the identity and namespace structure, while OperatorRoleManager determines which wallets are currently authorized to perform specific governance actions.

At the top of the hierarchy is `aegis.eth`, which represents the ultimate governance owner. The parent owner retains final control over the governance system and can add, remove, replace, or reactivate delegated operators. A separate delegated account, `operator.aegis.eth`, acts as an operator administrator and can manage pool operators without needing to be the ultimate owner.

Below that are active pool operators such as `alice.operator.aegis.eth` and `bob.operator.aegis.eth`. These wallets are authorized through OperatorRoleManager and can pause or unpause the governed Uniswap v4 pool. The HookGovernance contract checks their current authorization on-chain before allowing those actions.

This means revocation takes effect immediately. For example, the `aegis.eth` owner can remove Alice as an operator. Alice still owns and resolves to `alice.operator.aegis.eth`, but her authorization state becomes inactive. If she then attempts to pause the pool, the transaction reaches HookGovernance and reverts with `Unauthorized()`. If she is later reactivated, her governance authority is restored without needing to create a new ENS identity.

Aegis also includes `charlie.contributor.aegis.eth` to demonstrate that having a valid identity inside the wider Aegis namespace does not imply governance privileges. Charlie can connect to the application, resolve his ENSv2 identity, and use the pool normally, including executing swaps, but he cannot pause or unpause the pool. A governance attempt from Charlie is rejected on-chain by HookGovernance with `Unauthorized()`.

This creates a clear permission model:

`aegis.eth` → ultimate governance owner
`operator.aegis.eth` → delegated operator administrator
`alice.operator.aegis.eth` / `bob.operator.aegis.eth` → active pool operators
`charlie.contributor.aegis.eth` → identified participant with no governance authority

The Uniswap v4 integration is fully functional rather than simulated. The deployed pool uses ETH and a Sepolia MockUSDC token. Users can execute a real ETH-to-MockUSDC swap through the Aegis swap router. When the pool is active, the swap succeeds. When an authorized operator pauses the pool, HookGovernance's Uniswap v4 `beforeSwap()` callback detects the paused state and reverts the swap. Once another authorized operator unpauses the pool, swaps immediately work again.

This creates a simple but powerful live demo flow:

swap succeeds → Alice pauses the pool → the same swap is rejected → Bob unpauses the pool → the swap succeeds again.

The frontend also reconstructs the operator directory from on-chain `OperatorAdded` and `OperatorRemoved` events rather than hardcoding Alice and Bob into the interface. It then checks the current OperatorRoleManager state for each discovered wallet and resolves their ENSv2 primary names. This means the interface reflects current blockchain state rather than maintaining a separate off-chain permission database.

Aegis uses ENSv2 not simply as a naming system, but as a composable organizational identity layer. A project could create a namespace such as `project.eth` and organize wallets under roles such as `security.project.eth`, `trader.project.eth`, `liquidity.project.eth`, or `agent.project.eth`, while separate authorization contracts determine what each identity is actually allowed to do.

The same model can extend beyond human operators. Autonomous agents could receive readable ENS identities while being granted tightly scoped permissions such as swap-only access, liquidity management, emergency pause authority, treasury actions, or monitoring roles. Those permissions can then be revoked without destroying the agent's underlying identity.

Aegis therefore demonstrates a broader design for on-chain organizations: ENS provides readable, hierarchical identity; application contracts provide revocable authorization; and Uniswap v4 hooks enforce those permissions directly at the protocol execution layer.

The result is a governance system where users can understand who an account represents, what role it belongs to, and what authority it currently has, while every important permission remains verifiable and enforceable on-chain.

projects.title: safe402
projects.description: SAFE Protocol is the security layer between AI agents and the tools they use.
projects.project_description: SAFE402 is a security verification layer for AI agents that discover and use third-party tools such as MCP servers, agent skills, APIs, plugins, x402 services, and autonomous financial tools. The core problem is that an agent may discover a tool that claims to be harmless while actually performing undeclared actions such as reading environment secrets, accessing the filesystem, interacting with a wallet, spawning processes, or sending data to an unexpected network destination. SAFE402 verifies what a tool claims it can do against what it actually does. When an agent discovers a new tool, SAFE402 can analyze its code, execute it inside an isolated sandbox with synthetic secrets, wallets, credentials, files, and RPC endpoints, and observe its real behavior. The system converts those observations into a standardized capability manifest covering network, filesystem, secrets, wallet, process, and RPC access. It then compares declared and observed capabilities, calculates a risk score, explains any mismatches, and returns a machine-readable ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK decision. Verification is bound to an exact tool version and content hash so a previously verified release cannot automatically make a changed version trusted. The long-term goal is to make security verification a native part of agentic discovery: before an autonomous agent installs a tool, grants it access, pays it, or allows it to interact with a wallet, SAFE402 gives the agent verifiable evidence about what that tool actually does. The project is designed around one simple principle: AI agents should not blindly trust the tools they discover. SAFE402 gives them a security checkpoint before execution.
projects.how_its_made: SAFE402 is built as a modular security pipeline around an AI agent. A discovered tool first goes through a static scanner that looks for behaviors such as filesystem access, network requests, environment-variable access, shell or process execution, wallet or RPC interaction, suspicious dependencies, dynamic code execution, obfuscation, prompt injection, tool poisoning, and other agent-specific attack patterns. Static analysis alone is not treated as sufficient, so the tool is then executed in an isolated sandbox using controlled synthetic resources such as fake API keys, fake environment variables, decoy credential files, a fake wallet, and fake RPC endpoints. This lets SAFE402 observe whether the tool attempts actions that were never declared without exposing real user secrets. Those observations are passed into a capability engine that normalizes behavior into categories such as NETWORK READ/WRITE, FILESYSTEM READ/WRITE/EXECUTE, SECRETS ENV/CONFIG/CREDENTIALS, WALLET READ/SIGN/TRANSACT, PROCESS SPAWN/EXECUTE, and RPC READ/WRITE. A risk engine compares declared capabilities against observed capabilities and produces both a 0–100 risk score and human- and machine-readable reasons. The final result is returned through the SAFE API and SAFE MCP server as an ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK decision tied to the exact tool version and content hash. For partner technologies, SAFE402 uses Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows as the confidential verification layer for sensitive audit execution. The intent is to run adversarial tests and behavioral monitoring without exposing sensitive test fixtures, while producing a capability manifest, risk result, tool hash, and cryptographic attestation that can be verified externally. Hedera Consensus Service is used as the public verification registry. SAFE402 records compact verification data such as the tool ID, exact version, content hash, manifest hash, risk score, status, attestation hash, and timestamp. This creates an immutable audit history so agents can verify that a specific version was actually checked rather than trusting a generic “verified” label. The Graph is used as the security-intelligence layer. It indexes relationships between tools, versions, developers, audits, capabilities, attestations, incidents, and reputation so agents can query questions such as whether a previous version failed an audit, whether a developer has shipped tools that accessed wallet functionality, or which verified tools have no filesystem or wallet capabilities. x402 is used so the AI agent itself can pay for verification. Instead of a human checkout flow, SAFE402 can return a 402 Payment Required response, allow the agent to pay automatically, and then continue the verification workflow. World AgentKit is used for optional human-backed auditor or agent identity, allowing SAFE402 to distinguish anonymous automated participants from agents operating on behalf of a unique human. One of the more notable parts of the project is the adversarial sandbox design. Rather than only scanning code for suspicious strings, SAFE402 deliberately gives the tool believable but fake secrets, wallets, sensitive files, and credentials and watches what it tries to access or exfiltrate. This makes the security decision based on observed behavior, not just what the tool says about itself.

projects.title: Float
projects.description: Float is an overdraft layer that keeps AI agents running when their balance hits zero.
projects.project_description: Float is a credit layer for AI agents that lets them pay for services even when they don’t have enough funds. A human verifies their identity through World, then connects their agents to Float. Agents can make payments through Arc using USDC, while Hedera handles fast, low-cost machine payments and metered services. When an agent runs out of balance, Float can front the payment and record it as credit for that agent. The dashboard gives the human a clear view of their agents, credit limits, borrowed amount, repayments, and payment history. This allows agents to keep working without requiring them to be constantly funded, while keeping human accountability and spending limits at the center.
projects.how_its_made: Float is built as a full-stack Web3 application using Next.js, TypeScript, Solidity, Arc, Hedera, Circle Gateway, x402, and World. We built our own credit/loan layer and deployed the core smart contract on Arc to track agent credit limits, borrowing, and repayments. World’s Selfie Check is used for human verification, while AgentKit/AgentBook connects agents back to their human. For payments, agents use Circle Gateway and x402 with USDC on Arc, while Hedera + Blocky402 powers fast, low-cost machine payments and metered services. We also built a custom FloatSignerTS payment layer that automatically detects when an agent has insufficient funds and routes the payment through Float’s credit facility instead. The frontend dashboard brings the agents, credit limits, outstanding debt, repayments, and payment activity into one place.

projects.title: Blee
projects.description: Pay USDC over Bluetooth. No internet, wallet address or QR code required.
projects.project_description: Blee makes digital money work like cash. Today, sending crypto usually starts with friction: find a wallet address, scan a QR code, make sure both sides have connectivity, select the right network and wait for infrastructure to cooperate. Blee removes that interaction entirely. Open Blee and nearby people automatically appear through the Blee Bluetooth Mesh Network. Tap the person, enter an amount and send USDC. No wallet address needs to be exchanged. No QR code needs to be scanned. The phones can communicate directly over Bluetooth even when the sender and receiver do not have internet access. Under the hood, the sender cryptographically authorizes the payment and the payment packet can be carried across nearby Blee devices using store-and-forward networking. If another Blee device in the network has internet connectivity, it can broadcast the sender's already-signed transaction to Arc without ever controlling the sender's funds or paying the sender's gas. The result is a payment experience that feels much closer to handing someone cash: discover the person beside you, tap their name and pay. Blee is currently built around USDC on Arc Testnet, with a self-custodial wallet, durable offline transaction state and a native Android Bluetooth networking layer.
projects.how_its_made: Blee is an Android-first self-custodial wallet built with a React/Capacitor application layer and a native Android networking service. Nearby Blee devices discover each other using Bluetooth Low Energy scanning and advertising. Payments are transported through BLE/GATT with fragmentation, acknowledgement, retry and bounded store-and-forward routing. The native Android service owns networking so discovery and payment delivery are not dependent on the WebView remaining active. The financial state is persisted locally using SQLite with WAL, including the payment journal, signing intents, mesh inbox/outbox, seen packets, settlement jobs, peer identities and settlement receipts. This lets Blee survive application restarts and temporary connectivity loss without treating UI state as the source of truth. For payments, Blee uses USDC's EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization. The sender creates the payment authorization and, when settlement information is available, also signs an EIP-1559 transaction calling transferWithAuthorization. This enables one of Blee's most important properties: another Blee device can relay the payment and broadcast the sender's already-signed raw transaction when it reaches internet connectivity. The relay device cannot change the recipient or amount, never receives the sender's private key and never pays gas on behalf of the sender. Settlement currently runs on Arc Testnet (chain ID 5042002). Internet connectivity determines when blockchain settlement happens; it does not determine whether nearby Blee devices can create, persist, deliver or acknowledge a payment. We also built durable duplicate protection, signed mesh messages, encrypted wallet backup/recovery, native payment notifications and optional biometric unlock.

projects.title: Proof of Heart
projects.description: One verified human, one dating profile. AI twins screen your matches and pay per call onchain.
projects.project_description: Proof of Heart is a dating app with one structural rule: one verified human can hold exactly one profile — and your AI twin goes on the first date, not you. Romance scams work because one person can run many fake profiles cheaply. Photo checks raise the cost of each one but never cap how many a person holds. Signup — World ID Selfie Check (credential 11). Proofs are verified server-side, and the server asserts issuer_schema_id === 11 on what World actually issued, not on what the client requested, so a weaker credential fails closed. The nullifier is claimed atomically: a second signup with the same face is refused with 409 NULLIFIER_ALREADY_CLAIMED. Twins — World AgentKit / AgentBook. Each verified user's twin gets an agent wallet registered in AgentBook on World Chain, so anyone can resolve it back to a verified human. Agent keys stay server-side: a twin takes its turn while its owner's tab is shut. The screening date — Hedera x402 + HCS. Two twins hold a multi-turn conversation for their owners, then a final call scores compatibility and names friction points. Direct human chat unlocks only above a threshold. Every twin utterance is a paid call. The inference endpoint is x402-gated on Hedera: 402 challenge, the agent signs a transfer, Blocky402 co-signs and settles. Pricing is metered, not flat — base + prompt tokens + requested output tokens, quoted from the actual request before the challenge, so a four-turn screening costs more than a one-line reply rather than being subsidised by it. Each settled call publishes an HCS receipt with payer, agent id, price, tokens and a SHA-256 commitment to the request rather than its text, plus a HashScan link. Three things are enforced where the browser can't reach: proof verification; the AgentBook human-backing check, which returns 403 AGENT_NOT_HUMAN_BACKED before the 402 so an unbacked bot can't burn a real user's HBAR; and the screening verdict, which gates who messages whom. Because every utterance costs real HBAR, running twins at spam scale costs real money.
projects.how_its_made:
Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, Radix/Tailwind. No separate backend — the API routes are the server. Every sponsor SDK (@worldcoin/idkit + idkit-core, agentkit, @x402/hedera, @hiero-ledger/sdk, Anthropic) is a lazy await import() in try/catch with a fallback, keeping Node-only code out of the client bundle and degrading a missing key to a labelled sandbox path rather than a crash — the flow is clickable with a blank .env.local. The chain: Selfie Check yields a nullifier → the account id is derived from it → that account mints an agent wallet registered in AgentBook → the agent's key signs x402 payments for its own inference. Each step's output is the next step's credential. Notable:
• Selfie Check's preset string isn't published, so the preset is configurable and the server asserts issuer_schema_id === 11 on the issued proof — a weaker credential fails closed.
• x402 route config is built per-request, since price is metered from the body before the 402.
• HCS receipts commit to a SHA-256 of the request, never its text.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Proof of Heart is a dating app with one structural rule: one verified human can hold exactly one profile — and your AI twin goes on the first date, not you.

Romance scams work because one person can run many fake profiles cheaply. Photo checks raise the cost of each one but never cap how many a person holds.

Signup — World ID Selfie Check (credential 11). Proofs are verified server-side, and the server asserts issuer_schema_id === 11 on what World actually issued, not on what the client requested, so a weaker credential fails closed. The nullifier is claimed atomically: a second signup with the same face is refused with 409 NULLIFIER_ALREADY_CLAIMED.

Twins — World AgentKit / AgentBook. Each verified user's twin gets an agent wallet registered in AgentBook on World Chain, so anyone can resolve it back to a verified human. Agent keys stay server-side: a twin takes its turn while its owner's tab is shut.

The screening date — Hedera x402 + HCS. Two twins hold a multi-turn conversation for their owners, then a final call scores compatibility and names friction points. Direct human chat unlocks only above a threshold.

Every twin utterance is a paid call. The inference endpoint is x402-gated on Hedera: 402 challenge, the agent signs a transfer, Blocky402 co-signs and settles. Pricing is metered, not flat — base + prompt tokens + requested output tokens, quoted from the actual request before the challenge, so a four-turn screening costs more than a one-line reply rather than being subsidised by it. Each settled call publishes an HCS receipt with payer, agent id, price, tokens and a SHA-256 commitment to the request rather than its text, plus a HashScan link.

Three things are enforced where the browser can't reach: proof verification; the AgentBook human-backing check, which returns 403 AGENT_NOT_HUMAN_BACKED before the 402 so an unbacked bot can't burn a real user's HBAR; and the screening verdict, which gates who messages whom.

Because every utterance costs real HBAR, running twins at spam scale costs real money.

projects.title: Hermes v2
projects.description: Encrypted messaging for AI agents, now reasoning over live, spam-filtered DEX data from The Graph.
projects.project_description:
Hermes is an end-to-end encrypted, asynchronous messaging layer for AI agents. Every agent is an ENS name that publishes its encryption keys; messages are sealed, stored on 0G, and routed through a small inbox contract on Sepolia. A quorum of three agents (Architect, Pragmatist, Skeptic) answers a user's sealed question, and a coordinator writes the final report. PRE-EXISTING WORK: all of the above was built for ETHGlobal Open Agents (April–May 2026) and is everything up to git tag v1-baseline. It is disclosed in CONTINUITY.md. Judged diff: https://github.com/Red3lue/Hermes/compare/v1-baseline...ethonline-2026 BUILT DURING ETHONLINE 2026: Hermes agents now reason over live on-chain data from The Graph. A live DEX data service, packaged as an MCP server. It gives any AI client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor) live data for Uniswap v3, Curve and SushiSwap, using one query pattern across Messari's standardized dex-amm subgraphs. Numbers you can trust. The subgraphs' own TVL is wrecked by spam-token pricing (Uniswap v3 reports about $136B, and we have seen $1e43; the real blue-chip figure is about $466M). Hermes counts only pools whose every token is a blue-chip asset, matched by address, and reports real TVL, 7-day volume, market share, capital efficiency and the effective fee traders pay, stamped with the Ethereum block the data comes from. A grounded agent quorum. When a user asks a DeFi question, the coordinator fetches that data before fanning the question out, all three agents deliberate over the same numbers, and the report cites them and ends with the exact subgraphs and blocks used. In a live round, every figure the agents cited matched The Graph data, and when a question was underspecified they abstained and explained why instead of guessing. Live demo: https://hermes-web-734709088945.us-central1.run.app
Built with Claude Code as a pair programmer; details per file in AI_USAGE.md
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript pnpm monorepo. The new packages/mcp-server uses the MCP TypeScript SDK over stdio and queries The Graph Network gateway with a Subgraph Studio API key. Its data module is also imported by the existing agents-server, whose quorum coordinator grounds DeFi questions before fan-out. Both services run on Google Cloud Run. THE GRAPH: Messari's Standardized Subgraphs were the key. Every DEX shares the dex-amm schema, so one GraphQL pipeline serves Uniswap v3, Curve and SushiSwap unchanged, and adding a protocol is one registry entry with no new queries or normalization code. THE HACKY PARTS: Spam-token filter: protocol TVL from the subgraphs is unusable, so pools are kept only when every token is on an address allowlist (symbols get spoofed). Discovery off the hot path: finding those pools means sorting tens of thousands of pools by volume, which takes 10–20s and times out when indexers lag. It runs in the background with a checked-in seed list as fallback, so a round needs one fast query. Graceful degradation: each protocol gets a 12s deadline; if the gateway is slow, the last good result (at most 30 minutes old) is used and marked "(cached)", and a background refresher keeps it warm. Rounds start in seconds. RPC rate limits: on Cloud Run's shared IPs, the agents' inbox polling hit a public Sepolia RPC's limits, so the RPC now takes a fallback list (a keyed endpoint first, public second). The web app's inbox scans now cover only recent blocks and poll less often. ENSv2 surprise: Sepolia's default Universal Resolver now routes ENSv1 names through an ENSv2 mirror resolver that accepts reads but reverts writes, which broke setting user records from the app. We traced it and set records on the real v1 resolver. PRE-EXISTING STACK (Open Agents): viem, ENS NameWrapper subnames as the key directory, X25519-sealed envelopes signed with EIP-191, 0G Storage, the HermesInbox contract on Sepolia, Claude for agent reasoning, and a React frontend.

projects.title: Encore-RWA
projects.description: Fund live events, get paid automatically from ticket revenue — split on-chain, no under-reporting.
projects.project_description:
Encore is a programmable revenue-security protocol built on Hedera. Event organizers need cash before a single ticket sells — but banks won't lend against future ticket sales, and revenue-share deals rely on trusting the organizer's word. Encore fixes both: an organizer sells a token representing a fixed share of ticket revenue (say 18%), verified investors buy in upfront, and every ticket sale is split automatically on-chain by a TicketEscrow smart contract — the organizer's cut paid out immediately, the investor pool locked until settlement.
Built on Hedera's Token Service and Smart Contract Service, tickets are minted as NFTs with a built-in 10% resale royalty that keeps paying investors even after resale. Every transaction — every split, every payout — is publicly verifiable on HashScan and the Mirror Node. This demo walks through the full lifecycle on Hedera testnet: offering terms, KYC-gated funding, ticket sales, resale, compliance controls, settlement, and a live on-chain health dashboard.
projects.how_its_made:
Encore runs two Solidity contracts on Hedera's EVM — FundingVault.sol (the all-or-nothing raise: KYC-gated invest(), finalize(), refund-if-failed) and TicketEscrow.sol (splits every ticket sale between organizer and investor pool the instant it's paid, tracks an on-chain accounting
invariant, and lets holders claim() pro-rata payouts after settlement). Both are written and tested with Hardhat, then deployed to Hedera testnet.Alongside the EVM side, we lean hard on the Hedera Token Service for everything that doesn't need custom logic: the mUSD stablecoin, and the ticket NFT collection, minted natively with a built-in 10% resale royalty (a CustomRoyaltyFee with TicketEscrow as the fee collector) — so resale payouts to investors happen automatically at the protocol level with zero custom code, instead of us having to write and audit royalty-splitting logic ourselves. That's the clearest case of a partner technology (HTS) directly shrinking our attack surface and our code. The backend is Node/Express, orchestrating both worlds from one service layer: @hashgraph/sdk for native HTS operations (token creation, KYC, freeze, associate) and ethers.js over Hedera's JSON-RPC relay for contract calls — one request can touch both in sequence. Off-chain JSON state tracks display metadata (activity feed, settlement snapshots) that doesn't belong on-chain. The revenue-right security token runs in a MOCK mode standing in for Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, so the compliance flow (KYC/freeze gating transfers) is demoed against a lightweight mock contract with the same interface ATS would expose.The hackiest deliberate choice: there's no browser wallet in this build. Four pre-created testnet accounts (admin, organizer, investor1/2, fan) have their keys held by the backend, and a role-switcher in the UI picks which one signs each call — that's what makes a from-scratch live demo deterministic and fast instead of fighting wallet popups mid-presentation. Wallet connect (HashPack/MetaMask via the relay) is scoped as real future work, not a permanent shortcut. We also had to patch around a flaky quirk in Hedera's JSON-RPC relay, which occasionally throws a malformed unhandled rejection mid-poll for a transaction receipt — we catch it at the process level so one flaky relay response doesn't crash the whole
demo server.
