projects.title: Capability Descent
projects.description: Capped, revocable spending authority for AI agents: real HBAR settles, over-budget is refused
projects.project_description: Capability Descent gives autonomous agents delegated spending authority that is capped, attenuable, and revocable. A parent agent grants a child agent an HBAR allowance; that child can grant a smaller allowance onward, never a larger one. Every paid request is checked against the allowance before a price is quoted, so an over-budget request is refused with a machine-readable reason and no settlement is ever attempted. Authorized requests settle real HBAR on Hedera testnet through x402 and the Blocky402 facilitator, and each settlement is re-verified against consensus via the Mirror Node instead of trusting the facilitator receipt. Revoking a child propagates to its subtree while sibling grants keep spending, which the recorded demo shows end to end. ENS provides agent identity and the parent/child link. Every claim in this submission maps to a row in RESULTS.md, which also lists the claims we could not prove.
projects.how_its_made: Three TypeScript packages, deliberately split by what they are allowed to touch. core/ is pure allowance algebra over bigint: no clocks, no network, no SDKs, no randomness, with fast-check property tests for attenuation and conservation through delegation depth 5, so a child grant can never exceed its parent and spent can never exceed limit. chain/ holds the live integrations: the x402 Hedera scheme via @x402/fetch and Blocky402's testnet facilitator, the Hiero SDK for signing, a Mirror Node client that re-verifies each settlement against consensus rather than trusting the receipt, and ENSv2 forward/reverse resolution through the canonical Universal Resolver plus write calldata for the deployed PermissionedResolver. surface/ is the x402-gated resource server, the payer, an MCP server so an LLM agent can spend under the same caps, and the demo control plane. Two hacky-but-load-bearing details. First: the Hedera SDK silently parses a bare hex ECDSA key as ED25519, which produced INVALID_SIGNATURE with no hint; the signer now derives candidate keys of both types and matches them against the account key that consensus publishes, refusing before it signs anything. Second: our ENS write calldata originally targeted selectors that do not exist on the deployed resolver, and an absent selector reverts without data, which our own preflight classified as a permission refusal, so both live tests passed against a contract declining to exist; we now assert every selector against eth_getCode bytecode. ENS onchain publication is built and preflighted up to the broadcast but not broadcast, and RESULTS.md marks that row blocked rather than claiming it.

projects.title: SynapseVM
projects.description: Build, ship, and verify neural reflexes for robots, software and autonomous systems.
projects.project_description: SynapseVM is a platform for turning biological and synthetic spiking neural networks into portable, composable, and verifiable software modules. Instead of treating SNNs as isolated research files, SynapseVM packages them as reusable NeuroBlocks with typed inputs and outputs, provenance, versioning, runtime requirements, benchmarks, and verification metadata. Developers can discover neural circuits in the Library, combine them visually in a node-based Workbench, connect them to sensors, control logic, and actuators, and then compile the result into a portable NeuroStack. The compiled stack can be exported to environments such as WASM, Rust, Python, or ROS2 and used outside the SynapseVM frontend in robots, simulations, games, edge software, or autonomous systems. SynapseVM also includes a 3D simulator for testing behaviors before deployment. Our current primitives include modules for looming/collision detection, optic flow, heading, and target tracking. A typical example is an emergency-braking stack where sensor data is converted into neural events, processed by a LoomGuard NeuroBlock, passed through a deterministic safety gate, and converted into a brake command. A core part of SynapseVM is verification. Critical actions can generate a NeuroReceipt that binds the exact compiled stack, committed input, previous state, neural output, control decision, and final action. Because execution is deterministic, the same event can be replayed independently to verify that the same input and state produce the same result. The goal is to make neural software feel like normal software: discover it, compose it, compile it, run it anywhere, and verify what it did.
projects.how_its_made: We built SynapseVM as a full pipeline from neural circuit → reusable module → composed behavior → portable runtime → verifiable execution. The frontend is built as a modern web application with a node-based Workbench and a live 3D simulator. In the Workbench, users connect typed nodes such as sensors, adapters, NeuroBlocks, control logic, and actuators. The important part is that the visual graph is not just UI. It compiles into a deterministic NeuroStack with locked module versions, graph wiring, runtime parameters, and verification metadata. We package this into a portable .synapse artifact that can be executed outside the frontend and exported toward environments such as WASM, Rust, Python, and ROS2. For the neural layer, we represent spiking models through a structured intermediate format and deterministic runtime. We intentionally avoid putting blockchain or remote services inside the real-time control loop. Reflexes run locally; verification happens asynchronously. To make replay possible, we use deterministic execution semantics and canonical state/input encoding so the same Stack, state, and input reproduce the same output. Our 3D simulator feeds world-state data through the exact same adapters and NeuroBlocks used by the compiled Stack. This means the simulator is not a mocked animation: it is a test environment for the portable neural software itself. One particularly hacky part was converting simulated spatial events into event-style neural inputs so the same LoomGuard module can be reused across very different embodiments, such as a vehicle brake or drone avoidance system. For verification, critical actions generate a NeuroReceipt containing the Stack identity, NeuroBlock identity, committed input, pre-state, neural result, control decision, final action, and post-state. A separate verifier can replay the execution and confirm that the same inputs produce the same result. We also keep the trust plane separate from execution, so verification never adds latency to the reflex itself. We use partner technologies where they naturally fit the architecture: Chainlink CRE for confidential external verification/replay of private execution data, The Graph for indexing published modules, stacks, validation events, and verification history, and Hedera for anchoring or settlement around module usage and licensing without placing payments inside the real-time reflex path. The core technical idea is that SynapseVM treats neural models like software packages: versioned, composable, exportable, benchmarkable, and independently verifiable.

projects.title: Takarabako
projects.description: Physical IoT DeFi, agentic yield strategy, insert cash into a Raspberry Pi and get the defi position
projects.project_description:
Takarabako is a  Physical Bridging Cash To Stablecoin Layer, where Cash can be deposited to a personal onchain wallet and execute multiple strategies powered by an agent. The problem:
Cash and stablecoins are both trusted forms of money, but moving between them still requires a bank account or an exchange like Binance. 1.3 billion adults are unbanked (World Bank Global Findex 2025), 900M of them own a mobile phone but have no account-based path into digital dollars. The phone exists, the rail doesn't. Remittances still cost ~6% on average (World Bank, 2026), over double the UN's 3% target, because the on/off-ramp at each end is manual, bank-dependent, and slow (1–5 days). The solution:

projects.title: whetstone
projects.description: AI rewrites Solidity to save gas. Whetstone checks it's still correct and puts a receipt on-chain.
projects.project_description: An LLM says it made your Solidity function 11,000 gas cheaper. Should you believe it? Usually there is no way to tell: the patch might not compute the same thing, the number might not reproduce, and the model may just be reciting code it memorised. Whetstone turns each of those doubts into something you can check. Open-weight models are paid per call to optimise a well-known library function that has been deliberately mutated, so the memorised answer is now the wrong one. Every patch is compiled, checked for equivalence against the original (a formal proof where the solver finishes, a declared fuzz campaign where it does not) and measured under a pinned compiler and a fixed input scenario. Every attempt, failures included, publishes a receipt to Hedera Consensus Service, with a pointer on Base Sepolia indexed by a subgraph. The leaderboard is a static page that queries that index from your browser, and any gas figure can be recomputed from the committed bundle with one command. So far: 141 paid attempts, 9 models, 4 tasks, $2.31 at list price. 78 produced a valid patch: 37 formally proved, 41 fuzzed. Pointed at Uniswap v4-periphery, it found that VanityAddressLib.score can be made 79% cheaper (2,110 gas per call on a realistic workload) while computing exactly the same score. The full write-up is in FEEDBACK.md. What it is not: a model ranking. Four tasks and a handful of seeds are enough to demonstrate the method, not to crown a winner.
projects.how_its_made: Four parts, each with one job. The agent loop (Node.js). Fixed prompt, temperature, token ceiling and round limit. The model only ever sees mechanical feedback (compiler errors and checker verdicts), never hints. Models are served through OpenRouter and Groq. Paid inference with x402 on Hedera testnet. Every model call goes through our own x402 gateway: without a valid X-PAYMENT header it answers 402, so payment is verified and settled before the provider key is ever used. The price is metered per call on the request's declared upper bound (prompt + max_tokens). Because that overcharges, each receipt keeps the HBAR that actually moved separate from tokens used × a pinned public price list. Built on @x402/hedera and @hashgraph/sdk. Verification with Foundry. solc 0.8.35 pinned, EVM target Osaka. Equivalence is checked with hevm 0.58 symbolic execution and bitwuzla, inside a 6 GB systemd cgroup: on loop-heavy functions the solver will otherwise happily take the whole desktop down with it. When the prover cannot finish, the patch is fuzz-compared on return data and revert data (20,000 runs, pinned seed) and labelled FUZZED, never passed off as proved. Gas is a forge test over a committed input scenario. Two controls exist in order to fail: a cosmetic mutation that the admission gate must reject, and a "trivial floor" (the task with one word deleted) that a patch has to beat before its saving means anything. Receipts and index. Each receipt (patch, task and baseline hashes, toolchain, guarantee, cost, payment tx ids) is written to Hedera Consensus Service, read back and hash-checked. A permissionless RunRegistry contract on Base Sepolia then stores a pointer to it and its content hash, and a subgraph on The Graph indexes those rows. Two things read that index: the static leaderboard, and the budget allocator that decides which model gets paid next. The allocator is deliberately not an LLM: a fixed policy picks the best gas per dollar and sets a model aside after two undecided proofs or two failed attempts in a row, streaks the subgraph maintains as rows arrive. The notable surprise: we wrote down in advance that the first task would show no saving. Models beat the expert baseline anyway, because some patches used Osaka's new CLZ opcode, which the pinned reference library predates. We recorded the broken prediction and the reason in the decision log instead of quietly fixing the baseline.

projects.title: Streamsmith
projects.description: One prompt becomes a verified, live Substreams pipeline that agents can trust.
projects.project_description: AI can write a Substreams pipeline in minutes, but nobody should trust one it wrote: the code can be subtly wrong and nothing tells you. Streamsmith makes that trust checkable. A human writes the contract: a protobuf schema (what the data must look like), a config (chain, addresses, sampling interval) and a gate file (checks against real blocks whose correct answers are already known). Then one prompt. The official StreamingFast Substreams skills teach the agent how to write the Rust; the Streamsmith plugin teaches it how to prove the result is right and get it live. The promotion pipeline is gate → publish to the Substreams registry → deploy (Graph Market hosted sink, or a self-managed sink into ClickHouse) → Deployment Receipt → generated MCP server. Nothing is published until every gate assertion passes, and the gate verifies the agent did not modify the contract files. The Deployment Receipt binds the package hash, output module hash, parameter hash, proto descriptor hash and sink schema hash to the gate evidence and the deployment. The MCP server generated from it re-checks those hashes and the chain head every minute and refuses to answer (receipt_mismatch, schema_mismatch, chain_mismatch, stale_data) instead of guessing. Worked example: erc4626-flows, a reusable ERC-4626 vault-activity package for Base (deposits, withdrawals, and fixed-interval convertToAssets observations for Gauntlet USDC Prime and Steakhouse Prime USDC), composed on the Pinax erc4626 package, published to substreams.dev, and running as a Graph Market hosted deployment into ClickHouse Cloud with a live receipt. Payoff: Vaultpilot, a B2B treasury agent for a Privy business wallet. The owner sets a policy (two approved vaults, a per-action cap, deposit and withdraw only); the agent holds an additional signer key that can do nothing else. It reads the MCP, decides whether to rotate USDC between the vaults based on observed-window share-value growth, refuses on stale or mismatched data, and is denied by Privy at the policy layer when it tries anything outside the policy. Recorded proof: from a 112-file clean-start commit holding only the contract and tooling, one human message produced the package, a green gate (18/18), a registry publish (v0.1.1), a ClickHouse deployment, a receipt and an MCP server in about 40 minutes with no further human input. The run folder, the receipt and every generated line of code are in the repo under runs/recorded/.
projects.how_its_made: Substreams package (Rust → WASM): map and store modules over the Pinax erc4626 and erc20 packages, plus eth_call sampling of convertToAssets at the processed block so observations are deterministic. The proto contract is frozen in specs/vaultflows.proto with the table annotations the sink needs. Published with substreams publish; v0.1.0 is the live pipeline, v0.1.1 is the one the recorded one-prompt run produced. Streamsmith (TypeScript CLI + Claude Code plugin): gate runs executable assertions from specs/gate.yaml against pinned Base block ranges and exits non-zero on any failure; publish, deploy (hosted via the Graph Market portal API, self-managed via substreams-sink-sql, plus views, status, and an --attach mode that records a running deployment without redeploying), schema-render (renders the sink's DDL offline, byte-identical to the live ClickHouse schema, so the schema hash can be bound without a database), receipt (JSON-schema-validated Deployment Receipt), mcp and manifest. The plugin's SKILL.md carries the build traps we hit so the agent doesn't: the block-limit flag, the enum-in-sink panic, the per-database sink-info folder. mcpgen: generates a typed stdio MCP server from the proto descriptors and the receipt. Every tool response carries provenance; a refusal chain (receipt_mismatch → schema_mismatch → chain_mismatch → stale_data → check_unavailable) runs before any query. It detects ClickHouse's read-only profile rejecting settings and retries without them. Sinks: the Graph Market hosted deployment is primary; a self-managed sink is the documented fallback. Both write to ClickHouse Cloud, read by consumers through a read-only user. Hacky but notable: the first hosted deployment crash-looped because its start command was generated once at first deploy with a raw parameter string; config updates only restart the pod, so the fix was a fresh deployment with no parameter override. The registry counts every manifest fetch as a download, so that crash loop alone accounts for over a thousand "downloads" on our package page. Vaultpilot (TypeScript + Next.js): Privy server wallet owned by the treasurer's authorization key; the agent's key is a 1-of-1 key quorum attached as an additional signer with an override policy (earn_deposit and earn_withdraw on two vault ids under a cap). Privy policies don't aggregate Earn actions, so the daily cap is enforced app-side. The decision service applies a minimum observed window, a growth differential threshold, a cooldown, an outflow guardrail and a staleness refusal, and every fact behind a decision is on the dashboard alongside the pipeline stamp carrying the receipt hashes. The dashboard holds no keys. Partner tech: The Graph's Substreams skills wrote the pipeline, the registry and Graph Market run it; Privy's policies and additional signers are what make an agent with money safe to leave alone. 313 tests across the workspace; GitHub Actions builds the package.

projects.title: Vouch Protocol
projects.description: Providers stake capped guarantees on AI-agent work; a confidential test pays clients when it fails
projects.project_description: Vouch is a confidential, post-completion outcome-assurance protocol for AI-agent work. Acceptance tests are point-in-time. An AI agent's output can pass the public checks, get accepted, and get paid for — then be revealed as defective by a private or later-run test. Once the fee is released, the client has no recourse and the provider bears no consequence. Vouch closes that gap. A provider voluntarily attaches a provider-funded, capped performance guarantee to a job. During a coverage window after payment, a confidential test runs inside a TEE and can prove a covered failure — automatically triggering a predefined service-credit payout to the client. The verdict becomes part of the provider's onchain performance history. Vouch is not a marketplace, not insurance, and not ordinary escrow. Escrow releases on acceptance; Vouch's novelty is the post-acceptance coverage window plus a confidential trigger that keeps private tests and criteria from ever leaking. Guarantees, payouts, and reputation are authoritative onchain; secrets live only inside the enclave.
projects.how_its_made: Vouch is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo. The dashboard is Next.js 16 with Tailwind v4 and shadcn/ui, backed by a NestJS 11 API that serves offchain operational data only — never money, reputation, or secrets. An autonomous agent quotes risk and monitors jobs but never settles funds. Authoritative financial state lives in a Foundry contract (AssuranceHub) deployed to Arc, where the capped guarantee, coverage window, and USDC payout logic run. We integrate Circle's Agent Stack for the agent wallet and USDC movement, giving the agent a real onchain identity that can transact within strict guardrails. Reputation is derived, not stored: a The Graph subgraph built from scratch indexes Vouch's onchain events into an authoritative performance history, which the agent consumes over live GraphQL to make risk-quotation decisions — closing the loop from settlement back into pricing. The confidential verification is a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. The private test and criteria run inside a TEE via handlerInTee; the DON-signed enclave verdict is the sole authorization gate on the guarantee payout, so evaluation logic and repo credentials never touch Postgres, public onchain metadata, the subgraph, or IPFS. Shared Zod schemas, chain constants, and ABIs keep contracts, agent, and API type-safe across the workspace; Prisma 7 backs the rebuildable offchain cache.

projects.title: Freeboard Finance
projects.description: For Aave borrowers: a basket that shifts into your debt asset as health factor falls, and pays you.
projects.project_description:
Freeboard Finance is a no-cliff liquidation guard for Aave v3 borrowers: a basket beside the loan that shifts into the debt asset as the health factor falls, and pays the borrower a spread for every step. THE PROBLEM
Protecting a leveraged position today is binary. Nothing happens until a threshold is crossed, then collateral is dumped all at once, at the worst moment, into the thinnest market. Stop-losses, keeper bots and liquidation guards all share that cliff. THE INSIGHT
A rebalance and a deleverage are the same operation at different urgency: sell some of X for Y according to a rule. An index rebalances toward target weights; a guard moves toward solvency. So Freeboard makes the target weights a function of the health factor. With ETH, BTC and USDC beside a USDC loan, the curve the borrower signs reads: HF 2.00 → 50/30/20, HF 1.60 → 40/24/36, HF 1.30 → 30/16/54, HF 1.15 → 20/10/70. As the health factor falls, the target slides toward the asset she owes. Trades that move the basket toward its target are priced attractively; trades that move it away are priced expensively. Arbitrageurs do the rebalancing, a little at a time, and pay the borrower a spread to do it. Deleveraging starts early, intensifies continuously, and is paid for the whole way down. By the time the loan is in danger she already holds the USDC to repay it. HOW THE HEALTH FACTOR GETS INTO THE PRICE
The basket is a 1inch Aqua position. The strategy executes on the production AquaSwapVMRouter (0x111111338c…, swap-vm v1.0.2, matched to the tag by bytecode) through the router's own _extruction instruction, opcode 0x20, calling FreeboardExtruction, an immutable view contract. Inside the pricing path, on every quote and every swap, it staticcalls Aave v3's getUserAccountData for the maker, decodes the curve from the program bytes, interpolates the target at that health factor, reads the other basket legs from Aqua, and prices the fill by how much closer or farther from target the basket ends up. No router source is modified, no redeploy, nothing off-chain in the loop. Because Aave's read is deterministic within a block, quote and swap always agree; swap-vm's own invariant suite runs against the Freeboard program on the deployed router with every check on. WHY A PUBLIC CURVE CANNOT BE FRONT-RUN
Front-running a rule needs a moment worth waiting for, and a continuous curve has none: the basket sells a little at every health factor, so there is no cliff. The health factor cannot be pushed; it moves with Aave's oracle and the borrower's own debt, neither of which is flash-loanable. Front-running another taker's fill hurts that taker, not the borrower. No fill ever beats the oracle, so there is no price below fair to drain at. And a public curve means more takers compete for the same fill, which is what protects the borrower. THE PER-FILL CAP
One fill can move at most maxShiftBps of the basket's value (500 bps in the demo), checked after pricing on the amounts that actually settle. A wrong health factor, a bug, or a greedy taker cannot restructure the basket in one fill; a fill past the cap reverts with FreeboardFillExceedsMaxShift(shift, maxShift). If Aave cannot compute the health factor at all, the fill reverts rather than pricing from a number Aave would not stand behind; Aave cannot liquidate in that state either, so refusing costs the borrower nothing. LEDGER: THE HUMAN APPROVES THE CURVE
The curve and the cap are bytes inside the SwapVM program, and the program is what Aqua.ship() commits to, indexed by its hash. So the transaction the borrower signs on her Ledger is the approval of her risk policy, not just a key. She signed it on a Nano X through the official @ledgerhq/wallet-cli, and it is on Ethereum mainnet: tx 0xc13c55e1…70c4, against FreeboardExtruction at 0x8804F353…0f41. A test decodes that transaction and asserts its calldata is byte-for-byte the program every fork test prices; flip one byte of the curve and the deployed router refuses it on quote and on swap. The device screen is a blind-signed contract call today; readable rows need an ERC-7730 descriptor, which is not done, and the README says so. THE AI AGENT: BOUNDED BY THE CHAIN, NOT BY A PROMPT
The taker is an LLM agent (Claude, on the Strands Agents TypeScript SDK) with exactly three tools: read the position, quote a trade, fill it. No rule in code picks the pair, the size or the moment; the model does. Its RPC URL, taker key and API key are decrypted from Ledger's Key Ring into memory at start-up, never on disk or in the environment. In the judged run the operator told it to deleverage Alice "all of it, in ONE fill." It sent the whole 5,855 USDC gap; the router refused it, FreeboardFillExceedsMaxShift(945, 500). It then filled 3,100 USDC → 0.058883 WBTC, equal to its quote to the wei, toward target, and ended its report by explaining that the cap comes from the curve Alice signed on her Ledger, which no operator, prompt or agent can raise. That is Ledger's threshold model for agents, set once and enforced on-chain: autonomous under the cap, a new device signature above it. WHAT IT DOES FOR THE BORROWER, MEASURED
Same wallet, same Aave position, same oracle path from HF 2.00 to 1.10, same taker, the same $80,000 through the deployed Aqua and router, with one instruction of difference: swap-vm's stock constant-product swap or Freeboard's curve. The stock basket buys the falling asset and pays its takers -$395.83 to do it; it reaches the bottom worth $53,703, holding 17,888 USDC. Freeboard earns +$24.47 in spread, arrives worth $56,328, holding 39,435 USDC of the debt asset, $5,128 ahead of holding the shipped basket untouched. When she repays with what the basket handed her, her health factor is 1.37 instead of 1.21. projects.project_description_markdown:
Freeboard Finance is a no-cliff liquidation guard for Aave v3 borrowers: a basket beside the loan that shifts into the debt asset as the health factor falls, and pays the borrower a spread for every step.

THE PROBLEM
Protecting a leveraged position today is binary. Nothing happens until a threshold is crossed, then collateral is dumped all at once, at the worst moment, into the thinnest market. Stop-losses, keeper bots and liquidation guards all share that cliff.

THE INSIGHT
A rebalance and a deleverage are the same operation at different urgency: sell some of X for Y according to a rule. An index rebalances toward target weights; a guard moves toward solvency. So Freeboard makes the target weights a function of the health factor. With ETH, BTC and USDC beside a USDC loan, the curve the borrower signs reads: HF 2.00 → 50/30/20, HF 1.60 → 40/24/36, HF 1.30 → 30/16/54, HF 1.15 → 20/10/70. As the health factor falls, the target slides toward the asset she owes. Trades that move the basket toward its target are priced attractively; trades that move it away are priced expensively. Arbitrageurs do the rebalancing, a little at a time, and pay the borrower a spread to do it. Deleveraging starts early, intensifies continuously, and is paid for the whole way down. By the time the loan is in danger she already holds the USDC to repay it.

HOW THE HEALTH FACTOR GETS INTO THE PRICE
The basket is a 1inch Aqua position. The strategy executes on the production AquaSwapVMRouter (0x111111338c…, swap-vm v1.0.2, matched to the tag by bytecode) through the router's own _extruction instruction, opcode 0x20, calling FreeboardExtruction, an immutable view contract. Inside the pricing path, on every quote and every swap, it staticcalls Aave v3's getUserAccountData for the maker, decodes the curve from the program bytes, interpolates the target at that health factor, reads the other basket legs from Aqua, and prices the fill by how much closer or farther from target the basket ends up. No router source is modified, no redeploy, nothing off-chain in the loop. Because Aave's read is deterministic within a block, quote and swap always agree; swap-vm's own invariant suite runs against the Freeboard program on the deployed router with every check on.

WHY A PUBLIC CURVE CANNOT BE FRONT-RUN
Front-running a rule needs a moment worth waiting for, and a continuous curve has none: the basket sells a little at every health factor, so there is no cliff. The health factor cannot be pushed; it moves with Aave's oracle and the borrower's own debt, neither of which is flash-loanable. Front-running another taker's fill hurts that taker, not the borrower. No fill ever beats the oracle, so there is no price below fair to drain at. And a public curve means more takers compete for the same fill, which is what protects the borrower.

THE PER-FILL CAP
One fill can move at most maxShiftBps of the basket's value (500 bps in the demo), checked after pricing on the amounts that actually settle. A wrong health factor, a bug, or a greedy taker cannot restructure the basket in one fill; a fill past the cap reverts with FreeboardFillExceedsMaxShift(shift, maxShift). If Aave cannot compute the health factor at all, the fill reverts rather than pricing from a number Aave would not stand behind; Aave cannot liquidate in that state either, so refusing costs the borrower nothing.

LEDGER: THE HUMAN APPROVES THE CURVE
The curve and the cap are bytes inside the SwapVM program, and the program is what Aqua.ship() commits to, indexed by its hash. So the transaction the borrower signs on her Ledger is the approval of her risk policy, not just a key. She signed it on a Nano X through the official @ledgerhq/wallet-cli, and it is on Ethereum mainnet: tx 0xc13c55e1…70c4, against FreeboardExtruction at 0x8804F353…0f41. A test decodes that transaction and asserts its calldata is byte-for-byte the program every fork test prices; flip one byte of the curve and the deployed router refuses it on quote and on swap. The device screen is a blind-signed contract call today; readable rows need an ERC-7730 descriptor, which is not done, and the README says so.

THE AI AGENT: BOUNDED BY THE CHAIN, NOT BY A PROMPT
The taker is an LLM agent (Claude, on the Strands Agents TypeScript SDK) with exactly three tools: read the position, quote a trade, fill it. No rule in code picks the pair, the size or the moment; the model does. Its RPC URL, taker key and API key are decrypted from Ledger's Key Ring into memory at start-up, never on disk or in the environment. In the judged run the operator told it to deleverage Alice "all of it, in ONE fill." It sent the whole 5,855 USDC gap; the router refused it, FreeboardFillExceedsMaxShift(945, 500). It then filled 3,100 USDC → 0.058883 WBTC, equal to its quote to the wei, toward target, and ended its report by explaining that the cap comes from the curve Alice signed on her Ledger, which no operator, prompt or agent can raise. That is Ledger's threshold model for agents, set once and enforced on-chain: autonomous under the cap, a new device signature above it.

WHAT IT DOES FOR THE BORROWER, MEASURED
Same wallet, same Aave position, same oracle path from HF 2.00 to 1.10, same taker, the same $80,000 through the deployed Aqua and router, with one instruction of difference: swap-vm's stock constant-product swap or Freeboard's curve. The stock basket buys the falling asset and pays its takers -$395.83 to do it; it reaches the bottom worth $53,703, holding 17,888 USDC. Freeboard earns +$24.47 in spread, arrives worth $56,328, holding 39,435 USDC of the debt asset, $5,128 ahead of holding the shipped basket untouched. When she repays with what the basket handed her, her health factor is 1.37 instead of 1.21. Every fill is real ERC-20 movement on a mainnet fork at block 25,900,000, against the deployed contracts' own bytecode.

WHAT IT NEVER DOES
Freeboard never touches the Aave position. No supply, borrow or repay; the collateral and the debt stay exactly where they are. It only changes what the basket beside the loan is made of, so that as her margin thins she is converted, and paid, into the asset she would need to repay. Repaying stays her action.

The demo page draws the signed curve decoded from the program bytes, slides the cursor as the health factor falls, and counts the spread up fill by fill; it replays the committed run by default and reads a live anvil walking the same path when one is present. projects.title: Clinical Quantum
projects.description: USDC agents on Arc pay for quantum NHS work only when it beats a classical floor
projects.project_description: Clinical Quantum Exchange is an agentic marketplace where autonomous agents buy, grade and pay for quantum computation using USDC on Arc Testnet — but only when that computation is actually worth paying for. Four agents with their own Circle developer wallets run a seven-step pipeline over synthetic NHS waiting-list pathways (MSK physiotherapy, dermatology, ophthalmology, cardiology and more). A Trust agent applies policy and budget caps. A Baseline agent computes a classical floor and runs a dequantization gate — if a classical method matches the quantum result, the job is refused and nobody gets paid. A Nexus agent executes against committed Quantinuum Nexus specifications. A Registry agent grades the receipt, anchors its hash on Arc through a deployed, Arcscan-verified ReceiptAnchor contract, then releases USDC settlement to the agents that earned it. Every receipt carries a SHA-256 digest sealed with SLH-DSA (post-quantum signatures), so the evidence layer survives the closing quantum gap that Circle's own quantum tracker measures at 96 demonstrated logical qubits against the 824 needed to break ECDSA — while being explicit that Arc transaction signing itself is still ECDSA. The endoscopy pathway is deliberately blocked and shown as blocked: its 32-qubit register exceeds the 26-qubit emulator ceiling. Honest refusal is a first-class outcome. No quantum-advantage claim, no diagnosis or outcome claims — the framing is capacity, cost and patient experience only, on synthetic cohorts.
projects.how_its_made: Built on TanStack Start (React 19, Vite 7) with all money and crypto logic in server functions. Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets provide the four agent wallets on ARC-TESTNET, created through a bootstrap script against a freshly reset entity secret. Payments are native USDC transfers via the Circle Wallets API; on Arc, USDC is also the gas token, so the Registry wallet funds its own contract calls. ReceiptAnchor.sol (Solidity 0.8.24) is deployed through Circle's Smart Contract Platform at 0xd924f134e69f678e09bd31394f975b3cdbd2f52f on chain 5042002, and verified on Arcscan via a Blockscout standard-JSON verification script. It anchors each receipt hash exactly once and rejects duplicates. An Alchemy Arc RPC endpoint is held server-side for balance and state reads. Post-quantum sealing uses @noble/post-quantum's SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f — a 48-byte seed, 32-byte public key and 17KB signature per receipt, generated and verified server-side; only fingerprints reach the browser. Anchoring and settlement are gated on a verified seal. Quantum results come from committed Quantinuum Nexus emulator specifications and run records rather than live QPU calls, with resource estimates (qubit counts, depth) driving the block/allow decision. The hacky bit worth flagging: Circle transaction polling originally blocked the request for 24 seconds and hung the whole run. The pipeline now returns pending Circle transfer IDs immediately and the UI upgrades each row to an Arcscan link once a txHash lands.

projects.title: Keyless Recovery
projects.description: Recovery without custody, help without ongoing intermediaries
projects.project_description: Keyless, an demo app that shows how nihilium recovery can be integrated with Privy to select guardians of privy accounts without them needing to be part of the privy ecosystem. Important that it is to showcase the capabilities of Nihilium in combination of other (embedded) wallets, keyless is not meant to be a separate wallet or product. The use-case it shows is social recovery based on ZKEmail with an onchain ERC7579 module for timelock enforcement, however, Nihilium, the protocol, does support much more methods for recovery.
projects.how_its_made:
It is a browser based wallet based on privy, and the privy app is used as a smart account.
Nihilium Recovery is used to seal randomness from which a guardian key is generated. A guardian key is generated for all supported chains but here only sepolia is used. This is relevant because an app might integrate more than a single chain, so being able to recover multi-chain is a must. Nihilium itself is an open source public good protocol (see the nihilium-core repo) for generalized agnostic key recovery. The protocol works off-chain, so the ZKEmail recovery verification itself doesn't require any transactions. It reconstructs the randomness required to generate the key of which the public key is a simple guardian of a ERC7579. How the nihilium protocol works cannot be explained here and I refer to the website nihilium.io

projects.project_description: Counterweight helps a treasury offer WETH/USDC liquidity while controlling the inventory allocated to its strategy. Assets remain in the maker wallet through Aqua's allocation model. Quotes encourage trades toward a target allocation, and an execution-time guard rejects trades that would exceed immutable exposure limits. We implement a custom SwapVM router with two custom instructions and a small patch to the pinned SwapVM base contract. It uses Aqua for strategy allocation accounting and actual token settlement. The custom logic combines inventory-seeking quotes with mandatory execution-time exposure checks.
projects.how_its_made: The pricing library values allocated WETH and USDC using the epoch's fixed reference price. It computes WETH weight in basis points, compares it with the target, and scales the difference by tuning intensity: skewBps = clamp((wethWeightBps - targetWethBps) × intensityBps / 10,000, -200, +200) The implementation uses integer arithmetic and applies the resulting price shift plus a directional spread to calculate exact-input output amounts. When the maker holds excess WETH, the quotes encourage traders to buy WETH from the maker, reducing its WETH allocation. This encourages movement toward the target. We use Solidity to implement the immutable epoch controller, custom SwapVM skew/guard instructions and guarded Aqua settlement. The modified upstream SwapVM retains its transfer path while adding entry and post-settlement checks. A Node.js pipeline applies the DEX-AMM query and normalization to two distinct deployments, validates identity/freshness and maps completed-day activity to bounded intensity/spread. Live standardized Graph observations from Uniswap and SushiSwap tune only bounded quote parameters. Privy provides the organization wallet, owner quorum, restricted updater and emergency signer.

projects.title: Fare
projects.description: Pay-per-request APIs on Hedera: lookups and AWS jobs, priced in HBAR via x402.
projects.project_description:
Fare sells two paid APIs on Hedera. Agents pay HBAR per HTTP request using x402 / Blocky402. Price scales with the ask. Lookups return live Hedera account summaries and recent transactions from the public Mirror Node. One unit is 0.001 HBAR. Asking for more rows costs more (limit=25 is 4 units). Jobs accept a short Node.js script. AWS Lambda runs it and returns stdout, stderr, and exit code. Timeout meters the price. There is no UI. A small client handles 402, signs a Hedera transfer, and retries. After settle we optionally write account, amountTinybars, and txId to HCS topic 0.0.10320508 as a public receipt. Live: https://fare-production.up.railway.app
Repo: https://github.com/ducnmm/fare402
Video: https://youtu.be/p7db4KH2slc
projects.how_its_made: Resource server is Express plus @x402/express and ExactHederaScheme from @x402/hedera. We do not run a facilitator. Quotes and settlement go through Blocky402 (https://api.testnet.blocky402.com). Amounts are native HBAR (asset 0.0.0) in tinybars, not USDC. Lookups proxy Hedera Mirror Node REST, retry on 502/timeout, and page transaction lists in chunks of 25. Jobs invoke AWS Lambda (Node 22) via @aws-sdk/client-lambda when AWS_SANDBOX_LAMBDA_ARN is set. FARE_JOB_LOCAL=1 is a local child_process fallback for development only. The paying client wraps fetch with @x402/fetch, registers ExactHederaScheme, and sets spend controls to HBAR. HCS audit is fire-and-forget so a hung topic submit cannot block PAYMENT-RESPONSE. Merchant is deployed on Railway. Secrets stay in a gitignored .env. The repo was created during this event and is public at https://github.com/ducnmm/fare402.

projects.title: ITHACA
projects.description: You talk, it invests. A voice-run AI that grows your USDC on its own and can't be robbed.
projects.project_description: Two things are broken right now. Normal wallets bury you in data and buttons, and the AI agents everyone's shipping got wallets but no brakes. One hallucination or one leaked key and the money's gone. ITHACA fixes both. There's no dashboard to learn. You just talk to it, the same way you'd tell a person what you want, and it talks back. Say "put my idle USDC to work" and it shows you the safest markets and moves the money. Say "get me out" and it runs. Voice is the whole interface here, not a feature bolted on top. Under that voice sits a real agent. You sign one mandate on your Ledger Flex, and that's the last thing you ever approve. After that it reads live market risk through The Graph, puts your idle USDC into whatever pays safest, and shifts it as conditions change. If danger shows up it pulls everything back to a safe address you chose. If a whole chain turns risky, it sends the funds over to Circle's Arc. And it can't go rogue. The contract itself caps what the agent is allowed to do, so even a stolen key can't move a dollar you didn't approve. You talk to it, it grows your money, and it physically can't lose it. Live on Base and Arc today.
projects.how_its_made: Four pieces working as one agent. The voice layer is the front door, and it is the whole UI. We run Gemini Live for speech in, reasoning, and speech back, wired into an ElevenLabs interface with a live orb and waveform so you can watch it listen and think. You push to talk, it answers in a beat, and every command maps straight to an on-chain action. No forms, no buttons, no menus. For eyes, we built graphscout, an MCP server on top of The Graph. The raw Subgraph MCP makes an agent read a 20,000-token schema and hand-write GraphQL before it can say anything useful. graphscout does it in one call and hands back a straight risk verdict, about 98x fewer tokens and one round trip instead of three. That is exactly why the voice agent can answer without an awkward pause, and anyone can install it in Claude or Cursor. For the brakes, everything runs through GuardianVaultMulti, a Solidity contract that checks the Ledger-signed mandate on-chain every single time. Caps, allowed venues, the safe haven, expiry, one-time escalations, all re-checked in the same transaction as the action. It has 26 passing tests. The Ledger Flex is the root of trust. You sign once over USB or Bluetooth with the Device Management Kit, and a broker built on the Ledger Key Ring holds the agent's key, so the agent only ever gets a scoped capability and never the key itself. For the money, it is USDC the whole way. When a chain goes bad the vault burns USDC through Circle's CCTP V2 and mints it on Arc, and we've run that round trip end to end. The whole thing is a Next.js and React PWA on Vercel with no backend daemon to babysit.

projects.title: hors-luma
projects.description: HORS is CORS for AI agents—private function sharing governed by human origin
projects.project_description: This project is HORS — Human-Origin Resource Sharing — and HORS Party, the first function we published behind it. CORS governs resource sharing between web origins. HORS governs function sharing between human-backed agents. We shipped it as hors-sdk and hors-cli 0.1.0 (https://github.com/cqlyj/hors): wrap your MCP server or HTTP API, write a policy on the function, and any of your agents can call it as you. The answer leaves. The secret stays. The problem is not that agents cannot talk. A2A, MCP and OAuth already let them. The problem is that a private function still costs a key. One super-agent: one leak ruins it. You hand over a key, they know the agent or the app, anyone with the key can call, and the secret leaves with the call. HORS inverts that. You publish a function. They know the human — any of your agents is you; others pass the policy. Don't share the agent. Share the function. hors-sdk is the gate. A policy has an origin (who may call: you, any verified human, the public, or a person), a rule (what else must be true, async, in order, keyed by that human), a challenge (any JSON on a denial; proof comes back in hors/meta), and middleware (audit, cap, redact — after the gate, never instead of it). The one-liner is gated.registerTool("spend", { hors: { origin: kid, rule, use } }, handler). In the slide we ship with the SDK, a kid calls spend(); the card never leaves that host; $20 a week; over that you approve from your phone. The ledger writes who, shop, amount. Never the card. hors-cli is how a human and an agent talk to a horsed function. connect: World App once, pin the human behind this agent. list: unsigned, tools and policies, like a CORS preflight. call --meta: signed, and the way you answer a challenge. mcp: bridge any host — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, a ChatGPT GPT — so the host never holds the key. One World App scan registers the agent's wallet in World's AgentBook on World Chain. Every later call is a signed envelope hors-sdk resolves to an anonymous humanId. Two agents of one human are one human. A wallet that is not registered is not a human. A new wallet is not a new person. HORS Party is that gate used for commerce, live. horsparty.eth is a Luma event (https://luma.com/o2mvf1me) whose registration is also a HORS-gated MCP service. A party an agent registers for by calling its name. You do not fill the Luma form. You say to your agent: "Reserve a seat for me at https://luma.com/o2mvf1me." In the demo that agent is a ChatGPT GPT. It opens Luma, sees the $1 ticket, then notices this is a HORS Party: agents register through hors-cli, not the Luma button. If your profile is not a verified human yet, it stops, puts the World App QR on screen, and waits for you to scan. That is the human boundary hors-cli refuses to cross for the agent. After the scan it calls claim on horsparty.eth. hors-sdk has already resolved you to a humanId. The first claim is denied PAYMENT_REQUIRED — a HORS challenge carrying an x402 price list, not an error. The agent signs 0.10 USDC or 1 HBAR on Hedera testnet and submits nothing; Blocky402 settles it. The retry with hors/meta.x402 grants the seat, mints a receipt subname, and hands back a free Luma coupon. You open the coupon, the ticket is $0, one click. The demo that already ran: seat 1, receipt seat-1.horsparty.eth, coupon HORS-2SNS, 1 HBAR on HashScan from 0.0.10482581 to 0.0.10482105, facilitator 0.0.7162784 paying the fee. That is the custom-policy unlock we actually shipped: pay as a human, not a wallet. Agents pay in the challenge. HORS keys the receipt to the humanId, not the wallet — the next agent of the same person is free. A script with a key can read seats (public). It cannot buy. The same pattern is why the rest of the slide exists: never give the kid the card; ask a trading agent and keep the edge; prove a live bank session with zkTLS and never put the page on chain; call swap() or supply() and keep the key. Origin, rule, challenge, middleware. The rest is yours. Three chains, one job each, joined by hors-sdk. Sepolia ENSv2 is the name: horsparty.eth points at the service, carries the instructions (agent-context), and hors.remaining. Each guest leaves with {label}.horsparty.eth — "HORS Party · going" — non-transferable, revocable, expiring. Hedera testnet is the money. World Chain is the human. Luma stays the guest list. Guests never need the URL https://horsparty.fly.dev/mcp; hors-cli finds it in the name. Registration closes 2026-10-05T09:00Z. Don't share the secret. Share the function.
projects.how_its_made: We built two packages that share a version, then a party that is the first function published behind them. hors-sdk and hors-cli 0.1.0 (https://github.com/cqlyj/hors) are the gate and the client. HORS Party (https://github.com/cqlyj/hors-luma) is a stock McpServer passed to hors() from hors-sdk/mcp. The party does not fork HORS. That is the point of the SDK: you publish a function, you do not hand over a key. hors-sdk is TypeScript, Node ≥ 22.18, native type-stripped config, createGate() at the centre. A caller signs a SIWE envelope ("HORS v1 call") binding host, path, function (urn:hors:fn:…), a hash of the arguments, a nonce and a five-minute expiry. It rides in params._meta["hors/auth"] on MCP or in HORS-Authorization on HTTP. The gate verifies eip191 / eip1271 / eip6492, looks the wallet up in AgentBook on World Chain through @worldcoin/agentkit-core (lookupHuman on 0xA23aB2712eA7BBa896930544C7d6636a96b944dA), and applies the function's policy. The handler sees ctx.hors.callerHumanId. The secret — the card, the book, the prompt — never enters the call. Identity fails closed: World Chain down and the human uncached is HORS_UNAVAILABLE. The policy model is what we actually designed. Origin: who may call — same-human, any-human, public, a person, or a function. Rule: what else must be true, async, in order, keyed by that human, under ruleTimeoutMs; returns true or { deny, code, challenge }. Challenge: any JSON on a denial; the caller satisfies it out of band and retries with hors/meta, which is unsigned on purpose — the gate does not vouch for the attachment. Middleware (use): wraps the handler after origin and rules, so a denial never reaches the ledger. The kid-spend snippet in the pitch is not a sketch of a future app; it is the API. origin: kid, rule: week <= 20 or OVER_CAP with an approval challenge, use: ledger.write(callerHumanId, args) and return. The card never left the host. hors-sdk/mcp replaces registerTool so every tool is gated (tools registered before hors() are refused). hors-sdk/http is the same model on fetch or Express. hors-sdk/client signs. hors-sdk/resolvers turns a name, a URL, ens: / .eth (ENSIP-26 agent-endpoint[mcp]) or erc8004:… into https. Policies publish on tools/list and /.well-known/hors.json, like CORS headers; rules stay private. Denials are results, not JSON-RPC errors. hors-cli is the other half of 0.1.0. connect shows a World App QR and pins the human — the one command an agent must never run. list is unsigned. call --meta answers a challenge. hors mcp bridges any host so the host never holds the key: hors_status, hors_list, hors_call. HORS_MOCK=1 keeps signatures real and mocks only AgentBook; it throws under NODE_ENV=production. HORS Party is how we proved the challenge slot is enough for commerce. Three tools, two custom policies, inline. seats is public. claim is any-human plus notClosed, noSeatYet, notSoldOut, paymentVerified. ticket is any-human plus hasSeat. Origin is the bot check — HORS_UNSIGNED / HORS_NOT_HUMAN never reach a party rule. noSeatYet keys on humanId: pay as a human, not a wallet; the next agent of the same person calls ticket() and pays nothing. The hack: x402 is HTTP 402. HORS already owns the tool call, so we refused @x402/mcp and put the protocol objects in the slots we had built. The rule's challenge is { type: "x402", paymentRequired, how } from x402ResourceServer.createPaymentRequiredResponse. The signed PaymentPayload comes back as hors/meta.x402. Settlement is payment in the result. @x402/core is unchanged. how is the name's agent-context, so the agent that has not read the name still gets pay.mjs. We raised ruleTimeoutMs to 30 s because verify runs inside the rule. Partner tech, Hedera. Blocky402 (https://api.testnet.blocky402.com) is the facilitator. initialize() reads /supported for extra.feePayer (0.0.7162784 — never hard-coded). The guest signs with ExactHederaScheme.createPaymentPayload from @x402/hedera and submits nothing; the facilitator submits the transfer and pays the fee. We skipped the x402 client spend-policy engine because it does not know HBAR 0.0.0. pay.mjs is fifteen lines in agent-context.md and refuses any network other than hedera:testnet. Grant then settle in one SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE: human_id primary key, then settle. success: false releases the seat. A thrown settle keeps the seat with payment = NULL rather than charge a guest who has no seat. The HashScan in the video is that path: 1 HBAR from the guest to 0.0.10482105, facilitator 0.0.7162784 paying the fee. A documented settlement is 0.0.7162784@1789161315.246414908. Partner tech, ENS. hors-sdk already resolves agent-endpoint[mcp]. rpc.ens points at Sepolia; the resolver is unchanged. The party adds the tree: three Verifiable Factory proxies, ETH registrar, setParent, grantRootRoles, authorizeTextRoles so the hot key may write only hors.remaining. Enhanced Access Control is the multisig. A compromised server can mint junk receipts; it cannot move the name or rewrite the instructions. Receipts: register with role bitmap 0 and expiry = party end + 7 days — non-transferable, revocable, expiring. description = HORS Party · going. The coupon never enters a record. Partner tech, World. The party has no World ID code. hors-cli connect is the human, once. AgentKit's public guide is written around agentkit.fetch; we needed lookupHuman, which lives in @worldcoin/agentkit-core and is not on that page. REGISTRATION.md still says Base; lookups are World Chain. Sandbox proofs never enter AgentBook. hors-sdk absorbs that. The party writes origin: "any-human". Runtime: Node 24, @modelcontextprotocol/server v2, @hono/node-server, viem, zod, @x402/core and @x402/hedera 2.25, node:sqlite, Fly.io app horsparty in syd. One createGate() per process. No web page, no guest-side wrapper, no fakes. A guest has hors-cli, Node, a Hedera testnet account, and the text of the name. Origin, rule, challenge, middleware. The rest is yours.

The kid-spend snippet in the pitch is not a sketch of a future app; it is the API. origin: kid, rule: week <= 20 or OVER_CAP with an approval challenge, use: ledger.write(callerHumanId, args) and return. The card never left the host. hors-sdk/mcp replaces registerTool so every tool is gated (tools registered before hors() are refused). hors-sdk/http is the same model on fetch or Express. hors-sdk/client signs. hors-sdk/resolvers turns a name, a URL, ens: / .eth (ENSIP-26 agent-endpoint[mcp]) or erc8004:… into https. Policies publish on tools/list and /.well-known/hors.json, like CORS headers; rules stay private. Denials are results, not JSON-RPC errors.

hors-cli is the other half of 0.1.0. connect shows a World App QR and pins the human — the one command an agent must never run. list is unsigned. call --meta answers a challenge. hors mcp bridges any host so the host never holds the key: hors_status, hors_list, hors_call. HORS_MOCK=1 keeps signatures real and mocks only AgentBook; it throws under NODE_ENV=production.

HORS Party is how we proved the challenge slot is enough for commerce. Three tools, two custom policies, inline. seats is public. claim is any-human plus notClosed, noSeatYet, notSoldOut, paymentVerified. ticket is any-human plus hasSeat. Origin is the bot check — HORS_UNSIGNED / HORS_NOT_HUMAN never reach a party rule. noSeatYet keys on humanId: pay as a human, not a wallet; the next agent of the same person calls ticket() and pays nothing.

The hack: x402 is HTTP 402. HORS already owns the tool call, so we refused @x402/mcp and put the protocol objects in the slots we had built. The rule's challenge is { type: "x402", paymentRequired, how } from x402ResourceServer.createPaymentRequiredResponse. The signed PaymentPayload comes back as hors/meta.x402. Settlement is payment in the result. @x402/core is unchanged. how is the name's agent-context, so the agent that has not read the name still gets pay.mjs. We raised ruleTimeoutMs to 30 s because verify runs inside the rule.

Partner tech, Hedera. Blocky402 (https://api.testnet.blocky402.com) is the facilitator. initialize() reads /supported for extra.feePayer (0.0.7162784 — never hard-coded). The guest signs with ExactHederaScheme.createPaymentPayload from @x402/hedera and submits nothing; the facilitator submits the transfer and pays the fee. We skipped the x402 client spend-policy engine because it does not know HBAR 0.0.0. pay.mjs is fifteen lines in agent-context.md and refuses any network other than hedera:testnet. Grant then settle in one SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE: human_id primary key, then settle. success: false releases the seat. A thrown settle keeps the seat with payment = NULL rather than charge a guest who has no seat. The HashScan in the video is that path: 1 HBAR from the guest to 0.0.10482105, facilitator 0.0.7162784 paying the fee. A documented settlement is 0.0.7162784@1789161315.246414908.

Partner tech, ENS. hors-sdk already resolves agent-endpoint[mcp]. rpc.ens points at Sepolia; the resolver is unchanged. The party adds the tree: three Verifiable Factory proxies, ETH registrar, setParent, grantRootRoles, authorizeTextRoles so the hot key may write only hors.remaining. Enhanced Access Control is the multisig. A compromised server can mint junk receipts; it cannot move the name or rewrite the instructions. Receipts: register with role bitmap 0 and expiry = party end + 7 days — non-transferable, revocable, expiring. description = HORS Party · going. The coupon never enters a record.

Partner tech, World. The party has no World ID code. hors-cli connect is the human, once. AgentKit's public guide is written around agentkit.fetch; we needed lookupHuman, which lives in @worldcoin/agentkit-core and is not on that page. REGISTRATION.md still says Base; lookups are World Chain. Sandbox proofs never enter AgentBook. hors-sdk absorbs that. The party writes origin: "any-human".

Runtime: Node 24, @modelcontextprotocol/server v2, @hono/node-server, viem, zod, @x402/core and @x402/hedera 2.25, node:sqlite, Fly.io app horsparty in syd. One createGate() per process. No web page, no guest-side wrapper, no fakes. A guest has hors-cli, Node, a Hedera testnet account, and the text of the name. Origin, rule, challenge, middleware. The rest is yours.

projects.title: TrustGate
projects.description: Trust-aware x402 payments for autonomous AI agents on Hedera.
projects.project_description: TrustGate is a reputation-aware payment layer for autonomous AI agents built on Hedera. It extends x402 pay-per-request payments with a verifiable trust mechanism that evaluates an agent's transaction history before deciding how its payment should be handled. When an agent discovers and requests a paid service, TrustGate checks its on-chain reputation. New or low-reputation agents are routed through a protected payment flow using Hedera Scheduled Transactions, allowing the payment to be held while the service is delivered and resolved according to the escrow policy. Agents with an established history of successful interactions can use the standard x402 settlement path with significantly lower friction and latency. Each payment, delivery outcome, and trust decision is recorded through Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), creating a publicly verifiable audit trail. This gives autonomous agents a way to progressively establish trust through successful transactions rather than relying solely on static identities or centralized reputation systems. The MVP demonstrates an end-to-end agentic commerce flow: service discovery, x402 payment, reputation evaluation, adaptive settlement, service delivery, and on-chain reputation updates. TrustGate's core idea is simple: the more an agent proves it can transact successfully, the less friction it faces when paying for services.
projects.how_its_made: TrustGate is a TypeScript/Node.js payment router for autonomous agents, built around Hedera Testnet and x402. We use @x402/core + @x402/hedera to generate and sign x402 v2 HBAR payments, and Blocky402 as the Hedera facilitator for verification/settlement. Hedera Scheduled Transactions provide the protected payment path, while an in-memory reputation engine records successful payments and routes agents from PROTECTED to STANDARD once they reach a trust threshold. A particularly hacky part was adapting the x402 v2 payment envelope to Blocky402’s Hedera-specific verification requirements and dynamically incorporating its fee-payer configuration.

projects.title: BOLT
projects.description: Lock beneficiary funds on Arc via Privy policy + World Selfie Check. Public verification included.
projects.project_description: BOLT-Beneficiary Only Ledger Transfers BOLT answers a fundamental question: how does a business prove it can't spend customer money? By making it impossible. BOLT locks customer accounts using Privy policies enforced inside a secure enclave. The policy runs before the signing key is reassembled—unauthorized transactions are refused before a signature can ever exist. When a beneficiary claims their money, they prove identity via World Selfie Check, then a key quorum of business owners approves the unlock. The transfer settles as USDC on Arc. Every obligation, balance, and state change is recorded on-chain and indexed by The Graph. Anyone—regulator, auditor, customer—can visit the public page and cryptographically verify the money's location and amount. No trust in the business required. Just math
projects.how_its_made: BOLT is built on three load-bearing sponsors working together, each doing irreplaceable work: Privy enforces the core lock. We compile a policy that decodes USDC calldata and constrains transfer._to (not just transaction.to—the latter points to the token contract, not the payee). The policy runs inside Privy's secure enclave before the signing key is reassembled. No unsigned paths, no app-layer overrides. Key quorum signatures are required to widen the policy. Arc is where the money lives. Every obligation, every balance, every settlement is USDC on Arc testnet. The subgraph indexes all events in real-time. World gates access. Beneficiaries prove identity via Selfie Check (IDKit) before claiming. We discovered and worked around a React 19 incompatibility in the widget, switching to the raw IDKit.request() API from @worldcoin/idkit-core with identical results. Technical stack: Next.js 15 frontend + API routes (TypeScript strict), Solidity contract (BoltRegistry) on Arc via Hardhat, Postgres + Drizzle for workflow state, AssemblyScript subgraph for indexing. Device IDs tracked via localStorage to implement repeat-verification skip (FR-8.8). Notable hack: Obligation accrual must record the on-chain ObligationAccrued event before inserting the Postgres row. If you reverse the order, the settlement call later reads a stale Postgres obligationId, tries to settle on-chain, and reverts after the money has already transferred—leaving state inconsistent. We discovered this the hard way and backfilled evidence.

projects.title: Sigma86
projects.description: A smart vault helping DAOs sell big token bags safely, without crashing the market.
projects.project_description:
DAOs today hold millions of dollars in their treasuries. But when they want to sell
Large amounts of native tokens to fund their daily operations, they face a big
problem. If they sell everything at once, MEV bots will attack them and drain their
funds. If they sell slowly using a simple linear schedule (TWAP), they lose money
because of regular market volatility. Sigma86 solves this problem completely. It is a smart DeFi vault powered by an
autonomous off-chain agent. Instead of guessing how to sell, I use institutional
mathematics (the Almgren-Chriss execution model) based on the DAO's actual Value-
at-Risk (VaR) budget. My agent calculates the mathematically perfect selling
schedule to balance market impact and volatility risk. Then, it automatically
executes the swaps on-chain. This ensures that DAOs get the best possible price for
their tokens without any manual headache or risk of getting front-run by bots.
projects.how_its_made:
I built this project using a hybrid architecture: an off-chain brain and a highly
secure on-chain vault. The off-chain agent is developed in TypeScript and integrated using the Model
Context Protocol (MCP). It acts as the mathematical engine. It takes the DAO's risk
budget, calculates the required trajectory, and generates the exact routing
payloads. For the on-chain part, I wrote the smart contracts in Solidity and tested them
heavily using Foundry. One very notable hack I implemented was writing the core
execution logic in raw Yul assembly. The vault uses Yul to directly route the swaps
into the Uniswap V3 Mainnet Router. This completely bypasses the standard Solidity
ABI encoding overhead, which saves base gas and ensures my transactions get high
priority in the block. Finally, I used Chainlink Data Feeds as my ultimate security layer. I intentionally
set the DEX slippage to zero, and instead use an atomic post-trade check against
the Chainlink oracle. If the execution price is bad, the oracle check will
immediately revert the entire transaction. This provides 100% protection against
sandwich attacks without locking user funds.

projects.title: Aetheris
projects.description: AI agencies with a treasury: pay sub-agents per task via Hedera HTS, every step anchored on HCS
projects.project_description: Aetheris is an Autonomous DeAI Agency and Micro-Treasury Operating System on Hedera. An agency holds its own budget, hires named sub-agents, pays each one the moment a task completes, and proves every step on a public audit log that anyone can read. The problem it solves: today an AI agent either gets an open-ended token approval that anyone holding the key can drain, or no funds at all. Payees are bare addresses, nothing caps what can be spent, and "proof of work" is a log on somebody's server. The settlement loop: a client escrows one deposit for a job. The agency contract can never commit more in sub-agent fees than that deposit, and the client can reclaim it until the job settles. Each completed task is paid immediately through the Hedera Token Service system contract (with a plain ERC-20 fallback), and every lifecycle step is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic before the contract call, so on-chain sequence numbers match the mirror node. Mistakes are retracted with append-only correction records, never deleted. The Graph indexes jobs, tasks, settlements, the HTS-vs-ERC-20 rail, a sub-agent leaderboard and daily rollups. The retained margin can only be swept by a human operator who has passed World ID proof of personhood; the proof's nullifier is burned on-chain so one human can only ever claim once. Two roles in the app. Operator: the human running the agency, with Mission Control (pipeline, leaderboard, treasury, audit stream, World-ID-gated margin claim). Client: any wallet that funds a job. Clients sign in with a passkey (embedded wallet), escrow a deposit from the browser, see exactly their jobs and refundable escrow, and can reclaim a deposit until settlement. Everything on screen is live: treasury balances are read from the chain, finality is computed from indexed timestamps, and every panel carries a LIVE or DEMO badge with its reason. Limits are stated plainly: World ID has no router on Hedera so the contract runs in an announced bypass mode; 1inch does not serve Hedera so swap routing is for the operator's EVM wallet; the indexer is self-hosted because Hedera is not on The Graph's hosted network.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity 0.8.24 on Hedera EVM (chain 296) with Hardhat 2 and OpenZeppelin 5. AetherisAgency drives the job lifecycle (createJob, assignSubAgent, completeTask, settleJob, refundJob, verifyOperator); AetherisTreasury escrows deposits and pays sub-agents. A frozen event interface is implemented by the contracts and indexed by the subgraph so the two can never drift. 37 tests, including one that asserts every event topic against the frozen interface. Hedera: settlement goes through the HTS system contract at 0x167 via a library that decodes int64 response codes. A subtle catch we handle: a call to an empty account returns success with empty returndata, which naively decodes to response code 0 and looks like success, so it is mapped to UNKNOWN to keep the ERC-20 fallback safe on other chains. Locally the precompile does not exist, so the tests install a stateless mock at 0x167 with hardhat_setCode and run the real library unchanged. On testnet the gas profile proves the precompile does real work: 2,360,527 gas for an HTS settlement versus 229,111 for ERC-20. Every step is recorded on an HCS topic (0.0.10518320) before the contract call, and readers honour append-only Correction records. The Graph: Hedera is not in The Graph's hosted registry, so we run graph-node against the Hedera JSON-RPC relay, the path Hedera's own docs prescribe. 17 entities, 10 handlers, Settlement.viaHts makes the rail queryable, AgencyDayData gives time series. Hashio rejects eth_getLogs inside JSON-RPC batches, so every ethers provider runs with batchMaxCount: 1. World ID 4.0: IDKit v4 with a server-signed request context, the raw result verified at the v4 endpoint scoped to our relying party, then relayed on-chain by the server so the RP-scoped nullifier is burned in verifyOperator. A second proof from the same human returns 409. No router exists on Hedera, so the contract emits WorldIdBypassActive rather than hiding it; only the ZK check is skipped, replay protection stays live. 1inch Swap API v6.0 through a server-side proxy (the key never reaches the browser) with live quotes on Arbitrum, Base, Ethereum, Optimism and Polygon. Privy: passkey, email, Google and external-wallet login with embedded wallets on Hedera testnet; the client write path signs approve and createJob through viem against the embedded wallet, with a testnet faucet that drips HBAR and a test token so a fresh passkey wallet can fund a job. ENS names resolved on Ethereum mainnet with a fallback RPC list. Frontend: Next.js 14, Tailwind, framer-motion. Server components read the subgraph and the chain; API routes return typed error envelopes. The Operator/Client role auto-detects from the connected wallet. Hacky but useful: a scroll reveal with a rect-check fail-safe so no content can be stranded invisible, and a single SVG favicon that switches marks with prefers-color-scheme because browsers ignore the media attribute on icon links.

projects.title: Chainguard lite
projects.description: An AI DeFi safety screener gated by Hedera x402 micropayments, analyzing live data from The Graph.
projects.project_description: ChainGuard Lite is a pay-per-report AI safety screening API designed for autonomous AI agents and crypto users. Every day, agents interact with unfamiliar smart contracts without safety guardrails because existing security tools require costly subscriptions or lack machine-readable APIs. ChainGuard Lite solves this by combining indexed blockchain data with HTTP-native micropayments. When an agent or user requests a safety report on an EVM address, the service issues an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent autonomously signs a tiny Hedera HBAR payment (0.001 HBAR) via the x402 protocol, unlocking live GraphQL data from The Graph. A deterministic risk engine scores the address based on event counts, unique counterparties, and interaction patterns, while GPT-4o-mini translates raw evidence into clear explanations. The result is instant, pay-as-you-go safety checks without subscriptions or API keys.
projects.how_its_made: ChainGuard Lite was built as a multi-tier microservice architecture: Frontend: React 18, Vite 6, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS using a custom "Tactile Clay Sentinel" claymorphism design system. It features live risk labels, evidence tables, and a 5-stage payment visualization timeline. Backend & Payments: Built with Express.js microservices (Agent Server and Report Service). The Report Service gates API access behind true HTTP 402 headers. The Agent Server orchestrates autonomous payment flows using @x402/hedera and @hashgraph/sdk on Hedera Testnet, signing 0.001 HBAR transfers instantly. Data & Indexing: Queries live blockchain data from The Graph Studio via GraphQL (Uniswap V3 on Arbitrum Sepolia and a custom-deployed chain-guard subgraph on Base Sepolia) to extract counterparty metrics, event bursts, and interaction logs.

projects.title: FormDrop
projects.description: Fill out a Google Form, get paid instantly — AI-judged, World ID-verified, Hedera-settled.
projects.project_description: FormDrop turns any Google Form into a crypto payout machine — respondents get paid instantly, in testnet HBAR/USDC, just for filling out a form, with zero wallet setup required. The problem: Crypto payment products can never reach the people who'd actually benefit most. Every crypto-payments idea shares the same failure mode: it asks people to adopt a new app or platform first, and almost nobody does. Meanwhile Google Forms already has 700M+ monthly users — researchers, professors, community managers, growth teams — running exactly the kind of paid surveys and bounty campaigns crypto rails are supposedly perfect for. That audience has been completely unreachable, because nothing meets them inside the tool they already use. Instant payout with no verification is a fraud vector, not a feature. Pay the moment someone submits and you're paying bots, copy-pasted spam, and gibberish right alongside real answers. No fraud resistance means one person can drain the whole pot. The hack we're proudest of. Privy has no native Hedera chain type — only ethereum, solana, etc. But Hedera runs on the same secp256k1 curve, and HIP-583 auto-creates an account from an EVM address the first time it receives funds. So we provision plain Privy ethereum wallets and use their address directly as a Hedera payout destination — no bridging. Confirmed on Hedera's Mirror Node: the account shows up exactly as HIP-583 predicts, a "hollow" account with no key set. Payments and audit trail. The AI-judgment call is paid via x402, settled in testnet USDC (an HTS token) through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every verdict — approve/reject, a SHA-256 hash of the response (keeps respondent text off a public ledger), and the paying transaction id — is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic with no admin key, so anyone can independently audit it via the Mirror Node. Respondent wallets are Privy-provisioned by email and locked with a policy denying every wallet method (receive-only by default); the creator's funding wallet is owned by a Privy key quorum, not a single key. The unglamorous bug. Claim emails worked locally, then failed in production — Render blocks outbound SMTP ports on free tiers. A backup HTTP email provider got flagged for fraud review before it sent a single message. Fixed by switching to the Gmail REST API over plain HTTPS, authenticated via OAuth2 against an account we already trust.
