projects.title: Recon
projects.description: Verifies what AI agents claim vs. what they actually did — and what their mandate allowed.
projects.project_description:
RECON — Mandate Reconciliation for AI Agents Everyone is putting leashes on AI agents (spending caps, allowlists, session keys), but almost nobody verifies that the leash actually holds. RECON is a reconciliation layer that answers that question, rather than being yet another agent wallet. RECON reconciles three views of the same agent activity and turns any disagreement into independently re-verifiable evidence: Claimed — what the agent says it did (query, payment, action), recorded as HCS messages with canonical hashes. Actual — what really happened on-chain, read from PolicyVault execution events and Hedera transactions. Allowed — the mandate that was in effect at the moment of execution: budget cap, recipient allowlist, and deadline. Five deterministic rules (R1–R5) compare these three columns using one shared pure-TypeScript core: replaying a The Graph query at a pinned deployment and final block, checking each executed action against the mandate valid at that moment, verifying the claimed vs. actual executed set, validating HCS message ordering via a correlation state machine, and matching payment claims against settlement receipts. Any inconsistency produces a MISMATCH with a
deterministically derived evidenceHash; a down external service produces UNVERIFIABLE rather than being silently
passed or failed. The agent runs on a restricted signer with no owner keys: it performs a live The Graph query, pays an x402-gated RECON
verify-query API settled on Hedera testnet, selects a bounded action, executes through an on-chain PolicyVault (HBAR
budget, allowlist, deadline, stake), and publishes its evidence to an HCS topic under a single correlation ID. A public verifier — the same code the agent used — then replays everything from the Hedera mirror node, the Graph
gateway, and payment receipts, and presents the Claimed / Actual / Allowed reconciliation in both a CLI and a React
panel. Everything runs live against real services (real HCS messages, real vault transactions, real 402 payments) with no mocks presented as evidence.
projects.how_its_made:
RECON is TypeScript end to end, with one Solidity contract. The central design decision is that verification is a pure
function: src/core holds the canonicalization, SHA-256 hashing (via @noble/hashes), correlation state machine, and the R1–R5 reconciliation rules, and it never touches the network, environment variables, wallets, or the UI. Vendor
behavior lives behind narrow adapters (src/adapters/thegraph, src/adapters/blocky402, src/adapters/hcs), and module boundaries are enforced by ESLint import rules. The payoff: the agent and the public verifier literally run the same
code, so CLI/Web parity is structural rather than something we tested into existence by hand. The on-chain side is a PolicyVault in Solidity 0.8.34, compiled with Hardhat 3 and driven through viem over the Hedera
JSON-RPC relay. It separates owner / agent / verifier / operator roles, enforces an HBAR budget cap, recipient
allowlist, and deadline before any transfer, isolates the operator's pre-funded stake from the vault principal, and exposes a kill-switch that makes the next agent action revert with NotActive. Seven Solidity tests cover the mandate,
roles, stake isolation, slashing, and the freeze. The application layer is strict TypeScript (Node ≥ 22.13) with zod validating every JSON boundary, a Vite 8 + React 19
panel, and tsx-run scripts for probes and the live demo. The browser demo drives the whole loop through a single
backend process — Graph query → x402 payment → DeepSeek rationale → vault execute → five HCS events → verify — so no browser wallet is needed; slash and freeze are signed server-side from .env keys. The frontend implements no rules of
its own; it renders the same LiveSnapshot the CLI verifier emits. Partner technologies, load-bearing: Hedera — @hashgraph/sdk publishes the HCS evidence timeline under one correlation ID and reads it back from the
mirror node; PolicyVault runs on testnet (chain 296). The Graph — a GraphQL query drives the agent's decision and is replayed at a pinned deployment + final block as R1
evidence, using the same canonicalization and hash. x402 / Blocky402 — the verify-query API returns a 402 with exact/hedera:testnet requirements; the agent pays through
the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies and settles, and the response carries the on-chain settlement reference. Payment success is deliberately independent of verification pass. DeepSeek V4 Flash — picks between bounded EXECUTE_VAULT / STOP and writes a short rationale. The LLM never computes
an amount, address, hash, or policy result; that's all deterministic code. Notable/hacky bits: the x402 payment header is generated in memory inside the same code path the web server uses, so
the demo needs no separate api:start process or header round-trip. Hedera's public relay rejects wide eth_getLogs spans, so verify:live starts its vault-log scan at the vault's deploy block (resolved from the mirror node). We hit
the weibar-vs-tinybar trap — msg.value-style amounts are 18-decimal weibar while calldata amounts are 8-decimal tinybar — and handle both explicitly. And when The Graph gateway prunes historical _meta.block.hash, we record it as
null rather than fabricate it. Development was AI-assisted and disclosed; a human set scope and reviewed every change.

projects.title: Bajigur
projects.description: Design prompts marketplace an AI agent can buy on its own, one payment per prompt, settled on Hedera
projects.project_description: Bajigur is a shop for motion and web design prompts where the buyer can be a person or the AI agent working for them. Every prompt carries its own price, usually a few cents, and you pay for the one you use instead of a monthly plan. For a person it works like any website. You sign in with an email, Privy creates the wallet for you, we create and fund your Hedera account, and you claim a free name under bajigur.eth, for example claude.bajigur.eth. Buying is one button. There is no seed phrase to write down, no browser extension to install, and no signing popup on every purchase. For an agent it is three tools over MCP. Paste https://mcp.bajigur.xyz/mcp into Claude Desktop, Claude Code or Cursor and the agent can search the catalogue, list the prompts your wallet already owns, and fetch one. When it fetches a prompt you have not bought, the server answers with a payment request over x402, the agent pays on Hedera, and the text comes back in the same response with the transaction id attached. Nothing is cloned, nothing is installed, and no private key sits on the machine. The money goes straight to the creator. Their payout account is not stored in our database; it is the bajigur.hedera text record on their ENS name, read at the moment payment is quoted, so a creator changes where their next payment lands by editing a record they own. Every purchase mints an ERC-1155 licence to the buyer, so the same prompt is free to read again from any client afterwards, and that licence is what grants access rather than a row in our database. Creators build a public record too. A buyer who holds a licence can rate the creator, and the rating is written to the ERC-8004 reputation registry on Hedera, signed and paid by the buyer's own wallet so it cannot be faked by us or by the creator. The score comes back in the catalogue listing, which means an agent comparing two prompts can weigh who wrote them without a second lookup. Everything runs on public testnets and can be checked by anyone. The x402 challenge, the catalogue, the creator profiles and the discovery feed are all open endpoints, and docs/verify.md in the repo is a list of copy and paste commands that verify each claim against Hedera and Sepolia directly.
projects.how_its_made: The repo is a Bun workspace monorepo driven by Turborepo, around 9,300 lines of TypeScript and Solidity across 100 source files, plus the tests. apps/api is Bun with Hono. It is an x402 v2 resource server built on @x402/hono over @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Only GET /prompts/:id/unlock is paid; the price and the payTo are resolved per request from the prompt itself, so each creator is paid directly instead of through a platform account. Published prompt bodies live in Postgres on Railway, where the API is deployed. apps/mcp is the MCP server, Streamable HTTP and stateless, carrying the x402 client. It runs two ways: locally over stdio with your own Hedera key, or hosted at mcp.bajigur.xyz where you sign in with OAuth and the API signs for you, so the machine holds no key at all. apps/web and apps/landingpage are Next.js 16 with React 19, the React Compiler and Tailwind v4, on Vercel. contracts is Foundry: PromptRegistry, an ERC-1155 that records listings and issues licences, on Hedera testnet, and BajigurRegistrar, our ENSv2 registrar, on Sepolia. Both are verified. Hedera. Every prompt is priced twice, in USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) and in HBAR, and both appear in the 402 so the client chooses which asset to spend. After settlement the API writes one JSON record to an HCS topic and mints the licence. Contracts never sit in the payment path, because an x402 payTo on Hedera has to be a 0.0.x account and not a contract, so the facilitator settles a plain HTS transfer and the contract only records what happened afterwards. A returning buyer is checked with balanceOf through the mirror node's free contracts/call endpoint, so proving you already own something costs nothing and skips the 402 entirely. Privy. The user grants our signer on their embedded wallet, the API creates and funds their Hedera account and associates USDC, and from then on signs their x402 payments with secp256k1_sign. That is what removes the wallet popup from the purchase, and it is also what lets someone who has never held a token buy a prompt. ENS. bajigur.eth has its own ENSv2 subregistry on Sepolia behind BajigurRegistrar, which enforces the rules in Solidity: one free name per wallet, three to thirty-two characters, ten years. claimFor registers the name to the user's own wallet and writes their Hedera account into the bajigur.hedera record in the same transaction, with the platform paying the Sepolia gas, because a name without that record would send the owner's buyers to us by mistake. ERC-8004. Identity and reputation registries are already deployed on Hedera testnet as singletons, so this is Hedera and ERC-8004 at once, with HBAR for gas and HashScan for the receipts. The first time somebody rates a creator we mint their agent, write their ENS name into its onchain metadata, hand the token to the creator's own wallet, and write erc8004 onto their ENS name, so name and agent point at each other in both directions. Four things that cost us real time and are worth writing down. HBAR payments were refused while the account held 107 HBAR. The x402 client's default spend controls allow stablecoins only, and that filter runs before our payment selector, so the HBAR option was already gone by the time we tried to pick it. We proved it by running both versions against the real 402 and printing what each chose. The fix is one shared policy that names HBAR in allowedAssets and selects it, used by the MCP wallet and the web path alike. Privy's embedded wallets run in a TEE, where delegateWallet throws. The TEE equivalent is addSigners with a key quorum id, which is what we call, and it is idempotent, so reconnecting a wallet that is already granted is safe. Privy policies cannot gate secp256k1_sign, so spend caps could not live in Privy. Our API decodes the Hedera transaction body before signing and refuses anything that does not debit the user's own account, credit a known creator payout account, and stay under the cap baked into that user's token. The hosted MCP server does OAuth, and the first version kept registered clients and authorization codes in memory. That works in dev and fails in production, where every request can land on a different serverless instance: a client registered seconds earlier came back as invalid_client. Both are now self-contained strings sealed with AES-256-GCM, so any instance can serve any request, and we verified it by registering, waiting, and probing again. One last note on the browser. The x402 challenge travels in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header, and the API deliberately does not list it in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, so a page cannot read it cross-origin. The web app therefore runs the entire payment inside a route handler, which has the useful side effect of keeping the agent token in an httpOnly cookie and the Hedera SDK out of the client bundle.

apps/web and apps/landingpage are Next.js 16 with React 19, the React Compiler and Tailwind v4, on Vercel. contracts is Foundry: PromptRegistry, an ERC-1155 that records listings and issues licences, on Hedera testnet, and BajigurRegistrar, our ENSv2 registrar, on Sepolia. Both are verified.

Hedera. Every prompt is priced twice, in USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) and in HBAR, and both appear in the 402 so the client chooses which asset to spend. After settlement the API writes one JSON record to an HCS topic and mints the licence. Contracts never sit in the payment path, because an x402 payTo on Hedera has to be a 0.0.x account and not a contract, so the facilitator settles a plain HTS transfer and the contract only records what happened afterwards. A returning buyer is checked with balanceOf through the mirror node's free contracts/call endpoint, so proving you already own something costs nothing and skips the 402 entirely.

Privy. The user grants our signer on their embedded wallet, the API creates and funds their Hedera account and associates USDC, and from then on signs their x402 payments with secp256k1_sign. That is what removes the wallet popup from the purchase, and it is also what lets someone who has never held a token buy a prompt.

ENS. bajigur.eth has its own ENSv2 subregistry on Sepolia behind BajigurRegistrar, which enforces the rules in Solidity: one free name per wallet, three to thirty-two characters, ten years. claimFor registers the name to the user's own wallet and writes their Hedera account into the bajigur.hedera record in the same transaction, with the platform paying the Sepolia gas, because a name without that record would send the owner's buyers to us by mistake.

ERC-8004. Identity and reputation registries are already deployed on Hedera testnet as singletons, so this is Hedera and ERC-8004 at once, with HBAR for gas and HashScan for the receipts. The first time somebody rates a creator we mint their agent, write their ENS name into its onchain metadata, hand the token to the creator's own wallet, and write erc8004 onto their ENS name, so name and agent point at each other in both directions.

Four things that cost us real time and are worth writing down.

HBAR payments were refused while the account held 107 HBAR. The x402 client's default spend controls allow stablecoins only, and that filter runs before our payment selector, so the HBAR option was already gone by the time we tried to pick it. We proved it by running both versions against the real 402 and printing what each chose. The fix is one shared policy that names HBAR in allowedAssets and selects it, used by the MCP wallet and the web path alike.

Privy's embedded wallets run in a TEE, where delegateWallet throws. The TEE equivalent is addSigners with a key quorum id, which is what we call, and it is idempotent, so reconnecting a wallet that is already granted is safe.

Privy policies cannot gate secp256k1_sign, so spend caps could not live in Privy. Our API decodes the Hedera transaction body before signing and refuses anything that does not debit the user's own account, credit a known creator payout account, and stay under the cap baked into that user's token.

The hosted MCP server does OAuth, and the first version kept registered clients and authorization codes in memory. That works in dev and fails in production, where every request can land on a different serverless instance: a client registered seconds earlier came back as invalid_client. Both are now self-contained strings sealed with AES-256-GCM, so any instance can serve any request, and we verified it by registering, waiting, and probing again.

One last note on the browser. The x402 challenge travels in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header, and the API deliberately does not list it in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, so a page cannot read it cross-origin. The web app therefore runs the entire payment inside a route handler, which has the useful side effect of keeping the agent token in an httpOnly cookie and the Hedera SDK out of the client bundle.

projects.title: Agent Insure
projects.description: Insurance for AI agents against LLM prompt-injection fraud, built on Hedera, ENS and World
projects.project_description:
Agent Insure is insurance for autonomous AI agents that hold and spend money on their own. Insured Business App: https://insured-business.up.railway.app
Agent Insure App (Insurance Company): https://agent-insure-hq.up.railway.app Give an agent a wallet and it inherits a new risk: indirect prompt injection. Hidden instructions buried in ordinary content, like a vendor invoice or a webpage, can manipulate the agent into authorizing a payment nobody approved. It's not a patchable bug: an LLM reads instructions and data as one undifferentiated stream of text, which is why OWASP, Microsoft, and Palo Alto's 2026 research still call this unresolved. And a stablecoin payment has no chargeback, so the loss is instant and final. Agent Insure covers that loss. Each agent's spending scope (budget cap, approved vendors) is locked into its ENS identity as an enforceable record. Every transaction is logged immutably to Hedera Consensus Service. To file a claim, the company's human manager first need to pass a live World Selfie Check, so nobody can run the whole loss-and-payout loop through software alone. Investigation pulls the disputed payment from Hedera's Mirror Node, checks its destination against the ENS-locked vendor list, and rules fraud on a mismatch. Payout follows automatically from a shared risk pool. A good analogy would be autonomous vehicles, like Waymo: the car drives itself, but Waymo still carries liability insurance for when something goes wrong on the road. AI agents need that same structure. Once an agent, not a person, is the one deciding to spend money, someone still has to be liable when it gets that decision wrong.
projects.how_its_made: The project is a monorepo: an Express backend and two React 19 + Vite + Tailwind frontends, one for the insured company (Northbeam Distributors) and one for the insurer (Agent Insure HQ). One Playwright E2E suite drives both apps against the real backend, no mocks. PayableAgent decides who to pay by reading an invoice's extracted text through a tool-calling request to a local Llama 3.2 3B model served by Ollama, via the OpenAI SDK pointed at Ollama, at temperature 0 with a fixed seed for reproducible demos. The poisoned invoice hides its rerouting instruction as white text on a white background inside a real rendered HTML invoice, the same concealment trick used in real prompt-injection attacks. Every PayableAgent payment settles on Hedera and is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic. The investigation step pulls that history from Hedera's public Mirror Node API and compares the disputed payment's destination against the ENS-locked vendor account to rule fraud on a mismatch. Every vendor payment also sits behind a x402-gated micro insurance-coverage fee, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet: a bare request gets back a real HTTP 402 challenge, and PayableAgent's own signer completes and settles it in real mUSDC before the vendor payment proceeds. An agent's spending scope (budget cap, approved-vendor list) is written as ENS text records on a Permissioned Resolver on Sepolia at payableagent.agentinsure.eth. Locking it is not a UI toggle: it calls the resolver's revokeRootRoles to permanently give up the write-role bitmap, so the record becomes unwritable on-chain, verified against the resolver's Sourcify-published source. Filing a claim requires a live World Selfie Check for human KYC. Because IDKit's bundled React widget fails to load its WASM module under Vite's dev server, the flow calls its framework-agnostic createRequest() builder directly, renders its own QR code, and independently re-verifies the returned proof against World's API server-side.

projects.title: QUOTA
projects.description: Origin fraud isn't fake certificates, it's volume. QUOTA caps PDO claims at the actual harvest.
projects.project_description: Bronte pistachios are about 0.25% of world pistachio production. The harvest is biennial and small, roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes per cycle. Yet "Bronte" sells worldwide, all year round, every year. The protected designation was created in the late 1990s specifically to stop counterfeiting of the name. It didn't. In 2021 the Carabinieri seized 650kg being sold as Bronte DOP with nothing behind the claim. That seizure is enforcement working: one shipment, one inspection, one case. What nobody can see is the aggregate. How much product claims this origin at any given moment is not a number anyone can compute, because there is no ledger of DOP claims anywhere. Attestation can't fix this, because anyone can always issue one more certificate. QUOTA inverts the approach: instead of certifying, count. A consortium mints exactly one transferable origin unit per certified gram at harvest, as a Hedera token whose maxSupply is the certified harvest and which has no admin key, no wipe key and no pause key. The cap is enforced by network consensus, not by our code. Units move down the supply chain under KYC-gated transfer. Processing burns nothing: input units are retired and derived units minted against a yield ratio ceiling, so 1,000g of in-shell pistachio can become at most 450g of kernel. Units are retired at consumption into an account whose key is derived from a published, reproducible hash, making retirement final and independently verifiable. Policy lives in ENS. A season subname's expiry is the mint window. There is no timer and no closeSeason function, because the authority to mint simply ceases to exist. The cap and yield ratios are resolver text records the contract reads live. Authority is split three ways, and ENS enforces the split rather than our application logic. The consortium owns the denomination. An independent control body appoints and removes issuers but holds no minting right itself and cannot mint a single gram. Issuers can mint but cannot appoint anyone. The split mirrors EU geographical indication law, where an accredited control body verifies producers precisely so that a consortium cannot certify itself. Nobody ever hands over a key. Four refusals, one law. Minting past the cap is rejected by Hedera consensus. Minting without a minting right is refused before any transaction is sent. The control body, which decides who may mint, is refused when it tries to mint itself. And transforming above the yield ceiling reverts on-chain against a ratio read live from ENS. Prevention where possible, detection where not. An off-chain reconciler compares Hedera mint history against Sepolia anchor events and records any unmatched mint as an on-chain finding, indexed by a subgraph and surfaced in the dashboard. We proved it by minting directly on Hedera, bypassing the system entirely. It was caught. Everything is live on testnet. The README documents all four proofs with a real transaction link for each, states what's real and what's demo-scale, and shows how to verify every claim yourself in about 90 seconds. The interactive demo panel runs locally only, because it holds real signing keys; the video walks through it end to end.
projects.how_its_made: Four layers across two chains, because no single chain could do all of it. Hedera holds the asset. HTS tokens with FINITE supply, maxSupply set to the certified harvest in grams, plus KYC, freeze and supply keys, and an immutable custom fee for the consortium levy set at creation. No admin key, so nothing can be changed afterwards. Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio was the obvious choice and we abandoned it: its published SDK has a broken ESM entry point, is documented as monorepo-only, and ships a critical vulnerability. Using @hashgraph/sdk directly turned out better, because the cap became a protocol-level property rather than something we wrote and hoped was correct. Ethereum Sepolia holds QuotaAnchor, a minimal event-and-authorization contract that reads the cap and yield ratios live from ENS resolver text records and checks an EAC role before recording anything. Verified on Etherscan, Blockscout and Sourcify. ENS v2 is the policy layer, not decoration. Season subname expiry is the mint window. Text records are the canonical cap and yield ratios. EAC roles are the delegation mechanism, and they split authority three ways: a control body holds admin rights and can appoint or remove issuers without ever holding a minting right itself. Participant subnames are non-transferable, achieved simply by not granting ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN, which we confirmed by reading the verified registry source rather than guessing. The Graph makes it queryable, with one shared schema across multiple consortia and the same query working for any of them by changing only the consortium id. The genuinely hacky part is the bridge. Subgraph mappings are deterministic sandboxed WASM and cannot call REST, so they can't reach Hedera's mirror node. Reconciliation therefore happens off-chain: a script pulls full mint history from the mirror node, compares it against the full anchor-event history across every contract address this project has ever deployed to, and records unmatched mints as new Sepolia events the subgraph then indexes. The reconciler is the detector; the subgraph makes its findings queryable. We say so explicitly rather than implying the subgraph does something it structurally can't. What we'd most like read is the design history, because almost every decision here was forced by a measurement rather than assumed, and the rejected alternatives are documented with the status codes that killed them. Burning reopens mint headroom, since maxSupply caps circulating supply rather than lifetime issuance, so we retire instead of burn. Freeze is bidirectional and leaves retirement reversible until frozen, so we don't use it for finality. Hedera validates key satisfiability on both create and update, so a genuinely unspendable account is impossible. An empty KeyList returns KEY_REQUIRED, an impossible threshold returns INVALID_ADMIN_KEY. A discarded key was rejected on principle, not evidence, because "we deleted it" is unverifiable. A key derived from a published hash is worse cryptographically and better epistemically, since anyone can reproduce and check it. Auto-association can't bootstrap a KYC-gated token, since KYC requires prior association and association requires a signature. ENS role expiry works by version-shifting rather than an expiry branch. An empirical result contradicted our own source reading, and re-reading found the real mechanism. Admin-tier role bits cannot be granted through ordinary grantRoles at all, because the bit-shift overflows uint256. The only route is register()'s extraRoleBitmap, which grants to exactly one address at registration, so rotating an admin requires unregister and re-register. A final self-audit found the README claiming a full-history retirement-outflow reconciler that was never built. Only an opportunistic tripwire exists. We fixed the documentation rather than quietly building the component, and the asymmetry is now stated plainly. One more, found while assembling the evidence. Our cap-failure script never logged its own transaction ID, because submit was declared inside the try block and was out of scope in the catch. The transaction existed regardless, since Hedera recorded the failure whether or not we printed it, so we paged the mirror node's full mint history for the treasury account, found the single non-SUCCESS result among forty, and opened it on HashScan to confirm the page itself reads TOKEN_MAX_SUPPLY_REACHED before linking it. All four refusals are now independently checkable by someone who runs nothing.

projects.title: GrantLane
projects.description: A grants program that can't be gamed by fake applicants and pays out the moment work is verified.
projects.project_description: GrantLane is a milestone grant escrow where a claim has to survive a challenge before it pays out. A grantor escrows USDC against a list of milestones up front, and the money is released milestone by milestone without anyone approving each one by hand. An applicant applies with a pitch, a repo and proposed milestones, after passing a World ID Selfie Check so the queue is people rather than scripts. The grantor adjusts the scope and escrows the total in one transaction, which also commits a hash of the agreed milestone terms on-chain, so nobody can quietly rewrite what a milestone required. When a milestone is done, the grantee publishes their evidence (a summary plus a live link, demo video or repo) and claims it with a 1 USDC bond. The claim becomes an assertion on UMA's Optimistic Oracle V3, carrying a link to the evidence and its hash. The claim is then open to dispute for a set window: 5 minutes in the demo, 48 hours in real use. If nobody disputes it, it pays out and the bond comes back. Anyone who thinks it's false can dispute by matching the bond, and UMA decides; whoever was wrong loses their bond to the other side. A rejected milestone simply reopens for a better claim. This design came from throwing out an earlier version that scored evidence automatically. No automated scorer can tell whether work is actually good, so rather than pretend to judge, GrantLane makes lying expensive: the evidence is public, the claim is bonded, and the challenge is open to anyone. Two more things it enforces. Approved money is credited and withdrawn rather than pushed, so no failed transfer can block a settlement. And a grantor can't pull funds out from under a claim that's live or disputed. Settlement is open to anyone, and a Chainlink CRE workflow does it on a schedule. Everything runs live on Base Sepolia: escrow 0x85AC2a3e1EBc0959599025eB6eF36eD34c862840, with a full run of funding, claiming, disputing, settling and withdrawing recorded as real transactions in the repo.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin 5.1. GrantEscrow integrates UMA's Optimistic Oracle V3 directly: a claim pulls the bond from the grantee, approves the oracle, and asserts with the grantee as asserter so the bond returns to them. UMA's assertionResolvedCallback and assertionDisputedCallback are restricted to the oracle and ignore assertions the escrow didn't make, since anyone can name your contract as a callback recipient. Payouts are pull-payment, settlement is permissionless, and closeGrant is blocked while a claim is open. Two EIP-712 types (MilestoneClaim, PayoutWalletChange) let the server authorise actions without ever holding a key or paying gas. 60 tests: 45 against a mock oracle that mirrors UMA's bond and callback rules, 8 for the receiver, and 7 fork tests against the real UMA oracle and Circle USDC. The frontend is Next.js 14 (App Router) with wagmi v2, viem and Tailwind driven by CSS-variable design tokens. Applications and evidence bundles live in Upstash Redis. Evidence is content-addressed: /evidence/<hash> recomputes both the evidence hash and the terms hash and shows whether they match the chain, so a disputer doesn't have to trust the site. World ID uses IDKit 4.x with the selfieCheckLegacy preset. The rp_context is signed server-side, proofs are verified through World's Developer Portal API, and the server issues short-lived HMAC-signed tickets which are exchanged for the EIP-712 attestation the user submits themselves. For Chainlink, the plan was Automation, but its testnet service was sunset in June 2026. I confirmed that on-chain: the Base Sepolia registry had performed zero upkeeps. So settlement moved to a CRE cron workflow following Chainlink's migration path: it runs the escrow's checkUpkeep off-chain, signs a report whose payload is the escrow's own performData, and the forwarder delivers it to a receiver contract that can only call performUpkeep. Deploy access is still pending, so it currently runs from the CRE CLI with real transactions through the mock forwarder, which the UI and docs state plainly. The hackiest part was answering a UMA dispute on testnet. The sandbox oracle only accepts an answer for a price it actually requested, and the request's ancillary data is assertionId:…,ooAsserter:…, where ooAsserter turns out to be the assertion's asserter, not the oracle. I found that by tracing a failing fork test and comparing the bytes.

Payouts are pull-payment, settlement is permissionless, and closeGrant is blocked while a claim is open. Two EIP-712 types (MilestoneClaim, PayoutWalletChange) let the server authorise actions without ever holding a key or paying gas. 60 tests: 45 against a mock oracle that mirrors UMA's bond and callback rules, 8 for the receiver, and 7 fork tests against the real UMA oracle and Circle USDC.

The frontend is Next.js 14 (App Router) with wagmi v2, viem and Tailwind driven by CSS-variable design tokens. Applications and evidence bundles live in Upstash Redis. Evidence is content-addressed: /evidence/<hash> recomputes both the evidence hash and the terms hash and shows whether they match the chain, so a disputer doesn't have to trust the site.

World ID uses IDKit 4.x with the selfieCheckLegacy preset. The rp_context is signed server-side, proofs are verified through World's Developer Portal API, and the server issues short-lived HMAC-signed tickets which are exchanged for the EIP-712 attestation the user submits themselves.

For Chainlink, the plan was Automation, but its testnet service was sunset in June 2026. I confirmed that on-chain: the Base Sepolia registry had performed zero upkeeps. So settlement moved to a CRE cron workflow following Chainlink's migration path: it runs the escrow's checkUpkeep off-chain, signs a report whose payload is the escrow's own performData, and the forwarder delivers it to a receiver contract that can only call performUpkeep. Deploy access is still pending, so it currently runs from the CRE CLI with real transactions through the mock forwarder, which the UI and docs state plainly.

The hackiest part was answering a UMA dispute on testnet. The sandbox oracle only accepts an answer for a price it actually requested, and the request's ancillary data is assertionId:…,ooAsserter:…, where ooAsserter turns out to be the assertion's asserter, not the oracle. I found that by tracing a failing fork test and comparing the bytes.

projects.title: TrueTick
projects.description: Live fair-price & deviation for tokenized stocks across issuers and chains, sold to agents via x402.
projects.project_description: The same real-world stock is now tokenized by several issuers, on several chains, in several DEX pools — and they don't agree. NVDA alone exists as NVDAon (Ondo, Ethereum), NVDAx (Backed, on both Ethereum and Solana), NVDA (Robinhood Chain) and NVDAc (Coinbase B20, Base). A per-chain dashboard shows you one of them and tells you nothing about the other four. TrueTick puts all of them in one table, priced against the real-world reference, so you can see which price is real. Right now the reliable venues agree within about 0.5–0.8% of each other — and one NVDA pool prices at $1,153 against a real $218. That pool holds $27k and hasn't traded in 24 hours. TrueTick doesn't hide it: it shows the number and flags it as phantom-liquidity and price-divergence. The agreement between the honest venues is what makes the outlier legible. Two rules run through the whole system. Every price field is number | null , never 0 — a zero propagates silently through arithmetic and renders as a real price, which is exactly how two silent-$0 bugs in our own subgraph would have shipped unnoticed. And a bad price is always labelled, never dropped: market-closed, thin-volume, phantom-liquidity, subgraph-syncing, source-error. The headline spread is computed across reliable venues only, because including the broken pool would report a spectacular, meaningless "428% spread". The data is the product, so it's sold rather than given away. The price service sits behind x402: an agent requests it, gets HTTP 402, pays 0.01 HBAR settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, and receives the data plus a transaction id it can verify on HashScan. An MCP server lets Claude Desktop be that paying agent — it names a ticker, our server decides to spend, and the wallet key never reaches the model. Everything is live on-chain data. Nothing is mocked.
projects.how_its_made: The core is one normalized schema ( TokenizedStockPoint ) with one adapter per venue. Adding a chain or a DEX is a new adapter file plus registry rows — the schema, quality rules, HTTP service and UI are untouched. That isn't a claim, it's the record: adding Solana (non-EVM, base58 addresses, no chain id, a DEX with no swap event) required zero schema changes; the types file gained two optional fields. Four data sources, across two Graph products: • Ethereum (Ondo, Backed) — Uniswap v4 subgraph. v4 exposes no USD price, so it's derivedETH × Bundle.ethPriceUSD, cross-checked against the deepest traded pool's own ratio. Using the deepest pool by TVL instead flagged a false 4.97% divergence caused by an untraded memecoin pair. • Robinhood Chain (Uniswap V3) — Substreams. The Graph's networks registry lists "subgraphs": [] for eip155:4663, so no subgraph was possible. • Solana (Raydium CLMM) — Substreams. There's no swap event to decode, so price comes from vault balance deltas: decode the CLMM PoolState for the pool's two vaults, diff pre/post token balances, and skip same-sign pairs (those are liquidity adds, not trades). • Base (Coinbase B20, Aerodrome Slipstream) — a subgraph we forked, fixed and published ourselves, because none existed for that CL factory. So we're a Graph publisher, not just a consumer. Both Substreams adapters compose prebuilt StreamingFast foundational modules driven by query-string params — there's no Rust in the repo. The .spkg files are vendored so the pipeline doesn't depend on registry availability at runtime. Publishing the subgraph surfaced two bugs that would have produced a healthy-looking subgraph returning $0 everywhere: upstream whitelisted USDC at Avalanche's address (eth_getCode proves no contract exists there on Base), and getEthPriceInUSD loaded a Uniswap pool that an Aerodrome-only subgraph never indexes, so ethPriceUSD was 0 and every USD field with it. Payments: x402 v2 with the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, HBAR (asset 0.0.0), settled as a native HAPI TransferTransaction — so the receipt is a Hedera tx id, not an EVM hash, and the facilitator pays the network fee as co-signer. The client cross-checks the challenge's advertised feePayer against Blocky402's published signers before spending, because pointing at a generic x402 facilitator would still settle, still show real transactions, and silently miss the requirement. Settlement happens after the handler returns and is cancelled on a 4xx/5xx, so a failed request costs nothing. The MCP server exposes six tools to Claude Desktop. The hacky-but-necessary part: Claude Desktop cancels a tool call at 60s and a cold Substreams venue takes 105–120s. Paying first risked settling after the client gave up — charged, nothing shown. So get_deviation probes warmth with a free request first and refuses to pay while cold, and concurrent requests for a ticker are deduped into one fetch (three "parallel" calls were queueing on the 2-session cap and all looking like cold starts). Favourite bug: byAddress() lowercased its input, correct for EVM hex and silently wrong for base58 — 'Xsc9qvGR…' is not 'xsc9qvgr…', so every Solana lookup would have missed and the venue would simply have been absent.

projects.title: DEADMAN
projects.description: An x402 escrow whose refund is executed by the Hedera network itself. No keeper, no arbiter.
projects.project_description: Every x402 payment on Hedera eventually asks the same question: what happens if the seller just goes silent? Usually the answer is someone has to step in — the buyer, an arbiter, a hosted watchdog service — and now you're trusting that someone to notice, to act, and to stay online. DEADMAN removes that someone entirely. The moment a buyer pays into escrow, the contract schedules its own refund using Hedera's HIP-1215 (scheduleCall) — in the same transaction, before anything can go wrong. If the seller delivers and reveals the right key, they get paid and the scheduled refund cancels itself. If they never respond, nothing needs to happen — the network just executes the refund it already scheduled, on its own, with zero signatures. We proved this isn't theoretical by literally killing our own server mid-flow: the process holding the decryption key was gone, and the refund fired anyway, right on schedule. Built for a world where the buyer paying is an AI agent, not a person who can chase down a refund manually.
projects.how_its_made: DEADMAN is a HoldEscrow contract on Hedera, EVM-equivalent, wired into an x402 payment flow. The trick that makes the whole thing possible is HIP-1215 — Hedera's scheduleCall — which lets a contract arm a future call to itself inside the very transaction that accepts payment. No cron job, no relayer, no keeper bot polling a database. The network is the keeper. On top of that sits a hash-commitment scheme: before payment is even accepted, the seller commits to hashes of the key, the ciphertext, and the underlying message. Payout only unlocks by revealing a key that matches — and a mismatch is provable on-chain, not just taken on faith (see verify.ts). We spent most of our time not on the happy path but breaking it: fifteen adversarial spikes against real testnet behavior — gas floors that silently ate transactions, revert edge cases around scheduled calls, a mirror node that occasionally lied about its own state. We kept the ones that failed in the docs instead of hiding them. The live board and server are both deployed and talking to real testnet transactions, not mocked — including the demo where we kill the server mid-flow and the scheduled refund still fires with zero signatures.

projects.title: GroupBet
projects.description: Private prediction markets for small groups to create personalized events.
projects.project_description: We built private prediction markets that let small groups bet on events that cannot be covered by traditional prediction markets. The way it works is someone in the group can create a market with a description describing anything they want to bet on. Then, the members of the group can purchase contracts betting on a certain outcome, and once the outcome has happened someone can submit a photo as "proof" of the outcome. If the photo proves either the "Yes" or "No" decisions on the market the market will resolve and the bettors will be paid out.
projects.how_its_made: We used Privy to allow for easy onboarding by automatically creating and funding wallets for our users, and we used Bazantic to seamlessly integrate API calls from Privy and our own app. This allows humans and agents alike to use our platform. We built our own prediction markets from scratch on Solana, with pricing determined by an AMM with an LMSR algorithm. We used the OpenAI image API to create a description for the submitted resolution image, which is sanitized and passed back into the API to create a resolution for the market with a confidence level. We also support notifications through Telegram to notify users of important shifts in their predictions and groups.

projects.title: Repo Shield
projects.description: Know what a GitHub repo does before you run it, a  scanner for fake-interview malware.
projects.project_description: Fake recruiters send developers "take-home assignments" as GitHub repos. Opening the folder in VS Code or running npm install is enough to steal your SSH keys and drain your crypto wallet — the code looks completely normal. This is the Contagious Interview campaign (attributed to the Lazarus Group), and it's hitting engineers now: our submission includes real LinkedIn posts from people it happened to. Every existing scanner (Socket, Snyk) is built for the repo owner and needs an app or CI action installed. But when a "recruiter" invites you to a private repo as an outside collaborator, you have read access and nothing else — so you clone it blindly or walk away. RepoShield is the first candidate-side scanner. You paste a repo (public with no sign-in, or private via GitHub OAuth) and it reads what the code actually executes — install hooks, editor auto-run tasks, obfuscated payloads, credential-access patterns, typosquatted dependencies — using a two-phase pipeline: 38 fast static rules find the risky files, then an LLM reads only those and explains the execution flow in plain English. You get a 0–100 threat score, a verdict, and a copy-pasteable plan to inspect the repo safely without ever running it. Two things make it more than a linter: it can run the entire analysis inside a Chainlink CRE enclave, so a private/company repo is scanned without our servers or a public AI ever seeing the source; and it publishes verdicts to an onchain registry indexed by The Graph, which the LLM reads back — so a repo whose owner has a pattern of flagged repos is caught before its code is even read.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a TypeScript analysis engine (38 heuristics + a classifier + a Gemini phase-2 pass) inside a Next.js 16 app on Vercel. A key design choice: the engine is a pure function with zero I/O, so the exact same analyzeRepo() runs in the browser and inside a hardware enclave. Chainlink CRE (Confidential Workflows): the workflow is a handlerInTee running in an AWS Nitro enclave. It fetches the developer's GitHub OAuth token and the Gemini key from the Vault DON, reads the private repo over the confidential-HTTP capability (token never leaves the TEE), runs the full scan, and returns only a 7-field aggregate verdict to the DON — the findings quote source code, so they stay inside. Making the engine run in CRE's WASM runtime meant it couldn't use fetch, crypto, Buffer or setTimeout — all banned — so we hand-wrote SHA-256/base64/UTF-8 and inject an HttpClient. It compiles to WASM and simulates end-to-end via the cre CLI. We also implemented the ETH-signed JWT (alg: ETH) the gateway needs to trigger a deployed workflow. The Graph: a ScanRegistry contract (Foundry, on Sepolia) emits ScanPublished; a subgraph on Subgraph Studio indexes it. Before analysis, the app queries the subgraph live for prior verdicts on the repo AND its owner (name_starts_with), and feeds that into the LLM's prompt and the score — making The Graph a load-bearing decision input, not a display. Hacky bit worth mentioning: repos are fetched as one gzip tarball via GitHub's archive endpoint, which 302-redirects to codeload — unmetered against the API rate limit. A whole scan costs ~2 API calls instead of 15+, so we read 100% of a repo's files instead of a sample. Contracts use Foundry; the app and gateway signing use viem.

projects.title: NanoAffliate
projects.description: Affiliate payouts by the second, not the month — verified human, settled on Hedera.
projects.project_description: NanoAffiliate is a pay-per-second affiliate marketing platform built natively on Hedera. Instead of the usual pay-per-click model — where creators wait 30–90 days for commissions and sellers pay for traffic that's often fraudulent — we meter and pay out real, verified human attention in 5-second intervals, settled instantly on-chain. At the center is our Attention Trust Oracle: a real x402-gated service on Hedera that scores every 5-second interval of a reader's session — tab activity, interaction patterns, scroll behavior, device signals, and cross-session diversity — and returns a trust verdict. Our Hedera Agent calls it autonomously, pays for every call via x402, and when a session is verified, pays the creator directly through a native Hedera transfer from the seller's on-chain escrow. Sessions that stay ambiguous get escalated to a Selfie Check, a biometric liveness proof that also unlocks a premium, verified-attention pricing tier. Every affiliate link is its own dedicated Hedera Consensus Service topic — the same identifier a creator shares as a link is the identifier anyone can paste into a public Hedera explorer to see that link's complete, tamper-proof history of clicks, attention ticks, and trust decisions. Both the Oracle and the Agent carry portable HCS-14 identities, so the service relationship being paid for is provably real, not just an account number paying another account number. The result: creators get paid in real time instead of months later, sellers only pay for attention that's actually verified rather than guessed at, and the entire system is independently auditable by anyone — not because we ask you to trust our dashboard, but because you don't have to.
projects.how_its_made: NanoAffiliate is built entirely on Hedera's native services, deliberately avoiding smart contracts since none of the logic requires on-chain computation — the Consensus, Account, Crypto Transfer, and Schedule services do everything needed. The core loop: every affiliate link is its own dedicated HCS topic, created at link-generation time — the topic ID doubles as the shareable URL, so pasting a link into a browser redirects to the product, and pasting the same ID into HashScan shows that exact link's full, tamper-proof click/attention/trust history. Every 5 seconds a reader is on the page, our Hedera Agent (built on Hedera Agent Kit, running autonomously) calls our Attention Trust Oracle — a stateless Express service scoring tab state, interaction recency, scroll naturalness, device fingerprinting, and cross-session diversity. That call is gated by @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator — a real, metered, pay-per-call service, not a free internal function dressed up as one. When a tick passes, the Agent fires a separate, plain Hedera TransferTransaction from the seller's escrow to the creator — deliberately not x402, since there's no resource being gated on a push payment, just a payer and a payee. Identity: the Oracle and Agent each carry an HCS-14 UAID — a SHA-384 hash of six canonical fields (registry, name, version, protocol, native Hedera account ID, skills), deterministic and independently recomputable by anyone, with HCS-11 profile documents published to a shared identity-registry topic. Escrow: every seller gets their own distinct Hedera account, but all of them share one key — the Agent's own — so payouts need no per-seller secret lookup, while balances stay individually verifiable on Mirror Node. Partner tech: Blocky402 for x402 settlement, World ID's Selfie Check for the one fraud signal that's a genuine hard stop rather than a heuristic — a bot farm can defeat IP diversity with rotated residential proxies, but it can't hold a real face to a camera. Redis + BullMQ drive the 5-second tick scheduler and a rolling session-diversity aggregate. The hacky bit worth admitting: for the hackathon build, Amazon products are supported via manually-entered product data rather than the Product Advertising API, since PA-API now requires 10 qualifying sales in a trailing 30 days just to keep access — impossible for a fresh project. Purchase confirmation for those links is honestly self-reported, not webhook-verified, because Amazon exposes no real-time conversion API to third-party affiliates at all — a platform limitation, not one we could engineer around.

NanoAffiliate is built entirely on Hedera's native services, deliberately avoiding smart contracts since none of the logic requires on-chain computation — the Consensus, Account, Crypto Transfer, and Schedule services do everything needed.

The core loop: every affiliate link is its own dedicated HCS topic, created at link-generation time — the topic ID doubles as the shareable URL, so pasting a link into a browser redirects to the product, and pasting the same ID into HashScan shows that exact link's full, tamper-proof click/attention/trust history. Every 5 seconds a reader is on the page, our Hedera Agent (built on Hedera Agent Kit, running autonomously) calls our Attention Trust Oracle — a stateless Express service scoring tab state, interaction recency, scroll naturalness, device fingerprinting, and cross-session diversity. That call is gated by @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator — a real, metered, pay-per-call service, not a free internal function dressed up as one. When a tick passes, the Agent fires a separate, plain Hedera TransferTransaction from the seller's escrow to the creator — deliberately not x402, since there's no resource being gated on a push payment, just a payer and a payee.

Identity: the Oracle and Agent each carry an HCS-14 UAID — a SHA-384 hash of six canonical fields (registry, name, version, protocol, native Hedera account ID, skills), deterministic and independently recomputable by anyone, with HCS-11 profile documents published to a shared identity-registry topic.

Escrow: every seller gets their own distinct Hedera account, but all of them share one key — the Agent's own — so payouts need no per-seller secret lookup, while balances stay individually verifiable on Mirror Node.

Partner tech: Blocky402 for x402 settlement, World ID's Selfie Check for the one fraud signal that's a genuine hard stop rather than a heuristic — a bot farm can defeat IP diversity with rotated residential proxies, but it can't hold a real face to a camera. Redis + BullMQ drive the 5-second tick scheduler and a rolling session-diversity aggregate.

The hacky bit worth admitting: for the hackathon build, Amazon products are supported via manually-entered product data rather than the Product Advertising API, since PA-API now requires 10 qualifying sales in a trailing 30 days just to keep access — impossible for a fresh project. Purchase confirmation for those links is honestly self-reported, not webhook-verified, because Amazon exposes no real-time conversion API to third-party affiliates at all — a platform limitation, not one we could engineer around.

projects.title: Covenant_Hedera
projects.description: Covenant is a lending console for private credit where a program sets the collateral value
projects.project_description:
you would not lend someone money against their house and also let them tell you what the
house is worth. private credit runs close to that: a fund holds a pile of loans, values them
itself, and borrows against its own number. the Financial Stability Board found that the same
loan gets different marks at different managers, because the judgement behind the mark is the
manager's own (FSB, Report on Vulnerabilities in Private Credit, 6 May 2026, section 3.3). covenant takes that valuation out of self-marking. a confidential compute engine reads the
underlying borrower's revenue, EBITDA, total debt, cash and interest expense, and returns two
things only: a covenant pass or fail, and a haircut. both sides read the program before the
facility is struck. the lender never sees the financials behind the number, and can still
check that the published program produced it. what is live: a real note issued on Hedera testnet through the Asset Tokenization Studio,
against its deployed resolver and factory, no new Solidity and no contract deployed. the full
lifecycle runs: issuance, a transfer blocked by a compliance gate then granted then permitted,
a coupon priced and distributed, and a collateral hold created, released, created again and
executed on default. 21 transactions, signed by a human in MetaMask throughout, four gates
independently re-verified against Hedera's mirror node and the testnet json-rpc relay. every
hash is in EVIDENCE.md in the repository.
projects.how_its_made:
Hedera testnet, the Asset Tokenization Studio SDK (@hashgraph/asset-tokenization-sdk@8.0.0)
against its already-deployed resolver 0.0.9212226 and factory 0.0.9213391. we deploy no
contracts and write no Solidity: issuance, the KYC compliance gate, the coupon and the
collateral hold all run on ATS's own diamond, through the SDK. the benefit is concrete: a
compliance-gated, coupon-bearing, hold-capable security token is not something we built, it is
something ATS already gave us, correctly, on testnet, and we spent our time on the
confidential leg instead of reimplementing a compliance facet. Next.js 16 and React 19 for the console, with the confidential compute engine built as a plain
local service behind one swappable interface, CovenantEngine (lib/engine/types.ts). the entire
surface for a different implementation is one file, lib/engine/registry.ts: no caller names a
concrete provider. that is the shape a Chainlink CRE handlerInTee needs to drop into without
touching a single route or component, and we proved the swap. we did not ship it live inside
the build's timebox, and we say so rather than imply a deployment that did not happen: what
shipped is the interface a real handlerInTee would sit behind, not a running enclave. the hacky part, and it is the most interesting thing we found. ATS's own
Bond.createKpiLinkedRate cannot work on the deployed factory: it calls a factory function that
exists only in MockFactory.sol, a test-only contract, and the KPI-linked bond configuration is
registered in the deployed resolver but unreachable by any working path. we root-caused this
from source and on chain, filed it as B1, and routed around it by issuing on the working
variable-rate configuration instead, then driving the coupon rate through
setCouponRateType(FIXED) and a role-gated setRate, both called directly against the deployed
contract because the SDK exposes neither method. that single workaround is what makes the
coupon's rate provably token-enforced rather than caller-supplied: the token refused a rate
handed to it at setCoupon and stamped the value FixedRate.setRate had written 33 seconds
earlier instead, checkable on HashScan without trusting us. fifteen defects surfaced by building a working flow against the SDK, not by auditing it for
faults, filed in BUG.md as B1 through B15, two of which we investigated and withdrew after
finding the actual cause was ours, not the SDK's. the confidentiality boundary is enforced by a committed script, npm run scan:disclosure, which
builds the console for production and scans every asset the lender's and holder's pages ship
for the borrower's raw financial fields and figures. it was tested on itself: we deliberately
introduced a leak, confirmed the script failed on it, then removed the leak and confirmed a
clean pass, so the check is proven to fire rather than assumed to. built by one person, hao, directing a team of AI agent configurations running on Claude. the
agent definitions and the specs and prompts that drove this build are committed in the
repository, in .claude/agents/ and specs/, not written after the fact. every one of the 21
transactions on chain was signed by a human in MetaMask: ATS SDK v8 ships no local-key signer
(SupportedWallets.CLIENT is disabled in its source), so no agent could have signed any of
them, and this is independently checkable on Hedera's mirror node, not asserted. full account:
AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: Conduit
projects.description: Buy AI inference from a peer's GPU, paid per answer in USDC on Arc. No server, no cloud.
projects.project_description: Conduit is a serverless, peer-to-peer marketplace for AI inference. You buy an answer directly from someone else's GPU and pay them per answer in USDC. There is no server in the middle, no account on either side, and your prompt never touches a cloud  peers find each other over a DHT and the model runs on the seller's own machine. The core idea is that the payment is the access handshake: a seller's inference runtime sits behind a firewall that only opens for a buyer who has settled. A freeloader connecting without paying is refused at the handshake and gets zero bytes. PRE-EXISTING (built June–July 2026 for QVAC Hackathon I): the P2P marketplace itself — Hyperswarm discovery, the payment-gated provider handshake, the on-device capability prober that decides what a machine can sell, the ConduitEscrow payment-channel contract, and the Electron desktop app. NEW THIS HACKATHON (Continuity track): • Migrated settlement to Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), where USDC is both the gas token and the token answers are priced in — so a seller earns and spends one asset instead of earning one and paying fees in another. • Built a subgraph on The Graph indexing every channel the escrow has ever opened, so a first-time buyer can see how a seller treated everyone, not just themselves. Crucially it classifies withdrawals rather than counting them: probes and session renewals are indexed and visible but excluded from scoring, because a naive settled/withdrawn tally is trivially gamed. • Added a World personhood gate via AgentKit. A seller can require that a buyer is a verified unique human; the wallet resolves to an anonymous human id in AgentBook on World Chain - never an identity. This is what makes the reputation layer expensive to forge: buying a reputation now costs a person, not gas. • Removed the free local-answer tier entirely. Every answer is bought from a peer, so the market is never invisible. Demonstrated end to end across two machines: a Mac buyer is refused as an unverified human, verifies by scanning a QR in World App, then buys answers from a Linux GPU - settling six answers in two on-chain transactions
projects.how_its_made: Stack: TypeScript throughout. Hyperswarm/HyperDHT handles serverless peer discovery and NAT hole-punching. QVAC, Tether's on-device runtime, runs the models: Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B and Llama 3.2 1B. Inference is delegated over an end-to-end encrypted Noise link, so model weights never leave the seller and prompts never reach a cloud service. ethers v6 handles signing, Solidity + Hardhat handles the escrow, React + Electron powers the desktop app, and node:test runs the suite with 79 tests and zero new test dependencies. ARC: settlement. ConduitEscrow (0xdC48E5e5c3Cf91b6db9ec0f329a14188174632C2) is an EIP-712 payment-channel contract. A channel is opened once with a deposit, then every answer gets an off-chain signed voucher containing a cumulative total. The seller can redeem everything in a single claim. The reason Arc worked particularly well here is that USDC is both the gas token and the settlement token. A seller earns and spends the same asset, which makes sense for a machine selling compute. One subtle issue took some debugging: Arc exposes the same balance through two views, native at 18 decimals and ERC-20 at 6. The ERC-20 view is a floored projection, so gas accounting has to happen in native units or you can lose a base unit on each reading. THE GRAPH: reputation. AssemblyScript mappings index Opened, Settled, and Withdrawn events from the escrow. The interesting part is the classification, not just counting events. On the original Sepolia deployment, both real Withdrawn events came from the same buyer reopening 24 seconds later. That is loyalty, but a naive counter would classify it as abandonment and give the seller a 0.0 score. So withdrawals are split into qualified abandonment, probes, and renewals. Probes are sessions that were too short, too small, or came from a buyer with no settlement history. Only qualified abandonment affects the reputation score. The UI shows both the naive score and the hardened score, so the difference is visible instead of just being claimed. WORLD: personhood. AgentKit's createAgentBookVerifier resolves a wallet to an anonymous humanId through AgentBook on World Chain. There were two gotchas worth calling out. lookupHuman(0x0) returns a NON-ZERO id, so the zero address has to be rejected before the lookup. Otherwise, an unfunded wallet could appear to be a human. The second issue was validateAgentkitMessage. It compares only the URI host, not the path. That meant a proof issued for one seller could validate for another seller. We added an explicit seller binding check. Registration happens directly in the app. The engine spawns the AgentKit CLI as a managed child process. Since the CLI only draws an ASCII QR code to a TTY, the QR is generated client-side from the link emitted by the CLI. A few other hacky bits were needed to make the desktop builds actually work. npm does not preserve the executable bit inside published packages, so the bundled Bare runtime was shipped as 0644. The app then failed with EACCES inside a squashfs AppImage and EROFS on a read-only DMG. An afterPack hook now restores the executable bit. The macOS prebuild of the llama.cpp addon links Homebrew's OpenSSL using an absolute path. The same hook vendors the required dylibs into the bundle, rewrites the load commands to @loader_path, and ad-hoc re-signs the binaries. install_name_tool invalidates the signature, and without re-signing, Apple Silicon refuses to dlopen the addon. The runtime also cannot restart a provider inside the same process. So the seller proves it can actually serve by launching its own binary in a child process, loading the model, and exiting. The exit code becomes the answer. Finally, the firewall allow-list could not be amended once the provider was running. That meant a seller could only serve the first buyer who paid. The allow-list is now accumulated before the provider starts, so multiple buyers can connect.

There is no server in the middle, no account on either side, and your prompt never touches a cloud  peers find each other over a DHT and the model runs on the seller's own machine.

The core idea is that the payment is the access handshake: a seller's inference runtime sits behind a firewall that only opens for a buyer who has settled. A freeloader connecting without paying is refused at the handshake and gets zero bytes.

NEW THIS HACKATHON (Continuity track):

• Migrated settlement to Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), where USDC is both the gas token and the token answers are priced in — so a seller earns and spends one asset instead of earning one and paying fees in another.

• Built a subgraph on The Graph indexing every channel the escrow has ever opened, so a first-time buyer can see how a seller treated everyone, not just themselves. Crucially it classifies withdrawals rather than counting them: probes and session renewals are indexed and visible but excluded from scoring, because a naive settled/withdrawn tally is trivially gamed.

• Added a World personhood gate via AgentKit. A seller can require that a buyer is a verified unique human; the wallet resolves to an anonymous human id in AgentBook on World Chain - never an identity. This is what makes the reputation layer expensive to forge: buying a reputation now costs a person, not gas.

• Removed the free local-answer tier entirely. Every answer is bought from a peer, so the market is never invisible.

Demonstrated end to end across two machines: a Mac buyer is refused as an unverified human, verifies by scanning a QR in World App, then buys answers from a Linux GPU - settling six answers in two on-chain transactions

Stack: TypeScript throughout. Hyperswarm/HyperDHT handles serverless peer discovery and NAT hole-punching. QVAC, Tether's on-device runtime, runs the models: Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B and Llama 3.2 1B. Inference is delegated over an end-to-end encrypted Noise link, so model weights never leave the seller and prompts never reach a cloud service. ethers v6 handles signing, Solidity + Hardhat handles the escrow, React + Electron powers the desktop app, and node:test runs the suite with 79 tests and zero new test dependencies.

ARC: settlement. ConduitEscrow (0xdC48E5e5c3Cf91b6db9ec0f329a14188174632C2) is an EIP-712 payment-channel contract. A channel is opened once with a deposit, then every answer gets an off-chain signed voucher containing a cumulative total. The seller can redeem everything in a single claim.

The reason Arc worked particularly well here is that USDC is both the gas token and the settlement token. A seller earns and spends the same asset, which makes sense for a machine selling compute. One subtle issue took some debugging: Arc exposes the same balance through two views, native at 18 decimals and ERC-20 at 6. The ERC-20 view is a floored projection, so gas accounting has to happen in native units or you can lose a base unit on each reading.

THE GRAPH: reputation. AssemblyScript mappings index Opened, Settled, and Withdrawn events from the escrow. The interesting part is the classification, not just counting events.

On the original Sepolia deployment, both real Withdrawn events came from the same buyer reopening 24 seconds later. That is loyalty, but a naive counter would classify it as abandonment and give the seller a 0.0 score.

So withdrawals are split into qualified abandonment, probes, and renewals. Probes are sessions that were too short, too small, or came from a buyer with no settlement history. Only qualified abandonment affects the reputation score.

The UI shows both the naive score and the hardened score, so the difference is visible instead of just being claimed.

WORLD: personhood. AgentKit's createAgentBookVerifier resolves a wallet to an anonymous humanId through AgentBook on World Chain.

There were two gotchas worth calling out. lookupHuman(0x0) returns a NON-ZERO id, so the zero address has to be rejected before the lookup. Otherwise, an unfunded wallet could appear to be a human.

The second issue was validateAgentkitMessage. It compares only the URI host, not the path. That meant a proof issued for one seller could validate for another seller. We added an explicit seller binding check.

Registration happens directly in the app. The engine spawns the AgentKit CLI as a managed child process. Since the CLI only draws an ASCII QR code to a TTY, the QR is generated client-side from the link emitted by the CLI.

A few other hacky bits were needed to make the desktop builds actually work.

npm does not preserve the executable bit inside published packages, so the bundled Bare runtime was shipped as 0644. The app then failed with EACCES inside a squashfs AppImage and EROFS on a read-only DMG. An afterPack hook now restores the executable bit.

The macOS prebuild of the llama.cpp addon links Homebrew's OpenSSL using an absolute path. The same hook vendors the required dylibs into the bundle, rewrites the load commands to @loader_path, and ad-hoc re-signs the binaries. install_name_tool invalidates the signature, and without re-signing, Apple Silicon refuses to dlopen the addon.

The runtime also cannot restart a provider inside the same process. So the seller proves it can actually serve by launching its own binary in a child process, loading the model, and exiting. The exit code becomes the answer.

Finally, the firewall allow-list could not be amended once the provider was running. That meant a seller could only serve the first buyer who paid. The allow-list is now accumulated before the provider starts, so multiple buyers can connect.

projects.title: Veritas_IITD Markets
projects.description: On-chain prediction markets for campus events — real stakes for students, real signal for colleges.
projects.project_description:
Veritas (IITD Markets)
For students: put your money where your prediction is. Pick a side in any inter-hostel event — cricket finals, sports championships, any competition with a real outcome — and stake USDC on it. Win, and you don't just get bragging rights: you claim a proportional share of everyone who backed the losing side, after a 10% platform fee. It turns campus rivalry into something with actual stakes, and gives you a live, crowd-priced read on who's actually favored before the event happens. For institutions: Veritas isn't just a betting app for students — it's a plug-in engagement and insight layer for the college itself. Student councils and event bodies get a transparent, on-chain gauge of real sentiment (backed by real money, not casual polls) around their own events, which drives attention and participation toward those events in the run-up. It's a product a college can point to as infrastructure it runs, not just something students happen to use.
Two sponsor integrations are load-bearing, not decorative. Resolution is handled by a Chainlink CRE workflow that fetches the official result through a confidential-compute step and writes it on-chain via a DON-signed report through a Forwarder → Receiver contract, rather than a plain script or a trusted admin key. Uniswap V2 is used two ways: users can swap ETH for USDC and place a bet in one transaction if they don't already hold USDC, and every bet mints a transferable ERC20 "position token" that's listed on its own Uniswap pair — so a user can exit a position before resolution, or someone else can buy into a position on the open market and later claim the payout themselves, never having placed a bet at all. Payouts are claim-based rather than pushed to avoid unbounded gas costs as the number of bettors grows. The full stack — Solidity contracts, the CRE workflow, and a React/wagmi frontend with market list, betting, and results/claim screens — is tested end-to-end, including a headless-browser verification of the actual wallet-connected UI against a live local deployment.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is Hardhat + Solidity 0.8.24 for the contracts, a two-agent split repo (Chainlink resolution side / Market+Uniswap+frontend side, coordinated via AGENT_COORDINATION_*.md docs), and a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend using wagmi/viem for wallet and contract calls. Contracts: Market.sol owns the OPEN→CLOSED→RESOLVED lifecycle: USDC-denominated createMarket/placeBet/closeMarket, and a claim-based (never looped) payout so gas cost stays flat regardless of how many people bet. resolveMarket is gated to a single resolver address, designed from the start to eventually be CREMarketResolverReceiver rather than an EOA. Chainlink CRE: the resolution side is a Chainlink CRE workflow with a confidential-compute step that fetches and validates the official competition result, then writes on-chain via a DON-signed report through a Forwarder → CREMarketResolverReceiver.onReport → Market.resolveMarket. We built a mock resolver first (same validation logic, plain EOA signer) so the market side could be built and tested against a real call path before the CRE deployment existed, then verified the real receiver contract against it with a dedicated integration test. Uniswap: two integrations, both load-bearing. placeBetWithETH swaps ETH → USDC through a real Uniswap V2 Router and bets the actual received amount in one transaction. More ambitiously, every bet also mints a transferable ERC20 "position token" (OutcomeToken, 1:1 with USDC staked) that createMarket lists on its own Uniswap V2 pair against USDC — a genuine secondary market, not an internal ledger. claim() was reworked to pay out (and burn) whoever currently holds the winning token, not whoever originally placed the bet, since that's the entire point of making it tradeable. Notably hacky bits: Vendoring the real Uniswap V2 Factory/Router locally for tests hit the classic gotcha where UniswapV2Library's hardcoded CREATE2 init-code-hash only matches Uniswap's original 0.5.16 build — a different Hardhat/solc/optimizer config produces different UniswapV2Pair bytecode, so every swap silently resolved to the wrong (non-contract) pair address. Fixed by vendoring a patched copy of the library with the hash recomputed from our own build (scripts/lib/computeInitCodeHash.js), and wrote a script to regenerate it if compiler settings ever change. Listing an OutcomeToken on Uniswap at market-creation time had to degrade gracefully — a call to a Router with no code "succeeds" at the EVM level with empty returndata, and Solidity's try/catch can't catch the resulting ABI-decode failure (it's an uncatchable revert), so we added an explicit code.length check before attempting the call, so the stretch goal never blocks core market creation. Pulling in OpenZeppelin's Strings (for token symbols) transitively requires the MCOPY opcode, which isn't available under the default paris EVM target — had to explicitly set evmVersion: "cancun" in the Hardhat config. For frontend verification without a real wallet extension, we drove the actual UI in a headless Playwright browser using a ~40-line fake EIP-1193 provider that forwards eth_sendTransaction etc. straight to a live local Hardhat node (which auto-signs for its own known accounts) — this caught a real bug where the UI's "transaction confirmed" indicator flipped invisible the instant an approve transaction landed, before the user ever saw it.
