Chainlink CRE: the resolution side is a Chainlink CRE workflow with a confidential-compute step that fetches and validates the official competition result, then writes on-chain via a DON-signed report through a Forwarder → CREMarketResolverReceiver.onReport → Market.resolveMarket. We built a mock resolver first (same validation logic, plain EOA signer) so the market side could be built and tested against a real call path before the CRE deployment existed, then verified the real receiver contract against it with a dedicated integration test.

Uniswap: two integrations, both load-bearing. placeBetWithETH swaps ETH → USDC through a real Uniswap V2 Router and bets the actual received amount in one transaction. More ambitiously, every bet also mints a transferable ERC20 "position token" (OutcomeToken, 1:1 with USDC staked) that createMarket lists on its own Uniswap V2 pair against USDC — a genuine secondary market, not an internal ledger. claim() was reworked to pay out (and burn) whoever currently holds the winning token, not whoever originally placed the bet, since that's the entire point of making it tradeable.

Notably hacky bits:
1. Vendoring the real Uniswap V2 Factory/Router locally for tests hit the classic gotcha where UniswapV2Library's hardcoded CREATE2 init-code-hash only matches Uniswap's original 0.5.16 build — a different Hardhat/solc/optimizer config produces different UniswapV2Pair bytecode, so every swap silently resolved to the wrong (non-contract) pair address. Fixed by vendoring a patched copy of the library with the hash recomputed from our own build (scripts/lib/computeInitCodeHash.js), and wrote a script to regenerate it if compiler settings ever change.
2. Listing an OutcomeToken on Uniswap at market-creation time had to degrade gracefully — a call to a Router with no code "succeeds" at the EVM level with empty returndata, and Solidity's try/catch can't catch the resulting ABI-decode failure (it's an uncatchable revert), so we added an explicit code.length check before attempting the call, so the stretch goal never blocks core market creation.
3. Pulling in OpenZeppelin's Strings (for token symbols) transitively requires the MCOPY opcode, which isn't available under the default paris EVM target — had to explicitly set evmVersion: "cancun" in the Hardhat config.
4. For frontend verification without a real wallet extension, we drove the actual UI in a headless Playwright browser using a ~40-line fake EIP-1193 provider that forwards eth_sendTransaction etc. straight to a live local Hardhat node (which auto-signs for its own known accounts) — this caught a real bug where the UI's "transaction confirmed" indicator flipped invisible the instant an approve transaction landed, before the user ever saw it.

projects.title: AgentGate
projects.description: Privacy-first payment gateway that lets AI agents make stealth transactions.
projects.project_description: AgentGate is a privacy-focused payment gateway built for AI agents. It lets an agent initiate USDC payments using only a recipient’s normal wallet address, while AgentGate resolves the recipient’s registered stealth identity and generates a fresh ERC-5564 stealth destination for each payment. The system is built on Base Sepolia and exposes an agent-friendly MCP interface through Bazantic, while keeping transaction signing isolated from the agent-facing API.
projects.how_its_made: AgentGate is built with TypeScript, Node.js, a REST API, Supabase/PostgreSQL, and Base Sepolia smart contracts. The payment engine prepares USDC transfers and integrates ERC-5564 stealth payments through a custom helper contract that calls the canonical ERC-5564 Announcer. Bazantic provides the agent-facing Gateway, MCP server, and Recipe, allowing Codex and other agents to interact with AgentGate using natural-language payment requests. A separate signer handles transaction execution so private keys never enter the Gateway or MCP layer. The frontend is built with React, Vite, and Tailwind for wallet connection and payment-plan testing.

projects.title: WalletOS
projects.description: WalletOS an AI companion for w3 wallets makes your autonomous workflows smarter, safer, and easier!
projects.project_description: WalletOS is an agentic intelligence layer for crypto wallets. It gives users a way to connect their existing AI agent, such as Codex or Claude Code, to their wallets and dApps so the agent can understand context, investigate on-chain activity, recommend actions, and prepare transactions for user approval. Instead of building another wallet with a closed AI assistant, WalletOS turns the user’s own agent into the intelligence layer of the wallet. The agent can use installable WalletOS Skills for tasks such as transaction security, portfolio analysis, protocol research, risk management, and rebalancing. Our first skill focuses on transaction safety. When a user interacts with an unfamiliar dApp, WalletOS can provide the agent with the page context, contract interaction, calldata, and wallet request so it can compare what the website claims will happen with what the transaction will actually do. This helps users understand risky approvals, deceptive signatures, phishing flows, cloned protocols, and potential wallet-drain behavior before they approve anything. WalletOS also supports proactive financial workflows. An agent can analyze positions across wallets, identify concentration or idle capital, research protocols, recommend a rebalance, and prepare the required transactions for the user to review and approve. Sponsor technologies extend the agent’s capabilities: The Graph provides on-chain intelligence for protocol and wallet research, Ledger strengthens the security and trusted signing workflow, and Privy enables agentic wallet and execution use cases. The long-term vision is an open marketplace of Web3 agent skills, similar to extensions for an IDE, where developers can publish reusable capabilities and the user’s AI agent decides when and how to use them. Your wallet provides custody. Your agent provides intelligence. WalletOS connects both.
projects.how_its_made:
WalletOS is built as a browser extension + local desktop runtime. The extension captures dApp and wallet context, while the desktop companion runs local agents such as Codex and gives them access to WalletOS Skills. The key idea is the runtime: instead of hard-coding every blockchain integration into the app, WalletOS loads plugins/skills that tell the agent which tools to use for a task. A skill can combine CLIs, MCPs, APIs, and scripts, so new capabilities can be added without changing the core app. For example, our security skill uses Foundry tools such as Cast and Anvil to decode and simulate transactions. The Graph is used by research and portfolio skills to query on-chain protocol and wallet data. Ledger is integrated into the security and signing flow, including local testing with Speculos. Privy is used for agentic wallet and execution workflows. The most hacky part is that WalletOS does not run its own AI model. It launches the user’s existing local agent and turns it into a wallet-specialized agent by giving it runtime context plus installable Web3 skills. This lets us keep the core lightweight while making the system extensible across many protocols and partner technologies. BROWSER EXTENSION
↓
AGENT RUNTIME

WALLET ACTIONS

projects.title: Sigil
projects.description: Skills for AI agents, backed by staked USDC and verified on-chain, licensed per use via x402
projects.project_description: Sigil is a trust layer for AI agent skills. An agent extends itself by installing skills (small tools, MCP servers, snippets of code), and one bad skill can leak a cloud key or drain a wallet. Today an agent has two signals about a skill, the author's description and a scanner's opinion, and neither costs anything to be wrong. Sigil makes being trustworthy cost money. Anyone lists a skill for free; the gateway hashes its source into the skill id, pins the bundle on Hedera as an HCS-1 file and announces it on an HCS registry topic. A staker then locks USDC on Arc behind one machine-testable predicate about the skill: it reads no env var, opens no network connection, reads or writes no path outside an allowlist, starts no subprocess, runs no dynamic code. An agent buys the skill's source per request over x402 on Hedera, gets an HTS licence NFT, and runs the skill in a deterministic sandbox that records every env, file, network, subprocess and eval event and hashes the canonical trace. If the trace breaks the claim, anyone can dispute with a counter-bond and the trace; an independent verifier re-runs the exact bundle from the pinned source, and the contract pays stake plus bond to whichever side the evidence supports. A World Selfie Check nullifier is stored on every claim and dispute so one person cannot hold both sides of a stake. No model adjudicates anything: the only thing behind a claim is capital at risk, and anyone can re-run the evidence. Everything is live on Hedera testnet and Arc testnet: 17 skills listed, real x402 settlements through Blocky402, real USDC escrow on Arc, disputes settled both ways, and the whole loop (register, claim, probe, dispute, resolve, settle) works from the browser.
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm monorepo in TypeScript. The gateway is Express: a JSON index for skills, claims, disputes, resolutions and payments, with Hedera HCS as the audit log. Every event is an HCS message on the registry topic and on a per-claim topic; skill sources and dispute evidence are pinned as HCS-1 files; each buyer gets an HTS licence NFT minted on settlement; the agent carries an HCS-14 identity. Paid access is x402 via @x402/core, @x402/express and @x402/hedera, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator in HBAR or HTS USDC, priced per kilobyte of source; a licence gate reads NFT ownership from the mirror node so holders read free. The sandbox runs the skill in a scrubbed Node child process with an interposition shim that wraps process.env, fs, net.Socket.connect, dns, child_process and eval (the child also runs with --disallow-code-generation-from-strings); canary env vars are planted so a leaking error handler is caught red-handed; the trace is canonicalised and sha256'd, and we verified byte-identical hashes across processes, working directories and a Docker container. Stake custody is a Foundry/Solidity contract on Arc (SigilStake: openClaim, dispute, resolve; DisputeResolver records verdicts), and the agent signs every approve, dispute and resolve as an ERC-4337 user operation from a Circle Agent Stack wallet. The web app is Next.js 16, React, TanStack Query, wagmi/viem and Tailwind, designed as a printed ledger rather than a dashboard. Hacky and worth mentioning: the gateway exposes POST /claims/:id/probe, which runs the claim's skill in the same sandbox on the server, so a browser user gets dispute evidence without the repo; a headless agent cannot open the World widget, so its operator verifies once and lists the nullifier; and the same skill.json folders feed both the UI's example picker and the CLI registration script.

projects.title: Bond Desk
projects.description: Compliant bond desk on Hedera: KYC-gated order book, scheduled coupons, TEE risk monitor
projects.project_description: Bond Desk is a compliant corporate bond market on Hedera testnet, watched by a confidential Chainlink CRE enclave. The bond is a real Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) token, created through the live ATS factory on testnet, so it carries its own KYC list, freeze list and transfer rules. An on-chain order book trades it against USDC and asks the token's own compliance check (canTransferFrom) before every fill: KYC is enforced by the contract, not by the UI. Three bonds with different coupon schedules trade on the desk today, each with its own book. Coupons are paid by the Hedera Schedule Service: the lifecycle contract calls HIP-1215 scheduleCall, Hedera executes it at the due time, and the executed call schedules the next coupon from inside itself. Collateral is native HBAR held in a vault and valued against the live Chainlink HBAR/USD feed on Hedera. Risk is handled by a Chainlink CRE workflow running inside a TEE. It reads the coverage, compares it with thresholds that never leave the enclave, and signs an EIP-712 verdict (OK, WARN, FREEZE, DEFAULT). Anyone can relay the verdict; the RiskGate contract checks the signature and the nonce, not the sender, and a FREEZE halts trading for that bond only. The policy is private, the verdict is public and verifiable. The same desk is a web app (a dense trading terminal with full keyboard control), a public OpenAPI service, a paid Bazantic gateway with an MCP server, and a Bazantic Recipe that chains three gateways (Hedera Mirror Node, Bond Desk, Bank of Canada Valet) so an agent can find the best bond a wallet is allowed to hold and whether its coupon beats the sovereign benchmark. Everything ran on Hedera testnet with verified contracts and a receipt for every step: issuance through ATS, KYC grants, a rejected non-KYC fill and an accepted KYC fill, coupons paid by the Schedule Service on their own, WARN and FREEZE verdicts relayed, a fill rejected while frozen, an unfreeze. Both CRE workflows are deployed on the CRE network: the bond monitor runs hourly against Hedera, and the liquidation-protection workflow defends our position in Chainlink's Sepolia challenge every 30 seconds. For Hedera's harness track we also opened PR #62 on hedera-dev/hedera-harness, which makes the harness prove that a scheduled transaction executed and that its child transaction succeeded. Live app: https://wd6nrvmajt.ap-south-1.awsapprunner.com · Docs: https://bond-desk.mintlify.site
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Foundry, Solidity 0.8.28, OpenZeppelin v5. Six contracts (BondRegistry, BondMarket, CollateralVault, NavOracle, BondLifecycle, RiskGate) around ATS v8 bond tokens created through the existing testnet factory. ATS is treated as a black box behind its canTransferFrom, KYC, snapshot and freeze facets; we did not fork it. BondLifecycle is the Schedule Service payer: it calls scheduleCall on the 0x16b system contract and each executed coupon arms the next one. We hit the out-of-gas nested schedule and a block.timestamp lag on testnet and fixed both (4M schedule gas, a 10 s lag margin). RiskGate verifies EIP-712 verdicts: trusted signer, strictly increasing nonce per bond, freshness window. Chainlink CRE: TypeScript SDK, handlerInTee pinned to AWS Nitro, one batched JSON-RPC read per run because Hedera is not a CRE-supported chain, viem signing inside the enclave, secrets in the Vault DON. The same decide.ts policy module drives the Sepolia liquidation-protection workflow, which probes the challenge contract's onlyActive gate inside its read batch so it never spends gas outside a scoring window. The relayer (Node, viem) verifies the signature locally before paying gas; the deployed workflow can also deliver verdicts to Hedera itself. API and app: Hono on Node 22 with mirror-node history plus eth_call state, an OpenAPI 3.1 document that renders as an interactive reference in a browser and stays JSON for programs, served from one AWS App Runner image together with the Vite/React/wagmi app. The app is a trading terminal: sortable desk, depth ladders, keyboard for everything (j/k/Enter, b/s, arrows to nudge price), a compliance page that shows the token's own decision, a coupon page with the pending schedule, a risk page where anyone can paste and relay a verdict. Every write is simulated first, so a revert is decoded into a sentence before the wallet signs. Testnet self-service KYC works through EIP-191 signed messages and an officer key on the API. Bazantic: three gateways (Bond Desk API, Hedera Mirror Node testnet, Bank of Canada Valet, the last one written from scratch as an OpenAPI spec) and a Recipe with seven tool bindings, published through Bazantic's control MCP and tested on a KYC wallet and a no-KYC wallet. Hedera harness: our own Foundry harness with mocks for the 0x16b and 0x167 system contracts, a base test that fires due schedules, and doctor/verify/validate-schedule scripts (42 tests). Upstream, PR #62 on hedera-dev/hedera-harness adds a CHAIN-stage check that reads the scheduled child transaction at its execution timestamp on the mirror node, because the schedules endpoint cannot tell an executed-and-succeeded schedule from an executed-and-reverted one. We exercised the upstream branch end to end on testnet with real reverted fixtures. Hacky and notable: explicit gas overrides where hashio's estimator is wrong, the scheduling lag margin, splitting CRE secrets across two files to fit a 10-id cap, and discovering that cre execution logs returns confidential-handler logs once per DON node.

projects.title: Zikibols
projects.description: Fund real-world cashflows on Hedera: agent pays for diligence via x402, backers pledge with email.
projects.project_description: A backer should be able to fund an invoice bond or harvest share without a seed phrase, without trusting a screenshot of "DeFi history," and without receiving a meme ticker. Zikibols is that product: a crowdfunding app for tokenized real-world cashflows, built from scratch for ETHOnline 2026. One app, three load-bearing sponsor integrations — Privy for login and the pledge, The Graph for live diligence, Hedera for paid risk notes, an HCS audit trail, and the token lifecycle. It is not a general crowdfunding clone. A founder starts a campaign — a diligence-gated listing for invoice receivables or revenue-share assets. After funding, the campaign becomes a restricted token with a coupon that needs two people to release. Due diligence has two layers: The campaign (free). When a founder starts a campaign they publish the story, creator name, optional email, and Ethereum wallet. That is the public brief anyone can read without paying. Paid due diligence. Before pledging, a backer can Check this creator. The agent queries live DeFi books, searches the public web for that name and email, pays Hedera x402 for a written risk note, and hashes the result onto HCS. A backer can: Read the campaign, then Check the creator (live Graph + founder research + paid note) before sending money Pledge HBAR after logging in with email or social (no seed phrase) See the campaign turn into a restricted Hedera token, then a coupon that needs two people to release
projects.how_its_made: Zikibols is a Next.js 16 / React 19 app for tokenized invoice and harvest-share campaigns. The stack is three sponsor pipes, not a pile of demos: Privy gets a backer in, The Graph is the only on-chain source the diligence agent is allowed to trust, and Hedera is where money, the audit trail, and the security actually live. A founder publishes a free campaign brief (story, name, optional email, Ethereum wallet). A backer clicks Check this creator, which hits POST /api/agent. That agent queries Aave v3, Compound v3, and Spark Lend with one Messari lendingProtocols query and one account(id) query through the Graph Gateway. Same schema, three books; one subgraph can 500 without killing diligence. Adding a protocol is one subgraph id. There is no mocked Graph fallback — missing THEGRAPH_API_KEY fails on purpose. Those live books then become paid compute. A backer should be able to fund an invoice bond or harvest share without a seed phrase, without trusting a screenshot of "DeFi history," and without receiving a meme ticker.

Zikibols is that product: a crowdfunding app for tokenized real-world cashflows, built from scratch for ETHOnline 2026. One app, three load-bearing sponsor integrations — Privy for login and the pledge, The Graph for live diligence, Hedera for paid risk notes, an HCS audit trail, and the token lifecycle.

It is not a general crowdfunding clone. A founder starts a campaign — a diligence-gated listing for invoice receivables or revenue-share assets. After funding, the campaign becomes a restricted token with a coupon that needs two people to release.

Due diligence has two layers:
- The campaign (free). When a founder starts a campaign they publish the story, creator name, optional email, and Ethereum wallet. That is the public brief anyone can read without paying.
- Paid due diligence. Before pledging, a backer can Check this creator. The agent queries live DeFi books, searches the public web for that name and email, pays Hedera x402 for a written risk note, and hashes the result onto HCS.

A backer can:
- Read the campaign, then Check the creator (live Graph + founder research + paid note) before sending money
- Pledge HBAR after logging in with email or social (no seed phrase)
- See the campaign turn into a restricted Hedera token, then a coupon that needs two people to release

projects.title: Agentis
projects.description: Complete financial infrastructure for AI agents, usable via SDK, CLI, MCP or its dashboard
projects.project_description: Agentis gives AI agents wallets and the ability to pay for things—with spending controls set by their owner. Instead of handing an agent an unrestricted private key or manually paying for every request, users create named agents with separate wallets, budgets and permissions. Agents can operate automatically within those limits or request owner approval for each payment. A shared backend handles authorization, spending reservations, execution and transaction receipts across the dashboard, SDK, CLI and remote MCP. Hosted wallets use Privy, while Agentis enforces per-transaction, hourly, daily and total USD limits across each agent’s networks, including fees. Agents can send funds and access paid APIs through x402 and MPP without managing individual subscriptions or API keys for those services. For users who prefer local custody, the CLI also supports multichain wallets with keys kept on their own machine rather than in Privy. Local wallets support transfers, x402/MPP payments, shared USD spending limits and transaction history. They use owner-only file permisisons and do not require a hosted Agentis account. Optional capabilities are enabled per agent. The Uniswap integration adds swaps, manual portfolio rebalancing, recurring purchases, gas refill and swap-to-fund x402 payments—buying only the missing payment-token amount. The current implementation targets testnets across Base, Arc, Tempo and Solana, with Uniswap execution on Base Sepolia. The goal is practical financial autonomy for agents, with clear owner control and a traceable record of what was spent.
projects.how_its_made: Agentis is a TypeScript monorepo with a Bun/Hono backend, PostgreSQL and Drizzle for persistence, and Zod for input validation. The dashboard uses Next.js, React, Tailwind and TanStack Query. The SDK, CLI and remote MCP server all call the same backend operations rather than implementing separate payment logic. MCP uses the official protocol SDK and OAuth with PKCE; browser consent grants access only to explicitly selected agents and networks. Privy handles authentication and hosted wallet keys. Wallets use a user/server 1-of-2 ownership quorum, allowing server-authorized execution without a wallet-signature popup for every payment. Agentis—not the quorum itself—enforces spending rules. PostgreSQL transactions and owner-level locks reserve the payment amount plus maximum fees before execution. Amounts use bigint arithmetic and decimal strings, with fresh server-side prices for shared USD budgets. Approvals bind to the exact operation, and signed transaction data is persisted before broadcast so uncertain submissions can be reconciled instead of blindly resent. Viem handles EVM interactions, while Solana uses its own transaction adapter. x402 and MPP connect agents to paid HTTP services: discover payment requirements, authorize payment, retry the request and retain the payment record even if the service response fails. Local-custody CLI wallets use locally derived keys and a separate local policy ledger, without routing signing through Privy. Uniswap provides the trading layer on Base Sepolia. One practical workaround was using its deployed V3 Quoter and SwapRouter02 directly after the hosted Trading API returned upstream errors. We compare quotes across four fee tiers and construct bounded calldata ourselves, including exact token allowances, minimum outputs and native-token wrapping/refunds. Swap-to-fund buys only a payment's shortfall using exact output. PostgreSQL-backed schedules run through the existing worker and approval pipeline, so recurring purchases do not require an always-online AI agent or a separate scheduling service.

projects.title: StablePay
projects.description: WakaPay demo store for crypto checkout, webhooks, and merchant payment automation.
projects.project_description: This project is a demo merchant storefront built for the ETHGlobal hackathon to showcase how WakaPay can power real-world crypto commerce. It simulates a modern online store where users can browse different product types, add items to a cart, and complete payment through a secure WakaPay checkout flow. Behind the scenes, the app creates signed checkout sessions, redirects users to hosted crypto payment, and listens for payment webhooks to confirm transactions and trigger customer notifications. For a competition jury, the key idea is that this is not just a static UI demo, but an end-to-end proof of how merchants can integrate WakaPay into a production-style e-commerce experience for digital goods, subscriptions, services, tickets, and physical products.
projects.how_its_made: It is built as a Next.js web application with a marketplace-style frontend and a lightweight backend layer inside the same app. The frontend handles product browsing, filtering, cart management, and the checkout trigger, while the backend exposes API routes that prepare payment requests for WakaPay. When a user starts checkout, the server signs the payload with HMAC using the merchant credentials, sends it to the WakaPay/Wakari checkout API, and receives a hosted checkout_url for redirection. The project also includes a webhook endpoint that verifies Wakapay signatures, processes payment status events, and sends confirmation or reminder emails through SMTP. In short, it combines a modern React-based storefront, secure server-side payment integration, webhook handling, and email automation into one end-to-end merchant demo.

projects.title: Trelp
projects.description: Tranched Uniswap v4 liquidity, with a 1inch Aqua buffer that never leaves the vault.
projects.project_description:
Trelp splits a single Uniswap v4 liquidity position into two tradeable claims with
different risk profiles. THE PROBLEM
Being an LP is one blended bet. You earn trading fees, you lose money when the pair
moves against you, and you find out the net at the end. There is no way to buy only
the steady part or only the levered part. So two kinds of capital stay out: treasuries
that need predictable yield will not accept a position that can be down 20% because ETH
moved, and traders who want leveraged exposure to fee income have to borrow it elsewhere
and manage that separately. Both want the same position. They want different slices of it. HOW IT WORKS
Depositors choose a side. Senior is paid first at settlement and earns a capped return,
protected by junior's capital sitting underneath it. Junior absorbs losses before senior
feels anything, and in exchange keeps the entire upside above senior's capped claim.
Both sides hold ERC-20 claim tokens, so a position can be sold before the epoch ends. Senior's rate is not configured in advance. It is derived when the deposit window closes,
from how much of each side actually arrived. More junior capital means a thicker cushion,
so senior needs to be paid less for the risk. The derivation requires junior to beat an
unlevered LP at any fee yield, which makes the fee term cancel out, so the bound holds
regardless of how the epoch performs. Past roughly 50% junior there is no rate that leaves
both sides better off than simply LPing, and the vault refuses to start rather than sell
terms that do not work. A curator manages the position: picks the price range and moves it as the market moves.
Those powers are deliberately narrow. The curator never holds depositor funds, cannot
change terms once the epoch starts, is rate limited by a cooldown, and is blocked from
moving the range at all once the position is under stress. Every move has its cost
measured and recorded. The protocol never computes impermanent loss. At settlement it holds one number, the cash
balance after unwinding, and pays senior first up to its claim. Everything (fees, IL,
adverse selection, unwind cost) is already inside that number. Attributing it per user
would need path-dependent accounting and a counterfactual price oracle, and would change
nobody's payout. THE TWO INTEGRATIONS
Uniswap v4: a custom hook gates the pool to the vault's own position, overrides the LP fee
from a live solvency reading, and refuses swaps that would push more of the falling asset
onto the vault while still accepting trades that reduce risk. A dynamic fee is symmetric
and cannot skew, so a directional refusal is the only way to decline one side. A normal
pool has no way to say no, which is exactly how an LP ends up buying all the way down. 1inch Aqua: part of junior's capital works as a standing bid below spot. Aqua takes no
custody, so that capital is still sitting in the vault backing senior while it quotes. It
buys at a discount in calm markets, widens as the cushion thins via an Extruction target
that reads vault solvency at swap time, and stops bidding entirely when coverage breaks.
Anyone can then revoke it permissionlessly, turning it back into pure loss absorption. Both venues read the same coverage number from the same contract. One view of risk,
applied in two places. WHAT IS BUILT
Full protocol in Solidity with 98 tests across 11 suites, plus an opt-in mainnet fork suite
that runs the whole stack against the real v4 PoolManager and a real Aqua registry. Live
deployment on Base Sepolia with a working frontend: deposits, claim balances, live coverage,
on-chain event history, and redemption. A full epoch on a mainnet fork, with ETH falling 45%: coverage goes from 42.9% to negative,
the pool fee widens 30 to 90 bps, the hook refuses a swap, the buffer is revoked, and the
vault settles. Junior loses everything, senior finishes down 0.98%. That is the honest
shape of the product. Junior is a cushion, not a guarantee. KNOWN LIMITS
Senior's coupon is paid from realised gain, so a flat epoch returns principal and nothing
else. A CLO-style interest waterfall is the fix and is not built. There is no hedge during
a drawdown and no early settlement. One position per vault.
projects.how_its_made:
UNISWAP V4 HOOK
The hook is what makes the pool defensible. Gates liquidity so only our vault can LP in,
overrides the LP fee live off the vault's solvency, and refuses swaps that would dump more of
the falling asset on us while still taking trades that reduce risk. A dynamic fee is
symmetric and can't skew, so a directional refusal is the only way to decline one side. A
normal pool has no way to say no, which is how an LP ends up buying all the way down. v4 encodes hook permissions in the address, so we mine it with CREATE2 until it ends in
0x880. Pool also needs DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG or the fee override is silently ignored. 1INCH AQUA
ship() takes no custody, the tokens stay in your wallet. That's the whole reason this works:
junior's capital is a live standing bid and a loss-absorbing reserve at the same time,
because it never leaves the vault. The buffer is a SwapVM program, quote only. A two sided maker would hold inventory correlated
with the exact drawdown the buffer exists to survive. XYCConcentrateSwap derives virtual
reserves from its bounds, so a zero risky balance still quotes a working bid. Aqua strategies are immutable once shipped, so a spread tracking live coverage can't be a
strategy parameter. Extruction fixes that: it hands the swap registers to any contract mid
program, so our adjuster reads the vault at swap time and rewrites the output. Coverage-aware
pricing against the officially deployed SwapVM, no redeploy. We also had to anchor the bid to an oracle. With an unanchored curve the risk policy made
senior worse off (-15.43% vs -15.50%), because it underpaid for the risky asset so refusing
fills gave up as many gains as losses. Anchored, the same crash went -1.24% vs -15.44%. Those
two demo paths differ by one constructor argument. THE ANNOYING PART
v4-core pins solc 0.8.26, Aqua and SwapVM pin 0.8.30. No single file can import both. The
vault talks to both through hand written interfaces, every test suite takes one venue real
and mocks the other, and the one place both run together uses deployCode so no type crosses
the version line. activate() ships to Aqua and mints the v4 position in the same call, and
that path had never actually run until we wrote a combined test for it. STACK
Solidity, Foundry, Next.js 16, viem, Privy. Live on Base Sepolia, verified against forked
mainnet with the real PoolManager and a real Aqua registry. 98 tests. TWO THINGS THAT BIT US
Asset ordering. Pool price is currency1 per currency0, so which range bound exposes you to
the risky asset flips with token ordering. We had it as a constructor bool. Get it wrong and
the halt inverts silently, refusing the safe side and allowing the dangerous one. Derived
from the pool key now. settle() needed the risky balance at zero, but unwinding an in-range position returns both
tokens and nothing could convert them. redeem needs Settled, cancel needs Subscription. Funds
would have been stuck permanently. Tests missed it because the harness was impersonating the
vault to dump inventory. Added liquidate(), permissionless and floored against the oracle.

projects.title: Opaque
projects.description: Quantum-safe private USDC— from chain to IP. Still private when elliptic curves fail.
projects.project_description:
Opaque is a post-quantum private payments rail for USDC on Arc, built for the confidential-payments market.
Current systems can hide a transfer while leaving the authorization key, payment timing, RPC activity, or IP origin exposed. Opaque addresses these leak paths together while providing post-quantum security end-to-end.
Users control ERC-4337 smart accounts whose authority comes from FORS+C, a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme. Keys are generated and protected locally in the browser, while PQKeyRegistry and the account validator enforce key use, rotation, and bounded authorization on Arc. USDC is deposited and split into shared fixed-denomination pools—1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 USDC—so payments use interchangeable notes rather than a wallet-specific balance, which allows ring signatures to work.
For a payment, the wallet forms an eight-member same-denomination ring: one owned note and seven real decoys. projects.title: Sotto
projects.description: Sotto is a request-for-quote block-trading venue built on Hedera for ATS-issued securities.
projects.project_description: ATS, which is Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, lets an issuer mint a compliant bond. It does not let anyone trade one. Sotto is the missing secondary market. A bondholder escrows a block of an ATS-issued security and puts it up for bid. Dealers compete under commit–reveal: during the quote window only keccak256(price, quantity, nonce, dealer) reaches the venue, so nobody, including us — can read a price before the window closes. The window closes on a Hedera Consensus Service timestamp rather than our clock, so the venue cannot quietly extend it for a favoured dealer. Dealers then reveal, and each price is recomputed against its commit and must match exactly or the quote is void. The book is allocated on strict price priority across several dealers at once. In a live testnet run, a 30-unit block filled 3 units at 98.80 to one dealer and 20 at 98.55 to another, leaving 7 unfilled — each dealer paying its own quoted price, never a rival's and never a uniform clearing price. Every fill is a separate EIP-712 Trade with its own signatures, its own nonce and its own firmness deadline, and a dealer's firmness bounds its own settlement deadline on-chain rather than merely in our engine. Settlement is atomic delivery-versus-payment in a single transaction. Cash moves by transferFrom; the security moves by executeHoldByPartition on the ATS diamond, which runs compliance at the transfer itself. Any failure reverts both legs. There is no window in which the buyer holds the security and the seller has not been paid, and a revoked-KYC buyer fails inside the delivery call, taking the payment back with it. Compliance is enforced by ATS, not bolted on by the venue. A NAV band guard inside the settlement contract additionally refuses any trade priced more than 5% from an on-chain reference, with a staleness bound so an unmaintained mark blocks settlement rather than being trusted. Every stage — the request, the escrow, each sealed commit, the close, each reveal, the award and each fill — is timestamped on HCS topic 0.0.10383803. The venue is auditable after the fact without being transparent while the auction is live. The bond's whole lifecycle is on-chain too: coupons the contract schedules for itself through HIP-1215 scheduled calls, and redemption at maturity through the ATS Bond facet. Live on Hedera testnet at https://sotto-tau.vercel.app. Every claim in the README links to HashScan or to the HCS topic, so none of it has to be taken on trust.
projects.how_its_made:
Hedera testnet throughout, against the real Asset Tokenization Studio diamond (factory 0.0.7708432) and real Circle USDC (0.0.429274),  not a mock token. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 under Hardhat, all verified on Sourcify as exact_match: • SottoSettlement — EIP-712 verification of both parties, nonces consumed inside the settling call so a signature cannot replay, hold validation (escrow is self, amount sufficient, not expired), then transferFrom and executeHoldByPartition in one call. Every guard is a custom error, and the API decodes those four-byte selectors back into sentences for the UI.
• SottoNavOracle — administrator-published NAV with a staleness bound, behind an IPriceSource seam.
• ChainlinkPriceSource — reads live Chainlink AggregatorV3 feeds on Hedera testnet through that seam, so an asset with a real market price overrides the administrator's mark. A bond's NAV is not on a price feed and never will be, which is why the administrator path is primary and the feed is the override rather than the reverse.
• SottoCouponScheduler — schedules its own coupon payments using HIP-1215 scheduled contract calls via the Hedera Schedule Service system contract at 0x16b.
• SottoDealerBond — a dealer posts a bond and forfeits it to the seller, not to the venue, for failing to reveal. Two settlement paths, both live: Path A is EVM-native. The buyer approves exact USDC and anyone at all can relay the fully-signed trade, because the authorisation is the two signatures rather than the sender. Path B grants no allowance anywhere. The buyer signs a native HTS transfer of their own cash with a HIP-820 wallet session, the venue batches it together with the delivery call as a HIP-551 atomic batch, and the network provides the atomicity instead of a contract. The relay verifies the inner cash leg before batching — correct token id, exact debit and credit, exactly two transfers, no hbar movement, our batch key, already frozen — because without that check a buyer could sign a one-unit transfer and take the whole block. Backend is Fastify with ethers 6: the RFQ engine and allocator, an HCS audit writer, and the batch relay. Auction windows are judged against HCS consensus timestamps rather than the server clock. Frontend is Next.js 15 with Reown AppKit, wagmi and @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect, so a single ECDSA account serves both the EVM and Hedera-native namespaces from one wallet connection. The most useful thing we learned is in docs/ATS-SPIKE.md and is absent from Hedera's published docs: ATS v3.1.0 as deployed uses different role hashes from repo HEAD. Grants made with HEAD's constants land on hashes the deployed contract never checks — hasRole returns true and every guarded call still reverts, with no useful error. Only DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is stable across the two versions, which is what let us repair it from outside. One more that cost us a live trade: Hedera's JSON-RPC relay attaches no revert data to the error from a sent transaction, so a custom error's four bytes never reach the caller. Recovering them needs an eth_call replay against the same block, which the venue now does automatically whenever a revert comes back unexplained.

projects.title: Levantate Bridge
projects.description: AI agents post tasks; verified humans bid, deliver work, and get paid in USDC on Arc.
projects.project_description: Levantate Bridge is an agent-to-human task marketplace where AI agents autonomously post work, hire verified humans, and settle payment in USDC on Arc testnet—without a human operator in the loop on the agent side. When an agent hits a task it cannot complete alone (e.g. collecting neighborhood complaints, subjective judgment, or physical-world steps), it posts the task with a max budget and bidding window. Human workers browse open tasks, link a wallet they already control, and place bids. Every bid requires a fresh World ID Selfie Check bound to that task, round, and amount—identity comes from the proof, not the client, and each proof is spent once to block bot/sybil bidding. One World ID nullifier maps to one payout address. The agent selects a winning bid using live historical data from The Graph (completion rates, missed deadlines, typical payouts). Funds lock in a TaskEscrow smart contract on Arc funded by a Circle Developer-Controlled agent wallet. A separate Circle relayer wallet submits placeBid and submitWork for workers so they never need gas. Workers submit proof before a submission deadline; the agent evaluates it and calls approveWork, which releases USDC directly to the worker’s self-custodied wallet. If a worker misses the deadline, the agent can reclaim the task for a new bidding round—recorded on-chain and indexed for future scoring. All eight escrow events are indexed by a subgraph on Arc testnet. The agent uses that data for budgeting and bid scoring; write confirmation uses Arc RPC receipts. Settlement is USDC on Arc via Circle throughout—no bridging or swapping.
projects.how_its_made:
Overview
Levantate Bridge is a monorepo: contracts/ (Solidity escrow on Arc), backend/ (Node 22 API + agent + relayer), frontend/ (Next.js worker UI), subgraph/ (AssemblyScript indexer). Supabase Postgres stores workers, bids, proofs, and relayed tx state. One root .env.local configures everything. The agent chat, winner loop, and REST API all call the same escrow operations module. Circle + Arc
Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets on Arc testnet (chain 5042002, USDC 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000). Two wallets: Agent 0x42472b448b6ba8bb654483d4773db715901a64a7 — funds escrow, posts tasks, selects winners, approves/rejects work, reclaims, cancels
Relayer 0xd055b6cee7d72bc5111119ec7beb8c56b2f61ae1 — submits placeBid and submitWork so workers never hold gas
Escrow contract: 0xc8F1db364B14D7Aa4ea620bF9f649Ef3D7F14d52 (deploy block 61231705)
Explorer: https://testnet.arcscan.app/address/0xc8F1db364B14D7Aa4ea620bF9f649Ef3D7F14d52 Every write: Circle SDK → wait for tx hash → Arc RPC receipt (success = confirmed, revert = failed). Relayer uses a serialized nonce queue + idempotency keys so concurrent bids don’t race nonces. Benefit: Autonomous USDC settlement on Arc; workers paid to self-custodied wallets—the backend never holds worker keys. World ID (Selfie Check)
Every bid requires a fresh Selfie Check via @worldcoin/idkit (selfieCheckLegacy, sandbox World App). Backend signs mandatory rp_context, verifies at developer.world.org/api/v4/verify/{rp_id}. Signal per bid: bid:{taskId}:{round}:{amountMicro}. Nullifier comes from the proof, not the client. Each proof is spent once; fingerprints tied to task_id, cleaned up after pay/cancel/reclaim. Workers link a payout wallet with a free off-chain personal_sign before bidding. First bid binds one nullifier → one address. Benefit: Gates economic participation—blocks scripted bid floods without custodial worker wallets. The Graph
Subgraph slug levantate-bridge, network arc-testnet, indexes all 8 escrow events from the contract above. Published links: Subgraph Studio: https://thegraph.com/studio/subgraph/levantate-bridge/
Graph Explorer: https://thegraph.com/explorer/subgraphs/Fnr7E8tC1HbD1bvdAsTXMwe5R5kZdx98pH1bhmcWWGeL
Query gateway: https://gateway.thegraph.com/api/subgraphs/id/Fnr7E8tC1HbD1bvdAsTXMwe5R5kZdx98pH1bhmcWWGeL Agent uses live indexed data for:
Budget — median historical payout + submission window before postTask
Bid scoring — completion rate, missed deadlines, price vs median Benefit: Winner selection and budgeting use real on-chain history, not hardcoded rules. Stack & notable details
Next.js 16, viem, RainbowKit, Supabase, OpenAI agent at /agent. LLM proof review on submit. Two deadlines: bid (auction) vs submission (delivery); reclaimTask reopens bidding if a worker ghosts.

Signal per bid: bid:{taskId}:{round}:{amountMicro}. Nullifier comes from the proof, not the client. Each proof is spent once; fingerprints tied to task_id, cleaned up after pay/cancel/reclaim.

Workers link a payout wallet with a free off-chain personal_sign before bidding. First bid binds one nullifier → one address.

Benefit: Gates economic participation—blocks scripted bid floods without custodial worker wallets.

The Graph
Subgraph slug levantate-bridge, network arc-testnet, indexes all 8 escrow events from the contract above.

Subgraph Studio: https://thegraph.com/studio/subgraph/levantate-bridge/

Agent uses live indexed data for:
Budget — median historical payout + submission window before postTask
Bid scoring — completion rate, missed deadlines, price vs median

Benefit: Winner selection and budgeting use real on-chain history, not hardcoded rules.

Next.js 16, viem, RainbowKit, Supabase, OpenAI agent at /agent. LLM proof review on submit. Two deadlines: bid (auction) vs submission (delivery); reclaimTask reopens bidding if a worker ghosts.

projects.title: PinTool MM
projects.description: Sell your market-making strategy without showing it. Makers run it on Aqua with their own funds.
projects.project_description: PinTool Market Making removes the trust barrier between strategy creators and capital owners on 1inch Aqua. A Strategy Provider publishes a market-making strategy while keeping its activation rules, thresholds and sizing logic private. A Maker picks a strategy and sets private risk limits: total budget, maximum inventory share, per-fill caps and authorization lifetime. Neither side ever sees the other's inputs. A Chainlink Confidential Workflow intersects both policies inside a TEE (handlerInTee). Provider policies are Vault DON secrets; Maker limits are sealed in the browser and opened only inside the enclave. The workflow publishes only the minimal authorization the chain needs, a Guard report with allowed directions, per-swap caps, inventory caps and expiry, and it can only make the Maker's limits stricter, never looser. PinTool Guard sits behind SwapVM's Extruction instruction and checks every Aqua fill against that authorization, reverting anything outside it, so a strategy halts the moment the workflow stops renewing it. Funds never leave the Maker's wallet; one balance can back several strategies with at most one active at a time. Strategies are published under ENSv2 names on Sepolia so Makers pin a verified, immutable release. Everything runs end to end on Ethereum Sepolia with canonical WETH and Circle USDC: a public run of 40 transactions shows guarded swaps on two strategies plus an expected on-chain rejection, and the mandate service independently verifies every Guard report and Aqua receipt before the app shows it.
projects.how_its_made: Confidential workflow (workflow/, TypeScript, Bun, @chainlink/cre-sdk): a cron- or HTTP-triggered handlerInTee callback fetches the Provider strategy and the Maker limits with getSecrets(), reads live ETH/USDC market data from Kraken, runs a pure intersection function (the stricter side wins on every cap; inventory caps are derived from budget × share at the mid price; paused reports zero every cap), ABI-encodes the Guard report and crosses back with usingTheDons() so the DON signs it and the forwarder delivers it to PinTool Guard's onReport(bytes,bytes). The encoding is golden-tested byte for byte against the fixture the Solidity side decodes, and a leak-check script diffs every secret value against the simulation output. Local CRE CLI simulation broadcasts real reports through Chainlink's Sepolia simulation forwarder. Contracts (contracts/aqua-executor/, Solidity, Foundry): the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM sources are built unmodified at pinned commits. PinTool Guard implements the Extruction interface and is the terminal instruction of every Maker-approved program, so each fill is validated before any token moves. It enforces direction, per-swap amount, post-swap inventory and expiry per (maker, strategyHash), with strictly increasing nonces and standing authorizations the Maker can revoke. Official Aqua deployments require a KycNFT, so we redeployed Aqua and the SwapVM router on Ethereum Sepolia. Mandate service (orchestrator/, Node, Railway): validates requests, signs CRE HTTP-trigger calls, runs the confidential runner and independently verifies every Guard report and Aqua receipt from Sepolia RPC before the web app shows it, with a durable event outbox, serialized deliveries and restart recovery. Web app (frontend/, Next.js 15, React 19, Privy, viem, static export): marketplace, Provider Studio with an AI-assisted strategy builder (Vercel AI SDK + OpenAI), a Maker mandate flow that seals limits in the browser with noble ciphers, an activity monitor, and ENSv2 strategy names on Sepolia (namespace registrar, delegated version pointer, Maker-pinned releases). Hard parts: EVMClient has no TeeRuntime overload, so on-chain writes must cross out of the enclave; SwapVM's Extruction has no try/catch, so a veto must revert; the SDK's opcode table lagged the contract; and Extruction args are capped at 235 bytes, so the Guard report lives in PinTool Guard's storage and only a public envelope goes into the bytecode. Codex and Claude Code were used heavily across contracts, workflow and frontend, with the team owning product, privacy model and verification (see AI_USAGE.md).

projects.title: cackpass
projects.description: A decentralized event ticketing platform with USDC payments on Arc and on-chain proof of purchase.
projects.project_description:
CACK-pass is a Web2/Web3 hybrid event ticketing platform that lets organizers
create events, sell tickets, and settle revenue in USDC on Arc. We originally
ran on Lisk with a Paystack fiat rail, but Lisk Mainnet is being deprecated, so
we are migrating the whole platform to Arc — an EVM chain where USDC is the
native gas token and Circle-native rails are first-class. Buyers can pay two ways:
• Fiat via Flutterwave (card, USSD, bank transfer, mobile money)
• Native USDC on Arc via Circle App Kit, using a Privy embedded wallet Every crypto payment is written on-chain by our CackPassArcPayment contract,
which records the payer, amount, reference, event ID, ticket quantity, and
status (Pending → Confirmed → Failed). That gives organizers and attendees a
shared, tamper-proof audit trail for every ticket sale. Buyers without crypto can buy real USDC with a card through Privy's Fiat
Onramp (NGN / USD / EUR / GBP), delivered to their embedded wallet on Base
Mainnet. Tickets are stored on IPFS, verified by signed QR codes, and emailed
to the customer after purchase — no login required for guest checkout.
projects.how_its_made:
CACK-pass is a Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript app deployed on Vercel.
Auth and embedded wallets come from Privy — users sign in with email, Google,
or Twitter and get a wallet with no seed phrase to manage. Payments — Fiat: We migrated the old Paystack rail to Flutterwave v3. The
Flutterwave verify and webhook routes validate verif-hash signatures, create
Order + Payment + MyTicket records in MongoDB, and trigger a shared ticket
email. Card, USSD, bank transfer, and mobile money are all supported. Payments — Crypto (the hackathon core):
• Contracts: A new Hardhat project ( arc-contracts/ ) holds CackPassArcPayment.sol , deployed and verified on Arc Testnet
(0x084622e6970BBcBA510454C6145313c2993ED9E4). It exposes
initializePayment / confirmPayment / failPayment and emits
PaymentInitiated / PaymentConfirmed / PaymentFailed events. • Server side: lib/arc/client.ts wraps the contract with ethers v6 —
provider, signer, generatePaymentId, paymentIdToBytes32,
initializeOnChainPayment, confirmOnChainPayment, and getOnChainPayment
(with proper PaymentStatus enum decoding). • Client side: lib/arc/app-kit.ts wraps Circle App Kit —
sendUSDCWithAppKit(provider, contractAddress, amount) uses the Privy
embedded wallet's EIP-1193 provider to move USDC on Arc. Ticket price
and gas are both paid in USDC because USDC is the native gas token. • UX: components/payments/ArcPaymentButton.tsx orchestrates it —
gets the Privy provider, calls /api/payments/arc/initialize,
invokes sendUSDCWithAppKit, then redirects to
/payment/success?provider=arc&transaction_id=<hash>. Includes
double-click guards, wallet-not-ready state, and insufficient-funds
messaging. • Verification: /api/payments/arc/verify polls the contract, calls
confirmPayment as the platform owner, retries until the status is
Confirmed, mints MyTicket records, and sends the ticket email via
a shared /api/email/ticket-confirmation endpoint. • Fiat → Crypto onramp: The wallet dashboard uses Privy's
useFiatOnramp().fund() to buy real USDC with a card (NGN / USD / EUR /
GBP) on Base Mainnet. Base and Arc balances are shown side by side in
a dual-network dashboard so buyers can see exactly where their funds
live. Partner tech benefits:
• Arc — native USDC gas means zero-gas UX for buyers.
• Circle App Kit — the fastest way to move USDC into a contract-driven
payment flow.
• Privy — passwordless auth + embedded wallets + fiat onramp in one SDK.
• Flutterwave — reliable African fiat rails (card, USSD, bank, mobile money). Hacky bits worth mentioning: We solved a Mongoose strict-mode gotcha by
resolving the buyer email from multiple fallbacks (Order → Payment →
metadata.userEmail → User) so ticket emails never get dropped. We also
made the Arc verify step idempotent — if a payment is marked completed but
no ticket exists, we self-heal and re-process instead of silently failing.

projects.title: arbiter
projects.description: Arbiter lets clients escrow USDC on Arc for well defined tasks.
projects.project_description:
Digital work often ends with a subjective dispute: was it delivered, did it meet the agreed criteria, and who should get paid? Arbiter turns that question into a fixed, inspectable agreement.
A client commits the scope, acceptance criteria, worker, resolver, payment amount, and deadlines before the worker accepts. The scope can describe research, a website with required pages and performance characteristics, a copywriting brief with tone and messaging constraints, or a marketing campaign with agreed KPIs and reporting requirements. The client then deposits USDC into a non-upgradeable escrow on Arc. The worker submits an immutable Markdown deliverable or delivery record and commits its exact content hash onchain.
Arbiter evaluates the committed work against the agreed rubric. Deterministic checks can cover required sections, word limits, links, or other committed requirements. Semantic evidence records a pass, failure, or inconclusive result with criterion-level explanations and supporting excerpts. In this MVP, website and marketing work is assessed through the worker's submitted Markdown delivery record; independent URL crawling and KPI-provider integrations are future work. A pass proposes full payment; a failure proposes a full refund. Either party can challenge during the review window, which freezes automatic settlement and sends the agreement to the resolver. The resolver can pay, refund, or split the deposit. If the resolver times out, the pre-agreed testnet rule splits funds 50/50.
The deployed MVP uses public sample material and one Markdown submission per agreement. It makes deadlines, evidence commitments, transaction states, and resolver powers visible to both parties.
projects.how_its_made:
The core is a non-upgradeable Solidity escrow deployed on Arc testnet. It commits the
client, worker, resolver, USDC amount, research brief hash, source hash, evaluation-policy
hash, and separate submission, evaluation, challenge, and resolution deadlines. The contract
handles funding, report-hash submission, proposed outcomes, challenges, payment, refund,
resolver splits, and timeout settlement.
The web app uses React and viem for browser-wallet transactions. A Bun API stores immutable
Markdown reports and agreement material in SQLite, authenticated with wallet signatures and
one-time nonces. It hashes the exact submitted content before the worker commits it onchain. Evaluation is implemented as a TypeScript Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. Its handlerInTee processes the agreed rubric, supplied sources, report, model credential, and
structured model response. Deterministic checks validate sections, word limits, and source
references; semantic results include criterion-level outcomes, short reasons, and report
excerpts. Invalid or uncertain evaluation never triggers automatic payment and instead
routes the agreement to human review.
The public MVP is deployed on Fly.io with an encrypted SQLite volume. It runs on Arc testnet
and uses USDC for escrow settlement.

projects.title: Vesta
projects.description: Vesta utilizes a portion of CCA commitments for launch LP liquidity, by rewarding invested bidders.
projects.project_description: Vesta is a token launch strategy for CCAs. The auction discovers the launch price, then bidders can opt to escrow ETH plus a percentage of their allocation for for locked liquidity position using vesta. The team strengthens launch liquidity, and in return, bidders get rewards set by the team.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are built with Solidity and tested with foundry, locally and on Sepolia testnet. uniswap v4 and CCA repos are used to implement the vesta strategy and vault contracts, the frontend allows a launch team to manage any of their CCA launches directly from the site, and any participants to manage their CCA bids and their vesta commitments. The frontend uses React for the UI, wagmi and ethers for wallet connections and onchain calls/reads.

projects.title: x402 Work Receipts
projects.description: Signed work orders and receipts between two agents, paid with x402, verified by a stranger
projects.project_description: When two companies let agents act for them — one ordering work, one accepting and doing it — the record of what was ordered, agreed and delivered ends up inside one company's system, which can edit it, lose it, or simply be believed less than the other when the two accounts differ. x402-work-receipts is a working instance of the alternative: no single party owns the authoritative audit trail; a shared ledger records signed evidence of which agent, holding which mandate, received, accepted and executed which command. A customer agent turns a story card into a signed work order and pays an intake fee; a contractor agent verifies the signature, anchors the order's fingerprint on a Hedera consensus topic, and returns a signed acceptance. When the work exists, the customer pays the balance and collects a signed delivery receipt carrying both payments. Six anchors go on the topic — only hashes, no content — and a stand-alone verifier reaches the same verdict either party would, reading nothing but the public mirror node. Built for two organizations that already argue about what was agreed — an agency and its client — and, longer term, for any pair of agents transacting without a platform both of them trust. What the chain proves (wording taken from the source protocol spec §4.2): a sealed mandate with envelope hash eh existed at the sender no later than consensus time T1 and was accepted by the contractor, whose receipt with hash eh2 is fixed no later than T2; the counterparty's signature verifies independently. It does not prove the mandate's content (only its fingerprint), the quality or the fact of the work, or that a key belongs to a person. The payment profile adds: the intake and balance transfers exist on the ledger with the stated payer, payee and amounts. Try it without installing anything: https://x402-work-receipts.zeabur.app/verify loads the demo run and re-checks it against the public mirror node in the browser, with links to every anchor and payment on HashScan. This is not only a hackathon demo: two real companies have run the same signed work-order and receipt format in a private pilot since 8 September 2026 (their public audit topic on Hedera testnet: 0.0.10226839). The hackathon build is the open, self-contained slice of that format with x402 payment added.
projects.how_its_made: Node/TypeScript. Both agents speak x402 with the exact scheme on hedera:testnet , settled by the Blocky402 facilitator ( api.testnet.blocky402.com ) — not a payment demo, a real settled HBAR transfer per paid route, using the upfront flow so the handler can anchor the payment id inside the receipt it signs. Every step — order received, both payments, acceptance, delivery, receipt — is anchored as a hash-only message on a Hedera Consensus Service topic; a stand-alone verifier ( verifier/ ) reads only the public mirror node, seven checks, three exit codes (0 verified, 1 failed, 2 could not check). The contractor publishes an agent card at /.well-known/agent.json, so a customer agent discovers the service and pays for it with x402 without any API key. Envelopes are Ed25519-signed RFC 8785 canonical JSON; mandate.v1 and receipt.v1 are byte-identical copies of a pre-existing protocol (drift-tested by sha256), so the project extends a schema it does not own rather than inventing its own. Extras shipped after the base flow verified end to end: HCS-14 uaid identifiers so the verifier can tie a signature to a stable id instead of only a handle; a Scheduled Transaction retainer the customer authorises up front and the contractor releases after delivering; an MCP server exposing order / collect / verify as tools for any MCP-speaking agent runtime. The hacky bit: the base protocol schemas forbid any field that looks like money ( hour , rate , amount , usd , price , cost ), so payment.v1 is generated by a Python script that flattens the base schema's keywords into a new, self-contained schema, because JSON Schema 2020-12's unevaluatedProperties: false makes a plain allOf + $ref extension impossible. Claude Code wrote the modules under protocol/ , anchor/ , contractor/ , customer/ , verifier/ and demo/ from a written design and task-by-task plan kept in the repo; every task was reviewed, tested and checked against the public mirror node by hand before merging (see the "AI collaboration" section of the README).

Node/TypeScript. Both agents speak x402 with the `exact` scheme on `hedera:testnet`, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator (`api.testnet.blocky402.com`) — not a payment demo, a real settled HBAR transfer per paid route, using the `upfront` flow so the handler can anchor the payment id inside the receipt it signs. Every step — order received, both payments, acceptance, delivery, receipt — is anchored as a hash-only message on a Hedera Consensus Service topic; a stand-alone verifier (`verifier/`) reads only the public mirror node, seven checks, three exit codes (0 verified, 1 failed, 2 could not check). The contractor publishes an agent card at /.well-known/agent.json, so a customer agent discovers the service and pays for it with x402 without any API key.

Envelopes are Ed25519-signed RFC 8785 canonical JSON; `mandate.v1` and `receipt.v1` are byte-identical copies of a pre-existing protocol (drift-tested by sha256), so the project extends a schema it does not own rather than inventing its own. Extras shipped after the base flow verified end to end: HCS-14 `uaid` identifiers so the verifier can tie a signature to a stable id instead of only a handle; a Scheduled Transaction retainer the customer authorises up front and the contractor releases after delivering; an MCP server exposing `order`/`collect`/`verify` as tools for any MCP-speaking agent runtime.

The hacky bit: the base protocol schemas forbid any field that looks like money (`hour`, `rate`, `amount`, `usd`, `price`, `cost`), so `payment.v1` is generated by a Python script that flattens the base schema's keywords into a new, self-contained schema, because JSON Schema 2020-12's `unevaluatedProperties: false` makes a plain `allOf`+`$ref` extension impossible. Claude Code wrote the modules under `protocol/`, `anchor/`, `contractor/`, `customer/`, `verifier/` and `demo/` from a written design and task-by-task plan kept in the repo; every task was reviewed, tested and checked against the public mirror node by hand before merging (see the "AI collaboration" section of the README).

projects.title: Roll Call
projects.description: Every protocol has a pause button. Roll Call tells you whether anyone is still holding it.
projects.project_description:
Every protocol has a pause button, an upgrade path, a multisig. Almost none can tell you whether anyone is still holding it. Roll Call derives that from onchain history instead of reading the claim. Paste a protocol contract. Roll Call resolves the Safe above it, recovers which owners actually signed each transaction from the execTransaction calldata, tests whether those signers act independently or as one party, dates every signer's last onchain signal, and reads what the contract holds. Out comes the number that matters: the honest quorum, how many independent, awake parties are really required to move the money, against the threshold the protocol declares. Base's L1 Portal holds $1.92B. It can be upgraded by a 2-of-2 with zero margin and no timelock. Mantle's L1 Portal holds $411M behind a declared 6-of-14 that resolves to an honest quorum of 2, with 7 of its 14 signers showing no onchain signal in 180 days. Across 47 protocol contracts worth $4.82B, $2.38B sits behind a signer set with zero margin. Every number was read from chain state. Every number carries its tier: observed (chain state), tested (a calibrated permutation test with a published false positive rate), or inferred (the effective quorum curve). Nothing is a made-up score; the calibration endpoint is public. Ask it a question. "Who can freeze Mantle, and how many of them are asleep?" and an agent resolves the protocol to its keys, prices the report by the work it takes, reads what money sits behind those keys through The Graph, pays for the report over x402 on Hedera with its own wallet, and answers in plain English from the numbers, every step on screen. Every report also comes back as sentences, one per number, and as a path from the money to the people. It is a service agents pay for: metered by work, settled in HBAR or in RCC, an HTS token with a 2% fee schedule the network enforces; prepaid credits for runtimes that cannot sign; renewals by Hedera Scheduled Transaction; every report attested to HCS, and that archive doubles as the shared cache behind the enclave's signal. Roll Call is a registered ERC-8004 agent on Hedera testnet and Sepolia, with a discovery manifest at /.well-known/x402. Two Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows turn the measurement into action inside an enclave. One watches a private list of protocols and reports breaches. The other defends a live lending position in the official liquidation protection challenge on Sepolia, with a trigger no other protection has: if the market's own control surface degrades, it de-risks regardless of price. Both run end to end in the CRE simulator against the live contract. The Graph carries the population: a subgraph of Safe executions and approvals, and a registry of 84 verified Messari standardized deployments across 12 networks queried with one query string, every answer stamped with its deployment and indexed block. Seven MCP tools and a SKILL.md let any agent ask the same questions. Live: https://rollcall-pi.vercel.app
Repo: https://github.com/divyanshkhurana06/rollcall
Hedera Harness PR: https://github.com/hedera-dev/hedera-harness/pull/53
Harness before/after video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cqjV9rzSAkYKB_b_eQtC0rDgDpGZ_vvM/view?usp=sharing
projects.how_its_made: The load-bearing primitive is signature recovery. A Safe's execTransaction calldata carries a packed signature blob. Roll Call splits it by v-type (contract signature, approved hash, eth_sign, EIP-712), recovers each signer against the safeTxHash, and reconstructs who approved what, including nonce-zero signers that no explorer shows. Validated at 100% on every recoverable transaction in the test set. Independence is a permutation test: for each pair of owners, the observed co-signing count against a null that preserves the threshold (Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling), a co-submission artifact filter, and an empirical p-value with +1 smoothing. Calibration runs on synthetic signer sets and is published: 0% family-wise false positives at alpha 0.01, 100% power. Liveness is a binary search on eth_getTransactionCount over block history, with an explicit indeterminate state rather than a silent "never signed". Authority resolution walks EIP-1967 slots, Ownable and AccessControl grants; time to harm comes from timelock delays. Readers fail over across RPC providers and across the Safe API and its gateway, and a read that fails everywhere is reported as unreadable, never as an empty slot. Hedera: x402 v2 with strict PaymentRequirements through the Blocky402 facilitator; two settlement assets (HBAR, and RCC, an HTS token with a 2% fractional fee assessed by the network on a real settlement); a bearer credit store bought over x402; renewals by Scheduled Transaction verified on the mirror node; HCS attestations that double as the shared signal cache, which is what makes the serverless deployment stateless; ERC-8004 registration with the agent card inline as a data URI; and a PR to the Hedera Harness that makes doctor verify operator credentials against the mirror node. Chainlink: two Confidential Workflows on the TypeScript SDK. The liquidation strategy is written in the challenge contract's own integers, because at $1,800 the starting position has a health factor of 1.0029, which the contract truncates to 100 and liquidates; walked through the five published scenarios under both orderings of price update and liquidation check. One tick() engine runs inside the enclave, from a laptop, and in tests against an in-memory model of the contract that decodes every signed transaction. The hacky part: the simulator trapped for three days on every workflow including Chainlink's own scaffolds; the cause was the Bun version the SDK bundles with, isolated by reinstalling the old one and reproducing the trap. The enclave's plain HTTP budget is ten seconds, so the governance signal is served warm from HCS rather than computed on request. The Graph: a Safe subgraph in Studio, the Messari standardized deployments probed into a registry with per-deployment provenance, an MCP server with seven tools, and the Ask agent using the gateway as a step in a paid workflow. Web is React and Vite, API is Express bundled by esbuild into one Vercel function with a 300-second budget, web and API on one domain. Everything is testnet.

projects.title: Bridle
projects.description: x402 payment gateway for AI agents on Hedera. Blocks overspend, logs proof to HCS.
projects.project_description: Bridle is a deterministic policy firewall and hardware-confirmed trust layer designed to eliminate the "Soft Guardrail Fallacy" in autonomous agent payments. As LLMs gain the autonomy to procure compute, data, and APIs using crypto wallets, existing security models rely on system prompts like "do not spend over $10" or unconstrained private keys stored in .env files. These approaches fail when faced with prompt injection, context drift, or recursive loops. Bridle resolves this through a dual-rail economic architecture. Micro-payments of 1.0 HBAR or less settle autonomously at machine speed using the x402 protocol and the Blocky402 facilitator, enabling sub-cent, sub-second API access without pre-funded subscriptions. Whenever an agent attempts a high-value payment exceeding 1.0 HBAR, execution is instantly paused by hardcoded Python logic rather than probabilistic LLM prompts. The transaction parameters are routed to a Ledger hardware wallet—emulated via Speculos—requiring physical operator confirmation on the OLED screen before any funds move. Every operational decision, whether settled autonomously, signed via hardware, or vetoed by an operator, is immutably recorded to Hedera Consensus Service Topic 0.0.10474223 for verifiable auditability.
projects.how_its_made: Bridle is built across five interconnected layers spanning Python, Solidity, and Hedera native services. The cognitive engine runs on Google's Gemini 3.6 Flash within a Python agent that discovers endpoints, evaluates task relevance, and responds to standard HTTP 402 Payment Required challenges served by a FastAPI gateway. Rather than delegating spending guardrails to prompt engineering, the gateway and agent enforce spending limits strictly in Python runtime logic. For transactions exceeding 1.0 HBAR, execution is suspended and handed off to our custom Speculos emulator bridge (server/ledger_client.py and server/speculos_emulator.py), which exposes an interactive Web GUI and REST endpoints on port 5000 that emulate the Ledger Nano S+ chassis, OLED display, and APDU button flows. Approved transactions are broadcast to Hedera EVM Testnet (Chain ID 296) and settle against our Hardhat-tested BridlePaywall.sol contract deployed at 0x5442A862d2B11709045BE15015368c7dD6B9cfd8, which utilizes cryptographic nonces to prevent replay attacks. To solve asynchronous latency between EVM RPC transaction broadcast and Hedera Mirror Node indexing, the gateway integrates resilient exponential backoff polling (5 retries with 1.5s delay) to verify receipts reliably. Finally, the system leverages the Hedera SDK to commit structured audit messages directly to Hedera Consensus Service Topic 0.0.10474223, taking advantage of fixed USD-pegged fees and immediate ABFT consensus.
