projects.title: citable
projects.description: Prove you quoted correctly — per-paragraph position proofs on chain, ENS-named, any language.
projects.project_description: Citable is a provenance register for language. It does not try to answer "is this quote real?" — that question has no denominator, because nobody knows what share of everything a person ever said is available to check against. Citable inverts the burden of proof and answers a question that is actually decidable: "here is the proof that I quoted correctly." An author registers a statement. The text is split into paragraphs at blank lines, each paragraph is bound to its position and hashed into a merkle tree, and only the 32-byte root goes on chain — together with the author address, an ENS node, a timestamp, and the IPFS CID of a bundle holding the full text. The index sits inside the leaf: leaf = keccak256(keccak256(abi.encode(uint256 index, string segment))). That detail is the entire point. Sibling pairs get sorted when the tree is built, which discards their order, so without the index in the leaf a proof would show membership but not position — and position is what quoting out of context destroys. Verification runs as a cascade of three stages, and the interface never lets them blur into each other: Wording — is this paragraph in the statement, and where? A merkle proof, verified by the contract. Paragraph 5 of 7, with the neighbouring paragraphs shown next to it. Change a single character and the proof fails. Excerpt — is the fragment cut out of a registered paragraph? A fact, checked locally, with the full paragraph displayed beside the shortened quote. This is the common case of honest-looking distortion: the words are real, the meaning is not. Coverage — is the claim covered by the text, in another language or other words? A measurement, explicitly labelled as one, never as a proof. Stage 3 exists because a translation shares no bytes with its original. It runs entirely in the browser: embeddings (multilingual-e5-small) pick candidate paragraphs, a deterministic value check throws out claims that assert numbers or persons the paragraph never mentions, and an NLI model (mDeBERTa-v3-base-xnli) judges whether the claim is actually entailed by the text. Typing "Revenue rose by four percent last quarter." against a German paragraph scores 0.8253 entailment and reports paragraph 3 of 6. Changing one word to "forty percent" is not scored at all — the value check sees a 40 in a paragraph that says four and never lets the model near it. That design came out of a measurement, not a preference. Plain semantic similarity rated an invented confession ("Roth admitted the figures were manipulated") at 0.880 — higher than a faithful English translation of the same paragraph at 0.877. Similarity models measure what is being talked about, not what is being claimed. Built on similarity, the percentage would have endorsed the disinformation in exactly the case the project exists for. Entailment plus the value check separates the strongest false quote from the threshold by 0.235 instead of 0.072. A percentage from stage 3 means "no distorted quote in our 16-case test set reached this score" — not "83% true". The paragraph is always shown in full next to the number, so the reader judges, not the model. Identity comes from ENS. A signature alone is anonymous, and "key 0x7f3a… said this" convinces no reader. registerRoot is gated by an INameGuard, implemented against the real ENSv2 registry on Sepolia: the name holder may publish, and so may anyone the holder granted the publish role to — which is what a newsroom actually looks like, a volunteer publishing under the paper's name without owning it. The limits are on the landing page, not behind it. Stage 3 can be wrong. Spanish scores 0.562 against 0.821 for English and would be rejected at threshold 0.80. Irony and quote-within-quote are not handled. "Not registered" does not mean "fabricated" — and when nothing matches, the app says so with its denominator visible, naming how many statements and paragraphs it compared against.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts in Solidity with Foundry. CitableRegistry stores one record per statement — root, author, ensNode, timestamp, CID, segment count — and verifies position proofs on chain. Registration is gated by an INameGuard interface; ENSv2NameGuard implements it against the live ENSv2 registry on Sepolia. Both are deployed and verified on Etherscan, and all three registered statements went out with the guard armed. The single biggest technical risk is that the JavaScript and the Solidity disagree about a hash. If they ever drift, every statement already registered becomes unverifiable. So there is no hardcoded fixture anywhere: test/Leaf.t.sol shells out via Foundry FFI to script/js/leaf.mjs and compares the result against Leaf.leafOf, and test/ProofBridge.t.sol lets the JS segment a text, build the tree and produce a proof, then hands that proof to the contract. Segmentation, tree shape, pair sorting and the leaf formula are proven identical by forge test, not assumed. 55 Solidity tests, 60 JS tests for the client library. The client library (lib/citable/) is plain ESM on viem and merkletreejs, and the frontend imports it through an alias rather than copying it — a second copy of the leaf formula is exactly the drift the bridge test exists to prevent. Frontend is Next.js 16 with Tailwind 4, exported as fully static routes. There is no database, no server, no indexer: search by ENS name reads logs by the indexed ensNode topic straight from an RPC endpoint, the bundle is fetched from IPFS, and the tree is rebuilt in the browser. Verifying requires trusting no service at all. Three things were harder than expected and are worth naming: ENSv2 token ids are not labelhashes. The registry keeps a tokenVersionId in the lower 32 bits of the id, so ownerOf(labelhash(name)) returns 0x0 for every name that exists — a live Sepolia name currently sits at version 9. The guard therefore never derives an id; it asks the registry, which resolves the version itself. script/js/ens-probe.mjs proves this against names discovered from mint events, and a Sepolia fork test asserts the delegation path rather than assuming it. Registering the name itself was a second detour: the ENSv2 registrar on Sepolia prices in a test USDC that has a public mint, which is why wochenzeitung.eth could be acquired properly and the guard never had to be switched off. script/js/ens-register.mjs makes that path reproducible. transformers.js cannot be bundled here. env.js reads fs at import time to decide whether it is running on a server; Turbopack compiles a bare node builtin in a browser bundle to void 0, and Object.keys(void 0) kills the library before the first model byte arrives. resolveAlias does not help — the substitution happens before resolution. So stage 3 loads the library from jsDelivr and the weights from huggingface.co at runtime, about 400 MB on first use and only after the button is pressed. That is a real third-party dependency and it is stated on the page. Stages 1 and 2 depend on nothing but the chain and the bytes. CIDs are computed without kubo. A bundle below the chunk size is a single raw block, so its CID is sha256 with a four-byte header — verified against kubo 0.43.0, with its own vectors in the test suite. Above that size it throws rather than guessing a CID that points nowhere. publish.mjs refuses to broadcast until the CID this repo computes equals the one kubo computes, the bytes read back out of IPFS rebuild the root, and the deployed contract accepts a proof at the right index while rejecting the same segment at a different one. Availability is treated as a race, not a hierarchy. Public gateways, a Pinata dedicated gateway, and the app's own copy are all tried at once, and the first source whose bytes rebuild the on-chain root wins. A source serving anything else loses the race instead of being believed — which is why the app may ship its own copy at all: it buys reachability, not trust, and the screen names which source answered. Outage and forgery stay separate: "nobody answered" proves nothing, "someone answered with wrong bytes" is an accusation. One deliberate exception to the no-server rule: a browser must not hold a pinning key, so api/pin.mjs is a Vercel function that pins on the author's behalf before the transaction is offered. The order is the whole fix — earlier, the screen asked authors to download the bundle and pin it by hand, and nobody does that, which is how three statements ended up on chain with CIDs no node serves. The function accepts a bundle only if it rebuilds the root the client states, using the same verifyBundle a verifier runs, and pins the received bytes verbatim rather than a re-serialised object, because a round trip through an object could move the CID. The browser then compares the CID it gets back with the one it computed itself and refuses to register if they differ. It is a second point of centralisation next to the registry owner: it can refuse, it cannot forge. Partner technologies: ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia) supplies the identity layer without which a proof of authorship convinces no reader; IPFS holds the full text addressed by its own hash, so the chain only has to carry 32 bytes; Vercel hosts the static export plus the single pinning function. AI usage, declared honestly: contracts, frontend and tests were developed with Claude Code. Architecture, design decisions and verification by me.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts in Solidity with Foundry. CitableRegistry stores one record per statement — root, author, ensNode, timestamp, CID, segment count — and verifies position proofs on chain. Registration is gated by an INameGuard interface; ENSv2NameGuard implements it against the live ENSv2 registry on Sepolia. Both are deployed and verified on Etherscan, and all three registered statements went out with the guard armed.

The single biggest technical risk is that the JavaScript and the Solidity disagree about a hash. If they ever drift, every statement already registered becomes unverifiable. So there is no hardcoded fixture anywhere: test/Leaf.t.sol shells out via Foundry FFI to script/js/leaf.mjs and compares the result against Leaf.leafOf, and test/ProofBridge.t.sol lets the JS segment a text, build the tree and produce a proof, then hands that proof to the contract. Segmentation, tree shape, pair sorting and the leaf formula are proven identical by forge test, not assumed. 55 Solidity tests, 60 JS tests for the client library.

The client library (lib/citable/) is plain ESM on viem and merkletreejs, and the frontend imports it through an alias rather than copying it — a second copy of the leaf formula is exactly the drift the bridge test exists to prevent.

Frontend is Next.js 16 with Tailwind 4, exported as fully static routes. There is no database, no server, no indexer: search by ENS name reads logs by the indexed ensNode topic straight from an RPC endpoint, the bundle is fetched from IPFS, and the tree is rebuilt in the browser. Verifying requires trusting no service at all.

Three things were harder than expected and are worth naming:

ENSv2 token ids are not labelhashes. The registry keeps a tokenVersionId in the lower 32 bits of the id, so ownerOf(labelhash(name)) returns 0x0 for every name that exists — a live Sepolia name currently sits at version 9. The guard therefore never derives an id; it asks the registry, which resolves the version itself. script/js/ens-probe.mjs proves this against names discovered from mint events, and a Sepolia fork test asserts the delegation path rather than assuming it. Registering the name itself was a second detour: the ENSv2 registrar on Sepolia prices in a test USDC that has a public mint, which is why wochenzeitung.eth could be acquired properly and the guard never had to be switched off. script/js/ens-register.mjs makes that path reproducible.

transformers.js cannot be bundled here. env.js reads fs at import time to decide whether it is running on a server; Turbopack compiles a bare node builtin in a browser bundle to void 0, and Object.keys(void 0) kills the library before the first model byte arrives. resolveAlias does not help — the substitution happens before resolution. So stage 3 loads the library from jsDelivr and the weights from huggingface.co at runtime, about 400 MB on first use and only after the button is pressed. That is a real third-party dependency and it is stated on the page. Stages 1 and 2 depend on nothing but the chain and the bytes.

CIDs are computed without kubo. A bundle below the chunk size is a single raw block, so its CID is sha256 with a four-byte header — verified against kubo 0.43.0, with its own vectors in the test suite. Above that size it throws rather than guessing a CID that points nowhere. publish.mjs refuses to broadcast until the CID this repo computes equals the one kubo computes, the bytes read back out of IPFS rebuild the root, and the deployed contract accepts a proof at the right index while rejecting the same segment at a different one.

Availability is treated as a race, not a hierarchy. Public gateways, a Pinata dedicated gateway, and the app's own copy are all tried at once, and the first source whose bytes rebuild the on-chain root wins. A source serving anything else loses the race instead of being believed — which is why the app may ship its own copy at all: it buys reachability, not trust, and the screen names which source answered. Outage and forgery stay separate: "nobody answered" proves nothing, "someone answered with wrong bytes" is an accusation.

One deliberate exception to the no-server rule: a browser must not hold a pinning key, so api/pin.mjs is a Vercel function that pins on the author's behalf before the transaction is offered. The order is the whole fix — earlier, the screen asked authors to download the bundle and pin it by hand, and nobody does that, which is how three statements ended up on chain with CIDs no node serves. The function accepts a bundle only if it rebuilds the root the client states, using the same verifyBundle a verifier runs, and pins the received bytes verbatim rather than a re-serialised object, because a round trip through an object could move the CID. The browser then compares the CID it gets back with the one it computed itself and refuses to register if they differ. It is a second point of centralisation next to the registry owner: it can refuse, it cannot forge.

Partner technologies: ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia) supplies the identity layer without which a proof of authorship convinces no reader; IPFS holds the full text addressed by its own hash, so the chain only has to carry 32 bytes; Vercel hosts the static export plus the single pinning function.

AI usage, declared honestly: contracts, frontend and tests were developed with Claude Code. Architecture, design decisions and verification by me.

projects.title: Allowance
projects.description: A spending limit for AI agents — signed by a human, enforced before payment, and receipted forever.
projects.project_description: AI agents can spend money autonomously now. The x402 standard lets an agent hit an API, get told it costs a cent, pay, and carry on — no card, no human. That works beautifully, and it's the problem: x402 answers how money moves, and nothing answers whether it should. An agent reads a poisoned webpage and sends 500 HBAR to an attacker. Or it loops overnight and buys the same call four thousand times. Every one of those payments is correctly signed and correctly settled. The money is just gone. Spending limits do exist — Hedera's Agent Kit ships policies, x402 ships SpendControls — and they solve real problems. But in every case the limit is a setting the agent itself can reach. The thing being restricted holds the restriction. That's not a limit; it's a suggestion. Allowance is the layer that fixes it. A human writes spending rules — per-payment cap, rolling hourly budget, which counterparties are acceptable — and signs them as an EIP-712 message. The agent receives a sealed envelope it can read but cannot rewrite; change a digit and the signature breaks. Before every payment a guard checks the amount, the running spend, and the recipient's on-chain reputation from the ERC-8004 registry. Every decision is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic — including the refusals. That's the part everyone skips. If your agent is attacked at 3am and the guard holds, a success-only log shows you nothing, and nothing looks exactly like no attack happened. At $0.0001 per message, logging every denial is free, so the trail is complete instead of sampled. In the live demo the allowlist is deliberately empty. The agent pays an account its owner has never approved, because three independent reviewers on-chain rate it 910/1000 — then gets refused on the fourth call when the hourly budget is spent. The run finishes by replaying the topic from a public mirror node and recomputing the spend from scratch: it matches. The audit trail isn't a log kept beside the system; it is the system's memory.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo, npm workspaces, no build step — tsx runs sources directly. 94 tests, none requiring a network, because the evaluator is a pure function: no I/O, no clock, every fact passed in as an argument. Hedera does settlement, evidence, and reputation. HCS is the reason the project works at all — our claim is a complete audit trail, and on an EVM chain each log line is a gas-costing contract event, so denying a $0.002 payment would cost more than the payment. You'd batch or log off-chain, and the verifiability claim collapses. HCS is a native service at $0.0001/message and 10,000+ TPS, so recording every refusal stops being a cost decision. x402 — we didn't wrap the library. It publishes an async BeforePaymentCreationHook that runs before a payment payload is built and can abort with a reason; that signature is almost exactly our evaluator's, so our guard is an x402 hook. Settlement goes through the Blocky402 facilitator, which co-signs and submits every transfer — which is why our payment requirements advertise their fee-payer account. ERC-8004 answers "should we pay this stranger?" The registries turned out to be deployed on Hedera testnet at the same deterministic CREATE2 addresses used everywhere else, so reputation and settlement share a chain — no cross-chain hop on the payment path. We count distinct clients, not feedback entries: fifty five-star ratings from one address is one endorsement. Three things worth flagging as hard-won. ExactHederaScheme exists three times on different subpaths — /exact/client, /server, /facilitator — and the bare import gives you the client one, which fails on a server with a useless error. Two Hedera SDKs coexist (@hashgraph/sdk for receipts, @hiero-ledger/sdk transitively via x402), and instances can't cross that boundary. And a Hedera transfer can pass execute() and still fail at consensus, so the ALLOW receipt is written in onPaymentResponse after settlement confirms — writing it at authorization time would put a payment on a permanent audit trail that never happened. We also rewrote the reputation layer once. It originally scanned NewFeedback logs, on the belief getSummary() couldn't aggregate without a client list. getClients() returns exactly that list — and Hedera's mirror node caps topic-filtered queries at a 7-day window, so the log approach would have meant ~30 windowed queries per lookup on the payment path. Two eth_calls replaced all of it. The console is a single self-contained HTML file — no framework, no backend — so a judge can double-click it and see live receipts without running an install. Not finished: the owner's key still lives in .env, so "human-authorized" currently means a string on the same machine as the agent — the same weakness we criticise above. LedgerTrustRoot is written against Ledger's Device Management Kit and typechecks against their real packages, but never ran: no physical device, and Ledger's own Ethereum app doesn't build against their own SDK (C_chain_1_14px_bitmap undeclared, reproducing on both Nano targets). Details and the full error are in the README.

projects.title: Securtxn
projects.description: SecurTxn is control layer that verifies identity before money moves
projects.project_description:
THE PROBLEM About $226 billion a year moves in B2B stablecoin payments, and none of it can
be recalled. When a payout goes to the wrong recipient, there is no chargeback
and no reversal. What exists instead is a recovery industry: Binance processes
roughly 4,000 deposit-retrieval requests a month, and Kraken charges $200 to
$500 per attempt. Recovering a misdirected payment is a support ticket. Not
sending one is a control. Traditional banking solved this in 2020 with Confirmed Payee, which checks the
name on the account before a transfer goes out. Stablecoin rails have no
equivalent. A wallet address carries no identity, so nothing on the payment
path can answer the only question that matters: does this address actually
belong to the vendor on the invoice? https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/2026/08/06/why-stablecoins-still-have-a-payment-recovery-problem/ SecurTxn is that missing control layer. WHAT IT DOES SecurTxn sits in front of a stablecoin payout and refuses to let it proceed
until three independent questions are answered: Is the payee who they claim to be? Is a live human approving this specific payment? Is this address allowed to hold the asset at all? Each is answered by a different system, and none of them can be satisfied by
the person trying to get paid. HOW IT WORKS Onboarding. A vendor connects a wallet and completes a real DigiLocker consent
flow, which returns their Aadhaar and PAN documents with a verifiable XML
signature. They then sign an EIP-712 wallet control proof and an identity
binding that ties the DigiLocker subject to that specific address. Only the
combination makes a wallet CONFIRMED. Identity documents are encrypted at rest
and reduced to HMAC digests for matching. On-chain KYC (Hedera). The platform issues a verifiable credential for the
confirmed wallet and calls grantKyc on a tokenised bond deployed with the
Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (security 0.0.10444329, internal KYC
activated). This is the control that cannot be talked around: the token itself
rejects transfers to addresses that were never granted. An unverified wallet
does not fail our validation, it reverts on chain. Consent before matching. When a payment is raised, the payee is notified and
must accept it with an EIP-712 signature before any identity check runs. This
ordering is deliberate. Running a match without consent would turn the product
into a lookup service that tells a stranger whether a given address belongs to
a given PAN. The match (Chainlink CRE). The identity comparison runs inside a Confidential
Workflow on a Chainlink DON, in a TEE. The enclave never sees a name or a PAN.
It receives HMAC digests, compares them as opaque bytes, and returns one of
four verdicts: MATCHED, IDENTITY_MISMATCH, WALLET_NOT_ON_FILE or
VENDOR_NOT_FOUND. There is a single reason code for any identity failure,
because reporting which field mismatched would hand a prober a second bit of
information. The enclave has no crypto library and does no name scoring, so
there is nothing in it to leak. Proof of personhood (World ID). The sender passes a World ID Selfie Check on
every payment, unconditionally. The payee is challenged only when the risk
engine asks for one: a first payment from this sender, an amount above their
tier ceiling, a recently rotated wallet, a stale check, or a recent identity
mismatch. Signals are role-qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>, so one human acting as both sides of a payment cannot
satisfy both checks with the same proof. Settlement. The payout moves as an HTS token through an HTLC on Hedera testnet.
The payee claims it by revealing the preimage from their own key, which makes
the reveal itself the receipt. Nobody can produce it on their behalf, and an
unclaimed payment returns to the sender after the timelock. Evidence. Every decision writes an evidence record. Records are batched into a
Merkle tree and anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10454706).
Each anchor reads itself back from a mirror node after writing, so an anchor is
verified against the public record rather than merely submitted. Any single
record can produce a standalone inclusion proof, and altering a record after
anchoring makes its proof stop matching. Exception desk. A refusal is not a dead end. Blocked payments open a case with
the reason code, the evidence trail, and a path to resolution, because the
finance team still has an invoice to pay. WHAT IS REAL This is deployed and runs end to end at https://www.securtxn.com with no mocks
in the path. Two people have completed the full flow with their own DigiLocker
identities, their own World ID enrolments, a verdict from the deployed TEE
workflow, and a real token transfer on Hedera testnet. One thing stated plainly: the asset moved in the demo is stUSDC, a test
stablecoin we issued on Hedera testnet, not Circle's USDC. The mechanics are
identical, an HTS fungible token moving between KYC gated accounts through the
escrow contract, but it should not be described as transferring USDC. TECH STACK Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio bond with internal KYC, HTS token, HTLC
escrow contract, Hedera Consensus Service for evidence anchoring, mirror node
verification. Chainlink CRE: Confidential Workflow with a TEE handler, deployed to a DON,
secrets held in the Vault DON, digest-only matching. World ID: Selfie Check proof of personhood, role-qualified signals, nullifier
continuity enforced against enrolment. Identity: DigiLocker via the Sandbox aggregator, Aadhaar and PAN with XML
signature verification. Application: TypeScript, Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Next.js, viem, EIP-712
throughout.
projects.how_its_made:
ARCHITECTURE A pnpm monorepo. Fastify and Prisma over PostgreSQL (Supabase) for the API,
Next.js for the web app, viem for all chain work, Zod at every boundary, and a
shared package holding the EIP-712 struct definitions. Chain, compliance,
anchoring and identity are interfaces with a real and a mock implementation
selected by env var, so the test suite never depends on a public network being
up while the deployed instance always uses the real one. API and web run on
Render, the database on Supabase, the workflow on a Chainlink DON, the
contracts on Hedera testnet. CHAINLINK CRE, AND THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN The identity match runs in a Confidential Workflow on a TEE. The obvious design
was "encrypt the vendor record, decrypt inside the enclave, compare it." That
is impossible. The CRE SDK bans node:crypto outright, and the declared globals
are only TextEncoder/Decoder, Buffer, atob/btoa, URL and console. No
crypto.subtle, nothing. There is no primitive inside the enclave to decrypt
with. So we inverted it. At onboarding we store HMAC(pan, pepper) and
HMAC(normalise(legalName), pepper). At match time the API hashes the sender's
typed values the same way, and the enclave compares digest against digest. No
crypto is needed inside because the hashing already happened outside. The
pepper never leaves our server and the enclave never sees an identity. It is
not that the enclave is trusted with PII, it is that there is no PII in it to
leak. The cost is real and worth stating. Exact digests remove the near-miss band, so
a typo is now a flat mismatch rather than a 0.95 similarity score. We think
that is a net gain, because fuzzy name matching is precisely how a lookalike
payee slips through. Normalisation does the work instead: "MERIDIAN COMPONENTS
PRIVATE LIMITED" and "Meridian Components Pvt Ltd" reduce to the same digest. The second CRE problem is that the HTTP trigger is fire and forget.
workflows.execute returns an execution id and nothing else, and there is no API
to read a workflow's return value, so a workflow cannot be called as a
synchronous "is this payee verified?" RPC. The workflow POSTs its verdict to a
callback endpoint and the caller awaits the database row. That suits the
confidential design rather than fighting it, because the verdict is exactly the
one value that is supposed to leave the enclave. The callback has to be idempotent. In DON mode every observing node runs the
handler and every node POSTs the same verdict, so five callbacks arrive for one
logical answer. In TEE mode exactly one does. Both are correct, so later
callbacks are accepted and ignored. One trap worth naming: a CRE execution reaching SUCCESS only means the handler
did not throw. A matcher that always answered MATCHED would look identical
across every case. Our end to end script therefore asserts the verdict for five
different inputs rather than the execution status. The enclave authenticates to
the vendor lookup with a JWT held in the Vault DON and released directly into
the attested enclave. HEDERA Three separate uses, each doing something the others cannot. The tokenised bond is deployed with the Asset Tokenization Studio with
internalKycActivated set to true. That single flag is the integration: false and
the token enforces nothing, leaving grantKyc with nothing to gate. The issuing
account holds the KYC_MANAGER, INTERNAL_KYC_MANAGER and SSI_MANAGER roles and is
registered as an issuer, without which grantKyc reverts with AccountIsNotIssuer.
The demonstration that matters is the failure: a transfer to a wallet that never
went through grantKyc reverts on chain, not in our validation. The cash leg is an HTS fungible token moving through an HTLC contract. HTS
tokens answer the ERC-20 interface at their long zero address, 0x followed by
the token number in hex padded to 40 characters, which is how viem can talk to
them at all. Accounts are created with maxAutoAssociations set to -1, because a
receiver with no free association slots rejects an incoming token transfer. The
balance card surfaces that field for exactly this reason. Evidence anchoring uses the Consensus Service. Records are batched into a Merkle
tree and the root is submitted to a topic. Anchoring then reads itself back from
a mirror node and compares the published root against the recorded one. Mirror
nodes lag consensus by a few seconds, so the read back retries briefly, but a
root mismatch throws immediately and is never retried away: a disagreement
between our row and the public record is the one failure this whole mechanism
exists to surface. WORLD ID Selfie Check, with signals role qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>. This is not cosmetic. The nullifier uniqueness index is
(nullifier, action, signal), so a bare payment id means one human acting as both
sides of a payment collides with their own earlier proof. The asymmetry is
deliberate too: the sender is checked on every payment unconditionally, while
the payee is challenged only on risk, because the payee is the counterparty and
friction there costs you the payment. HACKY AND NOTABLE The EIP-712 structs live in one shared package imported by the signer, the
verifier and the tests. A second copy that merely reorders two fields produces
signatures that fail with no useful error, because the recovered address is
simply a different address. Next.js rewrites default to afterFiles, which runs only when no page matched. We
had pages at /vendors and /payments, so the API proxy was silently shadowed:
calls returned 200 with Next's HTML, JSON.parse produced a string, and the first
visible symptom was an undefined id three steps later. beforeFiles fixes it. The API's token minting endpoint is registered only when NODE_ENV is not
production, deliberately, because an approver token is what stands between a
payment and a human agreeing to it. That broke the entire deployed app, since
the web console minted its own tokens. The fix is a Next route handler signing
HS256 tokens server side for two roles only, agent and approver, never issuer or
bridge. The JWT is hand rolled with node:crypto rather than adding a library,
because the payload is two claims and a new dependency means a lockfile change
on a deployment that installs with a frozen lockfile. grantKyc is idempotent. The chain outlives our database and the wallet key lives
in the browser's localStorage, so a reset database plus a reconnected wallet
asks the chain for a state it is already in. The contract answers with a bare
custom error revert that surfaces as an unhelpful 500. A grant is a state, not
an event. Every foreign key is onDelete: Restrict, so evidence is never silently orphaned.
Even wiping the demo database has to be done in strict reverse dependency order. DigiLocker returned a 403 whose body we were deliberately withholding from logs
to avoid leaking PII. The actual message was "Insufficient credits." We now
surface the message and transaction id only, never the data. Separately, a user
who grants Aadhaar consent but not PAN produced an opaque 400 much later, so
there is now a pre-flight scope check naming the document that is missing.

unclaimed payment returns to the sender after the timelock.

Evidence. Every decision writes an evidence record. Records are batched into a
Merkle tree and anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10454706).
Each anchor reads itself back from a mirror node after writing, so an anchor is
verified against the public record rather than merely submitted. Any single
record can produce a standalone inclusion proof, and altering a record after
anchoring makes its proof stop matching.

Exception desk. A refusal is not a dead end. Blocked payments open a case with
the reason code, the evidence trail, and a path to resolution, because the
finance team still has an invoice to pay.

WHAT IS REAL

This is deployed and runs end to end at https://www.securtxn.com with no mocks
in the path. Two people have completed the full flow with their own DigiLocker
identities, their own World ID enrolments, a verdict from the deployed TEE
workflow, and a real token transfer on Hedera testnet.

One thing stated plainly: the asset moved in the demo is stUSDC, a test
stablecoin we issued on Hedera testnet, not Circle's USDC. The mechanics are
identical, an HTS fungible token moving between KYC gated accounts through the
escrow contract, but it should not be described as transferring USDC.


TECH STACK
==========

Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio bond with internal KYC, HTS token, HTLC
escrow contract, Hedera Consensus Service for evidence anchoring, mirror node
verification.

Chainlink CRE: Confidential Workflow with a TEE handler, deployed to a DON,
secrets held in the Vault DON, digest-only matching.

World ID: Selfie Check proof of personhood, role-qualified signals, nullifier
continuity enforced against enrolment.

Identity: DigiLocker via the Sandbox aggregator, Aadhaar and PAN with XML
signature verification.

Application: TypeScript, Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Next.js, viem, EIP-712
throughout.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ARCHITECTURE

A pnpm monorepo. Fastify and Prisma over PostgreSQL (Supabase) for the API,
Next.js for the web app, viem for all chain work, Zod at every boundary, and a
shared package holding the EIP-712 struct definitions. Chain, compliance,
anchoring and identity are interfaces with a real and a mock implementation
selected by env var, so the test suite never depends on a public network being
up while the deployed instance always uses the real one. API and web run on
Render, the database on Supabase, the workflow on a Chainlink DON, the
contracts on Hedera testnet.

CHAINLINK CRE, AND THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN

The identity match runs in a Confidential Workflow on a TEE. The obvious design
was "encrypt the vendor record, decrypt inside the enclave, compare it." That
is impossible. The CRE SDK bans node:crypto outright, and the declared globals
are only TextEncoder/Decoder, Buffer, atob/btoa, URL and console. No
crypto.subtle, nothing. There is no primitive inside the enclave to decrypt
with.

So we inverted it. At onboarding we store HMAC(pan, pepper) and
HMAC(normalise(legalName), pepper). At match time the API hashes the sender's
typed values the same way, and the enclave compares digest against digest. No
crypto is needed inside because the hashing already happened outside. The
pepper never leaves our server and the enclave never sees an identity. It is
not that the enclave is trusted with PII, it is that there is no PII in it to
leak.

The cost is real and worth stating. Exact digests remove the near-miss band, so
a typo is now a flat mismatch rather than a 0.95 similarity score. We think
that is a net gain, because fuzzy name matching is precisely how a lookalike
payee slips through. Normalisation does the work instead: "MERIDIAN COMPONENTS
PRIVATE LIMITED" and "Meridian Components Pvt Ltd" reduce to the same digest.

The second CRE problem is that the HTTP trigger is fire and forget.
workflows.execute returns an execution id and nothing else, and there is no API
to read a workflow's return value, so a workflow cannot be called as a
synchronous "is this payee verified?" RPC. The workflow POSTs its verdict to a
callback endpoint and the caller awaits the database row. That suits the
confidential design rather than fighting it, because the verdict is exactly the
one value that is supposed to leave the enclave.

The callback has to be idempotent. In DON mode every observing node runs the
handler and every node POSTs the same verdict, so five callbacks arrive for one
logical answer. In TEE mode exactly one does. Both are correct, so later
callbacks are accepted and ignored.

One trap worth naming: a CRE execution reaching SUCCESS only means the handler
did not throw. A matcher that always answered MATCHED would look identical
across every case. Our end to end script therefore asserts the verdict for five
different inputs rather than the execution status. The enclave authenticates to
the vendor lookup with a JWT held in the Vault DON and released directly into
the attested enclave.

HEDERA

Three separate uses, each doing something the others cannot.

The tokenised bond is deployed with the Asset Tokenization Studio with
internalKycActivated set to true. That single flag is the integration: false and
the token enforces nothing, leaving grantKyc with nothing to gate. The issuing
account holds the KYC_MANAGER, INTERNAL_KYC_MANAGER and SSI_MANAGER roles and is
registered as an issuer, without which grantKyc reverts with AccountIsNotIssuer.
The demonstration that matters is the failure: a transfer to a wallet that never
went through grantKyc reverts on chain, not in our validation.

The cash leg is an HTS fungible token moving through an HTLC contract. HTS
tokens answer the ERC-20 interface at their long zero address, 0x followed by
the token number in hex padded to 40 characters, which is how viem can talk to
them at all. Accounts are created with maxAutoAssociations set to -1, because a
receiver with no free association slots rejects an incoming token transfer. The
balance card surfaces that field for exactly this reason.

Evidence anchoring uses the Consensus Service. Records are batched into a Merkle
tree and the root is submitted to a topic. Anchoring then reads itself back from
a mirror node and compares the published root against the recorded one. Mirror
nodes lag consensus by a few seconds, so the read back retries briefly, but a
root mismatch throws immediately and is never retried away: a disagreement
between our row and the public record is the one failure this whole mechanism
exists to surface.

WORLD ID

Selfie Check, with signals role qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>. This is not cosmetic. The nullifier uniqueness index is
(nullifier, action, signal), so a bare payment id means one human acting as both
sides of a payment collides with their own earlier proof. The asymmetry is
deliberate too: the sender is checked on every payment unconditionally, while
the payee is challenged only on risk, because the payee is the counterparty and
friction there costs you the payment.

HACKY AND NOTABLE

The EIP-712 structs live in one shared package imported by the signer, the
verifier and the tests. A second copy that merely reorders two fields produces
signatures that fail with no useful error, because the recovered address is
simply a different address.

Next.js rewrites default to afterFiles, which runs only when no page matched. We
had pages at /vendors and /payments, so the API proxy was silently shadowed:
calls returned 200 with Next's HTML, JSON.parse produced a string, and the first
visible symptom was an undefined id three steps later. beforeFiles fixes it.

The API's token minting endpoint is registered only when NODE_ENV is not
production, deliberately, because an approver token is what stands between a
payment and a human agreeing to it. That broke the entire deployed app, since
the web console minted its own tokens. The fix is a Next route handler signing
HS256 tokens server side for two roles only, agent and approver, never issuer or
bridge. The JWT is hand rolled with node:crypto rather than adding a library,
because the payload is two claims and a new dependency means a lockfile change
on a deployment that installs with a frozen lockfile.

grantKyc is idempotent. The chain outlives our database and the wallet key lives
in the browser's localStorage, so a reset database plus a reconnected wallet
asks the chain for a state it is already in. The contract answers with a bare
custom error revert that surfaces as an unhelpful 500. A grant is a state, not
an event.

Every foreign key is onDelete: Restrict, so evidence is never silently orphaned.
Even wiping the demo database has to be done in strict reverse dependency order.

DigiLocker returned a 403 whose body we were deliberately withholding from logs
to avoid leaking PII. The actual message was "Insufficient credits." We now
surface the message and transaction id only, never the data. Separately, a user
who grants Aadhaar consent but not PAN produced an opaque 400 much later, so
there is now a pre-flight scope check naming the document that is missing.

projects.title: NotYet
projects.description: Scheduled agent authority — spend keys, API keys, any secret — that doesn't exist until its time.
projects.project_description:
NotYet gives an autonomous agent a budget on a schedule — without ever handing it a key it can drain early. The problem:
• Hand the agent the whole budget up front → one hack or prompt injection drains it all.
• Run a key server that releases keys just-in-time → that server is a honeypot holding every future key.
• Session keys solve expiry; nothing solves start — authority always exists the moment it's issued. Why it matters — every one of these was a key that existed before it was needed:
• Grok / Bankr wallet drain — May 2026, ~$175K.
• Lobstar Wilde trading bot — Feb 2026, ~$250K.
• Malicious LLM routers — Apr 2026, ~$500K. How NotYet fixes it:
• Each period's key is timelock-encrypted (drand/tlock) to a future round — before its time it doesn't exist in usable form, not even for the owner. Ask early → NOT_YET.
• Not just payments — the same lock seals ANY secret (an API key, a credential, a token): the agent holds only ciphertext up front and gets it at its time, not before. No key server to breach or coerce.
• Spends settle as real x402 pay-per-call on Hedera, gated on-chain by a PeriodVault (window + budget + per-tx cap) and audited on HCS.
• Hacked today = one period's budget. Never the treasury, never a future period.
projects.how_its_made:
• Issuance: each period's spend key is generated in software, its EVM address committed to a PeriodVault contract, then tlock-encrypted (tlock-js) to a future drand quicknet round and the plaintext wiped. The agent holds only ciphertexts.
• Unlock + spend: the agent calls withdraw(i, amount, sig); the vault enforces on-chain the time window (useless before AND after its period), ecrecover identity, per-period budget, and a per-tx ceiling. A real x402 pay-per-call then settles via the keyless Blocky402 facilitator; encrypted receipts land on HCS.
• Hedera: PeriodVault runs on Hedera EVM via @hiero-ledger/sdk (no ethers) — money, x402, HCS audit, and an optional HIP-423 scheduled-tx mode, all on one chain, no bridge.
• Ledger: the schedule is signed on-device via the Device Management Kit (headless on Speculos, RFC 6979, ERC-7730 descriptor); the device also co-signs over-cap spends and holds the audit view keys the agent can never reopen.
• Bazantic: wrapped as an MCP server + a published recipe chaining two services (NotYet + Hedera Mirror Node) — any agent integrates in one line.
• Stack: TypeScript ESM, viem, tweetnacl, drand-client, solc. Also an npm SDK: @keccak002/notyet.

projects.title: Wallet Vitals
projects.description: Aave risk copilot with health factors, stress tests, and verifiable onchain evidence.
projects.project_description: Wallet Vitals is a read-only Aave V3 Ethereum risk copilot. Paste a public address without signing in, connecting a wallet, or signing a message. The app returns a reconstructed health factor, liquidation buffer, fixed 5%/10%/20% collateral stress scenarios, and changes between comparable snapshots. The Graph supplies indexed positions, reserve indices and rates, liquidation parameters, and block metadata. The backend reads Aave oracle prices and the pool's account data at that same block hash, and cross-checks the reconstructed account before producing a report. Stale blocks, indexing errors, negative balances, unsupported eMode, and inconsistent accounts stop analysis instead of producing an unverified score. Every report carries an Evidence Receipt: subgraph and deployment identifiers, block number and hash, timestamps, calculation rules, assumptions, position references, oracle/pool addresses, and the contract cross-check. An optional AI layer explains precomputed facts; critical liquidation-boundary answers remain deterministic. Warning and danger labels are not presented as liquidation. The application is publicly deployed on Cloudflare with independent D1 storage, server-side API keys, expiring report links, explanation caching, and bounded public-demo usage. Live Graph/RPC/AI integration has been verified and all 50 tests pass in GitHub Actions. The video shows genuine public-deployment captures with English synthetic narration. This is a historical evidence snapshot, not a guarantee of current safety or financial advice. It never signs or executes transactions. The repository transparently discloses its retained upstream baseline and all new work in PRE_EXISTING.md. AI assistance was used during development.
projects.how_its_made: The implementation uses FastAPI and strict Pydantic contracts with deterministic Decimal/RAY math. A server-side GraphQL adapter queries the Aave V3 Ethereum Subgraph through The Graph Network and reconstructs accrued balances from scaled balances, reserve indices, rates, and source-block time. The Graph is load-bearing: without it, new analyses cannot discover positions. A notable integration finding was that indexed prices could be frozen even when the indexed block was current. We therefore obtain Aave's own oracle values using EIP-1898 eth_call requests pinned to the exact evidence block hash, resolve the oracle and pool from Aave's Ethereum addresses provider, and compare the reconstructed totals and health factor against the pool. There is no latest-block or fixture fallback. Unsupported eMode and material discrepancies fail closed. The local app runs on Python 3.12 with SQLite; production runs as a native Cloudflare Python 3.13 Worker with D1. A Fetch-backed httpx transport supports the same shared application code without sockets. The responsive UI uses server-rendered HTML, CSS, and dependency-free JavaScript. Production includes atomic request quotas, cached explanations, and 24-hour report links. OpenAI Responses receives precomputed structured facts. Numeric and identifier guards constrain narration, and deterministic explanations remain available. The boundary-critical 'What breaks first?' response is always deterministic. Keys never enter browser JavaScript. uv, Ruff, Pytest, GitHub Actions, and Docker support reproducibility; 50 tests cover risk math, data validation, oracle/account checks, API behavior, storage and quotas. Code was developed with AI assistance. Provenance: the repository retains the MIT-licensed dorukyy/telegram-wallet-tracker baseline under the upstream-baseline tag. The legacy Telegram bot is not the running product. The web app, Graph integration, Aave risk engine, same-block contract checks, tests, and Cloudflare deployment are new work in event-period commits. PRE_EXISTING.md describes the boundary; we do not claim the upstream code as original.

projects.title: DeDNS-over-DeVPN
projects.description: DDoV: anonymous browsing via attested, no-log relays - paid per-session on Arc via x402.
projects.project_description: DDoV (DeDNS-over-DeVPN) is a marketplace for anonymous internet access with enforceable, revocable permissions. A user pays for a time-boxed session at a chosen bandwidth tier (Lite/Standard/Turbo), and their device opens an encrypted tunnel to an authorized relay operator. That operator's tunnel-termination, DNS-resolution, and outbound-proxy logic runs inside a Chainlink CRE confidential handler, so the operator's own machine cannot read or log the user's traffic - attested and independently verifiable, not just promised. Which relays are currently authorized lives in an ENSv2 registry (hierarchical subnames like bob.dvod.eth) that separates the operational key (updates endpoint/capabilities) from the payout address (where earnings go), so a compromised operator key can't redirect funds. A permissionless watchdog contract - not a human admin - automatically revokes any relay whose attestation report stops matching its published, audited build hash, and the client fails over to a healthy relay within seconds. When you pay for a VPN with a your card, the payment itself ties your name to the service - you're exposing exactly the identity a VPN is supposed to protect. Paying in crypto avoids that: no card, no name, no linkage back to you, which is why DDoV settles exclusively through Arc/x402 rather than any card rail. Since payment is x402-gated and settles in USDC on Arc, as a single batched per-session purchase - never a per-packet or per-DNS-query transaction, so the latency budget for live browsing stays intact. The one-line pitch: browse without your ISP, your relay operator, or the sites you visit ever being able to link "who" to "what" — provably, not on our word. It's a full VPN-shaped privacy layer, not DNS-only, and the README states plainly which pieces (ENSv2, Chainlink CRE, Arc/x402, automatic vs. manual revocation) are genuinely live versus honestly labeled as simulated at demo time.
projects.how_its_made: DDoV is a pnpm + Turborepo TypeScript monorepo, built spec-first: the architecture, phase plan, and design system are laid out up front and drive implementation phase by phase, with small feature-branch commits merged into dev and tagged phase-completions merged into main -never a single end-of-day dump. The shared type layer (packages/session-spec) uses Zod to define the session, tier, and ENSv2 capability-record schemas, plus an explicit session state-machine transition table (BROWSING → QUOTED → PAID → TOKEN_ISSUED → TUNNEL_OPEN → ACTIVE, with RELAY_REVOKED/RELAY_UNREACHABLE both routing through an automatic FAILOVER_SELECT) so every transition is validated in code, not just diagrammed. Four partner technologies each do one job, deliberately non-overlapping: ENSv2 hierarchical subnames + permissioned resolvers register relay operators and separate their operational key from their payout address, so a compromised operator key can never redirect earnings; Chainlink CRE runs the tunnel/DNS/proxy logic inside a confidential, attested handler so the operator's own machine can't read traffic; Arc settles USDC; x402 gates session purchase/renewal only - never per-packet - to keep DNS/browsing latency real. The design system enforces its own discipline in code: an --accent token is reserved by convention to exactly three UI moments (countdown, tier highlight, failover/revocation), documented alongside the token values themselves rather than left to hope.

projects.title: Credence
projects.description: Onchain credit bureau giving autonomous agents identity, reputation, and financing.
projects.project_description: Credence is an onchain credit bureau for autonomous agents. It gives each agent a persistent ENSv2 identity, connects that identity to human-backed verification, and builds a transparent credit history from completed jobs. The CreditBureau contract records outcomes, calculates a score and spend limit, and freezes agents after repeated defaults. CreditEscrow enforces those limits at settlement time, so creditworthiness is not merely displayed in a dashboard. The Graph indexes registrations, outcomes, score changes, and limit updates for a live analytics experience. Once an agent proves its reliability, its receivables can be priced and tokenized through Hedera. The result is an end-to-end trust layer for agents: identity, verification, reputation, controlled credit, and financing.
projects.how_its_made: The core contracts are written in Solidity and tested with Hardhat. CreditBureau stores agent profiles, human-backing status, outcome history, score snapshots, spend limits, and freeze state. CreditEscrow checks the bureau before allowing settlement and records the outcome afterward. ENSv2 is integrated through a separate Foundry project because the ENSv2 contracts are distributed as a Foundry dependency. Our custom AgentSubnameRegistrar creates non-transferable agent subnames under a project-owned ENSv2 namespace, deploys per-agent resolver and registry proxies through the ENSv2 Verifiable Factory, and uses Enhanced Access Control role bitmaps to scope CreditBureau’s permissions. World provides the human-backing signal, while The Graph converts contract events into queryable entities consumed by the frontend and credit analyst. Hedera’s Asset Tokenization Studio is used to issue receivables whose pricing reflects the agent’s onchain score. The notable design choice is treating every boundary as enforceable infrastructure: ENS identity prevents ambiguity, EAC limits who can update records, escrow prevents unauthorized settlement, and indexing makes the full decision trail auditable.

The notable design choice is treating every boundary as enforceable infrastructure: ENS identity prevents ambiguity, EAC limits who can update records, escrow prevents unauthorized settlement, and indexing makes the full decision trail auditable.

projects.title: harbor
projects.description: Harbor: instant liquidity for redeemable assets and pending withdrawal rights.
projects.project_description:
Harbor is an onchain redemption-liquidity market connecting users who need liquidity now with capital willing to wait. Across DeFi, redeemable does not always mean immediately available. Yield-bearing assets can involve withdrawal queues, cooldowns and delayed settlement. Once a
user requests redemption, they may receive a pending withdrawal right instead of spendable funds. Harbor makes that waiting period tradable. Users can swap supported redeemable assets, sell eligible pending withdrawal rights for immediate liquidity, or buy available rights from pool inventory.
Liquidity providers deposit into a shared vault that supplies capital across approved strategies. The pool can resell acquired assets and claims or hold them
through redemption, sharing the resulting gains and losses with LPs. Harbor’s pricing engine considers expected recovery, remaining settlement time, operating costs and the pool’s existing exposure. It does not treat every claim
as guaranteed cash or assume every withdrawal takes the same time. As exposure grows, inventory-sensitive pricing makes further purchases more conservative and
adjusts resale prices to encourage reducing exposure. Ordinary token trading supports buying and selling with both exact-input and exact-output execution through Aqua and SwapVM. Eligible withdrawal NFTs trade as
whole rights through direct settlement using the same Book, pricing and risk accounting. Approved integrations do not require fresh governor approval for every
NFT. The Graph powers transaction-linked views of trading activity, strategy exposure, deposits, withdrawals and realized results. Privy provides embedded-wallet
onboarding alongside external-wallet support, with capability-aware batching and ordinary transaction flows. We also evaluated four pricing policies against frozen historical withdrawal data: fixed-delay pricing, age-based pricing, queue-aware valuation and Harbor’s
capacity-adjusted model. The presentation distinguishes simulated results from actual protocol activity and makes the assumptions and maker-versus-seller
tradeoffs explicit. The current demonstration runs on Hoodi. Harbor’s contracts are unaudited, and immediate liquidity depends on supported assets, valid pricing and available
capital. The core idea is simple: a user should be able to sell the right to wait, while the buyer receives a clearly priced and verifiable obligation.
projects.how_its_made:
Harbor is built with Solidity and Foundry, integrating official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts, Solady and OpenZeppelin primitives, The Graph, and a Next.js
frontend with Privy. The contracts separate economic responsibilities. HarborVault holds pool funds, issues LP shares and manages withdrawal liabilities. HarborBook owns portfolio
accounting, acquisition basis, exposure limits, pricing policies and settlement rules. A shared Executor coordinates trades across registered Book/Vault pairs.
Issuer adapters verify asset conversions, withdrawal ownership, claim status and actual recovery. A central accounting distinction runs through the system: nominal entitlement, estimated portfolio value and spendable cash are different quantities. A pending
claim can contribute to portfolio backing without becoming cash available for another purchase or an LP payout. Harbor combines discounted recovery valuation with an inventory-capacity adjustment. In simplified form: recovery_value =
nominal_entitlement
× sum(
scenario_probability × recovery_fraction
/ (1 + annual_funding_rate × remaining_days / 365)
) pool_bid =
recovery_value − operating_cost − buy_margin
− increase_in_capacity_penalty pool_ask =
recovery_value + operating_cost + sell_margin
− decrease_in_capacity_penalty The capacity penalty is zero below a utilization threshold and grows cubically above it. Its change across a trade adjusts the price according to how much
exposure the pool acquires or releases. Requesting redemption does not free that exposure merely because the asset changes representation. Authorized publishers provide reusable, bounded and expiring recovery-discount parameters. Contracts combine them with verified live state to calculate
executable amounts. Quotes do not depend on a backend signing every individual fill. Independent valuation remains responsible for LP accounting; publishing a
trading price cannot manufacture NAV. For ordinary ERC-20 swaps, Harbor builds a canonical SwapVM program using the official instruction set. Extruction invokes Harbor’s Book pricing logic, while
FeeProtocol handles the configured VM fees. The Vault is Aqua’s maker and publishes its strategy allocations. Aqua allocations and token approvals do not
replace Harbor’s cash, reserve and exposure constraints. Execution opens a shared operation lock, calculates the trade through the VM, authenticates callbacks, measures token movements and commits accounting only
after settlement checks pass. Exact-input and exact-output modes use explicit integer-rounding rules. Transient storage carries transaction-local authorization
and callback state, while fixed linked libraries keep substantial execution logic outside the Book’s runtime without introducing upgradeable dispatch. Raw withdrawal NFTs use direct settlement through the same Book because Aqua’s ERC-20 transfer path does not carry NFT IDs. The adapter verifies each claim’s
ownership, status and entitlement under an approved issuer policy. This avoids deploying a wrapper and publishing a separate Aqua strategy for every withdrawal
ID. The Graph indexes economic events into trade history, strategy-level activity, LP flows and realized results, with transaction hashes for verification. The data
layer also includes reusable standardized external-vault queries and a historical issuer pipeline. Historical finalizations use inclusive ranges and prefix
accounting to keep indexing work bounded. Exported research datasets carry provenance and reconciliation checks, and simulated pricing results remain separate
from live Harbor events. Privy manages embedded-wallet onboarding and connected external wallets. The transaction layer checks wallet capabilities before requesting atomic batches or
EIP-7702 authorization, with ordinary transactions available when batching is unsupported. Harbor’s Periphery handles native-token wrapping, unwrapping and
measured refunds without taking ownership of users’ signing keys. Foundry tests cover accounting lifecycles, all four trading modes, fee rounding, withdrawal funding, claim recovery, callback rollback and pool isolation. Fork-
based tests exercise real issuer and Aqua/SwapVM dependencies, while the Hoodi deployment demonstrates actual token and withdrawal-right transfers.

projects.title: ARC MAP
projects.description: Investigate Arc activity with sourced reports and a baseline you can revisit.
projects.project_description: ARC MAP turns activity on Arc into questions you can test. Start with a sourced signal on Today, run a read-only Hunter, inspect the transactions, then save a thesis with a fixed baseline and a finite check budget. Return later to see what changed without rewriting the original observation. In the recorded demo, The Graph returns 200 SUN transfer events, all from one transaction. ARC MAP reports that limit instead of treating the event count as independent activity. When the index advances but the transfer evidence stays unchanged, the thesis stays unchanged too. The current source also supports sharing one completed investigation: a contributor adds a public source and counterevidence, the owner reassesses, and revocation removes access while preserving the original report and contribution. This sharing flow was tested separately and is not shown in the recorded demo. The Graph supplies indexed transfer evidence; Arcscan and GitHub remain separate, labelled sources. You can explore without a wallet. Built-in analysis is rules-based; external agents can use the same bounded research operations through MCP.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript serve the browser and the research API. Node 22 workers run three loops: a public-source collector, an Arcscan radar, and a finite thesis checker with lease-fenced checks. SQLite stores observations, radar entries, private missions and theses; reports are immutable and comparisons are pinned to the baseline observed when the thesis was saved. The Graph supplies the transfer evidence. We deployed an ERC20 Transfer subgraph for the SUN token on Arc testnet (chain 5042002) in subgraphs/arcmap, and the Hunter queries it with bounded, dated samples. Arcscan and GitHub are separate, separately labelled evidence sources. A Graph outage is shown as a Graph error, never relabelled as an explorer result. Privy is wired for wallet login and viem for chain reads, but the submitted journey is read-only and performs no transaction. Contracts in contracts/ (Foundry) are the research-payment escrow developed during the event and are not exercised by this demo. Oscar set the product direction, workflow, visual direction, priorities and acceptance requirements. Codex and Cursor wrote most of the implementation and tests under his review, and Claude and Fable did source reviews. The product analysis is rules-based and does not call an LLM.

projects.title: Tabir
projects.description: Graduated liquidation protection with a policy no one can see. not even the node operators.
projects.project_description: Tabir protects a leveraged ETH/USDC position from liquidation without giving away how it does it. Most liquidation bots work off a single visible threshold: when health factor drops below some level, repay the debt. That survives the first shock, but it burns the borrower's emergency capital and closes out a position they wanted to keep. Worse, a public rule is a rule an adversary can probe, nudge the price just far enough to trigger a costly defensive action, repeat, and drain the protection budget without ever needing to liquidate anything. Tabir does two things differently. It responds in proportion to the actual threat rather than to a fixed level, using the rate of change in health factor to estimate time-to-breach and intervening only when a breach falls inside the reaction window. And it rations the emergency budget across the whole price path, holding reserve for a second shock it cannot see coming, so it survives multi-leg drawdowns that exhaust a naive strategy on the first dip. The protection policy itself, thresholds, buffers, sizing, budget caps, never leaves a hardware-isolated enclave. Observers see the action taken. They never see the reasoning behind it, or how much capital is left. The name is Indonesian for veil.
projects.how_its_made: Tabir is a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow in TypeScript, compiled to WASM with @chainlink/cre-sdk. It protects a leveraged vETH/vUSD position on Sepolia. A log trigger on PriceUpdate (with a cron fallback) calls handlerInTee. Inside the enclave, the workflow pulls the signer key, the RPC URL, and the policy from the Vault DON, then reads the position over JSON-RPC and rebuilds the price history from logs. It then runs decide() and signs the deposit or repay transaction with viem. The DON publishes a receipt with a salted hash of the policy, so we can later prove which policy ran without revealing it. decide() is pure bigint TypeScript, shared by the enclave and our rubric simulator, so the simulated scores describe the code that ships: 89.65 average, 0 of 11 scenarios liquidated. Why CRE: a public policy can be attacked by pushing the price just past its thresholds. The TEE keeps every threshold sealed, and only the action comes out. Hacky: the EVM write capability has no TEE support, so we send raw JSON-RPC and sign transactions inside the enclave. Every tick also runs the same path whether it acts or holds, so timing can't leak the thresholds.

projects.title: Superposition
projects.description: Aqua strategies backed by yield tokens: underlying asset discoverability, atomic re-deposit on fill.
projects.project_description: Superposition-Liquid is a meta-layer for 1inch Aqua that lets liquidity providers earn yield on 100% of their capital without giving up fill readiness. Today, when a maker ships a strategy on 1inch Aqua, their tokens sit idle in their wallet — Aqua is pure virtual-balance accounting and never takes custody. Superposition changes what backs that strategy. The maker points a per-token config at a yield venue (Aave v3, any ERC-4626 vault like Morpho or Euler, Stargate V2 pools, Pendle PT, or a Uniswap v4 hook), and every fill cycles that capital inside the swap transaction itself: a preTransferOut hook JIT-withdraws/redeems/unstakes exactly the delivery amount and hands it to the taker; a postTransferIn hook re-deploys whatever the taker paid back into the protocol. The maker's wallet holds tokens only for the duration of one transaction, idle balance stays zero, and the position earns protocol yield on top of swap fees. To routers and aggregators it reads as an ordinary ETH/USDC pool. It deliberately ships no pricing curve. Superposition wraps whatever SwapVM program the maker already writes — xyk, curved, flat-price, or a third-party curve — via two append-only meta-opcodes: YieldAdjustedRateXD (scales swap registers by the live exchange rate so quotes stay accurate while capital sits in yield tokens) and MakerCapitalGuardXD (makes quote() a complete fill-oracle: it reverts unless a real withdrawal of the delivery amount would succeed right now, so a passing quote is a strong fillability signal and a failing one returns the exact on-chain revert reason). Capability is abstracted behind one ILendingAdapter interface, so a new protocol is a single registry entry, not a router change. The adapters are pull-less: the router executes each adapter's pullPlan with its own allowance, so the maker approves once per token and never re-approves when switching protocols. Beyond supply, a side can be borrow-sourced: MakerConfig.BorrowConfig lets an Aave side quote an asset the maker doesn't hold, borrowing it against yield-bearing collateral, with the matching in-fill repaying the debt first — turning the same adapter into a delta-neutral/short inventory profile. Superposition also reaches into Uniswap v4: the SuperpositionUniAdapter exposes a concentrated-liquidity hook (which itself keeps 100% of pooled capital in ERC-4626 vaults between swaps) as just another yield venue the Aqua router can back a position with.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Solidity 0.8.30 + Foundry for the contracts; Next.js (App Router) + wagmi/viem + react-web3-icons for the landing page and a live maker console. Dependencies are pinned hard: 1inch/swap-vm v1.0.2, 1inch/aqua v1.0.0, OpenZeppelin v5.4.0, @1inch/solidity-utils 6.9.7. Piecing it together. The core is a modified redeploy of the SwapVM router (explicitly allowed by the 1inch rules). We append two custom opcodes to the end of the dispatch table — the deployed v1.0.2 has reserved no-op slots, so appending is append-only and never renumbers existing instructions. Around that we built ILendingAdapter and five implementations (Aave v3, generic ERC-4626, Stargate V2, Pendle PT, Superposition v4 hook), plus a MakerConfig registry mapping (maker, token) → adapter, and two router hooks (preTransferOut, postTransferIn) that orchestrate the JIT cycle. Each adapter resolves per-fill via one registry lookup, so routing never touches pricing math. Partner tech and why it helped. 1inch Aqua is the substrate: ship() allocates virtual balances with no token movement, and pull()/push() move real tokens only when a fill happens — exactly the seam we needed to swap "idle wallet" for "yield position" without changing the pool surface. Chainlink Data Feeds are our MEV guard: a price-sanity opcode reverts a fill if the implied swap price deviates beyond the maker's tolerance band from ETH/USD or USDC/USD (with per-feed staleness checks), so manipulation is rejected on-chain before execution. Uniswap v4 supplies a second engine entirely — the Superposition concentrated-liquidity hook — which we expose as a yield venue through the same one-token adapter interface. Notable, slightly hacky bits. (1) SwapVM hooks don't receive the final recipient and the default transfer always runs, so direct-to-taker delivery is impossible — we designed a "JIT-unwrap" pattern: the hook withdraws into the maker's wallet as preTransferOut, and SwapVM's own transfer delivers. (2) Aave tokens rebase, so shipping virtual balances in share counts while fills move underlying units produced a real unit mismatch; we fixed it by shipping in aToken count units and scaling quotes by rate(now)/rate(ship) on both quote() and swap(). (3) Borrow mode is implemented as the inverse of supply in the existing adapter (borrow on out-fill, repay-first on in-fill) rather than a new contract, keeping one code path and one source of truth. (4) The generic ERC-4626 adapter covers Morpho, Euler, Spark, and Yearn with zero protocol-specific code. Testing is where the design was validated. Real-vault fork tests caught two bugs mocks missed — the aToken unit mismatch above, and Pendle's callback conventions. The suite is 101 tests: unit + invariant fuzzing (256 runs over randomized fill sequences) + fork suites against live Base, Ethereum, and Arbitrum state. The whole stack is deployed to Ethereum Sepolia and verified via Sourcify (no Etherscan key), with an on-chain OrderBuilder so the console can ship() a real strategy through a browser wallet.

projects.title: Peaje
projects.description: The payment rail for AI agents: your site charges them, your agents buy for you.
projects.project_description: Peaje is the cash register of the agent economy: it lets any business charge AI agents per request, and lets any person run a buyer agent that spends from the same balance, with no payment code and no crypto knowledge required. Selling side: a business registers with an email and a URL, sets prices on links or API routes (or imports its sitemap), and gets a hosted gateway that answers HTTP 402 payment challenges via MPP, the machine-to-machine payment standard from Tempo and Stripe. Agents pay on their own in stablecoin (pathUSD on Tempo, USDC on Arc) and the gateway proxies the paid request to the original site. Peaje also makes the site discoverable to agents: agents.md, llms.txt, ard.json, an enriched openapi.json, an api-catalog, JSON-LD, Link headers and a paid-tools MCP server, all generated from the database and anchored at the business's own domain. The demo site's agent-readiness score (Ora) went from 40 to 73 after installing Peaje with a single prompt. The gateway also speaks the emerging agent-commerce protocols: UCP profile, ACP checkout sessions, and AP2 cart mandates signed with ES256. Buying side: every account gets one buyer agent with its own wallet. You type what you need in plain language ("this week's weather in Bogotá, three lines"), the agent searches roughly 15,000 real paid services across three sources (Peaje's own directory, Coinbase's x402 Bazaar, and the ERC-8004 identity registry via The Graph) and shows you what it would buy, at what price, and why, before spending a cent. A language-model veto rejects services that would not answer the request: buying nothing beats buying garbage. On approval it pays (MPP on Tempo/Arc, x402 with real USDC on Base mainnet), translates your request into the service's actual query parameters, reads what it bought, and returns a short human-readable answer with the on-chain receipt behind it. The agent's wallet balance is its budget: it physically cannot overspend. Peaje takes a 2% fee per transaction on the selling side. The full loop is live: an external agent paid for content on the demo business, that revenue funded the owner's buyer agent, and the buyer agent purchased real weather data and returned a three-line answer, every step with an on-chain receipt.
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo with three pieces: a multi-tenant Hono gateway (Railway) that does the charging, proxying, discovery generation and the whole buyer-agent engine; a Next.js dashboard (Vercel) with email-only onboarding; and a shared db package over Supabase. Wallets for businesses and agents are Privy server wallets, created invisibly at signup, exposed to code as viem accounts. Charging uses mppx (MPP's reference implementation): the gateway issues 402 challenges offering two rails per request, Tempo (pathUSD) and Arc (USDC via EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization), verifies receipts, credits a per-tenant ledger net of the 2% fee, and proxies to the origin. Discovery files are not static: they are generated per tenant from the database and served through the business's own domain via a reverse-proxy kit installed by pasting one prompt into any coding assistant, so the docs self-name at the business domain and agents never get pointed at our infrastructure. The buyer agent composes three discovery sources: our own directory, the full Coinbase x402 Bazaar index (~15 pages of 1,000 services, cached an hour: with the default 100 the agent only ever saw 0.7% of the market and bought junk), and ERC-8004 identity plus reputation read from Agent0 subgraphs on The Graph, which feeds on-chain reputation into every scoring decision. Deterministic keyword scoring picks a shortlist; Claude then acts as a veto gate ("does this service actually deliver the requested data?"), fills the winning API's query string (city coordinates, forecast variables, date ranges) and synthesizes the purchased content into a plain-language answer. Purchases pay via mppx on Tempo/Arc and via x402-fetch with real USDC on Base mainnet, from the same Privy account. Notable hacky bits: the agent's spend cap is not an accounting entry, it is the wallet's literal balance, so no bug can overspend; structured outputs silently reject open JSON schemas, so the query-builder had to move from a record type to closed key/value pairs (before that fix every purchase went out with an empty query and we paid for weather APIs that returned nothing); sweeping a Tempo wallet needs a fee buffer because gas is paid in the same token you are sweeping; and pending withdrawals are reconciled lazily against chain receipts from the scheduler tick, so the ledger heals itself.

projects.title: teecash
projects.description: User-friendly trustless privacy mixer combining TEE and cryptography
projects.project_description: This project combines blind signatures with TEE signing workflow to create seamless user experience while enabling trustless security, adding money and withdrawing are as simple as making regular wallet transactions and outputs are actual single-use wallets so long-term security of the funds does not depend on protocol details or additional at all (only mixing stage is dependent on that) and any functionality of a regular wallet is possible without extra engineering - if multiple outputs need to be combined to make a particular transaction those transfers are managed in the background USDC is used for gas on Arc avoiding any complexity with gas management.
projects.how_its_made: Chainlink confidential TEE workflow is used to trustlessly sign blind BLS signatures turning classic Chaumian eCash into fully-trustless construction. TEE-based Privy wallets complement it by providing managed output addresses with no need for client-side secret management (beyond the mixing operation). Arc is perfect chain for this type of service, using USDC for gas is essential for making withdrawals seamless and so it EIP-2537 precompiles support.
