projects.title: ProofOfHack
projects.description: ProofOfHack ensures hackers are not incentivised to hack platforms and then hold them to ransom.
projects.project_description:
ProofOfHack bridges the gap between protocol teams needing verified evidence before paying
bounties and security researchers needing payment certainty before disclosing findings. • Funded Bounty Escrows: Protocol teams create and fund immutable, fixed-reward USDC
bounties locked in onchain escrow contracts.
• Confidential Claim Submission: Researchers submit encrypted evidence packages that are
hidden from the protocol team prior to payment.
• Exclusive Claim Reservations: Submitting an active claim places a temporary, exclusive
hold on the bounty reward so multiple submissions cannot fight over the same reserved
funds.
• Confidential Verification: An isolated verifier service evaluates the claim against the
bounty policy and issues an onchain signed verdict without public disclosure.
• Permissionless Payouts: Qualifying claims credit the researcher directly in the escrow.
The researcher can collect USDC funds at any time without requiring protocol approval.
• Post-Payment Report Delivery: The private vulnerability report is released to the
protocol team's security reviewers only after payment finality is confirmed onchain.
• DeFi Vault Coverage & AI Assistant: Indexes live ERC-4626 vault deployments via The
Graph and uses a source-aware coverage assistant to recommend funding for uncovered vaults.
• Bounded Funding Automation: Enables automated policy funding via Circle Agent Stack
subject to strict onchain budget limits.
projects.how_its_made:
Core Technologies Used
• Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, viem for chain reads/encoding, and Lucide UI icons.
• Backend & Database: Fastify, Node.js (>=22.14), PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM, and pg-boss
for durable PostgreSQL-backed background job queues.
• Smart Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry (forge), and OpenZeppelin ERC-20 / Merkle /
ReentrancyGuard standards.
• Cryptography: libsodium-wrappers-sumo and Web Crypto API for client-side envelope
encryption and verifier signatures. Partner Technologies & Sponsor Integrations -> Arc (Settlement & On-Chain Escrow)
• Role: Arc testnet serves as the primary financial settlement layer.
• How it helped: Arc's near-instant finality and native stablecoin architecture enabled
atomic USDC bounty funding and payouts.
• Benefit: Ensures low gas fees and deterministic transaction finality for automated
report releases. -> Privy (Auth, Wallets & On-Chain Policy Controls)
• Role: Powers identity for protocol teams and researchers, embedded wallets, and smart
contract access rules.
• How it helped: We integrated Privy’s policy engine to enforce programmatic treasury
constraints (e.g., rejecting unauthorized funding actions or capping daily spending
limits).
• Benefit: Smooth Web3 onboarding without friction, paired with robust server-side wallet
management. -> The Graph (Live Vault/Cont Coverage Indexing)
• Role: Indexes ERC-4626 vault and general smart contract deployments across target EVM networks using custom GraphQL subgraphs.
• How it helped: Queries real-time vault TVL, asset balances, and contract metadata to
calculate which registered vaults/contracts lack funded bounty coverage.
• Benefit: Gives protocols an automated, data-driven view of their security coverage gaps. -> Circle Agent Stack (Autonomous Bounded Funding)
• Role: Powers an autonomous operations agent that monitors coverage gaps and top-ups
bounties.
• How it helped: Interacts with our BudgetController smart contract on Arc to execute
programmatic bounty deposits within daily budget caps.
• Benefit: Allows protocol treasuries to set rules once and let AI/agents handle routine
security top-ups automatically. How The Pieces Fit Together (Data & Control Flow) Discovery & Recommendation: The Graph indexes vault data → Circle Agent or Coverage
Assistant detects missing coverage → Recommends an approved policy. Escrow Funding: Protocol owner approves transaction via Privy → USDC is deposited into
the Arc Escrow Contract. Encrypted Claim Upload: Researcher selects a bounty → Encrypts evidence payload in-
browser using Sodium / WebCrypto → Ciphertext stored in object storage. Isolated Verification: Verifier Service (running in an isolated container context with
isolated keys) verifies the evidence payload against the target condition → Signs an on-
chain verification proof. Settlement & Report Release: Verifier proof is posted to Arc → Escrow pays USDC
directly to researcher's Privy wallet → Report Release Service captures the
PaymentFinalized block event on Arc → Unlocks decrypted report access to the protocol
reviewer. Hacky & Notable Implementation Highlights Cryptographic "Pay-Before-Reveal" Gate:
The report-release service enforces a cryptographic barrier: the server refuses to serve
the report decryption keys until it performs an independent RPC read verifying that the
payout transaction has achieved block finality on Arc. Isolated Verifier Sandbox vs. Trojanized Exploits:
To solve the issue of trojanized PoCs (where malicious exploit scripts target protocol
reviewers), we designed the verifier service as a headless, zero-trust runner. Proofs are
evaluated in isolated memory without human reviewers ever touching raw executable code on
local machines.

projects.title: OAO
projects.description: An AI agent that leverages The Graph and LangGraph to optimize your portfolio.
projects.project_description: This project automates the process of finding lending protocols, comparing markets and optimizing yield for the onchain assets in your portfolio. It leverages a LangGraph pipeline to orchestrate LLM discovery, The Graph onchain data and deterministic Python functions to analyze an Ethereum wallet and come up with a recommendation based on blockchain data.
projects.how_its_made: The project consists of a React frontend where the user can input their wallet address. This sends a request to the FastAPI backend which invokes the LangGraph graph (a pipeline of nodes with each their own functions in the process). The first step of the LangGraph graph is to analyze the wallet and its token holdings, it does so through The Token API from The Graph Protocol. Then it engages the LLM (Claude Sonnet 5) to discover relevant lending protocols for the assets in the wallet. Then the LangGraph graph engages the Subgraph MCP server to find subgraphs for the discovered protocols. The subgraphs are then queried to get real market data from the protocols, so that the optimizer node can use that data to make a decision based on yield and TVL. Finally the decision gets handed back to the LLM to create a human-readable recommendation. Each step of the process is being communicated back to the React frontend in real time through LangGraph streams and FastAPI Server-Sent Events.

projects.title: Retainer
projects.description: Your agent's access renews itself on-chain at 3am, with nobody awake.
projects.project_description: An agent can pay for something. An agent cannot subscribe to something. Every payment rail built for agents charges per request: 402, sign, retry, pay, repeat. That works for one call. For anything an agent needs continuously, a human keeps re-authorising it — by clicking, or by operating a cron job somebody has to keep alive. There is always a person behind the subscription. Retainer removes that person. It is a live x402-gated service on Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. An agent pays once. The server forwards that settled payment on-chain into a contract, which opens a subscription and arms a scheduled renewal through the Hedera Schedule Service (HIP-1215, the system contract at 0x16b). When the access window closes, the network itself calls renew() on the contract. No user. No server job. No cron. The network has renewed access 55+ times across 3 deployments with nobody awake, and is still doing it hourly. What it cost to learn, said out loud rather than hidden: The network charges the CONTRACT for each scheduled call, so the contract must hold gas to pay for its own future execution. Retainer books three separate pots: refundable to the subscriber, earned by the seller, and gas reserved for the next renewal. A renewal that re-arms the next one costs ~1.55 HBAR; one that does not costs ~0.05. Re-arming is ~97% of the cost, so at 1 HBAR per period this loses money on every renewal. That is the real economic constraint of on-chain self-renewal. One scheduled renewal reverted with our own Insolvent() guard when the three pots came within ~2.4 HBAR of the account balance. The contract correctly refused to spend money it had already promised elsewhere. It is disclosed as a limitation on /judge. Live: https://retainer.edycu.dev · For judges, 30 seconds: https://retainer.edycu.dev/judge Contract 0.0.10415845 / 0x433050c9bd203FBdd49FAB6b5E20eD3E1FB2a931
projects.how_its_made: Solidity contract (RetainerAccess) on Hedera testnet, a Next.js 15 App Router front end, and a TypeScript agent script, from the Scaffold-HBAR template as boilerplate. The engine is the Hedera Schedule Service. The contract books its own next execution through HIP-1215, the system contract at 0x16b, using three of its methods: scheduleCall arms the next renew() at the exact second the window closes, deleteSchedule releases the booking on cancel so reserved gas returns rather than being stranded, and hasScheduleCapacity asks the network whether the slot can be booked before committing — without that pre-check a full network turns a clean lapse into a revert. Tested locally against @hashgraph/system-contracts-forking, which is what made a system contract testable in CI at all. Payments are x402 over HBAR via @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Blocky402 advertised hedera:testnet with scheme exact and x402Version 2 on the standard /supported contract, so it dropped into the template's HTTPFacilitatorClient with no adapter — the swap was one environment variable — and it supplies its own fee payer, which removed a whole account from our setup. Wallet connection is native Hedera through @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect and Reown AppKit on the hedera namespace, not an EVM-address shim, so the account a user sees is a real 0.0.x id. The hacky parts worth naming: The agent signs exactly once. Rather than have it sign again to subscribe, the resource server takes the payment it just received and forwards it on-chain itself, so one signature becomes a self-sustaining subscription. Two transactions come back: the payment, and the subscription it became. Two different units for the same money. HBAR value on the wire is weibar (1e18) while the EVM sees tinybar (1e8), and getting that boundary wrong silently mis-prices everything. It is pinned by property tests that check every tinybar amount from 0 to 100,000 exhaustively, plus 100,000 randomised amounts across the whole uint64 range. A contract that pays for its own future needs an accounting model, not a balance. Three pots — refundable, earned, gas reserve — because "the contract has money" and "the contract can afford its next scheduled call" are different questions. We learned that from a live revert. The payment and the access it buys are two unrelated rows on the ledger. An x402 settlement is a CRYPTOTRANSFER and the subscribeFor it pays for is a CONTRACTCALL; nothing on Hedera ties them together. Both are now written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10440194, immutable, no admin key) sharing a settlement id, so the join is public. Writing it surfaced the hacky bit: the two records for one request can reach consensus in either order, so the verifier joins on settlement id rather than sequence number. It is off unless configured and can never reject a payment — an HCS outage must not cost a paying agent its access. The mirror node cannot see the thing being verified. Schedules a contract creates via scheduleCall do not appear under /api/v1/schedules, and /api/v1/contracts/{id}/results omits scheduled executions entirely — the first version of our verifier queried that endpoint, reported no renewals found, and looked entirely correct while doing it. Read the account's transactions, not the contract's results. 64 contract tests, 258 app unit tests including the property suite, and 58 end-to-end tests. The punctuality is measured rather than claimed: yarn bench needs no keys and reports that across all 30 renewals this deployment had armed as of the dated run on 2026-09-09, the network executed the scheduled call a median 64 ms — p95 151 ms — after the second it was asked for.

Payments are x402 over HBAR via @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Blocky402 advertised hedera:testnet with scheme exact and x402Version 2 on the standard /supported contract, so it dropped into the template's HTTPFacilitatorClient with no adapter — the swap was one environment variable — and it supplies its own fee payer, which removed a whole account from our setup. Wallet connection is native Hedera through @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect and Reown AppKit on the hedera namespace, not an EVM-address shim, so the account a user sees is a real 0.0.x id.

The hacky parts worth naming:

1. The agent signs exactly once. Rather than have it sign again to subscribe, the resource server takes the payment it just received and forwards it on-chain itself, so one signature becomes a self-sustaining subscription. Two transactions come back: the payment, and the subscription it became.

2. Two different units for the same money. HBAR value on the wire is weibar (1e18) while the EVM sees tinybar (1e8), and getting that boundary wrong silently mis-prices everything. It is pinned by property tests that check every tinybar amount from 0 to 100,000 exhaustively, plus 100,000 randomised amounts across the whole uint64 range.

3. A contract that pays for its own future needs an accounting model, not a balance. Three pots — refundable, earned, gas reserve — because "the contract has money" and "the contract can afford its next scheduled call" are different questions. We learned that from a live revert.

4. The payment and the access it buys are two unrelated rows on the ledger. An x402 settlement is a CRYPTOTRANSFER and the subscribeFor it pays for is a CONTRACTCALL; nothing on Hedera ties them together. Both are now written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10440194, immutable, no admin key) sharing a settlement id, so the join is public. Writing it surfaced the hacky bit: the two records for one request can reach consensus in either order, so the verifier joins on settlement id rather than sequence number. It is off unless configured and can never reject a payment — an HCS outage must not cost a paying agent its access.

5. The mirror node cannot see the thing being verified. Schedules a contract creates via scheduleCall do not appear under /api/v1/schedules, and /api/v1/contracts/{id}/results omits scheduled executions entirely — the first version of our verifier queried that endpoint, reported no renewals found, and looked entirely correct while doing it. Read the account's transactions, not the contract's results.

64 contract tests, 258 app unit tests including the property suite, and 58 end-to-end tests. The punctuality is measured rather than claimed: yarn bench needs no keys and reports that across all 30 renewals this deployment had armed as of the dated run on 2026-09-09, the network executed the scheduled call a median 64 ms — p95 151 ms — after the second it was asked for.

projects.title: beanie
projects.description: A multichain, non-custodial, permissionless stablecoin payment gateway.
projects.project_description: A multichain, non-custodial, permissionless stablecoin payment gateway. A merchant registers ONE destination address and ONE blockchain network to get dedicated, merchant-bonded non-custodial receivers on all supported blockchains; deposits settle through these receivers without Beanie ever having custody of users' funds. Incentivized keepers consistently call sweep() on pending balances to earn 0.05% of volume MEV reward. All chains share one pattern: A single factory deploys non-custodial receivers whose destinations are pinned to the merchant for good at deploy time. Receiver addresses derived from the merchant address. Funds ALWAYS sweep to the merchant Universal Beanie Webhook Registry, KV store for merchants' URL (as a 20-byte EVM address) Optional Stealth Account: Provides protocol-agnostic privacy on Beanie using PassKey Stealth Account Abstraction
projects.how_its_made: At its core, Beanie is a private intent layer. It allows anyone to announce an intent and uses JIT deployment to trigger actions when onchain conditions are met; in this case, it settles transfers. The exposed single function of the receiver is basically a deterministic turnkey and would do exactly the actions embedded without accepting external parameters. Beanie is grounded in efficient stablecoin infrastructures. Near-zero overhead of compute, network, or storage beyond the call function used to dispatch the announce events for direct wallet transfers using Chainlink CRE. No external ACID storage beyond the contracts deployed onchain, enabling a network of API providers and Keepers to serve as a convenience layer over Beanie contracts, without a privileged party. Starting beanie_api brings up the convenience layer; including the API, the workers, and the customer/merchant-facing UI. Receiver initialization is bundled with the first sweep() following a deposit; subsequent sweeps are cleared as a single transaction, ensuring that spam is a losing game for spammers On EVM, automations are orchestrated from Chainlink's CRE to ensure fast onchain delivery of assets, and signed webhooks are optionally delivered. UI and server authentication are through passkeys, and neither merchants nor users need native gas to make payments or receive payments on Beanie. Beanie processes direct transfers and gasless payments. Beanie abstracts all its complexity behind a single link that renders a payment widget for end users. Developers, merchants, and ordinary users can use any chain from any wallet. Zero sign-up friction during onboarding, merchants authorize with their passkey. The same PassKey is essential for Stealth Account Abstraction on Beanie

projects.title: Portcullis
projects.description: A security firewall that authenticates cross-chain settlement messages before value moves.
projects.project_description: Portcullis protects inbound cross-chain settlements at the receiving contract. Before an adapter transfers a token, PortcullisGuard verifies the signing authority, token and recipient allowlists, value bounds, replay protection, nonce order, per-source rate limits, and volume or policy conditions. Invalid messages are rejected before receiver state changes. The circuit breaker only latches on authenticated anomalies: a rate-limit breach, a volume spike, or an explicit policy denial. The project runs across Arc testnet, ENSv2 identity on Sepolia, Chainlink CRE private policy checks, and a Graph subgraph for inspection history and configuration.
projects.how_its_made: Portcullis is built in Solidity 0.8.36 with Foundry, Solady OwnableRoles, and OpenZeppelin. PortcullisGuard keeps the settlement state, while the inlined PortcullisChecks library evaluates six checks before an adapter can transfer value. The message digest binds block.chainid, the guard address, and the settlement payload; an ECDSA signature from the resolved authority proves the sender. EnsIdentityRegistry resolves guardian-allowlisted ENS names through ENSv2’s UniversalResolverV2. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow runs policy checks in a TEE and reports ALLOW, DENY, or MANUAL_REVIEW to CrePolicyConsumer. The Graph indexes guard and receiver events for the static Next.js guardian dashboard, built with viem and Privy. The project also includes Foundry unit, fuzz, invariant, and exploit-replay tests.

projects.title: Dry Powder
projects.description: Shared-reserve dip-buying strategies powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
projects.project_description: Dry Powder is a DeFi prototype for coordinating multiple buy-the-dip strategies from one shared stablecoin reserve. A maker can allocate one 10,000 mUSDC budget across ETH, WBTC, and LINK strategies, while each strategy remains independently fillable through Aqua. When one leg fills, the shared reserve state updates, reducing capacity and repricing sibling strategies automatically. This prevents overcommitted strategies from spending more than the maker’s real budget while still letting the maker express broader intent across multiple assets.
projects.how_its_made: Dry Powder is built with Solidity, Hardhat, TypeScript, 1inch Aqua, and 1inch SwapVM. The core is a custom DryPowderRouter with a custom SwapVM opcode that reads shared reserve state before settlement. Aqua handles strategy shipping and virtual balances, while the Dry Powder opcode enforces reserve budget, per-leg caps, maker wallet balance, tranche boundaries, and dynamic price multipliers. The demo deploys to Ethereum Sepolia using the official Aqua registry, mock ERC20 assets, and scripts for deploy, setup, quote, fill, and sibling repricing. The hacky/fun part is using independent Aqua strategies that appear overallocated, while one shared onchain reserve makes them collectively safe.

projects.title: Verdikt
projects.description: x402 marketplace: delivery verified per call in a TEE, auto-refunded on-chain, no disputes.
projects.project_description: Verdikt is a marketplace of x402-gated API services whose delivery is verified per call — not just self-reported at listing time. A proxy sits between a paying agent and an x402 provider at <slug>.verdikt.bond . When a payment header is present, the proxy recovers the payer from the payment signature and hands the call to a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow , which: Replays the payment against the provider from inside a TEE — once, because an x402 payment settles once Evaluates the response against the provider's own declared SLA Writes a PASS / FAIL / DOWN verdict to the on-chain registry on Arc If the SLA isn't met, the paying agent is auto-refunded from the provider's bonded deposit — capped at what was paid, booked as a credit rather than pushed, with no dispute or arbitration step. The SLA lives as a text record on the provider's ENSv2 subname ( <slug>.verdikt.eth ), scoped with per-key access control so only the provider can write it and only the verifier can write the derived reputation scores. An hourly workflow publishes conformance and availability ratios back to the same subname, and the marketplace ranks on them. It runs for real. Providers register self-serve through the dashboard: the wizard mints the ENS subname, publishes the SLA and posts the bond on Arc. The services listed front real third-party x402 providers (Alchemy, Allium, Syntalic and others). A Circle agent wallet has paid them through Verdikt, each call was judged inside the workflow, and the FAIL and DOWN verdicts drew real refunds out of the providers' bonds — all of it readable off Arc Testnet and Sepolia. Because verification is deterministic and code-enforced, consumers can pick a service based on its real track record instead of a provider's own marketing.
projects.how_its_made: Arc holds the registry, escrow, verdicts and refunds. USDC is Arc's native gas token, so bond, payment and refund are one asset moving as msg.value , with no approve / transferFrom . VerdiktRegistry is an IReceiver : verdicts arrive as DON-signed reports through the KeystoneForwarder, and a refund is booked as a credit the payer withdraws, or claims by an EIP-712 signature anyone can relay, never pushed, so a reverting payer can't erase its own FAIL. Ethereum Sepolia holds ENS : each provider's SLA lives only as the sla text record on <slug>.verdikt.eth , using ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver for per-key access control. The provider writes sla / url , the score writer writes conformance / availability , and cross-writes revert. VerdiktSubnameRegistrar mints subnames with exactly those roles; VerdiktScoreWriter is the IReceiver the hourly workflow reports to. Payment verification covers both exact transfer methods a real x402 challenge offers, plain ERC-3009 and Circle's GatewayWalletBatched , through one verifier that recovers the payer from the signature rather than reading it out of JSON. A contract-account payer is asked via ERC-1271 on the chain it paid on. Verification runs inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (TEE): it replays the paid call once, evaluates the response with a pure SLA engine, and writes the verdict to Arc. A 402 on the replay writes nothing, since the provider is saying it wasn't paid. A second, separate CRE cron workflow reads public VerdictWritten events and publishes trailing-window conformance/availability ratios to ENS, kept apart so the confidential path never depends on aggregate traffic timing. Deployment. The proxy is a Cloudflare Worker on *.verdikt.bond , with Durable Objects for the pending-verification rendezvous. The dashboard is a Lit + Vite static app reading Arc and ENS straight from the browser via viem, live at verdikt.bond. Workaround. Production CRE deployment access wasn't yet enabled, so we ran the confidential and cron workflows entirely through cre workflow simulate --broadcast , fronted by a small runner container that plays the role of Chainlink's gateway. It forwards the proxy's trigger into a long-lived simulate verify --listen process and runs the hourly aggregate as a scheduled job. Everything on Arc and Sepolia in this submission, every verdict, refund and published score, was produced by that simulator against the real live contracts, not mocked.
projects.project_description_markdown:
**Verdikt** is a marketplace of x402-gated API services whose delivery is verified per call — not just self-reported at listing time.

A proxy sits between a paying agent and an x402 provider at `<slug>.verdikt.bond`. When a payment header is present, the proxy recovers the payer from the payment signature and hands the call to a **Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow**, which:

- Replays the payment against the provider from inside a TEE — once, because an x402 payment settles once
- Evaluates the response against the provider's own declared SLA
- Writes a `PASS`/`FAIL`/`DOWN` verdict to the on-chain registry on **Arc**

If the SLA isn't met, the paying agent is **auto-refunded** from the provider's bonded deposit — capped at what was paid, booked as a credit rather than pushed, with no dispute or arbitration step.

The SLA lives as a text record on the provider's ENSv2 subname (`<slug>.verdikt.eth`), scoped with per-key access control so only the provider can write it and only the verifier can write the derived reputation scores. An hourly workflow publishes conformance and availability ratios back to the same subname, and the marketplace ranks on them.

**It runs for real.** Providers register self-serve through the dashboard: the wizard mints the ENS subname, publishes the SLA and posts the bond on Arc. The services listed front real third-party x402 providers (Alchemy, Allium, Syntalic and others). A Circle agent wallet has paid them through Verdikt, each call was judged inside the workflow, and the FAIL and DOWN verdicts drew real refunds out of the providers' bonds — all of it readable off Arc Testnet and Sepolia.

Because verification is deterministic and code-enforced, consumers can pick a service based on its **real track record** instead of a provider's own marketing.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**Arc** holds the registry, escrow, verdicts and refunds. USDC is Arc's native gas token, so bond, payment and refund are one asset moving as `msg.value`, with no `approve`/`transferFrom`. `VerdiktRegistry` is an `IReceiver`: verdicts arrive as DON-signed reports through the KeystoneForwarder, and a refund is booked as a credit the payer withdraws, or claims by an EIP-712 signature anyone can relay, never pushed, so a reverting payer can't erase its own FAIL.

Ethereum Sepolia holds **ENS**: each provider's SLA lives only as the `sla` text record on `<slug>.verdikt.eth`, using ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver for per-key access control. The provider writes `sla`/`url`, the score writer writes `conformance`/`availability`, and cross-writes revert. `VerdiktSubnameRegistrar` mints subnames with exactly those roles; `VerdiktScoreWriter` is the `IReceiver` the hourly workflow reports to.

**Payment verification** covers both exact transfer methods a real x402 challenge offers, plain ERC-3009 and Circle's `GatewayWalletBatched`, through one verifier that recovers the payer from the signature rather than reading it out of JSON. A contract-account payer is asked via ERC-1271 on the chain it paid on.

**Verification** runs inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (TEE): it replays the paid call once, evaluates the response with a pure SLA engine, and writes the verdict to Arc. A 402 on the replay writes nothing, since the provider is saying it wasn't paid. A second, separate CRE cron workflow reads public `VerdictWritten` events and publishes trailing-window conformance/availability ratios to ENS, kept apart so the confidential path never depends on aggregate traffic timing.

**Deployment.** The proxy is a Cloudflare Worker on `*.verdikt.bond`, with Durable Objects for the pending-verification rendezvous. The dashboard is a Lit + Vite static app reading Arc and ENS straight from the browser via viem, live at verdikt.bond.

**Workaround.** Production CRE deployment access wasn't yet enabled, so we ran the confidential and cron workflows entirely through `cre workflow simulate --broadcast`, fronted by a small runner container that plays the role of Chainlink's gateway. It forwards the proxy's trigger into a long-lived `simulate verify --listen` process and runs the hourly aggregate as a scheduled job. Everything on Arc and Sepolia in this submission, every verdict, refund and published score, was produced by that simulator against the real live contracts, not mocked.

projects.title: Arx
projects.description: Arx is a programmable transaction firewall and policy engine for on-chain AI agents.
projects.project_description:
An AI agent that can move money needs authority. The usual way to give it
authority is a private key or an API credential, which grants everything that
credential can do, for as long as it exists. That is a poor fit for a system whose behaviour is steered by text it did not
write. A poisoned invoice tells a payment agent the supplier's banking details
have changed. The agent believes it — it is not malfunctioning, it was convinced
— and signs. Better reasoning does not fix this, because the model is the part
that can be talked into things. The problem is not intelligence. The problem is authority. Arx sits between the agent and the signer and answers one question: is this exact
transaction inside the authority this agent was actually granted? It normalizes
the transaction, resolves the agent's capability, evaluates policy, inspects the
transaction bytes, scores risk from explainable signals, and produces one of four
outcomes in Ledger's own vocabulary — ALLOW, DENY, ESCALATE, or ABORT. Only an
approval cryptographically bound to those exact bytes can reach the signer, and
the Ledger device remains the final boundary. What makes it more than an allowlist is the set of checks a naive policy layer
gets wrong: The agent's own numbers are claims, not facts. An intent declares amountUsd;
Arx prices the actual transaction bytes through a Chainlink feed and refuses
the mismatch. An agent declaring $1 while moving 1000 ETH is caught. The recipient is often inside the calldata. In an ERC-20 transfer the payee is
an argument, not the to field, so an allowlisted token contract is otherwise
an open payment channel. A standing allowance is authority. An approve moves nothing now and lets the
spender move everything later, so the USD ceiling applies to it. Dependency failure is never permission. Every external adapter distinguishes
"checked, clean" from "could not check". Unknown resolves to DENY or ESCALATE,
never ALLOW. Silence is never approval. Arx also solves the credential half of the problem. Using the Ledger Key Ring, a
capability broker seals upstream secrets and hands the agent a short-lived token
bound to a hash of the policy in force — never the API key. The agent cannot leak
what it does not hold, and tokens die the moment an operator narrows the policy. Fourteen adversarial scenarios run as assertions, not printouts: prompt
injection, declared-value lies, calldata smuggling, address poisoning, a
double-sign race, replay, revocation mid-flight, and audit tampering. The suite
exits non-zero if any behaves differently from the documentation. A separate demo
drives a real AI agent that is genuinely prompt-injected, alongside an
unprotected control case that signs the attacker's transaction — because the
contrast is the argument.
projects.how_its_made:
TypeScript on Bun, Fastify, Zod, SQLite via bun:sqlite, viem for EVM primitives.
The authorization kernel makes no network calls and runs no model on the decision
path, so there is no prompt in it to inject into. Every decision is a pure
function of the capability, the intent, the transaction bytes and an injected
clock, which is what makes decisions reproducible from the audit log. Ledger is the core. The Device Management Kit (1.9.0), the Ethereum signer kit
(1.18.0), the first-party Speculos transport (1.2.1) and context-module (2.5.0)
are all pinned exactly, because the @ledgerhq packages publish a develop build
daily and a caret range drifts mid-event. Alongside the SDK path I implemented
the app-ethereum APDU protocol directly from its published specification and the
app's own C source, so the signing path is transparent and auditable rather than
opaque: BIP-32 path packing, 255-byte chunking, the EIP-2718 type-byte framing,
and the typed-transaction parity convention. Signatures are not accepted, they
are verified — the signer address is recovered from the exact signed digest and
compared to what the device reported. Because Docker was unavailable on the development machine, I built an in-process
implementation of the app-ethereum protocol that drives the same codec and is
keyed from the published Speculos test mnemonic. It derives
0xDad77910DbDFdE764fC21FCD4E74D71bBACA6D8D — the address Ledger's own fixtures
expect for that seed — which cross-checks the request encoding, BIP-32 packing
and response parsing against an external value. That mode produces real secp256k1
signatures that verify by address recovery, so the full pipeline is demonstrable
on any machine with no hardware, while reporting emulated: true and refusing to
start in production. The Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring) backs the capability broker. Its key
property is that after ring init, encrypt and decrypt need network but not the
device — which is what makes the "hosts with no USB port" story work: provision
once on a laptop, then unseal on a VPS with no hardware attached. Integrations plug into named seams — PriceOracle, NameResolver,
RiskSignalProvider, SignerAdapter, HumanVerifier, ExecutionVenue — and every one
returns an Availability<T> that keeps "checked, clean" distinct from "could not
check". ENSv2 on Sepolia resolves allowlist entries during authorization and
binds the resolved address, so a name re-pointed between approval and signing
aborts rather than redirecting funds. Chainlink aggregators are read directly
rather than through a convenience API, because latestRoundData returns updatedAt
and that lets Arx enforce its own staleness bound. The parts I would highlight as hacky or hard-won: hashing goes through an
RFC 8785-style canonicalizer rather than JSON.stringify, because otherwise a
digest depends on key insertion order and a reordered payload could be shaped to
match an approval bound to different bytes. Claiming an approval for signing is a
SQL compare-and-swap performed before any bytes reach the device, which is what
makes double-signing impossible under concurrency — verified with eight parallel
requests. The audit log is hash-chained so editing any historical decision
invalidates every hash after it, and GET /audit/verify recomputes the chain and
names the first break. An adversarial audit of this repository found six real defects during the build —
including a $100M standing allowance passing a $500 ceiling, and one agent being
able to sign another agent's approval. All six are fixed, each with a test, and
they are listed in the README rather than quietly patched.

opaque: BIP-32 path packing, 255-byte chunking, the EIP-2718 type-byte framing,
and the typed-transaction parity convention. Signatures are not accepted, they
are verified — the signer address is recovered from the exact signed digest and
compared to what the device reported.

Because Docker was unavailable on the development machine, I built an in-process
implementation of the app-ethereum protocol that drives the same codec and is
keyed from the published Speculos test mnemonic. It derives
0xDad77910DbDFdE764fC21FCD4E74D71bBACA6D8D — the address Ledger's own fixtures
expect for that seed — which cross-checks the request encoding, BIP-32 packing
and response parsing against an external value. That mode produces real secp256k1
signatures that verify by address recovery, so the full pipeline is demonstrable
on any machine with no hardware, while reporting emulated: true and refusing to
start in production.

The Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring) backs the capability broker. Its key
property is that after ring init, encrypt and decrypt need network but not the
device — which is what makes the "hosts with no USB port" story work: provision
once on a laptop, then unseal on a VPS with no hardware attached.

Integrations plug into named seams — PriceOracle, NameResolver,
RiskSignalProvider, SignerAdapter, HumanVerifier, ExecutionVenue — and every one
returns an Availability<T> that keeps "checked, clean" distinct from "could not
check". ENSv2 on Sepolia resolves allowlist entries during authorization and
binds the resolved address, so a name re-pointed between approval and signing
aborts rather than redirecting funds. Chainlink aggregators are read directly
rather than through a convenience API, because latestRoundData returns updatedAt
and that lets Arx enforce its own staleness bound.

The parts I would highlight as hacky or hard-won: hashing goes through an
RFC 8785-style canonicalizer rather than JSON.stringify, because otherwise a
digest depends on key insertion order and a reordered payload could be shaped to
match an approval bound to different bytes. Claiming an approval for signing is a
SQL compare-and-swap performed before any bytes reach the device, which is what
makes double-signing impossible under concurrency — verified with eight parallel
requests. The audit log is hash-chained so editing any historical decision
invalidates every hash after it, and GET /audit/verify recomputes the chain and
names the first break.

An adversarial audit of this repository found six real defects during the build —
including a $100M standing allowance passing a $500 ceiling, and one agent being
able to sign another agent's approval. All six are fixed, each with a test, and
they are listed in the README rather than quietly patched.

projects.title: Faregate
projects.description: Policy-governed AI agents autonomously transact for onchain data with human-in-the-loop controls.
projects.project_description: Faregate is a permission and payment gateway that lets AI agents autonomously purchase paid onchain data while keeping humans in control of what agents can access and spend. A human defines an agent's capability, including its allowed data scope, maximum cost per query, daily spending limit, and the amount above which human approval is required. The agent can then request blockchain data using natural language. An LLM interprets the request and produces a structured query, but it never makes the authorization decision. Faregate uses a deterministic policy engine to validate the structured query against the agent's capability, current spending ledger, query price, and approval rules. Requests can be denied, automatically approved, or paused for human approval. Once authorized, the agent pays for the query through x402 on Hedera using USDC, and Faregate retrieves the requested data from The Graph using the Messari standardized lending schema. The resulting data can be analyzed by an LLM, but the analysis is grounding-checked against the retrieved dataset so unsupported addresses or hashes are not presented as facts. Agent identity and capabilities are represented through ENSv2 passports on Sepolia, with live revocation checks on every request. The key idea is to give an AI agent a controlled capability instead of an unrestricted API key, wallet, or payment credential. Humans define the boundaries, deterministic code enforces them, and the agent operates autonomously within those boundaries. If the human revokes the agent, that revocation takes precedence even if the agent already holds an approved payment quote.
projects.how_its_made: Faregate is built as a TypeScript monorepo with an Express/TypeScript gateway, a Next.js dashboard, a separate demo agent, and shared domain logic. The gateway coordinates identity resolution, natural-language request interpretation, deterministic policy evaluation, pricing, payment, data retrieval, AI analysis, spend tracking, and audit logging. The agent sends a natural-language request to the gateway. OpenRouter with a structured-output LLM interprets the request into a validated query, but the model is deliberately excluded from the authorization path. A pure deterministic policy engine evaluates the agent's ENS capability, requested scope, query cost, daily spend, existing ledger, and human approval threshold. Pricing uses integer micro-USD values, avoiding floating-point rounding problems. For payments, Faregate integrates x402 with Hedera testnet and USDC, enabling machine-to-machine, per-query payments without API keys or subscriptions. ENSv2 subnames on Ethereum Sepolia act as agent passports, with capabilities stored in ENS text records and resolved through the Universal Resolver. The Graph is used as the data layer, with Messari's standardized lending schema allowing the same query documents to fan out across multiple protocol subgraphs. The project also includes several security-focused implementation details: policy is re-evaluated before quoting and again at payment release, payment nonces are single-use, requests are idempotent, human actions use wallet signatures, structured queries are validated and clamped, agents are rate-limited, and the gateway fails closed when identity resolution fails. AI-generated analysis is checked against the retrieved data to catch unsupported claims. The most notable design choice is the separation between AI reasoning and authorization: the LLM can interpret what the agent wants, but deterministic code decides whether it is allowed. ENS revocation is also checked live, so an agent can be rejected even after receiving an approved quote. The gateway never holds the user's funds or private keys; the agent pays from its own account.

projects.title: Mandate Agents
projects.description: Agent executes real on-chain financial actions for you, inside limits you set, with a ledger
projects.project_description: Mandate is bounded delegation for AI agents. You control what contracts an agent can call, how much USDC it can move, and which actions need your Ledger approval. The smart account enforces these limits on-chain, not the AI. Tell it: “Get me 100 USDC on Arc by Friday to pay Acme. Don’t sell my ETH.” It checks your positions, compares borrow rates, creates and simulates a plan, then executes safe steps on its own. For irreversible actions like bridging via CCTP, it pauses for a plain-text Ledger approval. The contract verifies the exact approval on-chain before executing. Everything is enforced on-chain: spending caps, allow-lists, replay protection, and guardian approvals. The agent never sees your keys or writes calldata.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Solidity + Foundry + OpenZeppelin, with a TypeScript/viem SDK powering deterministic action adapters and agent tooling. The core idea is bounded, verifiable execution: the AI only creates an intent; deterministic code builds the actual calls, while the smart account enforces allow-lists, per-tx/daily caps, replay protection, and guardian approvals. We use Circle CCTP v2 for Base Sepolia → Arc transfers and The Graph for standardized lending-rate data across protocols. Safe steps execute automatically; irreversible steps trigger a plain Ledger approval that the contract reconstructs and verifies byte-for-byte on-chain.

projects.title: Rug Radar
projects.description: Autonomous agent that pays per call for live DeFi drain and whale intelligence
projects.project_description:
Rug Radar An autonomous agent that pays per call for live DeFi drain and whale intelligence — settled on Hedera with x402, computed from The Graph's standardized subgraphs and Substreams, discovered through ENSv2. "Is the WETH/USDC pool being drained right now?" → the agent resolves api.rugradar.eth , hits a 402 , signs a 0.03 HBAR payment, gets a risk score with evidence, and every payment plus the final decision lands on a Hedera Consensus Service topic you can audit on HashScan. Built from scratch at ETHOnline 2026 for three bounties: Bounty What in this repo satisfies it Hedera — AI & Agentic Payments (x402) Live x402-gated service on Hedera testnet settled through the Blocky402 facilitator ( packages/service ), and an agent that pays for it ( packages/agent ). Extras: metered pricing (per protocol, per lookback day, per 15 s stream window), streamed micropayments , HTS USDC as an alternative asset, HCS audit trail of every settlement and every agent decision, ERC-8004 registration file, discovery directory via ENS. The Graph — Composable / Standardized Graph Products Every endpoint runs one query string across many protocols using the Messari Standardized Subgraphs ( dex-amm schema: Uniswap v3, Uniswap v2, SushiSwap, Curve; lending schema: Aave v3, Compound v3, Spark). The live whale wire composes Substreams ( ethereum-common package, filtered_events ) with a standardized subgraph for pricing. All data is live from The Graph Network gateway; nothing is mocked. ENS — Best Use of ENSv2 (Sepolia) The namespace rugradar.eth owns its own PermissionedRegistry and own PermissionedResolver (deployed through the VerifiableFactory). Services are expiring, non-transferable, revocable subnames ; their x402 endpoint, price list, pay-to account and audit topic are text records (ENSIP-26 agent-endpoint[x402] + agent-context ). Enhanced Access Control delegates exactly one text key ( x402.pricing ) to the service's own key. The agent discovers services by walking the registry and resolving through the Universal Resolver ; nothing about the paid API is hard-coded in the agent. Agents get their own identity subnames too. Demo UI — everything from one tab pnpm ui # → http://localhost:3001 One page, four panels, every button does the real thing and streams what happens over Server-Sent Events: Discover — resolves api.rugradar.eth live through the ENSv2 Universal Resolver, shows the records and the registry hierarchy ( ETHRegistry → our registry → our resolver , expiry, non-transferable), and a Prove Enhanced Access Control button where the service's own key edits x402.pricing and is refused on any other record. Pay per call — one-click paid requests: the 402 quote (HBAR and USDC options, pay-to, fee payer), the Hedera settlement id linked to HashScan, then the result summarized (risk score, whale list, lending stress). Plus a Whale wire button that pays for one 15-second SSE window. Ask the agent — the LLM run as a live feed: tool calls, quotes, payments, budget meter, then the verdict with a risk gauge, evidence, the payments list, and the HCS-anchored decision. One query, every protocol — the same standardized query fanned out to all seven protocols with timings. demo.md is the recording runbook; slides.html is the four-slide pitch (arrow keys). A real run (Hedera testnet + ENSv2 Sepolia + The Graph Network) 🛰 Rug Radar agent · wallet 0.0.10372230 on hedera:testnet · budget 1 HBAR · model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B ❓ Is the WETH/USDC pool on Uniswap v3 being drained right now? Should an LP exit? ⚙ discover_services({}) ENS discovery: 1 service(s): api.rugradar.eth ⚙ read_catalog(...) → GET https://…/v1/catalog (free) ⚙ pool_risk({"tokens":["WETH","USDC"]}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663313.356227872 · HCS 0.0.10372230@1788663360.527369081 ⚙ scan_whales({"protocols":["uniswap-v3"]}) paid 0.015 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663359.073787482 ⚙ pool_risk({"protocol":"uniswap-v3","pool":"0xe0554a47…"}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663385.026425010 **Verdict: Watch (not critical)** — the Uniswap v3 WETH/USDC 0.01% pool shows heavy LP churn but no drain: 24h withdrawals $2.49M (68% of TVL) are offset by $2.51M deposits (net +$22.9k), outflow is spread across many addresses, large swaps run both ways. projects.how_its_made:
Quickstart Requirements: Node ≥ 22, pnpm 11, one funded Hedera testnet account from https://portal.hedera.com (ECDSA or ED25519; set HEDERA_SERVICE_KEY_TYPE ), a Subgraph Studio API key, an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint ( LLM_BASE_URL , LLM_API_KEY , LLM_MODEL ; we use Qwen 3.8), and a Sepolia key with a little ETH for the ENS steps. pnpm install
cp .env.example .env        # fill in keys (see comments)

# 0. sanity: the same query across every protocol
pnpm graph:smoke

# 1. Hedera: a separate agent wallet (x402 needs payer ≠ payee), audit topics, optional USDC
pnpm hedera:agent-account    # creates a funded ECDSA account; paste HEDERA_AGENT_* into .env
pnpm hedera:topics           # paste HCS_SERVICE_TOPIC_ID / HCS_AGENT_TOPIC_ID into .env
pnpm hedera:associate-usdc   # optional; HBAR needs no association

# 2. run the paid service
pnpm service                 # http://localhost:4021/v1/catalog

# 3. ENSv2 on Sepolia: namespace, then publish the service + the agent identity
pnpm ens:deploy              # deploys our registry + resolver, registers <ENS_PARENT_LABEL>.eth, writes ens.deployment.json
pnpm ens:register api --url https://<public-url-of-service>
pnpm ens:register scout --agent
pnpm ens:resolve api.rugradar.eth
pnpm ens:list
pnpm ens:service-update api "<new pricing string>"   # EAC demo: the service key may edit only x402.pricing

# 4. pay for one call without the LLM ("curl with a wallet")
pnpm demo:curl "/v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC"

# 5. the agent — CLI or the demo UI
pnpm agent "Is the WETH/USDC pool on Uniswap v3 being drained right now? Should an LP exit?"
pnpm ui                      # http://localhost:3001 For a local run before ENS is set up, SERVICE_URL_OVERRIDE=http://localhost:4021 pnpm demo:curl "/v1/whales?protocols=curve" skips discovery (the UI honours the same variable). Public URL. The service is a long-lived process (facilitator sync at boot, open Substreams stream, SSE windows up to 120 s), so it does not fit serverless hosting. It runs on Render's free tier at https://rugradar-vibj.onrender.com (sleeps after 15 min idle; hit /health to wake it). Pushes do not auto-deploy there; run pnpm render:deploy . For a quick alternative, pnpm tunnel (cloudflared) prints a https://*.trycloudflare.com URL; set it as SERVICE_URL , restart the service, and republish the records with pnpm ens:register api --url <url> .

Agents get their own identity subnames too. | ## Demo UI — everything from one tab ```bash pnpm ui # → http://localhost:3001 ``` One page, four panels, every button does the real thing and streams what happens over Server-Sent Events: 1. **Discover** — resolves `api.rugradar.eth` live through the ENSv2 Universal Resolver, shows the records and the registry hierarchy (`ETHRegistry → our registry → our resolver`, expiry, non-transferable), and a **Prove Enhanced Access Control** button where the service's own key edits `x402.pricing` and is refused on any other record. 2. **Pay per call** — one-click paid requests: the `402` quote (HBAR and USDC options, pay-to, fee payer), the Hedera settlement id linked to HashScan, then the result summarized (risk score, whale list, lending stress). Plus a **Whale wire** button that pays for one 15-second SSE window. 3. **Ask the agent** — the LLM run as a live feed: tool calls, quotes, payments, budget meter, then the verdict with a risk gauge, evidence, the payments list, and the HCS-anchored decision. 4. **One query, every protocol** — the same standardized query fanned out to all seven protocols with timings. `demo.md` is the recording runbook; `slides.html` is the four-slide pitch (arrow keys). ## A real run (Hedera testnet + ENSv2 Sepolia + The Graph Network) ``` 🛰 Rug Radar agent · wallet 0.0.10372230 on hedera:testnet · budget 1 HBAR · model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B ❓ Is the WETH/USDC pool on Uniswap v3 being drained right now? Should an LP exit? ⚙ discover_services({}) ENS discovery: 1 service(s): api.rugradar.eth ⚙ read_catalog(...) → GET https://…/v1/catalog (free) ⚙ pool_risk({"tokens":["WETH","USDC"]}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663313.356227872 · HCS 0.0.10372230@1788663360.527369081 ⚙ scan_whales({"protocols":["uniswap-v3"]}) paid 0.015 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663359.073787482 ⚙ pool_risk({"protocol":"uniswap-v3","pool":"0xe0554a47…"}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement 0.0.7162784@1788663385.026425010 **Verdict: Watch (not critical)** — the Uniswap v3 WETH/USDC 0.01% pool shows heavy LP churn but no drain: 24h withdrawals $2.49M (68% of TVL) are offset by $2.51M deposits (net +$22.9k), outflow is spread across many addresses, large swaps run both ways. Recommended action: no exit needed. 💸 Spent 0.075 HBAR of 1 across 3 paid call(s) 🧾 Decision anchored on HCS: https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10372230%401788663436.746860424 ``` ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Agent["packages/agent · LLM agent (Qwen 3.8) with a Hedera wallet + demo UI"] A1["discover_services"] --> A2["read_catalog"] A2 --> A3["pool_risk · scan_whales · protocol_health · watch_whale_wire"] A3 --> A4["budget guard + HCS spend ledger"] end subgraph ENS["ENSv2 · Sepolia"] E1[("ETHRegistry
rugradar.eth")] --> E2[("our PermissionedRegistry
api · scout")] E2 --> E3[("our PermissionedResolver
agent-endpoint, x402.*, hcs.* records")] end subgraph Service["packages/service · x402-gated API on Hedera (Render)"] S1["GET /v1/whales"] S2["GET /v1/pool-risk"] S3["GET /v1/protocol-health"] S4["GET /v1/stream/whales (SSE)"] S5["onAfterSettle → HCS audit"] end subgraph Graph["The Graph"] G1[("Messari standardized subgraphs
4 DEX + 3 lending")] G2[("Substreams ethereum-common
filtered_events")] end subgraph Hedera["Hedera testnet"] H1["Blocky402 facilitator
verify + settle"] H2[("HCS topics
settlements · spend ledger")] end A1 -- "Universal Resolver" --> E3 A3 -- "402 → PAYMENT-SIGNATURE" --> Service Service -- "verify / settle" --> H1 S1 --> G1 S2 --> G1 S3 --> G1 S4 --> G2 S4 -. "token prices" .-> G1 S5 --> H2 A4 --> H2 ``` ### One paid request, end to end ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Agent participant ENS as ENSv2 (Sepolia) participant Svc as Rug Radar service participant Fac as Blocky402 facilitator participant Hedera participant Graph as The Graph Agent->>ENS: getEnsText("api.rugradar.eth", "agent-endpoint[x402]") ENS-->>Agent: https://…/v1 (+ x402.network, x402.payTo, x402.pricing, hcs.audit) Agent->>Svc: GET /v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC Svc-->>Agent: 402 · PAYMENT-REQUIRED (0.03 HBAR or $0.003 USDC, payTo, feePayer) Note over Agent: budget guard checks the quote before signing Agent->>Agent: sign Hedera TransferTransaction (ECDSA) Agent->>Svc: GET … · PAYMENT-SIGNATURE Svc->>Fac: /verify Svc->>Graph: liquidityPool + snapshots + withdraws (standardized query) Svc->>Fac: /settle Fac->>Hedera: submit transfer Svc-->>Agent: 200 · JSON risk score · PAYMENT-RESPONSE (tx id) Svc->>Hedera: HCS x402.settled {path, payer, amount, tx} Agent->>Hedera: HCS x402.paid {url, amount, tx} Agent->>Hedera: HCS agent.decision {verdict, payments} ``` If the upstream data fails (every protocol query errors, or the stream has no source), the handler returns a non-2xx status and the x402 middleware **cancels the payment** — the agent is never charged for nothing. ## What's metered and how much | Endpoint | Price (HBAR; USDC quoted alongside) | Data | |---|---|---| | `GET /v1/whales?protocols=…&minUsd=&lookback=` | `0.01 + 0.005 × protocols` | Largest swaps and LP withdrawals per DEX, one standardized query per protocol | | `GET /v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC` or `?protocol=&pool=` | `0.03 + 0.01 × extra lookback days` | Drain score 0–100 with factor evidence (7d TVL drawdown, 24h withdrawal pressure, withdrawer concentration, abnormal swaps, age) | | `GET /v1/protocol-health?protocol=aave-v3` | `0.02` | Lending stress: utilization, hot markets, liquidations | | `GET /v1/stream/whales?seconds=15..120` | `0.02 per 15 s window` | Server-Sent Events whale wire; re-request to extend = streamed micropayments | | `GET /v1/catalog`, `/.well-known/agent-registration.json`, `/health` | free | Discovery surface (also linked from ENS records) | Prices are computed per request (x402 dynamic pricing), so a one-protocol scan and a four-protocol scan produce different `402` quotes. ## The Graph: what the standard bought us - `packages/shared/src/protocols.ts` — seven protocols, one registry of subgraph IDs from Messari's deployment manifest, all verified at chain head. (Messari's Balancer v2 and PancakeSwap v3 Ethereum subgraphs are currently unhealthy on the network and were left out; re-adding one is a single JSON entry.) - `packages/shared/src/graph.ts` — three query strings (`whales`, `pool-risk`, `lending-health`) serve seven protocols. The only divergence we hit between schema majors is the event actor field (`from` in 1.3, `account { id }` in 4.0), handled by a one-line switch. Pool search uses the standardized `inputTokens_contains` filter with canonical token addresses on every DEX. - `packages/service/src/substreams.ts` — the live wire composes the reusable **`ethereum-common`** Substreams package (`filtered_events` with an `evt_sig:` query string) with the standardized Uniswap v3 subgraph for `lastPriceUSD`. Set `SUBSTREAMS_API_TOKEN` (Pinax or StreamingFast) to enable; without it the stream polls the standardized subgraphs so it is still live data. ## ENSv2 features exercised | Feature | Where | |---|---| | Own **PermissionedRegistry** (UserRegistry proxy via VerifiableFactory) as the subregistry of `rugradar.eth` | `packages/ens/src/deploy-namespace.ts` | | Own **PermissionedResolver** proxy with per-record EAC | same | | **.eth registration** on the ENSv2 ETH Registrar (MockUSDC, commit → 60 s → reveal) | same | | **Expiring** (30 d), **non-transferable** (no `ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN`), **revocable** (`unregister`) service subnames | `register-service.ts`, `revoke-service.ts`, `shared/src/ens.ts` | | **ENSIP-26** agent text records (`agent-context`, `agent-endpoint[x402]`) + namespaced `x402.*` / `hcs.*` / `erc8004.*` keys | `register-service.ts` | | **Enhanced Access Control** delegation of exactly one text key to the service's key (`authorizeTextRoles`), proven live by `packages/ens/src/lib/eac.ts` (CLI and UI button) | `register-service.ts`, `lib/eac.ts` | | **Universal Resolver** resolution and registry walking in the consumer | `packages/agent/src/discovery.ts`, `packages/agent/src/web.ts` | | **Agents as namespaces**: the agent has its own subname (`scout.rugradar.eth`) with its Hedera account and spend-ledger topic | `pnpm ens:register scout --agent` | ## Hedera: payment flow details - Scheme `exact` on `hedera:testnet`, facilitator `https://api.testnet.blocky402.com` (mainnet: `https://api.blocky402.com`). The facilitator acts as fee payer; the agent only needs HBAR for the price. - Two `accepts` per route: HBAR (canonical) and HTS **USDC** (`0.0.429274` testnet). The agent's policy prefers HBAR. - Server `onAfterSettle` hook → `TopicMessageSubmitTransaction` on `HCS_SERVICE_TOPIC_ID` with `{path, payer, amount, asset, settlementTx}`. - Agent decodes `PAYMENT-RESPONSE`, enforces `AGENT_BUDGET_HBAR` *before* signing (reads the `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` quote), mirrors each payment to `HCS_AGENT_TOPIC_ID`, then anchors its final verdict there as well. - `/.well-known/agent-registration.json` is an ERC-8004 registration file (`x402Support: true`); fill `ERC8004_REGISTRY` / `ERC8004_AGENT_ID` after registering with an Identity Registry. - The risk score is a transparent heuristic over standardized fields; every factor prints its evidence so an LP (or an LLM) can disagree with it. Testnet only; nothing here is audited. ## Live deployment (testnets) | What | Where | |---|---| | Service (Render free tier) | `https://rugradar-vibj.onrender.com/v1/catalog` | | ENSv2 namespace `rugradar.eth` (Sepolia) | registered on the ENSv2 ETH Registrar, tx `0x81c5442f…96df` | | Our PermissionedRegistry (UserRegistry proxy) | [`0x8ff7afe6ad9ED3D06caDFD487fdf059c1938Aa36`](https://sepolia.etherscan.io/address/0x8ff7afe6ad9ED3D06caDFD487fdf059c1938Aa36) | | Our PermissionedResolver proxy | [`0x132145725Cf0553E226B9e83C461C5F42250E0Ee`](https://sepolia.etherscan.io/address/0x132145725Cf0553E226B9e83C461C5F42250E0Ee) | | Service name | [`api.rugradar.eth`](https://sepolia.app.ens.domains/api.rugradar.eth) — expiring, non-transferable, `x402.pricing` delegated to `0x129d…9841` | | Agent name | [`scout.rugradar.eth`](https://sepolia.app.ens.domains/scout.rugradar.eth) | | Hedera service account (payTo) | [`0.0.5639476`](https://hashscan.io/testnet/account/0.0.5639476) | | Hedera agent account | [`0.0.10372230`](https://hashscan.io/testnet/account/0.0.10372230) | | HCS settlement audit topic | [`0.0.10372243`](https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10372243) | | HCS agent spend ledger | [`0.0.10372244`](https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10372244) | | Example x402 settlement (0.03 HBAR via Blocky402) | [`0.0.7162784@1788663313.356227872`](https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.7162784%401788663313.356227872) | ## Repository layout ``` packages/shared protocols registry, Graph gateway client + queries, risk scoring, ENSv2 constants/ABIs, HCS helpers packages/service Express + @x402/express on Hedera (Blocky402), metered routes, SSE stream, Substreams wire, ERC-8004 file packages/agent agent loop (OpenAI-compatible API, Qwen 3.8), ENS discovery, paying fetch with budget guard, HCS spend ledger, CLI (src/index.ts), demo UI server + page (src/web.ts, public/index.html), curl demo packages/ens deploy-namespace, register-service, lib/eac (EAC proof), revoke-service, resolve, list (viem, Sepolia) demo.md recording runbook · slides.html: four-slide pitch · hackathon.md: bounty analysis ```
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
## Quickstart

Requirements: Node ≥ 22, pnpm 11, one funded Hedera testnet account from https://portal.hedera.com (ECDSA or ED25519; set `HEDERA_SERVICE_KEY_TYPE`), a Subgraph Studio API key, an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`, `LLM_MODEL`; we use Qwen 3.8), and a Sepolia key with a little ETH for the ENS steps.

```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env        # fill in keys (see comments)

# 0. sanity: the same query across every protocol
pnpm graph:smoke

# 1. Hedera: a separate agent wallet (x402 needs payer ≠ payee), audit topics, optional USDC
pnpm hedera:agent-account    # creates a funded ECDSA account; paste HEDERA_AGENT_* into .env
pnpm hedera:topics           # paste HCS_SERVICE_TOPIC_ID / HCS_AGENT_TOPIC_ID into .env
pnpm hedera:associate-usdc   # optional; HBAR needs no association

# 2. run the paid service
pnpm service                 # http://localhost:4021/v1/catalog

# 3. ENSv2 on Sepolia: namespace, then publish the service + the agent identity
pnpm ens:deploy              # deploys our registry + resolver, registers <ENS_PARENT_LABEL>.eth, writes ens.deployment.json
pnpm ens:register api --url https://<public-url-of-service>
pnpm ens:register scout --agent
pnpm ens:resolve api.rugradar.eth
pnpm ens:list
pnpm ens:service-update api "<new pricing string>"   # EAC demo: the service key may edit only x402.pricing

# 4. pay for one call without the LLM ("curl with a wallet")
pnpm demo:curl "/v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC"

# 5. the agent — CLI or the demo UI
pnpm agent "Is the WETH/USDC pool on Uniswap v3 being drained right now? Should an LP exit?"
pnpm ui                      # http://localhost:3001
```

For a local run before ENS is set up, `SERVICE_URL_OVERRIDE=http://localhost:4021 pnpm demo:curl "/v1/whales?protocols=curve"` skips discovery (the UI honours the same variable).

**Public URL.** The service is a long-lived process (facilitator sync at boot, open Substreams stream, SSE windows up to 120 s), so it does not fit serverless hosting. It runs on Render's free tier at `https://rugradar-vibj.onrender.com` (sleeps after 15 min idle; hit `/health` to wake it). Pushes do not auto-deploy there; run `pnpm render:deploy`. For a quick alternative, `pnpm tunnel` (cloudflared) prints a `https://*.trycloudflare.com` URL; set it as `SERVICE_URL`, restart the service, and republish the records with `pnpm ens:register api --url <url>`.

projects.title: Hadera Code
projects.description: OpenCode overlay for Hedera Harness: idea to dApp, HTS tokens, beta persistent MetaMask for USDC.
projects.project_description: This is a contribution to hedera-dev/hedera-harness (open PR, not merged). The published harness is a long CLI run: you write a PRD and a recipe, then prove the wallet in Playwright Chrome with no MetaMask extension. This branch adds an OpenCode TUI overlay. You describe the dApp in natural language. The orchestrator interviews one question at a time, writes the PRD, generates one work unit, lints, boots next:dev, and walks you to RainbowKit Connect+Send in your own Chrome. Yarn install runs in tui install with no timeout so OpenCode never freezes. Existing HTS tokens (Circle testnet USDC, later any listed token) are looked up, converted via HIP-218, remembered, and baked — GENERATE does not invent a 0x. A beta persistent test wallet (Chromium + MetaMask extension, same profile across runs) is included so token flows can be signed on screen. It is a repeatable test vault, not your personal Chrome. The done bar is still Connect+Send in the human browser.
projects.how_its_made:
Built as an overlay on hedera-harness and sst/opencode, targeting scaffold-hbar (Next.js, RainbowKit, wagmi, Hedera Testnet 296). TypeScript CLI: tui install copies opencode.json, stage agents, slash commands, and a plugin with harness_* tools. Yarn Berry install runs in that terminal with no timeout; OpenCode bash denies yarn install. Hedera Docs MCP (SearchHedera) is first for protocol docs. Issuer token ids are not in that MCP, so harness_tokens does lookup → issuer webfetch → HIP-218 long-zero convert → .harness/tokens.json → bake evm=. OpenZeppelin Solidity MCP stays disabled until Contracts: solidity. Wallet path: RainbowKit in the user's Chrome (done bar). Beta extra: dappwright Chromium with MetaMask, persistent .harness/wallet/chrome-profile, provision on 127.0.0.1 (never paste keys in chat). EVALUATE drives .harness/e2e.json testids so any app's send form works, not only seed /payments. Playwright MCP is forbidden for wallet E2E because it has no extension. Tests cover overlay copy, token registry, UI contract, and yarn-install flags. Local nested dApps are gitignored.
PD: branch feat/hedera-harness-tui

projects.title: Hedera Lab
projects.description: Agent-ready Hedera testing with independent ledger verification, automated repair, and x402.
projects.project_description: Hedera Lab helps developers and AI coding agents test whether their Hedera applications actually do what they are supposed to do. The idea came from a simple problem: an application can look finished and pass its unit tests while still making the wrong transaction. A screen saying “Payment successful” does not prove that the right person received the right amount. We built Hedera Lab on top of Hedera Harness to make independent verification part of the development process. What it does Checks HBAR balances, NFT ownership, token associations and HCS messages. Connects browser actions, such as buying a ticket, to checks of the resulting ledger state. Supports in-memory simulation, a configured Solo local network and Hedera testnet. Produces readable reports showing which checks passed or failed, transaction evidence and cleanup results. Tests failure scenarios involving delayed responses, retries, concurrent requests and uncertain transaction outcomes. How a developer uses it The developer gives their coding agent the Hedera Lab skill and explains the expected behavior. For example: “Alice should receive 0.75 HBAR and Bob should receive 0.25 HBAR.” The skill guides the agent through inspecting the application, connecting its actual business logic and writing the verification files. A guided setup command automates this for supported JavaScript payment functions. Other supported workflows can use custom adapters and scenarios. The expected results come from the developer’s requirements, independently of the application’s output. This prevents the tests from simply repeating the same mistake as the code. When a check fails, the agent can inspect the findings, repair the application and run the same checks again. Optional paid verification We also implemented an x402 service for agents that want to purchase verification from a provider: The user authorizes required checks and spending limits. A purchasing client selects coverage and signs the payment locally. Blocky402 handles payment settlement. A separate worker executes the tests. A dashboard shows the results, payment evidence and actual network costs. This flow has been tested on a private deployment. There is currently no public paid-service endpoint, and the local testing tools do not require payment. What we demonstrated We tested a grant-payment application that passed all four of its ordinary tests despite sending incorrect amounts to recipients. Independent paid testnet verification caught the problem. A coding agent repaired the application, and the next verification passed without changing the approved requirements. That demonstration used a deliberately introduced defect. We also tested real testnet and Solo workflows, transaction recovery after process restarts, and guided onboarding without handwritten Lab files. Our goal is to make it easier to move from “the agent says it works” to clear, repeatable evidence that the application behaves as intended.
projects.how_its_made: We built Hedera Lab on top of Hedera Harness, keeping its code-generation and repair workflow while adding independent application verification. TypeScript and Node.js: Power the CLI, verification API, scenario runner and execution worker. YAML scenarios: Define disposable accounts, transaction steps and expected outcomes. Hiero JavaScript SDK: Executes real HBAR, NFT and HCS operations on Hedera testnet and Solo. Independent checks: Use receipts, account queries and Mirror Node data to verify what happened, rather than trusting the application’s success message. Playwright: Connects real browser actions to ledger checks through an authenticated local bridge. Agent skill and onboarding: Help coding agents generate adapters and verification files from user-approved requirements. JSON transaction plans: Let applications describe their intended operations without running application code inside the signing worker. x402 and Blocky402: Provide optional paid verification, with client-side signing, spending limits and payment settlement. Docker: Separates the private API and execution worker, with restricted resources and the execution key mounted only in the worker. The trickiest part was handling transactions that succeeded even though the client timed out. We added persistent recovery journals and original-transaction lookup, then tested recovery by deliberately killing processes. Hedera’s native services let us test payments, NFT ownership and audit messages without custom contracts for those examples. Solo supported local network testing, and Blocky402 enabled the real paid-request demonstration.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Hedera Lab helps developers and AI coding agents test whether their Hedera applications actually do what they are supposed to do.

The idea came from a simple problem: an application can look finished and pass its unit tests while still making the wrong transaction. A screen saying “Payment successful” does not prove that the right person received the right amount.

We built Hedera Lab on top of Hedera Harness to make independent verification part of the development process.

**What it does**

- Checks HBAR balances, NFT ownership, token associations and HCS messages.
- Connects browser actions, such as buying a ticket, to checks of the resulting ledger state.
- Supports in-memory simulation, a configured Solo local network and Hedera testnet.
- Produces readable reports showing which checks passed or failed, transaction evidence and cleanup results.
- Tests failure scenarios involving delayed responses, retries, concurrent requests and uncertain transaction outcomes.

**How a developer uses it**

The developer gives their coding agent the Hedera Lab skill and explains the expected behavior. For example:

> “Alice should receive 0.75 HBAR and Bob should receive 0.25 HBAR.”

The skill guides the agent through inspecting the application, connecting its actual business logic and writing the verification files. A guided setup command automates this for supported JavaScript payment functions. Other supported workflows can use custom adapters and scenarios.

The expected results come from the developer’s requirements, independently of the application’s output. This prevents the tests from simply repeating the same mistake as the code.

When a check fails, the agent can inspect the findings, repair the application and run the same checks again.

**Optional paid verification**

We also implemented an x402 service for agents that want to purchase verification from a provider:

- The user authorizes required checks and spending limits.
- A purchasing client selects coverage and signs the payment locally.
- Blocky402 handles payment settlement.
- A separate worker executes the tests.
- A dashboard shows the results, payment evidence and actual network costs.

This flow has been tested on a private deployment. There is currently no public paid-service endpoint, and the local testing tools do not require payment.

**What we demonstrated**

We tested a grant-payment application that passed all four of its ordinary tests despite sending incorrect amounts to recipients. Independent paid testnet verification caught the problem. A coding agent repaired the application, and the next verification passed without changing the approved requirements.

That demonstration used a deliberately introduced defect. We also tested real testnet and Solo workflows, transaction recovery after process restarts, and guided onboarding without handwritten Lab files.

Our goal is to make it easier to move from “the agent says it works” to clear, repeatable evidence that the application behaves as intended.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built Hedera Lab on top of Hedera Harness, keeping its code-generation and repair workflow while adding independent application verification.

- **TypeScript and Node.js:** Power the CLI, verification API, scenario runner and execution worker.
- **YAML scenarios:** Define disposable accounts, transaction steps and expected outcomes.
- **Hiero JavaScript SDK:** Executes real HBAR, NFT and HCS operations on Hedera testnet and Solo.
- **Independent checks:** Use receipts, account queries and Mirror Node data to verify what happened, rather than trusting the application’s success message.
- **Playwright:** Connects real browser actions to ledger checks through an authenticated local bridge.
- **Agent skill and onboarding:** Help coding agents generate adapters and verification files from user-approved requirements.
- **JSON transaction plans:** Let applications describe their intended operations without running application code inside the signing worker.
- **x402 and Blocky402:** Provide optional paid verification, with client-side signing, spending limits and payment settlement.
- **Docker:** Separates the private API and execution worker, with restricted resources and the execution key mounted only in the worker.

The trickiest part was handling transactions that succeeded even though the client timed out. We added persistent recovery journals and original-transaction lookup, then tested recovery by deliberately killing processes.

Hedera’s native services let us test payments, NFT ownership and audit messages without custom contracts for those examples. Solo supported local network testing, and Blocky402 enabled the real paid-request demonstration.

projects.title: WEIR
projects.description: Fair launchpad  Infra for  zero-custody presales, unruggable LP, and aut compounding yield staking.
projects.project_description: Weir is a launchpad built for the people who actually show up — not the bots that front-run them. Creators run a backing campaign before trading opens. Backers pledge money that never leaves their own wallet , putting down a 20% deposit as skin in the game. Stick with the pool and you get tokens far below what the public pays, with your deposit returned in full — no racing bots, no gas wars. Walk away and you lose the deposit and your tokens are burned forever, which makes the pool richer for everyone who stayed. After launch, a Uniswap v4 hook takes a cut of every trade and streams it to people who stake the token — real ETH/USDC, not more of the same token, and no impermanent loss. Stakers can opt into auto-compounding, which routes that yield back through 1inch SwapVM to buy and re-stake more of the token. Trading fees become standing buy pressure. And when a pool eventually goes quiet, the fees it earned don't die behind a lock. A prediction market — not a founder's key — decides whether stakers get let out early. The Problem: Launchpads Are Built to Extract, Not to Build Dead Pools Everywhere. Launchpads are littered with abandoned pools where liquidity sits trapped, dead, or rugged.
