Weir is a fair-launch memecoin launchpad built on a real Uniswap v4 hook and the
official 1inch SwapVM router, with no custom SwapVM opcodes. The launch path is a constant-product bonding curve (WeirV2BondingCurve) that gates
trading until a configurable open time and fences off a pool-seed reserve and an
optional backer commitment tranche. Backers commit pre-launch by signing a resting
SwapVM order (InvalidateBit + Deadline + StaticBalances + LimitSwap, byte-identical to
the official InstructionBuilder/MakerTraitsLib encodings) rather than transferring
funds up front — their pledge stays in their own wallet until our registry, acting as
taker, fills it against the official SwapVMRouter at graduation. We also support
Aqua's virtual-balance mode as an alternate authorization path on the same order
bytes, so a pledge can be honored without a signature at all. Graduation is a single atomic transaction: settle commitments through SwapVM, burn
whatever's unfilled, run a seed-preflight, then mint a full-range Uniswap v4 position
that's locked permanently — no external DEX migration. Post-graduation, a singleton
v4 hook (WeirV2MemeHook) intercepts afterSwap on every pool, takes a protocol/creator/
staker fee cut, and sweeps memecoin-denominated fees into quote using the pool's own
liquidity. Stakers can opt into auto-compounding, which routes their accrued reward
back through the same official SwapVM router to buy and restake more of the token —
so protocol fee flow becomes standing on-chain buy pressure with zero custom
infrastructure, just stock SwapVM instructions taker-filled against arbitrary
resting maker strategies. The hackiest part: encoding SwapVM orders deterministically from (campaign, backer,
pledge) instead of storing signed bytecode, so a pledge is rebuilt on-chain at
settlement time and verified purely by balance deltas — success isn't a return value,
it's "did the taker's balance change the way the fill implies."
projects.project_description_markdown:
**Weir is a launchpad built for the people who actually show up — not the bots that front-run them.**

Creators run a backing campaign before trading opens. Backers pledge money that **never leaves their own wallet**, putting down a 20% deposit as skin in the game. Stick with the pool and you get tokens far below what the public pays, with your deposit returned in full — no racing bots, no gas wars. Walk away and you lose the deposit and your tokens are burned forever, which makes the pool richer for everyone who stayed.

After launch, a Uniswap v4 hook takes a cut of every trade and streams it to people who stake the token — real ETH/USDC, not more of the same token, and no impermanent loss. Stakers can opt into auto-compounding, which routes that yield back through 1inch SwapVM to buy and re-stake more of the token. Trading fees become standing buy pressure.

And when a pool eventually goes quiet, the fees it earned don't die behind a lock. A prediction market — not a founder's key — decides whether stakers get let out early.

---

### The Problem: Launchpads Are Built to Extract, Not to Build

1. **Dead Pools Everywhere.** Launchpads are littered with abandoned pools where liquidity sits trapped, dead, or rugged. Nobody can reach it and nothing can be done with it.
2. **Zero Community Incentive.** Retail traders are treated as churn fodder. Long-term holders have no reason to stick around — holding pays nothing.
3. **FOMO Extraction as a Business Model.** Current launchpads only care about squeezing trading velocity out of degens before the coin crashes. The faster it collapses, the faster the next one launches.
4. **The "Big Backers Only" Gate.** MetaDAO and its peers only service big-ticket, institutionally-backed projects with heavy entry barriers. Average or niche creative ideas have nowhere to go.
5. **No Funding for Niche / Startup Ideas.** Creators with genuine ideas or small startups have no bridge between degen meme launchpads on one side and high-barrier venture DAOs on the other.
6. **Fake Social Engagement.** Existing social launch boards run on fake influencer shills with zero accountability. Creators have no way to verify genuine community interest before spending time and money deploying contracts.

The thread connecting all six: **there is no way to prove real commitment before launch, and no reason to stay after it.**

---

### The Breakthrough: Three Things Weir Does Differently

#### 1. Campaigns With Real Skin in the Game — Not Shills

A creator opens a campaign before trading goes live and calls for backers. Open to everyone, or allowlisted — the creator's choice.

To back a pool, you pledge an amount and post a **20% deposit**. The pledge itself stays in your wallet as a signed 1inch SwapVM resting order; only the deposit is escrowed.

- **Stick with the pool** → your order fills at a 20–40% discount to the public opening price and your deposit comes back in full. You never compete with a bot for the entry.
- **Walk away** → your deposit is forfeited and your allocated tokens are **permanently burned**. Supply drops, the forfeited money becomes quote backing everyone else's tokens, and the honest backers split it.

This is what replaces paid shills: **a backer count is a number with money behind it.** And because supply is fixed, more backers means fewer tokens left on the public curve — a lower threshold to graduate, and a faster launch for the creator.

> A failed backing round cannot leave public buyers worse off than no backing round at all.

#### 2. Auto-Compounding Staking — Yield For Coins That Have No Yield

If a token has real utility, it might have a yield strategy. **99% of them don't**, so there's nothing to pay the community with.

Weir generates yield in-house. A singleton Uniswap v4 hook (`WeirV2MemeHook`) intercepts every swap via `afterSwapReturnDelta`, takes a fee cut, and converts memecoin-denominated fees into quote using the pool's own liquidity. Stakers hold the token directly — **real ETH/USDC cashflow, zero impermanent loss.**

Opt into auto-compounding and that yield routes through the official 1inch SwapVM router to buy more of the token and re-stake it, without resetting your lock timer. The effect compounds: staked supply rises, circulating supply falls, and fee flow turns into continuous on-chain buy pressure — market cap, TVL and price all supported by the pool's own trading activity, with no external yield strategy required.

#### 3. Dead Pools: Don't Let the Yield Die With Them

There are hundreds of dead pools across every launchpad. The liquidity sits there, and so do the fees it earned — locked, unreachable, benefiting nobody.

Weir's liquidity is locked permanently by design (that's the anti-rug guarantee — the v4 position NFT goes into `WeirV2LaunchLocker` and there is no withdraw function). But the **accrued fees** shouldn't be hostage to that lock.

So the exit is governed by a market, not a person. Anyone can fund a MetaDAO-style binary LMSR decision market asking one question: *should stakers be allowed to exit early?* If PASS prices above FAIL, `unlockEarlyExit` fires and stakers can burn their stake to claim their share — shrinking supply on the way out. No team key, no multisig, no founder discretion.

> **Where this goes next:** extending the same decision-market machinery from the fee pot to the trapped principal itself — letting holders of a provably dead pool vote to recover the underlying liquidity, not just the yield it generated. That's the roadmap; today's contracts govern the fee pot.

---

### Key Technical Achievements

- **Uniswap v4 Native.** Custom bitmask permissions (`afterSwap: true`, `afterSwapReturnDelta: true`), transient flash accounting in `PoolManager`, internal fee-conversion swaps against pool liquidity, full-range LP via `PositionManager` + `Permit2`, permanent NFT custody in `WeirV2LaunchLocker`.
- **Zero Custom SwapVM Opcodes.** 100% stock 1inch SwapVM (`InvalidateBit`, `Deadline`, `StaticBalances`, `LimitSwap`), byte-identical to the official `InstructionBuilder` encodings. Orders are rebuilt deterministically on-chain from campaign parameters and verified purely by balance deltas. Aqua virtual-balance mode works on the same order bytes with no signature at all.
- **Atomic In-Place Graduation.** Settle commitments → burn what didn't honour → seed the v4 pool, in one transaction. No external DEX migration, no oracle, no window for bots to front-run the transition.
- **Honest Game Theory.** The 20% bond is a hardcoded protocol constant, not a creator knob (creator-set bonds race to zero). An aggregate exposure cap stops a backer pledging 5,000 against 100 of capital across multiple pools — closing the free-option hole that a per-pool bond alone leaves open.

projects.title: ShibbolETH
projects.description: Reference letters that cannot be deleted, written by verified humans, checkable as ENS names.
projects.project_description: ShibbolETH is a risk assessment platform for hiring and cold outreach, built on living references from verified humans. Before you trust a candidate or a counterparty, ask the people who vouch for them, verify at submission time that each is one real human, and set a policy the answer has to pass. In 2025 alone, North Korean operators stole a record $2 billion in crypto, much of it by placing IT workers inside companies through fabricated résumés, purchased identities and references nobody could check. Hiring and cold outreach run on social claims that cost nothing to fabricate and hours to verify, and the recommendations platforms show are free to create, reciprocal by custom, and deletable the moment they age badly. That is not evidence; it is marketing. ShibbolETH is a risk-assessment platform that attacks the other side of the claim: the corroboration. A candidate is vouched for by people who, at the moment of submission, prove they are one real human (World ID Selfie Check), sign under a permanent name of their own ( bob.shibboleth.eth , ENSv2), and put on chain a statement that cannot be deleted, only visibly withdrawn. References are living: the same person can update or revoke, every version stays readable, and the graph of who stands behind whom is public and scored. Trust propagates from verified humans the way the sybil-detection literature prescribes, so a ring of fabricated accounts scores zero and a farm behind one real person is worth one person. Employers and counterparties set policy, not gut feel: a minimum number of live vouches, attested work or platform accounts, a passed Selfie Check, a cap on critical readings, and screening questions the candidate must answer on the record. The signature question in the demo is the DPRK test: "What do you think of Kim Jong Un?", answered as a permanent ENS name under kju-is.shibboleth.eth , which an infiltrator under handler control cannot answer freely. A policy travels in the invite link, and the candidate's page shows whether they pass it, with every field independently resolvable by any ENS client or screening agent, no API of ours required. The attester runs as a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow: identity tokens and signing keys stay inside the enclave, only a signed record leaves. Privy gives every person a wallet they never see. Together this cuts the two riskiest moments in a company's pipeline, the hire and the first reply to a stranger, from "trust the résumé" to "check five verified humans who staked their own name on this person". Anyone can fabricate a résumé. Nobody can fabricate five verified humans who permanently staked their name on having worked with you.
projects.how_its_made: pnpm monorepo, five parts. Contracts (Foundry, Sepolia). Records live in Multipass, a name registry keyed per (domain, id) that verifies a registrar signature on every record. On top sits ENSv2: shibboleth.eth is the only registered name, and one wildcard RootAttestationResolver (ENSIP-10 resolve) answers the whole tree by deriving meaning from the path: <handle> is a person, <writer>.<candidate> a vouch, <handle>.kju-is an answer, <handle>.com.x.www an attested X account, private-www its masked mirror. Every other text key is forwarded to the stock ENSv2 PermissionedResolver; AttestationBridge registers the record and grants the wallet record-level ROLE_SET_TEXT on four profile keys in the same transaction, and writes the letter in that transaction too. AttestationReporter accepts Chainlink Keystone reports from the forwarder. 114 forge tests, 100% line coverage on the resolver. Registrar (pure TypeScript). (idToken, intent, signature, secrets) → { record, signature, viewCode? }. It verifies a Privy identity token (ES256 JWT with linked_accounts) offline, checks the wallet's EIP-712 intent and nonce, derives the record, and for a private account builds a one-time-pad masked name plus a commitment; the view code is HMAC(viewcodeKey, domain ‖ platformSubject), so it is re-derivable and never stored. The same module runs in two hosts. Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. onAttest runs in a Nitro enclave via cre.handlerInTee: secrets by runtime.getSecret, only the Multipass read and the report cross to the DON through runtime.usingTheDons(). A second TEE handler, onDisclose, is the only party that can open a private account for a permitted reader. The account has no deploy access, so we proved the write path with cre workflow simulate --broadcast through the MockKeystoneForwarder: two Sepolia transactions, one public record, one masked, landing through reporter → bridge → Multipass with no key of ours in the path. Hacky and worth noting: the reporter's forwarder is immutable, so a second reporter was deployed pointing at the mock forwarder purely to make the proof real. API (Hono, Node). The relay: same registrar code as the Node fallback, pays gas, submits through the bridge, indexes Multipass into a snapshot, and serves every read. World ID Selfie Check goes here: IDKit challenge signed as the app, proof verified against developer.world.org, nullifier bound to one wallet off chain, humanity record on chain keyed by wallet. The SybilScore is solved over the vouch graph from those proofs, trust-conserving after SybilRank/SybilLimit with EigenTrust-style weights from an LLM "council" that reads each letter as supportive/neutral/critical. Hacky: IDKit hashes a hex-looking signal as bytes, undocumented; we reimplemented hashSignal from idkit-core after every proof was refused. Also Multipass keeps a record's nonce after deletion, so the index remembers deleted nonces and the browser retries once with the number the revert names. Web (Next.js). Privy for login (email, Google, X, LinkedIn, GitHub), embedded wallet signs intents, useIdentityToken feeds the attester. Policies are URL query strings, so an employer's bar travels inside an invite link and different readers apply different standards to the same records. Journeys run in Playwright (174), the API against a docker stack (anvil + deployed contracts + the API image). CI on Forgejo; Coolify deploys both apps.

projects.title: Leverage
projects.description: LP-governed MEV auction hook that returns arbitrage value to affected liquidity providers.
projects.project_description: Levy is an LP-governed MEV auction hook built around a simple idea: liquidity providers should benefit from the value extracted when an AMM’s price becomes stale. AMM pools price assets based on the ratio of their reserves. When the external market price changes, the pool continues quoting its previous price until a trade corrects it. The first arbitrageur to trade against that stale price captures the difference directly from the pool’s reserves creating a recurring loss for LPs. Today, the right to capture that value is typically decided by gas auctions, private mempool access, and low-latency infrastructure. LPs bear the loss but have no say in who captures the opportunity or where the value goes. Levy replaces this race with an on-chain auction. During each epoch, arbitrageurs bid for the exclusive right to trade first against the pool. Instead of the arbitrage profit being silently extracted, the winning bid is distributed to LPs who were in the pool before the epoch began the same LPs who would otherwise have absorbed the loss.
projects.how_its_made: Levy is designed as an LP-governed MEV auction hook for AMM pools. Its core mechanism is organized around epochs: defined time periods during which the right to make the first arbitrage trade against a pool is auctioned on-chain. Rather than allowing arbitrageurs to compete through gas bidding, private order flow, or latency advantages, Levy creates a transparent bidding process for exclusive first-trade access. Arbitrageurs bid for the opportunity to correct a stale pool price after the external market moves. The winning bidder receives the right to execute that first trade for the epoch. The value paid by the winner is not treated as protocol revenue or captured by external infrastructure. It is distributed to liquidity providers who were already providing liquidity before that epoch started. This aligns the economics of arbitrage with the people whose capital is exposed to stale-price losses. The project is built primarily in Solidity, with a Foundry-based smart-contract development setup. The repository also includes tests, deployment scripts, and a frontend integration, allowing the auction-based MEV redistribution concept to be demonstrated as a complete application.

projects.project_description:
Reach is a stablecoin remittance app, you pick an amount, type the receiver's email, hit send. There's no wallet address to copy, no seed phrase to back up, and no separate step to buy gas before you can transact
Logging in with email creates a real wallet through Privy in the background the user never sees it as a "wallet" at all.
you can send to an email that's never touched Reach before. The backend resolves that email through Privy and, if it's genuinely new, pregenerates a real wallet for it right then so funds are already sitting there waiting the first time that person ever logs in.
The receiver gets a push notification the moment funds land, and a full transaction history that merges both Reach-routed sends and plain wallet deposits into one view.
projects.how_its_made:
The contract (Reach.sol, Solidity, Foundry, 30 tests) is a single-transaction payment router deployed and verified on Arc testnet: it pulls the sender's chosen token (USDC or EURC, admin-managed allowlist) and forwards net-of-fee straight to the receiver, with no escrow or claim step. The frontend is a Next.js 16 PWA using Privy for embedded-wallet auth and wagmi/viem for the send transaction, with contract reverts decoded into plain-language errors instead of raw selectors. The backend is Express + SQLite: it indexes the contract's events, resolves emails to wallet addresses via Privy (including pregenerating wallets for brand-new recipients), and sends web-push notifications. The trickiest problem was that Arc's USDC is the native gas token, so its ERC20 Transfer log effectively covers every transaction on the chain scanning it directly to catch plain wallet deposits blew straight through the RPC's per-query result cap. Deposits are instead synced per-address, on demand, from Arc's block explorer API, which already indexes both native sends and ERC20 transfers under one address-scoped endpoint.
I also turned off Privy's own confirmation modal (showWalletUIs: false) since the app already has its own Confirm step showing two separate "please confirm" popups for one send was pure friction, not an extra security boundary.

projects.title: ultratokenizer
projects.description: No proof, no mint. zkPDF in SP1, Groth16 on Hedera, and a receipt anyone can recheck offline.
projects.project_description:
Ultratokenizer is a token engine that physically cannot mint without a zero-knowledge proof that a real, signed document authorizes it. Today, tokenizing a real-world asset means trusting an operator's word that the paperwork exists. Ultratokenizer removes the word. The holder's signed PDF certificate never leaves their browser. A zkVM program verifies the RSA-2048/SHA-256 signature over the complete document revision, extracts the authorized quantity and holder, and proves the whole thing bound to one exact minting request. What reaches the chain is 224 bytes of public output and a Groth16 proof. The document does not. The Gate is the only authority. It re-derives the request digest in Solidity, checks the Groth16 proof against a registered program key, checks the holder's EIP-712 signature, checks a separate issuer permit, checks that the institution reserved exactly this quantity against a governed backing ceiling, burns a single-use claim identifier, and only then mints through a registered adapter. Any one failure reverts everything. There is no administrative mint function. The governor cannot bypass the proof, because no such path exists in the code. Every mint produces a receipt an outsider can recheck offline against their own trust pins, without our RPC, our site, or our word. Live on Hedera testnet right now, unpaused, with the real SP1 Groth16 verifier registered. Check it yourself before reading another line: Gate      0xE1e3a133335dC0FEeB20397163c16E69F74919e3
Verifier  0xC96613d470494347586839B275bFDc56E978c5Be
Token     0xa77e8a964606CE6994bd8d876445218dA3f9E64F  (ATS, 3 decimals, 1 mg)
Issuer    ERC-8004 agent #116 on 0x8004A818BFB912233c491871b3d84c89A494BD9e The verifier's on-chain runtime bytecode hashes to 0xebc2d3ce..., byte-identical to the SP1 v6.1.0 Groth16 verifier vendored in the repo. It is not a mock. What is honest about the current state: the source profile authenticates a synthetic, self-signed certificate capsule embedded in the signed PDF. The signature verification is real cryptography on a real PDF structure; the claim fields come from a fixture rather than a bank's live format. A production institution profile needs its own parser and its own program identity, and the Gate is built so that swapping it is a governed, versioned registry action rather than a code change.
projects.how_its_made: The spine is one canonical EIP-712 issuance request, and the same digest is computed independently in three languages that must agree. TypeScript (viem) builds and validates it. Rust recomputes it from scratch inside the SP1 guest with tiny-keccak, sharing no code with the TypeScript. Solidity re-derives it a third time in RequestHash.sol. A parity harness diffs all three across 64 adversarial cases -- non-canonical decimals, mixed-case checksums, boundary integers -- and CI fails if any disagree. Changing one field means editing three implementations and a Solidity ABI test, by design. zkPDF / SP1. The guest runs a strict PDF coverage parser before any crypto: it requires exactly one /ByteRange and one /Contents, requires the signed ranges to cover the entire supplied revision, and requires the excluded gap to be exactly a hex-string Contents value -- no appended revisions, no second signature, no arbitrary unsigned object. It then verifies an RSA-2048/SHA-256 CMS signature and derives the signer fingerprint from the canonical SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER, so a key embedded in the document is never its own authority. Output is 224 bytes of ABI-encoded public values decoded strictly on-chain. The Gate (Solidity 0.8.30, non-upgradeable, Foundry). Five append-only registries -- issuer keys, programs, source keys, policies, rights -- each with permanent revocation and no rewrite path. Replay protection runs across five independent namespaces: request digest, request ID, claim usage ID, holder nonce, permit nonce. Backing is real accounting: a reservation moves capacity into pending, a mint moves it pending to outstanding, and governance cannot lower the ceiling below live exposure. Signature checking supports EIP-1271 contract wallets and enforces low-s. Hedera ATS. The token is an Asset Tokenization Studio diamond. The mint adapter pins 15 runtime code hashes -- ten facets, four linked libraries, one resolver -- and re-checks every one immediately before and immediately after the mint, then asserts exact totalSupply and balance deltas. If any pinned contract changed mid-transaction, the mint reverts. We also built a native HTS adapter that creates a zero-supply token with a single contract-ID supply key and no admin key. ERC-8004 for identity only. The registry supplies issuer attribution and nothing else. We do not use reputation or validation -- those words appear nowhere in the source. The app reads a published index, then re-derives every claim from the Gate itself. A registry entry is attribution, not authorization. The hacky part worth mentioning: the synthetic claim capsule sits immediately after the PDF header, and we can prove it is inside the signed region without parsing PDF objects at all. The coverage parser requires the unsigned gap to begin with '<', and the capsule region contains no '<' byte, so the gap can only start after it. That turns a structural argument into an arithmetic one the zkVM can check cheaply. Polyglot monorepo, no workspace tool: five npm lockfiles, one Cargo workspace plus isolated crates, Foundry plus a separately compiled ATS package with checksum-locked solc. Risky surfaces get their own lockfile so a compromise there cannot reach the main install. Gates: 72 Foundry tests, 265 issuance, 225 web, 166 across domain and audit and institution, 64 parity cases, plus a hygiene check that rejects secrets and absolute paths in tracked files and commit messages.

projects.title: HarvestFi
projects.description: HarvestFi: Tokenized harvest forwards unlocking DeFi capital for Ugandan farmers
projects.project_description:
The Problem
Smallholder farmers in Uganda produce high-value cash crops like coffee, vanilla, and maize, but face a critical liquidity trap. Lacking access to traditional bank credit, they are forced to sell their harvest immediately at the time of harvest when market prices are at their lowest, just to cover immediate living and farming expenses. Meanwhile, global impact investors and DeFi users seek real-world yield but lack transparent, accessible, and trustless avenues to deploy capital directly into emerging market agriculture.
The Solution
HarvestFi bridges this gap by tokenizing future agricultural harvests into Real World Assets (RWAs). We enable farming cooperatives to issue "Harvest Forward Contracts" on-chain. These contracts are funded upfront by global investors using stablecoins (USDC), providing farmers with the working capital they need during the growing season. In return, investors receive a yield-bearing token (e.g., hCOFFEE) that is redeemed for a premium once the physical crop is delivered and sold to a verified off-taker.
How It Works
The Farmer (Invisible Web3): A cooperative in Uganda uses a simple WhatsApp bot to declare their expected yield (e.g., 1,000kg of Arabica coffee). Using Account Abstraction (ERC-4337), the backend creates a smart wallet for them in the background—no seed phrases or complex crypto knowledge required. They can even upload geotagged photos of their crop via WhatsApp, which are stored on IPFS as immutable proof of the asset.
The Investor (DeFi Yield): Global investors browse a sleek Next.js dashboard, review the IPFS-backed farm data, and fund the contract with USDC. Once the funding goal is met, the smart contract instantly routes the USDC to the cooperative's local mobile money wallet (MTN/Airtel) via a fiat off-ramp integration.
The Settlement (Trustless Execution): At harvest, the verified off-taker (e.g., a local coffee exporter) purchases the physical crop and deposits the final payment into the smart contract. The contract automatically burns the harvest tokens and distributes the principal plus the agreed-upon yield proportionally to the investors' wallets.
projects.how_its_made:
Architecture & Core Technologies
HarvestFi is a full-stack decentralized application bridging traditional agriculture with DeFi. The architecture is divided into three layers: On-chain smart contracts, a Next.js investor dashboard, and a Node.js WhatsApp backend for farmers.
Smart Contracts (Base & Foundry)
We built the core protocol using Solidity, tested rigorously with Foundry for fast, reliable execution. We deployed to Base (our L2 partner) because its low gas fees and native USDC integration are critical for micro-transactions in emerging markets. The core HarvestPool contract utilizes OpenZeppelin’s ERC20 and ERC20Permit standards to mint yield-bearing harvest tokens and handle gasless approvals, allowing investors to fund contracts without holding ETH for gas.
Frontend & Storage (Next.js, Privy, & Pinata)
The investor dashboard is built with Next.js and Tailwind CSS. We heavily leveraged Privy (partner tech) to implement Account Abstraction (ERC-4337). Privy allowed us to sponsor gas fees and enable social logins, completely abstracting the blockchain for the end user. For the Real World Asset (RWA) verification, we integrated Pinata (partner tech) to pin geotagged crop photos and cooperative documents to IPFS. The resulting Content Identifiers (CIDs) are stored directly in the smart contract, providing immutable, trustless proof of the underlying physical asset.
The "Hacky" & Notable: The WhatsApp-to-Blockchain Bridge
The most notable (and slightly hacky) piece of the project is how we solved the farmer UX. Smallholder farmers in Uganda do not use dApp browsers; they use WhatsApp. Instead of forcing them to download a wallet, we built a Node.js backend integrated with the Twilio WhatsApp API.
When a farmer sends a text or voice note like "I have 500kg of coffee ready in 60 days", our backend parses the intent using basic NLP. It then generates an EIP-712 typed data payload and uses a backend relayer to execute the transaction on their behalf via Privy. To the farmer, it’s just a chat interface; to the blockchain, it’s a fully signed, gasless smart contract interaction. We essentially turned a WhatsApp chat into a Web3 wallet.
Closing the Loop (Mock Off-Ramp)
To demonstrate the full financial loop during the hackathon, we built a mock API endpoint simulating a Mobile Money (MTN MoMo/Airtel) fiat off-ramp. This shows judges exactly how the USDC released by the smart contract upon settlement would instantly convert to Ugandan Shillings (UGX) and land directly in the farmer's local mobile money wallet, completing the bridge between DeFi and the real-world economy.

projects.title: LegitMate
projects.description: One click deploy specialized agents pre-configured with relevant skills, tools and plugins on cloud.
projects.project_description: LegitMate turns a specialist brief into a configured, owned Hermes workspace. A user chooses one of 279 Agency specialists, reviews its identity files, selects an approved model and capabilities, deploys the workspace, and verifies that the intended configuration reached the running instance.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, Shadcn, and Base UI. It gives people one clear five-step flow: search 279 Agency specialists, inspect the chosen profile, pick a model, add approved capabilities, and review the exact configuration before deploying. Agent37 handles the infrastructure. LegitMate provisions an isolated Hermes workspace, writes the selected SOUL.md, USER.md, AGENTS.md, default skills, plug-ins and runtime configuration to fixed server-owned paths. Users can reopen their owned instances and access chat, terminal, files, integrations, settings, lifecycle controls, and the Hermes dashboard. LLM can be API or BYOK (Bring your own Key and base url) Privy provides authentication and the embedded wallet identity used to scope every instance and action to its owner. The browser never supplies a trusted user ID, and secrets stay on the server. Funding and withdrawals are deliberately disabled unless the chain, asset, recipient, and production policy are explicitly configured. The Graph gives deployed specialists live Uniswap V3 market data with block-level source details, TVL, volume, and pool evidence. The agent’s analysis is shown beside that evidence instead of presenting an uncited AI answer. Surplus model discovery also runs server-side, so available models can be added without exposing provider credentials; the default Hermes models remain available if Surplus is not configured. The hackiest useful part is launch reconciliation. Agent37 can finish creating a workspace after a reverse proxy times out, so I attach a client request ID, search only the authenticated owner’s instances, and resume verification instead of blindly creating a duplicate. I also added a server-owned, tool-disabled readiness task so the product can prove the deployed specialist actually responds without accepting arbitrary prompts or commands. Everything runs on a VPS behind Nginx and Cloudflare, with GitHub Actions deploying pushes to main. Vitest, Playwright, TypeScript, ESLint, production builds, configuration receipts, and live health checks back the release. The result is not another agent picker or a mock dashboard. It is a practical way to choose specialist expertise, deploy it into infrastructure you own, and verify what actually landed.

projects.title: NULL
projects.description: Private distribution infrastructure for Ethereum. Distribute value, reveal nothing.
projects.project_description: A salary should arrive in someone's account without turning their income into a public spectator sport. On transparent blockchains, recurring payouts expose far more than transaction amounts: exact salaries, contractor rates, organizational hierarchies, and commercial relationships become permanently readable by anyone. Businesses require verifiable, audit-ready financial records. Contributors deserve personal financial privacy. NULL makes it possible to have both. NULL is an embeddable TypeScript toolkit and protocol that brings private, ENS-native payouts to Ethereum, with payroll and grant disbursements as its flagship use case. Instead of locking teams into a walled garden, NULL is built as an open developer toolkit. Available as an MIT-licensed npm package (@samarth208p/null-payouts), developers can embed private payouts directly into their own payroll platforms, DAO tooling, and enterprise treasury interfaces. For an organization, sending funds feels as intuitive as consumer banking: enter ENS names and amounts (manually or via CSV), verify the recipients, and authorize the payout. Each ENS name resolves to an onchain public encryption profile used to prepare that recipient's private allocation. The sender pays a human-readable ENS name; the recipient chooses their private exit wallet later. Behind the scenes, NULL compiles payments into funded distributions of eight fixed-size encrypted slots, padding unused positions so observers cannot infer team sizes or transaction structures. Larger rosters execute smoothly as consecutive batches with independent approvals, cryptographic receipts, and real-time progress tracking. Zero-knowledge proofs guarantee value conservation and authorization without ever exposing a plaintext payroll roster on chain. For recipients, NULL functions like a private payment inbox. Once users back up their local cryptographic keys and link their ENSv2 name, their browser scans public encrypted events. Recipients generate Noir UltraHonk zero-knowledge proofs to claim their funds against a global accumulator, completely hiding which batch their payout came from. Our latest deployment introduces private partial withdrawals: recipients can withdraw any exact amount to a fresh wallet while rolling the remainder into a newly generated private note. NULL is an unaudited testnet prototype on Sepolia. Senders naturally know what they paid, while deposits, exits, and ENS registrations remain public onchain events. Within those clear, practical boundaries, NULL eliminates public payroll surveillance on Ethereum.
projects.how_its_made: We built NULL as a high-performance TypeScript monorepo uniting a React and Vite reference application, modular SDK packages, Solidity smart contracts, five Noir zero-knowledge circuits, and dedicated services for governance and confidential compute. Our defining architectural decision was to build NULL from the ground up as an embeddable engine. The core SDK powers both external developer integrations and our reference web app, sharing a unified pipeline for name resolution, batch encryption, proving, and transaction reconciliation. ENSv2 serves as our identity and access-control backbone. Senders pay human-readable ENS names rather than unwieldy raw public keys. We engineered five specialized UltraHonk circuits on Ethereum Sepolia: shield, create_distribution, claim, withdraw, and withdraw_partial. Poseidon commitment trees track notes and distributions. projects.project_description_markdown:
A salary should arrive in someone's account without turning their income into a public spectator sport.

On transparent blockchains, recurring payouts expose far more than transaction amounts: exact salaries, contractor rates, organizational hierarchies, and commercial relationships become permanently readable by anyone. Businesses require verifiable, audit-ready financial records. Contributors deserve personal financial privacy. NULL makes it possible to have both.

NULL is an embeddable TypeScript toolkit and protocol that brings private, ENS-native payouts to Ethereum, with payroll and grant disbursements as its flagship use case. Instead of locking teams into a walled garden, NULL is built as an open developer toolkit. Available as an MIT-licensed npm package (@samarth208p/null-payouts), developers can embed private payouts directly into their own payroll platforms, DAO tooling, and enterprise treasury interfaces.

For an organization, sending funds feels as intuitive as consumer banking: enter ENS names and amounts (manually or via CSV), verify the recipients, and authorize the payout. Each ENS name resolves to an onchain public encryption profile used to prepare that recipient's private allocation. The sender pays a human-readable ENS name; the recipient chooses their private exit wallet later.

Behind the scenes, NULL compiles payments into funded distributions of eight fixed-size encrypted slots, padding unused positions so observers cannot infer team sizes or transaction structures. Larger rosters execute smoothly as consecutive batches with independent approvals, cryptographic receipts, and real-time progress tracking. Zero-knowledge proofs guarantee value conservation and authorization without ever exposing a plaintext payroll roster on chain.

For recipients, NULL functions like a private payment inbox. Once users back up their local cryptographic keys and link their ENSv2 name, their browser scans public encrypted events. Recipients generate Noir UltraHonk zero-knowledge proofs to claim their funds against a global accumulator, completely hiding which batch their payout came from.

Our latest deployment introduces private partial withdrawals: recipients can withdraw any exact amount to a fresh wallet while rolling the remainder into a newly generated private note.

NULL is an unaudited testnet prototype on Sepolia. Senders naturally know what they paid, while deposits, exits, and ENS registrations remain public onchain events. Within those clear, practical boundaries, NULL eliminates public payroll surveillance on Ethereum.

projects.title: chapter2
projects.description: Chapter 2 is a safety and approval system for crypto wallets controlled by AI bots
projects.project_description: As organizations and DAOs delegate real financial operations to autonomous AI agents such as paying for compute, data feeds, and service bills they face a dangerous all-or-nothing dilemma. AI models are non-deterministic, vulnerable to prompt injections, logic loops, and hallucinations. Because blockchain transactions are final and irreversible, giving an AI agent direct access to a treasury wallet means a single compromised instruction or software bug can instantly drain millions of dollars with zero recourse. Conversely, forcing humans to manually review and approve every single micro-payment creates an operational bottleneck that destroys the speed and autonomy of AI agents entirely. Chapter 2 solves this by establishing bounded autonomy through an asymmetric control system. Rather than treating wallet access as all-or-nothing, the system splits transactions into distinct risk tiers. Routine micro-payments, such as x402 web resource payments, proceed automatically without human delays, while any transaction that exceeds spending limits, sends funds to untrusted addresses, or shows anomalous intent is immediately halted for human sign-off. The platform coordinates this across an Ethereum and Base Sepolia smart contract foundation, a NestJS supervisory backend for policy checks and injection filtering, Privy and World ID for agent identity and human personhood verification, Flutter for mobile monitoring, and Ledger for hardware authorization. Smart contracts are essential because security guarantees cannot depend solely on off-chain servers that could crash, misconfigure, or suffer unauthorized tampering. Chapter 2 implements a custom transaction guard on Gnosis Safe that sits directly in the blockchain execution path. The contract enforces dual execution routes. Under the autonomous route, the contract verifies mathematical spending caps, including single-transaction limits and rolling 24-hour budgets, while strictly prohibiting administrative or contract-upgrade calls. If an action breaches these parameters, the smart contract immediately reverts the transaction unless it enters the human-approved route, which requires a valid EIP-712 cryptographic signature from the human owner. Mobile phones serve as the primary operational interface because autonomous AI agents operate around the clock, requiring immediate, portable oversight. When an agent attempts an action that exceeds its autonomous allowance, the human supervisor receives an instant push notification on their phone. Crucially, modern mobile devices provide hardware-isolated security environments, such as Apple's Secure Enclave on iOS and StrongBox Keystore on Android. Chapter 2 utilizes these dedicated hardware chips to store human authorization keys, gating every high-value approval behind native biometrics like Face ID or fingerprint scanning. This ensures that no software-level exploit on the backend can forge human approvals without physical biometric authorization. Ledger hardware wallets provide the final, highest tier of physical protection for high-value disbursements and core governance changes. While mobile biometrics handle daily operational alerts, high-value treasury reserves require true cold-storage isolation where private keys never enter internet-connected memory. Ledger devices support EIP-712 clear-signing, rendering the exact token, amount, recipient address, and stated purpose on an un-hackable, physical device screen. This prevents blind-signing attacks and gives human custodians ultimate, uncompromised physical authority over the treasury.
projects.how_its_made: Chapter 2 was built as a multi-tier monorepo designed to connect on-chain smart contracts, an event-driven supervisory backend, native mobile security hardware, and a cross-platform mobile client into a cohesive execution loop. The core protocol layer is written in Solidity using Foundry and deployed on Base Sepolia. At the center of the on-chain architecture is Chapter2Guard, a smart contract implementing the Gnosis Safe transaction guard interface. The contract acts as an immutable checkpoint that inspects all transaction calldata in real time, calculating rolling twenty-four-hour cumulative spend totals, checking single-transaction ceilings, and recovering EIP-712 cryptographic signatures directly in the pre-execution hook. The orchestration and policy logic are implemented in a NestJS backend written in TypeScript, using Ethers.js and Viem for on-chain interactions. When an autonomous agent attempts an action, such as buying server compute or paying an x402 HTTP resource fee, the backend intercepts the proposal before it touches the blockchain. The request passes through an intake pipeline that performs adversarial prompt-injection classification, semantic intent verification, and deterministic mandate validation. To prevent race conditions and double-spending across multiple concurrent agents, an atomic reservation engine locks required token amounts in memory. If an action is within safe spending caps, the agent submits it directly through the autonomous path on the Gnosis Safe. If the action exceeds limits or attempts an unapproved interaction, the backend serializes the request into an EIP-712 typed data payload and pushes an escalation event over a real-time WebSocket gateway. Partner technologies play a foundational role in enabling each layer of this architecture. Base Sepolia provides the low-latency, sub-cent transaction environment necessary for autonomous micro-disbursements and continuous on-chain guard checks. Gnosis Safe serves as the institutional treasury base, allowing us to enforce spending policies and signature thresholds at the EVM level without altering core Safe logic. World ID is integrated using proof-of-personhood verification, cryptographically binding every autonomous agent to a verified human principal to eliminate Sybil bot manipulation. Privy provides the agent key lifecycle and embedded wallet provisioning, authenticating agent owners through verified bearer tokens. Ledger hardware wallets and the Ledger Key Ring protocol provide physical cold-storage isolation, enabling EIP-712 clear-signing on device screens to neutralize blind-signing exploits. Furthermore, the x402 protocol enables standardized machine-to-machine HTTP micropayments, allowing agents to pay for live API endpoints and compute resources with verifiable cryptographic payment headers. The mobile command center is built in Flutter using the BLoC state management pattern, connecting directly to the backend WebSocket stream. To bridge the Flutter client to the device's physical security hardware, custom native modules were written in Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. These modules interface directly with Apple's Secure Enclave and Android's StrongBox Keystore. When an escalated transaction arrives, the human supervisor reviews the decoded parameters—recipient address, token type, amount, and business rationale—and authorizes the payment using Face ID or fingerprint biometrics. The native security module generates an EIP-712 signature directly inside the hardware enclave without exposing the private key to application memory, and the signed transaction is dispatched to the Gnosis Safe where Chapter2Guard validates the human signature on-chain. Several notable engineering challenges and clever workarounds were implemented during development. Inside Chapter2Guard, we built custom calldata parsers directly in Solidity to dynamically extract ERC-20 transfer targets and amounts from raw bytes during the pre-execution hook, allowing the contract to distinguish between autonomous agent micro-disbursements and human-signed multisig actions on the fly. To solve concurrency bottlenecks across fast-acting agents, we built an in-memory atomic reservation lock synchronized with on-chain twenty-four-hour timestamp windows, preventing parallel agents from exceeding daily limits through burst transactions. Additionally, we created a native mobile bridge that formats structured EIP-712 domain separators and typed schemas directly within hardware keystores, enabling biometric unlocks to generate Ethereum-compatible signatures without key leakage. Finally, for local agent tooling, we built a zero-plaintext subprocess adapter for the Ledger Key Ring CLI that passes encrypted payloads through memory buffers without writing plaintext keys or seed phrases to disk.

projects.title: MIRAGE
projects.description: Evidence before allocation: oracle checks, accounting consistency and Uniswap exit quotes
projects.project_description: An attractive lending rate does not tell an allocator whether its next market deserves a deposit. MIRAGE adds that missing decision step. Before USDC enters a Morpho Blue market, it checks available liquidity, the configured oracle, and a specified collateral sale against independent Uniswap prices and quotes. The Graph supplies live market discovery. MIRAGE turns those market IDs into a report with exact Ethereum calls, then applies the report to our existing allocation policy. Users can inspect the evidence, change the proposed amount, check another market, and compare the original decision with the admission gate. The workbench opens on 47 of those markets: every market that passed, plus the largest refusals. A market is refused when evidence is missing, when a check fails, or simply when its own supply is smaller than the entry it was offered. A wstETH example shows why route selection matters: the same input quotes about 5,928 USDC directly and 10,008 USDC through WETH. Its exit check passes after comparison; its unsupported oracle remains visible. Every result names its block, amount and coverage. Beyond the workbench set, we published all three check groups for all 697 Graph-discovered USDC markets at block 25938815, for a 10000 USDC scenario. The aggregate is 11 PASS, 95 BLOCK and 591 INSUFFICIENT. A market whose own supply is smaller than the proposed entry is refused whatever its other checks returned. Complete collection includes unavailable evidence; it is not a claim that every market can be assessed or admitted. The original snapshot, corrected diagnostics and audit records are public and can be replayed offline.
projects.how_its_made: MIRAGE extends our existing open-source USDC allocator and reuses the MIT-licensed EVM bytecode extractor from our second project, revert.pro. The original T1 decision policy still proposes an allocation. A new admission wrapper evaluates the market evidence and can veto that proposal when checks fail, are incomplete, or do not cover the proposed amount. This repository also carries our earlier MCDM allocator research, so its first commit predates the event. All MIRAGE code sits in mirage/ and contracts/: the first commit under mirage/ is 9 September 2026, the first under contracts/ is 13 September 2026, both inside the hacking window. The pre-existing part is the T1 policy being wrapped, which is unchanged and still makes the original proposal. A deployed Subgraph Studio subgraph indexes Morpho Blue CreateMarket events. Python discovers USDC markets at a pinned block hash, then makes individual RPC reads of market state, oracle contracts and interest-rate models. Supported oracle templates use factory membership, configuration getters and sampled historical prices. Unsupported bytecode goes through the existing 70-feature extractor for structural diagnostics. Uniswap v3 supplies a geometric TWAP and QuoterV2 sale simulations. MIRAGE compares direct and WETH routes with exactly the same collateral input, preserving both results and their raw calls. Offline replay rebuilds derived values from those calls. A Python server exposes the interactive workbench, evidence inspection and original-policy comparison. For the original frozen four-market capture, we independently reread 185 distinct contract calls and eight runtime-code reads through each of two RPC providers; all matched. Two small Sepolia contracts close the loop. MirageGate (0xe1b9031EeF64e376c37B4e3E849B35424f647901) records each admission decision on chain and prices it against the Chainlink ETH/USD feed through AggregatorV3Interface, inlined rather than imported. It refuses to record when the round is incomplete, the answer is not positive, or the update is older than the configured maximum age. ExecutionGuard is the reference consumer: its enter reverts unless the gate holds a fresh ALLOW for that exact market and amount, so an admission that was never granted cannot be spent. The separate full-universe capture covers all 697 discovered markets at block 25938815. Independent accounting and Uniswap calculations checked the saved raw observations, and expected exit outcomes matched production for every market. Both original and derived snapshots replayed successfully; the diagnostic migration preserved raw evidence, finding codes, severities and rates. These are offline checks, not a second-provider verification of the full universe. An optional stdio MCP server uses the official Python SDK to expose three reusable tools: get_saved_report, inspect_market, and preview_saved_allocation. An official SDK client successfully called all three, including a live Graph-to-RPC inspection of a PAXG market at block 25938274. The bundled client chooses its cases from the report the server just returned rather than from pinned market IDs, so the demonstration follows whichever evidence ships. AI agents can consume the same structured evidence and allocation comparison as the workbench. Findings are computed by explicit rules; no LLM or ML safety score decides admission.

projects.title: horofox
projects.description: An agent that cannot afford to answer you — until it earns the fee itself.
projects.project_description: CONTINUITY TRACK — DISCLOSURE UP FRONT. This project did not start from zero on day one, and the commit history says so plainly. The repository's first commit is 2026-08-31, four days before ETHOnline opened (2026-09-04 05:00 UTC). As of submission, 23 of 41 commits predate the event and 18 were made during it. The pre-event work is the trading agent and the self-funding ledger. Everything that makes this an ETHOnline submission was built during the event and is visible in git log from 2026-09-04 onward: the x402 payment layer on Hedera, the live paid production endpoint, the settled on-chain payments, and the demo. A commit dated 2026-09-04 in this repo is itself the written disclosure of the above. Nothing is hidden from the log; please read it. Every agent-payment project I could find solves one half of the problem: spending. Budgets, caps, allowances — how to stop an agent from spending too much. But an agent that can only spend is an agent on an allowance. Somebody else funds it. horofox closes the other half: it earns the money it spends, and until it has earned, it cannot answer you. The loop, end to end: A user asks a question. The agent checks its own quota ledger, finds zero credits, and refuses. That refusal is the production code path, not a mock. It earns. Every trade the agent routes carries a Hyperliquid builder code, and 0.1% of that flow accrues to us on-chain. No token minted, no fee invented — Hyperliquid pays it at the protocol level, so no rival can waive it to zero to squeeze us out. The fee converts into inference credit through an idempotent ledger. Settle twice and the second call grants zero, because the ledger already counted that money. To answer, the agent needs market data it does not have — so it buys it. x402 v2, exact scheme, on Hedera. It meets a 402, reads the requirements from the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, signs a Hedera transaction and settles. The facilitator co-signs and pays the gas, so the agent never has to hold HBAR. Now it answers, and one credit is consumed. This is live, not a mock. Real USDC has moved on Hedera testnet from the agent's account (0.0.10503338) into the service's (0.0.10503359), settling against the production endpoint at horofox.com — which returns a real, payable 402 to anyone who calls it. The data itself is worth paying for: Hyperliquid HIP-3 dexes carry tokenized equities, indices and pre-IPO markets that most price APIs do not list at all. These are perpetual futures, not shares — the service says so in its own llms.txt rather than letting an agent assume otherwise. One part of the loop is simulated, and the demo prints that on screen while it runs: registering a builder code requires a 100 USDC deposit in a Hyperliquid perps account, which has not been made, so the fee figure is injected into the real code path. Everything else — the refusal, the conversion, the payment, the answer — actually happens.

CONTINUITY TRACK — DISCLOSURE UP FRONT. This project did not start from zero on day one, and the commit history says so plainly. The repository's first commit is 2026-08-31, four days before ETHOnline opened (2026-09-04 05:00 UTC). As of submission, 23 of 41 commits predate the event and 18 were made during it. The pre-event work is the trading agent and the self-funding ledger. Everything that makes this an ETHOnline submission was built during the event and is visible in `git log` from 2026-09-04 onward: the x402 payment layer on Hedera, the live paid production endpoint, the settled on-chain payments, and the demo. A commit dated 2026-09-04 in this repo is itself the written disclosure of the above. Nothing is hidden from the log; please read it.

Every agent-payment project I could find solves one half of the problem: spending. Budgets, caps, allowances — how to stop an agent from spending too much. But an agent that can only spend is an agent on an allowance. Somebody else funds it. horofox closes the other half: it earns the money it spends, and until it has earned, it cannot answer you.

The loop, end to end:

1. A user asks a question. The agent checks its own quota ledger, finds zero credits, and refuses. That refusal is the production code path, not a mock.
2. It earns. Every trade the agent routes carries a Hyperliquid builder code, and 0.1% of that flow accrues to us on-chain. No token minted, no fee invented — Hyperliquid pays it at the protocol level, so no rival can waive it to zero to squeeze us out.
3. The fee converts into inference credit through an idempotent ledger. Settle twice and the second call grants zero, because the ledger already counted that money.
4. To answer, the agent needs market data it does not have — so it buys it. x402 v2, exact scheme, on Hedera. It meets a 402, reads the requirements from the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, signs a Hedera transaction and settles. The facilitator co-signs and pays the gas, so the agent never has to hold HBAR.
5. Now it answers, and one credit is consumed.

This is live, not a mock. Real USDC has moved on Hedera testnet from the agent's account (0.0.10503338) into the service's (0.0.10503359), settling against the production endpoint at horofox.com — which returns a real, payable 402 to anyone who calls it.

The data itself is worth paying for: Hyperliquid HIP-3 dexes carry tokenized equities, indices and pre-IPO markets that most price APIs do not list at all. These are perpetual futures, not shares — the service says so in its own llms.txt rather than letting an agent assume otherwise.

One part of the loop is simulated, and the demo prints that on screen while it runs: registering a builder code requires a 100 USDC deposit in a Hyperliquid perps account, which has not been made, so the fee figure is injected into the real code path. Everything else — the refusal, the conversion, the payment, the answer — actually happens.

projects.title: Turnstile
projects.description: Pay-per-call onchain analysis for AI agents. Sell the answer, keep the method.
projects.project_description: Turnstile is a marketplace where AI agents buy and sell onchain analysis one call at a time. A seller publishes an ENS name whose records are the offer: the price, the chains it accepts payment on, and the endpoint to call. A buyer's agent finds the seller, reads that price straight from the chain, calls the endpoint, gets an HTTP 402 back asking for payment, pays over x402 on Hedera or in USDC on Arc, and receives the answer. The agent spends from a wallet with a limit it can't raise on its own, and the premium scorer is built to run inside a Chainlink CRE enclave, so selling the answer doesn't mean giving away how you got it. The first seller is a Uniswap liquidity analyst powered by The Graph.
projects.how_its_made: The Graph is the data layer, twice. The analyst reads a Messari-schema Uniswap v3 subgraph I deployed to Subgraph Studio, through Subgraph MCP. Adopting Messari's schema instead of inventing my own meant the scoring code talks to standard entities, so any conformant AMM subgraph works as a subject. The other half is a Substreams module in Rust that normalizes ERC-8004 agent registrations across four networks. That's what fills the market page with 197 real agents. Only one of them publishes a price you can actually read, which is kind of the whole point. Payments go through a small PaymentRail interface with four methods, and the seller never knows which chain paid. I enforced that with a test that fails the build if any file on the payment path so much as mentions a chain. Hedera settles over x402 through Blocky402, and every sale drops a receipt on an HCS topic anyone can read. Arc settles USDC through Circle Gateway nanopayments, which batch sub-cent calls into one transaction. The agent wallet signs EIP-3009 authorizations offchain and has never sent a transaction, so its nonce is still 0 after eleven payments. Zero gas. The offer lives in an ENSv2 subname on Sepolia, minted by a registry and registrar I deployed. Price, rails and endpoint are text records, read fresh on every request. The hot key is scoped to exactly two of those records, so when it tries to change the payout address, the chain reverts it. A Forge fork test proves that against live Sepolia, not a mock. On the buyer side, the agent spends from a Privy wallet governed by two key quorums: one signature can't raise the spend cap, two can. The premium scorer runs in a Chainlink CRE enclave (simulated, because deploy access is gated). World Selfie Check caps each human at three listings.

projects.title: VibeDesk
projects.description: A security-first desktop app: AI trading agents, local wallets, live multi-source data — all local
projects.project_description: Wallet (account) + Data + AI = Agentic Trading A local-first desktop application where your AI agents read live multi-source market data, analyze the news, and — with your wallet's explicit approval — execute real on-chain trades. Your wallet, your AI, your data: nothing leaves your machine except signed transactions. Out of the box — the agent runtime ships inside the app, no server to install or run yourself. 01 · Safe Account Your keys. Your rules. Local-first wallet vault — manage multiple wallets on your own machine; seed phrases and private keys are generated locally and never shown in plain text Per-wallet agent approval — grant an agent access to a specific wallet with one click, revoke it anytime Process isolation — the agent and the wallet live in separate processes; the agent can only request signatures over IPC and can never read your secrets 02 · AI Agents that actually do things. Multi-agent by design — run a general chat agent, a trading agent and news bots side by side, each with its own context, tools and memory Powered by the Pi engine — a full agent runtime with persistent context and tool-calling built in Pluggable skills — extend any agent with data-source skills, strategy skills, or skills the agent builds for you on the fly (partially implemented) 03 · Data Every price. Every signal. One desk. Unified multi-source prices — Hyperliquid, Binance, Robinhood and more in a single view, refreshed in real time News & social feeds — watch the price and the narrative at the same time, on one screen AI-driven analysis — agents turn raw prices and headlines into actionable recommendations
projects.how_its_made: How it's made VibeDesk is an Electron + React desktop app with a hand-rolled Windows 95-style shell — a custom window manager with draggable multi-window layering, taskbar, start menu and desktop shortcuts built on top of React95. The whole "local OS" feel is just our own React state machine over DOM windows, which let us ship a demo where a trade agent window, a chat window and a live markets window all run side by side. Architecture: the wallet and the agents are strictly separated. The wallet vault lives in the Electron main process — keys are AES-encrypted on disk, decrypted in memory only, and never leave main; agents can only request signatures over IPC, they can never read the keys themselves. Agents are built on the mature Pi engine (the harness from the OpenClaw ecosystem), giving us a production-grade multi-agent runtime out of the box — persistent per-agent context, tool-calling, and a pluggable skill system we'll keep extending with more data sources, strategies, and agent-created skills. The data layer is also main-process-bound: a multi-source aggregator fetches live quotes from Robinhood, Yahoo Finance, Hyperliquid and Binance. We deliberately fetch from Electron main instead of the renderer, because public endpoints like Robinhood and Yahoo throw CORS errors in the browser — running Node fetch in main completely sidesteps that. Every tick is written into a local SQLite store (one point per symbol/provider/minute) so the price-history charts overlay multiple sources on the same time axis. One hacky note: better-sqlite3's native prebuild hung inside the Electron main process, so we swapped to sql.js via WASM, which turned out to be more reliable across rebuilds. LLM access is OpenAI-compatible — any base URL + key works, plus Ollama for fully local inference, plus a deterministic rule mode that runs with zero API keys (great for demo machines with no network key). Partner technologies. Arc (Circle) is our execution chain: real swaps run on the Arc testnet against the Minara deployment of Uniswap v4 — we call the V4 Quoter ( quoteExactInputSingle ) for live quotes including pool/hook fees, handle Permit2 dual approval (token → Permit2 → Universal Router), sign locally with viem, and broadcast; gas on Arc is native USDC, which makes the demo feel like a real agentic-trading OS. The same module already has mainnet placeholder configs for switching networks. The agentic trading loop. In the trade agent, a user can simply type "buy 1 USDC worth of ETH"; the Pi agent quotes, checks the authorized wallet, executes the swap in the main process, and returns the tx link while the balance panel refreshes live. Data + AI + Wallet = Auto Trading, all local-first.

projects.title: perjury
projects.description: AI agents post bonded claims; VRF peers verify them in a TEE. Lying costs ENS standing.
projects.project_description:
We trust what AI agents tell us about their own work. An agent says "Compound v3 utilization is 64.66%", another party acts on it, and nothing ever re-derives it. Logs do not help, because the agent writes its own logs. As agents start acting on each other's output, that gap becomes structural. Perjury closes it. An agent posts a claim with an economic bond; only the hash of the exact sentence goes on chain, so the claim cannot change once the money is down. The protocol assigns a random peer as witness — submitClaim has no witness parameter, so there is no code path to ask for one. The witness never sees the claimant's reasoning and independently re-derives its own answer from the same block. A Chainlink CRE confidential workflow opens both sealed submissions inside an enclave, recomputes each value from raw rows rather than trusting either stated conclusion, and publishes only a verdict and a commitment hash — never the evidence, never either methodology, never the disputed numbers. On a mismatch the claimant forfeits its bond and its stake, and its ENS standing drops, which makes it ineligible to audit anyone else in the next block. The forfeited ETH is paid to nobody. Not the witness, not the protocol, not us. The witness earns a flat fee whichever way the verdict goes. Paying the forfeit to the witness is exactly what would make fabricating disagreement profitable, and that is the single most important design decision in the project. Three constraints drive the rest, and each rules out a simpler approach: A claimant who picks its own auditor can always buy a pass, so assignment must be verifiably random.
An adjudicator that publishes evidence leaks each agent's methodology and hands future claimants a rubric to game, so the comparison must happen where the inputs stay sealed.
Reputation the subject can write is not reputation, so the record must be writable only by the adjudicator.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, Sepolia). ClaimRegistry escrows bonds and runs the claim lifecycle. WitnessRoster handles registration and assignment. VerdictSink is the only door a verdict can walk through. PerjuryStandingWriter is the only thing holding the ENS write role. No contract has an owner, a pause, an upgrade proxy, or an address setter — the claim "operators cannot influence a verdict" has to survive someone grepping for an escape hatch. 69 Solidity tests and 110 TypeScript tests, most of them asserting that things fail: a verdict from an EOA or the deployer reverts, assignment is unreachable except through the VRF callback, an agent cannot write its own reputation. That immutability is not free, and we paid for it three times. Each contract holds the next immutably and the registry's pointer at its verdict sink locks on first wiring, so a four-line change to the sink means redeploying everything and claim ids restart at 1. The site reads all three cascades rather than deleting the evidence of the earlier two. Chainlink. The CRE workflow is the tribunal — there is no second code path that produces a verdict. It is deployed to the DON and adjudicates inside an AWS Nitro enclave, not only in the simulator. Each scheduled run reads ClaimRegistry.pendingForTribunal() to find its own claim, fetches both sealed submissions over Confidential HTTP, opens them with an envelope key the Vault DON releases into the enclave and nowhere else, recomputes both values, and writes (kind, claimId, verdict, evidenceCommitment) through the production Forwarder. A verdict it settled: 0xf8dd4d0219ccfd9a723409fbd8d19c88a87c91547c123805e6ff16f3d1c657c5. VRF v2.5 draws every witness and every appeal panel. The callback walks the roster from seed % agentCount, skipping the claimant and anyone ineligible. On the claim the demo replays, the seed landed on the claimant itself and the walk stepped straight past it. The Graph. The facts under dispute. Live Gateway only, nothing mocked: 13 pinned deployments across 2 Messari schema families and 5 chains, all served by one standardized query pattern, so adding a protocol is a line in a config file rather than code. Where a subject has a second independently-indexed deployment we query both and require agreement — a deployment id is a hash of the mapping code, so two agreeing means something two RPC nodes agreeing does not. Divergence returns Unverifiable rather than a judgement. Every read is pinned to a block and the served block must equal the requested one, because state that legitimately moved between two honest reads is otherwise indistinguishable from disagreement. ENS. Each agent owns a real subname of perjury.eth, issued from a subname registry we deployed through the Verifiable Factory. Standing is a text record on a Permissioned Resolver, and Enhanced Access Control scopes the write per record key: the tribunal holds SET_TEXT on exactly two keys and has no grant on the issuance record, because the contract that can lower an agent's standing must not also decide whose standing it is. The operator that deployed everything and owns the name reverts when it tries to write standing. Agents get RENEW on their own subname and nothing else — an agent holding SET_RESOLVER could repoint its name at a resolver it controls and write whatever standing it liked.

VerdictSink is the only door a verdict can walk through. PerjuryStandingWriter is the only thing holding the ENS write role. No contract has an owner, a pause, an upgrade proxy, or an address setter — the claim "operators cannot influence a verdict" has to survive someone grepping for an escape hatch. 69 Solidity tests and 110 TypeScript tests, most of them asserting that things fail: a verdict from an EOA or the deployer reverts, assignment is unreachable except through the VRF callback, an agent cannot write its own reputation.

That immutability is not free, and we paid for it three times. Each contract holds the next immutably and the registry's pointer at its verdict sink locks on first wiring, so a four-line change to the sink means redeploying everything and claim ids restart at 1. The site reads all three cascades rather than deleting the evidence of the earlier two.

Chainlink. The CRE workflow is the tribunal — there is no second code path that produces a verdict. It is deployed to the DON and adjudicates inside an AWS Nitro enclave, not only in the simulator. Each scheduled run reads ClaimRegistry.pendingForTribunal() to find its own claim, fetches both sealed submissions over Confidential HTTP, opens them with an envelope key the Vault DON releases into the enclave and nowhere else, recomputes both values, and writes (kind, claimId, verdict, evidenceCommitment) through the production Forwarder. A verdict it settled: 0xf8dd4d0219ccfd9a723409fbd8d19c88a87c91547c123805e6ff16f3d1c657c5.

VRF v2.5 draws every witness and every appeal panel. The callback walks the roster from seed % agentCount, skipping the claimant and anyone ineligible. On the claim the demo replays, the seed landed on the claimant itself and the walk stepped straight past it.

The Graph. The facts under dispute. Live Gateway only, nothing mocked: 13 pinned deployments across 2 Messari schema families and 5 chains, all served by one standardized query pattern, so adding a protocol is a line in a config file rather than code. Where a subject has a second independently-indexed deployment we query both and require agreement — a deployment id is a hash of the mapping code, so two agreeing means something two RPC nodes agreeing does not. Divergence returns Unverifiable rather than a judgement. Every read is pinned to a block and the served block must equal the requested one, because state that legitimately moved between two honest reads is otherwise indistinguishable from disagreement.

ENS. Each agent owns a real subname of perjury.eth, issued from a subname registry we deployed through the Verifiable Factory. Standing is a text record on a Permissioned Resolver, and Enhanced Access Control scopes the write per record key: the tribunal holds SET_TEXT on exactly two keys and has no grant on the issuance record, because the contract that can lower an agent's standing must not also decide whose standing it is. The operator that deployed everything and owns the name reverts when it tries to write standing. Agents get RENEW on their own subname and nothing else — an agent holding SET_RESOLVER could repoint its name at a resolver it controls and write whatever standing it liked.

projects.title: Tessera
projects.description: Tessera: An MCP marketplace where AI agents pay for API tools per-call using Hedera & x402.
projects.project_description: Tessera is a decentralized, per-use tool marketplace built specifically for autonomous AI agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Today, the infrastructure of the web is stuck in human-centric patterns; when an AI agent needs to access a paid data source or run an API calculation, it cannot autonomously create a SaaS account, agree to a subscription, or enter a credit card. Tessera solves this by creating a true machine-to-machine economy. Instead of human signups, an agent connects to the Tessera MCP gateway, programmatically requests a tool, receives a per-invocation price quote, and instantly streams a micro-payment using the x402 protocol settled on Hedera. Once the payment is verified, Tessera securely executes the API call and feeds the clean data payload back to the agent in milliseconds. We chose Hedera because its fixed, ultra-low transaction fees make sub-cent micro-payments economically viable, unlocking a highly composable, zero-friction web where agents can seamlessly buy exactly what they need, one API call at a time.
projects.how_its_made: Tessera is built as an extensible Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway using Node.js and TypeScript. At its core, we mapped the standard JSON-RPC tool-calling cycle of MCP directly onto the open x402 payment standard. When an AI agent invokes an MCP tool, the Tessera proxy intercepts the request, assesses the metered cost, and intercepts the flow to throw a standard cryptographic payload via the x402 scheme. We deeply integrated Hedera as our foundational settlement layer, leveraging the @x402/hedera reference packages alongside the open-source Blocky402 facilitator on the Hedera Testnet. Hedera provides immense benefit to this architecture; its fixed, predictable, and ultra-low $0.001 network transfer fees are what actually make sub-cent micro-payments economically viable for rapid-fire API inference. A particularly notable, "hacky" engineering choice was how we bypassed traditional web authentication. Because AI agents lack persistent browser sessions or traditional Web3 extension injections (like MetaMask), we built a lightweight transport middleware that wraps the x402 402 Payment Required header challenge into an inline MCP error response framework. This allows the client-side agent framework to catch the payment request, sign an off-chain transaction authorization autonomously via its private key, and pass it back to the facilitator, completing the entire transaction, validation, and API data delivery natively within a single, continuous command-line routine without breaking the LLM’s execution context
