projects.title: StreamProof
projects.description: ZK-verified royalty tiers: prove stream thresholds privately, settle payouts via Arc + Privy.
projects.project_description: StreamProof is a zero-knowledge royalty settlement system for music streaming. Today, artists have no way to independently verify their royalty payouts, because platforms won't publish raw play-count data — doing so would expose competitively sensitive traffic and individual listener behavior. StreamProof resolves this tension directly: a platform commits streaming data as an on-chain Merkle root, and an artist generates a zero-knowledge proof showing their verified stream count crosses a specific payout tier — without revealing the exact count, to anyone, ever. A valid proof automatically triggers a USDC payout on Arc, settled directly into the artist's Privy embedded wallet. The artist's identity is anchored to an ENSv2 name where the platform holds narrowly scoped write-access to a single record, verified with both a positive and negative test. The result is verifiable, automated royalty settlement that never requires trusting a self-reported number.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a Noir circuit compiled with Barretenberg's UltraHonk backend, proving Merkle-tree inclusion plus a threshold comparison in one pass — the leaf hashes artist, track, period, verified count, and a salt using Poseidon2, chosen specifically because it has an independently verified TypeScript implementation that produces bit-identical output to the in-circuit hash, avoiding any mismatch between the off-chain tree builder and the on-chain commitment. Solidity contracts (Foundry, deployed on Arc Testnet) include a write-once CommitmentRegistry, a TierVerifier that checks proof roots against stored commitments before calling the generated Honk verifier, and a PayoutVault that releases fixed USDC amounts per tier. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control scopes the platform's write permission to exactly one text record on the artist's name — confirmed with a negative test that writing any other record correctly reverts. Privy provides the embedded wallet that actually receives the payout. The trickiest part was matching hash functions and proof formats exactly across the Noir circuit, the off-chain tree builder, and the generated Solidity verifier — a single mismatched flag anywhere in that chain silently breaks verification.

projects.title: PayProof
projects.description: Web3 freelance escrow with verified humans, secure wallets, and instant USDC payments.
projects.project_description: ProofPay is a Web3-powered freelance payment platform designed to make digital work more trustworthy, transparent, and secure. The platform connects clients and freelancers while solving one of the biggest problems in freelancing: trust between people who may have never met before. ProofPay uses World ID to verify that users are real, unique humans, helping reduce fake accounts, bots, and fraudulent identities. Users can complete verification through World’s identity infrastructure without exposing unnecessary personal information to the application. For wallet and authentication infrastructure, ProofPay uses Privy, allowing users to onboard easily and interact with Web3 wallets without requiring complicated blockchain setup. This makes the experience feel closer to a traditional Web2 application while retaining the benefits of blockchain. Payments are handled using Arc and USDC, providing a transparent and programmable payment layer. When a client creates a freelance agreement, funds can be locked into an escrow smart contract. The freelancer then completes the agreed work, and once the conditions are satisfied, the payment can be released. The goal of ProofPay is to create a trust-minimized freelance marketplace where identity, agreements, payments, and settlement are connected through programmable infrastructure. Instead of relying entirely on a centralized platform to decide who gets paid, ProofPay uses blockchain-based escrow and verification mechanisms to make the process more transparent. The platform can eventually support reputation, milestone-based payments, dispute mechanisms, and on-chain proof of completed work.
projects.how_its_made: ProofPay is built using a combination of Web3 identity, wallet infrastructure, backend services, and blockchain smart contracts. The frontend is built using React/TypeScript, providing the interface where clients and freelancers create profiles, create agreements, manage projects, and initiate payments. Privy handles authentication and wallet infrastructure. Users can sign in and receive or connect a wallet without needing to manually manage complex wallet setup. Privy provides the wallet interaction layer between the application and blockchain. World ID is integrated for human verification. During onboarding, users complete World's verification flow. The resulting proof is sent to the backend, where it is verified before marking the user's account as verified. The backend is built using Node.js and TypeScript. It manages users, projects, agreements, verification status, payment states, and communication with external services. A database such as PostgreSQL/Supabase stores application data. For payments, ProofPay uses USDC on Arc. Smart contracts implement the escrow logic: the client deposits funds, the contract holds them, and payment is released according to the agreement's conditions.

projects.title: Caplane
projects.description: A lien registry no one operates. Stops double-pledging without revealing the collateral.
projects.project_description: Offchain, double-pledging is caught by public lien registries like the UCC-1. Onchain there is none, and whoever ran one could rig it. Caplane is that registry with no operator: claims are sealed into an enclave, matched against active liens inside it, and the only function that can write accepts nothing but DON-signed reports. No owner, no pause, no operator wallet. Anyone can check that a claim is already pledged without learning what it is. A full receivables-financing flow runs on top, settling in USDC on Arc. Invoices are the demo; the registry is the project.
projects.how_its_made: Four contracts on Arc Testnet with no owner, pause, proxy or setter. A CI rule fails the build if governance appears. The registry's single write path accepts only DON-signed reports from a Chainlink CRE workflow running in AWS Nitro, with the chain selector and a permanent nonce carried inside the signed body, since the DON's signature commits to neither the chain nor the receiver. borrower comes from the event, never from the decrypted plaintext: a copyist replaying someone else's ciphertext would register the lien to themselves. The hacky part is the enclave. CRE runs Javy on QuickJS, not Node: no Intl (so localeCompare diverges without throwing), no Date , no secure entropy. Canonicalization is hand-rolled and proven byte-identical across bun → javy → node:wasi . EIP-712 recovery uses @noble/curves synchronously because viem's async verifiers collapse in Javy, and with default prehash it silently recovers a different valid address instead of erroring. ConfidentialHTTPClient doesn't compile inside handlerInTee despite being the client the docs name, so it's the normal HTTPClient on TeeRuntime . Claims match k-of-7 on peppered commitments. Measured false-match rate: 1/903 pairs at k=6, Clopper-Pearson 95% upper bound 0.524%, thresholds published on purpose so the rate is checkable. lienId is peppered because without it we brute-forced it against the real corpus in 71 ms. The fuzzy index posts to three positions only, since a fourth turned lookup linear at 30.9M gas, past the eth_call ceiling. The same schema takes vehicles by VIN at k=7, with no Solidity change and no redeploy. Debtor confirmation is collected before submission and rides inside the sealed envelope, because CRE can't suspend an execution. The EIP-712 signature is verified in the same run, requiring debtor ≠ submitter and exact agreement on claim, amount, currency and due date. Arc lets the registry and settlement share one chain (CRE supports it and the forwarder lives there), so there is no relayer anywhere in the trust path, and gas in USDC means one unit of account end to end. Privy organization wallets sit behind a 2-of-2 P-256 key quorum, and since organizations().create() requires default_key_quorum_id , that quorum is a prerequisite rather than an upgrade. A deny-by-default policy sits on top: the app signs up an org, provisions its wallet, and shows a transfer refused by policy. Privy signs but only ever sees ciphertext. Everything reads back without us: an npm SDK on viem alone that refuses any contract whose WORKFLOW_NAME() isn't the frozen one, an MCP server that returns the calldata and block for every answer, and a lookup page that reads chain state from the visitor's own browser in 552 bytes of hand-rolled decoding. Shut our backend off and the registry still answers.

projects.title: Sentinel402 Gateway
projects.description: Autonomous DeFi liquidity auditor using x402 micropayments, The Graph indexing, and ENSv2.
projects.project_description: As autonomous AI agents manage trading and DeFi operations, two primitives are missing: machine-native payment rails (agents cannot hold credit cards or KYC for API accounts) and verifiable proof of execution (downstream smart contracts need proof that an audit was computed against canonical state). Sentinel402 Gateway bridges this gap by combining RFC-compliant x402 micropayments, decentralized indexing from The Graph, and next-generation ENSv2 permissioned attestations: Bazantic x402 Micropayment Protocol: When an autonomous caller requests an audit, the gateway intercepts unauthenticated traffic with an HTTP 402 Payment Required challenge specifying cost (0.001 ETH) and the facilitator address. Once the agent provides a valid bearer token, execution proceeds without accounts or pre-shared keys. projects.title: RelayDesk
projects.description: Hand over an event link, not your wallet: ENSv2 URL permissions with verifiable revocation.
projects.project_description: RelayDesk helps community-event organizers hand over link maintenance without handing over their wallet or name ownership. An organizer delegates the url text key on a dedicated ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver to a separate volunteer account. The volunteer updates the event link; the organizer later revokes access while the last published URL remains available. The product separates a clearly labelled wallet-free simulation from actual Sepolia operations and public evidence. Judges can try the simulated grant, update and revoke workflow, then inspect the real test name, transaction receipts, role checks and Universal Resolver readback at /evidence. On September 8 we completed eight successful transactions against the dedicated ETHOnline deployment: mint, deploy, commit, approve, register, grant, volunteer edit and revoke. After revocation, read-only write simulations return EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, volunteer root/key roles are zero, and the last URL still resolves. The important boundary is explicit: URL-key authority covers the ENTIRE Resolver instance, not just one name. Separate activities should use separate instances; names sharing a Resolver are not isolated. Our verified result is one activity with distinct organizer and volunteer accounts. The two-activity comparison is unfinished, and we do not claim production security certification. September 5 evidence used a different deployment and is marked historical rather than used as current acceptance proof.
projects.how_its_made: We built RelayDesk with JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Node.js 24, viem and esbuild. The static public build runs inspected services in the browser with visitor-isolated simulation state; it has no server signing key. Real writes use the participant's browser wallet on Sepolia (chain ID 11155111), with fresh account/network checks and explicit transaction review. ENSv2 is the core authorization layer, not cosmetic naming. We use grantSetterRoles and revokeRoles for the url key and DNS-encoded names for setText(bytes,string,string). Registration follows a direct EOA path using the dedicated ETHOnline ETHRegistrar, VerifiableFactory and Permissioned Resolver. Factory implementation and deployment proofs are checked against verified ABI artifacts. Test-token approval uses the exact quoted amount. We inspect root/key roles and test the controlled fixture for registry resolver-management bypass authority. A key challenge was correcting assumptions about the deployed Factory ABI and the Resolver-wide permission scope. We migrated from an earlier deployment and reran the actual registration/delegation/revocation workflow on the event-specific contracts. Receipt verification checks the expected effects instead of treating a successful transaction alone as proof. Tests cover wrong networks, stale wallets, duplicate sends, deployment-proof binding, decoded authorization failures and permission boundaries; the last complete run passed 165 tests. AI disclosure: Codex and native helper agents generated and revised the application, tests and documentation; Claude cross-reviewed documentation, ABIs and implementation assumptions. The human participant supplied requirements, challenged and approved scope decisions, prepared accounts and the dedicated wallet, participated in operational checks, and recorded the Chinese narration. We do not claim the application was hand-written by the participant. See AI_USAGE.md and PUBLICATION.md in the public repository for attribution and history/privacy exclusions.

projects.title: Xovi Agents
projects.description: Agents pay over x402 to propose clips. Only a human confirms, and asserts it in an EAS attestation.
projects.project_description: Xovi (https://xovi.axolodao.org/) is a conservation dApp built around the public livestream of an axolotl museum in Mexico. People watch, mark behaviours they see, submit them as clips, and other people confirm or reject them. Xovi Agents adds a machine to that loop in the one position where a machine belongs: it proposes, and a person decides. A person connects a wallet on Base Sepolia and is offered an enrolment of three steps, each optional: verify with World ID in the page, with the proof bound to that wallet and checked on the server; take a name under xovi.eth, issued as a row and resolved through Zenbit's gateway with the ENS reference offchain resolver; and receive a machine credential minted by Xovi for that wallet. A wallet that declines still reaches the board and pays every read. The board offers screened windows of the museum's own footage by day and species, each cell carrying its recording and what one read costs, and never a count of what was withheld. Pay and run delegates one action: a paid read presents an x402 payment signed from the person's wallet as an EIP-3009 authorization in USDC, settled on Base Sepolia through the public testnet facilitator; a free read is proved from the wallet's own signature and settles nothing. The agent reads the windows of the cell it paid for, forms one proposal, submits it to Xovi under the wallet's own credential, and stops. A wallet whose credential was never minted ends at not submitted, as the disclosure states. A wallet a verified person stands behind gets free reads each day, two on the public deployment, counted against the person and not the keypair, and every read after that pays. A human operator confirms or rejects the proposal exactly as for a clip a person submitted. The operator asserts that confirmation in an EAS attestation anchored on Ethereum Sepolia with an onchain timestamp, a subgraph on The Graph indexes it, and the result is served through a paid query over MCP. The attestation asserts who confirmed and when; it certifies no identity, no reputation, no payment and no biological fact. Account shows the person's own settlements read back from the receipts ledger, Record shows the check a stranger can run, and Not yet names what the repository does not do. Nothing writes to a mainnet, nothing handles real funds, and no credential the agent holds can confirm or attest.
projects.how_its_made: The service is a Next.js application with route handlers and no middleware. The paid endpoint is an x402 resource server over @x402/core: an unpaid request gets a 402 with the price, asset, recipient and network in the challenge, and the client signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization for USDC on Base Sepolia that the public testnet facilitator verifies and settles. Two payers share one code path, the browser wallet on the page and a command line agent, and both refuse anything above a one dollar ceiling before signing. Every settlement is written to a receipts ledger keyed by the payer from the facilitator's settlement answer, guarded against a fabricated receipt, and the page's Account is drawn from that table alone. The per person allowance reads World ID's AgentBook on World Chain, where an agent address resolves to the nullifier of the person who registered it; the service keeps only a keyed digest of that identifier for thirty days and counts free reads against it, so a fresh keypair earns nothing new. The agent's identity is an ENS name on Ethereum Sepolia whose address record must equal the paying key, compared as an equality with the chain id checked first, never used as a lookup. Windows come from a small computer vision pipeline over the museum's recorded stream, screened by a person and signed off before a file is committed, and the board serves on offer or none per cell so no count leaks what was withheld. The human confirmation is a signed EIP-191 message recovered on the page, then attested offchain with EAS under a frozen schema and anchored with an onchain timestamp on Ethereum Sepolia; a subgraph on The Graph filters attestations by that schema identifier and an MCP server charges for the query with the same x402 rail, returning the 402 as a tool result. The delegated run is streamed to the browser as newline delimited JSON from the same invocation that does the work, so there is no shared state and no polling. Hacky and proud of it: the whole free read and settlement path was rehearsed against the real facilitator the night before the video, which is how the payer's own ceiling was found refusing the ruled price before it could sign.

projects.title: tokenize-it
projects.description: Tokenized ESOPs on Hedera: borrow against vested equity without selling it or leaving your wallet.
projects.project_description:
tokenize-it puts employee stock options on-chain on Hedera, then lets employees do two things that are close to impossible today: borrow against equity they have already earned without selling it, and get paid in the same stablecoin they borrow in. THE PROBLEM
Employee stock options are one of the most widely held private-market assets, and one of the worst served. A grant is a PDF, vesting lives in a spreadsheet, and an employee holding vested options in a private company usually can't sell them and can't borrow against them. The wealth is real but locked. WHAT IT DOES Issuance and lifecycle, enforced by the token itself. Options are issued as a compliant security token using Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio (ERC-1400 / ERC-3643). KYC and an issuer allowlist are enforced by the token, so a transfer to anyone who hasn't been onboarded simply fails. Our vesting contract places the whole grant in the employee's wallet up front, with each vesting tranche locked until its date. Once a date passes, anyone can release it, so vesting never depends on a trusted operator. HR can suspend an employee (vesting continues, transfers pause) or terminate them as a good or bad leaver: vested options stay theirs, and unvested ones can be clawed back into the option pool. Due process for leavers. A termination opens a dispute window before any clawback can happen. The employee can contest it in one click, at no cost. The ruling comes from an arbiter that the contract requires to be a multisig, and whoever made the termination is barred from judging the appeal. Every decision records the deciding address on-chain. Borrowing without giving up custody. An employee pledges vested options to the lending pool as an ERC-1400 hold over their own balance, not a transfer. The shares never leave their wallet; the pool holds zero shares while a loan is open, which anyone can check on-chain. The issuer keeps freeze and clawback rights over pledged equity. The pool lends stablecoin at up to 25% of the collateral's value. If a loan goes bad, liquidation executes the hold through the token's full compliance checks, takes only what is owed, and returns the rest. On testnet it seized 2,174 of 5,000 pledged shares and returned the other 2,826. Payroll in stablecoin, from a treasury nobody controls alone. Salary is paid from a Privy server wallet that can only act with a 2-of-2 quorum of officer keys. A Privy policy limits it to sending to the payroll contract and the stablecoin, so a compromised payroll wallet cannot touch the cap table. The payroll contract only pays employees on the issuer's allowlist. Paying wages in the same stablecoin the pool lends is what makes "borrow against your equity, repay from your salary" work in practice. A web2 experience. Employees sign in with an email and Privy creates a wallet for them. They never install anything, see a seed phrase, or hold HBAR: a relayer pays every network fee, and pledges and repayments are authorised with EIP-712 and EIP-2612 signatures. HR uses their own wallet in the issuer console, so every administrative decision is attributable to a person. HOW IT'S BUILT
Hedera testnet; the Asset Tokenization Studio for the security token; four Solidity contracts of our own (ESOPVestingController, ESOPLendingPool, EsopNavOracle, PayrollDisburser); a Next.js app with employee and issuer views; Privy for embedded wallets, server wallets, key quorums and policies; Chainlink's USDC/USD feed on Hedera for the stablecoin price; and a mirror-node indexer for the cap table. 165 tests pass, and every contract is deployed to Hedera testnet and verified on Sourcify/HashScan. Live at https://tokenize-it-git-main-balaji-shetty-pachais-projects.vercel.app/ WHAT'S STILL A STAND-IN A private company's share price has no public source. The share price feed has Chainlink's interface but is published by a valuation agent from an appraisal; every update is attributed and capped at a 30% move. The stablecoin price feed is a real Chainlink feed. The stablecoin is a testnet stand-in, and the arbiter is a stand-in multisig. Production would use real USDC and a Safe. Hedera's scheduled-transaction service (HIP-1215) isn't usable on testnet yet, so automatic vesting runs on a keeper. Because releasing a vested tranche is open to anyone, vesting is correct either way.
projects.how_its_made:
ARCHITECTURE
tokenize-it is four Solidity contracts sitting on top of Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS), plus one Next.js app that serves two audiences: employees at / and the issuer at /issuer. Everything runs on Hedera testnet. The ESOP token is an ATS security token: an EIP-2535 diamond (~100 facets) created through ATS's pre-deployed factory. We didn't write a token; we got KYC, an allowlist, freezes, forced transfers, and ERC-1400 locks and holds for free, and designed around those primitives. ESOPVestingController places a whole grant in the employee's wallet up front and locks each tranche until its vest date. Release is permissionless. Clawback force-releases unvested locks and moves them back into the option pool, rather than burning them, so the hard supply cap never runs out of headroom. ESOPLendingPool takes collateral as an ERC-1400 hold over the borrower's own balance, with the pool named as escrow. pledgeAndBorrow places the signed hold and opens the loan in a single transaction, so a failure can't leave shares held against a loan that never opened. Liquidation executes the hold through the token's full compliance stack, which meant onboarding the pool itself as a KYC'd, allowlisted institutional holder. EsopNavOracle speaks Chainlink's AggregatorV3 interface but is published by a valuation agent, with each update attributed and capped at a 30% move. PayrollDisburser pays salary on an accrue-then-withdraw basis, and only to addresses on the ESOP token's allowlist. The web app uses Next.js 16, React 19 and viem. Its API routes act as a relayer that pays every network fee, so employees never hold HBAR. There is one ABI definition for the whole app, after two copies drifted apart and silently broke the console. A small indexer builds the cap table from the Hedera mirror node, paging by timestamp. PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES AND WHAT THEY GAVE US Hedera and ATS: the lending design only works because ERC-1400 holds exist. The collateral never moves, so the lender never takes custody and the issuer keeps clawback and freeze authority over pledged equity. The pool's ESOP balance is provably zero while a loan is open (npm run proof:no-custody). Every contract is verified exact_match on Sourcify, which HashScan reads. Privy: on the employee side, embedded wallets with email login, and server-side token verification that resolves the wallet address itself, so a client can never claim someone else's equity. On the payroll side, a server wallet owned by a 2-of-2 key quorum of P-256 officer keys, plus a policy that only allows sends to the payroll contract and the stablecoin on chain 296. We tested both by trying to break them: one signature is refused with a 401, and a request to the equity token carrying a full quorum is refused with policy_violation. That policy is what makes the treasury structurally unable to touch the cap table. Chainlink: the stablecoin price comes from the live USDC/USD feed on Hedera testnet. Because our share-price oracle speaks the same interface, an issuer that later lists can swap in a real feed without touching the pool. THE HACKY AND NOTABLE BITS Hedera charges gas used, not gas offered. We measured it: the same mint at a 120k limit and a 900k limit cost an identical 0.03710687 HBAR. Meanwhile the estimator is not a safe bound: calls ran out of gas at 99.2% and 99.86% of the estimate, with empty revert data, while the same call simulated fine. So every write uses a generous explicit limit, which costs nothing extra. Hashio's RPC drops revert data, so failures arrive with no reason attached. Where we could, we check preconditions directly instead of decoding errors. For example, before funding a grant we check whether its tranche dates have already passed, because ATS refuses to lock tokens until a date that has gone by. With ATS's protected partitions, employees can't transfer directly at all. Every pledge is an EIP-712-signed hold relayed by a backend that holds the partition's participant role. ATS's EIP-712 domain version isn't "1" but the token's config version, so we read it from the chain at runtime. Repayment uses an EIP-2612 permit, so a borrower with no gas can still repay. ATS trap: freezing an address in whitelist mode removes it from the control list, while isFrozen() reads a different counter and reports false. So the app works out suspension from allowlist status plus grant status. Hold IDs must come from the event, not the hold count: the count drops when a hold is released while IDs keep climbing, and the two silently diverged. Hedera's Schedule Service (HIP-1215) lives at 0x16b with no bytecode, so eth_getCode says it doesn't exist; you have to probe it by calling it. On testnet, scheduleCall returns INVALID_CONTRACT_ID for every target, from a wallet and from contract code alike, while hasScheduleCapacity answers true. We built the scheduler anyway, then made a keeper the tier that actually runs. Because release is permissionless, vesting was never wrong without automation, only less automatic. The first transfer to an unused Hedera address creates a "hollow account", and that ran a plain HBAR transfer out of gas at 200k. A 37-tranche grant costs about 15.7M gas, over Hedera's 15M per-transaction ceiling, so funding is batched and resumable. ATS isn't vendored in the repo. A setup script clones it at a pinned commit, and a sync script runs our 165 tests inside ATS's own Hardhat project to reuse its deployment fixtures. One flag in those fixtures is the difference between a 45-second suite and a 36-minute one. We measured before optimising. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard saved 17,160 gas per call over our hand-rolled guard, so we switched. Hand-writing unchecked { ++i } saved a flat 44 gas on solc 0.8.28, because the compiler already does it, so we didn't.

2. Due process for leavers. A termination opens a dispute window before any clawback can happen. The employee can contest it in one click, at no cost. The ruling comes from an arbiter that the contract requires to be a multisig, and whoever made the termination is barred from judging the appeal. Every decision records the deciding address on-chain.
3. Borrowing without giving up custody. An employee pledges vested options to the lending pool as an ERC-1400 hold over their own balance, not a transfer. The shares never leave their wallet; the pool holds zero shares while a loan is open, which anyone can check on-chain. The issuer keeps freeze and clawback rights over pledged equity. The pool lends stablecoin at up to 25% of the collateral's value. If a loan goes bad, liquidation executes the hold through the token's full compliance checks, takes only what is owed, and returns the rest. On testnet it seized 2,174 of 5,000 pledged shares and returned the other 2,826.
4. Payroll in stablecoin, from a treasury nobody controls alone. Salary is paid from a Privy server wallet that can only act with a 2-of-2 quorum of officer keys. A Privy policy limits it to sending to the payroll contract and the stablecoin, so a compromised payroll wallet cannot touch the cap table. The payroll contract only pays employees on the issuer's allowlist. Paying wages in the same stablecoin the pool lends is what makes "borrow against your equity, repay from your salary" work in practice.
5. A web2 experience. Employees sign in with an email and Privy creates a wallet for them. They never install anything, see a seed phrase, or hold HBAR: a relayer pays every network fee, and pledges and repayments are authorised with EIP-712 and EIP-2612 signatures. HR uses their own wallet in the issuer console, so every administrative decision is attributable to a person.

HOW IT'S BUILT
Hedera testnet; the Asset Tokenization Studio for the security token; four Solidity contracts of our own (ESOPVestingController, ESOPLendingPool, EsopNavOracle, PayrollDisburser); a Next.js app with employee and issuer views; Privy for embedded wallets, server wallets, key quorums and policies; Chainlink's USDC/USD feed on Hedera for the stablecoin price; and a mirror-node indexer for the cap table. 165 tests pass, and every contract is deployed to Hedera testnet and verified on Sourcify/HashScan. Live at https://tokenize-it-git-main-balaji-shetty-pachais-projects.vercel.app/

WHAT'S STILL A STAND-IN
- A private company's share price has no public source. The share price feed has Chainlink's interface but is published by a valuation agent from an appraisal; every update is attributed and capped at a 30% move. The stablecoin price feed is a real Chainlink feed.
- The stablecoin is a testnet stand-in, and the arbiter is a stand-in multisig. Production would use real USDC and a Safe.
- Hedera's scheduled-transaction service (HIP-1215) isn't usable on testnet yet, so automatic vesting runs on a keeper. Because releasing a vested tranche is open to anyone, vesting is correct either way.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ARCHITECTURE
tokenize-it is four Solidity contracts sitting on top of Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS), plus one Next.js app that serves two audiences: employees at / and the issuer at /issuer. Everything runs on Hedera testnet.

- The ESOP token is an ATS security token: an EIP-2535 diamond (~100 facets) created through ATS's pre-deployed factory. We didn't write a token; we got KYC, an allowlist, freezes, forced transfers, and ERC-1400 locks and holds for free, and designed around those primitives.
- ESOPVestingController places a whole grant in the employee's wallet up front and locks each tranche until its vest date. Release is permissionless. Clawback force-releases unvested locks and moves them back into the option pool, rather than burning them, so the hard supply cap never runs out of headroom.
- ESOPLendingPool takes collateral as an ERC-1400 hold over the borrower's own balance, with the pool named as escrow. pledgeAndBorrow places the signed hold and opens the loan in a single transaction, so a failure can't leave shares held against a loan that never opened. Liquidation executes the hold through the token's full compliance stack, which meant onboarding the pool itself as a KYC'd, allowlisted institutional holder.
- EsopNavOracle speaks Chainlink's AggregatorV3 interface but is published by a valuation agent, with each update attributed and capped at a 30% move. PayrollDisburser pays salary on an accrue-then-withdraw basis, and only to addresses on the ESOP token's allowlist.
- The web app uses Next.js 16, React 19 and viem. Its API routes act as a relayer that pays every network fee, so employees never hold HBAR. There is one ABI definition for the whole app, after two copies drifted apart and silently broke the console.
- A small indexer builds the cap table from the Hedera mirror node, paging by timestamp.

PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES AND WHAT THEY GAVE US
- Hedera and ATS: the lending design only works because ERC-1400 holds exist. The collateral never moves, so the lender never takes custody and the issuer keeps clawback and freeze authority over pledged equity. The pool's ESOP balance is provably zero while a loan is open (npm run proof:no-custody). Every contract is verified exact_match on Sourcify, which HashScan reads.
- Privy: on the employee side, embedded wallets with email login, and server-side token verification that resolves the wallet address itself, so a client can never claim someone else's equity. On the payroll side, a server wallet owned by a 2-of-2 key quorum of P-256 officer keys, plus a policy that only allows sends to the payroll contract and the stablecoin on chain 296. We tested both by trying to break them: one signature is refused with a 401, and a request to the equity token carrying a full quorum is refused with policy_violation. That policy is what makes the treasury structurally unable to touch the cap table.
- Chainlink: the stablecoin price comes from the live USDC/USD feed on Hedera testnet. Because our share-price oracle speaks the same interface, an issuer that later lists can swap in a real feed without touching the pool.

THE HACKY AND NOTABLE BITS
- Hedera charges gas used, not gas offered. We measured it: the same mint at a 120k limit and a 900k limit cost an identical 0.03710687 HBAR. Meanwhile the estimator is not a safe bound: calls ran out of gas at 99.2% and 99.86% of the estimate, with empty revert data, while the same call simulated fine. So every write uses a generous explicit limit, which costs nothing extra.
- Hashio's RPC drops revert data, so failures arrive with no reason attached. Where we could, we check preconditions directly instead of decoding errors. For example, before funding a grant we check whether its tranche dates have already passed, because ATS refuses to lock tokens until a date that has gone by.
- With ATS's protected partitions, employees can't transfer directly at all. Every pledge is an EIP-712-signed hold relayed by a backend that holds the partition's participant role. ATS's EIP-712 domain version isn't "1" but the token's config version, so we read it from the chain at runtime. Repayment uses an EIP-2612 permit, so a borrower with no gas can still repay.
- ATS trap: freezing an address in whitelist mode removes it from the control list, while isFrozen() reads a different counter and reports false. So the app works out suspension from allowlist status plus grant status.
- Hold IDs must come from the event, not the hold count: the count drops when a hold is released while IDs keep climbing, and the two silently diverged.
- Hedera's Schedule Service (HIP-1215) lives at 0x16b with no bytecode, so eth_getCode says it doesn't exist; you have to probe it by calling it. On testnet, scheduleCall returns INVALID_CONTRACT_ID for every target, from a wallet and from contract code alike, while hasScheduleCapacity answers true. We built the scheduler anyway, then made a keeper the tier that actually runs. Because release is permissionless, vesting was never wrong without automation, only less automatic.
- The first transfer to an unused Hedera address creates a "hollow account", and that ran a plain HBAR transfer out of gas at 200k.
- A 37-tranche grant costs about 15.7M gas, over Hedera's 15M per-transaction ceiling, so funding is batched and resumable.
- ATS isn't vendored in the repo. A setup script clones it at a pinned commit, and a sync script runs our 165 tests inside ATS's own Hardhat project to reuse its deployment fixtures. One flag in those fixtures is the difference between a 45-second suite and a 36-minute one.
- We measured before optimising. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard saved 17,160 gas per call over our hand-rolled guard, so we switched. Hand-writing unchecked { ++i } saved a flat 44 gas on solc 0.8.28, because the compiler already does it, so we didn't.

projects.title: rewall
projects.description: Simple on-chain secret management with groundbreaking integrations
projects.project_description: Rewall is a serverless, on-chain secret management infrastructure. On Rewall, secrets are shareable by design. We use ENSv2's subname architecture for storing secrets and granting access. You share secrets by naming who may read them, and you take these permissions back by rotating the key. There are no accounts and no server in the middle. Nobody but the ENS names you chose can read a secret, and Rewall itself has nothing to read it with. In order to prove the strength of our design, we have tackled three privacy problems, and in one of them, we brought a whole new perspective to on-chain transfers: semi-confidential transactions. Rewall allows you to make confidential token transfers and share the details with whoever you grant access to. That means that while a third party can see your transfer, even the token receiver may not know who made the transaction as long as you do not give them permission. At its core, every person, team, and machine is represented by an ENS name that publishes a public key. A secret, such as an API key, password, private key, or two-factor authentication seed, is encrypted locally and stored as ENS text records under a subname you own, such as <provider>.rewall.alice.eth. Each secret is encrypted once with a randomly generated key. That key is then sealed separately to each authorized reader's public key, creating one small record per reader. Access is not something a centralized server checks. You either hold a sealed copy of the key or you do not. Revoking access means encrypting the secret again under a new key and sealing that key only for the readers who should retain access. Entire teams can also be granted access through subtree grants on parent ENS names. Rewall also introduces a recovery model without relying on a centralized custodian. A secret can have a recovery holder, such as a cold-wallet ENS name, or a group of guardians who each hold a piece of a recovery key. This means losing a wallet does not necessarily mean losing the secret. We also applied this architecture to two-factor authentication. Rewall can securely store 2FA seeds and generate live authentication codes while keeping the underlying seed encrypted and under the user's control. A browser extension can fill sign-in codes only on the exact site associated with the account. Another major use case is AI agents. Rewall allows an AI agent to use a secret without ever seeing the secret itself. Through the MCP server, the secret is decrypted inside the server process, used to perform the requested action, and then removed from the response. The agent receives only the result, with the sensitive value redacted. This means an AI agent can work with API keys, credentials, and other secrets without being able to expose, log, remember, or leak them. Around the core protocol, Rewall includes a dashboard at rewall.me for storing, sharing, revoking, managing secrets, managing live 2FA codes, and making private payments. A TypeScript SDK powers the rest of the ecosystem. The MCP server provides secret-safe access for AI agents, while the browser extension handles site-specific authentication. Rewall also includes a Chainlink CRE workflow that opens a secret inside an enclave and returns only a digest, as well as Ledger Key Ring enrollment that allows a server without a USB connection to join a key ring after explicit approval from a human on the Ledger device. If you want to learn everything about Rewall, refer to docs.rewall.me. It is our official documentation. We explain eight runnable examples, and refer to an Agent Skill that teaches AI assistants how to build on top of Rewall complete the project. Simply run npx skills add oynozan/rewall --skill rewall
projects.how_its_made: Rewall is built directly on ENSv2 on Sepolia. Each account owns a single PermissionedResolver, deployed through ENS's VerifiableFactory and reused across every name the account controls. This works because records inside the resolver are keyed by the namehash of the full name, so records belonging to different names cannot collide. A user's namespace, such as rewall.alice.eth, lives inside a UserRegistry controlled by that user, allowing new secrets to be created directly as subnames without involving a third party. Every read goes through UniversalResolverV2, following the standard ENS resolution path. Every write is a single PermissionedResolver multicall containing the encrypted blob, sealed data keys, reader lists, and the owner's signature in one transaction. Write delegation for an individual secret, or even an individual record key, is handled through ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control. Read access is deliberately not represented as an on-chain role: it is enforced entirely through cryptography. Names are registered through the Sepolia ETHRegistrar using its commit-and-reveal flow. Contract interaction is implemented directly with viem and typed ABI fragments using parseAbi, with interfaces verified against deployed bytecode. We avoid relying on ensjs for the protocol path because its registration flow targets a registry that the canonical ENSv2 root does not point to. The cryptography is deliberately built from standard, well-understood primitives. A user's identity key is deterministically derived from a single EIP-712 signature. The signature is reduced to canonical r and s values, hashed with SHA-256, and used as the material for an X25519 private scalar. The same wallet therefore derives the same encryption identity every time without permanently storing the key. Secret values are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a randomly generated data key. Before encryption, values are padded to a multiple of 256 bytes so that the ciphertext length does not reveal the approximate size of short credentials such as passwords, API keys, or 2FA seeds. The secret's own ENS name is bound into the ciphertext as authenticated data, preventing an encrypted blob from being copied to another name and successfully opened there. A key commitment stored inside the encrypted blob additionally ensures that only the intended data key can decrypt it. The data key is then sealed independently for every authorized reader using libsodium sealed boxes. Readers therefore never share a common private key, and adding a reader does not require re-encrypting the underlying secret. The owner also signs the reader lists together with the public key approved for each ENS name. This prevents a delegated writer from modifying the reader set to add themselves and then waiting for the owner to perform a future rotation. Revocation is cryptographic rather than administrative. The secret is encrypted under a fresh data key and that new key is sealed only for the readers who should retain access. No server has to enforce the decision. Recovery follows the same model. Guardian recovery uses Shamir secret sharing, with individual shares sealed to each guardian's ENS identity. Guardians re-seal and publish their shares on-chain for a replacement wallet, and recovery succeeds only when the reconstructed key produces the expected published public key. This allows wallet recovery without introducing a centralized recovery authority. The Rewall dashboard is a Next.js application using Privy for wallet connection. The derived identity key remains in memory for the active session and is never sent to the backend. A small set of server routes sponsors the initial ENS name registration and resolver deployment from a sponsor wallet. MongoDB is used only as the sponsorship spend ledger; those routes never receive or process secret material. The TypeScript SDK, built on viem and libsodium, is the canonical implementation of the protocol. The dashboard, MCP server, browser extension, integrations, and examples all build on the same SDK rather than independently implementing Rewall's encryption or ENS logic. The MCP server allows AI agents to use credentials without giving the model access to the credential itself. It supports both stdio and Streamable HTTP transports and enforces a host allowlist independently for each secret. It rejects IP literals and redirects to prevent destination bypasses, scans returned data for the secret across multiple encodings, and redacts any matching value before the result reaches the model. Just as importantly, the MCP server exposes no general-purpose signing capability. An AI model is never allowed to choose an arbitrary payload for the connected wallet to sign, because doing so would allow it to request the EIP-712 identity message itself, derive the user's encryption key, and gain access to every secret. The agent can use an authorized secret for a specific operation, but it cannot obtain the secret, the identity signature, or the underlying private key material. The browser extension is built with WXT. It detects one-time-password fields using heuristics modeled after Chromium and fills codes only when the current hostname exactly matches the hostname associated with the stored credential. Unlike the web dashboard, the extension can persist the identity key locally, but only in encrypted form under a user-provided passphrase. This makes 2FA another direct application of the same architecture. A TOTP seed can live as an encrypted Rewall secret, be shared or revoked using ENS identities, and generate authentication codes without exposing the underlying seed to a centralized password manager, application backend, or AI agent. ENS provides the naming, ownership, storage, and access-control foundation of the system. The ENS name is simultaneously the identity of a user, the namespace containing their secrets, the location of the encrypted records, and the reference used to determine who receives sealed access to them. Chainlink CRE extends that model into confidential computation. A CRE handlerInTee workflow reads Rewall's ENS records through the DON and decrypts the secret inside a trusted execution environment. The same sealed-box and AES-GCM construction is reimplemented using noble cryptographic primitives because the QuickJS runtime does not provide WebCrypto. The workflow can operate on the plaintext inside the enclave and return only the permitted result, such as a digest, without exposing the secret outside the TEE. Chainlink's Compliant Private Transfer architecture also forms the privacy rail behind Rewall's pay-by-name and semi-confidential transfer design. Its Sepolia vault and ACE policy engine provide the foundation for private transfers, while the current integration uses a local rail as a temporary substitute where the upstream indexer is unavailable. Semi-confidential transfers add selective disclosure on top of the private payment itself. The transfer can remain confidential while its receipt is represented as a Rewall secret. The sender then chooses exactly which ENS identities receive the sealed keys required to inspect that receipt. Transaction privacy is therefore not reduced to a binary choice between public and private: disclosure becomes programmable per participant. Ledger integration uses the Key Ring Protocol through the Device Management Kit. The enrollment flow runs against Ledger's genuine app-ledger-sync firmware inside the Speculos emulator, allowing the complete ceremony to be demonstrated end to end, including explicit human approval on the simulated device screen. This enables a server without direct USB access to become part of a hardware-backed key ring without weakening the approval model. Several infrastructure constraints also required protocol-level workarounds rather than mock implementations. ENSv2 does not currently provide subname enumeration, so Rewall maintains a single rewall.index record through the SDK and uses it to discover the secrets belonging to a namespace. Ledger tooling required inspecting the private wallet CLI implementation to confirm that its transport could not reach the emulator directly. The documentation stack also required correcting a Windows-specific Turbopack alias generated by Nextra. The documentation itself is built with Nextra and Mermaid, and the project includes runnable examples alongside an Agent Skill that can be installed with a single npx command to teach compatible AI assistants how to build against Rewall. Across all of these components, the same principle remains unchanged: ownership and metadata live on ENS, access is expressed through cryptography rather than a centralized authorization server, and sensitive material is revealed only at the exact point where it is required.

projects.title: Aletheia
projects.description: Privacy-preserving verification: prove claims without revealing your documents.
projects.project_description: Aletheia is a privacy-preserving credential verification protocol built around one simple idea: prove the claim, not the document. Instead of repeatedly sharing documents to prove facts like age or nationality, users generate Zero-Knowledge Proofs over trusted credentials and reveal only the claim a verifier needs. Ethereum provides the verification layer, ENS provides human-readable identity resolution, and The Graph indexes verification records. Phase 1 uses a clearly labelled development issuer, with DigiLocker planned as a future credential source.
projects.how_its_made: Aletheia is built from scratch as a TypeScript/React web application with an Ethereum-based verification layer. Credentials are normalized and signed by a quarantined development issuer, then used as private inputs to Circom 2.x circuits. We use circomlib, Poseidon hashing and EdDSA-Poseidon signatures with Groth16 proofs generated through snarkjs. Solidity contracts verify the proofs and emit ClaimVerified events on Ethereum Sepolia. The Graph indexes those events for verifier queries, while viem resolves existing ENS names to wallet addresses. No private credential fields are written to the blockchain, ENS or subgraph.

Credentials are normalized and signed by a quarantined development issuer, then used as private inputs to Circom 2.x circuits. We use circomlib, Poseidon hashing and EdDSA-Poseidon signatures with Groth16 proofs generated through snarkjs. Solidity contracts verify the proofs and emit ClaimVerified events on Ethereum Sepolia. The Graph indexes those events for verifier queries, while viem resolves existing ENS names to wallet addresses. No private credential fields are written to the blockchain, ENS or subgraph.

projects.title: Verdict.eth
projects.description: ENSv2 trust & verification registry for RWAs, enforced by autonomous AI agents.
projects.project_description: Verdict is an institutional verification registry and multi-agent consensus layer built natively on ENSv2 for tokenized Real World Assets (RWAs). Currently, protocols and autonomous agents must blindly trust raw contract addresses and static issuer PDFs. Verdict replaces this with machine-readable, canonical ENS profiles (e.g., buidl.rwa.verdict.eth) backed by an autonomous 4-agent inspection fleet evaluating Legal compliance, Custody reserves, and Technical security. By enforcing cryptographic separation between issuers and auditors, Verdict enables DeFi protocols like Aave and Morpho, RWA issuers like Ondo, and autonomous treasury DAOs to automate collateral onboarding and risk gating directly on-chain with zero counterparty tampering.
projects.how_its_made: Verdict is built natively on ENSv2 on Sepolia, leveraging Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control (EAC) to achieve strict cryptographic separation of authority. While issuers manage their asset profiles, only authorized auditor keys receive scoped setter roles for attestation records, making it mathematically impossible for issuers to forge audit scores. The application is built with Next.js, React Flow for interactive agent orchestration, Framer Motion, and Viem/Wagmi for on-chain resolution. We implemented an autonomous 4-agent quartet (Legal, Custody, Technical, and Consensus Synthesizer) along with an on-chain Agent Factory that lets users connect their wallet to mint custom sovereign subnames and apply tailored risk lenses directly into the consensus verdict.

projects.title: HandShake2
projects.description: Hedera and Graph-powered system enabling robots to facilitate x402 payments for physical-world work.
projects.project_description: HandShake is a platform where robots pay each other for physical world work, settled autonomously on Hedera via the x402 protocol. Robot A hands off a physical object. Robot B verifies the object's identity and legitimacy through an independent on-chain custody record indexed by The Graph, cross-checks the posted price and payee against what's physically written on the object, and only then signs and sends a real HBAR payment where no human approves the transaction. The goal is trustworthy machine-to-machine commerce for physical goods, not just digital ones.
projects.how_its_made:
The payment layer is x402 over Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator which was implemented by hand in Python since no official Hedera x402 SDK exists yet for that language, using hiero-sdk-python to build and sign the underlying HBAR transfer with the facilitator set as fee payer. Object verification runs on a separate ObjectCustody Solidity contract deployed to Base Sepolia, indexed by a custom subgraph on The Graph, so Robot B can independently confirm Robot A genuinely holds the object before paying, rather than trusting an HTTP claim. A physical QR sticker on each object carries its identity, price, and payee; Robot B's camera reads it directly and cross-checks it against Robot A's live quote, refusing the handoff on any mismatch. The robots themselves are JetCobot arms (Jetson + mycobot280), controlled via pymycobot, with the whole decision pipeline that includes scan, verify, quote-check, pay, while running as one script before any arm movement toward the object. Account for robot A: https://hashscan.io/testnet/account/0.0.10422144/operations?p1=1&k1=1789312060.240636104
Account for robot B: https://hashscan.io/testnet/account/0.0.10447952/operations

projects.title: Reshuffle
projects.description: Swap tickets without selling first — sign the outcome you'll accept, settle it on Arc.
projects.project_description: RESHUFFLE is a market for outcomes, not listings. Ticket holders who want to change tickets are forced to speculate. Resale makes you sell first and buy back, so the risk window is yours: sell your Friday pair and the Saturday pair may be gone, or buy first and you're carrying two sets. Official exchange usually requires the same event, venue and date at equal or higher price, so a date change falls outside it entirely. Worse, the trade that works often doesn't exist bilaterally. A holds Friday and wants Saturday, B holds Saturday and wants Sunday, C holds Sunday and wants Friday. Every pairwise negotiation fails; all three together clear. And even when a match exists, it stalls until every participant comes back online and approves that exact proposal. RESHUFFLE removes both. A user deposits their tickets into escrow and signs one EIP-712 intent describing the outcome they will accept: give up these tickets, only if I receive exactly two Saturday tickets in the same section with adjacent seats, and pay at most 30 USDC net, valid until Friday 18:00. Then they close the tab. A solver later composes many such intents — swappers, pure buyers, pure sellers, and unsold issuer inventory as a standing participant — into one reallocation where every signed condition holds simultaneously. The Settlement contract re-verifies each condition independently and either moves every ticket and every USDC payment in a single transaction, or reverts. The solver is untrusted; the contract is the trust anchor. That's the whole point: nobody is present to click confirm, so the outcome predicate has to be enforceable on-chain. On Arc Testnet we settled a three-party six-ticket reshuffle in one transaction, a four-party open chain with a pure buyer and pure seller, and confirmed that a non-adjacent allocation reverts with SeatsNotAdjacent. In the sign-and-leave demo, the participant browsers and signing process had exited before a separate solver settled — participant nonces unchanged, no new signatures required.
projects.how_its_made: RESHUFFLE is four Solidity contracts, a bounded TypeScript solver, a subgraph, and a Next.js app. Contracts (Arc Testnet, Foundry). TicketNFT is ERC-721 with seat metadata packed into one storage slot. Escrow holds deposited tickets; withdrawal is unconditional, but releaseBatch is onlySettlement — so Settlement is the only actor that can move an escrowed ticket to someone else. IntentRegistry.commit() is the only place a signature is ever checked (EIP-712, domain-bound to chainId and verifyingContract). Settlement.settle(Intent[], Leg[]) runs V0–V8 in the real transaction: intent state, escrow custody read at settlement time, redemption status, event/session/section masks, exact ticket count (exact, never a minimum), cohesion, seat adjacency, maxNetPay as a signed bound covering both payers and receivers, conservation, and USDC balance plus allowance capacity. Measured settle gas: 208k for a two-party exchange, 379k for a three-party six-ticket reshuffle. Arc / Circle. USDC is native gas, so a participant never needs a separate gas token, and cash legs settle in the same asset the constraint is denominated in. Net payments are grouped by wallet and are zero-sum excluding gas. The Graph. The registry stores commitment state and nonces but not an enumerable pool of matching conditions — those live in IntentCommitted. So an indexer is structurally required, not decorative. The subgraph indexes Ticket, Intent and Settlement; escrow custody is derived from NFT transfers. Three trust mechanisms: the shared hashIntent() recomputes every indexed commitment and rejects altered fields as HASH_MISMATCH; every read after a write is pinned with block: { number_gte: receiptBlock } so a stale snapshot can never replace newer state; and indexed discovery is always followed by chain reads and eth_call simulation before broadcast. A real transfer was observed indexed 7.3s after confirmation. Solver. Bounded search over the live pool — max 4 participants, 100 candidates, 2000ms — ranked by gross cash moved, then participant count, then intent-hash set. POST /api/solve/pool returns snapshotBlock, bounds, candidates, exclusions and simulation evidence. Agent. A read-only Claude agent with three tools (diagnose_intent, what_if, pool_overview) answers "why didn't this match?" from solver evidence, not from vibes. Every answer is pinned to one indexed block N, all balance reads use blockNumber: N, and a guard requires the answer to open with At Arc Testnet block #N, and to match complete evidence passages. Diagnosis works with no model key at all via a deterministic path. The agent has no signing capability. Hacky bits worth naming. foundry.toml sets evm_version = "paris" as a workaround for the open PUSH0 compatibility issue on Arc Testnet, even though Arc's docs describe Prague — flagged for re-test before mainnet. Gas estimation on some USDC writes is unreliable, so deployment scripts pass explicit gas limits. And Settled only emits hashes plus a participant count, so per-leg receipts and net USDC payments are decoded from transaction input and re-verified through RPC rather than indexed as entities.

projects.title: Foundereum
projects.description: Foundereum: A business account and metered toolbelt for AI agents, settled on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Give an AI agent (Claude Code, any MCP client or your AI Pipeline) a Privy secured wallet, a spending policy, and an x402 API key. Every tool it uses, swapping tokens, transferring funds, or pulling live on-chain data from The Graph, is paid for automatically with a sub-cent HTS payment via Blocky402, inside limits your team sets and can audit on HCS. No subscriptions, no shared API keys, no unbounded agent access to your treasury.
projects.how_its_made:
Foundereum is built in Go (API, Gateway, MCP server, Asynq worker) and React + TypeScript, backed by PostgreSQL  (double-entry ledger) and Redis (rate limits, nonces). AI agents connect via Model Context Protocol (MCP). Every tool call is metered through HTTP 402: the gateway issues a cryptographic challenge, the agent’s wallet signs the payment, and tools execute only upon verified on-chain settlement. Partner Tech: • Hedera: Sub-cent HTS USDC micropayments and public auditability. Every settled call is committed to a Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic (0.0.10442234) verifiable on HashScan. • Privy: Provisions split Treasury and Agent server wallets in TEE enclaves. Spending limits and allowlists are enforced at the hardware level (default_action: DENY), with WebCrypto multi-sig quorums for withdrawals • The Graph: Powers our agent data tools via Messari standardized subgraphs for live, cross-chain DEX pool intelligence. Notable Hack:
A zero-key automated x402 loop: the LLM never touches private keys or handles payment math. The gateway determines pricing from arguments, requests a TEE signature, settles atomically via Redis GETDEL (preventing replays), and returns verified data transparently.

projects.title: Wei
projects.description: An autonomous DevOps agent that automates Web3 PR reviews and pays bounties via smart contracts.
projects.project_description: Wei is a fully autonomous decentralized DevOps agent designed to eliminate the massive reviewer bottleneck in Web3 open-source governance (such as EIPs, GIPs, and RIPs). Currently, protocol upgrades and governance proposals suffer from painfully slow human review cycles and a lack of direct financial incentives for contributors. Wei solves this by providing a unified network where GitHub repositories can attach automated bounty pools to their issues. When a developer submits a Pull Request, Wei doesn't just passively read the code. It dynamically spins up an isolated AI sandbox environment using E2B to securely compile, run static analysis, and verify structural guidelines without any human intervention. Once the PR passes all strict automated checks, our backend acts as an off-chain oracle. It securely triggers our custom WeiBountyVault smart contract deployed on-chain to instantly distribute USDC or GRT directly to the contributor's wallet. To prevent bot-farming and sybil attacks, contributors must verify their unique human identity via World ID before claiming their automated rewards. Wei transforms open source by aligning instant trustless payments with rigorous automated code reviews.
projects.how_its_made: Wei is built with a highly decoupled architecture spanning a Next.js frontend, a Node.js backend oracle, and Solidity smart contracts. The user interface is built using React and Framer Motion, featuring a custom 3D roulette wheel to visualize active network bounties and integrated bots. For the core automation, we leverage E2B (Code Execution Sandboxes). Our backend listens to GitHub Webhooks, and upon detecting specific slash commands (e.g., /wei review), it spins up a secure E2B container to run AI-driven static analysis and tests on the submitted PR. For the Web3 infrastructure, we wrote custom Solidity contracts (WeiBountyVault.sol) to handle treasury management and distributions. Our Node.js backend acts as an off-chain oracle using ethers.js to trigger the distributeBounty function once the E2B sandbox returns a success signal. To guarantee Sybil resistance, we integrated @worldcoin/idkit on the frontend. When a user claims a bounty, they generate a Zero-Knowledge proof of humanity, and the resulting nullifierHash is passed to our smart contract to strictly enforce a "one human, one reward per PR" rule, completely neutralizing bot-farming attacks.

projects.title: Ecorestore Network
projects.description: Protocol for ecological restoration, where capital is released against verified restoration activity
projects.project_description: Ecorestore Network is a prototype tool that links nature restoration projects to payments. People pay for many kinds of restoration work, such as replanting forests, restoring riverbanks, and offsetting habitat loss. Funders need to know two things. First, did the land actually recover? Second, did it recover because of the project, or would it have recovered anyway? Today, these answers are often hard to check. They are also often kept apart from the payment itself. How Ecorestore Network works: First, a restorer makes a claim. For example: "Tree cover on our site grew by a certain amount." Second, a fixed set of rules checks the claim. The same inputs always give the same answer. The rules measure the site before and after the work. They compare the site with similar land nearby that was not restored. They check that the site and the nearby land changed in the same way before the work began. They take out any gain that would have happened anyway. Finally, they work out a range that shows how uncertain the result is. Third, payment uses the conservative number. The system uses the lowest value in that range, so funders do not overpay. Fourth, a methodology layer records the result. This layer is modelled on Hedera Guardian. It confirms that the right rules were followed and issues a record of that. Fifth, a smart contract handles the money. We call this contract a "Restoration Deed." It is on blockchain that holds the funder's money and releases only the approved amount. Only one approved account, chosen by the funder, can release it. Sixth, every step is saved and searchable. The Graph indexes the blockchain history, so anyone can trace what happened and why. Seventh, an AI assistant explains the results. The Auditor can look across a project's history, spot unusual patterns, and explain results in plain words. Ecorestore Network makes restoration results easier to check, easier to audit, and easier to fund. A working web app shows the whole process from start to finish. It uses a made-up restoration project on the Kootenay River in British Columbia. All environmental data is synthetic, not real field or satellite measurements. The demo runs on a test blockchain with test money only. It uses the self-hosted Hedera Guardian instance and does not touch real funds. Next steps are to deploy the contract to Arc Testnet, add digital signatures to strengthen the approval step, and quantify the spatial verification pipeline rigour with known restoration projects.
projects.how_its_made: Ecorestore Network is a TypeScript monorepo, with the following layers: Verification engine (TypeScript). A set of pure, deterministic functions checks a restoration claim. It compares the restored parcel with matched control parcels. It checks that both had similar trends before the work started. Then it measures the difference, removes gains that would have happened anyway, and applies an uncertainty range. Hedera Guardian (partner). Guardian holds the methodology, the workflow states and the credential. Guardian gave us a clear model for who may approve a result and in what order. It rejects a result if its hash no longer matches the evidence. Arc and USDC (partner). We wrote a Solidity RestorationDeed contract with OpenZeppelin and tested it with Hardhat. It holds USDC in escrow. It releases funds only when the verifier chosen by the sponsor submits a valid approval, and it blocks replayed approvals. Designing for Arc meant we could build around USDC settlement from the start. For now, it runs on a local chain with a mock USDC token. The Graph (partner). A subgraph indexes every deed event, running on a real Graph Node in Docker. The Graph gave us a queryable history without writing our own indexer. Our Auditor reads that history and compares it with the verification and Guardian records. Interface. A React and Vite app shows each stage, including a Leaflet map. Node server sends the app the real outputs of each layer. The server has no signing key. Docker Compose coordinates the whole stack, and GitHub Actions deploys it to the AWS EC2 host.

4. The Graph (partner). A subgraph indexes every deed event, running on a real Graph Node in Docker. The Graph gave us a queryable history without writing our own indexer. Our Auditor reads that history and compares it with the verification and Guardian records.

5. Interface. A React and Vite app shows each stage, including a Leaflet map. Node server sends the app the real outputs of each layer. The server has no signing key. Docker Compose coordinates the whole stack, and GitHub Actions deploys it to the AWS EC2 host.

projects.title: reCEPTION Swap
projects.description: reCEPTION Swap is a Real-Time Onchain Security Verification Layer for Dexs
projects.project_description: The project is driven by reCEPTION Hook, a native smart contract security layer designed to integrate with modern hook-enabled decentralized exchanges (such as Uniswap v4). It acts as a real-time shield, intercepting swap requests to dynamically detect and block malicious smart contracts before the transaction is finalized onchain. Powered by the reCEPTION AI Engine, the hook ensures that liquidity providers and retail users interact only with safe, verified assets, drastically reducing the financial impact of Web3 scams and exploits.
projects.how_its_made: reCEPTION Swap is built on Uniswap v4, using a custom reCEPTION Hook integrated with the PoolManager to bring smart contract security verification directly into the swap flow. The hook checks token security status before allowing swaps to proceed, connecting Uniswap v4’s hook architecture with reCEPTION’s existing verification layer. The frontend is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Wagmi, Viem, and the Uniswap SDK v4, while The Graph is used to query pool and liquidity-position data efficiently for the frontend. The broader reCEPTION platform supports multiple networks, including Ethereum and Hedera, with Hedera used by other reCEPTION features for on-chain infrastructure and data storage. The notable part of the implementation is tying an external security verification layer into the Uniswap v4 swap lifecycle so that unsafe or unverified tokens can be intercepted before the swap is finalized, rather than relying solely on a separate security-checking interface.

projects.title: SoulVault
projects.description: Local PII redact + wallet-gated rehydrate. Authorized wallets see granted fields.
projects.project_description: SoulVault is an event-driven coordination and continuity layer for AI agent swarms — plus a selective-disclosure document layer built on the same cryptographic core (secp256k1 ECDH + AES-256-GCM). The problem: Agent sessions are ephemeral and shared state is ad hoc. Multi-agent teams need verifiable coordination, encrypted continuity, and human-governed value flows — while the documents humans and agents exchange leak sensitive fields (PII, credentials, financial data) through every email and Slack copy. What we shipped: Selective disclosure for documents (Sepolia, this hackathon's focus). A browser dashboard runs local PII detection (presidio-web), produces a redacted artifact plus encrypted per-field slots, and anchors a docHash on a SoulvaultDocumentRegistry contract. The public bundle that travels is self-contained (registry address included), so any wallet — even outside the org — can request rehydration; the author grants per-slot keys wrapped to the requester's rehydration public key via SlotKeyGranted events, and only granted slots decrypt locally. Redaction runs are non-reversible by default; grants are explicit wallet capabilities. LKRP Swarm continuity upgrade. A swarm contract on Sepolia drives membership governance (join request/approve/remove), event-driven encrypted backups, a three-mode messaging bus (public/group/DM), and a fund-request lifecycle: agents file FundRequested, a bound SoulVaultTreasury approves and releases native funds onchain. ENS (org roots, swarm subdomains, ENSIP-11 multichain treasury discovery) and ERC-8004 provide public naming and identity. Recovery has been redesigned around Ledger's wallet-cli Key Ring (LKRP): the old model stored K_epoch as a physical secret that every member-custodian had to hold — losing custodians meant unrecoverable state, and kicked members kept copies. The Key Ring replaces stored epoch keys with ring-derived ones: the key is never stored, it's HKDF-derived from Ledger trustchain material with the key name (soulvault:epoch-recovery:<agentId>:epoch-<n>) as domain separation, so any enrolled machine — including ephemeral agents on a fresh VPS — can re-derive it with nothing to lose and nothing to escrow. Only the plaintext key name is durable metadata; harness-memory escrows are AES-256-GCM encrypted under it. Hardware & human gates. Ledger signing via Device Management Kit with clear-signing (verified against Speculos + a real Nano S Plus), and a World Selfie Check (incomplete) gate on rehydrate requests.
projects.how_its_made: Every encrypted thing — epoch keys, backups, group messages, DMs, document slots — uses the same primitive stack (ECDH + AES-256-GCM). Wire formats are locked to what the original node:crypto implementation produced, and enforced in both directions by cross-checked compat tests in packages/protocol/test/crypto-compat.test.ts. Slot IDs are deterministic per entity value, which is what makes same-redact-run detection work when a bundle is re-imported. Architecture. A pnpm workspace monorepo with a strict dependency direction: @soulvault/protocol (isomorphic crypto — @noble/curves, @noble/ciphers, @noble/hashes; no Node built-ins, runs identically in Node and browser) → @soulvault/node (contract calls, signers, ENS, state) → the surfaces that consume it: a Commander.js CLI and a Next.js dashboard. Contracts are Solidity with 60+ Foundry tests; all contract reads/writes in the browser go through viem. ENS as the config layer, not a database. On Sepolia, an org's configuration IS an ENSv2 subname registry (UserRegistry proxy deployed via the canonical VerifiableFactory, post-verified for ROLE_REGISTRAR before being trusted). Treasuries are discovered via ENSIP-11 multichain addr records (coinType = 0x80000000 | chainId), swarm/agent names carry epoch-bound expiries renewed on rotation, and EAC role bitmaps give per-name, per-role scoped delegation. Every ENS read/write dispatches through one v1↔v2 client (ensv2.ts) because v2's per-label string navigation silently breaks ported v1 labelhash walks. Event-driven everything. Both the CLI and the dashboard run off contract events ordered by (blockNumber, logIndex) — same-tx pairs like FundRequestApproved → FundsReleased render in order. The browser watcher (viem getLogs, chunked with learned per-provider range caps, 429 backoff, multi-provider round-robin transport) discovers sources at runtime. The biggest hack: deploy blocks for event-scan start are found by binary search over eth_getCode (~24 calls, cached per address in localStorage), because ENS records don't carry them. Partner technologies: Ledger DMK + Ethereum Signer Kit — hardware signing with clear-signing; verified against the official Speculos emulator (we built a test-only DMK transport over Speculos's APDU bridge since emulated devices never appear in WebHID) and a real Nano S Plus. Ledger wallet-cli Key Ring (LKRP) — the recovery redesign. Epoch keys stop being stored secrets: they're HKDF-derived from trustchain material with a key name as domain separation (soulvault:epoch-recovery:<agentId>:epoch-<n>). Any enrolled machine re-derives the key; a freshly-deployed ephemeral agent recovers its harness memories with nothing escrowed and no custodians to lose. ENSv2 — org→swarm→agent is a real registry hierarchy with EAC delegation, replacing a CBOR text-record list. ERC-8004 — public agent identity, mirrored into resolver records so ENS names reverse-resolve to agent profiles. presidio-web — in-browser PII detection feeding the redaction slots.
