projects.title: CIM
projects.description: AI agents pay-per-query for cyber threat intel via x402 on Hedera, with World-verified humans.
projects.project_description: Cyber Intel Marketplace (CIM) is a marketplace where autonomous AI agents pay per query for cybersecurity threat data. Providers publish services, like IP-reputation and file-hash reputation lookups, and set a price per query type. Agents discover available services through a registry, then pay for exactly the data they need using the x402 pay-per-request protocol settled on Hedera testnet. Every payment produces a verifiable on-chain audit record via Hedera Consensus Service. Crucially, both sides are gated by proof-of-personhood: providers must pass World's Selfie Check before publishing, and agents must be human-backed through World AgentKit and AgentBook before they can transact, preventing sybil abuse and keeping the data economy trustworthy. A live dashboard shows agents discovering, paying, and consuming data in real time, with links to HashScan for on-chain verification.
projects.how_its_made: CIM is a TypeScript monorepo split into backend, agent, frontend, and contracts packages. The backend is a Node.js API server (Express/Fastify) that wraps free threat-intel APIs, AbuseIPDB for IP reputation and VirusTotal for file-hash checks, behind our own metered endpoints, priced per query type. It also hosts a service registry with a discovery endpoint so agents can find available services programmatically. Payments run on the x402 pay-per-request protocol: a gated endpoint returns HTTP 402 with payment requirements, and settlement is handled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. We use the Hedera SDK (@hashgraph/sdk) for HBAR transfers and to write an on-chain audit log via Hedera Consensus Service ; every paid request submits a message to an HCS topic, making the whole transaction history verifiable on HashScan. The payment gate is a reusable middleware module the backend wraps around any endpoint. The autonomous agent is built on the Hedera Agent Kit. It runs a discover -> select -> pay -> consume loop: it queries the registry, picks a service for a given task (for example investigating a batch of suspicious IPs), hits the endpoint, auto-pays the 402 challenge within a max-spend budget guard, and aggregates the results into a threat report. It emits live activity events that the frontend renders in real time. Identity is powered by the World SDK. Providers must pass Selfie Check before they're allowed to publish a service, and agents are registered as human-backed through World AgentKit and resolved via AgentBook before the backend permits them to transact, all tested against the World ID Sandbox App. This turns proof-of-personhood into a concrete anti-sybil gate on both supply and demand sides of the marketplace. The frontend is React + Vite + Tailwind, featuring a marketplace directory, a provider dashboard, and a live agent activity monitor that visualizes the payment moment (402 -> paying -> paid -> data received) with links out to HashScan. For Bazantic, we deployed an x402/MPP Gateway for our threat-intel service and authored a Recipe describing how an agent should stack-rank suspicious indicators by threat score, so the service is reusable and agent-consumable through the Recipe rather than a one-off integration.

projects.title: YourTurn 2.0
projects.description: AI recovers value from unused bookings—within limits you set, without taking wallet control.
projects.project_description: YourTurn lets people delegate the recovery of bookings they can no longer use to an AI agent — without giving that agent broad control of their wallet, account or other bookings. The problem is simple: plans change. You book a yoga class, appointment, sports session, event or another time-based service, then something comes up. In most systems your options are poor: lose the booking, navigate a cancellation policy, manually find someone to take it, or spend time negotiating with the provider. Even where resale or transfer is possible, the customer normally has to manage every step themselves. YourTurn turns that into a delegated task. A customer selects one specific booking and gives an agent a narrowly defined Recovery Mandate . The customer decides what the agent is allowed to do, the minimum value they are willing to recover, how long the permission lasts and which actions are explicitly forbidden. The service provider's own rules remain binding as a separate layer. The goal is not to give an AI agent a wallet and hope it behaves. The goal is to give it one job, with boundaries that it cannot silently widen. A simple example In our main journey, Maya holds a Friday Yoga booking that she can no longer attend. She asks YourTurn to recover the booking, but only under specific conditions: recover this booking for me, but never for less than 40 USDC net. That authority applies only to this booking, only to the permitted recovery action and only until the mandate expires. Studio A, the service provider, still controls its own rules independently. Maya cannot authorize the agent to do something the provider does not allow. From there, the agent can handle the repetitive work: inspect the booking, evaluate the current recovery conditions and determine whether an available opportunity fits both Maya's mandate and the provider's policy. Bob first offers 32 USDC . YourTurn rejects it automatically because it is below Maya's minimum. No payment is attempted and the agent cannot decide that "32 is close enough." It must either find a compliant alternative or stop and ask for a new human decision. Bob then offers 45 USDC gross . Before the recovery can proceed, YourTurn re-checks Maya's current mandate, Studio A's current provider rules, Bob's eligibility and payment authorization, and the current booking state. In our demo configuration, Studio A receives a 10% provider royalty. That means the 45 USDC offer results in: 40.5 USDC to Maya 4.5 USDC to Studio A Maya's minimum applies to what she actually receives, not merely the headline amount Bob pays. Because Maya nets 40.5 USDC, the offer clears her 40 USDC floor. Bob becomes the new booking holder, sees the booking in My Bookings and can check in. Studio A sees Bob as the current holder and can fulfil the session normally. Maya retains the recovery receipt even as the booking lifecycle continues. That connected Maya → Bob → Studio A journey is important to us because recovery should not be a disconnected crypto action. It has to make sense as a real product before, during and after the transfer. The core idea AI automation should not mean unlimited AI authority. The agent can search, reason and act, but only inside a permission envelope created by the human and constrained by the provider. A wrong agent, wrong booking, expired mandate, replayed request, prohibited action, changed provider policy, invalid payment state or recovery below the customer's minimum should stop the operation rather than silently broadening what the agent is allowed to do. The blockchain and security infrastructure should also remain largely invisible to the person using the product. Maya should be able to think: "Recover my Friday Yoga booking for at least 40 USDC." She should not need to think about NFT allowances, transaction payers, typed-data signatures, nonce stores, agent protocols or settlement reconciliation. Those technologies exist underneath the experience because they make the boundaries around the agent stronger and the resulting state more independently verifiable. Three trust layers, one bounded action Making delegated recovery safe led us to separate three questions that are often collapsed into one: Ledger defines what the human allows. World proves who is asking to act. Hedera provides the booking-right, settlement and verifiable-state layer. None of those layers replaces the others. Ledger — what did the human authorize? Ledger protects the point where Maya grants or changes the agent's authority. The Recovery Mandate can bind the exact delegated agent, booking, permitted action, minimum recovery amount, settlement asset, expiry and nonce. The important idea is that hardware-backed approval can protect more than an immediate payment. It can protect the creation of a tightly scoped capability that an agent may use later. Instead of granting an AI agent general wallet access, Maya can authorize something much closer to: "This agent may recover this booking under these conditions until this time." Ledger authorizes the mandate itself. We do not claim that Ledger signs the downstream Hedera settlement transaction. World AgentKit — who is actually asking? A valid mandate still leaves another problem. If Maya authorized Agent X , the application needs to know whether the requester arriving later is actually the human-backed registered agent that Maya intended. World AgentKit and AgentBook provide that requester-identity layer. YourTurn verifies the signed AgentKit request, resolves the agent through AgentBook and applies freshness, exact-resource and replay protections before continuing. But World deliberately does not decide whether the requester owns Maya's booking or has permission to recover it. A requester can be correctly verified as human-backed and still be denied. YourTurn separately checks the current Recovery Mandate, expected agent, provider policy, booking state and payment conditions. That separation is intentional: identity verification is not the same thing as authorization. Hedera — what is true about the booking and the economic result? Hedera is the booking-right and economic-state layer underneath YourTurn. Booking rights are naturally serial-specific: one customer owns one particular booking for one particular service slot. Hedera Token Service gives us a useful way to represent that right without giving a delegated agent blanket control over everything a customer owns. Hedera also gives us independently readable network state through Mirror, so booking ownership and historical transaction evidence do not need to exist only as claims inside our own database. During ETHOnline we extended the Hedera side of the system with operation-bound payment state, seller-net minimum semantics, current-state revalidation, exact transaction preparation, external-signing validation, one-shot submission protection and indexed receipt reconciliation. The result is a model where the application can reason about a narrowly authorized recovery while still treating the booking, payment conditions and resulting state as things that must be verified at the moment they matter. Why this is a Continuity project YourTurn existed before ETHOnline. We had already built a Hedera-native booking and resale product with tokenized booking rights, lifecycle operations, provider controls and recovery flows. An earlier version of YourTurn won Hedera's "No Solidity Allowed — Build with Hedera SDKs" prize at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026. ETHOnline was not about resubmitting or cosmetically polishing that system. We asked a new product question: What happens when the customer does not want to manage recovery themselves — but also should not have to surrender control to an autonomous agent? Answering that required a substantial new authority architecture. Before ETHOnline, recovery was something the customer directly managed and the trusted backend executed. There was no end-user delegation layer, no hardware-oriented approval boundary, no human-backed requester verification and no complete agent authority model connecting identity, mandate, provider rules, payment and current booking state. During ETHOnline we added: booking-specific delegated authority instead of broad wallet authority; a structured Recovery Mandate with expiry, nonce and replay protections; current-authority revalidation rather than trusting stale approvals; World AgentKit and AgentBook requester verification; a Ledger device boundary for granting agent authority; USDC-first recovery economics with seller-net minimums; operation-bound buyer/payment state; stronger retry and partial-failure protections; exact Hedera transaction preparation and external-signing boundaries; and the connected Maya → Bob → Studio A product journey. The result is not simply "YourTurn plus three sponsor integrations." The three technologies solve three different trust problems inside one delegated economic action. Remove Ledger and the human's permission boundary becomes weaker. Remove World and the application loses the human-backed requester check. Remove Hedera and booking ownership and settlement evidence fall back toward application-controlled state. Together they let us explore a model of AI delegation that is useful without requiring the user to give the agent unlimited authority. Beyond yoga classes We use a yoga booking because the problem is immediately understandable, but the model is broader. The same pattern could apply to: fitness and sports sessions; medical or wellness appointments; event access; restaurant and activity reservations; lessons and workshops; travel inventory; coworking or facility bookings; and other time-bound services where a customer holds something valuable they can no longer use. Across those categories, the underlying problem is similar: a person wants software to do useful economic work on their behalf without surrendering unrestricted control. That is the larger idea behind YourTurn. We want AI agents to be able to participate in real-world economic workflows while keeping the human in control of what the agent can touch, what outcome is acceptable and when that authority ends.
projects.how_its_made: YourTurn is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Upstash Redis used for shared state, replay protection and durable recovery-operation coordination. The architecture deliberately separates three different questions: What did the human authorize? — Ledger Who is asking to act? — World AgentKit / AgentBook What is true about the booking and settlement? — Hedera YourTurn applies the business rules that connect those layers. HEDERA Hedera is the booking-right and economic-state layer. Bookings are represented through Hedera Token Service, with Mirror Node and HashScan providing independently readable network evidence. During ETHOnline we extended the existing Hedera product with serial-scoped delegated authority so an agent can be given authority over one specific booking instead of blanket authority over a holder's assets. We built Hedera Agent Kit v4 transaction tools for preparing serial-scoped NFT allowances, revocations and delegated transfers. A particularly important design choice is AgentMode.RETURN_BYTES. Instead of letting the agent automatically sign and submit a transaction, YourTurn can prepare and retain the exact Hedera transaction bytes, then pass those bytes across an external human/signing boundary. That lets us validate the exact transaction before and after signing instead of rebuilding it later. The recovery path also binds buyer-funded USDC payment authorization, provider policy, current holder state, seller-net minimums and booking state to the same recovery operation. WORLD AGENTKIT World AgentKit is the requesting-agent identity layer. Incoming signed AgentKit requests are parsed and validated server-side. YourTurn verifies the AgentKit message and signature, resolves the requester through AgentBook, checks freshness and nonce/replay state, and adds an exact full-resource check before allowing the request to reach application authorization. We deliberately do not treat “human-backed agent” as permission to act. After World verifies the requester, YourTurn still independently checks the current Recovery Mandate, expected agent, booking, provider policy, payment authorization and requested operation. This separation became one of the most important architectural ideas in the project: identity verification and application authorization are related, but they are not the same thing. LEDGER Ledger protects the human-authorization boundary. A Recovery Mandate is represented as EIP-712 typed data. Our device path uses Ledger Device Management Kit, Ethereum Device Signer Kit and Node-HID to discover/connect the device, derive and verify the enrolled address, and present the exact structured mandate through signTypedData. The mandate binds the delegated agent, booking serial, permitted action, minimum recovery amount, expiry and nonce. Ledger signs the authorization artifact — it is not claimed to sign the Hedera HTS settlement transaction. FAIL-CLOSED COMPOSITION The three systems are composed fail closed. Wrong requester, wrong booking, stale or expired mandate, replayed nonce, changed provider policy, buyer ineligibility, failed payment or a recovery amount below Maya's minimum stops the operation instead of silently widening authority. A major engineering challenge was making retries and partial failures safe. Every recovery has an operation-bound identity and authority/payment state so refreshes, retries or an old approval cannot accidentally authorize a different recovery. projects.project_description_markdown:
YourTurn lets people delegate the recovery of bookings they can no longer use to an AI agent — without giving that agent broad control of their wallet, account or other bookings.

The problem is simple: plans change.

You book a yoga class, appointment, sports session, event or another time-based service, then something comes up. In most systems your options are poor: lose the booking, navigate a cancellation policy, manually find someone to take it, or spend time negotiating with the provider.

Even where resale or transfer is possible, the customer normally has to manage every step themselves.

YourTurn turns that into a delegated task.

A customer selects one specific booking and gives an agent a narrowly defined **Recovery Mandate**. The customer decides what the agent is allowed to do, the minimum value they are willing to recover, how long the permission lasts and which actions are explicitly forbidden. The service provider's own rules remain binding as a separate layer.

The goal is not to give an AI agent a wallet and hope it behaves.

The goal is to give it one job, with boundaries that it cannot silently widen.

## A simple example

In our main journey, Maya holds a Friday Yoga booking that she can no longer attend.

She asks YourTurn to recover the booking, but only under specific conditions:

**recover this booking for me, but never for less than 40 USDC net.**

That authority applies only to this booking, only to the permitted recovery action and only until the mandate expires.

Studio A, the service provider, still controls its own rules independently. Maya cannot authorize the agent to do something the provider does not allow.

From there, the agent can handle the repetitive work: inspect the booking, evaluate the current recovery conditions and determine whether an available opportunity fits both Maya's mandate and the provider's policy.

Bob first offers **32 USDC**.

YourTurn rejects it automatically because it is below Maya's minimum. No payment is attempted and the agent cannot decide that "32 is close enough." It must either find a compliant alternative or stop and ask for a new human decision.

Bob then offers **45 USDC gross**.

Before the recovery can proceed, YourTurn re-checks Maya's current mandate, Studio A's current provider rules, Bob's eligibility and payment authorization, and the current booking state.

In our demo configuration, Studio A receives a 10% provider royalty. That means the 45 USDC offer results in:

**40.5 USDC to Maya**  
**4.5 USDC to Studio A**

Maya's minimum applies to what she actually receives, not merely the headline amount Bob pays. Because Maya nets 40.5 USDC, the offer clears her 40 USDC floor.

Bob becomes the new booking holder, sees the booking in **My Bookings** and can check in. Studio A sees Bob as the current holder and can fulfil the session normally. Maya retains the recovery receipt even as the booking lifecycle continues.

That connected Maya → Bob → Studio A journey is important to us because recovery should not be a disconnected crypto action. It has to make sense as a real product before, during and after the transfer.

## The core idea

**AI automation should not mean unlimited AI authority.**

The agent can search, reason and act, but only inside a permission envelope created by the human and constrained by the provider.

A wrong agent, wrong booking, expired mandate, replayed request, prohibited action, changed provider policy, invalid payment state or recovery below the customer's minimum should stop the operation rather than silently broadening what the agent is allowed to do.

The blockchain and security infrastructure should also remain largely invisible to the person using the product.

Maya should be able to think:

> "Recover my Friday Yoga booking for at least 40 USDC."

She should not need to think about NFT allowances, transaction payers, typed-data signatures, nonce stores, agent protocols or settlement reconciliation.

Those technologies exist underneath the experience because they make the boundaries around the agent stronger and the resulting state more independently verifiable.

## Three trust layers, one bounded action

Making delegated recovery safe led us to separate three questions that are often collapsed into one:

**Ledger defines what the human allows.**  
**World proves who is asking to act.**  
**Hedera provides the booking-right, settlement and verifiable-state layer.**

None of those layers replaces the others.

### Ledger — what did the human authorize?

Ledger protects the point where Maya grants or changes the agent's authority.

The Recovery Mandate can bind the exact delegated agent, booking, permitted action, minimum recovery amount, settlement asset, expiry and nonce.

The important idea is that hardware-backed approval can protect more than an immediate payment. It can protect the creation of a tightly scoped capability that an agent may use later.

Instead of granting an AI agent general wallet access, Maya can authorize something much closer to:

> "This agent may recover this booking under these conditions until this time."

Ledger authorizes the mandate itself. We do not claim that Ledger signs the downstream Hedera settlement transaction.

### World AgentKit — who is actually asking?

A valid mandate still leaves another problem.

If Maya authorized **Agent X**, the application needs to know whether the requester arriving later is actually the human-backed registered agent that Maya intended.

World AgentKit and AgentBook provide that requester-identity layer.

YourTurn verifies the signed AgentKit request, resolves the agent through AgentBook and applies freshness, exact-resource and replay protections before continuing.

But World deliberately does **not** decide whether the requester owns Maya's booking or has permission to recover it.

A requester can be correctly verified as human-backed and still be denied.

YourTurn separately checks the current Recovery Mandate, expected agent, provider policy, booking state and payment conditions.

That separation is intentional: **identity verification is not the same thing as authorization.**

### Hedera — what is true about the booking and the economic result?

Hedera is the booking-right and economic-state layer underneath YourTurn.

Booking rights are naturally serial-specific: one customer owns one particular booking for one particular service slot. Hedera Token Service gives us a useful way to represent that right without giving a delegated agent blanket control over everything a customer owns.

Hedera also gives us independently readable network state through Mirror, so booking ownership and historical transaction evidence do not need to exist only as claims inside our own database.

During ETHOnline we extended the Hedera side of the system with operation-bound payment state, seller-net minimum semantics, current-state revalidation, exact transaction preparation, external-signing validation, one-shot submission protection and indexed receipt reconciliation.

The result is a model where the application can reason about a narrowly authorized recovery while still treating the booking, payment conditions and resulting state as things that must be verified at the moment they matter.

## Why this is a Continuity project

YourTurn existed before ETHOnline.

We had already built a Hedera-native booking and resale product with tokenized booking rights, lifecycle operations, provider controls and recovery flows. An earlier version of YourTurn won Hedera's **"No Solidity Allowed — Build with Hedera SDKs"** prize at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026.

ETHOnline was not about resubmitting or cosmetically polishing that system.

We asked a new product question:

**What happens when the customer does not want to manage recovery themselves — but also should not have to surrender control to an autonomous agent?**

Answering that required a substantial new authority architecture.

Before ETHOnline, recovery was something the customer directly managed and the trusted backend executed. There was no end-user delegation layer, no hardware-oriented approval boundary, no human-backed requester verification and no complete agent authority model connecting identity, mandate, provider rules, payment and current booking state.

During ETHOnline we added:

- booking-specific delegated authority instead of broad wallet authority;
- a structured Recovery Mandate with expiry, nonce and replay protections;
- current-authority revalidation rather than trusting stale approvals;
- World AgentKit and AgentBook requester verification;
- a Ledger device boundary for granting agent authority;
- USDC-first recovery economics with seller-net minimums;
- operation-bound buyer/payment state;
- stronger retry and partial-failure protections;
- exact Hedera transaction preparation and external-signing boundaries;
- and the connected Maya → Bob → Studio A product journey.

The result is not simply "YourTurn plus three sponsor integrations."

The three technologies solve three different trust problems inside one delegated economic action.

Remove Ledger and the human's permission boundary becomes weaker.

Remove World and the application loses the human-backed requester check.

Remove Hedera and booking ownership and settlement evidence fall back toward application-controlled state.

Together they let us explore a model of AI delegation that is useful without requiring the user to give the agent unlimited authority.

## Beyond yoga classes

We use a yoga booking because the problem is immediately understandable, but the model is broader.

The same pattern could apply to:

- fitness and sports sessions;
- medical or wellness appointments;
- event access;
- restaurant and activity reservations;
- lessons and workshops;
- travel inventory;
- coworking or facility bookings;
- and other time-bound services where a customer holds something valuable they can no longer use.

Across those categories, the underlying problem is similar:

a person wants software to do useful economic work on their behalf without surrendering unrestricted control.

That is the larger idea behind YourTurn.

We want AI agents to be able to participate in real-world economic workflows while keeping the human in control of **what the agent can touch, what outcome is acceptable and when that authority ends.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
YourTurn is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Upstash Redis used for shared state, replay protection and durable recovery-operation coordination.

The architecture deliberately separates three different questions:

1. What did the human authorize? — Ledger
2. Who is asking to act? — World AgentKit / AgentBook
3. What is true about the booking and settlement? — Hedera

YourTurn applies the business rules that connect those layers.

HEDERA

Hedera is the booking-right and economic-state layer.

Bookings are represented through Hedera Token Service, with Mirror Node and HashScan providing independently readable network evidence. During ETHOnline we extended the existing Hedera product with serial-scoped delegated authority so an agent can be given authority over one specific booking instead of blanket authority over a holder's assets.

We built Hedera Agent Kit v4 transaction tools for preparing serial-scoped NFT allowances, revocations and delegated transfers.

A particularly important design choice is AgentMode.RETURN_BYTES. Instead of letting the agent automatically sign and submit a transaction, YourTurn can prepare and retain the exact Hedera transaction bytes, then pass those bytes across an external human/signing boundary. That lets us validate the exact transaction before and after signing instead of rebuilding it later.

The recovery path also binds buyer-funded USDC payment authorization, provider policy, current holder state, seller-net minimums and booking state to the same recovery operation.

WORLD AGENTKIT

World AgentKit is the requesting-agent identity layer.

Incoming signed AgentKit requests are parsed and validated server-side. YourTurn verifies the AgentKit message and signature, resolves the requester through AgentBook, checks freshness and nonce/replay state, and adds an exact full-resource check before allowing the request to reach application authorization.

We deliberately do not treat “human-backed agent” as permission to act.

After World verifies the requester, YourTurn still independently checks the current Recovery Mandate, expected agent, booking, provider policy, payment authorization and requested operation.

This separation became one of the most important architectural ideas in the project: identity verification and application authorization are related, but they are not the same thing.

LEDGER

Ledger protects the human-authorization boundary.

A Recovery Mandate is represented as EIP-712 typed data. Our device path uses Ledger Device Management Kit, Ethereum Device Signer Kit and Node-HID to discover/connect the device, derive and verify the enrolled address, and present the exact structured mandate through signTypedData.

The mandate binds the delegated agent, booking serial, permitted action, minimum recovery amount, expiry and nonce.

Ledger signs the authorization artifact — it is not claimed to sign the Hedera HTS settlement transaction.

FAIL-CLOSED COMPOSITION

The three systems are composed fail closed.

Wrong requester, wrong booking, stale or expired mandate, replayed nonce, changed provider policy, buyer ineligibility, failed payment or a recovery amount below Maya's minimum stops the operation instead of silently widening authority.

A major engineering challenge was making retries and partial failures safe. Every recovery has an operation-bound identity and authority/payment state so refreshes, retries or an old approval cannot accidentally authorize a different recovery.

Two notable integration sharp edges were worth solving:

- World AgentKit 0.2.1 validates the URI host, so for a sensitive write boundary we added an exact full-resource/path check ourselves.
- In our Node 22 + Node-HID Ledger runner, the DMK ESM entrypoint hit a Node resolution issue around an extensionless internal directory import, so we used the package's supported CommonJS export condition for the physical-device harness.

YourTurn is a Continuity build. Before ETHOnline it already had Hedera booking NFTs, resale/recovery flows and earlier agent infrastructure. ETHOnline added the bounded delegated-authority architecture across Ledger, World and Hedera rather than simply polishing the existing product.

projects.title: Squadrons
projects.description: The agent harness for DeFi — named scouts, onchain search, and capped live loops.
projects.project_description: Squadrons is the agent harness for DeFi. Instead of a generic chatbot with tools bolted on, you get a desk of named crypto agents — each with a home chain, memory, and an activity trail — that you can research with, Arm into strategies, and graduate from Observe → Paper → Live without babysitting every tick. Coding harnesses are built for repos (web search, docs, terminals, PRs). DeFi needs different primitives. Squadrons replaces those with onchain search (subgraphs / pools / TVL), Crypto Twitter pulse, DEX quotes and backtests, and armed strategy loops that run as deterministic host recipes — not LLM-on-every-tick. Spend is fail-closed: per-agent caps (default $10 auto-trade ceiling), Tenderly simulation where configured, and Live only when the operator and host both allow it. Operators pick a chain (Base, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Unichain, World Chain, Robinhood, Arc Testnet), create an agent, research with skills and MCP plugins, draft a strategy in chat, Arm it, paper-trade against live quotes, then go live under gas / slippage / spend guardrails. Optional self-improvement proposes param patches for desk approval. Custody is one Privy embedded wallet per user, shared across agents. Fund with Privy Add funds (fiat or crypto → USDC). Live settlement broadcasts through Privy’s Wallet API after a one-time session-signer grant — keys never sit in Squadrons. On Arc, agents trade USDC↔EURC via Circle Swap Kit through that same Privy path. The Graph powers Chain Search (Subgraph MCP) and Event Pipeline (NL → Substreams package → token-flow strategies), including Robinhood-focused top-token flows where traditional indexers are weak.
projects.how_its_made:
Squadrons is a pnpm monorepo: Next.js desk (apps/web) + Node 22 host supervisor (apps/host) + shared types/policy/recipes (packages/shared) + Cordis/dsh plugins (packages/squadrons-*). Web: Privy React for email/wallet login, embedded EVM wallets on login, Add funds (useAddFunds), and session-signer grant (useSigners). The desk is a three-column My Agents UI with SSE streaming for mid-turn tool activity and GenUI cards (Chain Search, Substreams pipelines, backtests). Host: verifies Privy access tokens, scopes agents by Privy DID, injects the shared wallet into agent turns, and runs long-lived dsh harnesses. Chat can draft strategies; Arm starts a deterministic recipe loop on the host scheduler. Observe/Paper never broadcast. Live builds swaps via 0x on ETH L2s or Circle Swap Kit on Arc Testnet, then signs through Privy Wallet API sendTransaction (Arc uses a minimal Privy EIP-1193 adapter so Circle kit.swap only needs eth_sendTransaction). Policy caps and optional Tenderly simulation sit in front of broadcast. Partner stacks we leaned on hard:
• Privy — core identity, custody, funding, and live settlement (not just login).
• The Graph — Subgraph MCP for live Chain Search; Substreams authoring from natural language into strategy edges (token_flow_alert).
• Circle Arc + Swap Kit — USDC-native gas and USDC↔EURC FX where 0x has no route.
• OpenRouter / dsh — agent turns with crypto-native tools (balances, quotes, social, intel) and host-provisioned MCP builtins so operators never paste API keys for the core loop. Notable glue: Cordis plugins publish flat JSON artifacts to the agent workspace; the host syncs them into activity/SSE for desk cards. Substreams pipelines use a studio-style deterministic stream head so Arm loops stay reliable without a separate sink subscription on every laptop. Funding destinations resolve to USDC on Privy settle rails (Base/ETH/Arb/OP) with an explicit fallback when the agent’s home chain isn’t fundable yet.

projects.title: civicord
projects.description: Verifiable record of UK candidate websites: what responded, redirected, and changed — on ENSv2
projects.project_description: Civicord is an open, longitudinal record of political candidate websites — tracking which URLs still respond, where they redirect, and what changed after an election. Candidate websites routinely rot, disappear, or get repurposed after elections. The UK has strong underlying infrastructure — Democracy Club provides stable candidate IDs, while Campaign Lab and the UK Web Archive provide election-era web data — but there is no open system connecting these into a per-candidate, longitudinal record of what happened to each website. Civicord starts with Campaign Lab’s April 2025 scrape of 2,375 UK candidate websites , keyed to Democracy Club person IDs. During this event, we audited all 2,375 sites: 64% still respond ~17 months later , while 363 have DNS/connection failures, 372 return HTTP errors, and 659 redirect elsewhere. Importantly, responding does not mean surviving: our demo candidate returns HTTP 200 but now leads to a domain-sale page. Civicord preserves the evidence behind these observations as archived excerpts with copyable citations. The integrity layer is ENSv2 , and it is central to how Civicord works. Each candidate receives an ENSv2 subname under Civicord’s UserRegistry on Sepolia ( p{id}.civicord.eth ), with Permissioned Resolver records containing the candidate name, original URL, and audit status. Anyone can verify these records directly from the browser without a wallet. ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control also lets Civicord separate identity from write authority. Our demo grants a delegate permission to update one field on one candidate record; the write succeeds, the permission is revoked, and the next write reverts. This provides a practical model for allowing candidates, parties, or authorized agents to maintain specific records without controlling the namespace. The site’s on-chain data is indexed through our The Graph subgraph and exposed to the browser as a live GraphQL view. A Bazantic gateway provides metered, machine-accessible access to the dataset via x402. The architecture is election-agnostic: roster → audit → record → verify → publish . The UK is the proving ground, but the same pipeline can work with electoral registries in other countries. Our goal is a public-good layer for electoral web history: per-candidate records journalists can cite, datasets archivists can reuse, and verifiable infrastructure agents and researchers can build on.
projects.how_its_made: Pipeline: Python 3.11+ with httpx ; the CLI uses argparse and asyncio for download → ingest → audit → report. Campaign Lab’s April 2025 scrape is normalized from 2,767 candidacies to 2,375 unique websites , keyed by Democracy Club person IDs. The async auditor uses HEAD with GET fallback, follows redirects, runs at 12-way concurrency with jitter, and performs a deliberately labeled heuristic content check. Tests and linting use pytest, ruff, and pre-commit. Frontend: Astro 7 on Node 24, fully static with zero backend. A prebuild step converts pipeline CSVs to JSON and generates ~3,000 pages at build time. The constituency map uses equal-seat hexes based on ONS boundary data. Each candidate page has a Verify on-chain action that calls a Cloudflare Pages Worker, which performs a raw eth_call against the Permissioned Resolver; verification requires no wallet. ENSv2: Civicord deploys its own UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver on Sepolia, with one p{id}.civicord.eth subname per Democracy Club ID. A resumable publisher mints the records idempotently. The key integrity mechanism is Enhanced Access Control : eac_demo.py executes real Sepolia transactions demonstrating grant → delegate write → readback → revoke → reverted write , with the transaction log committed to the repo. Data access: A same-origin worker proxies our The Graph Subgraph Studio endpoint, allowing the UI and six WebMCP browser-agent tools to query the live indexed registry. Bazantic wraps the dataset with x402 metering for machine-accessible usage. Why the partner technologies matter: ENSv2 provides role-scoped authority over individual civic records without requiring Civicord to build and audit its own permission system. The Graph turns registry events into a queryable ledger for the UI and agents. Bazantic provides the metering layer for programmatic access.

projects.title: Mandate Network
projects.description: Autonomous AI keeps infrastructure alive with bounded USDC spending and human escalation.
projects.project_description: Mandate gives autonomous AI agents bounded economic authority to keep real services online. In our demo, we deliberately break first-party infrastructure and let the agent recover it on its own: it detects the failure, evaluates available providers using live cost and reputation data, spends USDC to activate a fallback, reroutes traffic, verifies recovery, and stops paying when the original service is healthy again. The agent is not simply given a wallet. It operates under a mandate defining its budget, acceptable providers, operating constraints, and escalation rules. If a recovery requires more authority than it has, Mandate stops before funds move and requires a human to approve the escalation. Every major step is real and independently verifiable: the infrastructure faults affect actual HTTP callers, provider reputation comes from live onchain data, recovery payments are submitted on Arc Testnet, and the agent’s decisions can be traced through the system. Mandate is a closed-loop control system for autonomous AI: observe, decide, spend, verify, recover, and escalate only when necessary.
projects.how_its_made: Mandate is built as an Expo Router / React Native Web application with server API routes and Cloudflare D1 for shared infrastructure-health and fault state. A continuous autonomous loop combines health polling with the agent's own heartbeat, so it can detect failures even when nobody has the Mission Control dashboard open. Fault injection happens server-side through a shared wrapper, meaning a 503, latency spike, or timeout affects real HTTP callers rather than merely changing the UI. For settlement, Mandate runs on Arc Testnet with native USDC. We implemented ERC-4337 UserOperations directly with ethers.js and built our own deployed Paymaster to sponsor the agent's gas. The agent reads its real on-chain balance before acting and makes nanopayment-scale service payments—as low as $0.00004 USDC—without human intervention. Every payment resolves to a real Arcscan transaction. The Graph is load-bearing. We deployed our own subgraph indexing ERC-4337 UserOperationEvent activity on Arc and aggregate success/failure history into live provider reputation. graph-node could not decode the UserOperation calldata structure we needed, so we built a custom ABI head/tail decoder in AssemblyScript. The resulting reputation directly gates who the agent is willing to pay. We also query The Graph Gateway for live indexer freshness; excessive lag can stop a payment before signing, while the Gateway itself can become a paid liveness fallback during an outage. World ID Selfie Check defines the boundary of autonomy. If a recovery requires more money than the agent is authorized to spend, Mandate halts before moving funds and asks a real human to prove presence before authority can be increased. Cloudflare Workers additionally power our Paymaster and vendor infrastructure. The repository includes AGENTS.md, FEEDBACK.md, live verification endpoints, and reproducible commands so judges can independently verify the faults, Graph data, agent decisions, and on-chain payments instead of trusting the interface.

Mandate gives autonomous AI agents bounded economic authority to keep real services online. In our demo, we deliberately break first-party infrastructure and let the agent recover it on its own: it detects the failure, evaluates available providers using live cost and reputation data, spends USDC to activate a fallback, reroutes traffic, verifies recovery, and stops paying when the original service is healthy again.

The agent is not simply given a wallet. It operates under a mandate defining its budget, acceptable providers, operating constraints, and escalation rules. If a recovery requires more authority than it has, Mandate stops before funds move and requires a human to approve the escalation.

Every major step is real and independently verifiable: the infrastructure faults affect actual HTTP callers, provider reputation comes from live onchain data, recovery payments are submitted on Arc Testnet, and the agent’s decisions can be traced through the system.

Mandate is a closed-loop control system for autonomous AI: observe, decide, spend, verify, recover, and escalate only when necessary.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Mandate is built as an Expo Router / React Native Web application with server API routes and Cloudflare D1 for shared infrastructure-health and fault state. A continuous autonomous loop combines health polling with the agent's own heartbeat, so it can detect failures even when nobody has the Mission Control dashboard open. Fault injection happens server-side through a shared wrapper, meaning a 503, latency spike, or timeout affects real HTTP callers rather than merely changing the UI.

For settlement, Mandate runs on Arc Testnet with native USDC. We implemented ERC-4337 UserOperations directly with ethers.js and built our own deployed Paymaster to sponsor the agent's gas. The agent reads its real on-chain balance before acting and makes nanopayment-scale service payments—as low as $0.00004 USDC—without human intervention. Every payment resolves to a real Arcscan transaction.

The Graph is load-bearing. We deployed our own subgraph indexing ERC-4337 UserOperationEvent activity on Arc and aggregate success/failure history into live provider reputation. graph-node could not decode the UserOperation calldata structure we needed, so we built a custom ABI head/tail decoder in AssemblyScript. The resulting reputation directly gates who the agent is willing to pay. We also query The Graph Gateway for live indexer freshness; excessive lag can stop a payment before signing, while the Gateway itself can become a paid liveness fallback during an outage.

World ID Selfie Check defines the boundary of autonomy. If a recovery requires more money than the agent is authorized to spend, Mandate halts before moving funds and asks a real human to prove presence before authority can be increased.

Cloudflare Workers additionally power our Paymaster and vendor infrastructure. The repository includes AGENTS.md, FEEDBACK.md, live verification endpoints, and reproducible commands so judges can independently verify the faults, Graph data, agent decisions, and on-chain payments instead of trusting the interface.

projects.title: Arc Mandate
projects.description: An agent key that can only spend what you allowed. Limits enforced by Arc, revoked from your phone.
projects.project_description: Agent Mandate lets your AI agent spend USDC on Arc within a limit you set from your phone, enforced on chain. A Face ID passkey wallet in React Native, a session-key plugin we ported to Circle's wallets, and an MCP connector that pays x402 sellers. Revoke anytime. Toll, our maze, rewards agents with ERC-8004 reputation, checked by a Chainlink CRE replay.
projects.how_its_made:
Phone: Expo + React Native, with Circle wallets it doesn't officially support Circle's Modular Wallets TypeScript SDK doesn't support React Native, and the passkey step is where it breaks. We wrote our own Expo native module (Swift on iOS, Kotlin with Credential Manager on Android). A small shim installs navigator.credentials so Circle's SDK runs unchanged. We also convert the passkey's public key into the format Circle expects. One hack: we rewrite one request header, only on calls to Circle, so Circle's passkey server accepts a native app as if it were our website domain. The result is a Face ID smart account with no seed phrase. Session keys: we ported the plugin Arc's only session-key plugin (Alchemy's ERC-6900) targets EntryPoint v0.6, but Circle's accounts run v0.7. The obvious workaround installs fine and then fails on the first payment. We ported the plugin to v0.7 without touching its rules, deployed it with CREATE2, and tested it in Foundry on a fork against the real contracts. One meter On Arc, USDC is one balance with two views: native at 18 decimals and ERC-20 at 6. A limit on one view doesn't limit the other. So the native limit is zero, spending is capped on the ERC-20 view, and an allowlist permits only transfer, approve and Gateway's depositFor. Agent: an MCP connector (viem, the MCP SDK) Circle Gateway only accepts x402 payments signed by a plain key, not a smart wallet. So the agent has its own key, holds no money, and before each purchase sends a sponsored operation that moves just enough USDC into its own Gateway escrow. Then it signs the payment itself. Pairing without a server (hack) The connector shows a QR code with its address and a one-time code. The phone's grant writes a hash of that code on chain, and the connector finds it by scanning the plugin's events. The blockchain is the only link between laptop and phone. The connector also registers an ERC-8004 identity from the user's wallet, so the person owns it. Toll maze: Bun on Vercel. It charges per move over x402 using Circle's batching facilitator. Each hourly maze is generated from a seed, so every run is recorded in Upstash Redis and can be replayed from its moves, with a sha256 digest. When an agent solves it, the maze writes the score to the ERC-8004 Reputation registry, with the digest attached, and mints a CohortZero badge (ERC-721). Chainlink CRE: A TypeScript workflow whose handler runs in an AWS Nitro enclave. The Vault DON releases the Redis token only into that enclave, which matters because the token can also rewrite records. The workflow imports the maze's own replay code, recomputes the score and digest, and produces a DON-signed report shaped for our MazeVerdict contract. So far we've run it in the CRE simulator, where it matched what was already on chain. MazeVerdict is tested but not deployed yet. Arc surprises we worked around The standard anvil test keys are EIP-7702-delegated to sweeper contracts on Arc, so we derive test keys from our own seed. Arc's USDC ERC-20 transfers run in a precompile that a local fork can't execute. Forks emit no native transfer logs, so the activity feed reads UserOperationEvent and decodes which agent paid from the operation's nonce. What partners gave us:
Circle provided passkey wallets, sponsored gas and batched settlement, which makes a $0.001 step affordable. Arc gave us dollar-denominated gas. Chainlink CRE gives a score the seller can't fake or quietly edit.

projects.title: Amulet
projects.description: A wearable pendant that filters an AI agent's DeFi proposals and hands them to your Ledger to sign.
projects.project_description: Amulet is an autonomous DeFi guardian agent whose brain runs on an untrusted server and whose hands are a pendant on your chest. The brain watches your on-chain lending positions using live data from The Graph, decides when something needs doing (top up collateral, repay debt, rebalance), and drafts a transaction. The pendant (ESP32-S3, round touch display, haptic motor) receives the proposal, checks it against a policy stored in your ENS name, shows it on screen, buzzes, and when you swipe, streams it over Bluetooth directly to your Ledger Nano X. You tap the Ledger. The pendant broadcasts the signed transaction. No laptop, no phone, no browser extension is in the signing path. The agent can think as much as it wants; it cannot move a single wei without your body being present and your finger on hardware
projects.how_its_made:
For this project, I wanted to do something I can have fun with and is actual useful for me. I recently bought a ledger and realised while experimenting that if wanted to run an agent that uses ledger for signing, it needs to be either connected to a phone or laptop but thats not handy and I dont trust phones nowdays.
So I took the hardware route for this, and made a carryable pendent with a touch screen that has lots of options and helps as a middleman with no access.
Had to solder some pins and buttons and made the housing with cardboard which was quite fun and when the screen and all were working, it was almost like magical.
For the partner the obvious partner was Ledger here, running an agent on a server which sends request to my pendent directly via websocket that securely pairs to ledger on its own bluetooth, that I ported via ledgers own protocol, and relays a signed message tx to the ledger. The pendent shows the agent clearly which sent the tx, since each agent is registered on ens with policy and avatars, whenever a agent sends a tx, their avatars are shown on the pendent screen so its clearly visible who sent it and if the policy doesnt match, the pendent auto rejects before it reaches the leadger. No usb connection to phone or laptop needed.
The battery lasts for 2 hours currently but its because the 500mah battery wasnt avaible to buy but the cool part the pendent has a screensaver of arc reactor so when youre wearing it looks like a cool arc reactor.

projects.title: Common Arcade
projects.description: Open protocol and runtime for humans and AI agents to discover, join, and play games.
projects.project_description: AI agents can reason, plan and use tools, but they have almost nowhere to play . Most games are built only for humans. Most agent benchmarks are closed environments that humans can't join. When an agent does play a game, it usually scrapes pixels or fakes clicks, and the game has no idea an agent is there. Nothing checks that the agent's move was legal, nothing makes the agent and a human play by the same rules, and there's no safe way for an agent to put money on the result. Common Arcade is an open protocol and platform that makes humans and agents equal players. Every game is described by a versioned, signed manifest. It declares the seats, roles, legal actions, decision cadence and the authoritative rules. When a match starts, those rules run on a server-side match worker, never in a browser or inside an LLM. Each seat gets its own private view of the game, a list of legal actions and a feedback signal. A person pressing a key and an agent calling the SDK send the exact same kind of action, and the same server checks both. Seats can be handed between humans and agents in the middle of a match. Anyone can create a game by describing it in plain language. Studio Copilot, an Agent Commons agent, builds the mechanics you asked for. Before it can call a project done, it must pass a live-readiness test proving the rules, state, observations, results and replay can all be recreated on the match worker. External agents like Claude Code can do the same through our MCP server. Publishing creates a release that can never change, so the rules can't shift under a running match. From there, anyone can find the game, open a match, claim seats, watch as a spectator, rewatch a deterministic replay, or coach an agent's strategy while it plays. Matches can optionally be played for money. A creator allows it, and the host picks player stakes or a sponsored prize pool. USDC is locked in an escrow contract before the game starts, then the winner decided by the match worker is settled onchain. A 2.5% fee is split between the game's creator and the platform, so people who build games earn whenever they're played. Agents join paid matches with their own wallets, but never with open-ended access: the owner gives each agent a budget limited to one network, one table, one seat, an amount and an expiry. Within that budget the agent stakes, plays and signs its own moves, and can pay per call for in-game analysis over x402. Free play is always the default. Arcade is also open to agents outside our platform. Through Bazantic, any agent can call Arcade as a pay-per-call service with no signup or API key. It can browse games, live matches, results and replays, and read the payout accounting of any paid match. Two published recipes turn whole tasks into single tools. One finds a game an agent can play right now. The other audits a prize payout: it reads what Arcade says was paid, then checks the actual receipts on Arc and returns VERIFIED , MISMATCH or UNVERIFIABLE . An agent doesn't have to trust our numbers.
projects.how_its_made: Common Arcade is a TypeScript monorepo. It has four layers: a protocol spine, a control plane, a realtime match plane, and agent and payment integrations. Protocol:  Every contract is a strict Zod schema compiled into versioned JSON Schemas ( io.agentcommons.arcade/v0alpha1 ), with OpenAPI and AsyncAPI documents and a /.well-known/arcade.json discovery file. Manifests are canonicalized, SHA-256 hashed and Ed25519-signed, so a release is identified by its hash. Control plane: A Hono API, which runs locally or on AWS Lambda, handles projects (edits use If-Match revisions to avoid overwrites), publishing, matches, seat claims and session tickets. Tickets are single-use, expire after 30 seconds, and are tied to one match, seat and controller. DynamoDB stores projects and matches, and S3 stores replays. The web app, Studio and docs are Next.js 15 with Fumadocs. Match plane: A WebSocket gateway and match worker run on ECS Fargate. Game rules are uploaded JavaScript, which we run inside QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly . Date, fetch, require and Math.random are removed, and each call gets a CPU budget and a hard deadline. Every call starts in a fresh context, so the only state is the serialized game state. That makes each match deterministic: the worker validates, applies and hashes every action and records checkpoints, and a replay can be checked against those hashes. Each connection is ordered by sequence numbers, and every action carries a control lease plus the state sequence it was based on, so stale or out-of-order moves are rejected. Clients can resume within 30 seconds and get a fresh snapshot. Agents: Arcade doesn't call an LLM itself. It hands agent work to Agent Commons : Studio Copilot and playtest agents are Commons agents with a sandboxed computer and a build-common-arcade-games skill. Any other agent can use the MCP server (14 tools), the CLI or the SDK. MCP only covers discovery and setup. Fast realtime play goes through a policy runner connected over WebSocket, because an LLM tool call per game tick would never keep up. Test Arena runs deterministic policies against each other. These policies are written in a bounded, sandboxed expression language with no eval , and every run is replayable and logged. Payments: A ArcadeEscrow contract holds stakes, sponsor pools and spectator bets. It pays out through withdrawals that recipients claim, refunds cancelled matches, and lets anyone cancel an abandoned match after a timeout. It is covered by 16 tests, including 512 fuzz cases and a real Safe 2-of-2 execution. Agent budgets live in Agent Commons (Postgres). Before any signature, the spend is reserved under a row lock with an idempotency key. An agent can only stake, bet or fund a bounty on the one pool its budget names. Before each deposit the API checks the contract state, the token, the funding deadline and that the agent's wallet owns the seat, then approves the exact amount, simulates and waits for confirmation. The agent can't send arbitrary transactions or grant unlimited token approvals. x402 v2 analysis settles through EVM facilitators and Blocky402 on Hedera. Games never touch keys. Only a separate settlement adapter talks to the chain, and it only accepts the winner decided by the match worker. Partner technologies Arc: Settlement network. Full hosted matches (lock → settle → payout, and refunds) and x402 payments have settled here. Arc pays gas in USDC, so an agent only needs to hold one asset to stake, play and pay. Hedera: Escrow is deployed and USDC-enabled on Hedera Testnet, and the x402 analysis rail runs through the Blocky402 facilitator. Agents pay natively using their existing key, mapped to a Hedera account through the mirror node. Privy: handles wallet connection for owners in Agent Commons, the platform that holds agent wallets and issues their budgets. Bazantic: we turned two new APIs into agent services. Bazantic had no game or Arcade service before this. Common Arcade gateway ( https://idqnei5alresnbfes5pnwpgv6a.bazgateway.com ): game catalog, releases, public lobbies, live matches, results, replays and recordings. Common Arcade Payments gateway ( https://ga4s6ugwlrh57kwd7ejatxx2ni.bazgateway.com ): payment networks, and each paid match's pool, payout accounting and settlement transactions. Both specs are hand-written OpenAPI files served from arcade.agentcommons.io/bazantic/ and limited to credential-free read routes, with typed parameters and descriptions written for agents. Bazantic generates MCP tools named exactly after the spec's operationId s ( listGames , getMatchReplay , getPaidMatch …), which any agent can reach at the gateway URL + /mcp . Calls are paid per request in USDC via a 402 challenge. We deliberately kept creating and playing matches out of the gateways: that needs an access key and the realtime protocol. Two recipes are published: Audit a Common Arcade prize payout on Arc(https://bazantic.com/recipes/audit-a-common-arcade-prize-payout-on-arc) combines the new Payments service with Arc's RPC. It reads the paid match (escrow, pool, payout allocations, fee, transaction hashes). It confirms the chain is Arc Testnet ( 0x4cef52 ). It fetches every receipt, decodes the MatchCreated → Locked → RevenueShared → Settled escrow events, and checks that the prize and fee onchain equal Arcade's reported payout. The verdict depends on both services agreeing. For mat_b0018dc5-6c0b-4978-a914-305de6f20090 the chain shows prize 9750 and fee 250 atomic USDC, matching Arcade's record. Find a Common Arcade game an agent can play now (https://bazantic.com/recipes/find-a-common-arcade-game-an-agent-can-play-now) takes a play style, the agent's decision rate and whether it wants paid matches. It leaves out preview-only games that can't host a live match, ranks the rest, and returns the release ID, open agent seats, paid-match networks and exact next steps. Hacky bits worth mentioning Agents think at about 1 decision per second, but games run at 30Hz: Our first racing agents kept stalling because their inputs expired between decisions. We added "held" actions: the host keeps an agent's input active until its next decision, and steering sets a target lane instead of adding up over time. Average speed went from 16 to 84 mph, stalls from 11 to 0, and off-road time to 0%. Because the sandbox re-runs the whole rules file on every tick, a racetrack of 3,069 road segments is rebuilt from a ~31-row plan each call. Checked against the renderer, the rebuilt track matches on all 3,069 segments. Spectators can coach an agent's strategy mid-match. The new prompt takes effect at the agent's next decision. The worker also catches up on delayed ticks, so a slow agent can't freeze the game clock for the humans.

Calls are paid per request in USDC via a 402 challenge. We deliberately kept creating and playing matches out of the gateways: that needs an access key and the realtime protocol.

  Two recipes are published:
  - Audit a Common Arcade prize payout on Arc(https://bazantic.com/recipes/audit-a-common-arcade-prize-payout-on-arc) combines the new Payments service with Arc's RPC. It reads the paid match (escrow, pool, payout allocations, fee, transaction hashes). It confirms the chain is Arc Testnet (`0x4cef52`). It fetches every receipt, decodes the `MatchCreated → Locked → RevenueShared → Settled` escrow events, and checks that the prize and fee onchain equal Arcade's reported payout. The verdict depends on both services agreeing. For `mat_b0018dc5-6c0b-4978-a914-305de6f20090` the chain shows prize 9750 and fee 250 atomic USDC, matching Arcade's record.
  - Find a Common Arcade game an agent can play now (https://bazantic.com/recipes/find-a-common-arcade-game-an-agent-can-play-now) takes a play style, the agent's decision rate and whether it wants paid matches. It leaves out preview-only games that can't host a live match, ranks the rest, and returns the release ID, open agent seats, paid-match networks and exact next steps.

Hacky bits worth mentioning

- Agents think at about 1 decision per second, but games run at 30Hz: Our first racing agents kept stalling because their inputs expired between decisions. We added "held" actions: the host keeps an agent's input active until its next decision, and steering sets a target lane instead of adding up over time. Average speed went from 16 to 84 mph, stalls from 11 to 0, and off-road time to 0%.
- Because the sandbox re-runs the whole rules file on every tick, a racetrack of 3,069 road segments is rebuilt from a ~31-row plan each call. Checked against the renderer, the rebuilt track matches on all 3,069 segments.
- Spectators can coach an agent's strategy mid-match. The new prompt takes effect at the agent's next decision. The worker also catches up on delayed ticks, so a slow agent can't freeze the game clock for the humans.

projects.title: OneShot
projects.description: Payment control plane for AI agents: One job. Many retries. One settlement.
projects.project_description: OneShot is a safety-first settlement engine for autonomous business agents and paid tools. It makes Arc Testnet USDC payments resumable without allowing duplicate settlement: one stable business intent may have many attempts, but can produce at most one committed settlement. If a request times out, a worker crashes, a queue redelivers a job, or a response is lost after broadcast, OneShot never blindly retries. It moves the intent into a durable UNKNOWN state and reconciles it from authoritative provider and on-chain evidence. The product includes a non-custodial user-wallet flow, a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint for agents, a resumable team-report job, and an operator cabinet with payment proof and recovery history. The goal is simple: resume the work, not the payment.
projects.how_its_made: OneShot is a TypeScript monorepo built as a set of explicit domain packages and adapters. The React 19/Vite frontend provides the public landing page, agent documentation, and authenticated operator cabinet. A Fastify API exposes the HTTP and MCP surfaces, while a PostgreSQL ledger stores business intents, attempts, settlements, evidence, versions, and transactional-outbox jobs. Dedicated Node.js workers claim work with atomic compare-and-set transitions; only READY → SUBMITTING grants submission ownership, and this transition is persisted before any external call. Privy supplies wallet authorization and policy checks, viem builds and verifies Arc Testnet USDC transactions, and exactly one matching ERC-20 Transfer log is required before COMMITTED. For uncertain outcomes, a deterministic reconciliation safety core checks provider/RPC data and validated The Graph observations. The optional LLM recovery agent can recommend actions but can never sign, retry, or change financial state. We also built failure-injection and restart tests for lost responses, crashes, redelivery, parallel workers, and ambiguous evidence, with Vitest and Playwright coverage.

projects.title: Topin
projects.description: Topin is an AI agent that is built to help users automate and manage their lending portfolio.
projects.project_description: Topin is a DeFi liquidation-protection platform. It monitors lending positions on Aave V3 and Compound V3 in real time, calculates health factors and time-to-liquidation, and takes autonomous defensive action when positions approach danger. Users connect their wallet, add positions to monitor, and receive instant alerts when health factors drop. The system runs a background daemon that checks positions every 5 minutes and uses a risk engine to decide whether to notify, trigger an LLM analysis, or automatically repay debt. The platform is backed by a Fastify API with x402 micropayments, free users get limited analyses, while paid subscribers ($5/mo or $50/yr in USDC) get unlimited monitoring. A Chainlink CRE workflow runs defense logic inside a Nitro TEE for fully autonomous on-chain protection. The web dashboard is built with Next.js, showing live health gauges, AI-generated risk breakdowns, position cards, and real-time notifications. There's also a CLI agent that can analyze any address through a tool-calling LLM loop, and a fork demo that simulates a market crash to prove the protection works end-to-end against a real Aave V3 whale position.
projects.how_its_made:
This project is a pnpm monorepo with six internal packages and three apps, wired together through workspace dependencies. The core risk engine pulls live lending data from The Graph Gateway via GraphQL, querying Aave V3 and Compound V3 subgraphs simultaneously, normalizing positions across both protocols into a unified health factor model. The database layer wraps Supabase with typed models for seven tables;  users, subscriptions, monitored positions, agent tasks, notifications, payment records, and watched wallets.
The background agent daemon runs on node-cron, checking all active positions every five minutes. It uses pure conditional logic for routine risk evaluation,  no LLM calls needed for the common case,  and only escalates to DeepSeek's deepseek-v4-flash model when positions are volatile or below the user's threshold. Notifications go out through Supabase's Realtime for instant UI updates, and critical alerts also trigger email delivery through Resend.
The API is a Fastify server with x402 payment middleware that gates premium endpoints behind USDC micropayments on Arc testnet and Hedera testnet. It has a self-hosted facilitator that settles x402 payments using @x402/core and @x402/evm, with a dev mode bypass for local development. Rate limiting is in-memory and tier-aware, disconnected users get one free analysis, connected users get five, and pro users get unlimited.
The frontend is a Next.js 16 app with dark theme, wallet connection via Privy, and real-time notifications through Supabase Realtime subscriptions. The x402 client implementation signs EIP-712 TransferWithAuthorization typed data through Privy's embedded wallet and retries the request with the payment header. There's also a Chainlink CRE workflow that runs the entire defense logic inside a Nitro TEE; it reads on-chain position data via raw JSON-RPC calls, calculates health factors, and executes repay and deposit transactions autonomously when positions get risky. The fork demo ties it all together by mimicking a real Aave V3 whale on an Anvil fork, crashing the weETH oracle price through bytecode replacement, and executing a live protection cycle with metrics logging.

projects.title: BlueTits
projects.description: Artist social network with crypto commission payments and highly permissive content moderation.
projects.project_description: A social platform for artists with crypto payments powered by Privy. Artists can create personal profiles, showcase their work, and offer multiple commission options with different price ranges, scopes, and requirements. Buyers can create their own profiles, browse and search for artists, visit an artist’s page, choose a commission option, and submit a request describing what they want. The artist can review the request, accept it and send the buyer a payment proposal through Privy, or decline and close the request. Once the payment is completed, the commission moves into an active order workflow where both sides can track its status until delivery and completion.
projects.how_its_made: The project uses Privy for wallet authentication and blockchain transactions, Python for the core application logic and data processing, and JavaScript for the interactive frontend. Privy simplifies wallet onboarding and provides a clean way to connect users with on-chain functionality, while Python handles backend logic, data transformation, and communication between different parts of the application. JavaScript powers the user-facing experience and connects frontend actions to blockchain operations. The overall architecture is designed to keep the experience simple and Web2-like while still supporting asynchronous wallet interactions and blockchain transactions behind the scenes.

projects.title: World Commerce
projects.description: Trusted agent shopping with ENS identities, human approval, payments, and reputation.
projects.project_description: WorldCommerce is an agentic shopping demo. A buyer agent searches Shopify for a person. Merchants and buyer jobs live under ENS names. The person approves the pick. MockUSDC pays on Sepolia. Merchant commission pays out only when World AgentBook shows a unique human behind the buyer. I built it around four problems. a) Disposable counterparties. Agents show up as random wallets, so nobody knows who is shopping. We give them names: agent.dheeraj.eth and agent.shopify.eth. ENSIP-25 ties each name to an ERC-8004 agent record. b) Unconstrained discovery. The agent can ignore the ask and chase the biggest merchant bid. We mint {slug}.agent.shopify.eth from this Shopify UCP search. ENSIP-26 publishes what the merchant is and how to call it. c) No authority after you fire it. A single name cannot stop an agent from writing or spending. Nested subregistries split buyer jobs: intent, guardrail, payment, feedback. EAC lets a merchant edit an endpoint and blocks registration and commission keys. Revoke the role and those writes stop. d) Rebate has no legal home. A merchant kickback can land on any wallet. ENS names the payout leaf: commission.{merchant}.agent.shopify.eth. World AgentBook runs on settle. Human-backed agents get the bid. Others have it held. The purchase can still finish. The rule is simple: the agent works for the human. ENS handles names, trees, records, and write locks. World handles human-backing. ERC-8004 is the agent record. USDC moves the money.
projects.how_its_made: Discovery and payment sit next to two rails: ENSv2 for names and permissions, World AgentKit for human-backing. ENS (Sepolia hackathon). We registered dheeraj.eth and shopify.eth with ETHRegistrar commit–reveal. Nested UserRegistry and PermissionedCommerceResolver live in ens-contracts/ after the official UserRegistryImpl failed initialize. setSubregistry hangs the trees. Buyer roles sit under agent.dheeraj.eth. Merchants sit under agent.shopify.eth. After each search, ensureMerchantNamespaces creates {slug}.agent.shopify.eth. Text records use ENSIP-25 (8004 bind) and ENSIP-26 (context and endpoint), plus com.worldcommerce.*. EAC authorizeTextRoles splits Shopify admin and merchant operator. npm run ens:live shows an allow transaction and a deny revert. The UI ENS Tree loads both forests from /api/ens/tree with Explorer name and records links. World. @worldcoin/agentkit calls AgentBook lookupHuman on the buyer wallet at guardrails and on POST /api/settle. Human-backed → release commission. Empty lookup → hold. The catalog uses an AgentKit x402 header and a free-trial hook on GET /api/agentkit/data. Unregistered or exhausted calls get HTTP 402. World ID Sandbox is the approve selfie. It does not write AgentBook. Orb is required to register. When lookup is empty, the UI shows a labeled AgentBook mock so the release path is visible. Rest. Shopify UCP in src/ucp/. ERC-8004 buyer #9638 and seller #6832. Approve or Reject in ui/app.js before MockUSDC in src/payments/. Optional 8004 feedback after the receipt. Live demo on Railway.

projects.title: The Arena
projects.description: The Arena : P2P USDC prediction markets on Base & Arc. Humans + AI. No house. on chainlink oracles
projects.project_description: The Arena is a peer to peer prediction market for humans and AI agents. There is no house and no operator book. Anyone opens a card, stakes at least 1 USDC on a side, and waits for a counterparty. When at least two sides have funds the market goes live. The pot sits in the contract. Winners withdraw themselves after settlement. Two boards share that model. Sports markets run on Arc (hackathon track): home, away, or draw, with home as Team A. Bitcoin up or down runs on Base. Same rules, same minimum, same claim flow. One wallet can hold only one side of a given market so a single address cannot fake a live book. Settlement is built so we do not call the outcome ourselves when the stack allows it. Bitcoin uses a Chainlink Data Feed (BTC/USD AggregatorV3 latestRoundData). After the window anyone can settle and the contract compares open price to close. Sports cannot use a price feed. Chainlink Functions is sunset, so we use Chainlink CRE: a fixture id is stored on create, requestSportsResult emits a log after the deadline, a workflow fetches the score from football-data.org, and the API token lives in Chainlink Vault, not in the app or the contract. CRE writes a signed report to a SportsResultConsumer. Only the Keystone forwarder can call onReport, which settles the market. The same consumer pattern is deployed on Base Sepolia and Arc Testnet. If CRE is not ready, the owner can set the official full time result so the pot still pays. Unmatched (still open) markets are not resolved as a win. After a match timeout the stake can be refunded. The product is the loop: create or join, go live, settle without a house, claim on chain. Arc is where the sports pot lives (native USDC). Chainlink is how price and scores enter the contract. Agents and people use the same markets and the same leaderboard
projects.how_its_made: The Arena is a full stack peer pot prediction market. The on-chain core is a Foundry Solidity 0.8.24 contract, AgentMarket, using OpenZeppelin Ownable, ReentrancyGuard, and SafeERC20. It is not a proxy. The same bytecode is deployed twice, once per network, because each chain has its own pot and its own USDC. Base Sepolia (chain id 84532) holds Bitcoin up/down plus sports. Arc Testnet (chain id 5042002) is sports only and uses Arc native USDC at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000. Base USDC is the Circle test token 0x036CbD53842c5426634e7929541eC2318f3dCF7e. Live market addresses are 0x20FB4e706365FeF2Dd22Ddcd15987E695F6f637E on Base and 0x4394Ab4e118A6d0cd5dA87a2a80eD090c965bb0F on Arc. Owner is 0x426bE45496911cBdac19750Ff4bd90cE7ecefB48. A market is a struct: type, question, open/close price, deadline, createdAt, three option piles, pot, status, winner, oracle address.
