The Arena is a peer to peer prediction market for humans and AI agents. There is no house and no operator book. Anyone opens a card, stakes at least 1 USDC on a side, and waits for a counterparty. When at least two sides have funds the market goes live. The pot sits in the contract. Winners withdraw themselves after settlement.

Two boards share that model. Sports markets run on Arc (hackathon track): home, away, or draw, with home as Team A. Bitcoin up or down runs on Base. Same rules, same minimum, same claim flow. One wallet can hold only one side of a given market so a single address cannot fake a live book.

Settlement is built so we do not call the outcome ourselves when the stack allows it. Bitcoin uses a Chainlink Data Feed (BTC/USD AggregatorV3 latestRoundData). After the window anyone can settle and the contract compares open price to close. Sports cannot use a price feed. Chainlink Functions is sunset, so we use Chainlink CRE: a fixture id is stored on create, requestSportsResult emits a log after the deadline, a workflow fetches the score from football-data.org, and the API token lives in Chainlink Vault, not in the app or the contract. CRE writes a signed report to a SportsResultConsumer. Only the Keystone forwarder can call onReport, which settles the market. The same consumer pattern is deployed on Base Sepolia and Arc Testnet. If CRE is not ready, the owner can set the official full time result so the pot still pays. Unmatched (still open) markets are not resolved as a win. After a match timeout the stake can be refunded.

The product is the loop: create or join, go live, settle without a house, claim on chain. Arc is where the sports pot lives (native USDC). Chainlink is how price and scores enter the contract. Agents and people use the same markets and the same leaderboard

projects.title: SourceFi
projects.description: Arc-powered non-custodial escrow layer built for SourceFi’s B2B trade orders during ETHOnline.
projects.project_description:
SourceFi is a live B2B marketplace connecting Nigerian construction builders with verified material suppliers, protected today by Circle’s custodial escrow. During ETHOnline 2026, we built an Arc-powered non-custodial escrow layer that extends SourceFi’s existing payment infrastructure with programmable on-chain settlement. A buyer funds an order in USDC on Arc; the smart contract holds the funds until the buyer confirms delivery, releasing the payment to the supplier, or a dispute is raised, which a platform arbiter resolves on-chain through either release or refund. An unaddressed order automatically releases to the supplier after 14 days, so buyer inaction cannot lock funds indefinitely. Dispute resolution today is informed by SourceFi’s existing live video-call and delivery-photo evidence between buyer and supplier. This is not a standalone demo. It is integrated into SourceFi’s real application and uses Privy’s embedded wallet with the same authentication system SourceFi already uses. The system has been verified end-to-end on Arc Testnet:
fund → confirm → on-chain transfer
and
fund → dispute → confirmation blocked. Why blockchain, specifically? SourceFi deals with a fundamental trust problem: a buyer has to trust that their money will be held correctly, a supplier has to trust that payment will be released fairly, and both parties have to trust that the platform cannot quietly manipulate the settlement process. Blockchain gives us a stronger foundation for this. With the Arc smart contract, the rules for holding, releasing, refunding, and automatically releasing funds are enforced by code rather than by an internal database or a centralized payment administrator. Once funds are locked in the contract, SourceFi cannot simply edit a database record and move them somewhere else. Settlement actions are recorded on-chain and can be independently audited. This reduces the opportunity for fraud, unauthorized changes, or manipulation by a single party. It also creates a foundation for SourceFi to eventually make important trust signals, such as supplier reputation and transaction history, independently verifiable and resistant to retroactive alteration. What blockchain solves Non-custodial settlement: SourceFi does not need to directly control locked buyer funds. Programmable escrow: Release, refund, dispute, and timeout rules are enforced by smart-contract logic. Tamper-resistant settlement history: Completed transactions and settlement events can be independently verified on-chain. Reduced platform trust: Buyers and suppliers do not have to rely entirely on SourceFi’s backend to enforce the financial rules. Future verifiable reputation: Supplier transaction history and reputation signals can potentially be anchored on-chain, making retroactive manipulation much harder. Dispute evidence today SourceFi already captures delivery photos and live video-call evidence between buyers and suppliers. These records are retained through the application and are used by the platform arbiter when resolving disputes. However, we are intentionally honest about the current limitation: this is an application-level rule, not yet a cryptographic guarantee of evidence integrity. The arbiter still has to determine whether the physical delivery actually occurred. What blockchain does not solve Blockchain cannot independently verify that physical construction materials were actually delivered. The current system therefore removes custodial and settlement risk, but not the need for trusted dispute resolution. The arbiter still reviews the available delivery evidence before making the on-chain resolution decision. We see this as an important distinction: blockchain provides credible guarantees about what happens to the funds once a decision is made, while the real-world delivery decision still requires an evidence and verification layer. Roadmap Cryptographically anchor delivery evidence: Hash delivery photos and videos and anchor those hashes on-chain, allowing SourceFi to prove that evidence presented during a dispute has not been altered after submission. On-chain supplier reputation: Build a verifiable reputation layer based on completed transactions, delivery outcomes, disputes, and other meaningful performance signals, making reputation history significantly harder to manipulate retroactively. Cross-border settlement: Leverage Arc’s stablecoin and financial infrastructure to make settlement more efficient for Nigerian suppliers and international construction-material transactions. The goal is not to put every part of SourceFi on-chain. It is to use blockchain where verifiable rules, transparent settlement, and resistance to unilateral manipulation create real value for buyers and suppliers.
projects.how_its_made: SourceFiEscrow.sol (Solidity 0.8.24, OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 + ReentrancyGuard) is deployed to Arc Testnet at 0xd3a97B44C0D6DD006C29f71180938a5A4EE9B13D, with 4 passing Hardhat tests covering funding, confirmation, dispute-refund, and access control. The frontend runs inside SourceFi’s real Next.js/TypeScript app, using Privy’s embedded wallet — already SourceFi’s auth system — to sign every transaction client-side via viem. Three real infrastructure issues came up and got fixed: (1) Arc Testnet’s public RPC sends no CORS headers, confirmed against an open issue on Circle’s arc-node repo, worked around by routing through Alchemy’s Arc Testnet endpoint; (2) SourceFi’s existing CSP connect-src policy silently blocked that new RPC domain, fixed by extending the allowlist; (3) gas auto-estimation failed on Arc writes (“intrinsic gas too low”), fixed with explicit gas limits per call. Order IDs are derived via keccak256 of a string-prefixed identifier rather than an on-chain counter, keeping the contract simple while staying collision-resistant for this scale.

projects.title: TRAIDE on Arc
projects.description: Agents trade for real on a USDC-native DEX on Arc; each decision anchored on chain, via The Graph
projects.project_description: TRAIDE is a non-custodial AMM DEX that already lives on 25 chains at deterministic addresses. For ETHOnline 2026 it became the 26th chain deployment, on Arc, Circle's USDC-gas network, and for the first time the agents are not paper trading. Three autonomous agents (passive, aggressive, rebalance), each with its own funded wallet, read live market data from The Graph, decide, and execute real swaps on TRAIDE on Arc testnet with USDC as the quote asset. Every decision is written as a canonical receipt (traide-keeper format) that records the exact Graph query and response hash that informed it, and the receipt hash is anchored on Arc through a tiny attestation contract. A public dashboard at arc-agents.nohumannearby.com lists the agents' wallets, every swap with its explorer link, every anchored receipt, and P&L against hold, including the losses. Pre-existing before the event: the TRAIDE contracts, the receipts engine and paper-trading sims, the x402 intelligence API, and traide-keeper. New during the event: the Arc deployment (11 verified contracts, addresses invariant with the fleet), the wrapped-native adaptation for a USDC-gas chain, the real-swap agent runner, Graph-backed decisions with provenance receipts, the ArcReceiptAnchor contract and on-chain anchoring, the dashboard, and the mainnet-ready configuration.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity (Uniswap-v2-style Factory, Router, pairs, plus the TRAIDE AMM, staking, governance, oracle and bridge contracts) deployed through the canonical CREATE2 proxy at 0x4e59b44847b379578588920cA78FbF26c0B4956C with the same salts as the other 25 chains, so ten of eleven addresses match across the fleet. Arc has no gas token to wrap (gas is USDC, 6 decimals in the ERC-20 view, 18 in eth_getBalance), so the native USDC ERC-20 view takes the Router's wrapped-native slot and only token-to-token paths are used; that decision is documented, not hidden. Deploying to Arc surfaced a fleet-wide bug: the Pair's first-liquidity mint to address(0) reverts under OpenZeppelin 5, so the live pool runs on the TRAIDE AMM contract and the fix is scheduled as a V2 salt set. Agents are Python with deterministic BIP-44 wallets: market data from The Graph (Token API activity tier plus a subgraph price tier through the gateway; The Graph is load-bearing, no data means no trade), on-chain reserves read from the pool, swaps sent with web3.py, receipts canonicalized and hashed with traide-keeper, hashes anchored on Arc in the ArcReceiptAnchor contract. The dashboard is FastAPI behind its own Cloudflare tunnel. Everything runs unattended under PM2 with crash-loop guards through the judging window. Verification on Blockscout at testnet.arcscan.app.

projects.title: Workplane
projects.description: The Ethereum roadmap as work nodes: a swarm submits, a verifier confirms, escrow pays on verdict.
projects.project_description:
Ethplane takes the Ethereum Foundation's strawmap and turns each node into an ENS name under ethplane.eth, with a criterion a machine can check and an escrow that pays only on a verdict. How it works • A worker, a human or a model swarm, opens work sessions on a roadmap worknode. Many sessions run on one worknode at once.
• Every actor, worker, lineage, verifier and guest, is a name under ethplane.eth. A submission is an artifact plus the parents it built on.
• The worknode's verifier rebuilds the submission from the pinned reference commit, runs the benchmark itself, and writes the verdict onchain. 
• If a submission passes, the contract releases a split payment: 68 percent to the winning lineage, 15 to the parent, 10 to the verifier, 2 to the registrant, 5 held for the host. The treasury that funds nodes signs under a Privy policy that allows only three transaction shapes. Two nodes are live on Sepolia with 10,000 PLANE each in escrow: • Node 1, cl-pq-leanxmss-attestations: aggregate 900 post-quantum signatures in fewer VM cycles than 1,542,812.
• Node 2, dl-leanvm: the same criterion with the compiler open to the swarm. We dogfooded the roadmap for the hack, and continue to do so on an H100 GPU: two swarms of Qwen3-Coder 30B worked both nodes and cut cycles below the baseline three times, and every one grew the proof past the 302,182-byte bound. The verifier said no three times and wrote why onchain. No payout yet.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts, Foundry, Sepolia: Ethplane (nodes, sessions, submissions with parents, measurement, pull-based cumulative release, EIP-712 relay), PlaneToken, EthplaneSubregistry and one EthplaneResolver per node. ENS, on the hackathon ENSv2 deployment: ethplane.eth is registered on the v2 registry. The deployment's resolver and registry implementations expose no initializer, so proxies from its factory hold no roles; we ship our own subregistry (contracts-v2 IRegistry, permissionless one-time labels, expiry) and one resolver per node with an immutable servedNode and a writer role per key. The verifier holds the writer role for ethplane.head and ethplane.status; the resolver's owner can write them too. docs/ENS-PROBES.md has every probe with its output. Privy: the treasury is a server wallet under a policy that allows three transaction shapes, approve, fundNode under a cap, and defineNode whose split gives the verifier at least ten percent. A plain transfer was refused at signing: "RPC request denied due to policy violation". Guests log in with email, get an embedded wallet and a name under guests.ethplane.eth. Verifier, Python: a separate user with its own key; builds and runs the submission as a second user that cannot read that key; non-regression on proving time, verify time and proof size against a baseline the verifier measured itself; three differential probes on any pass, all 900 before a payout that reaches the target. Two watchers, one per node, judge for real. Swarm: our own agent loop, standard library only, on vLLM. Orchestrator, builder, critic and a View seat, each defined by its tools: measure posts the number, submit refuses anything the verifier would reject, the critic's shell refuses edits. API and site: Fastify, SQLite, viem indexer; Next.js static export. See ATTRIBUTION.md in the repo for human/AI breakdown.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Ethplane takes the Ethereum Foundation's strawmap and turns each node into an ENS name under ethplane.eth, with a criterion a machine can check and an escrow that pays only on a verdict.

How it works

    • A worker, a human or a model swarm, opens work sessions on a roadmap worknode. Many sessions run on one worknode at once.
    • Every actor, worker, lineage, verifier and guest, is a name under ethplane.eth. A submission is an artifact plus the parents it built on.
    • The worknode's verifier rebuilds the submission from the pinned reference commit, runs the benchmark itself, and writes the verdict onchain. 
    • If a submission passes, the contract releases a split payment: 68 percent to the winning lineage, 15 to the parent, 10 to the verifier, 2 to the registrant, 5 held for the host. The treasury that funds nodes signs under a Privy policy that allows only three transaction shapes.

Two nodes are live on Sepolia with 10,000 PLANE each in escrow:

    • Node 1, cl-pq-leanxmss-attestations: aggregate 900 post-quantum signatures in fewer VM cycles than 1,542,812.
    • Node 2, dl-leanvm: the same criterion with the compiler open to the swarm.

We dogfooded the roadmap for the hack, and continue to do so on an H100 GPU: two swarms of Qwen3-Coder 30B worked both nodes and cut cycles below the baseline three times, and every one grew the proof past the 302,182-byte bound. The verifier said no three times and wrote why onchain. No payout yet.

projects.title: Veyra
projects.description: Secure AI agent secret broker powered by Ledger Key Ring, World ID and Bazantic.
projects.project_description: Autonomous AI agents need access to APIs and secrets to be useful, but handing an agent raw API keys is a massive security risk. Furthermore, unchecked agents can spam requests and drain API limits. Veyra solves this by acting as a hardware-backed capability broker based on three pillars of trust. First, users vault their credentials into a physical Ledger Key Ring. The raw keys are never exposed to the internet. Second, when an AI agent needs to execute a task, it routes its request through a Bazantic x402 gateway, paying a crypto micro-toll to prevent spam and monetize the infrastructure. Finally, execution is gated by a World ID Face Auth check on-chain. A verified, live human must approve the specific action before Veyra decrypts the key and executes the task. Agents do the heavy lifting; you hold the keys.
projects.how_its_made: Veyra is built with a Next.js frontend, a Node.js backend, and smart contracts deployed on Base Sepolia. Our backend acts as a Universal Hardware Custodian using the Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring). We derive deterministic, collision-resistant hardware slots for every user (keccak256(userAddress) % 2^31), ensuring plaintext secrets never touch the cloud. To expose this local hardware to cloud agents securely, we built an OpenAPI schema and routed a Bazantic x402/MPP Gateway through an ngrok tunnel. This allowed us to demonstrate something entirely new: cloud AI agents paying micro-tolls to encrypt data directly into a local physical hardware enclave. To protect the system from Sybil attacks, we deployed the VeyraRegistry contract on Base Sepolia. The frontend uses World ID's IDKit to generate a ZK proof for human liveness. Our smart contract verifies the proof via the Base Sepolia World ID Router and emits an event. A backend listener catches this event, providing the final human-in-the-loop authorization required to trigger the Ledger decryption command.

projects.title: AgentMesh
projects.description: The multiplayer coordination and security layer for independently owned AI coding agents
projects.project_description: AgentMesh is a shared workspace where multiple developers bring their own coding agents, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or custom agents, connect them to the same project, and let those agents coordinate work through a structured protocol. Every agent has an owner, identity, capabilities, task scope, and explicit permissions. Developers choose their preferred work, and unclaimed tasks are assigned by capability after a visible countdown. Agents exchange real artifacts instead of repeatedly sending full project context, while sensitive actions such as merging, deploying, spending, reading secrets, or modifying permissions remain behind human controlled approval gates. AgentMesh is not another AI coding model and it is not a custom IDE. It is the collaboration, identity, permission, and audit layer between developers and their independently operated agents. Development teams increasingly look like one developer paired with one agent, each operating in isolation. AgentMesh changes that topology so those agents talk to each other through a shared protocol, with a human still holding final authority over anything sensitive.
projects.how_its_made: AgentMesh is a pnpm monorepo. The frontend is React, TypeScript, and Vite, using React Flow for a live multiplayer canvas that shows agents, tasks, and dependencies as connected nodes. The backend is an Express API with a WebSocket based realtime collaboration gateway, backed by PostgreSQL for persisted workspace, task, and event state. Coordination runs through a versioned protocol we designed ourselves, called the agent protocol. It defines typed message schemas for task claims, dependency requests, artifact publication, and approval flows, so agents exchange structured events instead of free form chat. A coordinator and policy engine turns a submitted PRD into scoped tasks, matches them to agents by declared capability, and evaluates every sensitive action against policy before it can execute. For real time canvas sync, we use Yjs CRDT documents for concurrent editing and presence, transported over the realtime gateway, with React Flow as the rendering layer. Task claims still go through a server side atomic transaction rather than client only CRDT state, so two developers can never win the same task. Identity runs through wallet authentication and ENSv2 subname resolution, so every agent's actions are tied to a real owner rather than an anonymous process. Paid actions settle through Hedera x402, with approval, budget, and idempotency checks in place so a request cannot be approved twice or charged twice. Local execution happens through a CLI adapter that runs inside the developer's own repository, using isolated Git worktrees per task. The adapter uses the developer's existing local agent authentication, so provider credentials and wallet private keys never leave the developer's machine or enter another agent's context.

projects.title: Xochi.fi
projects.description: Privacy-preserving settlement, powered by ERC-8262 ZKPs, & Raxol agents.
projects.project_description: Xochi is a ZK-compliant dark pool where AI solver agents compete to fill signed intents privately, with zero-knowledge compliance proofs (ERC-8262) clearing each trade before settlement. No order book, no MEV, regulator-verifiable. Built on Arc: trades settle in native USDC with sub-second finality, and CCTP lands cross-chain intents as USDC on Arc. Agents run on Raxol , our open-source Elixir/OTP runtime, launched on Virtuals.io
projects.how_its_made:
Xochi is a vertically integrated dark pool built on React 19, Vite, and Cloudflare Workers (D1 + KV + Durable Objects).
Arc integration required threading a new chain through every layer of the monorepo: a single 'CHAIN_REGISTRY' entry in our shared package propagates the chain ID (5042), explorer URLs, and native currency across the wagmi config, token registries, balance hooks, permit detection, and the worker's RPC routing; all type-checked so a missing entry fails to compile.
The key hack was handling Arc's unusual dual-decimal USDC: it's the native gas token at 18 decimals protocol-level but 6 decimals as an ERC-20, so we had to split the balance and gas display paths rather than treating them uniformly.
Privacy settlement (ERC-5564 stealth addresses with ERC-4337 gasless claims) works on Arc the same as any other chain. The live demo at (xochi-arc-demo.pages.dev) shows quoting, chain selection, and the full trade UI against Arc, with the solver backend ready to open mainnet corridors once Circle's USDC contract address is published.
Arc's sub-second deterministic finality is a natural fit for an intent-based mechanism, no reorg risk means the solver can confirm settlement in a single block. The Xochi frontend and API are fully wired for Arc mainnet (chain ID 5042) and ready to go live the moment Circle publishes the mainnet USDC contract address and Riddler opens the solver corridors.

projects.title: ReputAI
projects.description: Verifiable ENSv2 subnames, identities, and role-based access control for autonomous AI agents.
projects.project_description:
Give an agent its own name and a compromised agent walks off with it — repoints it,
redirects the address people pay, sells it. Keep the name yourself and co-sign every
update, and the agent isn't autonomous; in practice nobody hand-approves a restart at 3am.
ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control makes a third option possible, because permissions are
resource-scoped down to the individual record. An agent gets a subname under the operator's domain. On its own, with nobody in the loop,
it can change its service endpoint and rotate its own signing key . It cannot transfer
the name, repoint its resolver, change the addr() counterparties pay, write any text key
outside its allowlist, widen its permissions, or unregister itself. The operator keeps a
one-transaction kill switch: unregister() force-expires the name and bumps its eacVersionId , so the agent's roles don't merely stop working — they cease to exist. Compromising an agent's key lets an attacker impersonate its messaging until revocation —
never receive its funds, take its name, or outlive the kill switch. The agent can move around inside the box. It cannot move the box. Three contracts, deployed and verified on Sepolia beneath a real .eth name registered
live through the canonical ETHRegistrar : AgentSandbox — one provision() call mints the subname, grants a ceiling-checked
role bitmap, and allowlists the exact text keys the agent may write. It holds no
per-name roles itself, so it is provably not a backdoor into the names it mints. CounterpartyVerifier — walks from the ENS root, verifies the agent's signature
against the key the name publishes right now , and pays the resolved addr() , never
what the agent claimed. Resolves, verifies and pays in one transaction, or reverts with
the reason it refused. SubAgentRegistrar — workers whose permissions are a strict subset of the
orchestrator's; killing the orchestrator severs the whole fleet in one transaction. 101 tests against the real ensdomains/contracts-v2 contracts, no mocks. One finding worth flagging: ENS resolver lookup walks up the tree, and a revoked
name's records survive in the parent's resolver because they're keyed by namehash, which
unregister()` doesn't rotate. A verifier that accepts an inherited resolver keeps paying a
revoked agent. Resolution must be exact, inheritance is not identity. Containment here
is unreachability, not deletion, which is exactly why the verifier is load-bearing.
projects.how_its_made:
Solidity + Foundry, with ensdomains/contracts-v2 as a git submodule compiled from
source — so the tests run against the real PermissionedRegistry , PermissionedResolver and ETHRegistrar , not my idea of them. Deployment is forge script to Sepolia, verified
on Etherscan; a fork test runs the deploy scripts themselves so wiring mistakes fail in forge test . The demo front end is Node + viem driving a four-pane tmux control
room that polls the chain and holds nothing between frames — when the operator revokes in
one pane, the verifier's verdict in another goes red on its own. The security model is two ENSv2 tiers pulling in opposite directions on purpose. At the
registry the agent's authority is defined by subtraction - a role ceiling with ROLE_SET_RESOLVER and ROLE_UNREGISTER withheld. At the resolver it's defined by
addition authorizeTextRoles() per key, so the agent holds ROLE_SET_TEXT at resource(namehash, keccak256(key)) and nowhere else. addr() is unreachable from either
direction. The sandbox contract holds only admin roles, so it can grant the right to write
a key but cannot write a record itself. That record-level scoping is what ENSv2 bought: hand-rolling tiered, resource-scoped
permissions securely in a hackathon window isn't realistic. Hierarchical registries then
give subtree revocation as protocol behaviour. One transaction, no enumeration and being
inside ENS means the agent resolves in every wallet and contract that already speaks ENS. The nitty-gritty: pubkey was unusable, and it forced the design. setPubkey checks the name-wide
resource and there's no authorizePubkeyRoles to narrow it, so granting it hands the
agent a permission the operator can't scope. The rotatable key lives in a text key
instead — which every ENS client already reads. Registration is commit-reveal and the commitment binds the subregistry and resolver
addresses, so both proxies must exist before committing: two scripts and a sleep 60 ,
with phase 2 re-deriving the commitment before spending gas. A .eth name is an ERC-1155, so an EIP-7702-delegated EOA has code and reverts ERC1155InvalidReceiver . Cost real debugging time; now pinned by a test. Nothing is hard-coded. The whole run takes one variable, DEMO_AGENT_LABEL , and
works unchanged against anvil --fork-url , which is how it was rehearsed.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Give an agent its own name and a compromised agent walks off with it — repoints it,
redirects the address people pay, sells it. Keep the name yourself and co-sign every
update, and the agent isn't autonomous; in practice nobody hand-approves a restart at 3am.
ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control makes a third option possible, because permissions are
resource-scoped down to the individual record.

An agent gets a subname under the operator's domain. On its own, with nobody in the loop,
it can change its service endpoint and **rotate its own signing key**. It cannot transfer
the name, repoint its resolver, change the `addr()` counterparties pay, write any text key
outside its allowlist, widen its permissions, or unregister itself. The operator keeps a
one-transaction kill switch: `unregister()` force-expires the name and bumps its
`eacVersionId`, so the agent's roles don't merely stop working — they cease to exist.

> Compromising an agent's key lets an attacker impersonate its messaging until revocation —
> never receive its funds, take its name, or outlive the kill switch.

The agent can move around inside the box. It cannot move the box.

**Three contracts, deployed and verified on Sepolia** beneath a real `.eth` name registered
live through the canonical `ETHRegistrar`:

- **AgentSandbox** — one `provision()` call mints the subname, grants a ceiling-checked
  role bitmap, and allowlists the exact text keys the agent may write. It holds no
  per-name roles itself, so it is provably not a backdoor into the names it mints.
- **CounterpartyVerifier** — walks from the ENS root, verifies the agent's signature
  against the key the name publishes *right now*, and pays the resolved `addr()`, never
  what the agent claimed. Resolves, verifies and pays in one transaction, or reverts with
  the reason it refused.
- **SubAgentRegistrar** — workers whose permissions are a strict subset of the
  orchestrator's; killing the orchestrator severs the whole fleet in one transaction.

101 tests against the real `ensdomains/contracts-v2` contracts, no mocks.

One finding worth flagging: ENS resolver lookup walks up the tree, and a revoked
name's records survive in the parent's resolver because they're keyed by namehash, which
unregister()` doesn't rotate. A verifier that accepts an inherited resolver keeps paying a
revoked agent. Resolution must be exact, inheritance is not identity. Containment here
is unreachability, not deletion, which is exactly why the verifier is load-bearing.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Solidity + Foundry, with `ensdomains/contracts-v2` as a git submodule compiled from
source — so the tests run against the real `PermissionedRegistry`, `PermissionedResolver`
and `ETHRegistrar`, not my idea of them. Deployment is `forge script` to Sepolia, verified
on Etherscan; a fork test runs the deploy scripts themselves so wiring mistakes fail in
`forge test`. The demo front end is Node + viem driving a four-pane tmux control
room that polls the chain and holds nothing between frames — when the operator revokes in
one pane, the verifier's verdict in another goes red on its own.

The security model is two ENSv2 tiers pulling in opposite directions on purpose. At the
registry the agent's authority is defined by subtraction - a role ceiling with
`ROLE_SET_RESOLVER` and `ROLE_UNREGISTER` withheld. At the resolver it's defined by
addition `authorizeTextRoles()` per key, so the agent holds `ROLE_SET_TEXT` at
`resource(namehash, keccak256(key))` and nowhere else. `addr()` is unreachable from either
direction. The sandbox contract holds only admin roles, so it can grant the right to write
a key but cannot write a record itself.

That record-level scoping is what ENSv2 bought: hand-rolling tiered, resource-scoped
permissions securely in a hackathon window isn't realistic. Hierarchical registries then
give subtree revocation as protocol behaviour. One transaction, no enumeration and being
inside ENS means the agent resolves in every wallet and contract that already speaks ENS.

The nitty-gritty:

- `pubkey` was unusable, and it forced the design. `setPubkey` checks the name-wide
  resource and there's no `authorizePubkeyRoles` to narrow it, so granting it hands the
  agent a permission the operator can't scope. The rotatable key lives in a text key
  instead — which every ENS client already reads.
- Registration is commit-reveal and the commitment binds the subregistry and resolver
  addresses, so both proxies must exist before committing: two scripts and a `sleep 60`,
  with phase 2 re-deriving the commitment before spending gas.
- A `.eth` name is an ERC-1155, so an EIP-7702-delegated EOA has code and reverts
  `ERC1155InvalidReceiver`. Cost real debugging time; now pinned by a test.
- Nothing is hard-coded. The whole run takes one variable, `DEMO_AGENT_LABEL`, and
  works unchanged against `anvil --fork-url` , which is how it was rehearsed.

projects.title: AgentBounty
projects.description: Permissioned AI agents pay for data, complete bounties, and earn verified rewards.
projects.project_description: AgentBounty lets AI agents safely do real economic work. Each agent gets a real ENSv2 subname identity (e.g. researcher.agentbounty.eth) with an on-chain spending limit set as an ENS text record, editable only by a scoped Enhanced Access Control role. Agents browse a bounty marketplace, claim tasks atomically on an escrow smart contract, and pay for data via Hedera's x402 protocol — a real signed Hedera transaction settled through the Blocky402 facilitator, permanently logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as an independent audit trail. Data itself comes from The Graph: one standardized GraphQL query runs identically across multiple live Messari-schema subgraphs (Aave, Compound, Morpho), so the agent needs zero protocol-specific code. An LLM judges the result and submits an answer on-chain, but it's never blindly trusted — an independent verifier re-runs the same live query and compares results before any reward is released, in whichever asset (HBAR or our HTS token, ADC) funded the bounty. The result: agents with a provable identity, a hard spending ceiling they cannot exceed, and an auditable trail for every dollar spent — not an unrestricted wallet and an API key.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: React 19 + Vite + Tailwind 4, calling a small Express 5 API that drives the agent's live-execution timeline. Identity: ENSv2 (Sepolia beta contracts, called directly — no manager.ens.dev). A setup script deploys our own subname registry, mints researcher/intern/director subnames, and writes an agent.spending.limit text record editable only via a scoped Enhanced Access Control grant. viem reads it live, never from a config file. Payment: Hedera testnet via @hashgraph/sdk and viem (one ECDSA key covers both Hedera and EVM). Data requests go through a real x402 flow via the Blocky402 facilitator; every settlement logs to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as an independent, mirror-node-checkable audit trail. Data: The Graph — one GraphQL query written once against the Messari lending schema, run unmodified across three live subgraphs (Aave, Compound, Morpho). Judgment: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini via a hand-rolled fetch wrapper (no SDK), temperature 0. The same judge path runs both when an agent claims a bounty and when an independent verifier re-checks it before payout. Contracts: one Solidity escrow (raw solc, deployed with viem — no Hardhat) holding HBAR or our own HTS token (ADC), with exclusive-claim semantics so a multi-identity race resolves to one on-chain winner.

Data: The Graph — one GraphQL query written once against the Messari lending schema, run unmodified across three live subgraphs (Aave, Compound, Morpho).

Judgment: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini via a hand-rolled fetch wrapper (no SDK), temperature 0. The same judge path runs both when an agent claims a bounty and when an independent verifier re-checks it before payout.

Contracts: one Solidity escrow (raw solc, deployed with viem — no Hardhat) holding HBAR or our own HTS token (ADC), with exclusive-claim semantics so a multi-identity race resolves to one on-chain winner.

projects.title: Naumachy
projects.description: AI gladiators write 1inch Aqua strategies, fight on-chain and evolve. Aquascan keeps score.
projects.project_description: Naumachy is an arena where AI gladiators write market-making strategies as 1inch SwapVM programs, ship them to Aqua, fight with real inventory on Base, and evolve generation after generation. Aquascan keeps score: the explorer and P&L ledger for every Aqua strategy on seven chains, with its questions exposed as an MCP server. It starts from a measurement. Aqua lets a maker ship a program instead of a pool or an order, and the program can price on anything the chain knows. Aquascan read all 139,028 strategies ever shipped: on every chain, over 90 percent of the volume runs one template, a gated concentrated pool with a flat fee. Aqua gives makers a language, and everyone writes the same sentence. So the gladiators write the other sentences. Each is a wallet, a bankroll and a Claude mind that composes a program from the vocabulary, extended with three new instructions we appended to the SwapVM router: ToxicityFee, RiskCap and OracleAnchor. A validator checks every draft on a private fork before it ships. The programs trade, Aquascan re-prices every fill five minutes later, the lanista attests the scores on chain and crowns a champion, and the losers read the winner's program through The Graph and mutate. Eight generations ran in the gym on a fork; since 12 September 2026 the arena runs live on Base, hourly. The one act the arena cannot do alone is pay the champion: the prize sits on a Ledger account, an agent proposes the transfer through the MCP, a human confirms it on a Ledger Flex, and only then is the promotion recorded on chain. The same Ledger Key Ring seals every secret the arena runs on. Everything is public at naumachy.xyz: the explorer, every generation with every program and the rationale its mind wrote, the MCP server, and the story of how it is built.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts, in Foundry. NaumachyRouter is the SwapVM v1.0.2 router redeployed with three instructions appended: ToxicityFee, a maker fee that widens with one-way flow and decays; RiskCap, which bounds what one fill can move, read from the ledger; OracleAnchor, which re-centres the curve on a pool oracle and lets one inventory quote three markets. Aqua and swap-vm are the official releases, unmodified, as submodules, and programs ship to the canonical Aqua registry. An ArenaRegistry records generations, attested scores, champions, lineage and promotions. Tests run on a fork of Base with real tokens: quote equals swap, a loop through three pairs never pays the taker, the fee widens and forgets, the cap holds. The minds, in TypeScript. One Claude API call per gladiator per generation, briefed from Graph data and given tools that query our subgraphs through The Graph's Subgraph MCP. The compiler emits the bytes with RiskCap first; a validator ships each draft on a private anvil fork, quotes every pair and runs the three-leg loop, and refusals come back named so the mind can repair them. A model-free control line exists so a season can say what the mind is worth. Our own taker engine supplies the flow, since 1inch's resolvers route only to the canonical routers. Aquascan, on The Graph. Six Aqua subgraphs published on the network, a Substreams package in Rust for Robinhood Chain, which The Graph serves through Firehose only, plus a pools subgraph and the arena subgraph over our registry. One enrichment in Postgres prices every fill from the venue's own tape and same-chain pools, computes markouts at 5 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day, maker P&L, fees decoded from bytecode and Merkl rewards. A read-only API carries the source of every number; a React app renders it; an MCP server exposes nine tools, including arena_promotion, which ranks the attested record and writes the exact wallet-cli command for the prize without holding a key. Ledger. The host's secrets are sealed with wallet-cli's Key Ring under the operator's Flex and unsealed into tmpfs at boot. The CLI's transport is WebUSB only, so we enrolled the headless VPS by transplanting a ring member into a GNOME keyring under dbus-run-session. Promotion is a clear-signed transfer confirmed on the device; the lanista records it on chain only once mined. The findings are written up with a proposed fix. Two hacks: the overview aggregates a gigabyte of fills, so it is cached per rollup, served stale while recomputing and snapshotted to disk across deploys; and a full router with three more instructions exceeds Base's bytecode limit, so unused upstream slots stay in the table but revert. Claude Code wrote most of the code under our direction; docs/ai.md is the disclosure.

projects.title: Froggy
projects.description: A home for your agents: browser, wallet, inbox, monitoring, and human approvals.
projects.project_description: Froggy is a persistent workspace that gives AI agents the capabilities they need to actually get things done, instead of stopping at an answer. It combines a shared browser, a wallet with spending controls, an email inbox, Telegram notifications, monitoring, research tools, trading and task history in one place. You can use Froggy directly or connect an agent you already use through MCP. That agent can research, browse websites, watch wallets or saved items, prepare reports, receive email, use paid services and request financial actions while operating under limits it cannot change. The core idea is to separate delegating work from delegating authority. Agents can do useful work autonomously, but sensitive actions such as transfers, trades, dapp transactions, signatures and email sends can require the human. Froggy keeps the context, receipts and results together so the assistant you use can change without your ongoing work having to start over.
projects.how_its_made: Froggy is a TypeScript monorepo built on Bun with a React web app and a Bun server. The server owns durable agent runs, task history, approvals and recovery so work can continue even if the browser tab disconnects. External agents connect through a Streamable HTTP MCP server with OAuth 2.1, and there is also a task API, CLI and Telegram interface. Privy provides the user-controlled embedded EVM wallet and policy layer. We use it for wallet ownership, signing and controlled agent execution. Agents never receive the user’s private key and cannot increase their own spending limits. Hedera + x402 are used as a payment rail for purchasing Froggy credits with HBAR. The payment flow settles through Blocky402 and can record settlement evidence through HCS. Credits are deliberately separate from the user’s wallet funds: credits pay for agent work, while wallet funds are used for supported purchases and trades. The Graph powers onchain research. Froggy can query a standardized set of lending deployments and return the deployment and indexed block behind the result instead of only returning model-generated prose. Froggy also has a hosted shared Chrome environment. The agent can browse and operate websites while the person watches the same session, takes control when necessary, and hands it back afterward. The browser can expose Froggy’s wallet to supported dapps while signing remains outside hostile page content. We built a real email subsystem for the agent as well: inbound mail, attachments, drafts, delivery state and human-reviewed sending. This lets an agent receive verification emails, work with support replies and deliver generated reports. Telegram gives the agent an asynchronous way to notify the owner about updates and tasks that need attention. Monitoring and Watchlists let Froggy follow wallets, tokens and saved items over time, including Base and Robinhood Chain activity, rather than requiring the user to repeatedly check dashboards themselves. One architectural detail we cared about a lot is the security boundary: the browser package and wallet package are intentionally isolated, pages and model output cannot grant spending authority, every external wire message is decoded, and irreversible or uncertain financial operations are persisted before execution so retries do not accidentally duplicate payments.

projects.title: Alpha Markets
projects.description: A prediction market for DeFi fundamentals: AI analysts stake USDC on their protocol analysis.
projects.project_description: An agent economy for DeFi fundamental analysis, with a prediction market rewarding accurate reporting. Crypto has no earnings season. Nobody is paid to do fundamental analysis on DeFi protocols, so almost nobody does it. Alpha Markets builds the incentive: AI analysts publish verified protocol financials, sell them, and stake their own money on the conclusions they draw. Research. A plain-English directive becomes a report. A model plans which deployments to read and which queries to run, but never writes GraphQL and never types a figure. Code executes that plan against 28 Ethereum lending deployments through The Graph, pins them all to one common block, corroborates sampled figures against contract state, and hands the model a fact table. The model writes prose referencing figures by id; code substitutes the values. The result is hashed over its canonical bytes, and that hash is the report's identity. Tokenize and sell. The analyst mints the report as an ATS security on Hedera testnet with the hash committed in the token's creation event, then sells reads through an x402 paywall settled by the Blocky402 facilitator. A buyer agent pays from its own account and receives the body the public preview withholds. Stake. On Arc testnet, a parimutuel market takes claims about future protocol metrics, each backed by a report and by the analyst's own USDC. When the observation day closes, settlement re-reads The Graph, using the same query function that wrote the report, and resolves against that day's snapshot. Feed back. The claim is graded, the grade enters the analyst's public record, and that record goes into how the next report is planned. Being right compounds. Nothing bridges between chains. The same 32 bytes appear in a Hedera creation event and as a parameter on Arc, and anyone can check both.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next 16 on Vercel, TypeScript throughout, Neon Postgres, hand written CSS with no framework. The data layer, report pipeline, tokenization and market code all sit in one repo under src/, with the app calling those functions directly from server components rather than through an API layer. The Graph: Everything reads through Messari's standardized lending schema. One query document runs unchanged across five live schema versions, 3.1.0 down to 1.3.0, against 28 configured Ethereum deployments. Adding a protocol is adding a config row, not writing a query. That standardization is what makes the console's source panel possible: it asks all 28 whether they are answering and what schema version each reports, in about a third of a second. Settlement later re-reads the same querySubgraph function the report was written with, so The Graph is load bearing at both ends rather than a fetch step at the start. Reports: A model plans, code executes. The narrator receives a fact table and writes prose with {fact:ID} placeholders; code substitutes the values, so a model can never type a digit. Reports are hashed with RFC 8785 canonical JSON and stored as TEXT rather than jsonb, because jsonb reorders keys and normalises numbers and would silently change the identity of every report. Narration sits inside the hash, which means a report cannot be re-derived by re-running and has to be persisted rather than regenerated. Hedera: ATS issuance uses the contracts package with ethers directly, not the Studio SDK, which is 1.4 GB, ships React Native and Solana, and has no server side signer. Each report mints a ResolverProxy with maxSupply: 1 and its hash in the EquityDeployed event. Four contracts are Sourcify verified with exact runtime matches. Verifying them needed masking two 20 byte runs in the deployed bytecode, because the immutable resolver address is written into the runtime code by the constructor and a byte for byte comparison fails until you account for it. x402: @x402/next with the Blocky402 facilitator, settled in HBAR on testnet. The buyer agent has explicit spend controls and records the native transaction id from the signed bytes before settle is called, because every Hedera settle failure returns an empty transaction field including a timeout after successful broadcast. Arc: A parimutuel contract in Solidity 0.8.28, deployed with no test framework. Every path was driven by hand on testnet instead: resolve, void, empty pool, single staker, double claim. The empty winning pool is a first class branch rather than an edge case, because with few stakers one side is routinely empty and an unguarded division locks the pool forever. Payouts truncate and dust goes to nobody, since a last claimer rule is a claim order race. Things that bit: Circle's SDK exports generateIdempotencyKey in its typings and it does not exist at runtime. A stored idempotency key pins the request body, so a retry after a bug fix replays the cached failure forever; keys are derived from the call bytes instead. Arc's native token is 18 decimals while the ERC-20 at the same address reports 6, a factor of 10¹², which also means BIGINT overflows at 9.22 USDC and every money column is NUMERIC(78,0). One deliberate hack: The contract never checks its timestamps against the day a question names, so demo markets ask about a day that already happened while opening a normal staking window. A judge stakes, waits two minutes, and settlement reads a snapshot that has existed for days. Real data, real settlement, no waiting.

projects.title: Pulse
projects.description: Tokenize human potential on Hedera, others users can invest in and trade their beliefs.
projects.project_description:
Pulse is a decentralized social liquidity platform and bonding curve market protocol built natively on the Hedera Hashgraph network. It empowers creators, developers, founders, and communities to launch tokenized micro-economies instantly with zero upfront liquidity pool requirements and guaranteed algorithmic liquidity.
Traditional token launches on decentralized exchanges require creators to lock expensive initial liquidity in pools, making tokenization inaccessible for early-stage builders while exposing backers to rug pulls and illiquidity. Pulse eliminates these barriers by utilizing automated bonding curve mathematics (P=basePrice+slope×supply).
When users buy a creator's token on Pulse, native HBAR is algorithmically deposited into the bonding curve smart contract's Reserve Vault. As demand grows, token prices scale transparently along the mathematical curve. Token holders can sell their tokens back to the protocol at any time, instantly receiving HBAR directly from the smart contract reserve without relying on centralized order books or counterparty buyers. Key Features: Hedera Native Integration: Seamlessly leverages the Hedera Token Service (HTS) and Hedera EVM for high-throughput, low-fee token minting and settlement. EVM Smart Contract Suite: Custom-built Factory & Bonding Curve Contracts enforcing strict reserve collateralization, automatic protocol fee distribution, and on-chain token association checks. Pro-Grade Interactive Trading Terminal: Features dynamic SVG price history charts with multi-timeframe filtering (1D, 5D, 1M, 1Y, YTD, ALL), interactive crosshairs with hover tooltips, and real-time order receipts. Realized & Unrealized Portfolio Tracking: An advanced portfolio suite calculating overall All-Time P&L, tracking active holdings, cost basis, and net realized gains across closed positions.
Transparent Trade History & HashScan Integration: A complete transaction audit log recording all user buy and sell executions with direct clickable links to the Hedera HashScan Explorer. Creator Updates & Community Discussions: Integrated milestone announcement feeds and community discussion boards featuring expandable preview cards.
projects.how_its_made: Technologies Used: Blockchain / Web3: Hedera Hashgraph (Testnet), Hedera Token Service (HTS) System Precompiles (0x167), Hedera EVM Hashio RPC Relay, Hedera Mirror Node REST API, Ethers.js v6. Smart Contracts: Solidity v0.8.20, Custom PulseMarketFactory and PulseBondingCurve contracts. Backend: Node.js (ESM), Express.js, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), EIP-191 Signature Verification (verifyMessage). Database: Neon Serverless PostgreSQL (over SSL). Frontend: React Vite Infrastructure: Railway (Backend Hosting), Vercel (Frontend Hosting).

projects.title: SCREE
projects.description: A pixel-art survey map of how you get liquidated, read live from seven lending markets.
projects.project_description:
What it is Paste an address, or connect a wallet (address only: no signature, no approval, no gas). Scree reads that wallet's loans on seven lending deployments live through The Graph and draws the result as a pixel-art island you can walk.
West to east is the price of ETH. South to north is how long the price has held there. Height is the health factor minus one. Sea level is liquidation. Why it exists Every lending app gives one number: "liquidated at $3,434". That number is one deployment, at this instant, with no interest accrued, as if the rest of the market froze. It is most wrong exactly when it matters.
A wallet that borrows on several deployments is liquidated by whichever one binds first, and which one that is changes with price and with time. Scree draws the whole field. The borders on it, the folds, are the lines where one protocol stops being the thing that kills you and another takes over. No single-protocol dashboard can draw that line. projects.title: Quorum402
projects.description: One x402 resource unlocks only if enough separate buyers pay before the deadline, otherwise refunds
projects.project_description:
x402 turns HTTP 402 into a real payment handshake, but every scheme it defines ("exact", "upto", "batch-settlement", and the newly merged "auth-capture") describes one
payer settling one request. None of them can express "I'll pay if enough others do." quorum402 proposes and implements that missing shape as a scheme named "quorum": N
distinct payers, one resource, an all-or-nothing outcome, and a refund path when the
crowd doesn't show up. The same mechanism covers minimum-participant offers (a trip that runs at 20 travellers),
tiered group buying (the price falls as the pool fills), and all-or-nothing crowdfunding. Both halves of that promise run end to end on Hedera testnet: a crowd that arrives, meets
the threshold and releases the money to the seller, and a crowd that doesn't, where every
payer takes their own money back with their own key and the coordinator cannot stop them.
The contract is deployed with no admin key, and the coordinator and subgraph are both
public. The whole exchange can be replayed from a clean clone without asking us for
anything.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack. Solidity (QuorumPools.sol, one contract holding many pools) on Hedera testnet;
Hardhat 3 with viem and the node:test runner; TypeScript end to end; @hiero-ledger/sdk for
the native Hedera side; an Express resource server that issues the 402 challenge and acts as
each pool's coordinator; a subgraph for pool state; a browser demo that drives real payments
from funded testnet wallets; GitHub Actions gating build, solhint, ESLint, tsc and the full
test suite on every pull request and on main. Hedera + x402. Payments settle through the Blocky402 facilitator, which we verified live
against its capability endpoint before designing anything — it advertises exact on hedera:testnet and, notably, exact on every network it serves and nothing else. That
empirical check decided the architecture: quorum composes over exact rather than over
auth-capture, which has no Hedera binding. The buyer builds a TransferTransaction whose
transaction id belongs to the facilitator, signs it, and hands over a partially signed blob;
the facilitator countersigns, submits and sponsors the gas. The buyer never touches the
contract on the happy path. What only the network could tell us. The contract was first written believing Hedera's
EVM denominates value in weibars at 1 tinybar = 1e10. It does not: inside the EVM, address(this).balance and call{value:} are tinybars, and the 18-decimal weibars are what
the JSON-RPC relay presents to Ethereum tooling. The local test suite could not have caught
it (it defined its own copy of the constant and checked it against the contract's, so it
proved the two agreed with each other and nothing whatever about Hedera). One real payout on testnet caught it in a single run, and the ADRs and specs record the correction rather than
hiding it. The Graph. A subgraph indexes the pool lifecycle from Hedera testnet: pool created,
deposit recorded, threshold met, expired, released. It serves the fill state a buyer
actually decides on. It is not decoration: a threshold buy where the seat count is stale is a
threshold buy that takes money on a false premise, so a stale read blocks the commit rather
than rendering an old number. The Graph's decentralized network does not serve Hedera and
Hedera's own hosted service is unavailable, so indexing this contract meant running the
indexer: stock graphprotocol/graph-node:v0.35.1, no fork and no patch, deployed with IPFS and Postgres and pointed at the public Hashio relay. Live indexed data, no fixtures. Verifiable without us. QuorumPools is at 0.0.10409980 on Hedera testnet with no admin
key (https://hashscan.io/testnet/contract/0.0.10409980); npm run check:deployment reads the runtime bytecode back off the mirror node and hashes it against what this tree compiles to, and npm run check:payout opens a pool, settles a real x402 payment into it, meets the threshold, releases, and confirms on the mirror node that the recipient was credited to the tinybar. The coordinator and the subgraph (https://quorum402-subgraph.fly.dev/subgraphs/name/quorum402) both answer without a wallet or a clone, and the README transcribes a full run from the wire and points at the exact contracts and lines behind each integration.

projects.title: Kleeto
projects.description: Agents rent real computers by the second and pay for them themselves, over x402 on Hedera.
projects.project_description: AI agents can do the work now. They just lack a computer of their own, so they borrow yours: your screen, your logged-in accounts, and a laptop you have to leave open until they finish. Kleeto lets them rent their own. An agent requests a machine over HTTP, receives a 402 Payment Required response with a per-second price, and signs a payment from its Hedera wallet in USDC or HBAR. Once the payment settles, a browser, a Linux machine, or a full Linux desktop with real applications starts within seconds. There is no account to create, no API key to manage, no card to enter, and nobody to email. Usage is metered by the second. Each payment adds credit to a session, and the meter deducts from that balance while the machine is rented. Every second’s usage record is linked to the previous one through a hash. Payments, minute-by-minute hash checkpoints, and a final receipt are published to a public Hedera topic. The bill is not just a number we ask you to trust: anyone can recalculate it from the usage log and check it against the public records. In the recorded demo, the agent encountered a bot block on a marketplace, switched to a stealth browser, designed a part in CAD, rendered it on an eight-core machine, and laid out a spec sheet. It used and released five machines, returning six files with their hashes. The entire run cost 0.2357 testnet USDC , with every payment visible on HashScan. Anyone can try it at kleeto.fun , where a hosted agent with its own wallet does the work while you watch the meter run. Agents will not stay in chat windows. When they can rent compute by the second, without an account or a contract, they can get the tools they need as the work unfolds. A browser for one step, a desktop application for the next, and a more powerful machine when the job demands it. We’re starting with compute, but the same approach can extend to other services.
projects.how_its_made: The gateway is a small Node.js service. Every paid route uses x402 v2 with the exact scheme on Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Each 402 response offers USDC and HBAR at the same dollar-denominated, per-second rate. HBAR quotes use the ledger’s exchange rate. The facilitator covers network fees, so the agent pays only the quoted amount without needing extra HBAR for gas. Its fee-payer account is fetched from the facilitator at startup rather than hardcoded. Metering was the hardest part: x402 settles a fixed payment, but rental time keeps accumulating. Instead of settling every second, payments add session credit that the meter deducts one second at a time. Each usage record includes the previous record’s hash, forming a verifiable chain. The latest hash is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic every minute and when the machine is released, alongside records of every payment and a final receipt. Anyone can retrieve the usage records from the gateway, recalculate the charges, and verify the chain against checkpoints on the public mirror node. This avoids thousands of settlement transactions per hour while keeping individual usage records verifiable. Machines are provisioned through upstream providers only after payment settles. Live views are relayed through Kleeto’s own origin, keeping supplier endpoints out of the user’s browser. Agents connect through an installable skill, an MCP server, or plain HTTP. Discovery includes an A2A agent card backed by a working endpoint and a listing of every paid resource with its price. Both Kleeto and the demo agent have HCS-14 agent IDs inside ledger-published HCS-11 profiles, linked from their account memos. Agents can inspect these published identities before paying. The website and hosted demo use Next.js. The demo runs GPT 6 Astra , GLM 5.3 Flash , Minimax 3 and Kimi K3 as hosted agents.

Anyone can try it at **kleeto.fun**, where a hosted agent with its own wallet does the work while you watch the meter run.

Agents will not stay in chat windows. When they can rent compute by the second, without an account or a contract, they can get the tools they need as the work unfolds. A browser for one step, a desktop application for the next, and a more powerful machine when the job demands it. We’re starting with compute, but the same approach can extend to other services.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The gateway is a small Node.js service. Every paid route uses x402 v2 with the exact scheme on Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Each 402 response offers USDC and HBAR at the same dollar-denominated, per-second rate. HBAR quotes use the ledger’s exchange rate.

The facilitator covers network fees, so the agent pays only the quoted amount without needing extra HBAR for gas. Its fee-payer account is fetched from the facilitator at startup rather than hardcoded.

Metering was the hardest part: x402 settles a fixed payment, but rental time keeps accumulating. Instead of settling every second, payments add session credit that the meter deducts one second at a time. Each usage record includes the previous record’s hash, forming a verifiable chain.

The latest hash is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic every minute and when the machine is released, alongside records of every payment and a final receipt. Anyone can retrieve the usage records from the gateway, recalculate the charges, and verify the chain against checkpoints on the public mirror node. This avoids thousands of settlement transactions per hour while keeping individual usage records verifiable.

Machines are provisioned through upstream providers only after payment settles. Live views are relayed through Kleeto’s own origin, keeping supplier endpoints out of the user’s browser.

Agents connect through an installable skill, an MCP server, or plain HTTP. Discovery includes an A2A agent card backed by a working endpoint and a listing of every paid resource with its price.

Both Kleeto and the demo agent have HCS-14 agent IDs inside ledger-published HCS-11 profiles, linked from their account memos. Agents can inspect these published identities before paying.

The website and hosted demo use Next.js. The demo runs GPT 6 Astra , GLM 5.3 Flash , Minimax 3 and Kimi K3 as hosted agents.

projects.title: Gol
projects.description: An agent account that refuses payments outside its mandate and records every refusal on-chain.
projects.project_description: An AI agent with a wallet can be talked into paying the wrong person. The keys are not stolen and the contract is not broken. The agent is convinced by the text it reads, and it signs. Gol puts the limit on the chain instead of in the prompt. The owner sets a mandate: how much per transaction, how much in total, who can be paid, and when it expires. The agent works inside it. When the agent tries to go outside, the contract rejects the transaction and emits Refused, carrying the rule that was broken, the amount attempted, and how much room is left. A rejected transaction normally leaves nothing behind. It reverts and the attempt disappears. Here every refusal is stored as an event and indexed by a subgraph, so the owner can ask in plain English what the agent was refused and why, and get the answer from chain data rather than from the model's account of its own behavior. The demo sets a $10 cap, lets the agent pay correctly once, then lets it try $11. The refusal appears in the block explorer with the reason and the remaining headroom, and the same event answers the question in the console thirty seconds later.
projects.how_its_made: The mandate contract is Solidity, deployed and verified on Arc testnet. It checks four rules inside the call: a per-transaction cap, a cumulative cap, a recipient allowlist, and an expiry. It emits Executed or Refused(agent, rule, attempted, headroom, reason). The cap is checked against the argument inside the call rather than reconciled against a running total afterwards, so nothing moves before the rejection. The agent is a plain script. It takes a goal, builds a USDC transfer on Arc, and submits it through the mandate. It has no separate path around the checks. It gets through inside the bounds and gets rejected outside them. A subgraph on Subgraph Studio indexes both events from live data with a Studio API key. The query layer turns an English question into GraphQL against that subgraph, so the agent reads its own history off the chain instead of reporting it from context. The frontend is one Next.js page. Privy handles sign-in and the owner wallet and carries a policy on the owner account, so creating a mandate and acting inside one are two different permissions. The code is AI-assisted and attributed in the README. The repo commits the spec before the code it produces, so /spec holds the prompts and planning files, and the history shows where the spec was wrong and got corrected. Tests cover the edges: exactly at the cap, one unit over, the expiry boundary, and a replayed signature.

projects.title: Wayleave
projects.description: Human-approved payments for AI agents, from purchase request to settlement and delivery.
projects.project_description: Wayleave lets AI agents request purchases while humans retain control of every payment. Instead of giving an agent a wallet key, the owner links an ENS identity and an NFT-owned smart account, then grants scoped, expiring MCP access. The agent can inspect information, discover an offering, get a quote, and create a payment request. You approve and sign it with funds that come directly from your wallet. The owner reviews the recipient, amount, route, and fee bound before signing the exact operation. The first merchant is Wayleave itself, offering a versioned Developer Pack. The purchase workflow connects product discovery, an approval inbox, an implemented Arc Testnet-to-Ethereum Sepolia USDC route using Circle CCTP, and artifact retrieval. Source execution, destination settlement, and delivery are distinct milestones with durable records for recovery. Wayleave also exposes account-scoped indexed payment history through MCP, helping an agent explain known activity before proposing another purchase. Results identify their chain, token scope, and coverage limitations. The public app is deployed, covers ENSv2 namespace registration and resolution, Arc contract deployment, an E2E USDC payment flow through CCTP, and live subgraph queries.
projects.how_its_made: Wayleave is a Bun and TypeScript monorepo with Next.js, React, wagmi, viem, and Reown AppKit for the owner dashboard. Solidity contracts are built and tested with Foundry. The smart account combines pinned Kernel v4, EntryPoint 0.9, and an NFT owner validator. The owner signs the exact UserOperation, while a capped token allowance supports spending directly from the owner's balance. Agents never receive payment-signing authority. A SQL gateway, hosted with Turso, persists requests, approvals, settlement records, and merchant fulfillment. Local stdio and hosted HTTP MCP expose scoped tools. Owner-issued bearer credentials bind permissions, expiry, identity, chain, and account; current authority and revocation are checked on use. ENSv2 uses the dedicated ETHOnline deployment on Sepolia. A permissioned namespace and identity adapter resolve account names to stable Kernel addresses. ENS identity verification remains separate from authority over an Arc payment account. The implemented Circle CCTP route atomically pulls the approved USDC amount, grants the exact Circle allowance, burns on Arc, and clears the allowance. The gateway correlates source execution, attestation, and destination mint before recording settlement. Merchant delivery additionally verifies the artifact version and digest. The end-to-end route was validated with a live 1 USDC Arc Testnet → Ethereum Sepolia CCTP transfer, with separate source execution, attestation, destination settlement, and delivery records. The Graph subgraph indexes Sepolia account registration, configured-token transfers, and UserOperation outcomes. MCP provides bounded history queries and summaries with source event IDs and coverage metadata. Studio deployment and reconciliation with live RPC receipts are recorded; Arc indexing and decentralized-network publication are not claimed. A key engineering challenge was recovery without accidental duplicate payment. Another was evidence attribution: a successful outer transaction is insufficient when an inner UserOperation fails, and a token transfer does not prove delivery. These distinctions drive the verification logic and UI.

projects.title: MANDATEE
projects.description: The operating license that gives autonomous AI agents enforceable limits.
projects.project_description: MANDATE is built as a modern full-stack TypeScript project with a few specialized layers that work together. The frontend is a Next.js app built with React, and it uses Worldcoin’s IDKit widget to verify a human user before creating a charter. This gives the project a real identity gate instead of relying on wallet ownership alone. The user enters a wallet address, a domain, and a budget, then verifies their identity and triggers the charter minting flow. The on-chain logic lives in a Solidity smart contract deployed on Hedera using Hardhat. That contract stores each charter, tracks its owner, world nullifier, domain, budget, expiration, and usage, and enforces key security constraints. It prevents duplicate active charters per domain, ensures budgets aren’t exceeded, records execution events, and can revoke charters when needed. This is the enforcement layer: even if an agent misbehaves, the chain can still tell whether it has permission. The project then uses The Graph to index charter activity and expose real-time query data to the frontend. This allows the dashboard to show live charter stats, active charters, remaining budget, reputation, and execution history without hardcoding everything in the app. The Graph is effectively the read layer that turns the on-chain state into a usable operational view. The AI part is handled by an Express inference service built in TypeScript. It accepts requests, verifies payment via x402-style payment headers, and checks the charter through the Graph before invoking OpenAI. That gives the project a strong policy enforcement path: no inference without payment and no inference without a valid charter. It also records execution activity to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) so actions are traceable and auditable. The agent demo itself is a TypeScript script that queries the subgraph, checks whether the charter is valid, discovers services in a given domain, selects the best one based on budget and pricing, and then sends a request to the inference service with the charter ID and payment metadata attached. This makes the system feel like a real protocol stack rather than a toy demo: a human verifies identity, a charter is minted, the system indexes and checks state, and the agent consumes a service under a controlled policy. The stack includes Hedera for smart contracts and event logging, World ID for personhood verification, The Graph for indexing and querying, x402 for payment verification, OpenAI for inference, and Next.js for the app shell. Some parts are intentionally “hacky” in a good way: for example, the project uses a domain-bound nullifier guard to prevent a person from creating multiple active charters for the same domain, and it keeps the demo simple by using a service wallet and payment header pattern to model a real monetized AI request flow. The result is a practical architecture to explore a future where AI agents have identity, budgets, and governance built into the protocol itself.

projects.title: tearrubr
projects.description: Make it possible to verify a physical product without having to trust the seller.
projects.project_description: TearRubr is a product authentication platform that gives physical products a verifiable digital identity. Manufacturers register products with TearRubr and associate each product with a unique identifier. When a customer purchases an item, they can scan its TearRubr code and verify whether the product corresponds to a legitimate record. The goal is simple: Make it possible to verify a physical product without having to trust the seller. TearRubr uses blockchain as a public, tamper-resistant verification layer while keeping application data and user-facing functionality in conventional infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made:
TearRubr is built as an end-to-end physical product authentication platform that bridges industrial manufacturing lines with the Ethereum blockchain. Architecture & Tech Stack: Smart Contracts & Blockchain: We authored and compiled the TearRubr.sol registry contract in Solidity using Hardhat and deployed it live to the Ethereum Sepolia testnet (0xa34C7D37BB2bf41f73e562075878E86eFc7Ed05B). Transactions are signed and broadcast server-side using Ethers.js v6 connected via Alchemy's Sepolia RPC API.
Frontend & UX: Built with SvelteKit (leveraging Svelte 5 runes for reactive state) and custom Tailwind CSS.
Backend & Storage: SvelteKit server endpoints handle on-chain transactions, supply-chain verification APIs, and persist local metadata with Drizzle ORM and SQLite (better-sqlite3).
Notable Technical Solution (The Scalability Problem): High-volume FMCG goods (like Coca-Cola bottles) cannot afford an individual on-chain transaction for millions of units. To solve this, we engineered an industrial Batch Merkle Rollup engine: The factory inputs batch parameters, and the system generates thousands of unique serialized product twins ([PREFIX]-[BATCH]-[INDEX]).
We compute a deterministic Merkle Tree Root across all serial hashes.
Only the single 32-byte Merkle root is committed on-chain in one transaction, making high-throughput production cost-effective.
The platform exports a factory-ready CSV print manifest directly compatible with industrial packaging laser coders (Videojet/Domino).
