projects.title: CosmicGameSanctuary
projects.description: An indie game store where an agent buys games for you while you sleep, settled on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Cosmic Game Sanctuary is a storefront for browser games where the money and the ownership settle on Hedera instead of through a card network. The thing we think is actually interesting is that it's a games storefront where an autonomous agent is a first-class buyer, same as a person. For a person: browse with no login, sign in with just an email (no wallet popup, no seed phrase, no gas jargon), fund your wallet, buy a game, and it boots right there in the same tab a few seconds later, because the build is already pinned to IPFS and gets unpacked live in your browser. You get a GameKey, a real NFT, as proof you own it. You can also try a game minute by minute before buying, and every minute you already paid for a trial comes off the price if you decide to buy. For an agent: you put a game on your wishlist with a budget and walk away. The agent watches the store's public event feed on Hedera, and when something goes on sale it doesn't panic buy, it waits until the last responsible moment before the sale ends, checks what else you want and whether you can still afford both, asks a small model to decide only if the answer isn't obvious, then pays with its own wallet while the game itself lands in your account. It also has an ENS name of its own, and the ceiling it's allowed to spend is published as a record on that name and checked on chain before every purchase, not just asserted by us. For a developer: your build runs live in the page before you even publish it, you split revenue with your team by email (a teammate doesn't need a wallet yet, just an email, and the split locks the moment you publish, no editing it after), and your studio gets its own subname on ENS as its identity. We're deliberately not a web3 game, not GameFi. The goal is to feel like Poki or itch.io first and a crypto app never.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend is Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4. Backend is Node, Express, Drizzle over Postgres on Neon. Two of us, one repo each side, talking over a plain REST contract, with one deliberate exception below. Hedera is where the money and ownership actually live. We use the Hiero SDK (the renamed Hashgraph SDK) plus the official x402 packages for Hedera. Every game gets its own HTS NFT collection at publish time with no wipe, freeze, pause, or admin key on it, so "we can't take your game back" is something you can check on HashScan instead of something we just say. Buying a game, running a paid trial by the minute, and the agent paying for its own LLM call are all separate x402 gated routes, all settled through Blocky402 as the facilitator. The buyer never needs HBAR, the facilitator's own fee payer covers gas, and HIP-542 means a plain token transfer is enough to spin up a brand new Hedera account by itself. We also write to three public HCS topics, one for every listing and price change (so a sale's countdown is checkable by anyone watching the topic, not just printed on our own page), one for every settled sale, and one anchoring each agent's identity to the human who funds it. That last one is hand rolled against the HCS-14 spec, SHA-384 and Base58 over six canonical fields, because the standards SDK's install never finished in over four minutes and the spec explicitly allows offline derivation anyway. The agent calls Groq (openai/gpt-oss-20b) with structured output enforced, but only when a decision is actually contested, most rounds resolve without ever calling the model. It subscribes to the HCS listings topic directly instead of polling, so it costs the same whether there's 1 agent watching or 1000. Getting the decision timing right took three rewrites. The first version could only ever see one eligible option at a time, because two sales almost never start in the same second, so the hard choice the whole feature exists for never actually came up. The fix was scheduling the decision itself for the last responsible moment before a sale ends, and re-checking eligibility fresh every time instead of trusting a plan made earlier. ENS is ENSv2 on Sepolia, not just a name lookup. We deployed our own subregistry through VerifiableFactory and registered cgs-sanctuary.eth for real through commit reveal. Studio subnames mint on chain at signup with a role bitmap that only lets a studio point its own name and renew it, never unregister or transfer it away from us, same trust shape as the NFT keys above. Agents can claim a subname too, under that same scoped role, so an agent gets its own onchain identity the same way a studio does. Cosmic Game Sanctuary is a storefront for browser games where the money and the ownership settle on Hedera instead of through a card network.

The thing we think is actually interesting is that it's a games storefront where an autonomous agent is a first-class buyer, same as a person.

projects.title: Stryde
projects.description: A consumer fitness app combining onchain identity, ownership, and verifiable activities.
projects.project_description: We’re building Stryde, a mobile-first fitness app inspired by Strava, where athletes own their activity history, achievements, and reputation instead of having them locked inside one platform. Users can record runs, walks, and rides, build an onchain fitness identity, and compete through territory capture, seasons, challenges, achievements, and leaderboards. Activity metadata is stored on IPFS, while our contracts keep the important ownership and verification data onchain. We use The Graph to index our contracts and power profiles, activity history, territories, and leaderboards. Privy handles email login, embedded wallets, Smart Accounts, and sponsored transactions. ENSv2 provides human-readable athlete identities, while World ID Selfie Check is an optional verification layer for competitive features. The idea is simple: it should feel like a normal fitness app, with blockchain quietly providing ownership, identity, and verifiable history.
projects.how_its_made: Stryde is a Turborepo monorepo built with Expo, React Native, AntDesign, TypeScript, a Hono API, Solidity/Foundry contracts, and shared packages. Our contracts handle profiles, activities, territories, seasons, achievements, challenges, groups, and related assets. Larger activity metadata is stored on IPFS through Pinata, while the blockchain stores the important references and ownership data. For indexing, we use The Graph with both Substreams and Subgraphs. Substreams processes contract events, while our Subgraph models relationships between Stryde's entities. This lets us fetch things like an athlete's profile, activities, territories, contributions, and achievements together instead of making a bunch of RPC calls. Privy handles email authentication and embedded Smart Accounts, with Viem handling contract interactions. We also added retry handling around Smart Account initialization because of a provider timing issue we hit during development. ENSv2 is used for athlete identity across profiles, search, feeds, and leaderboards. World ID Selfie Check is integrated as an optional verification step for competitive features. The main goal throughout the build has been keeping the blockchain complexity out of the user's way.

projects.title: Evzi
projects.description: Intent-aware security layer that verifies AI agent actions against what the user actually wants.
projects.project_description: Evzi is an intent firewall for AI agents. The agent to worry about is not the malicious one. It is the honest one that read an instruction it could not tell was hostile — from a page, an email, a README, another API's response — and followed it in good faith. Prompt injection is not fixable with a better prompt: you cannot defend instructions using instructions. So the check has to live somewhere the agent's reasoning cannot reach, comparing the transaction against something the human froze first. You state a goal once. Evzi freezes it into an AuthorizedIntent — a hashed object carrying machine-readable constraints (chain, token, spend cap, allowed recipients, whether unlimited approvals are permitted at all), signed by the wallet whose funds it governs. The signature is what makes it hold: a hash is computed over public data, so anyone who edits a constraint can recompute it, but a signature cannot be recomputed without the key — and the key is the one thing an agent does not have. The verifier recovers the signer and refuses if it is not the wallet doing the spending. An agent then proposes transactions. Every proposal is checked against that frozen authorization, against live on-chain data from The Graph, and against Evzi's existing deterministic checks (calldata decoding, contract verification, simulation, origin trust), producing one policy: ALLOW, REQUIRE_APPROVAL or REJECT. The policy is derived from deterministic findings, not from a model — a confident LLM verdict cannot talk the pipeline out of a rejection. The demo shows exactly this. The agent reads a pool page saying "verify your wallet by sending your USDC to this address", believes it, and proposes the transfer — and is refused, because the human never authorized a recipient other than their own wallet. When it then tries an unlimited approval "so it does not have to ask again", that is refused too, and the agent narrows to exactly the 500 USDC that was authorized.
projects.how_its_made: A TypeScript monorepo: a Chromium MV3 extension plus a Hono worker on Cloudflare. The pre-existing part (May 2026, tag pre-ethonline-2026) decodes calldata, checks contracts against a curated registry and Sourcify, simulates on a Tenderly fork and classifies the origin. Built during ETHOnline 2026, on top of that: packages/intent (canonical-JSON hashing, EIP-191 signature recovery, the constraint verifier, derivePolicy), packages/onchain-context (The Graph), apps/ledger-signer (hardware signing daemon), and POST /verify, POST /agent/plan and /openapi.json on the worker. Tests went 128 to 313; the exact diff is git diff pre-ethonline-2026..HEAD. The Graph. Two products are composed and asked at once inside one budget, so the wait is the slowest single answer rather than the sum. The subgraph gateway reports the liquidity and volume behind a token in 200-500ms; the Token API reports holder counts, and /balances backs a warning about what an unlimited approval actually reaches — a wallet's whole balance, not just the amount being spent. The Token API was rearchitected mid-event by measurement: on 2026-09-10 it answered in about 10s, far too slow to hold someone waiting to sign, so it ran in the background filling a ten-minute cache; re-measured at 0.5-0.7s warm on 2026-09-12, so the verdict now waits for it and the holder count is there the first time. The cache and the fallback stayed: a source that misses the budget keeps filling the cache instead of holding the verdict, and a token counts as canonical if either product vouches for it, so one being unavailable does not blind the check. This is what catches a counterfeit USDC — its bytecode is fine and contract verification says nothing about it; only live market data separates it from the real thing. Ledger. apps/ledger-signer signs on the device but calls /verify itself first, rather than trusting whoever called it. On a REJECT the device is never contacted, so a compromised extension cannot even get a prompt onto the screen for something the authorization forbids — there is no tap to fool anyone into making. Verified end to end on a physical Nano S against the deployed verifier, recovering the signer address from the signature over the exact serialized transaction to prove the device signed what we asked. Bazantic. POST /verify is the reusable artifact: stateless, deterministic, no LLM in the loop, and it decodes the proposed calldata itself rather than trusting the caller's description of it. It is published as a Recipe with an MCP gateway that holds the API credential and injects it upstream, so a calling agent sends no key of its own. The required A/B is in apps/judge/ab — 11 proposals against one authorization, 3 trials each: the verifier took violations caught from 18/27 to 27/27. The honest result is that the Recipe layer measurably did not add accuracy on top of the raw API, and we report that rather than fish for a favourable configuration. Uniswap is used but not claimed: the v3 subgraphs and the protocol registry are load-bearing (without them every legitimate swap approval reads as a transfer to a stranger), but the integration is a consumer's, not a contributor's.

projects.title: ZoneGo
projects.description: The merchant pays $0.05 only when a verified human walks in. The visitor gets paid to explore.
projects.project_description: ZoneGo is a Web3 advertising network that flips how local ads work: instead of paying per click or impression, a merchant pays only when a real, unique, verified human physically walks into their store. A neighbor searches for what they need, picks a nearby store on a real map, walks over, and scans a QR the merchant shows at the counter. The merchant's device signs an EIP-712 visit signature on the spot, the contract verifies it on-chain, and USDC lands in the visitor's wallet in seconds — no app download, no seed phrase, no crypto knowledge required on either side. World ID's Selfie Check proves the visitor is a unique human before they can claim, closing the one attack that would otherwise kill the economics: a single person farming visits with many wallets. Privy gives both the merchant and the visitor an embedded wallet from just an email or phone number. The Graph indexes every visit and payout so the leaderboard and the merchant's own dashboard are provably not something we could fake or edit after the fact.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity on Base Sepolia. CampaignVault holds each merchant's USDC budget; VisitRegistry verifies the merchant's EIP-712 signature over (campaignId, nonce, expiry, geohash, visitor) and pays out — the merchant's own wallet signs the visit, so the backend never has authority to invent one. Tested with Foundry. Backend: FastAPI relay that pays gas on the visitor's behalf (a convenience, not a requirement — the visitor could submit the same signed call themselves). It calls World's Selfie Check to mint a short-lived attestation, and relays the claim to the contract using web3.py. Frontend: React + Vite. Campaigns are anchored to a merchant's real GPS location or to an address they type, geocoded with OpenStreetMap's Nominatim — no Google API key exists in this project, so the map itself is Leaflet tiles over OpenStreetMap too. Geohash encoding matching Solidity's bytes32 packing was written and verified from scratch, including a byte-for-byte check against a known-good on-chain transaction before ever sending a real one. The Graph indexes CampaignCreated/VisitRecorded/RewardPaid events for the leaderboard and merchant dashboard, so neither reads from a database we control. Notable hack: the QR shown to the merchant originally encoded the full EIP-712 domain and type definitions every time, which made it too dense for a phone camera to read off a screen. Since that schema never changes, we cut the payload roughly in half by hardcoding it on the scanning side instead of transmitting it — the difference between a QR that scans and one that doesn't.

projects.title: DriftFee
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that adjusts fees based on whether trades push prices further from equilibrium.
projects.project_description: DriftFee is a Uniswap v4 dynamic fee hook designed to reduce adverse selection against liquidity providers. Traditional AMMs charge the same fee to every trade, even though some trades may push the pool price further away from its recent equilibrium and potentially represent more informed or toxic order flow. DriftFee tracks a time-weighted reference price using the pool’s tick. For each swap, it compares the current price direction with this reference. Trades that push the price further away from the recent equilibrium pay a higher LP fee, while mean-reverting trades can receive a lower fee within predefined safety bounds. The goal is to make liquidity pricing more responsive to the direction and potential impact of order flow rather than relying only on static fees or symmetric volatility. All adjusted fees remain LP fees and flow directly to the pool’s liquidity providers through Uniswap v4’s native accounting. The project also focuses on adversarial safety. DriftFee is designed with bounded fees and tests around round-trip trading to ensure that fee discounts cannot be exploited to create an artificial profitable cycle.
projects.how_its_made: Tech stack: Solidity 0.8.26 (EVM Cancun), Uniswap v4 hooks, Foundry, OpenZeppelin utilities, CREATE2 salt mining. Architecture: The core challenge was pricing swaps by drift — how far they move the pool from equilibrium — without letting attackers manipulate the reference price via flash loans. The solution uses a time-decayed moving average of top-of-block ticks rather than spot price, sampled once per block.timestamp. The reference is folded forward with exponential decay, capped at 20% per update, so holding a manipulated price requires crossing many blocks against arbitrage. Two-step fee charging: beforeSwap sets a floor fee (minFee) that flows through the pool's normal accounting to LPs. afterSwap then measures the actual drift path the swap traced — integrating an adjustment over that path rather than pricing endpoints — and donates the remainder as an immediate top-up to in-range LPs. This prevents the owner from extracting fees; they're always donated. Path integration fixed two earlier attacks: Previous designs priced swap endpoints, which let traders split a trade 40 ways to collapse drift as O(V/N), recovering 67 bps against the hook. Integration over the path makes splitting a no-op — the cap sits inside the integral so clamping cannot be gamed. Crossing equilibrium isn't discounted (no net drift earned), killing the pre-move arbitrage. Testing: Adversarial review found and broke two earlier versions. The production design is covered by unit + fuzz tests, handler-driven invariants, and fork tests against the real deployed PoolManager on mainnet USDC/WETH (6/18 decimals, realistic prices). Deployment uses CREATE2 salt mining to hit the required permission bits.

projects.title: Tally
projects.description: A shop's revenue becomes a bond: Chainlink prices it privately, Hedera issues and repays it.
projects.project_description:
Tally turns a small business's real revenue into a short-term, fixed-rate bond. It's underwritten in private, priced in public, and pays itself back. THE PROBLEM
Many small shops have a year of steady card sales but no bank credit history. They can't borrow against the one thing that actually predicts repayment: their revenue. When they do get credit, underwriting is manual, opaque and one-off, and a good repayment record never follows them to their next lender. HOW TALLY WORKS Connect revenue. A business registers and connects its Stripe account through Stripe Connect. Tally reads its real charges directly; the business never types in a number. Underwrite. Tally boils the sales history down to three facts: revenue over the last 90 days, how many days of history exist, and how much daily sales swing (volatility). A fixed, transparent policy decides. It needs at least 30 days of history, at least $3,000 of 90-day revenue, and volatility under a cap. The coupon (interest) rate starts at 4% and rises with volatility. The same policy runs live on Chainlink's network as a CRE workflow. Nine independent Chainlink nodes read the revenue through an authenticated API and agree on the verdict, and only the verdict is reported, never the raw revenue. Issue. An approved business gets a real fixed-rate bond, issued on Hedera testnet through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, with its units minted to Tally's custodian account. Pay itself back. Each coupon payment is a Hedera Scheduled Transaction that waits for its due date. The Hedera network executes the payment by itself, with no bot, no cron job and nobody pressing a button, and sends real HBAR to the bondholder. Tally then uses the network's own timestamp to record whether each payment was on time, and writes that result on-chain. Resell. A secondary market lets bondholders list and sell their bonds. The bond token enforces compliance itself: a buyer who hasn't passed KYC is rejected on-chain by the token contract, not by our website. Build a public credit record. Every bond's lifecycle (issued, coupon paid on time or late, resold, redeemed) is indexed by a subgraph on The Graph, so any future lender can look up an issuer's repayment history before lending again.
projects.how_its_made:
Tally is a pnpm + Turborepo TypeScript monorepo: A Next.js 15 web app, deployed on Vercel, with its data in Postgres (Neon).
Four shared packages: seam (shared types and fixed-point money), underwriting (revenue snapshot and pricing policy), ats-client (Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio) and scheduler (Hedera Scheduled Transactions).
Solidity contracts built with Foundry, a subgraph, and a Chainlink CRE workflow.
Money is never a float. Every amount is a 6-decimal fixed-point bigint end to end, from Stripe charges through underwriting to the bond's face value. HEDERA — three services, each doing real work: Asset Tokenization Studio issues a genuine fixed-rate bond, not a token we made up. Compliance comes built in: KYC, whitelists and transfer restrictions are enforced inside the token itself, so when an account without KYC tried to buy on our secondary market, the token contract rejected it on-chain.
Scheduled Transactions with setWaitForExpiry(true) are the whole settlement engine. Each coupon payment executes by itself at its due date, with no keeper bot or cron job. Hedera won't schedule more than about 60 days ahead, so Tally stores the full coupon calendar at issuance and a background job schedules each coupon once it comes within range.
The Mirror Node is our source of truth. Whether a payment was on time comes from the network's own consensus timestamp, and the secondary-market order book is rebuilt from contract event logs rather than a database table.
THE HACKIEST PART — signing Hedera ATS transactions from a server:
The ATS SDK only signs inside a web browser: it checks for window, then needs a MetaMask-style window.ethereum. It fails in plain Node.js, and faking window only moves the error somewhere else. So Tally launches a real headless Chromium with Playwright, injects a minimal EIP-1193 wallet backed by an ethers wallet holding the custodian key, and loads an esbuild bundle of the SDK from http://localhost. It has to be localhost, because the SDK calls crypto.randomUUID(), which only works on a secure origin. Getting the SDK to bundle for the browser took four tricks: stubbing server-only logging and custodial-wallet modules it imports whether or not they're used
pointing the Hedera SDK import at its browser build by absolute file path, because esbuild ignores the browser field when exports is present
defining global as globalThis
working around an SDK quirk where a 0.0.x account ID resolves to a different EVM address than the one actually holding the tokens
CHAINLINK CRE — decentralised credit decisions:
The underwriting workflow is written in TypeScript with the CRE SDK and deployed live to Chainlink's private registry. Every minute it fetches a business's revenue snapshot using a secret held by CRE, applies the same policy as our underwriting package, and reports only approve/decline and the coupon rate, never the raw revenue. Nine independent nodes compute the verdict and reach consensus, so the credit decision doesn't depend on trusting our server. It's built to keep revenue inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) once Chainlink enables confidential execution for our private-beta workflow. THE GRAPH — a public credit record:
A subgraph indexes each bond's lifecycle events (issued, coupon, resale, redeemed, defaulted) into per-issuer standings: bonds issued, coupons on time and coupons late. Repayment history becomes a public, queryable record that follows the business to its next lender. Subgraph Studio can't index Hedera, so we also deploy the contracts to Ethereum Sepolia and index that copy. STRIPE:
Stripe Connect OAuth reads each business's charges from its own Stripe account. Charges are de-duplicated by ID, so revenue is never counted twice. For testing, Stripe Test Clocks create genuinely backdated paid invoices through Stripe's own API instead of fake database rows. SECURITY:
Any route that moves value (issuing a bond, arming coupons, listing or filling orders) refuses requests that come through a proxy or tunnel unless they carry an admin token, and the hosted site refuses them entirely. The revenue endpoint Chainlink reads checks its secret token in constant time.

projects.title: edgraph
projects.description: Autonomous depeg coverage: AI buys evidence when justified, transparent rules recommend approval.
projects.project_description:
EdGraph is an autonomous stablecoin depeg coverage system that detects potential depeg events, autonomously purchases additional evidence using HBAR micropayments, and uses an AI agent to evaluate the evidence and decide claim outcomes. Traditional insurance and coverage systems face three major problems: detection is slow, evidence is difficult to verify, and claim decisions are often opaque. EdGraph approaches the problem differently by giving an AI agent the ability to autonomously investigate and resolve claims while keeping its actions bounded by transparent, predefined policy rules. The core idea is simple: AI detects the opportunity, decides whether evidence is worth paying for, purchases the evidence, evaluates it against the policy, and decides the claim outcome. A user first connects their HashPack wallet and creates a coverage policy. The policy defines the covered stablecoin, depeg threshold, required duration, payout amount, and maximum evidence budget. These terms are registered through the Policy API into EdGraph's PolicyRegistry.sol smart contract on Hedera, creating an immutable on-chain reference for the coverage conditions and the maximum amount the AI can spend on evidence. Once a policy is active, EdGraph continuously monitors market conditions. A background Monitoring Worker queries The Graph for Base market data every 60 seconds and stores timestamped observations in SQLite. The Candidate Detector analyzes these observations to identify potential depeg events. It checks whether the price has remained below the policy threshold for the required duration, whether the observation window is complete, and whether there are significant monitoring gaps. When a potential claim is detected, the AI Claims Agent takes over the investigation. The first decision the agent makes is whether additional evidence is worth purchasing. It reads a live Graph risk snapshot containing information such as current price, liquidity, liquidity changes, and trading volume. Instead of blindly purchasing evidence for every potential claim, the agent performs a cost-benefit decision: "Is this event significant enough that I should spend HBAR to investigate it further?" If the agent determines that deeper evidence is justified, it autonomously purchases the evidence through x402 micropayments. The AI calls EdGraph's Evidence API, which responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required and specifies the required HBAR payment. The agent creates and signs a partial HBAR transfer, while the Blocky402 facilitator co-signs as the fee payer and submits the transaction to Hedera. Once the payment is verified, the Evidence API returns the requested evidence. The evidence contains deeper market information retrieved through The Graph, including historical prices, pool liquidity, swap activity, volume information, and provenance metadata such as the query hash, block range, and deployment ID. The AI Claims Agent then uses this evidence to evaluate the claim. Instead of relying purely on an LLM's subjective judgment, the agent is provided with transparent policy rules as guardrails. These rules describe the conditions that must be satisfied, such as the required depeg threshold, minimum duration, evidence completeness, provenance requirements, and allowed evidence budget. The AI reasons over the evidence while remaining constrained by the policy defined by the user. The agent ultimately produces one of three outcomes: ELIGIBLE — the evidence satisfies the coverage policy and the claim qualifies for payout. INELIGIBLE — the evidence does not demonstrate that the policy conditions were satisfied. NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW — the agent encounters an ambiguous, anomalous, or suspicious situation that should be escalated rather than resolved automatically. The important distinction is that the AI itself makes the final claim decision. The deterministic policy logic provides transparent constraints and structured checks, but the agent is responsible for interpreting the evidence, combining the available information, and deciding the outcome. Every step is recorded in SQLite, including market observations, claim state, the AI's evidence-purchase decision, x402 payment information, Hedera transaction hashes, Graph provenance, evidence reports, policy checks, and the final AI decision. This creates a complete audit trail showing what the AI observed, what it purchased, how much it spent, what evidence it received, and why it reached its final outcome. EdGraph therefore creates an autonomous coverage loop:
Detect → Decide → Pay → Verify → Evaluate → Resolve The system also demonstrates multi-chain coordination without requiring a bridge. Base provides access to liquid DeFi markets, The Graph provides indexed and verifiable market data, while Hedera provides the policy registry and HBAR settlement layer. The result is an insurance-like system where AI autonomously pays for the information it needs and uses that information to make bounded, auditable claim decisions.
projects.how_its_made:
EdGraph is built as a full-stack TypeScript monorepo using Scaffold-HBAR as the foundation, with custom services for The Graph integration, AI agents, x402 micropayments, policy management, and autonomous claim evaluation. The architecture is designed around a single autonomous agent loop. The monitoring infrastructure identifies potential events, while the AI Claims Agent handles the investigation and final claim decision. On-chain policy rules act as transparent constraints that bound what the agent can do. Policy Registry
Coverage policies are implemented through PolicyRegistry.sol, written in Solidity 0.8.28 and deployed on Hedera testnet. Each policy stores the covered stablecoin, depeg threshold in basis points, minimum depeg duration, payout amount, and maximum evidence budget in tinybars. Users connect HashPack and create policies through the Policy API. The policy is then registered on-chain through the Hedera smart contract. This gives the AI agent a reliable source of truth for the coverage terms and establishes a hard upper limit on how much HBAR it can spend on evidence. The application mirrors these policies into SQLite for efficient monitoring and claim processing, while the on-chain contract remains the authoritative policy registry. The Graph Monitoring Layer
EdGraph uses The Graph as its market observation and evidence layer. A custom GraphQL client queries a Uniswap V3 USDC/WETH pool on Base approximately every 60 seconds. The Monitoring Worker retrieves the pool information, calculates the current price, and stores timestamped observations in SQLite. The price calculation handles Uniswap V3's sqrtPriceX96 Q64.96 fixed-point representation. EdGraph converts the value into a human-readable USD price while accounting for token decimal differences and using BigInt to avoid JavaScript floating-point precision problems. Each observation can also retain Graph provenance information such as the query hash, block range, and deployment ID. This gives the AI agent access to both current market conditions and verifiable historical data. Candidate Detection
The Candidate Detector continuously analyzes the accumulated observations. It checks whether there are enough observations, whether the observations are complete, whether prices remain below the policy threshold, whether the required duration has been reached, and whether there are monitoring gaps larger than the permitted interval. For example, if a policy requires the stablecoin to remain below $0.98 for 30 minutes, the detector verifies that the observed price stayed below that threshold throughout the required window. If there is a significant data gap, the system does not simply assume that the missing period satisfies the condition. Once the conditions indicate a potential depeg event, the detector creates a POTENTIAL_CLAIM and passes it to the AI Claims Agent. AI Claims Agent
The AI Claims Agent is the core of EdGraph. It is an autonomous Node.js service responsible for both evidence acquisition and claim resolution. The agent first receives the potential claim and obtains a live Graph risk snapshot containing the current price, liquidity, liquidity changes, and trading volume. It then decides whether purchasing deeper evidence is justified. For example, a potential depeg accompanied by a significant liquidity drop and unusual trading volume may cause the agent to determine that additional evidence is valuable. Conversely, if the event appears to be a weak or temporary signal, the agent can avoid spending the evidence budget. Before making a purchase, the agent checks the maximum evidence budget defined by the on-chain policy. This creates an important safety boundary: The AI can decide how to investigate, but it cannot exceed the spending limit defined by the policy. After purchasing the evidence, the agent receives the detailed report and evaluates it against the policy. The agent is given structured policy constraints such as: required depeg threshold minimum duration required evidence fields provenance requirements liquidity anomaly conditions maximum evidence budget payout amount The deterministic policy logic provides these rules as structured checks and guardrails. The AI then reasons over the evidence and determines the final outcome. This means the AI is not simply returning an unconstrained LLM answer. It operates within a clearly defined policy boundary while retaining the ability to reason over multiple pieces of evidence. x402 Micropayment Flow
EdGraph uses x402 to allow the AI agent to purchase evidence on demand. When the agent requests deeper evidence, the Evidence API responds with:
402 Payment Required
The response specifies the required HBAR payment and payment information. The AI agent then creates a partial Hedera TransferTransaction and signs it using its ECDSA key. The transaction is sent to the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies the buyer's signature, co-signs as the fee payer, and submits the transaction to Hedera. The facilitator does not receive unrestricted control over the buyer's funds. It can only co-sign the transaction that the AI agent has already authorized. Once the payment is confirmed, the Evidence API returns the requested evidence. Payment amounts are represented in tinybars rather than floating-point HBAR values. Since one HBAR equals 100,000,000 tinybars, this avoids precision problems when constructing transactions. Every successful payment produces a Hedera transaction hash, which is stored in SQLite as part of the claim's audit trail. Evidence API The EdGraph Evidence API acts as a paid evidence service. After receiving a verified x402 payment, it performs deeper queries against The Graph. The resulting evidence report can contain: historical price observations depeg duration pool liquidity liquidity changes swap activity trading volume Graph query information block ranges deployment identifiers evidence timestamps This transforms The Graph from simply being a data source into a verifiable evidence layer that the AI can purchase on demand. The AI therefore does not need to permanently consume expensive or deep data queries. It can pay for additional evidence only when a potential claim justifies the cost. AI Policy Evaluation
After receiving the evidence, the AI Claims Agent evaluates the complete claim. The policy rules are exposed to the agent as deterministic constraints. For example, the agent can verify: Depeg condition: Did the stablecoin remain below the required threshold? Duration condition: Did the depeg persist for the required amount of time? Evidence condition: Does the purchased evidence contain the required information? Provenance condition: Can the evidence be traced to the expected Graph deployment and block range? Anomaly condition: Are there unusual liquidity or market conditions that make the result ambiguous? The AI combines these structured checks with the actual evidence and makes the final decision. The outcome is: ELIGIBLE when the evidence supports the claim, INELIGIBLE when the policy conditions are not satisfied, or NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW when the situation is too ambiguous or anomalous for safe autonomous resolution. The normal path is therefore fully autonomous. Human review is not the approval mechanism. It is only an exception mechanism. Particularly Hacky / Notable Autonomous evidence purchasing
The most important feature is that the AI agent does not simply consume unlimited data. It makes an economic decision about whether evidence is worth purchasing.
This turns the AI into an active economic participant rather than a passive chatbot. AI-driven claim resolution
The AI Claims Agent is responsible for the complete investigation lifecycle. It can detect the significance of an event, purchase additional evidence, interpret the evidence, apply policy constraints, and decide the final claim outcome.
The deterministic rules provide guardrails, while the AI provides the reasoning. Hedera-native x402
EdGraph uses native HBAR rather than ERC-20 payments for its x402 evidence marketplace.
The payment flow uses Hedera's partial-signature model, where the AI authorizes the transfer and Blocky402 acts as the fee payer.
This allows an autonomous agent to pay for a service without giving the facilitator unrestricted access to its funds. Uniswap V3 price calculation
EdGraph calculates prices from Uniswap V3's sqrtPriceX96 Q64.96 representation.
The system must carefully handle BigInt precision, token decimal differences, and fixed-point conversion to produce accurate prices. Continuous depeg validation
The Candidate Detector does not simply look for a single price below the threshold.
It validates a continuous observation window and rejects windows containing gaps larger than the permitted interval.
This prevents monitoring failures from being incorrectly interpreted as sustained depeg events. On-chain AI spending limits
The maximum evidence budget is part of the policy stored on Hedera.
This means the AI agent cannot arbitrarily increase its spending allowance through an application configuration change.
The policy defines the economic boundary within which the autonomous agent operates. Multi-chain coordination without a bridge
EdGraph observes Base DeFi markets, uses The Graph as its indexed data layer, and uses Hedera for policy registration and HBAR settlement.
The system therefore coordinates activity across ecosystems without requiring a token bridge for its core evidence-payment workflow. Complete auditability
Every major action can be traced through the system:
Market observation → potential claim → AI decision → x402 payment → Hedera transaction → Graph evidence → AI evaluation → claim outcome
This gives the autonomous system an auditable history instead of relying on an opaque AI response. Partner Technologies The Graph provides the market observation and evidence layer. EdGraph uses GraphQL queries to monitor Base liquidity pools and retrieve deeper historical evidence when the AI purchases it. Hedera provides the immutable policy registry and HBAR settlement layer. Coverage terms and evidence budgets are anchored on-chain, while x402 payments settle using native HBAR. Blocky402 provides the x402 facilitator infrastructure. It verifies the AI agent's payment authorization, provides the network fee, and submits the transaction to Hedera. Technology Stack Smart Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28, Hardhat, Hedera JSON-RPC Blockchain: Hedera Testnet, Base Mainnet Data: The Graph, GraphQL, SQLite Backend: Node.js 20, Next.js 14, TypeScript Frontend: React, TailwindCSS, DaisyUI, Reown AppKit AI: Autonomous Claims Agent with structured policy constraints and market-risk reasoning Payments: x402, @x402/core, @x402/hedera, Blocky402 Wallet: HashPack Infrastructure: Docker Compose, Yarn Workspaces Database: better-sqlite3

It then decides whether purchasing deeper evidence is justified. For example, a potential depeg accompanied by a significant liquidity drop and unusual trading volume may cause the agent to determine that additional evidence is valuable. Conversely, if the event appears to be a weak or temporary signal, the agent can avoid spending the evidence budget.

Before making a purchase, the agent checks the maximum evidence budget defined by the on-chain policy.

This creates an important safety boundary:
- The AI can decide how to investigate, but it cannot exceed the spending limit defined by the policy.
- After purchasing the evidence, the agent receives the detailed report and evaluates it against the policy.

The agent is given structured policy constraints such as:
- required depeg threshold
- minimum duration
- required evidence fields
- provenance requirements
- liquidity anomaly conditions
- maximum evidence budget
- payout amount

The deterministic policy logic provides these rules as structured checks and guardrails. The AI then reasons over the evidence and determines the final outcome.

This means the AI is not simply returning an unconstrained LLM answer. It operates within a clearly defined policy boundary while retaining the ability to reason over multiple pieces of evidence.

5. x402 Micropayment Flow
EdGraph uses x402 to allow the AI agent to purchase evidence on demand.

When the agent requests deeper evidence, the Evidence API responds with:
402 Payment Required
The response specifies the required HBAR payment and payment information.

The AI agent then creates a partial Hedera TransferTransaction and signs it using its ECDSA key.

The transaction is sent to the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies the buyer's signature, co-signs as the fee payer, and submits the transaction to Hedera.

The facilitator does not receive unrestricted control over the buyer's funds. It can only co-sign the transaction that the AI agent has already authorized.

Once the payment is confirmed, the Evidence API returns the requested evidence.

Payment amounts are represented in tinybars rather than floating-point HBAR values. Since one HBAR equals 100,000,000 tinybars, this avoids precision problems when constructing transactions.

Every successful payment produces a Hedera transaction hash, which is stored in SQLite as part of the claim's audit trail.

6. Evidence API

The EdGraph Evidence API acts as a paid evidence service.

After receiving a verified x402 payment, it performs deeper queries against The Graph.

The resulting evidence report can contain:
- historical price observations
- depeg duration
- pool liquidity
- liquidity changes
- swap activity
- trading volume
- Graph query information
- block ranges
- deployment identifiers
- evidence timestamps

This transforms The Graph from simply being a data source into a verifiable evidence layer that the AI can purchase on demand.

The AI therefore does not need to permanently consume expensive or deep data queries. It can pay for additional evidence only when a potential claim justifies the cost.

7. AI Policy Evaluation
After receiving the evidence, the AI Claims Agent evaluates the complete claim.

The policy rules are exposed to the agent as deterministic constraints.

For example, the agent can verify:

Depeg condition: Did the stablecoin remain below the required threshold?

Duration condition: Did the depeg persist for the required amount of time?

Evidence condition: Does the purchased evidence contain the required information?

Provenance condition: Can the evidence be traced to the expected Graph deployment and block range?

Anomaly condition: Are there unusual liquidity or market conditions that make the result ambiguous?

The AI combines these structured checks with the actual evidence and makes the final decision.

The outcome is:

ELIGIBLE

when the evidence supports the claim,

INELIGIBLE

when the policy conditions are not satisfied,

or

NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW

when the situation is too ambiguous or anomalous for safe autonomous resolution.

The normal path is therefore fully autonomous.

Human review is not the approval mechanism. It is only an exception mechanism.

Particularly Hacky / Notable
1. Autonomous evidence purchasing
The most important feature is that the AI agent does not simply consume unlimited data. It makes an economic decision about whether evidence is worth purchasing.
This turns the AI into an active economic participant rather than a passive chatbot.

2. AI-driven claim resolution
The AI Claims Agent is responsible for the complete investigation lifecycle. It can detect the significance of an event, purchase additional evidence, interpret the evidence, apply policy constraints, and decide the final claim outcome.
The deterministic rules provide guardrails, while the AI provides the reasoning.

3. Hedera-native x402
EdGraph uses native HBAR rather than ERC-20 payments for its x402 evidence marketplace.
The payment flow uses Hedera's partial-signature model, where the AI authorizes the transfer and Blocky402 acts as the fee payer.
This allows an autonomous agent to pay for a service without giving the facilitator unrestricted access to its funds.

4. Uniswap V3 price calculation
EdGraph calculates prices from Uniswap V3's sqrtPriceX96 Q64.96 representation.
The system must carefully handle BigInt precision, token decimal differences, and fixed-point conversion to produce accurate prices.

5. Continuous depeg validation
The Candidate Detector does not simply look for a single price below the threshold.
It validates a continuous observation window and rejects windows containing gaps larger than the permitted interval.
This prevents monitoring failures from being incorrectly interpreted as sustained depeg events.

6. On-chain AI spending limits
The maximum evidence budget is part of the policy stored on Hedera.
This means the AI agent cannot arbitrarily increase its spending allowance through an application configuration change.
The policy defines the economic boundary within which the autonomous agent operates.

7. Multi-chain coordination without a bridge
EdGraph observes Base DeFi markets, uses The Graph as its indexed data layer, and uses Hedera for policy registration and HBAR settlement.
The system therefore coordinates activity across ecosystems without requiring a token bridge for its core evidence-payment workflow.

8. Complete auditability
Every major action can be traced through the system:
Market observation → potential claim → AI decision → x402 payment → Hedera transaction → Graph evidence → AI evaluation → claim outcome
This gives the autonomous system an auditable history instead of relying on an opaque AI response.

Partner Technologies

The Graph provides the market observation and evidence layer. EdGraph uses GraphQL queries to monitor Base liquidity pools and retrieve deeper historical evidence when the AI purchases it.

Hedera provides the immutable policy registry and HBAR settlement layer. Coverage terms and evidence budgets are anchored on-chain, while x402 payments settle using native HBAR.

Blocky402 provides the x402 facilitator infrastructure. It verifies the AI agent's payment authorization, provides the network fee, and submits the transaction to Hedera.

Technology Stack

1. Smart Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28, Hardhat, Hedera JSON-RPC
2. Blockchain: Hedera Testnet, Base Mainnet
3. Data: The Graph, GraphQL, SQLite
4. Backend: Node.js 20, Next.js 14, TypeScript
5. Frontend: React, TailwindCSS, DaisyUI, Reown AppKit
6. AI: Autonomous Claims Agent with structured policy constraints and market-risk reasoning
7. Payments: x402, @x402/core, @x402/hedera, Blocky402
8. Wallet: HashPack
9. Infrastructure: Docker Compose, Yarn Workspaces
10. Database: better-sqlite3

projects.title: presign
projects.description: Agents send the unsigned tx, get a risk verdict with data provenance. Stale data can't say safe.
projects.project_description:
An autonomous agent holding a key signs whatever its planner hands it. presign answers one question before that signature - is this safe to sign? - and returns the thing nobody else does: how stale the evidence behind the answer was. The whole project in one line, live on the landing page right now: same call to the Aave V3 pool, freshness budget 30s  ->  low
same call, same data, same rules, budget 1s  ->  unavailable unavailable is a tier, not an error. A rule that cannot get fresh protocol data has no honest way to report "nothing found", so a green verdict without fresh evidence is impossible by construction. Everyone else returns a verdict computed on six-hour-old context that looks exactly like a fresh one. An agent POSTs an unsigned transaction (from, to, value, data, chainId). The service simulates it on a mainnet fork, reads the state diff, and runs four rules over it: approvals that are unlimited or reach a listed address, mutable logic behind a proxy, protocol invariants from indexed data, and unidentified counterparties. Back comes a tier, the findings, and provenance: which deployment answered, its lag behind chain head in seconds, and the age of the simulated block. CHECK IT YOURSELF - nothing here needs a key or an account: https://presign.dev
three transactions judged by that instance while you read, with the freshness slider that produces the pair above
https://presign.dev/quote?to=0xa0b86991c6218b36c1d19d4a2e9eb0ce3606eb48
the price before payment, itemised: simulation plus one unit per indexed deployment the verdict will read. Try a different address and the price moves
https://presign.dev/health
live sources, the Substreams watch window, the journal topic
https://presign.dev/llms.txt
the same service written for an agent rather than a person
https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10413192
every verdict this instance has issued, refusals included, timestamped by Hedera rather than by us. Same thing as raw JSON, if you prefer curl:
https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com/api/v1/topics/0.0.10413192/messages?limit=5&order=desc
https://basescan.org/address/0xCa73Fe3ccc9FB581Ef9C624a9D0B9EEAFAD0cDDa
the address that pays The Graph for the data behind those verdicts
https://github.com/n0ctr1/presign
npm run safety - the rules over twelve undisputed mainnet contracts (12 low, zero refusals); npm run latency; npm run coverage BY TRACK The Graph - an operational layer over indexed data, not a subgraph query. Discovery is not rebuilt: a registry supplies candidates, and on top of it conformance is checked by issuing the real query, liveness comes from _meta against an independently obtained chain head, and selection is capability-bound - "which deployments can answer this rule right now within N seconds of lag". Proxy-upgrade history streams from Substreams. The layer ships standalone as an MCP server with a SKILL.md. Fail-closed makes it load-bearing rather than decorative: no fresh indexed data, no green verdict. Hedera - x402-gated per call through the Blocky402 facilitator, priced by the data each verdict actually reads and quotable for free beforehand. Every verdict, refusals included, is journalled to HCS under a salted commitment to the paying transaction: checkable without exposing the payer, impossible to backdate. The service also pays The Graph on Base over x402, so both sides of the cost of one answer are visible. Ledger - the device is not a notification. medium blocks until a human approves the decoded transaction on a Nano X, a decline reads as 6985 (a decision, not a fault), and high never reaches the device at all. Keys live in the Ledger Key Ring rather than a .env; a ring that refuses to decrypt stops startup instead of falling back to a plaintext copy. The signing broker buys its own verdict for the exact transaction rather than trusting the one a model handed it. The service never holds a key and never broadcasts. It advises; the signature stays where the key is.
projects.how_its_made:
TypeScript throughout, an npm-workspaces monorepo of thirteen packages, no
framework beyond Hono for the HTTP service. Simulation: an Anvil mainnet fork with 'debug_traceCall' and the prestate tracer
in diff mode, so rules read the actual state diff rather than the calldata. That distinction is load-bearing - an approval buried inside a smart account's 'execute' is still an approval, and the diff shows it while the calldata does not. Mapping slots are resolved by computing keccak(key ‖ slot), with a bounded candidate scan; when candidates are truncated the rule returns 'unavailable'
rather than a confident guess. The Graph is the data layer, and an operational layer sits on top of it. Discovery is not rebuilt - 'subgraph-registry' runs as an MCP subprocess and supplies candidates - but its reliability score is economics, not liveness. So conformance is checked by issuing a real query for the fields a rule needs, liveness comes from '_meta { block hasIndexingErrors }' compared against an independently obtained chain head, and selection is capability-bound: the question is not "what is this subgraph" but "which deployments can answer this rule right now within N seconds of lag". Lag is read from the same GraphQL document as the data it qualifies, so the number cannot drift from the answer. Proxy-upgrade history streams from Substreams over gRPC. The whole layer ships standalone as an MCP server with a SKILL.md, so another team can ask that question without touching the rules. Hedera carries the money and the record. Inbound payments are x402 through the Blocky402 facilitator on testnet; pricing is metered - a base charge plus one unit per indexed deployment the verdict will read, counted before payment and quotable for free at GET /quote?to=<address>. Outbound, the service pays The Graph on Base over x402 (EIP-3009, facilitator submits), so both sides of the cost of one answer are visible. Verdicts go to an HCS topic under a salted commitment to the paying transaction: checkable without exposing the payer, and impossible to backdate. Ledger is used as two primitives, not branding. Device Management Kit over node-HID clear-signs 'medium' escalations - the human sees on the device screen what is being signed, and a decline reads as 6985, a decision rather than a fault. Service secrets live in the Ledger Key Ring instead of a .env: the key ring is consulted before any file, and a ring that refuses to decrypt stops
startup rather than falling back to a plaintext copy. Two things worth flagging as hacky-but-deliberate. First, the signing broker does not trust the verdict a model hands it - it buys its own verdict for the exact transaction and signs only through that, which is why each signature leaves two entries in the journal. Second, the escalation signs a
non-broadcastable approval nonce rather than the transaction itself wherever a signature would otherwise be broadcastable. Everything claimed is a command: 'npm run safety' runs the rules over twelve undisputed mainnet contracts (12 low, zero refusals), 'npm run latency' times whole verdicts cold and warm, 'npm run coverage' counts conforming deployments by querying them. The false-positive run is a release gate - it exits non-zero if anything reaches 'high'.

projects.title: Executor
projects.description: Receivership for autonomous agents. Same ENS name, redirected revenue.
projects.project_description: Autonomous agents are beginning to hold assets, earn revenue, make payments, and enter into economic relationships. But when an agent stops operating, there is no standard way to resolve what it leaves behind. Executor is a programmable resolution protocol for autonomous economic agents. Before operating, an agent can commit to a resolution plan that defines what should happen if it becomes inactive or unable to continue operating. When predefined failure conditions are met, Executor transitions the agent into a deterministic resolution process. The protocol can freeze further activity, account for assets and obligations, process pending settlements, collect available receivables, and distribute assets according to predefined priority rules. Executor separates an agent's execution process from its economic state. A running agent may fail, but assets, obligations, pending transactions, and contractual relationships can still require resolution. We are exploring a missing primitive for the emerging agent economy: what happens when autonomous software can no longer fulfill its economic responsibilities? Executor makes that outcome programmable, transparent, and deterministic.
projects.how_its_made:
ExecutorRegistry is a Solidity state machine on Sepolia (0x2946B46c2EB5Ec53
2093877223Ef043b13729e39), built with Foundry. Agent identity is keccak256 of
the label; a plan is locked at registration and the four authorities are checked
to be distinct. getPaymentDestination(bytes32) is a pure view over state —
cheap enough to sit in any payment path. ENS is what makes the redirect invisible to the payer. We deployed
ExecutorResolver against the ENSv2 beta PermissionedRegistry on Sepolia, using
the new role model: ROLE_SET_RESOLVER and ROLE_SET_RESOLVER_ADMIN. The resolver
answers addr() by calling straight into the registry, so the name resolves to
the treasury or the estate depending on live on-chain state, with no record
update and no key held by anyone. bindNode is one-way and deliberately so —
once a name is bound to an agent, nobody can quietly point it somewhere else.
ENSv2's per-role permissions are what let us hand out resolver control without
handing out the name. Hedera carries the money. The agent pays for model calls over x402 v2 through
the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Our DynamicPayTo hook resolves the
402 challenge's payTo field at request time out of the registry, so the paywall
charges 0.01 HBAR (1,000,000 tinybars) and settles it to whichever address the
agent's liveness currently dictates. Hedera's fixed, sub-cent fees are the
reason this works: destination-switching per request is only sane when the
settlement cost doesn't dominate the payment. The Graph is the dashboard's only data source — there is no RPC fallback
anywhere in the app, which we consider the honest test of a subgraph. Subgraph
v0.1.2 indexes registrations, heartbeats, state transitions, plan approvals and
plan executions, and uses dynamic data source templates with DataSourceContext
so each agent's estate contract gets indexed from the block it's created,without a hardcoded address list. PlanApproved and PlanExecuted are joined by
planHash, which is how the UI shows approval and execution as one story. The frontend is Next.js 14 App Router with viem and ISR, deployed on Vercel.
Registration is a real wallet transaction in the browser; the demo video signs
it with MetaMask on camera rather than scripting it. The hacky bit worth admitting: making the agent flippable inside a single
recording take. We register with a 30-second heartbeat interval and a
15-second grace period, which means the agent becomes eligible for
administration 45 seconds later — inside the same video. Getting that reliable
meant reading eligibility from the chain's own block.timestamp with a safety
margin rather than from the recorder's wall clock, because the two disagree by
enough to cause TooEarly() reverts.

projects.title: Ratchet Range
projects.description: A one-way liquidity band with partly permanent price impact.
projects.project_description: A custom curve opcode (0x52) that gives an AMM position permanent, one-directional price impact. It prices each fill exactly like 1inch's audited XYCConcentrateSwap over a band [sqrtLo, sqrtHi], then — after pricing — translates the entire band against the taker by grip times the fill's own sqrt-price move, so the markup never decays and the position never re-offers a zone it has traded through.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack. Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry end to end (forge for build/test/deploy/verify, anvil for the fork demo, cast for independent balance checks). 1inch SwapVM and Aqua come in as git submodules; OpenZeppelin 5.4.0 and @1inch/solidity-utils 6.9.10 via npm, because upstream remaps those into a node_modules/ that isn't vendored in the submodule. Compiler settings match upstream's exactly — via_ir, optimizer_runs = 700. What it is. RatchetRange is one custom SwapVM instruction at the free curve-bank slot 0x52. It prices a fill exactly like the audited XYCConcentrateSwap over a band [sqrtLo, sqrtHi], then — after the fill is priced — translates the whole band against the taker by grip × the fill's own sqrt-price move. The markup never decays, so the quote escalates with cumulative volume and slicing an order is strictly worse than sending it whole. Why 1inch's stack made this small. AquaOpcodes._runOpcode is internal virtual, so the whole extension is zero upstream diff: claim 0x52, super everything else, and every stock Aqua instruction keeps working. RatchetSwapVMRouter is AquaSwapVMRouter with one different opcode set. Because RatchetRange is a leaf (never calls ctx.runLoop()), it composes under stock wrappers — FeeFlatIn, Deadline, Salt, InvalidateBit — with no new plumbing. And Aqua's balance model does the inventory work for free: one maker wallet, one approve per token, balances keyed per (maker, app, strategyHash, token), so several positions account separately while the tokens never leave the wallet and the router never holds a maker approval at all. The hacky part worth mentioning: a self-staticcall to reuse audited math. The obvious build is to transcribe XYCConcentrateSwap.exec and swap in bounds read from storage — upstream parses its bounds out of bytes calldata, and a band held in storage has no calldata. That transcription would have been the single largest correctness risk in the design. Instead: XYCConcentrateSwap.exec only touches ctx.query.{tokenIn, tokenOut, isExactIn} and ctx.swap — never ctx.vm or ctx.fee — so the instruction builds a scratch Context and calls the audited function itself, through a self-STATICCALL that turns a memory value into real calldata: solidity
ctx.swap = IRatchetLeafPricer(address(this)).priceLeaf(
ctx.query, ctx.swap, abi.encodePacked(sqrtPriceMin, sqrtPriceMax)

projects.title: PayBound
projects.description: Capability-based payment isolation for AI agents. Separate reasoning from financial authority.
projects.project_description: Autonomous AI agents can now settle payments directly, but current architectures place an agent’s reasoning engine and its financial authority in the same trust domain. When an agent reads untrusted text—webpages, PDFs, tool responses, or invoices—prompt injection, poisoned context, or hallucinations can manipulate the agent into signing transactions to attacker-controlled addresses or draining balances. Rather than relying on fragile heuristic prompt filters, PayBound removes the agent's vocabulary needed to express an unauthorized payment. PayBound enforces capability-based payment isolation for autonomous AI agents. The untrusted agent environment never holds private keys, never accesses signing primitives, and never specifies payment parameters. Before the agent touches untrusted input, a trusted Broker pre-authorizes and issues an unforgeable, single-use, cryptographically bound Capability object. The agent’s payment tool accepts exactly one parameter: pay(capability_id). There are no destination or amount parameters for untrusted text to manipulate. When the agent invokes the capability, the Broker validates a formal 9-clause security invariant: Exact amount match (no dynamic price inflation). Fixed recipient address immutability. Pre-vetted resource ID matching. Canonical task definition hash binding. Attested sandbox workload session verification. Payment request digest match. Atomic single-use nonce burning (preventing replay attacks). Expiration timestamp validation. Global task cumulative spend budget cap. Even if an attacker achieves full prompt injection in the agent's context window, structurally zero unauthorized funds can move. PayBound settles payments over Hedera testnet via x402 and Blocky402, logs immutable audit trails to the Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), verifies enterprise spend policies inside a Chainlink CRE TEE enclave, and signs authorizations via Ledger hardware review.
projects.how_its_made:
PayBound was built as a strict-mode TypeScript monorepo on Node.js 24 LTS, managed with Turborepo and pnpm workspaces. Architecture and Core Technologies: Trusted Broker (apps/broker):
Built on Hono with @hono/zod-validator for strict runtime boundary schema checks. It runs a deterministic state machine (ISSUED -> RESERVED -> SUBMITTED -> SETTLED / FAILED / RECOVERABLE). Nonce-burning and budget enforcement happen atomically within a single synchronous SQLite transaction (better-sqlite3), preventing time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions. Isolated Sandbox & Agent Runtime (apps/sandbox):
The agent executes inside a containerized environment with strict Docker iptables egress policies that drop all outbound routes to RPC nodes, wallets, and payment facilitators—only allowing an authenticated channel to the Broker. The agent loop is driven by the Vercel AI SDK (ai) using Gemini Flash (with Groq fallback), exposing a strictly single-argument tool: pay({ capabilityId }). Hedera Settlement & x402 Micropayments (packages/settlement, apps/gated-content-service):
We built an x402-gated resource server on Hono serving paywalled research data on Hedera testnet. Payments settle via the Blocky402 facilitator using a two-signature fee-payer model: The Broker signs the exact HBAR transfer transaction (@x402/hedera). Blocky402 co-signs as the gas fee-payer (account 0.0.7162784) and submits directly to consensus. The Broker's settlement engine features two-stage reconciliation (consensus node receipt + mirror node REST polling fallback) and an idempotent startup recovery sweep for broker crash resilience. Immutable Audit Trail on HCS:
Every capability issuance, authorization decision, and settlement outcome is committed as a structured message to Hedera Consensus Service topics (0.0.10423726 and 0.0.10423727), verified via Hedera Mirror Nodes and HashScan. Hardware Review (packages/ledger-signer):
Broker payment authorizations route through Speculos, the Ledger device emulator running the native app-hedera.elf binary, performing on-device APDU screen review before cryptographic signature issuance. Confidential Policy Enforcement (cre-workflow):
Enterprise spend policies are evaluated using a Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) workflow compiled to WebAssembly via @chainlink/cre-sdk. Using handlerInTee, confidential spending thresholds are checked inside a hardware-isolated TEE enclave without exposing sensitive corporate caps to the host. Notable Engineering Highlights: Pluggable settlement seam (createX402Submitter) in apps/broker/src/settlement.ts allowed integrating x402 and Blocky402 without modifying the Broker's core state machine or widening the agent's single-parameter interface. Built an automated Speculos driver (global-setup.speculos.ts) that executes on-device APDU button presses over HTTP during end-to-end testing. Live adversarial testing proves prompt injections attempting to divert payments or alter amounts fail immediately at Invariant Clause 7 without needing heuristic filters.

projects.title: Agent Heights
projects.description: AI agent virtual office integrated with 20,000+ MCP server and EVM wallet capabilties
projects.project_description: Agent Heights is a virtual environment facilitating AI agent visibility and gamification. Players run their own office or visit other rooms and worlds to collaborate with other players and interact with their agents. Before the start of this hackathon, there was no EVM agent or broad DeFi capabilties. After, we have The Graph agent and Coinbase EVM agent. This duo is capable of complex defi strategy management including management of LP positions and dynamically trading based on volume or sentiment data.
projects.how_its_made: The game is a webui, Phaser based game interface. In the Market there is a collection of MCP server based agents that integrate with curated authenticated services, premium paid x402 endpoints, and over 22,000 MCPs from pulsemcp. Premium agents use paid services and balance is credited against the user. These payments are running through USDC micropayments using Circle's gateway service. The website is hosted on Railway, making use of websockets. Data is stored in a Supabase database We used The Graph MCP to query subgraphs which provides real-time DeFi data.

projects.title: Aukra
projects.description: AURKA lets treasuries provide liquidity without crossing predefined portfolio limits.
projects.project_description: AURKA lets users create token vaults called Spaces, set allocation ranges, and offer liquidity for swaps that respect those limits. It uses Aqua and SwapVM for settlement, with Privy trading wallets and an AI agent that evaluates and executes trades within user-approved limits. The Sepolia demo supports USDC and WETH.
projects.how_its_made:
We built AURKA with Solidity contracts, a React/TypeScript frontend, and a TypeScript backend. The frontend runs on Vercel, and the backend runs on Google Cloud. The demo uses Sepolia with mock USDC and WETH.
Each Space has a dedicated vault, allocation ranges, and a trading capacity limit. The contracts check whether a proposed swap stays within those constraints. Space creation uses a factory that deploys and initializes the vault in one transaction after the required token approvals.
We integrated Aqua and the upstream SwapVM router for liquidity and settlement. AURKA adds an execution guard so a trader cannot bypass the Space’s checks by calling SwapVM directly. We tested settlement, fee accounting, capacity consumption, and rollback when a trade fails.
Privy provides separate trading wallets for users. The backend handles wallet provisioning and policy configuration, while users authorize trading limits through signed controls. This lets an agent submit transactions without asking the connected browser wallet to sign every swap. The app also includes stop and recovery flows.
Vertex AI evaluates trading opportunities through structured tools. The model requests quotes and proposes trades; deterministic code checks the amounts, allocation limits, and execution conditions. The backend records evaluations and transaction outcomes so users can inspect the agent’s activity.

projects.title: Seed Agent
projects.description: AI talent search backed by transparent, verifiable onchain evidence.
projects.project_description: Seed Agent extends Seed Club Talent, an existing community directory, with an evidence-aware talent discovery workflow. Users describe who they need in natural language, find candidates from actual member records, resolve ENSv2 names to wallet addresses, inspect onchain activity through The Graph, and export a candidate report with traceable sources. Profile claims and onchain activity remain separate. AI interprets the search request; it does not invent candidates or missing evidence. Activity scores describe the returned protocol data, not a person's ability, credibility or identity. The current activity query covers Uniswap V3 on Ethereum mainnet. A successful empty query, an unqueried wallet and a failed request are treated as different states. Our demonstration resolves seedclub-ray.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia, matches its address to a member profile, checks protocol activity and exports the results. Address matching is not presented as proof of wallet ownership. The demo wallet has no evidence within the queried protocol scope, which does not imply that it has no activity elsewhere. This is a Continuity project. Accounts, member profiles and basic AI search existed before the event. During the hackathon, we added live onchain evidence, evidence-aware matching, ENSv2 discovery, and candidate reports with inspectable evidence. The repository documents the pre-existing baseline and event development history.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses Vite and vanilla JavaScript. The backend uses Tencent CloudBase authentication, PostgreSQL and cloud functions, with DeepSeek supporting natural-language processing. The Graph provides indexed Uniswap V3 data from Ethereum mainnet, including recent mint, burn and collect events and position data. Recent events cover a 90-day window; positions and earliest history are queried separately. Deterministic scoring keeps profile relevance separate from activity evidence. For AI searches requiring onchain evidence, the combined match score weights profile relevance at 70% and activity at 30%. We use viem to read ENSv2 through the Universal Resolver on Sepolia. Resolved addresses are compared with member records, and the interface exposes query blocks, resolver information and public name records. Our live demo uses seedclub-ray.eth, which I registered and configured during the event. A page-local shortlist connects discovery, activity checking and Markdown report export. Evidence details include query scope, timestamps, indexed blocks, score components and sample limits. Explorer links are included when transaction evidence is returned. Reports exclude contact fields, and failed requests are never treated as successful empty results. OpenAI Codex generated and revised most implementation code, tests and supporting documentation under my direction. I defined the product goals, made product decisions, performed manual deployments and acceptance testing, registered and configured the ENSv2 name, and recorded the demo narration. The repository documents this substantial AI assistance and distinguishes pre-event functionality from hackathon work.

projects.title: Prove to Earn Agent
projects.description: Autonomous agents that discover, execute and complete Prove to Earn quests for users.
projects.project_description: Prove to Earn Agent is an extension of P2E Inferno, our live Prove to Earn platform on Base. Today, users manually discover and complete onchain Daily Quest tasks. During ETHOnline, we are building an agent gateway and autonomous runner that lets a human authorize an AI agent once, then have that agent discover eligible quests, decide whether to act, execute supported onchain tasks from its own wallet, submit proof, claim rewards and complete the quest on the owner’s behalf.
projects.how_its_made: We are extending P2E Inferno’s existing Daily Quest engine rather than replacing it. The new agent gateway introduces owner-to-agent delegation, wallet-signature authentication, scoped and revocable permissions, typed API responses and x402-paid endpoints. A CDP AgentKit runner uses its own EOA wallet, The Graph informs execution decisions, and a custom Uniswap action preserves P2E Inferno’s existing Universal Router and fee path. World AgentKit proof-of-human is integrated into API pricing. Base is where the agent executes the onchain action. P2E Inferno’s existing Daily Quest verification logic checks that the submitted transaction satisfies the quest requirements, EAS provides verifiable attestations for task claims, and Unlock mints the final quest-completion key to the human owner.

projects.title: toll
projects.description: AI agents that autonomously pay for the data they need. Smart and Tidy!
projects.project_description: Toll is a working machine-to-machine payment system: an AI agent that autonomously buys live on-chain data, per query, with its own wallet and its own on-chain spending policy. The pain point is real. Agents today cannot pay for things by themselves. The moment an agent needs data — a price feed, a lending market snapshot, any API — a human has to step in with API keys, subscriptions, or a credit card. That breaks autonomy completely: no agent can do useful work overnight if it needs a human to approve a two-cent purchase, and the subscription model forces users to hand merchants their email, card, and signup just to let an agent read data. Toll replaces all of that with pay-per-request: the agent sees a price, checks its own rules, pays, and moves on. No accounts, no keys, no checkout, no human in the loop. How it works: you give the agent a task in plain English. projects.title: FirmDepth
projects.description: Bond-backed firm execution for Aqua’s reusable liquidity, powered by custom SwapVM logic.
projects.project_description: FirmDepth adds an optional execution-certainty layer to 1inch Aqua’s reusable liquidity model. Traders can use normal Soft execution, or upgrade an eligible quote into a short-lived, maker-signed Firm commitment with a minimum output, premium, expiry, and separate output-token Bond collateral. Aqua liquidity itself remains reusable rather than being reserved. At execution, FirmDepth rechecks current capacity: Aqua settles when it can satisfy the signed minimum, while the Bond path is used only for the protected output-capacity failure case. The project demonstrates real Sepolia execution, onchain token transfers, Bond locking/release, and deterministic Base-fork sponsor evidence.
projects.how_its_made: FirmDepth is built around the official 1inch Aqua model and a customized SwapVM execution path. We added two custom SwapVM instructions: FIRM_PRICE (0x52), which validates the signed pricing snapshot, and FIRM_GUARD (0x21), which binds execution to the accepted maker, taker, order, token pair, amounts, expiry, executor, router, and collateral constraints. The exact Firm program is 0x52002100. Firm quotes use EIP-712 signatures, a Registry tracks commitment state, and a BondVault manages separate performance collateral. The SDK reconstructs terminal receipts from Registry state, Aqua/SwapVM events, ERC-20 transfers, and Bond movement instead of trusting frontend status alone. The frontend is built in React/TypeScript, the quote service runs server-side, and the public demo uses real Ethereum Sepolia with dynamic EIP-6963 wallet discovery.
