projects.title: Agencia
projects.description: Connect your agent to every service it needs, even compute!!
projects.project_description: Connect your agent to every service it needs. Even compute. Buying API access today assumes a human: an account, a credit card, a subscription, someone to click "I agree." None of that works for an autonomous agent that needs to call a dozen services it discovered thirty seconds ago even Stripe does this but at a fortune of cost. Agencia throws out the billing relationship entirely and puts the payment inside the request where the cost lands with the merchants not the aggregators. Your agent shows up, sees a price, pays it, gets the thing. One call, one payment, done in under a second for a fraction of a cent. No account. No key. No subscription burning money while you sleep. It brings its own wallet and buys what it needs: reasoning, on-chain data, prices, web pages, live subgraph queries. And the part nobody expects — actual hardware. Your agent can rent a real Linux box by the second, run code on it, and hand it back. Not a quota. Not a plan. A machine, for eleven seconds, because that's how long it needed one. That changes what an agent can be. It stops being a thing that calls APIs you pre-arranged and becomes a thing that goes and gets what it needs, including compute it can think on. The economics go both ways. Have a machine sitting idle? Point it at Agencia, name your rate, get paid in HBAR every second someone uses it. Payouts land on-chain automatically when the lease closes. And it's all receipts. Every payment — yours and the supplier's — is written to a public consensus log. You can audit every cent your agent spent without trusting our dashboard, because the dashboard reads the same chain you do. The wildest part: your agent doesn't need to be told where anything is. Services announce themselves to a public topic on Hedera. Give an agent nothing but that topic and it'll find a service, read its menu, and pay it. No URL, no config, no integration. We built one that does exactly that. It buys its own reasoning, decides what to look up, and answers. Nobody told it which tools existed.
projects.how_its_made:
Build entirely on TypeScript the whole way down. Node + Hono for the service, the official MCP SDK so any MCP client can see the tools, @x402/core and @x402/hedera for payments, @hashgraph/sdk for chain work.
NVIDIA NIM behind the inference tools, Docker for the sandboxes. The payment trick. Naively, your agent pays the network fee to pay for a 0.002 ℏ call, which is silly. So the agent builds the transfer, points the transaction ID at the facilitat, and signs with only its own key. The facilitatorco-signs and submits. Your agent authorises the money without paying the gas and without its key ever leaving the machine. Compute was pretty tough we found aggregator willing to rent us and build the entire service behind hedera. For something fun we also have a cat walking across your macOS menu bar while a paid call is in flight, and sits down with its tail curled when nothing's being paid for. It's not a mock — registerPaidTool fires a loopback POST on verify and on settle, refcounted so two overlapping calls don't stop it early.

projects.title: CoopChain
projects.description: Onchain cooperative savings, risk-based lending, and tokenized investments.
projects.project_description: CoopChain is a blockchain-based financial infrastructure for cooperatives and SACCOs. It connects member savings, on-chain credit scoring, actuarial lending, stablecoin treasury management, tokenized investments, indexed financial data, confidential risk policies, and AI-assisted risk explanations into one modular system. The core principle: financial truth should be verifiable, risk decisions should be systematic, sensitive policies can remain confidential, and AI should explain rather than invent the decision. CoopChain models the full cooperative financial lifecycle — Membership → Savings → Credit Score → Loan Decision → Actuarial Calculation → USDC Lending → Investment Registry → Indexed Financial Data → Risk Engine → Confidential Policy → AI Explanation.
projects.how_its_made:
CoopChain is built with Solidity + Foundry (449 passing tests across 13 suites). Smart contracts: CoopVault, Savings, CreditScore, ActuarialEngine, LoanEngine, plus InvestmentRegistry, InvestmentToken, and InvestmentPool. The frontend is React + Vite + TypeScript. Sponsor integrations are functional components, not demos:
• Arc Testnet — USDC treasury and lending liquidity (ArcTreasury.sol)
• Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio — issued CCREF real-estate security on Hedera Testnet (ISIN KE0000000091, contract 0.0.10454483)
• The Graph — CoopChain subgraph indexes members, savings, loans, repayments, and investment positions; the Risk API reads indexed data instead of reconstructing state from RPC calls
• Chainlink CRE — confidential risk-policy evaluation inside an AWS Nitro TEE via handlerInTee; only the final risk tier is returned, private thresholds never leave the TEE
• OpenAI — AI Risk Agent that explains deterministic risk outputs, never invents them Backend: Node.js + TypeScript + Express + Ethers.js. Risk layer combines a deterministic engine (member risk, loan decision, investment risk) with the Chainlink CRE confidential layer. Notable: risk engines are strictly separated from AI explanation, and financial truth is never delegated to the LLM.

projects.title: varanasi
projects.description: Enforcement rail for AI agents: mandates verified at settlement, release gated on proof.
projects.project_description:
Varanasi is the enforcement rail for agentic commerce, infrastructure that lets humans hire AI agents with hard, on-chain spending limits instead of trust. Today, giving an agent work means handing it keys, allowances, or API credentials; one injected prompt or hallucinated address and the treasury drains. Varanasi moves the check to where the money moves. It works in four steps. A human signs an EIP-712 mandate, a cap, a work window, an expiry, and a nonce, and funds lock in the TaskEscrow smart contract, never in the agent's wallet. The agent works inside those bounds; replay is impossible because the nonce burns the moment it is used. An allowlisted validator scores the work, and release pays the merchant only when the score clears a threshold pinned at fund time, combined with a live identity and threshold re-check in the same transaction. Miss the bar and the human is refunded automatically, with evidence attached. One click revokes the agent's identity (AegisRegistry) and every downstream gate including a Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook (AegisHook) and RiskGuard closes.
The full stack ships together and is live: Solidity contracts on Sepolia (TaskEscrow, AegisRegistry, RiskGuard, AegisHook, all Sourcify-verified, 166 forge tests), a TypeScript agent engine that resolves ENS identity, pulls Uniswap intel from The Graph, pays $0.01 over the x402 rail on Hedera testnet, and returns ACT/SKIP verdicts with HashScan receipts (162 tests), an Express signal service with x402-gated alpha endpoints (5 tests), and a Next.js marketplace with Privy embedded wallets, a hire wizard, an agent roster with a 3D mascot, a documentation hub, a 23-brick public roadmap, and coming-soon Finance and Gold-backed-coin sections. Every claim links to a public record  proof, not screenshots.
projects.how_its_made:
Four surfaces, one repo, all wired together. Smart contracts are Solidity 0.8.30 via Foundry with via_ir (TaskEscrow's fund frame outgrew legacy codegen's stack limit  the IR pipeline keeps semantics identical). TaskEscrow (EIP-712 mandate escrow with nonce nullifiers, pinned per-task threshold/validator, last-write-wins scoring), AegisRegistry (ENSv2-backed revocable agent identities), RiskGuard (identity + score gate re-checked inline at release), and AegisHook (Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook verifying EIP-712 validator attestations from hookData)  deployed on Sepolia, Sourcify-verified, 166 forge tests including adversarial hardening.
The agent engine (TypeScript, Viem, Commander CLI) resolves agent identity through ENS, pulls live Uniswap pool intel from The Graph gateway, pays $0.01 USDC per signal over the x402 rail on Hedera testnet (with a neat fix: @x402/hedera's PrivateKey.fromString rejects 0x-hex ECDSA keys, so payer code uses fromStringECDSA, and prefers the USDC leg since facilitators reject HBAR in preflight), reasons to an ACT/SKIP verdict, and static-checks RiskGuard  162 vitest tests, all mocked/offline-safe.
The signal service (Express 5, TypeScript) serves x402-gated alpha endpoints with a file-backed receipt log plus mirrors of the shared finance types. The frontend (Next.js 14 App Router, Tailwind Colosseum theme, Privy embedded wallets so users sign in with email/Google/GitHub and get a self-custodial wallet, Viem contract calls, a procedural three.js robot mascot with zero model files) keeps a strict rule: demo finance state is simulated and labeled, and the agent's execute() throws until finance contracts deploy  so demo taps can never broadcast.
Partner tech that mattered: Privy (no seed phrases for mainstream users), The Graph (real pool data, not mocks), Chainlink CRE (the roadmap's quorum verdict layer), and patch-package pinning one Privy SVG attribute fix. Hackiest notable bit: the whole mandate replay story rests on a single usedNonce[signer][nonce] mapping plus chainId inside the signed struct  two lines of Solidity carrying the entire double-spend guarantee.

projects.title: Automator
projects.description: Build, simulate, and run onchain workflows on a visual canvas.
projects.project_description: Automator lets you connect contract calls, AI agents, forms, and logic on a canvas. You can build a flow by hand or ask the AI assistant to create and edit it. A flow can watch a token price and send an alert, collect a USDC payment through a mini-app, or query onchain data for an AI agent. Add screens to share it as an app, or define its inputs and return value to expose it through an API and MCP. You can simulate a flow, inspect each step’s output, and see where it fails. Onchain writes can be checked without sending transactions. Onchain transactions currently run on Base Sepolia and World Chain Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: I used TypeScript, Bun workspaces, and Turborepo for the monorepo. The frontend is built with Next.js, React Flow, Zustand, Coss UI, and Tailwind CSS. The backend uses Elysia on Bun and PostgreSQL, with shared TypeBox schemas for API validation. The workflow engine is a separate TypeScript package. OpenAI and OpenRouter power the AI integration, which converts tool calls into graph edits. Custom JavaScript runs inside QuickJS with time and memory limits. The MCP server uses the official TypeScript SDK and shares the HTTP API’s execution code. I used viem for EVM calls and transactions, Privy’s React and Node SDKs for authentication and wallet signing, and World ID’s IDKit for identity verification. Subgraph queries go through The Graph gateway; balance and price triggers use The Graph Token API and Chainlink feeds.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Automator lets you connect contract calls, AI agents, forms, and logic on a canvas. You can build a flow by hand or ask the AI assistant to create and edit it.

A flow can watch a token price and send an alert, collect a USDC payment through a mini-app, or query onchain data for an AI agent. Add screens to share it as an app, or define its inputs and return value to expose it through an API and MCP.

You can simulate a flow, inspect each step’s output, and see where it fails. Onchain writes can be checked without sending transactions. Onchain transactions currently run on Base Sepolia and World Chain Sepolia.

projects.title: Banshee Music
projects.description: AI-powered music launchpad for limited-edition songs, albums, and tickets on Uniswap v4.
projects.project_description: Banshee Music uses Uniswap v4 as the core liquidity and trading infrastructure for its music launchpad. BansheeHook , a custom Uniswap v4 Hook, manages the transition of ERC-1155 songs, albums, and tickets from their initial launch into active secondary markets, while enforcing Banshee-specific market rules and tracking trading activity. This allows each music release to become a liquid, onchain market while generating transparent activity that can contribute to Banshee’s Proof-of-Performance model.
projects.how_its_made: Banshee Music is built as an ERC-1155 music launchpad powered by Uniswap v4. Songs, albums, and tickets are represented as ERC-1155 assets, while our custom BansheeHook manages their launch lifecycle and connects each release to a Uniswap v4 market for liquidity and secondary trading. The hook tracks onchain activity such as primary sales and secondary-market trades, creating transparent data that can be used for Banshee’s Proof-of-Performance model. We used Solidity and Foundry for the smart-contract stack and built the frontend as a responsive Web3 application for artists and fans. The notable part of the architecture is adapting a Flaunch-style launch model—typically designed around fungible tokens—to music assets represented by ERC-1155, allowing a song, album, or ticket release to become its own onchain market.

projects.title: Sealed Books
projects.description: Close the books. Seal the truth. Nobody rewrites history. Tamper-proof accounting for real books.
projects.project_description:
Sealed Books is an institutional-grade double-entry accounting ledger that cryptographically guarantees financial period-close finality. In traditional ERPs like QuickBooks or NetSuite, accounting records sit in mutable SQL databases where database administrators or compromised credentials can quietly alter historical journal entries after financial statements are signed. Sealed Books eliminates this counterparty risk through mathematical zero-trust proofs. Key Capabilities:
- Strict Double-Entry Engine: All transactions validate Debits == Credits in integer minor units (cents) to avoid floating-point errors.
- Deterministic Binary Merkle Tree: Every balanced entry is canonicalized and hashed using SHA-256 into a cryptographic ledger root.
- Four-Eyes Multi-Sig Quorum: Period close enforces statutory separation of duties (2-of-2 multi-sig). Both the Financial Controller and an Independent Auditor must review and sign off.
- Frictionless Identity via Privy Enclaves: Users log in with standard passwordless email OTP. Sealed Books dynamically provisions Ethereum server wallets in Privy hardware enclaves governed by enterprise signing policies. No seed phrases, browser extensions, or gas tokens.
- Hedera Consensus Service Anchoring: The dual-signed seal is published directly to Hedera Testnet topic 0.0.10462941, securing an immutable, globally ordered consensus timestamp.
- Instant Forensic Tamper Detection: Anyone—an auditor, bank, or tax authority—can independently verify local database records against the public Hedera Mirror Node over standard HTTP. If a single entry is modified, deleted, or backdated, the verification engine instantly detects the tamper and pinpoints the exact record ID and discrepancy.
- Autonomous AI Audits via Bazantic: Features an x402 micropayment gateway and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI agents (Claude, Cursor, autonomous bots) can audit company books on demand with just an accounting period ID.
projects.how_its_made:
Sealed Books is engineered as a high-performance, memory-safe monorepo across Rust, TypeScript, and native desktop runtimes: Architecture & Tech Stack:
- Core Cryptography & Accounting (crates/core): Written in Rust with zero external dependencies for pure determinism. Implements balanced journal arithmetic, canonical JSON leaf sorting, deterministic binary SHA-256 Merkle trees, and trial balance calculations.
- Backend Server (apps/server): Built with Axum, Tokio, and LibSQL / SQLite. Features a custom REST API supporting both local embedded SQLite files and remote Turso clusters.
- Web & Native Desktop Clients (apps/web, apps/desktop): Built with React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, and Shadcn UI. The desktop client compiles into a lightweight native binary using Tauri v2. Partner Technologies & Integrations:
- Privy B2B Policy Server Wallets: Dynamically provisions isolated Ethereum server wallets via Privy's REST API during user registration and team invitations. Signing operations use secp256k1 via Privy's secure enclaves, enforced by organizational policy ID uqwuyziko7po5b6xtfbqug4z. The server enforces separation of duties (approver_1 != approver_2) so controllers cannot co-sign their own books.
- Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Dual-signed compact binary seal payloads are broadcast directly to Hedera Testnet Topic 0.0.10462941 via the Hedera Rust SDK. Verification is completely decentralized: the server queries the public Hedera Mirror Node (https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com) over HTTP without needing custom nodes or API keys.
- Bazantic MCP Gateway: Deployed an x402 micropayment gateway (https://sealed-books.bazgateway.com) exposing an MCP server. Published the "Sealed Books Accounting Period Audit" recipe enabling AI agents to verify books and inspect cryptographic proofs autonomously. Testing & Verification:
The codebase includes 72 automated unit, integration, and live enclave tests covering canonical serialization, Merkle tree construction, secp256k1 signature recovery, and real Hedera consensus verification.

projects.title: Basin
projects.description: Approve who you pay, not their wallet. Basin keeps payments safe as receiving addresses change.
projects.project_description: Basin is a safer way for companies to pay known people and organizations onchain. Today, approving a payee usually means storing a wallet address. That creates a fragile link between identity and infrastructure. If the recipient changes wallets, rotates keys, or moves funds elsewhere, the payer must update its records. Worse, a substituted address in an invoice or payment workflow can redirect money while still looking like a normal crypto transfer. Basin separates who is approved from where they currently receive money . A company creates an approved payment relationship with a recipient through a Basin identity such as maya.basin.eth . The payer approves Maya once. Maya controls her current receiving account underneath that identity. She can later change that account without asking every payer to update a wallet address. Payments do not simply resolve an ENS name and transfer funds. Basin checks the approved payer–recipient relationship, the current authorized receiving state, and the permissions required to execute the payment. A normal operator cannot silently replace the recipient or bypass the relationship with a different destination. This creates a simple rule: The company approves who. The recipient controls where. Basin is designed for real payment operations where the same counterparties are paid repeatedly: contractors, auditors, suppliers, contributors, and other trusted recipients. The result is a payment relationship that can survive wallet changes while still giving the payer control over who is authorized. If trust ends, the payer can revoke the relationship and future Basin payments are rejected. Basin turns an onchain address book into something stronger: a durable, enforceable payment relationship between two parties.
projects.how_its_made: Basin is built as a small end-to-end payment system around ENSv2 and Privy . ENSv2 provides the onchain identity and authorization layer. Basin creates names under .basin.eth and uses ENSv2 permissioned registry, permissioned resolver, and enhanced access-control primitives to separate control between the payer and recipient. The payer controls whether a payment relationship is trusted. The recipient controls the receiving information attached to their Basin identity. The permission model is designed so the payer cannot silently redirect the recipient, while the recipient can legitimately rotate receiving infrastructure without requiring payer-side updates. This is different from using ENS as a simple readable alias for one wallet. Basin treats the ENS state as part of an ongoing payment relationship with explicit authority boundaries and lifecycle rules. Privy provides the execution and wallet-control layer. Basin uses Privy-managed infrastructure and delegated authorization so routine payment operators can perform the actions they are allowed to perform without receiving unrestricted control of company funds. A payment must pass Basin's relationship checks before the authorized execution path can proceed. This lets us demonstrate an important failure case: an external payment attempt using substituted wallet details can be denied even when it comes from the normal operational environment. The application is built with Next.js and TypeScript in a pnpm workspace , with the frontend and backend kept in the same application through Next.js App Router and API routes. Basin also includes a small SDK so another application can create and submit Basin payments without depending on the Basin UI. For the ETHOnline build, settlement runs on Ethereum Sepolia , while the protocol design keeps the payment relationship separate from any single chain. One of the more unusual parts of the implementation is that changing a recipient's wallet is treated as a normal lifecycle event rather than a new contact. We can pay the same approved identity, change the receiving account, pay it again successfully, revoke that relationship, and then show a previously prepared payment fail. That sequence is the core technical idea behind Basin: identity remains stable while the infrastructure underneath it can change safely.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Basin is built as a small end-to-end payment system around **ENSv2** and **Privy**.

ENSv2 provides the onchain identity and authorization layer. Basin creates names under `.basin.eth` and uses ENSv2 permissioned registry, permissioned resolver, and enhanced access-control primitives to separate control between the payer and recipient. The payer controls whether a payment relationship is trusted. The recipient controls the receiving information attached to their Basin identity. The permission model is designed so the payer cannot silently redirect the recipient, while the recipient can legitimately rotate receiving infrastructure without requiring payer-side updates.

This is different from using ENS as a simple readable alias for one wallet. Basin treats the ENS state as part of an ongoing payment relationship with explicit authority boundaries and lifecycle rules.

Privy provides the execution and wallet-control layer. Basin uses Privy-managed infrastructure and delegated authorization so routine payment operators can perform the actions they are allowed to perform without receiving unrestricted control of company funds. A payment must pass Basin's relationship checks before the authorized execution path can proceed. This lets us demonstrate an important failure case: an external payment attempt using substituted wallet details can be denied even when it comes from the normal operational environment.

The application is built with **Next.js and TypeScript** in a **pnpm workspace**, with the frontend and backend kept in the same application through Next.js App Router and API routes. Basin also includes a small SDK so another application can create and submit Basin payments without depending on the Basin UI.

For the ETHOnline build, settlement runs on **Ethereum Sepolia**, while the protocol design keeps the payment relationship separate from any single chain.

One of the more unusual parts of the implementation is that changing a recipient's wallet is treated as a normal lifecycle event rather than a new contact. We can pay the same approved identity, change the receiving account, pay it again successfully, revoke that relationship, and then show a previously prepared payment fail.

That sequence is the core technical idea behind Basin: **identity remains stable while the infrastructure underneath it can change safely.**

projects.title: Assay-2
projects.description: A pay-per-query onchain credit bureau an AI agent buys from with only a wallet, no API key.
projects.project_description: Assay is a pay-per-query onchain credit bureau with an autonomous transfer agent. It scores any wallet's creditworthiness from live on-chain lending data — account maturity, leverage, past liquidations, portfolio quality, and counterparty hygiene — using a transparent, deterministic model. The LLM never computes the score, so any result is fully recomputable and a blocked user can be told exactly why. Scores are sold per query behind an x402 paywall: a caller pays a fraction of a cent in HBAR and gets a score back — no signup, no API key, just a wallet. That makes the bureau consumable by AI agents, not only humans. On top runs an autonomous agent that buys scores, underwrites a tokenized credit line (an ERC-20 whose transfers are gated by an on-chain eligibility list), and issues or revokes it on Hedera. The payoff: when a holder is liquidated, the agent re-scores them, revokes the line, and their next transfer reverts on-chain — off-chain intelligence, enforced on-chain.
projects.how_its_made: A single Next.js 15 / React 19 app plus a Hardhat contract, TypeScript throughout, Neon Postgres for the console read-model. Everything is dependency-injected so mock and live adapters share interfaces, backed by 169 passing unit tests. The Graph — scores are computed from the Messari standardized lending subgraph (Aave V3) via the gateway with Bearer auth. The account-level liquidation counter was unreliable, so we count liquidations directly from liquidates events — that fix is what makes the re-score → revoke beat real on live data. Hedera — the CreditToken (ERC-20 + Ownable, with an eligibility control-list enforced in _update) is deployed to Hedera testnet via the Hashio JSON-RPC relay and verified on Sourcify. Pay-per-query is x402, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator in native HBAR (feePayer partial-signing). Privy — a Privy server wallet is the autonomous agent that signs every issue/revoke. Privy signs but doesn't broadcast to Hedera, so we sign the chain-296 transaction with Privy and self-broadcast via ethers — that's what unlocked Privy-on-Hedera. Hacky bits: we reverse-engineered Blocky402's x402 v2 payload from its validation errors — native HBAR is asset id 0.0.0, and the v2 payload carries the chosen requirements under accepted, not top-level scheme/network. We build the Hedera payment with @x402/hedera + @hiero-ledger/sdk because hand-rolled @hashgraph/sdk bytes drifted from what the facilitator decodes.

projects.title: mandatei
projects.description: Ledger-backed x402 agents on Base: tap to fund, pay tools inside a cap keys never touch the LLM
projects.project_description: Mandate is a local operator for autonomous AI agents that spend real USDC on Base mainnet through the x402 payment protocol. You describe a goal in plain language; Mandate uses Vertex (Gemini) to plan which paid tools to call, shows you an upfront price preview, and only executes inside a Ledger-approved spending cap. Trust is split cleanly: your physical Ledger confirms your address and signs the initial USDC allowance via ERC-7730 clear signing (EIP-712); a Key Ring–sealed software wallet handles later micropayments to approved endpoints without repeated USB taps. The LLM never sees private keys. Live evidence comes from The Graph (including Agent0 registry lookups) and optional Hedera analysis; every tool call produces durable SQLite receipts. URL allowlists, per-call limits, rolling windows, and expiry are enforced by the broker—not by prompt instructions. When a run finishes, the agent profile is discarded; payment history and sources remain for audit. Built for ETHOnline 2026 Start Fresh: one npm start workspace on localhost, self-hosted x402 facilitator, and real device taps for funding—not mocked signing.
projects.how_its_made: Mandate is a Node 22 monorepo: packages/gateway (operator broker) + packages/facilitator (self-hosted x402 settlement), static UI in console/ , entry at scripts/start.mjs . Everything runs locally on :8410 ; SQLite holds mandates, payment receipts, and agent run checkpoints. Payments: We use Coinbase x402 v2 ( @x402/core , @x402/evm ) with the exact scheme on Base mainnet USDC (EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization ). The broker is the only component that can sign: it quotes unpaid 402 offers, reserves budget atomically, signs with a Key Ring–decrypted key via viem, and verifies settlement before accepting evidence. A loopback facilitator on :8406 batches settlement so the demo does not depend on a third-party endpoint. Ledger (partner stack): Physical device + DMK ( @ledgerhq/device-management-kit , HID transport) + Ethereum Signer Kit for address read and funding EIP-712. Spending keys live in @ledgerhq/wallet-cli Key Ring ( ring encrypt / decrypt over stdin pipes; password from macOS Keychain, never argv). Clear signing uses @ledgerhq/context-module CAL filters and a custom ERC-7730 descriptor ( docs/erc7730/ ) for “Authorize USDC transfer.” Without a partner LEDGER_ORIGIN_TOKEN , production CAL 403s—so we ship a loopback test CAL ( ledger:test-cal ) plus the ledger-dev Ethereum app ( CAL_TEST_KEY=1 ). We fail-closed on funding unless clear-signing is provable ( erc7730 or clear-basic ), not just “device connected.” Agent loop: Vertex Gemini ( gemini-3.5-flash via gcloud) plans tool steps; unpaid probes validate prices. Execution is adaptive: approved plan steps run sequentially, each paid through x402 to first-party tools on :8425 (The Graph subgraph queries, Coinbase spot prices, Hedera-backed analysis). Live Agent0 discovery uses Subgraph MCP; counterparty policy pools ERC-8004 feedback across chains before paying unknown recipients. Reports are generated from observed fields, not invented prose. Hacky but real: DMK close() hangs Node—we keep a singleton and resetDmk() instead. DMK returns v as 0/1; we normalize to 27/28 for USDC. CAL needs explicit EIP712Domain in types or the hash misses on device—we inject it without changing the x402 digest. DETECT_BLIND_SIGNING in traces is a reporter step, not proof of a blind screen. Address confirmation and funding are deliberately separate device actions so we never imply a tap signed money when it only showed an address.

Address confirmation and funding are deliberately separate device actions so we never imply a tap signed money when it only showed an address.

projects.title: Breakwater
projects.description: Treasury-owned Aqua liquidity that earns fees and enforces trading limits during stablecoin stress.
projects.project_description: Breakwater lets a treasury owner create liquidity with explicit risk limits while retaining custody of their tokens. The owner chooses an allocation, trading fee, safety trigger and permitted exit discount, then approves and activates the position through Aqua. Before creating, the owner can rehearse those same numeric settings against four historical USDC/USDT checkpoints without connecting a wallet. The comparison shows permitted behavior, original impairment, size-specific external quotes, estimated execution costs and the recovery tradeoff. It explicitly separates historical scenarios from Sepolia activation and leaves unavailable quotes unknown. It is a policy-explanation tool, not a return forecast or a claim that Breakwater beats a competent direct executor. While both assets satisfy the policy, trades can flow in both directions and the position records the retained input-token fee. When the asset becomes impaired, the same order refuses trades that add more of it and permits reserve-in, asset-out trades at an observation-bounded price, subject to backing and a willing taker. An unsafe reserve, co-depeg or invalid/stale observation halts trading. The owner can cancel even while trading is halted. The public Sepolia prototype exposes this owner journey, visible fee/exit accounting, owner-controlled sample-price scenarios and recent-position discovery. A separate wallet completed a 1 bUSD healthy trade, receiving 0.996975 rUSD while the position retained a 0.003 bUSD fee. Under sample stress, that same wallet paid 1 rUSD to buy 1.069175 bUSD from the same position: actual treasury balances confirm reserve received and impaired inventory reduced. The order then halted for an unsafe reserve and a co-depeg, and resumed quoting after healthy observations were restored. Impaired-input and halt checks use read-only execution calls, not mined failed trades. This was guided testnet testing, not verified unassisted use, adoption or demand. Tokens have no monetary value and the observations are not live market feeds. Exits and earnings are not guaranteed. The permitted discount is relative to an accepted observation, not a cap on total loss.
projects.how_its_made: Breakwater uses the pinned official Aqua contracts and a custom SwapVM router/instruction implementation. Aqua records virtual allocations while tokens stay in the maker's wallet. BreakwaterMakerAMM builds an order program combining the policy guard, SwapVM's flat-input-fee instruction, and the pegged liquidity curve. Stress changes the permitted instruction path of the existing order; it does not require replacing the order. BreakwaterPolicy checks independent USD observations for both assets and their relative price. Per-feed age limits, quote commitments, minimum output and deadlines address different failure modes. BreakwaterPositions records owner-created orders and accounts for healthy fees and exits using authenticated settlement hooks, with a commitment check across the transfer boundaries. Reverted settlement rolls back its accounting. The owner interface supports guided configuration, optional policy rehearsal, bounded token approvals, Aqua shipping, automatic quotes, explicit wallet actions, receipt recovery, scenario controls and cancellation. Transaction feedback retains the initiating wallet and position across wallet changes and pending-transaction reloads. Position sharing includes one-click copy and a manual fallback. Recent-position discovery uses bounded onchain event scans and displays current policy and backing. Expired samples explain owner-only refresh and offer recovery paths rather than an apparently executable trade form. Final CI passed 54 frontend tests and 74 contract tests; 12 optional fork tests were skipped. The actual-order differential test covers 60 arithmetic comparisons. Rehearsal and creation share one parsed settings object. The prior bounded historical study includes an unguarded fee-bearing curve, a halt/direct alternative, recovery tradeoffs and explicitly synthetic observation lag. The optional atomic-unwind executor remains experimental, not the main public workflow or a claim of superior returns. AI assistance: Codex substantially generated and revised contracts, tests, frontend code, graphics, configuration and documentation. File-specific attribution, reused upstream material and limits are documented in AI_DISCLOSURE.md and DEPENDENCIES.md in the repository. Human contributions included product direction, risk-policy and scope decisions, dedicated testnet funding, wallet-signed testing, usability feedback and coordination of external testing. We do not claim manual Solidity authorship, an independent security audit or verified independent adoption.

projects.title: Source Mark
projects.description: Paid Graph reads that refuse when provenance fails — x402 on Hedera, sources get paid.
projects.project_description: SourceMark is a paid read layer for onchain data that refuses to answer when it cannot prove provenance. Agents and apps that act on rates, TVLs, or other indexed metrics need more than a dashboard number: a stale or substituted subgraph answer is not a UI bug, it is a wrong transaction. SourceMark turns that into an HTTP product with real money attached. Callers request a metric over a schema family (for example Messari lending on Ethereum) from a single endpoint. The gateway looks up the family in a data-only registry of pinned The Graph deployment IDs that share a byte-identical schema IPFS hash, fans the same GraphQL query out to every ready source in parallel, and judges each response against live chain head for block lag and age. Sources that fail freshness, report indexing errors, or serve a different deployment than the pin are dropped with a reason. Families declare whether sources must agree (identical) or may differ (peer); identical disagreement refuses the whole read instead of papering over it with a median. Unpaid requests return a real HTTP 402 with x402 payment requirements on Hedera testnet (HBAR via the Blocky402 facilitator). No API key and no signup — the challenge is the onboarding. When a payment header is present, the gateway verifies with the facilitator first and does not settle yet. Only if the provenance gate passes does it settle, answer, and issue a signed receipt naming every contributing deployment, its block, the policy, and the payment. Digests can also be published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so existence-at-time is not only our database. If the gate fails, the response is 409 REFUSED and settlement is skipped — refusal is free by construction, so the service cannot profit from a guess. On success, revenue is recorded in SourcePayouts on Hedera: a routing fee, per-source shares, and a slashable unvested holdback. Demo source operators opt in with EIP-191 consent over their payout addresses and can claim cleared balances themselves. Anyone can dispute a receipt; the service re-queries The Graph at the recorded blocks. MATCH rejects with no slash. MISMATCH slashes holdback on the ledger and drives onchain openDispute, with arbiter resolveDispute or permissionless resolveAfterDeadline after silence. Buyers who pay in USDC on Base reach the same gate through Bazantic resale. Their rail cannot answer a Hedera x402 challenge, so the gateway uses api-key forward while sources are still paid in HBAR from an operator float — same provenance policy, same onchain split, receipt marked channel:resale. The live multi-page demo on Railway shows 402, paid read, forced refusal, resale, disputes, explore tables, and an SDK page.
projects.how_its_made: SourceMark is a TypeScript gateway on Hono (Node 22) with a multi-page static demo (home, demo, explore, sdk), a thin SDK package, and an MCP server plus SKILL.md for agents. The serving path never substitutes fixtures for live Graph data: if sources are unreachable or unpinned, reads refuse. Data layer — The Graph. registry/families.json maps a schema IPFS hash and query templates to pinned deployment IDs. Conformance is checked with The Graph’s network subgraph (byte-identical schemaIpfsHash), not marketing labels. At read time the resolver fans out through the decentralized gateway, reads _meta.deployment and enforces the pin, measures freshness against Ethereum RPC chain head (ANCHOR_MODE=rpc), and aggregates: median for identical families, TVL-weighted for peer families. That peer/identical split mattered: a naive median across Aave V3, V2, Spark, and a wound-down pool produced a rate none of them paid. Payments — Hedera + Blocky402. x402 v2 exact scheme on hedera:testnet via @x402/hedera and the Blocky402 facilitator. Verify and settle are separate calls: verify before Graph work, settle only after the gate. Buyer helpers ship with the product (CLI, loop agent, in-page demo) so the paywall is exercisable, not theoretical. Receipts and consent — viem. Answers and evidence are keccak-hashed over canonical JSON and EIP-191 signed. POST /v1/consent verifies a signature from the registered payout address. Optional HCS publish uses @hashgraph/sdk so digests land on a public topic. Liability — SourcePayouts.sol (Hardhat, Hedera testnet). recordRead locks the split and holdback; claim lets sources withdraw cleared balances; openDispute takes a bond; resolveDispute (arbiter) or resolveAfterDeadline (permissionless after disputeResolveSeconds) upholds or rejects. Dispute decisions are driven by Graph re-derive at receipt blocks, not arbiter opinion alone. A Hedera-specific unit trap mattered in production: msg.value arrives in tinybar while eth_getBalance is weibar; disputeBond must be stored in tinybar and sent as bond×1e10 weibar or openDispute reverts BadBond. Distribution — Bazantic. Registered from OpenAPI as api-key (not x402-mpp) because USDC-on-Base cannot satisfy a Hedera challenge. Same completeRead() path as direct buyers, so refusal cannot be skipped on resale. A multi-service recipe pairs SourceMark with Hedera Mirror Node; public recipe JSON lives in bazantic/. Notable hacks / hard-won details: free refusal via verify-then-settle; operator float ledger when rails do not meet; falsified-receipt demo that corrupts per-source anchors (hash-only tamper still MATCHed on value alignment); gas floors on Hedera resolve txs after under-estimated gas; dedicated DEMO_SOURCE_MNEMONIC payees instead of the public Hardhat phrase. Partners: The Graph (live data + schema identity), Hedera (x402, SourcePayouts, HCS), Bazantic (distribution and Mirror Node recipe).

projects.title: Sticker Bomb
projects.description: 🚦StickerBomb takes ideas from screens to streets with verified placement and instant USDC payouts.
projects.project_description: Cicada 3301 proved that an idea born online could send people into streets around the world searching for mysterious posters.⁠ ⁠StickerBomb turns that magic into quick commerce for physical advertising: upload your artwork, choose a city, and fund a campaign while local workers place it, independent workers verify it, and onchain escrow pays them automatically. From your mom’s basement, you can take your company from a screen to streets anywhere in the world. Brand side : Upload artwork, choose a city and fund the campaign. Track every placement, payment and QR scan from one dashboard. Gig Worker side : Claim a nearby job, place the poster and submit photo, QR and location proof. A different worker independently verifies it before both are paid.
projects.how_its_made: How it’s made We built StickerBomb as a full end-to-end pipeline connecting mobile-first street operations to trust-minimized, automatic payouts. Brand side: Brands create campaigns, choose approved locations through Mapbox, upload artwork, set rewards, and fund the campaign. They can track placements, payments, and scans from one dashboard. Gig worker side: Workers use our PWA to claim nearby jobs, scan the poster, and submit photo and GPS proof. A separate worker can independently verify the placement before payment. QR system: Every location receives a unique, artwork-styled QR that is tested before printing. Scans identify the exact poster, record privacy-safe attribution, and redirect visitors to the brand’s current destination. [1] World: Selfie Check binds one verified credential to one worker account, helping stop duplicate identities from claiming rewards. The escrow prevents the same job from being paid twice. [2] Chainlink CRE and escrow: Chainlink CRE privately checks the QR, geofence, evidence freshness, and installer/verifier proof. Its result reaches our Sepolia CampaignEscrow , which releases USDC only after approval. Privy: Privy provides brand treasury wallets, worker payout wallets, authentication, and controlled campaign funding—without requiring users to manage private keys. Infrastructure: The PWA runs on Vercel, campaign and job data lives in AWS RDS Postgres through Prisma, private evidence is stored in Supabase Storage, and Mapbox powers campaign locations and worker navigation. Stack: Next.js · Vercel · AWS RDS · Prisma · Supabase Storage · Mapbox · World · Chainlink CRE · Privy · Solidity · Sepolia · USDC. Hacky/notable: Every poster becomes a physical asset with an onchain payout condition, while sensitive evidence is verified inside a TEE—so workers are paid based on proof, not trust in our database.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
## How it’s made

We built StickerBomb as a full end-to-end pipeline connecting mobile-first street operations to trust-minimized, automatic payouts.

**Brand side:** Brands create campaigns, choose approved locations through Mapbox, upload artwork, set rewards, and fund the campaign. They can track placements, payments, and scans from one dashboard.

**Gig worker side:** Workers use our PWA to claim nearby jobs, scan the poster, and submit photo and GPS proof. A separate worker can independently verify the placement before payment.

**QR system:** Every location receives a unique, artwork-styled QR that is tested before printing. Scans identify the exact poster, record privacy-safe attribution, and redirect visitors to the brand’s current destination.[[1]](https://github.com/harshalbhangale/ethonline2026/blob/main/src/lib/assets/qr.ts)

**World:** Selfie Check binds one verified credential to one worker account, helping stop duplicate identities from claiming rewards. The escrow prevents the same job from being paid twice.[[2]](https://github.com/harshalbhangale/ethonline2026/blob/main/src/lib/world/selfie-check.ts)

**Chainlink CRE and escrow:** Chainlink CRE privately checks the QR, geofence, evidence freshness, and installer/verifier proof. Its result reaches our Sepolia `CampaignEscrow`, which releases USDC only after approval.

**Privy:** Privy provides brand treasury wallets, worker payout wallets, authentication, and controlled campaign funding—without requiring users to manage private keys.

**Infrastructure:** The PWA runs on Vercel, campaign and job data lives in AWS RDS Postgres through Prisma, private evidence is stored in Supabase Storage, and Mapbox powers campaign locations and worker navigation.

**Stack:** Next.js · Vercel · AWS RDS · Prisma · Supabase Storage · Mapbox · World · Chainlink CRE · Privy · Solidity · Sepolia · USDC.

Hacky/notable: Every poster becomes a physical asset with an onchain payout condition, while sensitive evidence is verified inside a TEE—so workers are paid based on proof, not trust in our database.

projects.title: AskChain
projects.description: AskChing turns DeFi questions into cited answers from live The Graph subgraphs.
projects.project_description: AskChing is an evidence-first DeFi research agent that transforms natural-language questions into transparent, cited answers from live Ethereum mainnet subgraphs. It compares lending markets across Aave V3, Compound V3, Spark Lend and Aave V2; analyses market conditions and historical trends; and discovers USDC yield opportunities across lending, Uniswap V3 and Curve. AskChing provides seven MCP tools for market comparison, research briefs, risk scanning, explainable analysis, 7- or 30-day trend analysis, cross-venue yield discovery and self-description. Every reported figure includes provenance such as its subgraph ID, block, timestamp and query hash. Calculations, confidence levels, caveats and data-quality gaps remain visible instead of being hidden behind an opaque score. Different products are not presented as directly equivalent: current lending supply APY and historical DEX LP fee APR are ranked separately. AskChing fails closed when it cannot obtain enough independent cited evidence, never invents unsupported data, does not execute transactions and does not present its output as financial advice.
projects.how_its_made: AskChing was built from scratch as a TypeScript pnpm monorepo. Its shared data layer queries six live Ethereum mainnet subgraphs through The Graph Gateway: Aave V3, Compound V3, Spark Lend, Aave V2, Uniswap V3 and Curve. The results are normalized into strict Zod schemas so rates, assets, units and rate definitions are validated before anything is compared or ranked. The MCP server exposes six research tools—compare_markets, research_brief, risk_scan, analyze_markets, analyze_trends and discover_yields—plus a get_info tool that explains the product and provides example prompts. A single tool-registration module powers both local stdio and remote Streamable HTTP transports, preventing their capabilities from drifting apart. The deployed Vercel endpoint can therefore be connected directly to MCP-compatible clients including Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Codex and Gemini CLI. A Grok tool-calling CLI forms the conversational orchestration layer. It interprets a natural-language request, selects the appropriate AskChing tool, supplies structured arguments and synthesizes the cited result. Deterministic fixture mode allows reliable demos and tests, while live mode uses The Graph API credentials. The evidence model is enforced in code: every observation carries its subgraph ID, block, timestamp and query hash, and quantitative comparisons fail closed unless at least two independent cited sources remain. Partial source failures become explicit gaps rather than disappearing silently. For DEX yield discovery, AskChing aligns Uniswap V3 and Curve snapshots to a shared completed UTC day and calculates historical fee APR from cited daily fees and TVL. A particularly practical hack was replacing a slow global Uniswap snapshot query with a two-stage process: discover eligible pools first, then fetch each pool’s snapshots in parallel. Lending APY and LP fee APR remain in separate rankings because their definitions and risks are fundamentally different. The repository includes Vitest unit and integration tests, behavioural evals, live-source probes, MCP transport smoke tests and deployment checks. Git history contains frequent incremental commits to preserve the ETHOnline Start Fresh development trail.

projects.title: Merxet
projects.description: End-To-End Encrypted Retail Protocol On Hedera with merchant-branded storefronts
projects.project_description: Merxet is an end-to-end encrypted retail protocol built on Hedera. It lets merchants sell products online and offline through a simple checkout, with payments handled on Hedera, private messages and sensitive order data protected by end-to-end encryption. Beyond distributing QR codes offline, sellers can create online storefronts for their product catalogs and customize them with the Merxet AI agent. Each store can have a short, unique ENS name, and sellers can verify themselves through World Selfie Check. Buyers use the Merxet app as a personal shopping cart with a built-in Hedera wallet. They can shop across different stores and pay with supported tokens, including HBAR and USDC. What makes Merxet different? Decentralized commerce with private order data. Sensitive order data is encrypted and stored on-chain. Only the buyer and seller can decrypt it. Transparent payments with predefined rules. Merxet's public payment protocol on Hedera uses escrow and predefined settlement rules, giving buyers and sellers a clear view of how payments are handled, without unexpected holds, extra platform fees, or verification delays. A fast, affordable way to start selling. Upload your products, generate QR codes for offline sales, and create an online storefront with AI customization, all within Merxet. projects.title: Honeybee pay
projects.description: AI-assisted crypto payments with buyer-approved rules and zero-knowledge privacy.
projects.project_description: Honeybee Pay aims to make everyday crypto payments simple, private, and secure. AI helps users prepare payments in plain language, while a payment firewall enforces the recipient, token, and amount the buyer approved. The AI cannot override those rules. A planned zero-knowledge proof layer will allow payment validity to be verified without publicly revealing selected transaction details. The first demo will compare three payments of 1 test USDC: a normal payment, a redirected payment in an intentionally unprotected demonstration, and the same redirection attempt blocked by the protected system. AI will explain why the payment was blocked. Development is underway; zero-knowledge privacy will be implemented and tested separately from the initial firewall demo.
projects.how_its_made: I’m building Honeybee Pay in GitHub Codespaces using Foundry to develop and test Solidity smart contracts. So far, I have documented the payment rules and demo scenarios and installed the development tools. The planned payment contract will check each payment against the buyer’s approval, including the recipient, token, amount, and expiration, and prevent approvals from being reused. AI will help prepare payment requests and explain blocked attempts, but it will not have authority to override the contract’s rules. The initial tests will compare normal payments with deliberately redirected payments using test USDC. The unprotected example will be kept separate from the protected payment contract. Zero-knowledge privacy is a separate planned phase; the proof system and its integration have not yet been selected or implemented. I’m using AI tools for development guidance and coding review. I will document their contributions alongside my implementation decisions, tests, and build progress.

projects.title: WISHMail
projects.description: Certified mail for agents across registries, anchored on Hedera Hashgraph.
projects.project_description: WISHMail is a protocol specification and reference implementation for verifiable messaging between software agents on the Hedera network. It defines a format for encrypted payloads transmitted via HCS-10 message operations, alongside an audit trail consisting of resolution proofs, consensus timestamps, return receipts, and attempted-delivery records. Using public consensus data from any Hedera mirror node, an external party can reconstruct a message exchange and verify the underlying cryptographic proofs without an encryption key, a stamp, a Hedera account, specialized credentials, or an intermediary broker. The protocol addresses a specific limitation in current agent frameworks: systems such as A2A cards, MCP tools, and agent registries establish discovery and communication channels, but they do not generate verifiable proof of delivery. Senders cannot cryptographically prove that a message was received, resolved to the intended recipient, or read. WISHMail provides this delivery verification via a consensus-witnessed transaction signed by the recipient. The protocol enforces two primary technical guarantees: Origin Integrity: An encrypted payload is cryptographically bound to its settlement transaction and the recorded address resolution. The resolution proof is stored within the payload’s Additional Authenticated Data (AAD); if the address was improperly resolved or the transaction improperly settled, the payload fails decryption. Deterministic Reconstruction: A message exchange forms an audit trail of proofs across public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topics, allowing any third party to replay the sequence using only the specification. The system supports multiple registry types. The specification defines address resolution as an input/output interface with three designated profiles: hcs14: The native profile, which resolves HCS-14 UAIDs by traversing HCS-11 and HCS-2 declaration chains on consensus. dns: Resolves names via the Domain Name System. nanda: Resolves records via a NANDA v2 index. A2A AgentCard: Supported as an extension profile. Each profile defines a specific trust classification. WISHMail does not host a registry, require a broker, or validate entries across external registries. In accordance with the honest degradation  standards of the specification, if a registry lookup cannot be independently verified from public data, the verifier must downgrade its trust classification. An operator's agent executes the buy_stamp function to pay for transmitting one directed message to one resolved address; broadcast messaging is not supported. Message fees are paid using $POSTAGE, a Hedera Token Service (HTS) token sold by a Postmaster account at a public rate that can be queried historically at the transaction timestamp. Inboxes use fee-gated topics (HIP-991) to prevent unsolicited traffic. Return receipts are implemented as long-term scheduled transactions (HIP-423) that execute automatically when the recipient appends the required signature. This transaction immediately logs the receipt to the recipient's manifest topic, linked directly to the first chunk of the original message. Recipients incur no network transaction fees unless they choose to acknowledge the receipt (then the recipient pays a small ScheduleSign fee). An agent initialized with only an HBAR balance can provision its account, mailbox, and postage tokens through a single buy_stamp function call. The architecture comprises four explicit roles and actions: The Assembler binds data into sealed payloads. The Consensus layer timestamps and records transactions. The Verifier parses data and reconciles cryptographic proofs. The Postmaster routes messages and covers fees on behalf of agents, no attestations. The protocol interfaces with external systems via six Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools: resolve, buy_stamp, send, inbox, ack, and verify. Five of the six, absent verify, are built for the MVP demonstration, with verify available by the CLI. Conformance is structured across four tiers, all of which depend on the base VERIFIER tier. The verification process requires no local configuration. The specification includes 17 formal invariants and 87 test suites, with every normative requirement mapped to a test case. The current implementation running on hedera:testnet demonstrates: A Postmaster account that sells and provisions mailboxes. Two autonomous agents running in separate Goose Desktop environments, each initialized from a fresh operator wallet funded only with HBAR. The end-to-end transmission, decryption, and signature verification of a test message containing the string: "Certified agent mail proven on Hedera." A third-party verification script that reconstructs the entire transaction history using data pulled from a public mirror node. Five operational test gates evaluated against pre-committed audit reports, with corresponding execution records and HashScan links for all deployed entities. The current deployment includes the following technical constraints: It does not claim formal conformance tier compliance, as the specification mandates two independent, interoperable implementations, and currently only one exists. It does not claim compliance with a formal resolution profile; consequently, the internal verifier flags the demonstration message as unverified, which reflects expected verification behavior under the specification. The DNS, A2A, and NANDA resolver modules are defined in the specification but are not implemented in the current transmission pipeline. The deployment operates strictly on the Hedera testnet. The protocol does not provide forward secrecy. The protocol guarantees only that messages are recorded on consensus and made available for recipients to read; it does not confirm physical consumption by an end user.
projects.how_its_made: WISHMail is organized as a single monorepo under a specification-first development model. The repository contains seven top-level directories and a set of root documents, divided between operational components and the historical development record. Components with Ongoing Function spec/: Contains the normative specification (RFC 2119 keywords are binding; all other text is non-binding), the working ledger of findings and decisions, 14 JSON Schemas tracking the specification, a pins.json file fixing every referenced standard to a specific commit hash, and 178 individual Architecture Decision Record files (D-1 through D-178). conformance/: Contains 87 test cases keyed to their respective invariants, nine captured fixtures (byte-for-byte mirror-node reads of live testnet correspondences), and DERIVATION.md (a pre-authored ledger defining the source and rationale for all test inputs, whether captured bytes, altered captures, in-memory ledger models, or reconstructions). Test bodies derive exclusively from specification sketches rather than implementation code. During initial test runs, the suite identified 11 implementation defects (including three normative MUST violations), all of which were resolved and validated against the identifying tests. Currently, 44 tests pass; the remainder either document specific clause failures or remain unexpanded with recorded rationales. No formal conformance class is claimed. app/: Contains the TypeScript reference implementation (Node 22), comprising a Postmaster counter (Streamable HTTP MCP server), a Correspondent agent (stdio MCP server running one process per agent as a Goose Desktop extension), an SDK, CLI utilities for each tool, and the native hcs14 resolver. It also contains OPERATIONS.md, an operations log documenting sequential gate reports and runs-of-record for every signed transaction on the testnet. scripts/: Contains three automated repository checks: generating and validating ENTITIES.md against deployment records, diffing the test register against the formal specification, and running a static grep that fails if any module outside the designated key-handling modules names agent private-key material. The Provenance Trail provenance/: Read-only, non-binding historical documentation. This directory preserves the day-one consolidation ledger (WISHMail v0.3, dated 2026-09-04) that preceded the specification and was used to backfill the first 41 decision records, the handoff document establishing the bridge thesis and invariant sets, legal research on U.S. Private Express Statutes informing the specification's informative postal-grounding section (§17), two Excalidraw design diagrams (the ratified scope map and the demo execution flow), the hackathon venue rules recorded on 2026-09-07, a dated trace of six pre-gate validation probes, and an outbound issue report documenting a normative contradiction in the pinned HCS-10 commit without prescribing a fix. Its recon/ subdirectory stores dated snapshots of all underlying standards (HCS-10, HCS-14, HCS-11, HCS-2, HCS-1, HCS-13, NANDA v2, the HOL broker, x402, and OpenConvAI), alongside derived draft pins and unresolved technical items. These snapshots directly inform spec/pins.json, and the ledger's digest of verified facts cites them by file and line. plans/: Stores eight approved planning documents verbatim, accompanied by a README mapping each plan to its executing commits and recording implementation divergences. Plans are strictly non-normative: each was formulated in plan mode, submitted with open questions, amended via human intervention, and executed. Discoveries made during execution were recorded directly in the decision register and git commit logs rather than updating retroactive plan files. docs/: Contains narrative documentation distinct from transactional records. GATE-RECORD.md provides an end-to-end procedural review of the five operational gates and the recorded demonstration, linking all identifiers to HashScan. OPERATOR-SCRIPT.md details the step-by-step instructions executed in Goose by the human operator. In any discrepancy between narrative documents and operational logs (app/OPERATIONS.md, ENTITIES.md), the logs govern. Root Documents CLAUDE.md: Committed standing instructions and system prompts loaded at the start of each agent session. STATUS.md: The one file in the repository permitted to rank open items by priority. LIMITATIONS.md: Itemized security and functional boundaries not defended by this deployment. CHANGELOG.md: Chronological modifications with per-entry contributor attribution. CONTRIBUTING.md: Governance rules for proposed code modifications. ENTITIES.md: Inventory of all testnet entities paired with creation transaction IDs and a table labeled "RESIDUE — NOT OPERATING" for diagnostic probe artifacts. Emancipation Proclamation: Committed as raw test payload data for the ten-chunk certified message executed in Gate Two. Versioning and Deployment The specification was frozen at version 0.5.0 on September 7, 2026, and incremented via patches to 0.5.13. All 14 schemas were registered on-chain under HCS-13 on September 9, 2026; once registered, no patch may alter them (§1.7), so any schema change is a new minor version. A mirror-node query of these records returns byte streams identical to the local files in spec/schemas/. The testnet deployment accounts for 75 recorded entities, each mapped to a creation transaction and an independent mirror-node read. Hedera Integrations and Core Functions HCS-10: Operates as the underlying transport layer pinned to a specific draft commit. WISHMail defines only the payload structure encapsulated within the operation data field. HCS-14, HCS-11, HCS-2, and HCS-1: Establish the decentralized address resolution chain, traversed via mirror-node queries without local client configuration. HTS: Mints $POSTAGE as a zero-decimal token lacking admin, freeze, pause, or wipe keys. HIP-991: Applies custom topic fees to gate inbound communication. The sender's payer transfers one $POSTAGE token to the treasury per connection request; the receiving agent's key is explicitly exempt. HIP-423: Executes return receipts through scheduled transactions. Senders assemble and fund the schedule transaction, which the network executes as soon as the recipient appends their signature, publishing the receipt to the recipient's manifest topic. Senders configure the receipt expiration window; expired, unsigned transactions indicate an unclaimed delivery rather than transport failure. HIP-542: Enables account auto-creation via token transfers, allowing an agent using an HBAR-only wallet to provision its account and asset balances in a single transaction. On-Ledger Exchange Rates: Calculates HBAR conversions using the network's consensus exchange rate at the transaction timestamp, replacing earlier off-chain DEX APIs to preserve deterministic third-party verification. Transaction Construction: All network interactions are built and signed using @hashgraph/sdk without Solidity or smart contracts. Cryptographic Architecture Payload encryption uses HPKE (RFC 9180 base mode: X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM) implemented natively via node:crypto and tested against RFC 9180 Appendix A.1 vectors. A third-party implementation (@hpke/core with @hpke/dhkem-x25519) was evaluated and eliminated due to documented nonce handling flaws. Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) consists of RFC 8785 canonical JSON containing the envelope header and the resolution proof hash; the envelope identifier is the resulting SHA-256 hash. Payloads are divided into ordered chunks capped at the 1024-byte HCS message limit, with each segment containing a cryptographic digest of the subsequent chunk. Canonicalization relies on the canonicalize package across both pricing calculations and payload envelopes. Operational Safeguards Every consensus transaction requires an immutable gate report committed to git prior to signature generation, followed by an operational run-of-record. Retroactive changes to gate reports are prohibited; updates require new dated log entries. Driver scripts capable of signing transactions default to --dry-run and dump their arguments prior to accessing key storage. This safeguard was introduced after an argument-passing defect on September 10, 2026, omitted a dry-run flag and executed an unauthorized agent deployment. Agent private keys generate within local memory during initialization and persist exclusively in the agent's local home directory. The Postmaster holds no agent key at any point; a static check fails if any module outside the designated key-handling modules names agent key material. ENTITIES.md is compiled by script and fails npm run check:entities if manual edits are detected. Goose Integration Accommodations The system resolves model-specific behaviors at the MCP protocol layer. Because the model parses object-level arguments into JSON strings, the server deserializes and validates incoming parameters at the API surface. Because the model occasionally modifies long base64 strings during output, the operator script enforces human verification of payload strings prior to token transfer. Identified Demonstration Defect The run-of-record for the testnet demonstration documents an operational fault: the recipient agent queried a mirror node only once before declaring its connection topic, creating six topics instead of the intended single topic. The root cause is cataloged by file and line number, with network fee deviations reconciled to three decimal places of HBAR. The defect remains unpatched in the demonstration build to preserve code freeze integrity. Development Protocol and Attribution The codebase was constructed with Claude Code under strict human architectural oversight. All protocol and design choices represent explicit human rulings; every code modification is structured for standalone verification without generative tooling. The working ledger categorizes assertions into three distinct states: RECORD (human directives), FETCHED (verified external documentation), and MINE (unverified model inferences). Git commits adhere to the Developer Certificate of Origin and Conventional Commits specifications, enforced via a commit-msg hook, with comprehensive change tracking maintained in CHANGELOG.md. The project is licensed under Apache 2.0. Work commenced after the opening of ETHOnline; no source code was imported, adapted, or extracted from prior repositories.

LIMITATIONS.md: Itemized security and functional boundaries not defended by this deployment.

CHANGELOG.md: Chronological modifications with per-entry contributor attribution.

CONTRIBUTING.md: Governance rules for proposed code modifications.

ENTITIES.md: Inventory of all testnet entities paired with creation transaction IDs and a table labeled "RESIDUE — NOT OPERATING" for diagnostic probe artifacts.

Emancipation Proclamation: Committed as raw test payload data for the ten-chunk certified message executed in Gate Two.

Versioning and Deployment

The specification was frozen at version 0.5.0 on September 7, 2026, and incremented via patches to 0.5.13. All 14 schemas were registered on-chain under HCS-13 on September 9, 2026; once registered, no patch may alter them (§1.7), so any schema change is a new minor version. A mirror-node query of these records returns byte streams identical to the local files in spec/schemas/. The testnet deployment accounts for 75 recorded entities, each mapped to a creation transaction and an independent mirror-node read.

Hedera Integrations and Core Functions

HCS-10: Operates as the underlying transport layer pinned to a specific draft commit. WISHMail defines only the payload structure encapsulated within the operation data field.

HCS-14, HCS-11, HCS-2, and HCS-1: Establish the decentralized address resolution chain, traversed via mirror-node queries without local client configuration.

HTS: Mints $POSTAGE as a zero-decimal token lacking admin, freeze, pause, or wipe keys.

HIP-991: Applies custom topic fees to gate inbound communication. The sender's payer transfers one $POSTAGE token to the treasury per connection request; the receiving agent's key is explicitly exempt.

HIP-423: Executes return receipts through scheduled transactions. Senders assemble and fund the schedule transaction, which the network executes as soon as the recipient appends their signature, publishing the receipt to the recipient's manifest topic. Senders configure the receipt expiration window; expired, unsigned transactions indicate an unclaimed delivery rather than transport failure.

HIP-542: Enables account auto-creation via token transfers, allowing an agent using an HBAR-only wallet to provision its account and asset balances in a single transaction.

On-Ledger Exchange Rates: Calculates HBAR conversions using the network's consensus exchange rate at the transaction timestamp, replacing earlier off-chain DEX APIs to preserve deterministic third-party verification.

Transaction Construction: All network interactions are built and signed using @hashgraph/sdk without Solidity or smart contracts.

Cryptographic Architecture

Payload encryption uses HPKE (RFC 9180 base mode: X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM) implemented natively via node:crypto and tested against RFC 9180 Appendix A.1 vectors. A third-party implementation (@hpke/core with @hpke/dhkem-x25519) was evaluated and eliminated due to documented nonce handling flaws. Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) consists of RFC 8785 canonical JSON containing the envelope header and the resolution proof hash; the envelope identifier is the resulting SHA-256 hash. Payloads are divided into ordered chunks capped at the 1024-byte HCS message limit, with each segment containing a cryptographic digest of the subsequent chunk. Canonicalization relies on the canonicalize package across both pricing calculations and payload envelopes.

Operational Safeguards

Every consensus transaction requires an immutable gate report committed to git prior to signature generation, followed by an operational run-of-record. Retroactive changes to gate reports are prohibited; updates require new dated log entries.

Driver scripts capable of signing transactions default to --dry-run and dump their arguments prior to accessing key storage. This safeguard was introduced after an argument-passing defect on September 10, 2026, omitted a dry-run flag and executed an unauthorized agent deployment.

Agent private keys generate within local memory during initialization and persist exclusively in the agent's local home directory. The Postmaster holds no agent key at any point; a static check fails if any module outside the designated key-handling modules names agent key material.

ENTITIES.md is compiled by script and fails npm run check:entities if manual edits are detected.

Goose Integration Accommodations

The system resolves model-specific behaviors at the MCP protocol layer. Because the model parses object-level arguments into JSON strings, the server deserializes and validates incoming parameters at the API surface.

Because the model occasionally modifies long base64 strings during output, the operator script enforces human verification of payload strings prior to token transfer.

Identified Demonstration Defect

The run-of-record for the testnet demonstration documents an operational fault: the recipient agent queried a mirror node only once before declaring its connection topic, creating six topics instead of the intended single topic. The root cause is cataloged by file and line number, with network fee deviations reconciled to three decimal places of HBAR. The defect remains unpatched in the demonstration build to preserve code freeze integrity.

Development Protocol and Attribution

The codebase was constructed with Claude Code under strict human architectural oversight. All protocol and design choices represent explicit human rulings; every code modification is structured for standalone verification without generative tooling. The working ledger categorizes assertions into three distinct states: RECORD (human directives), FETCHED (verified external documentation), and MINE (unverified model inferences). Git commits adhere to the Developer Certificate of Origin and Conventional Commits specifications, enforced via a commit-msg hook, with comprehensive change tracking maintained in CHANGELOG.md. The project is licensed under Apache 2.0. Work commenced after the opening of ETHOnline; no source code was imported, adapted, or extracted from prior repositories.
