projects.title: Tremor
projects.description: Two-sided continuous ETH realized-variance receipts hedging LVR on 1inch Aqua & SwapVM.
projects.project_description:
Tremor is a continuously priced market in ETH realized variance. It is a way to take a position on how violent the next week is, rather than which direction it goes. Volatility is one of the largest risks in crypto and almost nobody can trade it directly. You can bet on direction all day. But an LP bleeding to loss-versus-rebalancing, a desk short gamma, a treasury sizing its risk: none of them can take a clean position on variance itself without an options book and a counterparty to face. Tremor turns realized variance into an instrument. Each market is one observation window on the Chainlink ETH/USD feed carrying two complementary claims: LONG VARIANCE pays S × min(V / V_cap, 1)
SHORT VARIANCE pays S − LONG where V is the annualized realized variance actually observed and S is the cap payout. The two sides always sum to exactly S, which is $1.00, to the integer, in every state, because SHORT is computed by subtraction from LONG rather than rounded independently. Buying the pair can never win; selling the pair can never win. Settlement is computed, not quoted. At expiry anyone calls finalize, and the contract replays Chainlink's own round history on chain to compute realized variance and fix both payouts in a single call. There is no oracle write, no price feed of our own, and no privileged actor. The same is true of checkpointing the observation window: permissionless, bounded per call, and cheap. Anyone who wants a quote can make the call, because a market that is behind refuses to price. Prices move continuously, and every price the UI presents as executable is executable. This is not an order book. The market quotes off projected variance, meaning what has actually been realized so far blended with a forward for the time remaining. That is displaced by inventory skew and sits inside a spread that tightens as the window closes and the outcome becomes less uncertain. A fill is priced as the integral over a rising ask, so size pays impact honestly. The number on screen is read from the on-chain lens for that exact size, not estimated by the frontend. The indicative mark is shown separately and labelled an estimate, never offered as a cashout value. Both sides share one pot of collateral. Every claim is fully collateralized before it is sold, and the writer cannot withdraw what backs a live claim. Because long and short cannot both pay out, the market locks ceil(max(long, short) × S) rather than long × S + short × S. The saving is min(long, short) / (long + short) — up to half the capital for the same open interest when the book is balanced — and the terminal shows the actual figure read off the contract rather than a headline. That is the 1inch Aqua contribution: one vault, one reserve, two instruments. A built-in hedging tool sizes the position for the most concrete buyer: an LP's expected LVR is proportional to realized variance (E[LVR] ≈ P·σ²·T/8, for pool value P), so pool value and horizon in gives units and premium out, priced through the same lens.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry. TremorPortfolioMarketV4 holds the accounting and the fill legs; TremorPortfolioLensV4 is a separate read model, split out because the combined contract exceeded the EIP-170 24,576-byte limit by 746 bytes. PortfolioPricing is the whole pricing change and deliberately owns no new arithmetic: every integral, spread and clamp is the v2 VariancePricing library already pinned to reference vectors at 60 decimal digits. The bridge that let two generations compose with no seam is deriving the cap payout S = floor(unitNotional × capVariance / 1e18), which makes v2's perUnitPrice(V) and v3's S × min(V/cap,1) the same function of V. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM is the execution layer, not a wrapper. Each market ships six strategies, issue, exit and settle for both sides, and each one is a SwapVM program built from stock instructions: Salt · Deadline · Extruction. They run on the unmodified official AquaSwapVMRouter; we forked no router and added no opcode, which means this deploys against real Aqua today with no new audit surface and nobody's permission. The interesting part is where the pricing lives: the Extruction instruction calls back into the market mid-swap, so the curve is evaluated inside the swap itself. That is what makes preview and execution provably the same number. The frontend re-quotes through router.quote, which is the exact code path router.swap runs, immediately before signing. The vault ships each strategy hash-pinned, and the market verifies the returned hash matches what it built, so a fill cannot execute against a program the market did not author. Collateral sits in the writer's own TremorMakerVault, which grants Aqua an allowance the writer does not control the code of; the router pulls against that allowance when a leg fills. It is an allowance model, not escrow — which is exactly why a capped payoff fits it and a perp would not. Maximum liability is fixed at issuance, so a position is fully reserved from t=0, there is no leverage, and there is nothing to liquidate by construction. That is also what lets one reserve back two instruments. Chainlink is used as a historical record, not a price feed. The accumulator walks AggregatorV3 round history phase-aware, absorbs samples on a fixed per-market grid (sampleInterval, floored at 300 seconds; the demo markets use ten minutes, because the grid must be coarse enough that repeated rounds do not bias realized variance downward), and stores progress so checkpointing is idempotent and bounded. A market refuses to price against a window with unstored samples, so a stale quote reverts CheckpointsStale rather than filling at a number the feed has already moved past. All arithmetic is integer. WAD for variance, 6-decimal for USDC, bigint end to end with no floats anywhere in the stack. Rounding direction is chosen deliberately in every operation to favour the collateralized maker: takers pay ceil and receive floor, and the complement inherits that direction because it subtracts a floored term from a ceiled one. Backend: Rust, axum, alloy, sqlx/SQLite. An indexer plus an exact replica of the Solidity pricing, which is what lets the API serve history and previews without a chain round trip per request. The replica is pinned against the contracts' own vectors — 144 portfolio cases for the Rust replica, 60 series cases for the web replica, all generated at 60 significant digits — so a divergence fails a test rather than reaching a user. The API reconstructs price history per sample, on the window's own clock rather than the keeper's transaction time, and reports the anchor drift against on-chain state in ppm. A subgraph (The Graph, tested with Matchstick) mirrors the events. Frontend: Next.js 16, wagmi v3 / viem, Recharts, Playwright. The terminal is the product: chart with the executable band, an on-chain activity tape, a ticket that prices your exact size, and a collateral panel showing the shared-reserve saving against the separate-cap equivalent. The rule the whole UI obeys is that the Lens is the authority and the backend is a replica. Chain state is merged over API state, never the reverse, and an estimate is never rendered where a user will read an executable price. An oversized order is presented as a partial fill — the ticket prices what the router will actually sell, not the size that was typed. Notable details. Inventory skew is stateless: rather than storing a decaying signed skew with a half-life and a last-updated timestamp, the forward is displaced by impact × (long − short) derived from outstanding inventory, so it cannot drift from the book and reverses exactly on an exit. The E2E suite drives a real fill against an anvil fork through an EIP-1193 shim that forwards to the node under --auto-impersonate, so transactions are genuinely signed and mined, and the test asserts on the buyer's own receipt balance on chain rather than on the DOM. It also covers a refused signature and a slow wallet, and asserts that a quote which moves between display and signing stops the flow and asks for consent rather than signing the new number. To stress the design we built a harness that funds 1,000 scripted accounts on a local fork, against an earlier deployment of the same contracts, and runs each through the same call sequence the trading panel uses; the P&L report is reconstructed entirely from chain state, from USDC transfer logs and receipt balances, not from the harness's own memory. Verification: 290 contract tests across 26 suites including two Base-fork E2Es, 86 backend tests, 85 web unit tests, and 34 fixture-driven browser tests plus a live-fill suite that connects a wallet, signs and mines against a fork. A dedicated test decodes the shipped program bytes and asserts the opcode set, so the "stock instructions only" claim is enforced by CI rather than by a README.

The vault ships each strategy hash-pinned, and the market verifies the returned hash matches what it built, so a fill cannot execute against a program the market did not author.

Collateral sits in the writer's own TremorMakerVault, which grants Aqua an allowance the writer does not control the code of; the router pulls against that allowance when a leg fills. It is an allowance model, not escrow — which is exactly why a capped payoff fits it and a perp would not. Maximum liability is fixed at issuance, so a position is fully reserved from t=0, there is no leverage, and there is nothing to liquidate by construction. That is also what lets one reserve back two instruments.

Chainlink is used as a historical record, not a price feed. The accumulator walks AggregatorV3 round history phase-aware, absorbs samples on a fixed per-market grid (sampleInterval, floored at 300 seconds; the demo markets use ten minutes, because the grid must be coarse enough that repeated rounds do not bias realized variance downward), and stores progress so checkpointing is idempotent and bounded. A market refuses to price against a window with unstored samples, so a stale quote reverts CheckpointsStale rather than filling at a number the feed has already moved past.

All arithmetic is integer. WAD for variance, 6-decimal for USDC, bigint end to end with no floats anywhere in the stack. Rounding direction is chosen deliberately in every operation to favour the collateralized maker: takers pay ceil and receive floor, and the complement inherits that direction because it subtracts a floored term from a ceiled one.

Backend: Rust, axum, alloy, sqlx/SQLite. An indexer plus an exact replica of the Solidity pricing, which is what lets the API serve history and previews without a chain round trip per request. The replica is pinned against the contracts' own vectors — 144 portfolio cases for the Rust replica, 60 series cases for the web replica, all generated at 60 significant digits — so a divergence fails a test rather than reaching a user. The API reconstructs price history per sample, on the window's own clock rather than the keeper's transaction time, and reports the anchor drift against on-chain state in ppm. A subgraph (The Graph, tested with Matchstick) mirrors the events.

Frontend: Next.js 16, wagmi v3 / viem, Recharts, Playwright. The terminal is the product: chart with the executable band, an on-chain activity tape, a ticket that prices your exact size, and a collateral panel showing the shared-reserve saving against the separate-cap equivalent. The rule the whole UI obeys is that the Lens is the authority and the backend is a replica. Chain state is merged over API state, never the reverse, and an estimate is never rendered where a user will read an executable price. An oversized order is presented as a partial fill — the ticket prices what the router will actually sell, not the size that was typed.

Notable details. Inventory skew is stateless: rather than storing a decaying signed skew with a half-life and a last-updated timestamp, the forward is displaced by impact × (long − short) derived from outstanding inventory, so it cannot drift from the book and reverses exactly on an exit. The E2E suite drives a real fill against an anvil fork through an EIP-1193 shim that forwards to the node under --auto-impersonate, so transactions are genuinely signed and mined, and the test asserts on the buyer's own receipt balance on chain rather than on the DOM. It also covers a refused signature and a slow wallet, and asserts that a quote which moves between display and signing stops the flow and asks for consent rather than signing the new number. To stress the design we built a harness that funds 1,000 scripted accounts on a local fork, against an earlier deployment of the same contracts, and runs each through the same call sequence the trading panel uses; the P&L report is reconstructed entirely from chain state, from USDC transfer logs and receipt balances, not from the harness's own memory.

Verification: 290 contract tests across 26 suites including two Base-fork E2Es, 86 backend tests, 85 web unit tests, and 34 fixture-driven browser tests plus a live-fill suite that connects a wallet, signs and mines against a fork. A dedicated test decodes the shipped program bytes and asserts the opcode set, so the "stock instructions only" claim is enforced by CI rather than by a README.

projects.title: Sowee
projects.description: Waiting 90 days to get paid? Get cash today. Investors fund invoices at a discount.
projects.project_description: Sowee helps small businesses get paid sooner by turning unpaid invoices into bonds investors can buy. A business gets most of the money upfront, while investors receive the full invoice amount when the customer pays. The bond itself enforces KYC, so only verified wallets can hold or trade it. The flow is simple. A business submits an invoice and only its digital fingerprint leaves the browser. Sowee lists it as a bond, investors complete World Selfie Check and Sumsub KYC, then fund it with USDC. Investors can also trade the bond with other verified users before maturity. Everything runs on public testnets. Hedera provides the blockchain and public record, while Asset Tokenization Studio supports regulated securities. AI agents can also buy market data through x402 and fund bonds themselves, as long as their wallets pass the same checks. The same finance core also runs on Arc.
projects.how_its_made: Sowee has four main pieces that work together. The smart contracts handle the rules, turning each invoice into a bond token that checks KYC on every transfer. The web app lets businesses submit invoices and investors buy bonds, while the invoice itself stays in the browser and only its fingerprint is stored. The server handles the things a browser shouldn't, including signing quotes, running Sumsub KYC, verifying World Selfie Check, and providing market data to AI agents. Our agent can pay 0.01 USDC for the data, read it, and fund a bond on its own. Hedera provides USDC and HCS, which we use instead of a database to store and replay the system's records. Asset Tokenization Studio lets us issue regulated securities, Blocky402 handles agent payments, World Selfie Check adds an anti sybil layer, and the same finance core also runs on Arc. One of the more unusual parts is that there is genuinely no database, even issuer logos are stored on Hedera. We also spent a day chasing a vague World generic_error before finding that our own security settings were blocking the SDK.

projects.title: Tappy
projects.description: Tap to approve. An AI agent wallet where every onchain transaction needs a physical NFC tap.
projects.project_description: Tappy is a wallet for AI agents that the agent cannot drain. People are starting to hand real money to AI agents so they can buy things, pay for services, and move funds without being asked every time. But an agent can be talked into anything. A prompt injection hidden in a product listing, a web page, or an email can convince it to send the whole balance to an attacker, and it will do so confidently and immediately. The current answer is a policy file: a spending cap, an allowlist, a daily limit. Those help, but they are rules written in advance by someone guessing what will go wrong, and a policy file is not a person. Tappy puts a person back in the loop, physically. The wallet has two keys. The agent holds one. A human holds the other on a device they can put in their pocket, in our case a Flipper Zero. The smart contract executes a transaction only when both keys have signed the exact same transaction. The agent can propose anything it likes and can sign its half instantly, and none of that moves a single wei on its own. You chat with the agent in a normal web app and ask it to buy something, send money, or swap tokens. The agent works out what it wants to do and creates a proposal. That proposal appears on the Flipper's screen with the action, the amount, and who is receiving it. Press OK and the transaction goes to the chain, with the chat updating when it lands. Press Back and nothing happens at all, and the agent is told it was refused. The demo turns on what happens when the agent is compromised. A shop listing in our mock store contains a hidden instruction telling the agent to transfer the entire balance to an attacker's address. The agent does what it was told and proposes the transfer. The proposal shows up on the Flipper like any other, reading SEND, the full balance, to an address the human has never seen. The human presses Back, and the money stays where it was. The agent has exactly three abilities: propose a send, propose a swap, propose a purchase. There is no fourth tool that executes anything, so there is nothing an injection can talk it into that a human does not personally see and approve first. We did not add prompt-injection defenses to the agent, because whether the agent gets fooled does not change what can happen to the money. Around this we built a working demo economy: a chat interface, a wallet dashboard showing both keys and the live balance, a mock shop with items to buy, and a mock exchange to swap against, all deployed on testnet so the transactions are real on-chain calls. A physical NFC tag starts the purchase flow. Tapping a phone to a sticker opens the shop inside the app, so the interaction feels like paying for something in a real place. We chose a Flipper Zero because it has a screen, a button, and a radio, and because many people in this community already own one and enjoy hacking on it. Nothing in the design is tied to it. The same approval step could run on a phone, a hardware wallet, or a keyring NFC tag costing about a dollar. In this version the human key is stored on the laptop that talks to the Flipper, so the Flipper is the physical approval step and not yet the place the key lives. Moving the key onto the device itself is the obvious next step, and we have measured that the hardware can handle the cryptography, but it needs a toolchain we chose not to take on during a one-week build. Everything runs on testnet.
projects.how_its_made: Tappy is a 2-of-2 wallet for AI agents. The agent holds one key, a human holds the other, and nothing moves until both have signed the same transaction. Other agent wallets stop a runaway agent with a policy file, and a policy file is not a person. The contract is the whole security model in about eighty-five lines of Solidity, built with Foundry on OpenZeppelin's typed-data and signature-recovery libraries. Its one function takes a call plus two signatures, recovers both against a fixed agent address and a fixed human address, and reverts if either fails. Replay protection comes from a monotonic nonce combined with the chain ID and the contract's own address, and every proposal carries a deadline ten minutes out. Anyone can relay the call and pay the gas, because authority lives in the signatures and not in the sender. We left out spending limits and allowlists on purpose. Every competing product has those already, and none of them has a hand. The web app is a T3 stack: Next.js on the App Router, tRPC, Drizzle over Postgres, hosted on Vercel with Supabase behind it. Inside it a model tool-calling loop gives the agent three tools, one each to propose a send, a swap, or a purchase. It has no way to execute anything. Proposals enter a state machine as pending and sit there until a human decides. One library handles typed-data hashing and signing across the server, the laptop bridge and the tests, so the digest comes out the same way everywhere. What made a three-person week work was putting a single interface in front of the human approver, with one method that takes a summary and a timeout and returns a decision. Three things implement it: a mock that auto-approves or asks yes/no in a terminal, the real Flipper, and a future on-device signer. Two thirds of the project was built against the mock, so only one person ever needed the hardware, and plugging the device in changed nothing above it. The hackiest part is how the laptop talks to the Flipper. Its JavaScript engine cannot reach USB at all, since the serial module is wired to the GPIO pins rather than the host connection, so there is no socket to open and no way for a script on the device to receive anything from a computer. The bridge instead drives the Flipper's own command-line interface over the USB virtual COM port and uses its file commands to drop small JSON files onto the SD card. The app on the device polls for an inbox file three times a second, renders four short lines on the 128x64 screen, and writes the answer back to an outbox file. A sequence number makes it idempotent, so re-reading a file cannot double-approve. File-based IPC tunnelled through a serial terminal is an ugly way to do this, and it has been reliable. The hosting forced a similar inversion. Vercel cannot hold an open websocket, so the laptop polls upward twice a second and dials out instead of the server pushing approvals down. That also removes any need for an inbound tunnel to a laptop on hotel wifi. The endpoint takes a bearer token, and it separately recovers the submitted signature against the known human address, so a leaked token still cannot approve something the human never saw. NFC is how a purchase starts. A sticker carries a URL that opens the shop inside the app. Getting it readable on iPhones cost us an hour of confusion. The tag looked correct by every check we knew, Android read it instantly, and iOS did nothing at all. Dumping the raw pages by hand showed the stored address had two schemes in it: the encoding already carries a byte meaning "https", and we had typed the prefix in as well. iOS validates the address before it will show anything, and it reports no error when it throws one away. We now build the payload from the prefix code and a bare hostname. The risk we took most seriously was a byte-level disagreement between the TypeScript and the Solidity over how the signed message is encoded. One wrong hash and every transaction reverts with nothing useful to debug. We froze a shared test vector on day one and made both test suites check it, and nothing merged unless the two languages agreed. We built against a Flipper Zero, though nothing in the design depends on it. The second factor only has to do three things: show a human what is about to happen, take a yes or a no, and produce a signature. The Flipper is a convenient body for that because it has a screen, a button and a radio, and because a lot of this audience already owns one. The same interface could sit behind a phone, a hardware wallet, or a cheap NFC tag on a keyring, where tapping the tag replaces the button press. A tag has no screen, so you lose the ability to see what you are approving before you approve it. That trade buys a second factor costing about a dollar per user. The human key still lives on the laptop in this version, so the Flipper is the physical approval step and not yet the place the key is stored. Signing on the device is feasible, and we measured the curve maths at roughly a tenth to a quarter of a second per signature, but it needs a C toolchain we chose not to fight mid-build. Testnet only.

projects.title: Solvent
projects.description: Solvency-aware market making for 1inch Aqua: quotes widen as wallets thin and refuse past a floor
projects.project_description: 1inch Aqua lets a market maker commit liquidity to a strategy without depositing it. Tokens stay in the maker's wallet and Aqua pulls them only when a taker fills, so one balance can back many strategies at once. The catch is that no strategy knows about the others. SwapVM prices each one as if it owned the whole wallet, Aqua's ship() never checks the total against the balance, and the whitepaper says it plainly: the AMM keeps quoting on virtual balances without checking real balances or allowances. The documented fix is for makers to watch their wallets and dock strategies by hand. We measured how often this happens. We rebuilt every maker's balance sheet across Aqua's entire history on Base from primary data, reading each wallet's balance and allowance from an archive node. 115 makers shipped 443 strategies. 78 of the 88 books that ever held more than $100 were under-backed at some point, and 89% of all material observations were under-backed. One book advertised about $51,000 of USDC while holding nothing, for weeks, and every taker who tried it paid gas for a revert. The same pipeline, pointed at the identical Aqua contracts on Arbitrum and Optimism, finds 123 of 138 material books under-backed across the three chains. Solvent makes an Aqua position aware of its own balance sheet, inside the strategy bytecode: SolvencySkew, a new SwapVM instruction. The maker's utilisation (total committed across all strategies, divided by what the wallet holds and has approved) feeds into price. Below a threshold the quote is unchanged; above it the spread widens, because the last unit of a shared balance is worth more than the first. SolvencyFloor, a new SwapVM instruction. Above a maker-chosen utilisation the strategy declines at quote time, with a reason, instead of reverting at settlement after the taker has spent gas. It lives in the program bytes, so any taker can read the covenant before trading. It is the automatic version of the whitepaper's manual docking. The balance-sheet index. Both instructions need a maker's aggregate commitment, and Aqua cannot compute it on-chain. A subgraph maintains every maker's live book on Base, Arbitrum, Optimism and Base Sepolia, published on The Graph Network. A keeper publishes each maker's numbers to an on-chain oracle, SolventBook, where the instructions read them during the quote. Anyone can recompute the same numbers from the public index. The live demo has five views. Mainnet shows every real Aqua maker's book on Base, Arbitrum and Optimism right now, each capsule filled green only as far as the wallet can settle. How it works shows the deployed system, every component linked to its verified contract or logs. Quote desk runs live quotes from the deployed router on Base Sepolia: step through a healthy book, a wallet that drains (the spread widens from 3,106.67 to 3,202.86 at 87% utilisation) and a book past its floor (every quote declines with SolvencyFloor's reason), or connect a wallet and take a quote for real. Balance sheets and Settlement ledger show the numbers every quote reads and what actually settled, failed fills included. Makers get automated risk management instead of watching a wallet. Takers and agents get a pre-trade answer to whether a quote will fill. Aggregators can rank quotes by reserve ratio with one query and stop routing to phantom liquidity. The SDK, @aqua-solvent/core on npm, gives any app the same balance sheets on all four chains.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). SolvencyFloor and SolvencySkew are custom SwapVM instructions. We followed upstream's own extension pattern: each takes a reserved placeholder slot in the opcode table (Floor at 0x22 in the guards bank, Skew at 0xb5 in the rate-tuning bank), so no official opcode moves and stock Aqua programs run unchanged on our router. SolventRouter is the official AquaSwapVMRouter shape carrying the extended set, running against a pinned, unmodified deployment of the official Aqua contract on Base Sepolia. Floor is validation-only (no register writes, safe under staticcall), so a decline happens inside a free view call. Skew wraps the rest of the program and mirrors upstream's FeeFlatIn arithmetic branch for branch, so a skewed quote equals a stock program carrying the equivalent flat fee, and below its threshold it is a provable no-op. Both read SolventBook, a small oracle holding each maker's committed and backing per token, with a timestamp so consumers can judge staleness. Two more instructions (ReputationGate and ReputationPriceAdjuster) read SolventScore, a counterparty score built from what actually settled. Tests include differential suites for the book and score math, invariant tests, a regression suite from upstream 1inch running on our router, and a test that reproduces the core failure against the real contracts: one wallet holding 10 WETH ships three strategies advertising 30, each passes a backing check on its own, and the second taker reverts. The Graph. This is the piece that makes the rest possible. Aqua stores balances per (maker, app, strategyHash, token) with no enumeration and no per-maker total, so no contract call can tell you a maker's aggregate commitment. The subgraph handles Shipped, Docked, Pulled and Pushed. Instead of replaying deltas, every touch re-reads Aqua.rawBalances for that strategy and token at the indexed block and folds the difference into the maker's book, which is exact by construction and immune to event ordering and wrapper edge cases. Backing is min(balanceOf, allowance to Aqua), read in the same handler, because a revoked allowance fails a fill just like an empty wallet. Ship calldata is decoded only to learn a strategy's token list; strategies shipped through wrappers are picked up on their first Pulled or Pushed, which covers 442 of 443 real strategies. One schema ships as four manifests (Base Sepolia, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism), all published on The Graph Network. A parity check rebuilds the largest books on each chain from an archive node and requires agreement to the wei. The keeper. Wallets drain through plain transfers that Aqua never sees, so the index alone goes stale. The attestor reads every book from the index, re-reads each wallet on-chain, diffs against SolventBook and writes only what changed, so a quiet market costs no gas. It runs on GitHub Actions about once a minute: each run does eight passes and triggers the next run only on success, with a 15-minute cron as a backstop. Its key holds ATTESTOR_ROLE and nothing else. The console is Vite, React, viem, wagmi and RainbowKit on GitHub Pages. The quote desk simulates every fill before sending and decodes the revert, so a floored book shows SolvencyFloor's reason before any gas is spent. It reads the published subgraphs through The Graph's gateway with a per-request fallback to Studio, pauses polling on hidden or idle tabs, and caps each browser's daily gateway use to protect the query budget. The SDK (@aqua-solvent/core on npm) exposes the same books on all four chains and encodes Solvent strategy programs. Notably hacky: A reverted fill erases its own logs, so no subgraph can index a broken promise. SwapVM's transfer functions are private and swap() is not virtual, so a router cannot catch and re-emit the failure either. SolventRecorder records it from outside: a taker contract can try/catch its own swap and report the failure, or the attestor finds failed receipts aimed at the router and records them, citing the reverted transaction hash so anyone can check it on the explorer. The mainnet numbers came from a one-off analyzer that decoded every ship() transaction, applied every Pulled and Pushed as a delta, and read backing from an archive node at 34 heights plus each book's peak. Partner technologies: 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua's shared liquidity is what creates the problem, and SwapVM's instruction set is where the fix lives. Adding two opcodes put solvency inside the quote itself, with no change to Aqua. The Graph. The aggregate balance sheet cannot be computed on-chain, so an index is the only place it can exist. The Graph let us maintain it on four chains from one schema, publish it on the decentralized network for anyone to query, and feed it back on-chain through the keeper.

1inch Aqua lets a market maker commit liquidity to a strategy without depositing it. Tokens stay in the maker's wallet and Aqua pulls them only when a taker fills, so one balance can back many strategies at once. The catch is that no strategy knows about the others. SwapVM prices each one as if it owned the whole wallet, Aqua's ship() never checks the total against the balance, and the whitepaper says it plainly: the AMM keeps quoting on virtual balances without checking real balances or allowances. The documented fix is for makers to watch their wallets and dock strategies by hand.

We measured how often this happens. We rebuilt every maker's balance sheet across Aqua's entire history on Base from primary data, reading each wallet's balance and allowance from an archive node. 115 makers shipped 443 strategies. 78 of the 88 books that ever held more than $100 were under-backed at some point, and 89% of all material observations were under-backed. One book advertised about $51,000 of USDC while holding nothing, for weeks, and every taker who tried it paid gas for a revert. The same pipeline, pointed at the identical Aqua contracts on Arbitrum and Optimism, finds 123 of 138 material books under-backed across the three chains.

Solvent makes an Aqua position aware of its own balance sheet, inside the strategy bytecode:

- SolvencySkew, a new SwapVM instruction. The maker's utilisation (total committed across all strategies, divided by what the wallet holds and has approved) feeds into price. Below a threshold the quote is unchanged; above it the spread widens, because the last unit of a shared balance is worth more than the first.
- SolvencyFloor, a new SwapVM instruction. Above a maker-chosen utilisation the strategy declines at quote time, with a reason, instead of reverting at settlement after the taker has spent gas. It lives in the program bytes, so any taker can read the covenant before trading. It is the automatic version of the whitepaper's manual docking.
- The balance-sheet index. Both instructions need a maker's aggregate commitment, and Aqua cannot compute it on-chain. A subgraph maintains every maker's live book on Base, Arbitrum, Optimism and Base Sepolia, published on The Graph Network. A keeper publishes each maker's numbers to an on-chain oracle, SolventBook, where the instructions read them during the quote. Anyone can recompute the same numbers from the public index.

The live demo has five views. Mainnet shows every real Aqua maker's book on Base, Arbitrum and Optimism right now, each capsule filled green only as far as the wallet can settle. How it works shows the deployed system, every component linked to its verified contract or logs. Quote desk runs live quotes from the deployed router on Base Sepolia: step through a healthy book, a wallet that drains (the spread widens from 3,106.67 to 3,202.86 at 87% utilisation) and a book past its floor (every quote declines with SolvencyFloor's reason), or connect a wallet and take a quote for real. Balance sheets and Settlement ledger show the numbers every quote reads and what actually settled, failed fills included.

Makers get automated risk management instead of watching a wallet. Takers and agents get a pre-trade answer to whether a quote will fill. Aggregators can rank quotes by reserve ratio with one query and stop routing to phantom liquidity. The SDK, @aqua-solvent/core on npm, gives any app the same balance sheets on all four chains.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). SolvencyFloor and SolvencySkew are custom SwapVM instructions. We followed upstream's own extension pattern: each takes a reserved placeholder slot in the opcode table (Floor at 0x22 in the guards bank, Skew at 0xb5 in the rate-tuning bank), so no official opcode moves and stock Aqua programs run unchanged on our router. SolventRouter is the official AquaSwapVMRouter shape carrying the extended set, running against a pinned, unmodified deployment of the official Aqua contract on Base Sepolia. Floor is validation-only (no register writes, safe under staticcall), so a decline happens inside a free view call. Skew wraps the rest of the program and mirrors upstream's FeeFlatIn arithmetic branch for branch, so a skewed quote equals a stock program carrying the equivalent flat fee, and below its threshold it is a provable no-op. Both read SolventBook, a small oracle holding each maker's committed and backing per token, with a timestamp so consumers can judge staleness. Two more instructions (ReputationGate and ReputationPriceAdjuster) read SolventScore, a counterparty score built from what actually settled. Tests include differential suites for the book and score math, invariant tests, a regression suite from upstream 1inch running on our router, and a test that reproduces the core failure against the real contracts: one wallet holding 10 WETH ships three strategies advertising 30, each passes a backing check on its own, and the second taker reverts.

The Graph. This is the piece that makes the rest possible. Aqua stores balances per (maker, app, strategyHash, token) with no enumeration and no per-maker total, so no contract call can tell you a maker's aggregate commitment. The subgraph handles Shipped, Docked, Pulled and Pushed. Instead of replaying deltas, every touch re-reads Aqua.rawBalances for that strategy and token at the indexed block and folds the difference into the maker's book, which is exact by construction and immune to event ordering and wrapper edge cases. Backing is min(balanceOf, allowance to Aqua), read in the same handler, because a revoked allowance fails a fill just like an empty wallet. Ship calldata is decoded only to learn a strategy's token list; strategies shipped through wrappers are picked up on their first Pulled or Pushed, which covers 442 of 443 real strategies. One schema ships as four manifests (Base Sepolia, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism), all published on The Graph Network. A parity check rebuilds the largest books on each chain from an archive node and requires agreement to the wei.

The keeper. Wallets drain through plain transfers that Aqua never sees, so the index alone goes stale. The attestor reads every book from the index, re-reads each wallet on-chain, diffs against SolventBook and writes only what changed, so a quiet market costs no gas. It runs on GitHub Actions about once a minute: each run does eight passes and triggers the next run only on success, with a 15-minute cron as a backstop. Its key holds ATTESTOR_ROLE and nothing else.

The console is Vite, React, viem, wagmi and RainbowKit on GitHub Pages. The quote desk simulates every fill before sending and decodes the revert, so a floored book shows SolvencyFloor's reason before any gas is spent. It reads the published subgraphs through The Graph's gateway with a per-request fallback to Studio, pauses polling on hidden or idle tabs, and caps each browser's daily gateway use to protect the query budget. The SDK (@aqua-solvent/core on npm) exposes the same books on all four chains and encodes Solvent strategy programs.

Notably hacky:
- A reverted fill erases its own logs, so no subgraph can index a broken promise. SwapVM's transfer functions are private and swap() is not virtual, so a router cannot catch and re-emit the failure either. SolventRecorder records it from outside: a taker contract can try/catch its own swap and report the failure, or the attestor finds failed receipts aimed at the router and records them, citing the reverted transaction hash so anyone can check it on the explorer.
- The mainnet numbers came from a one-off analyzer that decoded every ship() transaction, applied every Pulled and Pushed as a delta, and read backing from an archive node at 34 heights plus each book's peak.

Partner technologies:
- 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua's shared liquidity is what creates the problem, and SwapVM's instruction set is where the fix lives. Adding two opcodes put solvency inside the quote itself, with no change to Aqua.
- The Graph. The aggregate balance sheet cannot be computed on-chain, so an index is the only place it can exist. The Graph let us maintain it on four chains from one schema, publish it on the decentralized network for anyone to query, and feed it back on-chain through the keeper.

projects.title: FindETH
projects.description: Brands/creators launch internet treasure hunts with on-chain prizes and collectibles.
projects.project_description:
FindETH is a Web3 treasure-hunt platform where businesses and creators turn their websites, products, and campaigns into interactive onchain discovery experiences. Creators/brands use AI to generate branded hunts with clues, locations, difficulty, prizes, and answer hashes. The AI workflow queries live The Graph analytics before generation, using historical completion rates, prize sizes, clue counts, and category performance to recommend better hunt designs.
Hunts are published through smart contracts on Sepolia, with clue answers protected as hashes and winners receiving verifiable NFT trophies. The platform combines wallet-based participation, Chainlink-powered mystery rewards, and backend metadata storage without exposing plaintext answers.
FindETH also uses ENSv2 to create hierarchical namespaces for creators, hunts, and AI agents. Each hunt can receive an ENSv2 subname containing metadata records, while Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control allow creators or delegated AI agents to update only the records they are authorized to manage.
projects.how_its_made: FindETH is built as a full-stack Web3 application. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Wagmi, Viem, and RainbowKit for the interface, wallet connection, contract interaction, ENS resolution, and Sepolia network support. Foundry and Solidity power the TreasureHunt and TreasureNFT contracts, including hashed clues, creator verification, prize handling, and Chainlink VRF-based mystery rewards. The backend is a FastAPI service using SQLAlchemy and Alembic with PostgreSQL/Supabase support. Gemini generates hunt drafts from real business content, while The Graph provides live onchain analytics before each generation so prize sizes, difficulty, and clue counts are informed by previous hunt performance. ENSv2 is integrated at the namespace level: creators receive hierarchical subnames for hunts and AI agents, with metadata stored in resolver text records. Permissioned Resolver and Enhanced Access Control enable delegated, record-specific updates. A notable security decision is that plaintext answers are never persisted in the backend. Only normalized answer hashes are stored onchain, while answers exist temporarily in the creator’s browser before publication.

projects.title: ENStrology
projects.description: AI horoscopes from your ENS name's onchain birthday the agent writes, but can't rewrite   you.
projects.project_description:
Every ENS name has an onchain birthday. ENStrology turns that real, verifiable date into a
playful AI horoscope and uses it to demonstrate a serious problem: how do you let an AI
agent create onchain content for someone without handing it control of their identity?
A user signs in with Privy, links the wallet that controls their ENS name, and ENStrology verifies both the name's control and its real registration date. After paying 0.01 demo USDC on Sepolia, the ENStrology Oracle generates a horoscope and stores it in real, expiring ENSv2 subnames.
The permission model is the point. Verified facts  source name, creation date, owner,  payment proof  live on a name the Oracle has no rights to at all. The horoscope lives on a sibling name where the Oracle holds a single scoped role. It can write the reading. It  cannot rewrite the facts, the owner, the resolver, or the expiry, and the user can revoke  its access at any time. All three cases are demonstrated as real Sepolia transactions,  including the one that reverts.
Readings can stay private or be published to the Cosmic Feed, a discovery page built entirely from contract events and ENS records — no database. Every result clearly separates verified onchain facts from AI-generated entertainment. This is entertainment, not prediction or financial advice.
projects.how_its_made:
ENStrology is a Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS app. Privy provides email and
social sign-in, embedded wallets, and external-wallet linking, so a user with a mainnet ENS
name can prove control of it from any linked wallet. viem handles all chain access: ENS
ownership and registration data are read from mainnet via The Graph's ENS subgraph with an
RPC fallback to registrar events, while every write happens on Ethereum Sepolia — the app
never sends a mainnet transaction. A Solidity payment contract, built and tested with Foundry, accepts 0.01 demo USDC, prevents
replay, and emits purchase and visibility events. The Cosmic Feed is built from those
events plus ENS resolution, so the contract — not a database — is the source of truth for
what is public. ENSv2 does the security work. Each reading is created as an expiring, non-transferable
subname in the Oracle's own namespace using the Permissioned Registry, with records stored
on a Permissioned Resolver. Because Enhanced Access Control scopes roles per name rather
than per record key, verified facts and AI content are deliberately split across two sibling
names: the Oracle is granted the Set Text role, as Manager only, on the horoscope name
alone. It holds no role on the facts name and no Admin rights anywhere, so it cannot grant
itself more. Attempting to write outside its scope reverts onchain, and the owner can revoke
the role at any time. The Oracle publishes its own purpose and endpoint as agent-context
and agent-endpoint records on its ENS name, following the ENS agent-record convention.
Horoscope text is generated with the Vercel AI SDK from verified structured facts only — the
model never chooses the name, the date, the payment, or the owner.

projects.title: Web3WAGMI Terminal
projects.description: A crypto terminal whose on-chain desks run on The Graph, with an assistant that shows its work.
projects.project_description: Web3WAGMI Terminal is a live crypto market terminal: around thirty desks covering price, funding, open interest, options, exchange flow, on-chain liquidity, ownership, fees and revenue, yields, unlocks and gas. It is public, free, and needs no wallet or login. The Graph runs the on-chain half, and every reading it powers answers a question no aggregator already answers. The flagship one is absorption. Exchange netflow is a standard metric that everybody publishes. Nobody publishes whether the market can actually absorb what just arrived. The deposits come from the Token API as indexed balance history across fourteen labelled exchange wallets. The liquidity that would have to take the other side comes from a Uniswap v3 subgraph through the decentralised gateway. Two Graph products, and neither answers the question alone. The second is composability shown rather than described. One literal GraphQL string is sent unchanged to nine Messari standardized subgraphs and every one of them answers, because they share a schema: a lending market, a DEX and a staking protocol all reply to the same request. The same string sent to Uniswap v3, which does not share it, is rejected by the gateway, and the panel shows that rejection as the measured cost of a bespoke schema. That shared schema also yields a reading no fee aggregator publishes, because only a shared schema defines supply side and protocol side as separate fields: the share of fees each protocol keeps rather than pays out. Aave v3 keeps 12%, Curve 52%, MakerDAO 88%. The fee board extends that to the whole market, and opening a row shows ninety days of fees, the chains they actually came from, and who holds the protocol's token, read from the Token API. Uniswap v4 took $107m in fees over thirty days and kept none of it. Lighter's token is 65% held by ten addresses; Aave's is 43%. An assistant answers in plain language using tools that read the terminal's own routes, so it cannot quote a figure the terminal cannot show, and it names which desks it read so the answer can be checked. It describes conditions and never recommends a trade.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript strict, Tailwind v4, standalone output on CapRover behind Cloudflare. Every upstream is read server side and cached per route, so traffic never multiplies cost: a route with a revalidate window costs the same for one visitor as for a thousand. Seven Token API endpoints. Historical balances and native balances drive the exchange flow desk. Holders and tokens give ownership concentration, since ten addresses holding a large number is not concentration until you divide by circulating supply. Hyperliquid open interest, liquidations and platform volume give the on-chain perp venue. Open interest is taken in contracts rather than dollars, because notional rises with price and would label every rally as new longs. The decentralised gateway serves a Uniswap v3 subgraph for pool liquidity, and nine Messari standardized subgraphs for the cross-protocol panel. Adding a tenth standardized protocol is one line: an id. The AI layer is an OpenAI-compatible tool loop with a primary gateway, a fallback, and key rotation. The hard part was never wiring up a model. It had a sign convention backwards twice. A coin arriving on an exchange is bearish and a stablecoin arriving is bullish, and it had that inverted; separately it called short covering downward pressure, when shorts buying back is upward. Both fixes were the same. Every reading now carries its interpretation decided in code and handed to the model with the number, so the model composes the sentence and never the conclusion. Details worth mentioning. The Token API's canonical host is unreachable from some regions, so the client resolves between it and the Pinax host at runtime and the payload names which one answered. The holders endpoint returns 500 intermittently on the largest tokens, so it retries three times, because losing the ownership read to one unlucky request wastes the most valuable thing the Token API gives this terminal. Multichain flow was built, measured and deliberately not shipped: on Base those labelled wallets hold airdrop dust, on Arbitrum only four of fourteen hold anything material, so the desk states its single-chain scope in its own header instead of implying coverage it does not have. With no Graph key at all the app still runs. The flow desk falls back to archive JSON-RPC and the payload says which source answered.

projects.title: Envoyage
projects.description: Hire a Uniswap v4 keeper without handing it your position. Scoped permission, not blanket approval.
projects.project_description:
To let a bot compound your Uniswap v4 position today, you call approve(keeper, tokenId).
That says WHICH position the keeper may touch. It says nothing about WHAT it may do. v4 makes this sharper than it sounds. Liquidity management goes through one entrypoint,
modifyLiquidities(bytes actions), and that bytes payload is an action array — a small
language with 26 opcodes. Restricting a keeper to "may only call modifyLiquidities"
restricts nothing, because that function is itself an interpreter. We traced all 26
opcodes to file and line: four of them (TAKE_PAIR, TAKE, SWEEP, MINT_POSITION) take a
recipient address straight from the caller. So an approved keeper can assemble
DECREASE_LIQUIDITY + TAKE_PAIR(..., its own wallet) and nothing on chain objects. That
is the Code4rena Revert Lend H-04 class, and the shape behind the ~$17M Aperture
Finance drain. Envoyage inverts who writes the instructions. The keeper never sends calldata — it
calls compound(mandateId, minFee), two integers. Envoyage assembles the v4 action array
itself, with the recipient as a constant in code. Misuse is not rejected by a check;
there is no field in which to express it. A mandate carries what an approval cannot: a fee cap in basis points of harvested fees
(never of the position), a fee recipient pinned at grant time, a cooldown, an expiry,
and a check that the position has not changed hands. Revocation is immediate. Each mandate is also published as an ENSv2 subname, so anyone can resolve it in any ENS
client and read the exact scope — without visiting our app or trusting our frontend.
projects.how_its_made:
Solidity 0.8.26 on Sepolia, Foundry throughout. The contract is immutable by
construction: no proxy, no admin, no upgrade path, no delegatecall, and no function
that accepts bytes or an address target. That is a security property, not an omission —
a contract aggregating many owners' approvals is a more attractive honeypot than those
approvals left scattered, so we assert it against the DEPLOYED BYTECODE rather than the
source: the runtime contains no DELEGATECALL, SELFDESTRUCT or CALLCODE, and no
arbitrary-call selector resolves. The opcode scanner skips PUSH immediates so a
constant containing 0xf4 isn't misread, and it carries a negative control that runs the
same scan over a contract which does contain DELEGATECALL — a scanner that finds
nothing proves nothing until you know it can find something. We started with an integration spike against real v4-periphery before writing any
protocol code, which is how we learned INCREASE_LIQUIDITY rejects a caller without
ERC-721 approval. That failure is the architecture: the authority has to live
somewhere, so the question is never whether someone holds it but who. Envoyage holds
it, and Envoyage cannot be told what to do with it. There is deliberately no swap leg, for two independent reasons: PositionManager does not
dispatch swap actions at all, and without a swap compound has no price, so no value can
leak through one. Uniswap reached a related conclusion itself, deprecating the
FROM_DELTAS variants as "vulnerable to sandwich attacks". Testing is 38 tests. The exploit replay is paired: every attack runs against NaiveUtils,
a comparator built vulnerable exactly as Revert V3Utils was, AND against Envoyage —
because a test showing we merely lack the vulnerable function is a tautology. The same
H-04 back-run steals 4.757902903361556095 token0 from the comparator and cannot be
encoded against us. The invariant suite fuzzes the keeper as an adversary over 12,800
calls; its anti-vacuity guard sits in a deterministic test rather than in
afterInvariant(), because Foundry evaluates invariants against the initial state and
afterInvariant reads handler counters at their post-setUp values — both placements
would have passed while proving nothing. ENSv2 (Sepolia beta) is where a mandate becomes publicly readable. We registered
envoyage.eth through the ETH Registrar's commit-reveal flow, deployed our own
UserRegistry via VerifiableFactory, and pointed the parent at it. A separate
EnvoyageNames contract mirrors mandates into subnames — separate on purpose, since
Envoyage is already deployed and immutable, and a mirror must never require edits to
what it mirrors. Every function on it is permissionless because it reads the truth out
of Envoyage rather than taking it from the caller, which is the same shape as the
contract it mirrors. The keeper is granted authorizeTextRoles on exactly one text key,
envoyage:lastRun; writing any other key reverts EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. That is
the same division the contract's gate enforces — the owner sets the scope, the keeper
touches only what cannot change it — expressed on a second substrate. Everything ENSv2 was transcribed from verified Etherscan ABIs, not from tutorials, and
that mattered: findTokenId is NOT keccak256(label) — the registry masks the low 32 bits
for versioning, so a locally computed id addresses a name nobody resolves through, and
it fails silently rather than reverting. Also shipped: a subgraph indexing the granted scope alongside actual behaviour (most
tooling can only index what a keeper did, because what it was allowed to do doesn't
exist on chain), a reference keeper bot verified compounding unattended on Sepolia, and
a web UI reading live state over two independent RPC operators with no backend or
indexer — two operators rather than several keys from one provider, because keys from a
single provider share a failure domain and the fallback never actually fails over.

That says WHICH position the keeper may touch. It says nothing about WHAT it may do.

v4 makes this sharper than it sounds. Liquidity management goes through one entrypoint,
modifyLiquidities(bytes actions), and that bytes payload is an action array — a small
language with 26 opcodes. Restricting a keeper to "may only call modifyLiquidities"
restricts nothing, because that function is itself an interpreter. We traced all 26
opcodes to file and line: four of them (TAKE_PAIR, TAKE, SWEEP, MINT_POSITION) take a
recipient address straight from the caller. So an approved keeper can assemble
DECREASE_LIQUIDITY + TAKE_PAIR(..., its own wallet) and nothing on chain objects. That
is the Code4rena Revert Lend H-04 class, and the shape behind the ~$17M Aperture
Finance drain.

Envoyage inverts who writes the instructions. The keeper never sends calldata — it
calls compound(mandateId, minFee), two integers. Envoyage assembles the v4 action array
itself, with the recipient as a constant in code. Misuse is not rejected by a check;
there is no field in which to express it.

A mandate carries what an approval cannot: a fee cap in basis points of harvested fees
(never of the position), a fee recipient pinned at grant time, a cooldown, an expiry,
and a check that the position has not changed hands. Revocation is immediate.

Each mandate is also published as an ENSv2 subname, so anyone can resolve it in any ENS
client and read the exact scope — without visiting our app or trusting our frontend.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Solidity 0.8.26 on Sepolia, Foundry throughout. The contract is immutable by
construction: no proxy, no admin, no upgrade path, no delegatecall, and no function
that accepts bytes or an address target. That is a security property, not an omission —
a contract aggregating many owners' approvals is a more attractive honeypot than those
approvals left scattered, so we assert it against the DEPLOYED BYTECODE rather than the
source: the runtime contains no DELEGATECALL, SELFDESTRUCT or CALLCODE, and no
arbitrary-call selector resolves. The opcode scanner skips PUSH immediates so a
constant containing 0xf4 isn't misread, and it carries a negative control that runs the
same scan over a contract which does contain DELEGATECALL — a scanner that finds
nothing proves nothing until you know it can find something.

We started with an integration spike against real v4-periphery before writing any
protocol code, which is how we learned INCREASE_LIQUIDITY rejects a caller without
ERC-721 approval. That failure is the architecture: the authority has to live
somewhere, so the question is never whether someone holds it but who. Envoyage holds
it, and Envoyage cannot be told what to do with it.

There is deliberately no swap leg, for two independent reasons: PositionManager does not
dispatch swap actions at all, and without a swap compound has no price, so no value can
leak through one. Uniswap reached a related conclusion itself, deprecating the
FROM_DELTAS variants as "vulnerable to sandwich attacks".

Testing is 38 tests. The exploit replay is paired: every attack runs against NaiveUtils,
a comparator built vulnerable exactly as Revert V3Utils was, AND against Envoyage —
because a test showing we merely lack the vulnerable function is a tautology. The same
H-04 back-run steals 4.757902903361556095 token0 from the comparator and cannot be
encoded against us. The invariant suite fuzzes the keeper as an adversary over 12,800
calls; its anti-vacuity guard sits in a deterministic test rather than in
afterInvariant(), because Foundry evaluates invariants against the initial state and
afterInvariant reads handler counters at their post-setUp values — both placements
would have passed while proving nothing.

ENSv2 (Sepolia beta) is where a mandate becomes publicly readable. We registered
envoyage.eth through the ETH Registrar's commit-reveal flow, deployed our own
UserRegistry via VerifiableFactory, and pointed the parent at it. A separate
EnvoyageNames contract mirrors mandates into subnames — separate on purpose, since
Envoyage is already deployed and immutable, and a mirror must never require edits to
what it mirrors. Every function on it is permissionless because it reads the truth out
of Envoyage rather than taking it from the caller, which is the same shape as the
contract it mirrors. The keeper is granted authorizeTextRoles on exactly one text key,
envoyage:lastRun; writing any other key reverts EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. That is
the same division the contract's gate enforces — the owner sets the scope, the keeper
touches only what cannot change it — expressed on a second substrate.

Everything ENSv2 was transcribed from verified Etherscan ABIs, not from tutorials, and
that mattered: findTokenId is NOT keccak256(label) — the registry masks the low 32 bits
for versioning, so a locally computed id addresses a name nobody resolves through, and
it fails silently rather than reverting.

Also shipped: a subgraph indexing the granted scope alongside actual behaviour (most
tooling can only index what a keeper did, because what it was allowed to do doesn't
exist on chain), a reference keeper bot verified compounding unattended on Sepolia, and
a web UI reading live state over two independent RPC operators with no backend or
indexer — two operators rather than several keys from one provider, because keys from a
single provider share a failure domain and the fallback never actually fails over.

projects.title: DeSci Proof Notebook
projects.description: Privacy-first research proof tool anchoring local file fingerprints on Base Sepolia.
projects.project_description: DeSci Proof Notebook is a privacy-first research proof tool for students, scientists, and independent researchers. It computes a SHA-256 fingerprint of a research file locally in the browser, then anchors that fingerprint, the creator address, a timestamp, and only the user-selected public title and note on Base Sepolia. The original CSV, image, or experiment file never leaves the user's device. Anyone can later upload the same original file to verify that its fingerprint matches the onchain proof, while the public history view lets people inspect available proof records without connecting a wallet.
projects.how_its_made: DeSci Proof Notebook is a bilingual web application hosted on GitHub Pages. It uses the browser Web Crypto API to compute SHA-256 locally, so the original file is never uploaded. The frontend connects to MetaMask on Base Sepolia and calls a Solidity smart contract that stores each fingerprint with the creator, block timestamp, public title, and optional public note. Read-only RPC calls allow verification and public proof-history lookup without a wallet. The contract source is verified on Base Sepolia. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow was built and successfully simulated with synthetic data to produce a commitment for a public file hash and private policy label. ChatGPT/Codex assisted implementation, documentation, bilingual copy, debugging, and UI iteration.

projects.title: OECL
projects.description: Verified evidence infrastructure for Ethereum agents and protocol composition research.
projects.project_description: OECL is an evidence infrastructure layer for Ethereum protocol research. It turns standardized live blockchain observations into machine-readable EvidenceReceipts that downstream agents, research systems and composition engines can admit or reject deterministically. During ETHOnline, OECL extended its pre-existing scientific laboratory with a standardized ERC-8004 observation pipeline powered by The Graph across Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Polygon and Monad. Each observation is independently checked against chain state before OECL classifies it as ADMISSIBLE, REJECTED or INCOMPLETE. Verified protocol presence is deliberately kept separate from compatibility or composition claims.
projects.how_its_made: OECL’s ETHOnline extension is built primarily in TypeScript with Next.js and React. A single standardized GraphQL query is reused across five Agent0 ERC-8004 mainnet deployments through The Graph. For each observation, OECL preserves indexed-block provenance and independently queries the corresponding chain through JSON-RPC, checking chain identity, block hash, Identity Registry runtime code and sampled agent ownership. A pure deterministic admission engine then maps available evidence to VERIFIED/ADMISSIBLE, MISMATCH/REJECTED or INCOMPLETE. Each result is exposed as a machine-readable EvidenceReceipt through an API and the web interface. The existing OECL V2.1 scientific corpus remains separate and deterministic; live evidence does not rewrite prior conclusions.

projects.title: DeFiCat
projects.description: DeFiCat: Telegram ENS agent. The Graph lookups, buy now or on drop, pay with x402.
projects.project_description: ENS data is public, but acting on it from chat is still painful: is kikoulol.eth free, who owns degen.kikoulol.eth, when does a name expire, can I buy it now, or sit on a taken name until it drops? DeFiCat is a Telegram agent for that loop. You ask in chat. The Graph is the read path: owner, expiry, and grace, for second-level names and subnames. ENS is the write path: if the name is available, the agent quotes then registers it (commit/reveal) from its own mainnet wallet, under a budget cap and a chat allowlist. If it is taken or over budget, you can arm a watch: Temporal waits until the name is eligible and the worker buys it without asking again. Lookups and quotes stay free. Spending is gated: Sign-In with Ethereum binds your Telegram chat to a wallet, you confirm an exact phrase, then you pay a service fee with x402 (1 USDC to buy now, 10 USDC to schedule the drop). The fee is USDC on Base Sepolia; the registration gas is ETH on mainnet from the agent. After payment, the agent auto-runs the intent: register now, or start the watch. This ETHGlobal Online 2026 demo targets The Graph and ENS. Paid DeFi services (swaps and the rest) are the same payment rails later, not this build.
projects.how_its_made: Two packages: a NestJS agents process (Telegram + HTTP + Temporal worker) and a Next.js UI for SIWE and x402. The bot is hexagonal. Domain rules (ENS label policy, budget, payment SKUs) never import Nest, viem, or LangChain. Telegram is a driving adapter; The Graph ENS subgraph is the lookup adapter (including subnames with no registrar row); viem talks to ETHRegistrarController for quote, commit, wait, re-quote, register. LangGraph tools (lookup_ens, purchase_ens, schedule_ens) cannot skip the gate: the LLM never chooses who may spend. Scheduled buys cannot live in bot memory. A second process polls Temporal. The bot only arms/cancels; the worker signs months later. Same EOA, so one worker (one nonce). Dev default is an in-memory scheduler that records watches and buys nothing. Telegram has no HTTP 402, so payment mirrors SIWE: the agent issues a one-shot token, the UI pays, the agent verifies with the public x402 facilitator, then replays the paid intent. Split-chain on purpose: SIWE + ENS on mainnet (CHAIN_ID), USDC x402 on Base Sepolia. Treasury is the same EOA as AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY. Hacky-but-intentional: exact confirmation phrases, fail-closed payment (the UI never tells the agent “paid”), and Temporal memos as the source of truth for watches instead of a second database.

projects.title: NameGate
projects.description: Tokenized bond on Hedera using ENSv2 subnames (roles, expiry, resolver records) as its KYC layer
projects.project_description: NameGate is a tokenized bond on Hedera where an investor's ENS name is the compliance layer, not a database entry. Each investor holds a subname on ENSv2, Sepolia. The issuer writes their KYC status, jurisdiction, accreditation expiry, and lock-up date onto that name as permission-scoped resolver records, not plain text anyone could edit. A permissionless beacon contract reads the name on-chain and ships the state to Hedera over Chainlink CCIP, where the bond's control list checks it before every transfer and coupon payout. Investor A gets paid. Investor B's transfer reverts with a reason string pulled straight from their ENS record, so you can point at the name and see exactly why. The issuer can't forge either side: they hold exactly one key on the name, the investor holds the rest, and one investor's KYC field is permanently locked against the issuer to prove that actually holds. Keeping compliance data outside the token isn't new; ERC-3643 and ONCHAINID already do versions of it. What's different here is the identity substrate: a human-readable, user-held name with role-scoped write access instead of an opaque identity contract, checkable by anyone who knows how to read an ENS record.
projects.how_its_made: Identity lives on ENSv2 (Sepolia): a custom UserRegistry issues non-transferable investor subnames pointing at a Permissioned Resolver, with Enhanced Access Control scoping exactly who can write which field. authorizeTextRoles grants the issuer a per-key role instead of a blanket write role, and ROLE_SET_RESOLVER is withheld so an investor can't repoint their own name to forge a record. A permissionless beacon contract on Sepolia reads the resolver's text records on-chain and forwards them to Hedera in the same transaction over Chainlink CCIP, so there's no off-chain relayer asserting what a record says. On Hedera, a Mirror contract implements Asset Tokenization Studio's own IExternalControlList extension point, plugged into the bond through its factory, not a fork. ATS's bond can declare and calculate a coupon but has no payout function at all, so we wrote a roughly 60-line CouponDistributor gated by the same control list the bond checks for transfers, plus a Hedera Schedule Service integration (ScheduleCreateTransaction with waitForExpiry) so a coupon can settle itself with no keeper. Privy runs the operational side: investors connect through embedded wallets with no seed phrase, and the issuer's own automation runs through an organization wallet whose policy restricts it to exactly two contract addresses, backed by a 2-of-3 key quorum in front of it. The most notable hacky bit: HBAR is 8-decimal tinybar inside the EVM, not the 18-decimal weibar the JSON-RPC relay reports externally, a documented 10^10 gap a local Hardhat network can't reproduce. Our first live payout reverted because of it; we now assert that exact gap in a regression test. Two more real bugs turned up the same way: an orphaned control list from a prior redeploy that silently blocked every transfer, and a stale per-key grant that survived a lock/unlock cycle. 194 tests total, 49 of them running live against Sepolia and Hedera testnet.

projects.title: PayRail
projects.description: AI accounts-payable agent that verifies suppliers and pays invoices in USDC on Arc
projects.project_description: PayRail is an agentic accounts-payable rail for wholesale B2B. An invoice arrives the way it does today, as an EDI 810 or a PDF. The buyer's AP agent parses it, three-way matches it against the purchase order and goods receipt, and resolves the supplier from an ENS name whose text records hold the supplier's USDC address on Arc, payment terms, and early-pay discount. Before the first payment, the agent checks that the supplier's agent is backed by a verified human through World ID. Payment runs from a Privy server wallet with policies set by the finance team: a recipient allowlist derived from ENS, a per-invoice cap, a daily cap, and a 2-of-3 human approval for anything above the cap. Small invoices pay themselves. Large ones wait for two signatures in the dashboard. On the supplier side, every approved invoice becomes a receivable token on Arc. A supplier waiting on net-60 terms can sell it into a USDC early-pay pool at a discount priced by days to due date and get paid today. Pool depositors earn the discount when the buyer settles. The whole rail is exposed as an MCP server, so any agent can submit, approve, pay, or finance an invoice with a single tool call. Built by a team that ships B2B order and invoice integrations for a living. The fixtures, the matching rules, and the payment terms are the real thing, not a toy.
projects.how_its_made: One monorepo, four packages. Contracts are Solidity with Foundry, deployed to Arc testnet where USDC is the native settlement asset. InvoiceRegistry tracks the lifecycle from Submitted through Approved to Paid or Financed to Settled. ReceivableToken is an ERC-721 minted to the supplier on approval; owning the token is the right to be paid. EarlyPayPool is a USDC vault that buys receivables at a discount and collects face value when the buyer pays, with the registry forwarding payment to whoever holds the token. The agent is Node 22 and TypeScript. Invoice parsing uses Claude with structured output to turn X12 810 segments and PDF text into a canonical invoice JSON, followed by a deterministic three-way match. Supplier resolution reads ENSv2 subnames and text records on Sepolia with viem. Human verification checks a World ID Selfie Check proof stored at supplier onboarding. Payment goes through Privy server wallets: the policy engine enforces allowlist and caps before signing, and an approver quorum handles anything above threshold. The supplier's agent runs on a Circle Agent Wallet so two companies with two wallet stacks can share one rail. The dashboard is Next.js with Privy React for buyer login and World IDKit for supplier onboarding. The MCP server exposes six tools over stdio and is published as a Bazantic recipe. A Graph subgraph indexes registry and pool events so the agent can answer questions like what is due this week without scanning the chain. Hacky bit worth mentioning: the ENS text records are the policy source. The Privy allowlist is regenerated from resolved ENS records, so adding a supplier is a name registration, not a config change.

projects.title: Batas
projects.description: An agent runs your 1inch Aqua position under limits it cannot widen and a name you can revoke.
projects.project_description: 1inch Aqua is a shared liquidity layer where the maker never deposits anything. Tokens stay in their own wallet, Aqua keeps a ledger of allowances, and it pulls directly from that wallet at settlement. That removes custody risk and concentrates a different one, because Aqua.pull() checks nothing beyond msg.sender. Whichever app the maker ships to may take their tokens. The entire security model is one sentence: you trust the app you ship to. Hand that app to an autonomous agent and the question gets sharp — what stops it, and where is the stop enforced? Most agent tooling answers "in the application layer", which means nowhere, because anyone can call the contract directly and skip your checks. Batas answers with a mandate: a size cap, a floor price, and an expiry. The mandate IS the Aqua strategy. Aqua.ship() hashes the strategy bytes you hand it, and Batas passes the encoded mandate as those bytes, so the mandate hash and the strategy hash are the same value. The terms are not metadata attached to the position — they are its identity. An attacker can compile a program with the limits removed, but that is a different strategy hash, and the maker never shipped a token to it. The limits are checked in the two places that gate the money. BatasApp validates them before AQUA.pull(), because after pull() the tokens have already left. And PolicyEnvelope, a new SwapVM instruction at third-party opcode slot 0x21, wraps the rest of the program: it delegates to runLoop() and inspects the settled registers when that returns. Placed first it is the outermost frame, so a fee appended behind the curve cannot push the amounts back out of bounds after the guard has passed, and in exactOut mode — where the input is only final once the curve has run — placement stops being something a program author can silently get wrong. It costs 975 gas. What that is worth, measured rather than asserted: the same attacker against the same reserves, twice. Under a mandate, two trades at an average rate of 1.662 and 83% of the position still there. With no mandate, sixty-four trades at 0.270 — a seventh of where the pool opened — and it is gutted. Every one of those was an ordinary constant-product swap that no application-layer check was there to stop. A second instruction at slot 0x22 makes the kill switch binding. The agent's authority is an ENSv2 subname: expiring, with the expiry compiled into the program's own deadline; revocable, because the grantor keeps ROLE_UNREGISTER; soulbound, because ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN is withheld. MandateName reads that registry during settlement, so revoking the name reverts the swap for every caller rather than only stopping an agent polite enough to ask. agent/killswitch.mjs --prove demonstrates it live: quote the position, revoke, quote again and get MandateNameNotHeld from a caller that has never heard of ENS, re-grant, and the position comes back at the same price. The agent reads the live position, derives its floor from measured price movement rather than a constant, compiles the SwapVM program itself, checks its bytes against the deployed router's hash before shipping, and publishes the grant to Hedera Consensus Service. Run with --watch it keeps running the position: it renews inside the expiry window, docks the mandate it replaces, and stops acting the moment the name is revoked without needing to be restarted by the person who just stopped it. A paid x402 endpoint on Hedera sells the one answer a counterparty cannot assemble alone: the decoded terms, the consensus timestamp on which those exact bytes became public, and the ERC-8004 identity behind the position with a check that it is held by the address that granted the mandate. 1inch Aqua is a shared liquidity layer where the maker never deposits anything. Tokens stay in their own wallet, Aqua keeps a ledger of allowances, and it pulls directly from that wallet at settlement. That removes custody risk and concentrates a different one, because Aqua.pull() checks nothing beyond msg.sender. Whichever app the maker ships to may take their tokens. The entire security model is one sentence: you trust the app you ship to. Hand that app to an autonomous agent and the question gets sharp — what stops it, and where is the stop enforced? Most agent tooling answers "in the application layer", which means nowhere, because anyone can call the contract directly and skip your checks.
