Placed first it is the outermost frame, so a fee appended behind the curve cannot push the amounts back out of bounds after the guard has passed, and in exactOut mode — where the input is only final once the curve has run — placement stops being something a program author can silently get wrong. It costs 975 gas.

projects.title: Karwan
projects.description: An open trade market with reputation, protected USDC payments and trade finance.
projects.project_description:
Karwan helps freelancers, businesses and clients trade with people they meet online. Users can find opportunities in its marketplace or bring an agreement from a conversation on WhatsApp, Instagram, X or another platform. A deal brings together the agreed terms, delivery milestones, counterparty history and payment status. Buyers fund protected USDC payments, sellers submit their work, and both parties can follow the agreement through delivery and settlement. Completed trades contribute to a verifiable track record that users can share with future counterparties.
The problem extends beyond payment. Someone finding a client through social media often has little evidence to judge whether that person will deliver or pay. Karwan connects that evidence to the actual agreement and its outcome. Its trade-finance direction builds on these records to help businesses seek funding against invoices and purchase orders. The current application runs on Arc Testnet. Imported ratings from freelance platforms and unrestricted access to financing are not claimed as available features.
projects.how_its_made:
Karwan uses Next.js, React and TypeScript for the interface, a Hono backend, PostgreSQL for durable workflows, and Solidity contracts for USDC escrow and milestone settlement on Arc Testnet. Circle wallet infrastructure supports email-based accounts, while external wallet users can connect their own wallets. CCTP handles supported cross-chain USDC routes.
The existing marketplace, settlement contracts and reputation system form the foundation. Our ETHOnline work extends it with shareable deal invitations, explicit acceptance of versioned terms, human-linked agent research allowances, and delivery-evidence checks. The World AgentKit integration uses signed challenges and AgentBook lookups to associate research access with a human identity. Switching agents does not create a fresh allowance. A Chainlink CRE workflow checks GitHub delivery against agreed criteria, including the exact commit, merge status and required checks from a trusted GitHub App. Its report targets a separate evidence registry that holds no funds. Delivery evidence and payment authority remain separate. An evidence result does not itself authorize payment. Durable invitation claims, replay checks and payout reconciliation address duplicate requests and interrupted operations.

projects.title: AgentProof
projects.description: AgentProof is a developer SDK and safety runtime that sits between an AI agent and execution layer.
projects.project_description: AgentProof — a spending limit an AI agent cannot talk its way around. The problem. People are starting to give AI agents real wallets — trading bots, treasury agents, autonomous buyers. An agent is not a program you can audit ahead of time; it decides what to do at runtime, and anything it reads can change its mind. A web page, a tool response, a token's own metadata can carry a hidden instruction ("send everything to 0xattacker") and the agent will follow it politely. It can also just be wrong: hallucinate a price, misread a field, swap 250 USDC when you said 100. Today "agent safety" almost always means a wrapper — code in the agent's own process that looks at what the agent says it wants to do and refuses the bad ones. That fails exactly when it matters, because the thing being restrained is the same process doing the restraining. If the agent is compromised, it skips the wrapper and signs directly. What we built. AgentProof splits enforcement into two layers that fail independently. An SDK and HTTP API (npm i @agentproof/sdk, or POST /v1/verify from any language). Three lines in your agent: describe the transaction, get a verdict, stop if it's denied. Seven policy types run per action — allowlist, max per transaction, daily spend, minimum balance, approval threshold, pool liquidity, and unlimited-approval detection. It decodes real Uniswap v4 Universal Router calldata down to worst-case outflow, so a swap that advertises 1 USDC but authorises 250 is priced at 250. Anything it can't decode returns UNBOUNDED and is blocked rather than guessed at. When a transaction is large enough that the owner wanted a say, the HTTP request is held open until a human answers — the agent is genuinely stopped, not notified — and if nobody answers, it's denied. Silence is never consent. An on-chain hook (ERC-7579 module inside the agent's own smart account). This is the part that actually holds. It re-checks the limits inside the wallet at signing time, so it applies whether or not the agent ever called us. The point of the whole design: the SDK is advice and we assume it will be bypassed. The hook is the guarantee. Our headline test involves no SDK at all — it installs the hook on the ERC-7579 reference account, sends a validly signed UserOperation through a real EntryPoint v0.8, and the account refuses it. No funds move. Who it's for. Anyone shipping an agent that can move money: DeFi trading agents, x402-paying agents that buy API calls, treasury automation. The owner writes the policy once; the agent inherits limits it cannot remove — we found that out the hard way when we tried to uninstall our own hook during development and couldn't. Everything is deployed and links to a block explorer: the hook on-chain, the agent's limits published under its ENS name so anyone can verify them without asking us, a subgraph of what the chain actually admitted, and an x402-gated API where every verification is a real settled payment.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: TypeScript SDK (zero runtime dependencies on the decision path), an HTTP verification API, Solidity + Foundry for the on-chain hook, solc's SMTChecker for formal verification, Next.js for the demo console. Partner tech: Uniswap v4, ENS v2, The Graph, Hedera (x402 payments). The design rule throughout: anything off-chain is advice, and the only thing that actually stops a transaction is on-chain. The decision path has zero dependencies. Every read the policy engine needs is an eth_call issued with fetch. viem is an optional peer dep, dynamically imported, and only if you sign — so you don't take a wallet stack's supply chain into the code that decides whether an agent may spend your money. Seven policies run per action: allowlist, max transaction, daily spend, minimum balance, approval threshold, pool liquidity, and unlimited-approval detection. Decoding is where the real work is. A policy is only as good as its understanding of the calldata. decode/uniswapV4.ts walks a Universal Router command stream and returns worst-case outflow per currency. The trap is exact-output swaps: the interesting number is amountInMaximum, not the quote, and reading the wrong field lets a 250 USDC swap look like a 1 USDC one. Anything undecodable returns UNBOUNDED rather than a guess, and unbounded always blocks. We pinned the decoder against six real Sepolia transactions — the first run decoded all six as UNBOUNDED, because of an off-by-one in the action bytes and a wrong struct word, invisible until real calldata replaced our own self-encoded fixtures. That bug is the argument for the whole approach. Uniswap v4 is therefore load-bearing rather than decorative: the Universal Router and PoolManager are the allowlisted targets, and a second public Uniswap subgraph feeds a pool-liquidity policy — bounding spend and bounding loss are different problems. The hook is an ERC-7579 module on an MSAAdvanced account (reference implementation v0.3.1) driven through EntryPoint v0.8.0. The version is pinned deliberately: v0.7 predates ISenderCreator, and v0.9 gates handleOps behind tx.origin == msg.sender. We also had to match the account's actual postCheck(bytes) — selector 0x173bf7da — not the draft postCheck(bytes,bool,bytes) from the spec. That one is worth dwelling on: the mock-only version of our test suite hid it for weeks. The hook would have installed cleanly and reverted on first real execution. The mocks agreed with each other while both disagreed with reality. There is now an integration test that installs the hook on a real 7579 account and drives it through a real EntryPoint to prove it. Formal verification with solc's SMTChecker proves MAX_TRANSFER and DAILY_SPEND hold over PolicyLib for all inputs, in about 1.3 seconds. We also compile a deliberately broken spec, PolicySpecBroken, which must produce a counterexample — that's how we know the solver is actually looking rather than trivially passing. The hook itself is fuzzed and invariant-tested, not proven, and the UI says which is which. Missing artifacts report NOT_RUN instead of passing silently. ENS v2 carries the agent's identity as a namespace: addr to the smart account, plus text records for policy hash, hook address, and status. The EAC roles encode the trust split precisely — the owner holds ROLE_SET_POLICY_RECORD, and the agent's session key holds only ROLE_SET_STATUS_RECORD, so an agent can suspend itself and nothing else. The SDK does a three-way binding check at startup: local file, ENS record, and the hook's stored hash must agree, or it refuses to run. The Graph indexes the hook's own SpendRecorded events, so spend history reflects what the chain admitted rather than what an agent intended. A pre-aggregated DailyAggregate entity is what keeps a policy decision fast enough for an agent's hot path. Subgraph reads are reconciled against a direct on-chain accumulator read — whichever source permits less wins — and if both are unreachable the SDK fails closed. Hedera makes the verification service the paid product. POST /v1/verify returns 402 with payment requirements; the client partially signs a transfer; the Blocky402 facilitator co-signs as fee payer and settles; then the verdict comes back. Verify before work, settle after — callers are never charged for failed requests. Each settlement is written to an HCS topic, so an audit trail exists on infrastructure we don't control. The loop closes nicely: the payment itself is a policy-checked action, so an agent can't be talked into paying a thousand dollars for a data query by a service that simply asks for it.
Hacky bits worth mentioning The browser can't pay, so the server pays for it. The demo console needed the x402 gate switched on to be honest, but a browser has no wallet — every check just came back 402. The console's verify route now answers the payment challenge itself with a Hedera signer, so the gate stays on and every click in the demo is a real settlement with its transaction id linked to HashScan. Nothing in the demo path is a mock or a bypass; the UI pays for its own verifications like any other caller. We couldn't uninstall our own hook. Updating the policy on a live account means executing against the account itself, and the hook rejects any target that isn't on the allowlist — including the account. uninstallModule is withHook on MSAAdvanced, so calling it directly re-enters the same check. The agent's session key cannot remove its own guardrails, which is exactly the property we wanted, with a consequence we hadn't planned: on this account the policy is fixed for the life of the account. We shipped it that way rather than weakening the check, and wrote up both escape routes in docs/future-work.md along with why neither is free.

The owner writes the policy once; the agent inherits limits it cannot remove — we found that out the hard way when we tried to uninstall our own hook during development and couldn't.

Everything is deployed and links to a block explorer: the hook on-chain, the agent's limits published under its ENS name so anyone can verify them without asking us, a subgraph of what the chain actually admitted, and an x402-gated API where every verification is a real settled payment.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Stack: TypeScript SDK (zero runtime dependencies on the decision path), an HTTP verification API, Solidity + Foundry for the on-chain hook, solc's SMTChecker for formal verification, Next.js for the demo console. Partner tech: Uniswap v4, ENS v2, The Graph, Hedera (x402 payments).

The design rule throughout: anything off-chain is advice, and the only thing that actually stops a transaction is on-chain.

The decision path has zero dependencies. Every read the policy engine needs is an eth_call issued with fetch. viem is an optional peer dep, dynamically imported, and only if you sign — so you don't take a wallet stack's supply chain into the code that decides whether an agent may spend your money. Seven policies run per action: allowlist, max transaction, daily spend, minimum balance, approval threshold, pool liquidity, and unlimited-approval detection.

Decoding is where the real work is. A policy is only as good as its understanding of the calldata. decode/uniswapV4.ts walks a Universal Router command stream and returns worst-case outflow per currency. The trap is exact-output swaps: the interesting number is amountInMaximum, not the quote, and reading the wrong field lets a 250 USDC swap look like a 1 USDC one. Anything undecodable returns UNBOUNDED rather than a guess, and unbounded always blocks. We pinned the decoder against six real Sepolia transactions — the first run decoded all six as UNBOUNDED, because of an off-by-one in the action bytes and a wrong struct word, invisible until real calldata replaced our own self-encoded fixtures. That bug is the argument for the whole approach.

Uniswap v4 is therefore load-bearing rather than decorative: the Universal Router and PoolManager are the allowlisted targets, and a second public Uniswap subgraph feeds a pool-liquidity policy — bounding spend and bounding loss are different problems.

The hook is an ERC-7579 module on an MSAAdvanced account (reference implementation v0.3.1) driven through EntryPoint v0.8.0. The version is pinned deliberately: v0.7 predates ISenderCreator, and v0.9 gates handleOps behind tx.origin == msg.sender. We also had to match the account's actual postCheck(bytes) — selector 0x173bf7da — not the draft postCheck(bytes,bool,bytes) from the spec. That one is worth dwelling on: the mock-only version of our test suite hid it for weeks. The hook would have installed cleanly and reverted on first real execution. The mocks agreed with each other while both disagreed with reality. There is now an integration test that installs the hook on a real 7579 account and drives it through a real EntryPoint to prove it.

Formal verification with solc's SMTChecker proves MAX_TRANSFER and DAILY_SPEND hold over PolicyLib for all inputs, in about 1.3 seconds. We also compile a deliberately broken spec, PolicySpecBroken, which must produce a counterexample — that's how we know the solver is actually looking rather than trivially passing. The hook itself is fuzzed and invariant-tested, not proven, and the UI says which is which. Missing artifacts report NOT_RUN instead of passing silently.

ENS v2 carries the agent's identity as a namespace: addr to the smart account, plus text records for policy hash, hook address, and status. The EAC roles encode the trust split precisely — the owner holds ROLE_SET_POLICY_RECORD, and the agent's session key holds only ROLE_SET_STATUS_RECORD, so an agent can suspend itself and nothing else. The SDK does a three-way binding check at startup: local file, ENS record, and the hook's stored hash must agree, or it refuses to run.

The Graph indexes the hook's own SpendRecorded events, so spend history reflects what the chain admitted rather than what an agent intended. A pre-aggregated DailyAggregate entity is what keeps a policy decision fast enough for an agent's hot path. Subgraph reads are reconciled against a direct on-chain accumulator read — whichever source permits less wins — and if both are unreachable the SDK fails closed.

Hedera makes the verification service the paid product. POST /v1/verify returns 402 with payment requirements; the client partially signs a transfer; the Blocky402 facilitator co-signs as fee payer and settles; then the verdict comes back. Verify before work, settle after — callers are never charged for failed requests. Each settlement is written to an HCS topic, so an audit trail exists on infrastructure we don't control. The loop closes nicely: the payment itself is a policy-checked action, so an agent can't be talked into paying a thousand dollars for a data query by a service that simply asks for it.
Hacky bits worth mentioning

The browser can't pay, so the server pays for it. The demo console needed the x402 gate switched on to be honest, but a browser has no wallet — every check just came back 402. The console's verify route now answers the payment challenge itself with a Hedera signer, so the gate stays on and every click in the demo is a real settlement with its transaction id linked to HashScan. Nothing in the demo path is a mock or a bypass; the UI pays for its own verifications like any other caller.

We couldn't uninstall our own hook. Updating the policy on a live account means executing against the account itself, and the hook rejects any target that isn't on the allowlist — including the account. uninstallModule is withHook on MSAAdvanced, so calling it directly re-enters the same check. The agent's session key cannot remove its own guardrails, which is exactly the property we wanted, with a consequence we hadn't planned: on this account the policy is fixed for the life of the account. We shipped it that way rather than weakening the check, and wrote up both escape routes in docs/future-work.md along with why neither is free.

projects.title: Genie Markets
projects.description: Genie Markets is a house-funded, $USDC-denominated number prediction market.
projects.project_description:
Genie Markets is a house-funded, $USDC-denominated number prediction market where users wager on digit outcomes derived from Chainlink VRF v2.5 randomness. The protocol eliminates traditional Web3 friction via Privy with gas-sponsored transactions and allows users to sign in with a Google account or email, creating a seamless Web2-like experience for non-native crypto users. When signing in, users have to choose either a Google account/email or an external wallet. The difference is that signing in via external wallets (e.g., MetaMask) will require users to pay their own gas fees. After users deposit $USDC funds, they can participate in five prediction types across two daily market windows: *Market Windows: Open Market: The open market window runs for 18 hours, allowing users to wager on Open Single, Pair, and Open Trio. Close Market: The close market window runs for 6 hours. Users can wager on Close Single and Close Trio during the Open market window, but the window to wager on Open Single, Open Trio, and Pair officially closes at the end of the Open market window and the start of the Close market window. Why open and close market? The open and close market allows for fun game types like the Pair. The whole market runs for 24 hours (Open 18 hours + Close 6 hours). The market windows can be adjusted according to user preference. *Prediction Types: Single Digits (0–9): Derived via (digit1 + digit2 + digit3) mod 10 for a 9x payout.
E.g., 1, 2, 3 = Single 6 ((1+2+3) % 10 = 6)
Single digits are of two types: Open Single and Close Single.
Single digits are derived from Trios. (123 in the above example is a trio; more on this below). Two Digit Pairs (00–99): Formed by combining the Open Single and Close Single outcomes for a 90x payout.
E.g., 1, 2, 3 = Open Single 6 ((1+2+3) % 10 = 6)
4, 5, 6 = Close Single 5 ((4+5+6) % 10 = 5)
The Pair becomes 65 (Open Single 6 & Close Single 5). Three Digit Trios (000–999): High-tier jackpot markets sorted canonically under Genie Ordering math (1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5 < 6 < 7 < 8 < 9 < 0). While there are 1,000 raw permutations from 000 to 999, enforcing canonical sorting reduces the pool to exactly 220 unique trio combinations. These offer tiered returns across three categories: Unique Trio (3 distinct digits, e.g., 123): 140x Twin Trio (2 identical digits, e.g., 100): 280x Jackpot Trio (3 identical digits, e.g., 000): 600x
There are only 10 Jackpot trios, 90 Twin Trios, and 120 Unique trios adding to 220 unique trios out of three digit trios from 000-999.
Trios are of two types: Open Trio and Close Trio. The Open Single and Close Single are derived from the Open Trio and Close Trio. Hence, the five prediction types are: Open Single, Close Single, Open Trio, Close Trio, and Pair. *Genie Market Round Flow Users wager on singles, trios, and pairs. First, the Open market is settled by Chainlink VRF. It returns a 3-digit number (e.g., 123)—this is the Open Trio. Based on this, the Open Single is derived (e.g., 6 in this case). In this step, the Open Single and Open Trio are settled. Secondly, the Close market is settled as well by Chainlink VRF. It returns another 3-digit number (e.g., 456)—this is the Close Trio. Based on this, the Close Single is derived (e.g., 5 in this case). In this step, the Close Trio and Close Single are settled, along with the Pair (derived from Open Single + Close Single, e.g., 65). The round settles as follows:
Open Trio 123, Open Single 6, Close Trio 456, Close Single 5, and Pair 65. *All wagers are locked in a non-custodial smart contract escrow. Payouts are pull-based and can be claimed within 30 days of round finalization. If a randomness request hangs past a 24-hour window, a permission less emergency recovery mechanism allows any user to trigger 100% wager refunds.
projects.how_its_made: Genie Markets is built with a modern Web3 stack combining Solidity smart contracts, Chainlink VRF, Privy for gas sponsored transactions and sign in via google/email, and a Next.js prediction terminal. *Smart Contracts (Solidity + Foundry): The core protocol lives in two contracts; "GenieMarkets.sol" is a a 5-phase round state machine (Open Betting → Open Pending → Close Betting → Close Pending → Settled) that handles betting, Chainlink VRF draw requests, settlement, claims, refunds, and bankroll management. All $USDC interactions use Open Zeppelin's "SafeERC20" and external transfers are guarded by "ReentrancyGuard". Winners pull their own payouts via "claimWinnings()" with in 30 rounds of round settlement. "GenieMath.sol" is a pure library that implements the custom Genie ordering math ( 1 < 2 < ... < 9 < 0 ), canonical trio sorting, single digit derivation via modular arithmetic, and trio type classification (Unique/Twin/Jackpot). *Frontend (Next.js + React): The frontend uses Next.js App Router with wagmi and viem for all smart contract reads and writes. Custom React hooks encapsulate contract interaction logic. The UI is built with Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui components, and Lucide React icons. *Chainlink VRF: Each round makes two VRF calls; one for the Open draw, one for the Close draw. The contract extends VRFConsumerBaseV2Plus and uses VRFV2PlusClient to request randomness with 3 block confirmations. A 24-hour staleness check lets anyone call cancelStaleRound() to refund players if VRF never responds. *Privy (Embedded Wallets + ERC-4337 Gas Sponsorship): This was the key integration for UX. Privy creates embedded smart accounts for users who sign in with Google or email; no MetaMask, no seed phrases. All transaction gas is sponsored through a custom use-smart-transaction hook that detects embedded vs. external wallets and routes transactions accordingly. Privy is wired into 14 components/hooks across the frontend for auth gating, wallet detection, and funding flows. External wallet users (MetaMask, etc.) are also supported but pay their own gas. *Partner technologies; Chainlink helped with VRF and Privy helped with UX.

projects.title: Mandate
projects.description: On-chain spending limits for autonomous DeFi agents that hold even when the agent is compromised
projects.project_description: Imagine you hire an AI agent to trade for you and tell it "only use Uniswap, and never risk more than $10,000 at a time." Normally that rule lives inside the agent itself, in its config or instructions. That's a problem, because if the agent gets hacked, tricked, or just makes a mistake, nothing stops it from breaking its own rule. This already happened in real life. In 2026 a compromised agent wallet lost about $150,000, twice. Another sent 1000 times more than it meant to after a crash. A wave of memory poisoning attacks drained an estimated $45 million from trading agents on Solana. Mandate moves the rule outside the agent's control entirely. The owner writes the agent's limits once, as a record on ENS. The agent can read it but cannot change it. A background service copies that record onto a smart contract so it can be checked instantly. Every time the agent wants to trade, the system checks the published limit and the agent's live reputation, pulled through The Graph. Only if both check out does the trade go through, settling in real USDC on Arc. If not, no money moves. The outcome writes back to the agent's public reputation either way, so its track record builds over time instead of being guessed at. We also built MandateGate, using 1inch's SwapVM. Instead of only checking permissions before a trade, this opcode checks them inside the swap itself, so the rule can't be skipped even by a bug elsewhere. We proved this with four real Sepolia transactions: one allowed trade that went through, one blocked trade that reverted on chain, one that only worked because we changed permissions after the contract was already live, and one against a real concentrated liquidity position instead of a simple swap. All contracts are verified and publicly viewable. Nothing here is simulated. The agent is really registered on Sepolia, the data feeds are live, and our public server returns real answers to anyone who queries it. We've completed 9 real settlements on Arc worth $12.71, and 10 real reputation entries written by a second account, since an agent can't rate itself. One honest gap: our dashboard still uses the simpler off-chain check for its own trades. MandateGate is proven on chain but not wired into the main app yet, a real capability sitting ready rather than something clickable today. Built for ETHOnline 2026. Submitting for ENS, The Graph, and 1inch.
projects.how_its_made: The app runs on Next.js and TypeScript, talking to the blockchain through Viem. The contracts are written in Solidity and built with Foundry. We run our own subgraph on The Graph, and also read from a separate public ERC-8004 subgraph on Base. The flow: an owner writes an agent's permission limits into an ENS text record on Sepolia, using ENSv2's newer per-name resolvers. A relayer copies that record into a contract called PermissionMirror, so it can be checked instantly on chain. When a trade is proposed, we combine two live signals into one trust score, our own subgraph's sync history and the agent's real ERC-8004 reputation. No reputation yet is treated as unknown, never as zero. If the trade passes, it settles in real USDC on Arc, whose native currency is USDC itself, so it's a plain value transfer with no token contract or approval step. The result then writes back to the agent's reputation from a second account, since an agent cannot rate itself. The part we're proudest of is "MandateGate", a custom opcode built on 1inch's SwapVM. Normally our check runs before a trade is attempted. MandateGate moves that same check inside the swap itself, so it cannot be skipped. We built it by reading the real SwapVM source directly, since the pattern we were originally told to follow does not actually exist in the codebase. We found the real one ourselves and extended 1inch's official router in code, without editing any of their files. To prove a blocked trade really reverts on chain, we had to broadcast a transaction we already knew would fail. Foundry's own tool refuses to send anything its simulation shows will revert, so we pulled the exact transaction data it had prepared and sent it manually with a fixed gas limit, skipping that check. That got us a real, mined, failed transaction instead of just a simulated one.

projects.title: Onchain Heartbeat
projects.description: Live blockchain pulse narrated by an AI agent that pays for its own data over Hedera x402
projects.project_description: Onchain Heartbeat turns blockchain activity into a vital sign, and gives the AI narrating it a wallet and a name. A circle beats in the centre of the screen. Its rhythm, amplitude and colour are driven by live Uniswap v3 swap flow on Base a slow cyan swell when the chain is quiet, fast crimson thumping when it's busy. You read the state of the chain from across the room, before anyone tells you what the numbers mean. Every 18 seconds an AI agent buys a fresh reading and calls the play in one line of commentary. It doesn't authenticate with an API key it pays. The reading sits behind an x402 paywall: the agent gets a 402, signs an HBAR transfer, Blocky402 settles it on Hedera testnet, and only then does the data come back. One payment per narration, never batched, each individually auditable. And it signs what it says. The narrator owns onchain-heartbeat.eth on the ETHOnline ENSv2 deployment, with avatar, description and url as text records an identity, not a label. When the chain's mood shifts, that call is published as its own subname, carrying the comment, the reading behind it, and the Hedera transaction that paid for it. Resolve any narration and you can check what the agent claimed, what it was looking at, and what that claim cost. It addresses two gaps. Chain data is a wall of numbers you have to read to understand. And AI agents can't sign up for API keys, can't hold subscriptions, and can't prove they said anything their output is unattributable by default. This is a small, complete demonstration of the alternative, running live rather than described. Verifiable settlement: 0.0.7162784@1788690223.769989855  confirmed on the Hedera mirror node.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind 4, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, viem, and the x402 v2 packages (@x402/hedera, @x402/next, @x402/fetch). Nine runtime dependencies total. The seam. Every data source returns the same { activityLevel, label }, so the visual never knows where its number came from. That contract absorbed three swaps during the build  mock to RPC, RPC to The Graph, and one ENS deployment to another and PulseVisual.tsx never changed once. The pulse itself maps 0–100 onto three CSS custom properties (--beat, --amp, --hue) and lets CSS keyframes animate, so the heartbeat runs on the compositor rather than in JS, with @property registrations easing amplitude and hue between readings. The Graph. A Messari standardized subgraph for Uniswap v3 on Base, queried server-side so the API key never reaches the browser. Swaps-per-minute is derived from the timestamp span of the last 500 swaps 500 rather than 100 because over a handful of integer seconds the rate quantises into coarse jumps (429, 600, 750, 1500). Thresholds were calibrated by sampling, not guessed: 341–652/min in the daytime, but 121 overnight, so the scale is logarithmic rather than linear. A linear window pinned half the day at zero and flatlined the pulse. Hedera x402. /api/chain-data is a real metered resource behind @x402/next, and the thing it sells is the subgraph reading so the payment buys indexed data, not a receipt. The client sets a hard 0.01 HBAR per-payment ceiling, because an agent paying on a timer should have one. scripts/buy-reading.mjs lets any third party with a funded testnet account buy a reading, so the endpoint isn't a private arrangement. ENSv2 and the hacky part. The hackathon's ENS app couldn't complete a registration, so we went straight at the contracts. None of the deployment is verified on Etherscan or Sourcify, so the ABIs were recovered by scanning PUSH4 selectors out of deployed bytecode and resolving them against a signature database, then cross-checked against a registration that had already succeeded on-chain argument order copied from a working call rather than guessed. That also isolated the app's defect: it encodes initialize's first argument as address,uint256 where the implementation expects (address,uint256)[], producing a selector that matches no function. Reported with a keyless repro (docs/ens-app-bug-report.md). Registration is commit-reveal paid in ERC-20, not ETH. Records live on a per-name Permissioned Resolver keyed by DNS-encoded name the shared PublicResolverV2 rejects the owner for every node derivation. The per-narration subnames need no registration at all: writing records on the parent's own resolver is enough for ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution to reach them, so no CCIP-Read gateway. Verification discipline. Every on-chain write is simulated before it's sent, and multi-step flows are checked together with eth_simulateV1 against one projected post-state which is the only way to verify a call against a resolver proxy that doesn't exist yet. Each dependency degrades instead of breaking: kill the subgraph, the facilitator, the LLM or the resolver and the pulse holds its last rate and keeps beating.

Onchain Heartbeat turns blockchain activity into a vital sign, and gives the AI narrating it a wallet and a name.

A circle beats in the centre of the screen. Its rhythm, amplitude and colour are driven by live Uniswap v3 swap flow on Base a slow cyan swell when the chain is quiet, fast crimson thumping when it's busy. You read the state of the chain from across the room, before anyone tells you what the numbers mean.

Every 18 seconds an AI agent buys a fresh reading and calls the play in one line of commentary. It doesn't authenticate with an API key it pays. The reading sits behind an x402 paywall: the agent gets a 402, signs an HBAR transfer, Blocky402 settles it on Hedera testnet, and only then does the data come back. One payment per narration, never batched, each individually auditable.

And it signs what it says. The narrator owns onchain-heartbeat.eth on the ETHOnline ENSv2 deployment, with avatar, description and url as text records an identity, not a label. When the chain's mood shifts, that call is published as its own subname, carrying the comment, the reading behind it, and the Hedera transaction that paid for it. Resolve any narration and you can check what the agent claimed, what it was looking at, and what that claim cost.

It addresses two gaps. Chain data is a wall of numbers you have to read to understand. And AI agents can't sign up for API keys, can't hold subscriptions, and can't prove they said anything their output is unattributable by default. This is a small, complete demonstration of the alternative, running live rather than described.

Verifiable settlement: 0.0.7162784@1788690223.769989855  confirmed on the Hedera mirror node.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Stack. Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind 4, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, viem, and the x402 v2 packages (@x402/hedera, @x402/next, @x402/fetch). Nine runtime dependencies total.

The seam. Every data source returns the same { activityLevel, label }, so the visual never knows where its number came from. That contract absorbed three swaps during the build  mock to RPC, RPC to The Graph, and one ENS deployment to another and PulseVisual.tsx never changed once. The pulse itself maps 0–100 onto three CSS custom properties (--beat, --amp, --hue) and lets CSS keyframes animate, so the heartbeat runs on the compositor rather than in JS, with @property registrations easing amplitude and hue between readings.

The Graph. A Messari standardized subgraph for Uniswap v3 on Base, queried server-side so the API key never reaches the browser. Swaps-per-minute is derived from the timestamp span of the last 500 swaps 500 rather than 100 because over a handful of integer seconds the rate quantises into coarse jumps (429, 600, 750, 1500). Thresholds were calibrated by sampling, not guessed: 341–652/min in the daytime, but 121 overnight, so the scale is logarithmic rather than linear. A linear window pinned half the day at zero and flatlined the pulse.

Hedera x402. /api/chain-data is a real metered resource behind @x402/next, and the thing it sells is the subgraph reading so the payment buys indexed data, not a receipt. The client sets a hard 0.01 HBAR per-payment ceiling, because an agent paying on a timer should have one. scripts/buy-reading.mjs lets any third party with a funded testnet account buy a reading, so the endpoint isn't a private arrangement.

ENSv2 and the hacky part. The hackathon's ENS app couldn't complete a registration, so we went straight at the contracts. None of the deployment is verified on Etherscan or Sourcify, so the ABIs were recovered by scanning PUSH4 selectors out of deployed bytecode and resolving them against a signature database, then cross-checked against a registration that had already succeeded on-chain argument order copied from a working call rather than guessed. That also isolated the app's defect: it encodes initialize's first argument as address,uint256 where the implementation expects (address,uint256)[], producing a selector that matches no function. Reported with a keyless repro (docs/ens-app-bug-report.md).

Registration is commit-reveal paid in ERC-20, not ETH. Records live on a per-name Permissioned Resolver keyed by DNS-encoded name the shared PublicResolverV2 rejects the owner for every node derivation. The per-narration subnames need no registration at all: writing records on the parent's own resolver is enough for ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution to reach them, so no CCIP-Read gateway.

Verification discipline. Every on-chain write is simulated before it's sent, and multi-step flows are checked together with eth_simulateV1 against one projected post-state which is the only way to verify a call against a resolver proxy that doesn't exist yet. Each dependency degrades instead of breaking: kill the subgraph, the facilitator, the LLM or the resolver and the pulse holds its last rate and keeps beating.

projects.title: LP Terminal
projects.description: Uniswap V3 LP scanner — track every position's range, status, and owner, plus pool balances.
projects.project_description:
This is a Uniswap V3 liquidity position scanner built for Robinhood Chain, focused on
solving a specific gap: there's no built-in way to see every LP position in a given
pool at once. The NonfungiblePositionManager tracks positions globally by tokenId, not
per-pool, so the project builts a data pipeline that scans NFPM event logs (Transfer,
IncreaseLiquidity, DecreaseLiquidity) alongside the pool contract's own Mint events,
correlates them by transaction hash to recover tick ranges, and reconstructs each
position's price range and current owner entirely from on-chain history — no
subgraph or archive node required. The frontend displays a live pool header (current price, token balances), a
paginated table of every position in the pool with its range and status (active
in-range, out-of-range, or closed), and a detail view for inspecting individual
positions with a visual range indicator. Data is fetched from the chain, written to
Supabase, and served to the frontend as a read-only snapshot — the UI shows exactly
which block range the data was scanned from, so it's transparent about being a
point-in-time view rather than claiming real-time accuracy it doesn't have.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is Next.js (React/TypeScript) for the frontend, Supabase (Postgres) for storage, ethers.js for all on-chain interaction, and uniswap-v3 sdk, targeting Uniswap V3 on Robinhood Chain. The core technical challenge was position discovery: Uniswap's NonfungiblePositionManager tracks positions globally by tokenId, with no built-in way to query "every position in pool X." The project solved this by scanning NFPM Transfer events (filtered on mint transfers from the zero address) to enumerate all tokenIds, then reading positions() to filter by matching token0/token1/fee for our target pool. The trickier problem was historical accuracy: calling positions() or slot0() at a specific past block requires an archive node, which our RPC provider didn't support (the project hits a "metadata not found" error mid-build). Rather than switching providers, the project rebuilts the data layer around pure event-log replay — summing IncreaseLiquidity and DecreaseLiquidity deltas to compute net liquidity per position, and correlating each NFPM mint's transaction hash with the pool contract's own Mint event to recover tickLower/tickUpper (which aren't included in any NFPM event directly). This means the entire position dataset is reconstructed from raw logs, with no archive node or subgraph dependency. The project used @uniswap/v3-sdk for tick-to-price conversion (tickToPrice) to display human-readable price ranges instead of raw tick integers, which handles the precision/decimal-scaling correctly rather than us re-deriving the 1.0001^tick formula by hand. Data is fetched via a standalone Node/TypeScript script (separate from the Next.js app, using a Supabase service_role key) and written to Postgres. The most "hacky but necessary" decision was scoping to a fixed, prefetched block range rather than live-fetching on every page load — this trades real-time freshness for demo reliability, and the UI is explicit about this by displaying the exact block/timestamp range the data was scanned from.

projects.title: Botvue
projects.description: Catches sites that answer AI crawlers with a 200 OK and nothing in it, then proves it.
projects.project_description: Botvue reports when a website serves AI crawlers a different, often empty, page than it serves browsers and Googlebot, while still returning HTTP 200, so the agent has no reason to doubt it succeeded. It fetches one URL six ways at the same moment: a browser, Googlebot, and four real AI crawler user-agents (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot). It compares the responses and classifies any difference on a five-level severity scale, from cosmetic markup residue up to prompt injection: text addressed directly to the AI reading it. Every finding carries a SHA-256 hash of the actual response body, so it can be independently re-verified rather than taken on trust. We measured 131 findings across a 567-property corpus of real news sites; the rest are clean or refuse crawlers honestly with a real 4xx, which isn't a problem since an agent that gets refused already knows it got nothing. Paid checks settle via x402 on Hedera testnet, and that settlement is independently re-confirmed against Hedera's public mirror node rather than trusted from the payment facilitator alone.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a Python/FastAPI gateway that fetches a URL as a browser and as five bot user-agents via httpx, extracts text with trafilatura, and classifies differences with a rule-based taxonomy before mapping the worst match to a pass/flag/block decision. Paid requests are gated by x402: a 402 response carries Hedera testnet payment terms fetched live from the Blocky402 facilitator's own endpoint, never hardcoded, and after settlement we independently re-verify the transaction against Hedera's public mirror node instead of trusting the facilitator's word alone, the same verify-don't-trust discipline as the content check itself. A second adapter, an MCP server, exposes identical logic as three tools for AI agents directly, including fetch_url, a drop-in fetch-tool replacement that withholds content when it doesn't match what a human would see. A GitHub Actions cron re-scans the full corpus daily. A third-party gateway, Bazantic, independently discovered our OpenAPI spec and now prices /check on Base and USDC as a second payment rail.

projects.title: ZubiDubi
projects.description: Self-custodial early exit liquidity for maturing DeFi assets, priced by time, risk, and exposure.
projects.project_description: ZubiDubi is self-custodial early exit liquidity for locked, delayed redemption DeFi assets like Pendle PT tokens, LRT receipts, and vault withdrawal shares. These assets are worth full value at maturity but illiquid before it, and today holders either wait or sell off-chain at an opaque discount. Generic AMMs cannot price this correctly because they have no concept of time to maturity. Built by modifying SwapVM itself, not wrapping it: a reusable instruction library adds oracle validation, exposure limits, and term-discount pricing as native opcodes. Many DeFi assets are transferable but not instantly redeemable: Pendle-like Principal Tokens, LST/LRT withdrawal receipts, vault withdrawal claims, bridge receipts, and other maturing positions. Holders who need liquidity early often must wait, sell into thin markets, or accept opaque OTC/RFQ pricing. ZubiDubi creates a programmable early-exit market for those assets. Makers publish liquidity strategies from their own wallets instead of locking funds into isolated pools. Sellers bring a maturing claim, and ZubiDubi routes the sale across makers who can actually deliver liquid USDC/WETH at that moment. The maker pays liquid tokens now and receives the maturing claim now, taking on duration and redemption risk in exchange for a discount. The core idea is a programmable term-liquidity book: makers define risk curves based on oracle-backed value, time to maturity, inventory, liquidity depth, risk tier, and exposure limits. The route executor checks real deliverable liquidity onchain, skips insolvent makers, splits fills across the best executable strategies, and reverts if the requested trade cannot fully settle. ZubiDubi also introduces shared term-risk budgets. A maker can assign sibling Aqua strategies to one global receipt/quote budget, so when one strategy fills, the rest lose capacity and start quoting worse prices as utilization rises. This turns wallet-held liquidity into a coordinated term-liquidity book rather than isolated strategies racing the same balance. The deployed demo includes verified Sepolia contracts, real Sepolia WETH/USDC/LINK-backed PT-style receipt assets, Chainlink oracle pricing, a deployed Graph subgraph, a hosted solver API, and a frontend for markets, selling, making strategies, portfolio issuance/redemption, and playground proofs.
projects.how_its_made:
ZubiDubi is built on the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM codebases, with SwapVM extended for term-liquidity markets. On the contract side, we modified the Aqua SwapVM router and added a reusable instruction library instead of one app-specific mega-opcode. The library has three modular instructions: BACKING_ORACLE_CHECK: validates the receipt/quote pair, reads oracle-backed par value, enforces stale-oracle protection, maturity bounds, and optional secondary-oracle deviation haircuts.
EXPOSURE_CAP: enforces maker max receipt exposure, max quote-token notional, available liquidity, and inventory limits.
DISCOUNT_CURVE_1D: computes the executable quote using base discount, annualized term rate, convexity, risk tier, inventory pressure, and liquidity-depth penalty. We also built ZubiDubiRouteExecutor, which is the onchain settlement layer. It receives candidate Aqua/SwapVM strategies from the solver, calls the router for quotes, checks deliverable maker liquidity as min(Aqua virtual balance, wallet balance, allowance), applies shared term-risk budget caps, sorts/fills routes, charges a DAO fee, and executes atomically. If the full route cannot be filled, the transaction does not partially settle. The instruction library and route executor are covered by Foundry invariant and fuzz tests proving discount never goes negative or above par, payout is monotonic in time to maturity, convex discount is always at least linear discount, maker payout never exceeds the minimum of wallet balance and allowance, routes settle atomically, fees are conserved, and no maker's liquidity is double counted across sibling strategies sharing a budget. The live Sepolia book includes multiple independent maker wallets, not just one maker publishing sibling strategies. We funded two additional maker EOAs and shipped six more live strategies across different receipt assets and payout tokens, all indexed as active on the subgraph, with the hosted solver actually routing a real request across three independently owned strategies at once. This proves genuine multi-maker competition and routing on real deployed contracts, not a single wallet simulating multiple counterparties. For demo assets, we deployed PT-style receipt contracts on Sepolia. These are real ERC20 receipt contracts backed by real Sepolia WETH, USDC, and LINK. Users can issue claims by depositing backing assets and later redeem after maturity. For production, the same flow maps to real delayed-redemption assets such as Pendle PTs, withdrawal receipts, vault claims, or bridge receipts. We used real Chainlink feeds and onchain ratio adapters for pricing, plus an optional Pyth adapter path for dual-oracle validation. We also added a mainnet-fork Pendle benchmark test using a real Pendle PT market, so we can compare ZubiDubi's maker curve against Pendle's implied PT pricing and show inventory-aware repricing after maker exposure changes. The Graph is the market reconstruction layer. Our deployed Subgraph Studio endpoint indexes Aqua strategies, SwapVM fills, routed fills, skipped makers, shared term-risk budgets, receipt issuance/redemption, maker exposure, market volume, and DAO fee accrual. This lets the solver and frontend discover the live term-liquidity book without scanning raw logs. The solver API is a hosted Node service on Railway. It queries The Graph for active strategies, decodes executable SwapVM order bytes, calls Sepolia RPC for fresh quoteExactIn checks, returns route splits and budget-pressure metadata, and builds maker strategy payloads for the frontend. The frontend is deployed on Vercel and uses Privy for wallet connection, Viem for contract calls, The Graph for indexed state, and the Railway solver API for executable quotes. The frontend includes live markets, a swap-style sell page, maker strategy creation with an interactive curve editor where makers drag discount, cap, convexity, and exposure handles directly on the chart, backed by the same pricing math used onchain so the chart and the shipped transaction can never drift apart, portfolio issuance/redemption, and a playground page with proof panels, route-split visualizations, pressure-budget badges, test commands, and live Graph-backed state. Everything is deployed: verified Sepolia contracts, Graph subgraph, Railway solver API, and Vercel frontend.

projects.title: Vouch
projects.description: Identity and reputation for AI agents: ENSv2 names, indexed evidence, x402-priced lookups.
projects.project_description:
Vouch makes AI agents prove what they’ve done, not just say it. Right now any AI agent can claim anything about itself. "I’m fast. I’m reliable. I’ve done 10,000 jobs."
With Vouch, an agent can’t lie about its track record because it doesn’t control the score.
Here’s how it works: Every agent gets a real name
When an agent registers with Vouch it gets a name under vouch.eth. It’s a real ENSv2 subname.
It can’t be sold, it expires, and it works like a credential — not an asset you flip.Tied to that name are records. But not all records are equal.
Who can write them is what matters. The agent controls its claims. We control the proof.
The agent’s own key can update things like:
agent:endpoint, agent:capabilities, agent:price That’s what it says about itself. But it can’t touch: agent:score, agent:disputes, agent:volume.
Only the Vouch scorer can write those. And the score isn’t made up. It’s pulled from real activity:  jobs settled, feedback from counterparties, disputes filed. All of that is indexed on-chain from Ethereum using a Graph subgraph built on the ERC-8004 registry. And this isn’t enforced by some backend we control. It’s enforced directly by ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control. The permission is set on each record in the agent’s own resolver.
If the agent tries to give itself a score of "999", the transaction just fails. There’s literally no way for it to rate itself.
3. Why this matters
x402 made it easy for one agent to pay another. Great.
But it didn’t answer the real question: "Should I trust this agent with my money?" Identity tells you who they are. It doesn’t tell you if they’ve ever done the job. That’s what Vouch sells. A reputation check. It’s an x402-paid endpoint on Hedera. About $0.001 per lookup, with 3-second finality.
Claims are free. Proof costs money. That’s the whole business model in one sentence.
4. What it looks like in practice
A buyer agent needs a seller.
It looks up 3 candidates by their ENS name, pays to check their reputation, sees one has a 60% dispute rate and drops it, then hires one of the others. No human in the loop. Later, if that hired agent messes up a job, the counterparty files a dispute on Sepolia. The subgraph picks it up, the scorer recalculates, and writes the new lower score back to the agent’s resolver. Next time a buyer checks, that agent gets skipped.
If the operator is done with the agent entirely, the name owner just revokes it and it stops resolving.
5. Three IDs, all linked vouch.eth name = what humans use HCS-14 Universal Agent ID = what agents use to route to each other ERC-8004 token ID = what all the on-chain evidence is attached to
projects.how_its_made:
The Graph doesn't index Hedera, so the project is split across two chains.
Identity and evidence on Ethereum Sepolia, payment and audit on Hedera testnet. On the ENS side I registered vouch.eth through the ENSv2 ETHRegistrar
(commit-reveal, paid in Sepolia USDC, it rejects native ETH), deployed my own
UserRegistry proxy through the VerifiableFactory and pointed the name's
subregistry at it. Every agent gets its own PermissionedResolver, and write
access is granted per text key with authorizeTextRoles() . To make a name
non-transferable you simply don't grant ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN. There's no
soulbound flag. The ENSv2 tutorial is out of date. register() takes six arguments, not the
five documented, with an undocumented registry pointer sitting between owner and resolver . I caught that because I pull verified ABIs from Sourcify
(Blockscout as fallback) and assert every function exists before calling it.
Every write is simulated first, so a wrong role bitmap fails for free. The subgraph indexes four contracts on Sepolia: ERC-8004's IdentityRegistry, my
VouchAttestations and VouchScoreAnchor, and my own ENS registry. I used
ERC-8004's entity shapes rather than inventing a schema, so the same query works
against any ERC-8004 deployment. A Subgraph MCP layer sits on top for
natural-language lookups. Two things stop agents gaming their own score. An AgentCounterparty entity means
uniqueCounterparties counts distinct raters instead of attestation volume, so
colluding agents rating each other repeatedly gets them nowhere. And attest() reverts if the caller owns the agent's ERC-8004 token. Hedera handles the money. x402 there uses a partially-signed TransferTransaction:

projects.project_description_markdown:
Vouch makes AI agents prove what they’ve done, not just say it.

Right now any AI agent can claim anything about itself. "I’m fast. I’m reliable. I’ve done 10,000 jobs."
With Vouch, an agent can’t lie about its track record because it doesn’t control the score.
Here’s how it works:

1. Every agent gets a real name
When an agent registers with Vouch it gets a name under vouch.eth. It’s a real ENSv2 subname.
It can’t be sold, it expires, and it works like a credential — not an asset you flip.Tied to that name are records. But not all records are equal.
Who can write them is what matters.
2. The agent controls its claims. We control the proof.
The agent’s own key can update things like:
agent:endpoint, agent:capabilities, agent:price

That’s what it says about itself. But it can’t touch: agent:score, agent:disputes, agent:volume.
Only the Vouch scorer can write those. And the score isn’t made up. It’s pulled from real activity:  jobs settled, feedback from counterparties, disputes filed. All of that is indexed on-chain from Ethereum using a Graph subgraph built on the ERC-8004 registry.

And this isn’t enforced by some backend we control. It’s enforced directly by ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control. The permission is set on each record in the agent’s own resolver.
If the agent tries to give itself a score of "999", the transaction just fails. There’s literally no way for it to rate itself.
3. Why this matters
x402 made it easy for one agent to pay another. Great.
But it didn’t answer the real question: "Should I trust this agent with my money?" Identity tells you who they are. It doesn’t tell you if they’ve ever done the job. That’s what Vouch sells. A reputation check.

It’s an x402-paid endpoint on Hedera. About $0.001 per lookup, with 3-second finality.
Claims are free. Proof costs money. That’s the whole business model in one sentence.
4. What it looks like in practice
A buyer agent needs a seller.
It looks up 3 candidates by their ENS name, pays to check their reputation, sees one has a 60% dispute rate and drops it, then hires one of the others. No human in the loop. Later, if that hired agent messes up a job, the counterparty files a dispute on Sepolia. The subgraph picks it up, the scorer recalculates, and writes the new lower score back to the agent’s resolver. Next time a buyer checks, that agent gets skipped.
If the operator is done with the agent entirely, the name owner just revokes it and it stops resolving.
5. Three IDs, all linked
- vouch.eth name = what humans use
- HCS-14 Universal Agent ID = what agents use to route to each other
- ERC-8004 token ID = what all the on-chain evidence is attached to

The Graph doesn't index Hedera, so the project is split across two chains.
Identity and evidence on Ethereum Sepolia, payment and audit on Hedera testnet.

On the ENS side I registered vouch.eth through the ENSv2 ETHRegistrar
(commit-reveal, paid in Sepolia USDC, it rejects native ETH), deployed my own

subregistry at it. Every agent gets its own PermissionedResolver, and write
access is granted per text key with `authorizeTextRoles()`. To make a name
non-transferable you simply don't grant ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN. There's no
soulbound flag.

The ENSv2 tutorial is out of date. `register()` takes six arguments, not the
five documented, with an undocumented registry pointer sitting between `owner`
and `resolver`. I caught that because I pull verified ABIs from Sourcify
(Blockscout as fallback) and assert every function exists before calling it.
Every write is simulated first, so a wrong role bitmap fails for free.

projects.title: PAI
projects.description: AI-native agreements that structure, fuzz, accept, fund, and settle through conversation.
projects.project_description: PAI is programmable agreement infrastructure for digital work. A user can describe an agreement in natural language, and PAI converts it into a structured Agreement Object, checks the terms for ambiguity and execution risk, asks for clarification when needed, and creates a canonical agreement with an immutable version and cryptographic hash. Each party independently reviews and accepts the exact same agreement before binding their wallet. PAI Core then manages the agreement lifecycle from DEFINE → ACCEPT → FUND → DELIVER → SETTLE, with an exception path for disputes and resolution. The architecture is designed to remain chain-independent: intelligence, agreement logic, acceptance and dispute workflows live in PAI Core, while settlement is handled through execution adapters. In the ETHOnline build, we demonstrate the full canonical agreement flow through READY_TO_FUND, an Arc Testnet settlement adapter, and indexed settlement history through The Graph.
projects.how_its_made: PAI is built as a modular TypeScript/Solidity system. The backend uses Node.js, TypeScript, Prisma and PostgreSQL, while the frontend uses React and Vite. Agreement intelligence runs through a local Qwen3 model, but the model is not trusted as the final authority: its structured extraction is followed by a deterministic Agreement Check that independently detects issues such as ambiguous currency, missing settlement assets and subjective acceptance criteria. After clarification, PAI persists a canonical agreement, creates immutable revision 1, computes a server-side SHA-256 agreement hash, and requires the CLIENT and CONTRACTOR to accept the same agreementId + agreementVersion + agreementHash tuple. Wallet ownership is then bound through the PAI Core lifecycle, progressing the agreement to READY_TO_FUND only after both parties have accepted and bound wallets. The blockchain execution layer is separated behind adapters. For ETHOnline we built an Arc Testnet settlement adapter for USDC approval and AgreementEscrow funding/settlement transactions. Arc settlement events are indexed with The Graph into Agreement, Milestone and SettlementEvent entities, giving PAI a verifiable read model for funding and settlement history. The demo includes live Arc transaction proof and a live Graph query showing a completed agreement, released milestone and indexed transaction history. Telegram is used as a lightweight agreement interface so users can create, clarify and accept agreements without starting from a traditional dApp UI. The main architectural goal was to keep PAI Core chain-independent so future Stellar, Solana and other execution adapters can reuse the same agreement lifecycle instead of rebuilding the product for every chain.

projects.title: Robinhood Predictor
projects.description: AI-agent parimutuel stock prediction market with Chainlink feeds and World ID anchoring
projects.project_description: Robinhood Predictor is a parimutuel stock prediction market live on Robinhood Chain mainnet (chain ID 4663), where users bet whether a stock's closing price will land above or below its opening price. The core contract went live on July 10, two to three days after Robinhood Chain itself launched, and it's been running continuously since — 91 commits and 88 real transactions across market creation, locking, and settlement. For ETHOnline we extended this live infrastructure with an AI agent that can place bets on its own. The agent reads live price data from Chainlink and trend signals from a Graph subgraph we built for this market, then decides whether to bet or sit out. If the two signals disagree, it holds off instead of forcing a trade. An autonomous agent placing bets raises an obvious question: who's actually behind it? Every agent bet has to pass through World AgentKit first. The relayer checks that the wallet is backed by a real, unique human before it will sign the transaction. No valid attestation, no bet. Settlement runs through Chainlink: the contract reads the price recorded when a market locked, compares it to the live closing price, and decides the winner on-chain. We also wrote an independent Python script that rebuilds the settlement logic from scratch, without touching our Solidity code, reruns it against every real transaction on mainnet, and seals the result with a SHA-256 hash. Before StockPredictionMarketV2.sol ever entered git history, we ran a self-audit pass modeled on our own audit-orchestrator methodology — recon, then fix. It caught two real issues pre-commit: a receive() function that would have permanently trapped any ETH sent to it by accident, and a missing zero-address check on the relayer address in the constructor. The contract shipped already fixed. Full notes: https://github.com/pplmaverick/robinhood-stock-prediction-market/blob/824e0d67e0fe2e8ba0c96760c44905ee1ee1b3d8/verification/self-audit/AUDIT_NOTES.md Full AgentKit feedback document: https://github.com/pplmaverick/robinhood-stock-prediction-market/blob/824e0d67e0fe2e8ba0c96760c44905ee1ee1b3d8/docs/feedback-agentkit.md
projects.how_its_made: The contract is Solidity, deployed on Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum-based L2 built for stock trading, first on July 10 and still live today. Settlement is parimutuel: winners split the losing side's pool, and Chainlink price feeds decide the outcome by comparing the price at lock time to the price at close. For ETHOnline we added a second contract, StockPredictionMarketV2, with a placeAgentBet function gated by a relayer-signed attestation — the caller supplies a signature that must recover to the relayer's address before the bet is accepted. Behind that relayer sits a small Node.js decision engine that pulls live price data from Chainlink and reads trend data from a Graph subgraph we built specifically for this market, indexing every bet and settlement event so the agent has something to reason against beyond raw price. If the price signal and the trend signal agree, the agent bets. If they disagree, it skips the market on purpose. The part that took the most work is the World AgentKit layer sitting in front of the relayer. Before the relayer signs an agent's bet, it checks that the agent's wallet is verified as backed by a real, unique human through AgentKit. If that check fails, the transaction never gets signed. Testing the backed path fully needs a physical Orb, which we didn't have during the hackathon, so that branch is currently verified through code review and unit tests rather than a live proof — we're writing this up honestly instead of claiming we tested something we didn't. Because the original contract already had a real transaction history before this hackathon started, we also wrote a standalone Python script that rebuilds the settlement math independently of our Solidity code, checks it against every transaction pulled from mainnet via eth_getLogs, and seals the result with a SHA-256 hash so the numbers can't be quietly edited afterward.

projects.title: Snitch
projects.description: Snitch: The Operating layer for Shared treasury and Onchain payments.
projects.project_description: Snitch is an operating layer that helps companies manage onchain payments from a single workspace. A company can create separate accounts for different departments, projects, regions or payment flows. Each account operates independently, with its own treasury, transaction history and wallet secured through Privy. This keeps funds, payments and financial records clearly separated. Within each account, finance teams can issue invoices, receive payments, pay vendors, manage global payroll and monitor transactions from initiation to confirmation. Role based access gives each team member the appropriate level of control while restricting sensitive wallet actions, such as private key export, to authorised roles. Snitch never takes custody of company funds or private keys. Privy protects wallet access and handles key export, allowing the company to retain control of its assets while Snitch provides the operational tools and records needed to manage them.
projects.how_its_made: Snitch is a non-custodial payment infrastructure that never stores private keys, recovery phrases, or wallet signing material. It also cannot move company funds independently. We use Privy as the wallet and key management layer for every Snitch account. When a company creates a new account for a department, project, region, or payment flow, Snitch provisions a dedicated wallet through Privy and connects it directly to that account’s treasury and transaction history. This allows companies to separate funds and financial activity without manually creating, securing, and managing multiple wallets. Privy is particularly important to our non-custodial design. It handles the underlying wallet infrastructure, transaction layer for treasury, and secure key access, while Snitch operates above it as the operational layer for invoices, vendor payments, payroll, and transaction management.

projects.title: Cordon
projects.description: Cordon helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
projects.project_description:
The problem:
AI agents can decide which tools to call, repeat failed requests, and delegate work to other agents. That flexibility makes their costs difficult to predict. A user may approve a task expecting a useful result, only to discover that the agents have exhausted the budget collecting information without completing the final output.
There is evidence that unexpected agent costs are a real engineering problem. A June 2026 research preprint catalogues 63 reported production budget-overrun incidents across 21 orchestration frameworks, including failures involving delegated work. This evidence concerns broader agent computation and orchestration costs, rather than specifically Circle marketplace payments, but it illustrates the financial consequences of poorly coordinated autonomous activity.
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04056 Delegation adds a coordination problem. If workers receive independent allowances without a shared total check, their combined purchases can exceed the owner’s intended task budget. Even when a shared limit exists, fixed worker allocations can waste available capacity: one worker may finish with money left over while another stops because its own allowance is exhausted.
Existing spending controls provide an essential foundation. Circle Agent Wallets, for example, document per-transaction, daily, weekly, and monthly limits, along with recipient restrictions. Cordon focuses on the task-management problem around those controls: how should an agent team adapt its work when the remaining budget changes?
Source: https://developers.circle.com/agent-stack/agent-wallets/wallet-operations/custom-policies What Cordon is and how it helps Cordon is a budget-aware companion for AI agents, designed for integration through an SDK and Model Context Protocol (MCP). Its goal is to help agents complete useful work efficiently within a shared budget while preserving the quality of the result. The owner defines a spending mandate for a task. Agents working under that mandate share its limits, and delegated agents can only receive narrower permissions. Their spending counts against the budget above them, so delegation does not create a fresh allowance outside the owner's mandate. Cordon checks paid-service requests and provides structured feedback when a request encounters a constraint. Our broader vision is to help agents use this feedback to choose a cheaper service, reuse available information, avoid unnecessary retries, or reserve enough budget for the remaining work. If additional spending is necessary, the agent can ask the owner for a specific exception. The current MVP establishes the foundation with shared spending controls, recorded refusals, and owner-approved releases. Cost-aware planning and alternative-service selection are the next capabilities we aim to develop. How we will evaluate Cordon We will compare three approaches: direct purchasing without Cordon, a conventional shared budget with a hard stop, and Cordon. Each approach will receive the same task, starting information, service options, and output requirements. Our main question is whether Cordon can reduce the total cost of completing a task while delivering an equally useful result. We will measure task completion, total spending, repeated or unnecessary purchases, completion time, and the number of times the owner needs to intervene. Total cost will include payment fees, gas, and any Cordon service fee. For deterministic tasks, such as retrieving a fixed dataset or performing a calculation, we will check whether the final outputs match exactly. For research and synthesis tasks, we will evaluate accuracy, completeness, source quality, and freshness against the same checklist. We will use fixed data or aligned timestamps where needed to make comparisons fair. We will also test difficult situations, including repeated failures, expensive services, and several agents drawing from one budget. A run that spends less because it stops early will count as incomplete, not as an efficiency improvement. These are planned evaluations. We will make this testing result as a path for cordon continuitity towards our end goal to help  helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
projects.how_its_made: Cordon is four layers where authority only flows downward — from the owner to the contract, never up from the agent. Three Solidity contracts on Arc testnet: MandateRegistry manages the agent tree and enforces narrowing, TreeVault holds funds and performs ancestor debit (every draw charges every node up to the root), and ConductRecord publishes refusals to ERC-8004's reputation registry. No proxy, no admin key, no upgrade path. The daemon (Node 23.6+, TypeScript, viem 2) is the only component that holds a private key. Agents call cordon_fetch(url) — the daemon reads the seller's x402 challenge, extracts price and payee from it (never from the agent), and asks the vault. There is no cordon_transfer or cordon_pay tool, and a test asserts each stays unregistered. An agent that can't express "send money to X" can't be talked into it. Arc testnet was essential — USDC as both gas and payment token means operators hold one asset, and sub-second finality makes per-purchase on-chain enforcement affordable. Privy powers the console wallet gate with embedded wallets via createOnLogin, so owners without a browser wallet can still sign mandates. Settlement runs through Circle Gateway and x402 with EIP-3009 authorization. The hacky bit: ancestor debit. A grandchild's $1 purchase debits $1 at every node up to the root, so headroom is always the tightest bottleneck across the whole path. We validated with 1,200 adversarial strategies across 45,360 draws — zero got past a bound. A hostile drill gave an LLM agent the daemon and told it to spend freely against a $0.02 mandate; it reached $0.007 before concentration stopped it.
