Our main question is whether Cordon can reduce the total cost of completing a task while delivering an equally useful result. We will measure task completion, total spending, repeated or unnecessary purchases, completion time, and the number of times the owner needs to intervene. Total cost will include payment fees, gas, and any Cordon service fee.

For deterministic tasks, such as retrieving a fixed dataset or performing a calculation, we will check whether the final outputs match exactly. For research and synthesis tasks, we will evaluate accuracy, completeness, source quality, and freshness against the same checklist. We will use fixed data or aligned timestamps where needed to make comparisons fair.

We will also test difficult situations, including repeated failures, expensive services, and several agents drawing from one budget. A run that spends less because it stops early will count as incomplete, not as an efficiency improvement.

These are planned evaluations. We will make this testing result as a path for cordon continuitity towards our end goal to help  helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Cordon is four layers where authority only flows downward — from the owner to the contract, never up from the agent.

Three Solidity contracts on Arc testnet: MandateRegistry manages the agent tree and enforces narrowing, TreeVault holds funds and performs ancestor debit (every draw charges every node up to the root), and ConductRecord publishes refusals to ERC-8004's reputation registry. No proxy, no admin key, no upgrade path.

The daemon (Node 23.6+, TypeScript, viem 2) is the only component that holds a private key. Agents call cordon_fetch(url) — the daemon reads the seller's x402 challenge, extracts price and payee from it (never from the agent), and asks the vault. There is no cordon_transfer or cordon_pay tool, and a test asserts each stays unregistered. An agent that can't express "send money to X" can't be talked into it.

Arc testnet was essential — USDC as both gas and payment token means operators hold one asset, and sub-second finality makes per-purchase on-chain enforcement affordable. Privy powers the console wallet gate with embedded wallets via createOnLogin, so owners without a browser wallet can still sign mandates. Settlement runs through Circle Gateway and x402 with EIP-3009 authorization.

The hacky bit: ancestor debit. A grandchild's $1 purchase debits $1 at every node up to the root, so headroom is always the tightest bottleneck across the whole path. We validated with 1,200 adversarial strategies across 45,360 draws — zero got past a bound. A hostile drill gave an LLM agent the daemon and told it to spend freely against a $0.02 mandate; it reached $0.007 before concentration stopped it.

projects.title: ZeroKeyMate
projects.description: An iPhone companion that proves your age privately and pays on Arc.
projects.project_description: ZeroKey Mate turns an iPhone into a companion that helps you act while keeping identity details private. Ask Mate for a beer. The on-device model proposes the supported order, while application code controls identity verification and payment. The phone authenticates a physical Japanese My Number card and creates an order-bound zero-knowledge proof that the cardholder is at least twenty. The shop receives the proof, not the card certificate, signature, name, address or date of birth. A deployed Age Gate contract verifies the proof before checkout proceeds. After the user approves this exact payment, a Privy embedded wallet signs a 0.10 test-USDC authorization and the shop settles through x402 on Arc Testnet. A physical-card purchase completed on September 13, with 12.0 seconds of local age-proof processing shown on the iPhone and a confirmed public Arc transaction. Further test payments completed, and the app links to their real explorer receipts. A DockKit stand adds the physical companion experience. The recorded demo combines actual device takes. This is an experimental testnet build: no real money or physical delivery. Payment approval remains explicit, and the supported purchase is one configured product and store. World ID authentication, smartphone My Number card support and unattended spending permissions are not integrated.
projects.how_its_made: The native iOS app uses SwiftUI, Apple Foundation Models, on-device Speech, AVFoundation, DockKit and CoreNFC. The local model produces a structured purchase proposal; deterministic code checks the item, merchant, network and amount. Card fields, proof witnesses and signing interfaces are never exposed to the model. Camera capture stops before NFC begins. The physical My Number card supplies a government-signed JPKI credential and signs a challenge bound to the order and nonce. Our Noir circuit checks the trusted root, RSA signatures, certificate validity, age of at least twenty and order expiry. ProveKit from World Foundation generates the proof on the iPhone, using a pinned experimental Groth16 backend and native Rust bridge. Identity evidence stays on the device; the shop receives the proof and public order inputs. This is not World ID authentication. Cloudflare Workers, D1 and a Durable Object run the store, preserve order state and serialize sponsored settlements. The Worker verifies the proof with the deployed Arc Age Gate contract through two independent RPC providers before returning x402 payment requirements. Privy supplies the embedded buyer wallet and signs the exact EIP-712 USDC authorization after user approval. The merchant sponsors gas. Signed transactions are persisted before broadcast, and receipt checks bind success to the actual transfer and authorization. A real-card certificate exposed a mandatory policy extension missing from our early fixture. We corrected both parser and circuit, regenerated matching proof artifacts and verifier, and completed the physical purchase. We also separated camera shutdown from DockKit motor commands to unblock NFC. Age verification is an eth_call enforced by the Worker, separate from the token transfer. The setup is single-party, certificate revocation is not checked, and the app still relies on network services for wallet login, store access and settlement. Source, reused public components, AI assistance and testnet evidence are documented in the repository.

projects.title: Agent-grid
projects.description: Agent grid is a coordination engine for agentic jobs, where agents behave like keepers
projects.project_description:
Built atop the teachings of KeeperDAO, we propose an agent platform where agents coordinate rather than compete in a zero-sum game
The full build suggests a flow where there are three main actors, a worker, a job poster, and liquidity providers.
On the proposed build, users can deposit liquidity, agents can bond to apply for jobs and earn reputation, and job posters make jobs for their protocols/verifiable off chain jobs depending on their needs. Once an agent is bonded, they'd be able to apply for jobs which ops cost < agent bond, this way the agent is allowed to borrow funds from the LP's against their collateral for the job cost, from where it diverges to two paths: NOTE: lending and the severity-graded arbiter are designed/built-dark, not shipped today — drawWorkingCapital always reverts; v1 reject() is a fixed 90/5/2.5/2.5 split. in the happy path, the agent completes the job, the LP's are repaid + a small tax, job poster validates and got what they wanted, and agent is free to unbond without slash In the unhappy path, the agent hallucinates, makes half the job, job poster is unsatisfied, calls reject(), arbiter comes to check, determines agent barely did half the job, rules the ops cost penalty on agent, agent hypothetical bond is $50 and loan was $25, slashed for the loan plus a graded fee — an honest failure costs a fraction of malice. Of course the plan outlined above is just two paths, there are at least 5 other rulings including mutual cancel, so we try to stay true to the keeper network in neutrality while also accommodating for the fact we have much more accessibility to on chain than what was the norm back then, which is why we built the matching engine/coordination engine/Job router as we like to call it, all on chain, no off chain matching, this makes it a first come first serve, reputation plays a role, direct hires too, but it remains that, early bird gets the worm.
projects.how_its_made: The smart contracts' early build relies purely on OpenZeppelin, with lending built but dark, there is no need for external dependencies or an oracle anywhere, slashing is the designed liquidation — bond = collateral. Meanwhile on the agent side, agents interact with tools that wrap over our protocol neatly, built on top of The Graph. we verify jobs purely based on-chain transactions, for now its only on the same chain where the protocol is hosted, however since its all evm, and agents are not bound by keeper mechanics, jobs can presumably be cross chain from the get go, give the correctly crafted spec/job description. We have a thorough test suite, invariants are fuzz tested using foundry enforcing I1-I9, only one token, USDC, and a vault for it, our original piece is the MCP server, any MCP client (Cursor, Claude Code) connects to our protocol, in the provided ONBOARDING.md anyone can try out our template job to fix a stale oracle, either as job poster or as worker. note: No price oracle anywhere in the value path, the oracle in the keeper job is the target , not a dependency. Reputation also comes into play often : deterministic first claim window: tier ≥ 3 gets (+10m), everyone else +20m, direct hires skip windows "early bird gets the worm" but with earned priority but basically NEUTRAL is zero weight, a mutual cancel buys neither party reputation, wash jobs are economically pointless (anti-wash by one line of econ design).

projects.title: Anora
projects.description: Anora tokenizes claims backed by verified warehouse receipts into private, permissioned tranches.
projects.project_description: Anora turns warehouse receipts into permissioned, investable credit. Commodity owners can raise working capital without selling inventory early or exposing private commercial records. Financing conditions are verified with zero-knowledge proofs, then the claim is issued as an ATS note with risk-based tranches. Eligible institutions can subscribe, trade positions through a compliance-gated secondary market, receive distributions, and follow the facility through repayment and collateral release. The prototype uses Indonesia’s Warehouse Receipt System (SRG) as its initial use case.
projects.how_its_made: Anora uses React and Vite for role-based Borrower, Capital Provider, and Compliance workspaces, with a Bun and Hono API coordinating the facility lifecycle. Noir generates zero-knowledge eligibility proofs, which are verified on Hedera testnet. Financing claims are issued as permissioned Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio notes with tranche-specific caps and transfer rules. Privy supports account and organizational authorization, while World ID contributes identity and uniqueness verification. The system also demonstrates allowlisted transfers, freezes, pauses, custom fees, secondary-market settlement, distributions, repayment, and redemption.

projects.title: Neltrix
projects.description: Onchain chart pattern analysis built from Uniswap swap data, sold per call via x402 on Hedera
projects.project_description: Neltrix is a market data and pattern intelligence layer built entirely from onchain DEX activity, with no centralised price feed anywhere in the stack. Every trade on a DEX is public, but there is no easy way to ask "give me hourly candles with support levels for this pool." You would have to replay huge numbers of swap events, deal with Uniswap V4 using a completely different schema from V3, and discover for yourself that some pools report negative TVL and that a meaningful share of published candles carry broken wicks. Neltrix does that work for you. It builds OHLCV candles for Uniswap V4, Uniswap V3 and SushiSwap pools from data indexed by The Graph. It then runs a rules-based pattern engine over them: candlestick patterns (engulfing, harami, hammer, shooting star, morning and evening star), chart patterns (double top and bottom, head and shoulders, triangles and wedges) and harmonic patterns (Gartley, Bat, Butterfly, Crab). It also clusters swing highs and lows into support and resistance levels and rolls everything up into a bullish, bearish or neutral verdict with a plain English summary. Onchain data is messy, so the pipeline detects and repairs problems like pool creation artifacts, single bad prints, negative TVL and wash-traded pools, and reports every repair in the response instead of hiding it. Data quality is a signal in itself: on the same pair and week, the thinner ETH/USDC 0.01% pool needed 7 wick repairs while the 0.05% pool needed none, which points to sandwiching. Browsing pools and charts in the web app is free. The full analysis endpoint is priced at 0.1 HBAR per request using x402 on Hedera, so an AI agent with no account, API key or subscription can discover the price from a 402 response, pay for one call and get the result. We included an autonomous agent that does exactly that. Neltrix does not trade or hold positions. The verdict has not been backtested, so its confidence measures how strongly the rules agree, not the chance of being right. The most reliable outputs are the price history, the levels and the data quality findings.
projects.how_its_made: The backend is Python with FastAPI, httpx and Pydantic. The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and Motion, and the candlestick chart is custom SVG. The payment gateway and the buyer agent are Node.js using the x402 SDKs (@x402/core, @x402/express, @x402/hedera) and the Hiero Ledger SDK. The Graph: Uniswap V3 and SushiSwap are both published by Messari on the dex-amm Standardized Subgraph schema, so we send one query string to both through The Graph's decentralized network gateway. Adding another dex-amm protocol only takes one line in a registry. The catch was that the deployments are on different schema versions (v4.0.1 vs v1.3.2), so the shared query can only use fields that exist on both. Uniswap V4 has no Messari deployment, so we wrote a separate adapter of about 250 lines for its native subgraph that produces the same internal shape. A single data source interface hides both schemas from the rest of the app. Uniswap: V4 is our main pool source. Its subgraph publishes real hourly and daily OHLC, so a full year of candles takes one query, and 4h candles are rolled up from hourly ones. Messari's schema has no OHLC, so for those protocols we rebuild candles by replaying raw swap events, capped at 10,000 swaps per request to keep things interactive. The API response always says which of the two paths was used. Pattern engine: everything is deterministic geometry, not machine learning. We find swing points, then match candlestick, chart and harmonic patterns (harmonics use Fibonacci ratio ranges). Raw matches are filtered hard: each category has a confidence floor, candlestick patterns only count if they close near a support or resistance level, and overlapping matches are reduced to the strongest one. In the verdict, repeated patterns with the same name are damped by 1/sqrt(n), because nine Bearish Haramis in one choppy week describe the same chop rather than nine separate signals. More recent patterns are weighted higher. Data cleaning: we drop candles with non-positive prices, zero volume or extreme high/low ratios, clamp bad wicks to a rolling median while keeping the candle body, rank pools by volume instead of TVL (the top V4 USDC/USDT pool reported -$24.7M TVL), and use a major token allowlist to filter out wash-traded pools. Failing indexers are retried with backoff and surface as a 502. Hedera: POST /api/analyse is the only paid route. An Express paywall sidecar returns a 402 with PAYMENT-REQUIRED (exact scheme, hedera:testnet, 10,000,000 tinybars), verifies the agent's partially signed HBAR transfer with the Blocky402 facilitator, forwards the request to FastAPI, then settles on chain and returns a PAYMENT-RESPONSE receipt. The facilitator pays network fees, so the payer's balance moves by exactly the price. Two things cost us real debugging time: x402 v2 uses unprefixed headers (not X-PAYMENT-*), and the client's default spend controls reject native HBAR. Rather than turning the controls off, the agent allows HBAR explicitly with a 0.5 HBAR per-call limit, so it refuses an overpriced 402 before it signs anything. We confirmed three settled payments on Hedera testnet through the mirror node, separately from our own code.

projects.title: Finch, Token Tracker
projects.description: Discover Robinhood tokens which landed in your wallet randomly
projects.project_description:
Finch snitches on where your tokens really came from. On Robinhood Chain, wallets receive tokenized stocks — NVDA, COST, GLD — they never bought, with no obvious cause. Here's why: someone launches a memecoin on Pons, it graduates to a Uniswap V4 pool paired against a stock, and the
creator's fee cut — paid in that stock — gets redirected through a holder-fee distributor to holders. A wallet just sees "+0.09 NVDA from 0xe25e…"; no block explorer says which memecoin that came from, or why that wallet. Finch is a Telegram bot (@FinchRH_bot) that reconstructs the route: it finds the transfer, resolves the payer on-chain (cross-checked against the official PonsHolderFeeManager registry, never inferred from a getter alone), and confirms
the creator-fee path from the Pons launch through its Uniswap V4 pool to the payout. Ask it "why did I get NVDA?" and it answers in plain language — with the technical trace available as a drill-down, and every response honestly labeled
confidence: "signal only - not a recommendation". It also surfaces Pons's own activity directly — recent launches and graduations to a live Uniswap V4 pool. The same backend is callable three ways: the Telegram bot, an HTTP API wrapped as a metered Bazantic x402 gateway, and an MCP server for Claude/Cursor — Finch is a peer other agents call, not a gatekeeper.
projects.how_its_made:
Finch is a Telegram bot backed by a Substreams pipeline indexing Pons launchpad activity on Robinhood Chain (EVM 4663). Stack: a parameterized Rust Substreams module (published finch-substreams@v0.1.1) → substreams sink postgres → Aiven
Postgres → a Node/TypeScript bot (grammy) with an HTTP API, MCP server, and Bazantic x402/MPP gateway, all deployed as systemd services on an AWS box behind Caddy. Partner tech: The Graph is load-bearing twice over — StreamingFast's Robinhood endpoint (via a thegraph.market Substreams token) is the only data source Finch has, and a separate call to The Graph's canonical ENS subgraph resolves
addresses to .eth names. Bazantic wraps the same HTTP API as a metered x402 gateway and hosts a published Recipe (FINCH_GRAPH_ENS) chaining both of Finch's own tools as one LLM-orchestrated call. Hacky/notable bits, honestly: we pivoted off subgraphs entirely mid-hackathon after The Graph's dev-rel confirmed a Goldsky-hosted subgraph doesn't satisfy the track — the whole query layer got rewritten from GraphQL to raw SQL against
the Substreams sink. The 1 GB free-tier Postgres meant the sink can't hold full chain history, so an hourly prune job truncates pool-swap tables and keeps only a rolling transfer window. Uniswap V4's singleton PoolManager has no
per-pool address to watch, so the Substreams module decodes Initialize events directly and filters by Pons's Meme Hook address to find only the relevant pools. And the Bazantic Recipe's LLM kept returning its answer wrapped in a
different ad-hoc JSON shape almost every run — fixed by parsing defensively by field role (a list of known key-name aliases) instead of chasing exact key names each time it drifted.

  confidence: "signal only - not a recommendation". It also surfaces Pons's own activity directly — recent launches and graduations to a live Uniswap V4 pool.

  The same backend is callable three ways: the Telegram bot, an HTTP API wrapped as a metered Bazantic x402 gateway, and an MCP server for Claude/Cursor — Finch is a peer other agents call, not a gatekeeper.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Finch is a Telegram bot backed by a Substreams pipeline indexing Pons launchpad activity on Robinhood Chain (EVM 4663). Stack: a parameterized Rust Substreams module (published finch-substreams@v0.1.1) → substreams sink postgres → Aiven
  Postgres → a Node/TypeScript bot (grammy) with an HTTP API, MCP server, and Bazantic x402/MPP gateway, all deployed as systemd services on an AWS box behind Caddy.

  Partner tech: The Graph is load-bearing twice over — StreamingFast's Robinhood endpoint (via a thegraph.market Substreams token) is the only data source Finch has, and a separate call to The Graph's canonical ENS subgraph resolves
  addresses to .eth names. Bazantic wraps the same HTTP API as a metered x402 gateway and hosts a published Recipe (FINCH_GRAPH_ENS) chaining both of Finch's own tools as one LLM-orchestrated call.

  Hacky/notable bits, honestly: we pivoted off subgraphs entirely mid-hackathon after The Graph's dev-rel confirmed a Goldsky-hosted subgraph doesn't satisfy the track — the whole query layer got rewritten from GraphQL to raw SQL against
  the Substreams sink. The 1 GB free-tier Postgres meant the sink can't hold full chain history, so an hourly prune job truncates pool-swap tables and keeps only a rolling transfer window. Uniswap V4's singleton PoolManager has no
  per-pool address to watch, so the Substreams module decodes Initialize events directly and filters by Pons's Meme Hook address to find only the relevant pools. And the Bazantic Recipe's LLM kept returning its answer wrapped in a
  different ad-hoc JSON shape almost every run — fixed by parsing defensively by field role (a list of known key-name aliases) instead of chasing exact key names each time it drifted.

projects.title: Keel
projects.description: On-chain Avellaneda-Stoikov pricing A SwapVM opcode on Aqua as a v4 dynamic-fee hook, via a subgraph
projects.project_description: Keel is the first on-chain market making position that prices its own inventory risk. Every market maker's real enemy is inventory, not spread. If you quote symmetrically around mid in a trending market, you are ground into holding more and more of the depreciating asset: you earn spread on every fill and still lose money on the position. Professional desks have solved this since 2008 with a reservation price (Avellaneda and Stoikov): as your inventory drifts away from target, you skew your quotes away from mid, so the trade that would hand you even more of what you already hold gets priced worse, and the trade that brings you back gets priced better. No on-chain venue has ever implemented this, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight. On a pool AMM the inventory belongs to the pool, not to any individual maker, so there is no "your position" for a reservation price formula to skew around. The usual workaround is a keeper bot that rebalances after the fact, which reacts late and pays gas to react. Aqua from 1inch is the first venue where this becomes possible. Tokens never leave the maker's own wallet, and aqua.safeBalances(maker, app, strategyHash, tokenIn, tokenOut) exposes a maker's real, live wallet inventory at quote time. That is a number no pool AMM design can offer. Keel is a custom SwapVM instruction that reads it, computes a reservation price skewed in proportion to how far the position leans, and quotes around that instead of raw mid. There is no keeper, no rebalancing transaction and no delay, because the defence is inside the pricing curve itself. Measured against an identical 120 fill adversarial flow, a stock constant product position ends at 0.2110 PnL down while Keel ends at 0.0620 down, an improvement of 0.1490. Both positions take on exactly the same inventory drift (token0 grows 84.39% for both); the entire difference is what each fill cost the taker. It is live on Base Sepolia against real Circle USDC and WETH, not mock tokens, with a shipped position that has taken ten exposed side fills and one covered side fill. The same pricing kernel also runs as a Uniswap v4 dynamic fee hook, so one set of maths serves two venues.
projects.how_its_made: The kernel. AvellanedaStoikov.sol is pure WAD fixed point maths: reservation price, half spread, soft bound penalty, and the balance re centring that applies all three. The full model's spread term needs a live order book arrival rate, which this build does not have, so that one term is replaced by a maker declared base spread. The inventory skew mechanism, which is the actually novel part, is implemented in full. Dropping the log and exp requirement meant plain WAD arithmetic was enough and no big number library was needed. The 1inch integration is the mechanism, not a wrapper. Keel is opcode 0x92, a reserved but unallocated slot in SwapVM's balance tuning family. KeelRouter inherits the real, unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and overrides _runOpcode, which upstream declares internal virtual for exactly this purpose: it intercepts 0x92 and delegates every other opcode to super._runOpcode, the stock dispatcher. A test proves that append only property against the real router. The official swap-vm and aqua repositories are cloned verbatim and never patched. Reading the real source changed the design twice. There is no shared price register in SwapVM: Context.SwapRegisters is only {balanceIn, balanceOut, amountIn, amountOut}, and stock instructions "adjust price" by mutating balances in place before a curve instruction consumes them. An early sketch split reservation price, spread and soft bound across three sequential opcodes writing to a shared register; with no such register, the second and third would have read back already mutated balances instead of live inventory. All three are now composed into one atomic transform in a single instruction. Separately, no accessor for live inventory was needed at all, because SwapVM already populates the context from AQUA.safeBalances() before any opcode runs. The bug worth mentioning. The instruction originally keyed its decimal scaling, its inventory sign and its exposed side test to the swap's in and out sides, which is only correct in the A to B direction. Covered side fills reverted at any realistic size. The fix keys all three to tokenA and tokenB instead, which required adding tokenA to the shipped program and therefore a full redeploy, since KeelRouter inlines the instruction as an internal library. The first covered side fill this project ever landed came from that router: 0.0001 WETH in for 3.372388 USDC out. The Graph. A subgraph decodes Aqua's Shipped payload, locates the InventorySkew opcode inside it, and re runs the same Avellaneda Stoikov formula ported to AssemblyScript, so a solver querying it gets the same number a live quote() would return. This answers a real routability problem: SwapVM liquidity is order based and distributed, so there is no single reserve to read. Pushed and Pulled are handled alongside Swapped, because without them the indexed values were deltas since ship rather than balances and could read negative. All router deployments stay in the manifest so historical fills are never orphaned. The official Subgraph MCP endpoint is wired to the same schema, so an agent can ask for a position's live reservation price in natural language. Verified live: deployment QmRFBHuUtSAgDkrLhCe5Ae2cn1Nwp2sqKfeMVvBD5fvZog, no indexing errors, 21 positions and 88 fills indexed. Uniswap v4. KeelSkewHook reuses halfSpreadWad and softBoundPenaltyBps through the dynamic fee override returned from beforeSwap, found by reading LPFeeLibrary directly. It deliberately does not reuse the curve re centring functions: those are specific to SwapVM's balance pair representation, and v4's concentrated liquidity has no equivalent without reimplementing v4's own swap math. That seam is stated rather than hidden. Testing and tooling. 38 Foundry tests and 5 SDK tests pass. The most important is a 2000 run fuzz test asserting that quote() and swap() agree across the whole inventory range, since a maker who quotes one number and settles another is worse than useless. A known limit is tested rather than left as a surprise: re centring can, for a misconfigured strategy, produce a virtual balance exceeding real holdings, and the test asserts it reverts safely instead of mispaying. packages/strategy-sdk builds ship and dock calldata in TypeScript and is byte verified against fixtures generated by the Solidity itself. The Next.js console lets a maker ship a real position from the browser, showing the live quote curve and the literal SwapVM bytecode updating together as parameters change. Special note: The checked in on chain results were decoded from the router's own fill events rather than copied from Foundry's broadcast log. That log prints the simulation pass, whose amounts differ slightly from what actually settled; summing the decoded events reproduces aqua.safeBalances() exactly, which is what makes the file trustworthy during a demo when an RPC may be unreachable.

projects.title: Co-Eco-Graph
projects.description: Explore smart contract ecosystems through interactive graphs and AI-powered storytelling.
projects.project_description: Co-Eco-Graph is an interactive Web3 exploration tool that reveals how smart contracts are used across the decentralized indexing ecosystem. Instead of examining a contract through isolated blockchain explorers or manually searching for related data, users can enter a contract address and discover the subgraphs that index it across The Graph Network. The application transforms this information into a visual graph connecting the contract with its subgraphs, data sources, event handlers, entities, and GraphQL fields. This makes it easier to understand what data is being indexed, how different subgraphs represent the same contract, and what information is available for further analysis. The project is designed to bridge the gap between raw blockchain indexing infrastructure and human understanding. It combines decentralized data discovery, structured schema analysis, interactive visualization, and AI-powered storytelling in a single lightweight application.
projects.how_its_made: Co-Eco-Graph is built with vanilla TypeScript, Vite, and SVG to create an interactive, framework-free graph visualization of smart contract ecosystems. The frontend communicates with a Vercel serverless API that queries The Graph Network to discover subgraphs indexing a contract, retrieves their manifests and GraphQL schemas from IPFS, and extracts entities, fields, data sources, and event handlers. The collected data is combined into a compact dataset and sent to Pollinations through its OpenAI-compatible API for AI-powered interpretation and fantasy-style image generation. The result is a visual, explorable map of how contracts are used across Web3, combining decentralized indexing, IPFS metadata, serverless processing, and AI storytelling in one lightweight application.

projects.title: ZKward
projects.description: AI-managed USDC vault: 7 agents hedge privately with post-quantum ZK and fund their own inference
projects.project_description: A vault that thinks for itself. Seven AI agents read prediction markets, hedge on perps, and pay their own inference bills via x402 on Hedera. Live on Sui mainnet with real money since June. Every hedge is sealed in post-quantum ZK, so nobody sees your position. No trusted setup.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js/Vercel, Solidity on Hedera, Python STARK prover, HCS as a free audit log. Mirror Node replaced rate-limited Hashio RPC with pre-indexed reads. Hackiest bit: our perp venue returns a valid orderHash for orders it silently drops, so we verify fills by delta. We are getting crowdsourced data for trading from prediction markets.

projects.title: Homeward
projects.description: A safety app for people living with dementia/Alzheimer's, and for lost children.
projects.project_description: A safety app for people living with dementia/Alzheimer's, and for lost children: when a stranger finds someone who appears lost or disoriented, the app matches a captured face against a caregiver-enrolled database and  automatically alerts next-of-kin — without ever revealing the person's identity to the stranger who found them.
projects.how_its_made:
Homeward is built using Nextjs for the Front End.  While homeward is a web based this can be easily adapted as a mobile application in the future.
Supabase is used as the database.  Where personal details and encrypted biometric facial details are stored. World Id Selfie check is used to gate or protect the App from abuse.  Users who find an individual who is lost or wondering will have to use selfie check to prove that they are human. this ensures that the tool isn't abused and use as a surveillance too. Chainlinks CRE is used to ensure privacy.
The operator of the supabase database doesn't have access to the biometric data its encrypted.   All facial matching is done in a TEE  Trusted Execution Environment .
Once a match is found the finder is alerted that a match is found.  No details about the lost indvidual is disclosed.  The system sends an email alert to the next of kind.  With the details of where the individual was found and a picture showing what image was used to confirm the match.

projects.title: Ground State
projects.description: Ethereum as a place: every address a spot, contracts as buildings, ground you dig for with CREATE2
projects.project_description: Ground State is a black-and-white world you walk through in the browser, with other people, where the map is the Ethereum address space itself. An address is forty hex digits; each digit picks one cell of a 4×4 grid, forty times over, so every address has exactly one place and neighbours share a prefix. Nothing about the map was designed: it falls out of how Ethereum names things. Everything standing in the world is real and follows the chain's own rules. A contract stands as a building: size from the length of its code, shape from the code's hash, darkness from its balance. A wallet lies as a plate with a post for every token it holds, the post as tall as that holding's share of the total supply, the name and amount cut into it. The current block crosses the sky in real time, every transaction a ribbon from sender to receiver; reverted ones shake and are drawn back. No scenery, no mock data, and no content we author. What the chain says is what stands, and what happens. Empty ground cannot be bought. It is dug for. A plot is a contract deployed with CREATE2, so its address, and therefore its place, is fixed by a salt before the contract exists. Digging searches salts on every core of your machine; every attempt is a place, the closest is kept, and there is no threshold: stop whenever you like, and one transaction on Sepolia makes the closest place found your contract, forever. It rises out of the ground as a blueprint of the building it will be. A plot is a proxy its owner can act on: write into it (the words stand out of the wall as the drawing becomes a building), name it under groundstate.eth via ENSv2, point it at any contract they deployed so that code runs at this very address, seal the code for good, or hand the plot on. A subgraph on The Graph Network indexes every plot; The Graph's Token API shows which wallets hold it. Other people are here as figures: their digging is seen, their claims stand up on every screen within seconds, and all see a place seen by one. World ID's Selfie Check says who here is a person: a person's word about a place is kept at once, a stranger's when five agree. It weighs; it does not gate. The world is thirteen digits deep today, a metre being one cell of the thirteenth digit. A depth switch is next: the same chain at any level, and every level down makes standing this close sixteen times the work, so ground dug beside something today is worth more with every level. This is an early version: the world stands, the game around it is not written yet, and writing it is the first work after the hackathon. Live at gs.bwtoken.io, open source under MIT.
projects.how_its_made: Everything is written during the event: one contributor, 288 commits, 132 tests. Disclosed per the rules: the concept and plan predate it (they were the application), and the monochrome palette and mark are reused from bwtoken.io by the same author. The world is a WebGL2 engine of our own in TypeScript, no framework, no textures, no models, no asset pipeline. Geometry is generated from what an account is. Terrain is the address tree hashed: six depths of the tree are the octaves; the height of a cell is the keccak of its address prefix so that anyone can compute the hill under an address. There is no colour, so everything is said with light: one low sun, filmic tone mapping instead of clipping, ordered dithering only against banding. Buildings stand on foundations rather than flattening the ground. The onboarding tour drives the world through a Driver interface (look, walk, type, press) so the same code plays itself. Digging is CREATE2 salt mining in an AssemblyScript WebAssembly module, on every core via workers, about seven million attempts a second per thread. The first twenty bytes of the salt must be the claimant's address, which the factory checks: a salt seen in the mempool is worthless to anyone else, and the check costs nothing because it is one hash per attempt rather than two. Finds are kept in the browser, filed by chain, factory and owner. The Plot contract (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry) is an EIP-1967 proxy: owner and implementation in the EIP-1967 slots, note and seal in a namespaced slot, so any implementation is written like an ordinary contract; seal() fixes the code for good. Verified on Sourcify and Blockscout. Two earlier factories stand as relics. The Graph: two products composed. A subgraph over three generations of the factory, every plot a dynamic data source, indexing owner, every inscription, implementation, seal, name and salt; the mapping decodes the address into 80-bit x/y coordinates and the metre cell and 256-metre tile, so "everything near here" is one query. Published to The Graph Network and read through the gateway. The Token API (Pinax) supplies what a mainnet wallet holds: every fungible token with its supply. Our live server (Node, ws) is the one asker for everybody, keeps the keys out of the browser, and streams holdings as ndjson, a line per token as each supply arrives, so a wallet's posts rise one by one. It pushes the whole world to every page over the socket on joining, then only what changed; Blockscout and the factory's logs are fallbacks. Subgraph Studio throttled the whole subgraph with 429s on day eight, which is why there is one asker and why the subgraph was published. ENSv2 on Sepolia, on its own terms. groundstate.eth is registered on the ENSv2 beta and points its subregistry at a PermissionedRegistry of ours, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. One contract, Names, holds the only ROLE_REGISTRAR and ROLE_UNREGISTER on it and is also the ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver for the whole subtree: addr is the plot, text(description) is what the owner wrote, text(url) opens the world there. Labels are registered with a role bitmap of zero, so a name's token cannot leave its place; about three hundred labels are reserved. The world resolves names through UniversalResolverV2 and travels by them. All ENS and chain calls are built by hand: a selector and a word, less code than a library. World ID Selfie Check, as a weight, not a gate. IDKit runs in a vanilla TypeScript page (no React); the RP signature is made on the live server with @worldcoin/idkit-server and the proof is verified against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify. The server keeps a token hash and its expiry for the credential's ninety days and nothing about anybody. A person stands in grey, a stranger in white; a person's word about a revealed place is kept at once, a stranger's counts a fifth. The first live check passed in production on 13 September. Our notes on the docs and the Developer Portal are in docs/world-id-feedback.md. Hacky and proud of it: the runes cut into posts and walls are a small stroke alphabet of our own, and the key is deliberately not documented; the walker turns into a spinning auger while digging, with ground chips whose rate is the hash rate; and the whole page turns over, black or white, world included.

A depth switch is next: the same chain at any level, and every level down makes standing this close sixteen times the work, so ground dug beside something today is worth more with every level. This is an early version: the world stands, the game around it is not written yet, and writing it is the first work after the hackathon. Live at gs.bwtoken.io, open source under MIT.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Everything is written during the event: one contributor, 288 commits, 132 tests. Disclosed per the rules: the concept and plan predate it (they were the application), and the monochrome palette and mark are reused from bwtoken.io by the same author.

The world is a WebGL2 engine of our own in TypeScript, no framework, no textures, no models, no asset pipeline. Geometry is generated from what an account is. Terrain is the address tree hashed: six depths of the tree are the octaves; the height of a cell is the keccak of its address prefix so that anyone can compute the hill under an address. There is no colour, so everything is said with light: one low sun, filmic tone mapping instead of clipping, ordered dithering only against banding. Buildings stand on foundations rather than flattening the ground. The onboarding tour drives the world through a Driver interface (look, walk, type, press) so the same code plays itself.

Digging is CREATE2 salt mining in an AssemblyScript WebAssembly module, on every core via workers, about seven million attempts a second per thread. The first twenty bytes of the salt must be the claimant's address, which the factory checks: a salt seen in the mempool is worthless to anyone else, and the check costs nothing because it is one hash per attempt rather than two. Finds are kept in the browser, filed by chain, factory and owner. The Plot contract (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry) is an EIP-1967 proxy: owner and implementation in the EIP-1967 slots, note and seal in a namespaced slot, so any implementation is written like an ordinary contract; seal() fixes the code for good. Verified on Sourcify and Blockscout. Two earlier factories stand as relics.

The Graph: two products composed. A subgraph over three generations of the factory, every plot a dynamic data source, indexing owner, every inscription, implementation, seal, name and salt; the mapping decodes the address into 80-bit x/y coordinates and the metre cell and 256-metre tile, so "everything near here" is one query. Published to The Graph Network and read through the gateway. The Token API (Pinax) supplies what a mainnet wallet holds: every fungible token with its supply. Our live server (Node, ws) is the one asker for everybody, keeps the keys out of the browser, and streams holdings as ndjson, a line per token as each supply arrives, so a wallet's posts rise one by one. It pushes the whole world to every page over the socket on joining, then only what changed; Blockscout and the factory's logs are fallbacks. Subgraph Studio throttled the whole subgraph with 429s on day eight, which is why there is one asker and why the subgraph was published.

ENSv2 on Sepolia, on its own terms. groundstate.eth is registered on the ENSv2 beta and points its subregistry at a PermissionedRegistry of ours, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. One contract, Names, holds the only ROLE_REGISTRAR and ROLE_UNREGISTER on it and is also the ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver for the whole subtree: addr is the plot, text(description) is what the owner wrote, text(url) opens the world there. Labels are registered with a role bitmap of zero, so a name's token cannot leave its place; about three hundred labels are reserved. The world resolves names through UniversalResolverV2 and travels by them. All ENS and chain calls are built by hand: a selector and a word, less code than a library.

World ID Selfie Check, as a weight, not a gate. IDKit runs in a vanilla TypeScript page (no React); the RP signature is made on the live server with @worldcoin/idkit-server and the proof is verified against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify. The server keeps a token hash and its expiry for the credential's ninety days and nothing about anybody. A person stands in grey, a stranger in white; a person's word about a revealed place is kept at once, a stranger's counts a fifth. The first live check passed in production on 13 September. Our notes on the docs and the Developer Portal are in docs/world-id-feedback.md.

Hacky and proud of it: the runes cut into posts and walls are a small stroke alphabet of our own, and the key is deliberately not documented; the walker turns into a spinning auger while digging, with ground chips whose rate is the hash rate; and the whole page turns over, black or white, world included.

projects.title: Capsule
projects.description: Launch AI agents in a minutes as ENS names with onchain permissions, spending limits, and recall.
projects.project_description:
“We give too much authority, data, permissions and execution control to 3rd party platforms and AI Providers while using AI. This directly contradicts Ethereum’s core principles. We should start to take it back as much as we can. Capsule is a small step toward this vision.” TLDR; You can launch your AI Agents in 2-3 minutes bu using your ENSv2 domain and these Agenst are going to get their permissions(e.g. spending cap, prompt) on-chain. So all authority is yours. Capsule is a launchpad for AI agents. It provides a platform to launch AI Agents in 2-3 Minutes. The agent gets an ENS Domain, on-chain permissions, and off switch. The Capsule solves two core problems:
1 - First, platforms control the agent's identity, settings, permissions, and shutdown.
2 - Second, running your own agent is difficult for ordinary users. It requires wallets, secrets, servers, deployment, terminals, cloud setups, secret management, DevOps skills and monitoring. Capsule solves both problems. Its guided flow makes the agent easy to launch. The control solution comes from ENSv2. The agent's identity and permissions stay under the owner's ENS name. Capsule can help run the service, but ENSv2 keeps ownership and control with the user. Capsule makes the Agent Running process into a five-step, no-code flow. Connect a wallet with ENS v2 Domain, set the model and prompt, mint the Agent's ENSv2 name, and start the runner. That's all. In a few minutes you will have a working AI Agent with Ethereum wallet. Then you can communicate with it on Telegram(for now, proof of concept). Also the Capsule has analyst page to ask about your agents current analytics. We use The Graph in order to turn public activity into useful data. The subgraph combines events while indexing. It tracks heartbeats, transaction signers, recalls, and timing. The dashboard and analyst use this index to answer what happened to the agent. So, in order to use the application:
1 - Go to https://capsule-ens.vercel.app
2 - Register your ENSv2 Hackathon domain: https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/register
3 - Connect your ENSv2 Domain to Capsule https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/connect
4 - Create your telegram bot(@BotFather) and get your AI provider API KEY
5 - And five steps Launch: https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/launch In a 2-3 minutes your Agent will be ready on your telegram bot.
Thats all! Pitch: https://capsule-pitch-v2-ethglobal.berkingurcan.chatgpt.site
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, ENS v2 beta on Sepolia): The whole on chain side is one contract, CapsuleMinter.sol. A single mint() call registers the subname in the parent's subregistry, writes the ENSIP 25, 26 and 27 records (class, schema, agent-model, agent-runtime, agent-prompt, agent-endpoint[capsule], agent-endpoint[web]), sets addr to the agent key, grants the human owner text and addr admin roles on their own name, and grants the agent write access to exactly one key, agent-heartbeat. There is deliberately no halt() function. The kill switch is the owner calling authorizeTextRoles(dnsName, "agent-heartbeat", agent, false) straight on the ENS resolver. So if our backend vanishes, every owner still has a working off switch through ENS alone. The minter holds no parent name of its own. Any .eth name connects itself with connectParent, which stores the registry, resolver and DNS name once as a triple. That ordering is the security model. If mint() took registry, resolver and parent name per call, someone could pass a real parent's registry next to a resolver they control, pass every permission check against their own resolver, and register a label inside somebody else's name. Storing the triple once behind an admin check makes that combination impossible to even express. The contract also builds its own ERC 7930 interoperable address in the constructor from block.chainid and address(this), so the ENSIP 25 registry id is right on every chain with nothing hardcoded. No vendored ENS code, only the functions we call declared in a local interface file, so it builds in about two seconds. Runner (TypeScript, viem, Docker, OpenClaw) The agent process is handed one environment variable, its own ENS name, and works out everything else from the chain. It reads through UniversalResolverV2 rather than a fixed resolver address, because every ENS name gets its own PermissionedResolver deployed as a UUPS proxy through VerifiableFactory, so the address is not knowable in advance. It refuses to boot if addr on the name is not the key it holds. Two cadences, because the check and the record are different jobs. Every tick it does a free eth_call with the same modifier and the same revert as the real write, so a revoke is caught in seconds for zero gas. Every heartbeat interval it writes beat-<n> as a real transaction, which is the part an outside observer with nothing but the chain can see. Only EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles counts as a revoke, everything else is assumed transient so a flaky RPC does not kill an agent live on stage. And before halting it confirms against the role table instead of trusting the revert, because the resolver's onlyPartRoles modifier names the wrong resource on purpose. A third case had to be split out too: a broke agent and a revoked agent both stop writing, so from the chain they look identical. The runner reserves a few heartbeats worth of gas that the model can never spend, precisely so an agent can never spend itself into looking revoked. The prompt injection boundary This is the part I care most about. The supervisor holds the agent private key. The OpenClaw gateway child process does not. buildOpenClawEnv builds the child's environment from nothing rather than filtering the parent's, so a new secret is excluded by default instead of having to be remembered, and a smoke test scans the child env for anything shaped like a 32 byte key. The model can still spend, but only by asking: a loopback HTTP broker on 127.0.0.1 with a fresh bearer token per boot, and every request passes checkSpend first. The limits come off the chain from two text records, agent-spend-cap and agent-spend-allow, which the owner can write and the agent cannot, because the agent's grant is per key and covers the heartbeat alone. Set the cap to zero and within one tick the agent is alive, beating, answering, and unable to move a wei. Everything in that module fails closed, so anything unparseable or absent resolves to zero and zero means no. We used plain JSON over loopback instead of MCP here on purpose. MCP is the tidier long term seam, but implementing the handshake blind risked a capsule that boots clean, heartbeats fine, and silently has no wallet tool, which is the worst possible demo failure. The agent's persona file is composed, not copied. Three sections in a fixed order: identity facts the supervisor states, live status rewritten every tick, then the owner's prompt body last under a heading that names it. The order is the security property, because the prompt body is the only part an attacker can reach. The file is written to a temp path and renamed, because the tick loop rewrites it while the gateway is reading it, and a reader caught in a torn write is a language model being told who it is. Subgraph (The Graph) A capsule's truth is spread across two contracts that never emit the same event, so the index is a join: CapsuleMinted and ParentConnected from the minter, TextChanged, EACRolesChanged and AddrChanged from the resolver. There is no single resolver address to point a manifest at, so handleParentConnected spawns a data source template the moment a name connects, which is the same discovery the runner does at boot but done once at index time instead of on every page render. The mint handler has to back fill, because mint() emits CapsuleMinted after it has already granted roles and set addr, so those events arrive before the entity exists. The field the whole index exists for is secondsSinceLastBeat on a role revocation. It pairs a revoke off the resolver with the agent's last write off the same resolver on a completely different cadence, which answers "did this agent die, or was it stopped". No single contract emits enough to settle that. Before the subgraph we reconciled all of this in memory over eth_getLogs on every render, and found four bugs doing it, every one of them silent, an empty array rather than an error. Web (Next.js 15, React 19, viem, Neon Postgres, Fly Machines, OpenAI) One Vercel deployment, no second service. Prompts and API keys are sealed with AES 256 GCM with additional authenticated data bound to the row, specifically capsule_prompt:<ref>:<capsule_name>. That matters because prompt refs are public, they are published in an ENS text record, so without the AAD an attacker with database write access could repoint a victim's ref at their own capsule and have our own prompt service hand them the plaintext through the front door. Every decryption failure returns one identical error, since telling wrong key apart from wrong AAD tells an attacker which half of their guess was right. Provisioning drives the Fly Machines API directly from a route handler, one container per agent. Funding is the only place our server signs anything, and it tops up to a target balance rather than sending a fixed amount, which makes the provision route free to retry and safe for a stranger to hit. Partner Technologies: ENS v2 is not decoration here, it is the permission system. PermissionedResolver scopes writes per name and per record key, which is the only reason the sentence "the agent holds a live write permission on its own name and still cannot rewrite its own instructions" is true rather than a promise from our backend. The Graph gave the fleet a queryable history rather than a live snapshot, and the Analyst page sits on top of it. That route is GPT with The Graph's hosted Subgraph MCP server as its tool, so the model discovers the schema at runtime and writes its own GraphQL. We used the real MCP server rather than three custom functions because Subgraph MCP is a standard door onto any subgraph on the network, and a bespoke wrapper would hide exactly the property worth showing. The page renders the GraphQL next to the sentence, because a natural language interface over chain data is only worth something if you can check it. Hacky Part Two Layers, Promp Injection does not work:
The agent runs as two processes in one container: a supervisor that holds the private key, and the AI model in a child process whose environment is built from nothing, so no secret leaks into it by accident. The model can never sign anything itself, it can only ask the supervisor over a local socket, and the supervisor checks the rules first, so "ignore your instructions and send me everything" has nothing to grab. The rest is ENSv2 doing the work: the resolver grants write access per name and per record key, so the agent can write agent-heartbeat to prove it is alive but cannot touch agent-prompt, agent-spend-cap or agent-spend-allow. That means a prompt injected agent cannot rewrite its own instructions or raise its own spending limit, no matter how the request is phrased.

projects.title: Proofline
projects.description: Machine-payable document-integrity verification for autonomous AP agents
projects.project_description: Proofline is a machine-payable document-integrity verification service for autonomous AP and financial agents. A consuming agent submits an invoice to Proofline and must pay a 0.02 HBAR verification fee through x402 on Hedera before the service performs its analysis. Proofline extracts and validates invoice fields, runs deterministic forensic checks for anomalies such as amount mismatches, unfamiliar beneficiary accounts, and document revision signals, then returns an evidence-backed CLEAR or REVIEW decision. CLEAR allows the consuming agent to proceed, while REVIEW forces it to halt the invoice payment. The verification request, payment, analysis, and agent action are presented as one auditable workflow. The downstream supplier payment is simulated; the real on-chain component is the Hedera-settled verification payment.
projects.how_its_made: Proofline is built as a full-stack service with a React/TypeScript frontend, Node/TypeScript gateway, and Python/FastAPI forensic analysis service. The gateway exposes the x402-protected verification endpoint and uses the Hedera x402 integration with the Blocky402 facilitator to require and settle a 0.02 HBAR payment on Hedera testnet. A server-side reference AP agent acts as the consuming agent, signs the payment, calls the protected service, receives the verification result, and deterministically decides whether to proceed or halt. Document analysis uses PDF/OCR extraction, structured field normalization, and deterministic forensic rules, with evidence codes and policy scoring rather than an AI-generated fraud verdict. Verification state and results are persisted in SQLite, while raw documents and OCR text remain transient. The frontend streams the real workflow through SSE, including payment, analysis, decision, and agent-action stages.

projects.title: Flyte
projects.description: Perpetual futures exchange that lets traders trade concepts and ideas instead of traditional assets.
projects.project_description: Flyte is a perpetual futures exchange with a twist - instead of trading traditional crypto assets Flyte lets traders trade the aggregate attention that concepts, ideas, events, and even people have on the internet. Think about trading the concept of 'Humanoid Robots' instead of BTC; or 'GTA6' instead of ETH. Imagine trading the usage and attention of an actual meme instead of a token merely spun up in response to it. Flyte makes all of this possible. Through the use of Chainlink Runtime Environment Confidential Workflows we can essentially "Oraclise" anything that has a footprint across news, social media, or anywhere online. And through the use of 1Inch new Aqua liquidity primitive we can provide Liquidity Providers with much better capital efficiency.
projects.how_its_made: Flyte was built using the following technologies... Smart Contracts: Foundry on WSL for building and writing our smart contracts. I used openzep for our dummy Aave USDC ERC20, and the interfaces for use in the PerpApp contract itself. Then I've imported the Aqua and SwapVM contracts from 1Inch. Our PerpApp.sol is a minimalist perp contract, as scope had to stay a bit tighter in a one-week build. However, it's broadly GMX-aligned (just with the GMX-style pool layer removed and we're using Aqua and a Request-for-Quote model instead). Deployed to Arb One mainnet. I didn't get to squeeze it into the video, but you can mint "dummy aUSDC" on takeflyte.xyz and use it on the platform! It is a rebasing ERC20 (1% every 15 mins - DeFi Summer style), as I wanted to illustrate on the platform capital efficiency and how you're still earning yield due to self-custody'ing the tokens until we pull them for a trade via Aqua. Frontend: Next.js. This is deployed to Vercel and live at takeflyte.xyz. It's a fairly standard Next.js app, with each 'box' being it's own component. State is read directly from the the deployed Arb One contracts as I didn't have time to spin up subgraphs or Ponder.sh. The design is a bold, "neo-brutalist" one. Chainlink (CRE) Confidential Workflows: we're using CRE Confidential Workflows for our 'Oracle Layer'. CRE simulation was run locally on a 15 minute cadence for a couple of hours prior to the demo video being filmed, so we actually got some live data in our charts, etc. The workflow packages up our API keys (Firecrawl and OpenRouter) and our proprietary algorithm. Essentially what we're doing it calling Firecrawl's /search API endpoint and passing in search params for that market (so for our "Humanoid Robots" market we pass in 'Humanoid Robots', 'Unitree', 'Tesla Optimus', etc., and pull the headlines for those), we then take the quantity + sentiment (via our OpenRouter API key) and produce a single-figure 'attention score'; and that's the oracle price traders trade against. 1Inch Aqua: we are using Aqua for our liquidity layer. Obviously you forgo the atomicity of 'swap' style strategies as we do pull the counterliquidity during a trade, but it avoids the "liquidity sitting in a pool" problem. projects.project_description_markdown:
Flyte is a perpetual futures exchange with a twist - instead of trading traditional crypto assets Flyte lets traders trade the aggregate attention that concepts, ideas, events, and even people have on the internet.

Think about trading the concept of 'Humanoid Robots' instead of BTC; or 'GTA6' instead of ETH. Imagine trading the usage and attention of an actual meme instead of a token merely spun up in response to it. Flyte makes all of this possible.

Through the use of Chainlink Runtime Environment Confidential Workflows we can essentially "Oraclise" anything that has a footprint across news, social media, or anywhere online. And through the use of 1Inch new Aqua liquidity primitive we can provide Liquidity Providers with much better capital efficiency.

projects.title: Petri
projects.description: Darwinian evolution for AI agents: harnesses mutate, get tested, and only verified winners survive.
projects.project_description: Petri is a petri dish for AI agent harnesses. A harness is the code around a model: the prompt, the retry loop, and the context it reads. In a lab, a scientist picks the traits they want, grows many cultures, and keeps only the ones that show those traits. Petri does the same for harnesses. A human picks the trait, the harnesses evolve, and only verified improvements survive. Today, when a team changes a harness, they usually say the agent "feels better". There is no baseline, no repeat count, and nobody else can check the claim. Failed ideas stay in one person's terminal, so the next engineer tries them again and pays for the same tokens. Step 1: Pick the dish. A human chooses the domain, the model, and the starting harness, for example Coding, Claude Sonnet 5, and the Petri harness. Step 2: Pick the trait. Each change states the trait it aims to improve: accuracy (more tasks solved) or token savings (fewer tokens used). The tree shows each change with a label for its direction and size, such as "accuracy +280%". The showcase trees show more traits a team could select for: speed, security, ethics, code quality, and trust. Step 3: Let it mutate. Every change is a new node in the tree. A node is a small mutation: it changes at most 2 files and 120 lines of its parent, and it starts from its parent's files. Each node holds a hypothesis in plain English, the result that would prove it wrong, a benchmark score, and signatures from the keys that re-ran it. Step 4: Select. The rule is strict and public. A verifier re-runs both the parent and the new version, 5 times each, and the median counts. The author cannot verify their own node, and two reports from one key count as one. A node survives only when 2 distinct keys each measure a gain of at least +1000 basis points. A drop of 1000 basis points or more is rejected as a regression. Anything in between is rejected as noise. Unlike a real dish, Petri keeps every failed culture. Rejected nodes are never deleted. The "petri digest" command turns the whole tree into instructions for the next agent: what survived, what failed and why, and which areas nobody has tried. The next generation starts from the survivors and does not repeat the dead ends. The recorded tree has 16 versions on a 20-task coding benchmark. The start version solves 5 of 20 tasks. Adding full symbol signatures and a worked example reached 19 of 20, and 2 keys accepted it. Removing them again was rejected and kept. Guards and the typecheck stopped 8 more mutations before they could run, and they stay in the tree as a record. The web app shows the dish as a lineage graph, with a stats chart of each generation. In the demo, a version with 1 of 2 keys survives live when a second key runs "petri verify".
projects.how_its_made:
Petri has two parts: a TypeScript engine with a CLI (the lab), and a Next.js 16 web app that shows the dish (the microscope). THE CONTRACT FIRST
Before any code, we wrote SPEC.md as a binding contract. It fixes the exact bytes that get hashed, the bytes that get signed, the acceptance rule, and the CLI surface. Then we built every module against it. This kept a fast, parallel build from drifting apart. THE ENGINE
The engine runs on Node with tsx and commander, and every stored object has a zod schema. There is exactly one canonical JSON encoder and one SHA-256 helper in the codebase. A node id is the SHA-256 of its identity fields only: parent, harness files, benchmark and hypothesis. Wall time and file paths are excluded, so the same experiment gives the same id on any machine. Keys are ed25519 from node:crypto, and every verification report is a signed envelope. SELECTION
The acceptance rule is one pure function in src/policy/acceptance.ts. It reads the signed deltas and returns accepted, rejected or pending. Every event goes into a hash-chained append-only log, and the tree state is rebuilt from that log. "petri fsck" checks every invariant, including that no node was deleted. The engine has 93 tests. MUTATION WITH GUARDS
A new version is a patch on its parent's files. Before anything runs, guards refuse a patch that changes more than 2 files or 120 lines, touches the frozen harness/contract.ts, or spawns processes or reads environment variables. A scratch typecheck then refuses code that does not compile. A refused mutation still becomes a node with its reason, so the dead end is recorded. THE SEALED DISH (THE HARDEST PART)
A harness must never see the benchmark tests, or it could cheat the selection. A TypeScript type is not a security boundary, so we used real process isolation. The harness runs in a child process under the Node --permission model, with a single read grant that covers only the prompt and harness files. The code the model writes runs in a second child process, and the test source is never written to disk. An early audit caught a harness that could read the tests. That audit is why this two-process design exists. REPLAY MODE (THE HACKY PART)
We wanted anyone to reproduce the tree with no API key. Replay mode stores recorded model answers keyed by the SHA-256 of the harness files. The tests still really execute in the sandbox; only the model call is replaced. When a mutation has no recording, Petri does not guess a number. It marks the node "not-scored", and "petri verify" refuses it. Live mode calls Claude Sonnet 5 through the Anthropic SDK. FEEDING THE NEXT GENERATION
"petri digest" flattens the whole tree into a text brief for the next agent: what survived, what failed and why, and which areas nobody has tried. "petri evolve --dry-run" prints the exact prompt a model would receive to propose the next mutation. THE WEB APP
The Next.js app runs the real "petri export" and "petri digest" commands on each request, so the page always shows the actual log. A picker selects the dish: domain, model and harness. The tree is an SVG lineage graph with a tidy layout. Each edge carries a label for its trait and size, such as "accuracy +280%". The stats chart plots only measured versions, generation by generation, against a goal line. Showcase trees for other domains use the same acceptance rule to set their statuses. They are clearly separated from the measured tree. PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES
The repo includes a Hedera Consensus Service topic client and World AgentKit code. Hedera is meant to give the verification log a shared order and timestamps that no single machine can rewrite. World ID is meant to prove that each verifier is a distinct human, not one person with many keys.

projects.title: Mandate-app
projects.description: Programmable authority for autonomous execution without transferring treasury custody.
projects.project_description: I started Mandate with a simple question: how can an AI agent act for a treasury without receiving its private key or taking custody of its funds? At the core is MandateAquaApp, a Solidity contract that turns the owner's instructions into hard onchain limits: who may execute, which tokens and venue may be used, the minimum rate, spending caps, and expiry. 1inch Aqua keeps the funds in the owner's strategy balance. When a valid call arrives, Mandate pulls only the approved input, performs the swap, and sends the measured output straight back to the owner. If any check fails, the whole transaction reverts. I use ENSv2 as a real permission layer, not just a profile name. Every execution checks that agent.mandate-test.eth is still active and still owned by and resolved to the dedicated gas-only agent. The owner can immediately stop that agent by revoking the mandate, docking the Aqua strategy, or changing the ENS identity. The app is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Privy provides the owner smart wallet, Alchemy sponsors the Sepolia setup calls, and viem/wagmi handle typed contract interactions. A separate authenticated agent service holds the dedicated signer. Hono powers the public API, while a worker and Supabase PostgreSQL store confirmed receipt evidence. The web app runs on Vercel; the API, worker, and agent run in isolated Docker services behind Caddy. The trickiest part was proving the 1inch integration honestly. 1inch Classic is not available on Sepolia, so the live demo uses official Aqua and ENSv2 with a clearly labeled fixed test venue. Separately, a Foundry test captures a real 1inch mainnet route at a pinned block and runs the same production contract against forked mainnet liquidity. I also published a Bazantic Recipe that first asks 1inch for a route, then asks Mandate to independently check that route against the authority. It returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN; 1inch supplies the route, but only Mandate decides whether the agent is allowed to use it.
projects.how_its_made: Mandate is an onchain authorization firewall for autonomous agents. We encoded each authority as an immutable StrategyV1 and built MandateAquaApp in Solidity 0.8.30. The strategy fixes the chain, app, maker, dedicated agent, token pair, venue target and selector, rate floor, per-call and total spend caps, and validity window. On every execution, the contract rechecks the strategy hash, live limits, and the agent's current ENSv2 identity before moving any token. 1inch Aqua is the settlement and accounting layer. The treasury owner keeps custody between executions while Aqua provides strategy-scoped virtual balances. During an approved execution, Mandate pulls only the exact input through Aqua, grants the venue an exact temporary allowance, measures the real ERC-20 balance delta rather than trusting a return value, clears the allowance, and pushes the measured output directly back to the owner. Any failed identity, cap, route, rate, accounting, allowance, or residue check reverts the entire transaction atomically. ENSv2 is load-bearing authorization, not a profile badge. MandateAquaApp reads the Permissioned Registry and resolver during every call, checking that the name is active and that both its current owner and resolved address match the dedicated gas-only agent. The owner can therefore stop execution through Mandate revocation, Aqua docking, or an ENS identity change. The owner experience is a Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. Privy provides the owner smart wallet, Alchemy sponsors the Sepolia setup transactions, and viem plus wagmi handle typed calldata, simulation, block-bound reads, and transaction state. A narrowly scoped agent signer runs separately from the browser and public API. Hono exposes validated inspection, simulation, receipt-audit, and route-assessment endpoints; a worker confirms receipts and handles reorg reconciliation; Supabase PostgreSQL and Drizzle store evidence without ever becoming the source of authority. The web app runs on Vercel, while the API, worker, and authenticated agent run as isolated Docker Compose services behind Caddy. Our Bazantic Recipe, mandate-1inch-route-assurance, composes two services in sequence: 1inch getClassicSwapRoute obtains a live Ethereum route, then Mandate assessOneInchRoute independently decodes the calldata and checks it against the immutable policy. The result is deterministic PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN; a route-provider response alone can never produce PASS. Bazantic provides the MCP gateway, Recipe orchestration, and x402/MPP payment rails. One notable engineering compromise was handling network reality honestly. 1inch Classic does not advertise Sepolia, so we did not disguise a test contract as live liquidity. The public Sepolia flow combines official Aqua, live ENSv2 authorization, and a clearly labeled fixed venue for deterministic execution. A separate reproducible Foundry proof captures a real 1inch mainnet route at a pinned block and executes the same production Mandate contract against official Aqua and forked mainnet liquidity. Foundry unit, fuzz, invariant, integration, and fork tests cover the contract boundary, while Vitest and Playwright cover the typed services and browser flow. Token amounts remain bigint or decimal strings end to end, incomplete evidence fails closed, and neither the app nor the agent retains strategy tokens after settlement.

projects.title: Proofwork
projects.description: Escrowed USDC bounties that pay the contributor and the reviewer the moment a pull request merges.
projects.project_description: Open-source bounties mostly do not pay. Of 529 open agent bounties surveyed in August 2026, 73% never settled. Agents made code cheap and review expensive, and the maintainer who reviews an AI-generated pull request is paid nothing for it. Proofwork escrows USDC on Arc against a GitHub issue before anyone starts, and splits it three ways when the work is merged: the contributor, the maintainer who reviewed it, and a protocol fee. The merge is the approval. Nobody signs off on a payout and there is no invoice. The loop: a funder picks an open issue and escrows USDC from their own wallet (approve, then createAndFund; Proofwork never holds their key). A contributor, human or agent, comments /claim on the issue, which GitHub has already authenticated, so the comment doubles as proof they control the login. They open a pull request whose body says Fixes #N. A maintainer merges. The merge webhook checks that the pull request closes the funded issue, that its author holds an active claim, and that the base branch is the one the repository ships from, and only then does the verifier wallet call settle. Three transfers, one transaction, a few seconds. Maintainers set their terms before work starts, not after: whether AI-assisted contributions are welcome, whether they must be disclosed, what an agent stakes to hold a claim, and how long a claim survives without a pull request. That is the part every previous bounty board skipped, and it is why a maintainer would list at all. It is live and it has paid. Issue #1 on the project's own repository was funded, claimed, fixed, merged and settled: $1.70 to the contributor, $0.30 to the reviewing maintainer, $0.06 protocol fee, in a single transaction on Arc testnet.
projects.how_its_made: ProofworkJobs is a Solidity 0.8.24 contract implementing ERC-8183 job escrow in full, plus the three-way settlement the standard does not model. It is deployed and source-verified on Arc testnet at 0x3Bc728A813a7aBe0cB898fd63967525e92353D85, with evm_version set to paris because Arc has no PUSH0. 35 Foundry tests cover the properties that matter: the split never leaves dust, a refund always returns budget and fee together, a fee change cannot reprice a job that is already funded, pausing stops new money entering but never blocks a refund, and a hostile payment token cannot reenter a payout. The API is Hono on Cloudflare Workers with Drizzle on Neon Postgres. A GitHub delivery is signature-verified, written down, and only then acted on, so a crash mid-handling leaves a record to replay. Settlement is signed by a Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet: the orchestrator lives in a package with no database, no HTTP and no chain client in it, every side effect behind an interface, which is what lets the code path that moves money be tested end to end without a network. The frontend is Next.js 16 on Cloudflare via OpenNext; the funder signs approve and createAndFund in their own wallet with wagmi, and the API only ever hands out calldata and reads the receipt back off chain. The genuinely hacky part was Cloudflare Workers. Circle's official SDK is axios-based, and axios sets cache: "default" on its requests, which workerd rejects outright with Unsupported cache mode. That surfaced only after a real merge, with the escrow already funded. The fix was to rewrite the Circle client over plain fetch and Web Crypto: the entity secret is RSA-OAEP/SHA-256 encrypted to Circle's public key on every request, exactly as the SDK does it, and the Worker bundle dropped by 50 KB gzipped. Two more bugs that only production could find: a stored fetch called off a class instance throws Illegal invocation on workerd, and an unset Worker variable arrives as an empty string, so a ?? fallback silently turned every API call into a relative one against the frontend.
