The merge webhook checks that the pull request closes the funded issue, that its author holds an active claim, and that the base branch is the one the repository ships from, and only then does the verifier wallet call settle. Three transfers, one transaction, a few seconds.

Maintainers set their terms before work starts, not after: whether AI-assisted contributions are welcome, whether they must be disclosed, what an agent stakes to hold a claim, and how long a claim survives without a pull request. That is the part every previous bounty board skipped, and it is why a maintainer would list at all.

It is live and it has paid. Issue #1 on the project's own repository was funded, claimed, fixed, merged and settled: $1.70 to the contributor, $0.30 to the reviewing maintainer, $0.06 protocol fee, in a single transaction on Arc testnet.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ProofworkJobs is a Solidity 0.8.24 contract implementing ERC-8183 job escrow in full, plus the three-way settlement the standard does not model. It is deployed and source-verified on Arc testnet at 0x3Bc728A813a7aBe0cB898fd63967525e92353D85, with evm_version set to paris because Arc has no PUSH0. 35 Foundry tests cover the properties that matter: the split never leaves dust, a refund always returns budget and fee together, a fee change cannot reprice a job that is already funded, pausing stops new money entering but never blocks a refund, and a hostile payment token cannot reenter a payout.

The API is Hono on Cloudflare Workers with Drizzle on Neon Postgres. A GitHub delivery is signature-verified, written down, and only then acted on, so a crash mid-handling leaves a record to replay. Settlement is signed by a Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet: the orchestrator lives in a package with no database, no HTTP and no chain client in it, every side effect behind an interface, which is what lets the code path that moves money be tested end to end without a network. The frontend is Next.js 16 on Cloudflare via OpenNext; the funder signs approve and createAndFund in their own wallet with wagmi, and the API only ever hands out calldata and reads the receipt back off chain.

The genuinely hacky part was Cloudflare Workers. Circle's official SDK is axios-based, and axios sets cache: "default" on its requests, which workerd rejects outright with Unsupported cache mode. That surfaced only after a real merge, with the escrow already funded. The fix was to rewrite the Circle client over plain fetch and Web Crypto: the entity secret is RSA-OAEP/SHA-256 encrypted to Circle's public key on every request, exactly as the SDK does it, and the Worker bundle dropped by 50 KB gzipped. Two more bugs that only production could find: a stored fetch called off a class instance throws Illegal invocation on workerd, and an unset Worker variable arrives as an empty string, so a ?? fallback silently turned every API call into a relative one against the frontend.

projects.title: ARCA
projects.description: Easily configurable, USDC-native recurring subscriptions and memberships for Web3.
projects.project_description: Overview Arca is a decentralized subscription and recurring billing infrastructure engineered to bring a seamless, Stripe-like checkout experience to Web3. While the traditional digital economy thrives on frictionless recurring memberships, Web3 has historically subjected users to manual monthly renewals, volatile dual-token gas requirements, and multi-chain liquidity fragmentation. Arca eliminates these barriers by uniting Circle’s CCTP , the Arc blockchain (native USDC gas settlement) , Circle Modular Wallets with passkeys , and an automated non-custodial AutoPay engine into a cohesive recurring payments protocol. The Problem Arca Solves The Dual-Token Gas Dilemma: In traditional Web3 dApps, users must acquire and manage volatile gas tokens (ETH, POL, AVAX) just to pay a $10 USDC monthly membership. If a subscriber runs out of native gas, their transaction reverts and their subscription lapses. Subscription Churn from Manual Renewals: Blockchains are fundamentally push-based; contracts cannot pull funds without an active signature. Forcing users to open their wallet and manually sign transactions every 30 days leads to catastrophic subscriber drop-off. Fragmented Multi-Chain Liquidity: A user's funds are often scattered across Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, or Ethereum, while the merchant’s contract lives on a specific network, forcing users through tedious, multi-step manual bridging. Lack of Turnkey Merchant Tooling: Web3 builders lack production-ready tooling—such as multi-tier plans, hosted checkout links, HMAC-signed webhooks, and developer API keys for gated access. Core Innovations & Architecture USDC-as-Gas on Arc Testnet: Transactions execute with sub-second finality and utilize USDC directly as the native gas token. Both merchants and subscribers operate purely in stable currency with zero native token volatility or secondary gas token requirements. Frictionless Cross-Chain Liquidity via Circle CCTP: Arca integrates Circle’s official Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol. Users can fund subscriptions using USDC held on 15+ supported testnets (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Ethereum Sepolia, Avalanche Fuji, Polygon Amoy, etc.) via 1:1 burn-and-mint bridging with zero slippage or third-party liquidity pool risk. Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine: Subscribers pre-authorize renewals through a scoped EIP-712 typed signature tied to a session key permission. When a subscription cycle expires, an autonomous off-chain relayer triggers the renewal on-chain using ERC-1271 smart account signature verification. Users get true "set-it-and-forget-it" automated billing while retaining 100% custody of their funds. Turnkey Merchant & Developer Platform: Multi-Tier Plan Creation: Merchants can launch custom plans with flexible billing durations, tiered pricing, and perk configurations in minutes. Hosted Checkout Links: Clean, responsive checkout pages ( /pay/[planId] ) with real-time balance calculations, passkey login, and single-click checkout. Enterprise Webhooks: Real-time, HMAC-SHA256-signed delivery notifications ( payment.succeeded ) with dedicated per-endpoint activity logs, response tracking, and payload inspection. Developer API Keys: Cryptographically hashed secret keys for programmatic subscriber gating and backend verification. Real-Time Analytics: Powered by The Graph, tracking active MRR, gross revenue, churn, and protocol fees on live dashboards. Why It Matters Arca bridges the gap between Web2 user convenience and Web3 self-sovereignty. It enables SaaS platforms, content creators, gaming studios, and DAOs to build sustainable, predictable recurring revenue streams without forcing their customers through Web3 onboarding friction.

All payments and protocol fees settle directly in native USDC. Frontend & Full-Stack Engine: Built with Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Shadcn UI, powering an intuitive merchant portal and checkout dashboard. On-Chain Client & Transaction Dispatch: Powered by Viem for contract encoding, EIP-712 typed data signing, and ERC-4337 smart account UserOperations via Circle's bundler. Data & Indexing Layer: The Graph Subgraph: Deployed directly on Arc Testnet ( indexer/subgraph.yaml ), indexing events like PlanCreated , Subscribed , and AutoPayExecuted into real-time metrics (MRR, active subscriber counts, historical revenue charts). This eliminated the traditional "dual-token" onboarding barrier: users never need a secondary native gas token (like ETH or MATIC) just to pay a subscription. Every membership fee and network cost is denominated and paid strictly in USDC. Circle Modular Wallets & WebAuthn Passkeys: Integrated @circle-fin/modular-wallets-core to deploy ERC-4337 smart accounts secured by biometric passkeys (FaceID / TouchID / Windows Hello), completely abstracting seed phrases. Leveraged Circle's Paymaster infrastructure so initial account deployments and token approvals are sponsored seamlessly without gas fees. Circle Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP): Integrated Circle’s official CCTP protocol to solve multi-chain liquidity fragmentation. Furthermore, manually setting gas limits ( callGasLimit , verificationGasLimit ) caused the bundler to invalidate its own paymaster signature (yielding AA23 reverts). We engineered a hybrid gas strategy: fetching gas prices from Circle's oracle ( getUserOperationGasPrice ) to enforce the 1 gwei priority floor, while leaving gas limits dynamic for the bundler’s internal estimator. Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine via EIP-712 & ERC-1271: Blockchains are strictly "push-based"—smart contracts cannot spontaneously withdraw funds without a transaction trigger. projects.project_description_markdown:
### Overview

Arca is a decentralized subscription and recurring billing infrastructure engineered to bring a seamless, Stripe-like checkout experience to Web3. While the traditional digital economy thrives on frictionless recurring memberships, Web3 has historically subjected users to manual monthly renewals, volatile dual-token gas requirements, and multi-chain liquidity fragmentation. 

Arca eliminates these barriers by uniting **Circle’s CCTP**, the **Arc blockchain (native USDC gas settlement)**, **Circle Modular Wallets with passkeys**, and an automated **non-custodial AutoPay engine** into a cohesive recurring payments protocol.

---

### The Problem Arca Solves

* **The Dual-Token Gas Dilemma:** In traditional Web3 dApps, users must acquire and manage volatile gas tokens (ETH, POL, AVAX) just to pay a $10 USDC monthly membership. If a subscriber runs out of native gas, their transaction reverts and their subscription lapses.
* **Subscription Churn from Manual Renewals:** Blockchains are fundamentally push-based; contracts cannot pull funds without an active signature. Forcing users to open their wallet and manually sign transactions every 30 days leads to catastrophic subscriber drop-off.
* **Fragmented Multi-Chain Liquidity:** A user's funds are often scattered across Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, or Ethereum, while the merchant’s contract lives on a specific network, forcing users through tedious, multi-step manual bridging.
* **Lack of Turnkey Merchant Tooling:** Web3 builders lack production-ready tooling—such as multi-tier plans, hosted checkout links, HMAC-signed webhooks, and developer API keys for gated access.

---

### Core Innovations & Architecture

* **USDC-as-Gas on Arc Testnet:**
  Transactions execute with sub-second finality and utilize USDC directly as the native gas token. Both merchants and subscribers operate purely in stable currency with zero native token volatility or secondary gas token requirements.

* **Frictionless Cross-Chain Liquidity via Circle CCTP:**
  Arca integrates Circle’s official Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol. Users can fund subscriptions using USDC held on 15+ supported testnets (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Ethereum Sepolia, Avalanche Fuji, Polygon Amoy, etc.) via 1:1 burn-and-mint bridging with zero slippage or third-party liquidity pool risk.

* **Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine:**
  Subscribers pre-authorize renewals through a scoped EIP-712 typed signature tied to a session key permission. When a subscription cycle expires, an autonomous off-chain relayer triggers the renewal on-chain using ERC-1271 smart account signature verification. Users get true "set-it-and-forget-it" automated billing while retaining 100% custody of their funds.

* **Turnkey Merchant & Developer Platform:**
  * **Multi-Tier Plan Creation:** Merchants can launch custom plans with flexible billing durations, tiered pricing, and perk configurations in minutes.
  * **Hosted Checkout Links:** Clean, responsive checkout pages (`/pay/[planId]`) with real-time balance calculations, passkey login, and single-click checkout.
  * **Enterprise Webhooks:** Real-time, HMAC-SHA256-signed delivery notifications (`payment.succeeded`) with dedicated per-endpoint activity logs, response tracking, and payload inspection.
  * **Developer API Keys:** Cryptographically hashed secret keys for programmatic subscriber gating and backend verification.
  * **Real-Time Analytics:** Powered by The Graph, tracking active MRR, gross revenue, churn, and protocol fees on live dashboards.

---

### Why It Matters

Arca bridges the gap between Web2 user convenience and Web3 self-sovereignty. It enables SaaS platforms, content creators, gaming studios, and DAOs to build sustainable, predictable recurring revenue streams without forcing their customers through Web3 onboarding friction.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
### 1. Core Architecture & Stack

* **Smart Contracts (Solidity / Arc Testnet):** The protocol is anchored by `SubscriptionGateway.sol`, which manages plan configurations, multi-tier pricing, flexible cycle durations, protocol fee routing, and permissioned renewals. All payments and protocol fees settle directly in native USDC.
* **Frontend & Full-Stack Engine:** Built with Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Shadcn UI, powering an intuitive merchant portal and checkout dashboard.
* **On-Chain Client & Transaction Dispatch:** Powered by Viem for contract encoding, EIP-712 typed data signing, and ERC-4337 smart account UserOperations via Circle's bundler.
* **Data & Indexing Layer:**
  * **The Graph Subgraph:** Deployed directly on Arc Testnet (`indexer/subgraph.yaml`), indexing events like `PlanCreated`, `Subscribed`, and `AutoPayExecuted` into real-time metrics (MRR, active subscriber counts, historical revenue charts).
  * **MongoDB:** Manages high-throughput off-chain state, including encrypted session pre-authorizations, developer API keys, hashed secrets, and webhook activity logs.

---

### 2. Partner Technologies & How They Fit Together

* **Arc Blockchain (Primary Execution Layer & Native USDC Gas):**
  * Arc provides sub-second finality and utilizes USDC as its native gas token.
  * This eliminated the traditional "dual-token" onboarding barrier: users never need a secondary native gas token (like ETH or MATIC) just to pay a subscription. Every membership fee and network cost is denominated and paid strictly in USDC.
* **Circle Modular Wallets & WebAuthn Passkeys:**
  * Integrated `@circle-fin/modular-wallets-core` to deploy ERC-4337 smart accounts secured by biometric passkeys (FaceID / TouchID / Windows Hello), completely abstracting seed phrases.
  * Leveraged Circle's Paymaster infrastructure so initial account deployments and token approvals are sponsored seamlessly without gas fees.
* **Circle Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP):**
  * Integrated Circle’s official CCTP protocol to solve multi-chain liquidity fragmentation.
  * If a subscriber’s USDC balance on Arc is empty, the client initiates a 1:1 burn-and-mint bridge from any of 15+ supported testnets (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Ethereum Sepolia, Avalanche Fuji, Polygon Amoy, etc.).
  * The application tracks the `DepositForBurn` event on the source chain, queries Circle’s Iris attestation service for the cryptographic signature, and executes `receiveMessage` on Arc to mint native USDC directly into the user’s account.
* **The Graph:**
  * Custom AssemblyScript mappings transform on-chain contract events into queryable GraphQL endpoints, powering real-time merchant analytics and buyer subscription tracking.

---

### 3. Notable Engineering Breakthroughs & Solutions

* **Bypassing Viem’s Gas Estimator for Circle's Arc Bundler:**
  Arc Testnet’s bundler strictly enforces a `maxPriorityFeePerGas >= 1 gwei`. Standard Viem fee estimation defaults to ~0.002 gwei on testnets, causing immediate bundler rejections. Furthermore, manually setting gas limits (`callGasLimit`, `verificationGasLimit`) caused the bundler to invalidate its own paymaster signature (yielding `AA23` reverts). We engineered a hybrid gas strategy: fetching gas prices from Circle's oracle (`getUserOperationGasPrice`) to enforce the 1 gwei priority floor, while leaving gas limits dynamic for the bundler’s internal estimator.

* **Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine via EIP-712 & ERC-1271:**
  Blockchains are strictly "push-based"—smart contracts cannot spontaneously withdraw funds without a transaction trigger. To achieve true Web2-style recurring renewals, we implemented an EIP-712 structured permission scheme. Users sign a typed authorization granting a renewal allowance over a defined cycle. An off-chain relayer continuously evaluates eligible expired subscriptions, verifies the authorization on-chain via ERC-1271 smart account signature validation, and executes `subscribeWithSignature()` on the user's behalf without holding custody of user keys.

* **Automated CCTP Attestation State Machine:**
  CCTP bridging requires waiting for finality on the source chain before Circle’s attestation service signs the message. We designed a resilient client-side state machine with exponential backoff and transaction hash recovery that bridges the tokens, captures the burn nonce, waits for attestation, and automatically triggers the destination mint and subscription checkout without forcing the user to leave the page.

* **HMAC-SHA256 Webhook Delivery Pipeline:**
  Modeled after Stripe’s webhook security, every on-chain subscription confirmation emits an event that triggers an internal dispatch queue. The queue constructs a timestamped payload, signs it using HMAC-SHA256 with the merchant’s unique endpoint secret, records execution latencies and status codes, and displays real-time delivery logs on a dedicated webhook inspection dashboard.

projects.title: TR4CE
projects.description: Verifiable ERC-4626 vault evidence for people and agents. Vault Activity data? Verified ✅
projects.project_description: Most vault products show a number without preserving enough context to verify it. And that's the main reason i built TR4CE. ERC-4626 standardizes how vaults are called, but a clean APY or successful preview does not prove that the data is complete, current, tied to the right asset, or comparable across different vault implementations. TR4CE traces Base mainnet vault activity and turns it into reproducible evidence reports. Each report keeps the vault address, chain, blocks, observation window, raw calculation inputs, policy version, provenance, and limitations. I then evaluate that evidence against five explicit rules covering the underlying asset, history, TVL, observed share-value return, and account withdrawability. Every rule returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN. I treat missing, stale, reverted, or unsupported data as UNKNOWN instead of guessing a value or hiding the gap. The committed evidence manifest currently covers four USDC-denominated ERC-4626 vaults across Morpho V2 and Yearn V3, backed by recorded Base contract reads and public transaction references. When someone wants to act on a report, TR4CE prepares exact deposit or redeem calldata and simulates it at a named block. It never signs or submits the transaction. The connected wallet owner still reviews and approves every action. I built it this way so the same evidence can help a person, wallet, or agent make a decision without giving TR4CE custody of funds or control of a private key.
projects.how_its_made: I built TR4CE as an evidence pipeline rather than another vault dashboard. The historical layer is a Rust and WASM package running on The Graph Substreams. It filters Base blocks to a configurable set of ERC-4626 vaults, then emits typed deposits, withdrawals, share transfers, and block-scoped snapshots through protobuf. Keeping vault addresses as runtime parameters means the same package can trace a different curated set without rebuilding it. The Substreams output uses the PostgreSQL Database Changes format. Raw observations and the stream cursor land together, while a worker promotes only confirmed rows into the application schema. If a deep reorganization changes a promoted block, dependent reports and prepared actions are invalidated instead of quietly serving stale evidence. I kept the evidence and policy logic in shared TypeScript packages. Token values stay in integer base units, ratios retain their original inputs, and missing data never becomes a convenient zero. The five policy rules always resolve to PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN, so the web app, API, and MCP tools all return the same decision from the same evidence. The interface uses Next.js and React, with Hono for the HTTP API and a generated OpenAPI 3.1 contract. I also built six MCP tools for vault search, evidence retrieval, policy evaluation, action preparation, and receipt status. viem handles contract reads and simulation, while wagmi hands unsigned calls to the connected wallet. TR4CE never receives a private key and has no transaction submission endpoint. The most time-consuming part was making the proof honest across Morpho V2 and Yearn V3. They share ERC-4626 interfaces but not identical behavior, so I kept versioned adapters and raw capability results instead of forcing everything into one score. I also found that substreams run --test-file was not enforcing assertions in the CLI version I used. I wrote a pinned live-check script that runs real Base blocks and compares the output with committed fixtures. That workaround became part of the reproducible evidence trail rather than something hidden from reviewers.

projects.title: Deflow
projects.description: Non-custodial compliance payment gateway for crypto checkouts.
projects.project_description: Deflow bridges the gap between regulatory requirements and Web3 privacy. We separate fund flow from compliance screening: money moves strictly between payer and merchant contracts, while checks run in an isolated enclave. Non-custodial: Deflow never takes custody of funds. Payments go into the merchant’s dedicated smart contract (MerchantGateway) during a short screening window. The contract has only two exits: forward to the merchant on approval, or refund to the payer if flagged or timed out. Funds cannot be frozen. Zero Data Liability: Personal documents and paid AML intelligence never touch the merchant's servers, Deflow's backend, or the blockchain. Verification executes inside a Chainlink CRE enclave (TEE). The blockchain only ever receives an opaque, single-use nullifier, a verified tier, and an expiry timestamp. Compliance: Deflow runs automated sanctions and fund provenance (KYT) checks out of the box for every payments in real time. Merchants toggle identity checks (Sumsub / World ID) only when transaction thresholds or local jurisdictions require it.
projects.how_its_made: Deflow combines Solidity gateways on Base Sepolia, a Next.js checkout and a Go Chainlink CRE confidential workflow running in a TEE. Sumsub KYC stays inside the enclave, only a merchant-scoped nullifier reaches the chain. KYT uses GoPlusScreener (instead of Sumsub AML because of costs) to score wallet risk before settlement. Privy provides merchant wallets and approval policies. Payments are escrowed, then settled or automatically refunded. World ID support was prepared but disabled because we were not granted access during the hackathon.

projects.title: Ottopus
projects.description: Stop juggling wallets to get one thing done. Let your agent plan; you review and sign.
projects.project_description:
You have assets spread across wallets and chains. Doing one thing onchain means remembering which wallet holds what, then comparing dapps/ protocols for a route, then reading calldata you can't read or using other simulation tools. Ottopus hands that work to your agent and keeps the decision with you. Link your wallets once, point any MCP-capable agent at Ottopus, and say what you want "Buy 500 USD worth Spacex token." Ottopus looks across every linked wallet, picks the one that makes the action cheapest, builds the route, decodes it, and hands back a review link with a one-sentence reason: "Recommended Trading wallet (…7A21) — already holds USDC on Base, avoids a bridge and an approval, saves about $4." You open the link, see in plain language what will happen, simulate it against live chain state, and sign it in your own wallet. The agent never holds a key and never sends anything tool calls produce plans, not transactions. It works with the wallets you already have: hardware, hot, or a multisig like Safe. Ottopus is not a wallet and takes no custody. It plans, explains and
simulates. You stay the signer.
projects.how_its_made:
A pnpm workspace with two deployables from one commit: a Next.js web app on Vercel and a Node service on Railway, over Supabase Postgres. The service holds everything that matters — the plan engine, the calldata decoder, external decoders, connectors to services like swap, earn protocols, simulation, and a remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP + OAuth 2.1) that
any agent host can add by URL. The web app renders what the service verified; it never computes a plan or touches the database. Auth is Privy. Plans are append-only and bound to an immutable hash, so a plan can't change between what you review and what you sign. Simulation runs through a provider
independent of whoever built the route.
projects.project_description_markdown:
You have assets spread across wallets and chains. Doing one thing onchain means remembering which wallet holds what, then comparing dapps/ protocols for a route, then reading calldata you can't read or using other simulation tools.

Ottopus hands that work to your agent and keeps the decision with you. Link your wallets once, point any MCP-capable agent at Ottopus, and say what you want "Buy 500 USD worth Spacex token." Ottopus looks across every linked wallet, picks the one that makes the action cheapest, builds the route, decodes it, and hands back a review link with a one-sentence reason:

"Recommended Trading wallet (…7A21) — already holds USDC on Base, avoids a bridge and an approval, saves about $4."

You open the link, see in plain language what will happen, simulate it against live chain state, and sign it in your own wallet. The agent never holds a key and never sends anything tool calls produce plans, not transactions.

It works with the wallets you already have: hardware, hot, or a multisig like Safe. Ottopus is not a wallet and takes no custody. It plans, explains and
simulates. You stay the signer.

projects.title: Agentic EMS
projects.description: Empower EMS with agentic layer for fixed income strategies safely and like a pro.
projects.project_description: Institutional-grade DeFi lacks a unified intelligence and execution layer. While traditional fixed-income traders rely on Bloomberg to monitor macro liquidity, assess underlying credit risks, and execute structured instruments, DeFi equivalents are forced to manually cross-reference fragmented data silos—DefiLlama for TVL, L2Beat for roll-up security, governance forums, and disparate on-chain analytics. This operational fragmentation makes sizing large allocations across liquidity pools, money markets, and yield protocols inefficient and structurally risky and time consuming. The Solution: welcome the  Agentic Execution Management System (EMS) This project rebuilds the Bloomberg terminal kind of experience for fixed-income and yield-focused DeFi allocators, powered by an autonomous, dual-agent architecture accessed through a natural language interface: Macro & Market Ingestion: An automated ETL engine aggregates real-time macro indicators across DeFi sectors ( using theGraph, defillama and other data providers): scraping TVL flows, fee yields, protocol governance shifts, and underlying L1/L2 systemic risk vectors. Predictive Intelligence: By pairing transformer-based language reasoning with time-series forecasting models, the system evaluates protocol counterparty risk and models multi-chain yield projections. Institutional-Grade Execution The agent synthesizes trader intent into an optimized execution strategy, deconstructing large capital allocations into multi-leg routing transactions using bridging solutions like CCTP, lifi, layerzero, OneInch SwapVM to minimize slippage and MEV exposure and can convert positions to stablecoin in less time risk. Continuous Portfolio Management:  Once on-chain legs settle, the platform tracks positions autonomously, surfacing dynamic hedging recommendations and automated rebalancing alerts.
projects.how_its_made: The platform is organized within a modular TypeScript-first Turborepo monorepo comprising five distinct applications: The Trading Desk UI: A high-performance dashboard that guides allocators through intent capture, visual portfolio payoffs, quantitative risk simulation parameters (vega, alpha, beta, gamma which are generated by the AI agent pipeline) and live execution tracking across categories of DeFi protocols (LP, lending, prediction markets, etc…). Serverless Inference Microservice: A dedicated engine hosted on Google Cloud product running multi-agent workflows that stream typed, step-by-step reasoning events directly to the interface. Predictive Risk & Indexing Service: An analytical back-end integrating temporal data retrieval, automated market indexing, and quantitative yield projections. Execution & Settlement Engine: A venue-agnostic transaction compiler that turns strategic goals into concrete on-chain routing instructions across standard bridging protocol (layerZero), standard bridge aggregators (Lifi), and CCTP. Chain Validation Harness: An automated environment that tests and verifies execution scenarios against live network state forks to ensure deterministic gas fees and possibility of other challenges like MeV sandwich attacks, etc. Partner Integrations: Data & Risk Aggregation: Instead of building ad-hoc indexers, we leveraged The Graph alongside Messari’s standardized subgraphs across ~200 deployments to normalize liquidity, lending, and derivative protocols. Macro risks and protocol vulnerabilities are sourced directly from DeFiLlama, L2Beat, and governance hubs. Sovereign Custody & Approval: We combined Privy (embedded wallets), Ledger (hardware clear-signing), and Safe (multi-sig smart accounts) so institutions retain total sovereignty: agents propose allocations, but devices approve them. Cross-Chain Settlement & Liquidity: Circle Arc and CCTP v2 provide native cross-chain settlement with zero bridge friction, while 1inch and Uniswap v4 serve as our programmable routing layer for deep liquidity and custom pool hooks. Inference layer: it runs on Google Vertex AI based Gemini-3.1 / 2.5 models for multi-step reasoning, orchestrated with LangGraph (as the multi-agent system doing custom analysis across the DeFi data analysis pipeline and order execution setup based on the risk parameters), traced via LangSmith (in order to provide the observability), and paired with TimescaleDB and Google’s TimesFM3 open source for continuous time-series yield forecasting. Resolutions to the challenges I faced during developing the app: Bypassing Ingestion Bottlenecks: Institutional governance forums and analytics dashboards aggressively rate-limit scrapers. We engineered a stealth Python worker running specialized browser virtualization to scrape critical governance signals, backed by cross-language schema tests to prevent data drift. Robust error / hallucination handling: That these AI / RAG agents are famously bad news when it comes to hallucination and lack of attribution of data. We have been very strict in terms of detecting all those generated hallucinated patterns, and we have defined very strict guardrails. Either the AI agent will generate the correct response (that is, the predictions for investment into a strategy) or generate the ER EIP-712 transaction typed data structure correctly, or it will give null as an error. We handle the AI agent orchestration and its reliability very seriously. Simulation of the APY’s of yields: To provide more comprehensive analysis for the fixing traders to define their backstops and other rebalancing strategies. The Times FM3 model provides them with the possibility to predict the potential API/APY yield for the future. It is a state-of-the-art model that can start predicting any time series data, provided it is sufficiently fine-tuned, starting from 10 time series data points of lending protocols, it will be able to do a simulation perfectly.

projects.title: BONE DRY
projects.description: A promise that can't bounce: cross-chain solvency for 1inch Aqua via Opcode 35 & Uniswap v4
projects.project_description:
Bone Dry: a promise that can't bounce Bone Dry makes sure a market maker on 1inch Aqua can't sell the same money twice. If a maker is promising more than their wallet can pay, their quote gets worse, and past a limit the trade is refused, on-chain, before anything breaks. The problem On 1inch Aqua, market makers don't lock their money in a pool. It stays in their own wallet, and they just publish a promise: "I'll trade up to this much." That's efficient, but nothing stops a maker from promising the same balance again and again. When several traders try to use those promises, the first trade goes through and the rest fail, because the money isn't there. We measured it. 7 of the 12 largest maker positions on Base were promising money they didn't hold. On Ethereum, about 102,000 WETH was advertised, but only around 4 WETH could actually be delivered. The fix: opcode 35 1inch Aqua strategies run on a small program called SwapVM. We added a new instruction to it, opcode 35. A maker can add it to any strategy, and every time someone trades against it, it: Checks what the wallet already owes to the maker's other strategies.
Widens the price as the wallet gets stretched. The more of the wallet is already promised, the less generous the quote.
Refuses the trade past a limit the maker chooses, for example 80%, so a promise the wallet can't cover never gets filled. Makers can still withdraw a promise at any time, in one transaction. Swapping through Uniswap v4 We built a Uniswap v4 hook called Tap. Its pool holds zero money. When someone swaps, the hook fills the trade straight from Aqua makers' wallets in the same transaction. If a maker refuses, the hook doesn't fail the swap. It records the refusal on-chain and fills the trade from the next maker that can pay. One wallet, two chains Bone Dry is live on Base and Ethereum, and the same wallet can make promises on both. For traders: before you sign, the app quotes your trade on both chains. It shows the price you'd get and how much of your trade each chain can actually fill, so you can choose.
For makers: the app shows your whole book across both chains, promised against what your wallet holds, and warns you before you publish a strategy that would be refused. The Graph Our Aquifer subgraph on Base reads every strategy as it's published. It spots the ones using opcode 35 and checks whether each one's list of the maker's other strategies is complete. It also records every opcode-35 fill and every refusal the hook catches, so the app can show what happened to each maker's strategies, with links to the transactions. Proof it works Live on Base mainnet and Ethereum mainnet (router and Uniswap v4 hooks on both).
First real trade through opcode 35 on Base: the quote was cut by 2.98% because the wallet was 60% committed (tx 0x95aab656…).
First real refusal on Base: a strategy at 90% committed was turned away against its 80% limit, and the swap still completed from another maker (tx 0xe29c843d…).
56 contract tests and 15 subgraph tests, all passing.
projects.how_its_made:
Built with: Solidity and Foundry · 1inch Aqua and SwapVM · Uniswap v4 (hooks and PoolManager) · The Graph (AssemblyScript subgraph) · Next.js 16, React 19, viem, wagmi and RainbowKit · Postgres for an Ethereum strategy index · deployed on Vercel. Opcode 35, added to 1inch SwapVM without forking it Extending, not copying: 1inch's opcode table is overridable, so our BoneDryRouter extends it and adds one new instruction at slot 35. The original opcodes 0–34 are untouched, so every existing 1inch strategy still runs on our router.
What a strategy carries: its settings are packed into its program as [declared total][sibling count][sibling hashes][max utilisation][widen bps]. On every trade the instruction:
reads the maker's other strategies on-chain (up to 6);
rejects a declared total lower than what it finds;
reads the wallet's real balance and allowance;
then widens the price or refuses.
Safe maths: it uses mulDiv so huge numbers can't overflow. The whole router is 19,793 bytes, under Ethereum's 24,576-byte contract limit, with nothing removed.
Events only on real trades: it emits EncumbranceApplied only on a real trade, never during a price quote, so the index only records trades that happened. A Uniswap v4 hook with an empty pool Mining the address: a v4 hook's permissions live in the last bits of its address. Our Foundry script searches salts until the address carries exactly "before swap" and "return a delta".
Filling the swap: the hook takes each swap in beforeSwap and fills it maker by maker. It pulls tokens from each maker's wallet through Aqua and settles with the PoolManager in the same transaction, so the pool never holds a balance.
Catching refusals: each maker's quote and fill is wrapped in try/catch. A refusing maker becomes a MakerSkipped(maker, strategy, token, amount, reason) event, and the trade moves on to the next maker. Normally a revert leaves no trace; this turns it into a record.
Two bugs we hit and fixed:
Rounding remainder: splitting a trade across makers left a few units unfilled, which made multi-maker swaps fail. The remainder now goes to the first maker.
Partial fills: in an empty pool, a partial fill would push the price to its limit and break the pool. Swaps are now all-or-nothing. The Graph: reading strategies as they're published No extra events needed: when a strategy is published, the subgraph walks its program bytes the same way the VM does. It finds opcode 35 and decodes its settings from the bytes alone.
Completeness check: it compares each strategy's list of siblings with the maker's actual live strategies and flags lists that are incomplete.
Fills and refusals: it indexes our router's EncumbranceApplied and both hooks' MakerSkipped, and collapses a refusal the hook retried within one swap into a single record. Mappings are covered by 15 Matchstick tests. The app Two books, never mixed: Aqua keeps balances per router, so 1inch's makers and our opcode-35 makers are separate books. The route API plans each one, re-checks every maker's real balance live, drops makers whose quote would fail, and picks the better book.
Both chains compared fairly: the same trade is quoted on Base and Ethereum and compared by price per unit actually filled, plus how much of the trade each chain can take.
Always a current quote: browsing uses a 20-second cache, so repeat quotes come back in about 36 ms. Pressing Swap always re-quotes fresh and stops if the price moved.
Your book on every chain: the maker book comes from the subgraph on Base, and from our Postgres index plus on-chain logs on Ethereum, with every amount re-read live.
Honest declarations: the strategy builder works out the declared total on the server from live balances, so a maker can't under-declare by mistake. Things we're proud of Refusals you can see: the hook turns a failed quote into an on-chain event, and the subgraph makes it searchable. The first real refusal on Base is indexed and shown in the app.
Cross-chain without a bridge: opcode 35 only rejects a declaration that's too low. So a maker can include what they owe on another chain, and the strategy will refuse when their whole book is overstretched.
Rehearsed before sending: every mainnet script ran on a fork first, with safety checks that abort rather than over-promise. The full Ethereum deployment cost about 0.0004 ETH, and our tests swap against the live Ethereum contracts.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Bone Dry: a promise that can't bounce

Bone Dry makes sure a market maker on 1inch Aqua can't sell the same money twice. If a maker is promising more than their wallet can pay, their quote gets worse, and past a limit the trade is refused, on-chain, before anything breaks.

1. The problem

On 1inch Aqua, market makers don't lock their money in a pool. It stays in their own wallet, and they just publish a promise: "I'll trade up to this much."

That's efficient, but nothing stops a maker from promising the same balance again and again. When several traders try to use those promises, the first trade goes through and the rest fail, because the money isn't there.

We measured it. 7 of the 12 largest maker positions on Base were promising money they didn't hold. On Ethereum, about 102,000 WETH was advertised, but only around 4 WETH could actually be delivered.

2. The fix: opcode 35

1inch Aqua strategies run on a small program called SwapVM. We added a new instruction to it, opcode 35. A maker can add it to any strategy, and every time someone trades against it, it:

Checks what the wallet already owes to the maker's other strategies.
Widens the price as the wallet gets stretched. The more of the wallet is already promised, the less generous the quote.
Refuses the trade past a limit the maker chooses, for example 80%, so a promise the wallet can't cover never gets filled.

Makers can still withdraw a promise at any time, in one transaction.

3. Swapping through Uniswap v4

We built a Uniswap v4 hook called Tap. Its pool holds zero money. When someone swaps, the hook fills the trade straight from Aqua makers' wallets in the same transaction.

If a maker refuses, the hook doesn't fail the swap. It records the refusal on-chain and fills the trade from the next maker that can pay.

4. One wallet, two chains

Bone Dry is live on Base and Ethereum, and the same wallet can make promises on both.

For traders: before you sign, the app quotes your trade on both chains. It shows the price you'd get and how much of your trade each chain can actually fill, so you can choose.
For makers: the app shows your whole book across both chains, promised against what your wallet holds, and warns you before you publish a strategy that would be refused.

5. The Graph

Our Aquifer subgraph on Base reads every strategy as it's published. It spots the ones using opcode 35 and checks whether each one's list of the maker's other strategies is complete. It also records every opcode-35 fill and every refusal the hook catches, so the app can show what happened to each maker's strategies, with links to the transactions.

6. Proof it works

Live on Base mainnet and Ethereum mainnet (router and Uniswap v4 hooks on both).
First real trade through opcode 35 on Base: the quote was cut by 2.98% because the wallet was 60% committed (tx 0x95aab656…).
First real refusal on Base: a strategy at 90% committed was turned away against its 80% limit, and the swap still completed from another maker (tx 0xe29c843d…).
56 contract tests and 15 subgraph tests, all passing.

projects.title: ALFQuote
projects.description: Hook-aware discovery, assessment, quotes, and protected Uniswap v4 swap dry-runs.
projects.project_description:
ALFQuote is a hook-aware integration toolkit for discovering, assessing, quoting, and safely simulating swaps through Uniswap v4 DualPool hooks on Ethereum.
DualPool hooks can keep assets in external ERC-4626 vaults and return liquidity to Uniswap only when a swap occurs. As a result, the standard PoolManager liquidity value can be zero even when the hook has usable capacity and can provide a quote. Integrators that inspect only vanilla PoolManager liquidity can incorrectly reject these pools.
ALFQuote provides a reusable TypeScript library and an alfquote command-line interface with four commands:
discover enumerates factory deployments or reconstructs a hook’s pools from onchain Initialize events.
assess reports compatibility, provenance, routing requirements, and upgradeability as four independent, evidence-backed fields. It never compresses them into a misleading “safe” verdict.
quote checks hook and pool liveness, applies the hook’s advertised gas bound, reads vanilla liquidity, reserves, and effective liquidity separately, and produces a hook-aware indicative quote.
swap builds protected Universal Router v2 calldata and performs a read-only simulation. It reports slippage protection, gas, decoded reverts, balances, ERC-20 allowances, Permit2 allowances, and all execution blockers. It never signs or broadcasts a transaction.
Every command supports readable terminal output and a stable JSON envelope for coding agents. Results include schema version, chain and block context, input data, warnings, status, and structured output or errors. Zero quotes, unavailable evidence, failed liveness, and identity mismatches fail closed rather than becoming usable prices.
The project includes live Ethereum mainnet verification, a successful protected swap on a controlled Tenderly mainnet fork, reproducible evidence, 235 automated tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send safety gates.
projects.how_its_made:
ALFQuote is an npm workspace written in TypeScript. It contains a reusable alfquote library, a Commander-based CLI, separate read-only verification scripts, and isolated Tenderly fork-evidence tooling. The onchain integration uses viem for Ethereum RPC reads, ABI encoding and decoding, event parsing, storage access, calldata construction, and transaction simulation.
The discovery service reads the official DualPool factory registry at an explicit block. For each deployment, it verifies provenance in both directions: the factory must recognize the hook, and the hook must report the expected factory. Pool discovery scans PoolManager Initialize logs, filters by the exact event signature, reconstructs every PoolKey field, and derives the PoolId to check it against the event. Explicit fixtures remain clearly labeled and never inherit a factory claim.
Assessment is deliberately conservative. ERC-165 support and required IALFHook views establish compatibility. Provenance, routing policy, and upgradeability remain independent. Proxy detection checks EIP-1967 implementation, beacon, and admin storage slots, plus EIP-1167 minimal-proxy bytecode. Failed or incomplete reads produce unknown or unverified, never a favorable guess.
The quote service checks isLive() and livePools(poolId) before quoting. It reads maxGas() and uses that value as the quote call’s gas bound. It then reports three different liquidity signals:
Vanilla PoolManager liquidity
Total DualPool reserves
Effective liquidity currently usable for swaps
The mainnet proof showed why this distinction matters: the selected PoolManager position reported zero vanilla liquidity while the DualPool hook had positive effective liquidity and returned a non-zero quote.
Protected swaps are encoded for Universal Router v2 using V4_SWAP, SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE, SETTLE_ALL, and TAKE_ALL. The release path always uses empty DualPool hookData. amountOutMinimum is calculated from the quote and an explicit slippage value. Simulation checks the sender’s token balance, ERC-20 approval to Permit2, Permit2 approval to Universal Router, and Permit2 expiration. Reverts are decoded and classified conservatively. The public library contains no wallet client, private key, signer, approval transaction, or broadcast function.
Tenderly was used as a controlled mainnet-fork environment because a read-only mainnet address did not have the balances and Permit2 approvals needed to prove successful execution. A fresh evidence run funded an isolated test address, submitted normal approval transactions, and executed a protected 1 USDC swap. The quote, minimum output, actual output, gas, balance changes, and hook events were reconciled. Mainnet remained read-only, and the successful fork simulation remains the primary execution proof.
The CLI uses Commander 15 and exposes injectable arguments, environment variables, and output sinks so command behavior can be tested without spawning processes. Human and JSON output come from the same structured result. Big integers are serialized as decimal strings, RPC credentials are redacted, and long calldata is preserved without truncation. Exit codes distinguish success, typed skips, invalid input, unavailable evidence, swap blockers, configuration problems, and internal failures.
The repository uses Vitest for unit and integration coverage. CI performs a clean install, type-check, build, 235 tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send scans. An offline end-to-end test drives all four commands through one mocked transport. An opt-in integration script verifies the complete journey against live Ethereum mainnet.
projects.project_description_markdown:
ALFQuote is a hook-aware integration toolkit for discovering, assessing, quoting, and safely simulating swaps through Uniswap v4 DualPool hooks on Ethereum.
DualPool hooks can keep assets in external ERC-4626 vaults and return liquidity to Uniswap only when a swap occurs. As a result, the standard PoolManager liquidity value can be zero even when the hook has usable capacity and can provide a quote. Integrators that inspect only vanilla PoolManager liquidity can incorrectly reject these pools.
ALFQuote provides a reusable TypeScript library and an alfquote command-line interface with four commands:
discover enumerates factory deployments or reconstructs a hook’s pools from onchain Initialize events.
assess reports compatibility, provenance, routing requirements, and upgradeability as four independent, evidence-backed fields. It never compresses them into a misleading “safe” verdict.
quote checks hook and pool liveness, applies the hook’s advertised gas bound, reads vanilla liquidity, reserves, and effective liquidity separately, and produces a hook-aware indicative quote.
swap builds protected Universal Router v2 calldata and performs a read-only simulation. It reports slippage protection, gas, decoded reverts, balances, ERC-20 allowances, Permit2 allowances, and all execution blockers. It never signs or broadcasts a transaction.
Every command supports readable terminal output and a stable JSON envelope for coding agents. Results include schema version, chain and block context, input data, warnings, status, and structured output or errors. Zero quotes, unavailable evidence, failed liveness, and identity mismatches fail closed rather than becoming usable prices.
The project includes live Ethereum mainnet verification, a successful protected swap on a controlled Tenderly mainnet fork, reproducible evidence, 235 automated tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send safety gates.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ALFQuote is an npm workspace written in TypeScript. It contains a reusable alfquote library, a Commander-based CLI, separate read-only verification scripts, and isolated Tenderly fork-evidence tooling. The onchain integration uses viem for Ethereum RPC reads, ABI encoding and decoding, event parsing, storage access, calldata construction, and transaction simulation.
The discovery service reads the official DualPool factory registry at an explicit block. For each deployment, it verifies provenance in both directions: the factory must recognize the hook, and the hook must report the expected factory. Pool discovery scans PoolManager Initialize logs, filters by the exact event signature, reconstructs every PoolKey field, and derives the PoolId to check it against the event. Explicit fixtures remain clearly labeled and never inherit a factory claim.
Assessment is deliberately conservative. ERC-165 support and required IALFHook views establish compatibility. Provenance, routing policy, and upgradeability remain independent. Proxy detection checks EIP-1967 implementation, beacon, and admin storage slots, plus EIP-1167 minimal-proxy bytecode. Failed or incomplete reads produce unknown or unverified, never a favorable guess.
The quote service checks isLive() and livePools(poolId) before quoting. It reads maxGas() and uses that value as the quote call’s gas bound. It then reports three different liquidity signals:
Vanilla PoolManager liquidity
Total DualPool reserves
Effective liquidity currently usable for swaps
The mainnet proof showed why this distinction matters: the selected PoolManager position reported zero vanilla liquidity while the DualPool hook had positive effective liquidity and returned a non-zero quote.
Protected swaps are encoded for Universal Router v2 using V4_SWAP, SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE, SETTLE_ALL, and TAKE_ALL. The release path always uses empty DualPool hookData. amountOutMinimum is calculated from the quote and an explicit slippage value. Simulation checks the sender’s token balance, ERC-20 approval to Permit2, Permit2 approval to Universal Router, and Permit2 expiration. Reverts are decoded and classified conservatively. The public library contains no wallet client, private key, signer, approval transaction, or broadcast function.
Tenderly was used as a controlled mainnet-fork environment because a read-only mainnet address did not have the balances and Permit2 approvals needed to prove successful execution. A fresh evidence run funded an isolated test address, submitted normal approval transactions, and executed a protected 1 USDC swap. The quote, minimum output, actual output, gas, balance changes, and hook events were reconciled. Mainnet remained read-only, and the successful fork simulation remains the primary execution proof.
The CLI uses Commander 15 and exposes injectable arguments, environment variables, and output sinks so command behavior can be tested without spawning processes. Human and JSON output come from the same structured result. Big integers are serialized as decimal strings, RPC credentials are redacted, and long calldata is preserved without truncation. Exit codes distinguish success, typed skips, invalid input, unavailable evidence, swap blockers, configuration problems, and internal failures.
The repository uses Vitest for unit and integration coverage. CI performs a clean install, type-check, build, 235 tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send scans. An offline end-to-end test drives all four commands through one mocked transport. An opt-in integration script verifies the complete journey against live Ethereum mainnet.

projects.title: Helico
projects.description: An agent trades and grows your idle capital without ever taking token custody.
projects.project_description: Helico lets an AI agent manage your capital without ever taking custody of it. Instead of granting an open-ended token approval to an external bot, you receive a counterfactual smart contract account at a precomputed address, allowing it to receive funds before deployment. You name Helico's agent — a contract, not a key — and explicitly whitelist allowed markets. The agent cannot call functions that transfer tokens elsewhere or specify arbitrary recipients—it can only allocate capital across your approved venues. Capital recovery is permanently guaranteed: the emergency escape hatch resides directly in the proxy rather than the implementation contract, meaning no upgrade can alter or remove it. Even when tested against a hostile implementation, the account owner retains full clawback authority. Execution is a Chainlink CRE workflow that registers handlerInTee — the handler is declared for the AWS Nitro enclave the network provides — and runs on Chainlink's DON. Every five minutes, it scans every account, evaluates real-time yields across four lending markets, and balances idle liquidity against active allocations. Strategy thresholds are secrets the Vault DON releases only to that handler; what leaves is only the final rebalancing decision — as a report the DON signs and writes to Arbitrum One through Chainlink's KeystoneForwarder, into the agent contract your account named. No key of ours is in that path: the forwarder is the only address that can reach the agent's onReport, a DON transmitter pays the gas, and the agent can only call the two functions your account lets an agent call. In practice it moves capital to whichever pays most — Morpho at 4.32%, Compound USDC at 2.83%, Aave at 2.69%, Compound ETH at 1.26% as of today. Fifteen such moves are on chain across five owners' accounts, sent by nine different DON transmitters under one policy hash, each with the account's own event confirming what moved; the latest landed 23 seconds after a fresh wallet's single signature. Allocated funds remain fully liquid and spendable. Through a 1inch Aqua mandate, your tokens never leave your wallet — the app holds a ledger entry, not money. When a taker executes a swap, the app unwinds the exact deficit from the lending venue mid-transaction, eliminating the traditional tradeoff between earning yield and staying liquid. Three such fills are on Arbitrum One: each one spent the account's idle cent first, redeemed exactly the shortfall out of Morpho inside the swap, paid the taker, and left the rest earning — and within two runs the network had restored the floor and lent out the ether the taker paid. A dedicated subgraph, published to The Graph Network, provides visibility across the system. Because Aqua balances are nested multiple layers deep without indexed event parameters, querying active mandates for a wallet is impossible directly on-chain; the indexing layer bridges this gap to surface full portfolio activity. The chat reads that index through The Graph's Subgraph MCP, so a question about your position is answered from the data, with the queries shown beside the answer.

Additionally, we added an on-chain instruction to a fork of 1inch's SwapVM—returning opcode 34 for AQUA_YIELD_COVER_OPCODE()—letting a concentrated position pay a taker directly out of an active lending position. The Graph A custom subgraph indexes both Aqua and our account factory. The frontend queries this index through an intermediate Go caching service with operation-name whitelisting to protect API quota limits. Two Graph products, composed. The subgraph is published to The Graph Network (id 7Qw2zNn9recjF81BVL), and the chat backend composes it with The Graph's Subgraph MCP server: a status question —"why has nothing moved?" — opens an MCP session, hands the model the subgraph's schema, and lets it write its own GraphQL against our subgraph, at most five queries, pinned to that one id. The answer comes back as the last step beneath the reply, with every MCP call shown as a step above it — initialize, schema, each qhether the schema accepted it — so the reads that produced the sentence are visible beside it.Asked what is left in a mandate a taker had just filled against, it answered the ledger's figure to the micro-unit. The enclave keeps its direct GraphQL read; the composition lives in the natural-language interface. Engineering Highlights Declared Asset Scope: The enclave batches every market and asset into a single eth_call, and a venue reverts when asked about an asset it does not list, so one refusal would fail the whole run. Markets now declare which assets they list, and a market that declares none serves them all. Declared rather than inferred ropped call, a paused venue, and a market that genuinely does not hold the asset all arrive as thesame silence. Precise Share Conversions: A share count is not an amount of money, so conversions go through tdeem rather than arithmetic copied out of it. Copied arithmetic works today and drifts from thecontract that actually burns the shares. Upgradeable Proxies: Both Aqua contracts and the agent sit behind the same lightweight 163-byteintegration tests proving active mandates persist across implementation upgrades and that areplaced agent implementation brings its own forwarder and workflow owner with it. AI assistance is logged in AI-USAGE.md, each entry naming what was asked for, what changed, and what was verified, and implementation plaplans/ before the code, 41 of them.

projects.title: WayFare
projects.description: Agents with hardcoded endpoints aren't a market. Wayfare's agent finds its providers at runtime.
projects.project_description: Every agentic-payments demo hardcodes its endpoints. The agent already knows every service it will ever call, which means there is no discovery, no choice, and no market — just a scripted workflow with a payment attached. Wayfare removes the config file. Its agent starts a run with a task, a budget, and no tools. It resolves an ENS parent name to enumerate providers it has never seen, reads each one's agent-context record to learn what it does and what it costs, and decides which are worth paying for. Payment happens per call over x402 on Hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every settled call is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, so the record of which provider was paid, how much, and for what is publicly verifiable rather than self-reported. Because nothing is hardcoded, the agent's behaviour changes with its environment. Add a provider while the demo is running and the agent finds it on the next run with no code change. Cut its budget and it makes a different choice — cheaper provider, fewer calls, or it declines to proceed. Providers cannot write their own reputation records; that permission is held separately, so track record is something earned rather than claimed. Wayfare is infrastructure, not an app. The agent is the demonstration; the discovery, settlement, and receipt layer underneath is the product.
projects.how_its_made: Wayfare is a TypeScript monorepo: an agent runtime, three independent x402-gated provider services, an ENS identity package, and a React frontend streaming over WebSocket. Hedera handles settlement. Each provider returns 402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED with its price; the agent constructs a transfer transaction, signs it with its own key, and deliberately leaves it incomplete so the fee payer can finalise it. That partially signed transaction goes back as proof of intent, and the provider forwards it to the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies it, adds its own signature to cover gas, and submits it. No provider in the system ever pays gas or settles on-chain itself. Pricing is metered per call rather than flat, so cost scales with the work requested. Every settled call writes a receipt to an HCS topic — provider name, amount, transaction id, result hash — confirmed via Mirror Node and linked to HashScan in the UI. ENS is the discovery layer, not decoration. Each provider is a subname carrying ENSIP-26 records: agent-context describing its capability and pricing in a form an LLM reads directly, and agent-endpoint[mcp] pointing at its callable interface. The agent has no provider list; it resolves one. Enhanced Access Control is what makes the reputation record trustworthy — the role permitted to write it belongs to the settlement recorder, not to the provider being rated. Bazantic sits between the agent and the providers. Each provider's API is registered as a gateway with a Recipe explaining when it's useful, what it needs, and how to read the result, exposed through Bazantic's MCP server. projects.project_description_markdown:
Every agentic-payments demo hardcodes its endpoints. The agent already knows every service it will ever call, which means there is no discovery, no choice, and no market — just a scripted workflow with a payment attached.

Wayfare removes the config file. Its agent starts a run with a task, a budget, and no tools. It resolves an ENS parent name to enumerate providers it has never seen, reads each one's agent-context record to learn what it does and what it costs, and decides which are worth paying for. Payment happens per call over x402 on Hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every settled call is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, so the record of which provider was paid, how much, and for what is publicly verifiable rather than self-reported.

Because nothing is hardcoded, the agent's behaviour changes with its environment. Add a provider while the demo is running and the agent finds it on the next run with no code change. Cut its budget and it makes a different choice — cheaper provider, fewer calls, or it declines to proceed. Providers cannot write their own reputation records; that permission is held separately, so track record is something earned rather than claimed.

Wayfare is infrastructure, not an app. The agent is the demonstration; the discovery, settlement, and receipt layer underneath is the product.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Wayfare is a TypeScript monorepo: an agent runtime, three independent x402-gated provider services, an ENS identity package, and a React frontend streaming over WebSocket.

Hedera handles settlement. Each provider returns 402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED with its price; the agent constructs a transfer transaction, signs it with its own key, and deliberately leaves it incomplete so the fee payer can finalise it. That partially signed transaction goes back as proof of intent, and the provider forwards it to the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies it, adds its own signature to cover gas, and submits it. No provider in the system ever pays gas or settles on-chain itself. Pricing is metered per call rather than flat, so cost scales with the work requested. Every settled call writes a receipt to an HCS topic — provider name, amount, transaction id, result hash — confirmed via Mirror Node and linked to HashScan in the UI.

ENS is the discovery layer, not decoration. Each provider is a subname carrying ENSIP-26 records: agent-context describing its capability and pricing in a form an LLM reads directly, and agent-endpoint[mcp] pointing at its callable interface. The agent has no provider list; it resolves one. projects.title: VaultBreaker
projects.description: AI agent capability broker protecting private keys via Ledger seed & Hedera on-chain spend limits
projects.project_description: Vaultbreaker is a scoped-capability broker designed to solve the single biggest security threat in autonomous Web3 AI agents: raw private key exposure. Today, any AI agent executing autonomous micropayments for pay-per-call APIs or services either holds a raw private key in memory (allowing prompt injections or compromised agents to drain the wallet) or a static API key (exposing credentials with no spend limits). There is no standard pattern for giving an agent narrow, expiring, spend-limited, and non-exfiltratable payment authority. Vaultbreaker solves this by combining Ledger hardware seed protection with Hedera on-chain budget enforcement and tamper-evident audit logging: DEVELOPER POLICY REGISTRATION: A developer registers a metered pay-per-call service (e.g., an AI inference endpoint) and defines a spend policy specifying maximum price per call, daily budget ceiling, and token time-to-live (TTL). LEDGER-PROTECTED CAPABILITY ISSUANCE: When an agent requests authority for a task, the Vaultbreaker broker invokes the Ledger Key Ring CLI ( wallet-cli ring ) to encrypt the underlying settlement credential using Ledger seed-derived hardware protection. The broker issues a short-lived, scoped capability token to the agent. The agent NEVER sees or holds the raw private key at any point. x402 METERED SERVICE EXECUTION: The agent presents its capability token + payment header to the x402-gated metered service. An x402 facilitator adapter validates the scope and remaining budget against the deployed smart contracts on Hedera Testnet ( CapabilityRegistry.sol ), decrementing the budget on-chain per call. REAL-TIME ON-CHAIN REJECTION (THE DEMO MOMENT): If the agent attempts a call after its budget is exhausted, expired, or explicitly revoked, the transaction is rejected ON-CHAIN in real time. The raw credential was never exposed, proving that limits are cryptographically and on-chain enforced rather than just a UI promise. HEDERA CONSENSUS SERVICE (HCS) AUDIT FEED: Every capability issuance, successful spend, on-chain rejection, and revocation event is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, producing an immutable, judge-legible audit trail rendered in real time on the frontend timeline.
projects.how_its_made:
Vaultbreaker is built as a three-plane architecture spanning smart contracts, a hardware-secured broker backend, and a cybernetic Next.js frontend: SETTLEMENT & ENFORCEMENT PLANE (Smart Contracts):
Built with Solidity 0.8.20, Foundry, and OpenZeppelin Contracts. CapabilityRegistry.sol : Deployed on Hedera Testnet (EVM Chain ID 296). Tracks capability policy hashes, remaining budget accounting, expiration timestamps, and revocation state. Reverts transactions on budget exhaustion ( InsufficientBudget ), expiry ( CapabilityExpired ), or revocation ( CapabilityRevokedError ). X402FacilitatorAdapter.sol : Serves as the thin adapter between x402 payment callbacks and CapabilityRegistry , ensuring payment settlement occurs only if capability spend checks succeed. Tested using a complete Foundry test suite (8/8 tests passing) covering time-warped expirations ( vm.warp ), budget exhaustion, and exact arithmetic. ISSUANCE & HARDWARE ENCLAVE PLANE (Broker Backend):
Built with Node.js, TypeScript, Express, Ethers.js v6, and Vitest. Ledger Key Ring Integration: Integrates the Ledger Wallet CLI ( wallet-cli ring ) as the root of trust to encrypt underlying settlement credentials. Includes a seed-derived AES-256-GCM fallback keyring to guarantee zero credential exposure across all environments. Policy Engine: Generates cryptographic policy hashes ( keccak256 ) and signs scoped, short-lived JWT capability tokens for the agent. Vitest Suite & E2E Runner: Includes 4/4 Vitest unit tests and an automated end-to-end integration test ( scripts/e2e-demo-test.ts ). AUDIT PLANE (Hedera Consensus Service):
Integrates @hashgraph/sdk to submit structured JSON audit events ( CAPABILITY_ISSUED , CAPABILITY_SPENT , CAPABILITY_REJECTED , CAPABILITY_REVOKED ) to a Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic. The backend auto-polls the Hedera Mirror Node REST API ( mirrornode.hedera.com ) to populate a live timeline with HashScan verification links. FRONTEND & UX:
Built with Next.js 16 (App Router + Turbopack), React 19, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide React. Features a Developer Console (policy registration & revocation), an Agent Terminal (simulated x402 micropayment runner with real-time budget gauges), a prominent "REJECTED ON-CHAIN IN REAL-TIME" Cyber-Alert modal for over-budget calls, and a live HCS Audit Feed timeline.

projects.title: ARCANUM
projects.description: Governed USDC wallets for AI agents on Arc, now with signed, offline-verifiable payment receipts.
projects.project_description: Arcanum is a wallet layer for AI agents that have to spend money. Instead of handing an agent a normal wallet and hoping the prompt holds, each agent gets a GuardedWallet contract on Arc with a policy attached by the owner: how much it can spend per payment, per day and per month, which vendor categories it can pay, whether the destination has to be on an allowlist, and the amount above which a human has to look at it. The contract checks all of that inside the same transaction that moves the USDC. Small routine payments just go through. Anything over the review threshold gets held on chain until someone on the council approves or rejects it. Unknown destinations get denied. There is nothing to bypass because the rule lives in the same place as the money. I have been building this for a while and the app was already live before ETHOnline, so this is a Continuity entry. The repo has a tag marking where the event started, and PRE-EXISTING.md in the root walks through what was there before and what I added during the event, commit by commit. What I added is payment decision receipts. The idea came from a gap I kept running into. The wallet enforces policy and the indexer shows what happened after the fact, but there was no way to prove what the policy said about one specific payment at one specific moment, especially for a deny, which reverts and leaves nothing on chain. So now, before an agent pays, it can ask for a receipt. The API evaluates the exact signed payment intent against the wallet's policy at one pinned block and signs the result. The receipt has the verdict (allow, escalate, deny or freeze), the reason code, the caps and spend counters it looked at, the vendor entry, whether the signer was authorized, the block number and hash, and the agent's own signature over the request. You can verify it offline against a published issuer registry, no account, no API call. There is a public verify page on the site that does it in the browser. The receipt id also goes into the calldata of the transaction that acts on it. Afterwards the API links the transaction back to the receipt as evidence: executed, escalated, reverted, and later the council's outcome. An auditor can put the decision next to what actually happened and see whether the chain agreed. One thing I want to be clear about: a receipt never authorizes anything. The contract has no idea receipts exist and evaluates policy again when the transaction lands. The receipt is a record of a decision, not a permission slip. Everything for this sits on the ethonline-2026 branch: the receipt format and verifier, issuance and evidence linking in the API, the SDK methods (requestPaymentReceipt, executePaymentIntentWithReceipt and attachPaymentReceiptEvidence, and the SDK verifies every receipt before it acts on one), the receipts pages in the dashboard with an evidence timeline, the public verify page, a Circle signer so the agent can sign from a Circle developer-controlled wallet instead of a key file on its own machine, and an inbound CCTP V2 funding flow so a governed wallet on Arc can be topped up from Sepolia USDC.
projects.how_its_made: The base is what Arcanum already was: Solidity 0.8.24 contracts built with Foundry (GuardedWallet, WalletFactory, PolicyEngine, VendorRegistry, EscalationManager, AnomalyOracle, all on Arc Testnet), a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js 15 app, tRPC with SIWE sessions, Supabase for the read models, a Ponder indexer feeding them, viem and wagmi on the client, and a TypeScript and a Python SDK. I did not touch the contracts during the event. Receipts live next to them. The receipt body is a strict schema. Unknown fields are rejected, addresses are lowercased, anything that can exceed 2^53 is a decimal string. It gets serialized with a subset of RFC 8785 (sorted keys, no whitespace, no floats) and hashed with SHA-256, so the digest comes out identical in TypeScript, Python or anything else. The issuer signs that digest with a plain EIP-191 personal signature over a fixed prefix plus the digest. Issuer keys are published in a registry with validity windows, per chain, so verification works offline and I can rotate keys later without breaking old receipts. The API refuses to issue if its configured key is not an active registry entry for the chain it is running on. To issue one, the API reads the wallet, the policy engine, the vendor registry and the escalation manager with normal eth_calls, all at the same pinned block. The annoying part was the spend windows. The contract rolls the daily and monthly counters over based on block timestamp, so the receipt has to do the same math at that block's timestamp or it would show numbers executeUSDC would never see. After the last read it checks the block hash again; if it changed, that is a CHAIN_READ_FAILED, not a wrong receipt. Envelopes are stored in a Supabase table with a trigger that blocks updates and deletes. Issuance is idempotent per intent reference, so asking twice gets you the original back flagged as replayed. Nothing goes on chain to issue a receipt. For evidence, the agent puts the receipt id inside the reason string of executeUSDC. To link, the client only sends a transaction hash. The API pulls the transaction and its logs from the Arc RPC itself, requires exactly one matching event from that wallet, notes whether the calldata actually names the receipt, and appends a row: executed, escalated, frozen or reverted, then later the escalation status, each with a flag for whether the chain agreed with the verdict. A denied executeUSDC reverts and emits nothing, so a deny only exists as a receipt, and a revert is evidenced from the transaction status alone. One transaction can only ever link to one receipt. In the SDK, verifyPaymentReceipt runs four separate checks: format, digest, issuer signature, and the agent's request signature. executePaymentIntentWithReceipt will not submit unless all four pass and the receipt actually answers the intent it just signed. It also will not act on a replayed receipt by default, because the earlier attempt may already have paid and the contract does not dedupe references, so a second executeUSDC is simply a second payment. The dashboard and the public verify page run the exact same verifier in the browser. Verification never talks to the API. The Circle piece is a viem local account whose signMessage, signTransaction and signTypedData get forwarded to a Circle developer-controlled wallet, so the agent's key lives in Circle's MPC setup and never on the agent's box. I treat Circle as a signing oracle, not something to trust: every signature has to recover to the wallet address, a signed transaction gets parsed back and compared field by field against what I asked for, the entity secret gets re-encrypted for every single request because Circle rejects reused ciphertext, and the SDK does gas estimation and broadcasting to Arc on its own. The thing that cost me the most time: the wallet has to be created on Circle's generic EVM-TESTNET identifier. Named chains like ARC-TESTNET do not support transaction signing, and it took a while to work out that this was what the error meant. The governed wallet, the policy and the receipts have no idea Circle is behind the signer. CCTP funding burns native USDC on Sepolia with CCTP V2 and mints straight into the governed wallet on Arc. I request Circle's Forwarding Service for the destination mint and keep a separately approved, gas-capped manual relay for when forwarding does not finish. Settlement is checked strictly against the attestation, the nonce and the MessageReceived log on Arc. One detail worth knowing on Arc: USDC is also the gas token, native balances are 18 decimals while the ERC-20 side is 6, and the funding code has to keep those apart or the amounts are off by a lot. On process: most of the event code, tests, the migration and the docs were written by an AI coding agent working from my written plan, with a second AI reviewing each slice. Design decisions, deployment, the testnet runs and the video are mine. No new npm dependencies were added. It is all written up in PRE-EXISTING.md.
