projects.title: AgentARC
projects.description: Agent to agent commerce on ARC: Identity,policy, nanopayments, and escrow.
projects.project_description:
AgentARC lets one agent pay another agent in USDC on Circle Arc. I built it around four problems in agentic commerce. Who to trust: every agent has a Circle wallet, and we only pay sellers we can identify.
What to buy: the agent reads your prompt, finds our seller on Arc, and checks Circle’s marketplace so we don’t overpay.
Whether to pay: small instant jobs go out right away; big or risky jobs hold the money first; bad identity or overspend never pays.
How to settle: we hold USDC, check the delivery, then pay the seller or send it back. After it’s paid, it stays paid, no chargebacks. Circle Agent Stack in the demo: Agent Wallets, USDC on Arc, Agent Marketplace, Nanopayments, and AuthCapture escrow.
projects.how_its_made: I built AgentARC as a TypeScript app running on Node 20 with two lightweight HTTP processes: a buyer orchestrator on port 5180 and an independent x402 seller on port 5181. I used Node’s native http module, vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, and Vitest to keep the stack simple. The flow is: user intent, discovery, ERC-8004 trust signals, deterministic policy, Circle Agent Wallet, USDC on Arc, x402 seller, verification and then receipt. I used Circle’s developer-controlled wallets for keys and transactions. USDC is both payment and gas on Arc Testnet. x402 gates paid seller APIs using HTTP 402. ERC-8004 data from 8004scan provides identity, feedback, validations, and x402 support as separate signals. CoinGecko provides live ETH pricing and OHLC data, while OpenAI is optional for intent parsing with a regex fallback. I kept payment decisions deterministic with a rules engine. It fail-closes when identity is missing or failures are high. Small objective jobs use direct nanopayments, while larger or subjective jobs use protected escrow-style flows. The hacky part was making this reliable on Arc testnet. When Circle’s x402 settlement and contract execution APIs failed, I implemented controlled USDC transfer and AuthCapture fallbacks. I also split the seller into a separate process after discovering that internal API calls could deadlock the original server.

The hacky part was making this reliable on Arc testnet. When Circle’s x402 settlement and contract execution APIs failed, I implemented controlled USDC transfer and AuthCapture fallbacks. I also split the seller into a separate process after discovering that internal API calls could deadlock the original server.

projects.title: Maneki
projects.description: Web3 job board for AI agents: open MCP + AgentKit-verified AI matching. Discover free, act human.
projects.project_description: Maneki (maneki.work) is a live Web3 job board — thousands of active roles scraped nightly from 60+ sources, browsed daily by human candidates. Job-hunting AI agents are coming, and recruiting spam from unverified automation is already here. This project gives agents a first-class way in, with World ID deciding who gets it for free. The Maneki Agent Gateway exposes two surfaces. Discovery is open, like the web: an MCP server (search_jobs, get_job, list_hiring_companies) that any AI assistant can use with no signup and no API key — just per-IP rate limits. Actions are human-verified: full search results with salary data and AI matching against a real CV sit behind x402. An agent registered on AgentBook — meaning a real, unique, Orb-verified human stands behind its wallet — gets a free quota tied to the anonymous human id, not the wallet address. Spinning up fresh wallets doesn't reset it: Sybil-resistant rate limiting with no accounts, no cookies, no API keys. Everyone else pays $0.01 USDC per request on World Chain or Base. The payoff: on the website, AI matching requires an email signup gate. For agents, proof of personhood replaces the account entirely. A verified agent posts a CV and gets back scored, ranked matches (23 matches judged from 1,940 candidates in our live demo) — and every application will carry proof that one real human is behind it. That's the spam filter recruiters actually need, and the foundation for continuity: a quota, a match history and a reputation that follow the human across wallets, agents and services. Live: https://maneki-agent-gateway.vercel.app (MCP at /api/mcp) · https://maneki.work/agents
projects.how_its_made: The gateway is genuinely registered — agentkit-cli + World App, transaction on World Chain — and the E2E demo runs a real PDF CV (pdf-parse) through agentkit.fetch. The job data never leaves as a dataset: the gateway queries a private, key-authenticated API on the Maneki Next.js app query-by-query (no bulk export, capped results, links point to Maneki job pages only — anti zero-click by design). The matching endpoint reuses Maneki's production pipeline: deterministic gates first, then LLM judging of shortlisted candidates against the CV. The hacky bit worth mentioning: @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1's client parses the 402 payment-required payload from the response body, but x402 2.25 servers emit it as a base64 response header with an empty body — the reference stack can't complete its own handshake. We ship a response middleware that mirrors the header payload back into the body so both client generations work, and documented it (plus Developer Portal and Sandbox access friction, and a facilitator cold-start timeout we hit in production) in FEEDBACK.md in the repo. Deployed on Vercel via the Hono framework preset after discovering the Node adapter buffers responses and kills MCP streaming — that migration story is in the commit history.

projects.title: HoldBook
projects.description: A prototype for tokenized asset issuance, KYC, and hold workflows on Hedera.
projects.project_description: HoldBook is a secondary-market prototype for fictional equity on Hedera Testnet. Eligible users sign NOVA/HBAR orders, which are matched by price-time priority. Sellers lock tokens through ATS Holds, and buyers pay for atomic delivery and settlement. Recorded tests cover normal trades, reverse trades, cancellation and expired-Hold recovery. KYC is synthetic, and reviewers can explore the demo without a wallet.
projects.how_its_made: Built with React, TypeScript, Hedera ATS SDK and MetaMask. A Go service authenticates signed orders, matches trades and stores results in PostgreSQL. A Solidity contract executes ATS Holds and HBAR payments atomically. GitHub Pages, Cloud Run and Neon host the application. AI assistance is documented, wallet actions require manual approval, and original software is MIT-licensed.

projects.title: Arbitra
projects.description: The AI-operated escrow court and reputation protocol for the agentic economy.
projects.project_description: Arbitra is a trust-minimized, auditable AI escrow and arbitration protocol for autonomous agents. Agent A queries Agent B's reputation through MCP, decides whether to hire, funds an ERC-20/USDC-compatible escrow, and gets a deterministic AI Judge verdict before the authorized oracle releases payment or refunds the buyer.
projects.how_its_made: We built Arbitra using a tri-layer architecture: EVM Smart Contracts, a Node.js AI Oracle, and an MCP Reputation Agent. Think of the protocol like a high-tech courtroom: the Smart Contract acts as the impenetrable vault holding the funds, the MCP Server is the private investigator running background checks, and the Node.js backend is the active judge rendering the final verdict. Technologies & Partner Integrations Arc Testnet & Circle: We deployed our ArbiterEscrow.sol contract to the Arc Testnet using Hardhat Ignition. Arc was incredibly beneficial because it treats USDC as a native system-level gas token (0x360...000) while remaining completely EVM-compatible. This allowed us to use standard OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 interfaces without rewriting any Solidity logic for custom token behaviors. The Graph: To satisfy the AI tooling track, we built an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that acts as an autonomous risk assessor. It seamlessly queries The Graph's Uniswap V3 and Aave V3 subgraphs to pull a seller's DeFi history. By combining live Graph data with our backend's escrow history, our AI can contextually reason about a wallet's risk profile—such as warning a buyer if a seller has zero escrow history but is heavily gambling capital on highly volatile meme coins. Backend Oracle: The core engine is a Node.js backend using Prisma and Ethers.js v6. It listens for DeliverableSubmitted events on-chain, fetches the associated work, evaluates it using Gemini 2.5 Flash, and signs a resolveEscrow transaction to release funds or issue a refund.

projects.title: T3 Trade
projects.description: An agentic trading environment for your existing AI subscriptions, with enforced risk limits.
projects.project_description: T3 Trade is an open-source agentic trading environment. It gives coding agents a trading workspace with charts, market research, backtests and missions that have a strategy, an expiry and a maximum-loss budget. You can use supported agent providers through their existing CLI logins. An agent can read the market, publish a plan and wake when a price level or candle condition changes. The server checks every proposed order before signing. Position increases require an exchange-native stop, retries use deterministic order IDs, and the user can pause, reduce, close or revoke a mission even when the agent is offline. Perpetual-futures execution is restricted to Hyperliquid testnet. Research works without a signer. T3 Forge extends this workflow to Ethereum research. Agents can build typed detectors that combine external sources with onchain swap facts from The Graph. Generated code must pass typechecking, tests and host-reviewed acceptance cases in an isolated container before installation. Each detector retains its evidence and can be armed or disarmed without granting permission to spend. The repository also contains a fixed Uniswap v4 fee hook for a dedicated Sepolia testnet pool, with expiring policies and an owner-controlled pause. T3 Trade is an alpha built on the open-source T3 Code workspace. The contribution is the trading and research system around that workspace, including deterministic risk checks, market-data recording, event-driven missions and sandboxed detector development. It does not promise returns or offer unattended trading with real funds.
projects.how_its_made: We forked T3 Code to reuse its agent conversations, repository workflows and desktop shell, then added the trading domain. The web client uses React and TypeScript, the desktop app uses Electron, and the server uses Effect services with SQLite persistence. Typed WebSocket contracts connect the client to server commands. Persisted events drive read models and queued side effects, so the UI sends intent while server-side services enforce policy. The Hyperliquid adapter owns exchange reads and local signing. A 17-check preview validates mission authority, sizing, leverage, market freshness, risk reservations and stop requirements before an order can proceed. Reconciliation treats exchange positions, orders and fills as authoritative. Pure accounting rules and property tests cover budget exhaustion and reservations. For Ethereum research, The Graph provides indexed Uniswap swap facts. Source adapters verify deployment identity, indexing errors and freshness before evidence can count as current. The repository includes a Rust Substreams package and a cursor-based ingestion path for pool observations. T3 Forge compiles agent-authored TypeScript detectors in a digest-pinned Docker image with no network, a read-only root and a non-root user. Generated tests and separate host-reviewed acceptance cases gate installation. Missing or stale evidence produces an unknown reading. The Solidity Uniswap v4 hook is fixed code. It binds to one pool, supports expiring fee policies and falls back to its baseline fee when a policy expires or the owner pauses it. Its authority is separate from Hyperliquid signing. General Uniswap swap drafts currently stop with an explicit broadcaster-missing refusal; a draft is not presented as an executed trade. The difficult part was separating what an agent may propose from what the host may execute. We kept permissions, spending limits, idempotency and reconciliation in typed services rather than prompts, and made the user's reverse actions work without a running model.

projects.title: SUBFLOOR
projects.description: A signed price floor enforced inside 1inch SwapVM settlement, so an agent cannot sell below it
projects.project_description: SUBFLOOR is a vault where an autonomous agent trades your whole portfolio and one thing is impossible by arithmetic: a fill below the worst price you signed. The floor is not enforced by the strategy, the agent, or anyone watching the mempool. It lives in the settlement function itself, the code no program can reach around, and a machine-checked proof covers every program that could ever run, not just the ones we tested. The authority to set the floor sits on a hardware device in your hand, so the machine that trades is never the machine that defines "worst." A public index recomputes every fill against every floor, so the guarantee is not our claim about our own execution, it is anyone's query. It runs live on mainnet with our own money. A detector can be wrong. A bound cannot. Prior art, named because it is real: CoW Protocol's settlement contract already enforces on-chain that no order clears worse than what it specifies. But that is taker-side and per discrete order, one signed order at a time. Nothing covers a delegated maker running continuous two-sided programmatic strategies on standing inventory, which is exactly what an agent-run book is. This property exists for taker orders. Nobody gives it to delegated makers. SUBFLOOR implements ERC-8377 (Reference-Relative Slippage Bounds), a draft standard I authored (ethereum/ERCs PR #1935, public since Aug 2026). The specification is public prior art; every line of implementation here was written during the event, and none of the ERC's reference implementation is reused.

projects.title: Stratus Finance
projects.description: Deposit gold + S&P 500 as one token, borrow with isolated per-asset risk on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Stratus Finance lets users deposit a Real-World-Asset basket (tokenized gold plus a tokenized S&P 500 index, minted via Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio) and borrow stablecoins against it. Existing lending protocols like Aave and Morpho only accept single-asset RWA collateral, because a combined basket is hard to price and hard to liquidate safely. Stratus solves this with look-through isolation: the vault decomposes the basket into two separate, independently configured lending reserves at deposit time, each with its own loan-to-value ratio and liquidation threshold. If gold crashes, only the gold reserve gets liquidated. The S&P 500 position keeps backing the loan, untouched. Built on a real, unmodified Aave v2 fork (Bonzo Finance), with real ATS tokens and real RedStone price feeds for gold and the S&P 500 index. Every stage, mint, deposit and decompose, borrow, and isolated liquidation in both directions, has been run for real on Hedera testnet with recorded transaction hashes, not just unit tested.
projects.how_its_made: The lending core is a real, unmodified fork of bonzo-finance-contracts (Aave v2), deployed through the actual upgradeable-proxy flow, not reimplemented. GOLD-x and STOCK-x are real Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) Equity diamonds, issued directly via @hashgraph/asset-tokenization-contracts, with control-list compliance gating navigated for every protocol contract: the pool, the vault, both aTokens, and the demo liquidator. Two new Solidity contracts, StratusBasketToken and StratusVault, handle the actual decomposition. Depositing the basket pulls the underlying ATS tokens and deposits each into its own isolated Aave v2 reserve on the user's behalf; recomposing reverses it. StratusRiskView is a read-only contract giving a per-component health-factor heuristic alongside the pool's real, enforced health factor. Price feeds are RedStone's real, signed pull-oracle feeds (gold tracks the real XAU spot price, the index tracks the real S&P 500 level via USA500.Y), chosen after checking every oracle actually integrated with Hedera: Pyth's Hedera receiver contract rejected valid Wormhole VAAs, a real infrastructure gap outside our control, and Chainlink and Supra had no RWA feeds on Hedera testnet at all. Chainlink stays wired in as a working alternate oracle. One genuinely hacky find along the way: a Pyth refund calculation silently rounded to zero because Hedera's 8-decimal tinybar ledger drops native-value amounts below 1e10 wei. We fixed it and contributed the check upstream to hedera-dev/hedera-harness.

projects.title: Kyro
projects.description: Wallet trust checks and advisory USDC limits before Arc payments.
projects.project_description: Kyro checks a wallet before you pay it. You give it an address or a Kyro username and the use case (payment, escrow, lending or marketplace). It answers allow, caution or block, with an advisory USDC limit and the evidence behind the answer. It can also write an immutable receipt of the check. Kyro is advisory and non-custodial. It never holds keys or funds and it cannot move or stop a transaction. Kyro has been live on Arc Testnet since before the event. The check at thekyro.co/check works without an account. The same answer is one anonymous GET on the public API, which has 10 operations, an OpenAPI 3.1 spec and a TypeScript SDK on npm. For ETHOnline I built two things, both in the public repo. The devkit: SDK source, spec, examples and docs. The agent gate: a small agent that pays USDC invoices on Arc Testnet through the Circle CLI and asks Kyro before every payment. Allow within the limit pays, caution or an amount over the limit holds for a human, block refuses. If Kyro does not answer, nothing is paid. On 9 September the gate paid 1.5 USDC live from a Circle agent wallet; the transaction hash and Arcscan link are in the README. A dry-run mode runs the same flow with no credentials. Mainnet activation is scheduled for 16 September. CHANGELOG-ETHONLINE.md lists what existed before the event and what was built during it.
projects.how_its_made: The product is a Next.js app with API routes and a Postgres evidence store. Indexers read wallet history from Arc RPC and a few other EVM chains. A verified attestation is a transaction hash on Arc that involves both wallets; Kyro checks the hash onchain and the other party has to accept it before it counts. Scoring is deterministic and versioned (identity_score_v1), so the same evidence always gives the same score. The decision model (decision_v0.4.1) turns score, coverage and freshness into the verdict and the advisory limit, with reason and warning codes a program can act on. Receipts are hashed and readable by id. The devkit is a pnpm workspace. packages/sdk is the source of @kyrodev/sdk: no runtime dependencies, typed methods for the 10 operations, a shared error type and rate-limit metadata. A drift check fails CI if the SDK and the vendored OpenAPI snapshot disagree. CI runs on Node 20 and 22. demos/agent-gate is TypeScript. A planner proposes invoices. A policy applies caps (5 USDC per transfer, 10 per run) plus a ten-minute duplicate guard. The SDK reads the Kyro decision anonymously. On proceed the executor spawns the Circle CLI once (circle wallet transfer on ARC-TESTNET) with a UUID idempotency key and parses the JSON envelope into submitted, failed or unknown. Timeouts, 429s, 5xx and malformed answers refuse the payment. Every intent and result is appended to a JSONL audit log. Tests run against fixtures and a stand-in CLI, so the suite never reaches Circle. The hacky part: the first live run on Windows died before the CLI started, because Node refuses to spawn batch shims without a shell (CVE-2024-27980). The gate reported failed and paid nothing, which is what it is for. The fix runs the .cmd shim through cmd.exe with checked arguments.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Kyro checks a wallet before you pay it. You give it an address or a Kyro username and the use case (payment, escrow, lending or marketplace). It answers allow, caution or block, with an advisory USDC limit and the evidence behind the answer. It can also write an immutable receipt of the check. Kyro is advisory and non-custodial. It never holds keys or funds and it cannot move or stop a transaction.

Kyro has been live on Arc Testnet since before the event. The check at thekyro.co/check works without an account. The same answer is one anonymous GET on the public API, which has 10 operations, an OpenAPI 3.1 spec and a TypeScript SDK on npm.

For ETHOnline I built two things, both in the public repo. The devkit: SDK source, spec, examples and docs. The agent gate: a small agent that pays USDC invoices on Arc Testnet through the Circle CLI and asks Kyro before every payment. Allow within the limit pays, caution or an amount over the limit holds for a human, block refuses. If Kyro does not answer, nothing is paid. On 9 September the gate paid 1.5 USDC live from a Circle agent wallet; the transaction hash and Arcscan link are in the README. A dry-run mode runs the same flow with no credentials.

Mainnet activation is scheduled for 16 September. CHANGELOG-ETHONLINE.md lists what existed before the event and what was built during it.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The product is a Next.js app with API routes and a Postgres evidence store. Indexers read wallet history from Arc RPC and a few other EVM chains. Scoring is deterministic and versioned (identity_score_v1), so the same evidence always gives the same score. The decision model (decision_v0.4.1) turns score, coverage and freshness into the verdict and the advisory limit, with reason and warning codes a program can act on. Receipts are hashed and readable by id.

projects.title: Air Index
projects.description: Create and own your index fund as an ENS name — composition lives entirely in the ENSv2 namespace.
projects.project_description:
Index products today are opaque and locked in. The composition of an ETF lives in a
provider's database, you cannot verify it, you cannot fork it, and you cannot take it
anywhere. Air Index makes the index itself a name. In Air Index, an index IS an ENS name. Create defi-blue.airindex.eth and you own an
index. Each constituent is a subname: weth.defi-blue.airindex.eth resolves to the
token's contract address, and its weight is stored as a data record on that same name.
There is no backend database. The entire composition of an index is the namespace, so
any wallet, app, or agent can read a full index with a stock ENS library — no Air Index
SDK required. Resolving weth.defi-blue.airindex.eth in viem returns the token address
directly. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control lets us split an index into the two things it actually
is: rules and numbers. The methodology is pinned to IPFS and written to the name's
contenthash, then permanently locked by revoking both the role and its admin role — after
that, nobody can change the rules, not even the creator. The weights, meanwhile, can be
delegated to a rebalancer with a permission scoped to a single record key, so the
rebalancer can adjust allocations but cannot swap in a different token, add a constituent,
or touch the methodology. Firing the rebalancer is one transaction. That rebalancer can be an AI agent, and it gets its own namespace:
rebalancer.defi-blue.airindex.eth holds the agent's address, and its mandate — cadence,
maximum drift, allowed asset classes — is published as text records on its own name. The
agent's on-chain permissions are exactly its published mandate, so what it is allowed to
do is publicly verifiable rather than a matter of trust. Two more things fall out of the namespace model. Short tickers work like they do for real
ETFs: dfbl.airindex.eth is a resolver-level alias of defi-blue.airindex.eth, sharing one
set of records with no duplication, the same way IBIT and "iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF" are
one product. And indexes are forkable: pointing a new name's subregistry at an existing
index's registry produces a fork that tracks the original, or you can branch and diverge.
Forking an index becomes as cheap as forking a repo.
projects.how_its_made:
Everything runs on the ENSv2 beta deployment on Sepolia. https://explorer.ens.dev/airindex.eth Structure. airindex.eth has a subregistry; every index is a subname token in it, so an
index is an ERC1155 the creator genuinely owns and can transfer or sell. Each index name
then has its own registry holding its constituents. We lean on ENSv2's longest-suffix
resolution: constituents inherit the nearest ancestor's resolver, so a constituent
resolves off the parent's resolver without needing its own, which keeps creating an index
cheap. Constituent data uses the standard profile — addr(60) for the token contract, a
data record for the weight — specifically so that nothing about reading an index requires
our code. Permissions. This is where ENSv2 does the heavy lifting. Resolvers in ENSv2 are per
account rather than per name, so we deploy one protocol-owned Permissioned Resolver
through the Verifiable Factory and scope each creator to their own index with
authorizeNameRoles. Rebalancer delegation uses authorizeDataRoles against a single record
key, which grants ROLE_SET_DATA for that key only — a name-level grant would have been a
superset and too broad. Locking the methodology calls revokeRootRoles with
ROLE_SET_CONTENTHASH OR'd with ROLE_SET_CONTENTHASH_ADMIN in one call; without the admin
role there is no path to granting it back, which is what makes the immutability real
rather than a promise. None of this was expressible in ENSv1 without the Name Wrapper's
coarse fuses. Aliasing. Tickers use setAlias at the resolver level, which required both names to sit on
the same resolver instance — one reason we went with a shared protocol resolver. Worth
noting for anyone building on this: aliases only resolve through the Universal Resolver's
resolve() path, so calling text() or addr() directly on the resolver with an aliased
namehash silently returns empty. That cost us an hour. Forking is the other kind of
aliasing — namespace-level — done by pointing a new index's subregistry at an existing
one, which is a tree operation that simply has no ENSv1 equivalent. Gotchas. ENSv2 token IDs are mutable and regenerate when roles change, so we never cache
them and always resolve to the current ID at transaction time via findTokenId. We also
never hardcode a resolver address, since a name's configured resolver is now its owner's
own deployment. Stack. Solidity with Foundry for the registrar and registry, viem plus ENSjs v4.2.3+ for
all ENS reads and writes, wagmi and Next.js on the frontend, and a public price API mapped
by symbol for portfolio valuation — prices are the only off-chain component, and index
composition is read live from Sepolia on every load, never from local state.

projects.title: ZKProofport
projects.description: Private ZK eligibility for people and AI agents using USDC financial services on Arc
projects.project_description: ZKProofport is a composable private eligibility infrastructure that enables humans and AI agents to prove required qualifications and conditions to services without revealing raw personal data or their credential wallets. In our current Arc demo, starting with Coinbase KYC, we separate the private wallet holding the KYC credential from the Arc wallet executing actual financial activities. Users can authorize a specific Arc wallet to use their KYC eligibility for a given service without disclosing their KYC wallet. AI Agents can then request and pay for the necessary proof, verify it on Arc, and execute USDC-based actions. Through this design, users reduce the exposure of sensitive personal data and credential wallets, while service providers can verify eligibility without directly collecting or storing unnecessary personal information. ZKProofport is not limited to KYC alone. We currently support Coinbase KYC and Country proofs, with plans to expand into various proof capabilities including organizational membership, balance thresholds, and RWA ownership. By allowing services to define required conditions and enabling agents to select only the necessary proofs, our goal is to build the foundation for a new generation of privacy-preserving applications on Arc—spanning RWAs, lending, payments, and gated access.
projects.how_its_made: We are expanding our agentic flow for Arc based on ZKProofport’s existing Coinbase EAS-based KYC circuit and mobile proving stack. The Noir circuit verifies targetWallet, audience, chainId, nonce, and expiresAt alongside the Coinbase KYC credential to bind the proof to a specific Arc wallet and service, while keeping the original KYC wallet as a private input. Proofs are generated using Noir and Barretenberg and verified on-chain via Arc’s EVM verifier. An AI Agent discovers the ZKProofport Prover Agent via ERC-8004 and pays a 0.001 USDC proof fee through an x402-compatible payment flow. The private witness is processed inside a TEE-backed Prover Agent, and the generated proof is verified on Arc before being used to execute KYC-gated USDC actions. We are designing this architecture to scale across Country proofs, organizational membership, balance thresholds, and RWA ownership—allowing Arc applications to compose and verify only the necessary eligibility criteria without directly handling raw personal data.

projects.title: PrivateSignal
projects.description: Private risk scores in a Chainlink TEE on  Graph data; Arc agents pay USDC and act only if cleared
projects.project_description:
PrivateSignal is confidential risk intelligence for on-chain agents. DeFi positions are public, but proprietary risk policy is not supposed to be. If scoring weights, thresholds, and cross-protocol rules are exposed, competitors copy them and agents leak intent before moving capital. Centralized black-box scorers restore secrecy but destroy verifiability.
PrivateSignal solves that with a narrow pipeline: live multi-protocol portfolio data from The Graph is aggregated across lending markets such as Aave V3 and Morpho Blue using standardized schemas and optional natural-language/MCP query entry. A proprietary risk model then runs inside a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, loading sealed model weights, thresholds, and policy profiles from Vault DON secrets. Only a public verdict leaves the enclave: score, recommendation, coarse reason codes, and execution metadata. Model internals stay sealed.
An Arc agent can pay a native USDC fee for that confidential result and is hard-gated by it. If the score clears policy, the action may proceed. If not, capital movement is blocked. The system fails closed when Graph data is missing or unreliable, rather than treating empty data as a healthy portfolio.
This is not a liquidation bot, MEV searcher, or generic dashboard. It is decision infrastructure: public market state in, private policy evaluation sealed, public verdict out, agent behavior constrained. The product thesis is composability across The Graph, Chainlink CRE confidential compute, and Arc’s native USDC agent environment.
projects.how_its_made:
PrivateSignal is assembled as a three-layer pipeline: public multi-protocol data intake, confidential scoring, and agent-side policy enforcement.
On the data side, TypeScript services query live The Graph decentralized-network subgraphs for Aave V3 and Morpho Blue. A schema mapper normalizes those responses into one UnifiedAccountData shape, and an aggregator derives cross-protocol features such as combined exposure and concentration. Natural-language prompts are routed through a Graph MCP-style path into structured queries so the judged entrypoint is not hand-written GraphQL.
The scoring core is a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow written against the CRE TypeScript SDK and compiled to QuickJS WASM. The handler is registered with handlerInTee under a Nitro TEE constraint. Inside the enclave, model weights, thresholds, and policy profiles are loaded from Vault DON secrets through batched getSecrets—a real fix we needed after sequential getSecret calls only resolved the first secret in the deployed runtime. The scorer is pure and fail-closed: missing or empty Graph data returns GRAPH_DATA_UNAVAILABLE instead of a fake healthy score. Only score, recommendation, coarse reason codes, and an honest non-claiming execution envelope leave the enclave.
The product API and Next.js frontend sit outside the DON. They prepare validated payloads, call the deployed private-registry workflow over the zone-a gateway with an authorized ECDSA EVM key, and display operator-vs-enclave boundaries without exposing sealed parameters. On Arc testnet, an agent wallet pays a native USDC fee and runs a hard allow/deny gate on the confidential result before any capital action.
Notable engineering details: secrets are the source of truth on the DON path rather than compiled constants; config targets were reconciled for local simulation vs private staging; and we deliberately avoided self-minted “verified” attestation theater. Partner stack benefit is composability: Graph for standardized public state, CRE for sealed policy evaluation, Arc for native-USDC agent enforcement.

projects.title: Bake your own memory
projects.description: Teach a foundation model one fact, it keeps it, and you are paid every time an answer uses it.
projects.project_description: Ainize compiles knowledge into a model's own memory table instead of retrieving it. We tested it on questions built from 15 Messari-standardized subgraphs pinned at block 25902936. On vault-asset questions the base model answered 0 of 13 correctly. The same model with one Ainize knowledge patch answered 11 of 13 — and only counting facts it got right across every held-out phrasing it was never trained on. It runs at $0.0000369 per question with zero network calls. On 30 facts deliberately withheld from training it scored 0/30, exactly like the base model, so the gain is the patch and not leakage. ENS mints a patch's name only if training proves it descended from its parent's checkpoint.
projects.how_its_made: Subgraph queries over 15 Messari deployments become {prompt, answer} training datasets carrying provenance — which subgraph, which query, which block, row hashes. A patch is a .npz of rows from the model's 51.2B-row n-gram memory table, where a single token addresses only 16 of 320M rows, written into a running vLLM through a live hook with no restart.

projects.title: ShelfSign
projects.description: Camera-attested stock marketplace with Hedera x402 pay-per-query and HCS receipts
projects.project_description: ShelfSign lets buyers see real, camera-attested warehouse stock instead of trusting a spreadsheet or a chat message. A warehouse camera is enrolled once by extracting its CMOS sensor's manufacturing-defect noise pattern (a PRNU-based physical fingerprint), which becomes that camera's account identity. To attest stock, our backend issues a fresh nonce; the Hikvision camera burns that nonce into its on-screen display, we OCR it back out of the captured frame, and we re-derive the camera's fingerprint from the live image to confirm it matches the enrolled sensor - not a phone photo, not a swapped camera, not a replayed video. A YOLO/PyTorch vision service then counts SKUs in the frame, and we publish a signed attestation (image hash, camera account, nonce, item counts, model hash) to Hedera Consensus Service so it is independently verifiable. Suppliers must lock a 10 HBAR bond via x402 before they can attest, and that bond is slashed if a previously Verified camera later fails an authenticity check. Buyers browse attested stock for free and pay a small Hedera x402 fee (about 0.01 HBAR) to trigger a live re-attestation on demand, then place orders against verified inventory. The result is a trust layer for supplier stock claims that is bound to physical hardware and to the current moment, not just a signature anyone holding a key could produce from an old photo.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend is a Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript app with Supabase Auth, split into supplier and buyer dashboards - warehouse/camera management and an attest wizard on the supplier side, a stock catalog and order flow on the buyer side. Backend is Node/Express + TypeScript, exposing nonce issuance, camera enroll/attest endpoints, warehouse/order APIs, Hedera HCS publishing, and an x402 payment gateway on the buyer live-attest endpoint. Vision is a Python FastAPI service running Ultralytics YOLOv8 for stock detection alongside a custom CMOS/PUF pipeline: calibration frames go through wavelet-domain PRNU extraction, a BCH fuzzy extractor turns the noisy sensor fingerprint into a stable secp256k1 keypair (the camera account), and a challenge-response flow re-derives that same key from a live frame to prove it is the same physical sensor. The camera is a Hikvision unit accessed over ISAPI; we use its OSD overlay to burn a server-issued nonce into the JPEG and OCR it back out, which stops replay of old full-shelf footage. All state lives in Supabase/Postgres with RLS. On the Hedera side we publish every attestation (type shelfsign.attestation.v1) to HCS so buyers can check image hash, camera account, nonce and counts on HashScan, and we use Hedera x402 (Blocky402) for payments - suppliers stake 10 HBAR into an escrow vault before they can enroll or attest, and buyers pay about 0.01 HBAR per live re-attest. The hacky part: since we cannot ask hackathon judges' or random suppliers' own Hedera accounts to hold real funds mid-demo, the escrow vault and slashing today run from a platform-controlled funder key rather than each supplier's own account - a limitation we call out directly rather than hide. We also built a fake-cam ISAPI stub so we can demo the CMOS-fingerprint rejection path (phone photo or wrong camera) live without a second real sensor.

Backend is Node/Express + TypeScript, exposing nonce issuance, camera enroll/attest endpoints, warehouse/order APIs, Hedera HCS publishing, and an x402 payment gateway on the buyer live-attest endpoint. Vision is a Python FastAPI service running Ultralytics YOLOv8 for stock detection alongside a custom CMOS/PUF pipeline: calibration frames go through wavelet-domain PRNU extraction, a BCH fuzzy extractor turns the noisy sensor fingerprint into a stable secp256k1 keypair (the camera account), and a challenge-response flow re-derives that same key from a live frame to prove it is the same physical sensor. The camera is a Hikvision unit accessed over ISAPI; we use its OSD overlay to burn a server-issued nonce into the JPEG and OCR it back out, which stops replay of old full-shelf footage. All state lives in Supabase/Postgres with RLS. On the Hedera side we publish every attestation (type shelfsign.attestation.v1) to HCS so buyers can check image hash, camera account, nonce and counts on HashScan, and we use Hedera x402 (Blocky402) for payments - suppliers stake 10 HBAR into an escrow vault before they can enroll or attest, and buyers pay about 0.01 HBAR per live re-attest. The hacky part: since we cannot ask hackathon judges' or random suppliers' own Hedera accounts to hold real funds mid-demo, the escrow vault and slashing today run from a platform-controlled funder key rather than each supplier's own account - a limitation we call out directly rather than hide. We also built a fake-cam ISAPI stub so we can demo the CMOS-fingerprint rejection path (phone photo or wrong camera) live without a second real sensor.

projects.title: Tare-Vault
projects.description: Tare traces DeFi vault positions, checks evidence, and explains what remains unverified.
projects.project_description: NOTE: The demo works when https://tare.visk404.dev/ is pasted directly into the browser’s address bar, but clicking an external link can trigger the origin error. What is behind my vault balance, how can I check it, and what should I investigate next? Tare is an evidence-first DeFi investigation tool for depositors, treasury reviewers and AI agents. A vault balance can hide several layers of allocations and shared lending dependencies. An accounting quote can also look reassuring without establishing custody, liquidity or full backing. Starting with a public wallet address, Tare discovers supported positions across Ethereum, Base and Arbitrum. Explorer examines one wallet–vault position, showing observed shares, contract conversion quotes, supported market exposure and eligible source checks. Investigate adds bounded multi-position analysis, shared-market relationships, comparisons between two observations, and historical share/accounting verification for Steakhouse USDC on Ethereum. The Graph supplies indexed observations for comparison with direct blockchain reads. Chainlink provides reference prices for eligible assets. An optional Bazantic Recipe explains the displayed evidence with fact citations, while the original report and limitations remain available. Tare separates observations, calculations, reference prices and unverified claims. Missing evidence stays missing; accounting agreement never becomes a universal safety score. Reports and captures can be downloaded, and compatible captures can be replayed without pretending they are fresh evidence. The public investigation flow is read-only and requires no wallet signing. A separate Chainlink CRE experiment demonstrates confidential policy evaluation and bounded execution on a dedicated Base Sepolia test control. Evidence before assumptions.
projects.how_its_made: Tare is built primarily in TypeScript, with a React/Vite interface, protected HTTP API, CLI and local stdio MCP server. Shared modules separate source acquisition, protocol adapters, integer calculations, verification and report formatting. Live acquisition and saved-capture replay reuse the same comparison logic. Discovery combines Morpho, enabled Euler supply discovery and configured ERC-4626 registry entries. RPC-backed adapters support Morpho V1 market exposure, bounded Ethereum USDC V2-to-V1 traversal and generic ERC-4626 accounting. Other supported V2 candidates receive an explicitly narrower accounting-only check rather than invented strategy coverage. Our AssemblyScript subgraph indexes Steakhouse USDC share transfers and vault/market accounting. A separate accounting-only deployment supports recent comparisons. The Graph Token API contributes wallet share-balance observations; Tare compares eligible data against block-pinned RPC, checking deployment identity, indexing errors and exact values. Historical verification joins share-ledger and accounting comparisons at one covered block. Chainlink valuation uses reviewed USDC/WETH feed mappings on Ethereum, Base and Arbitrum, with round, freshness and L2 sequencer checks. Separately, a CRE confidential handler processes authenticated Tare evidence and private policy thresholds. A retained hosted run delivered a bounded exit through Chainlink’s forwarder and our one-use Base Sepolia receiver; the latest retained configuration is paused. Bazantic exposes seven Tare gateway tools and reusable Recipes. The in-page assistant retrieves a consented, ten-minute report snapshot and returns a cited explanation. Tare checks response structure, citation IDs and complete context retrieval, without claiming these checks guarantee factual correctness. A separate Graph-to-Tare Recipe composes indexed acquisition with RPC comparison. No direct LLM provider dependency was added. Key engineering challenges were preserving exact units, handling indexing lag and block differences, distinguishing authorization from evidence, and retaining useful partial results without overstating verification.

projects.title: Moor
projects.description: Range orders on 1inch Aqua, Ledger-signed, ENSv2-named. Agent proposes, Ledger decides.
projects.project_description: Moor turns the waiting time of holding into productive capital. The holder defines a buy or sell strategy and authorizes it once from their Ledger; after that signature, the position runs on its own, asking for nothing else while it's active. Through 1inch Aqua, the holder is the maker of a price range: tokens never leave the wallet, but the position earns a fee on every trade that crosses that range, and once the price reaches the defined condition, the order fills with no additional signature. Every position is registered as its own name in ENS, with the strategy carried inside its records — readable by any application, not just Moor. An agent monitors price and state and can propose adjustments by writing directly onto that name, but it never has permission to sign anything or move capital: the agent proposes, the Ledger decides.
projects.how_its_made: The Live App is Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript. It never touches a private key — every write goes through Ledger's Wallet API (@ledgerhq/wallet-api-client-react), and every read goes through viem via TanStack Query. Position parameters and the model's output both validate against the same Zod schema, so the trust boundary is shared code, not a convention. The chain layer is 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, deployed unmodified from their official sources on Sepolia, plus a small custom MoorRegistrar — it's the only contract Moor wrote, and it never touches Aqua or holds an approval. ship/dock are always called by the holder's own wallet, so the maker is always the Ledger, never a Moor contract. Identity runs on ENSv2's Sepolia beta: each position is its own subname, and who can write which text record is an on-chain role, not an app-level rule — that's what lets an autonomous agent (a Supabase Edge Function, running every 5 minutes, with Groq's gpt-oss-120b for structured proposals) write exactly 8 keys and nothing else, provably, without trusting our backend. When the holder's EOA is EIP-7702-delegated to Simple7702Account — the one delegate Ledger's Ethereum app whitelists — the whole opening session (approve, ship, name) collapses into one executeBatch signature instead of three. Every signable function ships with an ERC-7730 Clear Signing descriptor, captured against an emulated Speculos and submitted to the community registry.

projects.title: Fashion Passport
projects.description: On-chain digital passports for fashion, proving authenticity, provenance and ownership.
projects.project_description: Digital Fashion Passport gives physical fashion items a verifiable digital identity that can follow them throughout their lifetime. Brands can create passports containing product information, materials and provenance, while owners can verify authenticity and transfer the passport when an item is resold. The goal is to create a transparent, persistent history connecting physical fashion with on-chain ownership.
projects.how_its_made: So the whole project is essentially an ERC721 contract deployed to Sepolia at 0x67ad5c6b250f08b1cfd749cc371cdd140d81a61f, hooked up to a bare-bones frontend built with just vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. I deliberately skipped frameworks, build tools, and any kind of backend to keep things simple. The contract itself, FashionPassport.sol, runs on Solidity 0.8.26. Every passport lives as a struct containing the brand, model, registrar, createdAt timestamp, and metadataURI, all mapped by token ID with an internal counter tracking the count. Because this was my first blockchain hackathon, I actually wrote the core ownership logic by hand first. I built my own mapping, transfer function, and require checks just to wrap my head around what an NFT really does under the hood before leaning on OpenZeppelin. Swapping it over later ended up being pretty painless: the custom struct and createPassport logic stayed untouched, token ownership shifted to OpenZeppelin through _safeMint, and I swapped out my custom transferPassport function for the standard transferFrom. On the tooling side, I stuck entirely to Foundry. I leaned on forge for building and running tests, anvil to spin up a local chain and rehearse deployments, cast whenever I needed to poke the contract from the command line, and a forge script to handle the actual deployment. To make sure nothing slipped through, I wrote five unit tests covering creation, initial ownership, checking that IDs start at 1 and increment properly, transfers, and ensuring nobody can move an asset they do not own. Sensitive keys stay locked away in a gitignored .env file backed by a committed example template, and CI takes care of formatting, builds, and test runs on every single push. For the frontend, ethers.js v6 pulls straight from a CDN to talk with the deployed contract. The browser just manages a provider, a MetaMask signer, and the contract instance itself. That means no private keys ever touch the browser, leaving users to sign everything directly through their own wallets. While Alchemy handles RPC duty during deployment and terminal scripts, the web UI relies completely on the user's active wallet connection. A few small implementation details are worth pointing out. I set passport IDs to start at 1 instead of 0 because Solidity mappings initialize empty slots to zeroed values, meaning a non-zero createdAt timestamp doubles as a clean existence check. Since transactions do not just hand back return values off-chain, the frontend grabs the newly minted token ID by decoding the Transfer event log with an interface parser. The gallery UI also rebuilds directly from live chain state instead of guessing with optimistic updates, which keeps the screen from showing phantom data that does not actually exist on-chain. On top of that, switching accounts quickly can fire off overlapping requests, so I tagged each fetch cycle with a sequence number to ensure only the latest load ever renders. Finally, any address input runs through ethers.isAddress so it validates the full checksum instead of just checking character length. Figuring out what belongs on-chain versus off-chain was definitely the hardest design choice. I decided to keep the core provenance data on-chain, specifically the brand, model, original registrar, creation timestamp, and the metadata link. Rich photos, lengthy descriptions, and decorative icons stay off-chain, mostly because burning gas to store display strings the contract never even touches made zero sense. That brings us to the registrar field, which is the real heart of the project. While ownership changes every time an item is sold, that original registrar never moves, meaning anyone down the road can trace a resale straight back to who actually made it.

projects.title: Breeja
projects.description: Cross-chain stablecoin settlement for agents and humans with gasless, route-optimized payments.
projects.project_description: Breeja is a cross-chain stablecoin settlement network built for both humans and autonomous agents. It lets a payer send USDC or another stablecoin across chains without needing gas tokens on the destination network, and without forcing the recipient to manually manage the transfer flow. The flow is simple: the payer signs an EIP-3009 transfer authorization, a relayer submits the deposit on the source chain and pays gas, and a router selects the best route based on live conditions like gas cost, destination liquidity, and user preference. The funds then arrive at the recipient on the destination chain as a single, seamless payment rather than a fragmented bridge experience. The platform is designed around one shared settlement layer for multiple front doors. A human can use the web app, while an agent or developer can integrate through the SDK, MCP tooling, or an x402-compatible flow. The SDK is the core product, with the browser app serving as just one client interface. Under the hood, Breeja treats each supported chain as both a source and a destination, using a relayer to provide liquidity and a routing engine to balance fast settlement against trust-minimized alternatives. It supports two main settlement modes: a fast custodial route backed by relayer-controlled liquidity, and a more trust-minimized CCTP-based route for users who want lower custodial risk. Breeja is therefore not just a token bridge; it is a programmable cross-chain payment layer for real-world settlement, with gas abstraction, route optimization, and agent-friendly integration built in. This makes Breeja especially well suited to ETHGlobal-style demos: it combines consumer UX, agent tooling, developer APIs, and blockchain infrastructure in one coherent product. The value proposition is that payments can be initiated from a natural-language prompt, a browser wallet, or an SDK call, while the underlying settlement remains deterministic, reusable, and consistent across client surfaces.
projects.how_its_made: Breeja is a cross-chain stablecoin settlement network for humans and autonomous agents. It lets a payer send USDC across chains without holding gas on the destination network, using signed transfer authorizations and a relayer that submits the payment and pays gas. A routing layer selects the best path based on gas price, liquidity, and user preferences, with either a fast custodial route or a more trust-minimized CCTP route. Breeja is built as a unified system: Solidity smart contracts for settlement, a TypeScript relayer for execution and liquidity coordination, a Next.js frontend for human UX, and an SDK that exposes the same payment flow to agents, MCP tools, and x402-style integrations. Partner technologies like CCTP, The Graph, Privy, ENS, and Ledger improve trust, identity, and infrastructure. The key design choice is that the AI layer interprets intent and explains the route, but does not authorize settlement or control the trust boundary.

projects.title: Attenuate
projects.description: AI agents get ENS names, not keys. Ask for more than your parent holds and the name never mints.
projects.project_description: An AI agent that spends money needs a key, and a key is all or nothing. There is no way to say "this agent may spend 200 USDC repaying my Aave loan and nothing else." The moment that agent delegates to a sub-agent, the sub-agent inherits the same key, so whatever limits you had in mind are gone. Attenuate makes a permission a name. Every agent is an ENSv2 subname carrying a grant: a capability bitmask, a spend cap, a query budget, an expiry, and how many further hops it may delegate. A child's grant must be a strict subset of its parent's, and that check runs inside the registry contract. The key design decision: we inherit ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and override register() to revert. The standard way of minting a name under ours does not work at all. The only entry point runs the subset check first, so an over-privileged subname is not rejected after the fact. It is never minted. Ask for one capability your parent lacks, or one wei more than your parent has left, and the name does not exist. Three properties follow. Attenuation is structural, not a policy we remember to apply. Budgets are conserved: a parent's remaining balance drops as children are minted, so it cannot hand the same money to two children. Revocation is O(1): bumping a parent's epoch kills the entire subtree in the same block, measured flat at 4,327 gas whether the subtree has 1 node or 15. Sub-agents are real OS processes holding their own keys, not function calls with names attached. Executor.execute requires msg.sender == agentOf(node), so a process that knows a name but not its key is refused NOT_AGENT on chain. A parent that delegates mints the child's name to a key derived for it, funds it, and spawns it as a separate process. LEDGER: one EIP-712 mandate signed on device establishes the root. initRoot recovers the signature and compares it to the device key. There is no owner function, no admin path, and no seed method that bypasses it, so without that signature the tree cannot exist. Escalations surface as a device prompt rather than a silent revert, and a rejection is a decision the code understands. Development runs against Speculos with no hardware. ENS: attenuate.eth is live on the ENSv2 Sepolia deployment, with every grant published as text records on its own PermissionedResolver. Reading them shows the capability mask narrowing at each hop: 0xff at the root, 0xd4 at risk, 0x54 at exec, 0x40 at probe, with each parent's remaining budget dropping as children are minted. No child ever receives ROLE_SET_RESOLVER, because an agent that can repoint its own resolver could rewrite the permissions its name publishes. THE GRAPH: a subgraph indexes the permission tree itself, including registries that did not exist when it was deployed, since a delegation tree grows at runtime. An MCP server exposes six tools so any agent in any framework can read its own scope and dry-run a proposed grant before spending gas, getting back the exact reason and which field to narrow. x402 payments debit the same on-chain query budget through the same Executor path that governs moving money. An LLM proposes what each sub-agent should be allowed to do. Its output is never filtered in TypeScript; whatever it asks for goes to the registry, and the registry is what refuses. In our run the model stayed in scope every time, which is the point: the guarantee does not depend on the model behaving.
projects.how_its_made: STACK: Solidity with Foundry for the contracts, TypeScript everywhere else (viem, Next.js, Node), AssemblyScript for the subgraph mappings, and the Model Context Protocol SDK for the agent-facing server. ENSv2. The core is AttenuatedSubregistry, which inherits ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and overrides register() to revert with UseRegisterWithGrant. That single override is what makes attenuation structural: the standard mint path does not exist, so the only way in runs the subset check first. GrantStore holds the state and the invariant, six requires comparing a child's capabilities, spendCap, queryBudget, expiry, maxDepth and readOnly against the parent's remaining values, not its totals. Checking against spendCap instead of spendRemaining is the bug that would let one parent hand its whole budget to two children, and we have a conservation invariant test for it. A registry cannot embed its own initcode, so delegating names get their child registry from a SubregistryFactory that the store authorises at grant time. Revocation bumps an epoch on the parent and every descendant compares its stored parentEpochAtGrant on read, so killing a subtree is one storage write: measured flat at 4,327 gas for subtrees of 1, 3, 7 and 15 nodes. isLive walks up to MAX_WALK ancestors and fails closed past it, bounded at 11,310 gas. Enhanced Access Control gave us a role split we actually use: the granting role and the revoking role are held by different keys, and no child ever receives ROLE_SET_RESOLVER or ROLE_SET_SUBREGISTRY, because an agent that can repoint its own resolver could rewrite the permissions its name publishes. Withholding ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN makes a permission non-sellable. Executor meters spending from calldata. Each capability is registered with a target, a selector, and the argument index holding the amount, so the contract reads the amount out of the call it is about to make rather than trusting a number passed alongside it. Capabilities can also pin an argument, which is how "approve, but only the pool" is expressed. LEDGER. One EIP-712 RootMandate signed on device, recovered in initRoot and compared to deviceKey. Signing goes through the Device Management Kit over the Speculos transport. Two things cost us a day each and are worth passing on. A DMK session signs exactly once: the second signTypedData in a process returns 0x6980, which reads like a device fault, and rebuilding the signer does not help because the old session still holds the transport. It only works if you explicitly call dmk.disconnect({sessionId}) first. Separately, a user rejecting on device arrives as EthAppCommandError 0x6985 "Condition not satisfied", so the obvious catch treats a deliberate human decision as a crash. THE GRAPH. The subgraph indexes the permission tree itself. The interesting part is that a delegation tree grows at runtime: child registries are deployed when a name is granted CAP_DELEGATE, so a static address list misses everything below depth one. An AI agent that spends money needs a key, and a key is all or nothing. There is no way to say "this agent may spend 200 USDC repaying my Aave loan and nothing else." The moment that agent delegates to a sub-agent, the sub-agent inherits the same key, so whatever limits you had in mind are gone.

Attenuate makes a permission a name. Every agent is an ENSv2 subname carrying a grant: a capability bitmask, a spend cap, a query budget, an expiry, and how many further hops it may delegate. A child's grant must be a strict subset of its parent's, and that check runs inside the registry contract.

The key design decision: we inherit ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and override register() to revert. The standard way of minting a name under ours does not work at all. The only entry point runs the subset check first, so an over-privileged subname is not rejected after the fact. It is never minted. Ask for one capability your parent lacks, or one wei more than your parent has left, and the name does not exist.

Three properties follow. Attenuation is structural, not a policy we remember to apply. Budgets are conserved: a parent's remaining balance drops as children are minted, so it cannot hand the same money to two children. Revocation is O(1): bumping a parent's epoch kills the entire subtree in the same block, measured flat at 4,327 gas whether the subtree has 1 node or 15.

Sub-agents are real OS processes holding their own keys, not function calls with names attached. Executor.execute requires msg.sender == agentOf(node), so a process that knows a name but not its key is refused NOT_AGENT on chain. A parent that delegates mints the child's name to a key derived for it, funds it, and spawns it as a separate process.

There is no owner function, no admin path, and no seed method that bypasses it, so without that signature the tree cannot exist. Escalations surface as a device prompt rather than a silent revert, and a rejection is a decision the code understands. Development runs against Speculos with no hardware.

Reading them shows the capability mask narrowing at each hop: 0xff at the root, 0xd4 at risk, 0x54 at exec, 0x40 at probe, with each parent's remaining budget dropping as children are minted. An LLM proposes what each sub-agent should be allowed to do. Its output is never filtered in TypeScript; whatever it asks for goes to the registry, and the registry is what refuses. In our run the model stayed in scope every time, which is the point: the guarantee does not depend on the model behaving.

projects.title: SettleOne-Protocol
projects.description: Risk-aware DeFi infrastructure that puts escrow capital to work before settlement.
projects.project_description: SettleOne is intelligent settlement infrastructure that enables escrow capital to be productively managed through risk-aware DeFi strategies while preserving explicit settlement constraints. Instead of leaving capital idle until a deal settles, SettleOne evaluates eligible strategies, applies a predefined risk policy, monitors positions using on-chain data, and manages controlled exits when risk or settlement conditions require it. The platform combines on-chain escrow, configurable risk policies, deterministic strategy selection, Aave-based yield generation, yield accounting and distribution, The Graph for blockchain data, and an AI risk-monitoring layer. AI is used to interpret and explain risk signals rather than directly control funds. Deterministic rules and smart contracts remain responsible for financial actions. A typical flow is: create a deal → fund escrow → define risk policy → evaluate strategy → deploy eligible capital → monitor yield and risk → exit when required → settle the deal → distribute eligible yield. The goal is simple: make settlement capital more productive without making yield more important than settlement safety.
projects.how_its_made: SettleOne is being developed as a full-stack Web3 settlement infrastructure platform using a Turborepo monorepo with React and TypeScript on the frontend and a Node.js/TypeScript backend. The frontend integrates RainbowKit, ethers.js and Web3 tooling for wallet connectivity and blockchain interactions. The backend uses Prisma and PostgreSQL for application data, JWT-based authentication, Redis and BullMQ for background processing, and Socket.IO for real-time updates. Google OAuth is used as part of the authentication flow, while Alchemy RPC provides reliable blockchain connectivity. The smart-contract layer is built in Solidity using Foundry and deployed on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. The contracts handle the core settlement infrastructure, including escrow state, deal lifecycle, settlement conditions, strategy interactions, and controlled fund movement. Chainlink Automation is being integrated for automated on-chain monitoring and execution where appropriate. The current DeFi implementation is being built around Aave, with the architecture designed around an extensible strategy layer so additional protocols can be integrated later. Pinata is used for decentralized storage where required. The platform is deployed using Vercel for frontend infrastructure and Railway for backend services. Two important components are currently under active development and are not yet part of the live deployed flow: the The Graph data layer and the AI risk-monitoring layer. The planned Graph integration will provide indexed on-chain/Aave data for the strategy and risk engines, while the AI layer will analyze structured risk signals, identify anomalies, summarize position health, and explain recommended actions. The architecture intentionally separates intelligence, policy, and financial execution. The deterministic risk and strategy engines evaluate predefined constraints, while AI is designed as a monitoring and explanation layer rather than an autonomous fund controller. Actual financial actions remain constrained by application logic and Solidity smart contracts. This separation ensures that an AI model cannot independently move funds or override the settlement and risk policies defined by the protocol. Current status: the core settlement, escrow, authentication, backend infrastructure, smart-contract system, Sepolia deployment, DeFi integration work, and supporting infrastructure are being actively developed, while The Graph integration and AI risk-monitoring layer are currently in development and will be integrated into the next stage of the system.

projects.title: Hanvil
projects.description: A local Hedera network in one 10 MB binary, with a coding-agent harness and an x402 rail built in.
projects.project_description:
hanvil is a local Hedera network that runs as a single 10 MB binary. It serves JSON-RPC (7546), mirror node REST (5551) and HAPI gRPC (50211) from one in-memory chain, on the same ports and with the same 30 pre-funded accounts and keys as hiero-local-node, so @hiero-ledger/sdk, viem, hardhat and foundry connect without config changes. First JSON-RPC answer 6 ms after exec, 5.8 MB resident. Why: hiero-local-node is 18 containers, 3.8 GB of RAM and about 50 s to boot, and it is deprecated as of this month. Its replacement, Solo, runs on Kubernetes and wants 12 GB of RAM and 6 cores. hedera-harness, Hedera's coding-agent harness, only runs against testnet, so every agent attempt costs HBAR and a network round trip, and a failed attempt leaves state behind for the next one. What is in the binary: hanvil: the network. evm_snapshot / evm_revert clone and restore the whole chain. --state FILE persists it across restarts. hiero-local-node supports neither. hanvil run: a Rust port of hedera-harness. Reads a schema-v3 recipe, boots the chain in-process, runs GENERATE / ASSERT / CHAIN / SMOKE / EVALUATE with claude, cursor or any command as the agent. Snapshot before each attempt, revert after a failed one, chain assertions read from the Chain struct instead of a mirror round trip. No testnet account, no HBAR. 0.21 s per attempt with a fake agent. hanvil toll: an x402 facilitator plus a metered service on the same chain, with payer, payTo and feePayer accounts preconfigured. A paid request settles in 0.081 s. The same service deployed on Railway against testnet settles in 4.91 s. hanvil_rejections: transactions Hedera refuses at precheck (duplicate transaction id, bad signature, expired valid-start window, and so on) never reach consensus, so on a real network they produce no record, no receipt and no mirror row. hanvil is the node, so it keeps them and exposes them over JSON-RPC as hanvil_rejections. The demo replays an x402 payment header and reads the DUPLICATE_TRANSACTION refusal back from that list. Recipes can also assert on decoded contract events and advance the chain clock between assertion sets. Numbers, same M-series Mac, hanvil vs hiero-local-node: boot to first JSON-RPC answer: 6 ms vs 50.6 s RSS: 5.8 MB vs 3,898 MB on disk: 10.1 MB vs 9.4 GB processes: 1 vs 18
225 tests. The command behind each number is in the README. Upstream: PRs #47 and #48 to hedera-dev/hedera-harness add network: "local" (run CHAIN against a local node) and per-attempt chain snapshots. Both are open. The demo runs the upstream TypeScript harness with those two PRs applied, green on hanvil. Not emulated: consensus, gossip, staking, the real fee schedule (flat 10,000 tinybar per HAPI transaction, 71 tinybar per unit of EVM gas), and HAPI bodies beyond the six implemented (the rest return NOT_SUPPORTED). The full list of 35 declared gaps is in the README under "What is emulated, and what is not".
projects.how_its_made: Rust. One Chain struct behind a RwLock. The JSON-RPC, mirror and gRPC listeners, hanvil run and hanvil toll all take the same lock, so a transfer submitted over JSON-RPC is visible from the mirror endpoints immediately. evm_snapshot clones the struct, evm_revert swaps it back. Nothing holds the lock across an .await. Crates: revm (EVM), alloy (ABI decoding, sender recovery), axum (the HTTP listeners), tonic + prost (HAPI gRPC over 130 vendored Hedera .proto files), clap, serde_yaml_ng (recipes), regex (secret scan). The node makes no outbound network calls. Hedera details that took the most work: The EVM runs in tinybar, not wei. eth_getBalance and eth_gasPrice multiply by 10^10 at the JSON-RPC boundary. A value that is not a whole number of tinybar is refused with the relay's own error, -32005. HAPI prechecks run in the order a real node runs them: node account, transaction id, valid duration, valid start, duplicate id, payer, supported body, signatures, payer balance. Signatures are verified for real: ECDSA secp256k1 over keccak256(bodyBytes), ED25519 over bodyBytes. Error codes map 1:1 to ResponseCodeEnum. A precheck failure leaves no record and no receipt, same as Hedera, but is appended to an in-memory list served as hanvil_rejections. Ports, account ids, EVM addresses and private keys are copied from hiero-local-node so existing configs and the SDK's forLocalNode() keep working. x402: on Hedera an x402 payment is a CryptoTransfer the client signs and the facilitator co-signs and submits as fee payer. hanvil toll implements the facilitator (:4020) and a metered service (:4021) against the in-process chain: 100000 tinybar per call, payer 0.0.1002, payTo 0.0.1003, feePayer 0.0.1004. The same code, pointed at testnet, is deployed on Railway (examples/toll, Dockerfile in the repo). The demo makes one paid request there and shows the receipt on HashScan. Harness: hanvil run reimplements hedera-harness's five stages. GENERATE spawns the agent CLI with the PRD as its prompt. ASSERT checks required and forbidden files, runs the static validators and the secret scan. CHAIN runs the recipe's deploy commands, optionally advances the chain clock, then evaluates the assertions against the Chain struct. SMOKE starts the app's dev server and drives it with @playwright/mcp in headless Chromium. EVALUATE runs a validator agent with the same MCP server. Subprocesses run in their own process groups so Ctrl-C kills the agent, the dev server and the browser together. Every attempt dumps chain state to logs/chain-state-attempt-N.json, and hanvil --state <file> boots from it. The signer's private key is written as <redacted by hanvil> in every prompt file. Process: solo, first commit 2026-09-07, written with Claude Code. The rules the code was held to are in .claude/CLAUDE.md (one Chain, one lock; ids as newtypes; no unwrap under src/; clippy -D warnings) and a pre-commit hook enforces them. Every commit carries a Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer. docs/research.md pins each claim about upstream behaviour to a file and line. CI runs cargo test on ubuntu and macos, runs the upstream TypeScript harness's CHAIN tier against hanvil with no secrets, and fails if median boot goes over 100 ms.

projects.title: ProofServe
projects.description: AI agents discover and pay for services run by recently verified, live humans.
projects.project_description: ProofServe connects autonomous agents with pay-per-request AI services operated by people who have recently completed World Selfie Check. It combines human-liveness eligibility with machine-to-machine micropayments. Providers register, create draft services, and complete Selfie Check. Service activation is a separate backend decision: unverified providers cannot activate their services, and discovery returns only currently eligible services. We treat Selfie Check as a low-assurance liveness signal—not a guarantee of unique identity or service quality. Our example service classifies support tickets. An agent receives a ticket and a maximum payment budget, discovers an eligible provider, handles an HTTP 402 payment challenge, and pays in HBAR on Hedera testnet through Blocky402. The application displays recorded execution events, a settlement receipt, and a HashScan transaction link. We completed a real end-to-end backend run that returned an AI triage result. The browser also preserves payment evidence when execution fails, rather than hiding the settlement or automatically repeating payment.
projects.how_its_made: We built ProofServe as a TypeScript npm monorepo with a Next.js/React frontend, Fastify API, embedded server-side agent, and a separate protected triage service. Shared Zod schemas validate requests, payment requirements, receipts, and AI results. World IDKit performs Selfie Check using a server-signed RP context. The backend verifies the returned proof through World before recording current provider eligibility. Activation remains explicit, and the agent rechecks eligibility before payment. The protected endpoint issues an x402 v2 HTTP 402 challenge. The buyer validates its offer against the registry, enforces an integer tinybar-denominated service-payment budget, and signs a Hedera testnet transfer. Blocky402 handles verification and settlement; Gemini generates the structured triage response. Network fees are separate from the service-payment budget. PostgreSQL stores agent runs and payment tombstones to preserve settlement evidence and prevent automatic payment retries after interruption. The browser communicates through server-side proxies without receiving the API bearer token. We used Codex-assisted development, GitHub reviews, Vitest regression tests, and automated formatting, linting, typechecking, and builds. Web, API, triage, and PostgreSQL are hosted on Render. The pinned demo’s provider registry remains process-local. Our latest browser run settled successfully but failed during AI execution; the UI correctly retained its receipt and reported the failure.

Our example service classifies support tickets. An agent receives a ticket and a maximum payment budget, discovers an eligible provider, handles an HTTP 402 payment challenge, and pays in HBAR on Hedera testnet through Blocky402. The application displays recorded execution events, a settlement receipt, and a HashScan transaction link.

We completed a real end-to-end backend run that returned an AI triage result. The browser also preserves payment evidence when execution fails, rather than hiding the settlement or automatically repeating payment.

We built ProofServe as a TypeScript npm monorepo with a Next.js/React frontend, Fastify API, embedded server-side agent, and a separate protected triage service. Shared Zod schemas validate requests, payment requirements, receipts, and AI results.

World IDKit performs Selfie Check using a server-signed RP context. The backend verifies the returned proof through World before recording current provider eligibility. Activation remains explicit, and the agent rechecks eligibility before payment.

The protected endpoint issues an x402 v2 HTTP 402 challenge. The buyer validates its offer against the registry, enforces an integer tinybar-denominated service-payment budget, and signs a Hedera testnet transfer. Blocky402 handles verification and settlement; Gemini generates the structured triage response. Network fees are separate from the service-payment budget.

The browser communicates through server-side proxies without receiving the API bearer token. We used Codex-assisted development, GitHub reviews, Vitest regression tests, and automated formatting, linting, typechecking, and builds.
