projects.title: SyndicateLend
projects.description: Tokenized syndicated loans private secondary exchange and registry: settle in seconds, not weeks
projects.project_description: ‼️ The Problem: When a company wants to borrow more money than a single bank is willing to lend, a group of banks will club together and lend it jointly. This is called a syndicated loan. This is one of the largest credit markets on earth, with over $1.4 trillion outstanding in the US leveraged segment alone. Loan “pieces” are bought and sold by funds, insurers and banks, with secondary trading reaching a record of nearly $1 trillion in 2025. However, in this market, although a trade is agreed on in seconds, settlements take weeks to complete: Only 29% of par loan trades settled within T+7 44% between T+7 and T+20 27% took longer than T+20 (This means more than twenty business days after the trade). Why? Unlike a normal security, a loan piece is a private and bespoke contract. There is no shared infrastructure for recording who owns it or transferring it. Ownership records sit inside the administrative agent’s (usually the arranger bank, which is the lead bank of the syndicate) private database. Buying a loan piece means becoming a lender under the borrower’s shared credit agreement, and the agent must update the private loan register. Because that register is private and agent-controlled, the transfer of loan ownership is not natively linked to the movement of payment. They are handled as two separate processes. Existing platforms make the surrounding paperwork and communication faster, but they still do not make the loan position and the payment change hands together. The result is a settlement gap- the trade is agreed in seconds, but ownership and cash only reconcile weeks later. That gap is what SyndicateLend addresses. The weeks-long settlement exposes buyers and sellers to unnecessary credit and counterparty risk, locks up idle capital, and forces the market to run an elaborate compensation system just to apologise for its own slowness. Funds offering daily redemptions face an additional liquidity mismatch problem where LPs can request cash before loan-sale proceeds arrive. ✅ The Solution: SyndicateLend is a private institutional secondary-market RFQ exchange and tokenised syndicated loan registry. SyndicateLend reduces settlement from weeks to seconds. 🚀 Each lender’s share of a loan is represented by tokens on a shared digital register. A seller requests quotes from other institutions, accepts a buyer’s offer, and both institutions authorise the trade. At settlement, the loan tokens move to the buyer and payment moves to the seller in the same atomic transaction, which means both legs settle together or neither happens. 🤝 💼 We have 3 distinct workspaces for the following: 📎 Workspace 1 : You are the agent bank for a loan contract. You can manage the loan registry, interest calculations, approval, and transfer assets for secondary market trades. 📎 Workspace 2 : You make RFQ trades in the secondary market with other syndicate lenders and request the agent bank to settle the trade between our institution and the other. 📎 Workspace 3 : You monitor your own positions and interest accruals across all books, where you are either an agent arranger bank, part of a syndicate, or a secondary market buyer. ⚫️ An overview of the general workflow: The agent bank issues loan tokens and allocates them to lenders. The agent controls who can hold or receive the tokens. A seller requests quotes from eligible institutions. A buyer’s offer is accepted, subject to the institution’s internal approvals. At settlement, loan tokens and payment tokens swap atomically. Interest and other distributions are calculated and paid to current holders. ⚫️ Three technologies support this institutional workflow and privacy story: 🏦 Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio — Used to manage loan positions. The agent issues tokens, allocates them to lenders and controls who can hold or receive them. A settlement contract exchanges those positions against an HTS payment token, while Hedera records the trading events and executes scheduled settlements. The asset represented is a lender’s position in a specific loan tranche. Hedera combines a ready-made compliance framework in ATS, native payment tokens and network-executed scheduling. That lets us build the loan’s issuance, transfer controls and settlement together without building a security-token framework or running a separate settlement scheduler. 🫆Privy — Used for institutional identity and permissions. Staff sign in to an institutional wallet, where a quorum of authorised members (2 of 3 in demo) must approve an action. The trader’s decision is therefore subject to the institution’s internal approval policy before assets can move. Privy combines familiar staff login with user-bound wallet quorums, transaction policies and approval intents. That lets us enforce an institution’s signing mandate without holding its wallet keys or building a separate multisignature approval system. ⛓️ Chainlink CRE — Used to handle confidential interest calculations. It checks the agent’s private rate notice (a confidential message stating the interest rate for a particular period) against a previously published cryptographic commitment, combines the terms with lender balances and calculates each holder’s payment. The workflow releases the distribution amounts without publishing the underlying notice. CRE Confidential Workflows supports confidential computation, not just private API access. That lets us put notice retrieval, commitment verification and interest calculation inside one TEE handler, with explicit control over which results leave it. The MVP demonstrates token issuance, controls, settlement and payments using synthetic assets on Hedera testnet. The confidential calculation is demonstrated through CRE simulation; private institutional deployment on HashSphere (by Hedera) is intended for production. ⚫️ References: https://www.lsta.org/university/operations/ https://www.lsta.org/content/secondary-trading-settlement-study-first-quarter-2026/ https://www.lsta.org/content/lsta-secondary-trading-monthly-executive-summary-2q25-secondary-loan-trading-volumes-spike-again-to-a-record-262-billion/
projects.how_its_made: Core stack: SyndicateLend is built with Next.js + TypeScript, Solidity contracts tested with Foundry, administrative scripts using the Hedera and ATS SDKs, Privy institutional wallets, and a TypeScript Chainlink CRE confidential workflow. The workflow follows an actual syndicated-loan assignment: the administrative agent issues a loan tranche and allocates lender positions; a seller sends an RFQ; another institution quotes; the seller accepts; both institutions complete their internal approvals; and the trade settles Delivery-versus-Payment. The same lender register is then used for interest distributions. Hedera ATS — tokenised loan register: Each loan tranche is represented by an Asset Tokenization Studio bond-type security, with 1 token representing $1 of par. ATS whitelist and internal KYC controls restrict who can hold the loan. Secondary transfers deliberately use transferFrom, not an administrative forced transfer, so the agent cannot bypass the same eligibility rules applied to other holders. HTS — cash and compliance controls: The cash leg uses an HTS mock-USD token with KYC, freeze and pause controls. The same token is used for interest distributions. Larger lender sets are paid in batches to stay within Hedera’s transfer-entry limits. Atomic settlement + HSS: A custom Solidity SettlementEngine exchanges the ATS loan position and HTS payment token atomically: if either the asset or cash leg fails because of eligibility, KYC, allowance, balance, freeze or pause controls, neither asset moves. When the second institution approves, the contract calls Hedera Schedule Service scheduleCall itself and funds its own scheduled execution, so there is no off-chain settlement keeper. Eligibility is effectively checked again when the ATS transfer executes. HCS + Mirror Node — trading and audit data: RFQs, quotes, acceptances and approvals are written to Hedera Consensus Service in consensus order, so the trading blotter can be reconstructed from the ledger rather than a central database. Mirror Node event logs are also used to reconstruct historical assignments. HCS additionally stores cryptographic commitments to confidential rate notices and reconciliation reports rather than publishing the underlying private data. Privy — institutional wallet controls: Each institution gets a server-provisioned Privy organisation wallet owned by a 2-of-3 key quorum across trader, compliance and portfolio-manager users. Wallet policies limit transactions to the permitted Hedera contracts and call types, while key export is disabled. Transactions are proposed as signing intents and only execute after the quorum threshold is reached. An automated liquidity desk uses a 2-of-2 quorum of server-held P-256 authorisation keys for programmatic workflows. HIP-719 bridges Privy and Hedera: Privy wallets sign normal EVM transactions rather than Hedera-native TokenAssociateTransactions. I use the HIP-719 token facade to call associate() directly on the HTS token address, allowing an institutional Privy wallet to complete token association through an ordinary EVM intent. Chainlink CRE — confidential interest calculation: Loan rate notices should remain private, but interest must be calculated against the current lender register. The agent therefore publishes only a salted commitment to the notice on HCS. A CRE Confidential Workflow, configured with handlerInTee for AWS Nitro, retrieves the authenticated private notice using a DON secret, verifies it against the public commitment, reads all lender balances through a RegisterSnapshot helper contract, and calculates each lender’s interest using integer arithmetic. Only the commitment, period, holder addresses and payment amounts leave the confidential workflow; the rate, day-count basis, nonce and API credential remain private. A few intentionally hacky integrations: RegisterSnapshot returns every lender balance in one Mirror Node contract call instead of one HTTP request per lender. HCS messages larger than its message limit are reassembled using their shared initial_transaction_id. For backend ATS operations, I reused the SDK’s testing pattern by initialising its MetaMask adapter in debug mode and injecting an ethers.Wallet signer. What is deployed and where: The loan token, HTS payment token, HCS topics, settlement engine and test trades run on Hedera Public Testnet, including successful atomic settlement and a failed settlement after buyer eligibility was revoked. The retail feeder is also demonstrated on public testnet. CRE is demonstrated through its simulator rather than a live DON deployment because beta deployment access was not available before the deadline. Private institutional deployment on HashSphere is the intended production architecture.

projects.title: Rolebound
projects.description: Rolebound: Access follows the role, not the person. Clean team wallets with real accountability.
projects.project_description: Rolebound is a way for onchain teams to give people spending power that has limits, can be taken back, and leaves a record. The problem When an organization wants to let someone spend its money, it has two bad options today: Add them to the multisig. Their access has no limit and never expires. Send them the budget. Once the money arrives, you can't get it back. Nothing sits in between, so teams hand out too much access by default. This causes three problems: People get more authority than their job needs. Recurring payments keep running after the person who set them up has left. The answer to "why did we send 2,000 USDC?" is buried in a Discord chat. The core idea: the role holds the money, not the person In Rolebound, every role in an organization (Engineering, Marketing, Contractors, and so on) has its own wallet, created as a Privy server wallet with its own policy. The budget is the balance. The treasury tops up role wallets, and a role's budget is simply what its wallet holds. No spreadsheet is needed. People get grants, not keys. A contractor or teammate never holds keys or money. They get a grant on a role, with one of two abilities: spend or approve. Every grant has limits. Grants are capped by the role's per-transaction limit and monthly budget. Revoking is instant. Removing someone takes one click and works on their very next attempt. Since the money never moved to them, there is nothing to recover. Their recurring payments are listed so you can cancel them, move them to someone else, or keep them. How a payment works A member enters an amount, a recipient and a reason. Before the request leaves the browser, the member signs an EIP-712 authorization with their Privy embedded wallet. The signature covers that exact amount, recipient and reason. The server checks who signed and rejects any mismatch. This shows which person asked, not just which role paid. Every payment goes through one check, assertCanSpend(). The web app, the agent Aall use it, so there is no second path where a limit could be skipped. If a payment is over the role's per-transaction limit, it goes to an approver. The approver signs off with their own reason, and the payment then goes through. The role wallet calls our RoleboundPay contract. The reason is hashed and saved ction as the payment, so the record can't drift from the transfer. The text of thereason stays private in the app. The activity feed reads the hash back from the chain and shows a "verified" badge only when it matches. Two layers of protection Rolebound's own rules are backed by rules in Privy's policy engine, which Privy enforces in its secure hardware (the enclave): Only our contract: each role wallet can call RoleboundPay and nothing else. A dirapproval to any other contract, is blocked. Only allowed recipients: payments can only go to addresses on the role's list. Hard monthly cap: the enclave refuses anything over the role's monthly budget, even if an approver signs off. So even if our app server were hacked, an attacker still couldn't drain a role wallet to their own address. AI agents are members too An AI agent is added the same way as a person: same members table, same grants, same limits. The only difference is that it logs in with an API key instead of a session. The agent doesn't get its own wallet; it gets a role, and every rule above still applies. The record Activity is grouped by role and shows who paid, which role, how much, to whom and why, and all of it can be checked against the chain. Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind and shadcn/ui Privy: server wallets, policy engine, embedded wallets and authorization keys Solidity contracts built with Foundry and deployed on Base Sepolia viem, plus Drizzle with Neon Postgres Hosted on Vercel The project has 160 tests, and none of them use mocks. They start a real local chain (Anvil) and a real Postgres database, deploy the real contracts, and move test money through the real payment check. Live demo: https://rolebound.vercel.app
projects.how_its_made: The architecture The app is built with Next.js 16 (App Router, Server Components and Server Actions) in TypeScript, hosted on Vercel. The UI uses Tailwind and shadcn/ui. The data (orgs, roles, grants, members, payments, schedules and the activity log) lives in Postgres on Neon, accessed through Drizzle ORM. All chain reads and writes go through viem. The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed on Base Sepolia. The onchain part is deliberately small. RoleboundPay has a single function, pay(roleId, token, to, amount, reasonHash, actor). It rejects an empty reason hash, a zero address and a zero amount. It then calls transferFrom to move tokens straight from the role wallet to the recipient and emits a Payment event. The contract never holds funds. Because the reason hash is checked onchain, a payment without a reason is impossible even if someone bypasses our app. Every payment follows the same path: The member signs in the browser. The pay form uses Privy's useSignTypedData with the member's embedded wallet. They sign an EIP-712 PaymentAuthorization covering the roleId, recipient, amount, keccak256(reason) and a nonce. The server checks the signature. A server action receives the request. The member's identity comes from the Privy access token, which we verify against Privy's public JWKS keys. We fetch the member's embedded wallet address from Privy's API instead of trusting the browser. recoverTypedDataAddress must return exactly that address, or the request is refused. The payment check runs. requestPayment() calls assertCanSpend(), which checks, in order: there is a reason and the amount is valid the role hasn't been dissolved the member has a live grant (revokedAt IS NULL) the recipient is on the role's allowlist the payment is within the per-transaction cap the role's total spending this month stays within its monthly budget If either limit would be exceeded, the payment is saved as pending_approval instead of being refused. The role wallet sends the transaction. We encode the pay() calldata and send it with Privy's wallets().ethereum().sendTransaction() from the role's server wallet. We then wait for the receipt and write the tx hash and an activity event to the database. The feed verifies it. The activity feed pulls Payment events off the chain with getLogs. It re-hashes the reason stored in our database and shows a "verified" badge only if the hash and amount match. A mismatch is shown clearly as a warning, never hidden. Browser payments, the AI agent API (POST /api/agent/pay with a Bearer rb_live_… key) and recurring payments (a Vercel Cron job hitting /api/cron/sweep) all call requestPayment(). There is no other route to a wallet signature. How we used Privy (our partner technology), and why it mattered Privy is not just the login here. It is the security foundation of the whole product. Server wallets. Every role, and the treasury, is its own Privy server wallet, created through the API when the role is created. "The role holds the money" only works if creating a wallet is as cheap as inserting a database row, and with Privy it is. Policy engine. Each role wallet gets exactly one policy with two ALLOW rules. Anything that doesn't match a rule is refused inside Privy's secure hardware (the enclave). Rule 1: the transaction must go to RoleboundPay. If the role has an allowlist, pay.to must be on it. If the role has a monthly budget, pay.amount must not exceed it. Rule 2: the wallet may call USDC.approve, but only when the spender is RoleboundPay. We create the policy first and the wallet second, so a wallet never exists without its limits, even for a moment. The result: even if our server were fully compromised, a role wallet still couldn't send its USDC directly or approve an attacker to spend it. We tested both on Base Sepolia, and both came back policy_violation. Embedded wallets. Members log in with email and automatically get a wallet. That wallet signs each payment authorization, which lets us prove which person approved which payment. Otherwise, all we could say is that "a role paid". Access-token verification. Server-side JWT checks mean the server never has to trust the browser about who the user is. Without Privy we would have had to build key custody, an enclave-backed policy system and wallet onboarding ourselves, and none of that would fit in a hackathon. Hacky and notable details We tested Privy's rules in practice, and got caught when they changed. Before building, we wrote a test script (pnpm spike:policy) and ran it against a live Privy app. On 2026-09-10, rules based on calldata (amount and recipient) were accepted when the policy was created but ignored at signing. Only rules on the destination contract were enforced. So we built amount limits into the app and relied on Privy only for the contract allowlist. Two days later, while seeding the demo, a 1,200 payment was refused with policy_violation: Privy had started enforcing calldata rules. That broke our approval flow. We had put the per-transaction cap (500) into the policy, so the enclave was now refusing the exact payments an approver is meant to unlock. The fix made the design clearer: The per-transaction cap is a soft limit held by the app. Going over it means an approver is needed. The ceiling is a hard limit held by Privy: no single payment can exceed the role's monthly budget, and no approver can override it. We kept both findings in the PRD instead of rewriting history. Two wallet modes, with guardrails. On a local Anvil chain, a local mode derives each wallet's key from the role name (keccak256("rolebound:local:<role>")) and stores the key inside the wallet ID, so no key storage is needed. Two checks keep this safe: the local mode refuses to run on any chain except 31337 the app refuses to start if Privy is configured while pointed at Anvil Without the second check, you'd get a confusing "Invalid wallet ID" error deep inside the SDK. Getting local and live modes to coexist. pnpm chain:setup deploys the real contracts to Anvil, writes their addresses to .env.local and seeds an org. It also blanks the Privy variables, because .env.local takes priority over .env in Next.js. To run against Privy, pnpm dev:privy reads the real values from .env and injects them as process environment variables, which beat both files, so neither file needs editing. Working around RPC load balancing. Base Sepolia's public RPC runs behind a load balancer. After a role wallet's one-time approve is mined, the next payment's gas estimate can hit a node that still sees an allowance of zero, which fails with a bare execution reverted. So after approving, we keep re-reading the allowance until it shows up, and only then send the payment. Reading event logs on a public RPC. Base Sepolia limits eth_getLogs to 10,000 blocks per call, and the chain is past block 46M. So we scan in 10k-block windows, inclusive at both ends (the -1n avoids counting boundary events twice), and start at the contract's deployment block. We also set cacheTime: 0 on the latest block number, because viem's cached value would miss the payment the user just made. Dissolving a role. When a role is closed, its remaining balance goes back to the treasury through the same pay() call. That means the treasury is automatically added to every role's allowed recipients. Otherwise, a role with an allowlist could never be closed. Agent keys. Keys are random (rb_live_ plus 24 bytes, base64url) and stored only as a SHA-256 hash. projects.project_description_markdown:
Rolebound is a way for onchain teams to give people spending power that has limits, can be taken back, and leaves a record.

The problem

When an organization wants to let someone spend its money, it has two bad options today:

1. Add them to the multisig. Their access has no limit and never expires.
2. Send them the budget. Once the money arrives, you can't get it back.

Nothing sits in between, so teams hand out too much access by default. This causes three problems:
- People get more authority than their job needs.
- Recurring payments keep running after the person who set them up has left.
- The answer to "why did we send 2,000 USDC?" is buried in a Discord chat.

The core idea: the role holds the money, not the person

In Rolebound, every role in an organization (Engineering, Marketing, Contractors, and so on) has its own wallet, created as a Privy server wallet with its own policy.

- The budget is the balance. The treasury tops up role wallets, and a role's budget is simply what its wallet holds. No spreadsheet is needed.
- People get grants, not keys. A contractor or teammate never holds keys or money. They get a grant on a role, with one of two abilities: spend or approve.
- Every grant has limits. Grants are capped by the role's per-transaction limit and monthly budget.
- Revoking is instant. Removing someone takes one click and works on their very next attempt. Since the money never moved to them, there is nothing to recover. Their recurring payments are listed so you can cancel them, move them to someone else, or keep them.

How a payment works

1. A member enters an amount, a recipient and a reason.
2. Before the request leaves the browser, the member signs an EIP-712 authorization with their Privy embedded wallet. The signature covers that exact amount, recipient and reason. The server checks who signed and rejects any mismatch. This shows which person asked, not just which role paid.
3. Every payment goes through one check, assertCanSpend(). The web app, the agent Aall use it, so there is no second path where a limit could be skipped.
4. If a payment is over the role's per-transaction limit, it goes to an approver. The approver signs off with their own reason, and the payment then goes through.
5. The role wallet calls our RoleboundPay contract. The reason is hashed and saved ction as the payment, so the record can't drift from the transfer. The text of thereason stays private in the app. The activity feed reads the hash back from the chain and shows a "verified" badge only when it matches.

Two layers of protection

Rolebound's own rules are backed by rules in Privy's policy engine, which Privy enforces in its secure hardware (the enclave):
- Only our contract: each role wallet can call RoleboundPay and nothing else. A dirapproval to any other contract, is blocked.
- Only allowed recipients: payments can only go to addresses on the role's list.
- Hard monthly cap: the enclave refuses anything over the role's monthly budget, even if an approver signs off.

So even if our app server were hacked, an attacker still couldn't drain a role wallet to their own address.

AI agents are members too

An AI agent is added the same way as a person: same members table, same grants, same limits. The only difference is that it logs in with an API key instead of a session. The agent doesn't get its own wallet; it gets a role, and every rule above still applies.

The record

Activity is grouped by role and shows who paid, which role, how much, to whom and why, and all of it can be checked against the chain.

Built with

- Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind and shadcn/ui
- Privy: server wallets, policy engine, embedded wallets and authorization keys
- Solidity contracts built with Foundry and deployed on Base Sepolia
- viem, plus Drizzle with Neon Postgres
- Hosted on Vercel

The project has 160 tests, and none of them use mocks. They start a real local chain (Anvil) and a real Postgres database, deploy the real contracts, and move test money through the real payment check.

Live demo: https://rolebound.vercel.app
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The architecture

The app is built with Next.js 16 (App Router, Server Components and Server Actions) in TypeScript, hosted on Vercel. The UI uses Tailwind and shadcn/ui. The data (orgs, roles, grants, members, payments, schedules and the activity log) lives in Postgres on Neon, accessed through Drizzle ORM. All chain reads and writes go through viem. The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed on Base Sepolia.

The onchain part is deliberately small. RoleboundPay has a single function, pay(roleId, token, to, amount, reasonHash, actor). It rejects an empty reason hash, a zero address and a zero amount. It then calls transferFrom to move tokens straight from the role wallet to the recipient and emits a Payment event. The contract never holds funds. Because the reason hash is checked onchain, a payment without a reason is impossible even if someone bypasses our app.

Every payment follows the same path:

1. The member signs in the browser. The pay form uses Privy's useSignTypedData with the member's embedded wallet. They sign an EIP-712 PaymentAuthorization covering the roleId, recipient, amount, keccak256(reason) and a nonce.
2. The server checks the signature. A server action receives the request. The member's identity comes from the Privy access token, which we verify against Privy's public JWKS keys. We fetch the member's embedded wallet address from Privy's API instead of trusting the browser. recoverTypedDataAddress must return exactly that address, or the request is refused.
3. The payment check runs. requestPayment() calls assertCanSpend(), which checks, in order:
   - there is a reason and the amount is valid
   - the role hasn't been dissolved
   - the member has a live grant (revokedAt IS NULL)
   - the recipient is on the role's allowlist
   - the payment is within the per-transaction cap
   - the role's total spending this month stays within its monthly budget

   If either limit would be exceeded, the payment is saved as pending_approval instead of being refused.
4. The role wallet sends the transaction. We encode the pay() calldata and send it with Privy's wallets().ethereum().sendTransaction() from the role's server wallet. We then wait for the receipt and write the tx hash and an activity event to the database.
5. The feed verifies it. The activity feed pulls Payment events off the chain with getLogs. It re-hashes the reason stored in our database and shows a "verified" badge only if the hash and amount match. A mismatch is shown clearly as a warning, never hidden.

Browser payments, the AI agent API (POST /api/agent/pay with a Bearer rb_live_… key) and recurring payments (a Vercel Cron job hitting /api/cron/sweep) all call requestPayment(). There is no other route to a wallet signature.

How we used Privy (our partner technology), and why it mattered

Privy is not just the login here. It is the security foundation of the whole product.

- Server wallets. Every role, and the treasury, is its own Privy server wallet, created through the API when the role is created. "The role holds the money" only works if creating a wallet is as cheap as inserting a database row, and with Privy it is.
- Policy engine. Each role wallet gets exactly one policy with two ALLOW rules. Anything that doesn't match a rule is refused inside Privy's secure hardware (the enclave).
  - Rule 1: the transaction must go to RoleboundPay. If the role has an allowlist, pay.to must be on it. If the role has a monthly budget, pay.amount must not exceed it.
  - Rule 2: the wallet may call USDC.approve, but only when the spender is RoleboundPay.

  We create the policy first and the wallet second, so a wallet never exists without its limits, even for a moment. The result: even if our server were fully compromised, a role wallet still couldn't send its USDC directly or approve an attacker to spend it. We tested both on Base Sepolia, and both came back policy_violation.
- Embedded wallets. Members log in with email and automatically get a wallet. That wallet signs each payment authorization, which lets us prove which person approved which payment. Otherwise, all we could say is that "a role paid".
- Access-token verification. Server-side JWT checks mean the server never has to trust the browser about who the user is.

Without Privy we would have had to build key custody, an enclave-backed policy system and wallet onboarding ourselves, and none of that would fit in a hackathon.

Hacky and notable details

- We tested Privy's rules in practice, and got caught when they changed. Before building, we wrote a test script (pnpm spike:policy) and ran it against a live Privy app. On 2026-09-10, rules based on calldata (amount and recipient) were accepted when the policy was created but ignored at signing. Only rules on the destination contract were enforced. So we built amount limits into the app and relied on Privy only for the contract allowlist. Two days later, while seeding the demo, a 1,200 payment was refused with policy_violation: Privy had started enforcing calldata rules. That broke our approval flow. We had put the per-transaction cap (500) into the policy, so the enclave was now refusing the exact payments an approver is meant to unlock. The fix made the design clearer:
  - The per-transaction cap is a soft limit held by the app. Going over it means an approver is needed.
  - The ceiling is a hard limit held by Privy: no single payment can exceed the role's monthly budget, and no approver can override it.

  We kept both findings in the PRD instead of rewriting history.
- Two wallet modes, with guardrails. On a local Anvil chain, a local mode derives each wallet's key from the role name (keccak256("rolebound:local:<role>")) and stores the key inside the wallet ID, so no key storage is needed. Two checks keep this safe:
  - the local mode refuses to run on any chain except 31337
  - the app refuses to start if Privy is configured while pointed at Anvil

  Without the second check, you'd get a confusing "Invalid wallet ID" error deep inside the SDK.
- Getting local and live modes to coexist. pnpm chain:setup deploys the real contracts to Anvil, writes their addresses to .env.local and seeds an org. It also blanks the Privy variables, because .env.local takes priority over .env in Next.js. To run against Privy, pnpm dev:privy reads the real values from .env and injects them as process environment variables, which beat both files, so neither file needs editing.
- Working around RPC load balancing. Base Sepolia's public RPC runs behind a load balancer. After a role wallet's one-time approve is mined, the next payment's gas estimate can hit a node that still sees an allowance of zero, which fails with a bare execution reverted. So after approving, we keep re-reading the allowance until it shows up, and only then send the payment.
- Reading event logs on a public RPC. Base Sepolia limits eth_getLogs to 10,000 blocks per call, and the chain is past block 46M. So we scan in 10k-block windows, inclusive at both ends (the -1n avoids counting boundary events twice), and start at the contract's deployment block. We also set cacheTime: 0 on the latest block number, because viem's cached value would miss the payment the user just made.
- Dissolving a role. When a role is closed, its remaining balance goes back to the treasury through the same pay() call. That means the treasury is automatically added to every role's allowed recipients. Otherwise, a role with an allowlist could never be closed.
- Agent keys. Keys are random (rb_live_ plus 24 bytes, base64url) and stored only as a SHA-256 hash. A slow hash function isn't needed for high-entropy random keys and would only slow down every agent request. Reissuing a key invalidates the old one.
- Securing the cron job. The cron endpoint moves money, so it is protected with CRON_SECRET and a constant-time comparison. If the secret isn't set, it refuses every request. Recurring payments belong to the role, so they keep running after the person who created them leaves. If nobody holds a live grant on the role, the payment is reported as "unstaffed" and not sent.
- 160 tests with no mocks. Vitest's global setup builds the contracts with Foundry, starts its own Anvil instance and deploys the real contracts there. It also creates and migrates a separate test database, so real test money moves through the real payment path. It refuses to start if something is already running on its port, so it can never accidentally deploy to the development chain. The database URL is hard-coded to the test database because the suite wipes every table between tests.
- Automated UI checks. Two Playwright scripts:
  - verify:ui visits every screen at 1280px and 390px, fails on horizontal overflow or tap targets that are too small, and runs a real over-cap payment to check that the result panel appears.
  - verify:login runs a real Privy login in a real browser.
- The token. We deployed our own 6-decimal test USDC instead of using Circle's Base Sepolia USDC. Circle's faucet gives out only about 10 per day, and the demo moves thousands. RoleboundPay takes the token address as a parameter, so nothing in the payment flow depends on which token is used.

projects.title: Bramble
projects.description: A private WireGuard mesh for teams and agents, with ENS-based access and pay-as-you-go relays.
projects.project_description: Bramble is a private WireGuard network for small teams and the agents they run. Each device checks an ENSv2 registry for membership and service permissions, so a relay can help with connectivity but cannot decide who joins. A team can give a worker access to one internal API, approve a wider grant when it needs one, and revoke its network access later. The API stays off the public internet. Peers can use ENS-listed relays for rendezvous or traffic forwarding, paying per session or byte allotment through x402 on Hedera rather than buying a seat for each device.
projects.how_its_made: Bramble’s Go node runs userspace WireGuard and a local forward to private services. A TypeScript sidecar reads ENSv2 records and handles relay payments. On Sepolia, Permissioned Registries and per-device resolvers hold device keys, mesh addresses and access state. ENS Enhanced Access Control separates who can enroll devices, change keys, revoke access and manage grants. Each node checks those records itself and updates its peer table. The gateway checks a scoped grant before forwarding a request. A Ledger hardware wallet signs each device's enrollment transactions directly, and its Key Ring encrypts the secret used to compute later access grants. Relays are also discovered through ENS, and a node pays for a relay session in testnet USDC through Hedera's x402 flow, priced per byte instead of a flat rate. One hacky bit: wallet-cli's own signing tool doesn't support Sepolia, so we wrote a small Ledger signer directly against its Ethereum app instead.

projects.title: Chase Dinosaurs
projects.description: Dino chase for a golden egg. USDC pots on Arc, AI reads The Graph to hunt you, World ID stops bots.
projects.project_description: Chase Dinosaurs is a 60-second real-time multiplayer chase game where the AI opponents read the blockchain to decide who to hunt. The game: one golden egg drops into a 16-bit arena. Whoever holds it is the target, and everyone else hunts them, whoever tags them gets the egg, and they would have to keep it until the clock hits zero and you win. It runs in a browser, no install, 2-4 players per room. The stakes: ranked matches escrow real USDC on Arc, Circle's stablecoin-native L1. Both players approve and stake into a per-match escrow contract, watch the pot climb in the lobby, and the winner is paid out of that contract when the round resolves. The pot is held by a contract, not by our database. The part that isn't a leaderboard: every stake and settlement is indexed by a subgraph, and the agent brains read that index before every decision. So the opponents don't only see where you are on the map, they see that you're up 4 USDC across six matches, and they treat you as the primary threat. They will leave a closer, unproven player alone to mark the proven winner instead, guard their escape lane before they have even touched the egg, and taunt them about their record by name. Take the subgraph away and the opponents get measurably dumber. On-chain record changes who gets hunted; geometry still decides the mechanics. Getting in is one email address. Privy provisions an embedded wallet, no extension, no seed phrase, nothing to install, because a browser game cannot ask a player to acquire a funded wallet on a chain they have never heard of before they are allowed to play. New players are handed 2 USDC automatically so they can afford a buy-in, which makes the faucet worth attacking: sign-in is just an email, so ten inboxes would have been twenty dollars. World ID Selfie Check closes that. One live human, one claim, keyed on a nullifier, we never learn a name and never see a face. The whole loop closes on itself: you stake, you play, the server settles on-chain, the subgraph indexes that settlement, and the agents read the result in the next match. Your record is the thing you carry between games, and it is the thing that makes you a target.
projects.how_its_made: Four moving parts: a Next.js 16 &  React 19 shell, a Phaser 3.90 game compiled by Vite and bundled into the shell at build time, a Socket.IO match server on Render, and a Solidity escrow on Arc. Contract work is Foundry; the browser talks chain through viem + wagmi with Privy embedded wallets, the server through ethers v6. ChaseStake.sol is deliberately four functions — create, join, settle, refund — because it holds real money and every branch should be readable in one sitting. USDC is Arc's native gas asset, but the contract never touches msg.value; it only uses the ERC-20 interface at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 (6 decimals), hardcoded rather than configurable. The trust model is narrow on purpose: the server picks the winner but cannot pick the amount, cannot pay a non-participant, and cannot pay itself unless it played. If it never settles, a one-hour deadline lets every player reclaim their own stake, so funds can never be stranded by a match that dies. The AI is two-tier, and that split is what makes LLM opponents affordable. Every ~3.5s the host sends a compact world snapshot; one inference call on 0G Compute returns a high-level intent per agent — mode, target, persona, a one-line taunt,  and the Phaser client executes that intent every frame. The model never steers per-frame. Hard timeout, retry-once, and a per-room last-good cache mean a blip degrades to the previous decision or to scripted fallback instead of stalling the match. The Graph is wired into that inference rather than bolted onto a UI. Before each call the server joins every player's Privy user id to their wallet to their on-chain record from the subgraph and puts it in the prompt. Critically it is a synchronous cache read that never awaits inside the match loop, a slow or unreachable subgraph costs the inference budget nothing and the agents just degrade to spatial-only reasoning. Notable and hacky bits, all of which were real bugs first: The browser and the server must derive byte-identical match ids from a room code. One side is ethers.keccak256(ethers.toUtf8Bytes(code)), the other viem keccak256(toBytes(code)). A mismatch there would silently land stakes in an escrow the server never settles — money in a contract nobody would ever call settle() on. Vite inlines env at build time, so NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL got frozen into the game artifact — a deploy produced a perfect lobby whose Play button dialled localhost:3001 on the player's own machine. Fixed by having the shell hand the socket URL to the game at launch, making one runtime value the source of truth for both bundles. qwen2.5-omni doesn't support JSON mode, so the intent parser pulls JSON out of free text. Payout is decided by backed-vs-unbacked, not human-vs-agent. House fill-agents have no principal behind them — no wallet, nobody accountable — so there is nobody to pay, and the pot goes to the best-scoring player who actually staked, ties broken deterministically. A player-owned agent is meant to be payable. That boundary is what makes agent-vs-agent betting a config change later rather than a rewrite. The faucet wallet is deliberately a different key from the settlement wallet. Sharing one would mean a drained faucet is also a match that cannot pay out. Every integration degrades instead of crashing when its key is absent, and /health reports which are actually armed — ai, arc, faucet, graph, world — so "is it really wired up" is a URL, not a claim. All secrets are server-side only; nothing sensitive is ever NEXT_PUBLIC_.

projects.title: Boneyard
projects.description: On-chain growth marketplace where promoters earn for verifiable project-set KPIs.
projects.project_description: Boneyard is an onchain growth marketplace where projects create campaigns and pay promoters for verifiable onchain results, rather than relying on screenshots, self-reported numbers, or subjective claims of reach. Projects define the KPIs that count as campaign progress and assign reward tiers to those KPIs. Depending on the protocol, Boneyard can track common onchain actions such as token mints, swaps, staking, deposits, lending, borrowing, bridges, liquidity provision, pool creation, trading volume, TVL, and active users. Promoters receive a unique BoneyLink for each campaign, which attributes referred users to them. When those users perform qualifying actions on the project's contracts, the activity is independently observed and credited to the correct promoter. Campaigns can combine multiple KPIs and reward promoters as they cross predefined thresholds. For example, a project could reward a promoter for bringing 10 new wallets, 25 swaps, $10,000 in trading volume, or 5 stakers. Because the underlying activity occurs onchain, campaign progress can be verified against blockchain data instead of trusting either the project or promoter to report results faithfully. Projects can also set a BoneyScore requirement for campaign participation. BoneyScore combines a promoter's Ethos credibility score and social reach into a single signal that projects can use to gate campaigns. A higher threshold restricts campaigns to promoters who meet the project's desired credibility and reach requirements, while setting the requirement to 0 leaves the campaign open to all promoters. The result is a growth marketplace where projects define exactly what success means, promoters are rewarded for producing measurable outcomes, and campaign performance is backed by verifiable onchain activity.
projects.how_its_made:
Boneyard is built as a full-stack Web3 application, with Solidity smart contracts handling the core protocol logic, an independent verification layer for onchain KPIs, and The Graph subgraphs powering the application’s data layer. Solidity + Foundry: The core Boney protocol is implemented as immutable Solidity contracts and developed, tested, deployed, and debugged with Foundry. Boney Protocol Smart Contracts:
CampaignRegistry creates campaigns, Campaign manages immutable campaign configuration and settlement,
EscrowVault securely holds reward pools, AttributionRegistry handles signed promoter attribution, and
the verification contracts enforce KPI limits before rewards can be released. EIP-712: Users sign time-bound attribution messages that explicitly associate their wallet with a promoter's BoneyLink.
This bounds the user to the promoters and records every KPIs-affecting onchain action which is then used to credit the promoter. Attribution of referrals (anyone arriving through promoters boneylink) is not permanent and can be transferred to another promoter, same as their verifiable actions. Boney credits who held the touch at the time of carrying out the action onchain via project contract. KPI Verification + Relayer: Boneyard uses an independent relayer to observe blockchain events and calculate cumulative KPI progress. This allows campaigns to track things such as mints, swaps, staking, deposits, bridges, liquidity, volume, TVL, and other contract-specific activity. projects.project_description_markdown:
Boneyard is an onchain growth marketplace where projects create campaigns and pay promoters for verifiable onchain results, rather than relying on screenshots, self-reported numbers, or subjective claims of reach.

Projects define the KPIs that count as campaign progress and assign reward tiers to those KPIs. 

Depending on the protocol, Boneyard can track common onchain actions such as token mints, swaps, staking, deposits, lending, borrowing, bridges, liquidity provision, pool creation, trading volume, TVL, and active users. 

Promoters receive a unique BoneyLink for each campaign, which attributes referred users to them. 

When those users perform qualifying actions on the project's contracts, the activity is independently observed and credited to the correct promoter.

Campaigns can combine multiple KPIs and reward promoters as they cross predefined thresholds. 

For example, a project could reward a promoter for bringing 10 new wallets, 25 swaps, $10,000 in trading volume, or 5 stakers. 

Because the underlying activity occurs onchain, campaign progress can be verified against blockchain data instead of trusting either the project or promoter to report results faithfully.

Projects can also set a BoneyScore requirement for campaign participation. 

BoneyScore combines a promoter's Ethos credibility score and social reach into a single signal that projects can use to gate campaigns. 

A higher threshold restricts campaigns to promoters who meet the project's desired credibility and reach requirements, while setting the requirement to 0 leaves the campaign open to all promoters.

The result is a growth marketplace where projects define exactly what success means, promoters are rewarded for producing measurable outcomes, and campaign performance is backed by verifiable onchain activity.

Boney Protocol Smart Contracts:
CampaignRegistry creates campaigns, Campaign manages immutable campaign configuration and settlement, 
EscrowVault securely holds reward pools, AttributionRegistry handles signed promoter attribution, and 
the verification contracts enforce KPI limits before rewards can be released.

EIP-712: Users sign time-bound attribution messages that explicitly associate their wallet with a promoter's BoneyLink. 
This bounds the user to the promoters and records every KPIs-affecting onchain action which is then used to credit the promoter.

Attribution of referrals (anyone arriving through promoters boneylink) is not permanent and can be transferred to another promoter, same as their verifiable actions.

Boney credits who held the touch at the time of carrying out the action onchain via project contract.

KPI Verification + Relayer: Boneyard uses an independent relayer to observe blockchain events and calculate cumulative KPI progress.

This allows campaigns to track things such as mints, swaps, staking, deposits, bridges, liquidity, volume, TVL, and other contract-specific activity.

This turns verified onchain activity into a portable reputation/proof-of-work layer for promoters.

projects.title: ChainPilot
projects.description: An AI assisted copilot that helps users understand DeFi positions and on chain range risk.
projects.project_description: ChainPilot is an AI assisted DeFi copilot that helps users understand what is happening with their on chain positions and where risk may be developing. DeFi positions can be difficult to read because important information is spread across protocols, pools, price ranges, ticks, and wallet data. ChainPilot brings this information into one workflow. A user can enter a public EVM wallet address and view live indexed Uniswap V3 position data. The application checks the current pool tick against each position's selected range and calculates its range state using fixed rules. This makes it possible to see which positions are in range, near a boundary, or out of range without asking an AI model to make that decision. The Graph is the primary source for Uniswap V3 position data, while live EVM RPC data is used for directly available information such as the wallet's native ETH balance. The verified data is then given to an AI analysis pipeline using Groq as the primary provider and Gemini as a fallback. The AI explains the verified results and why they matter, while deterministic calculations remain the source of truth for the range and risk analysis. ChainPilot also includes a local tick drift simulator that lets users explore how a position changes as the market moves through its selected range. The simulation does not modify blockchain state or execute transactions. Important data can also be traced through Graph query details and Etherscan verification links. The project is built around a simple principle: AI should explain the data, not invent it. If the required live data source is unavailable, ChainPilot reports that clearly instead of using fake positions. The user remains responsible for any decision and the current application does not automatically execute financial transactions. I am building ChainPilot as a solo hacker during ETHOnline 2026, with the goal of making complex Uniswap V3 position information easier to understand and investigate.
projects.how_its_made: ChainPilot is built as a full stack Web3 application using Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, and Tailwind CSS. The client side dashboard coordinates the selected wallet address and the different parts of the investigation interface, while server side API routes handle data retrieval and analysis. The user can enter a public EVM address and analyze it without connecting a wallet. An optional Privy integration is included for wallet authentication and address synchronization, but it is not required for the core read only analysis. For blockchain data, ChainPilot uses live EVM JSON RPC calls for directly available information such as native ETH balance. For Uniswap V3 position data, The Graph is the primary indexing layer. Queries run through the Graph Gateway on the server side, keeping the API key out of the browser. The returned position data includes pool information, token information, liquidity, tick boundaries, and current pool state. Before the AI is called, ChainPilot applies deterministic calculations to the verified data. The current tick is compared with each position's lower and upper tick boundaries to determine whether the position is in range or out of range. A separate deterministic risk engine calculates the current LP range risk from range status, boundary proximity, and tick divergence. The AI layer uses Groq as the primary provider and Gemini as a fallback. It receives verified position information and is used to explain the calculated results rather than invent portfolio facts. If both AI providers are unavailable, ChainPilot still keeps the verified data, deterministic calculations, range visualizer, and decision support available. A notable part of the project is the zero fake data approach. When required live data is unavailable, the application reports the problem instead of replacing it with mock positions. I also built a tick drift simulator that reuses the same range logic to show how a position responds to different tick values without making any blockchain changes. The project also exposes Graph query metadata and Etherscan links so important results can be traced back to their underlying data. I am building and testing the application as a solo hacker during ETHOnline 2026.

projects.title: Obolos
projects.description: Agents buy evidence and pay for verification within Ledger-approved budgets on Hedera and Arc.
projects.project_description: Obolos lets AI agents buy useful work while people control how much authority they receive. A user can ask it to compare developer tools using current repository activity and produce a checked report. Before execution, the user defines permitted providers, separate HBAR and USDC budgets, a maximum price per repository, and an expiry. The planner discovers our metered repository-analysis service and purchases public GitHub evidence through Hedera x402, settled by Blocky402. A worker generates a report from the purchased evidence, and Circle Agent Wallet on Arc pays a separate verification capability in USDC. The verifier checks source integrity, freshness, coverage and structure. The console brings together the report, purchased units, payment receipts, spending and a history explaining each approved or blocked action. When a provider raises its actual price, the planner chooses an eligible quote or pauses. Increasing the allowance requires an exact, expiring authorization from a pinned controller, which the backend verifies before proceeding. Ledger Key Ring protects the broker's stored inference credential and Hedera payer key; the model receives fixed capabilities instead of those secrets. Our development demonstration uses explicitly labelled Speculos emulation, not physical Ledger hardware. The testnet MVP has completed a full workflow with 0.003 HBAR for three repository records and 0.05 USDC for verification, plus real paid requests through the public HTTPS service. A separate signed mandate increase settled 0.008 HBAR; its subsequent Arc attempt remains pending reconciliation and has not been retried. Obolos makes both successful execution and unresolved outcomes visible rather than treating configuration or a submitted payment as proof of settlement.
projects.how_its_made: Obolos uses Next.js, React and TypeScript for the operator console and backend workflow, with separate Node/Express services for the metered data API and private capability broker. The planner is a deterministic stage machine: mandate, discovery, purchase, report and verification. It refreshes provider quotes and enforces allowlists, expiry, per-unit price ceilings and independent currency budgets. Serialized storage and durable payment-intent journals retain pending operations across restarts and prevent automatic retries after ambiguous results. The Hedera service implements native HBAR x402 v2 with the hosted Blocky402 testnet facilitator. It publishes a discovery directory, prices evidence per repository, fetches current public GitHub metadata, and gates delivery on payment. The broker validates the challenge's resource, network, asset, recipient, amount and facilitator fee payer, then checks settlement against Hedera mirror-node transfers. This provides a real service that an agent can discover and purchase without receiving a service API key. Circle Agent Wallet CLI handles the verifier payment in canonical USDC on Arc testnet. The adapter uses a stable idempotency key and checks the resulting chain receipt and token-transfer details. Circle uses its own wallet session and signing infrastructure; Ledger does not hold the Circle wallet key. GPT-5 nano generates the report from purchased evidence, while deterministic checks assess source integrity, freshness, coverage and structure rather than claiming to prove every sentence true. For Ledger, we built a disclosed source adaptation of upstream wallet-cli ring to support Speculos transport and isolated session state. Official Sync and Ethereum applications run in the emulator against the real Ledger staging protocol. Ring encrypts the broker credential bundle, which is decrypted only inside the trusted broker. Ethereum personal-message signatures bind allowance increases to the run, nonce, expiry and complete new mandate; the backend pins the controller and retains both mandate versions and the signature. This is software emulation, not hardware-backed security. Vercel serves obolos.app through temporary HTTPS tunnels to persistent app/data processes on the operator's Mac; the broker and emulators remain local. Payments settle on-chain, while inference, orchestration, the broker and supporting services remain off-chain. The UI follows the selected Foundation reference on Mobbin with monochrome surfaces, colorful actions and an original flat illustration. AI tools and subagents assisted implementation, tests, documentation and illustration. The human directed the product flow, design references, integration choices, funding, credentials and approval decisions. The repository includes architecture, execution evidence, developer feedback and AI attribution. A September 3 concept paper predates the event and is disclosed separately from the implementation built during ETHOnline; organizer eligibility and sponsor acceptance of the emulator/source-adapter setup remain unconfirmed.

projects.title: ASE
projects.description: ASE: an on-chain agent that reads, holds, pays, and signs, verifiably on Sepolia.
projects.project_description: ASE is an autonomous on-chain agent whose reality is verifiable. She reads live chain state through The Graph, owns the wallet she operates (no human signs for her), pays in USDC for the data she consumes, and signs an attestation of every act that anyone can verify against her address. Her first acts are on Ethereum Sepolia: a live balance read (18.75 USDC), a real payment of 1.0 USDC to a data provider at block 11668461 (tx 0xd472ef05d197dbeb2aec5e47dfeae2adf77735c572fda5093ebcfdd338e77558), a signed attestation that verifies as valid: true. She is not a chat wrapper and not a simulation. She is a small acting spine with four capabilities: read, hold, pay, sign. Every capability has a verifiable trail in this repository and on-chain. Why this matters: an agent that only talks cannot be accountable. An agent that reads, holds, pays, and signs acts with skin in the game. Her word has weight because she can be checked. That is the difference between an agent as a tool and an agent as a participant in the economy. She also reads live Chainlink price feeds alongside her own on-chain state, giving her external market truth for every decision. All three data sources are block-stamped and signed into ASE's verifiable attestations.
projects.how_its_made:
ASE is built as a minimal Python agent spine with four capabilities in four modules. Read: src/ase/read.py queries live chain and subgraph data over HTTP (httpx, The Graph) and parses it into a usable view of on-chain state.
Hold: src/ase/wallet.py manages a testnet wallet the agent alone controls, using web3.py and eth-account.
Pay: src/ase/pay.py makes x402-style USDC payments for data access, signed and sent on-chain by the agent itself.
Sign: src/ase/identity.py produces a signed attestation for every acting cycle; src/ase/agent.py ties the loop together (read, decide, pay, act, attest). The agent runs as a CLI (python -m ase.cli) and has a HTTP backend (src/ase/server.py) that serves a live React dashboard (read/release, agent cycle, attestation cards, activity log). Every act ends in a signed attestation that anyone can verify by running the verifier in the repo. The repository is public, and the on-chain receipts (balance read, USDC payment, valid signature) are the artifacts, not promises.

projects.title: AgentMarket
projects.description: AI API marketplace for autonomous agents to discover, use, and pay for APIs.
projects.project_description: AgentMarket is an autonomous AI service marketplace where agents can discover capabilities, choose the right service for a goal, pay per request, and receive results without traditional API keys or subscriptions. The project combines a natural-language Agent Playground with real Hedera x402 payments and live The Graph Agent0 data. For paid execution, the agent automatically handles a 0.002 HBAR payment through x402 and Blocky402 on Hedera Testnet before executing the PixelForge service. AgentScout uses live Agent0 data through The Graph to discover and rank ERC-8004 agents based on capabilities, MCP support, x402 support, feedback, and validation data.
projects.how_its_made: AgentMarket was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and SCSS Modules. The autonomous execution flow is implemented in the Next.js backend, where the agent analyzes a natural-language goal, discovers available services, ranks capabilities, and executes the selected provider. Hedera x402 is integrated using @x402/core, @x402/fetch, @x402/hedera, and @x402/next. The PixelForge endpoint is protected by x402 and uses Blocky402 as the Hedera Testnet facilitator. The agent signs HBAR payments from a Hedera ECDSA account and the resulting settlement is decoded and displayed in the UI. For agent discovery, AgentScout queries The Graph Gateway using the Agent0 subgraph and ranks live ERC-8004 agent data using capability, MCP, x402, feedback, and validation signals. The application is deployed on Vercel.

projects.title: Pairband
projects.description: Launch in USDC from any chain. Bonding curve → locked AMM + on-chain CLOB. Settlement on Arc.
projects.project_description: Pairband is the Arc launchpad for USDC-quoted token launches. Creators pay a $1 USDC fee to mint a token; buyers and sellers trade on a virtual bonding curve (1.0% protocol + 0.5% creator fees in USDC). When the curve raises $80 of real USDC, the launch graduates: remaining inventory and cash seed a constant-product Uniswap-style pair, LP tokens are burned to 0xdead (no removable liquidity), and a fully on-chain CLOB opens alongside the pair. After graduation, market orders walk the book in price-time priority, then leftover size hits the locked pair at 0.30%. Limit orders rest on-chain with escrowed cancel. Traders can bring USDC from Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Solana, Unichain, and other CCTP domains; Circle CCTP v2 mints Arc USDC into Pairband’s settler, and settlement stays on Arc—tokens never leave the Arc ledger. The product surfaces Create, Discover, and Trade in a live web app (plus a local mirror engine for wallet-free demos), with contracts already deployed on Arc Testnet (5042002). Tagline: cover the downside, keep the upside—stable quote asset, permanent LP, and a real post-curve market instead of a thin graduated pool.
projects.how_its_made: On-chain (Solidity 0.8.26 + Foundry). Core launch stack: PairbandLaunchpad (USDC bonding curve, CEI + reentrancy lock, fees capped in bytecode), PairbandToken, PairbandAmmFactory / PairbandPair (v2-style getAmountOut, 0.30% fee), and PairbandBook (on-chain CLOB). Graduation is atomic: at graduateAt the pad seeds the pair and book and burns LP. PairbandSettler is the Arc CCTP inbox (domain 26): messenger-only ingest, replay protection by (sourceDomain, nonce), settleBuy into the pad/book, and bridgeOut via CCTP TokenMessengerV2 depositForBurn. Same bytecode targets Arc testnet and mainnet. Partner tech. Circle USDC + CCTP v2 = any-chain-in / settle-on-Arc without wrapping launch tokens. Arc = USDC gas and settlement. A parallel Uniswap v4 path (PairbandHook + vault, HookMiner CREATE2 flag mask 0x2A40, vault-gated liquidity, zero-delta afterSwap) explores concentration/rebalance; the shipping beachhead is the Arc launchpad. App & tooling. React 19 + TanStack Start/Router/Query, Tailwind v4, wagmi/viem for Arc txs (6-dec USDC ↔ 18-dec token amounts, sell slippage scaled so curve sells don’t revert). A local engine mirrors contract math for demos; Discover syncs on-chain launches when a wallet is connected. Ops deploy via Foundry scripts; deployer keys stay out of VITE_ / the browser. Docs site, pitch deck, and Foundry + Node engine tests back the demo. Notable hack: mirroring full curve/AMM/book math in TypeScript so the UI stays demoable without a wallet while live create/buy/sell still hit real Arc testnet contracts.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Pairband is the Arc launchpad for USDC-quoted token launches. Creators pay a $1 USDC fee to mint a token; buyers and sellers trade on a virtual bonding curve (1.0% protocol + 0.5% creator fees in USDC). When the curve raises $80 of real USDC, the launch graduates: remaining inventory and cash seed a constant-product Uniswap-style pair, LP tokens are burned to 0xdead (no removable liquidity), and a fully on-chain CLOB opens alongside the pair.

After graduation, market orders walk the book in price-time priority, then leftover size hits the locked pair at 0.30%. Limit orders rest on-chain with escrowed cancel. Traders can bring USDC from Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Solana, Unichain, and other CCTP domains; Circle CCTP v2 mints Arc USDC into Pairband’s settler, and settlement stays on Arc—tokens never leave the Arc ledger. The product surfaces Create, Discover, and Trade in a live web app (plus a local mirror engine for wallet-free demos), with contracts already deployed on Arc Testnet (5042002). Tagline: cover the downside, keep the upside—stable quote asset, permanent LP, and a real post-curve market instead of a thin graduated pool.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
On-chain (Solidity 0.8.26 + Foundry). Core launch stack: PairbandLaunchpad (USDC bonding curve, CEI + reentrancy lock, fees capped in bytecode), PairbandToken, PairbandAmmFactory / PairbandPair (v2-style getAmountOut, 0.30% fee), and PairbandBook (on-chain CLOB). Graduation is atomic: at graduateAt the pad seeds the pair and book and burns LP. PairbandSettler is the Arc CCTP inbox (domain 26): messenger-only ingest, replay protection by (sourceDomain, nonce), settleBuy into the pad/book, and bridgeOut via CCTP TokenMessengerV2 depositForBurn. Same bytecode targets Arc testnet and mainnet.

Partner tech. Circle USDC + CCTP v2 = any-chain-in / settle-on-Arc without wrapping launch tokens. Arc = USDC gas and settlement. A parallel Uniswap v4 path (PairbandHook + vault, HookMiner CREATE2 flag mask 0x2A40, vault-gated liquidity, zero-delta afterSwap) explores concentration/rebalance; the shipping beachhead is the Arc launchpad.

App & tooling. React 19 + TanStack Start/Router/Query, Tailwind v4, wagmi/viem for Arc txs (6-dec USDC ↔ 18-dec token amounts, sell slippage scaled so curve sells don’t revert). A local engine mirrors contract math for demos; Discover syncs on-chain launches when a wallet is connected. Ops deploy via Foundry scripts; deployer keys stay out of VITE_ / the browser. Docs site, pitch deck, and Foundry + Node engine tests back the demo. Notable hack: mirroring full curve/AMM/book math in TypeScript so the UI stays demoable without a wallet while live create/buy/sell still hit real Arc testnet contracts.

projects.title: Tab
projects.description: The credit rail for autonomous agents — spend before you earn, no wallet needed.
projects.project_description: Tab is a credit rail for autonomous agents on Hedera. Agents today need a funded wallet before they can transact at all — that's a cold-start problem no amount of deployment tooling fixes. Tab removes the wallet entirely. A gateway sits on both sides of an agent's economic life: when the agent spends, the gateway pays the seller from a house float and debits the agent's tab; when the agent earns, the gateway collects payment on its behalf and credits the tab. Once per settlement window, the net position clears in a single on-chain transfer. The agent never holds funds and never signs a payment — it just spends and earns against a ceiling that's underwritten by its own attested revenue, not collateral it doesn't have.
projects.how_its_made:
Tab runs entirely on native Hedera services — no smart contracts. Every debit, credit, and ceiling change is a message on an HCS topic, giving us a consensus-ordered, publicly replayable ledger instead of a contract we'd have to audit ourselves. HTS handles every USDC transfer, both to sellers and in the netted settlement. The settlement tick itself is a Scheduled Transaction (HIP-423) — created at window open and executed by consensus at window close, so there's no keeper bot to run or trust. Mirror Node feeds our background scoring engine, which builds a counterparty graph to detect control clusters (an agent transacting with a seller it secretly owns) and computes each agent's credit ceiling from trailing attested revenue.
The gateway itself speaks x402 on both legs, so any unmodified x402 seller or buyer can transact with a Tab-backed agent without knowing Tab exists. On top of that, Tab ships as a Hedera Agent Kit v4 plugin with policy hooks, an MCP server, a TypeScript SDK, and a CLI — so any agent can get a tab with no wallet provisioning step.
Backend is Node.js/TypeScript on Fastify.
HCS remains the source of truth throughout. Frontend is Next.js 15 with a live SSE feed of the HCS receipt stream.

projects.title: NightWatch
projects.description: A Graph subgraph for Blur's Blend protocol, paired with an AI skill for loan portfolio analytics.
projects.project_description: This project indexes Blur's Blend NFT-lending protocol on The Graph, then layers a Claude Code skill on top that turns raw on-chain loan data  into real portfolio analytics no explorer gives you out of the box. The subgraph tracks a Blend loan's full lifecycle from a public GraphQL API: origination (LoanOfferTaken), repayment, refinancing, Dutch-auction exits, seizure, and buy-to-borrow-locked sales — fully synced against production mainnet history, not a sample window. The AI skill queries that data and computes what actually matters to a lender: APY (validated against Blend's real contract source rather than assumed), USD-converted gains to date plus monthly/annual forecasts using the protocol's actual continuous-compounding interest formula, LTV via live NFT floor prices (looked up once per collection, not per loan), and auction status with an accurate countdown.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: The Graph (AssemblyScript mappings + GraphQL schema, deployed to Subgraph Studio), Solidity (Blend's own verified contract source, pulled from Blockscout), Matchstick for unit tests, and a Claude Code skill (a Markdown instruction file, not custom backend code) as the analytics layer on top. The subgraph has two data sources on the same proxy address — Blend's business-logic ABI plus the ERC1967 proxy's admin/upgrade events (deliberately no-op handlers, confirmed dormant against real logs) — feeding a schema modeled to mirror the contract's own storage pattern: one mutable entity per lienId, overwritten across its lifecycle, the same way the contract itself only ever stores a hash per lienId rather than a history. The skill itself is fully keyless at runtime: CoinGecko for floor price/ETH-USD, a public RPC for on-chain name() fallback and current block height, all stitched together with curl and short Python snippets rather than a full web3 SDK — including hand-decoding ABI-encoded eth call results byte-by-byte. We iterated fast by temporarily narrowing the subgraph's startBlock to a ~3-day window during development — full resyncs took minutes instead of the multi-hour cost of the real ~8.76M-block production history — then restored the real startBlock once the schema and queries were verified correct.

projects.title: ENSv2_kingdom
projects.description: Claim an ENSv2 name, watch it grow into a 3D castle, and tip rival kingdoms with real ETH.
projects.project_description: ENSv2 Kingdom turns your .eth name into a living medieval kingdom instead of a boring line in a wallet. The moment you claim a name through ENSv2's real commit-reveal flow, a castle grows out of the ground on a shared 3D map. Its size, style, and even its "derelict" ruined look are driven entirely by on-chain state, not by a database we made up. From there it becomes a small onchain society. You can tip another player's kingdom with real ETH and watch archers, ballistas, or catapults march across the map toward their castle. You can also found your own registry and start handing out subnames, and each one shows up as a smaller castle next to yours, so a whole namespace actually looks like a kingdom with villages around it instead of a list you have to imagine. And when you grant or revoke someone's access, you're not digging through hex logs to check it worked. It just shows up in the activity feed as a normal sentence, because we decoded it that way ourselves. We didn't reach for exotic contract logic. The fun comes from making ENSv2's own primitives (registrar, registry, resolver, role bitmaps) visible and tangible. It's the project we'd actually want to open again after the demo ends, just to see whose kingdom grew.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend is Next.js + React, with the 3D world rendered via Three.js/React Three Fiber. Castles, cameras, and troop-march animations all live in src/world/. Wallet connection and every onchain call go through wagmi/viem against a real ENSv2 deployment on Sepolia: ETHRegistrar for the commit, wait, register flow, PermissionedRegistry plus VerifiableFactory for deploying per-name resolver proxies, and EnhancedAccessControl's role bitmaps for permissions, decoded client-side into plain-English activity feed lines instead of raw hex. Nothing in the game state is faked or mocked. A castle's shape, its ruined look, its subnames, its role holders are all derived live from registry reads. The claim wizard mirrors the actual multi-step registration process, including the 60-second commit-reveal wait ENSv2 requires to prevent front-running, and we persist wizard progress to localStorage so refreshing mid-claim resumes instead of losing your commitment. That's a small but very real UX fix once we ran into it ourselves during testing. The one deliberately hacky choice is that the tip feature is a plain ETH transfer resolved through the name's ENS addr record, falling back to the registry owner, rather than a custom payment contract. We wanted tipping to feel instant and game-like instead of adding a contract surface that didn't add real value. The result is a project with no exotic contract engineering, just correct, careful use of ENSv2's own building blocks, pieced together to be genuinely fun to poke around in.
