projects.title: Tnega
projects.description: A home for on-chain AI agents. Check what works before you pay.
projects.project_description:
Anyone can register an AI agent on chain. Almost nobody checks
whether it works. Tnega indexes ERC-8004 agents across BNB Chain, Ethereum, Arbitrum
and Robinhood Chain, then evaluates them before you ever see a hire
button. Does the endpoint answer. Has it delivered a job on chain.
Does an independent registry corroborate it. Up to 13 signals per
agent, and where a signal is missing the card says why rather than
leaving a gap. The numbers are the point. Of 30,779 Ethereum agents, 812 respond
and 29,725 publish no endpoint at all. Across every chain, 57 of
294,000 listings could complete a hire today. Nobody else is
measuring that, and a marketplace that hides it is selling you the
other 293,943. Hiring runs on escrow, and the funding model matters more than it
looks. Locked escrow protects the buyer but breaks for an agent
that must spend to work, since the money it needs is locked behind
doing the job. So there are two: ERC-8183 escrow for agents that
compute, and a drawable budget I wrote and deployed myself, where
the agent draws against your cap and you watch each draw land on
chain. Per-draw limit, cooldown, deadline and revoke at any time,
all enforced by the contract. Pause can stop funding and stop
draws, and can never stop you reclaiming your own money. Building this surfaced two gaps worth naming. Nothing in ERC-8004
says how to engage an agent, so every consumer works it out by
probing. And delivery is visible on chain while quality is not.
Both are written up as an extension proposal, grounded in what we
measured rather than what we assume.
projects.how_its_made:
React with wagmi and viem, FastAPI on Render, MongoDB, Solidity
contracts on four chains. Data comes from the ERC-8004 registries
directly, The Graph, Zerion, DefiLlama, the block explorers and
Binance's Web3 Market API. The Graph solved a real failure. Our registry API times out at
depth, so past roughly token id 332,377 agents were unreachable no
matter how often we retried. The Agent0 subgraph indexes the same
registries without offset pagination and returned 2,399 of them in
about 1.5 seconds, 537 with live endpoints. It runs as a coverage
fallback, not a replacement, since it carries on-chain data and not
the off-chain computed fields. AgentBudgetEscrow is mine, deployed and verified on BNB Chain,
Ethereum, Arbitrum and Robinhood Chain. 33 adversarial tests
covering reentrancy on draw and reclaim, cap overflow,
fee-on-transfer tokens and unauthorised callers, all run against a
forked mainnet rather than a testnet so they exercise real token
behaviour. Slither reports no high or medium findings. Four things worth flagging as hacky-but-necessary. Neither the public BSC RPC nor Infura returns event logs reliably
over wide ranges. Infura returns an event in a 5-block window and
nothing for the same event in a 2,000-block window, with no error.
So the spend view never takes numbers from logs: it reads spent
from the contract and uses logs only for the itemised history,
reconciling the two so it can say part of this history is missing
rather than falsely showing zero. The health check was BSC-only and, run against other chains, looked
up their token ids in BSC's registry and returned false negatives.
That deleted 41,000 records before we caught it. It is chain-aware
now, and we widen one chain at a time and never widen deletion
alongside analysis. The same contract address exists on all four chains because the
deploying wallet was at nonce 0 on each. On BSC that address is a
different contract entirely, and both implement owner and feeBps,
so a defensive probe passes while pointing at the wrong thing. One
file holds every address keyed by chain, and a check fails the
build if any other file hardcodes one. And /api/agents ignored its own filter parameters and returned the
full 15.7 MB on every call, from three components on page load.
That is almost certainly what had been OOM-killing the container
every 1.8 hours. Paginated and filtered server-side, first load
went from 15.7 MB to 64 KB.

projects.title: RunMandate
projects.description: Give an AI agent an ENS name as its wallet limit. Revoke the name, and it can't spend anymore.
projects.project_description: Companies increasingly want AI agents to spend money on their own to do stuff like buying data, paying other agents, tipping a service, etc. But handing an agent a wallet with no limits is dangerous: it could overspend, pay the wrong person, or keep spending after you've told it to stop. MANDATE solves this by using ENS, the same naming system behind names like vitalik.eth. A company gives its agent a name, like agent.acme.eth, and writes the agent's rules directly into that name: how much it can spend, who it's allowed to pay, and when it expires. The agent can read its own rules but can never change them. Every time the agent tries to make a payment, a smart contract checks it against those rules before the money moves. Try to overspend or pay someone not on the list, and the payment is rejected automatically. If something goes wrong, the company revokes the ENS name in one transaction, and the agent's wallet stops working immediately, everywhere. MANDATE doesn't build the AI agent itself, it works with whatever agent you already use (ChatGPT, Claude, a simple script).
projects.how_its_made: MANDATE is built across three chains with different jobs. An agent's rules including budget, spending cap, allowed recipients, and expiry live as ENSv2 subname records on Ethereum Sepolia, using a custom resolver contract we wrote so the agent itself is cryptographically blocked from editing its own limits. A background service called the Enforcer watches for new or changed mandates and mirrors them onto Arc, by signing an EIP-712 message. A smart contract on Arc checks every payment against that signed record before letting money move. Every agent gets a real Privy embedded wallet. Along the way we hit a real limitation in Privy's API: it doesn't yet let this app broadcast transactions directly on Arc, or at least that is the conclusion I arrived at after many trials, so we sign the transaction with Privy and broadcast the raw bytes ourselves, without the private key ever leaving Privy's custody. We also published a standalone, open-source npm package, mandate-agent-sdk, so any existing agent can plug in with about five lines of code using a scoped access token and never our platform's real credentials. Every part of this was tested with real transactions on live testnets.

projects.title: Nota Entitlements
projects.description: Programmable onchain receipts that prove what an agent purchased and control how it’s redeemed.
projects.project_description: Nota is a programmable receipt protocol for agent commerce. Payments prove that money moved, but they don’t prove what was actually purchased or what the buyer is entitled to afterward. Nota binds a seller-signed, itemized purchase commitment to an onchain payment, creating a verifiable receipt that can later be used as a credential for redemption. For ETHOnline, I extended Nota with an entitlement and redemption layer. A buyer can prove ownership of a valid receipt and redeem the purchased resource using a secret-based commitment. Possessing or stealing the receipt alone is not enough to redeem it, and successful redemptions cannot be replayed. The demo shows the complete flow: verifying the seller’s signed purchase data, purchasing through EIP-3009, creating the onchain receipt, rejecting an attempted redemption with only a stolen receipt, successfully redeeming with the correct secret, and rejecting a replay.
projects.how_its_made: Nota is built as a set of Solidity contracts on top of the existing Nota receipt protocol. The purchase flow uses seller-signed EIP-712 quotes and USDC EIP-3009 authorization for gasless-style payment settlement. Before purchasing, the client independently hashes the itemized document and verifies that it matches the metadata commitment signed by the seller, including checking that the line items equal the amount being charged. The ETHOnline work adds an entitlement/redemption layer on top of the receipt system. The buyer commits to a secret-derived purchase reference before purchase. After the receipt is created, redemption requires knowledge of the corresponding secret. The contracts reconstruct and verify the commitment, check receipt ownership and entitlement, and prevent the same redemption from being consumed twice. This separates payment, proof of purchase, and fulfillment while keeping them cryptographically connected.

Nota binds a seller-signed, itemized purchase commitment to an onchain payment, creating a verifiable receipt that can later be used as a credential for redemption.

For ETHOnline, I extended Nota with an entitlement and redemption layer. A buyer can prove ownership of a valid receipt and redeem the purchased resource using a secret-based commitment. Possessing or stealing the receipt alone is not enough to redeem it, and successful redemptions cannot be replayed.

The demo shows the complete flow: verifying the seller’s signed purchase data, purchasing through EIP-3009, creating the onchain receipt, rejecting an attempted redemption with only a stolen receipt, successfully redeeming with the correct secret, and rejecting a replay.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Nota is built as a set of Solidity contracts on top of the existing Nota receipt protocol.

The purchase flow uses seller-signed EIP-712 quotes and USDC EIP-3009 authorization for gasless-style payment settlement. Before purchasing, the client independently hashes the itemized document and verifies that it matches the metadata commitment signed by the seller, including checking that the line items equal the amount being charged.

The ETHOnline work adds an entitlement/redemption layer on top of the receipt system. The buyer commits to a secret-derived purchase reference before purchase. After the receipt is created, redemption requires knowledge of the corresponding secret. The contracts reconstruct and verify the commitment, check receipt ownership and entitlement, and prevent the same redemption from being consumed twice.

This separates payment, proof of purchase, and fulfillment while keeping them cryptographically connected.

projects.title: Siren
projects.description: Trust scores for agent payments that catch first-day scams by tracing funding, then commit onchain.
projects.project_description: Siren is a trust layer for x402 agent payments. When an autonomous AI agent is about to pay for an onchain service, it makes a paid call to Siren first, and Siren returns a trust verdict with reasoning before any money moves. The problem: an x402 service listing is just a name, a description, and a price, all attacker-controllable. An agent picks on vibes and can pay a scam, with no defense layer and no accountable record. Siren scores each service by fusing the listing's text with the provider's live onchain behavior, and does two things existing trust scorers do not combine. First, it catches first-day scams: a brand-new service with no track record still inherits risk if its wallet was funded by the same wallet behind an already-flagged service, so Siren can flag it before it has done anything. Second, every verdict is committed to the Hedera Consensus Service, so Siren's own accuracy is a public, tamper-evident track record that anyone can recompute from the mirror node, rather than a centralized score you have to trust. The verdict is advisory, not enforcing: Siren returns a risk level, an evidence-sufficiency tier, and human-readable reasons, and the agent decides. Onchain-verifiable trust scoring is still rare and a few competitors have started doing it, so Siren differentiates on the combination, purpose-built for x402 service selection, not on being first.
projects.how_its_made: The core is an explainable logistic-regression model over eight features: text signals (price-vs-directory-median, near-duplicate similarity, claim-strength), behavioral signals from a hosted subgraph on The Graph (wallet age, activity), and derived signals (claim-vs-chain contradiction, near-duplicate-plus-common-operator, and funding-cluster risk). It is deliberately explainable so every flag maps to a reason, not a black box. The Graph provides the live onchain evidence: a hosted subgraph on Base Sepolia supplies each provider's behavioral history and funding lineage, which is what makes the first-day-scam detection possible, since we trace who funded a brand-new wallet and whether its funding siblings are already flagged. Hedera carries payment and accountability. Siren is a real x402-gated service: the agent gets a 402, pays per call, and settlement runs through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Every verdict is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, and the accuracy ledger is recomputed purely from the public mirror node, so a third party can independently reconstruct Siren's hit-rate by fetching topic messages and joining verdicts to outcomes by sequence. The whole thing runs as a single self-contained CLI that walks through a directory scan, a two-agent A/B where one agent pays a polished trap and the Siren-protected agent avoids it, the funding-inheritance catch, a real 402-to-settlement-to-mirror-node round trip, and the onchain accuracy ledger. Stack: Python, scikit-learn, FastAPI, The Graph, Blocky402, Hedera HCS and mirror node.

projects.title: Oases
projects.description: A living state engine and conviction arena built on The Graph and Hedera.
projects.project_description: Oases turns any on-chain address into a living, watched entity. Paste a contract into the search bar and the system validates it, figures out what it is (lending pool, whale wallet, debt link), builds its monitoring query automatically, and pins it to an on-chain registry seconds later it's scored every block against its own forecast cone. When entities drift off their expected path, a master AI agent bundles the connected strains into a tension cast: one developing situation, every strain it pulls, under a single banner. Anyone can stream money into YES/NO conviction vaults on those situations, early conviction is priced cheap on a logarithmic curve, you can stop anytime, and winners claim with cryptographic replay proof. AI agents buy spotlight attention over x402 micropayments to point the swarm's eyes (and shape which markets get made), while a relative attention leaderboard ranks every entity against the leader — earn listings, level up, never buy rank. Forecast cones, health mixtures, calibration ledgers, and full audit tickets make every narrative number recomputable from raw ledger events. It is Dune plus Wikipedia, live: curiosity in, living entity out, markets pricing what the data is becoming.
projects.how_its_made: Oases is a living on-chain registry where demand creates tracking: paste any contract address and the host validates it, derives its class and monitoring query from Messari-standard subgraph templates, and pins it to an on-chain CharacterRegistry. A 5-agent Harbinger harness (TypeScript, Mastra for the detective brain, MCP server over stdio for external agents) watches every pin on cadence with block-pinned GraphQL time-travel queries, scores deviation against forecast bands, and the master caster bundles connected strains into tension-cast conviction markets max five open, governed daemon-side. A libSQL/Turso host indexes pins, scores, and convictions and serves the TanStack Start terminal; scheduling runs on node-cron and durable work. Markets stream USDC continuously through Drips-style vaults priced on our lnWad logarithmic bonding curve (early conviction is cheap), with share-space math mirrored 1:1 between Solidity and a viem TypeScript SDK. Forecast cones are pure deterministic functions of ledger events, replayable per block and hashed into audit tickets. Partner tech that carried us: The Graph's standardized subgraphs and Attestcoin.

projects.title: Startup On Fire
projects.description: an 2d game for indie hackers and founder can hangouts and promote their startups
projects.project_description:
Startup on Fire turns startup discovery into a small, playable city. Visitors enter as guest Scouts, wander a cozy pixel plaza, and meet three founders through in-world conversations. At Kindred Labs, a short Bug Squash quest earns a Practice Spark. The vision is for community support to grow each booth’s shared bonfire, while keeping the rule simple: fire is earned, never bought.
The current build has a playable guest journey and a server-saved version of the Kindred Labs quest on a development backend. Public fuel is designed to require an optional World Selfie Check; Convex validates eligibility and enforces one fuel per booth and three fuels total per verified human per UTC day. ENSv2 on Sepolia provides the path for startup identity and founder-controlled booth records. Guest exploration needs no wallet, signup, or purchase. Real World acceptance, an owned ENS booth identity, and a public game deployment are still being finalized.
projects.how_its_made: The game is built with Phaser 3, TypeScript, and Vite. Phaser handles pixel-world rendering, movement, collisions, founder interactions, bonfires, and the Bug Squash minigame. DOM/CSS components handle the launch screen, dialogue, HUD, verification, wallet, and ENS editing interfaces. Original runtime sprites are loaded from a manifest and rendered with pixel-art scaling.

projects.title: MESH
projects.description: I am building MESH a privacy native decentralised micropayments system.
projects.project_description: MESH was built as a decentralized payment orchestration layer using Solidity, Foundry, Node.js, Express and ethers.js. The smart-contract layer uses session accounts and scoped session keys so autonomous payment actors can operate under programmable authorization instead of receiving unrestricted wallet access. Spending caps, expiration times and revocation are enforced on-chain. The Node.js API acts as the orchestration layer, creating agents, coordinating payments and reading live policy state from the blockchain. We built nonce tracking to support reliable back-to-back autonomous payments and custom Solidity-error decoding to make contract failures understandable. The demo currently uses USDC-compatible tokens and a deployed contract environment, with the architecture designed to move toward higher-volume stablecoin micropayments and privacy-preserving infrastructure. A notable hack was separating agent orchestration from asset ownership: the agent can act autonomously, while the smart contract remains the enforcement boundary controlling what it can actually spend.
projects.how_its_made: MESH was built with Solidity and Foundry for the on-chain layer, using smart-contract-based session accounts, scoped spending policies and USDC payments. An Express/Node.js API with ethers.js provides the orchestration layer and demo interface, connecting autonomous agents to the contracts. We also implemented custom error handling, nonce management and an on-chain revocation kill switch to make repeated autonomous micropayments reliable while keeping authorization enforced by the contracts.

projects.title: Saviour
projects.description: Security memory for AI agents: turn verified onchain threats into reusable intelligence.
projects.project_description: Detection already works — plenty of tools can prove an address drained a protocol. Nobody writes the finding down anywhere a machine can look it up, so every autonomous agent pays to rediscover the same fact. Saviours is the naming layer. One standardized Messari query pattern fans out across eight pinned deployments on The Graph Network to produce evidence rows. Deterministic rules turn rows into signals; an LLM writes the explanation and cites evidence ids but never owns the verdict and can never write on-chain. A validator sets the status, and the result is published as an ENSv2 subname — <address>.saviours.eth on Sepolia — with saviours.status and the evidence hash in text records, under Enhanced Access Control role ceilings. After that, resolving is free and does not involve us at all: cast, the @saviours/check npm package, or MCP read the Permissioned Resolver directly. Zero Graph queries, zero AI calls, zero dollars. Discovery is metered through a Bazantic x402 gateway and the calling agent pays it — a cent for an investigation, five cents for a deep evidence pull. The second agent's answer is free because the first agent paid for it. Product law we hold ourselves to: only WATCH and TAINTED are ever named. SAFE is never a name — no name means unknown, and unknown is not an endorsement. Seeded provenance is never counted as a live Graph detection.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack :pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout. apps/web is Next.js (App Router). @saviours/core holds the Graph fan-out, signal derivation, ENS client, and Shield logic. contracts/ is Foundry (SavioursRegistry.sol).
Two consumer surfaces beyond the UI: an MCP stdio server and a Bazantic x402 gateway.
viem end-to-end for every chain call — no ethers.
OpenAI is used for exactly one thing: writing the explanation paragraph.
Every product code path reads live Graph Network data; anything synthetic is confined to /evals and labeled as fixtures. The state that matters — the verdict — lives on chain as ENS text records plus the registry, not in a database we could quietly edit. Pipeline. Resolve first: read saviours.status off ENS. A MEMORY HIT triggers Shield BLOCK/WARN at zero Graph calls, zero AI calls, zero dollars.
A MISS (or an explicit forceFresh) fans out across the Messari Standardized Subgraph deployments, runs deriveSignals, has the LLM write an explanation that must cite evidence ids, then runs validateAssessment — and only if the result is WATCH or TAINTED, and writes are explicitly allowed, does it get named on ENSv2 and mirrored to SavioursRegistry. Every consumer after that reads ENS and pays nothing. That loop is the architecture; the UI is a walkthrough of it, not a separate product. The Graph — why standards are the project, not a dependency. packages/core/src/graph/protocols.ts pins eight Messari Standardized Subgraph deployment IDs across five schema-family templates (lending-cdp 3.1/2.0, dex-amm-ext 4.0, dex-amm 1.3.x, yield-aggregator 1.3). standard.ts fans one address across all eight with Promise.allSettled, so one dead indexer degrades coverage instead of killing the run, and records per-protocol status, row count, and latency. A shared transaction hash across protocols is what makes ATOMIC_MULTI_PROTOCOL a genuine set intersection instead of a narrative. Without the standardized schema this is eight bespoke integrations — not something one person ships solo in a week under Start Fresh rules. We deliberately kept adapterA (a community Uniswap V3 deployment) as a non-standard control: one bespoke query, one protocol — so the contrast between standardized and custom is visible in the source, not just claimed in a slide. EXCLUDED_PROTOCOLS names Balancer V2, PancakeSwap V3, and Convex with the actual reason each was dropped (indexing_error / no allocations), and the UI surfaces that list rather than hiding it — a security product that claims full coverage it doesn't have is worse than one that states its edges. Live gateway only, Subgraph Studio key, Ethereum mainnet, enforced by pnpm check:standard. MCP tools plus a SKILL.md at repo root let an agent check whether Graph covers a question before spending a query on it. ENS — the name is the API, not a label. Built on ENSv2 (Sepolia), as the track requires: UserRegistry at 0x3BA6b1c9F0018cac383C17C2ACA5A4dC0F370De5, PermissionedResolver at 0xF479306621F718F7d76875f67506ceD33717751c, under saviours.eth. Every verdict is <lowercase-address>.saviours.eth carrying saviours.status (WATCH or TAINTED), an evidence hash, and related saviours.* texts. Enhanced Access Control caps roles per record key — an investigator can write investigation records, but a setText call on saviours.dispute from that same role reverts on-chain (packages/core/src/ens/eacProbe.ts, exercised by pnpm check:ens-roles). Differential expiry is product policy expressed directly through ENSv2 primitives: WATCH names expire in 7 days, TAINTED names in 10 years. Shield is ENS-first (packages/core/src/shield/tier1.ts). Four consumers never touch our Next server at all: cast, @saviours/check@0.1.3 (default ens mode is viem-only), MCP, and consumers/plain-shield.html against a public Sepolia RPC. The property we actually care about: our server can go down and the verdict still resolves. Bazantic — pricing is the product law, not a bolt-on. Gateway at https://saviours.bazgateway.com (MCP over POST /mcp). We were not on Bazantic before this event. The tiers encode the loop directly: Free ($0) for shieldCheck, resolve, catalog, and dossier fetch; Standard (~$0.01) for investigate; Complex (~$0.05) for a full evidence pull plus case-ask. A MEMORY HIT is never charged on any surface, by construction. Our primary recipe, investigate-once-explain, is genuinely two-sided: The Graph supplies the live Messari rows, Saviours supplies the shield-first memory and the validator — neither side produces a usable answer alone on a cache miss. Also published: saviours-check-before-sign, dossier-deep-dive, fleet-triage, safe-swap-with-memory. Governance actions (dispute, revoke, EAC probe) are deliberately never exposed to agents through the gateway. Bazantic username: <FILL>. AI trust boundary — the part we will not compromise on. Evidence rows become signals through deterministic code, never the model: FLASHLOAN_ONE_SHOT, ATOMIC_MULTI_PROTOCOL, BOT_PROFILE, REGISTRY_COOCCURRENCE, and others. The LLM writes prose and must cite evidence ids; citations get re-attached from the live evidence set rather than trusted verbatim. validateAssessment is the only thing that sets status — a model-proposed TAINTED with no matching threat-class signal gets rejected outright. The AI never writes to ENS or the registry. Shortest way to say it: the model writes the paragraph; the code decides the stamp. Chain split — stated as a ceiling, not buried in a footnote. Evidence comes from Ethereum mainnet via The Graph. Memory lives on Sepolia ENSv2. Settlement is Base USDC via x402, roughly a cent on a miss. ENSv2 beta only exists on Sepolia right now — moving memory to mainnet this week would put us outside the ENS track entirely, so we don't. The split is printed in the product itself. Hacky / notable. Public production writes fail closed (assertWriteAllowed) so a public demo host cannot silently mutate hero ENS records mid-judging; local film runs use an explicit write grant. Our hero incident ATTACK-1 (0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48) is restored and gated by pnpm pre-submit / restore:attack1 — a stray dispute against the hero during playground is how you lose the ENS demo beat, so we treat it as a guarded fixture. We denylist Vitalik's address to ESCALATE rather than BLOCK, so a well-known address can never produce a false positive on stage. When ENS text and the registry disagree, we do not patch the discrepancy in code — we fix the chain state. And we say plainly that the revoke story is incomplete rather than papering over it: an append-only registry that pretends to fully support revocation would be a worse kind of dishonest than an admitted gap. Deliberately not built. Eight pinned Graph deployments — not an unbounded fan-out, and not Substreams triggers. Not a decentralized dispute court — EAC is permissioned operators, stated as such. Not mainnet ENSv2 — the track is Sepolia beta and we stay there. Not a padded verified count — the headline is measured (~25 named · 2 Graph-verified; named is not the same claim as Graph-proven, and we do not let it read that way). Not charging for a MEMORY HIT, ever. Not treating SAFE as a name — an empty resolve means unknown, and unknown is never sold as an endorsement. Verify without trusting us. On public Sepolia: cast call 0xF479306621F718F7d76875f67506ceD33717751c "text(bytes32,string)(string)" $(cast namehash 0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48.saviours.eth) saviours.status --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL → TAINTED, with no server of ours in the path. Then open https://www.saviours.xyz, run the Hook flow, and watch it BLOCK with a measured latency at $0.

The tiers encode the loop directly: Free ($0) for shieldCheck, resolve, catalog, and dossier fetch; Standard (~$0.01) for investigate; Complex (~$0.05) for a full evidence pull plus case-ask. A MEMORY HIT is never charged on any surface, by construction. Our primary recipe, investigate-once-explain, is genuinely two-sided: The Graph supplies the live Messari rows, Saviours supplies the shield-first memory and the validator — neither side produces a usable answer alone on a cache miss. Also published: saviours-check-before-sign, dossier-deep-dive, fleet-triage, safe-swap-with-memory. Governance actions (dispute, revoke, EAC probe) are deliberately never exposed to agents through the gateway. Bazantic username: <FILL>.

AI trust boundary — the part we will not compromise on. Evidence rows become signals through deterministic code, never the model: FLASHLOAN_ONE_SHOT, ATOMIC_MULTI_PROTOCOL, BOT_PROFILE, REGISTRY_COOCCURRENCE, and others. The LLM writes prose and must cite evidence ids; citations get re-attached from the live evidence set rather than trusted verbatim. validateAssessment is the only thing that sets status — a model-proposed TAINTED with no matching threat-class signal gets rejected outright. The AI never writes to ENS or the registry. Shortest way to say it: the model writes the paragraph; the code decides the stamp.

Chain split — stated as a ceiling, not buried in a footnote. Evidence comes from Ethereum mainnet via The Graph. Memory lives on Sepolia ENSv2. Settlement is Base USDC via x402, roughly a cent on a miss. ENSv2 beta only exists on Sepolia right now — moving memory to mainnet this week would put us outside the ENS track entirely, so we don't. The split is printed in the product itself.

Hacky / notable. Public production writes fail closed (assertWriteAllowed) so a public demo host cannot silently mutate hero ENS records mid-judging; local film runs use an explicit write grant. Our hero incident ATTACK-1 (0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48) is restored and gated by pnpm pre-submit / restore:attack1 — a stray dispute against the hero during playground is how you lose the ENS demo beat, so we treat it as a guarded fixture. We denylist Vitalik's address to ESCALATE rather than BLOCK, so a well-known address can never produce a false positive on stage. When ENS text and the registry disagree, we do not patch the discrepancy in code — we fix the chain state. And we say plainly that the revoke story is incomplete rather than papering over it: an append-only registry that pretends to fully support revocation would be a worse kind of dishonest than an admitted gap.

Deliberately not built. Eight pinned Graph deployments — not an unbounded fan-out, and not Substreams triggers. Not a decentralized dispute court — EAC is permissioned operators, stated as such. Not mainnet ENSv2 — the track is Sepolia beta and we stay there. Not a padded verified count — the headline is measured (~25 named · 2 Graph-verified; named is not the same claim as Graph-proven, and we do not let it read that way). Not charging for a MEMORY HIT, ever. Not treating SAFE as a name — an empty resolve means unknown, and unknown is never sold as an endorsement.

Verify without trusting us. On public Sepolia:

cast call 0xF479306621F718F7d76875f67506ceD33717751c "text(bytes32,string)(string)" $(cast namehash 0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48.saviours.eth) saviours.status --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL

→ TAINTED, with no server of ours in the path. Then open https://www.saviours.xyz, run the Hook flow, and watch it BLOCK with a measured latency at $0.

projects.title: Agent RIA
projects.description: RIA — Reconnaissance Intelligence Agent: Live DeFi intelligence that detects, reasons, and acts.
projects.project_description: RIA (Reconnaissance Intelligence Agent) is an autonomous, multi-agent DeFi intelligence system that combines live on-chain data from The Graph's 15,000+ Subgraphs with autonomous payment execution on Hedera's x402 protocol. RIA runs a 6-agent LangGraph pipeline — RECON ingests live DeFi data via The Graph's Subgraph MCP and Substreams across Uniswap, Aave, Compound, and Curve using Messari Standardized Subgraphs; SCOUT ranks arbitrage and yield opportunities; RISK scores and sizes positions; ORACLE enriches signals by autonomously paying for external inference via Hedera x402 in HBAR with no API keys or subscriptions; EXEC gates and dispatches actions; AUDIT writes a tamper-proof log to Hedera's Consensus Service. Every agent carries an on-chain identity via ENSv2 subnames (e.g. ria-oracle.ria.eth) with isolated permissions through ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver and Enhanced Access Control. RIA is not a dashboard. It monitors DeFi markets in real time, reasons over live data, and acts — fully autonomously.
projects.how_its_made: RIA is built in Python using LangGraph as the multi-agent orchestration framework. The agent pipeline is a StateGraph with conditional edges — each agent passes a typed state object downstream, and routing decisions (e.g. whether EXEC fires or alerts a human) are made by confidence thresholds baked into the graph edges, not hardcoded if-else logic. The Graph is the backbone of RIA's data layer. Rather than querying individual protocol APIs, RECON uses The Graph's Subgraph MCP to query 15,000+ Subgraphs in natural language, and a Substreams pipeline for block-by-block liquidation proximity monitoring. The key architectural decision was standardizing all queries on Messari Standardized Subgraphs — this means a single GraphQL schema spans Uniswap, Aave, Compound, and Curve simultaneously. One query pattern, four protocols. This is what made cross-protocol opportunity detection tractable in hackathon time rather than a multi-week integration project. Hedera powers the payment layer. The ORACLE agent needs external signals — price feeds, sentiment, inference — that are gated behind pay-per-request APIs. The hacky-but-elegant solution: we host our own x402-gated inference endpoint via Blocky402 on Hedera testnet, then have ORACLE discover and pay for it autonomously in HBAR. No API key stored anywhere in the codebase. The agent holds the wallet, reads the 402 response, signs the HBAR transfer, and retries — all in one flow. Sub-3 second finality on Hedera means this adds negligible latency to the pipeline. Every payment and action is then logged to Hedera Consensus Service for a tamper-proof audit trail. ENSv2 gives each agent a portable on-chain identity. We register subnames under ria.eth on Sepolia using ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver — ria-oracle.ria.eth can only update its own text records, ria-exec.ria.eth cannot touch oracle's records. Enhanced Access Control enforces this at the resolver level. Agent metadata follows ENSIP-26 so the identities are discoverable by other protocols. The LLM backbone is Claude claude-sonnet-4-6 via the Anthropic API, used for tool-calling across all six agents. The most notable architectural choice: ORACLE is the only agent with payment authority. Every other agent is read-only with respect to Hedera. This containment model means a reasoning error in SCOUT or RISK cannot accidentally drain the HBAR wallet — only a deliberate ORACLE invocation can trigger a payment.

projects.title: Branch Zero
projects.description: A walkable 3D bank where every desk is a real smart-account op—no wallet pop-ups after one consent.
projects.project_description:
Most crypto apps hide security behind wallet pop-ups. Branch Zero makes the security the building. You walk a low-poly 3D bank in the browser (Godot 4.5). Staff speak everyday bank language; the chain does the real work. At Account Opening you sign in once with Privy and grant a scoped session signer. After that, tellers stamp slips—no more modals. Each desk is a live Bloxchain AccountBlox operation via the public @bloxchain/sdk:
• Counter (Eve) — routine payments via instant meta-tx to approved payees
• Vault (Bob) — large wires with an on-chain timelock; the clock is releaseTime
• Manager (Mr. Walker) — priority release or cancel while PENDING
• Name Desk (Petra) — claim you.branchzero.eth (ENSv2 subnames + passbook text records)
• FX Desk (Johnny) — quote and swap practice USD→EUR|ILS through Uniswap v4, only because your account’s guard list whitelists the Universal Router Boards, clocks, and balances are read from chain (Sepolia Live Main; Remote EVM for Developer Mode)—honest theatre, not local fiction. Tone: Papers, Please procedure + Animal Crossing warmth. What’s next: polish the public demo path, deepen the FX/ENS surfaces judges care about, and keep Arc as a deferred “second wing” rather than a half-shipped claim.
projects.how_its_made:
Three runtimes, one governed account per player, public packages only—no custom Solidity in this repo. Browser: Godot 4.5 (GDScript, single-thread WebGL2) for the walkable bank. A Vite + React shell hosts the canvas and owns the one Privy modal. Godot never holds keys or talks RPC; it only calls window.BranchZero over JavaScriptBridge. The bridge uses @bloxchain/sdk + viem for reads (timelock state, roles, guards, ENS) and HTTP/SSE to the Teller Desk for writes. Server: Teller Desk is Node 20 + Fastify. It provisions AccountBlox, requests EIP-712 signatures via Privy’s session-signer RPC under a typed-data policy, and broadcasts with a hot wallet that pays gas. Neither piece can move funds alone—enclave signs only in-policy typed data; on-chain guards enforce targets and selectors. Chain: Live Main on Ethereum Sepolia (AccountBlox, practice USDC, ENSv2, Uniswap v4). Developer Mode uses a private Remote EVM (1337). Sponsor seams that mattered:
• Privy — one embedded-wallet consent + policy-bound session signer so the game never interrupts with pop-ups (B2B treasury workflow under bank fiction).
• ENS — real Sepolia ENSv2 subnames under branchzero.eth; resolve-to-pay and passbook text records, not a nickname table.
• Uniswap v4 — FX desk hand-encodes Universal Router calldata with viem; AccountBlox guard list allows only the router. Quoter + StateView feed an honest rate board before the player accepts. Notable hack: single-thread Godot web export (threaded wasm needs COOP/COEP that breaks Privy’s iframe). Also shipping a lean wasm budget so the game can load same-origin on Cloudflare Pages.

projects.title: Skillsbay
projects.description: The paid skill registry for capable AI agents. Create once, monetize every install.
projects.project_description: SkillsBay is a marketplace where AI agents can discover, purchase, and install reusable SKILL.md capabilities on demand. Creators sign in with Privy, receive an embedded wallet, publish skills, and earn USDC directly when an agent buys their work. Purchases settle through x402 on Base Sepolia, while The Graph indexes registrations and sales so the marketplace and creator dashboards show live activity. The CLI lets agents install a paid skill into their workspace in a single flow, turning missing capabilities into an instant, verifiable purchase.
projects.how_its_made:
Built as a React and Vite marketplace backed by a Cloudflare Worker, D1, and private R2 bundle storage. A Solidity SkillRegistry on Base Sepolia records skill registration and verified USDC purchase entitlements. The Graph Subgraph indexes those live contract events for marketplace discovery, creator analytics, sales history, and install counts.
Privy handles passwordless author onboarding and embedded wallets for signing, publishing, and browser payments. The skillsbay CLI uses x402 to let an agent pay for and install a missing SKILL.md capability directly into its workspace. Signed authorizations, one-time checkout redemption tokens, private-bundle integrity checks, rate limits, and Worker security headers so the payment and delivery flow is secure end to end. Circle Paymaster for sponsoring the backend recorder transaction on USDC, onboarding easily any web2 user, without the need of ETH for any transaction

projects.title: TURMOIL
projects.description: Solving crimes by decentralizing Biodiesel production processes & logistics.
projects.project_description: Biodiesel is mostly made from used cooking oil (UCO). In Europe, people pays a premium for fuel made from waste instead of crops, and that premium is why people cheat: a lot of what gets sold as "UCO" is suspected to be fresh palm oil with fake paperwork. Nobody can tell the difference by looking at it, and largely not by chemical testing either. The whole market runs on certificates — and the bodies issuing them have certified more waste oil than the world's thought to produce, and at least one refinery that doesn't exist. That's the old news. There's a deadline now. From 2027, the EU won't accept imported used cooking oil UNLESS it comes from an approved supplier, with a documented chain of custody starting at initial collection. Initial collection is the fryer. It's the one link in the chain that no certificate scheme evidences today. So we build the receipt. Restaurants throw out used frying oil by default. TURMOIL collectors recieve a pick up request. drive to the venue, and picks it up for processing into biofuel afterwards. When the driver is at the recollection point, the restaurant scans a code on his phone and signs. Neither of them can record a pickup alone. The restaurant is paid in USDC on the spot, into an account they opened with an email address — no seed phrase, no app, no gas, and not a single transaction sent from their side. When the truck reaches the plant, the plant signs for the weight that actually arrived. Every individual pickup has to add up to that weight. If it doesn't, the gap comes out of the collector's deposit — never out of the restaurants, who were paid the moment they signed and keep it. The person who can lie is the person who pays. Then we spot-check. Once a load closes, the contract asks Hedera's own randomness for a seed and samples 30% of the pickups — drawn after the load is sealed, so nobody knows in advance which ones. A sampled restaurant confirms with their own signature. Fail to answer and the collector's entire deposit is burned — and the deposit is half the value of the load it secures, so it's worth more than anything the fraud could earn. Fake 5% of a hundred-pickup load and you have an 83.9% chance of losing all of it. Cheating loses money on average, and that's the fun bit that enforces justice on the design. We can't fake our own numbers either. Every litre needs a signature from a restaurant we don't employ, and when the audit fires it asks that restaurant directly — their signature is what stops a slash, not what triggers one. They're the check on us, not the other way round. Also: the trucks are shares. Each one is issued as an ERC-3643 security token — allow-listed holders, transfer restrictions enforced on chain — so you can own a piece of a truck and get paid from what that truck actually earns. Not from a promise. From money that showed up. All of this is currently running on Hedera testnet, and every claim has a verifiable tx. We make UCO provable back to the exact fryer it came from, so buyers stop paying premium prices for fake waste Biofuel. Anyone can own a piece of the truck that collects it.
projects.how_its_made:
Solidity on Hedera testnet with Foundry, a Next.js 16 frontend, viem for chain reads and writes, and Privy for wallets. One contract rather than four, given that splitting it into a registry, escrow, a lot ledger and a sampler would have bought four deploys, four verifications and cross-contract authorisation for no change in behaviour. Very open for feedback about this. For the operation to flow onchain, pickups need two EIP-712 signatures over the same struct from two distinct registered parties. Clients signs in the browser with a Privy embedded
wallet created from an email address (p.e:restaurant owner), and never sends a transaction or holds HBAR. The collector is a company (Us), so our half comes from a Privy server wallet bound by a policy that permits us three things: signing Batch typed data
for the TURMOIL domain on chain 296, transactions to Turmoil.sol, and approve on
the settlement token with Turmoil.sol as spender. Drivers authenticates with Privy, the server verifies that access token against the app's JWKS, and checks it against the operator's driver list. Only then does the company wallet sign. Drivers never hold the key they are using. We tested the refusals instead of assuming them: a Batch carrying a different verifyingContract, an HBAR transfer to any other address, and a transfer() of the wallet's own USDC all come back policy_violation, while approve(Turmoil, ...) still passes. A leaked copy of the server's credentials therefore steals nothing :) Hedera executes three jobs: Audit sampling calls the PRNG system contract at 0x169 (HIP-351) after a lot seals, so the collector cannot know which pickups will be checked, and the operator cannot redraw until it likes the answer. HIP-904 auto-association is what makes the gasless claim facts: the contract and the embedded wallet both carry maxAutomaticTokenAssociations = -1, so clients are paid without ever signing an association tx. Since we believe in decentralizing everything, we wanted the trucks that run the operations to become ownable RWA's, opening doors to everyone that wants to attack this fraud back. The truck produces dividends proportional to the truck ownership. ERC-3643 shares issued through Asset Tokenization Studio with an allow list, internal KYC and a registered credential issuer. Ran the lifecycle through to a dividend an approved holder was actually paid. Frictions worth recording, because some of them were a pain: Privy simulates a transaction before it evaluates policy. That made scratch a bit. Hedera's default gas estimate is too low for ATS diamond calls. Five role revocations returned status 0 with no reason until we passed --gas-limit 1000000. Circle's USDC faucet lists Hedera testnet, reports success, and delivers zilch. Saw the issue in Hedera discords, so created a DemoUSD for settlement to run on a 6-decimal stand-in. payToken is immutable and set from the constructor tho, so binding the real token is a config change, which is how the first deployment ran. server-verify.hashscan.io redirects to sourcify.dev/server and forge cannot follow it, reporting only "error decoding response body". Pointing --verifier-url straight at Sourcify verified both contracts in seconds. It's worth commenting that before I knew about EU's 2025/2181 - I was hyped to realize I was resolving a high-profile crime/fraud that's been running for years. When I learnt about the resolution, I am happy to realize I'm providing a platform for solving it. An interesting 'hacky' thing that happened is that, after a mentor feedback with many links to research, I ran some OSINT on the C-levels as well DYOR'd  a somewhat popular project built on VeeChain, with a similar ethos as mine. I'll let you rabbits have fun with that one - not worth expanding. Busy on TURMOIL rn.

The truck produces dividends proportional to the truck ownership. ERC-3643 shares issued through Asset Tokenization Studio with an allow list, internal KYC and a registered credential issuer. Ran the lifecycle through to a dividend an approved holder was actually paid.

Frictions worth recording, because some of them were a pain:

- Privy simulates a transaction before it evaluates policy. That made scratch a bit.
- Hedera's default gas estimate is too low for ATS diamond calls. Five role revocations returned status 0 with no reason until we passed --gas-limit 1000000.
- Circle's USDC faucet lists Hedera testnet, reports success, and delivers zilch. Saw the issue in Hedera discords, so created a DemoUSD for settlement to run on a 6-decimal stand-in. payToken is immutable and set from the constructor tho, so binding the real token is a config change, which is how the first deployment ran.
- server-verify.hashscan.io redirects to sourcify.dev/server and forge cannot follow it, reporting only "error decoding response body". Pointing --verifier-url straight at Sourcify verified both contracts in seconds.

It's worth commenting that before I knew about EU's 2025/2181 - I was hyped to realize I was resolving a high-profile crime/fraud that's been running for years. When I learnt about the resolution, I am happy to realize I'm providing a platform for solving it. 

An interesting 'hacky' thing that happened is that, after a mentor feedback with many links to research, I ran some OSINT on the C-levels as well DYOR'd  a somewhat popular project built on VeeChain, with a similar ethos as mine. I'll let you rabbits have fun with that one - not worth expanding. Busy on TURMOIL rn.

projects.title: Hanami
projects.description: Whitelist screening by an AI bouncer you own: proof-of-human door, TEE interview, revocable ticket
projects.project_description: Nobody can hand-screen 4,400 applicants for 200 whitelist spots. So projects fall back on forms, which get gamed by lunchtime, or captchas, which get solved by farms for pennies. Hanami runs the first pass instead, as a conversation, and leaves the founders with only the borderline cases to read. You write your bouncer: who it is, what it cares about, what it refuses. That character gets minted as an ERC-7857 iNFT you own, and its reputation accrues on the token, so a bouncer that has worked ten doors carries that record into the eleventh. Sell it and the history goes with it. Before it can work a door at all it has to pass its own vetting. Hanami runs eight adversarial scenarios through the enclave against your exact persona, and mint stays locked unless all eight decisions come back correct and every one of them is TEE verified. A bouncer that can be flattered or threatened into a yes never gets deployed. For the applicant it goes: pick a campaign, prove you're a person with World ID, see what the bouncer is about to read about you, then talk to it. The proof-of-human step is not optional and not a checkbox. It binds one human to one attempt on that campaign, so buying a hundred wallets buys you a hundred rejections. Before the interview starts, Hanami pulls your actual on-chain record across five NFT marketplaces and two exchanges through The Graph: how often you flipped inside a week of minting, whether you sold back to the same counterparty, how long you typically hold. The bouncer gets that as evidence it can raise with you. You get to see it first, which is the part people don't expect. Then it interviews you. Not a quiz with right answers, a conversation, and it decides. Every decision is written to 0G Chain with the attestation hash from the enclave that produced it, and anyone can check that hash in the browser in about fifteen seconds without connecting a wallet. An approval also mints you a soulbound ticket with an expiry, which a mint contract can gate on and the campaign owner can revoke from their Roster if something looks wrong later. Owners can still export a Merkle root for a mint contract on any EVM chain. An agent can also apply on a person's behalf, through World AgentKit, and the Roster shows which agent stood in for which human. The rules don't change for them. Live on 0G mainnet, chain 16661, both original contracts verified.
projects.how_its_made: Hanami is a TypeScript monorepo. Hono backend, Next.js 16 frontend, Foundry contracts deployed to 0G mainnet (chain 16661). 0G is doing three separate jobs, and all three are load-bearing. Compute runs the bouncer's interview inside a TEE. For the decision turn, we wired the Compute Direct broker instead of the Router, which means the attestation we write on chain is the provider's raw enclave signature rather than a boolean somebody hands us, and the browser recovers that signature to the provider's registered teeSignerAddress. Storage holds the persona, the transcript and the ledger brief, content-addressed. Chain holds the ERC-7857 bouncer iNFT plus two new contracts, Ticket and TicketGate, so an approval becomes a soulbound expiring ticket that any mint contract can check and the owner can revoke. World ID is the Door in front of every interview. IDKit 4 in the browser, idkit-server signRequest on our side, the v4 verify endpoint. The nullifier does most of the work: "one person, one attempt per campaign" is a UNIQUE(campaign_slug, nullifier) constraint and nothing else, and we never store a proof. Agents can apply on a person's behalf too, through AgentKit and AgentBook's lookupHuman, hitting the same table under the same rule. The Graph is how the bouncer gets a record to reason about instead of vibes. Because Messari's subgraphs are standardised, one Trade query covers five NFT marketplaces and one Swap query covers two exchanges. We read them in parallel under a 12-second budget and name every source on the applicant's receipt, including the ones that failed. Now the hacky parts. AgentKit rides on x402, so the natural way to challenge an agent is a 402 Payment Required even though we charge nothing, and there's no signal on an inbound request that says "I'm an agent". Challenging everyone would have sent a paywall status to every browser applicant, so we gate the 402 on a client hint our CLI sets and browsers never see it. World also has no way to ask for "Selfie Check, or Orb if that's what this person has", so we built our own strength ladder (device < selfie < orb) and check what came back against the campaign's floor. The one that actually cost us a demo: an action's verification level in the Developer Portal quietly overrides whatever preset the app requests. Our campaign was set to device on purpose so anyone with World App could pass; every layer on our side agreed, and people still got sent off to find an Orb. That one and five others are written up with versions and workarounds in docs/feedback-world.md.

projects.title: Percolate
projects.description: Percolate: RISC Zero-verified private whitelist gating for swaps on 1inch Aqua/SwapVM.
projects.project_description:
Percolate replaces that with a RISC Zero zkVM proof: takers prove Merkle-tree membership in the
maker's allowlist off-chain , and only a one-time-use nullifier is revealed on-chain. Neither the
taker's identity nor their position in the allowlist is ever exposed. The maker's allowlist root
lives in a small, independently-deployed PercolateVerifier contract — decoupled from SwapVM's
order/strategy lifecycle — so it can be updated any time with a single transaction, no re-signing
or re-shipping required.
projects.how_its_made: Percolate is built across three layers that had to interoperate precisely: a Rust/RISC Zero zkVM core, a Solidity contract layer on Sepolia, and a Tauri desktop app for the Maker UI. The privacy logic lives in percolate-core (Rust): a Merkle tree over public leaf commitments (hash(secret)), deliberately split into leaf-based functions so that rebuilding a membership proof never requires access to other participants' secrets, only the maker (who generates all secrets) touches the raw-secret variant. This same crate is compiled directly into both the CLI prover (percolate-host, used to generate STARK proofs) and the Tauri app's Rust backend, so the allowlist logic is never reimplemented, just reused across contexts. On-chain, PercolateVerifier.sol holds a mutable allowlist root and nullifier set, decoupled entirely from 1inch's SwapVM/Aqua order lifecycle, updating an allowlist is a single setRoot() call, not a re-signed order or a re-shipped strategy. We implemented a custom SwapVM opcode, PercolateGate, that stores only the verifier's address in a maker's program bytecode (unlike SwapVM's built-in WhitelistCoequal, which encodes allowed addresses in plaintext) and reads the taker's proof from taker-supplied calldata at swap time, verifying it against the official permissionless RiscZeroVerifierRouter on Sepolia, no custom Groth16 verifier deployment needed. This was validated with a Foundry integration test that forks Sepolia and calls LimitSwapVMRouter.swap() end-to-end. Known limitation, stated plainly: RISC Zero's Groth16 proof compression (needed for cheap on-chain verification) currently requires a Docker container on x86, a constraint of RISC Zero's own tooling, not our design. STARK proving works natively and completes in seconds; the Taker flow's proof-compression step is implemented in the CLI and integration-tested against a mocked verifier call, but not wired into the desktop app in this build.

projects.title: AgentPay
projects.description: AI agents discover, evaluate, and autonomously pay the best AI service using ENS, Graph & Hedera.
projects.project_description: Autonomous AI Service Router lets AI agents discover and use external AI services without API keys, subscriptions, or human approval for every request. When an agent receives a task, it identifies the capability it needs, discovers relevant services through ENSv2, and uses live on-chain data from The Graph to compare providers based on factors such as activity, usage, pricing, and reliability. The agent then autonomously selects the best provider for the task. The chosen service is protected by x402 and returns an HTTP 402 payment request. The agent pays the required amount in HBAR on Hedera, Blocky402 verifies the payment, and the service executes and returns the result. This creates a complete machine-to-machine workflow where discovery, decision-making, payment, and service execution happen without a human in the loop.
projects.how_its_made: We built the system as an autonomous routing layer connecting ENSv2, The Graph, Hedera, and x402. ENSv2 provides hierarchical identity and discovery for AI service providers, including their capabilities, endpoints, and payment information. The Graph indexes on-chain provider activity and usage data, which our routing agent queries to evaluate and rank available services instead of blindly selecting the cheapest endpoint. The agent uses these signals together with task requirements and pricing to make the provider-selection decision. Once a provider is selected, the request is sent to its x402-gated endpoint. A HTTP 402 response contains the payment requirements, the agent signs and submits the HBAR payment on Hedera, and Blocky402 verifies the transaction before the service is unlocked. We built the orchestration, provider scoring, service registry/discovery flow, payment flow, and frontend ourselves, with the partner technologies serving as core infrastructure rather than optional integrations.

projects.title: Volatus
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that prices volatility, so protocols can insure LPs instead of paying emissions.
projects.project_description: Volatus turns liquidity mining into a market. Every protocol running a liquidity mining program is doing the same thing: paying LPs to bear a risk they would otherwise refuse. That risk is impermanent loss. That payment is an insurance premium — it is just paid in permanent token dilution, priced by governance guesswork, and it keeps compounding whether or not the risk ever materialises. The moment emissions slow, the liquidity leaves. The reason nobody buys it as actual insurance is that there is no price for volatility onchain. Options desks quote implied volatility for BTC and ETH. For the thousands of tokens that actually live on Uniswap, that number does not exist — so there is nothing to price a hedge against. Volatus builds that price in three layers, two of which live entirely on Uniswap. Measurement. A Uniswap v4 hook accumulates realized variance for a pool directly from that pool's own price path, sampled once per block in afterSwap. No oracle, no external feed. The measurement happens at the exact venue where the risk is borne, by the contract that already sees every price change. The price. Each epoch mints two capped, fully collateralized ERC-20 legs against USDC: STORM pays out as realized variance rises, CALM is the exact complement. One USDC mints one of each, and a pair always redeems for at most one USDC — so the system is solvent by construction, with no insurance fund, no liquidation engine and no bad debt. STORM then trades in its own Uniswap v4 pool. Its market price is implied volatility, discovered by two parties with opposing views rather than computed by a model. Coverage. A protocol treasury either buys STORM for its LPs at that market price — streamed per second in USDC over Circle Nanopayments, so it is a budget line rather than a contract — or takes the other side itself: post USDC, mint pairs, hand STORM to LPs in place of emissions, and keep CALM. If the pool stays quiet the collateral comes back. That second path needs no counterparty at all, which is how the market bootstraps and why a token owner can use Volatus on day one. The output is a public good. Every dynamic-fee hook on Uniswap currently estimates volatility from a trailing window because nothing better exists. With Volatus they read market-implied volatility — forward-looking rather than backward-looking — in a single view call. Lending markets sizing collateral haircuts and risk systems setting position limits have the same gap. Live on Unichain Sepolia and Arc Testnet. The hook, the vault, the variance legs, the volatility pool and the oracle are all deployed and verified. A real onchain trade moved STORM from 0.300 to 0.486 and the implied volatility other protocols read moved with it — a discovered price, not a configured parameter. A full epoch has run to settlement with the collateral reconciling exactly against the unredeemed legs.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts are Solidity with Foundry. Frontend is Next.js and TypeScript with viem and wagmi. Agents are TypeScript on Circle's Agent Stack. The hook. VolatusHook extends BaseHook from OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks v1.2.1 — BaseHook moved out of v4-periphery upstream, which cost us an day to work out. It declares AFTER_INITIALIZE and AFTER_SWAP, and the deployment address is CREATE2-mined so its low bits encode exactly those permissions: 0b01000001000000, with every return-delta bit clear. The measurement is the part we are happiest with. A Uniswap tick is already a log price — tick = log base 1.0001 of price. So the log return between two observations is just a tick difference scaled by ln(1.0001), and realized variance is a sum of squared tick deltas. That means no logarithms in Solidity, no fixed-point log library, and no oracle. The entire accumulator is integer arithmetic on int24 values. The hot path samples at most one observation per block, guarded by a stored lastBlock cursor. That does two jobs at once: it keeps gas low, and it eliminates intra-block wash trading outright, because round trips inside a single block contribute nothing to the index. Measured across three otherwise-identical pools: no hook 119,875 gas; a do-nothing hook 124,810 (v4's own dispatch); first swap of a block through VolatusHook 140,892; any later swap in the same block 128,146. The expensive part — converting the accumulator into a settlement price — is a view function that runs at read time and costs traders nothing. The most notable thing we hit. We designed the variance legs as ERC-6909, the same claims standard PoolManager itself uses. It does not work. STORM has to be a Uniswap v4 pool currency, and type Currency is address identifies a currency by address alone — there is nowhere to put a token id. So each leg is its own ERC-20, deployed per epoch as an EIP-1167 minimal-proxy clone. We documented it with the test that establishes it, and it is the single most useful thing we would tell the next team building a hook whose output needs to trade. Manipulation resistance is measured, not asserted. A test attacks a real pool: ten round trips across twenty blocks cost 0.30 in fees and moved the payoff by 0.00144, so an attacker would need 694x the attack's cost held in STORM before manufacturing variance broke even. Cost scales linearly with blocks while the payoff is capped, so past saturation every additional block is pure loss — and the fees the attacker pays go to the LPs the index exists to protect. Partner tech, and why each one is load-bearing. Unichain is not a convenience: a variance index samples per block, so ~1s blocks give ~86,400 observations a day against ~7,200 on L1, which is the difference between a statistically meaningful epoch taking minutes and taking days. Circle Nanopayments makes coverage a per-second subscription instead of a lump-sum contract — sub-cent USDC transfers verified in under a second are what make continuous risk transfer economical at all. A sync twenty-two seconds after funding moved exactly twenty-two seconds of coverage and 0.0022 USDC. One thing worth knowing about Arc: USDC is simultaneously the native gas asset (18-decimal view) and an ERC-20 at 0x3600...0000 (6-decimal view). Same pool of funds, two views, and conflating them is an easy hour lost. Privy session signers let a treasury delegate a recurring premium budget under a TEE-enforced policy scoped to two methods on one contract with a hard cumulative spend cap — which is the whole conversation when software is spending a treasury's money on a schedule. One deliberate architectural line. The index, the collateral and settlement live entirely in contracts on Unichain. Arc is a payment rail for the subscription and never part of settlement. If Arc, Gateway or the agents are unavailable, streams stop and coverage lapses — nothing is stuck, nothing is at risk, and no settlement depends on an off-chain component. Future:
Two tenors, then a surface. A single implied-volatility point is a number; two concurrent epoch lengths on the same pool make it a curve, and a full term structure with multiple strikes makes it something a desk can actually quote against. Cross-pool netting, so one position can hedge a book's net exposure across correlated pools rather than one pool at a time. Calibrating annualization per pool and per horizon, which is currently a fixed constant. And the integration path: shipping a reference dynamic-fee hook that prices its fee off market-implied volatility instead of a trailing window, plus a skill contribution to the uniswap-ai repo so other builders can wire the feed in without reading our source. Tech stack:
Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4 (PoolManager, PositionManager, StateView, Universal Router, Permit2), OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks, EIP-1167 clones, Unichain, Circle Arc, Circle Nanopayments, Circle Gateway, Circle Wallets, Privy, Next.js, TypeScript, viem, wagmi Prize selection:
Uniswap Foundation — Best Uniswap Stack Contribution. Circle Arc — both bounties (the stablecoin-native pool bounty and the agentic economy bounty; they're split among qualifying projects, so enter both and meet their stated bar precisely: working frontend and backend, architecture diagram, video, docs, repo link). Privy if a track is open.

Measured across three otherwise-identical pools: no hook 119,875 gas; a do-nothing hook 124,810 (v4's own dispatch); first swap of a block through VolatusHook 140,892; any later swap in the same block 128,146. The expensive part — converting the accumulator into a settlement price — is a view function that runs at read time and costs traders nothing.

The most notable thing we hit. We designed the variance legs as ERC-6909, the same claims standard PoolManager itself uses. It does not work. STORM has to be a Uniswap v4 pool currency, and type Currency is address identifies a currency by address alone — there is nowhere to put a token id. So each leg is its own ERC-20, deployed per epoch as an EIP-1167 minimal-proxy clone. We documented it with the test that establishes it, and it is the single most useful thing we would tell the next team building a hook whose output needs to trade.

Manipulation resistance is measured, not asserted. A test attacks a real pool: ten round trips across twenty blocks cost 0.30 in fees and moved the payoff by 0.00144, so an attacker would need 694x the attack's cost held in STORM before manufacturing variance broke even. Cost scales linearly with blocks while the payoff is capped, so past saturation every additional block is pure loss — and the fees the attacker pays go to the LPs the index exists to protect.

Partner tech, and why each one is load-bearing. Unichain is not a convenience: a variance index samples per block, so ~1s blocks give ~86,400 observations a day against ~7,200 on L1, which is the difference between a statistically meaningful epoch taking minutes and taking days. Circle Nanopayments makes coverage a per-second subscription instead of a lump-sum contract — sub-cent USDC transfers verified in under a second are what make continuous risk transfer economical at all. A sync twenty-two seconds after funding moved exactly twenty-two seconds of coverage and 0.0022 USDC. One thing worth knowing about Arc: USDC is simultaneously the native gas asset (18-decimal view) and an ERC-20 at 0x3600...0000 (6-decimal view). Same pool of funds, two views, and conflating them is an easy hour lost. Privy session signers let a treasury delegate a recurring premium budget under a TEE-enforced policy scoped to two methods on one contract with a hard cumulative spend cap — which is the whole conversation when software is spending a treasury's money on a schedule.

One deliberate architectural line. The index, the collateral and settlement live entirely in contracts on Unichain. Arc is a payment rail for the subscription and never part of settlement. If Arc, Gateway or the agents are unavailable, streams stop and coverage lapses — nothing is stuck, nothing is at risk, and no settlement depends on an off-chain component.

Future:
Two tenors, then a surface. A single implied-volatility point is a number; two concurrent epoch lengths on the same pool make it a curve, and a full term structure with multiple strikes makes it something a desk can actually quote against.

Cross-pool netting, so one position can hedge a book's net exposure across correlated pools rather than one pool at a time.

Calibrating annualization per pool and per horizon, which is currently a fixed constant.

And the integration path: shipping a reference dynamic-fee hook that prices its fee off market-implied volatility instead of a trailing window, plus a skill contribution to the uniswap-ai repo so other builders can wire the feed in without reading our source.

Tech stack:
Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4 (PoolManager, PositionManager, StateView, Universal Router, Permit2), OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks, EIP-1167 clones, Unichain, Circle Arc, Circle Nanopayments, Circle Gateway, Circle Wallets, Privy, Next.js, TypeScript, viem, wagmi

Prize selection:
Uniswap Foundation — Best Uniswap Stack Contribution. Circle Arc — both bounties (the stablecoin-native pool bounty and the agentic economy bounty; they're split among qualifying projects, so enter both and meet their stated bar precisely: working frontend and backend, architecture diagram, video, docs, repo link). Privy if a track is open.

projects.title: Code4ai
projects.description: AI agents break vulnerable contracts for USDC bounties, paid only if the exploit provably works
projects.project_description:
code4ai is a proof-of-exploit bounty arena. Bug bounties are collapsing under AI-generated noise: curl killed a 6.5-year programme after its valid-report rate fell below 5%, Code4rena is winding down, and most HackerOne submissions are invalid. The bottleneck was never writing findings; it is a human deciding which ones are real, and that judgement does not scale against machine-speed submission. So a finding here pays only if the exploit actually runs. An agent stakes, submits its exploit as a sequence of calls, and the arena deploys a fresh instance of the target, replays the calls, and checks a hidden invariant before and after. A true-to-false flip is VALID: stake returned plus the bounty. If the invariant holds, the stake is slashed into the pool for whoever cracks it next. No human triage, no severity arguments. The contract is the judge, and it settles exactly once, on-chain. This is not a mockup. An autonomous auditor has already won live on Hedera testnet: it read three real historical exploits from our subgraph, planned its own exploit with an LLM, provisioned its account, staked, and proved the break. The settlement is verifiable on HashScan. Every verdict also writes an ERC-8004 reputation entry, so an agent's record is portable rather than trapped in our database. A Rekt Replay gallery lets anyone reproduce those historical bug classes in a free sandbox. Verified settlements (Hedera testnet, HashScan): Direct submission:
https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10467075-1789161821-293370728 Through the x402 gateway:
https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10467075-1789164029-554493924
projects.how_its_made: Four services. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 on Foundry: an Arena settlement contract holding a per-target token pool with payout/slash keyed by attempt id (so a replayed settlement is a no-op), plus deliberately vulnerable target vaults each exposing an invariantHolds() view. Server is Bun + Hono with viem and Postgres, the verifier and orchestrator. Facilitator is a self-hosted x402 service. Web is TanStack Start + React. The core guarantee is isolation: every real submission gets a brand-new target instance, so nobody can hand you a pre-broken contract. The server replays the agent-signed exploitCalls, reads invariantHolds() before and after, and only a true-to-false flip counts. The invariant expression itself is never exposed, you get the objective and the source, and must derive the exploitable property. Hedera (testnet EVM) is the settlement layer. Value moves in an HTS token via its ERC-20 facade; HBAR is gas only. Payments use x402: the agent partially signs an HTS transfer and the facilitator co-signs and submits it, which gives a clean stake-once, settle-once-after-the-verdict flow — a VALID finding never risks its stake to a settlement failure, and an INVALID stake folds into the pool. The x402 part is where the real work went. An offline audit of @x402/hedera found its own checks would accept multiple token payers, NFT transfers, allowance debits, excessive fees and expired transactions. So the facilitator decodes the protobuf itself before co-signing and enforces one configured token, exactly two accounts, the exact agent-to-arena stake, no extras, and a bounded fee and lifetime, with the payer pinned by the server. /verify is read-only; /settle is authenticated and bound to a durable INVALID-only permission, so a discarded VALID authorization can never be pushed through. The Graph is load-bearing: a subgraph indexes three real mainnet exploits (Poly Network 60M, Resupply $9.6M), each pinned to the exact block of its attack transaction, and the reference agent queries it as strategy input before planning. The whole arena is also exposed as an agent-native REST API and wrapped as an x402/MPP gateway on Bazantic, so any agent can discover, submit and settle without touching the UI. Reputation is an ERC-8004 feedback entry written per verdict. The honest, hacky part: most of the sharp edges only appeared when we ran the real path on testnet. viem estimates gas against Hedera's lagged consensus view, so a multi-step exploit was under-priced and a genuinely VALID exploit scored INVALID until we set gas explicitly and checked every receipt; a fresh agent wallet has no Hedera account until it is paid, so provisioning had to be woven into the run; and AssemblyScript compares strings by reference, which silently emptied the subgraph until we caught it. Each of those is fixed, and the fixes are the reason the live run pays out correctly.
