projects.title: Chain Hound
projects.description: ChainHound: AI wallet verification that traces funds, analyzes risk, and investigates activity data.
projects.project_description: Chain hound is an integration agent, other platfform can integrate and check any interacting wallets risk score and decide do they want to interact with that wallet or not. Every stolen crypto wallet leaves a trail, but almost every tool that reads that trail is a locked, human-only dashboard that won't explain how it reached its conclusion. ChainHound is different: give it a wallet address, and it tells you — with receipts — how risky that wallet actually is. Under the hood, it pulls the wallet's real transaction history live: on-chain transfers directly from an RPC node, plus swap and lending activity from The Graph's Subgraph MCP (Uniswap V3 and Aave V3). That evidence gets scored by an AI model, but the model never invents the number — it only explains a risk score and a set of flags that are calculated deterministically from the actual data. If the model can't score a wallet, it says so explicitly, rather than quietly returning nothing. There are two ways to investigate. Wallet Analysis checks a single address on its own history. Fund Trace goes one hop further: it independently re-verifies the wallet's most recent counterparties too, and rolls everything into one trail-level verdict — because a clean wallet fed by a risky one shouldn't get a free pass just because you only checked the first hop. Every wallet ChainHound touches also gets a real, human-readable identity: it's registered on ENSv2 (on Sepolia) with its own subregistry, and named with a pronounceable label instead of a 40-character hex string — so a report reads like names, not noise. Finally, this isn't just a website. The same risk-verification logic is published as paid, machine-callable APIs through Bazantic — an agent, a wallet app, or a protocol's withdrawal guard can pay a few cents, ask "is this wallet safe?" in code, and get back a verdict plus supporting evidence, with no login, no dashboard, and no human in the loop required.
projects.how_its_made:
ChainHound is a Next.js frontend (Vercel) talking to a Node/Express backend (Railway) that runs the actual investigation pipeline. Given a wallet address, it fetches on-chain transfers directly via ethers.js/Alchemy, pulls swap and lending activity from The Graph's Subgraph MCP, and feeds both into Gemini/Claude for risk scoring — the model only explains numbers we calculate deterministically, it never invents a score. A "Fund Trace" mode re-runs this same pipeline on the wallet's recent counterparties, one hop out, and rolls everything into one pass/fail trail verdict. Partner tech, and why it mattered: The Graph — Subgraph MCP gives us live Uniswap V3/Aave V3 data, not a cached snapshot. We run swaps and lending as two parallel Gemini conversations, each on its own API key, so one category hitting a free-tier rate limit doesn't block the other.
ENS — every wallet gets registered on ENSv2 (Sepolia) with a real subregistry: the root wallet owns its own namespace, counterparties become subnames under it. Addresses are turned into pronounceable labels (adjective-noun-number), and the registrar actually resolves a label back before trusting it's free, retrying on a genuine collision.
Bazantic — we exposed the same risk-verdict logic as priced x402 Gateways and wrote a Recipe that chains two of them: pull the risk verdict, and if it's flagged, automatically pull Uniswap activity as supporting evidence — one paid call, two services, one combined answer.
Hacky/notable bits: the browser UI streams NDJSON progress live as the pipeline runs (we hit — and fixed — a bug where our own Next.js proxy was silently buffering the whole stream, making "live" progress arrive all at once). We also deliberately strip ENS registration from the Bazantic-facing API, since sequential on-chain writes are the slowest part of the pipeline and an agent asking "is this wallet risky" needs a fast answer, not a pretty name.

projects.title: Pramaan
projects.description: Verifiable digital identities for physical products, from factory to resale.
projects.project_description: Pramaan is a physical-to-onchain trust and provenance platform built specifically for high-value luxury goods such as luxury watches, jewelry, handbags, collectibles, and other premium products where authenticity, provenance, ownership, and resale value are critical. The luxury market has a fundamental trust problem: counterfeiters can replicate physical designs, serial numbers, certificates, packaging, and even digital records, while genuine products can be diverted, replaced, or tampered with somewhere between the manufacturer and the final buyer. Pramaan creates a continuous, verifiable connection between the actual luxury product, its cryptographic identity, its supply-chain journey, its ownership history, and its financial settlement. At manufacturing, every luxury item receives a unique digital identity and an on-chain digital twin. The physical item is paired with a secure NFC identity, such as an NTAG 424 DNA tag. The NFC is not simply a QR-code replacement; it acts as the cryptographic bridge connecting the physical luxury item to its digital identity. For example, when a manufacturer produces a luxury watch, Pramaan creates a batch, mints a unique identity for that specific watch, and binds its NFC identity to it. This establishes the first trusted point in the lifecycle: this particular physical watch was registered by an authorized manufacturer and is associated with this particular on-chain identity. The manufacturing layer uses a smart-contract registry to maintain critical identity information on-chain. Batch creation, individual product minting, NFC binding, and tag status are represented as verifiable blockchain state and events. Operational information such as manufacturers, organizations, roles, permissions, and product metadata is maintained in Supabase/PostgreSQL, while the blockchain acts as the authoritative layer for critical identity and lifecycle state. The Graph indexes these blockchain events, providing an efficient, queryable provenance history for each luxury item. Instead of simply asking whether a serial number exists, participants can ultimately inspect the item's history and understand how its digital identity has evolved. Once the luxury item leaves the manufacturer, Pramaan follows that same identity through the authorized luxury supply chain. A product can move from manufacturer to distributor, logistics provider, another distributor, and finally retailer, with custody transitions recorded throughout the journey. At important handoffs, the product identity can be verified and the relevant custody state updated. This creates a continuous chain of provenance rather than disconnected shipping records, making every participant accountable for the product while it is under their custody. Pramaan adds an intelligent monitoring layer to the physical movement of luxury goods. During transportation, checkpoints generate telemetry such as location, timestamp, and movement information. The system evaluates this information against deterministic rules for suspicious conditions such as impossible travel speeds, unexpected route deviations, geofence violations, duplicate appearances, or other inconsistencies with the expected journey. These signals produce a risk assessment, while an AI agent interprets the evidence and explains why a shipment may be suspicious. The AI does not blindly determine authenticity; security-critical signals come from deterministic verification and supply-chain rules, while the agent provides intelligent analysis and orchestration. Hedera supports the scalable infrastructure required for supply-chain telemetry and agent activity. Instead of putting every operational event directly on an EVM blockchain, relevant high-frequency activity can be handled through Hedera. x402 enables machine-to-machine payments for agent and infrastructure services, allowing parts of the verification and monitoring ecosystem to become economically programmable. A key differentiator of Pramaan is that anomaly detection does not simply produce a warning on a dashboard. A detected anomaly can trigger a financial consequence. Imagine a luxury watch traveling through an authorized route from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the system suddenly receives evidence that the same watch appears in New York only twenty minutes later, the movement is physically implausible. Pramaan can identify the anomaly, generate a high risk score, have the AI agent explain the suspicious behavior, and trigger an on-chain response such as freezing the associated settlement. This creates Pramaan's core loop: Physical product → Cryptographic identity → Supply-chain telemetry → Anomaly detection → AI analysis → Blockchain action → Financial enforcement. For financial enforcement, Pramaan integrates Uniswap v4 hooks as a programmable settlement layer. When custody transitions and verification conditions are satisfied, settlement can proceed according to predefined rules. If a serious supply-chain anomaly occurs, the corresponding escrow or settlement can be frozen until the issue is investigated and resolved. This transforms supply-chain monitoring from passive visibility into an enforceable system where financial incentives are connected to the physical integrity of the luxury item. At the point of sale, the consumer becomes part of the verification loop. A buyer can interact with the item's NFC identity and verify it against its registered digital identity and provenance. Instead of relying only on a printed certificate, serial number, or retailer claim, the customer receives cryptographic evidence connecting the physical luxury item to its registered digital identity. The customer can also inspect its provenance and understand where it originated and how it moved through the authorized supply chain. Pramaan continues beyond the initial purchase through digital ownership and trusted resale. Luxury goods have significant secondary-market value, making authenticity at resale just as important as authenticity at the original purchase. The item's digital ownership follows the legitimate owner throughout its lifecycle. During resale, a buyer can physically verify the luxury item before the digital ownership transfer is completed. This creates a stronger connection between physical possession, authenticity, digital ownership, and settlement in the secondary market. The architecture gives each technology a specific responsibility. NFC anchors Pramaan to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts maintain authoritative identity, ownership, lifecycle, and settlement state; Supabase manages operational data and access control; The Graph provides the queryable provenance layer; Hedera supports scalable telemetry and agent infrastructure; x402 enables machine-to-machine payments; AI analyzes supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks connect product state to programmable financial settlement. Ultimately, Pramaan is not simply an NFT, NFC authentication system, or shipment-tracking dashboard. It is a trust infrastructure for the luxury economy, where a physical product carries a verifiable digital identity throughout its entire lifecycle. From manufacturing and NFC binding to logistics, anomaly detection, retail verification, ownership, and resale, Pramaan connects the physical and digital worlds into one continuous, verifiable product lifecycle.
projects.how_its_made: Pramaan is built as a partner-first Web3 infrastructure platform for luxury goods, where each partner technology has a specific role in connecting the physical product, its provenance, intelligence, and financial settlement. The frontend is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, with wagmi and viem providing wallet connectivity and communication with our EVM smart contracts. The application layer uses Supabase PostgreSQL for organizations, roles, permissions, product metadata, shipments, checkpoints, and operational state, while critical ownership, product identity, custody, and settlement logic is handled through smart contracts. At the physical layer, Pramaan uses NFC technology from NXP, specifically the NTAG 424 DNA family, to give every luxury item a cryptographically verifiable physical identity. During manufacturing, the item's NFC identity is bound to its unique digital product identity. This makes the NFC tag the bridge between the physical luxury item and its digital representation. Unlike a conventional QR code or printed serial number that can simply be copied, the secure NFC architecture provides cryptographic evidence that can be used during subsequent verification and handoffs. The core on-chain identity is implemented using Solidity and Foundry, with our Registry contract maintaining the relationship between batches, individual luxury products, and their NFC identities. Product and tag identifiers are represented using deterministic cryptographic hashes, keeping unnecessary product information off-chain while preserving verifiable relationships on-chain. The same identity created at manufacturing becomes the foundation for the product's subsequent logistics, verification, ownership, and settlement lifecycle. The Graph provides the provenance and indexing layer for Pramaan. Blockchain events generated throughout the product lifecycle can be indexed and exposed through GraphQL, allowing the platform to reconstruct a luxury item's history efficiently. This is particularly important for luxury goods because provenance itself contributes to value: a buyer should be able to understand not just whether an item exists, but where it originated, which authorized entities handled it, and how its ownership and verification history evolved. For the high-frequency physical supply-chain layer, Pramaan integrates Hedera. Logistics checkpoints and telemetry can generate significantly more operational activity than is practical to place directly on an EVM chain. Hedera provides an efficient infrastructure layer for this activity while the EVM remains responsible for the critical state that requires strong programmability and financial enforcement. This gives Pramaan a hybrid architecture in which operational scale and blockchain-level trust complement each other rather than competing for the same workload. We use x402 to introduce machine-to-machine economic interactions into the platform. Our supply-chain and AI infrastructure can require automated services such as telemetry processing, verification, or agent-driven operations, and x402 provides a mechanism for these services to participate in programmable payment flows. This allows Pramaan to move beyond a conventional supply-chain dashboard toward an ecosystem where autonomous software agents and infrastructure can interact economically. The intelligence layer is powered by an AI supply-chain agent. Pramaan continuously evaluates logistics information such as location, timestamps, expected routes, movement velocity, and checkpoint history. Deterministic rules identify objectively suspicious conditions such as impossible travel, route deviation, geofence violations, or duplicate appearances. The AI agent then interprets these signals, assesses the situation, explains the reason for the anomaly, and can initiate the appropriate protocol-level response. This separation is deliberate: deterministic logic establishes the security signal, while AI provides reasoning and orchestration rather than being treated as an unquestionable source of truth. The most important architectural connection is between AI-driven supply-chain intelligence and financial settlement. Through Uniswap v4 hooks, Pramaan can make settlement programmable according to the verified state of a luxury product's journey. In a normal journey, custody and verification conditions can allow settlement to proceed. If the system detects a critical anomaly, the protocol can enforce a corresponding financial action, such as freezing the associated escrow until the issue is resolved. This creates a direct relationship between the physical movement of a luxury item and the financial state of its transaction. For example, imagine a luxury watch moving from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the telemetry layer reports that the same watch appears in New York only minutes later, Pramaan can identify the movement as physically impossible. The anomaly is detected from supply-chain signals, the AI agent interprets and explains the event, and the resulting risk state can propagate into the blockchain settlement layer. Instead of an anomaly simply appearing as an alert that someone has to manually investigate, the financial system itself can react to the integrity of the physical supply chain. The platform also uses Supabase as the operational coordination layer. Manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, retailers, and other participants can be represented as organizations with wallet-linked profiles and role-based permissions. This provides the application with the context necessary to determine which participant is authorized to perform a particular operation, while smart contracts enforce the corresponding on-chain restrictions. The result is a hybrid authorization model combining organizational identity, wallet identity, and blockchain-level permissions. The final consumer experience brings all these layers together. A customer purchasing a luxury watch can interact with its NFC identity and verify the corresponding digital identity and provenance. The product's history can be presented through the indexed blockchain data, while its ownership can subsequently move to the legitimate buyer. Because luxury goods often retain significant value in secondary markets, Pramaan extends this identity beyond the initial sale: during resale, the physical item can be verified before digital ownership and associated settlement are transferred to the next owner. What makes Pramaan particularly notable is that none of the partner technologies are isolated features added simply for integration. Each one occupies a specific position in a single lifecycle: NXP NFC anchors the digital identity to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts establish authoritative product and financial state; The Graph makes provenance queryable; Hedera provides scalable infrastructure for supply-chain telemetry; x402 enables autonomous machine-to-machine payments; AI interprets supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks enforce programmable financial consequences. Together, these technologies create a continuous pipeline: Physical Luxury Item → NFC Cryptographic Identity → On-chain Digital Twin → The Graph Provenance → Hedera Telemetry → AI Anomaly Intelligence → Uniswap v4 Financial Enforcement → Verified Ownership & Resale. projects.project_description_markdown:
Pramaan is a physical-to-onchain trust and provenance platform built specifically for high-value luxury goods such as luxury watches, jewelry, handbags, collectibles, and other premium products where authenticity, provenance, ownership, and resale value are critical. The luxury market has a fundamental trust problem: counterfeiters can replicate physical designs, serial numbers, certificates, packaging, and even digital records, while genuine products can be diverted, replaced, or tampered with somewhere between the manufacturer and the final buyer. Pramaan creates a continuous, verifiable connection between the actual luxury product, its cryptographic identity, its supply-chain journey, its ownership history, and its financial settlement.

At manufacturing, every luxury item receives a unique digital identity and an on-chain digital twin. The physical item is paired with a secure NFC identity, such as an NTAG 424 DNA tag. The NFC is not simply a QR-code replacement; it acts as the cryptographic bridge connecting the physical luxury item to its digital identity. For example, when a manufacturer produces a luxury watch, Pramaan creates a batch, mints a unique identity for that specific watch, and binds its NFC identity to it. This establishes the first trusted point in the lifecycle: this particular physical watch was registered by an authorized manufacturer and is associated with this particular on-chain identity.

The manufacturing layer uses a smart-contract registry to maintain critical identity information on-chain. Batch creation, individual product minting, NFC binding, and tag status are represented as verifiable blockchain state and events. Operational information such as manufacturers, organizations, roles, permissions, and product metadata is maintained in Supabase/PostgreSQL, while the blockchain acts as the authoritative layer for critical identity and lifecycle state. The Graph indexes these blockchain events, providing an efficient, queryable provenance history for each luxury item. Instead of simply asking whether a serial number exists, participants can ultimately inspect the item's history and understand how its digital identity has evolved.

Once the luxury item leaves the manufacturer, Pramaan follows that same identity through the authorized luxury supply chain. A product can move from manufacturer to distributor, logistics provider, another distributor, and finally retailer, with custody transitions recorded throughout the journey. At important handoffs, the product identity can be verified and the relevant custody state updated. This creates a continuous chain of provenance rather than disconnected shipping records, making every participant accountable for the product while it is under their custody.

Pramaan adds an intelligent monitoring layer to the physical movement of luxury goods. During transportation, checkpoints generate telemetry such as location, timestamp, and movement information. The system evaluates this information against deterministic rules for suspicious conditions such as impossible travel speeds, unexpected route deviations, geofence violations, duplicate appearances, or other inconsistencies with the expected journey. These signals produce a risk assessment, while an AI agent interprets the evidence and explains why a shipment may be suspicious. The AI does not blindly determine authenticity; security-critical signals come from deterministic verification and supply-chain rules, while the agent provides intelligent analysis and orchestration.

Hedera supports the scalable infrastructure required for supply-chain telemetry and agent activity. Instead of putting every operational event directly on an EVM blockchain, relevant high-frequency activity can be handled through Hedera. x402 enables machine-to-machine payments for agent and infrastructure services, allowing parts of the verification and monitoring ecosystem to become economically programmable.

A key differentiator of Pramaan is that anomaly detection does not simply produce a warning on a dashboard. A detected anomaly can trigger a financial consequence. Imagine a luxury watch traveling through an authorized route from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the system suddenly receives evidence that the same watch appears in New York only twenty minutes later, the movement is physically implausible. Pramaan can identify the anomaly, generate a high risk score, have the AI agent explain the suspicious behavior, and trigger an on-chain response such as freezing the associated settlement.

This creates Pramaan's core loop:

Physical product → Cryptographic identity → Supply-chain telemetry → Anomaly detection → AI analysis → Blockchain action → Financial enforcement.

For financial enforcement, Pramaan integrates Uniswap v4 hooks as a programmable settlement layer. When custody transitions and verification conditions are satisfied, settlement can proceed according to predefined rules. If a serious supply-chain anomaly occurs, the corresponding escrow or settlement can be frozen until the issue is investigated and resolved. This transforms supply-chain monitoring from passive visibility into an enforceable system where financial incentives are connected to the physical integrity of the luxury item.

At the point of sale, the consumer becomes part of the verification loop. A buyer can interact with the item's NFC identity and verify it against its registered digital identity and provenance. Instead of relying only on a printed certificate, serial number, or retailer claim, the customer receives cryptographic evidence connecting the physical luxury item to its registered digital identity. The customer can also inspect its provenance and understand where it originated and how it moved through the authorized supply chain.

Pramaan continues beyond the initial purchase through digital ownership and trusted resale. Luxury goods have significant secondary-market value, making authenticity at resale just as important as authenticity at the original purchase. The item's digital ownership follows the legitimate owner throughout its lifecycle. During resale, a buyer can physically verify the luxury item before the digital ownership transfer is completed. This creates a stronger connection between physical possession, authenticity, digital ownership, and settlement in the secondary market.

The architecture gives each technology a specific responsibility. NFC anchors Pramaan to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts maintain authoritative identity, ownership, lifecycle, and settlement state; Supabase manages operational data and access control; The Graph provides the queryable provenance layer; Hedera supports scalable telemetry and agent infrastructure; x402 enables machine-to-machine payments; AI analyzes supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks connect product state to programmable financial settlement.

Ultimately, Pramaan is not simply an NFT, NFC authentication system, or shipment-tracking dashboard. It is a trust infrastructure for the luxury economy, where a physical product carries a verifiable digital identity throughout its entire lifecycle. From manufacturing and NFC binding to logistics, anomaly detection, retail verification, ownership, and resale, Pramaan connects the physical and digital worlds into one continuous, verifiable product lifecycle.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Pramaan is built as a partner-first Web3 infrastructure platform for luxury goods, where each partner technology has a specific role in connecting the physical product, its provenance, intelligence, and financial settlement. The frontend is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, with wagmi and viem providing wallet connectivity and communication with our EVM smart contracts. The application layer uses Supabase PostgreSQL for organizations, roles, permissions, product metadata, shipments, checkpoints, and operational state, while critical ownership, product identity, custody, and settlement logic is handled through smart contracts.

At the physical layer, Pramaan uses NFC technology from NXP, specifically the NTAG 424 DNA family, to give every luxury item a cryptographically verifiable physical identity. During manufacturing, the item's NFC identity is bound to its unique digital product identity. This makes the NFC tag the bridge between the physical luxury item and its digital representation. Unlike a conventional QR code or printed serial number that can simply be copied, the secure NFC architecture provides cryptographic evidence that can be used during subsequent verification and handoffs.

The core on-chain identity is implemented using Solidity and Foundry, with our Registry contract maintaining the relationship between batches, individual luxury products, and their NFC identities. Product and tag identifiers are represented using deterministic cryptographic hashes, keeping unnecessary product information off-chain while preserving verifiable relationships on-chain. The same identity created at manufacturing becomes the foundation for the product's subsequent logistics, verification, ownership, and settlement lifecycle.

The Graph provides the provenance and indexing layer for Pramaan. Blockchain events generated throughout the product lifecycle can be indexed and exposed through GraphQL, allowing the platform to reconstruct a luxury item's history efficiently. This is particularly important for luxury goods because provenance itself contributes to value: a buyer should be able to understand not just whether an item exists, but where it originated, which authorized entities handled it, and how its ownership and verification history evolved.

For the high-frequency physical supply-chain layer, Pramaan integrates Hedera. Logistics checkpoints and telemetry can generate significantly more operational activity than is practical to place directly on an EVM chain. Hedera provides an efficient infrastructure layer for this activity while the EVM remains responsible for the critical state that requires strong programmability and financial enforcement. This gives Pramaan a hybrid architecture in which operational scale and blockchain-level trust complement each other rather than competing for the same workload.

We use x402 to introduce machine-to-machine economic interactions into the platform. Our supply-chain and AI infrastructure can require automated services such as telemetry processing, verification, or agent-driven operations, and x402 provides a mechanism for these services to participate in programmable payment flows. This allows Pramaan to move beyond a conventional supply-chain dashboard toward an ecosystem where autonomous software agents and infrastructure can interact economically.

The intelligence layer is powered by an AI supply-chain agent. Pramaan continuously evaluates logistics information such as location, timestamps, expected routes, movement velocity, and checkpoint history. Deterministic rules identify objectively suspicious conditions such as impossible travel, route deviation, geofence violations, or duplicate appearances. The AI agent then interprets these signals, assesses the situation, explains the reason for the anomaly, and can initiate the appropriate protocol-level response. This separation is deliberate: deterministic logic establishes the security signal, while AI provides reasoning and orchestration rather than being treated as an unquestionable source of truth.

The most important architectural connection is between AI-driven supply-chain intelligence and financial settlement. Through Uniswap v4 hooks, Pramaan can make settlement programmable according to the verified state of a luxury product's journey. In a normal journey, custody and verification conditions can allow settlement to proceed. If the system detects a critical anomaly, the protocol can enforce a corresponding financial action, such as freezing the associated escrow until the issue is resolved. This creates a direct relationship between the physical movement of a luxury item and the financial state of its transaction.

For example, imagine a luxury watch moving from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the telemetry layer reports that the same watch appears in New York only minutes later, Pramaan can identify the movement as physically impossible. The anomaly is detected from supply-chain signals, the AI agent interprets and explains the event, and the resulting risk state can propagate into the blockchain settlement layer. Instead of an anomaly simply appearing as an alert that someone has to manually investigate, the financial system itself can react to the integrity of the physical supply chain.

The platform also uses Supabase as the operational coordination layer. Manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, retailers, and other participants can be represented as organizations with wallet-linked profiles and role-based permissions. This provides the application with the context necessary to determine which participant is authorized to perform a particular operation, while smart contracts enforce the corresponding on-chain restrictions. The result is a hybrid authorization model combining organizational identity, wallet identity, and blockchain-level permissions.

The final consumer experience brings all these layers together. A customer purchasing a luxury watch can interact with its NFC identity and verify the corresponding digital identity and provenance. The product's history can be presented through the indexed blockchain data, while its ownership can subsequently move to the legitimate buyer. Because luxury goods often retain significant value in secondary markets, Pramaan extends this identity beyond the initial sale: during resale, the physical item can be verified before digital ownership and associated settlement are transferred to the next owner.

What makes Pramaan particularly notable is that none of the partner technologies are isolated features added simply for integration. Each one occupies a specific position in a single lifecycle: NXP NFC anchors the digital identity to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts establish authoritative product and financial state; The Graph makes provenance queryable; Hedera provides scalable infrastructure for supply-chain telemetry; x402 enables autonomous machine-to-machine payments; AI interprets supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks enforce programmable financial consequences.

Together, these technologies create a continuous pipeline:

Physical Luxury Item → NFC Cryptographic Identity → On-chain Digital Twin → The Graph Provenance → Hedera Telemetry → AI Anomaly Intelligence → Uniswap v4 Financial Enforcement → Verified Ownership & Resale.

Pramaan is therefore designed not as a collection of Web3 components, but as a complete trust infrastructure for the luxury lifecycle, where physical authenticity, provenance, logistics intelligence, ownership, and financial settlement are connected into one programmable system.

projects.title: I'm The Mayor
projects.description: Fun mayor simulator for developers to unwind and escape doom scrolling during Claude sessions.
projects.project_description: Ever thought "If I was him ,would've done this better" or "Capitalism is bad /  "This place should've been governed by communists"? Time to put the money where the mouth is , cause you will be the mayor of the City and make your in between deep prompting time to something fun. I made this project especially for developers like me who get bored and doom scrolls like hell instead of using your brain to do something fun and entertaining Made to work like a Claude code sidebar , fun simulation game| Powered by ENSv2 ,Privy and Graph ( Subgraphs)
projects.how_its_made: Vanilla JS, Canvas 2D, zero npm packages in the browser, ~25 files on one window.MM global. State is a 48×48 grid plus thirty scalars, fully deterministic. smoke.js runs 500 game-days against a stub DOM — 225 checks, no browser, no network. The chain layer is a separate esbuild bundle loaded beside the game, never inside it. Pull the network out and it's the same game. ENS (ENSv2, Sepolia) is load-bearing. CityOracle.push() is the only path onto the chain and requires the write role on mayor.cityhall.eth — no name, no write. The office expires with the term, is non-transferable (an office can't be sold; a district deed can), and is revocable by the recall the sim already triggers. Nine districts each deploy their own registry. verify-gate.js proves it in 8 assertions, including a stranger's push reverting with NotTheMayor. Privy gets you in with email OTP, no seed phrase — and its ES256 token plus public JWKS became the auth for cloud saves. The Graph indexes nine ERC-4626 vaults and the oracle; the manifest is generated from the deployment so it can't drift.

projects.title: elpi.xyz
projects.description: Decentralized options with Uniswap v4 hooks, flash accounting, and idle LP liquidity vaults.
projects.project_description: elpi is a decentralized options protocol built on fixed agreements over disclosed risks, where every term and execution venue is immutably bound at mint. This project delivers the production-ready Uniswap v4 integration (OH_UNISWAP), solving the execution friction and capital inefficiency typical of on-chain derivatives: Flash Settlement Execution (UniswapV4VenueAdapter): Implements elpi's ISettlementVenue via Uniswap v4's singleton PoolManager. Using transient flash accounting (unlock, sync, settle, take), option settlements execute with zero persistent intermediate balances, strictly bounding single-position insolvency (Invariant I1). Zero-Fee Settlement Hook (OptionSettlementHook): A custom Uniswap v4 hook operating on dynamic fee pools that waives AMM swap fees (overrideFee = 0) specifically for authorized elpi PositionAccounts. This guarantees protocol fee withholding is restricted solely to profitable payouts (Invariant I4). Idle LP Capital Staging (V4LiquidityVault & V4LPRouterRestaker): Instead of letting collateral sit unproductive, uncommitted LP collateral is staged in Uniswap v4 AMM pools to earn trading fees. Collateral is atomically extracted as raw ERC-20 at mint and automatically re-staked post-settlement within a safe, gas-bounded try/catch boundary without risking oracle-free expiry recovery (Invariant I3). Continuous Clearing & Monitoring UI: Includes a full Next.js dApp featuring an asset onboarding wizard, real-time pool swap tracking, and TradingView charts displaying live strike and payoff zones.
projects.how_its_made: We built this integration using Solidity 0.8.26 targeting the Cancun EVM, Foundry for contract development and formal testing, and Next.js 14, Viem, and TradingView Lightweight Charts for the frontend application. Key architectural highlights and technical feats: Uniswap v4 Flash Accounting: We implemented UniswapV4VenueAdapter to interface directly with the v4 singleton PoolManager through unlock() callbacks, eliminating token wrapping overhead and multi-hop transfer costs. Hook Address Mining & Flag Verification: Using a custom CREATE2 mining script (MineHookSalt), we mined hook addresses matching the 0xC8 flag bitmask (BEFORE_SWAP, AFTER_SWAP, BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA). The hook verifies that swap callers are authentic ERC-6551 token-bound PositionAccounts before waiving the AMM fee. EIP-1153 Transient Flow Netting: We leveraged Cancun transient storage (tstore/tload) inside the settlement hook to net opposite option settlement flows within the same transaction, saving substantial gas and preventing market impact. Gas-Isolated Re-Staking: To uphold Invariant I3 (venue-free expiry recovery), V4LiquidityVault wraps post-settlement LP re-staking inside a strict 300,000 gas try/catch boundary. If Uniswap v4 modifications fail or run out of gas, option expiry settlement still succeeds without reverts. Robust Verification: Built a test suite with 62 passing unit, fork, and fuzz tests, including a 2,048-call invariant campaign with zero invariant violations.

1. Flash Settlement Execution (UniswapV4VenueAdapter): Implements elpi's ISettlementVenue via Uniswap v4's singleton PoolManager. 3. Idle LP Capital Staging (V4LiquidityVault & V4LPRouterRestaker): Instead of letting collateral sit unproductive, uncommitted LP collateral is staged in Uniswap v4 AMM pools to earn trading fees. projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built this integration using Solidity 0.8.26 targeting the Cancun EVM, Foundry for contract development and formal testing, and Next.js 14, Viem, and TradingView Lightweight Charts for the frontend application.

Key architectural highlights and technical feats:
- Uniswap v4 Flash Accounting: We implemented UniswapV4VenueAdapter to interface directly with the v4 singleton PoolManager through unlock() callbacks, eliminating token wrapping overhead and multi-hop transfer costs.
- Hook Address Mining & Flag Verification: Using a custom CREATE2 mining script (MineHookSalt), we mined hook addresses matching the 0xC8 flag bitmask (BEFORE_SWAP, AFTER_SWAP, BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA). The hook verifies that swap callers are authentic ERC-6551 token-bound PositionAccounts before waiving the AMM fee.

- Robust Verification: Built a test suite with 62 passing unit, fork, and fuzz tests, including a 2,048-call invariant campaign with zero invariant violations.

projects.title: Vectra
projects.description: Vectra turns complex group debts into fewer, smarter USDC settlements on Arc.
projects.project_description: Vectra is a simple group treasury and USDC settlement system built on the Arc Testnet. It changes how people handle shared expenses from basic “who owes whom” records to official settlement intents that are secure and authorized. In traditional expense-splitting apps, users can log expenses and calculate who owes what, but settling those amounts is still manual. People need to decide who pays whom, start several transfers, and check if everyone has paid. Vectra simplifies this by managing that final settlement step. Users can create or join a group, track shared expenses, and Vectra then calculates the net amounts each member owes or is owed. Instead of making individual payments right away, the backend creates a structured settlement intent. This intent includes the group ID, nonce, deadline, and clear transfer instructions. An authorized coordinator signs this intent using EIP-712 typed data. The signed intent is sent to the VectraTreasury smart contract on the Arc Testnet. The contract checks if the coordinator is authorized, ensures the deadline is valid, and verifies details to prevent replay attacks. It then processes the necessary USDC transfers all at once. This means the settlement either happens as authorized or fails, preventing partially completed payments. Vectra also uses an off-chain PostgreSQL database to manage groups, memberships, expenses, settlements, authentication sessions, and settlement status. After a blockchain transaction is submitted, the backend checks the transaction and the events from the contract before marking the settlement as complete. This keeps application status separate from blockchain actions while ensuring financial execution is clear and verifiable on-chain. The system uses wallet authentication, EIP-712 signatures, nonce-based protections, deadline enforcement, SafeERC20 transfers, and database-level protections for uniqueness and concurrency. The process looks like this: Shared Expenses → Net Obligations → Settlement Intent → EIP-712 Authorization → Arc Transaction → Atomic USDC Settlement → On-chain Verification. In summary, Vectra is more than just an expense splitter. It shows how stablecoins and blockchain transaction intents can act as a reliable settlement layer for shared expenses, with Arc providing the necessary execution environment and USDC serving as a stable payment method.
projects.how_its_made: Vectra is a full-stack Web3 application built around  Arc Testnet as the on-chain settlement layer, with Next.js/React on the frontend, an Express/TypeScript backend, PostgreSQL/Prisma for application state, and Solidity smart contracts for programmable USDC settlement. The frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, wagmi, and viem for wallet connection, EIP-712 signing, contract interaction, and transaction tracking. The backend manages groups, members, expenses, authentication, and settlement intents using Express, Prisma, and PostgreSQL. The core of Vectra is the settlement-intent flow on Arc. Instead of simply calculating balances, the backend converts a group's expenses into optimized net obligations and creates a structured intent containing the group ID, nonce, deadline, and exact USDC transfers. The authorized coordinator signs this intent using EIP-712 typed data. The signed intent is then executed by our VectraTreasury Solidity contract deployed on Arc Testnet. The contract verifies the EIP-712 signature, deadline, and per-group nonce before executing the required USDC transfers atomically. OpenZeppelin EIP712/ECDSA utilities provide signature verification, while SafeERC20 is used for secure token transfers. Nonces prevent replay attacks, and deadlines prevent stale settlement intents from being executed. Arc is therefore not just the deployment environment; it is the execution and settlement layer of Vectra. We use Arc's EVM compatibility to deploy our Solidity treasury contract and its blockchain execution to make the final USDC movement verifiable and programmable. USDC provides the stable settlement asset, while Arc provides the on-chain infrastructure where the authorized settlement intent becomes an actual financial transaction. A key design choice is that Vectra does not blindly trust a successful transaction response. After the settlement is submitted to Arc, the backend independently verifies the transaction and the smart contract's emitted events before marking the settlement as completed in PostgreSQL. This keeps the Web2 application state synchronized with the actual on-chain settlement. The complete architecture is: Expenses → Net obligations → EIP-712 settlement intent → Arc smart contract → Atomic USDC settlement → On-chain verification → Finalized application state. The notable part is turning an ordinary expense-splitting calculation into a cryptographically authorized, programmable settlement intent that is actually executed and verified on Arc.

projects.title: coldcascade
projects.description: A maker on HyperEVM that prices off Hyperliquid's book, hedges on the perp, and buys the cascade.
projects.project_description: coldcascade is an automated market maker on HyperEVM whose price is not set before the trade that takes it. Every automated maker is potentially arbitraged for the distance between its own price and the reference venue's, because its quote is written earlier and somebody is paid the difference. That's the loss-versus-rebalancing, and fees only scale it down. This maker reads Hyperliquid's own order book (best bid, best ask, mark and oracle) through the HyperCore precompiles inside the call that settles the swap, and clamps its quote to what crossing that book would have paid. Thus there is no earlier price to take. It is close to an oracle-pegged AMM, with one difference that decides everything: an oracle is an index of other venues' prices, and you cannot execute against an index. The book is the price you can actually get. On ordinary flow the two agree and neither is arbitraged: both zero across the live record. It takes a broken book to separate them, and to show that we reconstructed the whole liquidation cascade of 10 October 2025 and replayed it: over that session an arbitrageur takes $222 from the oracle-pegged maker, $3,558 from a plain curve, and $0 from this desk. One of our example transactions on mainnet can be used to represent the claim: the desk paid 79,539.60 against an L1 bid of 79,699.00, exactly its own 20 bps parameter, while its own constant-product curve wanted to pay 163 bps over the book. In the crash event, the same rule gets one condition inverted, and that lets it absorb a liquidation cascade: when forced sellers eat the bid, the desk quotes inside the gap they opened and becomes the best bid in the market, buying from people who have no choice but to sell. Protection and aggression are the same code with one boolean the other way round. projects.title: Shoalfi
projects.description: tells lending markets what their collateral is really worth if sold, and caps borrowing to it
projects.project_description: Last August, three lending protocols were drained the same way. Moonwell lost $8.7M. Morpho saw $36.4M of liquidations set off by about $320K of trades. Tectonic lost ~$75M and Cronos halted the whole chain. None of them were hacked. The price oracle was right every time. Nobody asked the second question: if this collateral had to be sold, how much would actually sell? That's what shoalfi measures. For every collateral token in a lending market, we check how much could really be sold on Uniswap before the price drops 10%, then compare it to how much has been borrowed against it. If a market has lent far more than the token can absorb, it shows up red. Right now we cover 134 tokens across 250 markets on Compound v3 and Morpho Blue. 14 are lent past what's safe. WBTC is the clearest: $412M borrowed against it, but only $29M could actually be sold. That's a 47× gap. The part we think matters most: 103 of those tokens have no Uniswap pool at all. We don't score them zero and call them safe, we show a dash and leave them out of the ranking, because we genuinely don't know. One is PT-reUSD, live on Morpho right now with $926K borrowed against it. That's the same kind of token that caused the $36.4M cascade three weeks ago. You can also just ask it questions in plain English, and the data comes from The Graph. We also put the number on-chain. A contract on Sepolia takes the $28.8M depth reading and turns it into an $8.6M borrow cap. If the reading goes stale for 15 minutes, the cap drops to zero.
projects.how_its_made: You open the dashboard and the first thing you see is a green pill: "live · block 25,963,881." That isn't decoration. Every response from our API carries the Ethereum block its numbers came from, in a header the browser is allowed to read. The pill is that header. If it ever goes stale, you'll know before you trust a row. Then you look at a row: WBTC, $412M borrowed, $29M sellable. That second number is the hard part. TVL and volume both lie about thin tokens, so we don't use them. We walk the real Uniswap v3 tick liquidity with Uniswap's own v3 SDK, starting at the pool's current price, crossing each tick, adjusting liquidity as we go, until we reach the price 10% down. That's genuinely how much would clear. The walker is tested against the closed-form math to prove it. The "$412M borrowed" side comes from The Graph, and this is what made a weekend build possible. Aave, Compound and Morpho all publish the same standardized schema, so one query reads all three, only the subgraph ID changes. We added Morpho Blue's 214 markets by setting one environment variable. No new code. You scroll down and hit a divider: "no uniswap venue found." 103 of 134 tokens sit below it, every column an em dash. This is the deliberate part. The API returns null, not 0, and the UI refuses to rank them, because they aren't safe, they're unmeasured. A zero here would be a lie, and that exact lie is what broke Morpho. You type a question in plain English and get a real answer. That's The Graph's Subgraph MCP wired into Claude, so it can query subgraphs live when the answer isn't already on screen. It has three fallbacks and always responds; the badge tells you honestly which path it took, and we never show the MCP badge unless a tool was actually called. Finally you click through to a contract on Sepolia. The $28.8M depth reading is published on-chain, and CapSteward turns it into an $8.6M borrow cap. Let that reading go 15 minutes stale and the cap returns zero, no fresh depth, no new borrows.

projects.title: NexGuard Sentinel
projects.description: Testnet incident response with live Graph data and pause-only smart contract protection.
projects.project_description: NexGuard Sentinel is a Base Sepolia incident-response prototype. A live The Graph Subgraph indexes withdrawals from a deliberately vulnerable, valueless DemoVault. Sentinel extracts bounded rolling features, requests a structured AI assessment, and applies deterministic pause-only policy. SQLite reservations, persisted signed transaction hashes, canonical receipts and confirmation checks make the action path auditable and prevent blind resends. Missing or invalid AI cannot authorize an action. Only the separate human owner can unpause. An Evidence API and MCP tools expose recorded incident data and payload integrity checks. A Ledger recovery CLI and schema-validated ERC-7730 descriptor support recovery preparation. Payment settlement, hardware Clear Signing demonstration, and final live AI-to-pause evidence are not yet verified. This Continuity project extends NexGuard Edge Resilience; the earlier IoT MVP and AI-assisted development are disclosed in the repository.
projects.how_its_made: Python 3.12, SQLite, httpx, FastAPI, web3/eth-account, Ollama structured output, Solidity 0.8.24 Guardian/DemoVault contracts on Base Sepolia, and a Graph Studio Subgraph built with AssemblyScript. The runtime validates canonical Graph snapshots, persists pending processing separately from ingestion, and records model inputs, prompt identity and classification results. Deterministic policy enforces a pause-only authority boundary, durable cooldown and action budget. The executor persists signed transaction identity before broadcast and reconciles canonical receipts and the final contract state. An outbox retries notification delivery. Tests exercise duplicate/concurrent delivery, restart, failed AI, confirmation timeout, reorg, state mismatch and durable notification retries. Foundry, pytest, Ruff, strict MyPy and Matchstick verify the components. Dependencies are locked and package assets are included. The pre-existing IoT resilience MVP is preserved alongside the new Sentinel module. New event work and AI assistance are documented in the SSD and disclosure records. Live Graph reads and historical contract receipts are verified; the final real-model end-to-end run, real A/B transcript and Ledger hardware demonstration remain pending.

projects.title: Tollgate
projects.description: Agents pay per API call in HBAR or an HTS token: x402 paywall, metered, no keys, no subscriptions.
projects.project_description: Tollgate turns an ordinary HTTP API into a pay-per-call resource that an autonomous agent can use with no account, no API key and no subscription. An unpaid request returns HTTP 402 carrying a machine-readable price for that exact request. The agent signs a Hedera TransferTransaction for the quoted amount and retries with an X-PAYMENT header; the server verifies and settles that payment through the Blocky402 facilitator and only then serves the data. Pricing is metered rather than flat — a base charge plus a per-record charge plus a surcharge for full detail — so a one-record query costs a fraction of a hundred-record one, and the schedule is published at /schedule so an agent can budget before it spends anything. The same request can be paid in HBAR or in X402T, a Hedera Token Service token that carries a 2% fractional fee. Both prices come from one meter — the token amount is derived from the tinybar quote — so choosing the token never changes what a request costs. The token was created with every key empty, so neither its fee nor its supply can be changed by anyone, including us. The demo endpoint is live on a public host and serves real Hedera mirror-node data. The server holds no private key at all: the buyer signs, the facilitator submits the transaction and pays the network fee, and every settlement is independently verifiable on the mirror node by anyone, without trusting us or the facilitator. Payments can also be recorded as receipts on a Hedera Consensus Service topic created with no admin key, so the trail is append-only and not even the operator can rewrite or delete a record after the fact. Writing receipts needs an operator key, so it is opt-in and switched off on the public demo, which keeps that box keyless. Reading needs no key, no account and no SDK: the /receipts endpoint hands back the raw mirror-node URL alongside its own answer, so anyone can audit the same trail from a source we do not control.
projects.how_its_made: Node.js with zero runtime dependencies — the server is plain ESM, deploys as about 100 KB with no node_modules directory at all, and runs under systemd on a 1 GB box. The Hedera SDK is a buyer-side dependency only, which is precisely what allows the hosted server to hold no key material. Settlement is native HBAR on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator (x402 "exact" scheme, CAIP-2 network hedera:testnet). We picked the native TransferTransaction over the EVM relay because a native cryptotransfer settles for roughly 107x less than an ethereumtransaction on this network. The repo carries the measurement tool rather than the claim: tools/measure-settlement-fee.mjs reads live transactions off the mirror node and reported a median charged fee of 129,394 tinybar over 100 successful transfers, which is what the base charge is pinned above so that a minimum request is never underwater on its own settlement. Verification never trusts the facilitator's own answer: the server reads the settled transfer list from the mirror REST API and sums every entry for each account, because Hedera transfer lists are double-entry and first-match reporting silently turns a gross figure into a wrong "net" one. Three things worth naming as hacky. The facilitator returns HTTP 200 for a rejected payment — the verdict is isValid in the body, not the status line — so a client written the obvious way (if (res.ok) serve()) accepts forged and underpaid payments while looking perfectly correct; only a literal true passes here. The replay key is claimed after verification passes but before settlement, and an indeterminate settlement deliberately does not release it, because a settle that timed out may still have landed and freeing the key would invite an honest buyer to pay twice. And the buyer supplies exactly one field, the signed transaction: every payment term is rebuilt from server config, so an attacker cannot hand us favourable terms and have the facilitator compare their claim with itself. 189 tests, no network in the test path, with negative controls that fail when the defence is removed. The token rail uses HTS token 0.0.10464963 (X402T) with a 2% fractional fee paid to collector 0.0.10464960, created during the event by the repo's own tools/create-fee-token.mjs. Two traps shaped it. A fractional fee marked inclusive is taken out of the transfer, so under the exact scheme the payee lands short and every settlement is rejected as underpaid; the server reads net_of_transfers off the mirror node and refuses such a token by name. And a token's treasury and fee collectors are exempt from its fees, so a demo they fund shows the fee never firing; both are refused as buyers. The buyer never names the asset: the server tries its own offers and the signature selects one, and a facilitator outage aborts instead of falling through to the other asset. On testnet a token settlement costs the facilitator about 2.8 million tinybar at steady state, against roughly a quarter of a million for HBAR. The first one cost 69 million because it included the payee auto-associating the token, a one-time cost we keep out of the per-request figure. Payment receipts go to Hedera Consensus Service topic 0.0.10446488 using the schema Hedera's own harness PRD specifies (x402.receipt.v1), rather than a shape we invented. Read and write are deliberately split. Reading is over the mirror REST API with no key at all, which is what makes an audit trail independently checkable rather than our word for it; writing needs an operator key and is therefore switched off on the hosted demo, and /health reports holdsPrivateKey and writeEnabled from the running config instead of as constants, so the box cannot advertise itself as keyless while holding a key. The topic has no submit key, so anyone can append to it, and the reader treats every message as untrusted input. The receipt operator is deliberately not the payee: it signs records and pays their sub-cent fees and can never move revenue. A receipt records the asset that actually moved: sequence 2 on the topic, written from a local instance with writing enabled, is a 300-unit X402T payment, not 300 tinybar. Emission happens after the buyer has been served and is never awaited, because a consensus round must not sit between a paying buyer and their data; a test injects an emitter that never resolves and asserts the response still lands.

projects.description: AI agents autonomously find, evaluate , negotiate and finance unpaid business invoices
projects.project_description: FACTORA is an autonomous agent-to-agent marketplace for invoice financing. Businesses list unpaid invoices as financing proposals, after which an AI Underwriter Agent evaluates the debt document, derives its economics, prices the credit risk, and uses live DeFi market data from The Graph to establish a capital hurdle rate. A Buyer/Investor Agent evaluates opportunities, negotiates discount terms, and decides whether to finance them. Agents can also pay for underwriting, reports, and market intelligence per API call through x402 on Hedera, without API keys or subscriptions. Once financed, the receivable is tokenized and managed on Hedera through Asset Tokenization Studio, covering issuance, compliance, clearing, settlement, and maturity, with HCS providing a verifiable audit trail.
projects.how_its_made: FACTORA is built as two connected services: a main TypeScript/Express application containing the marketplace, proposal service, Buyer/Matchmaking logic, AI Underwriter Agent, The Graph integrations, x402 payment layer, and World ID Selfie Check gate; and a dedicated factored-hedera Fastify sidecar that acts as the Hedera execution boundary. The Underwriter uses an OpenAI-compatible LLM with strict evidence-based tool calling, while The Graph provides live Messari-standardized subgraph data and Subgraph MCP queries for market yields used in pricing. Paid agent-to-agent services use the x402 protocol on Hedera with the exact scheme and Blocky402 facilitator, producing on-chain payment receipts. The Hedera sidecar uses the Asset Tokenization Studio SDK and Hedera SDK for receivable security issuance, KYC, clearing, settlement, and maturity operations, with HCS recording the lifecycle audit trail. World ID Selfie Check provides an identity and anti-Sybil signal at proposal creation. A notable implementation choice is the hard boundary between agents and Hedera: agents never construct ATS transactions, sign Hedera transactions, or manage role configuration.

projects.title: Proof of Spend
projects.description: An agent that spends money you can audit without trusting the auditor.
projects.project_description: Give an AI agent a wallet and you get two bad options. Fund it and hope — it can drain the account before anyone notices. Or approve every transaction yourself, which is just a slower you. Both are arguments about permission, and neither leaves you with evidence. When the spending is over and someone asks what happened, all you have is the agent's own account of itself. That is the actual gap. An agent's logs belong to whoever runs the agent. A spending limit enforced inside the agent's own process is a limit the operator can lift the same afternoon. If a purchase is disputed six weeks later, a justification pulled from that database was, as far as anyone outside can tell, written this morning. Proof of Spend closes the gap with ordering. Before this agent pays for anything, the spend decision — not the receipt, the decision, approved or declined — is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic and must reach consensus before the payment is allowed to settle. A justification written after a payment can be shaped to fit it. One timestamped by a public network before the settlement exists cannot. Three layers, three jobs. The rail moves the money: a live x402-gated store on Hedera testnet, quoting native HBAR in tinybar, and a buyer client that speaks exactly one rail. The ledger decides what may be spent and records what was: an external receipt ledger the agent queries but does not own, holding a running total, because fifteen payments of 0.15 drain a wallet exactly as one over-cap payment would. The notary proves the ledger did not change its mind: HCS, holding only hashes. No chain can do the ledger's job — a transfer knows an amount and two addresses, not "espresso", and cannot refuse a purchase before it happens. No database can do the notary's job, because it certifies itself. Concretely, four things become checkable by someone who trusts neither party. If the agent is told refuse and pays anyway, the anchored refusal plus the on-chain payment proves it disobeyed, and the operator cannot quietly delete the refusal. If a spend is disputed, the anchored approval's consensus timestamp proves it was authorised before the money moved. If an auditor asks whether spending controls were real, an anchored refusal cannot be manufactured retroactively — unlike a list pulled from the agent's own database the week the auditor calls. And if a vendor claims a purchase attempt never happened, the anchored decision names the amount, the currency and the payee, timestamped, checkable without access to either side's systems. The refusals are the half that usually disappears. When an agent is told no, nothing moves: no payment, no wallet entry, no trace on any chain. The only record that a limit did its job is a database the operator controls — unless it is anchored, which here it is, with the same rigour as an approval. Verification requires nothing from us, and that is a deliberate property of Hedera rather than a generic blockchain claim: the mirror node is an unauthenticated REST API. Two curl commands are the entire tool a third party needs — no wallet, no SDK, no account. Hand someone the receipt file alone and they can hash it themselves, confirm it against the topic, pull the settlement transaction, and re-run the decision-precedes-settlement comparison without asking us for anything. The topic itself is not taken on trust either. Every topic this agent creates carries a submit key scoped to its own key, so Hedera's consensus rules reject anything it did not sign. Reusing a topic goes through the same check on every anchor: the agent reads the topic's submit key from the public mirror node and refuses to anchor unless it genuinely matches — and refuses outright any topic that has an admin key, since that key could later clear the submit key and retroactively undo the guarantee for everything already anchored there. What it does not do, stated plainly: HCS proves integrity, not truth. A ledger that files a wrong receipt and anchors it has anchored a wrong receipt, immutably. This narrows what you have to trust. It does not eliminate it. Anchoring is best-effort by design — if HCS is unreachable the purchase still completes and the receipt is still filed, visibly unanchored, because an unanchored receipt is worth more than a lost one. The store is live and public, and the half that matters most costs a checker nothing: verifying an anchor needs no account, no key and no code of ours — a receipt, curl, and a public mirror node. Buying, naturally, needs a funded Hedera testnet account of your own and access to a receipt ledger.
projects.how_its_made: An npm workspace of four packages plus a runnable walkthrough, TypeScript executed directly by Node 24 with no build step, and 393 tests across 22 files under vitest. The package boundaries are load-bearing, not decoration. Two claims in this project would otherwise be assertions. packages/verifier depends on nothing of ours — its package.json lists one public Hedera SDK and node:crypto, so "the verifier agrees" means two independent implementations agree, checkable in five seconds rather than by reading imports across files. packages/buyer speaks exactly one rail: no registry, no funding seam, nothing pluggable — its dependency list has only ever had one rail in it. packages/anchor/src/hash.ts and packages/verifier/src/hash.ts are duplicates on purpose, and the README carries the canonicalisation as a written specification both were implemented from independently. Numbers are rejected outright — a JSON number has no single spelling, and amounts are the one thing in a receipt that must not be ambiguous, so they travel as decimal strings. Keys sort by Unicode code point, including the lone-surrogate case that a UTF-8 byte comparator gets wrong. Anyone can write a third implementation from that text and get the same digest. The store is an x402 service that answers every gated path with a 402 and a challenge quoting native HBAR (asset 0.0.0) in tinybar, settled through Blocky402's open testnet facilitator. It refuses to start unless the facilitator is reachable and actually settles exact/hedera:testnet — otherwise it would bind its port, look healthy, and fail every purchase. It deploys to Vercel as a single function built by esbuild, with CI failing if the committed bundle drifts from its source. Serverless has no boot, so the guarantee a long-running server gets for free had to be rebuilt: the first request of each cold start runs the facilitator preflight, and until it passes every request answers 503 with the reason. A deployment that cannot settle payments does not get to look healthy, and a failed preflight is not cached, so a facilitator outage recovers without a redeploy. The budget lives outside the agent, in a receipt ledger reached over MCP — check_budget before, save_receipt after. The agent refuses to buy at all when neither a ledger credential nor a caller-supplied verdict is present, because an agent that decides for itself whether it may spend is the thing this project exists to prevent. The sharpest thing we got wrong is worth stating: receipts were originally filed in USD while the budget rule counted in HBAR. The ledger filtered them out of its window, spend never accumulated, and the cap silently stopped binding — a failure that looks identical to working correctly from every log. Filing in HBAR was a one-line fix for a bug that would have quietly voided the entire control. The agent-facing contract ships in the repo as a skill, so any agent opening it follows the anchor-before-pay sequence and prints the same four-field report — and the report format is enforced by tests rather than merely documented. Supply chain: a seven-day min-release-age cooldown in .npmrc, with npm ≥ 11.10.0 enforced at preinstall because older npm silently ignores it.

projects.title: Aqua0
projects.description: One USDC deposit backs many stablecoin FX strategies on Arc, run by AI agents.
projects.project_description: We built Aqua0, a cross-chain shared liquidity layer, and brought it to Arc for stablecoin FX. One USDC deposit backs several FX strategies at once, such as USDC/ARS and USDC/BRL, without splitting capital, and tokens leave the vault only when a swap settles. Pricing comes from ForexCurve, a new 1inch SwapVM opcode at index 34 based on the Shell v1 and DFX v2 forex curve, which is stateless and solved in closed form. It values the book at the oracle price p, with x as the USDC balance, y = p · FX balance, and the ideal split I = (x + y) / 2. While each side stays within ±β of I, a trade gets exactly the oracle price with no slippage. Past that flat band, each side pays an inventory fee μ = min(δ · m / I, maxFee) · m, where m is its distance past the band, and the total fee is ψ = μx + μy. A trade that increases ψ pays the increase to the pool, and a trade that rebalances the book gets a share λ of the reduction back. Past the halt band ±α the swap reverts, as it also does on a stale or out-of-band oracle price, and every swap pays a proportional fee ε. The defaults are α 0.5, β 0.15, δ 0.5, maxFee 0.25, λ 0.3 and ε 30 bps, and the opcode matches all 979 reference vectors within a few wei. The Graph indexes the protocol, and our MCP server, published as the npm package @aqua0/mcp, a Claude Code plugin and a hosted endpoint, lets AI agents in Claude Code or Codex read liquidity, quote, swap and benchmark strategies against onchain markets while signing with Circle wallets. An autonomous keeper agent with its own Circle wallet pays for market data with Circle Nanopayments and rebalances the FX books on its own. As a result, cross-border and agent-to-agent payments can go from intent to a verifiable onchain FX trade without anyone juggling exchanges, indexers or wallets.
projects.how_its_made: Aqua0 is a cross-chain shared liquidity layer that lets an LP deposit capital once and use the same liquidity across multiple trading strategies, instead of fragmenting it across separate pools. For ETHGlobal Continuity, we extended Aqua0 onto Arc and built an FX-focused, agent-native execution stack around it. On Arc Testnet, we deployed Aqua0's shared-liquidity vault architecture with native USDC as the primary quote asset. The same USDC principal can back multiple FX strategies simultaneously, for example USDC/ARS and USDC/BRL, while the actual tokens remain in the vault and are pulled just in time when a swap settles. This gives much higher capital efficiency than creating an isolated liquidity pool for every currency pair. Users sign in with Privy and trade through Circle developer-controlled wallets, and USDC/BRL prices come from RedStone market data that is signed by 3 of its 5 primary signers and pushed onchain before each swap. For 1inch, we integrated the official Aqua and SwapVM stack and built a new SwapVM opcode specifically for foreign-exchange strategies. Our ForexCurve instruction, whose formulas are in the description above, prices a strategy at a live FX oracle, applies a base trading fee, charges an inventory fee as the book becomes imbalanced, refuses a stale or out-of-band oracle price, and halts swaps that would push the book past its halt band. Aqua0's adapter publishes these strategies into Aqua as virtual balances, while the underlying liquidity remains shared inside Aqua0's vaults. We have live USDC/ARS and USDC/BRL strategies and swaps running on Arc Testnet. For The Graph, we built an Arc subgraph on Subgraph Studio that indexes the state agents actually need, which includes LP deposits, liquidity commitments, strategy deployments, fills, fees and the liquidity backing each strategy. The Graph acts as the read layer for our MCP, so agents do not have to reconstruct protocol state from raw RPC logs. Our benchmark_fx_strategy tool also composes two Graph products by sending one Messari standardized DEX query unchanged through The Graph Network gateway to 12 subgraphs across 4 protocols and 6 chains, then combining the result with our Aqua0 subgraph. An agent can ask whether a 30 bps BRL strategy is competitive and get a verdict backed by numbers. In our run, BRL liquidity was thin, with about $118k in the deepest pool. Our MCP layer then turns this infrastructure into an agentic finance interface. An agent can inspect available liquidity, understand which strategies are backed by it, request live swap quotes, compare an Aqua0 FX strategy with liquidity available elsewhere onchain, and prepare or send the next transaction. It installs in one step as a Claude Code plugin or with npx -y @aqua0/mcp. We also built an autonomous FX book keeper. It holds its own Circle developer-controlled wallet, wakes when a swap tilts a forex book, and buys oracle and book signals per call with Circle Nanopayments, which use x402 payments batched by Circle Gateway on Arc. OpenAI gpt-5-nano chooses an action inside limits enforced in code, including a data budget, a maximum trade size, a cooldown and spend caps, and a rules-based policy takes over when the model's answer is invalid. The keeper rebalances from its own wallet, is funded with App Kit, and has an ERC-8004 identity that receives reputation feedback after each rebalance. In a live run, a 0.1 USDC swap tilted USDC/BRL to 265 bps, and the keeper brought it back to 30 bps with no human in the loop. A few parts were hacky. DFX finds each trade by iterating 32 times, but we solve the same curve in closed form as a quadratic per case so it can run as an onchain opcode, and it matches all 979 reference vectors within a few wei. The custom router came out at 24,418 bytes, just under Ethereum's contract size limit. On Arc, USDC is also the gas token, so a wallet's balance change mixes gas with the swap output, and we read the amount received from Transfer logs instead. Arc's public RPC rejects large log queries, so we added retries and caching, plus a request-splitting proxy for a self-hosted Graph Node. The longer-term use case is making cross-border payments and agent-to-agent service payments extremely simple. An agent paying a provider in another currency could inspect liquidity, find an efficient FX route, obtain a verifiable quote and execute the payment without a person manually navigating exchanges, bridges, indexers and wallets. The Continuity work therefore ties the integrations together. Arc and Circle provide the stablecoin-native execution environment and wallets, 1inch Aqua and SwapVM power the FX strategies, and The Graph plus our MCP make the liquidity and execution layer usable directly by agents.

projects.title: Quaestor
projects.description: Trading agents route through one governed endpoint. Attacked venues get priced up for everyone.
projects.project_description: Quaestor is a multichain control and observability layer for autonomous trading agents: a routing engine for agents and an Etherscan-style public explorer for everyone else. Owners give each agent a treasury with purpose-scoped allowances for DATA, INFERENCE and EXECUTION. Per-call and per-epoch limits are enforced by smart contracts, so an operator can act quickly but cannot exceed the authority its owner granted. Every successful spend emits a receipt that binds the payment to the keccak256 hash of the agent’s decision record. The public explorer lets anyone inspect the agent, its owner and operator, its policies, payment history, rationale and transaction proof without connecting a wallet. A wallet is only needed when an owner wants to manage an agent. Quaestor also introduces herd-aware routing. When one onboarded tenant reports an attacked venue, that venue’s permit price rises for every other agent. The price is calculated as base × (1 + k × distinct reporters). If the new price exceeds an agent’s owner-set cap, the governor refuses the transaction. This turns shared risk intelligence into an economic signal that agents can consume automatically. The system is live across X Layer, Arc and Base, with paid x402 decisions settled in HBAR on Hedera testnet. The same product exposes risk quotes, policy evaluation, venue comparison, agent histories and verifiable decision receipts through machine-readable routes and a public multichain explorer. projects.project_description_markdown:
Quaestor is a multichain control and observability layer for autonomous trading agents: a routing engine for agents and an Etherscan-style public explorer for everyone else.

Owners give each agent a treasury with purpose-scoped allowances for DATA, INFERENCE and EXECUTION. Per-call and per-epoch limits are enforced by smart contracts, so an operator can act quickly but cannot exceed the authority its owner granted. Every successful spend emits a receipt that binds the payment to the keccak256 hash of the agent’s decision record. The public explorer lets anyone inspect the agent, its owner and operator, its policies, payment history, rationale and transaction proof without connecting a wallet. A wallet is only needed when an owner wants to manage an agent.

Quaestor also introduces herd-aware routing. When one onboarded tenant reports an attacked venue, that venue’s permit price rises for every other agent. The price is calculated as base × (1 + k × distinct reporters). If the new price exceeds an agent’s owner-set cap, the governor refuses the transaction. This turns shared risk intelligence into an economic signal that agents can consume automatically.
