projects.title: Tool402
projects.description: Agent-ready APIs with x402 payments and tokenized funding on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Tool402 is a Hedera Testnet marketplace prototype connecting API providers, backers and software agents. Its goal is to help finance the creation or improvement of specific tools through a capped share of their paid usage, rather than a guaranteed yield. The prototype combines machine-readable tool discovery, an x402 consumer payment client, provider campaign workflows using Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio, and HBAR backing for open offerings. RiskScan Quick is our first example tool: it checks supplied disclosures about identity, pricing, limitations and evidence. Optional World Selfie Check adds a wallet-bound human-presence signal alongside MetaMask authentication. We keep payment confirmation, token allocation and revenue distribution separate. Backing records can be checked server-side against Hedera transaction evidence, but a confirmed transfer does not automatically issue tokens or distribute revenue. The project demonstrates the foundations of agent-driven API commerce and tool-specific financing, not a live investment product.
projects.how_its_made: Tool402 is a strict TypeScript monorepo with separate web, consumer-agent, core and backend packages. The interface uses Next.js 16, React, Tailwind CSS and nuqs, while Convex stores application records and workflow state. The consumer agent is a Node.js CLI built with @x402/core and @x402/hedera. It discovers RiskScan, evaluates the quoted network, asset and amount against an explicit spending policy, and handles the signed payment request and response validation. Blocky402 is the intended Hedera Testnet settlement facilitator. MetaMask handles wallet approvals and signed commands. Server-authenticated requests connect Next.js to Convex. For tokenization, we use the official Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio Factory contract artifacts with viem to encode deployBond and decode deployment events. A key engineering focus was making transaction evidence durable and preventing duplicate use. Backing verification checks the sender, recipient, amount and successful receipt, binds each transaction hash to one funding attempt, and supports status recovery without sending HBAR again. World IDKit provides optional Selfie Check, with server-side verification and a signed, wallet-bound cookie.

projects.title: Koven
projects.description: Credit and policy infrastructure for autonomous x402 agents on Hedera
projects.project_description: Koven gives AI agents financial autonomy without placing wallet keys in the model’s hands. An agent receives a mission, discovers paid x402 services and ranks providers using price, reliability and reputation. If it lacks funds, competing lender agents can offer working capital and Koven selects the best valid offer. Before any HBAR payment is signed, an isolated restricted signer verifies a Groth16 proof showing that the payment respects the mission’s spending cap and approved recipient policy. The provider settles the x402 payment on Hedera, returns the paid result, and an authenticated completion flow allows the loan to be repaid after settlement is independently confirmed. A live dashboard exposes the mission lifecycle, lender offers, provider selection, policy proof, payment status and Hedera transaction evidence. Koven combines agentic procurement, credit, policy enforcement and verifiable settlement into one end-to-end protocol for autonomous commerce.
projects.how_its_made: Koven is built as a TypeScript and pnpm monorepo containing a consumer agent, competing lender agents, an orchestrator, an x402 resource server, an isolated restricted signer, shared protocol packages and a Next.js dashboard. Services communicate through typed HTTP contracts validated with Zod, while SQLite provides durable mission, loan, idempotency, nonce and event storage. Payments use x402 v2 with the exact Hedera scheme and HBAR settlement through Blocky402. The Hedera SDK is also used to inspect and independently verify funding, payment and repayment transactions instead of trusting HTTP responses alone. Transaction IDs and signed bytes are persisted before submission so interrupted or uncertain operations can be reconciled safely without sending a duplicate payment. The wallet private key exists only inside the restricted signer. The consumer and orchestrator can request typed operations but cannot access or export the key. Before signing, the signer verifies a Groth16 proof generated with Circom and SnarkJS. The proof is bound to the mission, amount, recipient, resource and nonce, enforcing the spending policy at the wallet boundary even if the agent’s prompt is compromised. Provider ranking combines price, latency and event-derived reputation, while lender selection compares independently signed credit offers. Authenticated completion callbacks trigger an idempotent repayment workflow after Hedera settlement has been verified. The React and Next.js dashboard polls typed APIs to display the complete mission, credit, proof and settlement trail.

projects.title: Keryx
projects.description: Keryx pays cited sources and settles evaluated AI research jobs in USDC on Arc.
projects.project_description: Keryx turns a question and a USDC budget into an inspectable research job. Its agent discovers sources, explains BUY/SKIP/CACHE decisions, buys selected content through x402, and produces a cited answer. Creators receive weighted USDC rewards for cited contributions that pass the evidence checks. For ETHOnline, we extended an existing research engine with a buyer workspace and an independent buyer client. Buyers can inspect package pricing, prepare requests, follow jobs, review source decisions and quotations, and recover an existing purchase after losing a response. The client checks the recipient, network, asset and spending limit, records durable recovery state, and verifies portable receipts against the request and returned result. The workspace distinguishes a completed job from a sufficiently supported answer. It exposes quality limits, settled and pending creator amounts, and unused creator reserve. Packages are prepaid and fixed-price; unused reserve is not an automatic refund. This is not an on-chain escrow marketplace with evaluator-triggered release or refunds. Keryx is a Continuity Track project. The research engine, payment rails, registry and durable server jobs existed before the event. Event work includes buyer checkout and recovery, evidence-quality improvements, creator controls and operational hardening. Our demonstrations use owner-operated Arc Testnet pilots; we do not claim independent customer adoption or mainnet readiness. Pre-event baseline: 5e83d45 (September 2). Dated event log: https://github.com/tang-vu/keryx/blob/main/docs/ethonline-2026.md
projects.how_its_made: The app uses Next.js, React and TypeScript, with a SQLite database on the production VPS and a Supabase/PostgreSQL adapter available behind the same database interface. A durable asynchronous worker runs the research pipeline. Model-assisted planning and synthesis are combined with source decisions, quotation checks, explicit evidence coverage and bounded payment allocation. Arc Testnet is the deployed EVM network and USDC is the payment unit. The Solidity SourceRegistry records source ownership and payout configuration. viem connects application and wallet actions to Arc; Hardhat tests the contracts locally. Circle Gateway and the x402 batching tools connect paid source access and citation rewards to USDC payment flows. Cached content can avoid a new access toll while still earning a reward when cited. Our event work focuses on the buyer boundary: checking payment challenges against pinned terms, journaling before a purchase, retaining uncertain states after a lost response, and resuming the original job instead of buying again. Browser recovery uses durable local storage and cross-tab coordination. Portable receipt verification binds the saved request to the returned answer and payment ledger; it does not independently prove blockchain finality. Paid pilots exposed question-interpretation and receipt-projection defects, which drove targeted fixes and regression tests. Later work added creator authority checks, funding-recovery safeguards and incremental archive reads to reduce transient memory use. Vitest, Chromium checks, TypeScript, contract tests and production checks support the implementation. A revision-checked registry V2 is a separate tested candidate, not a deployed replacement. The public continuity log identifies the pre-event baseline and event changes.

projects.title: Inference Exchange
projects.description: Agents buy and sell inference from each other, paid per call in HBAR over x402 on Hedera
projects.project_description: Agent-to-agent payments usually mean a fixed price list. Real inference does not work that way: the same provider charges wildly different amounts for "write a haiku" and "analyse this design," and only the provider can judge which one it is looking at. Inference Exchange is a marketplace where AI agents hire other AI agents and agree a price for the specific task first. A buyer submits a prompt; every provider prices that prompt against its own backend and may refuse it outright. The buyer compares real per-task prices, picks one, gets the work, and pays in HBAR on Hedera. Three things make it more than a price list: The quote is binding on the provider. Whatever it estimates becomes the ceiling. If the job runs over, the difference comes out of the provider's margin, not the buyer's budget. Estimation risk sits with the only party able to estimate. Either side can walk. A provider can decline with a reason — too long, outside its competence — and a decline is a first-class outcome that is never scored against it as a failure. The buyer sees the price before committing to anything. Payment happens after delivery. A Hedera transaction is only valid for 180 seconds, but real agent work takes minutes. So dispatch is free and returns immediately, the work runs with no transaction in flight, and payment settles at collection. Verified with a 200-second job that settles cleanly — the thing that would be impossible with payment wrapped around the work. The spend policy lives in the broker, not in the buying agent. That is deliberate: an agent's task comes from its inputs, its inputs may be attacker-controlled, and it holds its own key — so a control shipped inside it is a suggestion. The broker is the only x402 resource server in the system, so there is nowhere else to pay. Every decision — refusals, declines, settlements — is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic and read back from a public mirror node , so a buyer auditing the exchange never has to ask the exchange what it decided. In the demo, three of the providers are real headless Claude Code agents at three model tiers, eachpricing the same prompt differently and settling real testnet HBAR to a real account.
projects.how_its_made: The broker is Go. It is the only publicly reachable component: x402 resource server, job store, dispatcher, spend policy and HCS writer. Providers dial out over a WebSocket and never listen on a port, so a laptop behind NAT can sell. 130 Go tests, no network required. x402 v2 on Hedera through Blocky402. The registry never opens the signed transaction — it authors payment requirements from its own job record and hands them to the facilitator, which checks the transfer against exactly those. Payment settles buyer → provider directly ; the exchange never holds funds, which is why the Go side needs no Hedera SDK on the payment path at all. The facilitator pays the network fee, so the buying agent never needs HBAR for gas. Buyer and seller are Node. The buyer client is the only component that touches a private key, because it is the only one that signs. An MCP server wraps it in six tools, so any MCP-capable agent can discover providers, compare quotes across several at once, delegate, and read its own decision log back off the chain. Provider backends are pluggable — claude-code (headless Claude Code, the flagship), the Anthropic API, Ollama, and a deterministic echo for testing. Pricing was calibrated against real runs: a headless Claude Code invocation burns ~14,200 tokens before doing any work, almost all of it the agent's own context, and opus varies about twofold run-to-run on the identical prompt. Those measurements are in the README, because they are the reason a static rate card cannot work.

projects.title: useOmnis
projects.description: Delegate financial tasks to AI with budgets, approvals, paid services, and proof.
projects.project_description: AI agents can already research, code and operate software, but financial tasks still break the delegation loop. The moment an agent needs to buy a service or move stablecoins, the user has to return to choose providers, manage wallets, enforce budgets, approve payments and verify what actually happened. Giving the model unrestricted wallet access is not an acceptable alternative. useOmnis is a bounded financial execution agent for builders, founders and operators who already delegate work to AI and use stablecoins. It can understand the request, determine what capability is needed, evaluate a bounded set of paid machine services, recommend one, purchase an allowed service, stop at human approval boundaries, complete the final payment and preserve the evidence. Groq’s GPT-OSS 20B handles conversational interpretation through strict JSON-schema structured output. Instead of allowing model text to become financial truth, useOmnis promotes extracted intent only after deterministic evidence validation checks the recipient, payment amount, asset, service budget, task state and approval requirements. Contextual follow-ups are slot-aware, so instructions such as “make the payment 0.3” or “use five cents for the check” update only the intended financial field. projects.title: Yucarn
projects.description: Businesses receive/use stablecoins; individuals send to any chain, from any chain.
projects.project_description: Yucarn is a browser-based, multi-chain payment portal and merchant platform that makes USDC payments simple across blockchain networks. It allows users to pay recipients on different supported blockchains without manually bridging assets, switching networks, or managing destination-chain gas tokens. Yucarn currently supports 52+ EVM blockchains, with Solana and Sui planned for future support. For buyers, Yucarn provides a simple payment experience where the user focuses on the recipient, amount, and destination blockchain rather than the underlying blockchain infrastructure. Using Circle’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) V1/V2, Yucarn burns USDC on the source chain and enables official USDC to be minted on the recipient’s destination chain. Its background infrastructure handles the required network fees, removing the need for users to hold gas tokens on the destination blockchain. For businesses and merchants, Yucarn provides tools to accept and manage cross-chain USDC payments. Merchants can create shareable invoices containing unique, tiny sub-cent tracking amounts that allow incoming payments to be identified and matched automatically. Businesses can also manage payouts, select the blockchain where recipients should receive their funds, and use Yucarn to pay employees, freelancers, suppliers, and other recipients directly on their preferred supported network. The platform also includes business-focused infrastructure such as a merchant dashboard built with Next.js, a NestJS backend, and PostgreSQL. Team payroll can be settled directly on Arc Testnet, while Web3 domain registration through ENSv2 allows businesses and users to establish human-readable blockchain identities. Privy provides the authentication layer, giving users a familiar Web2-style login experience while interacting with Web3 payment infrastructure. At its core, Yucarn abstracts away the complexity of cross-chain payments while keeping the destination blockchain explicit. Instead of requiring users to understand bridges, liquidity routes, network switching, gas tokens, or cross-chain settlement, Yucarn handles the underlying infrastructure so users can simply choose who they are paying, how much they are paying, and which blockchain the recipient should receive the funds on. The goal is to make stablecoin payments feel as straightforward as modern internet payments while preserving the benefits of blockchain-based settlement.
projects.how_its_made: Yucarn is built as a monorepo containing three main applications: a React 18 + Vite 6 + TypeScript client payment app, a NestJS backend API and blockchain watcher, and a Next.js merchant dashboard. TailwindCSS is used across the frontend applications, with Wagmi/Viem and Reown AppKit handling EVM wallet connectivity and transaction interactions. Circle’s Bridge Kit (@circle-fin/bridge-kit) and CCTP power the cross-chain USDC payment flow, allowing users to pay recipients on another supported blockchain without manually bridging or switching networks. Yucarn dynamically calculates transfer fees and applies a 0.024 USDC mint adjustment so the recipient receives the exact requested amount. The backend uses NestJS, Prisma, and PostgreSQL for APIs, business logic, and persistent data. A custom ArcWatcherService continuously monitors USDC transfer events on Circle Arc Testnet (chain ID 5042002, CCTP domain 26), allowing Yucarn to automatically detect and confirm merchant invoice payments. Arc also serves as the core settlement layer for the business side of the platform, supporting merchant transactions and payroll flows. Privy provides authentication and wallet management. The frontend uses @privy-io/react-auth to support social login, passkeys, and embedded wallets, while @privy-io/server-auth validates authentication tokens on protected backend requests. ENS is integrated as Yucarn’s human-readable identity layer. Users can pay using ENS names instead of long wallet addresses, while businesses can use ENS names for payroll recipients and register .eth names and subdomains through ENSv2 Sepolia contracts. One of Yucarn’s notable implementation tricks is its tiny-amount invoice nonce system. Each invoice is assigned a unique sub-cent amount difference, such as $10.0001 or $10.0002. When a payment reaches Arc, the watcher uses this deterministic amount as a lightweight identifier to match the payment to the correct open invoice, avoiding the need for a dedicated payment smart contract. We also implemented ENS registration as a managed two-step flow. Because ENS requires a commitment followed by a waiting period before registration, the NestJS backend coordinates the process while the dashboard presents it as a simple user flow. Together, CCTP handles cross-chain USDC movement, Arc provides business settlement and on-chain event verification, Privy handles authentication and wallets, ENS provides human-readable identity, and the three-part monorepo ties the payment, merchant, and infrastructure layers together.

projects.title: Tollgate Agent
projects.description: Let AI agents pay for useful services while you control how much and who they can spend it to.
projects.project_description:
AI agents can do useful work, but giving them access to money requires clear limits. Tollgate lets you give an agent a budget, choose who it can pay, and decide when its spending permission
ends. In our demo, an agent pays for a research report comparing Aave, Uniswap, and Morpho. You can follow each step, from requesting the report to making the payment and receiving the result. The spending rules are enforced by a smart contract. If an instruction asks the agent to spend more than allowed, the contract blocks it. The owner can also turn off the agent’s spending
access. The idea is simple: let agents buy what they need to complete a task, while keeping people in control of the money.
projects.how_its_made:
We built the interface with Next.js and React, and the backend with Node.js. The spending rules live in Solidity smart contracts on Arc testnet, with payments made in test USDC. Circle provides the agent’s wallet. The owner uses their own browser wallet to set the budget and approve payment recipients. For the research report, we get token activity data from The Graph and use an AI model running through Ollama to turn it into a readable explanation. We use an x402 payment flow: the service tells the agent what the report costs, the agent pays through Tollgate, and the service checks the payment before releasing the report. We adapted
this flow so every payment passes through the owner’s spending rules.

projects.title: Arcaidia
projects.description: Permissionless Cross-Chain Liquidity & Intelligence Market for Arc
projects.project_description: Arcaidia is a permissionless intent liquidity market for moving USDC across chains, and for turning it into a different token on the far side, built on Circle's CCTP V2 between Ethereum and Arc. A user signs one intent: "this much USDC from this chain to this recipient on that chain, at most this fee, by this deadline", optionally naming a token to receive instead of USDC and the minimum they will accept. The router pulls the USDC and initiates the canonical CCTP burn in the same transaction. From there the money arrives in one of two ways, tracked separately and never conflated: in seconds, if a liquidity vault advances it, or in minutes through canonical settlement if none does. The vaults are the market. Anyone deploys one through a factory, posts an immutable utilisation-tiered fee policy, deposits USDC, and runs the open-source solver. Solvers are autonomous agents: each discovers intents through The Graph, independently re-verifies the source transaction over RPC, prices the risk deterministically against its vault's live liquidity, exposure and settlement health, and signs a short-lived EIP-712 authorisation, through a Circle Agent Wallet for the house vault. The vault verifies that signature on chain, enforces the user's fee cap and its own posted tier, and pays the recipient from its own capital. The first valid fill wins on chain. When Circle's attestation lands, the settlement receiver proves the message, reads the intent from the CCTP hook data the router burned in, and reimburses whichever vault filled; if none did, it pays the recipient directly. No solver ever touches funds, and nothing in the protocol trusts a solver's word. Trade intents extend this with one adapter: for a non-USDC token out, the vault swaps through a Uniswap V2 market on the destination chain inside the same fill and falls back to delivering USDC if the swap cannot meet the user's floor. On top sits an agent economy: the relay computes ecosystem intelligence (liquidity, fee band, scarcity, settlement latency) from the indexed market, and sells it per request over x402 on Hedera. The house solver buys the view it decides with from its own Hedera account on every intent, and in selective mode uses it to hold under-priced fills when capital is scarce, while two independent operators run unpaid and fill the same intents. The site shows all of it: a console per vault with live solver telemetry, a liquidity page with the market state, an intelligence page where a visitor can pay for an answer from the browser, a self-service Earn flow that deploys a vault on both chains and hands the operator a one-command solver, and Transfer and Trade pages with live candles and the cross-chain spread. Three vaults, three solvers, a traffic generator, the market bot and the paywall have been running around the clock on both testnets.
projects.how_its_made: The protocol is five Solidity contracts (router, liquidity vault, vault factory, intent market, settlement receiver) deployed at identical CREATE2 addresses on Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet from one deployer, so the same bytecode serves both directions. The router calls Circle's TokenMessengerV2 depositForBurnWithHook, encoding the intent id and recipient in the hook so settlement is bound to the intent rather than asserted by anyone. The receiver calls receiveMessage on Circle's MessageTransmitterV2 with the real attestation and decodes the burn body; we learned the hard way that the header's recipient field is Circle's own contract, not ours, and carry the real 472-byte message as a golden test vector. Vault safety is enforced entirely on chain: reserve floor, per-fill and exposure caps as live percentages of total assets, replay nonces, expiry, signer allowlist, the user's fee cap and the vault's posted tier, checked before any transfer, with an atomic claim on the intent market so the race has one winner. Everything off chain is TypeScript in a pnpm monorepo. @arcaidia/domain is the single schema: canonical intent v1.1, decision types, ports, config and generated ABIs, shared by contracts tests, solver, relay, indexer views and web. The solver reads The Graph's Nest indexer (SQL over HTTP, hosted by the Graph team) for pending intents, vault state and settlement health, then checks every "pending" intent against the settlement receiver on chain because the indexer lags fills by independent vaults; that one check is what stopped all three solvers from wrongly refusing every fill as a settlement backlog. Risk is a pure function over deterministic inputs; every decision is logged with the exact inputs behind it. The house solver signs through a Circle developer-controlled Agent Wallet; independent operators use local keys generated in the browser on Earn. The Hedera piece uses @x402/express in front of the relay with the Blocky402 testnet facilitator and HBAR pricing, and @x402/fetch plus the Hiero SDK in the solver, which caps its spend per answer and records every settlement receipt into its decision narrative and telemetry heartbeat; the intelligence page pays from the browser with a polyfilled Buffer for the Hedera SDK. The Uniswap market is our own 0.8.28 fork of Uniswap V2 with four mock tokens against real USDC, a bot that trends and rebalances the pools so prices drift between chains, a price API that never emits a price as a JSON number (everything is an e18 string), and an ISwapAdapter the vault calls inside fastFill behind try/catch so a failed swap still delivers USDC. The solver's trade gate asks the deployed adapter about the post-fee amount, the same amount the vault will swap, which was a real bug we caught in the handoff. The frontend is TanStack Start with Privy as the wallet layer, viem for every read and write, lightweight-charts for the candles, and a hard rule that no number is ever fabricated: every figure is real or rendered as unavailable. The whole stack ships as one Docker image whose entrypoint is chosen by an env var, built on a laptop and streamed to a 4 GB AWS box behind Caddy, after we watched a 2 GB box spend an hour swapping while it tried to build seven images. Hackiest but honest: the relay and solver keep a list of retired receiver addresses and ask every one of them whether an intent settled, because the D12 receiver replacement left intents settled on a contract nobody points at any more.

projects.title: pebble
projects.description: Swap crypto on Uniswap V2 using chat, backed by automated risk rails and on-chain receipts.
projects.project_description: SwapChat is an AI-powered conversational decentralized trading terminal built on Ethereum Sepolia. It simplifies decentralized finance (DeFi) by allowing users to check balances, query live market prices, and execute on-chain token swaps entirely through intuitive natural language. Traditional DEX interfaces present complex forms, routing selectors, and manual slippage inputs that confuse newcomers and slow down traders. SwapChat solves this with a real-time conversational agent capable of: Conversational Balances & Price Discovery: Querying live ERC-20 token reserves and Uniswap V2 liquidity pools on Sepolia for real-time exchange rates. Intelligent Multi-Turn Intent Resolution: Handling incomplete prompts (e.g., "swap ETH for USDC") by prompting for missing amounts, computing routing paths, slippage tolerance, and generating interactive Trade Proposal cards. Secure On-Chain Execution: Signing and broadcasting transactions directly to the Uniswap V2 Router via funded burner wallets, instantly generating verified on-chain Trade Receipts with Etherscan verification links. Session Memory & Transaction Auditing: Persisting trade histories in local SQLite and conversational state, allowing users to ask "what was my last transaction" or "show my transaction history" to inspect past trades and live search filter session receipts.
projects.how_its_made: SwapChat is architected with a decoupled full-stack Web3 design combining a React frontend with a Node.js NLP and Web3 execution engine: Smart Contract & Web3 Layer: Built on Ethereum Sepolia using ethers.js v6 to interface directly with the Uniswap V2 Router (0xeE567Fe1712Faf6149d80dA1E6934E354124CfE3) and Uniswap V2 Factory. It features an automated burner wallet system with local key management for zero-friction testnet trading. Conversational NLP & State Machine: Engineered an intent parsing pipeline that handles entity extraction (amounts, token symbols, slippage) and multi-turn conversational session states. If a trade prompt is missing parameters, the session memory stores the context and prompts the user for clarification before constructing the proposal. Risk & Slippage Engine: Computes real-time reserves via Uniswap Pair contracts (getReserves), simulates expected output amounts using the standard constant product formula (x * y = k with 0.3% fees), and provides automated price impact warnings. Persistent Ledger: SQLite and in-memory session logging track all executed trades, gas used, transaction hashes, and block confirmations, enabling instant natural language history retrieval. Frontend: Built with React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, featuring glassmorphic trading cards, animated trade proposal modals, and live searchable receipt tables.

1. Conversational Balances & Price Discovery: Querying live ERC-20 token reserves and Uniswap V2 liquidity pools on Sepolia for real-time exchange rates.

3. Secure On-Chain Execution: Signing and broadcasting transactions directly to the Uniswap V2 Router via funded burner wallets, instantly generating verified on-chain Trade Receipts with Etherscan verification links.
4. Session Memory & Transaction Auditing: Persisting trade histories in local SQLite and conversational state, allowing users to ask "what was my last transaction" or "show my transaction history" to inspect past trades and live search filter session receipts.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
SwapChat is architected with a decoupled full-stack Web3 design combining a React frontend with a Node.js NLP and Web3 execution engine:

- Smart Contract & Web3 Layer: Built on Ethereum Sepolia using ethers.js v6 to interface directly with the Uniswap V2 Router (0xeE567Fe1712Faf6149d80dA1E6934E354124CfE3) and Uniswap V2 Factory. It features an automated burner wallet system with local key management for zero-friction testnet trading.
- Conversational NLP & State Machine: Engineered an intent parsing pipeline that handles entity extraction (amounts, token symbols, slippage) and multi-turn conversational session states. If a trade prompt is missing parameters, the session memory stores the context and prompts the user for clarification before constructing the proposal.
- Risk & Slippage Engine: Computes real-time reserves via Uniswap Pair contracts (getReserves), simulates expected output amounts using the standard constant product formula (x * y = k with 0.3% fees), and provides automated price impact warnings.
- Persistent Ledger: SQLite and in-memory session logging track all executed trades, gas used, transaction hashes, and block confirmations, enabling instant natural language history retrieval.
- Frontend: Built with React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, featuring glassmorphic trading cards, animated trade proposal modals, and live searchable receipt tables.

projects.title: DoubleQuote
projects.description: The same USDC quotes in two order books at once. Whichever fires first atomically unwinds the other.
projects.project_description: A Morpho Midnight maker buy-callback that parks a lender's capital in a Uniswap LP position instead of leaving it idle in a lending market, and unwinds exactly as much of it as is needed, just-in-time, when a fixed-rate offer is taken. Today a Midnight maker's capital is committed the moment they want to quote. doubleQuote removes that: the maker signs an offer that locks nothing, keeps earning Uniswap LP fees while it sits in the book, and only gives up liquidity at the instant a loan is actually filled — for exactly the size filled.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Solidity 0.8.34, Foundry, deployed and verified on Base. Uniswap v3 and v4 adapters, Midnight for fixed-rate lending, all bound through interfaces against already-deployed contracts — 207 tests, every one of them a fork of Base at a pinned block. Nothing is mocked. The hard part is quoting. Midnight asks a maker "how much can you source?" through buyerAssetsBound, an external view reached by eth_call. So we had to model a burn, a swap and a slippage check inside a view — and no official Uniswap quoter is view-callable, because every one of them is simulate-and-revert. QuoterV2 and V4Quoter both work by executing a swap and reading the revert payload, which a view cannot do. So we reimplemented the concentrated-liquidity swap loop and the tick-book walk as 812 lines of pure math (SourcingMathLib + TickBookLib), fed by storage getters. TickBitmap.nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord takes mapping storage self, so it's unusable off-storage too — the bitmap walk is ours. The bound is found by bisection on liquidity burnt, capped at 0.5 of active liquidity — above that the sourced amount stops being monotone and bisection is silently wrong. Park, route and reference are three independent venues. Where the position sits, where the residual swap executes, where the price is read. Parking is permissionless; routing and referencing are not — they're constructor immutables, unreachable through the maker-signed callbackData. That column is the safety envelope. The price reference is a 1800s v3 observe() TWAP, and never read from a hook on the parked pool, since a hook owner profits from breaking the feed. v4 does the whole unwind inside one unlock — burn, swap, settle, take — using flash accounting, so no intermediate token ever touches the callback. Notable hack: our foundry.toml scopes via_ir to Midnight's ratifier path to keep one compiler profile. It doesn't work. The deploy script reaches HashLib through a digest helper, so the whole unit compiles under the IR profile and every deployed contract is the IR build — confirmed by diffing on-chain runtime code against both artifacts with immutable slots masked: 14,225 bytes vs the default's 15,485. We found it during deployment, not before. Every sharp edge like that went into FRICTION.log as it happened, and FEEDBACK.md is 19 findings edited down from it — each with a file, a line, and a time cost.

projects.title: OBSIDEUM
projects.description: Trade, send, receive across 8 networks. Portfolio-first trading platform.
projects.project_description: OBSIDEUM is a portfolio-first trading platform. Not just another swap interface. A complete self-custody experience. You connect your wallet and immediately see your total balance across every chain, with the assets you hold pinned to the top automatically. From there you can swap any token, send to any address or ENS name, or receive on any of the 8 supported networks. Token discovery is fully automatic. When you switch chains, the top tokens surface themselves from Uniswap V3 liquidity data. The design is intentional. Every pixel. A custom WebGL visual engine, a glass design system. It looks like a product someone spent serious money on. It runs entirely in the browser. No backend. No server. Just the user and the chain.
projects.how_its_made:
Swap engine: direct on-chain via Uniswap V3. QuoterV2 probes three fee tiers in parallel and picks the best output automatically. If no direct pool exists it routes through WETH or USDC as an intermediary. Execution through SwapRouter02 with standard ERC-20 approval. No fees taken. Prices and token discovery: Uniswap V3 Subgraph via The Graph across 8 networks: Ethereum, Arbitrum One, Base, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Unichain. The subgraph surfaces top tokens by TVL per chain and user balances are detected automatically via balanceOf calls. Wallet: Privy handles everything.
injected wallets (MetaMask, Brave), embedded wallets, social login. Multi-wallet with active wallet switching. Identity: ENS resolution on send, type a name, get the address. ENSv2 subname registration on obsideum.eth is coming soon. Visual engine: built from scratch. WebGL crystal shards with cracks that leak violet light. (Not a library). Custom canvas price chart with pinch, zoom, drag, and crosshair (also not a library.) The entire project was built from a phone. No desktop. No IDE. Pure focus.
And yet the desktop experience is just as curated as the mobile. No compromises on either
With that being said.
This project isn't my ceiling. It's basically my floor.

projects.title: Ledger Guard
projects.description: Agent plans DeFi guards; you clear-sign on Ledger; Graph indexes; x402 keeper executes.
projects.project_description: Ledger Guard (Ledger Guardian Agent) is hardware-bounded delegation for autonomous DeFi exits on Base. You clear-sign stop-loss, take-profit, LP bounds, or buy-dip policies on a Ledger OLED. The master key never leaves the device. A headless keeper loads secrets from Ledger Key Ring (not .env), discovers live policies from our Receipt Graph on The Graph, checks Pyth bands, and only attempts execution after paying HBAR through an x402-gated POST /trigger (Blocky402 on Hedera). Every fill emits an on-chain ExecutionReceipt that the subgraph indexes so Activity can prove trigger, Pyth spot, fill price, slippage, and compliance against the clear-signed caps. One Ledger kill switch revokes all policies and session authority. An Agent room helps draft and explain protections; the LLM never pays and never broadcasts fills. Autopilot / pay-on-hit is the consumer that settles x402 and drives the keeper Driver. Demo: https://ledger-gaurd.vercel.app/ — Start from Scratch (net-new) for ETHOnline 2026, aimed at Ledger + The Graph AI Use Case + Hedera x402.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts on Base (Foundry): GuardianPolicyManager (ERC-7579-style policy + session path), Pyth price verify, Uniswap v3 SwapRouter02 for fills. Users sign setGuardianPolicy / killSwitch via Device Management Kit (DMK) WebHID in packages/web and packages/hardware-test, with ERC-7730 clear-signing descriptors for OLED labels. Frontend is Next.js (packages/web): Protect journey, Protections explorer, Activity timeline, Agent SSE UI, and a site-wide fill congrats overlay fed by Receipt Graph and Base ExecutionReceipt logs. Indexing: custom Receipt Graph (policies, kills, executionReceipts) on Subgraph Studio / Gateway — load-bearing for Autopilot, not decoration. Subgraph MCP + @lga/graph-data compose Messari lending/DEX decisions for the Solver path. Keeper (packages/keeper, TypeScript): Key Ring decrypt → capability broker (read:graph, read:pyth, pay:trigger, execute:policy). Roles: Composer/Clerk/Solver (LLM), Payer + Autopilot pay-on-hit (x402), Driver executePolicy. Host returns 402 unpaid; consumer pays HBAR via Blocky402, then Hermes/Pyth VAAs + session key fill on Base. Payment audits land on-chain / HashScan for the Hedera story. Notable: POLL_MS=0 so unpaid polling cannot burn Graph quota; pay-on-hit settles once per policy id; Graph policy list cached with cooldown on 429; master key never in keeper process — Key Ring holds keeper secrets.

projects.title: Transakt
projects.description: Transakt is a crypto management platform designed for families to make onchain finance accessible
projects.project_description: Transakt is a non-custodial family treasury designed to make crypto easier and safer for households. While crypto wallets are becoming more accessible, most are still designed around individual users who are expected to manage private keys, gas fees, and security themselves. Transakt takes a different approach by designing the wallet around how families actually manage money. A family can create a shared identity structure using ENSv2 , with a root identity such as smithfam.eth and individual subnames like alex.smithfam.eth and mom.smithfam.eth . These identities provide the foundation for organizing family members, permissions, and spending policies. Using Privy and ERC-4337 account abstraction , family members can onboard through familiar methods such as email or passkeys without managing seed phrases. Sponsored transactions remove the need for users to hold ETH just to pay gas. Transakt also introduces programmable family controls, allowing parents to define allowances, spending limits, and approval requirements for different members. For sensitive actions, World ID adds an additional human verification layer using zero-knowledge proofs, helping ensure that important transfers and permission changes are authorized by a real, unique person. By combining ENSv2 for identity, account abstraction for usability, programmable permissions for family finance, and World ID for human verification , Transakt turns a traditional crypto wallet into a family-oriented financial system while keeping users in control of their assets. Transakt is crypto infrastructure designed for families, not just individuals.
projects.how_its_made: Transakt is a mobile-first, cross-platform application built with **React Native (Expo)**and TypeScript, combining Account Abstraction (ERC-4337), ENSv2 decentralized namespaces, embedded wallets, and Zero-Knowledge Proof-of-Humanity. The system is organized into four integrated layers: 1. Identity & Wallet Layer | Privy Privy handles passwordless onboarding through email and 6-digit OTP authentication, while providing embedded wallets and secure key management. The same wallet infrastructure powers payments and asset management , allowing users to send and receive ERC-20 tokens without seed phrases or external wallet extensions. 2. Namespace & Delegation Layer | ENSv2 Transakt integrates with the ENSv2 Hackathon Registry contract on Ethereum Sepolia ( 0xa88553f454b77203b0d036a05c894d555eaaa2cc ). This layer handles name resolution, real-time pricing, and hierarchical subname issuance, enabling family structures such as: smithfam.eth alex.smithfam.eth mom.smithfam.eth These namespaces provide the foundation for organizing family members and their permissions. 3. Smart Account & Execution Layer | ERC-4337 Transakt uses ERC-4337 Account Abstraction to enable smart contract-based wallets and programmable transaction execution. This allows family accounts to support features such as spending limits, permissions, and automated transactions while abstracting away much of the underlying blockchain complexity. 4. Security & Guardrail Layer | World ID World ID provides Proof-of-Humanity and Sybil resistance through Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs. Sensitive actions, such as high-value transfers or permission changes, can require human verification through the World ID Sepolia Router, adding an additional security layer without exposing biometric information.
projects.project_description_markdown:
**Transakt is a non-custodial family treasury designed to make crypto easier and safer for households.**

While crypto wallets are becoming more accessible, most are still designed around individual users who are expected to manage private keys, gas fees, and security themselves. Transakt takes a different approach by designing the wallet around how families actually manage money.

A family can create a shared identity structure using **ENSv2**, with a root identity such as `smithfam.eth` and individual subnames like `alex.smithfam.eth` and `mom.smithfam.eth`. These identities provide the foundation for organizing family members, permissions, and spending policies.

Using **Privy and ERC-4337 account abstraction**, family members can onboard through familiar methods such as email or passkeys without managing seed phrases. Sponsored transactions remove the need for users to hold ETH just to pay gas.

Transakt also introduces programmable family controls, allowing parents to define allowances, spending limits, and approval requirements for different members.

For sensitive actions, **World ID** adds an additional human verification layer using zero-knowledge proofs, helping ensure that important transfers and permission changes are authorized by a real, unique person.

By combining **ENSv2 for identity, account abstraction for usability, programmable permissions for family finance, and World ID for human verification**, Transakt turns a traditional crypto wallet into a family-oriented financial system while keeping users in control of their assets.

**Transakt is crypto infrastructure designed for families, not just individuals.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Transakt is a mobile-first, cross-platform application built with **React Native (Expo)**and TypeScript, combining Account Abstraction (ERC-4337), ENSv2 decentralized namespaces, embedded wallets, and Zero-Knowledge Proof-of-Humanity.

The system is organized into four integrated layers:

### 1. Identity & Wallet Layer | Privy

**Privy** handles passwordless onboarding through email and 6-digit OTP authentication, while providing embedded wallets and secure key management.

The same wallet infrastructure powers **payments and asset management**, allowing users to send and receive ERC-20 tokens without seed phrases or external wallet extensions.

### 2. Namespace & Delegation Layer | ENSv2

Transakt integrates with the **ENSv2 Hackathon Registry** contract on Ethereum Sepolia (`0xa88553f454b77203b0d036a05c894d555eaaa2cc`).

This layer handles name resolution, real-time pricing, and hierarchical subname issuance, enabling family structures such as:

`smithfam.eth`
`alex.smithfam.eth`
`mom.smithfam.eth`

These namespaces provide the foundation for organizing family members and their permissions.

### 3. Smart Account & Execution Layer | ERC-4337

Transakt uses **ERC-4337 Account Abstraction** to enable smart contract-based wallets and programmable transaction execution.

This allows family accounts to support features such as spending limits, permissions, and automated transactions while abstracting away much of the underlying blockchain complexity.

### 4. Security & Guardrail Layer | World ID

**World ID** provides Proof-of-Humanity and Sybil resistance through Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs.

Sensitive actions, such as high-value transfers or permission changes, can require human verification through the World ID Sepolia Router, adding an additional security layer without exposing biometric information.

projects.title: TradeCharts
projects.description: Your wallet is the desk. AI drafts the map, rules check it, a close-kill can guard your perps.
projects.project_description:
TradeCharts is a live crypto desk. The story is at https://tradecharts.ai. You work the book at https://tradecharts.app: connect a wallet, see your coins and Hyperliquid perps, and map that book on a Binance tape (volume in coins, 24/7). AI is optional. It can draft an Elliott Wave map, plus Wyckoff, Fibs, internals, an events calendar, and tape indicators. A deterministic validator checks the proposal against Elliott rules before anything is drawn. You Confirm it. Long and Short both stay on the chart until a close takes one out. Recalculate cannot silently overwrite your locked dates. The problem: the chart, the wallet, and the perp stop still live in three places. Calls are screenshots. Hyperliquid stops fire on mark and wicks. Nothing answers “is this book fighting its own map?” Charts and venue stops already exist. We are connecting them — for a single wallet on this desk. This event (Continuity) makes that connection queryable. Two live Graph products compose the book against confirmed maps. A Chainlink Confidential Workflow decides flatten on a weekly close, not a wick. A World-backed agent is the human gate before funds. Flatten is not live on Hyperliquid. Desk Confirm is still a private save. See — The Graph. Watchlist is the wallet. Liquidation sits on the same pane as Long/Short invalidation. Each row is aligned, fighting, unmapped, or insolvent. We query two Studio products on Base — bag subgraph trade-charts-bag and maps subgraph trade-charts (MapConfirmed 0x78D7F79e50d2fd8cC065A01f15A6d21d0F6d3C7C) — and join them in application code (conflictOf). The desk Conflict board and Ask AI decide from that row. Judges paste any 0x into attest demo/ with no keys. https://tradecharts.app/docs/graph Stand behind — Chainlink. Invalidation is a weekly close inside a CRE Confidential Workflow (handlerInTee). A wick never fires. The decision is written onchain as KillSettled on Base Sepolia (0xe9CA1F6678EE6344e163f8F48CBDA12be2FA2167, first tx 0x6fc08432f522e46e19c38cc79e9c747c94bf5ca92a5fbb93ef9b49905dee1804). That write is keyed by the TEE output — not CRE consensus inside the workflow. https://tradecharts.app/docs/chainlink Stop — World. Who. The settlement agent must resolve in AgentBook (World ID) before anyone may settle. Sandbox App and the partner feedback doc are filled. Production register still needs an Orb-verified World ID. Device — Ledger. After World, before funds. A human pages and Signs on device (partner-sanctioned Speculos, Ethereum firmware, end-to-end recover). The agent may only flatten matching Hyperliquid risk. It cannot open, add size, or rotate. No leakable venue API key on the host. Wire: Confirm → Graph → Chainlink → World → Ledger → flatten. Sequential. The desk only reads. The live product:
https://tradecharts.app/ Roadmap:
https://tradecharts.ai/roadmap Docs:
https://tradecharts.app/docs
https://tradecharts.app/docs/beta
https://tradecharts.app/docs/graph
https://tradecharts.app/docs/chainlink
https://tradecharts.app/docs/world
https://tradecharts.app/docs/ledger Public code: https://github.com/AiAlchemist0/tradecharts-attest
projects.how_its_made:
The live desk is Vite + React + TypeScript. Catalog crypto is Binance coin-volume. Login is SIWE via WalletConnect. The book reads ETH/ERC-20s over RPC and Hyperliquid positions via their info API — read-only. Candles are lightweight-charts. The product line is a deterministic Elliott validator in TypeScript: schema first, then hard rules (H1–H5), then Fib and structure flags. Rejected proposals draw nothing. Confirm locks the map. Recalculate rescores without silently rewriting dates. Hackathon work that proves Graph, policy, and kill is open-source in https://github.com/AiAlchemist0/tradecharts-attest (no shared git history with the commercial UI). Judges clone that repo. That is the GitHub field on this form. A large share of Continuity work during the event also landed in the private commercial desk: the live Conflict board and Stop gate, Ask AI citing the compose row, book marks, and AI model training — a blueprint-library of learned map priors that warm-start Propose. The private repo is available to judges on request if they want to review that desk and training work. Do not treat a missing public tree as “nothing happened there.” src/graph/compose.ts — bag ⋈ maps → aligned / fighting / unmapped / insolvent (src/policy/conflict.ts)
Studio trade-charts-bag + trade-charts on Base — live, keyless version/latest
src/graph/prompt.ts — Ask AI must cite the compose row; it cannot invent fighting
demo/ + LIVE_GRAPH=1 npm test — same join, no mocked default path
cre/ — @chainlink/cre-sdk Confidential Workflow; bun test + cre workflow simulate
KillSettled 0xe9CA1F6678EE6344e163f8F48CBDA12be2FA2167 on Base Sepolia
world/ — AgentBook gate; world/feedback.md filled
ledger/ — device confirm after World; partner-sanctioned Speculos, EIP-191 Sign recovers the device address
src/policy/kill.ts — flatten only on a close; cannot open risk
src/validator/ — same render gate as production
Pre-existing (not judged as new): the commercial desk shell, Binance tape, SIWE, book reads, validator, Confirm as private JSON. This event: both subgraphs, compose, MapConfirmed records, live Studio consume, CRE decide + onchain kill record, World and Ledger gates in code, plus the private-repo desk consume and AI training above. We push attest often. I do not dump one giant commit on Sunday.

projects.title: Plumb AI Interface
projects.description: Plumb AI lets you execute DeFi with plain English: just type, review, and sign.
projects.project_description: Plumb AI is an execution interface for DeFi that lets you interact with DeFi using plain English. Instead of figuring out which platform to use, what buttons to click, or how to set up a transaction, simply type what you want to do. Plumb AI understands your request and turns it into clear, simple steps showing exactly what will happen. Once you're ready, you just review the steps and sign the transaction in your wallet for approval. You stay in control of your funds at every step. The goal is to make DeFi execution as simple as having a conversation. You don't need to understand all the technical details behind a transaction, you just need to explain what you want. Type what you want. Get the steps. Review. Sign. Done. Plumb AI brings a simpler, more accessible way to execute actions across DeFi, without making users navigate through complicated interfaces or multiple platforms.
projects.how_its_made: Plumb AI works as a translation layer between plain-English requests and on-chain DeFi transactions. A user first describes what they want to do in plain English. The request is sent to the Groq API, which identifies the user's intent and the required DeFi actions. Plumb then maps that intent to supported protocols and APIs, such as Uniswap, Aave, and Morpho. For each action, the backend fetches the required data through protocol APIs and RPCs, builds the transaction parameters and calldata, and sends the prepared transaction back to the frontend. Privy manages the user's wallet connection and signing flow, so Plumb never needs custody of user funds or private keys. For multi-step actions, Plumb breaks the request into individual transactions and presents them as clear steps before execution. The user reviews what is going to happen and signs each required transaction directly in their wallet. Under the hood, the main challenge was creating a common execution layer across protocols with very different APIs, contracts, parameters, and transaction formats. We built adapters around individual protocols so new DeFi integrations can be added without changing the core user experience. The result is a simple flow: plain English → intent → protocol selection → transaction building → user review → wallet signature → on-chain execution.

projects.title: Sprue
projects.description: Sprue turns plain-text logic into persistent, cross-chain APIs from multiple Subgraphs and sell it
projects.project_description: Sprue is an AI-powered platform for turning natural-language data requests into deployable and monetizable APIs. A user describes the data product they need, and Sprue discovers relevant Subgraphs, analyzes their schemas and pre-built aggregations, selects the appropriate entities and fields, and generates an inspectable structured DAG. Filters and sorting operations can be pushed down into GraphQL so that only the required data is fetched from The Graph. Before deployment, Sprue compiles and validates the DAG for cycles, schema mismatches, invalid operators, and source compatibility. A successful build produces an immutable executable version that queries The Graph in real time whenever the API is called. Creators can deploy a private API protected by a Sprue API key or publish an x402 endpoint on Hedera, allowing consumers to pay in HBAR and receive the API response automatically. Sprue also provides deployment controls, request testing, revenue statistics, transaction records, private deployment exports, and an hx402 CLI for calling and paying for compatible endpoints.
projects.how_its_made:
Sprue is built primarily in TypeScript. The frontend uses React 19, Vite, React Flow, Phosphor Icons, and Privy authentication. The backend runs on Node.js 24 with Express 5, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Redis, GraphQL, and Zod. Docker Compose connects the frontend, API, background worker, PostgreSQL, and Redis services, while Nginx serves the production frontend.
The Agent first inspects The Graph Subgraph schemas and available pre-built aggregate entities. Embeddings rank semantically relevant aggregates and entities before an OpenAI-compatible language model selects the best data sources, fields, and operators. Sprue then produces a typed, inspectable DAG. Compatible filters and sorting operations are pushed into GraphQL to reduce unnecessary source reads, while the remaining transformations stay visible in the workflow.
Our compiler validates node versions, typed ports, schemas, output contracts, reachability, and cycles before creating an immutable executable version and specification hash. The generic runtime can execute any valid compiled DAG, so deploying another API requires configuration rather than writing a new endpoint. Every request performs fresh, bounded queries against The Graph instead of reusing cached result rows.
Privy provides creator wallet authentication and transaction confirmation. Hedera testnet and Blocky402 are used to publish HBAR-priced x402 endpoints: clients receive an HTTP 402 payment challenge, submit a signed Hedera payment, and receive the protected API response after verification and settlement. We also built a standalone hx402-cli using the official x402 Hedera packages. It can create or import an encrypted wallet, obtain testnet funds, inspect payment requirements, enforce spending limits, pay compatible endpoints, and print their responses.
The most notable technical decision was separating API execution from individual endpoint code. Sprue treats each product as an immutable compiled DAG plus deployment configuration, allowing the same execution engine to serve private API-key endpoints, paid x402 endpoints, and self-hosted exports.

projects.title: TraceMind
projects.description: AI-powered onchain investigator that traces wallet activity with evidence.
projects.project_description: TraceMind is an AI-powered onchain investigator that lets users ask natural-language questions about a crypto wallet and receive an evidence-backed investigation report. The current MVP focuses on Aave V3 on Ethereum. TraceMind retrieves structured onchain activity through The Graph, performs deterministic financial normalization and aggregation, builds traceable evidence records, and uses Claude to investigate the retrieved activity and identify unusual behavior. Findings are linked back to the underlying onchain evidence so users can see what supports each conclusion.
projects.how_its_made: TraceMind is built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, The Graph, Anthropic Claude, Zod, and Vitest. The user enters a wallet address and investigation question through the frontend. The backend retrieves Aave V3 Ethereum activity from The Graph using cursor-based pagination. Token amounts are normalized using retrieved decimals and financial aggregates are calculated deterministically with exact decimal-safe arithmetic. The system then builds stable evidence records and sends the retrieved evidence, computed aggregates, and completeness metadata to Claude for investigation. Claude produces structured findings that must reference real evidence IDs, while the application validates those references before displaying the final report. This keeps blockchain facts, calculations, and AI interpretation clearly separated.

projects.title: BERT Community Layer
projects.description: Stake-backed communities for transparent proposals, voting, and automated USDC capital routing.
projects.project_description: BERT Community Layer brings transparent, stake-backed governance to online communities. Instead of relying on chats, polls, and trusted administrators, communities can make important decisions through an onchain lifecycle. Members join by locking USDC, admins or members create proposals, and member-submitted proposals are reviewed by independent validators before reaching a community vote. Once voting is complete, the protocol settles the result automatically. Depending on the outcome, USDC is routed between the community treasury, validator reward pool, global BERT reserve, and voter refund claims according to transparent onchain rules. Our demo uses a Minecraft Community example: members can propose features, validators approve eligible proposals, the community votes YES or NO with USDC, and the resulting capital flow is settled directly onchain. BERT turns community decisions into verifiable, stake-backed actions rather than promises made offchain.
projects.how_its_made: BERT Community Layer is built as a fully onchain community governance system. The core is written in Solidity and deployed on Arc testnet, using USDC as the asset for membership stakes, proposal bonds, and binary voting. Each community is created through a CommunityFactory that deploys and registers a CommunityHub and CommunityTreasury pair. The CommunityHub manages local roles, membership, proposals, validator approvals, voting, and lifecycle transitions, while the CommunityTreasury keeps USDC custody and separates membership-locked funds, execution funds, validator rewards, and voter refund claims. The frontend is built with TypeScript and Next.js, with wagmi and viem used to interact directly with smart contracts. No custom backend is required for the MVP: community data is read from contract views and onchain events. The project is tested with Hardhat and includes deployment scripts for Arc testnet and a dedicated demo community.

projects.title: Freelance Trail
projects.description: Verifiable freelance escrow: milestones, payments, and GitHub-proven contributions
projects.project_description:
FreelanceTrail is a blockchain-powered freelance platform that replaces trust with verification. Clients scope projects into milestones and fund each one in USDC
through a smart contract escrow on Arc Testnet — funds release only after a milestone is approved. Developers submit proof of work that's checked against their
real, merged GitHub pull requests, not a written claim. Every on-chain event is indexed through a Graph Protocol subgraph for fast, reliable syncing. AI agents
built on NVIDIA's models analyze contributions, generate a portable Developer Payment Passport summarizing verified earnings and reputation, and match clients
with developers based on real coding history instead of a resume.
projects.how_its_made:
The stack: NestJS + Prisma 7 (Postgres) for the backend, Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) + wagmi/viem + TanStack Query + Tailwind v4 for the frontend, and a
Solidity escrow contract (Foundry) deployed on Arc Testnet handling USDC milestone payments end to end.
Arc was the natural fit for the escrow layer since it's built for stablecoin settlement — USDC moves natively rather than as a bolted-on ERC-20, which matters
when you're locking and releasing funds per milestone instead of per project.
For on-chain sync, we started by polling Arc's RPC directly with viem — and hit its rate limits hard mid-hackathon once the escrow had real history to scan. We
replaced that with a hand-authored Graph Protocol subgraph indexing all six contract events, with the backend polling its GraphQL endpoint and persisting a sync
cursor for instant, rate-limit-free restarts. graph init's interactive wizard didn't work in our sandboxed shell, so we hand-wrote the schema/manifest/mappings
directly and verified correctness by getting graph codegen && graph build to actually compile, rather than trusting the docs blind.
Three AI agents (Mastra + NVIDIA NIM models) power contribution analysis, reputation generation, and freelancer matching. Getting NVIDIA's API reliable was its
own saga — we hit EOL'd models, unprovisioned models, and one reasoning model that hung for 12 minutes before we settled on nemotron-3.5-lightning. We also
chased down an intermittent ENOTFOUND that only Node's dns.lookup() (not dns.resolve()) triggered, fixed with a custom undici.Agent doing manual DNS resolution.
The most "hacky-but-real" design choice: milestone proof isn't free text. A developer must pick from their own verified, merged GitHub pull requests, and the
chain listener matches the submitted proof URL against that list before marking it verified — turning "trust me, it's done" into something actually checkable.

projects.title: Magic Internet Frens
projects.description: One v4 hook: swaps mint NFTs, self-liquidating perps, and one pool that outlives every token.
projects.project_description: Magic Internet Frens is an eternal token machine built as a single Uniswap v4 hook. Each generation — a token, an NFT collection and a pool that live and die together — runs until its volume dries up, then recycles its own liquidity into whatever the community votes to launch next. Five systems that normally need five protocols — a launchpad, an NFT mint, a perp DEX, a dividend stream and a treasury fund — all run inside one hook, off one pool, with no keepers, no external oracle and no off-chain sequencer. TRADING IS THE MINT. There is no mint button and no allowlist. Every swap through the pool accrues volume credit on a rising difficulty curve, and that credit forges sealed crystals which reveal into NFTs by rarity. You mint by using the thing. Buys are weighted above sells, and credit accrues to anyone who swaps — through our UI, through the Uniswap interface, or through an aggregator — because attribution falls back to the transaction signer rather than the router. THE HOOK PAYS HOLDERS, FOREVER. 2,222 hand-drawn MiFrens are the founding guild; half mint at genesis. Those holders take a cut of the swap fees of every generation that ever launches — not just the first — and can redeem at a ratcheting floor backed by an out-of-range reserve position that only ever grows. Enchant a fren and it earns; sell it and it settles to you at the exact block it leaves. PERPS THAT LIQUIDATE THEMSELVES. Leverage is borrowed from a community vault and marked against a manipulation-resistant TWAP written on every swap, not an external price feed. The novel part is that liquidations need no keepers and no bots: the hook sweeps the book inside ordinary swaps, so an unhealthy position is closed by the next person to trade the pool — and that trader is minted a Liquidatoor badge for it. Liquidations execute as real swaps against the same pool, so the chart tells the truth. THE COMMUNITY IS THE FUND MANAGER. The guild votes an envelope to rotate the LP's denomination — out of ETH into a stablecoin before a drawdown, into a synthetic equity for exposure, or back again. Rotation executes in capped slices, each floored at an oracle-derived price so a slice can never be filled into a manipulated venue, and the position is tracked as separate legs so the treasury can split, rebalance or merge back. AND WHEN A TOKEN DIES, THE NEXT ONE INHERITS EVERYTHING. When 24h volume falls below the death floor, the generation dies and anyone can call a permissionless relaunch(). One transaction drains the dying pool, deploys the winning proposal's token, seeds its pool from the recovered liquidity, and carries the genesis holders across. Liquidity is never abandoned — it is recycled into the next token. The machine has no owner, no off switch, and restarts itself indefinitely.
projects.how_its_made: ONE HOOK, FIVE SYSTEMS. CauldronHook is a Uniswap v4 hook whose address is CREATE2-mined so its permission bits live in the address itself. beforeSwap/afterSwap do the work: accrue volume credit, weight buys above sells, route fees to the dividend contract and the floor reserve, write the TWAP observation, and sweep liquidatable perp positions — all inside somebody else's swap. KEEPER-FREE LIQUIDATION. The sweep is a gas-reserved low-level call into the perp engine with its result deliberately ignored, so a failing liquidation can never revert a stranger's trade. tx.origin gets the badge, which means the liquidator is whoever happened to swap — no bot infrastructure, no MEV auction, no liveness assumption. Liquidation triggers on the worse of the TWAP mark or live spot: TWAP keeps its maintenance buffer so a flash push cannot liquidate a healthy position, while spot fires only past zero equity so a single large swap cannot outrun the average and strand unbounded bad debt. A position larger than the pool can absorb is closed partially, repeatedly, rather than reverting — otherwise it becomes unclosable by the liquidator, the sweep, and its own owner. LIQUIDITY THAT CANNOT GAP. Pools are seeded full-range and spot-straddling. We originally streamed liquidity as concentrated single-sided bands for anti-snipe and found in live testing that a buy larger than the streamed depth walks past the last band and the price gaps — measured 39x where constant product caps at ~8x, which then cascaded into unliquidatable perps. Bands are exhaustible by definition, and anything a perp mark, a liquidation engine, an NFT floor and a treasury rotation all read cannot sit on an exhaustible book. ROTATION. QuoteRotator swaps slices of the LP through a curated venue allowlist that fails closed, with minOut floored by a Chainlink-backed QuoteOracle that returns "cannot judge" instead of zero when a feed is stale — a confident wrong price is worse than a missing one. The registry tracks each destination as a leg, so a generation can genuinely hold ETH and a stablecoin simultaneously and rotate between them. SIZE WAS THE HARDEST CONSTRAINT. The hook and registry both sit against the EIP-170 contract-size ceiling, which drove the architecture more than anything else: functionality is split across linked libraries (PoolOps, PerpSwapLib, SeedLib, LegacyBuyLib) and a delegatecall facet reached through explicit forwarder stubs, since the registry deliberately has no fallback. Counter-intuitively, folding duplicated code into prunder the IR pipeline — de-inlining repeated structreads and packing a dynamic array into a single wordes that let the final liquidation fix land.OFF-CHAIN. A Ponder indexer on Railway is the singlerowser makes zero read RPC calls, so the frontendnever competes with the indexer for public nodes. Need through a factory subscription onCollectionDeployed, so a token summoned sixty secondhout redeploying anything — which is what makes aself-relaunching protocol observable at all. Frontenript with wagmi/viem and RainbowKit; Permit2 forPositionManager pulls; OpenZeppelin TimelockControllsted with Foundry.

PERPS THAT LIQUIDATE THEMSELVES. Leverage is borrowed from a community vault and marked against a manipulation-resistant TWAP written on every swap, not an external price feed. The novel part is that liquidations need no keepers and no bots: the hook sweeps the book inside ordinary swaps, so an unhealthy position is closed by the next person to trade the pool — and that trader is minted a Liquidatoor badge for it. Liquidations execute as real swaps against the same pool, so the chart tells the truth.

THE COMMUNITY IS THE FUND MANAGER. The guild votes an envelope to rotate the LP's denomination — out of ETH into a stablecoin before a drawdown, into a synthetic equity for exposure, or back again. Rotation executes in capped slices, each floored at an oracle-derived price so a slice can never be filled into a manipulated venue, and the position is tracked as separate legs so the treasury can split, rebalance or merge back.

AND WHEN A TOKEN DIES, THE NEXT ONE INHERITS EVERYTHING. When 24h volume falls below the death floor, the generation dies and anyone can call a permissionless relaunch(). One transaction drains the dying pool, deploys the winning proposal's token, seeds its pool from the recovered liquidity, and carries the genesis holders across. Liquidity is never abandoned — it is recycled into the next token. The machine has no owner, no off switch, and restarts itself indefinitely.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ONE HOOK, FIVE SYSTEMS. CauldronHook is a Uniswap v4 hook whose address is CREATE2-mined so its permission bits live in the address itself. beforeSwap/afterSwap do the work: accrue volume credit, weight buys above sells, route fees to the dividend contract and the floor reserve, write the TWAP observation, and sweep liquidatable perp positions — all inside somebody else's swap.

KEEPER-FREE LIQUIDATION. The sweep is a gas-reserved low-level call into the perp engine with its result deliberately ignored, so a failing liquidation can never revert a stranger's trade. tx.origin gets the badge, which means the liquidator is whoever happened to swap — no bot infrastructure, no MEV auction, no liveness assumption. Liquidation triggers on the worse of the TWAP mark or live spot: TWAP keeps its maintenance buffer so a flash push cannot liquidate a healthy position, while spot fires only past zero equity so a single large swap cannot outrun the average and strand unbounded bad debt. A position larger than the pool can absorb is closed partially, repeatedly, rather than reverting — otherwise it becomes unclosable by the liquidator, the sweep, and its own owner.

LIQUIDITY THAT CANNOT GAP. Pools are seeded full-range and spot-straddling. We originally streamed liquidity as concentrated single-sided bands for anti-snipe and found in live testing that a buy larger than the streamed depth walks past the last band and the price gaps — measured 39x where constant product caps at ~8x, which then cascaded into unliquidatable perps. Bands are exhaustible by definition, and anything a perp mark, a liquidation engine, an NFT floor and a treasury rotation all read cannot sit on an exhaustible book.

ROTATION. QuoteRotator swaps slices of the LP through a curated venue allowlist that fails closed, with minOut floored by a Chainlink-backed QuoteOracle that returns "cannot judge" instead of zero when a feed is stale — a confident wrong price is worse than a missing one. The registry tracks each destination as a leg, so a generation can genuinely hold ETH and a stablecoin simultaneously and rotate between them.

SIZE WAS THE HARDEST CONSTRAINT. The hook and registry both sit against the EIP-170 contract-size ceiling, which drove the architecture more than anything else: functionality is split across linked libraries (PoolOps, PerpSwapLib, SeedLib, LegacyBuyLib) and a delegatecall facet reached through explicit forwarder stubs, since the registry deliberately has no fallback. Counter-intuitively, folding duplicated code into prunder the IR pipeline — de-inlining repeated structreads and packing a dynamic array into a single wordes that let the final liquidation fix land.OFF-CHAIN. A Ponder indexer on Railway is the singlerowser makes zero read RPC calls, so the frontendnever competes with the indexer for public nodes. Need through a factory subscription onCollectionDeployed, so a token summoned sixty secondhout redeploying anything — which is what makes aself-relaunching protocol observable at all. Frontenript with wagmi/viem and RainbowKit; Permit2 forPositionManager pulls; OpenZeppelin TimelockControllsted with Foundry.

projects.title: GhostKey
projects.description: Give AI agents scoped, temporary authority without exposing permanent secrets or credentials
projects.project_description: GhostKey is a Ledger-backed trust and authorization layer for autonomous AI agents. Today’s agents often operate by receiving powerful, long-lived credentials such as API keys, cloud credentials, GitHub tokens, database secrets or wallet access. Once a secret enters an agent’s environment, prompt injection, malicious tools, logs or compromised dependencies can potentially expose it. GhostKey changes the model from giving agents secrets to giving agents authority. Each agent receives an ephemeral identity and narrowly scoped capabilities defining exactly what it may access, which actions it may perform, on which resource, and for how long. The underlying credentials remain protected and are consumed internally by GhostKey rather than exposed to the agent. Ledger provides the hardware-backed root of trust. Ledger Key Ring protects service credentials while allowing authorized agent workflows to operate headlessly. For sensitive operations, GhostKey escalates from autonomous execution to explicit Ledger-backed human approval. The prototype demonstrates this architecture with two providers: GitHub and AWS S3. An agent can inspect a repository, create an issue, list/read a specific S3 bucket, and operate across providers without receiving the GitHub PAT or AWS credentials. Unauthorized actions such as repository delete or S3 delete are blocked before any provider request is sent. The result is a new security boundary for autonomous software: agents get the minimum authority they need, for the minimum amount of time, without inheriting the user’s permanent identity.
projects.how_its_made: GhostKey is built with Next.js and TypeScript around a local capability broker. Every agent receives an ephemeral Ghost Identity. A capability engine binds that identity to a provider, resource, set of allowed actions and expiration time. Every operation is authorized against these constraints before a provider is contacted. Ledger Key Ring (wallet-cli ring) forms the secret-protection layer. Long-lived provider credentials are encrypted using Ledger-backed keys. When an authorized operation needs a credential, GhostKey decrypts and consumes it internally inside the provider adapter. The raw credential is never returned through the web interface, MCP tools or agent-facing APIs. Provider adapters separate authorization from credentials. GitHub demonstrates developer-platform authority with repository read and issue creation. AWS S3 demonstrates cloud-resource authority with list/read access to a scoped demo bucket. Destructive actions like github.repo.delete and aws.s3.delete are intentionally rejected with ACTION_NOT_ALLOWED before any provider call occurs. GhostKey also exposes an MCP interface so AI clients can discover and use capabilities without gaining access to the credentials behind them. For high-risk authority escalation, GhostKey uses Ledger hardware approval through the Ethereum app/device signing flow. A browser click alone cannot mint elevated authority; the user must physically confirm on the Ledger device. The resulting elevated capability is short-lived and expires automatically. One interesting design choice is separating secret access from authority: possession of a capability does not reveal the credential that makes the action possible. Capabilities are scoped, expiring and resource-bound, creating an authority-decay model instead of handing autonomous agents long-lived credentials.
