What is live today: all four contracts are deployed on Arc Testnet, the classify, hold, challenge and release loop has run end to end against a real Gmail inbox, and a real Selfie Check has been completed on a phone and recorded on-chain.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Postage is four independent pieces, each with its own install and no monorepo tooling. The only shared code is one TypeScript type, the gateway verdict.

Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry), deployed on Arc Testnet. PostageEscrow holds the USDC payments: a sender submits a price quote signed by the pricing server (EIP-712), the contract checks the signer against EnclaveRegistry, then splits the payment 20% to PostageVault and the rest to the recipient's claimable earnings. HumanRegistry records a World ID verified human as an address derived from their nullifier hash, so nothing on-chain links back to a real wallet. PostageVault routes its share 30% to treasury and 70% to a pool that refunds the relayer's gas; anyone may call refill because the funds can only ever go to one fixed address. The escrow and the registry deliberately use different EIP-712 domain versions so a signature for one can never be replayed against the other, and there is no ReentrancyGuard: every external call happens after state is written and events emitted, with a comment at each site saying not to reorder it. 68 Forge tests. Arc was a natural fit because gas is paid in USDC, so a sender uses one asset for both the postage and the transaction.

Mail path (Cloudflare Email Routing, an Email Worker, Workers KV). Inbound mail hits the Worker, which parses it, posts the fields to the gateway, and parks the raw bytes in KV. Message content never touches a database. When the gateway releases a message, the Worker re-sends the original bytes through Mailgun's raw-MIME endpoint with tracking and re-signing turned off. This is the hack I am most pleased with: Cloudflare's own send_email refuses a From: header you do not own, so relaying the untouched bytes through Mailgun is what keeps the sender's original DKIM signature valid at the far end.

Gateway and UI (Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, viem 2, a small libSQL database for everything except message content). The classifier is Claude (claude-opus-5) reading only the message's own headers, body and SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, and returning one of four tiers; if the API is unavailable a header-only fallback takes over, and it is not allowed to return the "dangerous" tier. Pricing takes the tier and scales it by the sender's history, read from a subgraph on The Graph that indexes all four contracts. The same subgraph powers the public /network page. Privy handles wallets and login, and the server verifies Privy's JWTs against Privy's own JWKS rather than trusting the SDK. Resend sends the challenge email.

World ID is the human lane. The challenge page opens IDKit with a Selfie Check, the server verifies the proof through the Developer Portal, then a relayer signs and submits attest() to HumanRegistry, so the sender never pays gas. One wrinkle worth knowing: Selfie Check currently issues v3 proofs and IDKit v4 rejects those by default, so it takes an explicit legacy opt-in. I wrote that up for the World team in docs/world-feedback.md.

Two honest caveats. The pricing signer is a plain server key registered in EnclaveRegistry under a placeholder measurement; the registry is shaped for a real Nitro enclave later but is not one today. And the deployed Selfie Check runs against World's sandbox, because the production World app does not have Selfie Check enabled yet.

projects.title: NextKey🔑🔒️
projects.description: Secrets handed to a person or an AI-agent, released by ENS rules, confirmed by a human on Ledger.
projects.project_description: You place a secret — a seed phrase, an API credential, a private message. Then you decide two things: who may open it, and under what conditions. Both are enforced by the protocol, not by our servers and not by anyone's goodwill. Who may open it is answered by cryptography, addressed through ENSv2. Sharing a secret with anna.eth wraps its key to the X25519 public key Anna publishes in her own ENS records — you share with a name, not with 0x7f3a…, and Anna never registers with us. ENSv2 enforces the other half: who may write that grant, revoke it, or delegate the right to. That is state in a registry you own, not a row in our database. Three independent runs are already on Sepolia, with transaction hashes in evidence/v2-onchain.log: a grant written from a phone with no wallet; one written in a browser on a name outside our own registry and opened from a command line by a key that was never in that browser; and a recovery in which two unrelated signer implementations, MetaMask and viem, reconstructed the same 32 bytes and the chain agreed. Live at nextkey.li — the playground writes real records on Sepolia without asking you for a wallet: a disclosed demo key with roles on a single resolver signs for you. Under what conditions is answered inside a trusted execution environment. A release agent can propose but never act alone. The condition — a guardian quorum, a time lock, prolonged inactivity — is evaluated in a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow on AWS Nitro, and the verdict carries the hash of the on-chain request it judged, so anyone can recompute it and see that the enclave decided that request and not a modified one. evidence/cre-decision.log has a passing run; evidence/release-loop.log has one where the binding fails on purpose and the release refuses. What leaves the enclave is the verdict and a coarse reason — never how far a request stood from its threshold. Honest scope: the guardian approvals are fixtures. The request is real and on chain; the people around it are not yet. Where your own key lives is your decision alone — a file on your machine, or a Ledger. The difference is invisible to whoever shares with you, because what they read is a public key in your ENS record and nothing else. On a device, opening a secret costs a deliberate button press, so software running on your laptop cannot do it while you are away from it.
projects.how_its_made: NextKey is a static site plus a set of Node tools; there is no backend, and that is a design constraint rather than an omission. Everything a server would normally hold is either public on chain or private on your own machine. The cryptography. A secret is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a content key. That content key is wrapped to the recipient with X25519 ECDH and HKDF-SHA256 — @noble/curves and @noble/hashes in Node, the identical code path in the browser via WebCrypto for AES and the same noble primitives for the curve. A grant made in the playground opens in the command-line tool and vice versa; 26 interop tests assert exactly that, 13 of them inside Chromium. What ENSv2 does that a database cannot. Three text records carry the whole handover: nextkey.eph, nextkey.secret, and the grant itself. The recipient is addressed by name — we read the X25519 public key she publishes under her own name, so she never registers with us and never learns we exist until she is told. Who may write, revoke or delegate those records is decided by ENSv2 roles on a Permissioned Resolver, so revocation is a protocol write rather than a promise from us. Resolution goes through the hackathon Universal Resolver, with the address overridden explicitly in viem — the built-in default resolves against production and silently returns the wrong answer, which cost us an evening early on. v2, and the leak it closes. In our first version a grant lived at a record name derived from a hash of the recipient's published key. The ciphertext was never the leak — the record name was: anyone holding Anna's public key could test every name for grants to her. In v2 the wrapping key and the record name are derived from the same ECDH secret, separated by HKDF info strings and salted with ephPub ‖ recipientPub, from one ephemeral keypair per name published once at nextkey.eph. Be precise about what this buys: the records are still public and still countable by an indexer. What is no longer computable is the mapping — whether a given grant belongs to a given person, or to anyone in particular. One scalar multiplication yields both the address and the unwrapping key, which is why a Ledger is asked to sign once instead of twice. Recovery without a stored file. The ephemeral private key can be re-derived from a deterministic wallet signature, so a name can be recovered with nothing but the wallet that created it. We tested this across two unrelated signer implementations: MetaMask published the key, viem reconstructed it, same 32 bytes, verified against the chain. Determinism here is measured, not assumed. The release condition, in a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. An autonomous agent can file a release request on chain under an ENS role that permits that one record on that one name and nothing else — it can propose, and it cannot act. The condition (guardian quorum, time lock, prolonged inactivity) is evaluated inside a Confidential Workflow on AWS Nitro, and the verdict carries the hash of the on-chain request it judged, so anyone can recompute that hash and confirm the enclave decided that request and not a modified one. scripts/release.mjs check performs that comparison and refuses to act when it fails — evidence/release-loop.log is a run where it fails on purpose. What leaves the enclave is a verdict and a coarse reason: quorum_not_met, never 1_of_2, because the distance to a threshold is itself useful to an attacker. Honest scope: CRE protects data during execution, not source code; the workflow is public, as it should be. And the guardian approvals in the fixture are stand-ins — the request is real and on chain, the people around it are not built yet. The hacky part we are least sorry about. The playground writes real records on Sepolia for a visitor who has no wallet, no account and no ether: a disclosed demo key holds root roles on exactly one resolver, used only by a pool of lent names, and the page says so on its face. That is what makes the on-chain step reachable from a phone in forty seconds. Where ENSv2 said no. We tried to delegate write access for grants with grantSetterRoles and could not: the role binds to the record key, but a v2 grant's key contains a tag that only comes into existence in the visitor's browser. Reproduced down to the revert selector — EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, 0x4b27a133. It is written up as Finding 11 in FEEDBACK-ENS.md, together with the rest of our feedback on the beta deployment. Two things that are unglamorous and saved the demo. A static host caches HTML and JS separately, so a page and its bundle drift; the symptom was Cannot set properties of null, which on a page about cryptography looks like broken cryptography. Every script tag now carries a content hash, and the bundle checks on load that the page matches it. And the site runs in nine languages with a merge tool and a checker, because a hand-edited 365 KB translation file is how one language quietly ends up a sentence short.

projects.title: Coalition
projects.description: Agents pool USDC to acquire shared compute and monetize unused capacity.
projects.project_description: Coalition lets AI agents pool money together to acquire shared compute they could not afford or efficiently use alone. It is a trustless coordination layer for funding, provisioning, and exchanging unused capacity. The problem is simple: compute infrastructure is usually priced for one owner, while many AI agents only need a fraction of a server. A powerful GPU server can cost around $20/hour, yet several agents may each need only a small share. Renting separately is inefficient, while purchasing the full resource alone may be unaffordable. Coalition makes it possible for agents to coordinate a shared purchase and divide the resulting capacity. Agents commit USDC toward a shared funding goal. Each commitment is locked in a smart contract, which tracks contributions and pays the compute provider once the pool reaches its target. If the funding goal is not reached before the deadline, participants can be refunded. This removes the need for a human intermediary to hold funds or manually settle a partially funded agreement. Once the resource is acquired, a Go orchestrator running on the VPS provisions each participating agent with a Docker container and enforces its allocated CPU and memory limits. Agents can therefore share the same infrastructure while retaining isolated execution environments. Coalition also addresses uneven resource usage. Agents may contribute equally but consume different amounts of the capacity they purchased. Instead of leaving unused capacity idle, an outside agent can purchase access to that spare capacity. The payment is settled atomically to the original participants according to the resale allocation, allowing agents that received less value from their initial contribution to recover more of their cost. In the current implementation, the funding model uses equal upfront contributions, while resale redistributes value based on unused capacity. A future extension will allow agents to choose between paying upfront for guaranteed access and recovering unused capacity through resale, or waiting for more participants and paying according to their actual allocation. ENS provides verified, human-readable agent identities tied to their funding wallets. The contract verifies that the ENS name resolves to the wallet participating in the pool, reducing the risk of impersonation or funding the wrong identity. The Graph indexes pool state and events, allowing the dashboard and participating agents to track commitments, funding progress, settlement, and capacity transactions transparently. Multicall3 is used for atomic resale settlement. Coalition turns “a group of AI agents want to share a resource” into an enforceable financial agreement: agents pool capital, smart contracts enforce the commitments, providers get paid automatically, unused capacity can be resold, and the economic history remains transparent and verifiable.
projects.how_its_made: Coalition is built as five cooperating programs: a Foundry Solidity ResourcePool contract on Arc, a viem-based TypeScript SDK, a Next.js dashboard, a stdlib-only Go orchestrator, and a The Graph subgraph. The entire application is hosted on a VPS. We initially planned to deploy the Next.js application on Vercel, but Coalition requires persistent application-level state, long-running orchestration, access to the agent pool services, and coordination with the shared compute environment. Vercel's serverless and edge-oriented execution model was not suitable for that architecture, so we moved the Next.js application onto the same VPS as the orchestrator and compute services. The VPS acts as the shared compute resource. Agents do not simply receive an on-chain entitlement; the Go orchestrator converts that entitlement into actual access to the VPS, allowing agents to run workloads inside Docker-enforced CPU and memory limits. The on-chain core manages funding rounds, participant commitments, exact-fill settlement, deadlines, dropouts, forfeitures, and refunds. Each round is isolated by roundId . The filling commit settles inline and pays the provider automatically, while expired rounds use pull-based refunds. Dropouts forfeit their committed stake, and the contract records ERC-8004 reputation feedback for completion or dropout. The contract has no owner, upgradeability, or pause authority; the provider is only authorized to start rounds. The TypeScript SDK is the shared integration layer. It uses viem for Arc interactions, keeps all USDC amounts as bigint atomic units, and handles the distinction between Arc's 18-decimal native USDC and 6-decimal ERC-20 USDC. It also integrates ENSv2 for identity resolution and ERC-8004 for agent identity and reputation. The Next.js dashboard performs all on-chain writes through server-side route handlers. Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets create and control the agent wallets, execute USDC approvals and contract calls, and replace the need for local private-key management. Funding uses parallel approvals but strictly sequential commits so the final commit can trigger inline settlement. The resale flow uses Multicall3 to execute multiple USDC transferFrom payouts in one atomic transaction, preventing partial payment states. Circle App Kit handles treasury transfers, while Circle's x402 Gateway is integrated into a Next.js route through an Express-compatible middleware shim for quota payments. The Go orchestrator is the bridge between blockchain settlement and real compute. It runs on the VPS, verifies an agent's purchased entitlement, reserves capacity, creates and manages Docker containers, and enforces CPU and memory limits. It maintains a concurrency-safe ledger, meters usage using integer micro-CU/MB accounting, confirms or rolls back reservations, and reaps workloads that exceed their budgets or lose authorization. This gives agents actual, controlled access to the shared VPS rather than merely recording resource ownership on-chain. The resale market calculates prices from the funding pool's target and ranks sellers by how unevenly their contributed share has been used. It generates a fill plan whose payouts sum exactly to the quoted amount, with division dust distributed deterministically. Once payment is verified, the orchestrator provisions the corresponding compute entitlement on the VPS. The Graph subgraph indexes pool commitments, settlements, dropouts, refunds, and reputation feedback. It is not just a dashboard data source: pool discovery, roster reads, and the autonomous resale decision loop depend on it. The agent loop fails closed when pool health is unavailable. Several implementation details were particularly hacky. Because Circle Contracts on Arc rejects Shanghai PUSH0 bytecode, we pinned the Solidity build to the Paris EVM. Because existing subgraph indexing depended on legacy event shapes, we emit both legacy and round-scoped events in the same transaction, preserving compatibility while supporting isolated rounds. Because resale involves multiple payouts that must either all succeed or all fail, we use one Multicall3 aggregate for the USDC transfers, and the Go service verifies the receipt's transfer logs in order. Because floating-point accounting and concurrent reservations can introduce nondeterminism, we use integer metering, explicit NaN/Inf rejection, and last-claimant dust absorption to keep concurrency and refund accounting deterministic. The result is a full path from agent identity and USDC commitment, through smart-contract settlement, to actual Docker-enforced workloads on a shared VPS and secondary-market resale of unused capacity.

projects.title: T-REX Capital Market
projects.description: Regulated capital markets on Arc, powered by Privy wallets and USDC.
projects.project_description: T-REX Capital Market is a tokenization platform for regulated digital assets, built for institutions, asset managers, issuers, and investors that want to bring financial products onchain while maintaining control over who can participate, hold, and transfer those assets. Most institutional tokenization is not a purely permissionless DeFi problem. Institutions operate within legal and compliance frameworks, their users are often not crypto-native, and issuers need control over the full asset lifecycle. They need to know who owns an asset, restrict who can receive it, enforce investor limits, onboard legal entities through KYC/KYB, and manage issuance, investment, transfer, and redemption. T-REX combines ERC-3643 regulated tokens, OnchainID identities, Privy embedded wallets, USDC settlement, and Arc into one institutional workflow. Users onboard through a familiar Web2-style experience using email and KYC/KYB . Privy creates and manages an embedded wallet for the user, so they do not need MetaMask, seed phrases, or prior Web3 experience. Once onboarded, an issuer can use the Token Issuance Wizard to configure and deploy an ERC-3643 regulated token on Arc Testnet . The issuer can define compliance rules such as jurisdiction restrictions, maximum investor balance, and maximum investor count. ERC-3643 enforces eligibility at the token layer, so only qualified identities can hold or receive the asset. Eligible investors can discover an offering, subscribe using USDC , receive the corresponding regulated tokens, and later redeem their position back into USDC. A wallet that does not satisfy the required identity or compliance conditions cannot participate, demonstrating that compliance is enforced onchain rather than only in the frontend . projects.project_description_markdown:
**T-REX Capital Market** is a tokenization platform for regulated digital assets, built for institutions, asset managers, issuers, and investors that want to bring financial products onchain while maintaining control over who can participate, hold, and transfer those assets.

Most institutional tokenization is not a purely permissionless DeFi problem. Institutions operate within legal and compliance frameworks, their users are often not crypto-native, and issuers need control over the full asset lifecycle. They need to know who owns an asset, restrict who can receive it, enforce investor limits, onboard legal entities through KYC/KYB, and manage issuance, investment, transfer, and redemption.

T-REX combines **ERC-3643 regulated tokens, OnchainID identities, Privy embedded wallets, USDC settlement, and Arc** into one institutional workflow.

Users onboard through a familiar Web2-style experience using **email and KYC/KYB**. Privy creates and manages an embedded wallet for the user, so they do not need MetaMask, seed phrases, or prior Web3 experience.

Once onboarded, an issuer can use the **Token Issuance Wizard** to configure and deploy an ERC-3643 regulated token on **Arc Testnet**. The issuer can define compliance rules such as jurisdiction restrictions, maximum investor balance, and maximum investor count. ERC-3643 enforces eligibility at the token layer, so only qualified identities can hold or receive the asset.

Eligible investors can discover an offering, subscribe using **USDC**, receive the corresponding regulated tokens, and later redeem their position back into USDC.

A wallet that does not satisfy the required identity or compliance conditions cannot participate, demonstrating that compliance is enforced **onchain rather than only in the frontend**.

USDC is used as the common payment and settlement asset for subscriptions and redemptions.

Arc is an intentional choice for T-REX because **USDC is both our settlement asset and the native gas token on Arc**. This creates a much simpler institutional experience. A user holding USDC to invest in a dollar-denominated financial product does not also need to acquire and manage a separate volatile gas token just to interact with the platform.

T-REX is not a hackathon-only proof of concept. It is a **fully functional product that we intend to launch on Arc Mainnet**.

T-REX also includes a wallet-management layer. Users can fund their Privy wallet through a **fiat on-ramp** and move USDC between **Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet using Circle CCTP**, giving the platform both traditional and cross-chain capital entry rails.

T-REX is not limited to traditional real-world assets. The same regulated ownership framework can support **private-market assets, tokenized funds, managed onchain portfolios, yield strategies, or other financial products** that require an identified and permissioned investor base.

The result is a complete regulated capital-market workflow where **identity, wallet onboarding, compliance, token issuance, stablecoin settlement, redemption, and cross-chain liquidity work together as one system.**

The **Node.js backend** acts as the orchestration layer between the application database, Privy, and smart contracts. It manages organizations, investors, compliance documents, token metadata, pricing, transaction records, and reconciliation. Application state and blockchain state are kept separate, with onchain activity treated as the authoritative source for asset ownership and transaction state.

The tokenization layer uses **ERC-3643/T-REX**. Each token is connected to its own `IdentityRegistry` and `ModularCompliance` configuration, so transfers, mints, and burns are permissioned based on investor identity and issuer-defined compliance rules.

We implemented reusable compliance modules including:

- `CountryRestrictModule`
- `MaxBalanceModule`
- `MaxInvestorsModule`

Investor identity is managed through **OnchainID**. An `IdFactory` creates deterministic Identity contracts for wallets, while investor eligibility is represented through signed claims. KYC/KYB documents remain offchain, so sensitive personal information is not stored inside token contracts. The blockchain only needs the identity and claims required to determine whether an investor is eligible.

**Privy provides email OTP authentication and embedded EVM wallets.** Privy's **ES256 identity token** is verified server-side, and the embedded wallet becomes the signer for blockchain transactions. This allows institutional and non-crypto-native users to interact with onchain infrastructure without managing seed phrases or browser wallets, while Privy's programmable wallet controls provide additional safeguards for institutional workflows.

For a purchase:

1. The investor approves USDC.
2. USDC transfers directly from the investor to the issuer.
3. The corresponding regulated tokens are minted to the eligible investor.

For a redemption:

1. The investor's regulated tokens are burned.
2. USDC is settled back to the investor using the issuer's approved allowance.

The controller coordinates the asset and settlement legs while ERC-3643 independently determines whether the investor is eligible to hold the regulated token.

T-REX smart contracts are deployed on **Arc Testnet**. **USDC has two responsibilities in the system:**

- Payment and settlement for investments and redemptions.
- Transaction fees on Arc.

This removes the need for institutional users to acquire an unrelated native token simply to pay gas.

The wallet-management interface integrates **Circle CCTP** for moving USDC between **Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet in both directions**. This allows users to bring cross-chain USDC liquidity into T-REX and use the resulting balance directly for regulated investments and settlement.

Indexing and reconciliation services track **token deployments, identities, claims, purchases, redemptions, and other blockchain events**. This allows application state to be reconciled against, and reconstructed from, onchain activity.

projects.title: Hunch
projects.description: The prediction market that pays early conviction, not last-second bots. From our whitepaper to Arc.
projects.project_description:
I'm Raj, founder of Hunch. This September we published a whitepaper, "The Vested Parimutuel", proposing a new way to settle prediction markets. For ETHOnline we took it from paper to production: the contract runs on Arc, Chainlink resolves it, The Graph indexes it, and humans and AI agents trade it through a live venue. THE PROBLEM WE FOUND IN OUR OWN DATA
Pool-based prediction markets reward whoever shows up last. In a classic parimutuel pool, a dollar staked ten seconds before close earns the same payout as a dollar staked at open, when the answer was still uncertain. On Hunch's own tape (5,291 markets, 779,549 trades), winners who bet in the final 10% of a market's life took a median 70.1% of the losing pool, and early winners lost a median 38.7% of their payout to them. THE MECHANISM
Each stake "vests" into the opposing side the moment it lands, and is only accepted up to the amount the other side can still cover. Anything above that is refunded immediately. Your payout is your stake plus whatever vested into your side after you entered, so early capital earns more and late capital earns less. The paper proves the key properties (payouts sum to the pool exactly, and a stake placed after the last opposing money is paid exactly its principal), then replays the rule on the same real tape: Last-decile winners' share of the losing pool: 70.1% → 0.08% Early-winner dilution: 38.7% → 0.00% Last-second bettors: paid 1.487× → exactly 1.000× Market creators who seed every outcome: median +248.4% return, negative in 0 of 5,173 markets. Opening long-tail markets becomes a business, not a subsidy.
It settles in constant time: 130k to 315k gas per entry at any book size, against 5.5M for the naive loop at 1,000 opposing positions. We released 118 conformance test vectors with it, and they all pass in our CI. WHY WE KNOW THIS MATTERS: HUNCH CUP
Hunch Cup is our prediction-market tournament for agents. Season 1 ran four weeks (July 8 to August 5, 2026) with paper money and a real $5,000 USDC prize pool on Base: 1,034,149 trades 7.68 billion pUSDC in paper volume 652,362 wallets, 470,983 of them trading 58,341 markets 469,886 agents vs 1,097 humans: 99.8% of traders were AI agents Peak of 55,687 daily active wallets That season taught us two things this project fixes. First, when 99.8% of the flow is agents, a pool that pays latency pays the fastest bot. The vested rule removes that edge. Second, an audit of our top 50 prize wallets found 47 belonged to just 4 operators. So agent identity here is tied to a verified human through World AgentKit: human-backed agents get higher limits, and farms don't. WHAT'S LIVE Contracts deployed and verified on Arc, settling in native USDC Markets resolved by Chainlink Data Feeds, relayed onto Arc by a Chainlink CRE workflow, with no human resolver A full trading venue: connect a wallet, see exactly how much of your stake will be accepted before you sign, enter, and claim The Graph subgraphs that serve the book as decision data (remaining capacity, implied odds, projected payouts), plus an ERC-8004 agent-identity subgraph for Arc An autonomous agent on a Circle Agent Wallet that researches, decides, trades and claims, paying for research with x402 nanopayments An SDK, MCP server and SKILL so any AI agent can trade the venue A classic parimutuel behind the same interface, so judges can see the same market settled both ways The venue never holds user funds. The SDK only returns unsigned transactions, and invariant fuzzing proves no contract lets anyone move another user's money. More than 1,350 tests, one CI gate. WHERE THIS GOES
Arc mainnet next. Then Hunch Cup Season 2 on this mechanism, settled on Arc, with prize eligibility tiered on human-backed identity. Then Hunch's whole agent API moves onto Arc without changing a single call for existing agents. Our goal is that when agents are most of the market, the market still pays the people who took the risk first. Links:
Website: https://vpm.playhunch.xyz
Whitepaper: https://playhunch.xyz/vpm-whitepaper
Github: https://github.com/rajkaria/hunch-vpm
X: https://x.com/playhunchxyz
projects.how_its_made:
It's a pnpm monorepo in three layers (settlement, indexing, agents), each usable without the ones above it, behind one gate: pnpm verify, which CI also runs. FROM PAPER TO CONTRACT
VestedParimutuel.sol is the whitepaper's reference implementation, copied byte for byte. The paper's 118 conformance vectors run against it on every push, so any edit breaks the build. Every property we claim in the paper has a test: Conservation.t.sol proves payouts sum to the pool exactly, Mechanism.t.sol proves late stake is paid exactly 1×, and Gas.t.sol regenerates GAS.md, showing flat entry cost against a naive implementation that grows about 5,000 gas per opposing position. SETTLEMENT (Solidity, Foundry, Arc)
On top of the mechanism I built: MarketFactory: opens a market and commits its resolution rules in one transaction, so stake can never land before the rules exist FeedResolver: feed, strike price, direction and staleness limit are hashed into the market ID, so nobody can change the rules after money is in. Anyone can trigger resolution, and the caller can't influence the result. ClassicParimutuel: the rule Hunch runs today, behind the same interface, for side-by-side comparison Swappable oracle adapters
A stale feed refuses to settle instead of voiding, and after a timeout anyone can void, so no market is ever stuck. ARC + CIRCLE
USDC is Arc's gas token, so the asset you bet with is the asset you pay fees in. One catch I found on-chain: native USDC on Arc uses 18 decimals, but its ERC-20 interface uses 6, so the two views of one balance differ by 10^12. The agent holds funds in a Circle Agent Wallet, and the entity secret is passed in already encrypted, so the raw secret never enters the process. It pays for market research per request with x402 / Gateway Nanopayments. CHAINLINK (the hacky part)
We started on Stork. Midway through, Stork's Arc testnet feeds stopped updating, and Arc testnet has no Chainlink Data Feeds. So I built a Chainlink CRE workflow: it reads BTC/USD and ETH/USD on Sepolia, reaches consensus across the DON, and delivers one signed report through Chainlink's KeystoneForwarder on Arc to our ChainlinkCreOracle. The adapter accepts only the production forwarder and one named workflow, keeps each feed's own timestamp so staleness reflects real feed age, and can lock its configuration. Oracles sit behind one interface, so the switch needed zero settlement changes. On mainnet, ChainlinkFeedOracle reads published feeds directly. A GitHub Actions keeper settles markets as they close, but anyone can. THE GRAPH
Our subgraph doesn't just index events. It computes decisions in the mapping: remaining capacity per side, implied odds from accepted stake, vesting so far, and projected payouts. Agents and the venue read answers instead of redoing the math. I also pointed Agent0's standardized ERC-8004 schema at Arc's three registries, so one query covers agent identity and reputation on both Base and Arc. A Rust Substreams package streams market and position tables off the same events. AGENTS + WORLD
@hunch-vpm/client gives typed reads and viem writes that never hold a key. On top sit three MCP tools and a SKILL that teaches any agent the mechanism. The agent's decide() is a pure function (no clock, no I/O) that returns every option it considered, so every trade can be audited. createArcRail exposes the same four verbs Hunch's existing agents already call (research, quote, positions, trade), so our off-chain book and Arc are swappable by config. World AgentKit checks AgentBook for a human behind each agent. Verified agents get higher rate limits and the full per-market cap, while anonymous agents still trade. This came straight from the Hunch Cup audit where 4 operators held 47 of the top 50 wallets. FRONTEND (Next.js, wagmi/viem, Vercel)
This contract can accept only part of a stake: offer 1,000 and 340 goes in. No DEX UI handles that, so I designed the pattern from scratch. Before you sign, the stake panel shows accepted, refunded, and which side's capacity limited you. After you enter, the UI shows "the round hasn't closed yet", because the contract only splits stake in a later block. It never claims a fill it can't know yet. CONTINUITY
Pre-existing: Hunch (live on Base), Hunch Cup, the whitepaper, its reference contract and its conformance vectors. Built during ETHOnline: everything else in the repo, including the Arc deployment, resolver, factory, oracles, CRE workflow, subgraphs, Substreams, SDK, MCP, SKILL, AgentKit tiering, agent, keeper and venue. The README has three commands a judge can run in about 60 seconds each. More than 1,350 tests across Foundry, Vitest, Matchstick and Rust.

projects.title: ModZero
projects.description: Permissionless content protocol: stake, fingerprint, license & challenge — no moderator, just proof
projects.project_description: ModZero is a decentralized content provenance and licensing platform that uses blockchain, fingerprinting, and watermarking to verify ownership, enable content licensing, handle disputes through community challenges, and provide transparent provenance without centralized moderators.
projects.how_its_made: We built ModZero as a full-stack decentralized provenance and licensing protocol. Solidity smart contracts on Ethereum Sepolia handle content registration, staking, licenses, claims, challenges, posts, and wallet-native usernames. A TypeScript/Express backend with SQLite indexes the blockchain state and integrates Hedera HCS for ordered provenance events. The frontend uses React, Vite, Tailwind, wagmi and viem for wallet interactions. We use dHash + invisible LSB watermarking for content matching. A particularly hacky part is binding license payments to contentId + requester at the transaction-data level, then independently re-verifying the payment on-chain before issuing the license, preventing cross-content payment reuse and replay.

projects.title: Glasshouse
projects.description: Glasshouse runs sealed-bid auctions in 1inch SwapVM: highest bidder wins, pays the runner-up price.
projects.project_description: Glasshouse is an on-chain sealed-bid auction mechanism for allocating the right to fill orders based on participant valuation rather than identity or timing. We compare three allocation gates on the same order: an allowlist, a time-based Dutch auction, and Glasshouse’s sealed-bid second-price auction. In Glasshouse, participants commit a hashed bid, reveal it during a defined window, and the highest bidder wins while paying the second-highest bid. The winner receives an exclusive window to fill the order; once it expires, anyone can fill at the base price. Across the same participants, the allowlist required 10,000 bps of base, the Dutch auction 10,618 bps, and Glasshouse 9,756 bps. More importantly, Glasshouse was the only mechanism where the participant with the highest valuation received the fill. The project also emphasizes reproducibility and honest measurement. Every published figure is tied to its underlying computation, with automated linting to prevent unsupported claims. Checks with no applicable data are explicitly reported as “not applicable” rather than treated as passes. The accompanying subgraph deliberately refuses to compute metrics such as market share, concentration indexes, or USD-denominated values when the contract does not emit sufficient data to support them.
projects.how_its_made: We built Glasshouse as a fully on-chain commit-reveal auction system integrated with 1inch Aqua on Base. GlasshouseBook is a standalone Solidity contract where commit stores a bid hash, reveal validates the bid, and settle determines the winner and second-price payment. It has no owner, admin, or upgrade path, and all parameters become immutable after a round opens. The contract is only 6,149 bytes, with CI enforcing the size limit. The auction is exposed through a custom SwapVM instruction, opcode 0x2e, in a redeployed AquaSwapVMRouter connected to the official 1inch Aqua contracts. We use Aqua to run Glasshouse alongside its existing identity and Dutch-auction allocation gates, allowing us to benchmark all three mechanisms under identical conditions rather than making theoretical claims. One of the more interesting engineering decisions was never re-implementing Aqua's order encoding in TypeScript. A Foundry fork test uses the upstream MakerTraitsLib and TakerTraitsLib against real Base state to generate the order encoding, which is then verified on chain before any transaction spends funds. We also use a LIVE_ROUND value in hook data to retry orders without changing semantic auction parameters. For indexing, we built a Messari-conventions subgraph covering all GlasshouseBook events and added an off-chain derivation of the top-two bidding rule, publishing whether it matches the contract settlement. The subgraph deliberately avoids unsupported metrics such as USD values, TVL, market share, and concentration indexes when the emitted data cannot answer them. The frontend is a fully static Next.js export with no backend or API key. It reads the contract directly through eth_call, while Vercel rewrites provide clean round and profile URLs. Bidding happens entirely in the browser using commit-reveal, with cryptographically secure salts stored and read back from localStorage before the wallet transaction begins. Our strongest verification layer is an independent verify-run script that reads raw contract logs from any RPC and reconstructs every auction outcome without importing the contract, subgraph, or frontend implementation. It verified 9 auctions with 8 passed, 0 failed, and 0 not-applicable. A second verifier compared the published subgraph against the same independent replay across 135 fields, with every comparison agreeing. We also added provenance linting, chain-call budget tests, a Uniswap V3 QuoterV2 benchmark as an external pricing reference, and automated contract-size checks. The final test suite contains 97 Solidity tests, 59 JavaScript tests, and the provenance lint, all passing.

projects.title: Mayarin
projects.description: Programmable payments for humans, apps, and agents. Pay with anything, settle your way.
projects.project_description: Mayarin is a programmable payment and clearing platform for internet commerce, built around a simple idea: pay with what you have, settle in what you need. Today, moving money across digital assets and blockchain networks still requires users and businesses to think about wallets, tokens, liquidity, swaps, networks, gas, and settlement paths. Mayarin abstracts that complexity behind a unified payment flow and simplify fragmented UI/UX for everyone. A payer whether a human, application, or autonomous AI agent creates a payment intent describing what needs to be paid. Mayarin handles the underlying process of discovering the payment context, determining an appropriate route, executing asset conversion when necessary, and settling the recipient in their preferred asset. For ETHOnline, we are extending Mayarin with agentic payments and intelligent payment routing. The Graph provides onchain data and context used by the payment flow, Uniswap provides liquidity and asset conversion for execution, and Arc provides stablecoin settlement infrastructure. Rather than treating these as separate integrations, Mayarin orchestrates them as parts of a single end-to-end payment lifecycle. We are also exploring how autonomous software can transact safely without simply giving an AI agent unrestricted control over a wallet. Mayarin introduces programmable payment authority, allowing applications and agents to operate within defined spending policies while the platform handles execution and settlement underneath. Our long-term goal is to make the underlying payment rail an implementation detail. Customers should be able to pay using the assets and networks available to them, merchants should be able to choose how they receive settlement, and software should be able to participate in commerce through the same programmable infrastructure. Mayarin is being developed as a real product beyond ETHOnline. The hackathon is being used to build and validate substantial new capabilities around agentic payments, routing, liquidity execution, and stablecoin settlement on top of the existing Mayarin foundation.
projects.how_its_made:
Mayarin lets a payer pay with whatever supported asset they hold while the merchant receives the exact stablecoin amount they configured. The core abstraction is the PaymentIntent, which keeps four concerns separate that most payment systems collapse into one: the payer's asset, the payment network, the execution route, and the merchant's settlement asset. The engineering core is the exact-output cross-asset flow. The merchant's settlement amount is locked first, Uniswap derives the payer-side maximum backwards from that fixed output, and the payer signs a bounded input with any residue refunded. A payment only advances after the on-chain receipt is read back and matched against the expected token, recipient, and amount successful transaction submission is never treated as proof of payment. Partner integrations The Graph, the settlement indexer queries Subgraph Studio with typed GraphQL for PaymentCompleted, ResidueRefunded, and rail observations, tracking _meta.block.number as its cursor instead of relying on direct RPC log scans. This matters most on Arc Testnet, where fast block production and RPC log-range limits make naïve polling unreliable. Uniswap, the liquidity and execution layer. Both V3 and V2 venues implement one SwapVenue port: on V3, QuoterV2's quoteExactOutputSingle prices the leg and Mayarin encodes SwapRouter02.exactOutputSingle; on V2-style pools — including the Arc Testnet EURC/USDC pair — getAmountsIn prices it and swapTokensForExactTokens executes. Either way the merchant's settlement amount is the fixed side and the payer's spend is the bounded one. Arc, supported as a stablecoin payment and settlement rail: chain configuration, USDC decimal behavior, wallet balances, deposit monitoring, PaymentRouter execution, and settlement confirmation on Arc Testnet. x402 agent payments, an AI agent receives a machine-readable payment requirement, signs one EIP-3009 authorization, and Mayarin verifies, broadcasts, confirms, and settles it through the same clearing engine. No account creation, no gas management on the agent side. Architecture, ports and adapters. Domain packages own the payment-intent lifecycle, quote locking, routing, clearing, the double-entry ledger, idempotency, and the settlement state machine. RPC providers, wallets, subgraphs, liquidity venues, and databases plug in as replaceable adapters. Stack are Bun, Hono, Zod, PostgreSQL + Drizzle, viem. Solidity and Foundry for the PaymentRouter, deposit forwarders, and settlement flows. Astro and React for the merchant dashboard and checkout. The flow that happens in the behind :
payer asset → quote and route → bounded execution → confirmed settlement → ledger and merchant receipt

projects.title: Copy Check
projects.description: Is that wallet worth copying? Scored after gas, and only on trades it makes after you find it.
projects.project_description: Copy-trading tools rank wallets by win rate and total PnL. Both mislead. One wallet we tracked closed 68 trades at a 38% win rate and still showed +0.033 ETH after gas. Remove its single largest winning trade and it became -0.083 ETH — to copy it profitably you had to be inside one specific trade, which is a timing problem, not a wallet-selection problem. Another wallet sat at -0.00001 ETH before gas and -0.00197 ETH after: 99% of the loss was gas. Copy Check scores a wallet under three rules the code enforces rather than merely documents: Forward-only. Registering a wallet pins the current block, permanently. Trades before that block are discarded and counted separately. A score computed over a wallet's past is a number you chose after seeing the answer. Gas is measured, not estimated. Measured gas per swap ranged 0.000030-0.003157 ETH, a 104x spread. Receipts that fail to fetch stay null and are counted — never filled with zero. Drop the single best trade. If a wallet only survives with its best trade included, it is reported as one-hit dependent, not as a pass. The tool also refuses to answer. It returns "withheld" when gas was not retrieved, "too few" under 20 closed round-trips, and skips bots entirely. A judgment without evidence is worse than a wrong one, because you cannot tell it is wrong.
projects.how_its_made: Python standard library only — no framework, no database, no server. The boundary that matters: verdict.py knows nothing about data sources. It takes a list of swaps, so it runs and self-tests with no API key and no network. Data comes from The Graph. We query the Uniswap v3 Ethereum subgraph for a wallet's swaps, then translate raw amount0/amount1 sign pairs into buy/sell decisions. Several things only measurement revealed: urllib's default User-Agent is blocked by Cloudflare with error 1010 before authentication is even reached; nested filters (transaction_: {blockNumber_gte}) take 40s and fail with "bad indexers" where timestamp_gte returns in 1.7s; ascending order silently truncates busy wallets, so we page newest-first and stop at the pinned block; and skip is capped at 5000, so the candidate scanner pages by timestamp cursor instead. transaction.gasUsed ships as 0, so tx hashes come from The Graph and gas comes from public RPC receipts with 12 parallel workers — 8.7 minutes of sequential lookups became 8.7 seconds. Per-wallet scoring went from 270-450s to 4.5-7.4s. The UI is a single static HTML file generated from the verdict JSON, with inline SVG icons and zero external requests, so it deploys anywhere and opens offline. Added during ETHOnline: a candidate finder that is blind to past profit by construction (it never reads prices, and counts round-trips by quantity alone), bot-fleet detection by token-basket fingerprint — found after seven addresses turned out to trade an identical basket to stay under the per-address bot threshold — a public live page, and daily automated re-scoring.

projects.title: Wizard
projects.description: Confidential B2B Campaign Factory using Privy and Chainlink Workflows on Base
projects.project_description:
The problem:
Cross-brand co-marketing ("spend $10 at Brand A, earn Y redeemable at Brand Z") gets negotiated constantly and built bilaterally, and every new partner pair means a new integration. That's months of engineering per partnership, upfront cost turned into permanent CapEx, and lock-in to whichever partner's API you built first. It also forces two competitors to share raw customer transaction data or stand up a joint PII pipeline just to answer "did this customer qualify?". And even when the integration exists, someone still reconciles receipts by hand at period end, against a ledger of record that belongs to one of the two companies, so neither side gets a proof the other has to believe.
Blockchain doesn't obviously fix this. Public chains are a non-starter: purchase data is personal data, it can't sit on a public ledger, and per-customer claim events leak the customer graph. Permissioned chains demand infrastructure most brands don't run, and still leave the ledger in somebody's custody. What we built:
Wizard replaces the bilateral integration with one shared on-chain factory plus confidential verification in a hardware enclave. A master CampaignFactory on Base Sepolia is the campaign clone generator: every campaign is an EIP-1167 clone of a shared CampaignEscrow , with terms fixed at launch, such as reward mechanic (percent rateBps or flat value), minimum spend, per-user cap with a calendar-anchored reset window (lifetime / day / week / month / year, span-N periods, anchor weekday, reset time-of-day), per-transaction cap, campaign-wide issuance cap, allowed days of the week (UTC bitmask), campaign start/end window, redeemable cashback vs. discount proof-of-savings, and a 2-party operating-cost split in basis points.
Purchase payloads don't go to a partner's server or a shared database. They're submitted to a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow by HTTP trigger into an attested TEE enclave. Inside the enclave the workflow reads the campaign's terms on-chain from the factory at request time (so new campaigns are picked up with zero workflow redeploys), evaluates the payload against them using the same clamp order the contract uses (per-tx cap → per-user cap → campaign-wide cap), and holds the one partner-held secret the Vault DON releases into the enclave: a master key used to derive a single-use claim nullifier H(HMAC(master, campaignId) || userAnchor || timestamp) . Raw payload facts, such as spend amount, item detail, prior earnings never leave the enclave. Only the verdict does (runtime logs currently exist, in production they wouldn’t).
On approval the enclave submits an execution proof via evm.write through the CRE Forwarder to the campaign's escrow on Base Sepolia. The escrow is not a passive log: it independently re-derives the earn and reverts InvalidReport unless the delivered points match bitwise, mints the ERC-1155 reward to the customer's wallet, and burns the nullifier, so a forged, replayed, or float-corrupted report cannot settle. Company B never sees Company A's customer records or transaction logs. It sees a settled on-chain claim against an escrow whose terms it agreed to, and it authorizes redemption on its own campaigns. Customer identity is a Privy embedded wallet created from an email OTP, so the customer manages no seed phrase and the merchant stores no password; the deposit handshake (each company funding its share of the operating deposit) is verified on-chain by exact sender, recipient, and wei amount before the campaign contract is ever deployed. Why the alternatives don't work:
Bilateral APIs: CapEx per partner, vendor lock-in, and full data sharing. CDP/loyalty SaaS (Segment, Braze, mParticle, LoyaltyLion): they unify customer data beautifully by requiring the data to move into a shared processor, which is exactly the thing two competitors can't agree to. Affiliate/offer networks and receipt-parsing reward apps: they can verify a purchase without a bilateral integration, but the trust sits in the network's own database, reconciliation is still manual, and settlement isn't programmatic. Public-chain settlement: leaks personal data. Permissioned chains: infrastructure burden, and a single custodian. Zero-knowledge proofs: the right cryptographic answer and the wrong 2026 economics at retail volumes, where there are proving cost, circuit work per campaign shape, plus you still need a trusted path for the input data. Confidential workflows are the practical middle: the privacy claim is honest and bounded (pseudonymous-but-linkable, not zero-knowledge; the enclave's trust assumption is hardware attestation), and the settlement side gets a proof that neither brand has to be trusted to produce. Where it goes (how the app would look like in production):
(1) N-party campaigns. The contracts already accept an arbitrary participant set and per-participant fee shares; the wizard exercises the 2-party case today. (2) One reward token across many campaigns, so a brand's points are a single fungible balance instead of campaign-scoped coupon tokens (the ERC-1155 minter role is already per-escrow, so this is an authorization change, not an architecture change). Deployment is split frontend/backend on Vercel with Neon as the database. Everything is wired through one Makefile (make db-up, make test, make typecheck) so a fresh clone runs with three commands. The request path, end to end:
A purchase starts as a JSON payload {campaignId, userAnchor, merchantId, amountSpent, timestamp, earnedInWindow} . The backend relays it, signs it, sends using CRE HTTP trigger, which fires an attested enclave. Inside the enclave, the workflow reads the campaign's terms live from the factory on-chain ( evmClient.callContract → factory campaigns(id) → escrow), so new campaigns need zero workflow redeploys; if the campaign has a campaign-wide cap it also reads campaignTotalEarned() from the escrow rather than trusting any caller-supplied number. It then evaluates eligibility: window, min-spend, day-of-week, per-tx cap, per-user cap, campaign cap; in exactly the clamp order the contract uses, derives the claim nullifier from a Vault-released secret, and crosses back to the DON for consensus. The DON signs the report and writeReport pushes it through the Chainlink forwarder to the escrow's onReport , which re-derives the earn itself and reverts InvalidReport unless the delivered points match bitwise, mints the ERC-1155 reward, and burns the nullifier. The frontend then confirms by reading the escrow's on-chain ledger rather than trusting any HTTP response. Chainlink CRE and how it's actually used:
This is the part I'd call the heart of the project. The workflow is a single HTTP-triggered cre.handlerInTee(...) handler running on { tee: 'nitro', regions: ['us-west-2'] } (currently deployed to Chainlink private registry), serving every campaign from one binary via a campaigns map in config. Three CRE capabilities do the work: runtime.getSecret() pulls CAMPAIGN_NULLIFIER_MASTER from the Vault DON straight into the enclave (never exposed to node operators or workflow-DON memory); the EVM client does the on-chain term reads; and runtime.usingTheDons() → donRuntime.report({encoderName: 'evm', signingAlgo: 'ecdsa', hashingAlgo: 'keccak256'}) → writeReport() produces the DON-consensus, DON-signed report. The confidentiality is structural: raw purchase facts ( amountSpent , items , earnedInWindow ) are evaluated inside the enclave and never leave it, only the verdict and a one-way nullifier are written on-chain. Trigger auth is ECDSA: every request must carry an authorized-key signature ( KEY_TYPE_ECDSA_EVM ), so merchants authenticate to the platform with API keys and never touch a key. What CRE bought us:
Before confidential workflows, the honest options for cross-brand verification were "share the data" (a non-starter between competitors) or "stand up a ZK proving pipeline" (real cryptographic cost per campaign shape, plus a trusted input path). CRE lets a purely stateless evaluator hold a partner-held secret and produce a settlement-grade proof, without the platform ever seeing the raw data. It also gave the project its cleanest architectural constraint: because the enclave can read on-chain state, the campaign rules live in one place (the factory), and the workflow never needs redeployment to learn new campaigns. Privy and how it's actually used:
Privy covers the entire identity-and-money surface. Customers and companies onboard with email OTP and get an embedded wallet, meaning no seed phrase, and no password stored anywhere. Two flows ride on it: the deposit handshake, where each company connects its Privy wallet and sends its share of the operating deposit via eth_sendTransaction (40:60 split → A sends 0.004 ETH, B 0.006 ETH), and the backend verifies each deposit on-chain, like the exact sender, exact recipient, exact wei, confirmed receipt, all before the campaign contract is even deployed; and the reward redemption, which is personal_sign over a human-readable statement ("Redeem 1.40 points from 0x… on campaign #5 (DayOfWeek Test) as Globex Books"), verified server-side by recovering the signer. The escrow does not exist until both deposits land, which makes Privy the actual activation switch for a campaign rather than a login screen. What was particularly hacky: Hand-rolling the CRE trigger JWT. Before the SDK exposed a client for firing deployed workflows, I reverse-engineered the gateway's signing scheme and reimplemented it byte-identically: alg: 'ETH' JWT, digest = sha256 of the body with keys sorted lexicographically at every nesting level, r||s||recoveryId base64url with yParity normalization. It's the difference between workflows.execute returning ACCEPTED and returning nothing at all. Discovering the report encoding the hard way. Wrapping the payload in onReport(...) calldata made the escrow see a 356-byte "report" that failed its length check; the working shape is a bare abi.encode(nullifier, recipient, amountSpentWei, eligible, pointsWei) . A verdict transport that doesn't exist on Vercel. Execution status lives behind the cre CLI, which can't run in a lambda. So the frontend was rewired to confirm claims by watching the escrow's own Claim events, with a backend probe that detects CRE-CLI availability and skips polling when it's absent. The on-chain ledger became the source of truth. Two id namespaces. Postgres row ids and the factory's sequential on-chain campaign ids are different numbers, and the workflow only knows the latter. So the payload route forwards the on-chain id, and the campaigns list verifies factory membership (escrow address match) to hide stale rows from superseded factory generations. The contract suite enforces calendar-anchored cap windows (day/week/N-week/month/year) with Hinnant's civil-date algorithm implemented in uint256 to avoid an oracle, and the escrow advertises IReceiver via a bare 0x805f2132 interface id (inherited IERC165 functions are excluded from type(IReceiver).interfaceId ) Tools and AI disclosure:
Built with Hermes Desktop as the harness, using GLM 5.3 Flash (code writing, README) and DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (technical spec and demo outline consolidation), full breakdown in AI_ATTRIBUTION.md . AI did the writing, cross-layer inconsistency checking between frontend/CRE/contracts, contract logic, test cases, and frontend boilerplate; I did the project and rule design, scope boundaries, naming, test-case design, production roadmap, and the CRE workflow deployment. Testnet ETH came from the ETHGlobal faucet. Local state runs Postgres 16 in Docker ( docker compose up -d, port 5433 ); the deployed app runs on Vercel with Neon Postgres. 67 Foundry tests (claim, caps, window resets including N-week anchors and DOW gates, redeem, redeemer whitelist, factory wiring), 27 workflow tests (3 demo campaigns × 5 payloads), and a backend suite covering launch validation, DOW-mask mapping, and wei conversion — all run by make test . The problem: 
Cross-brand co-marketing ("spend $10 at Brand A, earn Y redeemable at Brand Z") gets negotiated constantly and built bilaterally, and every new partner pair means a new integration. That's months of engineering per partnership, upfront cost turned into permanent CapEx, and lock-in to whichever partner's API you built first. It also forces two competitors to share raw customer transaction data or stand up a joint PII pipeline just to answer "did this customer qualify?". And even when the integration exists, someone still reconciles receipts by hand at period end, against a ledger of record that belongs to one of the two companies, so neither side gets a proof the other has to believe.
Blockchain doesn't obviously fix this. Public chains are a non-starter: purchase data is personal data, it can't sit on a public ledger, and per-customer claim events leak the customer graph. Permissioned chains demand infrastructure most brands don't run, and still leave the ledger in somebody's custody.

What we built: 
Wizard replaces the bilateral integration with one shared on-chain factory plus confidential verification in a hardware enclave. A master `CampaignFactory`  on Base Sepolia is the campaign clone generator: every campaign is an EIP-1167 clone of a shared `CampaignEscrow`, with terms fixed at launch, such as reward mechanic (percent rateBps or flat value), minimum spend, per-user cap with a calendar-anchored reset window (lifetime / day / week / month / year, span-N periods, anchor weekday, reset time-of-day), per-transaction cap, campaign-wide issuance cap, allowed days of the week (UTC bitmask), campaign start/end window, redeemable cashback vs. discount proof-of-savings, and a 2-party operating-cost split in basis points.
Purchase payloads don't go to a partner's server or a shared database. They're submitted to a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow by HTTP trigger into an attested TEE enclave. Inside the enclave the workflow reads the campaign's terms on-chain from the factory at request time (so new campaigns are picked up with zero workflow redeploys), evaluates the payload against them using the same clamp order the contract uses (per-tx cap → per-user cap → campaign-wide cap), and holds the one partner-held secret the Vault DON releases into the enclave: a master key used to derive a single-use claim nullifier `H(HMAC(master, campaignId) || userAnchor || timestamp)`. Raw payload facts, such as spend amount, item detail, prior earnings never leave the enclave. Only the verdict does (runtime logs currently exist, in production they wouldn’t).
On approval the enclave submits an execution proof via `evm.write`  through the CRE Forwarder to the campaign's escrow on Base Sepolia. The escrow is not a passive log: it independently re-derives the earn and reverts `InvalidReport`  unless the delivered points match bitwise, mints the ERC-1155 reward to the customer's wallet, and burns the nullifier, so a forged, replayed, or float-corrupted report cannot settle. Company B never sees Company A's customer records or transaction logs. It sees a settled on-chain claim against an escrow whose terms it agreed to, and it authorizes redemption on its own campaigns. Customer identity is a Privy embedded wallet created from an email OTP, so the customer manages no seed phrase and the merchant stores no password; the deposit handshake (each company funding its share of the operating deposit) is verified on-chain by exact sender, recipient, and wei amount before the campaign contract is ever deployed.

Why the alternatives don't work: 
Bilateral APIs: CapEx per partner, vendor lock-in, and full data sharing. CDP/loyalty SaaS (Segment, Braze, mParticle, LoyaltyLion): they unify customer data beautifully by requiring the data to move into a shared processor, which is exactly the thing two competitors can't agree to. Affiliate/offer networks and receipt-parsing reward apps: they can verify a purchase without a bilateral integration, but the trust sits in the network's own database, reconciliation is still manual, and settlement isn't programmatic. Public-chain settlement: leaks personal data. Permissioned chains: infrastructure burden, and a single custodian. Zero-knowledge proofs: the right cryptographic answer and the wrong 2026 economics at retail volumes, where there are proving cost, circuit work per campaign shape, plus you still need a trusted path for the input data. Confidential workflows are the practical middle: the privacy claim is honest and bounded (pseudonymous-but-linkable, not zero-knowledge; the enclave's trust assumption is hardware attestation), and the settlement side gets a proof that neither brand has to be trusted to produce.

Where it goes (how the app would look like in production): 
(1) N-party campaigns. The contracts already accept an arbitrary participant set and per-participant fee shares; the wizard exercises the 2-party case today. (2) One reward token across many campaigns, so a brand's points are a single fungible balance instead of campaign-scoped coupon tokens (the ERC-1155 minter role is already per-escrow, so this is an authorization change, not an architecture change). (3) Batch settlement at the merchant ingress to allow one DON consensus round for N receipts instead of N rounds, with a multi-claim report format on the escrow; this is what makes retail-volume economics work at all. (4) A merchant SDK that mirrors the rule gates client-side so obviously-ineligible transactions are never submitted (advisory only, the enclave stays authoritative). (5) Redemption privacy: `batchRedeem(bytes32[] commitments)` so the chain enforces supply conservation without learning who redeemed what. (6) Production gas: an ERC-4337 paymaster (e.g. CDP or Coinbase Developer Platform) sponsoring gas and settling in USDC, so companies never hold ETH, plus per-campaign workflow deployments for pause/upgrade isolation and per-campaign blast radius on trigger keys. (7) Production identity and authorization. Privy access tokens verified server-side and wallets bound to authenticated company accounts which also kills the demo's first-mover deposit-spoofing hole plus policies as enforced spend limits, and B's wallet as the escrow's authorized redeemer. Beyond that, Privy key quorums are what turn the platform's single relay key into a real org authorization model: an m-of-n threshold over authorization keys and user identities, enforced inside Privy's TEE infrastructure, with one level of quorum nesting so a "Brand Finance" quorum can sit inside an "Org Admins" quorum.
