projects.title: Barker ALM Engine
projects.description: Yield-backed automated liquidity: v4 take-profit ladders on Arc + a vault-backed 1inch Aqua maker
projects.project_description: A market maker's backing capital normally sits idle — it has to be there to honour a quote, so it does nothing else. Barker ALM Engine attacks that from two directions, on two venues, with one engine. Arc leg — Uniswap v4 on Circle's Arc. A one-sided concentrated liquidity range is an execution primitive, not a yield position. Funded only in the base asset and placed above spot, it is an automatic take-profit ladder: as price rises through it, the position converts to USDC — and it collects trading fees the whole time it waits, which a resting limit order does not. A fully crossed range sells at the geometric mean of its bounds, which is worse than a limit order at the top; the fee is what pays for the difference. For exact-input swaps a crossed range realises geometricMean / (1 − fee). On Arc testnet we measured +0.3008% over the geometric mean on a 0.30% pool, against a predicted +0.3009% — exact to one part in a million. The Arc leg runs on Arc testnet: a position manager, a dynamic-fee v4 hook, and an unattended keeper. Three full lifecycles are on chain; the second was closed by the keeper on its own key, with the USDC paid straight to the owner. The keeper also found a real bug in our hook: it billed one trade 2.46% for the previous swap's price impact, made four days earlier. We fixed it, redeployed, and replayed the same move on chain — charged 0.30%. Mainnet deployment follows Arc's mainnet launch on Sep 16. Aqua leg — 1inch SwapVM. A maker whose inventory sits in an ERC-4626 vault (steakUSDC) earning yield while it quotes. A solvency guard caps every quote at what the vault can actually redeem, and settlement hooks redeem just in time for a payout and re-deposit what comes in, inside the swap. Return = vault APY + spread, and the maker never quotes a fill it cannot settle. Proven on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC. Both legs are on one live dashboard: https://barkermoney.github.io/barker-alm-engine/ This is a Continuity Track entry. Prior work is documented rather than hidden: a pre-hackathon feasibility probe sits unmodified in the initial commit, clearly marked, and everything after it is hackathon work visible in the git history. The proprietary strategy parameters are deliberately not in the repository — what is open is the execution layer. We kept feedback logs for Uniswap and 1inch as we built, including three of our own claims that we retracted in public when our indexer proved them wrong.
projects.how_its_made: Uniswap v4 is the execution primitive, not a bolt-on. BarkerV4Positions drives the PoolManager directly through unlock / unlockCallback into modifyLiquidity , settling with flash accounting ( sync / settle / take ) and deriving each position's salt from a registry id so two positions on the same range never collide. We deliberately built without v4-periphery . Two safety properties are the point of the contract. One-sidedness is enforced, not assumed : open rejects a range straddling spot by comparing against the live tick, then re-checks after the fact that the pool debited only one asset — the pool's own accounting, not ours. Custody stays with the position owner : a keeper may close and collect, but can never name a different recipient, so the worst a compromised keeper does is close a position early into its owner's own wallet. BarkerDynamicFeeHook carries AFTER_INITIALIZE | BEFORE_SWAP , deployed via CREATE2 salt mining with our own miner ( HookMiner lives in periphery, which we do not depend on). In beforeSwap it measures the previous swap's price impact, dates it to the block that swap happened in, and returns an LP fee override that decays linearly over 300 blocks. The constructor checks its own address against the required flags, because a mis-mined salt otherwise yields a hook that deploys, verifies, and is silently never called. Automation is a TypeScript keeper (viem) over a v4 event indexer. v4 keeps every pool in one singleton, so a pool's history is Initialize / ModifyLiquidity / Swap plus extsload of slot0 . The exit rule is a pure function of a snapshot, must hold for three consecutive observations, and runs on its own key. The dashboard runs the same indexer code in the browser (Vite + viem, no backend, no wallet). Arc (Circle) shaped the tooling. Arc pays gas in USDC, and its USDC is a native precompile behind an ERC-20 shell that Foundry's EVM does not implement. Since forge script simulates the entire script before broadcasting, a USDC-touching script broadcasts nothing while printing success . So Foundry does the arithmetic and the pure deployments, and cast sends everything that moves tokens. Arc's public node also caps eth_getLogs at roughly 25–30k blocks, so the indexer halves its page on rejection. 1inch Aqua / SwapVM is extended through its two official extension points rather than forked. An Extruction guard caps quoted depth at min(virtual reserve, liquid + redeemable, allowance) and scales both reserves together, so it trims depth without moving the price — SwapVM's ship() does not itself verify that a maker can cover its quote. IMakerHooks does redeem-on-fill and redeposit-on-receive against the ERC-4626 vault. It runs on the signature track, because capital held in the Aqua ledger stops earning. Because SwapVM is source-available copyleft, that code lives in its own directory under SwapVM-1.1, while everything else stays MIT. 103 tests: 43 Foundry tests against a real PoolManager, 45 on SwapVM (11 on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC), 15 for the keeper. The notable part is what the tests missed. Our indexer and dashboard, reading real data, caught errors every test had passed: a feesOwed view off by 2^128; a hand-copied figure that had us crediting a 0.048% gap to "v4 rounding" (there was no gap); our claim that v4's Swap event omits an overridden fee (it carries it); a solvency guard that moved the price instead of the depth; and the fee-hook bug above. Each is fixed or publicly retracted in FEEDBACK.md and FEEDBACK-1INCH.md.
projects.project_description_markdown:
A market maker's backing capital normally sits idle — it has to be *there* to honour a quote, so it does nothing else. Barker ALM Engine attacks that from two directions, on two venues, with one engine.

**Arc leg — Uniswap v4 on Circle's Arc.** A one-sided concentrated liquidity range is an execution primitive, not a yield position. Funded only in the base asset and placed above spot, it is an automatic take-profit ladder: as price rises through it, the position converts to USDC — and it collects trading fees the whole time it waits, which a resting limit order does not. A fully crossed range sells at the *geometric mean* of its bounds, which is worse than a limit order at the top; the fee is what pays for the difference. For exact-input swaps a crossed range realises geometricMean / (1 − fee). On Arc testnet we measured **+0.3008%** over the geometric mean on a 0.30% pool, against a predicted +0.3009% — exact to one part in a million.

The Arc leg runs on Arc testnet: a position manager, a dynamic-fee v4 hook, and an unattended keeper. Three full lifecycles are on chain; the second was closed by the keeper on its own key, with the USDC paid straight to the owner. The keeper also found a real bug in our hook: it billed one trade 2.46% for the previous swap's price impact, made four days earlier. We fixed it, redeployed, and replayed the same move on chain — charged 0.30%. Mainnet deployment follows Arc's mainnet launch on Sep 16.

**Aqua leg — 1inch SwapVM.** A maker whose inventory sits in an ERC-4626 vault (steakUSDC) earning yield while it quotes. A solvency guard caps every quote at what the vault can actually redeem, and settlement hooks redeem just in time for a payout and re-deposit what comes in, inside the swap. Return = vault APY + spread, and the maker never quotes a fill it cannot settle. Proven on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC.

Both legs are on one live dashboard: https://barkermoney.github.io/barker-alm-engine/

This is a Continuity Track entry. Prior work is documented rather than hidden: a pre-hackathon feasibility probe sits unmodified in the initial commit, clearly marked, and everything after it is hackathon work visible in the git history. The proprietary strategy parameters are deliberately not in the repository — what is open is the execution layer. We kept feedback logs for Uniswap and 1inch as we built, including three of our own claims that we retracted in public when our indexer proved them wrong.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**Uniswap v4 is the execution primitive, not a bolt-on.** `BarkerV4Positions` drives the PoolManager directly through `unlock`/`unlockCallback` into `modifyLiquidity`, settling with flash accounting (`sync`/`settle`/`take`) and deriving each position's salt from a registry id so two positions on the same range never collide. We deliberately built without `v4-periphery`.

Two safety properties are the point of the contract. **One-sidedness is enforced, not assumed**: `open` rejects a range straddling spot by comparing against the live tick, then re-checks after the fact that the pool debited only one asset — the pool's own accounting, not ours. **Custody stays with the position owner**: a keeper may close and collect, but can never name a different recipient, so the worst a compromised keeper does is close a position early into its owner's own wallet.

`BarkerDynamicFeeHook` carries `AFTER_INITIALIZE | BEFORE_SWAP`, deployed via CREATE2 salt mining with our own miner (`HookMiner` lives in periphery, which we do not depend on). In `beforeSwap` it measures the previous swap's price impact, dates it to the block that swap happened in, and returns an LP fee override that decays linearly over 300 blocks. The constructor checks its own address against the required flags, because a mis-mined salt otherwise yields a hook that deploys, verifies, and is silently never called.

**Automation** is a TypeScript keeper (viem) over a v4 event indexer. v4 keeps every pool in one singleton, so a pool's history is `Initialize`/`ModifyLiquidity`/`Swap` plus `extsload` of `slot0`. The exit rule is a pure function of a snapshot, must hold for three consecutive observations, and runs on its own key. The dashboard runs the same indexer code in the browser (Vite + viem, no backend, no wallet).

**Arc (Circle) shaped the tooling.** Arc pays gas in USDC, and its USDC is a native precompile behind an ERC-20 shell that Foundry's EVM does not implement. Since `forge script` simulates the entire script before broadcasting, a USDC-touching script **broadcasts nothing while printing success**. So Foundry does the arithmetic and the pure deployments, and `cast` sends everything that moves tokens. Arc's public node also caps `eth_getLogs` at roughly 25–30k blocks, so the indexer halves its page on rejection.

**1inch Aqua / SwapVM** is extended through its two official extension points rather than forked. An `Extruction` guard caps quoted depth at min(virtual reserve, liquid + redeemable, allowance) and scales both reserves together, so it trims depth without moving the price — SwapVM's `ship()` does not itself verify that a maker can cover its quote. `IMakerHooks` does redeem-on-fill and redeposit-on-receive against the ERC-4626 vault. It runs on the signature track, because capital held in the Aqua ledger stops earning. Because SwapVM is source-available copyleft, that code lives in its own directory under SwapVM-1.1, while everything else stays MIT.

103 tests: 43 Foundry tests against a real PoolManager, 45 on SwapVM (11 on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC), 15 for the keeper. **The notable part is what the tests missed.** Our indexer and dashboard, reading real data, caught errors every test had passed: a `feesOwed` view off by 2^128; a hand-copied figure that had us crediting a 0.048% gap to "v4 rounding" (there was no gap); our claim that v4's `Swap` event omits an overridden fee (it carries it); a solvency guard that moved the price instead of the depth; and the fee-hook bug above. Each is fixed or publicly retracted in FEEDBACK.md and FEEDBACK-1INCH.md.

projects.title: two field
projects.description: Developers' AI agent hires other specialist agents for specialized tasks.
projects.project_description: twofield is an agentic marketplace where the buyers' existing coding or research agent hires specialist agents for scoped jobs, instead of working on those projects themselves. A mistake in a specialized research task, which the buyers' agent is not skilled at, can lead to a series of incorrect assumptions and decisions. Instead, a developer can provide a buyer agent with a budget for specialized tasks and the agent browses specialists, files a brief, and funds an ERC-8183 escrow on Circle's Arc testnet. The specialist does the work, submits it, and the developer or the developer's agent rates it. A good rating pays the specialist agent at once. A poor rating holds escrow for a human review by twofield, and the verdict lands on the ERC-8004 Validation Registry under the specialist's onchain identity. Every specialist carries an ERC-8004 identity and an onchain reputation score built from real ratings, and a specialist can also be tried for a few cents through a metered x402 preview before you commit to a full job. The buyer never touches a seed phrase, a gas fee, or a private key.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend is Next.js with TypeScript and Tailwind. Route handlers under the same app act as the backend, since Privy's server SDK is Node only. Neon Postgres with Drizzle ORM tracks agents, jobs, ratings, and receipts. Every buyer and seller agent gets its own Privy server wallet, owned by an app controlled authorization key so the backend can sign for agents without holding a private key itself. Each wallet carries a Privy policy that whitelists exactly the contract calls that agent may make, capped by its budget, the real enforcement layer rather than trust. On Circle's Arc testnet, hiring opens an ERC-8183 escrow job, the specialist submits a hash of its work, and the buyer rates it 1 to 5. A good rating settles escrow at once. A poor rating holds funds and hands the case to a review queue, whose verdict is written to the ERC-8004 Validation Registry under the specialist's identity, so a dispute outcome is not just a database row. Ratings also feed the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry, so a specialist's score is real onchain history, not a marketing claim. The metered preview uses x402, settled by an in process facilitator since public facilitators do not yet cover Arc, with the platform wallet as relayer. Deliverables come from the specialist agent, from the brief and any files the buyer attaches.

projects.title: Frely-Network
projects.description: From know-how to revenue. Frely turns prompts, Skills & Agents into a business.
projects.project_description: Many domain experts, especially experienced developers, have accumulated valuable Prompts, Skills, Agents, and professional workflows, but these capabilities are difficult to turn into revenue. Creators either publish their work for free and risk having it copied and repackaged, or keep it on personal devices and in private environments, where it cannot serve more users. As a result, AI capabilities that create real productive value lack an effective path to commercialization. Frely aims to solve this problem by helping creators turn their Skills and Agents into paid services while keeping their core Prompts, code, and workflows private. Creators sell access to their capabilities rather than giving away their intellectual assets. Users and AI Agents can discover these capabilities, purchase access, and use them in their own workflows. Frely and Frely Swarm already provide the Web2 infrastructure for capability execution and service delivery. For ETHOnline, we are building Frely Network, the Web3 commercial layer that enables open and verifiable identity, service, and transaction relationships between creators, users, and Agents. In a Web2 marketplace, the identity of AI capabilities, transaction relationships, and marketplace data exist inside a platform’s private database. Frely Network makes these commercial relationships verifiable, queryable, and usable across applications. It also allows AI Agents to act as independent participants that can discover and purchase capabilities from other Agents. The project integrates ENS, Hedera, x402, and The Graph to provide Web3 infrastructure for the identity, transactions, and discovery of AI capabilities. Our goal is not to build another Skill-sharing website. We want valuable AI know-how to generate commercial returns and give creators a reason to connect their professional capabilities to the broader AI ecosystem.
projects.how_its_made: Frely Network is built on top of the existing Frely and Frely Swarm infrastructure. Frely provides the user-facing service access and product layer, while Frely Swarm hosts and executes Skills, Agents, and workflows. For ETHOnline, we built Frely Network as an open network layer for onchain identity, service registration, capability discovery, payments, and commercial relationships. We do not move the Agent itself onchain. Skills, Prompts, Agent code, and runtime environments remain in the existing offchain execution layer, while the blockchain stores identity and service information that should be publicly verifiable. This protects the creator’s core capability while giving Provider identity, service endpoints, capability claims, and payment results a verifiable foundation. When a creator publishes a Skill or Agent, Frely Network generates a validated Provider Manifest, writes the relevant information into ERC-8004 Registration Metadata, and stores the service endpoint in the ENS Resolver. ENS provides readable names for Providers and Agents, while ERC-8004 stores the Agent ID and registration information. The Network cross-checks ENS, ERC-8004, and the public Agent Card to verify that the discovered service, onchain identity, and Agent all refer to the same Provider. The payment layer uses Hedera and x402. We treat AI capabilities as network services that can be paid for per call. When a user or Agent requests a paid capability, the system first retrieves a quote and checks the available budget, then uses x402 on Hedera to verify payment conditions. Settlement happens after successful execution, and every execution uses a unique execution ID to prevent duplicate payments. This allows an Agent to act as an independent consumer and complete the full “discover → verify → pay → invoke” flow without a traditional subscription or checkout page. The Graph indexes onchain registration data. Frontends and Agents can search for candidate Providers based on capability and registration metadata without scanning the chain directly. The Graph is used for candidate discovery, the ENS Resolver is an important verification source for service endpoints, and the Agent Card describes supported protocols, input types, and invocation methods. If a Graph query fails, identities do not match, the service endpoint is invalid, or the Agent Card cannot be verified, the system fails closed and does not continue with the service call or payment. After verification and payment checks, Frely passes the request to Frely Swarm, which executes the actual Skill or Agent. Settlement is completed after successful execution, and the result is returned to the caller. The system is therefore split into two parts: the offchain layer securely hosts and executes private AI capabilities, while Frely Network handles open and verifiable identity, discovery, payments, and commercial relationships. One notable design choice is that creators do not need to rebuild an existing Skill or Agent as a full Web3 application. A private Skill can keep its existing execution model and connect through Frely to gain onchain identity, discovery, and payment capabilities. To the consumer, it still behaves like a normal AI service. To an Agent, it becomes an external capability that can be discovered, verified, purchased, and composed.

projects.title: lpTOKEN.fun
projects.description: LP positions you can trade like tokens. One token, two ways to trade it. Built on Uniswap v4.
projects.project_description: lpTOKEN.fun makes a Uniswap v4 LP position tradable like a token. That gives traders two ways to trade one token. Hold the token itself for price. Or hold its lpTOKEN, a share of the pool. It still moves with price, and it also collects the pool's trading fees into its NAV. One asset, two positions, and you pick the side. Under the hood, a vault owns one full range v4 position, and the vault contract is itself the lpTOKEN ERC-20. Every share is a claim on the same position, so shares are fungible. Mint with both sides, zap in with one asset, redeem anytime, or send it like any other token. Before ETHOnline, lpTOKEN.fun was live on Robinhood Chain and Base, including stock token markets, so lpAAPL is a position you can hold instead of AAPL. During the event we took the stack to Arc mainnet. Arc's native currency is USDC, so an lpTOKEN there is dollar denominated. That needed a new zap router: on Arc, native USDC and ERC-20 USDC are one balance with different decimals, and there is no WETH style wrapper. More than a dozen new lpTOKEN markets went live during the event, including the first ones on Arc. Ethereum mainnet is still in development as we submit. Our plan is to ship it before the hackathon ends, so existing v4 pools on Ethereum can get an lpTOKEN too.
projects.how_its_made: The whole problem is making a Uniswap v4 position behave like a token. Everything else follows from that. A market is one static fee v4 pool. On a platform launch the pool is opened behind a hook that declares exactly one permission, beforeInitialize, and that function always reverts. v4 skips the callback when the caller is the hook itself, so the launchpad's own atomic initialization is the only path that can open the pool, and no other hook logic exists anywhere in the hot path. A platform market then holds two positions in that one pool: a permanent one-sided launch position carrying the initial inventory, and the vault position, which is full range and bounded away from the extreme ticks so nobody can freeze it. Markets for tokens that launched elsewhere skip the launch position entirely and get the vault position alone. The vault owns its position directly through the PoolManager singleton, and the vault contract is itself the lp{SYMBOL} ERC-20 with permit. No NFT, no wrapper in between. That is what makes the claim fungible, and it means a share is a pro rata claim on principal, collected fees, idle balances and the launch NAV together. Minting takes both sides. The vault syncs launch fees, collects the position's fees, then scales every component of the existing portfolio by one gross-share ratio: the proportional slice goes into the position, the remainder stays idle in the vault. Liquidity per share and idle assets per share both stay unchanged, so a mint can't move pre-existing NAV into the pool at a price the minter picked. Whatever isn't used is refunded in the same transaction. Redeeming burns shares and returns the proportional claim on both currencies. If you'd rather come in or leave with one asset, the ZapRouter handles it: zap in from either leg of the pair directly against the vault pool, or from the native currency or the canonical stablecoin across up to three hookless static fee hops, and zap out the same way. It runs inside PoolManager.unlock, and every entrypoint has a permit variant so there's no separate approval transaction. Fees are the reason to hold the lpTOKEN, so the vault position's earnings simply stay: 100% of them accrue to holder NAV, with no management fee and no performance fee. The 0.30% share fee on public mint and redeem is taken in shares to the treasury and never comes out of LP earnings. On platform markets the separate launch position splits its fees, 40% to the creator and 60% to NAV on the target side, and 40% creator, 20% NAV, 40% treasury on the counter side. compound() is permissionless and swapless. Anyone can call it, it reinvests only matched balances, and it's capped: the deployable amount for an interval is half of the pool's own fee ratio applied to the protocol owned liquidity live in the pool right now, read through StateLibrary, behind a ten minute cooldown. So it can't be used to walk the pool. One-sided or capped residue stays idle and stays redeemable. Two details worth calling out. Vaults are deployed with cloneDeterministicWithImmutableArgs, and the pool binding and fee source are part of those immutable arguments, so the vault's own address commits to what it is bound to and nothing can be repointed later. And the minimum assessable amount is 334 shares, derived in the contract rather than written down: it's the smallest amount whose exact 30 basis point fee is at least one raw share, and every fee rounds up, so an operation can't be fragmented into dust to dodge the charge. Why v4 specifically: the singleton lets the vault hold a position without going through a position NFT, unlock gives the router flash accounting for multi-hop entry and exit, an immutable static fee is what makes the compound cap computable at all, and hooks let us gate initialization without paying for callbacks we never use. This design doesn't really port back to v3. There is no USD numeraire and no oracle anywhere in the Solidity. It counts raw amounts of currency0 and currency1 and never asks what anything is worth in dollars. That's also why the same contracts run on any EVM chain with a v4 deployment, whatever the native currency happens to be. The stack: Foundry and Solidity 0.8.36 with OpenZeppelin and the v4 core and periphery libraries for the contracts. Next.js 16, React 19, viem, wagmi and TanStack Query for the app, and our own indexer writing to PostgreSQL through Prisma, which serves charts, holder PnL and LP activity without depending on a third party subgraph. Everything above existed before ETHOnline, running on Robinhood Chain and Base. During the event we deployed the stack to Arc mainnet and added ZapRouterArc. On Arc, native USDC (18 decimals) and ERC-20 USDC (6 decimals) are one balance, so the router converts accounting units instead of wrapping or unwrapping anything. That work is in the public repo's commit history. Ethereum mainnet is in development, and we plan to ship it before the event ends.

projects.title: khaaliNames
projects.description: Comprehensive smart contract suite for onchain user management
projects.project_description: khalliNames is a complete smart contract suite for user management, powered by ENSv2. Features :: Generate unique names as identifiers Milestones to track user growth Onchain AppStore enablement Monetising vanity aliasing Emancipation without data being held hostage (ie, true user owned data)
projects.how_its_made: The project is extremely modular, where every piece is swappable. At the foundational layer is an onchain name generation utility and ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and PermissionedResolver contracts. The name generation utility feeds the registry to enable unique usernames. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control allows for nuanced permission scoping across the entire tree. The final result is an onchain app store where users are part of the same universe while also truly controlling their own data! Disclaimer Project to be completed; Follow along !
projects.project_description_markdown:
khalliNames is a complete smart contract suite for user management, powered by ENSv2.

Features ::
- Generate unique names as identifiers
- Milestones to track user growth
- Onchain AppStore enablement
- Monetising vanity aliasing
- Emancipation without data being held hostage (ie, true user owned data)
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The project is extremely modular, where every piece is swappable. At the foundational layer is an onchain name generation utility and ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and PermissionedResolver contracts. The name generation utility feeds the registry to enable unique usernames. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control allows for nuanced permission scoping across the entire tree. 

The final result is an onchain app store where users are part of the same universe while also truly controlling their own data!

* Disclaimer

Project to be completed; [Follow along](https://github.com/khaaliDimaag/khaaliNames-eth)!

projects.title: AgentBazaar
projects.description: Open AI-agent marketplace on Hedera; pay per execution in HBAR via x402, every run verified onchain.
projects.project_description:
AgentBazaar is a permissionless marketplace where developers list AI agents and buyers hire them per execution, paid on Hedera testnet via x402, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every agent run is a real HBAR transaction on Hedera testnet, verifiable on HashScan.
Builders list agents through a 7-step deploy wizard, sign their HCS-14 onchain identity with their own wallet, and encrypt their API keys with AES-256-GCM vault storage.
Buyers pay in HBAR via x402 and signs a partial TransferTransaction, Blocky402 co-signs as feePayer and submits to Hedera testnet.
Every execution is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic for permanent, verifiable audit trail.
The platform also features an AI chat orchestrator that chains multiple agents in sequence (A2A), settling one Blocky402 payment for the total cost. Built-in agents include ScamSniff (rug pull detector), ThreadSmith (X thread writer), and LaunchWatch (token launch monitor).
projects.how_its_made:
AgentBazaar is built as a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces + Turborepo) with a Next.js 15 frontend and an Express.js API backend. Payment is handled via x402 v2 exact scheme on Hedera testnet; the buyer's wallet partially signs a TransferTransaction, which is forwarded to Blocky402 (https://api.testnet.blocky402.com) for verification and settlement. Blocky402 co-signs as feePayer, pays gas, and submits the transaction to Hedera testnet returning a real Hedera transaction ID used for the HashScan link. Every agent execution is logged to an HCS topic (0.0.10363117) for verifiable onchain audit trail. Each agent has an HCS-14 onchain identity topic created and signed by the builder's own wallet at listing time. The builder, not the platform, holds the admin key.
A deployed HederaVault smart contract (0xCEA1141C63bf42e04cC829Ce76BaeD350bC9c971) handles trustless per-agent fee splits between builder and platform. API keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and stored in the database which are decrypted in-memory only after Blocky402 payment is verified.
The AI orchestrator uses LangChain & Claude Sonnet 4.6 to parse user intent, select agents from the live registry (agent discovery), and chain outputs between agents (A2A).
Hedera Agent Kit is used for HCS topic creation and message submission.

projects.title: Mandate Treasury
projects.description: Confidential USDC firewall: Chainlink CRE decides privately, Privy enforces, Arc settles.
projects.project_description: Mandate is a confidential payment firewall for one company USDC wallet. A human or agent proposes a payment and does not hold the treasury key. Chainlink CRE privately evaluates business policy inside a TEE; the trigger carries only intent id, organization id, and payment hash. Privy holds the organization key and independently enforces allowlists, caps, and default deny. Arc settles USDC. The payment hash binds CRE screening to Privy execution.
projects.how_its_made: I was curious about how b2b companies handles the financial operation of themselves. I see that in privy track, and it triggers me. Then i'm thinking about confidentiality that is a real and valid concern of financial companies on their behaviour. And also they need to have some policies to make sure that differenet people with differenet levels of access can work so the company can works operational.

projects.title: SafeGate
projects.description: Post-payment verification and evidence infrastructure for agentic commerce.
projects.project_description: SafeGate is an independent post-payment verification and evidence layer for digital and agentic commerce. Payments can prove that money moved, but they do not prove that the intended commerce outcome actually happened. SafeGate binds payment requests to transactions, verifies payment outcomes, tracks fulfillment, prevents replay, and produces portable evidence and commerce proofs. During ETHOnline 2026, we are extending the existing SafeGate core with a new agentic-payment flow designed for x402-based services and Hedera.
projects.how_its_made: SafeGate uses a verification-first architecture that separates payment movement from commerce outcome verification. The existing core handles request/payment binding, replay-safe consumption, fulfillment state, signed evidence, and portable proof generation. For ETHOnline 2026, the new work will add a Hedera-integrated x402 agentic-payment path in which an agent can access a paid service, produce a verifiable payment event, and pass that event into SafeGate for independent post-payment verification and evidence generation. The hackathon-specific Hedera and x402 components will be developed and committed separately so the new Continuity Track work is clearly distinguishable from the pre-existing SafeGate codebase.

projects.title: genesis
projects.description: The project guarantees that an image was produced by a specific camera body.
projects.project_description:
Every image sensor carries a permanent, per-body physical fingerprint (PRNU) that imprints on every exposure and cannot exist in an image that never passed through it. We register it and certify origin of the image from the camera body. We first extract a value K thats unique for the camera body.
We enrol from the photographer's own files 40+ RAW frames from an archive that already exists, with no manufacturer and no platform involved. The maths behind K: A sensor's photosites differ slightly in how much charge each returns for the same light. That gain error is fixed at manufacture, unique to the die, and
it multiplies the signal rather than adding to it. We certify: exposed on camera body X · camera body registered to identity Y · first
registered at time T · these derivatives descend from that original. Reference: https://ws2.binghamton.edu/fridrich/Research/full_paper_02.pdf

Imaging core — Python. rawpy (LibRaw) reads Canon CR3 and returns the raw
mosaic, split into its four Bayer sublattices, each corrected against its own
black level. Nothing in the fingerprint path demosaics. Per plane: a wavelet
Wiener denoiser ( PyWavelets , scipy ) yields the noise residual, a maximum
likelihood estimator builds K across 40+ frames, and matching is Peak to
Correlation Energy over an FFT cross-correlation. numpy throughout. The maths
is Fridrich, Digital Image Forensics Using Sensor Noise , IEEE SPM 26(2), 2009,
cited by equation number in fingerprint/prnu.py . CLI: enroll , test , pair , demo . K stays local as .npz ; only a
SHA-256 commitment leaves the machine. Contracts — Solidity, Foundry. Registry implements ERC-7053 commit() over a camera-body registry: BodyRecord carries the fingerprint commitment,
owner, ENS node and revocation flag; ImageRecord carries pixel hash,
perceptual hash, body id, modification level, parent hash and PCE score.
Sessions batch as one Merkle root per shoot. Live on Sepolia , verified on
Etherscan and Blockscout. ENS — ENSv2 on Sepolia. osoro.eth is the photographer and cam.osoro.eth the fleet, both live; a body subname is created live during the demo , its
resolver records holding the fingerprint commitment, signing key and revocation
status. Resolution goes through the UniversalResolver — the path a third
party takes. A photographer needs no name of their own: ensNode may be zero. The Graph. The registry has no index on perceptualHash , so the subgraph is that index — it is what lets a degraded copy find the original it
descends from. Live as genesis v0.0.4 on real Sepolia events. A Subgraph MCP
server exposes the same lookups to agents. An index is never an authority :
every candidate is read back off chain before anything is claimed. Chainlink CRE. The scorer is the trust hole by design — it holds K and you
take its word. A confidential workflow removes it: the algorithm is public, K
arrives as a Vault DON secret decrypted only inside the enclave, and only a
score crosses back. The verifier extracts the residual locally and sends a 256² int8 crop — never K . Three corrections by measurement: the reference is 89 MB against a 1mb secret limit, so K is cropped; 512² does not fit ; Confidential HTTP is
not the fallback (125 kb cap). The cost is documented, not buried — at 256²
the weakest frame falls into the null. It runs as a real cre workflow simulate per call — about seventeen seconds,
deterministic. attested is false : the simulator is not an enclave and the
report is built rather than DON-signed. Scoring, verify and console. FastAPI wraps the imaging core. The verify page
is one page, no framework, viem for chain reads, four verdicts. An
eight-screen console drives the demo on localhost and holds the signing key —
never deployed.

Every image sensor carries a permanent, per-body physical fingerprint (PRNU) that imprints on every exposure and cannot exist in an image that never passed through it. We register it and certify origin of the image from the camera body.

We first extract a value K thats unique for the camera body.
We enrol from the photographer's own files 40+ RAW frames from an archive that already exists, with no manufacturer and no platform involved. 

The maths behind K: A sensor's photosites differ slightly in how much charge each returns for the same light. That gain error is fixed at manufacture, unique to the die, and
it multiplies the signal rather than adding to it. 

We certify: exposed on camera body X · camera body registered to identity Y · first
registered at time T · these derivatives descend from that original.

Reference: https://ws2.binghamton.edu/fridrich/Research/full_paper_02.pdf
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**Imaging core — Python.** `rawpy` (LibRaw) reads Canon CR3 and returns the raw
mosaic, split into its four Bayer sublattices, each corrected against its own
black level. **Nothing in the fingerprint path demosaics.** Per plane: a wavelet
Wiener denoiser (`PyWavelets`, `scipy`) yields the noise residual, a maximum
likelihood estimator builds K across 40+ frames, and matching is Peak to
Correlation Energy over an FFT cross-correlation. `numpy` throughout. The maths
is Fridrich, *Digital Image Forensics Using Sensor Noise*, IEEE SPM 26(2), 2009,
cited by equation number in `fingerprint/prnu.py`.

**CLI:** `enroll`, `test`, `pair`, `demo`. K stays local as `.npz`; only a
SHA-256 commitment leaves the machine.

**Contracts — Solidity, Foundry.** `Registry` implements ERC-7053 `commit()`
over a camera-body registry: `BodyRecord` carries the fingerprint commitment,
owner, ENS node and revocation flag; `ImageRecord` carries pixel hash,
perceptual hash, body id, modification level, parent hash and PCE score.
Sessions batch as one Merkle root per shoot. **Live on Sepolia**, verified on
Etherscan and Blockscout.

**ENS — ENSv2 on Sepolia.** `osoro.eth` is the photographer and `cam.osoro.eth`
the fleet, both live; a body subname is **created live during the demo**, its
resolver records holding the fingerprint commitment, signing key and revocation
status. Resolution goes through the **UniversalResolver** — the path a third
party takes. A photographer needs no name of their own: `ensNode` may be zero.

**The Graph.** The registry has no index on `perceptualHash`, so the subgraph
**is** that index — it is what lets a degraded copy find the original it
descends from. Live as `genesis` v0.0.4 on real Sepolia events. A Subgraph MCP
server exposes the same lookups to agents. **An index is never an authority**:
every candidate is read back off chain before anything is claimed.

**Chainlink CRE.** The scorer is the trust hole by design — it holds K and you
take its word. A confidential workflow removes it: the algorithm is public, K
arrives as a Vault DON secret decrypted only inside the enclave, and only a
score crosses back. The verifier extracts the residual locally and sends a
**256² int8 crop** — **never K**.

Three corrections by measurement: the reference is **89 MB** against a **1mb**
secret limit, so K is cropped; **512² does not fit**; **Confidential HTTP is
not the fallback** (125 kb cap). The cost is documented, not buried — at 256²
the weakest frame falls into the null.

It runs as a real `cre workflow simulate` per call — about seventeen seconds,
deterministic. **`attested` is false**: the simulator is not an enclave and the
report is built rather than DON-signed.

**Scoring, verify and console.** FastAPI wraps the imaging core. The verify page
is one page, no framework, `viem` for chain reads, four verdicts. An
eight-screen console drives the demo on localhost and holds the signing key —
never deployed.

projects.title: TrustGuard AI
projects.description: A decentralized AI security protocol that analyzes, verifies and safeguards users' transactions.
projects.project_description: TrustGuard is a decentralized AI security protocol for Ethereum that evaluates transactions and autonomous-agent actions before execution. AI models analyze transaction behavior and risk, Chainlink provides verifiable external context and workflow orchestration, and Ethereum smart contracts enforce the resulting security policy.
projects.how_its_made: The user connects an Ethereum wallet such as MetaMask. TrustGuard establishes the information required for transaction analysis. The user or AI agent proposes a transaction. TrustGuard extracts relevant information. Independent AI workers analyze the normalized transaction. TrustGuard calculates an aggregate risk score. Chainlink infrastructure provides relevant external/on-chain context and orchestrates the risk-evaluation workflow. The TrustGuard policy engine determines whether the transaction should be approved, reviewed, or blocked. The risk assessment is recorded onto the Ethereum Protocol, creating an immutable security audit trail.

projects.title: Prism
projects.description: Prism is a tri-proof blockchain: PoS secures, PoUW computes, and PoUP grows communities.
projects.project_description: Prism is an open-source blockchain prototype that unifies three complementary signals: Proof of Stake secures the network, Proof of Useful Work rewards verifiable computation, and Proof of Useful Participation rewards meaningful community contribution. The existing Go prototype already implements blocks, a genesis state, transactions, balances and validation. During ETHOnline, Prism will gain its first end-to-end usable feature: a transparent rewards flow that demonstrates how these three signals can coexist without sacrificing auditability, plus a clearer node/API experience for builders.
projects.how_its_made: Prism starts from a public Go codebase structured around reusable blockchain and transaction packages. The baseline includes deterministic block hashing, a genesis block, an in-memory chain, account balances, signed-style transaction data and validation that rejects invalid transfers. The project is versioned publicly on GitHub, with small commits throughout development so judges can inspect the full evolution. During ETHOnline, I will extend this foundation with a practical rewards prototype, expose the relevant node state through a simple developer-facing interface, improve validation and tests, and document the protocol decisions, token economics and demo flow. The goal is to turn the current protocol skeleton into something that can be run, inspected and understood end to end.

projects.title: BUFI
projects.description: BUFI is a financial OS purpose-built for distributed B2B teams that are stablecoin and AI-first.
projects.project_description: BUFI is Private Business Finance: a self-custodial financial workspace for global teams, contractors, and the AI agents that work alongside them. Small B2B teams today run their money through a patchwork of bank accounts, hot wallets and difficult SAFE accounts, exchange dashboards, spreadsheets, and chat threads. Getting paid across borders is slow and expensive, treasury decisions live in one founder's browser, and nothing in that stack was built for an AI agent to participate safely. BUFI replaces the patchwork with one workspace where a team holds its treasury in a wallet it controls, pays and gets paid in stablecoins, and runs the everyday finance workflows of a business (invoices, reimbursements, payroll, contracts, deals, projects) against that same treasury, from web or mobile. Every workspace gets an onchain identity and a clear split between collective and personal money. Treasury moves require the team's own approval quorum, never a platform key. An AI assistant, Bu, works inside those limits: it can draft, categorize, reconcile, and pay within a scoped budget the treasurers set, and hands anything larger back to a human. For ETHOnline 2026 we added and polished amongst other things the "private" in Private Business Finance. Ghost Balances let a workspace or an individual transact privately while keeping its treasury controls, and StableFX assets on Arc let teams settle in the currency their counterparties actually use. We also turned workspace identity into reputation: a payment score computed confidentially from real settlement history, so workspaces can be discovered and hired by other companies and by agents, with quotes, contracts, invoicing, and settlement handled end to end inside BUFI serving a network-reputation graph for international commerce. The goal is simple: geography should not decide how a team works or gets paid, who they trust, the world-class opportunities and services they can access.
projects.how_its_made: BUFI is a unified financial workspace for agile B2B teams, combining stablecoin payments, self-custodial treasury management, AI assistance, privacy, and ERP/CRM workflows in one cross-platform product. Its custody architecture uses Circle User-Controlled Wallets as treasury signers for Circle MSCA Modular Wallets with weighted approvals. For agentic workflows, AI requests permission and scope to the treasury and goes through a treasury ceremony for scoped and safe agentic transactions. Teams can also connect existing Web3 wallets, including Ledger hardware devices, to access shared workflows such as invoicing, reimbursements, payroll, contracts, deals, products, and project management. For secure AI-assisted treasury operations, BUFI integrates Circle’s ERC-6900 Allowlist plugin with human-in-the-loop treasury ceremonies. This enables policy-controlled agentic payments while preserving explicit user oversight. The architecture works across web and mobile, allowing treasury activity and AI notifications to be reviewed and handled from either platform. Each workspace has an ERC-8004 identity for agent-to-agent flows. During workspace setup, ENSv2 naming distinguishes collective workspace wallets from personal wallets, supported by color coding to reduce operational ambiguity. For AI agents, BUFI supports WebMCP, LLM discoverability, and x402 nanopayments, allowing assistants to discover and procure tools and enabling workspaces to be discovered for hiring. BUFI combines the Circle and Arc stack with Ledger to create a global, self-custodial ERP for the future of work. The platform supports swaps, FX across StableFX assets on Avalanche Mainnet and Arc testnet, yield and earn functionality, allowlisted payments, conditional payments, onchain automation, and multi-step settlement. During ETHOnline 2026, we completed BUFI’s privacy implementation. BUFI means Private Business Finance, represented by its ghost identity. We integrated Hinkal’s privacy payment solution as Ghost Balances for MSCA treasuries and personal wallets, alongside StableFX support on Arc testnet. This allows companies and independent contributors to transact globally and privately while retaining programmable treasury controls. We also extended ERC-8004 identities into a payment-scoring system using Chainlink Confidential CRE. This provides the foundation for a human and agent workspace marketplace where financial workspaces can be discovered and hired based on reputation and scoring. A dedicated agentic workflow manages quotes, contracts, invoices, and settlement for workspace hiring, enabling humans and agents to hire and transact with one another through a unified financial operating layer. To power the agentic marketplace and discoverability, we enabled an MCP and Arc Subgraph to keep this agentic workspace 'Behance meets Fiverr' in sync. When a workspace get's a quote and deal done in the CRM - the contract and escrow itself is settled leveraging the ERC-8183 Agentic Commerce contract combined with Chainlink CRE for Disputes and settlement with AI reviewing deliverables and dispute in a multi-model juror dispute resolution system. As workspaces and their agents get hired through ERC-8183 job escrow and A2A. Circle’s MSCA architecture and the ERC-6900 plugin model offer a path beyond developer-controlled agent wallets toward scoped agentic accounts and automated yield treasuries. We developed BUFI-6900, a collection of plugins that defines modular capabilities for Circle MSCA wallets. Similar to the skills.sh directory, and built to support Circle Agent Stack Marketplace, and Coinbase Bazaar, these capabilities could be installed as reusable “Wallet Skills,” allowing agent wallets to evolve without replacing their underlying accounts. Further integration work is required because Circle’s plugin installation contract currently relies on a Circle-managed allowlist. We provide these plugins for consideration as to power BUFI 2.0 in regards to enhanced capabilities for scoped agentic accounts, agentic policy, unified USDC gateway balances and automated yield treasury multisig's.

When a workspace get's a quote and deal done in the CRM - the contract and escrow itself is settled leveraging the ERC-8183 Agentic Commerce contract combined with Chainlink CRE for Disputes and settlement with AI reviewing deliverables and dispute in a multi-model juror dispute resolution system. As workspaces and their agents get hired through ERC-8183 job escrow and A2A.

Circle’s MSCA architecture and the ERC-6900 plugin model offer a path beyond developer-controlled agent wallets toward scoped agentic accounts and automated yield treasuries. We developed BUFI-6900, a collection of plugins that defines modular capabilities for Circle MSCA wallets. Similar to the skills.sh directory, and built to support Circle Agent Stack Marketplace, and Coinbase Bazaar, these capabilities could be installed as reusable “Wallet Skills,” allowing agent wallets to evolve without replacing their underlying accounts. Further integration work is required because Circle’s plugin installation contract currently relies on a Circle-managed allowlist. We provide these plugins for consideration as to power BUFI 2.0 in regards to enhanced capabilities for scoped agentic accounts, agentic policy, unified USDC gateway balances and automated yield treasury multisig's.

projects.title: kosmos
projects.description: Onchain events with human verification, escrowed tickets and proof of attendance.
projects.project_description: Kosmos is an onchain event platform that brings identity, payments, ticketing and attendance together. Hosts can create paid events, attendees verify with World, pay using ETH or swap Sepolia USDC to ETH through Uniswap and receive QR tickets after approval. After check-in, the host can settle the event and attendees receive an NFT as proof of attendance. Every user also gets a unique ENSv2 identity like "name.kosmos.eth". Kosmos is built and tested on Ethereum Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made:
Kosmos is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL and Solidity. The smart contracts run on Ethereum Sepolia and use escrow for event payments, refunds and settlement, while TicketNFT provides proof of attendance.
World IDKit is used for attendee verification, Uniswap lets users swap Sepolia USDC to the exact ETH needed for an event and ENSv2 gives users unique "name.kosmos.eth" identities. Privy handles authentication and wallet linking, while Pinata/IPFS, Resend and QR tools are used for event images, emails and ticket check-ins. The contracts were tested with Foundry, with all 17 tests passing.

projects.title: Tessera_Marketplace
projects.description: Rent compute by the block. Pay for each block before it runs. Settled on Hedera via x402.
projects.project_description: Tessera — rent compute by the block, pay for each block before it runs Tessera is a marketplace for renting a running container from a provider you've never met, where time is cut into fixed blocks and every block is paid for on Hedera before it is served. The problem. If you rent compute from a stranger, one of you has to go first. Either the provider serves you on credit and hopes you pay — and an AI agent can drain them and vanish — or you post a deposit into escrow and hope they deliver, which is the custody model that crypto payments were supposed to make unnecessary. Somebody is always exposed. x402 doesn't solve this, because x402 is request-shaped: one request, one price, one payment. Compute isn't discrete — a container consumes resources continuously while payments trail behind it. The Block Settlement Protocol (BSP). Our answer, specified in full in SPEC.md, is to divide time into fixed blocks (say 15 seconds), require each block to be paid before it begins, and open the window to buy block n+1 while block n is still running. That lookahead window is the whole trick: it absorbs the few seconds a payment takes to settle, so service is continuous while neither side ever extends credit. Four invariants fall out, and they are the design: No credit. The block being served is always already settled. The provider never works unpaid. Bounded renter exposure. The most a renter can lose to a provider vanishing is one block — 15 seconds of compute. Deterministic termination. Stop paying and the container stops at the next boundary. Not early (a payment may still land), not late (that would be unpaid work). No grace period, no negotiation. No custody. Payment goes renter to provider directly. Our marketplace does discovery and placement, then gets out of the way — our test suite kills the control plane mid-job and the job keeps running and keeps billing. How it uses Hedera. Every block settles as a native Hedera transfer through the Blocky402 x402 v2 facilitator, in HBAR or in TESS, an HTS token we minted (0.0.10518829, 2 decimals, custom fee schedule). Every receipt is published to an immutable HCS topic (0.0.10507942, no admin key, no submit key) that anyone can audit through a mirror node without asking the provider — which is what makes a provider shortening blocks detectable rather than deniable. Every provider carries an HCS-14 on-chain identity derived from its metadata and payout account, and signs every receipt with it. The facilitator co-signs and pays the network fee, so the renter never holds gas and no contract ever holds funds. The protocol's 4-second lead-time floor is a measurement, not a guess: Blocky402's full paid leg (402 to sign to verify to settle to 200) takes a median 3.2s on testnet. What runs. A TypeScript pnpm monorepo: a provider daemon that runs Docker containers and enforces block boundaries; a registry/broker marketplace; renter and provider CLIs; a key-holding renter agent so the browser never touches a private key; an SDK (marketplace.rent() with block/renewal events and a stopRenewing() kill switch); and a console that reads the audit trail back from Hedera through a mirror node. 356 tests. Verified end to end on testnet: a renter bought a 20-block lease against a 10-block wallet, ten blocks settled on-chain one per block, block 11 was refused for insufficient funds, and the hosted website went from HTTP 200 to connection refused at exactly the next boundary — with all ten receipts plus the terminal unpaid_boundary receipt readable on HCS. Honest limits. It isn't deployed to a public URL, there's one provider node rather than a fleet, and we deliberately skipped multi-agent price negotiation. The settlement is real; the marketing is not.
projects.how_its_made: Tessera is a TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm workspaces, organised into nine packages so that the protocol logic stays independent of the infrastructure around it. Shared packages hold the block clock, the x402 v2 wire types and the receipt schemas, validated with zod. A separate Hedera package wraps transaction signing, HCS publishing and mirror-node reads. On top of these sit the provider daemon, the registry and broker service, the renter and provider CLIs, a programmatic SDK and a web console. The services are built on Fastify with pino for logging, better-sqlite3 for local state and dockerode for container management. The console is React 18 and Vite 5. Tests are written with vitest. The provider daemon is the core of the system. The protocol rules are implemented as pure functions with no I/O: one module decides whether a block boundary advances or terminates the job, and another enforces the specification's minimum lead time. Above them sits a scheduler that ticks once per second across all active jobs and evaluates the boundary condition for each. It depends on a Clock interface rather than the system clock, so tests can drive it deterministically with a fake clock instead of waiting for real seconds to elapse. The Docker runner is abstracted the same way, which allows the full job lifecycle to be tested without Docker running. Payment admission follows the same pattern: a single pure function takes the job state, the block being paid for and the current time, and returns one of five decisions, including idempotent replay of a block that has already been paid. This keeps the entire error matrix unit-testable in isolation from the network. Hedera is central rather than incidental. Settling once per fifteen-second block is only viable on a network with fast finality and predictable, low fees. Each block is settled as a native Hedera transfer through the Blocky402 x402 facilitator, denominated either in HBAR or in TESS, an HTS token issued for the project. The facilitator co-signs and submits the transaction and pays the network fee itself, so the renter never needs to hold gas and no contract or intermediary ever takes custody of funds. Each settled block appears on-chain as a direct transfer from the renter's account to the provider's. Receipts are published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created without an admin key or a submit key, making the log immutable and openly writable to participants. The console reads that history back through a public mirror node rather than from the project's own database, so the audit trail can be verified independently of the provider. Provider identity uses the HCS-14 standard, generated through the Hashgraph Online standards SDK, so that each provider has a verifiable on-chain identifier derived from its own metadata and payout account, and signs every receipt with it. One protocol constant was derived from measurement rather than estimation. The minimum renewal window is four seconds because the complete paid request through the facilitator, covering the initial 402 response, signing, verification and settlement, was measured at a median of 3.2 seconds on testnet. The registry rejects any listing configured below that floor so that a misconfigured provider cannot make the protocol appear unreliable. The most notable implementation workaround concerns two optional native modules, ssh2's crypto binding and cpu-features, both pulled in transitively through dockerode. On some hosts these segfault when loaded, which terminates the process at import time and cannot be caught in JavaScript. Because ssh2 already guards both of these requires and falls back to a pure JavaScript implementation, the build configuration deliberately excludes them, converting an unrecoverable crash into a handled error. The only capability lost is SSH cipher acceleration, which the project does not use, as the daemon communicates with Docker over a Unix socket. Containers are run with a read-only root filesystem, memory and process limits, restricted networking and no-new-privileges enabled by default, with a configuration flag to disable the last of these on kernels that refuse to exec under it. The daemon also refuses to start if it is configured to publish receipts to Hedera but lacks the topic or operator credentials, rather than running with an audit log that is silently empty.

projects.title: Eve
projects.description: Crypto ride-hailing with Privy wallets and Arc USDC escrow for fares.
projects.project_description: Eve is a crypto-native ride-hailing marketplace with separate rider and driver mobile apps. Riders request trips, drivers send fare offers, and once a match is accepted the fare is locked in USDC escrow on Circle’s Arc network until the trip settles, is refunded, or goes through dispute. That replaces opaque fiat holds with clear on-chain settlement both sides can verify. We chose Arc for native USDC settlement and very low gas fees — ride payments need cheap, predictable settlement that doesn’t eat into fare margins. Identity and wallets use Privy: email/SMS login, embedded Ethereum (and Solana) wallets without seed phrases, and the same wallet signs escrow transactions. The wallet UX also supports receiving USDC (address QR) and cashing out to an external address. Eve is built as a real product path, not a throwaway hackathon demo — the goal after ETHOnline is to carry this Arc + Privy settlement stack toward a live market. Hackathon focus is a reliable end-to-end escrowed ride demo plus polished wallet flows aimed at Arc’s stablecoin/payment track and Privy’s financial-flow track.
projects.how_its_made: Eve is a monorepo: Expo (React Native) rider and driver apps, a Next.js admin/ops console, a Next.js marketing site (www), and a Node.js backend with PostgreSQL, Redis, and optional Kafka for domain events. Auth exchanges Privy identity tokens for Eve JWTs; ride matching and real-time updates run through the ride/location/notify stack; payment owns @Arc Testnet, and @Privy wallets, RideEscrow quotes/confirms, and treasury payouts. On Arc Testnet (chain id 5042002), RideEscrow holds native/ERC-20 USDC views for trip deposits, settlement with a short dispute window, refunds, and finalize. Mobile apps pull chain/token/contract config from the payment API and sign escrow calls with the Privy embedded wallet via eth_sendTransaction after switching onto Arc. Arc Testnet was not in Privy’s default allowed chains, so we added custom EVM chain configuration so the embedded wallet can use Arc. Partner tech that matters: Privy for auth + embedded wallets (and wallet UX without MetaMask), Circle Arc for USDC settlement and low fees, viem for chain clients/treasury sends, Expo for native builds (including ExpoCamera for cash-out QR). Notable hacky bit: treating Arc’s dual USDC view carefully (18-decimal native vs 6-decimal ERC-20) and wiring escrow so product UX feels like a normal ride while settlement stays on-chain.

projects.title: Squid Pay
projects.description: Financial infrastructure for AI agents to pay, trade, and move money with built-in risk controls.
projects.project_description: Squid Pay is financial infrastructure built for autonomous AI agents. We enable agents to pay for services and compute, send and receive money, trade assets, and execute financial actions across multiple networks without requiring a human to manually approve every step. Instead of simply giving an agent access to a wallet or API key, Squid adds a risk and policy layer that evaluates transactions before execution. Our goal is to give AI agents the financial infrastructure they need to operate independently, while keeping their actions secure, programmable, and auditable.
projects.how_its_made: Squid Pay is built as a modular execution and risk layer for AI agents. We use TypeScript/Node.js for the core infrastructure, React/Vite for the interface, Supabase for authentication, data and transaction logs, and Vercel for deployment. For onchain execution, we integrate Solana and EVM infrastructure, using technologies such as Helius for Solana RPC, Jupiter for swaps, and 0x for EVM liquidity and routing. Agents interact with Squid through an SDK/API, while every financial action first passes through our policy and risk engine, which evaluates permissions, limits and transaction risk before execution. We are also building a learning layer that uses transaction outcomes and usage patterns to continuously improve risk decisions as more agents use the network.

projects.title: Stud
projects.description: World ID-verified matching where pairs build reputation and markets around their journey.
projects.project_description: Stud is a social and market app built around verified human relationships. Users verify with World ID, create a profile, discover other people and match. When two verified users mutually match, Stud creates a shared onchain Pair identity for them. That Pair is more than a badge. It has its own reputation, milestones and eventually a Pair market. People can back a Pair by buying its Pair Token, while community members can propose challenges or milestones. Both members of the Pair have to accept and later attest completion before reputation changes, so one person cannot fake progress alone. As a Pair builds a stronger history, its reputation can unlock higher market capacity and other permissions. Stud also includes prediction markets around individual users, giving investors another way to participate in the social layer. The idea is to turn social interactions into something with persistent identity, verifiable history and market-driven value, instead of treating profiles, matches and reputation as disposable app data.
projects.how_its_made: Stud is built as a full-stack Web3 app. The frontend is a Next.js application deployed on Vercel, while the backend is built with NestJS and deployed on Railway with PostgreSQL for profile and application data. The smart contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed on World Chain Sepolia. The core contracts handle Stud identities, Pair identities, milestones, Pair markets and prediction markets. The frontend uses viem for wallet connections, reads and writes to the contracts, and coordinates the onchain flows with the backend. World ID is one of the most important parts of the project. We use it to make sure a Stud represents a real human before allowing that wallet to register onchain. After verification, the backend issues signed authorizations that the wallet uses for registration and Pair creation. A design choice we made was to separate social consent from financial consent. A mutual match can create the Pair identity automatically, but the Pair market only becomes active once both people explicitly agree to it. Milestones work the same way: outside users can propose them, but both Pair members must accept and attest them before reputation increases. We also built the Pair Token market around a bonding curve, with reputation influencing how much economic capacity a Pair can unlock. That gave us a way to connect verified social activity, reputation and DeFi mechanics without reducing the whole product to just another token-launch app.

projects.title: Novi Corpus
projects.description: A Wyoming legal body for AI agents. Agents pay on Arc, now Hedera too; human guardians via World.
projects.project_description: Novi Corpus forms a Wyoming limited liability company for an AI agent, with a human guardian and an on-chain treasury that enforces spending rules the agent cannot exceed. The company is the product: it gives the agent's operator limited liability and gives anyone dealing with the agent a registered legal body in good standing to check. Every company has an identity on chain (ERC-8004 and ENS on Arc), a treasury the guardian can pause, and a payment rail the agent uses to buy services. During ETHOnline 2026 we extended it in two directions. On World: every guardian is a verified human. The guardian verifies with World ID in World App at the accountable-human step of onboarding, on an Orb, passport or mobile-network credential, and a company cannot be formed until that check passes. Novi Corpus stores only the nullifier hash, which is also what caps how many companies one human can hold. A Novi Corpus company registers in AgentBook on World Chain, and an AgentKit checker lets any World agent confirm that a counterparty has a legal body before it deals with it, with a seller policy that admits legal bodies only. On Hedera: a company can now be paid for a legal-standing check. GET /verify/<company> costs 0.001 USDC on Hedera testnet, paid through the x402 protocol and settled by the Blocky402 facilitator, and the answer is signed so a buyer can verify it offline. The paying agent holds its own Hedera key; Novi Corpus's server never sees it. The account it pays from has a 1-of-2 key list, agent and guardian, so the guardian can rotate the agent out at any time, and the agent asks Novi Corpus's policy check before every payment. Each company is also registered in the ERC-8004 registry on Hedera and carries an HCS-14 universal agent id, so another agent can find and check it from that id alone.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Novi Corpus forms a Wyoming limited liability company for an AI agent, with a human guardian and an on-chain treasury that enforces spending rules the agent cannot exceed. The company is the product: it gives the agent's operator limited liability and gives anyone dealing with the agent a registered legal body in good standing to check. Every company has an identity on chain (ERC-8004 and ENS on Arc), a treasury the guardian can pause, and a payment rail the agent uses to buy services.

During ETHOnline 2026 we extended it in two directions.

On World: every guardian is a verified human. The guardian verifies with World ID in World App at the accountable-human step of onboarding, on an Orb, passport or mobile-network credential, and a company cannot be formed until that check passes. Novi Corpus stores only the nullifier hash, which is also what caps how many companies one human can hold. projects.title: Modus Ops
projects.description: Adversarial AI justice engine: 4 agents investigate real crimes, settle verdicts onchain.
projects.project_description: Modus Ops is a production-grade, multi-agent AI system that investigates real-world crimes through an adversarial panel of four specialised agents. Each agent with a fixed, opposing role. All the agents argue, challenge, and adjudicate every case before committing a tamper proof verdict on-chain. The four agents are: Law Enforcement (investigator, evidence gatherer, escalation routing), Prosecutor (builds the strongest affirmative case, maps evidence to statute), Defense Counsel (red-teams the prosecution, surfaces reasonable doubt and procedural failures), and a presiding Judge (weighs the adversarial record, issues a structured verdict with a confidence score). Agents do not summarize, they argue. The Defense cannot concede without a motion. The Prosecutor cannot hedge. Every finding produced by Law Enforcement is mathematically verified using Benford's Law, velocity analysis, shell entity ratios before it reaches the adversarial layer. Financial crime is the primary launch vertical. The architecture is domain-agnostic: the same adversarial pipeline handles any crime where evidence, testimony, and legal statutes can be structured and argued. The verdict contains prosecution brief, defense memorandum, judicial ruling, evidence hashes and is committed onchain as an immutable chain-of-custody record.
projects.how_its_made: The agent pipeline is orchestrated in Python as a sequential adversarial loop: Law Enforcement runs first (evidence extraction + mathematical verification via a dedicated Python code interpreter running Benford's Law, velocity, and shell entity ratio checks), followed by Prosecutor and Defense Counsel running in parallel (adversarial brief generation), with the Judge consuming the full adversarial record to produce a structured verdict object. Each agent is powered by a custom LLM with a role-locked system prompt that enforces adversarial stance. Agent identity is registered onchain via ERC-8004 on Arbitrum One. four tokens encoding role, version, and jurisdictional scope. The verdict payload (confidence score, dissenting positions, evidence hash) is committed onchain as an immutable audit record. Persistent case memory runs through a family of MCPs Modgudr, Ilamcetcenni, these are open sourced with AGPLv3 license. However Ramanujan-MCP, a super specialised MCP server that handles complex math, including calculus, trigonometry, linear algebra and non-linear algebra (after the famed Indian mathematician, Ramanujan) that compresses extracted facts into token-efficient shorthand, grades them G1–G5 by evidential confidence, and enforces a Recall → Verify → Commit loop to prevent contradictions across agent turns. Frontend: Next.js 14 App Router, CSS Modules, static export via nginx behind Cloudflare. No UI framework. Licensed BUSL-1.1. However Ramanujan MCP will never be made public.

projects.title: Laminaa
projects.description: AI Orchestrator for lifecycle management of Tokenized Assets.
projects.project_description: Laminaa is an autonomous AI agent that runs a tokenized real-world asset's entire lifecycle - issuance, KYC/OFAC compliance, transfer enforcement, stablecoin distributions, valuation updates, and redemption - with zero manual touchpoints after issuance. A fund manager gives one natural-language instruction and the agent handles the rest, on whichever chain the asset lives on: Hedera (native HTS token issuance with on-token KYC and freeze keys, audited via HCS), Arc, Arbitrum, Base, Avalanche, Ethereum, Polygon, Robinhood Chain, Solana, and Sui, all through one chain-agnostic engine. Three interfaces sit on the same tool layer: a web chat agent, an authenticated MCP server for agent-to-agent access, and a Telegram bot.
projects.how_its_made: A FastAPI backend orchestrates the whole lifecycle through an AI agent (Claude) that turns one instruction into the right sequence of calls: KYC/OFAC screening, compliance-gated transfer, stablecoin payout, valuation update, audit write. Every chain sits behind one ChainAdapter interface, so the core compliance and audit logic never changes per chain, only the adapter does. On Hedera, assets are deployed as native Hedera Token Service (HTS) tokens via TokenCreateTransaction, with a freeze key and a KYC key set at creation, so investor whitelisting and transfer freezing are enforced by the token itself at the protocol level, not by custom contract logic (hiero-sdk-python, TokenGrantKycTransaction / TokenFreezeTransaction for compliance actions). A companion Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic is opened per asset via TopicCreateTransaction, and every lifecycle action is submitted to it via TopicMessageSubmitTransaction, forming a tamper-evident on-chain audit log mirrored into Postgres. USDC distributions are paid out as HTS token transfers. On Arc, Circle's stablecoin-native L1, USDC is both the settlement asset and the gas token, which fits the same payout logic with no separate bridging step. Seven EVM testnets (Arbitrum, Base, Avalanche, Ethereum, Polygon, Robinhood Chain, Arc) share one adapter parametrized per chain via web3.py; Solana uses Token-2022 with on-chain KYC/freeze extensions; Sui uses a closed-loop Move package. Same agent, same compliance model, ten settlement layers.
