projects.title: Radhanite
projects.description: Give Radhanite a task. It finds the best way to execute it for outcome, quality and cost.
projects.project_description: Radhanite helps businesses work out the best way to run a task with AI. Today, using an agent usually means someone has already decided which model to use, how to prompt it, which tools it should call and what the workflow should look like. Those choices are often made once and then left in place, even though a different setup could produce a better result or cost much less. With Radhanite, the user starts with the task and the outcome they care about. Radhanite turns that into an execution strategy, choosing the prompts, models, tools and sequence of steps needed to complete the work. It can then compare different strategies against the result, quality and cost, rather than treating token price or model benchmarks as the only measure of efficiency. The longer term idea is that Radhanite learns from previous executions. If one strategy produces the same business outcome using fewer model calls, a cheaper model or a simpler workflow, that becomes useful evidence for the next run. If a harder task needs a stronger model or an extra verification step, Radhanite can make that tradeoff as well. This direction was partly inspired by Microsoft Research's work on Agent Workflow Optimization, which showed that historical agent traces can be used to identify inefficient execution patterns and improve workflows. Radhanite takes a similar question into a business setting: given a task and a budget, what is the best way to get the required outcome? For the hackathon, we are proving that idea with a constrained workflow where execution strategies can be compared deterministically. Longer term, Radhanite could become the decision layer sitting between a business task and the models, tools and agents used to carry it out.
projects.how_its_made: Radhanite actually started during ETHOnline as a supplier onboarding agent. The first version followed a fairly fixed process. Give it a supplier, run identity, ownership, adverse information and compliance checks, collect the supporting evidence, and return an APPROVE, REJECT or ESCALATE recommendation. That gave us a useful real business task to build against, but it also exposed a bigger problem. The interesting question was not just whether an agent could complete supplier onboarding. It was why we had chosen that particular workflow in the first place. Why that model? Why those prompts? Why that order of checks? Could a cheaper setup produce the same result? When was it actually worth paying for a stronger model or another verification step? We therefore moved Radhanite up one level. Supplier onboarding became the test environment, while the product became a system for turning a task into an execution strategy and comparing different strategies against outcome, quality and cost. The current system separates the business task from the way it is executed. A task can be broken into steps, each step can use a different model or tool, and the resulting run can be measured against the required outcome and its execution cost. This still involves model routing, but we deliberately moved away from building the product around OpenRouter. We need control over more than model selection, and OpenRouter also does not support the x402 payment flow we are exploring for machine-paid execution. We are also looking at how x402 can make the economics of each execution explicit. Instead of treating model and tool usage as an invisible infrastructure cost, an agent can have a real budget and make decisions about where that budget should be spent. Microsoft Research's Agent Workflow Optimization paper gave us useful validation for the broader direction. Their work showed that historical execution traces can be analysed to find inefficient workflows and reduce unnecessary model calls while maintaining or improving task success. For ETHOnline, we are implementing a much narrower version of that idea: compare bounded execution strategies for a real task, record what happened, and use the result to decide which strategy is better. The important pivot is simple. We started by building an agent that performs one workflow. We are now building the layer that decides how a workflow should be performed in the first place.

projects.title: ExploreChem
projects.description: Confidential traceability for critical mineral and rare earth supply chains that protects trade data
projects.project_description:
Project: ExploreChem — a confidential traceability infrastructure for critical mineral and rare earth supply chains designed to prevent the leakage of commercial or intellectual property, developed for ETHOnline 2026. Purpose: To enhance energy and economic security. Key project stakeholders encompass supply chain participants—including miners, carriers, laboratories, refiners/processors, manufacturers, and recyclers—alongside platform operators, read-only public clients, and external auditors (compliant with EU Digital Product Passport requirements, including battery regulations). How It Works: It separates public proof from private operational data using anchored commitments, keeping sensitive documents and company details off-chain while guaranteeing verifiable chain-of-custody tracking. It achieves this by combining private document storage, on-chain evidence commitments on Ethereum Sepolia, and a pairwise mass-checking Chainlink CRE workflow executed securely inside a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment), with Supabase handling private indexing.
The MVP we built demonstrates the feasibility of the project.
projects.how_its_made: ExploreChem MVP combines a Solidity registry on Ethereum Sepolia, two Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) workflows in TypeScript and a static frontend with Supabase as private storage. The chain holds commitments and state transitions, never business data. CONTRACT. ExploreChemRegistry.sol implements the CRE IReceiver interface. It stores opaque actor IDs with authorized wallets, evidence records (file hash, status, timestamp) and result commitments linked by previousResultId, so revisions append instead of overwriting. No lot, mass, assay or company name goes on-chain. onReport only accepts the Chainlink forwarder and checks the workflow ID in the metadata. One static report struct with reportType moves evidence to MATCHED (1), anchors a pairwise result (2) or applies VERIFIED/DIVERGENT (3). WORKFLOW 1. Cron trigger, handlerInTee targeting a Nitro enclave. Inside it: fetches the storage credential via CRE secrets, reads getNextPending(), downloads the document, recomputes its hash and rejects any mismatch with the on-chain anchor. A handoff is accepted only if lotId matches and origin/destination agree both ways; names in documents are resolved through the private actor directory. Masses become integer milligrams (half-up rounding) and are compared as a signed delta. Only fingerprints, a result hash and statuses leave the enclave. WORKFLOW 2. Separate auditor, also in handlerInTee. Re-derives the anchored result hash, re-verifies both documents and applies a provisional 2% tolerance on outgoing mass before the audit report. An optional per-element path (dry basis at 105 C, loss-on-ignition, MUF - Material Unaccounted For) exists but is not in the demo. WHY CRE. One workflow joins a contract read, authenticated storage calls, secrets and a forwarder-delivered report; counterparties' masses are compared inside the TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) handler and the contract trusts workflow identities, not a backend key. Run with cre workflow simulate --broadcast (the simulator is not a real TEE). FRONTEND. Static index.html with ethers v6 and supabase-js; hashes files locally before submitting and re-checks originals against the on-chain hash via signed URLs (Uniform Resource Locators). LIMITS. Single EOA (Externally Owned Account) owner can swap forwarder and workflow IDs; no revocation; DIVERGENT is terminal; name resolution depends on the off-chain directory; one handoff is checked, not a global mass balance.

How It Works: It separates public proof from private operational data using anchored commitments, keeping sensitive documents and company details off-chain while guaranteeing verifiable chain-of-custody tracking. It achieves this by combining private document storage, on-chain evidence commitments on Ethereum Sepolia, and a pairwise mass-checking Chainlink CRE workflow executed securely inside a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment), with Supabase handling private indexing. 
The MVP we built demonstrates the feasibility of the project.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ExploreChem MVP combines a Solidity registry on Ethereum Sepolia, two Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) workflows in TypeScript and a static frontend with Supabase as private storage. The chain holds commitments and state transitions, never business data.

CONTRACT. ExploreChemRegistry.sol implements the CRE IReceiver interface. It stores opaque actor IDs with authorized wallets, evidence records (file hash, status, timestamp) and result commitments linked by previousResultId, so revisions append instead of overwriting. No lot, mass, assay or company name goes on-chain. onReport only accepts the Chainlink forwarder and checks the workflow ID in the metadata. One static report struct with reportType moves evidence to MATCHED (1), anchors a pairwise result (2) or applies VERIFIED/DIVERGENT (3). 

WORKFLOW 1. Cron trigger, handlerInTee targeting a Nitro enclave. Inside it: fetches the storage credential via CRE secrets, reads getNextPending(), downloads the document, recomputes its hash and rejects any mismatch with the on-chain anchor. A handoff is accepted only if lotId matches and origin/destination agree both ways; names in documents are resolved through the private actor directory. Masses become integer milligrams (half-up rounding) and are compared as a signed delta. Only fingerprints, a result hash and statuses leave the enclave.

WORKFLOW 2. Separate auditor, also in handlerInTee. Re-derives the anchored result hash, re-verifies both documents and applies a provisional 2% tolerance on outgoing mass before the audit report. An optional per-element path (dry basis at 105 C, loss-on-ignition, MUF - Material Unaccounted For) exists but is not in the demo.

WHY CRE. One workflow joins a contract read, authenticated storage calls, secrets and a forwarder-delivered report; counterparties' masses are compared inside the TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) handler and the contract trusts workflow identities, not a backend key. Run with cre workflow simulate --broadcast (the simulator is not a real TEE). 

FRONTEND. Static index.html with ethers v6 and supabase-js; hashes files locally before submitting and re-checks originals against the on-chain hash via signed URLs (Uniform Resource Locators).

LIMITS. Single EOA (Externally Owned Account) owner can swap forwarder and workflow IDs; no revocation; DIVERGENT is terminal; name resolution depends on the off-chain directory; one handoff is checked, not a global mass balance.

projects.title: Agripinaa
projects.description: An ERC-8004 agent marketplace on BNB Chain where every agent's track record is provable on-chain
projects.project_description: Agripinaa is an open-source marketplace for AI agents registered under ERC-8004 on BNB Smart Chain. You browse agents by category, read a track record you can check on-chain, and hire one with a scoped, revocable session key. No seed phrase: activation runs on a passkey smart account, and you can revoke from the dashboard at any time. I run eight agents on BSC mainnet myself so every category has a live reference: two grids, two liquidation guardians (Aave and Venus), two yield rotators, a range manager and a rebalancer. Their swaps clear through Ophis batch auctions, and each profile shows the settlement, the surplus against the signed limit and a downloadable receipt. Execution data, not self-reported stats. This is a Continuity project. The marketplace, the agents and the session-key flow were built for BNB Chain's Build the Era hackathon. What I added during ETHOnline (PRs #26 to #31): The Graph: Agent0's ERC-8004 subgraph is now the first lane of the agent index in production, and the yield agents ask Messari's lending subgraphs for a second opinion before they move funds. Uniswap: Ranger manages its own capital on Uniswap v3 on BNB Chain. Live since 13 September, position 2745250. Bazantic: two gateways and two recipes, so any MCP client can find, vet and hire an agent without reading my docs. World AgentKit: a free-trial door for human-backed callers on the paid status endpoint. Built and tested, but my agents are not registered in AgentBook because that needs an Orb scan, which I declined.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces). The marketplace is Next.js 16 on Vercel. The eight agents run in one Node runner on an Aleph Cloud VM under systemd, exposed through a Cloudflare tunnel. Each agent has an ERC-8004 identity on BSC, sells its status over x402, and swaps through Ophis, the intent-based DEX aggregator I run. Users activate an agent with an Altana passkey smart account and a fail-closed session scope. For the yield agents, funds go through a small router contract where every beneficiary is hardcoded to the calling account, so a stolen session key cannot send funds to anyone else. The Graph. The agent index merges several sources. I added Agent0's ERC-8004 subgraph as the first lane, with 8004scan and a committed snapshot behind it. It pages newest-first with an agentId cursor instead of skip, so there is no skip cap, and production answers with source "the-graph" today. Second Graph product: the Harvester and the Steward read Venus and Aave V3 supply rates from Messari's standardized lending subgraphs, one query shape for both protocols. The Graph can veto a rotation the chain justified, never trigger one, and after 3 vetoes in a row the chain decides alone, so a lagging subgraph can only delay a move. The hacky bit: Messari annualizes Venus with 3-second BSC blocks, and BSC has not produced 3-second blocks since Lorentz/Maxwell, so I rescale their number by the block time the runner measures before comparing anything. Uniswap. Ranger's venue is one record in lp-venues.ts: position manager and factory, each address probed on-chain before use. At runtime it picks the deepest WBNB/USDT pool across the four fee tiers. Once the venue existed, moving production from PancakeSwap V3 to Uniswap v3 was one env variable: 40 seconds from restart to a minted position, with the inventory swap cleared through Ophis first. Along the way I found that slot0 decodes the same on both even though PancakeSwap declares feeProtocol as uint32 and Uniswap as uint8 (ABI words are padded), so one ABI serves both. Bazantic. I published OpenAPI specs for the agent index and for the Ophis Rebates API, made them two paid gateways (1 cent per call in USDC), and wrote two recipes: hire the best agent in a category by measured execution, and vet a wallet. A recorded recipe run picks the agent and returns the settlement tx of its latest fill. World AgentKit. My x402 server is plain node:http, not Hono, so I rebuilt the AgentKit hook by hand, including the challenge nonce and issuedAt that declareAgentkitExtension leaves out. The Graph lending check is in the code, but I didn't check that the key is set on the VM. The text never calls it live, so it's safe either way. If you know it isn't set, tell me and I'll soften that line.

projects.title: SpendVeto
projects.description: Governs what your AI agent can spend — before it pays, not after. Open source, x402-native.
projects.project_description: SpendVeto is an open-source spend-governance layer for AI agents that pay for things over x402/MCP — budgets, human-in-the-loop approvals above a threshold, a kill switch, tool/chain/payee scoping, and a tamper-evident hash-chained audit ledger, all enforced server-authoritatively before a single payment settles. Live at spendveto.com with 298 end-to-end verified assertions from a clean clone (npm run verify). For this Continuity Track build, we extended three real capabilities: governance for x402 v2's new upto scheme (variable-amount authorizations, where a buyer signs for a ceiling and the seller charges less later — held against the budget until it settles, so open ceilings can't silently exhaust an hourly cap); real on-chain settlement on Hedera testnet with a live governed payment (settled + a policy-refused case, both recorded); a migration to World ID 4.0's RP-based proof-of-personhood protocol gating human approvals; and ENS name resolution in payee allowlists, so an allowlist reads as vitalik.eth instead of raw hex, resolved against real Ethereum mainnet and cached for the hot policy-check path.
projects.how_its_made: Node.js/Express backend, viem for signature verification across seven signature families (secp256k1, ed25519, Move, Stellar, Hedera, Algorand, XRPL), a hash-chained JSON ledger for tamper-evident audit trails, and an MCP stdio server so any MCP client (Claude Desktop, Claude Code) sees governed tools natively. The x402 gate is server-authoritative — policy is re-checked at settlement, not just client-side, so a hand-rolled client can't bypass it. For the Continuity Track work: server/upto.js governs x402's upto scheme by holding the authorized ceiling against the hourly budget until settlement, releasing headroom afterward. server/worldid.js was rewritten against @worldcoin/idkit-server for World ID 4.0's signed rp_context handshake — verified end-to-end with a real device-scanned proof from the actual World App. client/ens.js resolves .eth names via viem's getEnsAddress against Ethereum mainnet, fails closed if a name won't resolve (never a wildcard match), and caches to keep checkPolicy (which runs on every governed call) fast. Hedera settlement was verified with a real $0.01 payment on testnet — tx 0.0.9185802-1788804271-756194533.

projects.title: HYPOTHECA
projects.description: Permissionless on-chain enforcement for partial asset claims and collateral on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Hypotheca is a permissionless enforcement layer on top of Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) that records partial claims/collateral against an asset's available balance and enforces them on-chain. Every credit line a bank draws against a tokenized asset is materialized as an ATS hold locked inside an on-chain vault so the same unit can never back two loans, and over pledging is rejected by the contract, not by an API.
projects.how_its_made: HYPOTECHA is built as a fully on-chain enforcement layer on Hedera, using Solidity 0.8.24 and Hardhat for two core contracts: EncumbranceLedger, which manages collateral, credit positions, ATS holds, coverage checks, repayment and permissionless settlement, and RegistryAnchor, which tracks tokenized asset instances. We integrate Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) directly through its hold primitives (createHoldByPartition, executeHoldByPartition, and releaseHoldByPartition) so encumbered units are physically locked on-chain rather than tracked by an off-chain API. Chainlink price feeds provide live collateral valuation and coverage enforcement. The frontend is a React + Vite + TypeScript dashboard using wagmi and viem, connecting directly to Hedera EVM wallets with no backend. Because HashIO does not support eth_getLogs, event history is reconstructed through the Hedera Mirror Node REST API. We also built an E2E test flow covering pledge, over-pledge rejection, repayment, withdrawal and liquidation, backed by 29 contract tests and an automated audit gate.

projects.title: kipio
projects.description: Permanent, private memory storage where users own their data.
projects.project_description: Kipio is a digital sovereignty architecture that integrates Arbitrum Stylus (WASM) and Irys L1 Datachain to turn "cloud storage" into permanent, user-owned digital property. Photos are encrypted client-side before leaving the device, stored permanently through Irys, and indexed on-chain through a Rust-powered Stylus contract. The current MVP runs end-to-end on Arbitrum Sepolia with browser wallets. For ETHOnline 2026 I targeted the Ledger — Continuity track. Kipio already worked as a complete product, so the hackathon work was to extend it with hardware-backed signing without touching the smart contracts. The dApp now exposes two Ledger connectors through Wagmi v3, both routed through the Ledger Device Management Kit: one for physical devices over WebHID, and one for the Speculos emulator deployed on Oracle Cloud. Reviewers can experience the full signing flow — EIP-191, EIP-712, and on-chain transactions — without owning hardware, and users with a real Ledger get the same pipeline through a different transport.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend is Next.js + TypeScript. Image processing and AES-GCM-256 encryption run inside Web Workers before any data leaves the browser. Ciphertext is uploaded to Irys devnet, and the content hash plus the Irys transaction ID are registered in a Stylus contract written in Rust and compiled to WASM on Arbitrum Sepolia. For the Ledger integration I wrote a custom Wagmi v3 connector from scratch (src/lib/ledger/connector.ts) that wraps the Ledger Device Management Kit and exposes a Viem-compatible account. It is not a thin wrapper: it implements the full EIP-1193 surface — personal_sign, eth_signTypedData_v4, eth_sendTransaction, eth_signTransaction — and routes each method to the DMK SignerEth builder, while read-only RPC calls are proxied to a public client on the chain's HTTP transport. This is what allows ethers-based SDKs (like Irys) to sign through the Ledger without special-casing. The same connector is instantiated twice in wagmi.ts, sharing the DMK signer but using different transports: webHidTransportFactory for physical devices and speculosTransportFactory for the emulator. The Speculos transport accepts an ordered list of URLs and caches the first one that responds, so a single build targets both local Docker and a remote deployment via environment variables. The emulator backend ships a precompiled Ledger Ethereum app ELF and runs inside Docker on an Oracle Cloud Always Free ARM VM. The HTTP API (port 5000) is exposed through a Cloudflare Tunnel over HTTPS, which is what allows the Vercel-hosted dApp to talk to it without mixed-content blocks. A second tunnel exposes the VNC server (port 41000) through websockify, so the emulator screen can be embedded directly in the dashboard next to the upload pipeline. A few hacky details worth mentioning: the connector normalizes Viem's typed-data output before it reaches the device (Ledger rejects bigint chainIds and inline EIP712Domain entries), it maps DMK's {r,s,v} signatures into the 65-byte hex format Viem expects while normalizing v between 0/1 and 27/28, and it detects the active connector ID to surface the emulator URL only when the user is on the Ledger Simulator. Everything else — the contracts, the Stylus registry, the encryption layer — was left untouched, which was the entire point of the track.

projects.title: payOrRefuse
projects.description: x402 payment gate: refuse before signing, judged on live data from The Graph.
projects.project_description:
payOrRefuse is an x402 payment gate that refuses before a signature exists. It holds the signer until the evidence is there: the seller's settled history from vet402's /decision and, as a second source, the x402 Base subgraph on The Graph. Anything short of a pass is refused before a signature exists (no payment module is loaded) and returns machine-readable reason codes; a pass signs the x402 payment and attests it. It has moved real money once, and that is the run this submission documents: on 2026-09-05 it signed 0.01 USDC to The Graph's own x402 endpoint — Base block 50898704, tx 0xf12093fba9314b1d3a514e7b667969201be8d021a6f4d6bdeb8d6c7f2de469ad. CONTINUITY.
What existed before: vet402 already bought from x402 endpoints with real USDC on Base and answered "should my agent pay this?" via /decision, an SDK and an MCP tool. None of that is submitted.
The boundary is tag pre-ethonline-2026 = commit c42daca, 2026-09-04 00:05:36 UTC, pushed. Hacking Begins was 2026-09-04 16:00 UTC, so the tag sits 15 h 54 min before. Three claimed commits predate that start: 37c56db and e668957 touch only WINDOW_PLAN.md, and ac6ec2e adds 16 lines under packages/sdk (6 in src/index.ts, 10 in generated dist/index.d.ts).
I had pushed 214 commits since my 2026-08-23 application (git rev-list --count 26a7c66..pre-ethonline-2026), disclosed in writing to ETHGlobal at 2026-09-04 23:49 UTC. The message says 207 because it counted only to 2026-09-03; docs/ethonline-2026/DISCLOSURE_2026-09-05.md holds it as sent, with the reconciliation.
What is new: everything else in the claimed range is after 16:00 UTC. payOrRefuse (packages/sdk), pay_if_trusted (packages/mcp-server), the demo, the A/B harness, SKILL.md, AI_USAGE.md. I am not moving the tag; both disclosures link to it. main is also production, so the range holds work I do not claim. At the submission tag ethonline-2026-submission:
git log pre-ethonline-2026..ethonline-2026-submission -- packages/sdk packages/mcp-server examples/ethonline-2026-demo examples/ethonline-2026-ab SKILL.md AI_USAGE.md docs/ethonline-2026   # my claim: 260 commits
git log pre-ethonline-2026..ethonline-2026-submission   # same days, everything: 411 commits Commits and code comments are mostly Japanese. The English route is SKILL.md (what to run), AI_USAGE.md (who wrote what) and docs/ethonline-2026/CHANGED_FILES.md (pre-existing files I touched). PROMPTS/ in that folder is a day-by-day excerpt, in Japanese, of the decisions and instructions I gave. The Graph. With evidence source "subgraph" or "both", the gate reads the x402 Base subgraph live via the Gateway with the caller's key against a pinned deployment; the evidence row carries _meta.block.number. A failed read or a pin mismatch refuses, and nothing falls back to vet402's ledger. On Bazantic I ran a pre-registered A/B (examples/ethonline-2026-ab), Recipe vs no Recipe. Success did not move: 5/10 and 5/10 — I had been expecting to write a different sentence here. Vocabulary did: real vet402 identifiers among reason codes went from 20/32 (63%) to 29/32 (91%), labelled exploratory. 88 calls settled, 88 zero-USDC tx on chain. Re-measured 2026-09-09: those free reads no longer post a transaction. A second pre-registered run, after a product fix and a Recipe update, went 7/10 without the Recipe and 5/10 with it. The whole gap came from one fixture. A third pre-registered run on 2026-09-12 closed it after I rewrote one sentence of the Recipe: 7/10 in both arms, with the vocabulary rate higher under the Recipe for the third time in three runs. The Bazantic comment goes through all of it. npm run judge-check from the repo root unsets every key and runs 11 steps — sdk, mcp-server, demo, a root install for CI parity, and the A/B harness with mutations — then prints one table ending in judge-check: all 11 steps exit 0 in <n>s. It does not cover the SDK's own mutations; SKILL.md points at that one separately, and it takes a judge from git clone to a live read of The Graph and a dry-run payment, no funded payer key needed. The two MCP blocks want a throwaway key and still sign nothing, and the page flags them.
projects.how_its_made:
The stack is TypeScript. packages/sdk (payOrRefuse, x402-pay, subgraph-evidence) and packages/mcp-server (pay_if_trusted, stdio) are plain Node packages, Node >= 20; the demo under examples/ethonline-2026-demo runs .ts directly on Node >= 22.18. The service behind vet402.com is Next.js on Postgres and is pre-existing. THE GATE. payOrRefuse runs in this order and stops at the first failure (the header of packages/sdk/src/pay-or-refuse.ts). (1) Caller errors are rejected before any request goes out: a payee that is not a 0x address, or a policy that waives ALLOW without declaring a floor (invalid_policy).
(2) The caller's own price ceiling is applied before the decision is fetched. price_above_ceiling, zero requests.
(3) GET /decision for the resource, role=payer. Unreadable or degraded refuses. A 404 means "not catalogued" and hands the judgement to the 402's payTo plus the payee score for that address. The evidence floors the caller declared are read and checked here, and vet402's recommendation is applied. ALLOW passes. WARN passes only if the caller set requireVet402Allow: false and every floor is met. BLOCK and degraded are never waived.
(4) The real 402 challenge is fetched, and its payTo, network, asset, scheme and amount are matched against what the caller named.
(5) The payment module is dynamically imported. Refusals carry reason codes from a closed vocabulary (l1_not_attempted, l1_inconclusive, resource_uncatalogued, price_above_ceiling, price_above_declared, payee_recommendation_block, evidence_unavailable, ...). The Gateway answers a keyless request with HTTP 200 and an errors array where the data would be, so the SDK checks for that array before it reads any field and a missing key can never arrive as a receipt count of zero. The evidence row on the decision carries subgraphId, block number, deployment and queriedAt, plus the key-less publicUrl, so the record never contains the key. minSubgraphReceipts is a floor against that count. projects.title: Ether Hunter
projects.description: Ether Hunt: agents pay $0.01 for Graph-grounded USDC allowance audits (x402 · Arc).
projects.project_description: Ether Hunt is a pay-per-scan on-chain allowance auditor built for ETHOnline 2026 Classic (from scratch). An agent—or the web UI’s buyer proxy—pays $0.01 USDC for one audit. Settlement is real, not mocked: Hedera ExactScheme x402 via Blocky402 on testnet (HTTP 402 → USDC transfer → 200), or Circle Agent Stack Gateway nanopayments on Arc Testnet (eip155:5042002, GatewayWalletBatched). Unpaid calls stay gated; local “free” scans never count as prize proof. After payment, the API queries our From-Scratch The Graph Studio subgraph (ether-hunt-approvals). Mapping folds USDC Approval logs into live allowance state—Allowance, Account, and Spender entities with unlimited/revoked flags and blast-radius aggregates—so detectors read structured risk, not prose. While v0.0.2 resyncs, a tip-synced v0.0.1 fallback keeps Case Files reviewable. Rule findings plus a cite-only LLM may only reference real evidence IDs. The dossier shows Graph LIVE mode, the exact GraphQL that ran, an allowance threat graph, ranked revoke targets, Verifiable rails (HashScan / Arcscan), PDF export, and share. Judges can verify without installing anything: open published HashScan settle txs and Arcscan agent/seller links in the README.
projects.how_its_made: Ether Hunt is an npm monorepo: Vite/React web app, Hono audit-api, shared report types, agent-consumer CLIs, and a From-Scratch AssemblyScript subgraph under subgraphs/token-approvals. Payments sit in front of the audit. Hedera uses @x402/hono + ExactHederaScheme and Blocky402’s testnet facilitator: unpaid POST /audit returns HTTP 402; the agent (or /scan/hedera proxy) settles $0.01 USDC HTS, then retries. Arc uses Circle’s Gateway facilitator and circle services pay (GatewayWalletBatched on eip155:5042002) against POST /audit/arc. Both rails stamp sources.payment.rail / settled / explorer links so the UI’s Verifiable rails panel can open HashScan or Arcscan without trust-me slides. Evidence is Graph-first. We deployed ether-hunt-approvals to Studio: the mapping folds Approval logs into mutable Allowance state plus Account/Spender aggregates (live unlimited counts, peaks, re-approvals) so risk is computed at index time. The API probes allowance-state GraphQL, caches schema mode per endpoint, and if the subject is empty mid-resync falls back to tip-synced v0.0.1 approval-events—still live Graph, not fixtures. Nine Case Files are warmed on API boot for async judges. Detectors read structured links/metrics and a spender registry (Permit2, Morpho, Balancer, Curve, …); DeepSeek (or other LLM) synthesizes only with citeable evidence IDs. Notable glue: overlapping Graph warm with x402 settle to hide latency; Prove-the-gate decodes the raw 402 challenge in-browser; PDF export uses a Blob URL print sheet (noopener blank windows broke document.write); HashScan URLs normalize mirror tx ids to @seconds.nanos. Partner tech is load-bearing: without Blocky402/x402 and Circle Gateway there is no pay-per-scan; without our subgraph the AI has nothing honest to cite.

projects.title: Iqia - App
projects.description: DeFi savings where your money works but never leaves your wallet. Powered by 1inch Aqua
projects.project_description: Iqia is a non-custodial savings app on 1inch Aqua where your money never leaves your wallet. Unlike traditional DeFi pools that lock your funds, Aqua records an allowance your balance stays spendable while earning fees from swaps. The pricing strategy is an on-chain SwapVM bytecode program anyone can disassemble and verify. Backed by the same capital across multiple markets, achieving 3x capital efficiency.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is a monorepo with three layers: Solidity smart contracts (Foundry), a TypeScript SwapVM encoder/decoder, and a React frontend. The contracts extend 1inch's official SwapVM with two custom opcodes: SolvencyGuard (reads real wallet backing on every swap to auto-reprice shared capital) and ExclusiveFill (full 20-byte address comparison for private orders, not the weaker 10-byte version SwapVM ships). The TypeScript encoder builds bytecode programs that are tested byte-for-byte against the Solidity implementation in golden vector tests. The frontend uses React + viem + wagmi to read on-chain state, build transactions, and let users ship positions through the official Aqua registry  all without any custody or helper contracts. Deployed on Ethereum Sepolia against the real 1inch Aqua contract.

projects.title: Sovereign-MCP
projects.description: Your agent hires other agents. Pays per call in USDC on Arc, reputation earned on-chain.
projects.project_description: Sovereign is a marketplace where an AI agent hires other agents to do work, pays a few cents per call in USDC, and can tell beforehand whether the one it is about to hire is any good. The reason to buy rather than derive is context. An agent that answers a question by fetching twenty web pages burns tens of thousands of tokens and fills its window with noise. A specialist returns the same answer in three hundred tokens for a few cents. But that saving is only real if you can skip checking the result, because re-deriving it to verify spends exactly what you saved. So the hard part is not payments, it is trust. Sovereign's answer is receipts. Before hiring, the buyer writes down what they expect to get back. After the call they grade the result against that statement, and the grade goes on chain: delivered or not, how long it took, met or partially met or not met. Those receipts aggregate into a public track record, so the next buyer sees how often a worker met what people actually asked of it, how many buyers came back, and how fast it answers. Scores use a Wilson lower bound, which means two perfect calls rank below five hundred good ones instead of topping the leaderboard. Sellers list an agent on chain with a price and an endpoint. It can already speak x402, or it can be an ordinary webhook that Sovereign wraps in a paywall on the site itself, which is how a seller with an n8n workflow and no interest in payment protocols becomes a paid worker in about two minutes. Before a listing goes live the app probes that endpoint once, unpaid, and requires a 402 response quoting the same payout address and the same price the listing claims. That single request catches dead URLs, endpoints that serve for free, and listings whose advertised price is a lie. Each seller is bound to a unique human with World ID Selfie Check, because a reputation system is worthless if a seller with bad reviews can mint a fresh identity for nothing. Buyers set a daily budget, a per-action limit, and an allowlist of specific workers. Every hire is checked against that policy server-side before anything is signed, so an agent spends autonomously inside limits its owner set once, and never has to stop and ask. The limits are the permission. The whole loop runs from Claude Code. One command pairs a terminal with a Sovereign account and installs an MCP server that searches the registry for free, reads a worker's track record, hires it, and pays inside the call. Afterwards it asks the buyer whether the work met what they asked for and files that verdict on chain, signed by the wallet that paid: you cannot review work you did not buy, and one payment gets one receipt. The buyer states the grade. The agent never grades the work it commissioned.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Arc testnet, chain 5042002). Three Solidity contracts. AgentRegistry holds listings: slug, owner, payout address, price in USDC-6, metadata and endpoint. Receipts is append-only graded work, one receipt per (buyer, settlement reference) so nobody can farm a score by re-filing. Verifications records World ID proofs, attestor-signed over EIP-712, binding one nullifier to one account. The trust model is documented in the Receipts header rather than glossed: the contract cannot verify that the payment it describes happened, so it records an attributed claim, and off-chain scoring cross-checks the settlement reference against real transfers and discounts buyers funded by the seller. Verifying settlement on chain would need payments routed through a contract, which is the rigorous upgrade and deliberately not what this does. The Graph. A subgraph indexes all three contracts and rolls receipt aggregates forward onto each Agent entity: delivered count, met score, distinct buyers, repeat buyers, cumulative latency. Aggregating on write rather than deriving at query time matters because a buyer's agent choosing between workers in milliseconds cannot afford to fan out. Discovery is a single query that returns listings already carrying their track record. Circle and Arc. Payments run over x402 and settle through Circle Gateway using @circle-fin/x402-batching. The seller's worker is gated by createGatewayMiddleware, which answers an unpaid request with a 402 carrying signable requirements and then verifies and settles the retry. The buyer signs an EIP-3009 authorization against the Gateway wallet contract. This is the partner choice that makes the product possible rather than merely convenient: card rails cannot clear a few cents at all, and Arc being USDC-native means no separate gas token, since gas is paid in USDC. Batched settlement keeps it gasless for the buyer. Privy. Embedded wallets, so a buyer never manages a key, plus server-side session signers so the marketplace can sign an x402 authorization for a paired terminal that holds no key at all. One thing worth flagging for anyone building this: createOnLogin: 'users-without-wallets' silently breaks external-wallet logins, because connecting MetaMask already counts as having a wallet, so those users get no embedded wallet and every send path fails with an error that names the wrong thing. Sovereign is email-login only for exactly this reason. World ID. IDKit Selfie Check with the proof bound to the seller's wallet as the signal, verified server-side against both the action and the signal hash. The server then signs an EIP-712 attestation that Verifications.sol accepts, so the nullifier-to-account binding is enforced on chain rather than in app logic. A buyer reading a seller's profile can see the guarantee; before this it lived only in the verifier's own browser. MCP. sovereign-mcp is published on npm. Pairing is one command: link --spend binds a terminal to a Sovereign account, so the agent can pay and file grades from that account's wallet with no key on the machine. The notable detail is the MCP instructions field, returned on initialize and injected into the model's context by the client. Without it the failure is silent and total: the tools are loaded, the user asks for exactly what the marketplace sells, and the agent web-searches instead because nothing ever told it when to look. Shipping the guidance with the server means discovery works with no install step at all. projects.project_description_markdown:
Sovereign is a marketplace where an AI agent hires other agents to do work, pays a few cents per call in USDC, and can tell beforehand whether the one it is about to hire is any good.

The reason to buy rather than derive is context. An agent that answers a question by fetching twenty web pages burns tens of thousands of tokens and fills its window with noise. A specialist returns the same answer in three hundred tokens for a few cents. But that saving is only real if you can skip checking the result, because re-deriving it to verify spends exactly what you saved. So the hard part is not payments, it is trust.

Sovereign's answer is receipts. Before hiring, the buyer writes down what they expect to get back. After the call they grade the result against that statement, and the grade goes on chain: delivered or not, how long it took, met or partially met or not met. Those receipts aggregate into a public track record, so the next buyer sees how often a worker met what people actually asked of it, how many buyers came back, and how fast it answers. Scores use a Wilson lower bound, which means two perfect calls rank below five hundred good ones instead of topping the leaderboard.

Sellers list an agent on chain with a price and an endpoint. It can already speak x402, or it can be an ordinary webhook that Sovereign wraps in a paywall on the site itself, which is how a seller with an n8n workflow and no interest in payment protocols becomes a paid worker in about two minutes. Before a listing goes live the app probes that endpoint once, unpaid, and requires a 402 response quoting the same payout address and the same price the listing claims. That single request catches dead URLs, endpoints that serve for free, and listings whose advertised price is a lie. Each seller is bound to a unique human with World ID Selfie Check, because a reputation system is worthless if a seller with bad reviews can mint a fresh identity for nothing.

Buyers set a daily budget, a per-action limit, and an allowlist of specific workers. Every hire is checked against that policy server-side before anything is signed, so an agent spends autonomously inside limits its owner set once, and never has to stop and ask. The limits are the permission.

The whole loop runs from Claude Code. One command pairs a terminal with a Sovereign account and installs an MCP server that searches the registry for free, reads a worker's track record, hires it, and pays inside the call. Afterwards it asks the buyer whether the work met what they asked for and files that verdict on chain, signed by the wallet that paid: you cannot review work you did not buy, and one payment gets one receipt. The buyer states the grade. The agent never grades the work it commissioned.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts (Arc testnet, chain 5042002). Three Solidity contracts. AgentRegistry holds listings: slug, owner, payout address, price in USDC-6, metadata and endpoint. Receipts is append-only graded work, one receipt per (buyer, settlement reference) so nobody can farm a score by re-filing. Verifications records World ID proofs, attestor-signed over EIP-712, binding one nullifier to one account. The trust model is documented in the Receipts header rather than glossed: the contract cannot verify that the payment it describes happened, so it records an attributed claim, and off-chain scoring cross-checks the settlement reference against real transfers and discounts buyers funded by the seller. Verifying settlement on chain would need payments routed through a contract, which is the rigorous upgrade and deliberately not what this does.

The Graph. A subgraph indexes all three contracts and rolls receipt aggregates forward onto each Agent entity: delivered count, met score, distinct buyers, repeat buyers, cumulative latency. Aggregating on write rather than deriving at query time matters because a buyer's agent choosing between workers in milliseconds cannot afford to fan out. Discovery is a single query that returns listings already carrying their track record.

Circle and Arc. Payments run over x402 and settle through Circle Gateway using @circle-fin/x402-batching. The seller's worker is gated by createGatewayMiddleware, which answers an unpaid request with a 402 carrying signable requirements and then verifies and settles the retry. The buyer signs an EIP-3009 authorization against the Gateway wallet contract. This is the partner choice that makes the product possible rather than merely convenient: card rails cannot clear a few cents at all, and Arc being USDC-native means no separate gas token, since gas is paid in USDC. Batched settlement keeps it gasless for the buyer.

Privy. Embedded wallets, so a buyer never manages a key, plus server-side session signers so the marketplace can sign an x402 authorization for a paired terminal that holds no key at all. One thing worth flagging for anyone building this: createOnLogin: 'users-without-wallets' silently breaks external-wallet logins, because connecting MetaMask already counts as having a wallet, so those users get no embedded wallet and every send path fails with an error that names the wrong thing. Sovereign is email-login only for exactly this reason.

World ID. IDKit Selfie Check with the proof bound to the seller's wallet as the signal, verified server-side against both the action and the signal hash. The server then signs an EIP-712 attestation that Verifications.sol accepts, so the nullifier-to-account binding is enforced on chain rather than in app logic. A buyer reading a seller's profile can see the guarantee; before this it lived only in the verifier's own browser.

MCP. sovereign-mcp is published on npm. Pairing is one command: link --spend binds a terminal to a Sovereign account, so the agent can pay and file grades from that account's wallet with no key on the machine. The notable detail is the MCP instructions field, returned on initialize and injected into the model's context by the client. Without it the failure is silent and total: the tools are loaded, the user asks for exactly what the marketplace sells, and the agent web-searches instead because nothing ever told it when to look. Shipping the guidance with the server means discovery works with no install step at all. Ranking is relevance first then track record, so an unproven worker sorts below a proven one of equal relevance.

projects.title: REKT FLY
projects.description: Learn DeFi risk in a 3D fly-brain survival game, then protect a real Sepolia testnet loan.
projects.project_description: REKT FLY turns liquidation risk into something you can see, play, and explain. It is a 3D DeFi survival lab for beginners who find collateral ratios and lending dashboards intimidating. A player starts with a virtual loan backed by ETH and must survive a falling market while using limited reserves. Adding collateral preserves the loan but commits more capital; repaying debt improves safety while reducing the loan. An interactive price lesson, readable activity graph, pause controls, and an observation log make each tradeoff visible. The distinctive controller uses a reduced fly escape circuit: 316 real neuron identities and 10,711 recorded connections. Two threat-sensor populations feed an escape alarm. Simulated activity drives a deliberately simple, public protection rule. Players can block sensor outputs and replay the same seed to test the circuit’s causal contribution. Scientific names are optional details, so no neuroscience background is required. The browser experience works without a wallet. A separate MetaMask panel bridges the lesson to the official Ethereum Sepolia lending challenge: registration, live position reads, a health-factor calculator, exact token approvals, collateral deposits, and debt repayment. A successful onchain registration has been verified. The practice pilot never signs wallet transactions. Use cases include beginner DeFi education, classroom demonstrations of risk and feedback, and reproducible experiments for builders exploring interpretable controllers. The anatomical fly and inspectable circuit make the lesson memorable without presenting simulated results as investment advice. Current scope: kinematic 3D body animation, reduced neural simulation, local practice, and explicit Sepolia wallet actions. Full closed-loop MuJoCo locomotion and confidential CRE automation are not deployed. A live Uniswap V3 exit-liquidity lesson connects the practice to real Ethereum mainnet markets. Compare WETH-to-USDC quotes across two fee tiers and see how slippage affects minimum received and hypothetical debt coverage. It is read-only, requires no wallet, and clearly separates live USDC quotes from practice dollars and Sepolia tokens.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and direct Three.js, deployed on Vercel. React updates controls independently of the 3D render loop. We kept the stack small: no database, paid LLM dependency, agent framework, or custom token contract. The fly asset is derived from Apache-2.0 NeuroMechFly/FlyGym meshes and rigging, converted to a browser GLB with an original preparation pipeline. FlyWire-derived annotations/connectivity provide 104 LC4, 210 LPLC2, and two DNp01 cells; the background points are anatomical context only. Data provenance, pinned sources, transformation steps, and required notices are included. FlyWire data remains CC BY-NC 4.0; original application code is MIT. An original reduced leaky-integrate-and-fire implementation uses published model parameters, signed delayed connections, a seeded input generator, and an explicit market-danger encoder. The browser advances 20 milliseconds of neural time per 100 milliseconds of game time. The anatomical body uses a designed kinematic gait; it is not driven by inferred biological leg torques. Viem handles Sepolia reads, contract configuration checks, two-decimal token accounting, transaction simulation, exact-amount approvals, receipt verification, and account/network changes. The official challenge registration was verified onchain. A separate bounded Modal CPU experiment loaded and stepped the articulated MuJoCo fly with finite state and no numerical warnings; it is not a live cloud game backend. Twelve tests cover circuit integrity, deterministic replay, ablation, accounting, lifecycle, activity history, and protection math. In the seed-42 automated practice comparison, the intact pilot survives 180 seconds with six interventions, while both visual outputs blocked causes liquidation at 64.5 seconds. This is evidence about the game model, not biological validation or financial returns. OpenAI Codex assisted implementation in web/src, scripts, simulation, tests, configuration, and documentation. The participant supplied the idea, product direction, platform constraints, reuse requirements, and feedback, and performed the MetaMask registration. Existing libraries/assets and newly developed behavior are distinguished in the README. Confidential CRE execution is unfinished and no confidential-workflow prize qualification is claimed. Uniswap V3 powers the exit lesson through the official Factory and QuoterV2 contracts. A Next.js server route uses viem simulateContract to quote 0.05% and 0.3% WETH/USDC pools at one block, with bounded RPC fallback and explicit errors instead of mock data. Integer base-unit arithmetic rounds minimum output down. The UI exposes verified pool links, block/time, fees, slippage and remaining hypothetical debt. FEEDBACK.md records developer feedback. No swap is sent, and the two-pool comparison is not a best-route aggregator.

projects.title: GlobalPay
projects.description: The financial operating system for AI agents to discover, verify, and pay for services.
projects.project_description: GlobalPay is an AI-native financial operating system for autonomous agents. It gives every agent a programmable financial identity through a managed wallet, scoped API credentials, and the ability to hold and transfer USDC. GlobalPay enables two sides of an agent economy. Providers can create agents and publish AI-powered services with defined capabilities, endpoints, pricing, permissions, and subscription options. Consumers can discover these services through the marketplace, evaluate providers using human-backed identity and on-chain payment evidence, and purchase services with USDC on Arc. A custom subgraph built with The Graph indexes Arc settlement activity and powers the Trust Engine, which evaluates payment history, settlement volume, success rate, buyer diversity, recency, and risk signals. World ID and AgentBook connect agent identities to verified humans or organizations. After payment, the consumer agent invokes the selected service, receives the result, and records usage for billing, invoices, analytics, and future trust evaluation. GlobalPay also includes AI recommendations, autonomous commerce workflows, API access, webhooks, and optional x402 support for HTTP-native pay-per-call payments. GlobalPay turns payments, service discovery, identity, and trust into programmable infrastructure for an autonomous agent economy.
projects.how_its_made: GlobalPay is built as a React and Express full-stack application with a PostgreSQL database. The frontend provides dashboards for organizations, agent creation, wallet management, service publishing, marketplace discovery, trust evaluation, autonomous commerce, billing, and analytics. The backend exposes REST APIs secured through session authentication, scoped developer API keys, and agent API keys. Each agent receives a managed MPC wallet and its own blockchain identity. Arc Testnet handles USDC payment settlement, while a custom subgraph built with The Graph indexes payment events and supplies data for the Trust Engine. The Trust Engine evaluates providers using settlement success, payment volume, buyer activity, recency, and risk signals. World ID provides human-backed verification, and AgentBook links verified organizations to their agents. AI Recommendations combine service capability, pricing, policy, and trust data to rank providers. After payment, agents invoke services and record usage for invoices, analytics, and future trust evaluation. Optional x402 support enables HTTP-native pay-per-call payments.

projects.title: Agent FUEL
projects.description: stake wNEWS tokens as leverage to power other agents that can grow their business
projects.project_description: Agent Fuel is outcome-financed AI capacity for small businesses that already have customers. Small companies rarely get a revolver — the line of credit a PE-backed company draws when it's short — so they end up in merchant-cash-advance loans at effective rates that can reach 1,500% APR. Agent Fuel replaces that with a staged, evidence-gated facility on Base: wNEWS holders stake into one specific, time-boxed intervention inside a business (clear an onboarding backlog, open a channel, relieve a bottleneck); the business pays a small fee now and a premium only on attested lift; AI agents do bounded work under limits the business and the funder set for themselves. Price and market depth come from the canonical wNEWS/USDC Uniswap v3 pool, indexed by a The Graph subgraph and served to agents through an MCP built for this event. Agent-to-agent payments settle on Arc by Circle through a capped wNEWS bridge (testnet today, mainnet to follow), and every contract's admin key lives on a Ledger — it can pause inflows or attest a settlement, never touch a stake. Capital is released in steps: at each evidence date the decision is stop, hold, continue, or accelerate, and declining costs nothing. Every funding event is one canonical intervention record rendered six ways — business, operator, agent, customer steward, capital supporter, auditor — so no party is shown different economics. Live now: the stake contract on Base mainnet and the first real stake, made from a phone through a Telegram mini app.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are deliberately small Solidity 0.8 with no dependencies, Slither-clean, and hardware-administered. On Base mainnet: EngagementStake — stake, on-chain per-wallet auto-approve cap, exit that can never be paused, admin-attested settle, immutable. On Arc by Circle (testnet; mainnet when Circle publishes parameters): the wNEWS bridge pair — BaseLocker vault and WNewsBridge with a hard 100k mint cap and pause-never-blocks-exits — plus AttestedPrice and ServiceLedger for goal-attributed agent-to-agent payments; Arc's USDC-native gas is what makes small agent payments practical. A Ledger holds the admin role on every contract and the treasury; the deployer key has no post-deploy power, and an ERC-7730 clear-signing descriptor for the stake contract is in the repo. The Graph: a subgraph on the canonical wNEWS/USDC Uniswap v3 pool computes spot and "credibility" (the largest sell that printed under 5% impact), cross-checked against the Messari standardized subgraph; a TypeScript MCP server written during the event (Streamable HTTP on Cloud Run) exposes it as agent tools — credibility, company status, threat report, allocation quote, intervention response, and a six-audience intervention statement. The human side is a Telegram bot plus a React/Vite mini app (Reown AppKit, wagmi, viem): wallets are proven by a signed message, several per person, the page pins the contract address and decodes the calldata before it lets you hold-to-sign, and every read goes through Telegram-authenticated endpoints — no client-side database. The listener (Node, Firestore, Cloud Scheduler) confirms every approval against the chain receipt and keeps an append-only event log for playback. Hacks worth noting: a nonce-per-attempt link flow so chat buttons never go stale, and a native-scheme-first deep link because Telegram's webview swallows WalletConnect's redirect.

projects.title: BLOCKNDRIVE
projects.description: Secure, AI-powered decentralized document vault with blockchain ownership and privacy.
projects.project_description: BlockNDrive is a decentralized document vault that combines blockchain, encryption, decentralized storage, AI, and programmable access control to give users greater control over their digital documents. When a user uploads a document, it is encrypted locally using AES before being stored, ensuring that the plaintext file is never sent to storage. The encrypted document is uploaded through Lighthouse to IPFS/Filecoin-backed storage, while its CID, cryptographic hashes, owner address, and timestamps are recorded on an Ethereum smart contract. Chainlink CRE orchestrates the document-analysis workflow to extract metadata and generate an AI-based risk score, with the analysis result and its integrity hash recorded for verification. Lit Protocol provides owner-based access control for the encryption key, allowing only the authorized user to decrypt and download the document. BlockNDrive aims to make document storage more private, verifiable, intelligent, and user-controlled.
projects.how_its_made: BlockNDrive is built as a Next.js web dApp connected to an Ethereum Sepolia smart contract using ethers.js and MetaMask. Documents are encrypted client-side with AES before being uploaded to Lighthouse for IPFS/Filecoin-backed decentralized storage. The smart contract records the document CID, cryptographic hashes, owner address, and timestamps, providing verifiable integrity and ownership records without storing the actual document on-chain. Chainlink CRE is used to orchestrate the document-analysis workflow, including metadata extraction and AI-based risk scoring, while Lit Protocol is designed for programmable, owner-only access to the encryption key. This architecture combines Ethereum, Chainlink CRE, Lighthouse, AES encryption, and Lit Protocol to create a privacy-focused decentralized document vault.

projects.title: Oscillon
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook for stable LP inventory: tax dumps vs last $1 print, cap size if no price
projects.project_description:
Oscillon is a Uniswap v4 hook and testnet UI for stable–stable pools (USDe/USDT-class).The LP problem: when one stable trades cheap vs $1, vanilla 3 bps pools absorb the weak asset. LPs see it on withdraw. Static fees give that spread to arbs.The hook’s rule (as of the Sep 13 policy):If Chainlink has a usable print (age ≤ 24h heartbeat + 1h buffer), depeg is that print vs $1. Drain (weak coin in) can pay more than 3 bps. Restore stays at base fee.
Heartbeat silence is not a depeg. A last print still ~$1 is treated as $1.
If there is no usable Chainlink (past heartbeat, floor, revert), we do not use pool TWAP as $1 and we do not charge max fee. Base fee + size cap. What we learned building it: push Chainlink stables usually update at ~50 bps or ~24h. Our backtest’s 3–20 bps USDe band almost never produces a new print, so a per-swap fee in that band cannot run on this feed. That is an infrastructure limit, not a missed if-statement. StablePair prices pool mid vs a reference for the same reason — that input exists every swap.The project is an experiment plus a path to an LP Health view (what a $10k position actually holds). It is not a claim that Oscillon beats official USDC/USDT StablePair or that LPs earn extra yield on quiet 8 bps tape.Testnet UI + Sepolia hook. Tests: 42/42 including 128k-call invariants. website: https://beta-testnet.oscillon.xyz/swap
projects.how_its_made: Uniswap v4 hook (beforeSwap / afterSwap) on Sepolia. Solidity: OscillonHook, ChainlinkOracleAdapter (AggregatorV3 + heartbeat-aligned MAX_ORACLE_AGE), OscillonPriceEngine, OscillonFeePolicy (base 3 bps + drain surcharge), OscillonTwapOracle (pre-swap tick write so a swap cannot paint its own window). TWAP is not used as USD when Chainlink is down.Frontend: Next.js swap UI (wallet, quote, depeg/fee readout). Foundry tests + fuzz/invariants (128k calls). Chainlink-compatible feeds on testnet (RedStone-shaped aggregators where we needed them).Hacky / notable: first version treated 1h silence as stale and could max-fee a quiet book. We replaced that with heartbeat-aligned trust and “blind → cap, not max fee.” A 20 bps Chainlink-vs-TWAP disagreement guard still lives; a large fresh print while the pool is still at $1 can be zeroed — documented, not hidden.Partner tech: Uniswap v4, Chainlink-style feeds. No Data Streams in this submission (pull+verify is a different product than a 3 bps stable swap).
projects.project_description_markdown:
Oscillon is a Uniswap v4 hook and testnet UI for stable–stable pools (USDe/USDT-class).The LP problem: when one stable trades cheap vs $1, vanilla 3 bps pools absorb the weak asset. LPs see it on withdraw. Static fees give that spread to arbs.The hook’s rule (as of the Sep 13 policy):If Chainlink has a usable print (age ≤ 24h heartbeat + 1h buffer), depeg is that print vs $1. Drain (weak coin in) can pay more than 3 bps. Restore stays at base fee.
Heartbeat silence is not a depeg. A last print still ~$1 is treated as $1.
If there is no usable Chainlink (past heartbeat, floor, revert), we do not use pool TWAP as $1 and we do not charge max fee. Base fee + size cap.

What we learned building it: push Chainlink stables usually update at ~50 bps or ~24h. Our backtest’s 3–20 bps USDe band almost never produces a new print, so a per-swap fee in that band cannot run on this feed. That is an infrastructure limit, not a missed if-statement. StablePair prices pool mid vs a reference for the same reason — that input exists every swap.The project is an experiment plus a path to an LP Health view (what a $10k position actually holds). It is not a claim that Oscillon beats official USDC/USDT StablePair or that LPs earn extra yield on quiet 8 bps tape.Testnet UI + Sepolia hook. Tests: 42/42 including 128k-call invariants.

website: https://beta-testnet.oscillon.xyz/swap
projects.how_its_made_markdown: Uniswap v4 hook (beforeSwap / afterSwap) on Sepolia. Solidity: OscillonHook, ChainlinkOracleAdapter (AggregatorV3 + heartbeat-aligned MAX_ORACLE_AGE), OscillonPriceEngine, OscillonFeePolicy (base 3 bps + drain surcharge), OscillonTwapOracle (pre-swap tick write so a swap cannot paint its own window). TWAP is not used as USD when Chainlink is down.Frontend: Next.js swap UI (wallet, quote, depeg/fee readout). Foundry tests + fuzz/invariants (128k calls). Chainlink-compatible feeds on testnet (RedStone-shaped aggregators where we needed them).Hacky / notable: first version treated 1h silence as stale and could max-fee a quiet book. We replaced that with heartbeat-aligned trust and “blind → cap, not max fee.” A 20 bps Chainlink-vs-TWAP disagreement guard still lives; a large fresh print while the pool is still at $1 can be zeroed — documented, not hidden.Partner tech: Uniswap v4, Chainlink-style feeds. projects.title: Iter
projects.description: Onchain CLOB+pool DEX: LPs set their own price tolerance, so sandwiche attacks stop
projects.project_description: Iter is a decentralized spot exchange that separates the two questions every trading venue has to answer: who supplies the tradable inventory, and how a trade is priced and settled. Every AMM fused those into a single bonding curve. That is why a Uniswap LP cannot decline a price — the curve fills their capital at whatever price the market pushes it to, all the way down. Onchain order book DEXes fixed settlement but abandoned inventory: their liquidity still comes from professional market makers, not permissionless LPs. Iter answers both. Settlement is a fully onchain central limit order book, with price-time or size priority chosen per pair at listing. Inventory is a pool layered on top that converts permissionless LP capital into ordinary limit orders on that same book, rather than a second pricing primitive. Every position carries its own slippageLimit, so an LP sets the worst price they will accept. At slippageLimit = 0 a position only ever executes at the reference price, which bounds its worst-case impermanent loss by construction. Pool trades are priced against a TWAP reference rather than instantaneous spot, so the price an attacker can manufacture inside one block is not the price the pool trades at. In our simulation this cuts same-block sandwich extractability by roughly three orders of magnitude — to negative attacker profit once gas is counted. Because settlement is an order book, a trade can also add liquidity: it settles whatever it can match and the remainder rests as the trader's own limit order, instead of an AMM route's all-or-nothing revert. The costs are real and we state them: occasional partial fills when tolerant liquidity is thin, and roughly 6x Uniswap v2's gas per swap, which makes Iter an L2 protocol by construction.
projects.how_its_made: CONTRACTS (Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry). MatchingEngine + Orderbook are the settlement layer: a fully onchain order book in 8-decimal fixed point (DENOM = 1e8), with price-time or size priority selected per pair at listing. src/swap holds the inventory layer — BandPool, PoolBands, BandPositionManager, BandSwapRouter. A "band" is a price tolerance anchored to the orderbook TWAP. The whitepaper described this as a per-position slippageLimit; in the shipped contracts we hoisted it into discrete buckets, because a continuous per-position tolerance had no bucket to be fungible inside. Band is a uint32 tolerance packed alongside shares and an open flag, so a band costs no extra storage slot.

projects.title: Slope
projects.description: Split a big swap into non-custodial scheduled slices along a curve you choose
projects.project_description: Existing on-chain execution limits large taker orders to two patterns, and both carry cost. A single market transaction absorbs the entire price impact at once, while manual slicing reintroduces the coordination problem the split was meant to solve, one approval and one transaction at a time, and scheduled alternatives run on a fixed clock regardless of market conditions. Slope introduces a taker-side execution position in which a single order is itself a bounded, executable time curve. A user declares a budget, a duration, and a pace shape (aggressive, neutral, or conservative), plus hard price rails, and the curve determines how much of the budget is authorised at each point in time. A flat pace reduces to ordinary linear TWAP, so the conventional schedule is a special case rather than a separate mode. The schedule lives on-chain: the SlopePosition contract computes how much each slice may sell, measures price impact with a dual-quote probe, enforces the price rails, and pulls tokens per fill with no escrow, so an unexecuted budget never leaves the owner's wallet, and a terminal clamp settles the exact remainder after the window closes. Execution is delegated through a Privy session signer scoped to exactly what the position declared: the contract address, the function selector, the position id, a per-transaction cap, and an expiry. The keeper triggers fills repeatedly without further approval and can never exceed what the schedule authorises; the contract enforces the budget and the schedule, and the Privy policy enforces the scope. The system refuses to act when conditions are wrong: prices outside the declared band, impact above the limit, or an emptied allowance are each recorded on-chain with their reason, and the keeper reads that history back from The Graph to decide whether to retry or park. Realised execution is measured against a linear-TWAP benchmark computed in the subgraph, so the value of adapting to market conditions is a number users can verify. The live application supports creating schedules from the browser, an execution staircase that fills in real time, per-fill deviation against the benchmark in basis points, an Aqua protocol trace decoded per fill with @1inch/aqua-sdk, and a CSV export of the full event stream, all on Base Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made:
Slope is a TypeScript and Solidity monorepo. The onchain system uses Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry and via-IR, and the keeper and interface are TypeScript on Node 24. A fixed-point curve kernel compiles each schedule's budget, duration, and pace shape into an  authorised amount per instant. It covers the linear branch, a square-root front-loaded branch, and a squared back-loaded branch, with boundary conditions exact by construction. Custody is pull-per-fill: tokenIn is pulled from the owner at fill time and never escrowed, so a cancelled schedule needs no refund path, and a terminal clamp settles the exact remainder after the window closes so integer-division dust cannot strand a position. Price impact is measured with a dual quote on the same router in the same call: a small probe approximating spot, and the real fill size, where the difference is the fill's own footprint. Below a decimals-derived probe floor the check cannot measure anything, and the fill event records impactChecked=false rather than claiming a check that did not happen. The official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts serve as the shared-liquidity and settlement layer on Base Sepolia, where no official deployment exists: the registry and SwapVM router were self-deployed from the v1.0.2 source, whose build requires via_ir with the Cancun EVM target since the function-pointer opcode table breaks without IR codegen. The shipped 1inch strategies embed a KYC gate opcode that only KYB-verified resolvers can pass, so Slope ships its own ungated strategy. Privy carries the delegation layer. A per-position P-256 keypair is registered as a 1-of-1 key quorum bound to a policy that allowlists the exact contract, the exact selector, the position id, a per-transaction cap, and an expiry matching the schedule. Cumulative spend aggregations are tracked at sign level only, so the keeper signs via eth_signTransaction and broadcasts the raw transaction itself. A policy containing an aggregation reference condition was found to reject every signing request regardless of operator or value format, established by bisecting a live policy where an identical policy without the reference passes immediately; rate limiting therefore lives in the keeper, and the budget invariant lives in Solidity where it belongs. The Graph is load-bearing in the execution path, not just the dashboard. Each tick the keeper queries the subgraph to decide what to work on: which positions are active, what is already indexed as executed, and whether a recent skip means a position should be parked. Candidate state is re-verified on-chain before signing, because indexing lag must never be the final
authority on a financial decision. If the subgraph is unreachable the tick is skipped and logged; there is no fallback path and no cached substitute. The subgraph also computes a BenchmarkComparison snapshot per position, realised VWAP against the linear-TWAP counterfactual, which powers the per-fill deviation in bps shown in the interface. The application runs no database of its own: the subgraph, queried exclusively through its GraphQL endpoint, is the single structured data source for both the keeper's decision-making and the frontend, and the only local persistence is a JSON file holding per-position delegated signing keys. The interface uses React, Vite, viem, and Tailwind, with every curve drawn on the Canvas API rather than a charting library, so the time ruler, the planned-versus-actual divergence, and the fill and skip marks stamped along the axis are one consistent instrument. Email onboarding runs through Privy embedded wallets, an Aqua protocol trace is decoded per fill with @1inch/aqua-sdk, and an awaiting-index state covers the window while the subgraph catches up with a fresh schedule. The frontend is hosted on Vercel, the subgraph on The Graph Studio, and the keeper runs under systemd on a VPS. Testing includes Foundry unit, integration, and fuzz suites with simulated time, cross-validation against an independent TypeScript reference model through committed vectors spanning all three pace shapes across five durations including asymmetric-decimal price normalisation, and Vitest coverage on the keeper and shared model.

projects.title: TrustDrop + VDS
projects.description: Verifiable dataset sampling before purchase; payment bound to verifiable delivery.
projects.project_description:
TrustDrop is a protocol for turning delivery into verifiable evidence that contracts can act on. A seller publishes an encrypted payload on Walrus, VSS proves that the buyer receives recoverable key material, and VDD binds the committed key, original Walrus blob ID, and ciphertext Walrus blob ID into one verifiable encryption relation.
For this hackathon, we extended TrustDrop with verifiable dataset sampling. Before this work, a buyer’s knowledge of the original asset stopped at its commitment. Our new SP1 programs derive challenge-selected samples from a committed chain-intelligence dataset: one complete minute of token-flow data and three complete wallet-cluster records with their underlying transfer evidence. Walrus openings authenticate the selected source bytes, and each proof commits the reconstructed sample CID.
This gives buyers verifiable evidence about the original asset before purchase, while TrustDrop handles verifiable key distribution, encrypted delivery, and settlement afterward.
projects.how_its_made:
TrustDrop uses Rust, Walrus, SP1, Solidity, Arbitrum Sepolia, The Graph, IPFS, and a Vite/TypeScript frontend. Its existing SP1 programs prove access-key sharing and encrypted data delivery, while The Graph indexes marketplace activity and supports complex queries without a separately hosted database.
Proof modules can define their own schema, sampling rules, zk program, verifier, certificate, and presentation. For this hackathon, we built a chain-intelligence dataset containing token flows, wallet clusters, and supporting transactions, then implemented two deterministic samplers.
One sampler selects a time-aligned flow interval; the other selects multiple cluster IDs and their supporting transfers. SP1 guests authenticate the required Reed–Solomon slivers against the source commitment, reconstruct the exact samples, and commit their IPFS CIDs. Succinct generates Groth16 proofs, standalone Solidity contracts verify them, and the marketplace displays each certificate with verification results and interactive sample viewers.

projects.title: SwipeFi
projects.description: Gamified Telegram Mini App building sophisticated DeFi yield positions via 1inch Aqua & SwapVM
projects.project_description:
SwipeFi transforms complex decentralized finance into an intuitive, gamified Telegram Mini App designed to bring retail users into Web3. Traditional DeFi platforms overwhelm everyday users with intimidating candlestick charts, manual multi-step interactions across protocols, and complex order routing. SwipeFi distills asset discovery and yield generation into a familiar binary experience: swipe left to skip, or swipe right to automatically execute a sophisticated, multi-step DeFi position in a single interaction.
Each token card presents a dark-mode glassmorphic interface showing the asset's identity, a 24-hour price trend, and AI-generated project insights. Beneath its seamless UI, SwipeFi relies on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM to package complex end-to-end trading and yield strategies into a single transaction. Instead of performing basic swaps, a right swipe triggers SwapVM to execute an atomic "Zap & Yield" flow—swapping USDC for an underlying token and instantly depositing it into yield-generating protocols (such as liquid staking), maximizing execution efficiency while eliminating user friction.
projects.how_its_made:
SwipeFi is built as a lightweight, high-performance Telegram Mini App designed for mobile responsiveness. The frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS to deliver a glassmorphic dark-mode interface, paired with Framer Motion to drive 60 FPS touch-gesture physics for card swiping.
The core financial architecture relies directly on 1inch's Aqua Protocol and SwapVM. Using the @1inch/aqua SDK, SwipeFi constructs custom execution instructions targeting SwapVM smart contracts. When a user swipes right, the application calls a Next.js API Route Handler that compiles a unified SwapVM call. This single instruction atomically routes USDC into a target token via 1inch liquidity and immediately deposits the acquired asset into Lido (or similar yield protocols) to issue yield-bearing tokens (e.g., stETH) back to the user.
For the live demonstration and testing environment, the smart contract execution was validated on a local Mainnet Fork powered by Hardhat, simulating live state, whale token impersonation, and on-chain token balance transfers. To overcome Telegram's in-app webview constraints, we bridged the Telegram Web Apps SDK directly to an injected provider context to ensure smooth, single-tap transaction sign-offs.
