projects.title: Reckon
projects.description: An agent manages a treasury under rules it can't forge. Refusing it is the whole point.
projects.project_description: If you hand money to an agent, you're trusting it not to do something dumb while you're asleep. Right now that trust sits in the agent's own code — an if-statement it can talk itself out of. reckon replaces that with a document. The owner writes a mandate in plain terms, signs it, and the agent holds a copy it can't alter. Six clauses: keep 60% in stablecoins, never more than 15% in one asset, max $500 a trade, only tokens older than 90 days with real liquidity, an hour between trades, and Uniswap only. What gets signed is the readable text plus a hash of the exact numbers, so every decision the agent makes can point back to the rules that were live at the time. Every clause is then enforced in three independent places. The evaluator checks the portfolio-wide limits against live data. Those same clauses compile into a Privy wallet policy, so the agent physically can't sign a transaction outside them — that refusal happens in Privy's signing enclave, not in our code. And anything the mandate merely bounds, rather than forbids, escalates to the owner, who signs an EIP-712 override good for one action, one token, one hour. Clause four is the one a price feed can't answer, so it comes from two Graph products composed together. The Uniswap v3 subgraph gives token age and the trough of daily TVL across thirty days — not today's number, because a pool that dropped to $40k last Tuesday isn't liquid however healthy it looks now. The Token API gives holder concentration. That second one taught us something: the top ten holders of WETH on Base own 52% of supply, but nine of the ten are bridges and protocol contracts, and real wallets hold 0.93%. The obvious metric rejects WETH for a reason that isn't real, so §4 counts wallets and the receipt records both figures. Execution is Uniswap v3 through SwapRouter02. The subgraph ranks fee tiers by TVL but doesn't get to set the price: we quote all four through QuoterV2 and take the best fill, which is about 0.6% better on WETH/USDC, with the winner flipping from 0.01% to 0.05% around $5,000. Four decisions in the demo, all against a fork of Base mainnet — real pools, real prices, real Privy signatures, fake funds. A $5 WETH rebalance clears every clause and executes. $5 of DEGEN is refused: trough liquidity was $493,000 against a $2M floor. A $12 WETH buy would put 34% into one asset against a 15% ceiling, so it stops and waits. Then the owner signs, the policy is widened for that single action, it executes, and the original policy goes back. Every decision appends a receipt: what it saw and where the data came from, what it wanted to do and why, which clauses it cleared or broke with the observed values and the limits, who authorised it, what it did on chain, and the hash of the mandate in force. The dashboard is that ledger and nothing else — no charts, no dials. One thing to be straight about: the planner that decides what to propose is written but not wired in, and has never been run — we had no API key. The four proposals in the demo are fixtures we wrote. So what exists is the layer that constrains an agent, with the decision-maker sketched in but not plugged in. It's called out in the README rather than left for someone to find.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript throughout, Next.js 16 for the dashboard, viem for anything touching a chain, zod for validating the mandate before it's ever hashed. The mandate is an EIP-712 document. What gets signed is a readable sentence per clause plus a keccak of the canonicalised clause values — keys sorted recursively, so the same rules always hash the same way. Every receipt cites that hash. Change one number and the hash changes, which is the whole point. Privy is where the mandate stops being a promise. We compile the clauses into wallet policy rules: §6 becomes a to allowlist of the Uniswap router, §3 becomes an amountIn ceiling, §4 becomes a tokenOut allowlist — and those last two are ethereum_calldata conditions, meaning Privy decodes the swap arguments with the ABI and compares them inside the enclave. That's what makes "the agent physically cannot" true rather than aspirational. Four things cost us real time there, none of them documented where we looked: A catch-all {method: "*", action: "DENY"} rule silently disables the entire policy. We added it as a safety net and every transaction started failing, including compliant ones. Bisecting it: a minimal policy with one ALLOW rule passes; add the catch-all and the same transaction is refused. A matching DENY overrides every ALLOW regardless of order, and policies are already deny-by-default, so the "safety net" only removes function. The failure is silent — policy_violation looks identical whether your conditions are wrong or an extra rule is eating them. Constraining only eth_sendTransaction leaves a hole: the agent can call eth_signTransaction and broadcast the signed payload through any RPC it likes. We emit rules for both. projects.project_description_markdown:
If you hand money to an agent, you're trusting it not to do something dumb while you're asleep. Right now that trust sits in the agent's own code — an if-statement it can talk itself out of.

reckon replaces that with a document. The owner writes a mandate in plain terms, signs it, and the agent holds a copy it can't alter. Six clauses: keep 60% in stablecoins, never more than 15% in one asset, max $500 a trade, only tokens older than 90 days with real liquidity, an hour between trades, and Uniswap only. What gets signed is the readable text plus a hash of the exact numbers, so every decision the agent makes can point back to the rules that were live at the time.

Every clause is then enforced in three independent places. The evaluator checks the portfolio-wide limits against live data. Those same clauses compile into a Privy wallet policy, so the agent physically can't sign a transaction outside them — that refusal happens in Privy's signing enclave, not in our code. And anything the mandate merely bounds, rather than forbids, escalates to the owner, who signs an EIP-712 override good for one action, one token, one hour.

Clause four is the one a price feed can't answer, so it comes from two Graph products composed together. The Uniswap v3 subgraph gives token age and the *trough* of daily TVL across thirty days — not today's number, because a pool that dropped to $40k last Tuesday isn't liquid however healthy it looks now. The Token API gives holder concentration. That second one taught us something: the top ten holders of WETH on Base own 52% of supply, but nine of the ten are bridges and protocol contracts, and real wallets hold 0.93%. The obvious metric rejects WETH for a reason that isn't real, so §4 counts wallets and the receipt records both figures.

Execution is Uniswap v3 through SwapRouter02. The subgraph ranks fee tiers by TVL but doesn't get to set the price: we quote all four through QuoterV2 and take the best fill, which is about 0.6% better on WETH/USDC, with the winner flipping from 0.01% to 0.05% around $5,000.

A $5 WETH rebalance clears every clause and executes. $5 of DEGEN is refused: trough liquidity was $493,000 against a $2M floor. Then the owner signs, the policy is widened for that single action, it executes, and the original policy goes back.

The four proposals in the demo are fixtures we wrote. So what exists is the layer that constrains an agent, with the decision-maker sketched in but not plugged in. It's called out in the README rather than left for someone to find.

projects.title: speculum
projects.description: Checks whether an AI agent's stated intent matches the transaction it is about to sign.
projects.project_description: In 40 consecutive Ethereum mainnet blocks on 13 September, speculum decoded 7,299 transactions. Of the 203 approvals that carried an amount, 59 were unbounded, nearly three in ten signatures granting a ceiling no token supply can ever reach. That traffic was not written for this project. It is what ERC-20 approval looks like on a normal morning. An agent says it will approve exactly 100 USDC. It emits calldata. The signer signs bytes that nobody ever compared against the sentence. Nothing in that flow is malicious and nothing reverts, which is why it keeps happening. speculum makes the agent declare what it is doing before it signs, then decodes the calldata on its own and compares the two. The decoder never sees the declaration, so the check cannot be circular. A match passes. A divergence blocks and escalates to a hardware confirmation. When the calldata cannot be decoded at all, speculum refuses rather than guessing, and says which of the two failures happened. Fifteen named divergence classes so far. Wrong recipient, wrong token, wrong spender, an amount larger than the one declared, an approval that came out unlimited when a specific figure was stated, native currency riding along undeclared, and calls that transfer ownership or upgrade a proxy behind an otherwise ordinary looking transaction. Simulators already tell a human what state will change. They do not know what the agent claimed, so they cannot tell you that the two disagree. That gap is the whole product.
projects.how_its_made:
The engine is Node and viem. decode takes a transaction and nothing else and returns what the bytes actually do. compare takes that plus the declared intent and returns a verdict with every reason attached. Calldata in the tests is encoded with viem rather than written by hand, so the bytes under test are real bytes and not strings that happen to parse. Two bugs came out of the tests rather than out of reading the code. The branch separating an unknown selector from unreadable arguments was structurally always true, so every unrecognised call was mislabelled. And the bitfield that crosses from JavaScript into the Solidity event needed a test of its own, because a silent disagreement there would have miscounted every indexed verdict without ever failing loudly. The contract stores nothing and emits everything, because the consumer is an indexer rather than another contract, and a check that costs twenty thousand gas is a check that gets skipped. It holds no funds and routes no calls, so it cannot become a point of failure inside a transaction it is judging. It also enforces one invariant: a clean verdict carrying findings, or a flagged verdict carrying none, is rejected rather than indexed as a contradiction. On AI use, since the rules ask for it. Claude was used to do some work here, including this text, since English is not my first language and I did not want mistakes in it. What it could not do is establish that any of it was true. Every fact in the repository README came from running something: the Ledger needing a physical confirmation and returning 0x6985 when refused was established by pressing both buttons and then pressing reject on a real device, eth_simulateV1 was probed across five endpoints and works on two, and the contract was funded and deployed by hand to Base Sepolia. The model had asserted several of those confidently before they were checked, and was wrong about some. Three errors were caught by eye rather than by tests, including a co-author still showing on the repository after the model declared the history clean, because it had verified commit messages instead of the page a person actually looks at. The problem, the decision to build from scratch, the partner choices and the name are mine.
The root of the service negotiates on the Accept header, so an agent gets the JSON descriptor it needs to discover the price and a browser gets a page, one URL with no second copy to drift. The consumer is in the repo too: hedera/agent.js sends the unpaid request first on purpose, takes the price from the 402 rather than anything hardcoded, signs, and refuses to sign the check it was told to block.

projects.title: Semantic ABI
projects.description: Ethereum type-checks bytes; Semantic ABI type-checks what evidence is allowed to mean.
projects.project_description: Semantic ABI is a type system for what one protocol’s evidence is allowed to mean when another protocol consumes it. Ethereum has an ABI for how contracts compose at the byte / execution level — but nothing checks meaning-level composition. A commitment, an attestation, a state-inclusion proof and an independent recomputation can each return true and carry completely different authority; today those distinctions live in prose and implementation discipline, and compositions silently upgrade one into another. Semantic ABI makes it machine-checkable. Every component declares a typed EvidenceClaim — authority_class, claim_type, scope, and a temporal boundary — plus an explicit does_not_establish set naming what it deliberately does not prove. A semantic linker checks a composition and throws a meaning-level TYPE ERROR, with a minimal counterexample, whenever an edge would upgrade authority with no evidence. A two-level runner keeps three values distinct that systems routinely collapse into one green light: the expected pair outcome, what a backend observed, and whether the backend conformed. The proof isn’t “we built X.” It’s that independently-built systems declare into the same schema and are checked by the same runner with no shared checker code — invinoveritas’s adapter is wired and reproduces a real historical bug live (a signed-commitment collapse), and the Vértice gateway maps the same real endpoints. Don’t trust it — recompute what you can, and label honestly what you can’t.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a zero-dependency Node/ESM engine (runs on clone, no install): a manifest loader + JSON-Schema, a semantic linker, and a two-level protected-relation runner, using node:crypto for content-addressing. Evidence is typed as EvidenceClaim<claim_type, authority_class, scope, issued_at | verification_time>. The linker’s one deliberate cross-class edge — recomputation → semantic verification — is claim- and scope-specific, never global; a global version would be the exact authority over-claim the tool exists to catch, so we refused it in the type system itself. Each system under test is wrapped by an adapter authored independently by its owner, mapping real endpoints to manifest declarations: invinoveritas (/review, /verify-proof, /ledger, a Bitcoin freshness beacon) and the Vértice gateway (EIP-712 L4 attestation, a Base-Sepolia anchor, a /verify recompute endpoint, ERC-8373 post-quantum key binding). There is no shared checker between adapters, so “N systems conform” means N genuinely independent systems, not one checked N times. Conformance vectors include negatives that must fail (prove-can-fail). The flagship reproduces a real, git-verifiable historical bug — invinoveritas pre-v18, where two structurally different REJECT verdicts (evidence-against vs merely-insufficient) produced the same signed commitment — as a live FAIL, fixed post-v18 as a PASS. It composes with the trustless-ai standards family it grew out of: WYRIWE / ERC-8299 (input provenance), ERC-8281 (on-chain anchoring), and a companion recompute-kit recipe that folds a genuine-enclave TEE inference (0G Compute) into an 8281 anchored manifest as an “attested, not recomputed” leaf. The notably-hacky-in-the-best-way part: during review the suite caught a real gap in its own checker — it gated the “not recomputed” disclaimer but not the “not judged correct” one — found by running the mirror case against itself. The thesis applied to itself; now fixed, with a proving negative.

projects.title: BlotChain-MEVShield
projects.description: 3D WebGL control plane detecting MEV sandwich threats & enforcing EIP-712 policies via v4 hooks.
projects.project_description: BlotChain-MEVShield is a 3D WebGL Spatial Control Plane and real-time threat monitoring dashboard designed to protect DeFi transactions on Arc Testnet and Uniswap v4 from MEV exploits, specifically sandwich attacks and mempool front-running. Users submit intents through an immersive 3D spatial interface built with React and Three.js. As intent payloads enter the system, our risk engine analyzes transaction paths, mempool activity, and pool states indexed by The Graph. When a high-risk sandwich attack scenario is detected, the visual HUD instantly highlights the targeted Uniswap v4 Hook node in red, calculates safe slippage parameters, and generates a cryptographically signed EIP-712 execution policy. This policy is verified on-chain within the Uniswap v4 hook before Swap trigger, neutralizing predatory bots before execution.
projects.how_its_made:
BlotChain-MEVShield is built using a modern decoupled architecture engineered for high availability and low latency: • Frontend & 3D Engine: Built with React, Three.js, @react-three/fiber, and Tailwind CSS for the glassmorphic spatial control plane UI, hosted on Vercel.
• Backend & Risk Engine: Node.js/TypeScript backend utilizing Viem and Wagmi for EIP-712 signature generation, combined with custom Subgraphs on The Graph to query real-time DEX pool states.
• On-Chain Hook: Uniswap v4 Custom Hook written in Solidity and deployed on Arc Testnet. The hook validates the EIP-712 execution policy inside the beforeSwap() function to enforce maximum slippage limits and prevent front-running.
• API Proxy & Resilience: Configured vercel.json rewrites for seamless API routing with zero CORS hurdles, supported by an automatic multi-tier fallback architecture to guarantee 100% UI availability.

projects.title: Usenami
projects.description: Live, signed market data from The Graph as the trust anchor for an AI trading agent's spend policy.
projects.project_description:
Usenami Signer seals exchange API keys inside an AWS Nitro Enclave. The signing secret never leaves the enclave, and every signing request is checked against policy before a signature exists. That policy engine isn't new for this hackathon — it's a Continuity project, live today, gating trade size and blocking withdrawals. We've proven it with real money: completed trades on Binance and Hyperliquid mainnet, and the full signing path proven on OKX.
For ETHOnline we're extending it with a new input: live market data from The Graph. An agent reads Uniswap V3 pool state through The Graph's x402 gateway — no API key, no account needed. The indexer's own response comes back signed, tied to the exact request and exact bytes: EIP-712, verified against the live on-chain DisputeManager and the indexer's real stake of 604,359 GRT. We build a canonical snapshot from that signed response and sign it ourselves, with a key whose address is published in our attestation. That snapshot is the designed input for the enclave's policy — the piece that lets "is this order priced sanely" become something a machine can check, not just a human watching a screen.
The layer that actually enforces a price bound from this data ships in the rotation after submission. What ships in the window is the producing half: read, pay, verify the indexer's signature, build the signed snapshot the enclave will consume next.
projects.how_its_made:
The core signer already runs a hard architectural boundary: the enclave has no network access at all, it only talks to its parent over vsock. Any external data - including a subgraph response - arrives from an untrusted party by construction. Trust can't come from "it's on-chain" or "The Graph served it"; inside the enclave that provenance is unobservable, only bytes are. Trust has to come from a signature the enclave can check with a baked-in key.
We read Uniswap V3 pool state (canonical, immutable factory 0x1F98431c8aD98523631AE4a59f267346ea31F984) through The Graph's x402 gateway — GraphQL directly, USDC on Base, $0.01 per query, no API key. The gateway response carries a graph-attestation header: an EIP-712 signature over (requestCID, responseCID, subgraphDeploymentID). We verified that signature end-to-end against two live paid responses. responseCID matched the exact response bytes on both. ecrecover against the current Horizon DisputeManager - 0x2FE023a575449AcB698648eD21276293Fa176f96 on Arbitrum, the address changed in a recent protocol migration and we caught the stale one before trusting it — resolved to an allocationID, and SubgraphService.getAllocation() resolved that to a real indexer staking 604,359 GRT on the exact subgraph deployment we queried. projects.title: Faultline
projects.description: Cross protocol liquidation contagion solver. Shock one protocol, see who else breaks.
projects.project_description: Every lending protocol reports solvency in isolation. Aave shows Aave health factors. Compound shows Compound collateral ratios. Neither can see that a wallet leveraged against an asset on one protocol and a completely unrelated wallet leveraged against the same asset on another protocol are exposed to each other through the market, with no direct link between them. Faultline builds that cross-protocol exposure graph from live Aave v3 and Compound v3 positions, applies a price shock, recomputes health factors, liquidates breaches, and prices the forced collateral sale against real Uniswap v3 tick liquidity, iterating to a fixed point. It's a deterministic solver, not a model: every liquidation mechanic is a published protocol parameter, not a prediction. Live proof, not a synthetic example: a 43.67% oracle shock to wstETH liquidates a real Aave v3 wallet. Because the wstETH/WETH Uniswap v3 pool's liquidity falls to under 5% of its starting depth after just 4 ticks, that wallet's forced 196 wstETH sale alone crashes the pool price from $1,718.78 to $0.50, a near total collapse independently verified against Uniswap's own QuoterV2 contract. That crashed price liquidates a second wallet sharing no protocol and no debt asset with the first; its own forced sale drives the price down to a final $0.0028.
projects.how_its_made: Python/FastAPI backend, React + react-three-fiber frontend. No ML or LLM anywhere in the solve path, a hard rule from day one: liquidation mechanics are published protocol parameters, so we solve the system deterministically instead of predicting it. Data layer: live positions pulled from Aave v3's and Compound v3's own subgraphs via The Graph. Three of our first four subgraph IDs, pulled from search results with plausible display names, turned out dead or pointed at a completely different schema (Messari-standardized instead of the protocol team's own). We rebuilt the rule after that: every subgraph and contract ID now comes only from the protocol's own docs or README, verified live before use. Live balances were harder than expected to get right. Aave's UserReserve.currentVariableDebt and Compound's PositionAccounting.baseBalance both look like live numbers but are snapshots written only on a wallet's last interaction, understating real debt by however much interest accrued since. We derive live values ourselves (scaled amount times the reserve's current index), verified to four decimal places against DeBank on real wallets. A second bug: Aave's eMode liquidation thresholds only apply to assets that specific eMode category lists as eligible, and our first query for that list silently truncated to GraphQL's default first-100 rows across the whole deployment, dropping a real eligible asset that happened to land outside the window. That produced a plausible-looking wrong health factor before we caught it. Uniswap v3's tick-level liquidity is what prices the forced sale for real, not a flat slippage assumption. We implemented the actual v3 constant-liquidity-within-a-tick-range swap math ourselves and verified it against Uniswap's own deployed QuoterV2 contract via a raw eth_call, matching our simulation to four significant figures. That check caught a real off-by-one in our own tick-crossing boundary (excluding the pool's current tick from a downward walk, producing impossible negative liquidity). Pool selection is address-verified too, not sorted by raw reported TVL: Uniswap's subgraph doesn't sanitize that field, and a real query surfaced a spam pool claiming ~$1.1 trillion TVL. We only treat a pool as eligible if both its tokens are governance-listed reserve assets already pulled from Aave or Compound. The solver is a fixed-point cascade: apply a price shock, recompute every wallet's health factor across both protocols, liquidate anything under 1.0 using Aave's own close-factor and seizure formulas straight from LiquidationLogic.sol, price the resulting forced sale against the real pool depth above, repeat until nothing new breaches. The reference case is externally reconciled against DeBank on both wallets. The frontend renders that cascade live with react-three-fiber: a shock slider calls the real solver on every drag, not a replay, and a wallet-lookup feature runs the full pipeline against any address typed in. Its honest-failure path (an asset with no Aave oracle price configured) was verified against a real wallet holding COMP as Compound v3 collateral, since COMP isn't a listed Aave v3 reserve at all: the app reports "health factor not computed" by name instead of showing a number built on an incomplete price. Partner tech: The Graph is what makes composing two independent lending protocols' full position state into one cross-protocol query pattern possible at all, that's the actual product. Uniswap v3's tick-level depth is what turns "the price moved" into an actual, mechanically-priced forced sale, and is what surfaced the concentrated-liquidity finding that became the second half of the demo.

projects.title: SPRY Finance
projects.description: Dynamic-fee Uniswap v4 hook that turns arbitrage-driven IL into LP revenue.
projects.project_description: Spry is a non-custodial Uniswap v4 hook that replaces flat swap fees with dynamic, per-swap pricing designed to better protect liquidity providers from impermanent loss and LVR. Instead of charging every trade the same rate, Spry measures how much a swap moves the pool and applies a four-zone fee curve: ordinary flow stays near a low base fee, while larger price-moving arbitrage and MEV trades progressively pay more. The additional fees accrue to LPs through Uniswap v4's native fee accounting. To prevent traders from bypassing the curve by splitting a large trade into smaller swaps, Spry tracks cumulative pool movement over a block window and prices each swap across that path using integral-based pricing. The mechanism is designed to be path-independent and splitting-resistant. Spry uses five fee tiers for different asset classes, requires no external oracle, makes no external calls from the hook, and never custodies user funds. Ref.: https://spry.fi/Spry-Whitepaper.pdf
projects.how_its_made:
Spry started from a simple problem: impermanent loss has always made LPing feel risky, especially when large arbitrage trades extract value from pools. When Uniswap introduced hooks, we saw an opportunity to change how swap fees work at the pool level. We built a hook that measures how much each swap moves the pool and adjusts the fee dynamically, so normal trades stay cheap while larger, more harmful trades pay more. The contracts are written in Solidity and tested with Foundry (covering unit, integration, attack scenarios, fuzz/invariant behavior, and fork tests).
The hook is non-custodial, uses only on-chain pool state, and does not rely on external oracles.

projects.title: fuda
projects.description: Membership as an on-chain right — issued in seconds, verified at the door with no server to trust.
projects.project_description: 🎫 Membership as an on-chain right. A venue issues a right, the member saves a standard pass to Apple Wallet, Google Wallet or the browser, and a scanner checks admission through fuda's API against the on-chain record. +Private adds a separate browser flow: unlock with a passkey, discover your rights and sign to enter. The right's on-chain validity can be checked independently of fuda. 🚀 Try a standard pass — no crypto wallet setup, no member account, no app install Claim your ETHOnline 2026 pass: https://app.fuda.sh/@ethonline2026/pass → The display a venue puts on its counter (scan it with your phone): https://app.fuda.sh/@ethonline2026/home → Slides (PDF): https://s.oboro.xyz/ethonline2026 → Member web app: https://app.fuda.sh → · Operator dashboard: https://dash.fuda.sh → · Gate scanner: https://gate.fuda.sh → Code: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh → · ENS: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/integrations/ens.md → · The Graph: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/integrations/thegraph.md → 🧩 The problem. Memberships live on a plastic card, a dedicated app or a vendor's database, so verification and revocation depend on the issuing system. fuda puts the right on-chain so another verifier can check it. The right should outlive the app. ⛓️ Independently verifiable rights. Each right is an EAS Entitlement on Base Sepolia, issued under an on-chain IssuerDelegation . The hosted gate calls the API, which reads both by eth_call and checks operational state in D1; required chain reads fail closed. Revoke on-chain and the same QR is rejected on the next scan. Anyone can check the on-chain records; reproducing the hosted admission verdict also needs its operational state. 🔐 Standard and +Private. Standard demos use Bearer verification: save a pass, present its QR. Signed adds holder proof through challenge-response, and +Private extends it with a fresh ERC-5564 stealth holder address per issued right, unlocked by a separate fuda PRF passkey prepared before issuance. Real iPhone captures show discovery of rights with distinct stealth holders, ADMIT for an active right and REJECT / REVOKED for a different, previously revoked one. Private issuance currently uses the admin API; its card-claim UI is not connected. Portable attendance records. Non-private admissions schedule an EAS Attendance attestation asynchronously, best-effort; a failed attestation does not undo admission. +Private emits no public Attendance; entry logs stay in D1. 🏷️ ENS names the relationship; EAS proves the right. ethonline2026.fuda.eth is an entry the venue claimed and owns in an ENSv2 User Registry on Sepolia — non-transferable, expiring, gas sponsored. The member number printed on the pass, <member-no>.ethonline2026.fuda.eth , is a free offchain name answered by a signed CCIP-Read gateway. Both resolve through the hackathon Universal Resolver from a plain viem client, and a manually provisioned +Private member name resolved to two different stealth addresses across two queries. Automated private issuance and naming remain unconnected. 📊 The Graph is on the read path, not beside it. The rights subgraph is what the member app queries for +Private discovery and what the dashboard queries for on-chain status; the API's own announcement cache was deleted when it landed. The app, dashboard, gate and API are deployed at *.fuda.sh , with rights on Base Sepolia and ENS on the hackathon Ethereum Sepolia deployment. Built in the event window on a fresh repo.
projects.how_its_made: All four surfaces are Cloudflare Workers — api, member app, dashboard, gate scanner — on Hono, Drizzle over D1, R2, valibot, viem. EAS on Base Sepolia holds rights and delegations; D1 holds cards, member records, challenges, single-use consumption, entry logs and stamp credits. Any required chain read that fails, fails closed. Code: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/tree/main/apps → · Architecture: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/architecture.md → Bearer and Signed verification. Standard Bearer rights use a counterfactual Coinbase Smart Wallet address computed by the factory with fuda's signer as its sole owner, so no member wallet setup or account deployment is needed to receive a pass; ownership transfer to the member is not implemented. Signed entry uses EIP-191 challenge-response through viem's verifyMessage , supporting ECDSA, ERC-1271 and ERC-6492. +Private: passkey before issuance. WebAuthn PRF output derives viewing and spending keys and a stealth meta-address on-device ( @noble/curves , WebCrypto). The issuer derives a fresh stealth address per right, attests the EAS right to it and publishes an ERC-5564 Announcement. The app fetches raw announcements from The Graph, matches locally, recovers the stealth signing key and signs an API challenge; the verdict shows in a modal on the member's device. Addresses differ per right, not per visit: issuer mappings and repeated presentations of the same UID are not hidden. packages/stealth-address . Wallet passes built from scratch. Google save links are RS256 JWTs; the Apple .pkpass is signed with a detached CMS SignedData assembled with pkijs on WebCrypto. The hacky bit: signing a .pkpass normally means shelling out to OpenSSL, which a Worker can't do, so the whole manifest-hash-and-sign path is pure WebCrypto at the edge. packages/pass . 🏷️ ENS — one hybrid resolver, two kinds of name. One FudaResolver (ENSIP-10 wildcard) serves the whole tree: an active claimed venue's addr() is read from the ENSv2 User Registry on-chain, while member names are answered offchain by a signed CCIP-Read gateway in the api, and the resolver verifies that signature before answering. The venue claims its name with its own transaction, gated by an EIP-712 voucher fuda signs; gas is sponsored through fuda's ERC-7677 paymaster endpoint (Alchemy's verifying paymaster pays). viem's built-in Universal Resolver is overridden to the hackathon one. packages/ens-contracts , spec: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/ens-naming.md → 📊 The Graph — composed Substreams. fuda_erc5564 extracts raw ERC-5564 Announcement events from the canonical singleton Announcer, parameterized by address, with zero fuda policy in it, so any ERC-5564 app can import the same .spkg without writing Rust. erc5564_eas_pipeline imports it by .spkg and composes it with an EAS Attested / Revoked module into one fuda_events stream, captured live from The Graph Market on Base Sepolia. The rights subgraph indexes EAS and the Announcer directly; the product's discovery path does not consume Substreams output. Spec: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/substreams.md → Raw and unfiltered on purpose. +Private discovery scans every announcement on-device; filtering per issuer or member inside the indexer would shrink the anonymity set. ADR: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-graph-push-query-lanes.md → Another hacky one. The subgraph's subgraph.yaml and schema-UID map are generated from the API's Sepolia configuration in wrangler.jsonc , and graph:prepare fails loudly while EAS_SCHEMAS or ANNOUNCER_FROM_BLOCK are unset, so the indexer and the Worker can't drift on which schema UIDs are live. Built spec-first: docs/specs/ and docs/adr/ are in the repo and the code comments cite them by section. https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/tree/main/docs →

- 🏷️ **ENS — one hybrid resolver, two kinds of name.** One `FudaResolver` (ENSIP-10 wildcard) serves the whole tree: an active claimed venue's `addr()` is read from the ENSv2 User Registry on-chain, while member names are answered offchain by a signed CCIP-Read gateway in the api, and the resolver verifies that signature before answering. The venue claims its name with its own transaction, gated by an EIP-712 voucher fuda signs; gas is sponsored through fuda's ERC-7677 paymaster endpoint (Alchemy's verifying paymaster pays). viem's built-in Universal Resolver is overridden to the hackathon one. `packages/ens-contracts`, spec: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/ens-naming.md [→](https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/ens-naming.md)
- 📊 **The Graph — composed Substreams.** `fuda_erc5564` extracts raw ERC-5564 `Announcement` events from the canonical singleton Announcer, parameterized by address, with zero fuda policy in it, so any ERC-5564 app can import the same `.spkg` without writing Rust. `erc5564_eas_pipeline` imports it by `.spkg` and composes it with an EAS `Attested`/`Revoked` module into one `fuda_events` stream, captured live from The Graph Market on Base Sepolia. The rights subgraph indexes EAS and the Announcer directly; the product's discovery path does not consume Substreams output. Spec: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/substreams.md [→](https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/specs/substreams.md)
- **Raw and unfiltered on purpose.** +Private discovery scans _every_ announcement on-device; filtering per issuer or member inside the indexer would shrink the anonymity set. ADR: https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-graph-push-query-lanes.md [→](https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-graph-push-query-lanes.md)
- **Another hacky one.** The subgraph's `subgraph.yaml` and schema-UID map are generated from the API's Sepolia configuration in `wrangler.jsonc`, and `graph:prepare` fails loudly while `EAS_SCHEMAS` or `ANNOUNCER_FROM_BLOCK` are unset, so the indexer and the Worker can't drift on which schema UIDs are live.

Built spec-first: `docs/specs/` and `docs/adr/` are in the repo and the code comments cite them by section. https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/tree/main/docs [→](https://github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/tree/main/docs)

projects.title: Aevum Protocol
projects.description: Cryptographic proof your trading strategy ran honestly — live on Ethereum Mainnet.
projects.project_description: Aevum Protocol's Verifiable Backtest Oracle (VBO) solves the credibility problem in algorithmic trading. Anyone can show a great backtest there's no way to know if it was cherry-picked after the fact. VBO makes that impossible. Traders commit a cryptographic hash of their strategy on-chain before the forward test window opens. Atlas Oracle cryptographically signs the BTC/USD price at both commit and attestation time using data from 905+ exchange sources. When the window closes, traders submit their logs and Aevum attests the results on-chain. The result is a permanent certificate proving the strategy ran honestly with zero look-ahead bias, independently verified benchmark prices, and no way to fake the timing. Live on Ethereum Mainnet since September 3, 2026. First mainnet commitment active. 4 contracts deployed and verified on Etherscan.
projects.how_its_made:
VBO v2 inherits Atlas Oracle's PullOracleConsumerStandard, making it the first trading strategy certification system with cryptographically signed benchmark prices. The architecture has 4 layers: Smart contracts AgentIdentity, ReputationOracle v2, ReputationController v2, and VBO v2 deployed on Ethereum Mainnet. VBO v2 uses Atlas Oracle pull-mode price feeds (BTC/USD feed #626, 905+ exchange sources, ConsensusScore verified).
Serverless Atlas integration a Vercel serverless function fetches the Atlas signed price payload server-side and builds the VBO calldata before sending to MetaMask. This solves the Atlas payload requirement without exposing API keys in the browser.
Frontend React/Vite on Vercel with WalletConnect via Reown AppKit. Agent registration gate checks on-chain identity before allowing strategy commits. Certificate page displays Atlas-verified BTC/USD prices with ATLAS VERIFIED badge.
Infrastructure Supabase for commitment tracking, Resend for transactional emails, Stripe for payment processing, ImprovMX for email routing. Two audits completed by Claude Opus 5 — 4 Critical, 6 High, 10 Medium, 8 Low findings all resolved. 36 Foundry tests passing. Hexens professional audit scoped, restarts at first investment close. Partner technology Atlas Oracle:
VBO v2 inherits PullOracleConsumerStandard from Atlas Oracle. This was the critical technical breakthrough without Atlas, BTC/USD benchmark prices on certificates would be self-reported. With Atlas, they are cryptographically signed by 905+ exchange sources and verified on-chain inside the smart contract. The atlasVerified flag on every Certificate struct proves both price points came from Atlas.

projects.title: UNICA
projects.description: Accept crypto, receive your asset. Uniswap converts, ENS names, The Graph indexes.
projects.project_description: UNICA is a testnet payment platform for ordinary businesses, live at https://unica.nfteria.click on Ethereum Sepolia. A business signs in with its wallet, and UNICA derives its identity, registers, payout wallet, and profile from on-chain ENS records. It can list one-off, recurring, or permanent products in an on-chain catalogue and share each product through a public shop, payment link, or QR code. Before signing, a customer sees exactly what they will pay and what the business is guaranteed to receive. Same-asset USDC purchases settle directly. Plain ETH can be wrapped to WETH when required, while supported cross-asset register orders can use the UNICA market on Uniswap v4. Two payments are demonstrated on Sepolia: a 2 USDC purchase that settled directly, and a register order paid in WETH that converted to USDC through the UNICA market on Uniswap v4, verified on-chain and indexed. A receipt says Paid only after UNICA's evidence rules verify the payment on-chain. Receipts identify the business and customer through forward-verified ENS names, include the transaction and explorer link, and report The Graph indexing only when the deployed subgraph returns that specific payment. Customers can view their purchases, while businesses can view payments and customers by verified ENS name. The holder of unica.eth can set up a new business through the application. The app derives the required ENS record and lineage operations from current chain state and presents each transaction for separate wallet approval. The market infrastructure is deployed and source-verified across five test networks; the submitted identity, catalogue, shop, and demonstrated purchase run on Ethereum Sepolia. Testnet only, no real value, and unaudited.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry: a market registry and factory, the UnicaMarketHook on Uniswap v4 (executor-only admission, the exact customer and amounts, a price band, an open unexpired sale), an executor, DirectSettlement for same-asset sales, ProductCatalog (one-off, recurring and permanent products with paidThrough, priced in ERC-20 assets whose deployed contracts expose readable metadata), TerminalAdmission (registers as ENS subnames with their own keys, revocable), and an ENSv2 resolver authority adapter read against the real Sepolia permissioned resolver. Vyper for the identity badge. Deployed stage by stage from the owner's own keystore after fork rehearsals, recorded into manifests, source-verified on Etherscan and Sourcify. The web app is static HTML and plain ES modules with no framework: an EIP-6963 wallet layer (MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet), hand-written ABI encoding, the ENSv2 universal resolver for reverse lookups with a forward check before any name is shown, avatar text records per ENSIP-12, a name-derived gradient when a name has none. The join screen plans a new business as exact calldata (setAddr, setText, three registerLineage rows) from the chain's current state, skips rows that already stand, and asks the wallet to sign each in turn; the product form reads any ERC-20's symbol and decimals by address before it lists; when WETH is required, the checkout wraps ETH first, waits for confirmation, then performs any required approval before initiating the purchase. A small Node companion, also deployed as a Vercel function, keeps the node URL server-side behind a same-origin RPC pipe, reads logs through Etherscan V2 with Blockscout as the fallback, derives businesses from the authority's lineage and resolver records, and applies the evidence rules that decide Paid. A The Graph subgraph indexes the hook's receipts, direct settlements and catalogue sales; the receipt panel, the customer's purchases and the business's customers read it. 670 web test cases and 729 Foundry tests, plus guards for secrets and claims, run in CI on every push. Two details worth saying: the register reads the direct settler's own OrderCreated log back rather than trusting a return value, and the checkout explicitly serializes wrapping, approval, and purchase confirmation so a subsequent transaction cannot race an unmined prerequisite. A converted sale is priced by the register from the deployment's two Chainlink feeds, crossed in the app, and the sale line names each feed, its raw answer and its publish time.

projects.title: ScalpLess
projects.description: Bot-proof Shopify drops: one human, one entry, fair onchain draws and resale capped at 110%
projects.project_description: Scalpless is a Shopify plugin and onchain protocol for hype launches like consoles, GPUs, sneakers and collectibles. When demand spikes, bots running thousands of accounts sweep the inventory in seconds and relist it at 2 to 5 times the price. CAPTCHAs, purchase limits and raffle apps don't stop them, because they are keyed to things bots can create for free: emails, cards, accounts and IP addresses. Real fans see "sold out", merchants take the blame, and resellers take the profit. Scalpless gives any Shopify merchant a fair drop in a few clicks: One human, one entry. Every entrant verifies with World ID. A uniqueness proof can only be made once per human, so each person gets one Credit Passport and one entry per drop, no matter how many wallets they use. Provably fair draw. Entrants lock a 10% refundable deposit. When entries close, a three-round weighted draw runs on Sui using onchain randomness. Losers are refunded in the same transaction and form a random waitlist. Winners must be human to claim. Winners re-confirm with World ID before claiming, so a bot that somehow farmed a win can't collect it. Flexible payment. Winners can pay in full, start a zero-default layaway (25% now plus 3 installments; a missed payment refunds 95% and passes the unit to the waitlist), or "borrow on yourself" with an uncollateralized loan backed by their World ID passport. Because the passport can't be reset, a defaulter can't escape with a new wallet: they lose access to future loans and drops. Credit limits start small and grow with on-time repayments, resale proceeds repay loans first, and lenders choose a senior or first-loss junior tranche. Resale without scalping. Each win is a claim on a real unit of the merchant's inventory, held as a non-transferable Sui object. It can't be sent to a bot or listed on an outside marketplace. Resale happens only inside Scalpless, capped at 110% of face value, and only to another verified human. Normal fulfillment. When a winner redeems, a paid Shopify order is created and the merchant ships it as usual. Every unit's lifecycle (won, paid, layaway, financed, resold, redeemed, shipped) is recorded on a public ledger and shown in the merchant dashboard. Shoppers can also pair an AI shopping agent that enters drops for them. The agent is tied to their one human identity and can enter, but only the human can claim a win.
projects.how_its_made: Scalpless is a pnpm monorepo with a Next.js web app, an Express backend, a Shopify app, a Move package on Sui testnet and a Solidity ledger on Base Sepolia. World ID (identity and agents): Shoppers verify with IDKit in the web app. On first use they create a session proof plus a one-time uniqueness proof, which mints a Credit Passport on Sui keyed to the human rather than the wallet. Winners re-verify before claiming. World ID for Agents and AgentKit let a person pair an AgentBook-registered shopping agent that can enter drops but can't claim wins. World ID is what makes uncollateralized lending viable: the "respawn problem" (default, then make a new wallet) disappears when identity can't be reset. Bridging World ID to Sui (the hacky part): Sui has no World ID verifier, so the backend verifies each proof with World's API and signs an Ed25519 attestation over a BCS payload shared between the backend and Move tests. Onchain, registry::verify checks the signature and returns an Attested "hot potato", a struct with no abilities that the protocol function must consume in the same transaction, scoped to one action on one object. This means an attestation can't be stored, replayed or reused elsewhere. The verifier key is rotatable via a script. Verifying Groth16 proofs directly onchain is on our roadmap to remove this trust assumption. Sui (draws, custody, payments, lending): The Move package handles the passport registry, drops, claims, market and lending pool, with 24 Move tests. The three-round weighted draw uses sui::random inside a private entry function, so nobody (including us) can reroll results, and losers are refunded in the draw transaction. Claims are key-only objects with no store ability, so they can only move through our module's functions; that is how the 110% resale cap and one-resale-per-human rule are enforced by the type system rather than by policy. During layaway and resale the protocol holds claims via transfer-to-object. The lending pool is a single shared object issuing SENIOR_LP and JUNIOR_LP coins, with installment repayment, an income router that applies resale proceeds and refunds to loans first, and permissionless late marking and default. We keep the invariant senior_assets + junior_assets == cash + outstanding_principal. For live demos the testnet pool uses a 10-minute loan term and 2-minute grace period so a full borrow, repay and default cycle fits in the pitch. Curvegrid MultiBaas (RWA ledger): Each claim is a tokenized unit of real merchant inventory. A mirror service follows Sui events and records every claim step and credit event on our ScalplessRWALedger contract (Foundry, 5 tests) on Base Sepolia. We deployed the ledger through MultiBaas, and the backend builds, signs and submits transactions through it, then reads MultiBaas's indexed events for the merchant dashboard. MultiBaas saved us from writing our own EVM indexer and gave the underwriting agent a queryable credit history. AI agents: An underwriting agent (Gemini) reads the borrower's onchain passport and MultiBaas-indexed credit history and proposes loan terms. It can only tighten the policy-defined terms (fees, limits), never loosen them. A keeper agent enforces repayment schedules when onchain conditions are met and explains each action. Shopify: The Shopify app includes a "Scalpless fair drop" theme app extension. Added to the product template, it reads the live drop directly from Sui in the shopper's browser (verified entries, units, required World ID level, countdown) and replaces Add to cart and Buy it now, so checkout bots have nothing to hit. Merchants launch a drop from any catalog product; our script tags it, adds it to a Drops collection and menu, and creates the Sui drop. When a winner redeems with a shipping address, the claim is burned on Sui and the backend creates a paid Shopify order for that variant, decrementing inventory. The merchant fulfills in Shopify admin as usual, and the buyer sees tracking. Known shortcuts: prices are currently in SUI rather than a stablecoin, backend state is stored in JSON files, and the app runs against public testnets from a single development store. Stablecoin settlement, a public Shopify App Store listing and trust-minimized onchain World ID verification are next.

projects.title: Iceberg
projects.description: Partially active AMM on 1inch Aqua & Uniswap v4: bots reach only the tip, the rest earns in Morpho
projects.project_description: Liquidity providers lose money to arbitrage bots every block. When ETH moves on Binance or Coinbase, an AMM's price is stale until someone trades against it. Bots trade first and keep the gap, a cost researchers call loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR). Iceberg implements the Partially Active AMM from a 2026 research paper (Ko, arXiv 2602.09887): in each block, only a fraction λ of the pool can trade. On the block's first trade the reserves are split into an active part and a passive part, and the passive part is frozen for the rest of that block. Bots can only take from the tip, so LPs lose less. The frozen part isn't idle: it sits in Morpho vaults earning yield until a trade actually needs it. The same kernel runs on two venues. On 1inch Aqua it's a set of custom SwapVM instructions; on Uniswap v4 it's a hook. A fee-aware keeper picks λ from the last six hours of real ETH prices at the pool's fee and publishes it on-chain for both venues. On Aqua, the maker holds only Morpho vault shares: each fill withdraws exactly what it needs and deposits the proceeds straight back. The same balance also backs a second strategy on 1inch's official router (Aqua shared liquidity). A weight-tracking rebalance retires the strategy when its ETH/USDC mix drifts and re-ships it balanced at the live price, without paying arbitrageurs to do it. On a minute-by-minute replay of a real day (21 Sep 2026) against a real plain Uniswap v4 pool, Iceberg cut LP losses to arbitrage by 17.6% at λ = 50% and 19.3% at λ = 39%, and the Aqua version lost exactly the same as the v4 hook. Iceberg is live on Base mainnet, and every demo trade is a real transaction on Basescan.
projects.how_its_made:
1inch Aqua / SwapVM: I wrote two custom SwapVM opcodes. PAActiveReserves (0x92) splits the strategy's balances into active and passive parts on the first fill of each block. It hands only the active part to 1inch's stock XYCSwap curve, and quotes never write storage, so a quote always equals the swap.
ChainlinkDeviationGuard (0x21) refuses to trade if the pool price drifts more than 1% from Chainlink.
IcebergRouter is 1inch's official AquaSwapVMRouter, unchanged, with these opcodes added in free slots; any other opcode falls through to 1inch's code. The router came out at 26 KB, over the contract size limit, so I moved λ policies into external ILambdaSource contracts. That brought it to 24,349 bytes, and a test fails if it grows past the limit. projects.project_description_markdown:
Liquidity providers lose money to arbitrage bots every block. When ETH moves on Binance or Coinbase, an AMM's price is stale until someone trades against it. Bots trade first and keep the gap, a cost researchers call loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR).

Iceberg implements the Partially Active AMM from a 2026 research paper (Ko, arXiv 2602.09887): in each block, only a fraction λ of the pool can trade. On the block's first trade the reserves are split into an active part and a passive part, and the passive part is frozen for the rest of that block. Bots can only take from the tip, so LPs lose less. The frozen part isn't idle: it sits in Morpho vaults earning yield until a trade actually needs it.

The same kernel runs on two venues. On 1inch Aqua it's a set of custom SwapVM instructions; on Uniswap v4 it's a hook. A fee-aware keeper picks λ from the last six hours of real ETH prices at the pool's fee and publishes it on-chain for both venues. On Aqua, the maker holds only Morpho vault shares: each fill withdraws exactly what it needs and deposits the proceeds straight back. The same balance also backs a second strategy on 1inch's official router (Aqua shared liquidity). A weight-tracking rebalance retires the strategy when its ETH/USDC mix drifts and re-ships it balanced at the live price, without paying arbitrageurs to do it.

On a minute-by-minute replay of a real day (21 Sep 2026) against a real plain Uniswap v4 pool, Iceberg cut LP losses to arbitrage by 17.6% at λ = 50% and 19.3% at λ = 39%, and the Aqua version lost exactly the same as the v4 hook. Iceberg is live on Base mainnet, and every demo trade is a real transaction on Basescan.

projects.title: Tap Pay
projects.description: Turn two Android phones into an ENS-verified NFC terminal with ETH-to-USDC payments.
projects.project_description: Tap turns two ordinary Android phones into a secure point-of-sale for cash-heavy merchants. A merchant enters a USDC price and broadcasts a signed payment request over NFC or QR. Before any Pay button appears, the customer’s phone verifies the request signature and resolves the merchant’s live *.tap.eth identity through ENSv2, ensuring that the name belongs to the signing wallet. Tampered, expired, foreign, or unresolved requests fail closed. The customer can pay directly in USDC or select ETH; Uniswap v3 swaps a bounded amount of ETH for the exact USDC requested, so the merchant receives the price they set. Both phones observe the onchain settlement and show success. Tap is also structured as reusable TypeScript SDKs that wallets and point-of-sale applications can integrate.
projects.how_its_made:
Tap is a Bun monorepo with an Expo/React Native Android application, a pure TypeScript core SDK, a React Native NFC SDK, and Solidity contracts tested with Foundry. Each phone creates and stores its own wallet key using Expo SecureStore. The merchant signs an EIP-712 payment request containing the merchant, token, amount, nonce, expiry, chain, contract, and ENS name. Android HCE broadcasts the request as an NDEF URL; the customer reads it using react-native-nfc-manager, with QR and verified Android App Links as fallback transports.
ENSv2 on Sepolia is the trust layer. We registered tap.eth, configured a dedicated UserRegistry and Permissioned Resolver, and used Enhanced Access Control to grant our custom TapMerchantRegistrar only the roles required to issue subnames and write merchant records. Merchants can self-register a direct *.tap.eth name from the app. During every payment, the SDK uses live ENS resolution to confirm that the signed merchant name resolves to the signing wallet. Nothing from the NFC payload is trusted or displayed before this verification succeeds.
Payments settle on Base Sepolia through TapPay, which validates signatures, expiry, amount, and replay protection before transferring USDC and emitting a merchant-specific Paid event. For ETH payments, our additive TapSwapPay adapter queries Uniswap v3 QuoterV2 across multiple fee tiers, selects the cheapest exact-output route, applies a visible maximum-input bound, and calls SwapRouter02 atomically. Unused ETH is refunded, while any swap or settlement failure reverts the complete transaction. The SDK also supports standard ERC-20 input through Permit2. This preserves the original signed request and ensures the merchant always receives the exact USDC amount requested.

projects.title: Waterline
projects.description: Proof of delivered compute. Verifies a rented GPU is the chip you paid for.
projects.project_description: GPU compute is increasingly financed, traded and lent against, but delivery is still self-reported. Waterline lets a renter verify it from inside the rented machine. One command runs a timed INT8 matrix challenge on the GPU's tensor cores. The GPU commits its answers, the API re-computes a random sample on a CPU, and a timing probe counts the cores to identify the chip. Result: PASS, DEGRADED (right chip, below rated speed) or FAIL (wrong chip or wrong answers). Each result is written to the GPU's own ENS name and rolled up to its provider. Failures require a World ID-verified person, and two independent reports, before a GPU is marked failed. Agents query the history through MultiBaas to avoid bad GPUs and providers. Providers can't write scores.
projects.how_its_made: Profiler (Python, CuPy, PyTorch): loaded into memory on the pod, nothing installed. Generates seeded 16k x 16k INT8 matrices bit-identical to the CPU reference, commits a Merkle root of per-row fingerprints before the sample is chosen, and counts SMs with a staircase kernel. API (FastAPI on Vercel, Redis): issues seeds, enforces the deadline, re-grades sampled rows and writes results onchain. ENSv2: our Marks contract on Sepolia is the wildcard resolver for waterline.eth, so every GPU and check resolves without registration. GPU nodes derive from provider nodes, giving per-provider roll-ups. Enhanced Access Control restricts score writes to our API. World ID for Agents: device-code approval verified server-side; per-GPU and per-provider voter IDs enforce one voice per person. A revocable mandate lets a person's agents report. Curvegrid MultiBaas: builds transactions we sign locally, indexes events and fires a webhook. Its event queries replace a backend database and drive the agent's GPU selection. 169 Python tests, Foundry contract tests, including against ENSv2 on a Sepolia fork.

projects.title: Axis
projects.description: AI treasury agent that trades on Uniswap and asks a World ID-verified human before big moves
projects.project_description: AXIS is an autonomous treasury agent with a human in the loop for the moves that matter. AI agents are starting to hold money, which forces an awkward choice: either a human signs every transaction (so the agent isn't really autonomous), or the agent can do anything (so one bug or bad decision can drain the wallet). AXIS puts a policy between the two. The agent manages a treasury of ETH and USDC on Sepolia and keeps it near a 50/50 target. Every cycle it values the portfolio with a live Uniswap quote. When the allocation drifts more than 10% from target, it proposes a rebalancing trade, and a policy engine sorts the trade into one of three tiers: Small trades (≤ 0.002 ETH) execute on Uniswap immediately, no human needed. Medium trades (up to 0.02 ETH) are held until the treasury owner completes a fresh World ID verification for that specific trade. The backend validates the proof itself; the browser's word is never trusted. Large trades, or anything over the 24h budget, are blocked outright and nobody can approve them. Before any of that, the agent is switched off. The owner turns it on by connecting Uniswap Wallet and signing a gasless EIP-712 "mandate" that sets a max per trade, a daily limit and an expiry. The policy enforces those limits, and the owner can revoke the mandate at any time with another signature from the same wallet, which pauses the agent immediately. A World ID approval is bound to a single proposal and can only be used once. It has to be recent (≤ 120s), and it must come from the same verified human who owns the treasury, matched on World ID's pairwise subject. If the user cancels, World ID returns an error, the approval window expires, or a different person verifies, the proposal is rejected and no transaction is sent. The dashboard shows treasury balances and allocation, the active delegation, trades waiting for approval, charts of allocation (with the target band and rebalance markers) and treasury value over time, a rebalance history with allocation before → after, who authorized each trade (the agent alone or a World ID-verified human) and Etherscan links, plus a live activity log of every decision and its reason.
projects.how_its_made: Backend: TypeScript on Node with Express, viem for chain access, and jose for JWT verification. The agent loop, policy engine, delegation, World ID and Uniswap client are small separate modules. State is kept in memory to keep the hackathon build simple. Uniswap: all pricing and execution go through the Uniswap Trading API on Sepolia. The agent calls /quote both to value the treasury (a small probe quote gives the USDC/ETH price) and to size each trade. For native ETH input it sends the swap straight away. For USDC input it checks the Permit2 allowance, sends a one-time approve if needed, signs the quote's permitData (EIP-712 PermitSingle) with the agent key, calls /swap and broadcasts the transaction. Without extra work, the API routed our trades through both v3 and v4 pools on Sepolia, and we show the route in the UI. World ID for Agents: we integrated the sandbox as a standard OpenID Connect provider. Each medium trade starts its own authorization-code flow with PKCE (S256), a random state bound to the proposal id, a nonce, prompt=login and max_age=120 to force a fresh verification. On the callback, the backend exchanges the code with the client secret (client_secret_basic), verifies the ID token signature against World's JWKS, and checks the issuer, audience, nonce and auth_time before it lets the agent execute. The first verified pairwise sub becomes the treasury owner, and later approvals must match it. The client secret never reaches the browser. Delegation with Uniswap Wallet: the frontend uses EIP-6963 to find the Uniswap Wallet extension even when other wallets are installed, and asks it to sign an EIP-712 Mandate { owner, agent, maxTradeWei, dailyLimitWei, expiry, nonce } with eth_signTypedData_v4. The backend verifies it with viem's publicClient.verifyTypedData. That covers plain EOAs, and should also cover a Uniswap smart wallet (Calibur via EIP-7702, checked through ERC-1271), though we only tested it with a plain EOA. The nonce is single-use, and revoking requires a personal_sign from the same owner. Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript served by the backend (no build step), with Chart.js for the allocation and value charts. It supports light and dark themes and works on phone-width screens. Hacky bits worth mentioning: The Uniswap extension refused to sign because the wallet's chain didn't match the chain ID in the typed data, so the page now asks the wallet to switch to Sepolia, signs for whatever chain the wallet is actually on, and the backend verifies against that chain. Replay is still prevented by the agent address and the single-use nonce. Testnet liquidity is thin and asymmetric (ETH→USDC and USDC→ETH quotes implied very different prices), so the agent always values the treasury with the same probe direction to keep drift measurements consistent. World ID needs an HTTPS redirect URI, so we ran the local server behind a cloudflared quick tunnel and serve a sector identifier document from the backend.

projects.title: OniBlock
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook where an AI prices toxic arbitrage every block, and loses power if it's wrong.
projects.project_description: Oniblock is a Uniswap v4 hook that protects liquidity providers from toxic arbitrage without making ordinary traders pay for it. The problem. When ETH moves on Binance, a Uniswap pool's price is briefly stale. Arbitrageurs buy the cheap side and LPs absorb the loss. On Ethereum this adds up to hundreds of millions of dollars in CEX–DEX arbitrage over the past two years. Private mempools protect traders from sandwiches, but they do nothing for LPs, because the arbitrage trade itself is the problem. Fixed fees and fixed thresholds are walls: they either tax everyone or let arbitrage through. How it works. Every block, an AI decides how sensitive the fee should be. A keeper sends the pool's state to Jev, TypeSafe's typed decision model, and asks two questions in one call: How likely is it that the next block brings flow that costs LPs money? What kind is it: CEX–DEX arbitrage, split arbitrage, backrun, JIT liquidity, sandwich, or none? The state it sends is the Binance mid vs the pool price, the arbitrage edge at the base fee, flow imbalance, trade size vs depth, volatility, and recent liquidity churn. The keeper signs the answer with EIP-712 and posts it on-chain. The contract turns that answer into two bounded knobs. k, the fee sensitivity, is 0.8 × p × confidence. Only swaps that move the pool toward Binance (the arbitrage direction) pay fee = 0.30% + k × live gap, capped at 1%. Everyone else pays the base fee. The JIT penalty window runs from 10 to 100 blocks. Liquidity removed inside its window forfeits its fees to the LPs who stayed, and each position is judged by the window in force when it was added. The AI has power only while it's accurate. A settler grades each prediction against what actually happened: was the trade profitable against Binance at that moment? It posts a Brier score on-chain and to ENS. A model scoring worse than a coin flip is demoted automatically and the pool falls back to base fees. No admin is involved. ENSv2 is the identity and permission layer. oniblock.eth has its own registry and subregistries for models and pools. The keeper and settler are authorised through custom Enhanced Access Control roles on quoter. and settler.oniblock.eth, which the hook checks on every post. Revoking a role is an instant kill switch. Only the settler may write the calibration.* records on each model's name (Permissioned Resolver per-key rights). An ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver serves live data from the hook for names that are never registered: jev-v1.live.oniblock.eth returns a model's live scorecard, weth-usdc.live.oniblock.eth returns the pool's current k, JIT window and fees. The keeper and settler have ENSIP-19 primary names, and the models carry ENSIP-26 agent records. Every swap emits a receipt with the gap, k, fee, model and signature, so anyone can re-check the pricing.
projects.how_its_made: Architecture. Four pieces: a Uniswap v4 hook (Solidity, Foundry), a keeper and settler (TypeScript, viem), an ENSv2 setup, and a Next.js app. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia against the real v4 PoolManager and the ENSv2 Sepolia contracts. The hook (OniblockHook.sol). Dynamic fee: beforeSwap returns fee | OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. The fee is computed only from on-chain state: the pool price vs the last attested Binance mid, and the attested k. Contracts can't call a model, so the model's opinion is pushed in beforehand as a signed attestation, and beforeSwap only reads it. Directional: only swaps that move the pool toward the mid pay the gap premium. Split-arb resistant: a per-block high-water anchor makes a split arbitrage pay the first sub-swap's fee on every part. Never reverts in the swap path: a stale oracle falls back to a conservative fee, and all data checks happen in the keeper's setAttestation transaction. beforeSwap hands the fee to afterSwap through transient storage, which emits a Receipt event with every input. JIT: built on OpenZeppelin's LiquidityPenaltyHook, with two changes: The penalty window is set by the model per block, and each position is judged by the window in force when it was added. When the last LP exits inside the window we park the penalty as ERC-6909 claims instead of reverting, so withdrawals never brick. Calibration gate: k comes from the model only while its node is allowlisted and its on-chain Brier score is under 0.25. Tests: 146 Foundry tests, including fork tests against real ENSv2 bytecode. The AI: our fine-tuned Kev-0.8B. Why Kev: Kev is an open-weights decision model, a LoRA adapter plus a pointer head on Qwen3.5. You send a state and typed questions, and it returns calibrated probabilities with no generated text. That's fast and cheap enough for a per-block decision, and we can fine-tune it ourselves. Fallback: a deterministic heuristic, posted under its own ENS model name so Kev is never blamed for it. Keeper and settler. Keeper: reads the pool, Binance and recent liquidity events, calls Kev, signs an EIP-712 attestation, and posts it first in the block with its own priority fee. It only posts when the new attestation would actually change pricing. Settler: grades each receipt against the Binance price at that swap's block (was the flow profitable against Binance after the fee?), computes Brier scores, and writes them to the hook and to ENS text records. Tests: 271 service tests. ENSv2 (partner tech). Registries: oniblock.eth is registered through the commit-reveal ETHRegistrar, with its own registry and subregistries deployed via VerifiableFactory. Roles: custom EAC role bits (ROLE_QUOTER, ROLE_SETTLER) on quoter. and settler.oniblock.eth are the hook's permission system, read through our EnsV2RoleOracle. Revoking a role is a kill switch. Per-key permissions: the PermissionedResolver grants the settler alone the right to write the calibration.* keys. Even the owner can't forge a model's score without a visible grant. Wildcard resolver: a custom ENSIP-10 resolver on live.oniblock.eth computes records straight from hook storage for names that are never registered: kev-v1.live.oniblock.eth returns Kev's live scorecard. projects.project_description_markdown:
Oniblock is a Uniswap v4 hook that protects liquidity providers from toxic arbitrage without making ordinary traders pay for it.

The problem. When ETH moves on Binance, a Uniswap pool's price is briefly stale. Arbitrageurs buy the cheap side and LPs absorb the loss. On Ethereum this adds up to hundreds of millions of dollars in CEX–DEX arbitrage over the past two years. Private mempools protect traders from sandwiches, but they do nothing for LPs, because the arbitrage trade itself is the problem. Fixed fees and fixed thresholds are walls: they either tax everyone or let arbitrage through.

How it works.
- Every block, an AI decides how sensitive the fee should be. A keeper sends the pool's state to Jev, TypeSafe's typed decision model, and asks two questions in one call:
  - How likely is it that the next block brings flow that costs LPs money?
  - What kind is it: CEX–DEX arbitrage, split arbitrage, backrun, JIT liquidity, sandwich, or none?

  The state it sends is the Binance mid vs the pool price, the arbitrage edge at the base fee, flow imbalance, trade size vs depth, volatility, and recent liquidity churn. The keeper signs the answer with EIP-712 and posts it on-chain.
- The contract turns that answer into two bounded knobs.
  - k, the fee sensitivity, is 0.8 × p × confidence. Only swaps that move the pool toward Binance (the arbitrage direction) pay fee = 0.30% + k × live gap, capped at 1%. Everyone else pays the base fee.
  - The JIT penalty window runs from 10 to 100 blocks. Liquidity removed inside its window forfeits its fees to the LPs who stayed, and each position is judged by the window in force when it was added.
- The AI has power only while it's accurate. A settler grades each prediction against what actually happened: was the trade profitable against Binance at that moment? It posts a Brier score on-chain and to ENS. A model scoring worse than a coin flip is demoted automatically and the pool falls back to base fees. No admin is involved.
- ENSv2 is the identity and permission layer.
  - oniblock.eth has its own registry and subregistries for models and pools.
  - The keeper and settler are authorised through custom Enhanced Access Control roles on quoter. and settler.oniblock.eth, which the hook checks on every post. Revoking a role is an instant kill switch.
  - Only the settler may write the calibration.* records on each model's name (Permissioned Resolver per-key rights).
  - An ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver serves live data from the hook for names that are never registered: jev-v1.live.oniblock.eth returns a model's live scorecard, weth-usdc.live.oniblock.eth returns the pool's current k, JIT window and fees.
  - The keeper and settler have ENSIP-19 primary names, and the models carry ENSIP-26 agent records.
- Every swap emits a receipt with the gap, k, fee, model and signature, so anyone can re-check the pricing.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Architecture. Four pieces: a Uniswap v4 hook (Solidity, Foundry), a keeper and settler (TypeScript, viem), an ENSv2 setup, and a Next.js app. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia against the real v4 PoolManager and the ENSv2 Sepolia contracts.

The hook (OniblockHook.sol).
- Dynamic fee: beforeSwap returns fee | OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. The fee is computed only from on-chain state: the pool price vs the last attested Binance mid, and the attested k. Contracts can't call a model, so the model's opinion is pushed in beforehand as a signed attestation, and beforeSwap only reads it.
- Directional: only swaps that move the pool toward the mid pay the gap premium.
- Split-arb resistant: a per-block high-water anchor makes a split arbitrage pay the first sub-swap's fee on every part.
- Never reverts in the swap path: a stale oracle falls back to a conservative fee, and all data checks happen in the keeper's setAttestation transaction. beforeSwap hands the fee to afterSwap through transient storage, which emits a Receipt event with every input.
- JIT: built on OpenZeppelin's LiquidityPenaltyHook, with two changes:
  - The penalty window is set by the model per block, and each position is judged by the window in force when it was added.
  - When the last LP exits inside the window we park the penalty as ERC-6909 claims instead of reverting, so withdrawals never brick.
- Calibration gate: k comes from the model only while its node is allowlisted and its on-chain Brier score is under 0.25.
- Tests: 146 Foundry tests, including fork tests against real ENSv2 bytecode.

The AI: our fine-tuned Kev-0.8B.
- Why Kev: Kev is an open-weights decision model, a LoRA adapter plus a pointer head on Qwen3.5. You send a state and typed questions, and it returns calibrated probabilities with no generated text. That's fast and cheap enough for a per-block decision, and we can fine-tune it ourselves.
- Fallback: a deterministic heuristic, posted under its own ENS model name so Kev is never blamed for it.

Keeper and settler.
- Keeper: reads the pool, Binance and recent liquidity events, calls Kev, signs an EIP-712 attestation, and posts it first in the block with its own priority fee. It only posts when the new attestation would actually change pricing.
- Settler: grades each receipt against the Binance price at that swap's block (was the flow profitable against Binance after the fee?), computes Brier scores, and writes them to the hook and to ENS text records.
- Tests: 271 service tests.

ENSv2 (partner tech).
- Registries: oniblock.eth is registered through the commit-reveal ETHRegistrar, with its own registry and subregistries deployed via VerifiableFactory.
- Roles: custom EAC role bits (ROLE_QUOTER, ROLE_SETTLER) on quoter. and settler.oniblock.eth are the hook's permission system, read through our EnsV2RoleOracle. Revoking a role is a kill switch.

- Wildcard resolver: a custom ENSIP-10 resolver on live.oniblock.eth computes records straight from hook storage for names that are never registered: kev-v1.live.oniblock.eth returns Kev's live scorecard.
- Primary names and agent records: ENSIP-19 primary names for the keeper and settler wallets, and ENSIP-26 agent-endpoint[web] records on each model name.
- Why it matters: ENS makes the AI an accountable identity with a public, tamper-evident scorecard, rather than an address in a config file.

The app. Next.js, server-side reads through UniversalResolverV2.
- A server-signed Swap button lets anyone trade without a wallet.
- Every trade is mirrored onto a plain v4 pool deployed next to ours, so the headline "Oniblock saved LPs" compares identical flow.
