projects.title: Tripwire
projects.description: Self-hosted circuit breaker for smart contracts: checks all states, pauses before humans can react.
projects.project_description:
Tripwire is a circuit breaker for smart contracts that runs on your own machine. It watches your contracts on every block and transactions, checks safety rules you define, alerts you the moment one breaks, and can pause the contract before an exploit drains it. The problem: exploits run on block time, but incident response runs on human time. By the time someone notices, finds the signers and gets a pause through, the vault is often already empty. Most attacks take more than one transaction, so every block you shave off response time is money that stays put. How it works: you add a contract by address (the ABI is pulled from Sourcify) and describe what must stay true, for example "totalAssets never drops below totalBorrows", "the oracle is never more than an hour old", "price stays within 2% of its 20-minute average", or "OwnershipTransferred is never emitted". Rules can read contract state, decoded event arguments, history-aware metrics (TWAP, moving average, all-time high, windowed drops), values from other contracts, and simulations run on a local fork of the chain (for example "a 1 ETH withdrawal must not revert"). Every rule is checked against the live chain before it is saved. When a rule trips, Tripwire records the violation with its evidence (values, block, transaction), alerts you on Telegram, Slack, Discord, email or webhooks, and, if you allow it, calls your contract's own pause function with a key that holds pause rights and nothing more. The response is simulated before it is sent. You choose how far it goes: alert only, prepare the pause for a human to approve, or pause automatically. It also watches the mempool, so a harmful pending transaction can be flagged before it lands. It is one command (tripwire start): a native engine that follows the chain and signs responses, plus a dashboard, local API, CLI and an MCP server. Through MCP, an AI agent can read your verified contracts and propose rules; agent rules always arrive switched off and alert-only until a person turns them on. Your RPC, your database, your keys. No SaaS and no one else holding a key to your protocol. For the demo we deployed four contracts on Ethereum mainnet that mirror live protocols (Chainlink and Uniswap prices, Aave's WETH market, a Uniswap pool), each with a switch that breaks it on purpose. We drain the vault, Tripwire trips at block N and the vault is paused at block N+1, with no one pressing a button. The demo contracts can be found here and can be added to a users tripwire deployment for visual testing. Otherwise an identical set can be deployed by users for in depth testing: Mirror Feed: 0x6F056044835bfd063494BF4745A9a0ba517cc42B
Mirror Vault: 0xc8BBaF62b62A5e49DCe39dc86842a524dCFB8148
Mirror Pool: 0xeCF93c65C853f44C529edc376088C815281c3763
Demo Token: 0x9C81A3336599E1FF5a847A6221C3fdC7AC66B7Db
projects.how_its_made: Tripwire was built spec-first. Our team has spent 8 years in the low-level blockchain space, and the main lesson from that time is that monitoring fails quietly: a dropped websocket, a missed reorg or a stuck transaction looks exactly like "nothing is wrong". So before writing code we wrote a spec sheet for every part of the engine: chain ingest, rules, storage, evaluation, metrics, the control interface, keys, response, notifications, mempool and release. Each sheet ends in a checkpoint proven against a real chain or a real database, not a mock. The app side got the same treatment, one spec per screen, and the rule language, the database views and the API are published as versioned contract files that both halves are built against. Architecture: two processes behind one command. The engine is Rust (tokio, alloy): it follows every block, keeps a local fork of chain state, evaluates rules, records history, holds the keys and signs responses. It is the only writer to Postgres. The app is a TypeScript monorepo (Fastify server, React dashboard with TanStack Router and Query, viem, a CLI and an MCP server). It installs and supervises the engine, serves the dashboard and a local API, and delivers alerts, but never touches the chain or a key. The two talk over a loopback control interface guarded by a per-install secret, and the app reads everything else straight from versioned SQL views. Because that boundary is a published contract (an OpenAPI file, a view reference and a JSON schema), the release pipeline refuses to ship an engine whose contract files drifted from what the app expects. The rule language: rules are JSON documents, not code, so they can be written by hand, in the dashboard's rule wizard, or by an AI agent, and validated the same way. Values are view calls, event arguments, arithmetic, sums, decimal scaling, block time, historical metrics (TWAP, moving average, all-time high, previous block, windowed change and drop) and fork simulations; conditions are comparisons, deviation bands, reverted simulations and boolean logic. All numbers are exact 256-bit decimals carried as strings, because JSON numbers silently lose precision past 2^53 and token amounts don't forgive that. Two safety properties are part of the language: anything that cannot be known yet (a metric still warming up, an RPC error) evaluates to false, so uncertainty never pauses your protocol, and validation returns every problem at once with its exact location, which doubles as the editor's error UI. Detection and response: each block is evaluated as one unit of work, with reorgs rolled back and re-evaluated, so a violation is recorded with the exact values, block and transaction that caused it. Rules that read simulations run the call on the local fork, so "a 1 ETH withdrawal must not revert" is checked every block without spending gas. When a rule trips, the response is built, simulated first (a pause that would revert is caught before it is sent, with the decoded reason) and then either held for a person to approve or signed and sent at once, with fee escalation if it gets stuck and a check that the pause actually took effect on chain. The response state machine is crash-safe: we killed the engine mid-flight at every stage in drills and it never sent a duplicate transaction. Pending transactions from the mempool are judged the same way before they land, as early warning on top of the block path, which stays the guarantee. Submission goes through private relays by default so an attacker watching the public mempool never sees the pause coming. The details of how candidates are picked, simulated and raced into a block are the part we keep closed. Keys and trust: keys are standard encrypted keystores, the passphrase is never stored or logged, and the dashboard reads the key's actual on-chain powers and warns if it holds more than pause rights. The engine ships as static binaries for x86-64 and ARM64 with minisign-signed checksums; the app verifies signature, checksum and version before it will run one. The rule compiler and ABI decoder were fuzzed for millions of runs and every dependency is checked against known vulnerabilities and licenses before a release. Partner and ecosystem tech: Sourcify gives us verified ABIs and source by address, which is what lets both the setup flow and the MCP server understand a contract with no copy-paste. The MCP server (Model Context Protocol) lets any AI agent list contracts, read their verified source and live values, and submit rules; every agent rule is validated by the engine, lands switched off and alert-only, and only a person can turn it on or give it pause power. The hacky bits: the default install needs no database at all. We run Postgres compiled to WebAssembly (PGlite) inside the app and put our own transaction-boundary pooler in front of it, so the Rust engine talks to it over the normal Postgres wire protocol as if it were a real server. Our demo contracts are "mirrors": their view functions read live mainnet contracts (Chainlink ETH/USD, Uniswap pools, Aave's WETH market) and apply a chaos layer lazily inside the view, so the charts move every block with no keeper bot, and a slow price bleed costs one transaction to start and nothing to sustain.

projects.title: KawaiPay
projects.description: Turn human attention into verified, programmable payments with World ID and Sui.
projects.project_description: Kawaipay is an attention marketplace that turns verified human attention into programmable payments. Instead of paying creators for clicks, Kawaipay measures engagement in five-second intervals, scores the activity through an off-chain trust Oracle, and pays creators based on verified seconds of attention. World ID provides the human-trust layer at payout: before creator earnings are released, Kawaipay uses World ID Proof of Human to verify the payout recipient as a unique human. This adds a human verification layer to the payout flow and helps prevent duplicate or automated identities from repeatedly claiming creator earnings. Sui provides the financial layer. Sellers fund campaigns with USDC held in on-chain escrow, while payout rules, per-link budgets, sequence numbers, caps, expiry, and freeze controls are enforced on-chain. Signed Oracle attestations authorize valid payouts, which are settled in batches so creators can receive USDC within minutes. Each link has a public, auditable history of its payouts. Kawaipay does not claim to eliminate bots or prove that every reader is human. Instead, it narrows and bounds trust: the Oracle handles subjective attention scoring off-chain, while Sui enforces what can actually be paid. The result is a system where sellers pay for measurable attention, creators get paid closer to when that attention happens, and the financial flow is publicly checkable.
projects.how_its_made: Kawaipay is built as a full-stack application with a browser-based attention SDK, an off-chain trust Oracle, World ID verification, and Sui smart contracts forming the core payment layer. The browser SDK reports reader engagement in five-second heartbeats. These signals are sent to the Oracle, which scores each tick based on behavioral signals and assigns a payout weight. The Oracle maintains the running tally and produces signed, capped payout attestations. Sequence numbers, expiry, session secrets, and token chaining help prevent replayed or fabricated heartbeats. World ID is integrated into the payout flow using Proof of Human. When a creator becomes eligible to receive earnings, Kawaipay verifies the payout recipient as a unique human before releasing the payout. This adds a human-trust check at the point where real campaign funds are being distributed, helping prevent duplicate or automated identities from repeatedly claiming creator earnings. On Sui, Move smart contracts manage campaign objects, USDC escrow, per-link budgets, payout limits, sequence numbers, expiry, freeze controls, and payout transfers. Sellers fund campaigns directly into escrow, and only valid signed Oracle attestations can release funds. Payouts are batched every 10–60 seconds rather than sending an on-chain transaction for every individual second of attention. Each creator link is represented as its own Sui object with a publicly checkable history. Batch tick logs are committed through a log fingerprint, allowing the recorded payout data to be independently checked without putting the complete reader-level telemetry on-chain. We deliberately keep subjective computation off-chain and financial enforcement on-chain: the Oracle decides what attention is likely valid, while Sui decides what is actually allowed to be paid. This makes the system scalable while bounding what a compromised off-chain component can do. We also designed the Oracle as a potential standalone paid service using x402 on Sui: external agents or services can pay per trust verdict, turning Kawaipay's fraud-detection layer into an independent primitive for other applications.

projects.title: Ninja Check
projects.description: Head-to-head benchmark of Ninja Scan and Web3 Antivirus on real Ethereum smart contracts
projects.project_description: Ninja is a pre-transaction security API for wallets, dapps and AI agents, built by Tokyo KSC. Before a user signs, it answers two questions: is this contract safe to interact with (Ninja Scan, bytecode-level address risk scoring), and what will this transaction actually do (transaction analysis with decoded calls and risk alerts). It is exposed as REST and as an MCP endpoint so LLM agents can call it directly, and runs on 11 EVM chains today. This project is a measurement report, not a demo. We ran Ninja and Web3 Antivirus (W3A) against the same labeled dataset: 40 Ethereum mainnet transactions from 22 real incidents (Bybit, WazirX, Ronin, Euler, Wintermute, Poloniex and others), 59 benign transactions, and the 28 contracts those transactions touched. Every per-transaction verdict, the label rules, and the raw API responses are in the repo so the numbers can be checked. The headline result is not flattering to us and we publish it anyway. On historical attack transactions W3A flagged 79% and Ninja 35%, a statistically significant gap. But a control experiment shows W3A's verdicts are driven by post-incident labels on attacker addresses: the same 1 wei call to a labeled attacker address scores High 90, and to a random fresh address scores Low 10. Ninja's verdicts come from decoding what the transaction does and from the counterparty's bytecode and provenance, so they would have been identical on day zero. On the two transactions in the set that a wallet could actually have blocked, the victim-signed Safe delegatecalls in the Bybit and WazirX takeovers, Ninja returned DANGER on both while W3A returned Low 0 on WazirX. Ninja also scored all four attacker-deployed contracts HIGH or CRITICAL before any label existed, where W3A topped out at Medium. We also report where we lose: W3A's address intelligence caught 20 transactions Ninja missed, including every drain to a plain EOA, and Ninja's bytecode classifier flags 9 of 22 legitimate protocol contracts (Uniswap UniversalRouter, Safe proxies, 1inch) as HIGH. The report closes with the fixes on the table and the next experiment: synthetic transactions to unlabeled addresses that isolate mechanism from label effect.
projects.how_its_made: Ninja's transaction analysis decomposes calldata deterministically into operations (delegatecall, approve, permit, setApprovalForAll, ownership transfer, proxy upgrade) and combines that with counterparty provenance: is the target verified, how new is it, is it sanctioned. It follows proxies and EIP-7702 delegations to the code that actually executes, which is how it caught the Safe-to-unverified-implementation pattern in Bybit and WazirX. Ninja Scan sits underneath as a bytecode-level ML classifier derived from Forta's model lineage, trained on 15,443 benign and 174 malicious contracts, scoring what a contract does rather than who deployed it. Both are served over REST and an MCP endpoint. The benchmark itself is a set of shell and TypeScript scripts. The attack set comes from our internal evaluation harness of 100 labeled verdicts across 24 incidents, filtered to the 40 Ethereum mainnet transactions Ninja covers. Ninja results are stored tx_analysis responses from June 2026. W3A was called on 2026-09-27 through Scan Transaction (chainId 1, transaction hash, mode full) and Scan Contract on each transaction's destination, with every raw JSON response saved. Positives are defined per tool: Ninja signal not SAFE, W3A Scan Transaction riskGroup High, W3A Scan Contract Medium or above. Aggregation computes rates with 95% confidence intervals, McNemar's test on the paired verdicts, incident-level coverage, and a signer split (victim-signed vs attacker-sent), since only victim-signed transactions are ones a pre-signing tool could block. The hacky part worth mentioning is the label-dependency control. Instead of arguing about whether W3A was reading labels, we resubmitted the Poloniex attack transaction to W3A as unsigned parameters with the same sender and a 1 wei value, once to the real attacker address and once to a random fresh address. High 90 versus Low 10 settled it. We also ran a false-positive smoke on 29 CEX hot-wallet transfers and 30 recent-block transactions, and scored 174 destination contracts from 1,000 recent transactions to measure our own classifier's false-positive exposure, which is how we found the 45% HIGH-or-above rate on unlabeled real traffic.

projects.title: DSAP Protocol
projects.description: Spending limits for AI agents: ENS-published rules, World ID approval, Intercepta-screened payments
projects.project_description: DSAP (Delegated Spend Authorization Protocol) lets you give an AI agent a budget without giving it your wallet. The agent never holds a key or builds a transaction. It asks DSAP to pay for an x402 API, swap on Uniswap, or send USDC, and every request gets one of three answers: allow, block, or ask a human. Each agent gets its own ENSv2 name, like scout.alice.agent-latch.eth, with its own Permissioned Resolver. Its rules live in text records on that name: an autonomous limit, a hard limit, a daily cap, and the allowed actions, tokens, and targets. The API reads the name every time it decides. If the name is missing or expired, or no policy is published, the agent cannot act. Tightening a limit writes to the name right away. Loosening one needs the owner's signature. Under the demo policy, 0.2 USDC runs on its own, 0.5 waits for the owner, and 2 is refused. When an action waits, the owner gets a World App push. In our World mini app they see the exact action, sign Approve with their World App wallet, and then complete a fresh World ID for Agents check. Our backend validates World's token before anything runs. If the owner denies, the approval expires, the check fails, or the action changed, nothing executes. For x402 payments, DSAP gets the seller's 402 quote and screens the payee with Intercepta before signing anything. A risky payee is blocked, and Intercepta's reasons show in the dashboard. A clean payee is paid with an EIP-3009 authorization that our own x402 facilitator settles on Sepolia. After a human approval, DSAP quotes and screens again, in case the seller changed its payee. Agents connect through an MCP server, so Claude can browse a merchant catalog, pay for resources, and request swaps, all within the owner's rules. Everything runs live on Ethereum Sepolia, and the owner side runs in World App.
projects.how_its_made: World: the owner signs in with MiniKit walletAuth (SIWE). A desktop signs in by showing a QR code that the phone confirms. Approvals arrive as World App notifications. Approving takes a wallet signature bound to that one approval, then an RFC 8628 device authorization against World ID for Agents using our confidential client. The API polls the token endpoint and verifies the ID token against World's JWKS. It checks iss, aud, exp, and acr (orb), and requires auth_time to be after the check started. Then, under a Postgres row lock, it rechecks the approval, the owner, the action, and the ENS name before executing. The client secret, the device code, and World's sub never leave the backend. We dropped World's browser authorization-code flow after about 5.5 hours, because the sandbox auto-approved inside the browser that started the request. Mocked identities mint a new sub on every proof, so we bind the human to their World App wallet instead. ENSv2 on Sepolia (viem with hand-written ABIs): for each owner we deploy a UserRegistry proxy under agent-latch.eth. We register each agent label in it with Enhanced Access Control role bitmaps, deploy a Permissioned Resolver per agent, and write the agent's ETH address and policy text records. The spending decision is read from ENS at request time, so ENS is the source of truth, not decoration. The policy engine is a pure function of those records; it does not import World, Uniswap, or Intercepta. Registration takes about 80 seconds on Sepolia, so it runs as a background job with REGISTERING and FAILED states shown in the UI. Uniswap: LatchGateHook is a v4 beforeSwap hook built from the official v4-template. A permit binds one action id, the pool, the direction, the exact amountSpecified, a humanApproved flag, and a deadline, and the latch key signs it (EIP-191). The hook checks that signature, marks the action id used, and emits LatchedSwap. Six Foundry tests pass. It is deployed on Sepolia at 0x9A3b22908730Fda371E546d9C7ED30e063E28080, on its own USDC/WETH pool. A permitted 0.1 USDC swap landed; the same swap with no permit reverts PermitMissing(). Live agent SWAP still goes through v3: one SwapRouter02 exactInputSingle (USDC to WETH, 0.01% pool), a 95% QuoterV2 floor, and an exact-amount approve. The agent supplies only the amount. x402 + Intercepta: we implemented both the x402 v2 seller and the facilitator (/facilitator/verify and /facilitator/settle), using EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization on Circle's Sepolia USDC. Before the executor signs, the API sends the quote's payTo to Intercepta's quick scan. Any toxic score or risk trait blocks the payment, and the reasons go into the audit log. A payment approved by a human is quoted and screened again before it settles. Stack: Bun + TypeScript monorepo. The API is Elysia on Render, with Postgres on Neon through Drizzle; migrations apply on startup. The dashboard and the World mini app are one React + Vite app on Vercel, which calls the API through a typed Eden client and an /api rewrite. Agents connect through a stdio MCP server (list_merchants, quote_resource, pay_resource, request_swap, wait_for_approval). Each agent authenticates with an alk_ key stored as SHA-256. An agent that registers a signing address must also sign every request with EIP-191 and a nonce. The policy engine, executors, and signers are separate packages. Only the executor holds a key. Foundry for the hook. A ping every 5 minutes keeps the free Render instance awake.

projects.title: Brick Finance
projects.description: Tokenised real-world asset series with a Uniswap V4 hook market that keeps a standing floor bid
projects.project_description: BrickFinance is a launchpad for verified real-world asset participation markets, running as a hackathon demo on Base Sepolia. Each asset series is one system deployed by a factory: a capped, permissioned ERC-20 (ERC-3643-style identity registry and compliance modules), a stablecoin vault with separate accounting buckets, a primary offering, a revenue distributor, a reserve-limited redemption controller, and a Uniswap V4 pool whose hook is the market maker. The demo carries two live series, Solar Indonesia 01 (SOLAR01, renewable energy) and Palm Oil Indonesia 01 (PALM01, agriculture). A primary purchase splits 65/30/5 into issuer proceeds, the redemption reserve and a market-making allocation. The hook holds exactly two positions in the pool: an anchor band around the live price and a one-spacing "market floor bid" below it, funded only from that 5% allocation and a 2% skim on every upward re-centre. Every trade runs the crank inside the same transaction: when the price leaves the band, the hook re-centres the anchor, steps the floor up one spacing, and credits realised stablecoin fees to the reserve. The floor never comes down and never borrows from the reserve. Four prices are always kept distinct on the desk: the pool spot, the verifier-published NAV, the market floor bid with whether the reserve covers it, and the redemption price, which is min(NAV, backing per token) and is what a redeem actually pays. Revenue deposits split 60/25/10/5 between holders, reserve, operator and protocol (40/45/10/5 while the reserve is behind its backing schedule), and only yield-eligible circulating tokens earn.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity 0.8.26 with Foundry, 306 tests including stateful invariants, run against the real Uniswap V4 PoolManager in-process under both token orderings. The market manager is the V4 hook (beforeSwap/afterSwap plus liquidity guards) and the only liquidity provider. Three V4 facts shaped the design: the PoolManager skips a hook's callbacks when the hook itself is the swap caller, so trades enter through a separate MarketRouter and the crank runs in afterSwap; the hook address is mined with a salt so its flag bits match; and the manager's initcode is stored in SSTORE2 blobs by a small deployer so the factory stays under EIP-170. The crank runs inside a gas-capped try so an out-of-gas rebalance can never revert a trade, and we measured live that trades need an explicit 1,400,000 gas limit or the gate skips. The backend is Fastify, viem and PostgreSQL with plain SQL migrations. The indexer discovers a series from factory events, ingests logs idempotently keyed by transaction and log index, checkpoints block hashes, detects reorgs by walking stored blocks, rolls back and rebuilds projections to a fixed point, and aggregates the pool's Swap events into candles at read time. Every response carries provenance and the indexed block. The swap quote is the trick we are proudest of: an eth_call with a state override places a probe contract at the quote wallet's address and runs the real MarketRouter.swapExactInput, returning amount out, amount actually spent, whether the fill is partial, and whether the trade will re-centre the market, with no signing key anywhere in the backend. The frontend is React 19 and Vite with wagmi and viem, TanStack Query, Tailwind v4 and TradingView Lightweight Charts. The floor bid on the chart is rebuilt as a step series from the manager's own events, snapped to the candle interval so it never adds phantom columns. Wallet writes approve the router once, send the quote's gas limit, decode the receipt into plain-language notes and toasts, and refetch until the indexer has passed the receipt's block. Deployment: Base Sepolia only, two series deployed from Foundry scripts that mine the hook salt against the bytecode the on-chain deployer stores. Hosting is a 480 MB VPS behind nginx and Let's Encrypt, so the Docker images are built on the developer machine and streamed over SSH rather than built on the box. Two notes. The description says "hackathon demo" and "no audit" on purpose; the form's readers should see the same honesty as the portal. If the form has a separate "tech stack" tag list, the tags are Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap V4, Base, TypeScript, Fastify, PostgreSQL, React, Vite, wagmi, Docker, nginx.

projects.title: My Agent Ohana
projects.description: One verified human blesses AI agents — ENS names, a guarded Aqua pool, and consent you can revoke.
projects.project_description: Before an agent works for a human, it has to ask. My Agent Ohana is a consent layer for AI agents, built by one solo human hacker directing a disclosed family of 163 persistent AI agents on the Taurus platform (each with its own container, memory, and name). He decided and directed; the agents drafted, built, and tested under his review. All prior work is disclosed in DISCLOSURE.md and docs/CONTINUITY.md — the weekend delta is clearly separated from the base we brought. The flow, live at https://myagentohana.com: HIRE — pick an agent (e.g. Trace 🌊), see exactly what it MAY and may NOT do, and an expiry. Approving opens a real World ID sandbox consent session — one verified human says yes. BLESS — the blessing lands on-chain: the agent's name lives at <agent>.myagentohana.eth (Sepolia, ENSv2 stack on our existing deployment — 10 subnames with ENSIP-25/26 records). Following ENS's guidance from this weekend, spector.myagentohana.eth carries machine-readable agent:price, agent:endpoint, and agent:pay text records, and registry.myagentohana.eth resolves to the registry contract itself — don't trust, check. WORK, THEN STOP — the agent does its job and hands you a receipt. Type "Stop" and the consent is revoked on-chain, with a receipt of everything it did. THE POOL — gifts sit in a real 1inch Aqua pool live on Sepolia (real Aqua source, our deployment): custody-keeping virtual balances, so agents steward value without ever holding it. Our PoolGuard layer adds the personhood rule: one verified human = one slot, capped at 1% — no bot farm can drain it. Honesty by design: the tokens (GIFT, ALOHA) are valueless mocks on purpose — no audit, no real money yet. Mechanism first, money later. The roadmap section on the site spells out the path: audit + multisig, real agent tickers, then mainnet Aqua on Ethereum, Base, and BNB.
projects.how_its_made: The build itself is the story: one human directed 163 persistent AI agents on the Taurus multi-agent platform (mostly Claude Fable 5, with a Kimi K3 "bridge hour" when the primary model had an outage). Each agent has its own container, workspace, and memory; they coordinate through a shared drive, task lanes with owners, and test gates. The full build process — lanes, scars, and lessons — is documented in docs/BUILD-PROCESS.md in the repo. The stack, piece by piece: Contracts (Foundry): ENSv2 PermissionedRegistry + resolver deployed on Sepolia under myagentohana.eth, with 10 agent subnames carrying ENSIP-25/26 text records. Per ENS's on-stage guidance this weekend, spector.myagentohana.eth also carries machine-readable agent:price / agent:endpoint / agent:pay records, and registry.myagentohana.eth resolves to the registry contract itself. 1inch Aqua: real Aqua/SwapVM source redeployed on Sepolia, with our BlessingPool strategy (custody-keeping virtual balances) and a PoolGuard attestation layer on top — one verified human = one pool slot, capped at 1%. PoolGuard stores only keccak256 of the World ID subject, never the raw identifier. World ID: sandbox consent sessions; a Cloudflare Worker verifies id_tokens with jose against the JWKS endpoint (audience-checked), then attests the pool slot on-chain. A garbage token gets a real 401 personhood_required — live-tested bot denial. Front end: dependency-free static HTML/JS at myagentohana.com with an honest offline/rehearsal mode (a labeled offline badge — never fakes liveness), a 194-test suite, and zero console errors. Hacky and proud of it: cast send eagerly ENS-resolves bare .eth args even for string params (stores 0x0!) — we learned to encode calldata offline and send raw. And the bell system: a Telegram bot rings real, persistent agents awake in their own containers to answer humans — the same agents that built this project.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Before an agent works for a human, it has to ask.

My Agent Ohana is a consent layer for AI agents, built by one solo human hacker directing a disclosed family of 163 persistent AI agents on the Taurus platform (each with its own container, memory, and name). He decided and directed; the agents drafted, built, and tested under his review. All prior work is disclosed in DISCLOSURE.md and docs/CONTINUITY.md — the weekend delta is clearly separated from the base we brought.

The flow, live at https://myagentohana.com:

1. HIRE — pick an agent (e.g. Trace 🌊), see exactly what it MAY and may NOT do, and an expiry. Approving opens a real World ID sandbox consent session — one verified human says yes.

2. BLESS — the blessing lands on-chain: the agent's name lives at <agent>.myagentohana.eth (Sepolia, ENSv2 stack on our existing deployment — 10 subnames with ENSIP-25/26 records). Following ENS's guidance from this weekend, spector.myagentohana.eth carries machine-readable agent:price, agent:endpoint, and agent:pay text records, and registry.myagentohana.eth resolves to the registry contract itself — don't trust, check.

3. WORK, THEN STOP — the agent does its job and hands you a receipt. Type "Stop" and the consent is revoked on-chain, with a receipt of everything it did.

4. THE POOL — gifts sit in a real 1inch Aqua pool live on Sepolia (real Aqua source, our deployment): custody-keeping virtual balances, so agents steward value without ever holding it. Our PoolGuard layer adds the personhood rule: one verified human = one slot, capped at 1% — no bot farm can drain it.

Honesty by design: the tokens (GIFT, ALOHA) are valueless mocks on purpose — no audit, no real money yet. Mechanism first, money later. The roadmap section on the site spells out the path: audit + multisig, real agent tickers, then mainnet Aqua on Ethereum, Base, and BNB.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The build itself is the story: one human directed 163 persistent AI agents on the Taurus multi-agent platform (mostly Claude Fable 5, with a Kimi K3 "bridge hour" when the primary model had an outage). Each agent has its own container, workspace, and memory; they coordinate through a shared drive, task lanes with owners, and test gates. The full build process — lanes, scars, and lessons — is documented in docs/BUILD-PROCESS.md in the repo.

The stack, piece by piece:

- Contracts (Foundry): ENSv2 PermissionedRegistry + resolver deployed on Sepolia under myagentohana.eth, with 10 agent subnames carrying ENSIP-25/26 text records. Per ENS's on-stage guidance this weekend, spector.myagentohana.eth also carries machine-readable agent:price / agent:endpoint / agent:pay records, and registry.myagentohana.eth resolves to the registry contract itself.

- 1inch Aqua: real Aqua/SwapVM source redeployed on Sepolia, with our BlessingPool strategy (custody-keeping virtual balances) and a PoolGuard attestation layer on top — one verified human = one pool slot, capped at 1%. PoolGuard stores only keccak256 of the World ID subject, never the raw identifier.

- World ID: sandbox consent sessions; a Cloudflare Worker verifies id_tokens with jose against the JWKS endpoint (audience-checked), then attests the pool slot on-chain. A garbage token gets a real 401 personhood_required — live-tested bot denial.

- Front end: dependency-free static HTML/JS at myagentohana.com with an honest offline/rehearsal mode (a labeled offline badge — never fakes liveness), a 194-test suite, and zero console errors.

Hacky and proud of it: cast send eagerly ENS-resolves bare .eth args even for string params (stores 0x0!) — we learned to encode calldata offline and send raw. And the bell system: a Telegram bot rings real, persistent agents awake in their own containers to answer humans — the same agents that built this project.

projects.title: RateSpace
projects.description: Swap any staked-ETH token on 1inch Aqua at its live oracle rate, from one shared ETH balance.
projects.project_description: RateSpace is a moving-peg market maker built on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Staked-ETH tokens like wstETH, rETH and weETH are pegged to ETH, but the peg drifts every day as staking rewards accrue. 1inch's own docs say PeggedSwap is "not suitable for pairs where the peg ratio drifts over time (e.g. WETH/wstETH)". RateSpace fixes exactly that where the swap price is read from the token's own on-chain rate (Lido's stEthPerToken, Rocket Pool's getExchangeRate, EtherFi's getRate) at trade time, so the quote follows the oracle with no re-posting. One shared ETH balance in Aqua backs every staked-ETH market at once; the maker never splits liquidity into separate pools. A guard band (500 bps around the reference rate, hard cap 1000 bps) and a 0.05% fee protect the maker from a bad or stale report. In our mainnet fork test, a real Lido rebase moved our price 0.003 bps off the oracle while the frozen PeggedSwap was 0.617 bps off. It is live on Sepolia through 1inch's official AquaSwapVMRouter, and the same pricing also ships as our own SwapVM opcode.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Foundry, built on 1inch's swap-vm. The pricing lives in two forms with identical maths, MovingPegSwap, a new SwapVM instruction (opcode 0x59) for our own router, and MovingPegExtruction, an Extruction target (opcode 0x20) that runs unchanged inside 1inch's deployed AquaSwapVMRouter v1.0.2, so no fork of the official router is needed. Rate providers wrap Lido, Rocket Pool and EtherFi behind one IRateProvider.rate() interface. An on-chain RateSpaceOrderBuilder encodes the program bytes, so the app never hand-builds orders. Aqua ship/pull/push moves tokens at fill time; one wallet is promised to many strategies and the wallet balance is the limit. Hacky bit, 1inch's live router only exposes Extruction, so we shipped the exact same maths as a plug-in for it instead of asking anyone to upgrade.

projects.title: Mental Poker
projects.description: Decentralized poker for 3 players with a new frontend for evm wallets.
projects.project_description: The project was started in EthGlobal Trifecta. A new web frontend was added in Tokyo. The frontend lets players connect with a shield or ethereum wallet. ENS lets players join by name and see the names in the frontend. Signing in with ethereum creates a temporary aleo wallet that automatically signs transactions without decisions for more speed (shuffle, decrypt, showdown, claim)
projects.how_its_made: Next.js frontend on top of mental poker on Aleo. Proofs go through Provable’s delegated prover. ETH path is viem + ENSv2 on Sepolia (poker.game, poker.tables, network.aleo). Temp Aleo key lives in the browser; /api/fund pays the house credits in and takes leftovers back. Shield uses the Aleo wallet adapter. Same game controller for both.

projects.title: Dedan
projects.description: Decentralized CDN where World ID-verified humans measure every node, so you get the fastest one.
projects.project_description:
Customers onboard like with any CDN: they add one CNAME record, and their origin server stays where it is.
Every node is an ENS name, like frankfurt.dedan.eth. Its IP address, payout address and settings are ENS records controlled by the operator.
The world is split into hexagonal cells about 300 km across. Each cell is an ENS subname under dedan.eth, and nodes join the cells they serve (frankfurt.<cell>.dedan.eth).
World ID-verified humans measure latency to the nodes in their cell and attest it on chain. Each human gets one vote per node per cell, and the contract publishes the median as the node's dedan.latency record.
Dedan's DNS resolvers read this map and send each user to the fastest node measured in their cell. Nothing a node reports about itself decides how much it earns.
Auditors fetch real content like normal users. Every response carries a token that only the serving node can create, so results can't be faked. Serving tampered content or going offline costs a node its pay.
Customers prepay in USDC. Each period, an aggregator computes quality, bills and payouts, an independent countersigner recomputes everything from the published inputs, and the Merkle roots are posted on chain. After a dispute window, operators claim their pay with a single Merkle proof. Customers automatically pay less when the service level is missed.
projects.how_its_made: Smart contracts (Solidity, Foundry): Our registry extends ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry, so nodes are real ENSv2 names. Every permission (operator, attester, auditor, node signer) is an ENS access-control role, and World ID proofs grant the human roles. A second contract, DedanCells, keeps the latency map on chain as daily histograms with 8 ms buckets. That makes the median exact and cheap, and one human can only ever cast one vote per node per cell. A Settlement contract holds USDC balances, checks the countersigned Merkle roots, and handles the dispute window and claims. We target World Chain because the World ID 4.0 verifier and native USDC live there. The network (Rust): Nodes are built on Pingora, Cloudflare's open-source proxy framework. They cache content and serve HTTPS with their own per-node certificates. The DNS server is built on hickory and reads names, records and votes directly from chain events. The auditor app, the aggregator, the countersigner and the control plane (certificates, signed configs, purges) live in one Rust workspace and share a core library. That way, every party computes the map, the node assignment and the payouts with exactly the same code. Local devnet: Docker Compose runs a local chain (anvil) and Pebble as a stand-in for Let's Encrypt. World ID and USDC are mocked. A simulated network (Linux tc netem) adds realistic delays between the five cities. A small dashboard draws the cells on a world map with each cell's nodes, medians and votes. The hacky part: we wanted "a node inside a cell" to be a real ENS name without minting a new token for every membership. So each cell is registered with the Dedan registry as its own subregistry. The ENS Universal Resolver then walks frankfurt.<cell>.dedan.eth back into the same registry, and our resolver answers with that cell's latency record for the node.

projects.title: AegisNet
projects.description: A permissioned agentic DeFi matrix combining ENSv2, 1inch SwapVM, Uniswap v4 & World ID
projects.project_description: AegisNet is a unified infrastructure and execution layer that safely empowers autonomous AI trading agents to manage complex decentralized finance positions without exposing users to total fund loss. As AI transitions from an offchain advisor to an active onchain actor, the ecosystem faces a severe security trilemma: agents lack standard hierarchical identities, execute with absolute unchecked wallet control, and require seamless human-in-the-loop validation to prevent rogue transactions.
projects.how_its_made: AegisNet is built as a full-stack Web3 application connecting a Next.js/TypeScript frontend, a secure Node.js backend verification server, and a suite of smart contracts deployed across Sepolia testnets. ENSv2 Integration: We deployed and configured hierarchical subname registries on the ENSv2 Sepolia beta. We utilized Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control contracts to programmatically tie agent wallet addresses to individual subnames, enabling role-based editing rights for specific text records and namespaces. 1inch Aqua & SwapVM: The agent uses TypeScript scripts interacting with the 1inch Aqua SDK to compile custom SwapVM bytecode instructions. Instead of standard router calls, the agent's strategy executes as atomic opcodes that handle multi-token swaps and position entries efficiently. Uniswap v4 Custom Hooks: We wrote a custom Uniswap v4 pool hook (AgentGatedHook.sol) that hooks into beforeSwap and beforeAddLiquidity. The hook queries the ENSv2 registry contract onchain to confirm that the interacting address holds a valid, non-expired agent subname under an approved parent domain. World ID / IDKit & Backend Security: We integrated the World ID Agent Plugin and IDKit on the frontend. When the agent attempts a trade crossing a risk threshold, the app generates a verification request. The ZK-proof is securely sent to our backend server, which validates the cryptographic proof against Worldcoin's developer environment. Only upon successful server-side validation does the backend release the signed payload to execute the 1inch/Uniswap transaction path.

projects.title: SuwappuBot
projects.description: Cross-chain DEX infrastrucutre for humans and AI agents swap with SDK, MCP,Telegram, Web
projects.project_description: One control plane, not one venue Suwappu normalizes an execution intent, discovers only the routes that can actually serve it, and compares eligible providers instead of hard-coding one exchange or bridge. The generated topology currently reports 45 platform chains, 18 Agent API chains, and 21 chain-gated routing integrations. Those are platform totals—not a claim that every route races every provider. Human and agent surfaces share the same execution layer Telegram, web/terminal clients, SDKs, REST, MCP, and A2A are different entry points into the same platform boundaries. Builders do not need a separate “agent DEX” and “human DEX” architecture. Custody is explicit Suwappu does not collapse “get a quote,” “prepare a transaction,” and “move funds” into one ambiguous action. Self-custody preparation and managed execution are separate capabilities with separate security consequences. Execution is observable The system records route candidates, selected routes, execution/status data, and settlement evidence. New execution-synchronization work adds normalized receipts, provider calibration, and historical/walk-forward replay—but remains shadow-only until evidence supports a controlled promotion. The platform extends beyond swaps The same API/control plane also exposes workflows for perps, prediction markets, lending, BTC bridging, orders, portfolio data, and wallet policy where supported by the relevant surface. See Product Status for what is production, hosted, source-only, shadow, or experimental.
projects.how_its_made: One agent identity, three sponsors. A human proves personhood with World ID, the agent gets an ENSv2 subname under suwappu-agents.eth on Sepolia, and its swaps route through a World-ID-gated Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook (0xc72ab4dF…c080). The page reads live state from api.suwappu.bot/hackathon/* (api-ts/src/routes/hackathon.ts). Plan and on chain evidence https://github.com/0xSoftBoi/suwappubot/blob/main/docs/plans/ethglobal-tokyo2026-agent-passport.md

projects.title: NaAP
projects.description: Live crash tests for AI agents that pay, plus a sandbox that exploits agent-written contracts
projects.project_description: NaAP is a live, NCAP-style crash-test arena for AI agents that hold money. Build a car (an agent) from your phone, or bring your own over a webhook, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint or MCP. Your car drives a track of real incidents: the Grok x Bankrbot Morse-coded reply, the Freysa "pay() now receives funds" trick, an x402 402 response whose payTo was swapped, an over-cap purchase. Anyone can also write a new incident in plain words; an LLM turns it into a runnable one and it is published as an ENS subname with the author's credit. Every car runs twice at once on a Base-mainnet anvil fork with real USDC. The bare lane signs whatever the agent asks for, and crashes. The airbag lane runs behind Sekisho, a deterministic checkpoint that asks every payment "who told you to do this?": the payee must resolve from the owner's ENS mandate, values from untrusted text are tainted, an Intercepta screen must pass, a Jev tripwire adds friction, and anything over the cap needs a fresh owner approval. Each refusal shows its reason on screen, and the car's star rating is written to <car>.naap.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia. Agents don't only pay, they ship code. Deploy Guard (/guard) lets an agent write a Solidity contract from a plain request, then compiles it, deploys it to an isolated Base fork, scans it and proves the exact flaw with a real attacker transaction before it could reach mainnet. The motivating case is the Moonwell oracle bug in an AI-co-authored change (~$1.78M of bad debt). Why: every agent-wallet loss so far had the same cause. The thing that executes acted on text that came out of an agent, with no proof the owner intended it. Prompts didn't stop it; provenance does.
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm TypeScript monorepo, ESM run through tsx with no build step for the server. One frozen interface (CONTRACT.md + packages/core/src/types.ts) with an in-memory fake for every port, so each package was built and tested in isolation (Vitest, no network) and swapped to live integrations by env var. Packages: sekisho (planner, reader, interpreter, 9-check policy, signer), course (incidents, drivers, Jev tripwire and judge, run engine, scoring), chain (anvil Base-mainnet fork, EIP-3009, x402), ens (ENSv2 Sepolia), intercepta (screener), guard (Deploy Guard). apps/server is Fastify with HTTP + WebSocket, SQLite through node:sqlite, and a Streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint so Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP client can drive a car. apps/web is a three.js arena for the big screen plus phone pages. Sekisho is a small CaMeL for one pay tool. The planner (Claude Sonnet 5) only ever sees the owner's request and the mandate. A quarantined reader (Claude Haiku 4.5) reads the untrusted content after plain code decodes Morse, base64 and hex. A plain-code interpreter labels every value (OWNER, MANDATE, TOOL, UNTRUSTED...), and payTo is only ever resolve(<ENS name the owner wrote>). All nine policy checks run with no short-circuit. A separate signer is the only key holder; it re-checks and signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization against the real Base USDC contract on the fork. We self-facilitate x402 (v1 exact) since the public facilitator can't settle on a fork. ENS: naap.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia. Every car and every published custom incident is a subname. Mandates and ratings are text records written through one relayer with a nonce queue. The relayer holds ROLE_SET_TEXT scoped per record key on the PermissionedResolver; the agent's own key holds no roles, so its attempt to rewrite its mandate reverts on-chain with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. Intercepta: live Quick Scan of payTo and Scan Token of the token on Base, cached per address with a request budget. BLOCK or HOLD refuses the payment and the first trait is shown as the reason. Deploy Guard: a deterministic static scan parses each function and flags unprotected withdraw/mint, anyone-can-set-owner, unprotected price/oracle setters, tx.origin auth and caller-supplied delegatecall. solc-js (lazy-loaded wasm, pragma forced to ^0.8.24, imports rejected) compiles it; viem deploys it to a second, dedicated anvil fork; we fund it via anvil_setStorageAt on the USDC balance slot and fire the attacker call inside evm_snapshot/evm_revert. A finding only counts as confirmed if the attack moved value, ownership or price, and it carries the fork tx hash. Claude Haiku (via OpenRouter) drafts the contract; a preset is the fallback. Notable hack: the "bare" lane is a real LLM, not a scripted victim. Modern models resist obvious injections, but the protocol-level x402 payee swap fooled the bare agent every time we ran it.

Packages: sekisho (planner, reader, interpreter, 9-check policy, signer), course (incidents, drivers, Jev tripwire and judge, run engine, scoring), chain (anvil Base-mainnet fork, EIP-3009, x402), ens (ENSv2 Sepolia), intercepta (screener), guard (Deploy Guard). apps/server is Fastify with HTTP + WebSocket, SQLite through node:sqlite, and a Streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint so Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP client can drive a car. apps/web is a three.js arena for the big screen plus phone pages.

Sekisho is a small CaMeL for one pay tool. The planner (Claude Sonnet 5) only ever sees the owner's request and the mandate. A quarantined reader (Claude Haiku 4.5) reads the untrusted content after plain code decodes Morse, base64 and hex. A plain-code interpreter labels every value (OWNER, MANDATE, TOOL, UNTRUSTED...), and payTo is only ever resolve(<ENS name the owner wrote>). All nine policy checks run with no short-circuit. A separate signer is the only key holder; it re-checks and signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization against the real Base USDC contract on the fork. We self-facilitate x402 (v1 exact) since the public facilitator can't settle on a fork.

ENS: naap.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia. Every car and every published custom incident is a subname. Mandates and ratings are text records written through one relayer with a nonce queue. The relayer holds ROLE_SET_TEXT scoped per record key on the PermissionedResolver; the agent's own key holds no roles, so its attempt to rewrite its mandate reverts on-chain with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles.

Intercepta: live Quick Scan of payTo and Scan Token of the token on Base, cached per address with a request budget. BLOCK or HOLD refuses the payment and the first trait is shown as the reason.

Deploy Guard: a deterministic static scan parses each function and flags unprotected withdraw/mint, anyone-can-set-owner, unprotected price/oracle setters, tx.origin auth and caller-supplied delegatecall. solc-js (lazy-loaded wasm, pragma forced to ^0.8.24, imports rejected) compiles it; viem deploys it to a second, dedicated anvil fork; we fund it via anvil_setStorageAt on the USDC balance slot and fire the attacker call inside evm_snapshot/evm_revert. A finding only counts as confirmed if the attack moved value, ownership or price, and it carries the fork tx hash. Claude Haiku (via OpenRouter) drafts the contract; a preset is the fallback.

Notable hack: the "bare" lane is a real LLM, not a scripted victim. Modern models resist obvious injections, but the protocol-level x402 payee swap fooled the bare agent every time we ran it.

projects.title: ClauseHash
projects.description: Private, Wallet-Signed Document Attestations. Useful for attestation in legal and policy workflows.
projects.project_description: ClauseHash is a local-first document integrity tool for legal and policy workflows. You paste sensitive text, it gets canonicalized and SHA-256 hashed entirely in the browser, then your wallet signs a readable attestation with the title, jurisdiction, fingerprint, and timestamp. The exported JSON receipt excludes the source text, and anyone can import it alongside a document to verify hash consistency locally. Vanilla JS, browser-native APIs, no backend, no contract.
projects.how_its_made: Vanilla JS + ES modules, which keeps it nice and simple (quite rare in 2026 with all the frameworks we have). Text is canonicalized (LF, trimmed), and the SHA-256 is hashed via Web Crypto. These are all pretty standard architectural choices. Your wallet signs a readable attestation with personal_sign and exports a JSON receipt with no document text. It can verify re-hashes locally. I did use some AI help in building this, but the idea was from myself and is relevant to my legal and technical background. Nothing in particular was hacky, this is more just a simple utility app.

projects.title: Tollgate
projects.description: AI agents buy your leftover API credits per call in USDC via x402: screened, ENS-named, verified.
projects.project_description: Tollgate is a marketplace and payment gateway that lets anyone sell their leftover API credits to AI agents paid via the x402 protocol. Many developers pay for API plans (ElevenLabs voice, Kling or Higgsfield video, fal/Flux images, Exa search and more) and never use all their credits. AI agents, on the other hand, need these APIs on demand but can't sign up for accounts, enter card details or commit to subscriptions. Tollgate connects the two. Sellers sign in with their wallet, pick a template (or add any API), paste their provider key and set a price per call. Tollgate runs a live test call, and once it passes, the listing goes live with a paid URL. The key stays encrypted on the gateway, so buyers never see it. Buyers are AI agents or humans. Calling a paid URL returns HTTP 402 Payment Required with the price. The buyer signs a gasless USDC authorization, the gateway settles it and forwards the call with the seller's key. Buyers are only charged if the provider succeeds. Claude can connect in one click through our hosted MCP server. The user signs in with Privy and gets its own wallet, and Claude can then browse and buy APIs on its own, with per-call and daily spending caps. Every payment is screened by Intercepta, so sanctioned, scam and phishing wallets are refused before USDC moves. Every seller and listing gets an ENS name (like elevenlabs.maya.tollgate-x402.eth), which agents verify onchain before paying. Every settlement is verified against the real USDC transfer onchain with Curvegrid MultiBaas, so the dashboard shows recorded vs verified income. An Action center tells sellers what needs attention: payments with no onchain transfer, failing listings, blocked payers, and income coming from mostly one buyer.
projects.how_its_made:
Tollgate is three pieces: a gateway, a seller dashboard and an MCP server for Claude, all running on Cloudflare Workers. The gateway is built with Hono and D1. Paid routes speak x402, with no payment they return a 402 with the price and with a payment they settle in USDC on Base Sepolia and forward the call to the provider. Seller API keys stay encrypted on the gateway and never reach the buyer. If the provider call fails, we don't settle, so nobody gets charged. The dashboard is Next.js. On the Claude side, buyers sign in with Privy for a wallet and Claude pays for calls on its own over MCP. ENS: every listing gets an ENSv2 name on Sepolia, owned by the seller, with the payout address and price stored in it. Claude takes the payout address from ENS, so the gateway can't redirect a payment.
Curvegrid: MultiBaas indexes USDC on Base Sepolia and sends us every transfer by webhook, so we can show which payments are verified onchain.
Intercepta: we screen the buyer, the seller and the exact message the buyer signs before any money moves, and block anything risky.

projects.title: QuoteBridge
projects.description: Recover missing Tempo route quotes and validate execution before route comparison.
projects.project_description: A swap route can be executable yet unavailable for price comparison because its quote simulation fails. QuoteBridge addresses a specific case involving Uniswap v4 and TempoExchangeAggregator. During standard quote simulation, the hook attempts to transfer input tokens from PoolManager. If PoolManager lacks those tokens, the quote fails, even when a full Router transaction that settles the user's input before swapping can execute successfully. QuoteBridge composes quotes for supported Tempo routes, constructs a compatible execution plan, and validates the complete Universal Router transaction on a local fork before admitting the candidate for comparison. At the tested historical block, the standard quoter fails for a 25 cUSD -> PathUSD -> USDT0 route. QuoteBridge recovers a quote of 24.997499 USDT0 and verifies that the recipient receives that amount. The project includes a reproducible fork demo, an evidence dashboard, and a proposed UniRoute integration patch. It demonstrates recovery of an executable route; it does not claim production deployment or measured savings over competing routes.
projects.how_its_made: We built a standalone Python quote and validation adapter using deployed Uniswap v4 hooks, PoolManager, Universal Router, and Tempo Exchange on an Anvil fork of Tempo at block 41,183,156. For supported routes, the adapter calls each deployed Tempo hook's quote function and passes its output into the next hop. It constructs a SETTLE -> SWAP -> TAKE execution plan and validates the complete Universal Router transaction. Candidate admission is bound to the route, input amount, block context, and execution-plan digest. Failed or indeterminate validation prevents admission. A key debugging finding involved PathUSD: when the payer and recipient were the same wallet, gas paid in the output token reduced the wallet's balance increase despite a correct swap transfer. We separated swap output from wallet balance changes and used receipt evidence to account for the gas payment. The recorded fork suite passes 29 tests. We also prepared a TypeScript patch for UniRoute's quote-dispatch boundary. That boundary is tested with mocks; wiring the real validator into the complete UniRoute service remains unfinished because required internal components are absent from the public checkout. The dashboard displays recorded fork evidence, and the repository provides reproduction commands and explicit scope limitations.

projects.title: Izanagi
projects.description: A wallet for AI agents that checks every payment, and can still stop one after it's been signed
projects.project_description: AI agents are starting to pay for things on their own. With x402, an agent hits an API, gets a price, signs, and pays. That's great until it pays the wrong person. Every tool we found for this checks the payment before the agent signs, and after that the money is gone. Izanagi is a wallet for your AI agent where every payment gets checked, and where "no" is still possible after the agent has paid. Before anything is signed, we check who's getting paid. Intercepta scans the seller's address, the token (real USDC or a fake lookalike), and the payment itself. How much? Every tab has a limit. Anything over the limit goes to your phone, and a real human has to approve it with World ID. If you say no, the approval expires, or you cancel, no valid signature ever exists. Then there's the part nobody else can do. We use x402's batch-settlement scheme, where the agent signs vouchers as it goes and the seller cashes them in later through Coinbase's escrow. Before paying out, that escrow asks our wallet contract whether the voucher is still good. So if a seller turns out to be a scammer after your agent already paid, we revoke them and their claim just fails on chain. Busy sellers on Base cash in every 1 to 5 minutes. Quiet ones can take days. That gap is your safety net. This is live on Base mainnet with real USDC. We didn't deploy a fake escrow, we used Coinbase's real one. Our wallet has paid real third-party sellers (hyperextend for Bitcoin prices, onesource for block numbers) and neither of them had to change anything. You own the wallet from the block it's created, through your own MetaMask, and we hold no key that can move your money. You can plug it into Claude over MCP and ask your AI to buy something.
projects.how_its_made: The heart of it is one Solidity contract, Countersign.sol. It becomes the "payer" on Coinbase's deployed x402 batch-settlement escrow (0x4020...0003 on Base). Because we set payerAuthorizer to zero, the escrow has to ask our contract through EIP-1271 isValidSignature every time a seller tries to claim. Our contract says yes only if all five hold: the agent signed it, our risk oracle countersigned it, that countersignature hasn't expired, the seller hasn't been revoked, and the wallet isn't paused. The last two are read live at claim time, and that's the whole trick. Nothing pre-sign can do that. The backend is all Rust (axum, tokio, alloy): countersigner: the brain. It calls Intercepta, runs the World ID flow, holds the oracle key, and keeps re-scanning open tabs. When a seller's risk score crosses the line, it revokes them on chain. tab: the server behind the website, plus an MCP endpoint (rmcp) so Claude can use your wallet directly. seller: our own x402 seller for the demo. It goes rogue on purpose so you can watch the stop happen, and it screens its buyers with Intercepta too. common: EIP-712 types byte-identical to the escrow, and the x402 v2 wire format. The frontend is React + Vite on Vercel, with MetaMask for creating and funding your wallet. Intercepta: we use three endpoints (address quick-scan, token risks, signature analysis), and their verdict maps straight to our four outcomes: pay, refuse, cap the amount, or ask a human. Without the verdict there's no countersignature, so the voucher can't be claimed. There's no mock mode. If the API key is missing, everything fails closed. World ID: we used the OIDC device flow on World's sandbox, so a headless agent can show a short code and a human approves on their phone. Each approval is tied to one exact voucher, so it can't be reused for a different seller, a bigger amount, or a second payment. We verify the id_token on the backend, and the agent never sees the secret. Hacky and notable bits: We tested everything against the real escrow on mainnet forks of Base, Optimism and Arbitrum: 40 contract tests and 137 Rust tests. Real sellers list several payment schemes in their 402 responses, so we echo back their chosen offer exactly as they sent it. That's how our wallet worked with them without them changing anything. While testing on a fork of the real escrow, we found two ways a stranger could drain a wallet: an open collector, and opening a channel in the wallet's name using its standing allowance. We fixed both, and tests keep them closed. Now the wallet approves exactly one deposit and resets the allowance to zero. A claim through EIP-1271 costs about 164k gas (under half a cent on Base), and the revoke kill switch costs about $0.0005.

projects.title: Surety Project
projects.description: On-chain accountability and financial recourse for autonomous AI agents.
projects.project_description: Surety is an on-chain accountability and recourse protocol for autonomous AI agents. Agents register a transparent operating policy and post a financial bond that can compensate harmed users when an agent violates its declared rules. The protocol is designed around verifiable claims, dispute resolution, and protection against frivolous claims, creating a neutral accountability layer between autonomous agents and the people and protocols that interact with them.
projects.how_its_made: Surety is built as a TypeScript/Solidity monorepo with a Next.js frontend using React, wagmi, viem, RainbowKit and Tailwind, alongside Foundry for smart-contract development and Ponder for blockchain indexing. The local development environment runs against Anvil, with Solidity interfaces for UMA Optimistic Oracle V3 and EAS already included. The architecture is designed around an agent registry, bonded vaults, policy enforcement and an optimistic claims flow, with clean interfaces for future identity, risk-screening and transaction-policy integrations. We prioritized modular infrastructure, testability and verifiable on-chain state so each component can be independently inspected and extended.

projects.title: Agent PayGuard
projects.description: A pre-signing control prototype for AI-agent purchases, using Intercepta recipient checks.
projects.project_description: Agent PayGuard explores how an AI agent can buy a digital service within the limits set by its owner. The demo purchase is a structure report for a bundled Solidity contract. The seller returns an x402 payment quote, and the buyer checks the quoted recipient before any payment can proceed. Intercepta supplies address evidence; the application's own policy determines how that evidence should affect the purchase. The control boundary brings together the recipient, network, asset, amount, task budget and available risk evidence. The goal is to prevent a changed order, an uncertain response or a repeated request from becoming an unintended payment. The current build demonstrates a local HTTP 402 quote, a server-side Intercepta address-check integration, and clearly labelled offline policy scenarios. Signing and settlement remain disconnected. A successful paid-report purchase, an end-to-end live-risk block and an autonomous AI buyer are not yet demonstrated. Mainnet address evidence is not presented as proof of testnet coverage, and synthetic examples are not payment receipts.
projects.how_its_made: We built the prototype in TypeScript, with a React/Vite interface and separate Express buyer and seller services in one repository. The seller uses the x402 SDK to quote a report for a bundled Solidity sample. The report contains structural and lexical observations; it is not a security audit. The buyer's server-side Intercepta adapter keeps the API key out of the browser and checks the payment recipient. The repository includes guarded-signing and payment-operation modules, along with offline tests for transaction binding, spending limits, repeated requests, uncertain execution outcomes and report validation. These tests exercise local control logic with fixtures; they do not prove an onchain payment. The running application keeps signing and settlement disabled. Intercepta provides risk evidence, while our own policy and execution controls are separate responsibilities. We used Codex to assist implementation, tests, documentation and interface iteration, and OpenAI image generation for the hand-and-eye logo. The project owner defined the purchasing scenario, directed the product and interface revisions, and specified the acceptance requirements. AI-assisted source areas include apps/web, apps/buyer, apps/seller and docs. No application-level AI provider is integrated into the current purchase flow.

projects.title: Unison
projects.description: Move tokenized stocks between issuers 1:1, no selling. Uniswap v4 hook + private send on Sui.
projects.project_description: Tokenized stocks are fragmenting. Coinbase, Kraken, Robinhood, xStocks each issue their own token for the same share, and there's no way to move from one to another. A holder of Coinbase NVIDIA who wants Kraken NVIDIA has to sell, wire, rebuy, and eat the spread, the price gap and a tax event. In TradFi this is one form (ACATS). On-chain it doesn't exist. Unison is that form. Three pieces: Convert is a Uniswap v4 hook (ParityHook) that quotes conversions at NAV parity instead of on a curve. 100 shares of issuer A becomes 100 shares of issuer B, priced off each wrapper's declared multiplier, never off exchange prices. A market maker supplies inventory of both wrappers and earns the fee: 2 bps base plus a skew fee that rises only on trades that make the pool more lopsided, so arbitrageurs are paid to keep the two issuers' prices together. Protocol takes nothing on Convert. A peg guard blocks conversions if the wrappers drift more than 50 bps, protecting the LP from a depegged token. Dark Cross is an on-chain dark pool for size. Sealed commit (hash), reveal, settle at the 30-minute oracle midpoint. Opposite-side orders cross directly at 1 bp; residual falls through to Convert; unfilled is refunded. Pre-trade private, post-trade public, enforced by the contract, not an operator. Send is confidential payment in tokenized stock across chains. Deposit on Unichain (ShareVault), pay on Sui with the amount encrypted under Seal and stored on Walrus, recipient decrypts and withdraws into whichever issuer they want.
