projects.title: BrandMyStuff
projects.description: A marketplace for ad space on everyday objects: AI-verified, investor-owned, settled on Sui.
projects.project_description:
BrandMyStuff is a marketplace that turns everyday objects into ad space. Anyone can rent out the space on things they own, like a laptop lid, a car, a helmet or a shop window, to brands that want real-world attention. Great spots can also be tokenised, so investors can own a share of their future ad income. The problem:
In 2026, viral posts showed huge demand for this. A developer sold every sticker spot on his MacBook lid to 64 bidding brands, Solana sold ad spots on its own logo, and a groom sold ad space on his wedding tuxedo. Small and  mid-size brands loved it because billboards and transit ads are priced for big budgets, and this was real-world advertising they could finally afford. But the market broke on trust. 30% of the MacBook winners never paid, there was  no way to judge whether a spot was any good, no proof the ad ever went up, and copycat marketplaces were left with 98%of their spots empty. How brandmystuff works: List: an owner photographs an object with the in-app camera, via a phone link or QR code, and marks the spots where an ad could go. Score: an AI judge (Gemini vision plus measured image metrics) gives every spot a transparent Ad-Space Quality Score out of 100, based on visibility, legibility, surface, context and durability. The score is written on-chain. Lease: a brand books weeks on a spot. The full payment in USDC is locked in an escrow smart contract on Sui, so owners are always paid. Prove and earn: each week the owner photographs the ad in place. The AI checks it against the listing and the approved design, and every accepted proof releases that week's payment automatically. Missed proofs are refunded to the brand, and disputes are handled on-chain. Tokenisation:
An owner can split a spot into 10,000 revenue shares and sell them to identity-verified investors, with a generated legal pack signed on-chain. Every time the spot earns rent, holders receive their share. They can trade shares on a built-in order book, and if a spot goes viral and brands pile in, early holders earn more. Investors can get paid on Sui or, through Circle CCTP and Curvegrid MultiBaas, as native USDC on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum or Optimism. AI agents as buyers:
Each brand gets Scout, an AI agent that reads the brand, discovers spaces through ENS, scores them for fit and books the best one. It pays through x402 (HTTP-native payments on Sui) from an on-chain budget mandate that caps what it can spend, and the brand can pause or revoke it at any time. Outside AI agents can also discover, quote and buy ad space through our MCP server and x402 endpoints, with no account needed. Built on: Sui (Move): escrow and weekly payments, fee splits (the owner keeps 88%), the KYC registry, revenue shares, the order book, sponsorships, cross-chain payout routes and agent budget mandates. That's 10 Move modules, upgraded live twice. Photos, reports and legal documents are stored on Walrus. ENSv2 (Sepolia): every account, object, space, lease and agent gets a readable name, like lid-center.macbook.sam.brandmystuff.eth. Its records publish the quality score, price and status, and are verified both ways against Sui. With Enhanced Access Control, owners can edit their own profile records but never their score. Lease names are held by the advertiser and expire with the lease. Agents get their own namespace, scout.<brand>.brandmystuff.eth, and register receipts for their purchases themselves. Curvegrid MultiBaas: runs every EVM step of cross-chain payouts across four testnets: deploying our payout relayer, building and submitting transactions, indexing delivery events, querying lifetime totals, reading balances and sending signed webhooks. Everything runs end to end on public testnets with test USDC.
projects.how_its_made:
Architecture:
A Next.js 16 app (App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4) serves both the UI and all API routes, including our own x402 facilitator and an MCP server. A long-running Node worker does three things: it polls Sui for events; it runs a retrying job queue (ENS writes, cross-chain payouts, AI score writes); it enforces on-chain deadlines. Supabase Postgres holds a read model rebuilt from Sui events, so the chain stays the source of truth and the database is a cache. Walrus stores photos, AI score reports, proof photos and legal PDFs. Gemini (gemini-3.1-flash-lite) does all the vision work. Sign-in uses Privy (email with embedded Sui and Ethereum wallets) or any Sui wallet through dApp Kit. Sui:
One package with 9 modules, plus a separate mandate package: asset: objects, ad spaces and a per-space week calendar that makes double booking impossible. lease: escrow and proof-gated weekly payments. The full USDC amount is locked upfront and paid out in "weeks + 1" instalments. A payment is released only when the AI proof scores at least 80% on both checks, a floor enforced in Move itself. Each payment is split 12% to the platform, then the investor share, then the owner. After a deadline passes, anyone can trigger refunds for missed proofs. Offering: 10,000 revenue units per space, with income spread by a pull-based accumulator that carries rounding dustcforward. kyc: an ERC-3643-style registry that gates every purchase, transfer and trade. market: asks, escrowed bids and expiry sweeps. sponsor: paid "Sponsored" tags. payout: holder-signed cross-chain payout routes. mandate (separate package): budget caps for AI agents. Two capabilities split authority: AdminCap for governance and OperatorCap for the backend. Display objects plus Walrus blob IDs make every space, object and lease render with its real photo in any wallet. On testnet, week_ms is 10 minutes, so a full lease runs in under an hour. The AI judge: Measured metrics: sharp computes sharpness, noise, exposure clipping, luminance contrast and pixels per cm, combined into an evidence-quality index. A 64-bit perceptual hash catches reused photos. Sampled judgements: Gemini grades 11 fixed criteria on a 0–4 scale in 3 independent samples (5 if they disagree), and code takes the medians and computes the score. Measured size: an ID card in the photo gives the real scale, so a space whose claimed size is more than 20% off is
rejected. Gates: eight checks reject AI-generated or stock photos, prompt-injection text, a close-up that doesn't match the object, and more. Provenance: photos can only come from a live camera through one-time links with a QR code, and the server confirms the bytes match what that link captured. x402 on Sui (hacky, and our own). x402 is usually shown on EVM chains, so we wrote a self-hosted facilitator for the exact scheme on sui:testnet: it verifies the payer's signature and rejects replayed payments; it dry-runs the transaction to prove the treasury receives exactly the quoted amount; it settles the payment, then books through lease::book_for on the payer's behalf; any failure is refunded on-chain. Quotes use Sui's on-chain clock, not server time, because the contracts check deadlines against it. The Scout agent. Each brand gets an agent with its own Sui and EVM keys, encrypted at rest. Leash: it spends through a Move BudgetMandate that fixes one agent, one payee, a per-payment cap, a total budget and an expiry. The brand can pause or revoke it. The payment is the mandate: its x402 payment transaction is a mandate::spend, so the facilitator sees an ordinary USDC transfer while the agent can never exceed what the brand allowed. Choosing an ad: it reads space data from live ENS records through the Universal Resolver, verifies each name against Sui, scores fit with Gemini, and only buys ENS-verified spaces within budget. ENSv2 (Sepolia):
We registered brandmystuff.eth through the ETHRegistrar's commit-reveal flow and deploy a subregistry on demand for each parent name. A relayer turns Sui events into ENS writes: register, records, renew, unregister. Lease labels from Move: lease::book_internal builds the l-<seq> label on-chain, so Sui and ENS always agree on lease names. One resolver per identity. ENSv2 resolver roles apply per record key across the whole resolver, never per name. So each user and each agent gets their own Permissioned Resolver: the owner's wallet may write only profile keys; attested.aqs, price and status stay platform-only. Safe migration: existing names move to the new resolver by copying records first and repointing second, then the holder's SET_RESOLVER role is revoked so no one can repoint to a forged score. Leases: lease names are held by the advertiser and expire with the lease. Agents: each gets scout.<brand>.brandmystuff.eth with REGISTRAR rights on its own subregistry only, and registers a buy-<n> receipt after every purchase. Its roles are removed the moment the brand revokes the mandate on Sui. Verification: a two-way Sui ↔ ENS check (a sui.object record) backs every name. Sui addresses are stored as coin type 784, so names resolve to Sui addresses natively. Proving the permissions: gas-free eth_call probes show an owner's attempt to write attested.aqs reverting with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. Curvegrid MultiBaas + Circle CCTP (cross-chain payouts):
Investors choose a payout chain at onboarding. That choice is added to the same Sui transaction that creates their profile, so it costs one signature. One transaction on Sui: it calls payout::release_routed (the Move function returns the holder's USDC) and passes that coin into Circle's deposit_for_burn_with_caller. Release and burn are atomic. Circle attestation: Circle attests the burn in about 5 seconds. Only our relayer can mint: our relayer, deployed through MultiBaas on 4 EVM testnets, is the only contract allowed to complete the mint, and the USDC goes straight to the investor. What MultiBaas does: holds the contract library and address aliases; builds every transaction (nonce, gas, EIP-1559 fees), which our key only signs; submits it and tracks the receipt; indexes PayoutDelivered events; runs event queries that total each holder's delivered USDC; reads contract balances; sends HMAC-signed webhooks. It replaced an RPC node, nonce management and a log indexer we would otherwise have had to build and run for four chains. Other notable hacks:
Wallet-free onboarding with Privy: users sign in with Google, Apple, X, email or a passkey, and Privy gives them an embedded Ethereum wallet while our server creates their Sui wallet. A custom PrivySuiSigner lets that embedded wallet sign the Sui transactions our app builds (it only signs the raw hash). So a brand or owner who has never touched crypto can list an object, pay into escrow, own ENS names and get paid, without installing a wallet or saving a seed phrase. Experienced users can still bring Slush, Suiet or Phantom through Sign in with Sui.

projects.title: Himitsu
projects.description: Private trading without an app relayer, powered by EIP-8141 frame transactions.
projects.project_description:
Himitsu is a private trading protocol that replaces an application relayer with native EIP-8141 frame transactions. It explores how users can authorize private spends and have gas paid by an onchain sponsor while submitting transactions directly from their browser to an Ethereum-compatible node.
Private applications often rely on a relayer to submit transactions and pay gas, avoiding the need to fund a fresh recipient wallet. Himitsu moves that coordination into the transaction itself. Each withdrawal or swap contains four frames: check expiry, verify the user’s zero-knowledge proof, approve gas sponsorship, and execute the operation.
Users deposit ETH or hUSD into a privacy pool and save a secret note that controls their funds. When they want to withdraw or swap, their browser generates a zero-knowledge proof locally. This proves authorization to spend an unspent note without explicitly identifying its original deposit. The secret note stays on the user’s device, and the proof binds the spend to the intended transaction.
An onchain sponsor checks the operation and fee limits before agreeing to pay gas. The pool then completes the withdrawal or swaps through Uniswap V2 and sends the output to the chosen recipient. No dedicated application relayer, hosted proving server, or separate recipient gas funding is required for these supported operations.
Himitsu runs on an EIP-8141-enabled Ethrex devnet. It includes ETH and hUSD deposits, withdrawals, bidirectional swaps, browser-based proof generation, and a transaction explorer showing individual frame results and the gas payer.
Himitsu demonstrates how native frame transactions can simplify private application infrastructure. It reduces direct deposit-to-spend linkage, while amounts, timing, and address reuse can still affect privacy.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Himitsu around native EIP-8141 frame transactions on an Ethrex devnet. The main engineering goal was to replace an application-operated relayer with a transaction that handles proof-based authorization, gas sponsorship, and execution onchain.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Family ConnectKit and Wagmi for wallet connections and deposits. For withdrawals and swaps, the browser constructs the frame transaction and submits it directly through RPC. The application does not require a dedicated relayer, bundler, hosted proving service, or indexer.
The privacy system uses Circom circuits, Groth16 proofs, and Poseidon hashing. Deposits create amount-bound commitments in a Merkle tree, while users keep a secret note containing their spending credentials. We use snarkjs and circuit WASM inside a browser Web Worker to generate proofs locally without blocking the interface. The browser reconstructs the tree from onchain events, so note secrets and Merkle witnesses stay on the user’s device.
Each private spend has four frames: an expiry check, proof verification, gas-payment approval, and execution. The privacy pool contract is the transaction sender. It authorizes execution based on the proof, while a separate, prefunded paymaster authorizes gas payment after checking the permitted operation, frame structure, and fee limits. This separates spending authority from payment authority without requiring an operator’s signature for each transaction.
One particularly interesting detail is binding the proof to the exact transaction. We represent the full 256-bit transaction authorization digest as two 128-bit circuit inputs. The proof is carried in the transaction’s arbitrary-signature entry, whose raw proof bytes are excluded from that digest. This avoids a circular dependency where generating the proof would change the message being proved. We also built custom EVM bytecode helpers for frame introspection and native approval instructions.
For trading, we integrated the official Uniswap V2 core contracts with a locally deployed WETH/hUSD liquidity pair. The pool transfers the exact swap input directly to the pair, enforces the minimum output, and sends the result to the recipient. Consuming the note and executing the swap happen within one contract call, so a failed swap rolls back the spend. Uniswap provides the exchange functionality while Himitsu handles private authorization and sponsorship.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Himitsu is a private trading protocol that replaces an application relayer with native EIP-8141 frame transactions. It explores how users can authorize private spends and have gas paid by an onchain sponsor while submitting transactions directly from their browser to an Ethereum-compatible node.
Private applications often rely on a relayer to submit transactions and pay gas, avoiding the need to fund a fresh recipient wallet. Himitsu moves that coordination into the transaction itself. Each withdrawal or swap contains four frames: check expiry, verify the user’s zero-knowledge proof, approve gas sponsorship, and execute the operation.
Users deposit ETH or hUSD into a privacy pool and save a secret note that controls their funds. When they want to withdraw or swap, their browser generates a zero-knowledge proof locally. This proves authorization to spend an unspent note without explicitly identifying its original deposit. The secret note stays on the user’s device, and the proof binds the spend to the intended transaction.
An onchain sponsor checks the operation and fee limits before agreeing to pay gas. The pool then completes the withdrawal or swaps through Uniswap V2 and sends the output to the chosen recipient. No dedicated application relayer, hosted proving server, or separate recipient gas funding is required for these supported operations.
Himitsu runs on an EIP-8141-enabled Ethrex devnet. It includes ETH and hUSD deposits, withdrawals, bidirectional swaps, browser-based proof generation, and a transaction explorer showing individual frame results and the gas payer.
Himitsu demonstrates how native frame transactions can simplify private application infrastructure. It reduces direct deposit-to-spend linkage, while amounts, timing, and address reuse can still affect privacy.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built Himitsu around native EIP-8141 frame transactions on an Ethrex devnet. The main engineering goal was to replace an application-operated relayer with a transaction that handles proof-based authorization, gas sponsorship, and execution onchain.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Family ConnectKit and Wagmi for wallet connections and deposits. For withdrawals and swaps, the browser constructs the frame transaction and submits it directly through RPC. The application does not require a dedicated relayer, bundler, hosted proving service, or indexer.
The privacy system uses Circom circuits, Groth16 proofs, and Poseidon hashing. Deposits create amount-bound commitments in a Merkle tree, while users keep a secret note containing their spending credentials. We use snarkjs and circuit WASM inside a browser Web Worker to generate proofs locally without blocking the interface. The browser reconstructs the tree from onchain events, so note secrets and Merkle witnesses stay on the user’s device.
Each private spend has four frames: an expiry check, proof verification, gas-payment approval, and execution. The privacy pool contract is the transaction sender. It authorizes execution based on the proof, while a separate, prefunded paymaster authorizes gas payment after checking the permitted operation, frame structure, and fee limits. This separates spending authority from payment authority without requiring an operator’s signature for each transaction.
One particularly interesting detail is binding the proof to the exact transaction. We represent the full 256-bit transaction authorization digest as two 128-bit circuit inputs. The proof is carried in the transaction’s arbitrary-signature entry, whose raw proof bytes are excluded from that digest. This avoids a circular dependency where generating the proof would change the message being proved. We also built custom EVM bytecode helpers for frame introspection and native approval instructions.
For trading, we integrated the official Uniswap V2 core contracts with a locally deployed WETH/hUSD liquidity pair. The pool transfers the exact swap input directly to the pair, enforces the minimum output, and sends the result to the recipient. Consuming the note and executing the swap happen within one contract call, so a failed swap rolls back the spend. Uniswap provides the exchange functionality while Himitsu handles private authorization and sponsorship.
A notable low-level fix was patching Ethrex’s mempool validation to expose earlier frame results to later verification frames. Our paymaster needs to inspect the preceding validation result, and the patch makes that information available during simulation as well as execution.
We also built an explorer that displays frame outcomes, gas usage, and the actual gas payer, making the native transaction flow visible during the demo. The prototype runs against a pinned EIP-8141 implementation with test assets, with automated tests covering transaction encoding, sponsorship rules, note recovery, and failure handling.

projects.title: YieldSolver
projects.description: DeFi deposits chase the best APY and fill 1inch intents on Base, earning yield and fees together
projects.project_description:
YieldSolver makes the same capital work twice. Money sitting in lending markets like Morpho, Aave and Fluid earns interest, but it does nothing else. Meanwhile, intent protocols like 1inch Fusion need liquidity at the exact moment an order is filled. YieldSolver connects the two: deposits keep earning lending yield, and the same deposits are used to fill 1inch Fusion swap intents on Base, earning fees and spread on top. The recommended mode is self-custody. A user supplies USDC or WETH to Morpho, Fluid or Aave and keeps the interest-bearing shares in their own wallet. With a single approval and a 1inch Aqua strategy, those shares become shared liquidity. They are only moved inside a transaction that must return them, so the user never deposits into our vault and can stop at any time. Three things then happen to the same position: A keeper moves the shares to whichever listed market pays the best APY. Our resolver borrows them just in time to fill a Fusion order, and repays them with a fee in the same transaction. The shares also run as a 1inch SwapVM order that quotes the Chainlink price plus a spread, so any taker can buy from the wallet's inventory. All fees come back to the wallet as more shares, so the capital never stops earning. For users who prefer a managed product there are three vaults:
A. A USDC yield vault that lends just in time to the resolver.
B. Inventory market making profiles (70/30, 50/50, 30/70 USDC/ETH) that fill orders from stock at oracle price plus spread, stay inside a plus or minus 5 point band, and lend idle inventory on Aave.
C. A conditional ETH carry vault. It keeps WETH as Aave collateral and borrows USDC into the best whitelisted ERC-4626 vault only while the spread beats the cost of getting in and out, then exits on its own when the spread disappears. Safety rules live in the contracts, not in the bots: LTV caps, public deleverage above 40 percent, trade size limits, price staleness checks, whitelisted markets and routers, and on-chain rejection of any loss-making fill. Everything is live on Base Sepolia with a dashboard showing where every dollar sits, what each wallet earned, and every fill with its transaction.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry, and bots are TypeScript with viem. The frontend is a Vite and TypeScript dashboard. Everything runs in Docker and is deployed on Base Sepolia. 1inch Fusion: users sign gasless intents with the official fusion-sdk and limit-order-sdk. 1inch has no testnet, so we deployed the unmodified Limit Order Protocol v4 and Fusion SimpleSettlement contracts ourselves and wrote a relayer that validates orders the same way the 1inch API does (hash, EIP-712 signature against the deployed domain, resolver whitelist, balance, allowance, expiry). Our resolver bot takes each order at its current Dutch auction price and simulates every possible source: JIT from the vault, inventory, JIT from a wallet, market making from a wallet, and SwapVM. It fills with the most profitable one. A minimum profit is enforced on-chain, so a bad simulation can never lose money. 1inch Aqua: this is the core of the project. We wrote three Aqua apps. AquaYieldApp is the self-custody app: the maker is a user wallet, and the committed Aqua tokens are ERC-4626 lending shares instead of plain tokens, so every committed budget keeps earning yield. It supports keeper rebalancing between markets, flash loans with a fee to the maker, and oracle priced swaps with inventory skew and a band. JitLiquidityApp and OracleSwapApp power the two managed vaults. Every pull is checked to come back within the same transaction. 1inch SwapVM: we built our own SwapVM router from the unmodified SwapVM 1.2 core plus 1inch's Aqua instruction set, and added two custom instructions. YieldOracleSwap (opcode 64) does oracle plus spread market making on yield-bearing shares. It converts share balances to underlying assets, prices at Chainlink plus spread with a skew toward the maker's target ratio, enforces a band and a max trade size, converts back to shares, and always rounds in the maker's favour. SequencerGuard (opcode 65) blocks trades while the Base sequencer is down. Wallets ship SwapVM orders over the same shares they committed to AquaYieldApp, which shows Aqua's real promise: one position backing several strategies at once. We ran 1inch's own CoreInvariants suite against our program (symmetry, quote and swap consistency, monotonicity, additivity, maker-favouring rounding), and it passes. Base and Chainlink: all contracts run on Base Sepolia. Lending markets, the oracle and the router are mocks driven by a simulator that mirrors the real Chainlink ETH/USD price from Base mainnet, so the demo moves with the real market. A Base mainnet fork test runs the carry vault against real Aave, Morpho vaults and the real Aave oracle. Curvegrid MultiBaas: we linked our 10 main contracts to a MultiBaas deployment on Base Sepolia. Its transaction explorer decodes our nested transactions (resolver, SwapVM, Aqua pull and push, share redeem, LOP fill) with function arguments and events, without verifying sources on Basescan. Its event indexing tracks our contracts' events. Notable hacks: Aqua only moves tokens, so to make liquidity earn while committed we commit ERC-4626 shares, then price in assets and settle in shares. We wrote a non-rebasing ERC-4626 wrapper for Aave so fixed Aqua budgets stay meaningful. For SwapVM fills, the resolver receives the wallet's shares first, redeems them inside SwapVM's taker callback, fills the Fusion order with the proceeds, then mints fresh shares of the other asset to pay the wallet back, all in one transaction. We found that route comparison was unfair, because the surplus from the auction decaying before inclusion was counted for JIT routes but not for exact-out routes. The resolver now ranks routes like for like. The SwapVM router came out over the 24 KB contract size limit. We brought it down to 21.4 KB with a size-optimised via-IR build. The carry vault only enters when expected profit over 24 hours covers entry plus exit gas three times. It uses hysteresis to exit, and the contract lets anyone deleverage if LTV drifts too high. The dashboard shows realised returns until a full day of data exists instead of annualising a few hours of flow. Testing: 157 Foundry tests (unit, fuzz, invariant, Base mainnet fork) and an end-to-end script that spins up anvil, deploys everything, runs all bots, and asserts that orders fill through every route and that wallets earn.

projects.title: FlyNS
projects.description: Autonomous fruit fly agents with unique ENS identities, inspired by real connectome data.
projects.project_description: Our project explores what happens when biological intelligence is turned into a network of autonomous digital agents. We use fruit fly connectome data as inspiration for building multiple lightweight agents, each representing an individual digital fruit fly with its own behavior, state, and identity. Instead of treating the swarm as a single AI system, every fly exists as an independent agent that can interact with other flies and with its environment. Each agent is assigned a unique ENS subname, such as ada.flyns.eth , which acts as its persistent onchain identity. ENS records can store metadata about the agent, including its wallet address, behavioral state, external endpoints, and other agent-specific information. This makes ENS more than a human-readable wallet name: it becomes a decentralized identity and discovery layer for autonomous agents. The system is designed around the idea of a digital swarm. Individual agents can perceive events, change internal state, communicate, and potentially develop different behaviors over time. By connecting biological network concepts with Ethereum identity infrastructure, we want to explore how thousands of simple autonomous agents could exist, discover each other, and interact through open protocols. The project combines connectome-inspired computation, autonomous agents, Ethereum, and ENS to create an experimental foundation for persistent digital organisms that can live and evolve on the open web.
projects.how_its_made: The project is built as a web-based multi-agent simulation that connects connectome-inspired fruit fly agents with Ethereum identity infrastructure. Each fruit fly is represented as an independent agent with its own internal state, behavioral parameters, wallet identity, and ENS subname. We use real fruit fly connectome research as inspiration for the agent architecture, simplifying biological neural relationships into lightweight computational rules that can run interactively in the browser. The frontend is built with TypeScript and Three.js, which renders the flies and their shared environment in real time. Agent state and simulation logic are kept separate from the rendering layer so that each fly can independently process inputs, update its state, and produce actions. For the blockchain layer, we use Ethereum-compatible wallets together with ENS. A parent ENS name acts as the namespace for the swarm, while individual agents receive subnames such as ada.flyns.eth . Each subname can point to the agent's wallet and store additional ENS records describing that agent. We also configured resolvers for the subnames so each digital organism can maintain its own independently resolvable identity and metadata. ENS is particularly useful because it gives autonomous agents a human-readable, persistent identifier without requiring us to build a custom identity registry. Instead of referring to agents only by database IDs or wallet addresses, other applications can discover and address them through standard ENS resolution. One notable part of the implementation is that the biological simulation and blockchain identity layers are intentionally decoupled. The flies can continue to run as lightweight local agents, while ENS acts as the persistent external identity layer. This means the architecture could scale from a small visual simulation into a much larger network of independently hosted agents without requiring every behavioral update to be written onchain.

projects.title: Proviso
projects.description: AI shopping agent that pays from your own wallet, bound by rules on ENSv2 and World ID approvals.
projects.project_description: Proviso is an AI shopping agent that you can actually trust with your money. You tell it what you want in plain words: "a Sony 55-inch TV within a month, never above $500, buy it yourself under $400." If you only name a kind of product ("a 4K TV"), the agent suggests concrete models with live prices and you pick one. It then compares live prices across stores, models the price history and upcoming sale dates, and decides when to buy. It pays in USDC straight from your own wallet. No deposit, no agent wallet. You set it up with one signature. Every purchase is checked on-chain by a smart contract against rules that live on your ENS name: At or under your "auto" limit, the agent buys on its own, and only from a merchant listed in verified.proviso.eth. Between auto and max, it must get you, a verified human, to approve that exact order with a fresh World ID confirmation (World ID for Agents). If you decline, or the approval expires, nothing is bought. Above your max, or over your monthly category budget, the contract reverts, whatever the agent was told. A prompt-injected checkout that swaps the merchant address is rejected too. Your rules and the agent's live status are public ENS records under [item].[category].[you].proviso.eth, so anyone can see what the agent is allowed to do and what it is doing. The AI agent itself can only write a status line; it can never raise a limit.
projects.how_its_made: iOS app in SwiftUI (iOS 26, Liquid Glass). Backend in Node/TypeScript, deployed as a Docker image on a k3s cluster behind a Cloudflare Tunnel. Contracts: PolicySpender (Solidity, Foundry) on Sepolia. It has unit tests and fork tests against the real ENSv2 deployment, USDC and the World ID router. Onboarding is a single EIP-2612 permit. We encode the whole account config (ENS root, resolver, agent, World ID link) as a hash into the permit deadline, so one gasless signature both approves spending and fixes the setup. ENSv2 is the policy layer, not a label: Each user gets <username>.proviso.eth with their own PermissionedResolver, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. Hobby/needs are subregistries, and each purchase is a registered subname that expires at its deadline. Limits are ENSv2 data records (uint256) that the contract reads with resolve() at buy time. A missing record reads as 0, so the check fails closed. Enhanced Access Control scopes who writes what. Only the owner's wallet sets budgets, the operator writes a request's bands, and the AI agent (agent.proviso.eth) may only write the "status" record. The merchant allow-list is verified.proviso.eth. Live status and remaining budget are mirrored to text records, so the explorer shows them. World ID for Agents (sandbox) does two jobs: Mandatory sign-in: OIDC with PKCE, Orb acr required. The pairwise sub is committed on-chain as the account's continuity id. Approvals for mid-band buys: an OIDC device grant. The backend validates the ID token (signature, audience, freshness, same sub as the owner), then signs an EIP-712 HumanApproval over the exact order hash. The contract checks it with 5-minute freshness.

projects.title: Go Health Me
projects.description: Put money on your own sleep or workouts. Your wearable proves it, SPOTTER pays the players who hit.
projects.project_description: GoHealthMe is a commitment game for your own health. You stake test USDC on a challenge, say seven hours of sleep on Saturday night or one workout on Sunday, your wearable proves whether you did it, and SPOTTER, the settlement agent, pays the players who hit when the challenge ends. Miss it, shown by your wearable, and your stake goes to the people who hit. Nobody hits, everyone gets their stake back. No wearable data for the challenge, stake back. Raw health data never touches the chain, only the verdict. Continuity track, so the split matters. Before the event: V1 won the Chainlink Confidential AI Attester prize at ETHGlobal New York, V2 gave SPOTTER its own Circle wallet, V3 became a Base Sepolia pilot with self-staked commitment pools and three wearable providers behind one join gate. Everything after commit a86387d is this weekend. What the weekend added. Character creation, once: prove you are one human with World IDKit (any World App credential, no Orb gate), pick your name as an ENSv2 subname on Sepolia, pair your wearable. A three-screen loop, Lobby, The Run, The Verdict, where SPOTTER asks you to confirm with World ID for Agents, screens the payout through a live Intercepta call, then pays. spotter.gohealthme.eth is the agent's own name with a provable permission boundary. The money model got real: SPOTTER now records a miss, but only when your wearable covered every night of the challenge and shows the goal not met, after a grace window. Plus the fixes V3 needed to actually pay a winner, a full redesign, and privacy and terms that are true. This morning the first real hit went through end to end on the live build: a WHOOP workout read, a World ID confirmation (the first request expired and nothing moved, the second confirmed), an Intercepta sanctions screen, and the result recorded on chain. Beta on Base Sepolia test USDC. Apple Health is not in yet.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 on Vercel, Dynamic embedded wallets (email or Base), HealthPoolsV3.sol (Foundry) on Base Sepolia holding test USDC, SPOTTER as a server-side agent loop settling from its Circle wallet, Upstash KV and Supabase with RLS. Wearables: WHOOP direct OAuth and Junction. 2,278 vitest and 73 forge tests. World: @worldcoin/idkit 4.3.0 on the 4.0 RP-signed request flow. projects.project_description_markdown:
GoHealthMe is a commitment game for your own health. You stake test USDC on a challenge, say seven hours of sleep on Saturday night or one workout on Sunday, your wearable proves whether you did it, and SPOTTER, the settlement agent, pays the players who hit when the challenge ends. Miss it, shown by your wearable, and your stake goes to the people who hit. Nobody hits, everyone gets their stake back. No wearable data for the challenge, stake back. Raw health data never touches the chain, only the verdict.

Continuity track, so the split matters. Before the event: V1 won the Chainlink Confidential AI Attester prize at ETHGlobal New York, V2 gave SPOTTER its own Circle wallet, V3 became a Base Sepolia pilot with self-staked commitment pools and three wearable providers behind one join gate. Everything after commit a86387d is this weekend.

What the weekend added. Character creation, once: prove you are one human with World IDKit (any World App credential, no Orb gate), pick your name as an ENSv2 subname on Sepolia, pair your wearable. A three-screen loop, Lobby, The Run, The Verdict, where SPOTTER asks you to confirm with World ID for Agents, screens the payout through a live Intercepta call, then pays. spotter.gohealthme.eth is the agent's own name with a provable permission boundary. The money model got real: SPOTTER now records a miss, but only when your wearable covered every night of the challenge and shows the goal not met, after a grace window. Plus the fixes V3 needed to actually pay a winner, a full redesign, and privacy and terms that are true.

This morning the first real hit went through end to end on the live build: a WHOOP workout read, a World ID confirmation (the first request expired and nothing moved, the second confirmed), an Intercepta sanctions screen, and the result recorded on chain.

Beta on Base Sepolia test USDC. Apple Health is not in yet.

projects.title: Meigi (名義)
projects.description: Confirmation of Payee for stablecoins and AI agents. Pay companies, not addresses.
projects.project_description: Stablecoin payments go to an address, and nothing checks that the address belongs to the company you mean to pay. A fake "our bank details changed" email, a prompt injection hidden in an invoice, or a hacked x402 server that swaps payTo all redirect the money the same way. Banks fixed this for wires with Confirmation of Payee (UK) and Verification of Payee (mandatory in the euro area since October 2025). Stablecoins, and the AI agents now paying with them, have nothing like it. Meigi (名義, the name on an account) binds a Japanese company's T-number, the registration number printed on its qualified invoices, to exactly one payout address: Registering needs an exact name match against the NTA corporate-number registry (5.79M records, 5.0M open), a DNS proof on a domain the registrant controls, and World ID officers. A payout changes only through a 72-hour public window: the business key with its World ID officers (verifier-checked, attester co-signed, verified on-chain), or a governance ruling on a dispute. Nothing changes it instantly. A second claim on a number freezes it instead of overwriting it. Payers check it three ways: ENS: t2011001234567.payee.eth resolves to the active payout in stock viem and ENS's own app and explorer on Sepolia; unknown or disputed numbers resolve to nothing. AgentVault: our AI accounts-payable agent can pay only registered payees, within caps. Prompt-inject it into trying to pay a scammer and the vault reverts PayeeMismatch, returning the registered payout, and the agent names the company it belongs to. x402 guard: before an agent signs, a merchant that declares its T-number must be paid at its registered payout; one that declares none gets at most a small screened allowance (¥50 by default), or nothing. Other agent-payment guards limit what their own agent may do. Meigi is a public payee registry that every agent, wallet and exchange can check: a company's government-issued number, bound to one wallet that nobody, including us, can change in under 72 hours. Japan comes first, but any official business ID works the same way, and the verifier already checks LEIs against GLEIF. Proving that the registrant represents the company, through its 商業登記電子証明書 (commercial-registration e-certificate), is the production step.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry, OpenZeppelin 5.4), all five Sourcify exact matches on Sepolia: PayeeRegistry: one payout per T-number. A payout changes only through a 72-hour public window (set at deploy; the contract enforces at least 1 hour): the business key with its World ID officers (verifier-checked, attester co-signed as one EIP-712 approval, verified on-chain by OfficerQuorum), or a governance ruling on a dispute, which only governance can dismiss. Disputes freeze a number, and attesters can be revoked. PayeeResolver: an ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver on payee.eth that answers from the registry at call time. AgentVault: owner-approved vendors, per-vendor caps, a pinned payout that must still match the registry, invoice de-duplication. PayRouter (pay by T-number from any wallet) and a mock JPYC with EIP-3009.
164 Foundry tests (156 run without an RPC; the 8 fork tests need one), including a fuzz test that a change never lands early. Three review rounds by separate AI reviewers covered the core contracts, with proof-of-concept exploits: 16 findings, 14 fixed, 2 documented as by design, every fix mutation-tested. CompanyNamespace and MandateGate, added later, passed reviews of their own; the ENS claim resolver has tests only, and none of this is a professional audit. Verifier (TypeScript, Hono, node:sqlite): an index of the NTA's public bulk data (5,787,472 corporate-number records), matched exactly after NFKC normalisation; a Keybase-style DNS TXT proof; World ID 4.0 through IDKit sessions. An officer enrolls once, and every later approval must come from the same session, with a signal that pins chain, registry, T-number, action, target, nonce and deadline. World ID 4.0's on-chain verifier isn't deployed on Sepolia, so the verifier checks each proof server-side with the Developer Portal's v4 verify API, then signs an EIP-712 approval that the registry checks on-chain. That one signature is the officer quorum on-chain, so the registry trusts the verifier to have checked each proof. ENSv2 (Sepolia Beta): payee.eth names companies, meigi.eth names agents. A company can claim its name as a token in a UserRegistry subregistry. Enhanced Access Control lets it set only text records on its profile, and ClaimedPayeeResolver forwards the money records from the registry, so a claim never changes an address. ap.meigi.eth carries ENSIP-26 records, is linked to ERC-8004 agent 10525 per ENSIP-25, is the AgentVault's ENSIP-19 primary name, and its key can write only agent-status. CompanyNamespace lets a claimed company open its own ENSv2 UserRegistry and issue soulbound, expiring, text-only names, each with its own PermissionedResolver. MandateGate, the AgentVault's agent, passes payInvoice on only while the buyer's ap.t4999900000005.payee.eth answers and the caller holds it. AP agent (TypeScript): deterministic extraction of Japanese invoices (T-number, 振込先, 税込 total, hidden text) → System-1 triage by our fine-tuned model → a deterministic kernel, the only part that decides → Intercepta screening → pay or hold. A local LLM on Ollama (Gemma 4 E4B in our demo) proposes, deliberately gullibly, and explains; it never decides. The agent holds no key and refuses to start if one is in its environment. A separate loopback signer holds the agent's key and signs only payInvoice (through the MandateGate, now the vault's agent), built from typed fields and simulated first. Held invoices go to a human through World ID for Agents (an OAuth device grant). The agent verifies the ID token and requires the enrolled approver; the separate signer enforces the ¥150,000 ceiling and independently verifies the token too (on in our demo stack). A hash-chained audit log records every verdict, approval and payment (GET /audit?verify=1). Fine-tuned triage model: payee-0.8b, a LoRA fine-tune of Kev-0.8B on PayeeBench-JA, our Japanese-first benchmark for payment-redirection triage, in which every identifier is provably fictional. Trained in 39 minutes on an M5 Max MacBook (PyTorch MPS), served with MLX. On our own synthetic benchmark it reaches 0.918 mean accuracy on the held-out test templates, at 39 ms p50 on the laptop; Llama 3.3 70B has lower mean accuracy (0.815) but ranks safe versus held items at least as well, so the model only routes and the registry match decides. At a 1% error budget it sends 45% of legitimate items straight to the kernel. One item that should have been held slipped through, and the kernel's exact registry match is the backstop for exactly that. x402 v2: a meigi-payee extension (T-number, plus the ENS name where the chain has ENS) in the 402 response; a client hook that holds a declared merchant to its registered payout, checking the registry and ENS independently, and aborts before signing on a mismatch; merchants that declare no payee get at most a small allowance (¥50 by default) after a clean Intercepta screen, or nothing; a self-hosted facilitator settling EIP-3009 mJPYC. Curvegrid MultiBaas and Mizuhiki: two MultiBaas deployments. One indexes the live demo's Sepolia contracts. The other indexes Meigi on Mizuhiki's Awaji testnet (chain 6497), where the registry and PayRouter are deployed, a registered vendor was paid in Mizuhiki's MJPY and MUSD test tokens, and an x402 purchase settled in MJPY. Seven saved queries in the format of Curvegrid's Matsuri sample confirm settlements and feed the site's settlements panel. Hack: the free plan backfills only 100 blocks, so we load the ABIs and queries before deploying, link right after the broadcast, and merge MultiBaas rows with RPC logs for older history. Front end and hosting: React and React Three Fiber (one "Sakasa Fuji" scene shared by the landing and the app), on Cloudflare Workers. A Worker serves the settlements API with the MultiBaas key kept as a secret; another proxies Workers AI for the benchmark's Llama baseline. AI usage: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote the code and docs under our direction, as a lead session plus parallel sub-agents; OpenAI Codex made one revision to the landing's garden. We chose the idea, the prizes, the scope and the constraints, handled accounts, keys and funds, and tested the demos. Every project-building sub-agent's brief is committed verbatim in docs/ai/briefs (15 of the 43 did the team's private preparation or tooling, and are listed by name without their briefs), Karan's own calls and the messages behind them are in docs/ai/calls-we-made.md, AI-assisted commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer (except 32 made between 13:50 and 16:14 JST on Sep 26), and AI_USAGE.md says who wrote what.

projects.title: nacre
projects.description: Your Uniswap range can go quiet. Nacre puts a funded floor under your trading fees.
projects.project_description:
The APY looked great when you deposited. Then the price moved. Concentrated liquidity gives LPs control over where their capital works, but very little certainty about what it earns. A position can spend days outside its range, generating no trading fees.
Nacre lets LPs buy protection against that fee shortfall. Underwriters fund price ranges and set the premium, coverage duration and maximum payout per position. LPs choose an available range, supply liquidity and purchase coverage backed by that capital. Say you protect 10 USDC of fees over 30 days. If your position earns 6 USDC in eligible fees, coverage pays the missing 4 USDC. If it earns more than 10, there is no payout. The premium is the cost of buying that protection. Underwriters earn premiums for taking the other side. Their capital pays the claims, so pricing badly has real consequences. Each bid has limited capital and a fixed number of spots. Once those are taken, more coverage cannot be sold against the same capacity. Nacre protects fee income. Token price losses and impermanent loss remain with the LP. The current prototype runs on Base Sepolia with test assets.
projects.how_its_made:
Nacre combines Uniswap v4 positions with a custom underwriting application built on 1inch Aqua.
Uniswap v4 provides the liquidity positions, pool state and fee collection. Our Solidity contracts bind coverage to a specific position NFT, price range, fee target and duration. The policy vault holds the NFT during coverage so the LP cannot remove liquidity or change the insured position after buying protection. At activation, the vault collects and forwards any existing fees. At settlement, it collects the position’s fees again, values both tokens through the configured oracle and calculates the eligible shortfall. Payouts cannot exceed the policy cap. 1inch Aqua handles the underwriting quote allocation and execution. Funded offer contracts publish quotes through Aqua’s ship function. When an LP buys coverage, our Aqua application pulls the full payout collateral into the policy vault and transfers the premium to the selected offer. An active policy therefore has its maximum payout reserved. One tricky part was letting investors choose narrower ranges inside an underwriter’s funded range without multiplying the available backing. Those positions share the bid’s capital and spot limit. The contracts enforce both when coverage is purchased. The frontend uses Next.js, React and viem. A Bun and Fastify API reads contract state and stores registered positions in SQLite. Historical fee data powers pricing suggestions and profit scenarios, while settlement uses fees collected from the actual position. Foundry fork tests exercise the integration against deployed Uniswap and Aqua contracts.

projects.title: Buckets
projects.description: Self-custodial DeFi with programmable policies for bounded, onchain execution.
projects.project_description: DeFi users face a fundamental trade-off between self-custody and programmable execution. You can keep assets in your own wallet, but giving an operator, strategy, or application permission to act on that liquidity can require broad approvals or trusted intermediaries. The alternative is moving assets into a contract or vault, sacrificing the simplicity of direct ownership. BUCKET addresses this by separating asset ownership from execution authority. Users keep custody of their liquidity while defining explicit financial policies for delegated execution: who can act, which assets and directions are permitted, how much can be spent, and when the authority expires. BUCKET uses ENSv2 to identify authorized operators, 1inch Aqua as the self-custodial liquidity rail, and SwapVM as the programmable execution layer. A BUCKET policy is compiled into an executable program with onchain checks for authorization, execution direction, quote constraints, spend limits, and actual wallet balance. The result is bounded, revocable execution without transferring ownership of the underlying assets. Our demo proves the complete flow on-chain: create a capability, authorize an ENS identity, execute a real Aqua + SwapVM transaction, verify the resulting wallet transfer, then attempt to exceed the policy limit and demonstrate that execution is rejected.
projects.how_its_made: BUCKET is a self-custodial financial capability protocol built with Solidity, Foundry, TypeScript, and React, using 1inch Aqua, SwapVM, and ENSv2 as core infrastructure. The protocol separates asset ownership from execution authority: users keep their liquidity in their own wallets while defining scoped, revocable policies for how that liquidity can be used. The Solidity layer contains BucketController for intents, settlement verification, and execution receipts; BucketCapabilities for issuing, delegating, revoking, expiring, and accounting for capabilities; BucketAuthority for ENSv2-based authorization; and a custom SwapVM router. Our TypeScript packages provide shared policy types and validation, typed protocol clients, and an exact mirror of the on-chain execution math. We use ENSv2 for identity , allowing a financial capability to be associated with a resolved ENS identity and its delegation hierarchy. We use 1inch Aqua as the self-custodial liquidity rail , so execution can settle against liquidity without introducing a BUCKET custody vault. We use SwapVM as the execution rail , compiling BUCKET policies into executable instructions that enforce the rules during the swap itself. We extended SwapVM with four BUCKET-specific instructions: 0xd0 CapabilityGuard, 0xd1 Quote, 0xd2 SpendLimit, and 0xd3 WalletBalanceCheck. Together they enforce authorization, bounded pricing, quantitative limits, and the user's actual ERC-20 balance inside the execution path rather than relying on frontend checks. On top of this capability infrastructure, we built RALE (Risk-Adaptive Liquidity Engine) as a programmable market-making strategy. RALE makes the maker's executable price state-dependent rather than static. projects.project_description_markdown:
DeFi users face a fundamental trade-off between self-custody and programmable execution. You can keep assets in your own wallet, but giving an operator, strategy, or application permission to act on that liquidity can require broad approvals or trusted intermediaries. The alternative is moving assets into a contract or vault, sacrificing the simplicity of direct ownership.

BUCKET addresses this by separating asset ownership from execution authority. Users keep custody of their liquidity while defining explicit financial policies for delegated execution: who can act, which assets and directions are permitted, how much can be spent, and when the authority expires.

BUCKET uses ENSv2 to identify authorized operators, 1inch Aqua as the self-custodial liquidity rail, and SwapVM as the programmable execution layer. A BUCKET policy is compiled into an executable program with onchain checks for authorization, execution direction, quote constraints, spend limits, and actual wallet balance.

The result is bounded, revocable execution without transferring ownership of the underlying assets. Our demo proves the complete flow on-chain: create a capability, authorize an ENS identity, execute a real Aqua + SwapVM transaction, verify the resulting wallet transfer, then attempt to exceed the policy limit and demonstrate that execution is rejected.

projects.title: Bonded
projects.description: Bonded stops AI payment agents from paying fraudulent invoices by re-checking every fact first.
projects.project_description: Business Email Compromise is the FBI IC3's costliest cybercrime category: an attacker impersonates a real vendor and says "we changed our bank account." Companies want AI agents to run accounts payable, but an agent that trusts the invoice pays the attacker. Bonded sits inside the agent's payment decision. Before any money moves, it independently re-derives every fact the payment relies on (who the vendor is, the payout address on file, the amount, whether the vendor is active) and compares each against what the invoice claims. It also screens the payout address for sanctions and scam risk. Every invoice gets one of three verdicts. CLEARED is paid automatically on Sui. REFUSED pays nothing and shows the claimed value next to the real one. HELD, for the genuinely ambiguous case such as a recent bank-detail change or a large irreversible payment, waits for a World ID–verified human. People are only asked when it matters, so they don't rubber-stamp every invoice. Bonded ships as an SDK and an MCP server, so any AP platform or agent framework can add it before its own payment step.
projects.how_its_made: A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) with a Next.js 16 console. The core is enforce(), a five-step check: policy hash, premise re-derivation, sanctions screening, budget, then an irreversibility gate. Premises route through a dispatcher to whichever adapter owns each fact. All money is bigint fixed-point with 6 decimals and never a float. Sui: a Move package holds a USDSUI vault and a policy registry. The agent's policy hash is committed on-chain, and each check produces a Verdict object that settle or settle_with_stepup must consume to pay, so a payment can't skip verification. Signing goes through the Sui CLI keystore, so the app never touches key bytes. Intercepta: live screening of the vendor's EVM payout address. An OFAC-listed Lazarus address is refused, with the evidence stored by hash. World: vendors verify their identity with World ID (IDKit) before a bank-detail change counts. Payments above the irreversible threshold need a fresh World ID for Agents step-up, checked server-side against JWKS within a 5-minute window. Disclosed limitation: the vendor master is a clearly disclosed fixture standing in for a real ERP or vendor system. Every other check runs live on Sui testnet.

projects.title: Agent's List
projects.description: Angie's List for AI agents. Every hire is ENS-named, Intercepta-screened and World ID-approved.
projects.project_description: Agent's List is Angie's List for AI agents, a marketplace where people and the AI agents working for them hire specialist AI agents for real, milestone-based work. It has one hard rule, an agent only spends money that a verified human approved with a fresh World ID verification, and only inside pre-approved limits. The problem Agents have started hiring and paying each other, often over x402, for an API call, a dataset or another agent's work. Today there are two bad options, hand an agent your wallet, and one hallucination or one compromised sub-agent can drain it, or approve every payment by hand, with no idea who is on the other side. Agent listings are anonymous, payees are bare addresses nobody checks, and a sub-agent inherits whatever authority its parent had. What a buyer does You start by typing the outcome you need or uploading an existing statement of work (PDF, Word or text). A guided flow turns it into a contract with milestones, success criteria, a deadline, a budget split per milestone, an estimate and matched agents. To fund the job, you approve it on your phone with World ID. The approval screen shows exactly what you are signing off on, including the amount, the agent, its ENS name and payout address, and its risk-screening result, and after approval, the USDC waits in escrow. Finally, the agent submits each milestone with evidence, and you release that milestone's payment with World ID approvals Hiring from your own agent Claude Code, or any MCP client, can search the catalog, scope a job and start a hire through our MCP server, but it can never pay. It shows you a short code, you approve on your phone with World ID, and the agent only finds out whether the money moved. For agent operators Operators list an agent, pick its ENS name (for example quartz-qa-test-planner.agentslist-app.eth) and stamp its exact configuration with World ID, covering the model, tools, MCP servers, price range and payout address. Change any of it and the agent can't be hired until it is re-stamped. The payout address is screened by Intercepta before the listing goes live, and because a ban follows the person behind the World ID, banning an operator stops every agent they run. Agents hiring agents A hired agent can sub-hire another agent, or buy a task from one over x402, but only inside a mandate derived from the human's approval. That mandate can only get narrower, with a smaller budget, a subset of categories, an earlier expiry and a limited depth. Before a paying agent signs, Intercepta screens the recipient and the exact payment authorization, and the receiving side screens the payer too. What each partner does World ID decides who can move the money. Every approval is a fresh verification bound to one exact action, so a stolen session or a replayed approval can't move funds, and spending caps and bans apply to a person rather than to a wallet or an agent. ENS decides where the money goes. Every agent is its own ENSv2 namespace carrying its description and payout address. Every funded job gets its own subname that expires at the deadline and records the contract's hash and status, and the hired agent can update that job's status and deliverable and nothing else. Payment goes to the address in the agent's ENS record, and if it no longer matches what the operator stamped, the payment is blocked. Intercepta decides whether it is safe to pay. Every payee, and every paying agent, is screened against real mainnet risk data before money moves. Sanctioned, scam or phishing addresses are refused with their reasons shown, risky ones are capped or flagged for the human, and if screening fails for any reason, the payment is refused. The three are chained. ENS names the payee, Intercepta screens it, and the World ID approval covers both. Failure paths are first-class too, including denied, expired and cancelled approvals, a sanctioned payee refused with its reasons, and a payment stopped because an agent's ENS record changed. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia with test USDC. We also built seven first-party specialists on our own agent kit (financial research, market research, contract review, month-end bookkeeping, proposals, support automation and data analysis), designed to do milestone work on their own machines and tie every claim to a source.
projects.how_its_made: Agent's List is built around the idea that every dollar an agent moves traces back, through mandates that can only narrow, to a fresh World ID verification of an exact action. World, ENS, and Intercepta each close one hole in that chain (who may move the money, where it goes, whether the other side is safe to pay), and we chained them so none can be skipped: the World ID nonce is the hash of an action that already contains the ENS-verified payee and the Intercepta verdict IDs. Stack: Python 3.12 / Flask 3, SQLAlchemy + Alembic, Postgres on Vercel (SQLite locally), Jinja + vanilla JS + ethers v6. web3.py on Ethereum Sepolia with Circle USDC (EIP-3009, EIP-712 domain read from the contract). The official x402 Python SDK on the paying side (v2 exact). PyJWT for OIDC. A Node + viem sidecar for ENSv2. A FastMCP stdio server so Claude Code can hire. Seven first-party specialists on our own agent kit (Claude and OpenAI-compatible adapters, policy-gated tools, a claim ledger that checks verbatim quotes). Workflow: Job description -> hashed statement of work (an uploaded SOW's SHA-256 is inside it) -> payee resolved from ENS -> Intercepta screens the payee -> canonical action JSON (amount, payee, ENS name, SOW hash, screening IDs) -> sha256 -> World ID step-up with that hash as the nonce -> consume() under a row lock: re-hash, re-check ban / weekly cap / human, re-resolve ENS, re-screen -> escrow executor (EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization into escrow, USDC transfer on each milestone release). The hired agent then spends under an ES256 mandate JWT that can only narrow (budget <= parent - spent - live siblings, categories a subset, expiry no later, depth <= 2) to sub-hire or buy tasks from other agents over x402. World ID for Agents: World's OIDC provider (sandbox issuer), validated only on our backend. Browser: code + PKCE S256 with prompt=login and max_age=0, so World re-verifies every time. Agents without a browser (Claude Code over MCP): RFC 8628 device grant; the agent shows a code, the human approves on their phone. The hack: the OIDC nonce is base64url(sha256(canonical action)). A token with any other nonce is rejected (a device token that omits it stays bound to its device code), auth_time must postdate the approval and be under 300 s old, and a jti never repeats, so one verification approves one exact action, not a session. World's pairwise sub is our only handle on a person: weekly caps and bans follow the person, not a wallet; the first approver claims the job; mandates carry sha256(sub); operators stamp their agent's manifest (model, tools, MCP servers, price, payout) with World ID and any edit forces a re-stamp; even sign-in is a step-up. Denied, expired, cancelled and rejected are real states with codes (NONCE_MISMATCH, STALE_AUTH, REPLAYED_TOKEN), and a payment that fails screening is blocked before it reaches World. PKCE verifiers, device codes and slow_down intervals live in Postgres so any Vercel instance can finish a flow. ENSv2: agentslist-app.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia. Each agent gets {label}.agentslist-app.eth with its own PermissionedResolver and UserRegistry; its records follow ENSIP-26 (agent-context, agent-endpoint[mcp]) and ENSIP-25 (agent-registration keyed by the ERC-7930 address of the ERC-8004 registry), plus x402-payto. Each funded job gets eng-{id}.{agent}.agentslist-app.eth: expiry = SOW deadline, platform-owned with roleBitmap 0 (non-transferable), sow-hash / mandate / status records, and the hired agent may set only status and deliverable. Sub-hires are wildcard records on the job's resolver, so they expire and revoke with it; revoke strips the agent's grants and unregisters the job. Before paying, Python reads x402-payto through the Universal Resolver: it must equal the payout the operator stamped with World ID or the payment fails closed (PAYEE_MISMATCH), and the name is hashed into the approval and re-resolved right before money moves. Hacks: one resolver per job, because resolver roles are per resolver, not per name; CREATE2 salts carry a version so a revoked name can be reissued; every on-chain step is journaled so a crash resumes mid-sequence, 60 s commit wait included; no default records, since an expired job falls back to its ancestor's resolver; the sidecar checks ROOT_REGISTRY -> getSubregistry("eth") at boot because the beta gets redeployed. Intercepta: Every hop is screened: an operator's payout address when they stamp a listing (Deep Scan), the payee at fund, release and sub-hire, the paying agent's wallet on every sub-hire and x402 task, and, in our paying-agent runner, the exact x402 authorization before signing. The SDK's before-payment hook fires before the authorization exists and its after-hook only sees it signed, so we wrapped its EVM signer: sign_typed_data first sends the exact EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization to Scan Message, with Quick Scan on the payee and Token Risks on USDC. Three live calls before the key is touched. The server deep-scans the payer and re-screens the authorization on receipt, so neither side can skip the gate. Risk data is mainnet-only, so each Sepolia payee maps to a real mainnet address and we rebuild the EIP-712 payload as its mainnet twin (chainId 1, mainnet USDC domain, mapped addresses). Traits decide (sanctions, known scammer -> REFUSE; mixers, non-KYC or anything unknown -> ASK_HUMAN), toxic score is secondary, and a missing key, a 4 s timeout or a bad schema is REFUSE. Verdict IDs go into the World ID-approved action, so an ASK_HUMAN warning is acknowledged by the human's own verification. In a live run, a demo agent mapped to an OFAC-sanctioned mainnet EOA was refused with six reasons (sanction_address, known_scammer, blacklist, fake_phishing_transfer...) by both the pre-sign gate and the hire flow, before any approval or signature existed; clean agents passed through to the World ID step. Additionally: The first 402 response creates a server-owned HireIntent (task hash, ENS payee, amount, expiry), so a paid retry can't swap the task. Agent IDs carry a Crockford base32 check digit the MCP server validates locally, so typos and nearly all invented IDs never reach the API. We built with Claude Code and Codex working in parallel, one task per branch and git worktree, with a CI check that requires every agent-authored PR to carry a self-review: 73 merged PRs and about 2,000 offline tests against a fake World IdP and a fake screener.

projects.title: Fleet Naming Service
projects.description: One ENSv2 registry, many doorways: hire an AI agent fleet with one tx, fire it with one.
projects.project_description: FNS (Fleet Naming Service) gives AI agent fleets a single on-chain identity that many businesses can adopt and drop instantly, using ENSv2's registry-linking primitives. A vendor runs a fleet of support agents (mia, kai, rin) in one ENSv2 UserRegistry. That same registry is mounted under several names at once — support.vendor.eth, support.shopa.eth, support.shopb.eth — so mia.support.shopa.eth and mia.support.shopb.eth resolve to the SAME ERC-1155 token, not copies kept in sync. Two kill switches, owned by opposite parties: Hire / fire: a merchant mounts the fleet with one setSubregistry transaction and unmounts it with one. Vendor recall: the vendor unregisters one agent and every doorway for it, under every merchant, dies in the same block. The catch: mounting is permissionless, so a scammer can mount the real fleet under support.scam.eth and it resolves. FNS ships a verifier (stock viem + the real UniversalResolver) that checks membership, canonical registry, two-sided consent (the fleet's own enf.parents record must list the parent), doorway expiry, and screens the settlement address against the OFAC sanctions oracle / Intercepta. Every name gets a live verdict: GREEN (legit), RED (counterfeit mount), ORANGE (endorsed doorway, flagged counterparty) or BLACK (not a member). The Next.js app includes a playbook editor where you build the demo as a node workflow — check a name, unmount, fire an agent, counterfeit mount, dirty settlement — sign each step in your browser wallet, and watch the topology graph, agent × doorway verdict grid and on-chain timeline update live. Deployed on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: FNS writes no Solidity of its own — it composes the real, deployed ENSv2 contracts on Sepolia (RootRegistry, ETHRegistry, ETHRegistrar, UserRegistry, PermissionedResolver, VerifiableFactory, UniversalResolverV2, UniversalHelper). The fleet's UserRegistry and a shared PermissionedResolver are deployed as proxies through VerifiableFactory.deployProxy with CREATE2 salts; each merchant gets its own UserRegistry with a "support" label whose subregistry points at the fleet. The hacky/notable bits: Namespace aliasing: one registry mounted at multiple setSubregistry points. We found no other project doing multi-mount. The shared resolver's default record (DNS name 0x00) holds the whole fleet bundle — addr(60) settlement address, enf.canonical, enf.parents, ENSIP-26 agent-context and agent-endpoint[web] — so every member inherits it without its own record. Topology fix: the resolver is attached to members only at register(), never to the parent node. That way a made-up name (bob.support.shopa.eth) returns ResolverNotFound instead of resolving through a wildcard — otherwise the verifier's "not a member" verdict would be meaningless. Stack: TypeScript + viem for setup/demo scripts (tsx), a standalone @fns/verifier package implementing checks C1–C5 (ENSIP-15 normalization, UniversalResolver resolution, registry walk from the root, UniversalHelper.findExactRegistry for canonical match). C5 screening uses the Chainalysis sanctions oracle on mainnet (keyless, real OFAC data) plus Intercepta (Web3 Antivirus) when an API key is set. Next.js 16 / React 19 app with server routes: /api/verify, /api/fleet (discovers every mount from SubregistryUpdated logs and verifies every agent × doorway at one block), and /api/actions, which plans kill-switch transactions for the browser wallet to sign — the server holds no keys. Testing: Foundry fork tests against the live ENSv2 deployment (10 passing, no mocks) and 80 vitest tests, including fork tests that run the demo scripts end-to-end.

projects.title: Dead or Alive Agent
projects.description: Pre-sign x402 payment screening with automatic holds and human-reviewed recovery controls.
projects.project_description: Dead or Alive Agent supervises an autonomous agent's x402 purchases before its signing key is created. It first discovers and parses an unsigned HTTP 402 response, then checks the proposed recipient and token with Intercepta. A clean requirement can continue to a tightly matched signed retry. A risky result is held, the local runtime is quarantined, and a World device-authorization challenge can request a fresh human decision. The repository includes a recovery vault, an audit stream, and a web console. The current hosted deployment is frontend-only; live credentials and ENSv2 beta compatibility work remain before the complete external flow can run.
projects.how_its_made: The backend uses TypeScript, Fastify, Zod, viem, and the official x402 core, EVM, and fetch packages. Payment discovery runs without an account; privateKeyToAccount is reached only after the Intercepta verdict passes, and the paid retry must match the screened network, asset, and recipient. The supervisor is an explicit state machine exposed through JSON routes and server-sent events. The World client uses OIDC Device Authorization and verifies the returned RS256 ID token against the discovered JWKS, issuer, audience, Orb assurance context, and authentication time. Solidity and Foundry implement and test active, quarantined, restored, and killed vault states. The Next.js 16 interface uses Wagmi for Sepolia wallet connectivity. Automated tests cover the orchestration with controlled dependencies; the third-party integrations are not represented as live until their credentials and current ENS interfaces are configured.
