projects.title: Swish
projects.description: Only wallet you will ever need for agentic economy, wallet where your agents are the account holders
projects.project_description: Swish is an allowance wallet for AI agents. An agent can only spend what it said it would spend it on. THE PROBLEM. Giving an agent a wallet is giving a wallet to no one. The usual answer is a spending limit, which bounds how much and says nothing about to whom or for what. The Grok/Bankr wallet was drained for $330K in March 2025 and $175K again in May 2026; a guardrail was built after the first attack and did not survive a later rewrite, because it lived in application code rather than in what could actually move the money. HOW IT WORKS. Before anything is signed, the agent declares exactly what it is about to pay — recipient, asset, maximum amount, expiry, reason — as a typed object on Sui. Swish then simulates the agent's real transaction and diffs the actual on-chain effects against that declaration. An undeclared beneficiary, a capability grant slipped into the same transaction block, or an asset the declaration never named is a violation, and a violation means no proof object is ever minted. WHY IT HOLDS. In allowance_vault.move, grep for "balance::split" finds three call sites. Two are execute_declared and execute_with_override; both take a Declaration and a proof object by value and destroy them on the way in, so there is no boolean to forget to check and no path a future refactor can quietly drop. The third is owner_withdraw, which asserts the caller is the vault owner and touches no agent machinery at all. WHAT IS LIVE. The Move package is published and upgraded in place on Sui testnet (0x896cf6e9...), with a shared Vault<SUI> at 0xa8db67c3... and 16 unit tests passing, negative cases written first. Both execution paths have been exercised on chain. SPONSOR TECHNOLOGIES. Sui is the whole enforcement layer: linear types make "this permission no longer exists" a fact the compiler checks, simulateTransaction over gRPC produces the effects that get diffed, and ed25519_verify checks the attestation on chain. World is the human gate — when a payment breaches its envelope it stops for one verified person rather than whoever holds a key, using IDKit v4 uniqueness proofs, with the nullifier recorded so a replay is recognised as the same human instead of dead-ending. Intercepta screens the counterparty before a signature exists rather than after; a known exploiter address returns 90/100, High, MALICIOUS_ADDRESS, and the payment never gets signed. THE WALLET AROUND IT. Each agent carries an editable AGENT.md brief fed to the model as instructions before every run. Guardrails cover per-payment cap, rolling window, daily and per-counterparty ceilings, risk threshold and allowed assets, plus limits the operator names themselves, each measured by the same engine and with the operator's own wording becoming the text of the refusal. Money lives in one vault and each agent gets a bounded allocation from it. The agent loop runs on Groq with tool order enforced by what the model is able to call, not by asking it nicely. Swish speaks MCP in both directions: it exposes a server so someone else's agent can ask this wallet for money and be told no, and it registers outside MCP servers your own agents call out to, with per-agent, per-tool permissions that form the tool set rather than filtering it. It ships as a Chrome MV3 extension registering through the Wallet Standard, so any dApp that can connect to a Sui wallet can connect to an agent with an allowance instead — demonstrated against an included storefront that knows nothing about Swish and simply gets refused. THE HONEST BOUNDARY. Swish does not judge intent. An agent that honestly declares a bad payment to an address you already cleared will execute. What it guarantees is that every outflow is either exactly what was declared to someone you pre-approved, or it stopped and asked a verified human. Testnet only.
projects.how_its_made: Sui Move 2024 for the contracts. Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4) for the wallet. @mysten/sui v2 and @mysten/dapp-kit for chain access. AI SDK v6 ToolLoopAgent on Groq for the agent loop. A Chrome MV3 extension for the Wallet Standard surface. THE CONTRACTS. Four modules: allowance_vault, declaration, proofs, agent_cap. The design rule is that a permission is an object that gets destroyed, not a flag that gets checked. Declaration and MatchProof/OverrideApproval are passed by value into execute_declared/execute_with_override and consumed there, so double-spending a permission is a type error rather than a bug you have to remember not to write. Attestations are signed off-chain with Ed25519 and verified on-chain with ed25519_verify, binding the proof to the exact effects digest we simulated. 16 unit tests, negative cases first. THE THING THAT COST THE MOST TIME. Sui testnet has fully retired JSON-RPC. Every method 404s, not just the exotic ones, which we only found after funding an address and seeing nothing. The whole chain layer was rewritten onto SuiGrpcClient, with simulateTransaction replacing devInspect/dryRun. That has a knock-on effect: dapp-kit's SuiClientProvider still builds a JSON-RPC client internally, so the demo storefront cannot broadcast in the browser. It posts the signed bytes to its own backend and submits over gRPC, which is what a real dApp backend does anyway and is genuinely Swish-agnostic: it takes bytes and a signature from any Sui wallet. HAND-ROLLED WALLET STANDARD. An injected page script cannot use npm imports without a bundler, so inpage.js dispatches wallet-standard:register-wallet and answers wallet-standard:app-ready directly. About twenty lines instead of a build step. A FINDING WORTH FLAGGING. dapp-kit's useSignAndExecuteTransaction never calls a wallet's sui:signAndExecuteTransaction. It always goes through sui:signTransaction and broadcasts the result itself. We had implemented sign-only as a deliberate refusal, which silently made the wallet useless to almost every dApp. The fix answers the original worry properly: before checking anything, Swish resolves the gas coin the site cannot know about, sets the transaction to expire at the end of the current epoch so a held signature cannot be replayed indefinitely, builds once, then simulates, diffs and signs those exact bytes. The Wallet Standard returns bytes alongside signature precisely so a wallet can hand back something different from what it was given. WHAT EACH PARTNER TECHNOLOGY ACTUALLY BOUGHT US. Sui is the only reason the guarantee is structural: linear types make "this permission no longer exists" a compile-time fact, and simulateTransaction gives the pre-flight effects that make the diff possible. World turns "ask a human" into one specific verified person rather than whoever holds a key; IDKit v4 took seven bugs to get right, the last being that action: "" is falsy in JavaScript, which silently swallowed the widget, and that a nullifier_replayed refusal is World recognising you. We now read the nullifier out of that refusal and treat it as recognition rather than a dead end. Intercepta screens counterparties before a signature exists rather than after; it is mainnets-only, so screening runs against a real EVM exploiter address and genuinely returns 90/100 MALICIOUS_ADDRESS. HACKY BITS, STATED PLAINLY. The vault's balance is decoded from raw BCS at a fixed byte offset: Vault<T> is id: UID (32 bytes) followed immediately by Balance<T> (one u64, little-endian), so bytes 32..39. gRPC returns object content as bytes and pulling in a full layout resolver was not worth it. The code says so and names the field-order assumption that would break it. Topping up the vault runs as a single programmable transaction because sui client split-coin needs a gas coin that is not the coin being split, so on a single-coin address it fails with "insufficient SUI balance" while sitting on plenty; splitting from gas inside a PTB sidesteps that and costs one gas payment instead of two. owner_withdraw shipped via sui client upgrade using the recorded UpgradeCap rather than a fresh publish, because republishing mints a new type identity and would have orphaned the live vault, its funds and its on-chain allow-list. AGENT KEYS. Real Ed25519 keypairs sealed with AES-256-GCM under an env secret and persisted to a server-side keystore. That last part was a bug fix: the browser's backup snapshot correctly strips secrets, so restoring from it handed back agents with no key, and every dev-server restart was permanently orphaning funded addresses. THE AGENT LOOP. prepareStep and activeTools restrict the model to exactly the next tool in sequence, so ordering is enforced by what it is able to call rather than by prompt instruction. Groq's free tier runs it; Anthropic is the fallback when the 8k-tokens-per-minute limit bites. Each agent's AGENT.md brief is composed into the instructions ahead of the hard rules, which are then restated after it, so a brief can narrow what an agent intends but never widen what it may do. MCP IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. A server exposing five tools so an outside agent can ask this wallet for money and be refused, and a client registering outside servers whose tools are granted per agent and per tool. Registration probes the server immediately with initialize then tools/list, and handles streamable-HTTP servers that answer a plain POST with an SSE frame, where a bare JSON.parse chokes on the data: prefix.

projects.title: Cypher Brain
projects.description: Give an AI agent an ENSv2-scoped, revocable wallet permission for one field. Never your funds.
projects.project_description: Cypher Brain is an existing open-source project that encrypts a personal AI "second brain" (gbrain) every night, then publishes a pointer to it so the brain can be restored elsewhere. That nightly job is run by an AI agent, not a human — which meant giving the agent broad, unverifiable trust: either the owner's real wallet key, or a centralized server nobody outside its operator could audit. This submission replaces that with ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control. The owner grants a separate agent wallet a role scoped to exactly one text-record key on the name's existing Permissioned Resolver — no custom smart contract. Routine pointer updates then use only the agent key; the owner's real key is never touched again. The scope is proven, not claimed: our ens-verify command reads the granted key back to confirm the write, then simulates a write to a different key and requires the resolver itself to reject it with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. We ran the full flow live on Sepolia — registered a real ENS name, granted three independent keys, wrote and verified each one, and captured every transaction hash. A stolen agent wallet can update one field. It cannot move funds, write anywhere else, or act as the owner.
projects.how_its_made: This project is a TypeScript CLI (cypher-brain) that already handled encryption and storage of a personal AI second brain; this submission adds four new subcommands on top of it: agent-wallet keygen, ens-setup, ens-set-text, and ens-verify. age encrypts the second-brain snapshot on-device before it ever reaches a storage backend (local file, Arweave/Turbo, or TON storage for this demo). The ENS text record only ever holds a pointer to that ciphertext — never the plaintext or its decryption key. For the ENSv2 side, viem talks to Sepolia and to the name's Permissioned Resolver. ens-setup lets the owner grant ROLE_SET_TEXT for one text key to a locally generated agent wallet, using a hidden interactive prompt so the owner's key is never written to disk. ens-set-text then lets that agent wallet alone write the granted key. ens-verify closes the loop: it reads the key back to confirm the value, then simulates (not broadcasts) a write to a different key, requiring the resolver's Enhanced Access Control to revert it with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. The hacky-but-deliberate part: we did not write a new smart contract. Everything here — the Permissioned Resolver, its Enhanced Access Control roles, the ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution path text records now go through — already existed in ENSv2's fresh Sepolia redeployment. We just wired an existing OSS project's agent wallet into permissions ENSv2 already offers, and proved the scope holds by making the agent try to break it and fail, live, on-chain.

This project is a TypeScript CLI (cypher-brain) that already handled encryption and storage of a personal AI second brain; this submission adds four new subcommands on top of it: agent-wallet keygen, ens-setup, ens-set-text, and ens-verify.

age encrypts the second-brain snapshot on-device before it ever reaches a storage backend (local file, Arweave/Turbo, or TON storage for this demo). The ENS text record only ever holds a pointer to that ciphertext — never the plaintext or its decryption key.

For the ENSv2 side, viem talks to Sepolia and to the name's Permissioned Resolver. ens-setup lets the owner grant ROLE_SET_TEXT for one text key to a locally generated agent wallet, using a hidden interactive prompt so the owner's key is never written to disk. ens-set-text then lets that agent wallet alone write the granted key. ens-verify closes the loop: it reads the key back to confirm the value, then simulates (not broadcasts) a write to a different key, requiring the resolver's Enhanced Access Control to revert it with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles.

The hacky-but-deliberate part: we did not write a new smart contract. Everything here — the Permissioned Resolver, its Enhanced Access Control roles, the ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution path text records now go through — already existed in ENSv2's fresh Sepolia redeployment. We just wired an existing OSS project's agent wallet into permissions ENSv2 already offers, and proved the scope holds by making the agent try to break it and fail, live, on-chain.

projects.title: yuin
projects.description: Privacy-preserving sign-in for any app — email or Google in, smart account out. No address mapping.
projects.project_description: Sign-in for apps that need real accounts, without making anyone learn crypto. Your users type an email and a password. They get a smart account with a passkey on it. No seed phrase, no extension, no gas prompt, nothing to understand. And nobody can take it from them. The password never leaves their browser, so no server holds the thing that unlocks the account. Creating one takes two independent parties agreeing — neither can mint an account alone, and both colluding get an empty one. Not "we promise not to look." We can't. Developers set up in one page. Claim a name on ENSv2, tick which sign-in methods you accept, done. Those rules are published where your users can read them before they trust you with anything. Inside the account, Uniswap quietly fixes the worst part of crypto UX: your user holds ETH, your price is in USDC, it just works. One confirmation. Like trusted vendors, but without the lock-in. Auth without the auth code.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity on Sepolia, Next.js on the front, two small Node services between them. Identity is a keccak hash of the email and an Argon2id stretch of the password, computed in the browser with WASM. The chain sees one hash and nothing else. It is written once, and only when two separately-keyed senders have each signed the same digest — chain id and contract address baked in, signers required in ascending order so one cannot sign twice wearing a hat. Accounts are ERC-4337 with an owner list instead of a single owner, and session keys whose spend cap the account itself enforces. Passkeys are genuine owners: the account rebuilds the exact bytes the authenticator signed, confirms the challenge really is in that clientDataJSON, checks the user-presence flag, then verifies the P-256 signature on chain through a deployed verifier — Sepolia has no RIP-7212 precompile, so the verifier is a contract using OpenZeppelin's Solidity implementation. ENSv2 is an ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver reading AppRegistry directly, so <app>.app.yuin.eth serves the app's sign-in rules as text records that cannot drift from the registry — it is the same storage, not a copy. Uniswap runs through the account's own execute. Swaps quote all three fee tiers and take the best, since Sepolia pool depth varies by an order of magnitude; ETH in is a single payable call, tokens in batch the approval and the swap into one transaction. Gas for a brand-new owner key is sponsored openly by a sender until a paymaster replaces it.

projects.title: AICity
projects.description: We make it dead simple to launch your own pop up city. It is Ethereum and AI agent native.
projects.project_description: We make it dead simple to launch your own pop up city. All you have to do is describe the name, location, mission statement, start and end date. It's easy to make a residency inside of it. Create a residency with a link to a listing (e.g. on AirBnB), list out the prices of each room, a deadline and min and maximum number of people to join each residency. When it's reached, then the funds can be released to the boundary. For the hardware POC, each residency comes with a visual dashboard that displays key information, number of residents, treasury balance, time until start and end date. Residents can access the phsyical space by unlocking the door with their Ethereum wallet, which we demonstrate using an air gapped raspberry pi zero wallet

projects.title: SuiDoBashi
projects.description: DeFi talent marketplace on Sui: local AI reads intent, your wallet signs every transaction safely
projects.project_description: Suidobashi is a DeFi talent marketplace on Sui, not a wallet. Users connect any Sui wallet they trust, inspect full transaction details in advance, and sign only approved actions. A local AI agent built with the QVAC SDK captures chat intention, applies deterministic policy and security checks, and routes requests to independent DeFi talents. Current talent coverage includes swaps, escrowed orders, Cetus CLMM position management, and DeepBook v3 grid authority with per-guard bands, quantity and budget bounds. For provenance and monetization, the architecture assigns SuiNS the publisher/agent registry and reputation anchor. Publishers and agents use readable leaf names with parent-controlled revocation; each identity binds an x402 recipient address; fulfillment receipts and service-fee payment events provide the evidence for ranking, preferring, and paying reliable agents. Walrus is the single source of truth bound to those SuiNS identities for each published agent install: versioned manifests, strategy grids, pre-prompts, action logs, receipts, and verification artifacts. A Sui registry maps identity to current pointer, blob ID, manifest hash, revision, and standing, keeping publisher names revocable while blobs remain immutable.
projects.how_its_made: Web app: React 19 plus Tailwind SPA served by the local Bun server, with connect, chat, policy, signing, talent, strategy, and activity panes kept separate from chain effects. Local agent: QVAC-powered model converts chat into structured intent; deterministic TypeScript gates check wallet balance, policy, venues, slippage, allowances, vault binding, position bounds, and order limits before submission. Wallet signing: users approve complete transaction bytes in their chosen Sui wallet; the server stores unsigned builds, receives signatures separately, and submits signed bytes. No server or repository holds user keys. Move package: sui_tokyo, edition 2024, with policy, order, spend vault, position, and DeepBook guard modules; tests cover gates, bounds, rotation, capability checks, revocation paths, budgets, and exits. Cetus: aggregator SDK and CLMM dependency for venue-aware swaps, positions, tick bounds, rewards, redemption, and direction-aware settlement. DeepBook v3: pinned source revision for grid authority; BalanceManager capabilities stay inside the guard while delegated operators receive bounded buy/sell only. Talent marketplace: independent talents with manifests, installed/marketplace states, strategies, runner plans, explicit refusals, and served-bundle verification. Identity, storage, and payments: SuiNS handles readable publisher/agent identities, revocation-safe leaf naming, recipient-address binding, and fulfillment-derived reputation; Walrus stores manifests, grids, pre-prompts, logs, receipts, and verification packets; the registry binds each identity to the current blob, hash, revision, and standing.

projects.title: MynaHealth
projects.description: Zero-knowledge medical eligibility for Japan: prove the condition, keep the record.
projects.project_description: MynaHealth is a medical proof primitive for Japan. It turns an issuer-signed dispensing record into a browser-generated Groth16 proof that a treatment rule is satisfied—without releasing the patient name, medication code, exact dispensing day, signature, or source document. A clinic, insurer, or online health service receives a narrow, independently verifiable answer instead of another copy of a sensitive record. The working demo generates eligible and ineligible proofs from synthetic Japanese records. The technical design composes an ENS-named policy, a World IDKit request bound to the medical proof digest, and a replay-protected Solidity gate. We also built a MyNaPortal medication-XML adapter and a second circuit that proves a hidden nine-digit medication code is in an allowed set and matches a blinded SHA-256 commitment. This is the foundation for attaching authenticated web provenance to the private medical proof.
projects.how_its_made: The core Circom 2 circuit checks an EdDSA/Poseidon issuer signature, medication allowlist, date window, and holder context using a private record witness. snarkjs creates the Groth16 proof in the React browser; an Express verifier independently checks the public policy inputs. A second compiled circuit proves SHA256(ASCII medication code || 16-byte blinder) and allowed-set membership while the code remains private; an altered public hash fails verification. The YZK-IF-002 adapter parses Japanese MyNaPortal medication XML locally. World IDKit 4 uses an RP-signed request tied to the medical proof digest, with backend World verification and a nullifier replay guard. viem resolves ENS policy metadata; Solidity and Forge model an ENS-resolved gate and test policy mismatch and double-spend rejection. We independently ran a TLSNotary fixture; binding a live authenticated medical response to the commitment is the remaining bridge. Built with Bun, Vite, TypeScript, Solidity, and Foundry.

projects.title: Levarac
projects.description: A peer-to-peer check of who was really there: phones that meet sign.
projects.project_description: Try it: install the Beid app from its public iOS beta (https://testflight.apple.com/join/2DNXhfTR), then open the human-check join page (https://alcor-human-check.levarac.workers.dev/, World ID staging). Code, deployments and verification steps: https://github.com/levarac/mizar Levarac answers one question for people who run events and apps: was this user really there, and did they actually meet anyone? Today the choice is an open allowlist that gets farmed, or a strong check built on private data that nobody outside can audit. Levarac is our ongoing project. Its Parallax protocol lets attendee phones record rotating Bluetooth identifiers of nearby phones and sign what they saw. An operator service anchors ordered commitments of those signed observations on Sepolia. That evidence layer, the Beid attendee app and the Barnard BLE library existed before this hackathon. At ETHGlobal Tokyo we built the part that turns this evidence into a fair, checkable reward list: Alcor, a human check. At join time the attendee proves with World ID (IDKit 4) that they are one person, and Alcor binds that World ID to exactly one event key for the event and publishes a signed credential list. A second key from the same person is rejected. Mizar, an evaluator and batch claim. A fixed public rule counts a key only if it has mutual, signed observations with at least N distinct credentialed partners, in at least B separate time windows per partner. The evaluator publishes a manifest, the eligible list and Merkle proofs; a root poster posts the root to a claim contract on Sepolia; each person then claims an EAS attestation with a signature from their event key. Anyone can recompute the list from the published inputs. Changing one bit makes verification fail. Ten phones held by one person still count as one person, and walking in without meeting anyone is not enough. What it does not do: it does not prove physical location, and it does not stop Bluetooth relays or verified people who agree to lie together. Alcor is a trusted attester in this version, because it verifies World ID off-chain. Claims link an event key to a wallet publicly. Status at submission: the claim contract and EAS schema are deployed on Sepolia (source verified on Sourcify), the Alcor service is live on World ID staging, and a read-only evaluation of the live demo event passed with 0 eligible keys because no phone had done the human check yet. The claim page, the first posted root and a live claim are still pending.
projects.how_its_made: Pre-existing: Beid, the attendee app (iOS/Android), public at github.com/levarac/beid. Its UI redesign continued in parallel during the event; that work is not part of this submission. Barnard, the BLE sensing SDK (Swift/Kotlin, MIT), public at github.com/levarac/barnard. The Parallax evidence layer: a Cloudflare Workers operator service and Solidity evidence contracts on Sepolia. This repository (levarac/parallax) is private, so judges cannot inspect it. Two evaluator files in Mizar carry "Ported from the pre-existing evidence-layer reference" headers, and the mutual-pair function follows its relation derivation; everything else in Mizar is new. Built during the hackathon: levarac/mizar (MIT), first commit 2026-09-25 23:53 JST: a Solidity claim contract (Foundry) that stores snapshot roots, checks a Merkle proof plus a typed signature from the event key, allows one claim per key, and calls EAS attest with a non-revocable schema; a TypeScript evaluator (ethers, @noble/curves, OpenZeppelin merkle-tree, CBOR/COSE parsing) that checks observation, commitment and credential signatures, applies the N/B rule, and has a verify mode that rechecks the posted root and RootPosted event on Sepolia; a claim page (Vite, viem, Cloudflare Workers); a local E2E runner on Anvil with a mock EAS; and a comparison of the same synthetic evidence under three rules. levarac/alcor (MIT), first commit 2026-09-25 23:53 JST: a Cloudflare Worker with D1 that verifies World ID proofs through the World Developer Portal v4 verify API, binds one nullifier to one event key per event with a unique constraint, and signs the credential list with Ed25519; and a join page using IDKit 4 ( @worldcoin/idkit-core 4.3.0). In Beid iOS: a small entry point that shows the request and signs a typed message with the event key for the join page and claim page (branch feat/event-key-signing-entry, commits 95b965a to ebcbfab, 2026-09-26 03:11 to 15:45 JST; not yet merged to Beid main). Partner technology: World ID is what makes the rule work. Without it, one person with ten phones is ten partners. With it, each event key needs its own verified human, and the evaluator only counts credentialed keys, including partners who never claim. Notable choices: eligibility is batched into one root per snapshot, but each person claims individually with their own signature, so wallets never appear in the public inputs. Rotating identifiers that are claimed by more than one signing key are dropped. World ID actions are derived from the event ID, so nullifiers do not link a person across events.

projects.title: Kakunin
projects.description: Projects publish their team on ENSv2. Anyone checks in 1s if a recruiter is really a member.
projects.project_description: Fake recruiters are how crypto teams get hacked: someone poses as a project member on Telegram, X or LinkedIn and gets a developer to run malware or sign a transaction. Takedown tools chase an endless list of fakes. Kakunin certifies the real ones instead: a short list each project publishes on ENSv2. Project side, self-serve. Any project can create its organisation at kakunin.xyz/create in about two and a half minutes (12 Sepolia transactions, gas sponsored on testnet): it picks an ENS name and the wallet that will own it. Kakunin registers <name>.eth to that wallet, not to Kakunin, deploys its org and team registries and resolvers, and gives a limited operator key just enough Enhanced Access Control roles to run the team. The owner signs in with a wallet signature (no gas) to add and revoke members; the operator can never touch the project's root name, and the owner can remove it on-chain at any time. Every member is a subname of team.<name>.eth, and the project's own ENS name is the attester. Member side. HR sends a one-time Telegram link (or QR). The member opens it from their own account, and their numeric Telegram ID (never the mutable @username) is attested on ENS. No wallet needed. Everyone else. Forward a suspicious message to the bot, use the web check, open the Telegram Mini App, or call the free public API. Answers: verified (with a proof anyone can re-check without trusting Kakunin), former member (revocation date read from ENSv2 events), lookalike (homoglyphs, typos) or unknown. Every failed check alerts the impersonated project. When HR revokes someone on-chain, every answer changes within seconds. Reporting. Anyone can report an account that impersonates a project, or an official member account that looks compromised (web check page, Mini App, bot /report and /compromised, API). A report only lands in the project's queue and alerts its admins on Telegram; nothing becomes public until an admin decides with a wallet signature. A confirmed impersonator is then answered as a reported impersonator by every check. For a compromised official account the admin's action writes org.status = compromised on the member's ENS name and revokes it, so every check answers "compromised account", recorded and dated on-chain. AI agents. The same check is sold per call over x402. The buying agent screens the destination with the live Intercepta API before it signs: a clean address is paid, a flagged one is refused, with the reason on record.
projects.how_its_made: ENSv2 (Sepolia), central to the product. Org and team registries are UserRegistry proxies deployed through the VerifiableFactory (kakunin-demo.eth -> team.kakunin-demo.eth -> member). HR gets ROLE_REGISTRAR | ROLE_UNREGISTER | ROLE_RENEW on the team registry root and ROLE_SET_TEXT on a separate team PermissionedResolver only; the dashboard reads the role bitmaps live to prove what HR cannot do. All reads go through UniversalResolverV2. An unregistered name leaves registry state, so "former member since..." is rebuilt from LabelRegistered / LabelUnregistered events and block timestamps. Self-serve multi-org provisioning. A resumable 7-task state machine (packages/core/src/provision.ts) registers <name>.eth to the owner's wallet via commit-reveal, deploys org and team UserRegistry proxies and two PermissionedResolvers through the VerifiableFactory, and grants a least-privilege operator that drops its setup rights on the org root at the end. The browser advances it one bounded step at a time to fit serverless limits, and tx hashes are saved before waiting so retries never double-send. Operator keys are sealed with AES-256-GCM. Verified live on kakunin.xyz: an organisation created through the public API in 155 s, then 24 end-to-end checks including a real attestation written from signed Telegram initData. Attestations. Implemented from the draft ENSIP "Text Record Attestations" (PR #85): DAG-CBOR payload, EIP-191 over keccak256, envelope Tag(0x61747374), stored as attestations[org.telegram.id][<org>.eth]. Telegram. grammY bot running as a webhook, plus a Mini App whose server validates Telegram's signed initData (HMAC-SHA256, replay window) on every request, so the account opening the app is authenticated and a member card cannot be requested for someone else. projects.project_description_markdown:
Fake recruiters are how crypto teams get hacked: someone poses as a project member on Telegram, X or LinkedIn and gets a developer to run malware or sign a transaction. Takedown tools chase an endless list of fakes. Kakunin certifies the real ones instead: a short list each project publishes on ENSv2.

Project side, self-serve. Any project can create its organisation at kakunin.xyz/create in about two and a half minutes (12 Sepolia transactions, gas sponsored on testnet): it picks an ENS name and the wallet that will own it. Kakunin registers <name>.eth to that wallet, not to Kakunin, deploys its org and team registries and resolvers, and gives a limited operator key just enough Enhanced Access Control roles to run the team. The owner signs in with a wallet signature (no gas) to add and revoke members; the operator can never touch the project's root name, and the owner can remove it on-chain at any time. Every member is a subname of team.<name>.eth, and the project's own ENS name is the attester.

Member side. HR sends a one-time Telegram link (or QR). The member opens it from their own account, and their numeric Telegram ID (never the mutable @username) is attested on ENS. No wallet needed.

Everyone else. Forward a suspicious message to the bot, use the web check, open the Telegram Mini App, or call the free public API. AI agents. The same check is sold per call over x402. The buying agent screens the destination with the live Intercepta API before it signs: a clean address is paid, a flagged one is refused, with the reason on record.

projects.title: Kido
projects.description: Kido turns complex cross-chain Web3 protocols into simple, secure actions anyone can use.
projects.project_description: Kido is a cross-chain Web3 agent platform designed to make advanced blockchain protocols usable by everyday users, not just developers. Instead of forcing users to understand different wallets, gas tokens, bridges, transaction formats, or protocol-specific interfaces, Kido lets them express what they want to achieve in simple language. Kido converts that intent into a structured agent plan that can interact with protocols across multiple chains, such as Uniswap and Morpho on Ethereum and Cetus on Sui. For example, a user could ask Kido to swap assets, move liquidity across chains, repay a risky lending position, or rebalance funds without manually navigating every protocol. Kido is paired with Amane, a universal financial authority layer that gives agents bounded permissions rather than unrestricted access to user funds. Amane creates chain-native accounts on Ethereum and Sui that share the same root controller and policy model. On Sui, an Ethereum wallet can authorize an action using a secp256k1 signature, while an untrusted relayer submits the actual Sui transaction and pays gas. The Amane Move package independently verifies the signature, account, amount, destination, adapter, nonce, expiry, policy, and budget before allowing the action to execute. This means Kido can automate sophisticated cross-chain workflows while keeping financial authority constrained and verifiable on-chain. The goal is to bring normal users closer to powerful Web3 protocols by hiding unnecessary technical complexity without hiding the security rules underneath.
projects.how_its_made: Kido is built as a cross-chain agent foundry with a separate financial authority layer called Amane. The core idea is that Kido can understand a user’s intent, turn it into a structured execution plan, and interact with protocols across different chains, while Amane independently limits what the agent is financially allowed to do. On the Ethereum side, we built Amane as a smart-account-style Solidity system on Sepolia. It supports bounded actions such as SWAP, REPAY, and PAY, with Root Policies, short-lived Leases, nonces, expiries, budgets, approved adapters, and exact action parameters. We integrated Uniswap v3 for swaps and Aave v3 for lending repayment, and designed the same adapter model to extend to protocols such as Morpho. On Sui, Amane is implemented natively in Move rather than trying to copy Ethereum account abstraction. Each user has a shared Amane account/vault object governed by a deployed Move package. We use Sui’s object model, typed assets, Programmable Transaction Blocks, and a hot-potato ActionTicket pattern. After an action is verified, the Move core creates a typed ActionTicket and releases only the exact controlled balance required for that operation. The approved adapter must consume the ticket within the same transaction, which prevents an untrusted executor from simply taking an unrestricted Coin object and redirecting it elsewhere. One of the more unusual parts of the project is cross-VM authorization. The user can keep an Ethereum secp256k1 controller, such as MetaMask, while still authorizing actions on their Sui Amane account. The Ethereum wallet does not sign a native Sui transaction. Instead, it signs a canonical Amane authorization containing the exact account, chain, asset, amount, destination, adapter, nonce, and deadline. An untrusted relayer then builds and submits the Sui PTB and can pay the SUI gas. The Amane Move package reconstructs the authorization digest on-chain, verifies the secp256k1 signature against the controller stored in the Sui account object, checks the policy and budget, and only then allows the action to proceed. This lets a user interact with Sui without needing a separate Sui wallet or holding SUI for gas, while the relayer remains outside the financial trust boundary. For Sui DeFi, we integrated Cetus CLMM for swaps. On Ethereum, Uniswap provides swap execution and Aave provides repay functionality. Our cross-chain architecture is designed so these can be composed into workflows such as using liquidity on Sui to protect or repay an Ethereum lending position. We are also building the transport layer around cross-chain messaging/bridging so a Kido plan can move value between chain-native Amane endpoints instead of treating each chain as an isolated wallet. Kido itself acts as the planning and orchestration layer. User requirements are converted into a canonical Agent Blueprint describing identity, protocols, assets, actions, permissions, privacy requirements, data sources, recovery behavior, and financial constraints. From that blueprint, Kido can generate protocol-specific execution plans, adapters, runtime configuration, tests, and monitoring logic. The runtime never receives unrestricted authority simply because the AI requested it; every financial action must still fit inside Amane’s on-chain policy envelope. We also built protocol and provider knowledge into the runtime so agents understand the exact protocols, chains, adapters, permissions, and limits they are operating with. For privacy-sensitive workflows, the architecture supports chain-native privacy providers, including Seal on Sui, with additional support being explored for confidential-compute systems such as Nautilus and CRE depending on the chain and trust model. A major engineering focus was making the system adversarial by default. Relayers and executors are treated as untrusted. They can construct malformed transactions, delay execution, or refuse to submit, but they should not be able to change the authorized amount, destination, adapter, account, or policy. We wrote negative tests for replay attacks, unauthorized adapters, wrong recipients, excessive amounts, expired permissions, and signature manipulation. We also added canonical signing tests so the TypeScript, Solidity, and Move implementations agree on exactly the same authorization bytes and hashes. The most “hacky” part is probably making an Ethereum wallet act as the root controller for a Sui-native programmable account without pretending that Ethereum and Sui are the same execution environment. We keep execution fully Sui-native—Move objects, PTBs, typed balances, Move adapters, and Sui gas—while making the owner’s financial authorization portable across VMs through secp256k1 verification. That gives us a universal account experience without relying on a trusted backend to custody funds or define authority.

projects.title: DayTrader
projects.description: A trading market for hosted assets. Hosts sell early, traders speculate, all settled on 1inch Aqua.
projects.project_description: DayTrader lets hosts of rental rooms and cars sell their future days before anyone books them. Each day of each asset is its own token (an ERC-20 with a supply of exactly one), created only when the host first lists that day. Every asset and every day also has an ENSv2 name, like 2026-10-03.demo-room.daytrader.eth. The name resolves to that day's token, so any wallet or tool can find a specific night by name, and the site discovers assets from the daytrader.eth root. Hosts create an asset, list days on a calendar, set weekday prices, and offer a discount for booking several days in a row. Traders place limit orders for one or more consecutive days, paid in USDC. Orders are posted to 1inch Aqua, so the money and the day tokens stay in each person's wallet until a trade settles. A matcher fills an order once the sellers' prices fit the buyer's limit. Our settlement contract, built on 1inch SwapVM, pays each seller and delivers every day in one transaction, and if any single day fails, the whole purchase is cancelled. Owners can resell days at their own price. When a guest books, the host marks the day as booked at a booking price that follows a price curve toward the date. Past days lock automatically, and every date runs on Tokyo time. Hosts get paid up front, and traders take over pricing future demand.
projects.how_its_made: DayTrader is a monorepo with three parts: Solidity contracts, a Node backend, and a Next.js website. Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.30). A RentalAssetFactory creates one RentalAsset per room or car, with a fixed 365-day calendar. Each day is its own ERC-20 DayToken with a supply of exactly one. Day tokens are created lazily at pre-computed addresses, and only the first time a host lists that day, so creating an asset costs almost nothing. The asset contract tracks who owns each day, the listing price, whether the day is booked, and a price curve that sets the booking price as the date gets closer. Past days lock automatically, and all dates are in Tokyo time. 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua was the key partner technology. Sellers and buyers publish their orders to Aqua, but their day tokens and USDC never leave their wallets. Aqua only records what each order allows to be taken, and it pulls the funds when a trade settles, so there's no escrow and no locked liquidity. Our DaySwapVM settlement contract reuses 1inch's SwapVM interpreter and its full-amount limit-swap instruction. We added our own pricing opcode, which reads each day's live price and the host's multi-day discount. One settlement fills a whole range of consecutive days in a single transaction, and if any single day fails, every transfer is rolled back. Nobody can end up with half a trip. ENSv2. Every asset is registered as <asset>.daytrader.eth and points to its contract, with its title, type and location stored as text records. Every day is <date>.<asset>.daytrader.eth and points to that day's token, so any wallet can find a specific night by name. The website reads its asset list from the root name. Backend and website. The website is Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4 and viem. Its API reads the chain through Darryl's backend code, and it rebuilds an in-memory index of contract events from the chain every time it starts, fetching events in batches of 500 blocks. So the whole site runs with no database. A separate worker (the 'taker') watches open orders, test-runs each fill first, and settles every order whose price now fits. The site is hosted on DigitalOcean App Platform and deploys automatically from main. Transactions open in a built-in Blockscout panel. Hacky parts worth mentioning. Our orders use a custom format that 1inch's standard router and resolver network can't read, so we wrote our own matcher. We register day names on ENS in batches of 73 so each transaction stays within gas limits. Our demo recordings are Playwright scripts. We built the project with AI coding agents: Cursor agents for the website and Codex for the contracts and backend, with every change landing as a small pull request.

projects.title: Lortnoc Tahc
projects.description: Private conversations in public places. Natural language encryption for any comment box.
projects.project_description: Public conversations are mass-surveilled. Manipulation campaigns sway public chatter, and when they don't like what you say, you become a target. Leaving the commons means losing your people. Lortnoc Tahc Everywhere lets you create a private commons within the public commons with natural language encryption. It is a browser extension: write anywhere on the internet, and you decide who reads it. Your message is encrypted, then turned into an ordinary post. To anyone scrolling past, it is people talking about the weather. Readers who pass the gate see the real conversation, decoded inline, and the site never sees it. Build a gate from any rule that can be proven. Two work out of the box: ENS v2 subnames for communities, and World ID for verified nationality. Readers prove they qualify without revealing who they are. Gates combine with passphrases and dates. A Space is a real ENS v2 name, bought on Ethereum mainnet, whose records hold its NFT collection and its bans. We created ethglobalhackers.space.lortnoctahc.eth for ETHGlobal Hacker Pack holders: every attendee can post there and read what is posted after one free wallet signature.
projects.how_its_made: Sealed posts. The message is encrypted with AES-SIV. Its key is split into XOR shares, one per rule, so rules combine as "this or that, and something else". The rule itself sits inside the ciphertext: a post carries no marker and no readable policy, and a reader's extension simply tries the keys it holds. Passphrases go through Argon2id. Natural language encryption. The ciphertext becomes cover text through our own reversible coder over a local GPT-2: at each step the model's top tokens form bins, and ciphertext bits pick among them. Decoding runs the same model backwards, byte for byte. The codec runs on Fly.io and only ever sees ciphertext. The gate (Node, Fly.io) holds key shares for rules that must be proven and releases them, sealed to a one-time X25519 key, only to readers who qualify. World ID: World's IDKit 4.3 widget runs in an extension tab, and readers connect once. The gate checks every proof twice, with World's v4 verify API and the WorldIDVerifier contract on World Chain (two of three RPCs must agree). Passport nationality works through Identity Check, including its World ID 3.0 fallback. ENS v2: every Space is a subname under space.lortnoctahc.eth with its own PermissionedResolver, deployed from ENS's VerifiableFactory. In one transaction our registrar writes the records, grants every role to the owner and revokes its own. The gate reads the collection and ban records through ENS's UniversalResolver and fails closed. Spaces are bought on Ethereum mainnet (the early bird is enforced in the contract), and a relayer issues the name. NFT holder checks read Ethereum, Base and Optimism. The extension is MV3 (Vite, CRXJS), released from public CI with a SHA-256 and build provenance. Every ENS record can be checked with curl on our ENS page.

The gate checks every proof twice, with World's v4 verify API and the WorldIDVerifier contract on World Chain (two of three RPCs must agree). Passport nationality works through Identity Check, including its World ID 3.0 fallback.

ENS v2: every Space is a subname under space.lortnoctahc.eth with its own PermissionedResolver, deployed from ENS's VerifiableFactory. In one transaction our registrar writes the records, grants every role to the owner and revokes its own. The gate reads the collection and ban records through ENS's UniversalResolver and fails closed. Spaces are bought on Ethereum mainnet (the early bird is enforced in the contract), and a relayer issues the name. NFT holder checks read Ethereum, Base and Optimism.

The extension is MV3 (Vite, CRXJS), released from public CI with a SHA-256 and build provenance. Every ENS record can be checked with curl on our ENS page.

projects.title: Secueji
projects.description: Secueji unifies AI code review, on-chain monitoring, and policy checks for Web3 operations.
projects.project_description:
Secueji is an agentic security platform that helps smart-contract teams investigate risks and make traceable decisions across their development and operational workflows.
Today, code reviews, on-chain monitoring, and administrative transactions often happen in separate tools. A reviewer sees a pull request, a monitoring service sees an event, and an operator sees a transaction request. Understanding whether these activities match the project's intended behavior requires connecting the evidence across all three.
Secueji brings these entry points into one project: Code review: Investigate GitHub pull requests against their exact code revisions, identify suspicious changes, and explain findings with source references. On-chain activity: Examine transaction receipts, logs, and related contract state to assess observed activity against the project's context and policies. Operations: Evaluate ABI-based administrative transaction drafts before execution, combining simulation results, deterministic rules, external risk intelligence, and AI analysis.
Specialized agents can investigate relevant repository files, blockchain data, and public security information through read-only tools. Their conclusions are validated before a separate policy layer produces an outcome: allow, human review, deny, or insufficient data. The agents do not hold signing authority or override policy.
Intercepta adds external risk intelligence to operation and chain-activity checks. Required screening runs independently of the agent, so a provider warning cannot disappear simply because the model overlooks it. The interface separates provider findings, agent interpretation, and the final policy decision.
Each case retains its evidence, policy version, analysis, and review history. Changed transaction parameters or stale evidence cannot silently reuse an earlier approval.
Secueji is a general-purpose platform. Our Base Sepolia token and escrow contracts provide concrete examples rather than defining the product's scope. It can gate operations routed through its execution path, but it cannot reverse completed blockchain transactions or block transactions that bypass it.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Secueji with Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, backed by PostgreSQL and Prisma. Clerk provides organization-based authentication, and server-side authorization scopes project data and actions to the active organization. A separate Node.js worker processes security jobs outside the web request lifecycle.
GitHub App webhooks and Alchemy webhooks feed the platform. We verify webhook signatures, deduplicate deliveries, and enqueue jobs in PostgreSQL. Worker leases and recovery logic let investigations continue independently of the browser while preventing an expired worker from publishing stale results.
Mastra powers specialized agents for code review, chain assessment, and policy judgment. Each receives task-specific instructions and case-scoped, read-only tools. These tools retrieve revision-pinned GitHub source, Alchemy-compatible RPC data, registered-ABI contract reads, project records, public pages, and OSV vulnerability information. The server controls credentials and access boundaries; the model chooses which available evidence to investigate. Our default model configuration uses Kimi K2.6 through Cloudflare Workers AI.
One notable engineering challenge was combining tool-driven investigation with strict structured output. Early tests showed that forcing JSON during investigation could lead to premature answers without meaningful tool use. We separated the stages: the agent investigates first, then a tool-free structured-output processor formats its report. Zod schemas, completion checks, and evidence-reference validation reject malformed or unsupported conclusions.
Mastra workflows connect evidence loading, fixed rules, agent judgment, policy decisions, and durable human-review suspension. PostgreSQL stores workflow state and traces alongside separately managed application records. Approvals bind to specific operation and policy versions rather than a mutable transaction request.
We use viem for ABI-driven transaction forms, calldata encoding, contract reads, and block-pinned simulations. Intercepta supplies an additional risk signal: configured checks run before agent analysis, persist independently, and feed the policy gate directly. Agents can also investigate related addresses and tokens through supplementary tools. Required missing or expired checks prevent authorization, while “no signal” remains distinct from a safety guarantee.
We verified a live Intercepta address response containing known_scammer and blacklist signals without sending funds. Our demo keeps payments on Base Sepolia and labels address intelligence separately from chain-specific transaction simulation. The full authenticated Intercepta-to-payment walkthrough remains pending validation.
Testing includes Vitest unit tests, PostgreSQL integration tests, Foundry contract tests, and browser-level component checks.

projects.title: lamble.fun
projects.description: Increase your chances of launching a successful token. Find the right narrative and launchpad.
projects.project_description: Lamble is a meta-launchpad for people and AI agents. It brings together market intelligence and token-launch orchestration to help creators decide what to launch, where to launch it, and how to structure it. Rather than replacing existing launchpads, Lamble provides a single starting point above them. The project starts with research. Its web dashboard compares 19 launchpads across multiple chains using fees, revenue, indexed launch activity, completion data, and historical trends. A narrative explorer groups related tokens, identifies their launch venues, and charts their combined trading volume over time. This gives creators a way to investigate which ideas and launch mechanisms are attracting activity before choosing a venue. The launch workflow is conversational. Users describe their idea through Telegram, the web application, or an AI agent connected through MCP. Lamble turns that intent into a reviewable proposal, compares compatible launch routes, and produces an itemized quote. Crucially, it preserves each launchpad’s native configuration rather than forcing every venue into the same generic form. Creator fees, holder rewards, initial purchases, allocations, and vesting are available according to the selected route’s capabilities. The execution layer implements Pump.fun on Solana and Clanker on Base, with direct funding. Planning, funding, and deployment are separate steps, and spending requires explicit user approval. Transaction verification, public launch pages, and creator profiles connect the original proposal to an inspectable outcome. The idea is simple: creating a token should not require starting from scratch on every launchpad. Lamble brings research, venue selection, configuration, and execution into one workflow.
projects.how_its_made: Lamble has two applications. The intelligence dashboard uses Next.js 16, React 19, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and customized shadcn components, with Lightweight Charts for historical data. The launch application uses React and Vite, backed by Hono on Cloudflare Workers. D1 stores launch state, proposals, approvals, and accounting records; R2 stores media; Cloudflare Workflows coordinates conversations and execution; and a recovery cron reconciles unfinished operations. The intelligence layer uses Frames MCP to discover and access data sources, including DefiLlama financial data and Codex GraphQL launchpad and token-market data. Research outputs are normalized into a validated snapshot consumed by the frontend, so rendering the website never triggers paid API calls. The pipeline preserves source evidence, measurement windows, and coverage limitations. Narrative charts aggregate hourly volume for identified token pools, while missing values remain unknown rather than becoming invented zeros. The current refresh process is agent-assisted, not a continuously running indexer. The launch backend separates language-model reasoning from transaction execution. An OpenAI-compatible model helps interpret intent and refine proposals, while typed application logic handles validation, quotes, approvals, and spending. Each launchpad adapter describes its capabilities, validates venue-specific settings, builds transactions, verifies their contents, and reconciles the result. Pump integration uses the Pump SDK and Solana libraries; Clanker integration uses the Clanker SDK and viem. This allows a shared conversational interface without losing the differences between launch mechanisms. One particularly hands-on challenge was getting the Solana dependencies to run inside Cloudflare’s Workers runtime. We replaced a native bigint-buffer dependency path with a pure-JavaScript implementation and configured Anchor’s browser-compatible entry behavior. We also found that Pump creation plus the initial buy exceeded the transaction-size limit in our implementation, so the execution engine represents them as dependent operations rather than incorrectly promising an atomic launch-and-buy.

projects.title: Accord
projects.description: Give people and AI agents a budget, with spending limits you control.
projects.project_description: Accord lets you give a person or an AI agent a budget while keeping control over how that money is used. You start by creating a Space: a shared pot of funds held in a smart contract. From there, you can set up an allowance for someone or give an agent money for tools and services. You choose the amount, spending limits and when access ends. For people, this can be a recurring allowance, a stipend or a grant. Recipients see what has been shared with them and verify with World ID each time they claim. The contract keeps track of how much they can claim in each period. For AI agents, you set a total budget, a daily limit, a limit for each payment and an amount above which the agent must ask for approval. Each agent gets an ENS name tied to its Space. It can make small purchases on its own, but larger ones appear in the owner's approval inbox. The owner reviews the exact amount and recipient, verifies with World ID and decides whether to approve or deny the payment. For example, a research agent can buy a repository snapshot for 1 tUSDC without interrupting you. A 20 tUSDC comparison pauses for your approval if you have set the threshold at 10. Once approved, the agent resumes the purchase and gets its report and payment receipt. You can revoke the agent's ENS identity to stop future spending, or close its allocation and recover the unspent funds. The aim is to make giving someone a budget feel straightforward, whether that someone is a person or an assistant. Developers can connect an assistant through our SDK or MCP tools. The live demo runs on Ethereum Sepolia with free test tokens and sponsored transaction fees. You can also explore the demo and its recorded payment evidence without connecting a wallet.
projects.how_its_made: Accord has three main parts: a Next.js web app, a TypeScript API built with Effect, and Solidity contracts on Ethereum Sepolia. The app handles Spaces, allowances and approvals. The API stores the workflow in SQLite, checks verification results and prepares signed payment permits. Each Space contract holds the funds and enforces budgets, daily and per-payment limits, expiry and replay protection. We use World in two places. People claiming an allowance complete an IDKit Selfie Check tied to that claim. This checks the presence and continuity of the enrolled person; it is not a claim about their legal identity. For agents, World ID for Agents lets the owner verify before granting a budget, increasing an agent's authority or approving a larger payment. Our backend validates the authentication result and requires a separate, explicit approval of the exact terms. The agent flow uses World's official event sandbox and its test identities. ENSv2 gives every Space a namespace and every agent a name under it. We use UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver contracts, with an adapter that checks the live name hierarchy when a payment executes. This makes ENS part of the spending rules: revoking an agent's name also blocks a payment permit that was signed earlier. Agents cannot transfer or renew their own names to get around those controls. The agent toolkit includes a TypeScript SDK, CLI and local MCP server. An assistant can inspect its budget, find services, request a quote, make a purchase and retrieve the result. Pending purchases keep their state so the assistant can resume after owner approval or a restart. Our demo research service collects public GitHub information and returns a report with sources and a matching onchain receipt. A transaction sponsor pays the network fees, and a faucet supplies tUSDC for the demo. The API is trusted to validate World verification and consent and to manage the ENS namespace; the contracts independently enforce signed permits, spending limits and live ENS authority. We tested both successful payments and failure cases, including denied approvals and a cached payment rejected after ENS revocation.

projects.title: Pawn Shop
projects.description: Lending and borrowing platform for vaulted collectibles and alt RWAs
projects.project_description: Pawnshop is a platform where collectors can borrow upto 35% of the fair value of the card. This enables collectors to access liquidity while holding onto their cards. The plan is to build other derivatives and assets leveraging alt RWAs. This includes a Pokemon Card Index and perp dex. Also exploring how tokenizing of RWAs can be made more efficient so we can own all parts of the stack.
projects.how_its_made: This was my first solo hacking experience. I learnt a lot designing the flow and definitely leveraged AI to accelerate the process. I had some difficulties setting everything up but figured it out eventually. Setting this up on testnet was a challenge since the cards didn't exist. The biggest problem with the project was the lack of a reliable price oracle for pokemon cards. The alt option was to used Realyse to fetch the latest fair value of the cards. But ended up fetching it all manually from PSA and using the last sale price. Used world ID to link wallets to user, this makes sure that we have a reputation graph built as the user uses the protocol more. Curvegrid MultiBass was super helpful as an index storing all data. ENSv2 helped us create sub registers and names for every contract in the protocol and gave it different permissions.

projects.title: Agentic World
projects.description: Onchain identities for AI agents: services verify the agent itself, owners set what it may do.
projects.project_description: Agentic World gives AI agents their own onchain identity, so they stop borrowing human credentials. Today, an agent that wants to use a service either gets its owner's password, API key or wallet, or it can't act at all. Agentic World replaces that with a separate account for each agent. The account is owned by a human, can be verified by any service, and the owner can limit what it does. Each agent is a smart account on Sepolia, created from a shared factory. Its signing key is a P-256 key held in the device's secure hardware: the Secure Enclave on macOS, or the TPM on Windows. The key never leaves the device, and the agent itself never sees it. When the account is created, the human's wallet is recorded as its owner. The owner can rotate or revoke the agent's key at any time and set an onchain spending policy: which contracts and functions it may call, up to what amounts, and which actions need the owner's own signature. Services integrate through our TypeScript SDK. A drop-in middleware protects any route. An agent that calls it gets a challenge back, signs it with its hardware key, and retries the same route with the proof attached. The service then checks the signature against the agent's account onchain and reads who owns it. Authentication tells the service which agent it is and whose it is. What the agent may do stays the service's own decision. No central Agentic World server sits in that path. Agents use Agentic World through an MCP server. It creates the identity, with the owner approving in their browser wallet; it signs service challenges; and it previews policy decisions. It only handles authentication, so it works with any service. To show real-world adoption, we integrated Agentic World into Curvegrid's Matsuri stablecoin demo, built on MultiBaas. AI agents sign in to Matsuri as themselves, never with a human's wallet or Matsuri's MultiBaas key. Owners connect MetaMask and switch each permission on or off for all their agents, or for just one. The permissions are: see balances and tickets, see history, buy vouchers, and redeem them. Matsuri prepares the exact transactions an agent may run. It's deployed on Vercel, with Upstash Redis holding sign-ins and permissions.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts.
The agent account is an ERC-4337 smart account written in Solidity on OpenZeppelin 5's ERC-7579 account base, using the canonical EntryPoint v0.8 on Sepolia. Factory: each agent is a minimal ERC-1167 clone of one shared implementation, which makes deploying an agent cheap and easy to verify. Validator module: verifies the agent's P-256 signatures with OpenZeppelin's P256 library, and answers ERC-1271 isValidSignature. That's how services check a sign-in proof. Policy module: a hook that checks every call against the owner's ordered rules. A rule covers the target, the function, the value and a token amount, with decisions ALLOW, DENY or REQUIRE_OWNER_SIGNATURE. Owner approvals are EIP-712 signatures with replay protection. Tooling: everything is built and tested with Hardhat 3, viem and Node's test runner, including end-to-end tests against a real EntryPoint. Hardware Keys.
The agent's key never exists in software. macOS: a small Swift helper creates the key inside the Secure Enclave. Windows: a Go helper does the same in the TPM, through the Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider, calling Windows' NCrypt API directly. It's shipped as a prebuilt, verified executable, so users need no compiler. What they sign: both helpers sign only structured sign-in challenges, never arbitrary data. SDK.
A TypeScript SDK in three parts: Core: the contract ABIs, proof formats and policy encoding. Agent: agent-side signing helpers. Service: the part services use. It pins the trusted implementation, checks that an account's code is an exact copy of it, and reads owner() and verifies the signature at the same block. It also consumes each challenge atomically and issues service-local sessions. Middleware: a drop-in Node/Express middleware runs the whole sign-in on the protected route itself. An agent without a session gets a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: AgenticWorld offer and a challenge, then retries the same route with proof headers. Services need no separate sign-in endpoints. MCP and portal. The MCP server is built on the official Model Context Protocol SDK, with zod for input validation, plus agent skills for Claude Code and Codex. Creating an identity: the MCP opens a one-time local approval page. There, the human's own browser wallet signs the account creation, so the MCP never holds a wallet key. Owner portal: a small esbuild-bundled page for aliases, policies and rotating or revoking the agent's key. Demo services. Services A, B, and C: plain Node HTTP servers. Misc Trusting an agent needs no registry. A service accepts an account only if its onchain code is byte-for-byte an ERC-1167 clone of the pinned implementation. The browser handoff on Windows needed special care: the approval flow stays open after handing off to Explorer. The MCP can't spend. It deliberately has no transaction or HTTP tool, only authentication, so a prompt-injected agent can't turn it into a way to spend money. Future Improvements The current MCP only acts as an authentication layer, future works would focus on upgrading the MCP to enable onchain transactions.

Agentic World gives AI agents their own onchain identity, so they stop borrowing human credentials. Today, an agent that wants to use a service either gets its owner's password, API key or wallet, or it can't act at all. Agentic World replaces that with a separate account for each agent. The account is owned by a human, can be verified by any service, and the owner can limit what it does.

Each agent is a smart account on Sepolia, created from a shared factory. Its signing key is a P-256 key held in the device's secure hardware: the Secure Enclave on macOS, or the TPM on Windows. The key never leaves the device, and the agent itself never sees it. When the account is created, the human's wallet is recorded as its owner. The owner can rotate or revoke the agent's key at any time and set an onchain spending policy: which contracts and functions it may call, up to what amounts, and which actions need the owner's own signature.

Services integrate through our TypeScript SDK. A drop-in middleware protects any route. An agent that calls it gets a challenge back, signs it with its hardware key, and retries the same route with the proof attached. The service then checks the signature against the agent's account onchain and reads who owns it. Authentication tells the service which agent it is and whose it is. What the agent may do stays the service's own decision. No central Agentic World server sits in that path.

Agents use Agentic World through an MCP server. It creates the identity, with the owner approving in their browser wallet; it signs service challenges; and it previews policy decisions. It only handles authentication, so it works with any service.

To show real-world adoption, we integrated Agentic World into Curvegrid's Matsuri stablecoin demo, built on MultiBaas. AI agents sign in to Matsuri as themselves, never with a human's wallet or Matsuri's MultiBaas key. Owners connect MetaMask and switch each permission on or off for all their agents, or for just one. The permissions are: see balances and tickets, see history, buy vouchers, and redeem them. Matsuri prepares the exact transactions an agent may run. It's deployed on Vercel, with Upstash Redis holding sign-ins and permissions.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts. 
The agent account is an ERC-4337 smart account written in Solidity on OpenZeppelin 5's ERC-7579 account base, using the canonical EntryPoint v0.8 on Sepolia.
- Factory: each agent is a minimal ERC-1167 clone of one shared implementation, which makes deploying an agent cheap and easy to verify.
- Validator module: verifies the agent's P-256 signatures with OpenZeppelin's P256 library, and answers ERC-1271 isValidSignature. That's how services check a sign-in proof.
- Policy module: a hook that checks every call against the owner's ordered rules. A rule covers the target, the function, the value and a token amount, with decisions ALLOW, DENY or REQUIRE_OWNER_SIGNATURE. Owner approvals are EIP-712 signatures with replay protection.
- Tooling: everything is built and tested with Hardhat 3, viem and Node's test runner, including end-to-end tests against a real EntryPoint.

Hardware Keys. 
The agent's key never exists in software.
- macOS: a small Swift helper creates the key inside the Secure Enclave.
- Windows: a Go helper does the same in the TPM, through the Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider, calling Windows' NCrypt API directly. It's shipped as a prebuilt, verified executable, so users need no compiler.
- What they sign: both helpers sign only structured sign-in challenges, never arbitrary data.

SDK. 
A TypeScript SDK in three parts:
- Core: the contract ABIs, proof formats and policy encoding.
- Agent: agent-side signing helpers.
- Service: the part services use. It pins the trusted implementation, checks that an account's code is an exact copy of it, and reads owner() and verifies the signature at the same block. It also consumes each challenge atomically and issues service-local sessions.
- Middleware: a drop-in Node/Express middleware runs the whole sign-in on the protected route itself. An agent without a session gets a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: AgenticWorld offer and a challenge, then retries the same route with proof headers. Services need no separate sign-in endpoints.

MCP and portal. The MCP server is built on the official Model Context Protocol SDK, with zod for input validation, plus agent skills for Claude Code and Codex.
- Creating an identity: the MCP opens a one-time local approval page. There, the human's own browser wallet signs the account creation, so the MCP never holds a wallet key.
- Owner portal: a small esbuild-bundled page for aliases, policies and rotating or revoking the agent's key.

Demo services.
- Services A, B, and C: plain Node HTTP servers.

Misc
- Trusting an agent needs no registry. A service accepts an account only if its onchain code is byte-for-byte an ERC-1167 clone of the pinned implementation.
- The browser handoff on Windows needed special care: the approval flow stays open after handing off to Explorer.
- The MCP can't spend. It deliberately has no transaction or HTTP tool, only authentication, so a prompt-injected agent can't turn it into a way to spend money.

Future Improvements
- The current MCP only acts as an authentication layer, future works would focus on upgrading the MCP to enable onchain transactions.

projects.title: Swap-Pay Invoice
projects.description: Billing module accepting token swap payment for merchants.
projects.project_description: Swap-Pay Invoice lets one merchant bill in native ETH or an accepted ERC-20. The merchant chooses which tokens to accept, then creates an invoice for a fixed amount, with an optional due date and an optional payer. If no payer is set, anyone may pay. The merchant sees each invoice’s amount, asset, due date, and status. A payer can settle a pending invoice before the due date, either in the invoice currency or by spending another accepted token that is exchanged into that currency in the same payment. The merchant receives the funds, and the invoice is marked paid. The same billing flow can be offered through an API as part of a digital asset management service. The merchant creates an invoice through the API and receives a link to the payment page. When payment completes, a webhook notifies the merchant’s existing system so the payment can be reconciled with the matching account or invoice.
projects.how_its_made:
Uniswap The app builds Uniswap v4 Universal Router calldata off-chain (V4Planner and RoutePlanner). The contract does not choose the pool. It pulls the payer's tokenIn through Permit2, calls Universal Router, and checks the result. Unspent tokenIn is refunded, and the Permit2 allowance is cleared before the call returns.
Local tests run against an Anvil mainnet fork so the script can use live v4 pool liquidity. MultiBaas Tested on Sepolia, as MultiBaas works with live testnets and does not support a local mainnet fork. On Sepolia, the invoice and accepted-token lists are retrieved through MultiBaas event queries rather than eth_getLogs, which helps overcome the limitations imposed by RPC providers on eth_getLogs.
MultiBaas makes it easier to query and retrieve data that would otherwise be difficult to access efficiently due to the limitations of smart contract data structures.
