projects.how_its_made_markdown:
# Uniswap
The app builds Uniswap v4 Universal Router calldata off-chain (V4Planner and RoutePlanner). The contract does not choose the pool. It pulls the payer's tokenIn through Permit2, calls Universal Router, and checks the result. Unspent tokenIn is refunded, and the Permit2 allowance is cleared before the call returns.
Local tests run against an Anvil mainnet fork so the script can use live v4 pool liquidity. 

# MultiBaas
Tested on Sepolia, as MultiBaas works with live testnets and does not support a local mainnet fork. On Sepolia, the invoice and accepted-token lists are retrieved through MultiBaas event queries rather than eth_getLogs, which helps overcome the limitations imposed by RPC providers on eth_getLogs.
MultiBaas makes it easier to query and retrieve data that would otherwise be difficult to access efficiently due to the limitations of smart contract data structures.

projects.title: Tokenise Tokyo
projects.description: An RWA tokenization platform that turns idle city spaces into programmable rights.
projects.project_description: Tokenize Tokyo is an RWA tokenization platform that puts Japan’s idle city spaces back to work. Instead of tokenizing a whole building, it turns a rooftop, a vacant floor or a parking bay into scoped, time-bounded usage and revenue rights: programmable, composable primitives that can be funded, traded, and managed on-chain. A rooftop could host solar panels. A vacant building could become a workshop. A parking space could serve a neighborhood business. Each opportunity needs clear agreements about the space, its purpose, its availability, and how income is shared. Tokenize Tokyo models each of these agreements as one such right. This is a Japanese social problem before it is a Web3 use case. Tokyo alone counted 896,500 vacant homes in the 2023 housing survey, its 23 wards reported 1,303 hectares of unused land in 2021, and only about 6% of detached houses had rooftop solar in FY2022. Aging owners, shrinking households and the cost of negotiating every arrangement one by one keep these spaces dormant while the city needs housing, renewable energy and room for neighborhood business. Tokenize Tokyo uses programmable rights to lower that coordination cost: an owner can share one use of a space without selling it, and the community can fund and operate it. Our application connects four workflows: tokenize your own asset, acquire rights in someone else’s project, manage your holdings, and monitor operations through a dashboard. For example, an owner can propose a rooftop solar project, define revenue-sharing units, and offer them to supporters. Holders can resell transferable units, claim revenue actually deposited into the project’s vault, or combine compatible revenue rights into custody-backed baskets. Once these rights are on-chain, four things become programmable. Ownership carries its own scope, purpose, period and transfer policy, and the contract rejects conflicting exclusive uses at issuance. Transactions settle rights and payment atomically, and transfer checkpoints keep income already accrued with the previous holder. Permissions are delegated through ENSv2 with limits on purpose, time and quantity, and can be revoked. Financial workflows compose: compatible revenue rights can be deposited into custody-backed baskets and redeemed for the underlying units. The dashboard connects these actions to operational data: funding progress, activation status, trading volume, deposited revenue, distributions, and transaction history. Charts help users understand both their holdings and activity across the platform. ENSv2 gives a connected space a hierarchical identity and revocable permissions for delegated work. An owner can authorize an operator to issue rights within defined limits, or authorize a reporter to update only an energy-report record. Tokyo is our starting point. City previews for New York and Hong Kong illustrate how the same model could extend to other cities. The live prototype runs on Sepolia using fictional properties, simulated property verification, and valueless test tokens. A separate wallet-free demo is available at /demo. Lending and collateral borrowing are presented as Coming soon.
projects.how_its_made: I built the frontend with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and MapLibre, using OpenFreeMap for the city basemap. Solidity contracts, developed and tested with Foundry, implement asset registration, verification, ERC-1155 rights, fixed-price trading, revenue distribution, and custody-backed baskets. Each right records its spatial scope, purpose, time window, supply, and transfer policy. Marketplace purchases exchange rights and MockJPY atomically. RevenueVault uses transfer checkpoints to preserve income already accrued to previous holders. BasketVault holds the underlying rights and supports share issuance and redemption. Curvegrid MultiBaas connects the application to these contracts. Foundry deploys the contracts; Forge MultiBaas and our linking scripts register their ABIs, addresses, and indexing configuration. The frontend uses MultiBaas for ABI-backed contract reads, unsigned transaction composition, event queries, dashboard aggregates, and receipt monitoring. Users approve transactions through their wallets. This let us build the market and operational dashboard without maintaining a separate event-indexing service. Curvegrid integration code: src/lib/multibaas.ts src/lib/queries.ts src/lib/projection.ts contracts/script/Link.s.sol Our ENSv2 integration uses the official Sepolia hierarchical registries and Permissioned Resolver. UrbanNamespaceAuthority validates the registered namespace’s binding to a specific asset and scope. Delegated issuance requires both an ENS role and an owner-defined application grant, with purpose, time, and quantity limits. A separate reporter permission allows updates only to urban.energyReport on a dedicated rooftop resolver. Reports are read through Universal Resolver V2, and revocation prevents further writes. ENS integration code: contracts/src/UrbanNamespaceAuthority.sol contracts/src/UrbanRightToken.sol src/lib/ens/reports.ts Live ENSv2 permissions demo Notable engineering work includes validating composed transaction calldata before signing, handling MultiBaas pagination and indexing delays, and combining verified historical logs with newly indexed events without double counting. I use Foundry, Vitest, and Playwright to check contract permissions, accounting, data projection, and browser workflows. Public transaction receipts provide reproducible evidence of the testnet flows.

projects.title: Tenjō
projects.description: Lose a ballot, gain a chance: gacha’s pity ceiling for ticket ballots, on World ID and Sui.
projects.project_description: Concert ballots and scarce drops make fans lose again and again, and every ballot forgets them. About 2.2 million people applied for the first Switch 2 lottery in Japan. By the fifth lottery, Nintendo had added a rule by hand: only people who had entered before and never won. That’s a pity system. Gacha games call it 天井, tenjō, the ceiling: keep trying and your luck builds. Tenjō makes that ceiling a primitive for any ballot. Each real person enters once. Your name goes in the draw once, plus once for every ballot you’ve lost in the same series (a tour, a shop, a product line), up to six chances. A win resets you to one. Yui, our example fan, has lost three ballots on a tour, so her next entry goes in four times. On paid drops you lock a refundable deposit: win and it pays for your seat, lose and it comes straight back. A pity counter only works if nobody can cheat it, and the two cheats need two networks. World ID stops one fan becoming fifty accounts that farm losses: each entrant proves they’re one unique human, and no name, email or document is stored. Sui stops anyone, us included, from fiddling the draw, the money or the counts: a Move package draws with sui::random, holds deposits in escrow, refunds every loser in the settlement transaction and keeps the loss ledger on-chain. A real World ID starts fresh in every drop, so a passkey on the fan’s phone remembers their losses. It never buys a second entry. For organisers (ticketing platforms, fan clubs, shops running lottery sales), Tenjō replaces three hacks: play-hour rules to stop bots, chasing winners who don’t pay, and “it’s rigged” complaints. Winners get a Ticket that can’t be transferred, which matters in Japan, where reselling specified event tickets above face value has been banned since 2019. It’s live at tenjo-azure.vercel.app on Sui testnet, with 22 World ID entries verified on production so far.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript end to end: Next.js 16 and React 19 on Vercel, Neon Postgres (PGlite locally) and a Sui Move 2024 package, tenjo::ballot. World ID: IDKit 4.3 in the browser. The server issues an RP-signed request, valid for five minutes and bound to one drop and purpose, then forwards the proof byte for byte to World’s v4 verify API. A 200 is never enough: the configured credential’s own result must succeed with a matching nullifier, action, environment, nonce and signal, and the request is consumed in the same database transaction as the entry. The nullifier is canonicalised and hashed into a 32-hex anonymous code. World ID 4 nullifiers are single-use per action, so real World IDs get one action per drop and a fresh code each time. To carry their losses we added WebAuthn passkeys (SimpleWebAuthn): the passkey signs over that drop’s World ID request and is checked before World is asked, so a refusal never spends the proof. A per-drop identity table stops a second passkey from buying a second entry. Sui: a shared Series keeps the loss ledger (Table<code, u64>) and each Drop<T> is an escrow vault over any coin type. For a paid entry, the server signs an Ed25519 permit over drop, code and sender after the World ID check, and ballot::enter rebuilds it with the real sender, so a copied permit fails. draw is a non-public entry function taking &Random that only stores a 32-byte seed. Its gas never depends on the outcome, so an unlucky draw can’t be aborted and retried. settle is public and deterministic: weighted picks without replacement from blake2b256(seed ‖ i), the winners’ deposits paid to the organiser as one coin, every loser refunded, winners with a wallet given a Ticket with key but no store, and every pity count updated, all in one transaction. The drop page re-runs settle in TypeScript from the seed and checks it matches. The server talks to Sui over gRPC with @mysten/sui and serialises organiser transactions with a Postgres advisory lock; fans pay through dApp Kit. Postgres mirrors the chain for fast pages. 31 TypeScript tests (one drives a software authenticator holding a real key), 22 Move tests and Playwright browser tests.

projects.title: Knowledge01
projects.description: A knowledge network stores what agents learn under your ENS - versioned, encrypted, and portable.
projects.project_description:
K01 (Knowledge01) is an open, vendor-neutral protocol that turns AI memory into versioned, portable knowledge owned by an ENS name, instead of locked inside one application's database. Today's assistants keep memories in isolated stores, where users can't see where a fact came from, who owns it, or who can read it. K01 treats knowledge the way the web treats pages: addressed by a hierarchical ENS name, stored on IPFS, and readable by any agent from any vendor. Developers integrate it three ways: SDK (@knowledge01/repo, with @knowledge01/storage): read, search and contribute versioned claims from TypeScript or Node.js.
MCP (@knowledge01/mcp): connect Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP client with one command, claude mcp add knowledge -e PINATA_GATEWAY=<gateway>.mypinata.cloud -- npx -y @knowledge01/mcp, so agents can read, search and cite namespaces.
CLI (@knowledge01/cli): create a namespace, set its policy, review proposals and publish. At its core, K01 stores knowledge as claims: single statements, each with its sources, contributor, reviewers and confidence. Claims are grouped into content-addressed commits on IPFS, and the ENS name's contenthash points at the current version. Each namespace has its own ENS v2 resolver, which enforces who can write on chain. The owner publishes and grants roles, a reviewer can publish what they approve, and a named contributor can write only a pointer to their own proposal. Reviews and approvals follow the namespace's published policy. K01 also lets agents pay each other for knowledge. Public namespaces are open plain text. Private ones are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the namespace key is sealed to each reader's public key with ECIES. Over the x402 protocol, an agent can buy read access to a paid namespace, such as fresh market data or research, with a USDC micropayment. The payment settles first, then the key is sealed to the buyer. Everything runs today on Ethereum Sepolia (ENS v2) and Base Sepolia (x402). The result is memory that outlives the app that wrote it, and that the next agent can verify and build on.

projects.title: GomiGo
projects.description: Tokyo has no public bins. GomiGo unlocks private dumpsters via World ID proof + ENSv2 registry.
projects.project_description: Tokyo streets have almost no public trash cans, convenience stores and apartment mansions restrict their dumpsters to prevent illegal dumping (fuhō-tōki). GomiGo turns those restricted private bins into a trustless public utility. Hosts register their bin as a hierarchical ENSv2 subname on Sepolia (e.g. bin-01-shibuya.gomigo.eth) with text records for capacity, hours, and accepted waste types. Tourists and commuters prove humanity once per ward per day using World ID (NFC Passport or Device credential) via IDKit, then receive a 10-minute dynamic access PIN, used to open a smart padlock, enter a keypad gate, or show to staff depending on the bin type. A ward-scoped nullifier cache on the server enforces the Sybil limit without storing any identity data.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. ENSv2 (Sepolia): We own gomigo.eth registered via ENSv2 ETHRegistrar using commit-reveal. A custom subregistry contract is deployed and wired via setSubregistry, enabling hierarchical wildcard resolution, each bin gets its own tokenized subname. A custom resolver stores bin-status, capacity, hours, and accepted-types as on-chain text records. Scoped roles from ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control restrict write permissions to the registered host address only; disposers get read-only resolution. World ID (IDKit v4): IDKitWidget runs verification_level "device" so NFC Passport credentials work without an Orb. Proofs POST to /api/dropoff/verify which calls the World v2 developer API. A ward-scoped in-memory nullifier Set enforces 1-pass-per-ward-per-day, duplicate nullifiers return HTTP 429 with an explicit rejection message. The viem library handles all Sepolia contract interactions.

projects.title: FinTessa
projects.description: A DApp router that atomically splits one token into a weighted basket —> one tx, zero dust.
projects.project_description: FinTessa is a DApp that splits one token into a basket of tokens in a single transaction. You pick how much of each token you want (weights in basis points, must add up to 100%), send one token in, and get all your output tokens out — no separate swaps, no partial fills. If any swap in the basket gets a worse price than you set, the whole thing reverts. Nothing sits in the router between calls; v4’s flash accounting means the input is pulled once and outputs go straight to your wallet. There’s a Next.js frontend where you move sliders to set your basket, see live price quotes from V4Quoter, and submit in two clicks.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts are in Foundry on top of Uniswap v4. The router calls PoolManager.unlock(), and inside that callback, it loops through each basket leg, calling poolManager.swap() once per token. When all swaps are done, it settles the input once and sends each output straight to the caller.
The deploy script spins up 5 mock ERC-20s, seeds four pools with liquidity, and dumps all the addresses and pool keys into a JSON file. A small npm script reads that file plus the Foundry build output and generates the typed config the frontend uses — so you never have to copy-paste addresses by hand.
The frontend is Next.js with wagmi and viem. Quotes are real on-chain simulations via V4Quoter, not hardcoded math. There’s a mock wallet connector pinned to a local Anvil account so you can test without MetaMask.

projects.title: sidekey
projects.description: Trade from the wallet you already own, signed with Google. No popups. Your key stays in charge
projects.project_description: Sidekey lets you trade from the wallet you already own with the speed of a Google-login app, without ever opening that wallet again. Apps like fomo made crypto feel instant: log in with Google, tap a token, done. But that magic lives in a fresh embedded wallet. Your real money, history, and positions sit in a MetaMask you've had for years, and that wallet still needs a popup for every approve, swap, and bridge. Sidekey closes that gap. How it works: Sign in with Google. Privy creates an embedded wallet that is upgraded in place to a ZeroDev Kernel smart account via EIP-7702. It signs headlessly, and a paymaster covers its gas. Connect your wallet and link it once. Your wallet signs a single scoped grant to the Google account: 5 USDC per day, plus a 50 USDC tier that stays locked. On MetaMask this is one ERC-7715 Advanced Permissions confirmation; on any other wallet it's gasless EIP-2612 permits. That is the last time your wallet opens. Buy. One sponsored UserOperation from the Google account pulls USDC from your wallet, swaps it on Uniswap v3, and delivers native ETH back to your wallet. Your address never changed, your funds never sat anywhere else, and no popup appeared. Go over the limit, prove you're human. A buy above 5 USDC opens World ID. Only after a verified proof does the server release the 50 USDC permission your wallet already signed. Cancel, and the cap stays at 5. Above 50 is refused outright. Your original key remains root: it can revoke the permission at any time, and the Google account can never do anything outside what you granted.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 16, viem 2.56, wagmi + RainbowKit, Privy (@privy-io/react-auth), ZeroDev (@zerodev/sdk 5.5, Kernel v3.3), World ID (@worldcoin/idkit 4.3 + idkit-server), Uniswap v3 SwapRouter02 + QuoterV2, Circle USDC on Sepolia, coss ui for the interface. Foundry and anvil for the fork-based audit before touching real chain. Two wallets, one grant. The Google side is a Privy embedded wallet. We use Privy's useSign7702Authorization to sign an EIP-7702 delegation to ZeroDev's Kernel v3.3 implementation, but we never send a type-4 transaction ourselves: the ZeroDev bundler carries the authorization inside the first UserOperation, so the wallet is upgraded and executes its first trade in one sponsored op. The paymaster sponsors everything, so the Google wallet holds zero ETH for the whole demo. The user's own wallet signs exactly one grant. On MetaMask we request ERC-7715 Advanced Permissions (wallet_requestExecutionPermissions, erc20-token-periodic) with two entries in one confirmation. On other wallets we fall back to two EIP-2612 permits on Circle's Sepolia USDC, which we verified exposes permit/nonces/DOMAIN_SEPARATOR on-chain. The 50 USDC "human" permission is signed at link time but held server-side, released only after a World ID proof is verified through the Developer Portal API. No private key exists anywhere in the app or env. The buy. One UserOperation from the Kernel account batches: permit (first time only) → transferFrom user → Kernel → approve router → multicall[exactInputSingle, unwrapWETH9] with recipient set to the user's wallet, so native ETH lands back at the same address that paid. Quotes come from QuoterV2 with 1% slippage.

projects.title: Resqueue
projects.description: Resqueue: An Economy where AI / Robots hire humans to perform tasks.
projects.project_description: ResQueue is a human-in-the-loop safety net for autonomous robots. Today, warehouse, delivery, and industrial robots handle most tasks on their own, but still get stuck on edge cases — a jammed gripper, a blocked aisle, an object they can't classify — and that usually means an expensive on-call specialist and a long wait. With ResQueue, every robot stays connected to an AI agent (like Claude or Codex) that constantly monitors its status. When a robot signals it's stuck, the AI agent reads the situation, decides whether a human is needed, and — if so — posts a priced job to an open marketplace in real time. Any human can claim that job, but only after verifying their unique personhood with World ID, which keeps the marketplace free of bots, farms, and duplicate accounts. Once claimed, the human teleoperates the robot remotely to resolve the issue and submits proof of completion. The same AI agent that raised the alarm then reviews the fix, scores it on speed, accuracy, and task difficulty, and releases a WLD payment sized to that score — automatically, with no manual invoicing or approval chain. The result is a global, on-demand workforce that lets autonomous fleets scale without needing to hire and staff round-the-clock human supervisors, while giving anyone with a WLD wallet and a World ID a way to earn by helping robots get unstuck.
projects.how_its_made: Resqueue is a marketplace where a stuck robot's own agent hires a verified human, and the whole thing runs as one Node process plus a browser front end. Physics in Node. The robot is a Unitree G1 humanoid running in MuJoCo compiled to WebAssembly, using the official @mujoco/mujoco bindings on the server, not in the browser. The server loads the official MJCF and 34 MB of STL meshes into an in-memory virtual filesystem, steps the simulation, runs an endless pick-and-place routine over 29 position-controlled joints, and streams body poses to clients over a WebSocket at 30 Hz. The browser renders those poses with three.js, loading the same STLs from the backend. Because physics is server-side, every viewer, the console and the phone see the same robot, and control authority can be enforced in one place. Getting stuck is physics, not a script. Three triggers pull the robot out of autonomy: a person's mocap body comes within 0.6 m of a hand, joint tracking error stays high for three seconds because a rail landed on the feeder, or the next box is more than 15 cm off its mark so the grasp misses. On any of these the robot holds position and hands its telemetry to its agent. The agent writes and reviews the job. The agent is Claude with structured output validated by Zod: title, brief, ordered steps, acceptance criteria, urgency and a reward between 0.05 and 0.1 WLD. It runs in one of three modes. It can call the Claude API directly, fall back to rules when no key is present, or run in "external" mode, where the server exposes a task queue over HTTP and a live Claude Code session polls it, reads the situation, and posts the JobSpec back. That last mode is how we demoed it: the developer's coding agent literally was the robot's onboard agent, watching the queue in a background monitor. Reviews time out to the rule-based verdict after 15 seconds so payouts never wait on a slow model. World ID is the trust layer. Accepting a job opens a QR built with @worldcoin/idkit-core. The backend signs the RP context with the SDK's signRequest, binds the proof to the job and browser session through the signal, and forwards the proof to the Developer Portal v4 verify endpoint. The RP-scoped nullifier becomes the worker's identity: same human, same nullifier, one balance, one payout wallet, so nobody farms rewards with multiple accounts. Teleop messages over the WebSocket are accepted only from the session holding the active verified claim. A tampered, replayed or foreign proof unlocks nothing and the job returns to the pool. Payouts on World Chain. Every approved job triggers an ERC-20 transfer of WLD from a treasury EOA on World Chain mainnet using viem. Payments are ledgered in Supabase Postgres through the transaction pooler, with the job, worker and explorer link, and failed transfers can be retried from the console. A finished job always pays the full reward. The score only shapes the summary. Phone controller. A PWA acts as a gamepad: two virtual sticks drive four joints of the selected limb, shoulder buttons switch limbs and joint pages, A/B/X/Y map to the job's actions, and a push-to-talk button streams Opus audio plus a live Web Speech transcript so the operator can literally talk to the person standing next to the robot. The console pairs a phone by showing a QR with a six-digit code; redeeming it hands the verified session's cookie to the phone. Hacky bits worth admitting. The G1's pelvis is welded to a stand so it can be posed freely without balance control. The grasp is kinematic: the held box is pinned to the hand, because the WASM bindings do not expose runtime constraint toggling yet. Raw STL data had to get MuJoCo's mesh_pos and mesh_quat inertial-frame transform applied by hand or every part rendered offset. World ID 4.0 uniqueness proofs are one per person per action, so every verification attempt gets its own action, registered on demand through the Developer Portal's MCP endpoint from inside the server. The pairing link asks the local ngrok agent for its tunnel URL at request time, so a fresh tunnel never needs a config edit. The phone cockpit forces landscape by rotating the whole app with a CSS transform against a measured viewport, since browsers rarely honour orientation lock.

projects.title: AquaVol
projects.description: AquaVol uses custom SwapVM instructions for self-custodial options with dynamic pricing.
projects.project_description: Onchain options are difficult to trade because liquidity is fragmented, pricing changes continuously with volatility and time, and many implementations stop at minting an option token without providing a programmable secondary market. AquaVol connects the full lifecycle: collateralized option creation, Aqua virtual liquidity, SwapVM-based pricing and execution, onchain trading, and exercise. Alice creates a covered WETH CALL by locking WETH inside an immutable OptionSeries contract. The resulting CALL tokens are exposed through Aqua as reusable virtual maker liquidity. Bob can then purchase the live CALL with avUSD through a custom SwapVM router. Instead of using a static option price, AquaVol extends SwapVM with custom pricing instructions. One instruction calculates Black-Scholes fair value from strike, expiry, guarded Uniswap V3 WETH/avUSD TWAP data, and registered implied volatility. A second instruction applies inventory-aware pricing using the maker’s remaining Aqua virtual balance. As CALL inventory decreases, the next ask automatically increases. AquaVol is deployed on Base Sepolia with a live WETH $4,000 CALL market. The frontend lets users connect MetaMask as either a Liquidity Maker or Option Buyer, execute real onchain trades, inspect Aqua balances, and verify transactions and contracts on BaseScan. It also includes a strategy workspace for exploring simulated strikes, PUTs, multi-leg positions, and expiry payoff diagrams while clearly separating simulations from the live market.
projects.how_its_made: AquaVol is built with Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry on top of the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts. The core innovation is a custom SwapVM router with AquaVol-specific pricing instructions. One instruction computes the option’s Black-Scholes fair value from spot price, strike, expiry, and implied volatility, while another applies inventory-aware skew using the maker’s live Aqua virtual balances. Together, these instructions turn SwapVM from a generic swap execution engine into a programmable options market maker. Aqua handles self-custodial virtual-balance accounting and settlement, while the computation-heavy option pricing logic is isolated in a dedicated pricing engine to keep the custom router deployable. The OptionSeries contract implements a fully collateralized European covered CALL. It locks one WETH for every CALL minted, accepts strike payment during the exercise window, burns exercised CALL tokens, transfers WETH to the holder, and allows the writer to redeem any remaining collateral after settlement. Spot pricing comes from a project-seeded Uniswap V3 WETH/avUSD pool on Base Sepolia. The oracle verifies the canonical factory, pool identity, token pair, fee tier, a complete 30-minute TWAP window, observation freshness, harmonic liquidity, tick deviation, and configured price bounds. A bounded volatility registry supplies the implied-volatility input consumed by the custom SwapVM pricing instruction. AquaVol programs are executed through SwapVM and settled using Aqua virtual balances. When a trader purchases CALL inventory, the maker’s Aqua balance changes; the inventory instruction reads that new state and automatically reprices the next trade. This makes each SwapVM execution state-aware rather than using a static option price. The pricing implementation is validated against an independent Python Black-Scholes reference model and deterministic test vectors. Foundry unit, fuzz, invariant, integration, and settlement tests cover the option lifecycle, custom SwapVM instructions, oracle safeguards, Aqua accounting, real token transfers, and inventory-based repricing. The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and viem. MetaMask signs transactions directly on Base Sepolia. A maker can mint CALLs, expose them as Aqua liquidity, refresh pricing inputs, and manage inventory. A buyer can approve avUSD and execute a protected exact-output CALL purchase through the custom SwapVM router, then inspect the resulting token transfers, Aqua balance updates, and confirmed settlement on BaseScan.

projects.title: suica os
projects.description: A fully hallucinated OS composed by a Jev for Sui DeFi; Type anything, get app in realtime
projects.project_description: Suica OS is a fully hallucinated, operating system where every app is an agent - realtime UI composed by a JEV. There is no landing page and nothing was built as a normal app. You boot into a retro desktop, open the Start menu, and type anything — "excel of vitalik.eth's portfolio" , "paint but roast vitalik.eth" , "doom but I'm shooting my losses" , "tetris game but my portfolio is falling" — and a working, on-chain app appears instantly as a chunky retro window, as fast as you can type. Why we built it. We're heading toward a future where we don't need apps for everything — agents do the work. But we still need interfaces: to see what our agents did, understand it, and approve or refuse it. So interfaces will be generated on demand — changing in real time, personal to whoever is using them. Suica OS is an experiment in that idea: an OS where every window is composed live, every app has an identity, and every dollar it moves is gated on-chain. Apps are places, not programs. Every app is really an agent : an ENSv2 name (its identity + a ~1 KB manifest stored in its text records) plus a Sui wallet (an AgentVault with spend caps). The UI is disposable — anyone who resolves the name can rebuild the exact UI instantly, no model call. suica.eth becomes a real filesystem: folders are ENS registries, sharing is Enhanced Access Control roles, and moving an app into a folder turns its old name into an ENSv2 alias — a symlink — so old share links keep working. The numbers are real. Portfolios, roasts and "losses" come from Ethereum mainnet (ENS + Ethplorer); balances, gas and payments come from Sui. Log on with Google (zkLogin — no seed phrase) and gas is sponsored , so you never hold SUI. Money only moves through one fixed signing dialog that is never generated; apps can only propose . An assistant, Tappy , acts on its own within a cap you set, asks when it's over, and if it ever tries to overspend the Move contract rejects it on-chain and you get a Blue Screen — no funds move. "Anything is possible." Ask for a program we don't have ("tetris but…") and it opens instantly in a built-in "compatibility mode" shell while an LLM writes the real shell in the background — sandboxed, tested, published to Walrus and named under shells.suica.eth , so it's instant for everyone after that. Tracks: Sui DeFi & Payments , ENS (Best Use of ENSv2, on Sepolia) , Curvegrid (Best Digital Asset Dashboard) .
projects.how_its_made: Frontend / OS shell. Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript. No UI framework — the "Windows 99" kit is hand-written CSS ( win99.css ) with a custom window manager, taskbar, Start menu, and a real BSOD. GSAP powers ~20 hand-built animation scenes. The real-time UI engine is Jev (TypeSafe AI), not an LLM. On every keystroke we make one call to Jev — a "System One" model that never writes text, it only answers ~20 typed questions ( choice / score / noul ) in parallel with calibrated probabilities in ~70–500 ms. Jev decides shell × function × target × vibe × risk ; a deterministic parser extracts the numbers (ENS names, tokens, amounts, leverage, schedules). Jev decides, code computes — a model never invents an amount. We route Jev through the Vercel AI Gateway . An offline keyword classifier with the identical output shape keeps the demo alive without a key. 6 data shapes (Table, TimeSeries, List, RiskyGrid, Gauge, Scene) let any of ~40 shells render any of ~30 functions — ~1,200 apps from one classifier call. ENS is the filesystem (ENSv2 on Sepolia). We registered suica.eth and deployed our own UserRegistry + PermissionedResolver . Apps and folders are minted as subnames; the full manifest lives in the suica.manifest text record and the app index is read from LabelRegistered events. Folders are their own registries; sharing grants Enhanced Access Control (EAC) roles (member can mint into a folder, manager can also share) — every mint/share request is EIP-191-signed by a per-browser device key , and the server enforces roles on-chain (mint into a folder without ROLE_REGISTRAR → 403). Each app deploys its own PermissionedResolver (creator's key holds root roles; the server keeps only argument-scoped setter roles, then revokes its root). Each user auto-claims a non-transferable username at <name>.users.suica.eth . Moving an app re-mints it and links the old name to the new record (an ENSv2 alias / symlink) , so old share links resolve live data. Sui is where the money moves. Enoki zkLogin (Google → wallet, key stays server-side, proxied through our API) + Enoki sponsored transactions (users never hold SUI). We wrote and published a Move package, AgentVault<T> : share tokens for depositors, an AgentCap permission slip (per-tx / per-day caps, recipient allowlist, expiry) and fee_bps to the creator. agent_pay aborts on-chain when it exceeds a cap — that Move abort is what drives the BSOD, and it's proven live (abort code 2 = EOverTxCap). We use PTBs for atomic multi-party settlement: Group Tab (settle each member in one sponsored PTB) and Programmable Payroll ( agent_pay per recipient in one batch — over-budget reverts the whole batch). Because DeepBook testnet has no liquidity, we deployed our own mock AMM pool (a susd coin + constant-price pool Move package) to make Rebalancer and DCA real, gasless SUI→SUSD swaps. An app's vault id is written into its ENS record under Sui coin type 784 , so grouptab.suica.eth resolves to its Sui vault. Sui reads/writes go over gRPC ( SuiGrpcClient ), since public JSON-RPC is deprecated. Generated shells run as an untrusted guest. When a prompt names a program we don't have, an LLM (via the AI Gateway) writes an HTML shell once, in the background. It's statically checked, smoke-tested in a hidden sandbox, then stored on Walrus with its sha256 and named at <label>.shells.suica.eth . It runs in a sandbox="allow-scripts" iframe with a no-network CSP — data is pushed in, and the only way out is proposing an action the trusted code already built. The dashboard (Curvegrid track). Task Manager shows every agent as a process with real balances and "End Process = revoke AgentCap"; My Computer shows the live AgentVault as a drive with a real balance + day-cap usage bar, reading on-chain vault/cap state (funds, fee_bps, caps, spent_today) every 15s. Hacky bits worth noting: we compile Move without a local Sui CLI by using a Dockerized mysten/sui-tools image with the framework vendored as a local sparse clone (the emulated container can't git-fetch); all tx-building/simulation/gRPC live server-side to dodge gRPC-web CORS (the browser only signs sponsored bytes and assembles the zkLogin signature); and the smoke-test iframe sits on-screen at 0.01 opacity because Chrome pauses rAF in hidden cross-origin frames.
projects.project_description_markdown:
![Suica OS — type anything, get an app](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fabianferno/ethglobal-tokyo-2026/main/docs/assets/suica-pipeline.png)

**Suica OS is a fully hallucinated, operating system where every app is an agent - realtime UI composed by a JEV.** There is no landing page and nothing was built as a normal app. You boot into a retro desktop, open the Start menu, and **type anything** — *"excel of vitalik.eth's portfolio"*, *"paint but roast vitalik.eth"*, *"doom but I'm shooting my losses"*, *"tetris game but my portfolio is falling"* — and a working, on-chain app appears **instantly** as a chunky retro window, as fast as you can type.

**Why we built it.** We're heading toward a future where we don't need apps for everything — agents do the work. But we still need interfaces: to *see* what our agents did, understand it, and approve or refuse it. So interfaces will be **generated on demand** — changing in real time, personal to whoever is using them. Suica OS is an experiment in that idea: an OS where every window is composed live, every app has an identity, and every dollar it moves is gated on-chain.

**Apps are places, not programs.** Every app is really an *agent*: an **ENSv2 name** (its identity + a ~1 KB manifest stored in its text records) plus a **Sui wallet** (an `AgentVault` with spend caps). The UI is disposable — anyone who resolves the name can rebuild the exact UI instantly, no model call. `suica.eth` becomes a real filesystem: **folders are ENS registries, sharing is Enhanced Access Control roles, and moving an app into a folder turns its old name into an ENSv2 alias — a symlink — so old share links keep working.**

**The numbers are real.** Portfolios, roasts and "losses" come from Ethereum mainnet (ENS + Ethplorer); balances, gas and payments come from Sui. **Log on with Google** (zkLogin — no seed phrase) and gas is **sponsored**, so you never hold SUI. Money only moves through one **fixed signing dialog** that is never generated; apps can only *propose*. An assistant, **Tappy**, acts on its own within a cap you set, asks when it's over, and if it ever tries to overspend the **Move contract rejects it on-chain and you get a Blue Screen** — no funds move.

**"Anything is possible."** Ask for a program we don't have ("tetris but…") and it opens instantly in a built-in "compatibility mode" shell while an LLM writes the real shell in the background — sandboxed, tested, published to **Walrus** and named under `shells.suica.eth`, so it's instant for everyone after that.

Tracks: **Sui DeFi & Payments**, **ENS (Best Use of ENSv2, on Sepolia)**, **Curvegrid (Best Digital Asset Dashboard)**.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
![Suica OS — how the tech fits together](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fabianferno/ethglobal-tokyo-2026/main/docs/assets/suica-architecture.png)

**Frontend / OS shell.** Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript. No UI framework — the "Windows 99" kit is hand-written CSS (`win99.css`) with a custom window manager, taskbar, Start menu, and a real BSOD. GSAP powers ~20 hand-built animation scenes.

**The real-time UI engine is Jev (TypeSafe AI), not an LLM.** On every keystroke we make **one** call to Jev — a "System One" model that never writes text, it only answers ~20 typed questions (`choice`/`score`/`noul`) in parallel with calibrated probabilities in ~70–500 ms. Jev decides *shell × function × target × vibe × risk*; a deterministic parser extracts the numbers (ENS names, tokens, amounts, leverage, schedules). **Jev decides, code computes** — a model never invents an amount. We route Jev through the **Vercel AI Gateway**. An offline keyword classifier with the identical output shape keeps the demo alive without a key. 6 data *shapes* (Table, TimeSeries, List, RiskyGrid, Gauge, Scene) let any of ~40 shells render any of ~30 functions — ~1,200 apps from one classifier call.

**ENS is the filesystem (ENSv2 on Sepolia).** We registered `suica.eth` and deployed our **own UserRegistry + PermissionedResolver**. Apps and folders are minted as subnames; the full manifest lives in the `suica.manifest` text record and the app index is read from `LabelRegistered` events. **Folders are their own registries; sharing grants Enhanced Access Control (EAC) roles** (member can mint into a folder, manager can also share) — every mint/share request is EIP-191-signed by a per-browser **device key**, and the server enforces roles on-chain (mint into a folder without `ROLE_REGISTRAR` → 403). Each app deploys its **own PermissionedResolver** (creator's key holds root roles; the server keeps only argument-scoped setter roles, then revokes its root). Each user auto-claims a non-transferable username at `<name>.users.suica.eth`. **Moving an app re-mints it and links the old name to the new record (an ENSv2 alias / symlink)**, so old share links resolve live data.

**Sui is where the money moves.** **Enoki zkLogin** (Google → wallet, key stays server-side, proxied through our API) + **Enoki sponsored transactions** (users never hold SUI). We wrote and published a Move package, **`AgentVault<T>`**: share tokens for depositors, an **`AgentCap`** permission slip (per-tx / per-day caps, recipient allowlist, expiry) and `fee_bps` to the creator. `agent_pay` **aborts on-chain when it exceeds a cap** — that Move abort is what drives the BSOD, and it's proven live (abort code 2 = EOverTxCap). We use **PTBs** for atomic multi-party settlement: **Group Tab** (settle each member in one sponsored PTB) and **Programmable Payroll** (`agent_pay` per recipient in one batch — over-budget reverts the *whole* batch). Because DeepBook testnet has no liquidity, we deployed our **own mock AMM pool** (a `susd` coin + constant-price `pool` Move package) to make **Rebalancer** and **DCA** real, gasless SUI→SUSD swaps. An app's vault id is written into its ENS record under **Sui coin type 784**, so `grouptab.suica.eth` resolves to its Sui vault. Sui reads/writes go over **gRPC** (`SuiGrpcClient`), since public JSON-RPC is deprecated.

**Generated shells run as an untrusted guest.** When a prompt names a program we don't have, an LLM (via the AI Gateway) writes an HTML shell once, in the background. It's statically checked, smoke-tested in a hidden sandbox, then stored on **Walrus** with its sha256 and named at `<label>.shells.suica.eth`. It runs in a `sandbox="allow-scripts"` iframe with a no-network CSP — data is pushed in, and the only way out is proposing an action the trusted code already built.

**The dashboard (Curvegrid track).** Task Manager shows every agent as a process with real balances and "End Process = revoke AgentCap"; My Computer shows the live **AgentVault** as a drive with a real balance + day-cap usage bar, reading on-chain vault/cap state (funds, fee_bps, caps, spent_today) every 15s.

**Hacky bits worth noting:** we compile Move without a local Sui CLI by using a Dockerized `mysten/sui-tools` image with the framework vendored as a local sparse clone (the emulated container can't git-fetch); all tx-building/simulation/gRPC live server-side to dodge gRPC-web CORS (the browser only signs sponsored bytes and assembles the zkLogin signature); and the smoke-test iframe sits on-screen at 0.01 opacity because Chrome pauses rAF in hidden cross-origin frames.

projects.title: ENS Verification
projects.description: Verifiable social and email records for ENSv2, with delegated permissions and sponsored updates.
projects.project_description: ENS Verification links social accounts and email addresses to ENSv2 names on Sepolia. Each identity record has a companion verification descriptor referencing evidence that clients can validate against current ENS ownership. The application supports wallet-signed GitHub gists and X posts, Farcaster proofs, DKIM-signed email evidence, and operator-signed OAuth attestations for Discord and Telegram. These methods have explicit, distinct trust models rather than treating every connected account as equally trustworthy. ENSv2 powers both ownership verification and delegated record updates. Users can authorize an HCA through resolver permissions and optionally submit sponsored updates through Pimlico. Verification checks live records, signatures, ownership and expiry instead of trusting a stored “verified” flag. The current authority profile supports active second-level .eth names.
projects.how_its_made: Built as a TypeScript monorepo with a React/Vite frontend, Effect backend, PostgreSQL and Drizzle. ENSForge handles ENSv2 resolution, registry reads, resolver permissions and batched record updates on Sepolia. Wallet signing and transaction approval remain in the frontend. A shared verification protocol defines descriptors, companion record keys and EIP-712 claims binding the name, record value, authority, proof target and expiry. Provider-specific verifiers validate the external evidence. Generic OAuth uses authorization-code flows with PKCE; Telegram additionally validates signed OIDC ID tokens. For sponsored updates, the app checks HCA deployment and permissions only when a write is requested, grants missing permissions during user-approved setup, and submits an ERC-4337 UserOperation through Pimlico. Each identity record and its verification descriptor are updated together in a resolver multicall.

projects.title: Radius
projects.description: Radius makes your ENS subname the credential for every piece of infrastructure in a network
projects.project_description: Most networks — corporate offices, university campuses, co-working spaces, event venues — still run on shared passwords, manual key distribution, and flat access for everyone. There's no per-person policy, no isolation between roles, no audit trail, no revocation without a full credential reset. Identity is an afterthought bolted on after the fact, if at all. Radius is an identity-gated network and API access control system. Any organization with an ENS name can use it — a company, a university, an event venue. Your ENS subname becomes the sole credential for everything: WiFi admission, bandwidth tier, sponsor or internal API access, SSH. The subname carries your role, your access policy, and your device group in ENS text records. The infrastructure reads ENS instead of a password database. No VPN client, no RADIUS server, no manual provisioning — mint a subname, walk in, connect. The system enforces access in three layers: a captive portal gates WiFi entry and assigns per-role bandwidth tiers at the kernel level, a resource proxy intercepts every API call and injects keys server-side so credentials are never exposed to end users, and an operator console lets administrators define groups, set per-identity and per-group daily quotas, rotate keys atomically, and revoke sessions in real time. Every admission, every proxied request, every quota check is logged against a session identity — not a bare IP — giving operators the first real audit trail without a dedicated security appliance. Critically, Radius gives everyone on the network a usable, role-appropriate slice of real bandwidth — so nobody has to fall back to their mobile hotspot. Role-based VLANs mean a staff member or VIP gets a dedicated high-bandwidth lane, isolated from general attendee traffic, while basic users get a fair share without being able to saturate or snoop on each other. One shared network, properly segmented — the way it should have always worked. The demo targets a crypto hackathon, but the enforcement model is identical for a corporate office, a university lab, or any physical location where identity-based access control matters.
projects.how_its_made: 1. Mint at check-in. Every attendee gets a subname under the event domain — philo.tokyo2026.ethglobal.eth . The organizer writes their role, bandwidth policy, SSH public key, and device group directly into ENS text records. No database entry. No password issued. The subname is the credential. 2. Captive portal reads ENS, not a password DB. When a device connects to the event WiFi, it hits the captive portal. The attendee signs an EIP-191 challenge with their wallet. The portal resolves the signing address to an ENS subname, reads the wifi-tier and wifi-bandwidth records, and maps them to an access group. That's the only auth check. 3. Network enforcement runs at the kernel level. Login triggers two things instantly: an iptables rule marks the device's traffic with an fwmark tied to its tier, and a tc HTB class enforces bandwidth — 5 Mbit for basic attendees, 10 Mbit for staff, 1 Gbit for VIP. Cross-tier FORWARD DROP rules prevent devices on different tiers from reaching each other at all. Device isolation is structural, not policy — there's nothing to misconfigure. 4. A resource proxy injects API keys server-side. All sponsor API access goes through a proxy layer. Attendees never see the keys. The proxy reads the active session, checks group membership and daily usage counters, then forwards the request with the key injected — into the URL path, query param, or header depending on the upstream. Limits are per-device and per-group, adjustable mid-day without a restart. Key rotation is atomic: stage a new key, commit it — zero downtime, old key invalidated in one swap. 5. The full audit trail is automatic. Every proxied request is logged against a session UUID (never a bare IP). Organizers see per-person API usage, bandwidth consumed, login/logout times — in real time, via the operator console. Nothing requires manual instrumentation.

Limits are per-device and per-group, adjustable mid-day without a restart. Key rotation is atomic: stage a new key, commit it — zero downtime, old key invalidated in one swap.

Every proxied request is logged against a session UUID (never a bare IP). Organizers see per-person API usage, bandwidth consumed, login/logout times — in real time, via the operator console. Nothing requires manual instrumentation.

projects.title: on-experiencenetwork
projects.description: A human-owned memory network that lets AI agents access lived experience with consent.
projects.project_description:
HEN, the Human Experience Network, is a privacy-preserving network for storing, discovering, and sharing real human experience. AI can generate unlimited information, but humans only live one life. Our failures, relationships, discoveries, professional intuition, and lessons learned are finite and often disappear with us. HEN turns those lived experiences into private, structured Experience Capsules that can be discovered by AI agents without exposing the original memory. Instead of asking an AI for another generic answer, imagine hearing: “137 people have experienced a situation similar to yours. Three closely match your circumstances, and two people have anonymously allowed their experiences to be used.” HEN connects AI not only to information, but to humanity’s accumulated experience. Users always remain in control. Memories are private by default, and AI can extract only approved, anonymized lessons. A person can choose to share, license, monetize, or simply keep an experience private. Declining is treated as a valid human decision, not an error. In the future, HEN can become a marketplace for rare human experience, where highly specific knowledge, failures, and long-tail expertise can become valuable assets while ownership stays with the person who lived them. Our principle is simple: Your memory is yours.
AI should not replace human experience.
AI should help preserve, discover, and value it.
projects.how_its_made: HEN combines decentralized identity, privacy-preserving memory storage, scoped AI agents, and onchain settlement into one human-controlled architecture. World ID is used as the human trust and consent layer. It proves that a real human is behind an experience and can also be used for fresh approval before sensitive agent actions. HEN does not need to store biometric data itself. When an agent requests access to an Experience Capsule, the user can explicitly approve or decline the request. ENSv2 provides the identity and permission structure for humans and their agents. A user can act as the root identity while specialized agents, such as research, broker, or care agents, operate under scoped subnames and permissions. This creates a clear hierarchy where the human remains the final authority. Memories are stored outside the public blockchain in a private vault. Only references, hashes, permissions, verification metadata, and licensing information need to be exposed onchain. AI transforms raw memories into structured Experience Capsules containing context, decisions, outcomes, mistakes, and lessons without requiring the original private data to become public. Monid gives our agents access to external services and tools through a unified integration layer. HEN supplies the human context, permissions, and memory, while Monid gives agents the ability to act across external applications. For the economic layer, we are exploring 1inch Aqua as a way to coordinate liquidity across multiple experience-bounty strategies. Unlike conventional markets where liquidity concentrates around popular assets, human experience has an unusual long tail: the rarest and least liquid experiences can sometimes be the most valuable. Aqua’s shared-liquidity model gives us an interesting foundation for experimenting with markets around those rare Experience Capsules. The result is a system where AI can search for relevant human experience, request access, negotiate terms, and execute actions, while every sensitive step remains subject to human permission.

projects.title: Agent Bank
projects.description: Agent Bank: Humans set the rules, AI move the money. AI pays bills and invests idle cash in DeFi
projects.project_description:
Agent Bank is business banking where a company delegates bill payments and the investment of surplus funds to an AI agent, and the agent can act only within the scope a World-verified human approved. Banks fear losing deposits to stablecoins and DeFi, crypto exchanges need recurring revenue beyond trading, and businesses are held back by hacks and key management. Agent Bank gives them a familiar bank account whose idle cash earns DeFi yield, run by an agent, with no keys to manage. The customer verifies with World and grants the agent access to specific invoice emails and specific card statements, as two separate scopes: email access alone cannot read card data. The agent extracts payee, amount and due date, forecasts recurring spend from payment history, and proposes one concrete plan: schedule every payment and invest the idle deposit in Aave until each due date. The human approves that plan once. From then on, the bank's policy engine re-checks the approved rules and balance before every action. Payments settle in tokenized deposits on a private chain, surplus is exchanged for stablecoins and invested in Aave on a public chain, and on each due date the agent redeems exactly what that bill needs while the rest keeps earning. The core rule is separating human approval of specific terms, delegation to the agent with scope and limits, and bank-side execution checks. Model output never grants permissions. Approvals are bound to account, content, version and auth generation, and replayed or expired approvals are rejected. Only the human can stop or revoke the agent, and wider scope needs a new approval. The live demo runs one month for a small business: two vendor invoices (Oct 1 and Oct 10) and a corporate card bill (Oct 20). The whole deposit is invested until needed, each bill is paid on its due date, and replaying a date never double-pays. How it's made
The app is a single Next.js 16 / React 19 TypeScript application with SQLite via Drizzle ORM for invoices, rules, delegations, intents and execution records, and viem for chain access. Features are plain modules (approvals, delegations, rules, invoices, cards, payments, investment, redemption) behind a small HTTP boundary. That boundary separates the human session (HttpOnly cookie) from the agent's dedicated credential: a human cookie cannot call agent APIs, and an agent credential alone grants nothing until a human delegates scope and limits. Payee, amount and operation are re-validated server-side before execution, with per-account execution locks. Private chain: Solidity contracts on OpenZeppelin, a Tokenized Deposit token (BankTD, 1 TD = 1 JPY) and a lock vault (TDLockVault), built and tested with Hardhat. A non-fork local Anvil chain stands in for the bank's private chain and is the source of truth for settled balances. To invest, TD is locked in the vault and the bank deploys matching stablecoin from its own inventory; locking never mints public tokens, and locked TD is never double-counted with invested assets. Redemption unlocks TD only after the stablecoin return is confirmed. Public chain: Aave on Base Sepolia with a test USDC-like token (not Circle USDC). Custody wallets are generated server-side and encrypted with a master key, bound to environment, account and chain, and never silently overwritten. Public sends are off unless explicitly enabled. AI: Gemini classifies requests and extracts invoice and card data. The model is treated as untrusted input, never as a source of authority. A deterministic stub mode runs the whole demo without external APIs. World: login and plan approval use World ID via IDKit 4 with Orb proofs verified through the Developer Portal. The signal is bound to account, operation and approved terms, with a per-operation nonce and expiry, so one proof cannot be reused for different terms. Nullifier reuse for the same person is expected, so replay protection lives in the challenge, not the nullifier. We also built a standalone World ID for Agents OIDC flow with openid-client: authorization code + PKCE S256, state, nonce, RS256 signature with non-repudiation checks enabled, issuer, audience, expiry, acr/amr and auth_time. It is the base for step-up approval of risky agent actions. Hosting: Cloudflare Containers behind a Worker. Each visitor gets a disposable container running the app, a local Anvil and SQLite, isolated from everyone else and put to sleep after 2 hours idle. The public demo uses stub assets; the Base Sepolia Aave path runs in local setups. The app stays bound to loopback, and a small proxy forwards only same-origin requests. Notable hacks: a bank-internal "change date" control fast-forwards through due dates without touching OS or chain time, re-verifying delegation and approval at every step, refusing to go backwards and halting on failure. IDKit 4.2.3/4.3.0 returned proof shapes that differed from what we had hard-coded, so we split SDK format checks from Portal cryptographic verification. We first built on IDKit sessions, but verification came back as verification_rejected regardless of credential type and we couldn't isolate the cause, so we switched to Orb + IDKit.request with a fresh, per-operation request bound to the exact terms being approved. The Agents OIDC callback only works when the same HTTPS origin starts and finishes the flow, because the auth cookie and the DB must match.
projects.how_its_made: Agent Bank lets users delegate everyday money management to AI while retaining control over what it can do. The agent reviews invoices, proposes payment schedules, and helps keep funds invested until they are needed. Users approve the plan, and the bank checks each action against that approval before execution. We integrated World ID into login and approval flows using IDKit. The backend verifies proofs and binds approvals to the user’s account and the specific action being authorized, rejecting expired or reused proofs. World ID supplies the proof-of-humanity layer; our bank application manages account access and financial permissions. Our World ID for Agents flow extends this model to external agents. After World authentication and bank account connection, users can grant scoped, revocable access for balance checks. They can also authorize a specific redemption to return invested funds to their original account. The agent receives a credential to execute that approved request, without the ability to change its amount or destination. The key implementation detail is that authentication and delegation remain separate. Connecting an agent does not automatically grant permission to move funds. The bank validates the credential, the user’s delegation, and the approved operation at execution time, with expiration and revocation checks throughout redemption. This makes World verification part of a concrete product flow: a human approves, an agent acts within that permission, and the bank enforces the boundaries.

projects.title: Phinary
projects.description: Binary markets AS Uniswap pools. No external oracle, no orderbook, no API, no service
projects.how_its_made:
The core is a Solidity hook for Uniswap v4. In beforeSwap, it calculates the option price from the underlying pool price, volatility and time to expiry. We use a Black–Scholes-based binary pricing model adapted to the average-price settlement window. The hook returns the swap amounts to PoolManager through custom accounting, replacing the usual AMM pricing curve for these trades.
Getting this pricing logic to work through Uniswap's existing swap flow was a key part of the build. V4Quoter provides quotes, Permit2 handles token permissions, and UniversalRouter executes swaps. We wrapped those interactions in a TypeScript SDK and modified a fork of the Uniswap interface to support option discovery and trading.
The price source is another Uniswap v4 pool. A dedicated oracle hook records the price at the start of each block and tracks volatility. Earlier swaps in the same block cannot change the price reported for that block. Settlement uses the average pool price over a window just before expiry. This still depends on the underlying pool's liquidity and resistance to manipulation.
For the testnet demo, a bot trades the underlying pools toward Coinbase reference prices, standing in for arbitrage in a live market. The option contracts read the pools; they do not call Coinbase or consume its API directly.
A shared USDC vault backs all four option tracks. Complete-set accounting reserves one USDC for each UP/DOWN pair, covering the winning side's payout. Once a market settles, the hook accepts the winning token through the swap path and returns one USDC per token. That lets the trader use the same interface for both entry and payout.
Bots keep the markets running by calling permissionless market-opening and settlement functions. The Next.js dashboard provides vault deposits, withdrawals and allocation views. Our Foundry tests cover pricing math, oracle behavior, the trade-to-settlement lifecycle and attack scenarios.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Phinary is a prediction market built from Uniswap pools, where betting on binary positions is just a token swap. There are no external oracles, off-chain APIs or order books: it runs entirely on Uniswap pools, and everything a market needs is calculated inside Uniswap v4 hooks.

Each market asks one question, such as "Will ETH be above $2,689.27 at 22:45?", and has two ERC-20 tokens, UP and DOWN, each trading against USDC in its own v4 pool. At expiry the winning token redeems for exactly 1 USDC and the losing one for nothing. Four tracks run on one hook and one vault: ETH and SOL, each with 1-minute and 15-minute markets.

Pricing with Black–Scholes:

The fair price of UP is the probability that the price ends above the strike. PredictionHook computes it on every swap with the Black–Scholes formula for a binary option. All three inputs come from Uniswap itself:

S, the underlying pool's price at the start of the current block;
K, the strike, which is the pool's price when the market opened;
σ, the volatility, which the oracle hook measures from the same pool's price history over the last 30 minutes.
A market settles on the average price over its final 10 or 30 seconds, not on a single instant, so the hook prices exactly that:

UP price = Φ( (ln(S/K) − ½σ²·T_D) / (σ·√T_V) )

Φ is the normal distribution. T_D and T_V are the time to expiry, adjusted for averaging over the settlement window. With no window, this is the textbook binary option price N(d₂). DOWN is priced as the mirror image of UP.

We wanted to make a new financial product available through infrastructure traders already use. Phinary puts option pricing and settlement inside a Uniswap v4 hook, with UP and DOWN　positions represented as tradable tokens. Our demo uses a fork of the Uniswap interface to show the full journey from purchase to payout.

Liquidity providers fund the other side. They deposit USDC into a shared vault through the Phinary dashboard and receive shares representing their stake. That vault backs multiple option markets. Its value changes with trading spreads and settlement payouts, so providing liquidity carries risk as well as the opportunity to earn returns.

The current deployment runs on Unichain Sepolia, with one-minute and fifteen-minute options for both ETH and SOL. We also built a TypeScript SDK so other applications can quote and execute trades against the same contracts.

projects.title: Kagi Wallet
projects.description: Give AI agents delegated keys from a self-custody MPC wallet. Spend more? Your ESP32s sign over IR.
projects.project_description: Kagi is an open-source threshold wallet for AI agents. It gives your agent its own spending key, capped and set to expire, while the key that actually controls your money stays split across hardware you hold. Agents need money to be useful, but today you pick between two bad options. Either you give the agent a hot key, and one prompt injection drains you, or you approve every transaction, and the agent is useless. Most crypto theft comes down to a stolen key, so we made sure no single device, server or phone ever holds one. Kagi splits every key with FROST threshold Schnorr signatures (the RFC 9591 family), and each half is useless on its own. Together they produce one standard BIP340 signature. Kagi works as a spending ladder: Under the cap: your agent pays on its own with an ephemeral session key. The smart account enforces the limit and the expiry on-chain, so the agent can't overspend even if it's compromised. Over the cap: the agent files an on-chain request with its reason. Your phone shows it, and you approve with your fingerprint plus a held button on your Kagi Wallet, an off-the-shelf $21.50 ESP32 stick. Together they form a 2-of-2 key. The treasury: needs a 3-of-3 key that includes a second stick, the vault. After setup the vault keeps its radio off and signs only over infrared, so you have to walk over and point your Kagi Wallet at it. Revoke: hold the revoke button on the phone, or hold B on the stick for 2 seconds. Any AI can use it. ChatGPT, Claude, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and VS Code connect through our MCP server with a personal connector link from the app. The agent can send ETH, check its allowance and ask for more. Kagi uses two partner technologies: Intercepta decides who the agent may pay. The cap limits how much it can lose. Every recipient is screened before the session key signs. Clean addresses pass. Risky ones are held for your approval on the phone and stick, even when the payment is under the cap. Sanctioned addresses and known scammers are refused outright. Curvegrid MultiBaas gives the agent a memory. It indexes every payment, limit request, approval and revoke, so you can ask your AI "what did my agent spend today, and who approved the raise?" MultiBaas Event Queries also power the Spending screen in the app. The website at kagiwallet.com lets you flash a stick straight from Chrome with no toolchain, connect your AI in a few clicks, and see what unlimited agent authority has cost people, drawn from real incidents. The Android app is on GitHub Releases. Everything runs on Sepolia, and the app can switch to Ethereum mainnet. Kagi is a working wallet you can use today, and a pattern for giving agents real money without giving them your keys.
projects.how_its_made: Hardware We used two M5Stack StickS3 boards (ESP32-S3), each with a screen, two buttons, a speaker and an IR transmitter and receiver. We flash the same firmware build to both, and a role saved on the device makes one stick the Kagi Wallet and the other the vault. The Kagi Wallet talks to the phone over Bluetooth LE. The vault joins the key once: we reshare it from 2-of-2 to 3-of-3 during a 2-minute radio window you open by holding a button on the vault. After that its radio stays off, and it signs only over infrared, after a press on the vault itself. We wrote the IR link ourselves on the ESP32's RMT peripheral: a 38 kHz carrier, NEC-style pulses, 4-byte frames with a sequence number, a CRC-8 and an acknowledgement, and retries, so a hand passing over the window slows a signature down instead of breaking it. Firmware The firmware is C++ built with PlatformIO. We wrote FROST ourselves on top of mbedTLS's big-number and elliptic-curve primitives, and used NimBLE for Bluetooth and M5Unified for the display, buttons and speaker. The IR link talks to the ESP32's RMT peripheral directly through ESP-IDF. Every approval is a deliberate hold on the button, and letting go early cancels it. The speaker stays quiet while the IR receiver is listening, because the StickS3 can't do both at once. Smart contracts The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built with Foundry. KagiAccount holds the manager key, the agent keys and their limits ( grant , spend , requestLimit , raiseLimit , declineLimit , revoke ). RootTreasury holds the 3-of-3 key. Ethereum has no Schnorr precompile, so we verify BIP340 signatures with the ecrecover trick, and that makes threshold Schnorr work on any EVM chain. The account supports ERC-1271 for the manager key only, which makes SIWE and Permit2 work. Agent keys are left out on purpose, because a signed permit would move money around the cap. There are 61 unit and fuzz tests, including the official BIP340 vectors and real FROST signatures made by the phone code. Mobile app The app is built with Expo and React Native. The phone's shard lives in secure storage behind a biometric unlock, and the app uses @noble/curves for FROST, viem for the chain and react-native-ble-plx for Bluetooth. The phone signs in TypeScript and the stick signs in C++, and the two must produce identical bytes. A shared test fixture catches it the moment they drift. The phone also keeps a small gas wallet and tops up each agent's key when it grants one, so we didn't need a relayer. Agent MCP server The server is Node, using the official MCP SDK and viem, and runs behind Caddy. Each person's connector link carries their own key, so one server can serve everyone. It finds each wallet's chain from where its contract is deployed, so the same link works on Sepolia and on mainnet. Intercepta Every payment runs a Quick Scan on the recipient, and a Deep Scan on anything that gets flagged. The result maps to pass, hold or refuse. A held payment goes through the contract's existing requestLimit → raiseLimit path, so it still needs the phone and the stick, and we didn't change the contract at all. If Intercepta can't be reached, the payment is held, never passed. Curvegrid MultiBaas Free public RPCs refuse or cap log queries, and one call to MultiBaas's events endpoint replaced all of that. Every user deploys their own wallet, so the server registers the ABI and links each wallet with MultiBaas the first time it connects. Event Queries add up spending by agent and by recipient, plus limit raises and requests, for the app's Spending screen and the get_spending_summary tool. Website The site is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, with Motion for animation, and is hosted on Firebase. esp-web-tools lets anyone flash a stick over Web Serial straight from Chrome or Edge. Hacks we're proud of Schnorr verification through ecrecover , a vault you can only reach by light, one firmware build that plays both roles, and FROST that matches byte for byte between TypeScript and C++.

Kagi is an open-source threshold wallet for AI agents. It gives your agent its own spending key, capped and set to expire, while the key that actually controls your money stays split across hardware you hold.

Either you give the agent a hot key, and one prompt injection drains you, or you approve every transaction, and the agent is useless. Kagi splits every key with FROST threshold Schnorr signatures (the RFC 9591 family), and each half is useless on its own. Together they produce one standard BIP340 signature.

Kagi works as a spending ladder:

- **Under the cap:** your agent pays on its own with an ephemeral session key. The smart account enforces the limit and the expiry on-chain, so the agent can't overspend even if it's compromised.

Any AI can use it. ChatGPT, Claude, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and VS Code connect through our MCP server with a personal connector link from the app. The agent can send ETH, check its allowance and ask for more.

Kagi uses two partner technologies:

- **Intercepta** decides *who* the agent may pay. The cap limits *how much* it can lose. Every recipient is screened before the session key signs. Clean addresses pass. Risky ones are held for your approval on the phone and stick, even when the payment is under the cap. Sanctioned addresses and known scammers are refused outright.
- **Curvegrid MultiBaas** gives the agent a memory. It indexes every payment, limit request, approval and revoke, so you can ask your AI "what did my agent spend today, and who approved the raise?" MultiBaas Event Queries also power the Spending screen in the app.

The website at kagiwallet.com lets you flash a stick straight from Chrome with no toolchain, connect your AI in a few clicks, and see what unlimited agent authority has cost people, drawn from real incidents. The Android app is on GitHub Releases. Everything runs on Sepolia, and the app can switch to Ethereum mainnet.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
#### Hardware
We used two M5Stack StickS3 boards (ESP32-S3), each with a screen, two buttons, a speaker and an IR transmitter and receiver. We flash the same firmware build to both, and a role saved on the device makes one stick the Kagi Wallet and the other the vault. The Kagi Wallet talks to the phone over Bluetooth LE. The vault joins the key once: we reshare it from 2-of-2 to 3-of-3 during a 2-minute radio window you open by holding a button on the vault. After that its radio stays off, and it signs only over infrared, after a press on the vault itself. We wrote the IR link ourselves on the ESP32's RMT peripheral: a 38 kHz carrier, NEC-style pulses, 4-byte frames with a sequence number, a CRC-8 and an acknowledgement, and retries, so a hand passing over the window slows a signature down instead of breaking it.

#### Firmware
The firmware is C++ built with PlatformIO. We wrote FROST ourselves on top of mbedTLS's big-number and elliptic-curve primitives, and used NimBLE for Bluetooth and M5Unified for the display, buttons and speaker. The IR link talks to the ESP32's RMT peripheral directly through ESP-IDF. Every approval is a deliberate hold on the button, and letting go early cancels it. The speaker stays quiet while the IR receiver is listening, because the StickS3 can't do both at once.

#### Smart contracts
The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built with Foundry. `KagiAccount` holds the manager key, the agent keys and their limits (`grant`, `spend`, `requestLimit`, `raiseLimit`, `declineLimit`, `revoke`). `RootTreasury` holds the 3-of-3 key. Ethereum has no Schnorr precompile, so we verify BIP340 signatures with the `ecrecover` trick, and that makes threshold Schnorr work on any EVM chain. The account supports ERC-1271 for the manager key only, which makes SIWE and Permit2 work. Agent keys are left out on purpose, because a signed permit would move money around the cap. There are 61 unit and fuzz tests, including the official BIP340 vectors and real FROST signatures made by the phone code.

#### Mobile app
The app is built with Expo and React Native. The phone's shard lives in secure storage behind a biometric unlock, and the app uses @noble/curves for FROST, viem for the chain and react-native-ble-plx for Bluetooth. The phone signs in TypeScript and the stick signs in C++, and the two must produce identical bytes. A shared test fixture catches it the moment they drift. The phone also keeps a small gas wallet and tops up each agent's key when it grants one, so we didn't need a relayer.

#### Agent MCP server
The server is Node, using the official MCP SDK and viem, and runs behind Caddy. Each person's connector link carries their own key, so one server can serve everyone. It finds each wallet's chain from where its contract is deployed, so the same link works on Sepolia and on mainnet.

#### Intercepta
Every payment runs a Quick Scan on the recipient, and a Deep Scan on anything that gets flagged. The result maps to pass, hold or refuse. A held payment goes through the contract's existing `requestLimit` → `raiseLimit` path, so it still needs the phone and the stick, and we didn't change the contract at all. If Intercepta can't be reached, the payment is held, never passed.

#### Curvegrid MultiBaas
Free public RPCs refuse or cap log queries, and one call to MultiBaas's events endpoint replaced all of that. Every user deploys their own wallet, so the server registers the ABI and links each wallet with MultiBaas the first time it connects. Event Queries add up spending by agent and by recipient, plus limit raises and requests, for the app's Spending screen and the `get_spending_summary` tool.

#### Website
The site is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, with Motion for animation, and is hosted on Firebase. esp-web-tools lets anyone flash a stick over Web Serial straight from Chrome or Edge.

#### Hacks we're proud of
Schnorr verification through `ecrecover`, a vault you can only reach by light, one firmware build that plays both roles, and FROST that matches byte for byte between TypeScript and C++.
