projects.title: Croquis (クロッキー)
projects.description: Draw a 3 minute sticker on your phone inside LINE and gift it to a friend as a one-of-one NFT.
projects.project_description: Croquis (クロッキー, Japanese for a quick sketch) is a daily drawing app that runs inside LINE, the messaging app most people in Japan already use. You get one blank canvas and a 5-minute timer. The clock starts on your first stroke and pauses if you leave the app. When time runs out, or you choose to finish early, the drawing is sealed. It's die-cut from your own strokes into a glossy sticker and becomes a one-of-one that can never be changed. It records who drew it, how long they spent and when. Stickers go on your sticker board, like stickers on the back of a laptop. The main thing to do with them is give them away. You can hand someone a physical drawing, but a digital one can be copied endlessly, so giving it means nothing. With Croquis, a gift actually leaves your board and moves to your friend's. You pick one friend in LINE's own friend picker. They get a gift message in your 1:1 chat with a frosted gift bag and an "Open your gift" button. They sign in with LINE, pull the tab on the bag, and the sticker is theirs. They don't need to already have the app or know anything about crypto. After receiving a sticker, you can send the artist gratitude through a combo mini-game inspired by Death Stranding's likes. Tap, stroke or shake a heart to build hits while a bar drains faster and faster, and the effects get more over the top as the combo grows. Gratitude is a public score on each person's stat board and the Explore leaderboards, and it can never be bought or sold. If the original artist is neither the giver nor the receiver, they still get 20% of the gratitude when their sticker is passed on. Every sticker has a transfer trail showing each time it was given and the gratitude it earned. Everyone gets 3 free daily tickets to draw. Extra tickets are sold in packs, priced in yen and paid in JPYC, a yen stablecoin. The whole design assumes artists who are suspicious of crypto. There are no wallets, seed phrases, gas prompts or "NFT" labels anywhere in the UI. Each person's handle is secretly an ENS name, each sticker is an ERC-721, and each gift goes through an onchain escrow, but it all feels like sending a sticker in LINE. The app is fully bilingual in Japanese and English.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: Vite, React 19 and TypeScript, running as a LIFF app (LINE Front-end Framework) inside LINE's browser on iPhone. The drawing canvas, die-cut sealing, the live resin/foil sticker look and the gratitude mini-game are all custom, with no drawing library. Sealing runs in a Web Worker: it traces the outline of your strokes, cuts the sticker shape out with a border and renders five images, including a timelapse. The mini-game reads taps, stroke passes and DeviceMotion shakes. Every string is in a typed Japanese/English catalog. Backend: A Hono REST API on Node 24, with Drizzle ORM on SQLite, deployed behind the LIFF endpoint. A typed client is generated from the routes, so the frontend and API can't drift apart. Identity and invisible wallets (Privy + LINE): We wrote a small auth server that checks the LINE ID token from LIFF with LINE, then issues a short-lived JWT for Privy Custom Auth (P-256, with a JWKS endpoint). That means signing in with LINE silently creates a Privy embedded wallet and a Safe smart account for each person, with no extra step. Gas is sponsored through a paymaster, so an artist with 0 ETH can still give stickers. Stickers onchain (Ethereum Sepolia): Written in Solidity with Foundry. StickerNFT is an ERC-721 whose original artist, content hash and metadata can't change after sealing. At seal time, a backend sealer key mints the NFT to the artist's smart account. The API waits for the receipt and checks the mint's Transfer event before telling the UI the seal worked, and a retry picks up an existing mint instead of minting twice. Typed ABIs are generated with wagmi CLI, and viem is used everywhere. Gift escrow: Giving sends the sticker straight into StickerGiftEscrow using ERC-721 safeTransferFrom receiver data (gift ID, claim hash, expiry), so the recipient doesn't need an account yet. A one-time gift claim token sits only in the LINE message link; our database and the contract keep only its hash. When the friend signs in with LINE, the API finds their smart account, signs a claim authorization bound to that recipient, contract, chain and deadline, and submits the claim. The sender can take a gift back while it's still waiting, and anyone can return an expired gift to its sender. ENS (ENSv2): Each person's handle is <name>.croquis.eth, permanent and non-transferable, with its own registry and resolver on ENSv2 (vendored at the commit deployed to Sepolia). Each sealed sticker gets its own name, <number>.<artist>.croquis.eth, which follows whoever currently holds the NFT. A waiting gift gets a temporary g-<id>.gifts.croquis.eth name that goes away when the gift is received or returned. A custom CroquisResolver answers sticker and gift names directly from the NFT and escrow contracts, and everything else through CCIP-Read from a signed gateway on our API. Our Forge tests build a local copy of ENS from ENSv2's own contracts. Ticket shop (JPYC on Sui): Reserve tickets are paid in JPYC on Sui from the person's Privy Sui wallet, using @mysten/sui. The API reads the payment contract's PaymentReceived events over Sui gRPC and checks the payer, amount and reference before handing out tickets. From the ticket shop, a person can open their ENS name and see their purchase history, read from Sui GraphQL and linked to Suiscan. So one person's identity covers two chains.

projects.title: Zigel
projects.description: Trusted transport payments: human verification, secure swaps, and verifiable Filecoin evidence.
projects.project_description: Eth Transport is a decentralized transport infrastructure platform connecting real-world road incidents, services, payments, identity, and verifiable evidence. For ETHGlobal, we are building  Eth Transport's Zigel, a trusted ETH↔FIL transport payment workflow: World ID verifies a unique human at critical trust moments; ENSv2 provides human, organization, and agent identities; 1inch and Uniswap provide DeFi swap and liquidity infrastructure; Intercepta screens transactions before users sign; and IPFS/Filecoin stores tamper-evident transport evidence, receipts, and incident data. The result is an end-to-end workflow where a human or authorized agent can initiate a transport action, securely move value, and leave a verifiable decentralized record.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Eth Transport’s Zigel as a modular Web3 application that connects a real-world transport workflow to identity, DeFi, security, and decentralized storage. The frontend orchestrates the user journey from a transport event or service request through human verification, identity resolution, payment, security screening, settlement, and evidence storage.
World ID / IDKit is integrated at consequential trust moments to verify that the requester is a unique human rather than using proof of humanity as a simple login. ENSv2 provides human-readable identities and namespaces for users, organizations, transport services, and future agents. This gives the payment and authorization flow an identity layer beyond raw wallet addresses.
For payments, we integrate 1inch for the Ethereum-side swap/routing workflow and Uniswap for DeFi liquidity and programmable swap infrastructure. We connect this with our existing Filecoin/IPFS transport infrastructure, allowing payments and services to produce decentralized, content-addressed receipts and evidence.
A key hackathon integration is Intercepta directly before transaction signing. Instead of checking security after a transaction happens, we screen the wallet/transaction/contract at the moment of authorization and expose the result before the user signs. This creates a security gate between payment intent and execution.
Underneath, the application combines Ethereum smart-contract interactions, wallet signing, ENS resolution, World ID verification, DeFi APIs/protocols, IPFS CIDs, and Filecoin persistence. Existing Transport DAO modules provide incident reporting, transport asset data, alarms, governance, and decentralized evidence storage.
The particularly hacky part is treating all these sponsor technologies as one trust pipeline rather than separate integrations:
World ID → ENS identity → payment intent → 1inch/Uniswap → Intercepta security check → transaction authorization → IPFS/Filecoin evidence.
This lets a human or future autonomous transport agent move from a verified real-world action to a secure financial transaction and finally to a verifiable decentralized record, while keeping each technology responsible for a distinct part of the trust model.

projects.title: Hank0
projects.description: ENS names as trading permissions for a Uniswap v4 permissioned pool holding a tokenized stock
projects.project_description: In September 2026 the SEC's Innovation Exemption defined a Tokenized Securities Venue as doing two things: running AMM pools for permissioned participants, and setting the standards for who may access them. Uniswap v4 permissioned pools cover the first. The second is left to the venue, and the interface Uniswap gives you is one function returning a flag for an address. Hanko answers that function with ENSv2. A cleared investor holds a name under let's say swap.tnvda.eth or lp.tnvda.eth, and the shape of the name is the permission. Every swap and every liquidity deposit resolves it live. Because it's ENS, three things come free. Names expire, so access lapses on its own. They're registered without the transfer role, so clearance can't be sold to a wallet the venue never cleared. And an investor can open names for their own trading bots / AI Agents inside their own registry without asking the venue. Revoke the investor and every bot under them stops in the same transaction, because a child of a lapsed name has nothing left to resolve through. Everything on the site is read from Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: The checker is a Solidity contract implementing Uniswap's IAllowlistChecker. checkAllowlist(account, token) turns the address into a lowercase hex label, looks it up in two ENSv2 UserRegistries, and returns the bytes2 flags (0x0001 swap, 0x0002 liquidity). If no direct name resolves, it tries agent delegation: the label is looked up in an index registry whose entries point at an investor's own registry through the resolver field, then walks back up to check the investor's name is still alive. Putting the pointer in ENS rather than a mapping means expiry and revocation semantics are inherited, not reimplemented. Each investor gets a UserRegistry proxy from ENS's VerifiableFactory, and names are granted with EnhancedAccessControl roles that deliberately exclude transfer. The pool is a real v4 permissioned pool on Sepolia: PermissionsAdapter wrapping a mock tNVDA, PermissionedHooks, PermissionedPositionManager. Two things cost us time and are worth writing down. UniversalRouter v2.1.2 is the default entry in Uniswap's deployment file and it cannot do permissioned swaps; you need v2.2. And the adapter has to be registered as a wrapper on the PoolManager itself, not just the router, which is only documented in Uniswap's own integration tests. 67 Foundry tests, most of them forked against live Sepolia so the ENS and Uniswap contracts under test are the real deployed ones. Frontend is Next.js reading state directly over viem, with the audit trail pulled from event logs.

projects.title: IC Pay
projects.description: Bringing stablecoin payments to everyday Japan through the IC cards people already carry.
projects.project_description: Japan already has the habit stablecoin payments need: tapping a card to pay. In its March 2025 report, JR East counted 112.3 million Suica cards issued , including mobile cards, and 2.07 million stores accepting interoperable transport e-money. That network recorded 253 million purchases in January 2025 alone . https://www.jreast.co.jp/e/investor/pdf/202503_e_suica_finance.pdf Stablecoin spending is growing quickly. Visa reported $5.2 billion in stablecoin-linked card spending in 2025 , up 319% year over year , with more than 130 programs across 50+ countries by March 2026. Yet this spending represented just 0.04% of Visa’s total volume , suggesting substantial room for adoption. https://www.visa.com/en-us/thought-leadership/innovation/stablecoin-linked-cards-monetize-money-movement Suica Pay brings crypto payments to a card people already carry. Users link a physical Suica to a crypto wallet, verify with World, and tap their card against a participating merchant’s iPhone to pay within approved spending limits. Merchants can accept payments and manage their own reward programs from the app. We built rewards around the familiar earn-and-redeem experience of Japanese loyalty programs. Customers accumulate merchant-specific points on qualifying purchases and redeem them toward later bills. Merchants choose the earning rate, reward caps, and expiry rules. For example, a 5% offer earns 5 points on a 100 icUSD purchase, which can cover 5 icUSD on a future visit. Customers can authorize automatic redemption and set limits on how many points each purchase uses. The app also supports NFT vouchers with redeemable merchant credit. Customers can spend part of a voucher’s credit and save the rest; collectible NFTs remain in their wallet after the credit is used. This is our RWA angle: representing a merchant’s promised discount or store credit onchain and redeeming it at checkout. One dashboard brings together wallet balances, points, vouchers, and payment history. The demo runs on Sepolia using icUSD test tokens.
projects.how_its_made: We built customer and merchant flows in one Swift/SwiftUI iPhone app. Core NFC reads a physical Suica’s FeliCa IDm, which the backend HMAC-hashes and links to a separate crypto wallet. Its transit balance stays untouched. Customers approve spending limits beforehand, then tap their card at the merchant’s iPhone. World IDKit Selfie Check handles onboarding and account recovery, with backend verification. The prebuilt Swift SDK dropped sybil_score , so we rebuilt the official Rust core and regenerated its UniFFI bindings to preserve the complete verification result. The TypeScript/Fastify backend uses PostgreSQL for accounts, invoices and payment jobs. Merchant phones sign invoice-bound requests with Secure Enclave P-256 keys; AWS KMS holds the operator-managed secp256k1 wallet keys. We built the adapter that converts KMS signatures into valid Ethereum transactions. Curvegrid MultiBaas constructs unsigned transactions, broadcasts signed transactions and indexes events for the dashboard. We used Curvegrid’s icUSD token and built payment and reward contracts with Solidity, OpenZeppelin and Hardhat on Sepolia. icUSD is an unbacked test token. Rewards include Japanese-art NFT vouchers and merchant points with fractional earnings, partial redemption and atomic payment settlement. Existing vouchers retain their credit and artwork; daily expiry buckets keep points processing bounded. Durable jobs, reservations and signed transaction journals prevent blind retries, and the app shows “Paid” only after verifying confirmed receipts. AWS Fargate runs the API and worker with private RDS PostgreSQL; a React/TypeScript dashboard on Amplify displays balances, payments and rewards. We tested against a real local EVM and PostgreSQL, and checked the native screens on both physical iPhones.

projects.title: Omamoris
projects.description: Give your AI agent a budget, not your keys. It shops on its own, only for what you asked.
projects.project_description: AI agents can finally shop, but nobody can safely let them. Checkout inside a chat makes you confirm every purchase, and a wallet with a spending cap can be talked into paying for anything inside the cap: a clean address, within budget, for something you never asked for. Omamori gives your agent a budget, not your keys. Your agent (Claude, or any MCP client) asks for an intent: what it may buy, where, how much and until when. You approve it once with one tap in World App, which also proves a real person said yes. The first time, it also creates your account, and a setup link deploys your own smart account on Base Sepolia, which you own and fund with USDC. From then on the agent shops on its own, paying x402 merchants from your account without ever holding a key. Every payment is checked against your intent before anything is signed, and the pipeline fails closed: idempotency, policy (budget, expiry, network), merchant binding, account funding, provenance, Intercepta address and token screening, a calibrated semantic intent check with TypeSafe Jev, and a fresh World ID approval whenever something is doubtful. A retry never pays twice, a second purchase needs an explicit purchase reference, and a new plan replaces the intent only after you approve it. You see every receipt with its reason, get gift card codes in your dashboard, and can revoke any intent. Proof: 49/49 end-to-end scenarios pass; Jev refused the key attack (matches_intent 0.02) while the legitimate purchase paid; one approval covered two real purchases on-chain; a World ID approval produced a payment bound by a StepUp attestation; and an independent verifier found no payment from the firewall wallet without a matching pay receipt. Testnet only.
projects.how_its_made: A bun + TypeScript monorepo with a firewall, an MCP server, an x402 store, a site, a demo agent and a Foundry contracts package. The firewall (Hono) runs the pre-signature pipeline. The agent never signs: it forwards the store's 402, the firewall re-fetches the merchant's own 402, runs every check, and only then builds the x402 payment payload (@x402 2.27, public facilitator, Base Sepolia USDC). The MCP server (official SDK, stdio and Streamable HTTP) exposes tools like request_promise, list_promises, pay_x402 and check_approval; the agent's credential stays in the server and is never returned to the model. Two Agent Skills packages on skills.sh (omamori-setup, omamori-purchase) teach any agent to connect and buy. OmamorisanAccount is a per-user smart account deployed with CREATE2 from a factory, owned by the user's wallet, with on-chain recipient and payment limits. It pays x402 through the unmodified public facilitator: USDC's EIP-3009 authorization is validated through the account's EIP-1271 signature check. Partners: World ID for Agents through the sandbox OIDC device flow (ID token verified with jose + JWKS and auth_time freshness), plus a signed StepUp attestation that binds each approval to its exact payment. AI agents can finally shop, but nobody can safely let them. Checkout inside a chat makes you confirm every purchase, and a wallet with a spending cap can be talked into paying for anything inside the cap: a clean address, within budget, for something you never asked for.

Omamori gives your agent a budget, not your keys. Your agent (Claude, or any MCP client) asks for an intent: what it may buy, where, how much and until when. You approve it once with one tap in World App, which also proves a real person said yes. The first time, it also creates your account, and a setup link deploys your own smart account on Base Sepolia, which you own and fund with USDC. From then on the agent shops on its own, paying x402 merchants from your account without ever holding a key.

projects.title: Wamia
projects.description: A liquidity backstop for yield trading that stops unfair liquidations.
projects.project_description: Wamia is a standing liquidity backstop for Pendle's PT (yield trading) markets, built for 1inch's "Build an Aqua App" track. On Aug 25, 2026, an attacker forced Pendle's router to sell millions of PT reUSD by repeatedly buying YT, pushing PT price down about 3% in roughly 9 minutes. Morpho's 15 minute TWAP oracle followed that dip down, and borrowers who had done nothing wrong got liquidated. $37.35M in debt became eligible for liquidation across 20 positions, even though PT's actual value at maturity never changed. Wamia addresses this by giving the market a bid that's always there. LPs ship idle capital (SY, Pendle's yield bearing wrapper token) to a Wamia strategy on 1inch Aqua, without locking it up. The strategy runs a pricing algorithm that reads live onchain Pendle, Curve and SY state on every trade and decides whether the current PT price looks like manipulation or a genuine repricing. When it judges a dip to be manipulation, it pays a small discount to fair value for PT; when the signals look more like a real depeg, a real loss in the vault's rate, or a real news driven move, the algorithm scales its discount down or stops quoting rather than absorbing the loss. When someone dumps PT into a thin pool and Wamia is willing to buy, a zero capital searcher sells that PT to Wamia and immediately buys it back on Pendle in the same transaction, helping pull the price back up before the oracle average can drag it down further. In a fork replay of the real attack, 5M SY of Wamia liquidity took liquidatable debt from $37.35M down to $0 in that scenario, while LPs earned an estimated 11.3% annualized (versus 10.58% at fair value) and the searcher made about 8,900 PT with no starting capital. Across a set of scripted collapse scenarios (a real depeg, a real drop in the vault's exchange rate, a real large repricing), the same algorithm held back or refused to quote, which is the behavior we're aiming for.
projects.how_its_made: Wamia runs entirely on 1inch's deployed, unmodified contracts: Aqua v1.0.0 and AquaSwapVMRouter (swap-vm v1.0.2). A Wamia strategy is a SwapVM order whose program is a single Extruction instruction pointing at WamiaQuoter, a stateless Solidity contract that prices every PT sale from maker-set parameters and live onchain reads: Pendle's spot, the SY exchange rate, and Curve's reUSD/USDC EMA price, never from taker-supplied data. Two optional v2 steps, WamiaRateGuard and WamiaSpendLimit, compose into the same program to add a high-water-mark check and a per-block spend cap. WamiaArb is the zero-capital searcher contract: it sells PT to Wamia through the router, and inside the router's preTransferInCallback immediately buys that PT back on Pendle with the SY it just received, keeping the leftover PT as profit or reverting if unprofitable. The contracts are built and tested in Foundry, with unit tests, a full local deployment of real Aqua/SwapVM release tags, and fork tests against live Pendle, Morpho and Curve contracts at the exact block of the Aug 25 attack. On the TypeScript side, @1inch/aqua-sdk and @1inch/swap-vm-sdk build the same order and program that the Solidity side produces, verified byte-for-byte (including the strategy hash) by a dedicated parity test. Fork replays use viem and anvil to mine block-by-block against forked mainnet state, comparing no-backstop, a reactive taker bot, and Wamia at several capital levels. The frontend is a Vite + React app with four screens (attack replay, LP shipping flow, market health dashboard, strategy inspector) that read committed replay data or talk to a locally deployed Wamia via npm run app:server. The full list of integration notes and suggestions we sent back to the 1inch team lives in FEEDBACK.md.

projects.title: MD Transfer Protocol
projects.description: Sign and publish Markdown under ENS names. Verify integrity and current team authorization.
projects.project_description: Markdown is becoming a shared working format for people and AI agents. Teams use it for instructions, research, and decisions, but plain Markdown provides no built-in proof of who signed a document, whether its content changed, or which published version the team intends people to follow. MDTP, the Markdown Transfer Protocol, connects two workflows through one team ENS namespace: signed in private and published in public. ENSv2 subnames identify team members, and current ownership determines whether their signatures or publications verify. Private documents stay offchain and carry two frontmatter fields: signer and signature. MDTP checks the signature over the normalized Markdown body against the current owner of the signer name. Changes to the signed content fail verification. Once a member's subname is revoked onchain, their signed files return Unauthorized on the next verification. Readers need no wallet to verify them. For public documents, MDTP stores Markdown in a Sepolia transaction and points the document name's mdtp text record to it. The transaction preserves that publication, while authorized publishers can update the ENS pointer to a new version. Readers can check the publisher, publication time, and recorded versions. The team chooses which publication to treat as its official source. Memona, our existing local-first Markdown app, is MDTP's first integration. It brings signing, publishing, verification badges, and mdtp:// links into the document workflow. Published documents can also be opened in the browser-based MDTP reader. Our demo follows a research team using fictional token data. Tom, an analyst, signs the team's portfolio strategy. After someone removes RUGY from its blocklist, Helen opens the shared copy and Memona flags it as Tampered. Eric, the team lead, restores the intended content, signs it, and publishes it under the team's designated document name as the official strategy. Without a wallet, Helen follows ENS links to that publication and checks who published it and when. She then asks the Folder Agent to use that strategy. Memona's mdtp_read tool returns the published document only when verification succeeds. Using that source, the agent screens 30 tokens, returns four candidates, and excludes RUGY. When the request points to the unauthorized ghost publication, the tool withholds the content and the demo agent stops without generating a report. Only published Markdown goes onchain; referenced images and videos remain on conventional web servers. The live demo runs on Sepolia. The MDTP core, CLI, WebAssembly bindings, and web demo are open source under the MIT license.
projects.how_its_made: MDTP has a Rust core with no network or filesystem I/O. It builds Ethereum calls and decodes responses, while the host application executes them. The CLI, WebAssembly bindings, web demo, and Memona integration reuse this core verification logic. For private files, we sign an EIP-191 personal_sign message containing the ENS signer name and the SHA-256 hash of the normalized Markdown body. Verification recovers the signing address and calls ENSv2's UniversalResolverV2.findOwner to check current ownership. We deliberately use ownership rather than the addr record: wildcard resolution can still return a parent's address after a child name has been revoked. Team setup deploys UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver contracts through VerifiableFactory and registers a name through ETHRegistrar using Sepolia MockUSDC. Members receive subnames with a zero role bitmap, preventing them from transferring or unregistering those names. Administrators manage membership through ROLE_REGISTRAR and ROLE_UNREGISTER. Separately, authorizeTextRoles grants resolver permissions for publishing to a document name's mdtp text record. Publishing sends two Sepolia transactions: a self-send containing the Markdown, followed by an authorized update of the document name's mdtp text record. The web reader discovers recorded versions from the current resolver's TextChanged logs, retrieves the referenced transaction content, and rechecks the publisher's current authorization. The Memona integration connects these two workflows to people and agents. Humans see verification badges and publication details. The mdtp_read tool checks a published document before returning its content to the Folder Agent. In the demo, the agent uses this tool to read the team's designated strategy and stops the report task when the tool refuses an unauthorized publication. Memona predates this hackathon. During ETHGlobal Tokyo, we built the open-source MDTP core, CLI, WebAssembly demo, and the Memona integration for signing, publishing, reading mdtp:// documents, and supplying verified published instructions to the Folder Agent. Claude Code agents wrote most of the implementation, tests, and documentation under our team's direction. Our team defined the product design, file format, and ENSv2 permission model and directed the development work. The repository documents the existing and new components and the AI assistance used.

projects.title: PDFi +
projects.description: A PDF invoice that pays itself, only to the vault its ENS name publishes, and sells on 1inch Aqua
projects.project_description: PDFi Plus is a PDF invoice that sends its own payment. It continues PDFi, which we built at ETHGlobal New York 2025: a PDF with form buttons that talks to a backend holding Coinbase CDP wallets. At Tokyo we rebuilt the invoice itself as a 1inch SwapVM order, checked the payee against ENSv2, and made unpaid invoices sellable through 1inch Aqua. The problem is invoice fraud. An attacker sends a copy of a real invoice with their own bank details and the accounts payable clerk pays it. The FBI's IC3 counted about $2.77B in business email compromise losses in 2024. It works because nothing links the invoice to the account printed on it. In PDFi Plus the merchant's wallet signs the invoice as an EIP-712 SwapVM order, and the money can only go to a vault created for that merchant and invoice number. At settlement our router resolves two ENSv2 names on-chain: acme-demo.eth has to point at the wallet that signed the order, and 1042.invoices.acme-demo.eth has to point at the vault. Edit the PDF and the signature breaks. Sign a new order with your own wallet and the ENS check reverts the payment. The clerk never compares account numbers, because the chain does it at the moment of payment. Paying is one step. In Adobe Acrobat the PDF has a Pay panel: the payer types their PDFi username and password, the PDF submits the form to our backend, and the backend sends the transaction from the payer's CDP server wallet. The payer needs no browser wallet and no ETH for gas. Every PDF also prints a pay link and QR code, so any viewer can pay on the web with a PDFi account or their own wallet. The payment terms live in the order: on a 2/10 net 30 invoice, paying in the first 10 days costs $980 instead of $1,000, and paying late adds 0.1% a day up to 3%, all computed on-chain when the payment lands. An invoice can be paid once. Unpaid invoices are also assets. Each invoice vault has a ClaimToken whose supply equals the face value. A financier ships one Aqua strategy that holds a single USDC balance and lists the claims of every invoice they are willing to buy. When a merchant clicks "Get paid now", the app quotes every strategy on-chain and sells to the best bid. When the customer pays, the financier redeems the full face value from the vault. The price comes from our discount-curve opcode: it rises toward face value as the due date gets closer and never exceeds what the customer would pay early. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia with demo USDC. The live demo has paid and factored invoices you can check on Etherscan.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Foundry, solc 0.8.30, via_ir). We forked 1inch SwapVM v1.0.2 and added three opcodes to the router's instruction table. Opcode 34, _paymentTermsXD, computes the amount due from the invoice terms and the block timestamp and records the payment, so a second fill reverts with AlreadyPaid. Opcode 35, _ensPayeeXD, takes DNS-encoded names from the signed order, finds their resolvers through ENSv2's UniversalResolverV2 and requires addr(merchant name) == order maker, addr(invoice name) == vault, and vault == VaultFactory.vaultOf(maker, invoiceId). Opcode 36, _discountCurveXD, prices ClaimTokens in Aqua mode as min(face x (1 - d), face x e^(-r x t)) with solady's expWad. One router handles both signed-order mode (paying) and Aqua mode (factoring). Opcodes can't read the order's traits or receiver, so the vault binding had to come from CREATE2 in VaultFactory. Fitting three extra opcodes under the EIP-170 size limit took via_ir and optimizer tuning (runs=700). PDFiPlusRouter, VaultFactory, InvoiceVault, ClaimToken and InvoiceLogic are verified on Sepolia Etherscan, and we use the canonical Aqua deployment at 0x1111113CCf1426A8E30e2bfF5E005d929bF6a90a. Aqua. Strategies are immutable and Aqua's safeBalances needs both tokens shipped, so a financier ships [USDC: X, CLAIM_1042: 0, CLAIM_1043: 0, ...]. Listing a new invoice means docking the old strategy and shipping a new one; the financier dashboard does both in one flow. Several financiers shipping strategies over the same claims gives the merchant a set of competing bids, and claim holders redeem pro-rata from the vault once the invoice is paid, late fees included. ENSv2 on Sepolia. Each merchant owns <label>.eth with its own resolver. Under it, invoices.<label>.eth has a separate registry and resolver, and each invoice is registered there with its vault as the addr record plus text records for the canonical order hash and the PDF hash. The backend holds a billing key with roles only on the invoices registry and resolver, so it can publish invoices but can't touch the merchant's main name, and the merchant can revoke it in two transactions. We gave invoices their own resolver because ENSv2 resolver roles apply to the whole resolver. A stolen billing key can break an open invoice by clearing its record, but it can't redirect money, because the opcode also checks the maker and the CREATE2 vault. Invoice names never expire, since an expired name would resolve to nothing and block payment. Backend (Express, TypeScript, MongoDB), carried over from PDFi: Coinbase CDP server wallets on ethereum-sepolia and a parser for the FDF forms Acrobat submits. New for Tokyo: accounts with usernames, scrypt password hashes, per-account and per-IP rate limits, signed sessions and wallet sign-in by signature; invoice publishing through the billing key; and a testnet faucet that gives new accounts gas and demo USDC. The backend generates each PDF with pdf-lib and embeds Acrobat JavaScript that calls submitForm with only the action and the data field. Our SDK (@pdfi-plus/sdk, viem) builds and decodes orders, quotes payments and factoring bids, and finds live strategies from Aqua's shipped and docked events in a single getLogs scan. Frontend: Next.js 15 and Tailwind v4 on Vercel, Dynamic for browser wallets. The backend runs in Docker Compose behind Caddy on an ARM VM and redeploys itself when main changes. The hacky part: of the PDF viewers we tested, only Adobe Acrobat desktop runs the form JavaScript, so the in-PDF payment works there and every PDF also carries a pay link and QR for the web pay page. PDF JavaScript is unsigned, so a tampered PDF could change the submit URL. That is why the pay page, which verifies the merchant's EIP-712 signature and shows the ENS-checked payee, is the primary path, and the in-PDF button is the convenience path for people without a wallet.

Fitting three extra opcodes under the EIP-170 size limit took via_ir and optimizer tuning (runs=700). PDFiPlusRouter, VaultFactory, InvoiceVault, ClaimToken and InvoiceLogic are verified on Sepolia Etherscan, and we use the canonical Aqua deployment at 0x1111113CCf1426A8E30e2bfF5E005d929bF6a90a.

Aqua. Strategies are immutable and Aqua's safeBalances needs both tokens shipped, so a financier ships [USDC: X, CLAIM_1042: 0, CLAIM_1043: 0, ...]. Listing a new invoice means docking the old strategy and shipping a new one; the financier dashboard does both in one flow. Several financiers shipping strategies over the same claims gives the merchant a set of competing bids, and claim holders redeem pro-rata from the vault once the invoice is paid, late fees included.

ENSv2 on Sepolia. Each merchant owns <label>.eth with its own resolver. Under it, invoices.<label>.eth has a separate registry and resolver, and each invoice is registered there with its vault as the addr record plus text records for the canonical order hash and the PDF hash. The backend holds a billing key with roles only on the invoices registry and resolver, so it can publish invoices but can't touch the merchant's main name, and the merchant can revoke it in two transactions. We gave invoices their own resolver because ENSv2 resolver roles apply to the whole resolver. A stolen billing key can break an open invoice by clearing its record, but it can't redirect money, because the opcode also checks the maker and the CREATE2 vault. Invoice names never expire, since an expired name would resolve to nothing and block payment.

Backend (Express, TypeScript, MongoDB), carried over from PDFi: Coinbase CDP server wallets on ethereum-sepolia and a parser for the FDF forms Acrobat submits. New for Tokyo: accounts with usernames, scrypt password hashes, per-account and per-IP rate limits, signed sessions and wallet sign-in by signature; invoice publishing through the billing key; and a testnet faucet that gives new accounts gas and demo USDC. The backend generates each PDF with pdf-lib and embeds Acrobat JavaScript that calls submitForm with only the action and the data field. Our SDK (@pdfi-plus/sdk, viem) builds and decodes orders, quotes payments and factoring bids, and finds live strategies from Aqua's shipped and docked events in a single getLogs scan.

Frontend: Next.js 15 and Tailwind v4 on Vercel, Dynamic for browser wallets. The backend runs in Docker Compose behind Caddy on an ARM VM and redeploys itself when main changes.

The hacky part: of the PDF viewers we tested, only Adobe Acrobat desktop runs the form JavaScript, so the in-PDF payment works there and every PDF also carries a pay link and QR for the web pay page. PDF JavaScript is unsigned, so a tampered PDF could change the submit URL. That is why the pay page, which verifies the merchant's EIP-712 signature and shows the ENS-checked payee, is the primary path, and the in-PDF button is the convenience path for people without a wallet.

projects.title: Plain Safe
projects.description: A local-first, privacy-focused Safe multisig UI with no backend.
projects.project_description: Plain Safe is a static, local-first interface for Safe multisigs. It replaces the hosted transaction service with a direct connection to an RPC chosen by the user. Add or create a Safe, build a transaction, review the exact call and its hashes, collect owner signatures through a link, code, or JSON file, and execute once the threshold is met. A co-signer can open a shared transaction and recompute its hashes and recover its signatures before connecting a wallet or making a network request. The review screen checks the Safe proxy and implementation against known code hashes, decodes calldata, highlights sensitive actions such as owner changes and delegatecalls, and simulates execution where the RPC supports it. It displays the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash, and Safe transaction hash so signers can compare them independently. The app also offers token balances, a local queue, onchain history rebuilt from RPC logs, an offline Verify page, and Uniswap swaps quoted from onchain contracts. There is no backend, analytics, or Safe Transaction Service. An in-app network guard allows the chosen RPC by default, blocks other destinations unless the user enables an explicit capability, and shows every attempted request in a live log. The app can be built as static files and distributed through IPFS.
projects.how_its_made: Plain Safe is a Vite/React/TypeScript static app. viem handles chain reads, Safe transaction hashing, ABI encoding and decoding, and contract calls; wagmi is used only for wallet connection, signing, chain switching, and sending transactions. Effect provides schemas for validating saved records and shared packages and services for RPC-backed work. IndexedDB stores settings, Safes, the transaction queue, and local history. TanStack Query coordinates reads, and wouter handles fragment routes so a compressed transaction package can travel after the URL's # without being sent to the host. We built a network guard that installs before the app and wraps fetch, WebSocket, XMLHttpRequest, EventSource, and sendBeacon. It starts with an empty allowlist, logs allowed and blocked attempts, and permits only configured RPC origins plus capabilities the user enables. Safe authenticity is inferred from the proxy and singleton bytecode hashes rather than trusting VERSION(). Imported packages are schema-checked, all three EIP-712 hashes are recomputed, signatures are recovered, and owners are checked against pinned-block chain state. Safety warnings come from decoded calldata rather than descriptive text. Simulation uses eth_simulateV1 where available and a Safe fallback otherwise. The Uniswap flow reads v3/v4 quotes onchain and builds a transaction, then decodes Universal Router commands for review. A Web Worker scans Safe events backward to reconstruct onchain history without an indexer. Tests cover pure transaction logic and Mainnet integration paths; the release tooling computes a reproducible IPFS CID.

projects.title: Sekisho
projects.description: Sekisho screens AI agent payments before signing and records the evidence behind each decision.
projects.project_description:
AI assistants can buy information and pay for online services, but businesses need control over who those assistants pay. A payment to a scammer or flagged recipient can create financial loss, investigation work and compliance concerns.
Sekisho places a policy checkpoint before an assistant signs an x402 payment. It gathers risk evidence about the other wallet, applies configurable business rules, and returns one of three decisions. ALLOW permits signing, HOLD pauses for review, and BLOCK refuses the payment. Seller-side checks also let a service screen the buyer before accepting payment.
Our browser demonstration follows an assistant purchasing a sample Ethereum-to-Japanese-yen market report for 0.05 test USDC on Base Sepolia. Visitors can run the demonstration without connecting a wallet. We verified both a successful purchase that delivered the report and a flagged purchase that stopped before signing.
Each decision preserves its supporting evidence and records a report fingerprint onchain through Curvegrid MultiBaas. This connects payment enforcement with an inspectable record of why the decision was made.
Sekisho also includes a private review console and escrow contracts. Deposit, clearance, release and refund were tested separately. The complete provider-triggered HOLD-to-escrow journey remains unverified. Sekisho is a working testnet prototype, not a guarantee of wallet safety or a replacement for a complete compliance programme.
projects.how_its_made:
Sekisho combines a Python FastAPI backend, a Python SDK with x402 payment hooks, Solidity contracts, a Next.js operator dashboard and a public browser trial.
The buyer-side hook runs before payment authorization is signed. It calls the backend to screen the recipient and binds the returned decision to the actual recipient, amount, token and network. The seller-side hook screens the payer before payment verification and acceptance. An unreachable gate or unusable Quick Scan response pauses payment rather than being treated as a clean result.
Intercepta supplies live wallet risk scores and traits. We supplement these with onchain sanctions-oracle checks and a bounded source-of-funds trace built from Blockscout transaction data. A deterministic policy engine evaluates the evidence. Language-model explanations are optional and cannot change the verdict. The hosted demonstration runs with the language model disabled.
The backend serializes each decision report into consistent JSON bytes and calculates a Keccak-256 fingerprint. Our ComplianceRegistry contract records the verdict, report fingerprint and policy identifier. Curvegrid MultiBaas provides runtime contract calls, transaction submission, indexed events and authenticated webhook delivery, allowing the Python application to maintain its audit trail without building a separate blockchain indexer. Foundry handles contract deployment and testing.
A separate ComplianceEscrow contract supports conditional release and refunds. Payment receipt verification independently checks the successful transaction and exact USDC transfer before marking a case paid. Recording a decision is therefore distinct from proving settlement.
The website runs on Vercel. A restricted Docker service on Render hosts the public trial with persistent SQLite storage. Server-managed testnet wallets let visitors try the flow without supplying credentials. Persistent spending reservations, request deduplication and fixed purchase limits prevent retries or redeployments from casually creating additional payments.
A useful engineering detail is the separation between mainnet risk research and testnet execution. We read risk evidence from Ethereum and Base mainnet while keeping all demonstration payments and contract writes on Base Sepolia. Reports identify live, cached and unavailable checks, and simulations are labelled separately.
Recorded verification includes 485 Python tests, 18 contract tests and successful hosted paid/refused flows with confirmed attestations and genuine MultiBaas webhook delivery. Claude Code and Codex assisted development under human direction, with development records and AI-use disclosures retained in the repository.

projects.title: IntentLinks
projects.description: Shareable links that give AI agents bounded, revocable spending power — enforced by Sui, not us.
projects.project_description: IntentLink is a link that carries a permission. You write what an AI agent may do with your money in plain English — how much, how often, where, for how long. You get back a shareable link with a QR code. Whoever opens it proves they're a real human, and then plugs in whatever agent they like. The limits aren't enforced by our code, our server, or the agent's good behaviour. They're Move asserts on Sui — nineteen of them, on every single spend. The problem Handing an agent money today means handing over the keys and hoping. "Only spend $50 a day" lives in a prompt. The API key does everything. You find out afterwards, and stopping it means rotating credentials. IntentLink is a valet key instead. The car starts, the boot stays shut — and it isn't a promise, it's the shape of the key. How Sui enforces it Four Move objects. A Vault holds the funds. A Capsule is the permission — key only, no store, so it can't be transferred, sold or wrapped. Access is by field, not ownership: the issuer may revoke, pause or tighten; the recipient may pause or hand back; only the holder address may execute. Every spend passes nineteen asserts: who's asking (3), is it alive (6), recurrence (1), soft caps (3), hard caps (2), scope (3), funds (1). An approved escalation lifts the soft caps and only those — nothing lifts the hard cap, not a permit, not the issuer at 3am, not a compromised backend. The centrepiece is a hot potato. begin_execute hands out the coin and an ExecTicket — a struct with no abilities at all. It can't be stored, copied or discarded, and only settle can destroy it, after checking the proceeds landed on the beneficiary fixed at mint. A transaction holding that ticket is structurally incapable of finishing unless the money goes to the right address. The agent isn't trusted not to skim; a transaction where it skims cannot be built. And because the swap is an ordinary call between those two, any venue works and we're coupled to none. Also on Sui: zkLogin and sponsored transactions, built ourselves — our own salt derivation, prover client and gas station with a reserved coin pool. Users sign in with Google and pay no gas. 43 Move tests, one per assert. How ENS publishes it Every capability is a subname under intentlink.eth, issued programmatically through an ENSv2 PermissionedRegistry. Its text records carry the vault, the capsule, the chain, the status, and il:policy — a hash of the terms. That same hash is written into the Sui object in the same flow. Before acting, the agent resolves the ENS name and halts if the two chains disagree. The recipient's page shows "Verified" only when the hashes match and our stored document matches the capsule field by field — a check on our own server, not just on the chain. Names are ERC-1155, so the tokenId is parsed from the TransferSingle mint event. Records go through a subtree resolver in a multicall, so a name is never half-updated. Reads use ENSIP-10 resolve(). We grant ourselves exactly ROLE_SET_RESOLVER | ROLE_SET_RESOLVER_ADMIN per name using Enhanced Access Control — only bit 24 is documented, so the layout was recovered by probing a fresh name. How World ID vouches for it At redemption, a live human is claiming the link — not a script, not a replayed credential. The load-bearing use is escalation. An agent can ask to exceed its limit; it can never approve. approve_escalation asserts ctx.sender() == capsule.issuer, and the frontend requires a fresh World ID proof whose signal is bound to hash(capsule, amount, nonce) — so a stored credential can't be replayed and a yes to 26 can't be stretched into a yes to 260. Using World sessions, the nullifier is comparable to the one recorded at mint, proving the same human, not just the same account. Every other approval mechanism is a bearer credential — and a bearer credential can be handed to the very agent you're constraining. A live human cannot. Bring your own agent claim() always accepted any address as holder, so a capability can be handed to an agent we didn't write and have never seen. Every permission is also an MCP server. One line of config into Claude Desktop or Cursor, and that assistant gains five tools generated from the capsule: get_permission, quote, execute, request_escalation, get_history. The tool list is scoped to the capsule — that's convenience. Underneath, execute meets the same nineteen asserts — that's the guarantee, and it holds for an agent that read nothing. Verified on testnet: a delegated key holding zero SUI traded 0.01 through MCP, and the same connection asking for 5 SUI was refused with E_OVER_ACTION_CAP, nothing moved. The demo Open Claude Desktop — an AI we didn't write, on someone else's laptop — tell it to spend ten times the limit, and watch Sui refuse it. Then revoke from the dashboard and watch the agent go quiet, because it cannot continue rather than because it agreed to stop. Anyone can build an agent that spends money. We built the part that says no.
projects.how_its_made:
How it's made Stack: Sui Move 2024 · Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) · TypeScript · @mysten/sui v2 over gRPC · viem for Sepolia · World IDKit v4 · Tailwind v4 · OpenAI structured outputs · Vercel with a private Blob store. The contract intentlink.move is ~1,200 lines and leans on Move's linear types rather than runtime checks. Capsule is key with no store, so a permission can't be transferred or wrapped. Permit has no drop, so execute_elevated consuming it by value makes replay unrepresentable rather than merely defended against. ExecTicket has no abilities at all — the hot potato that forces settlement to the beneficiary. One assert path (check_and_charge) is shared by the transfer and swap routes so they can't drift. 43 tests, one per assert. The bug worth admitting: the per-window budget bound nothing. roll_window used window_start_ms == 0 as its "never run" sentinel — and at a genesis-epoch test clock, zero is indistinguishable from unset, so the window silently reset on every call. Switching to windows_used == 0 fixed it. The tests caught it; reading the code hadn't. Sui JSON-RPC is deprecated on public fullnodes, so everything is SuiGrpcClient over GrpcWebFetchTransport, with responses arriving as tagged unions needing unwrapping. Enoki is paid, so we built its three parts ourselves: a salt service (HMAC(secret, iss|aud|sub)), a prover client, and a gas station — a pool of reserved coins so concurrent sponsored transactions don't collide. Users sign in with Google and pay no gas. Three things bit hard: listCoins is cached and returns stale versions. Reserving a gas coin now does a fresh authoritative version read first, or you get provided version doesn't match under any concurrency.
Google emits iss in two valid forms, so one person got two different Sui addresses on alternate sign-ins. A canonicalIss() normaliser fixed it.
getSecretKey() returns bech32, not base64. Round-tripping produced a key that looked fine and signed nothing — the sign-in button silently did nothing. Package upgrades have two traps. An upgrade mints a new package ID for calls while types keep the original, so PACKAGE_ID and PACKAGE_LATEST are separate config. Sharper: a struct introduced by an upgrade is named after the version that declared it. Executed stayed 0x2df6…, but EscalationRequested is 0x095f…. A history query filtered on one package returns a plausible, chronological, entirely incomplete timeline — missing exactly the newest events. It now queries both and merges on digest + event index. We measured DeepBook rather than assuming: SUI_DBUSDC had zero bids on testnet, so selling returned dust. We built a minimal constant-product AMM instead. The capability layer imports no DEX at all — the swap happens between begin_execute and settle, so changing venue is a one-line change. ENS — v2 specifically, on Sepolia Not the legacy registry; the differences are the whole integration. Hierarchical registries. intentlink.eth owns its own PermissionedRegistry, and every capability is minted as a subname inside it via register(label, owner, subregistry, resolver, roleBitmap, expires). Names are issued programmatically at runtime — thousands of them — rather than one vanity registration. Names are ERC-1155 tokens in v2. The tokenId only surfaces in the TransferSingle event, so it's parsed from the receipt to manage that name's roles later. Enhanced Access Control replaces v1's single owner with a role bitmap, and only ROLE_SET_RESOLVER (bit 24) is documented. We registered a throwaway name and probed it to recover the layout: roles sit at every fourth bit (0, 4, 8 … 28), admin at +128. Each capability gets exactly ROLE_SET_RESOLVER | ROLE_SET_RESOLVER_ADMIN — write its records, delegate that, nothing else. The v2 subtree resolver addresses names by DNS wire format, not namehash: setText(bytes dnsName, string, string). That ABI wasn't published usefully, so several were recovered from deployed bytecode. Writes go through multicall so a name is never half-updated — a capability whose il:status said active while il:policy said something else would be worse than no record. Reads use ENSIP-10 resolve(). What the name is for: it publishes il:capsule, il:vault, il:chain, il:status, il:expires, and il:policy — a hash of the canonical terms, written to Ethereum and into the Sui object in the same flow. The agent resolves the name before acting and halts if the two chains disagree. We also tried to freeze a name's records after issuance and found you can't: a subtree resolver authorises from the parent, so revoking write access on one name revokes it across the subtree. Removed rather than shipped as a fake guarantee. World ID v4 is protocol-level, not widget-level. Requests must be RP-signed server-side, and verification is POST /api/v4/verify/{rp_id} on developer.world.org — not the v2 {app_id} endpoint, which cheerfully answers "Action not found" for actions that plainly exist. signal_hash comes back hashed, and we were comparing it to the plaintext signal — which rejected every genuine approval until we hashed with IDKit's own hashSignal and compared hash to hash.
A v4 action allows one verification per human, with no API to raise it. So we mint a fresh action per request — which then makes nullifiers incomparable, since they're scoped to (user, app, action). The fix is World sessions: no action at all, and a session_nullifier stable for one human across every proof, which is what makes "the same human who set the limit approved raising it" checkable.
Bring your own agent, over MCP Each capability is exposed as an MCP server at /api/mcp/[token] — a JSON-RPC handler implementing initialize, tools/list, tools/call. The tool list is generated from the on-chain capsule with live figures, so a connected agent can't see an out-of-scope action. Connection tokens and delegated keys are derived (HMAC(secret, "mcp"|capsuleId)) rather than stored — surviving restarts without a table that can fall out of step, with constant-time comparison. Delegated agents hold zero SUI; their transactions are sponsored, because "fund this address before your agent can act" would undo the point of pasting one line of config. Deployment The intent store began as a JSON file. On Vercel that's fatal twice: the filesystem is read-only outside /tmp, and /tmp is per-instance — so a mint wrote to one lambda and the next click read an empty disk on another. Links 404'd while the capability was live on chain. It's now a private Blob (these records hold salts and emails; an unguessable public URL is a bet, not privacy), with a 2s cache collapsing repeated reads. Then the Git integration built the repository root, which has no Next app, reported Ready in five seconds, took the alias and 404'd everything. Setting rootDirectory via the Vercel API fixed it — and we pushed an empty commit specifically to prove a push no longer takes the site down. The NL compiler Intents are written in English and compiled with OpenAI structured outputs, each clause classified enforced / advisory / refused before anything is minted. The model kept inventing objections — reciting every limitation it had been briefed on, asked for or not — so a grounding filter keeps only clauses with real word-overlap against what the person actually typed.

Verified on testnet: a delegated key holding zero SUI traded 0.01 through MCP, and the same connection asking for 5 SUI was refused with E_OVER_ACTION_CAP, nothing moved.

The demo

Open Claude Desktop — an AI we didn't write, on someone else's laptop — tell it to spend ten times the limit, and watch Sui refuse it. Then revoke from the dashboard and watch the agent go quiet, because it cannot continue rather than because it agreed to stop.

Anyone can build an agent that spends money. We built the part that says no.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
How it's made

Stack: Sui Move 2024 · Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) · TypeScript · @mysten/sui v2 over gRPC · viem for Sepolia · World IDKit v4 · Tailwind v4 · OpenAI structured outputs · Vercel with a private Blob store.

The contract

intentlink.move is ~1,200 lines and leans on Move's linear types rather than runtime checks. Capsule is key with no store, so a permission can't be transferred or wrapped. Permit has no drop, so execute_elevated consuming it by value makes replay unrepresentable rather than merely defended against. ExecTicket has no abilities at all — the hot potato that forces settlement to the beneficiary. One assert path (check_and_charge) is shared by the transfer and swap routes so they can't drift. 43 tests, one per assert.

The bug worth admitting: the per-window budget bound nothing. roll_window used window_start_ms == 0 as its "never run" sentinel — and at a genesis-epoch test clock, zero is indistinguishable from unset, so the window silently reset on every call. Switching to windows_used == 0 fixed it. The tests caught it; reading the code hadn't.

Sui

JSON-RPC is deprecated on public fullnodes, so everything is SuiGrpcClient over GrpcWebFetchTransport, with responses arriving as tagged unions needing unwrapping.

Enoki is paid, so we built its three parts ourselves: a salt service (HMAC(secret, iss|aud|sub)), a prover client, and a gas station — a pool of reserved coins so concurrent sponsored transactions don't collide. Users sign in with Google and pay no gas.

Three things bit hard:

listCoins is cached and returns stale versions. Reserving a gas coin now does a fresh authoritative version read first, or you get provided version doesn't match under any concurrency.
Google emits iss in two valid forms, so one person got two different Sui addresses on alternate sign-ins. A canonicalIss() normaliser fixed it.
getSecretKey() returns bech32, not base64. Round-tripping produced a key that looked fine and signed nothing — the sign-in button silently did nothing.

Package upgrades have two traps. An upgrade mints a new package ID for calls while types keep the original, so PACKAGE_ID and PACKAGE_LATEST are separate config. Sharper: a struct introduced by an upgrade is named after the version that declared it. Executed stayed 0x2df6…, but EscalationRequested is 0x095f…. A history query filtered on one package returns a plausible, chronological, entirely incomplete timeline — missing exactly the newest events. It now queries both and merges on digest + event index.

We measured DeepBook rather than assuming: SUI_DBUSDC had zero bids on testnet, so selling returned dust. We built a minimal constant-product AMM instead. The capability layer imports no DEX at all — the swap happens between begin_execute and settle, so changing venue is a one-line change.

ENS — v2 specifically, on Sepolia

Not the legacy registry; the differences are the whole integration.

Hierarchical registries. intentlink.eth owns its own PermissionedRegistry, and every capability is minted as a subname inside it via register(label, owner, subregistry, resolver, roleBitmap, expires). Names are issued programmatically at runtime — thousands of them — rather than one vanity registration.

Names are ERC-1155 tokens in v2. The tokenId only surfaces in the TransferSingle event, so it's parsed from the receipt to manage that name's roles later.

Enhanced Access Control replaces v1's single owner with a role bitmap, and only ROLE_SET_RESOLVER (bit 24) is documented. We registered a throwaway name and probed it to recover the layout: roles sit at every fourth bit (0, 4, 8 … 28), admin at +128. Each capability gets exactly ROLE_SET_RESOLVER | ROLE_SET_RESOLVER_ADMIN — write its records, delegate that, nothing else.

The v2 subtree resolver addresses names by DNS wire format, not namehash: setText(bytes dnsName, string, string). That ABI wasn't published usefully, so several were recovered from deployed bytecode. Writes go through multicall so a name is never half-updated — a capability whose il:status said active while il:policy said something else would be worse than no record. Reads use ENSIP-10 resolve().

What the name is for: it publishes il:capsule, il:vault, il:chain, il:status, il:expires, and il:policy — a hash of the canonical terms, written to Ethereum and into the Sui object in the same flow. The agent resolves the name before acting and halts if the two chains disagree.

We also tried to freeze a name's records after issuance and found you can't: a subtree resolver authorises from the parent, so revoking write access on one name revokes it across the subtree. Removed rather than shipped as a fake guarantee.

World ID

v4 is protocol-level, not widget-level. Requests must be RP-signed server-side, and verification is POST /api/v4/verify/{rp_id} on developer.world.org — not the v2 {app_id} endpoint, which cheerfully answers "Action not found" for actions that plainly exist.

signal_hash comes back hashed, and we were comparing it to the plaintext signal — which rejected every genuine approval until we hashed with IDKit's own hashSignal and compared hash to hash.
A v4 action allows one verification per human, with no API to raise it. So we mint a fresh action per request — which then makes nullifiers incomparable, since they're scoped to (user, app, action). The fix is World sessions: no action at all, and a session_nullifier stable for one human across every proof, which is what makes "the same human who set the limit approved raising it" checkable.
Bring your own agent, over MCP

Each capability is exposed as an MCP server at /api/mcp/[token] — a JSON-RPC handler implementing initialize, tools/list, tools/call. The tool list is generated from the on-chain capsule with live figures, so a connected agent can't see an out-of-scope action.

Connection tokens and delegated keys are derived (HMAC(secret, "mcp"|capsuleId)) rather than stored — surviving restarts without a table that can fall out of step, with constant-time comparison. Delegated agents hold zero SUI; their transactions are sponsored, because "fund this address before your agent can act" would undo the point of pasting one line of config.

Deployment

The intent store began as a JSON file. On Vercel that's fatal twice: the filesystem is read-only outside /tmp, and /tmp is per-instance — so a mint wrote to one lambda and the next click read an empty disk on another. Links 404'd while the capability was live on chain. It's now a private Blob (these records hold salts and emails; an unguessable public URL is a bet, not privacy), with a 2s cache collapsing repeated reads.

Then the Git integration built the repository root, which has no Next app, reported Ready in five seconds, took the alias and 404'd everything. Setting rootDirectory via the Vercel API fixed it — and we pushed an empty commit specifically to prove a push no longer takes the site down.

The NL compiler

Intents are written in English and compiled with OpenAI structured outputs, each clause classified enforced / advisory / refused before anything is minted. The model kept inventing objections — reciting every limitation it had been briefed on, asked for or not — so a grounding filter keeps only clauses with real word-overlap against what the person actually typed.

projects.title: travely
projects.description: Live multimodal travel tracking with gas-sponsored USDC delay insurance on Sui.
projects.project_description: Travely brings flights, trains, coaches, and ferries into one calm, live travel timeline. Travelers can follow departure times, delays, gates, weather risks, connections, and vehicle details from a single mobile app. For supported flights, Travely also offers delay insurance with clear thresholds from 30 minutes to 6 hours or more. Users pay premiums in testnet USDC, while Travely sponsors the Sui network fees. Once the final arrival time is verified, eligible payouts can be claimed directly. Completed journeys are transformed into a visual travel passport with shareable stamps.
projects.how_its_made: Travely’s insurance system is built directly on Sui using a Move smart contract and Sui’s object model. Every delay threshold is represented by an onchain shared market backed by testnet USDC liquidity. Purchases create owned position objects for the traveler, while the contract calculates premiums, applies service and settlement fees, tracks reserves, and prevents payouts beyond available liquidity. Each market is cryptographically tied to a specific flight identity, including its operator, flight number, route, service date, and scheduled times. A protected ResolverCap authorizes resolution using the reviewed final arrival time. The contract then determines whether the selected delay threshold was reached, supports cancellation refunds, and lets winning travelers claim their USDC payout onchain. The Expo mobile app integrates Sui through the TypeScript SDK. Enoki zkLogin turns a familiar Google or Apple login into a Sui account without requiring a seed phrase. For every purchase or claim, the Bun and Hono proxy prepares a transaction, the user signs it with their zkLogin credentials, and Enoki sponsors the gas before submission to Sui testnet. Users therefore interact with real onchain markets and native testnet USDC without needing to hold SUI for network fees. Every confirmed action exposes its transaction digest and links directly to the Sui explorer for verification

projects.project_description_markdown:
CROSSPERMIT
One signature. Every chain. Nothing bridged.

An allowance isn't money. It's a number in a token's storage that says "this
spender may pull this much from me," and that number lives on one chain only.
Permit2 made granting it gasless, but a Permit2 signature can't leave its
chain: the EIP-712 domain includes chainId, so a signature valid on Base is
invalid on Arbitrum. Four chains means four signatures.

CrossPermit makes the permission portable. One signed message sets allowances
on many chains. Each chain keeps its own ledger, but a single signature
authorises all of them. No token moves and nothing is bridged. Bridges solve
"my money is on the wrong chain." CrossPermit solves "my authority is on the
wrong chain."


WHO NEEDS THIS
--------------

Funds managing client capital on-chain face two constraints that pull against
each other. They can't take custody, because the client's tokens must stay in
the client's wallet. And they can't ask for a signature per chain per
rebalance, because every wallet prompt adds friction, approval risk and
another audit line.

Today a four-chain move takes four signatures, four wallet sessions, and four
audit records that a risk committee has to trust describe one decision.

With CrossPermit it takes one signature and produces one audit record. The
desk never touches the tokens.


HOW ONE SIGNATURE TRAVELS
-------------------------

1. Pin the domain. Set chainId = 1 everywhere, so the digest names no chain.
   verifyingContract stays in the domain, so the contract address must be
   identical on every chain.

2. Prove the address. The ERC-2470 singleton factory gives the same address
   on every chain for the same init code and salt.

3. Merkle the rest. Each chain's permit bundle becomes a leaf, and the user
   signs the root. Anyone can submit a chain's bundle with its proof.
   CrossPermit rebuilds the root, recovers the signer and applies the bundle.
   No chain can apply another chain's leaf. Revocation works the same way:
   one signed LOCK covers every chain.

The test: Optimism Sepolia was added after the first two chains were live.
With the same salt, CrossPermit landed at the same address and returned a
byte-identical DOMAIN_SEPARATOR, with zero coordination.

  DOMAIN_SEPARATOR()
  0x4ce820a58ffb00fe1b6cb52f083bdd1cfd176732c34db34a84517668750aa5e4

It's identical on all three chains. Read it yourself.


LIVE TODAY
----------

One 65-byte signature goes to a relayer, which fans it out to Ethereum
Sepolia, Base Sepolia and Optimism Sepolia from a single HTTP request. A
Uniswap Universal Router deployed with permit2 := CrossPermit then spends the
allowance, including a real v4 swap on each chain.

The desk flow is:
  add a client -> send one link -> they sign once -> you allocate

  TRADE
    What it proves: v4 swap through the Universal Router's real V4_SWAP
                    settle path
    Status:         Live, 3 testnets

  INVEST
    What it proves: v4 LP position funded by CrossPermit.transferFrom, held
                    in the client's name
    Status:         Live, 3 testnets

  EARN
    What it proves: 10,000 USDC in, 10,032.65 out after 30 days on Aave v4
                    Core Hub
    Status:         Mainnet fork

  HOLD RWAs
    What it proves: Compliance-gated equity desk reading Ondo's live NVDAon
    Status:         Mainnet fork, venue mocked

Before the wallet opens, the client sees every per-chain grant in plain
language. That includes allowances already outstanding, so the grant is never
understated. The client can leave at any time: one signature locks the desk
on every chain, and a spend that worked a second earlier reverts.


WHY A RISK COMMITTEE SIGNS OFF
------------------------------

Every grant, lock and burned salt is a decoded row in MultiBaas. The
dashboard shows four sources side by side and never merges them:

  - Chain storage: what the allowance is now.
  - MultiBaas: how it got there, including grants that have lapsed.
  - PoolManager extsload: what the venue holds.
  - The desk's own records: what was requested. These are never treated as
    proof that anything was granted.

Where the sources disagree, the dashboard shows the disagreement. Any spender
that isn't the router or the liquidity desk is flagged.


WHY NOW
-------

v4 made the venue programmable, and the Universal Router made settlement
uniform. The remaining barrier to one-click multichain allocation is the
number of signatures. Removing it requires no change to the router's payment
path, only a router deployed with permit2 := CrossPermit.


LIVE
----

Chains:     Ethereum Sepolia, Base Sepolia, Optimism Sepolia
Salt:       keccak256("CrossPermit v1")
Compiler:   solc 0.8.27, optimizer 1e6 runs
