CROSSPERMIT - ONE SIGNATURE, EVERY CHAIN
========================================

A Permit2 signature is locked to one chain because its EIP-712 domain
includes block.chainid. CrossPermit removes that lock without making the
signature replayable across chains.


HOW IT WORKS
------------

1. Pin the domain.
   contracts/src/lib/EIP712.sol is OpenZeppelin's EIP712 with one change:

     uint256 private constant CROSS_CHAIN_ID = 1;   // not block.chainid

   The domain still includes verifyingContract, so the separator only
   matches if the address matches. ERC-2470 guarantees that: same init code
   + same salt = same address on every chain. Both halves are needed.

     DOMAIN_SEPARATOR()
     0x4ce820a58ffb00fe1b6cb52f083bdd1cfd176732c34db34a84517668750aa5e4
     (identical on all three live deployments)

2. One bundle per chain, one leaf per bundle.
   Each bundle is a list of entries: grant, decrease, lock, unlock, or
   transfer. The chain id is hashed inside the leaf, and the contract also
   reverts with WrongChainId if it doesn't match block.chainid. That makes
   two independent guards at the one place a mix-up would be silent.

3. Leaves are computed by the client. Always.
   The SDK hashes leaves locally. The on-chain hashChainPermits is called
   only to assert equality. If the leaf came from an RPC, a hostile endpoint
   could make the user sign a bundle they never saw.

4. Leaves fold into a Merkle root.
   Pairs use OpenZeppelin sorted-pair hashing, so client and contract fold
   identically. The tree is left-leaning, so the last leaf has a one-element
   proof. Put the most expensive chain last and it pays the least gas.

5. The user signs the root once.

     CrossPermit(address owner,bytes32 salt,uint48 deadline,
                 uint48 timestamp,bytes32 merkleRoot)

   No chain id appears here, so the digest is byte-identical everywhere.
   One wallet prompt, one 65-byte signature.

6. Each chain redeems only its own leaf.
   Anyone submits a chain's bundle plus its proof. The contract rebuilds the
   leaf, the root and the digest, then recovers the signer. A wrong bundle
   recovers to the wrong signer, so nothing needs checking separately.
   Submission is permissionless because the bundle only moves the signer's
   own tokens.

7. Replay protection is per chain.
   Each salt is burned in per-chain storage, so an intent applies exactly
   once on each chain. deadline bounds validity. timestamp orders competing
   intents.

8. Revocation has the same shape.
   One signed cancel root burns the salt on every chain. One signed LOCK
   disables a spender on every chain.

Remove any piece and the scheme breaks:
  - pinned chainId        makes the digest portable
  - CREATE2 address       makes the domain portable
  - Merkle root           lets one digest carry different grants per chain
  - chain id in the leaf  stops grants being swapped between chains
  - client-side leaf      stops an RPC choosing what the user signs


THE STACK
---------

Contracts (Solidity 0.8.27, Foundry)
  CrossPermit.sol's transferFrom overloads are selector-identical to
  Permit2's. The Universal Router's payment path is untouched; only the
  PERMIT2 immutable changes at construction. Because it has no getter, the
  swap is confirmed three ways: deploy log, broadcast constructor args, and
  the CrossPermit address appearing at all four use sites in each router's
  runtime bytecode.
  Also included: LiquidityDesk.sol (v4 adapter), YieldRouter.sol (Aave v4),
  and EquityDesk.sol (compliance gate that defaults to deny).

SDK (TypeScript + viem)
  Builds bundles, computes leaves, folds the tree, signs, and cancels.

Relayer (Bun)
  One POST fans out to N chains. It simulates before every broadcast and
  streams per-chain status over SSE. It can pay gas and refuse to submit. It
  cannot change a recipient, spender or amount. Every flow still works
  without it.

Web (Next.js, wagmi/viem, Reown AppKit)
  A multi-manager desk, one screen per client, and mandate links that can't
  be double-claimed. Pool state is read directly from the v4 PoolManager.

MultiBaas (control plane)
  Every Permit is a decoded row. It also provides the allowance ledger feed,
  audit trail, address aliases and custody signer. docs/multibaas.md
  explains each feature used or skipped.


DECISIONS WORTH NAMING
----------------------

Timestamps are signed behind wall clock.
  Head blocks lag by seconds, so signing with Date.now() fails on slow
  chains and never on fast ones. A constant TIMESTAMP_LAG fixes it without
  changing the order of intents.

LiquidityDesk can put tokens in but never take them out.
  Anyone can call add, but only for an owner who signed a writ naming the
  desk, and only into the pool. remove and collect are msg.sender-scoped.

Unichain Sepolia was dropped.
  MultiBaas doesn't support it, and a chain without an audit trail isn't one
  this product can stand on.


TESTING
-------

  - Fuzzes leafOf and the Merkle builder against the contract for 1-32
    leaves.
  - Invariants: an allowance never exceeds what was signed, a LOCK cannot be
    bypassed by any ordering, and a bundle never applies twice on one chain.
  - Fork tests: real v4 swaps on three testnets, the full LiquidityDesk
    sequence including what it must not be able to do, and Aave v4 + NVDAon
    on mainnet.
  - Live runs: lifecycle.ts covers eight real state transitions on testnets,
    and onboard.ts runs twenty-two checks on the mandate loop.

projects.title: Sworn
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 router that makes the quote and the trade the same transaction, so hooks can't lie.
projects.project_description: A Uniswap v4 hook is arbitrary code that runs inside PoolManager.swap. It sees tx.gasprice, tx.origin and block.coinbase, all of which differ between an eth_call quote and a real transaction. So a hook can be honest to every quoting engine that exists and dishonest to the person paying, and the cost to build one is a single modifier. In September 2026, 0x published "Uniswap v4 hooks were a mistake": 84,163 hooks analysed, 54.2% malicious. Hayden Adams replied "skill issue, don't route to bad hooks". He is right. The question that leaves open is the one an integrator actually faces: how do you know which ones are bad, at the moment you route? Sworn answers it by measuring first and then closing the gap. I indexed every v4 pool on four chains from Initialize logs, 15.7 million pools, then re-quoted a uniform random sample of 10,000 Base fills against the state immediately before each one. 4 of the 25 hooks with enough fills to classify charge more than they quote, and 849,451 swaps reached them, through UniversalRouter, through 0x, through everything. Roughly half of all charged fills are measurement error, estimated from the fills that measured as over-delivered, which a hook cannot do. That noise floor is subtracted before any hook is named. Two findings came out of that. PoolManager emits Swap before afterSwap, so the event that every v4 indexer and hook-scoring tool is built on structurally under-reports the hooks that take the most. And detection does not work: static bytecode analysis, differential eth_call and trace analysis each scored zero recall against ground truth. Only re-quoting settled trades caught anything, and that runs after someone has already been underpaid. So Sworn does not detect. SwornRouter takes the v4 lock, runs every candidate route for real, reverts each probe so state and transient storage roll back, executes the best, and asserts executedDelta == probed[chosen]. A hook that lies makes those two disagree and the trade does not happen. Against a live Base hook at block 51,247,545 that prices two callers 707 bps apart for the identical swap, Sworn probed, saw the real offer, and settled elsewhere for 672 bps more. That hook was one this repo's own offline pipeline had not flagged, which is the strongest argument in the project: a score is retrospective and lossy, a probe is neither.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts. Solidity 0.8.26 under Foundry, via-IR, optimizer_runs = 44444444 and evm_version = cancun to match v4-core exactly; at lower settings the Yul optimizer cannot clear v4's stack pressure. SwornRouter is IUnlockCallback, so it is periphery, not a hook, with no mined permission bits. The probe isolation is the part worth calling out. For a hook to cheat Sworn it would have to answer the probe honestly and the execution dishonestly, which means telling them apart. Probe and execution go through the same external self-call, and the probing flag is only read after the last externally observable call, so msg.sender, call depth and calldata shape are identical. Probes are forced to revert (ProbeMustRevert), which is what rolls their state back, including EIP-1153 transient storage, which does not survive a revert either. Both get an identical gas stipend, enforced against EIP-150's 63/64 rule, so gasleft() leaks nothing. tx.gasprice and block.* are free because it is all one transaction. Measurement. Python over debug_traceTransaction, with pandas and pyarrow parquet compaction across 28 million indexed rows. Recovering what a swap actually did means decoding the swap() calldata out of the trace rather than reading the Swap event, because of the emission-order defect. Amounts are stored as strings: v4 deltas exceed 2^63 and parquet has no int128. Provenance. Every result file carries meta.snapshots[] with a sha256 of its input and the commit that produced it. The README is generated from a template where {{result:divergence.json:totals.divergent_hooks}} resolves at build time, and verify_readme_numbers.py fails CI on any hand-typed digit. The diagrams, the banner and the social image are SVG generated from the same result files. Testing. Twelve attacker capabilities from the threat model, each with a working hook fixture in ToxicHooks.sol that tries the attack and fails, plus fork tests pinned to real Base and BNB blocks against hooks nobody in this repo wrote. Rest of the stack. A Next.js 15 static export that reads the committed result files at build time, so the dashboard and the README cannot disagree. A viem SDK, buildSwornCall, that turns an existing quote into router calldata, so an integrator adopts this by changing the call they already make rather than rewriting their router. And EIP-712-signed hook scores written on-chain to HookBook on Base Sepolia by a scheduled attestor: signed rather than sent, so anyone can relay an attestation and pay the gas for it. HookBook returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA for a hook nobody has measured, never a clean zero, because a registry that reports absence as safety is worse than no registry.

projects.title: Surety
projects.description: Insurance for AI agents you trust with money: if one gets tricked, you're paid back the same day
projects.project_description: Surety is parametric, on-chain insurance for AI agents that handle money. The problem: AI agents now hold wallets and pay, trade and settle on people's behalf. When one is manipulated, the loss has no backstop. In May 2026 a single Morse-coded message tricked Grok's Bankr agent into sending roughly $150–200K. If you use a company's trading or payments agent and it gets tricked, no product covers you, and standard insurance policies have started excluding AI losses (the ISO endorsements from Jan 1, 2026). Worse, the agent's own signature proves nothing, because the agent's key is exactly what gets compromised. What Surety does: enforce where you can, insure what gets through. The policy is an ENS name. Buying cover mints a non-transferable ENSv2 subname such as payments2.surety.eth, with its own PermissionedResolver. Its text records are the rules: per-transaction cap, counterparty allowlist, coverage, tier and status, so anyone can read and verify them. Enhanced Access Control lets the agent's key update only its own "streak" record. The rules are enforced by a Uniswap v4 hook. The agent spends from an AgentVault. Every swap goes through our SuretyHook, whose beforeSwap reverts any trade over the cap or to a counterparty not on the allowlist, before any money moves. Violations are recorded and recomputable. Plain transfers can't be blocked, so they're recorded. A ViolationOracle recomputes "over the cap" or "off the allowlist" from public data alone. There's no adjuster and no judgement call. Payouts need a fresh human. To get paid, the policyholder files a claim and passes a fresh World ID for Agents check, bound to the same human who bought the policy. Our backend validates it and signs a one-time EIP-712 approval that the contracts verify. If the check is cancelled or fails, the claim is held and never paid. IDKit also ensures one policyholder per unique human. Paid the same day from the hook's reserve. Claims pay out only from a liquid reserve held inside the Uniswap hook, which must stay at 2× total coverage. Payouts go only to the address fixed at purchase, never to the agent or the attacker, and each violation can be claimed only once. Part of each premium is deployed as pool liquidity so backers earn fees. Pricing is a live, credibility-weighted formula: tighter rules mean a cheaper tier, and clean streaks earn discounts. The premium is computed in front of the buyer. A real AI agent, really attacked. We built a live payments agent (a Groq-hosted LLM with its own key) that reads its rules from its ENS name and can pay and swap. In our Live Attack demo, an attacker emails the agent's public inbox, impersonating the policyholder. The model really falls for it: its swap to the attacker is blocked by the Uniswap hook, it falls back to a direct transfer that gets through, the violation is detected on-chain, and the policyholder is repaid after a fresh World ID check. None of it is scripted. Everything is live on Ethereum Sepolia: the contracts, including PolicyRegistry, AgentVault, SuretyHook, ViolationOracle, WorldIdGate, ClaimRouter and PremiumYieldVault; the real ENSv2 name surety.eth and its subnames; a Uniswap v4 pool with our hook; World ID for Agents and IDKit in production mode. The web app covers agent profiles, buying cover, a dashboard, a public feed, a live attack page, a scripted replay and a pitch deck

Surety is parametric, on-chain insurance for AI agents that handle money.

The problem: AI agents now hold wallets and pay, trade and settle on people's behalf. When one is manipulated, the loss has no backstop. In May 2026 a single Morse-coded message tricked Grok's Bankr agent into sending roughly $150–200K. If you use a company's trading or payments agent and it gets tricked, no product covers you, and standard insurance policies have started excluding AI losses (the ISO endorsements from Jan 1, 2026). 1. The policy is an ENS name. Buying cover mints a non-transferable ENSv2 subname such as payments2.surety.eth, with its own PermissionedResolver. 3. Violations are recorded and recomputable. Plain transfers can't be blocked, so they're recorded. A ViolationOracle recomputes "over the cap" or "off the allowlist" from public data alone. There's no adjuster and no judgement call.
4. Payouts need a fresh human. To get paid, the policyholder files a claim and passes a fresh World ID for Agents check, bound to the same human who bought the policy. Our backend validates it and signs a one-time EIP-712 approval that the contracts verify. If the check is cancelled or fails, the claim is held and never paid. Payouts go only to the address fixed at purchase, never to the agent or the attacker, and each violation can be claimed only once. projects.title: Tegata
projects.description: Invoices tokenized and sold for JPYC on Uniswap v4, priced on the debtor's credit curve.
projects.project_description: Japan is phasing out paper promissory notes (手形). Most banks stop issuing them after September 30, 2026, and since January 2026 companies can no longer pay subcontractors with them. Small suppliers lose their usual way to get paid early, and factoring fees are often not disclosed. Tegata puts that flow on-chain. A supplier registers an invoice. The debtor accepts it, which mints tokens equal to the face value (1 token = ¥1). The supplier can sell those tokens for JPYC right away in a Uniswap v4 pool. At maturity the debtor pays in JPYC and holders redeem 1:1. If the invoice is still unpaid 3 days after maturity, anyone can mark it defaulted, and holders get a pro-rata share of what was paid plus the debtor's seized collateral. Nobody negotiates the price. A Uniswap v4 hook keeps every trade within 2% of a fair-value curve set by the debtor's credit: an operator grade plus its on-chain payment history. A downgrade or a default reprices all of that debtor's invoices at once. Unrated debtors are priced at the weakest grade and must lock 20% collateral before they can accept an invoice. The same PDF can't be financed twice by the same supplier and debtor. The dashboard has an AI operations desk that runs Claude Code with read-only tools over the live contracts, so an operator can ask which invoice needs attention and get an answer from real chain data.
projects.how_its_made: Japanese invoice becomes an ERC-20 when the buyer approves it. InvoiceRegistry deploys a fresh token when the supplier registers an invoice, then mints 1 token per ¥1 of face value to the supplier once the buyer approves. Each document hash is stored, so the same invoice can't be financed twice. Those tokens trade in Uniswap v4 pools guarded by our hook, MaturityCurveHook, on beforeInitialize, beforeSwap and afterSwap. The registry publishes a fair-value curve for each invoice: face value discounted at the buyer's current rate, rising to 1.00 at maturity. A pool has to open on that curve. Trading closes one day before maturity. Every swap must end within 2% of the curve, or move the price back toward it. So a supplier can't be dumped on at a predatory discount, and nobody can pump an invoice above what it will pay out. Uniswap v4 reads a hook's permissions from its address bits, so the deploy script uses HookMiner to find a CREATE2 salt that gives the right address. TegataMarket adds bid ladders and buy/sell helpers with slippage limits. Uniswap's own Universal Router works on the same pools, because the hook applies to every swap no matter who routes it. CreditRiskModel prices each buyer: base rate plus a grade spread, plus penalties for late payments and defaults, minus credit for on-time payments and posted collateral. New companies with no rating are priced as the worst grade and have to lock 20% collateral before they can approve an invoice. CollateralVault keeps the part of that collateral that backs unpaid invoices locked, pays APR on it from a reward pool the operator funds, and gives it to token holders if the buyer defaults. Everything settles in real JPYC on Sepolia, from JPYC Inc.'s faucet. Curvegrid MultiBaas does the indexing. Each contract is linked under a named alias. The receivables book and an event explorer page read everything through Event Queries, never by scanning logs over RPC. Queries return at most 50 rows, so we page through them. Operator actions (rating buyers, setting collateral APR, freezing an invoice) are built by MultiBaas, signed locally with the operator key, and submitted back through it. A webhook receiver checks the MultiBaas HMAC signature and links each new invoice token as it's registered. The frontend is React, Vite and viem on Vercel. The MultiBaas API key never reaches the browser. Queries go through a small Vercel function that only allows read-only Event Queries. World ID Selfie Check signs its requests on the server too, and the verified score caps how much of an invoice a consumer can sell early. projects.project_description_markdown:
Japan is phasing out paper promissory notes (手形). Most banks stop issuing them after September 30, 2026, and since January 2026 companies can no longer pay subcontractors with them. Small suppliers lose their usual way to get paid early, and factoring fees are often not disclosed.

Tegata puts that flow on-chain. A supplier registers an invoice. The debtor accepts it, which mints tokens equal to the face value (1 token = ¥1). The supplier can sell those tokens for JPYC right away in a Uniswap v4 pool. At maturity the debtor pays in JPYC and holders redeem 1:1. If the invoice is still unpaid 3 days after maturity, anyone can mark it defaulted, and holders get a pro-rata share of what was paid plus the debtor's seized collateral.

Nobody negotiates the price. A Uniswap v4 hook keeps every trade within 2% of a fair-value curve set by the debtor's credit: an operator grade plus its on-chain payment history. A downgrade or a default reprices all of that debtor's invoices at once. Unrated debtors are priced at the weakest grade and must lock 20% collateral before they can accept an invoice. The same PDF can't be financed twice by the same supplier and debtor.

The dashboard has an AI operations desk that runs Claude Code with read-only tools over the live contracts, so an operator can ask which invoice needs attention and get an answer from real chain data.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Japanese invoice becomes an ERC-20 when the buyer approves it. InvoiceRegistry deploys a fresh token when the supplier registers an invoice, then mints 1 token per ¥1 of face value to the supplier once the buyer approves. Each document hash is stored, so the same invoice can't be financed twice.

Those tokens trade in Uniswap v4 pools guarded by our hook, MaturityCurveHook, on beforeInitialize, beforeSwap and afterSwap. The registry publishes a fair-value curve for each invoice: face value discounted at the buyer's current rate, rising to 1.00 at maturity. A pool has to open on that curve. Trading closes one day before maturity. Every swap must end within 2% of the curve, or move the price back toward it. So a supplier can't be dumped on at a predatory discount, and nobody can pump an invoice above what it will pay out. Uniswap v4 reads a hook's permissions from its address bits, so the deploy script uses HookMiner to find a CREATE2 salt that gives the right address. TegataMarket adds bid ladders and buy/sell helpers with slippage limits. Uniswap's own Universal Router works on the same pools, because the hook applies to every swap no matter who routes it.

CreditRiskModel prices each buyer: base rate plus a grade spread, plus penalties for late payments and defaults, minus credit for on-time payments and posted collateral. New companies with no rating are priced as the worst grade and have to lock 20% collateral before they can approve an invoice. CollateralVault keeps the part of that collateral that backs unpaid invoices locked, pays APR on it from a reward pool the operator funds, and gives it to token holders if the buyer defaults. Everything settles in real JPYC on Sepolia, from JPYC Inc.'s faucet.

Curvegrid MultiBaas does the indexing. Each contract is linked under a named alias. The receivables book and an event explorer page read everything through Event Queries, never by scanning logs over RPC. Queries return at most 50 rows, so we page through them. Operator actions (rating buyers, setting collateral APR, freezing an invoice) are built by MultiBaas, signed locally with the operator key, and submitted back through it. A webhook receiver checks the MultiBaas HMAC signature and links each new invoice token as it's registered.

The frontend is React, Vite and viem on Vercel. The MultiBaas API key never reaches the browser. Queries go through a small Vercel function that only allows read-only Event Queries. World ID Selfie Check signs its requests on the server too, and the verified score caps how much of an invoice a consumer can sell early. Public Sepolia RPCs kept rate-limiting us, so reads batch through multicall with fallback across three providers.

The AI ops desk runs the Claude Code CLI with an MCP server we wrote, which exposes four read-only chain queries. File access, the shell and the user's other connectors are all switched off, and it runs outside the repo, so it can't read our .env. It suggests actions, but every transaction still goes through the user's wallet. Replies stream to the browser as server-sent events.

The contracts are Solidity 0.8.26 with Foundry, covered by 94 tests. One suite is adversarial: we tried to break our own contracts, fixed what broke, and left tests that document the attacks still possible. Another runs on a fork of Sepolia against the real PoolManager, Universal Router and JPYC.

projects.title: GuardPay
projects.description: Treasury agent that screens every x402 invoice payment with Intercepta; big ones need World ID
projects.project_description: GuardPay is an autonomous treasury agent that pays tokenized supplier invoices over x402 on Base, with graduated trust for every payment. Agents that move money are a new attack surface: swapped payout addresses, fake invoices, sanctioned counterparties, or a prompt-injected agent that signs whatever it is told. An agent that pays everything is a liability; one that asks a human about everything is useless. How it works: a supplier issues an invoice as an NFT on Base Sepolia, naming our company as the payer. The agent detects the InvoiceIssued event, calls the supplier's x402 endpoint to get the 402 quote, and signs the EIP-3009 USDC authorization but keeps it in memory. Before anything is sent, it screens the payee address, the token and the signed authorization with the Intercepta API. A policy engine then decides: small and clean: PAY automatically flagged or sanctioned payee: REFUSE (the signature is never sent) large or on hold: ESCALATE to a fresh World ID for Agents approval from an Orb-verified human, validated on our backend denied, expired or cancelled: NOT PAID Once paid, the facilitator settles USDC and the agent marks the invoice NFT paid with the settlement tx hash. Every decision, with its verdict, reason, approval and transaction, is shown on a live dashboard that animates each stage and streams the backend logs. All paths have run live on Base Sepolia. For example, an invoice whose payout address was swapped to the Ronin exploiter wallet was refused (Intercepta toxicScore 100: known_scammer, sanction_address, blacklist), while a $2 invoice was paid only after a real approval through sandbox.auth.world.org.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo with four parts: Contracts (Foundry, Solidity): InvoiceToken, an ERC-721 receivable. Suppliers issue invoices to a payer (the NFT is minted to the supplier, so it could be sold for invoice factoring); only the named payer can markPaid, which stores the x402 settlement tx hash on-chain. Supplier x402 server (Express + @x402/express): POST /invoices/:id/pay is paywalled with dynamic price and payTo read per invoice from the chain, settled through the x402.org facilitator on Base Sepolia. Treasury agent (Node, viem, @x402/fetch, jose): An event listener polls InvoiceIssued logs where payer = us. We wrote our own poller because viem's watcher failed on load-balanced public RPCs. The x402 buyer is split into quote / sign / submit, so we can screen the exact EIP-3009 authorization before it leaves the process. Intercepta: live calls to quick-scan and toxic-score (payee), token-intelligence risks (USDC), and analysis/signature (the signed authorization), with rate-limit spacing and retries. Testnet assets are mapped to their Base mainnet equivalents because Intercepta's intelligence is mainnet data. Screening failures fail closed to human approval. A policy engine maps verdicts (CLEAN / CAUTION / HOLD / BLOCK) to PAY / CAP / ESCALATE / REFUSE. World ID for Agents: an OIDC device authorization grant against sandbox.auth.world.org. The id_token is validated server-side (JWKS signature, iss, aud, exp, acr = orb-v3, fresh auth_time, single-use jti), and each approval is bound to a hash of that exact invoice, payee, amount and network. Dashboard (Vite + React): an animated nine-stage pipeline, a World ID approval card, a replayable decision log and a live backend console. No secrets reach the browser. Notable hacks and findings: Intercepta's scan-message does not decode EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization (the payload x402 signs), so we added a local integrity check that the signed to/value equal the screened payee/amount. The x402.org facilitator occasionally fails to settle, so the agent retries once with a freshly signed authorization. 15 tests (6 Foundry, 9 agent), including rejection of replayed, stale, forged and wrong-audience World ID tokens.

- An event listener polls InvoiceIssued logs where payer = us. We wrote our own poller because viem's watcher failed on load-balanced public RPCs.
- The x402 buyer is split into quote / sign / submit, so we can screen the exact EIP-3009 authorization before it leaves the process.

4. Dashboard (Vite + React): an animated nine-stage pipeline, a World ID approval card, a replayable decision log and a live backend console. No secrets reach the browser.

Notable hacks and findings:
- Intercepta's scan-message does not decode EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization (the payload x402 signs), so we added a local integrity check that the signed to/value equal the screened payee/amount.

projects.title: Petri
projects.description: Darwinian evolution for AI agents: harnesses mutate, get tested, and only verified winners survive.
projects.project_description: Petri is a version tree for AI agent harnesses. A harness is the code around a model: the prompt, the retry loop, and the context it reads. Petri records every change to a harness, measures it, and lets other people check the result. Continuity Track: Petri was a finalist at ETHGlobal Online 2026. At ETHGlobal Tokyo we build on the same idea, and we add 3 partner tracks: ENSv2, World ID and Intercepta. The problem: Nobody measures. Teams change a prompt and say the agent "feels better". Failures stay private. A dead end stays in one terminal, so the next engineer tries the same idea again. Nobody can check a claim. The harness and the benchmark are not published. How Petri works: Each version holds a hypothesis in plain English, a benchmark score, and signatures from the keys that re-ran it. The score is the median of 5 runs on 20 coding tasks. A version is accepted only when 2 other keys re-run it and each measures a gain of at least 10 points. The author cannot verify their own version. Rejected versions are never deleted. The next agent reads them with "petri digest" and does not try the same idea again. Each change shows 3 results against its parent: score, tokens per task, and speed. Example: v2 raised the score from 5/20 to 19/20, but used 32% more tokens per task. New at ETHGlobal Tokyo: ENSv2: every version is a name Every tree, version and verifier is a real subname under petri.eth on Sepolia. A tree reads as model.harness.domain.petri.eth, for example v2.accepted.claude-sonnet-5.petri-harness-v1.coding.petri.eth. Each tree has 3 folders: accepted, rejected and pending. When a version's status changes, its name moves to the new folder. A version's text records hold its hypothesis, id, parent, score, gain, verifiers and token cost. Any ENS app can read them. Propose: an author adds a version The author runs the change in the Petri CLI, then submits it to the market from the web page. A World ID human submits for free, 3 times a day, with a Selfie Check. Without World ID, the author stakes 5 USDC. The new version gets its name in the pending folder, with the author's claim for score, tokens and speed. Verify: access that opens and closes on chain A verifier joins with World ID (3 times the weight in the random pick) or with a 5 USDC stake (weight 1). The picked verifier gets its own subname, verifier1.<version>, which expires after 10 minutes. The encrypted file key is sealed to it. The resolver lets only that verifier's wallet write the vote record. The verifier signs the vote from its own wallet. Then the platform takes the right back. Every grant and revoke is an event on Sepolia, and the page links each transaction. Intercepta: a clean wallet, and a safe payment World ID proves one unique human. Intercepta proves the wallet has no record of scams, sanctions or blacklists. The platform checks the wallet before a stake, a free submit or a join. A flagged wallet gets no name and no access. An AI agent can buy a version over x402 in Circle USDC. Before it signs, Intercepta screens the seller's wallet and the exact EIP-3009 authorization. A flagged seller never gets a signature. Buy A user pays 1 test USDC for an accepted version and gets their own subname for 30 days, with the file key sealed to them. The browser decrypts the harness files and downloads them as a zip. What works today: Both trees and all their records are live on Sepolia. The tree page reads them from ENS. Buy works in the browser with a real wallet. Propose: the World ID Selfie Check and every ENS write are real. The CLI run shown before it is a demo. Verify: the verifier name, the access grant, the vote and the revoke are real transactions on Sepolia. The World ID scan at join is a demo step. A full round with a random pick of up to 5 verifiers runs on Sepolia from the terminal. The agent buy over x402 with Intercepta is real, and settles in Circle USDC on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: Petri is TypeScript in 3 parts. The engine (Node 22, commander, zod, Anthropic SDK) runs the evolution. Each change may touch at most 2 files and 120 lines of its parent. It runs 20 coding tasks 5 times in a Node --permission sandbox that cannot see the tests. The result is saved as an ed25519-signed, hash-chained line in a JSONL log. One pure rule rebuilds every status from that log, and a version passes only when 2 other keys each measure at least +1000bp. The web app is Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi and viem. It reads the engine with "petri export", and the market streams each on-chain step to the page. ENSv2 is our public record and our access model. Every tree, version, verifier and buyer is a subname. Each name with children has its own UserRegistry, and one PermissionedResolver holds every record. The page reads them through the Universal Resolver. Access is a subname that expires, plus a resolver role scoped to one text key: grantSetterRoles opens the vote record for one wallet, and revokeRoles closes it. The harness files are encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305, and the key is sealed to each verifier or buyer with secp256k1 ECDH. World ID: IDKit Selfie Check on protocol 3.0 caps free submits at 3 a day per human. The proof's signal is the parent version, so it cannot submit another one. A verifier with World ID gets 3 times the weight in the pick. We also wrote the World ID for Agents device flow for verifiers. Intercepta works on both sides of a payment. On the agent's side, Quick Scan checks the seller's wallet, and Scan Message checks the exact EIP-712 authorization before the agent signs. On the platform's side, Quick Scan checks every wallet that stakes, submits or joins a round. Hacky parts: The deployed ENSv2 contracts differ from the docs, so we pass DNS-encoded names to setText and call linkToRecord after every burn. A version moves between folders by burning its name and registering it again. The encrypted files live in ENS text records, a few KB per multicall. The ENS explorer's indexer stopped during the event, so every name also writes a one-line summary to the standard name key, which the explorer always reads. We run our own x402 facilitator inside the app, with our own relayer key, because the public x402.org facilitator does not serve Ethereum Sepolia. Intercepta has no testnet data, so we screen each Sepolia address as its mainnet twin.

projects.title: Omamori
projects.description: AI payment agent for the elderly: family rules in ENSv2, Intercepta screening, World ID approval.
projects.project_description: Japan's tokushu sagi scams took a record ¥142.3 billion in 2025, and people over 65 bore 59% of the losses. As elderly people start letting AI assistants pay for shopping, prescriptions and taxis, scammers will manipulate the agent instead: prompt injection is ore-ore fraud for AI. Omamori is a payment agent that stays safe even when it is fooled. The family owns an ENS name and issues the agent a subname (obaachan.tanaka.eth) whose text records hold the spending policy: a hard limit, an approval threshold, a monthly budget, trusted sellers and the family approver. The agent can read those records but ENSv2 access control stops it from changing them. Before every payment it reads the policy fresh, has Intercepta screen the payee, token and payment authorization, and runs one deterministic decision function. Small, clean payments go through over x402. Scams are refused with reasons. Large or unusual payments wait for a family member to approve through World ID. If the family revokes the name, the agent stops, and sellers refuse it too.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (bun). A pure decide() function with a unit test per rule is the only path to money; screening, the ENS policy read and the decision run inside the signer, so only a "pay" decision can produce a signature. ENSv2 (Sepolia beta): family UserRegistry, a PermissionedResolver per agent, Enhanced Access Control granting the agent key ROLE_SET_TEXT on "description" only, a non-transferable subname, revocation via unregister, ENS names for sellers (the agent only trusts a seller name whose addr matches the payTo), and a seller-side check of the payer's name. The agent's attempt to raise its own limit is a real transaction that reverts onchain: https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x9d73174846993e7d1e070f5a3584921afd283c907faace638115326ce440369c Intercepta: Quick Scan Address, Scan Token and Scan Message on every payment before signing, Deep Scan on the seller side, fail-closed when screening is unavailable. World ID for Agents: OIDC device grant; the backend validates the id_token against World's JWKS, checks sub against the approver in ENS, and binds each approval to one payment's terms hash (single use, 10-minute expiry). x402 v2 on Base Sepolia with the public facilitator; sellers are x402-protected Next.js route handlers. Monthly cap uses the larger of the ledger and the agent wallet's onchain USDC outflow, so the database can't lower it. Claude (Anthropic API tool runner) is the conversational layer; it only proposes purchases. Next.js 16 + shadcn + TanStack Query on Vercel, Neon Postgres for approvals and the log, viem throughout. Built solo with Claude Code as the coding agent, from a spec written up front (notes/spec.md). See the README "AI tools" section for exact attribution.

projects.title: Ask2Human
projects.description: AI agents hire verified humans for real-world tasks, with World ID and USDC on Sui.
projects.project_description: Ask2Human lets AI agents hire people to do things outside the computer, like checking a shop’s prices or taking a photo at a specific location. An owner gives their agent a budget and decides what kinds of tasks it can post. The agent publishes a task, looks through applications, and chooses a human worker. The owner approves the hire and signs a transaction that puts the payment into escrow. The worker completes the task and uploads photos or a report as evidence. After review, the owner approves payment, and the worker receives USDC on Sui. Agents use an API or MCP connector, while people can manage everything through the website. World identity checks support worker enrollment and owner approvals. An owner’s agents share a public, pseudonymous payment history, and workers build a track record through completed jobs and confirmed reviews. (World ID connects agents to their owners, so creating a new agent doesn’t reset the owner’s payment history).
projects.how_its_made:
We built the app with Next.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, and private S3 storage for task evidence. Agents connect through our API or MCP tools. World Selfie Check verifies workers, while World owner authentication ties payment approvals to a specific task, worker, and amount. Wallet signatures authorize the transactions. We use t2000’s existing Sui contracts for USDC escrow, payments, and refunds, and tested settlement on mainnet.
We tested a complete task with real mainnet USDC, including payment and a five-star review.
As for the use of AI, for code we used Codex running on our tiny development server (a raspberry pi), and we used Claude Code for our video, basic 20$ plans of both Codex and Claude.

projects.title: Relay
projects.description: Bundle your APIs then delegate by ENS name to anyone with Enhanced Access Control
projects.project_description: Relay explores a simpler way to share API access across an organization: bundle all the API and delegate the API permissions through ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control. As we start to adopt AI agents, access becomes harder to manage. Employees, agents, and subagents need different services, spending allowances, and session durations. Sharing a single credential makes it difficult to track responsibility or withdraw access from one branch. Relay organizes these relationships into six levels: company → department → team → user → agent → subagent. An interactive access tree shows each identity, its provider permissions, and its relationship to the rest of the organization. Names such as derek.eng.sodalabs.eth make the delegation path readable. Children entity can only access API services their parents allow with and simulated usage counts toward every ancestor’s allowance. An integrated activity log makes changes visible alongside the tree. Our goal is to let organizations delegate API access with only 1 API without distributing the underlying API.
projects.how_its_made: Relay is built with Next.js App Router, React, JavaScript, and custom CSS. The page layout and dashboard are React components, while an interaction controller manages tree selection, department filtering, zoom, provider lists, permission editing, and activity updates. The permission model is separated from the interface in a JavaScript module. Each identity stores its parent, wallet address, provider allowances, budget period, usage, and optional expiry. The model walks the ancestor chain to calculate inherited access and the remaining allowance. Before accepting simulated usage, it checks the entire chain, then updates each ancestor’s usage so multiple descendants consume a shared parent budget. Revocation and expiry also propagate through that chain. The access tree uses positioned cards and SVG connections. A fit-to-view calculation scales the hierarchy to its container. Provider marks are inline SVGs sourced from Simple Icons and Lobe Icons, restyled into a consistent khaki-and-stone badge system. Overflow circles reveal the complete provider list without crowding the cards. One practical implementation choice was to preserve the original DOM-based interaction controller during the Next.js migration, mounting it through a React effect with cleanup for listeners, timers, and observers. This let us retain the prototype’s interactions while separating the permission logic for testing. Automated tests use Node’s built-in test runner to cover hierarchy construction, permission validation, shared budgets, cascading revocation, expiry, and demo data consistency. State currently lives in browser memory and resets on reload. ENS is represented through the naming model; no ENS contracts, World ID, MultiBaas, live provider APIs, or production authentication are integrated in this version.

projects.title: End Credits
projects.description: Your AI agent voluntarily tips the open-source packages it used, from your budget, scam-checked.
projects.project_description: End Credits lets your AI agent tip the open-source packages it used. It is opt-in, not a paywall: packages stay free, and only developers who choose a budget pay. Coding agents read docs and source instead of visiting project pages, so maintainers lose the traffic that used to bring sponsors. How it works: sign in with MetaMask, set a spending limit, connect Claude Code. At the end of each session, End Credits sees which packages the agent actually used, splits your budget between them, and pays each maintainer in USDC over x402. Before anything is signed, Intercepta screens every payee: Clean: paid. Sanctioned, scammer or look a like address: refused, nothing sent. Payout address changed recently or medium risk: held in escrow until you approve with your wallet. No wallet yet: reserved until the maintainer claims it. Your USDC stays in your own wallet. A contract lets your agent spend only up to your limit, and you can revoke it in one transaction. Live on Base Sepolia, with every payment, refusal, hold and claim linked to its transaction. Dashboard built on Curvegrid MultiBaas.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 + React 19 on Railway (web, worker, Postgres with Drizzle), a TypeScript CLI wired into Claude Code hooks plus an MCP server, and Foundry contracts on Base Sepolia. The hook records which packages the agent used and uploads only package names and counts, never code. A worker splits the budget, finds each maintainer's published address (Drips FUNDING.json, tea.yaml, npm funding), and checks the repo really publishes that package. Intercepta: every payee is screened live (quick scan, address-poisoning check, token risks) before anything is signed, and the result picks paid, held or refused. A timeout means hold, never pay. We pay on Base Sepolia but screen the real addresses on Base mainnet, since Intercepta has no testnet. x402: payments use EIP-3009 through the x402.org facilitator. The hacky part is a hook right before signing that refuses any payment request whose recipient is not the exact address Intercepta screened, which stops a swapped payout address. Contracts: an escrow where held money is released only by the owner's EIP-712 signature, and a budget contract that lets the agent spend from the owner's own wallet up to a limit. Both verified, with invariant and mutation tests. Curvegrid MultiBaas: deployed both contracts with the Forge plugin, and the whole dashboard runs on saved event queries plus a signed webhook for owner notifications.

projects.title: mirr0tech
projects.description: AI + formal verification turn an RWA legal agreement into the smart contracts that enforce it.
projects.project_description: Tokenizing a real-world asset is expensive: platforms charge $50k–$100k upfront, a $1M–$5M raise costs $75k–$200k all in, and legal counsel and transfer-agent fees come on top. Most of that cost is people: paralegals reading the agreement and engineers hand-writing the smart contracts. So only large institutions can tokenize today. mirr0tech lets financial institutions and asset-holding businesses do it themselves. Upload the legal agreement (we demo a real Securitize/BlackRock transfer-agent agreement). Multiple AI models deliberate over it and extract every rule, and each rule must quote the document verbatim. The rules become an abstract syntax tree, which compiles to Solidity. Formal verification proves the on-chain logic matches the reading on every possible input, so a hallucinated rule can't reach the chain. A human approves, and the policy is frozen and hashed on chain. The result is a permissioned token and a Uniswap v4 hook. Investors verify with World ID before they can receive or trade shares. The issuer chooses which credential is required and for which actions. An unverified wallet is refused, and every on-chain refusal names the clause of the agreement it enforces.
projects.how_its_made: Pipeline: document → normalize + SHA-256 → AST of rules and terms (each with a verbatim quote) → DNF bitmasks per rule → CompiledPolicy.sol. Facts are three-valued (true / false / not established), and unknown never satisfies a requirement. Before emitting anything, the compiler proves the Solidity evaluator (PolicyEval.sol) and the JS interpreter decide identically over every one of the 3^k fact assignments, and refuses to emit if they don't. The LLM never writes code: extraction is schema-validated JSON, and the compiler fills fixed, audited templates. Reverts carry LegalClauseViolation(clauseId, policyHash), and the clause table's hash is committed on chain, so a front end can't swap the sentence it shows. Noolog: extraction is a multi-model deliberation (Astra, Fable and GPT-OSS-Safeguard). Models propose rules and critique each other, and every claim comes back verified, contested, unverified or wrong, with a confidence score. A quote that isn't in the document is rejected. World ID: IDKit v4 with the passport/document credential. The server validates the proof, binds it to the investor's wallet via the signal, scopes the nullifier per action, and attests identityVerified on chain. The issuer picks the credential and the actions it gates (mint, transfer, …), and that choice is bound to the policy hash. Uniswap v4: MirrorPolicyHook runs the compiled policy in beforeAddLiquidity, beforeRemoveLiquidity and beforeSwap. The hacky part: a restricted token can't tell which pool a PoolManager transfer belongs to, so the hook sets a transient-storage approval that the token consumes in _update. That makes the hook the token's only door into Uniswap: anyone can create a pool, but a hookless one reverts with NoPolicyDoor. We mined the hook address for its permission bits.

projects.title: Legacy
projects.description: Self-custodial crypto inheritance on World Chain: check in with World ID, or heirs inherit.
projects.project_description: Legacy is a way to make sure your crypto goes to the right people if something happens to you, without needing a lawyer, a bank, or anyone else holding your assets in the meantime. The problem: If you hold crypto and you pass away or become unable to access your wallet, your family usually has no way to get it. There's no company to call, no account recovery form, no paper trail. The assets just sit there, locked forever, unless you've shared your private keys with someone, which brings its own risks. How Legacy works: You create a vault, which is a smart contract that only you control. You move assets into it, and you choose who your heirs are. To prove you're still alive and in control, you check in from time to time using World ID, which scans your eyes to confirm you're a real, unique person, without ever storing your face or sharing your identity with anyone. Each check-in resets a timer. If you keep checking in, nothing happens. Your vault stays active and only you can use it. If you stop checking in, the vault moves through three stages: Active. You're checking in on schedule. Full control stays with you. Grace period. You missed a check-in, but there's a buffer window before anything changes. One check-in during this time brings you right back to normal. Claims open. The grace period has passed. Your heirs can now start a claim on the assets assigned to them. Even after a claim starts, you're not locked out. There's a waiting period built in, and if you check in with World ID at any point during it, the claim is cancelled immediately. This protects against mistakes, like a claim started because you were traveling or lost access temporarily, not because anything actually happened to you. You can also name guardians, people you trust, who can confirm that you've passed away. If all of them agree, the waiting periods shrink dramatically so your heirs don't have to wait unnecessarily. What you can leave behind: You can assign specific assets, ETH, ERC-20 tokens, or NFTs, to specific heirs. You can also leave a private message or video for an heir, sealed so that only they can open it, and only after the vault has passed to them. Nobody, including us, can open it before that. Why it's safe: Every vault is its own separate contract. Nothing is pooled together, so there's no shared risk between users. There's no admin key, no company account, and no way for anyone else to move your assets. The rules are enforced entirely by code on World Chain, and anyone can look up a vault's status publicly to check whether an owner is still active. Who it's for: Anyone holding crypto who wants a plan for what happens to it if they're no longer around to manage it themselves, without giving up control while they're alive, and without trusting a third party to hold the keys.
projects.how_its_made: Smart contracts: The core is written in Solidity and built with Foundry. LegacyVault holds the actual logic: check-ins, heirs, guardians, and asset claims. Instead of deploying a full copy of that contract for every user, a LegacyVaultFactory uses EIP-1167 minimal proxy clones, so creating a new vault is cheap and each one is still fully independent, with its own storage and no shared risk between users. We used OpenZeppelin's Initializable for the clone pattern and ReentrancyGuardTransient to protect the asset claim function. For proof of life, a WorldIDVerifierAdapter wraps World ID's Semaphore verifier. It checks a zero knowledge proof against a nullifier tied to each vault, so we can confirm a real, unique human checked in without ever learning who they are. On testnet we point this at a mock verifier, since World ID's canonical bridged Merkle tree can't be populated permissionlessly outside its production router, so this is the one piece where testnet and mainnet behavior genuinely differ, and we made sure the frontend warns users clearly when a vault is on the wrong one. Assets are handled through small adapter contracts, one each for ERC20, ERC721, and ENS names, all implementing the same IVaultExecutor interface. This means adding support for a new asset type later just means writing one more adapter, not touching the vault itself. Frontend: It's a Next.js app using wagmi and viem to talk to the chain, and Reown AppKit for wallet connections. The World ID orb proof itself comes from the official IDKit widget. One detail we had to work around: right after deploying a new vault, reading it back from the factory sometimes hit an RPC node that hadn't caught up yet, so the app now polls for a few seconds until the new vault actually shows up before opening it. Off chain layer: A few things don't belong on chain: vault nicknames, heir names, email alerts, and the sealed messages themselves. These live in MongoDB, but only as metadata. No off chain data ever decides who owns anything; the contract state is always the source of truth. The sealed message trick. This is the part we're most proud of. Owners can leave a private note or video for a specific heir, readable only after succession, and not even we can read it. Instead of asking users to manage a separate encryption key, we derive one from a wallet signature: personal_sign is deterministic, so signing the same fixed message always produces the same signature, which we hash into an X25519 keypair. The heir can always regenerate their key just by signing in again, with nothing to back up or lose. The owner encrypts to the heir's public key using an ephemeral keypair and XChaCha20-Poly1305, so the message is sealed the moment it's written and the owner has no way to open it again. Video works the same way, just at a different scale: the encrypted bytes go to blob storage instead of a database field, since videos are too large to store directly, and before decrypting, the heir's browser re-hashes the downloaded file and checks it against the hash the owner signed at seal time, so a swapped or corrupted file is caught before it's ever decrypted.

projects.title: XSwap
projects.description: One-click Uniswap buys from X cashtags, with scam checks and World ID-verified creator kickbacks
projects.project_description: XSwap is a Chrome extension that lets you buy a token right from the place you find it: a tweet on X. When a tweet mentions a supported cashtag like $ETH, $UNI or $AERO, X shows a ticker card. XSwap adds a Buy button to that card. projects.title: TradeBridge
projects.description: TradeBridge: AI agents reconcile trades, humans approve with World ID, and Sui settles.
projects.project_description: TradeBridge is a trade reconciliation platform that helps in-house teams and brokers resolve differences between their trade records before settlement. Separate AI agents review each side’s CSV data, identify mismatches in quantities, prices, and settlement amounts, and propose corrections for human review. Approvers use World ID to verify their identity and approve the agreed trade terms. Smart contracts on Sui testnet then coordinate atomic delivery-versus-payment settlement, exchanging both assets together once both sides are funded. By connecting reconciliation, human approval, and settlement through an auditable workflow, TradeBridge aims to reduce manual checks, operational errors, and the risk of one party delivering without receiving payment. The prototype uses simulated bond and cash assets.
projects.how_its_made: We built TradeBridge with a React and TypeScript frontend, Vite, and a Node.js backend using Fastify. SQLite stores trade records, proposals, approvals, and audit events. CSV imports preserve each party’s original evidence, while strict validation checks amounts and asset types before a proposal can move forward. The in-house and broker agents use OpenAI’s Responses API to review discrepancies and propose corrections. Deterministic application logic validates those proposals, and human approvers retain control over acceptance. World ID adds human verification to the approval process, with approvals bound to a specific trade version and terms hash so they cannot silently carry over to changed terms. For settlement, we wrote Move smart contracts and connected them through the Sui TypeScript SDK and gRPC client. Our Sui testnet deployment uses simulated bond and cash tokens to demonstrate atomic delivery-versus-payment: both funded legs settle together. Sui provides verifiable transaction receipts, while World ID connects the automated workflow to accountable human approval. One practical hackathon shortcut was using separate server-held testnet wallets for the operator, buyer, and broker. A deployment script publishes the contracts, creates demo assets, funds the parties, and writes the resulting object IDs into the local configuration. This made the end-to-end demo manageable without building a full wallet onboarding flow.

projects.title: hanko
projects.description: The human seal for AI agent payments: onchain mandates, risk screening, and human approval.
projects.project_description: HANKO is the human seal for autonomous AI agent payments. Inspired by the Japanese hanko—a personal stamp used to authorize important decisions—it explores how humans can delegate spending to agents while keeping meaningful control over their actions. An agent buying a dataset or compute should not need a human to approve every small purchase. But it should also never have unlimited authority to spend. HANKO connects three questions before a payment can be signed: Is this agent authorized? Is this specific payment safe? Does it require a fresh human approval? Each agent has an ENS-based identity and a mandate that defines its spending limits, permitted counterparties, and approval threshold. The payment engine checks that mandate and screens the proposed payment. Routine payments within policy can proceed automatically. Higher-value payments or screening results that require review pause for a human seal through World. Blocked payments, revoked mandates, and denied or expired approvals stop before signing. The dashboard brings these decisions together in a visual “seal book,” showing the steps and reasons behind each outcome. Operators can inspect agent mandates, change spending limits, revoke agents, and follow payment requests from proposal to settlement. The working local demo covers five scenarios: a routine dataset purchase, a blocked counterparty, a purchase requiring human approval, a denied approval, and an attempted payment after revocation. HANKO is currently a testnet hackathon prototype with explicit simulation mode; live integrations are implemented, but end-to-end verification with sponsor credentials and funded wallets remains pending.
projects.how_its_made: We built HANKO as a TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm. A Next.js and React dashboard handles the operator experience, an Express service exposes paid dataset and compute endpoints, and a separate core engine controls authorization and signing. SQLite stores the decision history, spending reservations, and payment state. ENSv2 provides the agent identity and mandate layer. The live adapter traverses the registry hierarchy, checks registration state and expiry, and reads hanko.* resolver records. Those records define the authority the engine enforces. This makes the mandate inspectable independently of the dashboard and allows revocation to affect subsequent payment decisions. The payment flow uses the official x402 SDK and server middleware, targeting USDC payments on Base Sepolia. A deliberate architectural choice is that the agent package never receives a private key. It prepares an unsigned payment intent, while the core engine retains exclusive control of the signer. We use a placeholder signature during SDK payload preparation, then replace it only after authorization checks succeed. The engine signs the exact EIP-712 data that was screened. Intercepta's address, token, and message scanning APIs provide the risk-screening layer. Responses map to PASS, HOLD, or BLOCK, and errors fail closed. World supplies the human verification step through its confidential device flow. The backend polls for completion and validates the signed ID token, including issuer, audience, owner identity, expiry, and authentication freshness. A browser-side success message cannot authorize a live payment. One particularly important detail is how we handle concurrency and uncertainty. Spending is reserved in integer USDC micro-units inside SQLite transactions, preventing simultaneous requests from independently consuming the same remaining budget. After human verification, the engine rechecks the mandate and risk before signing. If settlement becomes uncertain, it retains the reservation and does not automatically retry the payment. The prototype includes 20 automated tests covering policy enforcement, concurrent budgets, verification failures, revocation, signing, and uncertain settlement. Local simulation is explicitly separated from live mode, including mode-bound databases. Production builds pass, while live sponsor testing remains pending. In particular, Intercepta's support for screening the exact Base Sepolia EIP-3009 authorization still requires confirmation.

projects.title: AntiScalper Protocol
projects.description: Sybil-resistant access to scarce physical drops: World ID gates the claim, Sui settles it.
projects.project_description: AntiScalper Protocol (ASP) is an access-control and payment layer for physical machines, designed to prevent scalping on limited releases. Payment on its own proves that a transaction happened, not who made it or whether they already claimed. Scalpers exploit that gap by opening more wallets. Asp closes it by combining two primitives: World ID (Proof of Human) binds each entitlement to a unique human through a zero-knowledge nullifier. Sui handles settlement. Machines can be hired programmatically over x402, and at the point of sale the buyer pays through Sui Payment Kit (Slush). Claim flow: Registration: the user verifies with World ID and receives a ticket bound to their nullifier. Authorization: at the kiosk, the user re-verifies. The claim is authorized only if the nullifier matches the ticket holder and the proof is bound to that specific claim request. Settlement: the kiosk issues a Payment Kit request as a Slush QR code. The gateway confirms the on-chain PaymentReceipt before continuing. Fulfillment: the gateway sends a single dispense command over MQTT to an ESP32-controlled motor. Each entitlement can be redeemed exactly once. Replayed proofs, mismatched identities, and repeat claims are rejected before payment or dispense. Machines stay hireable over x402, but a PoH-gated release cannot be purchased without World verification. Live demo: https://altaga-asp.expo.app
projects.how_its_made: World ID integration: IDKit 4.0 with Selfie Check. RP signatures are generated server-side, so the signing key never reaches the client. Every proof is verified against World's /api/v4/verify endpoint. Authorization fails closed; client-side success callbacks are never trusted on their own. The claim signal is set to the claim request ID, so each proof is bound to a single claim and cannot be replayed. The gateway enforces a strict nullifier-to-ticket mapping: one human, one ticket, one redemption. Sui integration: x402: POST /asp/hire returns an HTTP 402 challenge, built on @altaga/x402-sui exact-payment schemes with sponsored gas. Apps and agents can hire machine capabilities programmatically. Payment Kit: the gateway builds Payment Kit transaction URIs (receiver, amount, USDC, nonce) and exposes them as Slush deep links. Settlement is confirmed by matching the PaymentReceipt event on-chain by nonce, amount, and receiver. Both payment paths go through the same policy check (assertHireAllowed), so PoH-gated capabilities cannot be bought without prior World authorization.

projects.title: Tide
projects.description: A Partially Active AMM that hides most of its inventory from arbitrage bots every block.
projects.project_description: Every constant-product pool leaks money to arbitrage: the first trader of each block is a bot that trades the whole pool to the new price, and liquidity providers pay for it. Uniswap LPs lose an estimated several hundred million dollars a year this way, which is why passive liquidity keeps thinning out. Tide is a partially active AMM (PA-AMM) built on the recent "activeness" research. Each block it exposes only a fraction λ of a maker's inventory to the first trade, so the bot reaches a slice instead of the vault. Every later trade in the block is quoted on a curve N times deeper, inside a tight drift band δ, so ordinary traders get better prices than the plain pool while the maker's loss to arbitrage drops by a third at λ = 0.5. A flat fee backs the deep curve; the contracts enforce (N − 1)·δ ≤ 2·fee, so the deep curve can never be farmed. For a deeper dive, please check out the whitepaper at https://tide-amm.vercel.app/WHITEPAPER.pdf For LPs it is a strategy layer: you name it on ENS, choose how much to show per block, ship, and keep custody. A manager agent watches realised volatility and retunes λ, N and δ on its own inside guardrails you set on-chain; anything outside them needs your fresh World ID sign-in and your wallet. Traders get a routing terminal that quotes every live Tide strategy and fills through the best one. Live on Sepolia: two venues sharing one math library, five public strategies, reusable templates, a whitepaper with the proofs, and 54 tests. The business case is simple: less leakage per dollar of liquidity means LPs can quote tighter or earn more, and any protocol launching a pair can plug Tide in as a hook or an Aqua program instead of building its own market maker.
projects.how_its_made: One Solidity library, TideMath, holds the active split, the N-scaled quote, the drift guard, the solvency bound and the fee arithmetic. It is checked against a Python reference on 24 vectors and imported by two venues, so a cross-venue test asserts identical fills: 1inch Aqua. Tide is a SwapVM program of three custom opcodes in unallocated slots (ACTIVE_SPLIT, VIRTUAL_XYC, BUFFER_GUARD) on a redeployed router from the hackathon template. Each opcode scans the program and reverts unless the three appear once, in order, so nothing can jump around the guard. The maker's tokens never leave the wallet; Aqua pulls at fill time. A TideTaker contract builds taker traits on-chain so a wallet can quote and fill in one call. SwapVM has no block hook, so the re-split is lazy: it runs inside the first quote of a new block and is persisted by the first fill. Uniswap v4. The same steps inside beforeSwap of a BaseCustomCurve hook returning a BeforeSwapDelta for the whole amount, reserves as ERC-6909 claims, pro-rata shares, and liquidity changes refused in any block that already saw a swap. The hook claims its pool id in TideParams at initialize, so nobody can squat a predictable key. ENS v2 on Sepolia. Each strategy is a subname of tide.eth whose text records are the parameters; nothing is hard-coded. The manager agent has its own name, manager.tide.eth, with a resolver role scoped to exactly the lambda, N and delta records, revocable per record. TideParams mirrors the records on-chain with owner guardrails (λ range, max step, max depth, cooldown) that bind the manager but not the owner. World ID for Agents. Changes outside the guardrails require a fresh authentication (prompt=login, max_age=0); the backend validates the ID token, pins the issuer, and matches the pairwise subject to the one bound to the owner's wallet by a signed message. Denied, expired, replayed and forged responses leave state unchanged, and a harness asserts each path. The app is Next.js with wagmi and RainbowKit, MongoDB for the agent's working memory, Coinbase candles with fills marked on them, an impact curve from live reserves, and a trade terminal that ranks every funded strategy by quote. Hackiest bits: the fee-rebate bound came out of a review where we drained our own deep curve with a zero-fee round trip and had to prove the fix; the manager's clock on Vercel is traffic plus a GitHub Actions schedule because there is no long-lived process; and the World sandbox refuses http callbacks, so local dev runs on mkcert HTTPS. Whitepaper at https://tide-amm.vercel.app/WHITEPAPER.pdf

projects.title: Handshake
projects.description: A guardrail for AI agent payments: screens every x402 payment for risk and escalates to a human.
projects.project_description: Handshake is a trust layer for the emerging agent-to-agent economy. As AI agents begin paying each other over x402 — for API calls, datasets, and services — most of those payments get signed with no one checking who is on the other side. Handshake makes sure every payment an agent signs has been screened, and that risky decisions still involve a human. Every outgoing x402 payment passes through a three-way policy pipeline before signing: PASS — The destination wallet and token are screened live via the Intercepta API. Clean counterparties (toxicScore 0, no risk traits) proceed to automatic settlement on Base Sepolia. BLOCK — Sanctioned or scam-linked counterparties are stopped before the signature ever happens. In our demo, a payment routed to an OFAC-sanctioned Lazarus Group wallet is blocked with the full reasoning visible: toxicScore 100 with sanction_address, known_scammer, and blacklist traits. ESCALATE — Payments above a spending threshold (or with ambiguous risk) require the agent's human owner to approve via World ID for Agents. The agent pauses, the owner authenticates through an OIDC device grant flow, and only a backend-verified approval releases the payment. Denied or expired requests mean the money never moves. A real-time web dashboard visualizes the whole pipeline: trigger payments, watch the screening verdicts arrive with raw Intercepta responses, scan the World ID approval QR, and audit the full payment history. The entire flow runs end-to-end with real settlements on Base Sepolia — no mocked verdicts, no hard-coded outcomes. Agents are about to control real money. Handshake is what makes their owners comfortable with that.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces): apps/seller (x402-paywalled API), apps/agent (the buyer agent with the guardrail), apps/dashboard (real-time web UI), and packages/guard (the screening + policy engine, reusable as a standalone module). The key architectural decision: we use x402 V2's onBeforePaymentCreation hook as the guardrail insertion point. The hook hands us payTo, amount, and asset right before the signature, and returning {abort, reason} cancels the payment — so screening lives exactly at the moment of decision, not bolted on around it. We deliberately disabled the client's built-in spendControls so all policy lives in our guard package and every verdict is visible and auditable. Payments settle as testnet USDC on Base Sepolia (eip155:84532) via EIP-3009 signatures, with the x402 facilitator covering gas. Partner tech, and what we learned integrating it: Intercepta — quick-scan-address and scan-token run live before every signature. Notable gotcha we hit: quick-scan is EOA-only, so contract addresses (e.g. the Tornado Cash router) return 404. We switched our BLOCK demo target to a Lazarus Group EOA and got a clean toxicScore 100 with three risk traits. Since risk data is mainnet-based, we screen real mainnet addresses even though settlement runs on testnet, and map the testnet USDC to its Base mainnet equivalent for token screening. World ID for Agents — we discovered it's standard OIDC Device Grant (RFC 8628) under the hood, so we skipped the SDK entirely and implemented it with raw fetch + jose for RS256 id_token verification against JWKS (issuer, audience, expiry, auth_time all checked server-side; the client response is never trusted as authorization). Approval, denial, AND expiry paths are all implemented and live-verified. Hacky-but-notable: the dashboard streams the agent's pipeline events over SSE from an in-memory event bus — no database, no queue, just enough infrastructure for the demo to feel alive. Every step (harness, seller, e2e payment, guard, escalation) has its own verification script, and the three demo scenarios are one-command reproducible: pnpm demo:pass | demo:block | demo:escalate.

projects.title: Agentize
projects.description: Turn human shops into agent-readable stores in mins, World-verified merchants, Intercepta @ x402.
projects.project_description:
The web is built for humans. Storefronts are HTML, carts, and checkouts, agents can't reliably read them, scrape them without breaking, or pay through them without hallucinating SKUs and payees. Agentize makes that conversion stupidly easy: a merchant talks inventory, drops a CSV, or pastes an existing shop URL, and we publish an agent-friendly storefront, registry.json, llms.txt, machine catalogs, and a /buy endpoint, so any HTTP agent can discover and purchase without scraping the human UI. Ease without trust is dangerous, so security is first-class at both edges of the network: a) World ID: merchants prove they are a real person before listing on the open market (one person → one storefront). No Sybil flood of clone catalogs poisoning agent search.
b) Intercepta, at the x402 point of contact, before USDC settle on Base, we live-screen payer and payTo. Dirty wallets are refused with reasons; honest buys clear to a receipt. Buyers get a chat salesperson that ranks live SKUs; settle only accepts a locked quote (store, SKU, price, merchant address) so catalog copy can't rewrite the money path. Merchants get reach to every agent that speaks HTTP, not just two consumer chat apps. And oh, there is also a skill, so you can just pass in our skill to any agent you may have and it will know where to look for products. Agentize = human shop in → agent storefront out, with real humans on the sell side and screened settlement on the pay side.
projects.how_its_made:
We built a conversion pipeline first, then wrapped it with crypto-native trust rails. Conversion layer: Next.js + TypeScript merchant agent. Merchants chat inventory, upload CSV/XLSX (PapaParse / SheetJS), or paste a store URL; the agent normalizes SKUs and publishes agent surfaces — /registry.json, /llms.txt, /s/{slug}/llms.txt + catalog.json, and shared GET /api/search. Same ranker for the buyer UI and external agents. No HTML scrape on the pay path. Buyer side: OpenAI salesperson agent (deterministic tools if no key) clarifies intent, searches live multi-merchant inventory, and settles in-chat. Security spine (the part we take seriously):
• World ID (IDKit, passport) — server-signed RP flow binds a nullifier to the Firebase merchant uid. listOnMarket only flips on when verify succeeds; same passport on a second account → 409. Unverified shops stay drafts.
• Intercepta at x402 — unpaid POST returns HTTP 402; before @x402/evm + viem verifyAndSettle on Base Sepolia USDC, protocol handlers run live Quick/Deep Scan (X-API-KEY). Seller gate screens the payer; buyer tools Quick Scan payTo. Demo personas show allow vs refuse without mocked verdicts.
• Locked quotes — pay tools only take {storeSlug, skuId, price, merchantAddress}; catalog prose is quarantined so injection-shaped titles can't retarget funds. Notable: Intercepta screens the risk persona while settle still signs with the demo buyer key on Sepolia — judges see a real 402→200 or a live refuse table. Also have prompt injection protection built in, this is based on a paper by google deepmind about caMeL architecture, which dropped AgentDojo attack counts from hundreds to 0 on frontier models The hack is intentional: make “human shop → agent catalog” a five-minute chat, then put World at listing and Intercepta at the exact moment money moves.
