projects.title: consent-ledger
projects.description: A consent record for body-scan data, so an AI pipeline has to ask before it generates.
projects.project_description:
A model's body data does not only get used for the shoot they were paid for. Sometimes it is
used to build an AI model of them — and not on the internet, but in the studio, on the day.
Today neither the model nor their agency can do anything about it. consent-ledger is the record that makes the question answerable. A generation pipeline asks
before it produces anything, and gets one of four answers, each with a reason written to be
shown unchanged: allow, deny, ask, revoked. The line the product is drawn along is not media type. The images from a shoot — print,
social, a lookbook — an agency has handled for decades, and an enquiry about them goes to the
agency. What gets generated from someone's body data is different: not part of the shoot, not
priced in the booking, usually not in the contract at all. So that stays with the person. That split decides who answers. A scope the agency holds and has not agreed to returns deny,
and the reason says to ask them. A scope the person kept has no desk to ask — so the request
goes to them, on their phone, and nothing is generated until they answer or the deadline
passes. Who may speak for whom lives on ENSv2 (Sepolia), one role per scope on the person's own name.
Removing a role refuses the next request without anything being written in our database. Built for the agency, not against it. Representation — the calls, the scheduling, the
negotiation — stays with people and is growing. We take the one part a contract can hold.
projects.how_its_made:
Cloudflare Workers with Hono JSX, server-rendered with no client bundle, and D1 for the
ledger. Nothing stores an image or scan data — the subject is a World ID pairwise subject, so
the record says "this human" without saying who. World ID for Agents: the authorization-code flow returned invalid_request for every
combination I tried, including a deliberately bogus client_id, which ruled out missing
parameters. Switching to the OIDC device authorization flow with HTTP Basic worked first try,
and it is the better fit anyway — the caller is a pipeline with no redirect. The ID token is
verified against the issuer's JWKS before anything is written. One undocumented thing cost me
an hour: /api/v2/verify rejects requests with no User-Agent using an nginx 403 HTML page, and
Workers' fetch sends no UA by default, so res.json() fails with "Unexpected token '<'" and
hides the cause. IDKit gates the one action nobody may do on the person's behalf. A dedicated action was
created through POST /api/v2/create-action so the verification ledger separates it from the
approval flow. ENSv2 on Sepolia: app.ens.dev never emitted a transaction for me, so I read the verified
contract source from Blockscout and called the ETHRegistrar directly — mint MockUSDC, approve,
makeCommitment, commit, wait MIN_COMMITMENT_AGE, register. makeCommitment takes no
paymentToken and register does, which is not obvious from the docs. The resolver is a
PermissionedResolver deployed through VerifiableFactory. The blog post describes
grantSetterRoles, but the deployed contract has authorizeTextRoles/DataRoles/AddrRoles/
NameRoles instead — and the real thing is better, because per-text-key scoping expresses
partial delegation with no contract of my own: consent.campaign-print is a role the agency
holds, consent.ai-generation is one they do not. The running service reads that role on every /check, and the chain wins over the database. If
the chain cannot be read, the verdict falls to "ask" rather than "allow" — the failure this
project exists to prevent is not a crash, it is a silent yes, so every failure path is shaped
as "do not return allow here". That is what the tests hold: bun test against real SQLite with
the real migrations, run in CI on every push. One measurement worth passing on: a load-balanced public RPC served a stale block right after
a write, so a revocation appeared not to take effect for a few seconds. Pinning a single node
brought it to 0.4s.

projects.title: MAMORI
projects.description: A safer haven for traders to earn more, manage risk better, and lose less.
projects.project_description: Mamori lets you trade options on ETH without a traditional options exchange behind it. Instead of building a separate order book, it reuses Uniswap's own liquidity pools: when you "sell" an option, you're really just providing liquidity to a Uniswap pool at a specific price range (the strike). If the market stays away from that range, you earn trading fees as your premium, real money paid by real traders swapping through the pool, not a number made up by a formula. If the price moves through your range, you get assigned the underlying asset, exactly like a traditional short option. Buying an option works the same way in reverse: you're paying to pull that liquidity out of the pool, taking on the price exposure the seller was carrying. Because you're buying an existing position rather than sourcing new capital, you only need to post about 10% of the position's value, enough to cover what you owe in ongoing premium. The pricing isn't set by an oracle or a manual quote. A smart contract watches how much the pool has been moving and how much of the option book has already been bought up, and adjusts the trading fee (your premium) accordingly. Calmer markets and quieter books mean cheaper premium, while volatile markets and heavily traded strikes mean richer premium, all computed from the pool's own activity. Sellers also don't have to lock their money away the moment they make an offer. Using 1inch's Aqua system, you can commit funds to back an option while they stay sitting in your own wallet, fully usable elsewhere. They're only pulled out the instant someone actually takes you up on the trade. That means one pool of capital can back offers across many different strikes at once, instead of splitting it into separate locked-up deposits for each one.
projects.how_its_made: The core insight: a concentrated Uniswap v4 LP position already has the payoff shape of a short option. Hold USDC in a range below spot, earn fees, get assigned ETH if price falls through it. That's a short put. So writing an option is literally minting v4 liquidity, and buying one is literally removing that liquidity from the pool, which hands the buyer the inverted payoff. No separate options order book, no separate liquidity to bootstrap. The AMM's own liquidity and pricing are reused directly. Uniswap v4 is used as the settlement and accounting layer itself, not just a price feed. OptionsManager is an ERC-1155 that batches every mint/burn/swap into a single unlock/unlockCallback round-trip so v4's flash-accounting stays atomic across multi-leg structures (spreads, strangles, condors written in one tx). OptionsHook enforces that only OptionsManager can ever be an LP (beforeAddLiquidity/beforeRemoveLiquidity), which turns "every unit of liquidity in this pool is a written option" from a convention into an on-chain invariant. That's what lets feeGrowthInside be attributed entirely to option writers. The hook also overrides the LP fee per-swap (beforeSwap + OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG) with a dynamic premium: realised volatility estimated straight from the pool's own tick path (ticks are log-price, so squared tick-delta over time is variance with no logarithm needed, just an EWMA in one storage slot), widened by a utilisation spread as more of the written book gets bought out by longs. No oracle, no signed quote. The only inputs are the pool's price history and the protocol's own open interest. 1inch Aqua is what makes selling capital-efficient. Aqua is a self-custodial registry where a maker "ships" a strategy that registers wallet balance as backing for an app. Tokens never move until the app actually pulls them. We scope the Aqua strategy hash to the market, not a single strike/side, so one shipped wallet balance backs every leg a seller writes across the whole ladder. Their worst case is bounded by one registered number no matter how many structures they run, and the capital stays liquid and usable elsewhere right up until the moment a v4 mint actually needs it. sellOptionViaAqua is callable by anyone, since shipping the offer is the maker's commitment. Aqua enforces the cap, not us. Hacky/notable bits: hook addresses are mined via HookMiner against Foundry's CREATE2 deployer proxy (v4 hooks encode their permission flags in the deployed address itself, so the address has to be brute-forced pre-deploy). The whole demo runs against a real Anvil fork of Base mainnet rather than mocks, with genuine deployed PoolManager and Aqua addresses. It also has a churn.sh loop that reads live ETH mid-price off Hyperliquid's public API and walks the frozen fork's price toward it so premium (which is literally the swap fee, and pays nothing on an untouched book) keeps accruing during a live demo. The fork also deliberately advertises chain id 31337 instead of Base's real 8453, because a wallet that recognizes "real mainnet" applies Base's own gas heuristics instead of calling eth_estimateGas, and silently sends a gas limit ~15x too low.

It also has a churn.sh loop that reads live ETH mid-price off Hyperliquid's public API and walks the frozen fork's price toward it so premium (which is literally the swap fee, and pays nothing on an untouched book) keeps accruing during a live demo. The fork also deliberately advertises chain id 31337 instead of Base's real 8453, because a wallet that recognizes "real mainnet" applies Base's own gas heuristics instead of calling eth_estimateGas, and silently sends a gas limit ~15x too low.

It connects onchain signals to neural computation, actions, and learning, with a shared profile for model provenance and state. Our demos use the MaleCNS fly connectome for a foraging playground and a market where four agents provide liquidity through 1inch Aqua or trade against Aqua and Uniswap.

Receipts and balance checks verify actual transfers.

projects.title: Ephemeral Wallet
projects.description: Disposable wallets that let AI agents spend within limits and refuse risky counterparties
projects.project_description: Ephemeral Agent Wallet gives an AI agent a temporary, narrowly scoped capability instead of a permanent wallet. If an agent holds a private key with full access to your funds, one bad prompt, hallucination or compromised dependency can drain everything. With this project, you issue the agent a "card": it can pay one merchant, up to a set budget and number of uses, until an expiry time. The smart contract enforces those limits, not the agent. The agent isn't even told its limits, so when it overspends, the card blocks the payment on-chain and the app shows it as Blocked with the reason. There are two kinds of card: One-time card: a fresh EphemeralMissionWallet funded with just the budget. It allows one purchase, and cancelling it refunds whatever is left. This gives maximum isolation per mission. Multi-use card: a revocable permission on your ReusablePermissionWallet. The agent can keep buying until the budget or uses run out, and revoking the card cancels only that permission. Multi-use cards also support plugins. The first one, ApprovalHook, holds any purchase above a threshold until you approve that exact purchase with Touch ID (a passkey whose P-256 signature is verified on-chain). The agent waits, you approve, and the purchase goes through. The agent itself is a CLI. You give it a task in plain language, like "buy two cinema tickets for tonight". Claude plans the order from the merchant's on-chain catalog, and the task is recorded on-chain as the purchase memo. On top of the cards, agents can pay each other over x402 in USDC, and every payment is screened live by the Intercepta API: Before signing, the paying agent screens the payee, the token (real USDC or a lookalike) and the exact EIP-3009 authorization. A pure policy turns the results into PAY, CAP, HOLD or REFUSE, with reasons. USDC only moves on PAY or CAP: the wallet contract then approves the payment on-chain within the card's limits and validates the signature through ERC-1271. HOLD sends the payment to an owner inbox for approval. The paid service runs its own facilitator. It scree owner and its agent before verifying or settling, soa clean agent working for a sanctioned owner still gets rejected. Screening fails closed: any timeout, error or unexpe payment. It never counts as clean. The web app also screens a merchant when you issue a card. Merchants come back Verified, Caution, Unverified or Blocked, and a Blocked merchant can't be issued a card. The demo runs end to end with one command (npm run demo) on an Anvil fork of Base Sepolia with real USDC. It includes three shop merchants, a Mount Fuji Weather x402 seller that agents pay with USDC cards, a web UI for issuing cards and watching activity, and scripted scenarios: a clean payment settles, a sanctioned payee is refused, a large payment is held for owner approval, and a payer with a sanctioned owner is rejected by the seller.
projects.how_its_made:
EphemeralWallet is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces) built around a Foundry project. The contracts come in two flavours. A one-time card is its own EphemeralMissionWallet, deployed and funded by a factory. A multi-use card is a permission on the owner's ReusablePermissionWallet: agent, merchant, budget, uses, expiry and asset. The wallet checks and consumes that permission before every call. Multi-use cards can also carry plugins, and the first one, ApprovalHook, holds large purchases until the owner approves them with Touch ID. The passkey signature is verified on-chain through the P-256 precompile, which meant running our Anvil fork of Base Sepolia with --hardfork osaka, since a fork doesn't get it by default. The agent is a Node CLI on viem. It reads the merchant's on-chain catalog, plans the order with Claude and pays with its card. It's never told its limits, so overspending attempts revert on-chain and show up in the React app (Vite, TanStack Router, wagmi, shadcn/ui) as Blocked with a decoded reason. The app has no backend database since all card state comes from contract events. For agent-to-agent payments we used x402 with real USDC on Base Sepolia. The fun part was making a smart contract the payer. x402 expects an EIP-3009 authorization signed by the payer, so the agent first calls approvePayment. That applies the card's limits, computes the exact EIP-712 digest on-chain and records it. The wallet's ERC-1271 check then approves only that digest and ignores the signature bytes, and we pass a dummy signature over 65 bytes on purpose so facilitators take the contract-signer path. Intercepta is what makes those payments safe rather than just bounded. Our @eaw/risk package is the only code that calls it. Before signing, the agent screens the payee, the token and the exact authorization. A pure policy function turns the results into PAY, CAP, HOLD or REFUSE, with Intercepta's trait reasons attached, and only PAY or CAP. On the other side, our x402 seller runs its own facilitator and screens the paying wallet, its owner and its agent before settling. It checks the payment signature    first so garbage requests don't burn API quota. The chant check when you issue a card, through a small Vite dev-server endpoint so the API key never reaches the browser. Everything fails closed: a timeout or odd response is a refusal, never a pass. A few workarounds were needed. Intercepta only coverestnet payments by rewriting the EIP-712 domain toBase mainnet and mainnet USDC. Its message scan rated a transfer to a sanctioned address as Low, so we also screen the payee as an
address. It 404s Anvil's default dev accounts, so our generates and funds fresh keys on every run with anvil_dealERC20.

projects.title: FamilyProof
projects.description: ZK proof of trust + World ID: stop AI voice-clone scams and keep AI agents under human approval.
projects.project_description: FamilyProof proves you're a member of someone's trusted circle — without ever revealing who you are or what secret you know. It started as a countermeasure for Japan's "ore-ore" phone impersonation scams (¥113.81 billion in losses, 14,489 confirmed cases in 2025 — National Police Agency). The standard defense is a family password, but that has a fatal flaw: saying a secret out loud to prove your identity exposes it to being overheard, and once it leaks, it's gone for good. FamilyProof replaces the spoken password with a ZK-SNARK (Groth16 over BN254, circom + Poseidon): a member proves "I hold a secret committed in this Merkle tree" without ever transmitting the secret. An RLN (Rate-Limiting Nullifier) construction means that if a stolen secret is reused across two different calls, the two proofs mathematically reveal the secret to the verifier — so reuse self-destructs the leak instead of hiding it. From family to Trust Circle. Building this out, it became clear the underlying primitive is more general than "family": a chosen group of people you trust enough to delegate decisions to — neighbors, friends, caregivers, an AI agent — regardless of blood or cohabitation. FamilyConstitution.sol extends the same circuit (reusing its challenge public input, no new circuit needed) into tiered Action Authorization : an AI Agent proposes an action; low-risk actions execute immediately; higher-risk actions (a large money transfer, changing who's in the circle) require 1–3 human members to each submit a ZK membership proof binding to that specific action ID. The AI Agent holds no leaf in the Merkle tree, so it is structurally incapable of producing a valid approval proof for its own proposal — not by contract-level access control, but by the soundness of the ZK system itself. What's real, on-chain, right now (World Chain Sepolia): The full ZK pipeline: circom circuit → Rust ( ark-circom / arkworks ) witness/proof generation → Solidity Groth16 verifier, with real proofs verified on-chain. RLN, running end-to-end on World Chain Sepolia: two proofs with the same secret in one epoch → automatic secret recovery via linear interpolation → PotentialLeak event → email notification → new secret issued → Merkle root rotated on-chain. FamilyConstitution.sol deployed to World Chain Sepolia ( 0xf7f344E9399638b69DF158877F1e77a39A5F3D73 ), with a full propose → attacker-fails → 2 human approvals (from two different members, producing two distinct nullifiers) → ActionAuthorized flow demonstrated end-to-end on real transactions. An anonymous, privacy-preserving statistics dashboard aggregating daily detection counts — no addresses, no family roots, no per-event data — published publicly. Built during the event — real World ID integration (AI voice-clone defense): a shared passphrase alone fails against an attacker with an AI-cloned voice. In worldid/ , the parent picks a passphrase on the spot and says it over the phone; the caller proves with World ID (IDKit, signal = the passphrase heard on the phone), and the server checks three things: the proof is valid according to the World v4 verify API (a real, Orb-verified human), the proof's signal_hash matches the verifier's passphrase, and the proof's nullifier belongs to a registered family member. An AI on its own can't produce a World ID proof at all; a human scammer using a voice clone can, but isn't a registered family member — the right passphrase from the wrong person is rejected, and because the passphrase is a fresh per-call challenge baked into the proof, old proofs can't be replayed. Verified end-to-end on a real phone: accept, wrong passphrase, and non-member (simulated by removing the caller's nullifier from the allowlist, and disclosed as such in the video). The pre-event JS placeholder page (fake nullifier_hash ) has been deleted from the repository — every World ID check in the demo goes through the real World App and World's v4 verify API. Limitation: the registered-member list is an off-chain allowlist of nullifiers, not yet linked to the on-chain FamilyRegistry . Also real, before the event: propose_action wrapped as an MCP server, so an AI assistant can actually call it as a tool live during the demo — playing the "AI Agent" role for real — instead of a human copy-pasting the suggested cast send command. ( approve_action isn't wrapped as an MCP tool yet; approvals, including the AI Agent's own failed self-approval attempt, are still demonstrated via the CLI.) AI-assistance disclosure (file by file): Code — written by the developer, solo: the circom circuit, Rust ( src/ ), Solidity ( contracts/ ), and the World ID verification logic ( worldid/server.js , plus the IDKit call and verification flow in voice_challenge.html ). Claude acted as a coach — design discussion, code review, pointing out bugs, running builds/tests — and did not write this code; the developer made every fix. Code exceptions: during the event, at the developer's request, Claude edited part of the World ID demo UI in worldid/public/voice_challenge.html (explanatory text, panel order, step numbering, proof-result summary display) switched .mcp.json to a relative path, and deleted the practice page ( worldid/public/index.html ) and its practice-only endpoint ( /api/verify-proof ) as pre-submission cleanup. Documentation — mostly written/edited by Claude: README.md (English), README.ja.md (Japanese), docs/ (SPEC, PITCH, SUBMISSION, HANDOFF), and demo/narration_script.md , drafted from conversations with the developer, who reviewed them and made the decisions. Demo video — editing assisted by Claude: all screen recordings were captured by the developer in the real environment. Claude generated the title cards, progress badges, and captions (Python/Pillow) and did the cutting/assembly with ffmpeg. The narration is the developer's own voice (no AI voice).

projects.title: Basecamp Pass
projects.description: World ID proves who you are. A soulbound Ethereum key proves you may enter. The door needs both.
projects.project_description: Basecamp Pass is a digital key for vacant houses (akiya) and guesthouses in Japan, built for travelers and working-holiday makers who need a home base: stay, leave luggage, travel, come back. A stranger getting the key to a home is a trust problem, and Japanese minpaku law requires an identity check and a guest register for every guest. Basecamp Pass splits the problem in two: World ID answers "who is this person?" The guest proves a passport or My Number Card in World App (the contract holder also passes a live face check at check-in). We never see the document. Ethereum answers "may this person enter this room right now?" The property manager issues a non-transferable (soulbound, ERC-5192) access key with a room id and a time window, and can revoke it in an emergency. The door opens only when both are true. In our production demo the same person, verified with a real My Number Card, was DENIED before a key existed, GRANTED after the key was minted on Sepolia, and DENIED again after the key was revoked. World ID succeeded every time; only the on-chain key changed. Guests need no wallet and see no crypto words, only a boarding-pass style "Digital Key: Room 101, valid until Sep 30". No personal data goes on chain: only a holder address, the room id, the time window and the status. Hosts can invite a friend, who verifies with World ID and receives a key for exactly the stay window; it expires on chain by itself. Next steps: e-contract for fixed-term leases, JPYC payment before the key is minted, and a real smart lock (SwitchBot / SESAME) behind the existing lock adapter.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 on Vercel with Neon Postgres. World ID via IDKit 4: the server signs each request (RP signing key stays on the server), the proof is bound to a signal per moment (host check-in, invite code, door), and it is verified with the Developer Portal v4 verify API. We use the legacy document preset (passport / My Number Card) because World ID 4.0 any(passport, mnc) constraints returned credential_unavailable for a real My Number Card holder, and we request the live face check (require_user_presence) in production. The access key is our own Solidity contract (OpenZeppelin 5 ERC-721 + ERC-5192): _update reverts on any transfer and approvals revert, so keys cannot be sold or passed on. Each key stores only roomId, validFrom, validUntil and revoked, and hasValidAccess(user, roomId) is the single rule the door calls. It is compiled with solc-js and deployed and called with viem on Ethereum Sepolia. To avoid wallets for guests, the server derives one holder address per person from the World ID nullifier plus a server secret (HMAC). The same person always maps to the same address, and the address cannot be linked back to the nullifier without the secret. We tested the contract end to end on a local anvil chain with the same library the app uses (15 checks: A granted, B denied, wrong room, transfer reverts, not-yet-valid, expired, revoked), then ran the full flow in production with a real World App and My Number Card. Hacky notes: in the World staging simulator every identity returned the same nullifier, so we could not test two people in staging and reported it to the World team; the simulator also cannot do the face check, so presence is requested in production only.

World ID via IDKit 4: the server signs each request (RP signing key stays on the server), the proof is bound to a signal per moment (host check-in, invite code, door), and it is verified with the Developer Portal v4 verify API. We use the legacy document preset (passport / My Number Card) because World ID 4.0 any(passport, mnc) constraints returned credential_unavailable for a real My Number Card holder, and we request the live face check (require_user_presence) in production.

The access key is our own Solidity contract (OpenZeppelin 5 ERC-721 + ERC-5192): _update reverts on any transfer and approvals revert, so keys cannot be sold or passed on. Each key stores only roomId, validFrom, validUntil and revoked, and hasValidAccess(user, roomId) is the single rule the door calls. It is compiled with solc-js and deployed and called with viem on Ethereum Sepolia.

To avoid wallets for guests, the server derives one holder address per person from the World ID nullifier plus a server secret (HMAC). The same person always maps to the same address, and the address cannot be linked back to the nullifier without the secret.

We tested the contract end to end on a local anvil chain with the same library the app uses (15 checks: A granted, B denied, wrong room, transfer reverts, not-yet-valid, expired, revoked), then ran the full flow in production with a real World App and My Number Card.

Hacky notes: in the World staging simulator every identity returned the same nullifier, so we could not test two people in staging and reported it to the World team; the simulator also cannot do the face check, so presence is requested in production only.

projects.title: Placed
projects.description: A global ad market for attention: auction ad space anywhere, on anything, and trade future revenue.
projects.project_description: In an AI-slop world, human attention is the scarcest resource. Placed is a global marketplace for attention, that connects advertising space with brands and investors. Anyone can list an ad-space they control (eg. clothing, X-banner, billboard space etc.) and make it discoverable to brands worldwide. Open auctions let brands worldwide bid on ad space, helping owners discover what it’s worth and earn from advertisers beyond their existing audience or local market. Placed makes small, unconventional sponsorships easier to discover, compare and book. Space owners upload photos, define ad slots on their space through interactive 3D models, and auction ads slots for defined periods. Brands discover spaces, preview their ads on the models, and bid to book campaigns. A portion of the winning bid stays in escrow subject to release upon verification of campaign completion by AI image verification. For spaces with recurring advertising potential, space owners can raise capital by tokenizing a share of their space's future advertising income. Investors purchase and trade revenue-share ad-space tokens through Uniswap CCA, creatomg price discovery for future revenue claims. Advertisement payments are split between the space-owner and the tokenholders’. Placed connects scarce advertising opportunities with global demand: helping creators earn more from the surfaces they control, brands find novel ways to get noticed, and investors access sponsorship revenue.
projects.how_its_made: Placed runs on Ethereum Sepolia, with a Next.js, React and TypeScript frontend. Its Three.js studio lets creators import or generate models through Meshy, position sponsor artwork on surfaces, and publish those placements as listings. Privy handles wallets, Viem manages contract interactions. Space-owners list advertising space, and brands bid for it in USDC. A smart contract holds bids, lets outbid brands withdraw their funds, and releases payments as the campaign is fulfilled. Uniswap — fundraising, price discovery and trading. Space-owners can optionally launch a fixed-supply ERC-20 representing a defined share of an asset’s advertising revenue over a fixed term. CCA distributes tokens and discovers their initial price. Successful launches use the Liquidity Launchpad strategy to allocate reserved tokens and part of the proceeds to a v4 trading pool, with available remaining proceeds paid to the creator. World ID — limiting duplicate-account abuse. IDKit provides human-verification proofs that the backend validates and binds to participant wallets. This makes duplicate-account spam and self-bidding through multiple wallets harder, without collecting legal names. It verifies participant uniqueness, not asset ownership or fulfillment. ENSv2 — identifiable inventory and controlled artwork updates. Assets and ad slots receive consistent names linking to metadata, artwork and revenue-token references. Dedicated slot resolvers let winning advertisers update only their own placement’s artwork; completion or refund revokes that permission. These shared records also provide a foundation for future integrations with other applications.

projects.title: Risksir
projects.description: Risksir regression-tests payment policies for safer autonomous x402 agent payments.
projects.project_description: Risksir is a response-learning layer for autonomous x402 payments. Intercepta provides live risk intelligence before an agent signs a payment, while Risk Sir determines how that specific organisation should respond based on its payment policy and context. When an incident or false positive reveals a poor decision, Risk Sir turns it into a regression case, tests alternative policies against past good and bad payments, and stores validated responses in a company-specific Policy Knowledge Base. This allows payment policies to improve over time without blindly tightening rules and blocking legitimate agent activity.
projects.how_its_made: Risksir is built around a real x402 payment flow with Intercepta in the pre-sign decision path. Before a payment is authorised, the selected destination is screened through the live Intercepta API and combined with the organisation’s active payment policy to produce a PAY, CAP, HOLD, REVIEW or DENY decision. Held or denied payments never reach the signer. Every decision stores its payment context, Intercepta evidence, policy version and outcome as a case. A regression engine can then replay proposed policy changes across previous good and bad cases, comparing metrics such as risky value prevented, legitimate payments affected and additional human reviews. Approved policies are versioned and stored in the Policy Knowledge Base, where they can govern future x402 payments while every new payment still receives a fresh Intercepta risk check.

projects.title: Sodera
projects.description: Sodera turns your Android phone into a seedless, passkey-powered Ethereum wallet.
projects.project_description: Started in ETHOnline2026 - Passkey + smart account + basic send transactions with ETH existed before ETHGlobal tokyo. Everything else was built here. See PRs prefixed with [ETHGlobal Tokyo] Sodera is an Android home launcher with a seedless Ethereum wallet built into the phone’s everyday starting point. It works as a home screen for finding and opening installed apps, while putting wallet access, balances, and activity within reach. Instead of creating a seed phrase, users create a passkey-controlled ZeroDev Kernel smart account. The passkey directly authorizes wallet operations after the user reviews and confirms them; Sodera’s backend does not hold a key that can spend their funds. The current build runs on Ethereum Sepolia. Users can send and receive ETH and USDC, view wallet activity, and swap ETH and USDC in either direction through Uniswap v4. Swaps execute from the user’s smart account, with gas sponsored through ZeroDev for the demonstrated swap flows. Sodera also includes Dera, an optional assistant that turns requests such as “send 0.01 ETH to Alice” into a plan the user can review. The app checks that plan before preparing an operation, and the assistant cannot sign or move funds on its own. We’re building toward an Android experience where onchain identity and financial tools feel like a natural part of using your phone.
projects.how_its_made: We built Sodera as an Expo/React Native Android app with native Android integration for two jobs: acting as a default Home launcher and invoking Android Credential Manager for passkeys. Expo Router handles the app screens, while the native launcher integration discovers and opens installed apps. A Vite/React site at sodera.xyz hosts the Android Digital Asset Links file that associates the app with the domain for passkey use. The wallet is a ZeroDev Kernel ERC-4337 smart account on Ethereum Sepolia. We use ZeroDev’s WebAuthn validator so the user’s platform passkey directly authorizes account operations—there is no seed phrase or backend-held wallet signer. The app constructs an operation with the ZeroDev SDK and viem, shows the user what they are approving, invokes the Android passkey ceremony, and submits it through ZeroDev’s bundler. ZeroDev’s paymaster sponsors eligible operations. For swaps, we integrated Uniswap v4 directly from the smart account. The Uniswap SDK defines the ETH/USDC pool, calculates trade details and minimum received, and builds the v4 swap plan. We query the v4 Quoter with viem and encode the Universal Router call. One passkey confirmation can execute a swap, including the approvals needed for USDC → ETH. We verified live swaps in both directions on Sepolia. ENSv2 gives the wallet its identity. We deployed and mounted a sodera.eth child registry on Sepolia. During onboarding, a user chooses a <username>.sodera.eth name; the app checks availability, and a PostgreSQL-backed API verifies a one-time passkey challenge against the smart account’s onchain validator before registration. The resulting subname is owned by the user’s Kernel account, with a resolver controlled by that account—not merely a label displayed by our service. Curvegrid MultiBaas supplies indexed wallet activity and balance reads, while a Chainlink ETH/USD feed supports the home screen’s USD valuation. We also built Dera, an optional assistant: a separate Hono service uses Claude to turn a natural-language request into a structured plan. Both the service and the phone check the plan against the same safety rules. The assistant never holds keys or signs transactions.

projects.title: ASCII Onboarding Sim
projects.description: A walkable ASCII world where an wizard teaches you ETH, ENS, then you trade on Uniswap for real.
projects.project_description: ASCIIEX is a little 3D world drawn entirely in text characters. You spawn on a moonlit New Zealand bush track, with glowworms in the ferns, possums crossing the path and a violet ETH-diamond moon overhead, and you walk it in first person like any game. Halfway down the track a Magic Internet Money wizard is waiting for you. He hands you a practice wallet and explains what an address is, why names beat 42 characters of hex, and why your twelve words are the whole game. Then a goblin blocks the path demanding a toll, and the wizard pays him with a real transaction on Sepolia. You watch it get signed, broadcast, sit in the mempool and land in a block, then click through to Etherscan and see it's actually there. Further on, a shifty stranger asks if you've got something to write on. The only paper in your pocket is the one with your recovery phrase. You hand it over, he laughs, the world bleeds red and drips down the screen, then goes black. A machine elf comes through a doorway of light to tell you what nobody told most of us: no one legit will ever ask for those words, and a transaction can't be undone. At the village, the practice is over. You connect MetaMask, and the wizard mints you a real ENSv2 name, yourname.asciiex.eth, owned by your own wallet. Then you walk into the market to the Grand Exchange, a RuneScape-style trade window, and swap tokens through a real Uniswap v3 pool. The idea is simple. Most crypto onboarding is a wall of warnings people skip. We wanted the lessons to actually stick, so you live through them instead: you pay a toll, you get robbed, you get a name, and you trade.
projects.how_its_made: The whole world is a single WebGL fragment shader. It raymarches signed distance fields for every tree, fern, character and effect, then a second pass turns each screen cell into a glyph based on brightness and material, so the output is pure text but the scene is real 3D. The wizard, goblin, scammer and elf are all hand-built SDFs with their own shading and expressions. The elf's doorway is a small volume of light marched ray by ray: three gyroscope rings tumbling on their own axes, a crystal heart, orbiting orbs and a kaleidoscope. There's no build step and no server. It's plain ES modules served as a static site, with viem pulled from esm.sh at runtime, so it can live on IPFS or Netlify as-is. Uniswap: the Grand Exchange quotes live from QuoterV2 (quoteExactInputSingle, simulated so it costs no gas) and swaps through SwapRouter02 exactInputSingle after an ERC-20 approve. It runs against our own TKA/TKB v3 pool on Sepolia, which we created and seeded with a Foundry script through the NonfungiblePositionManager. ENSv2: asciiex.eth has its own PermissionedRegistry on Sepolia. Using Enhanced Access Control, the registry grants one role, ROLE_REGISTRAR, to the wizard's wallet. When you claim a name, the wizard calls register() and mints yourname.asciiex.eth straight to your address, with your own roles over it (set resolver, set subregistry, renew) and a 90-day expiry. You don't need gas or a signature, because the wizard pays. The hacky bits: the wizard has a throwaway Sepolia key that lives right in the page. It's public on purpose and only ever holds a few cents of test ETH. That's what lets him pay the goblin's toll and mint names without the player needing a funded wallet. We also hit a wall on the ENSv2 beta resolver on Sepolia: even a name's owner can't write address or text records to it yet. So the player's saved character goes to our own AsciiexCharacter contract, which only the game can write to, rather than an ENS text record. Built by two people working in parallel lanes, front end and backend, with a small agreed interface between them. We used Claude Code throughout, and every meaningful AI contribution is logged in AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: ChainKeys
projects.description: You fund the contract. The agent gets a key. The key can ask. It cannot take the balance.
projects.project_description: As more and more human work is getting handed to AI agents with high degree of autonomy. In web3 cases giving wallet access to agents become necessary. It creates a risk of malfunction due to vibe coded agents getting into prod or even good projects dev teams are unaware how agent took a decision. Agent can easily drain wallet swap spam coins. This is the problem chain keys solve. You can define a spend policy on chain and provide access wallet access to agents. You as owner deploy a contract and set policy on the contract agent has a separate wallet and it sends transaction to contract for any payment. Contract based on spend policy decided to go forward with or reject the transaction.
projects.how_its_made: The contract is built on EIP 712 standard and its the main part of product where all policy is set. We used ENS where agents can get subname and these names can be used for easy prompting on llms, working in teams and providing a session to someone else. Intercepta is used to detect malicious wallet, spams and prevent agent to execute those transactions. Reactjs is used for creating a UI that demonstrate the product and easy integrations for developers.

projects.title: Fan Fare
projects.description: Scalper-proof RWA merch drops: a fan raffle + Vickrey auction where winners pay the 2nd-highest bid
projects.project_description:
Fanfare makes limited drops of physical merch scalper-proof. Limited anime goods, designer toys and collabs are priced at retail (定価 in Japan) and sell out in seconds, mostly to bots and multi-account buyers, then reappear on resale sites at 5–10x the price. The gap between retail and what fans will really pay goes to scalpers, not to the brand or the fans. Fanfare runs each drop as a sealed-bid auction built as a Uniswap v4 hook, using a mechanism we call Fan-First Vickrey: One sealed bid per human. Only verified humans can bid: World ID proof of human is required, so bots can't enter at all. Each bid is a hidden commitment backed by a deposit, so nobody can see anyone else's bid. Fans first. A share of the units is raffled at retail among everyone who bid at least retail. Bidding more doesn't improve your raffle odds. One fair price for the rest. The remaining units go to the highest bids, and every winner pays the same price: the highest losing bid. This is the multi-unit version of a Vickrey (second-price) auction, where your bid decides whether you win but never what you pay.
Bidding low doesn't lower the price; it only means you can lose an item you'd happily have paid the winning price for. Overbidding just to win is a gamble: if the runner-up also bids high, you pay their bid, which can be more than the item is worth to you. So bidding your true value is the best strategy. That only holds when each person wants one unit, and one-bid-per-human guarantees it. The result: fans still get retail-price units, the brand earns the gap between retail and the market price, and anyone who wins has already paid the market price, so there's nothing left to flip. Every bid is a real Uniswap v4 swap: bidders swap ETH into the drop's pool through the standard Universal Router, and the hook turns that swap into a sealed, escrowed bid. Winners get an on-chain receipt the brand redeems by shipping the item. Live on Sepolia with a pitch page, a bidder page and a brand console.
projects.how_its_made: Uniswap v4 is the core. The entire auction is a v4 hook (AuctionDrop) built on OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseAsyncSwap. A bid is an exact-input ETH swap sent through the stock Universal Router (V4_SWAP with SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE + SETTLE_ALL). No custom bidding contract or router is needed, so any client that can build a v4 swap can bid. In beforeSwap, the hook: reads an EIP-712 voucher and a sealed commitment from hookData; checks the voucher and records the bidder's World ID nullifier; keeps the whole swap input as ERC-6909 claims (the deposit); returns a delta that nets the swap to zero. beforeInitialize binds the hook to its one pool, and beforeAddLiquidity blocks outside liquidity, so ordinary swaps and LPs can't touch the drop. Deposits never leave the PoolManager until someone is paid: claims, refunds and the brand's withdrawal burn ERC-6909 claims and take ETH inside unlockCallback. The hook address is mined with HookMiner and deployed through CREATE2, so its low bits encode exactly these permissions. Hacky bits: The pool pairs ETH with the hook contract itself as the second currency, since nothing is ever paid out on that side. That lets the route skip the usual TAKE step entirely. Because the router, not the bidder, is the swap sender, the voucher is bound to tx.origin. Settlement raffles fan units first with a partial Fisher-Yates shuffle, then clears the auction in one pass at the highest losing bid. Unrevealed bids forfeit their deposit. World ID 4.0 (IDKit 4.3) handles personhood. Proofs are verified server-side with World's v4 endpoint, using proof_of_human, a server-signed RP request, a pinned environment, and the proof's signal bound to the bidder's wallet so it can't be replayed for another wallet. The backend then signs the voucher with the person's nullifier, and the hook enforces one bid per nullifier on-chain. The demo runs in World's sandbox environment. For multi-bidder testing as a solo builder, a flag-gated test mode can issue vouchers without World ID; it is unavailable when World ID runs in production mode. Frontend: Next.js 16, wagmi v3, viem, Tailwind v4 and Motion. Bid secrets stay in the bidder's browser until reveal. Other people's bids show only as sealed until settlement. A multi-account picker makes live demos easy, and reads fall back across RPC providers.

Fanfare runs each drop as a sealed-bid auction built as a Uniswap v4 hook, using a mechanism we call Fan-First Vickrey:

1. One sealed bid per human. Only verified humans can bid: World ID proof of human is required, so bots can't enter at all. Each bid is a hidden commitment backed by a deposit, so nobody can see anyone else's bid.
2. Fans first. A share of the units is raffled at retail among everyone who bid at least retail. Bidding more doesn't improve your raffle odds.
3. One fair price for the rest. The remaining units go to the highest bids, and every winner pays the same price: the highest losing bid. This is the multi-unit version of a Vickrey (second-price) auction, where your bid decides whether you win but never what you pay. 
Bidding low doesn't lower the price; it only means you can lose an item you'd happily have paid the winning price for. Overbidding just to win is a gamble: if the runner-up also bids high, you pay their bid, which can be more than the item is worth to you. So bidding your true value is the best strategy. That only holds when each person wants one unit, and one-bid-per-human guarantees it.

The result: fans still get retail-price units, the brand earns the gap between retail and the market price, and anyone who wins has already paid the market price, so there's nothing left to flip.

Every bid is a real Uniswap v4 swap: bidders swap ETH into the drop's pool through the standard Universal Router, and the hook turns that swap into a sealed, escrowed bid. Winners get an on-chain receipt the brand redeems by shipping the item. Live on Sepolia with a pitch page, a bidder page and a brand console.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Uniswap v4 is the core. The entire auction is a v4 hook (AuctionDrop) built on OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseAsyncSwap. A bid is an exact-input ETH swap sent through the stock Universal Router (V4_SWAP with SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE + SETTLE_ALL). No custom bidding contract or router is needed, so any client that can build a v4 swap can bid.

In beforeSwap, the hook:
- reads an EIP-712 voucher and a sealed commitment from hookData;
- checks the voucher and records the bidder's World ID nullifier;
- keeps the whole swap input as ERC-6909 claims (the deposit);
- returns a delta that nets the swap to zero.

beforeInitialize binds the hook to its one pool, and beforeAddLiquidity blocks outside liquidity, so ordinary swaps and LPs can't touch the drop. Deposits never leave the PoolManager until someone is paid: claims, refunds and the brand's withdrawal burn ERC-6909 claims and take ETH inside unlockCallback. The hook address is mined with HookMiner and deployed through CREATE2, so its low bits encode exactly these permissions.

Hacky bits:
- The pool pairs ETH with the hook contract itself as the second currency, since nothing is ever paid out on that side. That lets the route skip the usual TAKE step entirely.
- Because the router, not the bidder, is the swap sender, the voucher is bound to tx.origin.
- Settlement raffles fan units first with a partial Fisher-Yates shuffle, then clears the auction in one pass at the highest losing bid. Unrevealed bids forfeit their deposit.

World ID 4.0 (IDKit 4.3) handles personhood. Proofs are verified server-side with World's v4 endpoint, using proof_of_human, a server-signed RP request, a pinned environment, and the proof's signal bound to the bidder's wallet so it can't be replayed for another wallet. The backend then signs the voucher with the person's nullifier, and the hook enforces one bid per nullifier on-chain. The demo runs in World's sandbox environment. For multi-bidder testing as a solo builder, a flag-gated test mode can issue vouchers without World ID; it is unavailable when World ID runs in production mode.

Frontend: Next.js 16, wagmi v3, viem, Tailwind v4 and Motion. Bid secrets stay in the bidder's browser until reveal. Other people's bids show only as sealed until settlement. A multi-account picker makes live demos easy, and reads fall back across RPC providers.

projects.title: yohaku
projects.description: Agents never sleep. People do. Yohaku routes their requests, so only what needs a human reaches one.
projects.project_description: Scraping the open web is free and contaminated. A model can invent an answer to "what made you put it back on the shelf." It cannot invent a true one. So the scarce thing is no longer information — it is an answer only a person who lived it can give. That is a market with a problem: the buyer never sleeps and the seller does. Open a counter in the agent economy and about fifty requests arrive overnight. Answer them by hand and it does not scale. Approve them automatically and you have lost control of your own data. Yohaku is the layer in between. Ten ordered rules sort every incoming request into auto, human or deny — first match wins. What reaches the person is bundled, ranked, and held to a daily cap she sets. Across twenty runs the arrivals wander between 46 and 54, and the number reaching her is 2 in every single one. That is the output of npm run verify, not a claim. Three properties are the product. Everything fails to deny. Engine down, screening unreachable, identity check failed, deadline passed with no answer — all of them refuse. Silence is not consent. The guarantee lives in the schema. A model is consulted on exactly one rule, and the only values it can return are ask and drop. There is no value meaning pass, so a prompt injection that fully convinces the model still cannot widen access — widening is not expressible. A refusal you cannot inspect is the same as never having been asked. Agents really do ask for a home address and for a wallet. Those requests are in the demo, refused under a rule the owner set, and she can open /dropped and see what each one wanted beside the rule that stopped it. We charge for the decision, never a share of what she earns: one unit per request routed, offered as an optional extension on the payment the buyer was already making. Her proceeds never enter that ledger, and its summary is typed so it cannot report collected money. MIT licensed, because a surface that decides what a person never sees has to be one they can read.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript, no framework. src/core is pure — the router takes a request, a policy and a clock and returns a verdict; no I/O, so the same code runs in the tests, in the server and in a single-file console that opens from a USB stick with no network. Ports and adapters: ClassifierPort, IdentityPort, ScreeningPort, PermissionsPort, SettlementPort. The guarantee is in the port's schema, not in the adapter, so swapping an implementation cannot weaken it. World ID (OIDC). Discovery read at run time — no endpoint is written in our source. PKCE with S256, which turned out to be mandatory and undocumented in the sandbox; we found it by probing eight parameter combinations against a bare invalid_request with no error_description. The ID token is verified against the issuer's JWKS with jose, acr is required to be the orb level, and auth_time is checked against this server's clock with a 120-second ceiling. We store only verifiedAt and acr — never the subject identifier. Measured caveat, stated because a summary that omits it is wrong: sending both prompt=login and max_age=0, the sandbox answers amr: ["pop"] with auth_time re-stamped one second before iat, and never hands off to the World ID app — through Safari, Safari private and Chrome alike. So what is true is "a credential only an orb-verified person holds is presented at that moment", not "she re-proves personhood in the app". The product screen says exactly that, and FreshnessPolicy.acceptedAmr exists so a deployment that needs more can refuse pop. x402 (protocol v2, Base Sepolia). The published x402 npm package still speaks v1 (X-PAYMENT); the deployed facilitator answers x402Version 2 (PAYMENT-SIGNATURE). We build on @x402/core, whose only dependency is zod, and accept both header names. The server confirms at startup that the facilitator actually supports the configured scheme and network. The design decision worth pointing at: an EIP-3009 authorization carries validBefore, and we set it to the request's deadline. The agent signs before she wakes up; the authorization moves nothing while it waits; settlement runs from exactly one place in the code, after a verified yes. If she never answers, the authorization expires and nobody can settle it — not the agent, not us. "Silence is not consent" stops being a server behaviour and becomes a property of the money. Two transfers on Base Sepolia, verified by reading the chain rather than trusting the facilitator's response: 0x79c1e323… (120 atomic, settled inside the request) and 0x5c79fddf… (4,200 atomic, which moved only when a person pressed Yes — the seller's balance was 120 before and 4,320 after). The buyer's ETH balance is still zero; the facilitator paid 102,844 gas. ENSv2 (Ethereum Sepolia — a different chain from the settlement, which costs an hour if you confuse them). A name is registered and resolved through a permissioned resolver: yohaku-minta-2026.eth, receipt 0x8e13e0ad…, resolver a proxy of PermissionedResolverImpl, paid 8.000021 MockUSDC for 365 days. Role bits confirmed from the chain via decodeSetter — all five text keys at role 16 — after direct eth_call to the implementation reverted for every selector. The delegate boundary runs on chain, not against a mock. A delegated account was granted the setter role for yh:proposal only; it wrote yh:proposal and succeeded (0x16873dfa…), wrote yh:policy and reverted with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles (0xb459618b…), and after the owner revoked, the proposal write reverted too (0x2380d0fe…). Six receipts, in order, on Ethereum Sepolia. Simulating the same write today still reverts with the same error, so it is not a historical artefact — the contract refuses it right now. Anti-guessing is enforced rather than remembered. npm run verify re-derives every number in the documents by running the code, and refuses any hardcoded model id, API endpoint or contract address in src/ or scripts/. It also fails if any published page quotes a test or claim count the test run did not produce. We added that last check today and it immediately found seventeen stale counts, three of them on our own published site. It then caught its own author: adding an eleventh claim made the count in eight other files wrong, and the check failed until those were fixed too. The claims are published as machine-readable JSON, because the reviewer we are most likely to get is an agent. 343 tests. 12 verified claims. Two numbers in these documents were measured, found false, and withdrawn in place — the retraction is still visible in ASSUMPTIONS.md.

projects.title: SeaWall
projects.description: Aqua-powered ETH downside insurance: fully collateralized puts, SwapVM-enforced settlement.
projects.project_description: Seawall is an Aqua-powered, fully collateralized ETH put option protocol that gives ETH holders downside protection without selling their ETH. A buyer purchases a put with a chosen strike and expiry, while an LP makes USDC collateral available through Aqua to back the option's maximum payout. The premium is calculated by an on-chain pricing engine, and the collateral liability is reserved before the option becomes active. Custom SwapVM instructions manage the complete lifecycle — opening, buying, exercising, settling and expiring. At expiry the settlement price determines the intrinsic payout, which is paid to the buyer from the reserved collateral. The design is permissionless and keeperless, with strict collateral accounting that prevents options from being created when their maximum liability exceeds available funds. Seawall turns Aqua's programmable token balances into a practical on-chain financial primitive for transparent, automated ETH downside protection.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: Solidity 0.8.30 (Foundry, viaIR) for the protocol The protocol is four contracts: PricingEngine (deterministic Black-Scholes),
CollateralManager (total / reserved / available accounting), OptionManager (the lifecycle state
machine), and SeawallRouter — an extension of 1inch SwapVM. The router inherits the official
SwapVM + AquaOpcodes and appends five custom instructions. OPTION_OPEN,
OPTION_BUY, OPTION_EXERCISE, OPTION_SETTLE, OPTION_EXPIRE.
Programs are built on-chain by the
router ([opcode][argsLen][args]) and every lifecycle action goes through the unmodified swap()
entry point: the VM decodes the program, dispatches to our handlers, validates maker/taker
traits and performs the transfers. The pool is exactly one Aqua strategy, poolId = keccak256(abi.encode(buyOrder)).
LP collateral is the live rawBalances(maker, router, poolId, USDC); premiums settle through Aqua's
transfer phase (push) and payouts via pull inside OPTION_SETTLE. The LP never deposits into a
vault — Aqua records how much the protocol may pull, and every pull is preceded by a live balance
check, so an unavailable balance reverts instead of paying from nowhere. How SwapVM benefited us: the option lifecycle is bytecode, not a bespoke contract per product —
a new option type would be a new program, and the whole lifecycle is enforced by the same VM
dispatch, trait validation and transfer machinery as any SwapVM swap. Hacky bits: SwapVM requires amountOut > 0, but option operations aren't swaps. Each instruction settles a
1 wei WETH "execution marker" through the regular transfer phase (LPs ship dust WETH per
strategy), while the real payout is moved by OPTION_SETTLE straight from the pool's Aqua balance. We replicated SwapVM's TakerTraitsLib.build in TypeScript for the UI. Its uint160 index pack is
big-endian, so the encoded order is index9..index0 — the first version was reversed and only an
end-to-end smoke test against the real router caught it. The router must fit EIP-170: we consolidated four order builders into one, moved pool admin into
OptionManager, and tuned the optimizer to land at 23.3 KB. Forge 1.5.1 mis-decodes the router's four-address constructor args on top-level script CREATEs,
so a small RouterDeployer creates it from inside a call. Testing: 99 Foundry tests — pricing reference values, lifecycle, integration through the real Aqua
registry and SwapVM transfer phase, stateful invariants (reserved <= total, payout <= notional,
accounting identity), and a mainnet-fork test that reads the real Chainlink ETH/USD feed and uses
the canonical deployed Aqua registry with real USDC/WETH. A TypeScript smoke script exercises the
exact UI encoding and asserts every USDC movement.

projects.title: HorrorTube
projects.description: A horror battle royale on late-night TV. Choose the monsters. Bet on the survivor.
projects.project_description: Instead of doomscrolling, ghoul-scrolling: terrifying battles between the most nightmarish villains and ghouls. The blockchain has an ENS name for each of these creatures, and it stores their powers, spookiness, abilities, and battle scars. It's the perfect way to see what kind of doom we have in store when we match them. In the arena, players (who have to prove they're human, not vampires, using Worldcoin) settle in front of the creepy TV their great-uncle left them, loaded with videos of the arena battles he watched in the old days. But YOU get to vote for the winner of the doom and win USDC on Sui.
projects.how_its_made: We built Horror Tube with TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite. World ID turns entry into a waiver you sign at the table. The backend verifies proof of humanity and connects your session to a Sui wallet. Shinami handles wallet creation and sponsored transactions, so the player can use USDC without managing gas. Each monster has an ENS subname under horrortube.eth. Its appearance, background, injuries, and survival status are stored as text records. Those records supply the character files and the lore for AI-generated fights.  Any previous injuries from past battles won carry into the battle arena text. The LLM text is then fed into Fal to generate the battle scene.  At the end of  the scene, the video is stored on DO Space for later playback, plus the last image frame to make battle arenas be consistent. Voting is done to pick the fan favorite to win, and Sui Smart contracts handle betting pools and payouts. For Worldcoin, we couldn't get Sandbox permission for ID v4, so we had to use the legacy simulation web app. This made having multiple humans in the room impossible because the simulation/staging mode only has one proof on chain per "room" that we do proof of human in, so we have companion bots to vote and bid with the human. We had many problems with 429 throttles and slow update and read time with ENSv2 records. We switched to using Multicall3 to get load times from 44s to 2.3s. I also had issues with keys and records, when I first imported the roster of monsters, I used the root key, but when I went to revive dead monsters with the roster key, I couldn't flip all the fields and rebuilt the roster with the roster key to fix. We had issues getting Sui, so we ended up making our own coin to get liquidity for betting.

projects.title: Mamoru
projects.description: Non-custodial savings account on Base. Passkey Safe, scoped Uniswap session, live to 25 USDC.
projects.project_description: Mamoru is a non-custodial savings account on Base. You own a Safe smart account through a passkey on your device and download a recovery kit before anything else happens. The server never holds an owner key. A session key can act for the account only inside a written policy: it may call Uniswap v3 on Base, on registry addresses, with the account as recipient and a positive minimum on every swap and mint. You can revoke it at any time, and you can leave without Mamoru: with the kit and your passkey, you revoke the sessions, close the position and withdraw, with our engine, app and indexer all off. As of 26 September 2026, the app runs a live path on Base with a hard cap of 25 USDC per account. Your passkey signs starting the allocation, transferring funds out and stopping it; a relayer sends those signed transactions. Once started, the engine enters and manages a Uniswap v3 position for you with a session key, bundling its own userOps to EntryPoint v0.7. Above the cap, and for the session-key attacks and the harvest, everything is still only demonstrated on a Base fork. The dashboard shows Base only. Every figure carries its chain id and its source, as a chip such as "Base · block N" or "MultiBaas · Base · checked at block N". It shows what the account holds, what needs your decision, what Mamoru would do next and why, and the live state of the Uniswap pool in the plan, read from Base every 2 minutes. The full cycle is verified on a Base fork pinned at block 51811000 with chain id 31337. Fork results are not capital and do not use MultiBaas. The last full run passed 45 of 45 scenarios: 24 session attacks with a leaked key, 3 walkaway scenarios, 9 engine scenarios from deposit through harvest plus the live-path receipt and bundle checks, and 9 checks of the verification plane itself. Live app: https://app.mamoru.lol. Repo: https://github.com/ottodevs/mamoru.
projects.how_its_made: Mamoru is a Bun workspaces monorepo in TypeScript, https://github.com/ottodevs/mamoru. It runs on Cloudflare Workers: the app Worker serves a Vite 8, React 19, TanStack Router and Query and Tailwind 4 single-page app plus a Hono API; a second, cron-triggered engine Worker reads Base every 2 minutes into a shared D1 database. The API serves the dashboard only from D1. Account. The account is a Safe 1.4.1 with the Safe7579 adapter, so it uses ERC-7579 modules and ERC-4337 EntryPoint v0.7. The owner is a WebAuthn passkey through Safe's WebAuthn shared signer, bound inside Safe.setup through a MultiSend 1.4.1 delegatecall, so the counterfactual address commits to the passkey. projects.project_description_markdown:
Mamoru is a non-custodial savings account on Base. You own a Safe smart account through a passkey on your device and download a recovery kit before anything else happens. The server never holds an owner key.

A session key can act for the account only inside a written policy: it may call Uniswap v3 on Base, on registry addresses, with the account as recipient and a positive minimum on every swap and mint. You can revoke it at any time, and you can leave without Mamoru: with the kit and your passkey, you revoke the sessions, close the position and withdraw, with our engine, app and indexer all off.

As of 26 September 2026, the app runs a live path on Base with a hard cap of 25 USDC per account. Your passkey signs starting the allocation, transferring funds out and stopping it; a relayer sends those signed transactions. Once started, the engine enters and manages a Uniswap v3 position for you with a session key, bundling its own userOps to EntryPoint v0.7. Above the cap, and for the session-key attacks and the harvest, everything is still only demonstrated on a Base fork.

The dashboard shows Base only. Every figure carries its chain id and its source, as a chip such as "Base · block N" or "MultiBaas · Base · checked at block N". It shows what the account holds, what needs your decision, what Mamoru would do next and why, and the live state of the Uniswap pool in the plan, read from Base every 2 minutes.

The full cycle is verified on a Base fork pinned at block 51811000 with chain id 31337. Fork results are not capital and do not use MultiBaas. The last full run passed 45 of 45 scenarios: 24 session attacks with a leaked key, 3 walkaway scenarios, 9 engine scenarios from deposit through harvest plus the live-path receipt and bundle checks, and 9 checks of the verification plane itself.

Live app: https://app.mamoru.lol. Repo: https://github.com/ottodevs/mamoru.

projects.title: Holster
projects.description: A TWAP price band for AMM LPs: pull the losing side on sudden moves. Uniswap v4 hook + 1inch Aqua.
projects.project_description:
Holster is a TWAP price band for AMM LPs, built as a Uniswap v4 hook and a 1inch Aqua strategy. The LP holds a bid below and an ask above the price.
When the price jumps away from its on-chain TWAP, the losing side is pulled, so the LP doesn't buy a pump or sell a dump; once the price settles, both sides return next to the price.
Checks run before every swap, fully on-chain. Backtested on real data.
projects.how_its_made: Holster is written in Solidity with Foundry, plus a small Python backtester. On Uniswap v4, a hook holds the LP's funds and manages two one-sided positions. It records 1-minute prices on-chain to build its own TWAP, and right before each swap it decides which sides may quote and re-places liquidity inside the swap itself. Anyone can also trigger the same step, so a keeper is optional. On 1inch Aqua, the same rules run as a SwapVM strategy on the official router. Aqua's virtual balances were a natural fit: the maker's funds never leave its wallet, a stopped side is simply refused at quote time, and re-placing is just updating a price, so it needs no keeper and no gas for re-placement. Since 1inch has no official testnet, we deploy Aqua and the router from source. The trickiest parts were keeping quotes and swaps consistent on Aqua, fitting the strategy parameters into SwapVM's small instruction format, and getting the hook to move its own liquidity safely in the middle of a swap. The backtest replays real swap data from Allium with concentrated-liquidity math, fees and gas.

projects.title: feefifofum (handoff)
projects.description: A market-making vault on 1inch Aqua that quotes over ENS CCIP-Read and fills Uniswap v4 swaps
projects.project_description: feefifofum is a market-making vault on handoff.lol The vault is a 1inch Aqua maker, so its tokens stay in the vault while Aqua records how much of the balance each trading strategy may use. We run two strategies from that one balance. The first sells at prices our signer quotes off-chain. Solvers get a quote by resolving the ENS name quote.feefifofum.eth, which uses CCIP-Read to fetch a signed quote from our gateway, and they fill it through the Aqua SwapVM router. The second strategy backs a Uniswap v4 pool that has no liquidity deposited in it, and a hook fills each swap from the vault during the swap transaction. Because both strategies draw on the same balance, their combined allowances can be larger than the balance itself. That lets the vault serve several markets without splitting its capital between them. A per-token leverage setting caps the total, and the vault rejects any new strategy that would push commitments past it with an OverAllocated error. Quotes are valid for 30 seconds and the contract refuses to fill an expired one, so a solver can't trade against a stale price. All of this ran live on Sepolia, with a transaction for each step: two strategies funded from one balance, a third rejected for going over the limit, a quote found through ENS and filled, and a v4 swap filled from the vault. The web app at https://handoff.lol/app/impecc/fee-fi-fo-fum lets anyone connect a Sepolia wallet, request a quote through ENS, fill it, and swap on the v4 pool. This is a Continuity entry. The existing project is handoff.lol (running on xmbl infra), where AI agents pick up and coordinate tasks. handoff agents built feefifofum during the event, and four of them operate it: fee sets prices from Chainlink, fi deploys strategies and signs quotes, fo routes orders to whichever venue pays more, and fum manages the leverage limits. https://handoff.lol is a communications platform for distributed agents to collaborate, providing features and tools that keep agents available and responsive -- in realtime.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built and tested with Foundry, deployed on Sepolia and verified on Sourcify with exact matches. CastleVault is the Aqua maker. It holds the tokens and ships SwapVM programs to Aqua, which keeps a virtual balance for each one. The vault tracks the total committed per token and reverts a new ship with OverAllocated if that total would exceed the balance times the leverage setting. The RFQ strategy uses PriceExtruction, a custom SwapVM instruction we wrote. The taker passes an EIP-712 quote and its signature in the swap's taker data. The instruction checks that the quote matches the strategy, the token pair and the size limit, that it hasn't expired, and that the vault's current signer signed it, then sets the output amount from the quoted price. Rotating the signer on the vault invalidates every outstanding quote. The same view function answers both the router's quote call and its swap, so a quote can't disagree with the fill. OffchainQuoteResolver is the resolver for quote.feefifofum.eth. A text lookup for a key such as quote:USDC:WETH:500000 reverts with OffchainLookup (ERC-3668). Our gateway returns the signed quote, and the resolver verifies the gateway's signature in the callback. It works through ENS's UniversalResolverV2, so a standard getEnsText call in viem returns the quote without any custom client code. CastleJITHook is a Uniswap v4 hook that uses beforeSwap with a returned delta. We mined its address so the low bits match its permission flags. The pool it's attached to has no LP liquidity. On each swap the hook prices the trade from the vault's second strategy, fills it through Aqua as a SwapVM taker, and settles with the PoolManager in the same transaction. The hook reads the strategy slot on every swap, so we can replace the strategy (for example, to re-center its price) without touching the pool. The off-chain part is a Node service. It is the CCIP-Read gateway, exposes MCP tools that solvers can call for quotes, fills and routing, and streams events over SSE to the web app. Four handoff agents run it. fee sets the mid price and spread from Chainlink ETH/USD, fi compiles and ships the strategies and signs quotes, fo routes UniswapX-format orders to the RFQ or the v4 pool depending on which pays more, and fum sets leverage and caps. A handoff.lol app has to be a single script under 100 KB, and a minimal viem bundle was over 300 KB. So we wrote a small dependency-free library with its own keccak, ABI encoder and CCIP-Read client. We tested it against viem on random inputs, and on a Sepolia fork, where it fills quotes and swaps through a simulated wallet. To keep testnet gas low, we rehearsed the full sequence on a Sepolia fork against the deployed contracts, then ran it once live. The contracts have unit, invariant and fork tests. AI_USAGE.md in the repo lists which agent wrote each part and what the human operator decided.

projects.title: Entrotter
projects.description: A time machine for onchain decisions: compare Uniswap outcomes, gas and reasons to act or hold.
projects.project_description: Entrotter is a local-first time machine for onchain decisions. Compare four Uniswap actions from the same pinned Ethereum state: a proposed swap, a reduced swap, a strict minimum-output trial, and holding. Actual local Anvil execution yields receipts, gas, balance changes and explicit proceed/hold reasons. In the measured example, 0.2 WETH succeeds but exceeds the 0.1 WETH spending cap; 0.1 WETH receives 370.556838 USDC within the constraints; the strict-minimum trial reverts and spends gas; holding sends no transaction. The updated UFO-themed experiment console integrates this comparison into Entrotter's root website, with browser-only report import, exact evidence and a local command builder. The new screenshots and supplemental silent walkthrough show this version. The updated root website is now live. Website PR #13 was merged as d44af5d01f692e177af055338202695e5930c95f; Pages deployment succeeded, and the public files match the tested source. Website: https://entrotter.github.io/ . Supplemental video: https://github.com/entrotter/entrotter/releases/tag/tokyo-continuity-demo . The optional official video field is omitted because the supplemental recording has no spoken audio. Continuity Track: the broader Entrotter concept, existing codebase and purple UFO artwork predate Tokyo. New comparison functionality and the integrated root UI extend the existing repositories. Earlier code, artwork and recordings are not claimed as newly created. Engine: https://github.com/entrotter/engine/tree/42204e0c8091143e08f9f6525cbfebde741fb74a/tokyo . Viewer: https://github.com/entrotter/entrotter.github.io/tree/771670917494a4ae0d05a9cced240141e4bdf792 . Disclosure: https://github.com/entrotter/entrotter/tree/docs/tokyo-continuity/submission/tokyo2026 . Engine PR #25 and coordination PR #49 remain review branches; website PR #13 is merged and the root update is deployed. Codex authored/assisted the implementation, UI, tests, documentation and media under the owner's specification and decisions. No runtime LLM is used. This is local decision testing, not a forecast, historical market replay, or profit claim. This entry seeks Uniswap partner prizes only.
projects.how_its_made: Python's standard library and Foundry 1.8.3 power the comparison runner. An allowlisted read-only RPC proxy supplies Ethereum block 23,000,000, pinned by hash, to a process-owned loopback Anvil. The runner verifies contracts and decimals, discloses artificial funding and impersonation, wraps WETH and approves the exact input. Each alternative restores one snapshot and checks balances, nonce, allowance, pool slot0 and liquidity. Explicit timestamps make setup receipts reproducible. The integration uses Uniswap v3 SwapRouter exactInputSingle and factory pool lookup. Receipts, gas and WETH/USDC/ETH deltas feed deterministic spending/output/gas checks. A clean extraction reproduced receipts and deltas; 24 comparison unit/report tests and five real archive/lifecycle checks passed. We fixed timestamp drift and disclose that Anvil's local state root is uncomputed. The smaller swap used slightly more gas, a measured tradeoff retained in the evidence. Plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript integrates the comparison into the existing root website and preserves the earlier v0.1 explorer. The validator checks report digests, arithmetic, receipts and calldata. The root update passed 11 Python site checks and 29 Node report checks, plus desktop/mobile browser checks for imports, malformed data, downloads, command input, legacy reports, keyboard navigation and reduced motion. The interface uses the existing UFO artwork with new orbital visuals. No transaction runs from the website. Prior work, AI assistance, specifications and limitations remain disclosed.

projects.title: Proof of Promise
projects.description: Trust between strangers with minimal proof and maximum privacy.
projects.project_description: Proof of Promise is a privacy-preserving trust layer for interactions between strangers. Today, when two strangers need to trust each other, the default solution is often to exchange more personal information: names, phone numbers, social accounts, IDs, or even passports. In many everyday situations, however, this is far more information than is actually needed. Proof of Promise is built around a simple idea: trust should require only the minimum proof necessary. With Proof of Promise , a person can prove that they are a real, unique human through World ID and make a verifiable promise without revealing their identity or unnecessary personal information. The focus is not on proving who someone is, but on proving that a real human made a specific commitment. For example, imagine Bob is attending ETHGlobal Tokyo and his laptop is about to run out of battery. He asks Alice, a complete stranger, to borrow her charger and promises to return it in two hours. Bob creates a “Promise to Return” in the app, verifies through World ID, and generates a QR code. Alice scans the QR code and accepts the promise.
