projects.project_description_markdown:
Writing a fully collateralised option today means locking the collateral in a protocol before anyone buys. The LPs with the most depth will not hand over custody, so option books stay thin.

VexiHakari turns 1inch Aqua into an options vault. An AquaVault is a shared vault whose own address is the Aqua maker: anyone deposits AAPL and USDG for shares, and the vault ships that one balance, as virtual balances, to two strategies at once. The first is an AquaWriter, an Aqua app that posts covered calls and cash-secured puts across a whole board of strikes and expiries. Posting moves nothing; when a buyer buys, Aqua pulls exactly the collateral of the contracts sold, inside the buyer's transaction, and at a buyback or at expiry Aqua pushes it home into the same strategy. The second is a SwapVM spot pool on the same balance, optionally concentrated with XYCConcentrate, which earns spot fees while the options wait.

The two must not sell the same token twice. ExposureGuard, a custom SwapVM instruction, shrinks the spot pool to what open option orders have not promised, at the same price, so a buyer who sees option depth can always fill it. It runs as an opcode on our router and, through SwapVM's Extruction, on 1inch's already-deployed router with no redeploy. DeltaSkew, a second instruction, leans the spot price against the delta the option book added.

In the trading app, every option is priced when it trades, never stored: VaultPricer computes Black-Scholes from the spot of the vault's own SwapVM pool, the clock and a volatility per expiry, with a spread and an inventory lean, bid and ask. A spot trade or a tick of time reprices the whole board with zero transactions. One MiniBook collects every vault's quotes; the app shows them as one book and routes each fill to the cheapest vaults first. Longs and shorts are ERC-1155 tokens in the wallets; settlement is physical, from Chainlink on mainnet.

A price read from a pool a taker can move is a price a taker can fake. We proved it on a fork of Robinhood Chain mainnet: in one transaction, a holder of 10 calls pushed the vault's pool 59%, sold the calls back at the pushed bid and pushed the pool back, taking 2,009.29 USDG over the fair bid of 114.96 for 58.81 USDG of swap fees. So the book is guarded by HAKARI (秤), its price layer on Uniswap v4. HAKARI started at this event as our study of what it costs to fake a v4 price: on Robinhood Chain's stock-token weekend of 2026-08-30, while minting was closed, pushing the HIMS/USDG pool 10% cost 12 USDG in fees, and later that night the pool stood at 54.50 against a Friday close of 28.84.

In VexiHakari, HAKARI does three things. First, an anchor: UniswapAnchoredPricer reads the v4 pool on the same pair through v4-core's StateLibrary before every ask and bid and refuses to quote when the vault's spot is more than 3% away; the round trip above then reverts, and the holder can only sell at the fair bid. Second, a band: StabilityBandPricer centres a band on the TWAP of a v4 pool that carries HAKARI's truncated-oracle hook, sizes it from realised volatility (the public repo uses a fixed, configurable 5% half-width), and tapers the book toward its edge (fewer contracts per trade, a wider spread) until it stops quoting past it. On the fork the same round trip reverts Paused(OutsideBand); inside the band the gain is bounded, derived and fuzz-tested: a push that moved the vault's spot 0.79% earned 10.40 USDG on ten calls, against 15.40 with the plain pricer. Third, settlement: HookTwapExpiryPrice settles a series on the hook's five-minute TWAP ending at expiry and refuses a window outside the band drawn before expiry, so a push at expiry only delays settlement to the next window (a +20% push is refused, and one window later the series settles at the honest price). It is for underlyings with no Chainlink feed (meme tokens) or a closed market (stock tokens on a weekend).

It runs on Robinhood Chain testnet 46630 with a public trail: a trading app with Create vault, Deposit, Spot swap, Buy and Sell back; shared vaults; two v4 AAPL/USDG pools, one with HAKARI's hook; the anchor, the band, and a book that settles on the hook's TWAP every 15 minutes. Every claim above has a fork test on Robinhood Chain mainnet 4663 against canonical Aqua, the deployed SwapVM router, the real TSLA/USDG v4 pool and Chainlink's TSLA feed.

That trading app is the Demo. The public repo, vexi-v1/vexi-hakari, holds the Aqua and Uniswap integration built at this event, with a wallet maker and fixed-premium quotes in place of AquaVault, VaultPricer, MiniBook, the anchor pricer and the Chainlink adapter (docs/extraction.md). Vexi existed before the event; this Continuity entry is the Aqua and Uniswap integration built during ETHGlobal Tokyo 2026 (docs/history.md).

projects.title: Mynachat
projects.description: Join a patient group by proving your diagnosis from Myna Portal, without revealing anything else
projects.project_description: Online patient groups can be a lifeline for people with rare diseases. They offer a community for sharing timely, valuable information, and provide emotional support and solidarity during difficult times. However, many patients would rather stay anonymous, and that forces a tradeoff. A public group can draw in people who don't have the disease, or who have conflicting interests, such as salespeople. A trusted private group is safer, but it is hard to find. It also needs someone to review each applicant, and that reviewer ends up holding sensitive medical information that could be misused. In short, online patient groups also have a trust problem. Mynachat is a permissioned message board where people with rare diseases can find each other and prove they belong, without revealing anything more about themselves.
projects.how_its_made:
Proving facts from the government portal (TLSNotary). Japan's Myna Portal has no API or signed data export, so we use TLSNotary's MPC-TLS. A Chrome MV3 extension (tlsn-wasm) acts as the prover and a Rust service (tlsn alpha.15) acts as the verifier. Together they run the TLS session with myna.go.jp using the patient's own login cookie, so the verifier knows the response really came from the government server. The patient reveals only the request line and one matching field. That field can be a prescribed drug name, a 指定難病 (designated intractable disease) certification, or a medical subsidy certificate (PMH). The cookie and the rest of the medical record stay hidden. A shared Rust criteria crate checks the revealed field against each group's rules in groups/catalog.json. A proof takes about 2 seconds in the browser, and we tested it against production.
One account per human (World ID 4.0). At signup the user verifies once with IDKit using the My Number Card credential. This is a World ID 4.0 credential requirement, and legacy proofs are turned off. After that they log in with a passkey. The World ID nullifier for the account action allows one account per person. Actions get a per-deployment prefix, so dev and production don't use up each other's proofs. Joining a group takes only the Myna proof, and the member picks a display name for that group. No real name, email or wallet is ever collected. Users can optionally link a World ID session, which lets them recover their account on a new device and register a new passkey. Board polls are secret ballots with one vote per person, enforced by a separate World ID action for each poll.
Web app. A Next.js app backed by SQLite (sql.js). It includes:
signup, login and recovery
enrollment for each group
a message board with threads, quoted replies, reactions and polls
disease search across all of ICD-10, with a waitlist for conditions that have no group yet
Japanese and English versions, including a live selective-disclosure demo on the landing page It's deployed on Fly.io. Audit report. Each proof produces a report that combines the verifier's record with the prover's view, with cookies masked. The verifier's record covers the TLS handshake, certificate chain, cipher suite, disclosed ranges and criteria verdict. The report checks that both sides saw the same revealed bytes, that the hidden bytes stayed hidden, and that the cookie was never revealed. It can be downloaded as a single HTML file.

projects.title: Truth Skills
projects.description: The first honest feedback loop for AI skills: graded from real usage, one World ID-verified human
projects.project_description:
Truth-Skills: the first honest feedback loop for AI agent skills The problem
AI agent skills (Claude Code skills, skills.sh, SkillsMP…) are multiplying fast, but nobody knows which ones actually help. Today the only quality signals are install counts and GitHub stars, and both are easy to fake. Even the official find-skills skill tells agents to trust a skill if it has "1K+ installs", comes from a "reputable source" or has "100+ stars". None of that says whether real people succeeded with the skill. Skill authors have the same blind spot: they never learn that users struggled, so skills don't get better. The solution
Truth-Skills is an MCP server that turns everyday agent usage into verified, honest feedback. Connect once with World ID. When you add Truth-Skills to Claude, you sign in with World ID. Your account is tied to a World ID nullifier, so one human gets exactly one account: no bots, no fake accounts, no vote farming.
Your agent grades, you never get interrupted. Connecting gives your agent one ability, the grade_skill tool. Whenever the agent sees you use a skill, it judges from the conversation whether the skill was relevant (+1) or whether you struggled with it (−1). You are never asked "did you like this skill?" and never have to sign anything again.
One human, one vote per skill. Skills are identified by their canonical name, as defined by the skills specification. Each verified human holds a single +1 or −1 per skill, updated as their experience changes. Private or in-house skills are excluded: only public, downloadable skills are ranked. Why it matters
For the first time, skill quality is measured by real outcomes from real, unique humans instead of popularity numbers anyone can inflate. A struggle counts as a −1 because a skill that people struggle with has a poor user experience, and that is exactly what its author needs to hear to fix it. Who benefits Users get a ranking of skills built by verified humans: which skills really work.
Skill marketplaces (skills.sh, SkillsMP…) can replace installs and stars with a trustworthy quality signal.
Skill authors finally get a feedback loop to improve their skills. How it's built
TypeScript and Express, using the official MCP SDK. We run our own OAuth 2.1 authorization server following the MCP Authorization spec: dynamic client registration, PKCE, short-lived JWT access tokens bound to our MCP endpoint, and rotating refresh tokens. World ID 4.0 handles sign-in: a uniqueness proof creates the account, then a World ID session lets the same human come back later without creating a second account. Data lives in Postgres, and codes and tokens are only ever stored as hashes. Users can see and delete their own grades.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack
TypeScript on Node 22, one Express 5 app, with the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @worldcoin/idkit-core 4.3, jose for JWTs, pg on Neon Postgres, and zod to validate config and every request body. Tests run with vitest and supertest against PGlite, an in-process Postgres, so the real SQL migrations run in every test without a database server. How it fits together
Claude Code talks to us in three roles, all served by the same process: Resource server. A stateless Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint (POST /mcp, no Mcp-Session-Id). A request without a token gets a 401 whose WWW-Authenticate header points to our RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata. That is how Claude Code discovers where to sign in. The bearer check runs before the JSON body parser, so unauthenticated bodies are never even parsed.
Authorization server. We run our own OAuth 2.1 server, built on the MCP SDK's router: RFC 8414 metadata, dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), PKCE S256, and RFC 8707 resource indicators. Access tokens are 1-hour HS256 JWTs (typ: at+jwt) whose audience is our /mcp URL, so they are useless anywhere else. Refresh tokens last 90 days, are rotated on every use, and are stored only as SHA-256 hashes, like authorization codes.
World ID sign-in. This is where our authorization server leaves the standard OAuth path (details below). Partner technology: World ID 4.0
World ID offers no OIDC provider, so our authorization server calls World directly and turns a World ID proof into an OAuth token. When Claude Code opens /authorize, we save the OAuth request as a "login request" row in Postgres, a small state machine, and send the browser to our sign-in page: Scan 1: uniqueness proof for the action truth-skills-account-v1. The server signs every proof request with the RP signing key, which never reaches the browser. It forwards the IDKit result untouched to the World Verify API, and creates the account from the returned nullifier. The nullifier is the same for a given human and action, and a unique key in the database makes a second account impossible.
Scan 2: a World ID session. We discovered that World App refuses to produce the same uniqueness proof twice. A returning human therefore can't simply sign in with scan 1 again. So right after signup we open a World ID session, store its session_id on the account and in an httpOnly cookie, and give the user a recovery link. From then on, a single session proof brings them back to the same account. World ID is what makes the whole idea work: "one human = one vote per skill" can't be enforced by installs, stars or email accounts. It also lets the agent grade skills in the background, because the human proved who they are once, at connection time, and never has to sign anything again. Hacky and notable details Sandbox without an Orb. Testing needed the World ID Sandbox app, an invite-code flow to enroll the tester (Selfie Check), and a 24-hour "staging verification window". We open that window from code through the Developer Portal's MCP tool (set_world_id_staging_verification) and send the returned token as x-staging-verification-token, only outside production. The docs barely mention any of this.
Replay protection for proofs. Every World ID request gets a fresh nonce stored on the login request, and the nonce is burned at verify time. A proof can be accepted once, for one sign-in, and only in the right step, otherwise the server answers 409 Login step out of order.
Race-free OAuth in single SQL statements. Issuing a code deletes the login request and inserts the code in one CTE, so one sign-in yields at most one code. Exchanging a code or a refresh token is a single update … where used_at is null returning, so two concurrent exchanges can never both win.
Migrations behind Neon's pooler. PgBouncer in transaction mode leaks session advisory locks, so the migration runner uses transaction-scoped pg_advisory_xact_lock instead.
A bug the tests caught. A forged token returned HTTP 500 instead of 401, because the SDK only maps InvalidTokenError to 401. Claude Code would never have re-authenticated. Every token failure is now wrapped in that error class.
Built as a stack of small PRs, one per step of the OAuth and World ID flow, each green on its own (118 tests at the top of the stack).

projects.title: Bailiff
projects.description: Any keeper can liquidate restricted-RWA loans via Uniswap v4. The RWA never leaves the allowlist.
projects.project_description: Restricted RWA tokens (ERC-3643 style) only move to wallets the issuer has allowlisted. On lending markets like Aave Horizon, seized RWA collateral can only go to the issuer's allowlisted holders. So liquidators must be KYC'd, pre-funded in stablecoins and able to hold the RWA. If that small group is slow or missing, lenders can be left with bad debt. Bailiff splits the trigger from the receiver. Any keeper can call the LiquidationAdapter, even with 0 USDC. In one transaction it sells the seized RWA on a Uniswap v4 permissioned pool, repays the liquidated debt and pays the keeper a USDC bounty. The keeper never touches the RWA. If the sale cannot cover the debt, everything reverts. Bailiff expands the keeper set without expanding the holder set. The issuer keeps control. On the liquidation side it flags one sell-only contract, the adapter, next to the pool's own wrapper, and never the keeper. The token's controls (allowlist, freeze, pause, forced transfer) and the issuer's bounded NAV oracle still apply. Revoke the adapter and the same keeper call reverts in Uniswap's hook. Bailiff is an extra route next to KYC liquidators, not a replacement. The buyer is the pool's allowlisted LP, a KYC market maker in the demo, whose USDC sits in the pool ahead of time. Aave's liquidationCall sends the collateral first and pulls the stablecoin from the caller at the end, with no callback in between. v4 flash accounting lets the adapter sell the RWA before it holds it, so the keeper fronts nothing.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.26 and Foundry on Uniswap v4-core and v4-periphery. No custom hook. The demo runs on an Anvil fork of Sepolia and the pinned tests on a Foundry fork, both at block 11782723, against Uniswap Labs' deployed PoolManager, PermissionsAdapterFactory and PermissionedHooks. My PermissionsAdapter comes from the real factory, and the adapter's constructor checks verifiedPermissionsAdapterOf. Inside one PoolManager.unlock, LiquidationAdapter: previews the exact repay and seize amounts swaps exactly the seize amount of vRWA (the PermissionsAdapter wrapper) for USDC. Flash accounting leaves the vRWA delta open, so it sells collateral it does not hold yet. No keeper capital, no flash loan. before any transfer: reverts if proceeds < repay; bounty = min(surplus * keeperBps / 10,000, the market's 6% bonus on repay); reverts if bounty < minBounty takes the USDC, repays the market, receives the RWA closes the vRWA delta: sync, RWA to the PermissionsAdapter, wrapToPoolManager, settle pays the keeper and pushes the rest to the borrower Notes: msgSender() returns the adapter, so Uniswap's hook checks the adapter, not the keeper. PermissionedV4Router checks allowedHooks and the deployed hook leaves that to callers. The adapter calls PoolManager directly, so it runs the same check (test_adapter_hookNotAllowed). MockRWA3643 (ERC-3643-style: HOLDER, freeze, pause, forcedTransfer; no ONCHAINID) is its own IAllowlistChecker. One issuer registry answers Uniswap's SWAP/LIQUIDITY flags and the token's HOLDER gate. The console's keeper has no swap permission, so it quotes by eth_call on the adapter, then sends with minBounty at 97% of the quote. Known gaps: No NAV execution floor yet: the swap has no price limit. The protocol-side guard is proceeds >= repay; minBounty only protects the keeper's cut. The surplus is pushed to the borrower's wallet, not credited, so a borrower that cannot receive USDC can block its own liquidation. projects.project_description_markdown:
Restricted RWA tokens (ERC-3643 style) only move to wallets the issuer has allowlisted. On lending markets like Aave Horizon, seized RWA collateral can only go to the issuer's allowlisted holders. So liquidators must be KYC'd, pre-funded in stablecoins and able to hold the RWA. If that small group is slow or missing, lenders can be left with bad debt.

Bailiff splits the trigger from the receiver. Any keeper can call the LiquidationAdapter, even with 0 USDC. In one transaction it sells the seized RWA on a Uniswap v4 permissioned pool, repays the liquidated debt and pays the keeper a USDC bounty. The keeper never touches the RWA. If the sale cannot cover the debt, everything reverts.

Bailiff expands the keeper set without expanding the holder set.

The issuer keeps control. On the liquidation side it flags one sell-only contract, the adapter, next to the pool's own wrapper, and never the keeper. The token's controls (allowlist, freeze, pause, forced transfer) and the issuer's bounded NAV oracle still apply. Revoke the adapter and the same keeper call reverts in Uniswap's hook. Bailiff is an extra route next to KYC liquidators, not a replacement.

The buyer is the pool's allowlisted LP, a KYC market maker in the demo, whose USDC sits in the pool ahead of time. Aave's liquidationCall sends the collateral first and pulls the stablecoin from the caller at the end, with no callback in between. v4 flash accounting lets the adapter sell the RWA before it holds it, so the keeper fronts nothing.

Solidity 0.8.26 and Foundry on Uniswap v4-core and v4-periphery. No custom hook. The demo runs on an Anvil fork of Sepolia and the pinned tests on a Foundry fork, both at block 11782723, against Uniswap Labs' deployed PoolManager, PermissionsAdapterFactory and PermissionedHooks. My PermissionsAdapter comes from the real factory, and the adapter's constructor checks verifiedPermissionsAdapterOf.

Inside one PoolManager.unlock, LiquidationAdapter:
- previews the exact repay and seize amounts
- swaps exactly the seize amount of vRWA (the PermissionsAdapter wrapper) for USDC. Flash accounting leaves the vRWA delta open, so it sells collateral it does not hold yet. No keeper capital, no flash loan.
- before any transfer: reverts if proceeds < repay; bounty = min(surplus * keeperBps / 10,000, the market's 6% bonus on repay); reverts if bounty < minBounty
- takes the USDC, repays the market, receives the RWA

projects.title: versu!
projects.description: Hardware-verified rhythm game on chain. Pay 1 USDC for 3 games. Entry fees fund the prize pool.
projects.project_description: versu! is a browser rhythm game with a verifiable Sui leaderboard. Players buy three ranked plays for 1 USDC. A trustable bridge hardware signs gameplay inputs, and a custom GKR proof verifies scores on-chain (Sui). World ID prevents duplicate prize claims; smart contracts split the daily prize pool among the top five.
projects.how_its_made: We built the game with React and PixiJS, using Mysten’s Sui SDK and WalletConnect for payments. BridgeOS (which belongs to the bridge hardware) records and signs USB HID inputs. a Rust prover generates a custom GKR/sumcheck score proof, which Sui Move verifies before recording a score. Sui contracts hold USDC and distribute prizes, while World ID prevent duplicate prize claims. The unusual part is binding a hardware-signed input trace to a proof Sui can verify. The current keys and proof setup are for a demo.

projects.title: Ticket
projects.description: Ticket is a UI for representing Options Trading in a more intuitive way.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: React 19 + TypeScript + Vite, with the chart drawn on a plain HTML canvas. There's no charting library, because the chart is the whole interface. Pricing is Black-Scholes written from scratch. It's deployed on Railway as a static build served by a small dependency-free Node server (server.mjs) with a health check. The Derive TypeScript SDK and ethers handle signing, and MetaMask provides the wallet. Architecture Data layer: the rest of the app only talks to a small MarketSource / Market interface (spot, candles, listed expiries and strikes, IV, quotes). There are three implementations:
Demo: a simulated random-walk market with a volatility smile.
Live: Derive mainnet.
Testnet: Derive's v3 API on Sepolia. Switching is a URL parameter, and the rest of the app doesn't know which one is running. Chart: a canvas that redraws from the current legs and view.
P&L heat map: computed on a grid of (time, price) cells and kept in an offscreen canvas, so it's only recalculated when the legs, prices or view change. The grid is coarser while you drag, so dragging stays at 60 fps.
Break-even line: where P&L crosses zero between grid cells.
Max profit/loss: found over the position's whole life (every expiry and the times in between), not just at the first expiry. That matters for positions with legs on different dates.
Strategy model: turns legs into a P&L function of (price, time), plus greeks, break-evens, chance of profit and max profit/loss. Derive integration (our exchange; not a prize partner at this event) Market data:
Everything goes over Derive's WebSocket JSON-RPC, including requests. Derive's REST endpoints don't send CORS headers, so a browser app can't call them directly.
Ticket loads the instrument list and each expiry's tickers (refreshed every 10 s), plus index price history, and subscribes to the live index.
v2 and v3 use different method names (e.g. get_all_instruments and get_index_chart_data on v3), so there's a small adapter for each.
Pricing that matches the exchange: Derive's own IV is computed against the forward price, and our model prices off spot. So for every listed option we solve for the IV that makes our Black-Scholes reproduce Derive's mark price exactly. The P&L map therefore starts from real exchange prices. Unlisted strikes interpolate IV between their neighbours.
Trading (testnet):
Connect: MetaMask switches to Sepolia and signs a Derive login. The app then generates a session key in the browser, and MetaMask authorises it with one EIP-712 signature (set_session_key).
Key limits: that key can trade on the orderbook and RFQ but can't withdraw, and it expires after 7 days. After that, orders sign without popups.
Review: each leg becomes a limit order on the right tick size and amount step. Derive's order_quote dry-runs every leg (validity, fill, fees) before anything is sent. Orders are then signed and placed one leg at a time, stopping at the first rejection.
Builder code: every order carries a referral code and extra fee, set by environment variable.
The SDK and ethers are lazy-loaded, so the chart doesn't pay for them until you connect.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Ticket: options trading that feels like trading perps

Options are powerful but hard to use. Most options UIs are a grid of strikes and expiries, and you have to picture the payoff in your head. Ticket turns the price chart itself into the order ticket, so building an options position feels as direct as opening a perp.

How it works

The screen is a large price chart. Past price shows as candles; the future side shows every listed expiry. Pick Buy/Sell Call or Put and click anywhere in the future: a leg is placed at the nearest listed strike and expiry. The whole future area is shaded as a P&L heat map over time and price: green where the position makes money, red where it loses, and brighter for bigger P&L.

On top of the map, Ticket draws:

a break-even line;
outlines where P&L is within 5% of the max profit or max loss, traced from the exact P&L right up to expiry;
hatching and tags when a loss (or profit) is uncapped.

Legs can be dragged, and the map morphs smoothly as you move them. A handle between legs drags a whole structure at once (e.g. slide a call spread to a new strike and date while keeping its width).

Compounding and tracking

Stack any number of legs into spreads, condors, calendars or custom shapes. A sidebar shows:

strategy name, net debit/credit, max profit/loss, break-evens, chance of profit and greeks;
presets for common structures, plus full undo and redo.

A Positions tab tracks open positions with live P&L, a P&L sparkline, and progress toward max profit. You can tick several positions to see their combined exposure on the chart together with a new trade.

Draw path

Draw where you think price will go, and Ticket builds the position that pays off along that path. It places a call butterfly on each listed expiry your line crosses, centred on your line's price at that date, with wings sized to the expected move. It then shows what you'd make if price follows your line.

Built on Derive

Live mainnet data: listed expiries and strikes, index price, price history, and each option's mark, bid, ask and implied volatility. Ticket prices with the implied volatility that reproduces Derive's mark, so the map matches exchange prices.
Testnet trading on Derive's v3 API (Sepolia): connect with MetaMask, sign in, and authorise a scoped, 7-day trading key created in the browser. That key can trade but not withdraw, and your wallet key never leaves MetaMask.
Order review: every leg gets a dry-run quote from Derive (validity, expected fill, fees) before signed orders are sent, as market or limit-at-mark. Your Derive positions and open orders appear in the app, and you can close or cancel them.
Builder code: every order carries a Derive builder code and fee.

A demo mode with simulated data works anywhere.


Transparency

AI use: the code was written with Claude Code, working from my direction; every commit is co-authored. I contributed the product concept, feature and design decisions, hands-on testing and bug reports, the Derive and MetaMask setup, and the deployment.
Earlier start: an early UI prototype was started shortly before the official start, and recreated in this repo in the first 9 commits. Everything after that was built during the event.

projects.title: Seikyu
projects.description: Sell unpaid invoices as ENSv2 names that expire on their due date, to World ID-verified investors.
projects.project_description: Small suppliers often wait 60 or 90 days to get paid on an invoice. Seikyu (請求, Japanese for "invoice") lets a supplier sell that receivable now. The invoice itself is an ENS name that expires on the due date, so the on-chain record lives for as long as the debt does and no longer. Issuing is one transaction. It mints an ERC-721 receivable into escrow, deploys an ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver for that invoice with seven text records (amount, currency, debtor, due date, status, token id, issuer), and registers inv-<id>.seikyu.eth in our own ENSv2 UserRegistry with the name's expiry set to the due date. An eighth record, ack, can only be written by the debtor's accounts-payable wallet. That permission is granted through the resolver's Enhanced Access Control and scoped to one key on one invoice, so the debtor acknowledges or disputes the invoice on ENS itself. Before buying, an investor verifies with World ID. The proof is checked server-side, tied to the investor's wallet through the signal, and stored on-chain as a nullifier, so one person gets one wallet and at most three open positions. The market contract then reads ENS before it allows the purchase: the name must still be live and ack must not be "disputed". The supplier receives the discounted price in the same transaction. When the debtor pays in full, the current holder receives face value, the token burns, and the ENS name is unregistered in the same transaction. If the due date passes with no sale, the name expires. If the invoice was sold and is still unpaid, anyone can mark it overdue; that renews the name for 30 days so the record stays readable while the debt is collected. All of this runs on Sepolia against the pinned ENSv2 contracts. Seven invoices covering every lifecycle state are live at https://seikyu.xyz, and 46 Foundry fork tests cover the full lifecycle.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Foundry, Solidity 0.8.27, OpenZeppelin v5.1. We built against a pinned tag of ENS's contracts-v2 repo (sepolia-deployment-2026-09-15) with hand-written minimal interfaces, checked for selector parity against that tag's ABI. The main branch has a different API, so the tag is the only ground truth. InvoiceRegistrar registers each invoice as a subname in our own UserRegistry (deployed through ENS's VerifiableFactory) and deploys one PermissionedResolver proxy per invoice. InvoiceMarket is the ERC-721 receivable plus escrow; the World ID gate and the position cap are enforced in its transfer hook. 46 fork tests run against Sepolia at a fixed block. All three contracts are Sourcify exact-match verified. Frontend: Next.js 15 (App Router), wagmi 2, viem 2, Tailwind 4, deployed on Vercel at seikyu.xyz. ENS records are read through UniversalResolverV2 (resolve with a multicall) and liveness through the registry's getState, so the UI can show a name whose records are still readable after it has stopped being live. World ID: IDKit 4.3 request widget with a server-signed RP context. The verify route hashes the signal with idkit-core's own hashSignal and compares it with the proof before calling /api/v4/verify, because World's endpoint does not check the signal itself. It then enforces environment and credential checks, and an operator wallet relays setVerified(investor, nullifier) on-chain. We designed around Passport and verified a real Passport proof live on Sepolia. The recorded demo runs the Proof of Human preset with legacy v3 proofs allowed, because in the staging Simulator's default v4 mode every test identity shares one nullifier, and a one-person-one-wallet demo needs distinct humans. Things we learned the hard way: (1) The deployed resolver scopes setter roles by record key only, not by name, so isolating the debtor's ack permission to one invoice requires a resolver per invoice. We found no cheaper way. (2) An expired ENSv2 name keeps its resolver storage and can be revived with renew(), so "mark overdue" is an ENS renewal that keeps an unpaid invoice's identity alive for 30 more days. (3) Staging World ID verification needs a 24-hour staging token that is only obtainable through the Developer Portal's MCP endpoint. We open the window there and send the token as a header on every staging verify call. (4) EIP-7702 smart-account EOAs cannot be issuers because the ERC-1155 registry mint rejects them; the issue form warns about it.

projects.title: NFTRanker
projects.description: Human-verified NFT voting with World ID: contextual checks, email-free sign-in, and verified feeds.
projects.project_description: NFTRanker turns NFT discovery into a community decision: people compare two NFTs, choose their favorite, and help shape collection rankings. This submission adds a World ID trust layer to that existing product. The key trust moment happens during rapid voting. When someone makes three same-side vote requests within ten seconds, the backend holds the third request before it can count. The interface offers World ID Proof of Human at that moment. People can also choose Not now and complete the existing security check, or close the prompt without counting the held vote. Successful server-validated verification lets the appropriate voting flow continue while preserving normal server restrictions. A guest who creates an account chooses the NFT again, so a pending guest vote is not silently cast under a new identity. World ID also supports email-free NFTRanker accounts, remembered-browser sign-in, and optional connection to an existing account. Newly accepted votes from signed-in, server-confirmed verified accounts receive a World badge and an app-scoped public alias in the voting feed. Proof of Human supplies the assurance needed for this interaction without requiring a passport or disclosing a real-world identity to NFTRanker. There is no one-person-one-vote quota. Verification does not prove every later vote is manual, and it does not remove all anti-bot controls. The goal is to introduce a useful human trust signal at the point where voting behavior warrants an additional check. Scope and status: NFTRanker and its NFT catalog, pairwise voting, rankings, email login, saved NFTs, and voting history predate this work. The new submission is the isolated World ID service, client components, account and voting adapters, migrations, tests, and documented integration patches. It runs in a local integrated preview; the World ID feature is not yet deployed to the public NFTRanker site. A real World App guest proof and upgrade of that verified guest into an NFTRanker account have been confirmed. A fresh account creation, sign-out, and returning-login phone walkthrough remains to be completed.
projects.how_its_made: The feature is built as a separate Node.js/Express service with persistent SQLite storage, plus React/TypeScript components and narrow adapters for NFTRanker. IDKit Core and the React widget are pinned to version 4.3.0. Vite builds the client library, and the World widget is loaded when needed. The backend creates and signs verification requests, binds each attempt to its server-derived participant and proof context, and validates the complete response with World before saving verification. Guest and account sign-in flows use World session proofs. Returning login requires a fresh proof of the stored session; a browser locator only finds that binding and is not an authentication credential. Attempts expire, cancellations remain cancelled, and replay and concurrency protections are enforced in storage. The host adapter derives identity from the existing application session, checks active accounts and request origins, and communicates with the feature service through an authenticated internal API. The feature service has its own database and does not open the host database. Explicit host migrations support email-free accounts, while the normal host session continues to authorize profile, saved-NFT, and voting-history access. Rapid-vote protection runs before the original vote handler. The third same-side request is held, and request receipts make an authorized retry idempotent. The alternative security-check path releases a hold only after the host server validates its original challenge. Browser flags, failed checks, and service outages cannot authorize a held vote. Feed attribution is captured from trusted server state at vote acceptance, not from a client-supplied World badge. A disposable integration runner applies the documented patches to copied application source and local data. This allows realistic testing without mounting the prototype into production. The current implementation record reports 96 passing automated tests, feature TypeScript and client builds, and an integrated Vite build. Automated provider responses are mocked; the separately confirmed real guest proof is distinct evidence. Cancellation, unchanged vote counts, mobile layouts, and the alternative-check transition have browser evidence. The main integration lesson was that one-time uniqueness actions cannot serve as repeatable guest verification or returning login. We moved those flows to stored World sessions and fresh proofs. Cross-browser account recovery and a full fresh-phone account lifecycle remain limitations. Codex assisted with implementation, tests, and documentation; the repository includes the prompt and scope history.

Guest and account sign-in flows use World session proofs. Returning login requires a fresh proof of the stored session; a browser locator only finds that binding and is not an authentication credential. Attempts expire, cancellations remain cancelled, and replay and concurrency protections are enforced in storage.

The host adapter derives identity from the existing application session, checks active accounts and request origins, and communicates with the feature service through an authenticated internal API. The feature service has its own database and does not open the host database. Explicit host migrations support email-free accounts, while the normal host session continues to authorize profile, saved-NFT, and voting-history access.

Rapid-vote protection runs before the original vote handler. The third same-side request is held, and request receipts make an authorized retry idempotent. The alternative security-check path releases a hold only after the host server validates its original challenge. Browser flags, failed checks, and service outages cannot authorize a held vote. Feed attribution is captured from trusted server state at vote acceptance, not from a client-supplied World badge.

A disposable integration runner applies the documented patches to copied application source and local data. This allows realistic testing without mounting the prototype into production. The current implementation record reports 96 passing automated tests, feature TypeScript and client builds, and an integrated Vite build. Automated provider responses are mocked; the separately confirmed real guest proof is distinct evidence. Cancellation, unchanged vote counts, mobile layouts, and the alternative-check transition have browser evidence.

The main integration lesson was that one-time uniqueness actions cannot serve as repeatable guest verification or returning login. We moved those flows to stored World sessions and fresh proofs. Cross-browser account recovery and a full fresh-phone account lifecycle remain limitations. Codex assisted with implementation, tests, and documentation; the repository includes the prompt and scope history.

projects.title: Rebind
projects.description: An agent job pool that only pays when the buyer and worker are two different humans.
projects.project_description: One person. Two agents. A sale to themselves. Rebind stops that sale from becoming revenue. A buyer agent escrows a reward and a worker delivers the job. Payment requires two different people, verified through sandbox World ID. If one person controls both sides, the work can finish, but the reward stays locked. Try the 40-credit demo: one human on both sides means zero paid. A second human verifies the buyer, and the same delivery gets paid. An on-chain demo enforces the same rule on World Chain Sepolia, with refunds after expiry. Its test tokens and fixture identities are separate from the live sandbox credit pool.
projects.how_its_made: We built the app with TypeScript, Express and viem, with Solidity contracts tested using Foundry. Three.js powers the 3D interface, MetaMask Connect handles wallet connections, and Vercel hosts the app. World ID for Agents supplies the settlement check. Our server starts a sandbox device grant and verifies the returned token's signature against World's JWKS, plus its issuer, audience and expiry. Payment requires delivered work and two verified, different pairwise subjects. Pending or denied requests attach no identity. Client-supplied subjects and differentHumans flags are ignored; settlement is recomputed from stored proofs. On World Chain Sepolia, an ERC-8183 ACP core holds DemoUSD, a test token separate from in-app credits. HumanRegistry stores keccak256(issuer + "|" + pairwiseSubject), keeping raw subjects off-chain. TwoHumansHook gates complete(): matching hashes revert with SameHuman; missing identities revert with Unproven. Refusal leaves the job Submitted and escrow untouched. claimRefund remains available after expiry. Explorer links show both a mined refusal and a successful payout. The credit pool accepts real sandbox World App approvals. The on-chain demo uses registrar-written fixtures; connecting live approvals to the registry is unfinished. Browser-carried state is signed with HMAC-SHA256, and automated tests use Node's test runner. The /flow walkthrough moves no money.

projects.title: Takarabako
projects.description: Takarabako helps turn your leftover travel cash into dollar savings
projects.project_description:
Leftover travel cash becomes dollar savings. Every trip ends the same way: a few foreign banknotes in your pocket. Too little to be worth exchanging, too much to throw away, and useless once you're home. Takarabako (宝箱, "treasure box" in Japanese) gives that cash somewhere to go. HOW IT WORKS FOR A TRAVELER
Sign up with just an email. You get a wallet without a seed phrase or an app, plus a personal ENS name like alice-1a2b.takarabako.eth. For example, at the Takarabako kiosk in Tokyo, scan your QR code and feed in your banknotes. Each note is converted at the live exchange rate and becomes a US-dollar balance on Ethereum, which earns a small base yield. You watch a lacquered treasure box on screen fill with gold as each deposit confirms. You don't need to know anything about crypto: the kiosk does the work, and your cash keeps its value after you fly home. For every dollar deposited you also receive tkCASH, a token worth one US dollar of the banknotes inside that specific machine. tkCASH is created only when a note goes in and destroyed when cash comes out, so the total supply always matches the cash the kiosks hold. WHY YOU CAN TRUST THE MACHINE
The kiosk is a verifiable machine. Its ENS name, tokyo-01.takarabako.eth, publishes the key it signs every note with, and that key was generated on the device itself. A deposit only counts if the signature matches the kiosk's name, so a fake box or a replayed signature can't create money. Every receipt shows "✓ tokyo-01.takarabako.eth". When an operator counts the cash box, the count is recorded on-chain. If it doesn't match, that kiosk stops accepting deposits until a human resolves it. You can always cash out, even from a paused kiosk. WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH YOUR SAVINGS Grow: put your balance to work as 1inch Aqua liquidity. Pick one of three beginner tiers (Steady, Balanced, Bold), each explained in one sentence, or draw your own price range on a chart. Send: pay anyone by their ENS name instead of a hex address. Give: every savings position has its own name, and sending that name hands the whole position to someone else. Cash out: take your money out as cash at the kiosk, or as USDC to your own wallet. Accounts can be verified as one real person with a World ID selfie check. Unverified accounts can move up to $1,000 a day. Verified customers have no daily limit and can log in at the kiosk with World ID. FOR OPERATORS
Every kiosk becomes a verifiable financial machine. A live proof-of-reserve dashboard shows the cash each kiosk holds, how fully tkCASH is backed, the banknotes coming in, daily cash flows, and who holds the token. An AI treasury agent answers operators' questions from live on-chain data and proposes actions (topping up the yield reserve, adjusting the base rate, pausing a kiosk, or adding USDC float). It can't execute anything: hard limits in code reject unsafe proposals, and a human approves every action. The agent also runs automatically when something looks wrong, like a reserve count that doesn't match. Takarabako turns the cash you forgot from your trip into savings you can actually use.
projects.how_its_made:
Takarabako has four parts: a physical kiosk, a Node/TypeScript backend, a Next.js 16 web app, and five Solidity contracts on Ethereum Sepolia (all verified on Etherscan). THE KIOSK (HARDWARE)
A Raspberry Pi 4 with a touchscreen drives a TB74 bill acceptor on its serial port (ICT protocol, 9600 8E1). A Python listener accepts a note only while a customer is logged in. Otherwise it refuses the note and the acceptor hands it back. It also reports unrecognized notes so the screen can tell the customer to try again. A small Node bridge on the Pi turns each accepted note into a deposit and signs it with a key generated on the Pi itself (EIP-712 NoteAccepted: kiosk, amount, currency, session, nonce, time). The Python code never sees account IDs or talks to the backend directly. CONTRACTS (Solidity, Foundry) TakarabakoVault: an ERC-4626-style vault holding each customer's USDC balance, with a base APY that accrues over time. TakarabakoCashReceipt (tkCASH): the cash in the box as a token. The treasury mints it in recordCashIn and burns it in redeem, updating that kiosk's on-chain reserve each time, so supply always equals total reserves. We fuzz-test this in Foundry. attestReserve records an operator's physical count and freezes the kiosk on any mismatch. Transfers between holders require both wallets to be allowlisted, stay under a $500/day limit, and stop when the contract is paused. Minting and burning skip those rules, so redemption is never blocked. Mock USDC and mock ETH (testnet stand-ins), plus mock risk tokens. BACKEND (Node, Express, TypeScript) Postgres for records. Redis with BullMQ for the deposit queue: each deposit is written to Postgres first, then a BullMQ worker credits the vault, mints tkCASH, retries failures, and streams pending to confirmed on the browser over server-sent events. If Redis is down, the Postgres row still records the cash we received, so no note is lost. Notes are converted from local currency to USD using live rates (open.er-api.com), cached for an hour. A fixed-rate override keeps the numbers from moving mid-demo. The backend creates each customer's wallet itself, so every account has a real wallet from its first login. FRONTEND (Next.js 16)
One app serves three audiences: Customer app: a 3D treasure box, yield with a draggable price-range chart, Send (pay by ENS name), History, a personal deposit QR, World ID verification, and Withdraw. Kiosk screen (/kiosk), which runs on the Pi's touchscreen, and a public deposit page (/deposit), where customers log in with their wallet QR or World ID. /ops: the operator dashboard.
Session tokens live in httpOnly cookies, so browser JavaScript never sees them. The treasure box is React Three Fiber + GSAP with custom GLSL shaders, and every animation is driven by real data: notes falling in on deposit.pending, melting into gold on deposit.confirmed, one orbiting gem per open position. Visitors who prefer reduced motion, or have no WebGL, get a plain layout. PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES AND WHAT THEY GAVE US Curvegrid MultiBaas:
Our contract layer and indexer. Every tkCASH write and every approved agent action is built by MultiBaas as an unsigned transaction, signed locally with the treasury key and submitted, so the key never leaves our backend and we don't need a hosted wallet. Saved Event Queries (cash in by kiosk and by note type, holders rebuilt from Transfer events, reserve attestations) power the dashboard. HMAC-signed webhooks, with replay protection, stream every event into Postgres, which feeds the live feed and wakes the AI agent when something looks wrong. One idempotent script (npm run mb:setup) uploads the ABIs, links the contract addresses, saves the queries and registers the webhook. ENS v2:
Our names live under takarabako.eth on the official ENS v2 Sepolia deployment, with our own registry (subnames are ERC-1155 tokens) and resolver, so any ENS-aware app can resolve them. ENS gave us three features: verifiable kiosks (the name resolves to the Pi's key, and the backend recovers the signer and compares), sending money by name, and positions as transferable deeds (aqua-<id>.takarabako.eth). When a kiosk is retired, it's marked as retired in ENS, and notes signed with the old name stop verifying. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM:
Customers provide ETH/USDC liquidity as SwapVM strategies registered in Aqua, using the Aqua and SwapVM SDKs. The advanced mode splits a customer's chosen price range into up to five concentrated strategies. Strategies entirely below the price hold only USDC and strategies entirely above hold only ETH, so a range below the current price becomes a "buy the dip" ladder. Token amounts come from SwapVM's liquidity maths, so every strategy starts at the market price. Because Aqua tracks virtual balances, the treasury can act as the market maker for every customer without moving tokens around. World ID:
A Selfie Check tied to the customer's wallet address. We store the nullifier uniquely (one human, one account), and the same proof also works as a kiosk login. Privy:
Login with Google or an email code in the browser, so travelers never see a seed phrase. Claude:
We use two models for two jobs. Haiku 4.5 explains each beginner yield tier in one sentence, and can never change the tier the customer picked. Opus runs the treasury agent, which calls tools in a loop. It has read tools (vault state, reserve status, treasury balances, MultiBaas event queries) and can only file proposals. The limits (APY ≤ 20%, ≤ $500/day of reserve funding, ≤ 10,000/day of minted float) are enforced in code and checked again at approval time, so a prompt injection can't get past them. If a request is declined, it runs again on Anthropic's fallback model instead of failing. HACKY BITS WORTH MENTIONING 1inch's SDK doesn't list Sepolia, and its hosted Swap API doesn't serve it. We found Aqua's SwapVM router still live at its previous address (v1.0.2) and talk to the contracts directly. Nobody trades on Sepolia, so our positions would never earn fees. We built a demo market maker: every 10 minutes the treasury trades against its own strategies, pulling mispriced ones back toward the live ETH price. Mock ETH is priced off the live ETH/USD rate. The Pi's default serial port can't do parity, which the bill acceptor needs. We disabled Bluetooth to free up the Pi's full serial port. World ID 4.0 isn't in most people's World App yet, so we request the 3.0 Selfie Check. The requested credential level isn't covered by the request signature, so the backend rejects weaker credentials, sandbox proofs in production, and proofs made for a different wallet. MultiBaas's free tier allows only five ABIs, so we designed around exactly five contracts. We started on Uniswap v3 (real LP positions), then moved to 1inch Aqua mid-hackathon. Our Uniswap and Aqua integration notes are in FEEDBACK.md. The kiosk moved from kl-sentral-01 to tokyo-01 on-chain: the old kiosk's reserve can still be cashed out, while its ENS record marks it as retired. Testing: 18 Foundry tests, including the supply == reserve fuzz test, and 78 backend tests (webhook signatures, policy limits, proposal lifecycle, monitor rules, World ID checks).

projects.title: PagoIntent
projects.description: A programmable obligation layer for agentic commerce on Sui.
projects.project_description: A user can say: buy this service for up to ¥3,000, only from a verified merchant, and only release the money when proof of delivery arrives. PagoIntent contacts a merchant, creates a Sui key for them if they do not have one, locks test USDC in a shared escrow, and releases it only when the predicate holds. If the merchant changes the price, the payment is aimed at another address, delivery never arrives, or nobody accepts before the deadline, the funds are not released. They return to the payer.
projects.how_its_made: PagoIntent is a Next.js application with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, connected to a Sui Move 2024 package running on devnet. I treated the blockchain as the core product: the frontend is mainly an interface for interacting with shared on-chain objects through Sui’s gRPC API.

projects.title: ENS Drive
projects.description: Google Drive - style sharing for ENS names: share with a team, not each subname with each person.
projects.project_description: ENSv2 already built the directory tree: every name can have its own registry, so names nest like folders (orbit-dao.eth › protocol › vault). What's missing is the sharing layer. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control (EAC) grants permissions one address on one name, in each folder's own registry, so there is no way to say "everyone on core-devs may manage every name under protocol, including the ones we create tomorrow." Today a team either copies every member onto every name and registry, or routes every action through a shared contract such as a Safe, where members stop acting as themselves. ENS Drive adds that permission layer with Cascade, a relationship-based access control (ReBAC) rule built into EAC itself. A name grants a role to a team contract, like sharing a folder with a group, and the team's members inherit that role on every name below it, checked live on every call: through up to three folders, up to four teams per folder, and teams inside teams. Add someone to a team once and they can manage every name; remove them once and their access is gone everywhere. Nothing is written to the names, and nothing EAC does today is replaced: the only new contract is a subclass of ENSv2's own PermissionedRegistry that overrides its role lookup. The live demo is a shared-drive view on real ENSv2 beta contracts on Sepolia, for a fictional DAO, orbit-dao.eth. A new contributor, alex.orbit-dao.eth, can't edit the protocol's contract names (vault, oracle, bridge). Dragged into core-devs, they can edit all three at once; moved into auditors, a team inside the security council that's shared one folder up on orbit-dao.eth, they still can; turning off "sharing flows into subfolders" takes it away. An attempt to add an always-yes group is refused on-chain. After each action an "On-chain, just now" card says in plain words what the contracts checked, and "Behind the scenes" replays the mined transaction's full call tree. The first, one-folder version is still there in a second tab.
projects.how_its_made: The core is one contract, CascadeSubregistryV2 (contracts/src/CascadeSubregistryV2.sol), a subclass of ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry built against ensdomains/contracts-v2@48b3e2d, the source matching the ENSv2 beta on Sepolia. It overrides EAC's role lookup, _getRoles, the documented hook the stock registry already overrides for approved operators, and its write-side check, _checkRoles. Because both are virtual, every permission check inside ENS's unmodified code runs the new version. It returns the caller's own grants, plus, for each team the registry names, the roles that ancestor registries grant that team on the path down to this registry, if the caller is a member. Cascade doesn't add a check; it changes the answer to the one check ENS already runs. The write-side check is lazy and role-aware: the caller's own roles first (owners pay no external lookup), then one folder at a time; a team is asked about membership only when its grants cover a role still missing, and the walk stops as soon as every requested role is covered. Because inheritance only adds roles, that gives the same yes/no as the full union; a differential fuzz test and a Halmos proof check it. Each level must point back down (getSubregistry on the parent returns the child) before its grant counts, so a registry can't claim a parent that doesn't claim it. Admin role bits are masked off, so members can use a role but never grant it; nothing is inherited at the registry root, so registering names, upgrading, or changing the teams stay native-only. Adding a team needs a dedicated root role and a contract that declares the team interface through ERC-165. projects.project_description_markdown:
ENSv2 already built the directory tree: every name can have its own registry, so names nest like folders (orbit-dao.eth › protocol › vault). What's missing is the sharing layer. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control (EAC) grants permissions one address on one name, in each folder's own registry, so there is no way to say "everyone on core-devs may manage every name under protocol, including the ones we create tomorrow." Today a team either copies every member onto every name and registry, or routes every action through a shared contract such as a Safe, where members stop acting as themselves.

ENS Drive adds that permission layer with Cascade, a relationship-based access control (ReBAC) rule built into EAC itself. A name grants a role to a team contract, like sharing a folder with a group, and the team's members inherit that role on every name below it, checked live on every call: through up to three folders, up to four teams per folder, and teams inside teams. Add someone to a team once and they can manage every name; remove them once and their access is gone everywhere. Nothing is written to the names, and nothing EAC does today is replaced: the only new contract is a subclass of ENSv2's own PermissionedRegistry that overrides its role lookup.

The live demo is a shared-drive view on real ENSv2 beta contracts on Sepolia, for a fictional DAO, orbit-dao.eth. A new contributor, alex.orbit-dao.eth, can't edit the protocol's contract names (vault, oracle, bridge). Dragged into core-devs, they can edit all three at once; moved into auditors, a team inside the security council that's shared one folder up on orbit-dao.eth, they still can; turning off "sharing flows into subfolders" takes it away. An attempt to add an always-yes group is refused on-chain. After each action an "On-chain, just now" card says in plain words what the contracts checked, and "Behind the scenes" replays the mined transaction's full call tree. The first, one-folder version is still there in a second tab.

projects.title: Aquantis
projects.description: Agentic RWA on 1inch Aqua protocol with Quantis QRNG by ID Quantique
projects.project_description: Aquantis is an application that runs trading strategies for Herculis Gold Coin (XAUH) [https://xauh.gold/] on the Aqua protocol, delivered as a Telegram Mini App with a built-in AI agent – a convenient, all-in-one Telegram experience for managing an XAUH gold portfolio. The system is built directly on top of XAUH, an Real-World-Asset (RWA) token that is already deployed and trading on Mainnet, so Aquantis operates against a live, gold-backed on-chain asset rather than a simulated or testnet environment. Herculis Gold Coin (XAUH) is a Swiss gold-backed payment token issued by Herculis Tokens SA [https://herculis.ch/herculis-tokens-sa], where each token represents one gram of 999.9-purity LBMA [https://www.lbma.org.uk/] gold that is refined, audited, stored, and insured in Swiss vaults. XAUH is already live across four networks – Ethereum [https://ethereum.org/], TON [https://ton.org/], TRON [https://tron.network/], and Polkadot [https://polkadot.com/], with JAMTON [https://app.jamton.network/] serving as the bridge connecting TON and Polkadot infrastructure. On Ethereum specifically, it's deployed as a verified ERC-20 token tracked on Etherscan [https://etherscan.io/token/0xa9b17f572341219703Bc951725Bdb3CA756B1A65], with an active XAUH/USDT liquidity pool on Uniswap [https://app.uniswap.org/explore/tokens/ethereum/0xa9b17f572341219703Bc951725Bdb3CA756B1A65] – giving Aquantis a live, tradable market to build its strategies on from day one. A key technical limitation of Aqua, 1inch's self-custodial shared-liquidity protocol, is that it does not natively support fee-on-transfer (FoT) tokens – assets that deduct a percentage on every transfer, so the amount received is less than the amount sent. Because Aqua's core contract and its AquaApps track maker and taker balances based on the amount specified in a swap rather than the amount actually delivered, an unhandled FoT token can desynchronize that internal accounting, breaking pricing logic and putting maker funds at risk; 1inch itself lists "Lack of support for Fee-on-Transfer (FoT) tokens" as out of scope in its bug bounty program, treating it as a known, unaddressed gap rather than a bug to be patched. Solving it matters because Aqua's own stated ambition is to become a venue for real-world-asset trading – letting users swap tokenized gold, equities, and other RWAs directly against each other – and fee-on-transfer mechanics are common in exactly that asset class, so leaving this gap unhandled quietly locks a meaningful share of RWA tokens out of Aqua's strategies. This is where Aquantis comes in: because XAUH is central to the product, Aquantis adds fee-aware transfer handling on top of Aqua so XAUH swaps settle accurately instead of relying on Aqua's default 1:1 transfer assumption. We already have a working prototype of the TMA – the Herculis XAUH Agent – and we're now adapting it to work with 1inch's Aqua Protocol. The agent is designed to support several functions, one of which is trading strategy selection for XAUH: the user picks a strategy from the options the agent presents, and the Herculis XAUH Agent processes that choice by routing it through Aqua Strategies, choosing whichever shipped strategies currently offer the most advantageous terms. In other words, the strategy choice stays with the user and the agent, while Aqua Strategies function purely as the execution layer that prices and settles the trade on-chain. Aquantis integrates ID Quantique's [https://www.idquantique.com/] quantum random number generator (QRNG) to bring true, physically-sourced randomness into two parts of the product. Inside the Herculis XAUH Agent, it is used to randomly assign which of the agent's trading strategies a user runs, so strategy selection can't be predicted or steered by anyone, including Aquantis itself. The more interesting use case is feeding that same quantum randomness into the auction-style strategies makers ship on 1inch's Aqua protocol, giving those auctions a genuinely unpredictable, tamper-resistant randomness source that today simply doesn't exist in that part of the protocol.
projects.how_its_made:
RWA support in the protocol. On the protocol side, the goal is to make XAUH – and any token with non-standard transfer behavior – tradable on Aqua without touching what already works, by treating fee-on-transfer support as an opt-in, backward-compatible layer rather than a rewrite.
First, SwapVM already prices fees through its Fee instruction, with flat, protocol, and dynamic fee types deployed today; we'd add a further, equally first-class "token transfer fee" instruction that a maker can wrap around a swap to declare that the input or output token deducts a fee on transfer and how that fee should be priced, while every other opcode – Controls, XYCSwap, XYCConcentrate, Decay, PeggedSwap, Extruction – and every strategy already built from them keeps running exactly as it does today.
Second, Aqua's settlement layer currently assumes a 1:1 relationship between the amount a push()/pull() call requests and the amount that actually lands, which is fine for standard ERC-20s but wrong for deflationary, fee-on-transfer, or rebasing tokens; reconciling based on the balance delta the token itself produces – checking the recipient's balance before and after the transfer instead of trusting the requested amount – makes settlement correct for XAUH-like assets while staying completely invisible for every token that already behaves normally.
Third, because a taker's input today typically crosses two transfers before it reaches the maker's balance – taker to router, router to maker – a fee-on-transfer token gets taxed twice, leaving the maker short of what the strategy expected; an additional single-hop settlement mode, where the taker's tokens go straight to the maker, or the router simply forwards on whatever amount it actually received rather than the amount originally requested, removes that double deduction, while the existing two-hop path stays the default for every token that doesn't need it. Aqua Strategies as execution layer. This is exactly what we mean when we describe Aqua Strategies as an execution layer: Aqua.sol only tracks virtual balances and access – a strategy is opaque, ABI-encoded bytes from its perspective – while the actual pricing and execution logic lives in SwapVM or a custom AquaApp, which is precisely the separation the Herculis XAUH Agent relies on when it picks "the most advantageous option." Concretely, Aqua's own strategy catalog already gives the agent more than one way to execute the same XAUH swap: a basic constant-product curve (what we're calling the 1D strategy – a single XYCSwap price curve, x·y=k) and a concentrated-liquidity variant (the 2D strategy – the XYCConcentrate opcode, which adds a bounded price range on top of that same curve for deeper depth around the current price). Both are built from the same SDK strategy builder (AquaXYCAmmStrategy.new() for the 1D version, .newConcentrate() for the 2D version), so shipping either one is a matter of parameters, not a different integration. When a user wants to trade XAUH, the agent calls SwapVM's free quote() against every currently shipped strategy that can fill the order – a 1D XYC pool here, a 2D concentrated position there – compares the amountOut each one returns after fees, and then executes swap() against whichever (maker, app, strategyHash) currently prices best; the strategy choice is entirely the agent's, Aqua and SwapVM simply settle whichever one wins. Random number generation in this context. Both of our quantum-randomness use cases plug into that same execution-layer picture. For strategy selection inside the Herculis XAUH Agent, a call to ID Quantique's Quantis QRNG returns a block of true random bytes, which we reduce (modulo, with rejection sampling to avoid bias) to an index into the agent's list of available trading strategies – the agent then executes that strategy the normal way, through whichever Aqua strategy prices best, exactly as described above. For the Aqua side, the SDK's strategy builders already expose a withSalt(...) parameter – salt is meant to be an arbitrary, ideally unpredictable value, which is exactly what a QRNG is for; instead of deriving that salt from something guessable (a counter, a timestamp, a locally-seeded PRNG), we draw it directly from the Quantis QRNG before the strategy is built and shipped, so the resulting strategyHash – and, in a Decay-priced strategy, the auction parameters riding alongside it – carry entropy that no party, including Aquantis, chose or could have predicted in advance. Because this all happens off-chain, in the same AquaProgramBuilder step every maker already uses before calling ship(), it's a drop-in substitution rather than a protocol change.

projects.title: Boss BoostPad
projects.description: Create a token pool and turn it into a boss raid. Fighters swap to attack and share the prize.
projects.project_description:
Boss BoostPad turns a token the creator already holds into a boss raid on Uniswap v4. A normal pool lets people trade, but it gives them nothing to defeat and no shared prize.
In Boss BoostPad, the creator opens the blacksmith, pastes that token, and sets three things: how many tokens go into the pool, the MockUSD volume the raid must reach, and what share of the deposit becomes the prize. Every boss has three fixed stages and the same default portraits. There is no expiry and no way for the creator to cancel the raid. Fighters enter from the garden hub and attack on the battle screen. An attack is a swap through that boss's pools. Each confirmed attack adds to that boss's eligible swap volume. A trade made in some other pool does not count. Holding the token, or sending it to someone else, does not count either. The volume target is three goals, sized 1, then 2, then 3. A 60 MockUSD target means stage goals of 10, 20, and 30. Clearing the first stage starts a shared 60-second cooldown. Clearing the second starts a shared 120-second cooldown. While the cooldown is running, the next attack waits. The sale tokens are already in the pool when the boss launches, and the price follows the pool as people buy. Clearing a stage starts the cooldown. It does not open a second hidden inventory, refill the pool, or reset the price. After the third stage, eligible fighters share the creator-funded prize, paid in the same token. They keep every token they bought during the fight. The claim is a separate reward credit, earned only by that fighter's attacks on that boss. Sending tokens to another wallet does not move that credit. The creator funds the prize up front and cannot take it back. The creator can later add or remove a separate liquidity position to change how deep the pool is. That position sits above the locked launch liquidity, and those changes do not count as attacks or prize credit. The garden hub, the blacksmith workshop, and the battle all run in the browser.
projects.how_its_made: Each Factory boss has a dedicated Uniswap v4 pool with its own BossHook. PoolManager invokes the Hook during boss-pool swaps, so the raid rules apply regardless of which website submits the attack. BossHook accepts swaps only from that boss’s dedicated BossRouter. Other interfaces can use the Router, but cannot bypass its checks. If an attack fails a check, both swaps and all resulting raid credit revert together. Trading the same token in another pool does not earn raid credit. Once the fighter has approved MockUSD, an attack executes in one transaction and one PoolManager unlock. It performs two swaps. The fighter first buys Attack Token in the shared MockUSD supply pool, then spends that Attack Token in the boss pool to buy the creator’s existing token. The Router returns unused MockUSD and Attack Token to the fighter. At launch, BossFactory deploys the boss’s Router, Hook, and collectible contract, takes the creator’s token deposit, escrows the prize in the Hook, and activates the full sale liquidity. Before the boss swap, BossHook verifies the authorized route, current stage, and shared cooldown. After the swap, it records the actual boss-token output, eligible MockUSD volume, and the fighter’s reward credit. Eligible volume counts the share of MockUSD spending attributable to Attack Token used in the boss swap: eligible volume = floor(MockUSD spent × Attack Token spent / Attack Token bought) The boss-token output determines damage and reward credit. No token is burned, and the fighter receives the purchased tokens. The creator’s volume target splits into three additional stage goals in a 1:2:3 ratio. For a 60 MockUSD target, fighters must contribute 10 MockUSD in stage one, another 20 in stage two, and another 30 in stage three. Clearing stage one starts a shared 60-second cooldown. Clearing stage two starts a 120-second cooldown. These pauses give the community time to regroup between phases. The Hook stores the reopening timestamp and rejects attack quotes and execution until that time. All sale liquidity is active from launch. Stage transitions preserve the pool’s price and liquidity, with no additional token allocation or price reset. Cooldowns control raid pacing without guaranteeing equal participation or preventing bots. The documented Boss deployment charges a 0.3% LP fee on each swap. The supply swap charges its fee in MockUSD, and the boss swap charges its fee in Attack Token. Both fees are included in the quoted output. For fully spent inputs, ignoring price impact and rounding, the combined fee-only output reduction is approximately 0.5991%: 1 − 0.997 × 0.997 = 0.005991 Actual output also depends on both pools’ prices, liquidity, execution limits, and unused-input refunds. ETH gas is separate and can still be charged when a submitted transaction reverts. Swap fees accrue to the LP positions. BossFactory charges no launch fee, and the creator funds the prize separately. Boss uses fixed fees and has no fee controller. The optional local demo uses an owner-controlled mock reference to adjust only the boss-pool LP fee. When the pool price is below the reference, the controller raises the fee to make discounted purchases more expensive. When the pool price is above the reference, the fee decreases and can reach zero. The supply-pool fee remains 0.3%. This demonstrates reference-based purchase pricing. It does not track a trustworthy live market oracle, reset the AMM price, or guarantee protection from arbitrage. The browser app uses Next.js and Phaser. Phaser runs the walkable garden hub. At /boostpad, creators inspect token metadata and balances, request a funding quote, approve the deposit, and launch a boss. Before launch, the SDK finds a CREATE2 salt that produces a Hook address with the required Uniswap v4 permission bits. The battle page reads contract state and submits attacks through viem on Base Sepolia. Confirmed contract execution determines whether an attack counts, and the browser displays that result. Factory prize rights are nontransferable credit recorded for each fighter by BossHook. After victory, a claim consumes that credit and pays a proportional share of the creator-funded prize in the creator’s token. The share depends on credited boss-token output, rather than MockUSD spending. Claiming requires no token approval or surrender of purchased tokens. Those tokens remain in the fighter’s wallet, and transferring them does not transfer prize credit. The older standalone demo uses transferable reward-bearing tokens and a MockUSD prize. Factory bosses use per-player credit.
