Fighters enter from the garden hub and attack on the battle screen. An attack is a swap through that boss's pools. Each confirmed attack adds to that boss's eligible swap volume. A trade made in some other pool does not count. Holding the token, or sending it to someone else, does not count either.

The volume target is three goals, sized 1, then 2, then 3. A 60 MockUSD target means stage goals of 10, 20, and 30. Clearing the first stage starts a shared 60-second cooldown. Clearing the second starts a shared 120-second cooldown. While the cooldown is running, the next attack waits. The sale tokens are already in the pool when the boss launches, and the price follows the pool as people buy. Clearing a stage starts the cooldown. It does not open a second hidden inventory, refill the pool, or reset the price.

After the third stage, eligible fighters share the creator-funded prize, paid in the same token. They keep every token they bought during the fight. The claim is a separate reward credit, earned only by that fighter's attacks on that boss. Sending tokens to another wallet does not move that credit. The creator funds the prize up front and cannot take it back. The creator can later add or remove a separate liquidity position to change how deep the pool is. That position sits above the locked launch liquidity, and those changes do not count as attacks or prize credit.

The garden hub, the blacksmith workshop, and the battle all run in the browser.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Each Factory boss has a dedicated Uniswap v4 pool with its own BossHook. PoolManager invokes the Hook during boss-pool swaps, so the raid rules apply regardless of which website submits the attack. BossHook accepts swaps only from that boss’s dedicated BossRouter. Other interfaces can use the Router, but cannot bypass its checks. If an attack fails a check, both swaps and all resulting raid credit revert together. Trading the same token in another pool does not earn raid credit.

Once the fighter has approved MockUSD, an attack executes in one transaction and one PoolManager unlock. It performs two swaps. The fighter first buys Attack Token in the shared MockUSD supply pool, then spends that Attack Token in the boss pool to buy the creator’s existing token. The Router returns unused MockUSD and Attack Token to the fighter. At launch, BossFactory deploys the boss’s Router, Hook, and collectible contract, takes the creator’s token deposit, escrows the prize in the Hook, and activates the full sale liquidity.

Before the boss swap, BossHook verifies the authorized route, current stage, and shared cooldown. After the swap, it records the actual boss-token output, eligible MockUSD volume, and the fighter’s reward credit. Eligible volume counts the share of MockUSD spending attributable to Attack Token used in the boss swap:

eligible volume = floor(MockUSD spent × Attack Token spent / Attack Token bought)

The boss-token output determines damage and reward credit. No token is burned, and the fighter receives the purchased tokens.

The creator’s volume target splits into three additional stage goals in a 1:2:3 ratio. For a 60 MockUSD target, fighters must contribute 10 MockUSD in stage one, another 20 in stage two, and another 30 in stage three. Clearing stage one starts a shared 60-second cooldown. Clearing stage two starts a 120-second cooldown. These pauses give the community time to regroup between phases. The Hook stores the reopening timestamp and rejects attack quotes and execution until that time. All sale liquidity is active from launch. Stage transitions preserve the pool’s price and liquidity, with no additional token allocation or price reset. Cooldowns control raid pacing without guaranteeing equal participation or preventing bots.

The documented Boss deployment charges a 0.3% LP fee on each swap. The supply swap charges its fee in MockUSD, and the boss swap charges its fee in Attack Token. Both fees are included in the quoted output. For fully spent inputs, ignoring price impact and rounding, the combined fee-only output reduction is approximately 0.5991%:

1 − 0.997 × 0.997 = 0.005991

Actual output also depends on both pools’ prices, liquidity, execution limits, and unused-input refunds. ETH gas is separate and can still be charged when a submitted transaction reverts. Swap fees accrue to the LP positions. BossFactory charges no launch fee, and the creator funds the prize separately.

Boss uses fixed fees and has no fee controller. The optional local demo uses an owner-controlled mock reference to adjust only the boss-pool LP fee. When the pool price is below the reference, the controller raises the fee to make discounted purchases more expensive. When the pool price is above the reference, the fee decreases and can reach zero. The supply-pool fee remains 0.3%. This demonstrates reference-based purchase pricing. It does not track a trustworthy live market oracle, reset the AMM price, or guarantee protection from arbitrage.

The browser app uses Next.js and Phaser. Phaser runs the walkable garden hub. At /boostpad, creators inspect token metadata and balances, request a funding quote, approve the deposit, and launch a boss. Before launch, the SDK finds a CREATE2 salt that produces a Hook address with the required Uniswap v4 permission bits. The battle page reads contract state and submits attacks through viem on Base Sepolia. Confirmed contract execution determines whether an attack counts, and the browser displays that result.

Factory prize rights are nontransferable credit recorded for each fighter by BossHook. After victory, a claim consumes that credit and pays a proportional share of the creator-funded prize in the creator’s token. The share depends on credited boss-token output, rather than MockUSD spending. Claiming requires no token approval or surrender of purchased tokens. Those tokens remain in the fighter’s wallet, and transferring them does not transfer prize credit. The older standalone demo uses transferable reward-bearing tokens and a MockUSD prize. Factory bosses use per-player credit.

projects.title: Reel Deal
projects.description: Relief fund for aquaculture farmers paid in JPYC upon trigger of specific environmental conditions
projects.project_description: Reel Deal is a relief fund for aquaculture farmers in Japan. Scallop, oyster and hoya farmers in fishing towns like Kesennuma can lose a whole season's harvest when the sea gets too warm, or when toxin levels are too high and shipping is banned. To protect their income, Reel Deal lets anyone donate to the fund or buy from a seafood marketplace where part of every sale goes into the fund. When public data shows a heatwave or shipping ban has hit a farm, the fund automatically pays the farmer in JPYC.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity, Foundry, OpenZeppelin v5 on Sepolia. Apps: Next.js 16 LINE mini-app (Drizzle + Postgres) on Railway, and an Astro + Solid.js + Storybook operator dashboard on AWS EC2. Data: Python FastAPI  ingesting JAXA satellite sea-surface temperature and Miyagi prefecture toxin-ban notices, with PostGIS for aquaculture plots. ENS (v2): individual plot registries (umi.eth → karakuwa.umi.eth → p1213-001..015). Each season the farmer receives a non-transferable, expiring slot from the coop,  and the pool reads it on-chain to know who to pay. World ID: IDKit v4 proofs. Selfie Check for level 1. It stops one person from claiming for too many plots. Caps are 3 vs 12 units per human, and only nullifiers go on-chain. JPYC (Ethereum Sepolia): donations in and payouts out of the ReliefPool. EIP-3009 gasless transfers mean farmers never need ETH. Curvegrid MultiBaas: indexes ReliefPool, HumanRegistry and JPYC events, powers the donor dashboard, and sends an HMAC-signed webhook that triggers the LINE payout message. Jev (TypeSafe AI via OpenRouter): a decision model used as a safety gate for payouts. Unsure triggers go to the co-op for human review, and it can never send money itself. It also routes farmers' LINE messages to fixed templates. Reown: AppKit + SIWE so anyone without LINE can connect their own wallet. LINE: LIFF + Messaging API. A wallet is created automatically when a farmer logs in, and payout notifications arrive as LINE messages. Farmer onboarding flow: add the co-op's LINE account → open the mini-app → LINE Login → wallet created automatically (one per LINE user) → request this season's slot for their plot → licence holder issues the non-transferable "2026" ENS slot to their wallet → verify with World ID (Selfie Check, optionally upgrade to level 2) → wallet bound in HumanRegistry → enrolled for payouts. Payout flow: Donors / marketplace sales → JPYC into ReliefPool → data pipeline sees a threshold crossed → Trigger signed 2-of-3 (pipeline, co-op, science) + Jev check → pool checks ENS slot + World ID → JPYC paid to farmer → MultiBaas webhook → LINE notification. Hacky bits: a fork-mode e2e (bun run e2e) replays the whole payout against a fork of live Sepolia in under a minute. Then we did it for real and paid a verified farmer ¥10,000 JPYC for the 2026 Karakuwa scallop shipping ban.

projects.title: OddsFlow
projects.description: Bet on many prediction markets with one balance, spent only when someone takes the other side.
projects.project_description: OddsFlow lets you bet on many prediction markets with the same money, and that money is only spent when someone takes the other side. The maker places fixed-price limit orders on as many Seer markets as they like, such as "YES at 0.40 here, NO at 0.25 there", and the same sDAI balance backs all of them at once. Through 1inch Aqua, each order is a strategy with its own virtual balance, and all of them draw on the maker's one real wallet balance. The sDAI never leaves the wallet: when a buyer takes the other side, only that order fills, and only for what it needs, in a single transaction. The maker's sDAI and the buyer's mint the outcome tokens together, each side gets its own, and every other order keeps running on what's left. Aqua's official router has no fixed-price instruction, so OddsFlow adds three SwapVM opcodes of its own. FixedPriceSwap trades at exactly the price the maker signed. OnlyUnresolvedCondition and OnlyUnansweredQuestion stop every order the moment the market resolves or anyone posts an answer on Reality.eth, so nobody can fill a maker with information from after the event. The rule that cannot fail: the maker's sDAI never leaves the wallet unless their tokens arrive in the same transaction, at their price.
projects.how_its_made: The app is Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript, with wagmi and viem for every read and write. It never holds a key. Order encoding lives in a shared packages/core, and a Foundry test writes a fixture that Vitest rebuilds byte for byte (program, strategy and hash). So the order the web shows is provably the order it publishes; that parity test caught a real divergence before the UI existed. The market list comes from Seer's public API, validated with Zod and cached for 5 minutes on the server. The Alchemy RPC stays server-only. The chain layer is the official 1inch Aqua on Gnosis Chain, untouched. On top of it we redeployed AquaSwapVMRouter v1.0.2 with three opcodes appended after the official set, so no official index moves. FixedPriceSwap takes the price as an argument instead of reading it from balances, which is why LimitSwap can't price an Aqua strategy. OnlyUnresolvedCondition reads Conditional Tokens, and OnlyUnansweredQuestion reads Reality.eth's getFinalizeTS. The router's ownership was renounced in the deploy run, so nobody can call rescueFunds. ship and dock are always called by the maker's own wallet, so the maker is always the user, never an OddsFlow contract. The one piece of glue is OddsFlowTaker. It sweeps up to 10 orders best-first, and inside SwapVM's preTransferInCallback it splits the maker's pulled sDAI plus the buyer's through Seer's GnosisRouter. That mints YES/NO/INVALID in the same transaction, and SwapVM reverts with AquaBalanceInsufficientAfterTakerPush if the maker's tokens don't arrive. It uses transient storage for its state and a callback guard, has no owner, holds nothing between transactions, and makers never approve it. Where the wallet supports EIP-5792, approve plus buy (or approve plus ship for several orders) goes out as one sendCalls batch, with a sequential fallback. Aqua has no testnet, so everything is tested on a Gnosis mainnet fork against the real Aqua and a real Seer market. That's 55 Foundry tests: every forbidden path reverts, SwapVM's own CoreInvariants run against our opcode, and a fuzz test shows the maker never pays more than their price. Contract coverage is 97%. A local script spins up the same fork with OddsFlow at fixed addresses, funded accounts and seeded orders, so the whole flow runs end to end in the browser without a wallet extension.

projects.title: Otomo
projects.description: Human-verified AI companions with ENS names, own wallets and 1inch Aqua savings.
projects.project_description: AI assistants forget you, cannot hold money, and anyone can spin up thousands of them. If an AI is going to run errands, hire other agents and move money for a person, we need to know a real human is behind it, give the agent a name others can find and trust, and make sure money only moves when that human agrees. Otomo ("companion" in Japanese) lets a World ID-verified human welcome up to three AI companions, each with a role (personal or work). Every companion is born with its own encrypted wallet and a non-transferable ENSv2 subname such as sora.otomo.eth. No wallet connection or blockchain knowledge is needed. Birth (World IDKit): the user names a companion, picks a role and verifies with World App. The backend verifies the proof, checks the one-time signal and nullifier, then creates the wallet and registers the ENS name on Sepolia. The same person signing up again is refused, and the app explains that this World ID already has companions and offers sign-in instead. Protected actions (World ID for Agents): anything that moves money (a job request, a reward, an Aqua strategy operation) becomes a pending action and runs only after a fresh World ID for Agents verification. Expired, cancelled, replayed or mismatched approvals execute nothing. Work between companions: sora (personal) asks taro (work) to write an introduction of Otomo. taro accepts, writes and delivers it; sora reviews it, and a separate approval pays 2 mUSDC from sora's wallet to taro.otomo.eth on Sepolia. Savings (1inch Aqua + SwapVM): the companion ships a strategy to the official Aqua registry. Tokens stay in the companion's wallet as virtual balances; a taker swaps through our SwapVM program with a 0.3% fee, moving real tokens; docking stops the strategy. ENS identity: each companion has its own Permissioned Resolver. Text records hold mood, role, skills, siblings and published work reputation, which companions read to find someone to hire. Friendly UI: a soft Three.js room where companions squish, bounce and answer when poked, in English, Japanese, Chinese and Korean. Honest notes: approvals use the World ID for Agents event Sandbox (mocked identity), not production identity assurance. Everything runs on Sepolia with test tokens that have no real value. The video's birth of momo was recorded on a local copy of the production database with a second World action, because the creator's World ID had already been used for the production birth action; the World App verification and the ENS registration are real.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 and TypeScript on Vercel, with Turso (libSQL) for companions, pending actions and strategies. World ID: IDKit 4 with RP signatures. The server issues a one-time birth challenge used as the signal, then verifies the proof via developer.world.org/api/v4/verify, checking action, signal and nullifier uniqueness. Companion limits are keyed by the verified nullifier. Money-moving actions use World ID for Agents OIDC (event Sandbox) with PKCE, nonce and single-use state, JWKS token validation, subject matching, prompt=login / max_age=0 and an auth_time newer than the pending action. A five-minute deadline and an atomic database claim prevent expired or replayed approvals from executing. ENSv2 on Sepolia: companions get subnames through the UserRegistry, each with its own Permissioned Resolver deployed by VerifiableFactory. The role bitmap omits transfer rights, so names can't be moved away. The address record points to the companion wallet; text records (otomo.role, otomo.skills, otomo.siblings, otomo.mood, otomo.reputation) are written by the companion and read by other companions to discover and hire each other. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: we wrote OtomoProgram in Solidity/Foundry (Deadline -> FlatFeeAmountIn 0.3% -> XYCSwap -> Salt) and an order builder. The SwapVM router is redeployed by us (allowed by the rules) against 1inch's canonical Aqua registry 0x1111113CCf1426A8E30e2bfF5E005d929bF6a90a. Aqua let us give companions a savings feature without taking custody of deposits: ship only records virtual balances, and tokens move only when a swap executes. The app checks strategy ownership, receipts and minimum output. Agent logic: a language model (Gemini) turns chat into structured intents validated with zod. The LLM output is never authorization: deterministic policy code decides whether an intent is automatic, rejected (e.g. the work companion cannot move savings) or requires World ID approval. Companion keys are AES-256-GCM encrypted and signed server-side with viem. Gemini also handles translation, speech and Gemini Live voice chat. Three.js renders the squishy companion room. x402 lets a work companion sell a service to other agents. Hacky bits: World's uniqueness proof can only be issued once per action, so later siblings are born from the already verified household session instead of a new proof. We also mapped World's generic errors (e.g. nullifier_replayed) to clear messages in the UI.

projects.title: YieldProof
projects.description: Human-verified RWA yield claims with on-chain attestation and reputation
projects.project_description: YieldProof is an on-chain verification protocol for real-world asset (RWA) yield claims. Issuers submit yield claims with supporting evidence, while independent attestors stake funds and verify the claims. World ID helps establish unique-human attestors and reduce Sybil risk, while ENSv2 gives verified attestors a portable on-chain identity and reputation. Multiple attestations are combined through protocol-defined consensus to produce a transparent, verifiable result on-chain.
projects.how_its_made: YieldProof is built with Solidity smart contracts and a web frontend, with RWA evidence committed through IPFS. The protocol manages claim creation, attestor registration, staking, attestations, consensus, rewards, slashing, and reputation on-chain. We integrated World ID/IDKit into the attestor onboarding flow so unique-human verification is an actual eligibility requirement rather than just authentication. ENSv2 is used to create portable attestor identities and expose reputation such as verification status, trust score, and verified claims. The frontend connects users to the deployed contracts through their wallets and provides the complete claim-to-verification workflow.

projects.title: Opti-om
projects.description: A Web3 marketplace for community-verified GPU optimizations that make local AI faster.
projects.project_description: Our project is a Web3 marketplace for GPU kernel optimizations that help locally hosted AI models generate more tokens per minute on existing hardware. It connects developers who create optimizations, community verifiers who test them, and users who want faster local AI without upgrading their GPUs. Running AI locally gives users more control over their models, data, and operating costs. However, configuring and optimizing those models requires technical expertise. Our goal is to make useful performance improvements easier to discover, evaluate, and install, while rewarding the developers who produce them. projects.title: TipRouter
projects.description: A thin tipping layer for Mastodon, Misskey, Concrnt, and the decentralized social web.
projects.project_description: Decentralized social networks such as Mastodon and Misskey solve an important identity problem: users do not have to depend on a single centralized platform. But the economic layer is still missing. Server operators pay infrastructure and moderation costs, creators have no interoperable way to receive value, and payment destinations exposed by a server still require trusting that server. TipRouter is a thin Web3 payment-routing protocol designed for existing decentralized and federated social services. A service host publishes its supported payment destinations and routing fee at /.well-known/tip-router , while users publish their own payment destinations in their profiles. A TipRouter client discovers both sides, finds a blockchain supported by both the user and the host, and routes a tip between them. Our first demo shows that this can work with existing services such as Mastodon and Misskey without moving the social network itself onchain. Entering a profile URL is enough to discover the user’s payment destination and the payment destination of the server hosting them. Concrnt, our existing decentralized social network, demonstrates a stronger version of the same protocol. Concrnt users already hold their own identity keys and cryptographically sign their posts and reactions. TipRouter payment destinations can therefore be published through the same signed mechanism, allowing clients to verify that a destination was actually authorized by the user instead of simply trusting the server. On top of this, we built Super Reactions: a fast tipping experience where a user selects an amount, authenticates with Face ID, and sends a visually prominent paid reaction to a post. Underneath the simple UX, TipRouter discovers, verifies, routes, and settles the payment between the creator and the service host. Before ETHGlobal Tokyo, Concrnt already existed as a decentralized social network but had no Ethereum integration or payment layer. During the hackathon, we built TipRouter, added blockchain key derivation to Concrnt, deployed the payment contracts, implemented signed payment destinations, created the Super Reaction UX, and built the Mastodon/Misskey interoperability demo.
projects.how_its_made: TipRouter is intentionally designed to keep the Web3 layer as thin as possible. Each participating service exposes a small JSON document at /.well-known/tip-router . For example, it contains a protocol version, a host fee in basis points, and payment destinations for supported networks: {"feeBps":500,"tipjars":{"ethereum":"0x...","sui":"0x..."},"version":1} Users expose their own per-chain payment destinations through their social profile or, in Concrnt, through a signed document. The client takes the intersection of the networks supported by the user and the host and selects a compatible chain. Settlement is handled by deliberately small TipRouter contracts, roughly 100 lines each, implemented separately in Solidity and Move. The contract atomically accounts for the creator and host portions of a tip using a pull-based model, so recipients can withdraw their accumulated balance later. We deployed the Ethereum implementation to Sepolia and implemented Sui as a second-chain example to validate that the protocol itself is not tied to a single network. For the Mastodon/Misskey demo, we treat a profile URL as the user entity. Fetching arbitrary federated profiles directly from a browser frequently fails because of CORS, so we built a Cloudflare Worker that resolves the remote profile and extracts the TipRouter information for both the user and their host. This lets an existing federated social account participate without requiring a custom blockchain integration in Mastodon or Misskey itself. Concrnt provides the stronger verification model. Concrnt already has an identity key system where users cryptographically sign every post and reaction. We publish TipRouter payment destinations using the same signed-document mechanism, which means a client can verify that a payment address was authorized by the user rather than merely asserted by their server. The Concrnt desktop app is built with Tauri. Private keys never enter the WebView and exist only inside the Rust layer. When the frontend requests a signature, the Rust side invokes Face ID or the platform biometric authentication mechanism and signs only after successful authentication. A Super Reaction roughly follows this flow: Click → select amount → create a signed Concrnt document → construct a TipRouter transaction bound to that document’s hash → commit the document → settle the tip. One of the most technically important decisions was what we chose not to put onchain. Instead of recreating social identities, posts, reactions, or ActivityPub on a blockchain, TipRouter starts from an action that already exists in the social layer and anchors only the information required for payment and settlement. The goal is to use as little Web3 as possible while still gaining verifiable ownership and programmable payments. This is also why TipRouter can work across very different trust models: Mastodon and Misskey can use it as a lightweight payment-discovery layer today, while a self-sovereign system such as Concrnt can additionally provide cryptographic verification of the user’s payment destination. No partner SDK is required by the core protocol; the multi-chain design is part of TipRouter itself.

projects.title: AquaTerm
projects.description: Fixed-rate term JIT lending with shared collateral across maturities, powered by 1inch Aqua
projects.project_description: AquaTerm is a fixed-rate, fixed-maturity just-in-time lending protocol built on 1inch Aqua. Borrowers can quote debt across multiple maturities without pre-locking separate collateral for every open order, while suppliers can quote the same liquidity across multiple term markets. Because Aqua orders use virtual balances rather than custodial escrow, uncommitted balances remain available until a match executes. That means both borrowers and suppliers can keep the same collateral and liquidity active in other Aqua strategies and continue earning yield on them. Collateral in the borrower's wallet remains free to use in Aqua strategies until it is actually pulled at fill time. AquaTerm only counts collateral already deposited in the app toward LTV; wallet balances enter the portfolio only when a match requires a top-up. The borrower specifies a maximum resulting portfolio LTV — an execution bound on leverage: the match reverts if, after the fill, total debt across all maturities would exceed this fraction of collateral value for that borrower. In practice, it works like slippage protection for leverage: if oracle prices move, multiple orders fill in sequence, or the required wallet top-up would leave the borrower more leveraged than they agreed to, the trade simply does not execute. It does not force a fixed collateral transfer — the app pulls only the shortfall from the chosen wallet token, using any collateral already deposited first. The loan asset, such as USDT, stays in the supplier's wallet while the order is open and can likewise participate in other Aqua strategies. On execution, USDT is pulled from the supplier to the borrower via Aqua; only then does the borrower receive spot liquidity. Simultaneously, maturity shares are minted just in time — ERC-4626 vault tokens representing fixed-maturity claims such as USDT-OCT30, USDT-NOV30, or USDT-JAN30. These shares are pulled from the borrower to the supplier as payment for the spot USDT. They are standard transferable ERC-20 tokens, tradable on a secondary market, and can be shipped into Aqua strategies like any other token. After maturity, each share redeems pro-rata against the vault's USDT cash via ERC-4626 redeem or withdraw . If all receivables are repaid in full, maturity shares redeem 1:1 against USDT. Each maturity is represented by an ERC-4626 vault whose shares are tradable maturity claims. For example, a supplier may exchange 480 USDT today for 500 USDT-OCT30, which becomes redeemable against the vault at maturity. The discount between spot USDT and the maturity claim determines the fixed rate. If bad debt occurs — for example, a borrower is fully liquidated and the remaining collateral is insufficient to cover the receivable — the vault writes down the unpaid portion. This reduces total debt and therefore the NAV of the maturity shares, causing current holders of that maturity to absorb the loss proportionally. A later repayment by the borrower can still restore vault value for the remaining holders. AquaTerm uses Aqua virtual balances to keep orders non-custodial until execution. Posting an order creates neither debt nor an additional collateral lock. When compatible borrower and supplier orders are matched, collateral is pulled only if required, maturity shares are minted just in time, and both sides of the trade settle atomically through Aqua. Borrower collateral is shared across debts of different maturities under a single portfolio health factor. Maturity claims are transferable and can be traded on the secondary market before expiry.
projects.how_its_made: AquaTerm is built around 1inch Aqua as its execution and liquidity layer. The core Solidity contract, AquaTermApp, uses Aqua virtual balances so borrowers and suppliers can post term orders without locking assets upfront. Their collateral and USDT remain available to other Aqua strategies while the orders are open, and real token transfers happen only when two compatible orders are matched. The most unusual part is how we handle fixed-maturity debt. Every maturity has its own ERC-4626 vault, such as USDT-OCT30 or USDT-JAN31. These derivative tokens are designed to redeem approximately 1:1 for USDT at maturity, assuming the underlying loans are fully repaid. Borrowers can advertise these maturity shares through Aqua before the shares actually exist. When a match executes, AquaTerm checks the borrower’s portfolio LTV, pulls only the additional collateral required, mints the maturity shares just in time, and immediately settles the trade through Aqua: the supplier’s USDT goes to the borrower, while the freshly minted maturity shares go to the supplier. This all happens atomically in a single transaction. The derivative tokens are implemented as ERC-4626 vault shares so that, in the event of bad debt, losses can be socialized across the current holders of the maturity claims. The maturity vaults track both cash and outstanding loans in their NAV, allowing the maturity tokens to behave as transferable fixed-income claims that can be traded before expiry. Risk is managed at the borrower portfolio level across multiple maturities and collateral types, with Chainlink price feeds used for collateral valuation, LTV checks, and liquidations. The contracts have no owner or admin setters; protocol parameters are fixed at deployment. We built a lightweight Python indexer using Flask, web3.py, and SQLite. It watches the AquaTerm contracts for borrower and supplier orders, reconstructs the live orderbook, and exposes it to the frontend. Matching is permissionless and incentivized: anyone can execute crossed orders, and the spread between the borrower’s minimum price and the supplier’s maximum price becomes the executor’s reward. The frontend is a lightweight static app built with vanilla JavaScript and ethers v6. It talks directly to the contracts for transactions and uses the indexer only for market discovery and orderbook data. The whole stack is intentionally simple and hackathon-friendly: Solidity and Foundry onchain, a small Python service for indexing, and a static frontend with no build pipeline.

projects.title: WakeStake
projects.description: An app that liquidates you if you don't get ur ass out of bed using a novel privacy mechanism
projects.project_description: WakeStake is an AI-powered, privacy preserving, social anti-snooze system that connects a wake-up alarm, an Ethereum wallet, and an X account, with additional features like a group chat set-up. Users can stake any amount of the erc-20 of their choosing. And can privately withdraw to a fresh account just like in a privacy pool. By creating a zero knowledge proof of their deposit. How ever the user also sets a wake-up time inside the private commitment. And share those secrets to a AI agent and/or their group chat of friends. They are allowed number of five-minute snoozes. How ever snooze for too long.... you lose! To prove they actually got out of bed, they must scan a QR code placed away from the bed, ideally in the bathroom. That QR code leads them to our app which prompts them to privately proof they woke up in time. But if they are too late, they zk circuit forces the withdraw to only be able to go through the pre commited donation address. Thier AI agent wil also analyzes the user’s X environment, such as posts, likes, follows, and audience, to select a legitimate charity the user is unlikely to personally support, making the financial consequence harsher. In group mode, the punishment charity can instead be selected by peer vote until the first penalty occurs. The smartcontract and circuit then enforces the transfers of the staked  tokens from the protocol, pre-funded wake-up stake to the selected charity. And WakeStake can automatically publish the failure to the user’s X account. The donation address also can use uniswap v3 to automattically swaps a erc-20 into a preffered asset so the donation address gets a clean token like usdc or eth. Incase the user uses a niche meme coin that donation recipients might not like Example tweet: “I voluntarily gave an AI control over my wallet because apparently I cannot be trusted with an alarm clock. WakeStake just donated 0.004 ETH from my wake-up stake to Vision for Israel because I refused to get out of bed. Proof of Snooze:etherscan.io/tx/0x… Also terrible at mornings? Use WakeStake: github.com/…” WakeStake also supports positive incentives: users can opt into success donations or sponsorships, allowing successful wake-ups to generate donations to causes they personally support. The idea is to combine financial commitment, social accountability, AI personalization, and verifiable on-chain consequences into a morning routine that is much harder to ignore than a normal alarm clock.
projects.how_its_made:
WakeStake is a Solidity contract, a Noir ZK circuit, a React mobile app and a Telegram bot. You lock tokens against a wake-up time. If you're up on time you keep them. If you oversleep, your stake goes to someone else. Groups are setup as contracts controlled by users who all get their own ens V2 domain with their own group subdomain. So for example emmy.wakkyuppygroup.wakestake.eth.
Entry to the group is gated by a minimum stake amount wich is enforced by another zk proof of minimum staked. And a group admin. On-chain (Hardhat 3 + viem, deployed and verified on Sepolia). Stakes don't sit in a public mapping. Each stake is a Poseidon commitment (token, amount, and a hash of the nullifier secret, secret hash, wake timestamp and donation address). It goes into a LeanIMT Merkle tree from zk-kit. Deploying took Hardhat Ignition modules that link five libraries: PoseidonT3/T4, LeanIMT, and the RelationsLib and ZKTranscriptLib that the generated verifier needs. ZK (Noir + Barretenberg UltraHonk). The circuit proves membership in the tree and then branches on time. If you wake up before your alarm, you prove you know a secret that only you hold. projects.project_description_markdown:
WakeStake is an AI-powered, privacy preserving, social anti-snooze system that connects a wake-up alarm, an Ethereum wallet, and an X account, with additional features like a group chat set-up.

Users can stake any amount of the erc-20 of their choosing. And can privately withdraw to a fresh account just like in a privacy pool. By creating a zero knowledge proof of their deposit.

How ever the user also sets a wake-up time inside the private commitment. And share those secrets to a AI agent and/or their group chat of friends. They are allowed number of five-minute snoozes. How ever snooze for too long.... you lose! 

To prove they actually got out of bed, they must scan a QR code placed away from the bed, ideally in the bathroom. That QR code leads them to our app which prompts them to privately proof they woke up in time. But if they are too late, they zk circuit forces the withdraw to only be able to go through the pre commited donation address. 

Thier AI agent wil also analyzes the user’s X environment, such as posts, likes, follows, and audience, to select a legitimate charity the user is unlikely to personally support, making the financial consequence harsher. In group mode, the punishment charity can instead be selected by peer vote until the first penalty occurs.

The smartcontract and circuit then enforces the transfers of the staked  tokens from the protocol, pre-funded wake-up stake to the selected charity. And WakeStake can automatically publish the failure to the user’s X account.

The donation address also can use uniswap v3 to automattically swaps a erc-20 into a preffered asset so the donation address gets a clean token like usdc or eth. Incase the user uses a niche meme coin that donation recipients might not like

Example tweet:

“I voluntarily gave an AI control over my wallet because apparently I cannot be trusted with an alarm clock.

WakeStake just donated 0.004 ETH from my wake-up stake to Vision for Israel because I refused to get out of bed.

Proof of Snooze:etherscan.io/tx/0x…

Also terrible at mornings? Use WakeStake: github.com/…”

WakeStake also supports positive incentives: users can opt into success donations or sponsorships, allowing successful wake-ups to generate donations to causes they personally support.

The idea is to combine financial commitment, social accountability, AI personalization, and verifiable on-chain consequences into a morning routine that is much harder to ignore than a normal alarm clock.

projects.title: Human Wall
projects.description: A guestbook where every verified human can leave exactly one message.
projects.project_description: Human Wall is a simple, anonymous guestbook powered by World ID. Every verified human can publish exactly one short message, while bots and duplicate users are prevented from posting repeatedly. It demonstrates how proof of personhood can make online public spaces more authentic without requiring usernames, passwords, or personal information. Visitors can read messages from other verified humans, write their own message, and verify their uniqueness before publishing it to the wall.
projects.how_its_made: Human Wall is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and World ID IDKit. The frontend lets a visitor write a message and launch the World ID verification flow. The proof is sent to a Next.js API route, which verifies it through the World ID Cloud Verification API. After successful verification, the message and its anonymous nullifier hash are stored by the server. The nullifier is used only to prevent the same human from posting twice and does not reveal their identity. Messages are displayed in a responsive guestbook-style interface.

projects.title: Kura
projects.description: Vault physical Magic cards, sell shards to verified humans, and buy out 80% to take the card home.
projects.project_description: Kura (蔵, "storehouse") is a vault for real Magic: The Gathering cards that gives them a market. Bring a card to a shop. The vendor scans it, Kura recognises the exact printing and prices it, and the owner gets an on-chain twin. The card itself stays in the vault. Split it into shards and half go on sale in a Uniswap auction. Only verified humans can bid, so bots can't sweep a Black Lotus. When the auction closes, the money raised and the other half of the shards open a Uniswap pool at the auction price. The owner becomes its liquidity provider and earns the trading fees, and the card now has a live price anyone can trade. Want the whole card? Get to 80% of the shards. Buying them from the pool pushes the price up. Then buy out the rest, everyone else gets paid, and you pick up the card at the counter with a World ID passport check. Every card has its own ENS name, like lightning-bolt-4ed-1.kura.eth, with its state, condition and appraisal in the records. And the vault reads like a market: value, volume, premium to market price, and how close each card is to a buyout.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity with Foundry, on Ethereum Sepolia. CardVault holds each card as an ERC-721, creates an ERC-20 for every sharding, and runs the auction, the buyout and the release. ShardMarket owns each card's Uniswap v4 pool. The tests fork Sepolia and run against the real Uniswap, Permit2, USDC and ENS contracts. Uniswap. Each sale is a Continuous Clearing Auction, and our validation hook only lets World ID-verified bidders in. At settlement ShardMarket opens a v4 pool at the clearing price and locks the owner's liquidity in it. It is also the pool's hook: it freezes trading once the card is bought out but always lets LPs withdraw, and it emits a trade event per card for our indexer. The fiddly part was turning the auction's clearing price into a v4 pool price for both token orders, and placing the leftover shards as a one-sided position. The app trades through the Universal Router with Permit2. World ID. Proof of Human gates bidding, one wallet per human. The Passport credential gates taking the card home. Our server checks each proof and signs a short-lived ticket that the contracts verify on-chain. ENS. kura.eth runs on ENSv2 with its own registry and resolver. Cards get non-transferable names that are revoked on release, and collectors claim handles. Rights are per record: the vendor edits condition, an appraiser agent writes appraisals, and nobody else can touch them. Indexer and app. A Ponder indexer on Railway feeds live SQL queries into a Next.js app on Vercel, so pages update as blocks land. The same indexer powers the analytics. Privy handles login and embedded wallets with sponsored gas. The hacky bits: Card recognition runs in the browser. A DINOv2 model embeds the webcam frame and matches it against about 45,000 Scryfall artworks stored as int8 vectors. Alpha cards have no collector number, so OCR was out. Prices respect finish and language. Foil and regular never mix, and a missing price falls back to the English printing before the condition discount. The appraiser can't send the same on-chain write twice: each one is claimed under a Postgres advisory lock with a fresh nonce.

projects.title: RealClanker
projects.description: Agents buy concert tickets only after World ID, named on ENS v2, settled on Sui.
projects.project_description: RealClanker is a concert box office for AI agents. A human proves they are real with World ID. That proof is bound to one ENS v2 agent, one concert, one ticket, and a short expiry. The agent buys through an MCP server. Sui takes the payment and mints the ticket. The same human cannot clear the gate twice, even from a second agent. Agents with no grant, an expired grant, or a grant for another show are refused. The live dashboard shows the sale as a race: cleared buyers reach the pool, and the rest go to jail. Organizers can replay how the sale happened.
projects.how_its_made: The organizer console is a Next.js app on Vercel. Agents call a stateless MCP endpoint at /api/mcp to list concerts, register an ENS name, fund a Sui wallet, and buy a ticket. World ID for Agents (sandbox.auth.world.org) runs an OIDC login. The callback verifies the ID token against the issuer JWKS before any grant is stored, and buy_ticket never trusts a subject an agent sends itself. Agent names are ENSv2 subnames of realclanker.eth on Sepolia. A platform wallet pays the gas and each agent's own EVM address owns the name. Each agent also gets a Sui devnet wallet. A Move package holds a shared ticket Pool. A successful buy pays the price and takes a Ticket object. A swarm mixes valid buyers with duplicates, expired grants, wrong-concert grants, and agents with no human at all. Concerts, grants, and wallets persist in Vercel Blob, and the race canvas can replay a saved sale without sending another chain transaction.

projects.title: Arkheion Dashboard
projects.description: Visual dashboard for Arkheion, a Spring/K8s-style framework for parallel-EVM smart contract systems
projects.project_description: Arkheion is a smart contract framework for the parallel-EVM era, built for financial institutions running complex on-chain systems — not one contract, but dozens of interdependent modules wired, versioned, and upgraded like backend services. Its CLI (init, cluster init, cluster auto, upgrade, rollback) does the real work: declaring dependencies instead of hardcoding addresses, auto-assembling entire contract clusters in one command, and hot-swapping or rolling back individual contracts without touching the rest of the system — the same relationship Spring has to Java beans, or Kubernetes has to containers. This project is the dashboard for that framework — not the framework itself. Exactly like kubectl and the Kubernetes Dashboard both sit on top of the Kubernetes control plane, the Arkheion CLI is the engine and this dashboard is its visual client. Every action here — mounting a workspace, deploying the cluster core, running auto-assembly, upgrading a contract, rolling it back — shells out to the exact same CLI command a developer would type in a terminal. It adds zero on-chain logic of its own. It exists because cluster auto produces real structure: a dependency graph with cycles, deferred links, and generation history that's genuinely hard to hold in your head from CLI logs alone. The dashboard makes that structure visible — live topology graphs, upgrade/rollback history, streaming logs — while the CLI stays the single source of truth on-chain.
projects.how_its_made: Arkheion Dashboard is a Vue 3 + TypeScript SPA on top of a small Express bridge server, sitting in front of the real Arkheion CLI — a Node.js framework that treats smart contracts as managed, versioned components with declared dependencies, the way Spring wires Java beans or Kubernetes reconciles containers. Architecture: Clean Architecture / DDD on the frontend (domain entities and repository interfaces with zero framework dependencies, infrastructure implementations behind them, Pinia stores orchestrating use cases, Vue components with no business logic). The Express server (server/server.js) is deliberately thin: every dashboard action spawns the actual arkheion CLI binary as a child process with stdin closed (so a command that would otherwise fall back to an interactive prompt fails fast instead of hanging the request forever), streams stdout/stderr back over a WebSocket for live logs, and returns the same success/failure the CLI itself reports. No on-chain logic lives in this app — it is a client, not a reimplementation. The trickiest real engineering was making the dashboard's data layer trustworthy. cluster list / cluster current print human-decorated text boxes for terminal use, not JSON, so the frontend can't parse them reliably — we instead run cluster graph (which the CLI already generates as a Mermaid diagram + HTML registry table from live on-chain reads) and parse that HTML server-side into structured nodes and active/passive edges. That HTML table doesn't carry generation numbers, so we cross-reference each contract's address against project.json's alldeployedcontracts to recover it — a small but real bug we caught by comparing dashboard output against direct chain queries ( eth_getTransactionReceipt , contractRegistrations ) rather than trusting either layer blindly. Stack: Vue 3 (Composition API), TypeScript, Pinia, Vite, ethers.js v6 for any direct chain reads, vis-network for the force-directed cluster topology graph, Express + ws for the CLI bridge and log streaming, and Hardhat as the local devnet the whole cluster deploys onto. The most "hacky but load-bearing" piece: a file-based cluster lock (a .arkheion-cluster.lock file with orphan-PID detection) in the CLI itself, so concurrent cluster auto / upgrade / rollback calls triggered from the dashboard can't race each other and leave the on-chain registry and project.json out of sync — a real failure mode we hit and fixed during development, not a hypothetical one.

projects.title: x402 Guard
projects.description: Intercepta screens every x402 payment before MetaMask Agent Wallet signs: pay, cap, ask, or refuse
projects.project_description: AI agents are starting to pay each other over x402, but nobody checks who is on the other side. x402-guard is a MetaMask Agent Wallet plugin that screens every x402 payment with the Intercepta API before the wallet signs it, shows the verdict with its reasons, and lets that verdict decide what happens: pay, cap, ask a human, or refuse. We started by testing the gap. x402 payments are EIP-3009 signatures, not transactions, and MetaMask's outflow limit doesn't count signatures. A real server wallet in Guard Mode, funded on Base, signed x402 payments to an OFAC-sanctioned Lazarus Group address, to a lookalike "USD Coin" contract, for 96% of its balance, and with a 1-year validity window. None of them triggered a prompt. USDC already freezes sanctioned addresses, and MetaMask's Blockaid scanning protects the signer from drainers. Nobody screens who the agent is paying. For each payment, x402-guard checks: the payee (payTo), with Quick Scan for sanctions, scammers and blacklists, and Deep Scan for mixer, sanctions-counterparty and scam exposure the token, with Scan Token, so only verified tokens like real USDC are paid the exact EIP-712 authorization about to be signed, with Scan Message our own limits: a per-payment ceiling by risk tier, a rolling 24h cap, and a 10-minute maximum validity Clean counterparties are auto-paid up to $1 and caution-tier counterparties up to $0.10. Blocked counterparties are never paid, and a refusal can't be overridden. Anything above a ceiling goes to a human, with an approval code bound to that exact payee, token and amount, so a seller can't swap the payee after approval. mm x402 screen <address> also gives a standalone counterparty risk profile. In the demo, an agent buys three reports. The clean seller is paid and settled on Base Sepolia. The seller whose payTo is the Lazarus Group wallet is refused before anything is signed. A wallet with 8 Tornado Cash deposits asks for $0.50, which is over its caution ceiling, so the agent stops and asks the human. Payments run on testnet, but every payee is a real mainnet address screened with Intercepta's mainnet data.
projects.how_its_made: x402-guard is a TypeScript plugin for the MetaMask Agent Wallet CLI (mm), built from MetaMask's official plugin template. It adds four commands: mm x402 pay, inspect, screen and config. Signing goes through the plugin's walletExecutor with a "typed-data" request, so MetaMask's own policy pipeline (Guard Mode, Blockaid, 2FA) still runs after our screen. The agent never touches keys. We ship a skill file (SKILL.md) that routes agents to mm x402 pay instead of raw sign-typed-data, and tells them to stop on a refusal and never approve on their own. The x402 client is a port of MetaMask's own x402_pay.py helper (exact scheme, EIP-3009, protocol v1 and v2). It builds the authorization first, so the payload Intercepta scans is byte-for-byte the one MetaMask signs. It never follows redirects, and it clamps the server's validity window. The Intercepta integration calls four endpoints in parallel: Quick Scan Address, Deep Scan Address (cached, with a timeout), Scan Token and Scan Message. It then folds traits into a clean / caution / blocked tier, because a raw toxicScore misses mixer exposure (it scores 0.4 to 15). Testnet payments are screened against the mainnet sibling chain. For the demo, a small Python x402 v2 seller verifies and settles real payments through the public x402 facilitator on Base Sepolia. Hacky and notable: The gap test: an adversarial x402 seller plus MetaMask's unmodified helper, run against a real Guard Mode wallet. We simulated each captured signature with eth_call on Base to prove it would actually settle. That's how we found Circle freezes OFAC addresses in USDC, which pointed us to unfrozen risk like mixer users. We found mixer-exposed test addresses by pulling recent depositors from Tornado Cash Deposit logs and deep-scanning them. The plugin SDK's executor and wallet-state types ship bundled, so we reverse-engineered the typed-data request and intent shapes from MetaMask's compiled CLI. projects.project_description_markdown:
AI agents are starting to pay each other over x402, but nobody checks who is on the other side. x402-guard is a MetaMask Agent Wallet plugin that screens every x402 payment with the Intercepta API before the wallet signs it, shows the verdict with its reasons, and lets that verdict decide what happens: pay, cap, ask a human, or refuse.

We started by testing the gap. x402 payments are EIP-3009 signatures, not transactions, and MetaMask's outflow limit doesn't count signatures. A real server wallet in Guard Mode, funded on Base, signed x402 payments to an OFAC-sanctioned Lazarus Group address, to a lookalike "USD Coin" contract, for 96% of its balance, and with a 1-year validity window. None of them triggered a prompt. USDC already freezes sanctioned addresses, and MetaMask's Blockaid scanning protects the signer from drainers. Nobody screens who the agent is paying.

For each payment, x402-guard checks:
- the payee (payTo), with Quick Scan for sanctions, scammers and blacklists, and Deep Scan for mixer, sanctions-counterparty and scam exposure
- the token, with Scan Token, so only verified tokens like real USDC are paid
- the exact EIP-712 authorization about to be signed, with Scan Message
- our own limits: a per-payment ceiling by risk tier, a rolling 24h cap, and a 10-minute maximum validity

Clean counterparties are auto-paid up to $1 and caution-tier counterparties up to $0.10. Blocked counterparties are never paid, and a refusal can't be overridden. Anything above a ceiling goes to a human, with an approval code bound to that exact payee, token and amount, so a seller can't swap the payee after approval. `mm x402 screen <address>` also gives a standalone counterparty risk profile.

In the demo, an agent buys three reports. The clean seller is paid and settled on Base Sepolia. The seller whose payTo is the Lazarus Group wallet is refused before anything is signed. A wallet with 8 Tornado Cash deposits asks for $0.50, which is over its caution ceiling, so the agent stops and asks the human. Payments run on testnet, but every payee is a real mainnet address screened with Intercepta's mainnet data.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
x402-guard is a TypeScript plugin for the MetaMask Agent Wallet CLI (mm), built from MetaMask's official plugin template. It adds four commands: mm x402 pay, inspect, screen and config. Signing goes through the plugin's walletExecutor with a "typed-data" request, so MetaMask's own policy pipeline (Guard Mode, Blockaid, 2FA) still runs after our screen. The agent never touches keys. We ship a skill file (SKILL.md) that routes agents to mm x402 pay instead of raw sign-typed-data, and tells them to stop on a refusal and never approve on their own.

The x402 client is a port of MetaMask's own x402_pay.py helper (exact scheme, EIP-3009, protocol v1 and v2). It builds the authorization first, so the payload Intercepta scans is byte-for-byte the one MetaMask signs. It never follows redirects, and it clamps the server's validity window. The Intercepta integration calls four endpoints in parallel: Quick Scan Address, Deep Scan Address (cached, with a timeout), Scan Token and Scan Message. It then folds traits into a clean / caution / blocked tier, because a raw toxicScore misses mixer exposure (it scores 0.4 to 15). Testnet payments are screened against the mainnet sibling chain. For the demo, a small Python x402 v2 seller verifies and settles real payments through the public x402 facilitator on Base Sepolia.

Hacky and notable:
- The gap test: an adversarial x402 seller plus MetaMask's unmodified helper, run against a real Guard Mode wallet. We simulated each captured signature with eth_call on Base to prove it would actually settle. That's how we found Circle freezes OFAC addresses in USDC, which pointed us to unfrozen risk like mixer users.
- We found mixer-exposed test addresses by pulling recent depositors from Tornado Cash Deposit logs and deep-scanning them.
- The plugin SDK's executor and wallet-state types ship bundled, so we reverse-engineered the typed-data request and intent shapes from MetaMask's compiled CLI.
- Local plugin installs crash with "window.addEventListener is not a function" because a symlinked install loads a second copy of the CLI. The official template hits it too, and it also refuses CLI 7.x. A small script re-links the plugin to the host's copy.
- Intercepta gotchas: Cloudflare blocks default user agents. Scan Message silently returns "Low" if you send message as a string, as the docs say. Sent as an object, it works and recognises x402's TransferWithAuthorization.

projects.title: Verifiable Blackbox
projects.description: Connect robot jobs, evidence, approvals, and payments across businesses.
projects.project_description: When a robot says “job done,” who checks the claim and authorizes the payment? Businesses buying robot services need more than an activity log. They need a clear connection between the work they requested, the evidence they accepted, and the payment they made. Verifiable Blackbox brings these records together in one traceable workflow. Inspired by an aircraft’s black box, Verifiable Blackbox connects physical robot activity to evidence-backed payments on Ethereum. Every job carries its own conditions, customer approval, evidence, signed verification result, and payment receipt—giving customers and operators a shared record they can inspect. Our demo brings this workflow into the physical world with a small M5Stack Rover. A customer creates a job and deposits a reward into escrow. The Rover is operated through a web interface, and the application connects its session records, video-motion assessment, and signed customer approval to that job. Phala checks the submitted evidence against the onchain job and returns a signed verdict. The Ethereum contract checks the signer, evidence hash, job details, and expiry before releasing the reward. A receipt connects the payment to its supporting evidence. The demo uses test mUSDC on Ethereum Sepolia. Each integration answers a practical business question. Which device signed the record? ENS resolves the robot’s registered public key for device-signature verification. Does this evidence belong to this job? Phala checks the correspondence and signs the result. What supports this payment? Curvegrid MultiBaas retrieves transaction receipts and events, allowing the ledger to connect payments with jobs and verification records. StegaVAR adds video embedding and reconstruction for visual evidence review, while a monthly accounting demo groups records by provider and exports them as CSV. Who may view the recorded evidence? A separate World IDP/OIDC disclosure workflow combines approver permissions with World authentication to grant five-minute access to sample recordings, with revocation and expiry controls. This keeps video access separate from payment authorization. Full authentication-to-disclosure validation in the World Sandbox is still pending. The result is a working prototype that connects robot operations with customer approval, verification, settlement, and accounting. Starting with one Rover, Verifiable Blackbox demonstrates the foundation for buying robot services across businesses: evidence customers can review, payments they can trace, and records they can use.
projects.how_its_made: We built four connected components: a physical rover, a web application, a verification service, and Ethereum smart contracts. Job identifiers and evidence commitments connect them. The stack includes M5Stack/ESP32 hardware, Python, Next.js, React, TypeScript, viem, Solidity, Foundry, and Phala Cloud with dstack. Privy supports authentication and wallet integration. The rover combines an M5StickC Plus2 with a RoverC Pro, its gripper, and a Unit CamS3-5MP camera. C++ firmware handles motor control, while a Python bridge handles Wi-Fi commands, telemetry, and camera access. Next.js API routes connect the application to this bridge, bringing job creation, robot operation, approval, and payment receipts into one interface. Settlement uses a Core, Hook, and Evaluator architecture inspired by the ERC-8183 job model. The Core holds the reward in escrow. The application checks the job owner’s approval signature, while the Phala service checks the evidence commitment, job-specific challenge, sequence, expiry, and onchain state. It signs an EIP-712 verdict only when those checks pass. The Evaluator validates the verdict against the target job before settlement. For Phala Cloud deployment, the verifier runs inside a TEE and derives its signing key through dstack KMS. Our independent attestation CLI checks a fresh nonce and expected signer, chain, Evaluator, and execution-environment values. Phala adds a way to inspect the environment producing the verdict, beyond trusting an API response alone. For device identity, the ESP32 signs job identifiers using P-256. We resolve the enrolled public key from an ENS vbb.device.p256 text record and verify the signature locally and through an ERC-7913 verifier deployed on Sepolia. This remains an independent verification component, separate from payment authorization. One practical hardware detail was moving signing into a separate task that runs while the rover is stopped, alongside stop monitoring independent of HTTP processing. Cryptography and network delays should not block stopping the robot. Curvegrid MultiBaas supplies receipts, events, and block information for selected Sepolia payments. We reconcile these records with the corresponding jobs and token transfers. A separate monthly sample dataset demonstrates aggregation by counterparty and CSV export. When bulk event retrieval hit an API limit, we used individual transaction-receipt endpoints to retrieve the existing payments without changing the settlement contracts. We also integrated an experimental StegaVAR video workflow. Recorded rover clips are embedded into cover videos, reconstructed, and analyzed on CPU using the recovered frames. This is currently a public sample comparison and analysis feature; it does not enforce confidentiality or authorize payments. We also added a World IDP/OIDC integration for controlled video disclosure. The workflow combines approver permissions with World authentication to grant five-minute access to a sample recording, with revocation and expiry controls. It remains separate from payment authorization. Full authentication-to-disclosure validation in the World Sandbox is still pending. Our Foundry, Python, TypeScript, and browser checks cover successful settlement, tampered evidence, expiry, verdict reuse, service recovery, and duplicate-payment prevention. The current verifier checks evidence and job consistency. Autonomous verification of physical movement or successful delivery remains an extension we are building toward.

projects.title: Pupille
projects.description: The Pupille iOS app uses secure hardware and World to prove that a pic was taken by a verified human
projects.project_description: Pupille is a native iOS capture and verification protocol for photos authored by unique humans. During enrollment, PupilleKit creates a persistent P-256 signing key inside the iPhone Secure Enclave and an Apple App Attest key. A World IDKit Proof of Human is generated with a signal that commits to the user’s pseudonymous handle and device public key. The backend verifies the World proof, its uniqueness/nullifier, and the Apple attestation before issuing an Ed25519-signed profile certificate. Photos can only enter the protocol through PupilleCameraView , which returns a controlled CapturedPhoto . When publishing, Pupille computes the SHA-256 hash of the exact JPEG bytes and caption, requests a one-time backend challenge, creates a fresh App Attest assertion, and asks Face ID to authorize the Secure Enclave signature. The backend independently recomputes the commitment, verifies the challenge, assertion, profile signature, and certified World identity, then issues a signed capture certificate containing the originating app ID. The proof is embedded directly inside the JPEG as a tagged APP11 segment containing the profile certificate, capture certificate, caption, and author signature. Verification does not trust a database “verified” flag: PupilleKit, our dependency-free TypeScript package, CLI, and browser verifier independently remove the proof segment, hash the original image bytes, validate both certificates and signatures, check the caption and author binding, and optionally enforce a list of trusted capture applications. Editing one pixel, changing the caption, relabelling the author, or copying the proof onto another image causes verification to fail. Inspired by Succinct’s ZCAM and designed as a path toward C2PA Content Credentials, the project includes the polished Pupille social proof-of-concept, a reusable Swift SDK, a web verifier, and a mock Amazon integration where verified-human customers can attach authenticated photos to product reviews with only a few SDK calls. The proof establishes byte integrity, attested app capture, device-key authorship, and World ID Proof of Human.
projects.how_its_made: We built Pupille to make authentic camera capture portable, human-verified and AI-resistant. We turn World ID’s Proof of Human into a reusable trust layer for authentic digital media, giving the World ecosystem a concrete new use case across social platforms, marketplaces, journalism, and user-generated content. Our iOS proof-of-concept captures a photo, hashes its exact bytes, signs the capture with a Secure Enclave key authorized by Face ID, and uses Apple App Attest to prove it came from our genuine app. World IDKit adds a privacy-preserving Proof of Human, binding one unique human to each pseudonymous profile. Our backend verifies the World ID and Apple evidence, then issues signed certificates that travel with each photo. We extracted this pipeline into a reusable Swift SDK and demonstrated its portability by integrating it into a mock Amazon app, where customers can attach cryptographically verified, human-authored photos to product reviews with only a few lines of code.

projects.title: Uniswap NameFlow App
projects.description: A fun, flowy, wavy app called NameFlow that displays Uniswap V3 pool info using Curvegrid and ENS.
projects.project_description: NameFlow is a fun, flowy, wavy app that displays Uniswap V3 pool activity using Curvegrid and ENS. It watches a set of V3 pools on Sepolia and shows every swap the moment it is indexed: a force-directed network of traders and pools with particles flying along the link when a trade lands, a Sankey of value flow from trader to pool to token, a per-pool timeline, live price and volume charts, a trade tape, and a pool card with the on-chain price, liquidity, tick range and net token flow. The twist is identity. Traders and pools appear under ENS names and avatars instead of hex, and the pool watchlist itself is not hardcoded: it lives in ENSv2 text records under nameflow.eth. Each pool is a subname such as weth-usdc-3000.nameflow.eth carrying its address and pair metadata, and the app verifies that metadata against the pool contract before trusting it. The namespace owner can add a new pool from the UI, which registers the subname in the ENSv2 registry and publishes its records in one transaction, while anyone else sees a read-only badge. That is ENSv2 access control made visible. Because a testnet is quiet, the app ships its own traffic: five ENS-named wallets run real swaps through SwapRouter02, alternating direction so the tiny testnet pools stay balanced, and a replay mode re-runs the indexed history through every view with a scrubber and speed control. All of it stays under about seven MultiBaas requests a minute at idle. For the next steps we planned to use webhooks and cloud wallets provided via Curvegrid, however since we were short on time we didn't have the time to implement this. The idea certainly has potential to improve upon further the name is catchy and the idea is fun!
projects.how_its_made: Frontend is Vue 3 with the Composition API, Vite, Tailwind, and D3 v7 plus d3-sankey for the force graph, Sankey, timeline and charts. Every chart is hand-built on D3 so we control the animations: new swaps are diffed by transaction hash and only those animate. All on-chain data comes through Curvegrid MultiBaas via the official TypeScript SDK. We linked the pool contracts and defined a saved event query over the Uniswap Swap event; the dashboard reads it with executeEventQuery, uses countEventQueryRecords as a one-request "anything new?" probe, and runs an arbitrary event query with server-side aggregators (add, min, max, last) grouped by contract for net token flow and tick range. Live price and liquidity come from callContractFunction on slot0() and liquidity(), and the pool card shows getEventIndexingStatus. This meant no indexer and no log scanning of our own. A Vercel edge function proxies the read endpoints so the API key never ships in the bundle. ENS is done with viem against Sepolia. The directory record on nameflow.eth lists pool and wallet subnames; pool records hold JSON metadata that we validate against token0(), token1() and fee() before use. Trader names use a managed reverse lookup at address.lookup.nameflow.eth, accepted only when forward resolution matches, with a standard primary-name fallback. Registration scripts create ENSv2 subregistries through the registry factory and grant role bitmaps, and the in-app "Add pool" flow does the same from a browser wallet with every write simulated first. The hacky parts: readiness for the swap simulator is derived from chain state in one multicall instead of a local flag, so a reload never re-funds wallets. Polling is a count probe first and rows only when the count moves, with visibility-aware back-off. ENS lookups are folded into multicall3 batches with a fallback list of public RPCs, which took a fresh load from 150 throttled requests to about ten. And Sepolia liquidity is so thin that a 5 USDC swap moved one pool 150%, so the simulator alternates direction per wallet and per round to stay net-neutral.

projects.title: DatingAppScamBusters
projects.description: DAS Busters lets users prove single status to dating apps and keep optional details private.
projects.project_description:
DAS Busters is a service that lets users prove their single status on dating apps. Self-declared profile information alone makes it difficult to confirm whether someone is actually unmarried. Our goal is to reduce relationship problems caused by false claims of being single and build trust in online dating.
Users receive signed digital certificates issued by public authorities or other authorized organizations through DAS Busters and store them on their own devices. When connecting to a dating app, they review the requested information and approve what they share. Proving single status is required, but optional attributes, such as “lives in Tokyo” or “in their 30s,” can remain undisclosed. The app receives only the proof results, never the certificate itself.
The same certificate cannot be used to register a second account on the same dating app. This prevents one person from maintaining multiple profiles with verified single status within that app.
By combining verification of relevant facts, limited disclosure, and duplicate-account prevention, DAS Busters supports trustworthy connections while respecting users’ privacy.
projects.how_its_made:
DAS Busters combines signed digital certificates, zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), and contracts deployed on Sepolia. The certificates use a custom format signed with EdDSA-Poseidon rather than the W3C Verifiable Credentials format. For this prototype, we used a simulated public authority as the issuer and implemented the complete flow: certificate issuance, receipt and storage, proof generation, and verification.
Users review the attributes requested by a dating app and choose what to disclose, then generate a ZKP from their stored certificate directly in their smartphone’s browser. Neither the certificate nor the user’s secret value leaves the device.
The proof circuit uses circom and Groth16 and contains 9,921 constraints. Proofs are generated with snarkjs and verified by a contract on Sepolia. Names, dates of birth, and other personal information are not recorded on-chain. The contract stores only a nullifier—an anonymous identifier determined by the combination of the user and the app. The same combination produces the same nullifier, preventing duplicate registration with the same certificate within a single app.
The frontend uses Next.js. We use Privy for Google login and World ID through IDKit 4 in the staging environment for human verification. Foundry supports contract development, while viem connects the frontend to the contracts.
A key implementation detail is that the nullifier is calculated from a secret value held only on the user’s device and an app-specific value. The issuer receives only a hash of that secret, so it cannot calculate the nullifier or identify the corresponding user on the dating app. We also bind each proof to a request-specific value to prevent it from being reused for a different request. For the prototype’s trusted setup, we used a single local contribution.
