By combining verification of relevant facts, limited disclosure, and duplicate-account prevention, DAS Busters supports trustworthy connections while respecting users’ privacy.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
DAS Busters combines signed digital certificates, zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), and contracts deployed on Sepolia. The certificates use a custom format signed with EdDSA-Poseidon rather than the W3C Verifiable Credentials format. For this prototype, we used a simulated public authority as the issuer and implemented the complete flow: certificate issuance, receipt and storage, proof generation, and verification.
Users review the attributes requested by a dating app and choose what to disclose, then generate a ZKP from their stored certificate directly in their smartphone’s browser. Neither the certificate nor the user’s secret value leaves the device.
The proof circuit uses circom and Groth16 and contains 9,921 constraints. Proofs are generated with snarkjs and verified by a contract on Sepolia. Names, dates of birth, and other personal information are not recorded on-chain. The contract stores only a nullifier—an anonymous identifier determined by the combination of the user and the app. The same combination produces the same nullifier, preventing duplicate registration with the same certificate within a single app.
The frontend uses Next.js. We use Privy for Google login and World ID through IDKit 4 in the staging environment for human verification. Foundry supports contract development, while viem connects the frontend to the contracts.
A key implementation detail is that the nullifier is calculated from a secret value held only on the user’s device and an app-specific value. The issuer receives only a hash of that secret, so it cannot calculate the nullifier or identify the corresponding user on the dating app. We also bind each proof to a request-specific value to prevent it from being reused for a different request. For the prototype’s trusted setup, we used a single local contribution.

projects.title: Jev Market Factory
projects.description: An AI agent turns news into prediction markets with instant 1inch Aqua liquidity priced by Jev
projects.project_description: Prediction markets have a long tail problem: most small questions ("Will next week's CPI print above 0.3%?", "Will this factory outage be fixed within a week?") never get a market, and the ones that do start with an empty book and no sensible opening price. Jev Market Factory closes that gap with an agent. For every news item, the Scout agent sends one request to Jev (TypeSafe AI's judgment-only model) asking three typed questions at once: is this an objectively resolvable future event (noul), which category (choice), and what is the yes-probability (noul). If it passes the threshold, the agent creates a YES/NO market on-chain, writes the probability to an oracle, and immediately ships liquidity for both YES/USDC and NO/USDC from a single market-maker USDC balance to 1inch Aqua. Aqua records virtual balances per strategy, so one wallet backs every market at once and tokens only move when a trade fills. Prices come from our custom SwapVM instruction JevPrice: it centers quotes on Jev's probability (p for YES, 1-p for NO), widens the spread as the deadline approaches, and halts trading when the signal is stale. A Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook reads the same probability and charges more for trades that push the pool away from it. After the deadline, the Resolver agent judges evidence text with Jev and settles the market; winners redeem 1 USDC per share. The web app (markets list, market detail with order panel, news intake, and a maker view showing one USDC balance vs. total virtual liquidity) reads everything directly from the chain.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, via_ir) run on an Anvil fork of Base mainnet against the official 1inch Aqua (0x1111113c...) and the official Uniswap v4 PoolManager, with real Base USDC. JevPrice (contracts/instructions/JevPrice.sol) is a custom SwapVM instruction (opcode 0x52, curve family). The Aqua build of the SwapVM router only wires a limited opcode set (no LimitSwap / oracle adjusters), so instead of adjusting a rate we compute the fill amount directly: center = p (YES) or 1-p (NO) read from JevSignalOracle, spread widens linearly over the last 24h before the deadline, buy = amountIn / (center + s), sell = amountIn * (center - s), rounding in the maker's favor, revert on stale signal or after the deadline. JevAquaRouter extends the official AquaSwapVMRouter and overrides _runOpcode to dispatch JevPrice (the router's _dispatch cannot be re-overridden). Aqua itself is unmodified. MarketFactory mints per-market YES/NO ERC-20s against USDC (split / merge / resolve / redeem). JevDynamicFeeHook (OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks BaseHook) returns an override fee from beforeSwap depending on whether the swap pushes the pool price away from Jev's probability. Agents are TypeScript + viem + @typesafe-ai/sdk. One Jev systemOne request mixes three typed questions (noul / choice / noul), so the Scout decides, categorizes and prices a market in a single ~150 ms round-trip. Scout creates the market, splits USDC into YES+NO and ships two Aqua strategies (Deadline + JevPrice program) from the same maker balance; Pricer re-judges on follow-up news and writes the oracle; Resolver judges evidence and settles. The web app is Next.js App Router with route handlers that read the fork directly via viem (no database: the chain is the source of truth) and call the agent CLIs for writes. Hacky bits: USDC is funded on the fork by writing the FiatToken balance storage slot; Aqua strategies are immutable byte strings, so price changes flow through the oracle instead of re-shipping. Built with Claude Code as a pair programmer.

projects.title: mantis
projects.description: Mantis is an AI DeFi agent that detects anomalies and gates swaps with World ID.
projects.project_description: Mantis is a signal-to-execution AI agent for safer DeFi automation. It monitors on-chain activity, detects anomalous or high-confidence signals, evaluates an execution intent, and routes approved swaps through Uniswap V3 on Arbitrum. Consequential actions require a fresh World ID for Agents approval. The backend validates the OIDC response, verifies nonce and issuer claims, binds the approval to the exact trade-intent hash, and fails closed on expired, denied, or mismatched approvals. Every decision is recorded through the agent identity and safety layer.
projects.how_its_made: Mantis is built as a Python service architecture using FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, web3.py, Docker, and Railway. Scout collectors monitor Mantle, Arbitrum, HashKey, and Ethereum. Signals flow through detection, enrichment, delivery, and Execute workers. Execute converts matching signals into canonical ExecutionRequests, runs deterministic safety guards, then requires a signed World OIDC approval artifact for protected actions. The approved Arbitrum path uses Uniswap V3 SwapRouter02 with QuoterV2 minimum-output protection. The World integration uses authorization-code OIDC, Client Secret Basic, S256 PKCE, JWKS ID-token validation, nonce checks, short-lived HMAC-signed artifacts, and exact intent binding. Dry-run mode is enabled for safe demonstrations.

projects.title: JPYC EC Agents
projects.description: AI shops through chat from your own wallet. World verifies you when an order needs your approval.
projects.project_description: JPYC EC Agents lets people delegate shopping to AI through familiar chat apps, using their own funds and their own rules. Users keep their assets in their own wallet and retain control of its private key. They set allowed merchants, a per-purchase limit, a budget for a defined period, and an expiry date, then delegate purchasing authority to the AI. The AI handles orders within those conditions automatically and pauses when an order requires the owner's decision. The existing JPYC EC platform already supported x402 payments and purchases by AI. An earlier prototype required funding an AI-controlled wallet and managing its key and balance. For this hackathon, I added a way for users to set the scope of delegation on screen while keeping their assets in their own wallet, without transferring funds to a dedicated AI account or managing a separate AI key themselves. For example, a regular item may be out of stock, and a substitute found by the AI may exceed the remaining budget for the period. The AI cannot expand its own authority. It presents the order and the reason for exceeding the budget, asks the owner for explicit consent to that order, and requests fresh authentication through World ID for Agents. The server verifies a match with the registered owner, fresh authentication, and consent to the specific order before allowing that single purchase. If the owner declines or cancels, or the authentication expires, the exception order is not executed. Verifying the owner when their decision is needed makes everyday shopping easier to delegate while keeping decisions about exceptions with the owner. EIP-7702 enables delegated execution from the owner's wallet, and ERC-7715 is used to request permissions. A custom PurchaseGate checks normal purchase conditions and approval tied to a specific order; payment is executed through ERC-7710 and x402. The implementation also includes conversion from USDC to the JPYC needed for payment through Uniswap, plus risk screening with Intercepta before payment. Orders involving a merchant outside the approved list, a swap-price deviation, or a risk warning eligible for owner approval are referred back to the owner. If screening results cannot be obtained, the purchase stops. LINE has 100 million monthly active accounts in Japan, whose population is approximately 123 million. By starting with a familiar chat app, we bring delegated shopping closer to an everyday interaction. LINE is the primary experience, with a Telegram demo for judges. Sources: Statistics Bureau of Japan population estimates and LINE's official service data . JPYC EC is a live e-commerce platform that accepts JPYC, a yen-denominated stablecoin. It has been publicly available for about six months since its March 2026 launch. As of September 26, cumulative activity, including usage before the public launch, totals 210 paid transactions worth 948,140 JPYC from 141 unique wallets. These figures describe the existing EC platform. Merchants already use it to sell products, receive payments, and manage orders. Connecting the new functionality to their products, inventory, and order management brings AI payments under the owner's control into real shopping workflows.
projects.how_its_made: I built the commerce platform with Next.js, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL, the purchase-control contracts in Solidity, and the signing and settlement services in Node.js. LINE provides an interface familiar to users in Japan, while Telegram lets judges try the experience on their own phones. The owner retains the private key that controls their assets. The AI's execution key is generated and stored encrypted in a separate signing service. Users do not have to manage a dedicated AI key themselves; the AI uses its delegated authority to sign authorizations for individual orders. One of the hardest parts was enforcing a normal budget while allowing only explicitly approved orders to exceed it. Permission redemption is restricted to PurchaseGate, which checks normal purchase conditions and exception approvals. The parent permission uses MaxUint256 as its amount limit, can only be redeemed by the Gate, and has an expiry. A separate owner signature registers a finite normal budget with the Gate. The initial setup screen explains that budget and exception enforcement depends on the Gate and the approval server. World ID for Agents verifies the owner immediately before a pending order is allowed to proceed. After recording explicit consent to the order, the system requests fresh authentication. The server checks the signature, issuer, audience, nonce, authentication freshness, and a match with the registered owner. It also rechecks the order, purchase policy, and risk assessment for changes before issuing an H signature bound to that order. World verification happens on the backend; the Gate validates the resulting backend signature, its match to the order, its expiry, and its single use. Declining, cancellation, expired authentication, or a different identity prevents the exception purchase. Revoked permissions and reused approvals are rejected. Uniswap v3 uses an exact-output swap to obtain the amount of JPYC required for the purchase. The implementation checks the maximum USDC input and swap-price deviation, and returns any unused USDC. Intercepta screening runs on the EC backend before payment. The original warning remains in the record even if the owner approves the purchase. Another challenge was that an onchain transfer and saving an EC order do not always succeed together. A transfer may succeed while its response is lost, or a database write may fail after payment. To handle these cases, the system persists the transaction before broadcasting it, follows that same transaction, and recovers the order. Retries avoid duplicate payments, and the merchant receives a single order. Regular purchases, owner-approved exceptions to the budget for a period, swaps, recovery from lost responses, and finalizing merchant orders have been tested on a local fork. Responses from World, risk screening, and other external services in those integration tests are fixtures. The World integration uses the event's development environment; its fake identities do not establish production identity assurance. The public chat demo is a simulation with no transfers or live World authentication. End-to-end verification on public Polygon Amoy testnet (chain ID 80002), including ERC-7715 on a physical device and an interactive World login through to a completed purchase, is still pending. I defined the requirements and chose the design. I used Codex for implementation, testing, research, and documentation.

projects.title: Patio Station
projects.description: Live audio and tiny video broadcast through Ethereum’s mempool.
projects.project_description: Patio is an experimental live radio that turns Ethereum's mempool into a broadcast medium. Instead of uploading a stream to a media server, Patio encodes live audio or tiny video directly into the calldata of pending Ethereum transactions. A listener watches those pending transactions, reconstructs the media in the browser, and plays the stream while the transactions are still moving through the mempool. Broadcasters can create Public broadcasts that appear in Patio's live directory, or Unlisted broadcasts that are accessible only through a shareable listener link. The result feels like a tiny internet radio where Ethereum itself becomes the transmission layer: you connect a wallet, check your microphone or camera, press Start, and another browser can listen to the signal through Hoodi. Patio is intentionally experimental. The point is not to compete with conventional streaming infrastructure, but to explore an unintended capability of Ethereum: what if the mempool itself could be a live medium?
projects.how_its_made: Patio is built as a Next.js + TypeScript web application using viem for Ethereum interactions and the browser's native media APIs for capture and playback. When a broadcast is prepared, Patio generates an ephemeral session EOA in the browser. The broadcaster's connected wallet temporarily funds this session, but does not sign every media packet. The temporary account is important because Patio deliberately manipulates transaction nonces and replacements. Media packets are encoded into transaction calldata and signed as future-nonce transactions. For each media window, Patio can replace the pending transaction with a newer candidate, effectively using Ethereum's transaction replacement mechanism as a tiny broadcast channel. For audio, the browser captures Opus/WebM with MediaRecorder. Video uses a deliberately tiny VP8/Opus WebM profile with aggressive compression, fragmentation and frequent keyframes so it can fit within the constraints of the transport. On Hoodi, the current transport uses QuickNode for transaction submission and txpool_contentFrom observation. The listener watches the broadcaster's temporary account in the pending transaction pool, validates Patio packets, orders and reassembles them, then feeds the resulting WebM data into MediaSource for playback. This means the audio/video bytes actually travel inside Ethereum transactions, it is not WebRTC or a conventional video stream with blockchain metadata added afterward. Patio also has a small onchain registry for Public broadcasts. Public sessions announce their stream metadata so they can appear in the Listen directory, while Unlisted sessions skip discovery and work directly from a shareable URL. At the end of a session, Patio uses replacement/cleanup transactions to consume the nonce range and returns the remaining temporary Hoodi ETH to the broadcaster where possible. Some of the hackier parts were making browser media behave over such an unusual transport: buffering WebM fragments without constantly seeking to the live edge, bootstrapping late video listeners, handling replacement transactions, preserving session state across cleanup, and keeping the whole thing usable despite the mempool being an intentionally unreliable place to build a radio. The result is deliberately strange: the wallet funds a transmitter, pending Ethereum transactions become packets, the mempool becomes the airwaves, and a URL becomes the frequency.

projects.title: Recycle CCA
projects.description: Recycle stranded capital from strictly outbid Uniswap CCA bids into fresh higher-limit bids
projects.project_description: This project extends Uniswap’s Continuous Clearing Auction (CCA) with a mechanism for recycling the unspent balance of a strictly outbid bid into a new higher-limit bid. In the current design, a bidder can deposit capital, partially execute, then become outbid as the clearing price rises. The remaining balance may be unable to execute under the original price limit, yet still remain locked inside the auction before graduation. Our extension allows the bidder to reuse only this provably unspent balance without withdrawing funds or adding new external capital. The original bid’s historical fills and accounting are preserved, while a fresh bid is created at the current checkpoint with a new maximum price, preventing any backdated allocation. The prototype compares two otherwise identical auctions: a baseline CCA where stranded capital causes the auction to fall short of its minimum funding threshold, and a modified CCA where that same capital is recycled into executable demand and the auction can graduate. The implementation also enforces key safety properties, including owner authorization, no recycling of active or clearing-price bids, no double-use of recycled credit, correct failure refunds, and preservation of historical fills.
projects.how_its_made: The project is built directly on top of Uniswap’s Continuous Clearing Auction Solidity contracts. I extended the existing bid lifecycle with a new recycling path that allows the owner of a strictly outbid bid to move only its provably unspent balance into a fresh bid at the current auction checkpoint. The implementation reuses the CCA’s existing checkpointing, fill calculation, clearing-price, settlement, and refund accounting rather than introducing a parallel accounting system. Historical fills on the original bid remain unchanged, while recycled credit is deducted from its future refundable balance and used to create a new child bid with a higher maximum price. This ensures the new bid receives no retroactive allocation and behaves like an equivalent fresh-money bid submitted at the same checkpoint. The main technical challenge was preventing the same deposited capital from being counted twice across bid chains. I added accounting to track recycled credit and covered repeated and descendant recycling, failed-auction refunds, unauthorized callers, active bids, bids exactly at clearing, rounding, and successful settlement. The prototype is entirely Solidity and test-driven, with no frontend. The core demo runs two otherwise identical CCA auctions using the same external deposits: the baseline auction strands an outbid bidder’s unused capital and fails its minimum raise, while the modified auction internally recycles that balance into executable demand and successfully graduates. A particularly useful validation was comparing a recycled bid against an identical new bid funded with fresh external ETH at the same checkpoint. Both produce the same terminal pricing, proceeds, and token fills, demonstrating that recycling changes capital efficiency rather than auction execution semantics.
projects.project_description_markdown:
This project extends Uniswap’s Continuous Clearing Auction (CCA) with a mechanism for recycling the unspent balance of a strictly outbid bid into a new higher-limit bid. In the current design, a bidder can deposit capital, partially execute, then become outbid as the clearing price rises. The remaining balance may be unable to execute under the original price limit, yet still remain locked inside the auction before graduation.

Our extension allows the bidder to reuse only this provably unspent balance without withdrawing funds or adding new external capital. The original bid’s historical fills and accounting are preserved, while a fresh bid is created at the current checkpoint with a new maximum price, preventing any backdated allocation.

The prototype compares two otherwise identical auctions: a baseline CCA where stranded capital causes the auction to fall short of its minimum funding threshold, and a modified CCA where that same capital is recycled into executable demand and the auction can graduate. The implementation also enforces key safety properties, including owner authorization, no recycling of active or clearing-price bids, no double-use of recycled credit, correct failure refunds, and preservation of historical fills.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The project is built directly on top of Uniswap’s Continuous Clearing Auction Solidity contracts. I extended the existing bid lifecycle with a new recycling path that allows the owner of a strictly outbid bid to move only its provably unspent balance into a fresh bid at the current auction checkpoint.

The implementation reuses the CCA’s existing checkpointing, fill calculation, clearing-price, settlement, and refund accounting rather than introducing a parallel accounting system. Historical fills on the original bid remain unchanged, while recycled credit is deducted from its future refundable balance and used to create a new child bid with a higher maximum price. This ensures the new bid receives no retroactive allocation and behaves like an equivalent fresh-money bid submitted at the same checkpoint.

The main technical challenge was preventing the same deposited capital from being counted twice across bid chains. I added accounting to track recycled credit and covered repeated and descendant recycling, failed-auction refunds, unauthorized callers, active bids, bids exactly at clearing, rounding, and successful settlement.

The prototype is entirely Solidity and test-driven, with no frontend. The core demo runs two otherwise identical CCA auctions using the same external deposits: the baseline auction strands an outbid bidder’s unused capital and fails its minimum raise, while the modified auction internally recycles that balance into executable demand and successfully graduates.

A particularly useful validation was comparing a recycled bid against an identical new bid funded with fresh external ETH at the same checkpoint. Both produce the same terminal pricing, proceeds, and token fills, demonstrating that recycling changes capital efficiency rather than auction execution semantics.

projects.title: BSA Gate
projects.description: A gate that checks who may pay and whether it's safe before USDC settles over x402.
projects.project_description:
BSA Gate is a compliance and safety checkpoint that runs before a stablecoin payment
settles. Today USDC moves blind: there is no check on who is paying, and no check on
whether the counterparty is dangerous. BSA Gate inserts one gate in front of settlement
and answers two questions. Who may pay. The payer holds an ENSv2 name that carries KYC attestations such as over 18
and jurisdiction. We issue these as an attestation authority: the user owns their name, but
only our issuer can write the attestation keys, so the claims cannot be forged and are
portable, issued once and trusted by any merchant. Real identity comes from an EU digital
identity wallet (EUDI): the user presents their ID credential, and we derive the
attestations from the verified birthdate and nationality without putting either on-chain. Whether it is safe. Before any money moves, the payer and payee are screened with Intercepta for sanctions, scams and mixer exposure. A risky counterparty is blocked with a clear reason,
and the screen fails closed. Only if both checks pass does the payment settle in USDC over x402, gasless for the payer.
The same gate protects a WooCommerce store, a Shopify store, and an autonomous AI agent paying another service, so a human shopper and an agent follow the exact same rules. An agent pays under a revocable, non-transferable delegation and a per-payment spend cap that only its principal can change, using a wallet that is its own and not the principal's. Remove ENSv2 and the product stops working: issuance, attestations, delegation, per-key write scoping and revocation all live in ENSv2.
projects.how_its_made:
The gate is a TypeScript facilitator (viem, Express). One pipeline runs five ordered steps:
verify the EIP-3009 authorization, enforce the agent spend cap, check ENS permission and
attestations, screen with Intercepta, then settle. It fails at the first check with a precise
reason and moves no money on a block. Identity and permissions (ENSv2 on Sepolia, sepolia-fix). We deploy a PermissionedRegistry
for bsagate.eth and a shared resolver through VerifiableFactory, with our issuer as admin.
After KYC, each principal gets their own UserRegistry and a name registered with RENEW only: no resolver swap, no sub-minting, no transfer. Attestations (over18, jurisdiction) are
resolver text records only the issuer can write, so the name owner cannot forge them. That
split between name owner and record writer is the core idea. We also use per-key roles
(authorizeTextRoles) so an attester can be scoped to a single record key. A principal
delegates a non-transferable, revocable agent (agent.alice.bsagate.eth, roleBitmap 0) that
inherits the principal's attestations by living under their name, and the principal keeps
ROLE_UNREGISTER as an on-chain kill switch. The gate walks the registries (getState,
getSubregistry) instead of trusting a resolver, so an unregistered name serving a default
record never passes. KYC from a real EU wallet (EUDI, OpenID4VP). The user scans a QR with an EU identity wallet
(tested with Procivis One), presents their PID, and the public EUDI reference verifier
validates it cryptographically. We decode the SD-JWT, derive over 18 from birthdate and
jurisdiction from nationality, and write only those derived attestations to ENS. A self-issue
demo path is kept for judges who do not have a wallet. Payments (x402, EIP-3009). The payer signs a gasless transferWithAuthorization on Circle USDC off-chain; the facilitator submits it, so the payer never pays gas. An autonomous agent client probes an x402 resource, gets 402 with the terms, signs with its own key, and retries with the X-PAYMENT header, all without a human in the loop. Spend cap. A per-agent, per-payment ceiling enforced by the facilitator. The principal signs
each cap change with an EIP-712 message, so a delegated agent can pay on its own but can never raise its own limit. Safety (Intercepta). Before settling, the gate calls the Intercepta Web3 Antivirus quick-scan
on both payer and payee. Sanctioned, scam, blacklisted or high-toxicity addresses are blocked. The risk data is mainnet, so we screen mainnet addresses even on a testnet build. Surfaces. A WooCommerce plugin (a PHP payment gateway with a REST settle route and a wallet order-pay flow, plus per-product required attestations), a Shopify pay service (a hosted pay page with Admin API write-back and a per-product metafield, not an installable app), an
autonomous agent-to-agent x402 client, and a Next.js web app: get-verified (EU wallet plus a
self-issue fallback, side by side), checkout, an agent console to delegate and spend-cap an
agent, and a live activity feed of settled and blocked payments with reasons. Engineering and delivery. 36 automated tests written test-first with vitest, run against a free
local Anvil fork during development. Deployed live: the facilitator on Railway (Docker, with a
persistent volume) in live mode against real Sepolia and the real Intercepta API, and the web
app on Vercel; both public and wired to the same gate. We proved real USDC settlements on
Sepolia across the agent, Shopify and WooCommerce surfaces, and every refusal live: not 18,
wrong jurisdiction, over the spend cap, and a real sanctioned payee (Intercepta toxicScore 100).

projects.title: Sui Cash
projects.description: The Merge of FeliCa & Sui: tap your Suica, show your face, pay on-chain. Verified with ZK proofs.
projects.project_description:
SuiCash turns the transit IC card already in every Japanese wallet into a key for a Sui wallet: tap your Suica, show your face, and pay on-chain. Tap you Suica card, take your face photo, then you can send money, even on chain. Japan already runs the electronic cash system based on FeliCa. Over 200 million transit IC cards (Suica and friends) are used every day, yet a few people in Japan have access to cryptocurrency. SuiCash connects them, and promotes the crypto mass adoption in Japan. The hard part: FeliCa is a proprietary standard built on symmetric-key (DES/3DES) mutual authentication. Blockchains assume public-key signatures and transparency. A Sui contract can't simply "check a Suica card.". So we utilized ZKP, and then we could finally fusion them. How we bridged it: FeliCa oracle – A terminal (Sony RC-S634 reader) runs the full FeliCa mutual authentication with the card through our oracle server (challenge → settle → attest). Zero-knowledge attestation – The oracle produces a Groth16 proof. The circuit very face the execution trace of authentication work inside the circuit. On-chain verification – A Sui Move package (felica_oracle) verifies the proof with Sui's native Groth16 verifier. This proves "valid FeliCa card was present" IDi-seeded Account Abstraction wallet – Each card's IDi deterministically maps to a Sui AA wallet. Anyone can top up a card by its printed number, with no app or seed phrase. Face binding – During registration, the user's face is linked to their IDi. At the payment terminal, card tap + face authentication together unlock the wallet. A stolen card alone isn't enough. What we built
What we built during the hackathon: the ZK prover and oracle server, the Move verifier contracts, a registration web app (card number ⇄ IDi, face enrollment, top-up), and a working payment terminal: a face-recognition device with a card reader.
projects.how_its_made: SuiCash can't be done without a spirit of reverse engineering. Hardware: we recently bought a health insurance reception terminal device. It incorporates a my number card reader, front facing camera , touch screen, and Android system with much vulnerabilities. While we research these vulnerabilities, we found the potential of interesting use case of FeliCa. We finally made Android app thanks to these vulnerabilities. FeliCa: FeliCa is actually a proprietary protocol. But KIRISHIKI Yudai's publication changed the situation. Protocols and cipher have been disclosed and developers can easily make softwares with felica. When we read his publications, we noticed that its authentication mechanism can be expressed with zkp constraints. Then we finally done it. ZKP Oracle: felica uses symmetric key cryptography, and it is inevitable to hold secrets. Oracle acts the role. It takes responsibilities to the secrets and makes zkp. Using arkworks, we implemented DES and 3DES as an R1CS circuit (~149k constraints) on BN254 Groth16. The circuit re-derives the FeliCa key schedule and checks the whole authentication transcript (3DES, MAC, transaction ID) inside the proof. Sui: Sui is a blockchain featuring high throughput. It matches the felica's characteristics. We implemented a groth16 verifier, and felica card bound wallet. So user can top up targeting to the card, on card can consume the balance on chain.

projects.title: Fuse
projects.description: NFT gacha: lock two away for good, an AI fuses them into one. Rerolling burns what you pulled.
projects.project_description: Fuse turns two NFTs you own into a single new one. Pick two, pay 0.001 ETH, and both parents move into a pool contract that has no way to send anything back out. It is not a burn address and not a promise in the docs: the pool's entire implementation is a single receive hook, with no withdraw, no approve, no owner and no upgrade path. A child NFT is minted to you in the same transaction, and an AI then fuses the two parent images into its artwork. If you don't like what you got, Remint burns that child and rolls a new one from the same two parents. It costs another 0.001 ETH, each child can be reminted at most three times, and there is no side-by-side comparison, no history and no undo. Exactly one result is ever on screen. That is the whole product: a gacha where the price of rerolling is the thing you already have. Half of the 26 starter pieces are sushi, on purpose. Two similar creatures fuse into something that could just be a third creature, and nobody watching can tell it happened. A creature fused with nigiri is obvious at a glance.
projects.how_its_made: Three Foundry contracts on Base Sepolia, all verified. FuseNFT is one ERC-721 holding both starter pieces and fused children. FusePool is where parents go, and its whole implementation is onERC721Received -- no withdraw, no owner, no upgrade -- so "they never come back" is the absence of code rather than a claim. Fuse owns fuse(), remint() and finalizeMetadata(), and splits authority three ways: the deploy key mints starters, the backend key can only write a tokenURI, anyone can fuse for 0.001 ETH. Fusion traits come from a seed derived on-chain from block data and a requestId. Off-chain is one Next.js app on Vercel, with OpenAI's image edit endpoint taking both parent PNGs and Cloudflare R2 holding the results. Vercel can't run a worker, so there is no event listener: the browser pokes /api/generate and the server checks the chain itself. The only way in is a tokenId somebody paid 0.001 ETH to put into Pending. There is no database either -- R2 conditional writes are the lock, and every step asks whether it already happened, so a timed-out generation resumes without a second mint or a second payment. What bit us: after a redeploy, requestIds restart at 1. A fresh fuse read the previous deployment's state record, saw "done", and never generated anything. R2 keys are now namespaced by chain id and contract address.

projects.title: StakePort
projects.description: Trustless secondary market for native ETH validator stake, settled by beacon-chain proofs
projects.project_description:
StakePort is a trustless secondary market for native Ethereum stake. Today, a solo staker or　institution that wants to exit a validator has to wait in the exit queue (days to weeks), and a
buyer who wants staked ETH has to wait in the entry queue. StakePort lets them trade the　validator position directly: the seller's stake is moved into the buyer's validator via an EIP-7251
consolidation, and the buyer's payment is released only once the beacon chain itself proves the
stake arrived. There are no custodians, no LST wrapper, and no trusted oracle. How a trade works: The seller delegates their validator's withdrawal EOA to a small EIP-7702 contract and lists an
order (fixed price or priced relative to wstETH). The buyer fills the order and pays in WETH, native ETH, or any token routed through Uniswap v4. Payment is held in escrow, and the same transaction submits the consolidation request
(source validator -> buyer's 0x02 validator) through the seller's delegated EOA. Checkpoint 1: an SSZ Merkle proof against an EIP-4788 beacon block root shows the request is in the beacon state's pending_consolidations queue. Checkpoint 2: a later proof shows the source validator was processed (withdrawable, balance
drained, not slashed). The escrow then pays the seller. If the request is ignored, the source is slashed, or nobody proves acceptance in time, the buyer is refunded. Anyone can relay the proofs, so settlement is permissionless. Pricing reflects queue economics. A buyer who skips the entry queue earns rewards sooner, so the seller can charge a premium: fair value = amount x (1 + APR x queue-time saved), with APR taken from Lido's public stETH APR feed. The UI shows live entry/exit queue lengths and this fair value. Liquidity venues:
- Uniswap v4 hook: buy stake with any token in one swap. The hook takes the input, swaps it    into ETH in the canonical pool, and fills the order. A v3 wstETH/WETH TWAP prices LST-relative orders.
- 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: buyers post standing bids (fixed or Dutch auction) backed by Aqua virtual balances, and sellers match their stake into the best bid.
- World ID: sellers can restrict an order to buyers verified with a World ID NFC document
credential (passport / My Number Card). The aim is to keep sanctioned jurisdictions out while
preserving privacy. It is not KYC: no identity data reaches the app or the chain. The demo runs on a mainnet fork one block before a real mainnet consolidation. Checkpoint 1 uses the real beacon state and a real proof; checkpoint 2 is simulated because it would take ~27 hours.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, EVM Prague; about 130 tests, including mainnet-fork tests):
- NativeStakeMarket: order book (EIP-712 or onchain listing), escrow, and a two-checkpoint
settlement state machine.
- Stake7702Delegate: the seller's EOA runs this code via EIP-7702. It can only call the EIP-7251
consolidation predeploy on behalf of the market.
- BeaconOracle + BeaconProofs: SSZ Merkle verification against EIP-4788 roots. The generalized indices are derived by hand for the Fulu BeaconState (38 fields): validators, balances, slot and pending_consolidations. They are cross-checked against Lodestar's SSZ types. Proofs: a TypeScript proof generator (Lodestar ssz and persistent-merkle-tree) builds the proofs. On real networks we don't download the ~250 MB beacon state. Instead we use the Lodestar proof API exposed by ChainSafe's public nodes to fetch compact multiproofs. Those nodes are not trusted: every proof is rebuilt locally and checked against the block header's state root, which the contract checks against EIP-4788. A relayer settles trades automatically, and an event indexer serves the frontend.

    - Stake7702Delegate: the seller's EOA runs this code via EIP-7702. It can only call the EIP-7251
      consolidation predeploy on behalf of the market.
    - BeaconOracle + BeaconProofs: SSZ Merkle verification against EIP-4788 roots. The generalized indices are derived by hand for the Fulu BeaconState (38 fields): validators, balances, slot and pending_consolidations. They are cross-checked against Lodestar's SSZ types.

    Proofs: a TypeScript proof generator (Lodestar ssz and persistent-merkle-tree) builds the proofs. On real networks we don't download the ~250 MB beacon state. Instead we use the Lodestar proof API exposed by ChainSafe's public nodes to fetch compact multiproofs. Those nodes are not trusted: every proof is rebuilt locally and checked against the block header's state root, which the contract checks against EIP-4788. A relayer settles trades automatically, and an event indexer serves the frontend.

projects.title: ENS402
projects.description: Discover x402 services on ENSv2, govern updates with EAC, and verify payments before agents sign.
projects.project_description: ENS402 is a public context and payment verification stack for x402 services. An HTTP 402 response tells an agent how to pay, but the server presenting the bill should not be the sole authority for its recipient and terms. ENS402 gives each provider and service a stable ENSv2 name. The service publishes a description, call format, endpoint, status and fixed payment terms on Sepolia. A native provider Registry groups services; a shared native PermissionedResolver stores separate records for each service. Enhanced Access Control lets an operations wallet update endpoints and descriptions while a Treasury wallet governs payment terms. Independent indexers can rebuild the supported service directory from public ENS state. Our reference Search API, SDK and MCP support keyword and semantic discovery. Before an agent signs a Base Sepolia USDC payment, Guard resolves the latest ENS records, compares them with the live HTTP 402 challenge and applies a separate risk signal. A mismatch in recipient, token, network or price stops the checkout. The project connects public discovery, scoped configuration governance and pre-sign payment verification in one agent workflow.
projects.how_its_made: We use the ENSv2 Sepolia deployment directly. The platform name points to a native Registry; each provider receives a child Registry and a native PermissionedResolver. Service names have distinct record bundles. Native EAC grants Ops only the endpoint, description, image and call-metadata writers, while a Treasury Safe receives the payment-record writer. A provider Admin manages registrations and grants. Our Solidity service registrar and TypeScript planners assemble native deployments, scoped permissions and service publication; Foundry and Anvil forks test both permitted and denied writes. An Envio event journal and bounded finalized RPC reconstruction build a PostgreSQL catalog; OpenAI embeddings add semantic ranking to keyword search. The Next.js reference app exposes provider onboarding, Search API, read-only MCP and buyer checkout. The TypeScript SDK freshly resolves ENS and compares the current HTTP 402 challenge before requesting a signature. x402 settlement uses Base Sepolia USDC. Privy is an optional hosted-wallet adapter; self signing remains available. Intercepta provides an Ethereum-mainnet address risk signal in the payment decision path, with its coverage shown separately from the Base Sepolia settlement checks. The public ENS402 platform Registry is linked on Sepolia; provider publication and a funded public end-to-end payment remain in progress.

projects.title: Nafuda
projects.description: ENSv2 title names for graded card slabs: tap to verify the slab and its owner; sell by transfer.
projects.project_description:
At a card show, a graded slab changes hands for cash in seconds, and the buyer has two questions nobody can answer on the spot: is this the slab the grader actually sealed, and is the seller its owner? A cert lookup only proves that the cert number exists. It says nothing about the slab in your hand, and clones copy the label perfectly. Nafuda gives every slab an ENSv2 name that works as its title. When a grader seals a card, it puts a chip inside the slab and issues <cert>.<grader>.nafuda.eth. The name records the chip's public key and resolves to the current owner. At the table, the buyer taps the slab: the chip signs a fresh challenge, and any ENS client checks the signature against the name's slab.chip record and the seller against its addr record. Selling the card is a transfer of the name, with the seller's declared price written into the transfer. ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control is the trust model: The holder gets exactly one role: transfer. Each grader's registry is emancipated, so the grader cannot unregister, re-point or claw back an issued title. Safe transfers only go through when the seller is the title's only role holder.
Every title page shows this live. A "who can do what" matrix simulates each party's call against the contracts and shows the contract's answer, and every buyer can run the per-title checks. Several graders share the namespace, each with its own registry and its own record schema. BGS-style subgrades and card categories (Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!, baseball…) are ENS text records. The collector app: explore, tap-to-verify, provenance flow, market map, signed offers. The grader console: intake board, issuing, trust panel, live access-control map. Curvegrid MultiBaas runs as an independent second witness of our index. Everything runs on Sepolia against the ENSv2 Beta. The three graders are simulated: they are modeled after PSA, BGS and CGC, and not affiliated with them. The chip is simulated in the browser. In production it would be an NFC chip, such as an Arx HaLo, sealed inside the slab.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, 32 tests) TitleController is each grader's issuing contract and the resolver of <grader>.nafuda.eth. Titles have no resolver of their own. The ENSv2 Universal Resolver walks nafuda.eth → grader registry → cert and finds the grader's resolver by wildcard (ENSIP-10). resolve() computes the addr and text records from registry state, so the holder record can never go stale. Each grader gets a UserRegistry, deployed through the ENSv2 VerifiableFactory. The controller holds ROLE_REGISTRAR, the holder receives only ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN, and the registry is emancipated. TitleControllerV2 adds grader-defined attributes (subgrades, card categories) and lists them in an attributes record. A one-way lock script revokes the remaining subtree powers. It was rehearsed on forks. Everything else is TypeScript, in one npm workspace A shared, unit-tested core: verification rules, the EAC permission model, EIP-712 intents and per-title integrity checks. Apps in React 19, Vite and Tailwind, with React Flow for provenance and the access map. viem talks to the chain, through our own EIP-6963 wallet provider (no wagmi). Title pages read everything from ENS in the browser. The Hono + Postgres server only indexes events for lists and charts, and stores signed off-chain intents (asks, bids, grading submissions). It all runs in Docker on a Mac mini, behind a Cloudflare Tunnel. Notable hacks The permissions matrix runs each action as an eth_call from each party's address, and shows the contract's own revert (for example EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles). The declared price rides in safeTransferFrom's data field, behind a 4-byte tag. Demo chip keys are derived from the cert, so tapping a slab, and cloning one, can be simulated in the browser. A market simulator trades between 16 demo collectors. Each has a <name>.nafuda.eth primary name, so the feeds show ENS names by reverse resolution. Curvegrid MultiBaas We linked the three grader registries in a MultiBaas deployment, and receive every transfer through its HMAC-signed webhook. The server reconciles both ways, and the result is public. Every event Curvegrid saw must be in our index, and every transfer we indexed inside its window must have been seen by Curvegrid. Choosing which events to link showed that our indexer ignored TransferBatch, which ENSv2 registries emit when one call moves several names. We fixed it. Testing Puppeteer e2e suites against the live site, and on Sepolia (submit → grade → issue → offer → transfer). An index-vs-ENS consistency check. Built solo. The code was written with Claude Code, a coding agent, under the author's direction. The planning docs and an AI-usage log are in the repo.

projects.title: watermark
projects.description: DAO treasuries market-make on Aqua, ENSv2 makes whitelists counterparties&agent tuning spreads.
projects.project_description: watermark turns a DAO treasury from a price taker into a market maker for its own assets. The problem. A multisig signs once per action. Selling in slices (DCA or TWAP) would mean another signature and another price for every slice, so the DAO hands the whole balance to an AMM or a solver in one trade. That sale is not free: the solver sets its own incentive first and comes back with the price that is left. A treasury-sized balance does not make the DAO the side that quotes. It is treated as the side that takes. In February 2023 ENS DAO sold 10,000 ETH (about $16.15M) through CoW Swap with a 2% slippage tolerance (EP3.3): a budget of up to $323k for the other side of the trade. What watermark does. The DAO's Safe signs once. That one signature ships a pricing program to 1inch Aqua. From then on the treasury quotes both sides, bid and ask, around an oracle mid at spreads the DAO sets itself, and market makers fill it in small pieces over time. Tokens never leave the Safe until the moment of each fill, and every fill is atomic. With a mid of 4,000 USDC and terms of 3 bp to sell and 10 bp to buy, the desk asks 4,001.2 and bids 3,996. One fill cannot move more than 50 ETH, so a large balance never leaves in one go. Who can trade. An open quote is a free option for the fastest bot. So only named counterparties can fill. Each market maker gets an ENS name under the desk, for example mm-a.clients.dao-treasury-a.eth. At every fill the router checks on-chain that the name is live and points to the wallet that is trading. A wallet with no name, or an expired one, is refused before a single token moves. Per-counterparty pricing. The Safe writes the terms once on each name (sell 3 bp, buy 10 bp, 50 ETH cap per fill) and a plain-English policy on the DAO's own name. After each fill, a risk agent looks at how that counterparty traded: how big, how often, and whether the price jumped its way right after. It writes that name's next spread to ENS, never outside the terms. Counterparties who trade fair get up to 3x tighter prices (1 / 4 bp instead of 3 / 10 bp). Counterparties who trade sharp stay at the edge. A spread written outside the terms is ignored, so the agent can never make a quote worse than the fence. The agent can only write spreads: it cannot change terms, addresses, expiries, the cap, the oracle or the policy, and it never needs another Safe signature. Guardrails. A 600-second oracle freshness window, a 50 ETH cap per fill, and an inventory floor: the desk stops selling ETH at a 70% ETH share. Every fill can be recomputed from public data. The app. A landing page, a treasury dashboard (quotes by counterparty, inventory, the terms fence), a six-step wizard that opens a desk as one Safe proposal, counterparty and agent views, a fills list with per-fill verification, and a trade screen for counterparties. Live on Sepolia, on the official Aqua registry. Not affiliated with 1inch or ENS.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). DeskRouter is a copy of 1inch SwapVM v1.0.2's Aqua router. Its opcode table keeps SwapVM's control instructions at their original numbers, switches off the fee and AMM slots, and appends two instructions of our own at 34 (EnsGate) and 35 (DeskPrice). The DAO's 2-of-3 Safe ships one SwapVM program to the official Aqua registry (0x1111113c...a90a, not redeployed). Aqua pulls tokens from the Safe and pushes the other side back in the same transaction, so the Safe keeps custody and our contracts store no configuration. EnsGate (#34) walks ENSv2's per-name registries on-chain (.eth registry, then the desk's registry, then the clients registry, then the resolver) and checks that the counterparty's name sits under this desk, has not expired, uses the pinned resolver, and that its addr is the taker Aqua passed for this swap (not tx.origin). DeskPrice (#35) reads two binary data records from the ENSv2 PermissionedResolver on the counterparty's name. desk.terms is abi.encode(uint8 version, uint16 sellBps, uint16 buyBps, uint128 cap). desk.spread is abi.encode(uint8 version, uint16 sellBps, uint16 buyBps, uint64 validUntil). A spread counts only if it is unexpired and inside the terms. The instruction then prices ask = mid x (10000 + sell) / 10000 and bid = mid x (10000 - buy) / 10000 from a Chainlink-style oracle with a freshness check, enforces the per-fill cap and the 70% inventory floor (selling ETH reverts at or below a 70% ETH share; buying still fills), and emits a DeskFill event carrying every input, so anyone can recompute the price. ENSv2. dao-treasury-a.eth has clients and agents subnames, each with its own registry, and one PermissionedResolver per treasury. The Safe owns every name and the root roles of the resolver and registries. The risk agent, risk.agents.dao-treasury-a.eth, is granted setter roles for exactly two record keys, desk.spread and desk.stats. ENSv2's per-record permissions are what make "an AI can tune prices but cannot move money or rules" enforceable on-chain rather than by trust. Agent (TypeScript, viem). A keeper scans DeskFill events from a cursor. It reads the fill, applies the plain-English sentences of desk.policy (inventory and suspicion rules), optionally asks TypeSafe's Jev model to pick a tier (tight, standard or fence), and writes the filler's next desk.spread and desk.stats. The next fill by that name reads the new record. Without a Jev key, a local tier rule is used. Read API and bot. A Node service stores every DeskFill in SQLite and serves read-only routes. The fill route recomputes each price from public on-chain data. A market-maker bot CLI quotes and fills as mm-a and mm-b. Frontend. React 19, Vite, viem and wagmi. The wizard builds the Safe transaction for the owners to sign. The landing page's clouds and sea were generated in Higgsfield (an image, then a Kling video), then turned into 1-bit animated PNGs by our own blue-noise (void-and-cluster) ditherer in Node. The motion graphics are live canvas simulations dithered every frame against the same 64x64 blue-noise mask, so still dots never flicker. Why the partners mattered. Aqua's shared liquidity means the treasury never deposits into a pool, and SwapVM let us add instructions instead of writing a new AMM. ENSv2 gave us identity for the gate and scoped, per-record delegation for the agent. Hacky bits: extending SwapVM's opcode table; storing pricing parameters as binary ENS data records that a swap instruction reads mid-fill; a policy written in plain English that an agent executes; and building the whole thing with one-requirement-per-PR cloud agents behind a clarity gate.

projects.title: Dim
projects.description: Confidential ETH UTXO research prototype with public Uniswap payments.
projects.project_description: This project studies confidential ETH transfers on Ethereum while keeping the relationships between consumed and created UTXOs public. The research prototype supports ETH deposits, confidential transfers, and public withdrawals. Its Uniswap integration exchanges a fixed amount of ETH for a public token, delivers all swap proceeds to a designated recipient, and lets the payer reuse the remaining confidential UTXO. It is aimed at developers and researchers evaluating functionality, cost, security, and the limits of amount confidentiality as a basis for future standardization. The public transaction graph and known amounts can reveal transfer amounts or remaining balances.
projects.how_its_made: The core tracks input existence and unspent status in contract storage and exposes UTXO consumption and creation relationships, following the core specification. Every operation checks valid owner authorization bound to its intended effects and execution context. ETH deposits create matching UTXOs, transfers conserve the input value, and withdrawals preserve the sum of the public withdrawal and any confidential remainder. Unauthorized spending, double spending, and replay of successful operations are rejected. Gas is paid separately in public ETH. Recipients discover, decrypt, and check receipt data using their keys and public history. The CLI distinguishes confirmed receipt from pending, failed, or unverified operations and supports resynchronization. The Uniswap integration binds the swap conditions to the owner's withdrawal authorization and rolls back all payment asset effects if the swap or delivery fails, following the integration requirements. The prior-EIP benchmark provides a separate measurement path for EIP-8182. Its Bash and JavaScript scripts build a pinned EIP-8182 reference implementation, generate Groth16 pool and demo-authorization proofs with snarkjs, and verify them on a local Anvil node using Foundry tools. They also exercise the reference demo's ML-KEM-768/X25519 receipt encryption and recovery from public logs. The comparison report records the reference code, measurement conditions, development-key assumptions, and limitations.

Unauthorized spending, double spending, and replay of successful operations are rejected. Gas is paid separately in public ETH.

Recipients discover, decrypt, and check receipt data using their keys and public history. The CLI distinguishes confirmed receipt from pending, failed, or unverified operations and supports resynchronization. The Uniswap integration binds the swap conditions to the owner's withdrawal authorization and rolls back all payment asset effects if the swap or delivery fails, following the integration requirements.

The prior-EIP benchmark provides a separate measurement path for EIP-8182. Its Bash and JavaScript scripts build a pinned EIP-8182 reference implementation, generate Groth16 pool and demo-authorization proofs with snarkjs, and verify them on a local Anvil node using Foundry tools. They also exercise the reference demo's ML-KEM-768/X25519 receipt encryption and recovery from public logs. The comparison report records the reference code, measurement conditions, development-key assumptions, and limitations.

projects.title: SUIJIN
projects.description: A shared liquidity on Sui that stays in your wallet until a trade settles.
projects.project_description: Suijin is a shared liquidity layer native to Sui. One self-custodial wallet balance can back several markets at once, and funds stay in the provider's own address until a trade actually settles. Today, putting tokens to work on-chain means depositing them into an AMM pool, an order book or a vault. Each deposit locks a separate slice of your balance, hands custody to a contract, and sits idle whenever that venue is quiet. Liquidity ends up thin and fragmented. Suijin replaces the deposit with a permission. Using Sui's new address balances and native Allowances, a provider grants one bounded, revocable, app-bound Allowance: a spend cap and an expiry that only the Suijin Move package can use. They then point several pricing strategies (fixed rate and a virtual constant-product curve) at that same Allowance. Each strategy advertises the full balance, so 1,000,000 tJPY backing two strategies shows a Shared Liquidity Ratio of 2.0x. That is not leverage: every fill draws on the same real balance and the same cap, so no combination of fills can spend more than exists. A trader signs once to create an order with an exact cap payment Allowance. A resolver finds the best executable quote across all strategies, and an executor settles both sides in a single PTB that pulls from the provider's and the trader's Allowances. The executor chooses when to settle, never what: Move recomputes every price, amount and recipient, and the whole PTB reverts if anything is off. The provider can revoke at any time, and every later fill fails. The web app covers Swap, Pay (send an exact amount paid in another coin), Earn (provide liquidity from your wallet), Limit orders and a Portfolio view. Everything runs live on Sui testnet with tUSD/tJPY test coins.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: two Move 2024 packages on Sui testnet. suijin has five modules: app binds Allowances to the package witness and is the only place a spend permit can be minted; math holds fixed-rate and virtual-curve pricing in u128; strategy stores pricing and limits per provider; order holds the trader's SwapOrder; settlement::fill is the atomic swap. mock_coins ships tUSD and tJPY (6 decimals) with open faucets. 26 Move tests cover every abort path. The core is sui::allowance with address balances, which are only enabled on testnet and devnet right now. We use propose_for_app so each Allowance is app-bound: it can only be spent through our package, so our Move rules gate every withdrawal, while the Sui framework enforces the cap, expiry and real balance. settlement::fill takes two tx.withdrawal inputs from allowances in one PTB, one for the provider's tJPY and one for the trader's tUSD, recomputes the output, checks the withdrawn balances match exactly, then sends funds to both sides. Hacky bits: allowance::issue returns nothing, so an order cannot reference the payment Allowance it creates in the same transaction. Instead, fill binds it by funder = trader, cap = exact quote amount, and expiry = order expiry. Curve math rounds the new base reserve up so rounding dust always stays with the provider, and the TypeScript SDK mirrors the Move math byte for byte with shared test vectors. The executor prices and settles from fresh fullnode state, and retries briefly because a fill request can race the order transaction to a different fullnode replica. Off-chain: a TypeScript SDK (@mysten/sui 2.33) builds every transaction and reads state, using GraphQL for objects and gRPC for balances and execution, since public JSON-RPC is off. One Bun server is both resolver (POST /v1/quote, any direction, exact input or output) and executor (POST /v1/orders/:id/fill); it holds the only spender key. The dApp is React 19 + Vite with dApp Kit v2 (@mysten/dapp-kit-react), deployed on Cloudflare. The landing page is TanStack Start on Cloudflare Workers, with a three.js particle scene (a water dragon rising from a pool, sampled from our logo) and GSAP ScrollTrigger animations.

projects.title: RFC Legends
projects.description: Idle rooster RPG with farm-signed records: onchain health attestations and ENS bloodlines.
projects.project_description: RFC Legends is an idle RPG with classic job/stat/card progression, live guild chat and a shared guild boss, themed around Thai native rooster breeds. You play as a trainer adventuring with a rooster companion; both level up automatically, even while you are offline. Your rooster belongs to one of five sire lines, and the rooster explorer shows the farm-registered birds of those lines — currently sample records with placeholder leg-ring IDs — each minted onchain only with two parties: the issuer submits it and the farm's key co-signs the registration (leg-ring ID, bloodline, hatch date). One leg-ring ID can only ever be one token, and the farm signs health and weight attestations anyone can relay onchain. Each bird carries an ENSv2 name; offspring are subnames of their sire, resolved through a permissioned resolver where only the farm key can write health records, so a bloodline is verifiable by anyone. Rare drops are the heart of the economy. Legendary items and monster cards mint from gameplay only — with a server-signed EIP-712 voucher and only to a World ID-verified wallet — and trade in an onchain Rare Market that splits every sale 90% seller / 10% RFC Club treasury inside the contract. One human, one account: a second wallet replaying the same World ID nullifier is rejected onchain, and every sale is indexed by Curvegrid MultiBaas, so the 90/10 split is readable straight from onchain events. Cartoon collectible art; premium items come only from gameplay drops, never a shop.
projects.how_its_made: The game is a Next.js 16 + React 19 app with a Phaser 3 canvas for the idle farm scene. A server-authoritative TypeScript engine simulates combat tick by tick and settles offline progress rate-based, so nothing about your progression is trusted to the client. State, guild chat and the guild boss live in PocketBase behind our API; wagmi and viem talk to five Solidity 0.8.28 contracts on Sepolia (a test-USDC, a World ID registry, an ERC-1155 for rare drops, a 90/10 marketplace, and an ERC-721 for the real roosters), all verified on Etherscan and covered by 105 Foundry tests at 100% line coverage. Three sponsor pieces do the heavy lifting. World ID gates the economy: the IDKit widget proves personhood, our server verifies the proof against World's API with the wallet as the signal (apps/web/src/server/worldid/verify.ts), then records the nullifier onchain in HumanRegistry — a second wallet replaying the same nullifier is rejected by the contract itself. ENSv2 carries the pedigree: each rooster has a name under rfclegends.eth and offspring are subnames of their sire (e.g. chick01.theprawang.rfclegends.eth), with a permissioned resolver where only the farm's key can write weight/health records (ens/src/ensv2.ts, ens/scripts/attest.ts), and the rooster pages resolve those records live. Curvegrid MultiBaas indexes the contracts' events and powers the market's sale history through saved event queries (contracts/scripts/multibaas-setup.mjs, apps/web/src/lib/contracts/multibaas.ts) — the 90/10 split of every sale is readable straight from indexed Sold events. Demo mode honesty: the live site runs with boosted EXP and drop rates so the full loop — leveling to 30, earning an MVP card, World ID verification, minting, listing, selling with the onchain 90/10 split — can be shown in minutes. The badge is always visible in the UI and the boosted rates are never presented as real. Everything onchain (contracts, verifications, sales, attestations) is real Sepolia activity; the birds shown are sample roosters with placeholder ring IDs until Ninlanee Farm's real records land.

projects.title: Machi Vouchers
projects.description: Japan's town shopping vouchers on Sui: shop-only, paid to the shop instantly, with a stamp rally
projects.project_description: Every year Japanese towns fund premium shopping vouchers: residents pay ¥10,000 and get ¥12,000 to spend at local shops. Most programs are still on paper, so shops count used vouchers and carry them back to get paid, and the city that funds the premium sees a final report rather than where its money went. Machi Vouchers rebuilds the program on Sui. A chamber of commerce launches a program; the city deposits the premium into a shared vault on chain; residents buy a set and get two kinds of voucher: small-shop vouchers (中小店舗券) that only work at small and independent shops, and any-shop vouchers (共通券) for every registered shop. Both are Sui Closed-Loop Tokens, so they can only be spent through the program's shop check and can't be sent to anyone else. When a resident pays, one transaction spends the voucher and pays the shop the same amount from the vault, so the shop is paid immediately. Staff give a stamp with +1 and Confirm. Stamps from five different small shops release a ¥500 bonus, and each shop also keeps its own stamp card. The resident's card can be added to a phone's wallet (tested in Google Wallet); the pass shows balances and stamps copied from Sui, its QR is the resident's Sui address, and the back links to the last transaction on Suiscan. The city dashboard shows what the subsidy achieved: subsidy deposited, sets sold, vouchers spent and the share at small shops, the vault, shops with no takings to follow up, and every onchain event behind the numbers. The live demo runs on Sui testnet with demo accounts that the server signs for, so anyone can try it without a wallet; every action is a real testnet transaction with a Suiscan link. Demo yen (dJPY) only.
projects.how_its_made: The core is a Sui Move package (edition 2024). A shared Program object holds the vault (Balance<DJPY>), the shop registry, stamp cards and the last-stamp table, plus both voucher TreasuryCaps, which move in at launch so vouchers can only be minted by buy and claim_bonus. Each voucher type has a TokenPolicy that allows only spend, and only with a ShopRule approval that pay_local / pay_any add after checking the shop is registered, active, small (for small-shop vouchers) and inside the use period. There is no rule for transfer, to_coin or from_coin. The shared Clock enforces sale and use windows and one stamp per shop per Japan-time day; the fifth distinct small shop sends a BonusTicket. 19 Move tests cover buying, payouts, the refusals, stamps, the bonus and the refund to the city at close. The app is Next.js 16 (App Router) on Vercel. Route handlers use the Mysten Sui TypeScript SDK over gRPC: they decode the Program object and dynamic fields from BCS, read each shop's dJPY takings, and count stamps per shop from the package's Stamped events. Payments are programmable transaction blocks that join and split the resident's voucher Tokens and call pay_local or pay_any in one transaction. Notably hacky: to let judges try it without a wallet, the server holds testnet keys for a demo resident and six demo shops and signs for them, one transaction at a time per signer with an explicitly chosen gas coin. Rule breaks are sent to the contract instead of being blocked in the app, so the refusal you see is the Move abort itself (for example check_shop abort 8), caught in the SDK's pre-signing check. Wallet passes are issued through PassEntry's API: the pass fields are copied from chain state after every payment, stamp and bonus, the QR is the resident's Sui address, and the back names the last transaction with its Suiscan link. Built solo with AI assistance (Claude Code), disclosed in docs/ai-usage.md.

projects.title: Airlock
projects.description: Human-consent gateway for AI agents. AI for power, humans for consent, blockchain for certainty.
projects.project_description: The human-consent gateway for AI agents: frontier AI for power, humans for consent, blockchain for certainty. AI agents leak confidential data the moment they call a frontier model. Airlock is an OpenAI-compatible gateway that any agent (LibreChat, Hermes, Claude Code) can point at instead of a model provider. It works in six steps: Local by default. Requests are answered by a local model. Redact. When an agent needs a frontier model, Airlock replaces names, companies, amounts and IDs with placeholders. Attack-test. The local model tries to re-identify the placeholders; a correct guess forces high risk. Read the policy from ENS. The agent's egress policy comes from ENSv2 records. Human approval. For confidential data, Airlock pauses the agent until a human approves through World ID for Agents. The approval is bound to the payload's hash, and the approver must hold a live ENS subname under the approver role. Revoke the subname and the approval fails. Send, restore and audit. Only the redacted text leaves, streamed. Real names are restored locally. Every decision is appended to a hash-chained audit log whose Merkle root is anchored to ENS. Anyone can run their own: sign in with a wallet, create a gateway and it becomes <name>.airlock.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia, with its own resolver, policy, approver role and audit anchor. Use the Airlock-hosted models (no keys needed) or bring your own local and frontier models, invite people with a role (member, approver, admin), and give each agent a per-member API key. Admins assign each member an agent whose ENS policy governs everything they send.
projects.how_its_made: Gateway: TypeScript monorepo with a Hono server that speaks the OpenAI API, including streaming. It uses a local Qwen 3.5 on vLLM (NVIDIA GB10) and a local codex-lb (gpt-5.6-sol) as the frontier upstream. Redaction: rules + company dictionary + optional Presidio + local-LLM tagging. A streaming rehydrator handles placeholders split across tokens. World ID for Agents: Human Continuity OIDC on the event sandbox, using the authorization code flow with PKCE. The OIDC nonce is a hash of the approval id and payloadHash. The ID token is verified in the backend against JWKS (iss, aud, nonce, auth_time), and state is single use. IDKit: World ID 4.0 Proof of Human is also supported, with the signal bound to payloadHash. It was verified with real staging proofs. ENSv2 on Sepolia: a script builds the whole name tree with viem: a UserRegistry per level, a PermissionedResolver, MockUSDC commit-reveal registration, and subnames with expiry. The Enhanced Access Control split lets only a security account change policy records, while the gateway may write only airlock.approver and airlock.auditRoot. Design finding: only leaf names get a resolver. Otherwise the wildcard lookup of the name-keyed resolver lets unregistered approvers keep resolving. Self-serve gateways: Sign-In with Ethereum (no shared token). Creating a gateway runs 11 resumable Sepolia steps: a PermissionedResolver and two UserRegistries of its own, <slug>.airlock.eth owned by the creator's wallet, policy., approvers., audit. and agents. subnames, the policy records, then a hand-over: on the resolver the platform key keeps only ROLE_SET_TEXT on airlock.approver and airlock.auditRoot (plus the approvers registry, to enroll and revoke approvers), so later policy changes and agent links are transactions the owner's wallet signs, which the server checks from the receipt. Per-gateway models and keys: local = Airlock-hosted or your own OpenAI-compatible URL (public addresses only on the hosted server); frontier = Airlock-hosted (no key, 5 frontier requests per person per hour) or Anthropic / OpenAI-compatible with the gateway's own key, AES-256-GCM sealed at rest. Per-member API keys (alk_…) pick the gateway, the person and the agent; identity headers from clients are ignored. Console: a single HTML page: sign-in, a create-gateway wizard, a Get started checklist, the chamber view with hold-to-approve, the linked redaction view, the hash-chained ledger, and Manage (members and invites, a live people → agent → ENS policy diagram, models, API keys). Tests: 35 unit tests (OIDC against a mock IdP, sign-in, role checks, API keys, agent assignment, owner-signed ENS changes, rate limits), plus end-to-end runs against the real World sandbox and Sepolia, and browser runs of the Console with a scripted wallet.

- Console: a single HTML page: sign-in, a create-gateway wizard, a Get started checklist, the chamber view with hold-to-approve, the linked redaction view, the hash-chained ledger, and Manage (members and invites, a live people → agent → ENS policy diagram, models, API keys).

projects.title: fuda [continuity]
projects.description: Membership as an on-chain right — issued in seconds, verified at the door with no server to trust.
projects.project_description: fuda turns memberships, tickets and loyalty cards into on-chain Rights that people carry as passes in Apple Wallet, Google Wallet or the browser. A member scans a QR and holds a pass seconds later: no app install, no wallet, no account. A gate reads the Right from the chain and admits. The Right outlives the app that issued it — anyone can verify it without asking fuda. That frictionless claim is the product's whole point, and it was also its blind spot. A Right proves a right exists ; it proves nothing about how many distinct people hold them . One person could claim the same Right on three phones, and the only thing in the way was a per-IP hourly budget — an abuse brake, not a uniqueness claim. What we built at this event: a Verified Human badge. A member who already holds a Right can attach a World ID Proof of Human to it. Claiming stays instant for everyone, including attendees with no World App; the gate keeps verifying from the chain alone with no call to World or to fuda's API; and a venue can now make a promise addressed to a person — one badge per attendee, a scarce benefit shared fairly — and have it mean something. The human check happens exactly once, at the moment it produces value, and never again.

Admission reads the chain, not our database, so a third party can verify a Right without our cooperation. The service. Cloudflare Workers running Hono, D1 through Drizzle, viem for chain access. Passes are built for Apple Wallet and Google Wallet; the browser pass is the fallback. The member app and the gate are hono/jsx/dom SPAs. Discovery runs through a subgraph on The Graph; issuer and member names resolve through ENS. The badge (new at this event). A badges table records one badge per (Right, kind) and enforces one subject per (verifier, scope) . A BadgeVerifier seam holds a single adapter for World. The member app uses the headless @worldcoin/idkit-core ; the Worker signs rp_context with signRequest from @worldcoin/idkit-server and forwards the proof to POST /api/v4/verify/{rp_id} server-side. The signal is the Right's EAS UID, so a proof minted for one pass cannot badge another. We store the nullifier and nothing else. Deliberately general. The schema separates what is claimed ( kind ) from who attested it ( verifier ), the column is subject_key rather than nullifier , and the routes are /badges/human rather than /world/* . The gate verdict carries a badges array from its first version so a second kind is not a breaking change. Hardware. The physical gate is a desk QR reader (a NETUM NT-5090) plugged into the machine showing the web gate. It presents as a keyboard: it types fuda:v1:<uid> and presses Enter, so the gate reads a scan whether or not a field has focus, and a scan arriving while a verdict is still on screen replaces it — a queue moves without anyone touching the screen. The reader speaks the same payload the camera path already did, and the admission decision is unchanged: the badge never touched it. What the badge changed is what the screen says afterwards. Everything built at this event is on the feat/idkit branch, not yet merged: github.com/oboroxyz/fuda-sh/compare/main...feat/idkit is exactly the event's diff.
