projects.title: New Friendship Tech
projects.description: Your trip to Tokyo is an expiring ENS name. Verified humans, dinner tables, a concierge agent.
projects.project_description: New Friendship Tech is a membership for people who travel and want to actually meet people in the city they land in. This build turns a trip into an on-chain object. When a member arrives in Tokyo they activate a trip, which mints maya.tokyo.<parent>.eth, a non-transferable ENSv2 subname whose expiry is their departure date. It exists only while they are in town and is only issued after a World ID proof of human, so every name in the city namespace is a verified person who is really there. Members host tables (coffee, breakfast, lunch, dinner) as data-only subnames under tables.tokyo.<parent>.eth. The attendee list lives in a text record, seats are approved by the host, and the bill is split from the names on the record and verified on chain. One concierge agent, published as concierge.<parent>.eth with ENSIP-26 records and aliased under every city, answers "who's around", finds you a dinner, and posts that you're free until 22:00. It never acts alone: every action that puts a member in a room goes through World ID for Agents, so the human approves with a fresh authentication. The concierge also exposes a read-only MCP endpoint, so any other agent can ask who is around and which tables are open. Names only, never wallets or contacts.
projects.how_its_made: The app is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Drizzle and PostgreSQL (PGlite in tests), with Privy for auth and wallet linking. ENSv2 is talked to through hand-written minimal viem ABIs for the registry, permissioned resolver and factory (the contracts-v2 package is a Foundry dependency, not npm), targeting the Sepolia ENSv2 beta deployment. A ChainAdapter interface has two implementations: SepoliaChain (viem, two wallet clients) and SimulatedChain (in-memory registry and resolver with role scoping enforced), so the demo and test suite run without an RPC. Trips are registered with expiry = departure, and the city entry carries no resolver, so an expired trip stops resolving instead of falling back to a shared resolver. A leased ENS job worker handles mint, extend, expire and record writes with a write proof (receipt, re-read, compare). The concierge has its own wallet that holds exactly two setter roles on the resolver (friendship.now and friendship.table); a write to any other key reverts. Record aliasing is used where it is honest: concierge.tokyo.<parent>.eth links to the concierge's record bundle with linkToNode, so a new city is one link, not a copy. World ID uses IDKit v4 with proofOfHuman and a passport preset as the Orb-free path, server-signed rp_context, verification against the v4 endpoint, signal hash bound to the city, and the nullifier stored to enforce one active trip per human per city. World ID for Agents is plain OIDC against the sandbox: a step-up is an authorization request with prompt=login and max_age=0 whose ID token is checked for auth_time, nonce and sub inside the same transaction that marks the approval consumed. Bill split settles in MockUSDC on Sepolia (the same token the ETH Registrar takes) with on-chain verification of the transfer; 0G Pay sits behind a flag. The MCP endpoint is hand-written JSON-RPC 2.0 on its own route because the app API enforces an exact Origin header that server-to-server MCP clients never send. The concierge brain is a swappable interface with a deterministic RuleBrain shipped and a custom loader for an LLM.

projects.title: Hmail
projects.description: Hmail: HORSed email. Your agents read it; your secret unlock only with your approval
projects.project_description:
Hmail is a HORSed email: a Gmail connector for AI agents where your assistant can read your mail, but login codes, sign-in links and password-reset links stay locked until you approve each one with a live World ID Selfie Check. Why: agents are now connected to everything. In September 2026, a personal agent (Instinct) with access to its user's Gmail took a one-time Luma login code from his inbox and signed in without asking. Full access to an inbox means full access to every account that inbox can unlock. How it works: Your "house" runs on your own computer. It syncs Gmail read-only, checks each sender's DKIM signature, and holds codes and sign-in/reset links in a sealed vault (AES-256-GCM). Nothing is stored on our servers.
Agents talk to the house through an MCP server gated by HORS (Human-Origin Resource Sharing, "CORS for agents"). Every call is signed and tied to the anonymous World ID human behind the agent, through World ID for Agents (AgentBook). Instead of sharing keys, the house shares functions, each with its own policy:
search / read: only your own agents (same-human); a redaction net replaces codes with [held · site · kind]
attachment: refused for mails that contain held codes
use_code(site, reason): needs a held code from that exact site, and your face
pair: a new assistant joins only after you approve a 6-digit confirm number
When an agent needs a code, use_code returns an approval challenge. The link and QR also appear live on your house page. You do a Selfie Check in World App, bound to that site, that reason and that one request.
Continuity: setup creates an IDKit session with a Selfie Check, and every release is proved inside that same session. The house checks the session id itself, so only the person who set up the house can approve, every time; a different face is refused. Proofs are verified server-side with World's v4 verify API (environment pinned), and each nullifier is accepted once.
The code is sealed to the agent's one-time key and typed straight into the verified site tab in Chrome over DevTools. The agent never sees the digits; its transcript only shows [held].
ENSv2: your ENS name is your mailbox's address for agents. Setup mints <you>.hmail.eth on ENSv2 (Sepolia) in about a minute, with a live transaction timeline. Each house gets its own PermissionedResolver, and the house holds setter roles for exactly two ENSIP-26 records (agent-endpoint[mcp] and [web]). The issuer renounces its rights, and hmail.eth is sealed. The house rewrites its own endpoint every time it restarts, so "you.hmail.eth" always finds your house even though its tunnel address changes. The approval page resolves the name to reject phishing links. Onboarding for non-technical users: copy one setup prompt into a local AI assistant, then on your house page connect Gmail, pick a name and scan your face. Copy one message to any assistant (including cloud ones like Grok); it links itself to your World ID once and asks to join. Tested failure paths: declined, expired, different face, replayed approval, a code requested for another site (NO_HELD_CODE), and phishing approval links. More uses: print an attachment from a computer that isn't yours without typing a password, and scam emails that try to trick your agent into forwarding a code get nothing. Built with hors-sdk and hors-cli 0.1.0, MCP, World IDKit 4.3 (Selfie Check sessions), World ID for Agents (AgentKit/AgentBook), ENSv2 on Sepolia with viem, and Vercel for the web pages, RP signer and name issuer.
projects.how_its_made:
Hmail is plain ESM JavaScript on Node 22 with no build step, in three parts: a local daemon (the "house"), a CLI for assistants, and a small web project on Vercel. The house (runs on your computer) An MCP server wrapped by hors-sdk (HORS 0.1.0, our own existing project). Each tool declares a policy: an origin (same-human or any-human), rules that return {deny, code, challenge}, and middleware. Rules share state with the handler through ctx.state. For example, the heldCode rule finds the code and the handler releases exactly that code. A redaction-net middleware scrubs anything code-like from every result. Unsigned tools/list publishes every policy, so any agent can see what it needs.
Gmail: desktop OAuth with PKCE and a loopback redirect. The house does the token exchange itself, so tokens never touch our servers. It syncs read-only every 15 s, verifies DKIM with mailauth (aligned pass only), strips hidden text against prompt injection, and classifies login codes, sign-in links and reset links into a held store.
State at rest is sealed with AES-256-GCM. A free cloudflared quick tunnel makes the house reachable. localhost:8390 redirects to the hosted house page with a per-run secret in the URL fragment, and the setup API also enforces the Origin header.
World (partner tech) IDKit 4.3 Selfie Check in a session gave us exactly the continuity question we needed: "is it still the same person who set up the house?" Setup does createSession; every release is a fresh Selfie Check proved in that session. The signal binds house, site, nonce and sha256(reason, recipient key). The house polls World's bridge itself and verifies with the v4 verify API, with the environment pinned. It also checks the session id and accepts each nullifier once. The RP signing key lives only on Vercel.
World ID for Agents (AgentBook, through HORS) tells the house which human is behind each assistant, with no accounts or API keys. hmail connect runs agentkit-cli register in agent mode and filters its output, so the assistant relays only the World App link.
Hacky bits: presets throw for sessions, so we build the request with .constraints(CredentialRequest("selfie", { signal })). IDKit loads its WASM with fetch(file://), which Node lacks, so we shim fetch. @hono/node-server swaps the global Request/Response and silently breaks IDKit, so we set overrideGlobalObjects: false. World's human-in-the-loop package needs Vercel Workflow, so we wrote our own approval loop for a local daemon.
ENSv2 (partner tech, Sepolia) The issuer (a Vercel function) mints <you>.hmail.eth in a UserRegistry under hmail.eth. It deploys a PermissionedResolver per house and grants the house setter roles for exactly two ENSIP-26 records (agent-endpoint[mcp] and [web]), then renounces its own rights. hmail.eth itself is sealed. The house rewrites its endpoint on every restart, so a free, changing tunnel URL gets a permanent, self-healing name that only the house can move. The approval page resolves the name to reject phishing links.
The issuer streams each step as NDJSON to the house page, which draws a live timeline with Etherscan links. Transactions go out in three batches (deploy and fund, register with records and grants, renounce), with explicit nonces.
Hacky bits: the load-balanced Sepolia RPC estimated gas against a stale node, so transactions failed. We now send fixed gas limits and retry reads until the chain catches up. A salt retry recovers half-finished deployments, and houses are funded only on fresh registration, so they can pay for their own record updates.
Releasing a code The code is sealed to the assistant's one-time X25519 key (HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, with site and approval id as associated data). The CLI's typist types it over the Chrome DevTools Protocol into the one visible https://<site> tab. It only types into a code field (never an email box) and checks that the code landed before pressing Enter. The agent never sees the digits.
Onboarding hack The whole setup is one prompt for a local assistant: npx -y -p node@22 -p github:cqlyj/hmail hmail up --background. Pulling node@22 as an npm package guarantees the right Node version on any machine. Pairing uses a 6-digit confirm number instead of codes. The approval QR is drawn locally with a vendored generator, because of a strict CSP.

projects.title: CryptoWill
projects.description: A dead man's switch for crypto inheritance: prove you're alive with World ID, or your heir inherits.
projects.project_description: When a self-custody holder dies, their crypto usually dies with them. The alternatives all require trust: hand over your seed phrase, give your funds to a custodian, or rely on a dead man's switch that only checks whether someone still holds a key. CryptoWill replaces "holds a key" with "is a living human". You lock funds in a will and name an heir by their World ID — only an anonymous identifier is stored on-chain, no name or wallet. You then check in with World ID on your own schedule. If you stop, the will moves through a grace period into a claimable state; your heir verifies with World ID and names a payout address. A final challenge period lets you cancel the claim with a single check-in if you're still here. After that, anyone can finalize and the funds go to the heir. There is no custodian, no admin key and no keeper: every rule is enforced by the contract, the phase is derived from timestamps, and every World ID proof is verified on-chain.

It verifies World ID proofs on-chain through the WorldIDRouter (Orb group), using two actions: one for the owner's liveness checks and one for the heir's claim. The usual World ID pattern treats a nullifier as a one-time ticket. We use it as an identity instead: the owner's nullifier is stored at creation and compared on every check-in without ever being consumed, which is what makes repeated proof-of-life possible. One-time claims are enforced by each will's state machine, so the same person can inherit from several wills. Proof signals bind the owner's proof to their wallet and the heir's proof to the payout address, so claims can be relayed by anyone but never redirected. Heirs have no address on-chain, so the contract keeps an index from heir nullifier to will IDs, letting heirs find their wills with a single scan. The frontend is Next.js 16 with wagmi and viem. It uses IDKit 4 with legacy proofs, plus a small serverless route that signs World ID requests so the RP key never reaches the browser. Before every transaction the app checks the proof's signal hash and simulates the call, so users never sign a transaction that would revert. Besides unit tests, we run fork tests against the real WorldIDRouter with real proofs generated in the World ID simulator.

projects.title: Staking Rewards Hub
projects.description: YieldReclaim: one-click harvesting of staking yields across all your positions,
projects.project_description: YieldReclaim is a decentralized application that solves a real pain point for Ethereum stakers: yield from staking positions accumulates across multiple protocols and validators, and claiming it means signing a separate transaction for every single position — paying gas each time and wasting time. With YieldReclaim, users connect their wallet and instantly see a unified dashboard of all their staking positions, including the accumulated (unclaimed) yield on each one. From there, they can harvest rewards from a single position or — with one click on "Harvest All" — batch every pending reward into a single transaction. Instead of N transactions and N gas fees, it's one signature and one fee. The interface shows a live summary of total pending rewards across all positions, per-position breakdowns, and a claim history, so users always know exactly how much they've earned and reclaimed. Toast notifications confirm each harvest, and claimed positions are visually marked to prevent double-claiming. The current build is a fully interactive demo: wallet connection, position fetching, individual and batch harvesting, and reward accounting all work end-to-end in the UI, demonstrating the complete user flow from connect to full yield recovery. The next step is wiring the batching layer to on-chain smart accounts / multicall contracts so the one-transaction harvest executes permissionlessly on mainnet. Built for ETHGlobal — because your yield should come home in one click.
projects.how_its_made: YieldReclaim is built as a single-page decentralized application on a modern full-stack React setup: TanStack Start (React 19 + Vite 7) handles routing, SSR, and type-safe route trees, with Tailwind CSS v4 and shadcn-style components for the UI layer. TanStack Query manages all async state — position fetching, pending harvests, and cache invalidation after each claim — so the dashboard stays consistent with zero manual state juggling. Toast notifications (sonner) surface every on-chain-style event the user triggers. The core UX flow is intentionally simple: connect a wallet, fetch all staking positions into a unified dashboard, then harvest rewards either per-position or via a single "Harvest All" action that collapses N transactions into one. Each row tracks accumulated yield, and a summary bar aggregates the total recoverable amount in real time. The hackathon version ships with a mocked wallet layer and simulated position data, which let us build and demo the complete end-to-end user journey — connect, view, claim, verify — without burning gas or waiting on a testnet faucet. The data model (positions, accumulated rewards, claim states) mirrors exactly what an on-chain indexer would return, so swapping the mock fetchers for real contract calls is a drop-in change with no UI rework. The next milestone is the part that makes the name true: wiring the batch harvest to a smart-account multicall so every position's claim executes in one signature, permissionlessly, on mainnet. Everything in the current codebase — the claim accounting, the optimistic UI updates, the aggregate totals — is structured around that single end state. Stack: TanStack Start, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query, sonner.

projects.title: Raindrop
projects.description: Together a community's judgments form a social graph of trust. We can let funding follow it.
projects.project_description: Raindrop is a cryptoeconomic mechanism that continuously allocates new token issuance according to a token-weighted trust network. Each round: The protocol computes global allocation weights using EigenTrust based on current balances and trust delegations New tokens are minted according to the configured issuance rate Tokens are distributed proportionally to the allocation weights The process repeats with updated balances This creates an adaptive, self-adjusting flow where influence is conserved with respect to capital, providing Sybil resistance without external identity systems.
projects.how_its_made: This project started as an idea that was sparked, but we used the hackathon as a way to harden the thesis, the protocol, the use-case and so much more. We spoke to open-source and DAO contributors and founders that have struggled with funding effectively throughout the event, which challenged the raindrop idea in many ways and finally got us to a point of confidence in its usefulness and stability. The end result is a whitepaper, simulations, and a battle-tested thesis so that the project is ready to be launched.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Raindrop is a cryptoeconomic mechanism that continuously allocates new token issuance according to a token-weighted trust network. Each round:

- The protocol computes global allocation weights using EigenTrust based on current balances and trust delegations
- New tokens are minted according to the configured issuance rate
- Tokens are distributed proportionally to the allocation weights
- The process repeats with updated balances
- This creates an adaptive, self-adjusting flow where influence is conserved with respect to capital, providing Sybil resistance without external identity systems.
projects.how_its_made_markdown: This project started as an idea that was sparked, but we used the hackathon as a way to harden the thesis, the protocol, the use-case and so much more. We spoke to open-source and DAO contributors and founders that have struggled with funding effectively throughout the event, which challenged the raindrop idea in many ways and finally got us to a point of confidence in its usefulness and stability. The end result is a whitepaper, simulations, and a battle-tested thesis so that the project is ready to be launched.

projects.title: PayGuard
projects.description: An on-chain vault for AI agent payments: auto-pay small bills, ask for big ones, block the rest.
projects.project_description: An AI agent that can pay is an agent that can empty the account. PayGuard is the vault in between. The owner deposits funds into a per-owner PayGuardVault and gives an agent bounded authority instead of a key: a hard total budget, an automatic limit, an escalation limit, and a list of merchants and categories it may pay. The agent never holds funds. For each payment, the merchant signs an invoice, the agent signs an intent, and the vault evaluates both on-chain before anything moves: ALLOW: small, in-policy bills settle on their own (demo: 0.50). ESCALATE: a larger valid bill waits until the owner signs that exact payment (demo: 180). The signature binds merchant, amount and route, so it cannot be reused or redirected. BLOCK: anything outside the rules (over budget, unknown merchant, duplicate invoice) never leaves the vault. No transaction is sent (demo: 500). The merchant always receives the exact invoiced amount. The owner can pay through three routes, each with its own vault and budget: a direct token transfer, a Uniswap v4 exact-output swap, or a 1inch Aqua/SwapVM swap. So an agent can pay in USDC while the owner's funds stay in another asset. The owner panel shows the remaining budget, the policy as read back from the vault, pending approvals, and activity that separates the policy's decision from what actually happened on-chain. The screen never decides anything. It shows what the vault decided. The relayer marks a payment paid only after a receipt exists. Built by the SuzuPay team (GustoDevelopment), which runs a live QR payment service with 100+ merchants in Fukuoka. PayGuard is the safety layer we want in front of those merchants as they start accepting agent payments.
projects.how_its_made: pnpm monorepo: Solidity contracts (Foundry), a Fastify API, a worker/relayer, PostgreSQL and a React 19 + Vite owner panel. Contract ABIs and EIP-712 types are generated once and shared, with drift tests so the frontend, backend and chain cannot disagree. Contracts. PayGuardVault (contracts/core-v4) holds owner funds and runs the whole decision on-chain: policy lookup, merchant/category bitmap, automatic and escalation limits, a hard budget, per-agent nonces and consumed-invoice tracking for replay defense. Invoices, intents and owner approvals are EIP-712 typed data. Owner approvals also accept ERC-1271 smart-wallet signatures. Settlement is atomic: if the route fails, the budget and state roll back. Foundry tests cover budgets, approvals, replays, negative evaluation, a malicious reentrant adapter, and invariants. Uniswap v4. PayGuardV4Adapter (contracts/core-v4/src/adapters) does an exact-output swap through the real PoolManager unlock/callback flow and settles all deltas. The vault caps the input it may spend, and the merchant gets exactly the invoiced output. The adapter is pinned to one pool and refuses hooks and non-standard fees, so a policy cannot be routed into an unexpected pool. 1inch Aqua / SwapVM. PayGuardAquaAdapter (contracts/aqua) is a taker-side adapter over AquaSwapVMRouter. It is bound to one maker and one SwapVM order, whose hash is computed at deployment, and uses SwapVM's exact-output max-input check. Its taker callback only accepts calls from the pinned router during its own settle(), and it leaves no allowance to Aqua after the call. Backend. The API handles SIWE sessions, policies, invoices, intents and approvals. The worker is a relayer with a transaction outbox and journal, crash recovery and a chain indexer that handles reorgs. It never treats HTTP 202 or a bare tx hash as success, only a verified receipt. The API and worker refuse to boot if an owner private key is present in the environment. Frontend. Every state comes from the API and the chain. Before the owner signs an approval, the panel recomputes the EIP-712 digest and checks chainId, verifying contract, signer, amount and recipient. Amounts are bigint strings throughout (6-decimal mUSDC and 18-decimal assets). Hacky bits. The API sends no CORS headers, so the panel runs behind a same-origin proxy (the Vite proxy in dev, a zero-dependency server.mjs in prod). A mock API lets us iterate on the UI without Postgres or Anvil. The demo runs on a local chain (31337) with mock tokens. No real funds move.

projects.title: ARCA
projects.description: ARCA turns projects into AI-assisted tasks, verifies contributions, and settles rewards in USDC.
projects.project_description: ARCA is an AI-powered outsourcing platform that turns company projects into structured tasks, records how people complete them with AI, and distributes rewards based on qualified contributions. Companies can choose the results that best fit their needs, while workers can earn rewards for meeting clearly defined requirements. When a company submits its goals and requirements, AI breaks the project into tasks based on the existing project context. This includes defining function interfaces, input/output JSON schemas, file requirements, and acceptance tests. These shared contracts help independently produced deliverables fit into the existing project. Once the company approves the plan, tasks are published, and participants work against the same requirements and completion criteria. Workers use a transparent desktop panel alongside their existing development tools to perform tasks with the platform’s AI. ARCA records the agents and models used, prompts, tool calls, file changes, and AI usage costs. This addresses a growing challenge in AI-assisted outsourcing: receiving code alone does not explain how or why it was created. Connecting deliverables to their work history supports review, accountability, and handover. ARCA uses World’s proof of humanity to support fair participation. It restricts the same person from entering the same task through multiple wallets and connects protected submission actions to human approval. Companies review submissions against predefined rules and qualification criteria, then select the result that best meets their needs. Rewards follow a differentiated distribution model rather than a winner-takes-all approach. Qualified contributors can participate in the reward pool even when their submission is not the final selection, with allocations varying by ranking. AI usage costs are accounted for within each worker’s gross reward allocation. Curvegrid connects payout plans with supporting evidence records, while Sui handles escrow-based USDC settlement. Together, these components connect project requirements, AI-assisted work, human review, and reward settlement into a traceable outsourcing workflow.
projects.how_its_made: We built ARCA as four connected components: a web platform for companies and workers, a desktop panel for AI-assisted work, a backend for task management and settlement, and blockchain adapters for partner integrations. The application uses TypeScript, a Next.js web interface, and Prisma to manage projects, tasks, participants, submissions, AI execution history, and settlement records. We separated the AI workflow into project analysis, task decomposition, execution, and review. During decomposition, the system produces structured requirements alongside natural-language instructions, including function interfaces, input/output schemas, permitted files, and acceptance criteria. Execution and evaluation reference the same task contract, making it possible to compare submitted work against the original requirements. The desktop panel lets workers interact with platform AI while using their existing development environment. Each execution records its model and agent, prompts, tool calls, file-change hashes, usage, and costs. These records are associated with the relevant task and submission, while proposed changes pass through human review and approval. One distinctive implementation detail is that client-submitted work history is checked against server-side AI execution records instead of being trusted on its own. For World, we integrated an IDKit-based proof request flow with server-side verification. Verified human identity is associated with task participation to restrict duplicate entries by the same person using different wallets. We deliberately separated wallet ownership from proof of humanity: wallets support accounts and transactions, while World supports person-level eligibility and protected submission approval. On Sui, we implemented Move smart contracts for escrow and settlement. Company deposits are associated with task budgets, and finalized allocation plans determine worker rewards, AI cost allocations, and refunds. The contracts include checks against duplicate settlement and spending beyond the available task budget. This makes reward execution verifiable through onchain transactions rather than only through changes in an application database. We integrated Curvegrid MultiBaas with a Solidity settlement-record contract. The backend records payout-plan and evidence hashes, then links the resulting Sui settlement receipt. MultiBaas provides the contract-call and transaction-query interface for this EVM audit layer. Prompts and private work files remain offchain; onchain records contain hashes and settlement information needed for verification. A significant engineering challenge was maintaining consistency between work evidence, reward calculations, and transactions across two chains. The EVM record and Sui payment are not a single atomic transaction. We therefore persist execution states and transaction receipts so that failed or uncertain operations can be reconciled before retrying. This adds coordination overhead, but helps prevent duplicate execution and makes settlement failures traceable. We validated the implementation through automated tests and separate partner integration checks. These covered application workflows, authorization, reward calculations, World verification through the official simulator, Curvegrid testnet writes and readbacks, and Sui testnet escrow transactions. We treated these as separate validation milestones rather than presenting individual integration checks as proof of a completed end-to-end USDC competition.

projects.title: Artwork Commons
projects.description: Platform for artists and galleries exhibit and sell physical art utilizing ENSv2
projects.project_description: Artwork Commons is a template for artists and galleries to run their own marketplaces for NFTs tied to physical artwork. An artist connects a wallet, chooses an ENS name they control, creates an artwork namespace such as art.eonmun.eth , and issues a named artwork record with its image and metadata on IPFS. A gallery uses its own ENS name to create exhibitions, invite artists to submit work, and offer accepted work for sale. Collectors can buy through an exhibition or directly from an owner. EON MUN is the example artist; the template is intended for others to use with their own names. The novel part is that ENSv2 names are the structure of the marketplace , rather than labels added afterward. ENSv2 permissioned registries let an artist control artwork subdomains and a gallery control exhibition subdomains independently. Its extended access control underpins narrowly scoped, expiring gallery permissions: an artist can authorize a gallery to exhibit, list, or sell a particular work while retaining ownership until a purchase. The artwork and exhibition records link to the relevant contracts, so a buyer can follow a work’s identity and attributed exhibition history across galleries. The contracts also enforce one standard artwork policy: the first sale can happen immediately, subsequent ownership transfers have a 180-day hold, and supported resales pay the original artist a 5% royalty. Gallery sales can include an agreed commission. The local blockchain demo exercises these rules with real contracts; the separate story demo uses staged data. Physical custody and historical claims are displayed as attributed records, not treated as blockchain proof that a painting was delivered or a past sale occurred.
projects.how_its_made:
We built Artwork Commons as a Next.js 16 and React 19 application, statically exported and served by Cloudflare Workers. The interface has separate artist, gallery, collector, and public browsing flows. viem connects the site to Ethereum: the wallet signs setup and sale transactions, while read-only RPC calls reconstruct artwork, exhibitions, permissions, listings, and ownership from contracts. Public deployments target Sepolia; a separate local mode runs the real ENSv2 contracts on Anvil so we can rehearse the entire flow without spending testnet ETH.
The Solidity contracts divide responsibilities. An artist’s ArtworkRegistry issues one ERC-1155 singleton token per physical work and fixes its creator, metadata, and standard terms. Its hierarchical permissioned registries let an artist publish works beneath their own name, such as blue-mountain.art.eonmun.eth, while a gallery publishes exhibitions beneath a different name. **Artwork Commons is a template for artists and galleries to run their own marketplaces for NFTs tied to physical artwork.** An artist connects a wallet, chooses an ENS name they control, creates an artwork namespace such as `art.eonmun.eth`, and issues a named artwork record with its image and metadata on IPFS. A gallery uses its own ENS name to create exhibitions, invite artists to submit work, and offer accepted work for sale. Collectors can buy through an exhibition or directly from an owner. EON MUN is the example artist; the template is intended for others to use with their own names.

The novel part is that **ENSv2 names are the structure of the marketplace**, rather than labels added afterward. ENSv2 permissioned registries let an artist control artwork subdomains and a gallery control exhibition subdomains independently. Its extended access control underpins narrowly scoped, expiring gallery permissions: an artist can authorize a gallery to exhibit, list, or sell a particular work while retaining ownership until a purchase. The artwork and exhibition records link to the relevant contracts, so a buyer can follow a work’s identity and attributed exhibition history across galleries.

The contracts also enforce one standard artwork policy: the first sale can happen immediately, subsequent ownership transfers have a 180-day hold, and supported resales pay the original artist a 5% royalty. Gallery sales can include an agreed commission. The local blockchain demo exercises these rules with real contracts; the separate story demo uses staged data. Physical custody and historical claims are displayed as attributed records, not treated as blockchain proof that a painting was delivered or a past sale occurred.

projects.title: Aquawrap
projects.description: Custom SwapVM opcode pricing wrapped-asset pools at the live oracle rate, on 1inch Aqua.
projects.project_description: AquaWrap is a custom SwapVM instruction that reads a live rate oracle (Uniswap V3 TWAP or wstETH wrap-rate + Chainlink) on every quote() and swap(), continuously re-anchoring the AMM curve so wrapped-asset liquidity stays accurate to real market prices. The problem: SwapVM's built-in PeggedSwap and XYCSwap fix the price at ship time, but wrapped assets (wstETH, cbETH, rETH) have exchange rates that drift as rewards accrue — a stale pool gets arbitraged and LPs bleed value. OracleSwap's curve (x + x0)·y = k with x0 = y/r − x makes the marginal price always exactly the live rate, while slippage still scales with trade size vs. reserve depth — a real AMM, not an RFQ. The official Aqua registry is used unchanged; only the SwapVM router is redeployed with the opcode appended (byte 0x22), which the bounty rules explicitly allow. Every existing opcode keeps its index, so existing programs behave identically. Quote/swap parity holds because the rate provider is a view call and the pricing kernel is pure. Includes a mainnet-fork test suite (ship → quote → swap → dock with real WETH/wstETH), viem scripts, and a zero-build HTML/JS dashboard.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.30 + Foundry, pinned against 1inch/swap-vm v1.0.2 (the exact tag the deployed router was built from) and 1inch/aqua v1.0.0 as git submodules. The core is an appended opcode: AquaWrapOpcodes overrides the virtual _opcodes() jump table, appending OracleSwap at index 34 (byte 0x22) — the first out-of-bounds index of the deployed router's 34-entry table, so OracleSwap programs only execute on our redeployed router. The pricing kernel is an oracle-anchored constant product: amountOut = y·r·net/(1e18·y + r·net), derived from the curve (x + x0)·y = k with x0 = y/r − x, so the marginal price equals the live rate at any reserve ratio. Notably, the naive approach of scaling balanceIn by the rate cancels out of constant product — the oracle would be decorative — so the curve is anchored through the rate instead. Rate providers: TWAPRateProvider reads Uniswap V3 observe() with TickMath inlined (v3-core v1.0.0 doesn't compile under solc 0.8.30), and WrapRateProvider combines wstETH.stEthPerToken() with the Chainlink stETH/ETH feed (18 decimals, 24h heartbeat). 27 tests pass, including a mainnet fork suite against the real Aqua registry and wstETH/WETH pool, a rate-drift test proving OracleSwap tracks the live rate while XYC stays stale, and a quote/swap parity fuzz. Client tooling is viem scripts (deploy, ship, quote+swap demo, OracleSwap-vs-XYC comparison) and a dependency-free HTML/CSS/JS dashboard.

projects.title: Whistle
projects.description: Trade player cards mid-match as goals and red cards move prices, or let your agent trade for you.
projects.project_description:
Whistle is a live football market with a built-in rule for fairness and a built-in rule for agents.
Before kick-off you mint player cards. Every card is a share of one pot, weighted by how that player performs, so a goal, an assist, a red card, a substitution or simply minutes on the pitch re-prices all 36 cards at once. At full time the pot is paid out by final score, and it empties to the last cent.
Every order waits for the referee. In-play markets have always had one problem: the person in the stadium sees the goal 30 seconds before the data feed does, and trades against everyone else. In Whistle nothing fills instantly once the match is live. Every order is queued and priced 30 seconds after it's placed, after the oracle has caught up with anything you could have seen. Orders in the same tick are netted against each other and filled at one price. Fifty people selling into a red card don't race each other, because being fast buys nothing.
Your agent plays it for you. Most fans won't trade for 90 minutes, so you hand an agent a playbook - Protect, Momentum or Contrarian, and a spend cap, and watch the game. Each agent is its own ENS name, agent-N.<you>.whistle.eth, with its own resolver and its own permissions. The Uniswap hook checks those permissions on ENS before every trade the agent makes. Pause writes its cap to zero; Revoke burns its roles, and its next order reverts on-chain. The records are split three ways: you set the strategy and cap, the agent writes its own action log, Whistle keeps its history, and none of them can edit the others'. A revoked agent keeps exactly enough authority to write, in its own record, that it was refused.
A human approves every increase in authority. Creating an agent, raising its cap or resuming it requires a fresh World ID verification, validated on our backend before the action runs. The new agent's ENS record then carries a private "human-backed" binding anyone can resolve. Lowering a cap, pausing or revoking never waits on verification.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, Sepolia).
Market economics. Each fixture is its own market: a settlement pot, 36 player cards as ERC-20 clones, and a market-maker vault. A card's reference price is the pot × the player's expected score ÷ Σ(expected score × supply). Expected score is closed-form in the match clock (banked points plus minutes accrued plus a decaying expectation), so the pot keeps two aggregates and re-prices every card in O(1) per event rather than looping over 36 players.
Invariants. Price equals mint price at kick-off; minting at the reference price leaves every other price unchanged; payouts sum to the pot. All three are fuzz-tested. Final scores are computed on-chain from the posted events, not trusted from the oracle.
Uniswap v4. Every card is a v4 pool with our WhistleHook and the dynamic-fee flag. Before kick-off it trades normally. Once the match is live, beforeSwap rejects direct swaps: orders go into the hook's queue, and a keeper's tick() nets buys against sells, fills the residual pro-rata from vault inventory, and executes every fill as a real PoolManager swap. The hook returns a BeforeSwapDelta that prices it at the oracle-anchored reference price and settles against the vault's ERC-6909 claims with take/settle.
The hacky part: a hook that calls swap itself gets no beforeSwap callback and silently fills against the AMM curve. We measured it on the Sepolia PoolManager: 987.16 out versus 750.00 at the hook's price. So fills go through a minimal WhistleFillRouter the hook trusts. That's written up in our FEEDBACK.md with the numbers.
Fees and gas. The fee is dynamic (base 30 bps, widening after events and with distance from the reference price) and split 90/10 between liquidity and protocol. Netting is also the gas optimisation: a card whose book nets skips an entire unlock and swap.
ENSv2 (Sepolia beta). whistle.eth points at our own Permissioned Registry; each user gets a subname registry; each agent gets a non-transferable subname and its own Permissioned Resolver deployed through VerifiableFactory.
Why a resolver per agent. Resolver roles are scoped per resolver instance and record key, not per name. A shared resolver would let agent-1 overwrite agent-2's records, so every agent gets its own.
How rights are split. Argument-scoped setText roles give you strategy, spend-cap and slippage; the agent status, last-action and pnl-live; Whistle matches-played, pnl-history and revoked-at. The registry drops its own write role in the same transaction that creates the agent.
What the hook checks. isAuthorized does a live ENS read on every order: roles, expiry and the remaining cap. So editing the agent's spend-cap in any ENS interface changes what the hook allows on the next block.
Other findings. The oracle's posting right is derived from the owner of oracle.whistle.eth, and that name is denied any trading role. Along the way we hit the beta's redeploy (so we pinned to the deployment tag), an EIP-7702 delegation collision on test addresses, and a linkToNode misreading — all in ENS_NOTES.md.
World ID for Agents. A confidential OIDC client using private_key_jwt (RS256), PKCE and max_age=0. The backend holds the pending action, exchanges the code, validates the ID token against World's JWKS (iss, aud, nonce, state, and an auth_time inside the attempt), and only then performs the protected action with the operator key. The browser never performs it. The pairwise sub is bound to the agent as a hashed human record on ENS. Denied, cancelled and expired paths make no chain call. Integration notes are in WORLD_DEBRIEF.md.
Oracle, keeper and agents (TypeScript, viem). A replay oracle posts the match from a JSON timeline: kick-off, heartbeats every five match minutes, goals, cards, substitutions, then postFinal. The keeper ticks the queue. The same logic runs as a stateless, browser-driven step function in the Next.js app, so the whole match can run from one screen: each call does one unit of work and derives everything else from chain state.
The rough edges we fixed.
Two events can share a minute (a heartbeat and a substitution at 65'), and the contract allows equal minutes, so a re-posted event would be applied twice. Every send is now checked against the fixture's MatchEvent history first.
A lagging load-balanced RPC node once did exactly that, doubling a goal. Reads are now pinned to a block no older than the newest receipt seen.
postFinal falls back to the chain's own scores if the replay and the chain ever disagree.
Agent logic. It's a pure evaluate(template, state, event, board) function; the three templates are equivalence-tested against the runtime. Agents sign with keys the server manages per fixture, so creating one is a single click with no key to handle.
Frontend (Next.js, Tailwind, wagmi/viem). A fixtures list; a pre-match screen where you mint, create agents and start the match on one page; a live pitch view with shirts coloured by state; agent profiles that read every ENS record live and show who wrote it; and a settlement screen that loads a build-time snapshot of settled logs so it paints instantly. Lighthouse accessibility is 100 on every screen.

projects.title: GuildAce
projects.description: AI agent marketplace: PM agents run B2B projects, World ID-verified humans review, ENS names agents.
projects.project_description: GuildAce is a B2B marketplace where AI agents take on real projects end to end. A client posts a case, and a PM Agent (powered by Gemini) breaks it into tasks, assembles a team of specialist agents, runs the work, delivers the results, and handles payment. Each task's funds are locked in an on-chain escrow contract on Sepolia and paid out automatically when the client approves. Work that only people can do, such as evaluating deliverables, arbitrating disputes, and completing human-only tasks, goes to real humans verified with World ID, and disputes are settled by a three-person jury. Every agent's name and public profile live on ENS (ENSv2), so clients can check who they are hiring before they commit.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. The web app is built with Next.js and supports Sign-In with Ethereum and World ID. The API is FastAPI on PostgreSQL and handles all on-chain work. The escrow contract and a mock USDC token run on Sepolia. The web app is hosted on Vercel, and the API and database are hosted on Render.

projects.title: Rivalry
projects.description: Race friends or human verified strangers across the world, same distance, same difficulty!
projects.project_description: This project is a blockchain enhanced irl version of zwift, initially designed for running but will expand to other sport disciplines. Say you're travelling in Sydney for a couple days, your friend is in  London and you're both training for a marathon. With Rivalry you can continue training together by racing an equally distanced equally difficult running route (adjusted for elevation gain) at the same time. Perhaps none of your friends are awake and you cant be bothered to search for running groups, you can select the stranger mode and be matched with someone who wants to run the same distance, to prevent running against a clanker you prove your humanhood, for races with greater time commitment, there are additional verifications so that you have greater reassurance.
projects.how_its_made:
Rivalry is an Expo (React Native, TypeScript) app for iPhone and Android.
Users sign in by email with Privy. The backend runs on Supabase: Postgres plus
Deno Edge Functions. Each function checks the user's Privy login token
itself, and the database tables are closed to direct access from the app.
Matching, readiness, the countdown, scoring and results are all handled in SQL
functions, so both phones always see the same race state. A scheduled
background job cleans up abandoned races and deletes precise GPS points once
results are saved. Routes come from openrouteservice. I trim each loop to the exact race distance
along its own path, so both runners race identical lengths anywhere in the
world. During the race, the server matches each GPS fix to the runner's own
private route, and friends see each other's position while strangers see only
progress. World ID is the trust layer: a fresh Selfie Check is required before two
strangers share a start time. The server signs each request, ties it to the
specific race, verifies the proof with World, and stores only the pass/fail
result. Hacky bits: IDKit's WebAssembly runtime runs in a hidden WebView that hands
the World ID link back to the app. I patched Expo's native iOS code to build
with an older Xcode. And the 10 km race is a 5 km loop run twice.

projects.title: StoikovHook
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that sets fees like a market maker: higher in volatile markets, skewed by direction
projects.project_description: Problem. A Uniswap pool is a market maker that never updates its quote: its fee is fixed when the pool is created. When the price moves elsewhere, arbitrageurs trade the pool back into line, and LPs fill those trades at stale prices. This loss is called loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR). A static fee is too high for regular traders in calm markets and too low for arbitrageurs when volatility spikes. Solution. StoikovHook gives the pool the two tools of an Avellaneda-Stoikov market maker. Every block it posts two fees, one per direction, computed only from the pool's own state. A volatility premium raises both. An inventory skew charges more to swaps that push the price further from its slow moving average, and less to swaps that bring it back. No oracle, no admin key, no token custody. Deployed and source-verified on Sepolia. Results. A deterministic Foundry simulation runs identical order flow through every pool, over 20 seeds of 400 blocks. Against a static pool that charges regular traders the same average fee, LPs end +0.160 ± 0.105 bps of pool value ahead, in 20 of 20 seeds. The extra fee income comes entirely from arbitrageurs (+0.175 bps); regular traders pay the same average fee. Problem. A Uniswap pool is a market maker that never updates its quote: its fee is fixed when the pool is created. When the price moves elsewhere, arbitrageurs trade the pool back into line, and LPs fill those trades at stale prices. This loss is called loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR). projects.title: coffer
projects.description: Policy-enforced autonomous treasury agents on Sui, with human approval for exceptions.
projects.project_description: Coffer is a policy-enforced autonomous treasury that lets organizations delegate routine financial operations to an AI agent without giving it unrestricted control of a wallet. The agent reads encrypted invoice context, extracts payment details, checks live treasury state, and chooses one of four outcomes: execute, request human authorization, hold, or reject. Sui Move contracts enforce spending limits, approved vendors, treasury buckets, mandate validity, policy versions, and revocation. Material exceptions require fresh, action-bound World authorization. Seal encrypts commercial documents and Walrus stores the ciphertext, while payment amounts and recipient addresses remain publicly auditable on Sui.
projects.how_its_made: Coffer combines Sui Move contracts, a TypeScript agent worker, Seal, Walrus, World, and a Next.js operations interface. Sui shared objects hold the treasury, payment requests, vendor policies, standing orders, and agent mandates. Owned capabilities define administrator, vendor, agent, and verifier authority. Before executing a payment, the worker retrieves ciphertext from Walrus, requests policy-controlled decryption through Seal, extracts structured invoice fields using Ollama or Anthropic, and evaluates them against current Sui state with a deterministic policy engine. Approved payments execute through Move, which independently rechecks the vendor, bucket, timing, policy version, per-payment limit, period limit, and human-approval threshold. When the agent reaches its delegated boundary, the backend creates a World authorization request bound to the exact treasury, payment request, vendor, amount, expiry, and nonce. The server validates PKCE, state, nonce, issuer, audience, freshness, action integrity, and replay protection before atomically executing the authorized Sui payment. The application includes Guided Replay for reliable demonstrations of all four outcomes and a restricted Live Testnet mode that creates a fresh request and payment transaction. A shared event ledger updates treasury balances, payment requests, and audit evidence across the workspace. Google account access is provided through Enoki zkLogin, while standard Sui wallets remain supported. Commercial document contents are encrypted, but Coffer does not claim confidential transaction amounts or recipient addresses.

projects.title: ReflexOS
projects.description: Neural reflexes you can compose, run, and prove for machines, software and autonomous systems.
projects.project_description: ReflexOS is the software layer for neural reflexes: tiny, deterministic brain circuits that machines and software can compose, run locally, publish under an ENS name, and prove. Digitized brains have left the lab. Fly connectomes now drive agents in Minecraft and Doom, and walk robots. These circuits are small (hundreds of neurons, not billions of parameters), fast (a decision within one control tick), deterministic (the same input always gives the same output) and light (they run on a CPU, with no GPU or cloud). That makes them a fit for a problem large models handle badly. Most systems don't need a giant model; they need a reflex: a car braking before a crash, a drone dodging an obstacle, an agent reacting to a critical event. Today these circuits can't be packaged, composed, shipped or verified the way software can. ReflexOS fills that gap. A Block is a neural circuit with a typed interface, locked by digest. LoomGuard, for example, is a collision reflex built from 780 real FlyWire neurons. In NeuroLab, Blocks are wired to sensors, control and actuators to form a Stack, either on a canvas or by describing it in plain words to an assistant, which asks a few questions and builds a graph the compiler has checked. Each Stack compiles to one canonical .reflex file containing the graph, the runtime plan and the exact model bytes, and it runs on a deterministic fixed-point runtime that behaves the same in the browser, in Node and in our npm package. A game or robot adds a reflex in two lines: npm install @reflexos/runtime, then EmergencyBrake.attach(car). ENS turns the library into something open and checkable. We registered reflexos.eth on ENSv2 with its own registry and resolver, plus branches for stacks, blocks, fleet and agents. Anyone can claim a namespace such as yourproject.reflexos.eth for free: their wallet signs a message and ends up owning the name, its registry and its resolver, while our server only holds a revocable publisher role with no admin rights. When a Stack is published, it gets its own subname, its SHA-256 goes into a text record, its file goes to IPFS through the contenthash record, and the owner's signature over the name and digest is stored on the name. Anyone can type the name, fetch the file from any IPFS gateway, and verify without trusting anyone that the bytes match the on-chain digest, that the owner signed them, and that recorded decisions replay to identical outputs. The Discover page lists every published Stack straight from registry events, with no database. Receipts make every critical decision accountable: they record what the reflex saw and why it acted, and anyone can replay them. The reflex path itself stays fully local; the chain is used only for publishing and proof, never between a sensor and a brake.
projects.how_its_made: ReflexOS is a TypeScript and Rust monorepo. The core is a deterministic spiking-neuron virtual machine: leaky integrate-and-fire neurons in Q16.16 fixed-point, with saturating integer arithmetic and weights in CSR sparse format. It exists twice with identical semantics, once in Rust (reflexos-core, with a Merkle crate for commitments and a CLI for run, replay and bench) and once in TypeScript for the browser and Node. Floating point never enters the tick loop, so a decision computed on a laptop, in a browser or on a companion computer is bit-for-bit identical, and that is what makes replay meaningful. Blocks are packaged by a Python compiler that turns circuit data into block.json: the CSR topology and weights, named input channels and output populations. LoomGuard, our collision reflex, is 780 neurons and 7,538 synapses from FlyWire FAFB v783 (LC4, LPLC2 and giant-fiber populations). A Stack is a typed graph of sensors, adapters, neural blocks, control nodes and actuators. The compiler checks port types, cycles, sample rates and the critical-path budget, locks every model by SHA-256, and emits one canonical JSON package with sorted keys and no floats. Its digest is the package's identity. The runtime schedules nodes on a 1 kHz clock and, on critical actuator changes, writes a receipt: an input commitment, state roots before and after, the actions taken, and a hash chained to the previous receipt, so a fresh runtime can replay the exact tick. The same runtime is bundled with esbuild into a dependency-free ES module and shipped as the npm package @reflexos/runtime, which our Three.js car game uses to brake with two lines of code. NeuroLab is Next.js 15 and React 19, with viem for everything on-chain. The Compose assistant is deliberately not an LLM wiring graphs. Free text, read either by a vocabulary extractor or by an optional model, fills a typed build spec. The dialogue asks only the questions that change the graph, and a deterministic planner builds the graph and runs it through the real compiler before anything reaches the canvas. There was no olfactory model to build the smell-tracking Stack from, so we engineered one: an 88-neuron circuit laid out like the fly's pathway, with bilateral receptors, antennal-lobe projection neurons, and interneurons that inhibit the receptor terminals so a dense plume doesn't saturate both sides. We tuned it by simulating it on the real VM until it steered the right way on every tick we measured. ENSv2 on Sepolia is the backbone of publishing, and it is our partner technology. We registered reflexos.eth through the ETHRegistrar's commit-reveal flow, paying in the testnet MockUSDC, and deployed our own UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver proxies through the VerifiableFactory with CREATE2 salts, one registry per branch (stacks, blocks, fleet, agents). ENSv2's hierarchy is the whole point: anyone can claim theirname.reflexos.eth, and it comes with its own registry and resolver owned by their wallet. Our operator holds only non-admin publisher roles, which the user can revoke. Publishing registers the Stack's subname, uploads the file to IPFS through Pinata, and in a single multicall writes the digest text record, the contenthash, and the owner's EIP-191 signature over the name and digest. Claiming and publishing are gasless for users: they sign messages in MetaMask, the server verifies each signature against the name's on-chain owner before spending any gas, and it rejects stale signatures so an old one can't roll a name back. Verification goes through the UniversalResolverV2, so anyone can check a Stack with nothing but its name. The hacky parts. The deployed ENSv2 contracts differed from the repository head: the resolver's initialize, setText and role layout had all changed, so we checked every function selector we call against the deployed bytecode and pulled ABIs from the exact deployment commit. On the deployed resolver, write permissions are scoped per record key, not per name, so a shared resolver would let any user overwrite anyone else's digest; that is why every user gets their own resolver. Registration normally cannot be simulated past the commit step, so before sending anything we rehearse the entire sequence with eth_simulateV1: deploy the contracts, mint, approve, commit, then jump the block timestamp past the commitment age, register, link parents, register the branches, and resolve the name back through the Universal Resolver, all on a fork. To list community builds without a database, we recovered the registries' event signature, LabelRegistered, by hashing candidate signatures until one matched the topics in real logs. Discover now scans those events and checks every entry live. Pinata stores small files as a single raw IPFS block, so a Stack's CID contains the very SHA-256 we publish as its digest, and the name's two records are two views of one fingerprint. Finally, the shared VM decoder injects loom signals into its danger population, which would have flattened the smell circuit's intensity. We route intensity through a different output population, and smooth the sparse per-tick spikes with an integer-only leaky integrator (ema += (x - ema) >> 3) that is stored in replayable state, so smell-tracking receipts still replay bit-exactly.

projects.title: PerkOS Runtime
projects.description: Seven AI agents research tokenized stocks with Uniswap; World gates authority, ENS proves identity.
projects.project_description: EQLTY Desk continues our ETHGlobal Lisbon project, EQLTY, as a Desk inside PerkOS Runtime. PerkOS Runtime is the app where Desks run: a desktop app for macOS, Ubuntu and Windows — the demonstration link is where you download it, and the video walks the whole journey. Each Desk is a team of agents with its own market and screens. You sign in with your wallet, pick the AI you want (Grok, ChatGPT, Claude, a model on your own machine, or PerkOS LLM when your wallet has access) and talk to Sparky, the assistant, by text or by voice. Turn memory on and Sparky's notes stay on your computer, encrypted under a key that comes from your wallet's signature. EQLTY Desk works tokenized stocks on Robinhood Chain. Seven roles share market facts, Uniswap quotes and an inspectable history. Analyze and advise turns use Scout, Risk, Quote, Trader and Auditor; launch analysis uses Scout, Risk, Hooks, Treasury and Auditor. A research turn never sends an order. The person reviews a fresh quote and explicitly holds to approve a buy. PerkOS validates the delegated wallet's authority, limits and transaction policy before signing permitted Uniswap v4 calls on Robinhood Chain. World protects a separate trust event: granting or increasing the selected Trader's wallet authority, with exact-parameter binding, backend verification and single-use approval. ENSv2 on Sepolia gives the team seven named identities, scoped evidence permissions and ERC-8004 associations verified through ENSIP-25. The owner can move the whole branch between authorized parents while keeping wallets and IDs, and published task packets stay verifiable at their original block. Runtime shows every ENS action with its signer, status, hash, block and an ENS Explorer link. We demonstrated live World sandbox approval and cancellation with both IDKit and World ID for Agents, and public Sepolia identity and evidence verification. Stock-buy execution is implemented and tested behind the owner's hold; we do not claim a live Tokyo swap receipt. Our Continuity disclosure separates the earlier EQLTY and PerkOS work from what we built at this event.
projects.how_its_made: Runtime is an Electron shell over a Next.js 16 app served on 127.0.0.1, started with Electron's own Node so it behaves the same on macOS, Ubuntu and Windows. Each launch mints a token that every local request carries, and the local API answers only loopback, same-origin calls. Persistent secrets stay in Electron safeStorage (Keychain, DPAPI or libsecret). Typed workspace packages sit under it: ai (Grok, ChatGPT, Claude, Ollama, LM Studio and PerkOS LLM providers), desk-contract (Desk contract v1 as zod schemas; Runtime refuses a desk answer that breaks it), perkos-client (the typed client for api.perkos.xyz), vault (memory encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a wallet-derived key sealed with a device secret) and ens (a keyless ENSv2 SDK that reads and verifies on its own). EQLTY Desk is a separate Hono and viem service that holds no keys. Its manifest declares the roster, turns and rules. It prices Robinhood Chain Stock Tokens in USDG and asks the Uniswap Trading API for V4-only quotes with V4_NO_HOOKS and X-Agent-Info (autonomous for quotes, human_mediated for swaps), and it checks every built swap (Universal Router 2.1.1, the swapper, chain 4663, zero value) before any calldata leaves. Runtime's turn engine fetches numbered facts (F1, F2, and so on), runs Scout and Risk with the Quote, Hooks or Treasury specialists in parallel, then Trader and Auditor with phase one's answers, and keeps every turn in History. PerkOS API owns authentication, the hosted agents, World verification and the signing boundaries. OIDC uses PKCE, a nonce and a public HTTPS callback; IDKit proofs are verified remotely; a fresh approval is consumed in the same transaction that saves the exact Trader rights. For stock orders the API reprices, checks a narrow policy (only V4_SWAP through Universal Router with Permit2, allowlisted contracts, a per-order cap) and simulates, and only then does a Dynamic delegated wallet sign under a Robinhood Chain signer rule. For ENS, each agent signs with its own Dynamic server wallet; the API persists every operation with nonce locks and reconciles receipts, while Runtime independently checks canonical pointers, scoped grants and ENSIP-25 associations. Runtime's launch flow drafts a stock-paired token through the Bankr Token Launch API, simulates it and waits for the owner's hold. Worth mentioning: our signer rule cannot list hook contracts, so quotes exclude hooked pools; measured live, that cost 0.27% of the output on AAPL and 0.04% on AMD. The ENS team moved to a new parent in 19 transactions without losing wallets, ERC-8004 IDs or grants, and its old evidence still verifies at the original block.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Runtime is an Electron shell over a Next.js 16 app served on 127.0.0.1, started with Electron's own Node so it behaves the same on macOS, Ubuntu and Windows. Each launch mints a token that every local request carries, and the local API answers only loopback, same-origin calls. Persistent secrets stay in Electron safeStorage (Keychain, DPAPI or libsecret).

Typed workspace packages sit under it: ai (Grok, ChatGPT, Claude, Ollama, LM Studio and PerkOS LLM providers), desk-contract (Desk contract v1 as zod schemas; Runtime refuses a desk answer that breaks it), perkos-client (the typed client for api.perkos.xyz), vault (memory encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a wallet-derived key sealed with a device secret) and ens (a keyless ENSv2 SDK that reads and verifies on its own).

EQLTY Desk is a separate Hono and viem service that holds no keys. Its manifest declares the roster, turns and rules. It prices Robinhood Chain Stock Tokens in USDG and asks the Uniswap Trading API for V4-only quotes with V4_NO_HOOKS and X-Agent-Info (autonomous for quotes, human_mediated for swaps), and it checks every built swap (Universal Router 2.1.1, the swapper, chain 4663, zero value) before any calldata leaves.

Runtime's turn engine fetches numbered facts (F1, F2, and so on), runs Scout and Risk with the Quote, Hooks or Treasury specialists in parallel, then Trader and Auditor with phase one's answers, and keeps every turn in History.

PerkOS API owns authentication, the hosted agents, World verification and the signing boundaries. OIDC uses PKCE, a nonce and a public HTTPS callback; IDKit proofs are verified remotely; a fresh approval is consumed in the same transaction that saves the exact Trader rights. For stock orders the API reprices, checks a narrow policy (only V4_SWAP through Universal Router with Permit2, allowlisted contracts, a per-order cap) and simulates, and only then does a Dynamic delegated wallet sign under a Robinhood Chain signer rule. For ENS, each agent signs with its own Dynamic server wallet; the API persists every operation with nonce locks and reconciles receipts, while Runtime independently checks canonical pointers, scoped grants and ENSIP-25 associations. Runtime's launch flow drafts a stock-paired token through the Bankr Token Launch API, simulates it and waits for the owner's hold.

Worth mentioning: our signer rule cannot list hook contracts, so quotes exclude hooked pools; measured live, that cost 0.27% of the output on AAPL and 0.04% on AMD. The ENS team moved to a new parent in 19 transactions without losing wallets, ERC-8004 IDs or grants, and its old evidence still verifies at the original block.

projects.title: Achilles
projects.description: Build cross-chain yield products with programmable Senior & Junior tranches.
projects.project_description: Achilles is a cross-chain structured-finance protocol that lets anyone build Senior and Junior tranche products from multiple sources of yield. Yield is fragmented across chains, protocols, and asset classes. LP positions, DeFi lending, tokenized stocks and ETFs, treasuries, private credit, and other yield-generating strategies may all live on completely different infrastructure. Achilles connects these opportunities through a modular adapter architecture. Each adapter represents a source of yield and can operate on any supported chain. Builders choose the adapters they want, combine multiple yield sources into a single portfolio, and structure that portfolio into Senior and Junior tranches. The Junior tranche takes first-loss risk in exchange for greater potential returns, while the Senior tranche receives priority in the yield waterfall and greater downside protection. This transforms a portfolio of heterogeneous yield sources into distinct, programmable risk-return profiles. For example, one Achilles product could combine an LP strategy on Base, lending on Ethereum, tokenized stock or ETF exposure, and another yield strategy on a different chain. Despite the underlying strategies operating across different networks, investors interact with them as one structured product with a Senior and Junior tranche. Achilles makes yield composable across chains and risk programmable through tranching. Instead of building a new protocol for every structured product, anyone can choose yield sources from across the ecosystem, combine them into a portfolio, configure how risk and returns are distributed between tranches, and launch their own onchain structured product.
projects.how_its_made: Achilles is built as a hub-and-spoke structured-finance protocol. The core idea is that yield can come from completely different chains, protocols, and asset classes, while investors interact with them as one Senior/Junior tranche product. On each supported spoke chain, a TrancheVault manages Senior and Junior shares. Both are ERC-1404 restricted tokens, so only eligible, allow-listed wallets can hold or transfer them. We use ERC-7540 asynchronous vault flows because not every yield source settles atomically. This is especially important for sovereign bonds, RWAs, cross-chain positions, and other strategies where settlement may happen asynchronously rather than within a single transaction. Each product has a CapitalAllocator that executes its strategy. A builder can define, for example, 30% LP yield on Ethereum, 25% lending on another chain, 20% tokenized equities, and 25% RWA yield. CapitalAllocator routes deposits and withdrawals to those sources in the configured proportions and triggers their settlement when required. The key abstraction making this possible is our YieldSource interface. Every external protocol or strategy is implemented as an adapter behind the same interface. The underlying source can be a Uniswap LP, lending protocol, tokenized stock or ETF, sovereign bond, private-credit strategy, or something entirely new. Each source can have different contracts, chains, settlement models, and internal logic without requiring changes to the tranche system itself. Uniswap is one of the first real YieldSource integrations we built. We integrate Uniswap v2/v3 liquidity pools on Ethereum Sepolia as LP yield sources. We also use Uniswap on Robinhood Chain Sepolia for tokenized-stock trading, demonstrating that the same underlying protocol stack can participate in very different Achilles strategies and asset classes. From the CapitalAllocator's perspective, these integrations are simply modular YieldSources that can be combined with other adapters into a single product. Cross-chain coordination happens through our private Hub chain. Each spoke connects through a VaultCoordinator, while the HubRouter manages cross-chain actions by product. The HubLedger stores canonical settlement data including NAV, tranche pricing, strategy configuration, requests, permissions, and approvals. Keeping this layer private lets builders protect proprietary strategy composition from unauthorized parties while maintaining a canonical data layer that can expose verified information to regulators and other permissioned participants. For blockchain data access on the application side, we integrated Curvegrid MultiBaas. MultiBaas provides the frontend with indexed blockchain data instead of requiring us to build and maintain a separate indexing stack for every spoke chain. This is particularly useful for Achilles because a single product may span multiple contracts, adapters, and chains. MultiBaas lets the interface surface onchain positions, transactions, vault activity, and other contract data while the protocol itself remains modular. At settlement, Achilles applies the tranche waterfall. Senior receives its configured fixed return first, while Junior takes the first-loss position and receives the remaining upside. We also integrate World IDKit Proof of Human for per-user tranche caps, allowing products to enforce allocation limits against unique humans rather than wallet addresses alone. The most unusual part of the architecture is that we deliberately do not force every yield source into the same execution model. Achilles normalizes them at the YieldSource interface and settlement layer instead. An instantly settling Uniswap LP, a tokenized equity position on another chain, and an asynchronously settling RWA can therefore become components of the same strategy. From the investor's perspective it is one structured product. Underneath, Achilles is coordinating multiple chains, settlement models, and financial primitives — and then applying one programmable Senior/Junior risk waterfall across the combined portfolio.

projects.title: say ur intent
projects.description: Sui DeFi in Codex and Claude Desktop: review transactions and approve them in your own wallet.
projects.project_description: Keep your AI. Keep your context. Keep your wallet. Say Ur Intent brings Sui DeFi tools and interactive transaction review into AI desktop applications. The integration targets MCP Apps-capable versions of the Codex desktop app and Claude Desktop. Users run Say Ur Intent on their own computer and connect it to their AI app through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which lets AI applications call external tools. MCP Apps lets those tools display interactive cards inside the conversation. Users continue with their existing AI service, model and conversation without creating a separate Say Ur Intent AI account or subscription. A user can ask to see their Sui wallet assets, check a DeepBook quote, and prepare a supported swap with an explicit amount and slippage limit. Asset and review cards appear in the AI app, while protocol information is returned to the conversation. A follow-up such as "Use a smaller amount; keep the other conditions" carries the earlier choices into a new request and a new transaction review. Before requesting wallet approval, the user sees what they will spend, the expected receive, the minimum receive if execution succeeds, the selected account, estimated gas and simulation findings. A graph of the Sui programmable transaction block (PTB) shows the underlying transaction commands for further inspection. The user requests approval from the Review card and signs that individual transaction in their own wallet. Say Ur Intent checks the returned transaction and signature against the reviewed transaction and selected account before submitting once. Confirmed execution facts return to the same conversation. The user can then ask about the transaction's actual asset changes and request fresh wallet balances without manually pasting a wallet result into the chat. Unconfirmed outcomes remain explicitly unknown. DeepBook and FlowX are the current swap adapters. A shared review and wallet workflow gives Say Ur Intent a reusable utility structure for AI tools and additional supported protocol adapters. Structured proposals from other tools can currently be reviewed; executing or signing those external proposals remains future work. The AI and cards receive transaction facts and status, never executable transaction bytes or wallet signatures. Each transaction requires the user's own approval, and estimates remain distinct from confirmed chain results.
projects.how_its_made: Say Ur Intent is a TypeScript application running locally on Node.js. The Model Context Protocol SDK exposes tools that an AI application can call, and MCP Apps supplies interactive views rendered inside the conversation. The AI desktop app provides the language model and conversation context; Say Ur Intent provides Sui data, transaction preparation, review and wallet interaction. The backend uses the Sui SDK for mainnet reads, transaction construction and simulation access. Pinned DeepBook and FlowX SDKs supply protocol-specific quotes and swap builders through shared adapter contracts. This allows each adapter to handle its protocol's concrete APIs while using the same review and approval workflow. Zod validates structured inputs and evidence contracts. Token quantities remain integer strings or BigInt values, with units derived from verified metadata. SQLite is the shared source of truth for accounts, cards, reviews and transaction requests. An explicit user action in the card records the exact review revision, transaction and account before a wallet signature is requested. WalletConnect carries a sign-only request between the private backend and the approved wallet. The backend recalculates the digest from the returned transaction bytes, verifies the selected account's signature and checks the mainnet connection before submitting once. The review binds human-readable facts and simulation evidence to the same transaction digest. PTB diagrams use @zktx.io/ptb-model and Mermaid to show transaction structure. Market charts use Lightweight Charts with official DeepBook Indexer candle data. Transaction bytes and signatures remain outside model-facing responses and card display state. A central engineering challenge is handling asynchronous wallet approval and uncertain network responses without repeating a financial request. Review revisions and atomic admission keep requests tied to the user's selection. Request status is stored separately from independently observed chain effects. Reopening a card reads stored state; a lost submission response leads to observation of the same transaction digest, not another submission. Tests exercise SQLite and signature verification with controlled wallet and chain dependencies. This Continuity project extends an existing open-source Sui evidence and review toolkit. Live end-to-end verification of the revised embedded wallet workflow has not yet been completed. OpenAI Codex was also used as a development assistant for implementation, tests, technical review and documentation. The maintainer defined the product requirements and reviewed implementation plans.
