projects.title: HumanOS
projects.description: Everyday AI workflows with ENSv2 agent identities, scoped permissions and human control.
projects.project_description: HumanOS is a local-first workspace for people who want useful automation without becoming prompt engineers. Describe an outcome, and HumanOS turns supported requests into reusable, typed workflows for research, writing, email and scheduled work. The experience is simple: delegate the work, review meaningful external actions, and keep the final say. Instead of asking a large language model to reinvent every step, HumanOS separates decisions from execution. Jev evaluates a finite set of server-defined blocks; DeepSeek generates written content; deterministic connectors perform the work. Workflows preserve their state, outputs and execution receipts, and pause when required information or a connection is missing. This is designed to reduce repeated model reasoning and make costs more predictable; we are not claiming a measured percentage of credit savings. ENSv2 gives each workflow agent a resolvable identity beneath a human namespace, with version-bound capability scope, expiry and revocation. This also applies to agents doing offchain work, such as writing or sending email. HumanOS checks the agent's authority before dispatching supported steps. Separate permissioned resolvers isolate agent records, while receipt hashes make execution evidence inspectable without publishing private message or booking details. ENS provides identity and auditable authority—not a guarantee that generated content is true. JAW account sign-in and World ID human verification serve separate purposes: proving account control versus establishing human assurance. The current prototype includes real-provider research and content runs, local scheduling, and a Resend email test with delivery evidence. Browser-assisted restaurant booking is in progress: the TableCheck integration currently supports guarded availability inspection, not a completed production reservation. Live booking and full live-chain acceptance are not claimed as completed demos. HumanOS makes unsupported or uncertain outcomes visible rather than inventing success.
projects.how_its_made: HumanOS is a TypeScript monorepo with a React/Vite frontend, a backend API, PostgreSQL-backed workflow state, shared schemas, model adapters, connectors and Solidity contracts. Flue is part of the local service architecture. Requests are normalized into deterministic intent and parameter bindings. Jev evaluates offered typed blocks and returns structured choices; it does not generate arbitrary executable plans. DeepSeek, accessed through OpenCode, handles content generation. The server validates the graph and controls which capabilities and connectors can execute. The durable runner records graph versions, attempts, outputs and receipts. Brave supplies web search and source links; Resend supplies email dispatch. External effects use exact payload review, account binding and final confirmation. Uncertain dispatch outcomes require reconciliation rather than an automatic retry that could duplicate an email or reservation. Local schedules retain their authorization context. ENSv2 is central to agent identity and authorization. The hierarchy is task-agent.human-root.parent.eth. The HumanOS registrar and adapter create isolated Permissioned Resolver instances and restrict agent setters to humanos.status and humanos.receipt, using Enhanced Access Control rather than granting registry administration. Application-level capability scopes are bound to the workflow version; the backend combines those scopes with live checks of ownership, controller, hierarchy validity, expiry and revocation. This distinction matters: ENS record-edit roles are not themselves permission to send email or spend funds. Agent keys are backend-managed in this prototype, and only opaque receipt hashes are published onchain. JAW signs users in through backend-verified SIWE sessions. World ID/IDKit is a separate human-verification integration with server-side validation; simulator coverage is not represented as production credential acceptance. Browser automation uses a dedicated Python Browser Use worker and Chromium, communicating with the API through a framed local protocol. It uses finite actions and guarded network policies, rather than an unrestricted autonomous browsing loop. The TableCheck adapter currently checks availability only; production submission, verification handoff and final booking confirmation remain unfinished. Tests cover local contracts, authorization boundaries, cancellation, replay and browser fixtures, while live-provider evidence is tracked separately. The key engineering tradeoff is deterministic execution with explicit failure states instead of treating plausible AI output as proof of an action.

projects.title: Soapay
projects.description: Privacy infrastructure for payments on chain. Get paid to a fresh address only you can open.
projects.project_description: Soapay is privacy infrastructure for payments on chain. Every payment lands on a fresh address that only you can open, and you can spend it without it ever linking back to you. On a public chain, anyone can see what you earn. A payroll batch on Base shows every recipient and every amount next to each other, readable forever, and your colleagues can see it too. A coworker who knows their own line can trace everyone else's, and at Gitcoin DAO a contributor put names to fifteen colleagues' exact salaries starting from nothing but their own pay address. So companies walk away. Visa calls the lack of privacy a dealbreaker for banks, and Toku says every CFO conversation ends the moment they realise payroll would be public. The fixes that exist (Base Ledgers, Tempo Zones, Toku on Aleo) are private ledgers for enterprises. They are permissioned, gated behind an application for access, so they are not for everyone, and they are not fully private, since every payment goes through the company running them, which sees the payment, keeps the books and, in a ledger, decides what you can withdraw. Everyone else still pays in public. With Soapay, a recipient shares one name, such as alice.soapay.eth, and nothing else. There is nothing to apply for and no account to open, so it is permissionless, and any name that carries the stealth records can be paid with no server of ours in the loop. Every payment to that name lands on a fresh stealth address that only the recipient can open and spend from. A coworker reading the same batch sees a list of never-before-seen addresses and cannot tell which line is theirs. The recipient scans the chain, finds their payments, and spends them without ever touching the wallet everyone already knows. Soapay is not another stealth wallet. A stealth wallet like Fluidkey uses the same ERC-5564 and ERC-6538 standards and also hides your wallet from strangers, but it is built for an individual receiving payments. Its server derives your addresses at name resolution and holds your viewing key, so it sees every payment you receive, and it never touches the batch, which is where a coworker reads your salary. Soapay works on the payer side of the same standards. The sender's browser derives every address and throws the ephemeral key away, only you hold your viewing key, and no server of ours sees anything beyond public chain data. One transaction pays and announces every recipient atomically. Amounts can be split into identical chunks and sorted so per-transaction totals never leak. A consolidation guard and a timing queue stop a spend from linking your addresses. A compliant exit through Privacy Pools, built and proven on a Sepolia fork, lets you cash out. Key rotation is attested by World ID. And everything, addresses, ledger and pool secrets, rebuilds from your seed with the public SDK, with no company in the loop. It works in three steps. First, onboarding happens once, usually from an employer's invite link. The recipient app derives spending and viewing keys from one seed, locks them behind a passkey, registers the stealth meta-address in the canonical ERC-6538 registry through a throwaway registrant, and issues an ENSv2 subname whose stealth text record holds the meta-address. The name has no addr record, so nobody can pay a static address by mistake. Second, payment happens in one transaction. The sender app takes names and amounts, resolves each name once and pins its meta-address, derives a fresh ERC-5564 stealth address for every line, sorts the lines so the order says nothing about who is who, and pays and announces them atomically. Plain EOA employers go through StealthDisperse, our one contract, which holds no funds, keeps no state and has no owner. Smart accounts and 7702 wallets send an EIP-5792 batch with no contract at all, and Safes get a transaction bundle to sign. Large runs are cut into transactions of at most 350 lines and never split by employee, because per-transaction totals would reveal salaries. Third, the recipient finds and spends. The scanner filters announcer events by view tag and reads real balances. On first spend a stealth address delegates to an audited ERC-4337 account through EIP-7702, and a paymaster pays the gas, sponsored on the Base Sepolia demo and taken in USDC by Circle's paymaster on Base mainnet, so the address never holds ETH and the main wallet never appears. A consolidation guard blocks a spend that would link your addresses to an identifiable destination and warns on the rest. Three integrations carry the design. ENSv2 on Sepolia gives per-resource access control, so an employee can rotate only their own stealth record and the issuer can only issue names. World ID Proof of Human sessions attest key rotations, so a stolen key alone cannot redirect pay. Soapay is privacy infrastructure for payments on chain. Every payment lands on a fresh address that only you can open, and you can spend it without it ever linking back to you.

On a public chain, anyone can see what you earn. A payroll batch on Base shows every recipient and every amount next to each other, readable forever, and your colleagues can see it too. A coworker who knows their own line can trace everyone else's, and at Gitcoin DAO a contributor put names to fifteen colleagues' exact salaries starting from nothing but their own pay address. So companies walk away. Visa calls the lack of privacy a dealbreaker for banks, and Toku says every CFO conversation ends the moment they realise payroll would be public. The fixes that exist (Base Ledgers, Tempo Zones, Toku on Aleo) are private ledgers for enterprises. They are permissioned, gated behind an application for access, so they are not for everyone, and they are not fully private, since every payment goes through the company running them, which sees the payment, keeps the books and, in a ledger, decides what you can withdraw. Everyone else still pays in public.

With Soapay, a recipient shares one name, such as alice.soapay.eth, and nothing else. There is nothing to apply for and no account to open, so it is permissionless, and any name that carries the stealth records can be paid with no server of ours in the loop. Every payment to that name lands on a fresh stealth address that only the recipient can open and spend from. A coworker reading the same batch sees a list of never-before-seen addresses and cannot tell which line is theirs. The recipient scans the chain, finds their payments, and spends them without ever touching the wallet everyone already knows.

Soapay is not another stealth wallet. A stealth wallet like Fluidkey uses the same ERC-5564 and ERC-6538 standards and also hides your wallet from strangers, but it is built for an individual receiving payments. Its server derives your addresses at name resolution and holds your viewing key, so it sees every payment you receive, and it never touches the batch, which is where a coworker reads your salary. Soapay works on the payer side of the same standards. The sender's browser derives every address and throws the ephemeral key away, only you hold your viewing key, and no server of ours sees anything beyond public chain data. One transaction pays and announces every recipient atomically. Amounts can be split into identical chunks and sorted so per-transaction totals never leak. A consolidation guard and a timing queue stop a spend from linking your addresses. A compliant exit through Privacy Pools, built and proven on a Sepolia fork, lets you cash out. Key rotation is attested by World ID. And everything, addresses, ledger and pool secrets, rebuilds from your seed with the public SDK, with no company in the loop.

It works in three steps. First, onboarding happens once, usually from an employer's invite link. The recipient app derives spending and viewing keys from one seed, locks them behind a passkey, registers the stealth meta-address in the canonical ERC-6538 registry through a throwaway registrant, and issues an ENSv2 subname whose stealth text record holds the meta-address. The name has no addr record, so nobody can pay a static address by mistake. Second, payment happens in one transaction. The sender app takes names and amounts, resolves each name once and pins its meta-address, derives a fresh ERC-5564 stealth address for every line, sorts the lines so the order says nothing about who is who, and pays and announces them atomically. Plain EOA employers go through StealthDisperse, our one contract, which holds no funds, keeps no state and has no owner. Smart accounts and 7702 wallets send an EIP-5792 batch with no contract at all, and Safes get a transaction bundle to sign. Large runs are cut into transactions of at most 350 lines and never split by employee, because per-transaction totals would reveal salaries. Third, the recipient finds and spends. The scanner filters announcer events by view tag and reads real balances. On first spend a stealth address delegates to an audited ERC-4337 account through EIP-7702, and a paymaster pays the gas, sponsored on the Base Sepolia demo and taken in USDC by Circle's paymaster on Base mainnet, so the address never holds ETH and the main wallet never appears. A consolidation guard blocks a spend that would link your addresses to an identifiable destination and warns on the rest.

Three integrations carry the design. ENSv2 on Sepolia gives per-resource access control, so an employee can rotate only their own stealth record and the issuer can only issue names. World ID Proof of Human sessions attest key rotations, so a stolen key alone cannot redirect pay. And an MCP server gives AI agents the same identities, with ENSIP-26 records and spending guardrails, so agents can be paid and can pay by name.

The trust model is simple. The employer is trusted and keeps its own records, so compliance stays where it already lives, and the only adversary is a coworker. The one contract we wrote holds no funds, keeps no state and has no owner, and everything else we call is a canonical, audited contract. Soapay is built for payroll and ready for any payout. Payroll is the first use case because it is where public payments hurt most, but nothing in the rail is specific to salaries. The same one-to-many flow already handles dividends and revenue share, token and equity allocations such as vesting unlocks and investor distributions, vendor and supplier payments, grants and bounties, prizes and airdrops, tips and creator payouts, and agents paying agents by name. The SDK plans all of them through one distribution module with payroll, dividend and grant presets, with vesting as a kind planned the same way, and a CLI runs any of them from a CSV. projects.title: Bizzet
projects.description: bizzet is a wallet built for business operations, from receiving sales to managing team funds.
projects.project_description: bizzet is a wallet designed around the actual operations of a real business. Sales go straight into each store's own wallet without a payment processor or settlement wait in between, and then flow up from each store to the headquarters wallet, including payments made on other chains, which are automatically bridged, converted to the currency the business chose, and gathered into a single ledger at headquarters. On top of the basics of receiving, holding, and sending funds, bizzet adds what a team needs to run a business. Organizations are modeled as groups (headquarters and its stores, including online shops), and each group has its own wallet. Members join a group with a role—Owner, Approver, or Viewer—that decides what they can see and do, and policies such as requiring two approvals for withdrawals from headquarters are enforced on-chain. Members sign in and approve transactions with a passkey on their own device, so no one has to manage private keys or seed phrases, and they never pay gas fees themselves. A dashboard shows balances, withdrawals, members, and funds still in transit between chains, scoped to each member's role and group. Payment settings such as the receiving currency and wallet address live in one on-chain name per store, so changing them once updates every sales channel.
projects.how_its_made: The repo is a pnpm monorepo ( apps/wallet , apps/dashboard , packages/contracts , packages/db ) managed with Biome and Lefthook. Both apps are SvelteKit + Svelte 5 + Tailwind v4, and the dashboard's login/session runs on better-auth backed by Drizzle ORM over Neon serverless Postgres. Each group's wallet is a Gnosis Safe, and packages/contracts (viem/ox + Hardhat) contains the raw calldata builders instead of relying on the Safe SDK, since we needed control that the SDK doesn't expose: encodeSafeInitializer bundles enabling the Safe4337Module (EntryPoint v0.7, for ERC-4337 gasless transactions) and creating each member's passkey signer into one MultiSend inside the Safe's own setup() call, so a group launches pre-configured — module enabled, owners set, passkey signers deployed — in a single transaction. We also hand-wrote the EIP-712 SafeOp typed-data struct for Safe4337Module v0.3, since no SDK covers it, and predictSafeAddress reproduces the factory's CREATE2 computation so the wallet can show a group's address before it's ever deployed. Members never hold a private key: passkeys (P-256, via SafeWebAuthnSignerFactory) become Safe owners directly, so a device's biometric signature is what satisfies the Safe's approval threshold, and an ERC-4337 Paymaster covers gas so members never touch it. For payouts, an on-chain name (ENSv2 subname per store) holds the receiving currency and address as text records, so every sales channel reads the same source of truth. Cross-chain sales are swept home by an external keeper (Gelato/Chainlink Automation) whose on-chain permission is scoped to a single destination — the home Safe — using Circle's CCTP v2 for the actual USDC transfer and Uniswap for any JPYC conversion, so the automation can move funds without ever being able to steal them.

projects.title: CorrFi
projects.description: correlation markets powered by Aqua shared liquidity and SwapVM.
projects.project_description:
CorrFi is a service that allows users to trade on how closely the prices of multiple assets move together. Rather than focusing only on whether individual assets go up or down, users can incorporate their views on the relationship between assets into their trading and risk management strategies. CorrFi is primarily designed for investors and traders who manage multiple assets. For example, even if someone holds different assets to diversify risk, those assets may all fall at the same time when markets become unstable. In other words, a portfolio may appear diversified while still being exposed to the same underlying risk. Some traders may also believe that two assets that have historically moved together will begin to move differently in the future. However, simply buying or selling the assets themselves means that the price movements of each individual asset also affect the trader’s profit and loss. This makes it difficult to express a view specifically on how the relationship between the two assets will change. CorrFi turns the degree to which two assets move together into a tradable instrument. Users select an asset pair and a time period, then trade either the side that benefits when the assets move more similarly or the side that benefits when their co-movement weakens. For example, instead of predicting whether both assets will rise or fall, users can trade on whether the tendency of the two assets to move in the same direction will continue.
At the end of the specified period, the degree of co-movement is calculated based on the assets’ actual price movements, and the final payout of the product is determined accordingly. However, having the correct market view does not necessarily guarantee a profit. Profit and loss depend on both the price at which the position was purchased and the final payout. CorrFi is also not an insurance product that directly compensates users for losses caused by falling asset prices. Rather, it is a tool for managing risks arising from the relationship between assets from a different perspective.
The other key group of users is market makers, who support trading by continuously providing bid and ask prices. A common challenge for market makers is capital fragmentation: if funds are allocated separately to each market, some markets may have excess capital while others may not have enough.
CorrFi aims to provide users with a way to trade the relationships between assets, while giving market makers a mechanism to support trading across multiple markets using shared capital.
projects.how_its_made: I built the core of CorrFi using Solidity smart contracts together with Python-based computation. I also integrated 1inch Protocol’s SwapVM and Aqua to enable capital-efficient market infrastructure, programmable pricing and settlement logic, and atomic execution. The protocol is currently deployed on Base Sepolia. CorrFi is a correlation derivatives protocol with multiple markets. In our MVP, each asset pair has three different maturities, which means even a single correlation pair creates three separate markets. As the number of asset pairs and maturities grows, the number of markets increases rapidly. A major challenge is that liquidity can become fragmented across these markets, making it difficult for market makers to provide sufficient liquidity to every market independently. We use Aqua to address this problem through shared liquidity. Instead of requiring market makers to allocate isolated capital to each individual market, Aqua allows liquidity to be shared across multiple CorrFi markets, significantly improving capital efficiency and enabling more flexible liquidity allocation. SwapVM is used to make the market-making logic programmable. It allows us to incorporate validation of calculated correlation values, risk-management rules, and incentive mechanisms directly into the quote-generation process. This enables market makers to set quotes based on the protocol’s correlation data while managing their exposure in a way that supports sustainable liquidity provision. SwapVM also allows this pricing and settlement logic to be composed into a seamless, atomic execution flow. By combining Solidity contracts, Python-based correlation computation, Aqua’s shared-liquidity architecture, and SwapVM’s programmable execution, CorrFi can support a large number of correlation markets without requiring completely separate liquidity for every market.

SwapVM also allows this pricing and settlement logic to be composed into a seamless, atomic execution flow. By combining Solidity contracts, Python-based correlation computation, Aqua’s shared-liquidity architecture, and SwapVM’s programmable execution, CorrFi can support a large number of correlation markets without requiring completely separate liquidity for every market.

projects.title: Hako 箱
projects.description: Every automation is an ENS name. The contract only pays when the name says so.
projects.project_description: Hako turns recurring token payments into ENSv2 names. Each user gets their own name like alice.hako-箱.eth, and every automation becomes a subname under it, like rent.alice.hako-箱.eth. The task's settings (token, amount, recipient, interval, status) live in the name's text records, its end date is the name's expiry, and deleting the task unregisters the name. A shared executor contract reads the name onchain before every payment, so a paused, expired or deleted task can never move money, no matter who calls it. Anyone can open a user's name and see exactly what's running on their behalf, with no backend or database. Users own their names, registries and resolvers, so their automations are theirs, not the app's.
projects.how_its_made: Built on the ENSv2 beta on Sepolia. hako-箱.eth points to its own UserRegistry, deployed through ENS's Verifiable Factory, and a registrar (adapted from the ENS contract-developer tutorial) issues user names. At sign-up, each user's wallet deploys its own registry and Permissioned Resolver and links them with setSubregistry, so the user holds every role and Hako holds none. Tasks are registered as subnames in the user's registry, and their settings are written to the resolver with multicall(setText). A hako.tasks record on the user's name indexes their tasks, so the React dashboard (viem + RainbowKit) reads everything straight from ENS. TaskExecutor (Solidity, Foundry) is callable by anyone. It checks that the user name and task name exist, that the task's owner is the user name's owner, and reads each setting via resolve(name, text(node, key)). Then it checks the status and interval before calling transferFrom. A small Node worker simulates execute for every task each minute and only sends when the simulation passes, so it has no power over funds. The hardest part: the Sepolia Permissioned Resolver writes with setText(bytes name, …) but only answers reads through ENSIP-10 resolve(); direct text() calls revert. We found this by tracing calls with cast and rebuilt the executor around resolve().

projects.title: UNMAPPED: Open World
projects.description: An endless open world an AI writes as you explore; remixes get ENSv2 names and Uniswap royalties.
projects.project_description: UNMAPPED (無界之地) is an open-source desktop game whose map has no edge, and nothing on it exists until someone walks there. The ground streams from a seed, so walking never waits for AI. The first time a player enters an unwritten place, a language model "witnesses" it: it names the place and writes its residents, a local custom, errands and foes. The model never writes code or JSON. It writes a small game DSL (OpenUI Lang dialects for scenes, dialogue, items and chapters). A parser checks every line, clamps every number to engine limits and sends errors back for at most two repair rounds; output that still fails becomes an honest error, never a stock scene. Once written, a place is saved and never needs the model again. Anyone can make a world from a few words: the model drafts seven editable world-bible cards, concept pictures for its art direction and 3-8 story chapters, then the app builds and publishes it. Every published world is an immutable, sha256-hashed cartridge on your own disk, and every save pins one exact revision. It runs on a cloud API or on your own machine: Apple's on-device model, inside the app, writes worlds, places and chapters, and a local Qwen 3.5 4B on llama.cpp also builds worlds. Play together. What a world holds is a signed, append-only history. Invite friends with a link and they walk what you witnessed with zero model calls, even while you are offline. A small world service only orders, checks and relays signed entries; it never calls a model. When two people reach an unwritten place together, one writes it and the other watches the same text arrive. Places nobody tends fade into fog and become legends, and residents pass on rumours of what friends really did. A world kept on one device can also join friends' worlds peer to peer over WebRTC, with a TURN relay so friends behind a VPN or a strict NAT still meet, and friends chat in both. A .world file carries a whole world, so it outlives any server. It is designed so a 70-year-old can play: four title entries, one list of worlds, one "Join a world" field that takes a friend's ENS name or 6-character join code, and one passkey. On chain (Sepolia) we give AI-made worlds provenance and a remix economy: ENSv2 names first: published worlds, remixes, saves and players get names in one tree under unmapped.eth (aether-land.unmapped.eth, moss-hollow.aether-land.unmapped.eth, kidney-run.aether-land.unmapped.eth, <you>.players.unmapped.eth). Text records hold only ids, versions and hashes; a save's name also carries its progress and join code. The app resolves names through the ENSv2 Universal Resolver, opens a world only if the hash matches the local bytes, and lets a friend join by typing the name. Naming a world deploys its own emancipated subname registry, so the family tree is the ENS hierarchy itself. Uniswap: a world's name holder can launch it from the app. Its token is priced by a Continuous Clearing Auction (via Liquidity Launcher's LBPStrategy), denominated in its parent world's token, then graduates into a v4 pool. Our v4 hook takes 1% of every swap and pays it up the family line (50/30/20) to whoever holds each world's ENS name. Live on Sepolia: the root world's auction cleared 86% above its floor with 4 passkey bids, and a 10 USDC buy paid exactly 1% to the name holder. No wallet and no key in the app: a player's passkey owns a smart account, and a gas station only pays gas for a fixed set of calls. A shared world's service can record a fingerprint of each beat on chain (WorldProvenance), and the app checks it against its own copy. The chain is optional: with nothing configured, the whole game still plays.
projects.how_its_made: UNMAPPED is an Electron app in TypeScript (Bun, electron-vite, React, zustand). The same land is drawn two ways: an HD-2D diorama in Three.js (painted chunk floors, shadow-casting sprites, bloom and tilt-shift built from three/examples) and a flat 16-bit canvas. Terrain is 32x32-tile chunks computed from seed + chunk coordinates, never stored and never generated by the model. AI: every model call goes through a Cordis-based harness (modelled on DeepSeek Harness) that assembles the prompt from ordered sections and exposes tools whose only way to change the world is a typed GameEffect. The model writes OpenUI Lang, parsed by @openuidev/lang-core against zod v4 schemas; one repair round sends back every kind of mistake at once (at most two rounds), and every number is clamped. Verified end to end with OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini. Apple's on-device model runs inside the app through our Swift bridge on FoundationModels. Its 4K context is too small for the full prompt, so there the model fills a JSON Schema derived from the DSL's own zod shapes (guided generation) and the host writes the answer back as an OpenUI Lang program the parser still checks. A local Qwen 3.5 4B runs on a llama.cpp sidecar the app starts. A local usage ledger records tokens and latency for every call, never prompts or keys. Mods are YAML + markdown prompt sections and declarative tools, never JavaScript. Data: published worlds are immutable sha256-hashed cartridges and saves pin an exact revision. Portable data is encrypted with a random AES-GCM Data Key wrapped by a passkey PRF or the macOS keychain. Shared worlds: a world is one sequenced, append-only log of signed events. Every device has an Ed25519 key; an event's id is the sha256 of its canonical JSON, and each log entry chains the previous entry's hash and carries the service's receipt signature. A Bun world service orders, validates (the same zod + DSL checks the app runs) and relays entries over one WebSocket; it never calls a model and never edits an entry. Folding the log is deterministic (integers, strict ISO dates, no floating-point trig, no locale compare), so the service and every device compute the same land, fog, legends and rumours. When two people reach one unwritten place, a short claim lets one write while the other watches the stream. Invite links carry a one-time secret that never enters the log. A .world file (a zip of the log and content packs) verifies offline and can bring a world up on another service. A phone-sized browser page joins by invite with a non-extractable WebCrypto Ed25519 key. Peer to peer: worlds kept on one device join as "continents", Yjs docs over y-webrtc. Nothing is exchanged until a peer's hello matches the continent code, protocol and physics version, and every entry is validated on arrival. We patched y-webrtc so only the lower peer id initiates (upstream glare left one-way data channels). A Cloudflare Worker mints short-lived Cloudflare Realtime TURN credentials and keeps the TURN key, so friends behind a VPN still connect: behind NordVPN, STUN alone never connected and the relay joined in 2.4 s. Chain (Ethereum Sepolia): Solidity compiled with solc-js, viem only in Electron's main process (keys never reach the renderer). ENSv2: names resolve through the Universal Resolver (DNS-encoded names). Names come first: LineageRegistry.register names a cartridge revision and deploys that name's own children's registry; recordSave names a player's save, held by their passkey account, with its hash, progress and join code as text records; player names are saves under players.unmapped.eth. Every registry it makes keeps only REGISTRAR | SET_PARENT, so every name stays an emancipated, safely transferable ERC-1155. We redesigned around this after hitting TransferUnsafeUntilRegistryIsEmancipated. Uniswap: LineageRegistry.launch (name holder only) starts a Continuous Clearing Auction through Liquidity Launcher LBPStrategy v3.1.0 and the CCA factory v2.1.0 (Uniswap's own Sepolia deployments), with their structs mirrored field for field. LineageHook (v4-periphery BaseHook) uses beforeInitialize (only LBPStrategy may open a world x parent-token pool), afterSwap + afterSwapReturnDelta for a 1% royalty split 50/30/20 up the line, and claim() pays the current ENS name holder. LineageRouter buys or sells along a whole family line inside one unlock. Passkeys: a PasskeyAccount verifies WebAuthn signatures with OpenZeppelin's WebAuthn library on the P-256 precompile (EIP-7951); main builds each batch and the passkey signs the digest. The gas station, a Cloudflare Worker, holds the only paying key: it builds each transaction itself, allows only a fixed list of targets, simulates first and caps gas and fees. WorldProvenance: a world service records each beat's log hash and fingerprint (never content); the app only reads it and compares with its own copy. Hacky bits: we mine the hook address with CREATE2 in TypeScript for flags 0x2044; initializeDistribution doesn't return the auction, so we recompute its address from LBPStrategy's salt rule; the whole market (deploy, three generations of launch/auction/graduation, swaps, royalties, name transfer, refusals) is replayed against Sepolia's real contracts with eth_simulateV1 before anything spends gas; Electron dev can't reach Touch ID, so main serves a localhost page the system browser opens for the one signature. The read-only Lineage Auction House is a static page on Cloudflare Workers that reads Sepolia directly. E2E runs drive the real app over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, with a virtual WebAuthn authenticator, a virtual gamepad and touch; one run takes a single world through Create, play, sharing, a co-owner, a phone and a .world move across six clients.

projects.title: Maat JEV Gate
projects.description: The pre-signing gate for AI agents that pay and trade. Unclear cases go to a World ID human.
projects.project_description: Maat is a gateway for AI agents that request paid resources or propose token swaps without holding a treasury key. The Agent sends an authenticated intent to the Gateway. For x402 payments, the Gateway reads the Merchant's payment requirements, screens the recipient and token with Intercepta, and uses JEV to compare the proposed payment with the Agent's task. It blocks unsafe requests, signs and settles approved Base Sepolia USDC payments, or asks a human to confirm through World ID. For swaps, Maat gathers live Ethereum mainnet quotes and risk evidence, then returns an allow, block, or escalate decision. Swap decisions are analysis only: this demo does not sign or broadcast trades.
projects.how_its_made: Maat is written in TypeScript with React and Vite interfaces, Fastify services for the Agent, Gateway, and x402 Merchant, and a Next.js Swap Guard. The Agent service submits fixed payment and swap scenarios to the Gateway with server-side credentials. On payments, the Merchant supplies an HTTP 402 quote; the Gateway checks Intercepta and JEV, then signs an EIP-712 USDC authorization with a server-only key. The Merchant sends the payload to an x402 facilitator for Base Sepolia verification and settlement. On swaps, the Gateway calls Swap Guard, which gets a Uniswap quote, reads Ethereum mainnet and explorer data, runs Intercepta scans and deployer forensics, applies risk rules, and asks JEV when needed. World ID's Sandbox OIDC flow verifies human approval before a pending payment proceeds; the callback goes to the Gateway, never to the Agent. Notable hacks: we implemented the x402 flow directly instead of using @x402/fetch. Payments settle on Base Sepolia through the public x402 test facilitator, while Intercepta screens Base mainnet USDC as a risk-data proxy for the testnet token. Swaps use live Ethereum mainnet quotes but are analysis only. If JEV is unavailable, Swap Guard falls back to labeled local rules. The blocked-recipient scene uses a known-risk address shared in Intercepta's ETHGlobal channel.

projects.title: FOI Attest & Tip
projects.description: On-chain proof of real disclosure requests via EAS, with tipping to support requesters
projects.project_description: Civic Disclosure Tip lets anyone file a real Freedom-of-Information / public-records disclosure request and permanently attest it on-chain via EAS on Base Sepolia, creating a tamper-evident, timestamped public record. Each request gets a shareable Case page where anyone can send ETH/USDC tips or reactions to support the requester, with on-chain leaderboards and referral tracking. We've already submitted and attested 6 real disclosure requests to Japanese municipal and prefectural governments (e.g. the Mayor of Anjo, Ichinomiya, and the Governor of Aichi Prefecture) using this system, and each request goes through an automated PII scan before submission to prevent accidental exposure of personal information.
projects.how_its_made: This project is a monorepo with a Python/FastAPI backend and a static HTML/JS frontend. Users sign directly with their own browser wallet, and each Freedom-of-Information disclosure request is recorded on-chain as an EAS (Ethereum Attestation Service) attestation on Base Sepolia, creating a tamper-proof public record with no server-side signing. Every request gets a public Case page where anyone can send ETH/USDC tips or reactions, also recorded on-chain as EAS attestations referencing the original request. Before submission, requests go through an automated PII scan to detect and warn about accidental personal-information leaks. The Google Gemini API powers on-the-fly translation on Case pages, so the original Japanese request text is also readable in English. We additionally built a custom OrgSubnameRegistryV2 contract that lets organizations (municipalities, NPOs) claim a human-readable ENS subname on-chain, so tip recipients aren't just raw addresses. Nothing is centrally custodied — every attestation and every tip is signed and paid for directly by the user's own wallet.

projects.title: Trinity Guardian
projects.description: Human-authorized AI agent payments with on-chain permissions, spending policies, and risk checks.
projects.project_description:
Trinity Guardian is a security and authorization layer for autonomous AI agent payments. It lets humans safely delegate spending authority to AI agents without giving them unrestricted wallet access. Each agent receives an ENS-based on-chain identity and programmable spending mandate, including per-payment limits, daily limits, and destination allowlists. Before a payment is executed, Guardian validates the agent's ENS permissions and passes the transaction through a risk checkpoint. projects.title: UnSui
projects.description: Unlock your Suica card's lost potential, collect unused funds as a crypto refund.
projects.project_description: Here is my story about experience in Japan (non-ai-generated) when it comes to visiting and re-visiting. My first even hackathon was in 2023 for ETHGlobal Tokyo. Since then transit card for Suica has been sitting with me with unused balance ever since! Only returning to the roots now I've realized that ths balances could have been used to a better purpose if it would be much easier to refund with minimal fees. And I'm not alone! There's thousands of tourists and visitors facing same issue with Suica cards unused balance on phisical cards. So this time coming back I've decided to solve this by building UnSui mobile app service that can help anyone with unused leftover balance to be transferred to any wallet of your choice on SUI (スイ) blockchain or Mizuhiki: The Japan Chain as an option. This works even better with Welcome Suica red card that by default only lasts 28 days without any refunds supported by JR East. UnSui is an NFC app that connects a Japanese Suica card to a crypto refund workflow. Hold a physical card to the phone to read the latest balance and recent journeys. Simply choose what to do with leftover balance any time even after you've left Japan or forgot to deal with the refund while in Japan (which is also not an easy thing to do). This can serve as on-board to crypto too! Think about it taking in account how much Yen depreciated in value over these 3 years and you could have utilized it or converted to Bitcoin or other currency instead. A sample-card demo works when no card is available. After a reading, you choose a wallet and network, review the yen conversion, and submit a refund request. A shared development ledger stores the receipt, tracks the remaining allowance, and blocks duplicate requests. Scanning works offline. Refunds need internet access that would communicate with backend to use SoftBank merchant ID where Suica card can be charged for remaining amount (minus fee) to access this as a service. Once Yen is secured we can issue SUI tokens on SUI blockchain or MIZU tokens on Mizuhiki Japan chain to wallet of your choice as a exchange transaction. World-ID identifications helps us with regulatory compliances when it comes to tracking funds and following the lawful practical use case according to the rules of merchant business where Suica can be used as source of payment.
projects.how_its_made: UnSui is a React Native 0.86 app. It reads a physical Suica card over NFC-F with react-native-nfc-manager and FeliCa system code 0003, decoding the balance and journey bytes on the phone then charging the card through SoftBank payment system (merchantID required). Station names come from a pinned, hash-checked Suica station table, with a small Tokyo fallback if that file is missing. A Node server on port 4100 is the refund ledger. It compiles the same TypeScript quote and allowance modules as the app, so the 2% fee, the network, and the remaining balance cannot drift between the phone and the server. Refunds above ¥1,000 open World’s official IDKit flow. The server verifies the proof with @worldcoin/idkit-core and binds it to the card, amount, recipient, and request id. Sui names resolve through Sui mainnet GraphQL. On a dGen1 phone, ethOS WalletProxy supplies the Ethereum Mainnet or Mizuhiki Awaji address. A Sui Move treasury is deployed on mainnet, and the backend can submit a payout through @mysten/sui using that same 2% fee. The contract stores a keyed card commitment, so the raw card id never goes on chain. The notable hack is treating the closed Suica record as a readable balance, then keeping one set of refund rules in TypeScript for both the phone and the server. Additinally there's a dashboard for user and admin to verify treasury, payouts or any activity in the UnSui service system so user does not need to use only phone UI if they wish to try desktop instead to view their refund history or card usag overall.

projects.title: Name Inheritance
projects.description: Heirs inherit an ENS name and the will sealed on it when the owner goes silent. No key holder.
projects.project_description: Conditional Name Inheritance lets the heirs inherit an ENS name, its subnames and the will sealed on it, when the owner goes silent. The owner seals the will on his ENSv2 name and checks in every week by writing a heartbeat record. The will is encrypted to a condition, not to a key: no heartbeat on the name for N finalized epochs. When the finalized chain shows that silence, anyone can open it. One transaction writes the disclosure record, hands the parent name to the main heir and the subnames to the other heirs, and the heir reads the will with her own key. Faking the condition means forging Ethereum finality, which Ethereum already slashes: with a third of the stake the attacker is slashed and the will stays sealed; with two thirds it opens, and at least 14.5 million of the 43.4 million ETH staked is burned. Built on the ENSv2 Sepolia beta: two names, records on the permissioned resolver of the owner with roles scoped to one key, the name handed over through the ETHRegistry, every read through UniversalResolverV2. The name tree with its lock runs on ENSv2 registry code on the local chain.
projects.how_its_made: Two Solidity contracts, 25 Foundry tests. Studio seals each envelope and writes the heartbeat and sealed records on the name through a role scoped to those two keys. Opener verifies the checker signature, writes the disclosure record once per window, and hands over a list of names through the registry. The name tree uses the vendored ENSv2 PermissionedRegistry and LabelStore code: the owner deploys his own registry, sets it as the subregistry of his name, registers the subnames, and revokes the registrar, unregister and set-subregistry roles so the tree cannot be changed later. Off chain, a Python checker turns the finalized chain into a witness with five checks: a finality certificate, a Merkle storage proof of the heartbeat record against the certified state root, the silence predicate, the horizon, and the beacon chain finalized checkpoint from two endpoints. A witness KEM prototype on the silence arithmetic derives the key, and PyNaCl seals the inner box to the heir key read from her name. The attack panel runs process_attester_slashing from ethereum/consensus-specs with 22 or 44 of 64 validators; on Anvil the two-thirds case rewinds the chain with a snapshot. A watchtower agent opens envelopes on Sepolia; three openings and one handover are on chain. The live page is viem on GitHub Pages, reading the chain in the browser.

projects.title: Kinjo
projects.description: Neighborhood mesh of cheap ESP32s that keeps people talking and transacting when the Internet fails
projects.project_description: Kinjo (近所, "neighborhood") is a local mesh network built from cheap ESP32 devices. When infrastructure fails, whether from a blackout like Spain and Portugal's in 2025, an earthquake, a typhoon or a deliberate shutdown, people a few meters apart often can't message each other or move money. Kinjo devices talk directly over ESP-NOW or could also do so through LoRa, with no router, cell tower or server and can forward each other's end-to-end encrypted messages, so relays carry traffic they can't read. ENS is the trust layer: every person has a name like alice.kinjo.eth and every device a subname that publishes its keys, so devices know whom to trust offline and owners can revoke a lost device. Devices that still have Internet act as gateways, carrying signed transactions from offline devices to Ethereum and sending receipts back over the mesh.
projects.how_its_made:
Kinjo has three kinds of devices. A handheld (ESP32 with a 2.8" touchscreen), a relay (XIAO ESP32-C3) and a bridge (another XIAO) plugged into a laptop, where the web app turns the laptop into a node too. They talk over ESP-NOW, the ESP32's built-in radio, so no Wi-Fi network or internet is needed. For the demo we force a 2-hop route (handheld -> relay -> laptop) so you can see the relay carry messages it can't read. Every message is end-to-end encrypted: X25519 key exchange, then ChaCha20-Poly1305. We wrote our own small wire format with a Python reference implementation and shared test vectors. The C++ firmware (Monocypher) and the TypeScript app (noble) both pass the same vectors, which is how three languages agree byte for byte. ENS is the trust layer. Our Solidity contract (Foundry) gives every user alice.kinjo.eth with their own ENSv2 registry and resolver. Each device becomes a subname whose text record holds its encryption key. Nodes resolve these keys to check who sent a message. Revoking a device in ENS makes everyone reject it, even though relays keep forwarding it. Users only sign EIP-712 messages. Our relayer pays the gas, so nobody needs testnet ETH. World ID (IDKit 4, Proof of Human) adds an optional "verified human" badge, checked server-side and stored as alice.verified.kinjo.eth. The team owns that name, so users can't fake their own badge. The web app is SvelteKit, installable and usable offline. It sets up the handheld over USB, and the handheld gets its name and contacts from ENS. Hacky bits:
Chrome's Web Serial kept dropping our boards on Linux, so we wrote a tiny Python helper that serves the serial ports over a local WebSocket.
In ENSv2 a deleted subname still falls back to the parent's resolver, so revoking also has to clear the key record.
The contract accepts signatures from normal wallets and from EIP-7702 smart accounts (ERC-1271), because one of our test wallets was a 7702 account.

projects.title: RealAddr for Agents
projects.description: A realistic rental address that enables contract execution solely through autonomous AI agents
projects.project_description: Currently, 57% of all web requests originate from bots and AI agents—humans are now the minority. To help AI agents operate offline as well as online, we have built a service that leases physical addresses to them. Contracts can be executed autonomously by AI agents using x402 payments. However, due to legal requirements, mail forwarding is permitted only for requests verified through human authentication via World ID. We also support secure x402 billing powered by Intercepta, as well as business support that links ENS domains to physical addresses using ENSv2. Currently, addresses across 11 locations in Japan are available for use.
projects.how_its_made:
Monetization via x402; Intercepta; curvegrid (MultiBaas)
Human verification using World ID
Low-cost linking and sale of ENS names and addresses using the ENSv2 hierarchical registry
GCP (Cloud Run, Firestore, Google Cloud Storage, Google Auth)
GitHub Actions; TypeScript
Support for Ethereum Sepolia and Base Sepolia via MultiBaas

projects.title: Ashiato
projects.description: Trace stolen crypto across BTC, ETH, Tron and 5 EVM chains to the exchange that can freeze it
projects.project_description: Ashiato (足跡, "footprints") is a crypto tracing tool for scam victims and the people who help them. When someone loses money to an investment or romance scam, the funds usually move through a few wallets and end up at an exchange. The exchange can freeze the account, but only if someone shows it where the money went. Commercial tools that do this cost thousands a year, so most victims never get that far. Paste an address or transaction hash (Bitcoin, Ethereum or Tron; Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BNB Chain and Polygon with Pro) and Ashiato draws the money as a graph. Click an address to see its transactions and counterparties, add the ones that matter, and build the trail hop by hop. Every address is checked against 120k+ open-source labels, the OFAC sanctions list and scam/drainer lists. Ashiato also spots exchange deposit addresses (the detail an exchange needs to identify the account holder), CoinJoins, Tornado Cash use, DEX swaps and cross-chain bridges (Bridgers, Across, Relay and deBridge hops are followed to the destination chain). Each address gets a 0–100 risk score with the reasons shown. Anyone can sign in with a wallet or email and add community labels ("this is a scam wallet"). Labels are signed with the user's wallet, so anyone can verify who said what, and other users vote on them. Cases are saved to your account and export as a printable report, CSV, GraphML or PNG to hand to police or an exchange. Everything a victim needs is free. Ashiato Pro (paid in USDC on Base or Ethereum, verified on-chain) adds watch alerts when traced funds move, a plain-English summary of the trace written by Claude, and the five extra EVM networks.
projects.how_its_made: Ashiato is a Next.js 15 (React 19) app on Vercel. The graph uses React Flow with a dagre layout; addresses you place by hand never move when new ones are added, and a select tool moves groups of nodes together. Chain data: Etherscan V2 for Ethereum and all the EVM chains (one code path, switched by chainid, including internal transactions and ERC-20 transfers), Esplora for Bitcoin (exact coin-level tracing through outspends) and TronGrid/Tronscan for Tron. Bridge hops are resolved through each bridge's public API (Bridgers, Across, Relay, deBridge), so a trail continues on the destination chain. Labels come from GraphSense TagPacks, eth-labels, the OFAC list, MyEtherWallet's darklist and ScamSniffer, merged into one lookup. Wallets and identity use Reown AppKit with wagmi and viem. Sign-In with Ethereum creates a session, and email/social sign-ins get a Reown smart wallet. Community labels are EIP-712 typed-data signatures, verified on the server with viem's verifyTypedData so they also work for smart-contract wallets (ERC-1271). The hacky part: labels started as EAS attestations on Sepolia, but asking a scam victim to pay gas and switch networks to flag a scammer put people off, so we moved to gasless signatures that stay publicly re-verifiable. Payments: there's no payment processor. The user sends USDC on Base or Ethereum from their wallet; the server reads the receipt, checks the Transfer log (payer, our address, amount, confirmations), credits each transaction once and stacks the paid months. Email wallets report chain IDs as "eip155:1", which broke viem, so we parse the chain ourselves and send with chain: null. Pro features: the plain-English summary uses the Anthropic SDK (Claude) with the trace's facts as input. Watch alerts use a Vercel cron job that checks watched addresses daily and flags funds that reach an exchange. Accounts, cases, labels, payments and alerts live in Supabase (Postgres via PostgREST, server-side only; no emails stored, only wallet addresses). This is a Continuity-track project: the tracing engine existed before the event, and everything above involving wallets, signatures, payments, Pro features, bridges, extra chains and the new graph tools was built during ETHGlobal Tokyo.

projects.title: Cordon
projects.description: Cordon helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
projects.project_description:
The problem
AI agents can decide which tools to call, repeat failed requests, and delegate work to other agents. That flexibility makes their costs difficult to predict. A user may approve a task expecting a useful result, only to discover that the agents have spent the budget collecting information without completing the final output. There is evidence that unexpected agent costs are a real engineering problem. A June 2026 research preprint catalogues 63 reported production budget-overrun incidents across 21 orchestration frameworks, including failures involving delegated work. This evidence concerns broader agent computation and orchestration costs rather than specifically Circle marketplace payments, but it illustrates the financial consequences of poorly coordinated autonomous activity. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04056 Delegation adds a coordination problem. If workers receive independent allowances without a shared total check, their combined purchases can exceed the owner’s intended task budget. And a limit written per wallet cannot express the rule that matters once work is delegated: a purchase made a few delegations down still counts against what the person at the top signed. The agent holds no key. Its only tool takes a URL; there is no tool that names a recipient or an amount, and there never will be. A daemon holds the operator key and asks the contract before any money exists.
A refusal is a transaction, not an error. The contract returns rather than reverts, so the refusal stays on chain and is published to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry, naming the draw that produced it. It also consumes no budget.
Readable by anyone. Every agent has an ENSv2 name whose records — cordon.live, cordon.headroom, cordon.boundBy — are computed from the contracts at resolve time, not stored. A seller can check a buyer with any ENS library, no account and no permission from us. The owner can also release one refusal (a signed exception) or cut a branch.
What is live today (testnet — Ethereum Sepolia and Arc): three contracts and a settlement rail on each chain, an MCP server on npm (cordon-mcp), a seller SDK (@cordon/verify), a console for the owner’s actions, a public name-resolve page, a real settled purchase read back from chain, and a hostile drill whose result is published whichever way it came out. What is next. Today a refusal tells an agent no with a reason. Our next step is to help agents use that feedback: choose a cheaper service, reuse information they already have, avoid retries that will be refused anyway, and reserve enough budget for the remaining work — or ask the owner for a specific exception. Cost-aware planning and alternative-service selection are the capabilities we aim to build on this foundation. How we will evaluate Cordon
We will compare three approaches: direct purchasing without Cordon, a conventional shared budget with a hard stop, and Cordon. Each receives the same task, starting information, service options, and output requirements. Our main question is whether Cordon can reduce the total cost of completing a task while delivering an equally useful result. We will measure task completion, total spending, repeated or unnecessary purchases, completion time, and the number of times the owner needs to intervene. Total cost will include payment fees, gas, and any Cordon service fee. For deterministic tasks, such as retrieving a fixed dataset or performing a calculation, we will check whether the final outputs match exactly. For research and synthesis tasks, we will evaluate accuracy, completeness, source quality, and freshness against the same checklist. We will use fixed data or aligned timestamps where needed to make comparisons fair. We will also test difficult situations: repeated failures, expensive services, and several agents drawing from one budget — and an agent that is prompt-injected or left running, since that is where the owner is the victim and the bound is what stops it. A run that spends less because it stops early will count as incomplete, not as an efficiency improvement. An earlier version of this test already exists as a gate: one task, split across a root and its workers, run under Cordon and under a plain shared cap, three runs each. With a worker stuck in a loop, the shared cap spent the total it was given and the other worker’s work never happened; under Cordon the loop was refused and the brief still completed. projects.title: Authentificate
projects.description: App that allows users to take accoutabilty in exchange of rewards.
projects.project_description:
World authentification allows any user to log in with just a wallet with guaranties of bein a human, this proces allows the owner of the wallet to give accoutability solo or with peers
on the review of ia generated code submited via smart contracts,
The review takes a minum amout to gain credibility to avoid spamers. This is subject to adjustments.
projects.how_its_made:
The smart contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry (via-IR, OpenZeppelin 5.1) and deployed on Sepolia. They are covered by 111 tests, including unit, fuzz and invariant tests. HumanRegistry enforces one human = one account. ValidationReceipts records every approval as an EIP-712-signed receipt. RewardToken is a soulbound token with no transfer function at all: tokens are keyed by humanId, and one cooldown per human is shared across every bounty, so tokens can't be farmed in parallel. Bounty holds the challenge code hash and link plus an ETH prize: reviewers with 5 tokens qualify for an equal split, and a judge can slash all tokens for approving failing code. The app is Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript) + viem. MetaMask signs every review, and a server-side relayer pays the gas. Storage is SQLite locally and Postgres in production (tested with PGlite). World ID (IDKit 4): a uniqueness proof gives the humanId, and a session proof becomes the account. Every proof is verified on our server against World's v4 verify API, and an attester co-signs an EIP-712 enrollment that the user's own wallet submits. We accept only World ID 4.0, because a legacy 3.0 proof yields a different nullifier, which would let one person enroll twice. A real proof passed on our test page. The demo runs a flagged "simulated" mode that is recorded on-chain as a distinct level, never Orb.
And a lot of latices and derivatives tied with orquestration (claude)

projects.title: Capital Pilot
projects.description: Shared AI intelligence with decentralized execution and risk
projects.project_description:
Capital Pilot is an autonomous on-chain asset management platform that combines shared AI market intelligence with transparent, verifiable smart-contract execution. Instead of having every trading vault independently call an LLM to analyze the market, Capital Pilot uses a shared AI intelligence layer. The platform continuously analyzes BTC market data once and publishes the resulting market insight and strategy decisions on-chain. Agent vaults can then consume the same verified decision, allowing multiple users to benefit from a common source of AI market intelligence without each vault separately paying the LLM analysis cost. The system continuously analyzes BTC market data and classifies the current market regime as either Trading or Market Maker. In Trading mode, an AI strategy agent evaluates the current conditions and selects one or more supported strategies, including Momentum, Technical Analysis, and DCA. Agent vaults configured for eligible strategies can then open positions based on the shared market decision. A separate exit agent evaluates existing positions and determines whether they should be held or closed. This creates a separation between shared intelligence and individual execution: AI market intelligence is shared across participating vaults.
Strategy configuration remains vault-specific.
Risk parameters remain user-specific.
Trade execution occurs independently through each vault's smart contract. Every market decision is recorded on-chain with its selected strategies, confidence score, rationale, and timestamp. Vault trades reference these decision records, creating an auditable connection between an AI-generated market insight and the on-chain transaction it ultimately produces. Users can connect MetaMask through the dashboard to create and fund agent vaults, view vaults across the platform, filter vaults by wallet, and monitor balances, strategies, market mode, open positions, realized PnL, and AI decision history. Why Capital Pilot?
Capital Pilot explores a different model for AI-powered DeFi: AI intelligence can be shared, while execution and risk remain decentralized at the vault level. Instead of repeatedly paying for the same market analysis across individual trading agents, one shared AI intelligence layer can generate a market view that multiple autonomous vaults can independently act upon. This creates a scalable architecture where intelligence is shared, decisions are transparent, and execution remains on-chain and user-controlled.
projects.how_its_made:
Capital Pilot consists of three connected layers: Smart Contracts
The Solidity contracts are developed and tested with Foundry. AgentFactory deploys and indexes user-owned agent vaults.
AgentVault manages deposits, withdrawals, trading positions, market-maker activation, realized PnL, and position history.
MarketRegimeRegistry stores timestamped AI market decisions and makes shared market intelligence available on-chain.
XYCSwap implements constant-product swaps using Aqua's shared-liquidity architecture.
AquaTradingAdapter connects agent vaults to the Aqua execution layer. Each market analysis receives a unique on-chain decisionId. The decision records the detected market regime, selected strategies, confidence score, rationale, and timestamp. When a vault opens or closes a position, the transaction references the corresponding decisionId. This creates an on-chain audit trail connecting: Market Data → AI Analysis → Strategy Selection → Vault Decision → On-chain Execution A strategy bitmask allows multiple strategies to be selected efficiently, while vaults validate that their configured strategy was actually selected by the shared AI strategy decision before opening a position. Every market-maker activation uses a unique salt, preventing reuse of an immutable Aqua strategy hash after docking. Shared AI Backend
The Node.js backend provides the shared intelligence layer. It consumes Binance candle data and calculates technical indicators including: RSI ADX ATR Bollinger Bands Momentum Volatility The backend coordinates three OpenAI-powered agents: LLM_A — Market Regime Agent: classifies the global BTC market regime as Trading or Market Maker.
LLM_B — Strategy Agent: evaluates the current regime and selects eligible trading strategies.
LLM_C — Exit Agent: evaluates existing positions and determines whether they should remain open or be closed. LLM_A and LLM_B generate a shared market insight rather than running independently for every user vault. The combined decision is recorded on-chain before eligible vaults execute trades. This architecture allows multiple agent vaults to leverage the same AI-generated market analysis, significantly reducing duplicated LLM calls and making AI-driven asset management more cost-efficient at scale. After a decision is confirmed on-chain, the backend submits the corresponding trading transactions through ethers.js using a nonce-managed signer. Each trade is linked to the confirmed market decision, preserving the relationship between the shared AI insight and the resulting execution. Frontend
The frontend is built with React, Vite, MUI, and ethers.js. The dashboard provides: MetaMask wallet connection and localhost network support Latest and historical market-regime decisions Shared AI market insights and strategy selections AI confidence scores and rationale Vault creation, token approval, and funding Global and wallet-filtered vault views Vault balances, market mode, and strategies Open positions and realized PnL PnL percentage Expandable position histories Links between individual trades and their underlying AI decisions Contract addresses and network settings are isolated in a frontend configuration file, allowing the interface to be deployed from localhost to compatible EVM test networks with minimal configuration changes.

projects.title: LIFELiNK
projects.description: LIFELiNK connects people in need with nearby helpers, using technology and Web3 to protect lives.
projects.project_description:
This is an AI-powered emergency assistance service that starts with a single press of an SOS button.
In an emergency, you may not have time to take out your phone, unlock it, open an app, and call the police.
With this service, you can simply press an SOS button on your phone or a keychain device to start the emergency response.
The AI automatically identifies the nearest police station and calls for help, providing your precise address, GPS coordinates, verified identity, and real-time information about the situation.
At the same time, your family and friends can follow what is happening through Discord, including your live location, the AI-police call, and live audio from the scene. If necessary, they can also contact the police directly.
The service uses World to verify that each account belongs to a real person, helping reduce false reports and misuse.
One press connects you to AI, the police, and the people you trust—when every second matters. ◾️Why We Created LIFELiNK
There are two main reasons why we created LIFELiNK. ・The first reason is simple.
We want to use technology to save more lives.
Every day, crimes and accidents happen around the world.
In some cases, a faster response could save a life.
So we asked ourselves
Can technology connect people who need help with people nearby who can help?
And can we do it faster?
That idea became LIFELiNK.
LIFELiNK is more than just a safety product.
In daily life, it gives people peace of mind.
In an emergency, it connects people quickly and helps turn that connection into real action.
We use different technologies to make this possible. ・The second reason is  Web3.

This is an AI-powered emergency assistance service that starts with a single press of an SOS button.
In an emergency, you may not have time to take out your phone, unlock it, open an app, and call the police. 
With this service, you can simply press an SOS button on your phone or a keychain device to start the emergency response.

At the same time, your family and friends can follow what is happening through Discord, including your live location, the AI-police call, and live audio from the scene. If necessary, they can also contact the police directly.
The service uses World to verify that each account belongs to a real person, helping reduce false reports and misuse.

projects.title: vet402
projects.description: An agent pays an x402 seller only while vet402's draft ENSIP-29 proof in its ENSv2 name holds.
projects.project_description:
I made vet402 put its proof inside the seller's own ENSv2 name. It buys from an x402 seller, checks what arrives, and signs the seller's offer record following the draft ENSIP-29. (x402 lets an API ask for payment with HTTP 402, so an agent can pay per call in USDC.)
An agent checks that proof before it signs. With vet402's API cut off, it still paid (Base Sepolia, 2026-09-26 00:29 UTC). After the seller changed one character of its offer (Sepolia block 11782719), the same command refused before signing.
vet402 and @vet402/sdk existed before the event. Here I built the ENSv2 path, a Base Sepolia profile, the /tokyo page and the demo. vet402 buys from x402 sellers to check their promises. In the 30 days to 2026-09-16 15:00 UTC, 426 of 1,008 comparable purchases did not match the declaration (42.3%). In the 30 days to 2026-09-26 it was 533 of 1,349 (39.5%). So the proof goes in the seller's name, where an agent can check it before it signs. The whole promise is one text record, x402-offer, with price, payTo and URL in one line. The attestation sits next to it. On 2026-09-25 vet402 did this for four sellers, and all four verify as VALID 7/7.
This depends on ENSv2: Enhanced Access Control works per record key. The seller's server key can rewrite its price, but writing the proof next to it with that key reverts with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles (eth_call, Sepolia block 11782193). The attestation cannot be forged anyway. The split adds least privilege. A leaked server key can change the price, and every agent then refuses, but it cannot restore an older offer together with the attestation that signed it.
The paying agent is also a name, agent-1.vet402.eth, with its own resolver and policy (trust atst.vet402.eth, at most 0.05 USDC). Then I tried to break it. With vet402 unreachable, the agent asked, got no answer, and paid, because the proof met its declared floor. One character changed: refused at step 7 (ens_attestation_signer_mismatch) without asking vet402. Try it on seller-d.eth at https://vet402.com/tokyo. Borrowing another seller's attested record with linkToRecord was refused, because the name is inside the proof (block 11782107). With the agent's name deleted, the parent's wildcard answered instead, and the agent refused (agent_policy_missing) because the answer was not from its own resolver (block 11782115). Intercepta screens first, every time. seller-e.eth's payee is sanctioned, so nothing is paid. seller-a.eth's payee has no history on Base, so the attester holds it for a person (block 11783180), and the agent pays it only at 0.01 USDC or less with a VALID proof. Two limits remain. vet402 is the only attester, so docs/tokyo-2026/attester-spec.md states what a second one must do. Every ENS name here is mine. The independent evidence is a real Base mainnet seller vet402 bought from unasked (2026-09-17 12:09 UTC, block 51428826), logged under obs.vet402.eth (block 11782167). This stays in payOrRefuse: it takes a name only through this check, and its payee field still rejects names. The agent does not need my server to answer. It checks my signature in the seller's name, and its own file decides which attesters it trusts. Requirements, every tx and a one-line check: https://github.com/kzmttkc/vet402/blob/tokyo-2026-submission/docs/tokyo-2026/for-reviewers.md
AI use: AI_USAGE.md (Tokyo), docs/tokyo-2026/human-log.md, docs/tokyo-2026/PROMPTS/.
Disclosure sent to ETHGlobal 2026-09-18 UTC, confirmed complete 2026-09-24.
projects.how_its_made: vet402 is a TypeScript monorepo: a Next.js app on Vercel (the API and the /tokyo page) and @vet402/sdk, the client an agent calls before it pays. The SDK has no runtime dependencies, and viem is an optional peer. The ENSv2 code loads through a dynamic import only when a caller passes a name, so callers that pay by address never load it. The ENSIP-29 codec carries its own small DAG-CBOR encoder. Its test compares the bytes with a fixture made once with @ipld/dag-cbor 9.2.6, which is not a dependency. Every ENS read pins one Sepolia block, the lower of two heads, on two independent public RPCs, and a value counts only when both return the same bytes. The current manager comes from UniversalHelper.findExactOwner. The offer and the attestation come through UniversalResolver.resolve, so linked records apply. That is why borrowing another name's record fails. The trust list is the consumer's own file of (name, address) pairs, with each address pinned locally and checked against the name's current addr. The public verifier accepts attestations up to 7 days old, while the demo agent's on-chain policy accepts 24 hours. That policy is read only from the agent's own resolver. An answer that reaches it through the parent's wildcard is refused. The attester buys before it signs, in six steps (docs/tokyo-2026/attester-spec.md). Payments are x402 on Base Sepolia in test USDC. In the demo agent, Intercepta screening runs before anything else. In the attester, it runs before anything is bought. No answer within 3 seconds, a 404 or an unexpected body means no payment. If vet402's API is unreachable (no connection, or HTTP 5xx), the caller's declared floor decides, and the decision line records vet402_unreachable and allowed_by_caller_policy. A 4xx, a degraded answer or a BLOCK that does arrive is never waived. The demo installs the SDK from a packed tarball with viem fixed at 2.55.1, so a clean clone runs on its own. Its --live commands check the chainId, simulate the transaction alone, check the signer's balance, and send nothing until a person types y. The first failing tests went in at b9d6fe74 (2026-09-25 12:08 UTC), before the code that makes them pass.
