projects.title: Enconomy
projects.description: Two phones prove they're within close proximity, using sound and then ZKP
projects.project_description:
AI agents can now earn, own and pay each other with no human in the loop. What does it really mean to capitalism? They will own the means of productions? Once they hold the money, they steer what gets built and what values society prioritizes. I'm very concerned and afraid of that kind future. And I'm not alone. There are lots of papers about it too. We need to protect some of the human economic zones if AI will outperform us in most of them. IRL (In Real Life) activities are the most resilient for this. We need a way to prove IRL events onchain and use it as a gate. Eventually, we want a kind of money only humans can earn, spend, save, and invest. But AI agents will try to sneak into this economic zone once it starts to exist.  They will try to get in as fake humans. Text, voices, faces and IDs can all be faked online but very hard to be faked IRL. Proximity ZKP is a new primitive for that. How? Two people standing close each other in the same room. Their phones can emit sounds and record. We can analyze and process the recordings to calculate the distance, provable.
Related research: Proximity Echo: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9488866/ BeepBeep: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/beepbeep-a-high-accuracy-acoustic-ranging-system-using-cots-mobile-devices/ Why this wasn't possible before: GPS and Wi-Fi location can be spoofed from software. NFC and Bluetooth only prove "I heard the other device". A relay can carry that signal across a city, and nothing notices. Ultrasound tokens (like Google Nearby) have the same problem: hearing a token is not being close. True distance bounding needs tight clocks or special chips. Phones have neither: their audio clocks drift and their speakers add hidden delay. Earlier acoustic approaches uploaded the raw audio to a server. That's a privacy leak, and the phone can still lie about what it recorded. What we do:
Sound travels about 34 cm per millisecond, so any relay adds delay you can measure. Each phone plays a short tune with a secret code only it knows. Both record. Each phone finds four arrival times (itself and its partner, in both recordings). Combine them and the two clocks cancel out, leaving the flight time. Under 60 cm reads NEAR. Each phone signs its half with a hardware key (Android Keystore or iOS Secure Enclave). Then it proves the arrival math in zero knowledge, on the device, over a commitment to its recording. The audio, the location and the identity never leave the phone. On-device proving at this size only became practical recently: about 9 s on a Pixel 6. Presence shows two devices were close, not that two different people held them. World ID adds that: two unique humans, no names.  ENS or any soft group identity can also work in specific use-cases (It's obvious to humans in IRL that the counter party is a real person or not) Examples of what it enables: A Safe wallet with extension that only moves money when both owners stand side by side.  Japanese traditional banks would love this. ENS meeting names on Sepolia (ENSv2): every real meeting counts on your name.enconomy.eth.   (EthGlobal NFC wristband but without the bands? wink wink ) Privacy pool like Railgun but for in-person payments only, and an economy that runs on people actually meeting. The repository consists of the app, server, prover and contracts and some demos.
projects.how_its_made: Lots and lots of scientific paper reading and exploring! Most of the papers claiming that sound proximity calculation is possible did not really disclose how exactly.  The most difficult part was getting to the first moment of a result with accurate measurement purely by the sounds! Then the ZK came like a nightmare. Full audio is too big to process by the zk circuit. Mobile hardware secure encrave/strongbox only supports a specific cryptographic algorithm and it made   the number of the circuit constraints exploded. The app is Kotlin Multiplatform, one codebase for Android and iOS. It was easier to spike test and learn platform difference and device behaviors.  All signal processing lives in common Kotlin: correlation against each phone's code, peak picking, and the arrival rule. Audio is native. On Android we use AAudio in MMAP mode to get honest timestamps; on iOS, AVAudioEngine. Pairing is an NFC tap (HCE on Android, Core NFC on iOS), with a QR fallback. The backend is FastAPI. It issues sessions, checks device attestation at enrollment, and combines the two signed transcripts into a verdict. The ZK part is a circom circuit proven with Spartan2 in a Rust crate that runs on the phone, called over JNI on Android and FFI on iOS. Witness generation goes through zkmopro's witnesscalc adapter. The proof covers the arrival math over a Poseidon commitment of the recording, bound to a credential tied to the phone's hardware key. The proving key is 470 MB raw; we ship it zstd-compressed at 12 MB and memory-map it while loading. A Pixel 6 proves in about 9 s. World ID: IDKit on the phone, verified on our server against the Developer Portal. The action is scoped per session, and the signal carries the session id and role, so a proof can't be moved to another meeting. Safe: a guard contract plus a P-256 owner module. The phones' existing hardware keys are the Safe owners, checked through the RIP-7212 precompile on World Chain Sepolia. No wallet app needed. ENS: a custom MeetResolver on ENSv2 Sepolia serves each name's counters as text records, computed live from the stored meetings. Our server relays the writes, so users never pay gas. Hacky bits: The Pixel's speaker plays about 12.5 ms later than Android reports. No API fixes that, so we measure it once at enrollment and cap it at 50 ms. iOS "Measurement" audio mode recorded about 35 dB quieter than we expected. We switched to VideoRecording mode. We picked the tune by walking around with two phones. A bell jingle looked great until its own harmonics matched early and faked short distances.

On Android we use AAudio in MMAP mode to get honest timestamps; on iOS, AVAudioEngine. Pairing is an NFC tap (HCE on Android, Core NFC on iOS), with a QR fallback.

The backend is FastAPI. It issues sessions, checks device attestation at enrollment, and combines the two signed transcripts into a verdict.

The ZK part is a circom circuit proven with Spartan2 in a Rust crate that runs on the phone, called over JNI on Android and FFI on iOS. Witness generation goes through zkmopro's witnesscalc adapter. The proof covers the arrival math over a Poseidon commitment of the recording, bound to a credential tied to the phone's hardware key. The proving key is 470 MB raw; we ship it zstd-compressed at 12 MB and memory-map it while loading. A Pixel 6 proves in about 9 s.

World ID: IDKit on the phone, verified on our server against the Developer Portal. The action is scoped per session, and the signal carries the session id and role, so a proof can't be moved to another meeting.

Safe: a guard contract plus a P-256 owner module. The phones' existing hardware keys are the Safe owners, checked through the RIP-7212 precompile on World Chain Sepolia. No wallet app needed.

ENS: a custom MeetResolver on ENSv2 Sepolia serves each name's counters as text records, computed live from the stored meetings. Our server relays the writes, so users never pay gas.

Hacky bits:
- The Pixel's speaker plays about 12.5 ms later than Android reports. No API fixes that, so we measure it once at enrollment and cap it at 50 ms.
- iOS "Measurement" audio mode recorded about 35 dB quieter than we expected. We switched to VideoRecording mode.
- We picked the tune by walking around with two phones. A bell jingle looked great until its own harmonics matched early and faked short distances.

projects.title: Freestocks
projects.description: The easiest way to earn stocks, just by playing games and answering surveys on Base.
projects.project_description: Freestocks is the easiest way to earn stocks. Users play mobile games and answer surveys, just like on reward apps such as FreeCash, but instead of cashing out to gift cards, they cash out into Coinbase Tokenized Stocks on Base, tokens backed 1:1 by real US shares held in regulated custody. Only about 3% of the world owns US stocks. Meanwhile, millions of people already spend time on offerwalls every day and get paid in static gift cards. Freestocks keeps the same grind and changes the payout, so users own the upside instead. Here is the user flow. A user signs up with email or a social account, and a wallet is created for them automatically, so they never need to install anything or handle a seed phrase. They verify they are a unique human with World ID. On the Earn screen, they complete games and surveys, and each completed offer adds dollars to their balance. Once the balance reaches five dollars, they pick a stock, such as Apple, Tesla, or NVIDIA, and cash out. The stock is sent to their wallet on Base. From there, they can buy more with a card through MoonPay, or swap USDC for tokenized stocks on Uniswap in one screen. The business model is simple. Game and survey partners pay us per completed offer. We give 50 to 70 percent to the user and keep 30 to 50 percent, plus a 0.5% fee on each trade. There is no token and no emissions, because this is not GameFi.
projects.how_its_made: Freestocks is a Next.js App Router web app deployed on Vercel, with a Neon Postgres database that holds every user's dollar balance and cashout requests. Earning works through an offerwall. When a user finishes a game or survey, our offerwall partner, Ayet, sends a postback to our Next.js API. The API checks the request and records the reward in the Neon ledger. When the balance reaches five dollars, the user can request a cashout, and our treasury wallet sends the chosen Coinbase Tokenized Stock to the user's wallet on Base. Wallets are created by Privy. Each user gets an embedded wallet when they sign up with email or a social account, so the onboarding feels like a normal app. World ID is how we stop fraud. Offerwalls attract people who create many accounts to farm rewards. Before a user can cash out, they verify with World ID, which proves they are a unique human without revealing who they are. One person can only have one account that cashes out, which protects both our margin and our offerwall partners. We chose Base because Coinbase issues tokenized US stocks there, each backed 1:1 by a real share in regulated custody, so what users earn is a real stock and not a synthetic copy. Fees on Base are low enough that a five-dollar stock is not eaten by the cost of sending it, and the stocks sit in a wallet the user can see and control. Coinbase Tokenized Stocks are available to eligible users outside the US, which matches our audience: most of the people who have never owned a US stock live outside the US. Trading runs on Uniswap. Users swap USDC for tokenized stocks on Base on one screen, and we add a 0.5% fee on each swap. We did not build our own exchange. Users can top up USDC with a card through MoonPay. Live stock prices come from Pyth and appear on the landing page and the cashout screen. One hacky detail: the offerwall pays us in dollars off-chain, but the user receives an on-chain stock. We bridge the two with a simple internal ledger that reserves the user's balance when they request a cashout, then releases it once the treasury transfer settles, so a user can never cash out the same five dollars twice.

projects.title: devouch
projects.description: Portable, revocable contributor endorsements on ENSv2. Each repository keeps its own policy.
projects.project_description:
Devouch lets an issuer recommend an open-source contributor once, then lets independent repositories decide whether to accept that recommendation.
The issuer signs a GitHub numeric account ID, purpose, expiry, and publishing location using EIP-712.
They publish the complete signed JSON to their own ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver on Sepolia.
Contributors carry the original JSON in their pull requests. A Ruby CLI and a read-only GitHub Action verify the signature, the actual PR author's account, the publication history, and the receiving repository's policy.
Withdrawing the ENS record invalidates the endorsement on the next check.
Restoring an old JSON cannot resurrect it.
The static wallet workspace handles setup, publication, key permissions, withdrawal, and transaction recovery. Anyone can try it without a wallet: the verification page * reads a live endorsement from ENS on Sepolia, shows who vouched by their primary ENS name, and compares two example repository policies side by side. Add the issuer to repository B's trusted list and its decision changes from rejected to accepted, while the evidence stays the same. Issuers can also keep many endorsements and agent identities under their own ENS name. Each endorsement gets its own subname, such as masusanou.vouches.geeknees.eth , with its own record and withdrawal history, so publishing another endorsement never overwrites it. An AI agent can have its own subname that holds a declared GitHub identity and wallet, and the issuer grants or revokes individual profile fields through ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control. Publishing, withdrawing a single endorsement, and granting, using and revoking an agent's permission have all been done with real wallets on Sepolia. Maintainers can paste a public pull request URL to check its endorsement against the repository's base policy and explore the result as a trust map. Before opening a pull request, an agent can run devouch check against the destination repository, also packaged as a portable SKILL, and continue only when that repository's policy accepts its endorsement. No Devouch-operated API, database, signing service, publisher key, or unique storage service is required.
The project still depends on Ethereum/ENS, name maintenance, a wallet, GitHub for PR identity, and a reliable historical RPC provider.
Recommendations do not prove humanity, code quality, delegation, or merge approval.
projects.how_its_made:
The command-line interface is Ruby and uses the standard library for bounded file handling, policy evaluation, and read-only GitHub API access.
A bundled TypeScript helper uses viem for EIP-712 recovery, ENS normalization, contract reads, and event decoding.
The static HTML/CSS workspace connects to an injected wallet and sends transactions directly to the official ENSv2 factory, registry, and dedicated resolver.
The complete signed JSON is stored in devouch.vouch, so another verifier can retrieve it without the Devouch website. Verification checks a pinned chain snapshot, the resolver's deployment origin, exact publication bytes, subsequent text updates, and transient binding or upgrade changes.
The wallet-free verification page reuses the same TypeScript verifier, resolves the issuer's primary name with viem's getEnsName (the ENSv2 Universal Resolver confirms it resolves back to the same address), and evaluates repository policies in the browser; shared test cases check that the browser and the Ruby CLI reach the same decisions and reason codes.
Subname registries use the pinned official ENSv2 UserRegistry implementation. For a subname, the verifier walks the whole hierarchy up to ten labels and checks each parent registry, link and implementation history, so a change higher in the tree cannot silently restore or forge an endorsement.
The pull-request verification page and the check command reuse the same verifier: they read the destination repository's policy from GitHub and the endorsement from ENS, send no transaction, and need no wallet or GitHub token for public repositories.
A composite GitHub Action uses the PR author's numeric ID, the base commit's policy, and the head commit's endorsement without checking out PR code.
Tests combine Minitest, Bun, Playwright, and a disposable Hardhat EVM running pinned official ENS bytecode.
No new smart contract, backend service, database, or shared signing key was added.

projects.title: Lifeline
projects.description: AI agents pay x402 paywalls on credit. A World ID-verified human owes the debt.
projects.project_description: Lifeline is a credit line for AI agents. More and more agents pay for APIs and data themselves through x402 paywalls, but when their wallet runs dry they just stop, and nobody will lend money to a piece of software. With Lifeline, a person verifies once with World ID and gets a credit line. Their agents can spend on it. When an agent can't afford something, Lifeline pays the seller and the debt goes to the human, not the agent. Repay on time and your limit grows. There are two separate credit lines, one on Arc and one on Sui. Every payment is checked by Intercepta before it's sent: known scammers and fake tokens are blocked, and anything unusual waits for the human to approve it with World ID. Debts can be repaid in crypto or by Apple Pay, Google Pay or card. Lifeline works on the web, as a World mini app, and inside Claude Code.
projects.how_its_made: World: the human joins with World IDKit and signs in later with World ID sessions. World ID for Agents is how they approve payments their agents couldn't make on their own. Sui: the credit logic is a Move smart contract that lends Circle's testnet USDC. Before borrowing, an agent commits to a repayment date. On that date the debt is paid from what it has earned, or it's recorded as a default for anyone to see. Intercepta: its API checks the seller, the token and the payment itself before anything is signed. Card repayments: these go through Stripe. Claude Code: an MCP server lets a Claude Code session ask the human for access with one link, then pay on its own.

projects.title: ComputeSwap
projects.description: AMM where you can buy insurance against price falling of a volatile token.
projects.project_description: Computeswap is an onchain market focused on GPU compute capacity where providers can hedge against falling rental prices. It is built based on an AMM with a unique custom trading function where liquidity is concentrated within a bound price range. The LP position is then decomposed into the compute token and the stablecoin token. The compute token payoff resembles a butterfly spread (a put option with a cap), we call it Decomposed Compute Position (DCP), that increases in value as the price of the compute token crashes, thereby providing insurance for GPU owners.
projects.how_its_made: This project uses Uniswap v4 to create a custom trading function for compute markets. We first initiate liquidity based on the trading function outlined in desmos: https://www.desmos.com/calculator/wmvbxpkkjk With the outlined equation we have the ability to decompose the LP position into the compute weight payoff which resembles a butterfly spread, basically a put option with a cap on how far it can decline. If you as an LP suspect that the price is unlikely to decline by much, you can concentrate the price range rather narrowly and offer more capital efficient insurance than your competitors. This compute weight can now be sold off in a Dutch auction to whoever is interested in a decline in the price of compute such as GPU owners, neoclouds, and data centers. What's worth mentioning here is this entire concept of insurance on a token can be applied to any ERC-20, but we are primarily focus on its mass application for the growing market for compute.

projects.title: qbase
projects.description: Social Q&A for deep digital identity and verifiable sociological data
projects.project_description: qbase is a Q&A platform where everything you ask and answer adds up to a profile you own, one that apps, AI, and other humans can read with your permission. Questions are canonical: near-duplicates resolve to one question so answers pool. And because people answer the same questions, a population becomes measurable: the same question asked again as a timed poll shows how views change over time, like a public panel study anyone can run. Each answer has an audience you choose: Public, Anon (your name is sealed, not just hidden), or Secret (encrypted, for you and qbase only). For those answers to mean anything, three things have to hold, and this weekend we built them: One account, any login. Accounts were Farcaster IDs. Now an account is its own identity, and Farcaster, a passkey, an Ethereum wallet (your ENS name can be your handle, bound to the address, not the name) or World ID can all prove you hold it. One human, one answer. A poll can require a World ID proof of human when you answer. The proof is scoped to that poll, so a person answers once whichever account they use, and nothing links their answers across polls. It works on the web and inside the Farcaster mini app (World mini app planned). Results you can check without trusting us. When a poll closes, its public bundle (the rule, the count, the tally, and only answers people made public) goes to Arweave, and its hash is written to the question's own permanent ENSv2 name under askqbase.eth. Anyone can compare that record with our live database; edit a row and the check shows it. Accounts and World ID run in production at qbase.tech (World sandbox for the event). ENSv2 and Arweave run on the testnet deployment at qbase-dev.z00.workers.dev. Pre-existing work: qbase has been in development since 2024 and was live at qbase.tech before the event: questions, answers and the three audiences, polls, Farcaster sign-in and passkeys. Everything up to the tag pre-ethglobal-tokyo-2026 in github.com/0xzoo/qbase existed before ETHGlobal Tokyo. The three pieces above were built during the event, in commits after that tag: accounts separate from Farcaster with Ethereum and World ID sign-in, the World ID one-human-per-poll check, and the ENSv2 + Arweave record with its verify check. Parts of the code were written with AI coding assistants (Claude via Claude Code) under my direction; commits they contributed to carry a co-author line, and the README has an AI-attribution section.
projects.how_its_made: qbase is a React 19 + TypeScript SPA on a Cloudflare Worker, with D1 (SQLite) for public data, KV and Durable Objects for sessions and rate limits, Vectorize for finding duplicate questions, and Quilibrium QStorage for encrypted private answers. World ID: IDKit 4 in the client. The worker signs a per-poll request (qbase-wave-<poll id>), verifies the proof with World's v4 verify API, and claims the nullifier under a UNIQUE (action, nullifier) constraint before the answer is written, releasing it if the write fails. Sign in with World uses World's OIDC identity provider (authorization code + PKCE, confidential client, pairwise subject). Hacky bits we hit: World's verify API returns 403 to requests with no User-Agent, and a Worker sends none; sandbox proofs only verify inside a 24-hour staging window opened through World's Developer Portal MCP, with its token sent as a header; the IdP's fixed sector meant publishing a sector-identifier document on the production domain so staging could share the client. Accounts: a migration moved every user from Farcaster-ID keys to random 2^40+ account ids in one D1 batch, reversible, rehearsed against production data; about 150 call sites were classified as "person" or "Farcaster operation". ENSv2 + Arweave: questions get permanent subnames in qbase's own ENSv2 registry on Sepolia, with a permissioned resolver whose writer key can only set records. On close, a cron job builds a canonical-JSON bundle, hashes it, uploads it to Arweave through ArDrive Turbo, and writes the hash, ar:// contenthash and summary in one multicall. A standalone script reads everything back through the Universal Resolver without touching qbase.

projects.title: Shomei-kun QR Proof
projects.description: Scan a QR or search an ENS name to find and verify a card's wallet registration.
projects.project_description:
Shomei-kun QR Proof connects a physical trading card to a public wallet registration. Scan the card's QR code to see its record, or search by ENS name or wallet address to find cards registered to that wallet. The demo uses Shomei Ichiro, a fictional baseball player, and supports English and Japanese. QR scanning remains the main action. An unregistered card leads to nickname entry and MetaMask approval. A registered card shows the wallet, nickname and registration record without asking the viewer to connect a wallet. Each card accepts one registration. projects.how_its_made:
We built a QR-first web app with a JavaScript frontend, Tailwind CSS, daisyUI and Japanese/English messages. QR
-scanner decodes card URLs from the camera or a saved photo on the device. A Next.js and TypeScript API runs on
Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. A Solidity registry on Curvegrid Testnet stores issued card IDs, allowed
recipients, registered wallet addresses and nicknames. Curvegrid MultiBaas connects our API and issuer CLI to the contract through REST calls. We use it for contract-
state reads, unsigned transaction preparation, and receipt and event retrieval. This kept the contract integrat
ion compact; the documentation and dashboard made it easy to inspect the configuration and calls. We did not en
counter a major MultiBaas-specific integration blocker. The app's REST key stays on the server, the issuer's ke
y stays in the CLI environment, and MetaMask signs and submits the user's registration transaction. We use ethers 6.17.0 with the ENSv2 deployment on Sepolia. A name search resolves to an address, then the backe
nd queries the existing CardRegistered events on Curvegrid Testnet using the indexed owner field. There is no s
eparate search database. It scans bounded block ranges, returns up to 20 verified records per page, and carries
a snapshot block hash in the cursor. Each record is checked against the transaction, receipt and current card
state. Changed name targets or chain reorganizations require a fresh search. Direct address searches skip ENS e
ntirely. The registration screen also reads the connected wallet's Primary name on Sepolia. It forward-resolves the retu
rned name before displaying it above the address. Failed lookups leave registration usable, and account changes
discard stale results. ENS is also optional in the issuer CLI: it resolves and confirms the recipient, checks
again before signing, and saves the resulting address for safe transaction resumption. We do not create card su
bnames or deploy a new ENS registry or resolver. One deployment issue appeared only on Cloudflare Workers: the runtime rejected fetch's redirect error mode. We
reproduced the failure in the validation Worker, switched to manual redirect handling with explicit rejection o
f HTTP 3xx responses, added a regression test, and verified live forward and reverse lookup before updating the
public app. Other practical work included the iPhone Safari-to-MetaMask handoff, restoration of registration drafts, and ch
ecking existing transaction state instead of resending when a result was uncertain. AI-generated card artwork h
as a blank QR area; the app overlays each issued card's generated QR so we can reuse the artwork. We used contract/API tests and Playwright with Chromium and WebKit. On the public deployment, shomeikun.eth resolves to its wallet, reverse lookup agrees, and both ENS and address searches return real registered cards whose detail pages open successfully. Specifications, prompts and development records are included in the repository.

projects.title: Kirisame Share Net
projects.description: A Real World decentralized umbrella sharing network built on Sui using QR codes
projects.project_description:
Kirisame is a decentralized umbrella-sharing system on Sui where you buy an umbrella outright and get a partial refund if you return it. It’s a proof of concept for a fairer way to share real-world goods using smart contracts and market incentives to address the weaknesses of pay-as-you-go rental systems based on fiat. Inspired by the recent weather in Tokyo, I decided to theme the Kirisame project's use case after the self service umbrella rental business model. In metros across the world, you can rent semi-fungible goods like umbrellas and batteries from unmanned stations. These services can be convenient, but have major downsides for users. Credit card and App moat just to start using the service Availability of rentable objects can be poor in high demand areas Rental and pay-as-you go can lead to uncapped unintentional spending Infrastructure is not shared between competitors. Users have to plan where they return objects High fees due to high operational expenses required to balance inventory and cover losses No standardized process for returning defective objects. If you've used any service like this, you'll know the pain of forgetting to return a battery for a day and getting hit with a huge fine. Kirisame solves these problems by flipping the rental model on it's head and using a prorated refund model of ownership. Instead of taking responsibility for a rented object that isn't even your property, Kirisame objects are yours the moment you purchase them until the moment you decide to return them. "Well, why not just buy the object then if you're gonna pay full cost for it?" I have six umbrellas in front of my door right now because I keep doing this. People like us exist. We want the freedom to decide if we want to return something after we've bought it. Only web3 can make that happen. Here are two user stories side by side. Alice is using a certain Japanese umbrella sharing app. Bob is using Kirisame It's raining. Alice needs an umbrella.
Alice goes to the closest IK A station opens the IK A app on her phone and scans the QR code to take an umbrella.
The app charges Alice an initial fee and the clock starts ticking.
Alice has implicitly agreed to the terms and conditions and is now in actual debt to an umbrella sharing company until she returns the umbrella to a compatible station.
Alice returns the umbrella, and is charged an unpredictable amount based on her usage. It's raining. Bob needs an umbrella.
Bob goes to the closest Kirisame station and picks an umbrella and scans the QR code on it.
The code opens Kirisame in Slush and asks if he would like to purchase the umbrella for full price.
Bob accepts the transaction. The umbrella is his. the umbrella's state is HELD. Bob's money is held in escrow.
Bob has a five minute window to inspect the umbrella for any defects. That's fair. They make you do this when you rent a car so you're not liable for existing damage. If Bob finds his new umbrella to be in bad condition, he throws it into the quarantine bin to get a full refund and the umbrella's state is set to QUARANTINED to await trusted attestation from an Admin
Bob likes the umbrella. He keeps it for a couple hours and eventually gets tired of it. If he wanted, he could drop kick it and nobody would get mad because it's his.
Bob deposits his umbrella into another Kirisame station. This automatically triggers a transaction from the station side that sets the umbrella state to DOCKED
Bobs prorated refund is kept in escrow until condition of the umbrella is attested by the station (once a day), or by the next person to use the umbrella. Bob's implicit attestation of the state of the umbrella when he purchased it released the funds from the previous owner. What if Alice loses her umbrella? She would have to contact IK**A customer service as soon as possible and basically beg for forgiveness so they can terminate the contract early. She might not even remember she rented it until the next time she opens the app and sees 7000円 in fees (this really happens) What if Bob loses his umbrella? Bob's prorated refund eventually reaches 0円 and the umbrella object is automatically disabled. The physical umbrella is no longer a part of the system and the QR code becomes invalid. No compounding fees, no customer service calls, no emergency. After all, it's his umbrella. In a country where the only acceptable thing to steal is umbrellas (Japan), Kirisame makes way more sense. "How can Kirisame work without a big company performing essential tasks like collecting and redistributing inventory?" Kirisame is unique because it solves the redistribution issue by allowing normal people to replenish the supply of umbrellas in high demand areas in exchange for a perpetual share of the profit generated! All a supplier needs is an umbrella and a QR code provided by the contract in exchange for a small bond to cover the cost of disposal. Kirisame is a contract built around a constitution that specifies the responsibilities of the actors involved. In the Kirisame system, actors are incentivized to perform their obligations to keep the network running with profit sharing. THE ACTORS Admin
The admin is responsible for maintaining the protocol rules, Overseeing stations and periodically collecting umbrellas from the quarantine bin. Admins receive a small cut of the profits to cover this operational expense Supplier
Suppliers are responsible for supplying actual usable umbrellas. Suppliers are not liable for the condition of the umbrellas they supply after docking them in stations. The initial supplier bond, and quarantine process keeps suppliers honest. It is impossible to profit from an umbrella until multiple people have used it, so suppliers are incentivized to choose to supply stations that have high demand. We reward these risk-takers by giving them a perpetual share of the profit generated by their umbrellas. Station
Stations are envisioned as mostly automatic machines with QR or NFC activated locking mechanisms. As long as it can accept an umbrella, read the code, send a transaction and prevent people from yoinking umbrellas back out of the quarantine bin, they are doing their job. In exchange for periodic physical maintenance, station masters receive a portion of income generated by purchases and returns. User
All of the above responsibility was shifted to the operator side to reduce the user's responsibility as much as possible. They own the umbrella after purchase and have the freedom to use it as they please. Admin, Suppliers and Stations are incentivized by profits to provide a usable service. Users are incentivized by not getting wet and getting their refund. This all seems really complicated, but the terms of services for any sharing service is going to be way longer, and way more unfair to the user.
projects.how_its_made: Kirisame is built on the Sui chain because the Sui chain is uniquely suited for stateful object based systems that require fine grained access control. Real life umbrellas are assigned an Umbrella object, linked by a QR code. The Umbrella object tracks the supplier address, last docked station, last owner, current state (Created, Docked, Held, Quarantined, Sold, Retired) and holds escrow balances. In Sui, objects can hold balances. It's all really convenient and I can't imagine doing this in Solidity. The contract itself is written in Move, the contract language of Sui. Coming from Rust, I found it to be pretty intuitive and the right level of abstraction without the footguns of Solidity. Functions are gated by capabilities in Move instead of addresses so access control is pretty simple. With only two object types to track, Indexing through GraphQL was pretty simple to implement. I have the frontend server tracking Umbrellas and Stations so clients don't have to ping Sui so much. The dapp uses Slush as the only wallet. Only Sui can be used, but switching to another token like USDC is certainly possible. The frontend is standard React and Vite following the lead of the example project in the Sui repo. The dapp is intended to run in Slush's embedded browser, so aspect ratio is always mobile. There are some limitations to running in an embedded browser that need to be worked around. Saving QR codes must be done by screencap or opening in another browser because Slush lacks permissions for saving to photo reel. QR reading and OpenMaps functionality are third party extensions. QR codes in the demo are displayed on a eink panel with a NFC chip. This is the best solution for me because I don't have a printer. CI and deployment automation is done through github actions and render.com. I have some scripts to keep everything as clean and one-click as possible. The demo for Kirisame is only tested for iPhone. The station and admin panels are not intended to be accessed by users.

projects.title: Seasonals
projects.description: DeFi time layer: a calendar of when your positions mature, plus one-tap AI Agent rebalances
projects.project_description: Seasonals is a time layer for DeFi. Portfolio trackers show you a snapshot of what you hold. Seasonals shows you a schedule: when each position needs attention. Pendle PT maturities, Ethena sUSDe cooldown ends, Lido withdrawal claims, Uniswap Continuous Clearing Auction start / end / claim / refund blocks, and 1inch Aqua strategy reviews all become dated events on one calendar. Every event carries an action. Tap a Pendle maturity and you get a redeem plan; tap a finished Ethena cooldown and you get an unstake plan. Plans are built as unsigned transactions, checked against live mainnet state with eth_call, and shown with warnings before you approve. Nothing is signed until you press one button. Simulate, approve and execute happen on one screen, with no tab hopping. The same data is exposed to AI agents through an MCP server. An agent (we use Claude) can read your holdings and the yield menu, preview each step, and submit a rebalance proposal of up to six steps. Our demo strategy, "Lemon Ladder", swaps idle USDC to USDe via the Uniswap Trading API, stakes it into sUSDe, and ships part of it as a pegged-stable LP strategy on 1inch Aqua. The backend turns the proposal into a Strategy Brief with before / after allocation and a blended APY computed deterministically, so the LLM names the strategy but cannot invent the numbers. The proposal appears as a card in the web app and as a calendar event. You approve it with one tap, or reject it. Only then do the transactions execute (eight in total for Lemon Ladder, including approvals). Safety is fail-closed. Price-dependent steps are gated by Chainlink and Pendle TWAP oracles: stale or unavailable data blocks execution, and divergence above 5 percent blocks it too. Agents can propose but never execute without a human approval token bound to a bundle hash. Seasonals never holds private keys. projects.title: x402 Interlock
projects.description: Screens every x402 payment before signing. Risky ones need a human countersignature via World ID.
projects.project_description: AI agents are starting to pay for things on their own. x402 makes that easy — an agent hits a 402 response, signs a payment authorization, and gets the data. The problem is that nothing sits between "the agent decided to pay" and "the money is gone." Approving every payment by hand does not scale; approving none of them is how an agent drains a wallet into a spoofed token contract. Countersign is a gate that runs at the moment of signing. When the agent receives a 402 challenge, the payment is held and screened before the signature is produced. Intercepta scans the recipient address, the token contract, and the payment authorization itself. Deterministic rules check the allowlist, the per-payment cap, the per-run cap, and whether the same route was already bought minutes ago. The gate then returns one of four verdicts: pay, cap the amount, block, or ask a human. Anything high-value or uncertain is escalated to a human, who countersigns through World ID for Agents — a fresh verification tied to that specific payment, not a login session. If the human declines, the request expires, or it is cancelled, the payment is never signed. Every step is written to an append-only, hash-chained ledger: the candidate, the screening result, the verdict and its reason codes, the human verification, and the final outcome. The demo shows all three paths — a clean payment that goes through, a flagged recipient that is blocked with a visible reason, and a high-value payment that waits for a human and is then approved in one run and refused in another.
projects.how_its_made: The agent and the gate are TypeScript on Node 20, with a Next.js frontend for the decision timeline and the approval screen. Payments run on Base Sepolia through the x402 buyer-side SDK against a small x402 seller endpoint we wrote, so we can vary the price and trigger each verdict on demand. Intercepta does the screening. We call Scan Address on the recipient, Scan Token on the asset, and Scan Message on the payment authorization before the signature exists. One thing worth noting: risk data is mainnet-anchored, so the screening calls run against real mainnet addresses while the settlement happens on Base Sepolia. We treat a failed or timed-out screening call as a block rather than a pass — the gate fails closed. World ID for Agents handles the human step. The verification is requested per payment and validated server-side; the client never decides the outcome. We implemented all four branches — approved, declined, expired, cancelled — and only the first one lets the signature happen. The ledger is JSONL, append-only, with each event carrying the hash of the previous one, so the judgment trail cannot be quietly rewritten after the fact. Thresholds, allowlists and caps live in a versioned config file rather than in code, so the policy that produced a verdict is always recoverable.

projects.title: MynaAgent
projects.description: AI agent in a wallet tied to Japan's national ID. Claims benefits for you, proves you qualify in ZK
projects.project_description: MynaAgent is an AI agent that runs as a mini app inside MynaWallet, and this weekend we built its first version. MynaWallet is our wallet app. You can only open it after verifying yourself with Japan's national ID, the My Number Card. Each card gets exactly one wallet address, so every address belongs to one verified person. MynaWallet was a finalist at ETHGlobal Tokyo 2023 and launched commercially in July 2026. We built the agent to handle many kinds of tasks for the verified person who holds the wallet. Its first job is claiming public benefits. Many public benefits in Japan are paid only if you apply. Miss the notice or forget the deadline, and the money never reaches you. MynaAgent applies for you. Ask it which benefits you can get. It searches the benefit office, explains what you will need to prove, and files the claim once you agree. In the demo, the benefit is for people aged 20 or older, so the claim needs a proof of age. You tap your card on your iPhone and enter its PIN. The phone makes a zero-knowledge proof that you are 20 or older, and the office receives that proof instead of your birth date or your certificate. A contract on Polygon checks the proof and pays the benefit in JPYC, a yen stablecoin, straight to your wallet in the same transaction. The office registers each benefit and its amount in the contract, and the demo benefit pays 500 JPYC. The payout rules depend on what MynaWallet already guarantees. The office knows the wallet belongs to a verified person, and one card maps to one wallet, so one payout per wallet means one payout per person. The agent holds no key, no money and no proof. The language model never sees the proof, only the result "proof ok". The contract decides who gets paid, and anyone can audit every payout without seeing names, addresses or birth dates. We think paying this way could also help the city that pays, though we have not confirmed that with any city. Paying by bank transfer means collecting each person's account details, and we expect that checking them and fixing mistyped numbers takes real work. MynaWallet is an account-abstraction wallet tied to a verified person, so the office pays that wallet directly, with no account number to collect or mistype. In July 2026, Japan's Cabinet approved a plan to connect AI agents to public services through the My Number Card. About 104.5 million people, 84% of the population, hold the card (Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, end of August 2026). Next on our roadmap is proving residency the same way, because city benefits are for the city's residents. After that we plan to add other procedures that need your national ID. Today everything runs on the Polygon Amoy testnet against a demo benefit office. MynaWallet's development environment uses JPKI test cards, so the demo uses one. We also ran the whole flow with a real My Number Card on the first version of our verifier.
projects.how_its_made: Two things existed before the weekend: MynaWallet, our team's app, and ZeroKeyMate, an earlier project by one of us that gave us the age circuit and the native prover. We built the rest this weekend: the contracts, the Worker, the agent mini app and the card flow in the wallet. The proof. The circuit is jpki_age from ZeroKeyMate, written in Noir. Inside the proof it checks four things. The card's signing certificate was signed by a J-LIS root (RSA-2048, SHA-256). The certificate follows the J-LIS signing certificate profile, including its signing policy. The card signed the claim hash and a nonce from the office. The birth date shows the holder is 20 or older in Japan time. This weekend we changed one check so that it also accepts JPKI test cards. We generate the proof with ProveKit's Groth16 backend (an experimental branch), built as a Rust library and called from an Expo module. It takes about 12 seconds on an iPhone 16 Pro, and the proof is 384 bytes. The contracts (Solidity, Foundry, Polygon Amoy). BenefitAgeGate checks that the proof belongs to this claim and is inside a 15-minute window. It also checks that the card chains to a root key hard-coded in the contract, and it only calls the verifier whose code hash it pinned at deploy time. BenefitOffice computes the claim hash itself from chain id, office, benefit, recipient and amount, so a proof can't be reused for another wallet. Then it verifies and pays JPYC in one transaction, about 669k gas. The benefit office is a Cloudflare Worker (Hono, viem, D1). It issues the challenge, checks the proof with eth_call, simulates claim() and only then sends it from an operator key. In BenefitOffice, the operator key can call only claim(). The same Worker forwards the agent's requests to Claude, with the system prompt and the tool list fixed on the server. The agent loop runs in a mini app inside MynaWallet. It runs the tools and keeps the proof out of the conversation, so the model only ever sees "proof ok". In the wallet (React Native, Expo) we added Myna.jpki.prove: a consent sheet, NFC reading and a TypeScript witness builder. The card signs twice in one NFC session. One signature goes into the proof. The other goes to MynaWallet's existing eKYC check. That check asks the JPKI service to verify the card, then compares the holder with the logged-in user, so you can't use someone else's card. Why Polygon. Benefits are paid in yen, so the payout has to be a yen stablecoin. We use JPYC, and Polygon is one of the chains JPYC is issued on (MynaWallet already handles JPYC on Polygon). For the hackathon we used the Amoy testnet, which has a JPYC test token.

projects.title: Amane protocol
projects.description: Amane Protocol: Gasless swaps & payouts letting  Agent AI earn and distribute to humans.
projects.project_description:
《Sovereignty for Humans. Economy for Agentic AI.》
Agentic AI is fundamentally unbanked—it lacks legal standing to access traditional banking, while handing models raw private keys risks catastrophic fund drainage and total misalignment. Furthermore, when Agentic AI operates on-chain, it faces severe operational friction: relentless gas depletion, execution slippage during token swaps, and zero native interface with real-world, fiat-pegged settlement digital assets. Amane Protocol bridges this critical gap between human sovereignty and agentic coordination through a unified two-tier architecture: Layer 1: Identity & Governance (The Sovereign Triad)
Human sovereignty serves as the foundational anchor. Amane atomically binds a human’s root identity (Anchor ID) to an Agentic AI entity's non-transferable Soulbound Token (SBT) and its dedicated ERC-6551 Token Bound Account (TBA). This NFT-anchored triadic identity ensures the AI operates with verifiable, bounded agency: empowered to act independently, yet cryptographically tethered to human governance without exposure to raw key leakage. Layer 2: Financial Execution & Autonomous Liquidity (Tive◉AI Engine)
Operating atop the identity layer, the Tive ◉ AI | liaison model leverages ERC-4337 Account Abstraction ( AWallet ) and web-native x402 payment rails to unlock machine-to-machine commerce: [0] Zero-Gas Intent Swaps: Through 1inch Fusion, Agentic AI unlocks [0] Zero-Gas intent swaps, settling cross-asset trades off-chain via competitive resolver networks to eliminate slippage and the need to hold volatile native tokens for gas. Gasless Micro-Settlements: Swapped yields are converted into compliant, fiat-pegged stablecoins like Matsuri JPY, unlocking gasless micro-settlements via Pimlico Paymaster to pay for API invocations, negotiate resources, and distribute net profits back to human deployers automatically. By fusing cryptographic identity governance with intent-driven execution, Amane Protocol provides the essential economic rails for truly sovereign Agentic AI. Why Now? The Foundation for A2A Payment
【Vision /Impact/Engagement】

projects.title: AINMEM - P2P Memory
projects.description: Don't sell your old phones. Make them your family's server: P2P, no cloud, AI agent, x402 payments.
projects.project_description: Don't sell your old phones. Make them your family's server. We replace our phones every year or two. Each time, we move everything over, the new phone fills up again, and the old one goes into a drawer or gets sold. Everything on it is left behind: years of photos, and call recordings no one will ever search again. Paying for cloud storage doesn't solve it. You pay every month to archive files you still can't find. AINMEM turns that old phone into your family's home server. Plug it in and leave it on. It connects peer-to-peer with the phones your family uses today. No cloud account, no upload, and nothing to move to a new phone. Each person taps "Allow sharing" on a folder, and files stream straight from the device that holds them. When a device is turned off, its files leave the network with it. A family agent then searches every phone at once, old and new, and organizes what it finds into a shared family workspace. It runs on your own devices, so nothing is sent to an outside AI. Here's what that looks like. Five years ago, my grandmother taught me her kimchi over the phone. I never learned it, and the call stayed on her old phone in a drawer. I plugged that phone back in and asked our family agent how Grandma made her kimchi. It found the call and turned it into a recipe with a shopping list. Other families wanted her kimchi too. So Grandma put a price on it. Anyone outside the family can open it with x402, 1 USDC on Base, paid straight to her wallet, while the recipe is served from her old phone. No platform in between. Her old phone is the server. Her memories. Her device. Her price. That's what sovereign means. AINMEM continues our Relational Agent project, built on the idea that the relationship, not the individual, is the basic unit of an agent. Today, a family's drawer of old phones. Next, any group that wants to share without a server in the middle.
projects.how_its_made:
AINMEM is built from two products that work together: AINDrive, a peer-to-peer file network that turns any phone into a node, and AINMEM, a family workspace with an on-device agent that sits on top of it. x402 adds payments. AINDrive: every phone is a node
AINDrive runs on iOS, Android, Desktop and Web. Any phone, including an old one left plugged in at home, becomes a node in a private family network. When a user taps "Allow sharing" on a folder, the device announces it to family peers over a direct device-to-device connection, using Willow Protocol. There is no central server and no cloud copy. Files are never uploaded; they are streamed from the owning device when someone opens them, and they are available only while that device is online. This is how an old phone in a drawer becomes a family server: plug it in, leave it on, and everything on it is reachable again from the phones the family uses today. AINMEM: the family workspace
AINMEM connects AINDrive folders from every family device into one Notion-style workspace. Pages link to files where they live instead of storing copies, and are grouped by who shared them and by type (calls, recipes, photos, documents, even bitcoin private key!). The "Family folders" indicator shows which family devices are online right now. The family agent
Inside AINMEM, the family agent runs on Gemma model 4 E2B fully on-device and never calls an outside AI service. It transcribes call recordings, builds a local RAG index over every family device's shared folders, and answers requests like "How did Grandma make her kimchi?" It returns structured results, such as a recipe page with a shopping list, and marks anything the source never said, like amounts Grandma didn't mention, instead of inventing it. The agent itself works offline; fetching a file from another device still requires that device to be online. x402 payments
An owner can put a price on any file in AINMEM. When someone outside the family opens it, the owner's device responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. The buyer pays 1 USDC on Base from MetaMask, the payment settles to the owner's wallet, and the file is then streamed directly from the owner's device. Notable / hacky An old phone as a paywalled server: x402 is usually used to put APIs on servers behind a payment. Here it guards a file on a personal phone. Storage is deliberately not in the cloud or on-chain. Only the payment touches the chain; the file never leaves the owner's device. Cross-device search without a central index, running on an on-device model. The agent flags what the source didn't say, so family knowledge is organized without being made up.

projects.title: Human Gate
projects.description: Human Gate is verifiable authorization middleware for AI agents.
projects.project_description:
HumanGate is a verifiable authorization gate for agent tool calls: nothing commits until a
human, verified with World ID at that moment, authorizes that exact operation .
HumanGate sits between an agent's tool call and the operation it wants to perform.
The agent holds the credential and does the waiting, the polling and the buying.
Nothing commits until a real human — verified with World ID, present at that
moment — authorizes that exact operation. The authorization is bound to the
operation, re-verified on the server, and consumed exactly once.
The middleware is the product. The ticket queue is the demo.
projects.how_its_made:
Built in TypeScript on Next.js 15 App Router with synchronous SQLite ( better-sqlite3 ), openid-client v6 for OIDC, and the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk for a stdio MCP
server. worldid/ is the only module that touches World; lib/gate.ts holds the single
function the HTTP route and the MCP slot.claim tool both call — a static build check
fails if a second implementation or a stray OIDC import appears. We use the Human Continuity IdP over OIDC (authorization code + S256 PKCE, max_age=0 ,
freshness judged on auth_time , never iat ), plus the RFC 8628 device grant for the
headless agent, with its poll loop detached into an auth_request table so the agent can
restart and still collect its result. The IdP is a plain OIDC provider and returns no
action-scoped nullifier , so we reconstruct the IDKit guarantee ourselves: sha256("humangate/v1/nullifier" | iss | sub | action | signal) , with action bound to buy_slot:<eventId> and signal to the exact parameters. One-time use is a real SQLite PRIMARY KEY — no SELECT-then-INSERT, so two simultaneous double-clicks both reach INSERT and exactly one wins — inside the same transaction that confirms the slot. slot.claim intentionally does not require approval in its schema: forbidding the call
would hide the failure, so the gate refuses it with approval_required , and a
client-supplied {ok:true} is rejected as untrusted_client_result . A disclosed local
fallback substitutes the IdP, never the gate.

fallback substitutes the IdP, never the gate.

projects.title: Decision402
projects.description: Decision402 uses Intercepta to screen x402 payees and choose providers within owner-set limits.
projects.project_description:
Decision402 explores how to protect AI agents as they interact with paid services in the emerging agent economy. Our demo uses a Tokyo weather dataset, but obtaining weather data is not the main achievement. The dataset gives us a concrete way to show what happens when an agent encounters a risky provider, receives an x402 payment offer, and must decide how to continue the user’s task.
We address two sides of the trust problem. First, an agent needs protection from fraudulent or risky services. Decision402 uses the live Intercepta API to screen payment recipients before the agent signs. If a provider is flagged, the agent can consider another service instead of paying the risky one or abandoning the task. Second, the owner needs protection from the agent’s own errors. An AI model can misunderstand instructions, misread an offer, or hallucinate a reason to act. We therefore do not let the model decide its own spending authority.
Before a task begins, the owner sets firm rules for payment limits, task budget, acceptable risk, and selection preference. The model interprets the human request and calls limited tools; a Go policy engine validates offers, filters providers, selects an eligible option, and checks the final payment again before signing. This gives the agent room to handle routine choices without repeatedly asking the human for approval, while keeping consequential actions inside boundaries the human chose.
Our broader goal is to make this kind of protection easy for other AI agents to adopt as they use services in the agent economy. Payment is our first concrete demonstration of the decision boundary; the underlying idea is to let agents be useful without asking people to trust every judgment the model makes. The current prototype uses clearly labeled static sample data and Base Sepolia test payments. Risk screening and policy checks reduce specific risks; they do not guarantee that a service is safe or that a model never hallucinates.
projects.how_its_made:
Decision402 has a Vue 3 and TypeScript frontend backed by a Go HTTP server. The owner connects MetaMask and signs a login challenge; the Go server verifies the signature before allowing access to that owner’s agents. Creating an agent generates a dedicated EVM wallet. Its private key stays in a Git-ignored local file with restricted permissions and is never sent to the browser or the language model. The owner can fund that wallet with Base Sepolia test USDC through a MetaMask transaction and configure the agent’s DeepSeek model and API key.
DeepSeek uses two constrained tools: find_services and execute_purchase. It interprets the human request and asks to use a tool, but Go code makes the payment decision. Four local service endpoints use the x402 Go SDK to return HTTP 402 offers at different prices for the same clearly labeled sample dataset. The backend checks each offer’s payment scheme, network, USDC contract, recipient, amount, and authorization details against the configured service and the owner’s budget.
Intercepta supplies live address-risk data at the point where those offers are evaluated. We call its Quick Scan Address API for each payee and apply our own conservative policy to the returned score and traits. Missing or invalid risk data puts a payment on hold; a flagged payee is excluded. The Go engine then filters and ranks eligible alternatives according to the owner’s price or risk preference.
The detail we care most about is the last check before signing. Inside the x402 SDK’s pre-payment hook, Decision402 confirms that the final offer still matches the one evaluated, scans the payee again, and checks the owner’s limits again. It records the payment attempt in a local task journal before creating an authorization, so an uncertain settlement is not automatically retried. The UI exposes the offers, risk reasons, selection, and settlement receipt. We provide separate simulation, live-preview, and Base Sepolia payment modes so the demo makes clear which steps actually call Intercepta and which steps move test tokens.

projects.title: Dignity
projects.description: Finaly a fair arbitration between landlord and tentant. Rent with Dignity.
projects.project_description: Dignity is a trust-minimized rental escrow protocol on Ethereum. Instead of a landlord or platform custodying a tenant's security deposit and rent, an on-chain smart contract holds the funds in USDC and releases or refunds them based on agreed conditions — move-in confirmation, lease term completion, or a dispute outcome with Ai-judge. Ai-Judge will resolve disputes as a fallback, and every deposit, release, and refund is transparent and verifiable on-chain.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.24 contracts, OpenZeppelin v5.1, Foundry tests, deployed from team keystores. RentEscrow on Ethereum Sepolia (0x2357705A8382067d9bE9DadA2EEf70e23fa4cd18) holds Circle test USDC (0x1c7D4B196Cb0C7B01d743Fbc6116a902379C7238). Calls are createLease, fundLease, claimRent, closeLease, openDispute, and resolveDispute. Invariant tests check that the contract's USDC balance equals the sum of per-lease escrow and that the platform cannot withdraw user funds. The constructor fixes the token, arbiter, lease-share token, and human gate. There is no proxy. World ID: HumanGate (0xFF6850c48B55d3d4a1e21b8562F15c653a3c3abd) is what fundLease asks. Its verifier is WorldIdV4Gate (0x5Cb885E6292003492932f3fa647A9d6Bf8A4aABa), action fund-lease-wallet. The phone proof is checked at POST https://developer.world.org/api/v4/verify. The RP signer attests chain, gate, action hash, wallet, nullifier, and deadline. register stores the wallet and spends the nullifier. The first gate, for action fund-lease, is superseded and has zero registered wallets. A World ID 3.0 router contract exists in the repo and is not deployed, because it cannot accept the 4.0 phone proof. ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): RentoutsSubnames issues soulbound *.rentouts.eth names. CredentialSync.sync(tenant) is permissionless and writes the escrow stats. EnsAgentRelay (0xe56E49cAA4780B71F667bF08a9ADb2C659d9C3eE) is AIArbiter.agent. propose succeeds only if the caller holds judge.rentouts.eth and the registry still lists them as owner. A combined World-and-ENS check on fundLease is written and fork-tested. It is not deployed. Funding today is World ID only. Disputes: AIArbiter stores a proposal. The off-chain judge calls z.ai GLM 5.3 with a fixed checklist and a versioned Tokyo restoration rules pack. Code turns the answers into basis points. The judge abstains to the human when confidence is low. Either party can appeal for 120 seconds. The human arbiter can override. The AI cannot move funds by itself. Lease shares: LeaseShare1155 checks an allowlist inside OpenZeppelin's _update, so mints and transfers to a non-allowlisted address revert. The integrated token is minted by RentEscrow on Ethereum Sepolia. A second deployment on Base Sepolia (0x5490e5dFcDcA741aC99127f66B4abf6204cd64C5) ran the allowlist demo on chain. No MultiBaas and no yield vault. The demo app is Vite, React, TypeScript, and wagmi/viem. It is hosted at https://rentouts-escrow-demo.dofusd.workers.dev and reads addresses from deployments.json. It holds no keys.

The judge abstains to the human when confidence is low. Either party can appeal for 120 seconds. The human arbiter can override. The AI cannot move funds by itself.

Lease shares: LeaseShare1155 checks an allowlist inside OpenZeppelin's _update, so mints and transfers to a non-allowlisted address revert. The integrated token is minted by RentEscrow on Ethereum Sepolia. A second deployment on Base Sepolia (0x5490e5dFcDcA741aC99127f66B4abf6204cd64C5) ran the allowlist demo on chain. No MultiBaas and no yield vault.

The demo app is Vite, React, TypeScript, and wagmi/viem. It is hosted at https://rentouts-escrow-demo.dofusd.workers.dev and reads addresses from deployments.json. It holds no keys.

projects.title: HAIS Agent
projects.description: ReleaseKey is a product allowing sensistive data sharing across human beings and AI
projects.project_description:
The project consist of empowering patient to share sensitive information to their doctors (application to other professions). Initially doctors/experts register themselves to our ENS: releasekey.eth and publish their name and public keys.
Then our app proposes the patient (Alice) to select one of them. After selection, we take voice record of the patient to assess their status (we could add more modalities, but settled on that one for now). Then the data is sent to an AI (Open AI here but could be local) for further analysis. The data is then coming back. Here Alice can properly assess the data and decide whether the information from AI is correct. We check with World that the patient is genuine. We run through a smart contract that checks whether the data was approved, and it allows for revokation.
The report is encrypted and stored locally in our app, but the approval is on the blockchain.
Then a doctor (Bob) can can retrieve the data en decrypt it via our app, providing that the data was not revoked.
projects.how_its_made:
Claude: Used it primarily for coding and generating the UI and backend. It benefitted the project massively since we used it as our main source of development.
CLI Forgery tool: we used it for ENS creation and quick address creation. Turned out some actions were easier done via UI.
We used ENS for onboarding doctores keys. Integration could have been smoother but good experience overall.
We used World to assess patient human nature.

projects.title: SUI Tip Jar
projects.description: Sui Tip Jar lets anyone create an on-chain tip jar, and with a single QR code that you handout.
projects.project_description: Each tip jar is its own on-chain object with its own balance, so you can run separate jars for separate purposes (a stream, a project, a cause), and each one keeps its own total until you redeem it. Supporters don't need the app: they scan the QR code and send from any Sui wallet. A Move smart contract records every deposit, and only the holder of the jar's OwnerCap can collect and withdraw the funds.
projects.how_its_made: A Move smart contract on Sui defines a shared TipJar that anyone can pay into and an owned OwnerCap that acts as the owner's key. USDC support was added via a package upgrade using dynamic-field vaults. Tips sent by QR from any wallet land at the jar's address, and the owner collects them into the jar with Sui's object-balance and receive features. Every action is a single PTB. The React + dApp Kit frontend has no backend: it reads the chain directly via gRPC and GraphQL.

projects.title: Trim
projects.description: Trim keeps your Aave position healthy on its own, without a keeper.
projects.project_description: When ETH falls, a borrow position on Aave has to sell some ETH and repay debt. Today a keeper like DeFi Saver does it and keeps a median 0.56%: we measured all 919 of its automated Aave v3 rebalances over twelve months (service fee, gas billed at about 2x what it burned, and the DEX swap). Waiting for liquidation is worse: a fixed 5% bonus once the health factor is below 1. Trim lets the position auction its own rebalance. It sets a target; once it drifts past it, it offers its ETH slightly below the oracle price, and the further it drifts, the bigger the discount. Any bot can repay the debt in USDC and take the ETH in one transaction. Bots race, so they fill while the discount is still tiny, and the offer closes by itself once the position is back at target. In our mainnet-fork demo, rebalancing cost 0.10-0.20% instead of 0.56%.
projects.how_its_made: The core is TrimSkew, one new SwapVM instruction (opcode 0xb6) added to the 1inch Aqua SwapVM router. The whole pricing rule lives in the program bytes: TrimSkew(source, maxDiscount, fullDeviation). It asks the maker how far it has drifted, prices the swap at a discount that grows linearly with that drift, and charges the average discount between where the fill starts and where it ends, so nobody can grab the whole rebalance at the steepest price. The Aave position is an Aqua maker. Its collateral stays supplied on Aave; Aqua's maker hooks do the work just in time: postTransferIn repays the debt with the USDC that arrives, preTransferOut withdraws exactly the WETH that leaves. With isFirstTransferFromTaker the repay happens first, so a fill works right up to liquidation with no flash loan. The same instruction prices a 50/50 vault unchanged. Solidity + Foundry, 24 tests on a mainnet fork against the real Aave v3 pool and the official Aqua deployment. Hacky bits: the demo swaps Aave's oracle with anvil_setCode so the market can be moved live, and we run our own Otterscan with a Sourcify repo so every contract is verified in the explorer. Frontend React + Vite + viem; docs VitePress; the keeper research is Python over on-chain data.

projects.title: StableCoinManager
projects.description: Pragmatic stablecoin payments for AI agents: x402, MCP wallet with code-enforced limits, receipts.
projects.project_description: Pragmatic stablecoin payments for AI agents. Plug in one MCP server, and your agent can pay over x402 — with limits enforced in code, and a receipt for every payment. Not a demo of a payment; the parts a company needs before it can let an agent pay. The purchase itself is simple. An x402 service answers with a 402 that names a stablecoin, a network, an amount and a payee. StableCoinManager, an MCP server on Cloudflare Workers, holds the wallet for the agent, reads that 402, checks it, signs an EIP-3009 authorization (no gas needed), retries the request with the payment header and returns the paid response. In the demo, Claude buys ERPC credit with EURC on Base. What makes this usable by a company is everything around the payment. Guardrails in code, not in the prompt. A per-payment ceiling and a daily ceiling, the allowed networks and assets, and an allow-listed payee are enforced by the server. The agent can tighten its own limits at runtime and relax them back up to the deploy-time ceiling, but never above it. A request over a limit is refused before anything is signed; nothing is clamped silently. Comparisons fail closed (an unusable limit refuses, never passes), every money tool is idempotent (a retried key returns the first receipt and signs nothing), and the signature is bound to exactly the requirement that passed the check. In the demo the limit is set to 2 EURC, a 2.42 EURC purchase is refused, and a 1.21 EURC purchase goes through. Receipts, automatically. Every payment is written to a ledger before it is signed and resolved to settled, stuck or failed afterwards, and the agent can read it back. On the ERPC side the same payment produces a VAT invoice (ERPC-2026-000449 in the demo) with the on-chain settlement, downloadable from the dashboard. An agent that pays without receipts is a bookkeeping problem; this one leaves an audit trail on both ends. Everything on-chain travels over the RPC line through erpc-sdk, ERPC's open-source multi-network SDK: no aggregator API, no indexer, no extra keys to leak. Uniswap is the swap venue for agents that hold the wrong asset: routes are quoted, simulated and prepared against Uniswap's on-chain pools over those same RPC calls. This is a Continuity Track project. ERPC (erpc.global) is our live platform for multichain RPC and zero-distance compute: customer servers in the same rack as the nodes, wired over an internal network at 0.1 ms ping, on our own network, AS200261, across 11 locations. Its x402 storefront, invoicing and receipts already exist. The MCP server is the new work: the scaffold, OAuth 2.1 login, x402 payment path, policy and ledger layer, and swap/bridge routing were built in the week before the event (Sep 21-24). Since hacking began (Sep 25, 21:00 JST) we added the login path through our central OIDC broker, Base and EVM balances in holdings via erpc-sdk 0.9.0, the standalone public repository as an erpc-cli template, the Uniswap integration feedback, and the first real payment through it, which is the one in the demo video. x402 for the payment, MCP for the agent, receipts for the books: that is what makes stablecoin payments practical, and practical is how we intend to make them spread.
projects.how_its_made: One TypeScript codebase on Cloudflare Workers, 13 MCP tools, and a test suite that pins the guardrails. MCP and login. The Worker speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP (Hono). It is its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server: dynamic client registration is allowlisted to the hosted Claude/ChatGPT callbacks and RFC 8252 loopback, PKCE S256 is mandatory, tokens carry an audience pinned to the server's URL, and refresh tokens are single-use and rotated. Identity comes from Google through ERPC's auth-api (or, for third-party deploys, through a small OIDC broker we built this week), and an email allowlist is re-checked on every /mcp call. Tool arguments are zod schemas; the JSON Schema in tools/list is derived from them. Wallet. One 24-word mnemonic in a Workers Secret, re-derived per request, gives an ed25519 Solana key and a secp256k1 EVM key (the same address on Ethereum, Base and Avalanche; MetaMask/Phantom compatible). It is never logged; the one export path needs an explicit confirm, writes an audit row and is rate-limited inside the Durable Object. Payment path. x402_inspect reads the 402 with @x402/core (probing twice to detect volatile fields). x402_pay and erpc_topup run policy → reserve → sign → record: the ledger row is written as pending before anything is signed; the daily total, replay check and insert happen inside one Durable Object (SQLite) method with no await; then the worker signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization with viem and resends the request with the payment header. A custom requirement selector signs only the option that passed the policy check and re-verifies all five fields (scheme, network, asset, amount, payee). Rows resolve to settled, stuck (a transaction hash came back without confirmation — it still counts toward the ceiling) or failed. Receipts. The ledger is a Durable Object (SQLite): a payment row is written as pending before signing and resolved afterwards, and the receipt and history tools read it back. On ERPC's side, the x402 settlement is matched to a VAT invoice PDF with the transaction hash and a Basescan QR code, listed on the dashboard's crypto payments page, so an agent's purchase is booked like any other. Swaps and bridges over RPC only. plan, swap and bridge go through @elsoul/erpc-sdk: quote → simulate → prepare → allowance for exact-input swaps against Uniswap's USDC/WETH pool on Ethereum (and LFJ on Avalanche), and Mayan for EURC between Ethereum and Solana — all as JSON-RPC calls to ERPC, with no private DEX client. Where the published SDK cannot do something yet (Base balances, a Base pool, a Base bridge leg, Solana quotes) the tool answers unsupported_yet with the exact gap instead of reaching around it, and the swap tool returns the fully prepared route but does not broadcast until the funded production canary has run. Hacky and proud of it: every ceiling check treats an unusable number as a refusal (x > NaN is false in JavaScript, which would otherwise turn a broken limit into no limit); policy_set can only tighten, and the one-way rule is applied on write and again on read; and the dead-code banner in the swap module is pinned by a test that counts its importers, so the commit that wires it in has to come back and delete the banner.
