projects.title: SubEtha Router
projects.description: Payment method shouldn't decide which APIs AI agents can use. The Router opens all of them.
projects.project_description:
THE PROBLEM
AI agents are starting to pay for APIs per call, using HTTP 402: the server answers "payment required" and says exactly what it wants, the agent pays, and the data comes back. No API key, no signup. The trouble is how you pay. Protocols like x402 and MPP (Machine Payments Protocol) are multiplying the options, from stablecoins through Bitcoin Lightning, with Block, led by Jack Dorsey, contributing Lightning payments to x402. Each provider picks a protocol, a chain and a currency, and it only accepts that combination. I will call one such combination a "rail". More choice does not mean the API you need accepts what you hold. The first mismatch is the protocol itself: you are set up to pay with x402, but the API only speaks MPP, so there is no way to hand over the money at all. Even when the protocol matches, the chain can still divide you. You might hold USDC on Base while the API wants USDC on Solana. Same protocol, same currency, different chain, and the endpoint is still closed. Not because of the data, but because of the rail. WHY I BUILT THIS
I ran into this while building SubEtha, another way for agents to pay, combining zERC-20 private transfers with x402. Building a new way to pay is only half the problem. A payment method is only as useful as the set of APIs that accept it. So I built SubEtha Router for this hackathon. It is not limited to SubEtha's private payments. If you pay with x402 or MPP, APIs that were closed to you become usable, without changing how you pay. HOW IT WORKS
The Router makes two separate payments for one request. You pay the Router on the rail you already hold. The Router then pays the provider, from its own funds, on the rail that provider demands. Both directions settle on testnet today: pay in MPP and reach an x402-only provider, or pay in x402 and reach an MPP-only one. This is not a swap or a bridge. Nothing is converted and nothing crosses a chain. The two payments are independent, each funded in advance on its own chain, which is why the Router keeps a balance on both sides instead of passing your money through. USING IT
The Router is already deployed and running. It is an MCP server, the standard Claude and other AI clients use to connect to tools, so there is nothing to install and nothing to run locally: you point your own AI at the hosted endpoint with one command and ask in plain language, "fetch the ETH price". The agent gets a quote, shows you the amount, and waits. The Router never holds your key. You sign each payment on your own machine and it receives only the signature. Nothing moves until you approve. That approval is tied to one specific quote, so an offer that changes afterwards is rejected rather than paid, and a durable log stops a repeated or concurrent request from paying twice. SCOPE, AND WHERE IT GROWS
Payments are on testnet today, and the Router covers the payment methods and routes it supports rather than every method or every API. That set is meant to grow, and growth compounds: each rail added is reachable from every rail already there, so the value of holding any one of them rises with the count. TRY IT YOURSELF
All of it is running right now. I host two sample providers, one accepting x402 and one accepting MPP, and the Router's MCP endpoint sits in front of them, all on public testnets. Bring Claude Code or any MCP-capable AI agent, connect in one command, and make a real payment yourself.
projects.how_its_made: Architecture. TypeScript on Node 22, ports and adapters. The core knows exactly two ports — inbound (take a payment) and outbound (make one) — and every protocol lives behind an adapter. x402 (@x402/core, @x402/evm, @x402/fetch) has both; MPP (mppx) has both. That is the entire reason both directions work: the core never learned a second protocol, it got a second pair of adapters. A third rail means writing adapters, not touching purchase logic. The asymmetry that shaped everything. x402 is signature-based — the payer signs an EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization, a facilitator submits it and pays gas, and the payer spends nothing until settlement. MPP is broadcast-based — the payer sends the transfer and pays the fee, so the money is gone the moment the credential exists, before the Router is asked to buy anything, with no refund on later failure. The same word "sign" means prepare on one rail and spend on the other. So the quote response carries a fundsMoveOnCredential boolean and the MPP path returns different guidance: get human approval before signing, not before purchase. Structured, because prose in a tool description gets skimmed. Safety. Approval binds to one quoteId; a purchase without it, with an expired one, or against an offer that changed after approval is rejected rather than paid at new terms. At-most-once is enforced by a durable journal holding an OS-level exclusive lock (flock(2), LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB via fs-ext), not an in-process mutex — a second Router process fails to start instead of racing the first. Repeats and concurrent requests re-send neither leg; an unconfirmable outcome stays unconfirmed rather than being blindly retried, because blind retry is how you pay twice. The outbound signer refuses typed data that doesn't match the approved quote, so a bug in the calling path can't redirect a payment — tested without spending anything. The key that isn't there. The hosted Router runs in Docker on EC2 behind Caddy (own TLS cert; fs-ext is compiled in a build stage so only the artifact ships). The container gets exactly one secret: the outbound key, which spends the operator's own funds. It never receives an inbound key — callers sign locally and send only the signature, and the source reads no private key from the environment for the inbound leg at all. A hosted Router cannot spend a caller's money even if it wanted to. MCP is served over Streamable HTTP (same wiring also available over stdio); statelessness cost us one relaxation — quote and purchase arrive as separate sessionless requests, so the typed client's "only execute quotes I issued" check became opt-in. That check is client-side convenience; the Router still rejects a wrong quoteId, an expired approval, an unissued nonce, an offer disagreeing with its config, and a repeated purchase. Providers. Both sample providers are ours: Hono with @x402/hono and mppx, on Cloudflare Workers — app.fetch is already the Workers entry point, so the same code runs under Node with no rewrite. CORS is allowed for unpaid reads only, from an allowlist, never on a request carrying a payment credential: a browser can read the 402 offer, it cannot be talked into paying. What bit us. Cloudflare's shared egress IPs are rate-limited by the public Tempo RPC, so the deployed MPP provider returned 500 while the transfer settled on chain — proven by contrast (25/25 from a residential IP, failures from Workers), fixed with an authenticated endpoint. The public x402 facilitator collides with its own pending transactions under rapid calls: 2 failures in 20 with no gap, 0 in 15 with three seconds between. Tempo fee variance is extreme — four identical 10000-unit payments cost 505, 945, 2283 and 23370 in fees, so we stopped quoting a range and now say it's unpredictable. And the one worth admitting: npm run sign was written for x402 and silently produced a wrong-chain signature for MPP, so the MPP route couldn't be bought through our own documented steps. It survived because x402 worked and nobody had run the other rail through the published instructions. Three separate places had the same bug for the same reason.
projects.project_description_markdown:
THE PROBLEM
AI agents are starting to pay for APIs per call, using HTTP 402: the server answers "payment required" and says exactly what it wants, the agent pays, and the data comes back. No API key, no signup.

The trouble is how you pay. Protocols like x402 and MPP (Machine Payments Protocol) are multiplying the options, from stablecoins through Bitcoin Lightning, with Block, led by Jack Dorsey, contributing Lightning payments to x402. Each provider picks a protocol, a chain and a currency, and it only accepts that combination. I will call one such combination a "rail".

More choice does not mean the API you need accepts what you hold. The first mismatch is the protocol itself: you are set up to pay with x402, but the API only speaks MPP, so there is no way to hand over the money at all. Even when the protocol matches, the chain can still divide you. You might hold USDC on Base while the API wants USDC on Solana. Same protocol, same currency, different chain, and the endpoint is still closed. Not because of the data, but because of the rail.

WHY I BUILT THIS
I ran into this while building SubEtha, another way for agents to pay, combining zERC-20 private transfers with x402. Building a new way to pay is only half the problem. A payment method is only as useful as the set of APIs that accept it. So I built SubEtha Router for this hackathon. It is not limited to SubEtha's private payments. If you pay with x402 or MPP, APIs that were closed to you become usable, without changing how you pay.

HOW IT WORKS
The Router makes two separate payments for one request. You pay the Router on the rail you already hold. The Router then pays the provider, from its own funds, on the rail that provider demands. Both directions settle on testnet today: pay in MPP and reach an x402-only provider, or pay in x402 and reach an MPP-only one.

This is not a swap or a bridge. Nothing is converted and nothing crosses a chain. The two payments are independent, each funded in advance on its own chain, which is why the Router keeps a balance on both sides instead of passing your money through.

USING IT
The Router is already deployed and running. It is an MCP server, the standard Claude and other AI clients use to connect to tools, so there is nothing to install and nothing to run locally: you point your own AI at the hosted endpoint with one command and ask in plain language, "fetch the ETH price". The agent gets a quote, shows you the amount, and waits.

The Router never holds your key. You sign each payment on your own machine and it receives only the signature. Nothing moves until you approve. That approval is tied to one specific quote, so an offer that changes afterwards is rejected rather than paid, and a durable log stops a repeated or concurrent request from paying twice.

SCOPE, AND WHERE IT GROWS
Payments are on testnet today, and the Router covers the payment methods and routes it supports rather than every method or every API. That set is meant to grow, and growth compounds: each rail added is reachable from every rail already there, so the value of holding any one of them rises with the count.

TRY IT YOURSELF
All of it is running right now. I host two sample providers, one accepting x402 and one accepting MPP, and the Router's MCP endpoint sits in front of them, all on public testnets. Bring Claude Code or any MCP-capable AI agent, connect in one command, and make a real payment yourself.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Architecture. TypeScript on Node 22, ports and adapters. The core knows exactly two ports — inbound (take a payment) and outbound (make one) — and every protocol lives behind an adapter. x402 (@x402/core, @x402/evm, @x402/fetch) has both; MPP (mppx) has both. That is the entire reason both directions work: the core never learned a second protocol, it got a second pair of adapters. A third rail means writing adapters, not touching purchase logic.

The asymmetry that shaped everything. x402 is signature-based — the payer signs an EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization, a facilitator submits it and pays gas, and the payer spends nothing until settlement. MPP is broadcast-based — the payer sends the transfer and pays the fee, so the money is gone the moment the credential exists, before the Router is asked to buy anything, with no refund on later failure. The same word "sign" means prepare on one rail and spend on the other. So the quote response carries a fundsMoveOnCredential boolean and the MPP path returns different guidance: get human approval before signing, not before purchase. Structured, because prose in a tool description gets skimmed.

Safety. Approval binds to one quoteId; a purchase without it, with an expired one, or against an offer that changed after approval is rejected rather than paid at new terms. At-most-once is enforced by a durable journal holding an OS-level exclusive lock (flock(2), LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB via fs-ext), not an in-process mutex — a second Router process fails to start instead of racing the first. Repeats and concurrent requests re-send neither leg; an unconfirmable outcome stays unconfirmed rather than being blindly retried, because blind retry is how you pay twice. The outbound signer refuses typed data that doesn't match the approved quote, so a bug in the calling path can't redirect a payment — tested without spending anything.

The key that isn't there. The hosted Router runs in Docker on EC2 behind Caddy (own TLS cert; fs-ext is compiled in a build stage so only the artifact ships). The container gets exactly one secret: the outbound key, which spends the operator's own funds. It never receives an inbound key — callers sign locally and send only the signature, and the source reads no private key from the environment for the inbound leg at all. A hosted Router cannot spend a caller's money even if it wanted to. MCP is served over Streamable HTTP (same wiring also available over stdio); statelessness cost us one relaxation — quote and purchase arrive as separate sessionless requests, so the typed client's "only execute quotes I issued" check became opt-in. That check is client-side convenience; the Router still rejects a wrong quoteId, an expired approval, an unissued nonce, an offer disagreeing with its config, and a repeated purchase.

Providers. Both sample providers are ours: Hono with @x402/hono and mppx, on Cloudflare Workers — app.fetch is already the Workers entry point, so the same code runs under Node with no rewrite. CORS is allowed for unpaid reads only, from an allowlist, never on a request carrying a payment credential: a browser can read the 402 offer, it cannot be talked into paying.

What bit us. Cloudflare's shared egress IPs are rate-limited by the public Tempo RPC, so the deployed MPP provider returned 500 while the transfer settled on chain — proven by contrast (25/25 from a residential IP, failures from Workers), fixed with an authenticated endpoint. The public x402 facilitator collides with its own pending transactions under rapid calls: 2 failures in 20 with no gap, 0 in 15 with three seconds between. Tempo fee variance is extreme — four identical 10000-unit payments cost 505, 945, 2283 and 23370 in fees, so we stopped quoting a range and now say it's unpredictable. And the one worth admitting: npm run sign was written for x402 and silently produced a wrong-chain signature for MPP, so the MPP route couldn't be bought through our own documented steps. It survived because x402 worked and nobody had run the other rail through the published instructions. Three separate places had the same bug for the same reason.

projects.project_description:
Reckn is an escrow for agent-to-agent payments where the arbiter is deterministic
re-execution. A buyer funds a deal with a floor; an agent does the work; the fee is released
only if replaying that work reproduces the agreed outcome. THERE IS NO KEY THAT CAN DECIDE
OTHERWISE — the escrow has no owner, resolver, admin, pause or upgrade, settleWithProof is
permissionless, and a build-time check enforces that rather than promising it. ERC-8004 reached Ethereum mainnet in January 2026 and gives agents identity and reputation. A
second address can submit feedback without establishing that any work happened. We build the
narrower condition here: a record's write right comes from a settlement. A completed job becomes a record under the agent's ENSv2 subname, and the right to write it
is an Enhanced Access Control role that the settlement creates and then destroys. The agent
cannot write it. Its client can, once, for that one record. Attempting otherwise reverts with
EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. The agent owns its name and holds only ROLE_RENEW on it: the
subname is issued without ROLE_SET_RESOLVER, so it cannot repoint its own name away from the
resolver that refuses it. See the residue paragraph below for the one thing that still
overrides that. Then the record is spent. A Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook reads it on chain, inside the swap,
synchronously and with no CCIP-Read, and refuses a swap from an agent with no settled record.
DELIVER, EARN A RECORD, AND THE RECORD IS THE PASS. WHY A POOL, AND WHY v4. A record that only says this agent did the work is a badge, and nobody
has to look at it. In front of a pool it is a key: it decides whether you can trade. That is the
difference between reputation and access. And the check runs INSIDE the swap, so it cannot be
skipped and cannot be delegated -- read the record off-chain and then route the trade, and the
party enforcing it is whoever operates the router, which is a party you have to trust in the one
place we removed one. v4 is the first version where the pool itself carries that rule. ALL OF THIS IS ON SEPOLIA, NOT ON A FORK. The hook is at
0x68116b8086283E51227c61FD791b6Da1A4230080, its address mined so that its low bits are exactly
the beforeSwap flag, on the real PoolManager with liquidity provided. Three transactions, the
same sender and the same pool and the same swap, and the only thing that changes between them
is whether the record exists: refused, then executed with 1.000000000000000000 in and
0.987158034397061298 out, then refused again once the record was cleared. Both refusals were
re-simulated at their own blocks, so we can say WHO refused and WHY rather than that something
failed: the PoolManager's ERC-7751 wrapper carries our hook as the target and our own
NoSettledRecord as the reason. The proving pipeline ran here too. A fresh Groth16 proof of the re-execution was generated on
2026-09-26 in 416.56 seconds over 15,972,262 constraints, and forty minutes later it settled a
deal on chain and paid an agent 250 USDC. Every other settlement in this repository was decided
by a proof committed before the event, which is disclosed; this one was not. The job that is proven runs on v3 SwapRouter02, which is the execution we have measured
through the zk guest. The pass is spent on v4. Earning and spending are different acts and
deliberately use different venues. WHAT IS NOT CLOSED, SAID BEFORE YOU FIND IT. The settlement grants the right to write the
record, not its contents: a buyer can write "reproduced" under a job whose proof said "failed".
The contents are checkable by anyone against the escrow and the proof; they are not enforced.
The hook cannot identify the swapper, because beforeSwap's sender is whoever unlocked the
PoolManager rather than the trader, so a second agent could trade behind the first one's
record. WE ASKED UNISWAP AND THEY ANSWERED: keep an allowlist of routers and call msgSender()
on them. We are declining it, because an allowlist is a party you have to trust and this project
exists to take that party out of a payment decision -- our own build check fails on the owner it
would need. An ENSv2 setter role is scoped to the key alone and never to a name, which we
measured; we pin the adapter to one name and put that name inside the record key, so a write
onto a foreign name is unattributable rather than impossible. WE ASKED ENS TOO, AND THE ANSWER
IS BETTER THAN OURS: partition names across resolver instances, because the resolver instance is
the trust boundary. This deployment is already that in its smallest form, one resolver serving
one name. And this is a testnet. THE RESIDUE, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. The account that is the agent also deployed the
registry and the resolver, and root roles override every per-key role above. While it holds
them, that account CAN write its own record and CAN repoint its own name — we measured both
rather than assume either. Root is renounced before this is submitted, and renouncing is
irreversible, which is why it is the last thing done and not the first. Do not take our word
for whether it happened: the demo page runs those three calls in your browser every time it
loads, and says which of them still succeed. Nothing above is a screenshot. The demo page reads Sepolia in your browser as it loads, and it
reports the residue that is still open by asking the chain rather than by telling you. Every
transaction is in a record generated from the chain, and a script checks in both directions

transaction the record holds is linked somewhere. PRE-EXISTING WORK IS DISCLOSED IN FULL BELOW. In short: this repository began on 2026-07-26;

projects.how_its_made: THE VERDICT. An SP1 zkVM guest runs real revm in-guest over a prestate MPT-verified against the block state_root — account proofs plus storage proofs — so the guest cannot be fed a state that never existed. Measured against Ethereum mainnet on 2026-09-08: a real SwapRouter02.exactInputSingle, witness of 7 accounts / 12 storage slots / 141 MPT nodes, 13,006,200 cycles, Groth16 end-to-end in 497.40 s on a laptop. That measurement predates the event and is disclosed as pre-existing. The pipeline also ran DURING the event: a fresh proof on 2026-09-26 in 416.56 s over 15,972,262 constraints, which then settled a deal on Sepolia and paid an agent 250 USDC forty minutes later. A Groth16 verifier checks the proof on chain and settleWithProof moves the money. The deal is bound to one execution — the token checked, the storage slot read (which is whose balance) and the calldata are all inside the binding, so a real proof of a different swap reverts with BindingMismatch() and nothing moves. DERIVING THE VERDICT WITHOUT BEING TOLD IT. The escrow's Deal has no outcome field, and the outcome exists only in an event, which contracts cannot read — and settlement is permissionless, so a third party may settle first. The record contract therefore re-verifies the proof itself through the verifier the funder named (pinned by codehash), and takes the outcome from verifyVerdict, never from its caller. It also refuses anything outside fundedAt + REFUND_AFTER, because a timeout refund writes the same terminal state as a real settlement and would otherwise be recordable as one. THE ENS SIDE. Each agent is a subname under a parent PermissionedRegistry we deploy, and its job records live on a Permissioned Resolver, which is itself an access-control surface. grantSetterRoles takes the setter's CALLDATA rather than a name, and decodeSetter returns the resource to revoke. We measured what that resource is derived from: the key alone. The same key under agent.reckn.eth and under victim.reckn.eth is one identical resource, so a setter role is never scoped to a single name. We handle it rather than claim otherwise -- the adapter's name is fixed at construction instead of taken from the caller, and the name is written inside the record key, so bytes placed on a foreign name sit under a key that names whose record it is and the canonical lookup for that name does not find them. The write onto a foreign name is not prevented; it is made unattributable. Records resolve through UniversalResolverV2, not by calling our resolver directly. THE UNISWAP SIDE. A beforeSwap-only hook, its address CREATE2-mined so uint160(hook) & ALL_HOOK_MASK == BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG, reads the record inside beforeSwap — synchronously, no CCIP-Read — and reverts NoSettledRecord. The PoolManager wraps that in ERC-7751 WrappedError, so our tests assert the wrapped target and reason, not the outer selector. beforeAddLiquidity is deliberately unflagged: THE GATE IS ON TRADING, NOT ON PROVIDING LIQUIDITY. HACKY AND WORTH MENTIONING. Before writing any of it we spent a day measuring against forked Sepolia, and the design was wrong twice. The deployed ENSv2 beta's ABI is not the main branch's (initialize and setText both differ); grantSetterRoles rejects a name with UnsupportedResolverProfile because its first argument is calldata; the resolver is UUPS, so an EIP-1167 clone dies inside onlyProxy with 210 gas and no revert data; and a name is an ERC-1155, so a contract owner without a receiver hook cannot register one. All of it is in FEEDBACK.md and spikes/tokyo-2026/FINDINGS.md.

DELIVER, EARN A RECORD, AND THE RECORD IS THE PASS.

WHY A POOL, AND WHY v4. A record that only says this agent did the work is a badge, and nobody
has to look at it. In front of a pool it is a key: it decides whether you can trade. That is the
difference between reputation and access. And the check runs INSIDE the swap, so it cannot be
skipped and cannot be delegated -- read the record off-chain and then route the trade, and the
party enforcing it is whoever operates the router, which is a party you have to trust in the one
place we removed one. v4 is the first version where the pool itself carries that rule.

ALL OF THIS IS ON SEPOLIA, NOT ON A FORK. The hook is at
0x68116b8086283E51227c61FD791b6Da1A4230080, its address mined so that its low bits are exactly
the beforeSwap flag, on the real PoolManager with liquidity provided. Three transactions, the
same sender and the same pool and the same swap, and the only thing that changes between them
is whether the record exists: refused, then executed with 1.000000000000000000 in and
0.987158034397061298 out, then refused again once the record was cleared. Both refusals were
re-simulated at their own blocks, so we can say WHO refused and WHY rather than that something
failed: the PoolManager's ERC-7751 wrapper carries our hook as the target and our own
NoSettledRecord as the reason.

The proving pipeline ran here too. A fresh Groth16 proof of the re-execution was generated on
2026-09-26 in 416.56 seconds over 15,972,262 constraints, and forty minutes later it settled a
deal on chain and paid an agent 250 USDC. Every other settlement in this repository was decided
by a proof committed before the event, which is disclosed; this one was not.

The job that is proven runs on v3 SwapRouter02, which is the execution we have measured
through the zk guest. The pass is spent on v4. Earning and spending are different acts and
deliberately use different venues.

WHAT IS NOT CLOSED, SAID BEFORE YOU FIND IT. The settlement grants the right to write the
record, not its contents: a buyer can write "reproduced" under a job whose proof said "failed".
The contents are checkable by anyone against the escrow and the proof; they are not enforced.
The hook cannot identify the swapper, because beforeSwap's sender is whoever unlocked the
PoolManager rather than the trader, so a second agent could trade behind the first one's
record. WE ASKED UNISWAP AND THEY ANSWERED: keep an allowlist of routers and call msgSender()
on them. We are declining it, because an allowlist is a party you have to trust and this project
exists to take that party out of a payment decision -- our own build check fails on the owner it
would need. An ENSv2 setter role is scoped to the key alone and never to a name, which we
measured; we pin the adapter to one name and put that name inside the record key, so a write
onto a foreign name is unattributable rather than impossible. WE ASKED ENS TOO, AND THE ANSWER
IS BETTER THAN OURS: partition names across resolver instances, because the resolver instance is
the trust boundary. This deployment is already that in its smallest form, one resolver serving
one name. And this is a testnet.

THE RESIDUE, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. The account that is the agent also deployed the
registry and the resolver, and root roles override every per-key role above. While it holds
them, that account CAN write its own record and CAN repoint its own name — we measured both
rather than assume either. Root is renounced before this is submitted, and renouncing is
irreversible, which is why it is the last thing done and not the first. Do not take our word
for whether it happened: the demo page runs those three calls in your browser every time it
loads, and says which of them still succeed.

Nothing above is a screenshot. The demo page reads Sepolia in your browser as it loads, and it
reports the residue that is still open by asking the chain rather than by telling you. Every
transaction is in a record generated from the chain, and a script checks in both directions
that every link in the repository names a transaction the record holds and that every
transaction the record holds is linked somewhere.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
THE VERDICT. An SP1 zkVM guest runs real revm in-guest over a prestate MPT-verified against the block state_root — account proofs plus storage proofs — so the guest cannot be fed a state that never existed. Measured against Ethereum mainnet on 2026-09-08: a real SwapRouter02.exactInputSingle, witness of 7 accounts / 12 storage slots / 141 MPT nodes, 13,006,200 cycles, Groth16 end-to-end in 497.40 s on a laptop. That measurement predates the event and is disclosed as pre-existing. The pipeline also ran DURING the event: a fresh proof on 2026-09-26 in 416.56 s over 15,972,262 constraints, which then settled a deal on Sepolia and paid an agent 250 USDC forty minutes later. A Groth16 verifier checks the proof on chain and settleWithProof moves the money. The deal is bound to one execution — the token checked, the storage slot read (which is whose balance) and the calldata are all inside the binding, so a real proof of a different swap reverts with BindingMismatch() and nothing moves.

DERIVING THE VERDICT WITHOUT BEING TOLD IT. The escrow's Deal has no outcome field, and the outcome exists only in an event, which contracts cannot read — and settlement is permissionless, so a third party may settle first. The record contract therefore re-verifies the proof itself through the verifier the funder named (pinned by codehash), and takes the outcome from verifyVerdict, never from its caller. It also refuses anything outside fundedAt + REFUND_AFTER, because a timeout refund writes the same terminal state as a real settlement and would otherwise be recordable as one.

THE ENS SIDE. Each agent is a subname under a parent PermissionedRegistry we deploy, and its job records live on a Permissioned Resolver, which is itself an access-control surface. grantSetterRoles takes the setter's CALLDATA rather than a name, and decodeSetter returns the resource to revoke. We measured what that resource is derived from: the key alone. The same key under agent.reckn.eth and under victim.reckn.eth is one identical resource, so a setter role is never scoped to a single name. We handle it rather than claim otherwise -- the adapter's name is fixed at construction instead of taken from the caller, and the name is written inside the record key, so bytes placed on a foreign name sit under a key that names whose record it is and the canonical lookup for that name does not find them. The write onto a foreign name is not prevented; it is made unattributable. Records resolve through UniversalResolverV2, not by calling our resolver directly.

THE UNISWAP SIDE. A beforeSwap-only hook, its address CREATE2-mined so uint160(hook) & ALL_HOOK_MASK == BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG, reads the record inside beforeSwap — synchronously, no CCIP-Read — and reverts NoSettledRecord. The PoolManager wraps that in ERC-7751 WrappedError, so our tests assert the wrapped target and reason, not the outer selector. beforeAddLiquidity is deliberately unflagged: THE GATE IS ON TRADING, NOT ON PROVIDING LIQUIDITY.

HACKY AND WORTH MENTIONING. Before writing any of it we spent a day measuring against forked Sepolia, and the design was wrong twice. The deployed ENSv2 beta's ABI is not the main branch's (initialize and setText both differ); grantSetterRoles rejects a name with UnsupportedResolverProfile because its first argument is calldata; the resolver is UUPS, so an EIP-1167 clone dies inside onlyProxy with 210 gas and no revert data; and a name is an ERC-1155, so a contract owner without a receiver hook cannot register one. All of it is in FEEDBACK.md and spikes/tokyo-2026/FINDINGS.md.

projects.how_its_made: The pre-event Itonami Bot economy already had x402 challenge admission, exact payee and asset policy, spending caps, a delegated signer boundary, and a simulated ledger. Event-time additions run in Cloudflare Workers and a Durable Object. Intercepta screens counterparties before signing; missing or risky verdicts hold or block. The World client is not yet registered, so the journey is shown only in controlled tests. The 1inch Aqua/SwapVM integration reads official Base contracts and virtual strategy balances; no Aqua strategy or trade is claimed. Public tests pass 16/16, private Durable Object tests pass 17/17, and the public CI is green. Intercepta live screening remains held until its sandbox key is configured. Codex assisted with code, tests and documentation; the concept and sponsor priorities came from the project owner.

projects.title: Halo
projects.description: Households hedge their own grocery inflation against an index built from receipts they already scan.
projects.project_description: Halo turns the receipts people already scan into a grocery-price index, and lets the households who feel inflation first take the other side of it. The gap is this. Inflation hedges exist — inflation-linked bonds, commodity futures, real estate — and every one of them needs a brokerage account, margin, a minimum size, or expertise. None of them reach someone buying rice. And to pay out when groceries get dearer you need a number: the official CPI is monthly, it lags, and in some countries it is politically exposed. For a corner shop in Lagos there is no online price to scrape at all. We did not start this weekend. We built Halo at ETHGlobal Buenos Aires last year as a mini app inside World App, where it was a top-10 finalist. A year later it is three mini apps — World App, MiniPay on Celo, and LINE on Kaia — with 417,000 users and 1,173,623 receipts. That is a real price, at a real shop, on a real date, from the people who actually paid it. What we built this weekend is the market layer. A household pays ¥1,200 and is paid the difference, up to ¥4,000, if rice rises more than 5% over three months. To them it is not a derivative; it is cover on the rice. Behind it: a matched-model index (same product, same shop, two periods — not a category average, which falls in the month you most need cover because shoppers switch to cheaper brands); an optimistic oracle that commits its rules before it sees the data, publishes the full leaf set under bond, and can be disputed; a Uniswap v4 hook that freezes the pool through the challenge window and prices its fee off the clock; and an ENSv2 name that re-reads that oracle and refuses a signed value one basis point off. The part we are proudest of is what it refuses to do. When the corpus is too thin the gateway will not publish a number — it returns the exact integrity floors it missed. A number that cannot say "I don't know" is not a number anyone should settle money against.
projects.how_its_made: Uniswap v4 — HaloHook, at 0xb8fd9d54093820e43Ca21B223468b78624198Ac4 on Sepolia. The address ends 8Ac4 because the low 14 bits are the permission set it declares; the deploy mines a CREATE2 salt until it lands on one. beforeSwap freezes the pool through the oracle's challenge window — a v4 pool is permissionless, so a hook is the only thing that can stop a race to front-run settlement. The dynamic fee is priced off the clock alone (flat until 7 days out, then linear to 200bp, returned with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG) so there is no input an attacker controls. afterSwap takes a 10bp backstop in the unspecified currency as ERC-6909 claims rather than transfers. beforeAddLiquidity and beforeRemoveLiquidity freeze too — leaving removals open would let whoever saw the data withdraw first. Two live pools on Sepolia, identical but for when they close: feeFor returns 500 and 11,642 pips, and the same 100 tUSD swap returns 99,750,349 against 98,639,473. The pools' own sqrtPriceX96 differ in the same direction. ENSv2, on Sepolia. halo is registered to us on the v2 ETHRegistry with HaloResolver attached, and our own UserRegistry subname registry deployed through VerifiableFactory hangs underneath. jp is minted to us; ng is delegated to a partner holding ROLE_SET_RESOLVER and nothing else — we hold zero roles on it and cannot point it back. findResolver offsets make the tree checkable: rice.jp.halo.eth resolves at offset 5, inheriting from jp rather than from halo at 8. The resolver implements ENSIP-10 and EIP-3668, and for a finalised epoch its callback re-reads HaloIndexOracle and reverts GatewayDisagreesWithOracle rather than trusting its own signature. World ID. The index's integrity model is counted in people — one observation per person per item, floors of 3 people per item and 30 per series — and all of that is worth exactly as much as a person is expensive to create. We were keying a person on their wallet address, which is free. A person is now an orb-level World ID nullifier, so two wallets belonging to one verified human collapse into one. Orb only: device attests a phone, not a person. Coverage is partial, so every epoch publishes verifiedPeople beside people. The stack is Hono on Cloudflare Workers, Postgres through Hyperdrive, a React mini app, and Foundry for the contracts. 119 contract tests, 317 API tests. Two bugs worth naming. The publication bond was computed in the wrong unit — every unit test passed because the stub used matching units, and only an integration test caught that a million dollars at risk asked for two millionths of an ether. And the matched-model index did not filter source = 'vision', so synthetic demo rows could have reached a figure that settles money on chain; the fix is in the committed rulesHash, because what data is admitted is the most load-bearing rule there is.

What we built this weekend is the market layer. A household pays ¥1,200 and is paid the difference, up to ¥4,000, if rice rises more than 5% over three months. To them it is not a derivative; it is cover on the rice.

Behind it: a matched-model index (same product, same shop, two periods — not a category average, which falls in the month you most need cover because shoppers switch to cheaper brands); an optimistic oracle that commits its rules before it sees the data, publishes the full leaf set under bond, and can be disputed; a Uniswap v4 hook that freezes the pool through the challenge window and prices its fee off the clock; and an ENSv2 name that re-reads that oracle and refuses a signed value one basis point off.

The part we are proudest of is what it refuses to do. When the corpus is too thin the gateway will not publish a number — it returns the exact integrity floors it missed. A number that cannot say "I don't know" is not a number anyone should settle money against.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Uniswap v4 — HaloHook, at 0xb8fd9d54093820e43Ca21B223468b78624198Ac4 on Sepolia. The address ends 8Ac4 because the low 14 bits are the permission set it declares; the deploy mines a CREATE2 salt until it lands on one. beforeSwap freezes the pool through the oracle's challenge window — a v4 pool is permissionless, so a hook is the only thing that can stop a race to front-run settlement. The dynamic fee is priced off the clock alone (flat until 7 days out, then linear to 200bp, returned with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG) so there is no input an attacker controls. afterSwap takes a 10bp backstop in the unspecified currency as ERC-6909 claims rather than transfers. beforeAddLiquidity and beforeRemoveLiquidity freeze too — leaving removals open would let whoever saw the data withdraw first.

Two live pools on Sepolia, identical but for when they close: feeFor returns 500 and 11,642 pips, and the same 100 tUSD swap returns 99,750,349 against 98,639,473. The pools' own sqrtPriceX96 differ in the same direction.

ENSv2, on Sepolia. halo is registered to us on the v2 ETHRegistry with HaloResolver attached, and our own UserRegistry subname registry deployed through VerifiableFactory hangs underneath. jp is minted to us; ng is delegated to a partner holding ROLE_SET_RESOLVER and nothing else — we hold zero roles on it and cannot point it back. findResolver offsets make the tree checkable: rice.jp.halo.eth resolves at offset 5, inheriting from jp rather than from halo at 8. The resolver implements ENSIP-10 and EIP-3668, and for a finalised epoch its callback re-reads HaloIndexOracle and reverts GatewayDisagreesWithOracle rather than trusting its own signature.

World ID. The index's integrity model is counted in people — one observation per person per item, floors of 3 people per item and 30 per series — and all of that is worth exactly as much as a person is expensive to create. We were keying a person on their wallet address, which is free. A person is now an orb-level World ID nullifier, so two wallets belonging to one verified human collapse into one. Orb only: device attests a phone, not a person. Coverage is partial, so every epoch publishes verifiedPeople beside people.

The stack is Hono on Cloudflare Workers, Postgres through Hyperdrive, a React mini app, and Foundry for the contracts. 119 contract tests, 317 API tests.

Two bugs worth naming. The publication bond was computed in the wrong unit — every unit test passed because the stub used matching units, and only an integration test caught that a million dollars at risk asked for two millionths of an ether. And the matched-model index did not filter source = 'vision', so synthetic demo rows could have reached a figure that settles money on chain; the fix is in the committed rulesHash, because what data is admitted is the most load-bearing rule there is.

projects.title: MaruMaru
projects.description: Borrower-owned financial passport proving financials qualify for loan without sharing any documents.
projects.project_description: MaruMaru (まるまる / 〇〇) is a borrower-owned financial passport for proving that you qualify financially without repeatedly handing over payslips, bank statements, or raw financial data. A borrower verifies themselves with World ID, proves financial facts such as income, savings and debt-service ratio, and receives an ENSv2 passport such as aiko.marumaru.eth. Instead of exposing the underlying numbers, the passport carries machine-readable qualification marks such as income ✓, savings ✓ and human verified. World ID anchors the passport to a human rather than just a wallet, allowing MaruMaru to enforce one live passport per person and make same-person activity across lenders visible. ENSv2 makes the passport borrower-owned, portable, soulbound by default, expiring, and equipped with revocable lender consent. MaruMaru is designed first for mortgage pre-qualification, where borrowers currently over-share sensitive documents simply to learn whether they qualify. It does not replace final regulated underwriting; it minimizes disclosure before that stage. The long-term direction is to extend the same borrower-controlled consent model to encrypted document release for the lender ultimately chosen by the borrower. This matches the guide’s intended positioning: the ENS name is the passport, the app is merely its control surface, and the product is explicitly a pre-qualification/disclosure-minimization layer rather than a replacement for regulated underwriting.
projects.how_its_made: MaruMaru combines World IDKit v4, Reclaim zkTLS, ENSv2, Solidity, Node.js and ethers into a single borrower-controlled verification flow. World ID is the human layer. The backend verifies the IDKit result against World’s v4 verification API, captures the achieved assurance tier, and derives a one-way humanKey from the World nullifier rather than storing or exposing the raw nullifier. MaruMaru deliberately matches proof strength to the action: Selfie Check or Passport can be used for lower-stakes shopping/pre-qualification, while Orb Proof of Human is required when uniqueness becomes load-bearing for underwriting. The World credential therefore changes application behaviour rather than acting as a login decoration. Reclaim is the financial-proof layer. Financial values are verified and reduced to policy results such as pass or fail, so the borrower does not need to disclose the underlying figure to every lender. We also bind the World verification and financial proof to the same MaruMaru issuance session, preventing unrelated or replayed proofs from simply being combined into a new credential. In the reproducible offline demo, the banking step uses a real authenticated 401→200 session, a real Ed25519-signed attestation and real cryptographic tamper rejection; the bank and attestor are simulated, and Reclaim’s TLS-session binding is explicitly disclosed as the property the offline stand-in does not reproduce. ENSv2 is the passport layer, not just a name attached to a database row. MaruMaruRegistrar.sol creates borrower subnames under our ENSv2 registry and writes scoped maru.* records for qualification marks. Enhanced Access Control restricts which records the registrar can write. Passports are soulbound by default by withholding transfer authority, carry freshness expiry, and lender grants can be created and revoked. We also withhold resolver-changing authority so a passport owner cannot point the name at a malicious resolver that fabricates passing marks. The contract also contains a stronger permissionless path, mintWithProofs, where the borrower submits their own World and Reclaim proofs and the Solidity contract verifies them, binds the financial claims to the caller, derives the marks against immutable policy thresholds, and mints the passport without trusting an off-chain issuer. The same World-derived human key powers one-live-passport-per-human enforcement and the protocol’s same-person-across-lenders signal. The application itself is split cleanly: app/handlers.mjs contains the shared World/bank/attestation/issuance/lender logic, app/store.mjs provides the local/Vercel storage seam, and demo/server.mjs is only a thin HTTP adapter. The borrower-facing UI then provides three views: create the passport, manage the passport and lender sharing, and let a lender look up an applicant by ENS passport name.

projects.title: Tora-x125
projects.description: Tora-x125: A secondary market for verified, tokenised impact investments
projects.project_description: Tora-x125 is a secondary market for verified impact investments. It tokenises green bonds, renewable-energy projects and carbon-removal assets into fractional, tradable digital assets, giving investors liquidity before maturity. Each asset links financial, risk and verified impact data on-chain. Tora-x125 integrates Uniswap v4 for secondary liquidity, 1inch for trading and stablecoin settlement, ENS for project identities, and World ID for investor verification.
projects.how_its_made: Tora-x125 is built around tokenised impact assets and programmable secondary liquidity. We use smart contracts to fractionalise green investments into tradable tokens, with project, financial and impact data linked onchain. Uniswap v4 provides liquidity pools and hooks for dynamic trading logic, while 1inch optimises swap routing and stablecoin settlement. ENS gives projects and issuers readable identities, and World ID supports privacy-preserving investor verification. We also explored a Sui implementation using Move, zkLogin and DeepBook for an alternative high-performance secondary market.

projects.title: Prophit
projects.description: Write a headline from the future. It becomes a token the market can trade.
projects.project_description: Prophit is a launchpad where every token is a headline from the future. Write one sentence, and it becomes a token anyone can buy or sell. The more people believe it, the higher the price goes. There is no oracle and nobody decides whether it came true. The price itself is the signal. Memecoins are fast but mean nothing. Prediction markets mean something but need approval and judging. Prophit gives you both: the speed of a memecoin and the meaning of a prediction.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry. Each headline is its own ERC-20 token, launched through Uniswap's Continuous Clearing Auction (CCA). Instead of a bonding curve that rewards whoever buys first, the auction finds one fair price over time. After the auction, the token trades in a Uniswap V4 pool with locked liquidity, and the author earns a share of the trading fees. We use ENS to name and store every prophecy (for example badges-2028.ringo.prophecy.eth). The sentence is written once and can never be edited. World ID makes sure each person gets only one prophet name. The frontend is React + wagmi + viem on Sepolia.

projects.title: Verdict
projects.description: USDC escrow on Arc that pays out only when two AI judges agree, verified on-chain byte for byte.
projects.project_description: Verdict is an escrow for work that's hard to judge automatically. Say you're paying someone 50 USDC to write an article, fix a bug or hit some performance target. You lock the money on Arc along with a written rubric that says what "done" means. When the other person finishes, they submit their evidence. Two AI models from different model families then judge that evidence against the rubric, and they don't see each other's answers. A third model checks whether their reasoning is actually backed by the evidence, and a fourth gives a confidence score. If both judges say yes, the reasoning holds up and confidence is above 85%, the contract releases the money. If they say no, the payer gets a refund. If they disagree or can't tell, nobody gets paid automatically. The escrow freezes and a named arbiter makes the call, and if the arbiter never does, the payer can take the money back after the deadline. What we cared about most is that you don't have to trust our server. Every model reply is signed over the hash of the exact request and the exact response. The contract re-hashes those bytes itself, recovers the signer with ecrecover and checks it against an on-chain registry. It also checks that the prompt referenced this particular escrow, so a valid verdict can't be replayed on a different one. Change a single byte and the signature check fails. We also added an x402 endpoint, so AI agents can pay 0.05 USDC per verdict and get back a signed verdict bundle they can verify themselves. Being upfront: the signer is pluggable. We fully built and tested the path where 0G Compute TEE enclaves sign the verdicts, but we couldn't get enough 0G testnet tokens to run it live. The live demo runs on Arc testnet use a self-attested signer over Groq models, and both the dApp and the verifier label those runs clearly.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are Solidity with Foundry. There are three: SignerRegistry stores which keys are allowed to sign and for which model, VerdictOracle does all the verification, and VerdictEscrow holds the USDC and handles open, settle, arbitrate and refund. The oracle is stateless and pretty minimal: two SHA-256 hashes, EIP-191, ecrecover, a check that the prompt contains the escrow's rubric and evidence hashes, and the quorum rules. We didn't want a JSON parser on-chain, so the prompt forces every model to start its reply with a fixed-width header like "VERDICT:Y;CONF:0.93;RUBRIC:0x…;EVID:0x…", and the contract reads it by byte offset. We have 20 Foundry tests covering tampered bytes, cross-escrow replays, revoked signers, the same model posing as two judges, and so on. The relayer is written in TypeScript on Bun with viem. Its main job is keeping the exact request and response bytes, since the signature only works on exactly what was hashed. It also checks everything locally before spending gas. One bug we hit: reasoning models sometimes quote a draft "VERDICT:" line inside their thinking field, so the relayer now rejects any reply where the first header in the raw JSON isn't the real one. For x402, it turned out Arc's USDC supports EIP-3009 (transferWithAuthorization), so our API acts as its own facilitator. It verifies the signed authorization and submits it on Arc. The frontend is a single HTML page using viem, with no build step. You can open escrows, submit evidence, act as the arbiter, and paste in any settle transaction to verify it yourself in the browser. It re-hashes every attestation and shows you who signed. The most hacky part was the 0G integration. The docs didn't match what the TEE actually signs, so we read the 0G broker source code (signChatWithKey) and found it signs sha256(request):sha256(response) as an EIP-191 message. That's why we call providers directly instead of going through the router, because the router rewrites the request and the hashes wouldn't match anymore. Partner tech: Arc for USDC escrow and gas, Arc Studio (it cloned the repo and ran our 20/20 tests), 0G Compute TeeML for the enclave signer path, and Groq for the free models used in the live runs.

projects.title: Unlinked
projects.description: Sends dapps' RPC reads over Tor, shows what they leak, and checks their code is the real one.
projects.project_description:
Whenever you open a dapp, your RPC provider can see your IP next to your wallets, your balances and the trade you're about to make. The page may also send your address to trackers, and you're trusting that the code you loaded is the code the team published. Unlinked is a browser extension that helps with all three. You keep your wallet, and the dapp doesn't need to change. Protect: it sends the page's RPC reads through Tor using anon-rpc. Each site and each account gets its own circuit, so your accounts are harder to link. If Tor is down, calls fail instead of leaking.
See: a small card shows which third parties the page contacted and which ones received your address.
Verify: it hashes the scripts the page ran and checks them against attestations on Arkiv. If one script doesn't match while the others do, the badge turns red.
projects.how_its_made:
Unlinked is a Chrome MV3 extension written in TypeScript, with no backend. A small script replaces window.fetch before the page loads and catches JSON-RPC calls. The service worker then sends them through anon-rpc, which checks the Tor client's hash against a contract on mainnet and runs it in a locked sandbox. Hiding the IP wasn't enough, so we split batched calls by account and rewrite request IDs, because both can link accounts. We also asked Tor's own check service which exit each request used: two accounts came out of two different exits. Arkiv stores the build attestations. Each record is owned by the wallet that vouches for it and expires after 30 days. Lookups go through Tor as one query, so checking a site doesn't reveal your IP to Arkiv. Without attesters you trust, a match shows amber instead of green, because anyone can write to Arkiv. The demo dapp is a plain Uniswap v4 page on Sepolia. It gets quotes from V4Quoter, so no API key ties them to you. The hacky parts: We find your address even when it's padded inside calldata.
We work out the chain from the RPC URL, so failover still works when a provider refuses Tor from the first call.
We wrote our own zip writer so anyone can rebuild the extension byte for byte.

projects.title: ENSure
projects.description: Owner-approved ENSv2 releases for IPFS sites, with public checks of release evidence.
projects.project_description: ENSure makes decentralized website releases reviewable and verifiable. It uses ENSv2 to separate preview and production publishing, IPFS to address static site builds by content, and a public verifier to check that the live site matches its recorded release evidence. A candidate build is published to the preview ENS name. ENSure fetches its build manifest and checks the declared files against their SHA-256 hashes before enabling owner approval. The current ENS parent-name owner signs an approval tied to the candidate’s CID, source commit, and build evidence. One resolver transaction updates production’s site pointer and approval records together. Visitors can verify the configured ENS names, resolver and ownership state, approval evidence, IPFS CID, build manifest, and fetched files without connecting a wallet. The app also shows release history and supports restoring a previously approved build through a fresh owner approval in the direct-owner flow. ENSure runs on ENSv2 Sepolia. Its verification checks file contents off-chain; ENS stores the pointers and permissions. A matching result establishes consistency with the release evidence, not that the site’s code is safe.
projects.how_its_made: The app is a React, TypeScript, and Vite frontend using wagmi and viem for wallet connection, ENSv2 reads, message signing, and resolver transactions. It reads the configured project on Sepolia, including ensure.eth, preview.ensure.eth, and prod.ensure.eth. Preview and production use separate resolvers. The owner can grant or revoke the configured CI wallet’s preview publishing roles. Promotion reads the live preview, retrieves its IPFS build manifest, checks the listed files, and requests an EIP-712 signature from the current ENS owner. The app submits a resolver multicall that updates the production content pointer and release evidence together, then independently reads back and verifies the result. Public verification does not require a wallet. It compares ENS records and approval evidence with the IPFS site CID, build manifest, and fetched file hashes. Release history is read from production resolver events. The current configuration uses direct owner approval; the newer release controller and Safe flow are not connected.

ENSure runs on ENSv2 Sepolia. Its verification checks file contents off-chain; ENS stores the pointers and permissions. A matching result establishes consistency with the release evidence, not that the site’s code is safe.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The app is a React, TypeScript, and Vite frontend using wagmi and viem for wallet connection, ENSv2 reads, message signing, and resolver transactions. It reads the configured project on Sepolia, including ensure.eth, preview.ensure.eth, and prod.ensure.eth.

Preview and production use separate resolvers. The owner can grant or revoke the configured CI wallet’s preview publishing roles. Promotion reads the live preview, retrieves its IPFS build manifest, checks the listed files, and requests an EIP-712 signature from the current ENS owner. The app submits a resolver multicall that updates the production content pointer and release evidence together, then independently reads back and verifies the result.

Public verification does not require a wallet. It compares ENS records and approval evidence with the IPFS site CID, build manifest, and fetched file hashes. Release history is read from production resolver events. The current configuration uses direct owner approval; the newer release controller and Safe flow are not connected.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Censorship-resistant, zero-ETH anonymous disclosures powered by EIP-8141 Alt-Mempool frame transactions, Anon-RPC over Tor, and a single-file verifiable walkaway frontend.

ZeroDrop lets a member of a group (a newsroom, a union, a government agency) publish sensitive evidence that anyone can verify came from **one of N verified members** without revealing which member posted it. 

### The Problem
Today, whistleblowers face an impossible trade-off: **credibility requires proof, but proof destroys anonymity**.
- **On-chain anchoring** requires gas (ETH), which requires an exchange account tied to government ID.
- **Centralized relayers** and **SecureDrop** log the source's IP address and can censor them under legal pressure.
- **Standard Mempools** reject transactions with high-gas verification rules.
For a confidential source, metadata leakage isn't an inconvenience — it's an arrest.


### The ZeroDrop Solution
ZeroDrop eliminates both the funding trail and the relayer:
1. **0-ETH Anonymous Writes:** The whistleblower proves membership using Semaphore zero-knowledge proofs. An **EIP-8141 Frame Transaction** makes the ZeroDrop contract both the sender and the fee payer (`from = ZeroDrop`, user balance = 0).
2. **Alternative Mempool (ERC-8421):** The verification frame burns ~370,000 gas on-chain. While rejected verbatim by canonical nodes (`MAX_VERIFY_GAS` exceeded), it is admitted and mined via the ERC-8421 alternative mempool (**Block 10041 on Chain 1337**).
3. **Anon-RPC over Tor:** Reads and writes route through an ephemeral Tor circuit via the official Ethereum Foundation Tor-JS contract.
4. **ETHBEAT CROPS Walkaway Standard:** The complete application compiles to a **single 1.98 MB static HTML file** with 0 external scripts, 0 external styles, and strict CSP. It runs offline from `file://` or decentralized IPFS gateways even if all servers disappear.

projects.title: Humdrop[Fairdrop]
projects.description: FairDrop: Walletless, proof-of-humanity claims for fair event merchandise distribution.
projects.project_description: FairDrop is a walletless, proof-of-humanity platform designed to make limited-edition event merchandise distribution fair, transparent, and resistant to duplicate claims. At hackathons, conferences, and community events, limited merchandise often gets distributed on a first-come, first-served basis, allowing individuals to claim multiple items while genuine attendees miss out. FairDrop addresses this problem using World ID to verify that each participant is a unique human without requiring them to connect or manage a crypto wallet. Organizers can create multiple merchandise campaigns with configurable supply limits and claim periods. Attendees verify their humanity through World ID and claim available rewards through a simple browser-based interface. A backend relayer handles blockchain transactions and gas fees, removing the need for attendees to hold tokens or pay transaction fees. The smart contract enforces campaign-specific claim uniqueness, supply limits, and date restrictions. This creates a transparent, verifiable distribution system where every eligible person gets a fair opportunity to claim limited rewards.
projects.how_its_made: FairDrop combines Solidity smart contracts, World ID verification, a backend relayer, and a browser-based frontend to create a walletless merchandise distribution experience. The smart contract is built using Solidity and OpenZeppelin's Ownable library. It supports multiple independent campaigns, campaign-specific nullifier tracking to prevent duplicate claims, supply restrictions, and configurable campaign time windows. World ID is used for proof-of-humanity verification. The backend handles proof verification and prepares authorized claim transactions through a relayer, so attendees don't need to connect a wallet or pay gas fees. We use Supabase for backend data integration and campaign-related application flows. The frontend provides interfaces for attendees to discover campaigns, verify their humanity, and claim rewards, alongside organizer functionality for managing campaigns. The project is designed for deployment on Ethereum Sepolia testnet. We also implemented automated testing using Foundry and Vitest to validate smart contract logic and application functionality.

projects.title: CORVEN
projects.description: Dependency-aware incident response for interconnected autonomous AI agents.
projects.project_description: Autonomous AI agents increasingly operate across interconnected systems, sharing permissions, credentials, resources, and downstream workflows. When one agent is compromised, the resulting exposure can extend far beyond that individual agent. CORVEN is an infrastructure-level incident response platform designed to address this problem. It maps relationships between agents, permissions, resources, and workflows to construct a dependency graph and calculate the potential blast radius of a compromised agent. Instead of relying on indiscriminate shutdowns or broad permission revocation, CORVEN identifies a minimum-safe containment boundary and generates an explainable response plan. The platform then executes supported containment operations, independently verifies whether malicious paths have been blocked, and checks that unaffected workflows remain operational. CORVEN also builds a verifiable incident evidence trail. ENS provides human-readable blockchain identity resolution, Arkiv provides decentralized evidence persistence, and Chainlink CRE supports independent workflow verification. Our goal is to make autonomous systems more accountable and resilient by connecting discovery, dependency analysis, containment, verification, and evidence into one incident-response lifecycle.
projects.how_its_made: CORVEN is built using a TypeScript-based backend and a modern web frontend, with Solidity smart contracts and dedicated blockchain integration adapters. The backend uses Fastify, TypeScript, Drizzle ORM, and PostgreSQL to manage agents, resources, dependencies, incidents, containment operations, and evidence. The dependency analysis and blast-radius calculations use deterministic graph logic rather than relying on an LLM to make security decisions. The frontend uses Next.js 15 and React 19 to provide an interactive security operations dashboard, including agent management, dependency visualization, incident investigation, containment planning, verification results, and evidence inspection. We integrated ENS for human-readable blockchain identity resolution, Arkiv for decentralized evidence persistence and read-back verification, and Chainlink CRE for independent verification workflows. Solidity and Foundry are used for Ethereum evidence anchoring and contract testing. Docker is used to containerize the application, with AWS ECR for image storage and AWS infrastructure for deployment. A key engineering decision was to separate analysis, authorization, enforcement, and verification. CORVEN does not assume that registering an agent means it is protected, nor does it claim that an operation succeeded simply because a transaction was submitted. Enforcement coverage and verification limitations are explicitly represented.

projects.title: Tracer AI
projects.description: Trade capped ETH volatility receipts on 1inch Aqua, not price direction.
projects.project_description: Tracer is a two-sided market for capped ETH realized-variance receipts built on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Writers fund a non-upgradeable vault and list three official-router programs: issue (USDC → receipts), exit (receipts → USDC before expiry), and settle (receipts → USDC at maturity from realized variance). Buyers and sellers trade at on-chain quotes that match swaps because pricing runs through TracerMarketEngine on the unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter.
projects.how_its_made: We built Tracer with Foundry contracts and a Next.js frontend. Each writer funds a non-upgradeable vault; the factory creates a receipt series and registers ISSUE, EXIT, and SETTLE SwapVM programs on the unmodified 1inch Aqua router in one transaction. TracerMarketEngine handles on-chain pricing, so displayed quotes use the same math as executed swaps. Each sale reserves the receipt’s maximum capped payout in the writer’s vault, and that reservation is released when the receipt burns on exit or redemption. At maturity, a permissionless accumulator processes Chainlink ETH/USD round history in bounded checkpoints to calculate realized variance and finalize the payout. An indexer and read-only API support the market and portfolio views.

projects.title: Blocktrack
projects.description: Privacy-preserving parcel tracking on a public chain. No backend.
projects.project_description: Status updates are verifiable and immutable. Names, phone numbers, addresses, parcel contents and courier notes are encrypted in the browser before they touch the chain. The only people who can decrypt an order are its customer, the operations admin, and the courier assigned to it. Built for a local Anvil demo with Foundry, React and client-side AES-256-GCM + ECIES. There is no API, no database, no account server, and no plaintext ever leaves the tab.
projects.how_its_made:
This is a working privacy-focused prototype, not a production logistics platform. No backend. A static React app talks directly to an Ethereum RPC endpoint.
The chain is the source of truth. Orders, status history, roles and wrapped keys are on-chain.
Encryption is the access control. Write permissions are enforced by the contract; read permissions are enforced cryptographically.
The public tracker is status-only. Anyone with a tracking ID sees state and timestamps, never personal data.
The demo data is fictional. Anvil's publicly known development keys are used for one-click demo accounts.

projects.title: Second-Witness
projects.description: Check the code in your browser against what independent witnesses recorded, before you sign.
projects.project_description: Second Witness is a Chrome extension that checks the code running in your browser before you sign a transaction. A website can serve your browser different code than everyone else gets. The page looks the same, but your money can go somewhere else. An altered Safe file was live on a public URL 44.7 hours before the $1.5B Bybit theft, and no signer's browser could tell. Second Witness is built for that moment, starting with multisig and treasury signers. You press one button before you sign. The extension hashes the exact scripts your browser loaded and compares them with what two independent witnesses recorded. The site doesn't have to sign up, and nobody learns which sites you check. You get one of six results: Same code: every file matches what two witnesses recorded. Don't sign: a file doesn't match, under a name that should never change. Not seen: witnesses haven't recorded this code, or a script comes from a host not on the site's list. New release: the code is under an hour old, or a recent release added addresses or hosts. Partial: the files match, but other code wasn't compared, or witnesses are behind. Can't check: the site isn't listed, or the records are missing or old. Witness records live on Arkiv as write-once records, so nobody can quietly change them, including us. The list of trusted witnesses lives on ENS under secondwitness.eth, so a witness can be revoked in one transaction with no extension update. There is no backend in the check. If we vanish, the records stay readable for 180 days and the check drops to Partial within an hour. We replayed 7 archived captures of Safe's real file through the same comparison code. The altered one reads Don't sign. We also found no false alarms: 0 hash-named files changed across about 532 URLs on 31 sites. Today it covers 24 listed sites, including Safe, Aave, Uniswap and Lido, and runs on testnets. We run both witnesses ourselves, and anyone can fork it with their own. It checks the code you sign through, not the transaction itself, so it adds to your review rather than replacing it.
projects.how_its_made: Second Witness is about 1,900 lines of TypeScript with 147 tests, split into witnesses, a Chrome extension and shared comparison rules. There is no backend in the check. Witnesses run in public GitHub Actions, one on Linux and one on macOS. They crawl 24 listed sites, including Safe, Aave and Uniswap, hash every JavaScript file with SHA-256 and write new hashes to Arkiv. The Manifest V3 extension attaches chrome.debugger only when you press the button, listens to Debugger.scriptParsed, reads each source with Debugger.getScriptSource and hashes what the engine actually parsed. That catches code served only to you, and altered code still running from cache after the server is cleaned. Arkiv is the record store. Hash records are created with the readonly flag and a 180-day expiry, so nobody can edit them, including us. The network sets $creator, so a record can't fake its writer, and the reader drops any hash record that isn't read-only or was updated after creation. Browsers call arkiv_query directly over CORS, so we run no server. The extension downloads every record and compares locally, so the RPC never learns which site you're checking. ENS is the trust list. secondwitness.eth is on ENSv2 on Sepolia with its own resolver. w1 and w2 are records on that resolver, read through wildcard resolution, with no registry or token for each one. Every browser reads the list on refresh, and one setAddress revokes a witness with no extension update. Notable hacks: the crawler finds lazy-loaded files without a browser by reading chunk maps inside JS bundles, and it paces itself using Retry-After after Cloudflare rate limits. We kept a site only if the crawl covered what a real Chrome loaded. We also replayed 7 archived captures of Safe's real _app file through the real comparison code, and the altered one reads Don't sign.

projects.title: Credra
projects.description: Verified invoices. Instant USDT financing. Every step onchain.
projects.project_description: Credra is invoice financing infrastructure built on Whitechain and Chainlink CRE. A business registers an invoice onchain — its document fingerprint goes to Whitechain Sepolia. A Chainlink CRE workflow reads the record, queries a simulated external registry, and compares issuer, buyer, amount, due date and document hash to return ELIGIBLE, REJECTED or MANUAL_REVIEW. Any failure defaults to MANUAL_REVIEW, never ELIGIBLE. The verdict is recorded onchain by a verifier wallet. An allowlisted investor funds the eligible invoice in official Tether USDT, paid directly to the business — the contract never holds funds. Repayment at the due date goes to whoever holds the ERC-721 receivable token. Zero platform fees. All three contracts are source-verified on the Whitechain Sepolia explorer.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, OpenZeppelin v5) on Whitechain Sepolia: InvoiceRegistry, InvestorAllowlist, and ReceivableFinance which mints an ERC-721 receivable and handles USDT funding. All three source-verified on Blockscout. Chainlink CRE workflow in TypeScript reads the invoice from Whitechain over RPC — declared as an experimental-chains entry since Whitechain isn’t in the supported-chains list. It queries a simulated external registry, compares every field, and fails safe to MANUAL_REVIEW on any error. Verdict is written onchain by the application verifier wallet, not a DON — clearly disclosed in the UI. Backend on Next.js + Vercel + Turso runs the CRE rules in-process, applies a risk engine, then calls recordVerification with the verifier key. Frontend uses Next.js 15, Tailwind v4, Privy (email + embedded wallets with showWalletUIs: false for silent signing), and wagmi/viem for all onchain calls.
projects.project_description_markdown: Credra is invoice financing infrastructure built on Whitechain and Chainlink CRE. A business registers an invoice onchain — its document fingerprint goes to Whitechain Sepolia. A Chainlink CRE workflow reads the record, queries a simulated external registry, and compares issuer, buyer, amount, due date and document hash to return ELIGIBLE, REJECTED or MANUAL_REVIEW. Any failure defaults to MANUAL_REVIEW, never ELIGIBLE. The verdict is recorded onchain by a verifier wallet. An allowlisted investor funds the eligible invoice in official Tether USDT, paid directly to the business — the contract never holds funds. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, OpenZeppelin v5) on Whitechain Sepolia: InvoiceRegistry, InvestorAllowlist, and ReceivableFinance which mints an ERC-721 receivable and handles USDT funding. All three source-verified on Blockscout.

Chainlink CRE workflow in TypeScript reads the invoice from Whitechain over RPC — declared as an experimental-chains entry since Whitechain isn’t in the supported-chains list. It queries a simulated external registry, compares every field, and fails safe to MANUAL_REVIEW on any error. Verdict is written onchain by the application verifier wallet, not a DON — clearly disclosed in the UI.
