projects.title: Nanite
projects.description: Email for AI agents: ENS identity + rules, signed mail, encrypted on Arkiv, owned by your wallet
projects.project_description: Nanite gives every AI agent its own email address, with an identity anyone can check and mail that belongs to its owner. The problem: agents now sign up for tools, answer support mail and follow up with customers, but when an agent emails you, you can't tell whose agent it is or what it may do. DKIM proves only the domain, and millions of senders share the same domains. Giving an agent OAuth access to your inbox hands over your whole mailbox, and inbox APIs for agents keep the mail and the rules in the vendor's database. Nanite fixes both: Identity on ENSv2. Every agent is an ENS name under its owner's, for example support.vikrantsingh.nanitecom.eth. Its rules are public text records: whom it may email (nanite.send: off, reply-only, allowlist or any), a daily limit (nanite.send-limit) and the key its mail is signed with (nanite.signer). The agent's own key can only change its description, so it can't loosen its rules. Signed mail. Every mail an agent sends carries X-Nanite-Agent and an EIP-191 X-Nanite-Signature. Anyone can check it against the agent's ENS record, with no Nanite server involved. Change one character and the check fails. Mail you own, on Arkiv. Every email is an Arkiv entity. Nanite creates it and transfers it to the user's wallet in the same transaction, so after that Nanite can't edit or delete it. The payload is ciphertext: a fresh key per email, sealed to the owner's key and the agent's key. Login codes expire on chain after 5 minutes and other mail after 2 days, unless the owner presses Keep. Any AI agent can use it over MCP: whoami, list_inbox, get_email, wait_for_email, get_latest_otp, send_email and extend_email. Hosted agents use Nanite's MCP endpoint. Self-hosted agents keep their key on their own machine, so Nanite only ever sees their ciphertext, and they sign their own mail. It is live on Sepolia ENSv2, Arkiv Rabdi and real email. On production, a self-hosted agent read a Gmail message that Nanite had stored only as ciphertext, replied through Claude Code, and the reply verified against ENS in Gmail. A copy with one changed character failed with signer_mismatch.
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo in TypeScript: a Next.js 16 web app (React 19, Tailwind 4, shadcn/ui) on Vercel, and a Hono API on Node with Postgres 17, in Docker on AWS Lightsail behind Caddy. Real mail comes and goes through Resend (inbound webhook, outbound with DKIM, SPF and DMARC). ENSv2 (Sepolia): we registered nanitecom.eth on ENSv2 with its own UserRegistry. Every user gets <user>.nanitecom.eth with their own registry, and every agent gets <agent>.<user>.nanitecom.eth with its own PermissionedResolver. ENSv2 resolver roles are scoped per key, not per name, so one resolver per agent is what makes least privilege possible: the agent's key gets SET_TEXT on agent-context only, and the chain rejects everything else with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles (tested). The operator holds only registrar and renew roles, which the user can revoke. The API reads the send policy fresh from ENS through UniversalResolverV2 before every send and fails closed if ENS can't be read. Revoking an agent removes its roles on chain. Arkiv (Rabdi): each email is one entity (schema nanite.email.v1) holding ciphertext, with only the attributes queries need: agent, type, time, thread id, reader key ids and a per-user pseudonym of the sender. The operator wallet creates the entity and calls changeOwnership to the user's wallet in the same executeBatch, so users need no tokens and Nanite gives up control. Expiry is the retention policy: login codes get 5 minutes, other mail gets permissionlessExtension so the owner's Keep (7, 30, 90 or 182 days) and the agent's extend_email work. Notable: anyone can write entities with our schema and transfer one into a victim's wallet, so every query is pinned to our creator address and the reader checks it on every row. Writes go through a single-flight queue, because key prediction depends on the nonce. We documented what hurt, with repro scripts, in arkiv/friction.md. Crypto: XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a fresh key per email, sealed per reader with X25519, with the reader list bound into the encryption. The user's key is generated in the browser and unlocked by one wallet signature per session (HKDF). Backups are a recovery code or a passphrase (Argon2id). Mail signatures are EIP-191 over a canonical string. We sign our own X-Nanite-Message-Id, because Amazon SES (behind Resend) replaces Message-ID, which broke our first signature version. MCP: hosted Streamable HTTP at /mcp with a bearer agent token, and a local stdio kit that decrypts and signs on the agent's machine for self-hosted agents. Mail content is always returned under an "untrusted" field. Everything runs in Docker, tested with lint, typecheck, API tests, Playwright end-to-end tests and live runs against Sepolia, Rabdi and Resend. Built with Claude Code: an orchestrating session planned and reviewed, Sonnet subagents wrote the code, and every architecture and security decision was made by a human.

projects.title: SenFund
projects.description: Turn invoices into USDT payment requests on Whitechain testnet, with simulated conversion and payout
projects.project_description: SenFund lets freelancers and small businesses send USD invoices that customers pay in test USDT on Whitechain Sepolia testnet (chain 1874). The merchant creates and signs an invoice in a Next.js workspace, and an LLM drafter can fill it from pasted invoice text. The merchant’s receiving address comes from an ENSv2 name on Ethereum Sepolia, such as merchant.senfund.eth. The customer gets a checkout link to a static page that reads the chain directly, so they can pay with their browser wallet and check the payment even when the merchant’s app is down. A verified settlement contract records each payment as a public, final event onchain. The merchant never has to trust a processor’s word that the customer paid. A Python backend matches those events to invoices and stores them. It also accepts a pasted transaction hash if a receipt is slow to appear. After a payment settles, a Chainlink CRE workflow picks a payout provider (for example Mudrex) and records the USD conversion and INR payout. That step is clearly labeled as simulated. Mainnet and live payouts are turned off. Users always sign transactions in their own wallet, and the app never signs on their behalf.
projects.how_its_made:
Next.js 16 and React 19 (with Framer Motion) power the merchant workspace. Its catch-all app/api/[...path] route proxies requests to a Python settlement service built on web3.py and eth-account. That service signs each invoice as EIP-712 typed data, stores invoices, and scans Whitechain blocks to match payments to invoices. The Solidity settlement contract is compiled with py-solc-x and verified on the Whitechain Sepolia explorer. It pulls test USDT and accepts each signed invoice only once, which blocks replays. Whitechain gave us cheap, fast testnet settlement and an official test-USDT token, so every receipt is a public event anyone can verify. ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia resolves the merchant’s payout address from merchant.senfund.eth. The checkout checks that name before paying, so rotating the record makes checkout refuse the old address. A Chainlink CRE workflow written in TypeScript (cre/payout) runs after settlement. It picks a payout route, such as Mudrex or a protected P2P fallback, and records a simulated USD-to-INR payout. The hacky parts: Checkout is a plain static page with the signed invoice in the link. It reads the chain straight from the browser, so customers can pay and verify while our backend is down.
After a restart, the backend scans recent blocks first and catches up on older ones in the background. You can also paste a transaction hash to force a match.
For local runs with no testnet, eth-tester and py-evm run a local chain.
Each invoice exports an evidence JSON with the transaction hash, block, route and fallback reason, and no personal data.

projects.title: StillWorks
projects.description: The sovereign CROPS storefront with automated escrow rails, 0G Private Computer TEE audits
projects.project_description: Stillworks is the store where you subscribe to open tools that publish a live passport and heartbeat. Backed by 0G Galileo smart contracts, subscription payments sit in non-custodial escrow that only releases when the tool is verified alive. If the service dies or misses a heartbeat, users claim an immediate pro-rata refund and download an encrypted walkaway bundle from 0G Storage Turbo to launch locally. Passports and exit bundles are audited in 0G Private Computer TEE enclaves (0gm- 1.0-35b-a3b), preserving client privacy under the strict Ethereum Foundation CROPS mandate without exposing code or personal data.
projects.how_its_made:
Browse & Audit: Users browse 10 seeded sovereign tools. Software passports and security postures are audited in real time via 0G Private Computer hardware TEE enclaves (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b) with sealed private trust mode. Escrow Subscriptions: Users deposit subscription fees into [SubscriptionEscrow. Automated Heartbeats: The founder's sovereign daemon periodically anchors
liveness proofs and encrypted walkaway bundle Merkle roots onto [StillworksHourlyProtocolHub. The Killswitch Demonstration: If the founder server or domain is terminated, the heartbeat expires. Subscribers immediately trigger an automated escrow refund and download their walkaway bundle from 0G Storage Turbo using the onchain Merkle root to run offline via Docker with zero downtime.

projects.title: p2p-Father
projects.description: Decentralized on-chain P2P crypto escrow inside Telegram & WhatsApp
projects.project_description: P2PFather – A Decentralized P2P Stablecoin Marketplace P2PFather is a decentralized peer-to-peer stablecoin marketplace that connects people who want to buy and sell cryptocurrencies using local fiat payment methods such as UPI and bank transfers. The platform already operates through a Telegram Mini App, Telegram bot, and web dashboard, with smart-contract escrow on Base and BNB Chain to make P2P transactions more secure and transparent. For this hackathon, we are extending P2PFather with Arkiv and World ID to improve the trust, transparency, and reliability of peer-to-peer trading. Arkiv is used to create and maintain decentralized records of trade-related activities, providing a verifiable history of transactions. World ID introduces proof-of-human verification to help reduce bot activity and strengthen user authenticity in the marketplace. We are building on top of an existing product rather than creating another standalone demo. Our goal is to make P2P stablecoin trading more accessible and reliable by combining decentralized escrow, verifiable trade records, and human verification. P2PFather aims to become a more transparent and trustworthy P2P marketplace where users can trade stablecoins, interact directly, and build a verifiable history of their transactions.
projects.how_its_made: P2PFather is built using Solidity smart contracts, React, TypeScript, Node.js, Express, and Supabase. The frontend is developed with React, Vite, Wagmi, and Viem, while the backend uses Node.js, Express, and grammY to power the web dashboard, Telegram Mini App, and Telegram bot. Our P2P escrow system uses Solidity smart contracts deployed on Base and BNB Chain to lock funds during trades and release them once the payment is confirmed. Supabase and PostgreSQL manage application data, user activity, and trade information, while Redis supports real-time operations. For this hackathon, we integrated Arkiv to maintain decentralized, verifiable records of P2P trade activities and World ID for proof-of-human verification. These integrations add an additional layer of transparency and help reduce automated or fake-user activity in the marketplace. Rather than building a standalone prototype, we extended an existing working product, integrating these technologies into its current architecture while retaining its existing escrow and trading workflows.

Arkiv is used to create and maintain decentralized records of trade-related activities, providing a verifiable history of transactions. World ID introduces proof-of-human verification to help reduce bot activity and strengthen user authenticity in the marketplace.

We are building on top of an existing product rather than creating another standalone demo. Our goal is to make P2P stablecoin trading more accessible and reliable by combining decentralized escrow, verifiable trade records, and human verification.

P2PFather aims to become a more transparent and trustworthy P2P marketplace where users can trade stablecoins, interact directly, and build a verifiable history of their transactions.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
P2PFather is built using Solidity smart contracts, React, TypeScript, Node.js, Express, and Supabase. The frontend is developed with React, Vite, Wagmi, and Viem, while the backend uses Node.js, Express, and grammY to power the web dashboard, Telegram Mini App, and Telegram bot.

Our P2P escrow system uses Solidity smart contracts deployed on Base and BNB Chain to lock funds during trades and release them once the payment is confirmed. Supabase and PostgreSQL manage application data, user activity, and trade information, while Redis supports real-time operations.

For this hackathon, we integrated **Arkiv** to maintain decentralized, verifiable records of P2P trade activities and **World ID** for proof-of-human verification. These integrations add an additional layer of transparency and help reduce automated or fake-user activity in the marketplace.

Rather than building a standalone prototype, we extended an existing working product, integrating these technologies into its current architecture while retaining its existing escrow and trading workflows.

projects.title: Dabba
projects.description: Own a stock basket on Uniswap v4 and earn from every trade, even Monday’s opening gap
projects.project_description: Dabbah is a token that holds a basket of stocks (Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft) plus USDC, a quarter each. Holders own a share of the basket. Traders swap against it at any hour, and every swap pays a fee that stays in the basket, so each share is worth a little more after every trade. You keep the stocks’ price exposure, and you can buy or sell your share for USDC whenever you want.
projects.how_its_made:
The core is one Uniswap v4 hook that runs six pools, one for each pair of NVDA, AAPL, MSFT and USDC. All six trade against a single shared reserve held as ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager. In beforeSwap the hook prices each trade with an equal-weight weighted-pool formula and returns a BeforeSwapDelta, so the hook does the pricing, not Uniswap’s default curve. Buying and selling the basket token with USDC alone uses the same formula, capped at 30% of the reserve per trade. A MarketClock contract stores each stock’s price and whether NYSE is open. A Chainlink CRE workflow fills it: nodes fetch the prices, agree on the median, work out NYSE hours (weekends, holidays, early closes), and sign one report that the clock accepts only from Chainlink’s forwarder. On every swap the hook reads the clock, picks the posted fee, measures the trader’s edge against Chainlink’s price, and keeps 80% of it, capped at 10% of the trade. On testnet we ran the workflow through the CRE CLI with one real broadcast, and a keeper pushes reports in the same format hourly. Arc settles everything in USDC with sub-second finality, and gas is paid in USDC too. We built the contracts and the React + viem frontend in Arc Studio. Testing: Contracts: Foundry unit, fuzz and invariant tests.
Frontend: a Playwright suite drives the live app with a real wallet and real Arc testnet transactions. Hacky bits: Arc’s USDC calls a precompile that Foundry can’t simulate, so transactions that move USDC go through viem scripts.
The app races the Arc explorer’s index against two RPCs to read history, because the free RPC tiers reject large log queries.
A replay script posts a Monday opening price to show the gap capture live.

projects.title: Jasoos
projects.description: Type a dream, walk into it: an AI detective world painted on 0G, saved on Arkiv, for humans only.
projects.project_description:
Every one of us was once a kid with a story we could see in our heads but never show anyone. ETH Jasoos turns that story into a world. You type one line, like “a rain-flooded night market in Mumbai, and someone wants my tiffin box”, and Jasoos paints it into an explorable mystery set in India. It has streets you can walk, rooms you can enter, suspects you can question, clues to collect, a sealed evidence box to crack, and one chance to name the culprit. Worlds are meant to be shared. A creator can make their world public, so anyone can play the case they dreamed up. Players like or dislike worlds, and the best stories rise to the top of the community gallery. Trust is built in, because a game of mysteries only works if it’s fair: One person, one detective. Every player proves they’re a unique human with World ID before they sign in.
Fair limits. Each human gets a fair free quota of worlds, one vote per world, and one accusation per case.
No shared answers. The evidence box needs a second, case-specific World ID check, so solutions can’t be farmed or passed around.
A secret answer. The culprit is sealed, so even the public database never gives it away.
projects.how_its_made:
asoos is a Next.js 16 / React 19 / TypeScript app with a canvas game engine. It’s deployed on Vercel, with generated images stored in Vercel Blob. It’s built around three sponsor technologies, each doing a job the game can’t work without. 0G Private Computer: the game engine
Every call goes through 0G’s OpenAI-compatible router, using the OpenAI SDK: 0gm-1.0 writes the world: the setting, the cast of suspects, the hidden culprit, NPC dialogue and the endings.
seedream paints every street screen, interior and character sprite.

projects.title: BuySpace
projects.description: Air rights NFTs on Hedera. Time-bound leases that expire on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: BuySpace lets property owners tokenize urban air rights above a parcel (views, vertical envelopes, not land) and lease them for a fixed term. On Hedera Testnet, an owner mints a Title NFT for the airspace envelope, then creates an on-chain lease listing priced in HBAR. A buyer pays from their own wallet and receives a Lease NFT for the term; the Title NFT stays with the owner. Lease offers are indexed on Arkiv Rabdi as queryable entities (schema airspace.mumbai.leases). Each offer expires with the commercial term, so stale listings drop out of the marketplace automatically without a cleanup job. The live demo is centered on Mumbai (BKC / Jio World Centre): tokenize on /tokenize, list on /lease/create, buy on /listings, then verify HashScan and Arkiv explorer links from the dashboard.
projects.how_its_made: BuySpace is a Next.js 14 app written in TypeScript. The frontend uses Tailwind for layout, and RainbowKit with wagmi so owners and buyers can connect a wallet on Hedera Testnet (chain 296). Settlement lives on Hedera. We deployed two contracts: AirspaceTitle , which mints a Title NFT for an airspace parcel, and AirspaceLeaseMarket , which handles listing and HBAR purchase. After a buy, the buyer receives a Lease NFT through Hedera Token Service ( @hashgraph/sdk ). We also kept an optional Asset Tokenization Studio path for title issuance. During the hackathon Hashio’s RPC was flaky, so we default to thirdweb’s 296 endpoint and point every tx at HashScan. Discovery lives on Arkiv Rabdi via @arkiv-network/sdk . Each open lease is an entity under airspace.mumbai.leases . Creating a listing writes the entity with an expiration matching the lease term; buying updates status and lessee, then extends expiry to the end date. The marketplace simply queries open entities, so when a lease ends the listing falls off on its own. API routes keep the Arkiv writer key on the server. A small local store is only a backup if Rabdi is unreachable. The home page map is Mapbox, zoomed to BKC and Jio World Centre for the Mumbai demo.

projects.project_description: It uses an EIP-8141 VERIFY frame flow to demonstrate why expensive post-quantum verification needs an alternative mempool admission path. The project includes a real Solidity wallet and verifier, gas measurements, canonical mempool rejection evidence, staking registry readback, ENS identity continuity with key rotation, Arkiv migration records, and a public Swarm passport. The UI presents all captured blockchain evidence honestly, including unavailable artifacts.

projects.title: Arena
projects.description: Social trading arena: AI agents trade on Flash, pay their own 0G compute, and are CRE-verified
projects.project_description: This project is a social trading arena where AI trading agents and human traders compete on one public leaderboard. Anyone can build an agent by picking a strategy template (Momentum, Mean Reversion, Breakout, Smart DCA or Social Sentiment) and tuning its sliders. Each agent then trades live on Base through Definitive Flash advanced orders: limit, TWAP, stop, take-profit, stop-loss, bracket and trailing stop. Every decision is an inference on 0G Private Computer, with a request ID you can inspect in the agent’s decision log.
projects.how_its_made: The project is a TypeScript monorepo with four parts. The web app has the leaderboard, agent builder, manual trading terminal and fork checkout. The agent runtime schedules ticks with BullMQ on Redis. Each agent gets its own Privy or Turnkey server wallet with spending policies that sign Flash EIP-712 orders. Five Solidity contracts on Base cover the agent registry, the performance registry, the treasury, the strategy marketplace and the risk oracle. Each tick pulls market data and indicators, plus a Flash quote and a Chainlink feed price. It then sends a JSON-mode request to 0G Private Computer in verified trust mode and stores the request ID and TEE flag. The proposal goes through the policy engine. Approved trades go to Flash as limit, TWAP or stop entries with an attached bracket, and fills are tracked over WebSocket. Chainlink CRE does the heavy lifting in two workflows. WF1 reads the registry on Base, pages through Flash fills, reads Chainlink feeds and computes FIFO PnL and a high-water-mark commission. It then writes a signed report to PerformanceRegistry, and that report is the only number the treasury will charge commission on. WF2 combines price feeds, an external market API and a 0G risk classification to write NORMAL, CAUTION or HALT to RiskOracle. The self-funding loop is where we got hacky. The agent collects commission into its treasury and calls topUp. A conversion relayer with a pre-funded 0G float then sends native 0G to the agent’s own 0G wallet. The agent deposits it into the 0G Payment Layer and its Router balance rises. Each agent has a capped sk- key with a daily credit limit, so spend caps are enforced by 0G itself. We used the float because bridging tiny commissions would cost more than the commission. Memory and lessons live in Postgres and 0G Storage, and share cards are generated on 0G image models.

projects.title: postcurve
projects.description: Bunker wallet: private payments into accounts only hash-based keys can spend, gas paid in USDC.
projects.project_description: Quantum computers, and AI-accelerated math, may break the elliptic-curve keys behind today's wallets sooner than expected (Justin Drake's "bunker mode", Vitalik's "prefer hash-only"). postcurve is a bunker for that day. Receive privately: Alice publishes a pq-sap stealth meta-address (ML-KEM-768). Every payment lands at a brand-new EIP-8141 account that only she can find. Spend with hash-only keys: each stealth account can only be moved by a 2-of-3 quorum of WOTS/XMSS one-time keys (browser, phone, paper recovery). No elliptic curve anywhere in a spend. Every key signs once and is burned on chain; a replay is refused by the mempool. No ETH needed: a staked postcurve paymaster verifies the quorum (~600k gas, allowed by ERC-8421's per-entity staked budget) in its pay frame, pays the gas, and takes its fee in the token being spent. To everyone else the account is a random address that never held ETH. Canary: a Chainlink CRE workflow watches large, long-dormant addresses whose public key is already exposed; a sudden sweep raises an alert (an early sign someone can break ECDSA), shown in the app. Everything in the demo is real: frame transactions on a local EIP-8141 devnet (ethrex), admitted by the ERC-8421 alt mempool sidecar.
projects.how_its_made: Signatures: WOTS (w=16) one-time keys in an XMSS tree (height 8, 256 leaves) over keccak256, written from scratch in TypeScript (SDK) and Solidity, with shared test vectors. Stealth: pq-sap commitment format 0x02 (EPF cohort 7), reproduced byte for byte against pq-sap's own vectors; ERC-5564 announcements, scheme 2; CREATE2 accounts bound to the commitment. Accounts and paymaster: Solidity 0.8.28 + Foundry, using hegota-support opcode helpers. The spend is one six-frame EIP-8141 transaction: only_verify (account) → pay (paymaster checks 2-of-3 hash-only signatures) → commit (burns the keys) → checkDeadline + transfer + fee (atomic batch). The paymaster is bounded: fee token only, minimum fee, max ETH cost, no ETH value in frames. Alt mempool: we patched the sidecar to implement ERC-8421 BUDGET-010 (per-entity validation budgets: 1,000,000 gas for staked entities) and opened an upstream PR (forshtat/mempool-workshop-sidecar#4). Canary: Chainlink CRE workflow (TypeScript SDK) simulated with the CRE CLI against the devnet and mainnet, plus a small service for state and the alert feed. App: React + Vite, keys in a Web Worker, browser storage records a key as used before it signs; a phone approver page pairs by QR and signs only what it shows; a local operator deploys accounts and funds test wallets. Tests: 85 Foundry tests, ~100 SDK tests, 43 app tests; an end-to-end script runs the whole spend on the devnet.

projects.title: SettleKit
projects.description: Screened USDT checkout with direct settlement, refunds, independent accounting and CRE recovery.
projects.project_description: SettleKit is a stablecoin payment gateway for merchants who need more than a successful wallet transaction. It combines hosted checkout, direct merchant settlement, mandatory wallet screening, signed webhooks, original-payer refunds and a responsive operations dashboard. Merchants can create payment links and invoices, manage contacts and API keys, inspect delivery failures and export reports. A separate store demonstrates durable, idempotent fulfillment: a redirect is never treated as payment proof. The settlement integration targets Whitechain Sepolia and its specified USDT. Arkiv Rabdi is the public receipt layer for minimal payment/refund evidence, with a separately served accountant that verifies source events and discloses history coverage. Chainlink CRE compares chain evidence, current payment eligibility and the separate merchant order API to recover failed notifications without charging again. Current evidence includes local payment/refund execution with a mock token, actual isolated Neon PostgreSQL, real CRE CLI recovery and exactly one store fulfillment. Public Arkiv SDK queries and Whitechain read-only checks have run. Funded Whitechain deployment/payment/refund, signed Arkiv receipts and public application hosting remain pending; local fixtures are not presented as live sponsor transactions.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript 5.9, backed by Neon PostgreSQL 17, Drizzle and pg. Wallet-signature login proves settlement ownership. viem/wagmi connect checkout and refunds to a Solidity router built with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin. Integer base units and short-lived, invoice-bound authorizations protect money handling. Stale or unavailable required screening blocks authorization. Private payment transitions and outbox jobs commit atomically. The observer verifies canonical chain evidence and handles reorg corrections. Signed HMAC webhooks are at-least-once; a separate durable merchant receiver deduplicates payments and checks current eligibility before fulfillment. Refund intents immediately hold new recovery. The official Arkiv SDK implements minimal public receipt publication and an independent accountant with trusted-writer/source verification, coverage and CSV. The actual CRE SDK compares HTTP/RPC evidence, current eligibility and a separate order API. Real local CRE CLI simulation recovered an injected notification failure and verified one fulfillment. CRE never moves funds. JS/REST/Python adapters are included. Verification: 114 root tests, 26 contract cases, 16 browser tests and 7 Python checks, plus isolated restores. AI assistance is disclosed in AI_USAGE.md. Funded Whitechain transactions, signed Arkiv receipts, public hosting and DON deployment remain unproven.

projects.title: Varada
projects.description: We built Varada. A launchpad for tokens supporting charity’s registered onchain via Endaoment.
projects.project_description: Varada (varada.eth) is a memecoin launchpad on Ethereum mainnet where every trade funds a charity. Each token launches into a Uniswap v4 pool. A custom hook sets a dynamic fee between 1% and 5% and sends the fees to an on-chain vault. The liquidity is locked permanently, so the creator can never pull it. Fees are converted to USDC and split by a fixed rule: 90% goes to the token's cause pool and 10% to the platform. At launch, each token picks a cause focus, such as hunger or endangered species, optionally tied to a region. Every week its holders vote on which nonprofit in that focus receives the money in the pool. The nonprofits are verified organizations listed on Endaoment. Ballots are private: Zama FHE (fully homomorphic encryption) keeps each choice hidden and reveals only the final tally. That means no single wallet's vote can be seen, traded against or used to pressure anyone. Once the week closes, the funds go straight to the winning nonprofit. We have registered hundreds of thousands of ENS's with this.
projects.how_its_made:
The project was built in a group of 2. First things first, we bounced ideas around and quickly concluded that we wanted to do something for the public good. From there, we looked towards charities, followed by DAOs. The idea originally involved a yield-bearing token using Uniswap v4 hooks, but we decided that it didn't quite align with our vision in a UX-friendly way. Other than that, we had a tricky time picking between Hisoka and Nym mixnet. We knew we wanted one of them, as it only made sense given how far we'd leaned into the CROPS side of things.
Besides those planning aspects, we agreed on each of our roles really early on: Tyrese working primarily on the graphics, slides and pitch, along with the related social media content. Camden working primarily on the contracts and integration.

projects.title: Tender
projects.description: Pay with any token, the merchant gets the exact stablecoin. Uniswap v4 hook, Whitechain USDT, x402
projects.project_description: Tender is a checkout where the customer pays with any token they hold and the merchant receives exactly the invoice amount in a stablecoin. projects.title: 0verwatch
projects.description: Overwatch: Contextual AI research and continuous monitoring for prediction markets.
projects.project_description: Overwatch is a Chrome Manifest V3 browser extension and backend intelligence platform that provides contextual multi-agent research Recon and persistent two-tier continuous monitoring Guard Watch + Sentry + Scouting for prediction markets, powered by decentralized inference on 0G Compute.
projects.how_its_made: Overwatch is built as a Chrome extension paired with a smart backend that continuously researches and monitors prediction markets. When you open a market page, the browser extension captures the market details and sends them to a Supervisor Agent (the Sergeant), which pulls live sports scores and match statistics using a set of approved data tools. A dedicated Research Analyst AI then evaluates these facts against the market's outcome rules to estimate probabilities and build a tailored Monitoring Plan. A persistent background worker (Guard Watch) regularly checks for live score or odds updates; when a significant change occurs, a lightweight Monitoring Agent (Sentry) triggers the Supervisor to run a full research update (Scouting) and send a Chrome notification straight to your screen. All AI inferences are powered directly by the user's connected 0G Compute credentials.

projects.description: USDT checkout on Whitechain: customers pay without gas, merchants refund, accountants export.
projects.project_description: Tazor is USDT checkout for businesses on Whitechain, told as one story: the customer pays without gas, the merchant refunds part of it, and the accountant gets the export. The customer pays without gas. A shop adds Tazor to its site in 15 lines: one script, one pay button and one event listener. The customer signs a single message (EIP-3009) from any wallet, or from a demo wallet inside the page, and holds no WBT. Tazor's relayer pays the gas. The signature commits to this merchant, this order and this amount, so nobody, including Tazor, can redirect or change it. It settles on Whitechain in about 4 seconds in the official USDT. The merchant refunds part of it. The merchant side is one more tag, <tazor-merchant-orders>. It shows orders read from Whitechain, one-click refunds and the CSV. A refund is one click and one signature from the merchant, also without gas. The contract sends a refund only to the customer who paid and never more than they paid. The customer can check it on a public receipt read from Whitechain. The accountant gets the export. Every payment and refund for the merchant comes straight from Whitechain, with dates, gross, refunds and net. It exports as CSV, plus Tally, Xero, QuickBooks and camt.054-style files. Because the ledger is the chain itself, the books can't disagree with the money. Merchants get signed webhooks at each step (order.paid, order.ready, order.refunded, order.finality) and choose finality by amount. Small payments are ready to ship as soon as Whitechain confirms them. Big payments wait until Whitechain has posted them to Ethereum. Also built and live on Whitechain Sepolia: Subscriptions: permit-based pulls that can't run early or exceed the plan, cancellable by signature at any time. The relayer renews due ones on a daily schedule. Pay from an exchange: every order has its own deposit address with an EIP-681 QR, so a plain transfer pays it and any overpayment is returned in the same transaction. AI agents paying per request over x402 (eip155:1874), with a spend cap. B2B invoices approved by WhiteBIT-verified people (WB Soul, simulated on testnet) using Face ID or fingerprint passkeys. Company roles live on ENSv2 and are proven onto Whitechain. An Ethereum fallback: if Tazor's servers disappear, a signed payment still lands on Whitechain through the OptimismPortal (measured at 69 s). Who it's for: Tazor serves businesses, and they serve their customers (B2B2C). A business starts in about a minute and gets a renews due ones on a daily schedule. Company roles live on ENSv2 and are proven onto Whitechain. An Ethereum fallback: if Tazor's servers disappear, a signed payment still lands on Whitechain through the OptimismPortal (measured at 69 s). Who it's for: Tazor serves businesses, and they serve their customers (B2B2C). A business starts in about a minute and gets snippet for its site, a hosted payment link and QR if it has no site, and its accountant export. The beachhead is cross-border SMEs, which today lose days and a 1–3% FX spread on every SWIFT payment. The first merchant is Healthsoft in India, a company I work with. It imports components from China and exports remote patient monitoring systems worldwide. Pricing is 0.5% per payment with gas included and no monthly fee. Trust model: the contracts have no owner and no upgrade key, so Tazor can't take or redirect money. The relayer can only refuse to submit, and anyone can submit the same signed payment instead. Everything runs on Whitechain Sepolia with the official USDT, and the README links every transaction.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry, OpenZeppelin 5.5), all source-verified on Whitechain's Blockscout: TazorCheckout is built on the track USDT's EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization. The authorization's nonce is a hash of the merchant, order reference, amount and deadline, so a relayer can't redirect a signed payment. We use receive... rather than transfer..., so only the checkout contract can submit it, which blocks front-running. Refunds are merchant-signed 3009 authorizations. The contract forwards them only to the stored payer and caps the total at the amount paid. Subscriptions take cycle 1 through 3009, then pull later cycles under an EIP-2612 permit. They can't be charged early or above the plan, and they cancel with an EIP-712 signature. The contract publishes its signing domain through ERC-5267. TazorDepositCheckout gives every order its own counterfactual deposit address, an EIP-1167 clone deployed with CREATE2. A plain transfer from an exchange or a "send-only" wallet pays the order. Anyone can settle it. The order amount goes to the merchant, and any extra goes back to the customer in the same transaction. B2B layer: OpenZeppelin ERC-7579 company accounts with a single PolicyHook. ERC-1271 approver accounts that verify passkeys (WebAuthn) through an ERC-7913 verifier on Whitechain's P-256 precompile. Payment and mandate modules that check WB Soul verification, the ENS role, an instant revocation list, two-approver thresholds and limits. No owner key and no upgrade key anywhere. Tests: 320+ Foundry tests. They include 20 fork tests against the real Whitechain Sepolia USDT that try the attacks: a redirected signature, a changed amount, double pay, over-refund, a forged refund, a stranger cancelling, changed plan terms. A Whitechain mainnet fork test impersonates WhiteBIT's operator to revoke a real WB Soul. Relayer (Node and TypeScript with viem, on Vercel): It's optional; anyone can submit the same signed payment. It runs every check before spending gas: signature, payer balance, unused nonce, a validity window of at most 1 h, and an eth_call simulation. It limits requests per IP, payer, merchant and order, and enforces a daily WBT budget and a balance floor. It sends Stripe-style HMAC-signed webhooks (order.paid, order.ready, order.refunded, order.finality). Missed webhooks are rebuilt from chain logs and re-signed. It runs a daily cron for subscription renewals. It's also our own x402 facilitator for eip155:1874 (/supported, /verify, /settle). SDK (@tazor/pay, viem): Framework-free web components: <tazor-pay-button> and <tazor-merchant-orders>. Order watching, EIP-681 payment QR codes, webhook verification and an x402 client. The demo shop integrates it in 15 lines. ERC-7730 clear-signing files describe every message a user signs. A test keeps them byte-identical to what the SDK signs. App: a Next.js static export with no server code. The merchant console, receipts, a customer portal and reports all read Whitechain directly through the CORS-open Blockscout API. Partner technologies: Whitechain: The official USDT's EIP-3009 and permit functions, with their bytes-signature versions that accept ERC-1271 smart-wallet signatures, make gasless pay and refund possible. The P-256 precompile verifies Face ID passkeys on-chain for about 3.5k gas. The L1Block predeploy and EIP-2935 let us prove ENSv2 roles from Ethereum onto Whitechain. The OptimismPortal gives a fallback when Tazor's servers are down. A payment checked on Ethereum by our EnsGate contract landed on Whitechain in 69 s. WB Soul: WhiteBIT's identity registry gates B2B approvers. It's simulated on testnet with a mirror that has the same interface. ENSv2 (Sepolia): each company is a sub-registry such as acme.taz0r.eth, and its APPROVER, ADMIN and AGENT roles authorise payments. Hacky bits: USDT's signing domain: the track USDT exposes no version() or eip712Domain(). We recovered its EIP-712 domain ("Tether USD", "1", chain 1874) by brute-forcing it against DOMAIN_SEPARATOR(). Proving Sepolia blocks: Sepolia's Glamsterdam upgrade added two header fields. We patched Unruggable Gateways' RLP header encoder to append blockAccessListHash and slotNumber, which made Sepolia block hashes match and ENS storage proofs verify on Whitechain. Whitechain RPC quirks: eth_getProof at latest fails on the testnet RPC, so we prove at a hex latest - 5. The RPC rejects decimal block numbers, and log queries are capped at 10k blocks, so we read in 9,000-block chunks. Passkey signatures: about half of WebAuthn signatures are high-s, which OpenZeppelin rejects. We convert DER to low-s (r, s) in the browser, and 100 out of 100 signatures verified on the precompile. Wallet warning: MetaMask's scanner flagged our Ethereum-fallback portal deposit, so we route that step through a public explorer's write-contract page instead.

projects.title: AutoNex
projects.description: 3D multi-agent engineering floor powered by 0G compute, Arkiv DB-Chain, and Ethereum Swarm.
projects.project_description: AUTONEX is a spatially-grounded, multi-agent autonomous software engineering floor. Today’s AI coding tools hit three systemic walls: single-brain saturation where one prompt hallucinating across disciplines causes context drift; black-box terminal dumps that leave engineers blind when agents deadlock; and brittle HTTP 429 rate limits that crash multi-agent simulations. AUTONEX solves this by transforming autonomous engineering into an observable 3D collaborative nexus with dual working modes: AUTONEX Office: A 4-agent agile squad (Diya leading PM, Rohan on backend, Kabir on frontend, Nisha on QA) executing hierarchical task DAGs in an isometric WebGL floor. Swarm Hall: An autonomous council of 10 to 50 specialized agents seated at a grand oval deliberation table executing a bounded 6-phase consensus protocol (Framing, Divergence, Semantic Clustering, Adversarial Critique, Weighted Borda Voting, and Code Synthesis). Instead of crashing on API rate limits, AUTONEX models latency physically: affected agents take a visual "3D Coffee Break" to the pantry while the gateway automatically fails over to fallback models. Every run, deliberation quorum, and permission audit is permanently anchored to the Arkiv Rabdi DB-Chain with zero-gas public reads, while heavy codebase deliverables are content-addressed on Ethereum Swarm with bit-for-bit SHA-256 verification, and inference is routed through 0G Private Compute.
projects.how_its_made: AUTONEX is built across a three-tier architecture: Frontend & 3D Spatial Presentation (React 18.3, Three.js, Vite 5, Zustand, TailwindCSS): We built a 96m x 70m isometric office floor across 14 zones and a 50-seat Swarm Deliberation Hall. To guarantee 60 FPS under heavy LLM event traffic, we decoupled the render loop using procedural low-poly forward kinematics and quaternion lerping over A* navmesh grids rather than heavy skeletal skinning. Asynchronous Mediation Bridge (Node.js/TypeScript & Python/FastAPI): Real-time seq-tracked WebSocket event bus with reconnection replay ( since_seq ). projects.title: Readmit
projects.description: Explains why an EIP-8141 transaction was rejected or failed, and fixes it before you send.
projects.project_description: Readmit is a debugger for EIP-8141 frame transactions on the Ethereum Foundation alt-mempool devnet. Frame transactions are new: one transaction is a list of frames (verify, sender call, paymaster), and when one is rejected by the ERC-8421 mempool rules, or fails on chain, the node gives a terse rule id or a bare revert. Readmit turns that into a plain answer. Paste a transaction hash and it shows what happened frame by frame, with gas used per frame, who paid, which mempool rule fired, and a fix. It also dry-runs a transaction before you send it, so you see the problem without broadcasting. Fixable problems, like a frame running out of gas, come with a machine-readable patch (used gas x 1.25, rounded up) that is applied and re-checked before sending. It also warns when your validation reads storage that someone else can change, such as a Uniswap pool price, which could invalidate a pending transaction. The engine is also available as a standalone TypeScript SDK, @readmit/sdk, on GitHub.
projects.how_its_made: Readmit is a Next.js and TypeScript app, deployed on Vercel, that talks straight to the public alt-mempool devnet (chain 1337). Reads and dry runs go to the ethrex node: ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction returns per-frame gas, success and the ERC-7562 access trace, and eth_getTransactionReceipt returns per-frame receipts. Mempool decisions come from the Skandha-based sidecar through skandha_explorer_getTransaction and listAdmissions. A pure diagnosis engine (diagnose.ts) combines these into findings with stable codes and machine-readable patches. Transactions are encoded and signed with @forshtat/hegota-support and viem, and sent to the sidecar in its wire format. Gas can be paid in a test token (tUSD) through a staked ERC-20 paymaster that we deployed with Foundry; it prices fees from a Uniswap v4 pool, which our fragility check flags. Wallet connection uses wagmi and RainbowKit. Something hacky: browser wallets cannot sign frame transactions yet, so sends are signed by a shared demo account, and the wallet only identifies the user. The engine is split out as @readmit/sdk with viem and ethers adapters and a golden-hash test proving it signs the same bytes as the app.

projects.title: Hundiiii
projects.description: Sell unpaid invoices to verified investors for USDT, atomically.
projects.project_description: Hundi is onchain invoice financing on Whitechain. An exporter usually waits 60 to 90 days to be paid after shipping goods. Selling the invoice at a discount to get cash early is established practice, and regulated platforms such as India's TReDS already support it. Hundi explores what a shared ledger can add. How it works: A verifier approves exporters, importers and investors, with a role, expiry and jurisdiction for each. The exporter issues an invoice with its face value, due date and discount. Only hashes of the reference and document go on chain, and a reference can be registered only once. The importer who owes the money confirms the invoice. No units exist before this, so nothing can be bought early. Verified investors buy all or part of the invoice. USDT goes to the exporter and units go to the investor in one transaction, or neither moves. Investors can resell to other verified investors. Transfers to unverified wallets are blocked by the contract, and transfers stop on the due date. On the due date, the contract collects USDT from the importer and pays whoever holds the units. Investors don't need to do anything, and anyone can trigger settlement. If the importer pays short, the invoice defaults after a grace period and holders share what was recovered, including later recoveries. A regular payment rail only moves money. It can't swap a claim for cash atomically or send repayment to the current holder. Here, both happen in one contract. This is a testnet prototype and doesn't claim to be production-ready. Double financing is only blocked inside Hundi, nothing prices the importer's credit risk, importers must pay onchain, and a token isn't a legal agreement. The README lists these limits in full.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin 5.4, and are deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874). There are two contracts. ParticipantRegistry is a KYB allowlist holding roles, expiry, jurisdiction and freeze status. HundiInvoice is an ERC-1155 where each token id is one invoice and one unit equals 0.000001 USDT of face value. All transfer rules sit in the _update hook, so direct and batch transfers can't bypass them. All units are minted to the exporter when the importer confirms, and funding simply moves them to investors, so partial fills need no special handling. Design details: holders are tracked on chain with EnumerableSet, so paying out needs no indexer. The USDT has a blocklist, so distribution uses trySafeTransfer and one blocked wallet can't stop everyone else being paid. A failed collection doesn't revert, so an invoice can't get stuck open. Claims are tracked per holder, so a holder who collects early still shares in later recoveries after a default. The frontend is Next.js 16 with wagmi, viem and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel, with a screen for each party and a public timeline per invoice. Every transaction is simulated first, so a contract rule appears as a clear message before the wallet asks for a signature. A small TypeScript keeper settles due invoices and pays holders, but settle and distribute are permissionless, so anyone can run them. Partner technology: Whitechain settles everything in its USDT. 1-second blocks make a multi-party flow feel instant, viem already includes the chain and Multicall3 handles batched reads. Blockscout verification worked on the first try. We tested against the real USDT on an Anvil fork before spending scarce faucet WBT. The USDT supports permit, so we also built and fork-tested fundWithPermit, though the app still uses approve then fund. Hacky bits: the public RPC rejects log queries over 10,000 blocks, which broke our approved list and invoice history once the chain passed that point, so the app now reads events in chunks. Short due dates and a 60-second grace period exist only for the demo. Fork testing used a window.ethereum shim to drive the UI without a real wallet. AI tools (Claude Code) generated most of the code, tests and docs under my direction, as documented in AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: GhostProof
projects.description: Bug bounties that pay on proof: exploits replayed on a chain fork, base reward paid on-chain
projects.project_description: Ghostproof is a bug-bounty platform where hackers get paid on proof, not on promises. Today, a researcher who reports a real bug often gets ghosted: no reply, no deadline, no pay. The company decides what the bug is worth after it has already seen it. Companies have the opposite problem: their inbox fills with spam, repeat reports and bugs that don't really work. Ghostproof fixes both. The company writes its rules before any bug is seen and locks a reward pool in a smart contract. One rule is mandatory: a stranger must never walk off with other people's money. A hacker submits the attack as a small runnable test. Before anything else, it passes three filters: World ID (one real human, one submission), a safety guard that blocks hostile code, and a duplicate check (the same attack, even reformatted, is only paid once). Our checker then replays the attack on a copy of the chain (a fork) and measures how much money moved. No AI decides this. If the attack breaks one of the company's pre-written rules, the pool contract automatically pays the hacker a base reward. That amount is set by the rule's severity, capped at the company's auto-pay limit and a monthly cap. An AI then writes a plain-language evidence report to help the company decide on any bonus, and the outcome is published to a public record on Arkiv. That record doubles as each company's reputation page. Hackers get a guaranteed incentive, fast feedback and full transparency. Companies get less noise, faster checking of reports, capped costs and a public track record that shows they pay. Runs on Ethereum Sepolia with test USDC, which has no real value.
projects.how_its_made: Three parts talking over HTTP and a contract ABI, built by three people on separate branches. Contracts (Solidity + Foundry, deployed to Ethereum Sepolia): a bounty pool that holds the company's test USDC, a rules contract with severity tiers, and a deliberately vulnerable vault as the demo target. The pool itself enforces the limits: the base payout is min(tier amount, auto-pay limit), further capped by the month's remaining allowance, and the pool is locked while a report is open. Backend (Node + TypeScript): the checker spins up a fork of Sepolia (anvil, with a direct forge test --fork-url fallback in case anvil misbehaves live) and runs the hacker's Exploit.t.sol against it, then decodes the run into a step-by-step replay of what the chain did. Every submission is treated as hostile: a guard rejects vm.ffi, vm.env, file cheatcodes and outside RPC calls before compiling, the sandbox has ffi = false and no file permissions, there is a size cap, and a hard timeout kills runaway processes. Duplicate detection hashes the exploit after stripping comments and whitespace, so reformatting an old attack won't earn a second payout. Partner tech: World ID: one verified human = one submission, which kills spam accounts. Proofs are verified on our backend only, never trusted from the browser (IDKit 4.x). Arkiv: the public record of every outcome. We use its built-in expiry so a report the company ignores expires on its own. The frontend reads it back to show each company's reputation stats. AI: one LLM call per report (via OpenRouter) turns the measured numbers into a readable evidence report. It is labelled "advice only" and never touches the money path, because mentors told us companies won't release funds on an AI's opinion. A pre-written fallback report keeps the demo alive if the API is slow. Frontend: Next.js, wagmi and viem, with a neo-brutalist UI. Three screens: company, hacker and public record. Hacky bits: the checker runs on one server standing in for a sealed computer (TEE). The payout function already has a signature slot reserved for a future sealed-checker signature. Built with help from Claude Code; see AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: OpenAid
projects.description: Zero-custody aid procurement & staged settlement eliminating corruption in charity.
projects.project_description:
Traditional humanitarian and disaster relief systems suffer from severe opacity, high administrative overhead, and the constant risk of fund misappropriation. In typical charity setups, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) maintain complete, unilateral custody over donated capital. If accounts are compromised, administrators are corrupt, or local officials demand kickbacks, donor funds can be siphoned or misallocated with zero auditability. Furthermore, procurement is often conducted behind closed doors without transparent price discovery, leading to inflated supplier margins, phantom deliveries, and kickback schemes. OpenAid Protocol (Pravaha) re-architects disaster relief as a trust-minimized, multi-actor state machine deployed on EVM-compatible blockchains. It enforces a strict separation of powers between Donors, NGOs, Suppliers, and Independent Ground Validators. THE CARDINAL PROTOCOL INVARIANT:
No participant—not even the NGO campaign creator, the protocol deployer, or any administrative multisig—shall ever possess the capability to unilaterally withdraw, sweep, redirect, or siphon escrowed funds to an arbitrary address. Escrowed donor capital can only leave the protocol under two strictly enforced, mutually exclusive mathematical conditions: Verified Staged Settlement: Payout is released directly to the winning supplier who submitted the lowest valid revealed bid and whose physical delivery manifest was verified by an on-chain validator quorum. Deterministic Proportional Donor Refund: Payout is returned proportionally to original donors via pull-based withdrawals if a campaign fails to fund, auction reveal fails, no supplier bids, delivery times out, or a challenge is upheld. CORE LIFECYCLE & WORKFLOW: Campaign Creation & Sub-Vault Isolation: An NGO defines supply specifications, budget ceilings, and delivery coordinates without touching capital. Multi-item relief drives (e.g., Food $50k vs. Blankets $30k) are partitioned into isolated sub-vaults—a supplier failure in one sub-vault never locks or drains another. Direct Escrow Funding: Donors deposit USDC directly into immutable smart contract escrow. The NGO’s balance remains strictly zero. Sealed Commit–Reveal Procurement Auction: Qualified suppliers submit cryptographic bid commitments (keccak256(bidAmount, salt, vendorAddress)), followed by a reveal window. This prevents front-running, bid-sniping, and supplier price-fixing. The lowest valid bid is programmatically awarded the contract. Physical Delivery & Tamper-Evident Evidence: The winning supplier fulfills the shipment and uploads GPS coordinates, multi-angle photos, and carrier waybills, pinning the root manifest CID to IPFS. Decentralized Multi-Node Evidence Verification (Chainlink CRE + Gemini AI): A specialized 4-node Decentralized Oracle Network (DON) cross-references carrier tracking APIs (verifying DELIVERED status), checks Haversine spatial geofences (verifying delivery inside the flood zone), and passes waybills to Google Gemini AI for optical character extraction and RFP specification matching. Sybil-Resistant Validator Quorum (World ID): A dynamic 5-member validator panel drawn from a pool of 14 verified individuals using the Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling algorithm reviews evidence and casts on-chain attestation votes. Beneficiaries submit zero-knowledge Semaphore proofs with anti-replay nullifier tracking. Two-Stage Payout with Challenge Timelock: Tranche 1 (70%): Released immediately to the supplier upon 3-of-5 validator quorum attestation to cover logistics and fulfillment costs. Challenge Window: A 72-hour timelock window opens during which any participant can submit counter-evidence. Tranche 2 (30%): Released automatically upon challenge window expiry without an active dispute. If a dispute is substantiated, the remaining 30% plus the defaulted vendor's slashed bond are refunded proportionally to original donors.
projects.how_its_made:
We built OpenAid Protocol to tackle a frustrating real-world issue: humanitarian aid disappearing into opaque NGO bank accounts. We wanted a system where code—not charity executives—holds custody and programmatically enforces delivery. The Nitty-Gritty & Architecture:
We started in Arc Studio to write and test our core settlement engine (OpenAidEscrow.sol), deploying it directly on Arc Testnet (Chain ID 5042002) with native Circle USDC (0x3600...0000, 6 decimals). The contract enforces a zero-custody invariant: donor capital routes into isolated sub-vaults (e.g., Food $50k vs. Blankets $30k) so one vendor's failure never stalls another's payout. Settlements are split into two stages: 70% immediate release upon 3-of-5 validator quorum attestation to cover vendor costs, and 30% locked behind a 72-hour timelocked challenge window. If a vendor defaults or delivery times out, donors pull back 100% of remaining funds through deterministic proportional math. Our frontend is a Next.js 14 App Router dashboard built with TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Ethers.js v6. Storing itemized bills of quantities and tenders on-chain would cost hundreds in gas, but using AWS or PostgreSQL would recreate the exact centralized point of failure we want to eliminate. We solved this with Arkiv: all tender RFPs, sealed bid commitments, shipping waybills, and audit logs live on Arkiv Rabdi Testnet (Chain ID 7794095) under the openaid.v1.* schema. Arkiv's native expiresAt TTL prunes expired tenders automatically, giving us decentralized queryability without recurring storage gas fees. How Partner Tech Leveled Us Up: Arc (Circle L1): Allowed us to build institutional-grade escrow with sub-second finality and native 6-decimal USDC accounting without bridging friction. Arkiv Network: Replaced custodial Web2 databases with cryptographically wallet-owned entities and automated state pruning. World ID & IDKit v1.3: Powers our Dynamic Validator Selection via the Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling algorithm (drawing 5 active validators and 3 alternates from a 14-member panel with conflict screening) and enables on-the-ground beneficiaries to generate zero-knowledge Semaphore proofs confirming receipt of aid. Chainlink CRE: Orchestrates our multi-node off-chain evidence pipeline before human reviewers vote, computing 3-of-4 Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus across logistics APIs, spatial geofences, and OCR matching. Particularly Hacky Things We Did: The AI-Oracle Handshake: Real disaster aid involves wrinkled paper bills of lading and handwritten carrier waybills. Inside our Chainlink CRE DON simulation, we wrote a specialized node that dispatches the uploaded delivery invoice to Google Gemini AI. Gemini extracts line items, quantities, and carrier stamps, and cross-checks them against the RFP specifications in Arkiv. If a supplier bid 500 blankets but the carrier invoice shows 420, the CRE node catches the discrepancy and fails BFT consensus! Venue Wi-Fi & PII Defense: To survive spotty hackathon Wi-Fi and automated GitHub Actions CI, we wrote an isomorphic TypeScript adapter for Arkiv with an in-memory deterministic fallback. We baked in a custom client-side regex interceptor (validatePublicSuitability) that screens payloads for PII (names, phone numbers, private keys) and aborts before sensitive data can leak onto the public DB-chain. projects.project_description_markdown:
Traditional humanitarian and disaster relief systems suffer from severe opacity, high administrative overhead, and the constant risk of fund misappropriation. In typical charity setups, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) maintain complete, unilateral custody over donated capital. If accounts are compromised, administrators are corrupt, or local officials demand kickbacks, donor funds can be siphoned or misallocated with zero auditability. Furthermore, procurement is often conducted behind closed doors without transparent price discovery, leading to inflated supplier margins, phantom deliveries, and kickback schemes.

OpenAid Protocol (Pravaha) re-architects disaster relief as a trust-minimized, multi-actor state machine deployed on EVM-compatible blockchains. It enforces a strict separation of powers between Donors, NGOs, Suppliers, and Independent Ground Validators.

THE CARDINAL PROTOCOL INVARIANT:
No participant—not even the NGO campaign creator, the protocol deployer, or any administrative multisig—shall ever possess the capability to unilaterally withdraw, sweep, redirect, or siphon escrowed funds to an arbitrary address.

Escrowed donor capital can only leave the protocol under two strictly enforced, mutually exclusive mathematical conditions:
1. Verified Staged Settlement: Payout is released directly to the winning supplier who submitted the lowest valid revealed bid and whose physical delivery manifest was verified by an on-chain validator quorum.
2. Deterministic Proportional Donor Refund: Payout is returned proportionally to original donors via pull-based withdrawals if a campaign fails to fund, auction reveal fails, no supplier bids, delivery times out, or a challenge is upheld.

CORE LIFECYCLE & WORKFLOW:
1. Campaign Creation & Sub-Vault Isolation: An NGO defines supply specifications, budget ceilings, and delivery coordinates without touching capital. Multi-item relief drives (e.g., Food $50k vs. Blankets $30k) are partitioned into isolated sub-vaults—a supplier failure in one sub-vault never locks or drains another.
2. Direct Escrow Funding: Donors deposit USDC directly into immutable smart contract escrow. The NGO’s balance remains strictly zero.
3. Sealed Commit–Reveal Procurement Auction: Qualified suppliers submit cryptographic bid commitments (keccak256(bidAmount, salt, vendorAddress)), followed by a reveal window. This prevents front-running, bid-sniping, and supplier price-fixing. The lowest valid bid is programmatically awarded the contract.
4. Physical Delivery & Tamper-Evident Evidence: The winning supplier fulfills the shipment and uploads GPS coordinates, multi-angle photos, and carrier waybills, pinning the root manifest CID to IPFS.
5. Decentralized Multi-Node Evidence Verification (Chainlink CRE + Gemini AI): A specialized 4-node Decentralized Oracle Network (DON) cross-references carrier tracking APIs (verifying DELIVERED status), checks Haversine spatial geofences (verifying delivery inside the flood zone), and passes waybills to Google Gemini AI for optical character extraction and RFP specification matching.
6. Sybil-Resistant Validator Quorum (World ID): A dynamic 5-member validator panel drawn from a pool of 14 verified individuals using the Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling algorithm reviews evidence and casts on-chain attestation votes. Beneficiaries submit zero-knowledge Semaphore proofs with anti-replay nullifier tracking.
7. Two-Stage Payout with Challenge Timelock:
- Tranche 1 (70%): Released immediately to the supplier upon 3-of-5 validator quorum attestation to cover logistics and fulfillment costs.
- Challenge Window: A 72-hour timelock window opens during which any participant can submit counter-evidence.
- Tranche 2 (30%): Released automatically upon challenge window expiry without an active dispute. If a dispute is substantiated, the remaining 30% plus the defaulted vendor's slashed bond are refunded proportionally to original donors.

We built OpenAid Protocol to tackle a frustrating real-world issue: humanitarian aid disappearing into opaque NGO bank accounts. We wanted a system where code—not charity executives—holds custody and programmatically enforces delivery.

The Nitty-Gritty & Architecture:
We started in Arc Studio to write and test our core settlement engine (OpenAidEscrow.sol), deploying it directly on Arc Testnet (Chain ID 5042002) with native Circle USDC (0x3600...0000, 6 decimals). The contract enforces a zero-custody invariant: donor capital routes into isolated sub-vaults (e.g., Food $50k vs. Blankets $30k) so one vendor's failure never stalls another's payout. Settlements are split into two stages: 70% immediate release upon 3-of-5 validator quorum attestation to cover vendor costs, and 30% locked behind a 72-hour timelocked challenge window. If a vendor defaults or delivery times out, donors pull back 100% of remaining funds through deterministic proportional math.

Our frontend is a Next.js 14 App Router dashboard built with TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Ethers.js v6. Storing itemized bills of quantities and tenders on-chain would cost hundreds in gas, but using AWS or PostgreSQL would recreate the exact centralized point of failure we want to eliminate. We solved this with Arkiv: all tender RFPs, sealed bid commitments, shipping waybills, and audit logs live on Arkiv Rabdi Testnet (Chain ID 7794095) under the openaid.v1.* schema. Arkiv's native expiresAt TTL prunes expired tenders automatically, giving us decentralized queryability without recurring storage gas fees.

How Partner Tech Leveled Us Up:
- Arc (Circle L1): Allowed us to build institutional-grade escrow with sub-second finality and native 6-decimal USDC accounting without bridging friction.
- Arkiv Network: Replaced custodial Web2 databases with cryptographically wallet-owned entities and automated state pruning.
- World ID & IDKit v1.3: Powers our Dynamic Validator Selection via the Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling algorithm (drawing 5 active validators and 3 alternates from a 14-member panel with conflict screening) and enables on-the-ground beneficiaries to generate zero-knowledge Semaphore proofs confirming receipt of aid.
- Chainlink CRE: Orchestrates our multi-node off-chain evidence pipeline before human reviewers vote, computing 3-of-4 Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus across logistics APIs, spatial geofences, and OCR matching.

Particularly Hacky Things We Did:
1. The AI-Oracle Handshake: Real disaster aid involves wrinkled paper bills of lading and handwritten carrier waybills. Inside our Chainlink CRE DON simulation, we wrote a specialized node that dispatches the uploaded delivery invoice to Google Gemini AI. Gemini extracts line items, quantities, and carrier stamps, and cross-checks them against the RFP specifications in Arkiv. If a supplier bid 500 blankets but the carrier invoice shows 420, the CRE node catches the discrepancy and fails BFT consensus!

We baked in a custom client-side regex interceptor (validatePublicSuitability) that screens payloads for PII (names, phone numbers, private keys) and aborts before sensitive data can leak onto the public DB-chain.
3. Beneficiary Anti-Replay Nullifiers: To prevent bad actors from re-submitting the same delivery proof to drain multiple sub-campaigns, we bound the World ID action hash to keccak256(campaignId, subVaultId, manifestCid) and built an anti-replay shield in our API routes that rejects recycled nullifiers with HTTP 409 Conflict.

Everything is tested and live: 115 automated tests passing across contracts and partner modules, with a live production deployment at pravahaprotocol.vercel.app.

projects.title: Numa
projects.description: Gasless USDT checkout that pays creators only when a real sale settles. Fake clicks earn $0.
projects.project_description: numa is a drop-in USDT checkout and creator marketplace on Whitechain Sepolia. Advertisers usually pay for clicks, and bots fake clicks, so merchants pay for traffic that never buys. With numa a creator earns a commission only when a real, buyer-authorized USDT payment settles on-chain. A merchant creates a campaign with a commission rate. Creators publish a profile and an offer, get approved, and share an attribution link. A buyer pays in USDT with one signature and no gas token: the merchant signs the order, the buyer signs an EIP-3009 authorization, and our relayer submits it. NumaRouter splits the payment atomically: the merchant's net, the creator's commission (held by the contract through a refund window, then released automatically) and a protocol fee. If a refund happens inside the window the held commission is clawed back. The business never holds the money in between. Every settled sale produces a public receipt, and a creator's reputation counts only conversions that match an on-chain OrderSettled event, so history cannot be faked. Merchants get an accountant-ready CSV export. Optional negotiation agents can haggle the commission over Arkiv inside private limits, and the merchant still signs the final on-chain step.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Foundry, OpenZeppelin): CampaignRegistry and NumaRouter, deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia. The buyer's EIP-3009 nonce is an EIP-712 commitment to the full order and split, which the router recomputes, so a relayer cannot swap the creator, amount or terms. 55 unit, fuzz and invariant tests. Backend (Node, Fastify, viem, Postgres): a relayer that only calls the router, verifies both signatures locally, simulates first, and enforces a gas ceiling, daily cap and per-address limit; a reconciler for uncertain sends; an indexer; and a keeper that releases commission after the refund window using chain time. We rehearsed the whole flow on an anvil fork of Whitechain Sepolia against the real USDT proxy, which caught a real out-of-gas bug before launch. Arkiv (SDK 1.0.1 on Rabdi): campaigns, offers, decisions, links, conversions, profiles, invites, endorsements and negotiation messages are wallet-owned entities with expiry. Anyone can write any entity, so every read checks the owner and, for money, the chain. Writes go through a serialized safe writer with explicit nonce, gas and gas price, and we verified browser-wallet-style writes. Frontend and SDK: React and Vite, plus an sdk-react checkout component and a demo shop that adds it in about 20 lines. Agents use a rules engine for every decision; Gemini or Claude only phrases a note. Hosted on Render and Vercel.

projects.title: Erodoro
projects.description: Buy the upside of a stock in $1 slices. One allowance per human, settled at Chainlink's price.
projects.project_description: Rips sell the upside of a tokenized stock in $1 slices. A stock holder locks stock in Erodoro's vault, which splits it into a capped claim they keep and an upside claim above today's price + 5%. Buyers pay $1 for slices of that upside; at expiry the vault settles at the stock's price and pays the upside out in the stock itself, so real stock backs every payout. Three things stood between that and something people can use: Who gets the small inventory. Each batch holds about $50 of upside. Without proof of personhood, one buyer with many wallets takes it all. With World ID, each person has one allowance per batch, counted across every wallet they verify. Who sets the settlement price. The house sells Rips, so it must not set the price it pays out. A Chainlink CRE workflow brings Chainlink's stock feeds from Base mainnet to the settlement oracle on Base Sepolia, and the vault settles at the first report after expiry. Getting out before expiry. Rips couldn't be resold. Each Rip now has a Uniswap v4 pool against USDC, behind a hook that only lets verified humans trade. Everything runs on Base Sepolia with real transactions: verify with World ID, buy Rips (any quantity, split across transactions), stay within the per-person limit, trade on Uniswap, and settle and redeem after expiry.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.28): CreSettlementOracle implements Erodoro's oracle interface, stores every CRE price report and returns the first one at or after maturity. HumanRegistry binds wallets to World ID nullifiers, takes reports from the CRE forwarder and caps each person's spend per batch; the Rips pool checks it before every sale. RipsResaleHook is a Uniswap v4 hook (beforeSwap, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeInitialize; address mined with CREATE2) that finds the real user through Universal Router's and PositionManager's msgSender() and requires a verified human. Chainlink CRE (TypeScript SDK): two workflows. rips-prices: cron, then latestRoundData on ten Chainlink stock feeds on Base mainnet, then one signed report to Base Sepolia. verify-human: HTTP trigger with the IDKit proof; it checks the action, Proof of Human and that the signal is the buyer's wallet, calls World's verify API through the HTTP capability with consensus (retried, since CRE caps HTTP calls at 10 seconds), and reports the result to the registry. CRE let us settle at a price the house doesn't control, and do World ID verification without running our own trusted backend. World ID (IDKit 4): IDKitRequestWidget requests Proof of Human, World ID 4.0 only, with the wallet as the signal so a proof can't be replayed for another wallet. A small verifier signs the request context with the RP key and starts the CRE workflow; the app itself is static. World ID is what makes "one allowance per person" possible when wallets are free. Uniswap v4: upside claims are wrapped 1:1 as ERC-20 and pooled against USDC at the house price, with full-range liquidity added through PositionManager. The app quotes with V4Quoter and swaps through Universal Router (V4_SWAP: SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE, SETTLE_ALL, TAKE_ALL) with Permit2. This gave Rips an exit before expiry without building our own exchange. App: Next.js 16, wagmi and viem. We tested by driving a real browser against Base Sepolia, and recorded the demo the same way with Playwright and a scripted cursor. Hacky bit: the CRE simulation forwarder accepts reports from anyone, so both on-chain receivers also pin the account that runs the simulation. With deploy access they switch to Chainlink's live forwarder and drop the pin.
