projects.title: LandChain
projects.description: LandChain: A Hedera-powered land marketplace for verified listings and fractional ownership
projects.project_description: LandChain – A Transparent, Blockchain-Powered Land Marketplace 1. Project Overview LandChain is a blockchain-powered digital land marketplace built on the Hedera network. It aims to make property discovery, document verification, transaction tracking, and fractional investment demonstrations more transparent, accessible, and trustworthy. The project addresses common challenges in traditional real estate transactions, including complex documentation, limited transparency, difficulties in verifying property-related information, dependence on intermediaries, and the high financial barrier to investing in valuable land. LandChain brings buyers and sellers together through a unified digital platform where sellers can list properties, submit supporting documents for verification, and make property information accessible to potential buyers. Buyers can explore listings, review verification reports, evaluate property details, and participate in a demonstration of fractional ownership using blockchain-based digital tokens. By integrating Hedera Smart Contract Service (HSCS), Hedera Token Service (HTS), Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), and Hedera Mirror Node, LandChain demonstrates how distributed ledger technology can improve the transparency, traceability, and accessibility of real estate-related digital workflows. 2. Problem Statement Traditional land acquisition and property investment involve several challenges: Complex Documentation: Property transactions require multiple documents, including ownership records, land records, supporting certificates, and other legal paperwork. Verification Difficulties: Buyers may struggle to independently assess the authenticity and completeness of documents submitted by sellers. Limited Transparency: Property-related activities and verification updates are often scattered across different parties and systems. High Investment Barriers: Purchasing an entire property requires substantial capital, making real estate investment inaccessible to many individuals. Lack of Traceability: Tracking document verification activities and transaction-related updates can be difficult when records are maintained through disconnected systems. LandChain explores how blockchain technology can address these challenges by creating a transparent, traceable, and digitally accessible property marketplace. 3. Our Solution LandChain provides a unified platform with two primary user roles: A. Sellers Sellers can: Register and create their profiles. Submit property information, including location, area, price, and description. Upload supporting property documents. Submit properties for document verification. View verification reports and their respective statuses. Make verified-status property listings available for buyer discovery. B. Buyers Buyers can: Register and connect their cryptocurrency wallets. Explore available property listings. View property information, pricing, and supporting verification details. Check whether submitted documents are Verified, Pending, or Rejected. Select investment units in the fractional ownership demonstration. Interact with smart contracts for simulated property purchase workflows. View blockchain transactions and token allocation records. 4. Document Verification System One of LandChain's important features is its document verification module. Sellers upload supporting property documents, which are evaluated against a predefined verification checklist. The system processes the submitted information and generates a verification report. The verification system categorises document submissions into three statuses: Verified: The submitted documents satisfy the predefined checks. Pending: Additional information or review is required. Rejected: The submitted documents fail the defined checks or require resubmission. For document integrity, LandChain generates cryptographic hashes of submitted documents and records these hashes on the Hedera network. This creates tamper-evident references that allow the platform to identify whether a document has changed after its hash was recorded. Importantly, a matching hash proves document integrity relative to the recorded version; it does not independently establish legal ownership, document authenticity, or government approval. Sensitive documents and personal information are not exposed directly on the blockchain. 5. Fractional Ownership Demonstration Real estate is traditionally an expensive asset class because purchasing an entire property requires significant capital. LandChain explores the concept of fractional ownership through blockchain-based digital tokens. Using Hedera Token Service (HTS), the platform creates digital tokens representing smaller units of a property's simulated value. For example, if a property is assigned a demonstration value of ₹10,00,000, the platform can divide its simulated value into 10,000 units, with each unit representing ₹100 of the demonstration value. Multiple participants can select and acquire different quantities of these digital tokens through the platform's demonstration workflow. The token allocation is recorded on Hedera, allowing participants to observe how blockchain-based tokenisation can represent fractional participation in a property-related asset. This feature demonstrates the technical possibilities of tokenisation. The tokens used in the current prototype do not independently provide legally recognised land ownership, title rights, or enforceable claims over the underlying property. 6. Hedera Technology Integration LandChain utilises multiple components of the Hedera ecosystem, with each service serving a specific purpose. 1. Hedera Smart Contract Service (HSCS) We use Solidity-based smart contracts deployed through Hedera Smart Contract Service to execute the simulated property purchase workflow. Smart contracts help manage predefined transaction conditions and the purchase demonstration process, reducing dependence on manual coordination for the on-chain workflow. 2. Hedera Token Service (HTS) HTS is used to create and manage digital tokens representing fractional units of a property's simulated value. It demonstrates token creation, distribution, and allocation among multiple participants. 3. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) HCS provides timestamped, consensus-ordered records of relevant platform activities, such as document verification updates and property-related workflow events. This enables transparent tracking of recorded events. 4. Hedera Mirror Node The Hedera Mirror Node allows the platform to retrieve and display blockchain transaction information, including relevant transaction details and token-related activity. It helps buyers and sellers inspect the history of recorded on-chain operations. 5. MetaMask Wallet Integration MetaMask enables users to connect their wallets and interact with the blockchain functionality of the platform. Users can initiate supported transactions and participate in the smart contract interaction workflow. 7. Complete Platform Workflow The LandChain workflow follows these steps: User Registration: Buyers and sellers register and access their respective dashboards. Property Listing: Sellers submit property details, including location, area, price, and descriptions. Document Submission: Sellers upload supporting documents for evaluation. Document Verification: The verification module evaluates submitted documents against predefined requirements and generates a verification report. Blockchain Integrity Recording: Cryptographic document hashes are recorded on Hedera to provide tamper-evident references. Marketplace Discovery: Buyers browse available listings and examine their property details and verification statuses. Fractional Unit Selection: Buyers select the quantity of demonstration investment units they wish to acquire. Smart Contract Interaction: The platform executes the simulated purchase workflow through Solidity smart contracts. Token Allocation: HTS manages the corresponding digital token allocation. Transaction Tracking: Relevant blockchain records can be retrieved through the Hedera Mirror Node and displayed to users. 8. What Makes LandChain Different? LandChain combines several blockchain capabilities into a single property marketplace demonstration rather than focusing on token creation alone. Its key differentiating aspects include: Combining document integrity tracking with property discovery. Providing a structured document verification workflow with transparent status reporting. Using cryptographic hashes to create tamper-evident document references. Demonstrating fractional property participation through Hedera Token Service. Using smart contracts to execute a simulated purchase workflow. Recording important platform activities through Hedera Consensus Service. Providing blockchain transaction visibility through the Mirror Node. Integrating wallet connectivity for blockchain interactions. The combination of these components demonstrates how blockchain infrastructure can support a more transparent and accessible digital real estate ecosystem. 9. Technology Stack Blockchain Network: Hedera Testnet Smart Contracts: Solidity Smart Contract Infrastructure: Hedera Smart Contract Service Tokenisation: Hedera Token Service Consensus and Activity Records: Hedera Consensus Service Blockchain Data Retrieval: Hedera Mirror Node Wallet Integration: MetaMask Document Integrity: Cryptographic hashing Document Processing: Automated checklist-based evaluation Platform: Web-based buyer and seller marketplace 10. Project Scope and Future Possibilities LandChain is currently a prototype demonstrating blockchain-based property workflows on Hedera Testnet. Future development could include: Integration with authorised government land-record databases. More comprehensive legal document validation and verification. Integration with trusted third-party verification agencies. Real-world property title verification. Legally compliant fractional ownership structures. Secure payment gateway and automated settlement integration. Multi-party property transaction management. Improved identity verification and fraud detection. Expansion to additional real estate asset categories. Any real-world deployment involving property ownership or investment would require appropriate legal structures, regulatory compliance, trusted verification authorities, and integration with official property registration systems. 11. Our Vision Our vision is to explore how blockchain technology can make real estate-related information, document verification activities, and digital transactions more transparent, traceable, and accessible. We believe that combining document integrity, decentralised infrastructure, smart contracts, and tokenisation can provide a foundation for a more accessible digital property ecosystem. LandChain – From Property Discovery to Digital Ownership. Powered by Hedera.
projects.how_its_made: How We Built LandChain* We built LandChain as a full-stack blockchain-powered land marketplace using Hedera Testnet, combining traditional web technologies with decentralized infrastructure to demonstrate transparent property verification and fractional ownership. 1. Frontend and Backend Architecture We developed a web-based application with separate Buyer and Seller dashboards. The frontend communicates with our backend through APIs to handle user registration, authentication, property listings, document uploads, verification status and transaction information. Users can register using mobile OTP authentication, connect their crypto wallets through MetaMask and select their roles. We also implemented a simulated KYC workflow for demonstration purposes. 2. Document Verification and Hedera Integration When a seller uploads property documents, our verification module checks them against a predefined checklist and generates a report with Verified, Pending or Rejected statuses. To provide tamper-evident document tracking, we generate cryptographic hashes of uploaded documents rather than storing sensitive documents directly on-chain. These hashes and verification activity records are submitted to Hedera for timestamped tracking. 3. Fractional Ownership Using Hedera Token Service One of our major implementations is fractional ownership demonstration using Hedera Token Service (HTS). We create testnet tokens representing smaller units of a sample property's simulated value. Buyers can select investment units, and the platform demonstrates token allocation and ownership percentage calculations. This showcases how Hedera can support digital asset creation and management. 4. Smart Contracts Using Solidity We use Solidity and Hedera Smart Contract Service to implement the simulated property purchase workflow. When a buyer selects investment units, the smart contract handles the transaction logic and records relevant information, including the buyer, seller, property ID and token allocation. 5. Hedera Consensus Service and Mirror Node We use Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) for timestamped verification and platform activity records. Hedera Mirror Node helps retrieve transaction information and display blockchain activity in our application. This allows users to explore transaction history and independently verify relevant activities through Hedera Testnet Explorer. 6. What Makes Our Implementation Interesting? Instead of building another conventional property-listing website, we connected property discovery, document verification, digital asset representation and blockchain transaction tracking into one workflow. Our interesting approach is the combination of off-chain document storage and on-chain cryptographic hashes. This avoids exposing sensitive property documents while providing a way to detect changes to the original files. We also distinguish between digital ownership representation and legally recognised land ownership. Our project uses fictional properties and testnet tokens to demonstrate the technology without claiming to transfer actual land titles. Partner Technology – Hedera Hedera is the core infrastructure behind LandChain. Its Smart Contract Service, Token Service, Consensus Service and Mirror Node allow us to demonstrate programmable transactions, digital token management, timestamped records and transparent transaction tracking within a single ecosystem. LandChain demonstrates how decentralized infrastructure can make property-related digital transactions more transparent, traceable and accessible.*

LandChain brings buyers and sellers together through a unified digital platform where sellers can list properties, submit supporting documents for verification, and make property information accessible to potential buyers. Buyers can explore listings, review verification reports, evaluate property details, and participate in a demonstration of fractional ownership using blockchain-based digital tokens.

By integrating Hedera Smart Contract Service (HSCS), Hedera Token Service (HTS), Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), and Hedera Mirror Node, LandChain demonstrates how distributed ledger technology can improve the transparency, traceability, and accessibility of real estate-related digital workflows.

## 2. Problem Statement

Traditional land acquisition and property investment involve several challenges:

- **Complex Documentation:** Property transactions require multiple documents, including ownership records, land records, supporting certificates, and other legal paperwork.
- **Verification Difficulties:** Buyers may struggle to independently assess the authenticity and completeness of documents submitted by sellers.
- **Limited Transparency:** Property-related activities and verification updates are often scattered across different parties and systems.
- **High Investment Barriers:** Purchasing an entire property requires substantial capital, making real estate investment inaccessible to many individuals.
- **Lack of Traceability:** Tracking document verification activities and transaction-related updates can be difficult when records are maintained through disconnected systems.

LandChain explores how blockchain technology can address these challenges by creating a transparent, traceable, and digitally accessible property marketplace.

## 3. Our Solution

LandChain provides a unified platform with two primary user roles:

**A. Sellers**

Sellers can:
- Register and create their profiles.
- Submit property information, including location, area, price, and description.
- Upload supporting property documents.
- Submit properties for document verification.
- View verification reports and their respective statuses.
- Make verified-status property listings available for buyer discovery.

**B. Buyers**

Buyers can:
- Register and connect their cryptocurrency wallets.
- Explore available property listings.
- View property information, pricing, and supporting verification details.
- Check whether submitted documents are Verified, Pending, or Rejected.
- Select investment units in the fractional ownership demonstration.
- Interact with smart contracts for simulated property purchase workflows.
- View blockchain transactions and token allocation records.

## 4. Document Verification System

One of LandChain's important features is its document verification module.

Sellers upload supporting property documents, which are evaluated against a predefined verification checklist. The system processes the submitted information and generates a verification report.

The verification system categorises document submissions into three statuses:

- **Verified:** The submitted documents satisfy the predefined checks.
- **Pending:** Additional information or review is required.
- **Rejected:** The submitted documents fail the defined checks or require resubmission.

For document integrity, LandChain generates cryptographic hashes of submitted documents and records these hashes on the Hedera network.

This creates tamper-evident references that allow the platform to identify whether a document has changed after its hash was recorded.

Importantly, a matching hash proves document integrity relative to the recorded version; it does not independently establish legal ownership, document authenticity, or government approval.

Sensitive documents and personal information are not exposed directly on the blockchain.

## 5. Fractional Ownership Demonstration

Real estate is traditionally an expensive asset class because purchasing an entire property requires significant capital.

LandChain explores the concept of fractional ownership through blockchain-based digital tokens.

Using Hedera Token Service (HTS), the platform creates digital tokens representing smaller units of a property's simulated value.

For example, if a property is assigned a demonstration value of ₹10,00,000, the platform can divide its simulated value into 10,000 units, with each unit representing ₹100 of the demonstration value.

Multiple participants can select and acquire different quantities of these digital tokens through the platform's demonstration workflow.

The token allocation is recorded on Hedera, allowing participants to observe how blockchain-based tokenisation can represent fractional participation in a property-related asset.

This feature demonstrates the technical possibilities of tokenisation. The tokens used in the current prototype do not independently provide legally recognised land ownership, title rights, or enforceable claims over the underlying property.

## 6. Hedera Technology Integration

LandChain utilises multiple components of the Hedera ecosystem, with each service serving a specific purpose.

**1. Hedera Smart Contract Service (HSCS)**

We use Solidity-based smart contracts deployed through Hedera Smart Contract Service to execute the simulated property purchase workflow.

Smart contracts help manage predefined transaction conditions and the purchase demonstration process, reducing dependence on manual coordination for the on-chain workflow.

**2. Hedera Token Service (HTS)**

HTS is used to create and manage digital tokens representing fractional units of a property's simulated value.

It demonstrates token creation, distribution, and allocation among multiple participants.

**3. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS)**

HCS provides timestamped, consensus-ordered records of relevant platform activities, such as document verification updates and property-related workflow events.

This enables transparent tracking of recorded events.

**4. Hedera Mirror Node**

The Hedera Mirror Node allows the platform to retrieve and display blockchain transaction information, including relevant transaction details and token-related activity.

It helps buyers and sellers inspect the history of recorded on-chain operations.

**5. MetaMask Wallet Integration**

MetaMask enables users to connect their wallets and interact with the blockchain functionality of the platform.

Users can initiate supported transactions and participate in the smart contract interaction workflow.

## 7. Complete Platform Workflow

The LandChain workflow follows these steps:

1. **User Registration:** Buyers and sellers register and access their respective dashboards.
2. **Property Listing:** Sellers submit property details, including location, area, price, and descriptions.
3. **Document Submission:** Sellers upload supporting documents for evaluation.
4. **Document Verification:** The verification module evaluates submitted documents against predefined requirements and generates a verification report.
5. **Blockchain Integrity Recording:** Cryptographic document hashes are recorded on Hedera to provide tamper-evident references.
6. **Marketplace Discovery:** Buyers browse available listings and examine their property details and verification statuses.
7. **Fractional Unit Selection:** Buyers select the quantity of demonstration investment units they wish to acquire.
8. **Smart Contract Interaction:** The platform executes the simulated purchase workflow through Solidity smart contracts.
9. **Token Allocation:** HTS manages the corresponding digital token allocation.
10. **Transaction Tracking:** Relevant blockchain records can be retrieved through the Hedera Mirror Node and displayed to users.

## 8. What Makes LandChain Different?

LandChain combines several blockchain capabilities into a single property marketplace demonstration rather than focusing on token creation alone.

Its key differentiating aspects include:

- Combining document integrity tracking with property discovery.
- Providing a structured document verification workflow with transparent status reporting.
- Using cryptographic hashes to create tamper-evident document references.
- Demonstrating fractional property participation through Hedera Token Service.
- Using smart contracts to execute a simulated purchase workflow.
- Recording important platform activities through Hedera Consensus Service.
- Providing blockchain transaction visibility through the Mirror Node.
- Integrating wallet connectivity for blockchain interactions.

The combination of these components demonstrates how blockchain infrastructure can support a more transparent and accessible digital real estate ecosystem.

## 9. Technology Stack

- **Blockchain Network:** Hedera Testnet
- **Smart Contracts:** Solidity
- **Smart Contract Infrastructure:** Hedera Smart Contract Service
- **Tokenisation:** Hedera Token Service
- **Consensus and Activity Records:** Hedera Consensus Service
- **Blockchain Data Retrieval:** Hedera Mirror Node
- **Wallet Integration:** MetaMask
- **Document Integrity:** Cryptographic hashing
- **Document Processing:** Automated checklist-based evaluation
- **Platform:** Web-based buyer and seller marketplace

## 10. Project Scope and Future Possibilities

LandChain is currently a prototype demonstrating blockchain-based property workflows on Hedera Testnet.

Future development could include:

- Integration with authorised government land-record databases.
- More comprehensive legal document validation and verification.
- Integration with trusted third-party verification agencies.
- Real-world property title verification.
- Legally compliant fractional ownership structures.
- Secure payment gateway and automated settlement integration.
- Multi-party property transaction management.
- Improved identity verification and fraud detection.
- Expansion to additional real estate asset categories.

Any real-world deployment involving property ownership or investment would require appropriate legal structures, regulatory compliance, trusted verification authorities, and integration with official property registration systems.

## 11. Our Vision

Our vision is to explore how blockchain technology can make real estate-related information, document verification activities, and digital transactions more transparent, traceable, and accessible.

We believe that combining document integrity, decentralised infrastructure, smart contracts, and tokenisation can provide a foundation for a more accessible digital property ecosystem.

**LandChain – From Property Discovery to Digital Ownership. Powered by Hedera.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
How We Built LandChain*

We built LandChain as a full-stack blockchain-powered land marketplace using Hedera Testnet, combining traditional web technologies with decentralized infrastructure to demonstrate transparent property verification and fractional ownership.

*1. Frontend and Backend Architecture*

We developed a web-based application with separate Buyer and Seller dashboards. The frontend communicates with our backend through APIs to handle user registration, authentication, property listings, document uploads, verification status and transaction information.

Users can register using mobile OTP authentication, connect their crypto wallets through MetaMask and select their roles. We also implemented a simulated KYC workflow for demonstration purposes.

*2. Document Verification and Hedera Integration*

When a seller uploads property documents, our verification module checks them against a predefined checklist and generates a report with Verified, Pending or Rejected statuses.

To provide tamper-evident document tracking, we generate cryptographic hashes of uploaded documents rather than storing sensitive documents directly on-chain. These hashes and verification activity records are submitted to Hedera for timestamped tracking.

*3. Fractional Ownership Using Hedera Token Service*

One of our major implementations is fractional ownership demonstration using Hedera Token Service (HTS). We create testnet tokens representing smaller units of a sample property's simulated value.

Buyers can select investment units, and the platform demonstrates token allocation and ownership percentage calculations. This showcases how Hedera can support digital asset creation and management.

*4. Smart Contracts Using Solidity*

We use Solidity and Hedera Smart Contract Service to implement the simulated property purchase workflow. When a buyer selects investment units, the smart contract handles the transaction logic and records relevant information, including the buyer, seller, property ID and token allocation.

*5. Hedera Consensus Service and Mirror Node*

We use Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) for timestamped verification and platform activity records. Hedera Mirror Node helps retrieve transaction information and display blockchain activity in our application.

This allows users to explore transaction history and independently verify relevant activities through Hedera Testnet Explorer.

*6. What Makes Our Implementation Interesting?*

Instead of building another conventional property-listing website, we connected property discovery, document verification, digital asset representation and blockchain transaction tracking into one workflow.

Our interesting approach is the combination of off-chain document storage and on-chain cryptographic hashes. This avoids exposing sensitive property documents while providing a way to detect changes to the original files.

We also distinguish between digital ownership representation and legally recognised land ownership. Our project uses fictional properties and testnet tokens to demonstrate the technology without claiming to transfer actual land titles.

*Partner Technology – Hedera*

Hedera is the core infrastructure behind LandChain. Its Smart Contract Service, Token Service, Consensus Service and Mirror Node allow us to demonstrate programmable transactions, digital token management, timestamped records and transparent transaction tracking within a single ecosystem.

LandChain demonstrates how decentralized infrastructure can make property-related digital transactions more transparent, traceable and accessible.*

projects.title: Noirwire
projects.description: Private BTC perp maker on Solana, hedged on Hyperliquid and 1inch Aqua, backed by an Arc USDC vault.
projects.project_description:
NoirWire is a private order book on Solana: resting orders, balances and positions stay hidden, and only fills are public. We offer a BTC perpetual with up to 10x leverage, and our house market maker takes the other side of every trade. That creates a problem every market maker has. Each fill leaves the maker with BTC exposure, and the money backing it sits on several chains at once. At this hackathon we built the system that hedges that risk and proves what it is worth. A trader buys BTC on the private book. The maker is now short BTC.
Hedge 1: a hedger reads the maker's real position and buys the same BTC on Hyperliquid, inside a price band. If it cannot see a fresh position, it waits.
Hedge 2: the maker posts a "we buy BTC" offer on Arbitrum with 1inch Aqua. 1inch traders sell BTC into it. Our HedgeGuard contract accepts only fills that reduce our risk and reverts the wrong way.
Depositors back the maker through one USDC epoch vault on Arc. A Solana depositor sends USDC over Circle CCTP V2 with hook data, and our HookExecutor delivers it into the vault.
A Chainlink CRE workflow reads the vault, the maker, the Hyperliquid account and the Aqua offer, computes the NAV and writes it onchain. If any source is missing or stale it writes nothing.
The vault settles each epoch at that NAV. A stale report or a price jump is refused.
Every number in the app carries a trust label (onchain, venue API or operator supplied), so depositors can see which parts are verified onchain and which they trust us for.
projects.how_its_made:
A TypeScript and Solidity monorepo (pnpm, Turborepo), built on top of our existing Solana order book, simulator and trading terminal. Arc (Circle): ShareVault, NavReceiver and HookExecutor in Solidity with Foundry, deployed on Arc testnet. The vault is an async epoch vault, not ERC-4626: deposits and withdrawals are requests priced at the next close, with a report age limit, closeId replay protection, a price-move pause and an internal ledger so a direct transfer never moves NAV. USDC is Arc's gas token, so depositors never hold a second token. Solana deposits arrive over CCTP V2 with hook data, and only our HookExecutor can deliver them.
1inch Aqua: the official Aqua registry and AquaSwapVMRouter, unmodified, on a fork of Arbitrum One, because Aqua has no testnet deployment. HedgeGuard is an Extruction target: a fill must match the allowed direction, fit the remaining size, sit inside a price band and stay near a fresh Chainlink BTC/USD price. Strategies are built with the Aqua SDK.
Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow combines an EVM read of Arc with HTTP reads of the Hyperliquid info API, the maker and the Aqua inventory, then writes a NAV report through the forwarder into NavReceiver.onReport. A sources hash lets anyone recompute what was signed. It runs with cre workflow simulate.
Hedger: a Node service that polls the maker's position, trades the BTC perp on Hyperliquid testnet with IOC orders, journals every order before sending it and stops trading when its data is stale.
Frontend: our Next.js trading terminal, now with the BTC market and a maker funding page that connects any EIP-6963 wallet and deposits USDC into the Arc vault with a real approve and requestDeposit.
The hackathon work is new code in the ethglobal-noirwire repo. The order book, simulator, terminal and wallet existed before the event. AI coding tools were used; the specs and prompts are in the repo.

projects.title: AgentHire
projects.description: Autonomous trust, discovery, and Hedera x402 micropayment network for AI agents.
projects.project_description: Overview & Problem Statement As artificial intelligence rapidly transitions from isolated conversational chatbots into autonomous, goal-oriented agentic systems, the software landscape faces a critical architectural bottleneck: the Specialization Dilemma. No individual AI agent can master real-time legal research, deterministic data analysis, secure code generation, and executive document synthesis without suffering from context-window bloat, prohibitive inference costs, and severe hallucination risks. To achieve real-world utility, complex workflows require multi-agent collaboration where specialized agents delegate and subcontract sub-tasks to each other. However, today’s Web2 infrastructure is built for human eyes with monthly SaaS subscriptions and credit cards. When autonomous AI agents need to hire other AI agents programmatically, there is no standardized machine-readable discovery layer, no Sybil-resistant publisher governance, and no mechanism for instantaneous, low-latency machine-to-machine micropayments. The AgentHire Solution AgentHire is an autonomous Agent-to-Agent (A2A) trust, procurement, and micropayment network that establishes a decentralized coordination and economic layer for artificial intelligence. It functions as an autonomous marketplace and execution mesh where AI agents can discover, evaluate, negotiate with, and hire specialist worker agents in real time, settling bounties peer-to-peer on-chain. Key Architectural Pillars: Master Orchestration & Intent Routing: At the entry tier, a Master Orchestrator Agent ingests user prompts, attached spreadsheets, or technical documentation. The Orchestrator conducts deep intent reasoning to decompose tasks, evaluates candidate agent capabilities, verifies domain relevance, and dynamically routes the workload to dedicated specialist workers: Research Agent: Autonomous web intelligence, cryptographic evidence gathering, and deep thinking. Coding Agent: Algorithmic function engineering, API implementation, and software architecture. Data Analyst Agent: Tabular spreadsheet computation, statistical distributions, anomaly detection, and numerical metrics. Report Generation Agent: Structured executive reports with verifiable citations and roadmap synthesis. Document Summarizer Agent: High-impact executive briefs and actionable takeaways from lengthy files. Native Hedera x402 Micropayments (Zero Solidity): AgentHire implements the open HTTP x402 Payment Required standard natively on the Hedera Hashgraph network. When an agent is invoked, contract terms are autonomously negotiated and settled using pure native Hedera SDKs ( @hiero-ledger/sdk ). Transactions are executed as direct TransferTransaction calls transferring exact tinybars (100,000 tinybars = 0.001 HBAR) with 2-second consensus finality. By avoiding Solidity and EVM smart contracts, AgentHire eliminates gas price volatility, contract re-entrancy risks, and execution latency, enabling friction-free machine-speed commerce. Cascading Multi-Agent Subcontracting: AgentHire demonstrates true autonomous recursive commerce. When a mission requires multi-domain expertise—such as conducting deep technical research and compiling the findings into an executive report—the primary specialist (Research Agent) acts as an autonomous general contractor. It receives funds from the Master Orchestrator, completes its intelligence phase, and autonomously hires and pays the downstream specialist (Report Generation Agent) on Hedera testnet in a secondary x402 transaction before synthesizing the final deliverable. Both transactions settle independently and generate verifiable on-chain consensus receipts. User Budget Control & Loss Minimization: AgentHire empowers users with a strict Task Spending Ceiling. The Orchestrator evaluates candidate agent price quotes against the user's defined tinybar budget. If a multi-agent cascade exceeds the cap, the system intelligently prunes subcontracts or reroutes workloads to maintain strict fiscal compliance, ensuring autonomous agents never exceed authorized spending policies. Sybil-Resistant Governance via World ID: In an open agent marketplace, malicious actors can easily deploy thousands of low-quality clone bots to manipulate ratings. AgentHire prevents Sybil attacks by requiring developers to complete a World ID Proof of Human zero-knowledge verification using IDKit v4 before publishing monetized agents. A cryptographically unique nullifier hash is verified on the backend, binding the listing to a verified human creator while preserving complete user privacy. Decentralized Identity via ENSv2: Every published agent is assigned a verifiable on-chain domain identity via the Ethereum Name Service (ENS). Using custom ENS text records ( agenthire.endpoint and agenthire.hedera ), the network binds the agent’s Ethereum name to its live webhook endpoint and its Hedera settlement account. This enables seamless cross-chain identity resolution between Ethereum namespaces and Hedera micropayment rails. Immutable Consensus Ledger & Transparency: Every task execution, log entry, and payment is recorded on the native Hedera network. Users and operators have full visibility through an interactive On-Chain Transaction Explorer ( /transactions ) and a Wallet & Earnings Ledger ( /analytics ), providing verifiable HashScan explorer links, consensus timestamps, and real-time financial auditing.
projects.how_its_made: Architecture & Core Technologies I built AgentHire as a high-performance monorepo powered by Turborepo and pnpm, structured across three specialized workspaces: @agenthire/api: A low-latency Fastify backend service executing agent reasoning, cryptographic verification, and on-chain settlement. @agenthire/web: A modern Next.js 16 (App Router) interface with Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming real-time agent thinking and HashScan consensus links. @agenthire/shared: Shared TypeScript type definitions, cryptographic schemas, and Bayesian math algorithms. Pure Native Hedera Implementation (Zero Solidity / No EVM) To target the "No Solidity Allowed" and "AI Agents That Pay: x402 on Hedera" tracks, I intentionally bypassed EVM and Solidity smart contracts completely. Instead, I built direct native Hedera consensus integration using @hiero-ledger/sdk: Live Micropayments via HTTP x402: I implemented an autonomous client-merchant negotiation protocol. In live-settlement.ts, when an agent is hired, the payer client (0.0.11331589) constructs a native TransferTransaction, deducting tinybars from the payer and crediting the merchant (0.0.11330954) with specific transaction memos. This achieves sub-3 second finality with near-zero network fees ($0.0001 per transaction). Autonomous Cascading Subcontracting: I architected a recursive payment loop in agent-orchestrator.ts. When a task requires both research and report generation, the Master Orchestrator triggers Transaction 1 to hire the Research Agent. Mid-execution, the Research Agent acts as an autonomous payer, hiring the Report Generation Agent via Transaction 2. Both transactions settle independently on Hedera testnet and are recorded in my local SQLite transaction store, immediately populating the live /transactions explorer. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Audit logs and task completion proofs are anchored as immutable topic messages to HCS Topic 0.0.11331471, providing verifiable sequence-level provenance. World ID (IDKit v4 & Proof of Human) To protect the marketplace against clone-bot spam and Sybil attacks without compromising developer privacy, I integrated World ID IDKit v4 on the /publish portal: When a developer monetizes an agent, my Fastify API generates a cryptographic challenge with relying party credentials (WLD_RP_ID & WLD_RP_SIGNING_KEY). The developer scans the zero-knowledge QR code via the World App simulator in staging mode. The server validates the ZK-proof, nullifier hash, and action signature, storing the verified human nullifier in SQLite to guarantee that one human publisher cannot flood the registry with duplicate agents. ENSv2 On-Chain Identity & Cross-Chain Routing I used viem to bind agents to Ethereum Name Service (ENS) domains on Sepolia: Agents are registered under human-readable names (e.g. nexus-agent.eth). I query ENS resolver text records (agenthire.endpoint and agenthire.hedera) via high-reliability RPC gateways (Tenderly). This creates a trustless bridge where an Ethereum ENS identity directly routes webhook calls and maps to native Hedera payment addresses. AI Orchestration & Proof-of-Competence Procurement (PoCP) LLM Reasoning: Powered by Groq's high-speed inference engine running Llama-3.3-70b and GPT-OSS models to classify intent, detect nonsensical inputs or gibberish, and perform real-time deliverable synthesis. Proof-of-Competence Procurement (PoCP): Located in apps/api/src/agents/pocp.ts, my procurement engine uses Bayesian reliability priors (Beta distributions) and predictive loss minimization to evaluate candidate agents. It can dispatch a 500ms paid synthetic micro-challenge before committing the user's full budget. Notable & "Hacky" Engineering Details True In-Flight SSE Cascading: Next.js streaming typically struggles with multi-stage backend awaits. I implemented an asynchronous event multiplexer using Fastify raw hijacked response sockets that streams Groq reasoning tokens, Hedera transaction consensus events, and markdown deliverables through a single unified SSE connection without buffering or blocking. Dual-Chain Identity Mapping: Binding ENS text records (EVM) directly to native Hedera account IDs (0.0.x) enables a hybrid identity layer where agents retain their Web3 identity on Ethereum while transacting with micro-cent finality on Hedera.

To target the "No Solidity Allowed" and "AI Agents That Pay: x402 on Hedera" tracks, I intentionally bypassed EVM and Solidity smart contracts completely. Instead, I built direct native Hedera consensus integration using @hiero-ledger/sdk:

- Live Micropayments via HTTP x402: I implemented an autonomous client-merchant negotiation protocol. In live-settlement.ts, when an agent is hired, the payer client (0.0.11331589) constructs a native TransferTransaction, deducting tinybars from the payer and crediting the merchant (0.0.11330954) with specific transaction memos. This achieves sub-3 second finality with near-zero network fees ($0.0001 per transaction).

- Autonomous Cascading Subcontracting: I architected a recursive payment loop in agent-orchestrator.ts. When a task requires both research and report generation, the Master Orchestrator triggers Transaction 1 to hire the Research Agent. Mid-execution, the Research Agent acts as an autonomous payer, hiring the Report Generation Agent via Transaction 2. Both transactions settle independently on Hedera testnet and are recorded in my local SQLite transaction store, immediately populating the live /transactions explorer.

- Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Audit logs and task completion proofs are anchored as immutable topic messages to HCS Topic 0.0.11331471, providing verifiable sequence-level provenance.


2. World ID (IDKit v4 & Proof of Human)

To protect the marketplace against clone-bot spam and Sybil attacks without compromising developer privacy, I integrated World ID IDKit v4 on the /publish portal:

- When a developer monetizes an agent, my Fastify API generates a cryptographic challenge with relying party credentials (WLD_RP_ID & WLD_RP_SIGNING_KEY).

- The developer scans the zero-knowledge QR code via the World App simulator in staging mode.

- The server validates the ZK-proof, nullifier hash, and action signature, storing the verified human nullifier in SQLite to guarantee that one human publisher cannot flood the registry with duplicate agents.


3. ENSv2 On-Chain Identity & Cross-Chain Routing

I used viem to bind agents to Ethereum Name Service (ENS) domains on Sepolia:

- Agents are registered under human-readable names (e.g. nexus-agent.eth).

- I query ENS resolver text records (agenthire.endpoint and agenthire.hedera) via high-reliability RPC gateways (Tenderly).

- This creates a trustless bridge where an Ethereum ENS identity directly routes webhook calls and maps to native Hedera payment addresses.


4. AI Orchestration & Proof-of-Competence Procurement (PoCP)

- LLM Reasoning: Powered by Groq's high-speed inference engine running Llama-3.3-70b and GPT-OSS models to classify intent, detect nonsensical inputs or gibberish, and perform real-time deliverable synthesis.

- Proof-of-Competence Procurement (PoCP): Located in apps/api/src/agents/pocp.ts, my procurement engine uses Bayesian reliability priors (Beta distributions) and predictive loss minimization to evaluate candidate agents. It can dispatch a 500ms paid synthetic micro-challenge before committing the user's full budget.


Notable & "Hacky" Engineering Details

- True In-Flight SSE Cascading: Next.js streaming typically struggles with multi-stage backend awaits. I implemented an asynchronous event multiplexer using Fastify raw hijacked response sockets that streams Groq reasoning tokens, Hedera transaction consensus events, and markdown deliverables through a single unified SSE connection without buffering or blocking.

- Dual-Chain Identity Mapping: Binding ENS text records (EVM) directly to native Hedera account IDs (0.0.x) enables a hybrid identity layer where agents retain their Web3 identity on Ethereum while transacting with micro-cent finality on Hedera.

projects.title: Stealth Pay
projects.description: Privacy-preserving crypto payments using ERC-5564 stealth addresses.
projects.project_description: Stealth Pay is a privacy-focused crypto payment platform that enables users to send and receive digital assets without publicly linking their primary wallet addresses to every transaction. It uses ERC-5564 stealth address technology to generate unique, one-time payment addresses for recipients. Receivers create a stealth identity and share their public stealth meta-address. Senders use this information to derive a unique destination address and transfer tokens without needing to know the receiver's main wallet address. The receiver's scanner detects incoming payments through on-chain announcement events and can locally derive the corresponding spending key to recover funds into their primary wallet. Stealth Pay integrates Whitechain Sepolia for testnet payments and Arkiv Rabdi for decentralized identity and payment-request data. Our goal is to make private crypto payments more accessible, practical and user-friendly.
projects.how_its_made: Stealth Pay is built using a full-stack Web3 architecture combining modern frontend technologies, smart contracts, cryptography and decentralized data infrastructure. The frontend is developed using Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, with MetaMask integration for wallet connectivity and transaction signing. The blockchain interaction layer uses Viem and Wagmi. Our core privacy mechanism implements ERC-5564 using secp256k1 elliptic-curve cryptography. It uses ephemeral keys, Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman shared-secret derivation and view tags to generate unique stealth addresses for individual payments. We developed Solidity smart contracts, including a StealthPaymentRouter and ERC5564Announcer, deployed on Whitechain Sepolia. The router handles ERC-20 token transfers and announcement emission atomically. A background scanner monitors blockchain events, identifies payments intended for the receiver and supports non-custodial recovery and sweeping of received tokens. For decentralized data, we integrated the Arkiv SDK on the Rabdi testnet to publish and retrieve receiver profiles and time-limited payment requests. Supabase/PostgreSQL supports application data where required. Private keys are generated and used client-side, while sensitive key material is encrypted before local storage. The project was tested using Whitechain Sepolia and a custom six-decimal TestUSDT demonstration token. The implementation also includes experimental or simulated integrations for selected ecosystem services such as Uniswap, ENS and BitGo MPC.

projects.title: Ownable
projects.description: Turn everyday purchases into investments in the companies behind them.
projects.project_description: Ownback turns everyday shopping into an opportunity to build investment ownership in the companies behind the products people buy. When a user purchases something, they can upload a receipt, take a photo, enter the details manually or connect their Gmail to find invoices. Ownback uses 0G Private Computer to read the receipt, identify the product and discover the companies involved in making it, including the manufacturer, suppliers and raw materials. For example, when someone buys an iPhone, Ownback can identify Apple as the manufacturer, along with companies such as TSMC, Qualcomm and Corning that contribute to the product. The user chooses what percentage of their purchase to invest, with a default of 5%. This amount is divided into investment allocations. By default, 70% goes to the product maker, 20% to the companies behind the product and 10% to the raw materials. USDC is allocated into individual investment jars managed by the OwnbackVault on Arc. Users can review their accumulated investments and approve when they want to buy. Before every purchase, Ownback shows the live price, quantity, fees and maximum purchase price. Every buy requires explicit user approval. Arc handles the vault and onchain investment logic, CCTP V2 supports cross-chain USDC transfers, and Arkiv maintains public records of companies, supplier relationships, verified tokens and investment proofs. Our goal is to make investing a natural part of everyday spending. Instead of only buying products from companies, people can gradually build ownership in the businesses and resources behind them.
projects.how_its_made:
Ownback uses 0G Private Computer for its AI processing pipeline. We use vision models to read receipts and invoices, language models to identify products and match them with manufacturers and suppliers, embedding models for matching and retrieval, and Whisper for voice input. The documented models include:
•⁠  ⁠Vision: 0GM-1.0-35B-A3B
•⁠  ⁠Language model: GLM-5.3
•⁠  ⁠Embeddings: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
•⁠  ⁠Speech recognition: OpenAI Whisper Large V3 AI processes purchase information and helps identify the companies and raw materials behind products. Its output is validated against structured schemas before being presented to users. AI never independently executes investments or moves funds. Users review the allocations and explicitly approve every investment. We use 0G Private Computer for these AI jobs so the receipt-reading and product-matching process runs through 0G's private inference infrastructure. Request IDs are also captured for tracing AI requests.

projects.title: Juicebox
projects.description: what did your ai get done this week? signed weekly receipts for all your tokenmaxxing
projects.project_description: everyone's token maxing right now. companies spend thousands a month per engineer on claude code and codex, and when someone asks "ok but what did we actually get for it?" the only answer is a token leaderboard. which literally rewards burning tokens, not shipping stuff. so we built juicebox. every person gets one signed weekly receipt of what their ai actually got done. it runs on your laptop, reads your claude code and codex sessions, and links them to the PRs and pushes they turned into. when you hit "write my week", a private ai on the 0G private computer (running inside a TEE) reads each session and writes one line: built, fixed, figured out, researched, wrote, planned or wasted. you pay for it from your own 0G credits, so you sign in with 0G and literally watch your balance go down by less than a cent. then you sign the whole week with a key made on your laptop (no wallet needed, and you can't drop or edit a line, that's the whole point) and send it. the full list goes to swarm, encrypted on your laptop, and arkiv gets a read-only record with the signed totals that you own, not your company. the company signs in with github and sees everyone's week, the PRs behind it and where the money went. never anyone's prompts. and since both sides have a reason to fudge the numbers, a chainlink CRE workflow checks every team once a month: it reads the receipts straight from arkiv, verifies every signature, asks github if what shipped is still there, and writes the score onchain on sepolia. nobody can change it. also for fun there's AI Wrapped, which tells you how much time you spend overthinking, treating ai like your therapist, or just saying hi :)
projects.how_its_made: it's a next.js + typescript app that runs right on your laptop. there's no juicebox server at all, which was kind of the point from day one. first it reads your claude code and codex logs, figures out what each session cost, and matches it to the PRs and commits it actually turned into on github. then 0G does the fun part. every session goes to a private ai on the 0G private computer, running inside a TEE, so your prompts never hit a normal ai api. it reads what you did and writes one line like "built the spend dashboard" or "went in circles on retries". and you pay with sign in with 0G, so it comes out of your own daily credits. you can literally watch your balance go down by less than a cent. every answer keeps its 0G request id, so you can check it later. you sign the whole week with a key made on your laptop, so nobody can quietly edit a line after. sending it was my favourite part to build. the full list gets encrypted on your laptop and goes to swarm. arkiv gets a read-only record with just the signed totals, and the record belongs to you, not your company, even though the company pays the gas. only the company's key can open the list. and because both sides could fudge the numbers, a chainlink CRE workflow checks every team once a month. it reads the receipts straight from arkiv, checks every signature, asks github if the stuff that shipped is still there, and writes the score onchain on sepolia where nobody can touch it. the hacky bits: CRE only takes 250 KB per response so we read arkiv in small pages, and swarm's own encryption puts the key inside the link, which you can't put on a public chain, so we encrypt it ourselves and seal the key to the company.

projects.title: FrameLabs
projects.description: FrameLab: replay expected pending-frame behavior twice, shrink mismatches, export CI bundles.
projects.project_description: FrameLab is a release-check workbench for EIP-8141 frame-transaction alt-mempool nodes. You write what should happen to pending frame transactions when the chain changes. It replays that sequence twice on a pinned local node, checks expected versus actual at each checkpoint, shrinks a mismatch to the smallest confirmed replayable case, and exports a CI bundle you can rerun after a fix. The first target is an alt-mempool node developer checking a change to admission, revalidation, or eviction. Scenario S1 funds a payer, queues keyed self-paid frame transactions plus a control, then drains the payer. Under the sidecar policy SP-BAL-ENFORCE, the newest unpaid frame transactions must be evicted and the older ones plus the control must stay. An expected eviction is a pass. The fail-and-fix demo uses a labelled local patch that reverses eviction order, never an upstream bug: shrink reduces the noisy case, then compare shows WRONGLY_EVICTED going back to PASS with the same scenario and rule pack. This is a Classic / From Scratch build for ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026, aimed at the EF prize Best use of the Frame Transaction Alternative Mempool. Tag v0.1-rc met 54/54 acceptance checks on CI. Try the read-only viewer at batcorps.batmnnn.live (injected shrink: batcorps.batmnnn.live ), a judge VM at lab.batcorps.batmnnn.live , or Codespaces from the repo. Qualifying frame tx: explorer.altmempool.wtf
projects.how_its_made: FrameLab is TypeScript on Bun, with YAML scenarios checked against JSON Schema and viem for RPC and signing. Each run starts a pinned ethrex node in Docker and the ERC-8421 workshop sidecar (a Skandha fork), applies an observation patch that only logs when a reconcile pass finishes, then drives blocks through ethrex's engine API. Assertions cite written sidecar policy, not model guesses. After a mismatch, shrink deletes steps until the same predicate still fails on two fresh runs, then export writes a checksummed bundle with replay.sh. compare checks that the same reduced case passes on the unpatched build. Vendor code stays pinned and uncommitted; setup-vendor.sh recreates it. The fail path is an injected patch that reverses newest-first eviction, so judges can see a real wrong outcome without claiming an upstream vulnerability. The hosted viewer at batcorps.batmnnn.live serves those exported bundles read-only. lab.batcorps.batmnnn.live signs a judge into GitHub and gives them a Linux VM with Docker, Bun, and FrameLab warmed up. A public-devnet command sends one qualifying frame transaction to the workshop alt-mempool. Partner benefit: the whole loop is built on the Frame Transaction Alternative Mempool stack (EIP-8141 frames, the workshop sidecar, ethrex, and the public explorer), which is the only way to test pending-frame lifecycle this way.

projects.title: Hedera Council Agent
projects.description: An AI agent holds one signing seat on a Hedera treasury council.
projects.project_description: An AI agent with a treasury key is a liability. One bad prompt, one dishonest proposer, one prompt injection, and the money is gone. Making a human approve every payment defeats the point of having an agent. This project sits between the two. The owner writes a standing instruction once, in plain words: "Pay registered vendors up to 50 HBAR each, at most 100 HBAR a month. Anything else goes to the council." 0G Private Computer compiles it into five checkable rules. The output is validated strictly, and invalid output creates nothing. The rules are shown back as a plain checklist written by code, not by the model. A council of World-ID-verified humans adopts the rules by majority vote, and every ballot is a World ID proof bound to the exact rules hash and the choice. The adopted hash is anchored in the Hedera audit log. After that, the agent decides alone. A payment inside the rules is co-signed with no vote. A payment outside them waits for a council vote. Before any signature, fixed code checks the transfer read back from Hedera against its description, checks the payee against the council registry, and checks the payment against the adopted rules. The agent pays a one-cent x402 check fee per payment, under a spending cap, and refuses an offer whose recipient is not the registered check service.

Anything else goes to the council." 0G Private Computer compiles it into five checkable rules. The output is validated strictly, and invalid output creates nothing. The rules are shown back as a plain checklist written by code, not by the model. A council of World-ID-verified humans adopts the rules by majority vote, and every ballot is a World ID proof bound to the exact rules hash and the choice. The adopted hash is anchored in the Hedera audit log.

After that, the agent decides alone. A payment inside the rules is co-signed with no vote. A payment outside them waits for a council vote. Before any signature, fixed code checks the transfer read back from Hedera against its description, checks the payee against the council registry, and checks the payment against the adopted rules. The agent pays a one-cent x402 check fee per payment, under a spending cap, and refuses an offer whose recipient is not the registered check service.

projects.title: NeverDown
projects.description: NeverDown: programmable resilience for any failure spot recover fast, then procure under policy.
projects.project_description: NeverDown is a programmable resilience operator for live Web3 apps. You attach it to a failure spot RPC, indexer, price API, or similar and encode what it’s allowed to do in a Resilience Contract: seller allowlists, per-payment caps, budgets, and allowed actions. When that dependency goes unhealthy, two planes run. The fast plane fails over to a preapproved standby immediately no LLM, no payment wait so the app keeps serving. The procurement plane then replenishes capacity: discover offers (Arkiv), verify seller identity (ENS), prove the endpoint works, authorize under policy, settle on Hedera via x402 if allowed, install the new standby, and leave an audit trail (HashScan + HCS). Bad sellers and over-budget attempts are refused before sign. RPC is only our ETHGlobal Mumbai demo vertical; the product is general dependency resilience under explicit policy, with an operator console and a separate @neverdown/sdk consumer example that shows the same failure stuck without the SDK and recoverable with it.
projects.how_its_made: We built NeverDown as a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm): Express gateway and seller adapters for the RPC demo, a PolicyEngine with durable budget reservations, a payment worker that keeps spend keys out of the browser via IPC, and a “Supreme Agent” loop for procure/deny. The web console is a five-act demo (contract → status → procure → deny → evidence) with a paced agent guide that reads live status/policy. A separate example app consumes only @neverdown/sdk and contrasts hard-coded retries vs monitor → ENS → Arkiv → prove → procure. Partner rails: Hedera testnet for x402-style cryptoTransfer settlement, budgets, and HCS authorize/settle (and deny) audit; ENS for seller texts (hederaAccount / x402Url) as the trust root; Arkiv for capability offer discovery. Capability is checked before pay (PoC). Gateway install uses an internal API after settle. Notable / slightly hacky: server-only SDK so spend keys never hit the browser; fail-closed allowlist/budget before any signature; demo UI streams each rail so judges can follow; hosted frontend on Vercel with a durable Heroku/backend path for the always-on operator. C3 isolation is still partially honest in our docs we don’t oversell that.

projects.title: Shikigami
projects.description: Any AI can now pay for you, with an undo button: escrow on Hedera, an open agent market on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Shikigami lets any AI act and pay for you, safely. Ask for anything in plain words: in our app (an installable PWA), in Telegram, or inside Claude through our MCP connector. The concierge finds agents on an open market, gets firm prices that each agent signs with its own key, and hires one over x402. The money never goes straight to the agent. It is held in escrow on Hedera, inside a spending limit you approved once with Face ID, and for 60 seconds one tap undoes it with a full refund. The agent does the real job (hotel bookings and cancellations via LiteAPI sandbox, flights via Duffel test mode, a price watcher that rebooks cheaper, bank-code lookups paid per answer), marks it delivered, and Hedera pays it by itself when the review window ends. Report a problem and you are refunded. Big spends need a real human: payments above 0.10 USDC, ratings and shops require World ID, so a bot, a stolen chat or a confused model can never spend alone. It also works on the street: pay any shop with a Live QR that a screenshot can't fake, or just by sound (a chirp). Anyone can plug in their own agent in minutes (docs + review on Arkiv). Everything is live on testnet today at https://heyshikigami.duckdns.org.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm, Turborepo): a Next.js 16 PWA, a Hono API, four agents and our own x402 facilitator, on Postgres/Drizzle, deployed with Coolify. HEDERA: payments use the x402 spec's transferExecutor method (official @x402 packages plus our own facilitator, because hosted ones only support cryptoTransfer). Every payment runs through MandateRegistry, our escrow contract: spending limits (budget, per-payment cap, allowed payees) that the AI key signs over (EIP-712), with the undo window inside the signed terms so nobody can shorten it. On delivery the contract calls Hedera's schedule service itself (HIP-1215), so the network pays the agent when the review ends, with no server in the middle. The facilitator simulates every call, then checks the ledger moved exactly the amount. Plus Face ID smart wallets that verify passkey (P-256) signatures on-chain (ERC-1271, sponsored gas), a public spend log on HCS, and ERC-8004 identities for every agent. ARKIV (SDK 1.0.1, Rabdi): the open market, not a log. Agents sign their own profiles, listings and quotes; every read checks $creator, so a forged offer is ignored; quotes expire on the network itself (10 min); our writer publishes receipts (pointing at the Hedera tx), pseudonymous verified ratings, disputes and our review of each agent. Typed schemas index only filter columns, and writes follow Arkiv's write-safety rules (gas floors, explicit nonces, no blind resends). WORLD ID (sandbox, OIDC device flow): a fresh human approval for payments over 0.10 USDC, one verified rating per human per agent, one shop per human; approvable from another device. AI: Claude Haiku runs the concierge (Messages API, our own tool loop, web search/fetch, vision). The same tools are an MCP server with OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, so Claude can hire agents within your limits; a Telegram bot runs the same concierge with live booking cards. HACKY BITS: in-person payments are a 24-byte request authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 (no elliptic curves, quantum-resistant). The chirp is ggwave tones (1.9-6.4 kHz, Reed-Solomon) at two speeds, with the mic's echo cancellation switched off. The Live QR hides a second code in 4x4 tiles that shift colour +-4 levels on the blue-yellow axis at constant brightness (about 0.13%), Manchester-coded with a Barker-7 sync: a fresh live code every 250 ms, so stickers and screenshots go stale in 3 seconds.

projects.title: CreatorAdvance
projects.description: Turn approved creator invoices into upfront USDT through a collateral-backed marketplace.
projects.project_description:
CreatorAdvance helps creators get paid today for work they have already completed. Creators often finish brand campaigns weeks before receiving payment. A sponsored video may already be published, the deliverables accepted, and the invoice approved-but the creator still has to wait 30, 60, or 90 days. During that gap, they need money to pay editors, cover production costs, and start their next project. CreatorAdvance turns that waiting period into a financing opportunity. It connects creators with approved investors who can purchase brand-confirmed receivables at a discount, with stablecoin settlement and receivable ownership managed on Whitechain. For example, a creator has an approved invoice worth 1,000 USDT due in 60 days. An investor offers 970 USDT for the receivable. The creator chooses whether to accept. Acceptance transfers the investor’s escrowed USDT to the creator and issues the investor an onchain receivable claim in the same transaction. When the brand repays, the contract routes payment to the current claim owner, less the disclosed platform fee. The product follows a complete business workflow: Businesses onboard first. They submit registration evidence for platform review, register their business profile onchain, authorize invoice signers, and deposit USDT collateral. Creators submit completed work. They select an approved business and upload their invoice, delivery evidence, and campaign brief. The application calculates document fingerprints automatically. Businesses confirm their obligations. An authorized signer approves the specific invoice terms. The contract checks the signature and reserves sufficient brand collateral before making the invoice financeable. Investors compete through funded offers. Approved investors escrow USDT when submitting offers, allowing creators to compare actual committed bids. Creators control acceptance. Funding and claim issuance happen atomically, preventing either side from receiving its part without the corresponding settlement. Repayment follows ownership. The contract supports partial repayments and restricts claim transfers to approved investors. After maturity and a seven-day grace period, default settlement can apply available brand collateral and record any remaining shortfall.
The current model requires collateral covering the invoice’s face value at approval. This makes the funding commitment explicit and prevents a business from promising the same collateral against multiple invoices. Each business has its own collateral accounting. Private commercial documents stay offchain. Their hashes bind the financing record to specific evidence without publishing the PDFs. Business verification and legal enforceability still require offchain processes; a document hash establishes integrity, not authenticity. CreatorAdvance is an Android-first testnet prototype. Its core issuance-to-funding flow has been demonstrated on Whitechain Sepolia using separate business, creator, and investor wallets and the organizer-provided USDT.
projects.how_its_made: CreatorAdvance combines an Android application, an authenticated backend, private document storage, and a Solidity financing contract. Each component has a specific responsibility: the application handles the user journey, the backend manages business records and access, and the contract enforces financial settlement. Mobile application and wallet integration The mobile client uses React Native, Expo, Expo Router, and TypeScript. Reown AppKit connects external wallets such as MetaMask, while Wagmi and Viem handle contract interactions, typed-data signing, token amounts, and transaction receipts. TanStack Query manages cached blockchain reads and refreshes them after confirmed actions. Wallet authentication uses Sign-In with Ethereum. A wallet connection identifies the connected account; a separate signed authentication message establishes its application session. The backend associates wallet addresses with their assigned business roles, while the contract independently checks privileged financial actions. Contract-enforced receivable financing The contract is written in Solidity 0.8.30 using OpenZeppelin components, including ERC-721, EIP-712, SafeERC20, access controls, pause controls, and reentrancy protection. Brand approval uses an EIP-712 typed-data signature covering the invoice’s business, creator, amount, dates, evidence hashes, nonce, and approval deadline. Domain separation binds that signature to the intended chain and contract. Nonces and deadlines limit replay and stale approvals. The contract maintains explicit invoice and offer states. Investors must be allowlisted, and offers require USDT escrow. When the creator accepts an eligible offer, the contract updates the financing state, mints the ERC-721 receivable claim, and transfers the escrowed payment atomically. The ERC-721 represents the application’s receivable claim. Transfer restrictions are enforced inside the contract’s ownership-update logic, so an ordinary NFT transfer cannot bypass investor eligibility checks. Repayments look up the current token owner rather than relying on the original investor address. Collateral accounting distinguishes a brand’s total deposits from its reserved commitments. Approval reserves the invoice’s face value, and withdrawals are limited to unreserved collateral. Repayment and default settlement update the outstanding balance and reservation accounting. Exact token-transfer checks protect the accounting from incompatible fee-on-transfer behavior. Backend, database, and private evidence The backend uses Fastify and TypeScript, with Zod validation and Prisma over Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL. It stores business applications, wallet-role relationships, invoice metadata, and synchronized chain events. The API is deployed on Vercel. PDFs are stored in a private Supabase Storage bucket. Signed upload URLs let the phone upload documents directly to storage, avoiding serverless request-body limits. Authorized backend processing calculates SHA-256 fingerprints for the invoice, delivery proof, and campaign brief; those fingerprints become part of the onchain approval payload. The API verifies transaction receipts and decodes contract events before updating its financial projections. Event records include block information for reconciliation, while the contract remains authoritative for collateral, escrow, claim ownership, and repayment balances. Whitechain integration and validation The deployment uses Whitechain Sepolia, chain ID 1874, with WBT for gas and the organizer’s six-decimal USDT contract for collateral and financing. Whitechain provides the shared execution environment in which stablecoin payment and receivable ownership can settle together. The supplied Ankr testnet endpoint is configured for application and backend RPC access. The recorded live demonstration financed a 5 USDT invoice with a 4.8 USDT investor offer. Creator acceptance paid the creator and minted the investor’s claim in one transaction. Foundry tests cover contract behavior and repayment accounting, including fuzz testing; repayment and default recovery still require live testnet validation. OpenAI Codex assisted extensively with research, implementation, debugging, documentation, and test execution under the developer’s direction. The developer supplied the product specification and directed the product workflow and integration decisions.

projects.title: meridian.trade
projects.description: Meridian — an exchange for LLM inference. built for ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026.
projects.project_description: The problem: provider credits (0G iAI, monthly plan allowances) expire and can't be cashed out. The product turns that idle capacity into a market: Sellers verify with World ID and list credits as MTokens (1M mixed tokens at 3:1 input/output), priced below list. Their API key is checked once, then sealed with AES-256-GCM. Buyers — agents or people — spend them through an OpenAI-compatible router, which fills from prepaid MTokens first and otherwise takes the cheapest ask across 0G, Command Code, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI and Zen/Go. Agents with no balance get an x402 402, pay USDC on Hedera, and the retry streams. Traders buy or resell MTokens on an order book at /trade, or hedge tomorrow's price with 5x oracle perps on 0G Galileo at /perps, indexed from a public HCS log and liquidated by a keeper. Humans approve cap raises and human-linking through World ID; /receipts recomputes the index in the browser from the log.
projects.how_its_made:
A pnpm workspace (apps/ , agents/ ) with four parts: apps/web — Next.js 16 App Router, TypeScript, no ORM magic beyond Drizzle on Neon Postgres. All domain logic lives in plain modules under apps/web/lib (ledger, book, bids, offers, rails, x402, hcs, world, approvals, payouts, perp, chain, secrets, auth), and the HTTP layer is thin route handlers under app/api/v1. The database is a double-entry-ish ledger: keys, listings, bids, offers, trades, prepaid, topups, usage, payouts, approvals, and perp_events, with balances stored as micro-USD bigint. Money — x402 via @x402/core + @x402/hedera: the router answers 402, the client signs an exact-scheme USDC transfer on Hedera testnet, the server settles through a facilitator and credits the key. Prepaid MTokens are spent first; the rest is settled against reported upstream usage. contracts — Foundry/Solidity: MockUSDC, IndexOracle (keeper-posted index), PerpMarket (5x, vault-backed, liquidations). Deployed on 0G Galileo 16602, driven from the web app with viem/wagmi and generated ABIs. keeper — one Node process (main.ts + jobs.ts) that publishes HCS rollups, posts the index, liquidates, matches resting bids, closes the day, schedules payouts and resets listings. It's the only index writer and a trusted component.
Request path: Bearer rk_… → SHA-256 lookup in keys → prepaid check → cheapest ask across rails → 402 or balance debit → stream from the upstream provider → usage settled → fill recorded → HCS log → index/perp feed. Seller provider keys are checked once, sealed with AES-256-GCM, and used custodied by the router. Identity is World ID (IDKit) for sellers and approvals, Privy + wagmi for wallets. Tests are node:test against real route handlers, plus live e2e scripts that spend testnet USDC.
