- contracts — Foundry/Solidity: MockUSDC, IndexOracle (keeper-posted index), PerpMarket (5x, vault-backed, liquidations). Deployed on 0G Galileo 16602, driven from the web app with viem/wagmi and generated ABIs.
- keeper — one Node process (main.ts + jobs.ts) that publishes HCS rollups, posts the index, liquidates, matches resting bids, closes the day, schedules payouts and resets listings. It's the only index writer and a trusted component.
Request path: Bearer rk_… → SHA-256 lookup in keys → prepaid check → cheapest ask across rails → 402 or balance debit → stream from the upstream provider → usage settled → fill recorded → HCS log → index/perp feed. Seller provider keys are checked once, sealed with AES-256-GCM, and used custodied by the router. Identity is World ID (IDKit) for sellers and approvals, Privy + wagmi for wallets. Tests are node:test against real route handlers, plus live e2e scripts that spend testnet USDC.

projects.title: TRACESEAL
projects.description: Turn HTTPS interactions into cryptographically verifiable evidence using TLSNotary and Hedera.
projects.project_description: TRACESEAL is a cryptographic evidence verification platform that transforms HTTPS interactions into independently verifiable digital evidence. In today's digital ecosystem, screenshots, API responses, and downloaded files can be manipulated, making it difficult to establish whether information genuinely came from a particular online source. TRACESEAL addresses this problem using TLSNotary, allowing users to generate cryptographic proofs of specific HTTPS interactions and verify that disclosed data originated from the claimed server. Users can submit TLSNotary proof packages containing an attestation, presentation, and request metadata. TRACESEAL runs these through a trusted verifier, validates the proof, and generates a canonical SHA-256 commitment using JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785). Each successfully verified evidence record receives a unique ts1_ identifier and is stored for subsequent retrieval and re-verification. TRACESEAL also integrates Hedera to introduce a public audit and accountability layer. Verified evidence can generate HCS audit events, with planned HTS NFT receipts and Mirror Node verification. Only minimal commitment and receipt metadata is intended for public anchoring; the underlying evidence remains stored separately. The key distinction is that TRACESEAL does not simply store screenshots or trust API responses. It verifies cryptographic evidence of an HTTPS interaction, making the verification process independently auditable.
projects.how_its_made: TRACESEAL is built using a Rust-based backend, an Axum HTTP API, a dedicated TLSNotary verifier integration, SQLite for persistent metadata, and filesystem-based artifact storage. The verification pipeline accepts a TLSNotary proof package containing attestation.tlsn, presentation.tlsn, and request.json. The backend invokes a pinned trusted verifier and accepts evidence only after successful cryptographic verification. It then generates a canonical representation using RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme, computes a SHA-256 commitment, and derives a unique ts1_ evidence identifier. The evidence can subsequently be retrieved and re-verified. The frontend provides an interface for submitting evidence, exploring verified records, viewing submission history, and inspecting blockchain anchoring status. projects.title: Neat Swap
projects.description: An AMM that adjusts its swap fee on every trade to undercut competing exchanges.
projects.project_description: neat swap is a token exchange that adjusts its trading fee for every swap instead of using a fixed fee. Before a trade, an off-chain service checks competing exchanges and calculates a fee just below the lowest one it finds. The idea is simple: give traders a lower fee while helping liquidity providers attract more trades. It’s deployed on Base, with a small live pool for testing. A lower fee doesn’t guarantee the best overall swap price, since liquidity and price impact also matter.
projects.how_its_made: We built neat swap with Solidity and Uniswap v4. A custom hook changes the pool’s fee when a swap happens. A Node.js service checks competing venues, calculates the fee and signs a quote. Our router passes that quote to the contracts, which use it to apply the fee. We used Foundry for contract development and testing, then deployed on Base. For now, the quote service is trusted, so the system depends on it providing accurate information.

projects.title: MitrAi
projects.description: MitrAI is an AI companion that grows with you and carries its public memory on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: MitrAI lets people create a character with a personality, voice, appearance and limited lifespan. Conversations gradually shape its traits and memories. Private chats stay private, while the owner can publish approved parts of the character’s mind to Arkiv. Other people can explore its public story, make an offer to continue it, and receive ownership through a wallet transfer. When its life ends, the character becomes a read only legacy. Offers and ownership transfers work in the current app, but payments are not built in yet.
projects.how_its_made: We built MitrAI with Next.js and React. Three.js renders the animated characters, including gestures, speech and lip sync. The conversation system uses 0G Private Computer to generate replies and displays a request ID for each 0G response. A small rules based engine updates traits and memories from conversation evidence. Supabase Postgres stores private chats and owner specific information. The Arkiv SDK stores the character’s approved public state and checkpoints on the Rabdi testnet, where wallet ownership can be verified and transferred. The owner controls what becomes public, so a new owner can continue the character’s story without receiving the previous owner’s private conversations.

projects.title: Resona
projects.description: Resona verifies event check-ins with World ID and phone sonar, then records attendance on Arkiv.
projects.project_description:
Resona is an event ticketing and attendance platform designed to make getting into an event feel as seamless as being there. Organizers create events and issue digital tickets, while attendees discover events, manage tickets in a mobile-friendly wallet and build a public record of the
events they attend. World ID connects a ticket to a verified attendee, helping support fairer access and one-person-per-event participation. At the venue, the attendee’s phone and the door’s phone use sound to confirm that the ticket holder is physically close to the entrance. Successful attendance is recorded on Arkiv, creating a verifiable foundation for event history and attendee profiles. Resona brings ticketing, identity, in-person check-in and attendance records together in one connected experience.
projects.how_its_made:
Resona combines event ticketing, human verification and proximity-based entry in a mobile web app. The frontend is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, and the backend is a Node.js/Express API. Attendees use a browser-held wallet to manage tickets and sign actions; viem verifies those
signatures server-side. Events, tickets, World-linked accounts, claims, payments and successful check-ins are represented as Arkiv entities on the Rabdi test network, so the app can query an event and its attendance history without relying on a conventional application database. Ticket
purchases use testnet payments, and the server checks the payment transaction on-chain before treating a purchased ticket as eligible for entry. For identity, World ID proofs are verified by the server and associated with the attendee’s wallet. The app uses that account identity when enforcing ticket-claim and purchased-ticket check-in policy, rather than treating a ticket’s browser-visible status as proof that a person is verified. Wallet signatures also bind check-in actions and holder reports to the ticket’s wallet. The central technical idea is phone-to-phone acoustic proximity checking. The door and attendee phones generate and play distinct seeded noise signals at scheduled times, capture audio in the browser and analyze the recordings with matched filtering and FFT-based correlation. Each side reports its detected signal timing; the server compares the reports to estimate distance and applies the proximity threshold before admitting the ticket. Fresh seeds and attempt numbers make recordings from earlier attempts unsuitable for a later check. A short pairing code helps connect the two phones, while a door token authenticates the door’s report and the attendee signs their own measurement. The novelty is in combining these mechanisms into one ticket journey: human identity helps limit duplicate participation, wallet signatures establish who is presenting a ticket, sound provides an additional indication that the attendee’s phone is near the door, and Arkiv records the resulting attendance. Rather than making a QR code or a name the whole security model, Resona uses the QR/pairing flow to initiate a check and makes admission depend on server-checked ticket eligibility, signed reports and the measured acoustic result. The design also keeps raw audio off-chain: Arkiv stores ticket and attendance data, not recordings.

projects.title: Clippo
projects.description: Clippo: brands fund USDC bounties, verified humans post clips, AI and Chainlink CRE settle on Arc
projects.project_description: Clippo is a clipping-and-bounty marketplace. A brand funds a USDC pool on Arc and tells its story. World-ID-verified creators post short clips about it. An AI verifier (Claude or Gemini) checks each clip against the brand's story, and sends low-confidence clips to a human. Views are reported on-chain by a Chainlink CRE workflow, and creators claim their own earnings from an escrow contract. Unspent funds go back to the brand. The escrow contract is the product. Per-view credits sit in a retention window, so a campaigner can dispute them before they become claimable. Pools can also be split across many creators, either by an explicit split or by views at close. The contract only pays the creator who earned the money. Clippo's wallet can trigger a payout and pay gas, but it cannot send funds anywhere else. Humans stay in control of the money. An AI agent can propose a split, but it never moves funds alone. Approving it needs a fresh World Agent Pass step-up (OIDC at auth.world.org), and the backend signs an approval bound to that exact split. Creators must prove they are real people with World ID (IDKit) before their wallet can be credited. USDC is both the payment and the gas token on Arc, so one faucet drop covers everything.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity with Foundry. ClippoEscrow handles funding, approval, per-view credits, a retention window, disputes, pool splits, claim and close. It uses EIP-712 signatures for human registration and split approval. The constructor rejects any token that does not have 6 decimals, so it only works with USDC. ClippoReportReceiver accepts Chainlink CRE reports and calls reportViews(). Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow (cron + HTTP trigger) reads Clippo's snapshot feed and writes view counts to the receiver. We read the transaction receipt, because the forwarder hides a failed onReport. We ran it in the CRE simulator. A local broadcast run on an anvil fork of Arc credited creators in the escrow, and an unlinked wallet was refused. It is not deployed and not broadcast to real Arc. World: IDKit v4 with backend verification for creator signup. The Agent Pass step-up is OIDC with PKCE against auth.world.org. The backend checks the ID token and issues a one-time token for that split. Tests use a local fake issuer. Web: Next.js, Prisma and Postgres, with viem for the chain calls. The API checks every transaction on-chain before trusting it. The AI verifier has free-tier protection: throttling, caching, retries, and a fallback to human review when the quota runs out. Something a bit hacky: the chain path switches on as soon as ESCROW_ADDRESS is set, so the same app runs as a demo or against real Arc. Honest limits: Arc Studio was not used (the contracts were written and tested in Foundry). The new escrow has not run end to end on real Arc. The Agent Pass step-up has not been run against the real issuer.

projects.title: Kakashi
projects.description: Pre-trade token risk checks: an AI agent buys x402 checks on Hedera within a World ID mandate.
projects.project_description: Kakashi checks a token before you trade it. Hedera tokens can carry issuer keys that freeze, wipe or pause balances or mint more supply, and they can carry hidden transfer fees. Most traders never check. An agent with a wallet could check for them, but it would spend whatever a prompt, a bug or a merchant talks it into, with no human sign-off and no receipts. You ask a question like "Should I put 2,000 USDC into 0.0.731861?". Kakashi turns it into the risks that matter, collects x402 quotes from four paid check sellers (KeyScan, HolderMap, TreasuryWatch and an adversarial InsiderAlpha), and lets sealed AI on 0G decide which checks the trade size justifies. It pays for them in USDC on Hedera and answers BUY, CAUTION or AVOID, citing a receipt for every purchase. Anything it did not check is listed as unknown. It only ever spends inside a mandate that a World ID-verified human approved: a total budget, a per-payment cap, an auto-approve cap, allowed merchants, a purchase limit and an expiry. Any check above the auto-approve cap needs a fresh World ID approval bound to that one purchase. The model only proposes. Plain code decides. A separate process signs. Every decision and payment can be proven on HashScan and in a hash-chained audit trail on the Hedera Consensus Service.
projects.how_its_made: Kakashi is a TypeScript (strict) pnpm monorepo on Node.js 22: a React 18 + Vite + Tailwind CSS 4 frontend, an Express 5 server that streams each run to the UI over server-sent events, four x402 check-seller merchants, and a separate signer process. State lives in SQLite (better-sqlite3) with append-only migrations and atomic budget reservations. zod validates every boundary, including all model output. 0G: plan, decide and synthesize run as sealed TEE inference on the 0G Router (OpenAI-compatible, private trust mode, verify_tee), with structured output and versioned prompts. Every decision carries a 0G trace ID. An eval scores 0G against a cheapest-first rule, which buys KeyScan every time and misses whales and treasury dumps. World: World ID Agent Pass over the OIDC device flow activates each mandate. The server verifies ID tokens with jose (JWKS, issuer, audience, fresh auth_time). Step-up approvals are single use and bound to one purchase hash. Hedera: the merchants answer with x402 v2 402 quotes (@x402/core, @x402/hedera) and settle in USDC on Hedera testnet through @hiero-ledger/sdk. The checks read real token data from the Hedera mainnet mirror node. Payments are reconciled against the mirror node, so a lost response is recovered instead of paid twice. Audit events are hash-chained and anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic. The hacky part: the model only proposes. Quotes are screened by 12 plain-code policy rules before the AI sees them, two-phase isolation stops prompt injection from merchant data, and an isolated signer pays only against a permit the policy engine issued.

projects.title: Blindspot
projects.description: Private whale alerts and copy trading on Ethereum. Your RPC provider never sees what you watch
projects.project_description: We kept running into the same problem. Every time a trading app checks a wallet, it asks an RPC provider like Infura or Alchemy. That provider sees everything: which wallets are yours, which whales you follow, even the trade you're about to make. That's valuable data, and it can be sold, leaked, or used to jump ahead of you. Anon-RPC is a great start because it hides who is asking. But the question itself still gives you away. "Give me the balance of this address" tells the provider exactly what someone cares about, even if it doesn't know who. So we flipped it around. Blindspot never asks about an address at all. Our relay grabs each new block once, and every user downloads the exact same copy through Anon-RPC. Your phone checks that the block is real, then looks for your wallets on its own. Nothing about what you watch ever leaves your device. On top of that one private core, we built the things traders actually want: Whale alerts: a pending alert about 6 seconds after a whale swaps, then a verified one once the block lands One-tap copy trading, signed on your phone and sent through the mixnet A private portfolio Private lookups of any wallet, using private information retrieval, so the server can't tell which address you asked about A Spy Panel, so you don't have to take our word for it. It shows side by side what a normal RPC learns (your IP and your addresses), what Anon-RPC alone learns (your addresses), and what our relay learns (block numbers, nothing else) It's live on Sepolia at useblindspot.xyz, works on desktop and phone, and needs no install or account. Go try it.
projects.how_its_made: The whole idea rests on one simple trick: if everyone asks for the same thing, nobody's question gives anything away. The relay: a small Node server fetches each new Sepolia block once, along with its EIP-7928 block access list and its receipts, and serves the same bytes to everyone. Phones only ever ask for "block N". Not trusting the relay: the phone checks every block itself. It verifies the header hash, the access-list hash and the receipts root (we wrote our own small trie for that), and checks the blocks link into a chain. Any block with real activity also gets confirmed against a second, independent provider. If the relay lies, the phone catches it. We tested this with tampered blocks on real Sepolia data. Anon-RPC (the partner tech that made this possible): every app read and every transaction goes through the Anon-RPC browser harness. That's what hides the user's IP, and it's why we could promise privacy end to end instead of just "trust our server". We use Nox by default. When we found Nox breaking on iPhone Safari, we built an automatic switch to Nym, plus a switch back once Nox recovers. It never falls back to a direct connection. In our measured session, 98.7% of requests went through the mixnet (230 of 233); the rest were startup reads the harness needs. Private lookups: we implemented private information retrieval using Paillier encryption with a square-root layout. The server computes over every record, encrypted, so it can't tell which one you wanted. A lookup takes 3 to 5 seconds and covers about 1,000 active addresses right now. Wallet history is hidden among 8 wallets, which is weaker, and we say so in the app. The hacky bits we're proud of: Pending alerts come from the relay's mempool feed in about 6 seconds, clearly labelled unverified. The app won't let you copy a trade until the block confirms it. The Spy Panel shows real logged requests, not a mockup. The "normal RPC" column is a deliberately leaky demo lane, locked to demo addresses. Each kind of request (block feed, lookups, quotes, sends) uses its own separate Anon-RPC session. projects.project_description_markdown:
We kept running into the same problem. Every time a trading app checks a wallet, it asks an RPC provider like Infura or Alchemy. That provider sees everything: which wallets are yours, which whales you follow, even the trade you're about to make. That's valuable data, and it can be sold, leaked, or used to jump ahead of you.

Anon-RPC is a great start because it hides who is asking. But the question itself still gives you away. "Give me the balance of this address" tells the provider exactly what someone cares about, even if it doesn't know who.

So we flipped it around. Blindspot never asks about an address at all. Our relay grabs each new block once, and every user downloads the exact same copy through Anon-RPC. Your phone checks that the block is real, then looks for your wallets on its own. Nothing about what you watch ever leaves your device.

On top of that one private core, we built the things traders actually want:
- Whale alerts: a pending alert about 6 seconds after a whale swaps, then a verified one once the block lands
- One-tap copy trading, signed on your phone and sent through the mixnet
- A private portfolio
- Private lookups of any wallet, using private information retrieval, so the server can't tell which address you asked about
- A Spy Panel, so you don't have to take our word for it. It shows side by side what a normal RPC learns (your IP and your addresses), what Anon-RPC alone learns (your addresses), and what our relay learns (block numbers, nothing else)

It's live on Sepolia at useblindspot.xyz, works on desktop and phone, and needs no install or account. Go try it.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The whole idea rests on one simple trick: if everyone asks for the same thing, nobody's question gives anything away.

The relay: a small Node server fetches each new Sepolia block once, along with its EIP-7928 block access list and its receipts, and serves the same bytes to everyone. Phones only ever ask for "block N".

Not trusting the relay: the phone checks every block itself. It verifies the header hash, the access-list hash and the receipts root (we wrote our own small trie for that), and checks the blocks link into a chain. Any block with real activity also gets confirmed against a second, independent provider. If the relay lies, the phone catches it. We tested this with tampered blocks on real Sepolia data.

Anon-RPC (the partner tech that made this possible): every app read and every transaction goes through the Anon-RPC browser harness. That's what hides the user's IP, and it's why we could promise privacy end to end instead of just "trust our server". We use Nox by default. When we found Nox breaking on iPhone Safari, we built an automatic switch to Nym, plus a switch back once Nox recovers. It never falls back to a direct connection. In our measured session, 98.7% of requests went through the mixnet (230 of 233); the rest were startup reads the harness needs.

Private lookups: we implemented private information retrieval using Paillier encryption with a square-root layout. The server computes over every record, encrypted, so it can't tell which one you wanted. A lookup takes 3 to 5 seconds and covers about 1,000 active addresses right now. Wallet history is hidden among 8 wallets, which is weaker, and we say so in the app.

The hacky bits we're proud of:
- Pending alerts come from the relay's mempool feed in about 6 seconds, clearly labelled unverified. The app won't let you copy a trade until the block confirms it.
- The Spy Panel shows real logged requests, not a mockup. The "normal RPC" column is a deliberately leaky demo lane, locked to demo addresses.
- Each kind of request (block feed, lookups, quotes, sends) uses its own separate Anon-RPC session.

Stack: a TypeScript monorepo with an SDK (verification, block feed, PIR, chain follower), the relay, and an installable React web app hosted on GitHub Pages. 90 automated tests.

What's honest to say: it's Sepolia only until block access lists reach mainnet, alerts need the app open (or Watch mode on a phone), and copy trades are public once they land. Next we want a light client so we don't need the second provider, faster PIR, and passkey wallets.

We built it with help from Claude Code, working from our own plan and architecture decisions.

projects.title: FreshMarket
projects.description: Second-hand marketplace: listings owned on Arkiv, USDT checkout on Whitechain, ENS seller names
projects.project_description: FreshMarket is a second-hand marketplace where sellers own their listings, buyers pay in stablecoins, and reviews come only from people who actually bought something. The problem. On today's marketplaces, sellers re-post the same item on every site, sold and abandoned listings stay up for weeks, the platform owns all the data, and anyone can leave a fake review. How FreshMarket solves it, using three networks: Listings on Arkiv (Rabdi testnet). Every listing is an Arkiv entity owned by the seller's wallet. Only that wallet can edit it, reserve it, mark it sold, extend it or delete it. The seller chooses how long it lives (15 minutes for demos, up to 30 days), and when it expires it disappears from every app with no cleanup job. Search uses Arkiv's indexed fields (category, brand, model, city, price range, condition, delivery), so buyers can browse without connecting a wallet. To show the data isn't locked into our app, SECOND LOOK, a separate static storefront with its own Arkiv client and none of our code, reads the same listings. Payments with USDT on Whitechain (Sepolia). Buyers click "Buy now with USDT" and pay through FreshPay, our verified escrow contract. It allows one paid order per listing, so two buyers can't pay for the same item, and it holds the payment until the buyer confirms the item arrived, or a hold period passes. The seller can refund all or part of it, and the refund goes straight back to the buyer's wallet. Payments are verified from the chain, never from what the browser reports. Sellers get a payments dashboard and buyers get a receipt page. The checkout is a reusable React widget and SDK that another app can embed in about 20 lines (live at /checkout-demo). Seller identity with ENSv2 (Ethereum Sepolia). We own freshmarket.eth, run our own subname registry, and give each seller a name like alice.freshmarket.eth with its own Permissioned Resolver, so sellers fully control their profile records. Using Enhanced Access Control, a seller can let a shop manager edit one specific text record and revoke that right later. A listing shows a seller's name only if it resolves back to the wallet that owns the listing. Reviews tied to real purchases. After a FreshPay order is released or refunded, the buyer can write a review. It's stored on Arkiv as a record the buyer owns, and it cites the FreshPay order number. A review counts toward a seller's rating only if that order on Whitechain names the same buyer and seller, so fake reviews are filtered out automatically. Live on testnets now. Realistic listings from several sellers across Mumbai, Pune and Bengaluru; real USDT orders including a partial refund; verified buyer reviews; and ENS registration, delegation and revocation transactions. Every transaction is linked in the README. Tech. Next.js, TypeScript, wagmi/viem, the Arkiv SDK, Solidity with Foundry (FreshPay contract, tests and a fork test against the real USDT), and ENSv2 contracts on Sepolia. The code is open source under the MIT license.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19 and TypeScript, Tailwind, wagmi + RainbowKit + viem for wallets, TanStack Query for caching, Vitest and Testing Library for app tests, and Foundry for the Solidity contract. The second storefront, SECOND LOOK, is a separate static Vite build. Deployed on Vercel. Three chains, each doing one job. Arkiv Rabdi stores listings and reviews, Ethereum Sepolia (ENSv2) stores seller identity, and Whitechain Sepolia settles USDT payments. Each chain gets its own read client and transport, and none of them reads the wallet's active network. So an ENS or Whitechain outage, or a user switching networks, never breaks Arkiv browsing. Each page declares the chain it needs, and the navbar badge switches the wallet only when the user clicks it. Arkiv. We defined a freshmarket.listings.v2 schema with the Arkiv SDK, using 10 indexed attributes so every search is a single indexed query instead of a client-side scan: Price is a u64 in USDT minor units (6 decimals), so price ranges are range queries on the chain. Categories are paths like pets/dogs/toys, so startsWith selects a whole branch. A small resolver maps free text, spacing and typos ("dogtoy", "dgo toy") to category paths. The repository validates every row it reads (seller must equal $owner, enums must be known values), because anyone can write the same schema tag. Expiry is a block height, and extending reads the current deadline and sets a new one. The UI never retries a wallet write, and it waits out indexing lag before refreshing. The wallet's Rabdi connection deliberately carries no access key, so the key never reaches the wallet; public reads use an origin-restricted key. Arkiv's ownership model is what makes the marketplace portable: SECOND LOOK reads the same entities with its own client and zero FreshMarket code. ENSv2. We own freshmarket.eth and deployed our own UserRegistry proxy through ENS's VerifiableFactory, then attached it as the subregistry. Each seller gets a dedicated PermissionedResolver proxy. Because Enhanced Access Control resources are scoped by record key, not by name, a resolver per seller is what stops a delegate from touching other storefronts. Sellers grant ROLE_SET_TEXT on the resource keccak256("freshmarket.description") to a shop manager and can revoke it. A name is shown only after reverse lookup, then forward resolution back to the same wallet, matched against the listing's Arkiv $owner. We pinned the ENSv2 Sepolia deployment and tested delegation against the real resolver bytecode with eth_simulateV1. Whitechain: the FreshPay contract. Solidity 0.8.28 with OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 and ReentrancyGuard, and no admin keys: Order IDs are sequential u64 values so they fit the orderId field of our Arkiv review schema; that's the cross-chain proof of purchase. activeOrder[merchant][ref] uses the Arkiv entity key as the reference, which gives every listing an atomic "stock of one" across all storefronts. Arkiv data alone can't enforce that. A quote deadline stops a stale checkout page from paying an old price. A balance-delta check rejects fee-on-transfer tokens. Escrow holds funds until the buyer confirms or a hold period passes. Partial refunds come from escrow, or from the seller after release. It has 21 unit and fuzz tests, plus fork tests against the official USDT on an Anvil fork of Whitechain. It's deployed and verified through Foundry's Blockscout verifier. Reusable checkout. src/freshpay/ is self-contained (it imports only react, viem and wagmi): a hook and widget that switch network, approve the exact amount, simulate before asking for a signature, pay, and then verify the order from the receipt and contract state, never from what the browser reports. There are also signed webhooks (HMAC-SHA256, idempotency keys, an outbox with a cursor and exponential backoff), tested for crash recovery. Notable hacks: Getting official test USDT. There's no faucet, and the docs list a different token. We traced the official USDT's owner to a USDTBridge contract, found a Uniswap V3 WWBT/USDT pool on Whitechain Sepolia, and swapped our own WBT through SwapRouter02 to get the USDT for real payments. Log history. Whitechain's RPC caps eth_getLogs at 10,000 blocks (under 3 hours), so order history comes from the Blockscout logs API, with a chunked RPC fallback. Live demo data. Seeded through opt-in Vitest scripts that reuse the app's own repositories. They're resumable from an evidence file and detect writes whose receipts were lost to rate limits, so nothing is posted twice. Proving a failed edit. Wallets won't broadcast a transaction that will revert, so we prove "a revoked delegate can't edit" with a read-only eth_call against the live resolver (npm run verify:ens-delegation). Reviews checked across chains. Each Arkiv review is checked against its Whitechain order, so ratings count only real, settled purchases.

projects.title: PACT
projects.description: Copy trading where your rules run first, Flash executes, and every fill is proven onchain.
projects.project_description:
Copy trading mostly works for the leader. A publisher-reported study of 100,236 copier outcomes on Binance, Bybit and MEXC found 97% of leaders in profit on their own PnL, but only 44% of them made money for the people copying them. Followers get someone else's size and a worse price, and they have no exit of their own. Sometimes they're the leader's exit liquidity. PACT copies the plan, not the trader. A leader publishes a structured plan: entry, stop, target, order type and a time window. Each follower has a mandate: their own rules per leader. That's how much to copy, how much per day, which order types, how far from the entry they'll pay, and how they exit. Up to ten leaders. When a plan arrives, PACT decides before asking for a price: copy, scale down, wait, decline or review, with the reasons. If it's a copy, Flash quotes the follower's exact size, the price has to agree with Chainlink, and the follower's own browser checks Flash's payload before the wallet signs. The follower gets their own Flash order: a TWAP or limit entry whose limit price is their maximum entry drift, with their own stop and target attached. PACT never holds keys or funds. What's new: Leaders are held to account. PACT reads the leader's wallet on Base. It flags anyone who sells into their followers' buys or trades well ahead of publishing a plan. Do it twice, and every follower's new copies of that leader are held. One human per leader. World ID (Proof of Human) means a leader can't blow up a wallet and come back fresh. Proof, not promises. Every number comes from Flash's fill records. Each copy gets a receipt that checks five promises against Flash's own report. Every decision goes into a hash-chained log the browser re-verifies. Flash stamps PACT's ERC-8021 builder code into each settlement transaction, so the chain itself shows the fill came through PACT. PACT's fee has to be earned. It's 10 bps, charged only on copies of proven leaders, and zero while a leader is on probation or flagged. It works with real money. On 7 Nov we copied a live ETH plan for $5 on Base: two TWAP slices, executed at $2,239.56 against the leader's $2,239.12 entry (+2 bps); $0.059 in fees; the stop and target live on Flash; 5 of 5 receipt checks matched. Fills:
https://basescan.org/tx/0x0d3ed912328e1379a60a8506eb6a53b24e52bb7a7d85c68878a376e05fe25474
https://basescan.org/tx/0x682b4fd438bc90dbe5b49d24bb09e565e5f7f76a28744f107e5f9a39225f3a81 Demo video: https://youtu.be/V1AYH5wm_vY
projects.how_its_made: PACT is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, wagmi and viem, with a Solidity layer using Foundry. Its architecture spans eight layers, from external integrations and evidence storage to policy, execution, wallet authority and the trading terminal. Definitive Flash is our execution layer and source of truth. We use its REST API and WebSocket for real quotes, TWAP and limit orders, TP/SL brackets, cancellations and fill tracking. Every copy decision is priced using a real Flash quote. Followers receive independently sized orders, with maximum entry drift enforced through the order's limit price. Finalized fills drive receipts, P&L and entry-drift accounting, preventing reorgs from being double-counted. Security is a core part of PACT. Before any wallet prompt, the browser independently decodes Flash's EIP-712 FlashOrder and Permit2 payloads and performs 33 checks covering recipients, tokens, chain, amounts, spender and deadlines. One end-to-end test inflates the order amount 20x on the server; the browser rejects it before signing. Our TypeScript policy engine handles proportional, fixed and stop-risk sizing, portfolio caps, probation, plan grades, style drift, revenge re-entry and a three-price check using Chainlink, pool data and Flash quotes, which must agree within 1%. We integrated World ID 4 (IDKit 4.6) for proof of human. Requests are RP-signed and verified through /v4/verify. The proof's signal is bound to the leader's wallet, while the nullifier ensures one human per leader address. It also provides human approval for Autopilot limits. For leader accountability, we inspect Base transaction receipts and ERC-20 Transfer logs against published plans and follower fills. PACT flags selling into followers (25%+ of a position during their fills) and potential front-running (30+ minutes earlier at a price at least 1% better). Every event is stored in a SHA-256 hash-chained evidence log, independently verifiable in the browser and exportable per order. We also built an experimental Autopilot using Foundry and Solidity 0.8.28. Its session account validates Flash orders and Permit2 permits through EIP-1271 within an onchain scope covering signer, expiry, tokens, amounts and recipient. It is tested against real Permit2 on a Base fork but remains in dry-run mode, not deployed. Some interesting engineering challenges came from real execution: bracketed limit orders require limitCrossPrice instead of limitNotionalPrice; market quotes can embed fees in execution prices, requiring custom cost accounting. We never blindly retry /order, since Flash may create or fill an order before returning an error. Instead, we snapshot and reconcile orders after failures. Our first real $5 execution exposed a fee-related price-bound mismatch, which we fixed with a regression test. ERC-8021 attribution is attached to every order using PACT's builder code and decoded from settlement calldata on Base. Our real fills carry both Definitive's code (bc_lv99qw8t) and ours (pactfi). We also configure flashIntegratorFeeBps per copy, charging 10 bps only on proven leaders and zero during probation or after conduct flags. PACT executes live on Base, with Arc (chain 5042) supporting the same flow up to signing. Validation: 197 unit tests, 10 live Flash integration tests, 14 Foundry tests (including Base-fork tests against real Permit2), 3 Anvil tests, 48 follower end-to-end checks, 40 UI checks and 22 World ID staging checks. We also completed one real $5 copy on Base, executing at $2,239.56 against the leader's $2,239.12 entry (+2 bps). Built with Claude Code as a pair programmer, with testing against real partner integrations wherever possible.

Some interesting engineering challenges came from real execution: bracketed limit orders require limitCrossPrice instead of limitNotionalPrice; market quotes can embed fees in execution prices, requiring custom cost accounting. We never blindly retry /order, since Flash may create or fill an order before returning an error. Instead, we snapshot and reconcile orders after failures. Our first real $5 execution exposed a fee-related price-bound mismatch, which we fixed with a regression test.

ERC-8021 attribution is attached to every order using PACT's builder code and decoded from settlement calldata on Base. Our real fills carry both Definitive's code (bc_lv99qw8t) and ours (pactfi). We also configure flashIntegratorFeeBps per copy, charging 10 bps only on proven leaders and zero during probation or after conduct flags.

PACT executes live on Base, with Arc (chain 5042) supporting the same flow up to signing.

Validation: 197 unit tests, 10 live Flash integration tests, 14 Foundry tests (including Base-fork tests against real Permit2), 3 Anvil tests, 48 follower end-to-end checks, 40 UI checks and 22 World ID staging checks. We also completed one real $5 copy on Base, executing at $2,239.56 against the leader's $2,239.12 entry (+2 bps).

Built with Claude Code as a pair programmer, with testing against real partner integrations wherever possible.

projects.title: ETHCraft
projects.description: A Minecraft city where AI agents gather, craft and build, powered by a Uniswap CITY-token economy.
projects.project_description: ETHCraft brings AI agents and an on-chain resource marketplace into Minecraft. Players explore a Mumbai-inspired city and give agents natural-language objectives, such as gathering materials, crafting items, constructing supported structures and delivering supplies. Agents act through game tools, observe their results and report progress. The marketplace connects this activity to a Uniswap v4 test-USDC/CITY pool. Players can acquire CITY and purchase stocked resources through Privy-managed game wallets, with approvals and checkout inside Minecraft. Arkiv makes selected agent progress publicly queryable and supports handoffs between workers. ETHCraft explores how games can make AI coordination and blockchain interactions understandable through familiar actions: requesting work, collecting resources and buying useful items. The current prototype uses test tokens on Unichain Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: ETHCraft combines a Java Paper plugin, Mineflayer agents and a Node.js backend. The plugin handles physical world interactions, inventory changes and player permissions. PostgreSQL and durable execution journals preserve identities and task history. Discord connects a player’s account to their Minecraft session, while Privy-managed wallets handle authorized testnet transactions. An orchestration layer routes decisions between economy and advanced models according to task complexity. 0G provides inference and work assessments. An optional voice pipeline connects 0G Whisper transcription to the same agent tools, then uses MiniMax speech synthesis for replies. Server-side policies enforce permissions and receiving-tool checks. Our Solidity integration uses Uniswap v4 on Unichain Sepolia. A custom hook applies elapsed-time price checks, liquidity requirements, trade limits and circuit breakers. Confirmed payment receipts are reconciled with native item delivery to prevent duplicate releases during retries. These controls reduce specific risks without claiming manipulation immunity or zero LVR. Arkiv stores structured, expiring progress snapshots that power the public dashboard and inform owner-requested agent handoffs. Minecraft remains authoritative for physical actions. The project extends earlier AgentCity code and uses attributed Arnis/OpenStreetMap map assets.

projects.title: Iva
projects.description: A Grocery agent on Telegram that finds the cheapest basket across apps, and she pays for her own AI
projects.project_description: Most AI agents stop working the day their owner stops paying the API bill. Iva pays her own. Iva is a Telegram grocery agent for India. Send her a shopping list as text, a photo of a note or a voice note. She checks Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto at your address, matches the same product across all three apps (different brands, names and pack sizes) and gives you the cheapest basket, the money you save and a link to each product. On a real 3-item list in Mumbai she found Zepto ₹213 vs Instamart ₹288, a ₹75 saving. How she keeps herself alive: each hunt costs 0.2 0G, paid into Iva's own wallet. She verifies the payment on 0G mainnet, then signs depositFor on the 0G Payment Layer to top up her own 0G compute account. No human tops her up. On mainnet a customer paid 4.8 0G and 7 seconds later Iva deposited 1.6 0G into her compute. A hunt costs her about 0.02 0G, so she earns roughly 10x what she spends. She reads her own balance before every job and picks the best brain she can afford: rich (glm-5.3 sealed in a TEE), lean (a model about 50x cheaper) or survival (no AI, still answers). Her API key has a 2 0G/day limit enforced by 0G, so she degrades instead of crashing. People come back: /watch re-checks your list every morning, and /deals shows live deals near you for free. Every winning price is published to Arkiv as an entity that expires after 6 hours, because grocery deals only last hours. She can also do the whole job: say "order" and she fills your Zepto cart through Zepto's official MCP, shows Zepto's bill and orders only after you reply YES. Without 0G, Iva can't understand your list, match products or pay for her own thinking. She would be a dumb keyword script.
projects.how_its_made: A Node.js agent running 24/7 as a service, plus a Next.js 16 website on Vercel. Shops: one shared headless Chrome (playwright-core) with an isolated context per shop and location. Instead of scraping HTML, we read the JSON that each shop's own search page fetches (Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto) and normalise it to one shape: price, MRP, pack, price per kg or piece, stock and link. Direct API calls are blocked by request signing and Cloudflare, so letting the real page do the fetch was the reliable route. AI on 0G Private Computer: the 0G Router (OpenAI-compatible). glm-5.3 sealed in a TEE reads lists and matches products across shops, qwen3-vl-plus reads photos, qwen3-omni-flash reads voice notes, and qwen3.7-flash is the cheap "lean" brain. We read each call's request ID and cost from x_0g_trace, show them to the user and log them in an append-only receipts file. Self-paying loop (viem on 0G mainnet): a treasury loop runs every 30 s and on every payment. It verifies the payment from its receipt (sent to Iva, succeeded, never claimed before), credits hunts, then calls depositFor on the 0G Payment Layer to top up her compute. Before each job she reads Router /account/funds and Payment Layer balanceOf to pick rich, lean or survival. The API key has a 0G-enforced daily credit_limit, and 402/429 responses drop her to survival instead of crashing. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet, @arkiv-network/sdk): schema iva.deal.v1 with indexed city, item, shop, unit price and time. Each hunt publishes up to 12 entities in one batched tx with a 6-hour expiry, through a queue, after the user already has their answer. Reads filter on Iva's wallet as owner, so nobody can inject fake deals. Zepto: an MCP SDK client for Zepto's official MCP server with OAuth (dynamic client registration + PKCE). It shows Zepto's bill, needs an explicit YES and never retries an order call. Hacky bits: some wallets underprice gas on 0G and their transactions never land, so the pay page sends legacy transactions with a gas-price floor and waits for the receipt. OKX Wallet's in-app browser returns fake hashes on 0G, so users can also pay from any wallet and paste the hash into the bot.

projects.title: Igris
projects.description: Discover which third parties receive your wallet address when you use a dApp.
projects.project_description: IGRIS is an open-source privacy intelligence platform for decentralized applications (dApps). It reveals what happens to your wallet identity when you interact with Web3 applications. Using isolated browser sessions and unique throwaway canary wallets, IGRIS observes how dApps expose wallet addresses to third-party services. It captures and analyzes wallet connections, RPC requests, signing interactions, network activity, and third-party tracking behavior. Instead of relying on static code analysis or generic security scores, IGRIS produces evidence-backed privacy reports that show which services receive wallet information, what information is exposed, and when the exposure occurs. Users can explore interactive timelines, connection relationships, privacy verdicts, and supporting evidence to understand the actual data flows behind a dApp. IGRIS also publishes versioned, independently re-verifiable scan reports to Arkiv, creating a persistent and transparent record of dApp privacy behavior. Our goal is to make Web3 privacy observable, understandable, and actionable for everyone.
projects.how_its_made: IGRIS is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm, with a modular architecture separating the frontend, scanning infrastructure, analysis engine, and report registry. The frontend uses Preact and Vite to provide an interactive interface for submitting dApp URLs, exploring scan results, visualizing privacy timelines, and inspecting evidence. The scanning engine uses Playwright and isolated Chromium browser sessions to interact with real dApps. Each scan uses a unique throwaway canary wallet implementing EIP-1193 and EIP-6963 wallet interfaces. This allows IGRIS to observe wallet connection behavior without requiring users to connect their actual wallets. Captured activity passes through an evidence pipeline that records wallet requests, RPC interactions, network activity, and third-party exposure. The core analysis package processes this evidence using modular detectors, relationship analysis, and verdict generation. We developed versioned data contracts for scans, evidence, wallet requests, and observed flows to maintain consistency and reproducibility across the system. For persistent transparency, IGRIS integrates Arkiv as its report registry, allowing versioned scan reports to be published and queried independently. The system also includes controlled test fixtures for validating detection behavior against known privacy leaks and expected outcomes. The entire project is open source under the MIT license.

projects.title: Monolith
projects.description: Privacy crash tests for Web3 apps to catch RPC leaks, fix routing, and verify the repair.
projects.project_description: Monolith is a privacy regression testing toolkit for wallet and Web3 checkout developers. An app can protect one blockchain read while a balance widget, receipt lookup or retry still contacts an RPC provider directly. Monolith helps developers find and reproduce those accidental bypasses. Its interactive Leak Lab runs useful blockchain reads, compares direct requests with a real Anon-RPC/Nym route, deliberately introduces a leaking widget, and demonstrates a bounded routing repair. Independent observations are checked against transport traces, so a successful repair must preserve useful reads and satisfy the privacy policy. Required-private reads stop when the worker or trusted discovery is unavailable. Arkiv supplies public EVM endpoint metadata with publisher, provenance and expiry checks. A dashboard, CLI and browser regression checks make results inspectable and repeatable. Monolith tests the network route; RPC providers still see request methods and payloads, and public blockchain activity remains public.
projects.how_its_made: We built Monolith as a TypeScript pnpm monorepo with a React/Vite dashboard, a Fastify observer, and shared transport, registry and analysis packages. MonolithTransport integrates the Anon-RPC browser harness with a real Nym worker. Chain-ID probes and application reads use the protected route or fail closed. Using the Arkiv SDK and viem, our importer published 100 public chain/RPC records from an MIT-licensed ethereum-lists/chains snapshot to Arkiv Rabdi. The reader validates publisher identity, source hashes and expiry before admitting endpoint candidates. The distinctive engineering trick is testing outside the transport wrapper: independent Chromium/Playwright observations detect widgets that bypass it entirely. The repair reruns the same useful operation while preserving the original failure. Vitest, static checks and browser regressions cover routing and trust boundaries. Optional EIP-6963 wallet support includes explicit Whitechain Sepolia network selection; payments remain disabled.

projects.title: Aftershock
projects.description: Stateful testing for EIP-8141 Frame Transactions and the Alternative Mempool.
projects.project_description:
Aftershock is a developer testing workbench for EIP-8141 Frame Transactions and the Alternative Mempool. Getting a transaction admitted is only the beginning: payer balances, nonce conflicts and replacements can affect what happens before inclusion.
Aftershock runs controlled experiments against real isolated nodes and checks expected behavior against actual observations. Our original suites test shared-payer affordability and keyed-nonce conflict/replacement lifecycles. Additional coverage includes replacement TTL expiry and refresh.
Developers can also upload compiled contract bytecode with an ordered test plan. Contract lab deploys the contract, executes calls, mined transactions or Frame Transactions, and checks declared return-data and storage assertions. Hosted execution runs through GitHub Actions, so visitors need only a browser.
Each run produces inspectable evidence, including transaction hashes, admission observations, receipts, assertions and cleanup results. The website separately supports live public-devnet inspection and bounded transaction/contract-call simulation.
Aftershock helps wallet, payer and mempool developers reproduce issues and catch regressions. It provides scoped testing against pinned implementations, not a general security certification.
projects.how_its_made:
Aftershock uses TypeScript, npm workspaces, Zod for input/report validation, viem for account and contract interactions, and the official @forshtat/hegota-support codec for EIP-8141 transaction encoding, signing and RPC serialization.
The scenario engine runs against an isolated EIP-8141-aware ethrex fork, the alternative-mempool sidecar and Lighthouse consensus. Tests create fresh accounts and controlled state transitions, then compare node observations with assertions derived from pinned implementation rules. Admission and successful execution are checked separately.
A lightweight HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend and bounded API functions run on Vercel. GitHub Actions provisions disposable Linux execution environments, runs Docker-based tests and returns validated report artifacts. Workflow identity, source commit and artifact integrity are checked; custom contract reports are also bound to the submitted plan’s SHA-256 hash. The CLI supports local execution, reports, comparison and scoped replay workflows.
We reuse upstream clients, the official codec and workshop assets. Our contribution is stateful scenario orchestration, invariant checks, evidence capture and the developer-facing test-plan workflow. Public-devnet submission and mined execution were also verified. AI assistance is disclosed in the repository.

projects.title: WhitePe
projects.description: Pay any merchant QR with crypto. Merchants receive USDT on Whitechain.            Convert to PDF
projects.project_description:
WhitePe enables customers to pay any registered merchant by scanning their existing payment QR code and using crypto from supported blockchain networks. WhitePe handles the conversion and routing, while merchants receive USDT directly on Whitechain. The problem
Merchants already use QR-based payment systems to collect payments, but these systems don't let customers spend crypto directly. Meanwhile, crypto holders face friction when trying to use their digital assets for everyday purchases. The solution
WhitePe bridges traditional QR-based merchant payments and multi-chain crypto. Merchants register their QR identity and connect a receiving wallet. Customers simply scan the QR, enter the amount, choose their preferred crypto asset, and pay. How it works Merchant onboarding: Register a business, upload or register an existing UPI or merchant QR code, and connect a Whitechain receiving wallet. Scan any merchant QR: Customers scan the merchant's existing payment QR through WhitePe. Choose how to pay: Enter the payment amount and select a supported crypto asset from available blockchain networks. Automatic conversion and routing: WhitePe handles the swap and cross-chain routing required to deliver the payment. Merchant receives USDT: The payment settles in USDT on Whitechain, with an on-chain transaction receipt.
projects.how_its_made: WhitePe is implemented using Next.js, TypeScript, Solidity, and viem , with Whitechain Sepolia as the settlement network. The frontend handles merchant onboarding, QR scanning, payment creation, wallet connections, and transaction tracking. Privy is used for embedded wallet authentication, while MetaMask and other external wallets are supported through wallet connectors. QR scanning is implemented using a browser-based QR scanner. The application parses the QR payload to extract merchant payment details, including the UPI ID or other supported merchant identifier. A merchant registry maps the extracted identifier to the merchant's registered Whitechain wallet. Smart contracts are written in Solidity and deployed on Whitechain Sepolia. The merchant registry stores merchant identifiers, wallet addresses, and registration status. The payment contract resolves the merchant's registered wallet, processes USDT settlement, prevents duplicate payments, and emits events for transaction tracking. Viem handles contract reads, transaction preparation, wallet interactions, and on-chain event monitoring. Cross-chain routing infrastructure is integrated to obtain swap quotes and route supported assets from source networks into USDT on Whitechain. The customer checkout flow calculates the required crypto amount, displays the routing quote, requests wallet authorization, and tracks the transaction until settlement is confirmed. The merchant dashboard listens for payment events and updates transaction history and receipts. The application is structured around reusable frontend components, dedicated contract interaction utilities, and a minimal backend for merchant data and transaction indexing.

projects.title: oscillon-auction
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that auctions the first trade at stock-market reopen and pays the bid to LPs
projects.project_description: Tokenized stocks like NVDA trade on-chain 24/7, but the real market closes overnight and on weekends. When it reopens, the pool price is stale, and the first arbitrageur trades at the old price and takes the gap straight from LPs. Reopen Auction Hook fixes that exact moment. When the market reopens, a keeper starts an auction on the pool. Normal swaps are paused for a few blocks while the price for the right to make the first trade falls every block (a Dutch auction). The first arbitrageur to accept pays the bid and makes their swap in the same transaction, moving the pool to the real price. The bid is donated straight to the pool's LPs. If nobody bids, the auction times out and the pool reopens on its own, so it can never get stuck. Why not just raise fees? A fee only returns a capped slice of the gap. projects.title: RentMeOut
projects.description: Rent Me Out tokenises rental rights so only the token holder can rent out a room.
projects.project_description:
Rent Me Out tackles a common rental problem in India and elsewhere: a tenant usually can't tell whether the broker in
front of them has any right to rent out a room. Duplicate brokers collect advances for the same room, and fake agents take
the money and vanish. We turn the right to rent out a room for a fixed period into a token. An owner verifies with World ID and submits their
property and deed, and a registrar reviews them. Once approved, the owner lists each room with its dates, price and map
location, and each listing creates one token. A broker who has verified with World ID buys that token with USDC, and the
payment and transfer happen in a single transaction, so neither side has to trust the other. Tenants need no account. They can open a public page to see who holds a room's rights, the rental period, the status and
the map pin. At a viewing, they can ask the broker to prove their World ID session against a fresh challenge and get a
signed match or mismatch. In a dispute, the registrar can freeze a room until it is resolved, and the token can be burned
once the period ends. The token only gives the right to rent out a room for that period. It does not transfer ownership of
the property. The app is live on Hedera testnet.
projects.how_its_made:
The frontend and API routes are built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with viem and MetaMask for wallet actions. The
contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed on Hedera testnet. Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio is the core of the project. Our RentalRegistry contract calls the ATS factory when a
listing is created, so a listing can't exist without its token. Each room gets its own token with a supply of 1 and zero
decimals, and the registry controls its transfers, freezes and burn. Each token's allowlist holds only its current holder,
so a broker has nobody to resell to. World ID 4.0 through IDKit handles uniqueness. Proofs are verified on our server, and one identity binds to one wallet
on-chain, so buyRoom rejects unverified wallets. We use Semaphore for private approvals: the registrar approves an
anonymous commitment, and the owner later proves membership in the browser without revealing which approved property is
theirs. The price, dates, payout wallet and coordinates are bound to that proof, so a relayer can't change them. Arkiv is our public data layer for searchable listings, the registrar queue and rights records, and entries expire with
the rental. Swarm stores deeds and application details. Public Swarm gateways disable its built-in encryption, so we
encrypt with AES-256-GCM on our server first and keep only a plain reference on Arkiv. If Arkiv is unavailable, rights
still come from Hedera, and a failed Arkiv write never undoes a sale. A few hacky parts are worth mentioning. World's signRequest doesn't let us choose the nonce, so we built a signed binding
that ties each World request to our own challenge. Each person can only complete a World action once, so we added a suffix
to our action names to rehearse repeatedly. We also pinned ATS to version 8.0.0 because newer structs change the
deployEquity selector, and we switched to partial token freezes after live testing showed that setAddressFrozen wasn't
doing what we needed.

projects.title: Kalypso
projects.description: Private data on Arkiv: encrypt on device, prove facts in zero knowledge, and delete for real.
projects.project_description: Arkiv is a public DB-chain: every attribute, owner and byte of calldata is readable by anyone, and deleteEntity only clears current state. Old blocks keep the data forever in every archive node.Kalypso is a TypeScript SDK and web app that makes private data work on Arkiv without changing Arkiv: Encrypt: records are encrypted in the browser (AES-256-GCM, size-bucket padding). Only ciphertext and a Poseidon2 commitment go on-chain. Each record key is split 2-of-3 between your device and two guardians, with shares sent over hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM-768 + X25519). Query: exact-match, range and COUNT search on encrypted fields, plus a relational layer (atomic multi-insert, 1:N and M:N blind foreign keys, batched JOIN, cascade). Everything compiles down to Arkiv's own indexed equality, OR and count, so Arkiv never sees a value. Prove: Noir circuits (UltraHonk) prove claims like "age ≥ 18" about a committed record, right in the browser. The proof is published on Arkiv, and anyone can verify it on a public page with no wallet and no key. Shred: the device and guardians destroy their key shares and sign attestations. One Arkiv transaction deletes the entities and publishes a public shred receipt. An archive node that kept the old calldata can try to decrypt it on the "Break it" page, and it gets only noise. Everything runs live on Arkiv Rabdi (chain 7794095), with real transactions and no mocks.
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo in TypeScript (pnpm workspaces): packages/crypto: AES-256-GCM via @noble/ciphers, HKDF, HMAC blind-index and range-tree tags, Shamir 2-of-3 over GF(2^8), hybrid ML-KEM-768 + X25519 share wrapping (@noble/post-quantum). packages/zk: Noir circuits for range and equality over Poseidon2 commitments, proved with Barretenberg UltraHonk (bb.js WASM in the browser). Verification keys are published on Arkiv, so verifiers fetch them from the chain. packages/core, vault, shred, sdk: the ArkivZK client on @arkiv-network/sdk 1.0.1, with typed schemas, record, proof, VK and shred-receipt entities, absolute expiry tied to the retention you choose, and native batches so a cascade shred is one atomic transaction. It also includes a query planner with IN-batching via OR (at most 18 terms), keyset paging, projections and explain(). guardian/: two small Node services that hold key shares, destroy them on request and sign attestations. archive/: an indexer that captures raw Kalypso calldata from Rabdi, plus an API that replays it and tries to decrypt, to show that shredding works against a real archive. apps/web: a Next.js 16 app with a vault, query explorer, prove, a public verify page, shred, and the archive "Break it" page. Reads go through a server-side RPC proxy, so the Arkiv access key never reaches the browser. Writes are signed by the user's wallet, or by one-time signers funded by a relayer, so records can't be linked to a wallet. Swarm: optional encrypted attachments uploaded to a Bee node. Only ciphertext goes to Swarm, and the reference is kept encrypted, never stored as-is on Arkiv. The notable trick is that encrypted search, COUNT and JOIN all run on Arkiv's own index. We store HMAC tags (blind indexoreign keys) as indexed attributes and compile queries to equality and OR, so nothing is downloaded and decrypted just to

projects.title: BinStep
projects.description: Shaped, auto-managed liquidity bins on Uniswap v4, with private wallet reads through Anon-RPC
projects.project_description: BinStep is a liquidity management app built on Uniswap v4 hooks. On a normal pool, an LP picks one price range and manages it by hand. BinStep lets an LP spread one position across up to 32 bins, each 0.10% wide, in a Spot, Curve or Bid-Ask shape, and see that shape on an interactive chart before depositing. Pools use a dynamic swap fee that rises with volatility, from 0.05% up to 1%, so LPs earn more when the price moves fast. LPs can opt in to automation: a keeper compounds earned fees back into the position and moves an out-of-range position beside the current price. The contracts only allow these actions when the price is stable, and rebalances have a cooldown. Each position shows how many times it has been compounded and rebalanced. The app also has swaps, a market list, and pool creation, so anyone can launch a test token and pool. Wallet-specific reads go through Anon-RPC by default, so an RPC provider can't easily link a wallet address to a user's IP. Public market data comes from the app's server and names no wallet. BinStep doesn't remove impermanent loss, and it doesn't aim to beat Uniswap on swap execution. Its goal is to give v4 LPs better control and less manual work. It runs on Base Sepolia with test tokens, and the contracts have not been audited.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed to Base Sepolia on the Uniswap v4 PoolManager. BinStepHook sets the volatility-based fee in beforeSwap, tracks volatility and a stable reference price in afterSwap, and only lets our manager add liquidity. We used HookMiner to find a hook address that encodes the right permissions. BinStepManager owns every position. Each bin is a separate v4 liquidity range, and the position id is used as the v4 salt, which keeps each position's fees separate. Compounds and rebalances run inside a single unlock callback, so many bins can change in one transaction. This costs more gas than a single-range position, and that is a trade-off we accepted to get custom shapes. BinStepRegistry lets anyone create a test token and pool. The frontend uses Next.js, wagmi and viem. Anon-RPC is integrated through @anon-rpc/browser-harness, trying the Nox worker and then Nym, and it never falls back to plain RPC without the user choosing it. Public market data and stats are served from Next.js API routes, because scanning a day of logs through a mixnet for each visitor would be too heavy. Transactions still go through the user's wallet RPC. The keeper and a demo trading bot are TypeScript services running on Railway, and the site runs on Vercel. The keeper reads every position, picks up to two useful actions per run, and reports what actually happened on-chain. The hacky parts: we started on Chainlink CRE, then replaced it with our own keeper because deploy access wasn't available. It still sends reports through a mock forwarder, which must be replaced before real funds. Swaps use a test-style router, and the bot creates the demo volume. Airdrops send tokens and starter gas in one atomic Multicall3 transaction.

projects.title: Quietpay
projects.description: Gasless Stripe-style USDT payments on Whitechain: checkout, links, subscriptions and refunds.
projects.project_description:
QuietPay lets a business get paid in USDT on Whitechain, from the first checkout through everything after it. Neither the customer nor the merchant ever pays gas or sees a seed phrase. Most crypto checkouts are a "pay" button that sends a plain transfer and leaves the merchant to sort out the rest. QuietPay handles the parts a real business needs once the first payment has gone through: Hosted checkout. The merchant's server creates a checkout session and redirects the customer. The customer logs in with Google, email or MetaMask, gets an embedded wallet (Privy) and pays with a single signature. Our relayer submits the transaction and pays the gas. Payment links and QR codes. A shop can sell at a physical counde. Subscriptions with failed-payment handling. The customer approves a plan once. A keeper charges each period automatically. If a renewal fails, the subscription goes past due and is retried during a grace perioid, the contract cancels it for nonpayment. Customers can cancelfrom the customer portal, also without gas.                                                                                                        Refunds. Partial or full refunds come from the merchant's own t caps the total refunded at the original amount. Receipts, signed webhooks with retries, CSV export and a merchant dashboard. The dashboard covers payments, subscriptions, plans, links, API keys, webhook delivery logs and a gas budget for each merchant. @quietpay/node SDK. A merchant integrates in about 20 lines. Money is never custodied. Funds go from the customer to our contract to the merchant's wallet within a single transaction. The rules are enforced not by trusting us: merchant-signed invoices, the exact amount, und caps and subscription spending limits. Our operator canregister merchants and plans, but it cannot move a customer's money without the customer's signature, and it cannot refund without the merchant's signature. To prove the integration is real, we built Swag Counter, a separhat talks to QuietPay only through the public SDK and HTTP, theway a real merchant would. All of these are real transactions in official test USDT on Whitechain Sepolia, with explorer links in our repo: a one-time
payment, a payment-link purchase, a new subscription, an automat and a partial refund. sdk docs: https://quietpay.gitbook.io/quietpay-docs

Chain and token. QuietPay runs on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) with the official test USDT (TetherTokenV2 proxy, 6 decimals). We never deployed a stablecoin of our own. Whitechain's USDT supports both EIP-2612 permit and EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization, which is what makes the whole product gasless: One-time payments: the customer signs an EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization. Because it requires msg.sender == to, only our contract can redeem the signature, so no one can front-run it and send the funds somewhere else. projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Chain and token. QuietPay runs on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) with the official test USDT (TetherTokenV2 proxy, 6 decimals). We never deployed a stablecoin of our own. Whitechain's USDT supports both EIP-2612 permit and EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization, which is what makes the whole product gasless:

- One-time payments: the customer signs an EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization. Because it requires msg.sender == to, only our contract can redeem the signature, so no one can front-run it and send the funds somewhere else.
- Subscriptions: the customer signs an EIP-2612 permit plus our own EIP-712 Subscribe message, which includes a maxAmount limit. The contract then pulls each period's charge with transferFrom.
- Refunds: the merchant's payout wallet signs an EIP-3009 authorization. Its nonce is built from the payment ID and a refund sequence number, so a refund
  can't be replayed.

Before building on the USDT EIP-712 domain, we checked that the the on-chain DOMAIN_SEPARATOR().

Smart contract. QuietPay.sol uses Solidity 0.8.30 with evm_versitechain for verification), OpenZeppelin v5 (EIP712,SignatureChecker, SafeERC20, Ownable2Step, Pausable, ReentrancyGuard) and Foundry. It handles:

- merchant-signed invoices, with one payment per order
- refund caps
- a subscription state machine: Active → PastDue → grace period → Canceled
- an optional fee capped at 1%
- a pause switch. Refunds still work while paused, so customers can always get their money back.

A failed renewal doesn't revert. It emits RenewalFailed and records the attempt, so the keeper's transaction still succeeds. Along with unit tests, we have a fork test that runs a real pay against the live USDT contract.and verified on Whitechain's Blockscout explorer.

Backend. The API uses TypeScript, Node 22, Hono, SQLite (better-m. It runs four workers:

1. Relayer. The only key that sends transactions. It decodes and broadcasting, and it has anti-drain checks: every merchant hasits own gas budget, backed by verified WBT deposits and reserved atomically before broadcast, so one merchant can't burn another's gas.
2. Indexer. Turns contract events into payment, refund and subsc
3. Keeper. Charges subscriptions when they're due and retries past-due ones.
4. Webhook dispatcher. Sends HMAC-signed webhooks and retries wim, 10m).

All amounts are decimal strings in the API and bigint base unitsJS floats for money.

Frontend. Next.js (App Router) and Tailwind for the hosted checkts, customer portal, merchant dashboard and admin panel. Privy(with Whitechain added as a custom chain) gives users Google/email login with an embedded wallet; MetaMask is also supported. Swag Counter is a separate
Next.js app that imports only @quietpay/node. CI enforces that by is a third-party integration.

Partner tech. Whitechain's fast finality makes a "paid" result fts USDT supporting EIP-3009 and EIP-2612 natively is what lets us build gasless payments, renewals and refunds without wrapping the token. We used Whitechain's official agent skill and its llms.txt docs while building. We logged documentation gaps we ran into in WHITECHAIN_FEEDBACK.

projects.title: Tennibot
projects.description: A tennis-ball rover in Isaac Sim whose zone decisions run on 0G, with logs hashed on 0G Chain.
projects.project_description: Tennisbot is an autonomous rover that finds and collects tennis balls on a court, avoiding obstacles and using the gaps at the sides of the net to cross. We built it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and trained it with reinforcement learning to drive and pick up balls using a simulated camera view and a memory of the balls it has seen. For this hackathon, we made 0G its decision layer. The trained policy still drives the wheels at 24 Hz, while 0G Compute chooses the next court zone. Each decision has a request ID and a TEE verification result. Each run's log is stored on 0G Storage, with its hash on 0G Chain, and a replay page rebuilds the mission and checks that hash. If 0G is unreachable or a proof check fails, the rover stops; there is no fallback brain. A live outage test confirmed this. On three courses, it collected 64 of 68 balls with 0G, against 58 for the policy alone. This is a small sample, and the policy alone is sometimes faster. The main gain is that the rover can take a mission, such as clearing the near side first. The rover, simulator environment and trained policy existed before the event. The 0G decisions, safe stop, mission logic, Storage and Chain logging, contract and replay page were built during the hackathon.
projects.how_its_made: Built with Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab and a PPO policy trained with skrl. A Python mission layer builds a short option list from what the rover has seen and calls the 0G Compute Router's /decisions endpoint using the laya model in sealed TEE mode. The chosen zone reaches the policy through its existing inputs, so no retraining was needed. 0G Compute makes the decisions in the loop, 0G Storage holds the episode logs, and our Solidity EpisodeRegistry contract on 0G Chain (Galileo testnet) records each log's hash and links runs together. Built with Foundry, the 0G Storage TypeScript SDK and ethers. Notable details: the next question goes out about 3 seconds before a zone finishes, so the rover usually keeps moving. The near-side rule is our own mission code, and laya chooses among the zones it leaves open. Rover position comes from the simulator, standing in for real localisation.

projects.title: Blast radius
projects.description: See which contract dependencies two positions share, with on-chain evidence stored in Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Blast Radius answers a question portfolios rarely ask: how many independent dependencies do my positions really have? Two reserve tokens can look unrelated yet run on the same implementation contract, so a single upgrade could affect both. We mirror a pinned subset of the Aave Address Book (Ethereum V3, MIT) into Arkiv and add what the registry does not contain: proxy and implementation relationships observed on mainnet at a pinned block, each with the raw storage value that supports it. In the published snapshot, 11 aTokens turn out to share one implementation. The app is a double bubble map. Pick two positions and see what they share in the middle and what is unique to each side. Two positions with an empty middle share no dependency. Every bubble opens the path and the on-chain evidence behind it. A controlled experiment on a local chain shows the effect: upgrading one shared beacon makes withdrawals revert in two vaults, while a third vault on its own beacon keeps working. Reachability means potential exposure, not proof of exploitability, and unknown contracts stay unknown.
projects.how_its_made: Everything is TypeScript. The importer pins an Aave Address Book commit, reads a finalized Ethereum block with viem, and runs small adapters: the ERC-1967 implementation slot, OpenZeppelin beacon proxies, and known Ownable beacons. Contracts the adapters do not understand are recorded as coverage gaps, never guessed. Arkiv is the shared source of truth. Five schemas (deployment, dependency, coverage, snapshot, scenario result) have indexed columns for the fields people filter on. The publisher writes in atomic executeBatch transactions, reads everything back, compares record counts and a digest, and only then writes a snapshot marker, so a half-finished import is invisible. Publisher identity comes from entity ownership, and reading needs only the public RPC: a keyless CLI and the browser app both query Arkiv directly, with no backend of ours. The controlled experiment uses Solidity and Foundry (OpenZeppelin UpgradeableBeacon and BeaconProxy) on a local anvil chain. A runner takes baseline and after-upgrade snapshots, runs identical withdrawals from the same state, and asserts the expected reverts before publishing. The frontend is React and Vite with a custom SVG double bubble map; react-force-graph-2d draws the second, graph view.
