projects.title: Lookout-Arkiv!
projects.description: Health verdict, expiry-aware disk forecast and phone alerts for Arkiv node operators
projects.project_description: Lookout is a dashboard that runs next to an Arkiv node and answers one question: is my node OK, and if not, what exactly do I do? Running a Rabdi node today, you can't see what matters. The entity store (GolemDB) exposes no size or entity metrics, expired entities don't give disk space back, failed RPC calls are counted but never logged, and the official node kit ships with metrics switched off. Lookout turns the node's raw readings into a single verdict (Healthy, Waiting, or Act now) with the next step, such as the exact command to run when Lighthouse has no peers. While the node syncs it shows a live race to the network head with an accurate "level in about X min". The Disk tab forecasts when the disk fills, two ways: at today's write rate, and if new writes reuse the space expired entities leave. It holds the forecast during catch-up so you don't get false alarms, and a what-if slider lets you shrink the budget until the real alert fires to your phone (ntfy, Slack or Discord). Traffic shows every RPC method with typical and slowest-1% latency and failures. Pool shows how Arkiv's load balancer sees your node (in rotation, lag, latency, data consistency, GLM owed) from the same public feed as nodes.arkiv.network. For Arkiv runs live query-language checks every 10 minutes (11 of 16 features behave as the spec says, with IDs matching Arkiv's conformance tracker). Alongside it we wrote 13 measured friction items, and a slow-query finder whose results go to Arkiv privately. Tested on a real Rabdi testnet node at the venue: 184,921 live entities, 27,300 blocks caught up while Lookout counted down.
projects.how_its_made: Lookout is a small Node 22 server (Hono) plus a single-page dashboard with no build step. A collector polls the node every few seconds: arkiv-reth's Prometheus metrics for RPC calls per method, latency and failures; JSON-RPC for head, peers and sync state; Lighthouse's beacon API for consensus peers and sync distance; and the node's data directory, measured in actually allocated bytes and split into entity data, chain database, old blocks, history index and expiry queue. History goes into node:sqlite, which ships with Node, so there's nothing extra to install. Entities and expiry come from the Arkiv SDK (@arkiv-network/sdk) and viem: Lookout counts live entities and buckets them by when they expire, which feeds the timeline and the expiry-aware disk forecast. The Pool tab reads the same public feed as nodes.arkiv.network and lines it up against what Lookout measures inside your node. Notable or hacky bits: We found by measurement that expiry frees space for reuse, not back to the disk: with all writes stopped, 295 entities expired in 7 minutes and the store grew by 168 KB. That's why there are two forecasts. The forecast detects catch-up and holds, because sync writes hours of history per minute and would otherwise trigger false alarms (we hit this on the real node and fixed it). The conformance checks deliberately send queries that should fail; Lookout subtracts its own failures so the Traffic tab only shows real ones. The what-if slider calls the real alert path, so you can test the push to your phone safely. Ships as Docker Compose: one command brings up a dev node, Lookout and optional demo traffic. Alerts go through ntfy, Slack or Discord webhooks. Styling uses SakaniUI tokens and Tabler icons (both MIT).

projects.title: Haven
projects.description: Private file sharing to ENS names: expiring stealth access, Arkiv index, Swarm files, Tor/Nym RPC
projects.project_description:
Haven: private file sharing with ENS names, with access that ends on its own. THE PROBLEM Google Drive and DocSend can see every file you share and everyone who opens it. Putting access control onchain is worse for privacy: anyone can read who was given your data room. Haven lets you share files with an ENS name (like alice.eth) without publishing who you shared with, and access ends on a date you choose. WHAT A USER DOES Sign in with a wallet (one message signature). Haven makes your encryption keys on your device. "Try it" works with no wallet, using two fresh identities in one tab. Claim a free you.haven.eth name (we pay the gas), or link an ENSv2 name you already own. Create folders, or "rooms": standalone folders with a random name and their own key, not linked to your identity. Upload files. They are encrypted (AES-256-GCM) and padded to fixed sizes in your browser before they leave the device. Share by typing an ENS name, a role (viewer, editor or manager) and an end date. You can also share with a group, or with everyone under a team's name (e.g. all subnames of acme.eth). Make share links for single files that stop working on their end date. Remove access early with one click, which also changes the folder's key. Works on the website and as an installable phone app. On Android you can send files to Haven from any app's share menu. ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): names are folders, roles are permissions Every folder is an ENS name with its own registry: our DriveRegistry contract, built on ENSv2's UserRegistry. Viewer, editor and manager are ENSv2 role bits. We added grantRolesUntil so roles end automatically. wasAllowed(account, role, time) tells any app whether an address had a role at a given moment. Private sharing: each share goes to a fresh stealth address made from the recipient's published Haven key, so the recipient's ENS name never appears in the role grant. Also used: namespace aliasing (mount a shared folder into your own tree), expiring subnames (share links), groups as their own registries, and syncing access with a team's subnames. ARKIV: a public database holding private data Arkiv holds the file index, welcome notes, key copies and member lists. Names, keys and member lists are encrypted. Only random IDs, addresses and sizes are visible. Writes are checked against ENS: a folder record only counts if its writer held the right DriveRegistry role when it was written. Other writes are ignored and counted in the public view. A guest's key copy and welcome note expire when their access does, so they drop out of normal Arkiv queries. haven.keylog: a public, signed, hash-chained history of each ENS name's encryption key. Any app can look one up with one query and spot a swapped key. 15 entity types in total. Swarm (Arkiv's Swarm bonus): file contents are stored on Swarm as padded, encrypted data. Encrypted Swarm "doorbell" messages tell members when to check for updates, with polling as a backup. ETHEREUM FOUNDATION: private networking and CROPS Anon-RPC: every Sepolia and Arkiv request can go through Nym, Nox or Tor, chosen in Settings. Each room and each stealth identity uses its own isolation key, so requests are harder to link to one person. Every request is labelled Private or Direct in the receipts panel. Haven doesn't hide what it can't protect. No analytics, trackers or third-party scripts. Fonts are self-hosted, with a strict Content-Security-Policy. MIT licensed. The contracts, API, website, phone app and Swarm node setup all run from the repo.
Nothing is mocked or pre-filled: every value on screen is read live from Sepolia, Arkiv and Swarm.
projects.how_its_made:
Haven is a TypeScript monorepo with a single Solidity contract. Everything private happens in the browser; the servers and chains only ever see ciphertext and random addresses. The contract is DriveRegistry, built with Foundry on top of ENSv2's UserRegistry. Every folder, room and group is its own ENSv2 registry under haven.eth, so the ENS roles on it are the file permissions. We added viewer/editor/manager role bits, grantRolesUntil so a role expires by itself, wasAllowed(account, role, t) so anyone can ask whether an address had access at a given time, and an upgrade freeze. ENSv2's role hooks aren't virtual, so we record the access history by overriding _grantRoles and _revokeRoles. We tested against the live Sepolia ENSv2 contracts with fork tests, not just mocks.
When you claim you.haven.eth, your own resolver publishes a haven.key text record. To share with you, someone derives a one-time stealth address from that key (Fluidkey's stealth-account-kit) and grants the role to that address, so your name never shows up next to the folder. Share links are subnames that expire, and mounting someone's folder into your tree uses ENSv2 aliasing. You sign in once, and that one signature derives every key on the device. Files are AES-256-GCM encrypted and padded to fixed sizes, from 64 KB up to 32 MB, before they leave the device. Folder keys change every epoch and can only be derived backwards. When your access ends, you're left holding an old key, so new files are unreadable to you without anyone sending a transaction. Arkiv holds the sealed file index, welcome notes, key copies, rosters, a public key log per ENS name, and signed website releases. Two things made it a good fit. Expiry: a guest's key copy is set to expire at the exact moment their access ends. And queries: every screen in the app is one indexed query. The catch is that anyone can write to Arkiv, so every entry is created read-only, and the client counts it only if its creator held the right ENS role when it was written. Swarm stores the padded ciphertext through our own Bee node, sends live updates through GSOC "doorbells" whose topics rotate every epoch, and also hosts a copy of the site. All Sepolia and Arkiv traffic goes through Anon-RPC on the Nox mixnet, with a separate isolation key per room and per stealth address. A receipts panel shows which calls went private and which went direct. Our small Hono API on Fly.io sponsors names, rooms and gas, and passes Arkiv and Sepolia calls through (the browser reaches it through the mixnet). It keeps no role on anything it registers, and the app checks that onchain.

Expiry: a guest's key copy is set to expire at the exact moment their access ends. And queries: every screen in the app is one indexed query. The catch is that anyone can write to Arkiv, so every entry is created read-only, and the client counts it only if its creator held the right ENS role when it was written. Swarm stores the padded ciphertext through our own Bee node, sends live updates through GSOC "doorbells" whose topics rotate every epoch, and also hosts a copy of the site. All Sepolia and Arkiv traffic goes through Anon-RPC on the Nox mixnet, with a separate isolation key per room and per stealth address. A receipts panel shows which calls went private and which went direct. Our small Hono API on Fly.io sponsors names, rooms and gas, and passes Arkiv and Sepolia calls through (the browser reaches it through the mixnet). It keeps no role on anything it registers, and the app checks that onchain.

projects.title: Kavach
projects.description: The A2A marketplace & payment firewall where AI agents hire workers and pay safely over x402.
projects.project_description:
Kavach ("shield" in Sanskrit/Hindi) is a two-sided Agent-to-Agent (A2A) marketplace and zero-trust payment firewall. THE PROBLEM
AI agents are starting to pay each other over HTTP 402 (x402) for summaries, translations, code reviews, data feeds, and bill settlements. That unlocks machine-speed commerce, but it creates a massive financial attack surface: a buyer agent can easily be tricked by prompt injection into paying a spoofed wallet, overpaying a rogue endpoint, or hiring a cheap worker agent that slips phishing links into its output. Today, standard a2a-x402 gives agents a way to sign payments, but zero way to verify if a counterparty is safe before money moves. THE SOLUTION
Kavach combines an open Agent Marketplace with a deterministic Payment Firewall in the middle: Discover & Propose (Requester Stays in Control):
Buyer agents discover skills via our A2A AgentCard (/.well-known/agent-card.json) and propose tasks with a maximum HBAR budget. Kavach suggests matching active Worker Agents from the registry (cheapest first). Nothing is paid until the requester accepts a worker—they can rule out workers, search again, edit the task, or withdraw at any time. The 6-Layer Payment Firewall:
Before a single HBAR moves to a worker or merchant, Kavach runs a zero-trust check: Probes the payee's own HTTP 402 challenge first (never trusting invoice/prompt text for who gets paid or how much). Reads the request privately inside 0G Private Computer (TEE mode) to extract payees, links, deadlines, and psychological pressure tactics ("URGENT", "share your OTP"). Autonomously hires independent Verifier Agents over Hedera x402 (paying 0.02–0.05 HBAR per check) to audit URLs for brand impersonation and query Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) for the payee's historical reputation. Enforces an Evidence Floor where AI models can raise risk, but can never lower deterministic fraud signals. Evaluates spending caps in a panic-free Rust/WebAssembly policy engine: low-risk payments under 2 HBAR settle automatically; medium/high-risk payments pause for a World ID Agent Pass approval bound to the exact SHA-256 payment hash. Screened Delivery & On-Chain Reputation:
Once paid over Hedera x402, the worker's output is stripped of control characters and scanned by our Rust link-intelligence engine so phishing links inside an answer are flagged before the buyer ever sees them. Every step is anchored to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS). THE BUSINESS MODEL
Kavach operates a three-sided agentic economy: Worker Agents monetize specialized AI skills (summarization, translation, code review, DePIN feeds) per task via x402 without building billing infrastructure. Independent Verifier Agents earn continuous micro-yield (0.02–0.05 HBAR per call) by selling threat intelligence, domain forensics, and wallet reputation to the firewall. Enterprise & Consumer Buyer Agents get a managed treasury guardrail ("Stripe Radar + Corporate Card Controls for AI Agents") with guaranteed spend caps and biometric human-in-the-loop escalation.
projects.how_its_made:
Kavach is built as a full-stack TypeScript (Next.js 16, React 19, Drizzle + Neon Postgres) and Rust-to-WebAssembly system, verified by 657 JavaScript unit/contract tests, 80 Rust unit/property tests, and 17 Playwright end-to-end browser tests. Safety-Critical Core in Rust + WebAssembly (rust/kavach-core & rust/kavach-wasm):
Because spending policy, approval binding, canonical JSON hashing, and phishing detection decide whether real money moves, we wrote the core engine in pure Rust compiled to WASM: Clippy enforces zero unwrap , expect , panic! , or unchecked indexing ( panic = "abort" in release). All money math uses exact integer tinybars ( i128 in Rust, bigint in TS, decimal strings on the wire—never floats). We implemented RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical JSON + SHA-256 in both Rust and TypeScript and ran a differential parity test suite ( tests/parity ) with fast-check and proptest over thousands of random inputs. This differential suite caught a real subtle bug where V8's JSON.stringify re-orders integer-like object keys ( "0" , "10" ) first regardless of insertion order! linkintel.rs is a pure Rust static URL forensics engine using idna , unicode-security , psl , and strsim (Damerau-Levenshtein) that catches homoglyphs, mixed-script labels, punycode tricks, redirect downgrades, and 1-edit lookalikes across 18 Indian and global brands (SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Axis, Paytm, PhonePe, NPCI, UIDAI, PayPal, Apple, etc.). Hedera x402 & Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): We used @x402/core , @x402/fetch , @x402/hedera , @x402/next , and @hiero-ledger/sdk with the Blocky402 testnet facilitator ( hedera:testnet , exact scheme, native HBAR 0.0.0 ). Because standard @x402/fetch will sign whatever a server asks for, we built a custom SpendGuard ( src/adapters/x402/guard.ts ) hooked into onBeforePaymentCreation . Each verifier call and worker settlement gets its own single-use guard pinned to the exact verified payTo account, asset 0.0.0 , and maximum tinybar amount. When third-party Worker or Verifier agents register ( POST /api/agents ), Kavach performs Proof of Control ( proveControl in src/marketplace/onboard.ts ): it sends an unpaid probe request and verifies the endpoint returns a valid x402 402 challenge paying the exact listed Hedera account at no more than the listed price, using a custom DNS-resolving createSafeFetch that blocks private/loopback IPs (SSRF protection). Every check lifecycle event and payee reputation outcome ( paid-ok vs flagged ) is encoded as <=1024-byte RFC 8785 canonical JSON and published to two Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topics, read back via the Hedera Mirror Node. 0G Private Computer (Confidential TEE Inference): Payment requests and task prompts contain sensitive PII and financial details. Our 0G adapter ( src/adapters/zerog ) connects to https://router-api.0g.ai/v1 with X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private ( TeeML attested models like glm-5.3 / 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b ). Prompts wrap untrusted user text inside strict data delimiters. Even if a prompt injection fools the LLM into rating a scam as low risk, our applyEvidenceFloor function guarantees the final risk verdict can never drop below deterministic verifier evidence ( link-intel , reputation , or payee-check mismatch). Furthermore, we implemented Corroborated Verifier Trust ( src/marketplace/trust.ts ): a third-party verifier's lone high risk claim is weighed as medium unless corroborated by a second independent verifier, preventing a malicious verifier from DoS-blocking honest merchants. World ID Agent Pass (Dynamic OIDC Step-Up & Action Binding): Using openid-client , Kavach requests dynamic OIDC acr assurance tiers matched to the payment's risk: max_age=0 + prompt=login for low-risk over-cap spend ( fresh ), orb for medium risk ( human ), and orb-face only to override high-risk blocks ( strong ). Because standard OIDC lacks transaction-specific authorization_details , binding.rs stores a PendingApproval containing the SHA-256 hash of the canonical BoundAction (checkId, payee, resource, amount, verdictHash, version). On callback, the hash is recomputed against the live payment state ( ACTION_CHANGED blocks mid-flight tampering) and transitioned from approved to consumed via a single atomic Postgres conditional UPDATE , making replay attacks impossible. To allow full offline judging and CI testing before live credentials are injected, we also built a spec-compliant in-app OIDC Simulator ( src/adapters/world/simulator.ts ) that signs real RS256 JWTs with PKCE and exercises the exact same verification code path ( source:simulated in audit logs).

projects.title: MemorySeal
projects.description: MemorySeal is a security protocol for AI agent memory, permissions, and verifiable provenance
projects.project_description: MemorySeal is a shared memory protocol for multi-agent systems built around one principle: memory is evidence, never permission. When agents exchange information, an observation can accidentally become authority. A browser agent might read a malicious instruction claiming that a payment was approved, save it as context, and pass it to another agent. MemorySeal separates that remembered information from the permissions the owner actually granted. Owners register agents, assign collection-specific access, and choose how incoming memories are accepted. Eligible low-risk observations can pass automatically under an owner-defined rule, while suspicious instructions, conflicts, and failed analysis are held for review. Agents can only retrieve memories that satisfy current access and eligibility checks. Each agent receives a real ENSv2 subname on Sepolia through sponsored backend registration. 0G analyzes ordinary memory content, while Arkiv stores public lifecycle metadata and commitments that users can query independently without exposing the memory text. The workspace includes an interactive parent–child memory map, readable activity history, organization roles, and a separate client-encrypted vault with recipient-specific key sharing and rotation. Python and TypeScript SDKs let developers integrate these workflows directly into their agents.
projects.how_its_made: The MemorySeal protocol is implemented through a Python FastAPI gateway, a TypeScript SDK, and a Next.js dashboard. Wallet signatures authenticate requests, while the gateway enforces the protocol’s collection permissions, memory acceptance rules, and payment policies. The protocol integrates ENS for readable agent identities on Sepolia. Agents receive persistent identities, and the demo displays their registration progress. Arkiv provides public provenance records containing content commitments, allowing users to inspect publication history without publishing private memory plaintext. The demo uses deterministic browser and finance reference agents to reproduce the same memory poisoning attack consistently. The browser worker fetches an invoice page and extracts its injected instruction. In the protected flow, the MemorySeal protocol checks the memory update, quarantines it, publishes provenance to Arkiv, and controls what the finance agent can retrieve. Sepolia transactions use viem with a dedicated server-side signing wallet. The signer restricts transactions to the configured network and recipient, enforces the protected payment policy, and journals transaction hashes before broadcasting to prevent duplicate sends. Streamed progress and live memory updates make each stage of the protocol visible in the dashboard.

projects.title: ShipLock
projects.description: AI agents pay for independent code reviews. Verified humans control exactly what gets merged.
projects.project_description: ShipLock — AI writes. Humans ship. AI coding agents can generate pull requests in minutes, but human review and release authorization haven't kept pace. As more agents write and modify code autonomously, engineering teams need a reliable way to delegate development without surrendering control over what reaches production. ShipLock is a release-security platform designed to bridge that gap. When an AI agent opens a GitHub pull request, ShipLock identifies the exact commit and initiates an independent security review. Using Hedera x402, the agent can autonomously purchase that review through a pay-per-request API, without a human manually approving every small payment. The resulting security findings are bound to the reviewed commit. Before merging, the maintainer verifies their humanity through World IDKit, passes a separate GitHub permission check, and explicitly authorizes the specific revision. ShipLock checks the live pull request again immediately before merging. If the agent has pushed new code after review or approval, the previous authorization is no longer valid, and the merge is blocked. Our vision extends beyond pull requests: the same approach could secure autonomous package publishing, production deployments, and smart-contract upgrades. ShipLock lets AI agents move fast while keeping humans in control of consequential actions.
projects.how_its_made: ShipLock is designed around three main integrations: Hedera x402 for autonomous payments, World IDKit for privacy-preserving human verification, and GitHub for commit-level release authorization. The application uses a TypeScript-based architecture with a web interface, backend APIs, a security-scanning service, persistent review records, and a policy engine. Hedera: An autonomous agent requests a paid security review. The review API responds with HTTP 402 payment requirements, which the agent satisfies through a Hedera testnet transaction using the x402 SDK and facilitator. The architecture records the settlement reference and binds the resulting audit to the reviewed GitHub commit. World IDKit: Before a sensitive merge operation, the maintainer completes privacy-preserving proof-of-human verification. Backend verification is combined with GitHub account authorization and explicit approval of the exact commit. GitHub: The application tracks pull-request head SHAs, associates findings with specific revisions, and uses GitHub's merge API with an expected SHA to prevent merging code that changed after authorization. AI-assisted development: Cursor AI handles application development and integration, while Hermes researches and implements the Hedera payment infrastructure. ChatGPT supports architecture, product design, documentation and coordination. The key design principle is that payment, review, human verification and merge approval must all be tied to independently checkable evidence.

projects.title: Synapse
projects.description: An AI agent that optimizes your AI agents, and pays for its own compute on 0G.
projects.project_description: Business processes are turning into AI agents, but most agents are written the obvious way: every step waits for the one before it, every call uses the biggest model, and the bill grows with every run. Synapse0g is a compiler and optimizer for AI agents that runs as a paid agent on 0G. A developer pastes or uploads a LangGraph agent with one sample input, or picks an example agent, and gets an itemised quote: the agent's steps, the price of a model call measured on 0G, the compute the job needs, and the optimizer's fee. They pay with one wallet transaction, depositFor on 0G's own Payment Layer, straight into the optimizer's 0G compute account, with no contract of ours in between. The server checks the payment on chain and starts the job by itself. Synapse0g traces the agent and lifts it into SIR, an effect-typed graph. Its edges are what each step really reads, and each step is labelled pure, read, write, external or irreversible. Twelve passes rewrite the graph, each only where its safety rule holds: independent steps run in parallel, pure steps are cached, unused context is dropped. Per-step model changes (hidden reasoning off, a cheaper model) are kept only if a firewall finds no task broken on held-out tasks. Irreversible steps, like placing an order, are flagged and never run. The optimized agent then runs on the customer's input. Every model call is paid from the optimizer's own balance, through its capped 0G Router key, with 0G's request id and exact charge shown live. The customer gets back the answer, the measured cost and time, and a zip with optimized_agent.py, generated from the optimized graph by the compiler (not an LLM), beside their original code. Spending is safe by design. Every call reserves its worst-case cost first, there are caps per job and per key, and when funds run low the job slows down or pauses, then resumes without paying twice. Measured on held-out tasks: the supplier-check agent ran 3.48× faster and 72% cheaper on 0G's bill, still 20/20 right. Changes that broke answers were blocked.
projects.how_its_made: The backend is Python 3.11. The compiler lifts LangGraph StateGraphs and plain Python functions into SIR, our effect-typed intermediate representation. For LangGraph it traces each step once on a sample input and records which state keys it really reads and writes, so the edges come from data flow rather than code order. Twelve passes (parallelize, memoize, cse, downgrade, context_prune and more) each declare a precondition checked against the effect lattice, and a runtime executes the optimized graph with parallel steps, a content-addressed cache, and irreversible steps stubbed. Every model call goes through our OpenAI-compatible proxy, which applies a per-step policy (reasoning off, routing to a cheaper model) and records tokens, latency, 0G's request id and the billed charge from the Router's x_0g_trace field. The policy is found by a search on tuning tasks and approved by a firewall: paired comparisons against an unchanged control run at the same moment, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, measured on held-out tasks. 0G is the payment and compute layer. Customers pay with depositFor on 0G's Payment Layer contract; we read its verified source to find the call, since the docs only show the dashboard. A payment desk matches each Deposited event to its quote by payer, amount and expiry, from the transaction receipt or a watcher scanning the chain, with an RPC fallback to dRPC because the public RPC rate-limits. Inference runs on the 0G Router (qwen3.8-flash, qwen3.7-flash) with the agent's own capped key, never the team's. A spend guard reserves each call's worst-case cost (request bytes × input price + max tokens × output price, in 0G wei) atomically in SQLite, against the job's cap, the key's cap and 0G's admission rule (0.01 0G minimum, 80% of the vault counted). It settles at 0G's billed charge and holds uncertain charges after timeouts. Hacky parts we're proud of: optimized agents are returned as real code by lowering the optimized SIR back into a LangGraph file, with parallel edges, cached steps, step-specific model settings and protected irreversible steps. Paused jobs replay the calls they already paid for, so they never pay twice. The frontend is React 19, Vite, Tailwind 4, React Flow for the live SIR graphs, and a three.js landing page tuned for Apple silicon. It's deployed as one Docker service on Render, with a persistent disk for jobs and payments.

The optimized agent then runs on the customer's input. Every model call is paid from the optimizer's own balance, through its capped 0G Router key, with 0G's request id and exact charge shown live. The customer gets back the answer, the measured cost and time, and a zip with optimized_agent.py, generated from the optimized graph by the compiler (not an LLM), beside their original code.

Spending is safe by design. Every call reserves its worst-case cost first, there are caps per job and per key, and when funds run low the job slows down or pauses, then resumes without paying twice. Measured on held-out tasks: the supplier-check agent ran 3.48× faster and 72% cheaper on 0G's bill, still 20/20 right. Changes that broke answers were blocked.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The backend is Python 3.11. The compiler lifts LangGraph StateGraphs and plain Python functions into SIR, our effect-typed intermediate representation. For LangGraph it traces each step once on a sample input and records which state keys it really reads and writes, so the edges come from data flow rather than code order. Twelve passes (parallelize, memoize, cse, downgrade, context_prune and more) each declare a precondition checked against the effect lattice, and a runtime executes the optimized graph with parallel steps, a content-addressed cache, and irreversible steps stubbed.

Every model call goes through our OpenAI-compatible proxy, which applies a per-step policy (reasoning off, routing to a cheaper model) and records tokens, latency, 0G's request id and the billed charge from the Router's x_0g_trace field. The policy is found by a search on tuning tasks and approved by a firewall: paired comparisons against an unchanged control run at the same moment, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, measured on held-out tasks.

0G is the payment and compute layer. Customers pay with depositFor on 0G's Payment Layer contract; we read its verified source to find the call, since the docs only show the dashboard. A payment desk matches each Deposited event to its quote by payer, amount and expiry, from the transaction receipt or a watcher scanning the chain, with an RPC fallback to dRPC because the public RPC rate-limits. Inference runs on the 0G Router (qwen3.8-flash, qwen3.7-flash) with the agent's own capped key, never the team's.

A spend guard reserves each call's worst-case cost (request bytes × input price + max tokens × output price, in 0G wei) atomically in SQLite, against the job's cap, the key's cap and 0G's admission rule (0.01 0G minimum, 80% of the vault counted). It settles at 0G's billed charge and holds uncertain charges after timeouts.

Hacky parts we're proud of: optimized agents are returned as real code by lowering the optimized SIR back into a LangGraph file, with parallel edges, cached steps, step-specific model settings and protected irreversible steps. Paused jobs replay the calls they already paid for, so they never pay twice.

The frontend is React 19, Vite, Tailwind 4, React Flow for the live SIR graphs, and a three.js landing page tuned for Apple silicon. It's deployed as one Docker service on Render, with a persistent disk for jobs and payments.

projects.title: Prophet
projects.description: A prediction Marketplace where you can bet on without worrying about chains using chainlink ccip
projects.project_description: The problem: prediction markets live on one chain, so liquidity is split. Someone with funds on Arbitrum has to bridge before they can join a market on Base, and every chain ends up with its own thin pool. Prophet keeps exactly one pool per market, in a hub contract on Base Sepolia, and lets anyone bet into it from Base, Arbitrum Sepolia or Ethereum Sepolia. A bet from another chain is a single Chainlink CCIP programmable token transfer: the stake and the bet travel together in one message, and the hub records the position when it arrives. There's no separate bridge step, and every bettor sees the same pool and the same odds. Settlement can't be gamed. After close, anyone can settle a market, and the contract only accepts the first Chainlink Data Feed round published at or after the close time, so nobody gets to pick the price
projects.how_its_made: used solidity 0.8.24 with foundry on chainlink contracts ccip 2.0 , chainlink data feeds and oppenzeppelin 5 Four contracts: PredictionHub (Base Sepolia) holds every market and pool. It's a CCIPReceiver: _ccipReceive checks the source chain and the trusted spoke address, then records a bet or processes a claim. PredictionSpoke (Arbitrum Sepolia, Ethereum Sepolia) turns each bet into a CCIP programmable token transfer: CCIP-BnM as the token, and the action, market, user and side as the data. Fees are paid in native gas, quoted with router.getFee, and any excess is refunded. Messages use GenericExtraArgsV2 with out-of-order execution. Payouts and refunds go back as a second CCIP transfer, with the fee paid in LINK by the hub and gasLimit 0, so the tokens land directly in the user's wallet with no receiver contract needed. FeedRelayer (Arbitrum) and RelayedFeed (Base) carry Chainlink SOL/USD rounds across chains. RelayedFeed implements AggregatorV3Interface, so the hub settles SOL markets exactly like ETH and BTC. How Chainlink helped: CCIP's programmable token transfers make a cross-chain bet atomic. The money and the instructions arrive together, so the hub never holds tokens without knowing what they're for. Data Feeds give a settlement price no bettor can pick, and CCIP let us bring a feed to a chain that doesn't have one.

projects.title: Canon Wallet
projects.description: Private Ethereum wallet: RAILGUN balance, Anon-RPC reads, an address per dapp, a DIY hardware signer
projects.project_description: Canon Wallet is a Chrome extension wallet built so that using Ethereum doesn't leak who you are. Private balance: funds live in RAILGUN's shielded pool. One Send screen works out from who you pay whether it is a public send, make private, send privately or make public. Proofs are built on your device. Private reads: every RPC call goes through Anon-RPC's Nox mixnet by default, so no RPC provider can tie your addresses to your IP. A Privacy screen counts what went through Nox and what didn't. One address per dapp: each site, over the injected EIP-6963 provider or WalletConnect, gets its own fresh address, so dapps can't link you by comparing addresses. Each site also gets its own network, and dapp network switches are accepted. Gasless dapp calls: site addresses become Calibur smart accounts with EIP-7702, with EIP-5792 batches, and a sponsor pays the gas. A site address can be funded straight from the private balance. Private swaps on Uniswap v4: one RAILGUN cross-contract call unshields, swaps and re-shields, so the swap never touches your public address. Free ENS names: claim <name>.canon.eth (ENSv2, Sepolia). Its org.railgun record holds your private address, so anyone can pay you privately by name. The sponsor's control is renounced after issue. Onboarding: new phrase with a word check, restore, a passkey (WebAuthn PRF) wallet with no phrase at all, or a hardware wallet. Hardware wallet: Buddy, an ESP32-S3 running BuddyOS, signs over USB or Bluetooth and clear-signs RAILGUN private transactions on its screen. Nothing that can spend leaves the device.
projects.how_its_made: Bun monorepo: the MV3 extension (React, Tailwind, esbuild), a sponsor service, and a mock hardware device. The wallet core (vault, RAILGUN engine, WalletConnect WalletKit, an encrypted account book) runs in the extension's offscreen document. The popup, side panel and onboarding tab only render pushed state and send whitelisted commands. Anon-RPC: the harness runs in PageWorker mode inside that same offscreen document, framing the null-origin sandbox page. One ethers.FetchRequest.registerGetUrl hook catches every JSON-RPC call. Hacky bit: RAILGUN require()s ethers while our code imports it, so the bundle had two ethers copies and one missed the hook. We alias ethers and axios to a single copy and install a fetch forwarder at the top of the bundle, because RAILGUN's GraphQL client grabs fetch at load. Proof-of-innocence lookups go through Nox too. If Nox is down, reads fail closed. RAILGUN (wallet SDK 11.3, engine 9.9.1): shield, private send, unshield, and cross-contract calls through Relay Adapt. Per-dapp addresses use RAILGUN's app-path derivation, keyed by the site's origin. The wallet submits its own proof-of-innocence proofs, as a broadcaster does, so funds are spendable again in minutes. Uniswap v4: RelayAdapt unwrapBase, then UniversalRouter V4_SWAP (exact-in single), then wrapBase and re-shield. Quotes come from the v4 Quoter through Nox. ENSv2 on Sepolia: we registered canon.eth with its own UserRegistry, then renounced the power to swap it. The sponsor issues subnames that set org.railgun to the user's 0zk address. Resolution goes through the Universal Resolver. Sponsor: a Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object queueing a single nonce. It relays RAILGUN transactions, including RAILGUN's EIP-7702 type-4 unshields, and executes Calibur batches (EIP-712 SignedBatchedCall plus a 7702 authorization). Passkeys: WebAuthn PRF output, run through HKDF, becomes the wallet seed and the vault keys. Hardware: our own framed JSON protocol over Web Serial and Web Bluetooth (GATT, encrypted and MITM-paired). RAILGUN clear-signing follows Ledger's clear-sign contract; the device computes commitments, encrypted notes and the EdDSA-Poseidon signature. A JS reference device built from RAILGUN's own primitives produces test vectors the C firmware matches byte for byte. Tests: Puppeteer end-to-end suites on real Sepolia and an anvil fork.

projects.title: Presign
projects.description: Plain English for what you sign, evidence for who you trust: a pre-signing checkpoint on Arkiv
projects.project_description: When you sign with a crypto wallet, you usually see an address and a wall of hex. Since EIP-7702, one signature can also hand your entire account to a smart contract. On October 29, a Binance hot wallet signed 50 such authorizations to an hours-old sweeper contract; Binance estimates about $6.3B was lost in the incident. PreSign is the checkpoint before every signature. It answers two questions before anything is signed: "What does this do?" We mirror the Ethereum Foundation's ERC-7730 clear-signing registry to Arkiv: 1,917 contracts on 143 chains, 201 of them audited by Cyfrin. Each entry carries a fingerprint (ERC-8176) that every reader re-computes, so raw calldata becomes plain English like "Wrap 0.001 ETH", and a tampered translation is blocked. "Who am I handing my account to?" The Delegation Radar doesn't ask who a contract claims to be. A Watchtower reads EIP-7702 delegations on-chain and publishes evidence about each delegate to Arkiv: same code as a known drainer (16 drainer families), upgradeable logic, and logic changes since first seen, written as readonly alerts that nobody can delete. It already found a live mainnet delegate whose bytecode is byte-for-byte the published CrimeEnjoyor drainer. The wallet vendors' own delegate lists (MetaMask, Coinbase, Uniswap, OKX, ZeroDev, Alchemy; 41 entries on 7 chains) are mirrored too, as one signal among several. check() turns this into the verdict a wallet, exchange or AI agent shows: verified, caution or blocked, with the evidence behind it. The Signer Guard refuses to sign anything that isn't verified. Everything lives publicly on Arkiv: any wallet can read it directly, with no PreSign server in between.
projects.how_its_made: PreSign is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces) built on Arkiv's Rabdi testnet with @arkiv-network/sdk and viem. core: Arkiv schemas and reader, ERC-8176 fingerprints (keccak256 of the JCS-canonicalized descriptor), the ERC-7730 formatter, bytecode code-family matching, and check(), the deterministic verdict engine. No AI at signing time; every verdict comes from verified data and fixed rules. importer: downloads the EF registry as one GitHub tarball at a pinned commit and reads it fully in memory. That's one request instead of ~1,000 API calls, and it avoids a macOS bug where two Morpho files differing only by letter case would overwrite each other on disk. Descriptors are gzip-compressed to fit Arkiv's 128 KiB limit and written in resumable batches, then read back to confirm. Cyfrin's EAS attestations are verified against our own fingerprints. Vendor delegates are only imported if the address is found in the vendor's own GitHub file at a pinned commit, with a per-chain code hash. keeper: re-syncs every source daily. Unchanged entries get their 7-day expiry extended, changed ones are superseded, removed ones stop being trusted immediately, and every change is written as a readonly Change record. If a source can't be read, nothing changes, so an outage can't "remove" trusted entries. watchtower (Delegation Radar): scans EIP-7702 authorizations, recovers who delegated, strips contract metadata and blanks embedded addresses so drainer clones match the same code family, detects upgradeable logic (EIP-1967 proxies and beacons), and writes readonly alerts when a delegate's logic changes. guard: wraps a wallet client and refuses to sign unless check() says verified, tested with real type-4 transactions on Sepolia. web: React + Vite. Every number and verdict is read live from Arkiv in the browser. MetaMask on Sepolia, and any transaction hash can be explained on 7 networks. Why Arkiv: a trust layer shouldn't need trust in us. Entities prove their publisher (readers filter with createdBy), expire unless re-confirmed, and alerts are readonly, so history can't be quietly rewritten. Hacky but notable: to prove the Radar works, we deployed a harmless delegate behind a beacon, delegated an account to it, then swapped the logic for a drainer. The address and code never changed, so an allowlist would still say it's fine, but the Watchtower caught the logic change and PreSign blocked it. We also rebuilt the whole mirror from a fresh clone with a brand-new publisher and got field-for-field identical data. 46 tests, CI on every push.

projects.title: Aven
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook pricing every swap from Hyperliquid's in-block oracle, so LPs stop losing to arbs
projects.project_description:
Aven is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook on HyperEVM that charges each swap a fee based on Hyperliquid's live perp market, read in the same block as the swap. THE PROBLEM
An AMM's price only moves when someone trades against it. When the market moves elsewhere, the pool goes stale, and arbitrageurs buy cheap or sell high against LPs at the same low fee. LPs lose that value (loss-versus-rebalancing, LVR). A fixed fee charges arbitrage and ordinary flow the same. Existing dynamic-fee hooks, such as Uniswap's VolatilePairHook, learn from the pool's own past trades, so they react after the damage is done. Oracle-based designs need a relayer, a keeper or a signer you have to trust. THE IDEA
Aven reads the market's present. HyperEVM gives smart contracts in-block access to Hyperliquid's perp oracle and mark prices through precompiles (0x807, 0x806). HyperCore and HyperEVM share one consensus, so there is no relay, no signer and no cross-chain delay. The fair price is already chain state. On every swap, AvenHook reads both prices and computes three signals: Fair-value gap: how far the pool's price is from the oracle, anchored to the top of the block. Charged only when the swap moves the pool toward fair, i.e. when it is arbitrage. Perp premium: mark vs oracle. Charged when the swap trades with perp-market pressure. Mark stress: how far the mark has moved from a time-weighted anchor (tau = 60 s). Charged above 50 bp. fee = clamp(0.05% base + gap term + premium term + stress term, 0.05%, 1%). The fee goes to LPs. Ordinary flow pays 0.05%; an arbitrageur closing a 1.5% gap pays up to 1%. If a price read fails, the swap never reverts: it pays a 0.30% fallback fee. Every input is emitted in a FeeComputed event, so anyone can recompute every fee. There is no owner, admin key, keeper, proxy, upgrade path or custody. Every config value is immutable. Two anti-gaming rules: a top-of-block gap anchor (splitting an arb into many swaps in one block doesn't lower the fee) and a time-weighted mark anchor (a dust swap can't reset the stress term). LIVE ON HYPEREVM MAINNET (chain 999)
AvenHook 0xfdd13cA6D7FcF4Ca710Bc8C77546592F42CF6080, deployed on Uniswap's own canonical v4 PoolManager. In the first live test, a shock pushed two identical pools about 188 bp off the oracle. The bot's arbitrage paid 9,950 pips (0.995%) on the Aven pool vs 3,000 (0.30%) on the plain control pool, so Aven LPs kept $97.25 more. That fee was recomputed off-chain from the event and matched exactly. Uniswap's own V4Quoter and Universal Router also route through the Aven pool. REPLAY ON REAL HISTORY
We replayed the Oct 29 2026 Binance-halt window (Hyperliquid mainnet data) through four identical pools. LP value vs holding: fixed 0.05% -$318, fixed 0.30% +$7, Aven with a 60 s-delayed price +$114, Aven live +$141. Live beats delayed, so the edge comes from reading the market in-block. On a calm day, Aven roughly matches fixed 0.30% while charging ordinary trades only 0.05%. No parameters were tuned on this data. THE APP
A web app with a trade terminal (market, limit, stop and TP/SL orders on the pools), swap, add liquidity, a live dashboard that shows the fee repricing in the same block as the oracle moves, the replay, an on-chain ledger and portfolio, and in-browser verification of any Aven swap. Limits: the pools trade open-mint demo tokens (aETH/aUSD), but the prices the hook reads are real Hyperliquid prices. There has been no third-party audit; our internal security review is in docs/SECURITY.md.
projects.how_its_made:
Aven has three parts: Solidity contracts, a TypeScript backend and a Next.js frontend, all written during the event in one pnpm monorepo. CONTRACTS (Solidity 0.8.26, Foundry) AvenFairValue is a pure fee library; AvenHook is the Uniswap v4 hook. It is built on OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseHook and implements Uniswap's IDynamicFeeHook, so anything that quotes Uniswap's dynamic-fee hooks can quote Aven. Permissions are beforeInitialize + beforeSwap only, so the hook address's low 14 bits must be 0x2080. We mined the address with v4-periphery's HookMiner through the CREATE2 deployer. Every beforeSwap return sets the override-fee flag (0x400000), the fallback included. A v4 dynamic pool's stored LP fee is 0, so one missing flag would mean free swaps. It has a dedicated test, an invariant and a mutation check. Precompile reads are hand-written staticcalls that never revert, forward exactly 30,000 gas and copy at most 32 bytes. hyper-evm-lib's PrecompileLib reverts on failure, so it is only used in tests. Reads can revert, return 0 bytes, return words wider than uint64 or burn all forwarded gas; each case has a test and falls back to a 0.30% fee instead of reverting the swap. beforeInitialize rejects any pool that isn't the configured pair with a dynamic fee, so the hook can't be attached to a pair it would misprice. Hook overhead is about 47k gas per swap; runtime size is 9.3 KB. PROOFS forge: 90 tests passing, covering unit, fuzz (1,000 runs), v4 integration in both token orders, nine named attack tests (split swaps, dust swaps, sandwich back leg, gas burn, preview == charged, and more), and invariants I1-I10 over random swaps, price moves and read failures. Mutation testing: we broke the code on purpose (no override flag, top-of-block reset every swap, anchor moving on a failed read) and confirmed the matching tests went red. Differential proof: the same fee math is ported to TypeScript with BigInt, integer-only. Solidity and TypeScript agree on 10,000 / 10,000 fee vectors and 2,000 / 2,000 anchor vectors, bit for bit. Verifier: pnpm verify <tx> rebuilds the inputs from the FeeComputed event, recomputes the fee, and checks it against the event (check A) and the PoolManager's own Swap fee (check B). Load tests: 2,318 swaps over 250 blocks with broken reads gave 0 reverts. They also found 4 real bugs, each fixed with a regression test: viem's ~4 s block-number cache, viem's 4 s receipt polling, a stampeding per-block cache, and gas estimates that missed the more expensive first-swap-of-block path. projects.project_description_markdown:
Aven is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook on HyperEVM that charges each swap a fee based on Hyperliquid's live perp market, read in the same block as the swap.

THE PROBLEM
An AMM's price only moves when someone trades against it. When the market moves elsewhere, the pool goes stale, and arbitrageurs buy cheap or sell high against LPs at the same low fee. LPs lose that value (loss-versus-rebalancing, LVR). A fixed fee charges arbitrage and ordinary flow the same. Existing dynamic-fee hooks, such as Uniswap's VolatilePairHook, learn from the pool's own past trades, so they react after the damage is done. Oracle-based designs need a relayer, a keeper or a signer you have to trust.

THE IDEA
Aven reads the market's present. HyperEVM gives smart contracts in-block access to Hyperliquid's perp oracle and mark prices through precompiles (0x807, 0x806). HyperCore and HyperEVM share one consensus, so there is no relay, no signer and no cross-chain delay. The fair price is already chain state.

On every swap, AvenHook reads both prices and computes three signals:
1. Fair-value gap: how far the pool's price is from the oracle, anchored to the top of the block. Charged only when the swap moves the pool toward fair, i.e. when it is arbitrage.
2. Perp premium: mark vs oracle. Charged when the swap trades with perp-market pressure.
3. Mark stress: how far the mark has moved from a time-weighted anchor (tau = 60 s). Charged above 50 bp.

fee = clamp(0.05% base + gap term + premium term + stress term, 0.05%, 1%). The fee goes to LPs. Ordinary flow pays 0.05%; an arbitrageur closing a 1.5% gap pays up to 1%. If a price read fails, the swap never reverts: it pays a 0.30% fallback fee. Every input is emitted in a FeeComputed event, so anyone can recompute every fee.

There is no owner, admin key, keeper, proxy, upgrade path or custody. Every config value is immutable. Two anti-gaming rules: a top-of-block gap anchor (splitting an arb into many swaps in one block doesn't lower the fee) and a time-weighted mark anchor (a dust swap can't reset the stress term).

LIVE ON HYPEREVM MAINNET (chain 999)
AvenHook 0xfdd13cA6D7FcF4Ca710Bc8C77546592F42CF6080, deployed on Uniswap's own canonical v4 PoolManager. In the first live test, a shock pushed two identical pools about 188 bp off the oracle. The bot's arbitrage paid 9,950 pips (0.995%) on the Aven pool vs 3,000 (0.30%) on the plain control pool, so Aven LPs kept $97.25 more. That fee was recomputed off-chain from the event and matched exactly. Uniswap's own V4Quoter and Universal Router also route through the Aven pool.

REPLAY ON REAL HISTORY
We replayed the Oct 29 2026 Binance-halt window (Hyperliquid mainnet data) through four identical pools. LP value vs holding: fixed 0.05% -$318, fixed 0.30% +$7, Aven with a 60 s-delayed price +$114, Aven live +$141. Live beats delayed, so the edge comes from reading the market in-block. On a calm day, Aven roughly matches fixed 0.30% while charging ordinary trades only 0.05%. No parameters were tuned on this data.

THE APP
A web app with a trade terminal (market, limit, stop and TP/SL orders on the pools), swap, add liquidity, a live dashboard that shows the fee repricing in the same block as the oracle moves, the replay, an on-chain ledger and portfolio, and in-browser verification of any Aven swap.

Limits: the pools trade open-mint demo tokens (aETH/aUSD), but the prices the hook reads are real Hyperliquid prices. There has been no third-party audit; our internal security review is in docs/SECURITY.md.

projects.title: ProofTrack
projects.description: Blockchain-powered product tracking with transparent, verifiable supply chain provenance.
projects.project_description: ProofTrack – Blockchain-Powered Supply Chain Transparency ProofTrack is a blockchain-based product provenance and supply chain tracking platform designed to bring transparency, trust, and accountability to modern supply chains. Today, customers often have no reliable way to verify where a product originated, whether it is authentic, or how it moved through different stages before reaching the retail market. Traditional supply chain systems are often centralized, fragmented, and dependent on information provided by individual organizations, making records difficult to independently verify and potentially vulnerable to manipulation. ProofTrack addresses this challenge by leveraging an Ethereum-compatible blockchain and smart contracts to create a decentralized, transparent, and tamper-resistant record of a product's lifecycle. Each product can be registered on the blockchain with a unique identifier, establishing a verifiable digital identity. As the product moves through the supply chain, important lifecycle events such as product creation, ownership transfers, and location updates are recorded as blockchain transactions. Because these records are stored on the blockchain, previously recorded information cannot be easily altered or manipulated. Every authorized participant in the supply chain can contribute relevant updates, while customers and other interested parties can independently verify a product's provenance and trace its journey. The platform aims to reduce counterfeit products, improve supply chain accountability, eliminate information asymmetry, and build greater confidence between manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and consumers. Ultimately, ProofTrack transforms traditional product tracking into a transparent and verifiable system where trust is supported by blockchain technology rather than relying entirely on centralized authorities. It provides a foundation for a more secure, accountable, and trustworthy supply chain ecosystem.
projects.how_its_made: How It's Made – ProofTrack ProofTrack was built using blockchain technology and smart contracts to create a transparent, decentralized, and tamper-resistant supply chain tracking system. The core of the application is an Ethereum-compatible blockchain, which acts as the source of truth for product provenance. We use smart contracts to manage product registration and record important lifecycle events, including product creation, ownership transfers, and location updates. Each product is associated with a unique identifier, allowing its journey to be tracked through different stages of the supply chain. Whenever a product is created or transferred, the corresponding information is submitted to the smart contract through a blockchain transaction. The smart contract validates the operation and stores the relevant information on-chain, creating a permanent and independently verifiable history. This eliminates the need to rely entirely on a centralized database or a single organization to maintain trustworthy records. The application interacts with the blockchain through Web3-compatible integration, allowing users to perform blockchain operations and retrieve product lifecycle information. Smart contracts handle the essential business logic, while the application layer provides an accessible interface for interacting with the tracking system. One of the most important technical decisions was using blockchain as the verification layer rather than treating it simply as a database. This ensures that product history is transparent and resistant to unauthorized modification. By combining smart contracts, unique product identifiers, and blockchain transactions, ProofTrack demonstrates how decentralized technology can solve real-world supply chain transparency challenges. The most interesting aspect of the project is its use of immutable lifecycle records to establish trust between otherwise independent supply chain participants. Instead of asking customers to blindly trust a manufacturer's claims, ProofTrack provides a blockchain-backed mechanism for independently verifying a product's journey.

projects.title: Corvex
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that queues stock-token orders while markets are shut, clears them at one price
projects.project_description: Stock markets close every Friday evening, but tokenized stocks keep trading on-chain all weekend. Liquidity providers sell into a stale price, and on Monday morning the first bot to arrive buys the whole overnight gap from the pool. Corvex is a Uniswap v4 hook that fixes this. While a stock's reference price is dark (weekend, holiday, halt, split pause or stale feed), trades that keep the pool within a 2% band still fill, and bigger trades are taken as claims and queued instead of filling at a stale price. When the price returns, anyone can run one cross. It clears the whole queue at a single fair price, matches buyers against sellers directly, swaps only the net imbalance against the pool and never past that price, and donates the surplus to liquidity providers. A falling-fee auction then closes what is left of the gap. Every open and close is also recorded as a Session Print, sent to Arbitrum and Base over Chainlink CCIP, and checked against the official exchange price by a Chainlink CRE workflow, so other chains can trust the price a stock opened at. Cross-chain buyers can queue orders from Arbitrum or Base, and their fills come back to their own chain. In our replay of one weekend with a 6% gap at the open, a pool with no hook loses 115.75 USDG and a Corvex pool loses nothing. With no queued orders, the falling fee takes an LP loss of 157.47 USDG down to 2.93. It runs live on Robinhood Chain Testnet, Arbitrum Sepolia and Base Sepolia, with a console where you can close the market, queue orders, run the cross and withdraw your fills.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity 0.8.26 with Foundry (104 tests, including fuzzing of cross settlement across four pool orientations). The core is a Uniswap v4 hook using beforeSwap with a return delta (to take a large trade as a claim instead of filling it), afterSwap as a band safety net, a per-swap dynamic fee for the gap auction, the queue held as ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager, an unlock callback that runs the cross, and donate() to pay LPs. The hook address is mined with CREATE2 so its permission bits are right, and we kept the code under the EIP-170 size limit. The pool leg of the cross uses a price limit equal to the cross price and a zero stored LP fee, so it can never cost more than the cross price. Anything above liabilities afterwards is the surplus donated to LPs. Chainlink does three jobs. Data Feeds give the reference price and the staleness and plausibility checks, and the cross only runs when the session is open, the oracle is unpaused, the feed is fresh and any announced split multiplier matches. CCIP 2.0 carries Session Prints to Arbitrum and Base (one failing destination never blocks the hook), carries schedules and orders to Robinhood Chain, and sends fills back to the buyer's source chain; each cross-chain user owns their orders through a small CREATE2 vault so credits stay attributable. A CRE workflow (TypeScript, cron plus EVM log triggers) fetches the official price from an external API, takes the median across nodes, compares it split-adjusted, and writes Attested or Disputed on-chain. We ran it with cre workflow simulate --broadcast, which wrote real attestations on Arbitrum Sepolia. The frontend is Next.js 16, Tailwind 4 and viem, with a three.js clay scene, a live replay chart whose P&L numbers follow the graph, and a one-screen console. 13 CRE logic tests and 5 Playwright tests walk a whole weekend through the UI on a local chain. Hacky parts worth knowing: Robinhood's testnet has no Uniswap v4, so we deployed the real v4-core PoolManager ourselves. The tokens, the price feed and the market-status keeper are mocks (in production the status would come from a Chainlink Data Streams adapter), and a localhost-only API route lets the console's Close and Reopen buttons act as that keeper without exposing the key. Uniswap wraps hook reverts, so we decode the real reason for users. We also documented what is not done: the fork replay of a real weekend, a CCIP token lane for the mock USDG, and a minimum order size to stop queue spam at the band edge.

projects.title: Tenor
projects.description: Tenor is the prop firm on Circle's Arc where skilled traders get funded with real capital.
projects.project_description: Tenor is a proprietary trading ("prop") firm built on Arc, Circle's stablecoin Layer 1. Its core promise is that it is the prop firm that can't trade against you. No B-book. Every funded trade is meant to be a real fill on an onchain venue (edgeX, Extended or Hibachi). Each funded account maps to its own venue sub account with a trade only key. Every loss is pre funded. A RiskReserve smart contract won't open a new funded account unless the USDC it holds covers the maximum possible loss of all live accounts plus the new one, with a 20% buffer. We only win when you win. After a one-time evaluation fee, Tenor earns only a share of real profits, and traders keep 80%. Fees come from a single public formula: pass rate × account size × max drawdown × buffers. The same formula runs in the UI, the server and an onchain PricingEngine contract, so prices are transparent and always cover the worst case. How it works for a trader: Sign in with Google. Pick a challenge: six account sizes, three plans (Classic, Turbo, Pro), 1-step or 2-step, or a free demo. Pay in USDC on Arc. The server verifies the payment onchain. Trade in an evaluation account. Fills are simulated against Extended's live order book, so execution is realistic. A rules engine enforces profit targets, static max drawdown, daily loss limits, TP/SL and daily rollover. A scheduled risk sweep keeps enforcing them while the app is closed. Traders who pass move on to a funded account trading real capital. Payouts settle in USDC or a local stablecoin through Circle StableFX.
projects.how_its_made: We have used TypeScript made up of three components: a Next.js 16 application (App Router, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4) deployed on Vercel, a pure TypeScript package containing the challenge catalog, rule definitions, execution math and pricing model and a Solidity 0.8.24 contract suite built and tested with Foundry.Arc integration: checkout is a native USDC transfer to the treasury on Arc testnet, verified entirely server side. The server prices the cart independently of the client and verifies an EIP-191 signature over the order to bind the wallet to the user. With viem, it then fetches the transaction receipt, decodes the ERC-20 Transfer logs and validates the token contract, sender, recipient and amount. A UNIQUE constraint on the transaction hash makes payment claims idempotent and prevents one payment from funding two orders. Arc's single-block finality allows accounts to be provisioned immediately on confirmation, and USDC as the gas token means users hold a single asset. Arc-specific handling includes using the 6-decimal ERC-20 view of USDC rather than the 18-decimal native balance, and enforcing a 20 gwei maxFeePerGas floor, since lower-priced transactions are silently dropped by the mempool. Extended integration: evaluation fills are simulated against Extended's live order book. Market orders walk the book level by level to produce realistic average fill prices and slippage. Real-time market data streams directly from Extended's public WebSocket to the client with automatic backoff reconnection and requestAnimationFrame-throttled rendering (about 30 fps). Client data is display-only; all fills and rule evaluation use an authoritative server-side read. Evaluation engine: rule enforcement runs inside Postgres transactions under a row lock on the account, in a deterministic order: TP/SL triggers, daily rollover, breach detection, then pass detection. Enforcement is suspended when any required mark price is unavailable, so stale or missing data cannot cause a breach. Gapped stop-losses fill at the worse of the stop price and the executable market price. Notable engineering decisions: Vercel's Hobby tier limits cron jobs to daily runs, so continuous risk enforcement is driven by a GitHub Actions workflow that calls a bearer-token-protected /api/cron/risk endpoint every five minutes. Sub-minute (30-second) candles are aggregated client-side from the live trade and top-of-book streams. RiskReserve is a USDC vault whose reserve() reverts unless holdings cover the aggregate live maximum loss plus the new account's maximum loss at a 1.2× buffer, making solvency an onchain invariant rather than a policy. ITenor.sol defines the interfaces for the full funded-account system: challenge registry, funded-account manager across edgeX, Extended and Hibachi, and payout module. CI runs unit tests and type-checking, and a separate integration suite exercises the engine against live venue data and the Arc testnet RPC.

5. A rules engine enforces profit targets, static max drawdown, daily loss limits, TP/SL and daily rollover. A scheduled risk sweep keeps enforcing them while the app is closed.
6. Traders who pass move on to a funded account trading real capital. Payouts settle in USDC or a local stablecoin through Circle StableFX.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We have used TypeScript made up of three components: a Next.js 16 application (App Router, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4) deployed on Vercel, a pure TypeScript package containing the challenge catalog, rule definitions, execution math and pricing model and a Solidity 0.8.24 contract suite built and tested with Foundry.Arc integration: checkout is a native USDC transfer to the treasury on Arc testnet, verified entirely server side. 

The server prices the cart independently of the client and verifies an EIP-191 signature over the order to bind the wallet to the user. With viem, it then fetches the transaction receipt, decodes the ERC-20 Transfer logs and validates the token contract, sender, recipient and amount. A UNIQUE constraint on the transaction hash makes payment claims idempotent and prevents one payment from funding two orders. Arc's single-block finality allows accounts to be provisioned immediately on confirmation, and USDC as the gas token means users hold a single asset. Arc-specific handling includes using the 6-decimal ERC-20 view of USDC rather than the 18-decimal native balance, and enforcing a 20 gwei maxFeePerGas floor, since lower-priced transactions are silently dropped by the mempool.

Extended integration: evaluation fills are simulated against Extended's live order book. Market orders walk the book level by level to produce realistic average fill prices and slippage. Real-time market data streams directly from Extended's public WebSocket to the client with automatic backoff reconnection and requestAnimationFrame-throttled rendering (about 30 fps). Client data is display-only; all fills and rule evaluation use an authoritative server-side read.

Evaluation engine: rule enforcement runs inside Postgres transactions under a row lock on the account, in a deterministic order: TP/SL triggers, daily rollover, breach detection, then pass detection. Enforcement is suspended when any required mark price is unavailable, so stale or missing data cannot cause a breach. Gapped stop-losses fill at the worse of the stop price and the executable market price.

Notable engineering decisions:
- Vercel's Hobby tier limits cron jobs to daily runs, so continuous risk enforcement is driven by a GitHub Actions workflow that calls a bearer-token-protected /api/cron/risk endpoint every five minutes.
- Sub-minute (30-second) candles are aggregated client-side from the live trade and top-of-book streams.
- RiskReserve is a USDC vault whose reserve() reverts unless holdings cover the aggregate live maximum loss plus the new account's maximum loss at a 1.2× buffer, making solvency an onchain invariant rather than a policy. ITenor.sol defines the interfaces for the full funded-account system: challenge registry, funded-account manager across edgeX, Extended and Hibachi, and payout module.
- CI runs unit tests and type-checking, and a separate integration suite exercises the engine against live venue data and the Arc testnet RPC.

projects.title: Mohar
projects.description: Any IoT device signs its own readings, an AI can only add caution, and a chain keeps the record.
projects.project_description: Mohar is a method that makes any IoT device verifiable. Today a device's reading reaches the people who rely on it through someone's server, and they take that server's word. Mohar removes the server from the trust path. The device has its own name on ENS, holds its own key, builds and signs its own reports, and sends them straight to a public chain through the Ethereum alternative mempool, with no backend, no custodial signer and no relayer. A 0G model gives a second opinion on every report, but it can only make the device more careful: it can never clear a hold, and if 0G is unreachable the device stops safely instead of guessing. Every decision is logged to 0G Storage with its request ID and can be replayed against the chain. Our demo device is a prepaid electricity meter. A Raspberry Pi Pico plays the meter's pulse output, and an ESP8266 does everything else on real hardware: it counts pulses, runs fixed checks, asks 0G, signs, and reports to a ledger that keeps credit, arrears and inspection holds. Swap the pulse input for any sensor and the rest stays. The meter is simulated, nothing measures real electricity, and nothing disconnects a supply.
projects.how_its_made: Firmware (C++ on an ESP8266, PlatformIO): Keccak-256, a custom hash-based one-time signature (Winternitz w=16, 67 chains, a Merkle tree of 256 keys, 2,400-byte signatures), an RLP encoder that builds the EIP-8141 frame transaction itself, and TLS 1.2 to a public RPC. Before signing, the chip saves its intent to flash so a power cut can never reuse a one-time key; we pulled the power three times mid-signing to prove it. A stack-overflow bug that caused resets was found by measuring free stack, and fixed. Contracts: MoharAccount and QuotaPaymaster in Yul (signature check in 89,161 of the 90,000 validation gas allowed), MachineLedger in Solidity. A frame transaction runs four frames: account verifies, paymaster approves, ledger records, paymaster settles. Ethereum Foundation track: the paymaster reads its own quota storage, which the canonical mempool refuses (StorageReadNonSender); the ERC-8421 alternative mempool admitted the same bytes and mined them on the public devnet. We built a local copy of the devnet and sidecar to test admission rules before funds arrived. ENS: ENSv2 on Sepolia, with a fleet registry, a Permissioned Resolver and Enhanced Access Control roles. meter-001.mohar.eth holds the ledger, paymaster, key root and log pointer; the dashboard finds everything from the name, and a maintenance key can edit only its own record. 0G: qwen3.8-flash on 0G Private Computer, chosen after testing 19 scenarios five times each, called by the device itself with a strict RUN or INSPECT allowlist. Episode logs go to 0G Storage and replay against the chain. Dashboard: Vite, React, TypeScript and viem, plus a three.js entry page.

projects.title: Leash-Out
projects.description: AI agents can spend money. Leash makes sure only your World ID can approve the big payments.
projects.project_description: AI agents now pay for things on their own, using standards like x402. Their wallets have a spending limit, and to raise it they send the owner a confirmation code by email. But the agent can usually read that inbox. So it reads the code and raises its own limit. Researchers at Cornell Tech and Yale showed this in October 2026 (I-HITL, arXiv 2610.35835), and we reproduced it with seven AI models: on a typical agent wallet, 20 of 21 runs raised their own limit. Leash fixes the approval step. The owner sets simple rules: how much the agent can pay on its own per payment and per day, and that a new shop always asks first. Payments inside the rules go through automatically from a small everyday wallet. Anything bigger, anything new, and any change to the limits waits for the owner. The owner approves with World ID on their phone, and the proof is bound to that one request, so the agent cannot fake or reuse it. Only then is the payment released from a vault that needs two of three keys on Hedera. Every decision goes to a public Hedera topic that nobody can edit. Every agent gets an ENS name (like shopper.leash.eth) with its status and wallets, and shops check that name on ENS directly. Revoke an agent and shops refuse it within seconds. In our runs on Leash, 0 of 45 moved money or changed limits without the owner.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo. An Express server holds the policy engine, approvals and co-signing, with SQLite for state. The web app is React and Vite. An agent SDK wraps fetch: when an API answers 402 Payment Required, it asks Leash before paying. World ID: IDKit 4 with server-side request signing and verification through the World developer API. Sign up is a uniqueness proof that also creates a World ID session. Sign in and approvals are session proofs. The hacky part: session proofs carry no action, so we bind each approval by putting the approval's ID in the proof's signal and checking the signal hash on the server. A proof for one payment cannot approve another, and nullifiers stop replays. Hedera: every agent gets an everyday wallet and a vault created with the Hedera SDK, no Solidity. The vault uses a 2-of-3 threshold key (agent, Leash server, owner recovery). The server only co-signs after a verified World ID approval, and only if the transfer exactly matches what was approved: payee, amount, token, payer and fee payer. Payments use x402 with the Hedera exact scheme, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every decision is written to an HCS topic as a tamper-evident audit log. ENS: we registered leash.eth on ENSv2 on Sepolia and pointed it at our own Permissioned Resolver, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. Each agent is a subname whose text records live on the parent resolver and resolve by wildcard through the Universal Resolver, so creating an agent costs one transaction. The demo shop reads those records from ENS itself before serving an agent, and checks that the paying wallet is one the agent publishes. We also built an experiment harness that runs the same task against a typical email-code wallet and against Leash, across Claude, Gemini, GPT-OSS, Gemma and Qwen models. Deployed on Vercel (web) and Railway (server).
