projects.title: Leafguard
projects.description: Post-quantum 2-of-3 smart wallet on EIP-8141 that blocks hash-based signature reuse on-chain
projects.project_description:
Leafguard (PQ-Vault) is a 2-of-3 guardian smart wallet where every approval is a post-quantum, hash-based signature. There is no ECDSA anywhere in the wallet and no seed phrase. It runs on EIP-8141 frame transactions submitted through the ERC-8421 alternative mempool.
Each payment is one transaction with three frames: VERIFY (guardian A's signature), VERIFY (guardian B's signature, which also approves payment) and SENDER (the transfer). Both post-quantum signatures are checked before the account pays any fee, so a missing, corrupted, stale or duplicate approval makes the transaction invalid and costs the wallet nothing.
Fast, compact hash-based signatures are one-time ("stateful"): a guardian key has a slot of 128 one-time leaves, and signing twice with the same leaf leaks the key. That is the classic failure mode, and it happens in real life through crashes, restored backups, cloned devices and rolled-back storage. Leafguard records each slot's high-water mark on-chain in a LeafLedger. The mark is checked in VERIFY and consumed in SENDER, so a leaf can never be accepted twice, even if the device holding the key forgets it used it. Anyone can submit an equivocation proof (two messages signed with one leaf) to revoke that slot. Keys renew automatically: a slot with 8 or fewer leaves left is rotated first, approved by the other two guardians. A key that runs out falls back to a larger, stateless SPHINCS-style signature, so the wallet never gets stuck. Two guardians can replace a lost one.
We measured it. In simulation, under stale restores, rollbacks and lost state, a baseline vault reached γ = 9 uses of a single leaf (forgery cost down to 35.6 bits) and hundreds of double-accepted signatures. Leafguard kept γ = 1 with zero double acceptances. We also ran the attack live on a local devnet: a vault without on-chain leaf state accepted two transactions signed with the same leaf after a stale backup restore. Leafguard rejected the same restored signer with StaleLeaf.
For the demo there are personal wallets (Alice, Bob, Carol) with send and receive, the fee explained, key health and shared 2-of-3 multisig vaults. There is also a block explorer that decodes frame transactions frame by frame, and a React Native phone app. The phone is a paired remote: the keys and signing stay on the wallet computer.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts are Solidity with Foundry (26 tests). PQVault holds the three guardians and does validate() for both VERIFY frames and execute() for SENDER. PQVaultFactory deploys accounts with CREATE2. LeafLedger stores the per-slot high-water marks and accepts equivocation reports. PQVaultFrameOps is a Yul helper for the EIP-8141 opcodes (TXPARAM, SIGPARAM, SIGDATACOPY, FRAMEPARAM, APPROVE). Signatures go in ARBITRARY signature entries and are checked against the protocol's canonical signature hash. We wrote no cryptography of our own: verification is upstream JARDIN's FORS and SPX verifiers, unmodified, and signing is JARDIN's Python reference signers, pinned as a git submodule.
Partner tech: we built on the ETHGlobal Mumbai alt-mempool workshop stack, namely forshtat's ethrex fork with EIP-8141 and a tracer, the hegota-support helpers and the skandha-based mempool sidecar. Two signature verifications cost more validation gas than EIP-8141's combined 100k cap: about 84k per VERIFY frame for a compact signature, about 292k for a stateless one. Reading the shared LeafLedger is also "storage not owned by the sender", which the canonical mempool refuses. So we implemented ERC-8421 [BUDGET-010] (a separate 1M-gas validation budget per staked entity) as a patch to the workshop sidecar: 7 new tests, all 393 executor tests passing, and a Docker image. The vault stakes itself when it is created. We measured that the canonical mempool and the stock sidecar reject the transaction, and the patched sidecar admits the staked vault while rejecting an unstaked copy.
On a local Kurtosis network (ethrex + Lighthouse + the patched sidecar), a payment uses VERIFY frames of 83,842 and 75,875 gas and a SENDER frame of 59,809. It is billed 379,513 gas, because frame transactions are charged by calldata size and post-quantum signatures are large. The first use of a key costs 97,920 more to create its ledger entry. The wallet's fee estimate reproduces 25 of the 26 frame-transaction receipts on the chain exactly (the one exception is a recovery transaction the wallet never sends). The off-chain toolkit is Python with no pip dependencies: an EIP-8141 frame-transaction encoder, checked against ethrex's test vector; a key store that records a leaf as used before signing with it (burn-before-sign); a devnet driver for rotation, recovery and the attack; the wallet servers and the frame-transaction explorer; 44 unit tests. Hacky but notable: Upstream JARDIN's hashing shares module-level buffers, so we serialise every call to it from our multi-threaded servers. The phone app is Expo, running in Expo Go. It reaches the wallet over an ngrok tunnel, paired with a code. The wallet treats any forwarded request as remote, so the tunnel can't bypass pairing. The research side is a simulator with fault injection plus a crash test that kills the signer 100+ times.

projects.title: ARCWEALTH
projects.description: Onchain alternative investment: auditable USDC strategy vaults and markets on Arc Testnet.
projects.project_description: ARCWEALTH is an onchain alternative investment platform built on Arc Testnet, where USDC is both the settlement asset and the gas token. Investors can trade live testnet assets and clearly labelled demo tokens, lend or borrow against cirBTC in a demo pool with a liquidation simulator, and invest from 10 USDC into three ERC-4626 Strategy Investment Funds: S1 Hybrid Long-Short (tokenized debt, covered calls and a tactical sleeve), S2 Asset Allocator (dXAU, dXAG, dCOPR) and S3 Aggressive Covered Call (dBTC, dETH, dSOL). Every number carries an honesty badge — LIVE-TESTNET, DEMO-ONCHAIN or SIMULATED-OFFCHAIN — so users always know what is real, what is a demo stand-in and what is modelled. Vault shares, NAV, cost basis and disclosures are recorded onchain; instant withdrawals are capped by the idle buffer, while larger exits are requested and fulfilled by a keeper. A keeper and log indexer keep prices, regimes, coupons, covered calls and NAV snapshots fresh, and the interface adds a portfolio dashboard, P&L, activity with explorer links and role-gated admin controls with a timelock. Unaudited testnet software; demo tokens have no monetary value and performance is illustrative, not investment advice.
projects.how_its_made: Built as a full-stack onchain application. The frontend is React 18 + TypeScript on Vite, styled with a custom Tailwind dark design system, React Router, TanStack Query, Recharts and Framer Motion. Wallet state and contract writes use wagmi v2 + viem v2 with ConnectKit, targeting Arc Testnet (chain ID 5042002). Contracts are Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin v5: ERC-4626 SIFStrategyVault, InvestorVault (onchain disclosure acceptance), RiskManager, StrategyManager, bond / covered-call / tactical / allocator modules, demo oracle, swap router, bond issuer, options counterparty and lending pool, plus a TimelockController for privileged changes. The backend is a Bun server exposing a REST API, keepers and a log indexer; it reads chain state via viem, uses a fallback RPC transport, forces type-2 EIP-1559 fees at or above Arc's 20 gwei floor, and runs Postgres when DATABASE_URL is set or in-process PGlite otherwise. Circle and Arc partner technology provides USDC, EURC and cirBTC plus the faucet; demo swaps route through our own oracle-priced router because live-token swaps need a Circle App Kit API key. Notable details: every figure is tagged by honesty tier; native 18-decimal USDC gas and 6-decimal ERC-20 USDC are never summed; approvals are exact, never unlimited; large withdrawals are queued, keeper-unwound and claimable; and the keeper writes NAV snapshots used for onchain performance charts. Scaffolded with Circle's Arc Studio, which sped up Arc Testnet and wallet wiring.

projects.title: TRACE
projects.description: Turn a Uniswap V3 wallet's on-chain history into an evidence-backed, backtested LP strategy.
projects.project_description: TRACE is on-chain strategy intelligence for Uniswap V3 liquidity providers. Blockchains show what happened, but not the strategy behind it: an LP's history is just separate mints, liquidity changes and fee collections. Paste any public wallet. TRACE reads its history from Ethereum Sepolia, rebuilds every V3 position (ranges, deposits, withdrawals, fees split from principal), and names the likely strategy as a hypothesis with a confidence score. Every rule links to the transactions behind it. TRACE then backtests the strategy on the pool's real swaps (observed replay vs simulated rules vs passive LP vs buy and hold) and checks, rule by rule, what 1inch Aqua can run. To execute, the user signs an EIP-712 authorization bound to the exact plan, approves exact token amounts and ships the strategy order to Aqua. Every step is confirmed from its Sepolia receipt. Nothing runs without the user's own wallet. Demo: wallet 0x4797...eb4c: 1 position and 12 events rebuilt; passive concentrated liquidity at 75% confidence; 793 real swaps replayed; Aqua ship confirmed on Sepolia. Honest status: no demo data anywhere. 0G inference and 0G Storage are integrated but currently blocked (no provider for our key's trust tier; storage uploader unfunded), so the app shows the evidence-only analysis and says so. Aqua taker swaps need 1inch's KycNFT and are not part of the flow.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind, wagmi + viem (Sepolia-only), TanStack Query, and a React Three Fiber 3D liquidity landscape drawn from real position events. Deployed on Vercel. Backend: Express API + BullMQ worker on Render, Postgres (Supabase), Redis (Upstash). Nine TypeScript packages: chain-config: single source of truth for Sepolia and every verified contract address (re-probed with eth_getCode at startup). chain-data: viem client with chunked eth_getLogs (Infura's 10k-block cap), a shared credit-based rate limiter and retries. uniswap-v3: order-independent position reconstruction with real token decimals; each Collect is split into owed principal vs fees, so fees are never double-counted. strategy-inference: deterministic "Strategy DNA" (range width, re-set frequency, time in range, fee cadence) plus a gated hypothesis step using the 0G router; only rules citing real transactions survive, confidence capped by the evidence. strategy-ir: immutable, content-addressed strategy versions. backtester: replays the pool's real Swap events with a look-ahead guard enforced in code and in the database; fees from real swap flow x fee tier x liquidity share. aqua-adapter: 1inch aqua-sdk and swap-vm-sdk; Uniswap TickMath ported to exact BigInt; compiles an AquaXYCAmmStrategy concentrate order from the position's real ticks, simulates approve/ship, verifies the Shipped event and virtual balances. authorization: server-verified EIP-712 with single-use challenges, expiry and replay protection. zero-g-storage: 0G Galileo uploads with Merkle read-back (references shown only after a real upload). Testing: 108 unit/API tests, a fork test of approve -> ship -> dock against the real Aqua contracts on an Anvil Sepolia fork, and live checks on Sepolia. projects.project_description_markdown:
TRACE is on-chain strategy intelligence for Uniswap V3 liquidity providers. Blockchains show what happened, but not the strategy behind it: an LP's history is just separate mints, liquidity changes and fee collections.

Paste any public wallet. TRACE reads its history from Ethereum Sepolia, rebuilds every V3 position (ranges, deposits, withdrawals, fees split from principal), and names the likely strategy as a hypothesis with a confidence score. Every rule links to the transactions behind it. TRACE then backtests the strategy on the pool's real swaps (observed replay vs simulated rules vs passive LP vs buy and hold) and checks, rule by rule, what 1inch Aqua can run.

To execute, the user signs an EIP-712 authorization bound to the exact plan, approves exact token amounts and ships the strategy order to Aqua. Every step is confirmed from its Sepolia receipt. Nothing runs without the user's own wallet.

Demo: wallet 0x4797...eb4c: 1 position and 12 events rebuilt; passive concentrated liquidity at 75% confidence; 793 real swaps replayed; Aqua ship confirmed on Sepolia.

Honest status: no demo data anywhere. 0G inference and 0G Storage are integrated but currently blocked (no provider for our key's trust tier; storage uploader unfunded), so the app shows the evidence-only analysis and says so. Aqua taker swaps need 1inch's KycNFT and are not part of the flow.

projects.title: QueryMint
projects.description: A decentralized data marketplace connecting multiple publishers through one query and payment.
projects.project_description: QueryMint is a decentralized, multi-publisher data marketplace built on Arkiv and Whitechain that enables buyers to discover, query and purchase data from multiple independent publishers through a single interface. Traditional data marketplaces often require buyers to integrate separately with different providers, negotiate pricing, manage access permissions and handle individual payments. QueryMint simplifies this process by introducing a unified discovery, authorization, quoting and settlement layer. Publishers connect their wallets, register on Whitechain, configure dataset pricing and access policies, and publish structured, encrypted records as publisher-owned entities on Arkiv. When a buyer submits a query, the QueryMint coordinator discovers matching records across registered publishers, verifies entity ownership, checks on-chain permissions, validates record hashes and calculates publisher-specific allocations. The coordinator then generates a cryptographically signed query manifest and a consolidated quote. Buyers can settle the purchase in USDT through a Solidity smart contract deployed on Whitechain. The contract verifies settlement instructions, publisher policies, coordinator permissions, expiry and replay protection before distributing payments directly to the respective publishers. After successful settlement, the buyer signs a separate delivery authorization. The coordinator verifies the confirmed transaction, retrieves the corresponding encrypted Arkiv records, validates them and delivers the authorized data. QueryMint also provides a developer SDK demonstration to make its buyer-side querying, quoting and settlement functionality reusable by other applications. My vision is to create an open data marketplace where independent publishers can monetize their datasets while buyers access multiple data sources through one query and one settlement.
projects.how_its_made: QueryMint is built using TypeScript, React, Vite, Node.js and Express.js, with Solidity smart contracts for on-chain settlement. The frontend consists of a buyer marketplace, publisher console and a separate SDK demonstration application. The backend coordinator, built with Node.js and Express, orchestrates publisher discovery, Arkiv queries, ownership verification, policy validation, quote generation, manifest signing and authorized data delivery. I use the Arkiv SDK to publish structured data as wallet-owned entities, including publisher profiles, dataset manifests and encrypted records. The coordinator queries Arkiv's indexer to discover matching entities across multiple publishers and validates ownership and content hashes before including records in a quote. Whitechain is used as the financial settlement layer. We developed and deployed a Solidity smart contract using Foundry on Whitechain Sepolia. The contract handles publisher registration, dataset policies, coordinator permissions and USDT settlement. Viem is used for EVM wallet interactions, contract calls and blockchain reads, while EIP-712 signatures authenticate coordinator-generated query manifests and buyer delivery authorizations. One important implementation detail is our separation of data discovery from financial settlement. The coordinator creates signed settlement instructions, but the smart contract independently validates the signature, publisher permissions, nonce, expiry and payout arithmetic before distributing USDT. I also implemented settlement-based delivery recovery, allowing the coordinator to reconstruct and verify a purchase using its confirmed blockchain transaction rather than relying entirely on temporary in-memory quote state. The project is deployed using Vercel for the frontend applications and Railway for the coordinator backend. The SDK is currently integrated as a private npm workspace package, with independent package distribution being prepared. We successfully demonstrated a live four-record purchase across two independent publishers, involving a total settlement of 4 USDT on Whitechain Sepolia, followed by buyer-authorized data delivery from Arkiv.

projects.title: ChainXray
projects.description: A Web3 debugging workbench to intercept wallet requests and inspect transaction execution.
projects.project_description: ChainXray is an open-source Windows desktop debugging workbench for Web3 developers and security researchers. Inspired by Burp Suite’s interception workflow, it focuses on supported requests passing between dapps and browser wallets. Developers can hold a request before wallet approval, inspect its method and parameters, edit supported fields, then forward or drop it. Captured transactions can also be copied to Repeater for isolated local testing. Request Flow connects the originating dapp, intercepted request, wallet and destination contract. Once the wallet returns a transaction hash, ChainXray automatically tracks receipts, execution status, gas usage and emitted events. Compatible RPC providers enable a nested contract execution tree with available decoded functions and revert details. The Uniswap Trading API integration provides read-only reference quotes that developers can associate with captured requests for manual comparison. The Arkiv integration lets users preview and publish sanitized observations as wallet-owned entities on Rabdi, then query them back without relying on a ChainXray-hosted database. Raw captures remain in a local workspace. Previously recorded requests, receipts and traces remain inspectable offline. ChainXray helps developers distinguish wallet rejection, contract execution failures and RPC limitations within one debugging workflow.
projects.how_its_made: ChainXray combines a Tauri desktop shell, a React and TypeScript interface, and a bundled Node.js engine. The desktop application communicates with an authenticated local API, while SQLite stores workspace evidence. Managed Chromium includes MetaMask and the ChainXray browser extension. The extension hooks supported injected wallet providers and MetaMask SDK connections. A key implementation challenge was that Uniswap’s MetaMask SDK connection bypassed the conventional window.ethereum request path. We added an SDK-specific adapter to hold those requests and correlate forwarding decisions with wallet outcomes. When a supported wallet returns a transaction hash, the engine retrieves the receipt and attempts contract tracing. It supports Geth-style debug_traceTransaction and a trace_transaction fallback, converting flat trace records into a nested execution tree. Viem handles Ethereum data encoding and supported ABI decoding. Anvil, Forge and Solidity tooling provide the isolated local lab. The Uniswap integration calls the Trading API quote endpoint, stores the reference response locally and optionally links it to a capture. It does not sign or submit swaps. Using @arkiv-network/sdk, ChainXray publishes an allowlisted protocol, category and summary to Rabdi as wallet-owned entities with seven-day expiration. The application also queries those entities, completing a user-visible write-and-read workflow. Raw requests, signatures and credentials are excluded from the public observation. For CROPS, the architecture keeps capture storage and saved-evidence inspection local, without requiring a ChainXray-hosted service. Live dapps, RPC reads and optional external integrations retain their network dependencies.

projects.title: Redline
projects.description: Continuous security testing for smart contracts. Proof, not opinion.
projects.project_description: Redline is continuous security testing for smart contracts. Install the GitHub App on a Solidity repo and every push gets attacked. A swarm of hunter agents reads the diff and the contract, pulls the shared attack-recipe library, and writes concrete attacks as Foundry tests: reentrancy, access control, oracle manipulation, accounting drift and more. Each candidate attack is then handed to a council of three independent referees that replay it against a forked deployment and measure balances before and after. A finding only turns red when the referees agree and real value moved. No value moved, no finding. Proof, not opinion. Every red finding lands as a GitHub check with a plain-English sentence, the amount at risk, a locked attack (the runnable form unlocks when you prove you own the repo) and a one-click "Fix it" that drafts the smallest patch as a diff. Reproduced attacks are saved as forever-tests so the same hole can never ship again. Two things are public by design. The recipe library the swarm learns from lives on Arkiv, so every installation makes every other one stronger. And the council's proof of each reproduced theft (votes and balance receipts, never the attack itself) is published on Arkiv, so anyone can verify a finding without trusting us. Live at https://redline.quantapar.com
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo): a Next.js 15 dashboard on Vercel, a Probot GitHub App that turns pushes and PRs into scans, a BullMQ worker that runs the pipeline, Postgres (Neon, Drizzle) and Redis. All the heavy work happens inside Foundry: hunters emit forge tests, referees run them against a fork with balance snapshots, and the deltas are what we vote on. 0G Compute powers the hunters. Each hunter is a separate model request through the 0G Compute router, so the swarm is diverse by construction rather than one model asked three times. Candidate attacks are deduplicated by target and weakness class before they reach the council. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) is the public memory. We define two schemas, redline.recipes and redline.proofs, with the Arkiv SDK. The worker queries redline.recipes on every scan before hunting, so the library is read from chain rather than from our database. When a finding turns red, the pipeline writes the council's proof entity in the same run. Both writes are idempotent on the Redline id, and the dashboard reads straight from Arkiv with Postgres as the fallback. Judges can query the library with a single select() against the writer address in the README. Hacky bits: Arkiv strings cap at 128 bytes, so titles and labels are clipped and the long parts (templates, proof JSON) ride in bytes columns. The runnable attack is redacted server-side before it reaches the browser, and the "Fix it" diff is generated from the same referee output that proved the theft, so the patch always targets the lines that actually moved money.

projects.title: Aquaprime
projects.description: Lend from your wallet, borrow cheaper as a verified human, and get liquidated only as much as needed
projects.project_description: AquaPrime is a zero-custody credit market built on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, designed around two simple principles: lenders should never have to lock capital into a custodial pool, and borrowers should never be wiped out by blunt liquidations. Traditional lending protocols force liquidity providers to deposit assets into shared smart contract vaults, creating systemic honeypots and fragmented capital. AquaPrime eliminates deposits entirely by leveraging 1inch Aqua’s balance virtualization. A lender’s capital stays securely in their own wallet, where a single signature allows the same USDC to simultaneously back three live strategies: an under-collateralized credit line, a liquidation backstop, and an AMM. This achieves three times the capital efficiency with zero dollars sitting idle in contracts. Capital moves only at the exact microsecond a borrower draws a loan: aqua.pull routes USDC straight from the lender’s wallet to the borrower, and repayments flow directly back via aqua.push. When positions go underwater, legacy protocols punish borrowers by dumping fifty to one hundred percent of their position at fixed penalties. AquaPrime replaces this with a mathematical scalpel inside the execution engine. We engineered a custom SwapVM opcode, 0xf0 (SolvencyDutchGuard), which dynamically calculates and auctions only the precise slice of collateral required to restore a position to a safe 1.02 health factor. It executes a Dutch auction ramping from a 1.5% to 6% discount over ten minutes, then asserts post-trade invariants to revert any fill exceeding the surgical cap. In our full-lifecycle integration tests, an insolvent borrower lost only 2.0 WETH out of 10, compared to roughly 4.6 WETH seized under standard close-factor rules. A second custom opcode, 0xf1 (OracleBackstopBid), lets LPs post standing oracle-priced bids that absorb this seized collateral, enabling keepers to execute zero-capital flash rescues across both orders in a single atomic transaction. To protect the protocol without invasive identity checks, we integrated World ID Proof of Human through IDKit. Verified humans unlock an 115% collateral tier alongside a three-minute grace window, compared to 150% for anonymous accounts. The proof is verified against World’s Developer Portal API and permanently attested on-chain via EIP-712, preventing Sybil attackers from farming the lower tier with multiple wallets while requiring zero KYC. For autonomous liquidation keepers, we introduced a cryptographic human-in-the-loop checkpoint using World ID Agent Pass. When an agent identifies an underwater position, it stages the auction and pauses. Before spending its hot key, it requires fresh human authorization via an OIDC step-up flow with PKCE, max_age=0, and an essential biometric authentication claim. The approval is bound to the exact borrower and action for 120 seconds. If cancelled, expired, or replayed, the backend fails closed with an HTTP 403 and refuses to broadcast. Because World’s enterprise portal gates production registration, the demo exercises our production-grade validation code against a standards-compliant local login server clearly identified in the interface. Privacy is enforced at the network layer. Every JSON-RPC read the browser makes—including balances, health factors, and simulated SwapVM quotes, is routed through the Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC Nox mixnet in a sandboxed, null-origin iframe. This closes a critical MEV attack vector where node operators surveil read queries to front-run profitable liquidations. The implementation is fail-closed, surfacing a clear notice rather than silently leaking traffic over cleartext if the mixnet drops. AquaPrime is fully deployed on Ethereum Sepolia against the canonical 1inch Aqua contract, native Circle USDC, and Chainlink ETH/USD, with all five contracts verified on Sourcify. The system is backed by 43 contract tests including a 40-position property test of the surgical math, 19 frontend unit tests, and an end-to-end browser test validating the complete lifecycle. The protocol generates sustainable revenue through a 10% reserve factor on interest and a 0.5% protocol fee on liquidated collateral, all without ever taking custody of user funds. Pitch: https://aquaprime-1.vercel.app/pitch
projects.how_its_made: AquaPrime was engineered from the ground up to push the boundaries of 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, combining low-level EVM assembly and bytecode manipulation with zero-knowledge identity and privacy-preserving networking. At the smart contract layer (Solidity 0.8.30, Hardhat, viaIR, Cancun EVM), we consume the canonical 1inch Aqua contract directly and redeployed the core SwapVM engine as AquaPrimeRouter. We overrode the router’s internal dispatch logic to inject an AquaPrime-specific opcode bank. Our primary custom instruction, 0xf0 (SolvencyDutchGuard), wraps the stock LimitSwap curve using a sandwich pattern: it invokes the VM execution loop from within itself. Before the curve runs, it asserts that the position is truly insolvent and that any human grace window has elapsed, then mathematically clamps the VM registers (balanceIn and balanceOut) to the exact surgical slice derived from x = (T·R·D − V)(1−d) / (T·R(1−d) − (1+f)). After the curve executes, it checks the filled amounts and reverts the entire transaction with SurgicalCapExceeded if the taker extracted more than the computed slice. Our second custom instruction, 0xf1 (OracleBackstopBid), allows liquidity providers to maintain a standing, oracle-priced bid directly from their wallet at a slight discount. The core lending market lives in CreditPositionRegistry, which inherits from AquaApp. Credit lines are native Aqua strategies shipped by lenders: borrowing triggers aqua.pull to draw funds directly from the lender’s wallet to the borrower, while repayments route back via aqua.push. When a position falls underwater, the registry dynamically ships a one-off 0xf0 auction order into Aqua. Upon execution, SwapVM’s postTransferIn maker hook executes on the registry to burn debt and distribute protocol fees. Our LiquidationExecutor contract ties the entire liquidation loop together in a single atomic transaction: it fills the 0xf0 auction, sells the seized collateral into the LP’s 0xf1 backstop order inside SwapVM’s pre-transfer-in callback, and settles the debt through Aqua, enabling keepers to execute liquidations with zero upfront capital. We encountered several non-trivial engineering hurdles while building this. First, both our router and registry initially exceeded the 24.576 KB EIP-170 contract size limit. We resolved this by hand-crafting an AquaOpcodes-compatible dispatch table (retaining only essential controls, decay, fee, and limit instructions), correcting opcode numbering collisions between stock SwapVM and AquaSwapVM (such as conflicting salt indices), and modularizing off-chain order construction into an external StrategyBuilder contract. Second, integer rounding dust in collateral accounting previously prevented completely liquidated positions from closing, causing bad debt to go unrecorded; we implemented a sweep threshold to clean dust and accurately book shortfall debt. To guarantee mathematical solvency under all market conditions, we wrote a 40-position property test verifying that the surgical formula always restores health factors between 1.00 and 1.03 regardless of price volatility. For identity, we integrated World ID 4.0 IDKit using proofOfHuman credentials with an RP-signed request. Proofs are validated server-side against World’s v4 Developer Portal API, binding the proof’s signal hash directly to the borrower's wallet. The backend then issues an EIP-712 attestation that the registry verifies on-chain, permanently storing a one-to-one mapping between nullifier and wallet without collecting personal data. During integration, we hit a subtle responsive bug where the stock IDKit modal collapsed into a mobile layout on screens 1024 pixels or narrower, inadvertently redirecting desktop laptop users to world.org; we resolved this by rebuilding the panel on IDKit’s headless useIDKitRequest hook, allowing our staging environment to open the World ID Simulator directly with the pre-loaded connect URL. For keeper security, we implemented the World ID Agent Pass specification as a full OIDC step-up flow featuring PKCE S256, max_age=0, essential biometric acr claims, and strict nonce freshness, binding single-use approvals to specific borrower actions for 120 seconds. Privacy is integrated at the transport layer via Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC. Using @anon-rpc/browser-harness, we run a hash-pinned Nox mixnet worker inside a sandboxed, null-origin iframe, routing all Viem contract reads through it with fail-closed security. During high-concurrency testing, public RPC rate limits occasionally broke the worker bootstrap; we engineered an ordered multi-RPC fallback mechanism that rotates the exit node's target provider while keeping all client traffic sealed inside the mixnet. On the server side, Next.js was aggressively caching chain reads across restarts; we enforced explicit no-store policies across all internal RPC fetch handlers to ensure instant state freshness. The frontend is built with Next.js 14, Viem, Wagmi, Tailwind, and Framer Motion. It features an interactive hero ocean powered by a custom GLSL shader in React Three Fiber (complete with Gerstner wave displacement, Fresnel sky reflections, and cursor wake physics), an animated canvas visualizer demonstrating virtual liquidity allocations across strategies, an interactive risk simulator matching the contract's fixed-point math, and a live SwapVM bytecode inspector that disassembles order instructions and reveals register transformations before and after 0xf0 execution. The entire system is backed by a one-command local orchestration script, a Playwright browser automation suite validating the complete borrower and rescue lifecycle, and a deterministic background keeper agent scanning blocks for liquidatable positions.

A lender’s capital stays securely in their own wallet, where a single signature allows the same USDC to simultaneously back three live strategies: an under-collateralized credit line, a liquidation backstop, and an AMM. This achieves three times the capital efficiency with zero dollars sitting idle in contracts. Capital moves only at the exact microsecond a borrower draws a loan: aqua.pull routes USDC straight from the lender’s wallet to the borrower, and repayments flow directly back via aqua.push.

When positions go underwater, legacy protocols punish borrowers by dumping fifty to one hundred percent of their position at fixed penalties. AquaPrime replaces this with a mathematical scalpel inside the execution engine. We engineered a custom SwapVM opcode, 0xf0 (SolvencyDutchGuard), which dynamically calculates and auctions only the precise slice of collateral required to restore a position to a safe 1.02 health factor. It executes a Dutch auction ramping from a 1.5% to 6% discount over ten minutes, then asserts post-trade invariants to revert any fill exceeding the surgical cap. In our full-lifecycle integration tests, an insolvent borrower lost only 2.0 WETH out of 10, compared to roughly 4.6 WETH seized under standard close-factor rules. A second custom opcode, 0xf1 (OracleBackstopBid), lets LPs post standing oracle-priced bids that absorb this seized collateral, enabling keepers to execute zero-capital flash rescues across both orders in a single atomic transaction.

To protect the protocol without invasive identity checks, we integrated World ID Proof of Human through IDKit. Verified humans unlock an 115% collateral tier alongside a three-minute grace window, compared to 150% for anonymous accounts. The proof is verified against World’s Developer Portal API and permanently attested on-chain via EIP-712, preventing Sybil attackers from farming the lower tier with multiple wallets while requiring zero KYC.

For autonomous liquidation keepers, we introduced a cryptographic human-in-the-loop checkpoint using World ID Agent Pass. When an agent identifies an underwater position, it stages the auction and pauses. Before spending its hot key, it requires fresh human authorization via an OIDC step-up flow with PKCE, max_age=0, and an essential biometric authentication claim. The approval is bound to the exact borrower and action for 120 seconds. If cancelled, expired, or replayed, the backend fails closed with an HTTP 403 and refuses to broadcast. Because World’s enterprise portal gates production registration, the demo exercises our production-grade validation code against a standards-compliant local login server clearly identified in the interface.

Privacy is enforced at the network layer. Every JSON-RPC read the browser makes—including balances, health factors, and simulated SwapVM quotes, is routed through the Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC Nox mixnet in a sandboxed, null-origin iframe. This closes a critical MEV attack vector where node operators surveil read queries to front-run profitable liquidations. The implementation is fail-closed, surfacing a clear notice rather than silently leaking traffic over cleartext if the mixnet drops.

AquaPrime is fully deployed on Ethereum Sepolia against the canonical 1inch Aqua contract, native Circle USDC, and Chainlink ETH/USD, with all five contracts verified on Sourcify. The system is backed by 43 contract tests including a 40-position property test of the surgical math, 19 frontend unit tests, and an end-to-end browser test validating the complete lifecycle. The protocol generates sustainable revenue through a 10% reserve factor on interest and a 0.5% protocol fee on liquidated collateral, all without ever taking custody of user funds.

Pitch: https://aquaprime-1.vercel.app/pitch
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
AquaPrime was engineered from the ground up to push the boundaries of 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, combining low-level EVM assembly and bytecode manipulation with zero-knowledge identity and privacy-preserving networking.

At the smart contract layer (Solidity 0.8.30, Hardhat, viaIR, Cancun EVM), we consume the canonical 1inch Aqua contract directly and redeployed the core SwapVM engine as AquaPrimeRouter. We overrode the router’s internal dispatch logic to inject an AquaPrime-specific opcode bank. Our primary custom instruction, 0xf0 (SolvencyDutchGuard), wraps the stock LimitSwap curve using a sandwich pattern: it invokes the VM execution loop from within itself. Before the curve runs, it asserts that the position is truly insolvent and that any human grace window has elapsed, then mathematically clamps the VM registers (balanceIn and balanceOut) to the exact surgical slice derived from x = (T·R·D − V)(1−d) / (T·R(1−d) − (1+f)). After the curve executes, it checks the filled amounts and reverts the entire transaction with SurgicalCapExceeded if the taker extracted more than the computed slice. Our second custom instruction, 0xf1 (OracleBackstopBid), allows liquidity providers to maintain a standing, oracle-priced bid directly from their wallet at a slight discount.

The core lending market lives in CreditPositionRegistry, which inherits from AquaApp. Credit lines are native Aqua strategies shipped by lenders: borrowing triggers aqua.pull to draw funds directly from the lender’s wallet to the borrower, while repayments route back via aqua.push. When a position falls underwater, the registry dynamically ships a one-off 0xf0 auction order into Aqua. Upon execution, SwapVM’s postTransferIn maker hook executes on the registry to burn debt and distribute protocol fees. Our LiquidationExecutor contract ties the entire liquidation loop together in a single atomic transaction: it fills the 0xf0 auction, sells the seized collateral into the LP’s 0xf1 backstop order inside SwapVM’s pre-transfer-in callback, and settles the debt through Aqua, enabling keepers to execute liquidations with zero upfront capital.

We encountered several non-trivial engineering hurdles while building this. First, both our router and registry initially exceeded the 24.576 KB EIP-170 contract size limit. We resolved this by hand-crafting an AquaOpcodes-compatible dispatch table (retaining only essential controls, decay, fee, and limit instructions), correcting opcode numbering collisions between stock SwapVM and AquaSwapVM (such as conflicting salt indices), and modularizing off-chain order construction into an external StrategyBuilder contract. Second, integer rounding dust in collateral accounting previously prevented completely liquidated positions from closing, causing bad debt to go unrecorded; we implemented a sweep threshold to clean dust and accurately book shortfall debt. To guarantee mathematical solvency under all market conditions, we wrote a 40-position property test verifying that the surgical formula always restores health factors between 1.00 and 1.03 regardless of price volatility.

For identity, we integrated World ID 4.0 IDKit using proofOfHuman credentials with an RP-signed request. Proofs are validated server-side against World’s v4 Developer Portal API, binding the proof’s signal hash directly to the borrower's wallet. The backend then issues an EIP-712 attestation that the registry verifies on-chain, permanently storing a one-to-one mapping between nullifier and wallet without collecting personal data. During integration, we hit a subtle responsive bug where the stock IDKit modal collapsed into a mobile layout on screens 1024 pixels or narrower, inadvertently redirecting desktop laptop users to world.org; we resolved this by rebuilding the panel on IDKit’s headless useIDKitRequest hook, allowing our staging environment to open the World ID Simulator directly with the pre-loaded connect URL. For keeper security, we implemented the World ID Agent Pass specification as a full OIDC step-up flow featuring PKCE S256, max_age=0, essential biometric acr claims, and strict nonce freshness, binding single-use approvals to specific borrower actions for 120 seconds.

Privacy is integrated at the transport layer via Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC. Using @anon-rpc/browser-harness, we run a hash-pinned Nox mixnet worker inside a sandboxed, null-origin iframe, routing all Viem contract reads through it with fail-closed security. During high-concurrency testing, public RPC rate limits occasionally broke the worker bootstrap; we engineered an ordered multi-RPC fallback mechanism that rotates the exit node's target provider while keeping all client traffic sealed inside the mixnet. On the server side, Next.js was aggressively caching chain reads across restarts; we enforced explicit no-store policies across all internal RPC fetch handlers to ensure instant state freshness.

The frontend is built with Next.js 14, Viem, Wagmi, Tailwind, and Framer Motion. It features an interactive hero ocean powered by a custom GLSL shader in React Three Fiber (complete with Gerstner wave displacement, Fresnel sky reflections, and cursor wake physics), an animated canvas visualizer demonstrating virtual liquidity allocations across strategies, an interactive risk simulator matching the contract's fixed-point math, and a live SwapVM bytecode inspector that disassembles order instructions and reveals register transformations before and after 0xf0 execution. The entire system is backed by a one-command local orchestration script, a Playwright browser automation suite validating the complete borrower and rescue lifecycle, and a deterministic background keeper agent scanning blocks for liquidatable positions.

projects.title: FrameFuzz
projects.description: FrameFuzz: AI-powered EIP-8141 admission testing across Ethereum mempools.
projects.project_description: FrameFuzz — Break the tx before the mempool does. Ethereum transactions can behave differently depending on which mempool evaluates them. With EIP-8141 frame transactions, programmable validation introduces new admission rules involving storage access, paymasters, staking, signatures, and execution context. A transaction that one mempool rejects may be perfectly acceptable to another. FrameFuzz is an agent-powered differential admission testing laboratory for EIP-8141.It helps Ethereum developers investigate these differences, understand the exact rule responsible, and preserve reproducible evidence. Developers can paste supported Solidity contracts, compile and analyze their source, investigate semantic mutations using four specialized AI agents, and prepare signed frame transactions for real admission testing. FrameFuzz compares two actual execution paths: Canonical ethrex: The public admission path. Alternative Skandha: An alternative mempool with its own admission and validation policies. Instead of simply reporting pass or fail, FrameFuzz captures RPC responses, validation rules, transaction identities, admission reports, frame receipts, and inclusion status. We demonstrated a real policy divergence using Uniswap v4. A staked EIP-8141 paymaster read StateView.getSlot0 during payment verification. Canonical ethrex rejected the transaction with StorageReadNonSender , while Skandha accepted the same signed transaction. The alternative path successfully included it, with a successful outer receipt and all three frame receipts succeeding. FrameFuzz also integrates Arkiv to publish, discover, verify, and reuse regression evidence, helping turn one-off findings into shared developer knowledge. The goal is to make EIP-8141 admission behavior observable, testable, and reproducible—before developers encounter unexpected transaction failures in production.
projects.how_its_made: FrameFuzz combines a React-based developer interface, a Node.js testing backend, Solidity compilation, AI-assisted mutation analysis, real EIP-8141 transaction construction, and two independent admission implementations. Frontend and developer experience We built a React and TypeScript interface using Material UI and Lucide icons. The Contract Playground supports Solidity source analysis, capability detection, admission-test preparation, real comparison results, evidence inspection, and regression workflows. The interface separates read-only investigation from explicitly authorized blockchain transactions. Solidity analysis and AI agents FrameFuzz compiles Solidity using solc, inspects compiler artifacts and ABI information, and identifies supported validator and paymaster patterns. Four independently invoked AI agents have specialized responsibilities: Contract Scout investigates contract behavior. Semantic Mutation proposes meaningful test variations. Feasibility Validator checks whether proposed experiments are executable. Evidence Critic challenges conclusions and distinguishes observed results from assumptions. We integrated OpenRouter for actual model calls, while deterministic tooling handles transaction encoding, signatures, RPC observations, and evidence classification. We deliberately avoid treating an AI prediction as a verified blockchain result. Ethereum Foundation / EIP-8141 We implemented a signed frame-transaction pipeline against the Ethereum Foundation workshop devnet, chain ID 1337, using the pinned EIP-8141 implementation. Canonical submissions use ethrex through eth_sendRawTransaction , while alternative submissions use the Skandha sidecar through eth_sendFrameTransaction . The comparison engine preserves signed transaction identity across paths, records actual rejection and admission responses, and queries receipts separately. It also handles shared-state nonce races, unsupported methods, duplicates, and simulation-only outcomes without misclassifying them as policy divergences. Uniswap v4 integration We built a Solidity paymaster whose PAYMENT verification path calls the genuine Uniswap v4 StateView.getSlot0(poolId) function. This introduces an external storage read during EIP-8141 validation. Using a deployed and staked paymaster, we captured canonical StorageReadNonSender rejection versus alternative Skandha acceptance for the same signed frame transaction. The live experiment produced Skandha admission ID 2065 , successful alternative-path inclusion, and three successful frame receipts. We also verified Solidity compiler settings, source and runtime bytecode binding, constructor parameters, and the deployed Uniswap integration contracts. This is a validation-time Uniswap integration, not a token swap or liquidity-management application. Arkiv integration We integrated Arkiv Rabdi, chain ID 7794095, for persistent, verifiable regression evidence. FrameFuzz can publish structured regression metadata through createEntity , query existing entities, verify content integrity, discover relevant findings, and import regression information without automatically signing a new transaction. Our implementation includes a confirmed real Arkiv publication and verified entity readback. Engineering and evidence The backend records signed transaction identities, raw JSON-RPC observations, admission classifications, simulation diagnostics, inclusion receipts, gas usage, source digests, and evidence provenance. A particularly important engineering challenge was preventing false positives: we encountered real endpoint-routing errors and shared-nonce races, corrected the adapters and comparison protocol, and preserved those observations rather than presenting them as policy failures. FrameFuzz demonstrates that AI-assisted smart-contract investigation can be connected to actual EIP-8141 admission behavior, with independently verifiable evidence rather than generated claims.

We also verified Solidity compiler settings, source and runtime bytecode binding, constructor parameters, and the deployed Uniswap integration contracts.

This is a validation-time Uniswap integration, not a token swap or liquidity-management application.

We integrated Arkiv Rabdi, chain ID 7794095, for persistent, verifiable regression evidence.

FrameFuzz can publish structured regression metadata through `createEntity`, query existing entities, verify content integrity, discover relevant findings, and import regression information without automatically signing a new transaction.

Our implementation includes a confirmed real Arkiv publication and verified entity readback.

**Engineering and evidence**

The backend records signed transaction identities, raw JSON-RPC observations, admission classifications, simulation diagnostics, inclusion receipts, gas usage, source digests, and evidence provenance.

A particularly important engineering challenge was preventing false positives: we encountered real endpoint-routing errors and shared-nonce races, corrected the adapters and comparison protocol, and preserved those observations rather than presenting them as policy failures.

FrameFuzz demonstrates that AI-assisted smart-contract investigation can be connected to actual EIP-8141 admission behavior, with independently verifiable evidence rather than generated claims.

projects.title: TrustOra
projects.description: Programmable trust infrastructure for secure work, AI evaluation and autonomous payments.
projects.project_description: TRUSTORA is a programmable trust infrastructure designed for the future of human and AI-driven work. It connects clients, freelancers and autonomous AI agents through secure agreements, milestone-based escrow, AI-powered deliverable evaluation and verifiable payment workflows. Using Arc, TRUSTORA enables USDC-based milestone escrow. 0G powers AI-assisted evaluation of submitted deliverables, while Hedera x402 enables policy-controlled payments between autonomous agents and services. ProofTrack connects project activity, evaluation results and transaction references into a traceable evidence history. Our goal is to make digital work more transparent and accountable by ensuring that agreements, deliverables, evaluations and payments are connected through verifiable workflows. AI provides recommendations, while important financial decisions remain under human control.
projects.how_its_made: TRUSTORA is built as a full-stack TypeScript application using Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS, with modular packages for blockchain integrations and backend services. Arc Testnet and Solidity smart contracts power USDC escrow workflows, including agreements, milestone funding, submission, release and dispute handling. The 0G Router API with GLM-5.3 provides AI-assisted deliverable evaluation. Hedera’s official x402 SDK powers HTTP 402 payment negotiation, policy-controlled HBAR transactions, facilitator settlement and Mirror Node verification. We use Ethers.js for EVM interactions, Prisma for application data management and ProofTrack for connecting evidence across workflows. The architecture separates AI recommendations from financial authorization: AI can evaluate work, but it cannot independently release escrow funds.

projects.title: Outvest
projects.description: Brands lock USDC upfront; Chainlink CRE verifies YouTube views; Arc pays creators automatically.
projects.project_description:
OutVest is escrowed pay for YouTube creators. A brand locks USDC in a smart contract first, and creators are paid automatically as their video views are verified. The problem. Creator payouts today are scattered and manual. View data lives in screenshots and private dashboards with no traceability. Payment depends on invoices and bank transfers that arrive late or never. And whoever holds the money and the data decides the number, so creators can’t check it and brands can’t verify what they’re billed. How it works. A brand creates a campaign on Arc and funds a vault with USDC. It sets a rate per 1,000 views, a cap per creator and an unlock schedule. The rules cannot be changed afterwards.
A creator signs in with email or Google through a Circle wallet. They pick a campaign, paste their YouTube link, and receive a unique code made from an onchain hash. They put that code in the video description to prove they own the video.
Clicking Verify emits an onchain event that triggers Chainlink CRE. CRE nodes each read the video from the YouTube API and must agree on the result. A signed report goes to our receiver contract, which only accepts reports from the Chainlink forwarder with the pinned workflow identity.
The vault binds the creator and pays 10% of their cap instantly. After that, earnings follow verified views, limited by a cap, a daily growth limit and a time-based unlock schedule. Snapshots, payouts and final settlement are scheduled CRE workflows.
Unused funds return to the brand. A deadman switch finalizes the campaign if the oracle goes silent. Chainlink CRE runs four workflows: bind (triggered by the onchain event), snapshot, final and payout (cron). Arc holds the escrow vaults, instant USDC settlement and the contracts that apply reports. CCIP lets a creator send a verifiable earnings receipt to Base Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack. Solidity 0.8.27 with Foundry (244 tests) for the contracts. TypeScript with the Chainlink CRE SDK 1.23 for the workflows. Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4 and viem for the app. Circle user-controlled wallets for sign-in and signing. Chainlink CCIP for cross-chain receipts. Everything runs on Arc Testnet, with USDC as the native stablecoin. How the pieces connect. Contracts: CampaignFactory deploys one CampaignVault per campaign. The vault holds the USDC and all the payout math. ReportReceiver is the only door for oracle data. It accepts calls only from the Chainlink forwarder and checks the workflow owner and ID against values the factory pinned once, with replay and timestamp checks on top.
Ownership proof: a creator calls requestBinding, and the vault stores keccak256(vault, wallet, videoId, nonce, chainId) as a challenge. They paste it into the video description. submitForVerification then emits VerifyRequested from the factory.
CRE: the wf-bind workflow has an EVM log trigger on that event. Each node fetches the video from the YouTube API (the key lives in CRE secrets) inside runInNodeMode. Results combine through ConsensusAggregationByFields: median for view counts, identical for the “challenge found” flag. The DON signs the report and the forwarder delivers it. Three more workflows (snapshot, final, payout) run on cron.
Payout rules: the vault credits views using the minimum seen across a rolling window of seven time buckets, so brief spikes don’t count, and limits growth per day. Pay then follows a time-based unlock schedule. 10% of the cap pays out in the same transaction as the bind.
App: the Circle SDK creates a challenge for each contract call and the user confirms with a PIN. The creator page reads vault state over a multicall to stay under RPC limits. What partner tech gave us. CRE meant no server of our own acting as oracle: consensus, secrets and signed delivery come built in, and the log trigger starts a check straight from a contract event. Circle wallets let creators sign in with email or Google, with no seed phrase or gas setup. CCIP gives a creator portable proof of earnings on Base Sepolia. Arc gives instant USDC settlement with USDC as gas. Hacky parts worth knowing. Chainlink deploy access isn’t enabled for us yet, so CRE can’t run live. The demo uses a relayer (bun run watch) that builds the same report envelopes and calls onReport from a wallet we set as the demo factory’s forwarder. It is a single-key oracle, not decentralized, and the real factory stays unlocked until CRE deploys.
CRE consensus has fixed fields, so view counts for up to 50 videos map to slots v0..v49 with -1 for missing. Workflows are also limited to 15 EVM reads per run, so shared code budgets reads across runs.
Free RPCs fought us. The public Arc endpoint rate-limits and free Alchemy allows eth_getLogs over only 10 blocks. The relayer scans in 10-block slices, catches up on missed requests through the Arcscan indexer, and batches reads into multicalls.
A mistake worth admitting: a shell quirk made my script create campaigns with default settings, so a few unfunded ones remain on-chain. The app hides campaigns that aren’t funded.

projects.title: Kizashi
projects.description: Bet on the whole curve, not just yes or no, and lock only the collateral you can actually lose.
projects.project_description: “Will Bumrah bowl over 145 tonight?” Yes or no. That’s the only question a prediction market lets you answer, and it’s the wrong question. You don’t think “over 145.” You think “probably 146 to 149, maybe a 150 if the pitch has pace, almost certainly not under 140.” That’s a curve. Every market today flattens it into one bit and throws away everything else you know. Kizashi doesn’t flatten it. You drag a curve over the outcomes you believe in, and you get paid according to how close reality lands to your shape. If you’d rather not think that hard, you can still take a plain yes/no bet on the same market. Market creators choose which format fits the question, and Kizashi tells them when they’ve picked the wrong one. The second thing that’s broken is money. On every venue, each position locks its full worst-case collateral, even when your positions partly cancel each other out. Hold a range bet and a hedge against it, and you pay twice for risk you don’t have. Kizashi prices every bet with one shared cost function and nets out the positions that offset, so you only lock what you can actually lose. Same money, more markets. Then there’s the engine. Tell it what you believe in plain English, hand it your rules as JSON or a PDF, and watch it go. “Will Bumrah bowl over 145 tonight?” Yes or no.

That’s the only question a prediction market lets you answer, and it’s the wrong question. You don’t think “over 145.” You think “probably 146 to 149, maybe a 150 if the pitch has pace, almost certainly not under 140.” That’s a curve. Every market today flattens it into one bit and throws away everything else you know.

Kizashi doesn’t flatten it. You drag a curve over the outcomes you believe in, and you get paid according to how close reality lands to your shape. If you’d rather not think that hard, you can still take a plain yes/no bet on the same market. Market creators choose which format fits the question, and Kizashi tells them when they’ve picked the wrong one.

projects.title: Cleverly Using Money
projects.description: Anonymous shared liquidity on 1inch Aqua: private LP notes, real yield, sandwich-resistant curves
projects.project_description: Cleverly Using Money lets LPs earn on their liquidity without revealing which position is theirs. Money in a privacy pool normally sits idle, and using it in DeFi means withdrawing and giving up anonymity. LPs deposit into a zero-knowledge vault and receive a private note. Every note is exactly one share of the vault, so all notes are identical and stay in one anonymity set as the share price moves. Withdrawing pays one share of every token the vault holds, to a new address with no ETH, while a relayer pays the gas for a 0.5% fee. No price oracle is needed: swap fees stay in the vault and raise what each note is worth. The vault is the Aqua maker, so one balance backs two SwapVM strategies at once: a concentrated WETH/USDC pair and a pegged USDC/USDT pair. Anonymous LPs can't watch a position and react to an attack, so the volatile pair uses SwapVM's decay instruction. In our fork demo, the same $1,000 sandwich makes the attacker $39.59 on the curve without decay and loses them $70.20 with it.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are Solidity, built with Foundry, and run against 1inch's deployed Aqua and SwapVM router on a Base fork with real WETH, USDC and USDT. Strategies are SwapVM programs composing concentrated liquidity, decay, a flat fee and PeggedSwap. The withdrawal circuit is Noir, proved with UltraHonk, using a generated Solidity verifier. The Merkle tree stores only its frontier onchain, and the client rebuilds paths from deposit events, so the RPC never learns which note is yours. The frontend is Next.js and viem, with noir_js and bb.js generating proofs on the user's device. 1inch's stack made the core design possible. Because Aqua strategies hold virtual balances, withdrawals never have to unwind a position, and one balance can earn in several strategies. The notable hacks: Mid-swap guard: vault balances are wrong between Aqua's pull and push, so a trader could buy a discounted share from inside a swap callback. We block deposits and withdrawals during a swap using SwapVM maker hooks with a transient counter, and the vault rejects any strategy that doesn't wire up the hooks. Contract size: Poseidon exceeded the 24KB limit under via_ir, so it's compiled separately and called through an interface. The generated verifier also has to compile outside via_ir. Sandwich demo: it runs real transactions inside Anvil snapshots and then rewinds, so both curves face the same attack from the same state.

projects.title: Unrelayed
projects.description: Relayer-free Tornado Cash withdrawals: a staked contract pays the gas via the ERC-8421 alt mempool
projects.project_description: If you want to withdraw from Tornado Cash privately, you withdraw to a brand-new wallet with no history. But that wallet has no ETH, so it can't pay the gas for its own withdrawal. Today the answer is a relayer: an off-chain server that sends the transaction for you and takes a fee. It works, but the relayer sees your IP address, can log you, can refuse to serve you, and can be shut down. The one part of the privacy flow that isn't trustless is the part that touches the network. Unrelayed removes the relayer. Instead of a server, a staked smart contract called TornadoExit sends every withdrawal itself. It uses EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool. A withdrawal is a single transaction whose sender is TornadoExit, and it has two frames: A verification frame, where TornadoExit decides whether to pay. It checks the Tornado zero-knowledge proof. It reads Tornado's state to confirm the Merkle root is known and the note isn't spent. It checks that the transaction has exactly the expected shape, that it names TornadoExit as the relayer, and that the fee covers the worst-case gas cost. Only if everything passes does it approve paying for the transaction. An execution frame, which calls the normal, unmodified Tornado withdraw, with TornadoExit as the relayer. Tornado pays the 0.1 ETH (minus the fee) to the fresh wallet and pays the fee back to TornadoExit. So TornadoExit gets its gas back plus a small margin on every withdrawal: about 0.0014 ETH per withdrawal in our tests. The user only generates the proof on their own machine and picks any fresh address. They don't sign anything, they don't need any ETH, and no server is involved. Why this only works on the alternative mempool: Gas: verifying the proof takes about 260k gas of validation, but the canonical EIP-8141 mempool allows 100k. Storage: the check has to read Tornado's storage, which the canonical mempool forbids. ERC-8421 allows both for a staked entity, so TornadoExit is staked in the ERC-8421 registry. Duplicates: the transaction's nonce key is the note's nullifier hash. Two attempts to spend the same note land in the same mempool slot, so the mempool itself refuses the duplicate. Spammers can't make TornadoExit pay for failed attempts or damage its reputation. What we showed on the public devnet, against the real Tornado 0.1 ETH pool, with real proofs: a withdrawal to a never-used wallet, with TornadoExit paying the gas; the same transaction rejected by the canonical mempool; an unstaked copy of the contract rejected; a duplicate spend refused; 15 kinds of malformed transactions (wrong relayer, low fee, bad proof, extra frames and so on) rejected before TornadoExit pays anything. The full suite runs end to end on the devnet, and every test with its transaction hashes is logged in the repo. Along the way we found a few things about the devnet: The predeployed pool uses its original 2019 verifier, so you need the matching v2.0 proving key. Its verifier uses a gas pattern the mempool bans, so we wrote a validation-safe copy of the same verifier for the check. The mempool won't let you read an empty account's code during validation. A recipient that reverts on receive could therefore make one withdrawal fail, but the nonce-key design limits that to one failed attempt per note. Limitations, honestly: The anonymity set on the devnet is tiny. You still need Tor or a private RPC to hide your IP from the node you submit to. Frame transactions aren't on mainnet yet. The design isn't specific to Tornado: it works for any Merkle-tree privacy pool that pays a relayer fee, and Railgun is the natural next target.
projects.how_its_made: The stack Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry. Frame opcodes: to use EIP-8141 from Solidity I used @forshtat/hegota-support. It wraps APPROVE, TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM and FRAMEDATACOPY as small Yul helper contracts that my contract deploys and calls. Its TypeScript codec handles the devnet's frame-transaction format. Client: TypeScript and viem. Prover: a separate Node 16 package using the original 2019 Tornado proving stack (circomlib, snarkjs, websnark's WASM Groth16 prover, fixed-merkle-tree). It's a straight port of tornado-cli's note, tree and proof logic. Network: everything runs on the public EIP-8141 devnet: ethrex as the execution client, and the ERC-8421 sidecar as the alternative mempool. How the pieces fit TornadoExit is the staked contract that sends every withdrawal. To withdraw, the client: rebuilds Tornado's Merkle tree from the pool's Deposit logs over plain RPC; quotes the fee (explained below); asks the Node 16 prover (a child process, JSON in and out) for a Groth16 proof with TornadoExit as the relayer; builds a two-frame transaction: a VERIFY frame calling TornadoExit.verifyWithdrawal(), and a SENDER frame calling Tornado's withdraw. Its nonce key is the note's nullifier hash; submits it with eth_sendFrameTransaction. In VERIFY, TornadoExit: introspects the transaction: frame count, frame 1's target, value, flags and gas limits, the exact withdraw calldata, and the nonce key; reads Tornado's root history and nullifier map; verifies the proof, then checks its own balance; only then calls APPROVE. What the alternative-mempool stack gave me Room for the check: a 1M-gas validation budget and read access to other contracts' storage once TornadoExit was staked in the ERC-8421 registry. The design isn't possible without those. Deduplication for free: keyed nonces mean two withdrawals of the same note collide in the mempool. Debugging help: the sidecar's admission reports and explorer showed exactly which rule rejected a transaction and for which entity, which saved hours. The hacky parts Probing the mempool from inside VERIFY. You can't log from a validation frame, so I wrote probe contracts that take an expected value as calldata and require(actual == expected). Admission means the value matched, rejection means it didn't. That's how I confirmed every TXPARAM and FRAMEPARAM value, the 256-bit nonce-key limit, stake-gated storage reads and SELFBALANCE, and how duplicates behave, all before writing the real contract. Finding the right proving key. Proofs from tornado-cli's key verified locally but failed against the devnet's Tornado Verifier. I decoded the verifying-key points from websnark's binary proving-key format (Montgomery form) and compared them with the PUSH32 constants in the deployed Verifier's bytecode. The pool turned out to be the original December 2019 deployment, which matches the tornado-core v2.0 key, not the later post-ceremony one. That key also only proves correctly with the websnark commit v2.0 itself used, so the prover pins that commit and checks the circuit files by sha256. A validation-safe copy of Tornado's verifier. The deployed Verifier calls the pairing precompiles with staticcall(sub(gas, 2000), …). The mempool bans GAS unless it's immediately followed by a CALL, so I wrote a copy with the same verifying key and the same input parsing that uses staticcall(gas(), …). To be sure it's really the same: a script disassembles the deployed bytecode and checks that all 28 key constants appear, in order; another fails the build if any GAS opcode isn't directly followed by a CALL; I compared the two verifiers on real and deliberately broken proofs, and they agree in every case. Fee quoting before the proof exists. The fee is one of the proof's public inputs, but the fee depends on the transaction's maximum gas cost, which depends on the calldata, which includes the proof. I break the loop by simulating the same transaction shape with every unknown calldata byte non-zero. That gives an upper bound on the cost; I add 10% and prove with that fee. Gas minimums from binary search. For a withdrawal that creates a new account and a new storage slot, ethrex reports about 307k gas used but fails with any limit below about 482k. I found the real minimum by binary-searching the frame's gas limit with ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction. TornadoExit refuses any transaction that gives the withdrawal frame less than that minimum plus a margin, so nobody can make it pay for an out-of-gas revert. Testing There are no mocks: every test runs against the live devnet with real deposits and real proofs. The end-to-end suite runs 77 checks covering the happy path, every malformed-transaction case, duplicate spends, the canonical-mempool and unstaked rejections, and fee accounting. It passes repeatedly.

Today the answer is a relayer: an off-chain server that sends the transaction for you and takes a fee. It works, but the relayer sees your IP address, can log you, can refuse to serve you, and can be shut down. The one part of the privacy flow that isn't trustless is the part that touches the network.

Unrelayed removes the relayer. Instead of a server, a staked smart contract called TornadoExit sends every withdrawal itself. It uses EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool. A withdrawal is a single transaction whose sender is TornadoExit, and it has two frames:

1. A verification frame, where TornadoExit decides whether to pay. It checks the Tornado zero-knowledge proof. It reads Tornado's state to confirm the Merkle root is known and the note isn't spent. It checks that the transaction has exactly the expected shape, that it names TornadoExit as the relayer, and that the fee covers the worst-case gas cost. 2. An execution frame, which calls the normal, unmodified Tornado withdraw, with TornadoExit as the relayer. Tornado pays the 0.1 ETH (minus the fee) to the fresh wallet and pays the fee back to TornadoExit. So TornadoExit gets its gas back plus a small margin on every withdrawal: about 0.0014 ETH per withdrawal in our tests.

The user only generates the proof on their own machine and picks any fresh address. They don't sign anything, they don't need any ETH, and no server is involved.

Why this only works on the alternative mempool:
- Gas: verifying the proof takes about 260k gas of validation, but the canonical EIP-8141 mempool allows 100k.
- Storage: the check has to read Tornado's storage, which the canonical mempool forbids. ERC-8421 allows both for a staked entity, so TornadoExit is staked in the ERC-8421 registry.
- Duplicates: the transaction's nonce key is the note's nullifier hash. Two attempts to spend the same note land in the same mempool slot, so the mempool itself refuses the duplicate. Spammers can't make TornadoExit pay for failed attempts or damage its reputation.

What we showed on the public devnet, against the real Tornado 0.1 ETH pool, with real proofs:
- a withdrawal to a never-used wallet, with TornadoExit paying the gas;
- the same transaction rejected by the canonical mempool;
- an unstaked copy of the contract rejected;
- a duplicate spend refused;
- 15 kinds of malformed transactions (wrong relayer, low fee, bad proof, extra frames and so on) rejected before TornadoExit pays anything.

The full suite runs end to end on the devnet, and every test with its transaction hashes is logged in the repo.

Along the way we found a few things about the devnet:
- The predeployed pool uses its original 2019 verifier, so you need the matching v2.0 proving key.
- Its verifier uses a gas pattern the mempool bans, so we wrote a validation-safe copy of the same verifier for the check.
- The mempool won't let you read an empty account's code during validation. A recipient that reverts on receive could therefore make one withdrawal fail, but the nonce-key design limits that to one failed attempt per note.

Limitations, honestly:
- The anonymity set on the devnet is tiny.
- You still need Tor or a private RPC to hide your IP from the node you submit to.
- Frame transactions aren't on mainnet yet.

The design isn't specific to Tornado: it works for any Merkle-tree privacy pool that pays a relayer fee, and Railgun is the natural next target.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The stack

- Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry.
- Frame opcodes: to use EIP-8141 from Solidity I used @forshtat/hegota-support. It wraps APPROVE, TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM and FRAMEDATACOPY as small Yul helper contracts that my contract deploys and calls. Its TypeScript codec handles the devnet's frame-transaction format.
- Client: TypeScript and viem.
- Prover: a separate Node 16 package using the original 2019 Tornado proving stack (circomlib, snarkjs, websnark's WASM Groth16 prover, fixed-merkle-tree). It's a straight port of tornado-cli's note, tree and proof logic.
- Network: everything runs on the public EIP-8141 devnet: ethrex as the execution client, and the ERC-8421 sidecar as the alternative mempool.

How the pieces fit

TornadoExit is the staked contract that sends every withdrawal. To withdraw, the client:

1. rebuilds Tornado's Merkle tree from the pool's Deposit logs over plain RPC;
2. quotes the fee (explained below);
3. asks the Node 16 prover (a child process, JSON in and out) for a Groth16 proof with TornadoExit as the relayer;
4. builds a two-frame transaction: a VERIFY frame calling TornadoExit.verifyWithdrawal(), and a SENDER frame calling Tornado's withdraw. Its nonce key is the note's nullifier hash;
5. submits it with eth_sendFrameTransaction.

In VERIFY, TornadoExit:

- introspects the transaction: frame count, frame 1's target, value, flags and gas limits, the exact withdraw calldata, and the nonce key;
- reads Tornado's root history and nullifier map;
- verifies the proof, then checks its own balance;
- only then calls APPROVE.

What the alternative-mempool stack gave me

- Room for the check: a 1M-gas validation budget and read access to other contracts' storage once TornadoExit was staked in the ERC-8421 registry. The design isn't possible without those.
- Deduplication for free: keyed nonces mean two withdrawals of the same note collide in the mempool.
- Debugging help: the sidecar's admission reports and explorer showed exactly which rule rejected a transaction and for which entity, which saved hours.

The hacky parts

- Probing the mempool from inside VERIFY. You can't log from a validation frame, so I wrote probe contracts that take an expected value as calldata and require(actual == expected). Admission means the value matched, rejection means it didn't. That's how I confirmed every TXPARAM and FRAMEPARAM value, the 256-bit nonce-key limit, stake-gated storage reads and SELFBALANCE, and how duplicates behave, all before writing the real contract.
- Finding the right proving key. Proofs from tornado-cli's key verified locally but failed against the devnet's Tornado Verifier. I decoded the verifying-key points from websnark's binary proving-key format (Montgomery form) and compared them with the PUSH32 constants in the deployed Verifier's bytecode. The pool turned out to be the original December 2019 deployment, which matches the tornado-core v2.0 key, not the later post-ceremony one. That key also only proves correctly with the websnark commit v2.0 itself used, so the prover pins that commit and checks the circuit files by sha256.
- A validation-safe copy of Tornado's verifier. The deployed Verifier calls the pairing precompiles with staticcall(sub(gas, 2000), …). The mempool bans GAS unless it's immediately followed by a CALL, so I wrote a copy with the same verifying key and the same input parsing that uses staticcall(gas(), …). To be sure it's really the same:
  - a script disassembles the deployed bytecode and checks that all 28 key constants appear, in order;
  - another fails the build if any GAS opcode isn't directly followed by a CALL;
  - I compared the two verifiers on real and deliberately broken proofs, and they agree in every case.
- Fee quoting before the proof exists. The fee is one of the proof's public inputs, but the fee depends on the transaction's maximum gas cost, which depends on the calldata, which includes the proof. I break the loop by simulating the same transaction shape with every unknown calldata byte non-zero. That gives an upper bound on the cost; I add 10% and prove with that fee.
- Gas minimums from binary search. For a withdrawal that creates a new account and a new storage slot, ethrex reports about 307k gas used but fails with any limit below about 482k. I found the real minimum by binary-searching the frame's gas limit with ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction. TornadoExit refuses any transaction that gives the withdrawal frame less than that minimum plus a margin, so nobody can make it pay for an out-of-gas revert.

Testing

There are no mocks: every test runs against the live devnet with real deposits and real proofs. The end-to-end suite runs 77 checks covering the happy path, every malformed-transaction case, duplicate spends, the canonical-mempool and unstaked rejections, and fee accounting. It passes repeatedly.
