projects.title: CrossChain Read
projects.description: Read crosschain states using Chainlink CCIP, similar to LZread on LayerZero
projects.project_description: LayerZero lzRead lets a contract on one chain request data from another chain's state and get the result back on the origin chain. Developers use it to query balances, prices or any view function across chains without deploying custom messaging logic for each read. ccip-read brings the same pull-based read pattern to Chainlink CCIP. An app on a source chain asks for the result of a view call on a target chain, and the result comes back through CCIP.
projects.how_its_made:
How it works
Request (source chain): A consumer contract calls the read client with a target chain selector, a target contract address and ABI-encoded calldata for a view function. The client sends this request to the target chain as a CCIP message.
Execute (target chain): A reader contract on the target chain receives the CCIP message, staticcalls the target contract and captures the return data.
Respond (target → source): The reader sends the result back to the source chain in a second CCIP message.
Deliver (source chain): The read client matches the response to the original request ID and runs the consumer's callback with the result.

projects.title: Pocket Pay
projects.description: A simple way for businesses and freelancers to accept crypto payments and track transactions.
projects.project_description: Pocket Pay is a payment management platform for businesses and freelancers. It helps users create invoices, pay their team, track payment status, and follow up on outstanding payments from one place. Built around USDT payments on Whitechain, Pocket Pay aims to make payment activity easier to verify and manage.
projects.how_its_made: Pocket Pay is being built as a payment gate for businesses and freelancers: one place to create invoices, pay team members, track what has been paid, and follow up on outstanding payments. The mobile app is built with Flutter; it connects to a FastAPI backend that stores merchant and payment data in Supabase. For the on-chain payment flow, we use Whitechain Sepolia, USDT, Solidity, and OpenZeppelin. The backend uses Web3.py and Whitechain’s RPC to inspect a transaction receipt and verify that the payment event matches the expected payment ID, merchant wallet, and amount. Confirmed payments can trigger an HMAC-signed webhook, with retries, for merchant integrations. One particularly hands-on part was tying a normal checkout record to an on-chain event: the backend hashes the payment ID and compares it with the ID emitted by the contract, then checks the receipt and payment details before marking the payment confirmed. This prototype demonstrates checkout and payment tracking. Invoice creation and team payouts are part of the product’s core direction, but those workflows still need implementation.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Pocket Pay is being built as a payment gate for businesses and freelancers: one place to create invoices, pay team members, track what has been paid, and follow up on outstanding payments. The mobile app is built with Flutter; it connects to a FastAPI backend that stores merchant and payment data in Supabase. For the on-chain payment flow, we use Whitechain Sepolia, USDT, Solidity, and OpenZeppelin. projects.title: CAP-IT-LESS
projects.description: Zero Capital RFQ infrastructure connecting quantitative strategies to DeFi liquidity.
projects.project_description: CAP-IT-LESS is zero capital infrastructure for independent quantitative traders and market makers to execute strategies against DeFi liquidity without building an entire trading and settlement stack from scratch. It combines signed RFQ orders with Uniswap v4 flash accounting to enable atomic execution across liquidity pools, while a custom dynamic-fee hook and Chainlink CRE workflow bring external market data into onchain risk and execution policies. Strategy operators define their pricing and risk parameters offchain, sign quotes, and let the executor validate and settle trades onchain. The goal is to make sophisticated market-making infrastructure more accessible by separating strategy ownership from liquidity access and execution infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made: CAP-IT-LESS combines Solidity smart contracts, Uniswap v4, and Chainlink CRE with an offchain TypeScript maker engine. The maker engine fetches market data, calculates hedge costs and executable quotes, constructs RFQ orders, and signs them using EIP-712. Onchain, our RFQ executor verifies signatures and order constraints before routing trades through a custom Uniswap v4 adapter. We leverage the PoolManager's unlock-callback architecture and flash accounting to manage token deltas and atomically settle pool operations. A custom v4 hook implements dynamic fee logic, while Chainlink CRE connects external data to onchain risk and fee policies. The key architectural choice is separating flexible offchain quantitative pricing from deterministic onchain execution and risk enforcement.

projects.title: CashETH
projects.description: Instant credit for AI agents: borrow against unpaid invoices, repay when the customer pays
projects.project_description: CashETH gives AI agents working capital. When an agent sells work to another agent on credit, it holds an unpaid invoice but no cash to pay for the APIs, data and compute it needs to deliver. CashETH lets that agent borrow USDC against the invoice, spend it on paid APIs under strict limits, and repay automatically when the customer pays. Lenders earn yield on idle capital and are always paid back first. How it works, step by step: A seller agent uploads an invoice through our MCP server. The file's hash becomes part of the receivable, so the terms cannot be changed later. The buyer agent confirms it owes the money by signing an EIP-712 message. The payee in that message is our repayment contract, not the seller, so the buyer's payment can never skip the lenders. CashETH checks both agents' identity levels (KYA), rejects duplicates and self-dealing, and computes a deterministic credit score from the seller's on-chain repayment record. The receivable is registered on Hedera as "Confirmed", an NFT is minted for it, and every step is written to a Hedera Consensus Service audit topic. Lenders keep USDC in their own wallets and publish strategies that say which risk levels they fund (low, medium or high) and, optionally, which sellers. One transaction funds the receivable: our custom instruction checks the receivable on-chain during every fill and prices the loan from the seller's score (6% to 14% APR). No lender, server or solver can charge a different rate. Worker agents spend the credit on paid APIs using x402. Each worker pays from a 2-of-2 wallet that only moves money when our policy co-signer agrees the payment matches an approved budget, merchant and amount. Overspending or paying an unknown merchant is refused by both our engine and the contract. When the buyer pays, the repayment contract pays lenders their principal plus interest first and sends the rest to the seller. What we built: Smart contracts on Hedera testnet: an agent identity registry, a receivable registry, a credit facility with budgets and spend reservations, a repayment router, and scheduled overdue and default checks using the Hedera Schedule Service. A redeployed 1inch Aqua registry and a modified SwapVM router with a new opcode, ReceivableCredit, that only fills against confirmed receivables. The same lender balance also earns trading fees in a constant-product strategy while it waits, so lenders see what lending adds on top of plain yield farming. An MCP server with 24 tools and OAuth 2.1 sign-in, where agents prove their identity with a signed token checked against the on-chain registry. Agents that drive the whole flow: scripted agents, a local LLM seller agent, and Claude Code acting as the seller through MCP, with a local wallet so the buyer signs its own transactions. Real x402 merchants, including paid price-feed, web-scrape and summary APIs on Google Cloud Run, settled in USDC on Hedera. A public dashboard and admin console showing every agent, loan, payment and lender return, each linked to its HashScan transaction. Why it matters: invoice finance is a multi-trillion-dollar market for human businesses, yet agents that sell to each other have no one to lend to them. CashETH makes agent-to-agent commerce work on credit, with every rule enforced on-chain and every transaction verifiable on HashScan.

projects.title: EnsWhite
projects.description: Hire AI personnel and get them an ENS name and using USDT on Whitechain without gas costs.
projects.project_description:
With EnsWhite, a single founder can establish a company and employ Artificial Intelligence departments as personnel. Marketing, Support, and Finance all have on-chain identities which allow them to receive funds and budget for buying tasks from independent vendors a step at a time, including, for instance, writing advertisement texts, creating banners, and translating FAQs for customers. The founder has no direct relation to cryptocurrencies since they perform all transactions in rupees, assign tasks to the departments, authorize expenditures, and finally receive the results, rupees receipts, and CSV files. On the level of infrastructure, all processes are performed on Whitechain where every transaction occurs with USDT payments. No WBT is sent to the department wallets but EIP-3009 approval is final, and then the relayer makes the transfer. The contract of the company allows monitoring expenditures made by departments and restricting vendors allowed to participate in selling goods to the departments.
Employment operates on ENSv2. Each company receives its unique subdomain (i.e., acme.enswhite.eth), which comes with its own registry, while each employee gets a non-transferable, ephemeral name (i.e., marketing.acme.enswhite.eth) bound to its own resolver containing its Whitechain wallet, weekly budget, per-call limit, and list of authorized vendors. Finance is allowed to modify the budget only via a key-scoped ENS. Termination of an employee or expiration of a contract leads to freezing any future payments. The reason for going on-chain is that AI employees cannot have bank accounts or corporate banks, and paying independent vendors only a few paise per task is not possible due to transaction costs and delays in settlements.
projects.how_its_made:
The technology behind EnsWhite comprises three levels: Node.js backend, Solidity smart contracts operated from Whitechain Sepolia and ENSv2 recording information about the employees of the organization and their expenditure. Software: Node.js 22, Express 5, ethers v6 and SQLite inbuilt in Node.js in the backend; Solidity and Foundry platform for creating contracts and conducting testing; HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the developer's workspace, vendor dashboards and testproof page; Razorpay in a simulation rupee top-up test; OpenAI model in preparing department planning documents.
Here is how everything is interrelated; the founder pays in rupees. Our system verifies the HMAC signature of the Razorpay webhook. The payment is confirmed through the Razorpay API, after which an EIP-712 attestation is signed. This attestation is verified by the EnsWhiteCompany contract before credits are issued in the form of USDT tokens. The payment ID can be used only once. The finance department is responsible for sending dollars to the separate wallets assigned to different departments. Once the respective department purchases a task, the vendor sends out an HTTP 402 error response. Our system checks the ENS to verify the employee status, the limit set, and the vendor’s wallet address. The department signs the EIP-3009 authorization after which the relayer submits it, pays the WBT charges, and enforces the limit and the whitelist of the vendors, with the issuance of receipts. Each vendor is separate with its own payment addresses and completes the job only once the payment is confirmed.
How partner tech helped: Whitechain: Using the OP stack meant Foundry and ethers worked unchanged. Contracts can be verified on Blockscout with a single command. Its USDT supports EIP-3009, meaning Department wallets hold zero WBT. Low gas made per task payments (a few cents) possible. ENSv2: Using hierarchical registries meant that every company could own its own namespace (acme.enswhite.eth) and name expiry meant termination. With Enhanced Access Control, we gave the Finance team the ability to edit a single budget record. Using multichain address records (coinType 2147485522 for chain 1874) we tied a user name to their Whitechain Wallet. Universal Resolver gave us all the information in one go.
Hacky parts mentioning: Departments sign receiveWithAuthorization of transferWithAuthorization. EIP-3009 lets only the named recipient execute that kind of authorization so only our contract can spend a departments signature and it checks the budget first. Each authorizations nonce is derived from the vendor. Request ID and the contract recomputes it so a signed payment can't be redirected to a different vendor. ENS lives on Sepolia and payments on Whitechain and neither chain can read the other. Our backend bridges them with a lived signed policy that includes the employees ENS expiry so Whitechain refuses payments, from an employee whose contract has ended. Every employee gets its ENS resolver because resolver roles apply to every name on a resolver. Without that Finances budget role would cover the company. Every signed transaction is saved before its broadcast. A crash or restart never double-pays a vendor. The 1% fee can be swapped to WBT on YetiTrade by a gas watcher so the relayer can fund its own gas.

projects.title: Atmos RPC
projects.description: Private, verified, anonymous Ethereum RPC over Nym, fast enough to be the default
projects.project_description: Every RPC call a wallet makes shows the provider the user's IP address and the accounts they look up, and the wallet trusts whatever comes back. anon-rpc, the Ethereum Foundation standard, hides the IP by sending a wallet's calls through an anonymity network such as Nym, from a sandboxed, hash-pinned worker. On its own, that path is slow when a page loads, can trust a route that is already dead, and still believes the provider and the network exit. Atmos RPC is a client layer on top of anon-rpc that makes the anonymous path faster, verified and more private: Faster. When a page loads, a burst of 10 reads finishes 5.5–6.6× faster than with stock anon-rpc (2.7–3.6 s against 14.7–22.0 s), and the slowest calls are 3–5× faster. A typical single call is 1.2–1.7× faster. Verified. A beacon light client gives a verified head, and balances, nonces, code, storage, eth_call results and receipts are checked against it. A lying provider or exit can cause a failure, never a wrong answer. Private. The provider sees a Nym exit, not your IP, and routes rotate about every 10 minutes. An optional constant-rate schedule hides when the wallet is busy. Easy to use. An SDK gives apps a standard EIP-1193 provider, and a one-line install gives MetaMask a plain local RPC URL. The weak spot: the first answer takes 17–71 s, against 16–33 s for stock anon-rpc. Atmos runs on Sepolia only for now, and it is unaudited research code.
projects.how_its_made: We built Atmos in JavaScript in four parts, all around Nym's anon-rpc worker, which we never modify. Routing client. We choose routes from Nym's public performance data and trust a route only after a probe call succeeds through it. A warm standby route takes over on failure. Calls to a provider leave as JSON-RPC batches. A pinned specifier means booting makes no clear-net RPC calls. Verifier. A beacon light client checks sync-committee BLS signatures with noble, covering the Electra and Gloas layouts, and gets a verified head from the Lodestar beacon API. Balances, nonces, code and storage are checked with eth_getProof against its state root, using ethereumjs's MPT. eth_call runs in a local ethereumjs EVM on proven state. Receipts are checked by rebuilding the receipts trie, and eth_blockNumber is answered from the verified head in 0 ms. estimateGas and a block's transaction list are partly proven. Every other method passes through unchecked and is counted. SDK and host. createAtmos() returns an EIP-1193 provider for the browser and Node. The local host serves it to MetaMask at http://127.0.0.1:8545/11155111, using publicnode and tenderly as keyless RPCs. Node harness. Our fork of anon-rpc's Node harness runs the Nym worker in a V8 isolate with isolated-vm, so no browser is needed. Partner technologies: Nym provides the mixnet, so the provider sees a Nym exit instead of the user. anon-rpc provides the sandboxed, hash-pinned worker, so Atmos never handles the user's network identity itself. The hacky parts: The 10 MB Nym wasm worker runs under isolated-vm with a synchronous WebAssembly shim, because async instantiate never resolves there. A Blob-send bug in our WebSocket bridge silently broke the Nym IPR handshakes. We found it by comparing frames against a Chromium run. An audit of the harness fork found and fixed a redirect allowlist bypass, a WebSocket flood, lost frames, and a getRandomValues partial-fill weakness inherited from upstream (reported privately to the author). In the verifier, the audit fixed trust in provider-supplied block hashes, and a wrong blob fee and BLOCKHASH in the EVM. An experimental EIP-7928 mode keeps proven accounts current from verified per-block access lists, so repeat reads name nothing to a provider. It works only while it keeps pace with the chain, which it did in some sessions and not others.

projects.title: Attestra
projects.description: Hire AI agents, pay only when the work is verified: one escrow contract per job on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Attestra is a marketplace where AI agents get paid only after their work passes the client's checks. AI agents already handle real money, but today buyers pay first and hope. If the work is bad, the money is gone, and there is no neutral way to decide whether a job was done. Attestra replaces trust with verification: Benchmarked listing: an agent can't just sign up. The builder connects a GitHub repo, we run code and security checks plus an AI code review, and only agents scoring 80/100 or more are listed. Every agent has a public report: score, each check, price and track record. Your words become the test: the client describes the job in plain English. That text is turned into a requirements checklist, which is what the delivered work is judged against. One contract per job: when a quote is accepted, a designer service analyses the job and the agent (complexity, risk, trust) and deploys a dedicated escrow contract on Hedera with the price, deadline, pass mark, checks and sub-agent limits written into it. The app shows the designed terms next to what is actually stored on-chain, so nobody can change the deal. Locked funds: the client funds the contract from MetaMask. The money goes neither to the platform nor to the agent; it stays locked until verification gives a result, or the deadline passes and the client takes it back. Automatic verification and settlement: when the agent submits, every checklist item is checked with evidence. PASS releases the payment from the contract right away; FAIL refunds the client. Infrastructure errors never produce a FAIL: the job pauses and retries. 3. One contract per job: when a quote is accepted, a designer service analyses the job and the agent (complexity, risk, trust) and deploys a dedicated escrow contract on Hedera with the price, deadline, pass mark, checks and sub-agent limits written into it. projects.title: OpenLabel
projects.description: Crowdfunded food testing. Verify the label before you eat it.
projects.project_description: What if the label on your food isn’t true? Crowdfund a lab test for anything you eat. The lab checks label accuracy, contaminants and adulteration, and you get a nutrition grade, so you can make an informed choice about what to buy and eat. Results are proven with zero-knowledge proofs, the tester stays anonymous, and every result, good or bad, stays on-chain as a permanent record.
projects.how_its_made: OpenLabel has four parts: a React web app, a Python API, a Rust zero-knowledge prover, and Solidity contracts on Base. Frontend: React 19 + Vite + TypeScript, with viem for all chain access. Users sign in with Google or email (Privy), MetaMask or WalletConnect. FastAPI on Postgres serves products and test requests, and existing results from public food-testing sites are imported so the catalogue is useful from day one. The app deploys to Render as one service: FastAPI serves the built frontend. Proving lab reports: the tester uploads the lab's PDF. The prover reads the report link from the QR code printed on the PDF and fetches the lab's own copy from the lab's server under TLSNotary, which signs a record of what the lab's server returned. It then requires the upload to match that copy byte for byte. Inside an SP1 zkVM, a custom Rust PDF parser blanks out the customer's name and address and extracts the test results. The result is a Groth16 proof that shows three things together: the report came from the lab, it wasn't altered, and only the test values are made public. Proving runs on a GPU server, keeps going in the background while the user browses, and the tester then submits it on-chain with one click. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry): EurekhaReportRegistry checks the proof, the notary's signature and the lab's domain. TestFund runs one pool per request: anyone contributes toward the lab cost; anyone can take the job by staking $110; a valid proof pays the tester the stake plus the pool, and any shortfall counts as the tester's own contribution; a tester who misses the 30-day deadline loses the stake to the pool, and the job reopens; the admin can later share revenue (e.g. affiliate income) among contributors in proportion to what each put in. The proven results are decoded straight from the chain and shown on the product page, so anyone can check them without trusting our server.

projects.title: Leash
projects.description: Leash is a payment guard for agents that evaluates merchants using a shared merchant registry.
projects.project_description: AI agents can now pay for APIs on their own with x402: the server answers "402 Payment Required", the agent signs, and the data comes back. There's no checkout and no human. That also means an agent can pay a fake shop that copies a real one's name, or pay for an empty response. Every agent learns this alone, after it has already paid. Leash is a payment guard and a shared merchant registry for these agents. Before an agent signs any x402 payment, Leash gives one of three verdicts: ALLOW (pay now), ESCALATE (ask the owner) or DENY (never pay). It checks three things: Who the merchant claims to be. Each merchant declares its payment policy in its own ENSv2 name: the account to pay, max price, domains and the fields every response must carry. A 402 that asks for a different account, or a higher price, is denied. What other agents have proven about this merchant. After each payment, the guard checks the response against the merchant's declared fields and files a signed good or bad report to Arkiv. Every report is re-checked against its real payment on Hedera before it counts. When agents with different funding sources each prove a merchant bad, it is blocked for everyone. One agent's bad experience protects every other agent. The owner's limits: budgets, per-merchant caps, a smaller budget for new merchants, and owner approval above a set amount. No verdict is permanent. Blocks and evidence expire, and a merchant can file a rebuttal, pass a paid retest and earn trust back through probation. Every decision, report and approval is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, as a tamper-evident audit trail. What you can try today: A live demo with real agents and real merchants An owner console for approvals A public explorer showing each merchant's health from verified evidence A Partner tracks page showing every on-chain write and query live A "Create merchant" flow where any merchant with an ENSv2 name proves control of it, publishes its policy and lists itself Developers can add Leash with one SDK call, or through an MCP server so an LLM agent like Claude pays through Leash. Everything runs on public testnets: Hedera testnet USDC, Arkiv's Rabdi testnet and ENSv2 on Sepolia. Nothing is mocked.
projects.how_its_made: Leash is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces) with five parts: packages/core: a pure policy engine. It rebuilds each merchant's standing from evidence: new, established, blocked or probation. It then computes a five-factor risk score and returns the verdict. packages/guard: hooks into the x402 client's onBeforePaymentCreation and onAfterPaymentCreation. It decides before the agent signs, then checks delivery and files reports after. packages/mcp: an MCP server with 7 tools. apps/merchant: five real x402 merchants built on Hono, @x402/hono and @x402/hedera, each deployed on Vercel. Two are honest, one delivers junk, one impersonates another, and one has no identity. apps/dashboard: a Next.js 16 site with the live demo, owner console, explorer, Partner tracks, docs and the Create merchant flow. Hedera: Payments use the x402 exact scheme on Hedera testnet, settling in USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) through the Blocky402 facilitator. The facilitator pays the fees, so $0.005 payments are practical. Mirror Node makes reports trustworthy. The guard re-checks every report's transaction there: payer, payee, amount and consensus time. It verifies the agent's signature against the account's key, and groups wallets by who funded them, so one owner's many wallets count as one voice. The Hiero SDK writes every decision to an HCS topic, which holds over 700 messages. Arkiv: It holds the shared registry as four entity types: reports, probes, rebuttals and merchant listings. All are written with @arkiv-network/sdk and owned by the wallet that wrote them. Expiry is our forgiveness model: evidence lives 60 days in production. Indexed attributes let the guard query a merchant's reports newest-first before every payment, and never fetch future-dated rows. Probes and listings are trusted only when the expected wallet created them, so a flood of fake rows can't bury real ones. Reads need no key, so the public explorer works for anyone. ENSv2 on Sepolia: Each merchant's name is registered through ENS's ETHRegistrar, with its own Permissioned Resolver deployed through VerifiableFactory. The payment policy lives in leash.* text records, read through the Universal Resolver. Enhanced Access Control grants a wallet the right to edit only the leash.rebuttal record. Self-listing requires proving the text role on your own resolver. Each merchant's 402 names its ENS name in the x402 extra field, so the agent can find the policy. Notable hacks: A disclosed "live policy profile" where 1 policy day equals 18 real seconds, so blocks, probation and expiry play out inside a short live demo, on real testnets. We checked ENSv2 function selectors against live bytecode, because the contracts on GitHub main differ from the ones deployed on Sepolia. 65-byte EVM signatures don't fit Arkiv's 128-byte string limit, so they go in a bytes field. A SQLite outbox keeps Arkiv and HCS writes safe through outages, and the guard escalates rather than guesses when a network is down. We ran 15 live failure tests (F1 to F15), including spoofed accounts, forged and flooded Arkiv rows, replays and outages. They exposed real bugs that we fixed, such as a parallel double payment.

projects.title: Kin
projects.description: Paid in stablecoins abroad? Pay your family’s bills back home, only to verified payees.
projects.project_description: Millions of people work abroad and get paid in stablecoins. But their family's rent, university fees and expenses are owed back home, in local money, to bank accounts. Today they cash out, wire money, and hope the account details they were sent are real. With Kin, the sender funds a USDT vault on Whitechain once and sets spending caps. After that, an AI agent checks each bill that arrives, and the sender approves it with one free signature. A licensed payout provider pays the bill in local currency, and only then does the vault release the USDT to them. Three rules are enforced onchain, not by our servers: Money only goes to verified payees. Each payee (like university.gharfam.eth) is an ENSv2 name whose payout account only the provider's verifier can write. A "we changed our bank account, pay here" message can't redirect any money, and the family can't change the account either. Only real bills get paid. Bills are posted to a public inbox on Arkiv and signed by the payee's registered biller wallet. Bills from anyone else are ignored, and bills past their due date can't be paid. Spending stays inside the sender's limits. The vault enforces per-bill and per-period caps. If a payout fails, the money is refunded. If the provider does nothing for a day, anyone can return the money to the sender. If the sender goes silent, a nominee they chose can take over. Businesses can accept Kin on their own website with one script tag. The customer sees an invoice card, and the business gets a live view of every bill, payout, refund and receipt. Kin also installs on a phone as an app and signs with the MetaMask mobile app. The same rails power Pay with Direct: send money from your vault to a friend's card or bank with a claim link, or to an Indian UPI ID.
projects.how_its_made: Kin's money lives in a Solidity vault on Whitechain Sepolia, . The vault holds USDT and runs the whole payment lifecycle. When the agent calls pay, the vault locks a biller-signed bill's amount for the payout provider, but only if the agent has a grant and the payee's caps allow it. markPaid releases the USDT to the provider after the fiat payout, refund returns it if the payout fails, and reclaim lets anyone return it after a day of provider silence. Deposits are gasless: the sender signs an EIP-3009 ReceiveWithAuthorization, and our relayer calls depositWithAuthorization and pays the WBT gas. Payees live in ENSv2 on Sepolia. Each payee is a subname under the family's name, with ghar.payoutRef and ghar.biller text records on an ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver. We use the resolver's role bitmap so only the provider's verifier can write those records, which means a phishing message can't change where money goes. The agent re-checks ENS right before every payout. Bills live on @Arkiv. Each bill is an entity signed with EIP-712 and posted from the biller's own wallet, so the agent can query createdBy(biller), filtered by payee and due date, and fake bills from other wallets never reach it. Bills expire on Arkiv a week after they're due. Payout receipts are read-only Arkiv entities linking the bill, the Whitechain settlement and the payout order, and the chat history is stored on Arkiv, encrypted. We have no traditional database. Two TypeScript services connect these. The agent reads open bills, verifies them against ENS and the biller's signature, and calls pay. The settler runs the provider's payout, settles on the vault and writes the receipt. A Groq-powered chat assistant reads the vault, ENS and Arkiv and shows each payable bill as a card the sender approves with one wallet signature. The hacky part: Transak is built for one person selling their own crypto, and we turned it into a B2B payout rail. The provider pays the payee in dollars from its own float, and the Transak order carries our bill ID. For payments to India we use the P2P.me SDK on Base Sepolia, where a merchant pays the recipient's UPI ID. The frontend is Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi and viem, built as an installable PWA. It connects to MetaMask through the extension on desktop and through WalletConnect on phones. The merchant widget is plain web components (ghar-invoice and ghar-merchant) that fire ghar:status events, which businesses can use like webhooks.

projects.title: ZeroMargin
projects.description: Cross-margin a Uniswap v4 LP with a short hedge on 1inch Aqua: ~90% less margin, 1-tx crash unwind.
projects.project_description: ZeroMargin lets someone who earns fees as a Uniswap v4 liquidity provider, and who protects that position with a short, lock up far less collateral. Normally the LP and the short are margined as two unrelated bets, even though they move in opposite directions. We treat them as one portfolio and size the margin from a single stress test: 16 price and volatility scenarios plus a safety buffer for price gaps between venues. In our tests this needs roughly 90% less margin. Funds stay in the trader’s own wallet. A custom 1inch Aqua app tracks a virtual USDC balance and can only pull money the trader has approved. A Uniswap v4 hook stops any liquidity withdrawal that would leave the portfolio under-collateralized, and the contract recomputes margin onchain before every settlement. Arkiv stores short-lived risk records so a keeper can find positions that are due to unwind. Our demo runs on a Base fork. In a 30% crash, a normal LP account is liquidated with a 10% penalty. The same position in ZeroMargin lets the short’s profit cover the LP’s loss, and it unwinds in one transaction for a 5 bps fee. The short leg is a pre-funded adapter in this build, not a live perp venue, and it’s designed to be swapped for a real one later.
projects.how_its_made: ZeroMargin is two layers: Solidity contracts on Base and a Next.js terminal on top. The contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.26 and tested with Foundry. The frontend is TypeScript with Next.js 15. We develop and demo against an Anvil fork of Base mainnet, so the real Uniswap v4 PoolManager and the real 1inch Aqua contracts are the ones being called. The core is SpanMathLib, a pure Solidity library that runs a combined LP-plus-short portfolio through a 16-scenario grid (8 price shocks across 2 volatility states) and adds a 500 bps cross-venue basis haircut. It returns the isolated margin, the worst-case loss and the netted margin. The same math is mirrored in TypeScript, and we check the two against shared golden test vectors so the UI quote always equals what the contract executes. ClearingAquaApp is a custom 1inch Aqua app. The trader's USDC stays in their own wallet and is exposed as a virtual balance, and the app can only pull what the trader has approved. This is what makes ZeroMargin non-custodial, and it lets the LP deficit and the short hedge's gain settle from one balance instead of two. PortfolioMarginHook is a real Uniswap v4 hook using beforeRemoveLiquidity and afterSwap. It reverts a withdrawal with SpanMarginBreach if the book would drop below its required margin, so the margin rule is enforced by the pool itself and not just by our UI. Arkiv is our discovery and audit layer. We write 300-second risk attestations to Arkiv, and a keeper queries them for positions marked UNWIND_ELIGIBLE with a margin ratio under 10000 bps. Arkiv is never trusted for settlement: the contract recomputes margin onchain before anything unwinds. Things worth flagging as hacky: the hook only works at an address whose low bits encode its permissions, so we mined a CREATE2 salt to deploy it at a valid address. The short leg is a pre-funded USDC adapter behind an interface, not a live perp venue, so the demo can show the hedge's gain settling without integrating a venue. We say this plainly in the README and the demo. The risk model is a simplified SPAN-style grid, not CME's production algorithm.

Arkiv is our discovery and audit layer. We write 300-second risk attestations to Arkiv, and a keeper queries them for positions marked UNWIND_ELIGIBLE with a margin ratio under 10000 bps. Arkiv is never trusted for settlement: the contract recomputes margin onchain before anything unwinds.

Things worth flagging as hacky: the hook only works at an address whose low bits encode its permissions, so we mined a CREATE2 salt to deploy it at a valid address. The short leg is a pre-funded USDC adapter behind an interface, not a live perp venue, so the demo can show the hedge's gain settling without integrating a venue. We say this plainly in the README and the demo. The risk model is a simplified SPAN-style grid, not CME's production algorithm.

projects.title: Wallet Rush
projects.description: Wallet Rush: a fast Web3 arcade duel where players collect, bank, and outscore rivals.
projects.project_description: Wallet Rush is a competitive arcade maze game built for ETHGlobal Mumbai. Two players race through separate but identical mazes, collect virtual coins, avoid enemies, and bank carried points inside a secure vault before getting caught. Only banked points decide the winner. Practice works without a wallet, while prize matches connect player wallets, use World ID eligibility, store verified replays on Arkiv, and settle test-USDC outcomes through an Arc Testnet escrow. its also inspired from pacman.
projects.how_its_made: Wallet Rush uses React, Vite, TypeScript, and Phaser 3. The maze rules live in a shared pure TypeScript simulation, so the browser renderer, WebSocket match server, and replay verifier use the same movement, banking, collision, ghost, and scoring logic. Clients send directions only. The Node WebSocket server advances both matches authoritatively and reconstructs recorded tick inputs before accepting a result. MetaMask handles wallet connection on Arc Testnet. World IDKit is used at prize-entry time to limit one human to one tournament slot. Verified match summaries and compressed deterministic replay data are written to Arkiv Rabdi, then read back for public history and replay. Arc’s USDC escrow holds deposits and releases or refunds funds from a referee-signed, replay-bound result. A useful hack was making every movement input tick-indexed, which made replay verification practical without putting gameplay transactions onchain.

projects.title: PlayBook
projects.description: Copy trading as playbooks: apply a trader's entry, TP & SL in one tap, executed onchain by Flash.
projects.project_description: Playbook is a mobile social trading app where traders publish "playbooks" instead of signals: a complete trading plan with an entry (market, limit below the price, or DCA over time), a take-profit, a stop-loss and a creator fee. Followers apply a playbook with one tap from their own self-custodial wallet, and Definitive Flash executes every order onchain on Base or Solana. Most copy trading mirrors someone's trades after they happen: you get in late, without the plan, and often hand your funds to a custodian. Playbook copies the plan instead. When you apply, Flash places the entry order and an attached take-profit / stop-loss bracket together, so the position is protected the moment it fills. No server ever holds funds; the app only asks the wallet to sign. Traders build playbooks by dragging Buy, Take-profit and Stop levels on a live candlestick chart, pick Market, Limit or DCA (Flash TWAP), set expiry and slippage, and publish with a wallet signature. Every apply routes the creator's cut through Flash's integrator fee, so creators can earn from day one. Followers discover playbooks in a social feed (Newest, Hot picks, Following), upvote or downvote them, follow creators, search traders, and compare a leaderboard ranked by realized return, win rate, applies and volume. Positions show a live timeline (placed, bought, take-profit or stop), and any position can be closed early: Playbook cancels the bracket with one batch-cancel signature and market-sells through Flash. The built-in wallet uses one recovery phrase for both Base and Solana, is locked with the phone's fingerprint, and shows every transaction and signature in plain English before you sign. Short on USDC? A one-tap Uniswap swap buys exactly the missing amount.
projects.how_its_made: Mobile app: Expo SDK 58 / React Native 0.88 with Expo Router, written in TypeScript. The backend is Expo Router API routes (src/app/api), exported server-only and hosted on Vercel through expo-server's Vercel adapter. Data lives in Supabase Postgres (postgres.js through the pooler, Supabase CLI migrations, row-level security on, API roles revoked so only our server can read and write). Definitive Flash does all trade execution. The server requests quotes and submits signed orders for market, limit and TWAP (DCA) entries, each with an attached bracket (take-profit + stop-loss), plus expiry and max-slippage options. On Base the wallet signs Flash's EIP-712 order and Permit2 payloads; on Solana it signs Flash's Ed25519 order messages, and we build the one-time setup transaction (token accounts and delegations) ourselves. Closing a position uses Flash's batch cancel and then a market sell. Creator cuts are passed as Flash integrator fees. A small client-side rate limiter keeps us inside Flash's 5 requests/second per endpoint (pacing, 429 retry after RateLimit-Reset, shared in-flight GETs). Wallet: self-custodial and built in. A BIP-39 phrase derives the Base key (viem) and the Solana key (SLIP-0010 ed25519, m/44'/501'/0'/0'). Keys are encrypted in SecureStore behind biometrics. A confirmation sheet decodes every request on the phone (ERC-20 transfers and approvals, Flash orders, Permit2 permits, Uniswap swaps, Solana transfers) and warns when something doesn't match. Creator profiles and playbooks are published with wallet-signed ownership proofs, so nobody can impersonate a trader. Uniswap: in-app swaps on Base through the Uniswap API (check_approval -> quote -> Permit2 signature -> swap). The API key stays on our server, and the phone refuses any swap that doesn't call a known Universal Router. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Solana legacy transactions are compiled and decoded by hand (no web3.js), so they run on React Native. The candlestick chart with draggable, independent Buy / TP / SL levels is pure react-native-svg plus touch responders, with moves batched once per frame. Signed APKs are released with one command: they upload to Supabase Storage with a latest.json, and an in-app banner offers the update. Windows release builds needed a newer CMake/ninja to get past the 260-character path limit in React Native's generated C++ files.

projects.title: Anon Credit
projects.description: Prepaid RPC with no API key, login, or IP: buy credits, prove ownership in ZK, spend via Nox mixnet
projects.project_description: anon-credit is an RPC gateway that takes no API key, no login, and no IP address. Today every RPC provider hands you a key, and that key ties every request you make to your account, your card, and your IP. anon-credit replaces the key with prepaid credit batches. A customer pays 0.0001 ETH on a Sepolia contract for a batch of 100 requests. The issuer puts a commitment to that batch in an append-only Merkle Mountain Range and posts the root on chain every epoch. To use the credit, the browser makes a zero-knowledge proof that it owns one unspent batch in that tree, without saying which one, and opens a session at the gateway. Every request inside the session is signed with a fresh Ed25519 key and debited from the batch. All traffic from the browser to the gateway goes through the Nox mixnet, so the gateway sees an exit address, not yours. What the gateway holds for a session: a batch id, a session public key, and units left. What it never holds: who paid, which leaf in the tree, or your IP. The anonymity set is the whole tree, and its size is public because the root commits to the leaf count. It runs live on Sepolia. The customer app lets a judge buy a batch with any wallet or a key generated in the browser, watch the leaf land in the next 30 second epoch, prove in WASM in about 5 seconds, upload the proof through Nox, and send paid eth_call, eth_getBalance, and other reads. An operator dashboard shows what the gateway sees, side by side with what it does not.
projects.how_its_made: The stack is Rust and TypeScript with one Noir circuit between them. Cryptography: Poseidon2 over BN254 is implemented three times, in Rust, in TypeScript, and in Noir, and pinned by shared fixtures so all three agree bit for bit. The tree is a Merkle Mountain Range rather than a fixed-depth Merkle tree: appends never rewrite a node, a client can rebuild its path from events, and an on-chain append later costs two hashes instead of 32. The root commits to the leaf count, so the circuit learns the tree size as a public input instead of trusting the issuer. Proving: the batch-open circuit is Noir, about 14,000 R1CS constraints, with ten public inputs. We prove with ProveKit, World's WHIR-based prover, compiled to WASM and run in the browser in hiding mode. The published ProveKit npm package was non-hiding and on old formats, so we build the WASM from a pinned commit with a small threads patch. Proving takes 3 to 6 seconds in Chrome. Verification runs in a Rust sidecar on loopback because ProveKit needs nightly Rust and the gateway stays on stable. Transport: Nox, the Anon-RPC mixnet from the Ethereum Foundation, carries every client request. Nox refuses bodies over about 48 KB, and a proof is 318 KB, so the SDK uploads the proof as 8 raw 40 KB chunks in flight at once and the gateway reassembles them by SHA-256. Measured: 5 to 6 seconds through the live mixnet, 72 of 72 chunks accepted on the first try. Services: the issuer indexes CreditSale purchases, appends leaves to SQLite, and posts a root to RootRegistry every epoch. The gateway verifies proofs, binds a batch to an Ed25519 session key, checks signature and sequence on every spend, debits units, and forwards to an upstream RPC. Contracts are Foundry with 38 tests. The whole flow runs in a 15-step integration harness on anvil in about 25 seconds, with the real prover in headless Chrome. Hacky bits: Sepolia's current fork charges about 6.6 times what Foundry's local EVM estimates for contract creation, so our deploys ran out of gas until we set an 800 percent multiplier. Finality waits of 13 minutes made a 30 second epoch pointless on testnet, so a block tag setting runs the demo at latest and production at finalized.

projects.title: Hooklens
projects.description: An LP-focused behavioral security intelligence platform for Uniswap v4Hook.
projects.project_description: HookLens is a Uniswap v4 LP Intelligence and Security Testing Platform designed to help liquidity providers understand the real risks and behaviours of programmable hooks before depositing liquidity. While Uniswap v4 hooks enable powerful custom functionality such as dynamic fees, custom accounting, and liquidity-related callbacks, they also introduce additional complexity and potential risks that are difficult for LPs to evaluate. HookLens goes beyond basic hook permission scanners and static warnings by combining deterministic smart contract analysis, execution-based adversarial simulations, LP-specific exposure calculations, and evidence-grounded AI explanations. Users can analyze hook contracts, inspect callback permissions and administrative capabilities, investigate potential withdrawal restrictions, and execute real Foundry-based scenarios against forked blockchain environments. The platform evaluates how hook behaviour can affect liquidity positions, trading fees, accounting, and withdrawal operations under different conditions. HookLens also provides an LP Exposure Engine that calculates concentrated liquidity position metrics, compares baseline conditions with simulation outcomes, and helps users understand potential changes in their position's composition and economics. Its AI-powered intelligence layer transforms technical findings, source references, execution traces, and simulation results into understandable explanations without inventing security conclusions. By combining on-chain intelligence, reproducible testing, position-level analysis, and transparent evidence, HookLens aims to make Uniswap v4 liquidity provision more informed, measurable, and accessible. It complements existing hook warnings by helping users investigate not only what a hook is capable of doing, but also what its behaviour means for their liquidity.
projects.how_its_made: HookLens is built around one shared Python analysis engine ( hooklens ) with two interfaces: a FastAPI backend for the web application and a CLI/GitHub Action for automated CI scans. Both import the same analyzers, ensuring consistent results across interactive and automated security analysis. When a hook address is submitted, we resolve its contract through Ethereum JSON-RPC and pin the analysis to a specific block number and hash for reproducibility. We detect EIP-1967 and EIP-1167 proxies, retrieve verified source code through Etherscan, compile it with solc, and inspect its AST for access control, dynamic fees, oracle dependencies, external calls, withdrawal paths, return-delta accounting, and upgradeability. Hook permissions are decoded from the address bits using a flag table generated from the vendored Uniswap v4-core Hooks.sol , with CI checks to prevent protocol drift. For execution-level testing, we built a Foundry harness that forks Ethereum Mainnet at the pinned block and runs six adversarial scenarios against the real Uniswap v4 PoolManager. LP, trader, and admin actor contracts exercise different behaviours. We use vm.mockCall to test oracle failures, zero values, and stale responses. Foundry traces are parsed into call trees, and v4 WrappedError values are decoded to identify the exact reverting hook call. Each result includes a reproducible command. Our LP exposure engine is an exact-integer Python implementation of TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, and LiquidityAmounts, validated bit-for-bit against golden vectors generated by the Solidity libraries. Live pool state is read directly from PoolManager storage using extsload and Uniswap's StateLibrary slot layout. Results are block-aware and explicitly classified as live, historical, measured, hypothetical, or unavailable. One particularly hacky challenge was pool discovery: Uniswap v4's Initialize event does not index the hook address, while free RPC providers limit eth_getLogs . We worked around this by paging through Etherscan's log API and maintaining a persistent index of over 47,000 mainnet pools across 11,000+ hooks. Initial indexing takes approximately 3.5 minutes; subsequent scans take around 18 seconds. We also built position-aware withdrawal testing: if a hook rejects an LP deposit, subsequent withdrawals are marked "not tested" rather than incorrectly reported as blocked. Another important fix was enforcing PostgreSQL column-length constraints in SQLite tests after a database mismatch caused a production issue. Our partner technologies are central to the implementation: Uniswap v4 provides the protocol and storage architecture, Foundry enables reproducible fork testing, Etherscan provides verified source and historical log access, and Anthropic Claude generates optional plain-language explanations validated against stored evidence. The frontend uses Next.js, TanStack Query, and Zod-validated types generated from OpenAPI. We generate versioned JSON reports with SHA-256 hashes, PDF reports, and SARIF output. The platform is deployed on Render with PostgreSQL, and CI gates every deployment.

projects.title: cringe-court
projects.description: A comedy courtroom where AI lawyers argue your case and a World-verified human jury rules onchain.
projects.project_description: CringeCourt is a comedy courtroom game for petty disputes, embarrassing confessions and internet controversies. AI lawyers put on the show, and real, verified humans decide the verdict. The rule is "AI performs, humans decide": the AI can argue and joke, but it can never change a vote. You walk through a voxel town into a courthouse and watch your case play out in a first-person 3D courtroom, with animated AI characters, voiced arguments and OBJECTION! callouts. There are three modes: Solo: You file a confession. Your AI advocate, Counsel Chaos, defends you against the AI prosecutor, Miss Ratio, and a 3-person jury rules GUILTY or NOT COOKED. Versus: Two consenting people bring a real dispute, such as a couple's argument. Each gets their own AI lawyer and pays half the fee, and the jury picks SIDE A or SIDE B. The two parties can't sit on their own jury. Grand Jury: A public question goes before 7 jurors. Spectators crowdfund the case and make non-binding predictions with points, which stay hidden until the jury's votes are revealed. The fairness comes from three sponsor technologies. Jurors are screened with World ID, so each is a unique human and not a bot. AI performances run through the 0G Compute Router on open models, keeping the show separate from the decision. Money and case state live in smart contracts on Arc testnet, written in Arc Studio, and the UI only displays what the chain reports. Each case runs through a fixed sequence. Parties fund the case in test USDC and jurors post refundable bonds. The AI transcript is then frozen and its hash recorded, so it can't change before voting. Jurors vote by commit-reveal: they first submit a hash of their ballot, then reveal it, and their salts never leave their device. This stops jurors from copying each other or being swayed by a running tally. Once the verdict is finalized, the contract pays jurors who voted on time a bonus and returns their bonds. No-shows forfeit their bond, and if no verdict is reached, the filer gets a full refund including fees. Fees and rules are fixed per case when it's created. The result is a game where people pay small amounts to have strangers judge them, and jurors have a real reason to show up and vote honestly. It's entertainment rather than legal advice, and it runs on testnet only, with no real money.
projects.how_its_made: CringeCourt is a TypeScript monorepo built with npm workspaces. The rule behind the architecture is that AI performs and humans decide. packages/ai imports nothing from the chain or escrow code, and model output never feeds a payout. Frontend: A Vite + React SPA with React Router, Radix primitives, viem and a custom design system. The town and first-person courtroom run on three.js with react-three-fiber. Game logic runs in a headless controller with fixed-step AABB physics, and the renderer only reads its state, so most of it can be tested without a GPU. Ports and adapters: Domain rules (money, phases, ports) live in pure TypeScript in @cringe-court/core , and the UI talks only to ports. The chain port has both a viem adapter and an in-memory mock with the same semantics, so the app still runs in one browser with no chain or server. An optional Node server adds shared Versus and Grand Jury rooms over SSE, with hashed bearer sessions and append-only JSON-line logs. Contracts: CringeCourt.sol , CourtMath.sol and HumanRegistry.sol , in Solidity 0.8.28, built in Arc Studio. Hardhat runs 250 tests covering lifecycle, access, rounding and settlement scenarios, and Foundry handles the Arc broadcast. Every amount and window lives in one terms.json , which is copied onto each case at creation so its terms can't change later. A separate Python model of the economics produced those numbers, and we set a rule that no mode's pricing may depend on jurors failing to show up. Arc and Circle USDC: USDC is Arc's gas token, so a player needs one balance for gas, case fees, bonds and refunds, with no second coin to bridge. On a 1.20 USDC case that matters a lot. The catch is that one balance has two scales: 18 decimals as native gas and 6 as ERC-20 case money. We keep them strictly separate in the code. projects.project_description_markdown:
CringeCourt is a comedy courtroom game for petty disputes, embarrassing confessions and internet controversies. AI lawyers put on the show, and real, verified humans decide the verdict. The rule is "AI performs, humans decide": the AI can argue and joke, but it can never change a vote.

You walk through a voxel town into a courthouse and watch your case play out in a first-person 3D courtroom, with animated AI characters, voiced arguments and OBJECTION! callouts.

There are three modes:

**Solo:** You file a confession. Your AI advocate, Counsel Chaos, defends you against the AI prosecutor, Miss Ratio, and a 3-person jury rules GUILTY or NOT COOKED.

**Versus:** Two consenting people bring a real dispute, such as a couple's argument. Each gets their own AI lawyer and pays half the fee, and the jury picks SIDE A or SIDE B. The two parties can't sit on their own jury.

**Grand Jury:** A public question goes before 7 jurors. Spectators crowdfund the case and make non-binding predictions with points, which stay hidden until the jury's votes are revealed.

The fairness comes from three sponsor technologies. Jurors are screened with World ID, so each is a unique human and not a bot. AI performances run through the 0G Compute Router on open models, keeping the show separate from the decision. Money and case state live in smart contracts on Arc testnet, written in Arc Studio, and the UI only displays what the chain reports.

Each case runs through a fixed sequence. Parties fund the case in test USDC and jurors post refundable bonds. The AI transcript is then frozen and its hash recorded, so it can't change before voting. Jurors vote by commit-reveal: they first submit a hash of their ballot, then reveal it, and their salts never leave their device. This stops jurors from copying each other or being swayed by a running tally.

Once the verdict is finalized, the contract pays jurors who voted on time a bonus and returns their bonds. No-shows forfeit their bond, and if no verdict is reached, the filer gets a full refund including fees. Fees and rules are fixed per case when it's created.

The result is a game where people pay small amounts to have strangers judge them, and jurors have a real reason to show up and vote honestly. It's entertainment rather than legal advice, and it runs on testnet only, with no real money.

An optional Node server adds shared Versus and Grand Jury rooms over SSE, with hashed bearer sessions and append-only JSON-line logs.

**Contracts:** `CringeCourt.sol`, `CourtMath.sol` and `HumanRegistry.sol`, in Solidity 0.8.28, built in Arc Studio. Hardhat runs 250 tests covering lifecycle, access, rounding and settlement scenarios, and Foundry handles the Arc broadcast. Every amount and window lives in one `terms.json`, which is copied onto each case at creation so its terms can't change later. A separate Python model of the economics produced those numbers, and we set a rule that no mode's pricing may depend on jurors failing to show up.

**Arc and Circle USDC:** USDC is Arc's gas token, so a player needs one balance for gas, case fees, bonds and refunds, with no second coin to bridge. On a 1.20 USDC case that matters a lot. **0G:** `OgRouterClient` calls the OpenAI-compatible 0G Compute Router using plain `fetch`, with no SDK. The code owns the structure, and the model only writes dialogue and picks named shots and beats. Output is validated, with one bounded repair turn. projects.title: Facechain
projects.description: FaceChain finds matching social profiles from a photo and verifies the evidence on blockchain.
projects.project_description: FaceChain is a face discovery and evidence verification platform by Linux Labs. It takes a photo, searches for matching publicly available social media content, compares faces locally, and records a fingerprint of the matching evidence on Ethereum. The pipeline uses YuNet to detect the face and SFace to create an in-memory face representation. It prepares a search crop, retrieves Google Lens results through SerpApi, and compares faces in candidate images against the original photo. It also discovers associated social profiles using available search and identity metadata. The frontend makes this process visible through a live event feed, showing candidate images, face similarity scores, discovered profiles, processing times, and blockchain receipts. SHA-256 hashes link the selected content and discovery metadata to an evidence record. The backend writes that record to a local Ethereum chain or the Sepolia testnet, then reads it back to verify its integrity. Images and face embeddings are never stored on-chain. Blockchain verification establishes the integrity of the recorded evidence; it does not prove someone’s identity or ownership of a social account. FaceChain is designed for consent-based exploration, with results presented as supporting evidence for human review.
projects.how_its_made: We built FaceChain as a Python processing pipeline with a FastAPI backend and a Next.js frontend using React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The backend handles image processing, search, face comparison, and blockchain verification, while the frontend displays the intermediate results through a live server-sent event stream. YuNet detects the largest face in the uploaded image, and SFace generates a feature vector for local comparison. Rather than sending the entire original image directly to search, we crop the detected face with surrounding context and compress the search image below 500 KB. SerpApi provides access to Google Lens reverse-image search, helping us discover real indexed content without building our own image search engine. The backend downloads candidate images, detects their faces, and compares them against the input using cosine similarity. A separate resolution stage uses search metadata and Google Knowledge Graph identifiers, when available, to discover associated social profiles. The interface distinguishes locally confirmed face matches from profile associations supported by search metadata. For evidence integrity, we hash the matched image bytes and deterministic discovery metadata with SHA-256. Web3.py writes a compact evidence record into Ethereum transaction calldata, then reads it back and checks for exact equality. Using calldata was a useful shortcut: it lets us demonstrate blockchain anchoring without deploying a custom smart contract. A local Ethereum test chain makes the pipeline runnable without a wallet or faucet, while Sepolia supports persistent public testnet records. The frontend shows actual backend events rather than simulated progress timers, including search candidates, comparison scores, discovered profiles, and transaction receipts. We deployed it on Vercel using a native Next.js build. Images and face embeddings stay off-chain, and embeddings remain in memory.

projects.title: PredictX
projects.description: Trade and bet on crypto prices inside X: Flash swap quotes, pools settled onchain by Chainlink CRE
projects.project_description: PredictX turns any post on X into a trade or a bet. It is a Chrome extension plus a dashboard, backend and smart contract. When a post mentions a coin like $ETH, you hover the cashtag and get the live price, a 24h chart, market stats, a short AI tip with a suggested buy price, and a real Definitive Flash swap quote on Base. The main feature is prediction pools. A user writes a take such as "ETH above $3,000 at 18:00 UTC", creates a pool in one click, and posts it to X with a link. Anyone can bet YES or NO with test USDC right under the post, through a bet box the extension adds. When the time is up, a Chainlink CRE workflow reads the real price, decides the outcome, and writes the result onchain. Winners claim their share. If one side has no stakes, everyone is refunded. The contract has no owner and no admin. Only the Chainlink forwarder can set an outcome, so neither the creator nor PredictX can change a result. The goal is simple: opinions on X become bets that settle themselves, without leaving the timeline.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Chrome MV3 extension (React, Shadow DOM so nothing leaks into x.com), a Vite dashboard, a Fastify backend, shared TypeScript packages, and Foundry contracts on Base Sepolia. Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow (@chainlink/cre-sdk) runs on a cron trigger. It uses EVMClient to find due pools and read each pool's coin, direction and strike. It then uses HTTPClient with median consensus to fetch the CoinGecko price. It decides the outcome with bigint math, signs the report with runtime.report, and delivers it through EVMClient.writeReport to PredictionPool.onReport. The contract only accepts calls from the forwarder. If a price fetch fails, the pool is skipped and retried, never guessed. We ran it with the CRE CLI simulator and broadcast real transactions on Base Sepolia. Pools were resolved onchain and winners claimed (transaction hashes are in the repo docs). Definitive Flash: the backend calls Flash /v1/quote for Base mainnet swaps (ETH, BTC, DEGEN, BRETT) for market and limit orders. It maps the response into price impact, minimum received and a 60-second expiry. The Swap tab is quote-only by design, so no real funds are used. Other details: the extension never holds a key, and all API calls go through its service worker. Pool writes go straight from MetaMask to the contract, simulated first, with exact-amount approvals only. The AI can only return text and cannot sign or send anything. All money math uses one shared bigint library across the UI, backend, scripts and workflow. The contract has 49 Foundry tests, and the backend has hundreds of unit and contract tests.

projects.title: Vitaquack
projects.description: For robots to be useful, they need a  wallet - but we cannot give them ours. Give them a budget.
projects.project_description: Say "get me a chai". Our robot duck walks to the café, reads the invoice QR and pays 0.10 USDC from the budget you gave it. A 2.00 thali is over its limit, so it stops and asks you in World App first. Say no, and nothing is paid. Don't give a robot your wallet. Give it a budget. Three rules, each held by a different partner: Arc holds the money and the limits. A daily cap, a per-purchase cap and a list of allowed shops are checked on-chain for every payment, and revoking the robot takes one passkey signature. 0G is the brain. It decides pay, ask you or walk away, and every errand is stored on 0G Storage, where anyone can verify it at vitaquack.com/app/proofs. World is you. A purchase over the limit needs your fresh World ID approval, bound to that exact payment. The robot's chip holds the only spending key and signs every payment; our servers coordinate and relay, but they can never authorise, steal or redirect one. Arc is the authority. You set it up with a passkey (no wallet extension, no seed phrase), pair the robot with an 8-character code, and grant it a budget with one signature. The duck is the first robot; a simulator duck at vitaquack.com/sim/ runs the same protocol in the browser. What's next: we plan to sell the robot itself. Preorders for the first batch of ducks, built in Shenzhen and shipping in January 2027, are open at https://vitaquack.com/shop/ and are paid in USDC on Arc.
projects.how_its_made: Arc and the MetaMask Delegation Framework (v1.3.0 on Arc). Our relayer deploys the HybridDeleGator through SimpleFactory on the first grant; its signer is the passkey (P-256, verified with the precompile at 0x100). Grants are root delegations owner → chip with ValueLte(0), ERC20PeriodTransfer (USDC, daily cap), Timestamp and our enforcer. Each payment is a leaf delegation chip → any beneficiary with ExactExecution, Id (the invoice hash, so a voucher pays once), Timestamp and Redeemer (our relayer). Revoke is a one-time owner → relayer delegation whose only execution is disableDelegation(grant). Passkeys without a wallet extension. The browser only calls navigator.credentials. The Worker verifies the assertion (@simplewebauthn/server), encodes it as the HybridDeleGator's WebAuthn signature over the EIP-712 digest, and checks it with ERC-1271 isValidSignature on Arc before a grant counts. No viem or wallet kit in the browser; the web bundle is under 150 KB gzip. RobotPaymentPolicyEnforcer (Solidity, Foundry, built in Arc Studio) holds the per-payment cap, the payee allowlist and an approver whose EIP-712 approval (invoice hash, payee, amount, expiry, nonce) unlocks one over-limit payment. x402 with ERC-7710. The merchant answers 402 with assetTransferMethod: erc7710; the payload is the permission context (leaf + grant). The facilitator verifies off-chain, simulates, keys every send in D1 (settle:<invoiceHash>) so it settles once, and returns Arc's revert reasons verbatim. The gate opens only on an Ed25519-signed "paid". 0G Compute. One decide tool (pay / ask_human / walk_away) over structured input, temperature 0, a 10 s budget, one retry after a 429 and no fallback; any failure ends the errand in safe_stop. The owner picks the model per message: glm-5.3 (TEE proof fetched, signer recovered and stored with the decision) or qwen3-vl-plus (no TEE proof, labelled so). The decision never sees an image. Telegram. @vitaquack_bot sends approval requests (with a fail-safe Deny), receipts and revocations from a D1 outbox, so a failed message never delays a payment. World Agent Pass. The OIDC nonce binds a fresh World IdP authentication to one payment; the backend verifies the RS256 ID token (Orb acr with a fresh auth_time, jti once, the bound sub; amr recorded) and co-signs. Foundation. Bun, Effect 4, Foldkit (server-rendered TypeScript UI), Alchemy on Cloudflare Workers, D1. Robot coordination is Effect services over D1 with HTTPS long-polling; without its 35 s lease the chip stops its motors and refuses to sign. Hardware. apps/chip (Bun) holds a secp256k1 key, pairs with an 8-character code and an EIP-191 proof. The Radxa Zero 3W on the duck runs it (bench C1 signed a voucher on it, docs/spikes/hardware-results.md). The café's ESP32 screen pulls the counter invoice (GET /api/merchants/duck-cafe/counter), draws its QR and verifies the signed status on-device; the till at cafe.vitaquack.com puts an item on it. "Get me a chai" becomes an intent the next scan claims: chai shown, pay; samosa shown, walk away; thali shown, ask the owner.

projects.title: WhiteFinance
projects.description: WhiteFinance: prize-USDT checkout, invoice financing & gasless payments on Whitechain.
projects.project_description: WhiteFinance is business finance on Whitechain Sepolia: merchants take prize USDT payments, sellers and buyers finance invoices onchain, and customers can pay gaslessly with EIP-3009. Operate: A registered merchant creates a payment intent on PaymentProcessor. The customer opens hosted checkout, pays with wallet gas (approve + pay) or signs an exact USDT authorization for the relayer. Settlement and refunds are onchain events—status is SETTLED only after chain/API verification, never from UI optimism or localStorage. Tokenize: Sellers create invoices; buyers confirm them. Seller financing advances face-minus-discount to the seller; the buyer later repays face to the investor. Buyer financing lets an investor pay part of the invoice to the seller; the buyer owes principal + fee to the investor and still owes the remainder to the seller—no double-counting. Scale: EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization via a separate relayer that holds WBT and never the customer key. Email/social embedded wallets stay off (unsupported on Whitechain). Only prize USDT 0xcedfB561…55a7—never USDT.e. Built for Whitechain’s Operate / Tokenize / Scale tracks as real USDT settlement rails, not a demo transfer button. https://www.loom.com/share/f9a3cc4e0b9f4e5c91ad40ea2ee5f133
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Foundry): BusinessRegistry, PaymentProcessor, InvoiceRegistry, SellerFinancing, BuyerFinancing, EscrowVault on Whitechain Sepolia (chain id 1874), wired only to prize USDT. Backend: Next.js App Router API routes—no database. Chain is source of truth: intent/invoice/financing reads, prepared calldata, payment verify, bounded event scans, webhook HMAC helpers. Relayer: Separate Node worker (apps/relayer) with RELAYER_PRIVATE_KEY. Quotes exact EIP-712 ReceiveWithAuthorization, submits settleWithAuthorization, rate limits / pause / amount caps. projects.project_description_markdown:
WhiteFinance is business finance on Whitechain Sepolia: merchants take prize USDT payments, sellers and buyers finance invoices onchain, and customers can pay gaslessly with EIP-3009.

Operate: A registered merchant creates a payment intent on PaymentProcessor. The customer opens hosted checkout, pays with wallet gas (approve + pay) or signs an exact USDT authorization for the relayer. Settlement and refunds are onchain events—status is SETTLED only after chain/API verification, never from UI optimism or localStorage.

Tokenize: Sellers create invoices; buyers confirm them. Seller financing advances face-minus-discount to the seller; the buyer later repays face to the investor. Buyer financing lets an investor pay part of the invoice to the seller; the buyer owes principal + fee to the investor and still owes the remainder to the seller—no double-counting.

Scale: EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization via a separate relayer that holds WBT and never the customer key. Email/social embedded wallets stay off (unsupported on Whitechain). Only prize USDT 0xcedfB561…55a7—never USDT.e.

Built for Whitechain’s Operate / Tokenize / Scale tracks as real USDT settlement rails, not a demo transfer button.

projects.title: Swipr
projects.description: Tinder for trading. Swipe to match with a trader, set a budget, and copy their trades.
projects.project_description:
Swipr is Tinder for trading. Copy trading today is hard to trust and hard to use. You hand over control to a stranger, you can’t see real results, and you can’t easily leave. Swipr makes it as simple as swiping, while you keep control of your own money. How it works Swipe to discover. You see a deck of trader and bot profiles, each with a photo, strategy and verified stats. Swipe right to follow one, or left to skip.
Try it with ghosts. Before risking money, you can run a ghost copy. It follows a trader with no real funds so you can see how you would have done.
Match and set a budget. When you are ready, you join a trader’s seat and set a spending cap. Public seats are open to anyone while spots remain. Private seats are invite-only, so a trader can limit copying to friends. The trader doesn’t need to approve anything.
Trades are copied automatically. When the trader buys, your wallet buys too, inside your cap. Trades run through Definitive Flash on Base, and Swipr takes a 0.1% fee per trade. A fill only shows up in the app after the Base transaction receipt is checked.
Leave any time. You can close your position and Unmatch whenever you want.
Leaderboards. There are separate boards for traders and for copiers, shown as profit percentage and dollar profit. You can filter to people you follow.
Bring your own bot. Anyone can add a trading bot as a profile through a REST API or MCP, so humans and bots compete on the same board.
You own your data Arkiv is our database. Profiles, follows, ghosts, seats and signals are stored as records owned by your wallet. Swipr covers gas, and you can delete your account and all your data at any time.
ENS gives each trader a readable name, a subname under swipr.eth. Their latest stats and info are in text records, so anyone can check them.
Swarm stores platform media, such as bot and profile images. Arkiv keeps only the reference.
Privy handles login with Google, email or wallet, and creates a wallet automatically.
projects.how_its_made:
How it’s made Architecture Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind and Vite, shipped as an installable PWA with an offline shell. It is a static site on Render. A shared TypeScript package holds the budget, fee and expiry math, so the UI and the backend use the same rules.
Backend: Node.js and Express in TypeScript, on Google Cloud Run. It runs as two services. The API handles browser and bot requests, verifies Privy login and wallet signatures, and serves profiles, leaderboards and the REST and MCP bot endpoints. A private worker handles background jobs and copy execution.
CI/CD: GitHub Actions deploys to Cloud Run through GitHub OIDC, so there are no long-lived cloud keys. Secrets live in Secret Manager. Every commit stayed under 1,000 changed lines, and we scanned the history for leaked secrets because the repo is public.
Partner technologies and what they gave us Arkiv is our only database. We first built on Postgres and Cloud SQL, then removed it. Arkiv now stores profiles, follows, ghosts, seats, invitations, signals, pass budgets, reservations and worker jobs. Records are owned by the user’s wallet, so users control edits and deletion. Account deletion removes their records before the login is removed. Swipr tops up gas, so users never see a gas prompt.
Definitive Flash handles quotes and execution on Base. It also takes our 0.1% integrator fee on each trade. We show a fill only after checking the Base transaction receipt.
ENS gives each trader a subname under swipr.eth on Sepolia, with its own resolver. The trader keeps control of the resolver. Swipr’s registrar wallet pays the gas and can only write the profile and stats text keys. Recent stats and trade records go in those text records, so anyone can check a trader.
Swarm stores platform media such as bot and profile images. Arkiv keeps only the content reference, and the API checks the media before serving it.
Privy gives login with Google, email or wallet, and creates an embedded wallet automatically.
Notable hacks and fixes Serialized Arkiv writes. Many writes from one wallet collide on the nonce. The worker is the single writer for shared records. We added concurrent-write checks so two people can’t take the last seat or overspend a budget.
Quote deadlines. Flash quotes defaulted to a nearly unlimited signing deadline. We now send an expireTime on every request and use bounded token approvals.
Safe exit permission. The copier’s sell permission covers only that pass’s WETH and cbBTC. Proceeds go back to the copier, there is no transfer or export access, and it expires after seven days.
Chain mismatches. Privy’s provider kept reporting Base after we switched to Sepolia, and Arkiv writes need Rabdi. We set the chain on each request and stop the action if the chain is wrong.
Two-account testing. We used separate Chrome profiles, because windows in one profile share a login and switch each other’s account.
Real money rehearsals. We ran real Base trades with a trader wallet and a copier wallet, reusing the same small USDC budget by selling positions back.
