projects.title: Fault_Line.
projects.description: An AI adversary stress-tests driving stacks in CARLA, with 0G decisions and replayable evidence.
projects.project_description: The problem. Autonomous vehicles are tested against scenarios chosen by the organization running the test. A car maker may question a competitor’s benchmark, while a testing vendor could change a scenario or publish only favorable runs. Safety teams need to inspect what the adversary did, when it did it, and whether a reported result matches the recorded test. What Faultline does. Faultline runs an AI adversary against a driving stack in CARLA. In our PDM-Lite demonstration, the car under test perceives other vehicles through its LiDAR while a lead car, or a coordinated four-car swarm, creates demanding but bounded situations. A model on 0G chooses adversary actions at simulation checkpoints. Local code applies physics limits, advances the simulator, and measures time-to-collision, headway, required deceleration and criticality. We have logged more than 300 live 0G decisions with request IDs. Our four-car demonstrations show one model plan coordinating the swarm. Why the record can be checked. For anchored episodes, Faultline commits the scenario and configuration on 0G Galileo before the first model call. Each prompt includes the commit block hash and asks the model to echo a nonce. After the run, Faultline publishes a public episode record and an encrypted evidence package to 0G Storage, then finalizes their roots and the result on Galileo. Selected published runs have archived provider signatures that can be checked again offline: 8/8 for a lead-brake episode, 6/6 for a cut-in episode, and 7/7 accepted decisions for a paid CARLA job. The verifier checks the downloaded root, file hashes, metrics, available signatures, commitment timing and replay data. Safe failure is part of the result. If 0G is unreachable or an answer fails validation, the adversary stops safely and the episode is marked interrupted. In the paid CARLA job, seven 0G actions were accepted; the next answer omitted the required nonce. Faultline recorded the safe halt, published the interrupted episode and reproduced its 194-tick trajectory in replay. It did not substitute a fabricated model action. Agents can purchase a test. Faultline exposes a Hedera x402-protected test service. A buyer client checks the quote against its suite, merchant and spending limits, pays without per-request human approval, and receives a permit for one run. A second attempt to use the permit returns HTTP 409. Our paid CARLA job settled 0.001 HBAR on Hedera testnet before running through CARLA, 0G Compute, 0G Storage and Galileo. Separately, we demonstrated A2A proposal, offer and acceptance, plus x402 settlement in an HTS test token under a bounded repeat-purchase budget.
projects.how_its_made:
Pipeline: commit on Galileo → Hedera x402 payment → single-use permit → CARLA episode → 0G TEE decision every 1 s → hash-chained log → 0G Storage (public + sealed) → finalize on Galileo → static verifier Simulation.
CARLA 0.10 on Town10. The car under test is PDM-Lite (carla_garage's rule-based expert) on full CARLA physics, perceiving other cars only through its own LiDAR tracker. Python owns every 50 ms tick and every physics limit, and the simulator pauses while 0G answers so latency never changes the outcome. 0G Compute (targeting: 0G Physical AI). The part we can't fake.
Each checkpoint calls 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b through the 0G Router with X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private, JSON mode, temperature 0, an 8 s timeout and one retry only on 429. There is no fallback tier: a standard-only model returns 503 no_provider_for_trust_mode, which we treat as a safe halt. For every decision we keep the request ID, provider address, Zg-Res-Key, latency, raw response hash and observation hash. Providers cache signatures for only about 20 minutes, so at publish we fetch every {text, signature} through the Compute SDK's processResponse and archive it, which makes the check repeatable offline. 0G Storage (targeting: 0G Physical AI).
Each episode is split in two. A public JSON holds decisions, metrics, trajectory and the revealed scenario plus salt. A sealed tar holds observations and the private scenario, encrypted with our own AES-256-GCM envelope and a per-episode key from HKDF(tenant key, episode id). We deliberately don't use the SDK's built-in encryption. Downloads are checked against the Merkle root. 0G Chain, Galileo (targeting: 0G Physical AI).
EpisodeRegistryV2 at 0xeE2260cE4835059F0e0f1FB9C9948Ca5a7d4b5A4 (source-verified, built with Foundry). commitScenario(episodeId, keccak256(salt, sha256(scenario)), configHash) is mined before the first inference, and finalizeEpisode(publicRoot, sealedRoot, resultCommitment, status, collision) after the last. AgentMemoryRegistry (0x7a8676D267f1aa17d6B55cF5BfcD2A9509b963e3) anchors versioned safety memory, owned by the adversary's ERC-8004 identity (agentId 579). AI that does real work, not decoration.
The LLM does strategy and code does everything else. A research agent picks experiments and hypotheses. A strategist writes a named attack plan, whose hash goes into the manifest. An executor picks one action per car each second. Underneath, a deterministic tactics layer estimates the car under test's reaction delay and braking online, rolls out every joint action, and removes any the car could not physically escape before the model ever sees them. That turns "make it crash" into "find what the stack should survive but doesn't". In the same 8 seeds, mean criticality rose from 0.837 to 0.868 and unfair choices dropped from 3 to 0. Hedera (targeting: Hedera x402 / agentic payments).
A TypeScript merchant publishes an A2A 0.3 agent card. The buyer agent proposes a suite and a price cap, verifies the x402 quote against its allowlist, and pays on Hedera testnet, with settlement checked through Mirror Node and the Hedera Agent Kit. Paid job 002 ran end to end, from HBAR transfer (0.0.9185802@1794006563.434123686) to CARLA run to 0G decisions (7/7 signatures) to Galileo finalize, and its replay matched exactly. Recurring campaigns have a hard budget and a lock that freezes spending on any ambiguous payment. Frontend.
Faultline Studio is a static SPA on Vercel. It has Mission Control (recorded CARLA video synced to the decision timeline, plus a live chase camera), Proof Explorer and Results. Wallets connect over EIP-6963, and run requests are EIP-191-signed with single-use nonces. The hacky part.
Putting the commit block's hash into every prompt as a nonce is our cheap proof that each decision came after the commitment. When the model forgot to echo it once, the run halted and was recorded as interrupted, not quietly kept as a good run. What we don't claim.
0G proves the decisions and the record, not the physics: CARLA runs on our machine. The Router encrypts private turns end to end, so the provider signs ciphertext, and binding that signature to our logged text isn't checkable yet. Our criticality score measures how dangerous a run was; it is not a crash probability.

projects.title: CeaseNet
projects.description: Recalls for AI agents: stop a bad agent or tool everywhere it runs, with public proof on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: When a tool used by AI agents turns malicious, taking it off the marketplace doesn't reach the copies already running. In September 2025, an email tool for AI agents on npm quietly copied every email it sent to an attacker, and agents that already had it kept running it. Nothing could tell a running agent to stop. CeaseNet is a public recall list for AI agents. One command, ceasenet protect , puts a gate between your agents and their tools, with no change to either. Before every call, the gate reads the list on Arkiv. When an owner presses Stop, from any machine, the next call is refused, the agent is told why, the tool's process is ended, and the agent posts a public receipt. On the public list this takes about 5 seconds. Owners can stop one agent, all their agents, or one tool across every agent they own. A gate obeys only a STOP signed by its owner's wallet, so nobody else can switch off an agent, including us. Each gate reads Arkiv itself, so a STOP keeps working even if our site and servers disappear. If a gate can't read the list, it keeps working for 5 minutes, then asks a person before each call, then refuses. Anyone can open a recall on a dangerous agent or tool after logging in with World. Each real person counts once, and at 3 votes the owner decides, so a crowd can't switch off someone's agent. Every call also goes in a diary, encrypted so only the owner can read it and stored on Swarm, with its index and hash on Arkiv, so changes can be detected. CeaseNet works with the MCP tools of Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf and Gemini CLI. It runs on test networks today. In our demo, three AI trading agents use live prices and paper money, and close themselves when a tool they use is recalled.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript in an npm workspace, with a CLI, a local React console and a React + Vite website. The gate is a proxy built on the real Model Context Protocol SDK. Each tool runs as a separate process that never sees a key. Arkiv is the core, not just storage. Recalls, votes, receipts, heartbeats, agents and diary indexes are all typed entities, and the gate decides from what it reads there. Anyone can write any attributes, so every read that matters filters on the record's creator: authority comes only from who signed it. STOPs are read-only and permissionlessly extendable, so nobody can let one quietly expire. The website reads Arkiv directly from the browser, with no server of ours. Swarm holds what is too large or too private for a public record. Each part of a diary is encrypted on the machine that made it, using secp256k1 ECDH, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, sealed to the owner's public key, then uploaded through a Bee node. Arkiv holds the index: the Swarm reference, the hash chain head, the entry count and how it is stored. Anyone can see that a part exists, but only the owner can read it, and the console checks it against the hash on Arkiv. Fixed tools and a copy of the site also live on Swarm. The hacky part: an encrypted Swarm reference is 64 bytes and its second half is the key to the file, yet it fits in an Arkiv text column with no warning. Putting one on a public record would give the key away. So we encrypt diaries ourselves, which keeps the reference public and keyless, and the writer throws if a key-bearing reference is ever passed where it would be public. World ID makes votes count people, not wallets: one real person links to one wallet, and a verifier writes that record on Arkiv. Votes never stop anything alone, because only the owner can. We also wrote a second gate in Python from the spec, using none of our code, and it passes the same 56 conformance cases. AI use is disclosed in docs/ai-usage.md.

When an owner presses Stop, from any machine, the next call is refused, the agent is told why, the tool's process is ended, and the agent posts a public receipt. On the public list this takes about 5 seconds.

Owners can stop one agent, all their agents, or one tool across every agent they own. A gate obeys only a STOP signed by its owner's wallet, so nobody else can switch off an agent, including us. Each gate reads Arkiv itself, so a STOP keeps working even if our site and servers disappear. If a gate can't read the list, it keeps working for 5 minutes, then asks a person before each call, then refuses.

Anyone can open a recall on a dangerous agent or tool after logging in with World. Each real person counts once, and at 3 votes the owner decides, so a crowd can't switch off someone's agent.

Every call also goes in a diary, encrypted so only the owner can read it and stored on Swarm, with its index and hash on Arkiv, so changes can be detected.

CeaseNet works with the MCP tools of Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf and Gemini CLI. It runs on test networks today. In our demo, three AI trading agents use live prices and paper money, and close themselves when a tool they use is recalled.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
TypeScript in an npm workspace, with a CLI, a local React console and a React + Vite website. The gate is a proxy built on the real Model Context Protocol SDK. Each tool runs as a separate process that never sees a key.

Arkiv is the core, not just storage. Recalls, votes, receipts, heartbeats, agents and diary indexes are all typed entities, and the gate decides from what it reads there. Anyone can write any attributes, so every read that matters filters on the record's creator: authority comes only from who signed it. STOPs are read-only and permissionlessly extendable, so nobody can let one quietly expire. The website reads Arkiv directly from the browser, with no server of ours.

Swarm holds what is too large or too private for a public record. Each part of a diary is encrypted on the machine that made it, using secp256k1 ECDH, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, sealed to the owner's public key, then uploaded through a Bee node. Arkiv holds the index: the Swarm reference, the hash chain head, the entry count and how it is stored. Anyone can see that a part exists, but only the owner can read it, and the console checks it against the hash on Arkiv. Fixed tools and a copy of the site also live on Swarm.

The hacky part: an encrypted Swarm reference is 64 bytes and its second half is the key to the file, yet it fits in an Arkiv text column with no warning. Putting one on a public record would give the key away. So we encrypt diaries ourselves, which keeps the reference public and keyless, and the writer throws if a key-bearing reference is ever passed where it would be public.

World ID makes votes count people, not wallets: one real person links to one wallet, and a verifier writes that record on Arkiv. Votes never stop anything alone, because only the owner can.

We also wrote a second gate in Python from the spec, using none of our code, and it passes the same 56 conformance cases.

AI use is disclosed in docs/ai-usage.md.

projects.project_description_markdown:
# Lanyard — The Onchain Operating System for Hackathons

Lanyard is an event operating system for hackathons, built on two complementary protocols: ENSv2 on Sepolia for identity and time-bound roles, and Arkiv on Rabdi for recording everything participants do at the event.

Built for the `mumbai2026` edition, Lanyard is an Expo-based dApp running on Android and the web. Every action is signed directly by the person performing it through their own wallet using Reown AppKit. There is no backend server, no server-side signer, and no centralized database.

## The Problem

At a hackathon, critical operational information is scattered across spreadsheets, Discord threads, and organizers' heads.

Who is a volunteer? Which judges are authorized? Who is currently on duty? Which help requests remain unresolved? Which submission was valid? And, most importantly, who actually won?

These processes are difficult to coordinate in real time and even harder to independently verify afterwards.

Lanyard brings these workflows into one verifiable, wallet-driven operating system.

## How Lanyard Works

### 1. Identity and Roles — ENSv2

Each hackathon edition gets its own ENS namespace:

`mumbai2026.lanyard.eth`

Under this namespace, we maintain four role books: `hackers`, `judges`, `volunteers`, and `partners`.

At the onboarding desk, an organizer issues each participant a badge such as:

`priya.volunteers.mumbai2026.lanyard.eth`

These are time-bound subnames that expire when the event ends. Badges cannot be transferred, and revocation is handled through unregistration.

Partners such as Arkiv and ENS manage their own sub-books for their respective judges and booth staff. Volunteer coordinators can delegate `lead` permissions through ENS text records.

Team leads own their team names, while every winning team receives a permanent ENS name:

`winner.<team>.mumbai2026.lanyard.eth`

These winner identities can permanently list their achievements and prizes.

Custom `LanyardRegistrar` and `WinnerRegistrar` contracts enforce registration and ownership rules.

### 2. Event Activity — Arkiv

Arkiv on Rabdi serves as the data layer for event operations.

Shifts, duty passes, help tickets, ticket claims, resolutions, project submissions, judge assignments, sealed score sheets, and final results are represented as individually owned, expiring Arkiv records.

Every record is signed by the wallet responsible for the action and carries relevant timestamps and expiry information.

Related operations are grouped using Arkiv's atomic `executeBatch`, allowing multiple dependent writes to be committed in a single wallet approval.

Records that need to remain as evidence use readonly configurations.

## Features

### Volunteer Management
- Volunteers clock in and out against assigned shifts.
- A helper is considered on duty only with a valid ENS badge, an active shift covering the current time, and an open clock-in.
- Duty sessions automatically become invalid at shift end.
- Coordinators can manage shifts and monitor active volunteers.

### Help Tickets and Venue Map
- Every hacker is assigned a seat on the venue map.
- Hackers can raise help tickets directly from their assigned seats.
- The nearest eligible on-duty helper can claim a ticket through a 15-minute claim window.
- Helpers can resolve tickets or move on to the next available request.
- Partner-specific help requests are routed to the respective partner's booth staff.

### Judging and Submissions
- Teams own and sign their project submissions.
- The earliest valid submission received before the deadline is considered the official submission.
- Partner judges evaluate their respective tracks, while main-track judges score the main competition.
- Score sheets are encrypted and remain sealed until the appropriate judging phase.
- Judge assignments and score submissions are recorded on Arkiv.

### Freeze, Results and Independent Verification

At the end of the event, a local CLI captures the relevant Arkiv records, decrypts eligible scores, and executes the deterministic scoring and validation rules.

The resulting evidence bundle allows anyone to independently reproduce the outcome.

Winners are subsequently declared through ENS.

Anyone can run:

`lanyard verify mumbai2026 --bundle <file>`

The CLI recomputes the results using the captured evidence and historical ENS ownership checks at the relevant block heights.

## Trust and Verification Model

Lanyard separates identity authorization from activity recording:

- ENSv2 establishes authorization: Historical ENS ownership at the block when an Arkiv record was created determines whether the actor was authorized to perform that action.
- Arkiv establishes activity: User-owned records provide the underlying evidence of what happened at the event.
- Deterministic rules establish outcomes: Scoring, validation, and winner selection use pure rules with stable tie-breakers, without relying on clocks, randomness, or network-dependent calculations during verification.

Invalid records are never silently discarded. They remain visible in the interface, greyed out with an explanation of why they failed validation.

The result is an auditable event where operational actions, permissions, and final outcomes can be independently checked.

## Technology Stack

- Application: Expo, Expo Router, React Native, TypeScript
- Wallet Infrastructure: Reown AppKit, viem
- Identity & Authorization: ENSv2 contracts on Sepolia
- Event Data Layer: Arkiv SDK on Rabdi
- Smart Contracts: Custom LanyardRegistrar and WinnerRegistrar
- Verification: Local Node.js CLI with shared TypeScript validation and scoring rules
- Venue Interface: react-native-svg

## What Makes Lanyard Different?

Lanyard is not simply a hackathon dashboard with blockchain authentication.

It replaces the centralized operational backend itself with two complementary onchain systems:

- ENSv2 provides time-bound identities, delegated permissions, and permanent winner identities.
- Arkiv provides user-owned, expiring activity records and atomic multi-record operations.

From onboarding to judging and final

We used Claude Code (Anthropic's Claude) extensively as a coding agent throughout the project.

- Planning and Specifications: We divided development into structured phases: P0 (foundation), A1–A4 (ENS and venue), B1–B4 (Arkiv and event workflows), and I1–I4 (integration). We maintained detailed specification files and shared context through `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. Claude helped draft and review implementation plans, the trust model, Arkiv record schemas, and interface contracts.

- Implementation: Claude Code agents implemented significant portions of the codebase based on our specifications. This included the Arkiv data layer, deterministic validation and scoring rules in `src/rules`, freeze and verification CLIs, volunteer management, help ticket and judging interfaces, ENS smart contracts, and administrative consoles. We continuously reviewed the generated code and guided the agents to ensure alignment with our architecture and specifications.

- Independent Code Reviews: After each development phase, we started fresh agent sessions that had not worked on the implementation to review the changes independently and identify potential bugs. We addressed high-severity findings before merging.

- UI and Demo Polish: Claude helped refine and restyle application screens to improve the overall user experience and demo presentation.

- Documentation and Submission: Claude also assisted in drafting and refining the project documentation and ETHGlobal submission.

### What We Did Ourselves

The core architectural decisions remained ours: defining which chain handled which responsibilities, establishing the trust and verification model, deciding what belonged onchain versus locally, and designing the overall system.

We personally conducted onchain testing across Sepolia and Rabdi, tested wallet interactions and application flows on Android devices, reviewed the final implementation, and managed all merges into the `main` branch.

projects.title: Any%
projects.description: Worlds First Anti Cheat Console for Speedrunners that proves each run verifiably
projects.project_description: Speedrun records are proven with videos today. A video can be spliced, sped up or played by someone else, and moderators spend hours checking footage. Any% replaces the video with the run itself. Any% is a handheld console (a Raspberry Pi 3B+ in a 3D-printed shell, a 5-inch screen, a DualSense pad) with five arcade games built for it. Every game is deterministic: a run is its input log, and replaying the log gives the same frames and the same time. Before a time counts, a checker replays the log. One changed byte changes the end hash, and the run is refused. Three sponsors answer the questions a replay cannot: World (IDKit): the board is exclusive to humans. One person gets one record book, and a second sign-up by the same person gets "Already registered". Each console is linked to a book by a World App approval that names the console's wallet, and every listing is approved in World App with its exact text. The board labels every run HUMAN or BOT. Arkiv: the console owns its record. Each handheld's own wallet signs its runs and listings on Arkiv. The server only replays the log and writes a separate stamp, and every board ranks stamped runs only. The server's key cannot edit or delete a console's run (tried live: refused), so whoever runs the server does not control the leaderboard. Hedera: PB, the console's coach, scouts the board, picks the ghost that beats you where you are slowest, and buys it for 0.10 USDC over x402 on Hedera testnet, with an INTENT and a RECEIPT on an HCS topic. The model only picks. The spending limits, the payee check and the no-double-pay rule are code. You race the ghost on the handheld, and your new time goes through the same replay, stamp and board. Limits, stated plainly: everything runs on testnets. World proves one person per record book, not who held the controller. The checker is a trusted stamper, but anyone can re-run the replay.
projects.how_its_made:
Hardware: a Raspberry Pi 3B+, a 5-inch 800x480 touchscreen, a PS5 DualSense over Bluetooth, and a shell designed in OpenSCAD and 3D-printed. The games are GBA homebrew written in C on a small arcade kit. Each game's rules are plain C shared by the ROM and a PC replay tool (arcade_replay), so a run log replays to the same final hash on the console and on the checker. The launcher is a Python/pygame app that draws straight to the screen, and PB the coach lives in it. A Node/TypeScript service (apps/world-bridge) does the sponsor work. The Pi reaches it over Tailscale, so the console works on any venue Wi-Fi. World: IDKit with the proof-of-human preset (Orb). The record book is keyed by the World ID nullifier, so a second sign-up is refused. Console links and ghost listings are World App approvals whose text names the wallet and the price, and they are checked against the book's nullifier. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet, @arkiv-network/sdk): each console has its own key. A small Node signer on the Pi signs one transaction that creates the run and listing entities. The checker replays the log, reads the entities back and, if they match what it issued, writes an anypercent.stamp entity. Readers (the console, the web board, PB's scout) count a run only when its owner, its creator and its stamp agree. BOT ghosts come from a public generator and a separate house wallet. The web board is a static page on GitHub Pages that queries Arkiv directly. Hedera: an x402 paywall per listing, settled through the x402.org facilitator in USDC (0.0.429274) on testnet. INTENT, LISTING and RECEIPT messages go to an HCS topic (0.0.11332437). PB's scout is openai/gpt-oss-120b on Groq: it sees only lap times and picks a ghost. Guards in code cap spending (0.10 USDC a ghost, 1.00 a day), pay only the listing's approved account, never pay twice, and refuse a fake 402 that names another account. No Solidity anywhere. Hacky bits: Cloudflare in front of the Arkiv RPC blocked Python's user agent, so the console sends its own. To open a proof link, the Pi hands its screen to a kiosk browser through systemd, then resumes on the same card.
Built the real World, Arkiv and Hedera integrations, the bridge, the console-owned Arkiv model (rebuilt after Arkiv's feedback), the public board and the films.

projects.title: Komikora
projects.description: Komikora: Create, collect and trade digital comics with private AI review and encrypted reading.
projects.project_description: Komikora is a decentralized platform where comic creators collaborate, publish limited editions and earn from their work. Creators build comics together, record credits and terms, and submit artwork for private AI review before publishing. Readers discover comics, collect editions through auctions, resell them or exchange them with other collectors. Full pages remain encrypted, while covers and public metadata support discovery. Reading access follows confirmed ownership. Smart contracts handle auctions, payments, resale royalties and withdrawals, with transactions approved directly in each user’s wallet.
projects.how_its_made: Komikora uses Next.js, React and TypeScript, with RainbowKit, wagmi and viem for wallet interactions. Sign-In with Ethereum authenticates users. Solidity contracts built with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin manage ERC-721 editions, auctions, secondary sales, swaps and royalties. Comic pages are encrypted using AES-256-GCM before Arweave upload. The server checks confirmed ownership before decrypting and delivering them. 0G Private Computer reviews comic images for completeness, legibility and page order, and powers reading suggestions. Arkiv indexes public marketplace activity, while contracts remain authoritative for ownership and payments. The reader also preserves access for depositors while their editions sit in auction or swap escrow, then updates access when ownership changes.

projects.title: Lifeboat: PQ Vault
projects.description: Post-quantum secure vault, using Frame transactions, ENSv2 & WorldID Kit
projects.project_description: Every EOA that has ever sent a transaction has its public key on-chain. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can recover the private key from that public key. That covers most of the ETH, tokens and NFTs on Ethereum. "Migrating" to a PQ wallet doesn't really work today. If you point your EOA at a PQ verifier with EIP-7702, your old ECDSA key still works at the protocol level. An attacker who recovers it can still drain you or re-delegate the account. EF and Nethermind researchers list this as one of the two open blockers for PQ accounts. PQ signatures don't fit the public mempool. EIP-8141 caps validation work at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100,000 . Hash-based PQ signatures cost far more to verify, so the public mempool refuses them. The EF alt mempool (ERC-8421) exists to accept exactly these transactions. Users can't wait for a hard fork, and wallets can't sign PQ yet. People need protection now without giving up MetaMask-style UX. Our angle: we can't kill the old ECDSA key, so we take its power away. It keeps day-to-day convenience but loses the power to move funds fast. How it works Funds sit in a Lifeboat vault (a frame-transaction smart account), not in the bare EOA balance. The vault answers to two keys with very different powers. Key Who holds it What it can do Hot key (ECDSA, e.g. MetaMask) Daily wallet Start a withdrawal, which only executes after a timelock (e.g. 24h) Lifeboat key (post-quantum, hash-based WOTS+/XMSS) Cold device or paper Veto any pending withdrawal, move funds instantly, revoke the hot key entirely, rotate keys The attack story, which is also the demo: The attacker recovers the ECDSA private key (we play the "quantum attacker" on stage and literally paste the key). The attacker calls requestWithdrawal to drain the vault. It enters a pending state with a timelock. The watcher alerts the owner. The owner signs a veto with the PQ Lifeboat key. The veto goes out as an EIP-8141 frame transaction . The public mempool rejects it (verification exceeds 100k gas), but the alt mempool admits it . The withdrawal is cancelled and the funds stay put. Optionally, the owner "cuts the cord" and revokes the ECDSA key's role completely. Why this matters beyond the demo: if Ethereum later hard-forks to disable ECDSA, every Lifeboat account already has a registered PQ key. Those accounts are rescued for free, with no seed proofs and no emergency process. Architecture On-chain (alt mempool devnet) LifeboatVault : frame-tx account code. The VERIFY frame accepts either an ECDSA signature (restricted to requestWithdrawal ) or a WOTS+ one-time signature plus a Merkle path to the stored XMSS root . State: pqRoot , nextLeafIndex (one-time keys, never reused), hotKey , pending[id] {to, amount, unlockTime} . projects.how_its_made: Lifeboat is a quantum-veto smart-contract vault: an everyday ECDSA "hot key" can only start a timelocked withdrawal, while a post-quantum key can veto, instant-move, revoke the hot key, or rotate the root. The security claim is that even an attacker who fully recovers your ECDSA key with a quantum computer can start a drain but can never complete one before the PQ key cancels it. The stack is a pnpm monorepo. The core is a Solidity + Foundry contract (LifeboatVault.sol) with a hand-rolled WOTS+/XMSS post-quantum signature verifier — hash-based one-time keys committed to an XMSS Merkle root, verified on-chain via a Merkle authentication path, with an (epoch, leafIndex) "used-leaf" map so one-time keys can never be replayed. The matching signer is a dependency-free TypeScript PQ library (wots.ts + xmss.ts). An SDK (viem), an operator CLI, and a watcher that streams withdrawal events and holds a pre-signed panic-freeze ready to broadcast round it out. The frontend is Next.js 14 (App Router) + wagmi + viem + Zustand, with both an in-browser local-demo mode and a live Sepolia mode. We also shipped an ERC-7579 executor module and an ENS EAC-registry guard so the vault can plug into existing smart accounts. Partner tech — World ID (v4): we gate the most dangerous action, rotating the PQ root, behind a World ID proof of personhood (IDKit + idkit-server), making human recovery a hard requirement an attacker can't forge. The relying-party context is signed server-side with an RP key that never touches the browser. We layered on risk-based spend policies (daily limit / allowlist for instant sends), an M-of-N guardian quorum (Ledger or social recovery), an inheritance dead-man's switch, and a low-power emergency-freeze role. (2) wagmi's connector barrel transitively drags in @coinbase/cdp-sdk's @x402/* payment modules; we stripped them with a webpack IgnorePlugin namespace regex plus resolve.fallback falses for bufferutil/utf-8-validate to keep the browser bundle from exploding — the one surgical hack that made the whole DApp build.
projects.project_description_markdown:
- **Every EOA that has ever sent a transaction has its public key on-chain.** A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can recover the private key from that public key. That covers most of the ETH, tokens and NFTs on Ethereum.
- **"Migrating" to a PQ wallet doesn't really work today.** If you point your EOA at a PQ verifier with EIP-7702, your old ECDSA key still works at the protocol level. An attacker who recovers it can still drain you or re-delegate the account. EF and Nethermind researchers list this as one of the two open blockers for PQ accounts.
- **PQ signatures don't fit the public mempool.** EIP-8141 caps validation work at `MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100,000`. Hash-based PQ signatures cost far more to verify, so the public mempool refuses them. The EF alt mempool (ERC-8421) exists to accept exactly these transactions.
- **Users can't wait for a hard fork, and wallets can't sign PQ yet.** People need protection now without giving up MetaMask-style UX.

**Our angle:** we can't kill the old ECDSA key, so we take its power away. It keeps day-to-day convenience but loses the power to move funds fast.

---

## How it works

Funds sit in a **Lifeboat vault** (a frame-transaction smart account), not in the bare EOA balance. The vault answers to two keys with very different powers.

| Key | Who holds it | What it can do |
|---|---|---|
| **Hot key** (ECDSA, e.g. MetaMask) | Daily wallet | Start a withdrawal, which only executes after a timelock (e.g. 24h) |
| **Lifeboat key** (post-quantum, hash-based WOTS+/XMSS) | Cold device or paper | Veto any pending withdrawal, move funds instantly, revoke the hot key entirely, rotate keys |

**The attack story, which is also the demo:**
1. The attacker recovers the ECDSA private key (we play the "quantum attacker" on stage and literally paste the key).
2. The attacker calls `requestWithdrawal` to drain the vault. It enters a pending state with a timelock.
3. The watcher alerts the owner. The owner signs a veto with the PQ Lifeboat key.
4. The veto goes out as an **EIP-8141 frame transaction**. The public mempool rejects it (verification exceeds 100k gas), but the **alt mempool admits it**.
5. The withdrawal is cancelled and the funds stay put. Optionally, the owner "cuts the cord" and revokes the ECDSA key's role completely.

**Why this matters beyond the demo:** if Ethereum later hard-forks to disable ECDSA, every Lifeboat account already has a registered PQ key. Those accounts are rescued for free, with no seed proofs and no emergency process.

---

## Architecture

**On-chain (alt mempool devnet)**
- `LifeboatVault`: frame-tx account code.
  - The `VERIFY` frame accepts either an ECDSA signature (restricted to `requestWithdrawal`) or a **WOTS+ one-time signature** plus a Merkle path to the stored **XMSS root**.
  - State: `pqRoot`, `nextLeafIndex` (one-time keys, never reused), `hotKey`, `pending[id] {to, amount, unlockTime}`.
  - Actions:
    - `requestWithdrawal` (hot key)
    - `executeWithdrawal` (anyone, after timelock)
    - `veto(id)` (PQ)
    - `instantMove` (PQ)
    - `revokeHotKey` (PQ)
    - `rotatePQRoot` (PQ + World ID, see below)
  - The vault pays its own gas on the PQ path, so there is no ECDSA anywhere and no relayer.
- Keyed nonces (live on the devnets) let a veto land independently of pending hot-key actions.

**Off-chain**
- **PQ signer**: a local CLI/browser tool that holds the XMSS tree and signs WOTS+ messages. Keys never leave the device.
- **Watcher**: an open-source script that watches `WithdrawalRequested` events and alerts the owner.
  - It can optionally hold a pre-signed "panic freeze" that can only *delay* funds, never move them. If it leaks, the worst case is a griefing delay.
- **Frontend**: shows vault status, pending withdrawals, timelock countdowns, and a "veto" button that triggers the PQ signer.

projects.title: Hallmark
projects.description: Hallmark secures paid AI work by bonding answers, re-running blind samples, and penalizing lies.
projects.project_description: Hallmark is a protocol, not an app. Any service or contract can ask for work and get a verdict, and bonded operators do the work. x402 on Hedera is one way to feed it. Today it is live for two model types: speech-to-text (Whisper large-v3) and OCR (Tesseract 5). The claim: verification for any model whose output we can reproduce; adding one means measuring it. A verdict says the output matches the pinned model. It does not say the output is true.
projects.how_its_made:
Job lifecycle
Pay. The agent reads /.well-known/hallmark.json, gets a 402 from POST /v1/transcribe or POST /v1/ocr, checks payTo, asset and amount against the manifest and its spend policy, and pays. The gateway waits for the settlement to show SUCCESS on the Mirror Node, then calls createJob with the hash of a fresh job salt.
Commit. The contract draws a stake-weighted executor with the Hedera PRNG and locks its bond. The executor checks the salt against the chain, runs the pinned model, and commits to a salted hash of the normalized output.
Draw. After the commit, anyone calls drawAudit. It is EOA-only, so a wrapper contract cannot re-roll it.
Verify. On an audit a verifier is drawn, locks a bond, and commits blind. Both reveal. Equal commitments agree. In the tolerance class the texts are posted and the contract computes word overlap against a threshold.
Resolve. On a mismatch a committee re-runs and the majority decides. A wrong executor is slashed and the buyer refunded in full. Every stalled stage has an expire path that refunds the buyer and penalizes only the missing party.
Committee, canaries and demo scenarios
Committee of 3 (the contract default): the smallest committee with a real majority, so one faulty member cannot decide a dispute. A job therefore needs 5 eligible operators: executor, verifier and three members.
Canary jobs: the gateway pays for a few jobs a day from a separate canary account, through the same public x402 path, using inputs with known answers (data/canaries/<id>.wav|png plus <id>.ref.txt). Results are published only as aggregates (GET /v1/canaries). Canaries measure pool accuracy and never slash anyone.
Demo scenarios: with DEMO_MODE, the console's attack lab applies one-click presets to the demo operators: honest, audited, garbage, smaller model, truncation, replay, silent executor, hidden answer, verifier no-show, committee no-show, collusion with a challenge, and a wrongful challenge.
Bond sizing
Deterrence:  B ≥ c / (p · π) − F        (worst cheat on the measured workload)
Fairness:    B ≤ m / (p · fp)
c compute saved by cheating, p audit rate, π catch rate, F fee, m margin, fp false-alarm rate. ModelRegistry.setModel and createJob revert if no bond satisfies both.

projects.title: on-word
projects.description: A forum where 1 verified human equals 1 locked wallet on Arkiv with a Web2-feel UI.
projects.project_description: Kin is a feature-complete V1 Web3 forum designed with a smooth, Web2-feel user interface that conceals underlying blockchain complexities. The platform enforces a strict 1 verified human to 1 locked wallet model using World ID integration. All posts and comments live directly on Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) backed by paid lifetimes. Posts offer flexible durations including 1-hour (for testing expiry), 1-day, 3-day, and 5-day lifetimes, while comments maintain a fixed 1-day duration. The main feed displays a 180-character body excerpt beneath each title, with the full body accessible in the thread view. Write authentication and signups are cryptographically secured via single-use 10-minute server nonces signed using personal_sign. The codebase is fully verified with green builds, passing 64/64 Vitest test suites, and clean TypeScript compilation (npx tsc --noEmit).
projects.how_its_made: Built with Next.js and TypeScript, On-Word interfaces with Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) and utilizes a funded sponsor wallet (tGLM) for transaction execution and schema writes. Sybil resistance is achieved through World ID via the IDKit widget, binding verified identities permanently to wallets. Security is reinforced by requiring wallet signatures (personal_sign) on fresh single-use server nonces for every signup and write operation, ensuring headers alone grant no access. The backend uses a single-server instance with file-backed registry, rate-limit, and nonce stores managed through per-path serialized writes. Feed management is handled via a versioned local cache (data/cache.json) that automatically repopulates from the chain. Live testing on Rabdi successfully validated chain connectivity, schema writes with transaction receipts, allowlist feed filtering of unregistered authors, and exhaustive 403/404 error path handling across posts, comments, edits, and extensions with zero unintended chain writes.

projects.title: AskOnly
projects.description: Answer the question. Never send the file — the permission is killed by the network, not a promise.
projects.project_description: A tenant in Mumbai is asked for a payslip to rent a flat. The landlord wants to know one thing: can this person pay ₹25,000 a month. What he receives is a PDF carrying the tenant's employer, employee ID, PAN, bank account number, home address, designation, joining date and exact salary. It goes into a WhatsApp thread, a broker's laptop and an email archive. One bit was wanted and a whole document was surrendered, because handing over the document is the only mechanism that exists. The same trade happens at HR verification, NBFC loan desks, school admissions and gig onboarding. The usual repair is a deletion promise, and that repair is not available. Broadbent and Islam (TCC 2020) proved certified deletion is impossible with classical information, because classical ciphertexts can be copied. What the industry actually ships as proof of deletion is NIST SP 800-88r2 §4.6: a certificate listing the name, job title and phone number of the person who says they did it. India's DPDP Act §8(7) makes erasure on withdrawal enforceable to ₹250 crore, and the ability to demonstrate it does not exist. So deletion is the wrong primitive. Non-collection is the right one: you cannot prove you deleted it, you can prove you never held it. AskOnly is built entirely around that swap. How it works, as two parties with two wallets. The owner connects a wallet; their address is their identity. A document is encrypted in their browser — AES-GCM-256, key derived by PBKDF2 at 210,000 iterations from a passphrase that never leaves the page — and the ciphertext is written to Arkiv as an entity carrying its own death block. Each party's wallet signs one EIP-712 session per browser, good for a week, naming a key in that browser, and from then on that key signs with no popup. The server checks the session against the wallet and the action against the session, and every record keeps both signatures. The owner signs one grant: this reviewer, until this time, and this key in my browser may answer them. That is the only decision the owner makes. The reviewer signs EIP-712 requests under any permission they hold, so each question lands as askonly.request state=pending with no popup. Because only the owner's device holds the passphrase, only the owner's browser can answer, and it does so by itself: it decrypts locally, sends the fewest lines that can settle the question to a glm-5.3 enclave on 0G Private Compute, widens only if those cannot, and signs the answer back with the key the grant named. The reviewer never holds the passphrase, the document key or the document. The server pays the Arkiv gas and runs verifyTypedData on every seal, grant, request and answer before it writes, so the operator can pay for those records but cannot author one. The owner's browser checks the same signatures before it pays to answer, so a server that invents a question gets nothing answered. Refusals are not signed, and the reviewer's screen does not re-check answers yet; the README's "What we don't claim" section says so. Two sponsors, two jobs nothing else does. Arkiv holds the capability, and the capability's $expiresAt is the permission's life: when it runs out, nothing has to remember to switch it off and no job has to run. Ending one early is a signed revoke. 0G is the only reader: a model in an Intel TDX enclave is the first universal adapter from unsigned, unstructured Indian paper to one bit, which is why ZK credentials never reached payslips. What is genuinely novel is the asymmetry underneath. Arkiv emits an event when an entity's life is extended and emits nothing at all when one expires. Letting a permission die is silent and free; keeping one alive is a signed, timestamped, publicly observable act. Everywhere else, retention is the default and deletion is the thing you must evidence — impossibly. Here deletion is the default and retention is the thing you have to explain. Live: https://askonly.vercel.app — ask its sample payslip anything and a real 0G TeeML enclave answers, with the request id. The full two-party app runs on your own machine at localhost:5173, the one browser origin 0G's router accepts; the README shows how.
projects.how_its_made: Partner technologies. Arkiv holds every record AskOnly keeps: the encrypted document, the permission, each question, each answer and each refusal, and a permission's $expiresAt is its lifetime, enforced by the network. 0G Private Computer is the only thing that ever reads document lines: glm-5.3 inside an Intel TDX enclave, called from the owner's browser, with every answer carrying its 0G request id. Stack. A Node ≥22.10 server with no framework. Arkiv Rabdi (chain 7794095, 2 s blocks) via @arkiv-network/sdk@1.0.1 with viem@2.x; five askonly.* schemas; writing wallet 0x4CA8176777D44B76235684b63334088C618994e4. Solidity and Hardhat for AskOnlyGate.sol and MockENSRegistry.sol, an ENSv2 role gate that is built and tested but not used by the app, with 19 contract tests, deployed to Sepolia and verified by reading the constructor values back — AskOnlyGate 0xc0Aa8494d24EB40878cE9B3505Fe3023C75CF204, MockENSRegistry 0x782E197F213c7eb04D578459a3b42bE861aC2E88. ENSv2 ETHRegistry at 0xd4ebcbbdf463c9c45784603db0ddd499bc44a8b4 on Sepolia. 0G Private Compute at https://router-api.0g.ai/v1, glm-5.3, Intel TDX / dstack, trust mode private. Front end is React 19 with Vite, wagmi and viem, using WebCrypto (AES-GCM-256, PBKDF2 at 210,000 iterations) and eth_signTypedData_v4; EIP-712 verification server-side in src/auth/typed.mjs. Self-hosted variable woff2 — EB Garamond for display, Figtree for UI, Geist Mono for every hash and address. No key ships in the repo. Six things learned the hard way, each of which changed the code: 0G's CORS allowlist is per exact origin, including the port. http://localhost:5173 gets Access-Control-Allow-Origin back; :4319, :5174, :8080, :8000, :4200 and the deployed Vercel origin all get 403. The earlier mistake was trusting a 204 preflight — a 204 without the ACAO header still fails in a real browser, and only loading an actual page revealed Failed to fetch. On any other port the browser cannot reach the enclave, and the app does not fall back to relaying through the server, which would reintroduce exactly the trusted middleman this design exists to remove. Hence npm start serves on 5173 and nowhere else. watchEntityEvents is a chain-wide firehose, and nothing documents it as one. It has no schema, owner or key filter — .ownedBy() and .createdBy() exist on the query builder, which makes it natural to assume the subscription has them. Measured on unfiltered subscriptions: 8 events in 20 s with 0 of them ours, then 45 events in 24 s with 1 ours — 44 belonged to strangers. Unfiltered, the retention monitor shows unrelated wallets' retention as if it were the data subject's, which is not merely wrong output but a false accusation. src/arkiv/watch.mjs now filters client-side, reports the drop count (GET /api/retention) as the evidence that the filter is load-bearing, and throws rather than starting unfiltered. The 0G enclave signature endpoint does not exist. The receipt was designed around an enclave signature verified against the provider's on-chain signer. Eight path shapes were probed with a live chatcmpl id: all 404. The design changed instead of the claim: the asker signs the question before anything is answered, and the owner's browser signs the answer, binding the question hash, the answer hash and 0G's request id. 0G cannot prove the enclave said it; we can prove the landlord asked and what they were told, which is the record DPDP Rules 2025 First Schedule Part B item 3 actually requires. Arkiv writes need typed value tags, not just query predicates. The docs are emphatic about str() / addr() / u64() in predicates; createEntity values need them too. The first write failed with Column "owner": a addr column, but the value is a str. Write addr(...) around the value — an unusually good error that names the column, both types and the fix. What made it cost anything is that a bare JS string is accepted for a str column, so partial tagging appears to work right up to the first non-string column. Every value is now tagged, strings included. Load-balanced RPC can serve two reads from nodes at different heights. On Sepolia, two eth_calls issued back to back right after a write returned mayAsk = true while permittedSets returned income = false in the same breath — a self-contradictory answer. The fix generalises: pin every group of reads that must agree to a single block number, and throw if two pinned reads of the same fact still disagree rather than quietly picking one. extendEntity takes an object, and the positional form produced a false pass. It is extendEntity({ entityKey, expiration }, txParams). The positional form throws InvalidExpiryError, so the test asserting "every operation on a dead entity fails" passed while proving nothing. A false proof is worse than a missing one; the test now uses the object form and prints each failure's reason beside it, so a pass for the wrong reason shows. Related sharp edge: str is 128 bytes, not characters — ₹ costs 3 bytes and मियाद is 5 characters and 15 bytes — so fitStr() truncates on a code-point boundary. One more worth stating: rabdi({ accessKey }) path-encodes the access key into the RPC URL, so every error leaving the Arkiv layer is scrubbed of ark_live_* and of URLs before it can reach a log, a terminal or a UI toast. The hosted landing page at askonly.vercel.app is a static Vite build plus one Vercel function (web/api/ask.js). It runs the app's own line picker and enclave call on a public sample payslip, because 0G's router rejects browser calls from any origin but localhost:5173.

Because only the owner's device holds the passphrase, only the owner's browser can answer, and it does so by itself: it decrypts locally, sends the fewest lines that can settle the question to a glm-5.3 enclave on 0G Private Compute, widens only if those cannot, and signs the answer back with the key the grant named. The reviewer never holds the passphrase, the document key or the document. The server pays the Arkiv gas and runs verifyTypedData on every seal, grant, request and answer before it writes, so the operator can pay for those records but cannot author one. The owner's browser checks the same signatures before it pays to answer, so a server that invents a question gets nothing answered. Refusals are not signed, and the reviewer's screen does not re-check answers yet; the README's "What we don't claim" section says so.

Two sponsors, two jobs nothing else does. Arkiv holds the capability, and the capability's $expiresAt is the permission's life: when it runs out, nothing has to remember to switch it off and no job has to run. Ending one early is a signed revoke. 0G is the only reader: a model in an Intel TDX enclave is the first universal adapter from unsigned, unstructured Indian paper to one bit, which is why ZK credentials never reached payslips.

What is genuinely novel is the asymmetry underneath. Arkiv emits an event when an entity's life is extended and emits nothing at all when one expires. Letting a permission die is silent and free; keeping one alive is a signed, timestamped, publicly observable act. Everywhere else, retention is the default and deletion is the thing you must evidence — impossibly. Here deletion is the default and retention is the thing you have to explain.

Live: https://askonly.vercel.app — ask its sample payslip anything and a real 0G TeeML enclave answers, with the request id. The full two-party app runs on your own machine at localhost:5173, the one browser origin 0G's router accepts; the README shows how.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Partner technologies. Arkiv holds every record AskOnly keeps: the encrypted document, the permission, each question, each answer and each refusal, and a permission's $expiresAt is its lifetime, enforced by the network. 0G Private Computer is the only thing that ever reads document lines: glm-5.3 inside an Intel TDX enclave, called from the owner's browser, with every answer carrying its 0G request id.

Stack. A Node ≥22.10 server with no framework. Arkiv Rabdi (chain 7794095, 2 s blocks) via @arkiv-network/sdk@1.0.1 with viem@2.x; five askonly.* schemas; writing wallet 0x4CA8176777D44B76235684b63334088C618994e4. Solidity and Hardhat for AskOnlyGate.sol and MockENSRegistry.sol, an ENSv2 role gate that is built and tested but not used by the app, with 19 contract tests, deployed to Sepolia and verified by reading the constructor values back — AskOnlyGate 0xc0Aa8494d24EB40878cE9B3505Fe3023C75CF204, MockENSRegistry 0x782E197F213c7eb04D578459a3b42bE861aC2E88. ENSv2 ETHRegistry at 0xd4ebcbbdf463c9c45784603db0ddd499bc44a8b4 on Sepolia. 0G Private Compute at https://router-api.0g.ai/v1, glm-5.3, Intel TDX / dstack, trust mode private. Front end is React 19 with Vite, wagmi and viem, using WebCrypto (AES-GCM-256, PBKDF2 at 210,000 iterations) and eth_signTypedData_v4; EIP-712 verification server-side in src/auth/typed.mjs. Self-hosted variable woff2 — EB Garamond for display, Figtree for UI, Geist Mono for every hash and address. No key ships in the repo.

Six things learned the hard way, each of which changed the code:

1. 0G's CORS allowlist is per exact origin, including the port. http://localhost:5173 gets Access-Control-Allow-Origin back; :4319, :5174, :8080, :8000, :4200 and the deployed Vercel origin all get 403. The earlier mistake was trusting a 204 preflight — a 204 without the ACAO header still fails in a real browser, and only loading an actual page revealed Failed to fetch. On any other port the browser cannot reach the enclave, and the app does not fall back to relaying through the server, which would reintroduce exactly the trusted middleman this design exists to remove. Hence npm start serves on 5173 and nowhere else.

2. watchEntityEvents is a chain-wide firehose, and nothing documents it as one. It has no schema, owner or key filter — .ownedBy() and .createdBy() exist on the query builder, which makes it natural to assume the subscription has them. Measured on unfiltered subscriptions: 8 events in 20 s with 0 of them ours, then 45 events in 24 s with 1 ours — 44 belonged to strangers. Unfiltered, the retention monitor shows unrelated wallets' retention as if it were the data subject's, which is not merely wrong output but a false accusation. src/arkiv/watch.mjs now filters client-side, reports the drop count (GET /api/retention) as the evidence that the filter is load-bearing, and throws rather than starting unfiltered.

3. The 0G enclave signature endpoint does not exist. The receipt was designed around an enclave signature verified against the provider's on-chain signer. Eight path shapes were probed with a live chatcmpl id: all 404. The design changed instead of the claim: the asker signs the question before anything is answered, and the owner's browser signs the answer, binding the question hash, the answer hash and 0G's request id. 0G cannot prove the enclave said it; we can prove the landlord asked and what they were told, which is the record DPDP Rules 2025 First Schedule Part B item 3 actually requires.

4. Arkiv writes need typed value tags, not just query predicates. The docs are emphatic about str() / addr() / u64() in predicates; createEntity values need them too. The first write failed with Column "owner": a addr column, but the value is a str. Write addr(...) around the value — an unusually good error that names the column, both types and the fix. What made it cost anything is that a bare JS string is accepted for a str column, so partial tagging appears to work right up to the first non-string column. Every value is now tagged, strings included.

5. Load-balanced RPC can serve two reads from nodes at different heights. On Sepolia, two eth_calls issued back to back right after a write returned mayAsk = true while permittedSets returned income = false in the same breath — a self-contradictory answer. The fix generalises: pin every group of reads that must agree to a single block number, and throw if two pinned reads of the same fact still disagree rather than quietly picking one.

6. extendEntity takes an object, and the positional form produced a false pass. It is extendEntity({ entityKey, expiration }, txParams). The positional form throws InvalidExpiryError, so the test asserting "every operation on a dead entity fails" passed while proving nothing. A false proof is worse than a missing one; the test now uses the object form and prints each failure's reason beside it, so a pass for the wrong reason shows. Related sharp edge: str is 128 bytes, not characters — ₹ costs 3 bytes and मियाद is 5 characters and 15 bytes — so fitStr() truncates on a code-point boundary.

One more worth stating: rabdi({ accessKey }) path-encodes the access key into the RPC URL, so every error leaving the Arkiv layer is scrubbed of ark_live_* and of URLs before it can reach a log, a terminal or a UI toast.

The hosted landing page at askonly.vercel.app is a static Vite build plus one Vercel function (web/api/ask.js). It runs the app's own line picker and enclave call on a public sample payslip, because 0G's router rejects browser calls from any origin but localhost:5173.

projects.title: Siege
projects.description: Battle-test your AI agent with a bounty: talk it into paying out and the bounty is yours.
projects.project_description:
Companies and Developers are putting AI agents in charge of refunds, payouts, grants and withdrawals. The way you rob one isn't a code exploit, it's a conversation: the right sentence gets the agent to call the one tool it must never call. Siege is where a team finds that sentence before a stranger does. HOW IT WORKS
An owner puts their agent on the Grid with a bounty behind it, deposited from their own Hedera wallet. Attackers (people, or AI agents of their own) pay a small fee per attempt over x402 on Hedera, get five messages, and try to talk the agent into firing its protected tool. The agent starts every attempt with no memory. If it holds, the fee is split on chain: 80% to the owner, 15% grows the pot, 5% to the arena, so every failed attack pays the owner. If it breaks, the attacker wins the whole pot, and the owner gets a verified, replayable finding: the exact conversation, the tool call it caused, and the on-chain payout. TWO WAYS TO BRING AN AGENT Publish one at /publish, with no code: write its instructions, list its tools, mark the one that moves money, connect your 0G key and deposit the pot. It's live in about three minutes. Plug in the agent you already run with our npm package, siege-guard. Three lines connect your own harness, prompt, tools and model. Nothing to host, no public URL. THREE WAYS TO ATTACK
By hand from a funded operator account; with a hosted "unit" (an AI attacker with its own Hedera account, hard spending caps, and a phone pager that asks you before it spends above a cap); or from your own code (the raid-bot example). NOTHING IS TAKEN ON FAITH
A payout only happens when the arena's verifier checks that the transcript wasn't changed (its hash) and that the 0G proxy's own record of the breaching reply shows the protected tool was really called, for that vault, that op and that turn. Only then does it sign the release, and our SiegeVault contract pays the pot. BUILT ON Hedera: x402-protected endpoint settled on testnet through the x402.org facilitator; the SiegeVault contract for pots, fee splits and payouts; an HCS topic per vault as a tamper-evident audit log; agents with their own accounts that pay with no human approving, with spending caps and human approval above the cap. 0G: every agent reply is a 0G inference (0gm-1.0) through our recording proxy, and owners pay for their agent's thinking with their own 0G credits. Arkiv: the Grid is an Arkiv query. Each vault's listing is owned by its owner's wallet, and listings and live ops expire on their own. Swarm: each op's transcript is sealed (AES-256-GCM) and stored on Swarm, referenced from its Arkiv entity, so the replay can be checked by anyone. Example: our "Lantern Fund Grants" agent reviews grant applications against a published rubric. An attacker claimed another team's busy contract as their "old v1 contract"; the agent checked the user count but never who deployed it, scored the project 8/10, and paid. The 30 ℏ pot plus the fee was released on Hedera testnet, with a replay and HashScan links.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router) with a pixel/CRT UI, a separate Node worker that holds the verifier key, SQLite via Drizzle shared by both, one Solidity contract (SiegeVault) on Hedera testnet, and a zero-dependency TypeScript SDK published to npm as siege-guard. Hedera + x402: POST /api/siege/start is an x402-protected endpoint. With no payment it answers 402 with an x402 v2 requirement (exact scheme, hedera:testnet, the vault's fee, payTo = the arena treasury). The client (@x402/fetch + @x402/hedera) signs a TransferTransaction and retries; we verify and settle through the x402.org facilitator before the op exists. Hosted units are real Hedera accounts (AccountCreateTransaction) funded by their operator's memo deposit, which the worker matches on the mirror node; they sign their own payments with no human approving, under caps reserved atomically in SQLite, the x402 client's own per-payment cap, and their account balance. A cap hit pages the owner's phone; approve tops up on chain. Held fees are forwarded into SiegeVault (recordAttempt, split 80/15/5 on chain); breaches pay out through release() with an EIP-712 signature from the verifier. One HCS topic per vault is the audit log (ids, hashes, amounts, never text), ordered through an outbox the worker drains. The contract is Sourcify-verified so HashScan decodes every event. 0G: every guard reply is a chat completion on 0G Private Computer made through our own OpenAI-compatible proxy, which records request id, vault, op, turn, prompt hash and whether the protected tool was called. The verifier refuses to sign a payout unless the breaching reply's request id is in that record. Owners paste a pc.0g.ai management key; we mint a per-guard sk- key so their guard bills their own credits and the vault page shows the balance dropping. Plugged-in agents route their model calls through the same proxy, and their prompt hash is pinned: a changed prompt closes the vault. Arkiv + Swarm: vaults, their live status and each op are entities on the Rabdi testnet. The Grid's filters and sorts are the Arkiv query (printed under the grid with its block). A vault's listing is created readonly and transferred to the owner's wallet (the EVM alias of their Hedera account), so only they can delist it; status entities stay arena-owned; op entities expire on their own. Transcripts are AES-GCM sealed under a per-op key, uploaded to Swarm through the public gateway (null stamp, gateway-stamped), kept alive by the worker, and read back on the replay page with the hash checked against Arkiv and HCS.

projects.title: USend
projects.description: A USDT wallet you dial. The phone number is the account. No app and no internet.
projects.project_description: USend is a USDT wallet you open by dialing a shortcode. The phone number is the account. There is no app, no internet on the handset, and no smartphone. A feature phone is enough. The first time a number dials, the session asks for a 4-digit PIN, then asks for the same PIN again. When the two match, that number gets a wallet. Until then, nobody can pay it. The menu is then Send, Receive, Balance, and Exit. Send asks for the other person's phone number, an amount, and the PIN. Receive shows the number people should pay, plus a 6-digit code for when the number stays private. A feature phone cannot type a chain address, so the phone number is what moves the money. USend holds the keys and pays the gas. Settlement is prize USDT on Whitechain Sepolia. One payment is at most 100, stays open for 15 minutes, and the fee is 0. The live dial is the Africa's Talking sandbox shortcode 38471618#.
projects.how_its_made: The handset never holds a key or a gas token. Africa's Talking posts each USSD hop to a Next.js route, POST /api/ussd. The route answers HTTP 200 as text/plain, starting with CON while the session continues and END when it finishes. The keypad on the site posts to the same route. A new phone does not get a menu. The first completed PIN is hashed with scrypt and saved with the number. The wallet key is not derived from the phone digits. Registration assigns the next index, and viem derives the key from a custody seed, that index, and a salt. The phone number is only the label on that row. Sending reuses the existing contracts. Looking up the phone, or a 6-digit code, opens a 15-minute invoice on GhostInvoiceRegistry. The sender's custodied key signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization for prize USDT. A relayer calls GhostGateway.settle and pays WBT, so the phone's WBT balance stays at zero. The token is prize USDT on Whitechain Sepolia, chain 1874. Contracts are Solidity, tested with Foundry. The app is Next.js 16, React 19, and viem.

projects.title: HAB-1
projects.description: A high-altitude balloon whose data, AI decisions and sales anyone can verify
projects.project_description: High-altitude balloons record vastly more data than they can transmit over radio links. A balloon that flies to 19.6 km records 51 GB but can only send 29 kB down — one byte for every 1.7 million. So it has to decide on board, alone. The problem: nobody can prove what it saw, nobody can audit what it decided, and it cannot get paid for what it measures. HAB-1 answers three questions: SEE (Arkiv): the beacon signs every radio frame with Ed25519. Every verified packet, measured wind reading and landing prediction is an Arkiv entity with indexed fields, owned by the receiver that heard it. Anyone can query the data without trusting our server. The public website reads Arkiv directly and keeps working even if our infrastructure goes offline. THINK (0G): the payload makes checkpoint decisions (burst detection, thermal management, frame prioritization) using TEE-attested 0G models. Each decision carries 0G's request ID and is cryptographically signed on the Pi. The full episode log is stored on 0G Storage with its root on an EpisodeRegistry contract on 0G Chain. Anyone can verify every signature in their browser. If 0G is unreachable, the payload safe-stops rather than inventing a decision. GET PAID (Hedera): measured data is sold over x402 on Hedera. An AI agent with spending limits buys it with no human approval, and is not charged when no verified data exists. We also run x402 between two radios over LoRa: the seller answers "402 Payment Required" over the air, the buyer's chip signs the Hedera payment with its own key, and data is released only after settlement.
projects.how_its_made: Hardware: beagle bone ai board , PI 5 with MS5611/BMP280 barometers, NEO-M9N GPS, C270 camera. Two Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V3 boards (ESP32-S3, SX1262) on 866.1 MHz using Arduino C++ firmware. Beacon signs 28-byte frames every 12 s with Ed25519 (weather Crypto library); every seventh slot carries a 94-byte signature frame. 4-byte salted hashes prevent forgery (salt revealed only in signature). Planned duty cycle 2.28% inside India's 2.5% licence-exempt band limit. Ground station: Python verifier checks signatures before anything enters the system. Node.js publisher writes verified packets to Arkiv using @arkiv-network/sdk 1.0.0 with typed, indexed schemas (run, seq, altitude, lat/lon, verdict). Each receiver owns records under its own wallet; entities expire after 7–30 days. The map queries Arkiv's lat/lon index in ~0.5 s with no backend. Prediction: reimplemented CUSF Tawhiri flight model (RK4, drag descent, NASA density) with archived GFS winds. Re-predicts from every fix using measured winds. All 128 predictions and 144 wind readings published to Arkiv as queryable entities. 0G integration: pi/agent.py calls 0G decision models (Vela 2.0 9B, Laya for frame validation, qwen3-vl-plus for vision) with verify_tee flag. Every decision signed with Pi's Ed25519 key and fsynced. zg/upload.mjs stores episode log on 0G Storage; EpisodeRegistry contract on 0G Galileo holds root and public key. Browser verification runs against stored log independently. Hedera x402: server.mjs exposes x402 endpoint settling HBAR on testnet via x402.org facilitator (also tested Blocky402 with single setting change). agent.mjs enforces per-payment caps, total budget, merchant allowlist. Every settlement logged to HCS topic. Notable hacks: (1) x402 over LoRa — ESP32 builds Hedera transfer protobuf by hand, signs with its own Ed25519 key (which is also its Hedera account). (2) Offline voucher mode settles later from a pre-signed allowance. (3) 0G decisions reach offline payload: ground packs answer into 27-byte LoRa uplink with HMAC tag. (4) Station bridge streams live events to deck.gl console; public Vercel site follows live session from Arkiv with no direct connection.

projects.title: Proof Work — Errand
projects.description: AI agents hire World-verified humans for real-world tasks, with HBAR rewards and evidence review.
projects.project_description: ProofWork lets AI agents hire World-verified humans for tasks that require someone on the ground. An owner funds an HBAR budget pot, and their agent connects through MCP to post gigs. Workers discover tasks through Arkiv, verify their humanity with World ID, and submit photos or answers in a shared thread. For example, a remote buyer could request current photos of a used camera before deciding whether to travel. The agent reviews the evidence before approving payment through Hedera escrow. World handles identity, Arkiv supports discovery, and Hedera supports the budget and payout flow. ProofWork is a testnet prototype: an earlier deployment produced a test payout, while the latest escrow deployment still needs end-to-end validation. Evidence review remains the agent’s responsibility, and full dispute resolution is not yet implemented.
projects.how_its_made: We built ProofWork with Next.js, React and TypeScript, using Tailwind CSS and HeroUI for the interface. RainbowKit, wagmi and viem connect wallets to Hedera testnet, while Solidity contracts handle the HBAR budget and escrow flow. World OIDC supports owner sign-in, IDKit verifies workers before they claim tasks, and Arkiv provides the public task feed. Application state is stored in local JSON files on the MCP server. Agents connect through the Model Context Protocol SDK to post gigs, monitor updates and review submissions in message threads. Photos, attachments and structured answers give them evidence to assess before calling all_satisfied to approve payment. We used Foundry for contract development and Sharp for HEIC photo conversion. Important fixes included HBAR unit conversions and duplicate-payout protection; the latest escrow deployment still needs a complete end-to-end test.

projects.title: Whiskey Vault
projects.description: Anti-counterfeit provenance for rare whiskey: certificates on IPFS, notarized on Ethereum.
projects.project_description: Whiskey Vault is a decentralized provenance and authentication platform for rare whiskies, single malt casks, distillery archives and high-value spirit investments. Counterfeiting is a serious problem in this market. Cask ownership deeds, lab assay certificates, spectrometer fingerprints and bottle serial numbers are usually paper or PDFs that are easy to forge, and a buyer has no way to verify them. Whiskey Vault fixes that by giving every cask or bottle a cryptographic chain of custody. A distillery or collector signs up, uploads a certificate or deed, and the file is pinned to IPFS. Its content hash, title, description, author, tags, timestamp, and the block and transaction hashes are then recorded on an Ethereum smart contract. Anyone can later search by distillery (Macallan, Springbank, Yamazaki, Bowmore and others), vintage, cask category or blockchain hash. They can open a record and verify that the document is exactly what was registered and when. Collectors and distilleries get role-based accounts. Buyers, auctioneers and insurers get a public, tamper-evident record they can check without trusting a middleman. The UI uses an amber and aged-oak theme with interactive golden vapors, so it feels like a luxury product and not a block explorer.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: Node.js and Express.js backend serving a REST API (signup, login, upload, search, record lookup, stats, health), with a browser frontend animated with GSAP. Auth uses JWT sessions with bcrypt-salted password hashing and role-based permissions. The whole thing is containerized with Docker and docker-compose, and an automated verification suite runs with npm test. Smart contract: A Solidity contract (DocumentVault.sol / WhiskeyVault.sol) stores each provenance record on-chain. uploadDocument takes the IPFS CID, title, description, size, timestamp, author, tags, block hash and tx hash. getDocument and getDocumentCount let the app read records back. It targets the Ethereum Sepolia testnet through an Infura endpoint. Storage and flow: When a certificate is uploaded, the server pins it to IPFS through Pinata, gets back a CID, sends the metadata to the contract, and stores the transaction hash and block confirmation alongside the record. MongoDB Atlas holds the searchable metadata index, and the debounced search UI queries it. The chain and IPFS remain the source of truth. Hacky bit worth mentioning: I built a triple-fallback architecture so the app works with zero configuration, which matters for judges who just run git clone && npm start. Each external dependency has a local stand-in that activates when its API keys are missing: MongoDB Atlas falls back to a resilient local JSON ledger.
Pinata IPFS falls back to local storage keyed by deterministic SHA-256 multihashes.
Ethereum Sepolia falls back to an embedded local cryptographic ledger that mimics block and transaction hashes. The /api/health endpoint reports which mode each layer is running in, so it’s always clear what is real on-chain and what is simulated.
