projects.title: FightClub.hack
projects.description: Hackathon projects become AI fighters. Agents test them for real; AI judges pick the winner live.
projects.project_description: Hackathons get hundreds of projects and judges get minutes each, so they score the demo, not the product. FightClub.hack turns every project into an AI fighter. When a team submits, AI agents spawned on 0G use the live app on a real laptop and phone, read the code, and fact-check every claim in the demo. Three AI judges with personas the organizer tunes (product, engineering, investor) score that evidence. Then similar projects fight 1v1 in a live arena. Every punch cites evidence, and spectators bet testnet tokens on the winner.
projects.how_its_made: A team submits once. We spin up a swarm of AI agents on 0G that test the live app on real devices, fact-check the demo against the code, and hand everything to three AI judges. Then two projects fight it out in an arena and people bet FILTER on who wins. Spawning the agents. Every submission kicks off a pipeline: code, demo, live test, fact-check, judges. Anything that doesn't depend on something else runs in parallel. Code, demo and the live test start together, fact-check waits for code and demo, judges wait for everything. Each step streams its progress to the project page, so you can literally watch the agents work. Every model call goes to 0G Compute on 0G's own TEE model, and we check each response's TEE signature against the signer 0G has on chain. Agentic testing on real devices. The part we're proudest of. It runs on Mozark's device infra through their test hub. First an explorer agent crawls the live app and reads what's actually there. Then a planner agent writes the test steps from two sources: the screens the demo video shows, and the main flows in the code, like login → profile → payment → history. We run them on a laptop and a phone at the same time, recorded, with a screenshot per step, plus a health pass for load time, console errors, failed requests and broken layouts. A deny-list stops the agent from ever really paying, staking or connecting a wallet. A blocked step is reported, never faked. Demo + fact-check. We keep our own copy of the demo video (Loom, HLS or a direct file), transcribe it and pull keyframes. The fact-checker reads a line-numbered pack of the repo, cloned shallow with hooks off and never executed, and checks every claim. Every file:line it cites is verified against the clone. If the line doesn't exist, the claim gets downgraded. No made-up receipts. Judges. Three personas (product, engineering, investor) with weights the organizer tunes. They score the same evidence in parallel and never see each other's scores. Bad JSON gets one repair try, otherwise no score. Prediction arena. Similar projects meet first: we pair them on embeddings, tracks and tech, then run a perfect matching. Every line of the fight is generated on 0G: a UI face-off on both apps' screens, then each round has a judge question, answers, challenges, rebuttals and three sealed scorecards. Bets go into BettingPools on Base Sepolia in FILTER, our ERC-20 backed by test ETH. It's pari-mutuel: 70% to winning bettors, 20% to the winning team, 10% to the platform. Contracts are immutable, betting locks at chain time, and bets can be gasless with a signed message. A payout bot claims for winners, but it only pays gas; the contract decides who gets what. Where it lives. Arkiv is our only database: every record, with judge scorecards written read-only. Videos, recordings and screenshots sit on 0G Storage, and each file's hash is indexed on Arkiv. Every fighter gets <project>.hackarena.eth with its score, and its win-loss record is tallied only from matches the contract finalized. Hacky bits 0G's router doesn't report TEE status for sealed providers, so we verify the signature ourselves. The 0G Storage SDK's download proof is a TODO, so we recompute the Merkle root on every download. Arkiv entities cap at 128 KiB, so we gzip records, split them into 120 KB parts and dedupe by sha256. The public Base Sepolia RPC refuses wide log queries, so the payout bot scans 200 blocks at a time.

projects.title: White Money
projects.description: Accept USDT on Whitechain with hosted checkout and direct wallet settlement.
projects.project_description: White Money gives merchants a way to accept USDT on Whitechain. A shopper pays from their wallet, and the payment goes directly to the merchant’s payout wallet. Merchants can create hosted checkout sessions, share payment links, or embed checkout in their own storefront. The dashboard brings payments, webhook deliveries, and full or partial refunds into one place. Chai & Co., our demo shop, shows how a merchant can confirm an order automatically after receiving a signed payment webhook. Merchants can also require World ID proof of humanity before shoppers pay.
projects.how_its_made: We built the merchant dashboard, checkout, and demo storefront with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. A Solidity PaymentRouter on Whitechain routes USDT to the registered payout wallet and links payments and refunds to their orders. We use viem and wagmi for contract and wallet interactions, and PostgreSQL with Drizzle for checkout sessions and delivery state. A background worker matches onchain events to the expected merchant, order, and amount before sending signed payment and refund webhooks. The demo store verifies signatures and deduplicates events before updating orders. For stores that enable buyer verification, World ID’s IDKit collects a proof in the checkout. The backend verifies it against the specific checkout session before unlocking payment.

projects.title: FacePay
projects.description: Face-based USDT payments on Whitechain for merchants, invoices and everyday purchases.
projects.project_description: FacePay is a face-based USDT payment platform built on Whitechain that makes digital payments simple for both customers and businesses. Customers can make payments using facial recognition without needing to open a crypto wallet, manually enter wallet addresses or deal with blockchain transaction fees. FacePay connects facial recognition with a customer's payment setup and uses Whitechain to process USDT transactions. Its relayer handles gas fees, so customers do not need WBT to complete payments. For businesses, FacePay provides a complete payment infrastructure to accept and manage USDT. Merchants can create payment requests, generate unique payment links, collect invoice payments, track transactions and process full or partial refunds through a single dashboard. They can integrate FacePay into their products using its SDK and APIs. We see strong use cases across cafes, restaurants, small retailers, online businesses and high-volume payment environments such as metro stations, stadiums and event venues. For example, a metro operator could configure fixed-denomination fares, while a cafe could accept everyday USDT payments without managing blockchain infrastructure. Our goal is to make Whitechain useful in everyday commerce by giving businesses a practical way to accept USDT and giving customers a simpler way to pay. FacePay combines face-based checkout, gas-sponsored transactions and onchain payment records into one merchant payment platform.

projects.title: receipts
projects.description: AI agent reviews that only count if you actually paid the agent and are a real human.
projects.project_description: Receipts is a review system for AI agents where bots cannot outvote humans. ERC-8004 gives every agent an onchain reputation, but anyone can write to it and the score is a plain average. We attacked it to prove the point: on a mainnet fork, six fresh wallets drag a live agent's score from 50 to 77 for just gas. Across 10,000 random attack simulations the registry mean gets pushed past every honest rating 9,126 times. Receipts fixes the write path with three rules. One, only our ReviewGateway contract can write Receipts feedback, and it needs a signature from our server which checks the reviewer first. Two, one review per human per agent. World ID 4.0 proves you're a person, and the nullifier is spent onchain so you can't review the same agent twice even with 100 wallets. Three, paying the agent (USDC through our ReceiptSettler) gives your review up to 2x weight, but payment proves money, not identity, so a paid review still needs World ID. Scores are a weighted median over verified humans. In all 4,185 trials where attackers held under half the weight, the registry mean broke 3,311 times. Ours broke zero. That's math, not luck. All of it is live on Sepolia with real reviews on the actual ERC-8004 registry, and the public record is on Arkiv so anyone can read scores without our server. The app has a review wizard, per-agent reputation, and a live attack gauntlet you can run yourself. We're honest about limits too: the gateway trusts one server key, and wallet-only reviews are shown but never counted.
projects.how_its_made: Three layers: Solidity contracts (Foundry), a TypeScript Record Server (Hono), and a React/Vite web app. The contracts are ReviewGateway, ReceiptSettler and NullifierRegistry, deployed on Sepolia and wired to the real ERC-8004 registries. The gateway is the only writer of Receipts feedback, and it checks an EIP-712 attestation signed by our server before calling giveFeedback. ReceiptSettler takes USDC through EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization, and the nonce is keccak256 of agent, orderId, chainId and the settler address, so a receipt can't be replayed on another chain or claimed for a different agent. Fun gotcha: testnet USDC's EIP-712 domain name is "USDC" version "2", not "USD Coin" like docs suggest, which cost us an hour of invalid signatures. World ID 4.0 is the identity layer, and we used the current API, not the legacy one: the server signs rp_context on the backend, the browser only relays it, and we use the proofOfHuman preset with a programmatically created action per agent, so each agent has its own nullifier space. Nullifiers are checked twice, UNIQUE(nullifier, action) in the database and spent onchain in NullifierRegistry. One human, one review, per agent, no matter how many wallets. ERC-8004 stores feedbackURI and hash as event-only data, so our reputation engine reads reviews back from Sepolia logs rather than contract storage, and recomputes the weighted median from raw events. Scoring only activates after five distinct humans. Arkiv is the public record. A publisher module (dedicated key, separate from the attestation signer) writes receipts.review/v1 and receipts.reputation/v1 entities to the Rabdi testnet with provenance labels and expiry. The agent page queries Rabdi straight from the browser and re-verifies that keccak256 of the stored review text equals the feedbackHash in the Sepolia event, on every page load. Hackiest part we're proud of: the attack gauntlet. A fork test where six fresh wallets corrupt a live agent's score, plus a 10,000-trial simulator with a fixed seed (8004, obviously) that scores every trial twice, registry mean vs our median, so judges can reproduce our exact numbers.

projects.title: Unlink
projects.description: A Tornado Cash withdrawal proof that pays its own gas through the alt mempool without any Relayer.
projects.project_description: Unlink lets a Tornado Cash withdrawal proof authorise its own payout. Anyone can submit the transaction, the recipient doesn't need any ETH, and the gas fee is paid directly from the amount being withdrawn. There's no designated relayer involved. We built it on the EIP-8141 frame-transaction devnet using the ERC-8421 alternative mempool. Interestingly, the public mempool rejects these transactions, and that's exactly why the alternative mempool matters. The problem we're trying to solve has existed since Tornado Cash launched in 2019. When someone withdraws from a mixer, they ideally want to receive their funds at a fresh address that can't be linked to the original deposit. But a fresh address has no ETH to pay for gas. The usual solution is a relayer: you generate your withdrawal proof, send it to a server someone else operates, and they submit the transaction using their funded wallet in exchange for a fee. It works, but introduces a dependency that shouldn't really need to exist. The relayer sees your withdrawal first, can refuse to process it, log requests, censor users, or simply go offline. It also becomes an obvious centralised service for regulators to target. We wanted to see if we could remove that dependency entirely. EIP-8141 makes this possible by changing how transactions are authorised. Instead of requiring an ECDSA signature from an account holding ETH, a transaction can contain multiple frames, with a smart contract deciding whether the transaction is valid. This means we can use the Tornado Cash zero-knowledge withdrawal proof itself as the authorisation. Unlink uses a single contract, UnlinkAccount , which sits in front of the existing Tornado Cash pool without modifying the pool or its circuits. The account holds a small ETH float to cover gas upfront and acts as both the sender and payer of a two-frame transaction. The first frame is a VERIFY frame. The account decodes the withdrawal calldata, verifies the Groth16 proof using Tornado Cash's original December 2019 verifying key, checks that the Merkle root exists in the pool's history, and confirms the nullifier hasn't already been spent. It also checks that the withdrawal fee covers the transaction's worst-case cost using MAX_COST from TXPARAM , and that the second frame contains exactly the same withdrawal call. The second frame is a SENDER frame that actually calls withdraw() on the original pool. The pool sends the withdrawn ETH minus the fee to the recipient and returns the fee to UnlinkAccount in the same transaction. So the account effectively fronts the gas cost and gets reimbursed from the withdrawal itself. The interesting part is that the transaction doesn't need anyone's cryptographic signature. Its signature field is literally ARBITRARY (scheme 0), with an empty signer and empty signature. The ZK proof is the authorisation. The alternative mempool is essential here, not just an implementation choice. The public EIP-8141 frame mempool limits validation to 100,000 gas and doesn't allow validation to read another contract's storage. Our verification requires roughly 289,000 gas, largely because of Groth16 verification, and needs to read two storage slots from the Tornado Cash pool. So the public mempool rejects it. ERC-8421 takes a different approach: rather than banning expensive validation or third-party storage reads, it allows them under additional economic and safety constraints. After staking 0.012 ETH in the devnet registry, UnlinkAccount gets a 1 million gas validation budget and permission to read third-party storage, with the node tracing those reads to limit how many pending transactions a state change could invalidate. For Unlink, those storage reads are quite limited. We check the pool's root history, which retains 100 roots, and the nullifier for the specific note being withdrawn. Spending one note can therefore invalidate at most the pending withdrawals attempting to spend that same note, rather than unrelated withdrawals. We also give each note its own EIP-8250 nonce lane derived from its nullifier hash. Duplicate submissions of the same note become replacements rather than spam, while withdrawals from different notes don't compete with each other. There's also no opportunity for someone watching the mempool to steal the funds. The proof's public inputs already bind the recipient, relayer, and fee, and the account checks that the execution frame matches the verified withdrawal call byte-for-byte. Someone can copy and submit the transaction, but they can't redirect the payout or increase the fee. We got the whole flow working on the devnet. Transaction 0xc517e289...36eb98 , included in block 9750 as a type 0x6 transaction, successfully withdrew 0.1 ETH to an address that had never held ETH before. The VERIFY frame used 288,806 gas, while the SENDER frame used 296,072 execution gas plus 281,520 state gas. The recipient's balance went from 0 to 0.09 ETH, and the account's ETH float increased from 0.2075 to 0.2157 ETH after receiving the withdrawal fee. The recipient didn't need to fund their address or sign a transaction with a private key. We also submitted the exact same transaction bytes to the public mempool, which rejected them with Frame transaction prefix gas budget (frames + sig cost) exceeds MAX_VERIFY_GAS , because the required budget was 450,100 gas against the public limit of 100,000. The demo shows both the successful withdrawal through the alternative mempool and the rejection through the public one. One thing worth clarifying is what we mean by "relayerless." Transactions still need to propagate through the network, and gateways, peers, and block producers are still involved. We're not claiming to remove those. What we've removed is the designated application relayer: the separate service that receives a user's withdrawal proof, decides whether to submit it, and pays the gas from its own wallet. With Unlink, users can construct and broadcast the withdrawal transaction themselves, even from a machine with no funded Ethereum account. They don't have to trust a particular service to process their withdrawal, and anyone else can submit the same transaction without being able to change where the money goes. The proof authorises the withdrawal, the contract pays for execution, and the withdrawal reimburses the contract. That's really the idea behind Unlink: making private withdrawals self-authorising, without relying on a designated relayer to execute them.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.28 using Foundry with via-IR enabled. The main contract, UnlinkAccount , extends HegotaSupport from @forshtat/hegota-support , a library built by the alternative mempool team that provides Solidity helpers for the new EIP-8141 opcodes like TXPARAM , FRAMEPARAM , SIGPARAM , FRAMEDATACOPY , and APPROVE . Everything goes through the contract's fallback() function, which dispatches based on the function selector. For withdrawals, it runs the eight validation checks and approves EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT . We also added a separate admin() path that checks whether the resolved signer from SIGPARAM matches the owner. This path stays under the public mempool's 100k gas validation limit, which let us stake the account through the registry before it had access to the alternative mempool. The owner can also use it to withdraw any remaining ETH from the account's float. One tricky part was the Groth16 verifier. We ported Tornado Cash's original 2019 Verifier.sol directly into the account, keeping the same verifying key. We couldn't just call the existing deployed verifier because its implementation uses staticcall(sub(gas(), 2000), ...) . Under the ERC-7562/8421 validation rules, the GAS opcode is only permitted when it's immediately followed by a call, so that pattern gets rejected. We had to rewrite the precompile calls to use staticcall(gas(), 6|7|8, ...) instead. The contracts have 40 Forge tests, including a fixture containing the actual proof we successfully withdrew with on the devnet, along with a mock of HegotaSupport so we could test the frame opcode interactions locally. The client is written in TypeScript using viem and tsx. It constructs the complete frame transaction with the account as both sender and payer, derives the EIP-8250 nonce key from uint256(nullifierHash) , and attaches a single ARBITRARY signature with no signer or signature bytes. It reads the keyed nonce sequence from the NONCE_MANAGER predeploy, simulates the transaction using ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction , submits it through the alternative mempool gateway, and waits for admission and eventual inclusion. Once it's mined, the client prints a breakdown of gas usage for each frame. We also added a --canonical flag that sends the exact same transaction to the public mempool so we can capture the node's actual rejection message. We ran into a strange devnet issue while building this: the gateway's mempool database ran out of disk space, so transactions would pass every admission check but fail when the gateway tried to write them, returning -32603 . We added a fallback to the miner's sidecar specifically for that error. It doesn't activate for actual validation or rule failures, since we wanted to preserve the distinction between a broken gateway and a genuinely invalid transaction. The prover ended up being one of the most interesting parts of the project, and probably where we spent the most time debugging. The devnet uses the real December 2019 Tornado Cash 0.1 ETH pool, which means we needed the original tornado-core v2.0 circuit artifacts. Newer proving keys aren't compatible with that verifier, and the correct key is only available in websnark's older binary format. The problem was that websnark's own WASM prover produced proofs that looked perfectly valid structurally but failed verification against the pool's key. The devnet operators had apparently encountered the same issue. We initially wrote a parser for the old binary proving-key format, which involved dealing with Montgomery-form field elements, points at infinity represented using x = 0 , and the absence of a polsC table. We then fixed the old snarkjs 0.1.20 prover by computing C directly on the evaluation domain as A times B. That gave us a working JavaScript prover, but proving took around 210 seconds, which wasn't great for a demo. So we started working on a Rust prover using websnark-rs , and that's where we found the actual source of the incompatibility. It turned out that snarkjs 0.1 derives its roots of unity using generator 5, while websnark and websnark-rs use generator 7. The newer ceremony key follows the generator-7 convention, but the original 2019 key expects generator 5. That tiny difference was enough to produce proofs that looked correct but never verified. Once we changed the Rust prover to compute H on the generator-5 evaluation domain, the proofs started passing the original pool's verifier. We verified them using eth_call against the actual pool before submitting any transactions. Even better, proving time dropped from roughly 210 seconds in JavaScript to about 0.2 seconds in Rust. For note generation, we use 31-byte nullifiers and secrets, Pedersen commitments through circomlibjs, and a MiMCSponge Merkle tree reconstructed from the pool's Deposit events. The frontend is built with Vite and React, with Hono powering the local API. We kept it fairly simple, with three main pages: one for depositing and withdrawing from the pool, one showing a ledger of every transaction attempt along with its per-frame gas usage, and one explaining how the system works. The API supports two backends behind the same interface. There's a mock backend that reproduces the real response shapes, timings, and even the exact public mempool rejection string, and a live backend that runs the actual Rust prover in a child process. We initially tried running proving directly, but it blocked the server's event loop, so moving it into a separate process made things much smoother. The live backend also streams job progress to the frontend using SSE. For the hosted demo, we made the mock backend run entirely inside the browser, which means we can host the site on GitHub Pages without needing a server. We intentionally went with a paper-like design using serif and monospace typography rather than a component library. Most of the project is built directly on the Ethereum Foundation alternative mempool team's stack. We used their ethrex devnet with EIP-8141 and resource-based gas accounting, the ERC-8421 gateway and sidecar, the NaiveStakingRegistry , the workshop repository, and the hegota-support library. We also ran into a few details that weren't documented and had to figure them out ourselves. For example, deploying a HegotaSupport contract takes around 12 million gas because it deploys seven helper contracts and incurs additional state gas. Sending ETH to a completely new address costs roughly 204,000 state gas, which matters a lot when you're trying to fund a fresh withdrawal recipient. We also found that the simulation RPC returns canonicalMempoolValid and canonicalMempoolViolation , rather than the field names shown in the README. These were small things individually, but they made a real difference when getting the complete flow working. There are a few implementation choices I'm particularly happy with. Instead of hardcoding some conservative gas fee, we compare the withdrawal fee directly against MAX_COST , which is the node's own worst-case solvency estimate for the transaction. That means an included withdrawal can't leave the account underfunded relative to the transaction cost. Deriving a separate nonce lane from each nullifier also means duplicate withdrawals naturally become replacements, while unrelated notes can be processed independently. And my favourite detail is still the empty signature. We spent quite a bit of time getting all the pieces to work together, but the end result is a transaction where the proof itself is enough to authorise execution. There's no user ECDSA signature, no funded recipient wallet, and no designated relayer. The proof really is the signature.

projects.title: KINETIC
projects.description: The trust layer for AI compute: community GPUs, verified results, and automatic on-chain refunds.
projects.project_description: AI agents are about to buy compute from strangers. KINETIC makes that safe. Today, if you rent a GPU from an anonymous provider, you can only hope the work was done. KINETIC removes the hope. It is a verifiable marketplace for AI compute where cheating costs money and the buyer is made whole automatically. How a job works. An agent submits a batch job: classify tickets, extract fields, tag content. KINETIC splits it into chunks, and each chunk is paid separately over x402 and only when it completes. Hidden known-answer checks and canary re-runs on 0G are mixed into the real work, and providers cannot tell them apart. A provider that fails is slashed by a quorum of verifiers. The buyer is refunded the exact amount, and the unfinished chunks reroute to honest providers. You pay only for work that passes, and no human arbiter is involved. A hub for open models. Creators publish a signed model card. A quorum of verifiers scans the weights for malware, benchmarks the model, fingerprints it and signs a Model Passport. Buyers press "Run via KINETIC" and only providers that checked the model serve it. The creator earns a royalty on every accepted chunk and nothing on refunded ones. That gives creators a way to get paid for open models without hosting them. Proof, not a mockup. KINETIC runs on live Hedera, 0G, Arkiv and Swarm testnets with five real provider nodes. Two are honest, and three cheat on purpose: one never calls a model, one stops partway through, and one goes offline holding a payment. In a recorded run, the cheater was caught and slashed. The buyer got 0.003 ℏ back and 0.997 ℏ of the cheater's bond was burned, executed by the vault's own scheduled call. Every payment, slash, refund and result is a public record, and each job ends with a Compute Passport anyone can verify offline. This is the trust layer that makes an open market for compute possible. Providers earn by being honest, creators earn by being useful, and buyers never have to take anyone's word for it.
projects.how_its_made:
KINETIC is a full-stack system spanning four networks, written in TypeScript (Node and Express services, a Vite dashboard) with a Solidity bond vault on Hedera. Each sponsor technology carries a load the product can't work without. Hedera: money and accountability. Buyers pay per chunk with x402 in HBAR. A custom bond vault holds each provider's stake. A slash needs 2 of 3 verifier signatures, followed by a dispute window, and then the vault's own Hedera scheduled call executes it, so no operator has to push the button. Refunds are exact, and model listing fees and creator royalties use the same rails. Every payment, canary result and Model Passport is written to an HCS topic. Agents get HCS-14 identities, and spending controls (price cap, job budget, allowlist, kill switch) are enforced and logged. 0G: the work and the judge. Providers do their work on 0G Compute (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, TeeML). The verifier re-runs hidden canaries on a different 0G model (glm-5.3) and checks each TEE signature against the signer in 0G's serving contract, so an agreeing cheater can't hide. Agents are registered with ERC-8004 on 0G Galileo. Users sign in with their 0G account, and their credits can pay for their own agent. Arkiv: the live market. Provider offers (which expire if the node goes quiet), the model registry, chunk claims, job state and reputation all live in Arkiv entities. Buyers discover providers by querying it, and the entire dashboard reads from it, so nothing on screen is animated from a script. Swarm: durable evidence and privacy. Swarm stores model weights, Model Passports, Compute Passports and encrypted chunk data. References on Arkiv are encrypted first, so public entities never leak where private data lives. The hard parts. Real adversaries. We run three real cheating nodes on live testnets. Providers can't tell the verifier's admission probes from job work, so we count both toward the slash threshold. A cheater is caught from its first fake chunk. We tried weaker real models as bad providers, but every 0G chat model we measured scored 100% on the labelled tickets, so the cheating is built into the node code. Each cheater labels itself in its Arkiv offer.
Two bugs found only by running live. 0G's glm-5.3 providers began registering a separate enclave signer, which left every canary unscored until we accepted either registered signer. And our self-settling slash never fired: the vault booked its call for the exact closing second, so it ran as a no-op. We fixed the vault (now v4) and covered both bugs with tests.
Honest limits, published. On testnet all three verifier keys are ours, and the README documents every such limit.
A clearly labelled in-browser synthetic replay keeps the dashboard working if any network is down.

Every payment, slash, refund and result is a public record, and each job ends with a Compute Passport anyone can verify offline.

This is the trust layer that makes an open market for compute possible. Providers earn by being honest, creators earn by being useful, and buyers never have to take anyone's word for it.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
KINETIC is a full-stack system spanning four networks, written in TypeScript (Node and Express services, a Vite dashboard) with a Solidity bond vault on Hedera. Each sponsor technology carries a load the product can't work without.

Hedera: money and accountability. Buyers pay per chunk with x402 in HBAR. A custom bond vault holds each provider's stake. A slash needs 2 of 3 verifier signatures, followed by a dispute window, and then the vault's own Hedera scheduled call executes it, so no operator has to push the button. Refunds are exact, and model listing fees and creator royalties use the same rails. Every payment, canary result and Model Passport is written to an HCS topic. Agents get HCS-14 identities, and spending controls (price cap, job budget, allowlist, kill switch) are enforced and logged.

0G: the work and the judge. Providers do their work on 0G Compute (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, TeeML). The verifier re-runs hidden canaries on a different 0G model (glm-5.3) and checks each TEE signature against the signer in 0G's serving contract, so an agreeing cheater can't hide. Agents are registered with ERC-8004 on 0G Galileo. Users sign in with their 0G account, and their credits can pay for their own agent.

Arkiv: the live market. Provider offers (which expire if the node goes quiet), the model registry, chunk claims, job state and reputation all live in Arkiv entities. Buyers discover providers by querying it, and the entire dashboard reads from it, so nothing on screen is animated from a script.

Swarm: durable evidence and privacy. Swarm stores model weights, Model Passports, Compute Passports and encrypted chunk data. References on Arkiv are encrypted first, so public entities never leak where private data lives.

The hard parts.

Real adversaries. We run three real cheating nodes on live testnets. Providers can't tell the verifier's admission probes from job work, so we count both toward the slash threshold. A cheater is caught from its first fake chunk. We tried weaker real models as bad providers, but every 0G chat model we measured scored 100% on the labelled tickets, so the cheating is built into the node code. Each cheater labels itself in its Arkiv offer.
Two bugs found only by running live. 0G's glm-5.3 providers began registering a separate enclave signer, which left every canary unscored until we accepted either registered signer. And our self-settling slash never fired: the vault booked its call for the exact closing second, so it ran as a no-op. We fixed the vault (now v4) and covered both bugs with tests.
Honest limits, published. On testnet all three verifier keys are ours, and the README documents every such limit.
A clearly labelled in-browser synthetic replay keeps the dashboard working if any network is down.

projects.title: jasmine
projects.description: A whatsApp agent that manages tokens across chains and remembers unfinished work.
projects.project_description: our project lets people manage tokens across blockchains through a WhatsApp conversation. you can ask it to check balances, send tokens, or manage a lending position for a set period. it shows you the plan and asks for approval before starting. for example, you can say, “manage my test tokens for 30 days.” the agent prepares a plan covering how much it can use, how much must stay untouched, which pools it can use, and how much it can spend on fees. once approved, it checks the pools on a schedule. it compares the expected extra earnings against the cost of moving and the time left in your plan. a higher interest rate alone is not enough to trigger a transfer. you can ask what happened, compare the pools, pause management, or request a withdrawal in the same chat. the agent tracks a transfer through to its destination and checks that the tokens reached the intended pool before reporting completion. the other important part is remembering unfinished work. encrypted task checkpoints are stored on Arkiv, so a restarted agent can recover saved progress. transaction records help it investigate an interrupted transfer without blindly sending it again. the current prototype runs on Ethereum Sepolia and Base Sepolia. we have completed a real testnet cross-chain transfer and destination deposit. the lending pools use simulated interest rates and do not earn real interest.
projects.how_its_made: we extended an existing Python agent with wallet tools, lending management, and blockchain-backed task storage. WhatsApp messages reach the agent through a separate messaging service and Redis. an OpenAI model interprets requests and calls tools with validated inputs. a background worker handles scheduled checks and follows transactions while the user is away. the lending calculations live in a shared TypeScript module. it checks balances, pool rates, fees, the remaining management period, and the user’s approved limits. amounts use integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point rounding errors. the application and Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) workflow use the same rules, so they do not maintain separate versions of the decision logic. the model handles the conversation, while code calculates whether a move qualifies. CRE reads contract state and validates the proposed operation. our prototype runs CRE locally, then relays the validated instruction through an application signer. it is not yet a workflow deployed to Chainlink’s decentralized network. Chainlink’s Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) carries the tokens and instructions between the two testnets. Solidity strategy contracts enforce limits, protect the reserved balance, reject repeated operations, and handle the destination deposit. we support both an encrypted agent wallet and a connected MetaMask wallet. approval is tied to the actual incoming user message and the specific review shown in that chat. the model cannot approve its own proposal. Arkiv stores encrypted task checkpoints and a separate encrypted lending activity history. this gives users a record outside our application database. private contents require the encryption key to read. SQLite holds local execution records, chat history, and transaction journals. one tricky bug was that a transaction could report success even when an inner contract call failed. we added checks for the expected contract events and token movements before marking an operation complete. we also save the signed transaction and its hash before broadcasting. if a response disappears, recovery checks that original transaction instead of creating another transfer. we used Foundry for contract tests, pytest for the Python agent, and Node and Bun tests for the TypeScript rules and CRE integration. recovery tests cover interrupted processes, missing responses, repeated approvals, and pending transfers.

projects.title: thehro
projects.description: Is a higher DeFi APY worth the switching fees? Find your break-even day, save it on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Thehro (ठहरो, Hindi for "pause") helps you decide whether moving your stablecoins to a higher-yield DeFi pool will actually earn you more money. The problem: DeFi apps advertise APY, and a pool paying 8% looks better than one paying 4%. But moving is not free. You pay gas, bridge fees, withdrawal and entry fees, and slippage. If you only hold the new position for a few weeks, those costs can be bigger than the extra interest. Chasing the higher APY leaves you with less money. Headline APYs are also often mostly temporary reward incentives that can end at any time. What Thehro does: Compares "stay" against "move" in dollars. You enter your amount, current APY, target APY, how many days you'll hold, and your switching costs. Thehro compounds both paths, pays the cost upfront on the move side, and shows which side wins and by how much. Calculates the break-even day: the day the higher rate has earned back the switching cost. A chart shows both balances over time. Pulls live markets from DeFiLlama's public yield feed: single-asset USDC pools with at least $1M TVL, refreshed every 5 minutes. You can search, filter by network, sort, and pick a real pool to compare against. Stress-tests the move. You can itemize withdrawal, gas, bridge, entry and slippage costs; exclude reward APY and use only the base rate; switch between today's rate and the 30-day mean; assume the rate falls by a percentage; and read a "What if the rate changes?" table, including a row where rewards end. Flags pools that may have lockups or eligibility limits, are mostly reward-driven, or have a current rate far from their 30-day average. Built on Arkiv: Connect a browser wallet and save the exact scenario (inputs, pool snapshot, fees and assumptions) as an expiring, wallet-owned receipt on the Arkiv Rabdi testnet. You choose how long it lasts, from 2 minutes up to 7 days, because a yield decision goes stale. The "My receipts" page queries Arkiv for entities owned by your wallet, so you can reopen a receipt and restore the same comparison or export it as JSON. When the lifetime ends, the receipt is no longer returned by queries. Expiry is enforced by the chain's block number, not by a cleanup job. A CLI script runs the same owner-filtered query, so anyone can reproduce the read. Without a wallet, the calculator still works. You can keep a local draft, share a scenario through a link (the data stays in the URL fragment and is never sent to a server), or export and import JSON. Thehro never deposits, withdraws, bridges, swaps, approves tokens or holds keys. The only transactions are the ones you sign to save receipts. It is a decision tool, not financial advice: it does not model taxes, depegs, smart-contract risk or rate changes beyond the scenarios you set. Stack: Vite with vanilla JavaScript, the Arkiv SDK, viem, DeFiLlama's yield API, and EIP-6963 wallet discovery with mobile wallet deep links. Built from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026 with AI assistance (Codex), as disclosed in the README.
projects.how_its_made: Thehro is a static, frontend-only app. There is no backend, no database we run, and no server-held keys. It's built with Vite and plain JavaScript (no React or other framework). Icons are Lucide, and the chart is hand-written SVG. The core is a small math module (src/math.js). APY is treated as an effective annual rate, so the balance after d days is P × (1 + APY)^(d/365). We use Math.expm1 and Math.log1p so small rates and short periods don't lose precision. The move side subtracts the switching cost before compounding, so the cost of spending those dollars upfront is counted. Break-even isn't found by trial and error. It is solved directly: days = 365 × ln(P / (P − cost)) / (ln(1 + target) − ln(1 + current)). The "What if the rate changes?" table re-runs the same math at lower target rates. Node's built-in test runner covers the formulas, edge cases and validation of untrusted input. Market data comes from DeFiLlama's public yields endpoint (yields.llama.fi/pools), fetched directly from the browser. The feed has more than 15,000 pools. We keep only single-asset USDC pools with no impermanent-loss risk and at least $1M TVL. Results are cached for 5 minutes and refreshed in the background while the tab is visible. We keep the base and reward APY split and the 30-day mean, which powers the "exclude rewards" and "30-day mean" stress tests. Simple heuristics on the pool metadata flag possible lockups or KYC limits, reward-heavy yields, and rates that are far from their 30-day mean. DeFiLlama is a data source only. It is not a second partner integration. Arkiv (the partner tech) stores the decision receipts. In src/arkiv.js, using @arkiv-network/sdk and viem: A named schema defines each receipt entity: name, source (indexed), savedAt (indexed u64), and a bytes field holding the full scenario as JSON. The user's injected wallet signs createEntity on the Arkiv Rabdi testnet (chain ID 7794095). We switch to the chain, or add it if needed, and confirm both the chain ID and the account before signing. Each receipt gets a native expiration (ExpirationTime.fromMinutes, from 2 minutes to 7 days) and is created with the read-only flag. "My receipts" runs an owner-filtered query (select … from schema, ownedBy the wallet, ordered by savedAt descending, paginated). The list comes only from Arkiv, not from local storage. Deleting a receipt is an owner-signed deleteEntity transaction. scripts/query.mjs runs the same schema and owner query from the command line, so judges can reproduce the read for any writer address. How Arkiv helped: a yield comparison goes stale quickly, and Arkiv makes expiry part of the data model. We didn't have to build a cleanup job or a backend. Ownership comes from the wallet, so receipts can be recovered on any device and any client can read them with the same schema. Notable or hacky bits: Expiry is decided by the chain, not by the browser clock. Receipts store an expiry block. We call getBlockTiming to estimate a wall-clock countdown from the block time. When the countdown ends, the app queries Arkiv again instead of hiding the receipt locally. Every receipt read from Arkiv is treated as untrusted. It is decoded, validated and size-limited (64 KB), and its queryable attributes are checked against the JSON payload. Any receipt that doesn't match is skipped and counted, not shown. Share links put the whole scenario into the URL fragment (#…) as base64url, so it never reaches a server. The same validator is used for share links, JSON imports and Arkiv receipts, so a scenario restores exactly. Rendering is plain template strings re-drawn from one state object. Epoch counters drop stale async results when you switch wallets or refresh during a request. Wallets are found through EIP-6963 so multiple browser extensions work. On phones with no wallet, we build deep links that reopen the page inside MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet or Trust Wallet. The schema keeps the project's original name (stayput.mumbai2026.receipts.v1) after the rename, so receipts saved earlier can still be read. The project was built from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai with AI assistance (Codex) for research, UI, implementation, tests and docs, as disclosed in the README.

projects.title: SAKA - DeFi AI Agent
projects.description: Your own AI DeFi agent on Uniswap that thinks on 0G and proves every move it makes.
projects.project_description: SAKA gives every user their own AI DeFi agent with a verifiable reason for every move. Sign in with a passkey, get a Privy agent wallet, and ask in plain English: "Swap $5 ETH to USDC", "Put $10 into ETH/USDC", "Is this hook safe?". The agent plans on 0G, builds transactions on Uniswap, and runs every action through a safety pipeline: a trade score, a hook safety score, a simulation, an independent AI guard and a deterministic policy. Small, safe actions under your limits run on their own after a 3-second countdown you can cancel. Anything bigger waits for your passkey approval, and risky actions are refused with a reason. Autopilot means the agent comes to you. Nine detectors watch each funded wallet every minute (dips, big moves, profit targets, idle USDC, LP out of range, new or changed hooks, better pools) and propose actions with Yes / Change / No, in the app and on Telegram. The Market Event Simulator lets you trigger a market event on demand: the event is simulated, the decision is real, and "no action" counts as a decision. The Hooks page explains Uniswap v4 hooks in plain words, each with a deterministic 0–100 safety score based on the Uniswap v4 Security Framework. Every decision, executed or refused, is stored on 0G Storage with every 0G request ID, check, policy result and transaction hash, so anyone can verify why the agent moved money without trusting us. Execution runs on Ethereum Sepolia; mainnet is read-only for market data.
projects.how_its_made: SAKA is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) with a React + Vite + Tailwind web app on Vercel, and a Fastify API, BullMQ worker, PostgreSQL (Prisma) and Redis running in Docker on one Azure VM behind Caddy. 0G is the brain. Every inference goes through the 0G Router (Private Computer) with verify_tee: true, our own client request ID, and a check that the X-Request-ID header matches the x_0g_trace request ID in the body. Otherwise the answer is rejected. GLM-5.3 in private trust mode is the planner, with 0GM-1.0 as a verified fallback. Vela 2.0 on the /v1/decisions endpoint is the guard: it returns a probability, blocks below 0.8, and fails closed if 0G is unreachable. 0GM-1.0 writes plain-English explanations. Each finished decision is serialized as canonical JSON (no personal data, no signatures) and uploaded to 0G Storage with the TS SDK; we check the returned root hash against our local Merkle root and show it on the card with an explorer link. Uniswap is the hands. We built our own MCP server, uniswap-agent-mcp, with 16 typed tools over the Trading API (client generated from the OpenAPI spec), the LP API, v4 V4Quoter / StateView / PoolManager / PositionManager and the v4 subgraph. It follows Uniswap's own uniswap-ai skills and is published as a plugin in our fork of Uniswap/uniswap-ai. The server is unsigned-only by design: a test fails the build if signing or broadcast code ever lands in it, so a hijacked model can only propose a trade. Permit2 flows return EIP-712 typed data plus an HMAC-signed resume token bound to the original arguments that expires in 120 s. score_hook reads the hook's 14 permission bits from its address and scores it against the v4 Security Framework. Privy server wallets hold funds under a per-wallet policy that only allows Uniswap contracts, Permit2 and allowlisted tokens. Passkeys (WebAuthn via SimpleWebAuthn) handle sign-in and step-up approvals. Telegram alerts use grammY. Notably hacky: the Market Event Simulator overlays simulated market data onto the real context reads, while the 0G planner, the pipeline and the Uniswap client stay real, so you can trigger a "3 a.m. crash" live and watch a genuine decision. The project has 600+ Vitest tests.

projects.title: Clinch
projects.description: Sybil-proof token launches and Uniswap v4 batch swaps where splitting wallets never helps.
projects.project_description: Every token sale on Ethereum has to decide who gets the scarce supply, and every common rule for that counts wallets. Per-address caps, pro-rata splits and whitelists are free to break: a whale makes fifty wallets and takes fifty allocations. Uniform-price auctions such as Uniswap’s CCA fix splitting but reward lying, because a large bidder who understates demand keeps the clearing price low and buys the rest cheap. Arbitrum’s airdrop lost 21.8% to 148,000 sybil addresses despite months of forensics, LayerZero ended up paying bounty hunters to inform on sybils, and the industry’s answer has drifted toward KYC and biometrics on what are supposed to be permissionless sales. Clinch is a sybil-proof, truthful auction engine built on the October 2026 adaptive-clinching result, which proves that if bidders’ budgets are enforceable, no set of fake identities beats one honest bid and bid order does not matter. On Ethereum, enforcing a budget is one line: escrow it. Each bidder deposits a budget and sets a max price. A price clock rises in steps, and at each step you clinch whatever remaining supply the other bidders can no longer afford, paying for those units at that price. The mechanism only ever sees the sum of everyone else’s escrowed money, so splitting across wallets changes nothing, shading your bid just drops you out earlier with fewer units, and there is no ordering to race for. In our simulations a whale gains 15x by splitting under a capped sale and 44% by shading under a uniform-price auction; under Clinch it gains nothing from either and slightly loses. For the proofs and the measurements, see the research notes at https://clinch-ur-token.vercel.app/whitepaper.pdf. Two products share one pure Solidity engine on Uniswap v4. ClinchLaunch sells a fixed supply on the clock, then in the same settle transaction initializes a full-range v4 pool at the discovered price with the proceeds and locks the liquidity forever. ClinchHook turns any v4 pool into a batch market: orders are escrowed for a few blocks, two-sided demand is matched by the same auction with the pool’s constant-product curve as the supply, and only the residual hits the pool in one swap inside unlock. Sandwich bots earn nothing because there is nothing to reorder, and the discretization surplus is rebated to traders. No admin keys; anyone can settle, and if nobody does, anyone can cancel and everyone is refunded in full. Clinch needs no identity to be honest, but some issuers still want a per-person cap, so the World ID arm runs the same launch with hUSDC, a 1:1 USDC voucher that only a verified human can mint, capped at 2,000 USDC per World ID nullifier, bound to one wallet and non-transferable between wallets. The core contracts are untouched; identity composes on top of a mechanism that no longer needs it. Watching a launch also leaks interest, since every price read tells an RPC provider which address is about to bid on which sale, so the app routes reads through the EF’s Anon-RPC when a specifier is configured. No trackers or analytics in the client. Live on Sepolia against Uniswap’s official v4 PoolManager with every contract verified: a six-bidder launch settled and seeded a CLNCH/USDC pool, a five-order two-sided WETH/USDC batch cleared in a single transaction, and the World ID arm is live with a success path and three rejection paths on chain. 99 Foundry tests with every claimed property fuzzed 2,000 times, Solidity checked bit-for-bit against a Python reference over 768 differential runs, an 80,000-strategy adversarial search that found no profitable deviation from honesty, and a sandwich bot that found no free lunch. The business case is simple: a launch where nobody can be cheated by whales, bots or sybils is a launch that does not need a credential, and any issuer on v4 can run one with a price and a budget instead of a KYC vendor.
projects.how_its_made: The whole thing is one pure Solidity library, ClinchEngine, that computes every allocation; ClinchLaunch and ClinchHook are thin wrappers around it and only touch Uniswap v4 inside settle(). We built the engine twice on purpose: first in Python as a research reference (research/clinch), then in Solidity, and the Foundry suite calls the Python engine over FFI and asserts the two agree to the wei. That differential harness is what let us iterate on the math without fear; every one of the 99 tests, including 2,000-run fuzzing per property, pins a named theorem from the paper. The frontend carries a third copy, a TypeScript port, so every number on screen is either read from the chain or computed by an engine that matches the chain exactly, which is how the post-settlement replay can show a “matches chain” badge. The mechanism is discretized adaptive clinching (Dobzinski, Lavi and Nisan 2008) with the AMM chord target and two-sided routing from arXiv 2610.36629. Prices are WAD fixed point over raw token units. The continuous price clock becomes a geometric ladder, capped so that every bidder’s limit lands exactly on a step, which the proportional exit rule needs. For the hook, the “supply” at each price is the constant-product pool itself: we solve a quadratic for the chord target, the rightmost point where a line of slope p through the cumulative (allocated, paid) point still sits on or above the pool’s cost curve, with two branches to keep the sqrt numerically stable. Because buyers pay the top of each ladder step, the engine leaves about 0.9·ε of volume above the curve; rather than let that leak, settle swaps everything the dominant side paid as exact input in one swap inside unlock and shares the pool’s actual output pro rata, so the discretization surplus comes back to traders. Settlement tolerates v4 rounding and any protocol fee via a single pips inequality. Check out the whitepaper at https://clinch-ur-token.vercel.app/whitepaper.pdf. Uniswap v4 (Build with Uniswap track) is the foundation and it shaped the design. The hook claims only three permissions: beforeInitialize so pools exist only through the hook, beforeAddLiquidity restricted to full range so the pool is exactly x·y = k, and beforeSwap that admits only the hook’s own settlement swap, which is what makes the batch guarantees hold between order and settle. Pools are fee 0 and ERC20 only because a fee breaks the chord geometry. The launch factory initializes a full-range pool at √P_X96 = √(price·2^192) and reserves the pool key on the hook in the same transaction, which closed a griefing vector where someone pre-initializes all 32 candidate tick spacings for a pair. Contract-level work bounds keep every accepted configuration under a 30M-gas block: (4·depth·1e14/ε + orders)·orders ≤ 10,000 for the hook, (ladder steps + maxBids)·maxBids ≤ 12,000 for the launch. A 32-order batch settles in 1.38M gas; the six-bidder demo launch took 99 steps and 3.68M. Our FEEDBACK.md records time-to-first-hook and the three doc gaps that cost us the most: the fee-0 constraint interaction, the hook address mining workflow, and swapping inside unlock from a hook’s own settle path. World ID (Best Use of IDKit track) went in as a token rather than a gate. HumanGate is hUSDC, a 1:1 USDC voucher only a verified human can mint, capped at 2,000 USDC per nullifier for life and transferable only to registered venues, so the cap lives in the money and cannot be split or lent. World ID 4.0 has no verifier contract on Ethereum Sepolia, so we route IDKit 4.6 Proof of Human through an RP-signed request (key never reaches the browser), verify at the Developer Portal, and have the server sign (chainId, verifier, signalHash, nullifier, externalNullifier) for an AttestedWorldID contract; the one-wallet-per-nullifier rule is enforced on chain regardless, and on a chain with the router the same gate takes verifyProof directly. Tested on Sepolia with real staging Proof of Human proofs: success path, same identity on a second wallet refused, replayed attestation reverts, OverCap and NotTransferable rejections. The Ethereum Foundation’s Anon-RPC (Best Use of Anon-RPC track) covers the leak the mechanism cannot: an auction is only neutral if nobody can see who is about to bid, and every “price if settled now” read tells an RPC provider which address is watching which sale. Reads route through @anon-rpc/browser-harness when a specifier is configured, with an honest unavailable state otherwise. The rest of the CROPS story is in the contracts: no admin keys, permissionless settle and cancel, no trackers or analytics in the client, and a keeper you can kill without the market noticing. The app is Vite, React 18, TypeScript, wagmi v2, viem v2, Tailwind v4, with a WebGPU shader hero and a Paper Shaders fallback. On public chains all reads go through Multicall3 so a page’s values come from one block even behind a load-balanced RPC. The optional keeper (app/scripts/keeper.ts) scans hook logs in chunks because free-tier providers cap eth_getLogs at ten blocks, and prints only the RPC host because provider URLs carry API keys. Hacky bits worth admitting: contract creation on Sepolia cost far more gas than forge’s local estimate, so deploys run with --gas-estimate-multiplier 1000, and the CREATE2 search for a hook address with the right permission bits needs --disable-block-gas-limit during simulation. An internal review turned up eight liveness issues (settle not fitting a block, liquidity removal mid-batch, tiny pools, slot griefing via ineligible orders, and so on); each is fixed or documented and pinned in test/Regression.t.sol. The one thing we refused to hack around: a certificate-only verifier for big launches would have been cheaper, but Lemma 4.12 certifies efficiency only and would quietly break sybil-proofness, so large launches wait for a multi-transaction ladder instead.

projects.title: DataLeases
projects.description: Data Leases lets AI agents discover data providers, negotiate prices, and request checkable answers.
projects.project_description: Data Leases is an open marketplace for recurring, evidence-backed data answers. Instead of buying an entire analytics subscription, users create a lease for a specific question. Each lease defines the required sources, update frequency, freshness limit, maximum price per answer, total budget, and end date. An autonomous buyer agent discovers compatible providers, compares offers, and negotiates machine-readable terms through the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Providers supply structured answers with their methodology and supporting evidence. Budget rules keep each request within the user’s authorized limits. The product architecture connects three services. Hedera x402 handles payments per request. Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) checks supported measurements against independently accessible blockchain state and external sources. Arkiv provides searchable provider listings and public-safe answer receipts that link the source, methodology, verification result, and payment record. Payment and verification are separate. Paying for an answer does not establish that it is correct. Verification reports identify which checks passed, failed, or could not be completed. The initial use case is Ethereum DeFi monitoring, particularly lending liquidity and utilization. Researchers, DAO treasury analysts, and AI applications can use data leases to follow specific metrics. A dashboard brings together the latest accepted answer, data freshness, spending, and verification status. Data Leases gives buyers a way to obtain specific, checkable answers while allowing independent providers to sell specialized analytics per request.
projects.how_its_made: We built Data Leases as a pnpm monorepo using Node.js and strict TypeScript. Its architecture follows the complete data request flow: discover a provider, negotiate terms, pay for a request, receive an answer, verify its evidence, and publish a traceable receipt. Shared Zod schemas define the messages and data exchanged between these stages. Discovery connects the buyer agent with providers that support the selected question. Arkiv’s role in the architecture is to hold searchable provider listings, including capabilities, pricing, and evidence requirements. We added Arkiv and hybrid discovery options to the shared contracts. The running implementation currently discovers providers through a local registry; Arkiv reads and writes are not yet implemented. The buyer and providers run as separate HTTP services using Express and the official A2A JavaScript SDK. Providers publish agent cards, and negotiation messages travel as structured A2A data parts over JSON-RPC. Deterministic rules enforce price ceilings, deadlines, and bounded negotiation rounds. Prices use integer strings and BigInt to avoid rounding errors, while SHA-256 hashes bind the accepted terms. After agreement, the architecture places Hedera x402 between negotiation and answer delivery. The buyer would complete an HTTP 402 payment flow under an authorized spending policy, linking the settlement receipt to the same request. This enables payment per answer without a subscription. Price negotiation is implemented, but the repository does not yet execute Hedera x402 payments. The provider returns a structured answer containing the value, units, methodology, and evidence references. For independent checking, we built a Chainlink CRE TypeScript workflow compiled to WebAssembly. It reads LINK token decimals from Ethereum at a specific block and compares the value with Uniswap token metadata fetched over HTTP. Recorded local CLI simulations demonstrate accepted, rejected, and inconclusive outcomes. The browser’s synthetic provider answers currently use a separate mock verification adapter. After verification, Arkiv’s second role is to store public-safe answer receipts linking methodology, sources, verification status, and payment records. This closes the documented workflow with a searchable history of what was delivered and checked. Payment and verification remain separate facts. The browser console uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript served by a Node.js gateway. It displays provider exchanges, agreed terms, answers, and verification details. One notable workaround was importing CRE’s final callback result because user logs could be dropped at shutdown. Request and transcript hashes bind each imported result to its inputs. Vitest covers negotiation rules, shared contracts, and verification integration.

projects.title: arkivector
projects.description: pgvector for Arkiv: similarity search over vectors stored on-chain, behind one REST call
projects.project_description: Your RAG embeddings are a row in someone else's database. One expired credit card and your retrieval layer has amnesia. Arkivector is pgvector for Arkiv. pgvector is the Postgres extension with more than 23,000 GitHub stars, and it is one of the most widely used pieces of RAG infrastructure there is. It adds vector similarity search to the database you already run, so retrieval becomes one line: ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5. No new service, no new query language. Now that agentic AI is everywhere, RAG matters more than ever. Agents need to look things up before they act, and pgvector sits underneath a huge share of those retrieval pipelines. Arkiv is a chain built for data, roughly "SQL on web3". Entities have typed attributes, an owner, and an expiry block, and you query them with a filter language instead of decoding raw contract storage. As far as I could find, it had no vector search. You could store an embedding there as bytes, but you could not ask which entities are closest to it. So I rebuilt pgvector for Arkiv, using pgvector's own C code for the math. Your app calls client.upsert(...). The daemon encodes the vector, signs an Arkiv transaction, and sends it. It mines on Arkiv, and the daemon indexes it once it reads it back from the chain. Then client.search(vector=..., k=5, filter=...) returns the nearest entities, ranked by L2, cosine, inner product, L1, Hamming, or Jaccard distance, in a single REST call, and there is an MCP endpoint so an AI agent can call search as a tool. Why Arkiv is the point, not a checkbox: Your RAG embeddings live on-chain. Nobody can delete or reprice them behind your back, and any Arkiv client can read them without Arkivector being online. Arkiv's expiry is native. When an entity's expiry block passes, it drops out of search automatically—a built-in data retention policy with no cron job required. Every search answer includes the block height, so you know exactly how fresh a result is. The daemon is only a cache; if you wipe it, it rebuilds the whole index from Arkiv. I tested all of this end-to-end. An upsert landed on-chain in under three seconds, synced back, and filtered vector search returned the right neighbours through both SDKs. It is honest about its limits. Searches currently perform an exact scan, which is correct but slow on huge collections. pgvector's HNSW graph is compiled into the daemon, and wiring it to collections is next.
projects.how_its_made:
The math is pgvector's actual C code, not a rewrite. The daemon is C11, because pgvector is C. The distance kernels, half-precision conversion, sparse and bit routines, and HNSW graph code are copied from pgvector 0.8.7 and compiled in unchanged, apart from a few marked lines, all listed in a provenance file. pgvector expects PostgreSQL around it (palloc, ereport, fmgr, lightweight locks), so I wrote a compatibility layer. palloc allocates from per-request arenas. ereport(ERROR) unwinds to a setjmp boundary and becomes an ordinary API error. A CI job diffs the copied files against upstream so they cannot drift. A parity suite of 97 tests runs the daemon's distances against real pgvector 0.8.7 in Postgres, and every result is bit-identical or within float32 rounding. Kernels are compiled once per CPU level (baseline, AVX2/FMA, AVX-512, aarch64) and picked at startup. Arkiv does the hard parts. Storage: Each item is a plain Arkiv entity with reserved attributes: a schema tag, an id, the vector as bytes, and the document. A halfvec(768) costs 1,544 bytes on chain. Syncing: A syncer thread bootstraps a collection through arkiv_query, then follows the chain through eth_getLogs on the Arkiv contract. It keeps a ring of recent block hashes to detect reorgs and roll back, and it runs periodic count checks to catch drift. Idle, it costs one cheap poll per block. Writes: The writer ABI-encodes execute((uint8,bytes)[]) calls, signs EIP-1559 transactions with secp256k1, and submits them. Arkiv's real contract accepts them. The first Rabdi write reverted until I found that the operation payload needs a 0x20 head offset, so the daemon runs on the live chain, not just my mock. Storage and Filtering
Entities live in memory-mapped segment files in pgvector's in-memory index. Attribute filters compile to roaring bitmaps "live at this block" before any distance is computed, using a worker pool so a slow scan never blocks the loop. The Slightly Hacky Bits
I wrote a custom node simulator with reorgs, expiry, and fault injection, so there is no behavior I cannot reproduce on demand. Everything is fuzzed: RPC, filters, vector literals, transaction calldata. It caught an allocation bug in the calldata decoder within seconds. An architecture film is generated at build time and played in the browser with Web Audio rather than shipped as a file process. The project was developed spec-first: the architecture and the API contracts were written before the code, with proposals and task lists in the repository and reviewed against those specs. CI enforces them with clang-tidy, cppcheck, sanitizers, fuzzers, and a 163-integration test suite. projects.project_description_markdown:
Your RAG embeddings are a row in someone else's database. One expired credit card and your retrieval layer has amnesia.

Arkivector is pgvector for Arkiv.

pgvector is the Postgres extension with more than 23,000 GitHub stars, and it is one of the most widely used pieces of RAG infrastructure there is. It adds vector similarity search to the database you already run, so retrieval becomes one line: ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5. No new service, no new query language. Now that agentic AI is everywhere, RAG matters more than ever. Agents need to look things up before they act, and pgvector sits underneath a huge share of those retrieval pipelines.

Arkiv is a chain built for data, roughly "SQL on web3". Entities have typed attributes, an owner, and an expiry block, and you query them with a filter language instead of decoding raw contract storage. As far as I could find, it had no vector search. You could store an embedding there as bytes, but you could not ask which entities are closest to it. So I rebuilt pgvector for Arkiv, using pgvector's own C code for the math.

Your app calls client.upsert(...). The daemon encodes the vector, signs an Arkiv transaction, and sends it. It mines on Arkiv, and the daemon indexes it once it reads it back from the chain. Then client.search(vector=..., k=5, filter=...) returns the nearest entities, ranked by L2, cosine, inner product, L1, Hamming, or Jaccard distance, in a single REST call, and there is an MCP endpoint so an AI agent can call search as a tool.

Why Arkiv is the point, not a checkbox:

Your RAG embeddings live on-chain. Nobody can delete or reprice them behind your back, and any Arkiv client can read them without Arkivector being online.

Arkiv's expiry is native. When an entity's expiry block passes, it drops out of search automatically—a built-in data retention policy with no cron job required.

Every search answer includes the block height, so you know exactly how fresh a result is.

The daemon is only a cache; if you wipe it, it rebuilds the whole index from Arkiv.

I tested all of this end-to-end. An upsert landed on-chain in under three seconds, synced back, and filtered vector search returned the right neighbours through both SDKs.

It is honest about its limits. Searches currently perform an exact scan, which is correct but slow on huge collections. pgvector's HNSW graph is compiled into the daemon, and wiring it to collections is next.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The math is pgvector's actual C code, not a rewrite. The daemon is C11, because pgvector is C. The distance kernels, half-precision conversion, sparse and bit routines, and HNSW graph code are copied from pgvector 0.8.7 and compiled in unchanged, apart from a few marked lines, all listed in a provenance file. pgvector expects PostgreSQL around it (palloc, ereport, fmgr, lightweight locks), so I wrote a compatibility layer. palloc allocates from per-request arenas. ereport(ERROR) unwinds to a setjmp boundary and becomes an ordinary API error. A CI job diffs the copied files against upstream so they cannot drift. A parity suite of 97 tests runs the daemon's distances against real pgvector 0.8.7 in Postgres, and every result is bit-identical or within float32 rounding. Kernels are compiled once per CPU level (baseline, AVX2/FMA, AVX-512, aarch64) and picked at startup.

Arkiv does the hard parts.

Storage: Each item is a plain Arkiv entity with reserved attributes: a schema tag, an id, the vector as bytes, and the document. A halfvec(768) costs 1,544 bytes on chain.

Syncing: A syncer thread bootstraps a collection through arkiv_query, then follows the chain through eth_getLogs on the Arkiv contract. It keeps a ring of recent block hashes to detect reorgs and roll back, and it runs periodic count checks to catch drift. Idle, it costs one cheap poll per block.

Writes: The writer ABI-encodes execute((uint8,bytes)[]) calls, signs EIP-1559 transactions with secp256k1, and submits them. Arkiv's real contract accepts them. The first Rabdi write reverted until I found that the operation payload needs a 0x20 head offset, so the daemon runs on the live chain, not just my mock.

Storage and Filtering
Entities live in memory-mapped segment files in pgvector's in-memory index. Attribute filters compile to roaring bitmaps "live at this block" before any distance is computed, using a worker pool so a slow scan never blocks the loop.

The Slightly Hacky Bits
I wrote a custom node simulator with reorgs, expiry, and fault injection, so there is no behavior I cannot reproduce on demand. Everything is fuzzed: RPC, filters, vector literals, transaction calldata. It caught an allocation bug in the calldata decoder within seconds.

An architecture film is generated at build time and played in the browser with Web Audio rather than shipped as a file process. projects.title: Agent Arena
projects.description: AI agents trade on Base via Flash orders; other agents predict if each trade profits. Verifiable.
projects.project_description:
AgentArena AgentArena is a social arena on Base where AI trading agents compete on real trades, other AI agents predict whether each trade will profit, and every result can be checked by anyone. The problem “My trading bot makes money” can’t be verified. Results can be cherry-picked, losing trades can be hidden, and track records can be faked. Strategies are valuable, so people won’t publish them. AgentArena keeps the strategy private and makes the results public and provable. How it works One human, one account (World ID).
An owner connects a wallet and verifies once with World ID’s Proof of Human. Our backend checks the proof and stores the nullifier, so one person can hold only one account. We don’t need to know who you are, only that you are one unique person. That stops anyone from farming the reward pool with extra accounts, or predicting on their own agents from a second one. Every agent has its own wallet.
The owner creates an agent and funds it with USDC on Base. Each agent gets its own wallet, so the most it can lose is what it was funded with. The owner sets per-trade, per-day and prediction limits, and can pause the agent or withdraw to their own address at any time. A policy engine is the only path to signing. It reserves budget atomically before each trade, and the signer refuses anything that isn’t a Flash order or a call to our own contracts. A sealed brain (0G Private Computer).
Every decision is made by a model running inside 0G’s attested enclaves, in private mode with TEE verification required. We store the request ID, provider, model and verification flag for each call. The agent chooses for itself whether to buy, predict or wait. The model only suggests: our code validates every field, rejects anything outside the rules, and clamps sizes to the owner’s limits. A prompt injection can’t widen those limits, because the model never sets them. Commit before trade.
Before any order is sent, the trade is committed onchain to our TradeLog contract, with the hash of the 0G request ID. Every commit must end as executed or failed, so a losing trade can’t be hidden or quietly dropped. Execution on Definitive Flash.
Flash is the engine. Because it is non-custodial, each agent signs its own orders and acts as its own funder. Bracket orders: the core trade is a market buy of WETH with a take-profit and stop-loss attached, signed and submitted in one go. Every market has defined risk and a clear end.
Limit entries: the agent can wait for a dip. The market opens only when Flash fills the order, and unfilled orders expire and are cancelled.
TWAP entries: the agent can spread a buy over time in tranches.
Streaming quotes: the agent races Flash’s live quote stream before it signs.
Risk flags: a token that Flash flags as risky is skipped.
Signed cancels: exits cancel the bracket, then market-sell. Expired limits and unwanted TWAP tranches are cancelled the same way.
Auto-cancel on a drained wallet: if the owner withdraws funds, Flash’s own auto-cancel ends the order and the market resolves cleanly. Free prediction markets.
When a buy fills, a market opens: “will this trade make money?” Predictor agents read the trader’s full record (trades, win rate, PnL, voids and failures) plus the trade itself, ask their own 0G model, and answer YES or NO with a probability. Nothing is staked. Predictions are written onchain with their 0G request ID, and they lock when the window ends or the trade exits, whichever comes first. Onchain, a prediction reverts if the predictor and the trader belong to the same human. On a TWAP, the predictors’ collective view can cancel the unfilled tranches, so the crowd sizes the position. Resolution from real fills.
The position closes at its target, its stop or a time limit. The resolver then computes realized profit or loss, net of fees, from Flash’s own fills of the committed trade. It never uses what the agent claims. The entry page shows a verification checklist and compares Flash’s receipt with our records, and a public script re-checks any entry from Base data, Flash fills and 0G attestation. An outcome is YES for a profit, NO otherwise, and VOID if the position couldn’t be closed. Leaderboards and rewards.
Traders are ranked by net return over the epoch, with a minimum number of trades. Predictors are ranked by Brier score, which rewards calibrated probabilities over lucky guesses. Losses and voids stay visible. Each epoch, the top three traders and the top predictor share a capped reward pool in USDC. At most one award goes to each human per epoch, enforced onchain, and owners claim from their verified wallet. Why someone comes back tomorrow Markets open continuously. Owners return to see whether their trader profited, whether their predictor called it, where they rank, what rewards are waiting, and to adjust limits for the next trade. Why it needs each partner
Definitive Flash: non-custodial signed execution, advanced orders, and the real fills that results are computed from. Without Flash there are no trades and no verifiable record.
0G Private Computer: every decision, with strategies kept private and proof of which model made each one. Without 0G the agents have no brain.
World ID: one verified human per account, which is what keeps rewards and predictions fair.
What makes it different Strategy stays private inside sealed inference, but results are public and checkable: committed before execution, filled on Base, scored from Flash fills, and decided by attested models. Predictions cost nothing to make, so the game is about skill and calibration rather than money.
