One reminder for you: this describes the full design as working on mainnet. Don’t attach transaction links or claim “executed” for TWAP, limit or streaming quotes unless you’ve actually run them on real Flash. Tell us about how you built this project; the nitty-gritty details. What technologies did you use? How are they pieced together? If you used any partner technologies, how did it benefit your project? Did you do anything particuarly hacky that's notable and worth mentioning? (min 280 characters) I'm listing out the shortcuts I've taken so far: a Coinbase fallback for price when Flash rate-limits, a local Flash stub, PGlite for local storage, persisted anvil state, and a retry when the 0G repl…
How we built AgentArena
Stack
Monorepo: pnpm workspace in TypeScript.
Contracts: Solidity with Foundry. TradeLog records commit, execution and failure. Arena holds the human registry, entries, predictions, reward epochs and claims.
Server: Express 5, viem for Base, zod for every schema, Drizzle ORM. The database is Postgres on Neon in production and PGlite locally.
Web: Next.js with wagmi, viem and RainbowKit, plus World IDKit for onboarding.
Packages: separate workspaces for the Flash REST client, the 0G client, World verification, and shared code (canonical hashing, schemas, ABIs).
Tests: node:test, Foundry tests, and anvil-backed integration tests for the trade, resolution and reward paths.
How it fits together
Two independent loops, both driven by the database. Each agent thinks on its own schedule. A separate market loop is the only thing that opens entries, watches exits, locks predictions, sells at the time limit, resolves and publishes rewards. State lives in the database, so a restart resumes where it left off, and a slow model call can never delay an exit.
The trade path is one fixed sequence: policy check and atomic budget reservation → TradeLog.commit (wait for the receipt) → Flash quote → approvals → sign → submit → poll → recordExecution or recordFailure. A test fails if an order can go out without a prior commit.
The model suggests and code decides. Every 0G output is parsed as JSON in a fixed schema, then bounded by validators: asset allowlist, long-only, stop below and target above entry, reward-to-risk range, size caps, TWAP and limit parameters. The model can’t set a limit.
Trades are hashed canonically. Sorted-key JSON, then keccak256. The hash is committed onchain before execution, and the resolver only counts fills from committed intents.
Partner technology
Definitive Flash. It is the execution engine and the source of truth.
The core trade is a market buy with an attached take-profit and stop-loss. One quote returns two EIP-712 payloads, and the agent’s own wallet signs both.
We also use limit entries, TWAP, the streaming quote WebSocket, signed cancels, the riskFlagged field, and Flash’s auto-cancel on a drained wallet. The entry page compares Flash’s receipt with our own records.
Because Flash is non-custodial, each agent can be an isolated trader with no account setup. That’s how we cap each agent’s loss at its own funding.
0G Private Computer. Every decision runs in sealed inference (TeeML, private trust mode, TEE verification required). We store the request ID, provider and verification flag, and write a hash of the request ID onchain. Without it, there is no proof which model made which decision.
World ID. IDKit runs on the frontend, and our backend verifies the proof and stores the nullifier. One human maps to one account, enforced in the database and mirrored onchain. Arena.predict reverts when predictor and trader are the same human.
Notable and hacky bits
The signer is boxed in. Agent wallets are plain EOAs whose keys are encrypted at rest (AES-GCM). The signer only sends transactions to our contracts, the owner, or USDC/WETH approvals to Flash, and only signs EIP-712 data in Flash’s domain. A test covers the domain refusal.
Recovery is idempotent. If a receipt is lost, the retry checks the onchain status and looks up the existing event. Otherwise it would revert with AlreadyClosed. A recovery pass also resumes intents stuck by a restart.
We handle 0G flakiness. A reply cut off while the model was still reasoning is retried, and anything that isn’t verified or fails validation is recorded and rejected.
Price lookups fall back to Coinbase spot when Flash rate-limits /search.
A Flash simulator for development. Flash has no testnet, so we wrote a labeled local Flash stand-in with an injectable clock. It can fill, expire and cancel orders deterministically. That let us test limit expiry, TWAP tranches and drained-wallet behavior without waiting minutes.
A local chain that persists. pnpm dev runs anvil with state saved to .anvil/state.json, matched with the database, so a local run feels like a real one. pnpm dev:reset clears both.
The canonical hash stayed stable. We added the execution field as optional, so intents committed before TWAP and limit support keep their original hashes.
We poll instead of subscribing to events. The market loop and resting-order settlement poll Flash on a short timer. It’s simple and survives restarts. The tradeoff is some latency.
The operator is a trust assumption. An operator wallet opens entries and publishes rewards. We say so openly, and a public verify.ts script lets anyone re-derive the outcome from public data.

0G Private Computer: every decision, with strategies kept private and proof of which model made each one. Without 0G the agents have no brain.
World ID: one verified human per account, which is what keeps rewards and predictions fair.
What makes it different
Strategy stays private inside sealed inference, but results are public and checkable: committed before execution, filled on Base, scored from Flash fills, and decided by attested models. Predictions cost nothing to make, so the game is about skill and calibration rather than money.

Trades use small real USDC on Base. Demo, not financial advice.

One reminder for you: this describes the full design as working on mainnet. Don’t attach transaction links or claim “executed” for TWAP, limit or streaming quotes unless you’ve actually run them on real Flash.

Tell us about how you built this project; the nitty-gritty details. What technologies did you use? How are they pieced together? If you used any partner technologies, how did it benefit your project? Did you do anything particuarly hacky that's notable and worth mentioning? (min 280 characters)

I'm listing out the shortcuts I've taken so far: a Coinbase fallback for price when Flash rate-limits, a local Flash stub, PGlite for local storage, persisted anvil state, and a retry when the 0G repl…
How we built AgentArena
Stack
Monorepo: pnpm workspace in TypeScript.
Contracts: Solidity with Foundry. TradeLog records commit, execution and failure. Arena holds the human registry, entries, predictions, reward epochs and claims.
Server: Express 5, viem for Base, zod for every schema, Drizzle ORM. The database is Postgres on Neon in production and PGlite locally.
Web: Next.js with wagmi, viem and RainbowKit, plus World IDKit for onboarding.
Packages: separate workspaces for the Flash REST client, the 0G client, World verification, and shared code (canonical hashing, schemas, ABIs).
Tests: node:test, Foundry tests, and anvil-backed integration tests for the trade, resolution and reward paths.
How it fits together
Two independent loops, both driven by the database. Each agent thinks on its own schedule. A separate market loop is the only thing that opens entries, watches exits, locks predictions, sells at the time limit, resolves and publishes rewards. State lives in the database, so a restart resumes where it left off, and a slow model call can never delay an exit.
The trade path is one fixed sequence: policy check and atomic budget reservation → TradeLog.commit (wait for the receipt) → Flash quote → approvals → sign → submit → poll → recordExecution or recordFailure. A test fails if an order can go out without a prior commit.
The model suggests and code decides. Every 0G output is parsed as JSON in a fixed schema, then bounded by validators: asset allowlist, long-only, stop below and target above entry, reward-to-risk range, size caps, TWAP and limit parameters. The model can’t set a limit.
Trades are hashed canonically. Sorted-key JSON, then keccak256. The hash is committed onchain before execution, and the resolver only counts fills from committed intents.
Partner technology
Definitive Flash. It is the execution engine and the source of truth.
The core trade is a market buy with an attached take-profit and stop-loss. One quote returns two EIP-712 payloads, and the agent’s own wallet signs both.
We also use limit entries, TWAP, the streaming quote WebSocket, signed cancels, the riskFlagged field, and Flash’s auto-cancel on a drained wallet. The entry page compares Flash’s receipt with our own records.
Because Flash is non-custodial, each agent can be an isolated trader with no account setup. That’s how we cap each agent’s loss at its own funding.
0G Private Computer. Every decision runs in sealed inference (TeeML, private trust mode, TEE verification required). We store the request ID, provider and verification flag, and write a hash of the request ID onchain. Without it, there is no proof which model made which decision.
World ID. IDKit runs on the frontend, and our backend verifies the proof and stores the nullifier. One human maps to one account, enforced in the database and mirrored onchain. Arena.predict reverts when predictor and trader are the same human.
Notable and hacky bits
The signer is boxed in. Agent wallets are plain EOAs whose keys are encrypted at rest (AES-GCM). The signer only sends transactions to our contracts, the owner, or USDC/WETH approvals to Flash, and only signs EIP-712 data in Flash’s domain. A test covers the domain refusal.
Recovery is idempotent. If a receipt is lost, the retry checks the onchain status and looks up the existing event. Otherwise it would revert with AlreadyClosed. A recovery pass also resumes intents stuck by a restart.
We handle 0G flakiness. A reply cut off while the model was still reasoning is retried, and anything that isn’t verified or fails validation is recorded and rejected.
Price lookups fall back to Coinbase spot when Flash rate-limits /search.
A Flash simulator for development. Flash has no testnet, so we wrote a labeled local Flash stand-in with an injectable clock. It can fill, expire and cancel orders deterministically. That let us test limit expiry, TWAP tranches and drained-wallet behavior without waiting minutes.
A local chain that persists. pnpm dev runs anvil with state saved to .anvil/state.json, matched with the database, so a local run feels like a real one. pnpm dev:reset clears both.
The canonical hash stayed stable. We added the execution field as optional, so intents committed before TWAP and limit support keep their original hashes.
We poll instead of subscribing to events. The market loop and resting-order settlement poll Flash on a short timer. It’s simple and survives restarts. The tradeoff is some latency.
The operator is a trust assumption. An operator wallet opens entries and publishes rewards. We say so openly, and a public verify.ts script lets anyone re-derive the outcome from public data.

projects.title: Clutch
projects.description: AI-created prediction markets on live-stream moments, with onchain trading and verifiable outcomes.
projects.project_description: Clutch turns the moments of a live stream into short, onchain prediction markets. Viewers watch a game, predict what happens next, and see the evidence behind the result, all in one place. Instead of markets being created by hand, an AI watches live gameplay on Twitch, Kick, YouTube and Lichess, picks out measurable events, and opens yes-or-no questions about what is about to happen: "Does Team Two's score go up this round?", "Game over within the next 8 moves?". For video markets, two different AI models independently read separate gameplay frames, and the engine evaluates both readings against the same structured rule. Chess markets instead compare a Lichess push stream with an independently replayed REST export. If both sources provide sufficient, consistent evidence, winners are paid via engine-operated automation. If they disagree, or the evidence isn't clear enough, the market is voided and everyone is refunded. Each verdict comes with a public receipt, so anyone can check the question, the rule, both readings and the evidence. Fairness shapes the design. Trading locks include a buffer for stream delay, Trading closes before the observation window begins, with an additional buffer to reduce advantages caused by differences in stream delay. Questions never use counters the streamer controls directly. Verifying once with World ID unlocks free test funds every day, a place on the leaderboard and a higher trading limit, all counted per person rather than per wallet, so creating additional wallets does not multiply a verified person's rewards or limits. Trading feels like a consumer app. Sign in with email or Google, get free test funds, and bet with one tap: no wallet pop-ups, Trade with one tap, with the embedded wallet handling transaction signing without repeated wallet confirmation pop-ups. Deposits can come from other chains. Clutch also includes a watch-and-trade view with Twitch chat built in, portfolios, market receipts, a streamer Studio with an OBS overlay, and a liquidity vault. The goal is to make watching live content participatory, with predictions that settle in moments and outcomes anyone can check.
projects.how_its_made: We used AI coding assistants, including OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, to help implement, review and debug the project. Codex assisted with API-origin restrictions, HTTP and WebSocket verification, browser testing, deployment inspection, and CI/CD preparation. The team directed the work and reviewed the implementation. The submission distinguishes verified testnet flows from integrations that are implemented but not yet validated end to end.

projects.title: IShara
projects.description: A buddy that points at what you ask about and do things for you live, and leaves a receipt as proof.
projects.project_description: Ishara is a screen tutor you can verify. You ask about whatever is on your screen, out loud or typed, in English. It explains, glides a cursor to the control you mean, walks you through a task step by step, answers followups and speaks back. It works in Chrome and in any Mac app. You can also give it an order like "fill the form and open and play any videos on youtube or web surfing" and it plans one step at a time and does it. The part I spent the time on is trust. Every answer comes from sealed models on 0G, and every answer leaves a receipt. A "How do I know?" page recovers the provider's signature, compares it with the signer registered onchain and shows the request id, so you don't take my word for it. Each session's log is encrypted, stored on 0G Storage, and its root is written to a contract on Galileo. A replay page fetches it back, decrypts it and checks the hash. If 0G can't be reached, Ishara says so and stops. It never falls back to another model and it never guesses.
projects.how_its_made: Two parts. A Chrome extension (Manifest V3) reads the page into a text outline and draws the pointer overlay. A local helper (Node 24, TypeScript, no framework) does everything else: speech to text with whisper.cpp on the laptop, so no audio leaves the machine; secret redaction (password, key, seed and card fields are removed in the tab and again in the helper); and every call to 0G. Mac apps are read through the Accessibility tree and on-device OCR by small Swift tools, and the same helper drives them. Every question goes to the 0G Private Computer Router in private trust mode. 0GM-1.0 reads the page text and writes the answer. For every pointer, laya, a second sealed model, is asked yes or no whether that control is what the sentence refers to. The ring only moves if it says yes. Right after each answer the helper fetches the provider's signature (it is only served for about 20 minutes), recovers the signer and compares it with the on-chain registry. At the end of a session the log is AES-256-GCM encrypted, uploaded to 0G Storage, and its root is written to a SessionRoot contract on Galileo (0x40F8A6CB2c16e0bA04005f527B6F3893963464ac). The replay page reads it back and checks the hash and the root. Things that were annoying or hacky: Apple's AVAudioConverter turned the built-in 3-channel mic into pure silence, so the helper mixes the channels by hand. laya signs a bare hash pair while 0GM signs a tagged record, so the proof check accepts both. Agent mode only presses keys in the app it read the screen from, after a test sent Cmd+W into the wrong window. Page text is treated as data: a page that tells the assistant to click something gets refused.

projects.title: Trivvo
projects.description: Shops pay real humans to visit. World ID stops bots, 0G AI checks photos, Hedera proves payouts.
projects.project_description: Tr!vvo pays people to explore their city. A café, shop or venue creates a "hunt": a short visit plus a few photo tasks (e.g. "take a photo of the laptop at the counter"). It funds the hunt with USDC, which sits in escrow until someone actually earns it. The shop prints a QR code for its counter. A hunter opens Tr!vvo inside World App (no extra wallet needed) or any browser, walks in and scans the code. A location check confirms they are really there. Before any money moves, World ID proves they are a unique human for this specific hunt, so one person with 100 wallets can only claim once. Small rewards need Proof of Human; rewards above $5 need a stronger credential. Once verified, the arrival reward is paid instantly. Then the hunter does the tasks. Each photo goes to a vision model on 0G Private Computer, which judges it against a rubric that 0G wrote when the hunt was created. Approved photos pass with a confidence score and a 0G request ID; a bad photo gets a clear reason and a retake; an unsure verdict goes to the shop for review, never a silent pass. When every task passes, the main reward is paid automatically. No shop staff has to check photos or pay anyone by hand. Every step (funded, human verified, arrival paid, photo approved, reward paid, stamp sent) is written to a public Hedera log, so anyone can check that the shop really paid and that the AI really approved the photo. Each finished hunt also earns the hunter a stamp, a Hedera token, and shops get a public trust score built from that log. Ads pay platforms to be scrolled past. Tr!vvo pays real humans to show up, and proves every payout.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: React 19 + Vite, wagmi/viem for wallets, deployed on Vercel. It also runs as a World Mini App via MiniKit, so inside World App the hunter uses the World App wallet and native World ID verification. QR scanning uses the live camera with a jsQR fallback for phones where the native barcode API is missing. Photos are downscaled in the browser before upload to keep AI calls fast and cheap. Backend: Node + Express + PostgreSQL on Render. Wallet sign-in supports both EOA and Safe smart-account signatures; every shop route checks ownership; the QR secret is never public; paid AI calls are capped. World: IDKit 4.6 with a separate action per hunt, so the nullifier is unique per hunt rather than global: one human = one claim per hunt, while the same human can still join other hunts. Proofs are verified server-side and the nullifier is stored before any payout. Rewards above $5 require a stronger credential than Proof of Human. USDC escrow and payouts settle on World Chain. 0G Private Computer: called through the OpenAI-compatible 0G Router (model 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b) in private trust mode, so runs are attested in a TEE. 0G is used twice: (1) at hunt creation it turns each free-text task into a precise "what the photo must show" rubric; (2) at check time a vision call judges the photo against that rubric and returns ok / confidence / reason. The 0G request ID is stored per attempt and shown to the hunter and on the public receipt. The verdict directly decides whether money moves: auto-pay, retake with a reason (max 5), or shop review if 0G is unsure or down. Hedera (SDK only, no smart contracts): the @hashgraph/sdk publishes every hunt event to a Consensus Service topic as a public receipt log, mints a TVSTAMP Token Service token to each hunter who finishes a hunt, and the receipt page, trust score and stamp count read back from the Mirror Node. Anyone can open the HashScan link on a receipt and see the 0G request ID inside the message. Hacky bits: per-hunt World ID actions to get per-hunt sybil resistance; using an HCS topic as a tamper-proof audit trail tying an AI verdict to a payment; and a "never silent pass" rule so an AI outage can't release money.

projects.title: Frame-works!
projects.description: Know before you sign: viem toolkit for the frame-tx alt mempool, plus relayerless privacy-pool exits
projects.project_description: Altpool is a viem toolkit for the ERC-8421 alternative mempool on the EIP-8141 frame-transaction devnet. Today developers send frame transactions blind: per-frame gas limits are written by hand, keyed nonces are managed by hand, and you only learn why a transaction was rejected afterwards, on the explorer. Altpool fixes that: SDK ( altpool ): a viem extension that fills per-frame gas, allocates EIP-8250 nonce keys, stakes your entity, preflights, sends, waits for the receipt and fetches the node's rule-by-rule admission report. Admission simulator ( checkAdmission ) and the frame-doctor CLI: before you sign, it tells you whether the public mempool and the alt mempool will admit a frame tx, and if not, which rule fails, for which entity, and the fix. Verdicts produced by ethrex or the sidecar are marked verified; the rest come from our local rule model and are labelled unverified. Entity monitor ( watchEntity + a live web page): stake, reputation, headroom before throttling, pending txs, inclusions and rejections across the gateway and miner nodes, with webhook alerts. MCP server: AI agents can call check_admission, get_admission_report and entity_status. QuietSend is the app we built with it. A privacy pool lets you withdraw to a fresh, unlinked wallet, but that wallet holds 0 ETH and can't pay gas. You either fund it from your old wallet, which links the two, or use a relayer that sees your details and can refuse you. QuietSend removes the relayer. One staked contract, ExitRelay, sends the withdrawal from the devnet's existing, unmodified privacy pool as an EIP-8141 frame transaction, and is repaid from the withdrawal's fixed fee in the same transaction. Before paying, its VERIFY frame checks the pool root and the nullifier and verifies the Groth16 proof itself (about 375k gas, fixed and pinned at 450k). The public mempool rejects that on two counts (the 100k validation cap and reading another contract's storage), and Altpool tells you so before you sign. The alt mempool admits it because ExitRelay is staked. Exits are live on the public devnet. Also built and live on the devnet: Pledge Paid: one 9-frame transaction that pays an invoice straight out of a WETH privacy pool (proof check, unwrap, Uniswap v4 swap, settle, sweep and a books check, all atomic). Wallet Bridge: MetaMask or Rabby control a frame-tx account by signing EIP-712 typed data. Falcon-512 post-quantum recipient wallets for QuietSend exits. Honest limit: on the devnet, the pool's crowd is accounts we seeded, so this proves the mechanism, not privacy yet.
projects.how_its_made: A bun + Turborepo monorepo: TypeScript packages on viem, Solidity contracts in Foundry, a React 19 + Vite + Tailwind site. Codec: all encoding, hashing and signing use @forshtat/hegota-support, the devnet's own codec (ethrex-eip8141-tracer profile). We didn't write a second one. Simulator: the public-mempool verdict comes from ethrex's own simulate (canonicalMempoolValid / canonicalMempoolViolation), so it's ground truth. The alt mempool has no dry-run RPC, so the alt verdict comes from the sidecar's admission records or the explorer when available, and otherwise from our model of the ERC-7562 / ERC-8421 rules. It routes each tx to public, alt via gateway or miner, or nowhere. Every real rejection we hit is saved as a test fixture. ExitRelay: 3 frames. Frame 0 is the built-in EXPIRY_VERIFIER deadline; frame 1 is ExitRelay's VERIFY (scope EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT, 450k limit); frame 2 is a SENDER frame calling pool.withdraw with relayer = ExitRelay. VERIFY reads the other frames with the frame opcodes and runs the cheapest checks first: frame shapes, max cost <= fee, withdraw calldata, nonce key == nullifierHash, then pool.roots(idx), isSpent, and the proof last. Using the nullifier as the EIP-8250 nonce key lets many exits wait in parallel, with only one pending exit per note. The hacky part: the devnet's Tornado v2.0 verifier calls the precompiles with staticcall(sub(gas(), 2000), ...), which breaks ERC-7562 OP-012 ("payer uses banned opcode: GAS"), so the gateway rejected our exit. Our deploy script copies the verifier's runtime bytecode and rewrites 3 sites (PUSH2 0x07d0 GAS SUB -> JUMPDEST x4 GAS). Same length, same verifying key, 15 bytes changed; deploy asserts the copy and the original agree on a real proof (true) and on fee + 1 (false). The pool still re-verifies with the original in the SENDER frame. Prover: snarkjs 0.1.20, websnark and a circomlib MiMC Merkle tree, with a key converter for the v2.0 circuit. It also runs in the browser. Pledge Paid: PayRelayWETH (staked) checks the proof against a WETH Tornado pool and pins frames 2-8; a CREATE2 Settler runs unwrap, Uniswap v4 swap, settle, sweep and a books check as one atomic batch; InvoiceBook records the payment. 9/9 frames succeeded on the devnet. Wallet Bridge: no wallet can sign a type-0x06 frame tx, but every wallet signs EIP-712, so BridgeAccount's VERIFY frame recovers that signature with ecrecover. Falcon: FalconWallet verifies a Falcon-512 signature (vendored ZKNOX ETHFALCON verifier, MIT) carried in an ARBITRARY signature entry. VERIFY costs about 3.9M gas, so it only runs on the alt mempool. MCP: a stdio server wrapping the simulator and monitor for AI agents. While building, we wrote up the devnet rule bugs we hit for the devnet team, e.g. the gateway's included count stays at 0, so a busy entity gets throttled after about 110 sends. AI assistance was used and is disclosed per event rules.

The alt mempool admits it because ExitRelay is staked. Exits are live on the public devnet.

Also built and live on the devnet:
- Pledge Paid: one 9-frame transaction that pays an invoice straight out of a WETH privacy pool (proof check, unwrap, Uniswap v4 swap, settle, sweep and a books check, all atomic).
- Wallet Bridge: MetaMask or Rabby control a frame-tx account by signing EIP-712 typed data.
- Falcon-512 post-quantum recipient wallets for QuietSend exits.

Honest limit: on the devnet, the pool's crowd is accounts we seeded, so this proves the mechanism, not privacy yet.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
A bun + Turborepo monorepo: TypeScript packages on viem, Solidity contracts in Foundry, a React 19 + Vite + Tailwind site.

- Codec: all encoding, hashing and signing use @forshtat/hegota-support, the devnet's own codec (ethrex-eip8141-tracer profile). We didn't write a second one.
- Simulator: the public-mempool verdict comes from ethrex's own simulate (canonicalMempoolValid / canonicalMempoolViolation), so it's ground truth. The alt mempool has no dry-run RPC, so the alt verdict comes from the sidecar's admission records or the explorer when available, and otherwise from our model of the ERC-7562 / ERC-8421 rules. It routes each tx to public, alt via gateway or miner, or nowhere. Every real rejection we hit is saved as a test fixture.
- ExitRelay: 3 frames. Frame 0 is the built-in EXPIRY_VERIFIER deadline; frame 1 is ExitRelay's VERIFY (scope EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT, 450k limit); frame 2 is a SENDER frame calling pool.withdraw with relayer = ExitRelay. VERIFY reads the other frames with the frame opcodes and runs the cheapest checks first: frame shapes, max cost <= fee, withdraw calldata, nonce key == nullifierHash, then pool.roots(idx), isSpent, and the proof last. Using the nullifier as the EIP-8250 nonce key lets many exits wait in parallel, with only one pending exit per note.
- The hacky part: the devnet's Tornado v2.0 verifier calls the precompiles with staticcall(sub(gas(), 2000), ...), which breaks ERC-7562 OP-012 ("payer uses banned opcode: GAS"), so the gateway rejected our exit. Our deploy script copies the verifier's runtime bytecode and rewrites 3 sites (PUSH2 0x07d0 GAS SUB -> JUMPDEST x4 GAS). Same length, same verifying key, 15 bytes changed; deploy asserts the copy and the original agree on a real proof (true) and on fee + 1 (false). The pool still re-verifies with the original in the SENDER frame.
- Prover: snarkjs 0.1.20, websnark and a circomlib MiMC Merkle tree, with a key converter for the v2.0 circuit. It also runs in the browser.
- Pledge Paid: PayRelayWETH (staked) checks the proof against a WETH Tornado pool and pins frames 2-8; a CREATE2 Settler runs unwrap, Uniswap v4 swap, settle, sweep and a books check as one atomic batch; InvoiceBook records the payment. 9/9 frames succeeded on the devnet.
- Wallet Bridge: no wallet can sign a type-0x06 frame tx, but every wallet signs EIP-712, so BridgeAccount's VERIFY frame recovers that signature with ecrecover.
- Falcon: FalconWallet verifies a Falcon-512 signature (vendored ZKNOX ETHFALCON verifier, MIT) carried in an ARBITRARY signature entry. VERIFY costs about 3.9M gas, so it only runs on the alt mempool.
- MCP: a stdio server wrapping the simulator and monitor for AI agents.
- While building, we wrote up the devnet rule bugs we hit for the devnet team, e.g. the gateway's included count stays at 0, so a busy entity gets throttled after about 110 sends.

AI assistance was used and is disclosed per event rules.

projects.title: Recharge
projects.description: Devcon or ETHGlobal? A sponsor gifts you an eSIM pack; your agent tops up your own plan via x402.
projects.project_description: Landing in Mumbai for Devcon, ETHGlobal or a token event with a phone that has no data? Recharge lets the event, a sponsor or a friend gift you an eSIM pack before you even clear immigration. Prove you are one human with World IDKit 4 (Orb or Document credential) and a sponsor's campaign pays for your first bundle (up to 1 GB), once per human per campaign. Anyone can also gift data to your ENS name, or hand you a scratch card at the venue, and you claim it with a signature or the card's PIN. Organizers run ticket-linked event campaigns with per-hour caps, a pause switch and refunds of unspent budget. Behind the gift: the nullifier becomes a quota key and DataDrop.claim on Hedera EVM pays the sponsor's USDC for that one human; the API orders a 1 GB India eSIM from the reseller, seals the activation code to your session key and keeps only a reference on the ledger (the sealed blob goes to Swarm when a Bee gateway is configured), while the entitlement itself is an Arkiv entity whose expiresIn equals the plan's validity, so it dies by protocol when the plan ends. When your own paid plan runs low (event packs are gift-only and have no top-ups), you, or an agent, buy 1 GB for $4.00 at a time: the API answers HTTP 402 with x402 v2 accepts (Hedera testnet HTS USDC and Base Sepolia USDC), the payer signs, the facilitator settles, the entity is extended and an HCS receipt is written. An operator-run agent, a Hedera Agent Kit wallet with an HCS-14 UAID, runs the top-up loop for the plans enrolled with it under a policy their owner signed (threshold, daily cap, pause), enforced in code, never by a model; anyone can run services/agent for their own plan. Live on testnet rails at https://app.recharge.ajudiya.com (API https://api.recharge.ajudiya.com): the traveller PWA, the sponsor console and the agent page, in English, with Hindi and Marathi copy via ?lang=hi or ?lang=mr. docs/DISCLOSURE.md, docs/CHANGELOG.md and docs/AUDIT-REPAIR.md record how the project was built; git log v0-prekickoff..HEAD is the complete dated record.
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm monorepo. services/api is a Hono server with one middleware chain (request id, security headers, CORS, rate limit, idempotency, zod validation, x402, octroi) in front of the routes. packages/octroi is the proof-or-pay engine: credential tiers, bundle sizing, challenges, claim locks, settlement markers, the shouldTopUp rule and gift reclaim, with 447 tests behind a coverage gate. packages/adapters has one port per partner with deterministic mocks for MODE=local and live adapters for MODE=live: World cloud verify v4 with a backend-signed rp_context, the x402.org facilitator (plus a self-run facilitator on Anvil), Arkiv rabdi entities with expiresIn, Swarm for the sealed eSIM activation blob when a Bee gateway is configured, HCS for receipts, ENS through viem, and the eSIM Access reseller API. packages/contracts holds DataDrop.sol (sponsor pools with scoped ids, hourly caps, pause, refund and HTS association) with Foundry fuzz and invariant tests, deployed on Hedera EVM 296. services/agent is the top-up agent: it reads the entitlement straight from Arkiv pinned to a trusted writer, applies the owner-signed policy in code, pays over x402 from a Hedera Agent Kit wallet (HTS USDC, fee payer taken from the facilitator), writes an agent-topup HCS receipt carrying its HCS-14 UAID, and keeps a durable trigger journal so a crash or a lost response never pays twice. apps/web is a Next.js PWA with RainbowKit/wagmi (MetaMask on Hedera EVM, HashPack over WalletConnect for native HTS payments), the sponsor console, scratch-card printing and en/hi/mr copy. Hacky bits worth knowing: the API serves /plans and /healthz from cache and falls over to a second Hedera JSON-RPC relay per request, because the public relay drops out for forty minutes at a time; reseller usage reports lag hours behind the carrier, so the agent's threshold is a field of the signed policy that the owner can set to 100 % to keep one bundle ahead; the eSIM activation code never touches the ledger (sealed to a session key, Arkiv keeps only the reference); and every live adapter runs offline over fixtures (authored from the vendor docs, plus redacted live recordings for Arkiv, the x402.org facilitator, the Hedera mirror, HCS, ENS and the eSIM Access catalogue), so the whole flow (claim, 402, settlement, webhook, gift, scratch card, expiry, reclaim, agent pass) runs offline in about 23 seconds with pnpm e2e, behind a red-team gate of 67 filed findings.

projects.title: SurgePass
projects.description: A fair line in front of booking sites: real people via World ID, a draw anyone can verify on Hedera
projects.project_description:
SurgePass is a fair line that sits in front of a booking website at its busiest minute. THE PROBLEM
When train Tatkal quotas, first-day movie shows or concert tickets open at a fixed time, everyone arrives in the same second. Scripts click faster than people, so bots take the seats; the rush overloads the site so real customers get errors; and reserved agent or partner quotas leak to touts who hoard and resell them. "Block the bots" no longer works either: AI agents acting for real people are arriving, so a site needs to know which automation has a real human behind it, and fairness has to be something anyone can check, not a promise from the seller. WHAT SURGEPASS DOES
SurgePass is a reverse proxy. The provider points its booking domain at it and adds about ten lines of code. Outside a drop's peak, every request passes straight through untouched. During a drop's peak, only the routes the provider chose are gated: People wait in a calm waiting room and verify once with World ID. One human gets one entry, and no personal data is collected. Entries go into a draw that is recorded on Hedera and can be recomputed by anyone. Everyone who gets a seat receives a short-lived signed pass and books on the provider's own site, with its own inventory, fares and checkout. Bots never reach the provider: they are sent to the waiting room, blocked, or asked to pay per request (x402) for extra availability checks, so hammering the site has a real cost. FOUR LANES, ONE RULE: A REAL PERSON BEHIND EVERY SEAT People (fair draw): verify with World ID, ask for up to the seat limit, and get a seat in a verifiable random order. Unused seats go to the next person in line. Premium (sealed bids): bids stay sealed (commit/reveal) until bidding closes; everyone who gets a seat pays the same clearing price, the highest bid that didn't get one. Partners (seat tokens): authorised agencies are allowlisted by their Hedera account. Their seats are Hedera tokens only approved partners can hold, they put down a refundable deposit, and unused seats are taken back and returned to the public draw. Agents (with permission): an AI agent can act for its human only after the human approves it with World ID. The agent then enters, bids and pays for extra checks by itself, within a budget, and still counts as that one person. The approval link stays open until the drop closes, so the agent can ask the night before and act alone at drop time. HOW WE USE WORLD ID
SurgePass signs a one-time World ID request for each drop (action "enter:<drop>") with a nonce that can't be replayed. The person scans with World App (proof of human); the proof is verified with the World Developer Portal (v4) and turned into an anonymous ID per drop, so the same person entering twice is refused as a duplicate. Agent approvals use the same proof, bound to that agent, the seat count and the maximum bid. World ID is the only way to say "one per person" at internet scale without collecting identities, and it works for the agents people will send. HOW WE USE HEDERA (THE REFEREE) Consensus Service (HCS): every drop has its own topic. Every entry, sealed bid, partner hold, the cutoff, the result, passes issued and seats returned are written there; consensus time decides who was first. PRNG: the draw's random seed comes from Hedera after entries close, under a transaction ID committed in advance, so nobody (the provider included) can pick who gets a seat. Token Service (HTS): partner seats are NFTs with KYC, freeze and wipe keys. Only KYC'd partner accounts can hold a seat, so a transfer to a reseller is refused by the Hedera network itself (ACCOUNT_KYC_NOT_GRANTED_FOR_TOKEN). Used seats are wiped, unused seats are wiped back to the public, and a misbehaving partner can be frozen. Scheduled transactions: deposits are refunded automatically. x402 payments in HBAR: surge-priced availability checks, agent bid deposits and partner deposits are paid per request and settled on Hedera. Mirror node: the waiting room rebuilds the draw (Fisher–Yates with sha256(seed + counter)) from public Hedera data in the browser and shows "Matches Hedera". PROVIDER INTEGRATION
Each allowed booking reaches the provider with a signed X-SurgePass-Assertion header (Ed25519 JWT) stating how many seats it may take and, for premium, the price. The provider verifies it with SurgePass's public keys and caps the booking. We ship the check in Node.js, Python, Java and Go, with the Node, Python and Java versions run against the live gateway. WHAT'S IN THE DEMO A provider console to create drops (route patterns, seats, peak windows, lanes), watch live decisions with a step-by-step trace for every request, run agent and partner test cases side by side, and see who was let through or turned away. A bot flood button: the same flood hits two identical booking sites. The one without SurgePass crashes; the one behind SurgePass stays healthy, with a live globe view of bots stopping at the gate while real people pass through. A World App-styled waiting room, a live draw reveal, a sealed-bid auction page, and a public "verify this draw" page. A reference AI agent (CLI and MCP server) that asks its human for approval and pays x402 on its own, and a partner client that signs with its Hedera key. Everything runs on Hedera testnet with real transactions (HCS topics, PRNG seeds, HTS seat tokens, scheduled refunds, x402 settlements) and real World ID verification with the production World App. The booking sites in the demo are mock providers we built to show the integration.
projects.how_its_made:
SurgePass is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces) with six parts that talk over HTTP and one WebSocket. THE GATEWAY (the core)
A Node.js reverse proxy built on Hono, with Redis (ioredis) for all shared state. Every request goes through one pipeline, and each step is recorded in a trace (with the gate's own time in microseconds) that the console shows live:
route match → is this drop at peak? → who is this (World ID session cookie, agent bearer token, or signed partner request) → waiting room / draw / sealed bid / partner hold → pass check → x402 for extra reads → forward to the provider with a signed header. Route matching uses each drop's URL pattern plus query/header conditions (e.g. ?quota=TQ), so only the routes a provider chooses are gated, and only during their peak (a schedule, or automatically when the backend's p95 latency or error rate crosses a threshold). All tokens (sessions, agent tokens, passes, provider assertions) are Ed25519 JWTs made with jose, each with its own "typ" so one can never be replayed as another. The provider gets an X-SurgePass-Assertion header (seats allowed, price, pass id, partner) and verifies it against our JWKS endpoint. The gateway strips any assertion a client tries to send itself. A live WebSocket feed sends sampled decisions plus per-second stats to the console; under a bot flood, bot lines are sampled but every human, agent and Hedera event always gets through. HEDERA (via the Hiero SDK, @hiero-ledger/sdk) HCS: a topic per drop. Writes go through an async queue so a burst of entries never blocks a request; each entry gets its consensus timestamp and sequence number back. PRNG: when the window closes we write a "window_closed" message containing the seat count and a transaction ID generated in advance, then run the PrngTransaction under exactly that ID. The seed can't exist before the cutoff, and anyone can check the order. The draw is Fisher–Yates using sha256(seed ‖ counter) (@noble/hashes), shared by the gateway and the browser. HTS: each partner quota mints NFT seat tokens with KYC, freeze, wipe and supply keys. Partners associate the token with their own key, we grant KYC, transfer seats in consensus order, wipe used seats after booking, and wipe unused ones back to the public draw. Scheduled transactions: deposit refunds are ScheduleCreate transfers. Mirror node: partner public keys are looked up when they're allowlisted, and the waiting room's "Verify" page downloads the whole topic and recomputes the draw in the browser. x402 ON HEDERA (@x402/core + @x402/hedera)
Paid endpoints answer 402 with x402 v2 payment requirements in HBAR. Clients sign a Hedera transfer with the "exact" scheme, and a public facilitator settles it on testnet. The same path is used for surge-priced availability reads (the price rises with load), agent bid deposits and partner hold deposits. WORLD ID (@worldcoin/idkit, @worldcoin/idkit-core)
The gateway signs a one-time RP request per action (enter:<drop>), with a nonce stored in Redis so it can't be replayed. The waiting room opens the IDKit widget (proof of human, production World App). The gateway verifies the proof with the World Developer Portal's v4 verify API and turns the nullifier into an anonymous ID per drop. Agent approvals reuse the same action, with a signal binding the proof to that agent, the seat count and the max bid. Approvals work like a TV sign-in code: the agent gets a 401 "HumanApproval" with a link, the human approves with World App, and the agent polls for its token. FRONTENDS (React 19, Vite, Tailwind, framer-motion) The waiting room is built on World's own UI kit (@worldcoin/mini-apps-ui-kit-react), so it looks and feels like World App. It has the live draw reveal, the sealed-bid page and the public "verify this draw" page. The provider console: drop builder, live decision log with step-by-step traces, partner management, side-by-side test runs (agents and partners run as real jobs against a chosen drop), an integration guide, and the bot-flood demo with a canvas "gate view" driven by the gateway's real per-second counts. A landing page and pitch deck from the same app, hosted on Vercel. AGENTS, PARTNERS AND LOAD A reference AI agent with a CLI and an MCP server (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk), holding its own Hedera account. It asks its human for approval, enters, seals bids and pays x402 by itself. A partner client that signs every request with its Hedera key (timestamp, method, path, body hash). A flood generator (undici) that hits two identical mock booking sites at once (one direct, one behind SurgePass), and a mock provider (Hono) that verifies the assertion in about ten lines. HOW THE PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES HELPED World ID gave us the one thing a ticket queue has never had: "one entry per real person" without collecting identities. It also made AI agents safe to let in, because every agent traces back to one verified human. Hedera turned "trust us, it was fair" into something anyone can check. Consensus timestamps give a fair order nobody can backdate, the PRNG gives a seed nobody controls, HCS gives a public record, and HTS KYC means a partner seat physically can't be moved to a reseller's account: the network refuses it, not our server. Fast finality and low, fixed fees made it practical to write every entry and settle per-request x402 payments during a rush.

The seed can't exist before the cutoff, and anyone can check the order. The draw is Fisher–Yates using sha256(seed ‖ counter) (@noble/hashes), shared by the gateway and the browser.
- HTS: each partner quota mints NFT seat tokens with KYC, freeze, wipe and supply keys. Partners associate the token with their own key, we grant KYC, transfer seats in consensus order, wipe used seats after booking, and wipe unused ones back to the public draw.
- Scheduled transactions: deposit refunds are ScheduleCreate transfers.
- Mirror node: partner public keys are looked up when they're allowlisted, and the waiting room's "Verify" page downloads the whole topic and recomputes the draw in the browser.

3. x402 ON HEDERA (@x402/core + @x402/hedera)
Paid endpoints answer 402 with x402 v2 payment requirements in HBAR. Clients sign a Hedera transfer with the "exact" scheme, and a public facilitator settles it on testnet. The same path is used for surge-priced availability reads (the price rises with load), agent bid deposits and partner hold deposits.

4. WORLD ID (@worldcoin/idkit, @worldcoin/idkit-core)
The gateway signs a one-time RP request per action (enter:<drop>), with a nonce stored in Redis so it can't be replayed. The waiting room opens the IDKit widget (proof of human, production World App). The gateway verifies the proof with the World Developer Portal's v4 verify API and turns the nullifier into an anonymous ID per drop. Agent approvals reuse the same action, with a signal binding the proof to that agent, the seat count and the max bid. Approvals work like a TV sign-in code: the agent gets a 401 "HumanApproval" with a link, the human approves with World App, and the agent polls for its token.

5. FRONTENDS (React 19, Vite, Tailwind, framer-motion)
- The waiting room is built on World's own UI kit (@worldcoin/mini-apps-ui-kit-react), so it looks and feels like World App. It has the live draw reveal, the sealed-bid page and the public "verify this draw" page.
- The provider console: drop builder, live decision log with step-by-step traces, partner management, side-by-side test runs (agents and partners run as real jobs against a chosen drop), an integration guide, and the bot-flood demo with a canvas "gate view" driven by the gateway's real per-second counts.
- A landing page and pitch deck from the same app, hosted on Vercel.

6. AGENTS, PARTNERS AND LOAD
- A reference AI agent with a CLI and an MCP server (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk), holding its own Hedera account. It asks its human for approval, enters, seals bids and pays x402 by itself.
- A partner client that signs every request with its Hedera key (timestamp, method, path, body hash).
- A flood generator (undici) that hits two identical mock booking sites at once (one direct, one behind SurgePass), and a mock provider (Hono) that verifies the assertion in about ten lines.

HOW THE PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES HELPED
- World ID gave us the one thing a ticket queue has never had: "one entry per real person" without collecting identities. It also made AI agents safe to let in, because every agent traces back to one verified human.
- Hedera turned "trust us, it was fair" into something anyone can check. Consensus timestamps give a fair order nobody can backdate, the PRNG gives a seed nobody controls, HCS gives a public record, and HTS KYC means a partner seat physically can't be moved to a reseller's account: the network refuses it, not our server. Fast finality and low, fixed fees made it practical to write every entry and settle per-request x402 payments during a rush.

projects.title: Ordin
projects.description: Automated recurring token payments on Whitechain with user automated terms
projects.project_description: Ordin brings recurring payments to Whitechain. Customers approve token access and authorize a payment policy specifying the merchant, recipient, amount, billing interval and optional expiry. Merchants can then collect eligible payments without requiring a new customer signature for every renewal. Funds stay in the customer's wallet until a payment succeeds. The contract enforces the agreed terms, permits only one successful payment per billing window and lets customers cancel future payments. Failed payments do not result in partial charges, and missed billing windows do not accumulate into debt. To demonstrate the experience, we built Frame, a software subscription app powered by Ordin. Payments unlock premium PNG generation and API access, while customers and merchants can manage billing, view receipts and track renewals. Ordin is deployed on Whitechain Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: Ordin combines a Solidity smart contract, a TypeScript SDK and a Node.js merchant service. The contract uses OpenZeppelin utilities for token transfers, signature validation and reentrancy protection. EIP-712 signatures bind payment authorizations to specific terms, with nonces and deadlines protecting against replay. It supports both standard wallets and ERC-1271 smart contract wallets. The SDK uses viem to prepare signatures, build transactions, inspect payment eligibility and decode contract events. Frame connects a browser interface to a merchant backend that relays signed authorizations, submits renewal transactions and tracks payment receipts. The merchant pays renewal gas, while customers currently pay for the initial token approval. Whitechain Sepolia provides the settlement network, with test USDT used for the subscription demo. For development, we use Hardhat, pinned Solidity compilation and automated tests covering payment rules, authorization, token interactions and subscription behavior. A useful demo detail is the accelerated billing schedule: Frame charges 1 test USDT per 120-second window for up to three windows, making renewals observable within a short demonstration.

projects.title: FrameCash
projects.description: Private eCash on EIP-8141: the pool sends your payment and pays its gas.
projects.project_description:
framecash is a Chaumian eCash wallet in which the pool contract, not the user, sends every
payment. You deposit ETH from any wallet with a set of blinded points. A mint, running as a
Chainlink CRE workflow, blind-signs them, and you unblind them into notes that nobody can
link to the deposit. To pay, you send one EIP-8141 frame transaction whose sender is the
pool. Its VERIFY frame checks the mint's BLS12-381 signature on chain, checks that the note
key signed this exact transaction, and approves paying the gas from the note. The SENDER
frame pays the payee and turns the rest into change, which the mint signs back into fresh
notes. There is no relayer, and no fresh address ever needs funding. The note's nonce key is its nullifier: the protocol consumes it when the pool approves, so
a note can't be spent twice. Validation reads no storage that payments write, so pending
payments never invalidate each other. All of the wallet's traffic goes through Anon-RPC over the Nox mixnet: reads, deposits,
the spent check, and the payment itself. The RPC node and the alt mempool never see the
user's IP next to a payment. Running on the EIP-8141 devnet (chain 1337). The browser app paid 0x8c7be807d1fc76e69a1b9b856d94aee26996b80c62a1990381a25b246d8f0410 (block 11030), with
the pool as payer and 43 RPC calls, all via Nox.
projects.how_its_made:
Contract (Solidity, Foundry). FramePool combines teecash's blind-mint deposit and
announce logic with a new pay path. Solidity can't emit the frame opcodes (APPROVE,
TXPARAM, SIGPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, FRAMEDATACOPY), so the pool deploys raw-bytecode helpers
of a few bytes each and calls them: APPROVE by delegatecall, the reads by staticcall. Gas. VERIFY costs 317k gas: hash-to-G2 and a pairing on the EIP-2537 precompiles,
plus introspection. That is over the canonical 100k cap. The pool stakes itself in the
ERC-8421 registry from its constructor, and the Skandha alt mempool admits it. Nullifier. The devnet doesn't support EIP-8250's single-use form, and we found that
a consumed key can be reused at sequence 1. So the pool accepts only sequence 0. Mint. A Chainlink CRE workflow in Go: a log trigger, blind signing in the
confidential handler, and WriteReport back to the pool. CRE has no forwarder on chain
1337, so we declared it under the CLI's experimental-chains setting with a forwarder of
our own. The workflow also mints change deposits emitted from inside frame transactions,
live. Client (TypeScript). Seed-derived note keys and blinding factors, so a new device
restores every note from the seed and a chain scan. A frame-tx codec, and a browser app on @anon-rpc/browser-harness . Anon-RPC. Nox is the default route. Nym drops the content-type header that Skandha
requires, and the tor-js demo gateway was down. We documented both. Tests. 22 forge tests, with BLS vectors produced by the TypeScript code over FFI, plus
TypeScript and Go tests. Each feasibility question has a probe with its result in research/ .
projects.project_description_markdown:
framecash is a Chaumian eCash wallet in which the pool contract, not the user, sends every
payment.

You deposit ETH from any wallet with a set of blinded points. A mint, running as a
Chainlink CRE workflow, blind-signs them, and you unblind them into notes that nobody can
link to the deposit. To pay, you send one EIP-8141 frame transaction whose sender is the
pool. Its VERIFY frame checks the mint's BLS12-381 signature on chain, checks that the note
key signed this exact transaction, and approves paying the gas from the note. The SENDER
frame pays the payee and turns the rest into change, which the mint signs back into fresh
notes. There is no relayer, and no fresh address ever needs funding.

The note's nonce key is its nullifier: the protocol consumes it when the pool approves, so
a note can't be spent twice. Validation reads no storage that payments write, so pending
payments never invalidate each other.

All of the wallet's traffic goes through Anon-RPC over the Nox mixnet: reads, deposits,
the spent check, and the payment itself. The RPC node and the alt mempool never see the
user's IP next to a payment.

Running on the EIP-8141 devnet (chain 1337). The browser app paid
`0x8c7be807d1fc76e69a1b9b856d94aee26996b80c62a1990381a25b246d8f0410` (block 11030), with

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
- **Contract (Solidity, Foundry).** `FramePool` combines teecash's blind-mint deposit and
  announce logic with a new pay path. Solidity can't emit the frame opcodes (APPROVE,
  TXPARAM, SIGPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, FRAMEDATACOPY), so the pool deploys raw-bytecode helpers
  of a few bytes each and calls them: APPROVE by delegatecall, the reads by staticcall.
- **Gas.** VERIFY costs 317k gas: hash-to-G2 and a pairing on the EIP-2537 precompiles,
  plus introspection. That is over the canonical 100k cap. The pool stakes itself in the
  ERC-8421 registry from its constructor, and the Skandha alt mempool admits it.
- **Nullifier.** The devnet doesn't support EIP-8250's single-use form, and we found that
  a consumed key can be reused at sequence 1. So the pool accepts only sequence 0.
- **Mint.** A Chainlink CRE workflow in Go: a log trigger, blind signing in the
  confidential handler, and `WriteReport` back to the pool. CRE has no forwarder on chain
  1337, so we declared it under the CLI's `experimental-chains` setting with a forwarder of
  our own. The workflow also mints change deposits emitted from inside frame transactions,
  live.
- **Client (TypeScript).** Seed-derived note keys and blinding factors, so a new device
  restores every note from the seed and a chain scan. A frame-tx codec, and a browser app on
  `@anon-rpc/browser-harness`.
- **Anon-RPC.** Nox is the default route. Nym drops the `content-type` header that Skandha
  requires, and the tor-js demo gateway was down. We documented both.
- **Tests.** 22 forge tests, with BLS vectors produced by the TypeScript code over FFI, plus
  TypeScript and Go tests. Each feasibility question has a probe with its result in
  `research/`.

projects.title: Rooted
projects.description: Rooted lets AI agents autonomously buy Ethereum block intelligence per request via x402 on Hedera
projects.project_description: Rooted is an agent-first data service for Ethereum block intelligence. It analyzes Sepolia blocks using ePBS payloads, EIP-7928 block access lists, native transaction replay, and conflict analysis, then produces an X-ray report showing validator and builder parallelism ceilings, execution-gas analysis, hot storage locations, and supporting evidence. A hosted Rooted instance exposes each report through an x402-protected endpoint: GET /api/paid/xray/{block_hash}. An autonomous agent can discover available reports through MCP, compare free summaries, choose a block, receive an HTTP 402 price quote, enforce per-request and daily spending limits, and sign the payment without human approval. The x402 facilitator verifies and settles the payment on Hedera testnet in HBAR or an HTS token, pays the network fee, and returns the report only after successful settlement. The client independently verifies the Hedera transaction through the mirror node and can append a tamper-evident purchase record to an HCS audit topic. Rooted demonstrates a complete pay-per-call economy where agents discover, evaluate, purchase, verify, and audit useful work autonomously.
projects.how_its_made: We built Rooted as a Go and TypeScript system. A Go backend runs beside Sepolia Nimbus and Geth, consumes ePBS payload envelopes and EIP-7928 block access lists, replays transactions with native Geth, analyzes read/write conflicts, and stores X-ray reports in PostgreSQL. A Next.js dashboard exposes the reports and hosts the x402 paywall. The paid route uses @x402/next, @x402/core, and @x402/hedera with the Hedera exact-payment scheme. Our autonomous Node.js client uses the Hedera SDK to sign payments, enforce per-request and daily budgets, restrict assets and recipients, prevent concurrent purchases, verify the returned report, and independently check the settled transaction through the Hedera mirror node. An MCP server lets an LLM agent discover free summaries and purchase a selected report as a tool call. Hedera provided fast, predictable settlement and facilitator-paid network fees, while HCS gave us a tamper-evident spending audit trail. The hacky part is the complete HTTP-native loop: the server returns 402 with a machine-readable quote, the agent signs and retries the same request, the facilitator settles only after the backend returns a valid report, and failed or invalid requests are never charged

projects.title: GPU4U
projects.description: AI agent that finds suitable GPUs and makes secure, policy-controlled x402 payments on Hedera.
projects.project_description: GPU4U is an AI-powered autonomous GPU marketplace router that simplifies GPU discovery, selection, and payment for AI workloads. Instead of manually browsing multiple GPU providers, comparing hardware specifications, checking availability, and calculating costs, users can simply describe their workload in natural language. GPU4U's AI agent understands the user's requirements, discovers available GPU offers through marketplace data, filters out unsuitable options, and identifies the most cost-effective GPU that meets the workload requirements. It then uses the x402 payment protocol to handle payments programmatically without relying on traditional manual checkout workflows. Integrated with Hedera, GPU4U enables secure payment settlement with independently verifiable transaction records. A facilitator handles payment verification and transaction submission while covering the network transaction fee. The agent also follows a policy-based spending system: payments within predefined limits can be processed automatically, payments above the automatic approval threshold require human authorization, and payments exceeding the hard spending limit or involving unauthorized recipients are rejected. GPU4U additionally provides payment verification through Hedera transaction records and maintains an auditable trail using the Hedera Consensus Service (HCS). Its goal is to make AI-driven compute procurement simpler, more transparent, and safer by allowing AI agents to discover suitable compute options and make controlled, verifiable payments on behalf of users.
projects.how_its_made: GPU4U is built using a Node.js-based AI agent and payment engine that connects GPU marketplace discovery with autonomous, policy-controlled payments on Hedera. For GPU discovery, we integrate the Aquanode marketplace API to retrieve available GPU offers. The GPU Router processes the user's natural-language workload requirements, validates the available offers against hardware and workload constraints, compares pricing, and selects the cheapest suitable option. The payment engine implements the x402 HTTP payment protocol. When a payment-protected endpoint responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required, the agent reads the payment requirements, checks the requested amount and recipient against its own quote and spending policies, and generates the required payment authorization. This connects the agent directly to the payment flow without relying on a conventional manual checkout process. We use Hedera Testnet for payment settlement. The Hedera facilitator verifies the payment authorization and handles transaction submission while paying the network transaction fee. After settlement, GPU4U independently checks the transaction through Hedera's public Mirror Node data to confirm that the transaction succeeded and the intended recipient received the expected amount. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) is used to maintain an additional audit trail of important payment events, while HashScan provides a human-readable way to inspect transactions. One notable implementation is the agent's spending-policy engine. It supports automatic payments within a predefined limit, human approval for payments above the automatic threshold, and rejection when a payment exceeds the hard spending ceiling or involves an unauthorized recipient. We also compare the server's x402 payment requirement against the agent's expected quote at the tinybar level, preventing unexpected price changes from being silently accepted. The combination of live marketplace discovery, an autonomous agent, x402, and Hedera creates a controlled payment workflow where an AI agent can discover compute offers and make verifiable payments without receiving unrestricted access to the user's funds.

projects.title: WalletDesk
projects.description: WalletDesk turns idle tokens in a wallet into Uniswap v4 liquidity without depositing them.
projects.project_description: Pools are only as deep as deposited capital. A large swap on a thin Uniswap v4 pool walks the curve and pays heavy price impact, while makers and treasuries sit on idle inventory in their wallets, because providing liquidity today means depositing it: custody risk, lockup and fragmented liquidity. Static on-chain quotes also get picked off once the market moves. WalletDesk fixes this with wallet-native liquidity. A maker ships a DeskBand strategy on 1inch Aqua: a custom SwapVM instruction that quotes a value-weighted price band with decay and a fee, while the tokens stay in the maker's wallet. Aqua only records virtual balances and pulls tokens when a fill happens. Our Uniswap v4 hook (OverflowHook) caps how much of an exact-input swap the pool fills and fills the residual from the best registered desk in the same transaction, through any v4 router, including Uniswap's stock PoolSwapTest. It advances the residual from PoolManager reserves, pays the maker through SwapVM (Aqua pull/push) and returns a BeforeSwapDelta that charges the caller. Before a desk fills, its quote must sit within the maker's limit of both the pool spot price and a reference price that a Chainlink CRE workflow writes on chain from Coinbase and Kraken (DON consensus), so a stale band is skipped instead of picked off. A desk can never revert a swap: unfunded wallets, failed fills and stale references all fall back to the pool, and every skip emits DeskSkipped(reason). Live on Unichain Sepolia with 31 verified transactions showing real overflow fills, plus a web app to make a desk, preview the pool/desk split, run live overflow swaps and claim optional USDC rebates.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are built with Foundry. OverflowHook is a Uniswap v4 hook (OpenZeppelin BaseHook) using beforeSwap + beforeSwapReturnDelta. It computes the residual above the pool cap, checks PoolManager reserves, quotes up to 8 registered desks per pool, and drops any desk outside its maxDeviationBps of the pool spot (from slot0) or the CRE reference, or whose wallet can't pay. It then takes the residual from reserves, settles the maker's output and returns a BeforeSwapDelta. If the SwapVM call reverts, it refunds via sync/settle with a zero delta, so swaps never break. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM v1.0.2: we wrote DeskBand, a new SwapVM opcode (value-weighted band in the v4 price unit, both directions, mixed decimals, decay and fee). The canonical AquaSwapVMRouter has no slot for it, so we redeployed a modified SwapVM (WalletDeskRouter) that inherits the unmodified SwapVM and only replaces the opcode table, as 1inch's rules allow. The hook verifies the strategy is really shipped and uses min(shipped, wallet balance, allowance) as deliverable inventory. On Unichain mainnet we use the live Aqua registry; on Unichain Sepolia (no Aqua code there) we deploy an unmodified Aqua ourselves. Chainlink CRE (TypeScript SDK): a cron workflow fetches Coinbase and Kraken prices per node over HTTP, takes a DON consensus median, writes it via an EVM write to DeskPriceFeed (an IReceiver consumer with replay-safe ordering) and reads it back. The hook fails closed on a missing or stale reference. The CRE simulation passed against the live Sepolia feed. The frontend is Next.js + wagmi/viem, with a viem keeper that indexes fills and skips; the web app is hosted on Railway. Testing: 38 local Foundry tests, the hook suite (21 tests) re-run on a Unichain mainnet fork against the live PoolManager and Aqua, 19 CRE workflow tests and 7 keeper tests, all in green CI. A one-command demo script forks Unichain, deploys, ships a maker, runs overflow swaps and starts the UI.

projects.title: BriefMint
projects.description: An interactive DAO workspace turning private ideas into owner approved, onchain opportunities.
projects.project_description: BriefMint is an interactive DAO coordination platform that transforms private project ideas into structured, publicly discoverable contributor opportunities. Built around an immersive isometric city, it addresses a common challenge in Web3 communities: turning scattered discussions, rough requirements and internal planning notes into actionable work. Using 0G Compute, BriefMint generates clearly defined deliverables, acceptance criteria and project requirements, while allowing organizers to review and approve exactly what becomes public. Once approved, opportunities are published to Arkiv as wallet owned, indexed records that contributors and external applications can discover independently. By combining AI assisted planning, human controlled publication and decentralized discovery within a visual workspace, BriefMint simplifies how DAOs organize work, communicate expectations and connect ideas with potential contributors.
projects.how_its_made: BriefMint is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Pixi.js, which powers its interactive isometric city and connects the planning, generation, approval and discovery workflows. Its backend uses Node.js, SQLite and Zod for authenticated private storage, structured data validation and revision management. We integrated 0G Compute Router with the 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model to generate contributor briefs from unstructured notes, requesting private routing with fallbacks disabled. Each generated proposal remains editable, and a canonical SHA256 hash binds the owner's approval to the exact public payload before publication. For decentralized discovery, BriefMint integrates the Arkiv SDK on Rabdi testnet, with MetaMask, wagmi and viem handling wallet authentication and owner authorized transactions. Approved opportunities are published as indexed Arkiv entities that can be retrieved independently of BriefMint's backend. We also implemented transaction receipt reconciliation, duplicate submission safeguards and strict separation between private notes and public records. The complete workflow was demonstrated through live 0G inference, owner approval, confirmed Arkiv publication and independent public readback, while independent cryptographic verification of 0G execution remains an area for further development.

projects.title: Proxima
projects.description: An agent wallet where AI agents can be tricked but can't move money outside the owner's ENS rules.
projects.project_description: AI agents now hold wallets, and they get tricked. Hidden instructions in a repo, an invoice, a web page or even a token's name can make an agent send funds to an attacker or grant a dangerous approval. Real incidents in 2026 (Grok × Bankr, the $7.5M jaredfromsubway drain) show that better prompts alone don't stop this. Proxima is an agent wallet built on the assumption that the agent will be fooled. Any agent connects through the ProximaSDK and a popup wallet; the owner approves the session. The agent holds no keys to the funds. It can only propose actions, and Proxima decides. Before anything is signed, the wallet privately simulates the transaction, lists every effect (payments, approvals, hidden balance changes), checks it against the owner's rules, compares it with what the agent claimed it would do, and traces which untrusted input (file, line, token name, page) led the agent astray. Each action is allowed, blocked, or sent to the owner for approval. The rules live on the agent's ENSv2 name (e.g. demo.proxima-demo.eth): approved payees, per-payment and daily caps, approval thresholds. With Enhanced Access Control the agent has zero roles and cannot change them; expiry and unregister act as its lifetime and kill switch. Funds sit in a Safe, and our ProximaModule re-reads the ENS rules on-chain before every payment, so violations revert even if the wallet is bypassed or the agent key is stolen. Every blockchain read goes through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC (Nox, with tor-js fallback), so the RPC never learns what the agent is doing. Self-serve 24-hour trial agents (tryN.trials.proxima-demo.eth) let anyone try it with tiny limits. Everything is live and verified on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: Proxima is a pnpm TypeScript monorepo plus a Foundry contracts project, all running against live Sepolia. On-chain (Solidity, Foundry): funds sit in a Safe v1.4.1. Our guard module (BlindspotModule) is the agent's only path to them (execute / executeBatch, 1-8 calls). On every call it checks the agent's ENSv2 name with getState (registered, owned by the caller, not expired), reads the owner's rules from the agent's ENS data record "blindspot.policy", and enforces allowed recipients, contracts and functions, per-transaction and daily caps, and "no leftover approvals" (ERC-20 allowances, NFT operators and approvals must be zero after the batch), reverting with named errors. The module is verified on Etherscan. A shared policy codec encodes rules byte-for-byte identically in TypeScript and Solidity. ENSv2 (central, not cosmetic): blindspot-demo.eth points to our own UserRegistry (deployed via VerifiableFactory). Each agent is a subname registered with zero roles and its own Permissioned Resolver; Enhanced Access Control lets the agent write only its agent.status text record, never its rules. Expiry is the agent's lifetime and unregister is the kill switch. Agents publish an ENSIP-26 agent-context record, payees are ENS names (vendor1.blindspot-demo.eth), and the owner changed the daily cap with one ENS setData, no redeploy. Self-serve trial agents live in a nested registry, tryN.trials.blindspot-demo.eth (24-hour expiry), created by a TrialProvisioner that holds only ROLE_REGISTRAR and a setter role on a separate trial resolver, so trials can never touch the demo agent's rules or vault. Wallet core (TypeScript, viem): every proposal is simulated with eth_simulateV1, reading balances and allowances in the same simulated block to get true post-state effects (catching tokens that move balances silently). Checks include rules, claim vs reality (what the agent declared vs simulated effects), look-alike addresses, proxy-upgrade detection via the EIP-1967 slot, rate limits and fail-closed on anything unrecognised. An origin trace tags every input as trusted or untrusted and points to the exact file, line or token name that introduced a bad recipient. Anon-RPC (Ethereum Foundation): every read and broadcast goes through the browser harness, Nox on Sepolia with an automatic tor-js fallback, and the worker hash pinned against the on-chain specifier. A per-session meter shows the anonymized share (~95-100%); the only excluded traffic is the declared bootstrap read, plus a manual, clearly bannered "Direct" mode for outages. Agent + SDK: the Proxima SDK connects any browser agent to the popup wallet over postMessage with origin checks; the owner approves a revocable session and the rules are handed to the agent at connect. Our example agent uses Groq gpt-oss-120b (model picker incl. custom/local endpoints) with tools like read_document, read_repo, token_info, propose and execute. Keys are encrypted in the browser (PBKDF2 + AES-GCM, memory-only unlock); the agent app never holds a key, and execute signs only an ALLOWed proposal re-checked just before signing. Hacky bits: deduplicating EIP-7708 ETH-transfer logs against eth_simulateV1's synthetic ones; one resolver per agent because resolver roles cover every name a resolver serves; a separate trial registry so trial keys can't call the demo module; skipping ENS's nested "nexus" submodule, whose file names break on Windows.
