projects.title: Octane
projects.description: An open gas market: makers compete to pay your gas, and you pay one fee in stablecoins.
projects.project_description: Octane is an open gas market. To move stablecoins today, you need a second token just to pay gas, and the usual fix is one company's relayer and one shared pool of funds. Octane replaces that with a market. Independent makers hold gas tokens and compete to pay your gas. You sign once, and you pay one fee in stablecoins inside the same transaction. There's no shared treasury, and no operator decides who can take part. It works in two places. On Whitechain Sepolia, a payer signs an EIP-3009 USDT authorisation bound to one maker. That maker relays it through a verified contract and pays the WBT gas. On the EF alt-mempool devnet, each maker runs its own staked EIP-8141 paymaster, which checks the payer's USDC balance during validation. The public mempool rejects that transaction, and the alternative mempool admits it. Live quotes, auction bids, fills and reputation all sit on Arkiv, so a crashed maker's price disappears within 30 seconds and anyone can read the market. Each maker's journal is stored on Swarm. People pay from a wallet in plain English or Hinglish. AI agents pay through an MCP server, including gas auctions where makers bid for the job. Merchants can cover the fee, and anyone can become a maker, setting their own rate or letting an AI agent price within hard limits. Try it at https://octane.rishabhprajapati.me. It runs on testnets with test tokens, the contracts are unaudited, and the demo makers all run on one server.
projects.how_its_made: Octane is a pnpm TypeScript monorepo with Solidity contracts built in Foundry. On Whitechain, OctaneRelay checks a signed EIP-712 quote and recomputes a nonce that binds the payment to the quote, merchant, amount, maker and fee payer. It then calls receiveWithAuthorization and pays the merchant and the maker in one transaction. Binding the nonce means a signature can't be used by another maker. There's no shared treasury to drain, because each maker spends its own WBT and is repaid in the same transaction. On the EF devnet, a factory deploys one staked EIP-1167 paymaster clone per maker, following the workshop's hegota-support patterns. The clone's pay frame makes six checks in 54,769 gas, inside the sidecar's 100k budget. This needs the alternative mempool because it reads USDC storage during validation. We saved the public mempool's StorageReadNonSender rejection beside the same transaction being admitted and mined. Arkiv is the market's shared state. It holds six entity types: quote, request, bid, fill, maker and makerStats. Ownership stops makers editing each other's prices or rating themselves, and expiry removes stale prices with no cleanup job. Clients verify every quote's signature. Swarm stores hash-linked maker journals, with the latest reference held on Arkiv, and pnpm recompute-fade rebuilds reputation from that public data. Makers are TypeScript services using viem. A formula with hard caps sets the price. Claude only picks a bounded risk buffer and writes a journal line. The wallet is built with Next.js and Tailwind, and agents connect through an MCP server. The hosted version runs on AWS EC2 with Caddy and systemd. Notable hacks: ecrecover wasn't usable during validation, so the maker's signature travels as a second signature entry and is read with SIGPARAM. Arkiv has no update that extends expiry, so each refresh is one atomic executeBatch of a patch and an extension. Whitechain's USDT has no eip712Domain(), so we assert the domain against DOMAIN_SEPARATOR(). AI usage: this was built by one person with heavy assistance from Claude Code. The README lists what AI generated, part by part. Timing disclosure: before hacking opened at about 21:05 IST on Nov 5, the repo received planning, tooling and setup commits, plus early code for the signed quote library and shared SDK modules. The commit history shows these.

projects.title: हिsaab
projects.description: Verifiable invoicing on Whitechain with gasless USDT payments and QR-based receipts.
projects.project_description: Hisaab is a blockchain-powered invoicing and payment verification platform that enables freelancers and contractors to issue invoices, receive USDT payments, and generate independently verifiable payment receipts. Built on Whitechain, Hisaab uses smart contracts to link invoices directly to their corresponding payments. Each invoice is cryptographically hashed onchain, ensuring that its contents cannot be tampered with without detection, while sensitive information remains privately sealed. Clients can pay invoices directly in USDT or use our gasless payment mechanism powered by EIP-3009, allowing them to complete transactions without holding native gas tokens. A relayer handles transaction submission and network fees. Upon full payment, Hisaab automatically mints an NFT receipt containing an onchain-generated QR code. Anyone authorized by the freelancer can scan this code to independently verify the invoice's payment status and transaction history against the blockchain, without relying on screenshots or trusting Hisaab's servers. We also integrate ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia to support verifiable organizational identities, subnames, and client acknowledgements. Hisaab combines Whitechain's payment infrastructure, gasless transactions, cryptographic verification, NFT receipts, and ENS-based identity to make financial documentation transparent, portable, and independently verifiable.
projects.how_its_made: Hisaab was built during ETHGlobal Mumbai over an intensive 36-hour development sprint, during which each team member managed approximately six hours of sleep. Our goal was to build more than an invoicing interface: we wanted to create an end-to-end system for issuing, settling and independently verifying invoices onchain. The application uses Next.js 16 and TypeScript, with Solidity smart contracts developed and tested using Foundry. We deployed two contracts on Whitechain Sepolia: HisaabRegistry, which manages invoice creation, payments and refunds, and HisaabReceipt, which automatically mints an NFT upon full invoice settlement. A key engineering challenge was implementing gasless payments. We integrated EIP-3009 with USDT and developed a custom TypeScript relayer that submits transactions on behalf of clients. The relayer performs authorization validation, balance and invoice-state checks, transaction simulation and rate limiting before submitting a payment. This allows clients to pay invoices without holding WBT for gas. We also designed the invoice architecture around privacy and tamper detection. Invoice documents are hashed using keccak256, while sensitive information remains sealed within the payment link. A salted commitment to the issuer's ENS identity is stored onchain. When a client opens an invoice, the application independently verifies its contents against the onchain hash before allowing payment. Another notable implementation is our onchain receipt generation. We developed SVG and QR code generation directly in Solidity, allowing the receipt NFT to carry a QR code linking to its independent verification page. This eliminates reliance on our backend for generating the receipt itself. For identity verification, we integrated ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia, supporting organizational identities, subnames, client acknowledgements, expiry and revocation. Our verification and PDF generation API runs on Render, while the Next.js application is deployed on Vercel. We also developed a shared TypeScript package for invoice hashing, document sealing, cryptographic signing, relayer logic and smart contract interactions. The contracts were validated with 35 Foundry tests. Claude Code assisted us as a pair programmer throughout development, particularly with implementation, testing and debugging. The architecture, product decisions and final code review were handled by our team. Building across two chains, implementing a custom gasless payment flow and generating verifiable receipts entirely onchain within 36 hours was an ambitious undertaking. It was also precisely what made building Hisaab worthwhile.

projects.title: Cinevest
projects.description: Fund independent films with milestone escrow, then pay only for the parts you watch.
projects.project_description: Cinevest connects independent filmmakers, backers and viewers through transparent film financing and pay-as-you-watch distribution. Creators publish a film proposal, set a funding goal and nominate an independent reviewer. Backers contribute test USDC into a smart contract escrow. If funding succeeds, production funds unlock in three milestone tranches: 30%, 40% and 30%. Creators submit evidence for review before further funds are approved. If the funding goal is missed, backers can reclaim their contributions. Once a film is ready, Chainlink CRE checks the campaign’s on-chain state and video delivery readiness before the reviewer approves its final release. Viewers can then buy full access or deposit a refundable viewing balance. Metered playback charges for five-second blocks of content watched, capped at the full-film price. Rewatching paid blocks adds no charge, and viewers can refund their unused balance. Viewing revenue is shared between the creator and backers under the campaign’s predefined terms, with capped backer repayments. Creator-owned listings make films discoverable through Arkiv, while public proposals, posters and milestone evidence are stored on Swarm. Cinevest currently runs on testnets using test USDC.
projects.how_its_made: Cinevest is an npm monorepo with separate Next.js applications for the frontend and backend, Solidity contracts built with Foundry, and a Chainlink CRE workflow. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, wagmi and viem for wallet connections and contract interactions. Arc Testnet provides USDC settlement. Each film has a campaign contract that manages contributions, production escrow, milestone approvals, purchases, viewing deposits, refunds and revenue allocation. Arkiv Rabdi stores creator-owned film listings, which the backend verifies against Arc before displaying them in discovery. Swarm stores public media and evidence, with references committed on-chain. PostgreSQL records publication progress, wallet sessions and viewing usage; Sign-In with Ethereum authenticates wallet owners. Mux processes uploaded films and provides signed video delivery. For metered viewing, we built an authenticated HLS gateway that rewrites playlists and checks each segment request against the viewer’s funded balance. This lets us enforce delivery limits without exposing unrestricted provider URLs. A background worker submits cumulative, meter-signed usage receipts to Arc, while the contracts cap charges at the deposited amount and full-film price. The Chainlink CRE workflow combines Arc contract reads with direct Mux API checks. It runs as a local CLI simulation through an authenticated runner; the independent reviewer still signs the approval transaction. One notable workaround was checking approval eligibility from public contract state because the simulator ignored the caller’s from field. We also built a resumable publication journal so interrupted Swarm uploads, Arc deployments and Arkiv listings can recover without blindly creating duplicate campaigns.

Once a film is ready, Chainlink CRE checks the campaign’s on-chain state and video delivery readiness before the reviewer approves its final release. Viewers can then buy full access or deposit a refundable viewing balance. Metered playback charges for five-second blocks of content watched, capped at the full-film price. Rewatching paid blocks adds no charge, and viewers can refund their unused balance.

Viewing revenue is shared between the creator and backers under the campaign’s predefined terms, with capped backer repayments. Creator-owned listings make films discoverable through Arkiv, while public proposals, posters and milestone evidence are stored on Swarm.

Cinevest currently runs on testnets using test USDC.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Cinevest is an npm monorepo with separate Next.js applications for the frontend and backend, Solidity contracts built with Foundry, and a Chainlink CRE workflow. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, wagmi and viem for wallet connections and contract interactions.

Arc Testnet provides USDC settlement. Each film has a campaign contract that manages contributions, production escrow, milestone approvals, purchases, viewing deposits, refunds and revenue allocation. Arkiv Rabdi stores creator-owned film listings, which the backend verifies against Arc before displaying them in discovery. Swarm stores public media and evidence, with references committed on-chain. PostgreSQL records publication progress, wallet sessions and viewing usage; Sign-In with Ethereum authenticates wallet owners.

Mux processes uploaded films and provides signed video delivery. For metered viewing, we built an authenticated HLS gateway that rewrites playlists and checks each segment request against the viewer’s funded balance. This lets us enforce delivery limits without exposing unrestricted provider URLs. A background worker submits cumulative, meter-signed usage receipts to Arc, while the contracts cap charges at the deposited amount and full-film price.

The Chainlink CRE workflow combines Arc contract reads with direct Mux API checks. It runs as a local CLI simulation through an authenticated runner; the independent reviewer still signs the approval transaction. One notable workaround was checking approval eligibility from public contract state because the simulator ignored the caller’s `from` field.

We also built a resumable publication journal so interrupted Swarm uploads, Arc deployments and Arkiv listings can recover without blindly creating duplicate campaigns.

projects.project_description: JanLekha 2.0 – Public Financial Transparency & Accountability Platform JanLekha 2.0 is a blockchain-powered public financial transparency platform designed to make government expenditure traceable, verifiable, and accessible to every citizen. Its core mission is simple: every taxpayer deserves to know where their money goes, how it is spent, who receives it, and whether the promised work is actually completed. Today, government budgets, procurement processes, contractor payments, and infrastructure project updates are often distributed across disconnected systems. Citizens may know how much money has been allocated to a project, but accessing its complete financial journey—from budget approval to contractor payment and verified project completion—is difficult. JanLekha addresses this transparency gap by connecting the entire public expenditure lifecycle through a unified platform. The platform provides six dedicated role-based workspaces for Government Administrators, Finance Officers, Procurement Officers, Contractors, Independent Auditors, and Citizens. Government administrators can register departments and projects, finance officers manage budget allocations and payment approvals, procurement officers publish tenders and evaluate bids, contractors submit bids and project milestones, and independent auditors verify submitted evidence and investigate potential financial discrepancies. What makes JanLekha particularly powerful is its citizen-first approach. Anyone can access the public portal without connecting a cryptocurrency wallet. Citizens can explore government departments, inspect project budgets, follow expenditure, examine procurement records, track contractor payments, review project milestones, access audit reports, and submit complaints. An interactive financial flow visualization helps users trace public money from government allocations through departments, projects, contractors, and payments. Built around a decentralized infrastructure, JanLekha combines multiple technologies: Arc Blockchain: Provides the blockchain infrastructure for recording and verifying approved public financial records, project events, procurement activities, and audit trails. The platform targets Arc Testnet and uses USDC for demonstrating blockchain-based settlement workflows, while maintaining government budgets and expenditure accounting separately in INR. Arkiv: Integrates a decentralized data layer for storing and retrieving relevant application records and supporting information. Swarm: Enables decentralized storage of project videos and visual evidence uploaded by government officials, helping preserve supporting material beyond a conventional centralized storage system. Image Compression: Compresses government-uploaded proof images to optimise storage requirements while retaining evidence for project monitoring and verification. Smart Contracts: Eight Solidity registries manage roles, budgets, projects, procurement, milestones, payments, documents, and audits. Document Verification: Uses SHA-256 hashing to verify document integrity and determine whether a document matches its previously registered cryptographic fingerprint. Risk Monitoring: An integrated risk engine detects potential discrepancies, including unusual budget variances, duplicate invoice hashes, unauthorised payment amounts, repeated milestone payments, delayed milestones, and missing supporting documents. JanLekha also incorporates separation of duties to reduce opportunities for misuse of authority. Contractors cannot verify their own work, auditors cannot modify original financial records, citizens have read-only access, and payment initiation is separated from payment authorisation. The ultimate objective is to transform government financial transparency from a matter of trust into something citizens can independently inspect and verify. Instead of merely publishing budget figures, JanLekha connects financial records with procurement activities, contractor accountability, project progress, supporting media evidence, and independent audits. JanLekha is built on the belief that public money should have a public trail. By combining blockchain verification, decentralized storage, cryptographic document integrity, and accessible citizen dashboards, we aim to create a more transparent, accountable, and trustworthy public financial ecosystem. Note: The current version is a testnet demonstration using synthetic government data and simulated USDC settlements. It does not represent actual government expenditure or move real funds.
projects.how_its_made: How We Built JanLekha 2.0 We built JanLekha 2.0 as a unified, citizen-first public financial transparency platform using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Solidity, Foundry, and a decentralized infrastructure powered by Arc, Arkiv, and Swarm. 1. Frontend and Application Architecture The application is built using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and React Router. We designed a unified application with a shared data store and six role-specific workspaces rather than building disconnected dashboards. The public citizen portal uses a light theme, while internal government workspaces use a dark, professional interface. Recharts powers financial analytics, while custom-built SVG components power our interactive Sankey money-flow visualization and geographical project explorer. 2. Arc Blockchain and Smart Contracts We chose Circle's Arc Testnet as our blockchain infrastructure, with chain ID 5042002. Using Solidity 0.8.24 and Foundry, we developed eight modular smart contract registries: RoleRegistry, BudgetRegistry, ProjectRegistry, ProcurementRegistry, MilestoneRegistry, PaymentRegistry, DocumentRegistry, and AuditRegistry. These contracts represent different stages of the government financial lifecycle. We integrated ethers.js and MetaMask-compatible wallet connectivity to interact with the blockchain. Our financial model deliberately separates INR-denominated government budgets from USDC-based settlement demonstrations. Native USDC is treated as the gas asset, while ERC-20 USDC uses six decimals. We also implemented a testnet deployment script that reads private keys exclusively from environment variables. 3. Arkiv and Decentralized Data Infrastructure We integrated Arkiv as a decentralized data layer to support the platform's record and information management. This complements Arc's on-chain financial accountability layer, allowing us to separate blockchain verification from application data storage. 4. Swarm and Evidence Storage One of our important design decisions was not to store large media files directly on the blockchain. Government officials need to submit photographs and videos as evidence of infrastructure progress, completed milestones, and project activities. We therefore incorporated an image compression pipeline to optimise uploaded photographs before storage and integrated Swarm for decentralized video storage. This allows supporting visual evidence to be handled separately from financial transactions while maintaining a path to associate evidence with relevant project and milestone records. 5. Document Integrity and Verification We implemented browser-based SHA-256 hashing for document verification. Citizens can upload a document or paste its hash to check its integrity against a registered reference. This creates a practical way to detect whether submitted evidence has changed without publishing confidential document contents directly on-chain. 6. Risk Detection and Audit Engine We developed a custom TypeScript risk engine that checks budget variances, duplicate invoice hashes, payments exceeding authorised limits, repeated payments against milestones, delayed milestones, and missing supporting documents. Each detected issue carries contextual information, evidence, risk severity, investigation status, auditor notes, and resolution history. Importantly, the system identifies potential discrepancies rather than automatically declaring fraud. 7. Role-Based Permissions and Separation of Duties We implemented a centralised permission system in src/lib/permissions.ts . It enforces role-specific actions in the demo, with clear separation between payment initiation and authorisation, contractor milestone submissions, independent auditor verification, and citizen read-only access. We also documented the need for server-side enforcement before production deployment. 8. Testing and Engineering Decisions We used Foundry to compile and test our Solidity contracts. Our test suite achieved 18 passing tests, with zero failures and zero skipped tests. We also built the frontend around a shared application context and browser localStorage, allowing all six workspaces to interact with the same demonstration state without requiring a separate backend server. What was particularly interesting about our implementation? The hackiest and most interesting engineering decision was connecting the entire government expenditure lifecycle into one coherent workflow instead of treating budgeting, procurement, payments, audits, and citizen transparency as separate applications. We also deliberately separated large evidence files from blockchain transactions, using compression and decentralized storage for media while keeping cryptographic verification and financial accountability as distinct concerns. We built the project with a strong emphasis on technical honesty: the Solidity contracts and wallet integration are real, but government figures are synthetic demonstration data and USDC settlements are simulated. Our architecture targets Arc Testnet, and the current demo does not move real funds or claim to represent actual government expenditure. Our goal was to demonstrate how blockchain, decentralized storage, cryptographic verification, and thoughtfully designed workflows can work together to make public financial accountability independently inspectable by ordinary citizens.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
# How We Built JanLekha 2.0

We built JanLekha 2.0 as a unified, citizen-first public financial transparency platform using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Solidity, Foundry, and a decentralized infrastructure powered by Arc, Arkiv, and Swarm.

**1. Frontend and Application Architecture**

The application is built using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and React Router. We designed a unified application with a shared data store and six role-specific workspaces rather than building disconnected dashboards. The public citizen portal uses a light theme, while internal government workspaces use a dark, professional interface. Recharts powers financial analytics, while custom-built SVG components power our interactive Sankey money-flow visualization and geographical project explorer.

**2. Arc Blockchain and Smart Contracts**

We chose Circle's Arc Testnet as our blockchain infrastructure, with chain ID 5042002. Using Solidity 0.8.24 and Foundry, we developed eight modular smart contract registries: RoleRegistry, BudgetRegistry, ProjectRegistry, ProcurementRegistry, MilestoneRegistry, PaymentRegistry, DocumentRegistry, and AuditRegistry.

These contracts represent different stages of the government financial lifecycle. We integrated ethers.js and MetaMask-compatible wallet connectivity to interact with the blockchain. Our financial model deliberately separates INR-denominated government budgets from USDC-based settlement demonstrations. Native USDC is treated as the gas asset, while ERC-20 USDC uses six decimals. We also implemented a testnet deployment script that reads private keys exclusively from environment variables.

**3. Arkiv and Decentralized Data Infrastructure**

We integrated Arkiv as a decentralized data layer to support the platform's record and information management. This complements Arc's on-chain financial accountability layer, allowing us to separate blockchain verification from application data storage.

**4. Swarm and Evidence Storage**

One of our important design decisions was not to store large media files directly on the blockchain. Government officials need to submit photographs and videos as evidence of infrastructure progress, completed milestones, and project activities. We therefore incorporated an image compression pipeline to optimise uploaded photographs before storage and integrated Swarm for decentralized video storage. This allows supporting visual evidence to be handled separately from financial transactions while maintaining a path to associate evidence with relevant project and milestone records.

**5. Document Integrity and Verification**

We implemented browser-based SHA-256 hashing for document verification. Citizens can upload a document or paste its hash to check its integrity against a registered reference. This creates a practical way to detect whether submitted evidence has changed without publishing confidential document contents directly on-chain.

**6. Risk Detection and Audit Engine**

We developed a custom TypeScript risk engine that checks budget variances, duplicate invoice hashes, payments exceeding authorised limits, repeated payments against milestones, delayed milestones, and missing supporting documents. Each detected issue carries contextual information, evidence, risk severity, investigation status, auditor notes, and resolution history. Importantly, the system identifies potential discrepancies rather than automatically declaring fraud.

**7. Role-Based Permissions and Separation of Duties**

We implemented a centralised permission system in `src/lib/permissions.ts`. It enforces role-specific actions in the demo, with clear separation between payment initiation and authorisation, contractor milestone submissions, independent auditor verification, and citizen read-only access. We also documented the need for server-side enforcement before production deployment.

**8. Testing and Engineering Decisions**

We used Foundry to compile and test our Solidity contracts. Our test suite achieved 18 passing tests, with zero failures and zero skipped tests. We also built the frontend around a shared application context and browser localStorage, allowing all six workspaces to interact with the same demonstration state without requiring a separate backend server.

**What was particularly interesting about our implementation?**

The hackiest and most interesting engineering decision was connecting the entire government expenditure lifecycle into one coherent workflow instead of treating budgeting, procurement, payments, audits, and citizen transparency as separate applications.

We also deliberately separated large evidence files from blockchain transactions, using compression and decentralized storage for media while keeping cryptographic verification and financial accountability as distinct concerns.

We built the project with a strong emphasis on technical honesty: the Solidity contracts and wallet integration are real, but government figures are synthetic demonstration data and USDC settlements are simulated. Our architecture targets Arc Testnet, and the current demo does not move real funds or claim to represent actual government expenditure.

**Our goal was to demonstrate how blockchain, decentralized storage, cryptographic verification, and thoughtfully designed workflows can work together to make public financial accountability independently inspectable by ordinary citizens.**

projects.title: Klarity
projects.description: Decentralized always-on clear-signing data for Ethereum wallets — the ERC-7730 registry
projects.project_description: Klarity is two things that need each other: an indestructible, untraceable Ethereum wallet , and the clear-signing security data that wallet depends on — both engineered so no single server, company, or court can take them down. Start with the wallet. Every wallet you've used loads its interface from a server that can be hacked, phished, domain-hijacked, or seized, and sends its RPC through a handful of providers that see your IP and your entire portfolio. Klarity removes both. Its UI is served directly from a smart contract via ERC-8244 ( html() as a gas-free view call) or from a content-addressed IPFS bundle — there is no website to compromise, and the interface lives in the same trust domain as the bytecode it drives. Its JSON-RPC rides an anonymizing transport (anon-rpc) in a hash-pinned, null-origin sandboxed worker, Tor- or Nym-routed, so the destination RPC never learns who is asking. It is reached as klarity.eth , whose ENS contenthash points at the pinned CID, resolvable through any ENS gateway ( eth.limo , Brave, ENS-native browsers) with nothing we host in between. The account itself is an ERC-4337 smart account controlled by a WebAuthn/passkey — no seed phrase to leak. Name-addressed, content-addressed, anonymized: a wallet with no off switch. Now the data that makes it safe. When a wallet shows "Approve unlimited USDC to 0x1f98…" instead of a wall of hex, it is reading an ERC-7730 clear-signing descriptor — the one safeguard standing between a user and blind signing, the single largest vector for drained wallets. If the wallet can't fetch that descriptor at signing time it doesn't stop and warn you; it silently downgrades to raw hex and asks you to sign anyway — exactly when an attacker's phishing calldata is in front of you. Yet today that security-critical dataset lives in one GitHub repo , and GitHub goes down routinely (its own status log shows repeated Git/API degradations in a typical two-week window; we cite only dated incidents, not an unverified annual figure). A wallet engineered to have no single point of failure cannot read its security data from one. So Klarity mirrors the entire ERC-7730 registry into Arkiv — a decentralized, permissionlessly-queryable entity store — keyed by (chainId, contract, selector) , byte-verifiable and provenance-pinned, with a two-way GitHub↔Arkiv sync for backwards compatibility (poll/webhook in, authorized pull-request back out). The whole path — UI, transport, and signing data — is equally un-takedownable. Around it: a MetaMask Snap that clear-signs at transaction time, a Next.js Explorer to browse and author descriptors, and attestation/reputation signals so consumers rank descriptors by verified trust.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript, end to end , across two repos: klarity (registry mirror, Fastify API, Arkiv client, EIP-712 auth, Explorer, Snap) and klarity-wallet (the ERC-8244 / anon-rpc / ENS wallet). The wallet (klarity-wallet) UI with no host — ERC-8244. contracts/HtmlHost.sol serves the wallet document from html() (selector 0x33c34ac3 ), a gas-free view . Because the document exceeds the EIP-170 24KB code cap, its bytes are stored as the runtime code of one or more SSTORE2 data contracts (each prefixed with a STOP guard so data can never execute) and stitched back with extcodecopy at read time. The host fetches html() through the anon transport (so even loading the UI is anonymized) and mounts it in a sandbox="allow-scripts" , null-origin iframe; per ERC-8244 the document is untrusted, so the origin address + chain id are rendered by the host outside the frame and every signing request is gated by a host-side confirmation. Anonymous RPC. src/lib/anonTransport.ts wraps @anon-rpc/browser-harness 's AnonRpcWorker — an anonymizing client in its own null-origin sandboxed iframe + Web Worker. A worker.fetch tunnels each request to a swappable, untrusted destination RPC; an on-chain specifier (content-addressed by keccak256) picks the carrier: passthrough (dev), torJs (real Tor through an operator-run gateway), or nym . anonViemTransport() exposes it as a viem custom transport, so both chain reads and the ERC-4337 bundler POST ride the anon network — no JSON-RPC leaves over clearnet at runtime. Name + content addressing — ENS + IPFS. The production build is a static, relative-path bundle; scripts/pin-ipfs.mjs pins dist/ as a wrapped directory → CIDv1, and scripts/set-contenthash.mjs encodes that CID ( @ensdomains/content-hash ipfs codec + packetToBytes ) into klarity.eth 's contenthash on an ENS v2 resolver (simulating first to surface a missing-role revert before spending gas). An ENS-aware gateway then resolves the name → contenthash → self-contained UI, server-lessly. The account is ERC-4337 + passkey/PRF ( src/lib/account.ts ). The registry mirror (klarity) Ingest + one hash, three jobs. The pipeline deep-merges every includes / $ref so stored records are self-contained, flattens each descriptor to one entity per (chainId, contract, selector) , and upserts to Arkiv's Rabdi testnet. Content-addressing is RFC 8785 (JCS) + keccak256 ( src/hash.ts ), reused identically by the Arkiv writer, the sync loop-guard, and the EIP-712 signature layer. Two-way sync. src/sync.ts keeps GitHub → Arkiv fresh (incremental compareCommitsWithBasehead poll + optional HMAC webhook); the signed-write path opens a cross-repo fork PR Arkiv → GitHub ( src/github.ts openDescriptorPR ), so the mirror stays backwards-compatible with the canonical registry. A one-shot backfill ( src/import.ts ) seeds ~740 files / ~16.4k entities behind a hand-rolled ~8-in-flight pool. Reads + writes. Reads run over Arkiv JSON-RPC via viem createPublicClient , each pinned .createdBy(REGISTRY_WALLET) — the impostor-entity trust filter. Writes are gated by an EIP-712 DescriptorWrite signature ( src/auth.ts , fail-fast: hash → deadline → allowlist → replay-nonce-last), with optional EAS attestation for reputation. The Snap. Decodes at onTransaction , reading ERC-20 decimals() / symbol() via two raw EIP-1193 eth_call s; offers an interaction-proven ranking vouch gated on the voucher's own mined transaction. Honest by construction. The decode never fabricates — any ABI/path/body failure degrades a field to labels-only; unresolved inner calls render an explicit "unknown" . Why Arkiv. Permissionless reads over plain JSON-RPC (the bounty's premise, which a Postgres box with an owner and a bill can't offer), on-chain provenance via .createdBy , always-availability vs. the GitHub single-point-of-failure, and permissionlessExtension: true — the community keeps the mirror alive without being able to edit a field.

**TypeScript, end to end**, across two repos: `klarity` (registry mirror, Fastify API, Arkiv client, EIP-712 auth, Explorer, Snap) and `klarity-wallet` (the ERC-8244 / anon-rpc / ENS wallet).

### The wallet (klarity-wallet)

**UI with no host — ERC-8244.** `contracts/HtmlHost.sol` serves the wallet document from `html()` (selector `0x33c34ac3`), a gas-free `view`. Because the document exceeds the EIP-170 24KB code cap, its bytes are stored as the runtime code of one or more **SSTORE2 data contracts** (each prefixed with a `STOP` guard so data can never execute) and stitched back with `extcodecopy` at read time. The host fetches `html()` **through the anon transport** (so even loading the UI is anonymized) and mounts it in a `sandbox="allow-scripts"`, null-origin iframe; per ERC-8244 the document is untrusted, so the origin address + chain id are rendered by the host *outside* the frame and every signing request is gated by a host-side confirmation.

**Anonymous RPC.** `src/lib/anonTransport.ts` wraps `@anon-rpc/browser-harness`'s `AnonRpcWorker` — an anonymizing client in its own null-origin sandboxed iframe + Web Worker. A `worker.fetch` tunnels each request to a swappable, untrusted destination RPC; an on-chain **specifier** (content-addressed by keccak256) picks the carrier: `passthrough` (dev), `torJs` (real Tor through an operator-run gateway), or `nym`. `anonViemTransport()` exposes it as a viem custom transport, so both chain reads and the ERC-4337 bundler POST ride the anon network — no JSON-RPC leaves over clearnet at runtime.

**Name + content addressing — ENS + IPFS.** The production build is a static, relative-path bundle; `scripts/pin-ipfs.mjs` pins `dist/` as a wrapped directory → CIDv1, and `scripts/set-contenthash.mjs` encodes that CID (`@ensdomains/content-hash` ipfs codec + `packetToBytes`) into **`klarity.eth`'s contenthash** on an ENS v2 resolver (simulating first to surface a missing-role revert before spending gas). An ENS-aware gateway then resolves the name → contenthash → self-contained UI, server-lessly. The account is ERC-4337 + passkey/PRF (`src/lib/account.ts`).

### The registry mirror (klarity)

**Ingest + one hash, three jobs.** The pipeline deep-merges every `includes`/`$ref` so stored records are self-contained, flattens each descriptor to one entity per `(chainId, contract, selector)`, and upserts to Arkiv's **Rabdi** testnet. Content-addressing is **RFC 8785 (JCS) + keccak256** (`src/hash.ts`), reused identically by the Arkiv writer, the sync loop-guard, and the EIP-712 signature layer.

**Two-way sync.** `src/sync.ts` keeps GitHub → Arkiv fresh (incremental `compareCommitsWithBasehead` poll + optional HMAC webhook); the signed-write path opens a cross-repo fork PR Arkiv → GitHub (`src/github.ts` `openDescriptorPR`), so the mirror stays backwards-compatible with the canonical registry. A one-shot backfill (`src/import.ts`) seeds ~740 files / ~16.4k entities behind a hand-rolled ~8-in-flight pool.

**Reads + writes.** Reads run over Arkiv JSON-RPC via viem `createPublicClient`, each pinned `.createdBy(REGISTRY_WALLET)` — the impostor-entity trust filter. Writes are gated by an EIP-712 `DescriptorWrite` signature (`src/auth.ts`, fail-fast: hash → deadline → allowlist → replay-nonce-last), with optional EAS attestation for reputation.

**The Snap.** Decodes at `onTransaction`, reading ERC-20 `decimals()`/`symbol()` via two raw EIP-1193 `eth_call`s; offers an interaction-proven ranking vouch gated on the voucher's own mined transaction.

**Honest by construction.** The decode never fabricates — any ABI/path/body failure degrades a field to labels-only; unresolved inner calls render an explicit *"unknown"*.

projects.title: Paradigm
projects.description: AI agents pay verified humans in USDC on Hedera to film short clips that teach robots.
projects.project_description: Robots learn from videos of people doing everyday tasks, but that data is hard to buy fairly. Paradigm is an exchange where a robot team's AI buying agent posts a paid task (for example "fold a T-shirt, filmed from above") and real humans earn by filming it on their phone. A contributor opens a task, proves they are a unique human with World ID, and films a 15–30 s clip with a live word + finger challenge so it can't be faked or reused. An AI verifier (Gemini) watches the clip, but code makes the final call, not the AI. Accepted clips are encrypted and stored on Swarm. The buyer agent finds accepted clips and pays the contributor directly in USDC on Hedera over x402. Its spending policy is plain code: up to 5 USDC it pays on its own, above 5 it asks its human to approve through World Agent Pass, above 10 it never pays. Only after settlement does the buyer get the decryption key. Every task, claim, verdict, receipt and licence is an open record on Arkiv, so anyone can audit who was paid for what. No Solidity, no wallet pop-ups for contributors, and it also installs as an Android app.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). apps/web is Next.js 16 on Vercel: task board, World ID claim, in-browser phone recorder, buyer console, explorer and the x402 endpoint. apps/worker (Hono + ffmpeg on Railway) runs the verification pipeline: probe, fingerprint + dedup, Gemini watching the clip, then deterministic verdict rules. apps/agent is the buying agent on Railway. Hedera: @x402/next withX402 turns GET /api/x402/clip/:key into a 402; price comes from the Arkiv task and payTo is the contributor's own Hedera account (alias + auto-association, created from their embedded wallet key). The agent pays with @x402/fetch, the facilitator settles USDC 0.0.429274, and only after settlement do we release the AES key and write the receipt. Every agent decision goes to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, through the Hedera Agent Kit with an SDK fallback. No Solidity anywhere. Arkiv: SDK 1.0.1 typed schemas for adx.task / claim / submission / verification / receipt / licence, all writes through one guard. Arkiv is the shared, queryable record any other agent can read. World: IDKit 4 proof verified server-side against developer.world.org (one human per slot), and World Agent Pass as the human approval step for payments above the agent's limit. Swarm: our own Bee 2.8.3 light node with our own postage batch; clips are AES-256-GCM encrypted before upload, so Swarm only ever holds ciphertext. Neon Postgres + Drizzle for app state. Android app is a Trusted Web Activity built with Bubblewrap from the same code.

projects.title: Ampere
projects.description: Flight recorder & frame admission diagnostics for Arkiv nodes & EIP-8141 alt-mempools.
projects.project_description: AMPERE is an open-source infrastructure flight recorder and admission diagnostic engine designed for high-performance decentralized database nodes and next-generation native account abstraction mempools. As the Ethereum ecosystem evolves, infrastructure complexity is compounding at two critical boundaries: specialized storage networks handling complex relational/graph state, and alternative mempools enforcing dynamic validation rules for native account abstraction. Today, operators and protocol engineers lack unified, low-overhead tools to capture what actually happens inside a node or during transaction admission. Public explorers only observe systems from the outside, treating bundler rejections, container saturation, and RPC degradation as opaque black boxes. AMPERE bridges this divide by providing an in-situ diagnostic pipeline across two key frontiers: 1. In-Situ Node Telemetry & Predictive Capacity Management Running directly alongside an Arkiv node instance ( arkiv-reth ), AMPERE interfaces with low-level container cgroups and the local JSON-RPC surface to observe what remote dashboards cannot: Predictive Storage Saturation Forecasting : Samples Docker container disk allocations for the node’s /data volume and calculates moving linear storage growth rates, firing urgent alerts when time-to-disk-exhaustion drops below 7 days. Granular RPC Method Profiling : Measures observed calls, failure rates, and p50/p95 latency distributions across core node interfaces ( net_peerCount , eth_syncing , and state operations). Private Workload Benchmarking with Zero Query Leakage : Features a loopback-gated benchmark harness to safely isolate, reproduce, and profile query latency under bounded concurrency. Raw query text is isolated within local storage and represented exclusively via opaque workload identifiers, preventing sensitive query shapes or potential DoS vectors from leaking into public diagnostics. Dual-Assertion State Verification : Interacts directly with node precompile interfaces ( execute(Operation[]) at 0x44...44 ) to seed and verify entity states, requiring both transaction receipt event topic extraction and immediate read-back assertions. 2. Native Frame Transaction Admission & Trace Diagnostics With EIP-8141, native account abstraction decouples transaction validation from standard EVM wrappers by delegating verification to autonomous execution frames ( VERIFY , SENDER , PAYMASTER ). Complex frame transactions—such as post-quantum smart wallets, high-verification-budget privacy protocols, and stateful paymasters—must navigate ERC-8421 alternative mempools governed by ERC-7562 staking and opcode validation rules. Frame Construction & Wire Serialization : Constructs and signs native multi-frame transactions using @forshtat/hegota-support and the ethrex-eip8141-tracer profile, packaging distinct VERIFY (execution & payment scope) and SENDER frames with explicit gas allocations and cryptographic wire formatting. Sidecar Admission & Rule Lifecycle Tracing : Submits transactions via eth_sendFrameTransaction to Skandha bundler gateways and queries skandha_explorer_getTransaction to parse discrete ERC-7562 validation rule checks, opcode boundaries, lifecycle state transitions, and sub-frame execution outcomes. Cryptographic Evidence Preservation : Binds RPC latency distributions, node resource snapshots, and mempool rule verdicts into deterministic canonical JSON records, cryptographically signed with Ed25519 for tamper-evident incident post-mortems and cross-team audits.
projects.how_its_made: AMPERE was built from scratch as an end-to-end TypeScript diagnostic engine comprising a local collector daemon, an isolated CLI benchmark harness, and a local Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19) diagnostic console styled with Tailwind CSS, operating entirely without hosted database dependencies. Core Architecture & Partner Technologies Arkiv Network ( arkiv-reth ) : We run a pinned local node instance ( ghcr.io/arkiv-network/arkiv-reth pinned by digest in compose.yaml ) on chain ID 1337 . The telemetry daemon connects directly to the host’s Docker socket/cgroups to extract live container metrics (CPU usage %, resident memory vs. limits, block I/O counters, process trees) alongside network peer counts and sync states. A linear regression forecast computes the discrete growth rate of the node's /data volume over sliding 60-second observation windows to calculate days-to-full storage alerts. EIP-8141 & ERC-8421 Alt-Mempool Stack : Built against the experimental devnet gateway ( altmempoolgateway.forshtat.com/rpc , chain 1337). Using @forshtat/hegota-support/profiles ( ethrex-eip8141-tracer ), the engine structures native multi-frame arrays—a VERIFY frame (scope: EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT , execution gas: 30k) and a SENDER frame (execution: 50k, state: 200k) with secp256k1Placeholder signatures. It submits via eth_sendFrameTransaction and interrogates skandha_explorer_getTransaction , parsing up to 200 rule checks (opcode constraints, account storage boundaries, ERC-7562 rules) and lifecycle timeline events. Netlify Cloud Relay : The Next.js console is configured for serverless deployment on Netlify, allowing node operators to push signed telemetry snapshots to an authenticated cloud dashboard over HTTPS without exposing inbound node ports or running public tunnels. Notable Engineering Breakthroughs & Hacky Details Uncovering the Silent SDK/Node Write Mismatch : While integrating Arkiv, we found that @arkiv-network/sdk@0.7.0 's mutateEntities dispatched compressed RLP to 0x...61726b6976 . Against the arkiv-reth node, this produced a deceptive 0x1 success receipt with 0 emitted logs and 0 entities created. We bypassed the SDK, reversed the node's underlying precompile, and wrote directly to execute(Operation[]) at 0x4400000000000000000000000000000000000044 with Viem, building a dual-assertion verifier checking both transaction event topics and state read-backs. Pre-Flight Frame Hash Locking & Multi-Frame Receipt Recovery : Experimental devnet bundlers frequently drop HTTP connections under load. Blind retries can trigger nonce collisions or duplicate submissions. AMPERE computes the deterministic frame transaction hash ( txHash(profile, tx) ) locally and writes an atomic lock to disk before transmitting wire bytes. If the connection drops, our inspector runs a recursive parser across internal frameReceipts to verify whether individual sub-frames ( VERIFY vs SENDER ) succeeded independently. Zero-Knowledge Private Query Benchmarking : To benchmark slow query shapes on owned nodes without leaking sensitive proprietary schemas or DoS patterns publicly, we built a loopback-only RPC client enforcing a 2s timeout and redirect rejection. Query texts are hashed into opaque workload IDs in .ampere/ , exposing only normalized p50/p95 latency distributions in public reports while keeping query text strictly confidential. Cryptographic Flight Recording : AMPERE normalizes all telemetry observations, method latency distributions, and mempool rule verdicts into deterministic canonical JSON, digests them with SHA-256, and signs them locally with Ed25519 ( @noble/ed25519 ), providing verifiable, tamper-evident proof of node state and transaction admission decisions.
projects.project_description_markdown:
# AMPERE is an open-source infrastructure flight recorder and admission diagnostic engine designed for high-performance decentralized database nodes and next-generation native account abstraction mempools.

As the Ethereum ecosystem evolves, infrastructure complexity is compounding at two critical boundaries: specialized storage networks handling complex relational/graph state, and alternative mempools enforcing dynamic validation rules for native account abstraction. Today, operators and protocol engineers lack unified, low-overhead tools to capture what actually happens inside a node or during transaction admission. Public explorers only observe systems from the outside, treating bundler rejections, container saturation, and RPC degradation as opaque black boxes. 

AMPERE bridges this divide by providing an in-situ diagnostic pipeline across two key frontiers:

### 1. In-Situ Node Telemetry & Predictive Capacity Management
Running directly alongside an Arkiv node instance (`arkiv-reth`), AMPERE interfaces with low-level container cgroups and the local JSON-RPC surface to observe what remote dashboards cannot:
- **Predictive Storage Saturation Forecasting**: Samples Docker container disk allocations for the node’s `/data` volume and calculates moving linear storage growth rates, firing urgent alerts when time-to-disk-exhaustion drops below 7 days.
- **Granular RPC Method Profiling**: Measures observed calls, failure rates, and p50/p95 latency distributions across core node interfaces (`net_peerCount`, `eth_syncing`, and state operations).
- **Private Workload Benchmarking with Zero Query Leakage**: Features a loopback-gated benchmark harness to safely isolate, reproduce, and profile query latency under bounded concurrency. Raw query text is isolated within local storage and represented exclusively via opaque workload identifiers, preventing sensitive query shapes or potential DoS vectors from leaking into public diagnostics.
- **Dual-Assertion State Verification**: Interacts directly with node precompile interfaces (`execute(Operation[])` at `0x44...44`) to seed and verify entity states, requiring both transaction receipt event topic extraction and immediate read-back assertions.

### 2. Native Frame Transaction Admission & Trace Diagnostics
With EIP-8141, native account abstraction decouples transaction validation from standard EVM wrappers by delegating verification to autonomous execution frames (`VERIFY`, `SENDER`, `PAYMASTER`). Complex frame transactions—such as post-quantum smart wallets, high-verification-budget privacy protocols, and stateful paymasters—must navigate ERC-8421 alternative mempools governed by ERC-7562 staking and opcode validation rules.
- **Frame Construction & Wire Serialization**: Constructs and signs native multi-frame transactions using `@forshtat/hegota-support` and the `ethrex-eip8141-tracer` profile, packaging distinct `VERIFY` (execution & payment scope) and `SENDER` frames with explicit gas allocations and cryptographic wire formatting.
- **Sidecar Admission & Rule Lifecycle Tracing**: Submits transactions via `eth_sendFrameTransaction` to Skandha bundler gateways and queries `skandha_explorer_getTransaction` to parse discrete ERC-7562 validation rule checks, opcode boundaries, lifecycle state transitions, and sub-frame execution outcomes.
- **Cryptographic Evidence Preservation**: Binds RPC latency distributions, node resource snapshots, and mempool rule verdicts into deterministic canonical JSON records, cryptographically signed with Ed25519 for tamper-evident incident post-mortems and cross-team audits.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
AMPERE was built from scratch as an end-to-end TypeScript diagnostic engine comprising a local collector daemon, an isolated CLI benchmark harness, and a local Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19) diagnostic console styled with Tailwind CSS, operating entirely without hosted database dependencies.

### Core Architecture & Partner Technologies
- **Arkiv Network (`arkiv-reth`)**: We run a pinned local node instance (`ghcr.io/arkiv-network/arkiv-reth` pinned by digest in `compose.yaml`) on chain ID `1337`. The telemetry daemon connects directly to the host’s Docker socket/cgroups to extract live container metrics (CPU usage %, resident memory vs. limits, block I/O counters, process trees) alongside network peer counts and sync states. A linear regression forecast computes the discrete growth rate of the node's `/data` volume over sliding 60-second observation windows to calculate days-to-full storage alerts.
- **EIP-8141 & ERC-8421 Alt-Mempool Stack**: Built against the experimental devnet gateway (`altmempoolgateway.forshtat.com/rpc`, chain 1337). Using `@forshtat/hegota-support/profiles` (`ethrex-eip8141-tracer`), the engine structures native multi-frame arrays—a `VERIFY` frame (scope: `EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT`, execution gas: 30k) and a `SENDER` frame (execution: 50k, state: 200k) with `secp256k1Placeholder` signatures. It submits via `eth_sendFrameTransaction` and interrogates `skandha_explorer_getTransaction`, parsing up to 200 rule checks (opcode constraints, account storage boundaries, ERC-7562 rules) and lifecycle timeline events.
- **Netlify Cloud Relay**: The Next.js console is configured for serverless deployment on Netlify, allowing node operators to push signed telemetry snapshots to an authenticated cloud dashboard over HTTPS without exposing inbound node ports or running public tunnels.

### Notable Engineering Breakthroughs & Hacky Details
- **Uncovering the Silent SDK/Node Write Mismatch**: While integrating Arkiv, we found that `@arkiv-network/sdk@0.7.0`'s `mutateEntities` dispatched compressed RLP to `0x...61726b6976`. Against the `arkiv-reth` node, this produced a deceptive `0x1` success receipt with 0 emitted logs and 0 entities created. We bypassed the SDK, reversed the node's underlying precompile, and wrote directly to `execute(Operation[])` at `0x4400000000000000000000000000000000000044` with Viem, building a dual-assertion verifier checking both transaction event topics and state read-backs.
- **Pre-Flight Frame Hash Locking & Multi-Frame Receipt Recovery**: Experimental devnet bundlers frequently drop HTTP connections under load. Blind retries can trigger nonce collisions or duplicate submissions. AMPERE computes the deterministic frame transaction hash (`txHash(profile, tx)`) locally and writes an atomic lock to disk before transmitting wire bytes. If the connection drops, our inspector runs a recursive parser across internal `frameReceipts` to verify whether individual sub-frames (`VERIFY` vs `SENDER`) succeeded independently.
- **Zero-Knowledge Private Query Benchmarking**: To benchmark slow query shapes on owned nodes without leaking sensitive proprietary schemas or DoS patterns publicly, we built a loopback-only RPC client enforcing a 2s timeout and redirect rejection. Query texts are hashed into opaque workload IDs in `.ampere/`, exposing only normalized p50/p95 latency distributions in public reports while keeping query text strictly confidential.
- **Cryptographic Flight Recording**: AMPERE normalizes all telemetry observations, method latency distributions, and mempool rule verdicts into deterministic canonical JSON, digests them with SHA-256, and signs them locally with Ed25519 (`@noble/ed25519`), providing verifiable, tamper-evident proof of node state and transaction admission decisions.

projects.title: Sitebound
projects.description: Killing the stablecoin checkout address and brining 3D Secured USDT payments for everyone.
projects.project_description: We are killing the checkout address. A crypto checkout shows a wallet address, and it lives in the page's code. Whoever controls the code decides where the money goes: one hacked script can swap the address, and a wrong paste is final. Compromised web code keeps costing users: Bybit, Feb 2025: about $1.5B, from malicious code in Safe's web app (BleepingComputer). BadgerDAO, Dec 2021: about $120M, from a script slipped into the front end (Rekt). Polymarket, Oct 2026: about $2.7M, from a swapped third-party script (The Hacker News). Ledger Connect Kit, Dec 2023: more than $610K, from a poisoned library (The Register). Curve, Aug 2022: about $570K, from a hijacked domain (Curve). npm, Sep 2025: address-swapping code reached packages with 2B weekly downloads. About $600 stolen, a near miss (The Hacker News). Crypto also has no card-style check of the site and amount, buyers need gas, and businesses must manage wallets. Sitebound is 3D Secure style USDT payments on Whitechain. There is no checkout address on the page at all. Every payment is bound to the registered site and its wallet, so a hacked page cannot redirect the money. Any website can accept USDT, a dollar stablecoin. How it works: Register the site with one DNS TXT record. The relayer checks it and registers the site on-chain; the wallet can be made in the browser. Paste one tag: <sitebound-pay amount="12.00" order="A123">. No address in it. The buyer links a USDT wallet once, then confirms each site and amount with a passkey (Touch ID). Chrome writes the site into the signed data; page code cannot change it. The contract verifies the passkey on-chain and pays only the wallet registered for that site. pay() has no payee field. The relayer pays the gas. Buyers hold and pay only USDT. Live on Whitechain Sepolia: Contract SiteboundV2 (verified): 0x64117398C837a8708a816818b31C36Df5a968596 App: https://sitebound-pay.pages.dev Demo: https://sitebound-demo.pages.dev Real shop: https://0xmujahid.xyz First real payment on testnet, a Whitechain Sepolia testnet transaction (3 USDT, buyer paid no gas): https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/tx/0x65a00ae0fec55014c6331f2767e815ea8c49e00241b6215d7a917e3076cd71d0
projects.how_its_made: Contract: SiteboundV2, Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry, deployed on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) at ``0x64117398C837a8708a816818b31C36Df5a968596 and verified on the Whitechain explorer and Sourcify (exact match). No contract owner, no proxy, no upgrade path. Passkeys: every passkey (P-256) signature is verified on-chain through the RIP-7212 precompile at 0x100, which Whitechain Sepolia has. The whole design rests on it. pay() checks that the signature came from the Sitebound frame (origin and crossOrigin:true), the RP ID, user verification, and a challenge that fixes the site, its config version, the order, the amount, the relayer fee and the deadline. It then moves USDT to the split registered for keccak256(topOrigin). EIP-712 binds a passkey to a wallet with a per-payment cap, a total cap and an expiry. The USDT allowance uses an EIP-2612 permit, so the buyer signs instead of sending an approve transaction. Relayer: a Cloudflare Worker (ethers 6). It checks the DNS TXT record, signs the site attestation, relays gasless payments and enforces daily caps. pay() is permissionless, so the relayer can refuse a payment but cannot redirect one. Frontend: static pages on Cloudflare Pages. The landing and setup pages use Preact. The checkout frame is vanilla JS with ethers 6 and runs on its own origin as a cross-origin iframe. Tests: 138 Foundry tests across v1 and V2 (100 for SiteboundV2, including 5 invariants). Notable hacks: forge test has no P-256 precompile, so the tests etch a Solidity P-256 verifier at 0x100. One test replays a real Chromium passkey assertion captured from a cross-origin iframe (virtual authenticator, not Touch ID). Whitechain USDT has no version() getter, so we found its permit domain (name "Tether USD", version "1") by matching DOMAIN_SEPARATOR. "Verify us" on the landing page reads the deployed bytecode, masks the immutables and compares it with the expected build hash, in the browser.
projects.project_description_markdown:
We are killing the checkout address.

A crypto checkout shows a wallet address, and it lives in the page's code. Whoever controls the code decides where the money goes: one hacked script can swap the address, and a wrong paste is final. Compromised web code keeps costing users:
- Bybit, Feb 2025: about $1.5B, from malicious code in Safe's web app (BleepingComputer).
- BadgerDAO, Dec 2021: about $120M, from a script slipped into the front end (Rekt).
- Polymarket, Oct 2026: about $2.7M, from a swapped third-party script (The Hacker News).
- Ledger Connect Kit, Dec 2023: more than $610K, from a poisoned library (The Register).
- Curve, Aug 2022: about $570K, from a hijacked domain (Curve).
- npm, Sep 2025: address-swapping code reached packages with 2B weekly downloads. About $600 stolen, a near miss (The Hacker News).

Crypto also has no card-style check of the site and amount, buyers need gas, and businesses must manage wallets.

Sitebound is 3D Secure style USDT payments on Whitechain. There is no checkout address on the page at all. Every payment is bound to the registered site and its wallet, so a hacked page cannot redirect the money. Any website can accept USDT, a dollar stablecoin.

How it works:
1. Register the site with one DNS TXT record. The relayer checks it and registers the site on-chain; the wallet can be made in the browser.
2. Paste one tag: <sitebound-pay amount="12.00" order="A123">. No address in it.
3. The buyer links a USDT wallet once, then confirms each site and amount with a passkey (Touch ID). Chrome writes the site into the signed data; page code cannot change it.
4. The contract verifies the passkey on-chain and pays only the wallet registered for that site. pay() has no payee field.
5. The relayer pays the gas. Buyers hold and pay only USDT.

Live on Whitechain Sepolia:
- Contract SiteboundV2 (verified): 0x64117398C837a8708a816818b31C36Df5a968596
- App: https://sitebound-pay.pages.dev
- Demo: https://sitebound-demo.pages.dev
- Real shop: https://0xmujahid.xyz
- First real payment on testnet, a Whitechain Sepolia testnet transaction (3 USDT, buyer paid no gas): https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/tx/0x65a00ae0fec55014c6331f2767e815ea8c49e00241b6215d7a917e3076cd71d0

- Passkeys: every passkey (P-256) signature is verified on-chain through the RIP-7212 precompile at 0x100, which Whitechain Sepolia has. The whole design rests on it.
- pay() checks that the signature came from the Sitebound frame (origin and crossOrigin:true), the RP ID, user verification, and a challenge that fixes the site, its config version, the order, the amount, the relayer fee and the deadline. It then moves USDT to the split registered for keccak256(topOrigin).

- Relayer: a Cloudflare Worker (ethers 6). It checks the DNS TXT record, signs the site attestation, relays gasless payments and enforces daily caps. pay() is permissionless, so the relayer can refuse a payment but cannot redirect one.

projects.title: Fulcrum
projects.description: Buy $1,000 of ETH with $100. Real spot, no perps, no funding rate. Lenders are paid first.
projects.project_description: Fulcrum is decentralised prop trading with spot-funded leverage. Buy $1,000 of ETH with $100. Lenders deposit USDC into an ERC-4626 vault. Traders put down a margin deposit and borrow up to 9x of it to buy real spot ETH or BTC. It is not a perp and has no funding rate: the trader holds actual spot assets, bought on Uniswap v4. Every position sits in its own isolated TraderProxy wallet, so one trader's position never touches another's. The first week of borrowing is free, then 8% APR. The loss order is what makes it work for lenders. The trader's deposit takes losses first, then the insurance fund. On close, lenders are repaid first. Profit is split automatically by the contract. Example (Trader level, $100 at 10x, $900 borrowed). If ETH rises 10%, the position is worth $1,100. Lenders get $910 (the loan plus 10% of the profit), insurance gets $1.50, Fulcrum gets $1.50 and the trader gets $187, against $10 unlevered. If ETH falls 8%, the contract sells at $919.08. Lenders get their $900 back in full, the keeper earns $0.50, insurance receives $18.58, and the trader loses their $100 and nothing more. Traders start small and earn their way up. Starter allows 5x on up to $50 of margin, Trader allows 10x on $250, Pro allows 10x on $1,000. Better traders keep more of their profit (80%, 87%, 91%). Levels are on-chain and owner-configurable. Lenders earn from borrowing fees (80% of the 8% APR goes to them), a cut of winning trades, and idle USDC yield. They never earn from trader losses, so they want skilled traders at size, and the levels are the filter. We replayed seven real crashes (COVID, May 2021, LUNA, FTX, Yen carry, Tariffs, Oct-10 2025) on 6.8 years of Binance 1-minute data, with 6,967 real Hyperliquid long positions from 342 traders. Lenders lost $0 in all seven crashes in every scenario, including all-10x stress with a thin pool and a 30-minute oracle outage. With lenders free to enter and leave, at a 10% lender return today's real trader demand supports an ~$86k vault (7.5% supports ~$169k, 5.5% ~$557k), and bear-year 2022 still made 10.0%. All results are published to Arkiv and the landing and /backtest pages read them live. Backtests are not guarantees.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.28, Base mainnet). PositionManager holds the position lifecycle: open, close, lazily accrued weekly rollover debt, oracle-gated liquidation, and the profit/loss waterfall. LPVault is an upgradeable ERC-4626 vault with deposit caps and an ERC-7540-style withdrawal queue. InsuranceReserve is the second-loss buffer. PositionManager and LPVault sit behind OpenZeppelin ERC-1967 proxies. All contracts are verified on Basescan. TraderProxy isolation. Each position gets its own TraderProxy wallet, an EIP-1167 clone of a shared implementation. The bought ETH or BTC lives there, not in a shared pool, so a bad position cannot drain another and settlement is a clean sweep of one wallet. We moved the proxy implementation out of PositionManager to fit under the EIP-170 size limit. Uniswap v4. Every trade and every liquidation executes on Uniswap v4. We wrote V4SwapRouter (100 lines), a router implementing IUnlockCallback. projects.project_description_markdown:
Fulcrum is decentralised prop trading with spot-funded leverage. Buy $1,000 of ETH with $100.

Lenders deposit USDC into an ERC-4626 vault. Traders put down a margin deposit and borrow up to 9x of it to buy real spot ETH or BTC. It is not a perp and has no funding rate: the trader holds actual spot assets, bought on Uniswap v4. Every position sits in its own isolated TraderProxy wallet, so one trader's position never touches another's. The first week of borrowing is free, then 8% APR.

The loss order is what makes it work for lenders. The trader's deposit takes losses first, then the insurance fund. On close, lenders are repaid first. Profit is split automatically by the contract.

Example (Trader level, $100 at 10x, $900 borrowed). If ETH rises 10%, the position is worth $1,100. Lenders get $910 (the loan plus 10% of the profit), insurance gets $1.50, Fulcrum gets $1.50 and the trader gets $187, against $10 unlevered. If ETH falls 8%, the contract sells at $919.08. Lenders get their $900 back in full, the keeper earns $0.50, insurance receives $18.58, and the trader loses their $100 and nothing more.

Traders start small and earn their way up. Starter allows 5x on up to $50 of margin, Trader allows 10x on $250, Pro allows 10x on $1,000. Better traders keep more of their profit (80%, 87%, 91%). Levels are on-chain and owner-configurable.

Lenders earn from borrowing fees (80% of the 8% APR goes to them), a cut of winning trades, and idle USDC yield. They never earn from trader losses, so they want skilled traders at size, and the levels are the filter.

We replayed seven real crashes (COVID, May 2021, LUNA, FTX, Yen carry, Tariffs, Oct-10 2025) on 6.8 years of Binance 1-minute data, with 6,967 real Hyperliquid long positions from 342 traders. Lenders lost $0 in all seven crashes in every scenario, including all-10x stress with a thin pool and a 30-minute oracle outage. With lenders free to enter and leave, at a 10% lender return today's real trader demand supports an ~$86k vault (7.5% supports ~$169k, 5.5% ~$557k), and bear-year 2022 still made 10.0%. All results are published to Arkiv and the landing and /backtest pages read them live. Backtests are not guarantees.

projects.title: Winterlock Wallet
projects.description: Post-quantum smart wallet where every one-time key is its own nonce, so payments can go in parallel
projects.project_description: Winterlock is a post-quantum smart wallet for Ethereum. Every payment is signed with a hash-based one-time key (WOTS+ under a Merkle tree), and you can use it from MetaMask Snap (Flask). The problem with one-time keys is simple. If you sign two different messages with the same key, anyone can forge a third one. So the wallet has to remember which keys are used. Most designs keep a bitmap or counter on chain, which means a storage write on every tx, and with a normal nonce you get only one pending tx per account. My idea: the key number is the nonce key. With EIP-8250 keyed nonces, leaf i can sign only a tx whose nonce key is i, at sequence 0. When the tx is approved, the protocol marks that nonce as used, so the key is dead also. The account writes nothing during verification. No bitmap, no counter. Since every payment has its own nonce key, one account can have many payments pending at the same time on the ERC-8421 alt mempool. On the devnet I sent 8 payments from one account. All 8 were pending together and landed in 2 blocks. Same burst on the public mempool: 1 accepted, 7 refused. While testing these lanes I also found a DoS gap in the alt mempool sidecar and opened 2 PRs upstream: a cap of 64 pending txs per unstaked sender (#6), and rechecking only the txs a new block actually touched (#5). Other things it does: A stuck payment is never fee bumped, because that means signing the same key twice. It waits for its deadline, the key gets burned and the retry goes out with a fresh key. Hot tickets for a phone or an AI agent. The device gets a few one-time keys and no seed. The account itself enforces a value cap, one allowed recipient, a fee cap and a kill switch, and rejects with the rule name (hot: value cap). Verification fits under the devnet's 100k gas verify cap (88,373 gas used). It is a hackathon prototype and not audited.
projects.how_its_made:
Winterlock is a smart account written in raw Yul, because solc can't emit the EIP-8141 opcodes yet, so I used verbatim for TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, SIGPARAM, SIGDATACOPY and APPROVE. Inside the VERIFY frame it copies a 2,594 byte signature entry, verifies 67 WOTS+ chains (keccak256, w=16) and a height-10 Merkle path, then calls APPROVE(3) for execution and payment. Verify takes 88,373 gas, so it fits the stock 100k cap with no stake, no budget raise and no sidecar patch. The main trick is that leaf i can sign only under EIP-8250 nonce key (epoch << 32) | i, at sequence 0. APPROVE consumes that nonce, so the protocol retires the one-time key in the same step. No SSTORE, no used-key bitmap, and every payment gets its own lane: 8 hash-signed txs from one account were pending together on the ERC-8421 alt mempool. Other pieces: Bounded verify: WOTS+ cost depends on the digest (worst case 1,005 chain steps), so the signer grinds a tx field until the digest needs ≤510 steps, then signs once. Hot tickets: a phone or agent gets a few leaves and no seed. VERIFY reads every later frame with FRAMEPARAM and enforces target, value cap, fee cap and a kill switch. Signer safety: each leaf is reserved in a file-locked journal before signing. No fee bumps; a stuck payment expires and is re-signed on a fresh leaf. chainId is hashed into every leaf. Cross-checked: Rust (CLI + WASM) and TypeScript signers, Yul and TS verifiers, vectors pass both ways, WOTS+ diff-tested against an audited Solidity implementation. 761 tests. MetaMask: Account Snap for Flask. The signed frame tx rides in the userop signature field and a keyless bridge sends the raw EIP-8141 bytes. Nothing ERC-4337 on chain. Upstream fixes: testing the lanes showed that a self-paying keyed sender had no per-sender cap in the sidecar, and the reconciler re-simulates every pending tx on every block. So one address could park unlimited lanes and make the node re-check all of them. I opened 2 PRs. #6 caps an unstaked sender at 64 pending txs (ERC-8421 LIFECYCLE-030) and closes a bypass through cancelled slots. #5 uses EIP-7928 block access lists to recheck only the txs a block touched: 4 simulations per block down to 0 on the devnet.

https://github.com/forshtat/mempool-workshop-sidecar/pull/5 Stack: Yul, Foundry, Rust, TypeScript, Bun, viem, React, MetaMask Snaps SDK.

projects.title: Tenbin
projects.description: Self-custodial index wallet that Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua trade at one price and nobody's watching
projects.project_description: Tenbin (天秤, the Japanese balance scale) lets Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua trade one wallet at one price PROBLEM : Earn trading fees on more than one exchange today, a market maker splits its coins into one pile per venue. Each pile gets its own price, the prices drift apart, and arbitrageurs live off the gap at the maker's expense while rebalancing is a job of its own, and every RPC provider the maker uses learns which book it runs and what it watches Tenbin removes the split.
