projects.how_its_made: "One price function, two venues, one wallet" Quant Knowledge: TenbinMath implements Balancer's weighted-pool formula (spot, exact-in, exact-out) in fixed point, using Balancer v3's LogExpMath for pow, with every rounding step in the maker's favour. It's checked against 111 vectors from an 80-digit Python reference. TenbinHook.quote() runs it over the wallet's real ERC-20 balances plus pending claims Uniswap v4: TenbinHook is a custom-curve hook. In beforeSwap it prices the trade from the wallet and returns a delta that cancels the pool's own curve, so the pool holds nothing. Output is paid straight from the wallet (sync, then Aqua.pull into the PoolManager, then settle). The trader's input is minted as ERC-6909 claims for the maker, counted as inventory immediately, and pushed into the wallet via Aqua.push on the next swap or a permissionless flush(). LP deposits are blocked and only the maker can open pools. A CREATE2 factory deploys one hook per maker, and the app mines the hook address in the browser. The official V4Quoter and Universal Router on Base Sepolia work unchanged; fork tests prove the quoter returns exactly the hook's quote 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: we wrote a new SwapVM instruction, PortfolioPrice (opcode 0xd0, in the unallocated bank), and added it to the official AquaSwapVMRouter without changing anything else (22.8 KB, under the 24 KB limit). It calls the same hook's quoteAndLock(), so both venues price identically, and it uses Aqua's virtual balance as that venue's selling limit. The maker's only approval is to Aqua. Aqua and SwapVM aren't on any testnet, so we deploy their official source on Base Sepolia The hacky part: our v4 hook also acts as an Aqua app. Aqua keys balances by the calling app, so the hook ships its own strategy and calls pull and push from inside the Uniswap swap. One inventory serves two protocols that were never designed to share one Security: our own audit found a critical cross-venue reentrancy bug (SwapVM calls the taker back after pricing but before moving coins, so a nested trade could price on stale balances; the PoC made $752.92). We fixed it with a fail-closed fill lock shared by both venues, and the PoC is kept as a test. 59 contract tests in total, including fuzzing, a 64-run invariant suite and 2 fork tests against live Uniswap v4 EF Anon-RPC: web/src/lib/anon.ts is the app's only read path, a viem transport built on @anon-rpc/browser-harness. It uses Tor by default and falls back to Nym if Tor can't start (the EF Tor gateway was down during the hackathon), and never silently to a non-private route. Each maker, pair and trader gets its own isolation key so the RPC can't link them. The Privacy page lists every read with its route, key and latency, and a small logging proxy shows requests arriving from anonymity-network exits App: Next.js 15 + viem, plain-SVG charts, static export to GitHub Pages. Tested with 18 Playwright browser specs, 27 headless user flows and 36 on-chain smoke checks. ./scripts/demo.sh forks Base Sepolia, deploys, launches a 40/30/30 index, trades on both venues and opens the app
projects.project_description_markdown:
Tenbin (天秤, the Japanese balance scale) lets Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua trade one wallet at one price

PROBLEM : Earn trading fees on more than one exchange today, a market maker splits its coins into one pile per venue. Each pile gets its own price, the prices drift apart, and arbitrageurs live off the gap at the maker's expense while rebalancing is a job of its own, and every RPC provider the maker uses learns which book it runs and what it watches

Tenbin removes the split. You hold a weighted index in your own wallet, for example 40% ETH / 30% BTC / 30% USDC while both Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua trade against that same wallet, priced by one function over its real balances, so both venues quote the same trade 0 wei apart

A fill on one venue changes the balances, so the other venue's next quote already knows. There is nothing to sync and no oracle.

Think of it as one water tank with two taps: the tank is your wallet, Uniswap and 1inch are the taps, and one gauge sets the price for both.

What you get:
- One inventory on two venues: your whole wallet, not half on each.
- Same price everywhere: 0 wei apart in every direction, exact-in and exact-out.
- Can't be gamed: every loop across both venues loses (a 1 ETH loop comes back -0.81%).
- Self-rebalancing: when prices move, traders buy what's cheap until the wallet is back on target, and pay the 0.30% fee for it (ETH +25% restores 40.01 / 29.99 / 29.99).
- Cheap re-weighting: glide 40/30/30 to 50/25/25 on $100k for $25 instead of $1,991.
- Self-custody: coins never leave your wallet; the only approval is to 1inch Aqua, which caps each venue.
- Private: every chain read in the app goes through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC.

It's for market makers, DAO treasuries and anyone holding a basket of coins who wants it to earn fees on more than one venue without splitting it.

Honest limit: Tenbin doesn't reduce LVR. When the outside price jumps, the traders who rebalance you keep the move and you earn the fee. The app says so.

Live on Base Sepolia with a working app: swap, launch your own index, live order book, arbitrage tester, privacy log and a guided six-step demo with real transactions.

projects.title: Aegis protocol
projects.description: Decentralized Web3 wallet intelligence to detect, report, and verify risk.
projects.project_description: Aegis Protocol is a decentralized Web3 security and wallet-risk intelligence platform designed to help users identify suspicious blockchain addresses before interacting with them. Traditional wallet security tools often provide fragmented information, limited transparency, and centralized reputation data. Aegis addresses this problem by combining on-chain verification with decentralized data storage. Built around Arc and Arkiv, Aegis uses Arc smart contracts to maintain a verifiable registry of wallet-related security reports and blockchain interactions, while Arkiv provides searchable, decentralized storage for report metadata and evidence references. Users can investigate wallet addresses, examine available risk signals, submit security reports, and verify recorded activity through on-chain transactions. The protocol is designed to support transparent community participation, evidence-based reputation assessment, and dispute handling. Aegis aims to create a more transparent and verifiable security layer for the Web3 ecosystem, helping users make better-informed decisions before sending funds or interacting with potentially malicious addresses.
projects.how_its_made: Aegis Protocol is built using a Web3 architecture that combines Arc blockchain infrastructure with Arkiv decentralized data storage. The frontend provides an interactive wallet investigation dashboard where users can connect their wallets, inspect suspicious addresses, view available risk indicators, and submit security reports. Arc is used as the on-chain execution layer. Solidity smart contracts manage the wallet report registry and the protocol's verification and security workflows. Users interact with these contracts through wallet-based transaction signing, allowing important actions to be independently verified on-chain. Arkiv is integrated as the decentralized data layer for storing searchable report metadata and evidence references. This allows the application to retrieve relevant security information without relying entirely on a centralized database. The frontend communicates with blockchain infrastructure using wallet connectivity and Ethereum-compatible libraries. Smart contract events and transaction logs provide traceability for important protocol activities. The architecture separates searchable evidence from authoritative on-chain state: Arkiv provides the data discovery layer, while Arc provides the transaction and contract execution layer. This combination creates a transparent foundation for decentralized wallet-risk intelligence.

projects.title: TRUTHLY
projects.description: Verified agent news becomes five-agent crypto decisions and protected onchain trades.
projects.project_description: TRUTHLY is an evidence-to-action network for crypto intelligence. Scout agents discover stories from RSS, GitHub and governance sources. Reporters file structured claims with independently owned sources and stake USDC behind their work. Herald verifies each claim, stores source hashes, and refunds or slashes the stake according to the evidence. Published intelligence can be purchased over x402, producing a story-specific receipt. Each eligible story is then analyzed by a five-agent Trading Intelligence Council: Alpha Hunter, Market Analyst, Macro Analyst, Risk Sentinel and Devil’s Advocate. They combine the verified news with live Definitive pricing and an independent Uniswap market reference to produce a deterministic BUY, SELL or HOLD decision. TRUTHLY displays evidence strength, agent votes, consensus, market divergence, risk/reward and a transparent Decision Quality score. Only a fresh executable BUY can reach the receipt-, mandate-, World-approval- and market-integrity-protected Definitive order path.
projects.how_its_made: TRUTHLY is built with Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript. Turso/libSQL and Drizzle store reporters, evidence, revisions, payments, entitlements, human principals, Council runs and execution audits. Scout collectors ingest RSS, GitHub and Snapshot discoveries. Reporters file structured evidence through x402 USDC payments on Base, while Herald performs source and claim verification and records immutable source hashes. A Groq-powered five-agent Council independently evaluates each real published story. Definitive Flash provides the execution quote and advanced limit order with attached take-profit and stop-loss protection. The Uniswap Trading API independently prices the same Base USDC→WETH notional through V2/V3/V4 liquidity; excessive divergence deterministically blocks execution. We strip permits, calldata and transaction payloads before storing Uniswap evidence. World IDKit creates a durable unique-human principal, while World Agent Pass authorizes exact high-impact actions using payload hashes, nonces, expiry and one-use consumption. Viem validates Definitive’s EIP-712 order data, token addresses, recipients, amounts, deadlines and bounded approvals before signing. An MCP server exposes the pipeline to agents, and a strictly separated Demo Mode uses real market quotes with paper-only execution.

projects.title: Nightshift
projects.description: NightShift: the trust layer where AI agents discover, hire, pay, and verify other AI agents.
projects.project_description: NightShift is an agent-to-agent service marketplace that lets AI agents discover, hire, pay, and verify other AI agents. A buyer agent can search for a needed skill-such as research, coding, translation, transcription, or data processing-then receive a quote, verify the worker’s ENS identity, and pay autonomously through x402 and USDC. NightShift adds safety controls including quote validation, replay protection, budget reservations, worker lifecycle checks, and settlement reconciliation. Job, payment, and completion records are anchored on Hedera, creating an auditable trust layer for autonomous agent work. The goal is to turn isolated AI agents into a connected economy where agents can work for and with each other.
projects.how_its_made: NightShift is a full-stack agent-to-agent commerce platform that enables AI agents to discover, hire, pay, and verify other AI agents autonomously. Built with TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Node.js, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and Solidity, it combines a marketplace interface with on-chain identity, payment coordination, execution, and auditable settlement. ENS provides verifiable worker identities and service discovery, while the buyer agent manages the complete transaction lifecycle: discovering workers, verifying identity, validating quotes, checking budgets, coordinating payments, executing tasks, and verifying results. The platform integrates x402 with USDC and Hedera for machine-to-machine payments and settlement, 0G Router for AI execution, and Hedera Consensus Service for tamper-evident, auditable event records. Privy enables secure wallet-based authentication. A core engineering challenge was making autonomous payments safe. NightShift uses Ed25519-signed quotes that cryptographically bind the worker, price, payment destination, network, expiry, and nonce. It also implements replay protection, atomic budget reservations, worker lifecycle checks, and settlement reconciliation to handle uncertain transaction outcomes without blindly retrying payments. Payment details are independently verified rather than trusted directly from provider responses. To validate the full system, we built a simulated full-stack environment that runs the real buyer and server logic while replacing external payment and execution providers with local test services. This allowed us to test complete buyer-to-worker journeys, including duplicate requests, payment failures, uncertain settlement, and fallback worker selection, without spending real funds. The result is more than an agent directory: NightShift is an integrated foundation for autonomous agent-to-agent commerce, connecting discovery, identity, pricing, payments, execution, and verification in one secure workflow.

projects.title: NodeRails
projects.description: The Most advanced crypto and stablecoin payments infrastructure
projects.project_description: NodeRails Payments is a non-custodial crypto and stablecoin payment infrastructure platform built for merchants, online businesses, platforms and finance teams that want to accept digital asset payments without dealing with the operational complexity of blockchains. Today, accepting crypto is still fragmented for most businesses. Customers hold different tokens on different chains, prices move between checkout and settlement, funds arrive in multiple wallets and networks, and finance teams are left with the difficult job of tracking, converting, bridging, refunding and reconciling every payment manually. NodeRails solves this by giving merchants one complete payment system that handles the full lifecycle of a crypto payment from the moment a customer starts checkout to the moment the merchant receives a clean, predictable settlement. With NodeRails, merchants can accept payments through hosted checkout pages, shareable payment links, invoices, subscriptions and API based payment flows. A customer simply opens the payment page, connects or uses their wallet, reviews the amount, authorizes the payment and completes the transaction using a supported chain and token. The experience is designed to feel familiar and trustworthy, closer to a modern online card payment than a raw blockchain transfer. Customers are not asked to send funds blindly to an address. They receive a clear payment status, a receipt, transaction references and a live tracking page where they can follow what is happening with their payment. This creates confidence for buyers and reduces support burden for merchants. At the core of NodeRails is a structured payment lifecycle. Every payment moves through clear stages such as created, authorized, captured, settled, refunded, disputed or expired. Funds are first captured into an escrow based flow rather than being sent instantly and irreversibly to the merchant. This creates an important safety window where merchants can review the order, start fulfilment, issue a full refund, issue a partial refund, or respond if a customer raises a dispute. This model brings important protections from traditional commerce into crypto payments while keeping the process transparent and verifiable onchain. It helps prevent situations where a customer pays, something goes wrong, and there is no clean way to reverse, partially refund or investigate the payment. After the settlement window, NodeRails automatically settles the payment based on the merchant preferences. This is one of the most powerful parts of the platform. A merchant does not have to receive the same scattered tokens that customers paid with. They can choose to settle to their wallet, settle into a stablecoin for predictable accounting, consolidate payments onto one preferred chain for simpler treasury management, or use bank oriented settlement where supported. For finance teams, this means fewer wallets to monitor, fewer tokens to manage, fewer manual swaps and bridges, and a much cleaner view of revenue. Instead of checking multiple chains and wallets at the end of the day, the business can work with a more predictable balance that fits their accounting and payout process. NodeRails also includes the tools businesses need to operate daily. Merchants get a dashboard to manage payments, customers, payment links, invoices, subscriptions, refunds, disputes, payouts, settlement settings, API keys, webhooks and team access. Payment links make it easy to collect money without building a full store. Invoices help service businesses and freelancers bill clients professionally. Subscriptions support recurring digital products and services. Payout tools help businesses send funds to recipients in a more organized way. Webhooks and APIs allow platforms and developers to integrate NodeRails into their own products and automatically react to events such as payment captured, payment settled, payment refunded, payment disputed and subscription updates. The platform is built for both sides of the transaction. Merchants get automation, control and clean settlement. Customers get transparency, receipts and a safer payment experience. Finance teams get better records, clearer statuses and less manual reconciliation. Developers get a structured payment model instead of having to combine wallets, chains, pricing, transaction handling, event tracking and settlement logic themselves. NodeRails brings these pieces together into one financial infrastructure layer for crypto commerce.
projects.how_its_made: NodeRails Payments is built with Next.js and TypeScript for the merchant dashboard, hosted checkout, customer payment tracking and admin experience. The backend uses Node.js services with PostgreSQL for payment records and Redis backed background processing for time based actions such as settlement, billing, notifications and webhook delivery. Smart contracts are written in Solidity using Foundry and handle the onchain escrow, settlement, refund, dispute and payout flows. The main product flow is create, authorize, capture, hold in escrow, settle and reconcile. A merchant first creates a payment through the dashboard, a payment link, an invoice, a subscription or the API. The customer then authorizes the payment from their wallet on the hosted checkout. Once captured, funds are held through an escrow based settlement window instead of being released instantly. This gives merchants time to review the order, issue full or partial refunds, and handle disputes before the payment becomes final. After the settlement window, the payment is settled based on the merchant preference, such as wallet settlement, stablecoin settlement, single chain consolidation or bank oriented settlement where supported. Blockchain activity is verified before final payment states are trusted, and merchants receive updates through the dashboard, receipts, payment tracking pages and webhooks. External providers are used where useful for areas such as asset pricing, liquidity, identity checks and fiat movement, while the core payment lifecycle, merchant controls and customer experience are handled by NodeRails. This keeps the system modular and easier to extend with new chains, tokens and settlement options over time, while giving businesses a cleaner and more predictable way to accept and manage crypto payments.

Finance teams get better records, clearer statuses and less manual reconciliation. Developers get a structured payment model instead of having to combine wallets, chains, pricing, transaction handling, event tracking and settlement logic themselves. NodeRails brings these pieces together into one financial infrastructure layer for crypto commerce.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
NodeRails Payments is built with Next.js and TypeScript for the merchant dashboard, hosted checkout, customer payment tracking and admin experience. The backend uses Node.js services with PostgreSQL for payment records and Redis backed background processing for time based actions such as settlement, billing, notifications and webhook delivery. Smart contracts are written in Solidity using Foundry and handle the onchain escrow, settlement, refund, dispute and payout flows.

The main product flow is create, authorize, capture, hold in escrow, settle and reconcile. A merchant first creates a payment through the dashboard, a payment link, an invoice, a subscription or the API. The customer then authorizes the payment from their wallet on the hosted checkout. Once captured, funds are held through an escrow based settlement window instead of being released instantly. This gives merchants time to review the order, issue full or partial refunds, and handle disputes before the payment becomes final. After the settlement window, the payment is settled based on the merchant preference, such as wallet settlement, stablecoin settlement, single chain consolidation or bank oriented settlement where supported.

Blockchain activity is verified before final payment states are trusted, and merchants receive updates through the dashboard, receipts, payment tracking pages and webhooks. External providers are used where useful for areas such as asset pricing, liquidity, identity checks and fiat movement, while the core payment lifecycle, merchant controls and customer experience are handled by NodeRails. This keeps the system modular and easier to extend with new chains, tokens and settlement options over time, while giving businesses a cleaner and more predictable way to accept and manage crypto payments.

projects.title: meter
projects.description: Marketplace for paid AI agents using Whitechain Sepolia payments & Ethereum Sepolia Uniswap DCA
projects.project_description: Meter is a marketplace being built to help people discover AI agents, pay for useful work, and automate recurring services using stablecoins. It connects creators who build specialized agents with users who want clear pricing, verifiable payments, and control over their funds. The product supports two complementary experiences. For individual tasks, users choose an agent, provide the required information, review a stablecoin price, and authorize payment. Meter is designed to handle the blockchain transaction fee behind the scenes, removing the need for users to acquire gas tokens or configure a network manually. Users gain a single interface for discovering services, managing subscriptions, following payment and execution status, and reviewing results. It does not promise bridging or atomic transactions between them. Currently under development for ETHGlobal Mumbai, Meter aims to make blockchain infrastructure feel practical and unobtrusive. projects.title: SeerAI
projects.description: A collar badge that listens while your phone is away. 0G remembers in a private TEE.
projects.project_description: LiveSub is a wearable memory for when the phone is in a bag. The LilyGO T-Display badge keeps one short clip, sends it to a laptop relay, and drops the audio. The relay calls 0G Private Computer twice, both with  trust mode private: whisper-large-v3 for the transcript, then a TeeML chat model for memory operations and, in Live, a translation. tee_verified has to be true. Both request_ids are stored. The audio buffer is wiped. Sound is never written. Each verified utterance is encrypted on the relay with AES-256-GCM and written to 0G Storage on Galileo. A KV index holds only what is still open: reminders and list items, each stamped with the time that sentence was said. The phone reads that index. It can dismiss a row or change its wording. It cannot add one. The key stays on the relay. The glass shows Companion, Live, Not linked, or MIC LOCKED: ENCLAVE OFFLINE. No transcript on the badge. If the relay drops, the badge cuts mic power and shows Not linked. If the enclave returns HTTP 503 or 502, or tee_verified is not true, it locks and writes nothing. It does not drop to trust mode standard.
projects.how_its_made:
The badge is a LilyGO T-Display v1.1. Firmware is PlatformIO on the ESP32. An INMP441 is powered from GPIO27, which the firmware drives high while the relay socket is up and low to cut the microphone. BCLK, word clock, and data are GPIO26, GPIO25, and GPIO33. A noise floor on the board drops silence. Speech becomes one 16 kHz WAV, leaves as a single binary WebSocket frame on /ws, and the buffer is reused. A short press on GPIO0 sends {"type":"press"}. The glass paints only the face the relay sends: Companion, Live, Not linked, or MIC LOCKED: ENCLAVE OFFLINE. The relay is TypeScript on Node 22, run with npm start in relay/. It owns the mode, the phone link, and the lock. Each clip is transcribed with POST /v1/audio/transcriptions?verify_tee=true on https://router-api.0g.ai/v1, model whisper-large-v3, header X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private. The audio buffer is zeroed when that request ends. A second private call, POST /v1/chat/completions with verify_tee: true and JSON output, sees the transcript, the timestamp, the mode, and the open reminders and list items. It returns memory operations and, in Live, a translation. tee_verified is read from x_0g_trace on the body. Operations apply only when that boolean is true. The working set updates in RAM, and a live line goes out on the /phone socket, before the storage write is awaited. Clips are transcribed one at a time. Storage uses the 0G TypeScript SDK against the Galileo Flow contract 0x22E03a6A89B950F1c82ec5e74F8eCa321a105296. The relay encrypts with AES-256-GCM first. The key stays in relay/data/aes.key. One ciphertext per utterance goes to the log, addressed by the SDK Merkle root, and a download asks for the proof. A KV value points at the open-item blob. GET /companion proof-checks that blob, decrypts it on the relay, and returns the reminders and list items. POST /companion dismisses a row or replaces its wording and keeps the original time. A failed proof, or a version 1.0 index from an earlier experiment, comes back empty. Private compute is what makes the memory believable. Each decision carries a request id and a TEE check, and the log binds that id to the ciphertext.
On HTTP 503, HTTP 502, or tee_verified other than true, the relay tells the badge to cut mic power and paint the red lock, and the index stays as it was. There is no local model waiting behind that check.

projects.title: Flashmob
projects.description: Copy crypto traders in one tap or on autopilot, on web and Telegram, with real orders on Base.
projects.project_description:
Flashmob is a copy trading platform built on the Definitive Flash API. Every
order a trader places is public and copyable, so their record comes from real
trades, not screenshots or signals. Traders: trade on the web or in Telegram, with market, limit, stop, bracket, TWAP and trailing orders Followers: get Telegram alerts and copy in one tap, or turn on auto-copy Auto-copy: places the trade with the follower's own size and spending limits, then follows the trader's sells, cancels and price changes Safety: copies with unusually high costs are skipped, and funds can only return to the user's own wallet Agents: AI traders with their own wallet, public profile, spending limits and a logged reason for every decision One wallet: the same embedded wallet works on web and Telegram
projects.how_its_made: Flashmob is a pnpm monorepo with two apps: a Next.js website hosted on Vercel, and a long-running Node worker that runs the Telegram bot (built with grammY). Both share a Postgres database on Neon through Drizzle. Definitive Flash is the trading layer, handling quotes, order execution and a live order stream on Base. Privy provides one embedded wallet that works on web and Telegram. Flash needs a signature on every order, so users approve a Privy server signer once, which lets auto-copy and Telegram orders sign while they are offline. When a trader places an order, the worker sees it on Flash's stream, applies each follower's size and spending limits, and places their copy. A few parts are hacky. Postgres doubles as the job queue, with jobs claimed using SKIP LOCKED and a unique index stopping a wallet from copying the same trade twice. The stream can miss orders that fill instantly, so the worker also reads recent orders every 5 seconds and sends both through the same path. Flash's stream needs our API key, so the server holds the connection and tells the browser when something changes. Before signing anything, the worker checks the order is on Base and that funds can only return to the user's own wallet.

projects.title: Trenchers AI
projects.description: Build, track and manage AI trading bots. Co-invest through the Arena across Solana and EVM.
projects.project_description: Trenchers helps traders build, paper-test, run and manage AI-assisted trading bots in one place. Users can turn an idea into a trading strategy, test it with simulated funds, track its performance and adjust how the bot trades before committing real capital. We started on Solana. For ETHGlobal, we’re extending Trenchers to EVM chains so users can manage their trading strategies across more networks through the same interface. We’re also building the Trenchers Arena, where strategy creators can make their bots available for others to discover and co-invest in. Creators bring the strategy, while other users can follow its performance and choose whether to participate without having to build a bot themselves. Paper results and live trading results will be clearly distinguished so users can understand what they’re evaluating. Our goal is to make the whole experience, from creating a first bot to tracking strategies and participating in the Arena, easy to use, with bot controls, performance tracking and investment management together in one place.
projects.how_its_made: Trenchers has a React and TypeScript frontend, a Rust backend for bot execution and monitoring, and a Python AI service built with FastAPI and Pydantic AI. Users can create trading strategies with AI assistance, paper-test them, run bots and track their performance through one interface. For our EVM integration, we use Alchemy to fetch onchain data. We use Uniswap v4 for swaps and Definitive Finance for trade execution. These integrations connect EVM trading to the bot creation and management workflow we originally built for Solana. PostgreSQL stores application data, ClickHouse supports trading analytics, and Redis handles caching. Our services run on Kubernetes. We’re also building the Trenchers Arena, where users can discover strategies, compare bot performance and co-invest in creator-run bots. The Arena connects strategy discovery with the execution and monitoring infrastructure, so users can manage their own bots and participate in other creators’ strategies from the same interface.

projects.title: Overdraft
projects.description: Credit lines for AI agents, repaid automatically from their x402 income on Hedera.
projects.project_description: AI agents have a cash flow problem. An agent pays for its AI before every job, but its customers pay after. So when a rush of paid work comes in, a perfectly profitable agent can run out of budget and start turning customers away, losing money it would have made. Overdraft gives these agents a credit line, so they can keep working through the rush and pay it back from what they earn. Here's how it works for an agent: It earns. Customers pay per job with x402 on Hedera. The money goes into a small contract set up for the agent, not its wallet. It borrows when it needs to. When paid jobs pile up faster than its budget, the agent borrows the shortfall by itself, within its limit. Nobody has to approve it. The loan can only be spent on AI. It goes straight into the agent's 0G compute account, which has no withdrawal. It repays without trying. Every payment that comes in sends the lender's share first until the debt is cleared. Each loan has a flat 5% fee and a seven-day term. Its ID is on the line. The agent's ERC-8004 ID is held as collateral while it owes. If it stops repaying, or reroutes its income, it defaults and the lender keeps the ID. Before anyone lends, Overdraft checks that the income is real. It traces where each customer's money came from, and if the "customers" were funded by the agent's own owner, that income doesn't count. Limits are set from verified income and start small, at most $5 for a new agent. Every application, decision, loan, repayment and default becomes a public record on Arkiv. Any lender, or anyone thinking of hiring the agent, can check its history without asking us, and old marks expire on schedule, like a real credit report. Owners get a dashboard showing their agents, what each one owes and where its ID is, plus a five-step enrolment with MetaMask. Agents can also find each other: a customer that knows only an agent's ID can look up its paid endpoint on the ID card and pay it directly. Everything runs live on Hedera testnet and Arkiv. On the 0G team's advice, the compute deposit is a dry run against 0G's live contract rather than a real transfer. You can watch the demo agent borrow and repay on its own, or enrol your own agent in a few minutes using a test endpoint I host.
projects.how_its_made: Overdraft runs on three networks, each doing the job it's best at. Hedera carries the money. Every job the agent sells is an x402 payment in USDC, settled through the official facilitator, which covers the fees so customers never need HBAR. The interesting part is where the money goes: the payTo isn't the agent's wallet, it's a contract I wrote for each agent, the IncomeSplitter. Every payment that lands there is split, 30% to the lender while there's debt, 20% back to the agent's AI budget, and the rest to the owner. A second contract, CreditLine, holds each agent's limit and debt, lends on request, and keeps the agent's ERC-8004 ID as collateral while it owes. Both are written from scratch in Solidity. 0G is where the loan goes. It's deposited into the agent's compute account through the PaymentVault's depositFor, which has no withdrawal, so a loan can only ever become inference. That's what makes lending to an agent safe. On the 0G team's advice I didn't spend real 0G during the hackathon: the relay runs the exact deposit as a dry run against their live mainnet contract (eth_simulateV1) and records the balances before and after. Arkiv is the memory. Every application, decision, loan, repayment and default is written there as a record owned by one bureau wallet, set to expire on schedule like an old entry on a credit report. Because it's public, any other lender can read an agent's history without going through us, and the website reads it straight from Arkiv too. Here's one loan end to end. Customers pay the agent through a TypeScript gateway built on the x402 packages for Hedera. When paid jobs pile up beyond its budget, the agent calls the CreditLine to borrow the shortfall and its ID gets locked. The relay sees the loan and makes the 0G deposit, and the bureau writes each step to Arkiv. A sweeper triggers the split on every payment, so the debt falls on its own, and once it hits zero the ID goes back to the owner. A watcher checks that agents keep paying into their splitter, and if one redirects its income, the line defaults and the lender keeps the ID. These services are Python (web3.py and FastAPI), and the site is Next.js with viem and MetaMask, hosted on Vercel, with the backend on Railway. A few things I'm proud of. Customer agents find where to pay by reading the agent's ERC-8004 ID card, so all they need is its ID number. The underwriter follows each customer's money three hops back on Hedera's mirror node, which is how it catches agents faking income with wallets their owner funded. Every credit decision gets a fingerprint stored both on Arkiv and next to the limit on Hedera, so anyone can check the explanation matches the limit. The splitter registers itself for USDC through Hedera's token service, which is what lets a contract, not a person, get paid over x402. And the public test endpoint that judges can enrol with pays the owner at first, then switches to the new agent's splitter on its own the moment it's enrolled.

projects.description: AI agents pay USDT within on-chain budgets, with human approval for larger payments
projects.project_description: How do you let an AI agent buy something on your behalf and still decide how much it can spend? With Countersign, you give the agent a spending mandate. You choose its budget, which merchants it can pay, and when it needs your approval. A smart contract enforces those rules when USDT moves. In our Whitechain Sepolia demo, an agent paid 0.50 USDT for an API resource on its own. A 1.50 USDT purchase reached the approval threshold and paused until the owner signed in through the World ID Agent Pass sandbox and approved that exact payment with their wallet. We also tested a stale sign-in, which the system rejected before any transaction was sent. The agent held zero USDT and zero WBT throughout. It signed the payment terms, the relayer paid for gas, and the merchant received USDT directly from the owner’s wallet. The agent’s ENSv2 name, "agent1.countersign.eth", publishes its endpoint and spending policy. The app compares supported policy records with the live Whitechain mandate and flags discrepancies.
projects.how_its_made: The agent signs an EIP-712 intent for an exact amount, merchant, and order. Our Solidity "Mandate" contract checks that signature againhe owner’s spending rules and verifies the merchant’s payout address through "MerchantRegistry". It checks the nonce, order ID, expiry, and mandate epoch to block replay and reject outdated approvals. If the checks pass, the contract transfers USDT from the owner’s allowance directly to the merchant on Whitechain Sepolia. For payments at or above the approval threshold, our Node.js API starts a fresh World ID Agent Pass sandbox sign-in using OIDC and PKCE. It checks the token’s signature and freshness server-side and confirms the World account belongs to the owner bound to the mandate. A separate attestor then signs the approval. The contract requires both the attestor and the owner to sign off on the same payment. We built GasGuard because sponsoring transactions gives the relayer its own budget to protect. It simulates each payment, sponsors only the Mandate’s "pay" function, and reserves gas against per-mandate and global budgets in SQLite before broadcasting. After three confirmations, the chain observer marks the payment settled. The merchant SDK handles payment requests and signed webhook verification, and the Next.js app provides the approval page and receipts. On ENSv2, we gave "agent1.countersign.eth" its own "PermissionedResolver". The agent can update its ENSIP-26 endpoint and context records, while the owner controls the spending policy records. The app reads both testnets live to check whether the published policy matches the contract that enforces it.

projects.title: Charter
projects.description: Git hosting on Arkiv where each repo's own on-chain rules decide merges, CI, bounties and releases.
projects.project_description: Charter is decentralized git hosting on Arkiv. A stock git push arkiv::<rid> and git clone arkiv::<rid> work end to end on the Arkiv Rabdi testnet with no server of ours in between. It is a redesign of the Radicle protocol in which Arkiv replaces gossip and seed nodes: every ref, patch, review and release is a signed entity on Arkiv, and every client verifies every signature and fails closed on rollback, expiry or missing data. What makes it more than "git on a chain" is repo programs. A repo's identity document pins a small deterministic Rhai program by hash, and every client enforces it on every push and fetch. A program can require a 2-of-3 delegate quorum on main, protect branches, require a passing CI attestation before a merge, pay an escrow bounty when a patch lands, or demand a zero-knowledge proof that a sealed patch meets a spec. The rules travel with the repo and nobody can quietly change them: re-pinning is itself a signed identity revision. Also live on Rabdi: Post-quantum signatures from day one: composite ML-DSA-65 + Ed25519 on identities, refs, anchors and ops. Private repos: MLS groups with X-Wing, ciphertext-only entities with blinded attributes, roles and member removal. AI agents as first-class contributors: scoped, revocable agent grants plus an MCP server (chart-mcp). A real headless Codex agent claimed a ZK-gated bounty through it and the escrow paid it on-chain. Arkiv-native CI and releases: a CI runner posts signed attestations to Arkiv, main only moves when the pinned program sees them, and release binaries carry signed, CI-attested release records that anyone can verify with chart release verify. Charter hosts its own source on Arkiv. Every change to main since the CI system landed went through an Arkiv patch, a CI attestation and the pinned program. GitHub is only a read-only mirror and the host of the release tarballs.
projects.how_its_made: Rust workspace, about a dozen crates. git-remote-arkiv is a git remote helper, so plain git talks to Arkiv. It packs objects, splits them into chunks under Arkiv's op body cap, writes them as entities with indexed ag.* attributes (repo id, kind, sequence, hash), and anchors each push with a signed, hash-linked head. Clones read entities back by attribute query and verify every signature and chain link. A local high-water mark plus Arkiv's entityNonce gives rollback and stale-view protection, because Rabdi has no historical reads. Arkiv access: the published Rust SDK targets the retired GolemDB ABI, so we wrote our own JSON-RPC client on alloy plus arkiv-bindings from the Arkiv node repo, pinned by commit. Rate limits, the 100-row query cap, the lack of NOT and no queryable $createdAt all shaped the schema (append-only signed chains, our own ag.at, key-ordered paging). The full friction log is in arkiv/friction.md. Crypto: composite ML-DSA-65 + Ed25519 signatures (both halves must verify), OpenMLS with X-Wing for private repos, RISC Zero receipts for ZK sealed patches, drand quicknet timelock. Repo programs run in Rhai, which is deterministic and sandboxed, with an op and time budget. The escrow agent pays program obligations on-chain and publishes an audit trail. Agents: chart-mcp is an MCP server (rmcp) exposing clone, patch, review, push and bounty tools, scoped by an on-chain agent grant that the repo can revoke. We tested it with a real Codex CLI agent, live. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Charter develops itself on Arkiv. Shell CI scripts run patch, runner, attestation, merge, then fast-forward a GitHub mirror. Release records are validated by the same pinned program as merges. The rename from arkiv-git to Charter shipped through that pipeline as v0.2.0 without touching the wire format.

projects.title: RegX
projects.description: Compliant invoice financing: ERC-3643 notes on Whitechain, settled in USDT, order book on Arkiv
projects.project_description: RegX is a compliant invoice-financing market. A small business (MSME) tokenizes a receivable as a regulated security, verified investors fund it in USDT at a discount, and the coupons and repayment are settled on-chain. Investors who want out before maturity can sell on a public order book that anyone can read. The problem. Invoice financing is slow and opaque. Investors can't see when an issuer misses a payment, and settlement goes through banks and back offices. Tokenizing a receivable only helps if the token keeps the rules a regulated security needs: who may hold it, how much each holder may own, and when it may move. Settlement also has to happen in a real stablecoin, not an IOU. How it works Issuance. Each invoice becomes an ERC-3643 (T-REX) note on Whitechain Sepolia: 1 USDT face value per unit, issued at 0.97 USDT, paying a 0.01 USDT coupon. Investors identify through ONCHAINID: a trusted claim issuer signs a KYC claim, and the identity is registered in the T-REX Identity Registry. Only verified wallets can hold or receive units. Subscription. During the subscription window, verified investors call subscribe(). Their USDT goes straight to the issuer and units are minted to them in the same transaction. The mint goes through T-REX compliance: identity check, a 150-unit holding cap per investor, and a module that allows minting only before the subscription deadline. An unverified wallet's subscription reverts on-chain. Secondary trading (DvP). Makers sign EIP-712 orders and publish them as entities on Arkiv, so the order book is public, queryable data owned by each maker, and orders expire with their Arkiv entity. A taker fills an order through the RegXDvP contract, which swaps note units for USDT atomically in one transaction. Before submitting, the app runs an on-chain checkFill pre-trade check that explains exactly why a trade would fail: buyer not verified, wallet frozen, token paused, compliance rule broken, or insufficient balance or allowance. Unverified buyers are blocked inside the transfer itself. Coupons and maturity. Coupon payment and maturity settlement are permissionless. Once a date passes, anyone can trigger them. USDT is pulled from the issuer's on-chain allowance and paid pro rata to every holder. At maturity, face value is repaid and the units are burned. A missed payment shows up as a public revert, not a quiet bank delay. Issuer controls. The issuer, acting as the T-REX agent, can freeze wallets and pause the token, and those controls are enforced in the contracts. Public history on Arkiv. A keeper mirrors every on-chain event into Arkiv as typed entities: fills, subscriptions, coupons, redemptions, freezes, pauses and KYC grants. Writes are idempotent, keyed by transaction hash and log index, so anyone can re-run the keeper and reproduce the dataset. The keeper also auto-settles coupons and maturity when they fall due. Why on-chain stablecoin settlement matters. Delivery and payment have to be atomic and auditable. USDT on Whitechain lets the same transaction that enforces ERC-3643 compliance also move the money. That removes settlement risk, and every subscription, coupon and repayment can be checked on the explorer. What's proven on testnet. The full lifecycle has run with real Whitechain test USDT: verified subscriptions a rejected subscription from an unverified investor an atomic DvP trade, plus a blocked buy from an unverified investor a coupon paid automatically to all holders maturity repayment of 15 USDT with the units burned All 12 contracts are verified on the Whitechain explorer, and 24 Foundry tests run against the real T-REX token. Stack. Solidity with Tokeny T-REX v4.1.6 and ONCHAINID; Foundry; viem and wagmi; a Next.js web app with views for markets, portfolio, issuer and activity; and the Arkiv SDK for the order book and event history.
projects.how_its_made: RegX is a TypeScript monorepo built with npm workspaces. It has four parts: contracts/ (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.17, EVM target paris): the smart contracts. shared/: ABIs, Arkiv schemas, EIP-712 order helpers and a revert-reason decoder, used by both the scripts and the web app. scripts/: deployment, keeper and lifecycle CLIs, run with tsx and viem. web/: a Next.js 15 app built with wagmi, viem, React Query and Tailwind 4. Contracts (Whitechain Sepolia, chain 1874). We used Tokeny's official T-REX v4.1.6 (the ERC-3643 standard) and ONCHAINID v2.2.1 directly rather than writing our own permissioned token. The setup is: One shared identity layer serves every note: an Identity Registry and its storage, a Claim Topics Registry (KYC is topic 1), and a Trusted Issuers Registry. Each note gets its own T-REX Token and ModularCompliance contract, with two custom modules attached: InvestorCapModule caps how many units one holder can own (150). RegXNote is the hacky part. We wrote it as a T-REX compliance module that is also the note's lifecycle contract. Because it sits inside the compliance hooks, it sees every mint, transfer and burn. It uses those hooks to keep an on-chain set of holders, which is how it pays coupons pro rata without an off-chain snapshot. It also enforces the lifecycle in the transfer path: minting only before the subscription deadline, transfers only before maturity, burns always allowed. On top of that it exposes subscribe() (USDT goes from the investor to the issuer, then units are minted), plus permissionless payCoupon(i) and settleMaturity(). Both pull USDT from the issuer's allowance and pay every holder, and maturity also burns the units. Since the note is a token agent, it can mint and burn directly. RegXDvP settles EIP-712 signed orders (domain RegX/1, bound to the chain ID). It supports partial fills, cancellation by nonce, and atomic swaps of units for USDT. It also has a view function, checkFill, that rebuilds what T-REX would check: paused, frozen wallets, free (unfrozen) balance, allowances, isVerified(buyer) and compliance.canTransfer. It returns a reason code, so the UI can explain why a trade would fail before the user spends gas. 24 Foundry tests run against the real T-REX Token, with a mock USDT. All 12 contracts are verified on Whitechain's Blockscout explorer by a script that calls its verification API. Whitechain (partner). We started on Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio and moved to Whitechain partway through. What Whitechain gave us: An EVM chain with roughly 1-second blocks and a 5 gwei base fee, so the full lifecycle (subscribe, trade, coupon, maturity) could run live within minutes on short-dated test notes. A real test USDT (6 decimals, with permit). Every payment in the demo is actual stablecoin settlement with explorer links, not a token we minted ourselves. Standard tooling that just works: Blockscout verification, and Multicall3, which the web app uses to batch its reads. Arkiv (partner). Arkiv is the market's data layer. We built on SDK 1.0.1's schema-first API on the Rabdi testnet with four typed schemas: regx.asset: the security's metadata and live stats. regx.order: the order book. regx.fill and regx.action: trades, and corporate and compliance events. Makers publish their signed orders as Arkiv entities from their own wallets, so each maker owns their order. Each entity expires when its order does, which means expired orders drop out of the book without a cleanup job. Arkiv strings are capped at 128 bytes, so signatures go in a bytes column. The web app queries the book with Arkiv's select().where().orderBy() and then reads each order's remaining size from the DvP contract, combining off-chain discovery with on-chain truth.
projects.project_description_markdown:
RegX is a compliant invoice-financing market. A small business (MSME) tokenizes a receivable as a regulated security, verified investors fund it in USDT at a discount, and the coupons and repayment are settled on-chain. Investors who want out before maturity can sell on a public order book that anyone can read.

The problem. Invoice financing is slow and opaque. Investors can't see when an issuer misses a payment, and settlement goes through banks and back offices. Tokenizing a receivable only helps if the token keeps the rules a regulated security needs: who may hold it, how much each holder may own, and when it may move. Settlement also has to happen in a real stablecoin, not an IOU.

How it works

1. Issuance. Each invoice becomes an ERC-3643 (T-REX) note on Whitechain Sepolia: 1 USDT face value per unit, issued at 0.97 USDT, paying a 0.01 USDT coupon. Investors identify through ONCHAINID: a trusted claim issuer signs a KYC claim, and the identity is registered in the T-REX Identity Registry. Only verified wallets can hold or receive units.
2. Subscription. During the subscription window, verified investors call subscribe(). Their USDT goes straight to the issuer and units are minted to them in the same transaction. The mint goes through T-REX compliance: identity check, a 150-unit holding cap per investor, and a module that allows minting only before the subscription deadline. An unverified wallet's subscription reverts on-chain.
3. Secondary trading (DvP). Makers sign EIP-712 orders and publish them as entities on Arkiv, so the order book is public, queryable data owned by each maker, and orders expire with their Arkiv entity. A taker fills an order through the RegXDvP contract, which swaps note units for USDT atomically in one transaction. Before submitting, the app runs an on-chain checkFill pre-trade check that explains exactly why a trade would fail: buyer not verified, wallet frozen, token paused, compliance rule broken, or insufficient balance or allowance. Unverified buyers are blocked inside the transfer itself.
4. Coupons and maturity. Coupon payment and maturity settlement are permissionless. Once a date passes, anyone can trigger them. USDT is pulled from the issuer's on-chain allowance and paid pro rata to every holder. At maturity, face value is repaid and the units are burned. A missed payment shows up as a public revert, not a quiet bank delay.
5. Issuer controls. The issuer, acting as the T-REX agent, can freeze wallets and pause the token, and those controls are enforced in the contracts.
6. Public history on Arkiv. A keeper mirrors every on-chain event into Arkiv as typed entities: fills, subscriptions, coupons, redemptions, freezes, pauses and KYC grants. Writes are idempotent, keyed by transaction hash and log index, so anyone can re-run the keeper and reproduce the dataset. The keeper also auto-settles coupons and maturity when they fall due.

Why on-chain stablecoin settlement matters. Delivery and payment have to be atomic and auditable. USDT on Whitechain lets the same transaction that enforces ERC-3643 compliance also move the money. That removes settlement risk, and every subscription, coupon and repayment can be checked on the explorer.

What's proven on testnet. The full lifecycle has run with real Whitechain test USDT:

- verified subscriptions
- a rejected subscription from an unverified investor
- an atomic DvP trade, plus a blocked buy from an unverified investor
- a coupon paid automatically to all holders
- maturity repayment of 15 USDT with the units burned

All 12 contracts are verified on the Whitechain explorer, and 24 Foundry tests run against the real T-REX token.

Stack. Solidity with Tokeny T-REX v4.1.6 and ONCHAINID; Foundry; viem and wagmi; a Next.js web app with views for markets, portfolio, issuer and activity; and the Arkiv SDK for the order book and event history.

- scripts/: deployment, keeper and lifecycle CLIs, run with tsx and viem.

Contracts (Whitechain Sepolia, chain 1874). We used Tokeny's official T-REX v4.1.6 (the ERC-3643 standard) and ONCHAINID v2.2.1 directly rather than writing our own permissioned token. The setup is:

- Each note gets its own T-REX Token and ModularCompliance contract, with two custom modules attached:
  - InvestorCapModule caps how many units one holder can own (150).
  - RegXNote is the hacky part. We wrote it as a T-REX compliance module that is also the note's lifecycle contract. Because it sits inside the compliance hooks, it sees every mint, transfer and burn. It uses those hooks to keep an on-chain set of holders, which is how it pays coupons pro rata without an off-chain snapshot. It also enforces the lifecycle in the transfer path: minting only before the subscription deadline, transfers only before maturity, burns always allowed. On top of that it exposes subscribe() (USDT goes from the investor to the issuer, then units are minted), plus permissionless payCoupon(i) and settleMaturity(). Both pull USDT from the issuer's allowance and pay every holder, and maturity also burns the units. Since the note is a token agent, it can mint and burn directly.
- RegXDvP settles EIP-712 signed orders (domain RegX/1, bound to the chain ID). It supports partial fills, cancellation by nonce, and atomic swaps of units for USDT. It also has a view function, checkFill, that rebuilds what T-REX would check: paused, frozen wallets, free (unfrozen) balance, allowances, isVerified(buyer) and compliance.canTransfer. It returns a reason code, so the UI can explain why a trade would fail before the user spends gas.

24 Foundry tests run against the real T-REX Token, with a mock USDT. All 12 contracts are verified on Whitechain's Blockscout explorer by a script that calls its verification API.

Whitechain (partner). We started on Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio and moved to Whitechain partway through. What Whitechain gave us:

- An EVM chain with roughly 1-second blocks and a 5 gwei base fee, so the full lifecycle (subscribe, trade, coupon, maturity) could run live within minutes on short-dated test notes.
- A real test USDT (6 decimals, with permit). Every payment in the demo is actual stablecoin settlement with explorer links, not a token we minted ourselves.
- Standard tooling that just works: Blockscout verification, and Multicall3, which the web app uses to batch its reads.

Arkiv (partner). Arkiv is the market's data layer. We built on SDK 1.0.1's schema-first API on the Rabdi testnet with four typed schemas:

- regx.asset: the security's metadata and live stats.
- regx.order: the order book.
- regx.fill and regx.action: trades, and corporate and compliance events.

Makers publish their signed orders as Arkiv entities from their own wallets, so each maker owns their order. Each entity expires when its order does, which means expired orders drop out of the book without a cleanup job. Arkiv strings are capped at 128 bytes, so signatures go in a bytes column. projects.title: ClearAudit
projects.description: Evidence-gated USDC settlement on Arc: lock funds, match an Arkiv fingerprint, pay, then forget.
projects.project_description: ClearAudit is an evidence-gated USDC settlement rail for situations where you cannot safely trust the other side with custody, and you cannot safely leave a permanent paper trail either. One party locks a fixed USDC amount in BountyVault on Arc Testnet (chain 5042002). The other side delivers an artefact and anchors only a fingerprint — with a thirty-day expiry — on Arkiv. Money leaves the vault only when a live fingerprint matches the on-chain terms (payee, payer, amount, criteria). Anyone can re-run that check at /evidence without a wallet. After thirty days Arkiv stops serving the fingerprint; the chain still shows who got paid. Bug bounties and freelance invoices can ride this rail. They are not the story. The story is incident settlement: recovery after an exploit, coordinated disclosure, a retainer under NDA, an agent task, a contest prize. Same vault. Different nouns. Live product surface: named deals, open tasks agents can claim, contests with split awards, payer release, settleAfterChallenge after the window, and a whitehat-only dispute path. The vault is non-upgradeable, 0% fee, no admin withdrawal. Settlement and gas are the same asset on Arc — the payee of a named deal never needs a separate gas token.
projects.how_its_made: Built as a Next.js 16 app (React 19, wagmi/viem, Privy) talking to a BountyVault on Arc Testnet and expiring report entities on Arkiv Rabdi. The Arc vault is the product: fund / commitEvidence / release / settleAfterChallenge / contests / dispute. Contracts were designed and first deployed with Arc Studio, then iterated with Foundry when Studio quota ran out — same sources, same network, no proxy. Live vault: 0x9D500710df8036e4BdF38Bf9A6CA7364Cd4e26C1. Arkiv holds the thirty-day fingerprint that gates payout. Only a hash and deal-matching metadata are written; the artefact body stays local. The app fail-closes through /api/release-guard and a public /evidence page that re-reads Arc + Arkiv before treating a payout as justified. Without Arkiv this gate would be “trust my Postgres.” For the Ethereum Foundation alt-mempool track there is a separate EIP-8141 research path on chain 1337 (/app/gasless): the researcher is a beneficiary in frame calldata, never tx.sender; the same Arkiv gate runs before a frame is built. Honest limit on the probed revision: PAYMENT-frame paymaster does not work, so the relayer pays gas — we do not claim ERC-4337 sponsorship on Arc. Notable pieces: CA- public refs derived from Arkiv entity keys, an operator-agent-as-payee path, seed deals for recovery / CVD / retainer / agent / contest, and Pip — a roaming companion that keeps the otherwise serious rail human.

After thirty days Arkiv stops serving the fingerprint; the chain still shows who got paid.

Bug bounties and freelance invoices can ride this rail. They are not the story. The story is incident settlement: recovery after an exploit, coordinated disclosure, a retainer under NDA, an agent task, a contest prize. Same vault. Different nouns.

Live product surface: named deals, open tasks agents can claim, contests with split awards, payer release, settleAfterChallenge after the window, and a whitehat-only dispute path. The vault is non-upgradeable, 0% fee, no admin withdrawal. Settlement and gas are the same asset on Arc — the payee of a named deal never needs a separate gas token.

Built as a Next.js 16 app (React 19, wagmi/viem, Privy) talking to a BountyVault on Arc Testnet and expiring report entities on Arkiv Rabdi. The Arc vault is the product: fund / commitEvidence / release / settleAfterChallenge / contests / dispute. Contracts were designed and first deployed with Arc Studio, then iterated with Foundry when Studio quota ran out — same sources, same network, no proxy. Live vault: 0x9D500710df8036e4BdF38Bf9A6CA7364Cd4e26C1.

Arkiv holds the thirty-day fingerprint that gates payout. Only a hash and deal-matching metadata are written; the artefact body stays local. The app fail-closes through /api/release-guard and a public /evidence page that re-reads Arc + Arkiv before treating a payout as justified. Without Arkiv this gate would be “trust my Postgres.”

For the Ethereum Foundation alt-mempool track there is a separate EIP-8141 research path on chain 1337 (/app/gasless): the researcher is a beneficiary in frame calldata, never tx.sender; the same Arkiv gate runs before a frame is built. Honest limit on the probed revision: PAYMENT-frame paymaster does not work, so the relayer pays gas — we do not claim ERC-4337 sponsorship on Arc.

Notable pieces: CA- public refs derived from Arkiv entity keys, an operator-agent-as-payee path, seed deals for recovery / CVD / retainer / agent / contest, and Pip — a roaming companion that keeps the otherwise serious rail human.

projects.title: Wisprr
projects.description: wisprr: private wallet-Stealth addresses, anon-rpc reads. No server and ENSv2 names
projects.project_description: wisprr is a privacy first wallet for Ethereum. Chrome extension, keys on your device, no server. Payments to you never land at the same address twice. You share a meta-address, not an address. Each payer derives a fresh one-time address from it, so ten payments leave ten unconnected addresses and nobody can total what you own. Three standards do the work here anon-rpc carries every read and broadcast through a mixnet, so the node answering never sees your IP. ENSv2 makes the meta-address shareable: wisprr.eth on Sepolia publishes the record, read through the Universal Resolver. ERC-5564 does the derivation, tested both ways against ScopeLift's SDK. Two things I haven't seen shipped elsewhere. A guard that refuses to sign a sweep if it would publicly tie a stealth address to you, because that's where 44 to 73 percent of these systems leak. And scoped grants: give an auditor a key for one date range that can read and cannot spend, and that expires. 67 tests. Interop checked both directions. Every crypto claim verified against live Sepolia, which is how I found my own derivation bug.
projects.how_its_made: I built wisprr as a Chrome MV3 extension. Keys live in the service worker. The popup is plain HTML and TypeScript, bundled with esbuild, and chain calls go through viem. Stealth math is ERC-5564 scheme 1 on secp256k1 (@noble/curves): ephemeral ECDH against the viewing key, a one-byte view tag, ETH to a fresh address, and an Announcement the recipient scans. I checked derived addresses and spending keys both ways against @scopelift/stealth-address-sdk, so a payment from their SDK opens here. The thing you share is the meta-address. It is registered on ERC-6538 and published on ENSv2 as the stealth-meta-address[1] text record. wisprr.eth is on Sepolia ETHRegistry with its own Permissioned Resolver. That resolver's setText takes a DNS-encoded name, and the wrong selector (the old namehash one) ate most of the ENS debugging. With the record set, typing the name resolves through UniversalResolver and the wallet derives a new stealth address from it. RPC goes through the Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC harness (@anon-rpc/browser-extension-harness) in an offscreen document, so the extension origin and the RPC host stay apart. It tries Nox, then Tor, then Nym. The mixnet socket drops often, so a dead tunnel falls back to a direct RPC and the send still lands. USDC on a stealth address usually has no ETH for gas, and a top-up would link it. ERC-3009 transferWithAuthorization lets the stealth key sign offline while someone else submits and pays gas. The service worker refuses the sweep if the destination is your own vault or the person who just paid you.

projects.title: NodeWatch
projects.description: One container next to your Arkiv node: health, live pool queries, and a phone call when it breaks.
projects.project_description: Nodewatch is an ops console for Arkiv community nodes. It runs as one extra Docker container on the same host as the node kit, needs no changes to the node, and gives the operator one screen for everything that normally gets watched by hand: whether the node is healthy and in sync, whether it is still in the load balancer's rotation, how full the disk will be next week, and what the pool is actually asking the node. The problem: the community node kit is easy to start and hard to keep alive. The tunnel to the load balancer dies, the disk fills up, a container restarts, and the node silently drops out of rotation. Operators usually find out when payouts stop. Nobody can see which queries the pool sends to a node or which ones are slow. What Nodewatch does: Watches the node. Execution, consensus and tunnel containers, head lag, peers, CPU, memory and disk, with a disk-full forecast, and the node's public status on the Arkiv node list. Alerts you. Every failed check goes to Telegram. Critical ones (a container down, the node out of rotation, a request slower than 3 seconds) open a PagerDuty incident that rings your phone and reads the incident out. Alerts resolve themselves and can be silenced from the console. Fixes things. For every failure the dashboard shows the exact command and a one-click fix: restart whichever container is down (tunnel, execution or consensus), and the same flow for a major outage where the whole node kit has to come back. Updating Nodewatch itself is also one click. Live queries. Nodewatch sits inline on the tunnel between the load balancer and the node, times every read request the pool sends, keeps the query text, and shows requests per minute, average and p95 latency, error rate, and the slowest query shapes. Any request over 750 ms is sent to Telegram with its text. Fleet view. A small Grafana Alloy container on each node pushes metrics and the per-request log to one central Grafana, so several nodes fit on one screen: who is slow, who is failing, what the pool is asking. Slow-query benchmarks. Nodewatch writes private datasets of 500 to 5,000 entities to Arkiv and runs 29 query shapes against them, measuring p95 per shape and how latency grows with dataset size. The report shows which shapes scale linearly, which ones to optimise, and the exact query text behind each number. Also: a heartbeat entity written to Arkiv so the node proves it is alive on-chain, backups, and wallet (SIWE) login for the console. Everything in the demo video ran on a live Rabdi node during the hackathon: the tunnel was stopped on purpose, the node left rotation, Nodewatch flagged it, the Telegram message and the PagerDuty phone call arrived, and the node came back after the one-click restart.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm) with a Fastify server and a React + Vite console, shipped as one Docker image. The server uses SQLite for state, viem for the chain, dockerode to inspect and restart the node kit's containers, prom-client for metrics and pino for logs. It runs on the same EC2 host as the Arkiv community node kit and talks to the node over the kit's compose network. Login is wallet-based (SIWE). The dashboard writes a heartbeat entity to Arkiv every 30 seconds from a small funded key, so anyone can verify on-chain that the node is alive. Alerting: a rules engine evaluates every check on an interval with thresholds and a "for" duration, so one flapping sample does not page anyone. Notifiers are Telegram (bot API) and PagerDuty (Events API v2). A critical rule opens a PagerDuty incident, which rings the phone and reads the incident aloud; the rule resolves the incident itself once the check has been quiet for five minutes. Each alert carries a fix: the exact command plus a one-click action that restarts the failed container (tunnel, execution or consensus) through the Docker socket, or brings the whole kit back after a bigger outage. The hacky part is "inline mode" for live queries. The load balancer reaches a node through an frpc tunnel container. Nodewatch rewrites the tunnel's frpc.toml so the tunnel's local target is Nodewatch's own proxy on the compose network gateway instead of the execution client, then restarts the tunnel. From then on every read request from the pool passes through Nodewatch, gets timed, parsed (arkiv_query text or params), and is forwarded to the node unchanged. The proxy is fail-open, strips accept-encoding so it can read JSON-RPC bodies, restores the original config if the switch fails, and a watcher re-applies the setting if the node kit rewrites the file. Per-request rows go to SQLite (48 h) plus an on-disk requests.jsonl; requests over 750 ms go to Telegram with the query text, over 3 s they trigger the critical rule. Benchmarks: Nodewatch uses the Arkiv SDK to create private datasets of 500 to 5,000 entities with typed, indexed columns, runs 29 query shapes against them with timed batches, and fits latency against dataset size per shape, so the report says which shapes grow linearly and which to optimise. Fleet view: a Grafana Alloy container on each node scrapes Nodewatch's /metrics (loopback-only unless a token is set) and tails requests.jsonl, then pushes to Prometheus remote-write and Loki behind Caddy basic auth on a separate small EC2. Dashboards are provisioned from the repo, so a new node appears on the fleet screen a minute after its agent starts. Arkiv specifics that shaped the build, and two things we hit: typed entities and arkiv_query drive the heartbeat and the benchmarks; the node caps query limits at 100, and eth_getLogs fails for blocks older than about a thousand, both measured on the live node and written up in arkiv/friction.md. The live demo and the 3-second phone call were produced on the real node by stopping the tunnel container and by pushing a 35-query batch through the proxy. All infrastructure, keys and on-chain writes were set up and approved by hand.

projects.title: chainroll
projects.description: The Ethereum chain list on Arkiv: queryable, signed, with live RPC checks and privacy labels.
projects.project_description: Chainroll puts the Ethereum chain list on Arkiv and shows whether you can trust it. Wallets and listing sites rely on ethereum-lists/chains, a folder of JSON files on GitHub. MetaMask, Chainlist and ethereum.org all read data built from it. But nothing checks that a listed RPC works, is on the right chain or is current, and anyone can copy the list and claim it is the real one. We tested every listed RPC: about 63% did not answer correctly, and the count was nearly identical from Mumbai and US West (2,612 vs 2,611). 1,815 of the 2,647 chains we could test had no working RPC in that survey. Chainroll mirrors all 2,855 chains, 4,219 RPCs and 2,536 explorers to Arkiv's Rabdi testnet, and adds Chainlist's 2,848 RPC URLs with their tracking labels and privacy statements, credited and kept under GPL-3.0. Each record is queryable with no API key: find L2s of a chain, chains with a reused ID, or Ethereum RPCs that pass right now. Trust is checkable, not assumed. The ENS name chainroll.eth names the publisher, a signed Sepolia transaction anchors the release, and a Merkle proof ties each Arkiv record to the exact upstream file. All 2,855 chains verify. The Verify page runs these checks in your browser, and a trust map lights up each step across Ethereum, Arkiv and GitHub. Two probers on Railway, in Southeast Asia and US West, test 958 RPCs in repeated rounds and publish signed readings. Each reading expires within 2 hours if its prober stops, so a stale green cannot linger. Apps only trust probers named by the publisher, and Arkiv's owner field keeps fake records out of what apps show. The site is static: your browser reads Arkiv and Ethereum directly, and shows the Arkiv query behind the network list.
projects.how_its_made: Chainroll is a TypeScript monorepo on Bun, with four parts: an importer, probers, a browser-safe read client (shared by the CLI and the site) and a React + Vite site. Importer: it reads ethereum-lists/chains at a pinned commit and splits each file into a core chain record plus separate RPC and explorer records, because RPCs churn and chain identity doesn't. The raw file is kept byte for byte with its git blob hash. It builds an OpenZeppelin Merkle tree over (chainId, shortName, sourceBlob), then writes to Rabdi with @arkiv-network/sdk in batches of 20. A re-run at the same commit writes nothing. Arkiv: this is the core of the project. Owner on every entity lets anyone write while apps only show the publisher and named probers. Per-entity expiry means a stopped prober's readings vanish within 2 hours, with no cleanup job. Patching keeps one health record per RPC per prober. Indexed, typed attributes make each registry question one query, and open browser reads mean we run no backend. ENS: we registered chainroll.eth on Sepolia's ENSv2 entirely from our CLI, including deploying the per-account resolver. Text records name the publisher and latest anchor. Probers are subnames, so one can be added or removed without a new release, and we tested a handover that leaves a hot key only the release records on a throwaway name. chainroll.eth itself has not been handed over. Probers: Dockerised on Railway in two regions, stamping their region from Railway's env. Each round sends eth_chainId, block 0 and latest block to 958 RPCs, signs readings with EIP-191 and keeps uptime history in SQLite. Site: static on Vercel, reading Arkiv and Ethereum straight from the browser. Verification runs client-side, reading ENS through two RPC providers. Hacky bits: The anchor is a transaction to self with readable calldata, "chainkiv/1 {json}", so you can read a release on Etherscan. Chainlist's data is a JS file. We parse it with acorn and read the AST, so its code never runs. Arkiv cursors break on the next block, so we page on $key instead. Rabdi's no-key budget is small, and our first site used over 2,000 requests per load. Now it checks the signed release and skips the full read if it matches its cached copy, cutting a visit to about 40. Verify waits out rate limits. A 64 KB response cap marked every Ethereum RPC down, because blocks were 88 to 104 KB. Pruned nodes refuse block 0, so an unknown first block is shown as "unconfirmed", never failed or passed. Tamper tests ran on a private arkiv-reth chain. Claude Code wrote most of the code and docs from our PRD and decisions.
