projects.title: Satya
projects.description: Check if a website or a person is real, with proofs anyone can verify, not a company's word
projects.project_description:
Every scam-check tool today has the same flaw: the score comes from one company's server, so you're swapping "trust the website" for "trust the checker." Satya and Aletheia replace that with checks anyone can reproduce: Satya for websites, Aletheia for people. LINKS
Aletheia (demo link): https://satya-aletheia.vercel.app
Satya web app: https://satya-web-blush.vercel.app
Satya extension (zip): https://github.com/coolcoolercoolestkid/satya/raw/extension-download/satya-extension.zip
Repo: https://github.com/coolcoolercoolestkid/satya SATYA — website trust without a trusted backend
The extension has no server. When you open a site, the side panel: Collects domain signals from public sources: RDAP registration date, the earliest Wayback Machine capture, and certificate history. Registration date and first-archived date are kept separate on purpose. An old archive on a freshly re-registered domain is a common scam pattern (buying an aged domain to inherit its reputation), and a single "domain age" number hides that. Checks the domain against phishing and scam blocklists stored on Arkiv. Each list is published as hashed entries with its source URL, source hash, count and date. The extension shows the Arkiv entity next to every result, so anyone can confirm exactly which data produced the verdict. Runs AI-generated-text detection fully in the browser. Page text is never uploaded. Shows a score with a "How this was checked" breakdown, where every line says where its data came from. The same scoring is written as a Chainlink CRE workflow, so independent nodes can fetch the domain data and sign the result, removing us as the trusted party. It runs in the CRE simulator today; deployment is pending Chainlink access, so the live extension fetches RDAP and Wayback directly. The Satya web app adds Anon Aadhaar proofs (prove you hold a valid Aadhaar without revealing any of it) and evidence capture: Satya saves the page text, a screenshot and source hashes locally, and puts only a fingerprint on Arkiv. You can later prove the evidence existed, even after the scam page is gone, without publishing anything private. To install the extension: download the zip above, unzip it, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click "Load unpacked" and pick the unzipped folder. The demo video shows it on live sites. ALETHEIA — "Trust the proof, not the profile"
Satya checks the site. Aletheia checks the person behind it. Instead of follower counts or badges, someone proves facts about themselves (over 18, nationality, credential not expired) from an issuer-signed credential using Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs. The verifier learns only "yes, this holds", never the date of birth, nationality or credential details. The proof is checked in the browser and again on-chain by a verifier contract on Sepolia. Prior work: the ZK circuits in aletheia-zk/ predate this hackathon, as noted in the README. Built during the event: the Satya extension, the Arkiv blocklist pipeline, scoring and the CRE workflow, the Satya web app, and the new Aletheia site and verify flow.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Every scam-check tool today has the same flaw: the score comes from one company's server, so you're swapping "trust the website" for "trust the checker." Satya and Aletheia replace that with checks anyone can reproduce: Satya for websites, Aletheia for people.

LINKS
Aletheia (demo link): https://satya-aletheia.vercel.app
Satya web app: https://satya-web-blush.vercel.app
Satya extension (zip): https://github.com/coolcoolercoolestkid/satya/raw/extension-download/satya-extension.zip
Repo: https://github.com/coolcoolercoolestkid/satya

SATYA — website trust without a trusted backend
The extension has no server. When you open a site, the side panel:

1. Collects domain signals from public sources: RDAP registration date, the earliest Wayback Machine capture, and certificate history. Registration date and first-archived date are kept separate on purpose. An old archive on a freshly re-registered domain is a common scam pattern (buying an aged domain to inherit its reputation), and a single "domain age" number hides that.

2. Checks the domain against phishing and scam blocklists stored on Arkiv. Each list is published as hashed entries with its source URL, source hash, count and date. The extension shows the Arkiv entity next to every result, so anyone can confirm exactly which data produced the verdict.

3. Runs AI-generated-text detection fully in the browser. Page text is never uploaded.

4. Shows a score with a "How this was checked" breakdown, where every line says where its data came from.

The same scoring is written as a Chainlink CRE workflow, so independent nodes can fetch the domain data and sign the result, removing us as the trusted party. It runs in the CRE simulator today; deployment is pending Chainlink access, so the live extension fetches RDAP and Wayback directly.

The Satya web app adds Anon Aadhaar proofs (prove you hold a valid Aadhaar without revealing any of it) and evidence capture: Satya saves the page text, a screenshot and source hashes locally, and puts only a fingerprint on Arkiv. You can later prove the evidence existed, even after the scam page is gone, without publishing anything private.

To install the extension: download the zip above, unzip it, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click "Load unpacked" and pick the unzipped folder. The demo video shows it on live sites.

ALETHEIA — "Trust the proof, not the profile"
Satya checks the site. Aletheia checks the person behind it. Instead of follower counts or badges, someone proves facts about themselves (over 18, nationality, credential not expired) from an issuer-signed credential using Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs. The verifier learns only "yes, this holds", never the date of birth, nationality or credential details. The proof is checked in the browser and again on-chain by a verifier contract on Sepolia.

projects.title: PaidX
projects.description: Tap-to-pay contactless crypto POS & AI agent payments with instant USDC settlement.
projects.project_description: PaidX is a non-custodial cryptocurrency point-of-sale (POS) protocol and agentic commerce network bridging physical retail counters, contactless NFC cards, and autonomous AI agents. In physical retail, PaidX allows customers to buy real-world goods—like a cup of chai—as easily as tapping a debit card. Customers tap a physical NFC card at an ESP32-powered countertop terminal or scan a dynamic QR code. Transactions settle in sub-second speed directly into native USDC on Base L2 and Ethereum Sepolia with zero gas headaches for the payer. Private keys never leave the customer's self-custodial wallet. Physical cards store zero keys and reference only salted cryptographic hashes, while ERC-4337 smart accounts and ERC-7715 session permissions enforce strict user-defined daily spending limits. Beyond physical retail, PaidX powers autonomous agentic commerce through a dedicated Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. External AI agents (Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT) can execute conversational payments on Hedera Testnet using the Hedera x402 exact payment scheme. Agent payments are governed by 2-of-3 MPC threshold signing, PostgreSQL row-level locked budget reservations, and immutable transaction audit logs published directly to the Hedera Consensus Service (HCS). The complete ecosystem includes a Next.js 15 customer and merchant console, virtual terminal keypad, hardware provisioning portal, on-chain merchant registry, and standalone ESP32 firmware.
projects.how_its_made: PaidX is built as an end-to-end decentralized point-of-sale protocol connecting physical retail, smart accounts, and AI agent commerce. On the hardware side, we created custom C++ firmware on an ESP32 microcontroller paired with a PN532 NFC reader and an ST7789 TFT display. The terminal reads contactless card UIDs, authenticates through a pre-shared hardware token, and sends a payment request to our Next.js 15 backend. To ensure non-custodial security without requiring customers to carry private keys, we implemented a cryptographic salting technique: the physical card UID is hashed using keccak256 with a secret salt before being recorded on our Solidity CardRegistry contract on Base L2 and Ethereum Sepolia. Using ERC-4337 smart accounts and ERC-7715 session permissions, our backend Session Relayer executes USDC settlements directly into verified merchant payout addresses up to the user's daily rolling allowance—enabling sub-second, zero-gas card taps at retail counters. For AI commerce, we built a standalone Model Context Protocol (MCP) server using Hono and Node.js. AI agents connect via Anthropic Streamable HTTP transport and execute payments on Hedera Testnet following the Hedera x402 exact payment scheme in HTS USDC. To solve concurrency and key management, we implemented PostgreSQL row-level locks (FOR UPDATE) for atomic budget reservations and a 2-of-3 MPC threshold signing architecture, logging every transaction immutably to the Hedera Consensus Service.

projects.title: session
projects.description: P2P battles win prompt credits inside your agentic session.
projects.project_description: Session is a multiplayer layer that lives inside a coding-agent session. Two people, on Cursor or Claude Code, leave their agents working on a prompt and use the wait to find each other and play. A prompt often runs for several minutes. User A might have about four minutes left and User B about three. During that overlap they battle in the editor: chess on one shared board, a game of flappy on the same course, or a puzzle that opens the moment the prompt is submitted. The person plays. The agent keeps writing code. Each session has an id and a display name. On the same Wi-Fi, sessions advertise themselves and show up as nearby. From anywhere else, a room code, a ping, or the prompt itself drops both players into one queue. The first prompt waits. The second prompt starts the round. Chess uses five-minute clocks. Flappy gives both players the same pipes. They fly on their own machines, and the higher score wins. Solo boards (sudoku, a crossword, KenKen, a maze, a mate) come from the games chosen in settings and rotate on every new prompt. The prize is tied to that prompt. A win or a solved board adds token credits, and those credits count only while the agent is still working. When the turn finishes, the cents become claimable. A claim pays them out as USDC, so the match can cover the prompt that was running beside it. Head-to-head games can also move a five-cent stake from the loser to the winner. Players can wear a name.session.eth subname, and the lobby of open challenges, room codes, and finished matches stays readable after the game.
projects.how_its_made: The repo is a pnpm workspace. packages/core is a TypeScript MCP server on stdio (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk). Cursor and Claude Code start it and call tools such as session_me, session_peers, session_ping, session_move, and session_poll. That process opens a WebSocket to one relay. The relay is Express plus ws, deployed on Railway at wss://sessionrelay-production.up.railway.app/ws. It is the authority for presence, room codes, pings, chess (FEN and clocks), flappy scores, and the USDC ledger. A 200ms sweep runs the clocks. Same-LAN discovery is separate: bonjour-service publishes a _session mDNS record whose TXT fields carry the session id, name, and host. Nearby is only a flag on the peer list. Every move still goes through the relay, which is what lets a Cursor window and a Claude Code window share one match. Cursor is two installs on that same socket. The agent plugin is a skill, a rule, and a stop hook: after a build step the agent polls, and if it is this session's chess turn it plays one UCI move and shows the unicode board from the tool reply. The editor UI is a VS Code webview extension (sidebar, board tab, credits), shipped as a .vsix and listed on Open VSX. Claude Code gets a real terminal pane on the same protocol. /session opens it. The person clicks pieces or flaps. The agent does not play. The hack that ties play to the prompt is a pair of files in ~/.session. A Cursor beforeSubmitPrompt hook writes agent-work.json with phase working and a generation counter, and writes puzzle-trigger.json with the next selected game. The extension watches those files, deals the board, and awards cents only while the phase is working. The stop hook marks the turn done, and the pending cents become claimable. The hook always prints {} and fails open, so a bad prefs file never blocks the prompt. Flappy is the other local trick. Physics run in the pane, frame by frame, using a mulberry32 stream seeded by the relay. Both machines generate the same pipes. Nothing is sent until the bird crashes, and the relay compares the two scores. USDC sits in SessionTreasury on Base mainnet (0xE2ca5C8ed8589Dc61abE1B2c2Dae309d2f86410c), written in Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry and called through viem. Deposits are plain USDC transfers. The relay credits each one once by scanning Transfer logs to the treasury over a rolling window of Base blocks and storing balances in a JSON bank. A claim is signed only by the relay's owner key. One cent of credit is 0.01 USDC, with a daily cap. On Base, sendReward is a direct transfer. For Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, and Polygon, the same function is a Chainlink CCIP 2.0 send whose receiver is the player's wallet, so there is no per-chain payout contract. The CCIP 2.0 extra-args are packed off-chain as a short blob (ExtraArgsV3: gas 0, finalized finality, empty verifier fields) and forwarded unchanged, so a Chainlink encoding change does not need a new treasury. forge test runs that blob through Chainlink's CCIP Local Simulator. An earlier wager path, SessionLock and SessionPayout, locks equal stakes on Base Sepolia and settles them on Ethereum Sepolia over CCIP. The opening coin-flip is Chainlink CRE plus VRF, so the relay is not the source of the random color. When two players pair, the relay spawns cre workflow simulate with the pair as an HTTP payload. The TypeScript workflow (@chainlink/cre-sdk) hashes both session ids, builds a report, and writeReports it to SessionMatchDraw on Base. That contract requests one VRF v2.5 word. An even word makes the player who waited white. The relay tails DrawFulfilled logs and applies the color. Names are a permissioned ENSv2-style registry: the subname owner is the only key that can edit the address and text records under session.eth. Arkiv stores the durable lobby. Challenges, rooms, and finished matches are wallet-owned entities filtered by kind, expiresAt, room code, and opponent, and the pane, the web lobby, and the board read those same entities. Live moves stay on the WebSocket, because a chess clock cannot wait on an entity write. The public site is Vite and React: a landing page for the extension, and a table view of who is in the room.

projects.title: Orryn
projects.description: Orryn helps teams find customer contracts still running old code and confirm when the fix works.
projects.project_description: orryn helps smart contract teams answer a practical question: which customer deployments still need a repair, and how can we tell when the repair actually worked? A supplier defines the affected deployments and the checks they expect to pass. orryn inspects each registered deployment, tests its behaviour, and explains what remains wrong. The customer keeps control of its contracts and must authorize any change. The project also includes a prototype for connecting verified repair results to supplier-funded grants.
projects.how_its_made: the web app uses next.js, react, and tailwind. the typescript backend uses fastify and postgres to manage wallet-authenticated verification jobs and their evidence. an isolated worker inspects the supported proxy and oracle-adapter setup, then runs behavioural tests in a local evm and signs the report. we use arc campaign contracts to manage funding, claims, challenges, and payouts. chainlink cre evaluates repair evidence, and ccip carries authenticated acceptance messages between the source-chain registry and the arc campaign. the customer’s wallet remains in control of contract repairs.

projects.title: Mivo
projects.description: MIVO uses a Raspberry Pi and camera to scan products, negotiate prices with AI, and pay using crypto
projects.project_description: MIVO is an AI-powered shopping assistant that finds products, negotiates better deals, and makes shopping effortless. Using AI agents, MIVO automates negotiations between buyers and merchants to reach mutually beneficial prices. With a Raspberry Pi-powered physical interface, users can initiate purchases that connect directly to the platform. MIVO combines 0G for decentralized AI, Arc for secure USDC payments, and 1inch for cryptocurrency swaps. From discovering products to negotiating prices and completing blockchain payments, MIVO brings everything together in one seamless experience. Our vision is simple: shopping should be something you ask for, not something you have to do!
projects.how_its_made:
We built MIVO by combining AI agents, IoT hardware, and Web3 into a unified shopping experience. Our Raspberry Pi acts as a physical interface, sending purchase requests to our Python-based backend through HTTPS APIs. The backend handles product discovery, buyer-to-merchant AI negotiations, and payment requests, while our web application provides an interactive interface for users.
We integrated 0G for decentralized AI inference and negotiation evidence storage, Arc Testnet for USDC payments, and 1inch for cryptocurrency swaps. MetaMask enables users to authorize transactions, while our backend independently verifies payments on-chain before confirming success. We used Neon PostgreSQL for data management and Vercel for deployment.
One of our biggest technical challenges was connecting a physical BUY signal to an AI-driven workflow and a real blockchain transaction. We designed the system so AI handles negotiation, users retain control over payments, and the blockchain provides verifiable settlement.

MetaMask enables users to authorize transactions, while our backend independently verifies payments on-chain before confirming success. We used Neon PostgreSQL for data management and Vercel for deployment.
One of our biggest technical challenges was connecting a physical BUY signal to an AI-driven workflow and a real blockchain transaction. We designed the system so AI handles negotiation, users retain control over payments, and the blockchain provides verifiable settlement.

projects.title: Baton
projects.description: Workers can fail. The entire job shouldn’t. Baton ensures one agent doesn't collapse the system.
projects.project_description: Imagine you're running a high-priority, high-responsibility job via a fleet of agents or agentic systems and an agent dies. Your job hits a standsill, context and progress remains ambigious and dependent on said agent's trustbase, and when real money is on the line, there is no quick verifiability protocol between claimed transactions and completed transactions. If only you had an infrastructure solution that could quickly hand over the rest of the incomplete job to the next available agent the moment your first agent dies, verifies and records all transactions on chain, encrypts and stores context on-chain (no sneaky work incase these servers shut temporarily!) and makes sure that just because an agent dies, your job doesn't have to. Presenting Baton. In one line, our tool helps long-running AI jobs survive worker failure. A buyer defines a job, milestones, and rewards; workers make progress and submit encrypted checkpoints containing manifests and artifacts. A checkpoint remains a candidate until the buyer accepts it (or assigns a contract that does so on their behalf), so an upload alone cannot replace the trusted recovery point or earn a reward. If a worker stops, an alternate worker is authorized for the job, is able to retrieve the accepted checkpoint, verify it, and continue from that state. BATON uses ENSv2’s job-scoped permissions to check worker authority and is building on Arkiv for encrypted, time-bounded checkpoint storage for quick queryability of centralised databases with the transparency of decentralized systems. The goal is to make recovery, ownership, and milestone payments inspectable instead of relying on one worker’s local files.
projects.how_its_made: BATON pairs a React, TypeScript, and Vite buyer console with a Node.js worker runtime and API, plus Solidity escrow contracts for milestones, accepted checkpoints, worker epochs, and payouts. EIP-712 signatures bind approvals and handoffs to the exact job state, while a SQLite ledger makes payment operations auditable and resilient to restarts. ENSv2’s Permissioned Resolver gives each job scoped worker permissions; Arkiv provides encrypted, queryable checkpoints with controlled lifetimes. The key design choice is that the escrow selects the canonical checkpoint: when a worker fails, its successor can verify that accepted state and carry the job forward while stale workers lose authority. Our most unconventional design choice was repurposing ENSv2’s hierarchical subregistry system as an agent authority tree, rather than simply using ENS for naming. Jobs become independent namespaces with scoped permissions for their workers and subagents, allowing authority to be delegated, revoked, and transferred as execution changes hands. We effectively turned ENS subregistries into a programmable coordination layer for autonomous agents, making the namespace hierarchy part of the protocol's security model rather than a decorative integration.

projects.title: Bell
projects.description: BELL pre-funds tokenized-stock liquidations before the closing bell, even if prices gap overnight.
projects.project_description: A stock can close on Friday and reopen much lower on Monday. If someone borrowed against that stock, the price can fall far enough to make the loan unsafe before a lender can sell the collateral. A price feed tells the lender what happened. BELL answers the next question: who has already committed cash to buy the shares? With BELL, a borrower can add optional cover to an existing loan during a window before market close. Buyers choose how many shares they will take, the price they will pay, and the premium they want. They lock USDC behind each offer. If the loan is healthy at the verified reopen, the buyer keeps the agreed premium and the committed cash is released. If the loan is unhealthy, the contracts use the reserved cash under the cover terms to repay debt and give the buyer a claim on the corresponding shares. The buyer can lose money if those shares are worth less than the agreed price.
projects.how_its_made: Chainlink CRE gives BELL’s contracts two facts they need together: what the stock traded at and which market session that price belongs to. A Friday price can support a loan or a cover offer. Settling that cover requires a separately verified reopening price. For the GoPro demo, we run the CRE workflow locally and broadcast its reports to Arc Testnet. The workflow reads BELL’s onchain asset configuration and session state, then fetches historical GoPro prices from Twelve Data and Yahoo Finance. It checks the ticker, currency, timestamp, and agreement between the two sources. We replay the historical observations on a compressed session clock so judges can follow the Friday-to-Tuesday gap in minutes. CRE submits distinct reports for the schedule, the borrowing and cover prices, the close, and the reopening benchmark. Each accepted report leaves an onchain record. BELL’s oracle emits a MarketEventAccepted event with the report type, sequence number, and report hash. We verify that event and the value stored by the oracle. That gives judges a way to trace a settlement back to the exact market observation that authorized it. Solidity contracts on Arc hold the test USDC and mock stock, reserve buyers’ funded offers, and calculate repayment and stock claims. We used Arc Studio to publish the React and TypeScript frontend and backend to Vercel. The backend indexes contract events and prepares transactions for each participant to sign in their own wallet.

projects.title: GPU Pool
projects.description: Pool everyday computers for AI inference, with human-verified credits and onchain payments.
projects.project_description: GPU Pool turns everyday computers into a shared AI inference network. People connect their machines into pools that distribute a model across available memory and compute, making it possible to serve models that a single participating machine cannot hold. Requesters access models through a chat interface or an OpenAI-compatible API. Contributors supply compute capacity and earn credits. World IDKit protects the starter-credit allocation: the backend verifies the result before granting credits, and a repeated verified nullifier cannot receive another starter grant. Arkiv provides discoverable listings of nodes, pools, and models. Hedera supports x402 payments, a public ledger of signed accounting events, and contract-based provider payouts. The website connects these services through account balances, network status, inference receipts, and payout views. The project explores a practical question: can people share the computers they already own while making access, contribution, and payment transparent? Blockchain payment demonstrations use testnet assets.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Hono gateway running on Node.js provides authentication, an OpenAI-compatible inference API, routing, credit accounting, and receipts. Shared Zod schemas define the interfaces between components, while SQLite transactions protect balance updates and prevent duplicate starter grants. Parallax supplies distributed inference across Apple Silicon and NVIDIA machines. We integrate it as a dependency, using launch scripts and runtime hooks for coordinated startup, telemetry, and layer reporting. One practical challenge was memory pressure on smaller Macs: reducing the KV-cache allocation helped stabilize distributed generation. World IDKit handles human verification. The gateway signs verification requests, validates results through World’s verification service, and associates normalized nullifiers with accounts. Its signing credentials remain on the server. Arkiv stores expiring discovery records, allowing routing to consider fresh pool and node information. Hedera provides HBAR payments through x402, asynchronous publication of signed ledger events through HCS, and Merkle-based provider claims through Solidity payout contracts. Automated tests cover identity outcomes, duplicate grants, accounting, and settlement behavior. Staging verification and full live-demo acceptance are documented separately from fixture-based tests.

projects.title: Lifeline
projects.description: Credit lines for AI agents backed by one verified human, so software can pay even when it's short
projects.project_description: Lifeline gives AI agents credit, backed by a real person. An agent can hold money, but it can't hold debt, because nobody can chase software for repayment. So one human, verified with World ID, takes on the credit line and authorizes their agents to spend on it. When an agent hits an x402 paywall, it pays from its own balance if it can. If it's short, Lifeline pays the seller and the human owes the price plus a 1% fee. Lines start at $0.50 and grow to $1 and then $2 as the human builds a repayment record, so a new borrower can only lose a small amount. Lifeline began at ETHGlobal Tokyo with credit on Arc and Sui. At Mumbai, we added: A real marketplace: agents can find and buy from 134 services that accept payment on Arc testnet. Deposit-backed credit: a $1 deposit adds $0.80 of credit, and if the human defaults, anyone can trigger that deposit to repay the debt. A lending pool: lenders fund loans and earn what borrowers pay. Cross-chain repayment: USDC on another chain can pay off Arc debt through Bridge Kit. Swap or borrow: before lending, Lifeline checks whether swapping the agent's other tokens on Uniswap would be cheaper, and the receipt says why it chose. Repay in any token: a human can repay from a wallet holding ETH, WETH or UNI, and agents can pay through a Uniswap Token Jar. USDT on Whitechain: an agent holding no WBT can buy, repay and pay for itself, because our relayer covers the gas.
projects.how_its_made: The app is Next.js and TypeScript, with Solidity contracts built and tested in Foundry. It also includes an MCP server, so agents like Claude Code can use their credit line directly. Arc: Nanopayments run through Circle Gateway using x402, and the Circle Discovery API supplies the marketplace. Arc Studio wrote, tested and audited the collateral vault and lending pool, then deployed them to Arc testnet. Its review found a real bug: a borrower could suspend their own profile to erase a default and block seizure. We fixed that by having the vault keep its own record of defaults. Bridge Kit handles cross-chain repayment, which we tested live from Base Sepolia. Deposits earn yield in an ERC-4626 Earn test vault. Uniswap: the Uniswap API prices swaps and builds the transactions, including Permit2 signing. We compare price impact, pool fees, gas and bridging against the cost of borrowing, then pick the cheaper option. We also integrated TJAR through Uniswap's real factory. Agents send tokens to the jar, and a keeper clears it for USDC when that's worth doing. We tested this on local forks using live API transactions, with no real money. Whitechain: we wrote our own x402 facilitator for USDT using EIP-3009. The relayer only spends gas after checking the merchant, payment size, signature and funds, and it has daily limits so it can't be drained. The credit facility is deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia, with real test USDT payments on the explorer. World: World ID proves each line belongs to one unique human, and session proofs handle sign-in after that. World ID for Agents adds a fresh human approval for held payments.

projects.title: RWAComply
projects.description: Onchain purchase limits shared across a person's wallets for tokenized asset markets.
projects.project_description: RWAComply is a platform prototype for controlling how much an individual can purchase in tokenized real-world asset markets. Instead of applying a limit to each wallet separately, it links multiple wallets to one pseudonymous investor allocation. An issuer defines a maximum USDC purchase amount for an offering. When an investor buys through the supported RWAComply purchase route, the smart contract checks their cumulative spending across linked wallets and rejects purchases that exceed the remaining limit. Each investor has a separate allocation. The project integrates World ID for proof of human, a wallet ownership signature, and onchain wallet registration. The allocation ledger tracks spending, while a Uniswap v4 hook and trusted executor enforce the limit during purchases. The current Sepolia deployment demonstrates the mechanism using mock USDC and RWA tokens. The broader multi-offering issuer marketplace is being developed and tested locally.
projects.how_its_made: RWAComply is built with Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4, Next.js, React, TypeScript, and viem. The smart contract layer consists of an AllocationLedger, a Uniswap v4 hook, and a trusted PoolExecutor. The ledger tracks cumulative USDC spending by pseudonymous allocation, while the hook checks the remaining budget before allowing a supported purchase. The executor is important because the hook needs to identify the actual trader even though the swap is initiated through a router. It passes the trader address through hook data, and the hook records the actual USDC spent from the swap's balance delta. This keeps the purchase check and spend recording within the same transaction. World ID is integrated through IDKit. The backend creates and signs verification requests, verifies returned proofs, maintains encrypted identity sessions, and issues EIP-712 wallet registration authorizations. Each linked wallet must separately prove ownership and register onchain. Arkiv, through its SDK on the Rabdi network, stores public offering metadata. The Ethereum ledger remains the source of truth for purchase caps and spending. The frontend uses Next.js API routes to connect these services without exposing signing keys to the browser. The core hook, ledger, and executor are deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and tested locally with Foundry and Anvil. The broader multi-offering marketplace contracts are currently tested locally, not deployed on Sepolia.

projects.title: safelyfy.gwei.limo
projects.description: Simple CROPS tool for upgrading your vault setup and inviting new memers with their devices to it.
projects.project_description: So, once someone at the family uses crypto and then wants to onboard more devieces or family members with their devices the process is quite tidious and not that many solutions are available for this. Safe wallet is one of the popular option but it's not new-user friendly at all. So we've built this very simple tool that is CROPS and helps new users safely add by now fixed, but in the future open-source variety of devices.
projects.how_its_made: This project uses local-first approach with no centralized servers as a compromise. It relies on anon-rpc for endpoint anonymization to ensure safety and privacy of the process. The project itself Is a wrapper around safe wallet creation process with different connectors that allow to easily add signing devices to a setup. There are no server and no intermediaries. At the same time ~57 signers can be added using Patricia Merkle Trie and hash in the URL that can be sent to a family memeber. After making an update family member sends the link back.

projects.title: AgentArena
projects.description: A social arena where AI agents trade on Base via Definitive Flash, and you copy the ones you trust.
projects.project_description:
Agent Arena is a social trading arena where AI agents trade real money on Base, and you choose who to follow. Every order goes through Definitive Flash advanced orders, every order has a stop loss, and every result is public and checkable onchain. THE PROBLEM
Copy trading and "AI trading bots" usually ask you to hand over your money and trust a black box. You can't see what the bot does, you can't limit it, and you rarely get proof of its results. WHAT AGENT ARENA DOES AI agents trade live: TrendHunter, DipBuyer and Contrarian Kaka read the onchain price every 15 seconds and place real orders on Base through Definitive Flash.
Build your own agent in a minute: pick a coin (WETH or cbBTC), a strategy (trend, dip, contrarian or "dip in an uptrend"), a take profit, a stop loss and a size. Test it on real onchain prices, with Flash's real costs, before it goes live. Your agent joins the leaderboard and anyone can copy it.
Watch, copy or invest: watch every trade on a live chart, copy an agent's trades, or invest so it trades every signal for you. You set your own size, daily cap and loss limit, and pause or stop any time. Large copies need a human approval.
Predict: vote on whether a trade will hit its target.
Auto-trade plans: pick a coin, a strategy, a budget, take profit and stop loss, and how long it runs, and it trades for you.
Trade from your own wallet: the app builds the Flash order and your wallet signs it (EIP-712). No key ever reaches the server.
FLASH ADVANCED ORDERS, END TO END
Market, limit, DCA (TWAP) and stop-buy entries, each with an attached take-profit and stop-loss bracket. Trailing stops, separate stop-loss and take-profit orders, a break-even stop that moves the bracket with a signed update, and one-tap "exit now" (signed cancel plus market sell). Order status streams over Flash's WebSocket, and live quotes come from Flash's quote stream. GASLESS AND SAFE BY DESIGN Sign in with any wallet using a free message. Add USDC with one free signature (EIP-3009). The arena's gas tank sends it, and Flash pays the gas of every order. You never need ETH.
Every user and agent trades from its own sub-wallet. Withdrawals can only go to your own address, and the API can never change it.
Never blind-signed: every Flash order is checked field by field before signing, approvals are capped, and a referee checks every trade first.
Risk rules on every automated trade:
stop loss within 5%;
a cost guard and a price check against the Uniswap v3 pool;
no new entries when the market swings too fast;
a pause after a losing streak;
a daily loss kill switch and a maximum hold time;
a circuit breaker on drawdown, an emergency stop, and a cap on total live spending.
TRANSPARENT AND SOCIAL
A risk-adjusted leaderboard (Arena Score = return minus half the biggest drop), a public feed of every decision saved with full history and search, share cards with link previews for X, Telegram and WhatsApp, and public signals by RSS, Discord and Telegram. An onchain proof page links every real order to its Flash order ID and its Base transactions on Basescan. REAL MONEY, NOT A MOCKUP
Tested with real money on Base mainnet: agent trades, a copied trade, a limit order whose bracket exit leg filled, and a gasless USDC deposit, all verifiable on Basescan. A paper mode uses real Flash quotes and real signing, with simulated fills, so anyone can try every flow safely. HOW IT'S BUILT
A Go backend using only the standard library, with hand-written EIP-712, secp256k1 signing and Base transaction encoding. It uses the Flash REST API and WebSocket, and reads prices and price history from the Uniswap v3 pool on Base. The frontend is an installable web app (PWA) with no framework, a strict security policy, no trackers, and support for MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet and other wallets. It is open source under the MIT licence. Agent Arena never promises profits: agents can lose, and that's exactly why every trade is limited, protected and public.
projects.how_its_made:
One Go binary (standard library only, no third-party Go modules) serves the API, runs the trading engine and serves an installable web app. The frontend is plain JavaScript modules and CSS, with no framework and no build step. Everything trades on Base mainnet through Definitive Flash. DEFINITIVE FLASH (the execution layer for every order) We use the Flash REST API for quotes, orders, order status with fills, single and batch cancel (EIP-191 signed messages), and bracket updates (a signed PATCH that moves the take profit and stop loss).
Two Flash WebSocket channels: "orders" for live status, and "quotes" for streaming prices, renewed about every 2 minutes.
Every advanced order type is wired up: market, limit, TWAP/DCA and stop entries with an attached take-profit and stop-loss bracket, plus standalone bracket, trailing-stop, stop-loss and take-profit orders.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Agent Arena is a social trading arena where AI agents trade real money on Base, and you choose who to follow. Every order goes through Definitive Flash advanced orders, every order has a stop loss, and every result is public and checkable onchain.

THE PROBLEM
Copy trading and "AI trading bots" usually ask you to hand over your money and trust a black box. You can't see what the bot does, you can't limit it, and you rarely get proof of its results.

WHAT AGENT ARENA DOES

AI agents trade live: TrendHunter, DipBuyer and Contrarian Kaka read the onchain price every 15 seconds and place real orders on Base through Definitive Flash.
Build your own agent in a minute: pick a coin (WETH or cbBTC), a strategy (trend, dip, contrarian or "dip in an uptrend"), a take profit, a stop loss and a size. Test it on real onchain prices, with Flash's real costs, before it goes live. Your agent joins the leaderboard and anyone can copy it.
Watch, copy or invest: watch every trade on a live chart, copy an agent's trades, or invest so it trades every signal for you. You set your own size, daily cap and loss limit, and pause or stop any time. Large copies need a human approval.
Predict: vote on whether a trade will hit its target.
Auto-trade plans: pick a coin, a strategy, a budget, take profit and stop loss, and how long it runs, and it trades for you.
Trade from your own wallet: the app builds the Flash order and your wallet signs it (EIP-712). No key ever reaches the server.
FLASH ADVANCED ORDERS, END TO END
Market, limit, DCA (TWAP) and stop-buy entries, each with an attached take-profit and stop-loss bracket. Trailing stops, separate stop-loss and take-profit orders, a break-even stop that moves the bracket with a signed update, and one-tap "exit now" (signed cancel plus market sell). Order status streams over Flash's WebSocket, and live quotes come from Flash's quote stream.

GASLESS AND SAFE BY DESIGN

Sign in with any wallet using a free message. Add USDC with one free signature (EIP-3009). The arena's gas tank sends it, and Flash pays the gas of every order. You never need ETH.
Every user and agent trades from its own sub-wallet. Withdrawals can only go to your own address, and the API can never change it.
Never blind-signed: every Flash order is checked field by field before signing, approvals are capped, and a referee checks every trade first.
Risk rules on every automated trade:
stop loss within 5%;
a cost guard and a price check against the Uniswap v3 pool;
no new entries when the market swings too fast;
a pause after a losing streak;
a daily loss kill switch and a maximum hold time;
a circuit breaker on drawdown, an emergency stop, and a cap on total live spending.
TRANSPARENT AND SOCIAL
A risk-adjusted leaderboard (Arena Score = return minus half the biggest drop), a public feed of every decision saved with full history and search, share cards with link previews for X, Telegram and WhatsApp, and public signals by RSS, Discord and Telegram. An onchain proof page links every real order to its Flash order ID and its Base transactions on Basescan.

REAL MONEY, NOT A MOCKUP
Tested with real money on Base mainnet: agent trades, a copied trade, a limit order whose bracket exit leg filled, and a gasless USDC deposit, all verifiable on Basescan. A paper mode uses real Flash quotes and real signing, with simulated fills, so anyone can try every flow safely.

HOW IT'S BUILT
A Go backend using only the standard library, with hand-written EIP-712, secp256k1 signing and Base transaction encoding. It uses the Flash REST API and WebSocket, and reads prices and price history from the Uniswap v3 pool on Base. The frontend is an installable web app (PWA) with no framework, a strict security policy, no trackers, and support for MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet and other wallets. It is open source under the MIT licence.

Agent Arena never promises profits: agents can lose, and that's exactly why every trade is limited, protected and public.

projects.title: Vigil
projects.description: News that expires in a week unless readers vote to keep it alive, built on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Vigil is a news app where every story has a lifespan. An editor posts a story with a one-week fuse. Readers watch it burn down and vote to keep it burning or let it fade. When voting closes with a day left, the count is frozen. If enough people took part and more than half chose keep, the story is renewed for another week. Otherwise it expires and disappears. Most news is read today and forgotten tomorrow, and the stories that matter most, like an unresolved water cut or a promised review that never happens, drop off the feed before anything is resolved. Vigil lets readers decide what stays visible, instead of an algorithm. A story survives only while people choose to keep it alive. An editor pulls candidates from live RSS feeds (starting with The Hindu's national feed) and posts them. Each story and each vote is a record on Arkiv, a Web3 database with built-in expiry, so a story's lifetime is a real property of the data, not a cron job on our server. Votes are public and anonymous: a vote stores only a choice and a salted hash, so anyone can recount the tally from Arkiv instead of trusting us. Status: the full loop works from RSS to Arkiv to voting to renewal or fade. World ID verification is simulated in this build (identity is a placeholder cookie). The vote path is built so a verified World ID nullifier can replace it.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4. The UI is a dark "night watch" design. Its signature element is a CSS "burn line", a fuse that shortens as a story runs out of time, with a tick marking where voting closes. Arkiv is our only database. Stories and votes are typed entities on the Rabdi testnet, written with @arkiv-network/sdk 1.0 and viem. Schemas use indexed columns for the fields we filter on, and a JSON bytes column for headline and summary, because string columns are capped at 128 bytes. Stories use the readonly flag and a 7-day expiration. We deliberately left permissionless extension off, since it would let anyone override the vote. Reads are scoped by $creator so only our editor and relayer wallets are trusted, because anyone can write entities under our schema name. Tallies use filtered count queries, and the keeper renews passing stories with extendEntity. Arkiv gave us expiry, queries and tamper-evidence with no backend database. Working: RSS inbox: a small standard-library RSS parser (no dependency) that handles CDATA and entities, and skips items missing a title, description, category, link or date. Editor page: a key-protected "Post to Vigil" route writes the story entity. Vote relayer: a separate wallet writes one readonly vote entity per voter per round, so readers need no wallet or gas. The voter id is a salted hash of identity, story and round, so votes can't be linked across stories or rounds. Keeper: a route plus a small Node loop script. After voting closes it reads the tally, applies the same rule function the UI uses, and extends the story if it passes. Arkiv emits no expiry event, so it polls. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Rounds without extra entities: each vote carries the story's expiry block as its round id. Extending a story changes that block, so a renewal starts a fresh empty round with no extra write. Rabdi write reliability: following Arkiv's own guidance, every write sets an explicit nonce read at "latest", plus gasPrice and gas. A per-wallet queue serializes writes so nonces never collide. Round length and quorum are environment variables, so a week-long vote can be demoed in about 10 minutes.

projects.title: Esperanto
projects.description: A Monero-to-Ethereum bridge using ERC-7984, helping users keep their balances private across chains.
projects.project_description:
Esperanto is a privacy-focused bridge designed to connect Monero with Ethereum through cwXMR, a confidential wrapped representation of XMR. The goal is to let users move between Monero’s private payment network and Ethereum’s programmable ecosystem while keeping their token balances and transfer amounts encrypted.
Users deposit XMR into a bridge vault to receive cwXMR on Ethereum. To move back, they redeem cwXMR and provide an encrypted Monero destination address.
The bridge is designed around independently operated vaults, with hardware attestation checking the software behind each mint. The current prototype targets Monero stagenet and Ethereum Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: The protocol has a TEE-based vault running on a Nitro enclave with on-chain attestation using Automata's Nitro attestation verifier contract (through an adapter). It allows multiple parties to run the service on their own, distributing the trust, as each instance will have its own vault on Monero and have minting rights to the contract. It uses Succinct’s SP1 to prove verification of AWS Nitro attestations, then verify those proofs on Ethereum through Automata. The bridge checks that each mint is bound to a fresh attestation from an enclave running approved vault software. I used Zama's FHE tooling and OpenZeppelin's ERC-7984 confidential tokens for the wrapped XMR token on Ethereum to make the balances stay private. Using Nym for communication between the browser and the service, and also for RPC calls from the service.

projects.title: Bull Street
projects.description: Tokenising Real Stocks. 24*7 & Cross Border Trades. Every trader can mint new tokens & arbitrage.
projects.project_description: Stock markets are only open a few hours a day. India's NSE is closed about 81% of the week, and if you live outside India, buying Indian stocks is hard: you need a local broker, paperwork, and you can only trade during their hours. Tokenized stocks help with this. A tokenized stock is a token on a blockchain that is backed by a real share, so it can trade at any hour and anyone with a wallet can buy it. But today only the issuing company can create new tokens, usually only while the stock market is open. So on weekends, when people want to buy, the token price drifts away from the real stock price. When the market opens again, the issuer mints new tokens, sells them into that gap and keeps the profit. On one weekend in August 2026 the Hims & Hers token traded at more than double the stock price. Bull Street lets every shareholder mint, not just one company. You pledge shares from your own demat account to a bonded broker. The broker confirms the pledge on-chain, and you can mint one token for each pledged share at any time of day, even on a Sunday. Your shares never leave your account. If the token trades above the stock, any shareholder can mint and sell, so the profit is shared by many people and the price stays close to the real one. Tokens trade peer to peer on an on-chain order book, settled in USDC. Anyone holding a token can redeem it for USDC: the broker sells the pledged shares when NSE next opens and pays out at that session's closing price. If a broker misses the deadline, their bond pays the holder 105%. To stop one person from playing both sides of a pledge, every minter and broker verifies with World ID, and one human can only hold one role. We are starting with Indian stocks (Reliance, TCS and Infosys on testnet) and plan to add other markets next. Everything runs on Arc testnet. There is no public API for pledging shares at CDSL (India's depository), so on testnet our API plays the depository's part.
projects.how_its_made: Smart contracts. 14 Solidity contracts, built and tested with Foundry (54 unit, scenario and invariant tests). The main ones: PledgeRegistry: pledges and minting. BrokerRegistry and BondVault: broker bonds. LevelBook and BullStreetExchange: the on-chain order book. One order can fill across several price levels in one transaction. RedemptionEngine: assigns each redemption to a pledge and enforces the deadlines. PriceOracle: NSE closing prices, signed by 2 of 3 signers. SessionClock: the NSE trading calendar. RoleRegistry: World ID roles. Arc. Everything is deployed on Arc testnet. USDC is the gas token on Arc, so a user only ever needs USDC: they pay fees, trade, post broker bonds and receive redemptions all in USDC. Since there is no second token to explain, the app is much simpler for people who are new to crypto. World ID. We use IDKit 4. The app asks the user to verify. Our API checks the proof with World's verify API, then signs a short EIP-712 attestation. The RoleRegistry contract checks that attestation on-chain and stores the person's nullifier with their role. Because of that, the same human can't register as both a minter and a broker, even from a second wallet. This is what keeps every pledge's two sides independent. Circle. Circle Modular Wallets give users passkey sign-in, so they don't need a seed phrase or a browser extension. Backend. Written in TypeScript: A Hono API that verifies World ID, stands in for the CDSL depository, finds a broker with free capacity for each pledge, and serves a cached snapshot of contract state. Workers: an oracle that fetches NSE closes from Yahoo Finance and Twelve Data and posts them signed; an indexer that writes events to SQLite; broker agents that confirm pledges and settle redemptions; a keeper that runs upkeep jobs. Frontend. Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, wagmi and viem. Hacky bits. Compressed calendar. Real NSE sessions are a day apart, so the testnet deployment uses a compressed calendar where each session lasts minutes. That lets you see a full pledge → mint → trade → redeem cycle in one sitting. RPC retries. The public Arc RPC rate-limits, so we spread reads across several RPC endpoints with viem's fallback transport. We also wrap transaction sends in our own retry, because viem never retries eth_sendRawTransaction.

projects.title: Pata
projects.description: Your door, shared only by consent: expiring, revocable ENS grants to your exact address
projects.project_description: Pata (पता, Hindi for "address") turns a home address into a permission you grant, not text you hand out. In India, couriers call to ask the way, and an address shared once with a shop stays with that shop, its couriers and its database forever. About 26% of cash-on-delivery orders are returned to the seller, and wrong or incomplete addresses are a main cause. With Pata, a household owns a permanent name such as calm-cloud.pata.eth on ENSv2. Anyone who looks it up, including in ENS's own app, sees only the area and PIN code, for example "Bandra Kurla Complex, 400051". The exact door is stored only encrypted: the map pin, its 4m x 4m DIGIPIN code, the room number, the written address, and directions in Hindi, Marathi and English that the phone reads aloud. When a shop or courier needs the door, the household approves a grant for that one requester, for a set time, and it can be stopped early. The grant is a random ENS subname with an expiry on chain. The courier gets a link that opens the door only while the grant is live. When the time runs out, the link shows only the area again, even if the household's phone is off, and nobody has to send a transaction. The household's "Who can find my door" screen shows each live link with a countdown and a Stop button. History lists every link it shared and how each one ended: "Ended on its own" or "Stopped by you". Requesters are named too. A shop gets its own Pata name with ENSIP-26 records saying who it is and where links go. The consent screen reads those records before the household approves, and it hands the link only to the page that name publishes. Later, the shop can prove it holds consent by signing a challenge with the grant's key, which anyone can check against ENS without seeing the address. That gives sellers proof of consent, which India's DPDP Act requires companies to be able to show. No server of ours can read an address. Once a link exists, the courier's page needs only ENS and Arkiv, read through the Anon-RPC mixnet.
projects.how_its_made: Pata is a Next.js 16 TypeScript PWA, exported as static files and served from Cloudflare, plus one small Cloudflare Worker. Everything runs in the phone's browser, and the household never needs a wallet. ENSv2 (Sepolia): we registered pata.eth and deployed its own UserRegistry through ENS's VerifiableFactory, then emancipated it and locked its subregistry pointer, so we can't take names back. Each household's phone deploys its own Permissioned Resolver (holding only the public area and PIN code) and its own grant registry from the same factory. The Worker then registers the name with no expiry. A grant is a random 8-character label in the household's grant registry, with an absolute expiry, owned by an address derived from a fresh session key. The courier page reads liveness from that registry, so expiry needs no transaction, and "Stop access" is an unregister. Role bitmaps (Enhanced Access Control) limit who can do what. Requester names carry ENSIP-26 agent-context and agent-endpoint[web] records, written when their resolver is deployed. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet, @arkiv-network/sdk): every exact record is an entity owned by the household's key, holding only AES-GCM ciphertext. The home record is sealed to the household key. Each grant is one entity, with a payload sealed to the session key and an index sealed to the household key, and it expires when the grant ends. Approving writes the grant and its read-only history entry in one batch. Owner-filtered queries build the live-access list and the history. Anon-RPC: every read the app makes goes through one @anon-rpc/browser-harness Nox worker, on both chains, on the household's phone and the courier's. Every page starts the worker when it opens. A failed read is retried through Nox, never directly, and a write is never re-sent. Writes still go direct for now; the README lists every exception. Address AI: the household taps "Use my current location" or types a nearby landmark, then types how to find the door. The area and PIN code are suggested from a table bundled in the app, so the location never leaves the phone. Claude Sonnet 5.5, called from the Worker, picks landmark pins only from real OpenStreetMap features (Nominatim and Overpass) and writes the directions in three languages. The room number never goes to the model. DIGIPIN encoding (India Post's open code), pin distances and expiry times come from plain, tested code; the model only proposes. The phone's own speech engine reads the directions aloud. The Worker holds the API keys, checks household signatures, and enforces a daily spend cap and a kill switch. It funds new households with Sepolia ETH and Arkiv tGLM, so nobody needs a wallet. It never logs the bodies of address requests. Notable hacks: The courier link carries its keys after "#", which browsers never send to a server, and the page clears it from the address bar at once. The link reaches a shop the same way: we open the page its ENS name lists, with the link after "#", instead of POSTing a key to anyone. The grant's owner key is derived from the link's session key, so the link is the only credential. Whoever holds it can prove it by signing a challenge, checked against the registry. A stop that's cut off halfway is checkpointed on the device and finishes on the next visit. Our 20-second stage grant needed a latency margin: one test grant had only 8 seconds left by the time it was mined. Frontend: MapLibre with OpenStreetMap data, plus a custom intro, a loader that morphs into a location pin, and page transitions, all of which respect reduced motion. Tested with nearly 600 Vitest unit tests, Foundry, and Playwright on phone and desktop. Code was written with Claude Code and Codex; the README says which parts.

projects.title: FrameShrink
projects.description: Shrink failing Ethereum frame transactions into smaller, reproducible tests.
projects.project_description: FrameShrink is a CLI debugger for Ethereum’s experimental EIP-8141 frame transactions. It helps developers answer: “What is the smallest example that still produces this failure?” The guided terminal flow lets users create or select a test wallet, request faucet funds, choose supported failures, and submit a test transaction to the public alt-mempool devnet. FrameShrink captures the rejection, reproduces it locally, and tries removing unnecessary frames and inputs. It keeps an edit only when the smaller transaction preserves the original failure fingerprint. Developers can inspect transaction previews and changes in their configured editor, export a reproducible regression test, and confirm submission of a corrected transaction to the devnet. The current version supports five controlled failures: application reverts, forbidden validation state writes, TIMESTAMP, NUMBER, and undeployed-account code access. Existing explorer links can also be inspected, although replay depends on having the required state and setup.
projects.how_its_made: FrameShrink is built with TypeScript and Node.js, packaged as an npm CLI. Inquirer powers the interactive terminal flow, viem handles Ethereum encoding, signing and RPC calls, and Zod validates transaction recipes and captured evidence. Execution runs through an existing EIP-8141-compatible Ethrex client in Docker, alongside the alt-mempool sidecar’s admission-policy checks. Ethrex provides execution evidence, while the sidecar identifies policy violations. FrameShrink adds the capture, reduction, comparison and regression-export workflow around those components. We built controlled Solidity fixtures that trigger specific failures. Each reduction candidate is rebuilt and signed again using development accounts, then evaluated against consistent local state. A structured fingerprint prevents the reducer from accepting an unrelated failure, such as a broken signature. A notable challenge was debugging combined failures: the first rejection can hide later ones. FrameShrink works through the selected failures in stages and verifies a passing control afterward.
