## Appendix A: Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `T`, `treeHash` | The VTREE sentence and its keccak hash |
| `S = derive(T)`, `specHash` | The VSPEC guarantees and their hash |
| `D_owner` | The owners' EIP-712 digest (§4.4) |
| `D_snapshot` | The attestors' EIP-712 digest over the snapshot root |
| `txCommit` | Commitment to every transaction field except frame 1's data |
| `path` | 1 stateless, 2 paymaster, 3 ERC-4337 |
| `consumed[·]` | Replay set, keyed by `D_owner` |

## Appendix B: Design decisions

| # | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | One snapshot trust model, two delivery paths, routed by gas | Stateless by default; the alt mempool for heavy renders |
| D2 | Explicit-digest owner signatures; every verifier rebuilds `D_owner` from its own render | Binds the render to the signature without `ecrecover` |
| D3 | `txCommit` blanks only frame 1 | Every verifier computes the same commitment; no padding or replay |
| D4 | Canonical expiry frame, device clock, TTL cap | A host-chosen block number proves nothing |
| D5 | No global epoch; per-call descHash | No mass invalidation |
| D6 | Revocation keyed by leaf hash, checked at execution, liveness-only | Immediate, with no effect on the mempool |
| D7 | Unattested targets are refused | The host controls any "effects-only" list, so that mode is unsound |
| D8 | TOKEN proofs are mandatory; flagged tokens are refused | Risk metadata can't be omitted silently |
| D9 | No standing approvals | The guarantees hold over time |
| D10 | No delegatecall, upgrade or 7702; ERC-1271 off | Removes the takeover class |
| D11 | Fee charged first; per-nonce tickets | Multiple pending transactions per sender |
| D23 | `consumed[D_owner]` | Replay protection that doesn't depend on keyed-nonce semantics |
| D24 | ENSv2 records govern attestors and revocations, checked at execution | ENS as the trust root, with no validation reads |
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Verbatim is a smart account where owners never sign calldata. They sign a hash of the sentence they read. Before admitting the transaction, the chain re-renders that sentence from the real calldata, and after the calls it enforces every promise the sentence made.

**Core: EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alt mempool.** A VERIFY frame reads the SENDER frame's calldata through the new introspection opcodes (FRAMEDATALOAD, FRAMEPARAM, SIGPARAM). It runs our on-chain renderer (DisplayVM), rebuilds the owners' EIP-712 digest from its own render, and APPROVEs only if every owner signature matches. Owner and attestor signatures are EIP-8141 explicit-digest entries, so the protocol verifies them before any frame runs. We never call ecrecover, which matters because the reference sidecar has no precompiles.

There are two paths:
- **Stateless:** Merkle proofs and attestor-signed snapshots ride inside the tx, so it needs no stake and reads no global state.
- **Paymaster:** a staked RendererPaymaster renders from its own cached snapshot. The canonical rules refuse that storage read, and ERC-8421 admits it.

Rotating the snapshot invalidated 50 of 50 pending transactions on the paymaster path and 0 of 50 on the stateless path. Everything fits the sidecar's 100k validation cap (85k transfer, 91k v4 swap). We also run an ERC-4337 version on Sepolia (Pimlico, Alchemy).

**Uniswap:** URRender, an on-chain decoder for Universal Router commands and v4 actions. It reads hook risk from the hook's address bits (afterSwapReturnsDelta → "HOOK CAN TAKE YOUR OUTPUT"), and refuses no-minimum swaps through such hooks. We tested it against Uniswap's official Sepolia contracts. We also rebuilt Uniswap's real web interface with a malicious build step: it quoted 26.19 USDC, an ordinary wallet got 0.026, and Verbatim refused the same bytes.

**ENSv2 is the trust root:**
- attestor sets and revocations live in ENS records;
- descriptor publishers must pass an exclusivity proof on their PermissionedResolver: one scoped setter, no root roles, locked resolver;
- recipient names are re-resolved forward and in reverse at execution.

**Stack:**
- Solidity 0.8.28 (via-IR) with Foundry, 191 tests including invariants and an attack matrix;
- TypeScript (viem): a renderer twin, an ERC-7730 descriptor compiler that compiles 1,898 of 3,035 registry functions, the snapshot builder, and an offline signer that is one HTML file;
- React + Vite on Vercel, Express on Render.

**Hacky bits:**
- **APPROVE without DELEGATECALL.** Solidity can't emit APPROVE (0xaa), and the account bans DELEGATECALL. We compile `log1(0,0,scope)`, which has the same stack shape, and our deploy tool patches that single byte from 0xa1 to 0xaa after checking there's exactly one LOG1.
- **One STATICCALL for frame data.** A Yul FrameReader returns the whole frame layout in a single STATICCALL, which helped bring the prefix from 109k down to 85k.
- **Real Uniswap code on the devnet.** We replayed mainnet bytecode for PoolManager, Universal Router and Permit2 onto the frames devnet.
- **Mined hook address.** SkimHook's address was mined to carry the exact permission bits.
- **Byte-for-byte fuzzing.** A differential fuzzer runs 10,000 cases per CI run to keep the Solidity and TypeScript renderers identical.
- **Rule findings.** We probed the sidecar's real limits (exactly 100,000 gas admitted, 100,001 refused) and turned what we found into four ERC-8421 rule findings and two ERC drafts.

projects.title: Sangam
projects.description: AI agents pay Indian merchants in USDC; Sangam verifies it on-chain and pays them rupees over UPI.
projects.project_description: AI agents hold crypto; Indian shops need rupees. Sangam bridges them. A merchant proves who they are with Self (zero-knowledge KYC) and gets an ENS name holding its price, payout address and UPI ID. A buyer's agent finds the shop by that name and pays USDC, over x402 on Hedera or from the buyer's own MetaMask within a spending cap they set. Before paying, the agent checks the invoice against ENS, so a hacked checkout can't overcharge. Sangam then verifies the payment on-chain, 0G decides whether to pay out or hold and refund, the merchant gets INR on UPI through Cashfree, and a hash-chained receipt is written to Hedera Consensus Service for anyone to audit.
projects.how_its_made: Sangam is built as a TypeScript monorepo: one Next.js 16 app (apps/web) plays every role — the merchant's x402 paywall, the settlement pipeline, the dashboards and the identity desk — with small packages for each integration (hedera, ens, og, ondc, mcp). Payment (x402 + Hedera): The merchant API serves HTTP 402 challenges with the @x402/* SDK (Hedera exact scheme, Blocky402 facilitator). The buyer agent reads the challenge, signs a USDC transfer with @hiero-ledger/sdk, and retries — no approvals, no deposit flow. Settlement pipeline: Every payment is confirmed against the Hedera Mirror Node (with retries for lag), then 0G Compute (@0gfoundation/0g-compute-ts-sdk) makes the payout-vs-hold decision. On hold — underpayment, or an ONDC order the seller never accepted — the USDC refund is a Hedera ScheduleCreateTransaction with no admin key: once created, nobody, including Sangam, can change or cancel it. On payout, RazorpayX pays the merchant INR over UPI. Tamper-evident receipts: Each HCS receipt carries prev — the sequence number and sha256 of the receipt before it. The dashboard replays the topic from the Mirror Node, not our own files, and checks every link: drop or reorder one receipt and the chain breaks visibly. Discovery & identity: Merchants are onboarded onto ENSv2 (Sepolia) — Sangam issues <label>.sangam.eth subnames, and each product gets its own subname holding its price and payout accounts; the storefront is rebuilt from ENS alone, so the chain is the database. The agent cross-checks every invoice against ENS before signing (shop verified, payouts match, bill ≤ ENS price). Identity uses the Self offchain SDK: a zero-knowledge proof from the Aadhaar QR or passport; our backend learns only the disclosed fields, and stores just the proof's nullifier.

projects.title: Confluence
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook whose pool depth comes from a maker's 1inch Aqua strategy, not locked liquidity.
projects.project_description:
A new token's Uniswap pool starts thin. To increase its depth, a market maker normally has to lock inventory inside that one pool, where it can't serve anything else.
Confluence is a Uniswap v4 hook that gets its depth from a maker's 1inch Aqua strategy instead. The maker's tokens stay in their own wallet and move only at the moment of a fill. On each swap, the hook buys part of the trade from the maker's Aqua strategy through 1inch's deployed SwapVM router, and the pool's own curve (x.y = k) fills the rest, all in the same transaction.
The maker's strategy includes a price band: an Extruction module we wrote refuses any fill more than 2% from the pool's live price, so the maker is never filled at a stale price. And Aqua can never break a swap: if the Aqua leg fails for any reason, it is undone and the pool fills the whole trade.

projects.title: Styx
projects.description: A vault on Arc where an AI agent can't raise its own limit or approve its own payments
projects.project_description: A recent study (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35835 , https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/11/01/ai-agents-bypassed-crypto-spending-limits-without-human-approval-researchers-find-in-a-new-test) found that AI agents with wallets often raise their own spending cap, for example by reading the approval code that was emailed to the owner. The limit and the approval were both somewhere the agent could reach. Styx moves them into the contract. You fund a vault on Arc, choose who can be paid and how much, and give your agent a key that can only spend inside those rules. It can't change them. If it needs to go over, you sign that exact payment in your own wallet, and the contract checks your signature before any money moves. Later, a reviewer can open one encrypted record and check it against the chain. We built it around supplier invoices, but it works for any payment an agent makes.
projects.how_its_made: The core is one Solidity contract, written with Foundry and deployed to Arc testnet from Arc Studio. The owner and the token are fixed at deploy. Each agent has its own policy (per-payment limit, daily limit, expiry, on or off), and a vault-wide daily limit sits on top of all of them. Every single payment carries the policy version and recipient version it was approved under, so changing a rule makes older requests invalid. Approvers are extra wallets the owner can allow to sign. The agent talks to a Python MCP server with tools like proposing a payment, submitting it, checking status, asking for approval, checking the approval. When a payment is over the limit the tools hand back "exception required" instead of sending anything. The server calls a Rust cli tool, and that tool is the only thing holding the agent's key. The research behind it: arxiv.org/abs/2610.35835, the CoinDesk write-up from 1 November 2026, and the Devcon 8 talk at cfp.devcon.org/devcon8/talk/HGQQNC. For the reviewer we wrote a Rust tool that opens a sealed record and checks it against chain data, using selective disclosure. In partner tech, Arc helped because USDC is the gas token there and it also has a normal ERC-20 interface. Arc Studio is where we wrote and deployed the vault, and the link to that workspace is in our submission. Arkiv stores the sealed record. We publish only the ciphertext to its Rabdi testnet, and a reviewer can fetch it with none of our servers running.

projects.title: Reputed
projects.description: Human-backed reputation for AI agents on Hedera. One World ID human, one creator record, no resets.
projects.project_description: Reputed ties every AI agent's reputation to a unique human who has been verified with World ID. AI agents can be spun up for free, so a bad one can disappear and come back under a new wallet. That makes agent reputation easy to game. With Reputed, a creator proves they are a unique human through World ID. The CreatorRegistry contract maps that World ID nullifier to exactly one wallet. There is no update or removal path, so a person can't start over with a new creator record. Agents register in the ERC-8004 Identity Registry on Hedera. Each one is linked to its verified creator and receives a non-transferable, frozen "Human-backed" credential NFT (HTS). Other users and agents leave reviews in the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry. A review only counts if the reviewer can prove they paid the agent. Review weight depends on the reviewer's own creator score. Each creator gets one vote per agent, and older reviews decay with a 90-day half-life. Misconduct is confirmed when two distinct creators report it. A confirmed incident lowers the agent's score and its creator's score too, so creators are accountable for what their agents do. Scores are published as reproducible snapshots on Hedera Consensus Service. The project includes: A web app with an agent explorer, creator pages, World ID verification, a review modal and an API key dashboard. An SDK with a counterparty gate, verifyCounterparty, that lets an agent check whether the other party is human-backed and reputable before it transacts. An MCP server for the same checks. @reputed/agent-kit, which onboards a Hedera Agent Kit agent with a single API key.
projects.how_its_made:
Monorepo. A pnpm and Turborepo workspace in TypeScript, with these packages: apps/web: a Next.js app.
apps/server: a Fastify server.
packages/contracts: Solidity contracts built with Foundry.
packages/shared: shared types, ABIs and helpers.
packages/sdk: the SDK and the MCP server.
packages/agent-kit: the Agent Kit integration.
Hedera. ERC-8004: We used the already-deployed ERC-8004 Identity and Reputation registries on Hedera testnet instead of writing our own. This makes Reputed interoperable with any ERC-8004 agent.
HTS: Our CreatorRegistry calls the Hedera Token Service system contract at 0x167. It mints, transfers and freezes the credential NFT in one atomic call. If any step fails, the whole call reverts, so a transferable credential can never exist. The collection has no admin key.
HCS: It stores signed review files and score snapshots.
Mirror Node: We read from the Mirror Node rather than the JSON-RPC relay. The relay's error responses lack CORS headers and it returns 400/502 while transactions settle. We confirm transaction outcomes through the Mirror Node.
World ID. The server signs the request and binds the proof's signal to the user's wallet.
Before calling World, it checks the action, the protocol version, the Orb credential and the nullifier range, plus an EIP-191 wallet signature.
Registering the nullifier on-chain is what enforces one human, one creator.
Retries are classified as resend (same proof) or restart (new scan), so a user doesn't burn their single verification on a network error.
Headless agent onboarding. The creator's browser generates an API key (rpk_test_…) and derives a signing key from it. Only the derived address goes on-chain, so the server never sees the key.
An agent uses that key to sign an EIP-712 LinkGrant and links itself to its creator. The agent's own account pays for the transaction.
The flow is crash-safe and idempotent. The chain is the source of truth, the local state file is only a hint, and an agent is never registered twice.
Indexer and scorer. A Mirror Node indexer stores events in append-only SQLite.
The scorer solves the circular dependency between creator scores and agent scores with a bounded fixed-point iteration. Published creator and agent scores are always consistent with each other.
Human-backed status is replayed from events, so each review is judged at its own consensus time.
Snapshots are hashed over canonical JSON, so anyone can reproduce them.
Notable hacks. isHumanBacked fails closed. Every call re-reads the ERC-8004 owner and wallet inside try/catch, because the registry doesn't notify our contract when they change.
Payment proof uses net flow, and each payment can back only one review.
Transaction IDs are normalized across three formats so one transaction can't be cited twice.
The web app never auto-resends a transaction whose outcome is unknown. It searches Hedera first.

projects.title: Clave
projects.description: A k-of-n multisig for Aztec where no single member can spend from or see inside the vault.
projects.project_description: Clave is a k-of-n multisig built for Aztec: shared custody that works with Aztec's private state. On Aztec an account has two kinds of authority. Spending is defined by the account contract through native account abstraction: its entrypoint decides which signatures authorize a transaction. Reading is defined by keys: incoming notes are encrypted to the account's address, and whoever holds the incoming viewing secret can decrypt them in their PXE. A multisig has to control both. Sharing the viewing secret among members means any member, including one you later remove, can read the treasury forever. Clave splits both kinds of authority across the members: Spending (k of n). The vault is a custom Aztec account contract, ClaveVault. Its private entrypoint accepts a transaction only when the auth witness carries valid Schnorr signatures from k registered members over the transaction's outer hash. The signer set and thresholds live in private notes, and the check runs inside the client-side proof, so the network never learns who the members are or how many signed. Viewing (t of n). The vault's viewing key is created by a distributed key generation between the members' keepers, and the result is the account's Ivpk, so the vault has an ordinary Aztec address. No one ever holds the secret. When a member's PXE syncs a note, its patched key store asks the keepers for threshold ECDH. Any t of them return address_secret × P computed from their own shares, each with a proof, which is exactly what Aztec's own key store would have computed. The note decrypts normally. The flow: members found a vault together (key generation, address derivation, deployment, on-chain config check). A member proposes a transaction. Each member's PXE rebuilds and simulates it independently before signing the approval message. Once k approvals are gathered peer to peer, any member builds the auth witness, proves locally and sends it, with fees paid through Aztec's sponsored fee payment contract. Removing a member reshares the viewing key in the same governance transaction that updates the signer set, so the removed member cannot read new notes and the vault keeps its address.
projects.how_its_made: Account contract (Aztec.nr v6, Noir). ClaveVault implements the account entrypoint and verify_private_authwit. The PXE serves a 49-field auth witness for the transaction's outer hash: up to eight signer keys, eight Schnorr signatures, and a deadline. The entrypoint checks that the keys hash to the signer-set commitment in the private config note, checks every slot (empty slots against the generator, so every vault size has one circuit shape), and requires at least k valid signatures over Poseidon2("clave.approval.v0", [vault, outer hash, config version, expires_at]). The config note is read without being nullified, so authorization also works in static authwit checks from other contracts. Config notes use constrained delivery so no member can be left without them. Config changes such as rotate_membership are #[only_self] and bump the config version, which voids old approvals. The entrypoint costs 27,176 gates. Threshold viewing (Rust, clave-crypto). Grumpkin arithmetic and a Feldman DKG with Schnorr proofs of knowledge. Each keeper holds a share of the address secret, including Aztec's preaddress offset and negation rule, so the shares combine to exactly the secret Aztec derives. For each note's ephemeral key P, a keeper returns share × P with a Chaum-Pedersen DLEQ proof, and the PXE combines t valid answers with Lagrange coefficients. Resharing moves the same secret to a new committee when members change. Point encoding, address derivation, the ECDH-to-AES step and tag derivation are checked byte for byte by golden tests against real Aztec 6.0.0 output. PXE integration (TypeScript). A minimal, marked patch to @aztec-labs/pxe swaps the key store: where Aztec would load the account's incoming viewing secret, it batches the ECDH requests to the keepers instead. A stock key store behaves exactly as before. The vault-wallet package registers the vault account, encodes the auth witness and drives proving. The Rust crypto reaches TypeScript through napi-rs bindings. Keepers and network (Rust). clave-keeper holds the sealed viewing share, runs the DKG and resharing ceremonies, answers decryption requests, and replicates signed proposals, approvals and receipts over a libp2p mesh (QUIC and TCP with Noise). The optional clave-relay gives circuit relay and sealed mailboxes for offline members and only ever sees ciphertext. Member tooling. claved is a per-member daemon that hosts the PXE, a passphrase-sealed signer (Argon2id with ChaCha20-Poly1305, optional Touch ID) and the proposal workflow. The Rust clave CLI drives it: found a vault, propose, review the rebuilt transaction, approve or reject, and execute.

projects.title: Dusk
projects.description: Unused 0G AI credits burn at midnight UTC. Dusk sells them as verifiable inference to anyone.
projects.project_description:
Dusk is a spot market for AI inference that would otherwise be wasted
Holders of 0G’s Infinite AI (iAI) receive compute credits every day. The credits reset at 00:00 UTC and nothing carries over, so whatever isn’t used is wasted. Dusk turns that waste into a market. A holder runs a worker, lists the models it can serve and its price per token, and anyone can buy inference from it. An escrow contract locks the payment and releases it only when the worker commits an output hash that matches the blob delivered on Swarm. Built for agents first. Our Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes dusk_market , dusk_submit, dusk_result and dusk_jobs. A frontier model can check live asks, fan tasks cheaply out to  models on 0G, and combine the results. An OpenAI-compatible proxy lets existing SDKs use Dusk by changing only their base URL. Identity and reputation use ENSv2 on Sepolia. Every participant gets a *.dusk.eth name with its own permissioned resolver. A controller role issues names. A separate revoker role can ban a wallet and burn its name in one atomic step. Reputation is computed from canary jobs and verifier evidence and published on chain, so anyone can read it back without trusting a single server Arkiv holds the whole market. The order book and the evidence trail live in Arkiv entities, so anyone can audit the market without a Dusk backend. Prompts and outputs stay on Swarm, encrypted for private jobs. Dusk is a liquidation market for a resource that expires daily, with escrow settlement, agent tooling, and on-chain reputation built in.
projects.how_its_made: The project is built as a web app with TypeScript end to end, plus Solidity for the two contracts that hold money and names. Inference runs on 0G Compute. Arkiv, the order book: Jobs, claims, receipts, worker ads and verifications all live as Arkiv entities. The engine stamps ownership, not our application code, so no Dusk server can hide workers, reorder claims or rewrite a receipt. Swarm, the payloads: Prompts and outputs live on Swarm. For private jobs, Arkiv keeps only a hash and an encrypted reference. Payments: A Solidity escrow on 0G Galileo funds the job when it is posted. A granted worker commits an output hash, and a challenge window stays open before settlement. ENSv2 on Sepolia, identity: A custom DuskIdentityController does commit-reveal registration of label.dusk.eth and deploys an isolated permissioned resolver for each holder. It enforces one name per wallet, expiry, and non-transferability. A separate revoker role, currently the reputation contract, can revoke a name and ban a wallet (bound to its generation) without touching the records. Reputation: Scores are computed off-chain from finalized evidence and canary verdicts, then published on chain through an authenticated workflow. Stuff we are proud of: The MCP server is the same buyer path as the web app, not a wrapper around it. An agent's jobs go through the same escrow and authorisation flow as a human's. projects.project_description_markdown:
Dusk is a spot market for AI inference that would otherwise be wasted
Holders of 0G’s Infinite AI (iAI) receive compute credits every day. The credits reset at 00:00 UTC and nothing carries over, so whatever isn’t used is wasted. Dusk turns that waste into a market. A holder runs a worker, lists the models it can serve and its price per token, and anyone can buy inference from it. An escrow contract locks the payment and releases it only when the worker commits an output hash that matches the blob delivered on Swarm.

Built for agents first. 
- Our Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes dusk_market , dusk_submit, dusk_result and dusk_jobs. A frontier model can check live asks, fan tasks cheaply out to  models on 0G, and combine the results. 
- An OpenAI-compatible proxy lets existing SDKs use Dusk by changing only their base URL.

Identity and reputation use ENSv2 on Sepolia. Every participant gets a *.dusk.eth name with its own permissioned resolver. A controller role issues names. A separate revoker role can ban a wallet and burn its name in one atomic step. Reputation is computed from canary jobs and verifier evidence and published on chain, so anyone can read it back without trusting a single server

Arkiv holds the whole market. The order book and the evidence trail live in Arkiv entities, so anyone can audit the market without a Dusk backend. Prompts and outputs stay on Swarm, encrypted for private jobs.

Dusk is a liquidation market for a resource that expires daily, with escrow settlement, agent tooling, and on-chain reputation built in.

Swarm, the payloads: Prompts and outputs live on Swarm. For private jobs, Arkiv keeps only a hash and an encrypted reference.

Payments: A Solidity escrow on 0G Galileo funds the job when it is posted. A granted worker commits an output hash, and a challenge window stays open before settlement.

ENSv2 on Sepolia, identity: A custom DuskIdentityController does commit-reveal registration of label.dusk.eth and deploys an isolated permissioned resolver for each holder. It enforces one name per wallet, expiry, and non-transferability. A separate revoker role, currently the reputation contract, can revoke a name and ban a wallet (bound to its generation) without touching the records.

projects.title: VoxMesh
projects.description: Voice-controlled multi-agent runtime: ENS identities, World ID gating, Arkiv tasks, 0G inference.
projects.project_description: VoxMesh is a decentralised, voice-driven multi-agent runtime. Every agent has an identity, every task has a trace, every delegation has context, and every execution leaves an auditable outcome. The problem: Most AI agent systems are black boxes. You can’t tell which agent did what, who authorised it, or whether the output can be trusted. Agents coordinate through private, centralised state, and anyone can trigger sensitive actions. What it does: You speak or type a command, such as “audit this smart contract”. A Supervisor agent plans the work and splits it into a DAG of tasks. It publishes those tasks as entities on Arkiv. Specialised Research and Security agents discover the tasks, claim them, execute them, and write their results back to Arkiv. The DAG orchestrator supports sequential and parallel steps, conditional skips, retries, timeouts, a call budget and a depth limit. A message bus with correlation IDs and allowlisted tools keeps each agent in its own lane.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: TypeScript end to end. The frontend is React 19, Vite 7, Tailwind 4 and shadcn/Radix. The backend is Node 22 with Express 5. Zod schemas in a shared shared/schemas.ts validate every request body, every query and every LLM output, on both client and server. viem handles wallet and chain work, Playwright drives MetaMask, and Vitest covers unit, integration and e2e tests. The server pushes live trace updates to the UI over SSE. How the pieces fit: A command, spoken (Web Speech STT/TTS) or typed, hits /api/orchestrator/execute. The Supervisor calls 0G for a JSON plan. The plan then goes through validatePlan(), which checks that each capability is actually offered by an agent discovered from the store, that dependencies reference earlier steps, and that the plan fits the call budget. The LLM only proposes. Deterministic code decides. The orchestrator runs the validated plan as a bounded DAG, with parallel layers, retries, timeouts, a call budget and a depth limit. Dependents of a failed task are marked cancelled. Arkiv as the coordination layer: Agents never message each other directly. The Supervisor writes all task entities and task.delegate messages in one executeBatch transaction. Each worker queries Arkiv for open tasks matching its capability, claims one (open → claimed), reads its dependencies back from the store, runs, and persists an execution record plus a result message. We defined six schemas: agent, task, execution, message, workflow and identity. Arkiv string attributes are capped at 128 bytes. So each entity has small indexed columns for querying plus a payload bytes column holding the full JSON. All writes go through one serial queue so the signer never races its own nonce. Claims are read-check-write inside that queue, and a second claim gets 409 CONFLICT. A full sequential workflow costs about 7 transactions. 0G: The adapter calls the OpenAI-compatible router with verify_tee: true and captures x_0g_trace.request_id, provider, billing and TEE status. Those are attached to the agent result, the trace, the Arkiv execution record and the workflow summary. A response with no trace ID is rejected, so IDs are never fabricated. World ID (IDKit v4): The server signs the RP context, so the signing key never reaches the browser, and remembers the nonce. The browser opens the IDKit widget. The server checks that the nonce is issued, unused and unexpired, then forwards the proof unchanged to the World verify endpoint. On success it opens an opaque session and stores an attestation on Arkiv with only a hashed subject. Agent registration and task writes require a verified human. ENSv2: From the Agents page, the user’s own wallet, with no server-held key, creates voxmesh.<parent>.eth and a hierarchy of supervisor, research and security subnames on Sepolia or Mainnet. Each agent gets text records through a Permissioned Resolver deployed via the Verifiable Factory. grantSetterRoles delegates edit rights for one agent’s endpoint key to a chosen address. Hacky and notable: Real MetaMask agent over CDP: The agent attaches Playwright to a separate local Chrome profile with MetaMask installed and a localhost debugging port. It opens a temporary tab and calls eth_sendTransaction through the injected provider. It never touches passwords or seed phrases, and a human approves the final transaction in the wallet.
Phone voice commands: Phones only allow speech recognition on HTTPS. So the server generates a self-signed cert for the laptop’s Wi-Fi IP and serves a locked-down phone page. A QR code pairs the phone, and the pairing token sits in the URL fragment so it never reaches the server. The phone listener exposes only a few routes and cannot register agents or reach identity endpoints.
Security in depth: Security Agent findings are cross-checked against an independent deterministic static scan, and the risk score is overwritten from validated output instead of trusting the LLM. Each agent has a tool allowlist, and no LLM-generated code is ever executed.
Prediction-market demo: Research reads Polymarket’s public Gamma API and persists a snapshot. A Liquidity agent then computes capped two-sided quotes from that stored result. It is simulation-only, with no order endpoint and no wallet access.

projects.title: Sky Proof
projects.description: Tamper-proof black box for autonomous drones: 0G records, Chainlink judges, Arc pays victims
projects.project_description: SkyProof is an independent, tamper-proof black box for autonomous drones, with automatic payouts when a drone breaks the rules. The demo uses a delivery drone, but any drone that acts on its own (agriculture spraying, inspection, filming over crowds, medical flights) works the same way: only the permit and the list of gated actions change. The problem: when a drone hurts someone, the only flight record belongs to the operator being investigated. It can be edited, lost or withheld. In a real 2019 case in France (BEA report 2019-0416), a drone fell on a festival crowd and injured 3 people, and investigators couldn't check the operator's "battery failure" story because the flight logs had disappeared. Victims are left waiting months for an insurer with no evidence. How it works: 0G decides and records. Before every safety-critical action (take off, reroute, drop a package, land), the drone (a PyBullet simulation) has to ask our flight computer. The flight computer sends the camera view and the flight permit to a vision model (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b) on 0G Private Computer. That model runs on a TEE-attested provider (Intel TDX, dstack) over a sealed channel. If 0G gives no answer, the drone stops safely, and the record says that no 0G decision is claimed. We never fake a decision. Every decision is added to a signed, hash-chained record. Every 15 seconds the record is encrypted and uploaded to 0G Storage, and its fingerprint is written to 0G Chain (FlightLog contract). Chainlink CRE judges. A victim files a claim on the website. When the claim window closes, a Chainlink CRE workflow fetches the record and checks it against the fingerprints on 0G Chain. It does not trust the operator, so a missing, edited or unreadable record counts as a breach in itself. It then applies fixed, tested rules, for example "dropped a package with a person in the zone" or "flew without a valid 0G approval". Arc pays. The operator stakes USDC in an escrow contract built in Arc Studio. If the judge finds a breach, the victim is paid automatically from that stake. If not, the claim goes to an insurer, who has to reply with a reason. The website (Next.js, live on Vercel) has pages for each role. Victims report a problem and track their payout. Insurers review the cases that weren't paid automatically. Anyone can replay a published flight in 3D and check every decision against the chain. Judges can start a real flight from the site (a fixed list of scenarios, one at a time, with a daily cap) and watch it go through all three steps. Proof it's real: every published flight on the site links to its 0G Storage upload, its 0G Chain transactions, the CRE verdict and the Arc payout transaction. A replay tool shows that changing or deleting a single record entry is detected. In one line: 0G decides and records. Chainlink judges. Arc pays.
projects.how_its_made:
SkyProof has five parts that talk to each other: a drone simulator, a flight computer, the 0G network, a Chainlink CRE judge and an Arc escrow. A Next.js website sits on top for victims, insurers and judges. Drone simulation (Python 3.12, PyBullet). A physics-simulated quadcopter flies fixed mission scenarios: a normal delivery, a person below the drop zone, and others. Every safety-critical action (take off, reroute, drop, land) goes through a safety gate. The drone can't do the action until the flight computer approves it. If no approval comes, it stops safely. Flight computer, "officer" (TypeScript/Node, ethers v6, ws). It holds the flight permit (who may fly, where, and the rules) and gets the drone's requests over WebSocket. For each request it asks a vision model on 0G Private Computer (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, on a TEE-attested Intel TDX / dstack provider, over a sealed channel). The permit names the model, and the officer refuses answers from any other model. Each decision is added to a hash-chained record (@noble/hashes) and signed with the drone's key. Every 15 seconds the new part of the record is encrypted and uploaded to 0G Storage (@0gfoundation/0g-storage-ts-sdk), and its root hash is written to our FlightLog contract on 0G Chain (Galileo testnet, along with a DroneRegistry contract, built with Hardhat). At the end of a flight the record is sealed. Judge (Chainlink CRE, @chainlink/cre-sdk, TypeScript). A small runner listens for the escrow's ClaimWindowClosed event and starts the CRE workflow. The workflow downloads the record and checks every part against the anchors on 0G Chain. It never trusts the operator's copy. A missing, edited or unreadable record is a breach in itself. The verdict rules are kept as pure functions in their own file (rules.ts) with unit tests (bun test), so the decision logic can be checked separately from the network code. Payouts (Arc, Arc Studio, Solidity). SkyProofEscrow holds the operator's USDC stake. When there's a breach verdict, the victim is paid automatically. When there isn't, the claim goes to an insurer, who must reply with a reason. Built and deployed in Arc Studio. Website (Next.js, React Three Fiber/drei/postprocessing, three.js, zustand, GSAP and Lenis, viem, deployed on Vercel). It has a full-screen 3D flight replay, and the HTML sections scroll over a fixed canvas. The 3D scene and the page share state only through a zustand store. Victims file claims with MetaMask. Published flights link to their real 0G Storage, 0G Chain, CRE and Arc transactions. How the partners helped: 0G made the black box independent. The decision comes from a model on attested hardware, not from the operator's server. The record lives on decentralised storage, and its fingerprint is on a chain the operator can't rewrite.
Chainlink CRE let us run a judge that neither we nor the operator control, with no backend of our own deciding claims.
Arc has native USDC and fast finality, so a victim gets paid in seconds instead of waiting months.
Hacky bits worth mentioning: The drone has to stop. If 0G doesn't answer, the drone stops safely and the record says "no 0G decision claimed". We chose not to fake an answer, even when it made demos fail.
Tamper replay tool. pnpm replay <flight> --tamper changes one byte of a stored record and --delete drops an entry. Either one makes the judge flag a breach, which is a live demonstration that the record can't be quietly edited.
Judges can start a real flight from the website. The site starts the Python simulator with a fixed scenario list and an argument array, never a shell string. Only one flight runs at a time, there's a daily cap and the drone needs a token, so a public button can't be used to run commands on our machine.
UI port. We ported an existing SvelteKit design system to React mid-hackathon, including GSAP scroll reveals, Lenis smooth scrolling and a loading screen that keeps animations paused until it lifts. We also had to fix scroll triggers that stopped working when pages grew after loading flight data.
Tests: 28 for the website, 8 for the flight computer, 9 for the CRE rules and 8 for the contracts.

projects.title: Animo
projects.description: Animo: Turn text prompts into AI-generated videos with interactive, audience-driven storytelling.
projects.project_description: Animo is an AI-powered video creation and audience engagement platform that transforms simple text prompts into fully narrated, professionally rendered videos. It combines AI-driven storyboarding, private 0G image generation, Edge-TTS voice narration, and Remotion-based video rendering to automate the entire content creation workflow. Users can edit individual scenes using natural-language instructions, preview changes, and manage revisions without losing previous versions. Animo also supports AI-generated Instagram captions and hashtags, video publishing, and audience-driven episodic storytelling through A/B choices, comment analysis, and voting. An integrated analytics dashboard provides insights into video generation, rendering costs, revisions, and audience engagement. Animo aims to make professional video production faster, smarter, and more interactive through AI automation.
projects.how_its_made: Animo is built using Next.js, React, TypeScript, and a modular AI-powered video generation pipeline. The AI director converts user prompts into structured storyboards, while 0G's decentralized AI infrastructure generates scene images in private trust mode. Edge-TTS handles voice narration and word-level caption timing, and Remotion combines images, camera movements, transitions, sound effects, background music, and captions into rendered MP4 videos using FFmpeg. We implemented a revision-based editing system that translates natural-language scene instructions into structured patches, regenerates only modified assets, and preserves previous versions. For audience engagement, we built an A/B voting engine that analyzes imported Instagram comments, detects votes, and generates subsequent episodes based on winning choices. A notable implementation is our experimental local Chrome automation for Instagram publishing, including dry-run support and verified permalink extraction. We also developed a local-first analytics and 0G cost-receipt tracking system to monitor generation expenses, revisions, and project activity.

projects.title: Arcline
projects.description: Arc DEX with auto-rebalancing USDC baskets, SIPs & Chainlink CRE risk guards. Built in Arc Studio.
projects.project_description:
Arcline is a spot exchange on Arc, built end to end in Arc Studio, for risk-managed portfolio investing that settles in USDC. Most people don't want to trade every day. They want a target mix (say 40% BTC, 30% gold, 30% EURC), want it kept in balance, and want to add money every month. On today's DEXs, they still have to do that by hand. Arcline makes it a smart contract.

projects.title: Onshift
projects.description: Expiring ENSv2 names as shift passes: staff and AI agents act for an org until the shift ends.
projects.project_description: Organisations hand out temporary power all the time: event cashiers, on-call responders, contract support, and now AI agents that issue refunds. That power is either a shared admin key, or a role someone has to remember to remove. A customer has it worse. Nothing lets them check whether the support agent in their DMs acts for the company right now, and fake agents use that gap. OnShift is that check, built as ENSv2 names on Sepolia. A shift lead gives a staff wallet or an AI agent a name like shift-0412.ops.onshift.eth, with a role, a spending cap and an end time, in one transaction. The pass can't be transferred, and an approved operator inherits nothing. The holder can refund an order only back to the wallet that paid, only up to the remaining cap, and only for actions the org allowed. They cannot choose a recipient. When the shift ends, the name stops working by itself. Nobody sends a revoke. Anyone can type the name into Public Check, with no account, and see On shift or Not on shift, the role and the time left. Look-alike organisations such as onshlft.eth are flagged. If something goes wrong, one break-glass transaction re-points the ops registry at an empty one so every pass fails, and quarantines the till so new payments stop. Refunds for orders already paid still return to the original payer. Recovery uses a fresh registry, so old passes stay dead. Playground lets any wallet issue a demo pass under demo.onshift.eth: Demo cashier or Demo agent, at most $5 and one hour. Demo passes use a separate gate and float and cannot refund production orders. It's live against the real ENSv2 contracts, with an admin console, a wallet-style staff app, a customer pay page, Playground and Public Check.
projects.how_its_made: OnShift is a set of Solidity contracts plus a React app that turn ENSv2 names into expiring shift passes. It calls the real ENSv2 contracts ENS deployed on Sepolia (UserRegistry, Permissioned Resolver, VerifiableFactory, ETHRegistrar and UniversalResolverV2). We wrote PassIssuer, PassResolverLib, ShiftGate, IncidentSwitch, Playground, the tests and the app for this hackathon. contracts/src/ensv2-local is an ABI-compatible test double so the suite can run offline; Sepolia does not use it. Each ENSv2 feature does real work: Hierarchical registries. Passes live in the ops UserRegistry under onshift.eth. IncidentSwitch.breakGlass re-points that subregistry at an empty registry, so every pass fails getState in one transaction. restore() deploys a fresh registry through VerifiableFactory, so old passes never come back. Record aliasing. The same switch aliases till.onshift.eth onto a pre-registered quarantine name with setAlias and writes till.status. ShiftGate.pay refuses while the till is not live. A watchtower can flip only to that quarantine name, never to an address of its choosing. Turning the till back on takes the org plus an auditor who has attested the gate's codehash. Expiring names. PassIssuer registers each pass with an expiry. ShiftGate treats a pass as live only when getState says REGISTERED and the expiry is still in the future. There is no cron and no required revoke. The issuer holds no renew role, and the scope record is bound to the same expiry, so a revived name fails with ScopeMismatch. Enhanced Access Control. Passes are registered with roleBitmap 0: no transfer, no resolver change, and nothing for an approved operator to inherit. The holder may write exactly one text record of that one name, shift.status. Permissioned Resolver, one proxy per pass. PassResolverLib deploys it through VerifiableFactory, writes the issuer-only records (treasury address, pass.scope, org, role, and agent-context on a production AI-agent pass), and grants the holder that single record. A fresh resolver is required because ENSv2 grants are keyed by namehash, so on a shared resolver a re-issued label would keep the previous holder's grant. ENSIP-26. A production AI-agent pass publishes agent-context. Playground calls issueDemo, which forces that record empty, mints only under demo.onshift.eth with the roles Demo cashier and Demo agent, and caps the pass at $5 and one hour. A second ShiftGate holds the demo float, so a demo pass cannot refund a production order. ShiftGate re-derives authority on every refund and check-in: follow the live ops or demo pointer, read getState, require the caller to be latestOwner, then read scope from that pass's own resolver. Spend is tracked per registry, label and expiry, so a re-issued label starts at zero. Order ids are derived on chain, and USDC can only go back to the wallet that paid, never for more than that order. Testing and tooling: npm test runs 88 Foundry tests on the local layer, including five Playground audit regressions. npm run test:fork runs the same suite against the real ENSv2 contracts on a Sepolia fork. npm run smoke:sepolia runs the live path (pay, issue, resolve, refund to the payer) and the blocked cases: redirect, raise the cap, transfer, unknown order, over-refund, over-cap, and refund after expiry. sdk/gate.mjs lets another agent repeat the liveness check with no key and refuse a name that is not live or whose till is quarantined. The app is React, Vite and viem. The console, staff app, customer pay page, Playground and Public Check all read the committed Sepolia deployment, and nothing in the UI is a fixture. A staff or agent device keeps a burner key in the browser, funded by a gas allowance sent with the pass and capped at 0.05 ETH. On Sepolia the org is one wallet; transferOrg moves that role to a Safe without redeploying. Hacky but notable: Sepolia prices deployed code at about 1,700 gas per byte, and EIP-7825 caps a transaction at 16.78M gas, so our first PassIssuer (about 10.4 KB) could not be deployed. Moving per-pass resolver setup into PassResolverLib, which runs by DELEGATECALL in the issuer's context, brought it to about 8.4 KB with the same permissions. AI tools: Cursor drafted and edited the contracts, tests, app and deploy scripts. We directed the design: a resolver per pass, getState as liveness, refunds bound to the paying wallet, and a demo namespace that cannot touch production. There are no spec-kit, OpenSpec or Kiro files and no prompt archive.
