projects.title: Chrono
projects.description: Duration-bound lending on Hedera: shorter loans unlock higher borrowing power.
projects.project_description: Your opportunity lasts an hour. Why should your collateral be priced for a month? A trader spots an arbitrage opportunity. A borrower needs liquidity until tomorrow. A long-term holder wants to make a move without selling their assets. These are different borrowing needs, with different time horizons. Yet conventional DeFi lending often applies the same collateral limits regardless of how long a borrower actually needs the money. Chrono makes time part of the lending equation. Built on Hedera, Chrono is a duration-bound money market where borrowers choose their borrowing window, and that choice helps determine how much capital their collateral can unlock. Shorter commitments can access higher borrowing limits, while longer positions receive more conservative limits. The idea is simple: shorter loans, bigger moves. The same collateral. More room to act. Imagine holding $1,000 worth of collateral and needing liquidity for a short-lived opportunity. With Chrono’s configured short-duration parameters, that collateral can support borrowing of up to $900 at 90% loan-to-value, before the opening premium and subject to market parameters and available liquidity. The difference comes from explicitly incorporating duration into the risk model. A short borrowing window gives price movements less time to accumulate than a long one. Chrono uses that distinction to offer a duration-dependent borrowing curve, connecting borrowing capacity to a defined repayment horizon. Shorter duration does not remove market risk. Instead, Chrono pairs the additional borrowing capacity with an explicit maturity and mechanisms for handling both deteriorating collateral health and unpaid debt. For borrowers, this creates a practical choice: choose a shorter window to unlock more capital, or choose a longer window for more time to execute a strategy. A loan with a timeline you can understand. The borrower’s journey starts with three decisions: what collateral to deposit, what asset to borrow, and how long to borrow it for. Before opening a position, borrowers can review their borrowing limit, opening premium, interest terms and repayment deadline. Once opened, the position has a defined maturity, and its liquidation threshold is determined at origination. That threshold does not tighten simply because the loan gets older, although changing collateral prices and accruing debt can still affect position health. Borrowers retain exposure to their deposited assets while using the borrowed liquidity elsewhere. They can repay before maturity, or use the configured grace period with its applicable late fee. Unpaid positions then become subject to expiry settlement. This makes Chrono useful for opportunities that have a natural time horizon: arbitrage, temporary liquidity needs, collateral rebalancing and short-term financing without immediately selling an existing position. Two risks. Two complementary settlement paths. A timed loan needs to answer two different questions: What happens if the collateral becomes unhealthy before maturity? And what happens if the borrower does not repay on time? Chrono addresses each through a separate mechanism. For price-driven risk, Chrono uses soft liquidation. When a position becomes unhealthy, its Dutch-auction mechanism allows collateral to be sold at an evolving discount. This path is designed to liquidate the portion needed to restore health where possible, rather than automatically closing the entire position. Buyers participate based on the auction’s available price, creating a mechanism for clearing collateral under market conditions. For maturity risk, Chrono uses scheduled expiry settlement. When a loan is opened, the protocol arranges its expiry execution through Hedera Schedule Service. The settlement architecture uses Stability Pool liquidity to absorb debt, with rules governing collateral allocation, penalties and any eligible borrower surplus. Settlement outcomes depend on the position and the available backstop liquidity. Together, these paths connect borrowing power to enforceable lifecycle rules: collateral health matters throughout the loan, and the repayment deadline matters at its end. A market with a role for every participant. Chrono brings together three complementary roles. Borrowers deposit collateral and select the borrowing window that fits their next move. Lenders supply the liquidity borrowers use and earn a share of collected borrower interest. Their returns respond to borrowing activity, while withdrawals depend on available pool liquidity. Stability providers supply the backstop capital used in default settlement. In exchange, they can receive collateral rewards and a share of opening premiums, while taking on a distinct risk of loss. These roles make Chrono more than a borrowing interface. They form a market that connects short-term demand for capital with liquidity supply and an explicit default backstop. Why Hedera is central to Chrono. Duration is only useful as a lending primitive if the protocol can act on it. Chrono uses Hedera’s EVM smart contracts for its lending logic, Hedera Token Service for supported testnet assets, and Hedera Schedule Service to arrange future expiry execution. Native scheduling is a core part of the design: the loan’s timeline is incorporated into its on-chain lifecycle when the position is created. The testnet application brings these mechanisms into a unified experience for borrowing, lending and Stability Pool participation. Chrono turns borrowing duration into a choice that matters. For the borrower, that means aligning a loan with the opportunity it is meant to fund. For the market, it means connecting capital efficiency to explicit deadlines and settlement rules. Your collateral. Your borrowing window. Your next move.
projects.how_its_made: We built Chrono around one architectural question: if a borrower commits to returning capital sooner, how can the protocol safely give that borrower more borrowing power? Answering that required more than adding a duration selector to a lending interface. Duration had to influence borrowing limits, interest pricing, liquidation rules and execution itself. Chrono’s core is written in Solidity and runs on Hedera EVM. We used Hardhat for contract development, deployment and testing, OpenZeppelin for standard access control and reentrancy protection, and PRBMath for fixed-point exponential calculations. The web interface uses React, Vite and ethers.js to connect the borrowing, lending and Stability Pool workflows to the contracts. Hedera Token Service supports the testnet assets, while off-chain services handle indexing, market-data updates and operational monitoring. We separated the protocol into contracts with specific responsibilities. BorrowVault holds collateral and position records. LendingPool manages supplied liquidity and outstanding principal. RiskEngine calculates borrowing limits and position health. InterestEngine handles rate evolution and debt accrual. LiquidationEngine coordinates the settlement paths, while StabilityPool supplies default backstop liquidity. ChronoRouter brings these operations together for users. We also separated maturity scheduling and schedule recovery from the financial accounting, so scheduling failures have an explicit recovery path. The first important choice was to configure risk by ordered collateral-and-debt pair. Borrowing USDC against ETH is a different exposure from borrowing ETH against USDC, so reversing the tokens should not automatically reuse the same settings. Each market can have its own duration bounds, LTV curve, liquidation thresholds, penalties and auction parameters. Within each market, the maximum LTV follows a bounded exponential curve based on the chosen loan duration. Short terms receive higher borrowing limits, and longer terms approach a more conservative baseline. We normalized the curve to reach its configured endpoints exactly. With the default parameters, that means 90% maximum LTV at the shortest allowed term and 75% at the longest. We deliberately separated the maximum borrowing LTV from the liquidation threshold. Opening a loan at its borrowing limit should still leave a buffer before liquidation. Registry validation checks both the endpoints and the relationship between the curves’ decay coefficients, keeping the liquidation threshold above the borrowing limit across the allowed term range. Another deliberate choice was to calculate the threshold using the original loan duration rather than the remaining time. A position should not become liquidatable merely because its clock is counting down. Price movements and accruing debt can still reduce its health, but elapsed time does not independently tighten its threshold. Maturity has its own enforcement mechanism. That distinction led to our two liquidation paths. Soft liquidation addresses an unhealthy position before terminal settlement. Our default mechanism is a public Dutch auction. Starting an auction records its price curve without immediately moving collateral out of the vault or closing the loan. The borrower can still repay or add collateral, and interest continues accruing. The auction starts above its reference oracle price and moves toward a discount. Instead of assigning every liquidation the same fixed bonus, this lets bidders decide when the collateral is attractive enough to purchase. The initial configuration moves from 105% to 90% of the reference price over 15 minutes, with configurable bounds. The more involved part is sizing the sale. We solve for the collateral amount needed to restore the remaining position to a target health factor of 1.05, accounting for the auction price, live collateral value, liquidation threshold and accrued debt. Selling collateral also removes collateral backing from the position, so simply repaying an arbitrary percentage of debt would not be sufficient. At execution, we recalculate the required lot, enforce the bidder’s maximum payment and minimum collateral limits, and reject a fill that cannot restore the required health. Repayment covers interest before principal, and the borrower retains unsold collateral. We also retained an alternative dynamic-discount liquidation mode, where the liquidator bonus responds to position health. Its Stability Pool route has additional protections, including a minimum health requirement and a reserve watermark for upcoming maturities. This prevents intermediate liquidations from freely consuming liquidity needed for imminent defaults. Hard liquidation handles a different event: the borrower has reached maturity and has not repaid within the grace period. It closes the position rather than trying to restore it. When collateral value and Stability Pool liquidity are sufficient, the pool repays the debt into LendingPool and receives the corresponding collateral plus its penalty allocation. The treasury receives its share, and eligible surplus collateral returns to the borrower. If that direct settlement cannot be supported, the protocol opens a separate two-phase Dutch auction. Auction proceeds follow a strict waterfall: lender debt first, then the penalty, then borrower surplus. We made this fallback explicit because scheduled execution cannot manufacture liquidity or guarantee a buyer. If an auction ultimately fails to recover the debt, the accounting must recognize the shortfall. Hedera Schedule Service is central to making this architecture possible. Ordinary EVM contracts do not wake themselves up at a future timestamp. A maturity check inside a contract only runs when someone submits a transaction. If higher borrowing limits depend on a defined borrowing window, relying entirely on an external bot to notice expiry would leave a critical part of the design outside the protocol. We therefore use HSS through Hedera’s schedule-service system contract to arrange future execution as part of opening a loan. Our maturity cron scheduler maintains one live schedule per position. If the final settlement time lies beyond the scheduling horizon, it creates an intermediate callback that schedules the next hop. The final hop calls the liquidation engine after maturity and the grace period. The implementation includes generation numbers to make stale or duplicate callbacks harmless, bounded searches for later execution slots when capacity is unavailable, and native-token reserves for execution funding. Opening a loan reverts if the initial scheduling requirements cannot be satisfied. If a later hop cannot schedule its successor, the failure is recorded in a recovery queue with its response code, allowing permissionless retries. Full repayment closes the scheduling job, while the liquidation engine independently checks eligibility so a callback cannot liquidate early. We also included small timing tolerances after investigating callback clock skew on testnet. These cron jobs reduce dependence on an always-online maturity keeper, but we kept the remaining dependencies explicit. Scheduled execution still needs funding, available network capacity, usable prices and settlement liquidity. Oracle updates, volatility updates, indexing and monitoring remain separate operational services. Interest pricing follows the same principle of separating different causes of risk. Each loan has a duration component fixed when it opens and a utilization component that changes with pool conditions. The duration component combines a declining short-term premium with an increasing term premium. Very short borrowing provides valuable capital flexibility and repeated turnover, so it should not become effectively free merely because the position is brief. Longer borrowing commits liquidity for longer and receives an increasing term charge. Combining these components allows the pricing curve to express both effects. The utilization component responds to liquidity scarcity. It becomes steeper above the target utilization, while its target rate also adapts over time. We checkpoint utilization before deposits, withdrawals, borrowing and principal returns, then integrate the rate between checkpoints. This prevents a new pool state from being applied retroactively to an earlier period and makes accrued interest less dependent on how frequently a position is touched. PRBMath supports continuous compounding, with explicit numerical bounds. Separately, we charge an upfront opening premium based on the position’s LTV and the pair’s recent realized volatility. This pays for exposure created when the loan opens, even if the borrower repays quickly. It is withheld from the proceeds while the recorded principal remains the requested borrowing amount. Borrowers provide a maximum acceptable premium, and the quote and execution share the same calculation path. The premium uses interpolated per-market tables and a minimum charging horizon. Early repayment does not refund it. The Stability Pool’s share vests gradually rather than becoming instantly claimable, reducing the incentive to deposit immediately before a premium arrives and withdraw immediately afterward. Unvested premiums are excluded from capital available to absorb defaults. We also spent time on accounting details that are easy to overlook. One bug we addressed concerned rounding direction. Small integer divisions must not repeatedly benefit users at the expense of the pools backing their claims. The intended rule is conservative: avoid overstating depositor claims or understating the shares that must be burned for a withdrawal. In Stability Pool accounting, payouts round down and required burns round up. These tiny differences matter because repeated operations can turn negligible rounding errors into an actual balance deficit. We normalized token amounts before cross-asset calculations because assets with different decimal precision cannot be compared directly. Borrowing limits, collateral seizure amounts, health calculations and premium quotes all need consistent units. We also capped settlement amounts against actual debt and available collateral and kept principal reduction synchronized with maturity bookkeeping. Finally, we ran simulations and historical market replays to examine borrower outcomes, lender outcomes, liquidation behavior, utilization stress and premium calibration. We also compared scenarios against an Aave reference implementation using matched market paths and seeds. These exercises helped expose trade-offs and guide parameter choices; they are simulation results rather than promises of live performance. The result is a lending architecture in which duration affects the entire position lifecycle. Borrowing limits define how much capital a chosen window can unlock, the interest model prices the liquidity commitment, premiums compensate the backstop, liquidation rules handle price deterioration, and HSS gives the repayment deadline an executable on-chain path.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Your opportunity lasts an hour. Why should your collateral be priced for a month?

A trader spots an arbitrage opportunity. A borrower needs liquidity until tomorrow. A long-term holder wants to make a move without selling their assets. These are different borrowing needs, with different time horizons. Yet conventional DeFi lending often applies the same collateral limits regardless of how long a borrower actually needs the money.

Chrono makes time part of the lending equation.

Built on Hedera, Chrono is a duration-bound money market where borrowers choose their borrowing window, and that choice helps determine how much capital their collateral can unlock. Shorter commitments can access higher borrowing limits, while longer positions receive more conservative limits.

The idea is simple: shorter loans, bigger moves.

The same collateral. More room to act.

Imagine holding $1,000 worth of collateral and needing liquidity for a short-lived opportunity. With Chrono’s configured short-duration parameters, that collateral can support borrowing of up to $900 at 90% loan-to-value, before the opening premium and subject to market parameters and available liquidity.

The difference comes from explicitly incorporating duration into the risk model. A short borrowing window gives price movements less time to accumulate than a long one. Chrono uses that distinction to offer a duration-dependent borrowing curve, connecting borrowing capacity to a defined repayment horizon.

Shorter duration does not remove market risk. Instead, Chrono pairs the additional borrowing capacity with an explicit maturity and mechanisms for handling both deteriorating collateral health and unpaid debt.

For borrowers, this creates a practical choice: choose a shorter window to unlock more capital, or choose a longer window for more time to execute a strategy.

A loan with a timeline you can understand.

The borrower’s journey starts with three decisions: what collateral to deposit, what asset to borrow, and how long to borrow it for.

Before opening a position, borrowers can review their borrowing limit, opening premium, interest terms and repayment deadline. Once opened, the position has a defined maturity, and its liquidation threshold is determined at origination. That threshold does not tighten simply because the loan gets older, although changing collateral prices and accruing debt can still affect position health.

Borrowers retain exposure to their deposited assets while using the borrowed liquidity elsewhere. They can repay before maturity, or use the configured grace period with its applicable late fee. Unpaid positions then become subject to expiry settlement.

This makes Chrono useful for opportunities that have a natural time horizon: arbitrage, temporary liquidity needs, collateral rebalancing and short-term financing without immediately selling an existing position.

Two risks. Two complementary settlement paths.

A timed loan needs to answer two different questions: What happens if the collateral becomes unhealthy before maturity? And what happens if the borrower does not repay on time?

Chrono addresses each through a separate mechanism.

For price-driven risk, Chrono uses soft liquidation. When a position becomes unhealthy, its Dutch-auction mechanism allows collateral to be sold at an evolving discount. This path is designed to liquidate the portion needed to restore health where possible, rather than automatically closing the entire position. Buyers participate based on the auction’s available price, creating a mechanism for clearing collateral under market conditions.

For maturity risk, Chrono uses scheduled expiry settlement. When a loan is opened, the protocol arranges its expiry execution through Hedera Schedule Service. The settlement architecture uses Stability Pool liquidity to absorb debt, with rules governing collateral allocation, penalties and any eligible borrower surplus. Settlement outcomes depend on the position and the available backstop liquidity.

Together, these paths connect borrowing power to enforceable lifecycle rules: collateral health matters throughout the loan, and the repayment deadline matters at its end.

A market with a role for every participant.

Chrono brings together three complementary roles.

Borrowers deposit collateral and select the borrowing window that fits their next move.

Lenders supply the liquidity borrowers use and earn a share of collected borrower interest. Their returns respond to borrowing activity, while withdrawals depend on available pool liquidity.

Stability providers supply the backstop capital used in default settlement. In exchange, they can receive collateral rewards and a share of opening premiums, while taking on a distinct risk of loss.

These roles make Chrono more than a borrowing interface. They form a market that connects short-term demand for capital with liquidity supply and an explicit default backstop.

Why Hedera is central to Chrono.

Duration is only useful as a lending primitive if the protocol can act on it.

Chrono uses Hedera’s EVM smart contracts for its lending logic, Hedera Token Service for supported testnet assets, and Hedera Schedule Service to arrange future expiry execution. Native scheduling is a core part of the design: the loan’s timeline is incorporated into its on-chain lifecycle when the position is created.

The testnet application brings these mechanisms into a unified experience for borrowing, lending and Stability Pool participation.

Chrono turns borrowing duration into a choice that matters.

For the borrower, that means aligning a loan with the opportunity it is meant to fund. For the market, it means connecting capital efficiency to explicit deadlines and settlement rules.

Your collateral. Your borrowing window. Your next move.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built Chrono around one architectural question: if a borrower commits to returning capital sooner, how can the protocol safely give that borrower more borrowing power? Answering that required more than adding a duration selector to a lending interface. Duration had to influence borrowing limits, interest pricing, liquidation rules and execution itself.

Chrono’s core is written in Solidity and runs on Hedera EVM. We used Hardhat for contract development, deployment and testing, OpenZeppelin for standard access control and reentrancy protection, and PRBMath for fixed-point exponential calculations. The web interface uses React, Vite and ethers.js to connect the borrowing, lending and Stability Pool workflows to the contracts. Hedera Token Service supports the testnet assets, while off-chain services handle indexing, market-data updates and operational monitoring.

We separated the protocol into contracts with specific responsibilities. BorrowVault holds collateral and position records. LendingPool manages supplied liquidity and outstanding principal. RiskEngine calculates borrowing limits and position health. InterestEngine handles rate evolution and debt accrual. LiquidationEngine coordinates the settlement paths, while StabilityPool supplies default backstop liquidity. ChronoRouter brings these operations together for users. We also separated maturity scheduling and schedule recovery from the financial accounting, so scheduling failures have an explicit recovery path.

The first important choice was to configure risk by ordered collateral-and-debt pair. Borrowing USDC against ETH is a different exposure from borrowing ETH against USDC, so reversing the tokens should not automatically reuse the same settings. Each market can have its own duration bounds, LTV curve, liquidation thresholds, penalties and auction parameters.

Within each market, the maximum LTV follows a bounded exponential curve based on the chosen loan duration. Short terms receive higher borrowing limits, and longer terms approach a more conservative baseline. We normalized the curve to reach its configured endpoints exactly. With the default parameters, that means 90% maximum LTV at the shortest allowed term and 75% at the longest.

We deliberately separated the maximum borrowing LTV from the liquidation threshold. Opening a loan at its borrowing limit should still leave a buffer before liquidation. Registry validation checks both the endpoints and the relationship between the curves’ decay coefficients, keeping the liquidation threshold above the borrowing limit across the allowed term range.

Another deliberate choice was to calculate the threshold using the original loan duration rather than the remaining time. A position should not become liquidatable merely because its clock is counting down. Price movements and accruing debt can still reduce its health, but elapsed time does not independently tighten its threshold. Maturity has its own enforcement mechanism.

That distinction led to our two liquidation paths.

Soft liquidation addresses an unhealthy position before terminal settlement. Our default mechanism is a public Dutch auction. Starting an auction records its price curve without immediately moving collateral out of the vault or closing the loan. The borrower can still repay or add collateral, and interest continues accruing.

The auction starts above its reference oracle price and moves toward a discount. Instead of assigning every liquidation the same fixed bonus, this lets bidders decide when the collateral is attractive enough to purchase. The initial configuration moves from 105% to 90% of the reference price over 15 minutes, with configurable bounds.

The more involved part is sizing the sale. We solve for the collateral amount needed to restore the remaining position to a target health factor of 1.05, accounting for the auction price, live collateral value, liquidation threshold and accrued debt. Selling collateral also removes collateral backing from the position, so simply repaying an arbitrary percentage of debt would not be sufficient. At execution, we recalculate the required lot, enforce the bidder’s maximum payment and minimum collateral limits, and reject a fill that cannot restore the required health. Repayment covers interest before principal, and the borrower retains unsold collateral.

We also retained an alternative dynamic-discount liquidation mode, where the liquidator bonus responds to position health. Its Stability Pool route has additional protections, including a minimum health requirement and a reserve watermark for upcoming maturities. This prevents intermediate liquidations from freely consuming liquidity needed for imminent defaults.

Hard liquidation handles a different event: the borrower has reached maturity and has not repaid within the grace period. It closes the position rather than trying to restore it. When collateral value and Stability Pool liquidity are sufficient, the pool repays the debt into LendingPool and receives the corresponding collateral plus its penalty allocation. The treasury receives its share, and eligible surplus collateral returns to the borrower.

If that direct settlement cannot be supported, the protocol opens a separate two-phase Dutch auction. Auction proceeds follow a strict waterfall: lender debt first, then the penalty, then borrower surplus. We made this fallback explicit because scheduled execution cannot manufacture liquidity or guarantee a buyer. If an auction ultimately fails to recover the debt, the accounting must recognize the shortfall.

Hedera Schedule Service is central to making this architecture possible. Ordinary EVM contracts do not wake themselves up at a future timestamp. A maturity check inside a contract only runs when someone submits a transaction. If higher borrowing limits depend on a defined borrowing window, relying entirely on an external bot to notice expiry would leave a critical part of the design outside the protocol.

We therefore use HSS through Hedera’s schedule-service system contract to arrange future execution as part of opening a loan. Our maturity cron scheduler maintains one live schedule per position. If the final settlement time lies beyond the scheduling horizon, it creates an intermediate callback that schedules the next hop. The final hop calls the liquidation engine after maturity and the grace period.

The implementation includes generation numbers to make stale or duplicate callbacks harmless, bounded searches for later execution slots when capacity is unavailable, and native-token reserves for execution funding. Opening a loan reverts if the initial scheduling requirements cannot be satisfied. If a later hop cannot schedule its successor, the failure is recorded in a recovery queue with its response code, allowing permissionless retries. Full repayment closes the scheduling job, while the liquidation engine independently checks eligibility so a callback cannot liquidate early. We also included small timing tolerances after investigating callback clock skew on testnet.

These cron jobs reduce dependence on an always-online maturity keeper, but we kept the remaining dependencies explicit. Scheduled execution still needs funding, available network capacity, usable prices and settlement liquidity. Oracle updates, volatility updates, indexing and monitoring remain separate operational services.

Interest pricing follows the same principle of separating different causes of risk. Each loan has a duration component fixed when it opens and a utilization component that changes with pool conditions.

The duration component combines a declining short-term premium with an increasing term premium. Very short borrowing provides valuable capital flexibility and repeated turnover, so it should not become effectively free merely because the position is brief. Longer borrowing commits liquidity for longer and receives an increasing term charge. Combining these components allows the pricing curve to express both effects.

The utilization component responds to liquidity scarcity. It becomes steeper above the target utilization, while its target rate also adapts over time. We checkpoint utilization before deposits, withdrawals, borrowing and principal returns, then integrate the rate between checkpoints. This prevents a new pool state from being applied retroactively to an earlier period and makes accrued interest less dependent on how frequently a position is touched. PRBMath supports continuous compounding, with explicit numerical bounds.

Separately, we charge an upfront opening premium based on the position’s LTV and the pair’s recent realized volatility. This pays for exposure created when the loan opens, even if the borrower repays quickly. It is withheld from the proceeds while the recorded principal remains the requested borrowing amount. Borrowers provide a maximum acceptable premium, and the quote and execution share the same calculation path.

The premium uses interpolated per-market tables and a minimum charging horizon. Early repayment does not refund it. The Stability Pool’s share vests gradually rather than becoming instantly claimable, reducing the incentive to deposit immediately before a premium arrives and withdraw immediately afterward. Unvested premiums are excluded from capital available to absorb defaults.

We also spent time on accounting details that are easy to overlook. One bug we addressed concerned rounding direction. Small integer divisions must not repeatedly benefit users at the expense of the pools backing their claims. The intended rule is conservative: avoid overstating depositor claims or understating the shares that must be burned for a withdrawal. In Stability Pool accounting, payouts round down and required burns round up. These tiny differences matter because repeated operations can turn negligible rounding errors into an actual balance deficit.

We normalized token amounts before cross-asset calculations because assets with different decimal precision cannot be compared directly. Borrowing limits, collateral seizure amounts, health calculations and premium quotes all need consistent units. We also capped settlement amounts against actual debt and available collateral and kept principal reduction synchronized with maturity bookkeeping.

Finally, we ran simulations and historical market replays to examine borrower outcomes, lender outcomes, liquidation behavior, utilization stress and premium calibration. We also compared scenarios against an Aave reference implementation using matched market paths and seeds. These exercises helped expose trade-offs and guide parameter choices; they are simulation results rather than promises of live performance.

The result is a lending architecture in which duration affects the entire position lifecycle. Borrowing limits define how much capital a chosen window can unlock, the interest model prices the liquidity commitment, premiums compensate the backstop, liquidation rules handle price deterioration, and HSS gives the repayment deadline an executable on-chain path.

projects.title: FLASHARB
projects.description: Flasharb executes atomic arbitrage between Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua using flash accounting
projects.project_description: FLASHARB executes atomic arbitrage between Uniswap v4 and 1inch Aqua, without traditional flash loans or upfront trading capital. Uniswap v4: Uses flash accounting to execute the first swap without immediately transferring tokens. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: Completes the second swap using liquidity from Aqua strategies. Atomic settlement: Both trades settle in a single transaction. If the arbitrage fails, everything reverts. Smart searcher: Automatically discovers price gaps, calculates optimal trade sizes, simulates execution, and estimates profit after gas. Live dashboard: Monitor opportunities, execute trades through MetaMask, and manage profits stored as ERC-6909 claims.
projects.how_its_made: FLASHARB is built using Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4, 1inch Aqua, SwapVM, TypeScript, viem, React, and Vite. Uniswap v4: Uses PoolManager.unlock() and flash accounting to trade without conventional flash loans. 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: Provides shared liquidity and executes the second swap. Searcher bot: Detects price gaps, optimizes trade sizes, simulates transactions, and calculates profit after gas. Dashboard React-based interface for live opportunities, MetaMask trading, and ERC-6909 profit tracking. Testing:Foundry, Anvil, automated bot tests, and Unichain fork tests. The clever part: Aqua sends tokens directly into Uniswap v4's PoolManager, while SwapVM's preTransferInCallback handles payment. Both swaps settle atomically with fewer token transfers. We also use ERC-6909 claims to store profits efficiently and are developing a Huff executor for further gas optimization.

projects.title: Conduence
projects.description: Personal agent for traders, a second brain to trade when you can’t, from events to execution.
projects.project_description: Conduence learns how a trader thinks, maps their preferences and reasoning, and transforms them into a decision framework agents can run on. Traders get access to the best tools and fast execution through our in-house pipeline, without requiring code, APIs, or dependence on complex trading software. Your agent wakes up within 850 ms of an activity occurring. We process events through to execution with a massive 70.5% reduction in cost compared with OpenClaw or Hermes-class agents. Some tools can deliver information to your agent up to five seconds before by reading from the mempool, while other tools helps with additional context enrichment.
projects.how_its_made: Conduence turns a user’s trading thesis into an autonomous agent that can research opportunities, execute trades within owner-defined limits. projects.title: Ponos
projects.description: Escrowed stablecoin payroll for AI trainers on Hedera: pay is locked first, and silence pays.
projects.project_description: People who label and review data for AI labs often wait weeks to be paid, and a reviewer who never responds can hold their pay indefinitely. Ponos (Byline Work) reverses that default: the money is locked before the work starts, and if nobody reviews by the deadline, the freelancer is paid automatically. How it works: Lock. An AI lab funds a batch of tasks in bUSD, a testnet dollar we issued with Hedera Stablecoin Studio (KYC, freeze, pause, wipe, a reserve and an HTS custom fee). An escrow contract pulls the pay plus a 3% platform fee before anyone can claim. Claim. A worker signs in with World ID, so each account is one unique human. Claiming a task over $100, or changing the payout wallet, needs a fresh World ID verification checked on our server. Submit. The work stays off-chain and only its hash goes on-chain. In the same call, the escrow schedules its own payout with Hedera's Schedule Service (HIP-1215). Paid. If QA passes or a reviewer approves, the worker is paid immediately. If nobody acts, Hedera executes the schedule at the deadline and pays the worker without any server involved. Only an on-chain hold with a reason stops it. Every task transition is logged on Hedera Consensus Service, and contributor scores are computed from that public log. AI agents can buy signed reserve, NAV, FX and escrow data over x402 on Hedera, with spending caps and no human approval. 0G provides an advisory second opinion on QA, with its request id stored in the report. It runs on Hedera testnet with a verified escrow contract. The lab, reviewer and compliance keys are held by the server for the demo, and the rupee payout is simulated.
projects.how_its_made: Ponos is a TypeScript project: a Solidity escrow contract, a small Node API, and a Next.js site. Hedera does most of the work. We issued our own testnet dollar, bUSD, with Stablecoin Studio, so we get KYC, freezing and a reserve out of the box. The escrow contract holds each task's pay. The fun part is Hedera's scheduled transactions: when a worker submits, the contract schedules its own payout for the deadline, so if nobody reviews, Hedera pays the worker on its own. Every step is also written to Hedera Consensus Service, which gives us a public log anyone can check. AI agents can buy our reserve and escrow data per request over x402. World ID makes sure each worker is one real person, and asks them to verify again before anything that moves money. 0G gives a second opinion when we grade work. The hackiest moment: our first scheduled payout fired right on time but paid nothing. Hedera's block clock was a couple of seconds behind the deadline, so the contract thought it was too early. We now schedule six seconds after the deadline, and it has paid every time since.

How it works:

projects.title: TrustMeBro
projects.description: TrustMeBro unlocks trade financing with Hedera x402 agents and Whitechain DeFi.
projects.project_description: TrustMeBro — AI-Powered, Onchain Trade Financing TrustMeBro is a decentralized trade financing platform that helps small and medium-sized exporters access working capital without waiting weeks or months for international buyers to pay their invoices. The Problem Imagine a coffee exporter in India who ships $50,000 worth of coffee to a European buyer. The shipment is already on its way, but the importer will only pay after 60 days. Meanwhile, the exporter needs money immediately to purchase raw materials, pay suppliers, manage operations, and fulfill new orders. Traditional trade financing often involves extensive documentation, manual shipment verification, lengthy approval processes, and limited accessibility for smaller businesses. Even profitable exporters can face severe cash-flow problems. Our Solution TrustMeBro transforms confirmed, shipment-verified trade invoices into tokenized financing opportunities. Investors can provide upfront liquidity to exporters, while smart contracts manage investment rights, repayment distribution, and importer reputation. The platform combines Hedera's x402 payment infrastructure for automated evidence purchasing with Whitechain smart contracts for decentralized invoice financing. How It Works Trade Creation: An exporter creates an invoice containing the trade amount, importer details, shipment reference, quantity, and commercial documentation commitments. Importer Confirmation: The importer reviews and approves the agreement on Whitechain, establishing a shared record of the transaction. AI-Agent Verification: An autonomous payment agent uses Hedera x402 to purchase shipment information from a verification service. The service checks relevant evidence, and an authorized verifier can produce a cryptographically signed attestation. Onchain Verification: Whitechain validates the attestation signature and checks that the shipment details match the agreed trade conditions. A successfully verified invoice becomes eligible for financing. Investor Financing: Investors fund eligible invoices using tokens on Whitechain. The advance amount depends on the importer's onchain Trust Score. The investor receives a tokenized receivable NFT representing their repayment claim. Repayment and Settlement: When the importer repays the invoice, smart contracts distribute funds to the current receivable NFT holder, the exporter, and the platform according to predefined financial rules. Reputation-Based Financing TrustMeBro introduces an onchain Trust Score for importers, starting at 60 and capped at 93. Repayment outcomes affect this score, which determines the percentage of invoice value eligible for upfront financing. For example, an importer with a Trust Score of 80 can enable an advance of $7,760 against a $10,000 invoice under the current financing formula. Investors earn a fixed 3% profit on the financed amount when the invoice is fully repaid, while TrustMeBro receives a 1% platform fee on the invoice face value at settlement. Technology and Integrations Whitechain: Trade agreements, financing, reputation, receivable NFTs, and programmable settlement. Hedera x402: Agent-initiated micropayments for shipment verification services. AI-Agent Workflow: Automated trade discovery, payment-policy checks, evidence purchasing, and verification coordination. EIP-712 Signatures: Cryptographically authorized shipment attestations. Tokenized Receivables: NFT-based representation of investor repayment rights. Current Prototype TrustMeBro has deployed its V2 smart contracts on Whitechain Sepolia and demonstrated invoice creation, importer confirmation, and an actual Hedera testnet x402 payment. The current shipment-verification integration uses explicitly labeled simulated evidence rather than authenticated live carrier data. Completing the full onchain verification-to-financing demonstration and integrating real logistics data are ongoing development goals. Our Vision We aim to make trade financing more accessible, transparent, and programmable, starting with small and medium-sized exporters in sectors such as agriculture, coffee, textiles, and manufacturing. Instead of allowing capital to remain locked in unpaid invoices, TrustMeBro creates a pathway for verified trade receivables to attract investment. Because a growing business shouldn't have to reject its next order while waiting to get paid for its last one.
projects.how_its_made: TrustMeBro is built as a cross-chain, agent-powered trade financing platform combining Whitechain, Hedera x402, Solidity smart contracts, TypeScript-based autonomous agents, and a Next.js frontend. The biggest engineering challenge was connecting two different processes: verifying that an international trade meets its agreed shipment conditions and allowing investors to finance that trade without relying on a centralized intermediary to manage the money. We divided the system into four interconnected layers: the trade-financing contracts, an autonomous verification agent, an x402-powered evidence service, and a user-facing application. Whitechain — The Financial Settlement Layer We developed and deployed three interconnected Solidity smart contracts on Whitechain Sepolia (chain ID 1874). TradePilotFinance.sol is the core financial engine. It manages trade creation, importer confirmation, verification status, funding eligibility, investor financing, and repayment distribution. ImporterReputation.sol manages the importer's onchain Trust Score. Every new importer starts with a score of 60, capped at 93. Repayment and default outcomes influence reputation, which determines how much financing can be advanced against future invoices. ReceivableNote.sol represents investors' repayment claims through restricted-transfer NFTs. When an investor finances an invoice, they receive a receivable NFT. The smart contract pays the current eligible NFT holder when the importer repays. We implemented a reputation-based financing formula: Base financing amount = 97% of invoice value. Available advance = Base amount × Importer Trust Score / 100. Investor profit = 3% of the funded advance. Platform fee = 1% of the invoice face value. For example, an importer with a Trust Score of 80 can unlock a 77.6% advance against a verified invoice. The importer repays the full invoice amount, and the contract atomically distributes funds to the investor, exporter, and platform. We use access controls, restricted NFT transfers, reentrancy protection, and transaction-level validation to protect the financing lifecycle. Hedera x402 — Autonomous Payments for Verification This is one of our most interesting technical integrations. International shipment verification normally involves requesting information from external services. Instead of requiring an operator to manually purchase and upload every report, we built an autonomous payment workflow using Hedera x402. Our agent is implemented in TypeScript and communicates with a verification merchant through HTTP. When an importer confirms a trade, the agent can discover the agreement on Whitechain and prepare a shipment evidence request. The merchant responds with an HTTP 402 payment requirement. The agent examines the quoted amount, merchant account, Hedera network, token, and spending policy before authorizing payment. We integrated Hedera testnet USDC payments, an x402 payment facilitator, and Hedera Mirror Node verification. Importantly, payment success is not assumed merely because an HTTP request succeeds. projects.project_description_markdown:
TrustMeBro — AI-Powered, Onchain Trade Financing

TrustMeBro is a decentralized trade financing platform that helps small and medium-sized exporters access working capital without waiting weeks or months for international buyers to pay their invoices.

The Problem

Imagine a coffee exporter in India who ships $50,000 worth of coffee to a European buyer. The shipment is already on its way, but the importer will only pay after 60 days. Meanwhile, the exporter needs money immediately to purchase raw materials, pay suppliers, manage operations, and fulfill new orders.

Traditional trade financing often involves extensive documentation, manual shipment verification, lengthy approval processes, and limited accessibility for smaller businesses. Even profitable exporters can face severe cash-flow problems.

Our Solution

TrustMeBro transforms confirmed, shipment-verified trade invoices into tokenized financing opportunities. Investors can provide upfront liquidity to exporters, while smart contracts manage investment rights, repayment distribution, and importer reputation.

The platform combines Hedera's x402 payment infrastructure for automated evidence purchasing with Whitechain smart contracts for decentralized invoice financing.

How It Works

1. Trade Creation: An exporter creates an invoice containing the trade amount, importer details, shipment reference, quantity, and commercial documentation commitments.

2. Importer Confirmation: The importer reviews and approves the agreement on Whitechain, establishing a shared record of the transaction.

3. AI-Agent Verification: An autonomous payment agent uses Hedera x402 to purchase shipment information from a verification service. The service checks relevant evidence, and an authorized verifier can produce a cryptographically signed attestation.

4. Onchain Verification: Whitechain validates the attestation signature and checks that the shipment details match the agreed trade conditions. A successfully verified invoice becomes eligible for financing.

5. Investor Financing: Investors fund eligible invoices using tokens on Whitechain. The advance amount depends on the importer's onchain Trust Score. The investor receives a tokenized receivable NFT representing their repayment claim.

6. Repayment and Settlement: When the importer repays the invoice, smart contracts distribute funds to the current receivable NFT holder, the exporter, and the platform according to predefined financial rules.

Reputation-Based Financing

TrustMeBro introduces an onchain Trust Score for importers, starting at 60 and capped at 93. Repayment outcomes affect this score, which determines the percentage of invoice value eligible for upfront financing.

For example, an importer with a Trust Score of 80 can enable an advance of $7,760 against a $10,000 invoice under the current financing formula.

Investors earn a fixed 3% profit on the financed amount when the invoice is fully repaid, while TrustMeBro receives a 1% platform fee on the invoice face value at settlement.

Technology and Integrations

- Whitechain: Trade agreements, financing, reputation, receivable NFTs, and programmable settlement.
- Hedera x402: Agent-initiated micropayments for shipment verification services.
- AI-Agent Workflow: Automated trade discovery, payment-policy checks, evidence purchasing, and verification coordination.
- EIP-712 Signatures: Cryptographically authorized shipment attestations.
- Tokenized Receivables: NFT-based representation of investor repayment rights.

Current Prototype

TrustMeBro has deployed its V2 smart contracts on Whitechain Sepolia and demonstrated invoice creation, importer confirmation, and an actual Hedera testnet x402 payment. The current shipment-verification integration uses explicitly labeled simulated evidence rather than authenticated live carrier data. Completing the full onchain verification-to-financing demonstration and integrating real logistics data are ongoing development goals.

Our Vision

We aim to make trade financing more accessible, transparent, and programmable, starting with small and medium-sized exporters in sectors such as agriculture, coffee, textiles, and manufacturing.

Instead of allowing capital to remain locked in unpaid invoices, TrustMeBro creates a pathway for verified trade receivables to attract investment.

Because a growing business shouldn't have to reject its next order while waiting to get paid for its last one.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
TrustMeBro is built as a cross-chain, agent-powered trade financing platform combining Whitechain, Hedera x402, Solidity smart contracts, TypeScript-based autonomous agents, and a Next.js frontend.

The biggest engineering challenge was connecting two different processes: verifying that an international trade meets its agreed shipment conditions and allowing investors to finance that trade without relying on a centralized intermediary to manage the money.

We divided the system into four interconnected layers: the trade-financing contracts, an autonomous verification agent, an x402-powered evidence service, and a user-facing application.

1. Whitechain — The Financial Settlement Layer

We developed and deployed three interconnected Solidity smart contracts on Whitechain Sepolia (chain ID 1874).

TradePilotFinance.sol is the core financial engine. It manages trade creation, importer confirmation, verification status, funding eligibility, investor financing, and repayment distribution.

ImporterReputation.sol manages the importer's onchain Trust Score. Every new importer starts with a score of 60, capped at 93. Repayment and default outcomes influence reputation, which determines how much financing can be advanced against future invoices.

ReceivableNote.sol represents investors' repayment claims through restricted-transfer NFTs. When an investor finances an invoice, they receive a receivable NFT. The smart contract pays the current eligible NFT holder when the importer repays.

We implemented a reputation-based financing formula:

- Base financing amount = 97% of invoice value.
- Available advance = Base amount × Importer Trust Score / 100.
- Investor profit = 3% of the funded advance.
- Platform fee = 1% of the invoice face value.

For example, an importer with a Trust Score of 80 can unlock a 77.6% advance against a verified invoice.

The importer repays the full invoice amount, and the contract atomically distributes funds to the investor, exporter, and platform. We use access controls, restricted NFT transfers, reentrancy protection, and transaction-level validation to protect the financing lifecycle.

2. Hedera x402 — Autonomous Payments for Verification

This is one of our most interesting technical integrations.

International shipment verification normally involves requesting information from external services. Instead of requiring an operator to manually purchase and upload every report, we built an autonomous payment workflow using Hedera x402.

Our agent is implemented in TypeScript and communicates with a verification merchant through HTTP.

When an importer confirms a trade, the agent can discover the agreement on Whitechain and prepare a shipment evidence request.

The merchant responds with an HTTP 402 payment requirement. The agent examines the quoted amount, merchant account, Hedera network, token, and spending policy before authorizing payment.

We integrated Hedera testnet USDC payments, an x402 payment facilitator, and Hedera Mirror Node verification.

Importantly, payment success is not assumed merely because an HTTP request succeeds. The workflow independently checks the payment settlement, recipient, token, and amount.

We successfully executed a real 0.30 test USDC x402 payment on Hedera testnet for our prototype.

The payment and evidence-processing logic are deterministic. We do not depend on an LLM inventing shipment details or arbitrarily deciding whether an invoice is trustworthy.

3. EIP-712 — Connecting Hedera Verification to Whitechain

Hedera handles the evidence-service payment, while Whitechain manages trade finance. Connecting these systems required a secure way to carry an offchain verification result into an EVM smart contract.

We implemented this using EIP-712 typed-data signatures.

After obtaining and validating a shipment report, our verifier service constructs an attestation containing:

- Whitechain trade ID
- Hash of the agreed trade terms
- Shipment document commitment
- Verified quantity and shipment stage
- Evidence report hash
- Unique nonce
- Timestamp and expiration

The dedicated verifier signs this structured attestation using an account authorized with "VERIFIER_ROLE".

The Whitechain finance contract exposes "verifyAttestation()", which validates the signature, authorized signer, trade commitments, nonce, timestamp, and shipment conditions.

Only an acceptable result can make the invoice eligible for financing.

We deliberately separate the verifier's signing authority from transaction submission. This allows the service to sign the evidence while a user or relayer submits the resulting transaction.

For our prototype, we implemented a manual MetaMask relay so a wallet owner can review and authorize the Whitechain transaction without sharing an Admin private key with the backend.

This creates an application-level connection between Hedera payments and Whitechain financial verification without requiring a conventional cross-chain token bridge.

4. Backend Architecture and Reliability

Our backend is built with Node.js and TypeScript, using separate services for evidence verification and agent execution.

The verification merchant serves paid evidence requests, validates shipment observations against agreed trade metadata, and produces signed attestations.

The Hedera agent manages trade discovery, payment policies, spending authorization, settlement verification, and durable execution state.

We implemented persistent jobs, duplicate-payment protections, payment reservations, transaction reconciliation, and explicit recovery states.

A particularly interesting challenge appeared during live testing: the merchant was caching a simulated observation, causing a report to become older than the permitted 300-second freshness window.

The Hedera payment had already succeeded, but the evidence was correctly rejected.

Rather than weakening validation or spending again, we fixed the merchant's fixture-loading behavior and developed a recovery mechanism that preserves the original paid report, rechecks the payment, and permits a separately authorized fresh demo attestation.

We also implemented versioned recovery history to prevent accidental overwrites or duplicate payment attempts.

This was important because paying for evidence and successfully verifying a trade are two separate outcomes, and the system must handle failures between them.

We also developed Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) audit components for recording payment and verification references, supporting a traceable history of agent activity.

5. Frontend and Developer Tooling

We use Next.js, React, and TypeScript for the user-facing application, alongside wallet interactions on Whitechain.

The application is organized around the main participants in trade financing:

Exporters create invoices and request financing.

Importers review trade agreements and manage repayment.

Investors inspect financing opportunities, fund receivables, and track their NFT-based claims.

Administrators and verification operators monitor shipment checks, transaction references, and verification outcomes.

We also built a separate React-based contract testing interface to exercise wallet connections, role checks, invoice creation, agreement confirmation, funding, repayment, and receivable NFT operations.

For Solidity development, we used Hardhat-based testing and contract integration tooling. We additionally wrote TypeScript backend tests covering payment failures, signature validation, stale evidence, duplicate transactions, and recovery behavior.

6. Partner Technologies and Their Benefits

Whitechain provides the EVM-compatible settlement infrastructure. It enables programmable financing, transparent repayment distribution, importer reputation, and tokenized receivable ownership.

Hedera provides the payment infrastructure for agent-initiated verification purchases. Its testnet token transfers and Mirror Node records allow us to independently verify payment execution.

x402 enables a machine-to-machine payment workflow where an agent can discover the price of a verification request and pay for the response without a traditional subscription or manual checkout.

EIP-712 lets us transform validated offchain shipment observations into structured, verifiable signatures that the Whitechain smart contracts can authenticate.

NFTs make investor repayment rights representable as onchain assets, with controlled transfers and settlement to the eligible current holder.

7. What Makes Our Implementation Different?

The most interesting part of TrustMeBro isn't simply combining an AI agent with DeFi.

It's connecting commercial evidence, autonomous payment, reputation-based financing, and programmable settlement into one workflow.

A trade starts as an agreement between two businesses. An agent purchases verification information. A cryptographic attestation binds the evidence to the trade. The financing contract determines funding eligibility and creates an investor repayment claim. Finally, a successful importer repayment distributes funds and updates reputation.

Instead of trusting an invoice just because someone uploaded it, the system is designed to require agreed trade commitments and authorized verification before financing.

Current Prototype and Next Steps

We deployed the V2 contracts on Whitechain Sepolia, tested invoice creation and importer confirmation, implemented the Hedera x402 purchasing workflow, and confirmed an actual Hedera testnet payment.

Our current shipment observations are explicitly labeled DEMO_SIMULATION. We do not claim that they represent independently authenticated live cargo movements.

The contract financing mechanics have been tested, while completing and validating the entire verification-to-financing lifecycle through the unified dashboard remains part of the integration work.

The next major production milestone is integrating authenticated logistics data providers and expanding the pilot to real exporters and financing participants.

Our goal is to turn verified trade activity into accessible, programmable working capital—where an agent can help establish the evidence, investors can finance the receivable, and smart contracts handle settlement.

projects.title: Supersonic
projects.description: Supersonic: real-time World Chain MEV intelligence with pay-per-analysis APIs for Arc.
projects.project_description: Supersonic turns any Chain(For this project we will use worldchain) activity into investigation-ready MEV intelligence for researchers, developers, and software agents. Instead of forcing users to reconstruct an incident from disconnected logs and contract calls, it indexes execution data directly from a reth ExEx, organizes it into queryable datasets, and connects analytics with an SGIP investigation interface. A user can begin with a World Chain transaction hash and move toward a structured investigation of the activity around it. For this Continuity feature, we built a TypeScript payment layer around the existing /v1/mev/analytics API. The layer introduces per-request x402 payment challenges, explicit payment and fulfillment states, idempotent retries, and stored responses and receipts. It is designed for Circle Gateway on Arc Testnet, with the Arc payment or Gateway transfer identifier kept separate from the World Chain transaction being investigated. The product opportunity is pay-per-analysis blockchain intelligence. An agent can request a specific investigation without a subscription or a custom billing integration, while developers gain a practical way to monetize high-value API work. Supersonic combines a specialized data pipeline, an investigation-focused user experience, and programmable access control in one product.
projects.how_its_made: We preserved the existing Supersonic core and added the payment feature at its API boundary rather than creating a parallel analytics product. A Rust reth ExEx streams World Chain execution data over gRPC on a Unix socket to the Rust tank-engine. ClickHouse stores the queryable datasets. Go services provide the REST and WebSocket APIs, with Valkey/Redis-backed caching, API keys, and rate limiting, while the Python SGIP interface supports investigation and MEV analysis. The new TypeScript seller uses a node:http adapter around the existing /v1/mev/analytics route. It parses PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, returns PAYMENT-REQUIRED challenges, and records PAYMENT-RESPONSE results. The seller engine binds idempotency to network|payer|nonce, validates route and payment terms before reservation, calls the Gateway settlement interface before upstream fulfillment, and commits fulfillment only for an upstream 2xx response. Same-binding retries return the stored response without another settlement or upstream call. Reliability was treated as part of the product, not an afterthought. The ledger uses lease owners, generations, fencing, and retry budgets; ambiguous submissions fail closed for reconciliation; and Gateway acceptance, batching evidence, and final settlement remain distinct. The HTTP adapter allowlists the paid route, caps request bodies, refuses redirects, keeps the upstream API key server-side, and applies upstream and settlement timeouts. Circle’s x402 batching SDK gives the integration concrete Gateway types and behavior to test against, while Arc provides the intended stablecoin-payment environment. The most useful implementation choice was to keep the seller thin and reuse the real analytics boundary. We also built deterministic concurrency regressions with controlled interleavings instead of timing-dependent sleeps. At the reviewed local HTTP checkpoint, 137 Vitest and fast-check tests passed, using a real local HTTP server and fixture upstream, with unit, integration, and SDK-contract testing kept clearly separated.

projects.title: Udhari
projects.description: Invoice financing for small businesses using Hedera and Chainlink.
projects.project_description: Udhari is an invoice financing platform that helps small businesses get paid immediately instead of waiting 30–90 days for buyers to pay their invoices. A business can submit an invoice linked to a GST e-invoice. Chainlink CRE independently verifies the invoice against the GST portal, checks the buyer's creditworthiness, and ensures the invoice hasn't already been financed. Once approved, the invoice is tokenized into an individual bond on Hedera using the Asset Tokenization Studio. Verified investors can purchase these bonds using stablecoins, allowing the business to receive its payment upfront. When the original buyer pays on the due date, investors can redeem their bonds for the full invoice value. Udhari also includes investor KYC verification, sanctions checks, duplicate invoice prevention, and automated monitoring for overdue payments. Our goal is to make invoice financing more accessible to small businesses that are often overlooked by traditional financial institutions.
projects.how_its_made: Udhari combines Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio with Chainlink CRE to build a verifiable invoice financing workflow. We built a frontend application where businesses can register, submit invoices, and track their financing status. A backend API handles application requests and triggers Chainlink CRE workflows. Chainlink CRE independently fetches and verifies invoice information from the GST portal, checks buyer creditworthiness, detects previously financed invoices, and performs investor verification through a KYC provider. Once the checks pass, our Hedera smart contract enforces the financing rules and tokenizes the approved invoice into an individual bond using the Asset Tokenization Studio. Investors connect their wallets, complete verification, and fund bonds using stablecoins. Funding transactions are sent directly from their wallets to Hedera. We also implemented smart contract restrictions so only verified investor wallets can hold the bonds, along with duplicate invoice prevention and redemption logic. Finally, Chainlink CRE monitors active deals for overdue payments and funding issues, allowing the platform to pause affected deals when necessary. The complete workflow is currently implemented and demonstrated on Hedera testnet.

projects.title: bagseven
projects.description: Payments, living entitlements, and spending permissions for apps and AI agents.
projects.project_description: Bagseven is a billing and entitlement infrastructure platform for applications and AI agents. It turns a verified payment into a clear, enforceable answer: what can this customer or agent use, how much can they use, and until when? Providers define plans that connect pricing directly to product access: a feature, USDT price, credit allocation, access duration, and receiving wallet. Customers pay the provider directly on Whitechain. Bagseven verifies settlement and creates a living entitlement on Arkiv—a queryable record of the customer’s rights, remaining credits, and expiry. The same entitlement powers access checks in an application, backend service, or MCP-connected assistant. The core innovation is separating three independent states: payment, renewal, and access. A successful payment proves settlement; it does not grant unlimited access. Cancelling renewal changes future billing intent; it does not remove an already-paid period. Access is determined by the living entitlement’s enabled state, remaining credits, and paid-through timestamp. This gives providers a consistent foundation for time-limited plans, prepaid credits, and metered features. Bagseven’s distinctive architecture separates the right to use a service from the authority to spend money. An agent consuming prepaid access uses entitlement credits without making another payment or requiring a funded spending mandate. When it requests a new payment, a separate authorization layer checks both the required entitlement and an owner-defined mandate. On-chain limits constrain purchases, spending windows, lifetime budgets, recipients, and delegated workers. World ID verifies the human behind authorization, Whitechain supplies payment evidence and spending enforcement, and Arkiv supplies living access records. Bagseven connects these through a unified billing lifecycle, SDKs, APIs, and MCP tools. Its core technical contribution is this payment-to-entitlement lifecycle and the separate enforcement of access rights and spending authority. Providers can monetize a service once and serve both people and agents through the same access model, while retaining control over pricing, usage, expiry, and automated spending.
projects.how_its_made: Bagseven is built around one core idea: a payment should create a precise, verifiable right to use a service—not just a successful checkout screen. We implemented a billing-to-entitlement lifecycle that applications and AI agents can both use. Providers define the commercial terms A provider creates a plan containing a feature identifier, USDT price, credit allocation, access duration, and receiving wallet. This connects the billing configuration directly to the product’s access rules. For example, a plan can sell 100 document-processing credits that remain valid for 30 days. Customers pay the provider directly Bagseven creates a checkout session for the selected plan and customer identity. The customer approves a USDT payment to the provider’s wallet on Whitechain. The backend verifies the transaction’s token, recipient, amount, payer authorization, and confirmations, and checks that the payment has not already been redeemed. Verified settlement becomes a living entitlement After payment verification, Bagseven creates an entitlement on Arkiv. It records who holds access, which feature it covers, how many credits remain, and when the paid period ends. Applications query this record instead of treating a historical payment receipt as permanent access. Applications and agents enforce the same access rules React, Node.js, and agent SDKs expose access checks and credit consumption. MCP tools make those capabilities available to assistants. Numeric features deduct credits as they are used; boolean features remain enabled until expiry. Server-side checks enforce access before protected work. A key architectural decision is that using prepaid access does not trigger another USDT payment or require a funded spending mandate. Entitlement credits represent service usage, not money. New agent payments require separate spending authority When an agent requests a new payment, Bagseven checks the required entitlement and a registered worker’s mandate. Solidity contracts on Whitechain enforce per-purchase, time-window, lifetime, recipient, and worker-allocation limits. Owners can delegate narrower allocations to child agents and revoke future spending. The core technical contribution is the separation of three clocks and two authorities. The three clocks are payment settlement, renewal preference, and current access. Cancelling renewal preserves the already-paid period; an expired or exhausted entitlement denies further usage even when its payment remains visible on-chain. The two authorities are permission to use a service and permission to spend money. Keeping them separate allows an assistant to consume purchased access without receiving unrestricted financial authority. We connected these flows using a TypeScript monorepo with Next.js interfaces, Fastify services, PostgreSQL, Redis, Solidity, and viem. World ID verifies the human authorizing access, Whitechain provides settlement and spending enforcement, and Arkiv stores living entitlement state. PostgreSQL tracks billing and agent records, while Redis coordinates payment claims and request idempotency. Providers can also authorize prefunded operating-gas accounts with encrypted delegated keys, expiry, and fee budgets. Those signing restrictions are enforced by the server; the mandate’s spending restrictions are enforced on-chain.
