Access is determined by the living entitlement’s enabled state, remaining credits, and paid-through timestamp. This gives providers a consistent foundation for time-limited plans, prepaid credits, and metered features.

Bagseven’s distinctive architecture separates the right to use a service from the authority to spend money. An agent consuming prepaid access uses entitlement credits without making another payment or requiring a funded spending mandate. When it requests a new payment, a separate authorization layer checks both the required entitlement and an owner-defined mandate. On-chain limits constrain purchases, spending windows, lifetime budgets, recipients, and delegated workers.

World ID verifies the human behind authorization, Whitechain supplies payment evidence and spending enforcement, and Arkiv supplies living access records. Bagseven connects these through a unified billing lifecycle, SDKs, APIs, and MCP tools.

Its core technical contribution is this payment-to-entitlement lifecycle and the separate enforcement of access rights and spending authority. Providers can monetize a service once and serve both people and agents through the same access model, while retaining control over pricing, usage, expiry, and automated spending.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Bagseven is built around one core idea: a payment should create a precise, verifiable right to use a service—not just a successful checkout screen. We implemented a billing-to-entitlement lifecycle that applications and AI agents can both use.

1. Providers define the commercial terms

A provider creates a plan containing a feature identifier, USDT price, credit allocation, access duration, and receiving wallet. This connects the billing configuration directly to the product’s access rules. For example, a plan can sell 100 document-processing credits that remain valid for 30 days.

2. Customers pay the provider directly

Bagseven creates a checkout session for the selected plan and customer identity. The customer approves a USDT payment to the provider’s wallet on Whitechain. The backend verifies the transaction’s token, recipient, amount, payer authorization, and confirmations, and checks that the payment has not already been redeemed.

3. Verified settlement becomes a living entitlement

After payment verification, Bagseven creates an entitlement on Arkiv. It records who holds access, which feature it covers, how many credits remain, and when the paid period ends. Applications query this record instead of treating a historical payment receipt as permanent access.

4. Applications and agents enforce the same access rules

React, Node.js, and agent SDKs expose access checks and credit consumption. MCP tools make those capabilities available to assistants. Numeric features deduct credits as they are used; boolean features remain enabled until expiry. Server-side checks enforce access before protected work.

A key architectural decision is that using prepaid access does not trigger another USDT payment or require a funded spending mandate. Entitlement credits represent service usage, not money.

5. New agent payments require separate spending authority

When an agent requests a new payment, Bagseven checks the required entitlement and a registered worker’s mandate. Solidity contracts on Whitechain enforce per-purchase, time-window, lifetime, recipient, and worker-allocation limits. Owners can delegate narrower allocations to child agents and revoke future spending.

The core technical contribution is the separation of three clocks and two authorities.

The three clocks are payment settlement, renewal preference, and current access. Cancelling renewal preserves the already-paid period; an expired or exhausted entitlement denies further usage even when its payment remains visible on-chain.

The two authorities are permission to use a service and permission to spend money. Keeping them separate allows an assistant to consume purchased access without receiving unrestricted financial authority.

We connected these flows using a TypeScript monorepo with Next.js interfaces, Fastify services, PostgreSQL, Redis, Solidity, and viem. World ID verifies the human authorizing access, Whitechain provides settlement and spending enforcement, and Arkiv stores living entitlement state. PostgreSQL tracks billing and agent records, while Redis coordinates payment claims and request idempotency.

Providers can also authorize prefunded operating-gas accounts with encrypted delegated keys, expiry, and fee budgets. Those signing restrictions are enforced by the server; the mandate’s spending restrictions are enforced on-chain.

projects.title: KneeDeep
projects.description: AI agents pay per query for live Mumbai flood reports from verified humans; reporters get paid.
projects.project_description: During Mumbai's monsoon, a delivery rider can lose an hour—or a vehicle—to a flooded subway that no weather API knows about. Weather data tells an agent it rained. It doesn't tell the agent whether a particular street is passable right now. KneeDeep is a paid, real-time API for street-level flood conditions, powered by human reports and built for AI agents. People verify their uniqueness through World ID and report conditions using five levels: dry, ankle, knee, waist, or road closed. Reports and votes are stored on Arkiv with a three-hour expiry because street conditions change quickly. AI agents call GET /v1/conditions . The endpoint returns HTTP 402, allowing agents to pay 0.1 HBAR per query through x402 on Hedera, using their own account. Responses include the condition, confidence, supporting evidence, and a vehicle passability verdict: safe, risky, blocked, or unknown. Our fusion engine combines independent reports, accounts for recency and disputes, and never treats missing data as safe. A safe verdict requires corroboration from at least two independent people. A dispatch agent checks six checkpoints across two routes, pays for the required queries, and chooses the safer route—or holds the delivery if all routes are blocked. 70% of eligible query revenue is allocated to contributors whose reports were corroborated by other verified people. A Chainlink CRE workflow independently recomputes conditions from public Arkiv evidence and publishes an attestation on Sepolia. The API exposes whether its results match the attestation. The demo runs on testnets and uses clearly labelled simulated scenarios. The CRE demonstration uses the simulator's trusted-sender configuration; production DON signature verification is a separate deployment step.
projects.how_its_made: KneeDeep is a TypeScript monorepo consisting of a NestJS API, PostgreSQL database, Vite + React + Leaflet frontend, standalone dispatch agent, and Chainlink CRE workflow with a Foundry smart contract. A single Docker image runs on Render, with the API serving the web application. Hedera + x402: The paid conditions endpoint uses @x402/express and @x402/hedera , with the Blocky402 facilitator. The agent signs HBAR payments from its own account using @x402/fetch , with per-query and per-trip spending caps. Invalid requests are not charged. Eligible reporter earnings are paid through the Hiero SDK using batched transfers. Database reservations, pre-generated transaction IDs, advisory locks, and Mirror Node reconciliation protect against duplicate payouts after failures. Arkiv: Reports and votes are public entities with native TTLs. Votes expire with their associated reports, so evidence expiration is handled by the data layer rather than a cleanup cron job. Agents and independent workflows can inspect the underlying evidence without relying on KneeDeep's API. World ID: IDKit Proof of Human is used to limit duplicate reporter identities. The relying-party request is signed server-side, legacy proofs are rejected, and the public reporter ID is derived from a salted nullifier hash. The nullifier itself is not stored. Fusion engine: A deterministic, dependency-free function combines reports and votes. Evidence recency decays with a 45-minute half-life, each human counts once, corroboration follows 1 − 0.5^n , and disputes count against a reported level. Ties resolve toward the more severe condition because routing decisions are safety-critical. Chainlink CRE: The same fusion logic is compiled into the CRE workflow. Each workflow node reads public Arkiv JSON-RPC data and recomputes area conditions for a shared scheduled timestamp. CRE consensus requires identical canonical results before publishing an attestation to the Sepolia contract. The API compares its condition results against the latest attestation. The current demonstration uses the CRE simulation forwarder with a trusted-sender restriction; production deployment would use the signature-verifying Keystone Forwarder. Engineering challenges: Identified and fixed a simulation-forwarder trust issue that could have allowed unauthorized attestations. Used PostgreSQL advisory locks and reservation rows to enforce one report per person per cell per 30 minutes despite slow Arkiv writes. Cross-checks agent trip records against the server's settled-payment ledger. 127 tests across the API, agent, contract, and workflow.

During Mumbai's monsoon, a delivery rider can lose an hour—or a vehicle—to a flooded subway that no weather API knows about. Weather data tells an agent it rained. It doesn't tell the agent whether a particular street is passable right now.

**KneeDeep is a paid, real-time API for street-level flood conditions, powered by human reports and built for AI agents.**

- People verify their uniqueness through World ID and report conditions using five levels: dry, ankle, knee, waist, or road closed. Reports and votes are stored on Arkiv with a three-hour expiry because street conditions change quickly.
- AI agents call `GET /v1/conditions`. The endpoint returns HTTP 402, allowing agents to pay 0.1 HBAR per query through x402 on Hedera, using their own account. Responses include the condition, confidence, supporting evidence, and a vehicle passability verdict: safe, risky, blocked, or unknown.
- Our fusion engine combines independent reports, accounts for recency and disputes, and never treats missing data as safe. A safe verdict requires corroboration from at least two independent people.
- A dispatch agent checks six checkpoints across two routes, pays for the required queries, and chooses the safer route—or holds the delivery if all routes are blocked.
- 70% of eligible query revenue is allocated to contributors whose reports were corroborated by other verified people.
- A Chainlink CRE workflow independently recomputes conditions from public Arkiv evidence and publishes an attestation on Sepolia. The API exposes whether its results match the attestation.

The demo runs on testnets and uses clearly labelled simulated scenarios. The CRE demonstration uses the simulator's trusted-sender configuration; production DON signature verification is a separate deployment step.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
KneeDeep is a TypeScript monorepo consisting of a NestJS API, PostgreSQL database, Vite + React + Leaflet frontend, standalone dispatch agent, and Chainlink CRE workflow with a Foundry smart contract. A single Docker image runs on Render, with the API serving the web application.

**Hedera + x402:** The paid conditions endpoint uses `@x402/express` and `@x402/hedera`, with the Blocky402 facilitator. The agent signs HBAR payments from its own account using `@x402/fetch`, with per-query and per-trip spending caps. Invalid requests are not charged. Eligible reporter earnings are paid through the Hiero SDK using batched transfers. Database reservations, pre-generated transaction IDs, advisory locks, and Mirror Node reconciliation protect against duplicate payouts after failures.

**Arkiv:** Reports and votes are public entities with native TTLs. Votes expire with their associated reports, so evidence expiration is handled by the data layer rather than a cleanup cron job. Agents and independent workflows can inspect the underlying evidence without relying on KneeDeep's API.

**World ID:** IDKit Proof of Human is used to limit duplicate reporter identities. The relying-party request is signed server-side, legacy proofs are rejected, and the public reporter ID is derived from a salted nullifier hash. The nullifier itself is not stored.

**Fusion engine:** A deterministic, dependency-free function combines reports and votes. Evidence recency decays with a 45-minute half-life, each human counts once, corroboration follows `1 − 0.5^n`, and disputes count against a reported level. Ties resolve toward the more severe condition because routing decisions are safety-critical.

**Chainlink CRE:** The same fusion logic is compiled into the CRE workflow. Each workflow node reads public Arkiv JSON-RPC data and recomputes area conditions for a shared scheduled timestamp. CRE consensus requires identical canonical results before publishing an attestation to the Sepolia contract. The API compares its condition results against the latest attestation. The current demonstration uses the CRE simulation forwarder with a trusted-sender restriction; production deployment would use the signature-verifying Keystone Forwarder.

**Engineering challenges:**
- Identified and fixed a simulation-forwarder trust issue that could have allowed unauthorized attestations.
- Used PostgreSQL advisory locks and reservation rows to enforce one report per person per cell per 30 minutes despite slow Arkiv writes.
- Cross-checks agent trip records against the server's settled-payment ledger.

127 tests across the API, agent, contract, and workflow.

projects.title: FairDrop
projects.description: FairDrop: Human-verified Web3 ticketing that fights bots and makes ticket distribution fairer.
projects.project_description: FairDrop is a Web3-powered ticketing platform designed to make event ticket distribution fairer, more transparent, and resistant to bots and Sybil attacks. Traditional ticketing platforms often struggle with bots and individuals using multiple accounts to claim several tickets, leaving genuine attendees with fewer opportunities. FairDrop addresses this problem by integrating World ID Proof of Human verification into the ticket-claiming process. Before claiming a ticket, users connect their EVM-compatible wallet and verify that they are a unique human. Our backend validates the World ID proof and checks whether that verified person has already claimed a ticket for the same event. This prevents duplicate claims across different wallets, helping ensure a fairer distribution process. FairDrop also uses Arkiv as a decentralized, queryable data layer for public event and ticket listing information. For payments, the platform integrates Arc and USDC, enabling stablecoin-based ticket purchases. MongoDB manages application data, reservations, and operational states, while World ID, Arkiv, and Arc provide human verification, decentralized data infrastructure, and blockchain payment capabilities. Our vision is simple: make event ticketing more accessible to genuine attendees by combining privacy-preserving human verification with transparent Web3 infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made: FairDrop is built using Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend, with an Express 5 and TypeScript backend. For human verification, we integrated World ID IDKit 4.0 and Proof of Human. The frontend initiates the verification flow, while the backend handles request signing and authoritative proof verification. Verified nullifiers are used to enforce event-specific uniqueness, preventing the same human from claiming multiple tickets for the same event, even when using different wallets. Arkiv is integrated through the official @arkiv-network/sdk to provide a decentralized and queryable data layer for event and ticket information. This allows public event records to be discovered independently of the application's private operational database. For payments, we use Arc infrastructure and USDC, with wallet connectivity built around EVM-compatible wallets such as MetaMask and other injected wallet providers. The Express backend separates verification, claims, Arkiv operations, and payment logic into integration modules. MongoDB is intended for private application state, reservations, and claim management, while blockchain infrastructure handles public records and payments. One important architectural decision is separating human identity from wallet identity: a wallet represents an account, but World ID helps establish that a claim comes from a unique human. This is central to FairDrop's approach to reducing Sybil-based ticket abuse.

projects.title: ACR
projects.description: Agent treasury and wallet holds $0, every bill priced on-chain, idle float earns until spent.
projects.project_description:
An AI agent with a funded wallet has a worst case equal to its balance. Give it a
spending limit and the worst case is the limit. Neither asks the question an
overcharge actually fails: is this a fair price? Float holds the budget in a vault instead. The agent's own wallet holds zero permanently, with a test asserting it before and after every payment the agent
causes. Each request names the printId of the compute price it was quoted
against. The vault recomputes the fair total itself, refuses anything above a
band, pulls the exact shortfall out of a real yield venue, and pays the
seller — in one transaction. 1 · It prices the purchase. A seller quoting 3× is refused on chain, in
English, with the fair counter-price attached. Transaction 0xb746116a… , block
70931213: Denied , code 10, reason "quote exceeds ACR fair band" , quote
3150000 against fair 1050000. 2 · It funds just in time. Transaction 0x364723c6… , block 70931234. Log 30
is Pulled(530250, 530250) from the Morpho Vault V2 position; log 32 transfers
1055250 USDC to the seller. The figures differ because the vault pulled the shortfall , not the payment — the rest was already in the buffer. That $0.53 was
earning yield in the previous block. Arc serves no debug_traceTransaction , so log order is the proof , which means anyone with an ordinary node can check it
rather than only someone with an archive node. 3 · What it cannot authorise, it parks. Over the per-request threshold a
request is not refused — a checkpoint opens on chain and waits for a verified
human's single-use EIP-712 signature, gated by World ID . The token is
validated against a fixed ladder of nine named refusals , and we report the first rung that failed rather than the last, because a stale auth_time and an
unverified issuer are different problems and "verification failed" cannot tell a
person whether to retry or stop. Denial, expiry and a failed verification are
each recorded on chain: a refusal is evidence, not silence. An approval widens the band; it never removes it. A person can authorise paying more than usual.
Nobody — including the approver — can authorise paying an unpriced amount to an
unapproved seller. Idle float sits in two tiers: a live Morpho Vault V2, and a USYC reserve sleeve
for Circle's tokenised treasury fund. That sleeve is real, written against the
Teller's verified ABI, and runs on Arc Testnet against a stand-in fund we deployed
and named SimUsycTeller so the explorer says so — because Circle's allowlist is
a 24-to-48-hour support ticket we could not clear during the event. We hold no
USYC, the production reserve slot is deliberately address(0) , and the acceptance
suite reports that on every run rather than letting the claim drift. Live on Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), every contract verified on Blockscout. 335
contract tests, 41 unit tests, and 15 acceptance checks that run against the live
chain and print what they observed rather than a tick. Honest limits. Prices are published per-provider list prices, not executed
fills — what the band constrains is what the vault will pay . The confidence
interval is a provider spread, not a forecast error bound. Float adds no yield of
its own; it shows accrued value, never a projected APY. requirePolicyCheckpoint is false on this chain, so the human-approval and guest-enrolment paths are
not exercised on Arc Testnet — they are covered by 80 contract tests and a
ten-leg local-chain walk, and the World submission says which chain it shows. And
one finding from our own audit, disclosed rather than buried: the executor can
resolve an open checkpoint, including writing EXPIRED over a signature a human
already gave. It is unrepaired.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts. Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry. FloatVault is the treasury: a
twelve-rung refusal ladder ( D_PAUSED =1 through D_DAILY_CAP =12, each a named
code in an event rather than a revert), EIP-712 checkpoint approvals, and an ISleeve interface — depositIdle / withdrawExact / valueUsdc — so the yield
venue is swappable without touching the treasury. The single unit conversion fairUsdc6 = priceWad * units / 1e12 appears exactly once and has a test pinning
it, because getting it wrong makes the fair band un-fireable while looking fully
implemented. Off-chain. TypeScript with viem 2.55 drives the keeper, the two demo agents,
the policy compiler and a 15-check acceptance suite ( node:test under tsx). The
dashboard is Next.js 16 / React 19 reading the chain directly through viem and
SWR — no server between the page and Arc — with the money path rendered in
three.js. A FastAPI + web3.py service holds the World ID gate. An MCP server
( acr-mcp , published to npm) exposes the tools to any agent host. Why Arc. USDC is the native gas token, so the treasury, the gas and the
payment are one asset — a forecast denominated in dollars is simultaneously a
forecast of gas. Arc Studio compiled the treasury policy from an English
sentence into JSON, audited the vault, and wrote two of the three dashboard pages.
Its output is checked, not trusted: our own validator refuses an invalid config
before a transaction is built — exactly the assurance Studio itself flagged when
it said, unprompted, "I didn't run it through a schema validator, but I checked
it by eye." Partner technology that actually changed the design. Morpho Vault V2 on Arc is
the working yield venue, and it is permissionless — all four transfer gates are
the zero address — which is what lets a contract hold shares, and is why the
just-in-time pull is one Solidity call instead of two transactions narrated as
one. An Eco Sauce compiled program asks that venue whether it could deliver a
given shortfall before anything is signed, with its Pot deployed on Arc (667,003
gas, verified). Pyth appears
as a negative result: deployed but dormant on Arc Testnet, every feed reverting PriceFeedNotFound() , which argues for a pushed print better than any benchmark
comparison could. Circle's USYC — the reserve tier, and what it cost to build honestly. Idle
float has two tiers and the second is Circle's tokenised treasury fund. UsycSleeve implements the same three-verb ISleeve interface as the Morpho
one, so the treasury gained a T-bill position without a line of it changing. Two
design decisions fell out of reading the Teller's verified ABI instead of
assuming one — Blockscout had not resolved the EIP-1967 proxy, so the
implementation came from storage slot 0x3608…2bbc → 0x238dc235…adf6 , 60
functions, and the verbs turned out to be deposit / redeem / previewDeposit / previewRedeem , not the buy() / sell() our own earlier notes had recorded.
First, no price oracle : the Teller previews its own redemption net of its own
fee, so the price comes from the counterparty that will honour it, and an oracle
would only add a trusted third party and a staleness window to a number already
published. Second, sizing by preview rather than by dividing through a NAV —
the redemption scales the share balance against the previewed value of the whole
position, rounded the way that cannot refuse a correct payment. Replacing that
with naive division fails two tests, one of them a real vault payment. It runs against a stand-in fund, because Circle's allowlist is a support ticket
with a 24-to-48-hour turnaround we could not clear during the event. SimUsyc and SimUsycTeller live in src/sim/ rather than test/ precisely because they leave the machine : a deployed contract shows its name on the explorer, and a MockUsycTeller sitting on a public chain would be the dishonest label. The
sleeve in front of them is the real UsycSleeve ( 0x6D2A34ed…972E ), unchanged,
with a real round trip on Arc Testnet — park 1 USDC, pull 0.5, valueUsdc reading 0 → 999999 → 499997. When the allowlist lands, one constructor argument
changes and nothing else does . The production vault's reserve slot stays address(0) meanwhile, and acceptance check T15 asserts that on every run, so the
claim cannot quietly drift into "we hold USYC". World ID — the human leg of the same product. The escalation path is gated by
World ID Agent Pass over an OIDC device flow. A parked payment names its own
request hash, a human authenticates freshly, and a FastAPI service validates the
token against a fixed ladder of nine named refusals — malformed_token , bad_signature , wrong_issuer , wrong_audience , expired , assurance_not_accepted , amr_not_accepted , auth_time_outside_window , not_the_enrolled_treasurer . The nine are pinned by a test rather than by prose: test_every_named_reason_is_reachable asserts set-equality between that tuple and
the reasons nine fixtures actually produce, so the count cannot drift away from
the sentence without a red test. The enrolled person is pinned on chain as keccak256("acr.treasurer::" + iss + 0x1f + sub) — one-shot, so a treasury names
its treasurer exactly once. The detail that justified building a ladder rather than a boolean: our live token
came back with amr = ["pop","user","mfa"] — the passkey shape, which World's
own docs say does not assert a fresh World proof — while acr claimed orb. The
spend cleared, correctly, because orb assurance is what that path asks for. The
same token is refused for a policy change , which requires face and forbids mfa . One token that can move money and cannot change the rules. The capability
split is deliberate too: the terminal holds the signing key and cannot move money,
the press holds the registrar key and cannot mint a request, so neither half can
issue a budget alone. The hacky parts worth naming. Arc serves no debug_traceTransaction , so just-in-time funding is proven by log order within one transaction. A weaker tool giving a stronger result: an
ordinary node can verify it. Arc's USDC at 0x3600…0000 is precompile-backed, so a forge script that moves
it dies in simulation with StackUnderflow and seeding has to go through cast . The same transfer emits two Transfer events — 2e18 from the
precompile and 2e6 from the ERC-20 view — one ledger with two decimals, visible
on chain. Arc silently drops transactions under 20 Gwei. No receipt, no error. Morpho Vault V2 returns zero from every max* function by design , so the
obvious maxWithdraw sizing reports an empty sleeve forever. valueUsdc converts the share balance instead. Shares are 18 decimals against 6-decimal
USDC, so convertToAssets must be fed shares and never an asset amount. USYC's Teller returned maxDeposit = 5,723,443 for an address whose
deposits revert NotPermissioned() . The obvious eligibility check is a lie;
the honest probe is a staticcall of deposit itself, and the revert selector
lives three levels down viem's cause chain on .data , not in .message . Our
stand-in Teller reproduces that non-zero maxDeposit on purpose — a double
that returned 0 when un-permissioned would quietly teach the wrong eligibility
check, which is the single mistake this fixture exists to make unrepeatable. printId is an incrementing id, not a timestamp, because two prints written in
one block share a timestamp — which keeps "stale print" and "print rotated"
separately enforceable rather than collapsing into one ambiguous refusal.

code in an event rather than a revert), EIP-712 checkpoint approvals, and an
`ISleeve` interface — `depositIdle` / `withdrawExact` / `valueUsdc` — so the yield
venue is swappable without touching the treasury. The single unit conversion
`fairUsdc6 = priceWad * units / 1e12` appears exactly once and has a test pinning
it, because getting it wrong makes the fair band un-fireable while looking fully
implemented.

**Off-chain.** TypeScript with viem 2.55 drives the keeper, the two demo agents,
the policy compiler and a 15-check acceptance suite (`node:test` under tsx). The
dashboard is Next.js 16 / React 19 reading the chain directly through viem and
SWR — no server between the page and Arc — with the money path rendered in
three.js. A FastAPI + web3.py service holds the World ID gate. An MCP server
(`acr-mcp`, published to npm) exposes the tools to any agent host.

**Why Arc.** USDC is the native gas token, so the treasury, the gas and the
payment are one asset — a forecast denominated in dollars is simultaneously a
forecast of gas. **Arc Studio** compiled the treasury policy from an English
sentence into JSON, audited the vault, and wrote two of the three dashboard pages.
Its output is checked, not trusted: our own validator refuses an invalid config
before a transaction is built — exactly the assurance Studio itself flagged when
it said, unprompted, *"I didn't run it through a schema validator, but I checked
it by eye."*

**Partner technology that actually changed the design.** Morpho Vault V2 on Arc is
the working yield venue, and it is permissionless — all four transfer gates are
the zero address — which is what lets a *contract* hold shares, and is why the
just-in-time pull is one Solidity call instead of two transactions narrated as
one. An **Eco Sauce** compiled program asks that venue whether it could deliver a
given shortfall before anything is signed, with its Pot deployed on Arc (667,003
gas, verified). **Pyth** appears
as a negative result: deployed but dormant on Arc Testnet, every feed reverting
`PriceFeedNotFound()`, which argues for a pushed print better than any benchmark
comparison could.

**Circle's USYC — the reserve tier, and what it cost to build honestly.** Idle
float has two tiers and the second is Circle's tokenised treasury fund.
`UsycSleeve` implements the same three-verb `ISleeve` interface as the Morpho
one, so the treasury gained a T-bill position without a line of it changing. Two
design decisions fell out of reading the Teller's **verified** ABI instead of
assuming one — Blockscout had not resolved the EIP-1967 proxy, so the
implementation came from storage slot `0x3608…2bbc` → `0x238dc235…adf6`, 60
functions, and the verbs turned out to be `deposit` / `redeem` / `previewDeposit`
/ `previewRedeem`, not the `buy()` / `sell()` our own earlier notes had recorded.
First, **no price oracle**: the Teller previews its own redemption net of its own
fee, so the price comes from the counterparty that will honour it, and an oracle
would only add a trusted third party and a staleness window to a number already
published. Second, **sizing by preview rather than by dividing through a NAV** —
the redemption scales the share balance against the previewed value of the whole
position, rounded the way that cannot refuse a correct payment. Replacing that
with naive division fails two tests, one of them a real vault payment.

It runs against a stand-in fund, because Circle's allowlist is a support ticket
with a 24-to-48-hour turnaround we could not clear during the event. `SimUsyc`
and `SimUsycTeller` live in `src/sim/` rather than `test/` precisely because they
**leave the machine**: a deployed contract shows its name on the explorer, and a
`MockUsycTeller` sitting on a public chain would be the dishonest label. The
sleeve in front of them is the real `UsycSleeve` (`0x6D2A34ed…972E`), unchanged,
with a real round trip on Arc Testnet — park 1 USDC, pull 0.5, `valueUsdc`
reading 0 → 999999 → 499997. When the allowlist lands, **one constructor argument
changes and nothing else does**. The production vault's reserve slot stays
`address(0)` meanwhile, and acceptance check T15 asserts that on every run, so the
claim cannot quietly drift into "we hold USYC".

**World ID — the human leg of the same product.** The escalation path is gated by
World ID Agent Pass over an OIDC device flow. A parked payment names its own
request hash, a human authenticates freshly, and a FastAPI service validates the
token against a fixed ladder of nine named refusals — `malformed_token`,
`bad_signature`, `wrong_issuer`, `wrong_audience`, `expired`,
`assurance_not_accepted`, `amr_not_accepted`, `auth_time_outside_window`,
`not_the_enrolled_treasurer`. The nine are pinned by a test rather than by prose:
`test_every_named_reason_is_reachable` asserts set-equality between that tuple and
the reasons nine fixtures actually produce, so the count cannot drift away from
the sentence without a red test. The enrolled person is pinned on chain as
`keccak256("acr.treasurer::" + iss + 0x1f + sub)` — one-shot, so a treasury names
its treasurer exactly once.

The detail that justified building a ladder rather than a boolean: our live token
came back with `amr` = `["pop","user","mfa"]` — the passkey shape, which World's
own docs say does not assert a fresh World proof — while `acr` claimed orb. The
spend cleared, correctly, because orb assurance is what that path asks for. The
same token is **refused for a policy change**, which requires `face` and forbids
`mfa`. One token that can move money and cannot change the rules. The capability
split is deliberate too: the terminal holds the signing key and cannot move money,
the press holds the registrar key and cannot mint a request, so neither half can
issue a budget alone.

**The hacky parts worth naming.**

- Arc serves no `debug_traceTransaction`, so just-in-time funding is proven by
  **log order** within one transaction. A weaker tool giving a stronger result: an
  ordinary node can verify it.
- Arc's USDC at `0x3600…0000` is precompile-backed, so a `forge script` that moves
  it dies in simulation with `StackUnderflow` and seeding has to go through
  `cast`. The same transfer emits **two** `Transfer` events — 2e18 from the
  precompile and 2e6 from the ERC-20 view — one ledger with two decimals, visible
  on chain.
- Arc silently drops transactions under 20 Gwei. No receipt, no error.
- Morpho Vault V2 returns **zero from every `max*` function by design**, so the
  obvious `maxWithdraw` sizing reports an empty sleeve forever. `valueUsdc`
  converts the share balance instead. Shares are 18 decimals against 6-decimal
  USDC, so `convertToAssets` must be fed shares and never an asset amount.
- USYC's Teller returned `maxDeposit` = **5,723,443** for an address whose
  deposits revert `NotPermissioned()`. The obvious eligibility check is a lie;
  the honest probe is a staticcall of `deposit` itself, and the revert selector
  lives three levels down viem's cause chain on `.data`, not in `.message`. Our
  stand-in Teller reproduces that non-zero `maxDeposit` **on purpose** — a double
  that returned 0 when un-permissioned would quietly teach the wrong eligibility
  check, which is the single mistake this fixture exists to make unrepeatable.
- `printId` is an incrementing id, not a timestamp, because two prints written in
  one block share a timestamp — which keeps "stale print" and "print rotated"
  separately enforceable rather than collapsing into one ambiguous refusal.

projects.title: dani.ai
projects.description: AI jobs with a guaranteed start time, paid through escrow, and a market to trade your place in line
projects.project_description: AI agents work to deadlines, but GPU time is rented by the hour and a queue promises nothing about when a job runs. An urgent job can sit behind work that could wait all day, with no way to move up. dani.ai is a market for GPU time built around one promise: every job gets a time it must start by. A provider measures its own slowest speed and plays its queue forward assuming every job runs as long as it possibly can. Where a new booking lands is its start-by time. Real jobs finish early, so tickets only ever start sooner, and new bookings never push back an existing promise. A job that runs long is never killed; the provider absorbs the overrun. Payment goes into escrow, not to the provider. Providers set their own prices by job size. You deposit the price of your job's maximum size, the escrow charges the size the job actually used, and the rest comes back. If the start slips, part of the charge is refunded: 25% up to 30 seconds late, 50% up to a minute, and everything if it's later, fails, or never starts. Lateness is judged by Hedera consensus timestamps, not by anyone's clock. An agent that's running late can buy an earlier place from one that can wait. The seller only accepts a later place that still meets its own deadline, and both places plus the payment move in one atomic transaction. Agents can also reserve capacity ahead at today's price and resell it if plans change. In the web app, people sign in with HashPack, approve a budget, and get their own agent. They can book a single job, a batch (one instruction over many files, lines or CSV rows), or a repeating job that reserves each run's place ahead. Anyone with a GPU can join as a provider with one command and their own wallet. Every provider gets a public track record built from the messages it signed on Hedera. It all runs on Hedera testnet, with Arkiv for discovery and public records.
projects.how_its_made: A TypeScript monorepo with five packages: shared (types and chain helpers), provider, agent, host and web. Provider: Built with Node.js, it works with any OpenAI-compatible model server. Our demo uses Ollama running Qwen2.5 0.5B. At startup, it calibrates its worst-case performance by keeping every worker busy and testing the longest inputs and outputs. Random prefixes prevent prompt caching from making performance appear faster than it actually is. Jobs stream over SSE, allowing the provider to monitor token generation and distinguish slow jobs from stalled ones. Scheduling uses a list-scheduling simulation of the entire queue, and bookings are only accepted if they don't increase the number of promises that could be broken. Hedera (@hiero-ledger/sdk): Handles all payments and execution proofs. x402 payments: Payments go into an escrow account through the blocky402 facilitator. An unpaid request to /book returns an HTTP 402 response containing the current price and promised start-by time, allowing agents to get a live quote for free. Signed HCS log: Each provider maintains a batched, signed log of bookings, starts, results and trades on its own HCS topic. Escrow keeper: Reads these logs and uses Hedera consensus timestamps to determine payouts. HTS NFTs: Queue positions are minted as NFTs only when traded. Afterward, they return to the treasury and are reissued by updating their metadata through TokenUpdateNfts , costing approximately one-tenth as much as minting new ones. Atomic trades: A single TransferTransaction handles two NFT transfers and the HBAR payment. The seller verifies the transaction details before signing. Budgets: Users provide their agents with HBAR allowances directly from their wallets, so funds remain in their wallets until a booking is made. Arkiv: Acts as the discovery layer. Provider offers: Providers publish their model, speed, pricing by job size and next available start time. Offers expire automatically, so offline providers disappear without manual cleanup. Places for sale: Buyers can find suitable tickets using a single typed query filtering by start time, seller deadline, size and budget. Public task records: No private content is stored. Since records are claims, agents verify each entity's owner against the provider's account before trusting it. Host: Runs one agent per signed-in user. Sign-in verifies HashPack signatures over one-time challenges. Agent keys are derived from a host secret, allowing accounts to be recovered through Hedera even if the database is lost. Storage uses PostgreSQL through Drizzle, with embedded PGlite when no database is configured. Web: Built with React 19 and Vite, using TanStack Query, view transitions and hedera-wallet-connect for HashPack. The wallet SDK and pdf.js (for reading dropped PDFs directly in the browser) are loaded only when needed.

projects.title: seiz3
projects.description: Hedged liquidations for tokenized stocks: seize on Morpho, short on Hyperliquid, sell via Uniswap v4
projects.project_description: eiz3 is an ERC-4626 USDC vault that handles these liquidations differently. When a Morpho loan backed by NVDAx goes underwater, the vault liquidates it and right away opens a matching short on xyz:NVDA on Hyperliquid's HyperCore, which trades around the clock. From then on the vault is price-neutral. If NVDA moves, the stock and the short cancel out. Then it sells slowly. The vault's NVDAx/USDC pool on Uniswap v4 runs our hook. When someone buys NVDAx, the hook fills them straight from the vault's stock at HyperCore's oracle price plus a small spread (0.10% while the market is open, 1% after the bell), and the vault buys back that much of the short. The hook only sells when the pool price is at or above its ask, so a buyer never pays more than the pool would have charged. Whatever no buyer takes, the keeper sells into the pool in small chunks and closes the short as it goes. The pool fee also goes up after hours. A Chainlink CRE workflow gives the contracts what they can't read on-chain: whether the US market is open, how much NVDA the HyperCore order book can absorb (this caps how big a liquidation the vault will take), and a signed snapshot of the hedge account. If that data goes stale, the vault stops liquidating instead of guessing. LPs deposit USDC and earn the liquidation discount without taking on stock price risk. It's live on Base Sepolia at seiz3.xyz, on Morpho's and Uniswap's own deployments. On /try you can get test tokens, borrow against NVDAx at the limit, get liquidated about 15 seconds later, see the short open on HyperCore testnet, and watch the vault sell back down to flat.
projects.how_its_made:
The contracts are Solidity 0.8.28 with Foundry. There are four: Seiz3VaultRemote is the vault. It liquidates on Morpho Blue, queues the hedge, and unwinds into v4.
Seiz3HookRemote is the Uniswap v4 hook.
HyperCoreGateway is the link to HyperCore.
RiskParams receives the CRE reports.
The hackiest part is the gateway. We started on HyperEVM, where contracts read HyperCore through precompiles and place orders through CoreWriter. Uniswap v4 isn't officially deployed on HyperEVM testnet, so we moved to Base Sepolia, which has both Morpho Blue and the v4 PoolManager. HyperCoreGateway copies HyperCore's precompile and CoreWriter interfaces on Base: The vault writes orders into the gateway.
A TypeScript relayer picks them up and places IOC orders from our hedge account on Hyperliquid. It uses the vault's cloid, so an order never goes out twice.
The relayer posts the account state back to the gateway along with an ack.
Reads come from the latest snapshot. If the snapshot is older than maxStateAge, reads revert and the vault fails closed. Because of this, the vault logic barely changed in the move. Uniswap: the hook uses beforeSwap with a returned delta to fill buyers off the curve. In one callback it sends the buyer's USDC to the vault, settles the vault's NVDAx into the PoolManager, returns the delta and sets the dynamic fee. v4's flash accounting is what made this possible: the liquidity lives in the vault, not in the hook or the pool. One catch we hit: the hook takes USDC before the swapper has paid, so the payout comes from the PoolManager's own balance. We cap each fill at that balance. Also, v4-periphery's HookMiner ran out of gas inside forge script when mining a salt for a hook this size, so we wrote our own miner that hashes the init code only once. Chainlink CRE: the workflow is written in TypeScript and runs on a cron. Market status comes from Data Streams (the NVDA regular-hours stream), and every node has to agree.
Each node pulls Hyperliquid's l2Book, and the DON takes the median bid depth inside our hedge band. That number becomes the vault's max liquidation size.
It also checks Chainlink's NVDA/USD Data Feed on Ethereum against HyperCore's oracle and sets capacity to zero if they drift apart. This check is off on testnet because HyperCore testnet's price is stale.
It writes two reports: one to RiskParams, and a hedge-account snapshot to the gateway that keeps things running if our relayer dies.
Without CRE, the contracts would have to trust one bot for all of this. For the hackathon it runs as cre workflow simulate --broadcast every minute instead of as a deployed DON. It reads at the latest block because Base Sepolia's finalized head lags by hours. Off-chain: the keeper, relayer, bots and API are TypeScript with viem. All ABIs are generated with wagmi from the forge output, so changing a contract breaks the TS build. A Hono API makes one Multicall3 call per second and streams the result over SSE to a Next.js 16 dashboard. Everything runs in docker compose behind a Cloudflare tunnel. Tests: the Foundry tests deploy real Morpho Blue and PoolManager bytecode, with a mock HyperCore behind a test relayer. They run a full round: weekend, borrow, crash, liquidate, short, hook fill, buy-back, Monday unwind, flat. Fork tests run the same round against Base Sepolia's real deployments. Testnet caveats: NVDAx and USDC are mock tokens, and the lending oracle is ours. On HyperCore testnet the other side of our hedges is our own market maker bot, because there's no real flow there. The orders themselves are real HyperCore orders. Other bots buy through the hook and keep the Morpho market at about 90% utilization, so a max borrow goes underwater in about 15 seconds and you can watch the whole flow live

projects.title: Ordo
projects.description: Open source tool for contributors and people eager to learn, prove your work on real pipelines
projects.project_description: Ordo is a open source tool for contributors and anyone eager to learn how real manufacturing works. you join a production pipeline (turbine blade casting, satellite integration, pharma batches and more), work on a stage and then prove what you did with one command, npx ordo-pow. an AI interviewer running on 0G private compute go through the machine's captures with you and asks about your work, your values get proven in zero knowledge so public only sees pass or fail not the numbers. a staked validator pick the valid record and a staked tester can challenge it, if they are right the validator gets slashed. good work earns rewards so learners and contributors get real credit for what they did. under the hood every stage runs on a machine (real one over MTConnect, recorded data or a virtual machine with its own 0G agent) which simulate the process, sign its photos, thermal, audio and video and buy supplies over x402 from its own Hedera account. agents watch telemetry and raise incidents but people decide by signing with there wallet (EIP-712). everything lands in a hash chained ledger anchored on Hedera HCS, money only move through scheduled transactions a manager approve, every org, person, role, machine and lot has a ENS name under ordo.eth and each lot ships with a public passport and QR minted as Hedera NFT.
projects.how_its_made: Its a typescript pnpm monorepo. server is Node 22 + Hono + Postgres, console is React + Vite, contracts in Solidity, CLI ordo-pow is plain node with zero deps. around 345 tests for server, contracts and CLI. login is Sign in with Ethereum and every human decision is a EIP-712 signature with single use nonce. ledger is hash chained and anchored on a Hedera HCS topic, checked through mirror node. Hedera: OrdoTrust for roles, stakes, cases and rewards, OrdoTreasury so budgets and topups are HIP-423 scheduled txns approved with HIP-755, OrdoWorkOrders lets the maintenance agent escrow vendor payments via Hedera Agent Kit, OrdoPayOnProof pays a Stablecoin Studio hold only after release, lot passports are HTS NFTs updated with HIP-657 and machines buy/sell over x402. 0G: agents reason on 0G Compute, sealed records and machine logs go to 0G Storage, agents are ERC-7857 iNFTs on Galileo and the proof of work interviews run through 0G Private Computer Router with a per session key. ENS: OrdoNames register names under ordo.eth on sepolia in batches, roles are names which contracts read, and OrdoRunResolver write the lot release on its name after checking signers and proofs. ZK: circom circuits with poseidon commitments and groth16 so pass/fail is public but values stay private. hacky part: virtual machines render there own PNG, WAV, MP4 and PDF with no native deps so they can run inside Vercel Sandbox. and the proof of work interviews run inside TEE providers through the 0G router, every turn comes back with a signed receipt which we verify so you know the interviewer was not tampered.

under the hood every stage runs on a machine (real one over MTConnect, recorded data or a virtual machine with its own 0G agent) which simulate the process, sign its photos, thermal, audio and video and buy supplies over x402 from its own Hedera account. agents watch telemetry and raise incidents but people decide by signing with there wallet (EIP-712).

everything lands in a hash chained ledger anchored on Hedera HCS, money only move through scheduled transactions a manager approve, every org, person, role, machine and lot has a ENS name under ordo.eth and each lot ships with a public passport and QR minted as Hedera NFT.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Its a typescript pnpm monorepo. server is Node 22 + Hono + Postgres, console is React + Vite, contracts in Solidity, CLI ordo-pow is plain node with zero deps. around 345 tests for server, contracts and CLI.

login is Sign in with Ethereum and every human decision is a EIP-712 signature with single use nonce. ledger is hash chained and anchored on a Hedera HCS topic, checked through mirror node.

Hedera: OrdoTrust for roles, stakes, cases and rewards, OrdoTreasury so budgets and topups are HIP-423 scheduled txns approved with HIP-755, OrdoWorkOrders lets the maintenance agent escrow vendor payments via Hedera Agent Kit, OrdoPayOnProof pays a Stablecoin Studio hold only after release, lot passports are HTS NFTs updated with HIP-657 and machines buy/sell over x402.

0G: agents reason on 0G Compute, sealed records and machine logs go to 0G Storage, agents are ERC-7857 iNFTs on Galileo and the proof of work interviews run through 0G Private Computer Router with a per session key.

ENS: OrdoNames register names under ordo.eth on sepolia in batches, roles are names which contracts read, and OrdoRunResolver write the lot release on its name after checking signers and proofs.

ZK: circom circuits with poseidon commitments and groth16 so pass/fail is public but values stay private.

hacky part: virtual machines render there own PNG, WAV, MP4 and PDF with no native deps so they can run inside Vercel Sandbox. and the proof of work interviews run inside TEE providers through the 0G router, every turn comes back with a signed receipt which we verify so you know the interviewer was not tampered.

projects.title: Ephemeral
projects.description: Healthcare data marketplace where AI trains on hospital data in a TEE
projects.project_description:
Ephemeral is a confidential healthcare data marketplace. AI teams can train models on hospital data without anyone, including us, ever seeing a patient record. The problem: hospitals hold some of the most valuable training data in the world, but privacy laws (HIPAA, GDPR, India’s DPDP Act) stop them from handing raw records to AI vendors. Meanwhile, AI models are running out of public data to learn from. Today’s answer is a centralized clean room or data broker, and that center is exactly what leaks. Datavant, a leader in health data linking, had a single phished employee mailbox expose names, Social Security numbers and health data, which ended in a $900K class-action settlement. Ephemeral removes the center: the model travels to the data, and the data never travels. How it works: A hospital publishes a dataset. The file is encrypted with AES-256-GCM in the browser, and the key is split into Shamir shares. The ciphertext is uploaded to Ethereum Swarm and locked with an Access Control Trie (ACT), so only keys on its grantee list can decrypt it. Buyers only ever see a synthetic preview of the schema. The dataset is then registered with its price on our coordinator contract on Base.
An AI company picks a dataset, uploads its model encrypted to Swarm, and pays in USDC. The coordinator’s factory deploys an isolated escrow vault for that job alone, so funds are never pooled. The payment is split on-chain the moment the job is funded: 95% to the hospital, 2.5% Ephemeral fee, and 2.5% storage reserve. The storage reserve is swapped through 1inch Fusion+ to xBZZ on Gnosis to keep the encrypted data paid for on Swarm.
Funding the vault emits an event that triggers our Chainlink CRE workflow, which runs inside a TEE (AWS Nitro). The workflow:
reads the dataset record from the coordinator
over Confidential HTTP, with a secret held in the Vault DON, adds the enclave’s key to the dataset’s ACT so only the TEE can decrypt
runs the job in memory and uploads the output encrypted for the builder
posts a DON-signed report on-chain
On success, the vault pays the hospital. On failure, the builder is refunded, and if the deadline passes the builder can reclaim the funds directly. Nobody approves payouts by hand.
Open datasets go through Arkiv instead. Public CSVs are split into 60 KB chunks and stored as Arkiv entities with a catalog entry. The marketplace queries them by owner and rebuilds them for free download, which brings AI teams in at zero cost. The whole app is censorship-resistant: its files live on Ethereum Swarm and are served through ENS at ephemeralglobal.eth.limo. The coordinator and vault factory are deployed on Base mainnet. Current status: the CRE workflow runs in simulation with a placeholder preprocessing step and a mock enclave measurement. Next, we’re deploying it to a production DON with real hardware attestation, supporting many concurrent jobs per dataset, and adding verified onboarding for hospitals and AI companies. Built solo with Solidity (Foundry), Chainlink CRE, Ethereum Swarm (Bee), Arkiv, Base, Gnosis, 1inch Fusion+, React, Astro and wagmi.
projects.how_its_made:
Ephemeral is a monorepo of four parts that I built and wired together : Solidity contracts, a TypeScript Ethereum Swarm library, a Chainlink CRE workflow, and an Astro + React frontend. Smart contracts (Foundry, OpenZeppelin) EphemeralBaseCoordinator on Base is the registry and lifecycle controller. Hospitals register datasets with their encrypted Swarm reference, ACT grantee list, ACT history ref, synthetic-schema ref, feed manifest and USDC price. When an AI company calls createTrainingJob(): EphemeralBaseVaultFactory deploys an isolated EphemeralBaseJobVault for that job, so funds are never pooled.
97.5% goes into the vault: 95% for the hospital and 2.5% as the mediator fee.
The other 2.5% goes to a storage executor that keeps the dataset’s Swarm postage stamp funded. The coordinator also validates a convergence config on-chain: the model profile (tree_ensemble, deep_vision_monai and others), the target metric (F1, ROC-AUC, accuracy, RMSE), an overfit-gap limit and a maximum of 25 tuning trials. The only way to settle is onReport(), callable only by the Chainlink CRE forwarder. It decodes an action enum: MarkRunning, Complete, Refund, Finalize or RefundWithActRoot. If CRE never answers, the builder can call reclaimRefund() on their vault after the deadline, even if the coordinator is paused. Failed jobs grant a retry credit, so a second attempt reuses the storage reserve already paid. Access is split into roles (dataset registrar, CRE forwarder, storage executor, storage oracle, mediator) with Ownable2Step admin, ReentrancyGuard and SafeERC20. The first version ran on Gnosis with native xDAI, next to Swarm; I then moved settlement to Base in USDC. Ethereum Swarm library (bee-js) I wrote my own pipeline on top of bee-js: ->AES-256-GCM encryption through WebCrypto with a random 12-byte IV
->My own GF(256) Shamir secret sharing that splits the dataset key 3-of-n
->ECDH so trained output can be re-encrypted to the builder’s public key
->Bee encrypted uploads (64-byte references) paid with postage stamps
->ACT grantee lists to gate decryption
Swarm feeds so each dataset has a stable manifest
A synthetic preview generator that publishes a 10-row fake sample of the schema, so buyers can evaluate a dataset without seeing real rows Chainlink CRE workflow (TypeScript, @chainlink/cre-sdk, viem) The workflow is registered with handlerInTee on AWS Nitro and fires on a log trigger for TrainingJobRequested. It then: Reads the dataset with EVMClient.callContract at the last finalized block.
Calls my Bee node through the ConfidentialHTTPClient. The Bee auth token is a Vault DON secret injected as a {{.SWARM_BEE_AUTHORIZATION}} template, so it never enters workflow memory or the compiled artifact.
Sends PATCH /grantee to add the enclave’s compressed secp256k1 key to the dataset’s ACT, which returns a new ACT history ref.
Runs the job and uploads the output encrypted.
Writes a DON-signed report that finalizes or refunds. The order of steps is deliberate. The output artifact is uploaded before the ACT is changed, so a failed upload can’t leave a stale ACT root. If the ACT grant succeeded but a later step fails, the refund path uses RefundWithActRoot, so the on-chain ACT root still matches Swarm. Arkiv (open data) Public datasets live on Arkiv as typed schemas (ephemeral.public-datasets.v1 and ephemeral.public-dataset-chunks.v1) with indexed fields. A publish script splits each CSV into 60 KB chunks, batches four entity creates per transaction, and stores the columns and preview rows as JSON bytes. The marketplace queries .ownedBy(mediator), fetches the chunks ordered by part and rebuilds the file in the browser. That gives a fully on-chain, queryable data catalog with no backend server. Frontend and hosting The frontend is Astro with React islands, wagmi/viem, HashRouter and Tailwind/shadcn. It has three workspaces: Healthcare, Marketplace and AI Company. The whole built site is deployed to Swarm behind a feed manifest and pointed to from ENS (ephemeralglobal.eth.limo). New deploys just update the feed; the ENS record never changes. That makes the app censorship-resistant, with no server to take down. How partner tech helped Chainlink CRE: gave me trustless orchestration. TEE execution, Vault DON secrets and DON-signed reports mean no Ephemeral server ever holds keys, data or the power to pay out.
Ethereum Swarm: handled encrypted storage, ACT access control and hosting in one stack.
Arkiv: gave me a queryable on-chain database for open data without running an indexer.
Base: made USDC escrow cheap.
1inch Fusion+: let me fund Swarm storage on Gnosis from USDC on Base. Hacky bits worth mentioning Cross-chain storage funding: a storage-reserve executor watches StorageReserveCommitted on Base. It swaps the 2.5% USDC reserve cross-chain to xBZZ on Gnosis with the 1inch Fusion+ SDK, calls PostageStamp.topUp() on the dataset’s batch, then reports back through a storage oracle with confirmStorageTopUp().
Contract size limit: the coordinator hit Ethereum’s 24,576-byte contract size limit (EIP-170), so I moved vault deployment into a separate factory. That brought the coordinator down to 24,267 bytes.
Exposing the Bee node: the CRE DON has to reach my Bee node, so the node is exposed through an ngrok tunnel with a skip-warning header.
Key handling: I convert uncompressed secp256k1 keys to compressed form by hand, because Bee’s ACT only accepts compressed keys.
Attestation placeholder: until real Nitro attestation is wired in, the attestation hash is keccak(enclave measurement, job tx hash, TEE public key, job ID), recorded on-chain with every job. What’s still simulated: the CRE workflow currently runs in simulation, with a placeholder preprocessing step (zero rows read) and a mock enclave measurement. Next steps are deploying to a production DON with real hardware attestation, supporting concurrent jobs per dataset, and adding verified onboarding for hospitals and AI companies.

projects.title: Vertigo
projects.description: Vertigo is prediction markets for every squad. Any group of friends, community gets its own market.
projects.project_description: Vertigo is prediction markets for every squad. Any group (friends, a hackathon team, a city community) gets its own onchain market over up to eight base events. Members buy single-event contracts or parlays, the paper's "joint contracts on the simultaneous resolution of several events", of up to three legs. Before paying, they see the exact payout for every outcome pattern, and they can sell a single-event position back before close. Every trader is a verified human through World ID, so nobody can farm a market with fake wallets. Each squad runs one engine priced by LOPMM, the Low-Order Parlay Market Maker. It "keeps a separate book for each combination of legs": one logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR) book per leg-set, with a common liquidity b. Each book stores its own parameter block r(S). The engine "shares information from lower-order parlays into the higher-order ones containing them", so a trade on one event reprices every parlay that contains it. We cap parlays at three legs to match the paper's low-order flow condition (most flow is in parlays of at most k legs). Because of that cap, the cost of a trade depends on the order m of the parlay, not on the number M of base events, and the operator's worst-case loss stays bounded. A buy is a full-trade: the trader states a target belief on their chosen pattern. The engine splits it into sub-trades, one for each lower-order book inside the parlay (seven for three legs), and settles them in the paper's buy-only realization with gauge shifts. The engine reserves each position's maximum payout so winners are always paid. Because a position also holds claims in the lower-order books, partial matches can pay. On top of the paper we add a graded target rule: other patterns are weighted by how many legs they match, so payouts rise in equal steps per correct leg instead of all-or-nothing. Selling back, an exact LMSR inverse on single-event books, is also our extension; the paper's mechanism is buy-only. Trades reach the same engine through two venues: 1inch Aqua with a custom SwapVM strategy, and a Uniswap v4 custom-accounting hook. The operator picks the venue for each squad in an admin portal, and the contracts enforce it. Squads get ENS names that point to their market. Squad events can be resolved by an EIP-712-signed outcome published to ENS, followed by a challenge-and-vote among verified members. Each position is an NFT that stores its payout for every outcome pattern, and winners claim after resolution. Everything runs live on Ethereum Sepolia: 14 squad engines, 155+ positions, buys and sells on both venues, and a deployed web app and admin portal.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). Engine. Each squad's LopmmEngine is a beacon proxy. It holds the squad's collateral and keeps one LMSR book per leg-set, each stored as a parameter block r(S) at a common liquidity b. A stateVersion counter stops stale quotes from filling. The engine reserves the maximum payout of every position and pays claims.
Positions. Positions are ERC-721 NFTs that record their payout for every outcome pattern.
Allowance. A CapacityGate enforces a daily spending allowance per verified human, using vouchers our backend signs after a World ID proof.
Math written twice. The LOPMM math exists in TypeScript and in Solidity with identical integer arithmetic (bounded log/exp, largest-remainder rounding). That covers the full-trade, its sub-trades into every lower-order book, the buy-only realization and the gauge shifts.
A 10,000-case differential test shows both give bit-identical quotes, next books and payouts.
A 70-digit Python Decimal oracle independently checks the TS model.
Size limit. To stay under the EIP-170 size limit, the engine calls a stateless LopmmEngineLens contract for all pure pricing and forwards its ABI-encoded return data unchanged.
1inch. The engine is an Aqua maker that ships one SwapVM strategy: a single Extruction instruction (opcode 0x20) that calls the engine for the price. The hacky part. ERC-20 and ERC-721 share the transferFrom(address,address,uint256) selector, so the position NFT is the swap's output.
Buys are exact-out swaps with amountOut set to the id of the NFT being minted.
Sells reverse it: an exact-in swap of the NFT for collateral, with a just-in-time approval of exactly the refund, so no standing allowance ever exists.
Side effects. We mapped what this trick could break: the engine only lets the freshly minted id move, only our router can pull, and no receiver callbacks run.
Uniswap v4. A custom-accounting hook with the flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta, at a CREATE2-mined address. Buys. In beforeSwap, the hook moves the trader's payment from the PoolManager into the engine, and the engine mints the NFT straight to the trader. The hook returns a BeforeSwapDelta that consumes the whole input, so the curve never runs and pools stay at 1:1 with no liquidity.
Sells are exact-output swaps for exactly the refund.
Charging the right person. The real trader comes from the trusted Universal Router's msgSender(), so the World ID allowance is charged to whoever paid.
Pricing beyond the paper. The paper's mechanism is buy-only, and its contracts pay only on their exact pattern. We added two things on top: Selling back. A single-event position can be sold back at the exact LMSR inverse of its purchase: refund = C(q) − C(q − payouts), minus the fee. A fuzz test checks that a buy-then-sell round trip never profits.
Graded target rule. For parlays, the trader's target belief p is pinned on the chosen pattern. The other patterns are tilted by how many legs they match, with weights q·w^matches and w solved by integer bisection. Routed through the sub-trades, this makes payouts rise in equal steps per correct leg.
Engines opt in onchain, and existing positions keep their payouts.
The price history replays each full-trade with the rule in force at its state version.
ENS. Squad names on an ENSv2 permissioned resolver carry text records that point to the engine. The owner can delegate writing a single record key.
A SquadVoteResolver imports the designated proposer's EIP-712-signed outcome from ENS through the Universal Resolver. It verifies the signature against the frozen event facts, then runs a challenge and a one-vote-per-human vote before resolving the engine.
App and infrastructure. App. A Next.js app with a three.js globe of squads, and live market charts rebuilt by replaying the position NFTs' full-trades, with no log indexing needed. An admin portal handles venue switching and resolution.
Backend. A Hono API (wallet auth, World ID verification, voucher signing) running on Vercel with Upstash Redis. Browser chain reads go through a read-only RPC proxy, so the RPC key stays on the server.
Libraries and deploys. Client libraries use viem and the 1inch SwapVM and Aqua SDKs. Deploys run from GitHub Actions on every merge.
Tests.
225 Foundry tests, including fork tests against live Sepolia Aqua, the PoolManager and the Universal Router.
150+ TypeScript tests.

1inch. The engine is an Aqua maker that ships one SwapVM strategy: a single Extruction instruction (opcode 0x20) that calls the engine for the price.

The hacky part. ERC-20 and ERC-721 share the transferFrom(address,address,uint256) selector, so the position NFT is the swap's output.
Buys are exact-out swaps with amountOut set to the id of the NFT being minted.
Sells reverse it: an exact-in swap of the NFT for collateral, with a just-in-time approval of exactly the refund, so no standing allowance ever exists.
Side effects. We mapped what this trick could break: the engine only lets the freshly minted id move, only our router can pull, and no receiver callbacks run.
Uniswap v4. A custom-accounting hook with the flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta, at a CREATE2-mined address.

Buys. In beforeSwap, the hook moves the trader's payment from the PoolManager into the engine, and the engine mints the NFT straight to the trader. The hook returns a BeforeSwapDelta that consumes the whole input, so the curve never runs and pools stay at 1:1 with no liquidity.
Sells are exact-output swaps for exactly the refund.
Charging the right person. The real trader comes from the trusted Universal Router's msgSender(), so the World ID allowance is charged to whoever paid.
Pricing beyond the paper. The paper's mechanism is buy-only, and its contracts pay only on their exact pattern. We added two things on top:

Selling back. A single-event position can be sold back at the exact LMSR inverse of its purchase: refund = C(q) − C(q − payouts), minus the fee. A fuzz test checks that a buy-then-sell round trip never profits.
Graded target rule. For parlays, the trader's target belief p is pinned on the chosen pattern. The other patterns are tilted by how many legs they match, with weights q·w^matches and w solved by integer bisection. Routed through the sub-trades, this makes payouts rise in equal steps per correct leg.
Engines opt in onchain, and existing positions keep their payouts.
The price history replays each full-trade with the rule in force at its state version.
ENS.

Squad names on an ENSv2 permissioned resolver carry text records that point to the engine. The owner can delegate writing a single record key.
A SquadVoteResolver imports the designated proposer's EIP-712-signed outcome from ENS through the Universal Resolver. It verifies the signature against the frozen event facts, then runs a challenge and a one-vote-per-human vote before resolving the engine.
App and infrastructure.

App. A Next.js app with a three.js globe of squads, and live market charts rebuilt by replaying the position NFTs' full-trades, with no log indexing needed. An admin portal handles venue switching and resolution.
Backend. A Hono API (wallet auth, World ID verification, voucher signing) running on Vercel with Upstash Redis. Browser chain reads go through a read-only RPC proxy, so the RPC key stays on the server.
Libraries and deploys. Client libraries use viem and the 1inch SwapVM and Aqua SDKs. Deploys run from GitHub Actions on every merge.
Tests.
225 Foundry tests, including fork tests against live Sepolia Aqua, the PoolManager and the Universal Router.
150+ TypeScript tests.

projects.title: Levee
projects.description: Hacked? It snaps back. Stolen stablecoins frozen and taken back in seconds on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Levee is a circuit breaker for stablecoin issuers on Hedera. It enforces one rule: no receipt, no movement. The problem: when a stablecoin issuer is hacked, the attacker uses the issuer's own keys or signing system to drain the treasury or mint fake tokens. Today that is stopped by hand and it is slow: Resolv (Mar 2026, ~$25M taken) took about 3 hours to stop, StablR about 8 hours to even respond, PlayDapp about 4 days. How Levee works: Every payment out of the treasury must get a receipt on Hedera first. A gate checks the requesting machine (signed request, allowed role, a live health pass on Arkiv), the amount caps and the recipient allowlist, writes the receipt to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, and schedules the transfer. A separate issuer signer adds the second treasury signature only after it finds that receipt on Hedera. A watcher reads every movement and every mint on the Mirror Node and matches it to a receipt written before it. Anything without a valid receipt (stolen keys, a rogue insider, an unauthorised mint) is contained automatically by a close-only smart contract that holds Stablecoin Studio's freeze and wipe roles: the treasury is frozen, the stolen tokens are wiped from the thief's account and the thief is frozen. The incident is published on Hedera. Only 2 of 3 admins together can reopen. The watcher can never unfreeze anything. Live on Hedera testnet: a theft was detected in about 2.5 s and taken back in about 5.6 s; a fake mint was wiped in about 4.8 s with supply restored exactly; 393 real payments ran with zero false alarms. The contract is verified on HashScan. The live dashboard shows it all and lets you run send, hack, unlock and fake mint yourself.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript end to end (Node services + a Vite/React dashboard), one Solidity contract, all on Hedera testnet with the Hedera JS SDK and Mirror Node REST. Hedera: the RUPC token is issued with Hedera Stablecoin Studio (v4 factory called directly) and its freeze/wipe/pause/cash-in roles are granted to our ContainmentController contract (verified on HashScan). Receipts, incidents and watcher heartbeats are three Hedera Consensus Service topics with submit keys, so consensus timestamps prove the receipt came before the money moved. The treasury is a 2-of-3 threshold key; normal payments use Hedera Scheduled Transactions so the gate and a separate issuer signer each add one signature, and the signer only signs after it independently finds the receipt. The watcher polls the Mirror Node; we found the public Mirror sits behind a CDN with max-age=1, so we cache-bust every read and prove from one ascending transaction listing that no receipt exists, which cut detection from ~7 s to ~2.5 s with zero false alarms. Arkiv: each payout machine runs an agent that sends signed health heartbeats every 60 s; a checker keeps a levee.pass.v1 entity alive on Arkiv with a 3-minute expiry, so a hacked or offline machine's pass simply disappears and the gate refuses it. Requests are signed by the machine's enrolled key and its role is checked. Ordering detail that mattered: a frozen account can't be wiped and a paused token blocks freeze/wipe, so the contract wipes then freezes, and pause is always last. 351 core + 279 dashboard tests run in GitHub CI. Built with Claude Code; images and the hero video were made with Google Flow.
