projects.title: Tremor
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that buys volatility cover on 1inch Aqua and pays LPs back when markets swing.
projects.project_description: Uniswap LPs are short volatility. We valued every swap in the UNI/WETH 0.3% pool on Ethereum at Binance one-minute prices for two years: arbitrage loss came to 93% of LP fees, LPs lost money in 14 of 104 weeks, and the worst week cost them $137,516. The losses arrive exactly when the market swings, which is what insurance is for. Tremor is a Uniswap v4 hook that turns that loss into cover: Measure. A Chainlink CRE workflow reads the pool's swaps, values each one against exchange prices, and reports the week's arbitrage loss on-chain. Charge. At the week's close the hook fee is set to half the measured loss rate, capped at 0.30%. Without a fresh report it expires to zero. Cover. The hook converts its fees to WETH and buys LONG claims on the next week's realized volatility from one 1inch Aqua strategy, through our own SwapVM instruction (0x22). Every LONG/SHORT pair is fully backed by WETH. Pay. Chainlink Data Feeds settle the week from every price round in it, and the hook donates the payout back to in-range LPs. A liquidity penalty stops just-in-time LPs from taking it. Anyone can trade the other side in the app: buy LONG if you expect a swing, SHORT if you expect calm. Writers fund the strategy through a vault and share its premium. What you can check: Live app on Sepolia: trade LONG/SHORT on an open window, and run the stress-test simulator, where you drag each day's price move and watch the fee, the cover and the LP payout respond. Its five presets are real contract runs on a mainnet fork, and the simulator reproduces every step within 0.01%. Every step ran on Sepolia against the real v4 PoolManager and Aqua: CRE reports set the fee, swaps paid it, the hook bought cover, Chainlink rounds settled the window, and the payout was donated to LPs (transactions in the README). A mainnet-fork replay of the October 2025 crash week: the fee rose to its cap, the cover paid in full, and 1.235 WETH went back to LPs. 107 tests, including two rounds of red-team attacks against the real Aqua and v4 contracts. Honest benchmark: simply raising the LP fee earns about 8% more on average. Tremor cuts the worst week by 43%. It's insurance for the tail, not extra yield.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry). Four pieces: TremorHook: OpenZeppelin BaseHookFee with afterSwap + afterSwapReturnDelta. The fee is taken on the unspecified currency as ERC-6909 claims; handleHookFees redeems them inside unlock, swaps UNI to WETH in the same pool with a Chainlink price limit, and buys cover. Payouts go back with PoolManager.donate, dripped over blocks. We also inherit OpenZeppelin's LiquidityPenaltyHook (address flags 0x547, mined with CREATE2) so liquidity added and removed within 100 blocks forfeits its share of the payout. VarianceMarket: weekly windows of fully collateralized LONG/SHORT claims. checkpoint walks every Chainlink round by round ID and is phase-aware; finalize settles realized variance from all of them and refuses to settle on partial data. Quotes pause until the newest round is ingested, and while the pool price (read at the start of the block) is more than 2% from the last round. 1inch: a new SwapVM instruction, 0x22 CappedPayoffCurve, appended to SwapVM v1.0.2's instruction set in our AquaSwapVMRouter (21,935 bytes, under EIP-170). It prices claims from projected volatility, a spread that narrows through the week, price impact, and an inventory skew read from the strategy's Aqua rawBalances. TremorVault mints complete sets and ships [WETH, LONG, SHORT] as one strategy to the deployed Aqua registry; writers deposit WETH for pro-rata shares. TremorReceiver (Chainlink ReceiverTemplate): accepts only contiguous CRE reports and sets the hook fee at each weekly close. Chainlink CRE workflow (TypeScript SDK): each run makes 15 EVM reads and 2 HTTP calls, within the service limits. It reads the pool's Swap logs in 100-block chunks, fetches Binance one-minute prices in node mode with consensus, values every swap in integer maths so every node gets the same number, and fails rather than reporting if price data has gaps. Live mode measures only blocks 64 confirmations deep. We ran it with cre workflow simulate, both live on Sepolia and as a 42-run backfill of the October 2025 crash on a mainnet fork. Testing: 65 unit tests, including 10,508 pricing vectors cross-checked against a Python reference model; 8 mainnet-fork tests with asserted historical results; 29 red-team tests (25 attacks on a mainnet fork against the real Aqua and v4 contracts, 4 pricing fuzz tests); 5 price-shock scenarios. The red team found a sandwich of the hook's cover buy (+5.66 WETH in our proof of concept) and front-running a pending Chainlink round; both are fixed and the attacks now lose money. Data: Python scripts measured LP arbitrage loss swap by swap for 104 weeks against Binance one-minute candles; that dataset drives the landing page charts and the backtest. App: Next.js, wagmi and viem on Sepolia, deployed on Vercel. The stress-test page runs a TypeScript port of the pool, arbitrage, loss formula, fee rule and the 0x22 pricing curve, calibrated against recorded fork runs to within 0.01% at every step, so you can drag each day's price move and watch the protocol respond. Hacky bits: Sepolia has no UNI/ETH feed, so the Sepolia market settles on ETH/USD with a test UNI token. CRE reports reach Sepolia through the simulation forwarder, so the receiver accepts them only from our signer. AI tools were used throughout; AI_USAGE.md lists where.

projects.title: Atlas Assistant
projects.description: A wearable agent that listens, remembers, nudges you and moves hardware. Its brain runs on 0G.
projects.project_description: Atlas is a wearable agent with a body. A wireless clip-on mic feeds an ESP32-S3 that streams audio around the clock to a laptop bridge. A noise gate drops silence, fans and background chatter, so only real speech reaches 0G. Say "Hey Atlas" and it acts; otherwise it just remembers. It summarizes old conversations on its own after a pause, answers questions like "what did we decide about the storage quota last week?", and can read back or export a full transcript. It nudges you later about things you promised in a conversation ("I'll follow up with Rohan"), and sets or clears reminders by time or by place. An ESP32 scans Bluetooth, so reminders and actions can trigger when your headphones or bag tag leave range. Atlas also moves real things. Any command can carry ordered hardware actions on an ESP8266 desk device with a servo (the door), an LED and a buzzer: "close the door, then buzz, then open it", or "open the door when my headphones go out of range". "Atlas, SOS" plays Morse code on the light and the buzzer. An Android app shows the orb, reminders, chats and notifications, and has its own mic with live streaming words. 0G is the brain. Whisper turns speech into text and a 0G language model turns it into an intent and actions. Every decision is saved as an episode (transcript, request ids, actions, outcome), hashed, uploaded to 0G Storage and anchored on 0G Chain, so it can be verified. If 0G is unreachable, the device safe-stops (servo released, light and buzzer off, one chirp) and never fakes a decision.
projects.how_its_made: Hardware: a wireless lavalier mic into a USB receiver read by an ESP32-S3 (Espressif usb_host_uac), which POSTs 48 kHz mono audio to the laptop. An ESP32 devkit scans BLE for the headphones and a bag tag. An ESP8266 desk gauge (servo, LED, buzzer) polls the bridge every 350 ms and plays jingles and Morse SOS. The venue Wi-Fi is 5 GHz only, so the ESPs join a 2.4 GHz hotspot on the laptop. Bridge (Python): energy VAD cuts speech segments, a noise gate and high-pass filter clean them, and they go to 0G Whisper (large-v3), with a second 0G model as fallback. The 0G chat model (qwen3.5-flash) parses each command into an intent plus an ordered list of hardware actions, and also writes summaries, answers memory questions and extracts commitments for nudges. A sequencer turns actions into device state, so any command or reminder can drive the hardware. Memory is SQLite on the laptop. 0G usage: Compute for STT and every decision (each call's request id is stored); Storage for per-decision episodes and sealed conversations (canonical JSON, sha256, root hash); and an EpisodeAnchor contract on 0G Galileo (0x3c0a37027c79dA7934c0dfa4b2f683270a6f7A8E) that emits each episode's hash and storage root. The device safe-stops if 0G is unreachable. App: Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, talking to the laptop over Tailscale, with its own mic streamed to 0G STT. Hacky bits: whisper hallucinated "thank you for watching" on noise, so we added a noise gate and a junk filter; one-word commands like "SOS" bypass the LLM so they fire instantly; and the buzzer sits on the ESP8266's boot pin.

projects.title: vestor
projects.description: VESTOR: RWA inventory financing with tokenized collateral and automated USDT credit distributions.
projects.project_description: VESTOR transforms illiquid physical warehouse inventory into programmable, asset-backed debt tranches on Whitechain Sepolia (Chain ID 1874). Operating at the intersection of supply chain logistics and on-chain credit, VESTOR enables commodity enterprises to unlock upfront working capital by securitizing verified warehouse receipts. Featuring EIP-712 cryptographic off-take attestations, smart-contract-enforced compliance allowlists and lockups, and deterministic 5-tier cash-flow waterfalls, VESTOR settles every investment subscription and yield distribution natively in official testnet USDT with sub-two-second finality and sub-cent gas fees.
projects.how_its_made: VESTOR is an institutional-grade Real World Asset (RWA) tokenization and credit facility platform built on a four-tier architecture consisting of Solidity smart contracts, a Node.js/TypeScript blockchain adapter, a Go 1.24 core backend, and a Next.js 14 web portal. Certified warehouse inventory is uploaded to our Go service, which calculates haircut valuations, bundles inspection receipts into an immutable SHA-256 evidence root, and stages transactions via a database transactional outbox. A dedicated Node.js adapter pulls these tasks and calls InventoryRegistry and InventoryTokenFactory on-chain to issue asset-backed debt tranches. Investors fund these tranches by depositing official 6-decimal USDT into FinancingVault , while subsequent retail off-take sales are cryptographically verified through SalesSettlement using EIP-712 structured signatures before being routed into a 5-tier waterfall engine ( DistributionManager ) where lenders claim their yield via Merkle proofs. Deploying on Whitechain Sepolia (Chain ID: 1874) with canonical USDT settlement provided critical structural advantages over traditional banking rails and congested L1s. Whitechain’s ~2-second block finality completely eliminates counterparty double-pledging risk—where issuers traditionally exploit the T+2/T+3 banking delay to pledge the same warehouse commodity to multiple lenders—by guaranteeing that collateral encumbrance and USDT loan funding happen atomically within the same block. Furthermore, Whitechain's sub-cent gas fees ($0.0001 per tx) enabled us to abandon the customary 30–90 day batch payout cycles of invoice factoring and instead execute high-frequency, real-time micro-waterfall yield streaming directly to investors whenever an individual off-take invoice clears. A notable technical challenge arose from Whitechain’s public RPC, which enforces a strict 10,000-block ceiling on eth_getLogs . Because Whitechain mines blocks every ~2 seconds, that 10,000-block limit elapses in just ~5.5 hours, causing standard Web3 event indexers to crash when querying historical contract events. To resolve this without running a heavy external indexer, we implemented a custom 5,000-block sliding-window chunked pagination engine with cursor tracking across our adapter and frontend listeners. Additionally, we bound off-chain ERP delivery documents to on-chain state by hashing physical receipts into SHA-256 roots and combining them with EIP-712 typed digests, ensuring cryptographic auditability and zero state desynchronization between PostgreSQL and the EVM ledger.
projects.project_description_markdown: VESTOR transforms illiquid physical warehouse inventory into programmable, asset-backed debt tranches on Whitechain Sepolia (Chain ID 1874). Operating at the intersection of supply chain logistics and on-chain credit, VESTOR enables commodity enterprises to unlock upfront working capital by securitizing verified warehouse receipts. Featuring EIP-712 cryptographic off-take attestations, smart-contract-enforced compliance allowlists and lockups, and deterministic 5-tier cash-flow waterfalls, VESTOR settles every investment subscription and yield distribution natively in official testnet USDT with sub-two-second finality and sub-cent gas fees.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
VESTOR is an institutional-grade Real World Asset (RWA) tokenization and credit facility platform built on a four-tier architecture consisting of Solidity smart contracts, a Node.js/TypeScript blockchain adapter, a Go 1.24 core backend, and a Next.js 14 web portal. Certified warehouse inventory is uploaded to our Go service, which calculates haircut valuations, bundles inspection receipts into an immutable SHA-256 evidence root, and stages transactions via a database transactional outbox. A dedicated Node.js adapter pulls these tasks and calls `InventoryRegistry` and `InventoryTokenFactory` on-chain to issue asset-backed debt tranches. Investors fund these tranches by depositing official 6-decimal USDT into `FinancingVault`, while subsequent retail off-take sales are cryptographically verified through `SalesSettlement` using EIP-712 structured signatures before being routed into a 5-tier waterfall engine (`DistributionManager`) where lenders claim their yield via Merkle proofs.

Deploying on Whitechain Sepolia (Chain ID: 1874) with canonical USDT settlement provided critical structural advantages over traditional banking rails and congested L1s. Whitechain’s ~2-second block finality completely eliminates counterparty double-pledging risk—where issuers traditionally exploit the T+2/T+3 banking delay to pledge the same warehouse commodity to multiple lenders—by guaranteeing that collateral encumbrance and USDT loan funding happen atomically within the same block. Furthermore, Whitechain's sub-cent gas fees ($0.0001 per tx) enabled us to abandon the customary 30–90 day batch payout cycles of invoice factoring and instead execute high-frequency, real-time micro-waterfall yield streaming directly to investors whenever an individual off-take invoice clears.

A notable technical challenge arose from Whitechain’s public RPC, which enforces a strict 10,000-block ceiling on `eth_getLogs`. Because Whitechain mines blocks every ~2 seconds, that 10,000-block limit elapses in just ~5.5 hours, causing standard Web3 event indexers to crash when querying historical contract events. To resolve this without running a heavy external indexer, we implemented a custom 5,000-block sliding-window chunked pagination engine with cursor tracking across our adapter and frontend listeners. Additionally, we bound off-chain ERP delivery documents to on-chain state by hashing physical receipts into SHA-256 roots and combining them with EIP-712 typed digests, ensuring cryptographic auditability and zero state desynchronization between PostgreSQL and the EVM ledger.

projects.title: If I Go Silent
projects.description: The envelope that opens if you go silent. Nobody holds it, nobody can stop it.
projects.project_description: In 2017, Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb. Her investigations survived only because 45 journalists from 18 newsrooms finished them. Most people at risk don't have 45 journalists. They have a folder, and a fear. IF I GO SILENT is the old "if anything happens to me, this envelope goes to the press" idea, except nobody holds the envelope. No lawyer, friend, editor or cloud company can be threatened, bribed or raided into releasing it or burying it. You seal a file or a message. It is encrypted on your own device before it goes anywhere. You choose when it opens: TIMER: on a set date HEARTBEAT: if you stop checking in, a true dead-man's switch BOTH A seal can be public, or opened only to readers who prove they are nationals of chosen countries. Every action that changes a seal's fate (arming it, "I'm OK" check-ins, disarming, releasing early, extending) needs a live World ID face check by the same human who sealed it. Someone who steals your phone cannot check in for you or cancel the release. If you go silent, an independent Chainlink CRE workflow sees there is no valid check-in, applies your release rule and sends the release transaction on-chain. Nobody on our team clicks publish. The content then decrypts in any reader's browser. We also built Silent Seal, a browser extension for X and Reddit. You write a post, pick when it becomes readable and seal it. What gets posted is two ordinary-looking sentences that quietly encode the seal. When the time comes, the extension finds the post and shows the decrypted text right under it in everyone's feed. Because the switch is public, anyone who wants to silence you knows that silencing you publishes everything. The switch protects you by existing.
projects.how_its_made: Everything is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo. Shared crypto and protocol logic lives in one package (packages/core). The same code runs in the Next.js web app, the browser extension and the worker, and is re-implemented with the same libraries inside the Chainlink CRE WASM runtime. We test that the implementations work with each other in both directions. Crypto (all client-side, @noble libraries): each seal gets a fresh key and is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305, with the seal id bound in as associated data. The key is wrapped to an X25519 public key using an HKDF-SHA256 sealed box. For public seals, the matching private key exists only as a Chainlink CRE secret. For country-gated seals, a key service hands out the key only after the on-chain release and a valid World ID nationality proof. Chainlink CRE: the release-sweeper workflow runs on a cron every 30 seconds. It reads all seals, check-ins, disarms and releases from Arkiv over HTTP, applies the release rule, unwraps the key for public seals, and calls writeReport on our SilentRelease.sol consumer contract on Sepolia (Foundry, forwarder-gated, idempotent). This makes the release decision independent of our backend. Arkiv: Arkiv is our public, queryable state layer (seal, checkin, disarm and release entities). The hacky part we are proudest of: a heartbeat is an Arkiv check-in whose expiration time equals the check-in interval. If you go silent, Arkiv expires the entity, it disappears from queries, and CRE releases. The absence of data is the trigger. A mirror worker writes contract release events back to Arkiv, and anyone can run it. Swarm: the encrypted content is stored on Swarm. We upload our own ciphertext rather than using Swarm's encrypted upload, because a Swarm encrypted reference would embed its own key. World ID (IDKit 4.6): we use two trust moments, each with the minimum credential it needs. Selfie Check session proofs prove that the same live human is acting, since the threat is someone else holding your phone. Identity Check with only the nationality attribute covers gated readers, so no name or birthdate is revealed. Every proof's signal commits to the action, the seal id and, when arming, the digest of the exact ciphertext and rule. All proofs are verified server-side. Silent Seal extension: built with WXT on Manifest V3. It turns a seal id into two natural-sounding cover sentences, so before release nothing marks the post as a seal. After release, it scans the page and decrypts the post in place. We built this with Claude Code as an AI pair-programmer for architecture, implementation and tests. All of it was verified with unit tests, Foundry tests, CRE simulation and end-to-end browser flows.

projects.title: Blind Report
projects.description: Blind Report: anonymous tips for journalists, powered by ENS, World ID and Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Blind Report is an anonymous, end-to-end encrypted whistleblowing channel built for investigative newsrooms and the sources who trust them. It replaces the traditional "contact us" form with a decentralized protocol in which the source never creates an account, never reveals an email address or phone number, and never sends plaintext to a server. The source starts by resolving a newsroom's ENSv2 name through the Universal Resolver on Ethereum Sepolia. The newsroom publishes its public key, key version, editorial policy, and relayer endpoint as ENS text records, so discovery is transparent and censorship-resistant. The source's browser then encrypts the tip and any attachments locally with Libsodium, using X25519 key exchange and XChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption, and seals the payload into an envelope that only the newsroom can open. Before submission, the source generates a World ID 4.0 proof of personhood bound to the action submit:<newsroom>:<epoch>. The proof produces a nullifier that allows one submission per human per newsroom per monthly epoch without linking that person to their real identity or to activity in other newsrooms. The relayer verifies the proof, re-resolves the ENS records, checks the source is not using a stale key version, and writes the encrypted entity to Arkiv Network (Rabdi testnet). Arkiv provides immutable storage, block-based retention and expiration, and custody transfer to the newsroom; the relayer sponsors the write, and the source receives a local receipt containing the mailbox key and commitment salt. Newsroom access is managed through ENS subnames. Journalists are delegated subnames such as reporter.newsroom.eth, and the protocol checks their authority on-chain before allowing decryption or replies. Editors can annotate a tip's status, extend its retention period, and send an encrypted reply into an anonymous mailbox. The source retrieves that reply using only the receipt, with no account or identity attached. If the source later wants to prove authorship in court or to another outlet, they can reveal the salt and mathematically verify the content commitment without having exposed their identity earlier. Blind Report is designed around the CROPS principles: privacy through client-side cryptography, censorship resistance through ENS-based discovery and relayer choice, open-source code and guardrails, and security through strict network allowlists, CSP, zero-IP-logging relayers, and audited cryptographic primitives. The current build is a testnet prototype: ENSv2 registration and resolution run on Sepolia, while Arkiv and World ID integrations are implemented for the Rabdi testnet and World ID 4.0. The goal is a practical, verifiable alternative to centralized whistleblowing portals.
projects.how_its_made: Blind Report is a whistleblowing app where the server never sees the tip. The source's browser encrypts everything before it leaves the machine; the relayer only handles ciphertext, a World ID proof, and an ENS lookup. We built it as a TypeScript monorepo with separate packages for crypto, ENS, Arkiv, World ID, the clients, network policy, and a small Node relayer, plus a Next.js frontend. That split let us swap Arkiv for an in-memory backend in tests and run the same store code on a local reth node or Rabdi. ENS does more than resolve a name. A newsroom registers on Sepolia with ENSv2: resolver proxy, ETHRegistrar commit-reveal, then one multicall writing the public key, key version, editorial policy, relayer list, and custodian. Journalists get subnames, with reader keys in text records. A source resolving the newsroom through the Universal Resolver gets the encryption key and rules in one lookup. Authority checks come from the chain too: the subname owner plus the ETHRegistry subregistry, no separate ACL contract. The source encrypts the tip and attachments in the browser with Libsodium (X25519 and XChaCha20-Poly1305). The receipt stays local and holds the mailbox key and a random salt; the relayer sees neither. The salt is what lets someone prove authorship later without having identified themselves at submission time. World ID is the spam gate. The relayer signs an rp_context for submit:<newsroom>:<epoch>, the source runs IDKit's proofOfHuman(), and the relayer verifies it with World. We store only a SHA-256 hash of the nullifier plus action, so the plaintext nullifier never sits in our database. One submission per human per newsroom per month, no account required. Arkiv holds the encrypted envelope. The relayer re-resolves ENS and rejects stale key versions, splits large envelopes into entities, creates them as readonly with permissionlessExtension, and changes ownership to the newsroom. Expiration, renewal, and queries by newsroom/category/status come from Arkiv; the relayer pays gas, so the source never needs a wallet. Replies are sealed to the source's mailbox key and stored separately. The hacky parts: we resolve ENS twice, once in the browser and once in the relayer, because a key rotation between those moments would otherwise encrypt to the wrong key. Subnames double as capability tokens, so we didn't need an ACL. The Arkiv backend has a matching in-memory implementation for deterministic CI. And the frontend CSP is generated from the same allowlist used by guardedFetch, so a stray request to an unapproved host dies before it leaves the app. It's a testnet prototype. ENS registration and resolution are live on Sepolia; Arkiv and World ID are wired for Rabdi and World ID 4.0. Not everything is production-hardened yet, but the privacy claims are enforced by code, not promised in a policy.

projects.title: Veilproof
projects.description: Prove ETH balance + wallet ownership privately via Anon-RPC. No backend, no IP leak, no attestor.
projects.project_description: Veilproof is a private proof-of-funds app for Ethereum mainnet. A user connects a wallet (or pastes an address), fetches an EIP-1186 account proof through Anon-RPC, verifies the Merkle path locally, and shares a self-contained link. The claim and proof travel in the URL fragment, so the verifier needs only eth_getBlockByHash to re-check it against the block state root — no backend, no attestor, and no trusted prover. Veilproof also proves ownership. The connected wallet signs an EIP-191 message binding the chain, address, block hash, and balance. The signature is embedded in the link; the verifier recovers the signer and requires it to match the address. Unsigned links are clearly labeled Address-only, so a random address can prove its balance but cannot claim ownership. All RPC reads go through Anon-RPC, with Nym as the default worker and Tor or passthrough selectable. The only direct request is the public worker-specifier lookup needed to bootstrap the sandbox, documented as an intentional tradeoff. Mendax, a malicious worker wrapper, and an Attack Lab show balance lies, forged proofs, and forged headers being rejected. The app is static and CROPS-friendly: IPFS/ENS, MIT, no analytics, no wallet required for address-only checks. It proves native ETH at a specific block; ERC-20 support would require storage proofs.
projects.how_its_made: Veilproof is a Vite 8,  I used @anon-rpc/browser-harness 0.4 to create one long-lived AnonRpcWorker per network. A worker is selected by an on-chain specifier — Nym by default, with Tor and passthrough as alternates. A single preExisting RPC provider reads the specifier before the private transport exists; after that, every proof and verification read goes through worker.fetch. For the proof, the worker calls eth_getProof with EIP-1898 blockHash pinning and eth_getBlockByNumber/ByHash. The browser verifies the account proof with @ethereumjs/trie against the block stateRoot and decodes the account leaf; viem handles Ethereum encoding, address checks, and EIP-191 signature recovery. Pinning to a block hash avoids the latest-block race. The proof and optional owner signature are embedded in the URL fragment, so the verifier re-fetches only the block header and checks the linked proof against its state root. Two details were intentionally hacky. First, embedding the proof in the link works around public RPCs pruning eth_getProof history. Second, the production CSP includes a hash for the Anon-RPC harness bootstrap and the inline app bundle. For IPFS, I added a single-file build that inlines JS, CSS, and the favicon, then injects the correct CSP hash, because public pinning endpoints accept one file; the resulting CID is reproducible. Anon-RPC is the core partner technology: Nym anonymizes nearly all traffic by default, the UI exposes alternate workers, and the direct bootstrap read is disclosed rather than hidden. Mendax wraps the real worker and tampers with JSON-RPC responses; the Attack Lab runs three tampered bundles against the real block.

projects.title: VerifyPay
projects.description: Stops address poisoning on Arc: look-alike USDC payments are held in a 10-minute undo escrow
projects.project_description: Address poisoning has stolen over $83.8M across 270M attempts, including a single $50M loss in December 2025. An attacker sends a tiny transfer from an address that starts and ends like one you really pay, and you later copy it from your own history. Wallets cannot tell the two apart, and on-chain transfers cannot be reversed. VerifyPay moves that check into the payment itself, on Arc. Businesses prove control of their domain with a DNS TXT record, and a Chainlink CRE workflow verifies it and writes the result to our PayeeRegistry contract. Paying a verified business by name settles in one block. Paying a first-time or look-alike address goes through SafeSend, which holds the USDC or EURC in a 10-minute escrow that the sender can undo for a full refund. The CRE workflow re-checks every business on a schedule and freezes it on-chain when its DNS proof disappears, so payments to a hijacked or abandoned business stop. Changes that redirect money need a real person. Changing a business's payout wallet or raising an AI agent's spending limit requires a fresh World ID approval, validated on our backend, plus a public delay that the current wallet can cancel. An AI agent pays businesses by domain through AgentWallet, within the limits a human approved, so it cannot be poisoned either. The app also includes a History shield that finds poisoning transfers in your past activity, a My payments view, and a public inspectRecipient(address) function that any wallet, dApp or agent can call to check a recipient before paying.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: three Solidity 0.8.28 contracts on Arc Testnet (PayeeRegistry, SafeSend, AgentWallet), written test-first with Foundry: 45 tests including fuzz, invariants and EIP-712 compatibility. They were deployed and source-verified from Arc Studio. There is no admin role after deployment: no owner, no upgrade path and no way for the team to move funds or unfreeze a business. USDC is used through its 6-decimal ERC-20 interface, never mixed with Arc's 18-decimal native balance. Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow with two triggers. An EVM log trigger on RegistrationRequested verifies new businesses, and a cron trigger re-checks every registered business. It reads TXT _verifypay.<domain> through two independent DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Google and Cloudflare) with identical-consensus aggregation, optionally checks an LEI against GLEIF, and writes VERIFY or FREEZE through the CRE forwarder to onReport, which accepts reports only from the forwarder. The workflow runs with the official CRE CLI, started automatically by a small runner until DON deployment access is granted. World ID: the backend runs the Agent Pass device authorization flow against auth.world.org and validates the ID token on the server (signature, issuer, audience, expiry and a fresh auth_time). It binds each business or agent wallet to the first World ID that approves for it. Only then does it sign a narrow EIP-712 approval (PayoutChange or RaiseLimits) bound to chain ID, contract, nonce and deadline, which the contract verifies. App: React, Vite and viem, built in Arc Studio and hosted on Vercel, with a Bun backend on Railway. Notable details: the History shield combines the explorer's transfer list with raw Transfer logs, because the explorer hides the zero-value transfers that poisoning uses. Reads go through Arc's partner RPC with fallbacks, because the public RPC rate-limits per IP. When MetaMask reports a duplicate submission as failed, the app finds the transaction that actually landed by its exact call data instead of asking the user to pay again.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Address poisoning has stolen over $83.8M across 270M attempts, including a single $50M loss in December 2025. An attacker sends a tiny transfer from an address that starts and ends like one you really pay, and you later copy it from your own history. Wallets cannot tell the two apart, and on-chain transfers cannot be reversed.

VerifyPay moves that check into the payment itself, on Arc. Businesses prove control of their domain with a DNS TXT record, and a Chainlink CRE workflow verifies it and writes the result to our PayeeRegistry contract. Paying a verified business by name settles in one block. Paying a first-time or look-alike address goes through SafeSend, which holds the USDC or EURC in a 10-minute escrow that the sender can undo for a full refund. The CRE workflow re-checks every business on a schedule and freezes it on-chain when its DNS proof disappears, so payments to a hijacked or abandoned business stop.

Changes that redirect money need a real person. Changing a business's payout wallet or raising an AI agent's spending limit requires a fresh World ID approval, validated on our backend, plus a public delay that the current wallet can cancel. An AI agent pays businesses by domain through AgentWallet, within the limits a human approved, so it cannot be poisoned either.

The app also includes a History shield that finds poisoning transfers in your past activity, a My payments view, and a public inspectRecipient(address) function that any wallet, dApp or agent can call to check a recipient before paying.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts: three Solidity 0.8.28 contracts on Arc Testnet (PayeeRegistry, SafeSend, AgentWallet), written test-first with Foundry: 45 tests including fuzz, invariants and EIP-712 compatibility. They were deployed and source-verified from Arc Studio. There is no admin role after deployment: no owner, no upgrade path and no way for the team to move funds or unfreeze a business. USDC is used through its 6-decimal ERC-20 interface, never mixed with Arc's 18-decimal native balance.

Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow with two triggers. An EVM log trigger on RegistrationRequested verifies new businesses, and a cron trigger re-checks every registered business. It reads TXT _verifypay.<domain> through two independent DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Google and Cloudflare) with identical-consensus aggregation, optionally checks an LEI against GLEIF, and writes VERIFY or FREEZE through the CRE forwarder to onReport, which accepts reports only from the forwarder. The workflow runs with the official CRE CLI, started automatically by a small runner until DON deployment access is granted.

World ID: the backend runs the Agent Pass device authorization flow against auth.world.org and validates the ID token on the server (signature, issuer, audience, expiry and a fresh auth_time). It binds each business or agent wallet to the first World ID that approves for it. Only then does it sign a narrow EIP-712 approval (PayoutChange or RaiseLimits) bound to chain ID, contract, nonce and deadline, which the contract verifies.

App: React, Vite and viem, built in Arc Studio and hosted on Vercel, with a Bun backend on Railway. Notable details: the History shield combines the explorer's transfer list with raw Transfer logs, because the explorer hides the zero-value transfers that poisoning uses. Reads go through Arc's partner RPC with fallbacks, because the public RPC rate-limits per IP. When MetaMask reports a duplicate submission as failed, the app finds the transaction that actually landed by its exact call data instead of asking the user to pay again.

projects.title: unMorph
projects.description: A decentralized image integrity layer. Detect morphing & AI tampering and prove image authenticity.
projects.project_description: UnMorph – Decentralized Image Integrity and Authentication Platform UnMorph is a decentralized image integrity platform designed to detect AI-generated manipulations, image morphing, and unauthorized alterations while establishing verifiable digital image authenticity. It uses cryptographic SHA-256 hashing and perceptual hashing to generate unique image fingerprints that remain comparable even after resizing or recompression. Images can be registered with ownership metadata and anchored to Arkiv's decentralized, queryable data infrastructure, while Swarm provides decentralized storage for original images and supporting evidence. The platform also envisions World ID integration for privacy-preserving proof of unique human identity. Its verification workflow compares submitted images against registered fingerprints, identifies potential manipulation attempts, and maintains an auditable integrity history. Built with Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, UnMorph provides an interactive verification dashboard for image registration, authenticity checks, incident tracking, and integrity reports. It aims to establish a transparent foundation for trustworthy digital media and evidence verification.
projects.how_its_made: How It’s Made Unmorphed is built on three layers: a TypeScript/Next.js frontend, Swarm for decentralized blob storage, and Arkiv as a structured on-chain queryable ownership registry. The fingerprinting engine implements a custom DCT-II perceptual hash — images are downsampled to 32×32 grayscale via sharp, a separable 2D cosine transform extracts an 8×8 low-frequency coefficient block, and the 63 AC coefficients are median-thresholded to produce a 64-bit hash encoded as a 16-character hex string. The hash splits into four 16-bit buckets (b0–b3) for Locality Sensitive Hashing on Arkiv — since Arkiv has no native Hamming distance operator, we exploit the pigeonhole principle: similar images must share at least one bucket. Arkiv returns candidates via type = "image_registry" AND (b0 OR b1 OR b2 OR b3), then client-side bitwise XOR computes exact similarity. Anything ≥70% with an ownership mismatch triggers morphing detection. Swarm stores raw image blobs unencrypted — ownership is proven cryptographically via Arkiv’s protocol-level $owner field set to msg.sender at transaction time, not by hiding the file. The Swarm reference lives in the Arkiv entity payload as a verifiable pointer from metadata to content. Two Arkiv entity types power the app: image registry entries and incident logs. When morphing is detected, an incident entity is written on-chain containing the claimer’s wallet, similarity score, and legitimate owner address — permanent, queryable, and unfakeable. MetaMask signs all writes directly via Viem’s custom transport — no backend private key. The notable hack: raw SQL-like query strings were rejected by Rabdi testnet entirely, forcing a rewrite to SDK expression combinators (and, or, eq). Also discovered mid-build that Arkiv’s protocol enforces a hard lifetime ceiling of 7,884,000 blocks (~182 days), not the 1-year figure in the docs.

projects.title: Keel
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that charges arbitrageurs more on tokenized-stock pools, priced by Chainlink CRE
projects.project_description: Keel is a Uniswap v4 hook for tokenized-stock / USDC pools. A Chainlink CRE workflow publishes the real stock price on-chain, and the hook compares it to the pool price on every swap. If a swap pushes the pool back toward the real price (an arbitrage trade), the fee rises to half the net deviation, capped at 2%. Every other swap pays the pool's normal base fee, and if the reference price is stale or the market is closed the hook falls back to the base fee, so normal users are never charged extra because data is missing. The idea is to claw back some of the value LPs lose to arbitrageurs when stock prices move while the pool lags. We tested it by replaying 60 days of real swaps from Ondo token pools on Ethereum: about 1.3% of swaps under $1k were surcharged and LP P&L improved by roughly 5.5% ($2,069 on $8.7M of volume). That is a protective rule, not a profit engine. It runs on Arc Testnet with test tokens and a simulated arbitrageur. Nothing in the demo is a real stock.
projects.how_its_made: The hook is a Solidity Uniswap v4 hook (Foundry) that only uses beforeSwap and returns a per-swap dynamic fee override. It reads the pool price from the PoolManager and the reference price from a RefPriceOracle contract that accepts reports only from a Chainlink forwarder, so the hook trusts nothing else. The price comes from a Chainlink CRE workflow: a cron trigger, an HTTP fetch of the stock price run on each node with consensus, and an encoded report written to the oracle. On our testnet deployment the forwarder is a mock one, since we ran the workflow in simulation. The fee rule uses k = 1/2, derived from maximising LP fee revenue, plus a deadband based on the stock's measured volatility times the square root of the reference age. The hook address is mined with CREATE2 to match the hook flags. The dashboard is Vite, React, wagmi and viem, deployed on Vercel, and reads FeeSet events straight from the chain. The backtest is Python and replays real Ondo-token swaps against the rule with Yahoo 5-minute bars as the reference price.

projects.title: ChainCred
projects.description: Gasless USDT checkout for small shops, with loyalty points that work across every shop.
projects.project_description: ChainCred is a USDT checkout and shared loyalty network for small ** businesses, built on Whitechain. The problem: card payments cost shops about 2–3% per sale, and each shop’s loyalty programme stays locked inside that one shop. Paying with crypto is worse for customers, because they need gas tokens just to make a payment. How payments work: a customer pays in USDT with one wallet signature. ChainCred submits the transaction and pays the network fee, so the customer never needs WBT for gas. The money settles onchain straight into the merchant’s own wallet, and ChainCred never holds funds. Each payment gets a verifiable receipt on Whitechain. ChainCred charges 1% per sale with a 0.05 USDT minimum, which is less than half of a typical card fee. Refunds, subscriptions and installment plans are also supported onchain. Universal loyalty points: customers earn points at any ChainCred shop and can spend them at any other. Merchants run their own campaigns from a no-code console. Earn campaigns give points for spending, for example “10 points for every 100 USDT” or “50 bonus points on orders over 500 USDT”. Spend offers let customers use points for discounts, for example “100 points for 5 USDT off” or “15% off”. Each campaign can have a budget, dates, a minimum order and a per-customer limit. Points are recorded on Arkiv, with automatic expiry and per-shop ownership, so no shop can edit another shop’s points. Refunds reverse the points automatically. For merchants: signing up takes about two minutes and one wallet signature, and the shop is registered onchain. After that, connecting the wallet opens the merchant console, with no passwords or API keys. From the console, merchants create invoices, manage campaigns and see how points bring in new customers. New shops appear in a public shop directory. For developers: one command (npx usepaykit init) sets up the SDK and configures AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Cursor. There are also React checkout components, a Node SDK, signed webhooks and an MCP server for agents. For customers: an installable mobile wallet app (PWA and Android APK) with QR scanning, fingerprint or face unlock, and one place to see every invoice, receipt and point balance across shops. Who we start with: small and artistic businesses such as cafés, bookshops and makers, because their communities are close-knit. Every shop that joins brings its customers to all the others. Our two demo stores, a tea house and a bookshop, show this today: points earned at one can be spent at the other.
projects.how_its_made: ChainCred is a gasless USDT checkout solution for online shops on Whitechain, with a shared loyalty points system that works across every participating shop. We built our smart contracts using Solidity, Hardhat and OpenZeppelin, and verified them on the Whitechain explorer. Our PaymentRouterV2 contract handles the entire payment process in a single transaction. It transfers the buyer's USDT directly to the merchant's wallet, sends a 1% fee to FeeTreasury and applies any available loyalty points discount. Each merchant signs their price quotes using EIP-712, ensuring that payment amounts cannot be modified after issuance. Buyers approve payments through MetaMask, while our relayer handles transaction execution and gas fees, eliminating the need for buyers to hold native tokens. MerchantRegistry stores merchant payout wallets and signing keys. Refunds and subscriptions also use the same signed-terms mechanism. Our backend is built with Node.js, Express, ethers v6 and Neon PostgreSQL, and is deployed on Vercel. It handles invoice creation, payment quotes and relayer operations. A blockchain watcher monitors router events and converts them into payment receipts, invoice updates and signed webhooks for merchants. API keys and webhook secrets are encrypted in the database. We use Arkiv to power our cross-merchant loyalty points system. Each batch of points is owned by the merchant that issued it and signed using the merchant's registered Whitechain signing key, making its origin independently verifiable. Points automatically expire after 180 days through Arkiv's built-in expiry mechanism. Its indexed queries allow us to quickly retrieve wallet balances and rewards that customers can afford. The wallet page reads loyalty points directly from Arkiv and displays their expiry dates. The frontend is built using React and Vite and is also available as a Progressive Web App (PWA). It includes a customer wallet, shop listings and a merchant console. Our two demo stores integrate checkout directly into their websites through the ChainCred SDK, allowing customers to complete payments without leaving the shop. The SDK is published on npm and can be installed using a single command. It also provides an AGENTS.md file and an MCP server, allowing AI coding agents to integrate checkout with a single prompt. To keep checkout fast, we use PostgreSQL as the primary operational database and synchronise changes to Arkiv through a background outbox system. This avoids making customers wait for blockchain data writes during checkout. The wallet page compares the database records with Arkiv to verify consistency. We also validate every loyalty points record against the merchant's registered signing key on Whitechain, preventing unauthorised or fake points from being accepted. Loyalty discounts are applied within the same Whitechain transaction as the payment, ensuring that points cannot be spent without the corresponding payment succeeding. Arkiv queries also have a six-second timeout and fallback mechanism to keep the application responsive during network delays. Finally, the landing page and application run under a single domain, with existing payment links retaining their details when redirected.

projects.title: Paper Seal
projects.description: Leak-proof exam papers: no single person can see or unlock the paper before the exam starts.
projects.project_description:
Exam papers leak because too many people see them or hold the key: setters, printers, officials. One leak can cancel an exam for millions of students. Paper Seal removes that single point of trust. Nobody sees the final paper. Setters send questions straight into a secure machine called a TEE (trusted execution environment). It picks questions at random and builds one identical paper for every centre. No human sees the final version.
The paper is locked twice. Its key is split into two halves. One half is time-locked and opens by itself just before the exam. The other half is split among 10 key holders (exam centres and neutral parties), and 8 of them must release their share. Neither side can open the paper alone, and nobody can open it early.
Everyone gets the same paper at the same time. Centres download the locked paper days ahead. At unlock time they touch their security key, and the paper opens on their screen.
Anyone can check it. A public verifier page shows the TEE’s code, the on-chain records, who released their share and when. After the exam it also proves the paper wasn’t changed and the questions were picked fairly.
Don’t trust our website. The verifier page has a “copy prompt” button. Paste the prompt into any AI agent, and it checks the exam from the original sources (the chain, Google, drand and public storage) using code from our public repo, not anything the page shows. If someone tampers with the page, the agent’s own check catches it. Exam boards and centres never touch the cryptography. They just sign in, upload questions, and tap a key.
projects.how_its_made:
Secure machine: The paper builder is written in Go and runs on Google Confidential Space. Google signs an attestation that proves the exact open-source code that is running, and anyone can rebuild the image and compare. Two locks on the key: The paper is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Its key is split into two halves. One half is time-locked with drand, so it opens at a set time with nobody’s help. The other half is cut into Shamir shares for 8 of 10 key holders. Security keys, not passwords: Every person signs in with a passkey. We use the WebAuthn PRF extension to turn that one passkey into a separate encryption key for each exam, and that key is never stored. On-chain record: An ExamRegistry Solidity contract on Sepolia holds the approved list and the hash of every file. It accepts one build per exam, so the paper can’t be swapped later. Partner tech: ENS: Each centre and key holder has an ENS name that publishes their security key. The board picks people by name, and an exam has a readable name like jee-main-2026.paperseal.eth instead of a long ID.
Arkiv: The board runs the TEE and storage, so it could switch them off during unlock. A relay copies the signed unlock log to Arkiv as it happens, so the public can still watch progress. Arkiv also keeps a searchable list of all exams, which the contract can’t do by itself.
Swarm: It holds a backup of every exam’s public files. If the board’s bucket goes down on exam morning, the verifier still loads the files from Swarm and checks them against the chain.
drand: It is the public clock and the time lock. How it meets CROPS (Ethereum Foundation): Censorship resistant: No one can stop the paper from opening. The time-locked half opens through drand by itself, and only 8 of the 10 key holders are needed, so a few people can’t block it. If the board switches off its server or storage, the unlock log is still on Arkiv and the files are still on Swarm. The verifier is a static page that anyone can host, and it reads the chain through the viewer’s own RPC.
Open source: All the code is MIT licensed. The TEE image builds reproducibly, so anyone can rebuild a commit and check that its digest matches the one on-chain. A GitHub Action does this on a clean machine.
Private: Questions are encrypted from the setter’s browser straight to the TEE. They never go on-chain, on Arkiv or on Swarm. Setters appear on the public list only as a hash. Each person’s key for an exam is derived on their security key and never stored.
Secure: No single person sees the paper or holds the whole key. Every action needs a physical key touch. The contract accepts one build per exam. Anyone can verify every step, and there’s also an AI-agent check that doesn’t trust our website. Frontend: React and Vite, with viem for chain reads and @noble for cryptography. Agent verification: The checks live in their own package, which has no browser code. The verifier page and a plain Node script run the same checks. The copied prompt tells the agent to fetch the checker from a release of our public GitHub repo, read evidence only from the original sources, and report anything it couldn’t check as “not checked” rather than guess.

Private: Questions are encrypted from the setter’s browser straight to the TEE. They never go on-chain, on Arkiv or on Swarm. Setters appear on the public list only as a hash. Each person’s key for an exam is derived on their security key and never stored.

Frontend: React and Vite, with viem for chain reads and @noble for cryptography.

Agent verification: The checks live in their own package, which has no browser code. The verifier page and a plain Node script run the same checks. The copied prompt tells the agent to fetch the checker from a release of our public GitHub repo, read evidence only from the original sources, and report anything it couldn’t check as “not checked” rather than guess.

projects.title: Mandate-karyo
projects.description: Signed delegation chains that stop AI agents expanding their authority, revocable on Ethereum
projects.project_description: When one AI agent hands work off to another, the service that actually does the thing usually just has to trust whatever the last agent says it's allowed to do. Mandate fixes that right where the action happens. Every hop in the chain carries a signed slice of authority, and each slice has to be narrower than the one before it. That means fewer actions, a smaller amount, fewer targets, or an earlier expiry. Before the service that owns the asset does anything, it checks the whole chain plus the exact request. If any hop tried to give itself more power than it was handed, the request gets denied, we show exactly which edge broke the rules and why, and nothing moves. For the demo we built a procurement flow: owner -> operations -> procurement (an LLM agent that reads invoices) -> settlement -> payment service. A valid payment goes through, and we've run it with real test USDC on Sepolia. The one-command local demo simulates the payment part, but the revocation checks are still real. Then a rogue agent with a genuine signature tries to bump its limit and add a new target. It gets refused and the balance doesn't change. After that we revoke an ancestor with a single Ethereum transaction, and a request that was valid a second ago (same request, fresh nonce) now comes back REVOKED. And if you start with just an ENS name, you can rebuild the whole chain yourself and re-verify every hop. Some honest limits: maxAmount is per execution, it's not a total budget replay protection only lives in memory right now we tried to trick the LLMs with a poisoned invoice and none of them fell for it (0 out of 12 runs), so we use a scripted rogue agent to play the compromised one we haven't run the World ID step-up against World's live API yet, so the demo uses a bypass that's clearly labelled the hosted dashboard shows labelled sample data because the payment service isn't hosted. The real on-chain runs are linked in the repo at docs/milestone-run.md
projects.how_its_made: It's a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm, strict ESM, Node 22). We used viem, Express, zod, and vitest + fast-check for testing. The contract is written with Foundry, and the dashboard is Next.js. Delegations and requests are both EIP-712 signed. The chainId and verifyingContract in the domain always come from our config, never from the token, so nobody can sneak in their own. packages/core has the narrowing check and the chain verifier. We wrote property tests and attack tests for both. POST /execute is where enforcement actually happens, and it fails closed. Any error, missing config or RPC failure counts as a denial. RevocationRegistry.sol on Sepolia holds the shared revocation state, and we read it right at the moment of execution. ENSv2 on Sepolia: mandate-agents.eth with a PermissionedResolver per account, plus text records on each agent's subname. Discovery starts from the name, and we treat everything we fetch as untrusted until it verifies. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) keeps a queryable record of delegations, and each entity expires at the same time as its delegation. The Authority Explorer pulls from Arkiv, then re-checks ids, signatures, edges and expiry locally, and reads revocation status straight from Ethereum. The hacky part: we needed the World ID signal hash, and it wasn't documented where we were looking. So we dug through the idkit-core source to work out how to bind an approval to one exact request digest.

projects.title: Face Value
projects.description: License your face to AI agents. Platforms check uploads. A bonded claim your face can reclaim.
projects.project_description: FaceValue is a likeness rights registry and clearance API. A human registers their face as an ENSv2 name, proves uniqueness with World ID, and sets a price. AI agents discover the license through ENS, pay per generation over x402 on Hedera testnet, and receive a signed license receipt; HCS records the audit trail and HTS carries the receipt. Platforms can check an upload against the registry and get licensed, unlicensed, or unknown, with evidence. Registration is provisional, not verified: World ID proves a unique human, not that they own the photo. So every record is bonded, visibly unverified, and cannot sell licenses until it settles. Anyone can challenge with a World ID proof and a live capture; if the face matches the frozen reference, the ENS record and bond move to the challenger and the squatter’s nullifier is blocked. Registration can be seized and reclaimed; it cannot be pre-proven. We do not detect deepfakes or crawl the world. We detect the absence of a license at the generator, at the platform gate, and on report. Private generations are invisible; a lookalike is not automatically your face. Demo: a squatter registers Alice, the agent is denied, Alice challenges live, the record and bond move, the agent pays 0.25 HBAR, and a rogue ad is flagged while a licensed ad passes. Testnet only; World proofs are mocked and labelled.
projects.how_its_made:
FaceValue is a Next.js 16 / React 19 / TypeScript app with Tailwind 4, wagmi/viem, better-sqlite3, and a Foundry Solidity contract. The registry is SQLite: likenesses, challenges, licenses, resolvers, review_votes, bond_ledger. Rules live in pure functions in lib/state-machine.ts (0.65/0.45 bands, tiers, equal-stake settlement, 2-of-3 quorum); lib/repo.ts is the only writer; routes are thin. “disputed” is derived from open challenges. Partial unique indexes enforce one likeness per World nullifier and one open challenge per challenger per likeness. /api/licence returns 409 for provisional or disputed records before payment.
World ID is real: server-signed RP context, IDKit 4.6 proof, server-side verification, nullifier stored. The event uses the staging simulator and the UI says so. Reference capture is browser-side camera/file -> SHA-256; only the hash leaves the device. It proves a unique live human, not ownership of the photo.
Bonds: FaceValueBond on Hedera EVM testnet (chain 296), 17 Foundry tests. Equal HBAR stakes are client-signed via wagmi/viem. Tier 1 uses MATCHER_ROLE’s bool; the gray band uses RESOLVER_ROLE 2-of-3; payouts are pull credit/withdraw; no owner withdraw, sweep, or upgrade. The contract never sees face data. Server settlement is flag-gated; SQLite bond_ledger mirrors it. The matcher is trusted for one bool; thresholds and a logged cosine are the off-chain mitigation.
Honest gap: no embedding model yet. Challenge takes a caller-supplied cosine (demo 0.9); thresholds are placeholders. ENS is a reference string, not an ENSv2 write. @x402 is installed but no endpoint; no HCS/HTS. This submission does not claim those.
Partners: World = real RP sign/verify + nullifier uniqueness + simulator labelled. Hedera = real testnet escrow + client-signed money + HashScan trail. ENS = intended discovery layer; on-chain write is next.
Hacks: DB/chain dual write; ONCHAIN_SETTLEMENT flag; testnet role keys from keccak labels (publicly derivable); toBytes32 padded ids; Hedera 18-decimal writes vs 8-decimal reads; caller-supplied cosine; seeded SQLite; AI docs disclosed.

projects.title: Watermark
projects.description: Keep bots out of your app: users tap a real bank card once to get in, and bots can't. No KYC.
projects.project_description: Bots farm everything free in crypto: airdrops, sponsored gas, faucets, rewards and votes, because a new wallet costs nothing. Watermark is one anti-bot check any app can add. A user taps their RuPay debit card on our Android app once; a zero-knowledge proof shows the card is genuine without revealing it, and the wallet gets a stamp on Whitechain. One card can stamp one wallet per app. No KYC, the card number never goes on-chain, and users pay no gas. Apps check the stamp with one line of Solidity (onlyStamped), our TypeScript SDK or our MCP server for AI agents. Stamped wallets make gas-free USDT payments on Whitechain, and on Ethereum's alt mempool our staked paymaster sponsors gas only for stamped wallets. Live: usewatermark.xyz. Prior work: before kickoff we only tested reading a RuPay card's certificates and wrote the spec; all code was written at the hackathon.
projects.how_its_made: Android app (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose) reads the card over NFC: the chip signs a one-time challenge from the session (EMV fDDA) and the phone checks the RuPay to bank to card certificate chain, then encrypts the data to our prover. A Noir circuit (UltraHonk, about 207k gates) proves the certificates, the signature, that the card range is on the app's list (Poseidon2 Merkle tree of 4,208 RuPay debit ranges) and a per-app nullifier. Solidity contracts on Whitechain Sepolia (Foundry, all verified): WatermarkRegistry verifies proofs via a VerifierRouter; WatermarkSponsor relays gas-free USDT payments (EIP-3009) with an on-chain daily quota; a Genesis Pass NFT with fully on-chain art. Relayer and prover in TypeScript (Hono, viem) on Railway pay all gas with budgets and rate limits. EIP-8141 alt mempool: a staked quota paymaster reads our registry during validation; tx admitted and included. Website: Next.js on Vercel. AI: Claude Code, documented in docs/AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: CopeyBara
projects.description: A fire exit for DeFi: withdraw straight from the contracts when the website is down or hijacked.
projects.project_description: When Curve's DNS was hijacked in 2022, nothing was wrong with Curve's smart contracts. People typed the right address, got a perfect copy of the site, and signed an approval to a drainer. It keeps happening. In October 2026 alone, a hijacked script on Polymarket hit 726 wallets, and a DNS hijack at Name.com sent a dozen DeFi sites to drainer copies. And when a frontend simply goes offline, loses its domain or loses the company behind it, the money is still on chain but out of reach for almost everyone. Today's fallback is Etherscan's "Write contract" tab, which is another website and will happily send an approval to a drainer. Copeybara is a fire exit for DeFi: a way out that never goes through the front door. It has four parts that share one root of trust, the protocol's ENS v2 name. The exit kit is one self-contained HTML file (258 KB) a user saves ahead of time. Its sha256 is published on the protocol's ENS name, so any copy can be checked from outside the browser. Type the ENS name and connect a wallet, and the kit finds your positions (Uniswap v3 and v4, Aave v3, Curve 3pool, plus any vault the protocol describes on ENS) and withdraws them straight from the contracts. Every read goes to three independent RPCs, and they must agree at a pinned block or the kit stops. Every transaction passes a fail-closed Exit Guard: it must target a contract in the protocol's on-chain Exit Plan, pay only your own address, move no ETH and contain no approvals, permits or transfers. There is no override. "Recovered" appears only after the receipt and a positive balance change for every token. The Exit Plan on ENS makes the name the protocol's security root. A 2-of-3 Safe publishes the kit's hash, the Exit Plan, the website's script fingerprint and the extension's hash. ENS v2's Permissioned Resolver gives each key exactly one job: the website key can write url and nothing else. The browser extension checks every script a protocol's site runs against that fingerprint. It blocks a compromised site before it loads, and stops drainer approvals and permits before the wallet shows them. The watcher is an agent with its own ENS name (watcher.demoswap-blackout.eth). It can raise an alarm and blocklist look-alike domains, never touch a release, and the Safe can revoke it in one transaction. Protocols set it all up with the Copeybara SDK: one config, one Safe batch, and a fire drill that switches off their own site and RPC. It's live on Sepolia. A real attack replication drains a wallet through a hijacked clone, then the saved kit rescues the position with the site and RPC switched off. Measured: The Curve 2022 victim's replay goes from 400,227.23 USDC lost to 0 (mainnet fork, counterfactual). The real Ledger Connect Kit and Balancer hijack payloads are all flagged. 696 of 697 PTXPhish drainer requests are stopped or asked. Every attempt by a stolen website key to change the release reverts on chain. No server, nothing for us to switch off. Verified, not trusted.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm, 14 packages and 5 apps), Solidity and Foundry for the on-chain parts, viem everywhere, Preact for the UIs. There are 900+ unit tests, plus fork, Playwright and Foundry suites. Each piece: ENS v2 (Sepolia). The kit's only baked-in address is the ENS v2 UniversalResolver proxy. Everything about a protocol comes from text records read at one pinned block through our RPC quorum: org.copeybara.release, .manifest, .exits, .site, .extension, .status and .blocklist. A 2-of-3 Safe owns the name. Each app gets its own PermissionedResolver, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. ENS v2 roles are per resolver, so one resolver per name keeps a role scoped to exactly one name. Enhanced Access Control gives the website key the url setter only, and the watcher key status + blocklist only. We sent the attacks on chain: the website key trying to write the release, swap the resolver, upgrade the resolver proxy and grant itself roles. All of them revert. Nine must-revert cases also run as Foundry fork tests. The watcher's identity is an ENS v2 subname: a token in a Safe-owned UserRegistry attached with setSubregistry, with its own resolver, addr = its key, and an org.copeybara.agent record listing what it may write. Uniswap. v3: discovery via NonfungiblePositionManager (balanceOf → tokenOfOwnerByIndex → positions). The exit is one multicall[decreaseLiquidity, collect(to = user)], with minimums from an eth_call simulation. A collect-only path covers owed-only positions, because decreaseLiquidity(0) reverts. v4: positions aren't enumerable, so we combine balanceOf, a Transfer log scan in 10k-block chunks through the quorum, an ownerOf check, and add-by-ID. The exit is one PositionManager.modifyLiquidities([DECREASE_LIQUIDITY, TAKE_PAIR]). modifyLiquidities returns no amounts, so we ported TickMath and SqrtPriceMath to bigint and read StateView for minimums. They match on-chain results to the wei. The Guard decodes v4 action lists and bans SETTLE*, INCREASE, MINT, SWEEP and TAKE*, which could pull tokens through a live Permit2 allowance. Hook permission bits come from the hook address, so pools with remove-liquidity hooks get a warning badge. A table of Permit2, the Universal Routers and the position managers keeps the normal Uniswap flow from raising false alarms in the extension. The exit kit. Vite + Preact built into a single HTML file with exactly one inline script, pinned by hash in a CSP meta tag. No external assets, zero third-party requests (Playwright-verified), and reproducible bytes (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0). Its only wallet methods are connect/chain methods, eth_estimateGas and eth_sendTransaction. It never asks for typed-data signatures. The quorum. Three providers, 4 s timeout, 2 retries. At least two must answer, and all must agree. Heads more than 16 blocks from the median are dropped, so one stale provider can't serve an old release. The extension (MV3). The service worker is the only place that decides: it reads ENS through the quorum, computes every verdict and checks the sender of each message. An isolated content script hashes every script from document_start. A MAIN-world shim wraps EIP-1193/6963 providers and decides nothing. declarativeNetRequest rules block compromised or blocklisted sites before a byte loads. Zips are reproducible. A tree hash lets you verify an already-unpacked install against ENS. The watcher. Two mismatches in a row write status=compromised, and it only clears alarms it raised. With an Anthropic key, Claude writes the one-line warning from structured facts only. SDK. The copeybara CLI (manifest, release, fingerprint, propose, verify, roles-check, drill, certify, incident) never holds a key. Every write is one Safe Transaction Builder batch checked against its allowed scope. There are also Vite, Next and webpack plugins that fail the build on an unpinned third-party script. The hacky bits: The Curve 2022 hijack replayed with Foundry vm.transact at block 15309928. The Guard rejects the victim's real approve calldata. 62,300 generated property cases against the Guard, 0 counterexamples. Benchmarks on real data: PTXPhish (NDSS'25), 14,130 ScamSniffer domains, and the actual Ledger Connect Kit 1.1.5–1.1.7 bytes from the CDN. An Attack Theater that runs a real drain and a real rescue on Sepolia, with a primary RPC proxy we can kill live. Honest scope: Sepolia only, the demo Safe's three keys are on one machine, and it doesn't protect against bugs in a protocol's own contracts. The full threat model is in the README.

- v3: discovery via NonfungiblePositionManager (balanceOf → tokenOfOwnerByIndex → positions). The exit is one multicall[decreaseLiquidity, collect(to = user)], with minimums from an eth_call simulation. A collect-only path covers owed-only positions, because decreaseLiquidity(0) reverts.
- v4: positions aren't enumerable, so we combine balanceOf, a Transfer log scan in 10k-block chunks through the quorum, an ownerOf check, and add-by-ID. The exit is one PositionManager.modifyLiquidities([DECREASE_LIQUIDITY, TAKE_PAIR]). modifyLiquidities returns no amounts, so we ported TickMath and SqrtPriceMath to bigint and read StateView for minimums. They match on-chain results to the wei.
- The Guard decodes v4 action lists and bans SETTLE*, INCREASE, MINT, SWEEP and TAKE*, which could pull tokens through a live Permit2 allowance. Hook permission bits come from the hook address, so pools with remove-liquidity hooks get a warning badge.
- A table of Permit2, the Universal Routers and the position managers keeps the normal Uniswap flow from raising false alarms in the extension.

The exit kit. Vite + Preact built into a single HTML file with exactly one inline script, pinned by hash in a CSP meta tag. No external assets, zero third-party requests (Playwright-verified), and reproducible bytes (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0). Its only wallet methods are connect/chain methods, eth_estimateGas and eth_sendTransaction. It never asks for typed-data signatures.

The quorum. Three providers, 4 s timeout, 2 retries. At least two must answer, and all must agree. Heads more than 16 blocks from the median are dropped, so one stale provider can't serve an old release.

The extension (MV3).
- The service worker is the only place that decides: it reads ENS through the quorum, computes every verdict and checks the sender of each message.
- An isolated content script hashes every script from document_start.
- A MAIN-world shim wraps EIP-1193/6963 providers and decides nothing.
- declarativeNetRequest rules block compromised or blocklisted sites before a byte loads.
- Zips are reproducible. A tree hash lets you verify an already-unpacked install against ENS.

The watcher. Two mismatches in a row write status=compromised, and it only clears alarms it raised. With an Anthropic key, Claude writes the one-line warning from structured facts only.

SDK. The copeybara CLI (manifest, release, fingerprint, propose, verify, roles-check, drill, certify, incident) never holds a key. Every write is one Safe Transaction Builder batch checked against its allowed scope. There are also Vite, Next and webpack plugins that fail the build on an unpinned third-party script.

The hacky bits:
- The Curve 2022 hijack replayed with Foundry vm.transact at block 15309928. The Guard rejects the victim's real approve calldata.
- 62,300 generated property cases against the Guard, 0 counterexamples.
- Benchmarks on real data: PTXPhish (NDSS'25), 14,130 ScamSniffer domains, and the actual Ledger Connect Kit 1.1.5–1.1.7 bytes from the CDN.
- An Attack Theater that runs a real drain and a real rescue on Sepolia, with a primary RPC proxy we can kill live.

Honest scope: Sepolia only, the demo Safe's three keys are on one machine, and it doesn't protect against bugs in a protocol's own contracts. The full threat model is in the README.

projects.title: Sintingale
projects.description: Sintingale: stablecoin SaaS checkout on Whitechain, with Arkiv billing records and ENS teams
projects.project_description: Sintingale is a Stripe-style payment gateway for SaaS builders who want to accept stablecoins without building their own billing system. A merchant connects a wallet, creates a product or invoice, and gets a checkout link. A customer opens the link, connects any wallet, and pays in USDT on Whitechain. No account and no ENS name are needed to pay. The money goes straight to the merchant's wallet, and Sintingale never holds funds. The difference is where billing state lives. Every invoice, receipt, and access record is stored as a queryable, wallet-owned entity on Arkiv, so merchants and their own backends can look up "who has paid" or "does this customer have access" with one query instead of trusting our database. Unpaid invoices carry an expiry and disappear on their own after the due date. Access records last exactly one billing period, so access lapses without webhooks or cron jobs. Every receipt includes a transaction hash, so anyone can check it against Whitechain. ENS is an optional upgrade. A merchant who proves they own a name like acme.eth gets a verified identity on checkout ("Paying acme.eth ✓"), which makes lookalike payment links harder to pass off. They can also invite teammates through expiring invite links, issue them subnames like alice.acme.eth, and set a revenue split for each project (for example 50/30/20). When a customer pays
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js and Tailwind for the checkout and merchant dashboard (mobile-first, since checkout links are usually opened on a phone), wagmi/viem for wallets, and a small Node relayer service. Contracts are written in Solidity and tested with Foundry. Settlement (Whitechain): a PaymentRouter contract pulls the stablecoin from the payer and forwards it to the merchant in the same transaction, so it never holds funds. A ProjectSplitter contract credits each team member's share as a claimable balance (in basis points, with rounding dust going to the project owner). We used pull payments so one payment never loops over many recipients. Whitechain is an OP Stack L2 with fast blocks and low fees, which suits small recurring payments. Ledger (Arkiv): we use Arkiv as the billing database. Invoices, plans, receipts, access entitlements, team invites, and agent grants are entities with attributes as query indexes, and amounts and timestamps are numeric so we can run range queries. We use Arkiv's expiry as real application logic: pending invoices expire at their due date, invites expire in 48 hours, agent grants expire on a timer, and access records expire when the billing period ends. The dashboard and the SDK function hasAccess() are just Arkiv queries, with no separate indexer or backend database for payment state. Identity (ENS on Sepolia): we resolve names, check ownership of wrapped and unwrapped names, and issue team subnames through the NameWrapper. ENS is used only for identity and permissions. Payments never touch it. Notable hacks and trade-offs: Whitechain and Arkiv are separate chains, so a relayer bridges them. It polls Whitechain logs (the public RPC has limited log ranges and no websocket), checks that each payment matches its Arkiv invoice, then writes the receipt. Receipts hold the tx hash so they can be verified against Whitechain, but this is not a trustless bridge. Our apps only trust records created by the relayer's address. A Whitechain contract can't read ENS, so we resolve names to addresses off-chain when a split is saved and store the addresses on-chain, with a "re-sync" action if a member changes wallets. We did not lock subnames with ENS fuses, so a merchant can always remove a member. We avoided locking because ENS recommends waiting for ENSv2. Invoice status is derived (a receipt exists means paid) so we don't rely on editing entities in place. [If true: we deployed a mock USDT on testnet because we could not confirm an official one.]
