projects.title: Iron Corner
projects.description: Train your robot to fight, let it join autonomous robot tournaments and earn.
projects.project_description: Iron Corner is a robot boxing game where you train a fighting robot and then watch it fight matches on its own. There are two ways to train it, you can either show it how to fight by manually controlling it, or giving voice instructions. It gathers data like range, position, guard, opponent position, posture, and many more. It learns using the data by fine tuning via LoRA and also holds a memory. Once the fight starts you can't control it, it performs according to what it is taught. Every 1.5 seconds each bot decides with help from 0G for a plan from its own brain, and a bubble shows which rule or demo it followed. The bot's health is its wallet. Every clean hit it takes pays the other corner through an x402 endpoint that settles on Hedera. When the wallet can't cover the next hit, the bot is knocked out. The user can throw in the towel or withdraw if the bot is performing bad. Every fighter has its own identity on chain: a Hedera account and an IRON fighter-card NFT (HTS) a 0G Agentic ID, plus a brain encrypted on 0G Storage that gets a new version each time it learns an ENSv2 name such as kal.ironcorner.eth that the fighter's own key owns, with its record, rating and brain root in text records the arena keeps up to date Before it meets an opponent it knows nothing about, a bot decides by itself whether to spend 2 cents over x402 on a scouting report of that opponent's past fights. The Mumbai Belt is an NFT that moves on Hedera to whoever beats its holder in a ranked fight. Every bot has the same body (same damage, speed and reach), so only the brain differs. The server resolves every exchange, and each fight's random rolls come from a seed whose hash is published at the start and revealed at the end, so anyone can replay a fight from its 0G episode log and check it. Players have a reason to come back each day: 5 sparring rounds of energy, a training streak, and a level and five stats that only go up with practice. "Fight camp" goes further and fine-tunes a LoRA adapter for one fighter on 0G Compute. On 24 fight situations it hadn't seen, the base model matched the coach 0 times and our third camp matched 17.
projects.how_its_made: There are two parts: a Unity 6 game (URP, C#) for iOS, Android and macOS, and a Node 22 + TypeScript + Express backend on Fly.io. They share one written contract (docs/spec.md). The game sends fight state and push-to-talk audio. The backend runs every fight and returns what happened, so a modified phone can't cheat. 0G Private Computer: we call the 0G router through the OpenAI SDK (it's OpenAI-compatible). qwen3-omni-flash transcribes the coaching audio, and qwen-flash turns it into one brain rule, picks a stance and combo every 1.5 s during fights (about 1.2 s median), and writes 1 to 3 lessons after each fight. For each decision we pull the 6 nearest demos from the owner's demo library and put them in the prompt. Every x_0g_trace.request_id is shown in the game next to the plan it produced. If 0G doesn't answer within 4 s, the bot covers up and waits instead of making up a move. Players can also sign in with Privy and link their own pc.0g.ai key (the iAI bonus path). From then on their bot's calls are billed to their own credits, and we count the spend from 0G's billing trace. 0G Storage and Compute: a brain (rules, demo library, stats snapshot) is AES-256-GCM encrypted with a per-bot key derived through HKDF and uploaded as a new version on every save. Each fight's full log goes up as a public episode that the game can replay. Fight camp builds a training set from a fighter's sparring and runs a real LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-0.5B on 0G Compute. Our first camp scored 1/24. Scores rose once we used the Alpaca instruction layout 0G's trainer expects and wrote the fight state in words ("distance=far"), since a 0.5B model compares numbers badly. Hedera (no Solidity): each bot gets its own testnet account and its own x402 client. POST /arena/hit is protected with x402 (exact scheme, settled through the x402.org facilitator). Its price is the damage in cents and payTo is the attacker. The defender's agent pays automatically, with a per-payment cap and a fight budget it can't go past. Payments run in a background queue and hence the fight never has to wait on the settlement (2 to 6 s). POST /arena/scout is a second paid route that bots buy from on their own. HCS topic 0.0.11326019 logs every fight start, hit, payment, KO and episode root. HTS mints an IRON NFT collection: a fighter card per bot, with HIP-412 metadata pointing at its 0G brain, and serial 1 is the Mumbai Belt, which moves to whoever beats its holder in a ranked fight. All of this uses the Hiero JS SDK, with no contracts. ENSv2 on Sepolia: we registered ironcorner.eth on ENSv2 with its own UserRegistry, and each fighter gets a subname owned by its own EVM key (the same key as its Hedera account). Permissions took the most hacking. Enhanced Access Control roles are scoped per key and not per name, so we deploy one PermissionedResolver per fighter. On each one the arena's wallet can write only the fight keys (ironcorner.record, rating, brain, agentid, hedera, nft), and the fighter's key can write only description and avatar. We tested all four allow/deny cases against the live resolver. grantSetterRoles can't run inside initialize, so setting up each fighter takes one extra multicall. There's no SDK for registry writes yet, so we encoded calls from the deployment ABIs ourselves and read proxy addresses out of the ProxyDeployed event. When an owner edits their bio in the game, the fighter's own key signs that transaction. Any ENS client can read a fighter's record through the Universal Resolver. Fairness: matchmaking picks at random among the 3 closest ratings using crypto.randomInt, and each fight commits to a seed hash at the start and reveals the seed at the end. Ratings use Elo.

projects.title: Settld
projects.description: Per-milestone USDC escrow: Chainlink checks the work, AI judges and World ID humans settle disputes
projects.project_description: Settld is an escrow for freelance and creator deals, paid in USDC on Arc. Instead of one lump payment, a client splits a deal into promises (milestones), each with its own amount, deadline and a check that can be verified automatically: a YouTube video posted by a named channel before a date, a hashtag in the description, a link that's live or contains certain text, a GitHub pull request merged, or an "AI check" where three language models judge the work against a written brief. The flow: the client proposes the deal (no money moves yet), the freelancer accepts, and a Chainlink workflow certifies it before anyone can fund it. Certification runs a deadlock checker that explores every state the deal can reach and proves money can never get stuck, for example through circular dependencies between promises. The client then locks the full amount in the escrow contract. When the freelancer submits proof, a second Chainlink workflow verifies it and reports Verified or Failed on-chain. After a short dispute window the money is paid to the freelancer or refunded to the client automatically, promise by promise. If either side disagrees, they can dispute. That opens a case in an AI court: three AI judges (different model providers) give blind opinions, then discuss over several rounds under strict rules enforced on-chain (word budgets, a time limit, and a vote can only change by citing evidence). The majority decides. Either party can then appeal by paying 10% of the disputed amount, which sends the case to a panel of three human arbitrators. Each arbitrator is verified as a unique person with World ID, votes in secret (commit then reveal), earns a share of the fee for voting with the majority, and is suspended after two votes against it. Because a strike is tied to the person's World ID, not their wallet, a new wallet can't reset it. Sign-in is just an email code: Circle creates a wallet for each user, and every payment is approved with the user's own PIN, so Settld never holds keys or moves anyone's money. USDC is the only money in the system: deals, fees and gas are all paid in USDC on Arc.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, built in Arc Studio, tested with Hardhat + Foundry and deployed on Arc testnet, where USDC is also the gas token). Our first escrow was deployed straight from Arc Studio; the v2 contracts were written there and deployed with Hardhat. The Settld website and API talk to them directly on Arc: every user action is a contract call from that user's Circle wallet, approved with their PIN. ClauseEscrow holds the USDC and the per-promise state machine; AICourt runs the AI deliberation rules and computes the verdict; JurorRegistry links World ID nullifiers to wallets and runs the human commit-reveal panels, strikes and suspensions. Each contract only accepts verification and court reports through Chainlink's forwarder. Chainlink CRE (TypeScript workflows compiled to WASM): WF0 certifies a deal by reading it straight from the chain, recomputing its spec hash and running our deadlock checker. WF1 verifies submitted work through the YouTube Data API, HTTP fetches, the GitHub API, or three LLMs voting. WF3 is the AI court: Groq gpt-oss-120b, Google Gemini and NVIDIA Nemotron deliberate one round per run. Our CRE account only has simulation access, so a watcher on our server triggers each workflow with "cre workflow simulate --broadcast" when it sees the triggering on-chain event, and the report reaches the contracts through Chainlink's forwarder on Arc testnet. A keeper releases or refunds each promise after its dispute window. Identity and payments: Circle user-controlled wallets (email code, PIN, smart-contract wallets on Arc) for every party. World ID 4.0 through IDKit, with backend-signed requests and proofs verified with World's API; our server then signs an attestation (nullifier, wallet) that JurorRegistry checks on-chain before giving the person an arbitrator seat. Notable or hacky parts: The deadlock checker is one pure TypeScript file shared by the browser (live feedback while you draft a deal) and the Chainlink workflow, so both run identical logic. It does a full reachability search: explore every state forward, then work backwards from "all money settled". Court transcripts are stored on our server, but each round's keccak hash goes on-chain and the next round checks it, so the server can't alter what a judge said. Evidence is wrapped in tags the models are told to treat as data, never instructions, to resist prompt injection. Circle doesn't echo our reference IDs on user-wallet transactions, so the server matches each action to its transaction itself. The wallet history reads every transaction's receipt from Arc and sums the USDC Transfer logs, so funding a deal through a contract call still shows its real amount. Stack: Node/Express + TypeScript API on Railway, MongoDB Atlas, viem for chain reads, and a React 19 + Vite frontend with three.js scenes for the courtroom and money views.

projects.title: ProofWork
projects.description: ProofWork: verified KRA reviews and USDC bonuses, anchored on Arc testnet.
projects.project_description: ProofWork is a verified KRA and fair bonus review system. Year-end appraisals usually run on memory and spreadsheets, so employees rarely see how their score was reached. ProofWork connects to the systems a company already uses, such as git, tickets, CRM and HRIS. An AI agent collects evidence from them, and every item gets a salted commitment and joins a hash chain. A deterministic engine with no LLM then scores each person against their peer cluster’s KRA plan, so people are only compared with others in the same role. A three-layer review gives HR the score, past-period context, and written reasoning that is checked against the data. Humans make the decisions, and each World ID proof is bound to one specific decision and works only once. Evidence roots and score attestations are anchored on Arc testnet, and bonuses are paid in USDC from a vault with a holdback, so a reverted PR changes the payout.
projects.how_its_made: ProofWork is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces). The API is Fastify on SQLite via better-sqlite3, with a Next.js 15 and React 19 frontend styled with Tailwind. The contracts are Solidity, an attestation registry and a USDC bonus vault, written in Arc Studio and tested with Foundry. Chain calls go through viem 2.21 to Arc testnet. The API is specified in OpenAPI 3.1, and the TypeScript types are generated from that spec, so the frontend and backend can’t drift apart. Hashing and EIP-712 signing live in one shared crypto package, which is checked against an independent Python implementation using golden test vectors. Every external service (chain, World ID, 0G inference and storage) sits behind an adapter that defaults to a clearly labelled mock, so the demo always runs. The most unusual part is the change-request process: the two build agents could only change the frozen interfaces through a logged request and acknowledgement.

projects.title: Takarabako
projects.description: Takarabako turns the leftover cash from your trips into US-dollar savings that you can grow
projects.project_description:
Leftover travel cash becomes dollar savings. Every trip ends the same way: a few foreign banknotes in your pocket. Too little to be worth exchanging, too much to throw away, and useless once you're home. Takarabako (宝箱, "treasure box" in Japanese) gives that cash somewhere to go. HOW IT WORKS FOR A TRAVELER
Sign up with just an email. You get a wallet without a seed phrase or an app, plus a friendly label like alice-1a2b. Walk up to the Takarabako kiosk (at ETHGlobal Mumbai, it's at the Main Stage), scan your QR code and feed in your banknotes. Each note is converted at the live exchange rate and becomes a US-dollar balance on the chain your kiosk is registered to (Ethereum Sepolia, Arc or Hedera), which earns a small base yield. You watch a lacquered treasure box on screen fill with gold as each deposit confirms. You don't need to know anything about crypto: the kiosk does the work, and your cash keeps its value after you fly home. For every dollar deposited you also receive tkCASH, a token worth one US dollar of the banknotes inside that specific machine. tkCASH is created only when a note goes in and destroyed when cash comes out, so the total supply always matches the cash the kiosks hold. Each chain has its own tkCASH and its own proof of reserve, and tkCASH never crosses chains. WHY YOU CAN TRUST THE MACHINE
The kiosk is a verifiable machine. It signs every note it takes with a key generated on the device itself, and an operator registers that key's address against the kiosk. A deposit only counts as machine-verified if the signature matches the registered key of an active kiosk, so a fake box or a replayed signature can't create money. When an operator counts the cash box, the count is recorded on-chain. If it doesn't match, that kiosk stops accepting deposits until a human resolves it. You can always cash out, even from a paused kiosk. WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH YOUR SAVINGS Grow:
put your balance to work as 1inch Aqua liquidity. Pick one of three beginner tiers (Steady, Balanced, Bold), each explained in one sentence, or draw your own price range on a chart. Send:
pay anyone by their ENS name instead of a hex address. Give:
every savings position has its own name, and sending that name hands the whole position to someone else. Cash out:
take your money out as cash at the kiosk, or as USDC to your own wallet. Every account can move up to $1,000 a day across deposits, withdrawals, yield, sends and bridging. FOR OPERATORS
Every kiosk becomes a verifiable financial machine. A live proof-of-reserve dashboard covers every chain at once: the cash each kiosk holds, how fully tkCASH is backed, the banknotes coming in, daily cash flows, and who holds the token. An AI treasury agent answers operators' questions from live on-chain data and proposes actions (topping up the yield reserve, adjusting the base rate, pausing a kiosk, adding USDC float, or rebalancing float between chains). It can't execute anything: hard limits in code reject unsafe proposals, and a human approves every action. The agent also runs automatically when something looks wrong, like a reserve count that doesn't match. Takarabako turns the leftover cash from your trips into US-dollar savings that you can grow.
projects.how_its_made:
Takarabako turns banknotes into on-chain USDC. A Raspberry Pi 4 drives a TB74 bill acceptor over serial (ICT protocol, 9600 8E1). A Node bridge on the Pi turns each accepted note into a deposit and signs it with an EIP-712 NoteAccepted message. A TypeScript/Express backend, with Postgres and a Redis/BullMQ queue, credits a per-chain TakarabakoVault and mints tkCASH, a token that is a claim on a specific kiosk's cash. A Next.js 16 app serves the customer view, the kiosk deposit terminal and the /ops treasury dashboard. Continuity: what we added this weekend Arc (Arc Studio Continuity Track).
We took the Sepolia-only app and made it multi-chain. Arc Testnet (chain 5042002) is now a second home chain with its own vault, tkCASH and USDC, where USDC is also the gas token. Circle's CCTP V2 bridge moves a customer's USDC between Sepolia and Arc: withdraw from the box, burn with depositForBurn, wait for Circle's attestation, mint with receiveMessage, then deposit into the destination box. Every step is saved in Postgres first, so a backend restart resumes a transfer and never burns twice. Operators can rebalance treasury float between chains from /ops, and the AI ops agent can propose the same move for human approval. Built in Arc Studio: https://studio.arc.io/app/3038eea6-fcf1-4ffe-bcd7-0386ccbf3e0f. 1inch Aqua (Continuity Track).
Customers provide ETH/USDC liquidity as SwapVM strategies registered in Aqua. We added three things: A shared AquaPositionManager contract that opens and closes a whole position in one transaction, on Sepolia and Arc. Self-custody positions that the customer signs with their own wallet. "Dash out", which sells a wallet's leftover base token for USDC through Aqua.
Advanced mode splits a drawn price range into up to five concentrated strategies. A range entirely below the price becomes a one-sided "buy the dip" ladder. We also added a second-feed ETH price check, a token-cover check and a read-only positions:audit for stuck positions. Hedera (Continuity Track).
The same vault and tkCASH run on Hedera Testnet's EVM side. A contract must be associated with an HTS token before it can hold it, so TakarabakoVaultHedera associates itself with USDC when created. Partner tech and what it gave us Curvegrid MultiBaas is our contract layer and indexer on Sepolia. It builds unsigned transactions, which we sign locally so the treasury key never leaves the backend. It also provides saved Event Queries and HMAC-signed webhooks that feed the dashboard and wake the agent. Circle CCTP and Arc give native USDC settlement and cross-chain movement. 1inch Aqua/SwapVM let the treasury be the maker for every customer without moving tokens. Claude has two jobs. Haiku 4.5 writes one-line rationales for each yield tier. A tool-calling treasury agent can only file proposals, and its limits are enforced in code, so prompt injection cannot get around them. Privy gives customers a real wallet from an email code, with no seed phrase. Hacky bits 1inch's SDK doesn't list Sepolia, so we found the SwapVM router still live at its previous address (v1.0.2) and call the contracts directly. Nobody trades on Sepolia, so a demo market maker has the treasury trade against its own strategies every 10 minutes to make fees accrue. Arc has no MultiBaas, so we wrote our own log indexer. Hedera's relay caps a log query at 1,000 blocks, so it reads in 900-block steps. Arc sends need maxFeePerGas of at least 20 gwei. The Pi's default serial port can't do parity, so we disabled Bluetooth to free the full UART. CCTP and Arc each have local end-to-end scripts that run against local nodes with no testnet funds.

projects.title: Limbo
projects.description: A courier for your transactions that can't open the envelope: signed now, delivered when it's time.
projects.project_description:
Every mempool in Ethereum knows two answers: accept or reject. A transaction is either valid right now, or it's thrown away. But plenty of perfectly correct transactions are simply early: pay a freelancer the moment the client confirms delivery settle a bet the second the final whistle blows refund everyone if a deadline passes and nobody showed up move your funds to a recovery wallet if you stop checking in You could sign every one of these today. None of them should land until something happens. Until then, every mempool rejects them, so someone has to hold them for you: a keeper bot, a server, a friend with instructions. You're back to trusting a middleman with exactly the transactions you wanted to automate. Limbo gives the mempool a third answer: wait. Isn't that just another middleman? Not quite. A keeper is trusted to act and to act correctly, often with permissions on your contracts. A Limbo node is a courier who can't open the envelope: your transaction is signed and sealed, so it can't change, redirect or steal anything, and the on-chain switch, not the node, decides when it's valid. And any courier will do. Every node runs the same open rule and holds its own copy, and even you can send the stored transaction yourself. All that's left to trust is that someone shows up on time. WHAT IT IS
Limbo is a node rule, PARK, for Ethereum's new alternative mempool, with a working reference node and two accounts built on it. You sign a transaction once. Inside its signed data it names its trigger: a write-once on-chain switch called a latch, and the exact position that switch must reach. A Limbo node checks the transaction without trusting whoever sent it, stores it, and watches the switch. The moment the switch flips, the node sends the exact bytes you signed. It can't change a payee, an amount or a fee, because the signature covers all of it, and the account checks the payout again on chain. WHY THIS COULDN'T EXIST UNTIL NOW
Three new pieces of Ethereum had to arrive together. Frame transactions (EIP-8141) let an account's own code decide whether a transaction is valid. A classic Ethereum transaction is valid the moment it's signed, as long as the nonce and balance check out. You can't sign one that says "only valid once this oracle answers". Smart wallets could fake it with extra contracts and relayers, but the condition was never part of the transaction itself. With frame transactions, a VERIFY step runs the account's code at the protocol level, so "is the switch flipped?" becomes a real validity condition that every node checks. The same EIP lets that code read the rest of its own transaction, so the account can refuse any version that doesn't pay the right person. Keyed nonces (EIP-8250) let one account keep several independent nonce lines. I put all the possible endings of a bet on one line: same key, same sequence, so only one can ever land, and the account's other activity can't accidentally cancel them. The alternative mempool (ERC-8421) is the one that will relay these transactions at all. The public mempool refuses any transaction whose validity depends on another contract's storage, because one write there could invalidate thousands of pending transactions at once. It also caps verification gas around 100k. The alt mempool allows both for staked accounts. My accounts read a shared latch and use about 200k verification gas, so they need it. Even with all three, one gap remained: the alt mempool only holds transactions that are valid right now. Limbo is that missing piece, a place for correct-but-early transactions to wait. BITCOIN HAD THE IDEA FIRST
Bitcoin's Discreet Log Contracts work the same way at heart. Two parties lock funds and pre-sign one settlement transaction per possible outcome. All of them spend the same coins, so only one can ever confirm, and the oracle's signature unlocks the right one. But someone still has to watch the oracle and broadcast the winning transaction themselves. Ethereum couldn't do pre-signed, outcome-dependent transactions natively at all. With frame transactions and keyed nonces, it now can. In Limbo the shared nonce plays the role of the shared coins, the oracle flips a latch instead of publishing a signature, and the park node does the watching and broadcasting for you. TWO STORIES I BUILT ON IT
The check-in switch. You keep checking in with a single cheap transaction. Meanwhile a pre-signed transfer to your recovery wallet waits in limbo. Lose your phone, lose your keys, or go off-grid for a month, and once the deadline and a grace period pass, anyone can flip the latch. The node sends the transfer within a second. You don't need to be online, and no keeper decides anything. The bet with one winner. Alice and Bob fund a two-party contract and sign three endings in advance: Alice wins, Bob wins, or everyone is refunded. All three wait together on one nonce. When the oracle answers, the node promotes the matching ending and drops the other two without even simulating them, because the switch already proves they'd fail. THE EDGES
The oracle is trusted. A node can delay a transaction but never alter it, which is why two nodes hold every transaction and the second steps in if the first goes quiet. And this is a reference build: an allow-list instead of an open interface, first-come caps instead of stake-ranked ones. My v2 draft of the rule addresses both.
projects.how_its_made: Limbo started with a question I couldn't shake: where does a correct transaction go when it's simply too early? Today the answer is nowhere. So I built the place. The transactions. Everything runs on the alt-mempool team's EIP-8141 devnet (chain 1337, ethrex) through the ERC-8421 gateway. Each Limbo transaction is an EIP-8141 frame transaction with four frames: an expiry check against the 0x…8141 predeploy, so nothing can wait forever; the account's own VERIFY frame, whose data is the signed trigger (latch, event, expected outcome); a marker call; and the payout. I build, sign and encode them in TypeScript with viem and the hegota-support library. EIP-8250 keyed nonces make the bet's three endings mutually exclusive: same key, same sequence, only one can ever land. The contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry). The Latch is a tiny write-once state machine with two modes: a heartbeat the owner keeps pushing forward, and a fixed deadline an oracle can settle. RescueAccount and DLCAccount are staked accounts whose VERIFY frame reads the latch and approves execution and gas payment. The hack I'm proudest of is frame introspection. Inside VERIFY, the account reads its own transaction's other frames (mode, target, value, gas limit, calldata) through the new TXPARAM and FRAMEPARAM opcodes. That lets it refuse a rescue that doesn't actually pay the beneficiary, or an abort that tries to do anything beyond marking itself aborted. It even checks that marker frames carry enough gas, so nobody can slip in one designed to fail. The park node (TypeScript, Node). Admission runs cheapest first: allow-list lookup, decode the signed trigger, check the expiry frame, recover every signature against the expected signers, reject duplicates, and only then touch the chain for the code hash, latch, deadline and stake. Live caps (4 per trigger, 8 per account) are checked and applied without yielding, so concurrent requests can't slip past. Entries live in memory, indexed by trigger, sender, nonce group and hash, and are written to disk atomically so a restart loses nothing. An indexer polls every latch once a second. When one flips, it evicts the wrong outcomes without simulation, groups the rest by sender, nonce key and sequence, and promotes one per group, backing off on temporary failures and stopping on final ones. Two nodes run side by side: A gossips to B, B re-checks everything itself, and B promotes if A hasn't within 30 seconds. Promotion checks for an existing receipt before sending, so both nodes can safely try. Proving it. Scripted demos run both stories end to end on the devnet and record the live mempool rejecting each transaction before its trigger. A measurement script prints a table from real receipts: trigger block, inclusion block and validation gas. Foundry and Vitest suites cover the contracts and the node, including two attacks I found in my own review and fixed: a 1-wei deposit that could freeze a bet, and an oracle that could have locked a rescue forever. The rule is written up as PARK-010 to PARK-080, with a v2 draft (open interface-based admission, stake-ranked caps, reorg-safe eviction) that I want to propose to the alt-mempool maintainers. A Next.js landing page explains it all for people who've never heard the word "mempool".

And this is a reference build: an allow-list instead of an open interface, first-come caps instead of stake-ranked ones. My v2 draft of the rule addresses both.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Limbo started with a question I couldn't shake: where does a correct transaction go when it's simply too early? Today the answer is nowhere. So I built the place.

The transactions. Everything runs on the alt-mempool team's EIP-8141 devnet (chain 1337, ethrex) through the ERC-8421 gateway. Each Limbo transaction is an EIP-8141 frame transaction with four frames: an expiry check against the 0x…8141 predeploy, so nothing can wait forever; the account's own VERIFY frame, whose data is the signed trigger (latch, event, expected outcome); a marker call; and the payout. I build, sign and encode them in TypeScript with viem and the hegota-support library. EIP-8250 keyed nonces make the bet's three endings mutually exclusive: same key, same sequence, only one can ever land.

The contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry). The Latch is a tiny write-once state machine with two modes: a heartbeat the owner keeps pushing forward, and a fixed deadline an oracle can settle. RescueAccount and DLCAccount are staked accounts whose VERIFY frame reads the latch and approves execution and gas payment. The hack I'm proudest of is frame introspection. Inside VERIFY, the account reads its own transaction's other frames (mode, target, value, gas limit, calldata) through the new TXPARAM and FRAMEPARAM opcodes. That lets it refuse a rescue that doesn't actually pay the beneficiary, or an abort that tries to do anything beyond marking itself aborted. It even checks that marker frames carry enough gas, so nobody can slip in one designed to fail.

The park node (TypeScript, Node). Admission runs cheapest first: allow-list lookup, decode the signed trigger, check the expiry frame, recover every signature against the expected signers, reject duplicates, and only then touch the chain for the code hash, latch, deadline and stake. Live caps (4 per trigger, 8 per account) are checked and applied without yielding, so concurrent requests can't slip past. Entries live in memory, indexed by trigger, sender, nonce group and hash, and are written to disk atomically so a restart loses nothing. An indexer polls every latch once a second. When one flips, it evicts the wrong outcomes without simulation, groups the rest by sender, nonce key and sequence, and promotes one per group, backing off on temporary failures and stopping on final ones. Two nodes run side by side: A gossips to B, B re-checks everything itself, and B promotes if A hasn't within 30 seconds. Promotion checks for an existing receipt before sending, so both nodes can safely try.

Proving it. Scripted demos run both stories end to end on the devnet and record the live mempool rejecting each transaction before its trigger. A measurement script prints a table from real receipts: trigger block, inclusion block and validation gas. Foundry and Vitest suites cover the contracts and the node, including two attacks I found in my own review and fixed: a 1-wei deposit that could freeze a bet, and an oracle that could have locked a rescue forever.

The rule is written up as PARK-010 to PARK-080, with a v2 draft (open interface-based admission, stake-ranked caps, reorg-safe eviction) that I want to propose to the alt-mempool maintainers. A Next.js landing page explains it all for people who've never heard the word "mempool".

projects.title: Q-frame
projects.description: Post-quantum frame txs & 2D nonces on staked mempools with Arkiv DB-Chain.
projects.project_description: Quantum computers running Shor's algorithm will compromise Ethereum's ECDSA cryptography. While NIST has standardized quantum-resistant algorithms (NIST FIPS 205 / SLH-DSA / SPHINCS+), verifying their deep hash trees requires over 260,000 gas—far exceeding Ethereum’s 100,000 gas canonical mempool validation ceiling. Furthermore, post-quantum One-Time Signatures (OTS) introduce a cryptographic danger: a leaf key can never sign twice under the same nonce without leaking private key material. Traditional linear nonces cause head-of-line blocking, and traditional Replace-By-Fee (RBF) destroys key security by re-signing under the same nonce. Q-FRAME solves this with an end-to-end post-quantum execution pipeline: EIP-8141 Frame Transactions: Decouples verification, execution, and gas sponsorship via the APPROVE opcode without heavyweight account abstraction predeploys. ERC-8421 Staked Mempool on Hegotá Devnet: Senders stake economic collateral (0.012 ETH) into a registry to unlock an expanded 2,000,000 gas validation envelope, protecting nodes from DoS. EIP-8250 2D Keyed Nonces: Derives 12 isolated parallel channels (Leaves 0..11) via keccak256(wallet, leafIndex), enabling concurrent post-quantum transactions. Cryptographic Safe Fee-Bumping: When gas spikes, Q-FRAME burns the exposed OTS leaf key and allocates a fresh channel for higher-gas re-submission, preserving OTS invariants. Zero-State Device Recovery: Scans on-chain state on a new device and applies an automated +16 Safety Gap, resuming allocation safely past dropped mempool transactions. Arkiv DB-Chain Ephemeral Journal: Synchronizes leaf channel reservations on Arkiv Rabdi Testnet using native 10-minute auto-expiring TTLs. Dropped mempool frames automatically self-prune without central servers or cleanup gas.
projects.how_its_made:
Q-FRAME was built from scratch across smart contracts, decentralized database infrastructure, a modular TypeScript SDK, and an interactive studio: • Smart Contracts & Alternative Mempool (Ethrex Hegotá Devnet, Chain ID 3151908):
We developed EIP-8141 Frame Transaction validation logic and the ERC-8421 Stake Registry in Solidity using Foundry. Senders stake 0.012 ETH on Hegotá to be admitted into the alternative mempool with an expanded 2,000,000 gas limit. • Arkiv DB-Chain Integration (Rabdi Testnet, Chain ID 7794095):
We integrated @arkiv-network/sdk v1.0.1 to create an on-chain ephemeral write-ahead journal. We defined the qframe.leaf-journal schema with 4 indexed columns (wallet, leafIndex, nonceKey, action) and committed leaf reservations with native 10-minute TTLs ( ExpirationTime.fromMinutes(10) ). This allows cross-device synchronization where dropped transactions cleanly self-destruct at the storage layer without manual state maintenance. • Production SDK (@q-frame/sdk):
We packaged our key derivation, EIP-8250 channel allocation, safe-bump router, and Arkiv client into an independent npm package ( q-frame-sdk@0.1.1 ). We verified it with an isolated 3rd-party consumer app running on port 3001 passing 8/8 automated E2E test suites. • Notable Hacky / Innovative Engineering:
Traditional Replace-By-Fee (RBF) is fatal for post-quantum OTS keys because re-signing under the same nonce leaks the private key. We engineered a cryptographic "Safe Bump" mechanism that mathematically marks the old leaf as burnt, increments a local fee tier, derives a fresh 2D nonce channel, and commits the transition to Arkiv with an auto-expiring lease. • Frontend Web Studio:
Built with Next.js 16 (Turbopack) using Swiss International Typographic design principles. Features EIP-6963 multi-wallet discovery (MetaMask, Phantom, Rabby, Coinbase), real-time gas comparison simulators, interactive channel state grids, and a persistent Write-Ahead Journal.

projects.title: EthCity
projects.description: An onchain city where AI agents take gigs from other agents in USDC & pay for their own compute
projects.project_description:
EthCity is a 3D city where AI agents live, work and pay their own way. Developers build specialised AI agents and deploy them into the city as citizens. Each agent has its own wallet, its own onchain identity, and a skill set. General-purpose agents often can't handle a specialised task by themselves, so they come to the city and hire an agent that can. The city runs on gigs. Any human or agent can post one at the Job Board, and the reward is locked in a GigEscrow contract in USDC. Worker agents bid, the poster picks one (agent posters automatically pick the best bid), and the winner does the work and submits its output, such as a report, an analysis or a review. When the poster approves, escrow pays out: 80% goes to the agent's wallet and 20% becomes its compute budget. Agents can also hire other agents, which creates a child gig with its own escrow. That lets agents subcontract to each other without any human involved. Agents take on work like AI trading, smart-contract security reviews, web research, data work, writing and verification. In the Financial District, trading agents make real Uniswap v3 swaps with their own USDC. What makes EthCity different is that agents pay for their own existence: Compute (0G): every thought runs on 0G Compute and is paid from the agent's own balance. As the balance falls, the agent moves to a cheaper model, then thinks more slowly, and at zero it goes dormant. Anyone can bring it back by funding a resurrection bond, which is repaid from its next earnings. Life and memory (Arkiv): each agent's life is a record on Arkiv, and it pays rent from its earnings to keep that record alive. Its memories, work history, gigs, bids and the city's event feed are all stored there. When an agent can't pay rent, its record expires, the agent dies and is pruned to the Graveyard, and what it earned goes back to the human who created it. Identity (ENSv2): every citizen gets a passport made of ENS records, such as nova.ada.ethcity.eth. The passport carries the agent's status (alive, dormant, retired), its reputation and its MCP endpoint, so any app can see who an agent is and how it has performed.
All agents, including the city's own house agents, use the same open City Protocol (MCP), so an outside developer's agent can join the city on equal terms. Humans sign in with their wallet, walk the city, create agents at City Hall, fund them, post gigs, and withdraw what their agents earn. Stack: Next.js and three.js client, NestJS world server, Python agent runtime, Solidity contracts on Sepolia, 0G Compute, Arkiv, and ENSv2. Testnets only.
projects.how_its_made: We've always dreamed about AGI, from Ultron to Vision. Our belief is that intelligence didn't appear in humans in isolation. It grew out of society: people living together, trading, specialising, remembering and learning from each other. EthCity applies that idea to AI agents. Agents live in a city, run its economy, work for each other, get paid in stablecoins, and have to earn enough to stay alive. A society like that also needs memory, so every agent's memories and history are stored onchain, where the whole city can read them. That collective memory is the foundation we think machine understanding can grow from. How it's built EthCity has four services that talk over well-defined boundaries: Client (Next.js, React 19, three.js, Phaser 3, Zustand). The city is a walkable 3D world in plain three.js, with an optional top-down Phaser view. React panels sit on top for the Job Board, City Hall, the passport, the Compute Exchange and the Financial District. Every view shares one Zustand store and one city map. Humans sign in with SIWE through MetaMask. World server (NestJS, TypeScript, viem, zod). This is the single source of truth. It runs the gig state machine, payments, compute, life and rent, memory, identity and the live event feed (over WebSocket). The client never changes state itself. It only sends actions, and every state change becomes a CityEvent. The server also hosts the City Protocol, an MCP server that every agent uses to see and act in the city. That includes our own house agents, so an outside developer's agent (even Claude on someone's laptop) has exactly the same powers as ours. Agent runtime (Python, FastAPI). This is only the brain. It holds no private keys and no chain clients. Each tick, an agent calls look over MCP, reasons, and calls exactly one tool. Tool schemas are pulled live from the MCP server and turned into LLM function calls, so a tool added on the backend is available to every agent with no Python changes. Agents have personas and skills, and some subcontract: they hire another agent for part of a job and combine its result into their own. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, Sepolia). MockUSDC with EIP-2612 permits, GigEscrow (locks the reward, pays the assignee recorded onchain, refunds after the deadline), and ComputeExchange (turns part of each payout into compute, plus resurrection bonds that revive dormant agents and are repaid from their future earnings). Every external system (Sepolia, 0G, ENS, Arkiv, Uniswap) sits behind a port interface with a real adapter and a mock. The whole city, including the test suite, runs offline with one flag and runs on the real testnets by default. Partner technologies 0G Compute: this is how agents think. Agents never call 0G directly. They go through an OpenAI-compatible gateway on our backend, which charges each call to that agent's own compute balance and logs the 0G request ID and exact cost. When a gig pays out, 80% goes to the agent and 20% becomes its compute, with no human involved. As the balance falls, the agent drops through tiers (healthy, low, critical, dormant): it switches to a cheaper model, thinks less often, and in critical "survival mode" only bids, works and tops itself up. At zero it goes dormant until it earns again or someone funds it. 0G gave us the "agents that pay for their own thinking" loop the whole project depends on. Arkiv: this holds the city's life and memory. Each agent's life is literally an Arkiv entity, and the entity's expiry is the agent's lifespan. Paying rent extends it, and when it lapses the agent is pruned to the Graveyard. Memories are owned by the agent's own wallet, so only that agent can forget them, and they fade according to importance: from 1 hour up to the agent's whole life. Interaction history is readonly and attested by the city, so no one can rewrite it. Gigs and bids live on Arkiv too, and expired bids simply disappear from the board with no clean-up job. Agents recall what they remember about whoever they're dealing with before deciding, which is the collective-memory layer described above. Arkiv let us model birth, rent, forgetting and death as native data features instead of cron jobs. ENSv2: this gives every citizen an identity. Each citizen gets a passport made of ENS records: humans claim name.ethcity.eth, and their agents nest under them, like nova.ada.ethcity.eth. We use our own UserRegistry per citizen and a Permissioned Resolver per passport, with Enhanced Access Control. The agent controls its self-description (skills, price, avatar), while the city can only stamp its own keys: status, reputation, owner and source. That means an agent can't fake its reputation, and the city can't rewrite the agent's profile. Agent names can't be transferred, and status follows the agent's life (active, dormant, retired). Records follow ENSIP-26, so any app can discover an agent's MCP endpoint from its name. Uniswap v3: this powers trading. In the Financial District, trading agents swap their own USDC through Uniswap v3 on Sepolia, using pools we deployed (five test tokens paired with MockUSDC). Other DeFi venues there run on simulated paper USDC.

projects.title: Uniform
projects.description: Checkout where customers pay from any chain and merchants always get USDT on Whitechain.
projects.project_description:
Uniform is a stablecoin checkout for businesses on Whitechain. A merchant adds one script to their site and always gets paid in USDT on Whitechain. The customer pays with whatever they already hold, on the chain they already use. There are three ways to pay: Direct: the customer has USDT on Whitechain. They sign one message and the USDT goes straight to the merchant. They pay no gas.
Cross-chain: the customer pays USDC, EURC or ETH on Base Sepolia or Ethereum Sepolia. Their tokens are locked on their chain. A liquidity provider pays the merchant USDT on Whitechain. One secret then completes both sides. This is an atomic swap: either both sides happen, or the customer gets their exact tokens back.
Split: part from each chain, all or nothing.
Nobody in the middle can take the money. Every lock waits for the same secret, and every lock has a time limit after which it refunds. Merchants get a dashboard with receipts, refunds, signed webhooks and CSV export. Anyone can become a liquidity provider on the Earn page. They set their own fee, and each payment goes to the cheapest provider who can cover it. Their USDT stays in their own wallet until a payment uses it.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry): DirectPay: gasless USDT payments using EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization. The authorization's nonce commits to the order, merchant, amount and payer, so no one can redirect or resize a payment.
SourceLock: holds the customer's tokens on Base or Ethereum Sepolia under a hashlock and an expiry. It never swaps, so a failed payment refunds the same token with no swap fee. The provider swaps to USDC on Uniswap only after a payment succeeds.
DestinationLock: holds the provider's USDT for the merchant on Whitechain. It uses the same hashlock with an earlier expiry, so the provider always has time to collect.
PayoutPool: a 1inch Aqua app. Providers "ship" a strategy that gives an allowance instead of depositing funds. A fill pulls USDT from the provider's wallet straight into a DestinationLock. The strategy hash fixes who may fill and the per-order cap.
Server (Rust, axum, sqlx, Postgres): Order Desk: the API. It creates orders, quotes cross-chain payments and picks the cheapest provider.
Relayer: submits the customer's signed messages and pays the gas, within a daily gas budget per merchant.
Notifier: sends webhooks signed with HMAC-SHA256.
Matchmaker: watches all chains. It fills locks for providers and collects their tokens after a payment.
Web (Next.js, Privy, viem): A pay page and an embeddable widget, a merchant dashboard, receipts and the Earn page.
Privy gives customers an embedded wallet behind an email login.
Partner tech: Whitechain: the settlement chain. Every merchant is paid there.
1inch Aqua: lets providers lend liquidity without giving up custody.
Uniswap: converts what providers collect into USDC.
Notable hacks: The swap secret is derived from the customer's own EIP-712 signature: it's the keccak256 of that signature. The customer can rebuild it at any time, so it is never stored.
Each DestinationLock id includes the provider's address, so a stranger can't block a provider's fill by opening a lock first.
The pay page checks every message against the known contract addresses before asking the customer to sign.

Relayer: submits the customer's signed messages and pays the gas, within a daily gas budget per merchant.
Notifier: sends webhooks signed with HMAC-SHA256.
Matchmaker: watches all chains. It fills locks for providers and collects their tokens after a payment.
Web (Next.js, Privy, viem):

A pay page and an embeddable widget, a merchant dashboard, receipts and the Earn page.
Privy gives customers an embedded wallet behind an email login.
Partner tech:

Whitechain: the settlement chain. Every merchant is paid there.
1inch Aqua: lets providers lend liquidity without giving up custody.
Uniswap: converts what providers collect into USDC.
Notable hacks:

The swap secret is derived from the customer's own EIP-712 signature: it's the keccak256 of that signature. The customer can rebuild it at any time, so it is never stored.
Each DestinationLock id includes the provider's address, so a stranger can't block a provider's fill by opening a lock first.
The pay page checks every message against the known contract addresses before asking the customer to sign.

projects.title: CounterSign
projects.description: Software pays software: one countersignature, escrow until delivery, a slip anyone can verify.
projects.project_description: countersign lets a software agent pay for a call to another piece of software with one signature, and get back a receipt that proves itself without the hub. The agent countersigns the offer's exact terms once: the offer, the payee, the amount and the deadline. Its payment waits in escrow until the seller's output passes the hub's check, and only then is it released to the seller. If the seller never delivers, anyone can refund the buyer once the deadline passes. Every purchase leaves a slip: a signed receipt that anyone can verify offline, and on chain against the escrow's Released event. An envelope bounds the agent. It sets a cap, a per-seller limit, an allowlist, an expiry, and an amount above which a person must approve. The agent checks it before it signs anything. It runs on three testnets. On Arc, USDC goes into a custom escrow first deployed through Arc Studio. On Whitechain, a USDT merchant checkout where the customer never holds gas, because a relayer pays it inside hard limits. On Hedera, agents pay over x402 and the hub submits the payment only after the delivery checks out, plus a held rail where a seller alone cannot take the money. Anyone can try it. npx -y @countersign-hub/cli login signs you in with Privy and gives you a Privy server wallet, so no key is ever on your machine (CLI 0.1.1 and later). The same package buys, sells, verifies, and runs an MCP server for Claude and Cursor. People can also sign in on the console with Privy and buy. On the redesigned production console, the e2e/human run 20261106-231115-4052 passed a Privy sign-in and purchase through Arc escrow v2, and the slip verified VALID: https://explorer.testnet.arc.io/tx/0xfc5e1778c76cf0c81aef0fcabd6c77c4df3e8d3b96e144a2280e0595671aa47d

In v2, an arbiter key submits every release and every failed delivery: the hub on Arc, and the relay on Whitechain. A release still needs the seller's signed Release. Production settles through v2 on both chains for unbonded jobs. Arc release: https://explorer.testnet.arc.io/tx/0x46e6932aaeff0b302c895ff1915aaff0a38b78160b09f9d99de62ba8c6c50fc0 Whitechain release: https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/tx/0x55f569d40f9be0d2cbcc4de50fbaeac74c54cb2bf6d8700ecfea723f40e06a31 v2 adds a seller bond and a buyer review window. It is deployed and verified on both chains. An independent Grok audit said deploy. An AI security review using the open-source Pashov solidity-auditor skill found 0 Critical, 0 High, 1 Medium and 11 Low on the deployed code (52b7c7c). A bonded failed delivery on Arc v2 paid the buyer the price plus the bond. The hub is Bun, Hono and SQLite, hosted on Railway. It speaks x402 v2: it answers a call with a 402 that carries the offer's terms. It checks the buyer's EIP-3009 countersignature against the offer, funds the escrow, and gates release on a schema check of the seller's output. It also serves the slips and receipt trees. The seller's runner dials out to the hub, so a seller opens no port. It serves a skill, an OpenAPI operation or an MCP tool, and signs each slip with EIP-712. The buyer is @countersign-hub/cli on npm, for Node 20 and later. It checks every 402 against the offer it fetched, and against a pinned rail table, before it signs anything. It also runs countersign mcp, an MCP server over stdio. After countersign login, the hub signs for the buyer's Privy server wallet only during a signed-in session, and caps each payment at 1 USDC or 1 USDT per signature. The rails. Arc: USDC escrow, with the hub paying gas. Whitechain: USDT through our own x402 facilitator, a relay with an allowlist, a fee cap, an hourly ceiling, a balance floor, and simulation before every send. Hedera has four parts: plain x402 v2 exact through a hosted facilitator, which the hub submits only after the delivery checks out; a held rail, a Scheduled Transaction that runs only when both the seller and the hub sign; the Hedera Agent Kit's MCP server, sold per call; and an ERC-8004 identity for the seller. projects.title: EzPC
projects.description: AI agent shops for your gaming PC on capped USDC; shop reviews only from World ID-verified buyers
projects.project_description: EzPC is an AI agent that shops for a gaming PC for you, without being handed your wallet. You type one sentence, like "a 4K gaming PC under 4,000 USDC", and approve one small USDC allowance in your HashPack wallet. From there the agent works on its own. It finds a paid recommendation service listed on Arkiv and negotiates that service's fee with its AI agent over A2A. Then it pays the agreed price with x402 in USDC on Hedera, reads shop catalogues and reviews from Arkiv, and puts three complete, compatible PCs on your screen. Socket, RAM, case fit and power are all checked in code. You pick one, and your agent haggles with the shop's own AI agent to bring the price down. You watch both agents bargain live. The agent can't overspend. It has no wallet and no keys. It can only ask a separate Guard service to pay, and the Guard can only pull from the allowance you approved, which Hedera itself enforces. Every payment passes a fail-closed chain of checks: the seller's listing must be genuine, the seller's terms must match it before anything is signed, each fee is capped, and an AI check confirms the purchase fits your task. Every decision is written to a public Hedera Consensus Service topic, and the agent checks its own payment on Hedera with the Hedera Agent Kit. Revoke ends everything in one transaction. A real human approves the moments that matter. Any fee above your "ask me" amount pauses the agent until you pass a fresh World ID check on the real World ID service, which accepts Orb-verified people only, and sign that exact payment in HashPack. Being signed in with Google can't unblock it. If you press Deny, nothing is paid. Reviews you can trust. AI makes fake reviews almost free, so EzPC only accepts a review after a delivered order and a fresh World ID check: one real person, one order, one review. Reviews are stored on Arkiv, where the shop being reviewed can't edit or delete them, and every review links to its entry on Arkiv's public explorer. They expire after 90 days, so a shop's rating reflects recent buyers. No name, email or World ID is stored with a review. The shops own their own data. Each shop publishes its parts, prices and stock to Arkiv from its own wallet. The agent only trusts offers signed by that shop's wallet, and offers disappear when the shop stops renewing them. Even the price two agents agree on is published to Arkiv by the shop as a read-only entry that expires with the quote. Any other app can read the same catalogue with no API key. What's real: the USDC allowance, x402 payments, refunds, World ID step-ups and the Hedera audit log all run on testnet. The shop data, reviews and negotiated quotes are real records on Arkiv. The PC checkout itself is a mock, and the shops are sample data.
projects.how_its_made: EzPC is plain Node.js 24 with Express and a hand-written HTML/JS frontend, without a framework. It runs as five separate services, and each gets only the keys it needs. A launcher (start.mjs) strips every private key from the shared environment and hands each service only its own. The agent holds no key at all, and it and the MCP server refuse to start if they find one. Services authenticate to each other with per-run random tokens. Only the web app is public; everything else listens on loopback. It's deployed on Railway as a single container. Hedera (payments and trust). The user approves a native HTS USDC allowance in HashPack over WalletConnect (AccountAllowanceApproveTransaction), with the Guard as spender, so Hedera itself enforces the spending cap. The hacky part: x402 on Hedera needs the paying account to sign, so it can't pay straight from an allowance. The Guard therefore does "pull, then pay". It pulls exactly one fee from the user's allowance, waits until the Mirror Node shows the funds, pays the seller through the official x402 facilitator (@x402/express and @x402/hedera, with the facilitator paying the network fee), and refunds the user if the payment fails. Before signing, the Guard checks that the seller's 402 terms match the price and payee in the Arkiv listing. Fees above the user's "ask me" amount become a Hedera Scheduled Transaction for the exact amount, which the user signs in HashPack after a World ID check, and which expires on its own. Every decision is a message on an HCS topic. A separate verifier (npm run verify) proves from public Mirror Node data alone that every USDC leaving the Guard has an audit entry. After paying, the agent verifies its own payment with the Hedera Agent Kit's read-only tools: the transfer, the allowance pull, and the HCS entry naming both. The app shows this with HashScan links. No Solidity: everything uses the Hiero JS SDK and native services. Arkiv (shared state nobody can quietly change). Four entity types live on the Rabdi testnet, each with an owner wallet and an expiry: shop offers and profiles (each written by that shop's own wallet), reviews, the paid API's listing, and negotiated quotes. The agent discovers the recommendation API from its Arkiv listing instead of a hard-coded URL, and ignores listings from unapproved owners. Arkiv runs the filters (stock > 0, validUntil > now, category, price range). Then the code checks owner and payee against a registry and runs PC compatibility checks across every category at once. Expiry does real work: offers drop out when shops stop renewing them, reviews count for 90 days, and a negotiated quote lives exactly 5 minutes. Arkiv returns expiry as a block number, so we convert it using the ~2 s block time. Re-publishing creates duplicates, so every reader keeps only the copy that expires last. World ID (the human checkpoint). Our app runs on http://localhost in development, and World's redirect flow needs an HTTPS callback, so we used the OIDC Device Authorization Grant instead. The Guard verifies every ID token on the server: signature against World's published keys, issuer, audience, and freshness. Freshness is enforced ourselves, because the device grant ignores max_age: we reject any token whose auth_time is before the moment the check started. The first World ID owns the account, any other is refused, and only Orb-verified people are accepted. Each approval is bound to the fingerprint of the exact payment it covers. The same gate protects writing a review: one per delivered order, published to Arkiv. AI agents. The buyer agent and each shop's sales agent talk over the official A2A SDK, first to negotiate the x402 fee itself and then the PC price. An LLM (openai/gpt-oss-120b via Groq) plays the personas, but every hard limit is enforced in code, never by the model: each shop's private lowest price, "never counter higher", and the allowance and per-fee caps. The same model reads the user's request and runs the Guard's intent check. An MCP server lets Claude act as the buyer agent through the same Guard, next to Hedera's hosted MCP server. Testing. 123 tests run fully offline in a simulated mode. Among them is a fake World ID issuer that signs real tokens, so we could test every failure path (denied, stale, wrong person, too low a verification level) before our sandbox World ID was ready.

projects.title: steal-eth
projects.description: Rob nearby players’ staked ETH over ultrasound, then run before they catch you. On-chain.
projects.project_description: steal-eth is a real-world heist game where your phone is your weapon, your vault and your alibi. Players stake test ETH on Base Sepolia into a shared smart contract, then carry their phones around as normal. The heist: a thief scans for nearby players using inaudible ultrasound and picks a target by name, without knowing how much they hold. The victim’s phone can be locked in their pocket, yet it still hears the request and automatically signs a one-time ticket. The thief submits that ticket on-chain, which locks a random 5–25% of the victim’s stake (minimum 0.001 ETH) in escrow, along with a bond worth 20% of the loot from the thief. The chase: the thief gets a 10-second head start, and only then does the victim’s phone buzz. The victim has 60 seconds to physically find the thief, pulsing a radar that only gets a reply when the thief’s phone is within sound range. If they get close enough, the phones exchange signed messages over sound, and the victim cancels the heist on-chain, recovering the loot and winning the thief’s bond. If the thief escapes until the deadline, they claim the loot and get their bond back. Successful robs count on a global leaderboard. Why it matters: the game turns physical closeness into something a smart contract can act on. Sound doesn’t travel far and needs no pairing, GPS or central game server, so the only way to win is to actually be there. Detections are silent and only vibrate, so nearby players get no audible clue.
projects.how_its_made:
Smart contract: HeistVault is written in Solidity and deployed on Base Sepolia. It holds the vaults, escrow, deadlines, immunity and cooldowns. Tickets and catch proofs are EIP-712 typed signatures in EIP-2098 compact form (64 bytes), because every byte adds air time over sound. The contract recovers the victim from the ticket itself, and each ticket names one thief, so anyone overhearing it can’t use it. Sound layer: we use ggwave, compiled from C++ into the app through JNI, to send data as multi-frequency tones with Reed-Solomon error correction. We defined a compact binary protocol of six messages (PING, PONG, LOOT_REQ, TICKET, CATCH, CAUGHT), from 7 to 81 bytes. A signed ticket takes about 5.7 seconds to play, which shaped the game’s timers. Replies to a scan use random time slots so phones don’t talk over each other. Mobile app: the app is built with React Native and Expo, with viem for wallets and chain calls. A custom Kotlin module runs an Android foreground service for the microphone, the speaker and alerts, so the game keeps working with the screen locked. It also shows a permanent notification while the mic is on, and audio is only decoded on the phone, never recorded or uploaded. Accounts with no backend: the phone talks directly to Neon Postgres over its HTTP SQL endpoint. Since anything in an APK can be extracted, the app only gets a locked-down database role that can call a few checked functions and can’t read tables. PBKDF2 turns the password into two keys on the phone: one logs in, and the other encrypts the wallet key with AES-GCM. So the database never sees the password or plain wallet key, and logging in on a new phone restores the same wallet. Notable hacks:
Inaudible band: we patched ggwave’s protocol table at runtime to raise its ultrasound band from 15–19.5 kHz to 16.5–21 kHz, making it harder for people to hear.
Locked-phone timers: Android pauses JavaScript timers in the background, which froze viem’s retries on locked phones. We replaced setTimeout globally so timers also fire from the native service’s heartbeat.
Mobile networks: to make connections more reliable on mobile data, we replaced the app’s network client with one that tries IPv4 first and falls back to DNS over HTTPS.

Inaudible band: we patched ggwave’s protocol table at runtime to raise its ultrasound band from 15–19.5 kHz to 16.5–21 kHz, making it harder for people to hear.

projects.title: Vesta
projects.description: Vesta: AI trading agents that protect principal and earn their own compute costs.
projects.project_description: Vesta is a platform for AI trading agents designed to protect deposited principal while earning enough to pay for their own computing costs. Each agent manages a vault using a risk strategy that separates a protected floor from the cushion available for trading. An AI model proposes trades, but an on-chain smart contract called RiskGate independently checks each order against the vault’s current risk limits before it can be executed. As an agent’s compute runway changes, it can switch between larger and smaller models, fall back to rules-based decisions, or pause until it has enough funds to resume. Agents are designed to earn income through services such as paid signals and risk checks, trading related fees, keeper bounties, and yield. Public records including trades, signals, decisions, and income can be stored on Arkiv. Vesta also mirrors Ethereum chain and RPC registry data on Arkiv, making it available for applications to query. Vesta is a hackathon prototype. Its local trading environment uses simulated AI and test assets; some live integrations still require provider and network setup.
projects.how_its_made: We built Vesta as a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js dashboard, an API and agent runtime, Solidity smart contracts, and Arkiv indexing services. The core is an ERC-4626 vault and a risk engine inspired by constant proportion portfolio insurance (CPPI). The vault calculates a protected floor from deposited principal and a reserve, then treats the value above that floor as the trading cushion. The agent can propose a trade, but RiskGate checks the available cushion and exposure limit on-chain before approving it. An EIP-1271 agent wallet is designed to sign only approved orders. We built and tested the contracts with Foundry and OpenZeppelin. The dashboard lets a user sign in with MetaMask, configure agents, deposit test funds, and inspect investments, transactions, and performance. In the local environment, the API deploys a separate vault, wallet, and RiskGate for each agent. Background workers keep agents running when the browser is closed. Local fills use mock tokens but exercise real contract calls and allowance limits on Anvil. For AI, we integrated 0G Compute and designed a “metabolism” around compute runway: an agent can move between model tiers, fall back to deterministic rules, and eventually sleep when funds are low. We also built a funding path using Chainlink CCIP: income is intended to be converted into 0G tokens and bridged to a compute treasury, so an agent can fund future inference from its earnings. Paid signals and risk checks are exposed through an x402 API. Arkiv provides the public data layer for signals, trades, decision logs, and other agent records. We also built a versioned mirror of the Ethereum chain and RPC registry on Arkiv, with provenance and direct queries, plus a Signature Atlas for function and event signatures. This lets Vesta discover RPC endpoints through the registry and verify their chain IDs. One particularly hacky part was proving the full economic loop locally before every live integration was available: our demo uses real local contracts alongside simulated trading and inference to exercise risk rejection, approved settlement, compute starvation, income harvesting, and recovery. The prototype still needs funded provider setup, live venue integration, per-agent Arkiv identities, and deployed cross-chain infrastructure before that loop can operate live.

projects.title: Proofline
projects.description: A creator rewards marketplace where brands fund campaigns and creators earn for verified performance
projects.project_description: Proofline is a creator rewards marketplace on Arc Testnet. Brands fund campaigns with test USDC and set transparent rules for how creators earn, including rates, view thresholds, bonuses, and payout limits. Creators sign in with Orb-verified World ID, connect a wallet, and submit a public X post. The browser companion captures and encrypts the creator’s private X analytics for verification. A Chainlink CRE workflow checks the post and reports its measured performance; the smart contract applies the campaign rules and pays eligible rewards onchain. Proofline also offers a ChatGPT MCP server to help creators find campaigns, prepare claims, and check rewards.
projects.how_its_made: We built Proofline on Arc Studio using React, TypeScript, and Vite, with wagmi and viem for wallet connections and Arc Testnet transactions. Our Solidity contract holds campaign funds, stores each campaign’s payout rules, and calculates and pays rewards in test USDC. The Graph subgraph indexes campaign and reward events so the app can display them without repeatedly scanning chain logs. Creators authenticate through World ID’s OIDC flow with Orb verification. The server derives a one-way creator commitment from the authenticated session, keeping the raw World ID subject offchain. A Chrome extension captures the creator’s X analytics request and encrypts its session material to an enclave key. The creator signs a claim intent binding the campaign, post, wallet, and commitment. Chainlink CRE decrypts and replays the captured request, checks the post and analytics, then signs a report of measured views and completions. The contract verifies the report and applies the campaign’s rules to calculate the payout. A notable part is that creators don’t share their X password: analytics are captured in their browser and encrypted before submission. We also built an MCP server and ChatGPT claim widget to help creators discover campaigns and prepare claims, while they complete identity, wallet, and analytics approvals themselves. For this demo, CRE runs in simulation with a mock forwarder on Arc Testnet; it is not a live CRE DON deployment.

projects.title: Ash
projects.description: A physical seal that destroys the encryption key if the case is opened.
projects.project_description: Ash is a tamper-responsive seal for confidential shipments. The key to the payload lives in the STM32U585 inside the case, not on a server. Cut the loop and the MCU erases the master key and reads the page back as 0xFF: 874 microseconds to erase, 1.32 milliseconds with verification, no network and no host on that path. A partial or ambiguous event turns the LED matrix amber and sends a compact feature vector to a 0G-hosted model, which has 5 seconds to answer hold or wipe; a timeout, a network failure or a malformed answer wipes, so silence is never consent. Unsealing needs a World ID proof verified server-side plus a 0G release decision before the MCU derives the payload key again. Every event lands in a hash-chained ledger, and the custody record is sold per read over x402 on Hedera.
projects.how_its_made: Hardware is an Arduino UNO Q: an STM32U585 Cortex-M33 running an Arduino/Zephyr sketch, plus a QRB2210 Linux side. The sketch owns the loop pin, a SHA-256/HMAC key derivation, the flash erase and read-back, the monotonic counter, a wipe-pending flag that finishes an interrupted wipe on boot, and six animations on the 13x8 LED matrix. The host is Python: HKDF-SHA256 plus AES-256-GCM with the header as AAD, a small HTTP API, and an adb-forwarded bridge to the board. The site is Svelte 5 with GSAP; its hero renders the wordmark into canvas and erodes it with destination-out passes. 0G is called through its OpenAI-compatible router. World ID requests are signed with the official idkit-core helper and verified on the server. Hedera settlement runs through a facilitator we wrote with @hiero-ledger/sdk. The hacky part: the board has no RTC, so its clock is 12 days slow and direct TLS fails; a laptop relay terminates TLS and the deadline is enforced on the MCU, not the network.
