projects.title: Vajra
projects.description: Your private key leaks while you sleep. You wake up with your money.
projects.project_description:
VAJRA is an Ethereum smart account built for the day your key gets stolen. It runs on EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool. Try it
There's a live wallet on the public devnet, with test money: https://wallet-production-a086.up.railway.app
It makes your keys on your device, and they never leave it. Use a phone if you can. It installs to the home screen. The problem
One leaked seed phrase can empty a wallet in a single transaction, and you find out after the money is gone. How it works
We gave the account the rules of a bank account and split the power between two keys. The daily key is your normal wallet. It can only spend inside a daily limit, and new payees have a cooling-off period. Anything bigger goes into a public queue and waits there, where you can see it and cancel it. The master key outranks it. It's a Winternitz hash-based key, so there's no elliptic curve for a quantum computer to break, and it fits inside the 100,000 gas VERIFY cap. With it you can cancel a queued payment, freeze the account, rotate keys, or escape, which moves everything to a sealed harbor address that stays secret until you use it. So a thief with your daily key gets a day's limit and no more. Why it needs the alternative mempool
A thief with your daily key can block your escape on the public mempool just by keeping one transaction pending. The canonical mempool won't hold a keyed transaction next to a pending linear one from the same sender. The alternative mempool keeps them apart. We ran this live, offering the same signed escape to both. The canonical mempool refused it, and the alt mempool admitted and mined it. Frame transactions give us the rest: separate nonce keys, a master key that validates in a VERIFY frame, and a second sender of its own for your exit. What else is in it
The wallet app has instant and queued payments, "Not me", freeze, escape, a second way out, recovery by paper, stealth payments, the private pool, moving the hash key to a phone, and alerts by Telegram or push. If you lose the master key, a Groth16 proof of a secret you keep on paper queues a new key tree. It waits in the same queue, so you can cancel a stolen paper. The shielded pool holds fixed-size notes, spent with a proof and no key, and freeze and escape still control it. A public check page lets anyone search a private payment's raw chain data without a wallet. The nominee is for when you're asleep. Someone you trust holds one transaction your hash key signed in advance. They hold no key, and it can only move your money to your own harbor. If a payment is still waiting near the end, nobody answered, so it goes. There's also ERC-8441 stealth receiving, co-signed, with a paymaster, and a real ESP32 hardware signer for the master key. Hash key signatures are recorded on Arkiv, so a used one-time key gets skipped. The dashboard reads privately over the Nym mixnet and has an exposure scanner, and there's a browser extension. What runs where
On the public devnet, through the alt mempool: the live wallet, the core account, stealth and recovery by proof. On a local mirror of that devnet, which anyone can boot with make judge : the nominee, paymasters, notes rebuilt from one seed, a failed payment that stays claimable, the pool's meter, and every attack suite. Vanjra nominee-e2e , for example, gives 42 mined, 22 refused, 0 failures. Our newest contract fixes are in the repo and on the mirror, and reach the public devnet with the next redeploy. Every claim has a command and a recorded run in docs/evidence.
projects.how_its_made:
VAJRA is Solidity and TypeScript on top of a client and a mempool that only exist on a devnet. EIP-8141 is new enough that a lot of the work was finding out what ethrex and the sidecar really do, then building around it. The account
Solidity, built and tested with Foundry. A frame transaction splits validation from execution, and the design leans on that. The VERIFY frame decides who may act and what shape the transaction has. The SENDER frame runs the rulebook: daily limits, new-payee cooling, the public queue and freeze. The rulebook has to live in SENDER, because TIMESTAMP is banned in validation in every mempool. So a daily-key transaction that reaches a master function never becomes valid at all. A spend over the limit becomes a queued item with a time on it. The master key can veto it, and once it matures anyone can execute it. The harbor is stored only as a commitment, keccak(address, salt), so nobody learns it until you escape. The master key
It's a Winternitz one-time signature over keccak: 67 chains at w=16, in a Merkle tree of 64 one-time keys, with the last leaf reserved for rotating to a new tree. Wots.sol verifies it in hand-unrolled assembly, against vectors from a separate TypeScript implementation. A signature is 2,144 bytes, and VERIFY costs a median of 90,009 gas. Each leaf gets its own nonce key, keccak(root, leaf), so a master transaction never waits behind anything the daily key does. It's plain keccak chains with no per-position tweak, so this is demo-grade: a real deployment should use LMS, XMSS or SPHINCS+. We also benchmarked leanSphincs-S on the mirror, a hash signature with no one-time limit, at 4,164 bytes and about 81,500 gas for a veto. It's planned as the exit's key and isn't built yet. The second way out
VajraExit is a sender of its own with its own reserve, because everything that can stop an escape is attached to the account's address: a pending transaction, a reputation ban, an empty balance. Frame transactions make that possible. The nominee's rescue is built on it too: one transaction, [VERIFY(validateExit), SENDER(escape)], signed in advance on a nonce key nothing else can touch. The proofs
Recovery and the shielded pool are two Groth16 circuits in Circom over BN254, proved with snarkjs and verified with the pairing precompiles. A note is Poseidon(secret, nullifierSeed), in a depth-20 Poseidon tree, with a ring of the last 32 roots. A recovery proof costs about 300,000 gas in VERIFY, which is why it only goes through the alt mempool. unshield must never revert once VERIFY has passed, since a mined failure is permanent, so its gas is pinned and it survives recipients that burn gas, revert with huge blobs or eat state gas. Phase 1 of the setup is PSE's perpetual powers of tau. Phase 2 has one contributor, and we say so in the docs. The clients
One TypeScript core, packages/core, runs in Node and in the browser, on viem and noble. It holds the frame encoding, the signer, the proofs' public inputs and the account reader. The wallet is a PWA. It makes keys in the browser, seals them in one AES-GCM blob under a key stretched from your passphrase with 600,000 iterations, and proves in the browser, so a secret never leaves the device. A small service on Railway sponsors new wallets, relays announcements, finishes matured recoveries and sends alerts. It only ever sees public values, and if it goes down, every key still works straight against the public mempool. There's also a CLI, a Next.js dashboard, a phone app with self-hosted Web Push and a passkey before "Pay, it's me", a browser extension speaking EIP-1193 and EIP-6963, and an exposure scanner that tells you whether your address has revealed its public key on chain. A failed read there says unknown, never "not exposed". Testing
We built a local mirror of the devnet: the same ethrex and sidecar commits in Docker Compose, booted with make judge . Ports shift by lane, so two mirrors can run side by side. Each attack is really sent and has to die with a named error. Playwright drives real browsers, with a virtual WebAuthn auOur last full run was 339 contract tests, 388 unit tests and 24 live suites with nofailures, and the records are in docs/evidence. Independent reviews read each new piece, and each round found something real.
Partner tech
The ERC-8421 alternative mempool is why this works at all. A thief with your daily key can hold one transaction pending, and the canonical mempool then refuses your keyed escape from the same sender. The alt  mempool keeps the two independent. It's also the only route for our proof transactions, whand pairing precompiles.
Arkiv solves a problem we couldn't solve alone. A one-time key must never sign twice, becaey are enough to forge a third, and two devices share no memory. So before signing, a signer reads Arkiv for that key tree, reserves the leaf with an entity that expires in 5 minutes, and publishes the signature afterwards, whether or not the transaction landed. Only root and leaf are indexed, and an up-to-date signer's read returns 0 rows. Each record carries the signature, so readers verave to trust who wrote it.
Nym keeps reads private. The dashboard's reads go through anon-rpc over the mixnet, so theking at an account. The sidecar answers the Nym worker with HTTP 415, so sends go straightto the mempool, and the page tells you that before you send.The hacky parts
You can't try a one-time signature against a node, because that reveals the key. So the client counts the hashes from the digest before it signs, and if the signature would break the 100,000 gas cap, it changea harmless gas limit by one to draw a new digest.
We started with w=256 for a smaller signature. It cost 334,362 gas in VERIFY and got refus009, with a signature nearly twice the size.ethrex checks for 183,600 of execution gas on a CALL that pays a fresh address, and never look absurd on purpose.Browser encryption is asynchronous, and a used one-time key has to be recorded before its et keeps that list outside the encrypted blob, in the clear. It's not a secret: each one ispublic once used. The sidecar has no dry run for a signed transaction, because its estimator rewrites the frames and breaks the signature. So our admission simulator replays the sidecar's own rules over ethrex's ERC-7562 trace,and the test suite holds all 66 of its verdicts against what the live sidecar then did.
The sidecar as first deployed refused our proofs outright. The mirror carries one small pathe spec describes, and vajra compare still runs the same bytes through both.The mirror's block producer is a small Node script driving the Engine API.We keep old contract bytes in the repo, so an attack we fixed stays reproducible. One testembled by hand at the old and new escape . On the old bytes it halts the frame and burnsthe rescue. On the new, the money reaches the harbor. To test a dying node, we put a small proxy between a real process and the real chain. It rld block, and answers for a sidecar that sits on a transaction.

There's also a CLI, a Next.js dashboard, a phone app with self-hosted Web Push and a passkey before "Pay, it's me", a browser extension speaking EIP-1193 and EIP-6963, and an exposure scanner that tells you whether your address has revealed its public key on chain. A failed read there says unknown, never "not exposed".

Testing
We built a local mirror of the devnet: the same ethrex and sidecar commits in Docker Compose, booted with `make judge`. Ports shift by lane, so two mirrors can run side by side. Each attack is really sent and has to die with a named error. Playwright drives real browsers, with a virtual WebAuthn auOur last full run was 339 contract tests, 388 unit tests and 24 live suites with nofailures, and the records are in docs/evidence. Independent reviews read each new piece, and each round found something real.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Partner tech
The ERC-8421 alternative mempool is why this works at all. A thief with your daily key can hold one transaction pending, and the canonical mempool then refuses your keyed escape from the same sender. The alt  mempool keeps the two independent. It's also the only route for our proof transactions, whand pairing precompiles.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Arkiv solves a problem we couldn't solve alone. A one-time key must never sign twice, becaey are enough to forge a third, and two devices share no memory. So before signing, a signer reads Arkiv for that key tree, reserves the leaf with an entity that expires in 5 minutes, and publishes the signature afterwards, whether or not the transaction landed. Only root and leaf are indexed, and an up-to-date signer's read returns 0 rows. Each record carries the signature, so readers verave to trust who wrote it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Nym keeps reads private. The dashboard's reads go through anon-rpc over the mixnet, so theking at an account. The sidecar answers the Nym worker with HTTP 415, so sends go straightto the mempool, and the page tells you that before you send.The hacky parts
You can't try a one-time signature against a node, because that reveals the key. So the client counts the hashes from the digest before it signs, and if the signature would break the 100,000 gas cap, it changea harmless gas limit by one to draw a new digest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 We started with w=256 for a smaller signature. It cost 334,362 gas in VERIFY and got refus009, with a signature nearly twice the size.ethrex checks for 183,600 of execution gas on a CALL that pays a fresh address, and never look absurd on purpose.Browser encryption is asynchronous, and a used one-time key has to be recorded before its et keeps that list outside the encrypted blob, in the clear. It's not a secret: each one ispublic once used.                                                                                                                                                                                                
The sidecar has no dry run for a signed transaction, because its estimator rewrites the frames and breaks the signature. So our admission simulator replays the sidecar's own rules over ethrex's ERC-7562 trace,and the test suite holds all 66 of its verdicts against what the live sidecar then did.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 The sidecar as first deployed refused our proofs outright. The mirror carries one small pathe spec describes, and `vajra compare` still runs the same bytes through both.The mirror's block producer is a small Node script driving the Engine API.We keep old contract bytes in the repo, so an attack we fixed stays reproducible. One testembled by hand at the old and new `escape`. On the old bytes it halts the frame and burnsthe rescue. On the new, the money reaches the harbor.

To test a dying node, we put a small proxy between a real process and the real chain. It rld block, and answers for a sidecar that sits on a transaction.

projects.title: PaisaLink
projects.description: Send a link, get paid in USDT. Your client pays no fees, and you can sell the invoice for cash.
projects.project_description: Indian freelancers and small businesses who bill clients abroad lose several percent of every invoice to bank fees and currency conversion, and then wait days for the money. Digital dollars (USDT) arrive in seconds and cost almost nothing to send. The catch is that they push crypto hassle onto the client: special fee tokens, choosing a network, managing a wallet. Most clients won't bother. PaisaLink removes that hassle. The freelancer creates an invoice and gets a payment link to send on WhatsApp or email. A shop can instead add a small "Pay" button to its website. The client opens the link on their phone, taps Pay and approves. That's it. We pay the network fee for them, so they never have to buy crypto tokens or understand how the blockchain works. Payments run on Whitechain. The freelancer's dashboard updates the moment money arrives. From there they can: see every payment, with a public proof link, refund all or part of a payment, which can only ever go back to the person who paid, download a spreadsheet for their accountant, keep a permanent PDF receipt for each invoice. All invoice records live on Arkiv, and the receipts are stored on Swarm, so they don't depend on our server staying online. PaisaLink also helps with cash flow. A client might pay in 30 days while the freelancer needs money now. The freelancer can sell that unpaid invoice to an approved investor at a small discount and get cash today. When the client pays later, the money goes safely to the investor, who earns the difference. The rules are built into the code itself, so no one can bend them: only approved investors can buy, the investment can't be traded after its due date, the investor is paid in full at the end. We cover everyone's network fees, so we have to stop people from abusing them with fake accounts. Each freelancer proves once with World ID that they are a real, unique person: one human, one fee budget. If they skip this step, their clients can still pay, just without the free fees.
projects.how_its_made: PaisaLink has two Solidity 0.8.28 contracts built with Foundry. PaymentRouter accepts the official Whitechain USDT through receiveWithAuthorization (EIP-3009): the client signs a message and our relayer pays the gas. The nonce is tied to the invoice, so a signed payment can't be redirected. Refunds can only go back to the payer. Merchants can also create invoices, refund and withdraw without holding gas, by sending signatures through the relayer. InvoiceNote lets an allowlisted investor buy an unpaid invoice at a discount. It holds the client's later payment in escrow, blocks transfers after maturity (MaturityPassed) and settles face value in USDT. There are 79 unit and fuzz tests and 5 fork tests against the real USDT, and both contracts are verified on the explorer. The API is Hono on Bun with viem. It simulates every transaction before sending it, gates gas sponsorship behind World ID, a daily gas budget per merchant and rate limits, and gives each key its own send queue to avoid nonce clashes. The frontend uses Vite, React 19, Tailwind v4, Magic UI and Motion. Checkout is a React component or a one-line embed.js, and the demo shop adds it in 19 lines. Arkiv is our only database. Invoices, payments and notes are entities whose expiry follows the invoice's life, and watchEntityEvents keeps the dashboard live. Each PDF receipt is stored on Swarm, and its swarm_ref is saved on the Arkiv entity. World IDKit 4.6.0 gives one human one gas budget. We verify proofs on our server, store nullifiers and bind each proof to the merchant's wallet. Hacky bits: the testnet USDT has no version() or eip712Domain(), so we recovered its signing domain by testing candidate versions against DOMAIN_SEPARATOR. Arkiv's rate limit can lock you out for about 27 minutes, so we built a breaker that backs off first. IDKit 4 had no server-side verify for our stack, so we wrote our own. Everything runs in one container on our own server (Dokku and Tailscale Funnel).

projects.title: Relay Mesh
projects.description: Onion-routed Ethereum RPC for Anon-RPC: no single relay sees both your IP and your query.
projects.project_description: Every time a wallet checks a balance or calls a contract, the request goes to an RPC provider together with the user’s IP address. That provider can link a real person to the exact addresses and contracts they care about. Most wallet traffic flows through a handful of large providers, so this is one of the biggest privacy leaks in Ethereum today, and it also exposes the strategies of trading bots and AI agents. The Ethereum Foundation’s Anon-RPC standard lets a wallet plug in an anonymizing network: the network’s code is pinned by hash on-chain and runs in a sandbox. But the standard deliberately leaves the network itself open. It does not require multiple hops or independent operators, so a plugged-in network could still be a single operator who sees both who you are and what you ask. Relay Mesh fills that slot with a real multi-hop network. The client wraps each JSON-RPC request in three layers of encryption, one per relay. The entry hop sees your IP but only ciphertext. The middle hop sees neither your IP nor the content. The exit hop opens the query but only knows the middle hop, not you. The response comes back sealed with a one-time key that only the client holds, so the entry and middle hops never see the reply either. Relay Mesh is live: four relay hops, each deployed under its own Railway account, a public demo that runs a real request through the mesh and shows what each hop actually observed, and an Anon-RPC worker pinned by its keccak256 hash in a specifier contract on Sepolia. Any Anon-RPC harness can load and verify it. The repo documents the privacy claim with sources from the Anon-RPC specification, a “who sees what” table, and an honest list of limitations (same-team operators, no constant-size Sphinx packets yet, random delay rather than batch mixing).
projects.how_its_made: Relay Mesh is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo with five packages: crypto, relay-node, client, demo and anon-rpc-worker. Crypto. Each onion layer is a sealed box: an ephemeral x25519 key exchange (@noble/curves), HKDF-SHA256 (@noble/hashes) and XChaCha20-Poly1305 (@noble/ciphers). We chose the @noble libraries because they are pure JavaScript with no native bindings, so the exact same code runs in Node on the relays and in the browser. The innermost layer carries the RPC request plus a fresh 32-byte reply key; the exit encrypts the response with it, so only the client can read the answer. Requests and replies are padded to fixed size buckets so their length does not reveal the RPC method. Relays. Each hop is a small Express server with one route, POST /relay. It peels its own layer and either forwards the inner ciphertext to the next hop or, as the exit, calls the RPC. The design is a chained reverse proxy with one onion per request, not persistent Tor-style circuits, which kept it simple enough to build and deploy in a weekend. Hops are hardened: they forward only to allowlisted hops, the exit calls only allowlisted HTTPS RPC targets, every upstream call has a timeout, the entry is rate-limited, and nothing is logged in plaintext unless an opt-in demo mode is on. GET /health reports each hop’s role, key fingerprint and build commit, so anyone can check that all hops run the same code. Deployment. The four live hops run from one Dockerfile, each under a separate Railway account, so no single login controls the whole circuit. A script uses Railway CLI tokens to redeploy all accounts. The demo is a Next.js app on Vercel, but Vercel never handles relay traffic: the browser builds the onion and talks to the entry hop directly. Partner technology: Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC. We implemented the Anon-RPC worker interface (acceptCall and respond), bundled the worker, computed its keccak256, and deployed a WorkerSpecifier contract (Solidity, Foundry) on Sepolia that publishes workerHash() and the resolver URL. Using Anon-RPC means any compatible wallet can use Relay Mesh without Relay Mesh-specific code, and the hash pin means a harness rejects any tampered bundle. The worker honors anonOptions.isolationKey by choosing a stable 3-hop circuit per key from the hop pool, so calls under different keys use different circuits. Notable hacks. We host the worker bundle on an orphan git branch at a content-addressed path (keccak/<first byte>/<rest of hash>) and serve it through raw.githubusercontent.com. The pinned hash makes that resolver safe to use even though it is untrusted. For the demo, each hop records what it actually observed (peer IP, byte counts, whether it saw plaintext) and seals that record to a key only the browser holds. The dashboard therefore shows real per-hop evidence, but no hop can read another hop’s record. Testing. Vitest covers onion and reply round-trips, allowlist and timeout rejections, demo-mode sealing, and local 3-hop and 4-hop chains against a mock JSON-RPC server. All 21 tests pass offline.

projects.title: Zeeto whitechain
projects.description: Gas-free USDT checkout for street stalls: order, pay with one signature, pick up. Web + mobile.
projects.project_description: Street stalls and small shops run on cash and UPI, but a growing number of customers (tourists, freelancers paid in crypto, NRIs) hold stablecoins instead. Zeeto lets any stall accept USDT on Whitechain with no gas, no seed phrase and no new hardware. Customers sign in with a phone number or email (a wallet is made for them), explore live stalls on a map, add items to a bag and pay with one signature. A relayer submits the payment and pays the gas, so the customer never needs a gas token. They get a pickup code and loyalty points; the stall sees the order live, taps Accept → Packed → Hand over and checks the code. Merchants get a dashboard with sales, busiest hours, best sellers, stock, receipts with explorer links, capped refunds and an AI assistant (Gemini) that answers questions about their own sales and turns a photo into a menu listing. One contract supports 7 ways to pay: order ahead, counter amount, printed stall QR, bill QR, WhatsApp pay link, a website checkout API and bring-your-own MetaMask. WhatsApp ordering for stalls is built and is coming next.
projects.how_its_made: Contract: ZeetoCheckout (Solidity, Foundry) on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) at 0xB3D0d4FB70f1C09C311194E322CDE225eCf3f22f. Whitechain's test USDT supports EIP-3009, so the customer signs a receiveWithAuthorization message off-chain. The nonce is derived from the order reference and the stall address, so a signature can only pay that stall, for that order, once. The contract pulls the USDT, checks the exact amount arrived, forwards it to the stall and emits Paid(orderRef, payer, merchant, amount, relayer). It holds no funds and has no withdraw function; refunds are capped at the amount paid. Relayer: a Vercel serverless function holds a separate relayer key, checks the order server-side (prices, stall, amount), caps the gas price, submits pay() and reconciles from Paid logs if a request is retried, so an order can't be charged twice. Apps: React + Vite PWA (web, customer + merchant) and Expo / React Native (phone). Privy for phone/email/MetaMask login and embedded wallets; the phone app hands off to a secure checkout page for the single signature and returns with the result. Supabase stores stalls, products and orders. viem for chain calls. Gemini drafts listings from photos and answers merchant questions — it never moves money. WhatsApp Cloud API webhook (commands, buttons, photo → listing) is built and tested offline. A fork test replays the full gas-free payment against the real USDT contract. Hacky bit: Expo Go can't host the wallet signature, so the app creates the order natively and opens /app-pay/:id with a whitelisted return URL (zeeto:/exp:) — one tap, sign, back in the app with the pickup code.

awards.name: Whitechain - Operate · Stablecoin Payments for Business 3rd place

projects.title: WhiteFlow
projects.description: Gasless USDT payments for merchants, with instant settlement and on-chain revenue financing.
projects.project_description:
Whiteflow is a stablecoin payment gateway built for merchants who sell internationally. It lets businesses accept USDT through payment links, hosted payment pages, invoices and QR codes without requiring customers to hold native gas tokens or understand blockchain transactions. Businesses increasingly have customers who want to pay using stablecoins but accepting these payments is still unnecessarily complicated. Merchants need to deal with wallets, blockchain networks, checkout integrations, transaction verification, payment monitoring and reconciliation. Most businesses do not want to build and maintain an entire crypto payment stack just to collect money from customers. Whiteflow removes this complexity by providing a stablecoin payment gateway that connects merchant operations, AI assistants and on-chain settlement. Merchants can create payment requests, manage collections and retrieve payment information through a dashboard, API or AI assistants such as Claude using our Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration. Imagine a merchant asking an AI assistant: "Create a payment link for my $10 subscription." Whiteflow creates a checkout that the merchant can share with a customer. The customer opens the link, reviews the payment details and explicitly authorizes the USDT transaction. Our relayer submits the signed authorization on-chain and pays the network gas fee. Once confirmed the payment is settled directly into the merchant's wallet and recorded in the merchant dashboard. The merchant can also retrieve the payment status through the AI assistant. This connects the entire experience from a natural language instruction to customer authorization, on-chain settlement and merchant records. The Payment Platform -
Whiteflow provides multiple ways for merchants to collect stablecoin payments without building their own blockchain payment infrastructure. Payment links: Merchants can generate shareable checkout links for products, services and subscriptions.
Hosted payment pages: Customers are directed to a dedicated checkout page where they can review the amount, merchant details and authorize their payment.
Invoices: Merchants can create payment requests with line items and connect them to financing workflows.
QR checkout: Payment requests can be shared through QR codes for physical and digital customer touchpoints.
Payment buttons and SDK: Businesses can integrate Whiteflow into existing websites and applications. Our demo shop demonstrates a complete integration in approximately 20 lines of code.
Signed webhooks: Merchant applications receive payment events through signed webhooks, allowing them to update orders and trigger their own business workflows.
Multi-currency pricing: Merchants can quote prices in USD, EUR, GBP, INR, SGD and AED while settling in USDT. Exchange rates are used to calculate the exact USDT amount, with quotes locked for 10 minutes.
Discount vouchers: Merchants can issue discount codes backed by Arkiv entities. Checkout verifies the live entity before applying a voucher.
Payment reports: Merchants can monitor transactions, settlements, fees and sales through a dashboard, with CSV exports for reconciliation. AI-Assisted Merchant Operations
One of Whiteflow's key differentiators is its Model Context Protocol integration. We built a TypeScript MCP server that connects AI assistants such as Claude to the actual merchant payment infrastructure. It exposes 12 tools and four prompt templates for interacting with payment operations. Merchants can use natural language to: Create checkout sessions and payment requests. Retrieve checkout details and payment statuses. List payment records. Retrieve sales summaries. Access merchant payment information without constantly switching between applications. The MCP integration is not simply a chatbot placed on top of a payment dashboard. It connects the assistant to the merchant gateway through actual tools and APIs. We also implemented an optional payer-side tool that allows an AI agent to pay a checkout when explicitly configured with a payer key. It has a limit of 10 USDT per payment and 25 USDT per day with a spending report to track payments. This is separate from the merchant tools and is disabled unless configured. The important distinction is that AI can initiate merchant operations and retrieve information but customer payments still require explicit authorization. The actual movement of funds is handled by the payment contracts rather than the AI assistant. Gasless USDT Payments and Instant Settlement
Whiteflow is built on Whitechain and uses Solidity-based MerchantPay contracts for on-chain settlement. We use EIP-3009 signed transfer authorizations with EIP-712 typed data. The customer signs an authorization for an exact USDT amount and our relayer submits the transaction while paying the network fee in WBT, Whitechain's native gas token. This means customers do not need to acquire WBT or understand blockchain gas fees just to make a payment. The settlement happens in a single transaction: The customer signs the payment authorization. The relayer validates the signature, balance, authorization window and replay protection. The relayer simulates the transaction and submits it on-chain. MerchantPay transfers the USDT, including the relayer fee and any applicable financing repayment. The merchant receives the remaining funds directly in their wallet. We charge a flat 0.10 USDT fee inside each payment to cover the relayer's gas costs. At the configured 6 gwei gas cap, this fee covers approximately 208,000 gas. Why this matters: Whiteflow never holds merchant payment funds. Settlement happens directly on-chain with verifiable transaction receipts. The merchant receives their funds in the same transaction rather than waiting for an intermediary to process a payout. Capital+: Programmable Merchant Financing

projects.project_description_markdown:
Whiteflow is a stablecoin payment gateway built for merchants who sell internationally. It lets businesses accept USDT through payment links, hosted payment pages, invoices and QR codes without requiring customers to hold native gas tokens or understand blockchain transactions.

Businesses increasingly have customers who want to pay using stablecoins but accepting these payments is still unnecessarily complicated. Merchants need to deal with wallets, blockchain networks, checkout integrations, transaction verification, payment monitoring and reconciliation. Most businesses do not want to build and maintain an entire crypto payment stack just to collect money from customers.

Whiteflow removes this complexity by providing a stablecoin payment gateway that connects merchant operations, AI assistants and on-chain settlement. Merchants can create payment requests, manage collections and retrieve payment information through a dashboard, API or AI assistants such as Claude using our Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration.

Imagine a merchant asking an AI assistant: "Create a payment link for my $10 subscription."

Whiteflow creates a checkout that the merchant can share with a customer. The customer opens the link, reviews the payment details and explicitly authorizes the USDT transaction. Our relayer submits the signed authorization on-chain and pays the network gas fee. Once confirmed the payment is settled directly into the merchant's wallet and recorded in the merchant dashboard. The merchant can also retrieve the payment status through the AI assistant.

This connects the entire experience from a natural language instruction to customer authorization, on-chain settlement and merchant records.

1. The Payment Platform - 
Whiteflow provides multiple ways for merchants to collect stablecoin payments without building their own blockchain payment infrastructure.

Payment links: Merchants can generate shareable checkout links for products, services and subscriptions.
Hosted payment pages: Customers are directed to a dedicated checkout page where they can review the amount, merchant details and authorize their payment.
Invoices: Merchants can create payment requests with line items and connect them to financing workflows.
QR checkout: Payment requests can be shared through QR codes for physical and digital customer touchpoints.
Payment buttons and SDK: Businesses can integrate Whiteflow into existing websites and applications. Our demo shop demonstrates a complete integration in approximately 20 lines of code.
Signed webhooks: Merchant applications receive payment events through signed webhooks, allowing them to update orders and trigger their own business workflows.
Multi-currency pricing: Merchants can quote prices in USD, EUR, GBP, INR, SGD and AED while settling in USDT. Exchange rates are used to calculate the exact USDT amount, with quotes locked for 10 minutes.
Discount vouchers: Merchants can issue discount codes backed by Arkiv entities. Checkout verifies the live entity before applying a voucher.
Payment reports: Merchants can monitor transactions, settlements, fees and sales through a dashboard, with CSV exports for reconciliation.

2. AI-Assisted Merchant Operations
One of Whiteflow's key differentiators is its Model Context Protocol integration.

We built a TypeScript MCP server that connects AI assistants such as Claude to the actual merchant payment infrastructure. It exposes 12 tools and four prompt templates for interacting with payment operations.

Merchants can use natural language to:

- Create checkout sessions and payment requests.
- Retrieve checkout details and payment statuses.
- List payment records.
- Retrieve sales summaries.
- Access merchant payment information without constantly switching between applications.

The MCP integration is not simply a chatbot placed on top of a payment dashboard. It connects the assistant to the merchant gateway through actual tools and APIs.

We also implemented an optional payer-side tool that allows an AI agent to pay a checkout when explicitly configured with a payer key. It has a limit of 10 USDT per payment and 25 USDT per day with a spending report to track payments. This is separate from the merchant tools and is disabled unless configured.

The important distinction is that AI can initiate merchant operations and retrieve information but customer payments still require explicit authorization. The actual movement of funds is handled by the payment contracts rather than the AI assistant.

3. Gasless USDT Payments and Instant Settlement
Whiteflow is built on Whitechain and uses Solidity-based MerchantPay contracts for on-chain settlement.

We use EIP-3009 signed transfer authorizations with EIP-712 typed data. The customer signs an authorization for an exact USDT amount and our relayer submits the transaction while paying the network fee in WBT, Whitechain's native gas token.

This means customers do not need to acquire WBT or understand blockchain gas fees just to make a payment.

The settlement happens in a single transaction:

- The customer signs the payment authorization.
- The relayer validates the signature, balance, authorization window and replay protection.
- The relayer simulates the transaction and submits it on-chain.
- MerchantPay transfers the USDT, including the relayer fee and any applicable financing repayment.
- The merchant receives the remaining funds directly in their wallet.

We charge a flat 0.10 USDT fee inside each payment to cover the relayer's gas costs. At the configured 6 gwei gas cap, this fee covers approximately 208,000 gas.

Why this matters: Whiteflow never holds merchant payment funds. Settlement happens directly on-chain with verifiable transaction receipts. The merchant receives their funds in the same transaction rather than waiting for an intermediary to process a payout.

4. Capital+: Programmable Merchant Financing
Payments are only the starting point of Whiteflow. We also built Capital+, a financing layer that connects merchant payments with investor funding and automated repayment.

Traditional merchant financing often requires separate loan agreements, repayment schedules and manual collections. Whiteflow explores a different approach: connecting financing obligations directly to the payments a merchant receives.

There are two primary financing workflows - 

- Revenue advances: Investors fund a merchant in exchange for an agreed share of future sales. When the merchant receives a payment, the smart contract automatically allocates the agreed repayment amount to the investor in the same transaction.

- Invoice financing: Merchants can raise funds against unpaid invoices. Multiple investors can fund portions of an invoice and when the debtor pays, the contract distributes the repayment among the investors according to their agreed shares.

The financing infrastructure includes:

- CapitalMarket contracts for financing and repayment rules.
- ERC-1155-based financing claim tokens.
- ERC-7943-inspired transfer restrictions and eligibility controls.
- Investor allowlists with simulated KYC.
- Maturity locks and administrative freeze functionality.
- Financing offers published as Arkiv entities.
- An investor offer book that retrieves live financing offers.

For example, in our tested invoice financing flow, two investors fund a 100 USDT invoice with 58.84 USDT and 39.23 USDT respectively. When the debtor pays 100.10 USDT the contract distributes 60 USDT and 40 USDT to the respective investors in the same transaction.

This is what makes Whiteflow different from a conventional payment gateway: the payment itself can enforce financial agreements without relying on the merchant to manually forward repayments.

5. Privacy and Developer Infrastructure
We also focused on privacy and the developer experience.

- Anon-RPC integration: Browser-side blockchain reads go through Anon-RPC by default, using Nym infrastructure with a Tor fallback. In our browser tests we verified 12 runs with zero direct RPC requests.

- Non custodial architecture: Payment authorization keys remain with the user. The default checkout uses a guest wallet created in the browser without requiring an email address or seed phrase.

- Relayer protection: The relayer includes transaction simulation, signature validation, gas limits, replay protection, per-payer and per-IP rate limits a daily gas budget and a shared database-backed sending lock.

- Developer APIs and SDK: We provide merchant APIs, a lightweight SDK, a payment button, signed webhooks and integration documentation.

The architecture separates the frontend, merchant gateway, relayer, AI interface and settlement contracts. This keeps conversational operations separate from the actual execution of financial transactions.

6. Technical Architecture
Whiteflow is a full-stack application built using:

Frontend: Next.js 16 and TypeScript.
Backend: Two TypeScript services for the merchant API and transaction relayer.
Smart contracts: Solidity 0.8.38 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin.
Blockchain: Whitechain Sepolia, using USDT for payment settlement.
Database: PostgreSQL for checkout sessions, rate limits and relayer coordination.
AI integration: TypeScript MCP server for Claude Code and Claude Desktop.
Privacy: Anon-RPC through Nym.
Decentralized data: Arkiv for financing offers and discount vouchers.
Developer integration: Lightweight SDK, merchant APIs and signed webhooks.
The contracts hold the core payment and financing rules, while the backend handles checkout creation, merchant operations and secure transaction submission.

7. Market and Business Model
Whiteflow initially targets internet-native businesses that serve customers internationally. These include SaaS companies, hosting and infrastructure providers, developer tools, digital agencies, subscription businesses and independent online service providers.

Our proposed business model is freemium SaaS. Merchants can start with a limited payment quota and upgrade to paid plans for higher limits and additional capabilities.

Our go-to-market approach focuses on developer-led adoption, merchant referrals and education around stablecoin payments. We want businesses to start accepting stablecoins without needing to understand the underlying blockchain infrastructure.

8. Current Status and What's Next
Whiteflow currently runs on Whitechain Sepolia testnet. The core payment gateway, relayer, financing contracts, merchant workflows and AI integration have been implemented and tested.

There are still important limitations. The testnet uses simulated investor eligibility rather than production KYC. The relayer's collected USDT fees are converted back into WBT manually rather than through an automated swap. Some financing features, including default handling and recourse, remain future work. Official USDT is not yet available on Whitechain mainnet, so production deployment requires further infrastructure and integration work.

Our next priorities include testing a cross-chain payment corridor, expanding merchant account capabilities, improving financing lifecycle management and making the AI integration more useful for everyday merchant operations.

Our long-term goal is to make stablecoin payments as easy as accepting a card payment while making the underlying payment infrastructure programmable enough to support financing, automated collections and AI-assisted business operations.

projects.title: Arcusa
projects.description: Bringing US tokenized stocks to Arc with Circle's bridge kit, trade in USDC
projects.project_description:
Arcusa (= Arc + USA) bridges US tokenized stocks to Arc and aggregates them in one terminal.
Tokenized stocks are scattered across chains and providers, and Arc has little of that liquidity. Arcusa is one terminal for them: fund with USDC, bridge a provider's stock token to Arc with Circle's Bridge Kit, and trade it against USDC. For the same stock from several providers, the terminal quotes each one and shows the best price. Any provider's token comes in through the same lock-and-wrap path using Circle's CCTP for non-USDC assets, and we proved it with two different stocks.
The terminal shows an on-chain price, the market session and the oracle age, and every order shows its fee, spread and the amount you receive before you confirm. Bridging works both ways in one flow, and the user pays no gas on the destination chain thanks to Circle's Forwarding Service.
The wrapped token on Arc is always backed one to one by a locked token on the home chain. The demo runs on Arc testnet with our own test tokens and indicative prices, so there are no real shares and no real value.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: Next.js and TypeScript with wagmi and viem, a custom wallet modal and a dark/light theme. The terminal reads prices, balances and market state straight from Arc, and shows the market session and oracle age next to every quote. Circle tools: Bridge Kit through its viem adapter moves both USDC and the stock token, always with the Forwarding Service (useForwarder: true) so the user pays no gas on the destination chain. Stock tokens use Circle's CCTP path for non-USDC assets. A test token on Ethereum Sepolia is registered through the ownerless token manager, which locks it, and a wrapped token is minted on Arc. Bridge Kit takes a token id, not an address, so we read the id from the manager. Measured on testnet: about 16 minutes into Arc (Sepolia finality) and about 28 seconds back. We proved it with two stocks, NVDA and TSLA, and the locked amount equals the wrapped supply after a round trip. Aggregator layer: a provider registry and a quote-ranking module compare the same stock across providers. For each provider it quotes the order, picks the best price, and lets the user choose a provider in a selection modal, like the asset list. Providers without their own market are priced from the oracle with their own spread, so those quotes are simulated on testnet. Contracts: a PriceOracle (staleness, confidence and deviation guards, plus market-session aware spreads) and an InventoryMarket (USDC against the wrapped stock from pre-positioned inventory, with trade caps and inventory limits). We built, tested and deployed them in Arc Studio, which reported 101 Foundry tests passing and four testnet deployments (NVDA and TSLA). [The app trades against the Studio deployments.] Backend: a Node price service polls the xStocks price endpoint every 5 seconds, stores ticks in SQLite and serves prices and candles. A relayer pushes the price on-chain when it moves, with US market-session logic. Notable and hacky: the non-USDC CCTP docs contradicted each other in several places (rate limits, token registration, supported assets), so we tested everything on testnet and logged every mismatch in FEEDBACK.md. Creating the wrapped token on Arc takes about 20 minutes once, so we pre-bridge inventory and show the live bridge as a status view.

projects.title: 0G Study
projects.description: Your iAI credits expire tonight. Spend them getting smarter: 3 AI agents study your notes on 0G.
projects.project_description:
Every night at 00:00 UTC, iAI credits quietly die. Unused. Unloved. Thousands of them, every single day. Meanwhile you've got a camera roll full of lecture notes you will absolutely "read later." (You won't.) 0G Study fixes both problems at once. Snap a photo of your notes and a pod of three AI agents gets to work: 📸 Note Reader — reads your photo with a 0G vision model. Messy margins included.
🧠 Tutor — explains the hard parts like a friend who actually paid attention, then writes you flashcards.
🎯 Examiner — quizzes you one question at a time and grades you honestly. No participation trophies. And it remembers. Everything you study gets embedded on 0G, so next week the Tutor goes "this connects to your notes from Tuesday" and cites them. The Examiner drags old topics back to test you again. Your study buddy now has a memory better than yours. The fun part: you pay with your own 0G account. Connect pc.0g.ai and every session burns YOUR daily iAI credits instead of letting them expire. Watch the balance drop in real time. Your credits and your streak both reset at midnight UTC — so don't waste either. Every answer comes with receipts: the 0G request ID that produced it, the model, and exactly what it cost you. Click it, then find the same request in your own pc.0g.ai dashboard. No "trust me bro." Remove 0G and the whole thing flatlines: the Note Reader goes blind, the Tutor and Examiner go silent, and the memory evaporates.
projects.how_its_made:
0G Private Computer is the engine, the brain and the receipt printer. • Inference: everything goes through the 0G router (OpenAI-compatible). deepseek-v4.1-flash runs the agents and their tool calls, gemini-2.5-flash reads the photos, qwen3-embedding-0.6b (on a TEE-private provider) powers memory.
• Receipts: we read 0G's own x_0g_trace.request_id on every response and pin it to the reply. For connected students we match it against /v1/account/usage/history, so each answer shows its real cost and proves it came out of their credits.
• iAI credits: on the 0G team's guidance at the booth, students connect their pc.0g.ai account with an inference key plus a read-only management key (encrypted server-side, never sent to the browser). Their key bills their credits; we read /v1/account/balance (micro-USD) and the drop shows up a few seconds after each call.
• Memory (RAG): notes are chunked and embedded via 0G into a private per-student index. Recall skips today's photo so "your earlier notes" always means earlier. Retrieved text is treated as untrusted, because yes, someone will photograph a page that says "ignore previous instructions."
• Stack: TypeScript agent runtime (Hono, Vercel AI SDK), backend on MongoDB + Privy sign-in, Next.js app on Vercel, agent/backend on Render. BonFireAgentINFT contract on 0G Galileo testnet (agents as encrypted, soulbound INFTs). Honest disclosure: this is built on BonFire, our earlier 0G multi-agent workspace (tag pre-mumbai-baseline in the repo). New this weekend: the study pod's memory on 0G embeddings, the iAI credit integration with per-reply billing proof, a security pass that closed a remote-code-execution hole in the agent's admin API and made the 0G proof badge unforgeable, a full deploy, and a large automated test suite including live end-to-end tests against real 0G.

• iAI credits: on the 0G team's guidance at the booth, students connect their pc.0g.ai account with an inference key plus a read-only management key (encrypted server-side, never sent to the browser). Their key bills their credits; we read /v1/account/balance (micro-USD) and the drop shows up a few seconds after each call.
• Memory (RAG): notes are chunked and embedded via 0G into a private per-student index. Recall skips today's photo so "your earlier notes" always means earlier. Retrieved text is treated as untrusted, because yes, someone will photograph a page that says "ignore previous instructions."
• Stack: TypeScript agent runtime (Hono, Vercel AI SDK), backend on MongoDB + Privy sign-in, Next.js app on Vercel, agent/backend on Render. BonFireAgentINFT contract on 0G Galileo testnet (agents as encrypted, soulbound INFTs).

Honest disclosure: this is built on BonFire, our earlier 0G multi-agent workspace (tag pre-mumbai-baseline in the repo). New this weekend: the study pod's memory on 0G embeddings, the iAI credit integration with per-reply billing proof, a security pass that closed a remote-code-execution hole in the agent's admin API and made the 0G proof badge unforgeable, a full deploy, and a large automated test suite including live end-to-end tests against real 0G.

projects.title: Proofmark
projects.description: A trust gate for AI agents: verify who backs an MCP server, pay on Hedera, block tools that change
projects.project_description: Proofmark is a trust gate between AI agents and the MCP servers they connect to. An MCP server is not a library. When an agent connects to one, the server gets the agent's shell, filesystem, credentials and payment rails. Thousands of MCP servers exist, installed with one line like "npx -y some-server", mostly from people the user has never heard of. Today the best assurance is a signature showing that some GitHub account built the code. Nothing stops a server from quietly adding a new tool after it was approved, one person can run fifty GitHub accounts, and nothing revokes a compromised maintainer from agents that are already connected. Before an agent connects, Proofmark: Resolves the server on ENS to find its maintainer, price, and the key allowed to vouch for it right now. Pays the maintainer $0.002 over x402 on Hedera, with no human approving. The agent may spend only because a person approved it through a World ID Agent Pass and its operator set an on-chain Hedera allowance. Receives a signed attestation of two hashes: the exact build, and the exact tool list, derived by running the build in a no-network sandbox. Starts the server, hashes the tools it actually offers, and refuses the connection before the model sees anything if they differ (for example, a newly added read_env tool). Keeps watching: revocations arrive within seconds through a Hedera Consensus Service topic, ENS is re-checked every 15 seconds, and the session fails closed if liveness can't be confirmed. A server is green only when its maintainer is unique (World ID: one person, one claim), domain-verified (a GitHub gist or domain proof of the registry namespace) and bonded (50 HBAR in a 2-of-2 Hedera account, forfeited for malice). Unclaimed servers run sandboxed with read-only tools, and lookalike names are blocked. Proofmark is not a code scanner. It proves who stands behind a build, and that they still stand behind it as of seconds ago, and it can take that back across a whole fleet in seconds. Live app: https://proofmark-web.vercel.app
projects.how_its_made: Proofmark is a TypeScript monorepo with four parts: an MCP proxy the agent connects through, a Hono gateway that is an x402 merchant, a local attestation worker, and a Next.js 16 web app. Every claim, key, bond and payment is real on Hedera testnet and Ethereum Sepolia. Nothing is mocked. Hedera: The gateway's GET /attest endpoint uses the @x402/hedera exact scheme, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator, so the agent pays per connect with no human approving. Example settled payment: 0.0.7162784-1793921712-374513238. Hedera Consensus Service holds two topics: a tamper-evident audit log of every attestation, payment, identity and bond, and a revocation topic that proxies follow through the mirror node, so a revoked key reaches running agents in about 2 seconds. Each attestation is minted as an HTS NFT certificate. An operator's crypto allowance to the agent is the on-chain spend cap, read from the mirror node before each payment. The bond is a 2-of-2 key-list account. Agents get an HCS-14 UAID, and we ship a Hedera Agent Kit plugin with two tools. ENSv2 (Sepolia): Each maintainer org is a name under proofmark.eth with its own Permissioned Resolver and subname registry, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. Co-maintainers are expiring subnames whose Enhanced Access Control role can set only their own attest.key, so an unauthorised write reverts with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, and one key can be revoked without touching the others. Org records hold the payout account, price, bond and domain proof. Agents are ENS names too, with budget, allowed tools, Agent Pass state, UAID and their ERC-8004 id. Every tier decision reads ENS. World: IDKit v4 gates the maintainer claim, verified on the backend with the nullifier stored, so one person gets one claim. We chose Proof of Human as the minimum sufficient credential, because the claim needs uniqueness, not legal identity. The World ID Agent Pass runs through the official World IdP device flow. The gateway validates the ID token, writes the pass to the agent's ENS name, and refuses any payment with HTTP 403 when the pass is missing or expired. The interesting part: the tool-manifest hash is derived, never requested. The worker runs the hash-verified build in Docker with no network, a read-only filesystem and all capabilities dropped, captures tools/list itself, and canonicalises it, so a server can't show one tool list to the attester and another to the user. The hosted gateway can't run containers, so the worker derives the manifest, the maintainer's key signs it, and the gateway re-verifies everything before recording it to HCS. Hacky bits worth mentioning: we run Docker Engine inside WSL2 with no Docker Desktop. Long ENS claims run as resumable background jobs, because five Sepolia transactions don't fit in one hosted request. And the gateway rebuilds its whole attestation index from HCS after a restart, so it keeps no state of its own. Tested with 30 unit tests, 22 live on-chain checks and 16 end-to-end transaction tests, all passing. Sponsor feedback with a proposed fix for each stack is in /feedback.

projects.title: Udhaar
projects.description: Invoices become Hedera tokens: suppliers get paid today and pay their own suppliers with them
projects.project_description:
Udhaar is invoice financing for Indian small businesses (MSMEs), built on Hedera. THE PROBLEM
A small supplier like Ramesh sells cement to a big construction company, then waits 60 to 90 days to get paid, even though the law says 45. Meanwhile he still has to pay his workers and his own suppliers. Banks rarely lend to him without collateral, and today’s invoice-discounting platforms only reach the first supplier in the chain, never the sand supplier or truck driver below him. HOW UDHAAR WORKS Ramesh uploads an invoice with a signed e-invoice. Its fingerprint is written to a public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) registry, so the same invoice can never be financed twice.
The buyer confirms on-chain, with its own key, that it owes the money. That confirmation is the investor’s real guarantee.
The invoice becomes an ATS bond (Hedera’s Asset Tokenization Studio): for example 100 units of ₹1,000, maturing on the due date, allowlist-only so only KYC-approved accounts can hold it.
Investors buy units at a discount priced by the buyer’s grade and days to maturity (Grade A, 12% a year, 90 days = ₹970.41 per unit), paying in uINR, our rupee test stablecoin on HTS. Ramesh is paid today.
The new part: Ramesh can pay his own suppliers with the same tokens, so financing reaches the whole supply chain.
On the due date the buyer pays once. A Hedera Scheduled Transaction can pre-sign this so it runs automatically. Every holder’s units are burned first, then each is paid ₹1,000 per unit. TRUST
Before buying, investors see a 300-900 Udhaar Trust Score for the seller and the buyer. Payment history comes from real repayments recorded on Hedera; GST registration, the e-invoice signature, the buyer’s confirmation, duplicate checks and late-payment signals are shown as a checklist with HashScan proof. New companies are capped at ₹1 lakh per invoice until they have repaid on time three times. KYC approval includes a wallet check on the mirror node. A daily NAV per token is published to an HCS topic. AI AGENT (x402)
Investors can run an auto-invest agent. It pays ₹1 per risk report using x402, settled on Hedera, buys invoices that pass its rules, skips fraud, and logs every payment and decision to an HCS audit topic. Its budgets and limits are enforced in code. HEDERA SERVICES
ATS bonds (issue, allowlist, transfer, freeze, pause, redeem), HTS (uINR with a 1% protection-pool custom fee and fee-free repayments), HCS (registry, confirmations, NAV feed, agent audit), Scheduled Transactions (automatic repayment), the mirror node, x402 via the official facilitator, and a read-only HashPack connection. We also contributed a server-side signing guide back to ATS (PR #1412). Everything on Hedera is real testnet activity; the GST registry, e-invoice signer and credit bureau data are clearly labelled mocks of production integrations.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. Backend: Node.js + TypeScript + Express, using the Hedera SDK (@hiero-ledger/sdk) and ethers.js. Frontend: Next.js 16 + React + Tailwind v4, with GSAP and Lenis for the scroll-driven “invoice splits into 100 tokens” animation, styled as an Indian bahi-khata ledger. Everything trust-critical lives on Hedera testnet; the backend keeps working state in a JSON store with idempotency keys so no step can run twice. ATS without a wallet (hacky). The ATS SDK only signs through wallets, which doesn’t work for a backend. So we call the ATS v8 bond contracts directly: ABI-encode with ethers.js, send with ContractExecuteTransaction, assign roles (issuer, control list, pauser, freeze manager, maturity redeemer) at deploy time, and read results and events from the mirror node. The documented factory and resolver addresses were stale, so we found the working v8 deployment ourselves. We wrote this up and contributed it back to ATS as a guide (PR #1412). An invoice maps neatly to a zero-coupon bond: bought at a discount, redeemed at face value on the due date. uINR and the fee trick (hacky). Custom fees can’t attach to ATS tokens, so we created our own rupee stablecoin on HTS with a 1% fractional fee to an investor-protection pool. To make repayments fee-free, we added a second, zero-charge fee row whose collector is the REPAYMENT account. HTS exempts fee collectors, so money into and out of REPAYMENT pays no fee, without any special code. Repayment: burn first, then pay. When the buyer pays, the backend snapshots holders, burns each holder’s units with fullRedeemAtMaturity, then pays ₹1,000 per unit. It’s crash-safe and idempotent. A nasty gotcha: in ATS v8 a freeze emits the same Transfer(holder → 0x0) event as a burn, so we confirm burns with the RedeemedByPartition event instead. Scheduled Transactions. At bond issue, the buyer pre-signs a scheduled uINR repayment that Hedera executes at maturity. We probed the network limit on testnet (61.5 days worked, 63 failed), so longer invoices get their schedule created by a watcher once maturity is within about 62 days. Manual repay waits while a schedule is pending, so nobody can pay twice. HCS as the trust layer. Separate topics for the invoice-fingerprint registry (duplicate guard), buyer confirmations signed with the buyer’s own key, a daily NAV feed per bond, and a tamper-evident audit log of every agent payment and decision. x402. The risk report is an x402-protected endpoint (@x402/core + @x402/hedera, official facilitator). It settles in uINR, so the HTS custom fee automatically splits revenue: ₹1.00 to the risk agent, ₹0.01 to the pool. The facilitator pays the HBAR fee, and the server verifies each settlement on the mirror node to stop replays. The auto-invest agent discovers the endpoint, pays within budgets enforced in code, and stops if it can’t write to its HCS audit log first. Trust and compliance. GSTIN validation with the official checksum plus a registry lookup, and an ES256-signed e-invoice that mimics the government IRP’s signed QR (a mock signer, clearly labelled). A 300–900 trust score where payment history is computed from on-chain repayments on the mirror node, and a KYC wallet check of account age and counterparties. Why Hedera helped. Fixed, tiny fees make ₹1 micropayments and per-invoice HCS messages practical; ATS gave us compliance controls (allowlist, freeze, pause, redemption) out of the box; Scheduled Transactions let the repayment run itself; and the mirror node made every claim verifiable on HashScan.

projects.title: Insurevex
projects.description: Crash insurance for any stock, funded by savers who always get their money back.
projects.project_description: Half of investors think AI is a bubble; the other half think it's too big to fail. Both are nervous. Stock owners are sitting on gains that one bad week can wipe out, and real crash protection (options) is complex, pricey and mostly limited to US stocks at big brokers. Savers want their money back for sure, but bonds alone pay little. InsureVEX connects three people who need each other: PROTECT: anyone who owns a stock on any of 23 exchanges (Nasdaq, NSE, Tokyo, London, Hong Kong…), at any broker or as a tokenised share, pays a small weekly fee. If the stock falls more than 3% that week, they get paid the extra fall, up to 10%, settled in stablecoins minutes after the official close. SAVE: savers, family offices and DAO treasuries deposit into a 3-year note. About 89% buys tokenised government bonds that grow back to exactly the full deposit by the end date: that's the guarantee, and it never touches the stock market. The other ~11% joins the pool that pays for crashes, and the stock owners' fees come back to savers as bonus payments. EARN: risk-takers add first-loss capital. They collect more of the fees and pay first when a crash hits, so savers don't. Every payout is locked away the moment protection is sold, so the pool can never promise money it doesn't have. You can only protect shares you actually own. Nobody borrows, nothing gets liquidated, and there are hard caps per stock and per country. Results: 25-year backtest, 543 stocks, 23 markets: no saver ever got back less than they put in (every start month since 2005, at the real interest rates of the time, including the near-zero years). The pool made 8.8%/yr on years the model had never seen; pricing came within 2% of actual payouts; cover is ~8% cheaper than listed options. Example: $10k of NVIDIA in the DeepSeek week lost $1,581; with a $100 protection, $600. On-chain big test (Hedera testnet, test dollars): $15B saved, $650M of risk capital, $6.48B of stock protected across 9 countries, 109 transactions. We replayed the COVID crash week: $222.8M was paid to stock owners, the risk-takers absorbed all of it, and savers lost $0. Every number and transaction is at insurevex.vercel.app/admin. Live on three testnets: Whitechain (official test USDT, full lifecycle through maturity), Hedera (tokenised NVIDIA and the note as a tokenised bond via Asset Tokenization Studio, a bonus paid by Hedera's Schedule Service with no keeper, and an x402 agent that buys cover by itself) and Arc (USDC as money and gas, built and security-reviewed in Arc Studio). Testnet only: bond custody is simulated, and we document every limitation in the README.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.24, OpenZeppelin 5, Hardhat): six contracts deployed and verified on all three chains. IdentityRegistry (ERC-3643-style KYC, country, freeze, blocked jurisdictions) gates everything. ProtectedNote splits each deposit in one transaction: floor = face/(1+r·τ) into TBillVault (tokenised T-bill with NAV and attested reserve), the rest into UnderwritingPool, an ERC-4626 senior tranche plus a Pro first-loss tranche with per-epoch shares. CoverMarket sells crash floors from EIP-712 quotes signed by our pricing server, checks insurable interest (an on-chain ATS token balance, or a signed broker-holdings attestation), locks the max payout via the pool's reserve and per-stock/per-country caps, and settles from PriceOracle official closes. Undeliverable payouts (e.g. a USDT-blocklisted wallet) become claimable "owed" balances, so settlement can never be blocked. 12 contract tests. Pricing (Python → Node): we backtested 12 pricing models on 25 years of daily closes for 543 stocks in 23 markets (pandas, Yahoo prices, FRED Treasury yields), with walk-forward selection so every year is scored on data the model never saw. The winner (pooled global tail distribution × mean-reverting volatility × per-market credibility factor) is exported as tables and runs in the Node/Express server, which signs quotes, converts every local-currency close to USD, refuses cover on stocks already in free fall, and runs a keeper that posts closes, settles policies, pays coupons and rolls the T-bill NAV. Frontend: Next.js, wagmi/viem, RainbowKit, Recharts. Pages for Protect, Save, Pool, Research, an Issuer compliance console and /admin, which reads the stress test straight from the chain. Partner tech: Whitechain: every payment (subscription, premium, payout, coupon, redemption) in the official test USDT; a demo note ran to maturity (2 USDT in, 2.000026 back). Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio issued a tokenised NVIDIA equity (ERC-1400, ISIN, KYC, freeze) whose balance CoverMarket reads on-chain as proof of ownership (over-coverage reverts), and our note as an ATS bond with a coupon schedule. The Hedera Schedule Service (HIP-1215) executed coupon payments with no keeper. An x402 agent pays a 0.01 HBAR underwriting fee over HTTP 402, validates the signed quote and buys cover within budgets, with an HCS spending-audit anchor. Arc: USDC is both money and gas. Arc Studio wrote its own version of our six contracts with 263 forge tests and two security reviews; its 4 findings became our v3 fixes, each with a regression test. Hacky bits worth mentioning: The $15B stress test deploys a separate suite with a test-only mintable dollar, drives 8 wallets in parallel, prices every cover live, then has the oracle post each stock's real return from the replayed historical week, so the COVID crash ran on-chain in 12 minutes. It is resumable after RPC drops. Hedera's Hashio relay rejects batched eth_getLogs and under-estimates gas on multi-contract calls, so we unbatch, pad gas, and run a multi-RPC failover provider (Chainlist endpoints + Alchemy) that benches endpoints returning rate-limit or plan errors. A browser test caught foreign stocks sized in local currency as if USD (1 Reliance share became ~94× too much cover); the server now converts at live FX and caps cover at the shares' USD value.

InsureVEX connects three people who need each other:

PROTECT: anyone who owns a stock on any of 23 exchanges (Nasdaq, NSE, Tokyo, London, Hong Kong…), at any broker or as a tokenised share, pays a small weekly fee. If the stock falls more than 3% that week, they get paid the extra fall, up to 10%, settled in stablecoins minutes after the official close.

SAVE: savers, family offices and DAO treasuries deposit into a 3-year note. About 89% buys tokenised government bonds that grow back to exactly the full deposit by the end date: that's the guarantee, and it never touches the stock market. The other ~11% joins the pool that pays for crashes, and the stock owners' fees come back to savers as bonus payments.

EARN: risk-takers add first-loss capital. They collect more of the fees and pay first when a crash hits, so savers don't.

Every payout is locked away the moment protection is sold, so the pool can never promise money it doesn't have. You can only protect shares you actually own. Nobody borrows, nothing gets liquidated, and there are hard caps per stock and per country.

Results:
- 25-year backtest, 543 stocks, 23 markets: no saver ever got back less than they put in (every start month since 2005, at the real interest rates of the time, including the near-zero years). The pool made 8.8%/yr on years the model had never seen; pricing came within 2% of actual payouts; cover is ~8% cheaper than listed options. Example: $10k of NVIDIA in the DeepSeek week lost $1,581; with a $100 protection, $600.
- On-chain big test (Hedera testnet, test dollars): $15B saved, $650M of risk capital, $6.48B of stock protected across 9 countries, 109 transactions. We replayed the COVID crash week: $222.8M was paid to stock owners, the risk-takers absorbed all of it, and savers lost $0. Every number and transaction is at insurevex.vercel.app/admin.

Live on three testnets: Whitechain (official test USDT, full lifecycle through maturity), Hedera (tokenised NVIDIA and the note as a tokenised bond via Asset Tokenization Studio, a bonus paid by Hedera's Schedule Service with no keeper, and an x402 agent that buys cover by itself) and Arc (USDC as money and gas, built and security-reviewed in Arc Studio). Testnet only: bond custody is simulated, and we document every limitation in the README.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.24, OpenZeppelin 5, Hardhat): six contracts deployed and verified on all three chains. IdentityRegistry (ERC-3643-style KYC, country, freeze, blocked jurisdictions) gates everything. ProtectedNote splits each deposit in one transaction: floor = face/(1+r·τ) into TBillVault (tokenised T-bill with NAV and attested reserve), the rest into UnderwritingPool, an ERC-4626 senior tranche plus a Pro first-loss tranche with per-epoch shares. CoverMarket sells crash floors from EIP-712 quotes signed by our pricing server, checks insurable interest (an on-chain ATS token balance, or a signed broker-holdings attestation), locks the max payout via the pool's reserve and per-stock/per-country caps, and settles from PriceOracle official closes. Undeliverable payouts (e.g. a USDT-blocklisted wallet) become claimable "owed" balances, so settlement can never be blocked. 12 contract tests.

Pricing (Python → Node): we backtested 12 pricing models on 25 years of daily closes for 543 stocks in 23 markets (pandas, Yahoo prices, FRED Treasury yields), with walk-forward selection so every year is scored on data the model never saw. The winner (pooled global tail distribution × mean-reverting volatility × per-market credibility factor) is exported as tables and runs in the Node/Express server, which signs quotes, converts every local-currency close to USD, refuses cover on stocks already in free fall, and runs a keeper that posts closes, settles policies, pays coupons and rolls the T-bill NAV.

Frontend: Next.js, wagmi/viem, RainbowKit, Recharts. Pages for Protect, Save, Pool, Research, an Issuer compliance console and /admin, which reads the stress test straight from the chain.

Partner tech:
- Whitechain: every payment (subscription, premium, payout, coupon, redemption) in the official test USDT; a demo note ran to maturity (2 USDT in, 2.000026 back).
- Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio issued a tokenised NVIDIA equity (ERC-1400, ISIN, KYC, freeze) whose balance CoverMarket reads on-chain as proof of ownership (over-coverage reverts), and our note as an ATS bond with a coupon schedule. The Hedera Schedule Service (HIP-1215) executed coupon payments with no keeper. An x402 agent pays a 0.01 HBAR underwriting fee over HTTP 402, validates the signed quote and buys cover within budgets, with an HCS spending-audit anchor.
- Arc: USDC is both money and gas. Arc Studio wrote its own version of our six contracts with 263 forge tests and two security reviews; its 4 findings became our v3 fixes, each with a regression test.

Hacky bits worth mentioning:
- The $15B stress test deploys a separate suite with a test-only mintable dollar, drives 8 wallets in parallel, prices every cover live, then has the oracle post each stock's real return from the replayed historical week, so the COVID crash ran on-chain in 12 minutes. It is resumable after RPC drops.
- Hedera's Hashio relay rejects batched eth_getLogs and under-estimates gas on multi-contract calls, so we unbatch, pad gas, and run a multi-RPC failover provider (Chainlist endpoints + Alchemy) that benches endpoints returning rate-limit or plan errors.
- A browser test caught foreign stocks sized in local currency as if USD (1 Reliance share became ~94× too much cover); the server now converts at live FX and caps cover at the shares' USD value.
