projects.title: Nainokot Wallet
projects.description: EIP-8141 privacy pool paymaster: a ZK proof pays your gas, so any account can transact privately
projects.project_description: Nainokot Wallet is a Chrome extension wallet that keeps your money private by never showing it to the apps you use. Your funds sit as private notes in a shielded privacy pool. When you connect to a site, the wallet gives it a brand-new account with zero ETH, never your funds’ address, and allows switching to a fresh account after every transaction, so a site can’t link your actions to each other or to your balance. How the gas gets paid: every transaction is an EIP-8141 frame transaction. The wallet makes a zero-knowledge proof on your device that you own a note in the pool, and the pool acts as the paymaster. A VERIFY frame checks the proof and approves payment, your calls run as SENDER frames from the empty account, and a final DEFAULT frame marks the note’s nullifiers spent and adds a change note back to the pool. The pool has a second, pre_verify shape, where the nullifiers are marked before payment is approved. A staked payer on the alternative mempool (ERC-8421) only admits one pending transaction per (payer, nullifier), so one note can’t be used to flood the pool with double spends. Apps get more than a payer. Through ERC-5792 wallet_sendCalls, a dapp can ask for an expiry frame (the 0x8141 verifier: the transaction is only valid until a deadline) and for atomic batches, where several calls land together or not at all. The pool can also act as the sender itself, for withdrawals to any address and for private transfers between wallets, spending two notes at once. To show it working we built Framecaster, a small X-style app with posts, threads, replies and likes. A three-post thread is one transaction: an expiry frame, then three calls in one atomic batch, paid from the pool. The wallet’s send window shows each frame as a card you can tap, and History shows every transaction’s frames as they ran on chain. Built with Yul and Solidity contracts, a TypeScript client, and on-device proofs, on a local chain running forshtat/ethrex (the alt mempool client). The repo includes smoke tests (frame shapes, 10 attack cases refused before the pool pays, cross-shape double spends) and a full browser end-to-end test.
projects.how_its_made:
Nainokot runs on EIP-8141 frame transactions, on a local chain 1337 running forshtat/ethrex, the alternative mempool (ERC-8421) client. The shielded pool is based on minimal-shielded-pool: we reuse its note format, Merkle tree, circuit and TypeScript prover, so proofs are made in the browser (about 1.4 s on a MacBook). Contracts: the pool is a small Yul dispatcher in front of a Solidity logic contract (PrivacyPoolLogic). The dispatcher reads the whole transaction with the frame opcodes (TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, FRAMEDATALOAD) and decides which shape it’s in: Sponsored: [sender VERIFY] [pool VERIFY: 288-byte proof, approves payment] [your SENDER calls] [pool DEFAULT: settle]. The pay frame reads the proof’s statement (root, nullifiers, fee, change note) straight out of the last frame’s calldata, so proof and settlement can’t be split. It also pins settle as the last frame with enough gas, and refuses already-spent nullifiers before it pays.
pre_verify: a DEFAULT frame checks the proof and marks the nullifiers before the VERIFY frame approves payment, the ERC-8421 pattern for a staked payer that writes during validation.
Pool as sender: for withdrawals and private transfers. The two nullifiers double as the transaction’s EIP-8250 nonce keys, so the protocol itself refuses a replay.
Expiry: if frame 0 targets the 0x8141 expiry verifier, every other index shifts by one. The wallet is a Manifest V3 Chrome extension built with esbuild. It exposes EIP-1193 and ERC-5792 (wallet_sendCalls, getCapabilities, getCallsStatus) with a privacyPaymaster capability, atomicRequired for batches, and an expiry capability. Each site gets a new key with zero ETH. The send window builds the transaction, runs a dry run, and shows each frame as a tappable card with decoded calldata. Partner tech: EIP-8141 frames gave us payment as a verify step, so an empty account can transact with no relayer, no bundler and no 4337 EntryPoint. The alt mempool’s staking rules let the pool use 2.5M gas for validation (the proof check alone uses 250k) and touch its own storage.

projects.title: LookOut
projects.description: Check before you sign: a private, community-owned scam check for wallets and AI agents, on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Lookout is a pre-sign safety check for wallets and AI agents. Before you send money or sign a request, it tells you whether the target is flagged (block, warn or unknown), why, and which Arkiv records back that up. It never says "safe", only "nothing found". The problem: scam sites and drainers live for hours, but vendor lists lag by days (a 2025 study found Google Safe Browsing took 4.5 days on average to flag the phishing sites it caught). One company owns the list and can see what you check. And open reporting is easy to game with thousands of fake wallets. How Lookout answers each one: Community owned. Reports, trusted-source verdicts, owner disputes and rulings are Arkiv entities, each with an owner and an expiry, so stale flags disappear. The lookup table is rebuilt from Arkiv alone. Private. The check runs over two-server PIR, so neither server learns which address you asked about. Verifiable. The table's root is published on Arkiv and the client checks every answer against it. Hard to game. A report locks a deposit in an escrow contract and only counts as confirmed when an independent trusted source flags the same target afterwards. A thousand fresh wallets weigh nothing and can only ever produce a warning. Agent ready. An AI agent calls one check_target tool and gets the same verdict as JSON, and aborts on block. World ID proves one human per wallet, so verified people earn bounties.
projects.how_its_made: It is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces, Node 24) with a Next.js 16 / React 19 app and about 440 tests plus an attack simulation, all gated by one npm run verify. Arkiv is the source of truth. We defined seven entity schemas on the Rabdi testnet with the Arkiv SDK. An indexer reads them by attribute query into a SQLite cache and applies trusted-writer rules, always checking $creator, because Arkiv records who created an entity but not whether they were allowed to. Expiry does real work: spam reports vanish in 24 hours. The private lookup is two-server XOR PIR over a table of 16,384 buckets of 512 bytes with two-choice hashing. The client sends each server a random bit vector (one differs by a single bit), XORs the answers, always asks for both candidate buckets so a hit and a miss look the same, then verifies the bucket against a hash table and the table against a root the indexer publishes on Arkiv as a snapshot entity. We check wiping the cache and rebuilding gives the same root. Hacky but worth noting: indexers disagreed on roots because block times drift from 2 s, so snapshots are built as of a 300-block epoch using the epoch block's real chain timestamp. Scoring is a pure function shared by the indexer, wallet and agent tool. The escrow is Solidity on Sepolia (deposits, refunds, bounty pool, tested with Foundry), settled by an operator service whose rulings carry public reasons. World ID (IDKit) ties one human to one wallet. Our attack simulation caught a real bug: a flood of farmed reports could push a genuine scam's signals out of the table, downgrading a block to a warning. We fixed it and kept the test. The demo uses one wallet for several roles. Much of the code was written with Claude Code under our direction.

projects.title: Comment Desk
projects.description: World ID–gated public comment desk with ENS names and Arkiv-backed, tamper-evident records.
projects.project_description: CommentDesk is a public-comment platform for dockets (regulatory filings, proposals, policy drafts) where every comment is tied to a verified, unique human — or an AI agent acting only with that human's fresh, in-the-moment approval. Verified members get a readable ENS name (like maya.commentdesk.eth) instead of an anonymous ID, and every comment, join, and agent-assisted draft is written to Arkiv so the record is queryable and tamper-evident rather than living in a database only the platform controls. Dockets can require different credential strength (Proof of Human vs. Selfie Check) depending on how high-stakes the topic is, and tallies are computed live from the on-chain-backed record.
projects.how_its_made: The backend is a Hono/Node service (TypeScript) that gates two moments with World ID 4 (IDKit): joining the registry (uniqueness proof, mints an ENS name) and posting a human-typed comment (credential level set per docket). Each proof's signal binds the member and a hash of (docket, topic, position, text), so proofs can't be replayed for different words, and the nullifier is scoped per (docket, topic) so re-use is refused server-side. For AI-drafted comments, posting requires a separate World ID Agent Pass step — a real OIDC step-up against auth.world.org with max_age=0 and a nonce frozen to the draft's hash, so the signed ID token itself commits to the exact text approved; the agent itself can never call the post endpoint. Verified joins and comments are persisted through Arkiv (DB-Chain) as the source of truth, with ENS names minted/resolved via a dedicated naming service on Sepolia. An optional built-in drafting agent (Groq, Gemini, or Claude, tried in that order with failover) interviews the member and proposes comment text in their own words, but every draft still requires the human's Agent Pass approval before anything is posted. Frontend is Next.js; the whole repo is an npm workspace monorepo (frontend, backend, contracts).

projects.title: Cordon
projects.description: Seal one malicious npm version on chain, and every guard blocks it before it runs.
projects.project_description: Cordon is a circuit breaker for npm dependencies. Independent detectors each vote that one exact package version is malicious, with an evidence hash. When a quorum of distinct detector keys agrees, the SealRegistry contract marks that version Sealed. A guard then blocks it in three places: cordon install checks every lockfile entry, transitive ones included, before npm runs and installs with scripts disabled; a sidecar makes running services that depend on it fail their health check; and cordon audit finds copies already installed. Seals are per version, so 1.4.0 stays installable when 1.4.1 is sealed, and the guard proposes a rollback without editing files. If the RPC is down, the guard blocks from a signed snapshot; if our watcher is down too, from its cached copy. A false seal is an outage we caused, so the contract has a quorum, a seal rate limit, vote expiry and a dispute window before a guardian can unseal. This is a testnet prototype on Base Sepolia (SealRegistry 0x07DCC100d48fBA912fEf3e14F61d1162596a0E8F). In the demo all three detectors and the guardian key are run by our team, the detectors are labelled simulated, and only npm lockfile v2 and v3 are supported.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin v5 AccessControl for SealRegistry, with frozen roles, quorum, vote lifetime, dispute window and a daily seal limit, deployed on Base Sepolia and verified on Sourcify. TypeScript on Node 22 for the guard CLI, the detectors service and the watcher, using viem, zod, Fastify and node:sqlite. The three detectors are a static reader of install scripts, a Docker sandbox that installs the package with a canary value and no real files, and an OSV lookup that counts only MAL advisories. The watcher polls the registry and the chain in parallel, signs snapshots of the Sealed list, and keeps a stopwatch from publish to first block. The dashboard is Next.js with wagmi and reads SealRegistry directly; it has a read only mode with no backend. A Chainlink CRE workflow runs the OSV check across nodes that agree on the MAL ids and writes the vote through a receiver contract; it runs in the CRE simulator only. We built it with Claude Code; docs/ai_usage.md lists every AI generated file.

projects.title: Bid3
projects.description: All the thrill of a live auction, with onchain receipts anyone can check.
projects.project_description: The hammer falls. One person wins. Everyone should be able to check the result. Bid3 is a live auction where bidders raise physical paddles, and every accepted bid, the hammer result and the payment end up in a public record anyone can check. It combines handheld hardware paddles, wallet-owned listings, a big-screen live room, auctioneer controls, phone-wallet payments and a results explorer. We built it for charity fundraisers, college festivals, community events and collector auctions, where people care about both the experience in the room and the fairness of the outcome. A seller connects their wallet, adds an item's details and sets an opening price. The listing is published on Arkiv and owned by the seller's wallet. Buyers can browse the catalogue, filter by category and price, and follow each lot from "up next" through to its final outcome. Each bidder holds an ESP32 paddle with a slide switch and a single BID button. Bidding needs no app, wallet or login. Switching the paddle on joins the room, and each press bids the next price. Every press is signed with the paddle's own key and sent over Bluetooth to a gateway with its own display, which passes it to the auction engine. The engine alone decides the order, price, countdown and winner. Public records show only a fresh alias for each paddle, such as K7 or M4, never a name, wallet or device ID. The auctioneer opens bidding on one lot at a time from an admin console. A shared live-room screen shows the current price, leading paddle, accepted bids and hammer countdown, and moves to the next lot by itself when bidding opens. The first accepted bid takes the opening price. Each following bid raises the price by exactly 5% and restarts a ten-second countdown. The leading bidder wins when that countdown ends. If nobody bids within the auctioneer's chosen window, the lot closes unsold and goes back to the seller. The rules also cover the awkward moments at real events. Switching a paddle off cannot withdraw a bid that was already accepted. A paddle that loses signal can't place new bids while everyone else carries on, and it must sign a fresh join to come back. projects.project_description_markdown:
The hammer falls. One person wins. Everyone should be able to check the result.

Bid3 is a live auction where bidders raise physical paddles, and every accepted bid, the hammer result and the payment end up in a public record anyone can check. It combines handheld hardware paddles, wallet-owned listings, a big-screen live room, auctioneer controls, phone-wallet payments and a results explorer. We built it for charity fundraisers, college festivals, community events and collector auctions, where people care about both the experience in the room and the fairness of the outcome.

A seller connects their wallet, adds an item's details and sets an opening price. The listing is published on Arkiv and owned by the seller's wallet. Buyers can browse the catalogue, filter by category and price, and follow each lot from "up next" through to its final outcome.

Each bidder holds an ESP32 paddle with a slide switch and a single BID button. Bidding needs no app, wallet or login. Switching the paddle on joins the room, and each press bids the next price. Every press is signed with the paddle's own key and sent over Bluetooth to a gateway with its own display, which passes it to the auction engine. The engine alone decides the order, price, countdown and winner. Public records show only a fresh alias for each paddle, such as K7 or M4, never a name, wallet or device ID.

The auctioneer opens bidding on one lot at a time from an admin console. A shared live-room screen shows the current price, leading paddle, accepted bids and hammer countdown, and moves to the next lot by itself when bidding opens. The first accepted bid takes the opening price. Each following bid raises the price by exactly 5% and restarts a ten-second countdown. The leading bidder wins when that countdown ends. If nobody bids within the auctioneer's chosen window, the lot closes unsold and goes back to the seller.

The rules also cover the awkward moments at real events. Switching a paddle off cannot withdraw a bid that was already accepted. A paddle that loses signal can't place new bids while everyone else carries on, and it must sign a fresh join to come back. An outage of the gateway, bridge or engine pauses the whole room. If the engine restarts, an unfinished auction comes back paused instead of trusting an old deadline.

As bidding happens, Bid3 publishes the frozen auction rules, accepted bids and final result to Arkiv. These writes happen in the background, so a press never waits for blockchain confirmation. Short-lived public snapshots also give a fallback view when the live stream is unavailable.

After the hammer falls, anyone can open the results explorer and inspect the published evidence. Their browser checks the publisher's identity, recalculates the rules hash, rebuilds every price on the bid ladder, compares the winning bidder and hammer price with the history, and verifies a fingerprint of the published bid transcript. Missing or inconsistent evidence fails the relevant checks. The catalogue, bid history and results explorer read directly from Arkiv, so published records stay independently accessible for their configured lifetimes, even when the live auction engine is offline.

The winner pays the seller on the Sepolia testnet. Tapping a phone on the paddle's NFC sticker opens that paddle's seat page, which creates a wallet in the phone's browser and links it to the paddle with one signed tap. When that paddle wins, the page pays the seller automatically, with MetaMask available as a fallback. The payment is signed and saved before it is broadcast, so a reload or retry cannot pay twice. Bid3 checks the transaction's sender, recipient, amount and auction reference before marking the lot paid. If the winner doesn't pay within ten minutes, the lot stays with the seller. Paid and unpaid outcomes are both published to Arkiv. The demo defaults to a zero-value transfer plus testnet gas, and paddles without a linked wallet can still bid.

We ran it end to end on real hardware. In lot bid3-004, two paddles traded 11 bids from 100.00 to 162.89, the lot sold to M4, and the rules, every bid and the result were read back from Arkiv. Publishing that whole round cost 0.00444 tGLM in testnet gas.

A losing bidder can revisit the sequence. A seller can check the hammer price. An organiser can point everyone to the same published evidence, even after the crowd has gone home.

projects.title: Racconpay
projects.description: Non-custodial USDC/EURC payments, vesting, escrow and yield suite on Arc
projects.project_description: RacconPay is a non-custodial stablecoin suite on Arc for teams, freelancers and finance departments. Pay many people in one transaction, stream salary with leave and pause controls, lock USDC or EURC in milestone escrow, send invoices, split bills and swap between USDC, EURC and cirBTC. Locked funds can optionally earn yield through Aave V4. Built with Arc Studio, it uses USDC as gas for predictable fees and sub-second finality, and runs on Arc Mainnet
projects.how_its_made: RacconPay is a React 18 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind app with no backend. It uses wagmi v2, viem v2 and ConnectKit for wallets, with optional WalletConnect. The contracts are Solidity 0.8.28 with OpenZeppelin 5.1, built and tested with Foundry (unit, fuzz and invariant tests) and deployed to Arc Mainnet. I used Arc Studio to extend an existing Arc Mainnet app. I added a vesting console (leave and pauses, bulk CSV upload, address book, activity reports), milestone escrow for USDC or EURC with an arbiter, and a swap through Circle App Kit with its viem adapter, limited to USDC, EURC and cirBTC. The yield feature is the part I'm proudest of. VestingStreamV2Yield deposits 70% of a stream into an ERC-4626 vault and keeps 30% in the contract, so the payee is always paid first. I pointed it at Aave V4's Core USDC Tokenization Spoke, which is an ERC-4626 wrapper over the Aave Hub

projects.title: framilier
projects.description: Framilier gives wallets a fair turn when an alternative mempool verifies EIP-8141 transactions.
projects.project_description: What happens when one wallet sends eight expensive transactions just before another wallet sends one cheap transaction? If the node starts checking transactions in arrival order, the second wallet can wait behind the entire burst. Framilier lets Ethereum alternative-mempool operators give each sender a turn and measure what that choice costs. In a local benchmark with two wallets paying their own fees and 20 rounds per policy, switching from first-come, first-served scheduling to sender rotation reduced the second wallet’s 95th-percentile admission time from 678 ms to 238 ms. The busy wallet’s median batch time increased from 593 ms to 622 ms. At framilier.dev, you can see exactly when the second wallet got a turn, inspect the transaction receipts, and explore a second scenario where both wallets use the same gas sponsor.
projects.how_its_made: We extended the Ethereum Foundation’s alternative-mempool workshop sidecar with a TypeScript scheduler. Before ethrex simulates an EIP-8141 frame transaction, the scheduler chooses the next check from queues grouped by sender. Our benchmark gives the node four simulation slots and allows one sender to occupy up to two of them with expensive checks. The Framilier CLI submits the same signed transactions on fresh private ethrex chains under three policies: scheduling off, first-come first-served, and sender rotation. A Solidity wallet verifies a Keccak hash chain that consumes about one million VERIFY gas. We record when each simulation starts and when the sidecar admits each transaction, then check the mined receipts separately. For the sponsored scenario, each wallet signs its own transaction and a shared staked paymaster authorizes payment in a separate VERIFY frame. We check that both wallets’ receipts name the same payer and that the fees add up to the change in its balance. This lets us test the distinction at the heart of that demo: two wallets can share a gas sponsor and still get separate turns.

projects.title: Human Club
projects.description: Petitions and fundraisers only humans can sign: one press on a device you own, no account.
projects.project_description: The Human Club at club.getknock.dev is a working social app where the scarce thing is being human. Anyone can read a petition or a fundraiser; only a verified human can start one or add a signature, and each human counts once per petition. Two ways in. A Wedgie — a small open device, a Pico with a 240×240 screen and a Trust M secure chip running the Knock app — shows the site's origin, its owner presses green, and it signs the site's single-use challenge with a P-256 key held in the chip. Or a visitor proves with World ID 4.0 through IDKit, enrolls a wallet with SIWE, and signs from there. Both paths resolve to the same World ID nullifier, so a Wedgie knock and a World App proof are the same human, counted once. Under it is Knock, the protocol that makes the club possible. A wedgie's key is bound to a human through KnockBinding on World Chain and named in ENSv2 on Ethereum mainnet, for example wedgie.itzraj.eth. The club's own verifier reads the ENS records and the binding on World Chain; it does not ask Knock's server. Fundraisers accept mainnet gifts, and the counter, the human and the act are written in one transaction. Everything is live and MIT open source: the app, the contracts, knockd, two verifiers, the Door SDK, the Console that binds and names a device, the docs, and the Human Club itself. It keeps no email, password or real name. Honest limits: no PIN on the device, proof farming is unsolved, the public nullifier is linkable across sites in Bound mode, and the Wedgie is not an audited hardware wallet.
projects.how_its_made: The club. Next.js 16 and React 19, deployed on Vercel. Vercel functions hold the petition and signature logic; Turso (libSQL) keeps members, petitions, signatures and fundraiser totals. Sign-in is SIWE with EIP-6963 wallets, World ID comes through IDKit 4.6, and a fundraiser's gifts are matched on Ethereum mainnet. Starting or signing writes the counter, the human and the act in one transaction. The device. A Wedgie runs a MicroPython app built from Safe Signer's parts. Its own P-256 key lives in Trust M slot KEY4; it draws the origin on screen, takes a green press, and signs an EIP-712 KnockPass. The computer talks to it over Web Serial. The protocol. KnockBinding is Solidity 0.8.30 built with Foundry (via_ir, OpenZeppelin P256) on World Chain. A first World ID proof enrolls a human and starts a session; later acts are session proofs. ENSv2 naming and the kill switch are transactions from the user's own wallet on mainnet, with EIP-5792 batching where supported. knockd is Rust (axum, alloy, p256) on Fly.io and signs RP requests. Verification. @knock-dev/verify for a site's own JavaScript server (memory or libSQL stores), knock-verify as a Rust crate, and knock-verifier as a small HTTP service. The club uses the JS package. Tests: 181 TypeScript, 34 Rust, 30 Foundry, plus live runs on real hardware.

A wedgie's key is bound to a human through KnockBinding on World Chain and named in ENSv2 on Ethereum mainnet, for example wedgie.itzraj.eth. The club's own verifier reads the ENS records and the binding on World Chain; it does not ask Knock's server. Fundraisers accept mainnet gifts, and the counter, the human and the act are written in one transaction.

Everything is live and MIT open source: the app, the contracts, knockd, two verifiers, the Door SDK, the Console that binds and names a device, the docs, and the Human Club itself. It keeps no email, password or real name. Honest limits: no PIN on the device, proof farming is unsolved, the public nullifier is linkable across sites in Bound mode, and the Wedgie is not an audited hardware wallet.

The club. Next.js 16 and React 19, deployed on Vercel. Vercel functions hold the petition and signature logic; Turso (libSQL) keeps members, petitions, signatures and fundraiser totals. Sign-in is SIWE with EIP-6963 wallets, World ID comes through IDKit 4.6, and a fundraiser's gifts are matched on Ethereum mainnet. Starting or signing writes the counter, the human and the act in one transaction.

The device. A Wedgie runs a MicroPython app built from Safe Signer's parts. Its own P-256 key lives in Trust M slot KEY4; it draws the origin on screen, takes a green press, and signs an EIP-712 KnockPass. The computer talks to it over Web Serial.

The protocol. KnockBinding is Solidity 0.8.30 built with Foundry (via_ir, OpenZeppelin P256) on World Chain. A first World ID proof enrolls a human and starts a session; later acts are session proofs. ENSv2 naming and the kill switch are transactions from the user's own wallet on mainnet, with EIP-5792 batching where supported. knockd is Rust (axum, alloy, p256) on Fly.io and signs RP requests.

Verification. @knock-dev/verify for a site's own JavaScript server (memory or libSQL stores), knock-verify as a Rust crate, and knock-verifier as a small HTTP service. The club uses the JS package. Tests: 181 TypeScript, 34 Rust, 30 Foundry, plus live runs on real hardware.

projects.title: Litmus Protocol
projects.description: Trustless validation for AI agents, turning adversarial testing into verifiable on-chain reputation.
projects.project_description: Litmus is a trustless validation protocol for AI agents that turns adversa,rial testing into verifiable on-chain reputation. Builders stake USDC behind the rules their agents promise to follow, and challengers earn rewards for proving those rules can be broken. Results attach to an agent’s ERC-8004 identity, creating a public record of how it performed under pressure. As AI agents gain access to wallets, private information, and external tools, their reliability becomes more consequential. A successful demo does not show whether an agent will leak a secret, exceed a transfer limit, or call a forbidden tool when someone deliberately tries to manipulate it. Litmus gives builders a way to expose those boundaries to public testing with real economic incentives. A builder creates a contest, defines the agent’s rules, and stakes USDC. Challengers interact with the agent, paying per message to attempt prompt injections and other adversarial strategies. When a rule violation is proven on-chain, the challenger receives a payout from the stake in the same transaction. Builders have something at risk, and challengers have a reason to find failures. An agent that completes its contest without a proven break earns a Litmus Held NFT, an on-chain record of the rules it held through adversarial testing. Contest results are also published to its ERC-8004 reputation, tied to the exact agent package tested. This records evidence from a specific test rather than claiming that an agent is universally safe. Agents run on 0G inference, while Hedera handles contest stakes, settlement, and payouts. A Chainlink CRE workflow audits each finished contest on Sepolia. Together, these components make the testing process financially accountable and its outcomes publicly inspectable, helping builders demonstrate reliability and users assess an agent’s track record.
projects.how_its_made: We built Litmus to turn AI-agent behavior into verifiable outcomes: a proven rule violation triggers a payout, while an agent that holds through adversarial testing earns a record of what was tested. The architecture separates agent execution, financial settlement, and evidence auditing. A Next.js frontend connects to a Hono gateway backed by SQLite, a private runner executes the agent, and Solidity contracts developed with Foundry manage stakes and payouts on Hedera testnet. The core smart contract holds HTS USDC for each validation’s prize pool, agent vault, and builder bond. We implemented three mechanically checkable rule types. Transfer-limit violations are detected inside the agent’s vault-send function, while invoking a forbidden emergency-withdraw tool directly triggers a breach. Secret leaks use commit–reveal: the challenger commits a hash bound to their address and a salt, then reveals the recovered secret in a later block. This prevents someone from copying a pending reveal to claim the reward. A verified breach updates the validation state and pays the challenger in the same transaction. Each adversarial message follows an x402 payment flow on Hedera. The gateway verifies the signed payment, asks the runner to execute the agent, and settles only if the response arrives within the charging deadline. Slow or failed runs are not charged. This required controlling verification and settlement separately rather than relying on middleware that automatically charges on a successful HTTP response. Settled fees reach the smart contract through retryable background jobs, with shares allocated to the prize pool, treasury, and refund escrow. 0G Compute powers the agent’s tool-calling loop. Builders select from the live model and provider catalog and can pin a provider for the validation period; pinned runs do not silently switch to another provider or model. We request TEE verification and preserve 0G request IDs and returned trace metadata in signed attempt records. The runner keeps agent secrets in an AES-256-GCM encrypted store, separate from the public gateway. Periodic canary tasks check that the agent remains functional, with failed rounds triggering refunds and repeated failures invalidating the validation run. On-chain settlement alone cannot establish that the gateway’s published evidence matches the original commitments. We therefore built a TypeScript Chainlink CRE auditor that retrieves the finalized log and revealed validation data, reads Hedera contract state, and compares log hashes, canary commitments, secret hashes, and deposited-message counts. Because CRE does not natively support Hedera, we access its JSON-RPC relay through the HTTP capability and use the EVM capability to write an attestation to Ethereum Sepolia. The current workflow runs through the CRE CLI simulator with broadcast enabled and the Sepolia simulation forwarder. When an agent completes the validation period without a proven breach, the gateway requires a passing audit before minting its Litmus Held NFT. This soulbound ERC-721 uses on-chain SVG artwork and records validation metadata, including the tested package hash. For linked ERC-8004 agents, eligible results are also published as reputation feedback, connecting the outcome to the agent’s identity and the exact package tested. We also handled failures across payment and settlement boundaries: reused payment authorizations are rejected, failed fee deposits are retried, and unsuccessful payouts become withdrawable credits so one recipient cannot block settlement. The repository includes Foundry contract tests, Vitest service tests, and fixture-based CRE audit tests. The frontend exposes inference request IDs, payment transactions, and audit status so users can inspect the evidence behind each validation result.

projects.title: ScoobyDAO
projects.description: AI investigates rugs; stake on the verdict, keep the principal side, and trade the yield side as YT
projects.project_description: ScoobyDAO: sniff out the rug before it pulls, and get paid while the case runs. Rug pulls cost crypto users billions every year: nearly $6B in 2025 by mid-April alone, according to DappRadar. Today’s warnings don’t help much. Scanners give you a risk score with no one accountable for it, anyone can call a token a scam on X, and audits are paid for by the project and stop after launch. Nobody does the digging, puts their name on the call and has money riding on being right. Inspired by Hindenburg Research, which published deep investigations and backed them with money, ScoobyDAO does that for tokens, in the open. It starts with AI agents investigating suspicious tokens. Our detective, Sniff, leads the pack. The Scout watches new tokens and pools, runs quick checks and ranks the most suspicious ones. The Investigators then write a case file covering five areas: trading patterns, onchain history, fundamentals, statistical risk and contract code health. They record what they found, what is still unknown and what points the other way. Every report is fingerprinted with SHA-256, so any change creates a new version. No AI can publish an accusation by itself. A real person reviews the report and confirms each step with World ID, and that approval is tied to that exact report version. If they deny it or let it expire, nothing happens. Once it’s approved, the report is published onchain and its market opens. Then the market decides. Anyone can stake dUSD, our test stablecoin, on Yes (“this is a rug”) or No. After 30 days a result is proposed with evidence, anyone can challenge it during a challenge window, and then it’s finalized as Yes, No or Void. The winning side gets its stake back plus 80% of the losing pool. For example, with 80 dUSD on Yes and 20 on No, each Yes dUSD returns 1.20. If the result is Void, everyone gets their money back. Here’s the twist that makes ScoobyDAO different: your stake keeps working. A case takes a month, so stakes would normally sit idle. ScoobyDAO splits every stake in two, like Pendle’s principal and yield tokens. The principal side is your Yes/No position: it pays out on the verdict and can’t be transferred. The yield side, called YT, is minted one-to-one when you stake. It earns the interest on the locked stake whatever the verdict, and it’s freely tradable. YT trades on our custom Uniswap v4 hook, which prices it on an interest-rate curve that moves with demand and shrinks as maturity approaches. You can even stake and sell your YT in a single transaction. You keep your vote and get dUSD back right away, so less of your money is at risk. YT buyers get exposure to the yield, and liquidity providers earn the yield on YT held in the pool. Because the YT price reflects interest and not the verdict, the market for truth and the market for yield stay separate. You can also stake from another chain. With Chainlink CCIP you can stake from Arbitrum Sepolia, and a vote counts only once it’s credited on Ethereum. Late messages become withdrawable receipts instead of votes, and malformed ones are held safely. What’s live today: the report registry, stake vault, yield token and Uniswap v4 hook market on Ethereum Sepolia, plus a CCIP sender on Arbitrum Sepolia with a delivered cross-chain vote. There’s a Next.js app for cases, reports, staking, YT trading, cross-chain tracking and claims, and a FastAPI backend that runs the agents and human checkpoints. We’re upfront about the demo: dUSD is a test token, the yield is simulated, and the demo roles are held by the team wallet. Built with World ID, Chainlink CCIP and Uniswap v4.
projects.how_its_made:
ScoobyDAO is built across four repositories that fit together. ScoobyDAO-web is the Next.js app. ScoobyDAO-backend is the Python service that runs the AI agents, the World ID human checkpoints and the publisher. SmartContracts is the Foundry suite deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and Arbitrum Sepolia. ScoobyDAO-seed is a private repository of hash-pinned evidence packages for our six historical reference cases. It holds captured third-party data, so it stays private for licensing reasons, but every package is pinned by SHA-256 and the backend checks those hashes before anything is shown. The core rule across all of them is that only a verified human can turn an AI’s investigation into an onchain market. -> SmartContracts (Solidity, Foundry, Ethereum Sepolia + Arbitrum Sepolia) ReportRegistry stores each published case: a report hash, a claim hash and its timings (cross-chain cutoff, lock time, result deadline, challenge period). It only accepts a publish call from the publisher, with a reviewer’s EIP-191 signature over the exact report, a single-use nonce and an expiry, so nothing can open a market without a fresh approval.
RiskFiStakeVaultV2 is the market. A stake in dUSD records a non-transferable Yes/No position (the principal side) and mints the same amount of YT (the yield side) to the staker in the same transaction. It also handles settlement. After maturity the resolver proposes Yes, No or Void with an evidence hash. Anyone can challenge within the window, and an adjudicator decides. Anyone can finalize, and a case that passes its deadline becomes Void. Winners get their stake back plus 80% of the losing pool, with a 20% fee taken from the losing pool only. Claims stay open for 90 days. A StakeReceiptREP token lets users deposit dUSD 1:1 now and stake later, or withdraw any time.
StakerYieldToken (YT) uses a global yield index with per-holder checkpoints on every mint and transfer, so a late buyer can never claim yield earned before they held the token. Yield is paid whatever the verdict. That is the PT/YT split, modelled on Pendle’s principal/yield tokenization but adapted so a losing voter still forfeits principal.
YieldCurveHookV2 is a custom Uniswap v4 hook that owns its own YT/dUSD inventory and uses v4 custom accounting instead of normal concentrated liquidity. It prices YT on a bounded interest-rate curve: the implied rate is an anchor plus a slope times net YT bought, clamped between a minimum and a maximum. The YT price is that rate multiplied by the time remaining, so it decays toward maturity. Liquidity providers get RF-YLP shares and earn the yield on YT held by the pool through a yield-per-share index. YieldCurveFactoryV2 deploys the hook at a mined CREATE2 address with the required v4 permission bits. A custom YieldSwapRouter settles input inside the PoolManager unlock callback. StakeAndSellRouterV2 stakes, mints YT and sells it through the hook in one transaction, so a user keeps their vote and gets dUSD back immediately. Slippage protection reverts the whole action.
CCIPStakeSenderV2 on Arbitrum Sepolia and CCIPStakeReceiverV2 on Ethereum Sepolia carry funded votes. dUSD is a Chainlink Cross-Chain Token with a BurnMintTokenPool, so the same token exists on both chains. The receiver checks the router, source chain, sender and token, and blocks replays by source nonce. A valid on-time message is credited as a vote. A late one becomes REP receipts for the payer instead of a vote. A malformed one is held and can be recovered. A delivered message is never counted as a vote until it is credited.
Tests include eight-voter end-to-end workflows (local plus CCIP votes, yield, settlement and claims), Void and challenged verdicts, principal-loss scenarios, 256 fuzzed buy/sell round trips with quote/swap equality, and fork tests against the deployed state. All contracts are verified on Etherscan and Arbiscan. -> ScoobyDAO-backend (Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, Huey worker, Docker, Render)
The Scout (discovery) module watches new tokens and pools, runs deterministic checks and ranks cases by how actionable they are. Cases that meet a strict policy (several independent verified concern groups) go straight to investigation; the rest wait for a human. The Investigation module researches five pillars: market microstructure, onchain mechanics, fundamentals and sentiment, statistical risk and technical health. It uses source adapters plus a bounded LLM reasoning step, and keeps evidence, unknowns and counterevidence. Output follows a frozen, versioned JSON schema (report v0.2). Every artifact is hashed with SHA-256 over the exact bytes, and a renderer produces HTML and PDF case files with a portable evidence index. A durable job queue runs investigations with lease-based workers. -> ScoobyDAO-seed (private evidence packages)
The six reference cases in the app replay real research from captured evidence: price histories, model outputs and source snapshots. That data comes from third parties we can’t redistribute, so it lives in a separate private repository. Each package is pinned by SHA-256 in a manifest. The backend imports it into its data volume and re-checks every hash before rendering, and the web app shows an integrity error instead of the data if anything doesn’t match. This keeps the public repos open source while the licensed evidence stays private, and anyone can still verify that what they see matches the pinned bytes. -> World ID integration (the human checkpoints, in ScoobyDAO-backend)
We integrated World ID through auth.world.org OpenID Connect. Our agents are headless, so we use the OAuth Device Authorization Grant: the backend starts a request, and the reviewer approves it in World App with a short code. The client authenticates with private_key_jwt (RS256), never a shared secret. Every ID token is validated against World’s JWKS for issuer, audience, expiry, authentication time and assurance level. Tokens that carry delegation claims are rejected, so an agent can never pass as the human.
World App only shows the requesting app and the code, not what is being approved. So we bind each approval on our server to the exact case or report digest, decision, audience, nonce and expiry, and show that digest to the reviewer before the code. The result is checked again on confirmation and recorded as an append-only receipt; database triggers block edits. Permission is separate from identity: an enrolled-reviewer allowlist with scopes (case investigation, report review, publication) decides what a verified person may do. Session and device codes are stored only as hashes. There are three checkpoints: “go for investigation”, “report sign-off” and a separate “publish” sign-off. After approval, an attestor key signs the registry’s approval digest, and a fenced outbox publisher sends publish() exactly once, using the onchain nonce as a backstop against duplicates. Denied, expired or cancelled attempts start nothing and publish nothing. The whole flow is tested against a fake World issuer with its own keys (200+ backend tests). -> ScoobyDAO-web (Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, wagmi 2 + viem, RainbowKit, TanStack Query, React Three Fiber, Vitest, Vercel)
All chain access goes through one protocol adapter layer, so pages never touch raw ABIs. ABIs come straight from the SmartContracts deployment bundle and are checked against a SHA-256 manifest. On load, a deployment check confirms the vault, hook, routers, receiver and sender are wired to each other as expected, and disables writes if they aren’t. Every transaction is a planned set of steps (approve, then act) that is simulated and gas-estimated before sending. Reverts are replayed at the failing block to show the real reason. Market phases and countdowns come from the latest block timestamp, never the user’s clock. The browser recomputes the SHA-256 of the report bytes to check them against the published hashes. A CCIP tracker follows each cross-chain vote through sent, in transit, credited, deferred-as-REP or held. The landing page has a 3D scene with a 2D fallback, and respects reduced motion. -> How the partner technologies helped
World ID lets us prove that a live, unique human approved a specific accusation, not an agent holding someone’s password. That is the trust anchor for publishing claims about real tokens. Uniswap v4 hooks let us build a market for yield, not just a swap: custom accounting, our own pricing curve and atomic stake-and-sell. Chainlink CCIP let us accept funded votes from another chain with clear, recoverable outcomes, and its Cross-Chain Token standard gave us one dUSD across both chains. -> Hacky and notable details
Our first live CCIP delivery ran out of callback gas and had to be retried manually. We raised the receiver’s callback gas to 1.5M and rebuilt Chainlink’s packed GenericExtraArgsV3 encoding byte for byte in TypeScript. CCIP chain selectors are larger than JavaScript’s safe integer range, so they live as strings and BigInts. The hook-owned v4 market can’t be routed through Universal Router, Permit2 or V4Quoter, so we wrote our own router and read quotes straight from the hook. The real market has a 30-day maturity, so we deployed a second, flexible registry and vault with minute-long windows to show the full lifecycle (stake, propose, challenge window, finalize, claim) live on testnet. We split licensed evidence into a private hash-pinned repo so the rest of the project could be fully open source. We built a fixture chain that enforces the same rules as the contracts for offline demos, and aliased an optional wallet SDK dependency to a stub to get the Next.js build passing.

Tests include eight-voter end-to-end workflows (local plus CCIP votes, yield, settlement and claims), Void and challenged verdicts, principal-loss scenarios, 256 fuzzed buy/sell round trips with quote/swap equality, and fork tests against the deployed state. All contracts are verified on Etherscan and Arbiscan.

-> ScoobyDAO-backend (Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, Huey worker, Docker, Render)
The Scout (discovery) module watches new tokens and pools, runs deterministic checks and ranks cases by how actionable they are. Cases that meet a strict policy (several independent verified concern groups) go straight to investigation; the rest wait for a human. The Investigation module researches five pillars: market microstructure, onchain mechanics, fundamentals and sentiment, statistical risk and technical health. It uses source adapters plus a bounded LLM reasoning step, and keeps evidence, unknowns and counterevidence. Output follows a frozen, versioned JSON schema (report v0.2). Every artifact is hashed with SHA-256 over the exact bytes, and a renderer produces HTML and PDF case files with a portable evidence index. A durable job queue runs investigations with lease-based workers.

-> ScoobyDAO-seed (private evidence packages)
The six reference cases in the app replay real research from captured evidence: price histories, model outputs and source snapshots. That data comes from third parties we can’t redistribute, so it lives in a separate private repository. Each package is pinned by SHA-256 in a manifest. The backend imports it into its data volume and re-checks every hash before rendering, and the web app shows an integrity error instead of the data if anything doesn’t match. This keeps the public repos open source while the licensed evidence stays private, and anyone can still verify that what they see matches the pinned bytes.

-> World ID integration (the human checkpoints, in ScoobyDAO-backend)
We integrated World ID through auth.world.org OpenID Connect. Our agents are headless, so we use the OAuth Device Authorization Grant: the backend starts a request, and the reviewer approves it in World App with a short code. The client authenticates with private_key_jwt (RS256), never a shared secret. Every ID token is validated against World’s JWKS for issuer, audience, expiry, authentication time and assurance level. Tokens that carry delegation claims are rejected, so an agent can never pass as the human.
World App only shows the requesting app and the code, not what is being approved. So we bind each approval on our server to the exact case or report digest, decision, audience, nonce and expiry, and show that digest to the reviewer before the code. The result is checked again on confirmation and recorded as an append-only receipt; database triggers block edits. Permission is separate from identity: an enrolled-reviewer allowlist with scopes (case investigation, report review, publication) decides what a verified person may do. Session and device codes are stored only as hashes. There are three checkpoints: “go for investigation”, “report sign-off” and a separate “publish” sign-off. After approval, an attestor key signs the registry’s approval digest, and a fenced outbox publisher sends publish() exactly once, using the onchain nonce as a backstop against duplicates. Denied, expired or cancelled attempts start nothing and publish nothing. The whole flow is tested against a fake World issuer with its own keys (200+ backend tests).

-> ScoobyDAO-web (Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, wagmi 2 + viem, RainbowKit, TanStack Query, React Three Fiber, Vitest, Vercel)
All chain access goes through one protocol adapter layer, so pages never touch raw ABIs. ABIs come straight from the SmartContracts deployment bundle and are checked against a SHA-256 manifest. On load, a deployment check confirms the vault, hook, routers, receiver and sender are wired to each other as expected, and disables writes if they aren’t. Every transaction is a planned set of steps (approve, then act) that is simulated and gas-estimated before sending. Reverts are replayed at the failing block to show the real reason. Market phases and countdowns come from the latest block timestamp, never the user’s clock. The browser recomputes the SHA-256 of the report bytes to check them against the published hashes. A CCIP tracker follows each cross-chain vote through sent, in transit, credited, deferred-as-REP or held. The landing page has a 3D scene with a 2D fallback, and respects reduced motion.

-> How the partner technologies helped
World ID lets us prove that a live, unique human approved a specific accusation, not an agent holding someone’s password. That is the trust anchor for publishing claims about real tokens. Uniswap v4 hooks let us build a market for yield, not just a swap: custom accounting, our own pricing curve and atomic stake-and-sell. Chainlink CCIP let us accept funded votes from another chain with clear, recoverable outcomes, and its Cross-Chain Token standard gave us one dUSD across both chains.

-> Hacky and notable details
Our first live CCIP delivery ran out of callback gas and had to be retried manually. We raised the receiver’s callback gas to 1.5M and rebuilt Chainlink’s packed GenericExtraArgsV3 encoding byte for byte in TypeScript. CCIP chain selectors are larger than JavaScript’s safe integer range, so they live as strings and BigInts. The hook-owned v4 market can’t be routed through Universal Router, Permit2 or V4Quoter, so we wrote our own router and read quotes straight from the hook. The real market has a 30-day maturity, so we deployed a second, flexible registry and vault with minute-long windows to show the full lifecycle (stake, propose, challenge window, finalize, claim) live on testnet. We split licensed evidence into a private hash-pinned repo so the rest of the project could be fully open source. We built a fixture chain that enforces the same rules as the contracts for offline demos, and aliased an optional wallet SDK dependency to a stub to get the Next.js build passing.

projects.title: Earlyout
projects.description: Sell your pending fund redemption today for USDC on Arc, at a price that explains its own risks.
projects.project_description: Tokenized private credit funds only let investors out on a schedule. Apollo's ACRED, for example, repurchases at least 5% of the fund each quarter and pays once the underlying fund pays. An investor who needs cash before the next window has no exit. Earlyout is that exit. The holder deposits the fund token; Earlyout files the redemption with the issuer and mints an ERC-1155 claim for that fund and payout date. The holder sells the claim to an ERC-4626 USDC vault on Arc and is paid USDC in the same transaction. The vault waits, collects the full amount from the issuer at the payout date, and the LPs who funded it earn the discount. Price = real NAV from Chainlink minus a spread with four named parts shown on screen: base, vault utilisation, time to payout, issuer credit. Every quote starts with a verdict: BUY, REFUSE (over the fund's cap or no idle USDC) or HALT (issuer reports failure or NAV is stale). When an issuer fails, one transaction writes its claims down for every LP at once. A public book of open claims lives on Arkiv and expires on its own at each payout date. Ten funds are listed on Arc testnet, each priced off its own Chainlink NAV feed on Ethereum mainnet. The fund token, issuer and issuer status API are stand-ins because real ones only serve KYC-approved wallets; the NAV, USDC, every contract and the Arkiv book are real. We sell the wait; we do not make the fund liquid.
projects.how_its_made: Seven Solidity contracts (OpenZeppelin v5, Foundry, 63 tests) drafted with Claude Code, then installed, tested, security reviewed and deployed in Arc Studio, which fixed five Medium findings and executed all 34 deployment transactions from a Circle developer-controlled wallet before handing ownership to our ops wallet. Everything settles in USDC on Arc: the Vault is ERC-4626 over USDC with virtual shares, claims are carried at USDC cost in totalAssets() so the share price moves only on USDC that arrives, idle USDC is tracked apart from deployed USDC to drive the REFUSE verdict and the withdraw cap, and markImpaired writes a failed fund down to its recoveryBps for all LPs in one transaction. NavOracle is a Chainlink CRE receiver (onReport plus ERC165): a CRE TypeScript workflow reads latestRoundData from each fund's NAV feed on Ethereum mainnet, fetches the issuer status from our API with identical consensus, ABI-encodes (fund, nav, decimals, updatedAt, status), signs a report and writes it to NavOracle on Arc, simulated with --broadcast through the CRE simulation forwarder (issuer OK, FAILED and restored; transactions on the explorer). Moving to the production KeystoneForwarder on Arc is one setForwarder call.. The Book screen reads only from Arkiv: a Next.js indexer writes claims, funds and NAV history with @arkiv-network/sdk, claims expire at their payout date via ExpirationTime.atDate, and the README has the writer wallet and a runnable query. Frontend is Next.js, wagmi and viem on Vercel. Hacky bits: Arc's USDC blocklist precompile breaks Foundry's local simulation of USDC transfers, so the deploy script ran step by step from Studio; a 15-minute demo window fund lets settlement be shown live.

projects.title: PaperAi
projects.description: Voice-first form filling for people who can’t read, with tamper-proof records on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Paper AI helps people fill in paperwork just by talking. It is built for two groups who struggle with forms every day: older people whose eyesight is too weak for small print, and people who never learned to read but can listen and speak. Today they have to ask someone else to fill in their forms and simply trust that it was done right. They have no way to know if the document is changed later. How it works: Scan: The app opens straight on the camera, with no account and no menus. It finds the page, takes the photo by itself and straightens it. Explain: Within seconds it says out loud what the document is, in simple Hindi or English: what it is for, what it asks, and which papers to bring. The person can ask questions by voice. Fill by voice: It asks one question at a time and listens for the answer. Important answers are read back to confirm ("Date of birth: 12 March 1960. Is that correct?"). The person can say "repeat", "skip" or "change my name". Nothing is ever written that the person did not say. Check and sign: The completed PDF is shown next to the original and the key details are read aloud. The person signs with a finger. A key kept on the phone also signs the PDF, so no wallet or account is needed. Already have a filled form? "Already filled? Sign it" skips the questions. Save and share: When the person saves, the document's fingerprint, their consent and their signature are recorded on Arkiv in one transaction. They can then send a short-lived link or QR code to family or the bank. A witness or guarantor can co-sign from their own phone, and that co-signature is also recorded on Arkiv. Verify: Anyone receiving the PDF can check it at /verify. The file is fingerprinted in their own browser and checked directly against Arkiv, so they do not have to trust us. If even one letter has been changed, the check fails. Privacy: The form itself never goes on chain. The PDF is stored encrypted and opens only on the phone that saved it. Arkiv holds only its fingerprint, the consent record, the signatures and share links that expire on their own. Built from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026 on the Arkiv Rabdi testnet.
projects.how_its_made:
Paper AI is a Next.js 16 app (TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Radix components) deployed on Vercel. It is built phone-first: the client handles the camera, the microphone and the signing key, and the server handles AI, PDFs and Arkiv writes. Postgres stores only metadata, through Drizzle, with embedded PGlite for local development. No names, answers or document text are ever stored in the database. Scanning: The document scanner is written from scratch in plain TypeScript, with no OpenCV download. It finds the page edges with Hough lines, warps the perspective to straighten the page, removes shadows, and takes the photo automatically once the page stops moving. Understanding the form: Claude (claude-opus-5-5, fast mode) reads the page images and returns schema-validated output (Zod). We split this into two calls. A small one says what the document is and is spoken in about 8 seconds, while full field extraction keeps running in the background, so the person is never left waiting in silence. Tesseract.js (English + Hindi) adds OCR word positions. Answers are placed on the page from the form’s own fillable fields first, then by finding each label on the page with OCR, and only then from the model’s estimate. Conversation: “The AI interprets, the code decides.” Claude only turns what the person said into a typed intent and value. A plain deterministic state machine, shared by browser and server, decides what happens next. That is how we guarantee one question at a time, a read-back of important answers, and that nothing is written that the person did not say. Voice: Live speech recognition streams 16 kHz audio over a WebSocket using a single-use token, so API keys never reach the browser. It uses OpenAI realtime transcription for listening and ElevenLabs for speaking. We picked those defaults by benchmarking Hindi and English accuracy ourselves. If one service fails there is a fallback chain: batch transcription, then browser speech, then typing. PDF: pdf-lib fills real form fields or draws text onto scanned pages, and fontkit shapes Hindi (Devanagari) text correctly. Partner technology, Arkiv: Arkiv is the trust layer, and every Arkiv feature we use changes something the person sees. Fingerprint, consent and signature are written in one atomic executeBatch. We use predictEntityKeys so the consent and signature records can reference the fingerprint record inside the same transaction. A save either records fully or says “could not be recorded”, never half.
Fingerprint and consent records are created read-only, so even we cannot rewrite history.
Each entity’s expiry matches the retention the person chose (1 week, 1 month or 6 months). Share links are Arkiv entities whose expiry is the link lifetime, so links stop working on their own. The “kept until” date on the receipt is read back from Arkiv, not from our database.
The /verify page fingerprints the PDF in the viewer’s own browser and queries Arkiv’s public RPC directly. Every query is filtered to records created by our writer wallet, so a forged record can never turn a tampered document green. A bank clerk can verify a document without trusting, or even reaching, our server. Notable hacks: No-wallet signing: a key generated and kept on the phone signs the finished PDF with EIP-712. On Arkiv the signature is stored as the signer’s address plus the 65-byte signature, so anyone can re-check it in their browser.
Co-signing over a live share link: a witness or guarantor co-signs by adding their own signature record next to the owner’s, but only while the share-link entity is still alive.
Crypto-shredding deletion: each PDF is encrypted with its own AES-256-GCM key. “Delete” destroys that key first, then the encrypted file, then the Arkiv records.

projects.title: Pied Piper
projects.description: Private decentralised LLM inference utilizing low end devices.
projects.project_description: Any device can join the network, from a browser tab with no install, and lend its spare compute to run a large language model for the whole swarm. No single device holds the model: it is cut into blocks of consecutive layers, each device holds one block, and every question travels through one holder of each block, like a torrent for inference. Devices earn PIPER for the compute they provide and spend it to ask. PIPER trades against USDC in a Uniswap v4 pool, so the price of inference is set by a market. A gas sponsor pays every transaction, so a phone only ever signs and never needs ETH. The result is plug and play: open a link, and your phone is serving a 2-billion-parameter model and earning for it.
projects.how_its_made:
The network serves one LLM, divided into blocks. Each block is a run of consecutive transformer layers; the first block also holds the embedding and the last one the output layer.
The tracker is the coordinator. It serves the web app and the weights, gives each joining device a block, and the device downloads only that block's weights (cached in the browser, so a reload takes a second). The tracker monitors the swarm, picks a route for every question and relays the hidden state from each block to the next, over WebSocket. Phones never need to know the route: each one runs its block and hands the result back. Every device gets a wallet on its first visit, kept on that device. It is a Privy guest wallet that can be made permanent by signing in with email or phone, or, without Privy, a key kept in the browser with a "Back up its private key" button to import it into any other wallet app. Devices earn PIPER for the computation they provide and spend it to ask. PIPER can also be bought in the liquidity pool, and its price there describes the market for inference: demand for answers pushes it up, and supply of compute brings more PIPER into circulation. Kernels for matrix multiplication run in WebAssembly SIMD, with int8 weights: about 4× faster per token than plain JavaScript and 12× faster on the prompt.

projects.title: Truce
projects.description: Invoices a buyer can verify before paying, then pay gaslessly in USDT on Whitechain.
projects.project_description: Truce stops invoice payment-redirection fraud: an attacker copies a real invoice, swaps in their own wallet, and the buyer pays the wrong address. A merchant publishes one small file on its own domain, /.well-known/truce.json, listing the wallet that signs its invoices and the wallet that gets paid. Every invoice is an EIP-712 signature over the amount, payout wallet, due date and domain. Before paying, the buyer's page runs ten checks against that domain file and shows PASS or FAIL. Change the amount, swap the payout wallet or point to a lookalike domain, and the invoice fails and Pay is disabled. The browser also remembers a merchant's wallets and warns if they change since the last payment. On PASS the buyer signs one EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization for USDT: no approval and no gas. A relayer submits it and pays the WBT fee. Our InvoiceSettler contract verifies the merchant's signature again on chain, pays only the signed payout wallet, and settles each invoice once. A swapped payout reverts even if someone bypasses the app. Merchants get a dashboard (create, status, CSV export), a 10-line SDK for their own app, optional pay-on-due-date with a pre-due balance check, and capped refunds. Live on Whitechain Sepolia testnet with test USDT. Example merchants are fictional. A signed authorization is a commitment, not locked funds.
projects.how_its_made: Contract: InvoiceSettler, written from scratch in Solidity with Foundry (49 tests), deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) at 0xCbe41B98D2333a1BD92d51Fbb6FE668c5170ff9d. It recomputes the EIP-712 invoice hash, checks the merchant signature, then calls USDT's receiveWithAuthorization with itself as the recipient (the token requires msg.sender == to) and forwards the funds to the signed payout wallet only. A settled-once map blocks replays; refunds are capped at the amount paid. Whitechain specifics: we reconstructed the track USDT's EIP-712 domain ("Tether USD", version "1", chain 1874, the proxy address) and matched it against the on-chain DOMAIN_SEPARATOR before writing any code, then ran a live gate test: redeem, replay rejection, wrong-payee rejection, time-window rejection and a signed cancel. 1-second blocks make settlement feel instant. Gas is paid in WBT by our relayer, so buyers need only USDT. Real settlement: tx 0x837bdd3c07787486124245c2adb5d49c446f9243d292252c309ea82d1294fc22 (settle, block 12404546). Shared TypeScript library (invoice-lib, 74 tests) for signing and the ten verification checks, used by both the browser and the server. Server: Node/Fastify REST API, viem relayer with simulation before sending, a daily gas budget, an RPC fallback, a due-date scheduler, and an SSRF-guarded fetch of the merchant's domain file (205 tests). Frontend: Vite + React + TypeScript, EIP-6963 wallet discovery, signing through MetaMask (106 tests). SDK: createInvoice() for merchant apps, with an example app. Hacky bits: a payment link can carry the whole signed invoice in its URL fragment, so the verify page works without our server storing anything. The Soul (WhiteBIT KYC) badge is mocked and labelled as such, because the registry isn't readable on testnet yet.

On PASS the buyer signs one EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization for USDT: no approval and no gas. A relayer submits it and pays the WBT fee. Our InvoiceSettler contract verifies the merchant's signature again on chain, pays only the signed payout wallet, and settles each invoice once. A swapped payout reverts even if someone bypasses the app.

Merchants get a dashboard (create, status, CSV export), a 10-line SDK for their own app, optional pay-on-due-date with a pre-due balance check, and capped refunds.

Live on Whitechain Sepolia testnet with test USDT. Example merchants are fictional. A signed authorization is a commitment, not locked funds.

Contract: InvoiceSettler, written from scratch in Solidity with Foundry (49 tests), deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) at 0xCbe41B98D2333a1BD92d51Fbb6FE668c5170ff9d. It recomputes the EIP-712 invoice hash, checks the merchant signature, then calls USDT's receiveWithAuthorization with itself as the recipient (the token requires msg.sender == to) and forwards the funds to the signed payout wallet only. A settled-once map blocks replays; refunds are capped at the amount paid.

Whitechain specifics: we reconstructed the track USDT's EIP-712 domain ("Tether USD", version "1", chain 1874, the proxy address) and matched it against the on-chain DOMAIN_SEPARATOR before writing any code, then ran a live gate test: redeem, replay rejection, wrong-payee rejection, time-window rejection and a signed cancel. 1-second blocks make settlement feel instant. projects.title: sayLess
projects.description: The wallet your AI agent can spend from: hard budget, World ID owner, public receipts.
projects.project_description:
Agents increasingly need to buy things to finish a task: data, tools, compute, APIs. Today there’s no safe way to let them. Hand over a card or private keys and you risk unbounded loss. Approve every purchase by hand and you lose the point of an agent. Pre-pay one vendor and the agent is locked to a single seller, so it can’t shop around per task. sayLess is the wallet your AI agent can spend from, with four guarantees:
• A real person owns the agent. Creating an agent needs a World ID check, so there’s exactly one human per agent.
• Nothing is bought without the owner. The agent drafts a plan, and the owner approves that exact plan.
• Spending is bounded. Every task has a hard budget that can never exceed the wallet balance.
• Every cent is accountable. Receipts are public on Arkiv, and the agent’s spending rules live on ENS, where the agent itself can’t edit them. In a full-stack testnet run with the real World App, the agent planned $9.61 across five services against a $20 budget and settled them after a single World ID approval. Testnet only, no custody of real funds.
projects.how_its_made: sayLess is a TypeScript monorepo: a Hono agent runtime plus a mobile-first React PWA (the wallet). The flow: the agent discovers services, ranks them with real inference on 0G Compute (paid from a ledger it funded), and drafts a plan under the task budget. The owner approves that plan with a World ID session proof bound to the exact plan, single-use and verified server-side, never in the browser. The plan is parked as an Arkiv entity with a 15-minute approval window, after which it can no longer be approved. Approved purchases then settle per call across the rails: x402 in USDC on Hedera, official USDT on Whitechain through our verified X402Receiver, Circle Gateway nanopayments in USDC on Arc, and a Uniswap v3 swap-to-pay on Sepolia when a rail needs a token the agent lacks. Every decision (paid, skipped, declined) is written to Arkiv as an entity owned by the agent’s wallet, so no one can inject fake receipts. The Receipts screen reads them back live. Each agent is a soulbound ENSv2 subname (name.dotslashlab.eth) whose resolver publishes its budget, threshold, and live spend. Enhanced Access Control lets the agent key write only its spend record, so it can’t raise its own budget. Spend decisions are also mirrored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as a tamper-evident audit log, and recurring charges use Hedera Scheduled Transactions. Partner tech, one job each: World ID (human owner + plan approval), Arkiv (public agent-owned receipts), ENSv2 (immutable rules + identity), Hedera (x402 USDC, HCS audit, scheduled payments), Whitechain (USDT business rail), Arc / Circle Gateway (pay-per-use discovery), Uniswap v3 (swap-to-pay), 0G Compute (the agent’s own reasoning).

projects.title: pinesign
projects.description: Prove you sent something and the other party downloaded it.
projects.project_description: Pinesign proves a file was delivered. Alice invites Bob with a signed entry on Arkiv. Bob replies to one email; his provider's signature (DKIM) proves it's him. One EIP-8141 transaction checks that signature on-chain and releases the file key. Bob downloads the encrypted file from Swarm and opens it. No transaction, no key. v0.1 (ETHRome) used Google sign-in, Circle and our own server. Now: passkeys, no vendors, and delivery is enforced by a transaction, not by us.
projects.how_its_made: Passkeys derive all keys in the browser. Invites and Bob-signed accepts live on Arkiv. Files are encrypted on-device and stored on Swarm. Bob's reply reaches verify@pinesign.xyz; an EIP-8141 transaction checks its DKIM signature on-chain (~56k gas), a paymaster pays gas, and the key is released. The transaction needs no wallet signature. Reads go through Anon-RPC.

projects.title: Guard-Rail-Pay
projects.description: GuardRail Pay secures x402 payments through verified merchants and controlled payout rotation.
projects.project_description:
GuardRail Pay is a security layer for autonomous AI-agent payments that prevents recipient substitution and unauthorized payout changes.
When an AI agent receives an HTTP 402 payment request, GuardRail Pay's buyer-side PayeeGuard independently verifies the requested recipient ( payTo ) against the merchant's trusted ENSv2 payment profile. It validates the payment origin, recipient address, network, asset, amount limits, profile version and payout rotation status before the buyer's signer is invoked. The guard produces deterministic PASS, HOLD, BLOCK or UNVERIFIABLE verdicts, failing closed whenever verification cannot be completed.
Merchants can propose payout changes through a controlled rotation process involving authorization, public announcement, a timelock and human approval using World ID Agent Pass. ENSv2 provides the merchant's payment identity and access-control layer, while Hedera supports autonomous payment execution and settlement verification.
GuardRail Pay also uses Arkiv as a decentralized shared risk-intelligence layer. Merchants can publish suspicious wallet signals and other participating systems can query this information before authorizing payments. This enables cross-merchant threat awareness rather than relying exclusively on isolated merchant databases.
By combining pre-signing payment verification, merchant-authorized payout identities, controlled rotation and shared risk intelligence, GuardRail Pay makes autonomous agent payments more resistant to recipient manipulation.
projects.how_its_made: GuardRail Pay is built using TypeScript, Solidity, ENSv2, Hedera and Arkiv, with three major integration layers. ENSv2 — Merchant payment identity: Merchants publish payment profiles containing their service endpoint, supported network, asset, active payout address, amount limits, profile version and rotation status. ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control separates permissions: the treasury role can propose payout changes, while the RotationController controls updates to the active payout address. Hedera — Payment execution and verification: Our buyer-side PayeeGuard intercepts payment requirements before signing. It validates the requested recipient, asset, network, amount and merchant authorization against the trusted payment profile. Legitimate payments are executed through the Hedera transaction flow, and the backend independently reconciles settlement using Hedera Mirror Node data. Transaction evidence can be inspected through HashScan. Arkiv — Decentralized shared risk intelligence: We implemented named Arkiv schemas for RiskSignal and WalletRiskState. When a suspicious wallet is detected, an authorized publisher writes a risk signal to Arkiv. Other participating systems can query the trusted risk state before signing and block payments involving flagged wallets. We also implemented deterministic idempotency handling and a dashboard for inspecting published risk records. World ID Agent Pass — Human authorization: Sensitive payout rotations require authenticated human-operator approval. This prevents an autonomous agent or unauthorized party from silently changing a merchant's payout destination. The key architectural decision is placing deterministic verification immediately before signing. A tampered recipient, untrusted merchant, stale payment offer or unverifiable trust state must never reach the signer. Our T1–T11 test matrix includes recipient-substitution attacks, payout rotation, authorization failures, RPC failures and replay attempts.
