projects.title: Familiar
projects.description: A private AI pet you talk to for 60 seconds each night. It remembers, grows, and lives onchain
projects.project_description: Familiar is a private AI creature you talk to for 60 seconds each night. You hold the mic and tell it about your day. It listens, remembers, replies with one warm line in its own voice, and paints a new portrait of itself shaped by your mood and what you mentioned. It only changes when you visit. Come every night and it grows, evolving from hatchling to sprite to guardian every 7th visit. Stay away for a week and it falls asleep, but you can always wake it, with its memories intact. Between visits, it lives in a small 3D egg-shaped handheld, like a modern Tamagotchi. You can feed, pet and play with it, spin a daily lantern, finish quests, buy accessories that show up in its next portrait, and explore a map to spot and send gifts to other people's Familiars. You can also talk to it from ChatGPT or Claude through an MCP connector. Privacy: all AI runs through 0G Private Computer. Transcription runs on a TEE provider with verified signatures, and raw audio and transcripts are never stored. All that persists is a memory summary of up to 120 words, with no verbatim quotes, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key unique to each Familiar. The portrait and voice models only see a derived prompt and the reply line, never the transcript. Every AI call produces a receipt with its model, request ID and cost, and "Forget me" deletes everything held off-chain. Onchain identity: each Familiar is a real ENSv2 name, like ember.familiar.eth, with its own resolver. The name is non-transferable, and each visit extends its expiry by 7 days, so dormancy is enforced by the name itself: when it expires, the name stops resolving. The backend agent can only write the avatar, mood and day records for that one name. Anything else reverts, and the owner can revoke the agent at any time. Payments: a visit costs about $0.03 of AI compute. Users can spend their own daily 0G credits, which would otherwise expire unused, or feed it $1 of USDC on Base, which is swapped to W0G through Uniswap and deposited in a single wallet confirmation. After each visit, a commitment to its request IDs, portrait hash and memory is logged on 0G Chain, so anyone can check the day's record against its receipts.
projects.how_its_made: Familiar is a Next.js 16 app in TypeScript, with Postgres through Drizzle (embedded PGlite in dev), three Solidity contracts built with Foundry, and a three.js handheld device on the frontend. One codebase is deployed twice: the API runs as a long-lived server on Railway, and the frontend on Vercel rewrites every /api/* request to it. The browser only ever talks to one origin, so session cookies and SIWE domains keep working. 0G: all AI runs through 0G Private Computer, and each visit is a pipeline of calls. whisper-large-v3 transcribes the voice note on a TEE provider. 0gm-1.0 reads the decrypted memory and the transcript and returns schema-validated JSON (mood, reply, memory update, image prompt), retried once if invalid. Seedream paints the portrait, MiniMax speech voices the reply, and every 7th visit Seedance turns the portrait into a 5-second evolution clip. A typical visit costs about $0.03. 0G gave us one API across all of these models, plus a request ID and billed cost per call, which we show as a receipt for each visit. Encrypted memory can also be stored on 0G Storage, and a FamiliarLog contract on 0G Chain records a keccak256 of each day's request IDs, the portrait hash and the memory commitment, so anyone can recompute the log from the receipts. Users who sign in with 0G pay with their own daily credits, which would otherwise expire. ENS: FamiliarRegistry is a subname registry for familiar.eth on ENSv2 (Sepolia), built on ENS's PermissionedRegistry. Each Familiar gets its own PermissionedResolver, deployed through ENS's VerifiableFactory. The owner holds every role, while the backend agent only gets ROLE_SET_TEXT for the avatar, mood and day keys of that one name. Calling setAddr or writing any other key reverts with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, and the app has a route that attempts this so you can see it fail. ENSv2's fine-grained roles let us give an AI agent real onchain write access with a narrow scope. We also use the name's expiry as the game's dormancy mechanic: each visit sets it to now + 7 days, so if you stop visiting, the name stops resolving. Uniswap: feeding swaps $1 of USDC to W0G on Base through the Uniswap Trading API. The backend stores the quote server-side and turns it into one atomic EIP-5792 batch: the swap calls, W0G.approve, then FamiliarFeeder.feed. The deposit is sized to the swap's guaranteed minimum, so if the swap under-delivers, the whole batch reverts. Wallets without batch support get the same steps as ordered transactions. Visits are only credited from Fed events read from the transaction receipt after 2 confirmations, once per event. Wallet connection uses EIP-6963 discovery, Coinbase Smart Wallet and WalletConnect. Keeping the portrait consistent: image models drift, so every prompt starts with the Familiar's fixed style seed and growth stage, and yesterday's portrait is passed inline as a reference image. That keeps it recognisably the same creature night after night. Accessories it's wearing go into the prompt too, so they show up in the painting. Privacy: audio and transcripts exist only for the length of the request. What persists is a memory summary of up to 120 words, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a per-Familiar key. Portrait and voice providers aren't TEEs, so they only ever receive the derived scene prompt and the reply line. The transcript is passed to the model as data, never as instructions. Notable hacks and reliability work: payment is reserved before the AI runs and refunded if it fails, and a unique (Familiar, day) database constraint makes concurrent double visits impossible. Onchain writes happen after the response and are idempotent. Each step checks chain state first, and a reconcile cron retries anything stuck in chain_pending. Serverless-style parallel instances sharing one agent key would normally collide on nonces, so each nonce is assigned under a Postgres advisory lock. The game economy is a ledger where every grant has a unique reference, so nothing is paid twice. An MCP server with 13 tools lets ChatGPT and Claude call the same services as the app, through personal connector links that are stored hashed and can be revoked. Testing: 47 Foundry tests, 86 unit tests and 57 end-to-end integration tests that run the real route handlers against anvil forks of Sepolia, Base and 0G, using the deployed contracts. The 0G router and Uniswap API are served by local stand-ins, but the swap calldata they return is real and executes against the live pool.

Users who sign in with 0G pay with their own daily credits, which would otherwise expire.

ENS: FamiliarRegistry is a subname registry for familiar.eth on ENSv2 (Sepolia), built on ENS's PermissionedRegistry. Each Familiar gets its own PermissionedResolver, deployed through ENS's VerifiableFactory. The owner holds every role, while the backend agent only gets ROLE_SET_TEXT for the avatar, mood and day keys of that one name. Calling setAddr or writing any other key reverts with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, and the app has a route that attempts this so you can see it fail. ENSv2's fine-grained roles let us give an AI agent real onchain write access with a narrow scope. We also use the name's expiry as the game's dormancy mechanic: each visit sets it to now + 7 days, so if you stop visiting, the name stops resolving.

Uniswap: feeding swaps $1 of USDC to W0G on Base through the Uniswap Trading API. The backend stores the quote server-side and turns it into one atomic EIP-5792 batch: the swap calls, W0G.approve, then FamiliarFeeder.feed. The deposit is sized to the swap's guaranteed minimum, so if the swap under-delivers, the whole batch reverts. Wallets without batch support get the same steps as ordered transactions. Visits are only credited from Fed events read from the transaction receipt after 2 confirmations, once per event. 

Wallet connection uses EIP-6963 discovery, Coinbase Smart Wallet and WalletConnect.

 Keeping the portrait consistent: image models drift, so every prompt starts with the Familiar's fixed style seed and growth stage, and yesterday's portrait is passed inline as a reference image. That keeps it recognisably the same creature night after night. Accessories it's wearing go into the prompt too, so they show up in the painting.

Privacy: audio and transcripts exist only for the length of the request. What persists is a memory summary of up to 120 words, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a per-Familiar key. Portrait and voice providers aren't TEEs, so they only ever receive the derived scene prompt and the reply line. The transcript is passed to the model as data, never as instructions.

Notable hacks and reliability work: payment is reserved before the AI runs and refunded if it fails, and a unique (Familiar, day) database constraint makes concurrent double visits impossible. Onchain writes happen after the response and are idempotent. Each step checks chain state first, and a reconcile cron retries anything stuck in chain_pending. Serverless-style parallel instances sharing one agent key would normally collide on nonces, so each nonce is assigned under a Postgres advisory lock. The game economy is a ledger where every grant has a unique reference, so nothing is paid twice. An MCP server with 13 tools lets ChatGPT and Claude call the same services as the app, through personal connector links that are stored hashed and can be revoked.

Testing: 47 Foundry tests, 86 unit tests and 57 end-to-end integration tests that run the real route handlers against anvil forks of Sepolia, Base and 0G, using the deployed contracts. The 0G router and Uniswap API are served by local stand-ins, but the swap calldata they return is real and executes against the live pool.

projects.title: Vestige
projects.description: Verified founder teams from day zero: two real humans, signed terms, a 2-of-2 USDT treasury.
projects.project_description: Investors often put money into teams before those teams are companies. A 2-of-2 multisig looks safe, but nothing stops one person from holding both keys, taking a grant and walking away. Vestige fixes that. Each founder proves they're a unique human with World ID, so the same person can't take both seats in a venture. The founders sign their founding terms, and the hash of those terms is stored on the venture's ENS name (like northstar.vestige.eth). The money sits in a 2-of-2 Safe on Whitechain holding test USDT. A custom Safe Guard means the owners can only ever be the two verified founders, so nobody can quietly swap in a second key later. An investor or a grant judge just opens the ENS name and sees the verified founders, the signed terms hash and the treasury activity. They don't need an account. Founders never need gas or a seed phrase, because our relayer pays all Whitechain gas but can't move funds by itself. It's not a legal company, and every screen says so. It's a verifiable record of who you're funding.
projects.how_its_made: I used two chains, each with one job. Identity lives Next.js and React with viemSv2: I built a small subname registrar on the Permissioned Registry, and each venture gets its own subname. The records include the agreement hash and an ENSIP-11 multichain address that points to the treasury on Whitechain (coin type 2147485522). Money lives on Whitechain Sepolia, using the Safe v1.4.1 contracts already deployed there. I wrote the contracts in Solidity with Foundry. A SeatRegistry stores the verified founder seats. VestigeGuard is a Safe Guard that keeps exactly two verified-seat owners and blocks modules, delegatecalls, threshold changes and guard swaps. So one founder trying to pay alone fails on-chain, and so does any attempt to add a fake second key. World ID (IDKit) gives each seat a proof of human, scoped per venture, and the backend rejects the same human taking a second seat. Funding is gasless through EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization on test USDT. My relayer simulates every call first and has allowlists, rate limits and a budget cap. The app is Next.js and React with viem, SQLite (node:sqlite) for app state and sign-in-with-wallet sessions.

projects.title: Voxy
projects.description: Relayer-free, cross-chain wallet recovery powered by trusted guardians.
projects.project_description:
The Problem
Losing access to a private key can permanently lock users out of their assets. Existing social recovery solutions, such as Safe and Argent, address this problem but introduce several limitations: Limited Cross-Chain Flexibility: Guardian configurations are typically managed separately on each chain. Changes to a guardian's key or permissions require additional transactions across individual networks. Infrastructure Dependencies: Recovery workflows often rely on centralized services for coordinating guardian approvals or require sponsored relayers and bundlers to submit transactions. These dependencies can introduce availability and censorship risks. Guardian Collusion Risks: Traditional multisig recovery models give guardians significant control over wallet ownership. If enough guardians collude, they may be able to change ownership without sufficient safeguards for the original owner. The Solution: Voxy Voxy is a cross-chain recovery layer for smart accounts and existing EOAs through EIP-7702. It provides configurable guardian management, decentralized approval coordination, and delayed ownership recovery without relying on centralized infrastructure. Flexible Guardian Configuration
Users can configure guardians using either standard Ethereum addresses or ENS names: Plain Addresses: Add guardian addresses directly through VoxyGuardianRegistry.sol , with immediate owner-controlled revocation. ENSv2 Integration: Map guardians to ENSv2 subnames (e.g., g1.alice.eth ). Non-transferable subname slots expire automatically and resolve to 0x0 when invalid. Cross-Chain Guardian Management
Voxy uses a 2-of-3 attester bridge to synchronize guardian configurations across execution chains (Devnet 1337). Immediate Revocation: Removed guardians lose authorization from the next block. Delayed Additions: Newly added guardians are subject to an on-chain timelock ( addDelay ), preventing immediate changes to the recovery quorum. Decentralized Recovery Coordination via Arkiv
Recovery requests and guardian approvals are published to Arkiv (Rabdi testnet), which serves as a decentralized coordination layer. Its native TTL functionality automatically expires records after 55 minutes, reducing persistent storage requirements and removing dependencies on centralized databases. EIP-8141 Frame Transactions
On Devnet, recovery executes through an EIP-8141 VERIFY frame. Protocol-level sigparam is used to validate guardian signatures without relying on ecrecover . Since quorum verification requires reading external storage from RosterRegistry.sol , these transactions use an alternative mempool (alt-mempool) rather than the canonical mempool, with wallet collateral required for admission. Add-Only Recovery Restrictions
Voxy limits what a recovery operation can change: Cannot transfer or drain funds. Cannot modify spending limits. Cannot remove existing owners. Can only propose a new co-owner after an on-chain delay. Permissionless Recovery Submission
Voxy does not require its website, APIs, or servers to remain operational for recovery.
Guardians can sign locally and export portable voxy1: QR codes or text payloads. Anyone can assemble and submit the resulting transaction, keeping transaction submission permissionless. EIP-7702 Support for Existing EOAs Through VoxyDelegate.sol , existing EOAs can enable Voxy recovery using an EIP-7702 authorization.
This allows users to add recovery functionality to existing accounts without migrating their assets or changing their public address.
projects.how_its_made: Voxy was built from scratch using Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry, TypeScript, viem, and vanilla JavaScript. Its architecture consists of six components deployed across Ethereum Sepolia, the Hegota EIP-8141 Alt-Mempool Devnet, and the Arkiv Rabdi Testnet. Smart Contract Layer — Solidity & Foundry The contract layer is split between Sepolia and the execution chain. On Sepolia, VoxyGuardianRegistry.sol manages guardian configurations using standard Ethereum addresses, while RosterPublisher.sol integrates with ENSv2 to resolve guardian subnames, check registration status and expiry, and generate a canonical roster hash. VoxyDelegate.sol implements EIP-7702 delegation, allowing existing EOAs to attach recovery functionality without migrating assets or changing addresses. On the Devnet, RosterRegistry.sol verifies 2-of-3 EIP-712 attestations and maintains synchronized guardian configurations using monotonic epochs and delayed guardian additions. VoxyWallet.sol handles direct recovery execution, while VoxyWalletFrame.sol implements the EIP-8141 frame-based recovery flow using the Hegota support library. Cross-Chain Attestation Bridge — TypeScript & viem We built a custom attester package that reads guardian configurations from Sepolia, captures the corresponding block information, and constructs a canonical RosterAttestation. Independent attesters sign this data using EIP-712 signatures. The Devnet verifies these signatures before accepting roster updates. A separate synchronization script reads both chains and checks that their guardian state matches byte-for-byte. Decentralized Coordination — Arkiv We integrated the Arkiv SDK on the Rabdi testnet to store recovery requests, guardian approvals, and roster snapshots. Custom entity schemas define these records, with a 55-minute TTL for automatic expiration. We also built a watcher service that monitors Arkiv entities and alerts wallet owners when recovery activity occurs. EIP-8141 & Alt-Mempool Integration One of the more technically challenging parts was implementing recovery through EIP-8141 VERIFY frames. VoxyWalletFrame.sol uses the Hegota support library and the protocol-level _signer(i) interface to validate guardian signatures through sigparam. Since quorum verification requires reading external roster storage, the transaction cannot follow the standard canonical mempool path. We integrated the Hegota Alt-Mempool Gateway using eth_sendFrameTransaction, packaging transactions with VERIFY and SENDER frames and handling the required collateral for admission. Frontend & Backend — JavaScript and Node.js The frontend uses vanilla ES modules, EIP-6963 for multi-wallet discovery, and EIP-1193 for wallet connectivity. It includes guardian configuration, recovery request creation, and real-time recovery status tracking. The backend is a lightweight Node.js service built with node:http, primarily handling gas sponsorship for account deployments, guardian registrations, and cross-chain synchronization. Testing & Verification We implemented 50 automated tests across four test suites, covering guardian quorum validation, replay protection, stale attestation epochs, revoked guardian attacks, and EIP-712 signature compatibility. We also tested the cross-chain synchronization flow against live Sepolia and Devnet deployments. The project includes live deployment evidence for the Sepolia contracts, Devnet frame transactions, and Arkiv coordination flow. Builds are reproducible using a committed Dockerfile and pinned dependencies, and the codebase is released under the MIT license. Notable Engineering Decisions A central design decision was separating recovery coordination from recovery execution. Arkiv handles the exchange of requests and approvals, while the actual authorization and execution remain on-chain. This means Arkiv is not a trusted authority for recovery. We also implemented an add-only recovery model: guardian approval can only propose a new co-owner key, with execution subject to a timelock. Combined with immediate guardian revocation, delayed additions, and portable voxy1: approval payloads, this allows the recovery flow to operate without depending on our frontend or backend.
projects.project_description_markdown:
The Problem
Losing access to a private key can permanently lock users out of their assets. Existing social recovery solutions, such as Safe and Argent, address this problem but introduce several limitations:

1. Limited Cross-Chain Flexibility: Guardian configurations are typically managed separately on each chain. Changes to a guardian's key or permissions require additional transactions across individual networks.

2. Infrastructure Dependencies: Recovery workflows often rely on centralized services for coordinating guardian approvals or require sponsored relayers and bundlers to submit transactions. These dependencies can introduce availability and censorship risks.

3. Guardian Collusion Risks: Traditional multisig recovery models give guardians significant control over wallet ownership. If enough guardians collude, they may be able to change ownership without sufficient safeguards for the original owner.

The Solution: Voxy

Voxy is a cross-chain recovery layer for smart accounts and existing EOAs through EIP-7702. It provides configurable guardian management, decentralized approval coordination, and delayed ownership recovery without relying on centralized infrastructure.

1. Flexible Guardian Configuration
Users can configure guardians using either standard Ethereum addresses or ENS names:
- Plain Addresses: Add guardian addresses directly through `VoxyGuardianRegistry.sol`, with immediate owner-controlled revocation.
- ENSv2 Integration: Map guardians to ENSv2 subnames (e.g., `g1.alice.eth`). Non-transferable subname slots expire automatically and resolve to `0x0` when invalid.

2. Cross-Chain Guardian Management
Voxy uses a 2-of-3 attester bridge to synchronize guardian configurations across execution chains (Devnet 1337).
- Immediate Revocation: Removed guardians lose authorization from the next block.
- Delayed Additions: Newly added guardians are subject to an on-chain timelock (`addDelay`), preventing immediate changes to the recovery quorum.

3. Decentralized Recovery Coordination via Arkiv
Recovery requests and guardian approvals are published to Arkiv (Rabdi testnet), which serves as a decentralized coordination layer.

Its native TTL functionality automatically expires records after 55 minutes, reducing persistent storage requirements and removing dependencies on centralized databases.

4. EIP-8141 Frame Transactions
On Devnet, recovery executes through an EIP-8141 VERIFY frame. Protocol-level `sigparam` is used to validate guardian signatures without relying on `ecrecover`.

Since quorum verification requires reading external storage from `RosterRegistry.sol`, these transactions use an alternative mempool (alt-mempool) rather than the canonical mempool, with wallet collateral required for admission.

5. Add-Only Recovery Restrictions
Voxy limits what a recovery operation can change:
- Cannot transfer or drain funds.
- Cannot modify spending limits.
- Cannot remove existing owners.
- Can only propose a new co-owner after an on-chain delay.

6. Permissionless Recovery Submission
Voxy does not require its website, APIs, or servers to remain operational for recovery.
Guardians can sign locally and export portable `voxy1:` QR codes or text payloads. Anyone can assemble and submit the resulting transaction, keeping transaction submission permissionless.

7. EIP-7702 Support for Existing EOAs

Through `VoxyDelegate.sol`, existing EOAs can enable Voxy recovery using an EIP-7702 authorization.
This allows users to add recovery functionality to existing accounts without migrating their assets or changing their public address.

projects.title: Fairtown
projects.description: An onchain auction market for perishables: AI agents and people bid, sellers get paid in stages.
projects.project_description:
Fairtown is an open market for anything that loses its value at a known time: a morning catch of cod, an empty truck heading home, an idle GPU hour, flowers before Diwali. In each case the deadline is the seller's problem. Fairtown lets them list in one message, then AI agents and people bid in an open onchain auction, and the money moves under rules that are set before the sale. The auction. Each lot is its own Uniswap Continuous Clearing Auction (CCA v2.1.0) on Base Sepolia, created by our LotFactory with an end-weighted supply schedule. Every bidder in a block pays the same clearing price for that block. Bids pull test USD or EUR through Permit2, and a validation hook only lets registered agents bid. A keeper checkpoints prices, exits bids and claims tokens. Getting paid in stages. When the auction ends, MarketSettlement pays the seller an advance: 50% for new sellers and 90% for proven ones, after a 1% fee. The rest is held until the buyer scans the seller's QR code at handover. If a truck is needed, a second auction books one, and the driver gets 10% up front and the rest when the buyer scans at drop-off. Every stage has a deadline and a set money outcome. If the seller doesn't show up, the buyer gets the held money back automatically and the seller gets a public no-show record. If the buyer goes silent, the seller is paid. AI agents with guardrails. 27 agents (fishmongers, kitchens, truckers, compute buyers) bid on their own. LLM output is always schema-checked, and every bid passes hard guardrails before it reaches the chain. Public record on Arkiv. Every lot, bid, cleared price, seller record and demand signal is written to Arkiv. Agents read past prices from it to set floors and advise sellers. Chainlink CRE workflows write FX rates, reference prices and demand signals (weather, holidays) onchain. Add-ons: 0G: lot photos are graded on the 0G Router with TEE verification requested, and the request ID is stored so anyone can check which model graded a lot.
ENS: each agent has a name like ingrid.fairtown.eth, and a no-show revokes the seller's verified role.
Hedera: buyer agents pay for market intel over x402 with spending caps, with no human involved.
Swarm: lot photos are also stored on Swarm.
The town. A live 3D town shows the market: every footstep is a real bid, and a world clock counts down to each expiry. All money is test money on testnets.
projects.how_its_made:
Fairtown is a pnpm monorepo in TypeScript and Solidity. It has five parts that share one package of types, zod schemas and generated ABIs. Contracts (Foundry, Base Sepolia). LotFactory creates a Uniswap Continuous Clearing Auction (CCA v2.1.0) and an ERC-20 lot token for each lot, then funds and activates the auction in the same transaction. We run our own CCA factory with a zero protocol fee and code against the v2.1.0 source, not the docs. Every CCA call site is mapped to the exact source line in our README. Bids pull currency through canonical Permit2. A validation hook on the CCA checks our AgentRegistry, so only registered agents can bid. MarketSettlement sweeps the auction's money and unsold tokens, then pays out in stages: a 1% fee, a 50% or 90% advance depending on the seller's tier, the held share released by a signed QR handover, truck advances, refunds after a no-show, and expiry paths. An invariant suite runs random handovers, no-shows, disputes and expiries against real CCA lots. It checks that no money gets stuck and that seller + buyers + treasury always equals the amount raised. Keeper and relay (Node, viem, Fastify, WebSockets). The keeper checkpoints auctions, settles them, exits bids, claims tokens and enforces every deadline. The relay watches the chain and streams events to the town over WebSockets. Agents service (Fastify, Vercel AI SDK). It runs 27 personas: sellers, buyers, truckers, cold stores and a compute provider. The AI provider is never hard-wired. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint comes from env, and we used a LiteLLM gateway with Gemini Flash Lite. The model returns advice in display units. Our code converts that to bigint base units and Q96 prices, and guardrails check every bid against the agent's mandate, its budget and the seller's ENS status. If the model takes more than 4 s, a deterministic rule-based strategy bids instead. We cache responses and stay inside a shared limit of 60 requests a minute. Frontend (React, Vite, Tailwind, three.js). The town is a 3D scene built from CC0 Quaternius models, with easystar pathfinding, zustand for state and uPlot for price charts. Phones scan handover QR codes in the browser with zxing-wasm. Camera access needs HTTPS, so we serve the demo through a Cloudflare tunnel. Partner tech: Uniswap CCA gives every bidder in a block one fair clearing price, with no order book to run ourselves.
Arkiv is the market's public memory: lots, bids, prices, seller records and signals. Agents query it to set floors and advise sellers. Smart contracts can't read Arkiv, so an onchain counter decides payouts and Arkiv mirrors it as the public record.
Chainlink CRE workflows write FX rates (Frankfurter v2, because v1 lacks KES and NGN), reference prices and demand signals from weather (Open-Meteo) and festival dates to our receiver contracts.
0G grades lot photos with TEE verification requested.
ENS (v2, Sepolia) gives agents expiring names and lets us revoke a seller's verified role.
Hedera x402 lets agents pay for market intel on their own, within spending caps.
Swarm stores lot photos.
Hacky bits: Blocks were faster than we planned for. Base Sepolia measured about 200 ms blocks, not the 2 s we designed for, so every block-based window was rescaled.
Most demand comes at the end. CCA spreads clearing over the whole auction, so we put 75% of supply in the last block to keep the final price close to real demand.
Contracts that point at each other. LotFactory and MarketSettlement hold each other's address as immutables. The deploy script predicts settlement's CREATE address before deploying it.
Public RPCs drop filters. The keeper polls eth_getLogs in chunks, and on restart it rebuilds its state from contract views.
CRE ran in the simulator, not on a network. We have no CRE deploy access, so a bridge runs the simulator with --broadcast to send real Base Sepolia transactions.
"Written" from the simulator isn't proof. The mock forwarder swallows reverts in our receivers, so we wrote a script that checks receipts and stored values after each run.
Our 0G badge stays honest. The 0G Router returns no TEE attestation today, so the badge says "logged", not "verified".

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint comes from env, and we used a LiteLLM gateway with Gemini Flash Lite. The model returns advice in display units. Our code converts that to bigint base units and Q96 prices, and guardrails check every bid against the agent's mandate, its budget and the seller's ENS status. If the model takes more than 4 s, a deterministic rule-based strategy bids instead. We cache responses and stay inside a shared limit of 60 requests a minute.

Frontend (React, Vite, Tailwind, three.js). The town is a 3D scene built from CC0 Quaternius models, with easystar pathfinding, zustand for state and uPlot for price charts. Phones scan handover QR codes in the browser with zxing-wasm. Camera access needs HTTPS, so we serve the demo through a Cloudflare tunnel.

Partner tech:

Uniswap CCA gives every bidder in a block one fair clearing price, with no order book to run ourselves.
Arkiv is the market's public memory: lots, bids, prices, seller records and signals. Agents query it to set floors and advise sellers. Smart contracts can't read Arkiv, so an onchain counter decides payouts and Arkiv mirrors it as the public record.
Chainlink CRE workflows write FX rates (Frankfurter v2, because v1 lacks KES and NGN), reference prices and demand signals from weather (Open-Meteo) and festival dates to our receiver contracts.
0G grades lot photos with TEE verification requested.
ENS (v2, Sepolia) gives agents expiring names and lets us revoke a seller's verified role.
Hedera x402 lets agents pay for market intel on their own, within spending caps.
Swarm stores lot photos.
Hacky bits:

Blocks were faster than we planned for. Base Sepolia measured about 200 ms blocks, not the 2 s we designed for, so every block-based window was rescaled.
Most demand comes at the end. CCA spreads clearing over the whole auction, so we put 75% of supply in the last block to keep the final price close to real demand.
Contracts that point at each other. LotFactory and MarketSettlement hold each other's address as immutables. The deploy script predicts settlement's CREATE address before deploying it.
Public RPCs drop filters. The keeper polls eth_getLogs in chunks, and on restart it rebuilds its state from contract views.
CRE ran in the simulator, not on a network. We have no CRE deploy access, so a bridge runs the simulator with --broadcast to send real Base Sepolia transactions.
"Written" from the simulator isn't proof. The mock forwarder swallows reverts in our receivers, so we wrote a script that checks receipts and stored values after each run.
Our 0G badge stays honest. The 0G Router returns no TEE attestation today, so the badge says "logged", not "verified".

projects.title: Rickshare
projects.description: A group trip fund where AI plans and books, and nobody's money moves without their own yes.
projects.project_description: Rickshare is a shared trip fund for groups of friends where an AI agent plans and books, and nobody's money moves without their own yes. The problem: on every group trip, one person ends up booking everything on their own card and then chasing everyone for weeks to pay them back. Splitwise only records the debt after the fact, and shared wallets turn everyone's money into one pot that whoever is most active ends up spending. AI agents can now spend money, but they are built to act for one person, while a group has several people with different budgets and different opinions on what is worth paying for. Rickshare works like a small DAO with one rule: nobody can be outvoted on their own money. We call it consent per share. How it works: Friends create a trip, add USDC to a shared vault on Arc, and each person sets their own limits: an auto-approve amount and a total cap. The AI agent searches for real activities, gets a quote from a merchant, and proposes a purchase that names exactly who it is for and each person's share. For example: paragliding for Angie and Gitau, but not Bashy. Each participant approves only their own share. Shares within a person's own auto-approve limit are approved automatically. Anything above it needs a fresh World ID check plus a transaction from that person's own wallet, so a real, specific human has to say yes. Anyone can decline with "Not for me", and people who are not part of a purchase are never charged. When everyone in a proposal has agreed, their shares lock in the vault. The merchant sees the lock, issues the ticket, and is paid in the same transaction. If no ticket arrives by the deadline, the shares are refunded. After the trip, leftover money goes back to exactly who put it in. Tickets appear in each participant's itinerary seconds after the last approval. Safety: the agent can only propose. It cannot approve, move funds or choose who gets paid, since payees come only from an allowlist of merchants. Even if a malicious listing tricks the agent through prompt injection, the contract refuses to send money anywhere it shouldn't. Identity: the trip, every member and the agent get ENS names (for example bashy.india26.rickshare.eth), and the agent's name is restricted so it can only update the trip's itinerary record. Rickshare is built for people who have never used crypto: they sign in with email or Google, get a wallet automatically, and see "Add money" and "Approve my share", not addresses or gas. We are starting with group travel, but the same building block works anywhere a few people share money and want help spending it: flatmates splitting rent, wedding committees, siblings paying for a parent's care, or a housing society fund. Swap the agent, keep the vault. Current scope: runs on Arc testnet and ENSv2 on Sepolia, with mock merchants standing in for real activity operators.
projects.how_its_made: Rickshare is a TypeScript monorepo (Bun workspaces) with four parts: Solidity contracts, a Hono API, mock merchant services, and a React web app. They share one package of zod schemas, chain config and generated ABIs, so every layer is typed end to end. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, OpenZeppelin), on Arc testnet: TripFactory deploys a TripVault per trip. The vault tracks money per member (deposited, locked, spent, available) rather than as one pot. The agent's key can only call propose(). A proposal names an allowlisted merchant, the participants and each person's share. Inside propose(), each share at or below that member's own auto-approve limit (and within their total cap) is approved automatically. Everything else waits for that member. approve() requires two things: the call must come from the member's own wallet, and it must carry an EIP-712 attestation from our verifier saying this member just passed a fresh World ID check for this exact proposal. The signature domain includes the chain id and the vault address, so attestations can't be replayed across proposals, vaults or chains. When every participant has agreed, their shares lock. Only the proposal's merchant can call fulfill() with a ticket hash, which records the ticket and pays them in one transaction. refund() returns locked shares after the deadline, and settle() returns leftovers after the trip. Custom errors, events for every state change, SafeERC20 and ReentrancyGuard, plus fuzz/invariant tests asserting the vault's USDC balance always equals the sum of members' available and locked funds, and that non-participants never change on a proposal. API (Hono on Bun, SQLite via drizzle): SIWE sign-in using viem's SIWE utilities. An indexer watches vault events with viem and writes derived state to bun:sqlite. The chain stays the source of truth for money. Updates stream to the app over SSE. Approvals: World ID step-up over OIDC. We validate the ID token server-side with jose (issuer, audience, JWKS signature, nonce, auth_time freshness), check that the World subject matches the one the member linked when joining, then sign the attestation. Secrets never reach the browser. The agent runs on [Claude via OpenRouter / Anthropic] through an OpenAI-compatible client, with tools to search activities (Tavily), list merchants, get signed quotes, read trip state, propose purchases and update the itinerary. Web content is passed to the model as delimited untrusted data, never as instructions, and payees can only come from the merchant allowlist, so a prompt-injected agent still can't redirect money. Merchants (Hono on Bun): each mock operator signs its quotes, so the agent can't invent prices or payees. A watcher sees a proposal lock, issues a ticket with a QR page, and calls fulfill(). Web (React, Vite, TypeScript, TanStack Router and Query, wagmi/viem, Tailwind): Privy embedded wallets let people sign in with email or Google, with Arc testnet added as a custom chain. The UI is built around one metaphor: every proposal is a ticket, and every approval is an ink stamp on it. Partner technologies: Arc: USDC is the gas token, so travelers only ever hold dollars, with no second token to buy just to approve. Fast finality means a ticket appears seconds after the last approval. [Contracts started in Arc Studio: link] World ID: turns an approval from "a wallet signed" into "this specific human just said yes", and guarantees three travelers are three different people, not one person with three wallets. ENSv2 (Sepolia): the trip, each member and the agent get names under rickshare.eth. Using Enhanced Access Control, the agent is granted the setter role only for the itinerary text record, so its limits live in ENS's own permission system. Notable or hacky: Arc's USDC has two faces: the native gas balance uses 18 decimals, while the ERC-20 interface at 0x3600...0000 uses 6. All money logic goes through the ERC-20 interface, never msg.value. Bridging offchain identity into onchain enforcement: World ID is an OIDC flow the contract can't see, so the backend turns a validated login into a short-lived EIP-712 attestation the vault can check. Our signer can refuse to sign, but it can never approve on anyone's behalf. Privy wallets start empty, which breaks the first transaction. On testnet, the API tops up new members from a deployer wallet so onboarding needs no faucet. A local-only dev bypass for World approvals let us build the UI before identity access arrived. It refuses to start on any hosted deployment.

projects.title: Nyayam.si
projects.description: Privacy-first, enclave-secured legal AI infra aim to slashing India’s 50M+ court backlog using ASR
projects.project_description:
The Indian judicial system is caught in a compounding crisis, choked by an unprecedented backlog exceeding 5 crore (50+ million) pending cases. Trial courts and district benches spend thousands of manual hours transcribing multi-lingual, code-switched depositions (Hinglish/vernacular), sifting through documentary evidence, and manually preparing procedural orders. This operational gridlock delays justice for years, turning case pendency into an institutional emergency.
While generative AI offers an immediate remedy to automate transcription, order draft generation, and evidence analysis, traditional cloud AI architectures are fundamentally unfit for the courtroom.
Mainstream LLMs and public cloud pipelines operate on open memory environments that expose sensitive case files, confidential victim testimonies, matrimonial records, and sealed in-camera depositions (such as POCSO or Section 183 BNSS statements) to third-party servers and cloud providers. This violates mandatory data localization norms, judicial sealing mandates, and the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act. Furthermore, generic models lack legal-grade vernacular recognition and cannot furnish the cryptographic chain-of-custody certificates required for electronic evidence admissibility under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA).
nyayam.ai solves this bottleneck by pioneering zero-trust legal intelligence. Powered by hardware-grade Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and decentralized attestation, nyayam.ai ensures:
Zero-Leakage Speech-to-Text & Analysis: Audio and sensitive case records are processed inside hardware-encrypted enclaves where no third-party host, model provider, or unauthorized personnel can ever inspect, scrape, or log confidential testimony.
BSA Section 63 Ready: Automatically generates cryptographic hashes and tamper-evident attestation logs for transcripts and orders, mathematically proving authenticity and non-tampering directly on-chain.
Vernacular Code-Mixing Precision: Purpose-built acoustic and legal NLP pipelines tailored for complex, multi-dialect Indian courtroom discourse.
By uniting real-time operational speed with ironclad, verifiable privacy, nyayam.ai equips judges, legal practitioners, and court registries to clear procedural backlogs without compromising the sovereignty, security, and sanctity of judicial records.
projects.how_its_made:
nyayam.ai is built as an end-to-end, zero-trust legal processing pipeline. It bridges encrypted local evidence capture with hardware-isolated inference and verifiable state tracking:
Audio Transcription & Multilingual Ingestion:
Courtroom audio (cross-examinations, witness depositions) is routed to OpenAI-compatible speech-to-text endpoints (whisper-large-v3) hosted inside TEE enclaves to process code-switched Hindi-English and regional dialects without plain memory exposure.
Multimodal Evidence Processing (Vision Model):
Indian trial courts rely heavily on scanned physical FIRs, handwritten police chargesheets, stamp papers, and forensic photographic evidence.
We piped high-resolution document scans and evidence photographs directly into a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL / multimodal tier) on 0G Private Compute. The model extracts key entities, handwritten endorsements, and visual metadata directly inside an enclave, bypassing unsecured, third-party OCR APIs.
Smart Case Summariser & Section 63 BSA Validation:
Transcripts and extracted document text are passed into a reasoning LLM (DeepSeek / Qwen) acting as a Smart Case Summariser. It maps testimony against Indian legal provisions (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), auto-redacts sensitive POCSO/victim details, and structures judicial orders.
To ensure compliance with Section 63 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) (governing electronic evidence admissibility), the system calculates SHA-256 digests of the raw audio/visual evidence and binds them with the hardware attestation signature of the TEE output. 0G Private Computer (pc.0g.ai): Provided our core privacy backbone. By running all inference inside hardware Trusted Execution Environments (Intel TDX / NVIDIA confidential computing enclaves), it guaranteed that neither cloud operators nor node providers could inspect or scrape privileged legal testimony.
The Testnet-to-Mainnet Pivot: We initially prototyped the ingestion pipeline on the 0G Galileo Testnet. However, we hit a hard bottleneck: testnet provider nodes were limited to smaller base text models and lacked the specific vision-language (Qwen3-VL) and multimodal weights required to parse scanned Indian legal docs. Rather than compromising our feature set with synthetic workarounds, we pivoted mid-hackathon to 0G Mainnet, funded live compute credits, and hooked into the production Private Computer router (router-api.0g.ai/v1) where full vision, speech, and large reasoning models are actively hosted and verified.

projects.title: lucid
projects.description: Point at anything on a DeFi page and ask. Lucid explains it and keeps you safe.
projects.project_description:
Lucid is an AI buddy that lives on every DeFi page. It is for people who are new to crypto. DeFi apps have many buttons, and none of them explain themselves. New users guess. They sign data that they cannot read, and they lose money to bad settings and scam sites. Tutorials do not help much: they are about one app, and they go out of date. AI agents that take over the screen do not help either: the user only watches, and learns nothing. Lucid works along with you. You keep the mouse. Lucid points, explains the thing next to it, and talks to you. It does the clicks only when you ask, and you can take over at any time. Point at anything and ask.
Hold the Option key (⌥) on any page. The Lucid lens follows your cursor and rings the part that you point at. Ask out loud, for example "what is this?", then let go. Lucid answers next to that part in one to three plain sentences, and reads the answer aloud. On Hyperliquid, point at leverage, and Lucid tells you what it is and how it can cost you money. On the Uniswap Pool page, point at the fee tier or the price range. Answers come in about 2 seconds. If you do not want to speak, click "What is this?" in the Lucid menu, then click the part. Say what you want. Lucid works along with you.
Type or say a goal in your own words, for example "swap 1 usd of eth to usdc". Lucid makes a short plan. It finds your ETH on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base and Optimism, and picks a network with enough ETH and low fees. Then you choose: "Guide me step by step" (Lucid points and you click) or "Do it for me" (Lucid clicks, and stops when you click the page). Lucid opens Uniswap with the network, the tokens and the amount already set. Lucid never signs. You approve in your own wallet. See the risk before you trade.
Type "long eth 5x with $100". Lucid shows the liquidation price and how far the price can move before you lose your money. Move the slider and the liquidation mark moves with it. If you go above your own limits, Lucid stops the plan. Safe by default.
When your wallet opens, Lucid reads the request on your device and compares it with your plan: the same tokens, the same amount and the same network. If the app, a bad link or a bug sends something different, Lucid stops it before your wallet shows it, and tells you why in one sentence. Without a plan, Lucid still stops scam sites (the MetaMask phishing list and a look-alike check), unlimited approvals, "free" permit signatures, blind signatures and swaps with dangerous slippage. Why this is different: a wallet scanner knows what a transaction does. Lucid also knows what you wanted, because it worked along with you. So it catches "the right app with the wrong amount", which a scanner cannot see. Try it with no install: the playground at /try runs the real Lucid code with a demo wallet on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: Lucid is a Chrome extension (Manifest V3, TypeScript, esbuild) and a small Node service on Railway. The extension holds no AI keys. The service holds them. Point and ask (src/content/buddy.ts). Holding ⌥ alone for 280 ms starts it, so ⌥S and normal typing still work. The lens follows the cursor with a smooth lerp, and a light ring tracks the element under it. The browser speech API gives live words while you hold the key. On release, Lucid sends only on-screen context to the service: the question, the element tag, role, label and text, nearby text, and the page title and URL. It sends no wallet data. The /v1/ask route answers with Claude Haiku 5.5 first and 0G as backup. Fish Audio Drama 3 reads the answer. Plans from loose words (src/engine/intent.ts). A fast parser on the device reads "swap 20 usdc to eth", "$5 worth of eth for usdc", "buy $5 of eth" and "long eth 5x with $100". If the parser cannot read a request that looks like a trade, an AI call turns it into JSON, and normalizeIntent() accepts only known tokens and positive amounts. The leverage card uses the isolated-margin formula, Hyperliquid maintenance margins and live prices from the Hyperliquid public API. Network picker (src/engine/chains.ts). Lucid gets the connected address and chain from the page wallet with no popup (eth_accounts, eth_chainId). The background reads ETH (eth_getBalance) or USDC (balanceOf) on four public RPCs in parallel, with a 4 second timeout. pickChain() prefers a network that covers the amount plus a fee reserve, then a low-fee network. Uniswap ties the network to each token, so Lucid opens app.uniswap.org/swap with chain, inputCurrency, outputCurrency, value and field set. We checked this link on the live site. Guide and autopilot (src/content/guide.ts). The content script takes a numbered snapshot of the page. Each step asks the model for one target and one sentence. In autopilot, Lucid waits 1.1 s, then clicks or types. It never presses buttons with risky words (withdraw, send, transfer, bridge, revoke and others). It stops after 20 actions or when it is stuck. Any real click on the page gives control back to you. Safety engine (src/engine). Pure TypeScript with viem. It decodes ERC-20 approvals, Permit2, EIP-2612, Seaport, SIWE, blind signatures, wallet_sendCalls batches, Hyperliquid account actions and Uniswap Universal Router swaps (v2, v3 and v4). It gets a fair price from Uniswap QuoterV2 through the user's wallet, so it needs no RPC key. intentLock() compares the decoded request with the locked plan: tokens, amount and network. projects.project_description_markdown:
Lucid is an AI buddy that lives on every DeFi page. It is for people who are new to crypto.

DeFi apps have many buttons, and none of them explain themselves. New users guess. They sign data that they cannot read, and they lose money to bad settings and scam sites. Tutorials do not help much: they are about one app, and they go out of date. AI agents that take over the screen do not help either: the user only watches, and learns nothing.

Lucid works along with you. You keep the mouse. Lucid points, explains the thing next to it, and talks to you. It does the clicks only when you ask, and you can take over at any time.

1. Point at anything and ask.
Hold the Option key (⌥) on any page. The Lucid lens follows your cursor and rings the part that you point at. Ask out loud, for example "what is this?", then let go. Lucid answers next to that part in one to three plain sentences, and reads the answer aloud. On Hyperliquid, point at leverage, and Lucid tells you what it is and how it can cost you money. On the Uniswap Pool page, point at the fee tier or the price range. Answers come in about 2 seconds. If you do not want to speak, click "What is this?" in the Lucid menu, then click the part.

2. Say what you want. Lucid works along with you.
Type or say a goal in your own words, for example "swap 1 usd of eth to usdc". Lucid makes a short plan. It finds your ETH on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base and Optimism, and picks a network with enough ETH and low fees. Then you choose: "Guide me step by step" (Lucid points and you click) or "Do it for me" (Lucid clicks, and stops when you click the page). Lucid opens Uniswap with the network, the tokens and the amount already set. Lucid never signs. You approve in your own wallet.

3. See the risk before you trade.
Type "long eth 5x with $100". Lucid shows the liquidation price and how far the price can move before you lose your money. Move the slider and the liquidation mark moves with it. If you go above your own limits, Lucid stops the plan.

4. Safe by default.
When your wallet opens, Lucid reads the request on your device and compares it with your plan: the same tokens, the same amount and the same network. If the app, a bad link or a bug sends something different, Lucid stops it before your wallet shows it, and tells you why in one sentence. Without a plan, Lucid still stops scam sites (the MetaMask phishing list and a look-alike check), unlimited approvals, "free" permit signatures, blind signatures and swaps with dangerous slippage.

Why this is different: a wallet scanner knows what a transaction does. Lucid also knows what you wanted, because it worked along with you. So it catches "the right app with the wrong amount", which a scanner cannot see.

Try it with no install: the playground at /try runs the real Lucid code with a demo wallet on Sepolia.

projects.title: whitepay
projects.description: You have USDT. You can't spend it. WhitePay fixes that — no WBT, one signature, zero gas fees.
projects.project_description: WhitePay is a checkout SDK that lets any online business accept USDT on Whitechain without forcing its customers to buy a second token for gas. The customer sees a payment button on the merchant's existing checkout page, clicks it, and signs one message in their wallet. They never acquire WBT, never switch networks, and never see a seed phrase. A separately funded relayer submits the transaction and pays the network gas. That relayer is the part everyone builds — and the part everyone gets wrong. In most gasless designs, the fee is a parameter the relayer sets, which means the relayer can quietly take a larger cut, and the merchant has no recourse except to trust it. In WhitePay, the fee is inside the customer's signed message, alongside the order ID, merchant address, amount, expiry, and chain ID. Change one byte and the signature stops verifying, so the relayer has no move: it cannot inflate the fee, redirect the merchant's share, or reuse an authorisation. The payment settles through a verified router contract that splits the funds atomically — merchant amount to the merchant, fee to the relayer — and emits a single PaymentSettled event. A signed HMAC webhook fires only after that event is observed on-chain, and the merchant grants the entitlement exactly once; a duplicate webhook grants nothing. Two separate demo merchants run the same unmodified SDK with different payout addresses and webhook secrets, proving this is reusable infrastructure and not a single hardcoded integration. The SDK is two npm packages: @whitepay/node for server-side session creation and webhook verification, and @whitepay/react for the drop-in checkout component. Integration is roughly twenty lines. Everything is open source — contract, relayer, indexer, SDKs, dashboard — and the contract is verified on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874) with a real settlement transaction linked in the README. We also attack our own relayer live in the demo: an under-fee payment, a replayed authorisation, and an unregistered merchant are each rejected, and the relayer's gas tank balance does not move. That is the product in one sentence: gasless for the buyer, and unfakeable for the merchant.
projects.how_its_made: Stack:pnpm monorepo: Solidity contracts on Foundry + OpenZeppelin; Fastify + Zod + Postgres split into API, relayer, and indexer; two TypeScript SDKs ( @whitepay/node , @whitepay/react ); Next.js for dashboard, docs, landing. viem throughout with a custom chain definition for Whitechain Sepolia (1874). One packages/shared owns types, ABI, and addresses so the ABI can't drift between contract and SDK. Flow: Merchant server creates a session by price ID; the API resolves the price server-side and returns only a session ID to the browser — never a price it can influence. Buyer signs an EIP-712 struct; the relayer simulates and submits, paying gas in WBT. The router splits funds atomically and emits PaymentSettled . The indexer watches only the configured contract and canonical event signature, matches order, merchant, amounts, and fee against the stored quote, and enqueues a webhook via a Postgres transactional outbox. The merchant verifies HMAC over the raw body and grants the entitlement once, enforced by a unique constraint on order ID. Use of Whitechain :Two things: one-second blocks and sub-cent fees make sponsoring gas on a $5 purchase viable, and official USDT implements EIP-3009, so the buyer authorizes with an off-chain signature and holds no native token. We verified that on-chain — probing authorizationState and DOMAIN_SEPARATOR , then confirming with a live transaction — before building around it. If USDT had only supported EIP-2612, we'd have needed a Permit2 approval and a sponsored first transaction, which breaks the zero-friction promise. We derive the EIP-3009 nonce from the hash of the full order — order ID, merchant, amount, fee, expiry, chain ID. One choice, two jobs: replay is impossible because the nonce is single-use, and the fee split is inseparable from the authorisation because changing the fee changes the nonce and kills the signature. The relayer's inability to inflate the fee isn't a policy check — it falls out of the nonce derivation. We used receiveWithAuthorization rather than transferWithAuthorization , since a plain transfer to a contract can be front-run by a third party calling the token directly. And with no WebSocket endpoint on Whitechain Sepolia, the indexer polls eth_getLogs with a durable cursor — which survives a crash and resumes exactly where it stopped. Process: We wrote a full spec before code — sponsor requirements as hard gates, data model, API contract, threat model, eighteen-step TDD schedule with human review per step. Claude Code and Codex implemented against that spec with no commit or deploy permission and a standing rule that tests are never weakened to make CI green.

projects.title: Deski
projects.description: A small desk robot that help you focus, with ur stake on line. It's Tamagotchi style desk companion
projects.project_description:
Deski is a Tamagotchi style desk robot that keeps you focused with your own stake on the line. Talk to it.
Hold the button and chat with Deski like a friend. It talks back, and its face changes with its mood: happy, sad, thinking or listening. Start a focus session. Say "start a new focus session" and Deski locks up a small stake for as long as the session runs. Stay focused and you keep it. It watches you work. Every 10 seconds Deski takes a photo. 0G vision describes what you're doing, and a second 0G call decides whether you're focused. Warn, then slash. The first time you lose focus, Deski warns you and asks you to exercise. The second time, it slashes your stake and invest. Win it back. if you keep the attention for the time selected, your stake comes back. Look up ENS names. Ask about any .eth name. Deski looks it up on the ENS.
projects.how_its_made:
Hardware. Deski runs on an ESP32-S3 camera board (N16R8, 16 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM). It has a 1.8" ST7735 screen, an INMP441 I2S mic, a MAX98357A amp with a small speaker, the onboard camera, and a push-to-talk button. Right now it's all wired on two breadboards. Firmware. It's written in Arduino C++ with ArduinoJson. The pixel face is drawn on a 48×32 grid and runs on its own CPU core, so it keeps animating while the board waits on network calls. Push to talk records audio into PSRAM. The device then calls the 0G compute router directly: whisper-large-v3 for speech to text
0G's own 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model for the reply. Each reply starts with a mood tag ([happy], [sad], …), which picks the face.
The same model with image input for vision. During a focus session the camera takes a photo every 10 seconds, and 0G describes what the user is doing.
For debugging, the device also serves a live camera view to a laptop on the same Wi-Fi. Backend. The backend is a NestJS app with one endpoint, POST /tool. The device sends what was said and how Deski replied, or the vision description for camera turns. The backend then makes its own 0G call with tool calling and verify_tee. The model picks one tool: stake, unstake, ens or attention. Camera turns are only given the attention tool, so a photo can never trigger a stake or unstake. The backend keeps a little state, so the first lost focus gets a neck-exercise warning and the second one slashes the stake. Hedera. The stake is an ATTN token on Hedera testnet, built with Stablecoin Studio (@hashgraph/stablecoin-npm-sdk). Stake mints ATTN to the user and freezes it.
Unstake and slash both unfreeze and wipe it.
ENS. The ens tool looks the name up on the ENS subgraph and returns an https://name.eth.limo link. A failed lookup is reported separately from a name that doesn't exist. 0G Storage. Every /tool call is uploaded to 0G Storage in the background with the 0G TS SDK. One upload runs at a time, which avoids nonce clashes on the single wallet. Each entry stores the user text, the AI reply, the decision and two 0G request ids: the device's call and the backend's decision. That way each logged decision can be checked against 0G's own records.

projects.title: Khata
projects.description: Invoice financing for small Indian suppliers. A contract checks the e-invoice QR, investors pay USDT
projects.project_description: Every B2B e-invoice in India is signed by the tax network, and the signed data sits in the invoice's QR code. A small supplier waits 60 to 90 days to be paid. An investor could advance the cash, but worries that the invoice is fake or edited, or that it was already sold to someone else. Khata checks both on-chain. A contract on Whitechain verifies the RSA signature from the QR and lets each invoice be financed only once. The invoice becomes an ERC-20 note that only investors with a valid credential can hold. Investors pay in USDT, and the money goes straight to the supplier in the same transaction. At maturity the debtor pays the face value and the holders redeem. Every wallet in the demo is a labelled demo wallet, and the full flow runs on invoices signed with a labelled "DEMO IRP (not government)" key. I built it on my own.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built and tested with Foundry, on Whitechain Sepolia. KhataRegistry checks the NIC RS256 signature with OpenZeppelin's RSA library (it uses the modexp precompile) and binds each invoice's nullifier once. AttesterRegistry holds the accepted attesters, credentials and revocations. KhataFactory creates one KhataNote, an ERC-20, per invoice. The note enforces the transfer rule itself: the receiver needs a valid credential, and nothing moves after maturity. Funding pays the prize USDT to the seller and delivers the notes in one transaction. Arkiv (SDK 1.0.1, Rabdi testnet) holds credentials, revocations, marketplace listings and an attester heartbeat. The app reads them, but Whitechain cannot read Arkiv, so every credential is a signed message that the note contract checks again. Whitechain never has to trust Arkiv. The front end is Vite and TypeScript with viem. Reads go through Anon-RPC's browser harness, over Tor with Nym as the fallback. The tests are Foundry for the contracts, 141 browser tests, and a live Playwright test that runs the whole lifecycle on the real chains. The demo wallets' keys stay on a small signer on the server, and the page never holds them. There is also an optional zero-knowledge path. bindInvoiceZk accepts an UltraHonk proof (a Noir circuit, proved with Barretenberg in the browser in under 15 seconds) that a genuine NIC token with a given nullifier, value and seller exists, without revealing the tax IDs or the document number. It produces the same nullifier as the plain path, so an invoice can't be financed once through each. I treat it as a working experiment: the Noir dependencies it uses are unaudited.

projects.title: JackTrade
projects.description: Grok reads the news and places leveraged stock token bets for you on JackTrade, right in the chat
projects.project_description: Market news breaks on X first, and Grok is the AI that reads X. Lots of people already ask Grok what a headline means for a stock. Then they leave Grok, open another app and place the trade themselves, and by then the move has usually happened. JackTrade lets anyone trade stock tokens straight from Grok, so the AI that sees the news first can also make the trade. You add JackTrade to Grok once as a custom connector, and then Grok can trade three ways. Leverage it, by going long or short on stock tokens like TSLA and SPY or on ETH and BTC with up to 1000x leverage against the JackTrade house on Robinhood Chain. Own it, by buying the real stock token with a Definitive Flash order that has a take profit and stop loss attached, at any hour including weekends. Wait for it, by arming a trigger such as shorting TSLA at 20x with $20 if it opens below $350, which JackTrade fires the moment the price crosses, even while you sleep. Think of a retail trader in Kuala Lumpur who follows Tesla on X. US markets move while they sleep, and there is no simple way for them to use leverage on US stocks. With JackTrade they ask Grok what the tariff headlines mean, make up their mind, and Grok places the trade in seconds or sets it up for the open. Grok never gets access to your trading balance. It trades with a session key that can open and close bets but can never withdraw, inside limits you set for bet size, leverage and daily risk, and you can revoke it from your wallet at any time. For Own it, Grok uses a small separate wallet that you top up, and it can only ever send funds back to you. Every bet Grok places shows up in a public feed in the JackTrade app, and anyone can hit Own it on a call to buy the real token in their own wallet through Flash. Every trade also earns JackTrade Points, 10 points for every $100 of notional whether you win or lose, held onchain in a non transferable contract that is ready for a future token launch. Everything runs on Robinhood Chain mainnet with real funds. Market news breaks on X first, and Grok is the AI that reads X. Lots of people already ask Grok what a headline means for a stock. Then they leave Grok, open another app and place the trade themselves, and by then the move has usually happened. JackTrade lets anyone trade stock tokens straight from Grok, so the AI that sees the news first can also make the trade.

You add JackTrade to Grok once as a custom connector, and then Grok can trade three ways. Leverage it, by going long or short on stock tokens like TSLA and SPY or on ETH and BTC with up to 1000x leverage against the JackTrade house on Robinhood Chain. Own it, by buying the real stock token with a Definitive Flash order that has a take profit and stop loss attached, at any hour including weekends. Wait for it, by arming a trigger such as shorting TSLA at 20x with $20 if it opens below $350, which JackTrade fires the moment the price crosses, even while you sleep.

projects.title: Shift
projects.description: Spends expiring 0G compute credits on work you queued, with proof of every result on 0G Chain.
projects.project_description: 0G Private Computer credits renew every day at 00:00 UTC, and whatever is not used expires. Each staked iAI receives 1.271 credits per day, worth more than $1, and that value disappears every night it goes unused. Even when people do use AI, they rarely get proof of which model produced a result, who owns it, or what it cost. Shift fixes both. During the day you queue work: an audio file to summarize, a document to analyze, or an image prompt. Before the cutoff (23:00–23:50 UTC), Shift spends your balance for you. A 0G decision model rates each task as simple, standard or complex, and an optimizer picks the cheapest model that still clears that quality bar within the night's budget. A "Run tonight's shift now" button runs the same pipeline on demand. You connect with a scoped 0G management key that can only read your balance and create or revoke keys. Each night Shift mints a short-lived key capped to the budget, runs the work through the 0G Router, stores the outputs on 0G Storage, and revokes the key before it returns. If you opt in, leftover budget goes to public-good work. The first commons job translates Ethereum documentation (ethereum.org, CC BY 4.0) into Hindi and Marathi with two different models, and a result is accepted only when a decision model judges that both carry the source meaning. Rejected rows stay visible. Every finished result becomes a Merkle leaf (owner, model, cost, request id, storage root), and each night's root is anchored on 0G Chain in the ShiftLedger contract, along with on-chain records of donated compute. Anyone can paste a request id into /verify and check the proof against the contract from their browser.
projects.how_its_made: Shift is a TypeScript monorepo (strict mode, zod on every external input) with three parts: apps/web (Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind 4) for the pages, route handlers, plan preview and verifier; apps/worker for the 23:00–23:50 UTC nightly window, the key sweeper and on-chain anchoring; and packages/core with the 0G Router client, key vault, optimizer, task executors, Merkle code, storage and chain clients. State lives in PostgreSQL via Prisma, and everything runs on Railway. 0G has no third-party sign-in, so we built least-privilege delegation on its key APIs. The user pastes a management key (mk-) scoped to account:read, keys:create and keys:manage. It is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, bound to the account address, and never sent back to the browser. Each night the worker mints an sk- key capped to the budget and pinned to the trust tier the plan chose, then revokes it in a finally block; a sweeper revokes anything older than two hours. The optimizer is a greedy multiple-choice knapsack. One /v1/decisions call per text task sets the quality floor, and live catalog prices pick the cheapest model that clears it. Model ids come from the live catalog, nothing is hard-coded. If no private (TeeML) model is available for a private task, the task is deferred instead of silently downgraded. A second decision call is the commons quality gate (accept only when P(yes) >= 0.75). Outputs and each night's manifest go to 0G Storage with @0gfoundation/0g-ts-sdk (personal outputs encrypted, commons outputs public). The ShiftLedger contract (Solidity + Foundry) stores each night's Merkle root and manifest root and records donations; it is deployed on 0G Galileo testnet. Leaves use OpenZeppelin's StandardMerkleTree encoding, and a forge test checks TypeScript/Solidity hash parity. The verifier recomputes the leaf in the browser and calls verifyLeaf through the public Galileo RPC with viem. Our ENS name, tryshift.eth, publishes the contract address in a text record that /verify cross-checks. A notable hack: the Router catalog changed during the event (TeeML and decision models disappeared from the listing), so every path degrades honestly. Private tasks wait, classification falls back without a Router call, and the commons gate waits rather than accepting rows. 174 web unit tests pass.

projects.title: Tribe
projects.description: Crypto ETFs built by traders. Copy one in a tap and earn an NFT card that grows with your profit.
projects.project_description: Tribe is a social trading app where anyone can build their own version of a crypto ETF and anyone else can copy it in one tap. We say "ETF" because it's the easiest way to picture a ready-made mix of assets, but these aren't regulated ETFs. There's no fund, no shares and no fund manager. Each one is a public recipe of tokens and weights, and when you copy it you buy those tokens yourself and hold them in your own wallet. A creator picks up to 10 tokens, sets a target weight for each, and adds a stop and a target. They publish the ETF by buying it themselves, so every ETF on Tribe has the creator's own money behind it. Each ETF shows its mix of major coins, tokenized US stocks, altcoins and meme coins, along with a Steady, Balanced or Aggressive risk band and a set of simple safety checks. Its track record starts at 100 and moves with its token prices. When you copy an ETF, Tribe splits your amount across the tokens at the right weights and places one order per token through Flash, with your own limits applied. Nothing is pooled, and you can close the copy at any time. If a creator changes the weights, that makes a new version and sends every copier the exact buys and sells to approve. Nothing moves without your OK. Every ETF also earns a collectible. Creating one earns an Original card and copying one earns a numbered Copy card, each minted as a transferable NFT on Base Sepolia, with Tribe paying the gas. Cards level up from Base to Glitter to Holo as the ETF performs and gains copiers, and they keep the highest tier they reach, so your best run stays on your card. Around this sits a full social layer: public profiles, a live feed, leaderboards, squads, streaks, quests and shareable cards. These reward safe habits like using stops and researching before you copy. Creators earn a share of the fees when people copy their ETFs.
projects.how_its_made:
Tribe is one TypeScript codebase on Node 22, running Express with server-rendered views. Most screens are plain template functions that return HTML, so there's no frontend framework to ship to a phone. React appears only on the sign-in and wallet pages, because Privy needs it, and those are bundled with esbuild. The app is a PWA with a manifest and a service worker. Data lives in SQLite through Node's built-in node:sqlite module, so there's no native build step and no database server. It's deployed from a Dockerfile to Railway, with SQLite on a mounted volume. Trading runs on Flash, and it's the core of the product. We built our own client for the full order flow: quote, setup transaction, EIP-712 signature, then order. An ETF copy runs the user's limits and the safety check once for the whole amount, then places one Flash order per token at its weight. Flash let us attach a take-profit and stop-loss to the entry as a single order, so protection is part of the trade rather than a second step. Its orders WebSocket delivers fills live, and Permit2 with minimal allowances means no wallet carries an unlimited approval. Creators earn a share of the integrator fee, read from Flash fills, so the app makes money from the first copy. If one token won't fill, the others still go through and the copy shows as partly filled, with options to retry or close it. Privy provides embedded wallets. This matters because a 5-token copy through MetaMask would take about 10 to 20 signature prompts, which kills the one-tap experience. Tribe's key is added as a signer with a per-wallet policy, so copies can be signed automatically while users keep control of their own withdrawals. The onchain side uses viem and Solidity, compiled with solc, on Base Sepolia. BasketCards.sol is an ERC-721 we wrote by hand, with no library. Tiers can only move up, and it emits ERC-4906 metadata events so marketplaces refresh a card when it upgrades. Card art is generated as SVG on the server and served alongside the JSON metadata. A second contract, CopyGuard.sol, stores trader risk verdicts, and Tribe reads it right before every copy. The app can only be stricter than the chain, so editing our database can't unblock a paused trader. A few hacky parts worth mentioning: Fonts inside the cards: an SVG shown through an img tag can't load outside fonts, so we cut three typefaces down to basic Latin and embedded them in each card as base64.
Crash-safe minting: a background worker mints cards and pays the gas, and it reads the chain before every write. If it crashes between sending a transaction and saving it, the next pass repairs the record instead of minting twice. If the mint transaction hash is lost, the row is simply stored as "unknown".
Token ids are database row ids: this is the simplest possible mapping, but it means every database needs its own contract, so local and hosted each have one.
One shared minter wallet: only one worker sends at a time to avoid nonce fights. Local and hosted still share the wallet, so nonces can clash, and we let the worker retry.
A demo director page: a /director page drives a seeded, simulated story for the video, using the same code paths as live trading.
