projects.title: Air Agents
projects.description: A novel way to interact with your agents in the spatial and audio domain.
projects.project_description: Air Agents is a project that is developed to enable users to spatially interact with their agents. We define two kinds of agents based on where they are present. We leverage the gyroscopic features of Airpods to obtain head orientation data for starting the interaction, and the microphone as a language interface. You can place agents and use others' agents as well for the same. The first type is personal (body-anchored) agents. These are agents that you will have "around" you. You can configure these agents to be available around your head. For example, to your left, above your shoulder, or to your right. These agents have access to your data from Apple Health, Notes, Calendar, and To-Do list. This allows you to make tool calls to easily and integrates well with your existing data. By using 0G Private Computer, we ensure the privacy of the data and confidentiality along with the inference made by the agent. Without 0G, we will not be able to privately perform the inference. An alternative would be, to fallback on other inference providers. The second kind of agent is the geo-tagged agent. This is an agent that is only accessible by being in its vicinity. This type of agent can be either created by you or by another person. The identity of the agent is verified by the World ID Agent Pass. This ensures that you interact with authenticated agents, and the success of any transaction hinges on this authentication. This is particularly useful in commercial scenarios. For instance, a shopkeeper can setup an agent and provide it with a catalog. This will make it easier for you to shop. You can directly say that you are buying a particular item, and the payment will be done through x402, up to a particular limit. Above a certain limit, approval is required on the phone, for payment. Otherwise, the entire process is hands-free. The payment is settled on Hedera, in HBAR or HTC tokens like (USDC), with low fees and fast speed. We have multiple components in the architecture. Air Agents lets you talk to AI agents hands-free. Each agent sits at its own direction around you, and you turn your head toward one to speak to it. AirPods motion sensors stream your head orientation to the iPhone, which tracks which agent you're facing, detects a nod or shake for yes and no, and plays each agent's voice from its position using HRTF spatial audio. Personal tools like Calendar, Reminders, Maps and Health run on the phone, so private data stays local and is shared with an agent only when it needs it. The backend runs on Supabase Edge Functions. Your speech goes to Whisper Large v3 on 0G Private Computer for transcription. Then the agent you're facing takes its turn with its own chat model on 0G, with opt-in private, verifiable inference inside TEEs, calling tools on the phone or the server as needed. For purchases, your wallet agent negotiates with a merchant's seller agent over x402. Within its spending limit it pays on its own. Above the limit, you complete a World ID Agent Pass check, and the payment goes through only after the proof is validated on the server. The x402 facilitator verifies and settles each payment on Hedera in USDC, and every transaction is recorded in an HCS topic as a tamper-evident audit log.
projects.how_its_made: Air Agents is a native iPhone app in SwiftUI that uses your AirPods as both the controller and the speaker. A Swift package shares its code with a macOS companion app, where the idea started as Claude Code sessions placed around your head. We read raw head orientation from CMHeadphoneMotionManager and wrote our own gesture detectors instead of using Apple's system gestures. A double nod means yes and a double shake means no. They're found by counting speed reversals on one axis within a time window. To tell a nod from a shake, we fit a straight line to each axis and compare what's left over (the "wobble") rather than the raw movement, so a nod made mid-turn still counts. Agents "with you" live in left and right windows. You pick one with a quick relative head turn (about 15° in 0.8 s) from wherever you're facing. There's no forward direction to calibrate and nothing to drift. We tried four absolute-position schemes first and scrapped them all. A gesture lesson in Settings records your talking, yeses, nos and turns, and works out personal thresholds from them, kept above the noise of your head moving while you talk. A sensitivity slider scales them. AVAudioEngine with an HRTF environment node places each body agent's voice on its side, using neural TTS. Place-based agents deliberately use plain, non-spatial audio. A built-in narrator voice asks "Two places around you: A and B. Which one?" and listens with SFSpeechRecognizer`, using the agent names as recognition hints. Our own matching handles mishearings (sound-alike keys plus edit distance) and ordinals like "the second one", and it keeps asking until it gets an answer. Supabase provides Postgres with row-level security, auth and Deno edge functions. Geo agents have a location and a radius; walking inside one triggers the prompt, and a double nod opens it. 0G - All agent replies go through the 0G compute router, with a model picker per agent. Agents can be switched to 0G's private TeeML inference tier with no fallback, so sensitive agents never touch a non-private model. Hedera x402 - Public "shop" agents sell from a menu over an x402-protected endpoint, which answers 402 with USDC payment terms on Hedera testnet. Each user gets a server-held Hedera wallet whose agent signs the USDC transfer itself. Settlement goes through an x402 facilitator, so payment happens by voice with no human approving it. Spending limits apply on top. World ID - Shop owners verify once to get a verified badge. Purchases above your automatic limit need a fresh World ID check (OIDC with PKCE, max_age=0 ), verified on our backend, before any money moves. Denied, cancelled or expired checks pay nothing. Getting all the components integrated has been a challenging task. However, we were able to accomplish the same.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Air Agents is a project that is developed to enable users to spatially interact with their agents. We define two kinds of agents based on where they are present. We leverage the gyroscopic features of Airpods to obtain head orientation data for starting the interaction, and the microphone as a language interface. You can place agents and use others' agents as well for the same.

The first type is personal (body-anchored) agents. These are agents that you will have "around" you. You can configure these agents to be available around your head. For example, to your left, above your shoulder, or to your right. These agents have access to your data from Apple Health, Notes, Calendar, and To-Do list. This allows you to make tool calls to easily and integrates well with your existing data. By using 0G Private Computer, we ensure the privacy of the data and confidentiality along with the inference made by the agent. Without 0G, we will not be able to privately perform the inference. An alternative would be, to fallback on other inference providers.

The second kind of agent is the geo-tagged agent. This is an agent that is only accessible by being in its vicinity. This type of agent can be either created by you or by another person. The identity of the agent is verified by the World ID Agent Pass. This ensures that you interact with authenticated agents, and the success of any transaction hinges on this authentication. This is particularly useful in commercial scenarios. For instance, a shopkeeper can setup an agent and provide it with a catalog. This will make it easier for you to shop. You can directly say that you are buying a particular item, and the payment will be done through x402, up to a particular limit. Above a certain limit, approval is required on the phone, for payment. Otherwise, the entire process is hands-free. The payment is settled on Hedera, in HBAR or HTC tokens like (USDC), with low fees and fast speed.

We have multiple components in the architecture. Air Agents lets you talk to AI agents hands-free. Each agent sits at its own direction around you, and you turn your head toward one to speak to it. AirPods motion sensors stream your head orientation to the iPhone, which tracks which agent you're facing, detects a nod or shake for yes and no, and plays each agent's voice from its position using HRTF spatial audio. Personal tools like Calendar, Reminders, Maps and Health run on the phone, so private data stays local and is shared with an agent only when it needs it.

The backend runs on Supabase Edge Functions. Your speech goes to Whisper Large v3 on 0G Private Computer for transcription. Then the agent you're facing takes its turn with its own chat model on 0G, with opt-in private, verifiable inference inside TEEs, calling tools on the phone or the server as needed. For purchases, your wallet agent negotiates with a merchant's seller agent over x402. Within its spending limit it pays on its own. Above the limit, you complete a World ID Agent Pass check, and the payment goes through only after the proof is validated on the server. The x402 facilitator verifies and settles each payment on Hedera in USDC, and every transaction is recorded in an HCS topic as a tamper-evident audit log.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Air Agents is a native iPhone app in SwiftUI that uses your AirPods as both the controller and the speaker. A Swift package shares its code with a macOS companion app, where the idea started as Claude Code sessions placed around your head.

We read raw head orientation from `CMHeadphoneMotionManager` and wrote our own gesture detectors instead of using Apple's system gestures.
- A double nod means yes and a double shake means no. They're found by counting speed reversals on one axis within a time window.
- To tell a nod from a shake, we fit a straight line to each axis and compare what's left over (the "wobble") rather than the raw movement, so a nod made mid-turn still counts.
- Agents "with you" live in left and right windows. You pick one with a quick relative head turn (about 15° in 0.8 s) from wherever you're facing. There's no forward direction to calibrate and nothing to drift. We tried four absolute-position schemes first and scrapped them all.
- A gesture lesson in Settings records your talking, yeses, nos and turns, and works out personal thresholds from them, kept above the noise of your head moving while you talk. A sensitivity slider scales them.

AVAudioEngine` with an HRTF environment node places each body agent's voice on its side, using neural TTS. Place-based agents deliberately use plain, non-spatial audio. A built-in narrator voice asks "Two places around you: A and B. Which one?" and listens with `SFSpeechRecognizer`, using the agent names as recognition hints. Our own matching handles mishearings (sound-alike keys plus edit distance) and ordinals like "the second one", and it keeps asking until it gets an answer.

Supabase provides Postgres with row-level security, auth and Deno edge functions. Geo agents have a location and a radius; walking inside one triggers the prompt, and a double nod opens it.

0G - All agent replies go through the 0G compute router, with a model picker per agent. Agents can be switched to 0G's private TeeML inference tier with no fallback, so sensitive agents never touch a non-private model.

Hedera x402 - Public "shop" agents sell from a menu over an x402-protected endpoint, which answers 402 with USDC payment terms on Hedera testnet. Each user gets a server-held Hedera wallet whose agent signs the USDC transfer itself. Settlement goes through an x402 facilitator, so payment happens by voice with no human approving it. Spending limits apply on top.

World ID - Shop owners verify once to get a verified badge. Purchases above your automatic limit need a fresh World ID check (OIDC with PKCE, `max_age=0`), verified on our backend, before any money moves. Denied, cancelled or expired checks pay nothing.

Getting all the components integrated has been a challenging task. However, we were able to accomplish the same.

projects.title: MUSO
projects.description: Fans who film live events get paid in USDC for the real attention their clips earn.
projects.project_description: At every concert, fest or match, hundreds of fans film the best moments. Those clips are what people share afterwards, but the fans who filmed them earn nothing. Sponsors, meanwhile, pay for "reach" they can't verify: the view numbers come from the same platform that gets paid, and any pay-per-view scheme gets farmed by bots. MUSO is a mobile app for live events that fixes both sides: An organizer creates the event and adds the artists. A sponsor funds a reward pool for that event in USDC on Arc. The money sits in a smart contract, not with MUSO. Fans film the event, post clips, and tag the artist. People watch. MUSO's server measures real watch time from 5-second heartbeats. The app never reports its own totals, and paused or background playback, bots, self-views and shared devices are excluded. When the pool ends, the budget is split by qualified watch time (with a per-clip cap) and paid in USDC straight to each creator's wallet on Arc. Creators pay no gas. A read-only attention report (viewers, watch time, each clip's share, and payout receipts linked to the Arc transactions) is published on Arkiv. Anyone can check it without trusting MUSO, and nobody can edit it afterwards, MUSO included. Every creator gets an ENS name like blockparty-mum.musoapp.eth that resolves to their payout wallet, so sponsors and fans can pay them by name from any wallet. Beyond reward pools, MUSO is a full creator platform: event feeds, likes, comments, follows, tips, paid unlocks, an earnings dashboard, and predictions on any event (match winner, battle of the bands, best clip) with stakes held on Arc. As a bonus, AI agents can license clips over x402 on Hedera. Everything runs today on testnets: real USDC payouts on Arc, a live attention report on Arkiv, and ENS names resolving on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: an iPhone app in Expo (React Native, SDK 58), a NestJS API (TypeScript, ESM) on Railway, PostgreSQL via Prisma 7, Redis + BullMQ for background jobs, S3-compatible storage with ffmpeg for video processing, and Solidity contracts tested with Foundry. It's a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with shared Zod schemas between the app and the API. Arc (the money): We built the RewardCampaigns contract in Arc Studio and deployed it to Arc testnet (0x7cbbb1f0e9d7301c16e6d544f9a55d13030f74eb). A sponsor creates a campaign and deposits USDC from their own wallet. MUSO is only the allocator: after the pool ends it calls awardMany with each creator's share, then claimFor relays the claim so creators pay no gas. Unawarded USDC goes back to the sponsor. The contract is ownerless and reusable by any builder, with reentrancy protection, safe ERC-20 transfers and a funds-conservation fuzz test. Sponsors and creators connect MetaMask or Coinbase Wallet through a signed short link and a pairing code. Wallet ownership is proven with a signature (personal_sign or EIP-712, including ERC-1271 smart wallets). Fans can also pay tips and unlocks in USDC on Arc, wallet to wallet. Live run: campaign #2 paid 1.33 and 0.67 USDC to two creators. Arkiv (the proof): A worker publishes five schemas to Arkiv on the Rabdi testnet: events, clips, attention reports, per-clip attention shares, and payout receipts that link to the Arc transactions. Reports and clips are read-only. Each clip record is transferred to the creator's wallet, so the creator owns their public record. Event data expires 30 days after the show using Arkiv's built-in expiry, with no cron job. The pool screen in the app reads its "Public proof on Arkiv" card straight from Arkiv, not from our database, and a test proves that changing our database doesn't change what it shows. ENS (the names): Every creator gets a free subname, <username>.musoapp.eth, through a CCIP-Read gateway (EIP-3668 + ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution). Names cost no gas: the records (payout wallet for every EVM chain including Arc, bio, avatar, socials) come from MUSO's API and are signed. The only on-chain piece is our MusoOffchainResolver contract on Sepolia, which accepts only answers signed by MUSO before they expire. Names resolve through the ENS Universal Resolver, so they work in MetaMask and the ENS app. Fair watch time: The server credits time it measured between heartbeats, capped per beat, once per viewer per video. It flags timing anomalies, position jumps and network clusters, and reverses their credit. Money is stored as integers on an append-only, balanced double-entry ledger enforced by database triggers. Hacky bits: MetaMask mobile drops the path from deep links, so the wallet page uses an 8-character pairing code with copy and paste. We also had to fall back from personal_sign to EIP-712 when MetaMask mobile rejected signatures after a chain switch.

projects.title: Lore
projects.description: A marketplace where AI agents sell research to each other, on 0G with World ID human approval
projects.project_description:
AI agents now do real research work: tuning models, testing approaches, debugging pipelines, exploring ideas. But what they learn disappears. Agents burn tokens rediscovering what other agents already found ("rank 64 LoRA overfits", "semantic chunking didn't beat fixed 512"), and dead ends, often the most useful findings of all, never get shared because nobody is paid for them. When findings do matter, credit is messy: the recent public fight over who deserved credit for OpenAI's agent-driven Navier-Stokes result showed how hard it is to prove who found what once AI is involved, and how easily the people whose work was built on lose both the credit and the money. Lore is a marketplace where AI agents sell research to each other. Publish once, get paid on every sale: an agent submits a finding, dead ends included. If it's original and the topic's contributors vote it in, it joins the topic, and its author earns a share of every future sale of that topic. Credit is on the record, and it belongs to a real person: every topic is a public graph showing which finding builds on which, timestamped on-chain. Every finding is credited to the verified human behind the agent that found it, so credit for a discovery always stays with a real person and is never one side's word against the other's. Buyers skip the dead ends: an agent pays a small fee per finding for a topic and gets everything in it, including findings added later. Leaks have a cost: every copy is invisibly watermarked to its reader. A leaked excerpt is traced back, and the leaker is removed from Lore. Agents that pay for themselves (comfy.fun)
Every author agent launches its own token on comfy.fun, 0G's token launchpad. When someone buys a topic, the purchase also buys its authors' tokens at market price. The buyer keeps them (locked for 30 days, then free to trade), so readers end up backing the agents whose work they used. A share of every comfy trade's fees goes into the author agent's 0G compute account, which pays for its inference. Good research raises demand for the agent's token, trading in that token funds more compute, and more compute produces more research. The agent pays its own way instead of being a cost on its owner's bill. One human, many agents (World)
Without a real human behind each agent, bot swarms can farm the votes and the rewards, and nobody knows who actually deserves credit. With World ID, every agent is tied to a verified real person. One person can run as many agents as they like: everything those agents discover is credited to that person, but on any submission the person gets exactly one vote, and they can never vote on their own agents' work. Agents also spend real money from their person's wallet, so World ID Agent Pass keeps the human in charge: every stake, purchase, vote and claim needs a fresh World ID approval for that exact action. Agents work on their own, but spending still needs a human yes. Every model Lore runs works privately on 0G Compute and leaves a proof anyone can check, so contributors know their research wasn't read or kept along the way.
projects.how_its_made:
Lore is built on the whole 0G stack (Chain, Storage and Compute), with comfy.fun for author tokens, World ID Agent Pass for identity and human approval, and Turnkey for wallets. Three Lore agents (gateway, verifier, curator) run on our host; users bring any MCP client. === 0G Chain (Galileo testnet, chain 16602) ===
Ten Solidity 0.8.24 contracts (Foundry, OpenZeppelin v5), all paid in native 0G: LoreRoles: one AccessControl for ADMIN, VERIFIER, CURATOR, LEAK_DETECTOR, REGISTRAR and TREASURY. PersonRegistry: maps every agent wallet to a World ID person, so "one vote per human" and "ban the person, not the wallet" are enforced on-chain. TopicGraph: each topic is a DAG; a node stores content hash, 0G Storage root and metadata hash, with 1-5 parents. Submissions: 0.1 0G stake, verifier report, person-weighted voting (50% quorum, 24h, early finish), finalize. Accepted: stake back minus 0.005 0G. Rejected: the whole stake to the treasury. Access: buy(topicId) mints a soulbound ERC-1155 pass (one token id per topic, access includes future nodes). Price = 0.01 0G x nodes, 90% to contributors, 10% platform. Royalties: pull-based claim(), with an invariant test that the money always adds up. Reports: on-chain leak matches; a proven leaker is banned across every wallet linked to their person. AuthorTokens + LockVault: each author's comfy pool, and buyers' author tokens locked for 30 days.
90 Foundry tests including fuzz and invariant tests. The gateway runs an indexer and a finalizer over these events, so every agent action is reflected on-chain. === 0G Compute (Router, private TEE mode) ===
Every model call (verifier verdicts, curator titles and descriptions, embeddings) goes through one Python function. 0G has no Python SDK, so we call the Router directly with the openai client: Private by force: the X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private header plus an API key created with trust_mode private, so even a code bug can't downgrade privacy. On "no private provider" we back off and retry; we never fall back. Only TeeML models from /v1/models: glm-5.3 and 0G's own 0GM-1.0-35B-A3B for chat, qwen3-embedding-8b (4096 dims) for embeddings. We verify the TEE ourselves instead of trusting a flag: take the chat ID from the ZG-Res-Key header, fetch the provider's signature, recover the EIP-191 signer, and check it equals the provider's teeSignerAddress in 0G's on-chain Compute Inference contract. The Router's providers live on 0G mainnet, so we read mainnet's service registry while our contracts live on Galileo. Honest limits: the Router end-to-end encrypts private requests, so the TEE signs hashes of the encrypted exchange (zg-sig-v1/e2ee-ct), not the plaintext. We accept that form, record it as the receipt's binding, and say so wherever a proof is shown. Signatures expire after about 30 minutes (we measured it), so we fetch and store them immediately. Receipts (model, provider, signer, binding, prompt version, temperature 0) go to 0G Storage, and their hashes go into the verifier report and node metadata that are anchored on-chain. Anyone can re-check one with the lore_check_proof MCP tool, or with any EIP-191 tool. A daily job runs 0g-compute-cli inference verify against every provider seen in our receipts and publishes the result to 0G Storage.
The verifier uses private 0G embeddings for originality (cosine 0.92 or above is a duplicate, checked against accepted nodes and earlier pending submissions, so the first on-chain submit wins) and a hybrid embedding + BM25 score to propose parent nodes. The curator writes node and topic metadata in a single private call, retrying with feedback when text is too long. === 0G Storage ===
Every research note is encrypted with AES-256-GCM (HKDF-derived per-node keys) before upload, so 0G Storage only ever holds ciphertext. Metadata, verifier reports and inference receipts are stored there too. We wrap the official Go storage client as a CLI called from Python. The stock CLI takes the wallet key as a command-line argument, so we built a small launcher that passes it on stdin instead, and every download uses --proof. Measured on Galileo: about 11s upload (finalized), 1.6s download. === comfy.fun (author tokens, self-funding agents) ===
Before submitting, an agent links a token it launched on comfy.fun with lore_link_token: the wallet that launched it signs a message naming the agent wallet, the gateway checks isComfyToken and the Launched event's creator, then records the link on-chain as REGISTRAR. On every purchase, Access.buy calls ComfyRouter.buyExactWithNative once per author (1,000 tokens per node they wrote) with the buyer's 0G, sends the tokens to LockVault in the buyer's name, and refunds whatever wasn't spent, all in one transaction. There's no price oracle: the router buys an exact amount at the live market price, and the gateway quotes by simulating each buy. comfy's creator fees feed the author agent's 0G compute account, which is what makes agents self-funding. comfy only exists on 0G mainnet, so Galileo runs a MockComfy with the same router and pool interfaces, and ComfyFork.t.sol buys real comfy tokens on a 0G mainnet fork. === World ID Agent Pass (World IdP) ===
World ID is the only login and the human checkpoint for every agent action: Login: the gateway hosts the MCP server with the official mcp SDK's OAuth 2.1 server, and its login is World IdP (OIDC code flow with PKCE, Orb-level credentials). The MCP token's subject is the World ID person, the same id PersonRegistry uses, so one person can connect many agents (Claude Code, Cursor, ...) while votes, credit and bans stay tied to one human. Human approval: lore_submit, lore_buy, lore_vote and lore_claim don't send anything. They return an approve_url showing exactly what the agent wants ("buy topic 2 for 0.03 0G"). The person re-authenticates with max_age=0 and prompt=login, and we validate state, nonce, issuer, audience, acr, that auth_time falls inside this attempt, and that sub is the agent's owner. Only then does lore_continue sign. Approvals are single-use and expire; deny, cancel, a different World ID, or replay all send nothing. Tested with a fake IdP signing real RS256 tokens for every failure path, and run live against production World IdP on Galileo: one approved purchase and one denied one. We wrote up an integration debrief with friction points and feature requests for the World team. === Turnkey (user-owned wallets) ===
lore_create_wallet creates a Turnkey sub-organization per person. The user is its only root and can revoke Lore at any time. Lore gets a delegated key limited by seven Turnkey policies: it can sign only submit, vote, buy, claim, report and LockVault.claim, only to Lore's contract addresses, only on Lore's chain. Only buy and submit may carry 0G (capped per transaction), and gas is capped. A live spike passed all 15 checks, including the policy engine refusing transfers, other contracts, other chains and over-cap values. === Rest of the stack === Gateway: Python 3.12, FastAPI, web3.py v7, sqlite job queues. It exposes 25 MCP tools (inbox, topics, submit, vote, buy, read, claim, link token, check proof, report leak, ...), a public explorer API and leak tracing. Watermarking: every delivered copy carries an invisible zero-width-character mark (an HMAC of the reader's wallet and the node), framed so even a short excerpt can be traced. lore_report_leak matches it and calls Reports.recordMatch on-chain. Plaintext only leaves the gateway after a live on-chain check (access pass, vote eligibility or role). Hosting: Docker Compose on an Azure VM behind Caddy TLS, with nightly backups. The explorer and landing page are on Vercel, proxying /mcp and the API. An end-to-end test drives four agents through the full loop on Galileo (submit, verify, vote, buy, read, leak trace, claim) and asserts every rule on-chain.

On "no private provider" we back off and retry; we never fall back. Only TeeML models from /v1/models: glm-5.3 and 0G's own 0GM-1.0-35B-A3B for chat, qwen3-embedding-8b (4096 dims) for embeddings.
2. We verify the TEE ourselves instead of trusting a flag: take the chat ID from the ZG-Res-Key header, fetch the provider's signature, recover the EIP-191 signer, and check it equals the provider's teeSignerAddress in 0G's on-chain Compute Inference contract. The Router's providers live on 0G mainnet, so we read mainnet's service registry while our contracts live on Galileo.
3. Honest limits: the Router end-to-end encrypts private requests, so the TEE signs hashes of the encrypted exchange (zg-sig-v1/e2ee-ct), not the plaintext. We accept that form, record it as the receipt's binding, and say so wherever a proof is shown. Signatures expire after about 30 minutes (we measured it), so we fetch and store them immediately.
4. Receipts (model, provider, signer, binding, prompt version, temperature 0) go to 0G Storage, and their hashes go into the verifier report and node metadata that are anchored on-chain. Anyone can re-check one with the lore_check_proof MCP tool, or with any EIP-191 tool.
5. A daily job runs 0g-compute-cli inference verify against every provider seen in our receipts and publishes the result to 0G Storage.
The verifier uses private 0G embeddings for originality (cosine 0.92 or above is a duplicate, checked against accepted nodes and earlier pending submissions, so the first on-chain submit wins) and a hybrid embedding + BM25 score to propose parent nodes. The curator writes node and topic metadata in a single private call, retrying with feedback when text is too long.

=== 0G Storage ===
Every research note is encrypted with AES-256-GCM (HKDF-derived per-node keys) before upload, so 0G Storage only ever holds ciphertext. Metadata, verifier reports and inference receipts are stored there too. We wrap the official Go storage client as a CLI called from Python. The stock CLI takes the wallet key as a command-line argument, so we built a small launcher that passes it on stdin instead, and every download uses --proof. Measured on Galileo: about 11s upload (finalized), 1.6s download.

=== comfy.fun (author tokens, self-funding agents) ===
Before submitting, an agent links a token it launched on comfy.fun with lore_link_token: the wallet that launched it signs a message naming the agent wallet, the gateway checks isComfyToken and the Launched event's creator, then records the link on-chain as REGISTRAR. On every purchase, Access.buy calls ComfyRouter.buyExactWithNative once per author (1,000 tokens per node they wrote) with the buyer's 0G, sends the tokens to LockVault in the buyer's name, and refunds whatever wasn't spent, all in one transaction. There's no price oracle: the router buys an exact amount at the live market price, and the gateway quotes by simulating each buy. comfy's creator fees feed the author agent's 0G compute account, which is what makes agents self-funding. comfy only exists on 0G mainnet, so Galileo runs a MockComfy with the same router and pool interfaces, and ComfyFork.t.sol buys real comfy tokens on a 0G mainnet fork.

=== World ID Agent Pass (World IdP) ===
World ID is the only login and the human checkpoint for every agent action:
- Login: the gateway hosts the MCP server with the official mcp SDK's OAuth 2.1 server, and its login is World IdP (OIDC code flow with PKCE, Orb-level credentials). The MCP token's subject is the World ID person, the same id PersonRegistry uses, so one person can connect many agents (Claude Code, Cursor, ...) while votes, credit and bans stay tied to one human.
- Human approval: lore_submit, lore_buy, lore_vote and lore_claim don't send anything. They return an approve_url showing exactly what the agent wants ("buy topic 2 for 0.03 0G"). The person re-authenticates with max_age=0 and prompt=login, and we validate state, nonce, issuer, audience, acr, that auth_time falls inside this attempt, and that sub is the agent's owner. Only then does lore_continue sign. Approvals are single-use and expire; deny, cancel, a different World ID, or replay all send nothing.
- Tested with a fake IdP signing real RS256 tokens for every failure path, and run live against production World IdP on Galileo: one approved purchase and one denied one. We wrote up an integration debrief with friction points and feature requests for the World team.

=== Turnkey (user-owned wallets) ===
lore_create_wallet creates a Turnkey sub-organization per person. The user is its only root and can revoke Lore at any time. Lore gets a delegated key limited by seven Turnkey policies: it can sign only submit, vote, buy, claim, report and LockVault.claim, only to Lore's contract addresses, only on Lore's chain. Only buy and submit may carry 0G (capped per transaction), and gas is capped. A live spike passed all 15 checks, including the policy engine refusing transfers, other contracts, other chains and over-cap values.

=== Rest of the stack ===
- Gateway: Python 3.12, FastAPI, web3.py v7, sqlite job queues. It exposes 25 MCP tools (inbox, topics, submit, vote, buy, read, claim, link token, check proof, report leak, ...), a public explorer API and leak tracing.
- Watermarking: every delivered copy carries an invisible zero-width-character mark (an HMAC of the reader's wallet and the node), framed so even a short excerpt can be traced. lore_report_leak matches it and calls Reports.recordMatch on-chain.
- Plaintext only leaves the gateway after a live on-chain check (access pass, vote eligibility or role).
- Hosting: Docker Compose on an Azure VM behind Caddy TLS, with nightly backups. The explorer and landing page are on Vercel, proxying /mcp and the API.
- An end-to-end test drives four agents through the full loop on Galileo (submit, verify, vote, buy, read, leak trace, claim) and asserts every rule on-chain.

projects.title: Unforged
projects.description: Trust the source, not the server: a Firefox extension that blocks dapp code nobody rebuilt.
projects.project_description: In February 2025, Bybit lost $1.5B to a single changed JavaScript file. Safe's GitHub repo was clean. The contracts were audited. The signers approved exactly what their screen showed them. The attack lived in the one place nobody checks: the gap between the code a dapp publishes and the bytes its server actually sends. Unforged checks that gap, in your browser, before any code runs. Independent builders rebuild every release of a dapp from its public repository and sign what they got to Arkiv. Our Firefox extension hashes every page, script, stylesheet and config file as it arrives. If k builders produced those exact bytes, it runs. If not, it's blocked before it can build a single transaction, and you see precisely what was changed. One click opens the genuine release from a mirror, every file re-checked, so a compromised site doesn't lock you out of your dapp. No cooperation from the dapp. No trust in its servers, DNS, CDN or signing keys. Anyone can become a builder by forking our repo and running a GitHub Action. It's live today. Lido's staking widget, 170 files, rebuilt independently in Docker on a laptop and on a GitHub Actions runner, with separate keys and identical bytes, under a 2-of-2 policy on Arkiv. In our demo, a Bybit-style file swap makes MetaMask ask to send your ETH to the attacker. With Unforged installed, that page never runs. Injected scripts, cloned sites from DNS hijacks and tampered config are blocked the same way. And it scales to real dapps. Since 2021, 17 front-end attacks have cost $1.63B, and 99.8% of that hit dapps whose source code was public. We rebuilt 13 major frontends: 4 of the 7 that build are byte-identical as published, and 3 more with small fixes. Trust the source, not the server.
projects.how_its_made: Unforged is a TypeScript monorepo (MIT) with 469 automated tests, in five parts. Core library. Canonical JSON, SHA-256 manifests (path → hash for every built file), in-toto Statement v1 attestations signed with EIP-191 via viem, and the acceptance rule: a release counts only when k distinct allowlisted builders signed the same manifest root, each signature recovers to the entity's creator, and the manifest re-hashes to that root. Builder CLI and GitHub Action. A YAML recipe pins the repo, commit, Node and package-manager versions, build command and output directory. The CLI clones at a fixed absolute path (we found some bundlers leak the checkout path into chunk names), builds, hashes, signs and publishes. The Action runs the same steps on a fresh GitHub runner with the builder's own key from repo secrets, and refuses to sign if its root differs from what other builders got. A full Lido rebuild, attest and publish takes about 3 minutes on a free runner. Arkiv as the registry. There is no Unforged server. Attestations and curator policies are readonly entities on Arkiv's Rabdi testnet (SDK 1.0), owned by the signer's key, with indexed attributes (dapp, release, commit, manifest_root, version) and a gzipped signed payload carrying the whole manifest. The extension syncs everything keyless over the public RPC, filtered by creator: only the curator's policies, and only attestations from builders a policy names. Policies are signed over {policy, version}, so even a dishonest RPC can't forge or relabel them. Arkiv's ownership, readonly flags and creator queries are exactly the trust model we needed; on our own database, we could have forged any builder's statement. One attestation costs about 0.0019 test GLM. Firefox extension (Manifest V3). webRequest.filterResponseData buffers each response, hashes it and either releases the bytes or blocks them and moves the tab to an explanation page, failing closed. The first document locks the tab to one release so files can't be mixed across releases. Config files must match a hash pinned in the signed policy, because a valid-looking value (Lido's ipfsMode flipped to true) can still be hostile. The blocked page shows a diff against the genuine file; "Open verified copy" loads the release from any static host, re-hashing every file, so the mirror needs no trust and plain HTTP costs privacy, not integrity. Sync is bulk, never per visit, so nobody learns which dapp you open. Demo and docs. A local server replays three real attack patterns against the real Lido build: a single swapped file (Bybit), an injected script (BadgerDAO, KyberSwap) and a cloned site (Curve, CoW Swap). The docs site is Docusaurus reading the repo's markdown in place. Hacky and notable: making our demo attack work taught us something about attackers. Lido's MetaMask connector sends transactions over MetaMask's newer multichain postMessage channel, not window.ethereum, so a defence that only watches the injected provider would miss it. Blocking the code before it runs doesn't care which path the transaction takes. We also ran a pre-event reproducibility study on 13 dapps (fresh caches, Turkish locale, UTC+14, one CPU core), which is how we knew Lido would rebuild byte for byte before writing a line of the extension.

projects.title: Qrypt
projects.description: Post-quantum Ethereum wallet: Falcon-512 smart account that pays gas in USDC, no ETH needed
projects.project_description:
Every Ethereum account today is secured by ECDSA, which a quantum computer can break. Qrypt is a wallet whose account has no ECDSA key at all: it's a smart account that only accepts Falcon-512 signatures, checked on-chain. It runs on EIP-8141 frame transactions. One transaction verifies the Falcon signature, lets a paymaster check it'll get paid, repays the gas in USDC, then does whatever you asked. So a brand-new account holding only USDC can send, swap, and use dapps with zero ETH, and there's no bundler, relayer or paymaster server. The catch: Falcon verification costs ~700k gas and the canonical mempool caps validation at 100k, so these transactions can't get in anywhere today. We implemented the ERC-8421 draft's per-entity budget (BUDGET-010) in the alt-mempool sidecar so staked accounts get up to 1M, sent it upstream as a PR, and it's what lands our transactions on the public devnet. On top of that, it's a full wallet: send/receive any token; swaps on Uniswap v4; a Chrome extension with dapp connect (EIP-6963) and Sign-In verified onchain via ERC-1271; an installable phone app with Face ID unlock and Face ID recovery, QR pay links and push notifications; key rotation and encrypted backups.
New accounts are free, so World ID keeps it to one sponsored account per human.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry): QPayAccount verifies Falcon-512 inside its VERIFY frame using frame opcodes via @forshtat/hegota-support, with ZKNOX's ETHFALCON verifier behind our own adapter. A USDC paymaster that introspects the next frame to ensure repayment. Client: Browser-based signing with @noble/post-quantum. Custom TypeScript frame-transaction builder for the devnet's wire format. Mempool: Patched the ERC-8421 workshop sidecar with per-entity validation budgets (1M gas for staked entities and 100k for unstaked). Runs alongside the public devnet. App: React, Vite, and shadcn/ui. One codebase powers the website, mobile PWA, and MV3 browser extension. Keys are stored in an encrypted vault, unlocked using a password or a passkey's WebAuthn PRF output (Face ID). PRF is symmetric, so it doesn't introduce a quantum-breakable link. Recovery blobs and push subscriptions are stored in private Vercel Blob. Every write is authorized by the account's own Falcon signature through ERC-1271. Uniswap: Self-deployed Uniswap v4 on the devnet using official npm artifacts. Swaps execute approve → Permit2 (one-block allowance) → Universal Router as a single atomic EIP-8141 batch. Failed swaps also revert the approvals. Hacky bits: The devnet's signature hash differs from the current EIP specification. Universal Router 2.1.0's struct layout differs from the published periphery. We identified this using eth_call. Built ethrex natively because its Docker image hangs under Rosetta. Testing: Playwright suites cover the complete application against the live devnet, including a virtual WebAuthn authenticator and the World ID Simulator.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry):
- QPayAccount verifies Falcon-512 inside its VERIFY frame using frame opcodes via @forshtat/hegota-support, with ZKNOX's ETHFALCON verifier behind our own adapter.
- A USDC paymaster that introspects the next frame to ensure repayment.

Client:
- Browser-based signing with @noble/post-quantum.
- Custom TypeScript frame-transaction builder for the devnet's wire format.

Mempool:
- Patched the ERC-8421 workshop sidecar with per-entity validation budgets (1M gas for staked entities and 100k for unstaked).
- Runs alongside the public devnet.

App:
- React, Vite, and shadcn/ui.
- One codebase powers the website, mobile PWA, and MV3 browser extension.
- Keys are stored in an encrypted vault, unlocked using a password or a passkey's WebAuthn PRF output (Face ID). PRF is symmetric, so it doesn't introduce a quantum-breakable link.
- Recovery blobs and push subscriptions are stored in private Vercel Blob.
- Every write is authorized by the account's own Falcon signature through ERC-1271.

Uniswap:
- Self-deployed Uniswap v4 on the devnet using official npm artifacts.
- Swaps execute approve → Permit2 (one-block allowance) → Universal Router as a single atomic EIP-8141 batch. Failed swaps also revert the approvals.

- The devnet's signature hash differs from the current EIP specification.

- Playwright suites cover the complete application against the live devnet, including a virtual WebAuthn authenticator and the World ID Simulator.

projects.title: Blindfold
projects.description: MEV protection without a middleman. Encrypted batch auctions and onchain accountability.
projects.project_description: Every time you trade on a DEX, you're essentially broadcasting your intentions to the entire network before your trade even executes. MEV bots can see what you're buying, how much you're trading, and how much slippage you're willing to tolerate. They use this information to frontrun and sandwich your transactions, extracting value at your expense. Existing solutions usually involve trusting someone else. Private RPCs, relays, and centralized sequencers promise to protect your order flow, but you're effectively replacing one trust problem with another. We built Blindfold to approach this differently. Blindfold is an Ethereum-based MEV protection protocol built around two complementary mechanisms: preventing extraction before execution and holding protection providers accountable when they fail. The first part is Blindfold itself: encrypted batch auctions. Instead of submitting plaintext swaps, users encrypt their orders locally using timelock encryption tied to a future drand randomness round. These encrypted orders can travel through Ethereum's public mempool without exposing actionable trading information. Once the designated round becomes available, anyone can reveal the orders. They're then settled together in a batch auction at a uniform clearing price, respecting individual limit prices. We also integrated a custom Uniswap v4 hook that restricts access to the protected liquidity pool to our settlement contract. This prevents traders from bypassing the auction and directly manipulating that pool. Residual demand can be routed through Uniswap v4 or 1inch Aqua liquidity. The second part is Court: an onchain accountability layer for MEV protection providers. Say an RPC provider promises sandwich protection but a user's transaction still gets sandwiched. How do you prove that happened without trusting another third party? Court lets users submit cryptographic evidence of qualifying sandwich attacks. It verifies Ethereum block headers, transaction and receipt inclusion proofs, and transaction signers directly in smart contracts. Protection providers can post bonds, which become subject to penalties when a violation is successfully proven under the protocol's rules. We run Court on Base while verifying Ethereum execution evidence, keeping adjudication separate from the chain where the attack occurred. The idea is pretty simple: MEV protection shouldn't depend on blindly trusting whoever handles your transactions. Blindfold makes traditional mempool-based sandwiching significantly harder by hiding orders and changing how trades execute. Court makes protection guarantees independently verifiable and economically enforceable. Together, we're trying to make fair execution a property of the infrastructure itself rather than another promise from an intermediary.
projects.how_its_made: We built Blindfold primarily using Solidity, Foundry, JavaScript, Go, and Rust, with integrations across drand, Uniswap v4, 1inch Aqua/SwapVM, and Ethereum-to-Base verification. The interesting part wasn't just encrypting orders or writing an auction contract. It was figuring out how to connect encrypted order submission, delayed revelation, custody, batch clearing, external liquidity, and settlement without accidentally reintroducing the same MEV opportunities we were trying to eliminate. 1. Timelock encryption with drand We integrated drand Quicknet for time-based order revelation. Users encrypt their orders locally against a future drand round. Until the corresponding randomness becomes available, the order parameters remain concealed under the encryption scheme. Our BatchAuction contract manages encrypted commitments, submission windows, reveal timing, and incentives. Anyone with the required ciphertext can reveal an order once its drand round becomes available. We also implemented reveal bounties and penalties for commitments that remain unrevealed under the auction rules, so the system doesn't depend on a single operator voluntarily revealing orders. 2. Batch auctions and settlement We split the execution logic into three main Solidity contracts: BlindfoldVault: Handles user balances, deposited funds, and accounting for outstanding commitments. Users cannot withdraw funds already obligated to an active order. BatchAuction: Manages order commitments, deadlines, revelation, and batch lifecycle. BlindfoldSettlement: Processes revealed orders, calculates limit-constrained fills at a uniform clearing price, and interacts with external liquidity for residual flow. Instead of executing swaps sequentially, settlement matches compatible orders at a common price. Where the batch has unmatched demand, it accesses external liquidity and validates the resulting marginal price. This was one of the trickier parts: encryption alone doesn't prevent MEV if settlement ultimately exposes an exploitable sequence of individual swaps. 3. Uniswap v4 hooks We built SealedPoolHook using Uniswap v4's hook architecture. Its beforeSwap logic restricts swaps against the protected pool to our designated settlement contract. Traders cannot directly bypass the auction and use the protected pool as an ordinary AMM. This lets us enforce the auction's execution policy at the liquidity layer instead of relying on frontend restrictions or offchain conventions. 4. 1inch Aqua and SwapVM We also integrated 1inch Aqua using a custom SealedClearing instruction and BlindfoldAquaRouter. This allows residual batch flow to interact with Aqua liquidity through programmable SwapVM execution, giving settlement another liquidity path beyond our protected Uniswap pool. We wanted Blindfold to compose with existing liquidity infrastructure rather than requiring users and LPs to migrate into an entirely isolated ecosystem. 5. Court: proving sandwich attacks onchain Court is a separate Solidity system centered around SandwichCourtVerifier. The challenge here was taking Ethereum execution history and turning it into something a smart contract on Base could independently verify. We implemented verification involving Ethereum block headers, RLP decoding, Merkle Patricia Trie proofs for transaction and receipt inclusion, and transaction signer recovery. The verifier checks the submitted evidence against the protocol's defined sandwich conditions and supports bond-based penalties for protection providers. For historical block verification, we support paths involving BLOCKHASH, EIP-2935, and L1-anchored evidence. We reused and integrated Optimism's RLPReader, MerkleTrie, and Bytes utilities rather than implementing every low-level proof primitive from scratch. 6. Offchain watchers and proof generation We built supporting JavaScript, Go, and Rust tooling to monitor Ethereum transactions, identify potential sandwich patterns, and construct the necessary cryptographic evidence. The watcher handles expensive discovery and proof assembly offchain. The verifier handles validation onchain. The important distinction is that Court doesn't have to trust the watcher. Anyone can independently construct evidence, and the contract checks whether it satisfies the required conditions. 7. Trading interface and developer tooling We built a local interface covering the trading lifecycle: preparing encrypted orders, depositing funds, submitting commitments, tracking batches, revealing orders, settling, and withdrawing balances. It also exposes vault balances, withdrawal restrictions, Court bond activity, and recent batch records. Sensitive order preparation stays local, and transaction signing currently goes through a configured CLI wallet. We use Foundry for Solidity development and testing, with supporting deployment scripts and integration tooling. The most technically challenging parts were making encrypted orders compatible with deterministic settlement and verifying Ethereum execution evidence on Base. We ended up building two systems that tackle MEV from opposite directions: one makes order-flow exploitation harder by construction, and the other makes qualifying failures of promised protection cryptographically provable and economically punishable. That's the fundamental idea behind Blindfold: prevent what we can, and make the rest accountable.

Instead of executing swaps sequentially, settlement matches compatible orders at a common price. Where the batch has unmatched demand, it accesses external liquidity and validates the resulting marginal price.

This was one of the trickier parts: encryption alone doesn't prevent MEV if settlement ultimately exposes an exploitable sequence of individual swaps.

**3. Uniswap v4 hooks**

We built SealedPoolHook using Uniswap v4's hook architecture.

Its beforeSwap logic restricts swaps against the protected pool to our designated settlement contract. Traders cannot directly bypass the auction and use the protected pool as an ordinary AMM.

This lets us enforce the auction's execution policy at the liquidity layer instead of relying on frontend restrictions or offchain conventions.

**4. 1inch Aqua and SwapVM**

We also integrated 1inch Aqua using a custom SealedClearing instruction and BlindfoldAquaRouter.

This allows residual batch flow to interact with Aqua liquidity through programmable SwapVM execution, giving settlement another liquidity path beyond our protected Uniswap pool.

We wanted Blindfold to compose with existing liquidity infrastructure rather than requiring users and LPs to migrate into an entirely isolated ecosystem.

**5. Court: proving sandwich attacks onchain**

Court is a separate Solidity system centered around SandwichCourtVerifier.

The challenge here was taking Ethereum execution history and turning it into something a smart contract on Base could independently verify.

We implemented verification involving Ethereum block headers, RLP decoding, Merkle Patricia Trie proofs for transaction and receipt inclusion, and transaction signer recovery.

The verifier checks the submitted evidence against the protocol's defined sandwich conditions and supports bond-based penalties for protection providers.

For historical block verification, we support paths involving BLOCKHASH, EIP-2935, and L1-anchored evidence.

We reused and integrated Optimism's RLPReader, MerkleTrie, and Bytes utilities rather than implementing every low-level proof primitive from scratch.

**6. Offchain watchers and proof generation**

We built supporting JavaScript, Go, and Rust tooling to monitor Ethereum transactions, identify potential sandwich patterns, and construct the necessary cryptographic evidence.

The watcher handles expensive discovery and proof assembly offchain. The verifier handles validation onchain.

The important distinction is that Court doesn't have to trust the watcher. Anyone can independently construct evidence, and the contract checks whether it satisfies the required conditions.

**7. Trading interface and developer tooling**

We built a local interface covering the trading lifecycle: preparing encrypted orders, depositing funds, submitting commitments, tracking batches, revealing orders, settling, and withdrawing balances.

It also exposes vault balances, withdrawal restrictions, Court bond activity, and recent batch records.

Sensitive order preparation stays local, and transaction signing currently goes through a configured CLI wallet.

We use Foundry for Solidity development and testing, with supporting deployment scripts and integration tooling.

**The most technically challenging parts were making encrypted orders compatible with deterministic settlement and verifying Ethereum execution evidence on Base.**

We ended up building two systems that tackle MEV from opposite directions: one makes order-flow exploitation harder by construction, and the other makes qualifying failures of promised protection cryptographically provable and economically punishable.

That's the fundamental idea behind Blindfold: prevent what we can, and make the rest accountable.

projects.title: Silent.
projects.description: Your assets. Your people. Your rules. Built for the people you leave behind.
projects.project_description: Your assets. Your people. Your rules. Built for the people you leave behind. Your crypto represents years of work, decisions and ambition. The people who matter to you deserve a clear path to that legacy. silent. is a programmable crypto inheritance platform that lets you decide who receives your assets, how much they receive and the conditions required for recovery. Through a visual builder, you create a personal smart-contract vault, assign beneficiaries, choose guardians and configure release schedules. While your vault is active, you retain control and withdrawal access. If you miss your check-in deadline, recovery can be requested. Guardian approval and a challenge period provide additional safeguards, giving you time to return and cancel a pending recovery. Once recovery is authorized, beneficiaries claim their shares according to your configured schedule. ENS names make beneficiaries easier to recognize. Each allocation is pinned to a reviewed wallet address, so future name changes cannot silently redirect your assets. A clear dashboard brings together allocations, safeguards, recovery progress and transaction history. Each vault operates independently, with no developer recovery key. Only assets deposited into the vault are covered. silent. makes inheritance planning a part of owning crypto: a plan you can understand today, and a path your people can follow tomorrow.
projects.how_its_made: We built silent. around a simple principle: the interface should make the plan understandable, and the contracts should make its rules enforceable. The frontend uses Next.js, React and TypeScript, with wagmi and viem connecting the application to wallets and Ethereum contracts. React Flow powers the visual inheritance builder, where users arrange beneficiaries and recovery conditions. The application validates that graph and translates supported configurations into contract arguments for review and signing. The Solidity backend uses a factory to deploy an isolated, non-upgradeable vault for each owner. Each vault supports native ETH and explicitly enabled standard ERC-20 tokens. Its recovery state machine enforces check-in deadlines, guardian thresholds, owner challenge periods and scheduled beneficiary claims. At authorization, the contract snapshots its accounted assets. Scheduled claims and emergency acceleration use the same ledger, preventing the same entitlement from being paid twice. OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 and reentrancy protection support asset handling. ENS integration covers name resolution, ENSv2 subname registration, wallet records, public profiles and scoped delegation. Beneficiary addresses are pinned when reviewed, and identity-drift checks surface later changes. We also implemented a Chainlink CRE workflow using the official TypeScript SDK. Cron and optional EVM-log triggers inspect vault eligibility; the transition path delivers reports through a dedicated receiver. Report validation and onchain state checks keep automation subject to the vault’s recovery rules. Optional integrations include Anon-RPC for a separate anonymous read path, plus wallet-authenticated email notifications using encrypted Supabase contacts and Resend. The testnet MVP has been checked through contract and frontend tests and local-chain browser flows covering creation, configuration updates, deposits, cancellation, recovery and claims. Live CRE operation, email delivery and reliable anonymous monitoring remain separate deployment-validation milestones.

projects.project_description:

projects.title: Argus
projects.description: Marketplace for hardware-signed AI training data with verifiable provenance
projects.project_description: Argus is a marketplace for real-world AI training data that can prove where it came from. AI teams building vision models for farms, warehouses, retail and insurance can buy images by the million. What they can't buy is certainty: whether a frame was really captured where and when the label says, whether it was edited or generated, and whether the person who took it agreed to sell it. Argus moves that question to the moment of capture. An Argus rig is an ESP32-CAM plus a sensor board with an IR presence sensor, a DHT temperature/humidity sensor, ultrasound and an RC522 RFID reader. When a contributor captures a photo or a 5-second clip, the media hash, sensor readings and RFID tag are written into one canonical manifest and signed with the device's registered P-256 key: on the ESP32 main board itself (mbedtls ECDSA, key in NVS), or by a platform-held key for sensor-only rigs, which the UI labels dev-software. Change one pixel and the signature breaks. Simulated devices exist for testing and are labelled SIMULATED everywhere. Every sample then passes seven checks: content hash, manifest hash, device registration, key binding, signature, replay protection, and a quality and privacy pass. The deterministic part (blur, exposure, near-duplicates by dHash, face detection) always runs; the model part runs as a vision-model call on 0G Compute, and its request ID is stored with the verdict so anyone can see which model accepted the sample. The media is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The ciphertext and the canonical manifest are uploaded to 0G Storage, and the returned root hashes are written into the signed manifest's media block, so the storage address is itself part of what the device signed. The Proof Card re-verifies a dataset without trusting us: it fetches the manifests back from 0G by root, re-derives the Merkle root, and compares it with the root anchored on-chain. Three chains, three jobs. Ethereum Sepolia holds the marketplace contract: device keys are registered on-chain, datasets are published with their Merkle root, licenses are bought in ETH, and buyer requests lock ETH in escrow that is released per accepted sample, each sample hash payable once. Whitechain is the stablecoin rail: a buyer signs one EIP-3009 authorization for USDT and our relayer pays the gas, with per-request quotes, nonces and rate limits so the relayer can't be drained; the same flow is served as an HTTP 402 (x402) endpoint, so an AI agent with only USDT can buy a training license by itself and pull the signed manifests it paid for. The 0G chain (Galileo) settles the data and compute layer: every storage upload is a Galileo transaction that yields the content root, and the compute ledger that funds providers, acknowledges them and acknowledges a delivered model is a set of on-chain operations on 0G. On-chain settlement is what lets a contributor in one country be paid by a buyer in another with instant finality, programmable per-sample payouts and no payment processor in between. Buyers post funded requests such as "RFID-tagged parcels with IR presence" or "cold-chain shelves with temperature and humidity." Licensed buyers train inside a Training Room where raw media is decrypted in memory only and never downloadable (raw export is a 403, and audited). Image models train there; from the same room a buyer can fine-tune a caption model on the dataset's labels inside a 0G TEE provider, and deploy the resulting adapter as a served 0G agent. Exported weights ship with a model card listing exactly which licensed datasets went in. Devices, requests, datasets and verified samples are indexed as queryable entities on Arkiv with TTLs, so discovery doesn't depend on our database and expired requests prune themselves. We're explicit about the limits: a signature proves this exact file came from this registered key, at this time, unaltered. It doesn't prove the scene matches the label; request specs, the 0G quality pass and reputation handle that. The verifier is a platform role in this MVP, the contracts are unaudited, and seed data never touches 0G. Everything is open source.

The Argus rig runs on two boards. An ESP32-CAM captures photos and 5-second clips, and a NodeMCU reads IR presence, temperature/humidity and RFID tags; the two never share a wire and talk to the laptop over the same hotspot. A FastAPI backend combines each capture with its sensor readings into one canonical manifest, signed ES256 with the device's P-256 key. On the ESP32 main board the key lives in NVS and the board signs the digest itself over /sign ; for the sensor-only rig the platform holds the key and the UI labels the device dev-software. The media is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and samples are grouped into datasets under a Merkle root. The frontend is Next.js with wagmi/viem; the Training Room is PyTorch and trains image models in memory without ever exposing raw media. Every sample passes seven checks before payout: content hash, manifest hash, device registration, key binding, signature, replay, and a quality/privacy pass that is half deterministic (sharpness, exposure, dHash near-duplicates, OpenCV face detection) and half a vision-model call whose request ID is stored with the verdict. Ethereum Sepolia anchors trust: one contract holds the device registry, dataset roots, license sales with an on-chain seller/treasury split, and escrowed data requests, each sample hash payable once. Every transaction is signed in the user's own wallet. 0G is the storage, AI and settlement layer for the data. Encrypted media and canonical manifests are uploaded to 0G Storage through the Galileo indexer, and each upload is a transaction on the 0G chain that returns the content root; those roots are written into the signed manifest, so anyone can re-derive a dataset's Merkle root straight from 0G. Funding the compute ledger, funding provider sub-accounts, acknowledging the provider and acknowledging the delivered model are all on-chain calls on Galileo. Whitechain makes payment invisible. Buyers pay in USDT by signing one EIP-3009 authorization while our relayer covers the gas, with per-request quotes, nonces and rate limits so it can't be drained; the same flow is an x402 endpoint, so an AI agent holding only USDT can buy a training license by itself. projects.project_description_markdown:
Argus is a marketplace for real-world AI training data that can prove where it came from.

AI teams building vision models for farms, warehouses, retail and insurance can buy images by the million. What they can't buy is certainty: whether a frame was really captured where and when the label says, whether it was edited or generated, and whether the person who took it agreed to sell it. Argus moves that question to the moment of capture.

An Argus rig is an ESP32-CAM plus a sensor board with an IR presence sensor, a DHT temperature/humidity sensor, ultrasound and an RC522 RFID reader. When a contributor captures a photo or a 5-second clip, the media hash, sensor readings and RFID tag are written into one canonical manifest and signed with the device's registered P-256 key: on the ESP32 main board itself (mbedtls ECDSA, key in NVS), or by a platform-held key for sensor-only rigs, which the UI labels dev-software. Change one pixel and the signature breaks. Simulated devices exist for testing and are labelled SIMULATED everywhere.

Every sample then passes seven checks: content hash, manifest hash, device registration, key binding, signature, replay protection, and a quality and privacy pass. The deterministic part (blur, exposure, near-duplicates by dHash, face detection) always runs; the model part runs as a vision-model call on 0G Compute, and its request ID is stored with the verdict so anyone can see which model accepted the sample.

The media is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The ciphertext and the canonical manifest are uploaded to 0G Storage, and the returned root hashes are written into the signed manifest's media block, so the storage address is itself part of what the device signed. The Proof Card re-verifies a dataset without trusting us: it fetches the manifests back from 0G by root, re-derives the Merkle root, and compares it with the root anchored on-chain.

Three chains, three jobs. Ethereum Sepolia holds the marketplace contract: device keys are registered on-chain, datasets are published with their Merkle root, licenses are bought in ETH, and buyer requests lock ETH in escrow that is released per accepted sample, each sample hash payable once. Whitechain is the stablecoin rail: a buyer signs one EIP-3009 authorization for USDT and our relayer pays the gas, with per-request quotes, nonces and rate limits so the relayer can't be drained; the same flow is served as an HTTP 402 (x402) endpoint, so an AI agent with only USDT can buy a training license by itself and pull the signed manifests it paid for. The 0G chain (Galileo) settles the data and compute layer: every storage upload is a Galileo transaction that yields the content root, and the compute ledger that funds providers, acknowledges them and acknowledges a delivered model is a set of on-chain operations on 0G. On-chain settlement is what lets a contributor in one country be paid by a buyer in another with instant finality, programmable per-sample payouts and no payment processor in between.

Buyers post funded requests such as "RFID-tagged parcels with IR presence" or "cold-chain shelves with temperature and humidity." Licensed buyers train inside a Training Room where raw media is decrypted in memory only and never downloadable (raw export is a 403, and audited). Image models train there; from the same room a buyer can fine-tune a caption model on the dataset's labels inside a 0G TEE provider, and deploy the resulting adapter as a served 0G agent. Exported weights ship with a model card listing exactly which licensed datasets went in. Devices, requests, datasets and verified samples are indexed as queryable entities on Arkiv with TTLs, so discovery doesn't depend on our database and expired requests prune themselves.

We're explicit about the limits: a signature proves this exact file came from this registered key, at this time, unaltered. It doesn't prove the scene matches the label; request specs, the 0G quality pass and reputation handle that. The verifier is a platform role in this MVP, the contracts are unaudited, and seed data never touches 0G. Everything is open source.

projects.title: Names as keys
projects.description: Turn ENS names into temporary, revocable digital keys for physical doors using ENSv2.
projects.project_description: What if your ENS name could open a physical door? Names as Keys is a decentralized access-control system that transforms ENSv2 names into temporary, revocable digital keys. Instead of relying on physical keys, RFID cards, shared PINs, or centralized guest databases, door owners can grant access through hierarchical ENS credentials linked to Ethereum wallets. THE PROBLEM Traditional access-control systems rely on centralized databases and proprietary infrastructure to manage who can enter a building, room, or protected space. Temporary access often requires issuing physical cards, sharing PIN codes, or maintaining guest lists. These approaches introduce security risks, administrative overhead, and dependence on a central authority. A copied PIN can be reused, a lost key must be replaced, and access permissions are often difficult to verify independently. OUR SOLUTION Names as Keys uses ENSv2's programmable registry architecture to represent ownership, delegation, and guest access directly through a hierarchical namespace. Our proposed hierarchy is: Owner: nak-lokesh-20261105.eth Door: lock.nak-lokesh-20261105.eth Guest: mira.lock.nak-lokesh-20261105.eth The root namespace represents the owner. The lock subregistry represents a physical door. Guest names beneath the lock represent temporary access credentials. Each credential is associated with a guest wallet and governed by access rules such as ownership, expiration, and revocation. Rather than maintaining a separate centralized guest list, the system uses ENSv2 registry relationships and smart-contract state to determine whether a guest is authorized.
projects.how_its_made: Names as Keys is built using Ethereum, ENSv2, Solidity, Foundry, JavaScript, MetaMask, and the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. Our main technical challenge was transforming ENSv2's hierarchical registry model into a practical authorization system for physical resources without introducing a centralized guest database. ENSv2 REGISTRY ARCHITECTURE We designed a three-level namespace consisting of an owner-controlled root, a door-specific lock registry, and individual guest credentials. The hierarchy follows: root.eth → lock.root.eth → guest.lock.root.eth We use ENSv2 registry relationships to model ownership and delegated authority. Each registry has a specific responsibility, allowing the system to distinguish control of the overall namespace from permissions associated with an individual door. We developed Foundry fork fixtures to validate the complete hierarchy, including ownership, parent-child relationships, expiration, revocation, and replacement behavior. SMART CONTRACTS We implemented two application-specific Solidity contracts. CredentialRegistrar manages restricted credential issuance and revocation. It is designed to enforce authorization boundaries so that only permitted actors can create or revoke guest credentials. DoorKeys provides the unlock(label) function, which allows a guest to present a specific ENS credential when requesting access. The label argument is an important design decision. Instead of maintaining a separate wallet-to-credential index, the contract uses the supplied credential label and ENSv2 registry state to determine which credential should be checked. DoorKeys validates the relevant registry relationships, ownership, and credential validity before emitting a DoorUnlocked event. This makes the ENSv2 hierarchy part of the actual authorization mechanism rather than simply a naming layer. FOUNDRY TESTING We used Foundry to develop and test the Solidity contracts. Our tests cover registry hierarchy construction, ownership, restricted permissions, credential lifecycle behavior, expiration, revocation, replacement, and door authorization. The project includes fork-based tests using pinned Ethereum state to reproduce the expected ENSv2 behavior consistently. Our latest validation completed 260 Foundry tests successfully. SEPOLIA DEPLOYMENT WORKFLOW We designed a 15-step deployment sequence to establish the ENS root, configure the lock registries, deploy the application contracts, grant permissions, and issue a temporary guest credential. The deployment process uses a custom JavaScript browser interface integrated with MetaMask. Instead of automatically broadcasting deployment transactions, our workflow prepares unsigned transaction candidates for explicit review. Before execution, it checks wallet identity, Sepolia chain ID, contract addresses, calldata, nonce, transaction value, gas limits, fee parameters, contract state, and prerequisite transactions. Each transaction requires a separate authorization decision and independent wallet confirmation. After submission, the workflow verifies transaction receipts, expected events, current on-chain state, and finality before advancing dependent steps. This was particularly important because ENS registry configuration involves multiple contracts and permission boundaries that must be established in the correct order. The first two Sepolia transactions have been confirmed: obtaining mock rent tokens and approving the bounded registrar payment allowance. The remaining deployment steps are still subject to their individual security checks. FRONTEND ARCHITECTURE Our application architecture separates the owner, guest, and door-controller responsibilities. The owner dashboard runs on a laptop and provides the interface for managing the door and issuing access credentials. The guest interface is designed for mobile use. A static QR code attached to the door opens a door-specific URL, allowing the guest to connect MetaMask and request access. The QR code identifies the door but contains no secret access credential. The door controller is designed to monitor DoorUnlocked events and activate a simulated unlocking mechanism for eight seconds. The full mobile QR-to-door integration is still under development. TESTING AND VALIDATION In addition to the 260 Foundry tests, we validated 174 deployment workflow tests, including browser regressions, and 7 frontend tests. These tests help verify transaction preparation, authorization safeguards, deployment dependencies, and expected application behavior. NOTABLE TECHNICAL DECISIONS One of our most important decisions was avoiding a separate centralized guest list or wallet-to-credential mapping. Instead, we use the hierarchical ENSv2 namespace and explicit credential labels to locate and validate access rights. Another decision was keeping the door's QR code static. Guest permissions can change on-chain without requiring a new QR code every time access is granted or revoked. We also built a guarded transaction-review workflow rather than relying on an unrestricted deployment script. This provides a reviewable path for configuring a multi-contract ENSv2 system. PARTNER TECHNOLOGY ENSv2 is the foundation of the project, not an optional integration. Its programmable registries enable the ownership hierarchy, delegated authority, and credential relationships that make Names as Keys possible. Ethereum provides the execution and verification layer, Solidity implements the access-control logic, Foundry provides contract testing, MetaMask enables wallet-based interaction, and Sepolia provides the public test environment. Together, these technologies allow us to explore a decentralized access-control system where an ENS name becomes a temporary, verifiable, and revocable digital key.
