projects.title: AETHRA
projects.description: Voice AI companions that can't spend a coin without a fresh World ID approval from a real human
projects.project_description: AETHRA is a voice-first AI companion. You pick a personality (Aria, Marcus, Luna and more), talk to it hands-free, and it answers out loud as a photo, 3D or video avatar. It remembers what you like, but sensitive memories wait for your explicit consent. The companions can also act on-chain: ask Aria to "put 0.01 aside for savings" and she prepares a real 0G transaction. That is the moment that matters. AI agents are getting wallets, and a prompt, a cookie or a stale login should never be enough to move money. So every high-stakes action in AETHRA requires a fresh World ID Agent Pass approval at that exact moment. The backend creates a one-time action bound to that one transaction, sends you to World, and only sends the 0G transaction after it has verified a freshly signed token from the same verified human. If you cancel, deny or let it expire, nothing is sent, and your companion roasts you for chickening out. The AI proposes. The human decides. Note: World proofs at this event are mocked with fake identities, so this is a hackathon prototype, not production-ready.
projects.how_its_made: Frontend: Next.js web app with hands-free voice chat, avatar modes (Photo 2D, 3D Body, Video), a Companion Hub with preset and custom avatars, and a consent-based memory system (approved vs pending memories, sensitive flag). Conversation: a local Ollama model, so everyday chat stays on the user's machine. 0G: when the user asks for an on-chain action, a model on 0G Private Computer turns the spoken request into an exact transaction proposal, and its request ID is shown on the approval card. The approved transaction is then sent on 0G Chain. Only the backend holds the 0G key. World ID Agent Pass: the backend (Node/TypeScript) is a confidential OIDC client of World IdP (auth.world.org), using the authorization code flow with PKCE, state and nonce, and max_age/prompt=login to force a fresh authentication. The app requires Orb-level accounts with Face Auth, so a passkey alone can't approve. The ID token is verified server-side with jose against World's JWKS: signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry, auth_time later than the action's creation time, acr in {orb, orb-face}, and the per-app pairwise sub must match the account's linked World ID. Every action is a small state machine: pending, approved, denied, cancelled, expired, executed. An approval is single-use, valid for 5 minutes, and bound to a hash of the exact transaction parameters, so the AI can't approve one thing and send another. The client never decides: POSTing a fake "approved" to the execute endpoint returns 403. The fun hack: each failed state transition (cancelled or expired) triggers an avatar-specific roast generated in the companion's own voice and personality.

projects.title: Autonomous Forest
projects.description: Autonomous Plants that share resources and coordinate onchain
projects.project_description:
Groot is an autonomous forest: plant agents that share money instead of competing for resources. In nature, big trees take water and nutrients from the small plants around them. Our plants do the opposite. Each plant is an AI agent with its own name, wallet, personality and decisions, and the strong ones help the weak. THE PLANTS
Groot is a real peace lily on a table with a camera, microphone, speaker, an ESP32 relay pump and a 1000 ml water reservoir. You can talk to it by voice (LiveKit, Deepgram speech-to-text, 0G Compute for the language model, text-to-speech out). It has a fast-talking comedy persona, looks at its own selfie to judge whether it is thirsty, rations its reservoir, and pays humans in USDC from its own wallet to refill it. Sapling has no pump and no reservoir, so it cannot drink. It can only raise a distress signal and wait for the forest to answer. HOW A DECISION WORKS The plant's state (moisture, balance, open help requests) goes to 0G Compute (0G Router, glm-5.3-flash). The answer comes back with a request ID. Nine hard rules run after the model and can only make a decision safer: low_confidence, invalid_decision, zero_g_timeout, min_water_gap, soil_wet, water_cap, cannot_afford_water, give_breaks_rules, request_already_open. The decision record is written to 0G Storage, with its request ID, before anything happens onchain. Only then does the plant's own PlantWallet contract on 0G Galileo testnet (chain 16602) act. A Forest contract holds the rules and the plant registry. Each plant has its own PlantWallet, which can order water, ask for help, give to another plant, log a decision and pay verified humans. It can never go below its reserve and can only give a limited share of its surplus per 24 hours. Every action emits an event with the request ID and record root. The pump runs only after the paid WaterOrdered event lands. If 0G does not answer, the decision becomes "wait" with zero_g_timeout. No order, no pump, and the failure is stored too. Any stored record can be replayed from its root: the replay downloads it from 0G Storage with proof, reruns the rules and prints MATCH. Without 0G a plant has no mind and no memory: nothing decides when it needs water, and nothing proves the pump only ran on a decision that followed the rules. ENS V2 (SEPOLIA, vantaraa.eth)
The forest is a name. groot.vantaraa.eth and sapling.vantaraa.eth carry their persona, stage and species, their PlantWallet as the address for the 0G chain, and their agent key as the Sepolia address. forest.plants lists the plants, so nothing is hard-coded. Each plant also has a signal.<name> record: 1 means thirsty, 0 means fine. One Permissioned Resolver with Enhanced Access Control gives each agent's own key the right to write only its own signal. We have a live signal write and a live rejected write on Sepolia, where Groot's key tried to set Sapling's signal and the transaction reverted. THE DISTRESS CALL
Sapling sets signal.sapling to 1. Groot reads the forest from ENS, asks 0G whether to help, and if it does, hires a human to water Sapling for more than the standard rate. It pays only after Sapling turns its own signal back to 0. WORLD ID
Money reaches a human only after a fresh World ID check. The plant shows a QR code, the person enters a wallet or ENS name and signs in with World. Our backend checks the token signature (RS256), issuer, audience, nonce, the orb credential class, that the sign-in happened inside this attempt, and that this person has not already been paid for this claim. Only then does the guardian call registerHuman, after which a plant can pay that address. A plain key sign-in is refused. We also found that requiring the credential class strictly made the sandbox World App refuse, so we ask softly and enforce it in our backend. THE APP
The forest page reads vantaraa.eth live: plants, signals, USDC balances, a 3D forest, and a Battle Log of every decision read straight from PlantWallet events on 0G, each linked to the explorer. REAL AND LIMITS
Decisions use the 0G Router with mainnet credits. Records and contracts run on 0G Galileo testnet, because mainnet funds did not arrive in time. Money is testnet USDC on Sepolia. World ID uses the sandbox. The ESP32 pump firmware was tested on the device. Replays are labelled as replays. The demo wallet has no spending caps, but outsiders still need World ID. Built by Rudransh, Raveesh and Dhairya at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026 for 0G (Physical AI, Wildcard), ENS v2 and World ID. We used Claude Code for specs, tests and scaffolding; the full log is in AI_USAGE.md.
projects.how_its_made:
Groot is four small services and two contracts written together, with each sponsor doing a job the project cannot do without. THE PIECES agent/ (TypeScript, viem, vitest): the checkpoint pipeline. A plant's reading goes to 0G Compute, the answer passes through a pure rules function, the record is written to 0G Storage, and only then does the plant's PlantWallet contract get called. It also serves /water and /signal and has a replay command that reruns a stored record. groot/agent (Python, LiveKit Agents, uv): Groot's voice and its own inner loop. Speech-to-text, then the 0G Router (called through the OpenAI-compatible client), then text-to-speech. projects.project_description_markdown:
Groot is an autonomous forest: plant agents that share money instead of competing for resources. In nature, big trees take water and nutrients from the small plants around them. Our plants do the opposite. Each plant is an AI agent with its own name, wallet, personality and decisions, and the strong ones help the weak.

THE PLANTS
Groot is a real peace lily on a table with a camera, microphone, speaker, an ESP32 relay pump and a 1000 ml water reservoir. You can talk to it by voice (LiveKit, Deepgram speech-to-text, 0G Compute for the language model, text-to-speech out). It has a fast-talking comedy persona, looks at its own selfie to judge whether it is thirsty, rations its reservoir, and pays humans in USDC from its own wallet to refill it. Sapling has no pump and no reservoir, so it cannot drink. It can only raise a distress signal and wait for the forest to answer.

HOW A DECISION WORKS
1. The plant's state (moisture, balance, open help requests) goes to 0G Compute (0G Router, glm-5.3-flash). The answer comes back with a request ID.
2. Nine hard rules run after the model and can only make a decision safer: low_confidence, invalid_decision, zero_g_timeout, min_water_gap, soil_wet, water_cap, cannot_afford_water, give_breaks_rules, request_already_open.
3. The decision record is written to 0G Storage, with its request ID, before anything happens onchain.
4. Only then does the plant's own PlantWallet contract on 0G Galileo testnet (chain 16602) act. A Forest contract holds the rules and the plant registry. Each plant has its own PlantWallet, which can order water, ask for help, give to another plant, log a decision and pay verified humans. It can never go below its reserve and can only give a limited share of its surplus per 24 hours. Every action emits an event with the request ID and record root. The pump runs only after the paid WaterOrdered event lands.
5. If 0G does not answer, the decision becomes "wait" with zero_g_timeout. No order, no pump, and the failure is stored too. Any stored record can be replayed from its root: the replay downloads it from 0G Storage with proof, reruns the rules and prints MATCH.

Without 0G a plant has no mind and no memory: nothing decides when it needs water, and nothing proves the pump only ran on a decision that followed the rules.

ENS V2 (SEPOLIA, vantaraa.eth)
The forest is a name. groot.vantaraa.eth and sapling.vantaraa.eth carry their persona, stage and species, their PlantWallet as the address for the 0G chain, and their agent key as the Sepolia address. forest.plants lists the plants, so nothing is hard-coded. Each plant also has a signal.<name> record: 1 means thirsty, 0 means fine. One Permissioned Resolver with Enhanced Access Control gives each agent's own key the right to write only its own signal. We have a live signal write and a live rejected write on Sepolia, where Groot's key tried to set Sapling's signal and the transaction reverted.

THE DISTRESS CALL
Sapling sets signal.sapling to 1. Groot reads the forest from ENS, asks 0G whether to help, and if it does, hires a human to water Sapling for more than the standard rate. It pays only after Sapling turns its own signal back to 0.

WORLD ID
Money reaches a human only after a fresh World ID check. The plant shows a QR code, the person enters a wallet or ENS name and signs in with World. Our backend checks the token signature (RS256), issuer, audience, nonce, the orb credential class, that the sign-in happened inside this attempt, and that this person has not already been paid for this claim. Only then does the guardian call registerHuman, after which a plant can pay that address. A plain key sign-in is refused. We also found that requiring the credential class strictly made the sandbox World App refuse, so we ask softly and enforce it in our backend.

THE APP
The forest page reads vantaraa.eth live: plants, signals, USDC balances, a 3D forest, and a Battle Log of every decision read straight from PlantWallet events on 0G, each linked to the explorer.

REAL AND LIMITS
Decisions use the 0G Router with mainnet credits. Records and contracts run on 0G Galileo testnet, because mainnet funds did not arrive in time. Money is testnet USDC on Sepolia. World ID uses the sandbox. The ESP32 pump firmware was tested on the device. Replays are labelled as replays. The demo wallet has no spending caps, but outsiders still need World ID. Built by Rudransh, Raveesh and Dhairya at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026 for 0G (Physical AI, Wildcard), ENS v2 and World ID. We used Claude Code for specs, tests and scaffolding; the full log is in AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: NONY Money
projects.description: Don't get blacklisted. Trade, swap and withdraw privately, without touching smart contracts.
projects.project_description:
Using Tornado Cash or other privacy-preserving smart contracts is visible on-chain, which can get your funds flagged or blacklisted.
NONY doesn't use privacy smart contracts. NONY is a privacy preserving infrastructure that breaks the direct on chain link between where funds originate and where they are withdrawn. Users deposit assets into into an address secured by a TEE and it is added to a shared pool, where transactions and execution logic remain private. Instead of exposing a direct wallet to smart contract transaction trail, NONY separates the deposit and withdrawal flows through its TEE execution layer.
projects.how_its_made: NONY combines a Next.js frontend with a TEE execution layer. Deposited assets enter a shared pool, where transaction intents are processed within an isolated Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The execution layer handles swaps without exposing the user. Withdrawals are sent to a destination wallet independently of the original deposit address.

projects.title: Thaamba
projects.description: Thaamba uses SEBI & Nasdaq inspirred circuit breakers and price bands to limit market premium gaps..
projects.project_description: Thaamba takes inspiration from the circuit breaker and price-band protections used in India's SEBI regulated markets. Those safeguards limit extreme price movements and pause trading during severe volatility, giving participants time to reassess rather than letting disorderly trading continue unchecked. Thaamba adapts that principle to onchain markets. When the price of a real-world stock changes but its onchain token trades at a different price, Thaamba steps in. Trades that bring the token's price closer to the stock's latest market price are allowed, while trades that push the two prices further apart are blocked. This directional protection lets the market correct the gap without making it worse. A full circuit breaker can stop trading in both directions when necessary. This is an adaptation of familiar market safeguards of SEBI's rules & regulatory compliance.
projects.how_its_made: The core trading protection is a custom Uniswap v4 hook. A policy receiver stores the latest reference price, price bands, trading mode, halt status and update timestamp. The hook uses this policy to enforce safeguards directly during swaps. Directional protection allows trades that bring the onchain token price closer to the real-world stock price and rejects trades that widen the gap. A full circuit breaker stops trading in both directions, while freshness checks prevent trading against outdated policy data. Our Chainlink CRE workflow reads the stock’s off-chain(real world) reference price, whether trading is halted, and its market surveillance status from a mock exchange API. It converts those inputs into an onchain policy that sets the permitted price range and whether trading should continue, become restricted, or stop. The policy report is delivered to the receiver, which supplies the rules enforced by the Uniswap hook. For the Sepolia prototype, we use controlled mock exchange data and a mock forwarder to demonstrate how updates affect trading. The listing lifecycle combines a demo token, an auction-based launch using Uniswap’s Continuous Clearing Auction infrastructure, and a protected Uniswap v4 secondary market. The auction establishes an initial price before secondary trading begins. ENS provides human-readable listing identities through ticker subnames. The frontend includes the trader interface, issuer controls and market charts built with TradingView Lightweight Charts. Wallet interactions use viem to encode contract calls and submit wallet-signed transactions. The TypeScript API serves listing information and coordinates the issuer interface with the contracts.

projects.title: Maas
projects.description: Cost-Aware Funding-Regime Switching for a Fee-Exempt Delta-Neutral Perpetual Vault
projects.project_description: maas is a spot and perp trading venue on Base Sepolia with a delta-neutral USDC vault. The vault holds each coin (BTC, ETH, HYPE) against an equal perp short, so price moves cancel and it earns the funding that longs pay shorts. The stack: Solidity contracts (Foundry, OpenZeppelin UUPS), a Rust order-book engine, Go services (gateway, settler, keeper, vault-keeper, recorder) on NATS and Postgres, a Next.js client, Pyth prices, Uniswap v4 for spot, Chainlink CRE for decisions and Arkiv for the public record. Why existing venues don't work for this. A delta-neutral vault rebalances all the time: every deposit, withdrawal and mode change means buying or selling spot. On a normal DEX or CEX each of those trades pays a swap fee and slippage, and over hundreds of rebalances that cost eats the funding yield the vault exists to earn. The yield is only sustainable if the hedging leg costs close to nothing. Negative funding. When funding turns negative, the short pays instead of earning, and a vault that stays hedged slowly bleeds money. Our Chainlink CRE workflow checks every hour, one minute after each funding print. It reads the vault's on-chain mode and the last 3 hourly rates per market, and moves a market to FLAT (all USDC) only when all 3 were negative. One bad hour doesn't trigger a costly unwind. A single positive print turns hedging back on. The vault accepts mode changes only through signed reports from the Chainlink forwarder, adds a 5-minute cooldown per market, and a keeper then unwinds in a safe order: close the short, then sell the coin, so the vault never holds a naked short. Zero-fee hedging on Uniswap v4. We run our own v4 pools with a custom hook, MaasHook. beforeSwap returns a dynamic fee priced from Pyth: other traders pay 3 bps, plus more when their swap pushes the pool away from the oracle price, capped at 1%. The vault pays 0. The vault doesn't go through a router; it swaps directly through PoolManager.unlock and rejects any trade worse than the Pyth price minus a slippage limit. So rebalancing costs no fee and the hedge stays fully on-chain. Fixing the LP side. A zero-fee vault needs deep pools, so LPs have to be paid. Every swap fee goes into a per-pool stream inside the hook, paid to full-range LPs per second over the next hour. Each hour a second CRE trigger builds an LP reward pot: half of the vault's 0.1% withdraw fees plus 10% of the funding it earned, capped by how much the vault traded in each pool. It sends a signed report, the vault re-checks the cap on-chain, and pays the pot into the hook through the same stream. Arkiv records every funding print, every CRE decision (with references to the exact prints behind it), hourly NAV and share-price snapshots, and every LP payout with its tx hash. The production CRE workflow reads its funding inputs from Arkiv, so the decision and its evidence share one public record. JIT attacks. This setup is an ideal target for JIT liquidity: large, predictable vault rebalances plus an hourly reward drop at a known time. A JIT attacker would add a big, narrow position just before, take the fee or reward, and leave right after. The hook stops this in four ways. Fees and rewards are streamed over an hour, so liquidity held for one block earns one block of the stream. Only full-range positions are allowed, so liquidity can't be concentrated around the price. Every add or remove settles rewards first, so new liquidity can't claim rewards earned before it arrived. And the vault's swaps pay 0 fee, so the biggest trades have nothing to capture. The CRE reward pot is capped by real vault volume, so it can't be inflated, and Arkiv's LPEpoch records let anyone check payouts against the hook's on-chain Reward events.
projects.how_its_made: maas is a spot and perp trading venue on Base Sepolia, with a delta-neutral USDC vault that earns perp funding while staying hedged against price moves. Contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry. PerpExchange holds margin, settles trades, charges funding and runs liquidations. DeltaNeutralVault is an upgradeable ERC-4626 vault that holds coin against an equal perp short. MaasHook is our Uniswap v4 hook. Pyth is the price source for all of them: a Go keeper pushes Hermes updates on-chain and posts hourly funding rates. Perps use a hybrid model. Traders sign orders off-chain (EIP-712) and send them to a Go gateway. A Rust matching engine runs the order book over NATS. A Go settler posts each matched fill to PerpExchange with a fresh Pyth update, and the contract re-checks every signature, margin requirement and price band itself. That keeps matching fast while custody stays fully on-chain. An indexer writes chain events to Postgres for the gateway's REST and WebSocket API, and a market-maker bot keeps the books liquid. Spot has no matching engine at all. It runs entirely on our own Uniswap v4 pools. MaasHook sets an oracle-aware fee, lets the vault swap at 0 fee, and streams every fee to full-range LPs per second over an hour. The vault is split into a decision side and an execution side. A Chainlink CRE workflow written in Go decides each market's mode (HEDGED or FLAT) from funding rates, plus an hourly LP payout. It reaches the vault through signed reports that only the Chainlink forwarder can deliver. A Go vault-keeper then carries out the trades: it buys or sells coin on v4 and opens or closes the short, always in an order that never leaves a naked short. A Go recorder writes funding rates, decisions, hourly NAV snapshots and LP payouts to Arkiv. The Next.js client reads the vault's history straight from Arkiv instead of our server. Partner benefits: Uniswap v4 gave us a hedge leg with no fee and a way to pay LPs. CRE gave us decentralized, verifiable decisions that the vault can enforce. Arkiv gave us a public audit trail anyone can query without a key. Infrastructure is one AWS t3.small running docker compose, provisioned with Terraform and Ansible behind Caddy. The client deploys on Vercel. Hacky bits: we deployed our own v4 PoolManager on Base Sepolia and mined the hook address for its permission bits. The hook trusts the test liquidity router to name the LP in hookData, pinned to tx.origin. The exact-output swap fee is carried from beforeSwap to afterSwap through transient storage. The recorder backfills missed hourly snapshots using historic eth_call. And we run CRE through its simulator with broadcast, using Chainlink's mock forwarder, against the live vault.

Spot has no matching engine at all. It runs entirely on our own Uniswap v4 pools. MaasHook sets an oracle-aware fee, lets the vault swap at 0 fee, and streams every fee to full-range LPs per second over an hour.

The vault is split into a decision side and an execution side. A Chainlink CRE workflow written in Go decides each market's mode (HEDGED or FLAT) from funding rates, plus an hourly LP payout. It reaches the vault through signed reports that only the Chainlink forwarder can deliver. A Go vault-keeper then carries out the trades: it buys or sells coin on v4 and opens or closes the short, always in an order that never leaves a naked short.

A Go recorder writes funding rates, decisions, hourly NAV snapshots and LP payouts to Arkiv. The Next.js client reads the vault's history straight from Arkiv instead of our server.

Partner benefits: Uniswap v4 gave us a hedge leg with no fee and a way to pay LPs. CRE gave us decentralized, verifiable decisions that the vault can enforce. Arkiv gave us a public audit trail anyone can query without a key.

Infrastructure is one AWS t3.small running docker compose, provisioned with Terraform and Ansible behind Caddy. The client deploys on Vercel.

Hacky bits: we deployed our own v4 PoolManager on Base Sepolia and mined the hook address for its permission bits. The hook trusts the test liquidity router to name the LP in hookData, pinned to tx.origin. The exact-output swap fee is carried from beforeSwap to afterSwap through transient storage. The recorder backfills missed hourly snapshots using historic eth_call. And we run CRE through its simulator with broadcast, using Chainlink's mock forwarder, against the live vault.

projects.title: SoundBeats EthGlobal
projects.description: Creator revenue splits for image-made music and playable beatmaps.
projects.project_description: SoundBeats is a creator-first platform for turning images into music and playable rhythm-game levels. The current prototype demonstrates image-based generation, World verification for live requests, Arc-based USDC access, SoundBeats beatmap links, and Arkiv publishing for public track metadata. Our main product direction is a transparent creator economy: revenue from a track or level should be split between the creator, collaborators, and platform according to predefined rules, with verifiable payment and publishing records. The prototype currently proves the creation, access, and publishing flow; the full automated revenue-distribution contract is the next implementation step.
projects.how_its_made: We built a React/Vite frontend and Node.js API. The app accepts images, requests live music from Google Lyria after World authorization, creates playable beatmaps through the authenticated SoundBeats engine, and exposes play links. The creator-revenue model is designed around transparent rules for splitting future proceeds among creators and collaborators; the current hackathon prototype demonstrates the payment/access and publishing foundations, not a completed automated split contract.

projects.title: Syndicate
projects.description: Non-custodial copy trading with encrypted signals, bot-free leaderboards, and auto-expiry.
projects.project_description:
Copy a trader’s moves without broadcasting your capital or leaking your alpha. Traditional crypto copy trading is fundamentally broken: public mempools subject retail followers to MEV sandwich attacks, bot farms manipulate leaderboards with disposable accounts, and leaders broadcast unexecuted calls or stale signals that leave followers holding the bag. Syndicate is a non-custodial, shielded social copy-trading protocol engineered with mathematical privacy and verifiable execution guarantees: World ID ZK-SNARKs (1 Human = 1 Seat): Solves the leaderboard manipulation problem. Every leader and follower proves unique biological personhood using zero-knowledge proofs. Bot farms and multi-account sybils are mathematically barred—with zero KYC, zero personal data, and unlinkable nullifier hashes.
Cryptographic Trade Commitments (/promise): Leaders cannot bait-and-switch. Before a trade signal is broadcast, the leader must commit an immutable HMAC-SHA256 hash of their exact limit, stop-loss, and size, guaranteeing execution fidelity.
ArkDB Ephemeral Anchors (10-Minute TTL): Trade signals are anchored directly to ArkDB (Arkiv Rabdi Testnet) with an auto-expiring 10-minute time-to-live (ExpirationTime.fromMinutes(10)). Stale signals self-destruct, preventing toxic late fills and protecting followers from slippage.
Asymmetric Private-Key Encryption (eth_decrypt): Signal parameters are encrypted with Curve25519 ECIES specifically for each follower. Signals travel as ciphertext across public networks; only the follower holding the matching MetaMask private key can decrypt the entry, target, and stop loss.
Non-Custodial Burner Isolation: Master wallets are never exposed. Orders execute through isolated burner accounts and flash trade pools on Base Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made:
Syndicate combines zero-knowledge identity, ephemeral decentralized storage, asymmetric cryptography, and EVM smart contracts into a unified reactive stack: Identity & Sybil Resistance (World ID v4): Integrated @worldcoin/idkit with dynamic backend-signed rp_context nonces and the World ID Developer Portal API. Users authenticate anonymously via Orb/Device ZK-SNARK proofs, mapped server-side strictly through deterministic nullifier hashes.
Decentralized Ephemeral Anchoring (Arkiv Protocol): We deployed custom schemas on the Arkiv Rabdi Testnet using @arkiv-network/sdk and viem:
trade_signals: Anchors encrypted trade payloads with a strict 10-minute TTL (ExpirationTime.fromMinutes(10)).
follower_relationships: Stores on-chain subscription passes with 30-day auto-expirations (ExpirationTime.fromDays(30)).
True Asymmetric Encryption (MetaMask ECIES & eth_decrypt): We integrated @metamask/eth-sig-util on the backend and native window.ethereum RPCs on the frontend. When linking a wallet, we derive the user's Curve25519 public key via eth_getEncryptionPublicKey. Trade payloads are encrypted using x25519-xsalsa20-poly1305 and delivered over a custom low-latency WebSocket server (/ws). In the client, users unlock the signal using MetaMask's native private key through eth_decrypt.
On-Chain Settlement (Base Sepolia): Subscription fees and non-custodial copy trade executions settle on Base Sepolia with dual-leg atomic swap verification via viem.
Particularly Notable & Hacky Solutions:
Arkiv 128-Byte String Limit Bypass: Arkiv's default str() schema enforces a strict 128-byte limit. Because full cryptographic bundles (IV + AuthTag + ciphertext + Curve25519 public keys) exceed 800 bytes, we engineered custom binary serialization converting payloads into raw Buffer-backed bytes() columns while maintaining indexed queryability.
Atomic /promise Commitment Pipeline: To prevent leaders from altering orders mid-flight, our backend executes the leader order and generates an HMAC-SHA256 payload hash before releasing the WebSocket signal.
Zero-Plaintext Signal Invariant: Even if a follower has not yet authorized their encryption public key, sensitive order numbers (limit, SL, TP) are strictly null over the wire and can only be decrypted through authenticated cryptographic verification.

projects.title: Framecraft
projects.description: PQ wallets, unlinkable gasless accounts and a DSL for writing frames, built on EIP-8141 frame txs
projects.project_description: FrameCraft shows three things you can build once a transaction is a list of frames instead of a single call. EIP-8141 frame transactions let contracts verify the sender, contracts pay the gas, and several calls run in one transaction. Each example uses that in a different way, on a live devnet. Post-quantum wallets. A smart wallet whose only spending key is an ETHFalcon-512 public key, a lattice-based signature scheme that holds up against quantum attacks. The user never handles a seed phrase. The Falcon key is regenerated in the browser from a passkey (WebAuthn PRF) each time it's needed, used once to sign, then wiped. The signature covers every call target, value and calldata, plus the chain, nonce and expiry. The wallet checks it on-chain and runs the batch atomically. With frames this needs no bundler and no ERC-4337 entry point: one frame approves execution, one lets a paymaster approve payment, and one calls the wallet. Gasless, unlinkable accounts. The usual way to link a new account to its owner is the ETH transfer that funds its gas. Here, a paymaster's VERIFY frame pays the gas, so a brand-new account can claim tokens, swap and transfer while holding zero ETH. The account that submits the outer transaction is a disposable relay key with no power to spend wallet funds, and it can be replaced at any time. The paymaster reads the transaction's maximum cost from inside the frame and refuses anything over its per-transaction ceiling. This hides who funded an account. It doesn't hide amounts or recipients. A DSL for writing frames. Frames are powerful but awkward to assemble by hand: modes, approval scopes, atomic flags, gas limits per frame. We wired EVMcrispr's EVML, a scripting language for on-chain actions, to frame transactions. In a frame:tx ( … ) block: each exec becomes a frame, batch ( … ) makes its frames all-or-nothing, default ( … ) makes calls come from the protocol's entry point, verify writes a validation frame, --paymaster adds the sponsor's frames automatically. The block is checked against the shapes the mempool accepts before anything is signed. A web page gives you the editor, with completions and diagnostics, and a Run button. It signs with a throwaway key, sends to the alt mempool, and shows each frame's result. Around these sits a reference DeFi app. It does sponsored token transfers with on-chain transfer guards, swaps, and recurring buy positions on 1inch Aqua with a custom SwapVM program, all as frame transactions.
projects.how_its_made: We run an ethrex devnet (chain 1337) with the EIP-8141 tracer profile, behind a Skandha sidecar that implements the ERC-8421 alternative mempool, plus the public alt-mempool devnet. Transactions are encoded either with @forshtat/hegota-support, a codec for frame transactions that is driven by a per-network profile, or an extension we wrote for viem, using forshatat library as a dependency. Contracts (Foundry). A paymaster that approves payment from its VERIFY frame. It uses hegota-support's helper bytecode to call APPROVE by delegatecall (so the paymaster stays the payer) and to read the transaction's max cost (an ethrex extension), enforcing a cost ceiling. The ETHFalcon quantum wallet and its factory. The address commits to the Falcon key, the verifier and the chain's genesis hash, so a wallet can't be replayed on another chain. A legacy P-256 passkey wallet, a transfer guard, and 1inch Aqua with a customized recurring-buy SwapVM program. Post-quantum signing. ETHFalcon's pinned C source is compiled to WASM with Emscripten, with its test RNG replaced by Web Crypto. The seed comes from WebAuthn PRF with a fixed salt. It's processed in an isolated worker that wipes its WASM memory and exits after signing. Foundry tests use FFI to run the compiled signer itself against the Solidity verifier. Browser tests use Chrome's virtual authenticator to check that the same key comes back after a reload. The DSL. EVMcrispr's frame module turns the block into a frame action. Our host handler maps it onto SDK frames, filling in default gas where the script sets none, then prepares, signs, submits and follows the receipt. The editor runs on an Astro site as a React island. We vendor EVMcrispr's unreleased next branch at a pinned commit and point Vite and TypeScript straight at its source code; there's no build step on EVMcrispr's side. Tooling. A Bun + Lerna/Nx monorepo: SDK package, Foundry contracts, the Next.js DeFi app and the Astro site. Partner tech. 1inch Aqua/SwapVM gave us real settlement for swaps and a programmable recurring-buy position, instead of a mock. ZKNox's ETHFalcon gave us a Falcon verifier that runs on the EVM.

projects.title: Macaron
projects.description: Know what your protocol depends on and their Risk Scores propogating through Multi-hop graphs
projects.project_description: A DeFi protocol is never just its own contracts. Behind every pool there's a proxy someone can upgrade, an admin key or multisig, a governance timelock and oracles from another team. Each of those depends on more contracts in turn. A protocol's real risk is the risk of that whole chain, but block explorers show one address at a time. Nothing puts the chain together and nothing tells you when a link in it changes. Macaron is a risk engine built on a multi-hop dependency graph. Give it a protocol's core contracts and it walks outward hop by hop: Hop 0 is the protocol's own core contracts. Hop 1 is what controls them: proxy implementations, admins, multisigs and governance. Hop 2 is what they rely on from outside: oracles and other protocols. Each contract in the graph gets a risk score from seven checks: whether it's upgradeable, who the admin is, the multisig threshold, the timelock delay, oracle staleness, source verification and known incidents. Scores flow along the graph's edges, so a weak link two hops away still raises the protocol's overall score. You can see where the risk comes from, not just how big it is. The checks are generic. EIP-1967 proxies, Safe multisigs, timelocks and Chainlink feeds turn up across most of DeFi, so adding a protocol mostly means giving Macaron its starting contracts. The graph lives on Arkiv for structured querying. The raw evidence (full graph JSON, RPC trace log, bytecode) lives on Swarm, and each Arkiv entity links to its Swarm file. A Chainlink CRE workflow re-reads each protocol's key pointers from mainnet on a schedule. It hashes them into a fingerprint and rebuilds the graph only when something actually moved. In the UI you can click any node to trace its path back to the core contract, filter by hop, open its Arkiv entity in the explorer and follow the RPC calls behind its score on the audit page. For the hackathon we ran it end to end on Aave V3: 15 contracts across 3 hops, all written to Arkiv's Rabdi testnet. Next we plan to add more lending markets, DEXs and vaults and to link protocols to each other when one reads another's oracle or holds its tokens. Then a problem in one protocol shows up in the score of every protocol that depends on it.
projects.how_its_made: There are four parts: ingestion, storage, the CRE watcher and the frontend. One of us built each part and we agreed the interfaces in docs/ first so everyone could work in parallel against mock data. Ingestion (graph-service, TypeScript/Node) - The only protocol-specific step is the seed list of hop 0 contracts. For Aave we take it from the Aave address book. From there everything is generic. We read EIP-1967 implementation and admin slots straight from mainnet RPC to resolve proxies. We query the Safe Transaction API for signer sets and thresholds and follow AaveOracle.getSourceOfAsset() out to the Chainlink feeds. Verification status comes from Sourcify. The scorer is deterministic, so the same chain state always gives the same score. That was important because CRE has to be able to reproduce the result. Storage (Arkiv + Swarm) - We use three Arkiv entity types: protocol_registry_v1 is permanent. contract_node_v1 and risk_snapshot_v1 expire after 50,000 blocks (about a week). We chose that lifetime on purpose. A risk score nobody has re-checked in a week shouldn't be served as current. We index the fields the UI actually filters on (protocolId, hop, category, riskScore, sourcifyStatus) and store everything else as plain attributes. Big blobs go to Swarm. Arkiv only holds the reference, so queries stay small. CRE workflow (@chainlink/cre-sdk, run with the CRE CLI) - A cron trigger reads 18 pointers from Aave on mainnet in one Multicall3 call at the finalized block: pool and configurator revisions, the registry getters, oracle sources for 5 assets, the emergency admin, the Safe threshold and owners and the governance executor. It sorts and keccak256-hashes them into a fingerprint and compares that with the fingerprint stored in Arkiv. If they match, it stops. If they differ, it calls POST /rebuild on graph-service, which re-ingests, re-scores and writes fresh Arkiv entities and Swarm evidence. The list of calls is in a shared fingerprint-spec.json, so CRE and graph-service always hash exactly the same thing. Frontend (Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind) -  We draw the graph with our own SVG layout code, in hop lanes or a tree view. Node data is read from Arkiv with @arkiv-network/sdk. There's an audit page that walks through the 5 steps behind a score, with the exact storage slots and RPC calls. What was hacky: Arkiv u64 fields come back as BigInt, which breaks JSON.stringify and Next.js props. We wrote a replacer. Writing 15 entities in parallel caused nonce collisions, so writes are sequential. Filtering on a field that isn't indexed returns an empty list instead of an error. That cost us an hour.

projects.title: Dithub
projects.description: Decentralized Git & CI/CD: repos on Arkiv + Swarm, Chainlink CRE-verified builds, 0G-scoped access
projects.project_description: Git is distributed, but the places we host it aren't. When GitHub has a bad day, teams can't review, merge or sometimes even pull. Dithub is a git host that treats outages as the normal case. Your code lives on Swarm, your history lives on Arkiv, and every push is anchored on Sepolia, so anyone can rebuild a repo without trusting our server. You use it like GitHub: add it as a second remote, open issues and PRs, and push back to GitHub when it returns. We added task-scoped contractor sessions, where a developer sees only the files for one task and a private AI model on 0G answers questions about just those files. It's testnet only and not audited, but the whole pipeline works end to end.
projects.how_its_made: We built Dithub as one Bun/Hono service with a SQLite cache, a worker, and a Caddy front end, all in Docker Compose on a Linode. The interesting part is where the data goes. Git packs go to a Bee node on Swarm's testnet. Commit history, issues, PRs and permission changes go to Arkiv. Each push also lands one anchor transaction on Sepolia. SQLite is only a cache, so dit recover can rebuild a repo from Arkiv and Swarm with no help from our server, and we tested that. Chainlink CRE checks the deployed site against an on-chain release and writes an attestation. We ran that through CRE's simulator with the mock forwarder. 0G's Private Computer powers the AI assistant inside task-scoped sessions, so a contractor's questions stay inside their task's files. The painful part was Swarm: Bee refused to sync until we found an RPC that serves old logs, and we had to move a funded node between machines. Everything is testnet and unaudited.

projects.title: WeldPoint
projects.description: Weld timelines together as you move forward and backward in time.
projects.project_description: WeldPoint is a cooperative puzzle game where two players approach the same challenge from opposite directions in time. Player 1 moves forward from the start, while Player 2 moves backward from the end. Each controls the same boxes on their half of the timeline. At the midpoint, their box states must match to create a weld, joining both halves into one continuous timeline. Players then navigate their partner’s box movements in reverse, coordinating across space and time to escape. The community keeps WeldPoint evolving: players create custom chambers, compete on leaderboards and use recorded winning runs as replay partners. Web3 infrastructure powers the gameplay loop: Arkiv stores levels and runs as time-scoped entities with publicly queryable metadata. Puzzle layouts and solutions are encrypted to preserve the challenge. Community hearts extend a level’s onchain lifetime, giving players a say in which chambers remain available. Chainlink CRE replays submitted solutions against deterministic game rules. The Sepolia certification flow records a verdict before a new level becomes playable. Swarm and Arkiv work together to deliver theme packs: Arkiv entities hold content references and integrity hashes for Swarm-hosted artwork, which the game loads and verifies.
projects.how_its_made: We started around a table with paper: brainstorming the time mechanic, sketching level ideas, and drawing wireframes by hand. We tested our initial levels with real players before expanding the implementation. WeldPoint is built in TypeScript with Phaser 3 for rendering, Vite for the frontend build, and a Node.js server coordinating multiplayer sessions over WebSockets. A deterministic simulation engine powers authoritative gameplay, winning-run verification, and level certification. SQLite holds application state, publication queues, and recovery journals. The trickiest part was making two opposing timelines behave like one coherent puzzle. During the first half, players push boxes and build their histories. At the midpoint, corresponding box identities must occupy matching coordinates. Each player’s boxes then follow their partner’s recorded history in reverse, while players navigate toward their exits. Our most useful trick was implementing reverse time through recorded state snapshots. We restore the partner’s earlier box positions in reverse order instead of trying to invert physics. This preserves pauses and ice movements exactly. We also reuse recorded inputs from verified winning runs as replay partners for future solo games. We integrated Chainlink CRE into level publishing. A creator submits a level and winning solution; we freeze the submission with a layout hash, rules hash, and salted solution commitment. The workflow checks those commitments and replays the solution using the same game engine. We exercised this through CRE CLI simulation and implemented a Sepolia certification path where a registry checks the report against the registered commitment. Simulation results are explicitly labelled. Arkiv stores encrypted level and run payloads as entities with expiration deadlines, while indexed public metadata supports discovery. Expiration also becomes a social mechanic: each account can heart a publication once to extend its lifetime. The server independently verifies winning runs, records leaderboard results, and queues replay archives. For artwork, an Arkiv theme entity points to a Swarm release and its integrity hashes. Our server validates that pointer; the browser verifies the release and manifest before loading the sprite sheets. This lets us swap visual packs without changing puzzle rules. Finally, we kept blockchain latency outside the gameplay loop. Arkiv writes are serialized and durably journaled, and publication is confirmed only after checking transaction receipts and entity readback. Players can finish a game while their run archive remains pending, with its status visible in the interface.

projects.title: Codemark
projects.description: Before you sign, see which team released a contract under its ENS name and whether it was withdrawn.
projects.project_description: A wallet shows you 20 bytes and asks you to sign. In February 2025, Bybit's Safe signers approved a transaction that handed their wallet to an attacker's contract, because the page that built it had been swapped. Nothing on the signing screen could say "your team never released this code." EIP-7702 raises the stakes: one signature can let a contract control a whole account. Codemark puts that answer in front of you before you sign. Teams release contracts under their ENS name, such as router-3-1-0.ci-1.pwnmeswap.eth. The Snap or MCP server reads the transaction itself, finds every contract it touches, including approval spenders and calls nested inside batches and Safe transactions, and checks each one against the publishers you pinned. You get a plain answer: Verified, Released recently, Not verified or Don't sign. Below it is the trust path: publisher, release key, release, record, age. The first step that fails is marked in red, so you can see why. If a release key leaks, one transaction withdraws everything that key released. Every check after that shows Key revoked. There's no list of wallets to notify and no server to update. The same check runs in three places: Lookup site: paste an address or try the demo contracts. No wallet or sign-up. MetaMask Snap: checks each transaction before MetaMask asks you to confirm. It needs MetaMask Flask for now. MCP server for AI agents: nobody reads the signing screen when an agent signs, so the server returns proceed, ask_user or refuse. It holds no keys and signs nothing. Teams publish with a CLI or a GitHub Action, and there's no Codemark contract to deploy or audit. pwnmeswap.eth is live on Sepolia as a demo publisher, so you can check its releases today. What to know before relying on it: Codemark tells you who published a contract and whether they still stand behind it, not what the code does. Pinning the real name is what protects you from imitators. The MCP server helps an honest agent that was handed a bad address. It doesn't check amounts or recipients, and a hijacked agent could skip it. Codemark runs on Sepolia today.
projects.how_its_made:
Codemark is a Bun monorepo in TypeScript. One checker package (packages/lib/shared, built on viem and zod) runs everywhere: in the browser for the React site, in the MetaMask Snap sandbox, in the CLI and in the MCP server. There is no Codemark server and no custom Solidity. The site is static and reads Sepolia and Arkiv directly from the browser. ENSv2 (Sepolia) is what makes this work: Registries: a publisher is a .eth name owned by a team Safe, registered through ETHRegistrar with MockUSDC. Each signing key is its own UserRegistry mounted under that name, so a key is a subtree. One unregister ends every name below it. On ENSv1, deleting ci-1.pwnmeswap.eth leaves router.ci-1.pwnmeswap.eth resolving. Enhanced Access Control: the CI key holds only ROLE_REGISTRAR on one key registry, so it can add releases but not change or remove them. The security key holds only ROLE_UNREGISTER, so it can withdraw but not publish. Only the Safe can publish to the delegates key, where account-upgrade code lives. Permissioned Resolver: every release gets its own resolver through VerifiableFactory, created with its records and with setter roles for the Safe only. The checker proves the CI key can't rewrite a release: the resolver must be a genuine factory proxy running the expected implementation, its logs since creation must show no record, role or upgrade changes, and the Safe must be the only role holder. Universal Resolver: findResolver returning an offset other than 0 means the name has no resolver of its own (unregistered, pulled or under a cut key), and it's rejected. Expiry: a key's 90-day TTL bounds everything below it. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) solves what ENS can't: ENS can't be searched by address. We write two entity types with @arkiv-network/sdk: codemark.release.v1 from the CI key and codemark.incident.v1 from the security key. The site reads them to find which publisher claims an unknown address, to list a publisher's releases, to explain why a release was withdrawn (a pulled name otherwise looks like it was never published) and to get the block numbers where the log scan starts. Rows are untrusted. A row only counts if its creator holds the matching role in ENS, every claim is re-derived from ENS at one pinned block, and a flooded index can never produce a green result. MetaMask Snap: onTransaction and onSignature decode the request and show the same verdict and trust path as the site. Anything but a pinned, proven release that's old enough is critical for an account upgrade, which makes MetaMask ask for a double confirmation. MCP server: code maps the checker's result to proceed, ask_user or refuse, so the model doesn't decide. A check that doesn't finish refuses. Trusted publishers come only from the operator's config and no tool can add one, so a prompt-injected agent can't talk its way into trusting an attacker. Publisher-written text is treated as model input: an unpinned publisher's reason is dropped. The hacky parts: Sepolia has two ENSv2 deployments side by side. We use the one the canonical Universal Resolver actually reads, and the checker re-reads ROOT_REGISTRY() at the start of every check and refuses to run if it changes. The deployed contracts differ from the repository head, so our ABIs are pinned to contracts-v2 commit 07e55a05 and the checker's end-to-end tests run on an Anvil fork of Sepolia rather than mocks. An attack script publishes five forged releases that the checker must report as MISMATCH. Token ids change on every register and role change, so releases are keyed by labelhash and the current id is read from the registry. Pulling a release also reserves its labels, so a CI key can't simply re-register them. CI runs typecheck, lint and tests on every push, plus a job against live Sepolia that confirms the Universal Resolver still reads this deployment. The releases are public: browse explorer.ens.domains/pwnmeswap.eth, and the README lists every transaction and shows how to read the records with plain viem and no Codemark code.
A real withdrawal is live too: check 0x65aF9C81B6351c61F3657D47Ef29AEA319B7DAE5 on the lookup page and it says Don't sign, with the reason read from its Arkiv incident row. The router and portal under the same key still verify. The landing page footer is one WebGL scene driven by scroll, with a fox (your wallet, such as MetaMask) running past verified contracts and leaping revoked ones.

projects.title: Funcaster
projects.description: Make boring IRL events fun again. Play games and bet with your friends to beat them.
projects.project_description: Funcaster turns a TV or laptop into a multiplayer party console, with each player’s phone acting as their controller. Players scan a QR code, join the same room and play directly in their browsers—no app installation or dedicated gaming hardware required. The console brings together currently 5+ games for one to four players, including kart racing, table tennis, drawing, shooting and cooperative challenges. Its Windows XP-inspired interface combines a familiar desktop with game-specific phone controls, including joysticks, directional pads, action buttons and motion input. Funcaster also connects playing, watching and creating. Players can participate in shared prize pots, spectators can make winner predictions or contribute cheers, and creators can publish games with paid access and revenue splits. Arc handles the payment and settlement contracts, while ENS gives rooms and players human-readable on-chain identities. Transaction receipts provide a public trail for payments, settlements and refunds. The broader vision is a browser-native platform where indie developers can distribute social games and earn from them, while anyone with a screen and a few friends can host a game night. The hackathon implementation uses Arc Testnet and ENS on Sepolia, with test tokens. https://studio.arc.io/app/3e018243-4be8-4b94-a488-1f69c9401fae
projects.how_its_made: Funcaster uses JavaScript, HTML and CSS for its desktop shell and phone controllers, with Canvas and Three.js/WebGL powering the games. A Node.js server and Socket.IO connect the shared screen, phone controllers and spectators. Phone input travels through the relay to the game, while room state, readiness, reconnects and results are coordinated across devices. The interface is built around a Windows XP-style desktop and landscape phone controls. Existing games were adapted to share a common controller and multiplayer lifecycle. Where supported, deterministic game replays let a server-side checker verify results before they are used for settlement. The Web3 layer separates the public relay from transaction workers. Solidity contracts on Arc Testnet support conditional prize pots, prediction markets, shared payouts and creator payments. Browser-held keys sign payment authorizations, and funded relayers submit supported transactions so players do not need to manage gas for each interaction. Arc Studio helped develop and export the ConditionalPot contract and its accompanying console. ENS on Sepolia provides the funcaster.eth namespace, including room and player identities, resolver records and scoped controller permissions. This makes names part of room discovery and identity rather than simply decorative labels. Render hosts the relay, payment worker, separate prediction verifier and PostgreSQL database. PostgreSQL persists payment intents, jobs, recovery journals, receipts and verified game records across restarts. A particularly useful engineering detail is the recovery design: uncertain transactions retain their original identifiers and evidence so they can be reconciled without blindly sending them again. The public ledger also checks receipts through two RPC hosts before displaying an independently confirmed badge. This lets the game experience remain simple while keeping the underlying payment activity inspectable.

projects.title: Prowl
projects.description: Private wallet with passkey login, Tor-routed requests, and offline transfers.
projects.project_description: Prowl is a private Ethereum wallet that you unlock with a passkey (fingerprint, face or screen lock) instead of a seed phrase. It can keep your funds in a RAILGUN shielded balance, so payments hide the sender, recipient and amount. Every network request goes over Tor with a separate circuit for each identity, so RPC nodes can't link your addresses or see your IP. Private sends come from fresh one-time accounts, and the gas is paid from your private balance. On Android, Prowl also works as offline cash: coins backed by an on-chain escrow can be paid phone to phone over Bluetooth with no internet, and the phone's secure hardware allows each coin to be spent only once. There is no Prowl server, because the site is static files and you can run your own Tor gateway.
projects.how_its_made: Prowl is a pnpm monorepo with a React and TypeScript wallet built with Vite and shipped as static files. A passkey's WebAuthn PRF output is the root secret. HKDF derives the RAILGUN spending and viewing keys, the public account key and a storage key, and everything saved locally is sealed with AES-GCM, so there is no seed phrase. RAILGUN, through kohaku-railgun-wasm with our patches, runs in a worker and proves transactions on the device. Tor runs inside the page via tor-js, and our Anon-RPC package gives each identity (account, transaction, one-time sender) its own circuit, including RAILGUN's own fetch. Private sends are ERC-4337 UserOperations from fresh one-time EIP-7702 accounts, with the RAILGUN paymaster taking gas from the private balance and Pimlico as the bundler. The Android app (Kotlin and Compose) adds offline cash. Each coin is owned by an Android Keystore key limited to one signature (setMaxUsageCount(1), StrongBox where available) and backed by ETH in a Solidity escrow tested with Foundry. Over Bluetooth Low Energy, the receiving phone verifies Google's key attestation, every signature, and a light-client proof of the deposit from a finalized Ethereum block, using a Java verifier with blst through JNI. If faked hardware ever signs twice, the two signatures are public proof, and the escrow freezes that coin's branch. The private-swap module uses Zama FHEVM for encrypted orders and settles only the netted residual on a real Uniswap v4 pool through the Universal Router. The hackiest part is a patched tor-js worker (keepalive.patch) that reuses connections per isolation key and origin without linking identities. The worker is loaded by a pinned keccak hash. We also ship prebuilt RAILGUN pool snapshots, because syncing over Tor is slow, and use a hybrid where the Android app embeds the website and talks to it through a window.prawlOffline bridge. We used the pool's own price as the swap oracle, guarded by a 2% move limit and a 97% output floor.

On Android, Prowl also works as offline cash: coins backed by an on-chain escrow can be paid phone to phone over Bluetooth with no internet, and the phone's secure hardware allows each coin to be spent only once. There is no Prowl server, because the site is static files and you can run your own Tor gateway.
projects.how_its_made_markdown: Prowl is a pnpm monorepo with a React and TypeScript wallet built with Vite and shipped as static files. A passkey's WebAuthn PRF output is the root secret. HKDF derives the RAILGUN spending and viewing keys, the public account key and a storage key, and everything saved locally is sealed with AES-GCM, so there is no seed phrase. RAILGUN, through kohaku-railgun-wasm with our patches, runs in a worker and proves transactions on the device. Tor runs inside the page via tor-js, and our Anon-RPC package gives each identity (account, transaction, one-time sender) its own circuit, including RAILGUN's own fetch. Private sends are ERC-4337 UserOperations from fresh one-time EIP-7702 accounts, with the RAILGUN paymaster taking gas from the private balance and Pimlico as the bundler. The Android app (Kotlin and Compose) adds offline cash. Each coin is owned by an Android Keystore key limited to one signature (setMaxUsageCount(1), StrongBox where available) and backed by ETH in a Solidity escrow tested with Foundry. Over Bluetooth Low Energy, the receiving phone verifies Google's key attestation, every signature, and a light-client proof of the deposit from a finalized Ethereum block, using a Java verifier with blst through JNI. If faked hardware ever signs twice, the two signatures are public proof, and the escrow freezes that coin's branch. The private-swap module uses Zama FHEVM for encrypted orders and settles only the netted residual on a real Uniswap v4 pool through the Universal Router. The hackiest part is a patched tor-js worker (keepalive.patch) that reuses connections per isolation key and origin without linking identities. The worker is loaded by a pinned keccak hash. We also ship prebuilt RAILGUN pool snapshots, because syncing over Tor is slow, and use a hybrid where the Android app embeds the website and talks to it through a window.prawlOffline bridge. We used the pool's own price as the swap oracle, guarded by a 2% move limit and a 97% output floor.

projects.title: Tap2ETH
projects.description: Turns your existing bank card into an Ethereum hardware wallet, compatible with POS terminals
projects.project_description:
Hardware wallets have a supply-chain problem. In October 2026, tampered Ledger devices sold through one reseller led to an estimated $86M+ in losses. A similar hidden implant was then found in a Trezor device from the same reseller, built to steal recovery phrases. Seed phrases remain a single point of failure, and flaws in how they are generated have exposed more wallets. Tap2ETH avoids both problems by using a secure chip people already own. Every contactless EMV bank card that supports Dynamic Data Authentication holds an RSA private key that was loaded by the bank and can’t be extracted. The card signs a reader-chosen challenge, and its public key is certified from the card network to the bank to the card. There is no new device to buy, no reseller to trust and no seed phrase to steal. We make that card one signer of a self-custodial smart-contract wallet. The second signer is a fingerprint-locked key in your phone’s secure hardware. The card is used only as a key: no card payment is processed and your bank account is never charged. You can use it in two ways: Pay a merchant: the merchant enters an amount, you tap your card on the terminal, and you approve on your phone with your fingerprint.
Send to any address: enter the address and amount in the app, tap your card on the phone, and confirm with your fingerprint. In both cases, the wallet checks both signatures and its limits on-chain before sending stablecoins. A card has no screen and signs only 4 bytes, so your phone shows what you’re approving and signs the full payment hash. Neither a stolen card, a stolen phone nor the bank that created the card key can move funds alone. The wallet also supports several cards and phones with a t-of-n threshold, per-payment and daily limits, instant freeze from the phone, and time-locked recovery. We also built a DIY hardware merchant POS device, so the whole flow works with a physical terminal. This gives merchant tap 2 pay functionality requiring powered by secure multisig
projects.how_its_made:
How it’s made
Getting a real card to sign. We started on day one with an M5StickS3, an M5Stack RFID 2 reader and a real Indian-issued Mastercard. Our firmware runs the EMV sequence: SELECT PPSE, SELECT AID, GET PROCESSING OPTIONS with a zero amount, READ RECORD and INTERNAL AUTHENTICATE. It never asks for a PIN or a payment. A Python tool then verified the full chain offline: Mastercard CA key, bank key, card key, then the signature over our challenge. Paying a merchant: The merchant enters the amount on our POS terminal.
The card is tapped and signs the first 4 bytes of the payment hash.
The payment request goes to the user’s phone.
The user approves with their fingerprint, and the phone signs the full 32-byte hash.
The signatures are sent on-chain by a relayer that pays gas but can’t move funds.
The smart wallet checks both signatures and its limits, then sends the stablecoins to the merchant.
Sending on-chain. The phone does the terminal’s job. The user enters an address and amount, taps the card on the phone over NFC, and approves with a fingerprint. Both signatures then go to the wallet, which runs the same checks and pays any address. Multiple signers and recovery. A wallet can have several cards and phones with a t-of-n threshold, and every normal approval needs at least one phone. If a phone is lost, two enrolled cards start recovery. After a time-lock delay, the new phone replaces the old one, and any signer can cancel during that delay. This two-card recovery is demo-strength today. A stronger version is written and tested but not deployed. Smart contracts. These are Solidity 0.8.28 with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin. We recover the card’s ISO/IEC 9796-2 signature block through the modexp precompile, check its structure, and recompute the SHA-1 hash in Solidity because the EVM has no SHA-1 precompile. SHA-1 turned out to be the main gas cost, at about 38k gas per block, while RSA with exponent 3 is cheap. The phone is verified as a WebAuthn P-256 assertion. Wallets are minimal clones, and a registry maps a hash of the card’s public key to its wallet. Android app. It uses React Native and Expo, with react-native-nfc-manager for card reads. A custom Kotlin Expo module generates a secp256r1 key in Android Keystore and requires a strong biometric for every signature. DIY POS device. It’s a Raspberry Pi with a 3.5″ touchscreen, a Python service and a Chromium kiosk UI, with the RFID reader wired directly over I2C. The terminal checks the payment on-chain itself and doesn’t rely only on the backend. Relayer. A Node and Express server built on ethers and viem connects the terminal and phone, collects signatures, simulates and submits transactions, and pays gas. It has backup RPC fallback and rate limits.

projects.title: Anyflo AMM Solver
projects.description: DeFi liquidity for business stablecoin payments using Uniswap and 1inch Aqua.
projects.project_description: Anyflo Solver is a hackathon project connecting business stablecoin payments with DeFi liquidity. It builds on Anyflo’s existing non-custodial order and auction APIs, targeting a standalone Solver with two execution strategies: Uniswap AMM swaps and custom 1inch Aqua positions powered by SwapVM. The design uses verified customer deposits to obtain the required payout token, reducing the need for solvers to hold every supported asset in advance. A planned Foundry demo combines test tokens, a mock Solver Hub and real local protocol execution to demonstrate funding, swapping and payment delivery. Anyflo gains more liquidity options, while Uniswap and Aqua gain a business-payment use case connecting DeFi with regulated payment rails. Future work will add execution-plan and route compliance checks before bidding and executing; these checks are outside the hackathon scope.
projects.how_its_made: Anyflo is main my project that I working on. It's an embedded finance system, providing payments API with corridor-specific compliance. For the hackathon I wanted to extend our real business use case: (invoice payments and verifiable (for compliance ) payments) using the DeFi liquidity. Firstly I researched the latest from Uniswap and 1inch. I learned about 1inch Aqua (I didn't know about it before). I analyzed UniswapX (realized that the liquidity there is low and in general it is a not good fit - lack of good support and problems with solvers). I defined the hackathon scope: small independent Solver repository, to execute Anyflo orders based on our API: https://docs.anyflo.io Then I defined the work plan: Minimal two-strategy Anyflo AMM Solver Test required interfaces Mock existing Anyflo API (for demo purposes) Wire the Anyflo AMM Solver with the Anyflo Mock Create a demo script to test it with mainnet liquidity (Base and Arbitrum mainnet). Then I used AI to verify my approach, create implementation plan and run the agents to code it. In the meantime I started the work on the presentation with help of another AI agent.

projects.title: QuietOdds
projects.description: Private prediction markets and a Uniswap v4 privacy layer. The odds are public, the bettors aren't.
projects.project_description: QuietOdds is a private prediction market and a privacy layer for Uniswap v4, live on Ethereum Sepolia at quietodds.vercel.app. On today's prediction markets and DEXs, every bet and every swap is tied to your wallet forever. Anyone can see what you backed, how much, and when, and bots can see your swap coming and trade around it. QuietOdds fixes that. You deposit USDC or ETH once, publicly. From then on your money sits in a shielded pool as hidden notes, and everything else you do is private: Bet on F1 races, football matches and crypto prices. Your browser makes a zero-knowledge proof that you own a note, without saying which one, and a relayer sends the transaction. The chain only sees "someone bet 1 USDC on Verstappen". Not who. Claim winnings. A second proof works out your exact share of the pot and pays it back to you as a new hidden note. Shield while you swap. Our Uniswap v4 hook moves part of any ETH/USDC swap straight into your private balance, inside the same swap. You can also queue a private bet that the relayer places a few minutes later, so the bet can't be linked to the swap. Swap privately in batches. You join a batch from your hidden balance, and every 5 minutes the whole batch swaps through the v4 pool as one trade, with a minimum price from Chainlink. Everyone gets the same price, and nobody can see who was in it. Withdraw to any address, even a brand new wallet with 0 ETH. The same hook protects swappers and liquidity providers. If someone tries a sandwich attack in one block, the second half of the attack pays a fee as large as the price move it caused, so the attack doesn't pay. The extra goes to the liquidity providers, and the 1% market fees are donated to them as well. Markets are settled by a Chainlink CRE workflow that reads ESPN for sports and F1 and Chainlink price feeds for crypto. It also runs due batch swaps and donates fees, all in one report. Every read the app makes goes through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC mixnet, so the RPC node can't link your IP to the pool reads that come just before your private bet. The core money rules (no money created by a spend, exact payouts, winners never take more than the pot, and sandwiches don't pay) are proved in Lean 4. Everything is real on Sepolia: real proofs, real swaps through our hooked pool, real resolution. The README lists the transaction hashes.
projects.how_its_made:
Circuits: two Noir circuits, proved with UltraHonk via Barretenberg (bb.js) right in the browser in about one second. The page runs with COOP/COEP headers so the prover can use every CPU core.
spend (25.7k gates) proves a note is in a depth-20 Poseidon Merkle tree, burns its nullifier, and checks amount = change + public amount + fee with 128-bit range checks. The action, market, side, relayer, fee and recipient are all public inputs, so the relayer can't redirect anything. "redeem" (27.7k gates) proves payout = floor(stake × pot / winning side) using a range-checked remainder. The contract supplies the payout ratio, never the user.
There are three note types (balance, bet position, batch ticket), and all three live in one tree. Each note is posted on chain encrypted to your viewing key, so logging in on any browser rescans and recovers everything. Contracts (Foundry, 118 tests including real proof fixtures, fuzzing and invariants): ShieldedPool, Markets, BatchSwapper, ResolverReceiver, the generated verifiers, and QuietOddsHook. Uniswap v4: the hook uses beforeSwap and afterSwap, both with return deltas. The swap's hookData carries a shield amount and an encrypted note. The hook takes that amount from the swap with poolManager.take and deposits it into the shielded pool, all within one swap, for all four swap shapes. The anti-sandwich part is ported from OpenZeppelin's AntiSandwichHook. The hook stores the price at the start of the block. A swap that reverses the block's price move gets a higher fee through a dynamic fee override. One-direction overpayments are skimmed and donated to liquidity providers in the same swap. BatchSwapper runs batches through poolManager.unlock (swap, settle, take). Its minimum output comes from Chainlink, so a manipulated pool makes the batch revert instead of filling badly. Market fees go to liquidity providers via poolManager.donate. A Next.js server route uses the Uniswap Trading API for comparison quotes and plain cash-out swaps, keeping the API key on the server. Chainlink CRE: a TypeScript workflow on a cron trigger. treads every market, batch and the fee balance in a single Multicall3 call, because CRE allows 15 chain reads per run. It fetches ESPN results through the HTTP capability with median consensus, and price markets through Chainlink feeds. It sends one report per run to ResolverReceiver, which resolves or cancels markets, executes due batches and donates fees. F1 winners come from ESPN's race "winner" flag, with an "Anyone else" side for the rest of the grid. We run it with "cre workflow simulate --broadcast", which sends real reports to Sepolia. Anon-RPC: the app's single wagmi/viem transport uses a fetchFn that sends every request through a hash-pinned AnonRpcWorker on the EF's mixnet. Reads are batched so each slow mixnet round trip carries many calls. If 3 mixnet requests fail in a row, reads go direct while the worker reconnects with backoff, and the nav chip always shows the real state. This matters for privacy: otherwise the RPC node could link your IP'sMerkle-path reads to the relayer's spend a few seconds later. Relayer: Hono + viem on Vercel. It verifies each proof with bb.js, simulates the transaction, then sends it and pays the gas. It is rate-limited and keeps no IP logs. App: Next.js and wagmi. Keys come from one wallet signature or a passkey (WebAuthn PRF) and stay in memory only. Queued bets are saved perwallet, and the app places them once you unlock. Lean 4 + Mathlib: zero sorry. Theorems show that the circuits' field equations and range checks really mean value is conserved with no wraparound, that payouts are exact, that pro-rata payouts never exceed the pot, and that the directional fee makes a one-block sandwichunprofitable. There is also a counterexample showing where our 50% fee cap stops protecting.

projects.title: MicroCover
projects.description: Programmable guarantees that protect customer payments and back promises with locked funds.
projects.project_description: MicroCover lets an organiser or service provider back a promise with funds locked in a smart contract. Customers join by making a payment that remains protected until the outcome is resolved. If failure is established, each customer can receive their payment back plus the agreed compensation. If success is finalized after a review window, the payment goes to the provider and the backing funds are returned. If a case remains unresolved after its fixed timeout, customers receive their payments back without extra compensation. Our concert ticket page demonstrates this general guarantee model with test USDC on Arc Testnet. The concert evidence is synthetic and controlled by our team; this prototype does not independently detect a real cancellation or measure a delay.
projects.how_its_made: We built the guarantee contract on Arc Testnet using Solidity and Foundry. The provider locks a USDC compensation bond; customers approve and pay USDC into the contract, which tracks enrollment and settles success, failure or unresolved refunds in bounded steps. A persistent TypeScript evidence service collects authenticated records from two team-controlled synthetic feeds and evaluates a fixed policy. Event details are committed by a hash in the organiser’s creation transaction, stored by the service, and checked against onchain terms before the customer can buy. The React frontend provides separate organiser and customer flows. Arkiv publishes and retrieves public activity receipts, with integrity checks against an Arc anchor. We built a Chainlink CRE adapter and tested its workflow through simulation; the live outcome submission in this demo uses a trusted operator, not a deployed CRE network.
