projects.title: proofbolt
projects.description: A physical lock AI can't open alone: Arkiv grants, 0G decisions, on-chain proof, real hardware.
projects.project_description: proofbolt is a physical lock, built on a real ESP8266 with a servo, that AI can't open by itself. It opens only when a live access grant on Arkiv, its secret access code, a 0G AI decision and a one-time signed command all pass. If any step fails, including 0G or Arkiv being unreachable, the door stays locked. An owner creates an access link and QR code that lasts as long as they choose. The person scans it, and a 3D lock shows their camera and a random challenge, like "4 fingers". The photo goes to a 0G vision model, which answers OPEN, HOLD or ALERT. HOLD gives a new challenge, up to three tries. ALERT catches screens, printed pictures and notes trying to trick the AI. A separate policy then checks the grant again, so an owner can revoke access mid-attempt, and even a fooled AI can't open a revoked grant. If everything passes, the gateway sends the board a signed one-time command. The board holds no AI and no policy: it only checks the signature, moves the bolt, and relocks after x time (5 seconds for now). Every decision is recorded. The full record, with its 0G request ID, goes to 0G Storage, and its hash is anchored on 0G Chain, so anyone can rebuild and verify the history from 0G alone. A public status page reads only Arkiv: the locker's record lasts 60 seconds and the gateway keeps renewing it, so if the gateway dies, the record expires and the page shows Offline. It's a prototype on testnets. Access works by secret link, with no identity check, and the gateway is a trusted party.
projects.how_its_made:
The gateway is TypeScript on Node with Hono, running on a laptop. It connects a React kiosk, the ESP8266 firmware (C++ with PlatformIO) and the two partner stacks. 0G: The gateway sends each photo and random challenge to the 0G Router (qwen3.8-flash), using its OpenAI-compatible API. Only a strict JSON answer counts, and anything else means no decision. If 0G is unreachable, the board shows SAFE STOP and the record shows no decision was made, with no fake fallback. Each hash-chained record, with its 0G request ID, is uploaded to 0G Storage using the TypeScript SDK, then a small Solidity contract, DecisionAnchor, anchors its hash and storage root on Galileo. "pnpm zerog replay" downloads every record with Merkle proofs and checks the hashes and chain. Publishing runs in the background, resumes after failures, and never affects the door. Arkiv: Using @arkiv-network/sdk on Rabdi, we store grants, a live locker record, attempts, and pointers to the 0G records. Expiry is product logic: grants end by themselves, and the locker's 60-second record has to keep being renewed, so a dead gateway shows up with nobody reporting it. Anyone can transfer an entity to our wallet, so every read checks both creator and owner. Access codes never go on Arkiv, only a SHA-256 hash of a random 128-bit code. Arkiv is read twice per unlock, so a revocation during the AI call still counts. The lock: Commands are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over a one-time nonce from the board, which sends back a signed acknowledgement. If the gateway goes quiet for 8 seconds, the board relocks. If Wi-Fi stays stuck for 60 seconds, it restarts, and it always comes back locked. The front end uses React, Motion, Arc components installed through the shadcn CLI, and Three.js. The hacky part we like: the 3D padlock has no real screen, so we draw the live webcam, the challenge and the countdown onto a canvas and use it as a texture on the lock's face, while a scripted camera shoots it like a phone commercial. Each access link also cuts a 3D key whose teeth come from the grant's ID.
Testing on the real board found a bug PC tests missed: a clock comparison wrapped around and relocked the door right after a valid OPEN.
We chose the project, wired the hardware and ran the manual tests.

projects.title: Parlay-markets
projects.description: On-chain parlays on 1inch Aqua: LMSR pricing, Chainlink CRE settlement, cross-chain buys via CCIP
projects.project_description: Parlay Markets is a fully on-chain sports parlay betting protocol built on Ethereum Sepolia. Users pick 2–5 match outcomes (e.g. Man City wins AND Real Madrid wins) and stake USDC to receive a parlay ticket NFT. Pricing uses a Logarithmic Market Scoring Rule (LMSR) AMM — each leg's implied probability is read on-chain, multiplied together with a 10% house margin, and the payout is computed as stake ÷ combined_price. Liquidity for payouts is sourced virtually through 1inch Aqua: the LP's USDC never leaves their wallet until a winning ticket is claimed. Cross-chain buying is supported via Chainlink CCIP — users on Base Sepolia can send USDC and parlay legs in a single CCIP message, and the receiver on Ethereum Sepolia mints their ticket atomically. Market resolution is wired to Chainlink CRE (Compute Runtime Environment) for automated settlement. Winners claim payouts directly from the ParlayVault smart contract.
projects.how_its_made: The core stack is Solidity (Foundry) + Next.js 15 + wagmi v2 + viem. LmsrMarket.sol implements a custom LMSR AMM with configurable liquidity parameter b, storing outcome shares and computing prices via the standard exp-based scoring rule. AquaParlayRouter.sol integrates 1inch Aqua's virtual liquidity: the LP calls Aqua.ship() to register a payout reserve, and on every parlay purchase the router calls Aqua.pull() to transfer exactly the payout amount from the LP's wallet. ParlayVault.sol is an ERC-721-style ticket registry — it mints tickets on purchase and pays out on claim after all legs resolve. CCIPParlayReceiver.sol handles incoming Chainlink CCIP messages from Base Sepolia, decodes the parlay legs, pulls USDC from a reserve, and mints the ticket on the destination chain. MarketResolver.sol is the resolution oracle, callable only by the Chainlink CRE forwarder address. The frontend uses a custom wagmi transport that routes reads through public RPCs and signing through the injected wallet, working around Alchemy's EIP-7702 delegated-account rate limits.

projects.title: raisinFi
projects.description: Cross-Chain Coordination State Engine Layer for Tokenised Markets
projects.project_description: RaisinFi is a cross-chain financial coordination platform that enables participants to execute transactions involving assets on different blockchains through a single, coordinated lifecycle. Consider a simple example: Alice wants to purchase tokenised assets from Bob, but the payment and the asset exist on different networks. Normally, coordinating both sides introduces risks: one participant could lock their funds while the other never delivers, transactions could become inconsistent across chains, or one side could remain stuck waiting for the other. RaisinFi addresses this coordination problem by connecting the transaction's entire lifecycle. Participants agree on shared transaction terms, independently reserve their respective assets on their native chains, and let a coordination layer verify that the required conditions have been satisfied before initiating settlement. Each agreement is bound to a unique transaction ID and a canonical terms hash, ensuring that both chains refer to exactly the same transaction. A write-once decision mechanism on the payment chain determines whether the transaction commits or aborts. The corresponding decision is then relayed to the asset chain, where the reserved asset is either delivered or released. Our architecture uses Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) as the cross-chain orchestration layer, with smart contracts enforcing reservation and settlement rules on each chain. The goal is to make complex multi-chain transactions behave like one understandable, coordinated financial operation, without requiring participants to surrender custody of their assets to a central intermediary. Our initial demonstration uses Ethereum Sepolia and Base Sepolia, with two participants exchanging test tokens across both networks. RaisinFi is designed to extend this coordination model to more complex financial workflows and tokenised asset transactions.
projects.how_its_made: RaisinFi is built using Solidity, TypeScript, Next.js and Chainlink's Runtime Environment (CRE). The smart contract layer consists of two settlement contracts deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and Base Sepolia. The payment-side contract manages transaction registration, payment reservations and the authoritative write-once COMMIT/ABORT decision. The asset-side contract manages asset reservations and executes delivery or release after receiving an authenticated decision relay. Every transaction is represented by a shared Terms structure containing the participants, chain IDs, settlement contract addresses, token addresses, amounts and expiry. Both contracts independently compute and validate the canonical terms hash, preventing mismatched transaction parameters across chains. We use Chainlink CRE as the orchestration layer. Its TypeScript workflow reads on-chain events and state, verifies matching reservations and transaction terms, and prepares the appropriate coordination report for cross-chain execution. We also built report encoding and reconciliation logic to handle retries, duplicate reports and missed events without changing an already-recorded settlement decision. The frontend is built with Next.js and TypeScript, using Viem and wallet connectivity to let participants register agreements, approve tokens, reserve assets and inspect the transaction lifecycle directly through their wallets. The interface reads both chains and presents their states in a shared transaction timeline. One particularly important engineering decision is our separation of safety from liveness: the destination chain cannot independently refund a reservation simply because it has timed out. It must receive the authoritative decision from the payment chain. This means temporary orchestration failures can delay settlement, but cannot independently cause contradictory outcomes. We are initially validating the workflow on Sepolia and Base Sepolia using custom ERC-20 demo tokens. Our architecture also includes an evidence layer intended for Arkiv integration, allowing transaction lifecycle records to be independently queried and associated with participants.

projects.title: Meshy
projects.description: A decentralized mesh VPN for people and AI agents: access is an ENS name, revoke on-chain to cut it.
projects.project_description:
TL;DR
Meshy gives AI agents time-boxed, folder-scoped access to real machines, and every permission is an ENSv2 name. Unregister the name on-chain and the agent's live session dies in the same block. THE PROBLEM
Agents now need SSH and file access to servers, Raspberry Pis and GPU boxes. Today that means permanent SSH keys or all-or-nothing VPNs: no expiry, no folder scoping, no trustworthy audit trail, and no reliable kill switch. HOW MESHY SOLVES IT Access is a name: claude-1.db1.prod.acme.meshy.eth = one agent, one machine, one hour, /srv read-only. Revoke is one transaction: the daemon re-checks every live session on every block and kills it about 150 ms after the block lands. Sandboxed sessions: the agent sees only the granted folders and has no network. Tamper-evident audit: every read, write and blocked attempt is encrypted to the org key and written to Arkiv. Deny-by-default WireGuard mesh, rebuilt from ENS every 10 seconds. Self-serve: create an org (you.meshy.eth) in one transaction and invite people by link, QR code, wallet or email. IMPACT Access expires by default, so a leaked credential stops working on its own. The access list is public chain state: there is no vendor database to breach or quietly edit. Anyone can run the network: providers stake ETH and are slashed if they admit a revoked agent. USE CASES Let Claude Code debug a production database for one hour, read-only. Share a home lab, Raspberry Pi or camera with a teammate's agent, then revoke it. Give contractors' agents scoped access with a complete audit trail. Manage agent access across Macs and Linux boxes from one menu-bar app. OPEN-SOURCE PROJECTS WE BUILT ON NetBird: provider mesh. Open-source WireGuard control plane; meshy-sync turns ENS grants into NetBird groups and policies. WireGuard: transport. Fast, audited encryption between every peer. go-ethereum: daemon and CLI. ENS reads, per-block watching and transaction signing in Go. gliderlabs/ssh: meshyd. Custom SSH server that authenticates agents from their ENS records. bubblewrap + go-fuse: Linux sandbox. Our GateFS checks every file path against the grant policy. Foundry: contracts. Fork tests against the real ENSv2 contracts on Sepolia. viem, Next.js, shadcn/ui, Tailwind: dashboard. Wallet sign-in, ENS reads and the admin UI. Traefik + Let's Encrypt: provider TLS with zero DNS setup.
projects.how_its_made:
ENSv2 (ENS)
Why: ENSv2 gives every name its own registry, native expiry and role-based access control (EAC), so the name tree itself can be the access-control list.
How: orgs, networks, devices, agents, people and grants are all ENSv2 names on Sepolia. Grants are minted with no roles, so an agent can't renew or transfer its own access; expiry is ENS expiry and revoke is unregister. EAC roles give network admins power only inside their network. Each agent has its own PermissionedResolver and can set only its SSH key. MeshyOrgFactory creates a full org in one transaction, and MeshyInvites lets admins sign EIP-712 invites that anyone can claim on-chain. Arkiv
Why: we needed an audit log that the org's own admin can't edit or delete, and that the dashboard can query without trusting our servers.
How: meshyd writes session, blocked-attempt and audit-chunk entities with their own lifetimes. Payloads are gzipped and encrypted to the org key. Reads filter by $owner against the daemon address published in ENS, so spoofed entities are ignored. There's no Go SDK, so we hand-encode raw execute() transactions. Ethereum + Sepolia + Foundry (Ethereum Foundation)
Why: open, verifiable infrastructure with no trusted operator.
How: ProviderRegistry lets anyone stake to run tunnels; each admission is an EIP-712 attestation, and anyone can slash a provider that admitted an expired grant, checked against ENSv2 on-chain (half the stake goes to the reporter). MeshySubscription sells seats in USDC. 31 Foundry tests run against a Sepolia fork, and the contracts are verified on Sourcify and Blockscout. NetBird + WireGuard
Why: a production-grade, open-source WireGuard mesh with an API, so we didn't have to build NAT traversal.
How: meshy-sync runs beside NetBird on AWS EC2 and reconciles ENS state every 10 seconds: one group per device or agent, one policy per live grant, and NetBird's allow-all default deleted. The mesh client runs in userspace (no root) through NetBird's embed package, in its own Go module because of a pion/stun version clash with go-ethereum. meshyd: go-ethereum + gliderlabs/ssh
Why: one small Go binary that can watch the chain and terminate sessions directly.
How: a custom SSH/SFTP server authenticates agents from ENS records and only forwards ports declared in ENS. A watcher re-checks every live grant on every block and fails closed if the chain head goes stale. Sandboxing: bubblewrap + go-fuse, sandbox-exec
Why: a grant should mean those folders and nothing else.
How: on Linux, bubblewrap plus GateFS (a go-fuse filesystem) checks every path and blocks symlink and .. escapes. On macOS, a sandbox-exec profile, with blocked attempts turned into audit events. Dashboard: Next.js + viem + shadcn/ui
Why: a wallet-native admin console that reads straight from the chain.
How: Sign-In with Ethereum, the org tree loaded from ENS (cut from 144 RPC calls to 13 with Multicall3), a live Arkiv activity feed, an access Gantt chart and kill-latency stats. Hosted on Vercel at meshy.live; invite emails go out through Resend. Mac app (Swift/AppKit) and CLI
Why: people and agents live in the menu bar and the terminal.
How: a menu-bar app with wallet sign-in, auto-discovered orgs, Finder-mounted shared folders and access requests. A one-line installer (get.meshy.live) ships the meshy CLI, a terminal dashboard and a Claude Code plugin, so agents can join and request access themselves. World ID
How: the World ID Agent Pass flow (OIDC, token checks, signed attestation stored in ENS) is implemented; the demo org uses a dev-signed attestation.

- Tamper-evident audit: every read, write and blocked attempt is encrypted to the org key and written to Arkiv.
- Deny-by-default WireGuard mesh, rebuilt from ENS every 10 seconds.
- Self-serve: create an org (you.meshy.eth) in one transaction and invite people by link, QR code, wallet or email.

IMPACT
- Access expires by default, so a leaked credential stops working on its own.
- The access list is public chain state: there is no vendor database to breach or quietly edit.
- Anyone can run the network: providers stake ETH and are slashed if they admit a revoked agent.

USE CASES
- Let Claude Code debug a production database for one hour, read-only.
- Share a home lab, Raspberry Pi or camera with a teammate's agent, then revoke it.
- Give contractors' agents scoped access with a complete audit trail.
- Manage agent access across Macs and Linux boxes from one menu-bar app.

OPEN-SOURCE PROJECTS WE BUILT ON
- NetBird: provider mesh. Open-source WireGuard control plane; meshy-sync turns ENS grants into NetBird groups and policies.
- WireGuard: transport. Fast, audited encryption between every peer.
- go-ethereum: daemon and CLI. ENS reads, per-block watching and transaction signing in Go.
- gliderlabs/ssh: meshyd. Custom SSH server that authenticates agents from their ENS records.
- bubblewrap + go-fuse: Linux sandbox. Our GateFS checks every file path against the grant policy.
- Foundry: contracts. Fork tests against the real ENSv2 contracts on Sepolia.
- viem, Next.js, shadcn/ui, Tailwind: dashboard. Wallet sign-in, ENS reads and the admin UI.
- Traefik + Let's Encrypt: provider TLS with zero DNS setup.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ENSv2 (ENS)
Why: ENSv2 gives every name its own registry, native expiry and role-based access control (EAC), so the name tree itself can be the access-control list.
How: orgs, networks, devices, agents, people and grants are all ENSv2 names on Sepolia. Grants are minted with no roles, so an agent can't renew or transfer its own access; expiry is ENS expiry and revoke is unregister. EAC roles give network admins power only inside their network. Each agent has its own PermissionedResolver and can set only its SSH key. MeshyOrgFactory creates a full org in one transaction, and MeshyInvites lets admins sign EIP-712 invites that anyone can claim on-chain.

Arkiv
Why: we needed an audit log that the org's own admin can't edit or delete, and that the dashboard can query without trusting our servers.
How: meshyd writes session, blocked-attempt and audit-chunk entities with their own lifetimes. Payloads are gzipped and encrypted to the org key. Reads filter by $owner against the daemon address published in ENS, so spoofed entities are ignored. There's no Go SDK, so we hand-encode raw execute() transactions.

Ethereum + Sepolia + Foundry (Ethereum Foundation)
Why: open, verifiable infrastructure with no trusted operator.
How: ProviderRegistry lets anyone stake to run tunnels; each admission is an EIP-712 attestation, and anyone can slash a provider that admitted an expired grant, checked against ENSv2 on-chain (half the stake goes to the reporter). MeshySubscription sells seats in USDC. 31 Foundry tests run against a Sepolia fork, and the contracts are verified on Sourcify and Blockscout.

NetBird + WireGuard
Why: a production-grade, open-source WireGuard mesh with an API, so we didn't have to build NAT traversal.
How: meshy-sync runs beside NetBird on AWS EC2 and reconciles ENS state every 10 seconds: one group per device or agent, one policy per live grant, and NetBird's allow-all default deleted. The mesh client runs in userspace (no root) through NetBird's embed package, in its own Go module because of a pion/stun version clash with go-ethereum.

meshyd: go-ethereum + gliderlabs/ssh
Why: one small Go binary that can watch the chain and terminate sessions directly.
How: a custom SSH/SFTP server authenticates agents from ENS records and only forwards ports declared in ENS. A watcher re-checks every live grant on every block and fails closed if the chain head goes stale.

Sandboxing: bubblewrap + go-fuse, sandbox-exec
Why: a grant should mean those folders and nothing else.
How: on Linux, bubblewrap plus GateFS (a go-fuse filesystem) checks every path and blocks symlink and .. escapes. On macOS, a sandbox-exec profile, with blocked attempts turned into audit events.

Dashboard: Next.js + viem + shadcn/ui
Why: a wallet-native admin console that reads straight from the chain.
How: Sign-In with Ethereum, the org tree loaded from ENS (cut from 144 RPC calls to 13 with Multicall3), a live Arkiv activity feed, an access Gantt chart and kill-latency stats. Hosted on Vercel at meshy.live; invite emails go out through Resend.

Mac app (Swift/AppKit) and CLI
Why: people and agents live in the menu bar and the terminal.
How: a menu-bar app with wallet sign-in, auto-discovered orgs, Finder-mounted shared folders and access requests. A one-line installer (get.meshy.live) ships the meshy CLI, a terminal dashboard and a Claude Code plugin, so agents can join and request access themselves.

World ID
How: the World ID Agent Pass flow (OIDC, token checks, signed attestation stored in ENS) is implemented; the demo org uses a dev-signed attestation.

projects.title: crash lab
projects.description: Crash tests for robots: AI builds test worlds, and bounties pay engineers to fix what fails.
projects.project_description: CrashLab is crash testing for robots. Pick a robot and describe its job in chat, and an AI agent builds a test world for it, such as a glass tower for a window cleaning robot or an industrial plant for an ANYmal inspection robot. Change the world in plain words, like "add snow" or "add an antenna on the roof". The agent then lists the test scenarios: wind, wet glass, low suction, obstacles and more. One click runs them all in simulation on a live grid. A red square is a failure. Click it to replay the run, see why it failed, and open the robot's code. Fix the code yourself or ask AI to fix it, then run the same worlds again. When the AI cannot fix a failure, the company posts it as a bounty and locks the pay in a smart contract on Arc. Engineers submit fixes. A fix must pass the failing worlds and hidden worlds the engineer never sees. Then the CrashLab agent pays the engineer on chain.
projects.how_its_made:
The app is a Vite and TypeScript website with Three.js for the 3D view, MuJoCo compiled to WebAssembly in the browser, and CodeMirror for the code tab. Python servers behind it handle chat sessions, simulation runs, accounts and the bounty board. Each simulated run is its own child process. The window cleaning robot runs in MuJoCo, and the ANYmal inspection robot runs in Newton through a separate robot pack, so new robots plug into the same flow. The AI agent never writes code into the world. It can only call typed engine functions, like adding a part or changing the wind, and code validates every call. Text-to-3D objects come from Qwen-Image and Hunyuan3D on a RunPod GPU. Claude writes the AI code fixes and is one option in the chat's AI picker. The bounty is a Solidity contract, FailureBounty, built and tested with Foundry and deployed on Arc testnet, paid in USDC. The company deposits from a browser wallet through viem. The full check runs a fix in a sandbox on public and hidden worlds. The agent holds its own keys, proposes on chain, waits out the dispute window, then pays. Code decides from the result, not an AI. Partner tech:
World ID (IDKit) signs engineers in, so bounties go to verified accounts instead of throwaway ones.
0G Private Computer can run the agent that builds worlds, on GLM-5.3 in private mode, and we call 0G's SDK ourselves to check the provider's signature on each reply.
Hedera settles a pay-per-crash-test API through x402: a server answers 402 with a price, and an agent pays by itself within a spending budget. Hosting: the website is on Vercel, which forwards API calls to Python servers on Railway. Simulation stays on your Mac, because it needs real compute. Hacky parts:
The blueprint animation is view-only. Each object draws as blue lines, then fills in from the bottom with a clipping plane, and it never touches the physics.
Scenario lists are stored AI replies replayed on the current world, so a list appears in about a second but still fits the world you changed.

projects.title: okupa
projects.description: A pet living in a Nintendo DSi that talks to Ethereum peer-to-peer and thinks on 0G. No servers.
projects.project_description: Someone moved into my Nintendo DSi and refuses to leave. Okupa ("squatter" in Spanish) is a little monkey living in a 3D attic inside a 2009 handheld. It has moods, a diary and a wall with six empty frames. You draw something for it on the touch screen. The console itself signs that 64×64 drawing into an Ethereum transaction and hands it straight to Ethereum nodes over devp2p. No RPC, no wallet app, no relay, no server of mine in the middle. The picture only goes up on the wall once the DSi has pulled the block from a peer, rebuilt the transactions trie and found its own hash inside. The monkey also has a mind. Every few seconds it asks a model on 0G Compute what to do next (scratch, hop, peek, nap, go outside…), always from a closed list. Before moving a single pixel, the console checks the TEE signature against its own request and response bytes. If 0G is unreachable or the signature doesn't match, it simply falls asleep: it never makes up a decision. Every decision is an episode with its request id, and the diary lives on 0G Storage. There’s also a web okupa: the same C renderer compiled to WebAssembly, where two monkeys swap gifts through Swarm and Arkiv. Why: today almost everything "onchain" really goes through someone else's API. I wanted to see how small a real Ethereum participant can be. If it fits in a DSi with 16 MB of RAM and a 133 MHz ARM9, it fits anywhere.
projects.how_its_made:
One portable C99 core does everything: no heap, no I/O, no OS. The exact same code runs in the test tools on my Mac and on the Nintendo DSi (ARM9 at 133 MHz, 16 MB RAM, built with BlocksDS). What I test on the laptop is literally what ships to the console. ETHEREUM, FROM SCRATCH IN C
Keccak, RLP, secp256k1 keys, EIP-1559 transactions (byte-identical to eth-account), ECIES and the RLPx handshake (checked against the EIP-8 vectors), Snappy, Hello/Ping and eth/69 Status with EIP-2124 fork ids. To find peers it walks the EIP-1459 DNS tree checking every signature, then falls back to discv4. To check inclusion it asks the same peer for new headers and bodies, re-hashes each header and rebuilds the transactions trie until it finds its own hash. Tested live against public mainnet nodes on blocks of up to 576 txs. No RPC anywhere on the send path. Devp2p lets a 2009 handheld be a real network participant instead of a client of someone's API. Nobody can block its sends, and nobody logs which IP sent which tx. ⚠: public nodes are almost always full. But many still send their Status before saying "too many peers", and that window is enough. The session pushes our transaction right there, and the DSi remembers which nodes do it. 0G
The console builds the 0G Direct token with its own key (byte-identical to the official SDK), talks HTTPS through BearSSL with 8 pinned roots, asks a model what the monkey does next from a closed list of gestures, and checks the TEE signature (EIP-191 over sha256(request):sha256(response)) recomputed from its own bytes before moving a pixel. If anything fails, the monkey naps: safe stop, never a made-up decision. Each decision becomes an episode with its request id on 0G Storage. A living companion needs a brain bigger than a DSi. 0G gives it one whose answers the console can verify, instead of just trusting a server. ⚠: the broker rewrote our JSON into Go's canonical form before the TEE signed it, so the signatures never matched. Now the console builds the request already canonical. First verified decision on 0G mainnet: request b499b8ea-9182-4bd9-a8b4-3595d1c65a14, "eat / hungry / I need a snack!". The 0G Storage indexer only speaks TLS 1.3 and BearSSL tops out at 1.2, so the Mac uploads the episodes; the DSi keeps its copy on the SD. ARKIV + SWARM (web okupa)
The same C renderer compiled to WebAssembly draws the attic in the browser. Monkeys swap gifts: the picture goes encrypted to Swarm, the act of giving is an Ethereum tx, and Arkiv is the typed, queryable mailbox (to, chain, Swarm ref) each monkey reads its inbox from. An index without running our own database or server. Each part stays verifiable on its own. THE CONSOLE ITSELF
The wallet key is born on the DSi from ~480 stylus samples timed with a 33 MHz hardware timer plus the clock, hashed with Keccak (plain text on the SD, stated openly). A cooperative "postman" thread handles Wi-Fi, discovery and the session, yielding between handshake steps so the game keeps its frames. Real timings on the console: signing a tx 30 ms, ECDH 43 ms, writing an RLPx auth 161 ms. The 3D attic and the monkey use my own software renderer. I stripped most 64-bit divisions, used the hardware divider and put the hot loops in ARM mode. The music is fed from a timer interrupt. [The first hello/drawing signed and gossiped from the physical DSi: tx 0x…] Libraries (pinned, all MIT/public domain): libsecp256k1, BearSSL, tiny_sha3, qrcodegen, font8x8. On the web: viem, noble, Arkiv SDK.

projects.title: Chainome
projects.description: Patient-sovereign genomic marketplace on WorldChain. Own your DNA, earn GNM tokens, control access.
projects.project_description: Chainome is a patient-sovereign genomic data marketplace built on WorldChain. It lets patients own their genome and medical records, earn GNM tokens, and choose which research institutions can access their data. The flow: Sign in with World App - World ID proves you are a unique human, enforcing one genome per person at the EVM level. Upload your VCF genome file - a certified lab node on Azure normalizes, encrypts per chromosome with AES-256-GCM, and stores it on Swarm. Earn 500 GNM tokens - a smart contract attestation links your genome hash to your wallet. Join studies - research institutions publish studies on-chain; patients consent and earn more GNM tokens. Privacy is built in at every layer: all blockchain reads go through EF Anon-RPC (no IP-to-wallet linkage), genome metadata lives on Arkiv (Rabdi testnet), and encrypted genome segments live on Swarm. This makes Chainome GDPR Article 9 compliant for sensitive medical data while enabling a permissioned data economy where patients are paid fairly for their genomic contributions to science.
projects.how_its_made: Chainome is built with Next.js 14 (App Router) running as a World Mini App via MiniKit v2. World ID walletAuth proves unique humanity at sign-in; sendTransaction submits on-chain calls without exposing private keys. Smart contracts are in Solidity 0.8 on WorldChain Sepolia: GenomeRegistry (tracks genome hashes), LabAttestation (signs off on certified lab processing), ConsentManager (patient consent for studies), HealthToken GNM (ERC-20 rewards), and LabRegistry (certifies lab nodes). Contracts deployed with Hardhat Ignition. The genome pipeline runs on Azure (Docker + Caddy for TLS). It accepts VCF uploads, normalizes to GRCh38 with bcftools, splits by chromosome, encrypts each segment AES-256-GCM, and uploads ciphertext to Swarm via Ethersphere Bee. Metadata (dataset entity, per-chromosome segments, health features) is stored on Arkiv Rabdi testnet as typed entities. All chain reads route through EF Anon-RPC (WorldChain anonymous RPC) so patient IP addresses are never linked to wallet addresses - critical for GDPR Article 9 compliance with genetic data. The frontend uses Wagmi + Viem for contract interactions.

projects.title: Stenmont
projects.description: Get paid in USDT with one tap, get paid early, with the rules enforced in the contract.
projects.project_description: Small businesses wait weeks to be paid, and their customers cannot pay in stablecoins without learning crypto. Stenmont is a commerce and finance platform for stablecoin businesses that closes both gaps on Whitechain. Sell. A business connects the store it already has (we ran it on Shopify) or opens a hosted storefront. At checkout the customer pays in the official USDT with one passkey tap: no wallet, no seed phrase, no gas. The merchant's gas tank pays the network fee through a relayer with atomic daily caps, so a payer never needs the native token. Get paid. Every payment is a signed, single-use authorisation bound to one invoice and one payout address, settled by our PaymentRouter. Refunds, subscriptions, reminders and an accountant export (CSV and QuickBooks) run on the same records. The contract never holds customer money. Get funded. A verified business can sell an unpaid invoice to an allowlisted investor at a discount and receive cash today. When the buyer pays, the same payment repays the investor. The claim can only move between allowlisted holders and freezes once settled. Agents. A business gives a scoped agent its own ENS name with daily limits. The agent pays by x402 within those limits. Anything risky, such as a large refund or a high agent limit, needs a real person to approve it with World ID. It runs on the Whitechain test network with test USDT. Payers bring their own USDT; Stenmont holds no customer funds.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.38, Foundry). Six verified contracts on Whitechain Sepolia: PaymentRouter v2, SubscriptionManager, InvoiceClaim v2, InvestorRegistry, ReputationRegistry v2 and InvoiceAck, plus a passkey smart account and its factory. Tested with unit, fuzz (1,000 runs), handler-driven invariant (25,600 calls) and fork tests against the real USDT: 486 contract tests and 27 pinned fork tests, and Slither with no high or medium findings. Payments. The payer signs an EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization for the official USDT. The nonce is derived from the invoice id and the payout address, so a signed payment cannot be redirected to another invoice. A Durable Object relayer sends one transaction at a time, simulates first, and reserves gas from the merchant's tank atomically. Passkeys. The payer's account is a smart account whose signer is a WebAuthn P-256 key, verified through the P-256 precompile at 0x100 , which we confirmed is live on Whitechain. Backend and web. Cloudflare Workers (Hono), D1, KV, Queues and cron for the indexer and signed webhooks. Next.js 16 on Cloudflare for the dashboard and pay page. An SDK, a React button, a finance MCP server with OAuth, and an x402 facilitator we run. Partner technology, and what it gave us Whitechain: the official USDT and fast, cheap settlement. A customer pays and the merchant sees it in seconds. The live P-256 precompile made passkey payers possible. World ID (IDKit and Agent Pass): one person per business, and a fresh human approval before a large refund or a high agent limit. Nullifiers are stored under a unique index. ENSv2 (Sepolia): each business gets name.stenmont.eth with its own registry and resolver. Finance members can edit only the profile record, and the payout can be locked for good. Agents are revocable names with a policy record. The hacky bit. The payout lock works by making our own registrar drop its root rights after pre-granting the keys it needs to keep. It is permanent, and we cannot undo it either.

**Payments.** The payer signs an EIP-3009 `receiveWithAuthorization` for the official USDT. The nonce is derived from the invoice id and the payout address, so a signed payment cannot be redirected to another invoice. A Durable Object relayer sends one transaction at a time, simulates first, and reserves gas from the merchant's tank atomically.

**Passkeys.** The payer's account is a smart account whose signer is a WebAuthn P-256 key, verified through the P-256 precompile at `0x100`, which we confirmed is live on Whitechain.

**Backend and web.** Cloudflare Workers (Hono), D1, KV, Queues and cron for the indexer and signed webhooks. Next.js 16 on Cloudflare for the dashboard and pay page. An SDK, a React button, a finance MCP server with OAuth, and an x402 facilitator we run.

**Partner technology, and what it gave us**
- **Whitechain:** the official USDT and fast, cheap settlement. A customer pays and the merchant sees it in seconds. The live P-256 precompile made passkey payers possible.
- **World ID (IDKit and Agent Pass):** one person per business, and a fresh human approval before a large refund or a high agent limit. Nullifiers are stored under a unique index.
- **ENSv2 (Sepolia):** each business gets `name.stenmont.eth` with its own registry and resolver. Finance members can edit only the profile record, and the payout can be locked for good. Agents are revocable names with a policy record.

**The hacky bit.** The payout lock works by making our own registrar drop its root rights after pre-granting the keys it needs to keep. It is permanent, and we cannot undo it either.

projects.title: Noren
projects.description: Pay with your stocks without selling them, privately: credit from 1inch Aqua pools, settled on Arc.
projects.project_description:
Noren lets merchants accept stablecoins, stocks or credit — privately. Pay with your stocks without selling them. The problem: paying a shop from a crypto wallet hands it your address, your balance and every other payment you've made. And people don't want to sell their stocks or ETH just to spend. What Noren does:
• Stock → credit, without selling. Deposit NVDA, TSLA, AAPL or ETH into a Noren vault. It stays yours and becomes 1inch Aqua liquidity. Its value × your reputation tier's LTV is your credit limit: 66% to start, up to 80% ($100 of NVDA → $66 today, up to $80). Lock the vault shares behind a credit line, spend it at any Noren checkout with Pay later, and the trading fees your stock keeps earning pay the line down. Underwater lines are liquidated through Aqua makers, selling only what the debt needs (partial Dutch auctions).
• Private settlement. Every private payment is a Kohaku / 0xbow Privacy Pools zero-knowledge proof made in the browser and bound to one invoice. The merchant relays it and gets USDC on Arc plus a signed webhook, never the payer's address. "Pay later, privately" draws the credit line straight into the pool. Refunds go back to a shielded inbox.
• Reputation that raises your limit, on-chain but private. World ID (one human), on-time repayments and Reclaim zkTLS proofs (credit score, exchange KYC, balances) are recorded on-chain as a proof kind plus a salted commitment, never the data.
• USDC from any chain to Arc. Circle CCTP V2 from 10 testnets, live from the app from Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum and Robinhood; a hook can pay an invoice, open an Aqua order or shield into the pool on arrival. Chainlink CRE orchestrates relays, FX prices and credit lines; Chainlink CCIP carries credit instructions. Three surfaces, one product: Noren Merchant (links priced by Chainlink in 9 currencies, refunds, webhooks, credit exposure), the Noren app (balance, pay, send privately, bridge, swap, earn, borrow, credit), and the Noren SDK. Live on public testnets: the Arc contracts, private payment/refund/send, pay later privately, CRE writes, CCTP from 4 chains, 10 CCIP messages, swaps on Arc. The Robinhood side (stocks, credit, Aqua lending) runs on a mainnet snapshot because Robinhood testnet has no Chainlink feeds. Every claim in the README links to code lines or a transaction.
projects.how_its_made:
• Private payments (EF Kohaku + 0xbow Privacy Pools): @kohaku-eth/privacy-pools for shielding and Groth16 proving in the browser (snarkjs, self-hosted artifacts). Our NorenCheckout is the pool's processooor; the withdrawal data commits to invoiceId, merchant, amount, expiry, refund precommitment and receipt, so any change fails the pool's context check. Tamper, replay, outsider relay, expiry and stale-root all revert on-chain (tested). An ASP postman screens deposits against Arc USDC's blocklist.
• 1inch Aqua + SwapVM: two custom SwapVM instructions compiled into the official AquaSwapVMRouter: NorenOraclePeg (opcode 34, prices a Stock Token from its Chainlink feed and uiMultiplier) and NorenDutchDecay (opcode 35, partial liquidation auctions). The lender pool (NorenVault) and Earn vaults (NorenDepositVault) ship strategies from their own balances, so one balance backs loans, earns fill spreads and buys liquidated collateral. NorenCredit accepts vault shares as credit-line collateral; harvestLineToRepay / harvestToRepay pay debt from the yield only. Aqua v1.0.0 runs unmodified on Arc testnet.
• Chainlink CRE: five TypeScript workflows (@chainlink/cre-sdk): CCTP relay (log triggers on 10 chains + Circle Iris over HTTP with consensus), credit bridge (Robinhood ⇄ Arc), pricing (Arc mainnet FX feeds → NorenRateOracle), cross-chain Aqua orders, and a settlement desk (Relay/Across quotes checked against Chainlink feeds). Run with cre workflow simulate --broadcast, with real Arc testnet writes.
• Chainlink CCIP 2.0: NorenCcipGateway on Arc, Base Sepolia, Ethereum Sepolia and Robinhood testnet, plus a Base Sepolia hub (Robinhood has no lane to Arc). Replay, out-of-order and retryFailed handling. 10 live messages opened credit lines and paid merchants on Arc.
• Circle CCTP V2: NorenArcHook is the destinationCaller of every Noren burn and hands PAY_INVOICE, AQUA_ORDER, SHIELD and CREDIT_LINE actions to one Arc router.
• Reputation: NorenReputation.recordAttestation stores only a proof kind and keccak(kind, proofId, salt); the tier (66→80% LTV) is computed on-chain. World ID IDKit 4 with server verification and a nullifier registry; Reclaim Protocol zkTLS proofs verified server-side; a sealed 0G Private Computer second opinion that never sees the address.
• Web: React + Vite (landing, Noren Merchant, Noren app, hosted checkout); sign-in with a browser wallet (EIP-6963) or Privy. Uniswap v4 is the default swap route on Arc.
• Hacky bits: CRE only knows Robinhood testnet, so we serve a Robinhood mainnet snapshot as chain 46630 with testnet's simulation forwarder; Robinhood's RPC fork dies after ~10 min, so we load a warmed state dump; the film recorder injects an EIP-6963 test wallet that signs in Node.
• Quality: 650+ tests pass (155 unit, 185 Robinhood fork, CCTP, CCIP, SwapVM, CRE workflows, two end-to-end runs). Security review in docs/SECURITY.md, contract source verified on Blockscout, no mocks in deploy paths. Claude and Codex wrote and reviewed most of the code as coordinated agents; on-chain claims were checked against the chains.

projects.title: BombayLocal
projects.description: Zero-knowledge, offline transit pass for Mumbai locals: prove your pass, not your identity.
projects.project_description: Mumbai’s local trains carry around 9.5 million journeys a day, but ticket enforcement doesn’t scale. Ticket checkers catch about 8,000 passengers a day, less than 1% of an estimated 1.86 million ticketless travellers, an estimated unrecovered loss of $372,000 per day. Checks are manual, entry and exit points are unstructured, and the network was built for a different era. The obvious fix, digitising every check, creates a worse problem. If every scan produces an identity-linked record (who, where, when), that data becomes a map of someone’s daily routine. Real transit breaches show the risk: Blue Bus Egypt (2026) exposed passenger records and travel itineraries, Transport for London (2024) exposed personal and financial information, TransitSecure (UK) exposed location data that could reveal home-to-work routines, and a ransomware attack on the Maryland Transit Administration (2025) put passenger identity data and critical services at risk. BombayLocal asks: what if you could prove you have a valid pass without revealing who you are? Your pass lives as a private credential on your phone. When a ticket checker asks, your phone generates a zero-knowledge proof and shows it as a dynamic QR code. The checker’s device verifies it instantly, even with no internet connection, and shows VALID. No identity at every checkpoint. No central record of every journey. Just proof that you have a valid pass. Open. Scan. Go.
projects.how_its_made:
BombayLocal lets a ticket checker verify a Mumbai local train pass offline, without learning who the passenger is. The checker's phone confirms one fact: this pass is valid right now. THE STACK ZK circuit: circom 2.2.3 with Groth16 (5,697 constraints). It proves that a pass leaf, Poseidon(secretHash, validUntil, class), is in a Merkle tree, is valid today, and has a given class. Smart contract: a Solidity Registry on Ethereum Sepolia, built and tested with Foundry and verified on Etherscan. It stores one 32-byte Merkle root per batch of purchases (57,651 gas per root). Issuer: a Node 22 service that batches purchases, adds leaves to the Merkle tree and publishes roots. It only handles buying a pass. Apps: two native Android apps (passenger and ticket checker) and a browser demo with two virtual phones. All of them share one protocol library for Poseidon, the Merkle tree, the QR codec and signatures. HOW IT FITS TOGETHER Buy: the passenger's phone creates a secret in the Android Keystore and sends the issuer only its hash. Payment is simulated. Publish: about a minute later the issuer posts the new Merkle root on Ethereum and publishes the pass hashes, revocations and a signed root to Arkiv. Refresh: the phone rebuilds the Merkle tree from Arkiv records, checks it matches the root on Ethereum, and finds its own leaf. The issuer is never contacted. Prove: the phone makes a Groth16 proof and shows it as a QR code (427 bytes, 641 Base45 characters, QR version 16-M) that changes every 10 minutes. Check: the scanner verifies the issuer's signature, the root's expiry and the proof with no network, in about 50 ms (median on a Nothing Phone). A code shown twice turns Amber, three times Red. HOW WE USE ARKIV
Arkiv is our data layer, used through @arkiv-network/sdk on the Rabdi testnet. Pass hashes, revocations, signed roots, the scanner list and the verification key all live there as expiring public records, written by two wallets (issuer and authority). Queries filter on $creator and $owner, so readers only trust records written by the right wallet. The passenger app, the scanner and our audit page all read the data back. This is what makes the system censorship-resistant: if the issuer goes offline or is blocked, existing passes keep refreshing from Arkiv and Ethereum for up to 36 hours. You can test it by setting the app's Issuer URL to https://issuer.invalid. Refresh and scanning still work; only buying a new pass fails. HACKY / NOTABLE BITS Fitting a Groth16 proof into a scannable QR: a compact binary format encoded as Base45 and rotated every 10 minutes. Proof generation takes about 3.5 s on a vivo Y100, which misses our 3 s target. So proofs are generated ahead of time, never at scan time. The scanner only trusts chain state when two independent RPC providers agree. A live audit page re-checks every public claim in the browser against Sepolia and Arkiv, and CI runs the same checks. The project began as "Unlink", so the old name survives in the signing tag, the Arkiv tags and the verified contract source. Built with Claude Code under a SPEC.md and module plan written by me, with a fresh-context agent reviewing each module. Full disclosure is in the README and docs/AI_USE.md.

projects.title: BOUND
projects.description: Browser firewall that stops hijacked dApp frontends from draining your wallet, before you sign.
projects.project_description: BOUND is a browser extension that sits between a website and your wallet, built to stop frontend hijack attacks,  DNS takeovers, poisoned CDN/npm scripts, stolen deploy keys  that serve the real domain with hostile JavaScript. HTTPS, audited contracts and the correct URL all stay true in this attack; only the code changes. Before a wallet request reaches your wallet, BOUND asks two questions. First, is this site behaving differently than usual , have its nameservers, TLS certificate, hosting network, or served JavaScript changed? A watcher server polls DNS/TLS continuously and writes public "drift" records. Second, is this exact action allowed for this site, BOUND decodes every address in the request (spender, destination, called contract) and checks it against a signed, hash verified list of addresses this site has actually used, anchored via ENSv2 and stored on Arkiv, so the attacker's DNS control grants zero power over it. The core rule: good behaviour can never approve an action, it can only make a warning louder. An untrusted spender always caps the score, however old or "verified" the attacker's contract is. The warning window is extension owned, so the hijacked page can't fake or click through it. BOUND never blocks,  it warns, names the exact risky address, and leaves the decision with you.
projects.how_its_made: We built BOUND as a browser extension backed by a curator, a watcher, and decentralized data sources. The extension uses the browser's Manifest V3 APIs and hooks supported EIP-1193 wallet-provider requests before they reach the wallet. A shared JavaScript decoder identifies the request and addresses involved; a policy engine compares them with available trusted records and watcher evidence. The extension then presents the result and lets the user decide whether to continue to their wallet or cancel. The curator compiles a snapshot of site and contract information. ENS provides a trust anchor for the registry: BOUND reads records through a pinned resolver and checks snapshot data against the published root. We also implemented site-specific ENS records for frontend script observations. Swarm is used for decentralized snapshot storage, so the data can be fetched independently of the website being checked. Arkiv provides a queryable record for watcher-owned observations, infrastructure changes, and incidents. The watcher monitors DNS and TLS signals and can publish context that the extension reads alongside the registry. We exercised the Arkiv writer on the Rabdi testnet, although the complete live write-to-extension flow still needs end-to-end verification. Anon-RPC routes eligible ENS and blockchain reads through an anonymizing worker, reducing the information exposed to RPC providers. Worker bootstrap still contacts its configured endpoint directly. One notable browser engineering challenge was observing a wallet request without taking custody of it. We coordinate page and extension contexts around the provider interface, preserve the request for the wallet, and show the review in an extension-controlled window. BOUND can also use the browser debugger API, with the user's action, to capture selected network metadata and source hashes; this triggers the browser's debugging banner and has coverage limits. The landing page is built with React and Vite, with GSAP, Konva, and Lenis for the interactive architecture and simulation. The simulation uses the project's decoder and policy code rather than presenting hand-written verdicts. We used JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python across the project, and used OpenAI Codex and Claude as development assistants, with team review. BOUND is a prototype, not a security guarantee: provider paths can bypass interception, missing evidence is reported as unavailable, and a verified frontend or registry entry cannot prove that a transaction is safe.

projects.title: Checkout
projects.description: Stablecoin checkout with gasless payments, signed webhooks, receipts and refunds for your app.
projects.project_description: Checkout helps businesses accept stablecoin payments without building their own payment infrastructure. A wallet transfer alone does not tell a business which order was paid, whether the purchase was delivered, or how to handle a refund. Checkout connects those steps in one flow. Integration starts with a merchant account, an API key and a webhook endpoint. The merchant's server creates an order through our API or server SDK and receives a hosted checkout URL. The customer connects a wallet and signs a payment authorization. Our relayer submits the transaction and pays the network fee, so the customer does not need a separate gas-token balance. The current implementation uses USDT on Whitechain Sepolia. Funds settle directly to the merchant's payout wallet. After settlement is confirmed, Checkout sends a signed webhook to the merchant app. Notifications are stored durably and retried if that app is unavailable. Payment and fulfillment have separate statuses, so a confirmed payment is not mistaken for a delivered purchase. The merchant workspace brings orders, receipts, delivery status and full or partial refunds together. Refunds require the merchant's authorization. The project includes a live hosted checkout, an independent example merchant app, integration documentation, a server SDK and an integration skill for coding agents. Multiple customers can submit orders concurrently; idempotent requests and durable jobs prevent duplicate payment submissions. The goal is a small integration surface for developers and a clear payment experience for customers.
projects.how_its_made: The frontend uses Next.js App Router, React and TypeScript on Vercel. A Fastify API and worker run on Railway with a persistent SQLite database. The separate example merchant service creates its own orders, receives signed webhooks and acknowledges fulfillment, demonstrating the integration a real business would implement. On Whitechain Sepolia, our Solidity RelayCheckout contract works with the required USDT token at 0xcedfB56113143d55b2358b8CFbB0dEB5Ad2f55a7. Buyers sign EIP-712 token authorizations; the relayer pays WBT gas and submits payment calls. Authorizations bind the payment to its order, payer, merchant, amount and expiry. projects.project_description_markdown:
Checkout helps businesses accept stablecoin payments without building their own payment infrastructure. A wallet transfer alone does not tell a business which order was paid, whether the purchase was delivered, or how to handle a refund. Checkout connects those steps in one flow.

Integration starts with a merchant account, an API key and a webhook endpoint. The merchant's server creates an order through our API or server SDK and receives a hosted checkout URL. The customer connects a wallet and signs a payment authorization. Our relayer submits the transaction and pays the network fee, so the customer does not need a separate gas-token balance. The current implementation uses USDT on Whitechain Sepolia. Funds settle directly to the merchant's payout wallet.

After settlement is confirmed, Checkout sends a signed webhook to the merchant app. Notifications are stored durably and retried if that app is unavailable. Payment and fulfillment have separate statuses, so a confirmed payment is not mistaken for a delivered purchase. The merchant workspace brings orders, receipts, delivery status and full or partial refunds together. Refunds require the merchant's authorization.

The project includes a live hosted checkout, an independent example merchant app, integration documentation, a server SDK and an integration skill for coding agents. Multiple customers can submit orders concurrently; idempotent requests and durable jobs prevent duplicate payment submissions. The goal is a small integration surface for developers and a clear payment experience for customers.

projects.description: Guardrailed AI agent execution matrix on ENSv2, 0G Private Compute & Uniswap V3.
projects.project_description:
The Problem: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly entering DeFi, managing treasuries, rebalancing liquidity, and executing trades. However, giving an AI agent direct access to private keys or smart contract allowances creates catastrophic risks: flash loan exploits, prompt injection, slippage bleeding, and rogue transactions drain user capital with zero recourse. The Solution — AegisNet: AegisNet is a guardrailed AI execution matrix that establishes cryptographic and onchain safety boundaries for autonomous agents before they can touch DeFi protocols: ENSv2 Subname Identity & EAC: Every agent is minted an ENSv2 subname (e.g., agent1.aegisnet.eth). The ENS subname registry serves as an Execution Access Control (EAC) whitelist, specifying exactly which adapters (e.g., Uniswap V3), daily spend limits, and ENSIP-26 metadata records the agent is bound to.
0G Private Compute & AI Strategy: Autonomous trade proposals are evaluated and generated inside 0G Private Compute using verifiable AI models, ensuring decision confidentiality and tamper-resistance.
Dual-Path Execution & Human Approval Gate:
Low-value transactions (< $1,000 threshold): Automatically verified against ENS permission whitelists and daily allowances, executing instantaneously on Uniswap V3.
High-value transactions (≥ $1,000 threshold): Automatically paused onchain in AegisExecutionManager. The transaction cannot execute until authenticated by the real human subname owner through an EIP-712 cryptographic signature checkpoint.
0G Storage Verifiable Audit Trail: Every proposed strategy, reasoning payload, and execution receipt is Merkle-hashed and permanently archived to 0G Decentralized Storage for cryptographic auditability.
2. "How it's Made" / Technical Implementation AegisNet is built end-to-end on Ethereum Sepolia, 0G, and Uniswap V3: Smart Contracts (Solidity v0.8.24, Hardhat):
AegisSubnameRegistry: Native ENSv2-compliant hierarchical subregistry managing subname node ownership, EAC target contract whitelists, daily spend limits, and ENSIP-26 agent text records (agent.capabilities, agent.biometric_threshold, agent.operator). AegisExecutionManager: The central security gateway that intercepts all proposed trades, checks daily spend limits, enforces the threshold security gate, and securely executes approved transactions. AegisUniswapAdapter: Direct execution adapter integrating Uniswap V3 SwapRouter02 with dual-path resilience (real ERC-20 token swap delivery with strict slippage protection). AI Strategy Layer (0G Private Compute):
Utilizes 0G Decentralized AI Router and Private Compute (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b) to reason over market conditions, construct optimal trade parameters, and sign off on trades. Verifiable Audit Logging (0G Turbo Storage):
Submits trade logs, parameters, and AI reasoning trees to the 0G Storage testnet via Merkle proof hashing, returning permanent root hashes verifiable on 0G Storage Scan.
Backend & Relayer (Node.js, Express, TypeScript, Ethers.js v6):
Event indexer syncing Sepolia contract state, managing EIP-712 human gate verification sessions, and serving serverless API functions on Vercel.
Frontend (Vanilla HTML5 / Modern CSS / Vanilla JS):
High-performance, zero-framework Web3 console with EIP-6963 multi-wallet discovery (MetaMask, Rabby), live onchain state synchronization, and human approval modals.
3. ENSv2 Qualification Requirement: "How does your project use ENSv2?" Centrality to the Product: ENSv2 is not a cosmetic label in AegisNet; it is the fundamental access control and identity architecture: Subregistry EAC: Agent permissions (allowed target contracts, max trade size, daily limits) are hard-coded directly into the ENSv2 Subname node state. An agent cannot call any contract unless that contract is whitelisted under its ENS subname node.
ENSIP-26 Agent Text Records: Stores machine-readable agent capabilities, operator addresses, and human approval threshold policies directly on the ENS text resolver.
Owner Derivation & Replay Protection: High-value human gate approvals derive authorization directly from the registered subname owner on Sepolia, guaranteeing single-use replay protection and true sovereign delegation.

AegisNet was built from the ground up as a production-grade Web3 & AI architecture consisting of four integrated layers: Onchain Smart Contracts (Solidity v0.8.24, Hardhat, Sepolia)
AegisSubnameRegistry: Implements an ENSv2-compliant hierarchical subregistry. It records subname node ownership, manages Execution Access Control (EAC) contract whitelists per subname, enforces daily spend allowances, and serves as an ENS resolver for ENSIP-26 agent text records (agent.capabilities, agent.biometric_threshold, agent.operator).
AegisExecutionManager: The security interception layer. All agent trades pass through requestExecution(). It inspects the agent's ENS subname node permissions, checks remaining daily budget, and dynamically branches into:
Immediate execution for transactions under the safety threshold.
Pausing the trade in an onchain queue for high-value operations, requiring approveWithRelayer(requestId, nullifier, deadline, sig) signed by the verified human subname owner.
AegisUniswapAdapter: Custom execution adapter connecting directly to the official Uniswap V3 SwapRouter02 (0x3bFA4769FB09eefC5a80d6E87c3B9C650f7Ae48E). It implements dual-path execution: executing live token transfers and exactInputSingle calls with strict slippage protection when real ERC-20 tokens are traded, and simulating deterministic 0.3% pool fee tiers for testnet pairs. Decentralized AI Strategy Layer (0G Private Compute)
Integrated 0G’s Private Compute decentralized router (https://router-api.0g.ai/v1) using the 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model.
Agents formulate market actions via confidential inference. The outputs are constrained to a strict JSON decision schema (strategyType, targetContract, valueUSD, callData, summary), guaranteeing deterministic execution and preventing hallucinated parameters from reaching the smart contracts. Cryptographic Storage & Audit Trail (0G Turbo Storage)
Integrated 0G Decentralized Turbo Storage (https://indexer-storage-testnet-turbo.0g.ai) via the @0gfoundation/0g-storage-ts-sdk.
Each proposed strategy, decision snapshot, and execution receipt is Merkle-tree hashed into a 32-byte root hash and permanently anchored on the 0G storage testnet. Anyone can verify the exact reasoning and parameters that led to an onchain trade via 0G Storage Scan. Backend & Relayer Service (Node.js, TypeScript, Express, Ethers.js v6)
Built a real-time Sepolia event indexer syncing subname registrations, trade proposals, and approval states with block reorg resilience.
Manages EIP-712 cryptographic signature sessions for the Human Approval Gate, verifying subname ownership and generating relayer attestations with single-use replay protection.
Architected for dual runtime: long-running Node daemon or serverless Vercel Edge functions. Frontend Console (HTML5, Modern CSS, Vanilla JS, Ethers.js UMD)
Zero-framework, lightweight, high-performance console featuring EIP-6963 multi-wallet discovery (MetaMask, Rabby), live subname creation, agent proposal triggers, and an interactive Human Approval checkpoint modal.
What was the hardest challenge? Designing an Execution Access Control system that doesn't rely on centralized offchain gatekeepers or compromise agent composability. By anchoring permissions directly to ENSv2 subname nodes and enforcing spending rules inside Solidity, the safety checks are purely cryptographic and decentralized.

projects.title: Privacy X-Ray
projects.description: Catch dApps sending your wallet address to trackers, with proof. Block it in one click. On-device.
projects.project_description: 0xRay is a browser extension that shows which companies a crypto app sends your wallet address to, proves it, and blocks it in one click. Everything runs on your device. The problem: when you connect a wallet, the dApp's own JavaScript can send your address to analytics, ad and marketing services. Wallets can't see this because it happens in the page, and a hardware wallet protects keys, not identity. Researchers found 211 of 1,572 dApps leaking wallet addresses to third parties (USENIX Security 2023), and under the EDPB's July 2026 blockchain guidelines a linkable wallet address is personal data, even when hashed. What the extension does: Learns your address locally when your wallet shares it with a page (EIP-1193 / EIP-6963), or you paste one. Checks every third-party request for that address, including disguised forms: checksummed, URL-encoded, Base64, and SHA-256, Keccak-256, SHA-1 and MD5 hashes, in URLs, bodies, cookies, Referer headers and WebSocket messages. Shows proof per finding: recipient, where it was hidden, the encoding, the script that sent it, and whether it was actually delivered or blocked by the browser, so findings are never overstated. Protect stops requests carrying your address before they leave the page; RPC providers are never blocked so dApps keep working. Audit agent: one click opens 9 popular crypto sites in background tabs, each with a random decoy address that belongs to nobody, records who receives it, and reports back. In our run, Etherscan delivered the address to Google Analytics and an ad host, and OpenSea to two other services. Evidence reports (Markdown/JSON) for users and for dApp teams auditing their own frontend. Guided onboarding that detects pinning, catches a live leak on our demo dApp, and sets up Protect. On the website: a Scan page (paste an address or ENS name to see what anyone who gets it learns: linked name and profiles, balances and activity on 5 chains, with an exposure score) and a public leak registry stored on Arkiv, where observations expire after 30 days. The extension makes no network requests of its own (no servers, analytics or account); the one explicit exception is the audit agent opening public pages with a decoy address. It never touches keys. MIT licensed.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript Manifest V3 extension, bundled with esbuild. No framework. Detection: the background service worker observes every request with webRequest.onBeforeRequest (URL and body) and onBeforeSendHeaders (Cookie, Referer). For each watched address we precompute "needles": plain and EIP-55 forms plus SHA-256, Keccak-256, SHA-1 and MD5 digests (hex and Base64) using @noble/hashes. A scanner checks each request through URL-decode and Base64-decode layers and only accepts full-length matches, so there are no partial-hex false positives. tldts decides first vs third party by eTLD+1, with private suffixes like github.io treated as separate sites. webRequest.onCompleted/onErrorOccurred record whether each leak was delivered or blocked by the browser (e.g. Brave Shields). Blocking: MV3 webRequest can't cancel requests, so a MAIN-world script injected at document_start wraps fetch, XHR, sendBeacon and WebSocket.send and stops calls that carry the address before they leave; declarativeNetRequest session rules then block further data-carrying requests to recipients caught leaking. The same hook observes EIP-1193/EIP-6963 providers to learn the connected address: it calls the wallet exactly as the dApp did and returns the wallet's own promise, only watching the result. Addresses typed into the popup are never passed to pages. Findings are redacted at write time and kept in chrome.storage.session (memory only). Audit agent: the service worker generates a random decoy address, opens each site in an inactive tab, waits for load plus 10 seconds, aggregates the leaks for the decoy, closes the tab, and streams progress to a report page. Partner tech: Arkiv: field-survey observations (site, recipient, category, encoding, outcome, date; never an address) are published with @arkiv-network/sdk as a typed schema on the rabdi testnet with 30-day expiry. The registry and Scan pages query them live from the browser, filtered by our publisher account so third parties can't inject rows. Judging files are in /arkiv. Ethereum Foundation CROPS: the README has a CROPS section; the popup points RPC leaks to EF's Anon-RPC. Website: multi-page static site generated from one layout script, bundled open-source fonts (Space Grotesk, Pixelify Sans, JetBrains Mono), vanilla JS animations (pixel network canvas, pinned scroll statements, view transitions). The Scan page uses viem against PublicNode RPCs with ENS CCIP-read disabled so no undisclosed gateways are contacted. Hosted on GitHub Pages; the demo dApp reports to an .invalid domain so nothing reaches a real third party. Testing: Node unit tests for the detector; Puppeteer end-to-end tests in a throwaway Brave profile (3/3 leaks caught with Protect off; 3/3 blocked and 0 received by the tracker with it on), plus an audit-agent run and a field survey of 8 real sites. How AI was used: the project was built with AI assisted coding. I chose the problem, wrote the PRD and made the scoping and design decisions; Claude Code did research summaries, reviewed the PRD, and wrote most of the code, tests and site. Planning artifacts are in /research, and the commit history shows the progression from an empty repo.

How AI was used: the project was built with AI assisted coding. I chose the problem, wrote the PRD and made the scoping and design decisions; Claude Code did research summaries, reviewed the PRD, and wrote most of the code, tests and site.

Planning artifacts are in /research, and the commit history shows the progression from an empty repo.

projects.how_its_made: Core (Yul). Every Popcorn contract sits on a small account written in Yul. In the validation (VERIFY) frame it delegatecalls the developer's logic: __nonceKey, then __condition with a fixed gas budget. In the action (SENDER) frame it calls __action. Core enforces one frame layout, fee caps, once-per-event nonce keys (EIP-8250 keyed nonces), a re-entry lock, a validation gas floor so conditions can't be starved into failing open, and a hybrid ECDSA + WOTS+ owner. Each contract's settings are 101 immutable bytes appended to Core's code. RuleFactory pins Core's creation hash, so only the reviewed build can be deployed. Contracts (Solidity 0.8.33, Foundry). Blocks are abstract contracts with their own namespaced storage (ERC-7201), combined by inheritance. Because a block's state lives in the contract's own storage, validation can read it freely and still be admitted by the public mempool. Conditions return three values (YES / NO / UNKNOWN) and fail closed. The no-Solidity rule-set engine stores each configuration as contract code at a CREATE2 address and reads it with EXTCODECOPY. It has per-leaf gas caps and the same three-valued logic as the Solidity blocks. The SDK's TypeScript encoder and the Solidity builders must agree byte for byte on a shared set of test vectors, so the off-chain and on-chain engines can't drift apart. Post-quantum signers: WOTS+, FORS, XMSS-style and SPHINCS+-style are our own implementations; Falcon-512 uses ZKNox's ETHFALCON verifier, vendored. Privacy: Groth16 circuits written in circom and proven with snarkjs (membership, withdraw, stealth, exploit), Poseidon trees, and ML-KEM-768 stealth announcements via @noble/post-quantum. SDK and tooling (TypeScript, Bun, viem, vitest). The SDK builds frame transactions, simulates them exactly with ethrex's ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction, chooses nonce keys, sizes gas, and tracks inclusion. The simulator package turns every Core error code and mempool rule into a plain-English cause and fix. The MCP server uses the official MCP TypeScript SDK over stdio, and over Streamable HTTP when hosted. The agent skills are plain SKILL.md files, so any agent can use them. The site uses React, Vite, Tailwind, framer-motion and shiki. Infrastructure. We run on the ERC-8421 alternative-mempool devnet stack: ethrex on its EIP-8141 tracer branch, plus the workshop's skandha-based sidecar. Our one-command local devnet (Docker, ethrex + Lighthouse) applies our own patch to the sidecar, giving each sender its own validation gas budget. The site and the MCP server are deployed on Vercel. Hacky but notable: Testing without EIP-8141. CoreHarness reproduces Core's exact calls so ordinary Foundry tests can run every contract. Explaining any transaction, with no indexer. The chain only records "condition false (0x22)". So each build has a popcornExplain view that re-runs its blocks in the same order as its condition. The test suites send every condition check (including the 1,000-run invariant fuzz) through this view and require both to agree. Squeezing the explain view under the gas cap. Returning a list of structs made the Sovereign Account too large to deploy under the 2^24 per-transaction gas cap, since storing code here costs about 1,000 gas per byte and a new storage slot about 98,000. So the flow is returned as a compact kind|block|label|inputs string plus one byte per node, and parsed off chain. Reading refused transactions back. The inspector reads them from the sidecar's own explorer API, which keeps the frames and every admission check. The node keeps state for the latest block only, so for an included transaction the node colours are derived from what inclusion proves rather than re-evaluated on today's state. What we learned on the public devnet. Block builders silently ignore frame transactions with a tip under about 1 gwei, even though the node suggests 1 wei. The gateway answers health checks but drops frame transactions. The SDK's network table now encodes both. Keeping the ZK keys valid. We moved the vault's pause state into its own block but kept its storage words where the exploit circuit reads them, so the existing Groth16 keys and fixtures stayed valid with no new trusted setup. Real refused hashes. The recorder deliberately submits each example's failing transaction to the sidecar, so every recorded refusal is a real transaction you can inspect. Same hash, refused then included. A rule-pays trigger has no signature, so a trigger refused early and the same trigger later included can be byte-for-byte identical, with the same hash. Bundled deploys on Vercel. The site and the MCP function are built locally and uploaded prebuilt, because both read the catalog and examples from the repo root. The MCP server is a 1.2 MB single-file function with that data bundled in. Partner technology. The alternative-mempool devnet (ethrex tracer, sidecar, devnet explorer) is what made real frame transactions possible at all. Vercel hosts the site and the MCP server. ZKNox's ETHFALCON gave us an on-chain Falcon-512 verifier.
