projects.title: Bramble
projects.description: Private WireGuard access for agents, authorized by ENS and revoked live, with a Hedera audit trail.
projects.project_description:
Bramble gives devices and automated workers (including AI coding agents) private network access without making a coordination server the authority. THE PROBLEM
Private-network tools such as VPN meshes rely on a central coordinator that decides who may join and what each member may reach. Whoever runs that coordinator can add a member, keep a revoked one, or be compelled to do either. An AI agent that needs a private service usually receives that service's credential, so a leaked agent leaks the backend. WHAT BRAMBLE DOES
Bramble is a userspace WireGuard mesh. Device identities, revocation and scoped service grants live in an ENSv2 Permissioned Registry on Sepolia. Every peer resolves that registry itself and updates its own WireGuard peer table. No coordinator and no relay can add a member or keep a revoked one. We make a "no trusted coordinator" claim, not a "no infrastructure" claim: we still depend on an RPC endpoint, relays and an administrator. HOW IT WORKS A tailnet is an ENSv2 registry. Each device is a subname (for example worker.<tailnet>.eth) with its own Permissioned Resolver. Enhanced Access Control gives separate accounts narrow rights: enrollment, key rotation, revocation, access rules and relay registration. Access records hold digests of service names, never plaintext names, hosts or ports. Relay endpoints sit in a separate registry, so device records never publish network topology. A worker or agent asks for access to a service. A human approves the request in the approval console. The grant is written to ENS, and each peer picks it up on its next resolution without a restart. The agent reaches the private service without ever holding the backend credential. The human revokes the grant in the console. Peers re-read ENS and drop the worker. The demo shows the next call fail. Public relays are discovered through ENS and paid per session or byte allotment through x402 on Hedera testnet (USDC, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator). The client enforces asset, network and per-payment limits before it signs. WHAT EXISTED BEFORE THE HACKATHON
This is a continuity entry. Baseline: tag pre-mumbai (commit 28e2a8f). It already had the Go WireGuard nodes and relay (brambled/, relay/), the ENS and x402 sidecars (sidecar/, relay-sidecar/), an admin CLI (admincli/) and a read-only dashboard (dashboard/). Sepolia ENS authorization and Hedera testnet x402 relay payments already worked. List new work with: git log pre-mumbai..HEAD WHAT WE BUILT DURING THE HACKATHON Approval console and activity feed: access requests, approve and revoke, device join and enrollment. Agent access: an MCP server that lets a coding agent request private access and call the private service, with per-agent spend caps and HashScan links. Tor control plane (EF CROPS upgrade): the sidecar sends ENS reads and payment HTTP requests through Tor with separate isolation keys, and CCIP-Read is disabled so no off-chain lookup bypasses Tor. The RPC provider no longer sees node IP addresses. Requests fail closed until Tor is ready. Hedera Consensus Service audit trail: for each grant, revoke and settled payment, the approval service posts a salted hash commitment to an HCS topic. The console checks a retained opening against the mirror node and links the entry on HashScan. Only commitments are public. Distribution: self-contained device binaries, a curl installer, bramble up , an embedded local web UI, and operator-sponsored capped relay sessions. Demo infrastructure: cloud nodes, a logging RPC proxy, a public console and a preflight check. MEASURED RESULTS (reported 6 November 2026) On the cloud nodes, the first failed call came 36.6 s and 37.0 s after revocation began (build 4928612). Revocation over Tor, two 600 s runs on one machine: replayed median detection 7.0 to 11.5 s, worst observation 29 s, excluding chain confirmation. KNOWN LIMITATIONS Revocation is not instant. It depends on the ENS poll interval, RPC behavior and Tor. Tor covers the control plane only. WireGuard, STUN and relay UDP stay outside Tor, so relays see peer IP addresses. The RPC provider still sees names, requested records and timing. Payments expose the payer account. HCS does not enforce access and does not prove that every event was logged. Node, admin and Hedera payer keys are software keys. The demo shows a worker running as a Unix user, not a proven autonomous agent session. LINKS
Repository: https://github.com/WhyAsh5114/bramble
Demo tailnet: bramble-dev-c91e55e9.eth (Sepolia)
projects.how_its_made:
ARCHITECTURE
Bramble is a monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) with a Go data plane and a TypeScript control plane. brambled/ (Go): the node daemon. It runs userspace WireGuard (wireguard-go), so it works on a laptop with no kernel module. It admits or drops each peer based on what the sidecar reports from ENS. sidecar/ (TypeScript on Bun, Hono, viem): one sidecar per node, local HTTP only. It is the Go daemon's only path to ENS state. We used raw viem, not ensjs, because it was the only client proven against the custom ENSv2 deployment addresses. relay/ and relay-sidecar/ (Go + TypeScript): a rendezvous relay for candidate exchange and a data relay that forwards opaque UDP. Both are metered through x402. approval/ (Next.js): the approval console and service. A human approves or revokes access requests. The service writes grants to ENS and posts audit commitments to Hedera. It writes grants but does not enforce them. agent-mcp/ (TypeScript): an MCP server that lets a coding agent request access and call the private service. The agent never holds the backend credential. hedera-audit/ (TypeScript): the HCS writer and reader. admincli/, dashboard/, rpc-proxy/: an admin CLI, a read-only dashboard, and the logging RPC proxy we use to show what an RPC provider sees. HOW A GRANT FLOWS An agent calls the MCP server to request access to a service. The request appears in the approval console. A human approves it. The approval service writes the grant to the device's ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver on Sepolia. The record holds an ACL digest of the service, never a plaintext name. Every node's sidecar polls ENS every 5 s. The Go daemon updates its WireGuard peer table from the result. On revoke, the record is removed. Each peer sees the change on its next poll and drops the worker. HOW PARTNER TECHNOLOGY HELPED ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): ENS is the authorization source, so no server has to be trusted. Permissioned Registries and Resolvers give each device its own record. Enhanced Access Control splits rights across accounts: enrollment, key rotation, revocation, access rules and relay registration. Separate registries for devices and relays keep topology off-chain. A scripted test checks that each role can do its own writes and no others. Hedera: x402 payments settle on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator, with testnet USDC as the asset. Fees are low enough to meter relay sessions per byte allotment. The client enforces asset, network and per-payment limits before it signs. The new HCS audit trail posts one 95-byte message per grant, revoke or payment: {"v":1,"kind":"grant","c":"<64 hex>"}. The commitment is an HMAC-SHA256 keyed by a fresh 32-byte salt over a length-prefixed encoding of the event. A retained opening can be checked against the mirror node and linked on HashScan. Only kind and timing are public. The writer is unit-tested against a fake Hedera client. Tor (Ethereum Foundation CROPS upgrade): the sidecar sends ENS reads and x402 payment requests through Tor, with one isolation key per purpose ('ens' and 'pay'), so a provider cannot link a node's reads to its payments. NOTABLE AND HACKY DETAILS Tor inside the sidecar, no daemon: we use tor-js 0.4.4, which runs Arti (the Tor Project's Rust client) as WebAssembly. Bun's fetch has no SOCKS support, and a system tor daemon would add a process and a disk state directory to every node. We replaced tor-js's socket layer. Its close() leaves direct TCP sockets open, so we give it our own socket provider that dials every relay itself and destroys all sockets on shutdown. No disk, no CDN: tor-js loads its WASM from node_modules and uses in-memory storage. By default it downloads the binary from a CDN in the clear and caches it under ~/.local/share. Our CI check (pnpm check:no-local-state) fails if the node runtime writes local state. The cost is a full Tor bootstrap on every restart. Bootstrap quirks: a failed tor-js client caches its rejected bootstrap and cannot be retried, so we close it and create a new one. A timed-out bootstrap cannot be cancelled, so we keep waiting on the same client. Isolation-key rotation: about 1 in 10 first requests failed in our spike. torFetch retries once under a fresh isolation key, because Tor keeps reusing a failed circuit. Fail closed: until Tor is ready, torFetch rejects instead of connecting directly, and every sidecar route except /health answers 503 with Retry-After. brambled waits up to 7 minutes for Tor at startup, and keeps its last-known peer set if a later resolve fails. CCIP-Read is disabled in the ENS client, so no off-chain lookup can bypass Tor. Guardrails as code: pnpm check:no-endpoints fails if any mesh endpoint (topology) appears on-chain, and pnpm check:no-local-state enforces the no-local-state rule. pnpm verify runs typecheck, lint, format, build and tests across Go and TypeScript. Relay trust is simple on purpose: the ephemeral relay port is the authorization, allocated only after a real payment. The first two distinct UDP sources win the two slots. This does not weaken mesh admission, because a relay cannot complete a WireGuard handshake without a peer's private key. HONEST LIMITS
Revocation takes time: the first failed call came 36.6 s and 37.0 s after revoke began on the cloud nodes (reported 6 November 2026), and Tor-path detection measured a median of 7.0 to 11.5 s on one machine. Tor covers the control plane only; WireGuard, STUN and relay UDP stay outside it. Node, admin and payer keys are software keys. STUN discovery exists, but separate-NAT hole punching and relay-fallback acceptance are not yet verified.

- Revocation over Tor, two 600 s runs on one machine: replayed median detection 7.0 to 11.5 s, worst observation 29 s, excluding chain confirmation.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS
- Revocation is not instant. It depends on the ENS poll interval, RPC behavior and Tor.
- Tor covers the control plane only. WireGuard, STUN and relay UDP stay outside Tor, so relays see peer IP addresses. The RPC provider still sees names, requested records and timing. Payments expose the payer account.
- HCS does not enforce access and does not prove that every event was logged.
- Node, admin and Hedera payer keys are software keys.
- The demo shows a worker running as a Unix user, not a proven autonomous agent session.

LINKS
Repository: https://github.com/WhyAsh5114/bramble
Demo tailnet: bramble-dev-c91e55e9.eth (Sepolia)
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
ARCHITECTURE
Bramble is a monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) with a Go data plane and a TypeScript control plane.

- brambled/ (Go): the node daemon. It runs userspace WireGuard (wireguard-go), so it works on a laptop with no kernel module. It admits or drops each peer based on what the sidecar reports from ENS.
- sidecar/ (TypeScript on Bun, Hono, viem): one sidecar per node, local HTTP only. It is the Go daemon's only path to ENS state. We used raw viem, not ensjs, because it was the only client proven against the custom ENSv2 deployment addresses.
- relay/ and relay-sidecar/ (Go + TypeScript): a rendezvous relay for candidate exchange and a data relay that forwards opaque UDP. Both are metered through x402.
- approval/ (Next.js): the approval console and service. A human approves or revokes access requests. The service writes grants to ENS and posts audit commitments to Hedera. It writes grants but does not enforce them.
- agent-mcp/ (TypeScript): an MCP server that lets a coding agent request access and call the private service. The agent never holds the backend credential.
- hedera-audit/ (TypeScript): the HCS writer and reader.
- admincli/, dashboard/, rpc-proxy/: an admin CLI, a read-only dashboard, and the logging RPC proxy we use to show what an RPC provider sees.

HOW A GRANT FLOWS
1. An agent calls the MCP server to request access to a service.
2. The request appears in the approval console. A human approves it.
3. The approval service writes the grant to the device's ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver on Sepolia. The record holds an ACL digest of the service, never a plaintext name.
4. Every node's sidecar polls ENS every 5 s. The Go daemon updates its WireGuard peer table from the result.
5. On revoke, the record is removed. Each peer sees the change on its next poll and drops the worker.

HOW PARTNER TECHNOLOGY HELPED
- ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): ENS is the authorization source, so no server has to be trusted. Permissioned Registries and Resolvers give each device its own record. Enhanced Access Control splits rights across accounts: enrollment, key rotation, revocation, access rules and relay registration. Separate registries for devices and relays keep topology off-chain. A scripted test checks that each role can do its own writes and no others.
- Hedera: x402 payments settle on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator, with testnet USDC as the asset. Fees are low enough to meter relay sessions per byte allotment. The client enforces asset, network and per-payment limits before it signs. The new HCS audit trail posts one 95-byte message per grant, revoke or payment: {"v":1,"kind":"grant","c":"<64 hex>"}. The commitment is an HMAC-SHA256 keyed by a fresh 32-byte salt over a length-prefixed encoding of the event. A retained opening can be checked against the mirror node and linked on HashScan. Only kind and timing are public. The writer is unit-tested against a fake Hedera client.
- Tor (Ethereum Foundation CROPS upgrade): the sidecar sends ENS reads and x402 payment requests through Tor, with one isolation key per purpose ('ens' and 'pay'), so a provider cannot link a node's reads to its payments.

NOTABLE AND HACKY DETAILS
- Tor inside the sidecar, no daemon: we use tor-js 0.4.4, which runs Arti (the Tor Project's Rust client) as WebAssembly. Bun's fetch has no SOCKS support, and a system tor daemon would add a process and a disk state directory to every node.
- We replaced tor-js's socket layer. Its close() leaves direct TCP sockets open, so we give it our own socket provider that dials every relay itself and destroys all sockets on shutdown.
- No disk, no CDN: tor-js loads its WASM from node_modules and uses in-memory storage. By default it downloads the binary from a CDN in the clear and caches it under ~/.local/share. Our CI check (pnpm check:no-local-state) fails if the node runtime writes local state. The cost is a full Tor bootstrap on every restart.
- Bootstrap quirks: a failed tor-js client caches its rejected bootstrap and cannot be retried, so we close it and create a new one. A timed-out bootstrap cannot be cancelled, so we keep waiting on the same client.
- Isolation-key rotation: about 1 in 10 first requests failed in our spike. torFetch retries once under a fresh isolation key, because Tor keeps reusing a failed circuit.
- Fail closed: until Tor is ready, torFetch rejects instead of connecting directly, and every sidecar route except /health answers 503 with Retry-After. brambled waits up to 7 minutes for Tor at startup, and keeps its last-known peer set if a later resolve fails.
- CCIP-Read is disabled in the ENS client, so no off-chain lookup can bypass Tor.
- Guardrails as code: pnpm check:no-endpoints fails if any mesh endpoint (topology) appears on-chain, and pnpm check:no-local-state enforces the no-local-state rule. pnpm verify runs typecheck, lint, format, build and tests across Go and TypeScript.
- Relay trust is simple on purpose: the ephemeral relay port is the authorization, allocated only after a real payment. The first two distinct UDP sources win the two slots. This does not weaken mesh admission, because a relay cannot complete a WireGuard handshake without a peer's private key.

HONEST LIMITS
Revocation takes time: the first failed call came 36.6 s and 37.0 s after revoke began on the cloud nodes (reported 6 November 2026), and Tor-path detection measured a median of 7.0 to 11.5 s on one machine. Tor covers the control plane only; WireGuard, STUN and relay UDP stay outside it. Node, admin and payer keys are software keys. STUN discovery exists, but separate-NAT hole punching and relay-fallback acceptance are not yet verified.

projects.title: Autolysis
projects.description: A loan that pays for its own liquidation. Borrowers keep most of the 5% bonus bots take today.
projects.project_description: Liquidation is the one moment a borrower can least afford to lose money, and it's exactly when DeFi charges them the most. When a loan gets risky, an outside bot repays it and walks away with about 5% of the debt. Aave alone liquidated around $429M in a single crash week this February. That bonus doesn't pay for anything essential. It exists because a loan can't act on its own: someone has to watch it, sign a transaction, bring capital and pay gas. Autolysis lets the loan do it itself. Every market has a contract account that authorizes and pays for its own liquidations, using EIP-8141 frame transactions on the ERC-8421 alternative mempool. Nobody signs anything. Anyone can broadcast the transaction, because the account's validation code checks that it's the one allowed liquidation for a position that's genuinely unhealthy at a fresh oracle price. The market then sells just enough collateral to bring the loan back to health, through a Uniswap v4 hook. The hook fills the sale at the oracle price: first from 1inch Aqua makers, whose USDC sits in their own wallets until a liquidation needs it, then from a backstop, and only then from the pool's curve. A custom SwapVM opcode means those makers can only be filled by a liquidation, so nobody can pick them off when the oracle lags. The borrower pays gas and a small spread instead of the bonus. Lenders keep a classic liquidation as a fallback if self-liquidation ever stalls. It runs on the EF devnet. A keyless, self-paid liquidation was included in block 2865. In a 12-position crash, the canonical mempool rejected all 12 (StorageReadNonSender, because validation reads live market and oracle state), and the alternative mempool included all 12 from a single account. Five attack transactions were all rejected. The Uniswap and Aqua parts are proven against the official contracts on a Unichain mainnet fork. I'm also proposing EXO-010, a narrow reputation rule for the alt mempool, so a sender isn't punished when an oracle update cancels its pending liquidations.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity with Foundry for the contracts, TypeScript for the transaction kit, and a small dashboard. Solo build, with Claude Code as a pair programmer and a lot of review rounds where I tried to break it. The account (EF frames + alt mempool). AutolysisAccount is both the sender and the gas payer. Its VERIFY frame reads the transaction through Alex Forshtat's hegota-support helpers and approves exactly one shape: two frames, the selfLiquidate call with the right arguments, one nonce key equal to hash(market, position), a recent oracle round inside a price band, a position unhealthy at both the cited and latest price, and a max cost under the fee cap. Every rule has a mutation test. The first version cost 131k gas on our mock, over the sidecar's 100k validation cap, so I rewrote it to read 15 fixed parameters into a fixed-size struct instead of decoding whole frames. On the devnet it measures 94,168. TIMESTAMP is banned during validation, so freshness comes from the oracle's round index, and wall-clock checks live in the execution frame. The signature is a single ARBITRARY entry: the code is the authorization. One EIP-8250 nonce key per position is what lets one account keep 12 liquidations pending at once. Gas is billed from the borrower's WETH collateral, unwrapped and sent to the account, capped at 0.3% of what's sold. A failed attempt can be billed at most once per price round, so nobody can grind a position down. The sale (Uniswap v4). V4Venue settles the collateral before calling swap, so the hook can pay makers in real tokens inside beforeSwap instead of handing them ERC-6909 IOUs. BackstopHook authorizes on the swap's sender, never on hookData, and uses beforeSwapReturnDelta to run the waterfall. Anyone else sees an ordinary pool. Invariants check that every swap nets to zero and that the hook ends each liquidation holding nothing. The buyers (1inch Aqua + SwapVM). Tier 1 calls our fork of AquaSwapVMRouter with one new opcode, LiquidationGate (0xf9): an order only fills if the taker is our hook and a liquidation is in progress. Makers ship strategies to the official Aqua registry and get paid WETH straight into their wallets in the same transaction. The fun part: SwapVM needs solc 0.8.30 and v4-core pins 0.8.26, so the hook talks to the router through an ABI-only interface, and the tests deploy the 0.8.30 build artifacts with vm.deployCode. Hacky but notable: our first devnet liquidation was admitted and then never included. The gateway sidecar runs in manual bundling mode, so I rebuilt the exact signed bytes, checked the hash matched, and relayed through the miner sidecar. With Alex's tip to retry with fresh entities, it landed in block 2865. The crash scene now checks whether the sidecar already has a transaction before retrying, so a network blip can never liquidate twice. Testing: 165 tests plus 12 stateful invariants, green in CI, including differential tests (TypeScript vs Solidity math) and fork tests against the official Uniswap PoolManager and Aqua registry on Unichain. One honest gap: replacing a pending liquidation with a fee bump is designed in but wasn't demonstrated on the devnet, so I don't claim it.

projects.title: Wick
projects.description: An AI market maker on Base that pays for its own brain with the fees it earns
projects.project_description: Most AI agents stop the day their owner stops paying the API bill. Wick is an AI agent that earns its own. Wick runs a W0G/USDC market on Base. Every five minutes it asks its brain, a TEE-verified model on 0G Private Computer, for a spread, a size and a lifetime. Code centres both prices on the Uniswap v3 600 second TWAP and the agent signs them as one EIP-712 pair. The 0G request id, the provider and the TEE verdict are hashed into the price itself, so every fill on Base traces back to one sealed AI run. The price is binding. Our own SwapVM instruction, running on the deployed and unmodified 1inch AquaSwapVMRouter, fills a swap only at the signed price, only before it expires and only within 800 bps of the onchain TWAP. The tokens never leave the agent's wallet. A SwapVM taker gate (WickGate) keeps the strategy closed to bots and open to Wick's own doors. Every fill pays a 0.30% fee, and the fee is what keeps Wick alive. The agent swaps fees to W0G on Uniswap, bridges them to 0G over Chainlink CCIP, unwraps them and deposits them into the 0G Payment Layer account that bills its next decision. One AI decision costs about $0.00079; the live dashboard shows fuel, runway and every paid decision, read straight from both chains. Anyone can trade with it: on the Wick app (a real wallet swap from the app: Base tx 0xe3ceac64cf0077c0305d677a11c1ad338cb81fbbcd06ab060094b924adfee7b1), through any Uniswap router via our v4 hook, or by buying the signed price over x402 for 0.01 USDC.
projects.how_its_made: Pricing runs on 0G Private Computer. A TypeScript agent calls the 0G router with verify_tee on 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b (Intel TDX provider). The model returns four numbers: bid half-spread, ask half-spread, size, lifetime. It never writes a price. composeQuotes builds both rates around the Uniswap v3 600 second TWAP, refuses anything past 790 bps, and the pair is signed once as EIP-712. The 0G request id, provider and TEE verdict are bound into inferenceId = keccak256(abi.encode(requestId, provider, verdict)) and stored on AgentQuoteBoardV2 beside the quote, so anyone recomputes a price's provenance with cast keccak. An answer without tee_verified true, or without a request id, is refused before the signer. Execution is a custom SwapVM instruction, AgentQuoteExtructionV2, invoked at Aqua opcode 0x20 on the deployed, unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter v1.0.2. Each fill checks the agent's epoch, expiry (900 s max), the signed rate against observe() on the Uniswap v3 pool, maxAmountIn and strategy depth, then charges 30 bps. A test pins the router's real opcode table. The live strategy sits behind SwapVM opcode 0x0e (_onlyTakerTokenBalanceNonZero), a taker gate whose WickGate token the v4 hook and maker hold, a shape 1inch's Aqua team pointed us to. Uniswap shows up three ways: the v3 TWAP band, SwapRouter02 and QuoterV2 for funding swaps, and an AquaAggregatorHook on BaseAggregatorHook that turns the Aqua strategy into a v4 pool. The pool holds nothing; the hook is the SwapVM taker and settles to the PoolManager. Fork tests run through the deployed Universal Router 2.1.2. The money loop is a Cloudflare Workers cron every five minutes. It reads TWAP, spot, vault, gas and board, and once fees reach 3x the live bridge cost it steps a persisted machine: swap fee USDC to W0G, ccipSend to the 0G chain, W0G.withdraw, PaymentLayer.depositFor(agent). A 1 0G daily spend cap drives NORMAL, LOW, CRITICAL and PAUSED tiers: a cheaper model and wider spreads, then no inference. LI.FI supplied gas on the 0G chain. A wick-quotes Worker sells signed prices over x402, each settlement bound to the payer's AuthorizationUsed event. The hack we like most: the chain, not the server, enforces the agent's leash. Pull 0G away and every fill and every v4 swap reverts StaleQuote. Stack: Solidity and Foundry (69 contract tests with fuzz, invariants and Base fork runs, 20 hook fork tests), TypeScript, viem, Next.js, Cloudflare Workers and KV.

projects.title: Dapping
projects.description: Dapping (dapp.ing): the verified professional graph for builders in Web3 and AI.
projects.project_description: Dapping (dapp.ing) is the verified professional graph for builders in Web3 and AI. It's a professional network where every claim shows what backs it. Verified companies confirm the roles builders held with them and issue participant, winner and role records (speaker, judge, mentor and more) for their events, hackathons, grants, bounties and accelerators. Builders link their own GitHub and dev.to: their dev.to articles appear on their profile, and pull requests merged into repositories they don't own count toward their Karma. Verification marks and Karma are earned from proof, and no plan can buy them. Around those profiles sit jobs, grants, hackathons, bounties, accelerators and events, so builders, companies and Projects connect in one graph. Sign in with email, X, or an EVM or Solana wallet. Free for builders.
projects.how_its_made: Dapping is a TypeScript monorepo (Turborepo + pnpm) with five apps: the Next.js 16 App Router web app (React 19), an Express 5 API with Socket.io for real-time chat, an admin console, a Strapi CMS for the blog, and Mintlify docs. Auth runs on Dynamic, so one account can sign in with email, X, or an EVM or Solana wallet. Data lives in Postgres, queried through Drizzle with file-driven, checksummed migrations: every migration is dry-run, applied and then verified against a ledger, and nothing is ever pushed straight to the schema. The proof layer is the core. Company attestations, participation records and Karma are computed server-side, and Karma deliberately counts only pull requests merged into repositories the builder doesn't own, so self-merges can't inflate it. dev.to articles are linked only when the dev.to profile names a GitHub or X account the builder has already verified. Production runs on Vercel (web) and a Hetzner host with Docker Compose (API and Postgres), behind Cloudflare, with media and backups in Cloudflare R2, Sentry for errors and PostHog for product analytics.

projects.title: Sidequest
projects.description: An expiring, wallet-owned task board for builders to find collaborators and ship faster.
projects.project_description: Sidequest helps builders find the person who can unblock their next step. During hackathons, small requests often disappear into group chats: a wallet integration needs debugging, a design needs feedback, or a demo needs testing. Sidequest gives those requests a searchable board with clear ownership and a useful lifetime. Builders can publish focused tasks, add relevant skills, set an expiry, discover requests by category, claim work and mark it complete. Search, status filters, sorting and personal activity views make it easy to find a useful contribution. Live tasks and actions are stored as public, wallet-owned entities on Arkiv. Other applications can query the same schema without depending on a Sidequest account. Expiration keeps time-sensitive requests from becoming permanent clutter. A separate Practice mode lets visitors try the complete workflow without connecting a wallet. Optional bounty amounts communicate an offer; Sidequest does not process payments or provide escrow.
projects.how_its_made: Sidequest uses React and TypeScript for the interface, with Vinext and Vite handling the application build. Cloudflare Workers serves the frontend and API routes, while Cloudflare D1 stores the session-isolated Practice workspace. SQL migrations define the practice database, and prepared queries keep each visitor’s records scoped to their session. The live board uses the official Arkiv SDK and viem on the Arkiv Rabdi testnet. Browser wallets sign live writes, while the backend queries Arkiv to reconstruct the board. Tasks have indexed attributes for discovery, structured payloads for their details and native expiration matching their requested lifetime. During hackathons, small requests often disappear into group chats: a wallet integration needs debugging, a design needs feedback, or a demo needs testing. Sidequest gives those requests a searchable board with clear ownership and a useful lifetime.

Builders can publish focused tasks, add relevant skills, set an expiry, discover requests by category, claim work and mark it complete. Search, status filters, sorting and personal activity views make it easy to find a useful contribution.

Live tasks and actions are stored as public, wallet-owned entities on Arkiv. Other applications can query the same schema without depending on a Sidequest account. Expiration keeps time-sensitive requests from becoming permanent clutter.

A separate Practice mode lets visitors try the complete workflow without connecting a wallet. Optional bounty amounts communicate an offer; Sidequest does not process payments or provide escrow.

projects.title: Commons
projects.description: A Nostr social app with a built-in multichain wallet: email login, gasless USDC, BTC + Solana.
projects.project_description: Commons is a mobile social app built on Nostr where every account comes with a self-custodial wallet, without seed phrases or gas. People sign in with email or Google; behind the scenes Privy creates embedded wallets on EVM, Solana and Bitcoin (both Native SegWit and Taproot) for them. The social side is a full Nostr client: a home feed of people you follow, posting, replies and threads, likes, profiles, search across Nostr (people, posts, npub, NIP-05), notifications, and end-to-end encrypted DMs (NIP-17). Every post and profile can be tipped in USDC with no gas, and the tip shows up on Nostr for everyone to see. Your Nostr identity is derived from your Privy wallet, so logging in with the same email on a new phone gives you the same npub, with no nsec or seed phrase to manage. The Wallet tab shows one total balance across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, Solana and Bitcoin, with native tokens and USDC, plus per-network deposit sheets with QR codes and clear network warnings. Transactions are gas-sponsored: a brand-new user holding 0 ETH and 0 SOL can still move USDC, because the app pays the fees.
projects.how_its_made: App: Expo SDK 58, React Native 0.88 (New Architecture, React Compiler), Expo Router with native tabs and protected routes, TypeScript strict, TanStack Query. Auth + wallets: Privy (@privy-io/expo) with whitelabel email-OTP and Google login. Wallets run on Privy's TEE infrastructure; the app creates EVM, Solana and Bitcoin (extended-chain) wallets itself after login. Nostr identity from Privy: Nostr needs a raw key in the app (Schnorr signatures, NIP-44 ECDH), which a remote signer can't provide. The app asks the Privy EVM wallet for a personal_sign over a fixed message and runs it through HKDF-SHA256 to get the Nostr secret key, cached in the iOS Keychain. The signature is deterministic (checked in-app), so the same login gives the same npub on any device. Nostr client: nostr-tools with one shared relay pool, publish-on-first-ack so slow relays never block the UI, batched profile loading, one query for a whole feed's likes/replies/tips, optimistic follows and likes. Signatures are verified only for events the app shows, because BigInt Schnorr checks are slow in Hermes. DMs are NIP-17: one kind-14 rumor sealed and gift-wrapped for both sides and sent to the recipient's kind-10050 relays; messages from strangers go to message requests. Search uses NIP-50 relays plus npub/NIP-05 lookup. Gasless USDC tips without a backend: the Expo SDK has no sponsor flag yet, so the app calls Privy's Wallet API rpc directly, each request signed by the user's own authorization key. On EVM Privy sponsors via EIP-7702; on Solana the fee is paid by the sponsor. Tips are announced as a kind-7 reaction with a tip tag (amount, CAIP-2 chain, tx hash), so they show up in notifications and on the post. Signature lab: an in-app test suite that signs with every method Privy offers and verifies each result on-device with viem and @noble/curves: Nostr key derivation, EIP-191, EIP-712, EIP-1559 tx, raw secp256k1, EIP-7702 authorization, Solana message + tx (ed25519), Bitcoin SegWit (ECDSA) and Taproot (BIP-340 Schnorr against the tweaked output key), plus sponsored sends on Base Sepolia and Solana Devnet. 12/12 pass. Bitcoin testnet trick: Privy only issues bc1 addresses, so the app re-encodes the witness program with the tb prefix (bech32/bech32m) to use the same keys on Testnet4. Balances: keyless public RPCs (publicnode, Solana RPC, mempool.space) batched per chain, CoinGecko for prices and token logos; images load from CDNs and are disk-cached, nothing bundled.

projects.title: Inphinity
projects.description: Index funds over tokenized stocks on Arc: create your own, earn fees, or just invest in USDC.
projects.project_description: Inphinity lets anyone invest in index funds built from tokenized stocks, and lets anyone create their own index fund and earn a fee from it. Why: in India most people invest through mutual funds and index funds, not single stocks. Tokenized stocks are coming onchain, but there is no fund layer on top of them. Inphinity is that layer, on Arc, in USDC. Investors browse the funds, invest USDC and get fund shares at NAV. Performance is NAV per share since inception (every fund starts at 1.00). Redeem any time for USDC. Creators pick 2 to 10 stocks, set weights and a fee of up to 2% a year, paid to them as fund shares. Every fund gets an ENS name like bchip.inphinity.eth. Stocks: 16 mock US stocks issued on Base and bridged to Arc with Circle CCTP and Bridge Kit (burn and mint, not wrapped). Prices: Chainlink CRE fetches real market prices and writes them onchain every 5 minutes, so funds move with the market. Names: a Chainlink CCIP message names each fund in ENSv2 on Sepolia, and the fund page verifies the name against Arc. Mock tokens priced from real data. US stocks today, Indian stocks next.
projects.how_its_made: I started by bringing tokenized stocks to Arc. I issued 16 mock US stocks on Base Sepolia as Circle CCTP cross-chain tokens, and moved them to Arc with Circle Bridge Kit. The token is burned on Base and minted on Arc at the same address, so it's bridged, not wrapped, and I didn't have to build my own bridge. Only the issuer does this bridging, from an issuer console in the app. Investors just use USDC. Then I built the index fund contracts on Arc with Arc Studio. It wrote, tested (145 Foundry tests) and deployed them. There's an exchange that holds the stocks and a USDC reserve and trades at the oracle price, so prices follow the real market instead of a thin testnet pool. Anyone can create a fund with 2 to 10 stocks, set the weights and charge up to 2% a year. Each fund is its own token. When you invest, it buys the stocks by weight and gives you shares at NAV. When you redeem, it sells your part and pays you back in USDC. For prices I use Chainlink CRE. A workflow fetches real stock prices from Yahoo Finance, takes the median, caps any jump at 5% and writes them onchain to the exchange every 5 minutes. That's what moves the NAV of every fund. The part I'm most excited about is the ENS side. I made inphinity.eth an ENSv2 registry, and every index created on the app gets its own subname. If someone creates a fund called Indian Stocks, indian-stocks.inphinity.eth gets created. It holds the fund's contract address on Arc, the stocks, their weights, the fee and the creator. The fund's page reads these records and checks them against the contract on Arc, so you get a double verification and a public page for every index. The creator owns the name but can't point it somewhere else, so nobody can use it to phish. The funds are on Arc and ENS is on Sepolia, so I use Chainlink CCIP to connect them. Creating a fund on Arc sends a CCIP message in the same transaction, and my receiver contract on Sepolia writes the name. The frontend is React, Vite, TypeScript and wagmi/viem, hosted on Vercel. The hacky thing I did is pointing every index at its own ENS subname, so ENS becomes the registry and public record for every fund on the app.

projects.title: Tessera
projects.description: An open collective to empower fellow hobbyists. Shared compute, Shared freedom.
projects.project_description: Apparently, we live in an era where RAM held by consumers and fellow hobbyists is RAM wasted. We boldly disagree. Tessera is an open collective where hobbyists pool their spare laptops to train machine learning models together, without having to trust each other. Training good models usually takes a data center. We think a community of ordinary machines can do it too, and that the people who contribute the compute should own the result and get paid for it. A requester posts a job and locks a budget in TOD, priced from the job's spec at 1 TOD for at least 1 GFLOP (a billion floating-point operations) of training. Each round, a group of nodes is seated and each one trains on its own slice of the data, commits to a hash of its checkpoints, then reveals it. Verifiers replay that work with a deterministic kernel that produces the same bytes on x86 and ARM, so a lazy or cheating node gets caught and loses its stake, while honest nodes are paid onchain. Owners verify with World ID, and one owner can't hold two seats in a round, so nobody can fill a round with their own machines. Finished models are indexed on Arkiv for fast lookup and stored on Swarm, so anyone can find, download, check and build on them. Anyone can also host a competition: the host locks a prize and a salted hash of the hidden labels, entrants commit their predictions, and a contract with no admin scores the entries and pays the winner. Joining takes one command: install the node, pair it with your wallet, verify, stake and run. Every contributor gets a public profile with their nodes, verified work and earnings, so reputation is built from real work rather than claims. Everything is open source, trains on public datasets and is verified in the open, which makes it a platform for hobbyists, by hobbyists. Shared compute, shared freedom.
projects.how_its_made:
The contracts are Solidity, built and tested with Foundry and OpenZeppelin. The token, node registry, job market and competitions contract are deployed on Base Sepolia. The registry and market handle stake, slashing, commit-reveal and payouts. The coordinator is Python with FastAPI and SQLite. It seats nodes, stores specs and weights by hash, and prepares each round's settlement, which two verifiers replay and co-sign with EIP-712 signatures before it goes onchain. Everything it serves can be checked against hashes recorded on the chain. Nodes run a Python CLI that ships as a multi-arch Docker image (amd64 and arm64), so joining needs nothing but Docker. Job code runs in a throwaway container with no network, a read-only root and capped CPU and memory. The web app is Next.js, wagmi and viem on Vercel, and there's also a terminal UI for operators.
The hacky part is the exact kernel. Normal ML libraries don't give identical floats across machines, so we wrote a fixed-order training kernel on numpy. Every PR runs the tests natively on both x86 and ARM runners and compares the hashes byte for byte. It's far slower than BLAS, but it means a verifier can replay a round and match it exactly. Even the data order is fixed: each node's batches come from a seeded shuffle derived onchain, so nobody picks their own data. Because the steps are fixed, we can count a job's operations from its spec alone, a bit like gas, and price the job in GFLOP from that count instead of trusting anyone's self-reported compute. Accepted updates are combined with a trimmed mean, and a validation gate drops any update that makes the model worse. For GPU training we're adding a second replay mode that checks results against measured tolerance bands, since GPUs can't be made bit-exact.
World ID gives us one person per owner, which stops one person filling rounds with fake nodes. Arkiv is our public index of finished models and job data, so anyone can query it without going through our servers. Swarm holds the actual files, referenced from those Arkiv records. The competitions contract scores entries itself by checking each reveal against its commitment and counting correct answers, so it needs no oracle or trusted scorer. One more small hack: a new node's operator key starts with no ETH, so on first start it asks the coordinator for a small gas top-up, rate limited per node.

projects.title: QRAFT
projects.description: Private ETH payments with one unified balance in ERC 8286 PQ wallets and EIP-8141 frame transactions
projects.project_description: QRAFT—Quantum-Resistant Anonymous Frame Transactions—is a private ETH payment protocol built around ERC-8286 post-quantum wallets and EIP-8141 frame transactions. Users add ETH to one unified private balance, send exact amounts to other users, and withdraw to a public address. Funds are held in a shared pool and represented by encrypted notes. The wallet automatically discovers incoming payments, selects notes for spending, and returns any leftover value as private change. Users interact with a balance rather than managing individual notes. Recipients share a QRAFT receiving address, and their wallets discover payments when they next connect. QRAFT uses ML-DSA-44 signatures to authorize public-account actions and ML-KEM-768 receiving keys to protect incoming payment notes. A passkey unlocks the wallet and protects its encrypted backup. Spending proofs are generated locally in the browser. Private payments use a shared proof-authorized account as the transaction sender, avoiding exposure of the user’s public wallet address in that field. The browser submits EIP-8141 transactions through Nym Anon RPC to the alternative mempool, without an application relayer. An onchain paymaster sponsors account setup and transaction gas. The complete flow—account creation, funding, private payments, change, recovery, and withdrawal—has been tested through real Nym connections. Post-quantum protection applies to account signatures and receiving encryption; the current Groth16 proof system is not post-quantum. Public deposits and withdrawals remain visible onchain.
projects.how_its_made: We built QRAFT with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Solidity contracts running on the EF EIP-8141 development network. The browser handles key management, note discovery, encryption and proof generation. We use viem for contract encoding and RPC interactions. The private pool uses a Circom join/split circuit with Groth16 proofs generated locally through snarkjs and WebAssembly. Notes contain an amount, owner commitment and random value. Poseidon commitments are recorded in a Merkle tree, while nullifiers prevent double spending. The circuit proves ownership and value conservation without revealing the input notes or private payment amounts. A payment creates a note for the recipient and, when needed, a change note for the sender. For the ERC-8286 PQ wallets, we use ML-DSA-44 for account authorization and ML-KEM-768 for receiving encryption, implemented with @noble/post-quantum. ML-KEM establishes a shared secret, HKDF-SHA-256 derives an encryption key, and AES-256-GCM encrypts each note. The recipient scans pool events, decrypts matching notes, checks their commitments, filters out spent notes and calculates one unified private balance. WebAuthn passkeys protect the locally encrypted master secret through the PRF extension. EIP-8141 lets us separate authorization, gas sponsorship and execution into native transaction frames. Public deposits use the user’s PQ account. Private sends and withdrawals use a shared, keyless proof account that validates the spending proof instead of requiring a public-wallet signature. The browser submits directly through Nym Anon RPC to the alternative mempool, so no application relayer signs or submits payments. The factory deploys accounts, and the paymaster funds both their setup stake and transaction gas. One integration challenge was making proof verification work within the alternative mempool’s restricted verification phase. We replaced gas-dependent calls in the generated Groth16 verifier with fixed precompile gas allowances and tested them with real proofs. We also use action-specific nonce keys for private payments, allowing independent transactions without a shared server-side nonce counter. For reliability, the wallet saves the exact transaction before submission and reconciles it after a timeout or reload. We tested this by deliberately dropping a submission acknowledgement, clearing browser storage, restoring with the original passkey, and completing a withdrawal. The project passed 93 unit tests, native transaction checks and a full browser-to-chain flow through real Nym connections.

Funds are held in a shared pool and represented by encrypted notes. The wallet automatically discovers incoming payments, selects notes for spending, and returns any leftover value as private change. Users interact with a balance rather than managing individual notes. Recipients share a QRAFT receiving address, and their wallets discover payments when they next connect.

QRAFT uses ML-DSA-44 signatures to authorize public-account actions and ML-KEM-768 receiving keys to protect incoming payment notes. A passkey unlocks the wallet and protects its encrypted backup. Spending proofs are generated locally in the browser.

Private payments use a shared proof-authorized account as the transaction sender, avoiding exposure of the user’s public wallet address in that field. The browser submits EIP-8141 transactions through Nym Anon RPC to the alternative mempool, without an application relayer. An onchain paymaster sponsors account setup and transaction gas.

The complete flow—account creation, funding, private payments, change, recovery, and withdrawal—has been tested through real Nym connections. Post-quantum protection applies to account signatures and receiving encryption; the current Groth16 proof system is not post-quantum. Public deposits and withdrawals remain visible onchain.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
We built QRAFT with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Solidity contracts running on the EF EIP-8141 development network. The browser handles key management, note discovery, encryption and proof generation. We use viem for contract encoding and RPC interactions.

The private pool uses a Circom join/split circuit with Groth16 proofs generated locally through snarkjs and WebAssembly. Notes contain an amount, owner commitment and random value. Poseidon commitments are recorded in a Merkle tree, while nullifiers prevent double spending. The circuit proves ownership and value conservation without revealing the input notes or private payment amounts. A payment creates a note for the recipient and, when needed, a change note for the sender.

For the ERC-8286 PQ wallets, we use ML-DSA-44 for account authorization and ML-KEM-768 for receiving encryption, implemented with @noble/post-quantum. ML-KEM establishes a shared secret, HKDF-SHA-256 derives an encryption key, and AES-256-GCM encrypts each note. The recipient scans pool events, decrypts matching notes, checks their commitments, filters out spent notes and calculates one unified private balance. WebAuthn passkeys protect the locally encrypted master secret through the PRF extension.

EIP-8141 lets us separate authorization, gas sponsorship and execution into native transaction frames. Public deposits use the user’s PQ account. Private sends and withdrawals use a shared, keyless proof account that validates the spending proof instead of requiring a public-wallet signature. The browser submits directly through Nym Anon RPC to the alternative mempool, so no application relayer signs or submits payments. The factory deploys accounts, and the paymaster funds both their setup stake and transaction gas.

One integration challenge was making proof verification work within the alternative mempool’s restricted verification phase. We replaced gas-dependent calls in the generated Groth16 verifier with fixed precompile gas allowances and tested them with real proofs. We also use action-specific nonce keys for private payments, allowing independent transactions without a shared server-side nonce counter.

For reliability, the wallet saves the exact transaction before submission and reconciles it after a timeout or reload. We tested this by deliberately dropping a submission acknowledgement, clearing browser storage, restoring with the original passkey, and completing a withdrawal. The project passed 93 unit tests, native transaction checks and a full browser-to-chain flow through real Nym connections.

projects.title: Hydra
projects.description: Your dApp's watchdog: warns you before you sign if a site's code isn't the team's release.
projects.project_description: Hydra is your dApp's watchdog. Not every update comes from the team. The biggest frontend hacks never touched a smart contract: attackers changed the website instead. BadgerDAO lost $120M to an injected script (Dec 2021), Curve users were sent to a cloned site through a DNS hijack (Aug 2022), and Bybit lost about $1.5B when one JavaScript file in Safe{Wallet}'s web app was changed. Bybit's own post says the attack "masked the signing interface", showing the right address while changing what was signed. Last week Polymarket said a compromised third-party provider hit 726 wallets, with $2.7M taken. Four hacks, same weak spot: the page looked normal, so users signed and lost funds. Today nobody can check whether the site they sign on is the build the team actually shipped. Hydra checks every script against the published build, in four steps: Publish: the team's CI sends each build to Hydra with one API key. No wallet in CI, no gas. Record: the SHA-256 of every file goes to Arkiv, a public, tamper-evident data layer, and the full build manifest goes to Swarm. Check: our browser extension re-hashes every script the page loads, including scripts injected after load, and our indexer re-checks live sites on a schedule. Warn: green if every script matches; red, naming the changed file, before the user signs. Before Hydra, a hacked page looks normal and users sign and lose funds. With Hydra, the same page shows a red warning in 3.8 seconds (measured on our live demo), and the protocol team gets an early alert on Telegram, Slack, Discord or a signed webhook, so they can act before more users are hit. When the team redeploys the right build, the site turns green again and Hydra sends a recovery alert. Live today, for everyone: Explorer (hydra-registry.vercel.app): anyone can search a domain, app name, file hash or Swarm reference and get a clear verdict, "Good to go" or "Warning: do not trust this site right now", read straight from Arkiv. No install, no wallet. Extension for everyday users (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Opera): checks every dApp you open while you browse. If our API is unreachable it shows grey (unverified), never a false green. Console for teams: sign in with your wallet and choose where alerts go. Teams prove they own a domain by serving /.well-known/hydra.txt, so nobody can publish a "release" for someone else's site. Try it: mouli51ch.github.io is an untouched published site and shows Good to go; our staged hijack of hydra-demo-dapp.vercel.app turns red and names /app.js.
projects.how_its_made: Hydra is a TypeScript/JavaScript monorepo built from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai, in two halves: publish once, then watch every load. Publish once: a team connects a wallet on the explorer's publish page (RainbowKit + wagmi), names its app and signs one message. The Hydra API (Node.js, plain node:http, on Render) turns that signature into a signed, expiring API key bound to that app name, verified with viem. The team adds one GitHub Actions workflow (hydra.yml) with the key as the repo secret HYDRA_API_KEY. On every push to main, our action (packages/action) hashes every file in the build output and sends the manifest to the API. The API uploads the build and a hydra-manifest.json to Swarm through the public gateway, then writes release, file and app-claim entities to Arkiv (Rabdi testnet) with @arkiv-network/sdk from its own testnet-funded wallet, so teams never need tokens or chain knowledge. Arkiv is our only database. Every release, file hash, app-name claim, indexer observation and alert subscription is an Arkiv entity, with expirations on the short-lived ones. Readers trust only entities created by Hydra's two wallets (publisher and indexer), so anyone can verify the record without trusting our server. The explorer is a static site on Vercel with no build step: it loads the Arkiv SDK from a pinned CDN version and queries Arkiv directly from the visitor's browser. Swarm holds each build's manifest, and its reference is stored on the Arkiv release, so a check can be rebuilt from Arkiv and Swarm alone. Watch every load: the Chrome MV3 extension sees each script a page loads through webRequest (including scripts injected after load), fetches it again without cookies, hashes it with Web Crypto SHA-256 and compares it with the release. Its red warning banner lives in a closed shadow root, so the page cannot hide or restyle it, and script bytes are only hashed, never run. The indexer re-checks published domains plus the top DeFi protocols by TVL from DefiLlama, writes only changed observations to Arkiv, and sends Telegram, Slack, Discord or Standard-Webhooks-signed alerts that teams set up in the console. Hacky bits worth mentioning: the Swarm gateway refuses to serve HTML (an anti-phishing redirect), which costs us nothing because Hydra only reads the JSON manifest and compares hashes. Domain ownership is proven by a /.well-known/hydra.txt file, checked at publish time and on every indexer run. We tested the wallet sign-in with freshly generated real wallets and real signatures through Playwright instead of mocks. The extension zip builds deterministically, so anyone can rebuild it and compare its SHA-256.

projects.title: Aegis
projects.description: A personal AI agent that acts intelligently but keeps humans in control.
projects.project_description: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of executing tasks independently, but autonomy without accountability creates serious risks. What happens when an AI makes a sensitive decision, sends a message, accesses private information, or initiates a financial action without human approval? AEGIS introduces a Human-in-the-Loop control layer for personal AI agents. AEGIS is a sovereign personal AI agent platform designed to combine private AI intelligence with human-controlled execution. Its architecture is built around 0G Private Computer for private, verifiable AI inference and World ID Agent Pass for human verification before sensitive or irreversible actions. Instead of allowing an AI agent to execute every action independently, AEGIS evaluates actions against user-defined autonomy policies. When an action requires human authorization, the agent pauses and requests fresh human verification. If verification succeeds, the protected action can proceed. If approval is denied, cancelled, or expires, the action is aborted. Users can interact with their agent, configure autonomy policies, monitor execution, and review a detailed activity and audit history. Our vision is simple: AI should be powerful enough to act, but never beyond the control of the human it serves. AEGIS — Your AI. Under Your Control.
projects.how_its_made: AEGIS is built using Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion. The application uses a modular architecture with a cinematic landing page, personal AI agent dashboard, autonomy policy editor, human verification interface, and activity audit timeline. The core architecture separates AI reasoning, action planning, authorization, and execution. Agent actions are evaluated against user-defined risk policies. Sensitive actions enter a Human Gate state and cannot proceed until the required human authorization succeeds. Denied, cancelled, and expired verification attempts lead to safe cancellation. The intended intelligence layer uses 0G Private Computer for private and verifiable inference, while World ID Agent Pass provides the human verification layer. The current application includes demo-mode simulations of these integrations so judges can explore the complete user journey. These simulations are clearly distinguished from live protocol integrations. Framer Motion powers transitions, loading states, and the cinematic verification experience. The interface is designed as a premium AI control center rather than a conventional chatbot.

projects.title: TouchStone
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hook that holds a refundable deposit on informed swaps and settles it on a signed price
projects.project_description: Every automated market maker has a quiet leak: a pool learns the price only from the trades it receives, so after the market moves it keeps quoting the old price until a bot trades against it. The bot keeps the difference and the liquidity providers pay for it. Touchstone is a Uniswap v4 hook that recovers part of that value without changing the price any trader gets. When a swap looks informed (large, first in its block, part of fast one-sided flow, or moving toward a stale price), the hook takes a small refundable deposit out of the swap's own output, in the same transaction and with a single wallet signature. A few seconds later anyone can settle it with a signed Pyth price. The trade is measured against that price: if its markout beats a margin, part of the excess goes to the liquidity providers and the rest returns to the trader. Benign flow is refunded in full and can earn a rebate. Around that core sit four markets: clawback on informed trades, a rented arbitrage licence that pays rent to the pool, rebates for benign flow, and quote integrity. For the last one, previewDeposit, a URC-4 indicative quote and a guarded router show the deposit before the user signs and enforce limits inside the transaction. Backtested on 184,145 real Ethereum USDC/WETH swaps from a held-out window, the trigger flagged the trades carrying 98.9% of toxic markout while asking a deposit on 23.4% of swaps (historical backtest, pre-registered). Seven verified contracts run on Arbitrum Sepolia, with a dashboard that executes a real swap and follows its settlement.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are Solidity 0.8.26 built with Foundry on Uniswap v4. The hook uses the beforeInitialize, beforeSwap, afterSwap and afterSwapReturnDelta permissions: beforeSwap snapshots price, liquidity and fee. afterSwap derives the notional from the actual currency deltas, evaluates four triggers (first touch per block, directional leaky-bucket flow, drift against a Chainlink reference, closed market) and returns a delta in the unspecified currency. The deposit is minted to the hook as an ERC-6909 claim in the PoolManager, so it is atomic with the swap and needs no second approval. The hook address is mined with CREATE2 to carry its flag bits, and the deploy script predicts nonces to wire seven contracts in one pass. Settlement is a separate contract. It verifies one signed Pyth update through the unique-update call and applies a confidence margin. It clips an overshooting swap to its in-the-money leg, so padding cannot dilute the markout. It splits the retained amount into a tip, a rebate pool and LP income that vests over time through a donation. The hook rechecks that the payout conserves the deposit exactly before paying. Partner technologies: Uniswap v4: PoolManager, StateView and V4Quoter. Pyth: settlement prices. Chainlink: the swap-time reference. Arbitrum: ArbSys supplies L2 block numbers for the first-touch rule. Notable engineering: The hook is 23,993 bytes against the 24,576-byte limit, because URC-4 quotes are served through its fallback to a lens contract. A tick-walking lens sizes trades across liquidity bands. Transient storage carries first-touch state through a transaction. A Rust simulator replays settlement against contract bytecode. Off-chain: A TypeScript keeper (viem, zod) fetches Hermes updates and settles records. An indexer with a read-only API and a Discord alert monitor watch the pool. CI runs 254 forge tests, invariant suites, Slither, coverage and gas gates, and dependency audits. The dashboard is Vite, React and viem with a WebGL ray-marched illustration. Its Simulation page calls previewDeposit, signs once, and shows t, the markout and the payout. The research is pre-registered Python with fixed seeds and hashed inputs. These counts are from my earlier runs: 254 forge tests, a 23,993-byte hook and seven contracts verified on Arbiscan. The 98.9% / 23.4% backtest figu2 results.

projects.title: Lala Fi
projects.description: Private payments on the chains you already use: deposit on Ethereum, Base or Arbitrum, exit on any.
projects.project_description: Privacy shouldn't require moving to a new chain. Today, every on-chain payment is public: your salary, your savings, who you pay. The usual fix is "move to a privacy chain". That means new wallets, thin liquidity, a new bridge to trust and an ecosystem nobody uses. People want privacy on the chains where their money already is. LalaFi is one shielded pool shared by Ethereum, Base and Arbitrum.
projects.how_its_made: ZK circuit: circom + snarkjs (Groth16 on BN254), adapted from Tornado Nova. It has 2 notes in, 2 out, a depth-24 Merkle tree and Poseidon hashes, and proves in about 1 s in the browser. The proof locks in the recipient, destination chain and fees, so a relayer can't redirect funds. Contracts: Solidity + Foundry. The hub on Ethereum holds the single Merkle tree and the global spent list, and checks every proof. Spokes on Base and Arbitrum take deposits and pay out, trusting only messages that arrive through the rollups' native bridges. A staked validator fast lane makes L2 deposits usable in minutes, and validators are slashed 100% if they lie. Tested with about 265 tests, including fuzzing, 14 invariants and attacks where every validator colludes. Partner tech: native Base and Arbitrum messaging means no third-party bridge to trust. Circle CCTP V2 rebalances USDC between chains. Off-chain: a TypeScript SDK (viem), a React web app, a CLI wallet, and a relayer, validator, finalizer and keeper.

projects.title: WaveFund
projects.description: A treasury run by a market of AI agents where the market decides which agent trades.
projects.project_description: Wavefund is a treasury where a market, not a token vote or a single fund manager, decides what the fund does next. The problem: DAO and on-chain treasuries hold billions, but allocation decisions come from token votes that are slow, low-turnout and easy to capture. AI agents can now write good proposals almost for free, so the bottleneck has moved from generating ideas to choosing between them. Normal decision markets can't solve this, because every proposal needs its own capital, so a trader with $1M cannot meaningfully back hundreds of options. Our answer is Quantum Markets, a design from Paradigm's research. Only one proposal is ever executed, so one deposit can count in every proposal market at once. In each Wavefund round, AI agents propose portfolio allocations (for example 30% ETH / 70% USDC). Anyone can deposit USDC once, claim credits in every proposal, and go LONG or SHORT on how the vault would perform under each one. When trading closes, the proposal with the best final-window average price wins, but only if it beats a "hold" baseline by a margin; otherwise the vault does nothing. The vault then executes the winning allocation through Uniswap v4, the losing markets are voided, and the winning market settles against the vault's realised return. Forecasters who were right get paid. The same engine can steer DAO treasury sleeves, protocol parameters, agent selection and grants, with token holders setting the guardrails and the market choosing inside them. This is a hackathon prototype on Arc testnet with no real funds. The demo interface can run in a simulated mock mode.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.26, Foundry, OpenZeppelin) on Arc testnet. QuantumRound runs each round: one USDC deposit gives credits in every proposal (each capped at the deposit), credits mint complete sets of LONG + SHORT tokens, and at settlement LONG pays π and SHORT pays 1 − π, where π maps the vault's realised return (clamped to a range such as -5% to +5%) onto 0 to 1. Only the winning market settles. Complete-set accounting and fuzzed solvency invariants keep payouts within deposits plus seed. Uniswap v4 does three jobs. (1) Every proposal market is its own v4 LONG/SHORT pool governed by a custom hook, WaveHook, which gates trading to the round window, bounds price to 0.01-0.99, and records price integrals in afterSwap so the final-window TWAP used for selection is computed on-chain. We mined the hook address flags with CREATE2 and HookMiner. (2) The winning allocation executes through a real v4 USDC/tETH pool with a 500 bps oracle-relative slippage cap; a breach cancels the round and deposits redeem at par. (3) One protocol-owned reserve seeds every proposal pool, so a single pot of liquidity gives all markets depth. Hooks let us put the market rules inside the AMM instead of wrapping a stock pool. Wavefund is a treasury where a market, not a token vote or a single fund manager, decides what the fund does next.

The problem: DAO and on-chain treasuries hold billions, but allocation decisions come from token votes that are slow, low-turnout and easy to capture. AI agents can now write good proposals almost for free, so the bottleneck has moved from generating ideas to choosing between them. Normal decision markets can't solve this, because every proposal needs its own capital, so a trader with $1M cannot meaningfully back hundreds of options.

Our answer is Quantum Markets, a design from Paradigm's research. Only one proposal is ever executed, so one deposit can count in every proposal market at once. In each Wavefund round, AI agents propose portfolio allocations (for example 30% ETH / 70% USDC). Anyone can deposit USDC once, claim credits in every proposal, and go LONG or SHORT on how the vault would perform under each one. When trading closes, the proposal with the best final-window average price wins, but only if it beats a "hold" baseline by a margin; otherwise the vault does nothing. The vault then executes the winning allocation through Uniswap v4, the losing markets are voided, and the winning market settles against the vault's realised return. Forecasters who were right get paid.

The same engine can steer DAO treasury sleeves, protocol parameters, agent selection and grants, with token holders setting the guardrails and the market choosing inside them.

This is a hackathon prototype on Arc testnet with no real funds. The demo interface can run in a simulated mock mode.

projects.title: ghosty.xyz
projects.description: Ghost on every app. Ghosty keeps your onchain actions private on the apps you already use.
projects.project_description:
On Ethereum, nothing you do is private. Anyone can look up your wallet and see your balance, your trades, your loans and the exchange you withdrew from. Bots copy traders within seconds, and people hunt positions they can see. A second wallet doesn’t give you anonymity either, because the money that funds it leads straight back to you. Privacy tools exist, but they make you leave the apps you use. You install a separate privacy wallet, move your money into it, and hope your app is supported. Most people give up and stay public. Ghosty brings privacy to you instead. It’s a browser extension that sits next to the apps you already use and keeps your money in a private balance (USDC shielded in Railgun). When you open Lighter, Uniswap or Compound, you choose Ghosty from the app’s usual wallet list and tap Go ghost. Ghosty funds the app from a proxy account with no history and no link to you. The app works exactly as normal, but it can’t see who you are, what else you hold, or where the money came from. When you’re done, Ghosty moves what’s left back into your private balance, and the next app starts clean. You stay on the same app and the same network. There’s nothing new to learn, and no server of ours in the middle. Your keys never leave your browser, and every blockchain lookup goes through Anon-RPC over the Nym mixnet, so even the data provider can’t tie your activity to you.
Ghosty protects your anonymity, not the trade itself: your positions on the app are still public, and the app can still see your IP address.
projects.how_its_made:
Ghosty is a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) built with WXT, React and TypeScript, with viem for chain work. One rule drove every design choice: nothing the user does should leak who they are.
Three parts:
The background service worker holds the encrypted vault and runs each action as a saved step-by-step process, so closing the browser mid-action resumes it instead of stranding funds. An offscreen document does the heavy work: the zero-knowledge proofs, the Railgun engine, and the Nym client for Anon-RPC. A content script adds Ghosty to each app’s own wallet list through EIP-6963, so the app treats it like any normal wallet. The private balance: Railgun is the main privacy pool. We run its engine and prover inside the extension, so the proof that moves money out of the private balance is built on your machine and your notes are never sent anywhere. Privacy Pools by 0xbow is built in as a second option, through its SDK and relayer. It adds compliant privacy: deposits are screened, so honest users can prove their funds are clean without giving up their anonymity. While building it, we found that leftover change from a withdrawal keeps its original screening approval, so one approved deposit can fund action after action without waiting for the next screening round. Existing Privacy Pools users can recover their account with a single MetaMask signature.
The apps: for Lighter, Ghosty funds the account through Lighter’s deposit address and signs with Lighter’s official signer, compiled to WebAssembly so it runs inside the extension. For Uniswap and Compound, Ghosty funds an unused Arbitrum address that you connect like any wallet, and shields whatever is left back into the private balance afterwards.
The way back: returning funds to the private balance pays its gas in USDC, using EIP-7702, an ERC-4337 bundler (Pimlico) and Circle’s Paymaster, so that step needs no ETH.
Anon-RPC: every blockchain read goes through Anon-RPC over the Nym mixnet, so the RPC provider can’t connect your lookups to your IP. If Anon-RPC is down, Ghosty refuses to move money rather than quietly falling back to a normal RPC, because a silent fallback would break your privacy exactly when you think you’re protected. We found that the Anon-RPC hop drops the content-type header, which rules out Arbitrum’s own public RPC, so we route through a gateway that accepts it. Ghosty also checks every new address for past activity through Anon-RPC rather than asking Lighter, because a burst of lookups from one IP would itself link the addresses together. The hacky part, and what’s next: Railgun normally holds new deposits for about an hour while it screens them, and its broadcasters enforce that wait. Ghosty sends its own transactions, so it can move sooner. The cost is that each new account needs a little ETH for gas, and today that ETH comes from the previous account, which links the two. Moving that gas to a sponsored paymaster is our next fix, so every account stays fully anonymous.

projects.title: DreamScape
projects.description: Tell your phone a dream when you wake. 0G paints it in private and hangs it on a wall you own.
projects.project_description: You wake up from a vivid dream, and by breakfast it's gone. Dreamscape keeps it. Each morning your phone nudges you. Hold the gold button and say the dream, or type one line, and pick how it felt. That's the whole habit: ten seconds. A few minutes later it hangs on your wall as a painting, with your voice kept beside it. 0G Private Computer hears it, reads its themes and paints it, all sealed, and your own iAI credit pays once you sign in with your 0G account. Your 0G credit resets at midnight UTC, and whatever is left expires. So three hours before, Dreamscape spends it on three pieces: a poster of your week's sky, a four-panel comic of your newest dream, and a moving portrait. They wait in Drafts for your yes. Each morning lights a star, the month fills in like a calendar, and a sealed Morning Note compares your week with what most people dream. Everything you keep is yours, and you can check it. Each dream is stored encrypted on 0G Storage and anchored on 0G Chain. Your gallery is an ENS name, yourname.dream-scape.eth, and each day is a name under it that points at that day's dream. Sell numbered editions of a piece for USDC: each edition is an ENS name the buyer owns, listed on Arkiv so anyone can search by theme, and they can give it to a friend. Share your whole gallery with a pass, an ENS name minted to a friend, who knocks and gets in for ten minutes or an hour. Without 0G, Dreamscape can't hear, read or paint a dream in private, keep it encrypted, or pay for tonight's art, so the dream is forgotten by breakfast and the credit expires at midnight. Live at dreamscape.hacklabs.in, with an Android app. Every receipt: dreamscape.hacklabs.in/proof.html
projects.how_its_made: Dreamscape is a Next.js 16 app (React 19, Tailwind v4) with a SQLite store (node:sqlite) and a worker that runs every model call, upload and transaction as a retried job. The Android app is a Capacitor 8 shell around the live site that adds the microphone permission and a morning reminder the phone schedules itself (@capacitor/local-notifications). 0G Private Computer. Every call goes through router-api.0g.ai/v1, OpenAI-compatible, with the trust mode set to private, so a sealed provider runs it or it waits. whisper-large-v3 transcribes the voice note, 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b reads the themes and titles the dream, z-image-turbo paints it with verify_tee, tencent/hy-image-3.5-preview draws the comic panels from reference images so the hero looks the same in every panel, and bytedance/seedance-2.0 animates the moving portrait. Each step keeps its x_0g_trace request ID, TEE result, cost and who paid, shown under "How it was made" on every piece. When providers went down during the event, each job fell back to an ordered list of backup models, and the piece says which one stood in. Sign in with 0G. The sign-in uses 0G's own Privy app. The server checks the token with jose against Privy's JWKS, trades it at /v1/auth/privy for a router session, and creates a scoped key on the dreamer's own account (POST /v1/api-keys, with a daily credit_limit), stored sealed. The 0G Pay SDK 0.4.0 reads the balance: telling one dream took it from $4.91 to $4.90, with the sealed reading at about $0.0001 and the sealed painting at about $0.009. 0G allows that sign-in only on localhost, so the live site signs in with the same wallet through our own wallet-only Privy app, and the key keeps paying. The nightly run starts at 21:00 UTC, three hours before the credit resets, inside a $1 daily budget. 0G Storage and Chain. Each dream record and painting is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a per-dreamer key (HKDF from the server's master key) and uploaded with @0gfoundation/0g-storage-ts-sdk 1.2.13. DreamRegistry, our Solidity contract on 0G Galileo, anchors each dream's storage roots. ENS v2 on Sepolia. dream-scape.eth has its own DreamscapeRegistry. Each gallery, name.dream-scape.eth, is registered to the dreamer's wallet with its own resolver. Day names like 2026-11-06.name.dream-scape.eth are answered by that resolver's wildcard text records (dreamscape.root, date, scope), written by a scribe key whose roles allow only those keys, and read through the Universal Resolver. Editions are names in each gallery's editions registry, minted by our NightMarket contract, so they move between wallets as ERC-1155 transfers. Passes are names in a passes registry, minted to the friend. NightMarket and Arkiv. NightMarket takes Circle's USDC, sends 95% to the dreamer and 5% to a commons fund, and mints the edition. Listings, vendor stalls, knocks and timed visits are Arkiv entities on Rabdi (SDK 1.0.1), so the market is searchable by theme, kind and price without our server. Image models garble text, so comic panels come back with no words, and the app letters the page itself. Tested on anvil forks of Sepolia against the real ENS contracts, NightMarket and USDC (names, sales, passes, commissions), and on a local Arkiv node.
