projects.title: HunterVerse
projects.description: Hunt AR creatures, win real discounts. Businesses get footfall and brand awareness in return
projects.project_description: HunterVerse turns your city into a treasure hunt. Local businesses drop 3D creatures on the map; players walk to them, catch them, and unlock real discount codes – a game where every catch is a coupon worth something. For businesses: launch a campaign in minutes. Pick a 3D model, set rewards per rarity (Common, Rare, Epic, Legendary), choose exactly how many of each, and drop it on the map. Chainlink VRF shuffles the rarities on-chain, so nobody (not even the business) knows which creature is the Legendary one. Businesses choose "Auto settle" (catches are delivered instantly) or "Approval" (they approve each catch), and they're notified of every claim and resale. And get the Footfall For players: log in with World ID, so only real, unique humans can play – no bot farms, no multi-wallet grinding. The map shows one creature per business within 500 m. Get within 50 m, tap it, see its 3D model and reward, and hit "Claim it". The smart contract checks your distance, makes sure you only catch one creature per campaign, and gives you the next creature in the VRF-shuffled order, so rarity can't be sniped. Your creatures live in your Profile. Redeem one to reveal its encrypted discount code (redeeming is permanent), or keep it and sell it on the built-in Marketplace. Buyers pay the seller directly on-chain, and ownership moves automatically. Every creature's data is checked against the chain before it can be listed, so tampered or fake creatures can't be sold. A real-world loyalty game that brings people through the door.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity contracts (Foundry), a Node.js worker, a business app (Vite) and a player app (Next.js + React), all on Base Sepolia. Chainlink VRF v2.5: when a business launches a campaign, the contract requests randomness and runs a Fisher–Yates shuffle inside the VRF callback, so the exact rarity counts are preserved but their positions are provably random. We then made the map always show a campaign's NEXT creature in that shuffled order, which makes rarity un-snipeable without needing a second VRF call per catch. World ID (IDKit v4): players prove they're unique humans, and the proof is bound to their wallet (wallet address as the signal, verified server-side against World's API, one human = one wallet). Our server then signs an EIP-712 "claim ticket" that the CreatureMarket contract requires, so even someone calling the contract directly can't skip the human check. Arkiv: every creature is an Arkiv entity (rarity, location, reward, Swarm model reference, plus catched / listed / redeemed / price flags), created by the business's own wallet so $creator proves authenticity. Hacky bit: for Auto settle we predict the entity keys before signing, so creating the creatures and handing them to our settler wallet happens in ONE atomic Arkiv transaction. The settler then mirrors the chain: on a claim, sale or unlist it transfers the entity and repairs any field that doesn't match the chain. Swarm: the 3D .glb models are uploaded to Swarm, with a unique per-creature copy stamped with its ID, verified by re-downloading and hashing. Contracts: CreatureMarket (built with OpenZeppelin) handles claim, redeem, list and buy. The 50 m check runs on-chain with integer-only math (an equirectangular projection plus Bhaskara's cosine approximation), and the frontend uses the exact same formula with BigInt, so the "Claim it" button lights up if and only if the contract will accept it. Security touches: discount codes are AES-256-GCM encrypted before they ever reach the chain, and are only revealed to the creature's owner after an on-chain redeem. Marketplace listings need a signed attestation from our settler confirming the creature's data is untampered. The map is Mapbox with a three.js player avatar and floating 3D creatures. 54 contract tests (including fuzzing), 80+ unit tests and a full end-to-end test cover the whole flow.

Swarm: the 3D .glb models are uploaded to Swarm, with a unique per-creature copy stamped with its ID, verified by re-downloading and hashing.

Contracts: CreatureMarket (built with OpenZeppelin) handles claim, redeem, list and buy. The 50 m check runs on-chain with integer-only math (an equirectangular projection plus Bhaskara's cosine approximation), and the frontend uses the exact same formula with BigInt, so the "Claim it" button lights up if and only if the contract will accept it.

Security touches: discount codes are AES-256-GCM encrypted before they ever reach the chain, and are only revealed to the creature's owner after an on-chain redeem. Marketplace listings need a signed attestation from our settler confirming the creature's data is untampered. The map is Mapbox with a three.js player avatar and floating 3D creatures. 54 contract tests (including fuzzing), 80+ unit tests and a full end-to-end test cover the whole flow.

projects.title: Lifeboat PQ
projects.description: Move an exposed Ethereum account to quantum-safe keys in one free, all-or-nothing transaction
projects.project_description: Every Ethereum account that has sent a transaction has published its public key. A large enough quantum computer could turn that key back into the private key and empty the account. You can't fix this by changing keys: the address is derived from the key, so the funds have to move. Lifeboat is that move. First it checks, privately, whether an address has exposed its key: the reads go through Anon-RPC over the Nym mixnet or Tor, so the RPC provider never learns who asked. Then one sponsored transaction creates a quantum-safe account and moves all the ETH and tokens into it. Everything moves or nothing does, and a sponsor pays the fee, so even a wallet holding only tokens can get out. The new account checks a hash-based signature on every transaction. In hybrid mode it also requires the old key, until the owner flips a one-way switch to quantum-safe only. In the demo we hand an attacker the old private key, exactly what a quantum computer would recover: a forged signature and a replayed real one are both refused by the network. Completed moves can be listed, opt-in, on a public log on Arkiv, so the record outlives the test network, and each row can be checked against the chain from the site. It runs end to end on the EIP-8141 alt-mempool devnet. Keys are made and kept in the browser. MIT licensed.
projects.how_its_made: The signature is XMSS with WOTS+C, written from scratch in TypeScript and verified in Solidity using only keccak256. Each account holds 1,024 one-time keys in a Merkle tree. Instead of a checksum, the signer searches for a counter that makes the message's base-4 digits add up to a fixed total, so verification always walks the same 144 hash steps: a fixed 48,600 gas per signature (an earlier w = 16 version averaged 101k and didn't fit the budget), with a 4,424-byte signature. The account is an EIP-8141 frame account that checks this signature in its VERIFY frame and only accepts the one-time key matching the transaction's nonce, so a key can't be reused. The move is a single frame transaction that creates the account through a CREATE2 factory and moves ETH and tokens atomically. A staked MigrationSponsor pays the gas only if the sender's key is exposed, the destination is a real Lifeboat account and it's that account's first move. Checking that means reading the factory's storage during validation, which the public mempool refuses (StorageReadNonSender) and the ERC-8421 alt mempool allows for a staked sponsor. The site shows the same signed transaction refused by one and mined through the other. The account itself fits the public mempool's 100k validation budget; only the sponsor needs the alt mempool. The exposure check makes five mainnet reads through Anon-RPC (@anon-rpc/browser-harness), Nym first and Tor as a backup, with the address as the isolation key; stalled reads retry over a fresh route. The opt-in public log uses the Arkiv SDK on the Rabdi testnet; the publisher re-derives every field from the mined transaction before writing. Frontend: React and Vite, keys generated in a Web Worker in about 5 seconds, signing in the browser. Contracts compile with solc-js and are tested in-process with @ethereumjs/evm (no Foundry); 24 tests. Claude Code helped write and test the code and draft the docs; details in the README.

projects.title: Topi
projects.description: True on-chain financial privacy engineered to survive the quantum era.
projects.project_description: Topi is a post-quantum private payment system built on Ethereum. It allows users to deposit, hold, and privately withdraw ETH without exposing their transaction history, their physical network location, or their wallet identity. The Problem Existing on-chain privacy protocols (such as Tornado Cash and Railgun) suffer from three critical vulnerabilities: The Quantum Threat : They rely on elliptic-curve pairings (BN254/Groth16) and classical ECDSA signatures. When quantum computers arrive, every historical and active note in these pools can be unmasked and drained. Network Layer Leakage : Transactions are sent directly to RPC nodes and public mempools, broadcasting the user's IP address, ISP, and timing metadata. The Relayer & Gas Bootstrapping Dilemma : To withdraw to a fresh address without linking identity, users need a way to pay gas. Traditional relayer networks are fragile, centralized, and constantly targeted for censorship. What Topi Delivers Topi eliminates all elliptic curves, pairings, and trusted setups across the entire transaction path—replacing them with hash-based, lattice-based, and symmetric constructions from packet transmission to on-chain execution. How the System Works Shielded Deposit : A user deposits ETH into the pool alongside a blinded precommitment. The smart contract assigns an index, computes the note commitment, and appends it to an incremental Poseidon2 Merkle tree (the pool tree) and an association tree. Zero-Knowledge Spend Proof : To withdraw, the user’s wallet syncs Merkle roots from on-chain event logs and generates a zero-knowledge withdrawal proof locally. Using Spartan-WHIR over the 31-bit KoalaBear field, proving completes in ~1 second (450 MB RAM) on consumer hardware, proving ownership of an unspent note without revealing which note it is. Post-Quantum Mixnet Routing : Instead of sending the ~1.3 MB proof to an RPC node, the wallet breaks it into ~280 fixed-size 8 KB onion packets. These packets are routed across a 4-node mixnet (Gateway → Mix → Exit) encrypted with X-Wing (ML-KEM-768 + X25519). Packets are mixed, shuffled in batches every 1.5 seconds, and padded with dummy cover traffic to defeat traffic analysis. Anonymous Rate-Limiting : To prevent DDoS attacks without requiring accounts, the gateway verifies a Binius64 zero-knowledge ticket over SHA-256 once per 10-minute epoch. A single 164-byte token on the first packet unlocks a 512-packet continuation budget. NAT-Friendly Replies : The first packet embeds a Single-Use Reply Block (SURB). The exit sends an acknowledgment back through a reply relay to a mailbox on the gateway. The client polls the gateway, so withdrawals work seamlessly behind firewalls and mobile cellular uplinks without opening inbound ports. Exit Aggregation & Recursion : An exit operator pulls two pending spends from its queue and runs leanVM recursion. It folds both client proofs into one compact terminal proof (~100 KB), amortizing the verification gas on-chain. EIP-8141 Settle & Alternative Mempool : The exit submits a frame transaction where the pool contract itself is the sender. Gas is sponsored by a post-quantum paymaster verified via a 5.6 KB stateless leanSPHINCS signature. Because verifying this signature requires 160,100 validation gas (exceeding standard public mempool limits), transactions route through a dedicated ERC-8421 alternative mempool that gossips transactions over libp2p. Mathematical Assurance : The state transition rules are modeled in Lean 4 with machine-checked proofs guaranteeing that no nullifier can ever be double-spent and the pool balance invariant is strictly preserved.
projects.how_its_made: Topi was engineered across four distinct technological environments: Rust for network and cryptographic transport, Yul/Solidity for EVM smart contracts, Python/Rust for recursive proving pipelines, and Lean 4 for formal verification. 1. Cryptographic Proving Pipeline Client Prover : Implemented with ethereum/spartan-whir over the KoalaBear field (p = 2^31 - 2^24 + 1). It proves the Privacy Pools withdrawal relation against 82 public fields, producing a compact transaction digest in about 1 second. Exit Prover : Uses Client-Side-Proving/leanVM. The exit operator verifies two client proofs in the VM and executes a grouped root recursion into a single Keccak-based WHIR terminal proof. Proving takes about 2.5 minutes on a 32-vCPU AWS c7i.8xlarge spot instance. On-Chain Verifier : Generated using ethereum/sol-whir-p3 (LeanVmGroupedTerminal_KeccakPow28T6Lean, 59 KB bytecode). StatementBinding.sol uses unrolled Poseidon1 and Poseidon2 permutations to cryptographically bind the terminal proof's applicationRoot to both spends' 82 fields inside the EVM. 2. Network Transport and Rate-Limiting Stack (Rust) crates/sphinx : Implements KEM-Sphinx packet serialization using the hybrid X-Wing cipher (NIST ML-KEM-768 lattice KEM combined with X25519). Packets are strictly 8,192 bytes. Per-hop keys (MAC, payload, and header stream) are derived using BLAKE3. crates/mixnet : Implements four node roles (gateway, mix, exit, reply-relay). Mix nodes batch packets over 1,500 ms windows and shuffle them. Gateways emit Poisson-distributed cover traffic (mean 700 ms) and run an internal key-value reply store for SURBs. crates/ratelimit : Implements anonymous epoch tickets using binius64 (Binius ZK proofs over SHA-256). 3. EVM Smart Contracts and EIP-8141 Frames (Yul / Solidity) Yul Account Abstraction : PoolAccount.yul and PQPaymaster.yul enforce EIP-8141 frame validation policies. Hash-Based Signatures : We integrated the leanSPHINCS verifier from nconsigny/SPHINCS-. The paymaster reads a 5,684-byte witness from an ARBITRARY signature entry and validates it on-chain using Keccak-based SPHINCS+. ShieldedPool.sol : Manages dual depth-32 incremental Merkle trees, checks historical roots, updates nullifier registries, and processes dual-recipient balance payouts. 4. Alternative Mempool (ERC-8421) Built by extending the open-source ERC-8421 sidecar (forshtat/mempool-workshop-sidecar, a Skandha fork for frame transactions). We wrote a custom admission engine (mempool/src/policy.ts) that verifies nullifier freshness, Merkle root validity, fee recipient commitments, and leanSPHINCS signatures before gossiping over libp2p. 5. Formal Verification (Lean 4) Modeled in lean/PoolModel/. We proved theorems (only_settle_runs_as_pool, run_distinct, settle_preserves_inv, pq_pool_tx_has_no_ecdsa) directly against Lean's kernel axioms (propext, Quot.sound). We paired this with differential testing scripts comparing Lean's pool-policy engine against ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction over 500+ mutated transaction vectors. Notable Hacks and Engineering Challenges Emitting Unreleased Opcodes via Yul verbatim : EIP-8141 introduces brand-new EVM opcodes (TXPARAM 0xB0, APPROVE 0xAA, FRAMEDATALOAD 0xB1, SIGDATACOPY 0xB5). Because solc has no native syntax for these opcodes, we hand-crafted the validation accounts in strict Yul assembly and injected raw opcode byte sequences using the verbatim builtin with pinned solc 0.8.28 compiler steps. Preventing Griefing via Storage-Based Nullifiers : Under EIP-8141, transactions can declare nonce keys. Initially, we considered setting the spend nullifier directly as an EIP-8250 nonce key. However, this introduced a severe denial-of-service vector: an attacker could copy a victim's nullifier from the mempool and submit it inside a transaction with a garbage proof. Frame validation would pass, consuming the nonce key, but the transaction would revert, permanently bricking the victim's note. We resolved this by keeping nullifiers strictly in contract storage inside ShieldedPool.settle. If a settlement fails, zero nullifiers are consumed. Patching Skandha's P2P Gossip Frame Cap : Settle transactions carrying the recursive terminal proof are about 104 KB in calldata. The upstream Skandha sidecar had a hardcoded 64,000-byte frame-data ceiling and dropped our transactions silently on the gossip network. We patched the sidecar to expand the gossip frame buffer to 128 KiB and increased the validation budget parameter maxVerifyGas from 100k to 200k. Bypassing the Devnet Code Deposit Gas Limit : On the public ERC-8421 devnet (chain 1337), state gas rules impose about 1,530 gas per byte of code, creating a ~37 KB contract deployment cap under the 60M block gas limit. Our terminal verifier is 59 KB and the pool logic is 50 KB. To deploy on chain 1337 without breaking up the verifier, we deployed the contracts on a local Anvil instance, extracted the contract state dumps, and injected them directly into the devnet's genesis allocation (deployments/1337/genesis/). Self-Contained Ratatui Terminal UI : We built crates/console (topi), which embeds the prover bash scripts, the Bun sidecar patches, and contract bytecodes directly into the compiled Rust binary. On non-repo machines, it automatically unpacks the environment into ~/.topi, controls background AWS spot instances, and renders a live ASCII world map tracking packet propagation across Mumbai, Frankfurt, N. Virginia, and Singapore.

projects.title: Sableye
projects.description: Stripe for USDT on Whitechain: checkout, invoices, subscriptions, refunds, straight to your wallet.
projects.project_description:
Sableye is Stripe for stablecoins: a drop-in SDK that lets any business accept USDT on Whitechain without ever handing its money to a middleman. The problem. Businesses that want to take crypto payments today have two bad options. A custodial gateway holds their money and can freeze it. Or they paste a wallet address and check an explorer by hand: no invoices, no refunds, no receipts, no accounting. Sableye gives them the full Stripe experience (invoices, a checkout widget, refunds, subscriptions, webhooks, emails, a dashboard) while every payment goes straight from the customer's wallet to the merchant's wallet. Sableye never holds funds. How it works. The merchant's server signs an EIP-712 invoice with its own key: amount, token, order ID, expiry, payout address. Signing costs no gas and needs no transaction. The customer pays it through our PaymentProcessor contract, which checks the merchant's signature, the expiry and the exact amount, and moves USDT directly to the merchant. Each invoice can be paid only once, refunds are capped on-chain at what was paid, and the contract never holds tokens. The checkout picks the best payment path automatically: gasless: EIP-3009, where the customer holds no gas token and the merchant's server pays a fraction of a cent; permit: one transaction; approve: works with any token. The server confirms each payment from the chain before fulfilment, never from the browser. What a merchant gets (one npm package: npm install sableye): invoices and payment links with QR codes; a styled <Checkout> component with themes, plus a one-line <script> drop-in for plain HTML sites; mobile wallets via WalletConnect; gasless payments; full and partial refunds; recurring subscriptions with a customer-approved spending cap, charged automa keeper; coupons; signed webhooks with replay; email invoices, receipts and "you got paid" notices with PDFs; revenue analytics (MRR, churn), reconciliation and CSV export. Built for AI coding agents. npx sableye init asks the merchant what they need: ting, checkout look. It writes their settings, then sets up their coding agentwith version-matched docs, an AGENTS.md and a skill, and prints a prompt that wires Sableye into the app's existing payment step without redesigning it. In our evaluation, Claude Code
integrated Sableye correctly in 12/12 trials across four real-shaped apps: Nexterver, Express, and a static HTML site. Merchant-owned records on Arkiv. Every paid invoice, refund and subscription is the merchant's wallet and written by the merchant's own server. Public fieldsare only what is already public on-chain. Order details and customer data are encrypted with a view key derived from the merchant's wallet signature. Our Books page reads these records
directly from Arkiv in the browser with no Sableye code, verifies each one again, and decrypts with the merchant's wallet. The merchant's books survive even if every Sableye server goes offline. A paid invoice costs about 0.00038 GLM per year on Arkiv. Verified, not just tested. The contracts are deployed and fully verified on Whitechain Sepolia, and the source on the explorer is byte-identical to our repo. PaymentProcessor: 0x8312552Ec716F0c159D88F73230Fff98C4aeCfB5 SubscriptionManager: 0x4E2571F08f6399b769F5F04ED7a54CE55729Bb78 Beyond unit, fuzz and invariant tests: we proved the core properties with Halmos (symbolic execution) and SMTChecker Gambit mutation testing: our test suite killed 165 of 165 mutants; we model-checked the SDK's indexer and subscription keeper with Quint/Apalach That process found and fixed eight real bugs. Try it. The live sandbox at https://sableye.xyz runs a real merchant on Whitech create and pay invoices with real test USDT, use gasless checkout, refund, and subscribe with renewals every 5 seconds; watch webhooks and emails arrive; see everything in the merchant's Client view; open the merchant's books on Arkiv.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, OpenZeppelin). PaymentProcessor checks an EIP-712 signed invoice (merchant, payout, token, amount, expiry, nonce): Signatures: SignatureChecker, so both normal wallets (EOAs) and smart-contract wallets (ERC-1271, e.g. Safes) can be merchants. Transfers: SafeERC20 moves tokens straight from payer to payout. The processor never holds a balance. Three payment paths: pay (approve), payWithPermit (EIP-2612), and payWithAuthorization (EIP-3009, gasless, with the authorization bound to the invoice hash so a relayer can't redirect it). Refunds are capped at what was paid, and revocation works via nonce bumps. SubscriptionManager stores a customer-approved spending cap and lets the merchant's keeper charge one period at a time, with on-chain timing checks. Deployment: both are deployed and verified on Whitechain Sepolia. We confirmed the explorer's verified source is byte-identical to the repo. Formal verification, done for real during the hackathon: Halmos symbolic proofs (17), with symbolic block time and number. Proofs that pass vacuously are a classic trap, so we planted 13 deliberate bugs and confirmed every proof catches them. solc's SMTChecker. Gambit mutation testing: we wrote a parallel worker-queue runner, and the test suite killed 165 of 165 mutants. projects.title: Tremor Mesh
projects.description: Residents' phones become a tamper-proof vibration witness: a tremor counts only when many agree.
projects.project_description: Metro lines and redevelopment shake Mumbai's old buildings every day. When residents complain about cracks, the only records belong to someone else: the contractor's site log, the authority's monitor, a spreadsheet. Each can be edited or withheld by one party, and residents' own phone readings get dismissed as "not accurate enough" (MMRC, 2017). TremorMesh turns the phones residents already own into a shared vibration record that nobody can rewrite, not even us. SENSE: each flat keeps one phone lying on the floor, running our web app (no install). It filters the motion sensor, computes peak particle velocity (mm/s) and fires only on a sudden change. A phone that is tilted or held in a hand is labelled "handling" and can never count. AGREE: one phone proves nothing. An event is confirmed only when k registered phones (k = 3 on our demo site) feel it within the same window (2000 ms). A 3-tone sound chirp aligns phone clocks, even offline. PROVE: the building committee invites each phone with a one-time QR; the phone gets its own ENSv2 subname, and the site rules (k, window, max phones) are public ENS text records. Every reading is signed by a key that never leaves the phone and written straight to Arkiv. Every viewer's browser recomputes the quorum; no server of ours decides anything. A revoked phone's new readings are refused, but what it witnessed before still stands (as-of rule). Confirmed events are sealed as evidence packs on Swarm, with the pack hash on Arkiv. Switch our servers off and a single offline HTML file rebuilds and verifies everything from Arkiv, ENS and Swarm. MAP (disaster mode): when a stronger quorum detects an earthquake, our companion Android app lets phones mesh over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi with no internet, relaying signed "I'm safe" / "I need help" check-ins and showing who hasn't been heard from; everything syncs to Arkiv when any phone reconnects. Next: using signal strength between phones for relative distances, to show rescuers where someone was last. Tested live at ETHGlobal Mumbai: 4 phones on a table, 141 readings, 137 refused (79 lone phone, 44 handling, 14 not registered), 1 event confirmed by 3 phones at 23:00:41 and sealed on Swarm. The dashboard can replay that recorded session. What we claim: a corroborated event in a vibration band at a time, co-signed by registered flats. Not a finding that a legal limit was exceeded, and not geophone-grade.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces): packages/core (pure logic, unit-tested), packages/chain (Arkiv, ENSv2, Swarm), apps/web (Vite web app + Vercel functions). Live at tremor-witness.vercel.app. Sensing (packages/core): the browser's Generic Sensor API (LinearAccelerationSensor, ~60 Hz). Each axis is band-passed (2 Hz high-pass removes tilt and hand sway, 25 Hz low-pass), integrated to velocity with a second high-pass against drift, and an STA/LTA detector fires on sudden changes. Peak velocity (PPV) and dominant frequency are reported. Handling rejection uses tilt (>15°) and the share of energy below 3 Hz. Quorum: a pure, deterministic function. Sort valid triggers, slide a window from each anchor, take the first trigger per phone; at least k distinct registered phones means an event. Because it is pure, every dashboard, the offline viewer and the Android app compute the same answer from the same signed data. Sound sync (hacky part): phone clocks were seconds apart. A phone plays a 3-tone chirp (3/5/7 kHz); the others detect it with a Goertzel filter on the mic and write sync anchors, so readings are aligned to one shared instant with no internet. Arkiv: every reading is an Arkiv entity written and signed by the phone's own in-browser key, so $creator is the phone itself, with no relayer. Raw triggers expire; confirmed events last longer. The quorum is literally a query over Arkiv, recomputed by every viewer. Invite issue/use is also logged on Arkiv. ENSv2 (Sepolia): <phone>.<site>.tremorwitness.eth subnames are the registry of who counts. Site rules live in text records (tw.k, tw.window_ms, tw.max_phones, plus tw.dk / tw.dwindow_ms for disaster mode). The as-of rule only counts a reading if the name was registered to its writer both at the claimed time and when Arkiv recorded it, so revocation stops future readings without rewriting the past, and a revoked phone cannot backdate. Swarm: confirmed events are packed (members, readings, ENS snapshot) and uploaded to Swarm; the keccak hash goes on an Arkiv event entity. The report page and scripts/verify-event.ts check the pack against the hash. Servers are optional: our Vercel functions only drip test gas, sign invites and register names. A single-file offline viewer reads Arkiv, ENS and Swarm directly. Disaster Mesh Android app (Kotlin, extensions/disaster-mesh): built on SafeMesh, our earlier GPL-3.0 fork of bitchat-android, for its Bluetooth / Wi-Fi multi-hop mesh. We added site join via the same invite QR (ENS mesh- subnames), a Kotlin port of the quorum checked against 307 shared test vectors, signed check-ins, a roster of who hasn't been heard from, and Arkiv sync on reconnect. Website: the team's own design, run through a small Preact runtime. AI assistance is documented in docs/AI_USE.md.

projects.title: GuardLink
projects.description: Cooperative health protection with private claims, independent appeals and verifiable payouts.
projects.project_description: GuardLink started after my father’s eye surgery. We had the paperwork, yet our claim kept stalling and my family borrowed while waiting for reimbursement. When it finally came, it felt like a favour. I wanted families to know what they were covered for, what was missing, and when payment would arrive. Over the past year, I reached 10,000 people directly and collected around 200,000 prospective contacts through community outreach. Conversations with women and families in Kerala’s self-help communities shaped the early prototype. At ETHGlobal Mumbai, I’m continuing that work through the Continuity Track and deploying the new version on Arc Testnet. A verified member contributes test USDC, receives a policy NFT and follows a private claim under one case ID. The evidence assistant requests missing documents, human jurors decide, and an independent panel can hear an appeal. The public ledger shows confirmed payouts. The demo uses synthetic claims. https://guardlink.ajnasnb.com/ledger/
projects.how_its_made:
Arc Studio helped build and deploy the Arc Testnet contract. Arc keeps USDC contributions, policy NFT issuance, jury authority and payout settlement verifiable. My coverage shows the NFT minted to the contributing wallet. The frontend, API Worker, evidence workflow and contract are in the public GuardLink monorepo. The evidence assistant accepts PDFs and photos, checks for missing document categories, and flags unreadable evidence and discrepancies with source references. The completeness score counts the required document types. Reviewers verify the sources and vote. Arkiv makes public milestones and governance queryable. Swarm stores encrypted evidence, and Arkiv links to the ciphertext reference. We are requesting the existing-project Arkiv + Swarm bonus. Uniswap v3 converts supported tokens into the pool’s settlement currency. The demo swaps WETH on Base Sepolia, bridges USDC with CCTP, then records a separate Arc contribution that issues policy #3. My coverage → Another way to contribute shows the three receipts. Continuity baseline: the founder’s research, direct outreach, cooperative insurance concept and prior prototype predate the event. Baseline commit: 370a135a7eb1fa883a4fca00111a3a8c2e5c226b. Mumbai added the Arc member and claims workflow, independent appeals, prospective governance, Arkiv and Swarm, and the verified conversion route. Codex helped with implementation, tests, documentation and editing. Arc Studio assisted contract development. The demo includes synthetic records, generated illustrative artwork and the founder’s narration. Arc Studio: https://studio.arc.io/app/5b1cd267-eb2b-4f67-82cf-0f0d2b15252d
Architecture: https://github.com/AjnasNB/GuardLink/blob/main/docs/ethglobal/ARCHITECTURE.md
Public Arc Studio app preview (open the Vercel app if the embed is blocked): https://studio.arc.io/share/arc-integration-deployment-sandbox-5d41cde3zs

projects.title: Kusari
projects.description: Onchain limits and an ENS kill switch for AI trading agents.
projects.project_description: Kusari lets an AI agent propose trades while an owner keeps enforceable control over its money and permissions. Funds stay in an owner-controlled vault. A Uniswap v4 hook checks the signed trade against a public ENSv2 policy: authorization, per-trade and daily spending caps, an allowed pool, price impact and minimum output. Revoking the agent’s ENS role blocks its next trade after confirmation. The live Sepolia demonstration uses real Gemini decisions and public transaction receipts. A normal trade succeeds within policy; a staged poisoned-news challenge demonstrates rejection when the model requests an over-limit trade. Anon-RPC/Nox carries the agent’s chain reads and submissions, while transactions remain public. The default demo is one shared funded workspace whose restricted agent key is held by Kusari’s runner. Visitors sign only a bounded run request and supply no trading funds. Separate-owner isolation has also been tested on live Sepolia: freezing agent A blocked A while agent B continued trading, with separate ENS labels, resolvers, vaults and spending counters. The README links the receipts. Personal self-service onboarding is an optional beta and is not required to use the shared demo.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts are written in Solidity around Uniswap v4 PoolManager and a required PolicyHook. AgentVault fixes its owner, agent and hook at deployment. The agent signs an EIP-712 SwapIntent binding the vault, pool, amount, minimum output, nonce and expiry. The hook checks authorization and spending before execution, then checks the real output and pool-price movement after execution; a revert rolls back the entire swap. ENSPolicySource pins an ENSv2 parent registry and reads policy data through ENSIP-10 resolution. A narrow registry marker role authorizes trading; the owner can revoke or restore it without changing the model. Agent privileges do not include editing the policy or moving the vault’s funds directly. The Kusari parent namespace remains a disclosed trust dependency. The TypeScript/viem runner on Fly calls Gemini and uses the Anon-RPC browser harness with Nox for chain reads, simulation and signed transaction submission. Next.js on Vercel supplies the interface and a fixed-route server proxy. Direct wallet-provider network/account checks pin owner actions to Sepolia. Shared runs use single-use signed challenges, cooldowns and service quotas. The public repository includes tests, deployment manifests, FEEDBACK.md and live isolation receipts. Codex assisted implementation, UI, tests and deployment tooling; the README discloses AI assistance and distinguishes automated rehearsals from user-confirmed MetaMask actions.

Next.js on Vercel supplies the interface and a fixed-route server proxy. Direct wallet-provider network/account checks pin owner actions to Sepolia. Shared runs use single-use signed challenges, cooldowns and service quotas. The public repository includes tests, deployment manifests, FEEDBACK.md and live isolation receipts. Codex assisted implementation, UI, tests and deployment tooling; the README discloses AI assistance and distinguishes automated rehearsals from user-confirmed MetaMask actions.

projects.project_description_markdown:
# Faultline

Faultline is an on-chain parametric earthquake catastrophe bond built on Hedera using Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS). It replaces traditional SPVs, manual calculation agents, and fragmented reporting with automated, auditable smart contracts.



### The Problem

Traditional catastrophe bonds transfer disaster risk to capital markets, reaching $65.5B outstanding by Q3 2026. However, issuance remains slow and expensive. High-risk emerging regions like India lack sovereign cat bonds or parametric cover, despite active seismic zones like Kutch (site of the 2001 M7.7 Bhuj earthquake).



### How It Works

1. **Deposit & Issuance:** A sponsor funds an HTS stablecoin coupon reserve. KYC-cleared investors deposit stablecoin into `FaultlinePool`, which mints ATS bond units 1:1.
2. **Immutable Rules:** Terms are hashed on-chain (`termsHash`) at issuance. The Kutch rule covers coordinates 22.5–24.5° N, 68.5–71.5° E (depth ≤ 70 km) with a linear payout from 0% loss at M7.0 to 100% at M8.0 (USGS-reviewed).
3. **Oracle Attestation:** Post-quake, the calculation agent ingests USGS data, signs an EIP-712 attestation, and logs it to an HCS topic. A relayer forwards this to `FaultlineTrigger`.
4. **Challenge Window:** A time-locked dispute window allows the trustee to pause or veto erroneous reports (bounded trust).
5. **Instant Settlement:** Calling `execute()` applies an O(1) global loss index, writing down all holders and releasing payout to the sponsor in one transaction.
6. **Maturity:** Investors redeem remaining principal plus accrued coupon yield.



### Hedera Architecture

* **ATS v8:** Regulated security token, KYC verification, and lifecycle management.
* **HTS:** Stablecoin collateral, coupon distributions, and disaster payouts.
* **HCS:** Tamper-proof, ordered audit log for signed oracle data.
* **EVM Contracts:** Pool and trigger settlement logic.
* **Mirror Node:** Fast queries for the Next.js/MetaMask dashboard (Investor, Sponsor, Trustee, Replay, Evidence, Issuer).



### Testnet Results & Metrics

* **Historical Replay:** Replayed 2001 Bhuj event (`usp000a8ds`) with an exact 70% loss settlement.
* **Trustee Veto:** Successfully intercepted and vetoed a synthetic invalid trigger.
* **Balance Audit:** Zero-leakage accounting across 34 live test transactions ($501 = 500 deposits + 1 reserve).
* **Verification:** Smart contracts verified on Sourcify (exact match).
* **Test Suite:** 436 Hardhat, 83 Oracle, 99 Unit, and 11 Playwright tests.



*Note: Faultline is an unaudited prototype for demonstration only. Not a licensed insurance or securities product.*
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
# Faultline Architecture & Implementation


### Tech Stack

* **Smart Contracts:** Solidity 0.8.28, OpenZeppelin Contracts v5

* **Testing & Deployment:**
* **Hardhat 2:** Compilation, unit testing, security checks, and fast-check invariant fuzzing (436 tests)
* **Hardhat 3:** Testnet execution using an encrypted keystore (zero plaintext private keys)


* **Oracle CLI:** TypeScript, Hedera SDK (@hashgraph/sdk 2.81), ethers v6, Zod
* **Frontend Dashboard:** Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, ethers v6; tested via Vitest and Playwright; hosted on Vercel

---

### System Integration & Lifecycle

* **Token Lifecycle:** The bond is an ATS v8 security token deployed via the ATS factory. FaultlinePool holds the exclusive issuer role to mint tokens 1:1 against HTS stablecoin deposits and burns them at maturity using controllerRedeem
* **O(1) Accounting:** Scalable settlements avoid looping over holders (O(n)). The pool updates a single global loss index and coupon index; all balance and payout adjustments evaluate on-demand from index deltas
* **Trigger Verification:** FaultlineTrigger validates oracle EIP-712 signatures against termsHash (RFC 8785 canonical JSON + keccak256), managing dispute windows, trustee pauses, vetoes, and replay protection
* **Deterministic Terms:** The termsHash logic resides in a shared TypeScript library imported across contract tests, the oracle, and the dashboard to guarantee consensus on parameter rules

---

### Integrated Ecosystem Services

* **Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS):** Handles regulatory compliance, KYC gating, role partitioning, and controller-directed redemptions
* **Hedera Token Service (HTS):** Native ledger support for stablecoin collateral, coupon distributions, and payout transfers
* **Hedera Consensus Service (HCS):** Serves as an immutable, sequential audit trail for oracle attestations; the client verifies EIP-712 signatures directly from mirror node streams
* **Infrastructure & Data:**
* **USGS ComCat:** Authoritative source for earthquake magnitude, coordinates, and depth
* **Hedera Mirror Node:** Backs dashboard event streams and HCS feeds
* **RPC Layer:** Hashio JSON-RPC relay with automatic failover to thirdweb
* **Contract Verification:** Fully verified with exact bytecode matches on Sourcify



---

### Engineering Solutions & Edge Cases

1. **Testnet Historical Replay:**
* Shrunk the real 2001 Bhuj event (usp000a8ds) into a 30-minute testnet risk window via timeOffsetSec
* Hardcoded chain-ID guards prevent replay terms from ever executing on mainnet


2. **Automated Trustee Pause:**
* Pre-signed pause transactions execute instantly upon oracle attestation broadcast, confirming within 6 seconds of a 120-second challenge window (114 seconds remaining)


3. **HTS Empty Revert Handling:**
* HTS system calls revert with empty data in the EVM, obscuring KYC or freeze failures
* Decodes failure reasons via mirror node trace analysis to display actionable UI error states instead of raw EVM reverts


4. **1.3× Gas Buffering:**
* Compensates for EIP-3529 storage refund anomalies in ATS execution paths by applying an automatic 1.3× buffer over standard eth_estimateGas values to eliminate INSUFFICIENT_GAS failures


5. **Non-EVM Workflow Fallbacks:**
* To work around lack of HCS EVM precompiles, the dashboard outputs prefilled CLI commands for HCS topic creation, HTS KYC granting, and oracle binding directly from the issuer portal


6. **Decoupled Wallet Execution:**
* The frontend handles read simulations, gas estimation, and receipt polling across dedicated RPCs with automatic retries; browser wallets are used solely for signature authorizations


7. **Idempotent Deployments:**
* All deployment and interaction scripts default to dry-run mode unless explicitly flagged (EXECUTE=1), supporting clean, repeatable demo states

projects.title: SPICA
projects.description: One SDK to discover services, control spending and execute autonomous USDC payments.
projects.project_description: SPICA acts as a payment and spending-control layer for AI agents. First, an AI agent searches for the API or service it needs through marketplace discovery. SPICA then inspects available providers, compares their pricing, and generates a quote. Before making a purchase, its Spending Firewall checks the agent's budget, provider permissions, spending limits, and approval requirements. Once authorized, SPICA coordinates the USDC payment through Arc and Circle's payment infrastructure. After payment is confirmed, the agent accesses the service and receives the result. Finally, SPICA records transaction events on Hedera through HCS, creating a tamper-evident audit trail. Its npm SDK makes these capabilities easier for developers to integrate into their AI agents.
projects.how_its_made: SPICA is built as an intelligent payment and trust layer for autonomous AI agents. We developed the application using React, Vite, TypeScript, and a backend API that connects service discovery, spending policies, and payment orchestration. The working flow starts when an AI agent searches for a service through the Circle Agent Marketplace Discovery API. SPICA retrieves available providers, inspects their details, compares pricing, and generates a purchase quote. Before any transaction, our Spending Firewall validates the agent's budget, provider permissions, per-transaction limits, and human approval requirements. For payments, we integrate Arc and Circle's USDC payment infrastructure, enabling agents to access services through a programmable payment flow. We use Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) to record transaction events, creating a tamper-evident audit trail that improves transparency and accountability. Our biggest focus is making autonomous payments controllable rather than simply automated. Instead of allowing an AI agent to spend freely, SPICA enforces spending rules through the backend. We are also developing the @SPICA/agent-sdk npm package to help developers integrate service discovery, quotes, purchases, budget checks, and transaction history into their own AI agents. The combination of programmable USDC payments, policy-based spending controls, and Hedera's audit infrastructure makes SPICA a foundation for safer autonomous commerce.

projects.title: Ruma
projects.description: Anonymous FIAT payments between Ecuador, Perú, Colombia, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia and Venezuela
projects.project_description: 6B dollars are being moved inside LATAM in remittances, most neobanks use a centralized provider or target only US-LATAM and Europe-LATAM corridors. Ruma is the app for all payments inside LATAM with decentralized, private KYC and stablecoin rails. With Ruma, a user can send dollars from a local bank in Ecuador and it arrives as pesos in Argentina directly to MercadoPago, all throughout a trusted peer network from all these countries with dispute resolution in the background. It also allows paying local QRs by spending the balance deposited to Ruma, this way travelers or debanking users get to spend USDC as locals. A user in Ecuador deposits money (USDC) from another wallet into Ruma, and then scans a DeUna QR and then this gets sent to a peer who will pay the QR for them, and receive the USDC in exchange. All within minutes.
projects.how_its_made: Ruma is a NextJS PWA with no backend server and a self-custodial, anonymous-first design. To create a Ruma account we use Privy to allow users to onboard with an email or passkey. The money sending layer is the most important thing, and for this we have integrated P2P.me SDK, which is a decentralized protocol for buying and selling USDC on Base. WIth this we can give one example of sending money from Ecuador to Colombia: Daniel from Ecuador wants to send money to Miguel in Colombia. Daniel deposits $100 on Ruma through a peer (he sends the FIAT to the peer's bank account and the peer transfers USDC automatically to Daniel's balance at buy price) and gets 100 USDC (at buy price 1USD=1USDC). Daniel has added Miguel as a contact with his Bre-B number (local payment method in Colombia), and he touches "send" this will initialize a USDC transfer from Daniel to a peer in Colombia, which wll then take the USDC and send the FIAT (pesos colombianos) to Miguel Bre-B. Payment details are stored in device only, transfered encrypted only to the peers to manage payments. This is all done by the P2Pme SDK. Alchemy is being used to fetch the transfers and then parsed into a readable format for activity tab on the app. I added usernames with ENSv2 for easy transfer between existing Ruma users. All users get a .rumalatam.eth username but I present it without this suffix inside the app, so they remember only the username part. It also works for depositing money into Ruma, in which screen displays the full ENS name. I deployed a Permissioned registar contract with a custom rule to not generate two identical usernames, no default username and some other smaller rules.

projects.title: Rover Hire
projects.description: Rover for Hire :Claude can think, but it has no wheels and no eyes. So it rents some.
projects.project_description: Claude can think, but it has no wheels and no eyes. So it rents some. You type one sentence into Claude: "Inspect parcel #3 and send me 5 photos. Spend at most 0.80 USDC." Claude finds a small robot car listed on Hedera, agrees a price with it, and hires it. The rover drives around the room, finds the box marked #3 among look-alike boxes, and photographs it from every side. Each photo shows up in your chat a few seconds after it is taken. Built for ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026, for 0G's Physical AI: Agents with a Body and Hedera's AI Agents That Pay: x402 on Hedera.
projects.how_its_made: We built Rover for Hire as an autonomous physical-AI marketplace where AI agents can discover, negotiate with, hire, and securely pay real-world robots to perform tasks. The system is built around three major components: Claude as the buyer agent, Hedera as the agent-commerce and payment layer, and 0G as the verifiable AI execution layer. On the commerce side, we integrated Hedera's ERC-8004 agent registry to discover registered rovers, A2A (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) for price negotiation, and x402 for per-action USDC payments. The buyer agent uses the Hedera Agent Kit to interact with these services. We also integrated Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) to maintain public payment and spending records. Users can choose between Hedera, Base, and Solana testnets for every mission. On the physical-AI side, we connected a camera-equipped 4WD rover to 0G Compute , where a vision model processes camera frames and generates individual movement decisions. These decisions are executed inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) , with cryptographically signed responses. The rover independently verifies the signature and payment before activating its motors. No model response or valid payment means no movement. The most interesting engineering challenge was implementing a strict pay-before-act and verify-before-act pipeline . Every movement requires a fresh AI decision, a valid TEE signature, and a confirmed payment. We also implemented a second, independent visual verification before taking each photograph: the model must confirm that the box number matches the requested parcel. Incorrect identification means no photograph and no charge. We built a multi-chain payment mechanism that validates the seller's wallet address against both its ERC-8004 registration and its shop listing, preventing payments to mismatched addresses. Every mission event, including camera frames, AI decisions, signatures, payments, and photographs, is persisted using 0G Storage , while an EpisodeLog anchors the mission record on 0G Galileo. Finally, Claude delivers photographs directly to the user as they are captured and leaves an on-chain agent review on Hedera after the mission. Partner technologies were fundamental to the architecture: Hedera enabled agent discovery, negotiation, reputation, and programmable payments; 0G provided verifiable AI inference and decentralized storage; and the physical rover brought the entire agentic workflow into the real world.

projects.title: Nod
projects.description: A crypto wallet where someone you trust gives a nod before a risky payment goes out.
projects.project_description: Nod is a wallet for people who are new to crypto and easy targets for scams, like newbies, parents and older relatives. When you sign up, you pick one person you trust as your trustee. They can never touch your money, but risky payments wait for their nod. Every payment is checked before it goes out. Your first payment is capped at $10, and someone you've never paid can get at most $10 in their first 24 hours. If the address is on a scam list, looks like a copy of someone you've paid before, or the amount is over the limit your trustee set, the payment goes to your trustee along with your answers to three quick questions. They can allow it once, or deny it. When they deny a flagged payment, the address gets reported, so it's flagged for every Nod user. Trustees can also paste any address into Nod to see if it's a known scam before anyone pays it. Signing in is just Google, so there's no seed phrase to lose.
projects.how_its_made: The app is built with Expo and React Native, so the same code runs on Android, iOS and the web. Everyone signs in with Google through Privy, which gives each person an embedded wallet. Payments are USDC on Ethereum Sepolia. The backend is a Supabase Edge Function (Hono on Deno) with Postgres. It runs the payment rules: the $10 first payment cap, the $10 limit for someone new in their first 24 hours, the trustee's limit, scam lists, and a check for copycat addresses that share the first and last 4 characters with someone you've paid. When a payment passes, the backend sends it as a signer on the user's Privy wallet, with gas sponsored by Privy. Arkiv holds the parts that need to be shared and provable. When a payment needs the trustee, the app writes an approval request to Arkiv from the user's wallet, encrypted to the trustee with tweetnacl, and it expires on its own after 24 hours. The trustee answers by writing a decision from a separate key made just for that pair, so nobody can link the trustee's main wallet to the person they protect, but the backend can still check who wrote it. It only accepts an Allow it can verify on Arkiv, so even our own server can't fake an approval. Scam reports also live on Arkiv, where any wallet can read them: about 780 imported from OFAC and eth-labels, plus reports from trustees when they deny a flagged payment. A few hacky bits: the trustee's encryption key is made from a Privy signature, so it comes back on a new phone with no backup. Privy can't sponsor gas on Arkiv's chain, so the backend tops up wallets with tGLM itself. A cron job renews scam reports on Arkiv before their 180 days run out and keeps a permanent copy in Postgres. We also check addresses with GoPlus, send pushes with Expo and invite emails with Brevo, and host the site on Cloudflare Pages.

Arkiv holds the parts that need to be shared and provable. When a payment needs the trustee, the app writes an approval request to Arkiv from the user's wallet, encrypted to the trustee with tweetnacl, and it expires on its own after 24 hours. The trustee answers by writing a decision from a separate key made just for that pair, so nobody can link the trustee's main wallet to the person they protect, but the backend can still check who wrote it. It only accepts an Allow it can verify on Arkiv, so even our own server can't fake an approval. Scam reports also live on Arkiv, where any wallet can read them: about 780 imported from OFAC and eth-labels, plus reports from trustees when they deny a flagged payment.

A few hacky bits: the trustee's encryption key is made from a Privy signature, so it comes back on a new phone with no backup. Privy can't sponsor gas on Arkiv's chain, so the backend tops up wallets with tGLM itself. A cron job renews scam reports on Arkiv before their 180 days run out and keeps a permanent copy in Postgres. We also check addresses with GoPlus, send pushes with Expo and invite emails with Brevo, and host the site on Cloudflare Pages.

projects.title: WondrPay
projects.description: UPI for digital dollars: pay anyone's name in USDT on Whitechain with a PIN. No gas, ~3 s to settle.

MetaMask works too, guarded by a WondrPay PIN. Pay anyone by scanning a QR, or by typing a name or address. Every person and shop gets a chat-style payment thread, like Google Pay. A PIN or fingerprint on every payment, plus World ID above a limit you set (default $100), so a stolen unlocked phone can't drain you. Deployed on Vercel. Every feature was tested with real testnet transactions (73+ scripted checks). Whitechain (chain 1874): we wrote and verified a PaymentRouter, a MerchantRegistry and an Autopay factory. A shop signs an EIP-712 Order. The payer signs USDT's EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization with nonce = the order digest, so that signature can settle only that exact order, and only through the router (no front-running). Allow-listed relayers pay the WBT gas, so users hold only USDT. Autopay uses one EIP-2612 permit per subscription contract, and the keeper can never charge early or above amount x cycles. Every read filters on our writer address, and payers re-hash each request and check the merchant signature on-chain before signing. ENS v2 (Sepolia): wondrpay.eth has its own UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver. Every shop or person gets name.wondrpay.eth with their Whitechain address under ENSIP-11 coinType 2147485522, resolved live at payment time. API secrets are stored as SHA-256 hashes, and every approval is a single-use wallet signature. Webhooks are SSRF-guarded and EIP-191 signed, and the SDK is SRI-pinned. projects.title: cybazaar
projects.description: Hire AI agents for useful work, verify their deliveries, and pay them in USDC.
projects.project_description: Argo Hiring Desk opens an existing AI agent company to outside clients. Today, Argo's agents work through a private team roster, message board and task system. Hiring Desk is designed to let people and other agents discover selected providers, post a brief, accept an offer, receive a verifiable result and pay in USDC, without needing access to Argo's internal systems. Our first use case is a bounded research assignment: compare three supplied public documents and produce a cited Markdown brief. The proposed workflow combines a public storefront with a private operator desk. The client agrees to a provider and price; the operator approves execution, reviews the result and releases it. Each assignment runs in a fresh worker with only its approved inputs, tools and budget, keeping private company memory and credentials outside the job. The architecture gives each public integration a specific role. Arkiv holds the public job lifecycle, Swarm stores released deliverables, ENS provides discoverable names, ERC-8004 supplies agent identity and a reputation integration, and Arc provides USDC settlement. A client should be able to inspect the job, delivery hash and payment evidence independently of the private dashboard. The hackathon scope is one complete hiring transaction with an Argo-operated provider and testnet payment. It uses direct payment after delivery, with no escrow or payment guarantee. Wearable operator controls and Hedera x402 metering are later extensions.
projects.how_its_made: We are building Hiring Desk as an optional addon to the existing Second Brain engine, with shared TypeScript contracts connecting the private operator interface, a separate public client application and an isolated worker service. This reuses Argo's existing agent-company infrastructure while defining a separate protocol for external work. The implemented foundation includes package and build wiring plus a versioned desk/v1 protocol. Its shared types and validation cover public records, client acceptance, lifecycle transitions and payment evidence. Foundation checks recorded in the build log include shared, server and web builds, declaration and ESM smoke checks, and 14 standalone protocol tests. These are package-level results; the integrated hiring flow still needs verification. The planned adapters connect Arkiv job records to Swarm delivery references, ENS names, ERC-8004 identities and Arc payments. The protocol binds acceptance to the job, provider, price, network and recipient. Amounts travel as integer strings, and a submitted transaction is kept distinct from a confirmed payment. The execution design separates the agent doing the work from the services holding authority. A disposable worker receives approved public documents and narrow tools. A gateway enforces access and spending limits, while a separate broker publishes approved output and handles permitted signing operations. Publication approval is bound to the exact result hash, so changing the output requires another review. The main engineering challenge is reconciling public job records, private operational state and payment receipts without treating them as one atomic transaction. The design uses explicit states, repeat-safe processing and restart reconciliation. Live adapter checks, worker isolation tests and the complete testnet demonstration remain the final integration gates.

projects.title: palm.fi
projects.description: Hack-proof vaults on Arc, compromised private key is no longer an empty treasury.
projects.project_description:
Palm fi : hack-proof USDC vaults on Arc. A compromised private key no longer means an empty treasury. THE PROBLEM Almost every major treasury hack ends the same way: the attacker gets valid signatures, and the money is gone before anyone notices. On Oct 29, 2026, attackers got an exchange’s own signing infrastructure to sign for them, and billions left hot wallets in under an hour. Multisigs, MPC and HSMs all protect the key. Once the key is compromised, there is nothing left to stop the outflow. OUR APPROACH palmfi protects the vault, not the key. We start from the assumption that the attacker already has valid signatures, and make that survivable. Unless an attacker controls more than half of an organisation’s wallets, the most they can take is a small instant budget. Everything else waits until the team has had a chance to say no. HOW IT WORKS Deposit: an org (e.g. “nvidia”) registers at least 3 wallets, each with one vote, and deposits USDC into its Vault on Arc. It receives a 1:1 Protected token (nvidiaUSDC). The token can only move between the org’s own whitelisted wallets and the payment pool, so there is no side door for transfers.
Instant budget: small payments go out immediately, up to a rolling 24h / 7d limit. That limit is all a single stolen key can ever move right away.
Delayed requests: anything above the budget becomes a request, with a 1 USDC bond. It defaults to the maximum 72h delay until it is scored.
Anomaly scoring with Chainlink CRE: the Sentinel workflow reads the vault’s own onchain history (its last 32 outflows, how often each destination has been paid, business hours, wallet ages, pending config changes) and computes a “surprise score” in bits. The delay starts at 15 minutes and doubles every 2.5 bits. Routine payroll scores about 3 bits and clears in about 30 minutes. A $3M payment at 3am to a brand-new address scores about 30 bits, which triggers a FLAG: the vault freezes and the destination is blocklisted. An attacker’s unusual withdrawal never gets the fast path.
The team decides: while a request waits, a majority of the org’s other wallets can veto it, or a majority of all wallets can fast-track it. Above a hard cap, at least 24h applies unless fast-tracked. Every voter gets a Telegram alert on long delays, FLAGs and settings changes, so honest wallets are present to vote.
Paying other orgs: orgs pay each other by name through a single Orbital pool, Paradigm’s N-token stablecoin AMM, built as a Uniswap v4 hook. You pay in your token and the payee receives theirs. The swap counts against your instant budget, so the pool can’t be used to get around the rules. Issuers settle in USDC later.
Recovery: a FLAG freezes the vault. An optional cold recovery key, which can never spend, can unfreeze it or migrate funds to a recovery vault fixed at onboarding. WHO IT’S FOR DAOs, exchanges, fintechs and any team holding stablecoins in hot wallets: anyone who needs payments to go out fast day to day but can’t afford one leaked key emptying the treasury.
projects.how_its_made:
We designed palmfi backwards from one assumption: the attacker already has valid signatures. So no component trusts a signer on its own. The Vault trusts its budget and its voters, the Hub trusts only Chainlink CRE reports, and the Uniswap hook trusts only the Vault’s budget check. There are three layers: Solidity contracts on Arc, two Chainlink CRE workflows, and a Next.js app. ARC: THE VAULT THAT CAN’T BE EMPTIED IN ONE GO Foundry contracts deployed on Arc testnet (chain 5042002). VaultFactory clones a Vault and a ProtectedToken for each org. A single Hub is the network directory, maps org names to vaults, holds the blocklist, and is the only contract that accepts CRE reports. Every vault reports its events through the Hub, so one CRE workflow can watch every org.
The Vault holds USDC, tracks the rolling 24h/7d instant budget, queues requests, counts votes, and freezes on a FLAG. The ProtectedToken enforces the whitelist in its own transfer function, so funds can’t leave through a side door.
Why Arc: a treasury product shouldn’t make its users hold a volatile gas token. On Arc, USDC is the gas, so an org only ever touches USDC. One wrinkle: Arc exposes USDC both natively (18 decimals) and as an ERC-20 (6 decimals). We use only the ERC-20 interface and reject msg.value, so gas amounts and token amounts can never be confused.
Arc Studio: we drove it from Claude Code through the arc-studio CLI. Studio built our Foundry project, ran the full suite on an Arc fork, and ran a security review that came with runnable PoCs. All 8 PoCs reproduced against our code. We fixed 7 with regression tests (AuditFixes.t.sol), recorded the 8th as a design decision, and redeployed. Getting exploit PoCs during a hackathon is unusual; it caught real bugs. CHAINLINK CRE: SPOTTING THE DRAIN BEFORE IT LANDS Sentinel (log-triggered): fires on RequestQueued, ConfigChange and Outflow events from the Hub. It reads the vault’s onchain scoringContext (the last 32 outflows, destination counts, business hours, wallet ages, pending config changes) and computes a deviation score in bits. The delay starts at a 15-minute floor and doubles every 2.5 bits. A score of 28 bits or more, or a blocklisted destination, means FLAG. The Sentinel then signs a SET_DELAY or FLAG report, which reaches Hub.onReport through the Keystone forwarder.
Every CRE node has to reach the same result, so scoring is pure integer math in milli-bit fixed point, with no floats anywhere.
Reconciler (cron): writes a heartbeat, scores any request the Sentinel missed, checks that reserves match token supply, and checks voter wallets for unexpected EIP-7702 delegations (a sign of a compromised wallet).
Alerts on DELAY and FLAG go out over Confidential HTTP to our /api/notify endpoint, which sends Telegram messages to every voter.
Why CRE: anomaly detection needs offchain computation, but the result has to be trustworthy onchain. CRE gives us decentralised, deterministic scoring that writes straight back to the contracts. No single server decides whether your treasury freezes.
A fixture suite simulates the failure matrix: CRE offline, malformed or stale reports, missed events. The Hub ignores bad reports, and if no score arrives, requests stay at the 72h maximum delay. When anything fails, the outcome is slower payments, never faster ones. UNISWAP V4: CLOSING THE SIDE DOOR Orgs pay each other through one Orbital pool (Paradigm’s N-token stablecoin AMM), built as a single v4 hook. Every two-token PoolKey is a facade over one set of shared reserves, held as ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager. Adding an org only adds facades over the same liquidity instead of fragmenting it into new pools.
beforeSwap is a NoOp custom curve. It does closed-form trades on the sphere invariant, or, when LPs provide liquidity in tight ticks, solves Paradigm’s torus invariant by bisection (OrbitalTicks.sol).
Inside the swap, the hook calls the payer vault’s chargeOutflow, so a payment through the pool uses the same budget as a withdrawal. A frozen token halts trading. Issuers settle foreign inventory in USDC later (deferred settlement).
We wrote our own minimal OrbitalRouter so the hook can trust msgSender() to identify the real payer.
Why v4: hooks let us replace the AMM curve entirely and enforce treasury rules inside the swap itself, so payments through the pool can’t bypass them. WEB
Next.js, wagmi and viem. Dashboard, voting with a per-term breakdown of each score, an incident view, pay-by-name and onboarding. /api/notify plus a Telegram bot for voter alerts. NOTABLY HACKY The Vault exceeded the 24 KB EIP-170 contract size limit, so we split it into Vault + VaultModule and joined them with delegatecall. Every contract is now under 24 KB.
The scoring model exists twice, in TypeScript in the Sentinel and in the UI, to explain scores. A drift test fails CI if the two copies diverge.
So the full flow can run live with cre workflow simulate --broadcast, the testnet Hub trusts CRE’s simulation forwarder. In production, Hub.pinWorkflow pins the real Keystone forwarder and workflow identity.
Faucet amounts are tiny, so the testnet FLAG threshold is 18 bits instead of 28. Otherwise our demo drain wouldn’t look scary enough to trigger a FLAG.
For uneven pools, the Orbital pool keeps a 20× virtual concentration so it stays on the curve.

A fixture suite simulates the failure matrix: CRE offline, malformed or stale reports, missed events. The Hub ignores bad reports, and if no score arrives, requests stay at the 72h maximum delay. When anything fails, the outcome is slower payments, never faster ones.

UNISWAP V4: CLOSING THE SIDE DOOR

Orgs pay each other through one Orbital pool (Paradigm’s N-token stablecoin AMM), built as a single v4 hook. Every two-token PoolKey is a facade over one set of shared reserves, held as ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager. Adding an org only adds facades over the same liquidity instead of fragmenting it into new pools.
beforeSwap is a NoOp custom curve. It does closed-form trades on the sphere invariant, or, when LPs provide liquidity in tight ticks, solves Paradigm’s torus invariant by bisection (OrbitalTicks.sol).
Inside the swap, the hook calls the payer vault’s chargeOutflow, so a payment through the pool uses the same budget as a withdrawal. A frozen token halts trading. Issuers settle foreign inventory in USDC later (deferred settlement).
We wrote our own minimal OrbitalRouter so the hook can trust msgSender() to identify the real payer.
Why v4: hooks let us replace the AMM curve entirely and enforce treasury rules inside the swap itself, so payments through the pool can’t bypass them.

WEB
Next.js, wagmi and viem. Dashboard, voting with a per-term breakdown of each score, an incident view, pay-by-name and onboarding. /api/notify plus a Telegram bot for voter alerts.

NOTABLY HACKY

The Vault exceeded the 24 KB EIP-170 contract size limit, so we split it into Vault + VaultModule and joined them with delegatecall. Every contract is now under 24 KB.
The scoring model exists twice, in TypeScript in the Sentinel and in the UI, to explain scores. A drift test fails CI if the two copies diverge.
So the full flow can run live with cre workflow simulate --broadcast, the testnet Hub trusts CRE’s simulation forwarder. In production, Hub.pinWorkflow pins the real Keystone forwarder and workflow identity.
Faucet amounts are tiny, so the testnet FLAG threshold is 18 bits instead of 28. Otherwise our demo drain wouldn’t look scary enough to trigger a FLAG.
For uneven pools, the Orbital pool keeps a 20× virtual concentration so it stays on the curve.

projects.title: Hugo
projects.description: AI-powered rewards for meaningful open-source contributions, funded and paid in USDC.
projects.project_description: Open-source programs depend on contributors, but incentive-driven participation can sometimes lead to floods of low-quality pull requests, overwhelming maintainers and making it harder to recognize meaningful work. Hugo makes rewarding genuine open-source contributions automatic, transparent, and sustainable. Instead of attaching a fixed bounty to every issue, Hugo allows maintainers and organizations to fund repositories through dedicated USDC treasuries. Project owners configure a maximum reward per pull request and can start or stop funding at any time. When a pull request is merged, Hugo uses AI to evaluate its impact, quality, correctness, testing, and complexity. A deterministic reward engine then calculates a payout based on the evaluation, recent donations, available funds, and the project's immutable reward cap. No manual reward approval is needed. Contributions merged while funding is active can receive automatic rewards; contributions merged while funding is stopped are ineligible. Contributors with registered wallets receive payments automatically. New contributors don't need to sign up beforehand: their rewards are reserved until they authenticate through GitHub, receive an embedded wallet, and claim their USDC. Hugo also supports multiple eligible contributors per PR, allowing rewards to be shared fairly rather than attributing all the work to one author. By combining AI-assisted assessment with programmable stablecoin payments, Hugo makes it easier for maintainers, DAOs, and sponsors to support meaningful open-source development without manually managing every payout. Fund open source. Reward meaningful contributions. P.S. Hugo is named after the character from A Plague Tale ;)
projects.how_its_made: Hugo is built using Next.js, TypeScript, Supabase, Vercel, GitHub Actions, thirdweb, Arc, Arkiv, and Chainlink CRE, with an AI evaluation layer that supports 0G Private Computer and OpenAI as configured inference providers. GitHub Actions initiates the workflow whenever a pull request is merged. The workflow submits contribution evidence to Hugo's hosted API, which evaluates the changes and persists the AI assessment. Our AI evaluation engine scores contributions across impact, quality, correctness, tests, and complexity. Rather than allowing an LLM to decide how much money to transfer, we separate AI scoring from financial calculations. A deterministic reward engine uses the quality scores, recent seven-day donation activity, treasury availability, and a hard per-PR cap to calculate the actual reward. Arc Testnet powers our programmable USDC treasuries. Each repository has a dedicated smart contract supporting funding deposits, owner-controlled funding intervals, capped allocations, onchain reward reservations, signed claims, and automatic payouts. Previously reserved rewards remain claimable even after funding stops. thirdweb provides GitHub-linked embedded wallets. Existing contributors with verified wallet associations receive rewards automatically. New contributors can authenticate later and claim reserved earnings without setting up MetaMask or sharing wallet addresses publicly. Arkiv Rabdi Testnet provides independently queryable contribution and settlement attestations. We implemented actual entity writes and a public verification interface that reads Arkiv records through its SDK, rather than relying only on our private Supabase database. Sensitive identity mappings and individual reward amounts are kept outside Arkiv. Chainlink CRE provides an additional verification layer. Our workflow retrieves an authenticated Hugo reward report and checks its repository identity, report hash, funding eligibility, reward reservations, and payout limits against finalized Arc blockchain state. We successfully demonstrated this through a CRE CLI simulation returning CRE_VALIDATED. For infrastructure, Vercel hosts the Next.js application and API, Supabase stores program and reward metadata, and GitHub Actions handles post-merge integration. One important design choice was keeping payouts independent of contributor onboarding: Hugo can reserve a reward for someone who has never visited our application and allow them to claim it later through their verified GitHub identity. The result is an end-to-end testnet prototype connecting ordinary GitHub contributions to AI-assisted evaluation, programmable stablecoin rewards, automatic settlement, and publicly verifiable contribution records.

projects.title: Rally
projects.description: Rally gets people off their phones and out the door, with others who want to do the same thing.
projects.project_description: Rally helps people get off their phones and into the real world to do activities with the right people! With more than 18 users already using rally! 🏁 Rally's Formation Intelligence Engine uses 6 diverse touchpoints understands the personal, activity and other feedback loop contexts and associates the right people together to do the right thing for the right world! Everyone chooses whether to join. Once enough people agree and the host sets a meeting point, the group can see where to meet. You can also browse a public map of open Rallies, where each dot represents a real plan and shares a playful invitation based on its title. After the activity, the Rally finishes automatically. Group members can leave an optional vouch or submit photos for group rewards ( RALLY Tokens ). The aim is simple: spend less time looking for people and more time doing things together.
projects.how_its_made: ✅ We built Rally as a mobile-friendly website using Next.js and React, with a TypeScript server handling plans, invitations, and rewards. PostgreSQL, hosted on Supabase, keeps the shared record of who has joined and which seats are available. Privy handles wallet sign-in. ✅ We use 0G Compute to make the Agentic Harness to understand people’s plans, choose useful questions, compare preferences, write the map’s invitations, and assess optional group photos for proof of work ( using 0g Image Models ) . ✅ Arkiv helps us publish and discover open activities without sharing people’s names, personal preferences, or exact meeting points. We check those listings against our database before showing them. ✅ We also integrated Arc Testnet for recording supported reward actions. Completion points work in the app; recording those on-chain requires the compatible reward contract. ✅ One useful detail is that invitations don’t reserve seats. When someone accepts, the server checks availability and capacity again before adding them. This prevents two people from accidentally taking the last seat. ✅  A background check runs every two minutes to look for missed matches, while unchanged results are reused to avoid unnecessary AI calls. ✅  We also fixed a subtle problem with follow-up questions: Rally now keeps details it already understood. If someone says “carrom in 17 minutes,” it carries that game and start time forward instead of asking for them again.
