projects.title: Sereno
projects.description: Every developer always had a wallet, they just got to know it now.
projects.project_description: Sereno turns every GitHub account into a crypto wallet, and every SSH key on a GitHub profile into the key that spends from it. No app, no seed phrase, no signup. Anyone can pay a developer by GitHub username: type "torvalds" on the pay page, or send to torvalds.sereno.eth, and USDC lands in a smart account at an address derived from their numeric GitHub ID. The developer doesn't need to have heard of us. The account doesn't need to exist yet; it's a CREATE2 address, the same on every EVM chain, and it can't be hijacked by renaming because GitHub IDs never change. To spend, the developer signs a short, human-readable payment text with the tools they already have: ssh-keygen -Y sign , a hardware security key, or a phone acting as a passkey. The contract rebuilds that text, verifies the SSH signature on-chain (P-256, phone/security keys, ed25519 and RSA), checks that the key is really on their GitHub profile, and pays. A relayer submits the transaction for a small fee that's written into the signed text, and anyone can self-submit instead. The favourite part: a signed git commit IS a payment. Write the payment text as the commit message, git commit -S , git push . GitHub shows its green "Verified" badge, our relayer sees the commit and the money moves. The push is the broadcast. Keys stay in sync with GitHub through a Chainlink CRE workflow: the nodes agree on each user's current key set and write key hashes on-chain, so a key you delete on GitHub stops working at the next sync. A key first seen less than 72 hours ago can't move more than 50 USDC, which limits the damage of a stolen GitHub account. Names are real ENSv2: <user>.sereno.eth resolves for everyone through a wildcard resolver and a CCIP-read gateway, and a developer can claim theirs as a real ENSv2 subname owned by their account, with its own PermissionedResolver, by signing with a phone or security key. If a username changes hands, the name fails loudly for 15 days instead of paying a stranger. On top of that: Issue bounties: fund any GitHub issue with USDC; when a merged PR closes it, a CRE workflow confirms it with GitHub and the PR author is paid by GitHub ID. A browser extension that adds "Pay" buttons to GitHub profiles, PRs, commits and issues. The sereno-ak CLI on npm ( npx sereno-ak send 1 friend --as me ). Escrow with a refund if the recipient never claims. Everything is deployed on Base Sepolia and Arbitrum Sepolia at the same addresses, with ENS on Sepolia.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.37, Foundry): an on-chain SSHSIG verifier implementing OpenSSH's PROTOCOL.sshsig byte format, dispatching by key type: P-256 through the RIP-7212/EIP-7951 precompile at 0x100 (~47k gas); phone/security keys (sk-ecdsa) by rebuilding the FIDO authenticator data; RSA through the modexp precompile; ed25519 through a vendored Solidity Ed25519 library compiled separately under solc 0.6.
A P-256 payment costs ~189k gas on Base. SshAccount accounts come from a factory whose CREATE2 salt is the GitHub ID; every contract is deployed through the Arachnid deterministic deployer with fixed salts, so all addresses match on Base Sepolia, Arbitrum Sepolia and Sepolia, and one ENS answer works on every chain. We pin solc exactly and strip the metadata hash, because a teammate's newer compiler would otherwise change every account address. Commit-as-payment: git signs commits as a normal SSHSIG in the "git" namespace over the commit object minus its gpgsig header. The account's executeCommit takes the headers plus the signature and requires that the intent is the whole commit message, not a paragraph hidden in a longer one. The relayer reads the exact signed bytes from GitHub's commit verification API. Hacky bit: git signs with SHA-512 by default, which costs ~640k extra gas in Solidity, so we set gpg.ssh.program to a 3-line wrapper that adds -O hashalg=sha256 only when git asks it to sign. GitHub still shows "Verified". Chainlink CRE: two TypeScript workflows. "github-keys" fetches each user's authentication and signing keys from the GitHub API (token from CRE secrets) with consensusIdenticalAggregation, and writes keccak256(key blob) hashes on-chain. The KeyOracle clears removed keys (revocation), keeps first-seen times for the 72h new-key delay, and maps login to ID so nobody can claim someone else's ENS name. "github-bounty" uses GitHub GraphQL to confirm that an issue was closed by a merged PR, and records the author as the winner.
Because the simulation forwarder doesn't check DON signatures, we put a ReportGate in front of our receivers that routes by workflow name and allowlists the broadcasting EOAs. A sync worker on our laptop pulls jobs from the relayer and runs the CRE simulation with --broadcast on demand, so "Sync my keys" on the site works in about 17 seconds per chain. ENSv2 (Sepolia): sereno.eth has an ENSIP-10 wildcard OffchainResolver that reverts with EIP-3668 OffchainLookup to our Bun gateway (username → GitHub ID → CREATE2 address, signed responses, every EVM coin type). It also has a UserRegistry subregistry from ENS's VerifiableFactory. A permissionless NameRegistrar checks an SSH signature plus the oracle's login mapping, then registers <user>.sereno.eth to the user's account with its own PermissionedResolver proxy, all set in one transaction because initialize skips role checks. Stale names after a GitHub rename can be released by anyone and are quarantined for 15 days. Ed25519 doesn't fit Sepolia's per-transaction gas cap, so name claims use P-256 or phone keys. The phone works as a FIDO key through Win32-OpenSSH 10: QR code, then a fingerprint. Clients: Pay page: Vite + React + viem, on Vercel; it resolves our testnet names itself, since stock wallets don't. CLI: Bun, bundled for Node and published to npm; it finds your key in ~/.ssh and shells out to stock ssh-keygen and git. Relayer and gateway: Bun on Railway, one Docker image. MV3 extension: React, a P-256 browser key in a password vault, buttons injected into GitHub pages. Shared: a TS package holds the intent builder (tested byte-for-byte against the contract), ABIs and addresses.
Partner tech: Circle USDC on every chain.

projects.title: lowki
projects.description: 🌾 CROPS embedded wallets on Kohaku: a drop-in for Privy where users own their keys and privacy.
projects.project_description: Embedded wallets made onboarding easy, but at a cost: one company holds a share of every user's keys, sees every app each user signs into, and every app can see the user's whole on-chain history. Lowki keeps the developer experience of Privy and removes the trust. Lowki is a CROPS wallet SDK (Censorship-resistant, Open source, Private, Secure) built on Kohaku, the Ethereum Foundation's privacy wallet framework. Our Rust key worker implements Kohaku's Host, and Kohaku's Privacy Pools plugin runs on it unchanged, with a WebGPU prover and Anon-RPC transport in place of the defaults. Same SDK. @lowki/react-auth implements Privy's React API (PrivyProvider, usePrivy, useWallets, useSignMessage, useSendTransaction…). Moving an app over is one import. Our demo app Lowki Tips was written for Privy; a second app written straight from Privy's docs type-checks against both the real Privy SDK and Lowki. Keys stay on the device. The wallet is created and used inside a Rust/wasm Web Worker and locked with the passkey's WebAuthn PRF output. Sign-up is one passkey: no email, no seed phrase. Our server only stores a blob it can't open, so it can never sign. A wallet per app. Every app gets its own address and a pairwise user ID, so apps can't follow users across each other. Only the user's wallet home sees all their apps. Private payments. Tip a creator at chai.lowki.eth: the ENSv2 name resolves to a fresh stealth address on every lookup, verified on chain, so a public name doesn't become a public payment history. Or tip from a private balance through Privacy Pools (via Kohaku), with the zero-knowledge proof made in the browser on WebGPU in ~0.17 s (3.6x faster than snarkjs). Private connection. Wallet reads and broadcasts go through Anon-RPC (Nox / Nym / tor-js), so the RPC provider can't see the user's IP. Get tipped too. Claim your own name.lowki.eth (gas sponsored, live on Sepolia); anyone can pay it from any wallet and only your wallet can find the payments. CROPS by design. Censorship-resistant: self-hostable, plain EOAs, ragequit can't be blocked, stealth addresses verified on chain. Open source: MIT/Apache-2.0, one Rust server binary, no third-party scripts or trackers. Private: per-app wallets, stealth names, Privacy Pools, Anon-RPC. Secure: Rust for every key operation, zeroized secrets, passkey-gated unlock, pinned circuit files. Live: lowki.eth, its ENSv2 contracts and the creator names are on Sepolia. The private withdrawal runs on a Sepolia fork because Sepolia's Privacy Pools ASP currently publishes placeholder data; the contracts, the proof and Kohaku are real.
projects.how_its_made:
Built on Kohaku and designed against the CROPS principles. Rust everywhere keys or proofs are involved; TypeScript only as bindings. Each crate is tested against vectors from the reference implementations. lowki-keys: BIP-39/32, per-app account derivation, passkey-PRF key wrapping (HKDF -> AES-GCM). lowki-shares: 2-of-3 Shamir, byte-compatible with Privy's shamir-secret-sharing. lowki-stealth: ERC-5564 stealth addresses and scanning (6.2x faster than ScopeLift's SDK in the browser). lowki-pp-core: Privacy Pools v1 notes, Poseidon, LeanIMT. lowki-groth16 + lowki-gpu: a snarkjs-compatible Groth16 prover on wasm and WebGPU; proofs are byte-identical and accepted by the on-chain verifier, about 3.6x faster than snarkjs in Chrome. lowki-aa: ERC-4337 / EIP-7702 user operations. lowki-worker: the wasm key worker (unlock with PRF, per-app accounts, signing, proving). lowki-server (axum + sqlx): passkeys via webauthn-rs (including passkeys created inside an app's iframe, accepted only for registered apps), sessions, ES256 app tokens + JWKS (what app backends verify, like Privy's), encrypted app lists, sponsored ENS name claims, and the ENS CCIP-Read gateway. lowki-ens: ENSIP-30 stealth records, CCIP-Read client, registrar/owner-account signatures. Wallet UI: Leptos (Rust -> wasm) in an iframe/popup on its own origin.
SDK: @lowki/react-auth with Privy's provider, hooks and types, an EIP-1193 provider and a wagmi connector, plus useSendPrivately.
Kohaku: our Host (network, storage, keystore, provider) backed by the Rust worker; Kohaku's Privacy Pools plugin runs unchanged on top, with its prover swapped for our WebGPU one and its provider carrying Anon-RPC.
ENSv2 on Sepolia: lowki.eth registered via ETHRegistrar; a VerifiableFactory proxy of ENS's UserRegistryImpl as an emancipated subregistry; LowkiRegistrar for sponsored, owner-signed registrations; an EIP-7702 owner account so the whole name setup is one sponsored transaction; Fluidkey's StealthResolver (ENSIP-30 draft) in verified mode.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Embedded wallets made onboarding easy, but at a cost: one company holds a share of every user's keys, sees every app each user signs into, and every app can see the user's whole on-chain history. Lowki keeps the developer experience of Privy and removes the trust.

Lowki is a CROPS wallet SDK (Censorship-resistant, Open source, Private, Secure) built on Kohaku, the Ethereum Foundation's privacy wallet framework. Our Rust key worker implements Kohaku's Host, and Kohaku's Privacy Pools plugin runs on it unchanged, with a WebGPU prover and Anon-RPC transport in place of the defaults.

- Same SDK. @lowki/react-auth implements Privy's React API (PrivyProvider, usePrivy, useWallets, useSignMessage, useSendTransaction…). Moving an app over is one import. Our demo app Lowki Tips was written for Privy; a second app written straight from Privy's docs type-checks against both the real Privy SDK and Lowki.
- Keys stay on the device. The wallet is created and used inside a Rust/wasm Web Worker and locked with the passkey's WebAuthn PRF output. Sign-up is one passkey: no email, no seed phrase. Our server only stores a blob it can't open, so it can never sign.
- A wallet per app. Every app gets its own address and a pairwise user ID, so apps can't follow users across each other. Only the user's wallet home sees all their apps.
- Private payments. Tip a creator at chai.lowki.eth: the ENSv2 name resolves to a fresh stealth address on every lookup, verified on chain, so a public name doesn't become a public payment history. Or tip from a private balance through Privacy Pools (via Kohaku), with the zero-knowledge proof made in the browser on WebGPU in ~0.17 s (3.6x faster than snarkjs).
- Private connection. Wallet reads and broadcasts go through Anon-RPC (Nox / Nym / tor-js), so the RPC provider can't see the user's IP.
- Get tipped too. Claim your own name.lowki.eth (gas sponsored, live on Sepolia); anyone can pay it from any wallet and only your wallet can find the payments.
- CROPS by design. Censorship-resistant: self-hostable, plain EOAs, ragequit can't be blocked, stealth addresses verified on chain. Open source: MIT/Apache-2.0, one Rust server binary, no third-party scripts or trackers. Private: per-app wallets, stealth names, Privacy Pools, Anon-RPC. Secure: Rust for every key operation, zeroized secrets, passkey-gated unlock, pinned circuit files.

Live: lowki.eth, its ENSv2 contracts and the creator names are on Sepolia. The private withdrawal runs on a Sepolia fork because Sepolia's Privacy Pools ASP currently publishes placeholder data; the contracts, the proof and Kohaku are real.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Built on Kohaku and designed against the CROPS principles. Rust everywhere keys or proofs are involved; TypeScript only as bindings. Each crate is tested against vectors from the reference implementations.

- lowki-keys: BIP-39/32, per-app account derivation, passkey-PRF key wrapping (HKDF -> AES-GCM).
- lowki-shares: 2-of-3 Shamir, byte-compatible with Privy's shamir-secret-sharing.
- lowki-stealth: ERC-5564 stealth addresses and scanning (6.2x faster than ScopeLift's SDK in the browser).
- lowki-pp-core: Privacy Pools v1 notes, Poseidon, LeanIMT.
- lowki-groth16 + lowki-gpu: a snarkjs-compatible Groth16 prover on wasm and WebGPU; proofs are byte-identical and accepted by the on-chain verifier, about 3.6x faster than snarkjs in Chrome.
- lowki-aa: ERC-4337 / EIP-7702 user operations.
- lowki-worker: the wasm key worker (unlock with PRF, per-app accounts, signing, proving).
- lowki-server (axum + sqlx): passkeys via webauthn-rs (including passkeys created inside an app's iframe, accepted only for registered apps), sessions, ES256 app tokens + JWKS (what app backends verify, like Privy's), encrypted app lists, sponsored ENS name claims, and the ENS CCIP-Read gateway.
- lowki-ens: ENSIP-30 stealth records, CCIP-Read client, registrar/owner-account signatures.

Wallet UI: Leptos (Rust -> wasm) in an iframe/popup on its own origin.
SDK: @lowki/react-auth with Privy's provider, hooks and types, an EIP-1193 provider and a wagmi connector, plus useSendPrivately.
Kohaku: our Host (network, storage, keystore, provider) backed by the Rust worker; Kohaku's Privacy Pools plugin runs unchanged on top, with its prover swapped for our WebGPU one and its provider carrying Anon-RPC.
ENSv2 on Sepolia: lowki.eth registered via ETHRegistrar; a VerifiableFactory proxy of ENS's UserRegistryImpl as an emancipated subregistry; LowkiRegistrar for sponsored, owner-signed registrations; an EIP-7702 owner account so the whole name setup is one sponsored transaction; Fluidkey's StealthResolver (ENSIP-30 draft) in verified mode.

projects.title: teammate-finder
projects.description: Post who you are and who you need. Posts vanish after 24h, so every teammate is still looking.
projects.project_description: Teamfinder is a small board for hackathon attendees who are missing a teammate. You post your role, your skills, a short note and how to reach you, and you say which role you need. Everyone else can filter by the role they are looking for, search by skill, and copy your contact in one click. The point is freshness. Every post disappears after 24 hours, so the board never fills up with people who already found a team. Only the wallet that created a post can delete it, so nobody can remove or edit someone else’s listing. There is no signup: you connect a wallet and you are in. The app has a landing page, a board with live stats (open posts, most wanted role, posts expiring soon), filters, a new post form, and a demo mode with sample data so it is usable even with no wallet or network.
projects.how_its_made: The front end is Vite, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind v4. The whole UI is built only from the 1st-Pouf component library (a shadcn-style registry of claymorphism components): screens use variant props and never raw HTML, classNames or inline styles. The back end is a small Express API on MongoDB Atlas. Posts carry an expiresAt date and a TTL index deletes them after 24 hours, with the API also hiding expired ones in between sweeps. There are no accounts: writes are signed with the user’s wallet (personal_sign) over a message that includes the address and a timestamp, and the server verifies it with viem. Only the author’s signature can delete a post, and signatures older than 5 minutes are rejected. A demo mode with built-in sample data lets the UI run with no wallet or network. Notable details: filters are validated on the server against the allowed roles, skill search runs in the browser, and the build is served by the same Express process for a single deploy. Vitest covers the helpers and API tests for bad signatures, wrong wallet, expired signature, invalid fields, owner-only delete and expiry.

projects.title: Poincaré
projects.description: A Uniswap v4 hook that detects trends and makes trend-chasing swaps pay a spread to the LPs
projects.project_description:
What we have made Poincaré is a Uniswap v4 hook that turns an ordinary two-asset pool into one that responds to the market. It runs a live WETH/USDC pool on Unichain Sepolia.
The hook has a trend detector built on CUSUM, a change-point method introduced by E. S. Page in 1954 and later proved optimal by Lorden and Moustakides.
When the detector confirms a real trend from the pool's own price, the hook charges a spread to swaps following that trend and keeps it in the pool for its liquidity providers. If there is no trend, the pool trades like a normal one with a small fee that follows volatility.
No oracle, keeper or off-chain service is involved and everything that the pool decides comes from its own price, inside the swap. We have around the hook built a complete product: PoincareLens: a quoting contract whose quotes match executed swaps to the wei. PoincareDCA: a contract for DCA orders that can wait out the trend spread and catch up later. Developer tools: a TypeScript SDK, an HTTP API, an MCP server so AI agents like Claude can read the market and manage orders, and a Claude skill that teaches the agent to use it safely. Platform: http://www.poincaretrade.in, with a trading app, a pool and liquidity screen, an analytics report built from the detector's own on-chain records, and full documentation with step-by-step guides. The contracts have went through a scoped review by SFS-Labs and an Olympix pre-audit scan, with entire project being open source under the MIT licence. Once per block, before the first swap, the hook reads the pool price and computes how far it moved since the last sample.
It clips extreme values so one wild block cannot dominate, then feeds the return into two CUSUM statistics, one looks for an up-trend and one for a down-trend.
Each statistic adds a block's move only when that move exceeds a small noise allowance, and drains back toward zero when the market chops or reverses. Evidence therefore builds only when the price keeps moving the same way. A trend is declared when a statistic crosses a threshold. That threshold is set from a target false-alarm rate, not from a fixed number of blocks, so the moment it fires depends on the data and cannot be predicted or gamed. Because volatility alone can make CUSUM's evidence rise, the hook also measures directional efficiency.
This is actually the net distance the price travelled divided by the total distance it covered, smoothed over recent blocks. It is close to one in a clean trend and close to zero in back-and-forth noise.
The spread engages only when the CUSUM evidence is past its threshold and directional efficiency is above a floor chosen from how noisy that measure is in a market is when there is no trend. A control law then maps the evidence to a spread: zero at the threshold, rising to a hard cap of 5%, limited in how fast it can change from one block to the next, and fading back to zero as the trend ends. So when a swap arrives, the hook prices it itself on a constant-product curve, instead of letting the pool use its built-in liquidity math. Every swap pays a fee proportional to recent volatility, capped at 0.30%. A swap pushing in the direction of the confirmed trend also pays the spread; a swap going against it does not.
The hook returns this result to Uniswap as the swap's final amounts and settles through ERC-6909 claims. It also keeps its own record of every amount it settles, so tokens sent to it from outside cannot distort prices or the detector. We feel there is a need for this as Liquidity providers are the backbone of every AMM, and they lose money in a way most of them never see. Prices move first on large centralised exchanges and a Uniswap pool keeps quoting the old price until arbitrageurs trade against it to close the gap, and every such trade transfers value from the LPs to the arbitrageur. (loss-versus-rebalancing or LVR). It is worst during trends, when the price keeps moving the same way and arbitrageurs can take the gap again block after block. A standard pool cannot defend against this, because it charges the same fee to everyone at all times and cannot tell a calm market from a trending one, or a trader bringing the price back from one chasing the move. Raising the fee for everyone drives away the ordinary traders who make providing liquidity worthwhile. Existing fixes either rely on an external price oracle (another trust assumption and point of failure) or use dynamic fees that react to volatility without knowing which direction the risk is coming from. But a pool that can confirm, from its own price and with a known false-alarm rate, that a real trend has started, can then charge only the flow that profits from it. For liquidity providers, Poincaré targets their biggest loss. During a trend, the swaps that would have taken value from them now pay a spread that stays in the pool and grows every LP's share. In calm markets the pool stays cheap and competitive, so LPs keep earning from normal trading. In a four-year replay of real ETH/USDC prices, with the same price path and order flow for every pool, a $2 million Poincaré position finished about $185,000 ahead of a standard 30 basis point pool. Arbitrageurs took 32% less, and Poincaré stayed ahead in each of the four years separately, through a doubling, a sideways market and a 38% drawdown. This is a simulation with modelled flow rather than live results, but the advantage built up steadily rather than coming from one lucky period. For traders, the pool is fairer rather than simply more expensive. Anyone trading against the trend, or trading when there is no trend, never pays the spread. Because the Lens quotes exactly what will execute, there are no surprises at execution.
PoincareDCA goes further: a regular investor can set up a recurring buy that automatically waits whenever buying would cost the spread and catches up once the trend passes. They get the same total on the same schedule without paying the trend premium. For builders and the wider ecosystem, Poincaré shows that a pool can manage its own risk using only its own data, with a detector backed by decades of statistics rather than hand-tuned rules. The SDK, API, MCP server and Claude skill make that market signal available to bots, apps and AI agents. They can read whether a trend is under way, quote swaps, and run spread-aware strategies without understanding the maths underneath. Because it is open source under MIT, anyone can study, fork or build on the design.
projects.how_its_made:
Written in Solidity and tested with Foundry. Inside it are four small libraries: Cusum, the trend detector; DirectionalSignal, which measures how one-directional the price move is; ControlLaw, which turns the evidence into a spread capped at 5%; PriceLib, for the price maths. On every swap, the hook reads the pool's own price, updates the detector, works out the spread and prices the swap itself. There's no oracle and no keeper. A Lens contract reuses the exact same maths, so quotes match real swaps to the wei. We tuned the parameters with Python back-tests on four years of real ETH/USDC prices. Tech stack
-> Contracts: Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4 core and periphery, OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks, Solady, and HookMiner (to mine the hook address).
-> App: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind, wagmi and RainbowKit.
-> Backend: Supabase (Postgres plus edge functions) for the trade history, the HTTP API, a DCA keeper, and a function that checks every database write against the chain before saving it.
-> Developer tools: a TypeScript SDK, an MCP server so AI agents can use Poincaré, and a Claude skill.
-> Hosting and analytics: Vercel and PostHog.
-> Uniswap v4: the custom-curve pattern (beforeSwapReturnDelta) let us replace the pool's pricing entirely while still using v4's settlement and ERC-6909 claims. A pool that reacts to trends wasn't possible before v4 hooks.
-> OpenZeppelin's base contracts: they handled the accounting for us, so we could focus on the maths. Hacky BITS The detector looks at each block only once, using the reserves from before that block's first swap. A flash trade that's undone in the same block never reaches it. The hook keeps its own record of its reserves instead of reading its token balances, so tokens sent in from outside can't move prices. Every block, the hook emits an event with the detector's full state. Our analytics charts are rebuilt from those events, so the page doesn't depend on our own database. Testnet gas estimates came out wrong for transactions that go through the hook, so the app sets explicit gas limits and approves exact amounts. There's no swap log to read for a custom-curve pool, so the hook emits its own HookSwap event, and the trade history is built from that.

projects.title: Meeti
projects.description: Connecting people through AI agents, discovery, and permission-based introductions.
projects.project_description: Meeti is an AI networking workspace that starts with what a person wants to achieve. Instead of searching through profiles or exchanging contacts immediately, each owner reviews a public intent and lets a personal representative discover complementary opportunities. A job seeker and a recruiter, or someone seeking help and someone offering expertise, have different intentions even when their words look similar. Owners control their profile context, document excerpts and sharing policies. Public discovery uses expiring Arkiv records. ENSv2 agent identities and current permissions constrain protected actions independently of the language model. Semantic relevance helps rank candidates, while bilateral requirements, direction, visibility and authorization determine eligibility. A recommendation is a candidate introduction, never consent. The interface supports profile and private-file setup, reviewed intent publication, discovery, agent activity, qualification briefings, version-bound mutual approval and explicit meeting-time agreement. There is no fabricated calendar invitation. Private contact and original files remain protected. Current demo status: two separate hosted accounts authenticate and retain private data. ENSv2 identities and real Arkiv testnet records have live evidence. Hosted DevRel discovery has now executed real Arkiv reads at blocks 314475 and 314476 and actual 384-dimensional MiniLM embeddings. The bounded retrieval scanned two candidates and returned one possible match with cosine similarity 0.6873; missing preferred evidence remains explicit, and similarity is not a probability. One real model-generated qualification message has been accepted and persisted; a later provider request failed. Full conversation, consent and meeting-flow acceptance remain pending. World remains paused after the existing HTTP 403 blocker, so protected private release is unavailable and no human-verification claim is made.
projects.how_its_made: Meeti uses Next.js 16, TypeScript and Node.js 24, deployed on Vercel. Wallet authentication verifies nonce-based signatures with domain and chain binding, expiry and replay protection before issuing opaque sessions. Server-side account authorization keeps separate users isolated. Supabase Postgres persists application state, while private Supabase Storage holds encrypted original documents. AES-256-GCM encryption and backend disclosure rules protect private context. ENSv2 on Sepolia is the live authority for agent identity and delegated permissions. Dedicated subnames and resolvers separate agent records, with narrow status-record delegation, expiry and revocation checks. Approved public agent context uses ENSIP-26 records. ERC-8004 registration identities and ENSIP-25 association checks bind the claimed ENS name to the exact network, registry and agent identifier. These associations do not establish professional credentials or grant access to private data. Arkiv Rabdi is the authoritative discovery source. Approved public intents use a versioned schema, indexed scope and intent-direction attributes, writer/owner validation, explicit expiry, confirmed writes and read-back. Queries retrieve bounded active complementary candidates instead of requiring every optional tag to match. Private conversations, raw files and secrets are not public intent payloads. The backend runs real 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings through CPU ONNX and computes cosine similarity. Complementary direction and bilateral hard requirements are checked separately from semantic ranking. Similarity is not presented as a probability. Model-driven qualification has bounded turns, evidence citations, persistent checkpoints and recoverable failure states; its current hosted run has one accepted message followed by a provider failure rather than replaced by scripted success. Consent is tied to a current proposal version, and deterministic interval overlap is used for meeting-time proposals. ENS authority and intent freshness are checked again before protected actions. World remains explicitly disabled after the existing 403 blocker, preserving its final release gate. Verification boundary: hosted DevRel discovery now has real Arkiv and MiniLM embedding evidence, with one possible match at cosine 0.6873 from a bounded two-candidate scan. Qualification has one accepted message, followed by a provider failure. A complete hosted agent conversation, mutual-consent and meeting flow is still pending; provider errors are not replaced with scripted success.

World remains explicitly disabled after the existing 403 blocker, preserving its final release gate.

Qualification has one accepted message, followed by a provider failure. projects.title: ParlayMarket
projects.description: Build parlays on any prediction markets you’re browsing, priced live and backed by an LP vault.
projects.project_description: Prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi now offer parlays, but mostly on sports and only in combinations they choose to list. If you believe a crypto price target, an election result and a tech launch will all happen, you still have to buy three separate positions and get three small payouts. Prediction markets can’t list every possible combination: that would fragment liquidity and multiply market-maker risk. ParlayKit lets you combine any bets on any market: politics, crypto, sports, culture, all in one parlay. It is a venue-agnostic browser extension. You browse a prediction market as usual, and ParlayKit detects every market on screen and pops up an offer to combine them. You tap Yes/No on any two or more markets and watch the combined probability, odds and payout update live from the venue’s order book. Then you place the parlay from your own wallet in one transaction. The venue doesn’t need to list anything or change anything. Venues plug in through lightweight adapters: one finds the markets on the page, one reads their prices and resolution data. v1 ships with a Polymarket adapter and a demo venue. One liquidity pool backs every combination on every supported venue. Each leg is priced at its live best ask, which is what buying that leg alone would cost. In v1 the parlay price is the product of the leg prices plus a small per-leg house edge. This is the independence special case of the ParlayMarket automated market maker (Rana et al., 2026). In v2 we plug in its pairwise model to price correlated legs coherently from the same pool. The counterparty is an ERC-4626 vault anyone can deposit USDC into. LPs earn the house edge on losing parlays and pay out winners. On-chain risk limits keep the vault solvent: a per-parlay risk cap, a utilization cap, and withdrawal caps that keep potential payouts reserved. Each parlay is a transferable ERC-721 ticket. Settlement is permissionless. The contract reads the same on-chain resolution data the venue pays out from. A losing leg settles the parlay immediately, a 50/50 market pays half, and a full win pays whoever holds the ticket.
projects.how_its_made:
The main idea comes from my research paper ParlayMarket (published in AFT2026) that allows pricing the parlays. Now about the technical parts:
ParlayKit has three parts: Solidity contracts, an off-chain quoter, and a Chrome extension. A plug-in venue-adapter layer runs through all three. Contracts (Solidity 0.8.26, Foundry, OpenZeppelin v5), deployed on Polygon Amoy. ParlayEngine takes an EIP-712 signed quote. The quote binds the buyer, the stake, the legs (each a market id, an outcome and a price), a 90-second deadline and a single-use nonce.
The engine doesn’t just trust the quote. It re-prices the parlay on-chain (product of leg prices × (1 + edge)), rejects duplicate or already-resolved markets, and checks vault risk limits. Then it moves the stake into the vault and mints the parlay as a transferable ERC-721 ticket.
settle() is permissionless. It reads each leg’s payout vector from the Conditional Tokens contract the venue settles on, and pays maxPayout × Π(numerator/denominator). That one formula handles full wins, early settlement on any losing leg, and 50/50 resolutions.
ParlayVault is ERC-4626 with two extra ledgers. pendingPremium keeps open stakes out of the share price until they settle. lockedPayout caps LP withdrawals so a winner can always be paid.
14 Foundry tests, including a fuzz test that the house never pays more than the fair independent payout. Quoter (Node + ethers v6). Venue sources turn what the extension found on the page into markets, outcome ids and live order-book prices. The Polymarket source reads the Gamma API and prices each leg at the outcome’s best ask, i.e. what buying that leg alone would cost. The quoter’s BigInt pricing math matches the contract’s bit for bit, so the payout the user sees is exactly what the contract pays. It never trusts prices sent by the client: it re-reads them, rejects resolved markets and correlated same-event legs, signs the quote, and dry-runs the exact transaction with eth_call before returning ready-to-send calldata. Extension (Chrome MV3, zero-dependency vanilla JS). Site adapters find the markets visible on any page, from event pages to category feeds, so the “combine these” pop-up works wherever you’re browsing. The UI is rendered inside a Shadow DOM so it never clashes with the host site. A tiny script running in the page’s own context bridges to the user’s wallet (window.ethereum) over postMessage, so the extension never touches keys. It handles network switching, USDC approval, buying, claiming, and LP deposit/withdraw. Pricing roadmap. v1 uses the independence special case of the ParlayMarket AMM (Rana et al., 2026). The pricing is isolated in one function, and the contract already accepts a signed per-leg price vector, so the pairwise correlation model can be dropped in without contract changes. Hacky bits. The quoter returns fully encoded calldata, so the extension needs no ABI library and no bundler: load it unpacked and it runs. We built a fictional demo venue plus a dev-wallet shim that routes to a local test chain (anvil), which let us test the whole flow (LP deposit → quote → buy → forged-signature revert → resolve → claim) in headless Chrome without MetaMask. On testnet, a mock Conditional Tokens contract exposes the exact getters of the real one, so going to mainnet is just swapping two addresses. AI tools. We used Claude as an agentic coding assistant to generate the contracts, quoter, extension and docs from our spec, and to run the test suites. Details are in AI_USAGE.md.

projects.title: Mohar (PoL)
projects.description: Teacher eligibility checks a school can prove years later, even after the platform is deleted.
projects.project_description: In April 2025 India’s Supreme Court upheld the cancellation of 25,753 school appointments in West Bengal. The records that could have separated honest appointees from fraudulent ones had been destroyed, so everyone lost their job together. In September 2025 the same Court ruled that every in-service teacher must hold the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) by 31 August 2028, and every school in the country will have to show that it checked. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Rules add a duty, commencing 13 November 2026, to keep tamper-evident records of consent. Mohar is the record of that check. A teacher holds an eligibility credential signed by the issuing body and presents only the eligibility claims to a school, under a purpose-scoped consent; the certificate’s date of birth, category, family names and marks stay hidden. The school verifies the credential and signs a receipt. Each term the school re-checks the credential’s status and signs a re-check receipt, so a cancelled certificate is caught mid-year. Commitments to the consent, the presentation and the receipts are written to an append-only log whose batch roots are anchored to Ethereum Sepolia and to Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps. An inspector verifies any receipt against both anchors with nothing from the platform. In the demo, the platform’s databases are deleted on camera and the receipt still verifies. The live inspector page carries a sample bundle whose Bitcoin proof is complete, and anyone can repeat the check. What Mohar does not do: it does not issue credentials, does not decide eligibility, and does not make a certificate honest. The issuer in this version is simulated. Mohar provides a cryptographic record of timing, authorship and consent, not a claim of legal compliance.
projects.how_its_made: Node 22, plain ESM JavaScript, no framework. Credentials are SD-JWT verifiable credentials (RFC 9901) issued with @sd-jwt/core and signed with Ed25519 through jose. The issuer is a did:web with a static DID document; the teacher and the school are did:key. Selective disclosure lets the teacher reveal five eligibility claims and withhold the rest of the certificate, and a key-binding token ties each presentation to the school’s nonce and to the consent record. Credential status is an IETF Token Status List served as a static file; the verifier reports not_revoked, revoked or unknown, and never shows unknown as valid. The log service receives only commitments: SHA-256 over a domain tag, a 32-byte random salt and the signed record. A public root reveals nothing about the record, even to someone who already holds it. Entries form a hash chain; each batch closes into a Merkle root bound with the batch header, and the batch root is written as calldata in an ordinary Ethereum Sepolia transaction and stamped with OpenTimestamps. Every accepted commit returns an acknowledgement signed by the operator key, which the teacher and the school keep; two acknowledgements for one sequence number with different entries are a proof of rollback, and a CLI subcommand produces it. The inspector is one self-contained HTML file built with esbuild (about 1 MB, 1,471 bundled modules) hosted on GitHub Pages. It checks the receipt signature, the chain entry, the Merkle path, the Sepolia calldata, the Bitcoin proof and the acknowledgement, each as a separate pass or fail line, with the OpenTimestamps verification done in the browser through a block explorer. The school and log services run on Railway with SQLite on persistent volumes. Tests run with node --test; the privacy tests run first in CI and include deleting both databases and verifying an exported bundle offline. Worth noting: the anchor is calldata rather than a contract, and the verifier fetches one transaction and compares bytes. The demo deletes the live log on camera. Salted commitments and signed acknowledgements were both added during the event after audit findings, with the earlier batches discarded and re-anchored. No partner technologies were used. The code was written by AI coding agents working from me instructions. The author made every design decision, commissioned every audit (each run by a separate AI agent) and ruled on its findings.

projects.title: xMarket
projects.description: Autonomous AI agent executing verified onchain bracket trades from breaking social event triggers
projects.project_description: When breaking macroeconomic or crypto news hits social media—like Fed rate announcements, regulatory rulings, or protocol exploits—markets react in milliseconds. Retail traders are consistently too slow, while traditional bots blindly market-swap into massive slippage and MEV sandwich attacks. Worse, current "AI trading bots" act as opaque black boxes where users have zero proof of whether a trade was executed based on real sentiment analysis or developer front-running. PumpIt solves this by creating an autonomous, event-driven trading agent powered by verifiable AI inference and automated bracket execution: Intent Configuration: Traders set up a catalyst trigger by choosing a target source (e.g., @federalreserve), catalyst event, minimum confidence threshold (e.g., ≥ 75%), and bracket risk parameters (+5% Take-Profit / -2.5% Stop-Loss). Verifiable Sentiment via 0G Private Computer: A live sentinel monitors incoming posts and routes them through 0G Private Computer (TEE). It evaluates economic polarity (Hawkish/Dovish) and returns a cryptographic request ID. This provides tamper-proof proof onchain that trades were triggered by objective AI reasoning rather than hallucination or manipulation. MEV-Protected Bracket Execution via Definitive Flash: When confidence criteria are met, PumpIt immediately fires a non-custodial trade via Definitive Flash on Arbitrum One. Instead of an unprotected market swap, it automatically attaches Take-Profit and Stop-Loss orders with built-in MEV protection. Self-Sustaining Economy ("Agents That Pay for Themselves"): Every filled Definitive Flash order earns a 0.1% (10 bps) integrator fee rebate. PumpIt routes these rebates directly into its 0G compute balance vault, autonomously funding future inference costs without requiring manual human top-ups.
projects.how_its_made: PumpIt is built with Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring a real-time reactive terminal interface with live sentiment monitoring, intent wizardry, and position tracking. Under the hood, two core partner technologies power the agent: • 0G Private Computer: We integrated the 0G Compute OpenAI-compatible router API (router-api.0g.ai) running open-weights LLMs (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b) inside Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs). The agent extracts sentiment scores, action signals (BUY/SELL/HOLD), and cryptographic request IDs. If 0G were removed, the system would lose all verifiability, turning into an untrusted black box prone to developer manipulation and front-running. • Definitive Flash API: Rather than routing swaps through standard AMMs where high-volatility news spikes cause devastating slippage, we integrated Definitive Flash (flash.definitive.fi) on Arbitrum One. We wrap every trade into an Advanced Bracket Order with atomic Take-Profit (+5%) and Stop-Loss (-2.5%) limits, protecting capital from whipsaws with institutional-grade MEV protection. • Autonomous Fee Flywheel: We configured Definitive's 10 bps integrator fee rebate to route straight into the agent's 0G Compute Vault. Each executed trade generates revenue that re-deposits into the 0G balance, creating a perpetual, self-funding autonomous agent with built-in daily spend caps. Notable & Hacky Solutions: Live Demo Reliability: Hackathon demos often stall waiting for real-world tweets or fighting Twitter API rate limits. We engineered a hybrid sentinel engine that can poll live X accounts or instantly ingest real-time custom test tweets from a built-in interactive drawer. Zero-Setup Testing for Judges: We included an in-app API Key modal allowing judges to test using their own 0G and Definitive keys without touching terminal configs, backed by a robust fallback heuristic engine to ensure zero crashes during live testing.

projects.title: GraphPay
projects.description: AI agents with ENS identities check a GraphQL Arkiv, then pay USDT on Whitechain, Web2-easy.
projects.how_its_made: Whitechain Sepolia (pay). GraphPayCheckout, a Solidity contract built - verified on the Whitechain explorer one-signature orders settled by a relayer through a Permit2 witness (payee, amount, deadline and order id inside the signature), refunds capped by the order, re-orders as children of a paid order, subscriptions renewed by a relayer and cancelled by the subscriber's signature, and per-agent daily caps the contract enforces, recording a refusal on the chain. Our own x402 facilitator runs on Vercel: the shop answers HTTP 402 with one quote, the agent signs once, the facilitator checks the ENS gate, verifies and settles, and its relayer pays the gas under a balance floor and a daily gas budget (https://graphpay-event.vercel.app/api/facilitator/health). The first agent payment through our facilitator, in real test USDT: https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/tx/0x87505ef2457b6e925fa7378a55fd91419e83c37fb8effc06d901884700c72c00 ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia (identify). Our own subname registry under graphpay.eth, a registry and resolver per owner, a resolver per agent, and agents as namespaces (payer.vitalik.graphpay.eth, risk.<shop>.graphpay.eth) with expiring, non-transferable names. Scoped setter roles (Enhanced Access Control) let an agent set only its agent-context and its Whitechain address, so it cannot raise its own cap. ENSIP-26 records publish our MCP server from the root name. A wildcard resolver serves synthetic agents with no per-agent transaction. The gate reads status, registry state, expiry, cap and the payee address live with stock viem; a watcher keeps the on-chain policies in step, so a killed agent stays dead. Every transaction: https://github.com/Zugzwang-world/graphpay/blob/main/docs/sessions/identity/namespace.md Arkiv Rabdi (remember). A mirror turns each Whitechain event between named actors into a readonly receipt plus tallies for both ends, the pair link and a checkpoint, in one atomic batch, so a restart never double-counts. Arkiv has no SUM or GROUP BY, so the tallies make a city-wide top 10 two reads where plain code needs five. Every read is scoped to our writer wallets; expiring rows drive "open now", agents at work and quotes; GraphQL and MCP routes return an explain trace of every Arkiv call. Menus, with their storefront and dish photos, live on Swarm through the public gateway, with their content hash on Arkiv. Two SDKs, built and published during the hackathon. @graphpay_ethglobal/arkiv-graph 1.0.0 is a generic graph layer over Arkiv: you define the nodes, edges and running totals; it writes them atomically with a safe writer, reads only rows from wallets you trust, explains every read, and ships ArkivSim, an in-memory Arkiv node for tests, plus a non-payments leaderboard example. @graphpay_ethglobal/agentpay 1.0.0 is a two-sided kit for agent payments in USDT on Whitechain: on the buyer side, an AI agent pays an HTTP 402 with one signature and no gas under an on-chain spending pass, with refunds and subscriptions; on the merchant side, any route gets a price and settles through a facilitator, with refunds, renewals and a CSV export; its tools are also exposed to agents over MCP. GraphPay itself uses both through their public APIs: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@graphpay_ethglobal/arkiv-graph and https://www.npmjs.com/package/@graphpay_ethglobal/agentpay The stage. Next.js on Vercel: one screen telling one story in eleven scenes, the pitch in the middle and the two phone apps (React, Vite, Tailwind) for the customer and the shop on either side. A director moves the middle in step with the live errand, both phones and the shop's live feed. No database of our own: state lives on the Whitechain contract and on Arkiv, and the website only runs code. How we built it. All code, including both SDKs, was written during the hackathon, in a public repository started at kickoff, with small, frequent commits: https://github.com/Zugzwang-world/graphpay/commits/main Notable hacks: the payee comes from ENS at the moment of payment; every Arkiv receipt names its Whitechain transaction in a ref attribute, so anyone can re-derive the tallies from the chain; the graph node is the ENS name plus its epoch, so a re-registered name cannot inherit an old reputation (fork-tested); a shop's "open now" is a row that expires unless the shop keeps it alive.
projects.project_description_markdown:
AI agents are starting to pay for us, in stablecoins. They need three things they don't have yet: an identity their owner controls, a shared record no company owns, and a fast way to check who they are paying. On a plain Web3 database, every check means reading the whole ledger again, and the ledger grows with every payment.

GraphPay gives agents all three. Identify (ENS): every agent has a name under its owner, a daily cap it cannot raise, and an off switch. Remember (Arkiv): every payment becomes a line between two names, with running scoreboards updated in the same write, so a city-wide ranking takes two reads instead of re-reading every receipt; in our pre-event lab benchmark at 9,612 payments, that answered 1.8 times faster with about 30 times less data. Menus and photos live on Swarm, pointed to from Arkiv. Pay (Whitechain): shops get paid in USDT, with refunds, re-orders and renewals, and the person never sees a wallet or pays gas.

Live demo, open to everyone with no passcode: https://graphpay-event.vercel.app

The story: Vitalik types one sentence on his phone: "Just landed in Mumbai. Get me the best masala dosa near BKC under 6 USDT, delivered within an hour." His agents find the shops near him on Arkiv, ask the money graph for each shop's orders, refunds and on-time rate, refuse the trap shop with its reasons, and pay the good shop 4.80 USDT with one signature and no gas.

The shop's agents check the buyer back on the same graph and on ENS before they bill, and the shop dispatches on chain once paid. It refunds part of an order and exports a CSV for its accountant. A subscription on a labelled 2-minute demo clock renews on its own and is cancelled with the subscriber's own signature.

The human stays in charge. Pausing an agent is one ENS record, and so is lowering its daily cap, which the chain then follows. The owner can kill an agent by unregistering its name: the watcher revokes its pass on Whitechain, and its next payment is refused and recorded on Arkiv. An agent cannot raise its own cap, because its ENS resolver refuses the write. The payee is read from the shop's ENS name at pay time, never hard-coded.

Every agent payment becomes a receipt on Arkiv that cannot be edited, linked back to its Whitechain transaction, plus running tallies for both sides, written in one atomic batch. Any agent can ask the graph over GraphQL or MCP and see the exact Arkiv reads behind each answer.

Both SDKs we wrote are on npm, MIT, testnet only: 
@graphpay_ethglobal/arkiv-graph (a generic graph on Arkiv with explain traces) and 
@graphpay_ethglobal/agentpay (agent payments over x402 on Whitechain). 
Every claim above, with its evidence: https://github.com/Zugzwang-world/graphpay#verify-each-claim
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Whitechain Sepolia (pay). GraphPayCheckout, a Solidity contract built - verified on the Whitechain explorer one-signature orders settled by a relayer through a Permit2 witness (payee, amount, deadline and order id inside the signature), refunds capped by the order, re-orders as children of a paid order, subscriptions renewed by a relayer and cancelled by the subscriber's signature, and per-agent daily caps the contract enforces, recording a refusal on the chain. Our own x402 facilitator runs on Vercel: the shop answers HTTP 402 with one quote, the agent signs once, the facilitator checks the ENS gate, verifies and settles, and its relayer pays the gas under a balance floor and a daily gas budget (https://graphpay-event.vercel.app/api/facilitator/health). The first agent payment through our facilitator, in real test USDT: https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/tx/0x87505ef2457b6e925fa7378a55fd91419e83c37fb8effc06d901884700c72c00

ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia (identify). Our own subname registry under graphpay.eth, a registry and resolver per owner, a resolver per agent, and agents as namespaces (payer.vitalik.graphpay.eth, risk.<shop>.graphpay.eth) with expiring, non-transferable names. Scoped setter roles (Enhanced Access Control) let an agent set only its agent-context and its Whitechain address, so it cannot raise its own cap. ENSIP-26 records publish our MCP server from the root name. A wildcard resolver serves synthetic agents with no per-agent transaction. The gate reads status, registry state, expiry, cap and the payee address live with stock viem; a watcher keeps the on-chain policies in step, so a killed agent stays dead. Every transaction: https://github.com/Zugzwang-world/graphpay/blob/main/docs/sessions/identity/namespace.md

Arkiv Rabdi (remember). A mirror turns each Whitechain event between named actors into a readonly receipt plus tallies for both ends, the pair link and a checkpoint, in one atomic batch, so a restart never double-counts. Arkiv has no SUM or GROUP BY, so the tallies make a city-wide top 10 two reads where plain code needs five. Every read is scoped to our writer wallets; expiring rows drive "open now", agents at work and quotes; GraphQL and MCP routes return an explain trace of every Arkiv call. Menus, with their storefront and dish photos, live on Swarm through the public gateway, with their content hash on Arkiv.

Two SDKs, built and published during the hackathon. @graphpay_ethglobal/arkiv-graph 1.0.0 is a generic graph layer over Arkiv: you define the nodes, edges and running totals; it writes them atomically with a safe writer, reads only rows from wallets you trust, explains every read, and ships ArkivSim, an in-memory Arkiv node for tests, plus a non-payments leaderboard example. @graphpay_ethglobal/agentpay 1.0.0 is a two-sided kit for agent payments in USDT on Whitechain: on the buyer side, an AI agent pays an HTTP 402 with one signature and no gas under an on-chain spending pass, with refunds and subscriptions; on the merchant side, any route gets a price and settles through a facilitator, with refunds, renewals and a CSV export; its tools are also exposed to agents over MCP. GraphPay itself uses both through their public APIs: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@graphpay_ethglobal/arkiv-graph and https://www.npmjs.com/package/@graphpay_ethglobal/agentpay

The stage. Next.js on Vercel: one screen telling one story in eleven scenes, the pitch in the middle and the two phone apps (React, Vite, Tailwind) for the customer and the shop on either side. A director moves the middle in step with the live errand, both phones and the shop's live feed. No database of our own: state lives on the Whitechain contract and on Arkiv, and the website only runs code.

How we built it. All code, including both SDKs, was written during the hackathon, in a public repository started at kickoff, with small, frequent commits: https://github.com/Zugzwang-world/graphpay/commits/main

Notable hacks: the payee comes from ENS at the moment of payment; every Arkiv receipt names its Whitechain transaction in a ref attribute, so anyone can re-derive the tallies from the chain; the graph node is the ENS name plus its epoch, so a re-registered name cannot inherit an old reputation (fork-tested); a shop's "open now" is a row that expires unless the shop keeps it alive.

projects.title: Rival
projects.description: Every swap is an auction. Sign once, solvers race, and Sepolia proves you beat TWAP.
projects.project_description: Rival turns every swap into a public auction. You sign one gas-free intent — sell this much tWETH, and take no less than this much tUSDC — and competing solvers race to fill it on Ethereum Sepolia. The order book is Arkiv: wallet-signed, expiring, SQL-queryable entities any solver can read. Solver identity is ENSv2 (rival.eth is live; atlas is registered). Settlement only pays if the fill clears a decaying price curve pegged to a Uniswap v4 TWAP, plus a hard floor the contract always enforces. Permit2 pulls your tokens, the winning solver sources liquidity from the v4 PoolManager, and the fill emits a receipt: amount out, fair-value reference, and improvement in basis points. A live absolute fill is already on Sepolia (0xeadff32d9c91c28bab2c9dc8136c7d1a2ef2c0091085f1a0e2d891645e9500ec). Open the demo, spin up an in-browser wallet, sign an intent, and watch the curve fall.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity and Foundry on Sepolia. RivalOracleHook is a Uniswap v4 hook (permissions afterInitialize and beforeSwap only, flag mask 0x1080). beforeSwap records at most one TWAP observation per block inside try/catch and never reverts the swap; consult and quote expose the mean tick. RivalSettlement prices the intent, then Permit2 permitWitnessTransferFrom pulls the input with the intent hash as the witness. UniswapSolver is the fill callback: the solver account delegates to it, unlocks PoolManager, swaps, settles the input, and takes the output. Solver names sit on an ENSv2 PermissionedRegistry we deployed (non-transferable, 30-day expiry, 100 tUSDC bond); SolverRegistry.isListed reads ownerOf and fails closed. The public book is Arkiv Rabdi via @arkiv-network/sdk 1.0.1: intents (rival.intent.v1) and solver presence (rival.solver.v1). The app is Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind, and viem, with a decay chart in Recharts. A Hono runner on Fly publishes intents, proxies Arkiv reads (browser CORS), and heartbeats solvers. The notable trick is EIP-7702 delegation: atlas stays an EOA and still runs the solver contract inside the settlement callback. The production site is still the previous build, and the faucet is empty, so redeploy before judges open that link.

projects.title: Veil
projects.description: Privacy for the wallets and dapps you already use, one Tor circuit per account.
projects.project_description: Veil makes the wallets and dapps you already use private by default, with no change to them. Every read your apps make to an RPC provider normally carries your IP and the addresses you look up, and because a handful of providers serve many apps, one of them can tie your main, trading and airdrop wallets to one person, and to where you are. Veil routes those reads through the Ethereum Foundation's anon-rpc over Tor and gives each account its own circuit and exit, so a provider sees unrelated strangers instead of one person. When a provider refuses Tor, Veil re-routes the read to a Tor-friendly provider on the same chain, only after a real block, and it never falls back to a direct connection without asking you first. It ships as a Chrome and Brave extension: turn it on once and the apps you already use are private today, instead of waiting for every app to adopt privacy itself. Veil is honest about its limits. Providers still see which addresses you query (hiding that needs private information retrieval, which is on the roadmap), and the Tor gateway can see that you use Tor, but not what for. The whole thing runs with no accounts, no telemetry, and no Veil server anywhere in the path.
projects.how_its_made: Veil is a Manifest V3 browser extension written in TypeScript and bundled with esbuild. At document_start, before a dapp's own scripts run, it installs a MAIN-world shim that wraps window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest, so a single hook catches the JSON-RPC reads made by viem, ethers v5/v6 and raw XHR with no per-app integration. For each read it finds which account the request is for, from the params or from inside eth_call calldata (ignoring the zero address), and assigns it an anon-rpc isolation key, so the same account always rides the same Tor circuit and two accounts never share one. It also blinds the JSON-RPC id, because viem numbers requests from one global counter and leaving ids untouched would let a provider stitch the per-account routes back together. The read is relayed from the MAIN world to an isolated content relay, to the background service worker, to an offscreen document running the Ethereum Foundation's anon-rpc harness (@anon-rpc/browser-extension-harness): a null-origin sandboxed iframe hosting tor-js, a full Tor client compiled to WebAssembly whose code is fetched at runtime but hash-pinned on-chain and verified before it runs, with no access to your keys, DOM or cookies. It reaches the provider through a blind KPS gateway that relays only encrypted bytes, never your traffic or destination. The gateway is a runtime setting (self-hostable, built from the EF's tor-js-gateway), so it can be swapped without rebuilding the extension. A chrome.proxy hook for routing a wallet's own opaque traffic by host is built but stays inert until a raw-stream path lands, so nothing is ever sent in the clear. Partner technologies: anon-rpc and tor-js from the Ethereum Foundation did the hard cryptographic and transport work, which let Veil focus on per-account routing, page interception, and honest fallback behaviour rather than reimplementing Tor in the browser. We tested on real apps with real browser sessions (never spoofing headers or forging Origin): Lido, ENS, Compound, Morpho and Spark read cleanly over Tor, Aave's provider blocked all 16 of our test reads, and Veil's re-route recovered it, which is exactly the block-then-reroute path the product is built around.

projects.title: MolBhav
projects.description: Your agent haggles the stall and pays in HBAR, so the morning line doesn't wait on one bargain.
projects.project_description: MolBhav (मोलभाउ, "haggling") lets a street stall serve a packed morning line without one customer holding the counter. At a busy stall, one buyer asks about a single item, then bargains, while others stand and listen. The shopkeeper cannot weigh or take the next order until that talk ends, and the price said out loud becomes the price for everyone waiting. UPI starts only after the talking: scan a QR, type the amount, enter a PIN. The shopkeeper still has to check that it arrived. Before opening, the shopkeeper sets an asking price and a private floor once. A Bluetooth sign on the stall broadcasts its agent id and ENS name a few meters, so a phone knows which counter it is facing and whether it is open. Each buyer's agent haggles with the stall agent on its own. The line never hears the next person's deal. When they agree, the buyer pays that amount in HBAR on Hedera through x402, from their own wallet to the stall. Cash and UPI stay for anyone who wants to pay by hand.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js and TypeScript on the web, Postgres for stalls and deals, Redis for agent cards. Gemini writes the bargaining lines. The server checks every price against the stall's floor and the buyer's limit before it sticks. A shopkeeper signs in with Magic and gets a Hedera wallet. Their UPI ID is hashed into the stall's agent id, so the agent is the same person who already takes payments. Saving the stall mints a name on ENSv2 (Sepolia), like ram-lal-chai.molbhav.eth, pointing at the A2A agent card and the Hedera account to pay. An ESP32 on the counter broadcasts that agent id and ENS label over Bluetooth LE, a few meters, with no pairing. The iPhone app is a Capacitor shell. iOS often sends the name and the manufacturer data in different packets, so the scan stitches them. Closed stalls are dropped. The two agents talk rfq, counter, and accept over A2A. The deal is in rupees. Pay turns it into HBAR and returns HTTP 402. The buyer's Magic wallet signs an HBAR transfer with @hiero-ledger/sdk. The x402 facilitator on Hedera testnet pays the network fee and settles it. We never see the key. One catch: Magic's EVM address is not the account that can spend, so pay-to is the 0.0.x account from Magic's admin API. Auto-pay runs in the open browser tab, because that is the only place the key exists.
