projects.title: Pearl
projects.description: Tamper-proof black box for AI robots, with insurance payouts only a verified human can claim
projects.project_description: Pearl is a tamper-proof black box for AI-driven robots, with insurance built in. Robots are leaving their cages and working next to people. When one hits something or someone, nobody can prove what really happened. The logs sit on the owner's computer and can be edited. Nobody can show which AI made which decision. A bot can file an insurance claim as easily as a person can. Pearl fixes this in five steps: 0G AI decides. At each step of a task (plan, check the grasp, check the placement, rate an incident) the robot sends its camera image and sensor readings to an AI model on 0G. The model runs in verified mode inside secure hardware (a TEE). The arm only moves after a valid answer. If 0G is unreachable, or the answer is invalid or unverified, the robot stops safely and records "no decision". It never invents one. The robot keeps its own record. Every decision (with its 0G request id) and every camera frame goes into a hash-chained log. The robot encrypts the log with a fresh key for each run that only the owner can unlock, and signs it with its own key. The sealed file goes to 0G Storage, and its fingerprint is anchored on 0G Chain under the robot's own address. Anyone can check it. The robot writes a public entry for each run on Arkiv, with labels only: robot, outcome, severity and time. That makes runs and incidents searchable without a central database. A shared proof link lets anyone confirm a record is untouched without being able to read it. Change one byte and verification fails. Only a real human can claim. The robot's own safety loop freezes the arm when a hand enters the work zone or the base is knocked, and the AI rates how serious the incident was. The owner can then file a claim. That needs a fresh World ID Agent Pass check, proving it is really the account owner, and an IDKit Proof of Human, so one person gets one claim per incident. A person at the insurer unlocks that one run (the owner shares only that run's key), then approves or declines with a reason. A contract on 0G Chain pays a fixed amount by severity. Each claim is a live Arkiv record, updated at every step. It works without internet. The robot pre-signs its 0G and Arkiv transactions into a sealed bundle. A laptop relay, a phone over Bluetooth or another robot (a mesh, for future multi-owner fleets) carries it to the first device that's online. Carriers can't read or change anything. Pearl runs on an ESP32-S3 robot arm and in a MuJoCo physics simulation. In the simulation, the rendered camera image is exactly what the AI sees. The web app has a landing page aimed at insurers, an owner workspace, an insurer workspace and labelled demo workspaces, so anyone can try it without World ID.
projects.how_its_made: Robot program and server: TypeScript on Node 22. The robot side runs as its own program, just as the ESP32 does, and the dashboard server never signs robot data. The arm layer can drive a TypeScript simulator, a MuJoCo 3.3.7 physics arm (Python) or the real board, all over the same line protocol. 0G Compute: Each checkpoint calls the 0G Compute Router with the camera frame and telemetry, using model 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, trust mode "verified" and the TEE check turned on. The model returns a named action as JSON, never joint angles, and the answer is checked against a schema (zod). If the provider fails, the same prompt and image go to other 0G vision models (qwen2.5-vl-72b, gemini-2.5-flash-lite) within one time budget. Every attempt is recorded. A bad answer is never retried. It becomes a failsafe. 0G Storage and 0G Chain: The encrypted log and frames are uploaded with the 0G Storage SDK. Two Solidity contracts (Foundry) run on Galileo, both source-verified on chainscan: EpisodeAnchor is a write-once record keyed by the robot's address. It stores the log's fingerprint and a hash of all the 0G request ids. RewardPool pays approved claims after re-checking the anchor. The arm is also registered in 0G's zerobot registry, so a run can start from an on-chain command. Arkiv (@arkiv-network/sdk) is the public, queryable index: The robot's own wallet writes one read-only entry per run (pearl.episode.v2). The insurer desk writes one patchable record per claim (pearl.claim.v1), updated at every status change. The owner's run list, incident filter, home counters, claim status and the insurer's queue are all live Arkiv queries. No private data goes on Arkiv. World: Agent Pass uses OIDC with the device grant against the World IdP. We validate the ID token ourselves: signature, issuer, audience, freshness, the orb level, and that the subject is the owner. IDKit v4 runs in the browser. The backend signs the request and verifies the proof with World's v4 API. The action is claim-<run id> and the signal is the payout wallet, so one human gets one claim per incident. Reused proofs are rejected. Encryption: AES-256-GCM with a fresh key for each run. The key is wrapped for the owner's P-256 key (ECDH + HKDF), and the robot signs with EIP-191. The same WebCrypto code runs in Node and the browser. When the owner files a claim, the browser re-wraps only that run's key for the insurer. Firmware: ESP32-S3 N16R8 (PlatformIO, Arduino core 3). The safety loop needs no network: a VL53L0X distance sensor watches the hand zone; an MPU6500 motion sensor detects bumps; a heartbeat watchdog catches lost connections. On top of that, the board has a full device-first core in C++: the 0G call, sealing, signing, the 0G Storage upload, the anchor transaction, Arkiv calldata, bundles and Bluetooth (BLE GATT). An iPhone streams snapshots over Wi-Fi as the robot's camera. Web app: React 19 + Vite, plain CSS and a three.js arm view. The frontend is on Vercel and the backend on Render. Hacky bits worth mentioning: We ported the robot's crypto and chain code to C++. To prove it matches, the TypeScript code generates test vectors and host tests check the firmware against them, byte for byte. Offline robots pre-sign raw EIP-1559 transactions. We capture Arkiv's signed transaction with a custom viem transport, so anyone can broadcast it later without holding a key. Uploads kept "succeeding" while files never appeared on 0G Storage, because nodes from another shard reported them as finalized. We now upload each segment to every node of the correct shard, and count only those nodes. There's also a direct node-download fallback for when the indexer can't find a file. The MPU6500 on our board reports a chip ID the standard library rejects, so we wrote a small register-level driver. The owner's wrapped key is embedded in the sealed file's header. That makes claims work even when the robot is offline: the dashboard reads everything it needs from Arkiv, 0G Chain and 0G Storage.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Pearl is a tamper-proof black box for AI-driven robots, with insurance built in.

Robots are leaving their cages and working next to people. When one hits something or someone, nobody can prove what really happened. The logs sit on the owner's computer and can be edited. Nobody can show which AI made which decision. A bot can file an insurance claim as easily as a person can.

Pearl fixes this in five steps:

1. 0G AI decides. At each step of a task (plan, check the grasp, check the placement, rate an incident) the robot sends its camera image and sensor readings to an AI model on 0G. The model runs in verified mode inside secure hardware (a TEE). The arm only moves after a valid answer. If 0G is unreachable, or the answer is invalid or unverified, the robot stops safely and records "no decision". It never invents one.

2. The robot keeps its own record. Every decision (with its 0G request id) and every camera frame goes into a hash-chained log. The robot encrypts the log with a fresh key for each run that only the owner can unlock, and signs it with its own key. The sealed file goes to 0G Storage, and its fingerprint is anchored on 0G Chain under the robot's own address.

3. Anyone can check it. The robot writes a public entry for each run on Arkiv, with labels only: robot, outcome, severity and time. That makes runs and incidents searchable without a central database. A shared proof link lets anyone confirm a record is untouched without being able to read it. Change one byte and verification fails.

4. Only a real human can claim. The robot's own safety loop freezes the arm when a hand enters the work zone or the base is knocked, and the AI rates how serious the incident was. The owner can then file a claim. That needs a fresh World ID Agent Pass check, proving it is really the account owner, and an IDKit Proof of Human, so one person gets one claim per incident. A person at the insurer unlocks that one run (the owner shares only that run's key), then approves or declines with a reason. A contract on 0G Chain pays a fixed amount by severity. Each claim is a live Arkiv record, updated at every step.

5. It works without internet. The robot pre-signs its 0G and Arkiv transactions into a sealed bundle. A laptop relay, a phone over Bluetooth or another robot (a mesh, for future multi-owner fleets) carries it to the first device that's online. Carriers can't read or change anything.

Pearl runs on an ESP32-S3 robot arm and in a MuJoCo physics simulation. In the simulation, the rendered camera image is exactly what the AI sees. The web app has a landing page aimed at insurers, an owner workspace, an insurer workspace and labelled demo workspaces, so anyone can try it without World ID.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Robot program and server: TypeScript on Node 22. The robot side runs as its own program, just as the ESP32 does, and the dashboard server never signs robot data. The arm layer can drive a TypeScript simulator, a MuJoCo 3.3.7 physics arm (Python) or the real board, all over the same line protocol.

0G Compute:

- Each checkpoint calls the 0G Compute Router with the camera frame and telemetry, using model 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, trust mode "verified" and the TEE check turned on.
- The model returns a named action as JSON, never joint angles, and the answer is checked against a schema (zod).
- If the provider fails, the same prompt and image go to other 0G vision models (qwen2.5-vl-72b, gemini-2.5-flash-lite) within one time budget. Every attempt is recorded.
- A bad answer is never retried. It becomes a failsafe.

0G Storage and 0G Chain:

- The encrypted log and frames are uploaded with the 0G Storage SDK.
- Two Solidity contracts (Foundry) run on Galileo, both source-verified on chainscan:
- EpisodeAnchor is a write-once record keyed by the robot's address. It stores the log's fingerprint and a hash of all the 0G request ids.
- RewardPool pays approved claims after re-checking the anchor.
- The arm is also registered in 0G's zerobot registry, so a run can start from an on-chain command.

Arkiv (@arkiv-network/sdk) is the public, queryable index:

- The robot's own wallet writes one read-only entry per run (pearl.episode.v2).
- The insurer desk writes one patchable record per claim (pearl.claim.v1), updated at every status change.
- The owner's run list, incident filter, home counters, claim status and the insurer's queue are all live Arkiv queries. No private data goes on Arkiv.

World:

- Agent Pass uses OIDC with the device grant against the World IdP. We validate the ID token ourselves: signature, issuer, audience, freshness, the orb level, and that the subject is the owner.
- IDKit v4 runs in the browser. The backend signs the request and verifies the proof with World's v4 API.
- The action is claim-<run id> and the signal is the payout wallet, so one human gets one claim per incident. Reused proofs are rejected.

Encryption: AES-256-GCM with a fresh key for each run. The key is wrapped for the owner's P-256 key (ECDH + HKDF), and the robot signs with EIP-191. The same WebCrypto code runs in Node and the browser. When the owner files a claim, the browser re-wraps only that run's key for the insurer.

Firmware: ESP32-S3 N16R8 (PlatformIO, Arduino core 3). The safety loop needs no network:

- a VL53L0X distance sensor watches the hand zone;
- an MPU6500 motion sensor detects bumps;
- a heartbeat watchdog catches lost connections.

On top of that, the board has a full device-first core in C++: the 0G call, sealing, signing, the 0G Storage upload, the anchor transaction, Arkiv calldata, bundles and Bluetooth (BLE GATT). An iPhone streams snapshots over Wi-Fi as the robot's camera.

Web app: React 19 + Vite, plain CSS and a three.js arm view. The frontend is on Vercel and the backend on Render.

Hacky bits worth mentioning:

- We ported the robot's crypto and chain code to C++. To prove it matches, the TypeScript code generates test vectors and host tests check the firmware against them, byte for byte.
- Offline robots pre-sign raw EIP-1559 transactions. We capture Arkiv's signed transaction with a custom viem transport, so anyone can broadcast it later without holding a key.
- Uploads kept "succeeding" while files never appeared on 0G Storage, because nodes from another shard reported them as finalized. We now upload each segment to every node of the correct shard, and count only those nodes. There's also a direct node-download fallback for when the indexer can't find a file.
- The MPU6500 on our board reports a chip ID the standard library rejects, so we wrote a small register-level driver.
- The owner's wrapped key is embedded in the sealed file's header. That makes claims work even when the robot is offline: the dashboard reads everything it needs from Arkiv, 0G Chain and 0G Storage.

projects.title: Formless
projects.description: Conversational surveys: 0G AI extracts indicators, Chainlink CRE anchors them. verify onchain
projects.project_description: Formless replaces rigid humanitarian survey forms with natural conversation, while keeping the structured, comparable data that fair aid targeting needs. Today, organisations decide who receives aid using fixed questionnaires in tools like KoboToolbox, which reduce a family's situation to checkboxes such as "income: irregular" and lose the story behind it. Once data is cleaned, recoded and scored, nobody outside the organisation can check what the family actually said, how it became data, or whether it was changed later, and excluded households can't see why. In Formless, a trained enumerator talks with the household instead of reading out a questionnaire. After each answer, AI running on 0G Private Computer in sealed TEE mode tracks which of five vulnerability dimensions have been covered (social, economic, physical, environmental and political) and suggests neutral follow-up questions, while the enumerator stays in charge. When the conversation ends, 0G turns it into ten fixed indicators. Each value is linked to the exact quote that supports it, or marked unknown, and the server rejects any quote that doesn't appear word for word in the transcript. The enumerator then reads every value and its quote back to the family, who confirm or correct it. Once the household confirms, a Chainlink CRE workflow anchors the record on Ethereum Sepolia. The workflow fetches only de-identified values and hashes, never the transcript. It reads the published scoring rule's hash onchain and refuses to use any other rule, and it recomputes the record's fingerprint and Aid Score independently of our server. It then writes a signed report to our SurveyRegistry contract, which accepts reports only from the CRE forwarder and only once per record. The onchain eligible flag is what triggers aid, so the organisation can't quietly change a score or rewrite history. The family receives a QR receipt containing its own answers but never a name. Our static verifier page recomputes the fingerprint and the score in the browser and checks them against Sepolia. Every read goes through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC on the Nox mixnet, so the RPC provider can't link a check to a vulnerable household. The check works even with our backend switched off, which is the censorship-resistance property at the heart of our CROPS design. Programme staff get a dashboard with a ward-by-dimension heat table of vulnerability indices, and a recheck button that compares every database record with its onchain anchor, so any tampered row shows up immediately. Each sponsor technology closes a specific trust gap. 0G proves which model interpreted a family's words, because every request ID and TEE provider is sealed inside the anchored fingerprint, and it keeps sensitive conversations away from the AI operator. Chainlink CRE means the organisation can't score its own homework. Anon-RPC and the static verifier let a household prove its own record privately, even if the organisation refuses to help or disappears. The AI never decides who gets aid: it only suggests questions and extracts values, a published rule does the scoring, and political indicators, limited to access to documents and public services and never opinions, are excluded from aid scoring. The project is live. The enumerator app, dashboard and verifier run on Cloudflare Pages, the API runs on Railway, and records are anchored through cre workflow simulate with broadcast. With real 0G inference using the 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model, it extracted 58 of 60 indicators correctly on our test households. The proof of concept uses invented households only, an illustrative scoring rule, and English typed input. Automatic USDC payouts to eligible households are the next step.
projects.how_its_made: Formless is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo. The enumerator app and the verifier are React, Vite and Tailwind static sites on Cloudflare Pages. The API is Hono on Node 22, with Node's built-in SQLite, running in a Docker container on Railway. The contract is Solidity with Foundry on Ethereum Sepolia. A shared core package holds the survey template, scoring rule, hashing and receipt format as pure TypeScript, so the exact same code runs in the browser, on the server and inside the Chainlink workflow's WebAssembly runtime. Records are fingerprinted with canonical JSON and keccak256, and golden test vectors checked in both Vitest and Forge keep Solidity and TypeScript agreeing byte for byte. 0G Private Computer is called through the OpenAI SDK pointed at the 0G router, in private trust mode with TEE verification, using 0G's own 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model because it is one of the few chat models served by sealed TEE providers. Turning off the model's hidden reasoning pass cut response time from 28 seconds to about 2, which made live follow-up suggestions practical. Every request ID, provider address and sealed-encryption header is stored inside the anchored fingerprint, so we can prove which sealed model interpreted each family's words. Every quote is checked against the transcript before the family sees it, and extraction reached 58 of 60 correct indicators on our test households. The Chainlink CRE workflow, written with the CRE TypeScript SDK and compiled to WebAssembly, uses an HTTP trigger and an HTTP fetch with consensus. It reads the published rule hash onchain, recomputes the fingerprint and Aid Score with the shared core library, and writes a DON-signed report to our SurveyRegistry contract. The contract accepts reports only from the forwarder, only under the published rule, and only once per record. Getting it onto Sepolia took two fixes: reading the latest block instead of the last finalized one, since our contract was only minutes old, and raising the gas limit to cover the forwarder's overhead. Our most notable hack bridges the hosted app to a CLI-only Chainlink simulation. The hosted API queues each interview, and a small runner on any machine logged in to CRE runs the real simulation with broadcast and reports the transaction hash back. The API trusts nothing the runner says: it marks a record anchored only after confirming on Sepolia that the transaction emitted our registry's event with that record's exact fingerprint. For the Ethereum Foundation's CROPS track, the household receipt is self-contained. It holds the family's answers in the URL fragment, which is never sent to a server, so the verifier needs only the chain and keeps working with our backend switched off. We plugged EF's Anon-RPC browser harness into viem as its fetch function, so every read travels through the Nox mixnet, and a build check confirms there are no trackers or CDNs. We tested the whole flow end to end in headless Chrome, on a local chain and then on Sepolia, and finally on the live deployment.

projects.title: Booker Bob
projects.description: Agents team up on real-world proofs, choose privately, earn limits. Bob pays helpers, buys things.
projects.project_description: Agents need multiplayer. They hire and pay strangers, and history is cheap to fake. Headwater is a set of contracts that anchors an agent's history in facts and in what real people paid, so good work compounds and a payment alone adds no weight. Booker Bob finds and pays helpers for you, and he is the first agent on it. Bob went to pay a test store 31.23 test USDC, above his limit. A contract stopped him. A real person said yes in World on an iPhone, the payment cleared on Arc testnet, and store order #1081 landed with the transaction in its note. Steal Bob's key and the same limit still binds the thief. Your USDC stays in your wallet under an allowance, and each helper gets a limit read from its standing. Above it the payment waits for your yes, bound to that one payment. A replay is refused, a no cancels, and silence expires. Small Discovery payments run outside CapEscrow: Bob enforces that limit, with the Gateway deposit as the ceiling. Standing starts with reviews from paying people, verified with World, with context proved from internet history through REP, rated anonymously, once per helper. The live market is seeded test people, tagged as test people, on test money. Each context has its own ranking, and your view is the mix you choose. Payments between agents pass weight on, so a circle has none to pass. Tests hold it at zero. Your phone reads every context through a mixnet and works out your list locally. With a private reason, your contexts and why Bob chose stay off chain, and a Jolt proof in zk mode shows the payee was the best candidate in your committed view. A private reason runs from a laptop. The payment, payee, amount and address stay visible on chain, and the money can be traced. The market runs on Arc for speed. Ethereum Sepolia keeps its history, every round so far, and the market can restart there, with limits building up again from new ratings. Try it, with no World App and no wallet. /cheat runs a circle of payments on the live contract with test money. /prove makes a Jolt proof on your own device. /check verifies a proof an iPhone made, in your browser. make judge runs the tests and the evil operator run, with no keys and no sign-ups. The README marks each claim Live, Local or Not run. The Booker Bob name comes from our earlier hackathon entries (hackathon alter ego XD), linked in the README; this is a new project and no code carried over. The test store and visual rules were reused, and REP is used only as an external issuer.
projects.how_its_made: Four decisions shaped the build. Rank is checked on chain. It is a personalized PageRank seeded by reviews, with payments carrying half. A solver submits each round's list and Headwater checks it as a fixed point in one pass, so anyone can submit and a list that fails the check is refused. capturePrice states the people, issuers and dollars the top spot would cost. Nobody has run that attack. A yes belongs to one payment. World's token carries the payment's intent hash as its nonce, and the gate and WorldTokenVerifier both check it, the second on chain. A replay reverts, with the transaction on record. A private reason has a bonded check. There is no Jolt verifier on the EVM here, so a bonded verifier attests, the release waits out a 15 s challenge window, anyone can re-verify and challenge, and a named arbiter rules. With nobody watching, a bad attestation pays once the window ends. The arbiter is a trusted role, and on the laptop path the laptop holds both the view and the bonded verifier's key. One such payment ran on Arc: $1, opened by a script, from a laptop, paid 44.0 s after the intent. The market can leave Arc. Arc is permissioned, so HistoryAnchor on Sepolia keeps every round so far, and make anchor-rebuild with no Arc RPC gave 37 groups, 225 members, 312 nullifiers and all 6 submitted lists exact, through round 5979951. On Sepolia the owner's stop ran with yes, no and silence.  After Arc is gone, a forged consistent history cannot be caught from Ethereum alone. Proving speed, on a generated 56-node market. /prove is a separate page that makes a proof in the browser: 34 s plus 13 s of load on a real iPhone on the live site, 31.5 to 37.9 s in earlier runs, 18.0 s in Chrome on a Mac, about 0.6 s to verify in a browser. Natively on an iPhone 15 Pro Max it takes 8.87 s. These are measurements, and no payment uses them. Public Jolt needs two small changes to run in wasm, and one fixes a multiply that wraps to 0 on wasm32. We also ran a market simulation: 20 players on 7 models, up to 8 moves each, with play money against a snapshot of the test market. Payments gave none of them weight. Paying people to rate was outside it, so it shows no attack resistance. Code and results: docs/market-sim.md. Contracts, Solidity with Foundry, on Arc testnet and Sepolia: CapEscrow pays from the owner's allowance, enforces limits and stops above them. Headwater records receipts, anonymous reviews and payment edges, and checks rank. SeedRegistry lists issuers and contexts. WorldTokenVerifier checks World tokens. BondedApprover runs the verifier's bond and the challenge window. AgentCredentials, deployed on Arc, answers "rated by at least n" with one view call. Its checks are tested on a local chain. HistoryAnchor, on Sepolia, keeps each round of Arc's history, chained. The phone is a web app in TypeScript with viem. Keys are made on the device. Semaphore gives anonymous group membership and one-use nullifiers. Every context's list and each agent's signals go through the official anon-rpc harness, over Nox in desktop Chrome and Nym on an iPhone. If a network fails, the read goes direct and the screen says so. The gate is a small TypeScript server on Fly for World checks, relays, funding and the store. Bob and his key run inside it, and he picks from his own list for now. The list your phone works out stays on the phone, and Bob has yet to read from it. Anyone can close a round. Bob finds services through Circle's Discovery API. One of them, BotPay, is ranked by seeded test people who paid it through the escrow, the rest stay listed unranked, and Bob pays per call with Gateway nanopayments over x402. Discovery, catalog and checkout run over UCP on a test Shopify store. Payment and the paid order run off-protocol, through CapEscrow and the Shopify Admin API, with the transaction in the order note. Spending proofs from REP arrive as signed verdicts from internet history, checked against the issuer's keys. The band and amount stay off chain. One real verdict joined on Arc. ENS and Coinbase checks are built and tested, and no screen joins with a wallet yet. Trust left in place: on this deploy the arbiter, the gate and issuers 1 and 2 are one key. On a grant naming VoucherApprover that key can approve any payment the agent opened, up to the grant's ceiling each round. The app's allowance is unlimited, so round after round that can reach the whole balance until the owner revokes. WorldTokenVerifier's admin sets World's keys, so it could forge a yes, until the final deploy drops it. make evil runs those keys against the real contracts and prints each refusal. External services are listed in the README, new and reused work are separated there, and AI use is documented per file in AI-USAGE.md with prompts in specs/prompts.

One of them, BotPay, is ranked by seeded test people who paid it through the escrow, the rest stay listed unranked, and Bob pays per call with Gateway nanopayments over x402. Discovery, catalog and checkout run over UCP on a test Shopify store. Payment and the paid order run off-protocol, through CapEscrow and the Shopify Admin API, with the transaction in the order note.

Spending proofs from REP arrive as signed verdicts from internet history, checked against the issuer's keys. The band and amount stay off chain. One real verdict joined on Arc. ENS and Coinbase checks are built and tested, and no screen joins with a wallet yet.

Trust left in place: on this deploy the arbiter, the gate and issuers 1 and 2 are one key. On a grant naming VoucherApprover that key can approve any payment the agent opened, up to the grant's ceiling each round. The app's allowance is unlimited, so round after round that can reach the whole balance until the owner revokes. WorldTokenVerifier's admin sets World's keys, so it could forge a yes, until the final deploy drops it. `make evil` runs those keys against the real contracts and prints each refusal. External services are listed in the README, new and reused work are separated there, and AI use is documented per file in AI-USAGE.md with prompts in specs/prompts.

projects.title: PennyAgent
projects.description: AI agent with its Hedera wallet and a hard budget that pays for data over x402, no human in loop.
projects.project_description: Agents can reason, but they cannot pay for anything without a human holding the card. PennyAgent gives an AI agent its own Hedera wallet and makes it safe to trust with money. You ask a question and set a budget. The agent reads a catalogue of paid data endpoints, decides which are worth buying, and pays for each one over x402: the server answers HTTP 402 with a price, the agent signs a Hedera transfer, and a facilitator settles it. It answers from what it bought, mints a receipt NFT for the run, and logs every payment to a public HCS topic. The interesting part is the guardrails. Every rule is enforced in code before anything is signed, never in the prompt: a run budget, a per-purchase cap, an allowlist of payees, a process-wide ceiling, a bound so a server cannot charge more than it advertised, and an optional "ask me above X" human approval. Spending is reserved atomically, so parallel purchases cannot overspend. Agents can also pay agents: our Analyst agent sells a combined briefing over x402 and pays the data server out of its own wallet, two hops, both on-chain. And an MCP server lets any MCP client (such as Claude) use the same guarded wallet.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo. Payments use the x402 exact scheme for Hedera ( @x402/hedera , @x402/express , @x402/fetch ) settling HBAR on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator. The data server wraps free public APIs (Open-Meteo, CoinGecko, Hacker News) behind an x402 paywall. The agent is a Claude tool-use loop; its spending guard plugs into the x402 client's hooks to reserve the exact amount being signed, commit it once the payment is sent (even if the server then errors), and refuse anything off-policy. Hedera services: HCS for the audit log and the agent's identity profile (a UAID following the HCS-14 draft), HTS for per-run receipt NFTs, the Mirror Node REST API for the dashboard's audit view and health checks. No Solidity. The dashboard is React + Vite. We ran two code reviews (one independent) and fixed every finding; the payer is tested with the real x402 client against a mock x402 server.

projects.title: pool-watcher
projects.description: Private crypto accounting: scan RAILGUN txs with a viewing key into a Beancount ledger.
projects.project_description: NOTE: I could not finish this in time for the deadline. pool-watcher is a privacy-preserving accounting system for RAILGUN V2, the private-transaction protocol on Ethereum. RAILGUN hides who sent what to whom, which is great for privacy but terrible for bookkeeping: a merchant receiving private payments has no normal way to produce a ledger, because the on-chain data is encrypted. This project closes that gap end to end. The core idea is viewing-key-based trial decryption. A wallet's viewing key can see its own transactions but can never spend funds. We use that asymmetry to build a read-only accounting pipeline that never touches spending authority. The system has four parts. First, a local test bed: an Anvil chain with a fresh RAILGUN V2 deployment and a scripted scenario that shields 1000 test tokens to wallet A, sends five private transfers from A to B with product memos, then unshields 50 from B to a public address, exporting the resulting logs, steps, and viewing keys as ground truth. Second, a stateless scanner: a Node/TypeScript service that trial-decrypts RAILGUN Shield, Transact, and Unshield logs for a single viewing key. It holds no database, no Merkle tree, no RPC access, and no state, making it a pure decrypt primitive. It speaks NDJSON over a Unix socket (init, scan, pubkey, ping) and returns one event per decrypted note, including direction, memo, sender and receiver, and the unshield fee split. A Rust handle crate defines the wire contract and is the production client. Third, a Rust integration app: an actix-web UI where the merchant pastes their viewing key. The browser seals that key client-side to the scanner's X25519 public key using X25519, HKDF-SHA256, and XChaCha20-Poly1305, so the plaintext key never crosses the socket or touches disk. An alloy listener backfills and live-subscribes to chain logs, feeds them to the scanner, and a writer turns the decrypted events into a Beancount ledger. Fourth, Fava serves that ledger as a real accounting UI. Incoming private transfers appear as product-narrated sales, the unshield appears as a withdrawal to the bank with the fee booked as an expense, and change notes are excluded. The ledger is idempotent: events are deduped in memory and the file is atomically rewritten, so restarts rebuild cleanly from backfill. Why it matters: it demonstrates that private on-chain payments can still be reconciled with double-entry accounting. bean-check passes, balances tie out (185 TST remaining, 235 in sales, 50 minus fee to the bank), and spending keys are never exposed and plaintext viewing keys never leak. The scanner is also chain-, asset-, and pool-agnostic, and its KeyService seam is designed to swap the sealed-box demo for a future Nitro enclave, where the viewing key would be decrypted inside attested hardware. In short: private money, public-grade books. A complete demo that takes encrypted RAILGUN activity and turns it into an auditable merchant ledger, with privacy preserved at every step.
projects.how_its_made: How I built pool-watcher The stack at a glance. The project is four cooperating pieces: a Nix/devenv-managed local test bed, a Node/TypeScript decryption scanner, a Rust integration app, and a Beancount/Fava accounting UI, wired together with Docker Compose. The through-line is RAILGUN V2, the privacy protocol whose encrypted events we turn into a ledger. The test bed (ground truth). We needed real RAILGUN history to build against, so we built a reproducible local chain. devenv.nix pins Foundry (Anvil and cast), Node 22, Yarn, Rust, and jq; scripts/install.sh is idempotent and does the heavy lifting. It checks out a pinned RAILGUN contracts submodule (vendor/contract), applies a patch, installs the Hardhat 2.x/ethers v5 toolchain, compiles the contracts, and installs the demo's TypeScript deps. scripts/chain.sh starts Anvil with --state .state/anvil.json so history survives restarts. scripts/deploy.sh runs hardhat deploy:test, parses the deployed proxy/delegator/testERC20 addresses out of Hardhat's log, and records them plus a deployment block in .state/deployment.json. The scenario itself uses the official @railgun-community/wallet SDK (10.4.0) with snarkjs and leveldown for proof generation and the engine DB. scripts/scenario.sh shields 1000 test tokens to wallet A, sends five private A-to-B transfers with product memos, unshields 50 from B to a public EOA, then exports balances, keys, and the raw proxy logs. Those exports (out/steps.jsonl, out/keys.json, out/logs.json) are the ground truth every other component is tested against. The scanner (stateless trial decryption). The scanner is a Node/TypeScript service that imports only the decryption primitives from @railgun-community/engine — ShieldNote.decryptRandom, TransactNote.decrypt, getNoteHash, serializeTokenData — not the wallet/engine runtime. It holds no database, no Merkle tree, no RPC, and no state: it is a pure decrypt primitive. For each Transact ciphertext it derives a shared key from the viewing key and the blinded receiver key, tries isSentNote=false, then the blinded sender key with isSentNote=true; a passing AES-GCM auth means the note belongs to the wallet. Shields use the shieldKey the same way. The wire protocol is deliberately boring: NDJSON over a Unix domain socket, one JSON object per line, one response per request, with init, scan, pubkey, and ping ops. One process and one socket per viewing key, single-flight (extra connections queue). We used zod to validate requests and ethers' Interface to parse the RAILGUN ABI. The Rust railgun-scanner-handle crate is the source of truth for the wire contract; the Node scanner mirrors it, and the same crate is used as the cross-language protocol test client. The app (Rust: actix-web + alloy + Beancount). The integration app is a Rust binary. actix-web 4.18 serves a small UI and API; alloy 2.5 does the chain I/O; tokio runs the async runtime; bigdecimal and chrono handle money and dates. The flow: the browser fetches the scanner's X25519 public key, seals the pasted viewing key client-side, and POSTs only ciphertext to /api/init. The app relays it to the scanner over the socket; the scanner opens it, derives the 0zk wallet address, and becomes ready. The plaintext viewing key never crosses the socket and never touches disk. Once initialized, an alloy listener backfills eth_getLogs from the deployment block, then keeps a live eth_subscribe WebSocket stream. Logs are grouped by block, each block's timestamp is fetched for the Beancount date, and batches are sent to the scanner. A ledger writer maps events to double-entry Beancount: incoming notes with product memos become sales, the unshield becomes a withdrawal with the fee split to Expenses:Fees, and change notes are excluded. It dedupes by txHash:logIndex:hash:direction and rewrites the file atomically (temp + rename), so Fava reloads on the rename and restarts rebuild idempotently from backfill. Fava runs in its own container and waits for the ledger file to appear. How it's pieced together. Docker Compose runs scanner-b, app, and fava; Anvil stays on the host. The scanner and app share a Unix-socket volume; the app mounts .state read-only and a ledger volume that Fava also mounts. The app's Dockerfile uses the repo root as build context because the Rust crate path-depends on scanner/crates/handle. A multi-stage build compiles the browser seal bundle with esbuild, then embeds it into the Rust binary with include_str!. The scanner's KEY_SERVICE is a build arg baked into the image (local for tests, sealedbox for the demo), never a wire input. Partner technologies and why they helped. RAILGUN is the whole point: its viewing-key model gives us read-only visibility without spending authority, and its engine gave us battle-tested note decryption instead of reimplementing the cryptography. Foundry/Anvil gave us a fast, state-persistent local chain with cast for scripting. alloy gave us typed HTTP + WS providers and log subscriptions in Rust with minimal glue. actix-web gave us a tiny, fast UI/API server. Beancount + Fava gave us a real, auditable double-entry ledger and a polished accounting UI for free. @noble (curves/hashes/ciphers) let the exact same sealed-box code run in the browser and the scanner. Nix/devenv made the whole toolchain reproducible. The notably hacky bits. The test-artifacts tarball was dead (HTTP 525), so we patched the contracts repo to drop @railgun-community/circuit-artifacts and make loadAllArtifacts a no-op, then wrote register-vkeys.ts to fetch production vkeys from IPFS and register all 54 non-POI variants directly. eth_estimateGas lied: it estimated ~87k for delegator.callContract(proxy, setVerificationKey, 0) when the real cost was ~1.2M, so the inner call silently ran out of gas while the outer tx succeeded; we send an explicit gasLimit of 5,000,000 and assert the VerifyingKeySet event. The engine's exports map blocks deep imports, and getSharedSymmetricKey, poseidon, and encodeAddress aren't exported, so we reimplemented the small primitives: X25519 scalar multiplication + SHA-256 for the shared key, Poseidon via circomlibjs, and bech32m 0zk address encoding. Unshield attribution: the public Unshield event has no sender, so we attribute it to the wallet that can decrypt a note in the same transaction (the change note) — otherwise wallet A would see B's withdrawal. Unshield amounts are net: the contract emits base already net of fee; we report value = base + fee (gross leaving the private balance) and fee separately so the ledger can post net to the bank and fee to expenses. Change notes decrypt both ways, producing an in and an out event that cancel in the balance arithmetic. Anvil's --state reload doesn't preserve historical eth_getCode, so a binary search for the exact proxy block fails after restart; we record the pre-deploy block as a safe lower bound. V3 addresses don't exist in the pinned contracts, so lib.ts disables V3 at runtime by mutating both the top-level and the wallet SDK's nested shared-models copy. Bridging sync and async: the Rust handle is deliberately synchronous (std::UnixStream, no tokio), so the app owns it on a dedicated thread and talks to it over an mpsc channel with oneshot replies, serializing all scans. Custom sealed-box envelope: ephemeralPub(32) || nonce(24) || ciphertext, key = HKDF-SHA256(shared, info="railgun-scanner-vk"), AEAD = XChaCha20-Poly1305 — identical code in seal.ts and the scanner. Meta-hack: we built the project with a ticket-driven "Ralph loop" (scripts/ralph.sh) over a git-native ticket board (tk), where opencode implements each ticket and a separate verifier run must end with VERDICT: PASS before the ticket closes and commits. The result is a demo where bean-check passes, balances tie out (185 TST left, 235 in sales, 50 minus fee to the bank), and privacy is preserved end to end.

projects.title: Flexx
projects.description: Flexx: A privacy-first AI wallet for secure payments on ethereum and L2s
projects.project_description: Flexx is an AI wallet for Ethereum that keeps your data on your own machine. You type what you want in plain English, like "send 50 USDC to Alice", "bridge 10 USDC to Base Sepolia" or "pay rent every month", and it turns that into a transaction you approve. We built it for the Ethereum Foundation's "Access Layer for AI and Ethereum Wallets" problem. For now it runs on testnets (Sepolia, Base Sepolia and Arbitrum Sepolia) with USDC and ETH. The problem we wanted to fix is that most AI wallets send your prompts, balances and contacts to a cloud model, and one hallucination or malicious input could move real money. In Flexx the AI is useful but never trusted, and your private data stays local. The model is an open-source one (Qwen, run through Ollama) on your own device, so nothing goes to a cloud LLM. Before it sees a request, amounts, addresses and group names are replaced with random placeholders, so it only ever works with labels. It also doesn't act freely. It runs inside a fixed pipeline, its output is forced into a strict schema, and code re-checks everything: balances, daily limits, address validity and name uniqueness. Text from outside, like a pasted invoice or message, goes to a separate quarantined model. Anything it returns is marked untrusted, needs your explicit confirmation, and can never fund an autopay. Recipients are resolved through your private address book or ENS (ENSv2), and you can pay a whole group through an ENS parent domain. You then see a plain-language summary and confirm it. Only after that does a stripped hand-off with on-chain fields go to the execution layer. Names, context and your original prompt are never included. Flexx handles one-time and group payments, bridging between chains, recurring autopays (through a delegated executor contract and Chainlink CRE automation) and cancelling autopays with a refund. Everything goes through an EIP-7702 account with spending limits you set. Everything is stored in one encrypted local database, and session data like placeholders and prompts is wiped when the session closes. Balances are fetched through anon-rpc so lookups don't reveal who you are. We're shipping it as a local CLI.
projects.how_its_made: We wanted to answer one question: can you hand your wallet to an AI without trusting the AI? Our answer was to treat the model like a smart but unreliable intern. It gets to read and interpret, but it never touches a key, and everything it produces gets checked by code that assumes it's wrong. Flexx is a TypeScript monorepo on Node 22 with three parts: an agent, a wallet, and a shared protocol package, all talking over authenticated HTTP on localhost. We built it like a small engineering org made of AI agents, with parallel work lanes, versioned contracts between them, and separate agents writing and reviewing the code, so nothing graded its own homework. The agent is a Fastify service on an encrypted SQLCipher database, with the key in the OS keychain. A local Qwen model on Ollama does the understanding, but it's on a very short leash: 13 fixed steps, narrow questions, and a JSON schema on every answer. Before the pairing step, real amounts and addresses are swapped for placeholders, and we generate a fresh schema per request that only allows those placeholders. The model can't hallucinate a recipient there because the decoder physically can't emit one. Untrusted content like pasted text, files and web pages goes to a quarantined model call with no tools, so a prompt injection has nothing to grab. The wallet is the paranoid half. It decodes the exact calldata about to be signed and runs it through eth_simulateV1 against Alchemy, QuickNode and PublicNode, requiring two of three to agree at the same pinned block. If the intent, the bytes and the simulated transfers don't all match, nothing gets signed, and there's no "simulation is down, send it anyway" path. Partner tech did the heavy lifting. MetaMask let us delete key management altogether: it holds the key and approves atomic EIP-7702 batches, and we verify the mined transaction afterwards. ENSv2 turns a name into a payment group, so iitr.eth can be your payroll list with no contacts database. Chainlink CCIP gave us real cross-chain USDC, and we delivered a live transfer from Sepolia to Base and track it to finality. Chainlink CRE is the backbone of autopay: a cron with no spending key that can only run plans the user registered on our IntentExecutorV3 contract. The workflow compiles to WASM and is waiting on deploy access. Now the fun part, the hacks: Tor circuit trick: we vary the SOCKS credentials per query type, which gives each one its own Tor circuit, so an RPC provider can't easily link your balance reads, ENS lookups and simulations by exit address. Pretending the upgrade already happened: first-time accounts are simulated with a state override that gives them their EIP-7702 code before they've actually upgraded. Time travel: we simulate registering an autopay, jump the clock forward, and watch the first run pay. For cancels, we jump past the cancel and require that the next run doesn't pay. Smuggling a batch through MetaMask: a one-call batch gets sent directly, so we pass our whole checked batch wrapper as that single call. The event log is the database: the contract stores only a hash and a schedule, and emits the full calldata in an event. The cron rebuilds its entire plan list from chain logs and keeps no state of its own. Off-by-one in a delegation: the time-window enforcer's bounds turned out to be exclusive, so we sign start - 1 and end + 1 or lose the first and last valid seconds. Taming RPC providers: Sepolia's node and the others report traced ETH transfers from different pseudo-addresses, so the decoder accepts both. Our log scanner also shrinks itself to fit provider limits, down to the 10 blocks we hit on Alchemy. We tried hard to break it. Local chain tests run MetaMask's real contracts on Anvil at their real addresses, and we kill -9 the wallet with a payment in flight to prove it can't pay twice. A 50-person autopay used 2.15M gas on its first run and produced a 27.9 KB report, inside CRE's limits. We also discovered that forked chains can't prove bridged USDC arrives, because the fork never mints it, so we stopped trusting the fork and did a real send. The code passes 2,603 agent tests, 208 security and privacy audit checks, and 385 wallet unit tests, and a 154-prompt evaluation against the real model got zero wrong handoffs in its last full run, before we moved to the v2 envelope. And because a wallet for people who live in the terminal should feel like it, flexx is hand-rolled: a custom renderer, an animated ASCII opening that dissolves into dust, and no TUI library.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Flexx is an AI wallet for Ethereum that keeps your data on your own machine. You type what you want in plain English, like "send 50 USDC to Alice", "bridge 10 USDC to Base Sepolia" or "pay rent every month", and it turns that into a transaction you approve. We built it for the Ethereum Foundation's "Access Layer for AI and Ethereum Wallets" problem. For now it runs on testnets (Sepolia, Base Sepolia and Arbitrum Sepolia) with USDC and ETH.

The problem we wanted to fix is that most AI wallets send your prompts, balances and contacts to a cloud model, and one hallucination or malicious input could move real money. In Flexx the AI is useful but never trusted, and your private data stays local.

The model is an open-source one (Qwen, run through Ollama) on your own device, so nothing goes to a cloud LLM. Before it sees a request, amounts, addresses and group names are replaced with random placeholders, so it only ever works with labels. It also doesn't act freely. It runs inside a fixed pipeline, its output is forced into a strict schema, and code re-checks everything: balances, daily limits, address validity and name uniqueness. Text from outside, like a pasted invoice or message, goes to a separate quarantined model. Anything it returns is marked untrusted, needs your explicit confirmation, and can never fund an autopay.

Recipients are resolved through your private address book or ENS (ENSv2), and you can pay a whole group through an ENS parent domain. You then see a plain-language summary and confirm it. Only after that does a stripped hand-off with on-chain fields go to the execution layer. Names, context and your original prompt are never included.

Flexx handles one-time and group payments, bridging between chains, recurring autopays (through a delegated executor contract and Chainlink CRE automation) and cancelling autopays with a refund. Everything goes through an EIP-7702 account with spending limits you set.

Everything is stored in one encrypted local database, and session data like placeholders and prompts is wiped when the session closes. Balances are fetched through anon-rpc so lookups don't reveal who you are. We're shipping it as a local CLI.

We wanted to answer one question: can you hand your wallet to an AI without trusting the AI? Our answer was to treat the model like a smart but unreliable intern. It gets to read and interpret, but it never touches a key, and everything it produces gets checked by code that assumes it's wrong.

Flexx is a TypeScript monorepo on Node 22 with three parts: an agent, a wallet, and a shared protocol package, all talking over authenticated HTTP on localhost. We built it like a small engineering org made of AI agents, with parallel work lanes, versioned contracts between them, and separate agents writing and reviewing the code, so nothing graded its own homework.

The agent is a Fastify service on an encrypted SQLCipher database, with the key in the OS keychain. A local Qwen model on Ollama does the understanding, but it's on a very short leash: 13 fixed steps, narrow questions, and a JSON schema on every answer. Before the pairing step, real amounts and addresses are swapped for placeholders, and we generate a fresh schema per request that only allows those placeholders. The model can't hallucinate a recipient there because the decoder physically can't emit one. Untrusted content like pasted text, files and web pages goes to a quarantined model call with no tools, so a prompt injection has nothing to grab.

The wallet is the paranoid half. It decodes the exact calldata about to be signed and runs it through eth_simulateV1 against Alchemy, QuickNode and PublicNode, requiring two of three to agree at the same pinned block. If the intent, the bytes and the simulated transfers don't all match, nothing gets signed, and there's no "simulation is down, send it anyway" path.

Partner tech did the heavy lifting. MetaMask let us delete key management altogether: it holds the key and approves atomic EIP-7702 batches, and we verify the mined transaction afterwards. ENSv2 turns a name into a payment group, so iitr.eth can be your payroll list with no contacts database. Chainlink CRE is the backbone of autopay: a cron with no spending key that can only run plans the user registered on our IntentExecutorV3 contract. The workflow compiles to WASM and is waiting on deploy access.

Now the fun part, the hacks:

- Tor circuit trick: we vary the SOCKS credentials per query type, which gives each one its own Tor circuit, so an RPC provider can't easily link your balance reads, ENS lookups and simulations by exit address.
- Pretending the upgrade already happened: first-time accounts are simulated with a state override that gives them their EIP-7702 code before they've actually upgraded.
- Time travel: we simulate registering an autopay, jump the clock forward, and watch the first run pay. For cancels, we jump past the cancel and require that the next run doesn't pay.
- Smuggling a batch through MetaMask: a one-call batch gets sent directly, so we pass our whole checked batch wrapper as that single call.
- The event log is the database: the contract stores only a hash and a schedule, and emits the full calldata in an event. The cron rebuilds its entire plan list from chain logs and keeps no state of its own.
- Off-by-one in a delegation: the time-window enforcer's bounds turned out to be exclusive, so we sign start - 1 and end + 1 or lose the first and last valid seconds.
- Taming RPC providers: Sepolia's node and the others report traced ETH transfers from different pseudo-addresses, so the decoder accepts both. Our log scanner also shrinks itself to fit provider limits, down to the 10 blocks we hit on Alchemy.

A 50-person autopay used 2.15M gas on its first run and produced a 27.9 KB report, inside CRE's limits.
