projects.how_its_made: Canary is a Chrome extension written in TypeScript. It runs on a shared core library that also powers our agent gateway and SDK. Before the page's own code runs, Canary injects a script into every frame that wraps the page's network APIs, including fetch, XHR, WebSocket and beacons. It examines outgoing requests and passes JSON-RPC calls to the extension's background worker. The worker decides what happens next: handle the request privately, block it, or allow it while recording what was sent. This gives Canary a per-tab record of what each party received, both with and without protection. Some requests, such as tracking pixels and script tags, cannot be intercepted through these APIs. For those, Canary uses browser-level blocking rules to catch URLs containing the wallet address, including the different formats commonly used by trackers. The popup and dashboard are built with React. Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC and tor-js Canary's private connection uses the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC worker, powered by tor-js, a WebAssembly build of Arti, the Rust Tor client. It creates Tor circuits directly in the browser and connects to relays through a gateway using WebRTC. Before the worker runs, Canary resolves it from an on-chain registry and checks its hash. It runs inside a null-origin sandbox in an offscreen document, separate from both the webpage and the extension's privileged APIs. This lets Canary run a real Tor client in the browser without asking users to install anything or requiring dapps to change their code. Canary does not simply forward a dapp's reads to its original RPC provider. Those provider URLs often contain API keys that identify the dapp. Instead, Canary handles supported read calls using a public endpoint for the correct chain. The dapp's original provider never receives those requests, and the RPC endpoint sees a Tor exit rather than the user's IP address. Each wallet address gets its own Tor circuit, keeping requests from different addresses separated. Getting Tor fast enough for everyday dapp usage took a significant amount of engineering. While profiling requests, we found that tor-js closed its connection after every request. That meant each read had to open a new Tor stream and complete another TLS handshake. We improved the request pipeline in a few ways. Canary batches, caches and removes duplicate reads, reducing twenty individual reads from roughly 50 seconds to around two seconds. It also starts building a Tor circuit as soon as it learns a wallet address and retries stalled reads through a fresh circuit. We also contributed two patches to tor-js: HTTP keep-alive within each circuit, which reduced a warm read from 827 ms to 234 ms. A gateway liveness check that detects when a gateway silently stops responding, preventing circuits from hanging indefinitely. Another issue appeared during failover. Even after switching gateways, tor-js could continue routing an address through the dead gateway. We handle that recovery inside Canary. When the Ethereum Foundation's demo gateway stopped working during the hackathon, we set up and ran our own gateways instead. Answering requests on the correct chain Replacing an RPC provider only works if Canary knows which blockchain that provider serves. Getting this wrong would mean returning data from the wrong chain. Canary first checks well-known provider URLs and then asks the endpoint directly over Tor. Some dapps use their own servers that do not accept Tor connections. We encountered this with 1inch, so in that case the page contacts the server directly with a request that does not contain a wallet address. Canary also does not assume that a wallet's currently selected chain is the only one the dapp uses. Real applications often read from several chains at the same time, so each endpoint needs to be handled independently. ENSv2 We use ENSv2 to make privacy promises public and independently verifiable. A dapp's ENS name stores its privacy manifest, which describes who should receive the user's wallet address. It also stores a signed verdict from an independent verifier describing what the site actually does. The website and its ENS name reference each other, giving users a way to check that the records belong to the site they are visiting. Our scanner loads a site with and without Canary using Playwright, mitmproxy and a fake wallet containing a synthetic address. It records which services receive that address and compares the observed traffic with the site's manifest. The verifier then signs the result and publishes it to the ENS name. ENSv2's role-based permissions let us give the verifier a key that can update one specific record, without giving it control over the rest of the name. This means a compromised verifier cannot change the dapp's privacy manifest. Its permission can also be revoked, and readers can check whether the key still has permission. For dapps that have not published a manifest, Canary creates signed labels under its own ENS namespace. This gives users access to the results of our scans even when a site has not published its own privacy information. We use the same approach for AI agents. An agent's ENS manifest defines the privacy policy its gateway must enforce, and the gateway publishes signed reports about the traffic it handles. The extension also checks these ENS records through the ENS Universal Resolver over Anon-RPC. This means checking a site's privacy information does not reveal to the RPC provider which site the user is visiting. Uniswap v4 Canary Swap demonstrates how a private trading flow can work without sending a wallet address to a quote server. It gets quotes using the Uniswap v4 Quoter and StateView through ordinary contract calls that do not include the user's address. Trades are executed through the Universal Router with Permit2 on our own v4 pool on Sepolia. The page also shows the network requests made while generating a quote. Its ENSv2 name contains a verified privacy manifest, so Canary can show that the observed requests match the site's declared policy. Our example AI agent can perform the same swap through the Canary gateway, with its signed transaction broadcast over Anon-RPC. AI agents The agent gateway runs the same Anon-RPC worker inside headless Chrome. It exposes a JSON-RPC endpoint and an HTTP(S) proxy, so an agent can use it by changing its RPC URL and proxy settings rather than changing its underlying implementation. We also built a TypeScript SDK with a viem transport, an ethers provider and an LLM pseudonymizer. The pseudonymizer replaces wallet addresses in prompts with placeholders before they are sent to an LLM. Some of the less obvious engineering work A few problems required solutions beyond the main request pipeline. Switching wallet accounts safely: When a user switches accounts, Canary temporarily holds the wallet's account announcement until the blocking rule for the new address is installed. This prevents the new address from reaching a tracker before protection is ready. Handling eth_accounts locally: Remote RPC nodes do not hold wallet keys, so their response to eth_accounts would be empty. Canary handles this call locally instead of sending it to a remote endpoint. Running gateways with UDP support: The tor-js gateways need inbound UDP for WebRTC and QUIC. We could not find a free hosting provider that supported this setup, so we run our gateways in Docker behind a UDP tunnel, with the Ethereum Foundation's gateway available as a fallback. Failing closed: If the private connection stops working, Canary returns an error rather than silently sending reads through the normal connection. Users can choose to allow direct access for a particular site.
projects.project_description_markdown:
# Canary — Privacy I

Your wallet protects your private keys, but it doesn't necessarily protect your wallet address when you interact with decentralised applications.

Dapps built with wagmi and viem send blockchain reads such as `balanceOf(you)`, allowances, and positions directly from your browser to their RPC providers. Many also send your wallet address to analytics platforms and third-party trackers, where it can be associated with your IP address. Your wallet's RPC settings do not control this frontend traffic.

A USENIX Security 2023 study found that 211 of 616 dapps leaked wallet addresses to third parties. Our own scans of five leading dapps identified 12 third parties receiving wallet addresses.

**Canary is a browser extension that protects users across dapps without requiring a fork, integration, or changes to the dapp's code.**

## Private reads
Canary routes the dapp's supported Ethereum RPC reads through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC over Tor. Instead of connecting directly to the dapp's RPC provider, supported reads travel through an anonymous network path. The RPC endpoint sees a Tor exit address rather than your original IP address.

## Leaks blocked
Protecting RPC requests alone isn't enough. A dapp can still expose your wallet address through unrelated third-party requests. Canary detects and blocks requests carrying your address across the communication channels available to a page, including Fetch, XMLHttpRequest (XHR), WebSocket, beacons, and tracking pixels.

## Measured coverage
Canary measures what happens to every inspected request and classifies it as:
- **Protected:** Routed through Anon-RPC.
- **Blocked:** Prevented from reaching its destination.
- **Exposed:** Reached a destination without the intended protection.
- **Not inspected:** Could not be reliably inspected or classified.

Each request also receives a receipt documenting what the relevant endpoints observed with and without Canary.

## Making Tor fast enough for a dapp
Privacy protection is only useful if the application remains responsive. We measured where the latency comes from and optimised the request pipeline, circuit management, and gateway infrastructure.

**Batching, caching and deduplication:** Canary groups reads arriving within 15 ms into a single JSON-RPC batch. It caches values that do not change, such as chain IDs and deployed contract code, briefly caches block numbers, and deduplicates identical requests already in flight. On `app.uniswap.org`, 20 of 24 RPC calls were exact duplicates.
- 20 sequential reads went from 43–55 seconds to 1.6–2.1 seconds when batched.
- On a real dashboard firing 20 reads simultaneously, the page settled in 1.7 seconds instead of 3.2 seconds.
- All 80 answers were returned instead of 73.

**Pre-warmed Tor circuits:** Canary maintains a separate Tor circuit for each wallet address. The first read on a new circuit initially took approximately 2.0 seconds, compared with 1.15 seconds for subsequent reads. Canary now builds the circuit as soon as it learns the wallet address, before the dapp makes its first request.

**Hedged reads:** If a read receives no response within three seconds, Canary sends it again through a fresh circuit. The new circuit maintains the same per-address isolation, helping prevent a slow relay or gateway from stalling the application.

**Faster startup:** The extension includes a Tor directory snapshot, saving approximately 11–13 seconds on first startup compared with using EF's gateway.

**Our own gateways:** EF's demonstration gateway initially took 18–43 seconds to start Tor and stopped working on 6 November. We deployed our own public gateways, bringing Tor startup time down to approximately four seconds. Today, a warm private read takes approximately 0.85 seconds.

## What we found in EF's tor-js
While profiling Anon-RPC, we identified several performance and reliability issues in EF's `tor-js` implementation. We developed two patches intended for upstream integration and implemented an additional recovery improvement within Canary.

**1. Connection reuse:** Previously, `tor-js` closed its connection after every request using `Connection: close`. Every read therefore had to establish a new Tor stream, a new TCP connection from the exit, and a new TLS handshake, adding approximately one second of overhead. Our keep-alive patch reuses connections while maintaining strict address-level isolation: a connection belonging to one address is never reused for another.
- Warm reads improved from 827 ms to 234 ms.
- With per-address circuit isolation, reads improved from 1,140 ms to 203 ms.
- 20 parallel reads improved from 2.0 seconds to 0.98 seconds.

**2. Detecting dead gateways:** Previously, when a gateway died without properly closing its connection, `tor-js` only detected the failure after the WebRTC connection timed out. Until then, circuits and reads using that gateway could remain stuck. Our liveness patch checks gateways that have gone quiet and removes them after two missed checks.
- Each gateway failure now causes one failed read instead of two.
- Recovery time improved from 17–31 seconds to 10.5–14 seconds in five of six tests.

**3. Faster recovery after gateway failure:** After a gateway failed, Tor continued assigning an address to its circuit through the dead gateway. Consequently, every subsequent read had to wait for the three-second hedge. We fixed this within Canary: when a hedge succeeds through a new circuit, that working circuit becomes the address's circuit for subsequent reads. Recovered reads improved from approximately 4.2 seconds to 0.8 seconds.

**4. EF gateway reliability:** EF's demonstration gateway could not reliably reach Tor guard relays and, on 6 November, stopped completing connections. This requires a fix from EF's gateway operator. Canary therefore runs its own gateways, retaining EF's gateway as an optional fallback.

**Upstream integration:** The Anon-RPC worker is pinned on-chain by its hash. This means the two `tor-js` patches cannot simply be shipped inside Canary; they need to be integrated upstream first. Our builds are reproducible: an unpatched `tor-js` build produces exactly the hash of the currently deployed on-chain worker.

## ENSv2 privacy promises
Canary also makes a dapp's privacy promises independently verifiable. A dapp publishes the parties that should receive its wallet address in an ENSv2 text record called `privacy.manifest`. Canary's independent verifier scans the dapp, compares its observed traffic against the declared manifest, and publishes a cryptographically signed verdict.

The verifier receives permission to modify only the verdict record through ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control. This allows it to publish findings without receiving control over the dapp's other ENS records. The dapp can revoke that permission, and Canary can detect the revocation.

Most dapps will never publish their own manifests. For these applications, Canary maintains signed privacy labels under its ENS namespace, such as `app-aave-com.labels.canary.eth`. These labels contain the verifier's findings and are displayed by the extension when the dapp accesses the user's wallet address.

## Canary Swap
We built Canary Swap to demonstrate a privacy-preserving alternative to conventional Uniswap integrations. `app.uniswap.org` sends the user's wallet address to its quote server as the `swapper` parameter before the user signs anything. Canary Swap takes a different approach: it obtains quotes directly from the Uniswap v4 Quoter on-chain, without including the user's wallet address in the request.

## AI agents
The same privacy problem applies to autonomous AI agents. Their blockchain reads can reveal their strategy before they execute a trade.

Canary extends its Anon-RPC infrastructure to agents through a local gateway and SDK. Each agent receives an ENSv2 name whose `privacy.manifest` defines the policy enforced by its gateway. The gateway retrieves the policy, routes the agent's reads through Anon-RPC, and publishes signed reports describing where its traffic went.

This provides agents with policy-controlled access and a verifiable record of their network activity.

## Results
- **Address leaks:** Across five leading dapps, third parties receiving wallet addresses went from 12 to 0.
- **RPC coverage:** On 1inch with a wallet connected, 237 RPC calls went through Anon-RPC, with none held back.
- **Batching:** 20 reads improved from 43–55 seconds sequentially to 1.6–2.1 seconds batched.
- **Tor startup:** Improved from 18–43 seconds through EF's demonstration gateway to approximately four seconds using our own gateways.
- **Connection reuse:** A warm private read improved from 827 ms to 234 ms with our `tor-js` keep-alive patch.

## Live deployments
- **LeakyDash:** A deliberately leaky demonstration dapp.
- **Canary Swap:** A privacy-preserving swap application deployed on Vercel.
- **12 ENSv2 names:** Deployed on Ethereum Sepolia.
- **Public Tor gateways:** Our own gateway infrastructure supporting Canary's anonymous RPC connections.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Canary is a Chrome extension written in TypeScript. It runs on a shared core library that also powers our agent gateway and SDK.

Before the page's own code runs, Canary injects a script into every frame that wraps the page's network APIs, including fetch, XHR, WebSocket and beacons. It examines outgoing requests and passes JSON-RPC calls to the extension's background worker. The worker decides what happens next: handle the request privately, block it, or allow it while recording what was sent. This gives Canary a per-tab record of what each party received, both with and without protection.

Some requests, such as tracking pixels and script tags, cannot be intercepted through these APIs. For those, Canary uses browser-level blocking rules to catch URLs containing the wallet address, including the different formats commonly used by trackers. The popup and dashboard are built with React.

### Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC and tor-js

Canary's private connection uses the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC worker, powered by tor-js, a WebAssembly build of Arti, the Rust Tor client. It creates Tor circuits directly in the browser and connects to relays through a gateway using WebRTC.

Before the worker runs, Canary resolves it from an on-chain registry and checks its hash. It runs inside a null-origin sandbox in an offscreen document, separate from both the webpage and the extension's privileged APIs. This lets Canary run a real Tor client in the browser without asking users to install anything or requiring dapps to change their code.

Canary does not simply forward a dapp's reads to its original RPC provider. Those provider URLs often contain API keys that identify the dapp. Instead, Canary handles supported read calls using a public endpoint for the correct chain. The dapp's original provider never receives those requests, and the RPC endpoint sees a Tor exit rather than the user's IP address. Each wallet address gets its own Tor circuit, keeping requests from different addresses separated.

Getting Tor fast enough for everyday dapp usage took a significant amount of engineering. While profiling requests, we found that tor-js closed its connection after every request. That meant each read had to open a new Tor stream and complete another TLS handshake.

We improved the request pipeline in a few ways. Canary batches, caches and removes duplicate reads, reducing twenty individual reads from roughly 50 seconds to around two seconds. It also starts building a Tor circuit as soon as it learns a wallet address and retries stalled reads through a fresh circuit.

We also contributed two patches to tor-js:

- HTTP keep-alive within each circuit, which reduced a warm read from 827 ms to 234 ms.
- A gateway liveness check that detects when a gateway silently stops responding, preventing circuits from hanging indefinitely.

Another issue appeared during failover. Even after switching gateways, tor-js could continue routing an address through the dead gateway. We handle that recovery inside Canary. When the Ethereum Foundation's demo gateway stopped working during the hackathon, we set up and ran our own gateways instead.

### Answering requests on the correct chain

Replacing an RPC provider only works if Canary knows which blockchain that provider serves. Getting this wrong would mean returning data from the wrong chain.

Canary first checks well-known provider URLs and then asks the endpoint directly over Tor. Some dapps use their own servers that do not accept Tor connections. We encountered this with 1inch, so in that case the page contacts the server directly with a request that does not contain a wallet address.

Canary also does not assume that a wallet's currently selected chain is the only one the dapp uses. Real applications often read from several chains at the same time, so each endpoint needs to be handled independently.

### ENSv2

We use ENSv2 to make privacy promises public and independently verifiable.

A dapp's ENS name stores its privacy manifest, which describes who should receive the user's wallet address. It also stores a signed verdict from an independent verifier describing what the site actually does. The website and its ENS name reference each other, giving users a way to check that the records belong to the site they are visiting.

Our scanner loads a site with and without Canary using Playwright, mitmproxy and a fake wallet containing a synthetic address. It records which services receive that address and compares the observed traffic with the site's manifest. The verifier then signs the result and publishes it to the ENS name.

ENSv2's role-based permissions let us give the verifier a key that can update one specific record, without giving it control over the rest of the name. This means a compromised verifier cannot change the dapp's privacy manifest. Its permission can also be revoked, and readers can check whether the key still has permission.

For dapps that have not published a manifest, Canary creates signed labels under its own ENS namespace. This gives users access to the results of our scans even when a site has not published its own privacy information.

We use the same approach for AI agents. An agent's ENS manifest defines the privacy policy its gateway must enforce, and the gateway publishes signed reports about the traffic it handles.

The extension also checks these ENS records through the ENS Universal Resolver over Anon-RPC. This means checking a site's privacy information does not reveal to the RPC provider which site the user is visiting.

### Uniswap v4

Canary Swap demonstrates how a private trading flow can work without sending a wallet address to a quote server.

It gets quotes using the Uniswap v4 Quoter and StateView through ordinary contract calls that do not include the user's address. Trades are executed through the Universal Router with Permit2 on our own v4 pool on Sepolia.

The page also shows the network requests made while generating a quote. Its ENSv2 name contains a verified privacy manifest, so Canary can show that the observed requests match the site's declared policy.

Our example AI agent can perform the same swap through the Canary gateway, with its signed transaction broadcast over Anon-RPC.

### AI agents

The agent gateway runs the same Anon-RPC worker inside headless Chrome. It exposes a JSON-RPC endpoint and an HTTP(S) proxy, so an agent can use it by changing its RPC URL and proxy settings rather than changing its underlying implementation.

We also built a TypeScript SDK with a viem transport, an ethers provider and an LLM pseudonymizer. The pseudonymizer replaces wallet addresses in prompts with placeholders before they are sent to an LLM.

### Some of the less obvious engineering work

A few problems required solutions beyond the main request pipeline.

**Switching wallet accounts safely:** When a user switches accounts, Canary temporarily holds the wallet's account announcement until the blocking rule for the new address is installed. This prevents the new address from reaching a tracker before protection is ready.

**Handling eth_accounts locally:** Remote RPC nodes do not hold wallet keys, so their response to eth_accounts would be empty. Canary handles this call locally instead of sending it to a remote endpoint.

**Running gateways with UDP support:** The tor-js gateways need inbound UDP for WebRTC and QUIC. We could not find a free hosting provider that supported this setup, so we run our gateways in Docker behind a UDP tunnel, with the Ethereum Foundation's gateway available as a fallback.

**Failing closed:** If the private connection stops working, Canary returns an error rather than silently sending reads through the normal connection. Users can choose to allow direct access for a particular site.

projects.title: Stabrix
projects.description: One curve, 8 stablecoins, zero deposits: idle wallets on 1inch Aqua that catch depegs via Chainlink.
projects.project_description: Stabrix puts every stablecoin on one curve, straight from idle wallets on 1inch Aqua. The same coins also stand ready to buy any coin that depegs, and Chainlink CRE decides when that happens. THE PROBLEM Hundreds of billions of dollars of stablecoins sit in wallets, treasuries and DAOs earning nothing. Earning swap fees today means locking them in a pool, where your coins leave your wallet and can do only one job. When one coin depegs, traders dump it into the pool and drain the healthy coins, so LPs are left holding the broken coin and the market loses its liquidity exactly when it needs it most. ONE BALANCE, TWO JOBS Stabrix gives one wallet balance two jobs at once, and the coins never leave the wallet. Both jobs are 1inch Aqua strategies over the same balance. FX range (new SwapVM instruction, opcode 34) One strategy prices 8 stablecoins on a single curve, 56 swap directions in all: USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS and USDe at $1 EURC, BRZ and IDRX at live euro, real and rupiah rates It uses the sphere AMM from Paradigm's research paper on AMMs for many stablecoins, computed in closed form inside SwapVM. Liquidity is concentrated up to 301x. Every swap is checked onchain so the LP can never lose value. Peg backstop (new SwapVM instruction, opcode 35) Dormant while coins are healthy. The moment Chainlink CRE flags a depeg, it buys the broken coin at market price minus a discount the LP chose in advance. It pays only in healthy coins and never pays above face value. At the same instant every FX range refuses the broken coin, so LPs are never dumped on and healthy pairs keep trading. The result is something no pool can offer: a buyer of last resort for every stablecoin, funded by idle wallets. Every day the coins earn FX fees. On the day a coin breaks, they are the liquidity that stays. BUILT ON 1INCH AQUA AND SWAPVM Stabrix only works because of Aqua. Anywhere else a backstop is idle capital waiting for a crisis, and nobody funds it. On Aqua it costs nothing to keep, because the same coins earn fees every day until they are needed. Two new SwapVM instructions, packed under SwapVM's 255-byte argument limit for 8 coins. Both instructions also run on 1inch's official AquaSwapVMRouter, without changing a single 1inch contract. One swap fills makers on our router and 1inch's router in a single transaction. A maker opens a strategy with one Aqua ship call and closes it with dock. There are no deposits, withdrawals or LP tokens. CHAINLINK CRE A Go workflow is the brain of the system. It sets the FX rate every swap uses and decides when a coin is broken. Every 30 seconds it: reads every Chainlink feed in one call; checks those prices against CoinGecko and DefiLlama, with consensus across nodes; writes a signed report onchain. No single API can halt or un-halt a coin. The onchain oracle accepts reports only from the CRE forwarder and the registered workflow, and rejects any rate that drifts from Chainlink's feed. LIVE On Base Sepolia, USDe was crashed to $0.93 and every FX range refused it instantly. A fresh wallet sold 5,000 USDe to the backstops for 4,549.25 USDC, in one transaction across our router and 1inch's. Every swap through the app receives exactly what was quoted, to the wei. Real CRE CLI runs halted a coin, resumed it, and wrote live prices onchain. Every one of the 56 swap directions was filled with real tokens on 1inch's official Aqua and router. The repo has 80 Foundry tests with fuzzing, a TypeScript SDK with 145 tests that matches the Solidity math byte for byte, and a 21-test CRE workflow. The full app covers swapping, opening ranges and backstops from your own wallet, live pool depth, an activity feed of every CRE report, and a depeg lab that crashes a coin and runs the real workflow.
projects.how_its_made: Stabrix has four parts that fit together: Solidity contracts on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, a Chainlink CRE workflow in Go, a TypeScript SDK, and a Next.js app. CONTRACTS (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry) 1inch Aqua is the liquidity layer, and SwapVM is where the pricing runs. A maker never deposits. Opening a strategy is one Aqua.ship call that records an allowance per coin, and closing it is dock. On a fill, Aqua pulls the input token into the maker's wallet and pushes the output to the taker in the same call. Because Aqua only tracks allowances, one wallet balance backs several strategies at once. We wrote two new SwapVM v1.0.2 instructions: StabrixTick (opcode 34) is the sphere AMM from Paradigm's research paper on AMMs for many stablecoins, built for Aqua: Each coin's virtual balance is v = x·ρ + m, where x is the maker's live Aqua balance, ρ is the oracle's USD price, and m is a virtual floor that sets the concentration (301x on the Tight preset). The invariant is Σ(r − v)² = r². The pool keeps no state: the radius r is re-derived from live Aqua balances on every swap, so the curve always prices what the maker really holds. Swaps are closed form, two integer square roots and no iterative solver. After every swap the contract re-checks r' ≥ r, so a trade can never make the LP poorer. Non-dollar coins (EURC, BRZ, IDRX) sit on the same curve by scaling with ρ, which turns a multi-stablecoin AMM into a multi-currency FX market. StabrixBackstop (opcode 35) asks the oracle for a depeg price, and the oracle reverts until the coin is halted. The discount grows linearly as the cap fills. It is priced at the midpoint of the trade, d = d0 + (d1 − d0)(A + a/2)/C, so splitting a sale into pieces never gets a better price than selling it whole. It pays at min(market, face value), and only in coins that are not halted. Notable engineering: Configs packed under 255 bytes. SwapVM caps an instruction's arguments at 255 bytes, so we bit-packed the configs. Eight coins, their decimals, the oracle, the floor, the edge, the fee and the exposure cap fit in 219 bytes for a range and 209 for a backstop. Running on 1inch's official router without modifying it. We use its Extruction opcode, which hands pricing to an external contract. The exact same pricing library runs natively on our router and on 1inch's deployed AquaSwapVMRouter, and tests assert both quote identically. One transaction across both routers. StabrixBatchTaker fills makers on both routers in a single transaction, with a minimum output and a deadline. Wallet check per fill. checkWallet confirms the maker still holds the output coin, so a maker who spends their coins elsewhere is skipped instead of breaking the swap. Rounding always favours the maker. Ceiling division on inputs plus a 1-wei buffer on outputs means split trades can never beat a whole trade. Fuzzing proves it. StabrixLens reads every strategy, balance and quote in one call for the app. 80 Foundry tests, fuzzed at 2,000 runs, check that: the LP never loses value; round trips never profit; splits never beat the whole trade; the router never drains an LP; the backstop never pays above the discounted market. Nine more tests run against a Base mainnet fork with real USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS, USDe, EURC, BRZ and IDRX on 1inch's official Aqua and router, and every pair fills. How 1inch helped: Aqua is the reason the backstop can exist. In any pool, standby depeg liquidity is idle capital nobody would fund. With Aqua's shared liquidity, the same wallet balance earns FX fees in ranges every day and backs the depeg market at no extra cost, without ever leaving the wallet. SwapVM let us ship the whole AMM as two instructions instead of a new protocol, and Extruction let those instructions run on 1inch's official router, so Stabrix liquidity is fillable by any taker of 1inch's AquaSwapVMRouter from day one. CHAINLINK CRE (Go, cre-sdk-go) The workflow depeg-sentinel is the orchestration layer. It sets the FX rates and decides when a coin is broken. Every 30 seconds a cron trigger runs one Multicall3 read that returns every Chainlink feed and the oracle's current status per coin in a single EVM call. Then two HTTP fetches, CoinGecko at full precision and DefiLlama, are aggregated across nodes with median consensus, plus a check that every node saw the same set of prices. The policy is pure Go and unit-tested: Halt: at 3% off peg. An offchain halt needs every API to agree; a Chainlink feed can halt alone. If both sources are past 0.75%, that also halts. Resume: only when every source is back within 0.25%, so one lagging API cannot lift a halt. FX rate push: on a 2 bp move, or every 10 minutes as a heartbeat. The report goes through the CRE forwarder to StabrixOracle.onReport, which accepts only the forwarder plus the registered workflow owner. It uses a CRE rate only when it is fresh and within 0.5% of the Chainlink feed, refuses to trade on a stale feed, and takes the lower of the CRE price and the market feed for depeg purchases. Chainlink made this possible in two ways. The feeds give us trustworthy FX rates for euro, real and rupiah stablecoins. CRE gives us a decentralized, consensus-checked signal for "this coin is broken", which is exactly what a backstop needs before it can safely buy. To simulate on a Base fork, we deployed the oracle with Chainlink's CRE simulation forwarder and the simulator's workflow owner. cre workflow simulate --broadcast then writes real reports onchain, and the halt and resume runs are logged in the repo. The same workflow also wrote live CoinGecko and DefiLlama prices to the oracle on Base Sepolia. SDK (TypeScript, viem) The SDK has a bigint port of the curve and the backstop math, checked byte for byte against Solidity using generated test vectors (145 tests). Its router splits a trade into 64 slices. Each slice goes to the strategy with the best marginal price across every maker on both routers. Slices are halved near a range edge, and strategies the trader owns are skipped. The result is executed through the batch taker. Quotes equal the amount received onchain to the wei. APP (Next.js 15, Tailwind v4, React Query, viem) The app has six pages: Swap: live routing across both routers. Liquidity: open FX ranges and pledge backstops straight from your wallet. Pool: reserves and depth by depeg tolerance. Activity: swaps, strategies and every CRE report read straight from chain logs, with Basescan links. Docs. Depeg lab: crashes a coin through a local price API, runs the real CRE workflow, and charts backstops buying it. Other details: Wallets: any wallet connects through EIP-6963 discovery and is switched to the right network automatically. One site, both networks: a single deployment serves both networks with a switch in the header. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Test coins in one click. "Get test coins" mints $10,000 of all 8 test stablecoins in one transaction by batching the mint calls through Multicall3's aggregate3. Frozen feeds on a fork. A Base fork freezes Chainlink feeds while block time follows the clock, so the fork oracle is deployed with a 30-day feed age and the demo never goes stale. Working around the public RPC. Base Sepolia's public RPC caps eth_getLogs at 200 blocks, which breaks strategy discovery, so everything reads through a public RPC with a larger range. Deploying 1inch on Sepolia ourselves. 1inch has not deployed Aqua on Base Sepolia, so our deploy script deploys 1inch's unmodified Aqua and AquaSwapVMRouter source next to Stabrix. The official-router path then works identically on testnet.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Stabrix puts every stablecoin on one curve, straight from idle wallets on 1inch Aqua. The same coins also stand ready to buy any coin that depegs, and Chainlink CRE decides when that happens.

THE PROBLEM

Hundreds of billions of dollars of stablecoins sit in wallets, treasuries and DAOs earning nothing. Earning swap fees today means locking them in a pool, where your coins leave your wallet and can do only one job. When one coin depegs, traders dump it into the pool and drain the healthy coins, so LPs are left holding the broken coin and the market loses its liquidity exactly when it needs it most.

ONE BALANCE, TWO JOBS

Stabrix gives one wallet balance two jobs at once, and the coins never leave the wallet. Both jobs are 1inch Aqua strategies over the same balance.

1. FX range (new SwapVM instruction, opcode 34)
- One strategy prices 8 stablecoins on a single curve, 56 swap directions in all:
  - USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS and USDe at $1
  - EURC, BRZ and IDRX at live euro, real and rupiah rates
- It uses the sphere AMM from Paradigm's research paper on AMMs for many stablecoins, computed in closed form inside SwapVM.
- Liquidity is concentrated up to 301x.
- Every swap is checked onchain so the LP can never lose value.

2. Peg backstop (new SwapVM instruction, opcode 35)
- Dormant while coins are healthy.
- The moment Chainlink CRE flags a depeg, it buys the broken coin at market price minus a discount the LP chose in advance.
- It pays only in healthy coins and never pays above face value.
- At the same instant every FX range refuses the broken coin, so LPs are never dumped on and healthy pairs keep trading.

The result is something no pool can offer: a buyer of last resort for every stablecoin, funded by idle wallets. Every day the coins earn FX fees. On the day a coin breaks, they are the liquidity that stays.

BUILT ON 1INCH AQUA AND SWAPVM

- Stabrix only works because of Aqua. Anywhere else a backstop is idle capital waiting for a crisis, and nobody funds it. On Aqua it costs nothing to keep, because the same coins earn fees every day until they are needed.
- Two new SwapVM instructions, packed under SwapVM's 255-byte argument limit for 8 coins.
- Both instructions also run on 1inch's official AquaSwapVMRouter, without changing a single 1inch contract.
- One swap fills makers on our router and 1inch's router in a single transaction.
- A maker opens a strategy with one Aqua ship call and closes it with dock. There are no deposits, withdrawals or LP tokens.

CHAINLINK CRE

A Go workflow is the brain of the system. It sets the FX rate every swap uses and decides when a coin is broken. Every 30 seconds it:
- reads every Chainlink feed in one call;
- checks those prices against CoinGecko and DefiLlama, with consensus across nodes;
- writes a signed report onchain.

No single API can halt or un-halt a coin. The onchain oracle accepts reports only from the CRE forwarder and the registered workflow, and rejects any rate that drifts from Chainlink's feed.

LIVE

- On Base Sepolia, USDe was crashed to $0.93 and every FX range refused it instantly. A fresh wallet sold 5,000 USDe to the backstops for 4,549.25 USDC, in one transaction across our router and 1inch's.
- Every swap through the app receives exactly what was quoted, to the wei.
- Real CRE CLI runs halted a coin, resumed it, and wrote live prices onchain.
- Every one of the 56 swap directions was filled with real tokens on 1inch's official Aqua and router.

The repo has 80 Foundry tests with fuzzing, a TypeScript SDK with 145 tests that matches the Solidity math byte for byte, and a 21-test CRE workflow. The full app covers swapping, opening ranges and backstops from your own wallet, live pool depth, an activity feed of every CRE report, and a depeg lab that crashes a coin and runs the real workflow.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Stabrix has four parts that fit together: Solidity contracts on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM, a Chainlink CRE workflow in Go, a TypeScript SDK, and a Next.js app.

CONTRACTS (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry)

1inch Aqua is the liquidity layer, and SwapVM is where the pricing runs. A maker never deposits. Opening a strategy is one Aqua.ship call that records an allowance per coin, and closing it is dock. On a fill, Aqua pulls the input token into the maker's wallet and pushes the output to the taker in the same call. Because Aqua only tracks allowances, one wallet balance backs several strategies at once.

We wrote two new SwapVM v1.0.2 instructions:

- StabrixTick (opcode 34) is the sphere AMM from Paradigm's research paper on AMMs for many stablecoins, built for Aqua:
  - Each coin's virtual balance is v = x·ρ + m, where x is the maker's live Aqua balance, ρ is the oracle's USD price, and m is a virtual floor that sets the concentration (301x on the Tight preset).
  - The invariant is Σ(r − v)² = r².
  - The pool keeps no state: the radius r is re-derived from live Aqua balances on every swap, so the curve always prices what the maker really holds.
  - Swaps are closed form, two integer square roots and no iterative solver.
  - After every swap the contract re-checks r' ≥ r, so a trade can never make the LP poorer.
  - Non-dollar coins (EURC, BRZ, IDRX) sit on the same curve by scaling with ρ, which turns a multi-stablecoin AMM into a multi-currency FX market.
- StabrixBackstop (opcode 35) asks the oracle for a depeg price, and the oracle reverts until the coin is halted.
  - The discount grows linearly as the cap fills.
  - It is priced at the midpoint of the trade, d = d0 + (d1 − d0)(A + a/2)/C, so splitting a sale into pieces never gets a better price than selling it whole.
  - It pays at min(market, face value), and only in coins that are not halted.

Notable engineering:

- Configs packed under 255 bytes. SwapVM caps an instruction's arguments at 255 bytes, so we bit-packed the configs. Eight coins, their decimals, the oracle, the floor, the edge, the fee and the exposure cap fit in 219 bytes for a range and 209 for a backstop.
- Running on 1inch's official router without modifying it. We use its Extruction opcode, which hands pricing to an external contract. The exact same pricing library runs natively on our router and on 1inch's deployed AquaSwapVMRouter, and tests assert both quote identically.
- One transaction across both routers. StabrixBatchTaker fills makers on both routers in a single transaction, with a minimum output and a deadline.
- Wallet check per fill. checkWallet confirms the maker still holds the output coin, so a maker who spends their coins elsewhere is skipped instead of breaking the swap.
- Rounding always favours the maker. Ceiling division on inputs plus a 1-wei buffer on outputs means split trades can never beat a whole trade. Fuzzing proves it.
- StabrixLens reads every strategy, balance and quote in one call for the app.

80 Foundry tests, fuzzed at 2,000 runs, check that:
- the LP never loses value;
- round trips never profit;
- splits never beat the whole trade;
- the router never drains an LP;
- the backstop never pays above the discounted market.

Nine more tests run against a Base mainnet fork with real USDC, USDT, DAI, USDS, USDe, EURC, BRZ and IDRX on 1inch's official Aqua and router, and every pair fills.

How 1inch helped: Aqua is the reason the backstop can exist. In any pool, standby depeg liquidity is idle capital nobody would fund. With Aqua's shared liquidity, the same wallet balance earns FX fees in ranges every day and backs the depeg market at no extra cost, without ever leaving the wallet. SwapVM let us ship the whole AMM as two instructions instead of a new protocol, and Extruction let those instructions run on 1inch's official router, so Stabrix liquidity is fillable by any taker of 1inch's AquaSwapVMRouter from day one.

CHAINLINK CRE (Go, cre-sdk-go)

The workflow depeg-sentinel is the orchestration layer. It sets the FX rates and decides when a coin is broken. Every 30 seconds a cron trigger runs one Multicall3 read that returns every Chainlink feed and the oracle's current status per coin in a single EVM call. Then two HTTP fetches, CoinGecko at full precision and DefiLlama, are aggregated across nodes with median consensus, plus a check that every node saw the same set of prices.

The policy is pure Go and unit-tested:
- Halt: at 3% off peg. An offchain halt needs every API to agree; a Chainlink feed can halt alone. If both sources are past 0.75%, that also halts.
- Resume: only when every source is back within 0.25%, so one lagging API cannot lift a halt.
- FX rate push: on a 2 bp move, or every 10 minutes as a heartbeat.

The report goes through the CRE forwarder to StabrixOracle.onReport, which accepts only the forwarder plus the registered workflow owner. It uses a CRE rate only when it is fresh and within 0.5% of the Chainlink feed, refuses to trade on a stale feed, and takes the lower of the CRE price and the market feed for depeg purchases.

Chainlink made this possible in two ways. The feeds give us trustworthy FX rates for euro, real and rupiah stablecoins. CRE gives us a decentralized, consensus-checked signal for "this coin is broken", which is exactly what a backstop needs before it can safely buy.

To simulate on a Base fork, we deployed the oracle with Chainlink's CRE simulation forwarder and the simulator's workflow owner. cre workflow simulate --broadcast then writes real reports onchain, and the halt and resume runs are logged in the repo. The same workflow also wrote live CoinGecko and DefiLlama prices to the oracle on Base Sepolia.

SDK (TypeScript, viem)

The SDK has a bigint port of the curve and the backstop math, checked byte for byte against Solidity using generated test vectors (145 tests). Its router splits a trade into 64 slices. Each slice goes to the strategy with the best marginal price across every maker on both routers. Slices are halved near a range edge, and strategies the trader owns are skipped. The result is executed through the batch taker. Quotes equal the amount received onchain to the wei.

APP (Next.js 15, Tailwind v4, React Query, viem)

The app has six pages:
- Swap: live routing across both routers.
- Liquidity: open FX ranges and pledge backstops straight from your wallet.
- Pool: reserves and depth by depeg tolerance.
- Activity: swaps, strategies and every CRE report read straight from chain logs, with Basescan links.
- Docs.
- Depeg lab: crashes a coin through a local price API, runs the real CRE workflow, and charts backstops buying it.

Other details:
- Wallets: any wallet connects through EIP-6963 discovery and is switched to the right network automatically.
- One site, both networks: a single deployment serves both networks with a switch in the header.

Hacky bits worth mentioning:

- Test coins in one click. "Get test coins" mints $10,000 of all 8 test stablecoins in one transaction by batching the mint calls through Multicall3's aggregate3.
- Frozen feeds on a fork. A Base fork freezes Chainlink feeds while block time follows the clock, so the fork oracle is deployed with a 30-day feed age and the demo never goes stale.
- Working around the public RPC. Base Sepolia's public RPC caps eth_getLogs at 200 blocks, which breaks strategy discovery, so everything reads through a public RPC with a larger range.
- Deploying 1inch on Sepolia ourselves. 1inch has not deployed Aqua on Base Sepolia, so our deploy script deploys 1inch's unmodified Aqua and AquaSwapVMRouter source next to Stabrix. The official-router path then works identically on testnet.

projects.title: X402 API Marketplace
projects.description: A decentralized API marketplace enabling instant, subscription-free USDC micropayments.
projects.project_description: x402 API Marketplace is a decentralized platform that enables developers to monetize their APIs using instant, on-chain USDC micropayments powered by the x402 protocol. It creates an open marketplace where API providers can register their services, define custom pricing, and receive payments directly to their crypto wallets whenever someone accesses their APIs. On the consumer side, developers can discover and consume paid APIs without traditional subscriptions, centralized payment gateways, or manually managing API keys. The platform integrates x402 payment middleware to handle HTTP 402 Payment Required responses, payment verification, and seamless API access. It also features a dashboard for managing registered APIs and monitoring API calls and earnings. Built using React, Tailwind CSS, Node.js, Express, MongoDB, and EVM-based payment infrastructure, the project aims to make API monetization permissionless, transparent, automated, and accessible to developers worldwide.
projects.how_its_made: We built the x402 API Marketplace using a React + Vite frontend with Tailwind CSS v4 for a responsive dashboard, and a Node.js + Express backend for API registration, routing, and payment orchestration. MongoDB Atlas stores API metadata, wallet addresses, pricing information, and usage statistics. The core payment infrastructure is powered by Coinbase's x402 protocol, integrating @x402/express middleware and @x402/evm for EVM-based payment verification on Base Sepolia. API providers register endpoints, specify USDC pricing, and receive payments directly to their wallets. On the consumer side, we integrated @x402/fetch , which intercepts HTTP 402 Payment Required responses, automatically handles payment authorization and signing, and retries the API request after payment. We also developed a proxy layer that connects registered endpoints with the payment middleware and tracks API usage and earnings. projects.title: BlackBox
projects.description: A flight recorder for AI robots: decisions proven on 0G, searchable on Arkiv, checkable by anyone.
projects.project_description: Blackbox is a flight recorder for AI robots. AI drones already inspect solar farms, bridges and power lines, and an AI decides what they see: a cracked panel or just dust. Those calls move money through repairs, warranty claims and insurance payouts. But the only record lives in the operator's own database, so the owner, the insurer and the panel maker have to take it on trust. Blackbox fixes that: Acts only on verified AI. The drone moves only on an answer from 0G's sealed AI model that it has checked itself. Forged commands are refused. Fails safe. If 0G can't be reached, the drone flies home instead of guessing, and later resumes where it stopped. A record nobody can rewrite. Every decision is signed by the robot, stored on 0G Storage and anchored on 0G Chain. Searchable on Arkiv. Every finding is also written to Arkiv, so anyone can ask "what's the history of panel r2m13?" or "do the cracks cluster in one maker's batch?". The site owner's asset register lives there too, owned by their own wallet. Anyone can check it. Scan a QR code and the whole flight is re-checked in the browser. The demo is a solar farm inspection where we try to break it: a forged command is refused, an edited log is caught, and cutting the AI link sends the drone home. Next is an SDK so any robot can plug in.
projects.how_its_made: Robot (Python). A Skydio X2 drone simulated in MuJoCo. Before it moves, its interlock checks that 0G's answer is strict JSON, echoes the robot's nonce, and carries a valid signature from an allowlisted 0G TEE signer. A lease watchdog safe-stops the drone if no valid answer arrives in time. Every event becomes a robot-signed, hash-chained log entry. Core (TypeScript). Calls 0G's sealed vision model 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b (TeeML on Intel TDX) through the 0G Compute Router, fetches the TEE signature, and reads the signer from 0G's on-chain InferenceServing contract. Logs and encrypted camera crops go to 0G Storage. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry). BlackboxRegistry on 0G Galileo registers each mission, anchors the log every two decisions, and closes the mission with its trajectory hash. It checks robots against 0G's zerobot RobotRegistry. Arkiv. With @arkiv-network/sdk on the Rabdi testnet we write each finding (queryable by panel, label, severity, maker and batch), the site owner's asset register (from their own wallet), a mission board, and a copy of every 0G Storage file. Writes are batched and expire after 90 days; 0G keeps the proof forever. UI. A React and three.js 3D console with live Arkiv history and analytics, plus a public browser verifier with no backend. Hacky bits. 0G's Router adds trace fields to each response, so we strip them and re-marshal the JSON Go-style to rebuild the exact bytes 0G signed, letting the robot verify the signature itself. If 0G Storage is down, the verifier reads the Arkiv copy but still checks every hash against 0G Chain, so the backup can't change the verdict. Arkiv has no joins, so we copy each panel's maker and batch into every finding.

projects.title: Relayless
projects.description: Pay anyone privately from a wallet with zero ETH. No relayer. Built for the EIP-8141 alt mempool.
projects.project_description:
Paying someone privately on Ethereum today forces a bad choice. To withdraw from a privacy pool, you either fund your fresh wallet with gas, which links it straight back to you, or you trust a relayer: a middleman who sees your IP, can censor you, and is a single point of failure. That one problem is a big part of why everyday private payments on Ethereum still don’t happen. Relayless removes that choice. It’s a privacy pool built on EIP-8141 frame transactions (Ethereum’s native account abstraction), where the pool itself sends the withdrawal and pays the gas out of the money being withdrawn. The receiving wallet never needs a single wei of ETH, and there is no relayer at all. How it works, in one transaction: A VERIFY frame checks a zero-knowledge proof that you own a note in the pool, against a recent root (EIP-8272), and approves paying gas from that note.
The note’s nullifier is used as the transaction’s keyed nonce (EIP-8250), so a double-spend isn’t a failed transaction someone pays for: it’s simply invalid.
A SENDER frame pays the recipient, adds a change note, and refunds unused fee.
Verification costs about 253k gas, far above the public mempool’s 100k limit, so the pool is a staked entity in the ERC-8421 alternative mempool, the only place this transaction can live. Relayer-less withdrawals have been prototyped by researchers. Relayless is the layer that makes them usable by real people: One seed, nothing new to back up: your wallet signs once, and every note can be recovered from the chain on any device.
Pay any amount: partial payments leave change notes, and larger payments split across notes, all pending at once from the same pool.
See how hidden you really are: an anonymity meter based on min-entropy (not a feel-good number) with plain advice like “wait” or “split”, plus an optional rule enforced inside the proof: only withdraw once at least k deposits follow yours.
Compliance without doxxing: a World ID–gated association set proves a unique human is behind a deposit, nothing more, and anyone excluded can always exit publicly, so funds are never trapped.
ENS as the directory: anyone can run an association-set provider, discoverable by name and verified against the on-chain pool, and you can pay alice.relayless.eth at a fresh, unlinkable address every time (ENSv2 on Sepolia).
Optional Nym mixnet routing hides your IP from the RPC for name and directory lookups. Built on, and for, the alternative mempool. Every user shares one pool sender, so its reputation is everyone’s. We designed out every way a withdrawal could be admitted but not mined: always proving against the latest root, a generous fee with a refund, a gas reserve, simulating before sending, and a payout that can’t revert. Building it also surfaced real issues, which we shared with the alt mempool authors: The public gateway can’t admit any Groth16 privacy withdrawal today: its 100k cap applies even to staked senders, and precompiles are rejected during validation. There’s a minimal repro, plus a patch and a safety argument.
Fee-bump replacements were counted as new reputation events. The authors confirmed this as a bug, and we fixed it in our patch with a test.
We measured how a note owner can grief a shared sender’s reputation across nodes, and proposed a rule change. Relayless ships with a viem-based SDK (deposit, pay, anonymity, recover) that simulates admission before sending, a CLI, a mobile-friendly web app, and a one-command local stack tested from a fresh clone. It’s fully open source, with CROPS, threat model, limitations and prior work documented in the README. Relayless: private payments, no relayer, no history.
projects.how_its_made:
Relayless is a TypeScript monorepo with five parts: Circom circuits, Foundry contracts, a viem-based SDK and CLI, a Vite/React web app, and scripts that bring up a full EIP-8141 stack locally. The withdrawal transaction (EIP-8141 frame transaction, pool as sender): Frame 0, VERIFY: verifies a Groth16 proof and calls APPROVE for execution and payment, so the pool pays gas from the note being withdrawn. The validation reads no storage at all: the root comes from an EIP-8272 recent-root reference instead of contract storage, and the verifying key is hardcoded in code. That’s what lets many withdrawals from the one shared sender be pending at the same time.
The nullifier is the EIP-8250 keyed nonce. The protocol consumes it atomically with payment approval, so a double-spend is an invalid transaction, not a paid failure, and we don’t need a nullifier mapping at all.
Frame 1, SENDER: pays the recipient, inserts the change note into a LeanIMT and publishes the new root. It’s designed and fuzz-tested so it cannot revert after APPROVE, because a payout failure after approval would cost the shared pool reputation.
Frame 2, DEFAULT: refunds unused fee. Circuits: adapted with attribution from 0xbow’s Privacy Pools (commitment, withdraw, association-set membership), then reshaped for native AA. We removed the relayer, fee and refund public inputs, and bound the proof to the transaction’s sigHash instead. The proof travels as an ARBITRARY signature entry, which avoids the circular dependency between the proof and the hash it commits to. We published the root as H(treeRoot, leafCount) so the circuit can enforce an optional “at least k deposits after mine” rule. Verification measures about 253k gas, compared with the roughly 211k research floor for a single-note withdrawal; the extra public inputs for the k-gate, association set and change note account for the difference. Partner technologies and how they helped: EF alternative mempool (ERC-8421) and ethrex with EIP-8141: these are the whole reason the product can exist. Without stake-based admission, a 253k-gas privacy verification can’t propagate at all. We built and debugged against the workshop sidecar and its admission reports, and the SDK simulates admission before broadcasting, so a failing withdrawal is never sent and never burns the pool’s reputation.
World IDKit: Proof of Human gates the association set, the minimum credential that stops one person from flooding it with sybil deposits. It’s verified server-side, with the cancelled, invalid, duplicate and never-approved paths all handled, the last one by a public exit.
ENSv2 on Sepolia: a Permissioned Registry for an association-set provider directory (world.asp.relayless.eth and others), Permissioned Resolvers holding each provider’s root and policy, and Enhanced Access Control so each operator can edit only its own records. The app discovers providers from ENS and cross-checks each root against the on-chain pool. Private receive names store a stealth meta-address, so every payment to alice.relayless.eth lands at a fresh, unlinkable address, and EAC lets the app edit only that record.
Nym mixFetch: swapped in as the fetch transport under viem, so ENS and directory reads can go through the mixnet. It’s off by default, and if the mixnet is unreachable the app asks you instead of silently falling back to a direct connection. Notably hacky: The public gateway rejects every Groth16 withdrawal: the 100k cap applies even to staked senders, and COD-010 bans the pairing precompile. We wrote a small sidecar patch that adds per-entity budgets and a precompile allowlist, and documented why pure, stateless precompiles are safe for block builders.
While measuring griefing on our own stack, we found the sidecar counted fee-bump replacements as new “seen” events. The alt mempool authors confirmed it as a prototype bug, and our patch fixes it with a test that fails without the fix.
ethrex lost block-number lookups for a run of blocks on two fresh chains, so the SDK reads around the gap and fails loudly if pool data is affected. We wrote this up for the authors.
Sends fall back across Sepolia RPCs automatically after one provider refused real transactions and another rate-limited us.
A one-command local stack (scripts/local-stack.sh) builds the chain, waits about 11 minutes for frame transactions to activate, stakes the pool and deploys. It’s tested from a fresh clone. Testing: circuits, contracts with fuzzing, SDK and ASP server unit tests; a local end-to-end suite (29/29) covering deposit, private payment, double-spend rejection, change notes and concurrency; and an ENS end-to-end suite on real Sepolia (48/48). AI usage: Claude Code was used for implementation, testing and documentation under my direction; I designed the system, made the decisions, and reviewed and validated the work.

projects.title: WAVE
projects.description: The next secure standard of no-seed-phrase wallets via EIP-8141, ERC-8286, EIP-8250 and EIP-8272.
projects.project_description: WAVE is a smart wallet built on EIP-8141 frame transactions, with EIP-8250 keyed nonces and EIP-8272 recent roots. ERC-4337 wallets still depend on an EOA: every UserOperation reaches the chain inside a normal transaction that a bundler's EOA signs. With EIP-8141, the account itself is the transaction sender. Your payment needs no EOA signature and no EntryPoint contract, and you have no seed phrase. You choose how you approve: World ID, a passkey with Face ID or Touch ID, a security key, or any mix. The highest-ranked method becomes the owner. You set simple rules, like Wise. Up to an amount, one method approves. Above it, a stronger method approves. A daily limit stops every method, and an optional wait lets you cancel risky changes. The smart contract enforces these rules, not the app. WAVE also gives AI agents their own wallets. You create an agent wallet from your main wallet, then use it from Claude Code through a local MCP server. The agent can send alone up to its limit. Above that limit, Claude Code shows a QR code and you approve with World ID Agent Pass. A script watches the approval each second and reports the result back to the agent. Above the daily total, the contract refuses the payment, and no human can override it. If approval is denied or expires, nothing is sent. Every action shows its transaction hash.
projects.how_its_made: WAVE is built on five standards. EIP-8141 (frame transactions) is the core. A type 0x06 transaction holds ordered frames, and its sender is the smart account. ERC-4337 wraps a UserOperation in a transaction that a bundler's EOA signs, and an EntryPoint contract runs it. EIP-8141 removes both from the user's transaction. A VERIFY frame runs the account's own validation and calls APPROVE. A SENDER frame then runs the transfer. A failed VERIFY frame means the transaction is invalid and is never mined. A failed SENDER frame mines with status 0x0. ERC-8286 (frame validators) defines how an account runs a validator by DELEGATECALL in a VERIFY frame. This lets one wallet accept many signature types. EIP-8250 (keyed nonces) gives an account parallel nonce streams. WAVE puts the validator address in nonce_keys[0], and the account reads it with TXPARAM. The key picks the method, so methods do not block one another. EIP-8272 (recent roots) lets a transaction reference a recent World ID Merkle root. The validator reads it with the RECENTROOTREFLOAD opcode (0xB6), through a small Yul helper. This avoids a storage read in another contract, which mempool rules restrict. ERC-8421 (alternative mempool), with rules in the style of ERC-7562, admits frame transactions that the public mempool refuses. WAVE needs it, because World ID verification costs far more than the public 100k limit. We wrote three validators. The passkey validator checks a WebAuthn P-256 signature through the 0x100 precompile. Its 512-byte fixed witness keeps sig_hash stable. The World ID validator verifies a Semaphore Groth16 proof on BN254 onchain, with the signal bound to sig_hash, so each proof approves one exact transaction. It uses the 0x06, 0x07 and 0x08 precompiles and costs about 237k gas in VERIFY. The agent key validator uses secp256k1. WavePolicy holds spending tiers, a hard daily limit, a delay queue and recovery. Wallets are CREATE2 clones whose address commits to their setup. A gas station paymaster sponsors gas on the local network. We ran a local stack: ethrex, Lighthouse and the alt mempool sidecar. The sidecar needed two patches: a higher verification gas budget, and a precompile list, because precompiles have no code and failed its rule check. Hacky parts: a local dev key deploys wallets, publishes World ID roots and runs the test faucet, and the sponsor signs with secp256k1. So the user's payment needs no EOA, but this local support code does. The frontend is Next.js 16 with a Vite and React phone UI. World ID uses IDKit 4. Human approval for agents uses World ID Agent Pass, with OIDC device flow, validated on the backend. The first approval links a World ID to the agent. Later, a scan by the same person sends the payment. The MCP server has no approval tool, and it holds no secrets. A Claude Code Stop hook polls each second and returns the result to the agent. The contracts have 78 Forge tests.

EIP-8250 (keyed nonces) gives an account parallel nonce streams. WAVE puts the validator address in nonce_keys[0], and the account reads it with TXPARAM. The key picks the method, so methods do not block one another.

EIP-8272 (recent roots) lets a transaction reference a recent World ID Merkle root. The validator reads it with the RECENTROOTREFLOAD opcode (0xB6), through a small Yul helper. This avoids a storage read in another contract, which mempool rules restrict.

ERC-8421 (alternative mempool), with rules in the style of ERC-7562, admits frame transactions that the public mempool refuses. WAVE needs it, because World ID verification costs far more than the public 100k limit.

We wrote three validators. The passkey validator checks a WebAuthn P-256 signature through the 0x100 precompile. Its 512-byte fixed witness keeps sig_hash stable. The World ID validator verifies a Semaphore Groth16 proof on BN254 onchain, with the signal bound to sig_hash, so each proof approves one exact transaction. It uses the 0x06, 0x07 and 0x08 precompiles and costs about 237k gas in VERIFY. The agent key validator uses secp256k1.

WavePolicy holds spending tiers, a hard daily limit, a delay queue and recovery. Wallets are CREATE2 clones whose address commits to their setup. A gas station paymaster sponsors gas on the local network.

We ran a local stack: ethrex, Lighthouse and the alt mempool sidecar. The sidecar needed two patches: a higher verification gas budget, and a precompile list, because precompiles have no code and failed its rule check.

Hacky parts: a local dev key deploys wallets, publishes World ID roots and runs the test faucet, and the sponsor signs with secp256k1. So the user's payment needs no EOA, but this local support code does.

The frontend is Next.js 16 with a Vite and React phone UI. World ID uses IDKit 4. Human approval for agents uses World ID Agent Pass, with OIDC device flow, validated on the backend. The first approval links a World ID to the agent. Later, a scan by the same person sends the payment. The MCP server has no approval tool, and it holds no secrets. A Claude Code Stop hook polls each second and returns the result to the agent. The contracts have 78 Forge tests.

projects.title: ATLAS-Omiiii
projects.description: Ethereum, decoded with receipts. Search, decode and trace source evidence via Studio, CLI, SDK & API
projects.project_description: ATLAS is an Ethereum Developer Intelligence Platform built around one fundamental question: when a blockchain tool tells you what a transaction means, can you trace that answer back to its source? Ethereum developers regularly switch between signature databases, ABI references, blockchain explorers, RPC providers, and documentation to understand smart-contract interactions. ATLAS brings these workflows together through four connected developer interfaces: a visual Studio, command-line interface (CLI), TypeScript SDK, and REST API. Our core innovation is a provenance-backed Ethereum signature registry powered by Arkiv. Rather than returning only a possible function name, ATLAS connects canonical signatures to pinned Solidity source files, original Git commits, source locations, licenses, deterministic record hashes, and wallet-created Arkiv entities. We demonstrated a real Arkiv Rabdi transaction for the OpenZeppelin function getRoleMember(bytes32,uint256), selector 0x9010d07c, including an indexed write, on-chain receipt, API readback, and Studio lookup. Our importer additionally validated 3,892 Solidity function and event declarations across pinned OpenZeppelin and Ethereum ERC sources in offline analysis. These declarations have not all been uploaded to Arkiv. ATLAS provides deterministic calldata decoding, signature search, event and log interpretation, Ethereum transaction inspection, and clearly separated community suggestions from 4byte.directory. When multiple signatures could match, ATLAS exposes that ambiguity instead of inventing verification. Beyond Arkiv, we implemented supporting workflows across four additional technologies: Swarm: A content-addressed artifact reader that retrieves public files from a Bee-compatible gateway and computes SHA-256 digests to verify the received bytes. A complete postage-backed upload and Arkiv-linked artifact publication are separate steps. ENSv2: Read-only permission checks using Enhanced Access Control on supported Ethereum deployments. ATLAS can inspect publisher-related registry roles and distinguish authorized accounts from unauthorized ones without making permission-changing transactions. Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC: A browser-based Nym worker integration for supported privacy-oriented Ethereum reads, including an optional Transaction Lab privacy workflow. Regular backend RPC analysis remains separately identified rather than falsely presented as anonymous. 0G Private Computer: A server-side, opt-in explanation adapter that can send deterministically decoded calldata evidence for model interpretation. The interface separates local illustrative explanations from genuine provider responses, which require configured model access and credits. ATLAS is designed around transparent evidence, not fabricated certainty. Its public interface makes each developer workflow accessible, while its integrations expose real connectivity states and meaningful failures. Our vision is to make Ethereum interactions easier to investigate, understand, and integrate while preserving the technical evidence behind every interpretation.
projects.how_its_made: ATLAS is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces. Shared packages provide schemas, validation, signature processing, decoding, blockchain access, and consistent error handling to four interfaces: Developer Studio, CLI, TypeScript SDK, and REST API. The Developer Studio uses React, Vite, TanStack Router, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and Lucide icons. It includes a responsive public landing page, light/dark appearance support, Signature Explorer, Calldata Decoder, Event Inspector, Transaction Lab, developer documentation, integration diagnostics, and settings. The public landing page provides direct access to the CLI, SDK, REST API, and Studio. The backend uses Fastify, TypeScript, Zod, and viem. It provides validated routes for canonical function lookup, signature search, calldata decoding, event lookup, log decoding, transaction analysis, sponsor integration diagnostics, and supported extension workflows. Domain errors, upstream failures, missing configurations, and timeout conditions are handled explicitly. Arkiv is our primary decentralized data integration. We use @arkiv-network/sdk with the Rabdi testnet to maintain a searchable signature registry. Our importer extracts canonical function and event declarations from pinned, legally redistributable Solidity sources, including OpenZeppelin Contracts and Ethereum ERC specifications. Each record preserves its source repository, commit, path, license, and deterministic provenance hash. A real Rabdi testnet write was completed for getRoleMember(bytes32,uint256), selector 0x9010d07c. We verified the transaction receipt, indexed readback, matching entity key, and corresponding API result. Records are creator-scoped, indexed for lookup, and use an explicit expiration policy. The full offline source dataset is not represented as live Arkiv data. For Swarm, ATLAS includes a bounded, read-only Bee artifact adapter exposed through the REST API, SDK, CLI, and Studio. It retrieves public content by Swarm reference, validates response limits, and computes a SHA-256 digest. We also implemented an approval-gated workflow for future postage-backed uploads, Arkiv entity linking, and readback verification. This avoids confusing artifact retrieval with completed decentralized publication. For ENSv2, the backend uses viem to call genuine registry and Enhanced Access Control view functions on supported Ethereum deployments. The role inspector can use block-pinned reads to examine registry addresses, account permissions, resources, and role bitmaps. ATLAS exposes these results through its API, SDK, CLI, and Studio without claiming that a permission result independently proves ABI authorship. For Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC, ATLAS integrates a browser-based Nym harness. It provides a privacy-oriented read path for supported operations and an explicitly labeled direct RPC comparison. The Transaction Lab also distinguishes Nym-based reads from standard backend RPC analysis. Failed private requests do not silently fall back to direct reads. For 0G Private Computer, we developed a server-side explanation adapter. The system first performs deterministic calldata decoding using ATLAS's canonical evidence, then optionally submits structured context for real model inference. The integration includes input validation, timeout handling, rate-limit and credit errors, safe response parsing, and evidence separation. Local explanation previews are deliberately labeled as illustrative, while actual 0G inference requires configured provider credentials and returns its genuine response metadata. The CLI is distributed through the scoped npm package @omghotekar/atlas-cli and provides signature lookup, decoding, transaction tools, diagnostics, and additional evidence workflows. The TypeScript SDK reuses the shared contracts, providing typed requests, schema validation, timeouts, and structured errors. We used GitHub for version control, Vercel for deployment, and Vitest, ESLint, Prettier, and TypeScript checks for verification. The project also includes an npm packaging smoke test and reproducible source-provenance documentation. The distinctive engineering challenge was connecting decentralized source metadata, deterministic EVM decoding, publisher permissions, artifact verification, privacy-oriented RPC experiments, and optional AI interpretation without blurring the boundary between proven facts, unverified suggestions, and unavailable services.
