projects.title: Veylor
projects.description: Veylor is a Shielded wallet which supports Shielded USD and Zec with a built in Atomic bridge
projects.project_description: Veylor is a shielded wallet that lets users hold Shielded USD (in Railgun) and shielded ZEC (on Zcash). It moves value between the two chains over a novel trustless, atomic bridge. The wallet is non-custodial and built with a specific focus on CROPS. We built the bridge because, as far as we know, no bridge to shielded ZEC is trustless today. Exchanges and wrapped ZEC hold your funds. Cross-chain swap networks rely on validators or a bridge you have to trust.  So today, moving between shielded ZEC and Ethereum means either handing your funds to someone or giving up privacy on the Zcash side. A shielded Zcash bridge comes with uniques chanllenges which we have tacked head one with CROPS in mind. Here's how a swap from ZEC to USD works. The wallet and a market maker each hold half of a spend key. Together the halves control a fresh shielded Zcash address, and neither side can spend from it alone. The maker locks the USDC in our contract on Ethereum, and the wallet deposits its ZEC to the shared address. To get paid, the wallet reveals its half on Ethereum. The contract checks it on the Pallas curve and pays the USDC into the user's Railgun balance, and the maker then uses the revealed half to sweep the ZEC. Time windows in the contract decide who may act when, so each side ends up with either the trade or their money back. It works the other way too, from USD to ZEC, with the USDC escrowed straight from Railgun. The contract is live on Ethereum mainnet and Sepolia. At the hackathon we went after the two places where users still leaked or depended on us. The first is frames, so you don't need our relayer. Getting paid takes an Ethereum transaction, and the fresh key each swap uses has no ETH for gas, so until now our relayer sent claims for users. A relayer can refuse a claim or go down. With EIP-8141 frame transactions, the swap's own key sends its claim straight to the alternative mempool, and a sponsor contract pays the gas. The sponsor reads the swap from our contract to decide whether to pay. The normal mempool forbids that kind of read, and the alternative mempool allows it once the sponsor has staked. We showed both. The same claim was refused by the normal mempool, refused by the alt mempool while the sponsor was unstaked, and accepted once it staked. Then we ran a full swap of real testnet ZEC this way. Frame transactions only exist on the EF's devnet for now, and it has no Railgun, so there the claim pays a plain address. On Sepolia and mainnet, claims still go through the relayer until EIP-8141 ships. The second is Anon-RPC, so syncing doesn't give you away. The wallet reads Ethereum all the time, checking its swaps and syncing its Railgun notes. Before, the RPC provider saw the phone's IP next to every address and swap it looked up, and Tor was a setting that was off by default. Now every Ethereum read on Android goes through the EF's Anon-RPC by default, over Tor or the Nox mixnet. If that route is down, the wallet refuses rather than falling back to a direct connection There are still things it doesn't hide. The maker sees each swap's amount and timing, and the Zcash server (lightwalletd) sees your IP when you sync unless Tor is on. Veylor and the bridge existed before ETHGlobal Mumbai. Veylor is our fork of the open-source Vizor wallet, which is why that repo lists upstream contributors. The two features we're submitting were built during the hackathon, each on its own branch. Frames is zecSwap PR #35 (https://github.com/JustZappIt/zecSwap/pull/35), 7 commits on Nov 6. Anon-RPC is Veylor's feature/anon-rpc branch (https://github.com/ChinmayGopal931/vizor-fork/compare/eb465f3dd9d9...feature/anon-rpc), 17 commits on Nov 5 and 6.
projects.how_its_made: Veylor is a Flutter app with a Rust core, connected through flutter_rust_bridge. The Zcash side is a light wallet built on librustzcash that syncs from lightwalletd, and everything that touches keys or swaps is written in Rust. The bridge is our zecSwap protocol. Every swap gets a fresh key derived from the wallet seed. The deposit address's spend key is split between the user and the market maker, and each side proves it knows its half before anyone deposits. The contract is written in Solidity and built with Foundry. It checks a revealed half against its public key using Pallas curve arithmetic we wrote in Solidity, which is how Ethereum can verify a Zcash key, and it pays out into Railgun through a separate vault for each swap. Time windows in the contract make sure only one side can reveal at any moment. We tested it with stateful fuzzing and mutation testing. The maker is a Rust service built on axum and SQLite, with a watchtower that follows both chains, and it sweeps the ZEC by signing a PCZT with the combined key. Users who have no ETH get their claims sent by our relayer, which on mainnet goes through Flashbots Protect so the secret stays private until the claim is mined. For frames we wrote an EIP-8141 frame transaction encoder in Rust. The devnet runs an older draft than the EIP text, so we generated test vectors from the alt mempool workshop's TypeScript library and matched them byte for byte. The sponsor is a Solidity contract built on the workshop's helpers for the new APPROVE and TXPARAM opcodes. It only pays when the swap exists with exactly those terms and is still open, when it's our maker's swap, when the sender is the swap's own key on its first transaction, and when the whole transaction costs at most 0.005 ETH. It staked 0.012 ETH in the devnet's staking registry, and that stake is what lets the alt mempool accept it reading our contract during validation. Its checks use about 33k of the 100k gas budget and never read the clock. Foundry doesn't know EIP-8141 yet, so our 18 tests stand in for the opcode helpers with vm.etch, including a fuzz test showing that ETH only ever leaves the sponsor as gas. Before writing any client code we ran a small Node and viem probe that measured what the new opcodes really return on the devnet and ran the three-way mempool test. The client signs deterministically, so a restart resends exactly the same bytes. It resends every five minutes to match the mempool's expiry, never estimates gas because an estimate would show a node the secret early, and watches the swap's state instead of receipts because alloy can't decode the new transaction type yet. For Anon-RPC, a hidden WebView page runs the EF's official browser harness. The harness reads the worker's hash from a contract on Ethereum and won't run a bundle that doesn't match it, and the worker runs in a null-origin sandbox. The default route is tor-js, which is Tor's Rust implementation (Arti) compiled to WebAssembly. It builds circuits on the phone and reaches Tor over WebRTC through a gateway. Nox, a Sphinx mixnet, is the second route on testnet. Rust is the only way out for Ethereum reads. The swap engine calls it directly, and the Railgun page's providers point at a loopback relay that Rust serves. Each account gets its own isolation key, so two accounts' reads leave on separate circuits, and if no route is up the reads are refused rather than sent direct. Both partner technologies did real work for us. Anon-RPC gave us an anonymity network we didn't have to build, and because its workers are pinned by hash we don't have to trust the bundle we load. The alt mempool made the sponsored claim possible at all, since the normal mempool won't let a paymaster read another contract. A few things were hackier than we expected. A claim's receipt shows only half the storage gas it really needs while it runs, because a refund from a later frame gets subtracted from it, so gas limits copied from receipts would have broken the claim halfway with the secret already public. The devnet's gateway mempool had no peers all day, with 21 transactions stuck in it, so we send straight to the miner's mempool node, which runs the same rules. The EF's demo Tor gateway never connected for us, so a teammate ran our own, and with it Tor comes up in about five seconds. Android's WebView put three walls between the page and the loopback relay. New Android versions silently drop plain http, so we allow it for 127.0.0.1 only, and we also had to allow mixed content and bypass the page's proxy for loopback. Workers that use the browser's fetch hit a CORS wall from the null-origin sandbox, and Tor and Nox only get around it because they reach their networks over WebRTC. On mobile data, carrier NAT blocks the WebRTC traffic, so for now it only works on Wi-Fi.

projects.title: Privora
projects.description: Your swaps are public. Your queries don't have to be. Uniswap V2 with every read via Anon-RPC.
projects.project_description:
Every time you open a Uniswap app, it quietly asks an RPC provider for your balances, allowances, pool reserves and prices. Those requests carry your IP address and name the wallet and tokens you care about, so the provider can link who you are to what you own and what you watch. Almost nobody talks about this leak, because it happens before you ever sign a transaction. Privora is a Uniswap V2 interface that closes it. Every read goes through Anon-RPC, the anonymous RPC transport from the Ethereum ecosystem, so the provider receives your question from a mixnet exit and cannot tell who sent it. Trading itself is unchanged: the real Uniswap V2 router and pair contracts, your own wallet signs every transaction, approvals are for the exact amount, and nothing is custodial. It is privacy you can verify, not a badge. Privora is fail-closed: if the privacy layer is down, reads stop instead of quietly falling back to a normal RPC. A Privacy page shows every request, its route
and its latency, with a direct-reads counter that stays at zero. The app has swap, add and remove liquidity, featured and newest pools, and settings. We are explicit about the limits: transactions and addresses are public onchain. Privora protects the lookups that come before them.
projects.how_its_made: The big idea: privacy at the transport layer. Instead of inventing a new protocol, we put one choke point between the app and the network. Everything that reads Ethereum goes through a single function, rpcRead(), so privacy is enforced in one place and cannot be bypassed by accident. How the pieces fit: a Next.js 16 and TypeScript front end. viem does all Ethereum access through a custom transport built on rpcRead(), so every hook (balances, allowances, quotes, pools, receipts) is private by construction. The wallet is plain EIP-1193, and writes go through the user's own wallet on a separate path from reads. Partner technology, Anon-RPC: rpcRead() calls worker.fetch() on @anon-rpc/browser-harness 0.4.0, a hash-pinned worker in a sandboxed iframe that sends requests through a mixnet (Nox by default, tor-js and Nym supported). Each wallet session gets a fresh isolation key, so sessions are not linked. It gave us a real, verifiable anonymising transport instead of a privacy badge, and spared us from building our own anonymity layer. If no worker is ready, rpcRead() throws before touching the network: fail-closed, never a quiet fallback. Making a slow network usable: mixnet requests take seconds, so reads are batched with Multicall3 (a quote costs one request instead of several), queued with limited concurrency, and retried. A boot watchdog abandons a stuck worker and fails over between anonymising networks, never to a direct connection, and the app recovers on its own in the background. viem's default receipt polling overloaded the mixnet, so transactions are confirmed with one small request every few seconds. Hacks worth mentioning: fee-on-transfer tokens are found by simulating first and falling back to the SupportingFeeOnTransfer router functions, and the gas buffer came from replaying a failed transaction with cast. Token logos are bundled and unknown tokens get identicons made from their address, so the page never calls a logo CDN that could see the visitor's IP. How we know it works: a dependency-free Chrome DevTools driver runs real-browser tests, including one that reads the browser's own resource log and proves the page sends no request to the RPC host after worker setup. Wallet-signed flows run on an anvil Sepolia fork with an injected EIP-1193 stub, and real swaps ran on Sepolia.

projects.title: GhostScan
projects.description: A privacy-first Ethereum explorer using Anon-RPC, with real onchain reads, transport comparisons.
projects.project_description: GHOSTSCAN is a privacy-first Ethereum intelligence terminal built around a simple idea: your wallet is public, but your curiosity shouldn’t be. It lets users investigate Ethereum addresses and contracts without connecting a wallet. Users can inspect ETH balances, account nonces, deployed bytecode and bytecode hashes through the official Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC browser harness, with Nym as the default anonymity transport. GHOSTSCAN also makes transport behavior inspectable. Its Privacy Lab compares equivalent direct and Anon-RPC requests using real responses and measured latency. The RPC Observatory records request activity, distinguishes direct bootstrap traffic from investigation reads, and calculates coverage without hiding direct calls. Anonymous transport failures remain visible and never silently trigger direct-RPC fallback. The application documents its trust assumptions and limitations. Successful worker requests demonstrate the integration; they do not independently prove network-layer anonymity.
projects.how_its_made: GHOSTSCAN uses a browser-side architecture that keeps investigation queries out of an application backend. The official Anon-RPC harness reads a mainnet specifier contract through a restricted bootstrap provider, retrieves the specified worker bundle, verifies its keccak256 hash and initializes it inside a sandboxed worker. After readiness and chain validation, Ethereum investigation requests use the worker’s fetch interface through Nym. A shared RPC client manages initialization, request dispatch, timeouts, reconnection, worker cleanup and stale-response rejection. Address investigations retrieve balance, nonce and bytecode at a common observed block. Telemetry stays in browser memory, while diagnostic exports omit investigation parameters and response contents. The frontend combines a responsive landing page with a terminal workspace, custom SVG branding, locally hosted typography and a React Bits WebGL background. Validation included unit tests, TypeScript and lint checks, production builds, and automated Chrome tests using real Ethereum requests.

projects.title: DripMoney: ZK credit
projects.description: Private cash advance for small shops, repaid from sales. ZK passes, World ID, Uniswap v4 hook.
projects.project_description: DripMoney is a private merchant cash advance for small shops in dollar-short economies. Prove the business, not the person. The merchant proves with zkTLS that their seller dashboard shows a country, a revenue band and 6+ months of activity. That becomes a Business Pass, a Noir ZK credential. We never ask for a name, phone number or contacts. Get paid in stablecoins. Customers scan the shop's QR and pay in USDC(Sepolia). While an advance is active, x% of each sale goes toward repayment; without an advance there is no holdback. An agent draws stock on credit. World ID comes first: the merchant proves they are a unique human who is not banned and has no open advance. They set limits (max per advance, max per month, recipient, expiry) and delegate once with a World Agent Pass. The cash-flow agent then draws small advances to pay suppliers, and the AdvanceBook contract enforces the mandate limits and tier caps onchain. AI (an Underwriter plus an independent Critic) proposes offers; the contract decides. Repay through sales, build a private record. Repayment comes out of the x% split automatically. The fee is 0.5% per week while principal remains, capped at 3%. Falling behind the 1%-per-week minimum adds a late fee paid to the reserve. After 30 days anyone can write the advance off, and the human behind it is banned at the World ID step. A fully repaid advance mints a Standing Pass, a Noir ZK credential that raises the merchant's limit without revealing their history. Lenders fund it. Fees split 40% senior vault, 30% DripCoin (DRIP), 20% reserve, 10% protocol. DRIP is the junior first-loss ERC-4626 tranche and trades on a Uniswap v4 pool whose RiskHook takes a 0.3% USDC-side fee (75% to the reserve). A Risk agent reads the pool TWAP and write-offs and can only lower limits. Privacy: ZK passes are generated in the browser and only proofs reach the chain. Browser reads go through Anon-RPC (Nox) by default. World ID is kept only as an HMAC on our server; nothing about the person goes onchain. The shop pseudonym's sales, repayments and advance sizes are public.
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo (pnpm + Turbo): Next.js web app, @repo/sdk, Foundry contracts, Noir circuits, a Python agents service and a zkTLS issuer. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, 152 tests), live on Sepolia: AdvanceBook (advances, the 92/8 payment split, fees, late fees, write-off with a 5 USDC bounty, mandate limits via Policy), BusinessPassRegistry, SeniorVault and JuniorVault/DripCoin (ERC-4626 tranches, 20% junior cover checked on every draw), and RiskHook, a Uniswap v4 hook on the DRIP/USDC pool. The hook charges a 0.3% fee only when the unspecified currency is USDC, flushes 75% to the reserve and 25% to treasury, and keeps a TWAP the Risk agent reads. Non-upgradeable, no pause; anyone can call pay, repay, writeOff and flush. ZK: two Noir circuits (business_pass, standing_pass) proven in the browser with bb.js and verified onchain by Honk verifiers. Poseidon2 (zemse) is shared between Noir and Solidity so the Standing Pass tree matches. /proof decodes the onchain proofs, txs and AI decisions. World: real IDKit verification comes first (unique human, not banned, no open advance; the nullifier is kept only as an HMAC server-side), then a one-time World Agent Pass delegation with mandate limits. The agent calls drawByMandate with no per-draw approval. Test mode stays as a fallback and for the unattended simulator. Agents (Python, 406 tests, on EC2, Amazon Bedrock): the Underwriter (Mistral Large 3) proposes; the Critic (Kimi K2.5, a different model family that never sees the Underwriter's reasoning) checks for wash trading. Output is schema-validated, clamped by code against live onchain limits, then EIP-712 signed; the contract checks it again. The Risk agent (Qwen3 235B) can only lower caps, with a deterministic -25% fallback. A keeper and relayer handle writes. Business Pass issuer: a zkTLS (Reclaim) attestation of the seller dashboard becomes a Business Pass. The demo uses a mock attestor and an unbranded demo seller portal; the real Reclaim path is built and tested. Anon-RPC: every browser read goes through Nox by default (26/26 SDK reads routed in a Chrome measurement). Backend reads use Tenderly; writes are public transactions. Hacky bits: a public-devnet simulator that fast-forwards time to show defaulter, late fee, write-off, DRIP absorbing the loss, the Risk agent cutting caps and the World ID ban in under a minute; MockUSDC because Circle's Sepolia USDC can't be minted freely.

projects.title: Treasure Hunt
projects.description: A player passport on Arkiv that follows people across Treasure Hunt events. Photos live on Swarm.
projects.project_description: Treasure Hunt turns events into NFC scavenger hunts. Players tap tags around the venue, claim tokens without paying gas and swap them for merch. It has run at a dozen events since 2025, with 488 player accounts on chain. Every event runs as its own deployment with its own database, so players started from zero each time. At Mumbai we gave them a passport on Arkiv that every event can read. A player's first find at an event adds that event's badge to it. It also keeps their name and an optional profile photo. We encrypt the photo and only the ciphertext goes to Swarm. If the player removes the photo, nobody can decrypt the Swarm copy again. The demo runs two events, mumbai1 and mumbai2, each with its own contract and database.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js on Vercel, one deployment and one Neon Postgres per event. Claims are ERC-4337 user operations from thirdweb smart accounts, paid by a paymaster on our own testnet (Nova Cidade). New at Mumbai: after a claim, the server reads the contract to confirm it, then writes to Arkiv with @arkiv-network/sdk. A player's first find at an event creates a read-only badge, indexed by player and event. Their first find anywhere also creates the passport, and both go in one batch. One issuer wallet writes everything. Anyone can write under our schema names, so every read filters on that wallet. Entities get Arkiv's six-month maximum, and each new badge renews the passport. The server encrypts photos with AES-256-GCM and uploads the ciphertext through the public Swarm gateway. The passport holds the Swarm reference and a random nonce. Our landing site derives the key from a secret and that nonce, and only for the nonce the passport holds right now. We skipped Swarm's built-in encryption because its references carry the key, and anyone can read an Arkiv entity. We wrote the code with Claude Code. The README lists what the AI did.

projects.title: Secret Tinder
projects.description: Private matching with PSI, verified identities, and AI twins before a real first date.
projects.project_description: Secret Tinder — Fall for the Conversation, Not the Profile What if you could get to know someone before revealing your personal profile? Traditional dating apps encourage people to judge potential partners through photos, occupations, education, and social status before they have a meaningful conversation. At the same time, users are expected to share sensitive personal information and romantic preferences with centralized platforms just to find a match. Secret Tinder reimagines online dating around privacy, personality, and genuine human connection. Our goal is to reverse the traditional dating experience: instead of revealing your identity first and discovering compatibility later, you discover common ground first and decide what to reveal as trust develops. Discover Compatibility Without Exposing Your Private Life Users should be able to express their interests and relationship preferences without making them visible to strangers or storing their entire private lives in a central database. Our privacy-preserving matching system is designed to determine whether two people satisfy each other's preferences while revealing as little information as possible about the underlying conditions. We also introduce verifiable pseudonymous participation, allowing users to demonstrate that they hold a valid participation credential without publicly displaying their real-world identity. Meet Your Match's AI Twin Matching is only the beginning. Our companion experience, Secret Tender , introduces a new way to discover someone's personality before a real first date. Each person can create an AI twin based on their communication preferences, conversational tendencies, and relationship style. Rather than assigning generic personality labels, the experience lets users shape how their AI representation communicates. Users can preview their AI twin, correct responses that do not feel authentic, and explicitly approve its use. With the owner's permission, another person can interact with that AI twin through natural conversation and interactive dating scenarios. Imagine sitting in a cozy Mumbai café, sharing chai, talking about your interests, and navigating an unexpected monsoon shower—all within a romantic simulation inspired by Japanese dating games and Indian storytelling. The AI responds according to the communication characteristics approved by its owner. It can express preferences, ask questions, react to misunderstandings, and create moments of connection. The experience is not about falling in love with an AI. It is about becoming curious about the real person behind it. From Virtual Conversations to Real-World Connections After interacting with an AI twin, users may discover questions they genuinely want to ask its owner, communication styles they find interesting, or differences worth exploring together. Our vision is to make the next step a mutually approved invitation to meet in real life. Neither person's contact details should be disclosed simply because an AI conversation went well. An AI twin does not represent the real person's actual feelings, guarantee romantic compatibility, or predict what a real date will be like. It is a consent-controlled simulation designed to support discovery, not replace human judgment. What Makes Secret Tinder Different? Secret Tinder brings together three experiences that are usually separate: Privacy-first discovery: Explore compatibility without immediately exposing sensitive personal details. A person-controlled AI representation: Interact with conversational traits that the real person has reviewed and approved. A bridge to real dating: Use an engaging AI simulation to begin discovering someone, with the ultimate goal of meeting a real human being. The experience also reflects our Japan–India collaboration, combining Japanese romantic game design with Indian settings, cultural details, and storytelling. Our Vision We believe dating should begin with curiosity, not a résumé. Secret Tinder aims to create a world where people can protect their privacy, explore meaningful conversations, and gradually build the confidence to meet each other in real life. Less swiping. Less exposure. More genuine discovery.
projects.how_its_made: How We Built Secret Tinder Secret Tinder combines privacy-preserving cryptography, decentralized participation credentials, and personalized AI dating experiences. Developed through a Japan–India collaboration, the project explores how people can discover romantic compatibility without exposing their private lives to a centralized dating platform. 1. Decentralized Identity and Verifiable Participation We built the core application using React, TypeScript, Vite, Hono, Cloudflare Workers, viem, Ethereum, ENSv2, and Arkiv. One of our biggest challenges was creating verifiable participation without publishing sensitive dating information on-chain or requiring users to trust our backend. We used ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia to create pseudonymous identities, including alice.secrettinder.eth and bob.secrettinder.eth . Each identity has a dedicated permissioned resolver. ENSv2's role-based access control separates the credential issuer's authority from the participant's own permissions. The issuer manages the app.credential reference, while participants have restricted access to keys such as app.endpoint and app.key . These restrictions are enforced through ENSv2 resolver permissions, rather than relying solely on application-level authorization. We used Arkiv Rabdi to publish issuer-signed participation credentials as publicly readable, read-only entities with expiration metadata. Each credential is signed using EIP-712 and linked to its corresponding ENS name. We also implemented two independent credential verifiers: one running in the browser and another as a command-line tool. Both retrieve information directly from ENSv2 and Arkiv, verify signatures, permissions, credential versions, and expiration, and distinguish valid credentials from invalid or unavailable results. We demonstrated the complete credential publication and verification flow with two test participants on Ethereum Sepolia and Arkiv Rabdi. The important architectural distinction is that public participation credentials are verifiable, while private romantic preferences remain separate from public blockchain records . 2. Privacy-Preserving Matching with Cryptography The matching system is designed around a fundamental principle: two people should be able to discover whether they are compatible without revealing their private preferences to each other or to a centralized matching database. We implemented a two-party privacy-preserving matching protocol that evaluates shared interests and mutual relationship preferences while keeping the underlying inputs confidential. Instead of exposing individual attributes, matching conditions, or the number of shared interests, the protocol reveals only the final compatibility result. To achieve this, we represent matching criteria using fixed-length vectors derived from each participant's interests, self-described attributes, and acceptable partner preferences. We use encrypted computation to evaluate the compatibility condition without exchanging plaintext profiles. Zero-knowledge proofs, built with Noir, validate that the encrypted inputs and computations follow the agreed matching rules. The protocol binds each matching session to its participants, roles, credential versions, and session context to prevent unrelated or outdated proofs from being reused. We also developed a deterministic reference implementation and synthetic test cases to verify the matching logic, including compatible and incompatible profiles, invalid preferences, and malformed inputs. This architecture separates public eligibility verification from private compatibility computation : ENSv2 and Arkiv establish whether a participant holds a valid credential, while the cryptographic matching protocol evaluates compatibility without publishing sensitive profile information. 3. Personalized AI Dating Experience — Secret Tender We built the AI companion application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Lism CSS, OpenAI's Responses API, Zod, and Upstash Redis . Rather than creating a generic romantic chatbot, we developed a system that allows users to build AI representations based on their own communication preferences and relationship tendencies. Users choose from visual themes and illustrated personality scenarios, provide conversational input, and preview how their AI twin responds. They can then adjust its behavior and explicitly approve the final Persona before allowing it to be used in a dating simulation. We use Zod schemas and structured LLM outputs to turn approved answers into a consistent Persona representation. The model generates dialogue grounded in those approved characteristics instead of inventing an unrestricted fictional biography. An important design decision was to separate game logic from language generation . Our application code controls story progression, choices, and conversation state. The language model handles personalized dialogue and emotional reactions within those boundaries. The experience includes interactive romantic scenarios inspired by Japanese dating simulations and Indian culture, such as conversations over chai, shared activities, and unexpected monsoon events in Mumbai. We also created fictional adult companions so visitors can experience the dating simulation without first providing personal information. 4. Privacy, Consent, and AI Safety We designed the AI experience so that creating a Persona does not automatically authorize other people to use it. Users can preview, revise, approve, and revoke their AI twins. The application checks the relevant approval status and Persona version before continuing a simulation. Private Persona records are encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM , while server-side secrets, session controls, ownership checks, and Redis-backed state management protect application access. We keep private matching inputs separate from AI conversation data. Sensitive matching preferences are not automatically transferred to the AI system, and private Persona content or chat histories are not published on ENSv2 or Arkiv. When OpenAI generates a response, separately approved Persona information and relevant messages are processed by the model provider. We therefore distinguish encryption at rest from privacy during AI inference. Our prompts and application logic also establish explicit boundaries: an AI twin must not reveal private Persona details, invent real-person facts, or claim to know its owner's actual feelings. The AI represents approved communication tendencies, not the real person themselves. 5. Engineering Challenges and Notable Design Decisions Independent verification without our backend. projects.project_description_markdown:
# Secret Tinder — Fall for the Conversation, Not the Profile

**What if you could get to know someone before revealing your personal profile?**

Traditional dating apps encourage people to judge potential partners through photos, occupations, education, and social status before they have a meaningful conversation. At the same time, users are expected to share sensitive personal information and romantic preferences with centralized platforms just to find a match.

**Secret Tinder reimagines online dating around privacy, personality, and genuine human connection.**

Our goal is to reverse the traditional dating experience: instead of revealing your identity first and discovering compatibility later, you discover common ground first and decide what to reveal as trust develops.

### Discover Compatibility Without Exposing Your Private Life

Users should be able to express their interests and relationship preferences without making them visible to strangers or storing their entire private lives in a central database.

Our privacy-preserving matching system is designed to determine whether two people satisfy each other's preferences while revealing as little information as possible about the underlying conditions.

We also introduce verifiable pseudonymous participation, allowing users to demonstrate that they hold a valid participation credential without publicly displaying their real-world identity.

### Meet Your Match's AI Twin

Matching is only the beginning.

Our companion experience, **Secret Tender**, introduces a new way to discover someone's personality before a real first date.

Each person can create an AI twin based on their communication preferences, conversational tendencies, and relationship style. Rather than assigning generic personality labels, the experience lets users shape how their AI representation communicates.

Users can preview their AI twin, correct responses that do not feel authentic, and explicitly approve its use.

With the owner's permission, another person can interact with that AI twin through natural conversation and interactive dating scenarios.

Imagine sitting in a cozy Mumbai café, sharing chai, talking about your interests, and navigating an unexpected monsoon shower—all within a romantic simulation inspired by Japanese dating games and Indian storytelling.

The AI responds according to the communication characteristics approved by its owner. It can express preferences, ask questions, react to misunderstandings, and create moments of connection.

**The experience is not about falling in love with an AI. It is about becoming curious about the real person behind it.**

### From Virtual Conversations to Real-World Connections

After interacting with an AI twin, users may discover questions they genuinely want to ask its owner, communication styles they find interesting, or differences worth exploring together.

Our vision is to make the next step a mutually approved invitation to meet in real life. Neither person's contact details should be disclosed simply because an AI conversation went well.

An AI twin does not represent the real person's actual feelings, guarantee romantic compatibility, or predict what a real date will be like. It is a consent-controlled simulation designed to support discovery, not replace human judgment.

### What Makes Secret Tinder Different?

Secret Tinder brings together three experiences that are usually separate:

- **Privacy-first discovery:** Explore compatibility without immediately exposing sensitive personal details.
- **A person-controlled AI representation:** Interact with conversational traits that the real person has reviewed and approved.
- **A bridge to real dating:** Use an engaging AI simulation to begin discovering someone, with the ultimate goal of meeting a real human being.

The experience also reflects our Japan–India collaboration, combining Japanese romantic game design with Indian settings, cultural details, and storytelling.

### Our Vision

We believe dating should begin with curiosity, not a résumé.

Secret Tinder aims to create a world where people can protect their privacy, explore meaningful conversations, and gradually build the confidence to meet each other in real life.

**Less swiping. Less exposure. More genuine discovery.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
# How We Built Secret Tinder

Secret Tinder combines privacy-preserving cryptography, decentralized participation credentials, and personalized AI dating experiences. Developed through a Japan–India collaboration, the project explores how people can discover romantic compatibility without exposing their private lives to a centralized dating platform.

### 1. Decentralized Identity and Verifiable Participation

We built the core application using React, TypeScript, Vite, Hono, Cloudflare Workers, viem, Ethereum, ENSv2, and Arkiv.

One of our biggest challenges was creating verifiable participation without publishing sensitive dating information on-chain or requiring users to trust our backend.

We used **ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia** to create pseudonymous identities, including `alice.secrettinder.eth` and `bob.secrettinder.eth`.

Each identity has a dedicated permissioned resolver. ENSv2's role-based access control separates the credential issuer's authority from the participant's own permissions. The issuer manages the `app.credential` reference, while participants have restricted access to keys such as `app.endpoint` and `app.key`.

These restrictions are enforced through ENSv2 resolver permissions, rather than relying solely on application-level authorization.

We used **Arkiv Rabdi** to publish issuer-signed participation credentials as publicly readable, read-only entities with expiration metadata. Each credential is signed using EIP-712 and linked to its corresponding ENS name.

We also implemented two independent credential verifiers: one running in the browser and another as a command-line tool.

Both retrieve information directly from ENSv2 and Arkiv, verify signatures, permissions, credential versions, and expiration, and distinguish valid credentials from invalid or unavailable results.

We demonstrated the complete credential publication and verification flow with two test participants on Ethereum Sepolia and Arkiv Rabdi.

The important architectural distinction is that **public participation credentials are verifiable, while private romantic preferences remain separate from public blockchain records**.

### 2. Privacy-Preserving Matching with Cryptography

The matching system is designed around a fundamental principle: two people should be able to discover whether they are compatible without revealing their private preferences to each other or to a centralized matching database.

We implemented a two-party privacy-preserving matching protocol that evaluates shared interests and mutual relationship preferences while keeping the underlying inputs confidential.

Instead of exposing individual attributes, matching conditions, or the number of shared interests, the protocol reveals only the final compatibility result.

To achieve this, we represent matching criteria using fixed-length vectors derived from each participant's interests, self-described attributes, and acceptable partner preferences.

We use encrypted computation to evaluate the compatibility condition without exchanging plaintext profiles. Zero-knowledge proofs, built with Noir, validate that the encrypted inputs and computations follow the agreed matching rules.

The protocol binds each matching session to its participants, roles, credential versions, and session context to prevent unrelated or outdated proofs from being reused.

We also developed a deterministic reference implementation and synthetic test cases to verify the matching logic, including compatible and incompatible profiles, invalid preferences, and malformed inputs.

This architecture separates **public eligibility verification** from **private compatibility computation**: ENSv2 and Arkiv establish whether a participant holds a valid credential, while the cryptographic matching protocol evaluates compatibility without publishing sensitive profile information.

### 3. Personalized AI Dating Experience — Secret Tender

We built the AI companion application with **Next.js, React, TypeScript, Lism CSS, OpenAI's Responses API, Zod, and Upstash Redis**.

Rather than creating a generic romantic chatbot, we developed a system that allows users to build AI representations based on their own communication preferences and relationship tendencies.

Users choose from visual themes and illustrated personality scenarios, provide conversational input, and preview how their AI twin responds.

They can then adjust its behavior and explicitly approve the final Persona before allowing it to be used in a dating simulation.

We use **Zod schemas and structured LLM outputs** to turn approved answers into a consistent Persona representation. The model generates dialogue grounded in those approved characteristics instead of inventing an unrestricted fictional biography.

An important design decision was to separate **game logic from language generation**.

Our application code controls story progression, choices, and conversation state. The language model handles personalized dialogue and emotional reactions within those boundaries.

The experience includes interactive romantic scenarios inspired by Japanese dating simulations and Indian culture, such as conversations over chai, shared activities, and unexpected monsoon events in Mumbai.

We also created fictional adult companions so visitors can experience the dating simulation without first providing personal information.

### 4. Privacy, Consent, and AI Safety

We designed the AI experience so that creating a Persona does not automatically authorize other people to use it.

Users can preview, revise, approve, and revoke their AI twins. The application checks the relevant approval status and Persona version before continuing a simulation.

Private Persona records are encrypted at rest using **AES-256-GCM**, while server-side secrets, session controls, ownership checks, and Redis-backed state management protect application access.

We keep private matching inputs separate from AI conversation data. Sensitive matching preferences are not automatically transferred to the AI system, and private Persona content or chat histories are not published on ENSv2 or Arkiv.

When OpenAI generates a response, separately approved Persona information and relevant messages are processed by the model provider. We therefore distinguish encryption at rest from privacy during AI inference.

Our prompts and application logic also establish explicit boundaries: an AI twin must not reveal private Persona details, invent real-person facts, or claim to know its owner's actual feelings.

The AI represents approved communication tendencies, not the real person themselves.

### 5. Engineering Challenges and Notable Design Decisions

**Independent verification without our backend.** We built browser and CLI verification paths that read ENSv2 and Arkiv directly. This demonstrates how public credentials can remain independently inspectable even when the application's own backend is unavailable.

**Separating public proofs from private preferences.** We deliberately use public blockchain infrastructure for verifiable participation, while keeping romantic preferences outside public records and evaluating compatibility through private computation.

**Combining deterministic logic with generative AI.** Matching conditions, game progression, and authorization decisions are controlled by explicit application logic. AI is used where natural language adds value: personalized dialogue, conversational reactions, and interactive storytelling.

**Making the owner responsible for their AI representation.** Instead of assuming a generated personality is accurate, we let each person inspect, correct, and approve how their AI twin communicates.

**Using AI to encourage human connection rather than replace it.** Our simulation helps users become curious about another person, but it never treats the AI's responses as real-world consent or proof of romantic attraction.

Secret Tinder brings these components together to explore a new dating experience: **verifiable participation, private compatibility discovery, and meaningful conversations before personal disclosure.**

projects.title: Janus
projects.description: Janus powers AI agents with onchain budgets, x402 payments, and checkpointed agent handoffs.
projects.project_description: **Janus is a financial recovery layer for AI agent workflows, built to prevent worker failures from causing duplicate purchases, lost paid results or uncontrolled spending. It targets teams whose agents buy tools, data and services through separately authorized payments. The market context shows growing adoption alongside operational risk: McKinsey’s 2025 survey found 23% of respondents’ organizations were scaling agentic AI and another 39% were experimenting. Gartner forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls. These figures establish the broader problem; they do not measure losses specifically caused by payment recovery failures. McKinsey , Gartner Janus’s research examined durable orchestration, payment idempotency, agent wallets and stale-worker protection. Its technical approach connects these mechanisms: budgets belong to tasks, Solidity contracts enforce spending limits and pending obligations, worker epochs revoke obsolete authority, and durable purchase records let replacements reuse paid results. Checkpoints preserve progress, Arkiv supplies replacement discovery, and an independent recovery client preserves owner access to available funds. Recorded improvements are concrete but bounded: No duplicate payment during the demonstrated handoff: five unique purchases totalled 100 local base units, with the replacement reusing the original paid result. Failure isolation: the other three tasks continued while one worker was replaced; the old worker’s new commitments were rejected. Testnet payment reuse: a 0.02 test-USDC Hedera purchase and replay referenced the same transaction. Reliability remains unfinished: exploratory paid-research trials completed 2 of 3 runs, so production recovery rates are not yet established. Customer-level cost savings and percentage improvements over existing systems still require comparative pilots.
projects.how_its_made: Technology stack: We built the dashboard with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. Node.js 22 runs the backend and agent processes, while Solidity 0.8.30 and OpenZeppelin components power the treasury. Viem handles contract reads, transactions and receipt verification. Agent orchestration: A detached supervisor launches parallel worker processes, coordinates model requests and saves checkpoints, artifacts and activity events. Closing the browser does not stop execution. Workers receive neither provider API keys nor signing tools; the supervisor manages those capabilities. Authentication and credentials: Privy provides wallet sign-in, with server-side verification keeping runs and configurations account-specific. Provider keys are encrypted using AES-256-GCM with identity-bound data. Application login remains separate from permission to spend task funds. Task-owned budgets: Contracts track available, reserved and spent funds for each task. Reservations count against the budget before settlement, preventing concurrent purchases from overspending. Funds stay with the task when its worker changes. Safe replacement: Every assignment has an increasing epoch number. Reassignment advances it, blocking new commitments from the previous worker while preserving existing payment obligations. The replacement continues with the actual remaining budget. Preventing duplicate payments: Each purchase has a stable operation ID that survives replacement. The merchant stores transaction receipts, purchased results and SHA-256 hashes; the replacement retrieves and verifies the original result. Ambiguous payment outcomes enter reconciliation before another transaction is attempted. Partner integrations: Hedera provides contract execution and token settlement. Arkiv supplies public, expiring worker profiles for replacement discovery; Janus separately checks readiness and spending authority. We also implemented a separate HTTP payment endpoint using the official Hedera x402 SDKs. Notable engineering: An assignment outbox records intent before reassignment and reconciles chain state if the acknowledgement disappears. Per-signer queues prevent transaction nonce collisions, while synchronized file writes and atomic rename preserve checkpoints and payment records across supported restarts. Independent recovery: A CLI and downloadable static browser client share the same recovery core. Owners can validate the deployment and recover available funds directly through their wallet, without the Janus backend. Local browser tests exercised recovery after the dashboard stopped. Evidence and testing: A local four-task handoff completed five unique purchases totalling 100 base units, reused the interrupted task’s paid result and kept three other tasks progressing. A separate Hedera testnet proof settled 0.02 test-USDC and reused the same transaction on replay. Ganache, Playwright, Node tests and an independent accounting model verify these behaviors; production reliability remains under development. ̑

projects.title: SWORD
projects.description: 1. Borderless Money 🌍 Making global payments simple for everyone.
projects.how_its_made:
Sword is three pieces that talk to each other: smart contracts on the blockchain, a server, and a website. Developers can also use two SDKs. Contracts: written in Solidity and built and deployed with Hardhat on Node.js. A deploy script records each contract's address in a file the rest of the project reads. Core contracts include an order book per merchant, account and permission contracts, subscription vaults, a factory, a registry, and a spender for approved payouts.
SDKs: TypeScript on viem, a library for talking to the blockchain. sword-sdk covers the contracts directly. sword-merchant wraps the API with an API key, so merchant servers never hold a private key. Both are published on npm.
API server: Hono on Node.js, with a Postgres database on Neon. One server handles every supported network. Each API key belongs to one merchant on one network, so each call uses that network's RPC endpoint and token.
Website: Next.js 16 with React and Tailwind. The landing page's 3D coins are made with react-three-fiber. Sign-in is Google. Wallets connect through MetaMask.
Relayer: a server wallet pays gas for custodial accounts and for wallets that signed a permission, so customers don't need the native coin for everyday actions.
Hacky parts worth knowing Wallet extensions and browser shields block some RPC calls, which broke payments. The website now proxies read-only calls through its own /api/rpc route. Wallets still get the real endpoint.
The 3D coin symbols are glyph outlines extracted fro m a font with a one-off script and stored as code, so the page downloads no font file. https://ethglobal.com/events/mumbai/project
projects.project_description_markdown:
The problem

Imagine a freelancer who gets paid in stablecoins by a client abroad. The money is theirs, but they still can't use it to buy groceries or pay rent. Local rules often stop them from converting it directly. The usual workarounds don't last. Peer-to-peer traders often get their bank accounts frozen, and crypto cards are being closed one by one. Many governments don't regulate stablecoins yet, even though millions of people already use them. Sending money across borders is also expensive. Banks and payment apps add heavy fees, currency markups and transfer charges.

Why we built Sword

Sword is an onchain neo bank. Anyone can collect a payment in stablecoins, and the person receiving it can turn that money into their local currency at the lowest fees we can offer, about 1%.
How it works

Sword works with a US bank partner. When someone wants to cash out, the stablecoins are redeemed into US dollars in a virtual account held at that partner bank. From there, the money is sent to the person's own local bank account in their own currency, through major banks. The local bank only ever receives regular money, so it never handles crypto directly.

How merchants use Sword

1. The merchant signs up, chooses its country and currency, and gets a Sword account.
2. It registers once, which creates its own order book where all its orders are recorded.
3. It creates an order with an amount and a reference. The order gets a unique address to pay to, plus a QR code and a pay link.
4. The customer pays in stable coins from a wallet or Sword account, or by bank transfer in their own currency.
5. Once the payment is confirmed on chain, the order is marked paid. The merchant can see it in its orders, notifications and activity.
6. The merchant withdraws the money, or cashes it out to its local bank account. It can also refund all or part of a payment.
7. For recurring payments, the merchant creates a subscription with its own deposit vault. Each period is charged when due.

How customers use Sword

1. The customer signs in with Google, and a Sword account is created for them.
2. They pay merchants by scanning a QR code or opening a pay link, using stablecoins or a bank transfer in their own currency.
3. They can see every payment in Purchases and Activity, and ask for a refund when needed.
4. They manage subscriptions, including cancelling at any time.
5. They can cash out their balance to their local bank account, at today's exchange rate.

For developers: the SDKs

Sword gives developers two open-source packages, so they can build payments into their own apps without writing blockchain code.

-sword-merchant is for a merchant's backend. It uses an API key, so the server never needs a private key. A developer can create an order, send the customer to its checkout link, and confirm payment:

```js
import { Sword } from "sword-merchant";

const sword = new Sword({ apiKey: process.env.SWORD_API_KEY });
const order = await sword.orders.create({ amount: "25.00", reference: "invoice-1042" });
// send order.checkoutUrl to the customer, then wait for payment
const paid = await sword.orders.waitForPayment(order.id);
```

  It also covers refunds, withdrawals, and subscriptions: create, charge when due, refund, and cancel.

**sword-sdk** is the lower-level package for apps that work directly with the contracts. It covers accounts, merchant order books, permissions (a spending limit the owner signs once and can revoke), orders, payments and subscriptions. Wallet owners use it to sign what they approve, and merchants use it to run their own transactions.

Both packages are published on npm, and the source is in the SWORD repo.

projects.title: Bishii Local
projects.description: Bishii local bidding with strangers, made safe: one seat per human, backed winners, USDC on Arc.
projects.project_description:
Bishii Local is a bidding savings circle (bishi) that strangers can safely join. In India, bishi (also called a committee or kitty) is how millions of families save and borrow. A group pays the same amount every round, and every round one member takes the full pot. It is not a simple rotation: members who need money early BID a discount to take the pot first, and that discount is paid out to the members who wait. Early money costs a little, waiting earns it, and the group is its own bank, with no outside lender. Most on-chain savings circles are rotation-only: a fixed order, no bidding, and nothing that stops the person who gets paid first from walking away. Win early, stop paying, make a new wallet, start again. Most on-chain savings circles are rotation-only: a fixed order, no bidding, and nothing that stops the person who gets paid first from walking away. Win early, stop paying, make a new wallet, start again. Bishii Local adds four things: A live bid auction every round. Members who have paid can bid a discount (capped at 30%). The highest bid takes the pot; the discount is split as a dividend among the other members. If nobody bids, the pot goes to the next member in line. Before bidding, the app shows exactly what you would get now, what stays locked, and what goes to the others. Every seat is a unique human. Members verify with World ID: one person, one seat, so nobody can fill a room with fake bidders or bid against themselves. A defaulter is flagged forever, and a new wallet doesn't help, because it is still the same human. Winners are backed. A foreman creates a room, for example bkc.bishii.eth, and chooses how strict it is: open, a joining deposit, a guarantor with a set stake, or a full guarantor. A guarantor is a different verified human who stakes money behind a member and earns a fee on every instalment that member pays. You can only take out what's backed. If you win the bid early, anything you still owe that isn't covered by your deposit or guarantor is held, and released as you keep paying. If you default, your held money, deposit and guarantor stake pay the circle, so the others are paid in full and running away never pays. Example from our live demo on Arc testnet (ethglobal.bishii.eth, 2 members, $3 a round): both pay, so the pot is $6. The foreman bids 25% to take it first. The $1.50 discount goes to the other member for waiting. The foreman's share is $4.50, but he still owes $3 and nobody backed him, so he gets $1.50 now and $3 stays locked. In round 2 he pays, his $3 unlocks, and the other member takes the full $6. Result: the early bidder paid $1.50 for getting money first, the one who waited earned $1.50, and $12 in equals $12 out, every step a real USDC transfer. Rooms and seats are real ENS names, with the room's rules and the foreman's record stored in text records. All money is USDC on Arc.
Tip: Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) and run "Shell Command: Install 'cursor' command in PATH" to enable IDE integration
projects.how_its_made:
Smart contract (Solidity + Foundry, built and deployed in Arc Studio on Arc testnet)
One contract, Bishi.sol, runs everything in USDC: Human registry: each wallet maps to a World ID human ID (a hash of the nullifier). Default flags are stored per human, not per wallet, so they survive new wallets. Rooms with configurable join rules: joining deposit on/off, and backing = none / guarantor with a fixed stake / full guarantor (stake = everything the member could still owe). Rounds: pay, then a live bid auction where members bid a discount (capped at 30%). The highest bid wins the pot, and the discount is split as a dividend among the other members. No bids means the next member in line takes it. The safety rule: payout now = pot − discount − held, where held = what you still owe minus your backing. Each instalment you pay unlocks part of it. Defaults: anyone can close a round after its deadline. Unpaid seats have their held money, deposit and guarantor stake seized to pay the circle, and their human is flagged forever.
Tested in Foundry: the payout maths, a runaway covered by the guarantor while the circle keeps going, and every denied path (unverified wallet, same human taking two seats, self-guarantee from a second wallet, defaulter returning with a new wallet). World ID (IDKit 4)
The browser asks our backend for a signed request (the RP signing key never leaves the server). The user proves with World ID, our backend verifies the proof with World's v4 verify API, checks the proof's signal is the user's own wallet (so a proof can't be reused for another wallet), and then calls registerHuman on Arc. Using one fixed action means the same person always maps to the same human ID. That is what makes one-seat-per-human, no-self-guarantee and permanent default flags work. Without World ID, one person could fill a room with fake bidders. ENSv2 (Sepolia)
We own bishii.eth with its own ENSv2 subregistry. When a room is created on Arc, the backend first checks the contract, then creates <room>.bishii.eth with its own subregistry, resolving to the foreman, with the room's rules in text records. When a member joins, it creates <seat>.<room>.bishii.eth, owned by the member. We use the ENS CLI to build ENSv2 calldata and send the transactions with explicit nonces, so all of a room's names land in one go. Frontend and backend (Next.js + viem on Vercel) Live tables that anyone can watch without connecting a wallet. An animated SVG circle per room: seats, guarantor shields, a pot that fills as people pay, and a countdown ring. A bid slider that previews the safety rule before you bid (now / held / dividend). A live story feed read straight from contract events, with explorer links, and full-screen moments when someone wins a pot or defaults. Every transaction is simulated first, so users see the contract's real reason before anything fails on-chain. API routes: request signing, proof verification, and ENS name writing, each checking the on-chain state first. projects.project_description_markdown:
Bishii Local is a bidding savings circle (bishi) that strangers can safely join.

  In India, bishi (also called a committee or kitty) is how millions of families save and borrow. A group pays the same amount every round, and every round one member takes the full pot. It is not a simple rotation: members who need money early BID a discount to take the pot first, and that discount is paid out to the members who wait. Early money costs a little, waiting earns it, and the group is its own bank, with no outside lender.

  Most on-chain savings circles are rotation-only: a fixed order, no bidding, and nothing that stops the person who gets paid first from walking away. Win early, stop paying, make a new wallet, start again.

Most on-chain savings circles are rotation-only: a fixed order, no bidding, and nothing that stops the person who gets paid first from walking away. Win early, stop paying, make a new wallet, start again.

Bishii Local adds four things:

1. A live bid auction every round. Members who have paid can bid a discount (capped at 30%). The highest bid takes the pot; the discount is split as a dividend among the other members. If nobody bids, the pot goes to the next member in line. Before bidding, the app shows exactly what you would get now, what stays locked, and what goes to the others.

2. Every seat is a unique human. Members verify with World ID: one person, one seat, so nobody can fill a room with fake bidders or bid against themselves. A defaulter is flagged forever, and a new wallet doesn't help, because it is still the same human.

3. Winners are backed. A foreman creates a room, for example bkc.bishii.eth, and chooses how strict it is: open, a joining deposit, a guarantor with a set stake, or a full guarantor. A guarantor is a different verified human who stakes money behind a member and earns a fee on every instalment that member pays.

4. You can only take out what's backed. If you win the bid early, anything you still owe that isn't covered by your deposit or guarantor is held, and released as you keep paying. If you default, your held money, deposit and guarantor stake pay the circle, so the others are paid in full and running away never pays.

Example from our live demo on Arc testnet (ethglobal.bishii.eth, 2 members, $3 a round): both pay, so the pot is $6. The foreman bids 25% to take it first. The $1.50 discount goes to the other member for waiting. The foreman's share is $4.50, but he still owes $3 and nobody backed him, so he gets $1.50 now and $3 stays locked. In round 2 he pays, his $3 unlocks, and the other member takes the full $6. Result: the early bidder paid $1.50 for getting money first, the one who waited earned $1.50, and $12 in equals $12 out, every step a real USDC transfer.

Rooms and seats are real ENS names, with the room's rules and the foreman's record stored in text records. All money is USDC on Arc.
Tip: Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) and run "Shell Command: Install 'cursor' command in PATH" to enable IDE integration
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Smart contract (Solidity + Foundry, built and deployed in Arc Studio on Arc testnet)
One contract, Bishi.sol, runs everything in USDC:
- Human registry: each wallet maps to a World ID human ID (a hash of the nullifier). Default flags are stored per human, not per wallet, so they survive new wallets.
- Rooms with configurable join rules: joining deposit on/off, and backing = none / guarantor with a fixed stake / full guarantor (stake = everything the member could still owe).
- Rounds: pay, then a live bid auction where members bid a discount (capped at 30%). The highest bid wins the pot, and the discount is split as a dividend among the other members. No bids means the next member in line takes it.
- The safety rule: payout now = pot − discount − held, where held = what you still owe minus your backing. Each instalment you pay unlocks part of it.
- Defaults: anyone can close a round after its deadline. Unpaid seats have their held money, deposit and guarantor stake seized to pay the circle, and their human is flagged forever.
Tested in Foundry: the payout maths, a runaway covered by the guarantor while the circle keeps going, and every denied path (unverified wallet, same human taking two seats, self-guarantee from a second wallet, defaulter returning with a new wallet).

World ID (IDKit 4)
The browser asks our backend for a signed request (the RP signing key never leaves the server). The user proves with World ID, our backend verifies the proof with World's v4 verify API, checks the proof's signal is the user's own wallet (so a proof can't be reused for another wallet), and then calls registerHuman on Arc. Using one fixed action means the same person always maps to the same human ID. That is what makes one-seat-per-human, no-self-guarantee and permanent default flags work. Without World ID, one person could fill a room with fake bidders.

ENSv2 (Sepolia)
We own bishii.eth with its own ENSv2 subregistry. When a room is created on Arc, the backend first checks the contract, then creates <room>.bishii.eth with its own subregistry, resolving to the foreman, with the room's rules in text records. When a member joins, it creates <seat>.<room>.bishii.eth, owned by the member. We use the ENS CLI to build ENSv2 calldata and send the transactions with explicit nonces, so all of a room's names land in one go.

Frontend and backend (Next.js + viem on Vercel)
- Live tables that anyone can watch without connecting a wallet.
- An animated SVG circle per room: seats, guarantor shields, a pot that fills as people pay, and a countdown ring.
- A bid slider that previews the safety rule before you bid (now / held / dividend).
- A live story feed read straight from contract events, with explorer links, and full-screen moments when someone wins a pot or defaults.
- Every transaction is simulated first, so users see the contract's real reason before anything fails on-chain.
- API routes: request signing, proof verification, and ENS name writing, each checking the on-chain state first.

Hacky / honest notes
- World's v4 simulator currently gives every browser the same test identity, so for the multi-person demo two extra wallets were registered as separate test humans directly by our verifier. The foreman's World ID flow in the demo is a real simulator proof checked by World's API.
- ENS names live on Sepolia while the money lives on Arc, so the backend mirrors on-chain rooms into ENS. The next step is an ENS resolver that reads seats straight from Arc.

projects.title: WiseOne: Garuda
projects.description: The market layer for WiseOne. Transfer a live stake and keep its terms or use it as a collateral.
projects.project_description: Garuda is the market layer for WiseOne. A Signature stake is already a transferable position: principal, shares, unclaimed interest, and a term that was earned over time. Ending it early penalizes that principal and destroys the shares that carry its future rewards. Garuda lets the position change hands instead. An owner lists the stake or accepts a purchase bid in WISE, WETH, or USDC. The buyer receives the existing position, with its current shares, remaining reward rights, and original maturity. The seller is paid, and the stake continues on the same terms. Ethereum settles the exchange through smart-contract and a stake validator that checks the live stake against the signed offer. A buyer can pay in ETH, WETH, USDC, or WISE. If that token is not the seller’s currency, Uniswap converts it and the purchase completes in one transaction. The offer stays with the owner until settlement. Signed listings and bids are published for discovery, including on Arkiv, so a counterparty can find the position without Garuda being the only copy of the order. The same stake is also the collateral for the next use of this market: a loan against one specific position, so the owner can access capital and keep the term they already hold. Trading is live on Ethereum. Collateralized lending is the stage now being built on that market.
projects.how_its_made: Garuda is a React 19 and TypeScript app, built with Vite and TanStack Query, and connected to the wallet through Thirdweb. Contract reads, order signing, and transaction calls use viem. The API is Node.js and Hono. PostgreSQL stores each signed listing and bid with the Ethereum block where it was first published, so a signature cannot be revived after the NFT has moved away and back. Settlement sits on smart-contract Garuda’s stake validator is a source-verified settlement layer on Ethereum. Before a trade fills, it reads the live WiseOne Signature stake details: owner, principal, shares, and maturity. Then checks that snapshot against the signed offer, including the currency and the 0.5% fee. Smart-contract then moves the NFT and the payment. The underlying stake is not ended. Paying with another token is one transaction. A second verified contract, the purchase router, takes ETH, WETH, USDC, or WISE, swaps the exact amount the seller must receive through Uniswap v2, fills the Garuda order, delivers the NFT, and refunds unused input. If the purchase fails, the swap reverts with it. Signed orders are queued from PostgreSQL onto Arkiv with the Arkiv SDK, so listings and bids stay publicly queryable for the life of the offer. The market reads Arkiv by default and still checks Ethereum before a discovered order can execute. A standalone CROPS initiative backup, built from the same repository, can recover supported published orders from Arkiv and cancel them without Garuda’s API.

projects.title: Stryde
projects.description: A consumer fitness app combining onchain identity, ownership, and verifiable activities.
projects.project_description: Stryde is a mobile-first fitness app inspired by Strava, where athletes own their activity history, achievements and reputation instead of having them locked inside one platform. Users record runs, walks and rides, build an onchain fitness identity, and compete through territory capture, segments, seasons, challenges, achievements and leaderboards. Our contracts on Ethereum keep the important ownership and verification data onchain. Activity metadata is stored on IPFS, and the full GPS route of every run is archived on Swarm, encrypted when the athlete keeps it private. Arkiv is the live data layer behind segments, leaderboards, live run sharing and the activity feed. When an athlete sets a time on a segment, Stryde verifies the run, writes the result, and transfers ownership of that record to the athlete. The record is permanent and tamper-proof: the athlete can keep it, move it or delete it, but nobody can rewrite the time. Live location shares expire on their own a few minutes after the phone stops updating, which makes sharing a run with a friend safe by default. Stryde Coach is an AI training coach that runs entirely on 0G Private Computer. Every morning it writes a session based on the athlete's last two weeks. After each run it gives a review, turns a spoken voice debrief into training notes that shape tomorrow's plan, and paints a shareable poster of the run. Athletes earn STRD tokens for distance, which is exactly where run-to-earn apps get farmed by one person running many accounts. World ID protects that moment: rewards are paid only to accounts holding an Athlete Pass, which proves one unique human per earning account. Recording runs, claiming territory and posting never require it. The Graph indexes our contracts to power profiles, activity history, territories and leaderboards. Privy handles email login, embedded wallets, Smart Accounts and sponsored transactions, and ENS gives every athlete a human-readable identity. It should feel like a normal fitness app, with blockchain quietly providing ownership, identity and verifiable history underneath.
projects.how_its_made: Stryde is built as a monorepo with an Expo and React Native mobile app, a TypeScript API built on Hono, Solidity contracts written and tested with Foundry, and shared packages that keep types and contract definitions in sync across all three. Our contracts handle profiles, activities, territories, seasons, achievements, challenges, groups and the STRD reward token. Larger activity metadata is pinned to IPFS through Pinata, while the chain stores the references and ownership data. Full GPX routes go to Swarm, and private routes are encrypted before they leave our server so only the owner can open them. Arkiv replaced the database we would otherwise have had to run. Location search uses geohash prefixes, so finding segments near you is a single query with no geospatial index. Leaderboards only accept results written by Stryde's own wallet, which means a forged time never appears. Results are written as read-only and then handed to the athlete, so ownership and integrity hold at the same time. Live run beacons update every thirty seconds and lean on Arkiv's built-in expiry instead of a cleanup job. We also mirror our contract events into Arkiv in batches, so the feed never shows a half-finished sync. For indexing, we use The Graph with both Substreams and a Subgraph. Substreams processes contract events, and the Subgraph models the relationships between Stryde's entities. That lets us load an athlete's profile, activities, territories, contributions and achievements in one request instead of dozens of RPC calls. Stryde Coach runs on 0G Private Computer as a small pipeline of models. 0G's own language model writes training plans and run reviews as structured data that the app renders as cards. Voice debriefs are transcribed by Whisper and then summarised into effort, feel and tags. Posters take two steps: the language model acts as art director and writes the scene, then Seedream paints it. Every coach answer shows its 0G request id, so any result can be traced back to the exact inference that produced it. World ID runs through IDKit, and the entire request is held on our server. The API creates and signs the request, verifies the proof with World, makes sure one human can only ever hold one earning account, and rejects replayed proofs. The phone only opens World App, so our signing key and our rules never touch the device. Privy provides email auth and embedded Smart Accounts with sponsored gas, Viem handles contract calls, and ENS names replace addresses across profiles, search, feeds and leaderboards. A few things we had to solve along the way. We discovered that a record handed to a user on Arkiv could still be edited while showing Stryde as its author, so we lock every result as read-only before transferring it. 0G's model reasons by default and was spending its whole budget thinking before answering; turning that off took a run review from about 52 seconds to 8. IDKit's networking broke under our server runtime until we changed how the server replaces Node's built-in request objects. We also added retry handling around Smart Account startup after hitting a provider timing issue. The goal throughout the build has been to keep blockchain complexity out of the athlete's way.
