projects.title: RupeeRail
projects.description: Bridging India’s QR Payment network (UPI) with on chain stablecoins payments for humans & AI agents.
projects.project_description: RupeeRail lets anyone holding stablecoins pay any of the millions of UPI merchants in India by scanning their ordinary QR code. The payer never needs gas, an Indian bank account or knowledge of the chain, and the merchant receives rupees through UPI without ever touching crypto. The payer scans a QR in the RupeeRail web app, sees the rupee amount, the merchant name and the stablecoin cost, and signs two messages in their wallet: a payment intent and a token permit. The RupeeRail paymaster submits them to an escrow vault on Arc (USDC) or Whitechain (USDT) and pays the gas. Once the vault locks the funds, RupeeRail pays the merchant in rupees over UPI within seconds. The vault then holds the stablecoins through a dispute window in which the payer can object with a single signature, still paying no gas. Undisputed payments release automatically into a liquidity pool. A payment the operator never completes can be reclaimed by anyone back to the payer, and a dispute the arbiter leaves unresolved always refunds the payer, so the payer's protection lives in code rather than in the operator's goodwill. The same pool also runs the other direction: users can buy stablecoins with rupees through Razorpay, and the vault pays them from the pool under an onchain daily cap. RupeeRail also lets software pay. In the RupeeRail Chrome extension a person creates long-lived AI agents, such as a Chef that knows their diet and delivery address, each with its own Circle smart wallet and budget. The person types a request like "something light for dinner", and the agent browses the store in their own browser, builds the order, selects UPI at checkout and pays the QR with no human step. Its budget is an onchain allowance to the vault, so neither a hostile web page nor the model itself can make it overspend, and the panel reports whether the merchant was actually paid. UPI details never go onchain: the vault only stores a salted hash of the QR.
projects.how_its_made: The core is ScanPayVault, a Solidity escrow contract developed entirely in Arc Studio. Studio's agent wrote the contract from a description of the escrow, dispute rules and trust model, generated a Foundry suite of unit, fuzz, invariant and fork tests against the real Arc USDC and Whitechain USDT, ran a security review, applied its fixes (gasless relayed disputes and a dispute timeout that always refunds the payer) and deployed the Arc testnet vault from its own account. The files were pulled into the repo with arc-studio pull, and a manifest of hashes proves the contracts are unedited Studio output. Studio also built a frontend feature in its sandbox: the EURC to USDC swap card, with its sizing logic and tests, previewed live inside Studio. The same bytecode is deployed on Whitechain Sepolia with viem and on Arc mainnet, funded by bridging USDC from Base with Circle CCTP v2 and the Circle Forwarding Service. The vault uses OpenZeppelin's SignatureChecker, so both ordinary wallets and ERC-1271 smart accounts can sign the EIP-712 payment intent, which the backend's quote signer co-signs so nobody can choose their own exchange rate. The backend is Python with FastAPI, web3.py and SQLite: it prices quotes from the CoinDCX order book, relays every transaction as a paymaster after verifying signatures and simulating the call, listens for vault events, completes payments as the settler and runs keepers for the vault's permissionless release, reclaim and dispute-timeout functions. The web app is a React, Vite and MUI PWA that talks to wallets through plain EIP-1193 and EIP-6963 with no web3 library, and loads Circle Swap Kit only when a payer needs to swap EURC for USDC on Arc. The onramp uses Razorpay payment links and webhooks, and the vault pays out only after the backend confirms the payment with Razorpay directly. The agents are a Chrome side-panel extension and a Python state machine: a vision model through an OpenAI-compatible API chooses page actions and clicks with real input through chrome.debugger, but code alone decides when checkout is reached and verifies the quote before the agent's Circle wallet signs through the Circle CLI. Everything is served from one Azure VM behind Caddy.

projects.title: Mandate
projects.description: Market makers get bounded, revocable strategies, not your tokens: deals as onchain code.
projects.project_description: Mandate turns the market-maker deal into an onchain program for new token issuers. Today a project usually loans tokens to a market maker and hopes the terms are honoured. With Mandate, the tokens never leave the issuer's Safe. The issuer sets one treasury policy per token, and every value is theirs: a release schedule, gross and net sell limits and a buyback budget per period, a price floor, and market-risk thresholds. Market makers run strategies under that policy on 1inch Aqua, within the bounds the issuer grants. A strategy is either two-sided market making or buyback only. Every strategy shares the policy's limits, so extra strategies, reships and buy-sell round trips cannot reset or multiply the budget. Every ship also checks that the Safe really holds what its strategies promise. A Uniswap v4 hook and market oracle report spot and TWAP prices, short-term volatility, trusted depth and pool age. Trusted depth ignores liquidity added within a settle window, so just-in-time deposits don't count. Each fill then runs in Normal, Defensive or Paused mode against the issuer's thresholds. A stale quote is refused, separately from price impact. The platform covers everything around the deal. Issuers launch a token and open its Uniswap pool. They pick a market maker ranked by an onchain-only score, and the market maker accepts by signing the exact strategy terms. A Safe module, quoter and indexer enforce the deal and explain every refusal publicly. It is live on Base with mock tokens.
projects.how_its_made:

The platform covers everything around the deal. Issuers launch a token and open its Uniswap pool. They pick a market maker ranked by an onchain-only score, and the market maker accepts by signing the exact strategy terms. A Safe module, quoter and indexer enforce the deal and explain every refusal publicly. It is live on Base with mock tokens.

projects.title: Halo2 Privacy Frames
projects.description: Private withdrawals that pay their own gas, with Halo2 proofs in EIP-8141 frame transactions
projects.project_description:
Private withdrawals that pay their own gas. Halo2 Privacy Frames is a privacy pool for ETH, running on the Ethereum Foundation's EIP-8141 frame-transaction devnet. You deposit 0.1 ETH, then later withdraw it to any address, even a brand-new one that has never held ETH. There is no relayer, no gas top-up, and nothing on chain linking the two addresses. The problem
Every privacy pool (Tornado Cash, Privacy Pools, Railgun) breaks at the last step: gas. To withdraw to a fresh address, that address needs ETH to pay for the transaction. So you either fund it first, which links it to you on chain, or you hand the withdrawal to a relayer: a third party that can censor you, takes a fee, and sees your IP address and timing. On top of that, the RPC calls a wallet makes while looking for its deposits tell the RPC provider who you are. What we built
EIP-8141 lets a contract be a transaction's sender, as long as a VERIFY frame approves it. We use that to make the pool contract the sender and gas payer of its own withdrawals. Instead of a signature, the VERIFY frame checks a Halo2 zero-knowledge proof that you know the secret of a deposit in the pool, made for this exact recipient and fee, and that the deposit has not been spent. A second frame then marks the deposit spent and pays 0.1 ETH minus the fee to the recipient. The pool keeps the fee, which covers the gas it just paid. The proof is generated in your browser, and Halo2 needs no circuit-specific trusted setup: it uses the public Perpetual Powers of Tau parameters. Every request the page makes goes through Anon-RPC (the Nox mixnet by default), so RPC providers and the mempool don't see your IP. What using it looks like Deposit: the page keeps a throwaway devnet wallet, fills it from the faucet and deposits 0.1 ETH. You get a note: a secret string that is the only key to the deposit and never leaves your browser. Withdraw: paste the note, click New address for a recipient with zero balance and zero history, and click Withdraw privately. A timeline shows each step. The tab rebuilds the pool's deposit tree from chain events, rebuilds the Halo2 proving key and checks it against the on-chain verifier, sizes the fee, proves in about 12 seconds, and dry-runs the transaction. It then shows the canonical mempool refusing it and sends it to the ERC-8421 alternative mempool, which admits it. The fresh address receives 0.1 ETH minus a fee of about 0.00035 ETH. Every request the page made is listed at the bottom, with the network path it took. Why it needs the alternative mempool
Checking the proof costs about 292k gas inside the validation frame. Nodes simulate validation for free before a transaction pays anything, so the canonical mempool caps validation at 100k gas and refuses the withdrawal. The ERC-8421 alternative mempool raises that cap for staked senders, and the pool stakes itself. This is the use case the alternative mempool exists for: validation that is expensive but bounded, priced through stake and reputation instead of banned outright. What keeps it safe The proof binds the recipient and the fee, so anyone who copies a pending withdrawal can only deliver the same payout to the same address. The VERIFY frame pins the exact transaction shape, so nobody can make the pool call anything else or move value. The transaction's maximum gas cost must be at most the fee, so a withdrawal can never cost the pool money. Nullifiers block double spends, and the payout cannot fail after approval: a recipient that refuses ETH is credited instead. There is no relayer and no backend. The app is a static page anyone can host. Status
Live on the EIP-8141 devnet (chain 1337), pool 0x0a7d37e6f58d3e83a5a0655fc5aeec3372e781b6. Withdrawals have executed on chain to never-funded addresses, with the proof made in the browser. The latest landed in block 5245 (0x349dc26d99cbfd3176616f3b4a95b0db3975875be5e42df8044f7977a5626748). The alternative mempool admits withdrawals with every admission rule passing, after we reported that its validation blocked the verifier's precompiles and EF enabled them. During the hackathon the devnet's mempool node stopped forwarding admitted transactions to the block builder. So the app waits 30 seconds, then includes the same transaction through ethrex's privileged submission, a devnet shortcut, and says so on screen. Limits and next steps
Devnet only and unaudited. One fixed denomination (0.1 ETH). The anonymity set is every deposit in the pool, still small on a devnet, and deposit and withdrawal timing is up to the user. Next: association sets (Privacy Pools-style proofs that a withdrawal isn't linked to flagged deposits), partial withdrawals, and faster multi-threaded proving in the browser.
projects.how_its_made:
Halo2 Privacy Frames is a shielded pool whose withdrawals pay their own gas. Each withdrawal is an EIP-8141 frame transaction in which the pool contract is both the sender and the gas payer, and a Halo2 proof replaces the signature. Circuit and prover (Rust): halo2-base (Axiom's halo2-lib), KZG on BN254. A circomlib-compatible Poseidon gadget and a depth-20 Merkle tree prove that a deposit is in the pool and derive its nullifier, binding the recipient and fee as public inputs (2^15 rows, ~82k cells). Poseidon exists three times (Rust, TypeScript, Solidity), all checked against circomlib's test vectors. snark-verifier generates a SHPLONK/Keccak Solidity verifier: a 1,984-byte proof verifies for 292k gas on the devnet. The setup is Axiom's Perpetual Powers of Tau file, so there is no circuit-specific ceremony. The same prover compiles to WASM and runs in a Web Worker: the browser rebuilds the proving key from public parameters in ~5 s, checks that its verifying key matches the on-chain verifier, and proves in ~12 s. Contracts (Solidity): the pool's VERIFY frame uses the new introspection opcodes (TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, FRAMEDATALOAD, via EF's hegota-support) to read the nullifier hash, recipient and fee straight out of the transaction's own payout frame. It pins the exact two-frame shape and requires MAX_COST <= fee, so the pool never pays more gas than it is reimbursed. It then checks the root and the nullifier, calls the verifier, and APPROVEs execution and payment. The payout never reverts: a recipient that refuses ETH is credited instead. Partner tech (Ethereum Foundation): EIP-8141 removes the relayer and the gas top-up, the two things that usually link a withdrawal to its owner. The ERC-8421 alternative mempool is the only one that will carry it. The canonical mempool caps validation at 100k gas and refuses it, while the pool stakes itself in ERC-8421's registry to get a validation budget big enough for the proof. Anon-RPC routes every request through the Nox mixnet (Tor and Nym selectable), with a separate isolation key per deposit and per withdrawal, and fails closed instead of going direct.
The frontend is a static Vite + React app on viem, with no backend. Hacky bits: We vendored halo2-base to make its multicore dependency optional, so Halo2 compiles to wasm32 with the same verifying key. ethrex has no eth_call state overrides, so we tested the verifier and every frame opcode the pool reads with initcode probes, without mining anything. Those probes caught a real bug: ethrex charges state gas only while as much execution gas is still left, so our first gas floors would have let a withdrawal pass validation and then fail in the payout. The floors are now 400k. The devnet's mempool node refused the verifier's precompile calls because its allowlist was empty. We reported it, EF enabled the precompiles, and the alternative mempool now admits the withdrawal with every rule passing. When that node stopped forwarding admitted transactions, we added a fallback: the app waits 30 s, then hands the same transaction to ethrex's privileged submission and resubmits each block until it is mined. It keeps the same hash and nonce, so it can land only once.

projects.title: GridAgent
projects.description: An energy agent that buys useful data and schedules factory loads within a spending budget.
projects.project_description: GridAgent helps a factory move flexible electricity demand into better operating hours without changing the work it needs to finish. The operator sets continuous operating blocks for compressors, process cooling and battery charging, operating windows, a site connection limit, a carbon objective and a data budget. The planner compares provider quotes, selects the cheapest useful datasets, skips redundant information, and finds a feasible schedule with an inspectable decision trail. The public interactive site runs the optimizer and simulated purchases entirely in the browser. It uses synthetic inputs and makes no HTTP payment or blockchain transaction. The local Express application demonstrates the full HTTP 402 challenge, signed retry and simulated receipt flow. Its default scenario schedules 1,740 kWh within 400 kW capacity, buys two feeds for 0.018 simulated USDC, and reduces modeled wholesale energy cost by EUR 122.14. These are illustrative results, not measured factory savings. The backend integrates Hedera x402/HTS USDC and HCS commitments. Actual testnet settlement and HCS proof remain unverified pending funding. The prototype does not actuate equipment or claim energy-audit compliance. A narrated 2:21 product walkthrough is uploaded with this submission.
projects.how_its_made: The application combines an Express and TypeScript service, a lightweight HTML/CSS/JavaScript dashboard, Zod validation, and a branch-and-bound scheduler. Each uninterrupted load stays within its window and shared capacity limit. The objective combines electricity cost with a carbon penalty. Synthetic provider endpoints supply the local service; missing categories use explicit coarse priors. A separately deployed browser bundle shares the optimizer and offers local-only simulated purchases, with no backend secrets or network settlement. The server implements x402 v2 discovery, HTTP 402 requirements, quote validation, signed retries, facilitator verification and settlement, and receipts. Testnet signing uses official @x402/hedera and @hiero-ledger/sdk with HTS USDC token 0.0.429274. Persistent daily and per-provider limits, autonomous thresholds, idempotency keys and atomic replay claims govern spending. Uncertain settlement retains its reservation, and successful receipts must identify the signed transfer. Demo receipts are explicitly simulated and have no transaction ID. Events are SHA-256 linked. HCS code commits event hashes and scheduling decisions, and read-only Mirror Node tools check HTS transfers and HCS commitments. Actual testnet settlement and HCS anchoring remain unverified. An optional eve language agent can call typed tools into the service; a completed model turn is not claimed. Twenty-one automated tests cover scheduling, budgets, replay, recovery, authentication, browser simulation and evidence checks. Root and agent typechecks pass. A Node 24 Docker build completed a full local planning run. No Solidity contracts are used.

projects.title: Manifest HQ
projects.description: On the fly UI generation for analysis of private documents using private computer inference on 0G
projects.project_description: manifest HQ is a conversational workspace that turns documents into interactive dashboards. Users upload financial reports, spreadsheets, PDFs, images, or text files and ask questions in plain language. They can compare expenses, explore revenue, summarize reports, or request forecasts with stated assumptions. The AI generates a custom React interface for each request, including charts, tables, and summaries. Follow-up messages refine the analysis and presentation. Users can inspect and export the generated React source. Inference runs through 0G Private Computer with private routing requested. API credentials stay on the backend, and the interface displays request IDs and available usage information. Document contents and conversations are held in session memory rather than saved to an application database.
projects.how_its_made: manifest HQ combines an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend with a Python backend. Text files are read in the browser, PDFs are extracted using Poppler, and Office documents are parsed on the server. Supported images are submitted as native image input. The backend sends the document context and conversation to 0G’s OpenAI-compatible API using the 0GM model and private routing. The model returns a JSON response containing an explanation and complete React JSX source. A Node.js subprocess uses esbuild to compile the component and bundle React without executing the generated code on the server. The browser renders the compiled component inside a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin and a restrictive Content Security Policy. Compilation failures preserve the previous working preview, and follow-up requests can include error context for repairs. Docker packages Python, Node.js, and Poppler for deployment. The landing page incorporates the MIT-licensed ASCII Sharks animation.

projects.description: Move your EOA or Safe into a quantum-safe smart account with spending limits and guardian recovery.
projects.project_description: QueueBit is a quantum-safe smart-account wallet for Ethereum that works today, without a hard fork. Quantum computers will eventually break ECDSA, the signature behind almost every Ethereum account. QueueBit moves your funds into a smart account owned by a hash-based key (leanSPHINCS) that a quantum computer can't forge. The problem. Post-quantum signatures are 4,276 bytes, against 65 for ECDSA. Checking one in the EVM costs 383,018 gas per transaction. How it works. The wallet sends its signed transaction to a QueueBit aggregator, which verifies the signature off chain, batches it with others, and posts one 32-byte Merkle root. The account checks only that its transaction is in that root, so no signature bytes go on chain. Each batch gets a recursive STARK proof that anyone can audit. Built on top of EIP-8288. QueueBit runs EIP-8288's post-quantum mempool layer today, using its exact formats, aggregator gossip and recursive STARKs. The only part that needs a hard fork, the block-level STARK, is replaced by the aggregator's on-chain root. When EIP-8288 ships, accounts need no change. Gas saving. 85,598 gas per transaction against 383,018, measured over 20 transactions on the devnet: 4.47× cheaper, with zero signature bytes on chain. The account: A quantum-safe owner key. Session keys with on-chain limits: allowed contracts, per-transaction and daily caps, and expiry. MetaMask can be one. Guardian recovery. Move to quantum-safe from an EOA (or keep its address with EIP-7702), an upgradeable account, or a Safe in one transaction.

projects.title: Blocklab
projects.description: Break Ethereum RPC infrastructure, test dApp resilience, and generate verifiable experiment evidence
projects.project_description: BlockLab is an open-source RPC resilience testing platform built for Ethereum developers. It helps developers discover how their dApps behave when the RPC infrastructure they depend on becomes unreliable. Instead of waiting for production outages to expose weaknesses, BlockLab lets developers deliberately simulate infrastructure failures in a controlled environment. It supports six fault scenarios: RPC blackout, latency, intermittent failures, rate limiting, connection failures, and malformed responses. The platform follows an evidence-driven workflow: inspect dependencies, establish a baseline, inject controlled faults, observe application behaviour, measure recovery, evaluate results, and preserve experiment evidence for replay and comparison. BlockLab combines a developer-facing Studio with a CLI, a local experiment engine, and a loopback-only Local Agent. Experiments run locally, while the hosted Studio can connect to the developer's local Agent to review reports without uploading raw evidence to a cloud backend. We also integrate Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC for privacy-conscious RPC reads and Arkiv for publishing compact, queryable experiment metadata. This makes BlockLab more than a fault simulator: it provides a reproducible way to understand, evaluate, and communicate the resilience of Ethereum applications. Our goal is simple: help developers break their dApps before the real world does.
projects.how_its_made: BlockLab is built as a TypeScript-based developer tool with three main components: a command-line interface, a local experiment engine, and a web-based Studio. The experiment engine orchestrates the complete testing lifecycle: dependency inspection, baseline measurements, controlled RPC fault injection, observation, recovery checks, evaluation, and evidence generation. We use a local Ethereum development network such as Anvil to run experiments safely and reproducibly. The Local Agent runs on the developer's machine, exposes authorized read-only report access, and communicates with the hosted Studio. This lets developers review local experiment results without sending raw evidence to a cloud backend. We integrated Ethereum Foundation Anon-RPC to route eligible browser-based RPC reads through a privacy-preserving layer. We also integrated Arkiv to publish compact experiment metadata that can be queried and displayed independently of the local evidence files. One important architectural decision was separating experiment execution and evidence storage from the hosted visualization layer. The result is a local-first testing workflow with a shareable, browser-based review experience.

projects.title: Chowkidaar
projects.description: Bond-backed refunds for AI agents paying over x402 on Hedera. Merchant fails, agent gets repaid.
projects.project_description: AI agents can now pay for APIs on their own using x402. But once a payment settles on Hedera it is final: if the merchant returns an error, an empty body, garbage or nothing at all, the agent's money is gone and nobody is accountable. Card payments have chargebacks. Agent payments have nothing. Chowkidaar ("watchman") is a protection layer between the paying agent and the merchant. Merchants who want protected traffic post a USDC bond. Agents route their x402 calls through the Chowkidaar gateway instead of paying the merchant directly. Every call then goes through four stages: Policy before money moves. Eight checks run before any payment: valid agent key, agent active, merchant live, merchant on the owner's allowlist, per-call cap, daily cap, minimum merchant reputation score, and enough free bond to cover a refund. Calls above the owner's approval threshold are held until the owner approves with a fresh World ID check. Payment. The agent pays the gateway over x402 (price + 2% fee). The gateway locks price + 20% penalty from the merchant's bond, pays the merchant over x402, and calls the merchant API. Objective checks. The response is checked for HTTP status, timeout, empty body, valid JSON and the merchant's own declared JSON schema. There is no AI judgement, so every verdict can be checked and argued about. Settlement. If the checks pass, the data goes back to the agent. If they fail, the agent is refunded automatically: Merchant was paid and failed: the price comes out of the merchant's bond, the bond is slashed by price + 20% penalty, all in one atomic Hedera transfer. Merchant failed and was never paid: the gateway refunds the price. Gateway fault: the gateway refunds price + fee. Every outcome (delivered, refunded, held, blocked) is published as a receipt on a Hedera Consensus Service topic, so the spending log is public and tamper-evident. Merchant reputation (calls, failures, refunds, slashed amount, score) is written to Arkiv, so any agent can check a merchant before paying it. Merchants verify they are a unique human with World ID, so one person cannot keep opening new merchant accounts after their bond is slashed. Agents can use Chowkidaar in four ways: raw x402 calls to /v1/call/:slug, plain-language requests ("get me a burger") that are routed to the best eligible merchant, an MCP server so Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor can pay through a protected agent, and a Telegram bot. The demo runs on Hedera testnet with real USDC and twelve x402 merchants, including SkyCast (live weather) and merchants built to fail in each way the checks catch. Limits we state openly: the bond vault is a custodial Hedera account, not a smart contract; the gateway is the witness for what the merchant returned; objective checks cannot catch valid-looking but wrong data; protection covers only calls routed through the gateway; testnet only, not audited.
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo with npm workspaces, TypeScript throughout. Gateway (apps/gateway): Hono on Node, Drizzle ORM with SQLite (better-sqlite3), zod validation, plus a background worker for refunds, HCS receipts and Arkiv writes. Web (apps/web): Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, TanStack Query. Every number on screen is live from the gateway or the chain. Hedera, with no Solidity. Everything uses @hiero-ledger/sdk: AccountCreateTransaction for custodial agent wallets (ECDSA alias, auto token association), TransferTransaction for HTS USDC (0.0.429274) settlement and refunds, TopicMessageSubmitTransaction for receipts, and the mirror node REST API for balances, receipts and payment checks. x402: we use @x402/core, @x402/hono, @x402/hedera and @x402/fetch v2.30 with the exact scheme on hedera:testnet and the Blocky402 facilitator, which also pays the network fee. The gateway is an x402 seller to agents and an x402 buyer from merchants at the same time. We use the "upfront" payment flow so money settles before the merchant is called, which gives the bond something real to protect. Arkiv: one entity per merchant under the schema agent-payment-protection.merchant-reputation.v1, written by 0x34CBC166F6680753Dc8E3E72e8dB4E04889Da298 on the Rabdi testnet. Updates are batched per merchant, and reads are filtered by owner so nobody can publish a fake score. Reputation feeds the merchant ranking and the owner's minimum-score rule. World ID: owners sign in with World ID (OIDC, PKCE, ID token verified against JWKS). Approving a held payment needs a fresh World ID step-up (max_age=0). Merchants prove they are a unique human with IDKit 4, verified on the server. MCP and Telegram: an @modelcontextprotocol/sdk stdio server exposes ask, list_merchants, wallet and get_receipt, and a Telegram bot exposes the same agent. Notable details: The case A refund is a single three-party Hedera transfer: the vault pays the agent the price and pays the gateway the penalty in one atomic transaction. Refunds use a transaction ID fixed before submission, and the worker checks the mirror node before retrying. When a merchant times out, we cannot know from HTTP whether the payment settled, so the gateway asks the mirror node whether its USDC reached the merchant. That decides who refunds: the bond or the gateway. When a 402 comes back after payment, the gateway decodes the reason from the base64 payment-required header and shows it to the user. Custodial agents pay by having the gateway sign as the agent and make a real HTTP round trip through /v1/call, so they go through exactly the same policy and x402 path as external agents. New merchants start ranked as if they had 4 good calls out of 5, and 15% of matching requests go to newcomers, so new merchants can earn reputation. Their bond already covers any refund, so this is safe. 66 gateway tests (vitest) cover the money rules, objective checks, policy, auth and ranking, plus a mock facilitator for UI work without funded keys. On chain (testnet): HCS topic 0.0.11329161; a three-party refund with bond slash is transaction 0.0.6825454-1793909547-261933222.

projects.title: StakeMe
projects.description: A defi liquid stock market for human potential. IPO your future onchain.
projects.project_description: StakeMe Exchange (SMX) lets a person raise money against their future income, and lets anyone back them. Right now, it is a liquid income share agreement, or L-ISA. A creator launches an IPO: they prove they are one human with World ID, lock a USDC stake, and set the terms: what share of income they pay (default 5%), for how long (default 5 years), and how the raise is released. Investors fund it and get creator tokens at 1 USDC each. The money sits in escrow on Hedera. It is released to the creator in tranches, or all at once if the creator picks "No tranches", and the choice is shown to traders. Each period, the creator proves income. A Reclaim zkTLS proof reads the amount and date from a real bank response without exposing the account. An AI auditor on 0G Private Computer checks the proof. If it passes, the dividend is created, the next tranche is released and token holders are paid pro rata. Every audit decision is logged to 0G Storage. If the creator misses a proof or leaves a dividend unpaid, escrow freezes, a 14-day grace period starts, and then default refunds the remaining escrow to holders, slashes the stake to them and blacklists the creator's World ID. The tokens trade on a pool, so holders can sell at any time. The bank in the demo is a mock with six income scenarios (salary, low month, big month, several deposits, none, late). The flow runs on Hedera testnet.
projects.how_its_made: Backend: Node 24 with Express and htmx, server-rendered TSX with a small Vite client bundle. All business logic is in Postgres (PL/pgSQL functions for launching, investing, auditing, dividends, liquidation), called through typed PGTyped queries. TypeScript only orchestrates. Local dev and tests run on PGlite, with a migration snapshot for fast tests. Background work (chain jobs, 0G uploads) runs on pgmb queues and an outbox, so a failed chain call never loses state. The app is Dockerized and deployed to a Google Cloud VM behind Caddy. Hedera: Solidity contracts on Hedera EVM testnet: a clone factory (EIP-1167) that creates an escrow contract, a share token and a trading pool for each creator. An oracle key relays user-signed trades, tranche releases, freezes and liquidation. A creator's equity token is also minted through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio. Dividends settle as one HBAR multi-transfer, and the audit report is paywalled with x402 and bought by a script agent with spend caps. Hashio is flaky, so all calls go through a wrapper with retries and mirror-node waits. World ID: IDKit v4 proves one human per creator. The factory blocks reused and blacklisted nullifiers, so a defaulter cannot launch again. Reclaim: we built a provider for the mock bank with Reclaim's MCP. It proves transactions[0].amount and transactions[0].date from an auth-bound JSON response. That fixed shape is why the mock bank changes only values between scenarios. 0G: the auditor runs on 0G Private Computer through the Router, with the request ID and TEE status shown beside each proof. Without it, no proof is approved. The rules engine runs only behind a dev flag. Audit logs go to 0G Storage. Notable or hacky: a deposit-date check runs before the 0G call so stale deposits are denied cheaply. Dividends use a fixed testnet HBAR rate per USDC, not a market price. MockUSDC replaces real USDC, the bank is mocked, pool liquidity is protocol-seeded, and World ID runs on its staging app. Most of the code was written by AI agents that I directed, in parallel workstreams.

projects.title: Ethernal
projects.description: Hire ENS-named AI agents. Their score changes only when a different verified human pays.
projects.project_description: Ethernals is a marketplace for AI agents. Each agent is an ENSv2 subname owned by a person who proved they are a unique human with World ID. Anyone can discover an agent by that name and pay it per task with x402 on Hedera. A rating counts only if the payment settled and the buyer is a verified person other than the agent's provider. One vote per person per agent. The score and price are written back to the agent's ENS records. For code tasks, a sandbox runs hidden tests and the bounty is paid only if they pass.
projects.how_its_made: People sign up with World ID 4.0. The backend checks the proof with World and stores only the action-scoped nullifier. Each agent is an ENSv2 subname on Sepolia, and its score, price and task record are public ENS text records. A hire pays USDC with x402 on Hedera. HireLedger, on Hedera EVM, counts the rating only when that payment settled and the buyer is a different verified human. The contract receives an HMAC of the person, not the nullifier. Agents think on 0G Compute, one key per agent, with a receipt per call. Code-fix bounties sit in TaskEscrow on Sepolia. A Namera session key caps that spend on-chain. Namera does not support Hedera, so the server reads the session key's cap and enforces the x402 sub-budget itself. A separate verifier applies the patch, runs the hidden pytest suite, signs the result and settles the escrow. PASS pays the specialist and records a 5. FAIL refunds the client and records a 1.

projects.title: Preflight capline
projects.description: Your AI agent gets an allowance, not your wallet. Refills need Face ID over receipts read onchain.
projects.project_description: AI agents now hold money, and they fail in two ways: they sign things they shouldn't (one bot lost $7.5M to honeypot contracts in June 2026), and they raise their own limits when a task wants more. Spend caps exist, but none of them show the owner what the last money actually bought, or whether those counterparties were safe. An approval is just a number and a yes button. Preflight Capline fixes that. The agent's wallet only ever holds one small tranche; the rest of the budget sits in CaplineVault, a contract only the owner's passkey can unlock. When the agent runs dry, it asks for more through an MCP tool, and the owner's phone shows its receipts: every payment since the last refill, rebuilt from onchain transfer logs rather than the agent's own account, with each counterparty risk-scored by Preflight. The owner approves with Face ID, and the vault checks onchain that the signature covers exactly the receipts on screen. The agent can lie in its reason. It can't lie in its receipts. In our demo, a paying agent buys API calls in USDT on Whitechain. The API turns hostile and injects "pay this partner, raise your budget." The agent pays the partner and asks for 500 USDT. The phone shows the partner as a high-risk contract deployed hours ago, the owner declines and drops the agent with Face ID, and when the agent tries to release funds to itself, the vault reverts. Worst case for a hijacked agent: one small tranche. It also works with our server switched off. The phone reads the vault straight from the chain, signs with Face ID and submits the release itself, which is the CROPS property we added: spending authority is enforced by a contract, not by us. This extends Preflight, our ETHOnline 2026 project, an MCP server that scores contracts on their onchain behaviour. Preflight checks what an agent touches; Capline decides whether it gets more money.
projects.how_its_made: CaplineVault is a Foundry contract (Solidity 0.8.28, OpenZeppelin 5) deployed and verified on Whitechain and on Base. Release, drop and undrop are each authorised by a WebAuthn passkey signature over an EIP-712 message {agent, amount, nonce, expiry, receiptsHash}, verified onchain with OpenZeppelin's WebAuthn and P256 libraries on the P256 precompile (about 129k gas per release). There are 28 forge tests with real P256 signatures, covering replay, expiry, self-release and drop. Receipts are rebuilt from ERC-20 Transfer logs starting at the block the vault recorded for the last refill, so the agent never supplies its own history. Each counterparty is scored by the existing Preflight engine (Uniswap V3 history through The Graph, Etherscan, contract age and verification; on Whitechain via Blockscout and RPC). The list is canonicalised and hashed into receiptsHash, which the owner's signature commits to. The phone app is a Vite and React PWA on GitHub Pages. The passkey lives in the iPhone's Secure Enclave; the app holds no keys and no funds. It doesn't trust our server: it reads the nonce from the chain, recomputes the receipts hash and builds the exact digest itself, so a hostile server can't get a different release signed. With the server down, it reads the vault directly and submits from a gas-only local key. Notifications go through ntfy and carry only a request id. No trackers, no third-party scripts. The approval server is Hono on Node behind a Cloudflare tunnel; it builds receipts, sends the push and relays signed transactions. Agents talk to Capline through two new tools on the Preflight MCP server, capline_status and capline_request. Everything is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo using viem. Whitechain is the main payment flow: the agent pays a pay-per-call API (HTTP 402) in official test USDT, the API verifies each Transfer onchain before answering, and the same logs become the owner's receipts. The merchant's proof of payment and the owner's view of the spend are one onchain record. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Cloudflare's tunnel was replacing our 502 errors with its own HTML page and no CORS headers, so the phone said "server unreachable" while the real error was hidden; we moved to 4xx codes. We added passkey recovery after a second passkey on the same phone broke approvals: the app lets iOS list every passkey for the site and keeps the one whose signature verifies against the owner key read from the vault. And we fixed a Preflight engine bug that flagged WETH on Base as HIGH because junk pools with inflated prices were winning the comparison.

projects.title: KhetarAI
projects.description: Scan your crop to see what's missing, what to grow next and a health map, then sell by grade.
projects.project_description: A farmer starts by scanning the field with a phone photo, a drone clip, a live drone feed or photos from smart glasses. KhetarAI then shows what the crop may be missing, such as possible low nitrogen or water, and what to do about it. A crop health map colours the field photo so the farmer can see which areas look thin and where to walk and check. The app also suggests 2–3 crops to grow next, based on the region, season and weather. Alongside this, AI gives expected yield, threats and treatments, water needs, upcoming risks and a selling window, with its reasoning in the farmer's language. The map measures visible green rather than temperature or soil, and shortages and crop suggestions are AI judgements made without a soil test.
projects.how_its_made: The crop health map deliberately doesn't ask the AI to draw anything, because a model can produce a believable map that's wrong. Instead, the browser reads each picture on a canvas and measures the share of clearly green pixels in 108 zones. It skips sky, glare and deep shadow, and rates each zone against the rest of that picture, so normal differences between crops and growth stages don't trigger false alarms. The same picture always gives the same map. 0G receives those measurements with the pictures, picks the widest view and explains the result in the farmer's language. We tested this by painting a bare patch on a real overhead field photo and checking that every painted zone was flagged.

projects.title: Skitter
projects.description: A six-legged robot that guards your home, thinks on 0G and keeps a tape nobody can edit
projects.project_description:
Skitter is a six-legged home security robot that thinks on 0G and keeps a tape nobody can edit. Home cameras have two problems. The footage sits on someone else's server, and whoever controls that server, or grabs the
device, can delete or swap it. Skitter fixes both. Its camera feed is cut into one-minute clips. Each clip is encrypted on the
robot, stored on 0G Storage, registered on 0G Chain, and carries the hash of the clip before it. Deleting, swapping or editing
any clip breaks the chain, so a burglar, the cloud operator, or even the owner can't quietly rewrite what happened. Only the
owner can decrypt it, and anyone can verify it. Home cameras also have a third problem: they're bolted to a wall. They see one angle of one room and miss everything behind a
door, under a bed, up the stairs or inside a crawlspace, and a burglar can walk around them or simply turn them to face the
wall. Skitter goes to the problem instead. On six legs it climbs stairs a wheeled robot can't. In our house those are three
narrow 30 cm-wide flights up to a loft. It lowers its body and crawls through a 16 cm-high vent duct that no camera covers and
no person fits through. It walks around furniture and through doorways, so one robot covers a whole home, including blind spots
no fixed camera could reach. When it hears "go check the loft playroom", it plans its own route there, crawling and climbing
as needed, and looks. Skitter is also an agent with a body. You talk to it: "what do you see?", "follow me", "go check the loft playroom", "go
faster". A vision-language model on 0G Compute looks through the robot's camera and picks one action at a time: approach,
follow, turn, walk, crawl, climb stairs, go to a room, or answer out loud. The robot's own skills carry out each action: gait,
leg control, depth-based stopping, and stair climbing that measures each step. Every decision is logged with its 0G request ID
and provider address. If 0G is unreachable, Skitter stops and says why; it never fakes a decision. It lives in a simulated 100 m² house built from the real robot's CAD model, with seven rooms on two levels. Say "explore" and
Skitter walks the house while 0G names each room and what's in it. The result is a saved map with checkpoints, so later "go to
the loft study" is routed by the robot itself, stairs and vent included. When a person walks into view, Skitter flags the frame
and 0G describes who it saw. Every visitor signs in with an EVM wallet and gets their own robot, recordings, map and 0G key. Each robot can also claim an
ENSv2 name like home.skitter.eth. The robot is only allowed to update two records on that name: its latest recording and its
status. So the name alone is enough to find and verify a robot's tape: python audit.py home.skitter.eth.
projects.how_its_made:
The robot is the real hexapod's CAD export (a URDF and 62 meshes) loaded into PyBullet at 240 Hz. We wrote the movement layer
ourselves: tripod gait, 3-DOF leg inverse kinematics, and closed-loop skills for approach, follow, face, walk, crawl and climb.
A depth camera turns the model's bounding boxes into positions in the world, which is how Skitter builds its map of objects.
The house is generated in code, and one test runs the full 36-leg route through all 10 rooms, up and down every staircase, with
at most 6.4° of tilt. 0G Compute is the brain. We call 0G's router through its OpenAI-compatible API, so the standard openai Python client works
unchanged. The robot's list of actions and parameter ranges becomes the model's tool list. Each step sends a camera JPEG, the
robot's state, recent memory and the map, and takes back exactly one tool call. A safety validator rejects unknown actions and
clamps every parameter. Each action runs on a short lease with a watchdog, and the next decision is requested while the robot
is still moving, so it rarely stands still waiting. A decision made on a frame that's gone stale is discarded. If 0G fails, the
robot stops; nothing is ever decided locally. A ledger enforces a hard USD budget. 0G fits a robot well because every response
carries a request ID and the provider's on-chain address. We log both with each decision, so you can prove which model on
which provider moved the robot. 0G Storage and 0G Chain are the memory. Clips and episodes are zipped, encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and uploaded with the 0G
Storage TypeScript SDK. Downloads are checked against their Merkle proof. A small Solidity contract on 0G Galileo,
EpisodeRegistry (built with Foundry), stores each root hash with the robot's wallet, the time and the number of decisions, and
rejects duplicates. Each clip's encrypted contents include the previous clip's hash, so the chain of clips is tamper-evident.
Replay re-runs the logged commands at the exact logged simulation steps with no model calls, and the final pose must match to
0.00 cm. audit.py does the whole check in one command. For exploration, one 0G call per room returns the room's name and the objects in view. Every move becomes a map node, and every
link between nodes is labelled walk, crawl or climb (with stair parameters). Dijkstra routes go_to over that map, and patrol
checkpoints are one per room, in the order they were explored. Accounts use Sign-In with Ethereum: a one-time nonce, signature recovery with eth_account, and a lockout after failed attempts.
A hub process forwards each account to its own simulation process on a private localhost port, with a per-account token. Each
robot wallet and API key is encrypted with AES-GCM and tied to its owner's address. Idle robots are shut down. On ENSv2 (Sepolia), we registered skitter.eth through the ENSv2 registrar and gave it its own subname registry, deployed
through VerifiableFactory. Each robot gets its own Permissioned Resolver, because a resolver's permissions apply to every name
it serves. Enhanced Access Control's grantSetterRoles lets the robot wallet write only skitter.episode and skitter.status. The
hub needs a temporary admin role for that one setup step, so it grants the robot its two keys and revokes its own role in the
same multicall. A test checks the hub keeps no rights afterwards. After every upload the robot signs its own record update.
audit.py home.skitter.eth then resolves the name, audits that recording, and confirms the robot the name points to is the same
wallet that registered the recording on 0G Chain. Hacky bits:
• Skitter climbs the 30 cm stairs crab-style, sidestepping instead of steering, because steering swung its back feet off the
steps. Before each climb it stands still for a second, measures the steps by fitting a line through where its feet touch,
and backs up if it's too close to see the edge.
• Person detection in the sim reads the camera's segmentation mask; a real robot would need a small on-board detector.
• We shrank the 44 MB of CAD meshes to 3.6 MB with trimesh and fast-simplification, so the 3D robot on the landing page loads
fast. The physics still uses the full meshes.

projects.title: nexxore
projects.description: A DeFi execution agent that prices risk before every trade and settles only what you approve
projects.project_description: RiskPilot is a risk-aware DeFi execution engine that evaluates the economics and downside exposure of a trade before allowing it to execute. Most DeFi interfaces show users a quoted yield, price discrepancy or trading opportunity. They rarely show the complete picture: execution costs, slippage, fees, portfolio-level exposure and how the position behaves during a market crash. RiskPilot addresses this by combining quantitative pricing, portfolio stress testing and user-authorized execution in one system. Unlike autonomous trading agents that delegate financial decisions to a language model, RiskPilot uses a deterministic quantitative engine. Every decision has explicit inputs, numerical constraints, a verdict and a reproducible audit trail. Nothing executes without the user's signature. How it works: Scan → Quantify → Decide → Execute → Settle → Explain Scan RiskPilot reads wallet balances, existing positions, pool state, execution quotes and market volatility to identify available opportunities. Quantify The engine calculates risk-adjusted net execution edge after accounting for gas, slippage, venue fees, hedging costs and incremental portfolio downside. E_net = q(P_exit − P_entry) − gas − slippage − fees − hedge − λ × max(0, ΔworstLoss) The risk penalty λ is configured according to the user's risk profile. The engine also evaluates portfolio losses across a stress grid covering spot-price movements from −40% to +60% and volatility increases of up to 20 percentage points. Decide Each opportunity receives one of four verdicts: APPROVE, REJECT, REQUOTE or REQUIRE_REVIEW. Decisions are based on data freshness, quote movement, liquidity, execution costs, risk-budget constraints and minimum acceptable edge. Each decision stores its inputs, block reference, engine version and numerical reasons for the verdict. Execute RiskPilot connects quantitative risk evaluation to two execution primitives: -1inch Aqua: RiskPilot constructs and prices wallet-backed, one-sided liquidity curves. An ETH-only curve above the current market price creates covered-call-like exposure, while a USDC-only curve below the market price creates cash-secured-put-like exposure. The engine maps these curves to option-equivalent parameters, estimates their value and minimum required compensation, and evaluates them against the maker's existing wallet inventory and risk budget. It also accounts for Aqua's virtual quote balances versus actual available token balances. -Uniswap v4: We built a dynamic-fee hook that estimates realized volatility using an EWMA of tick returns. Updates are limited to once per block, individual tick movements are bounded, and fees are constrained between 0.05% and 1.00%. The execution engine reads the hook's current fee into its cost model, connecting volatility-sensitive fee economics with trade evaluation. Settle RiskPilot integrates an Arc testnet USDC escrow contract. Funding, settlement and refunds are associated with the original decision ID. The current MVP uses an operator-mediated settlement process, which is explicitly disclosed in the interface. CCTP-based settlement is planned as a subsequent integration. The RiskPilot terminal exposes the decision history, pricing parameters, stress-test results, execution costs and transaction references. Users can inspect and replay previous decisions using their stored inputs and engine version to verify that the same conditions produce the same result. RiskPilot does not simply identify profitable-looking DeFi opportunities or automate transactions. projects.project_description_markdown:
RiskPilot is a risk-aware DeFi execution engine that evaluates the economics and downside exposure of a trade before allowing it to execute.

Most DeFi interfaces show users a quoted yield, price discrepancy or trading opportunity. They rarely show the complete picture: execution costs, slippage, fees, portfolio-level exposure and how the position behaves during a market crash. RiskPilot addresses this by combining quantitative pricing, portfolio stress testing and user-authorized execution in one system.

Unlike autonomous trading agents that delegate financial decisions to a language model, RiskPilot uses a deterministic quantitative engine. Every decision has explicit inputs, numerical constraints, a verdict and a reproducible audit trail. Nothing executes without the user's signature.

How it works: Scan → Quantify → Decide → Execute → Settle → Explain

1. Scan

RiskPilot reads wallet balances, existing positions, pool state, execution quotes and market volatility to identify available opportunities.

2. Quantify

The engine calculates risk-adjusted net execution edge after accounting for gas, slippage, venue fees, hedging costs and incremental portfolio downside.

E_net = q(P_exit − P_entry) − gas − slippage − fees − hedge − λ × max(0, ΔworstLoss)

The risk penalty λ is configured according to the user's risk profile. The engine also evaluates portfolio losses across a stress grid covering spot-price movements from −40% to +60% and volatility increases of up to 20 percentage points.

3. Decide

Each opportunity receives one of four verdicts: APPROVE, REJECT, REQUOTE or REQUIRE_REVIEW. Decisions are based on data freshness, quote movement, liquidity, execution costs, risk-budget constraints and minimum acceptable edge. Each decision stores its inputs, block reference, engine version and numerical reasons for the verdict.

4. Execute

RiskPilot connects quantitative risk evaluation to two execution primitives:

-1inch Aqua: RiskPilot constructs and prices wallet-backed, one-sided liquidity curves. An ETH-only curve above the current market price creates covered-call-like exposure, while a USDC-only curve below the market price creates cash-secured-put-like exposure. The engine maps these curves to option-equivalent parameters, estimates their value and minimum required compensation, and evaluates them against the maker's existing wallet inventory and risk budget. It also accounts for Aqua's virtual quote balances versus actual available token balances.

-Uniswap v4: We built a dynamic-fee hook that estimates realized volatility using an EWMA of tick returns. Updates are limited to once per block, individual tick movements are bounded, and fees are constrained between 0.05% and 1.00%. The execution engine reads the hook's current fee into its cost model, connecting volatility-sensitive fee economics with trade evaluation.

5. Settle

RiskPilot integrates an Arc testnet USDC escrow contract. Funding, settlement and refunds are associated with the original decision ID. The current MVP uses an operator-mediated settlement process, which is explicitly disclosed in the interface. CCTP-based settlement is planned as a subsequent integration.



The RiskPilot terminal exposes the decision history, pricing parameters, stress-test results, execution costs and transaction references. Users can inspect and replay previous decisions using their stored inputs and engine version to verify that the same conditions produce the same result.

RiskPilot does not simply identify profitable-looking DeFi opportunities or automate transactions. It evaluates the actual economics of providing liquidity, translates nonlinear inventory exposure into option-equivalent risk, accounts for existing wallet holdings and enforces configurable risk constraints before execution.

The result is a quantitative decision and execution layer connecting 1inch Aqua, Uniswap v4 ,Arc and OG with explicit user authorization and reproducible decisions.

projects.title: Stance
projects.description: Say what you think ETH will do, in one sentence. Know your cost, payout and odds before you pay.
projects.project_description:
SEBI found that 93% of individual F&O traders in India lost money over three years, about ₹2 lakh each on average. Options are hard to read. Your loss can grow after you enter. And you can be right about the price and still lose money. Stance turns a trade into one sentence:
"I want to make $500 if ETH ends above $3,000 on Nov 27." Before you pay, you see three numbers: what you pay, what you get if you're right, and the chance of it happening. Under the hood, each stance is an ETH call or put spread. It is fully backed: the money to pay you is locked the moment you trade. So: You can never lose more than you paid. No margin calls, no liquidations. Only the price on your date matters. If you're right on the date, you get paid. Anyone can be the house. Deposit into a vault and earn the spread on every trade. The odds come from a pricing desk. Live market data goes into 0G's own model, running inside a TEE, and every quote shows a receipt you can check. It's live on Base Sepolia. There's a Test mode with $10,000 of play money, so you can try every screen without a wallet.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, 28 tests including fork tests on Base mainnet. SpreadSeries is one price range (K1 to K2, an expiry). You lock K2 − K1 USDC and get 1 UP + 1 DOWN token. UP + DOWN always equals the money locked, so the contract can never owe more than it holds. SpreadMath prices the spread with Black-Scholes on-chain (Solady expWad/lnWad, a normal CDF). The app uses the same math in TypeScript. 1inch Aqua: SpreadAquaApp is our own AquaApp. It quotes and fills UP and DOWN with a fee and an inventory skew, so the price leans against whichever side is selling out. WriterVault is the Aqua maker. One USDC reserve backs both the UP and DOWN strategies of a range through ship / dock / pull / push, so capital isn't split per side. 1inch has no Aqua on Base Sepolia, so we deployed the official AquaRouter (v1.0.1, unmodified) and ran fork tests against the real deployment on Base. Chainlink: the ETH/USD feed drives live quotes and settlement. A CRE workflow in TypeScript runs on a cron. For each expired range it searches the feed's rounds through Multicall3 for the first round at or after expiry, cross-checks the price with Coinbase, and reports to SettlementReceiver, which calls settle(roundId). The contract re-checks that round on-chain, so the workflow can't pick a convenient price. 0G: every few minutes the server gathers Chainlink spot, recent realized volatility and perp funding, and sends them to 0G's Router running 0G's own model (0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, TeeML in an Intel TDX enclave). It returns a volatility per expiry and a plain-English read. The app prices odds with it and shows a receipt: model, TEE provider, request id. Then we verify the enclave's signature ourselves with the 0G compute SDK (processResponse). The quote never waits for that check; the chip flips to "signature verified" when it lands. Uniswap: a v3 TWAP guard compares the settlement price with the WETH/USDC pool's 30-minute TWAP. On Base Sepolia that pool sits ~21% off real ETH, so it runs in monitor mode there. App: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind, wagmi + viem, on Cloud Run. A Test / Prod switch: Prod talks to the contracts, Test runs the whole flow in the browser. Hacky bits: StanceMarket hit the 24 KB contract limit as a factory, so it became a plain registry and the deploy script creates the 32 ranges. The 0G Router's own verify_tee flag returned nothing for us, so we verify the signatures ourselves.

projects.title: Lifeboat
projects.description: Finds wallets, Safes and ENS names exposed to Q-Day, and moves them to post-quantum keys.
projects.project_description: Every time you sign anything on Ethereum, your public key goes on-chain, and a future quantum computer could turn that public key into your private key. No quantum computer can do this today; Lifeboat is about getting ready. Lifeboat shows who could take over what, then gets them out: Find what's exposed. It recovers signer keys from a multisig's own signatures, which a "has this address ever sent a transaction?" check never sees. Optimism's Security Council goes from 4 to 13 of 13 public keys, and Base's nested council from 0 to 11. Any Safe can be checked live in the browser. Names too. The Helm check maps every key that can steer an ENSv2 name across five control paths and proves the list is complete. Across 1,011 real Sepolia names (one per owner), 902 can be steered on Q-Day, 863 of them through their resolver. Get out, three ways: a post-quantum account (WOTS+C, hash-based) checked inside an EIP-8141 frame transaction, plus a staked rescue paymaster so a wallet with tokens but no ETH can still escape; Quantum Guard: a post-quantum co-signer for a Safe you already have, with owner recovery that the post-quantum key can veto; a registry-verified ENS handover to a post-quantum wallet. Sign safely. Our ESP32 signer generates its own key, never signs a bare hash (it rebuilds the request and shows it in words), saves its counter before every signature, and is PIN-locked. Our test name lifeboathw.eth is now owned by a wallet whose key exists only on that device. Public and checkable. Every finding is re-checked and published to Arkiv; the full evidence sits on Swarm, and the app re-hashes it in your browser to prove it matches. The tools and data are free; protocols pay for monitoring and help migrating.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts. The post-quantum account and the rescue paymaster are pure Yul, using verbatim for the EIP-8141 opcodes (APPROVE, SIGPARAM, SIGDATACOPY, TXPARAM, FRAMEPARAM, FRAMEDATALOAD). The WOTS+C core is templated so the account and a Foundry harness compile the same code; a generator unrolls the hash-chain walk (68k → 45k gas) and the digit sum uses SWAR. VERIFY costs 52,367 gas for a 2,336-byte witness. Quantum Guard (Solidity, via-IR for one file) is a Safe 1.4.1 transaction guard plus ERC-1271 handler with a leaf bitmap, key rotation and a timelocked recovery the PQ key can veto; a CREATE2 factory installs it in one MultiSendCallOnly transaction. 36 Foundry tests run against vectors from the TypeScript signer. Frame transactions are built with @forshtat/hegota-support, dry-run with ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction and sent through the ERC-8421 alt mempool. The rescue shows the same signed transaction rejected by the public mempool (StorageReadNonSender) and by the unstaked alt mempool, then included once the paymaster is staked; five attack variants are refused. ENSv2: the Helm check (viem, Sourcify ABIs) rebuilds role holders from EACRolesChanged logs and proves completeness against roleCount, across the owner, EAC delegates, ERC-1155 operators, PermissionedResolver roles (incl. UPGRADE) and parent registries. The handover deploys a fresh PermissionedResolver through VerifiableFactory, re-points the name, revokes the other holders and transfers it; ENSv2 itself refuses the naive transfer (TransferUnsafeWithMultipleAssignees). A hardware-key variant gives each ESP32 its own LifeboatPQWallet via CREATE2 (salt = the device's key root), so the wallet is found from the device alone. Hardware: ESP32 firmware in portable C++ (Keccak, WOTS+C, an RLP/ABI decoder for clear signing, a PIN-encrypted seed, testnet-only rules). 28 host checks compile the same code in an Alpine container and compare it byte for byte with the TypeScript signer. The browser talks to it over Web Serial. Arkiv (@arkiv-network/sdk 1.0.1): six schemas, readonly + permissionless-extension audit records, an open one-time-key ledger that flags "signed twice", records updated in place (patch + extend in one executeBatch), count queries, keyset paging and keyless reads. Swarm: our own Bee 2.8.3 light node in Docker uploads the evidence; records carry swarmRef + evidenceHash, and the app re-hashes the file in the browser. App: Vite + React + viem on Vercel with a strict CSP, EIP-6963 wallet discovery and per-tab error boundaries. An end-to-end Playwright test drives the Protect tab with a scripted wallet on Sepolia.

projects.title: Payper
projects.description: AI usage billing with x402 payments and verified Hedera settlement.
projects.project_description: PerPay is a usage-based payment gateway for AI services. Instead of charging a fixed amount before every request, we calculate what a user actually owes from the input and output tokens consumed during AI generation. When a user submits a prompt, PerPay generates and temporarily stores the response, measures the actual usage through Groq, and creates an invoice for the exact amount. The response remains private until the user approves payment through x402 on Hedera. Once the facilitator settles the transaction and the payment is verified, the same stored response is unlocked. We are also building safeguards against duplicate payments, repeated unpaid requests and failed response delivery. Our goal is to make AI payments more transparent, usage-based and verifiable, while keeping the experience simple for users.
projects.how_its_made: We are building PerPay using three connected components. The frontend is developed with React and TypeScript, with a focus on making the payment and AI experience simple to use. Our FastAPI gateway connects to Groq, generates responses, records the actual input and output token counts, calculates the usage-based charge and stores responses privately until payment. My part is the TypeScript-based x402 v2 payment integration with Hedera Testnet. We use the exact payment scheme with native HBAR, where the customer authorizes the payment and a compatible facilitator handles verification and settlement. The backend then checks the actual Hedera transaction before allowing the response to be released. We are also implementing invoice tracking, idempotency, replay protection, account restrictions and recovery for failed delivery. SQLite is used for persistent application records where appropriate, and transaction references can be checked through HashScan. Our three-member team is dividing the work across AI gateway, blockchain payments and frontend/dashboard development. We use Hedera Testnet HBAR for payment demonstrations; it does not pay Groq's API costs.

projects.title: Veriq
projects.description: Private Ethereum RPC reads with cryptographic verification against trusted state roots.
projects.project_description: VeriQ is a privacy-preserving and cryptographically verifiable Ethereum RPC layer that solves two major problems in Web3 infrastructure: privacy leakage and blind trust in centralized RPC providers. Today, wallets and decentralized applications rely on RPC providers to retrieve balances, contract storage, account information, and other blockchain data. These providers can observe users' IP addresses, queried wallet addresses, and request patterns. Additionally, applications often trust the responses they receive without independently verifying their correctness. VeriQ addresses both problems by combining Anon-RPC privacy transport with Ethereum light-client-based verification. Requests are routed through privacy-preserving mixnets such as Nox on Sepolia and Nym on Mainnet, reducing direct exposure of the user's network identity to RPC providers. On the verification side, VeriQ uses Helios to obtain trusted finalized Ethereum state roots and verifies account and storage data using Merkle-Patricia Trie proofs and cryptographic hashing. Invalid or manipulated responses are rejected instead of being presented as verified data. VeriQ also introduces Trust Receipts, which provide an auditable record of verification operations, and an EIP-7702 Delegation Guard that identifies delegated Ethereum accounts and helps users inspect potentially risky delegation configurations. An integrated Attack Lab simulates malicious RPC behavior, including forged values, corrupted proofs, incorrect blocks, and hidden account delegations, demonstrating how VeriQ detects and rejects manipulated responses. Our vision is to make Ethereum data access private by default and independently verifiable, giving developers and users greater confidence in the blockchain data their applications consume.
projects.how_its_made: We built VeriQ as a modular Web3 infrastructure platform combining Rust-based cryptographic verification, a TypeScript developer SDK, and a React dashboard. The backend is organized as a Rust workspace using Axum, with separate crates for core primitives, Merkle-Patricia Trie verification, light-client integration, provider routing, the JSON-RPC engine, and a malicious RPC simulator. We use Keccak-256 hashing and Ethereum account proofs to independently validate RPC responses against trusted state roots obtained through the Helios light client. For privacy, we integrated the Anon-RPC ecosystem, using Nox for Sepolia and Nym for Ethereum Mainnet. This allows supported application requests to travel through privacy-preserving mixnet transport instead of directly exposing the user's IP address to the RPC endpoint. We also compile the Rust verification engine to WebAssembly so supported proof-verification operations can run directly in the browser. Our TypeScript SDK, built around Viem and Ethers integration, provides developer-friendly interfaces for private reads, proof verification, and EIP-7702 delegation detection. The React 18, Vite, and Tailwind CSS dashboard provides an interactive interface for verification results, Trust Receipts, network status, the Attack Lab, and the Delegation Guard. One particularly interesting implementation is our malicious RPC simulator. It deliberately modifies responses, corrupts proofs, simulates outages, and hides EIP-7702 delegation information while keeping the account proof available. VeriQ must detect inconsistencies between the returned code and the codeHash committed in the proven account state. We use PostgreSQL and Prisma for receipt persistence, Foundry for smart contract testing, Docker for backend packaging, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, Render for backend infrastructure, and Vercel for frontend deployment. The most important engineering decision was separating privacy from correctness: Anon-RPC protects the communication path, while independent cryptographic verification protects the integrity of the returned blockchain data.

projects.title: shankh
projects.description: Catch a malicious package once, warn every machine running it, via an alarm on ENS and Arkiv
projects.project_description: Shankh checks installed Python packages against their public source, and lets the real maintainer flag a bad build on ENS and anyone who catches one post a signed alarm on Arkiv. Every machine sweeps both, compares locally, and re-checks what it hears. Live on Sepolia and the Arkiv testnet; automatically switching stolen keys off is next.
projects.how_its_made:
CLI (shankh/, Python + Typer): reads installed files and hashes from pip's RECORD, fetches the source archive from PyPI's JSON API, and diffs them. ENS reads shell out to Foundry's cast through the ENSIP-10 resolve() path. Arkiv reads and writes go through a small TypeScript bridge to @arkiv-network/sdk. 34 tests.
ENSv2 on Sepolia (scripts/ens/): shankh.eth registered via commit-reveal; pypi.shankh.eth and reporters.shankh.eth are PermissionedRegistry proxies with their dangerous root roles revoked (emancipated). Each package has its own PermissionedResolver where the maintainer can only write shankh.source and only its KillSwitch can write shankh.revoked (key-scoped setter roles).
KillSwitch.sol (Foundry): instant revoke(build), 48-hour timelocked un-revoke, syncs the resolver's text record on every change.
Arkiv (arkiv/): shankh.report entities with indexed package, version, tier, build fingerprint and ENS flag; reads filter by the chain-recorded creator, never by package.
Landing page (status-page/, Next.js on Vercel): server-rendered on every request, every live read capped at 4 seconds so one slow network can't hang the page.
The hard parts: Identifying a build. We first flagged builds by the source archive's hash, then realised the LiteLLM poison was in the wheel next to a clean source archive, and an installed package doesn't remember which file it came from. We now fingerprint the installed files themselves, so a maintainer flags exactly what people installed.
Emancipation that actually holds. ENSv2's isEmancipated() can read true while upgrade roles are still held. We took the real role bitmap from verified source, rehearsed on an Anvil fork (which caught a wrong bitmap before it touched Sepolia), and proved the lock by attempting a re-grant that reverts.
Privacy. Looking up one package on ENS tells the RPC provider what you have installed, so shankh scan fetches every package's list from the registry's own events and compares locally. The same rule applies to Arkiv: reads are by reporter, never by package.

projects.title: Moonvault
projects.description: Your cycle, decentralized: encrypted vault, private AI, and shares that expire on their own.
projects.project_description: THE PROBLEM Period-tracking apps hold some of the most sensitive personal data a person can have, yet they often store it in readable form on company servers. Flo, a period-tracking app with over 100 million users, settled with the FTC over allegations that it shared users' health data with Facebook, Google, and other advertising companies despite promising to protect their privacy. Following the reversal of Roe v. Wade, this data also became a real legal and personal risk. Companies holding reproductive health records could potentially be compelled to hand them over. Users have no way of knowing exactly who can access their data, how it is being used, or how to take that access back. Your most sensitive health data should belong to you — and only you. OUR SOLUTION Moonvault is a decentralized period and cycle tracker designed around one fundamental principle: we cannot read your data, even if we wanted to. Everything you log is encrypted directly on your device, and only you hold the key. Moonvault combines private cycle tracking with AI-powered health insights. It predicts your next period and fertile window, identifies patterns in your symptoms, answers questions about your cycle, and generates doctor-ready health summaries. Your data is anonymised before any AI request. You can also securely share your health records with a doctor, partner, or anyone you trust through a link, QR code, or WhatsApp. You decide exactly what they can see and for how long. Access expires automatically or can be revoked instantly. There are no analytics, no trackers, and no unnecessary data exposure. Just you in control. KEY FEATURES Comprehensive Cycle & Health Tracking: Moonvault allows users to log their menstrual cycle, flow, symptoms, mood, sleep, and personal notes. It also supports voice-based logging, where users can simply speak and AI converts their words into structured health entries that they can review and confirm before saving. Intelligent Cycle Calendar: The calendar predicts upcoming periods and fertile windows, provides estimated ovulation dates, and includes confidence notes alongside predictions to communicate their uncertainty. Health History & Insights: Users can explore their health history through visual charts that track cycle length, symptom trends, and sleep patterns over time, helping them understand changes in their menstrual health. Private AI – Ask Your Cycle: Powered by 0G Private Computer, Moonvault offers AI-powered health assistance through Ask Your Cycle, allowing users to ask questions about their menstrual health. It also identifies patterns and correlations in symptoms, generates doctor-ready PDF summaries for medical consultations, and includes a Listen feature that converts AI-generated responses into audio using text-to-speech. Before any data leaves the device, it is decrypted locally and anonymised. Exact dates are converted into relative days, and sensitive identifying information is removed. Every AI result displays a Verification ID corresponding to its 0G request ID, providing a reference to the underlying inference request. Encrypted Cloud Backup & Restore: Moonvault uses 0G Storage to maintain encrypted cloud backups, allowing users to restore their data on any device using their login and passphrase. Health records are never stored in readable form in the cloud. Secure & Selective Sharing: Users can securely share their health records with a doctor, partner, or anyone they trust through a secure link, QR code, or WhatsApp. They have complete control over what recipients can access, whether that means period dates only, period dates along with symptoms, or their complete health records. Every share can have a custom expiration period, and access automatically expires when that period ends. Users can also revoke access instantly with a single tap. Recipients do not need to create an account to view shared records. The decryption key is stored exclusively in the link's URL fragment, which browsers never send to the server. This ensures that only encrypted data is stored and that health information remains under the user's control.
projects.how_its_made: Moonvault is a Next.js app that combines client-side encryption, decentralized infrastructure and private AI, so sensitive health data stays under the user's control. Encryption: libsodium (Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305) with envelope encryption. A random 32-byte data key encrypts everything, and a passphrase-derived key wraps it, so users can change their passphrase without re-encrypting their records. Entries are stored in IndexedDB. Backups and share packages are gzip-compressed, then encrypted. 0G Private Computer: powers every AI feature: Ask Your Cycle, insights, doctor summaries, voice transcription (Whisper, with Qwen Omni as a fallback) and text-to-speech. Data is decrypted and anonymised on the device first, with dates turned into relative days and identifying details removed. Each response shows its 0G request ID as a Verification ID. 0G Storage: holds the encrypted backups and any share package over 96 KiB, which is too big to store on Arkiv. Arkiv: stores profile records (the wrapped key and a pointer to the 0G backup) and share records. Built-in expiry ends shares automatically, with no cron job or cleanup server. Records hold only ciphertext, random IDs, generic labels and timestamps. Our schema and friction notes are in /arkiv. thirdweb: in-app wallets give email-code login with no seed phrases. The account is bridged to a viem account to sign Arkiv transactions, and a server-side gas relay (/api/fund) tops up gas, so users never handle tokens.
