Moonvault is a Next.js app that combines client-side encryption, decentralized infrastructure and private AI, so sensitive health data stays under the user's control.

Encryption: libsodium (Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305) with envelope encryption. A random 32-byte data key encrypts everything, and a passphrase-derived key wraps it, so users can change their passphrase without re-encrypting their records. Entries are stored in IndexedDB. Backups and share packages are gzip-compressed, then encrypted.

0G Storage: holds the encrypted backups and any share package over 96 KiB, which is too big to store on Arkiv.

thirdweb: in-app wallets give email-code login with no seed phrases. The account is bridged to a viem account to sign Arkiv transactions, and a server-side gas relay (/api/fund) tops up gas, so users never handle tokens.

projects.title: ForkTheFirstArtist
projects.description: Fork any artist in the garden: a name they own, a 0G steward, x402 tips on Hedera, 96.31% to them.
projects.project_description: Fork the First Artist turns Open Source Orchestra's garden circle (the artists of the Devcon 8 music space) into a place where every artist can be "forked": an ENS name they own, an AI steward that answers fans for them, and a tip jar that pays 96.31% straight to them. OSO takes 0%. No token. Continuity: the 3D garden circle existed before the hackathon. New this weekend is everything underneath it: Fork layer: tap any artist for their fork card (<name>.osoartist.eth, 96.31/3.69/0 split) and a panel with live proofs. Pay this artist (x402 on Hedera): an issued artist's card has "pay <name>", which runs the whole loop from the browser for any amount (0.01-10 testnet HBAR). A fan agent gets HTTP 402 and pays with x402, no human click; the steward pays a 0G meter its 3.69% per inference, forwards 96.31% to the artist and logs the split to HCS. The payout never comes from the browser: it is read live from the artist's own ENS name before every payment, and refused without active consent. 0G steward: 0G Private Computer answers grounded only on the artist's public profile, each with its 0G request ID. That answer is what the fan's tip buys. Arkiv: encrypted, expiring, revocable steward invitations, plus a trust ledger of every invitation, consent and approval, re-verified in the browser. Chain of trust + ENS: the owner of osoartist.eth is the root steward (/admin). A steward invites, the artist signs consent with their own wallet (/consent, where they add a Hedera testnet payout or leave it empty to be paid at their own wallet address), a steward approves; only then is <label>.osoartist.eth issued on ENSv2 mainnet, owned by the artist with their own resolver. Live now: shaka.osoartist.eth is issued on Ethereum mainnet through the full chain (Arkiv records + signatures), and real testnet tips from the production site have landed in his Hedera account 0.0.11347291. Other artists appear only after their own consent. Team and individual contributions (git history at github.com/Open-Source-Orchestra/fork-the-first-artist): Shaka Lei Kaumaka: product vision and the Open Source Orchestra origin; the 96.31% / 3.69% / 0% economics and the consent rules; directed and reviewed the AI agents; code-owner review and merges; live account setup, the root steward of osoartist.eth, and the demo. Rajarshi Roy (rajarshi-tech): payments and agent core. The x402 Hedera payment gate, the paywall and pay-per-call inference meter, exact atomic money math, the spend ledger and HCS audit trail, the provider-agnostic steward with prompt fencing, a three-ceiling spend budget, the tool loop and degradation ladder, and the x402 payer and demo scripts. Prince Keshri (princekeshri00): frontend and claims. The artist home and local draft editor, the MetaMask and HashPack wallet connections, steward invites and service-freeze records moved onto encrypted Arkiv entities, ENS ownership design, and agent consent/budget fixes and integration. Utkarsh Tiwari (utkarshhs): the Hedera Agent Kit steward that forwards 96.31% to the artist and logs the split to HCS (hedera-steward/). His testnet account also funded the live demo accounts. Yuuki Shimizu: main hacker on our ENS integration (osoartist.eth on ENSv2: artist-owned names, resolvers and payout records).
projects.how_its_made: Monorepo (TypeScript + Python + buildless static frontend); offline Node/pytest suites + Playwright browser tests; live proofs in docs/. Frontend (Continuity): the garden circle is Open Source Orchestra's existing Three.js circle (disclosed in frontend/SOURCE.md). New: fork.js/fork.css adds the ribbon, per-artist fork card and fork panel on top through a one-line event hook, plus /admin, /consent, /arkiv, /trust and /steward pages. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Hedera (x402 + Agent Kit + HCS): payments/ is a resource server on @x402/core and @x402/hedera against the x402.org facilitator, in native HBAR with exact integer tinybar math. agent/ holds the autonomous fan payer and the steward, which pays a 0G meter per call. hedera-steward/ (Hedera Agent Kit + hiero-sdk) verifies settlement on the mirror node, forwards 96.31% to the artist and logs the split to HCS. A Cloudflare Worker (oso-tip-loop) runs the fan and steward agents server-side so anyone can trigger a real loop from /pay; a Durable Object enforces a per-run gap, a daily run cap and a daily HBAR budget. For "pay this artist" the Worker resolves <slug>.osoartist.eth through the ENS Universal Resolver (addr 3030 -> ENSIP-11 Hedera EVM -> ETH address, fail-closed on consent/pause/network) and pays an EVM payout as a Hedera alias. Hacky: alias-created accounts are "hollow" and the facilitator rejects them until each pays one own-key tx, so we finalize them first; and public mainnet RPCs rate-limit Cloudflare egress, so ENS reads go out as one JSON-RPC batch over a 6-endpoint fallback, with the last live read kept in the Durable Object (refusals never fall back). 0G Private Computer: the steward's brain is 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b via the 0G router, behind a Cloudflare Worker; every answer returns its 0G request ID and cost. Open questions returned empty until we disabled hidden thinking (enable_thinking=false). Artist data and fan text are fenced against prompt injection. Arkiv: claims/ stores invitations as encrypted, expiring entities on Rabdi with atomic replace-plus-audit transitions (issue, revoke, freeze). record-trust.mjs writes signed invitations, consents and approvals as public oso.trust.v1 entities; /trust queries Arkiv and re-verifies each EIP-191 signature in the browser. ENS + trust: one module builds every signed message for pages and issuer. ens/onboard.mjs refuses issuance without a valid steward invite, artist consent and steward approval, then issues <label>.osoartist.eth on ENSv2 owned by the artist, with their own resolver (Hedera payout via coin 3030 or the ENSIP-11 Hedera address). Fork-tested first, then live on mainnet: our UserRegistry was activated by the parent owner's setSubregistry and shaka.osoartist.eth is issued (tx 0x1d2156d8...65968). AI agents helped with code, tests and docs; disclosed in commits.

New: fork.js/fork.css adds the ribbon, per-artist fork card and fork panel on top through a one-line event hook, plus /admin, /consent, /arkiv, /trust and /steward pages. Hosted on GitHub Pages.

Hedera (x402 + Agent Kit + HCS): payments/ is a resource server on @x402/core and @x402/hedera against the x402.org facilitator, in native HBAR with exact integer tinybar math. agent/ holds the autonomous fan payer and the steward, which pays a 0G meter per call. hedera-steward/ (Hedera Agent Kit + hiero-sdk) verifies settlement on the mirror node, forwards 96.31% to the artist and logs the split to HCS. A Cloudflare Worker (oso-tip-loop) runs the fan and steward agents server-side so anyone can trigger a real loop from /pay; a Durable Object enforces a per-run gap, a daily run cap and a daily HBAR budget. For "pay this artist" the Worker resolves <slug>.osoartist.eth through the ENS Universal Resolver (addr 3030 -> ENSIP-11 Hedera EVM -> ETH address, fail-closed on consent/pause/network) and pays an EVM payout as a Hedera alias. Hacky: alias-created accounts are "hollow" and the facilitator rejects them until each pays one own-key tx, so we finalize them first; and public mainnet RPCs rate-limit Cloudflare egress, so ENS reads go out as one JSON-RPC batch over a 6-endpoint fallback, with the last live read kept in the Durable Object (refusals never fall back).

0G Private Computer: the steward's brain is 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b via the 0G router, behind a Cloudflare Worker; every answer returns its 0G request ID and cost. Open questions returned empty until we disabled hidden thinking (enable_thinking=false). Artist data and fan text are fenced against prompt injection.

Arkiv: claims/ stores invitations as encrypted, expiring entities on Rabdi with atomic replace-plus-audit transitions (issue, revoke, freeze). record-trust.mjs writes signed invitations, consents and approvals as public oso.trust.v1 entities; /trust queries Arkiv and re-verifies each EIP-191 signature in the browser.

ENS + trust: one module builds every signed message for pages and issuer. ens/onboard.mjs refuses issuance without a valid steward invite, artist consent and steward approval, then issues <label>.osoartist.eth on ENSv2 owned by the artist, with their own resolver (Hedera payout via coin 3030 or the ENSIP-11 Hedera address). Fork-tested first, then live on mainnet: our UserRegistry was activated by the parent owner's setSubregistry and shaka.osoartist.eth is issued (tx 0x1d2156d8...65968).

AI agents helped with code, tests and docs; disclosed in commits.

projects.title: AXIS
projects.description: Decode Arkiv. Discover on-chain insights. Turn blockchain data into your next big discovery.
projects.project_description: AXIS - this  is all about making blockchain data easier to explore and understand. Built on Arkiv Network, it brings everything together in one place, helping you explore on-chain activity, discover useful insights, and see what's happening across the network. Whether you're building, researching, or just curious about the Blockchain network. AXIS makes the experience simpler, more intuitive and more engaging. No complicated data, just a better way to explore Arkiv and discover what lies beneath the surface.
projects.how_its_made: We built AXIS with one simple idea in mind : exploring blockchain data shouldn't feel complicated. We wanted to create something that makes Arkiv Network easier to understand while still being powerful enough for developers and Web3 enthusiasts. We connected our frontend and backend with Arkiv's network infrastructure and designed an interactive analytics experience where users can explore on-chain data through dynamic dashboards and visualizations. A lot of our efforts were put into making AXIS not just look good from the outside, but to also perform exceptionally on the backend. We refined the way blockchain data is fetched, processed, and presented to ensure users get accurate, reliable, and meaningful insights. Our focus was on building a tool that users can genuinely rely on to explore Arkiv Network, rather than just another dashboard that displays data.

projects.title: StarProof for Wedgie
projects.description: A space game and toolkit for hardware-signed decisions using Wedgie’s Trust M chip.
projects.project_description: Starproof turns space exploration into a hands-on demo of hardware-signed game actions. Pilot a rocket across 20 worlds, meet 18 strange neighbors, recover artifacts and manage your fuel. A connected Wedgie uses its OPTIGA Trust M chip to sign your expedition’s launch. Configurable switches choose whether travel, artifact collection, refuelling and scavenging also need device confirmation. The game is a playable reference for our reusable Wedgie toolkit. A live airdrop demo also lets each verified chip claim 1,000 STARPROOF on Base to a selected Safe without switching device apps. The browser and MicroPython source show developers how to implement the full flow: on-device approval, certified-chip proofs, server verification, gas-sponsored submission and permanent onchain claim tracking.
projects.how_its_made: We built Starproof with vanilla JavaScript, HTML/CSS and Canvas for the game, Node.js 24 for the authoritative API, and MicroPython for the Wedgie app. Web Serial connects the browser to the device. Each signed action binds the mission, origin, destination, cost, sequence, expiry and a random challenge. The device validates the action and asks for physical green-button approval; the server verifies its P-256 signature and Infineon factory certificate chain. This establishes participation by a certified Trust M chip. We extracted the transport, action protocol and certificate verifier into wedgie-actions, and published the installable device app separately. First-run installation uses pinned GitHub source and SHA-256 checksums. We reused Wedgie’s MIT USB helpers and 3D model with Three.js, and built the game’s procedural planets, monsters and effects around them. The project was built with Codex assistance. Vercel hosts the browser and API; private Upstash Redis stores missions and atomically consumes challenges. Two notable hacks keep the device usable: USB cancellation remains responsive inside approval prompts, and installation reconnects to the same board after a USB restart. The joystick doubles as a flight controller, while the idle device screen displays live game stats. Demo switches allow selected unsigned actions, explicitly labeled in the diary; launch remains signed.

projects.title: Redress
projects.description: Redress detects wrongful DeFi liquidations and automates evidence based refunds.
projects.project_description: Imagine losing your crypto because a price oracle made a mistake. Your collateral gets liquidated, even though the market conditions didn't justify it. Today, recovering those funds can involve slow, manual governance decisions. Redress is an automated restitution layer designed to make DeFi fairer and more accountable. It monitors lending protocols for liquidation events, compares the protocol's oracle prices against independent market data, and reconstructs the borrower's position to determine whether the liquidation was justified. When a wrongful liquidation or excessive seizure is verified, Redress calculates the minimum provable loss and triggers reimbursement through a smart contract connected to a funded vault. Every decision is backed by verifiable evidence and recorded onchain, making the process transparent and independently auditable. For DeFi protocols and DAOs, Redress offers a potential plug-in risk and restitution solution. For borrowers, it provides something equally important: confidence that an oracle error doesn't have to mean an unfair financial loss. We aren't trying to reverse blockchain transactions. We're building a way to make users whole when the information behind those transactions was wrong.
projects.how_its_made: Redress combines smart contracts, decentralized oracle infrastructure, independent market data, and decentralized storage to create an evidence-driven refund workflow. Smart contracts: We use Solidity and Foundry to develop the RedressVault and VerdictMath contracts. The vault receives verified reports, independently recalculates compensation, enforces payout limits, prevents duplicate payments, and transfers eligible reimbursements from its funded reserve. Chainlink CRE:CRE coordinates the verification workflow. It monitors Aave liquidation events, retrieves relevant blockchain state and external price data, and combines multiple sources into an authorized onchain report. Uniswap: Uniswap v3 TWAP provides an independent market-price reference. This helps us compare the price used by the lending protocol with actual market observations rather than trusting a single oracle. Arkiv and Swarm: Arkiv stores searchable records of incidents, verdicts, and reimbursements. Swarm stores detailed evidence bundles, including source observations and calculation data, so decisions can be independently reviewed. Application and testing: We use TypeScript, viem, Bun, and Next.js for event processing, workflow integration, and the user interface. Foundry and Anvil support contract testing and historical mainnet-fork simulations. One particularly interesting part is our historical incident replay: instead of relying only on a hypothetical scenario, we aim to replay Aave's March 10, 2026 wstETH liquidation incident and evaluate how Redress would have classified and reimbursed the affected borrowers. The result is designed to be more than a monitoring dashboard: it's an automated, auditable restitution system for DeFi.

projects.title: QRAC.me
projects.description: Post-quantum accounts for Ethereum, working today and ready for EIP-8141 frame transactions.
projects.project_description: QRAC.me (QR Accounts) is a dApp that gives you a post-quantum Ethereum account today, on the current network, and that already works with EIP-8141 frame transactions for when Ethereum gets native account abstraction. The problem: every normal Ethereum account is controlled by one ECDSA key. If that key leaks, or a quantum computer breaks it one day, everything in the account is gone, and changing that at the protocol level will take years. How QRAC.me works: you create a 24-word seed (256 bits, independent of any wallet). The dApp turns it into 1,024 one-time post-quantum keys (LMS / LM-OTS from RFC 8554, only hashes, nothing that a quantum computer breaks). You mint a small smart account (a 45-byte clone of shared logic, address known before it exists) whose only owner is the root of that key tree. To move funds, call a token, an NFT or any contract, or run a batch of calls, you sign the exact action with a one-time key. The account verifies that signature on-chain before doing anything. Any wallet can deliver it and pay the gas, but no wallet owns the account: the deployer's or funder's ECDSA key can't move a single wei. One-time keys are never reused (they are reserved before signing), a failed transaction never locks you out (sign a replacement with a fresh key), you can cancel a pending action, and you can rotate to a new key tree before the keys run out. It runs on Sepolia today: a real transfer authorized only by a post-quantum signature, accounts minted through the factory (738k gas instead of 10.5M), and simulated attacks with a leaked deployer key all refused. The same account idea goes further with frame transactions. On the EIP-8141 devnet the QRAC.me account validates its own transactions in a VERIFY frame: the transaction carries only the post-quantum signature (zero ECDSA), the account approves and pays its own gas, and each one-time key is used as an EIP-8250 nonce key, so the network itself refuses to accept a key twice. The post-quantum check needs about 250k gas of validation. The public mempool refuses it (limit 100k) and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool accepts it, which is exactly what we show in the dApp side by side, with the explorer link of the admitted transaction. The frame-ready contract is the same QRAC.me account plus native frame validation, so it works with today's transactions and with frame transactions. The goal is that the account you create now keeps its address and funds when the migration happens. Testnets only, not audited.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, with inline assembly where it matters): -LMSVerifier: a stateless LMS / LM-OTS verifier (RFC 8554, SHA-256 parameter sets) that calls the SHA-256 precompile in tight assembly loops. About 172k to 220k gas per signature with H10/W4 (1,024 keys, 2,508-byte signatures). It checks the official RFC 8554 test vectors on-chain, including on Sepolia and on the devnet.
-QRACAccount: the account. One state-changing entry point (submit), no owner, no admin, no upgrades. It keeps the key root, an epoch, a nonce and a bitmap of used one-time keys, and it runs batches of calls all-or-nothing.
-QRACFactory: mints ERC-1167 clones with CREATE2 (salt = hash of the public key) and initializes them in the same transaction.
-QRACFrameAccount + QRACFrameFactory: the account plus a VERIFY-frame entry for EIP-8141. It reads the signature hash (TXPARAM) and our signature from an ARBITRARY signature entry (SIGDATACOPY), checks that the transaction uses exactly the nonce key bound to that one-time key with sequence 0, verifies with the shared verifier and calls APPROVE. Solidity can't emit the new opcodes, so we used HegotaSupport (MIT, vendored), which reaches them through tiny helper contracts with delegatecall. That works even through our clones (clone, implementation, helper). Python, used as the reference and the test bench: our own LMS implementation that reproduces the RFC 8554 Test Case 2 key tree and signature byte for byte; the authorization encoder; a frame-transaction codec (RLP and signature hash), checked against the devnet by sending a transaction and getting back exactly our hash; 101 tests on an in-memory EVM (py-evm through eth-tester, solc through py-solc-x), including an attacker holding the deployer's key and every account test repeated on standalone, minted and frame accounts; a small JSON-RPC dev node for offline demos; and a devnet script that funds, deploys, mints, stakes, sends and runs attacks. dApp: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no build step and no backend. ethers v6 from a CDN. SHA-256 and LMS written in JavaScript (WebCrypto is too slow for about a million hashes), the key tree built in a Web Worker in 1 to 3.5 seconds, and BIP-39 and HMAC key derivation with WebCrypto. A signer journal in localStorage reserves each one-time key before signing and is exported as a JSON file after every signature. Before signing, the dApp asks the contract for the exact message bytes and refuses to sign if they differ from its own. A self-test page checks the browser against the Python references. Partner tech (EF frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool): the devnet, the sidecar's eth_sendFrameTransaction, ethrex_simulateFrameTransaction to show the public mempool's verdict before submitting, the faucet, the staking registry and the explorer. Without the alternative mempool our wallet simply can't exist with frame transactions, because validation needs about 250k gas. Hacky bits worth mentioning: -The verifier compiles with default Remix settings (no viaIR) because we packed parameters into one word and moved the hot loops into Yul functions.
-We measure verification gas on any chain with a read-only eth_call whose creation code deploys a temporary verifier, verifies and reverts with the gas used. No funds, nothing stored.
-One-time keys mapped to EIP-8250 nonce keys give a hash-based wallet protocol-level single use, without storage writes in a static VERIFY frame.
-The account stakes itself for the alternative mempool through its normal-transaction path, because a staking frame transaction would itself need more validation gas than an unstaked sender gets.

projects.title: Notchi
projects.description: A desktop pet in your MacBook notch that shows sponsored hooks while your AI coding agent thinks.
projects.project_description: Notchi turns the time developers spend waiting on AI coding agents into something useful. A tiny pixel pet lives behind a hidden door in the MacBook notch. When Claude Code starts working, the door opens, the pet drops out and walks a sponsored hook across the screen like a news ticker. It reacts live to the agent: working, waiting for approval, done or failed. When the agent finishes, it climbs back into the notch and reminds you to return. Brands fund campaigns in a contract on 0G Galileo. Notchi writes three hooks for them on 0G Private Computer, each with a verifiable request ID. Impressions settle onchain to the pet’s wallet, and the pet’s mood follows its real balance. Unspent budget refunds to the brand. Every pet needs a World ID proof, so one human gets one pet, and brands pay real screens rather than bot farms. Nothing in the main flow is mocked: if 0G is unreachable, the pet sleeps and says why.
projects.how_its_made: A native Swift macOS app (transparent overlay window, notch geometry from NSScreen safe-area insets, sprite-sheet animation, menu-bar popover with avatar picker and settings) runs a local hook server on 127.0.0.1:47474. User-level Claude Code hooks POST every agent event with a 1-second curl timeout, so the pet can never slow or block the agent, and hooks never return a decision. A Node/TypeScript server handles campaigns, impressions, settlement and World verification. A small brain package calls the 0G Compute Router (Private Computer / TEE) for every pet decision and for ad hooks, choosing the model by mood and safe-stopping on any error. CampaignVault.sol (Foundry, 20 tests including fuzzing) on 0G Galileo holds brand budgets, pays verified pets per impression and refunds unspent budget; only the human owner can change a pet’s payout address. The Next.js web app does World ID v4 (IDKit with a relying-party signature from the server) and brand checkout with viem. Hacky bits: wallets couldn’t estimate gas on Galileo, so we set it explicitly; World legacy vs v4 proof shapes; the reasoning model used its whole token budget thinking, so ad hooks get a larger budget; per-pixel hit-testing so the pet reacts to hover and clicks without blocking clicks anywhere else on screen.

projects.title: Frontrun
projects.description: Social trading on Arc mainnet where every call is backed by real position & reputation lives onchain
projects.project_description: Frontrun is a mobile-first social trading app on Arc mainnet. Sign in with Gmail, deposit USDC, and trade tokens across 8 chains in one tap. projects.title: Daak
projects.description: Every parcel handoff on India's buses proven, and drivers paid by the km and kg at each handover.
projects.project_description: In UP and Bihar, manufacturers send parcels to small-town shops on buses, often across two buses with a driver-to-driver handoff at a bus stand. Nobody signs at the handoff, every driver quotes a different rate, drivers are paid in cash with no record of their work, and when a parcel arrives torn, everyone blames the next person. Daak puts a meter, a receipt and a payout on the network that already runs. A shop taps a new parcel with its Android phone, picks the receiver and the best-rated driver for each stretch, enters the parcel's weight and size (priced on every charged kg, so each driver's pay follows the parcel), and its agent pays the exact booking over x402 on Hedera from the shop's prepaid rupees. Drivers join with their Google account; no wallet, no sticker. At every bus stand, the driver taps the parcel's NFC sticker, scans the next person's code (a QR their phone signs, good for two minutes and once) and photographs the lid, so both phones sign the handoff with keys in their secure hardware, and GPS is added. With only one phone, the next person taps their badge instead. A sealed vision model on 0G checks the photo: right parcel, right stop, still sealed. If 0G cannot answer, the handoff is recorded as "not checked by AI" and the money waits; nothing is faked. Each driver gets 50, 70 or 90% of their stretch's pay the moment the next person confirms the handover (more as their public record grows) and the rest after delivery, held in a Hedera scheduled transfer that releases itself unless the shop files a claim; then the responsible driver's held pay repays the shop. Pay is redeemed to UPI. Drivers can save in Bachat and unlock fuel advances from their proven record, and vouch for new drivers on their corridor, staking their own record on it. IDs are read by the same sealed AI before an operator verifies them. Every booking pays its own share of the AI checks: 2% of its fee on Hedera, the same value in 0G into Daak's own compute account. The receiving shop tracks the parcel by tapping it with any phone. Nobody sees a wallet or a token. Live on testnet: https://daak-ethglobal.vercel.app (every delivery read-only at /live , the network map at /network ).
projects.how_its_made: Android app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose: NFC reader mode, the system camera, GPS, Hindi or English with Hindi text-to-speech, an offline outbox, a P-256 key in the Android Keystore that signs every handoff. People sign in with Google (Credential Manager, token verified on the server) or a badge; at a handoff the other person shows a QR their phone signs, so both phones sign, with a badge tap as the one-phone fallback; vouching by scanning a newcomer's code. Next.js 16 on Vercel for the API and the web pages; no database: Arkiv is the store. Hedera with the JavaScript SDK and no Solidity: x402 bookings settled in dINR (Daak's HTS rupee-credit token with a 2% fractional custom fee) through the official facilitator, per-shop agent accounts with spend controls and catalogue discovery, escrow, advances, holdbacks as long-term scheduled transactions (waitForExpiry) that execute themselves, refunds by deleting the schedule, an HCS topic as the public log, the mirror node for balances and work records. 0G compute for a sealed (TeeML) vision check in private, TEE-only mode, with a 20 second budget and a safe-stop, and 0G Storage for the decision log; Daak's own 0G Direct compute account, topped up by every booking, pays for the checks. Arkiv for people, bookings, handoffs, daily orders and preferences, with expiry; Swarm for the lid and ID photos, encrypted, with the reference sealed before it reaches Arkiv. Data for the network map: India Post's pincode directory (GODL-India), OpenStreetMap bus stations (ODbL), OSRM road routes. The landing page's one-minute hero film is rendered in code by raea (React on Bevy) as cut paper, with its captions laid over it from the same timeline. Hacky bits: the meter charges road km taken from OSRM; the holdback release needs no server at all, because the schedule waits for its own expiry.

projects.title: Odyssey
projects.description: Real-world AI training data, signed at the sensor, verified by stake, owned by its capturers.
projects.project_description: AI models have read the internet. Now they’re running out of verified data, and they’ve never had senses. Odyssey gives them sense organs: smart glasses that capture first-person clips of the real world, signed by a hardware key at the moment of capture. Each device is tied to one human through World ID, and every batch is anchored on-chain, so nothing can be faked or quietly edited. Labs subscribe to datasets in 0G, and 70% of every payment goes to the people wearing the glasses.
projects.how_its_made:
What we built: a micro-monolith for IoT data. At its center is one core that every device shares: signature checks, device registry, World ID enrollment, storage on Arkiv and 0G, the dataset marketplace and rewards. It is designed so that each type of device plugs into the core as an extension, which defines what the device captures and how it signs and uploads. Adding a new device means writing an extension, not a new backend. Our first extension is smart glasses: an ESP32 running our own C++ firmware. Contracts are Solidity, tested with Foundry. Our partner technologies are Arkiv, 0G and World ID. The Next.js app: The core is a single Next.js app on Vercel. Its API routes are the gateway, handling ingest, enrollment, devices, datasets, samples, subscriptions and rewards, and its pages are the product. Contributors enroll their glasses with World ID and a payout wallet at /enroll, check each capture’s signature and content hash at /capture, and track earnings per reward epoch at /analytics. Labs browse and subscribe to datasets at /datasets, search samples by place on a map at /explore, and follow payments at /activity. The live pages ask for a wallet sign-in and read directly from Arkiv and 0G Galileo. The app also includes an interactive 3D model of the glasses, step-by-step ESP32 wiring lessons with reference firmware, and protocol docs. API and UI ship in one deploy, which is what makes the core a monolith. How it fits together: A device captures a sample and signs it with its key at the moment of capture. The core verifies the signature, checks that the device is enrolled, and writes the sample to Arkiv as a readonly entity carrying its metadata, signature, geohash and encrypted payload. Labs subscribe through our OdsySubscriptions contract on 0G Galileo, which splits each payment on the spot: 70% to a contributor pool and 30% to the treasury. At the end of each epoch we publish one Merkle root that splits the pool by sample count, and every payout wallet claims its share with a proof. How the partners helped:
Arkiv gave us a queryable data layer instead of a blob store. Samples, devices, datasets and reward epochs are all entities we can filter, and expiry lets us keep only the samples worth paying for while banned data simply expires.
0G runs our money and our big files: both contracts live on Galileo, and payloads over 96 KiB go to 0G Storage, with the root kept on Arkiv.
World ID solves the fake-device problem: one human per device, and two provable strikes ban that human. Why a micro-monolith: The core is one codebase and one deploy, so a small team can ship it in a weekend. The extensions keep it open: a dashcam, a weather station or a wearable can each be added without touching the core. Because the core keeps its data on Arkiv and 0G, every device’s samples land in the same verifiable layer and the same marketplace. The hacky parts: Our prototype glasses are a cheap sunglasses frame braced with ice cream sticks, carrying an ESP32 and a small display. It cost almost nothing, and it signs every clip it captures.
The World ID proof’s signal is the device’s own address, so a proof made for one device can’t be replayed to enroll a second one.
Location search runs on a geohash prefix index we built on top of Arkiv’s attribute queries.
Rewards use one Merkle root per epoch instead of one transaction per contributor, so payout cost stays flat as contributors grow.
ConsensusRegistry takes the median of validator scores per hex tile, so a single lying validator can’t swing a verdict.
24 Foundry tests across the two contracts.

projects.title: pUSDC
projects.description: A seatbelt for your stablecoins: big pUSDC sends are delayed and cancellable by your backup.
projects.project_description: Protected Token (pUSDC) makes large ERC-20 transfers cancellable, so a stolen key or a wrench attack can't drain a wallet in seconds. Any holder can switch on a public, on-chain "protected" flag. After that, transfers under a daily limit go out instantly. Anything bigger is scheduled: it arrives after a hold window, during which a pre-registered backup wallet can cancel it. An emergency button sweeps the whole balance to the backup and locks it there. Turning protection on is instant. Weakening it (turning it off, changing the backup, raising the limit) takes a delay of at least 7 days in production, so a thief can't just switch it off. Incoming transfers are always instant. ProtectedWrapper wraps any ERC-20 1:1 (USDC → pUSDC). Big sends from MetaMask are scheduled automatically, and contracts pulling funds over the limit get a clean revert. Unprotected accounts behave like a plain ERC-20 and work with Uniswap as-is. ScheduledSwap lets protected holders make big Uniswap v4 swaps: the swap waits out the hold, and the output always goes to the owner. The app (live on Base Sepolia) reads the chain through anon-rpc over a mixnet, so an RPC provider can't link a backup wallet to the wallet it watches.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Solidity + Foundry on OpenZeppelin's ERC20Permit. All the rules live in one abstract ProtectedERC20 that overrides OZ's _update hook, so the limits apply to every balance change: transfer, transferFrom and permit alike. ProtectedWrapper wraps any ERC-20 1:1 (USDC → pUSDC), with no permission needed from the issuer. Tricks: No keepers: delayed setting changes are applied lazily by a _sync() at the start of each call. O(1) cancel-all: scheduled transfers record an epoch, and stress() just increments it. The hacky part: when a protected EOA sends over its limit, transfer() returns true and the transfer is queued, so MetaMask just works. This only happens if msg.sender == tx.origin and the account has no code (so not EIP-7702). Contracts get a revert, so no DEX is ever fooled. Uniswap v4: ScheduledSwap uses flash accounting (unlock → swap → settle → take), and take() pays the output straight to the owner, so anyone can execute but only the owner gains. Only hookless pools are allowed. The tests run against the real PoolManager on a Base Sepolia fork. Frontend: React + Vite + wagmi/viem, static, with no backend. anon-rpc plugs in as viem's fetchFn, so app reads go through the Nox mixnet, and the RPC provider can't link a backup wallet to the wallet it watches.

projects.title: Idlecash
projects.description: Self-custodial control panel for 1inch Aqua: sign, ship and dock LP strategies, verified on-chain.
projects.project_description:
IdleCash is a self-custodial control panel for 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer where a maker’s tokens stay in their own wallet while the same balance backs swap strategies. The problem: Aqua lets liquidity providers keep custody, but managing strategies today means building raw calldata, signing by hand and checking block explorers to see whether anything actually happened. IdleCash gives makers a mobile app for that workflow, so they never have to hand assets to a centralized platform. What it does: A Flutter wallet app and a TypeScript backend use the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM SDKs to build a WETH/USDC constant-product strategy and prepare the ERC-20 approvals and the Aqua ship() call.
The maker’s own wallet signs every transaction. The app and backend never hold keys or funds.
After each transaction, the backend checks the receipt and the Aqua event. A strategy only shows as active once its Shipped event is confirmed, and as docked once Docked is confirmed. Anything unverified stays unverified.
One wallet can run several strategies, each with its own hash, status and transaction history.
The app can fetch a SwapVM quote and prepare slippage-limited swap calldata.
The portfolio view shows wallet balances separately from Aqua allocations, so the same tokens aren’t counted twice. How it was tested: Aqua has no listed testnet deployment, so we ran a local fork of Base mainnet using Base’s real Aqua and SwapVM contracts. The transactions are local, not on Base mainnet. What it does not do yet: it is an unaudited prototype. It doesn’t claim fee earnings, completed taker swaps, or shared execution across independent makers. The next milestones are a verified taker fill, a small-value run on Base mainnet, and verified fee and execution reporting.
projects.how_its_made: Stack Frontend: a Flutter app (Android debug build). It connects to the maker's wallet through Reown, signs transactions in that wallet, and saves the wallet session, strategy records and balance snapshots on the device. Backend:a TypeScript/Express API with routes to prepare a deposit, prepare a dock, verify a transaction, and prepare a swap. 1inch SDKs: @1inch/aqua-sdk and @1inch/swap-vm-sdk , using the official Aqua and SwapVM deployments on Base. Dev environment:Ganache forked from Base mainnet, plus scripts to start the backend against the fork and fund a development account. How it fits together The user picks a strategy size in Flutter. The backend builds an AquaXYCAmmStrategy with a random salt, wraps it in an SwapVM Order , encodes and hashes it, and uses AquaProtocolContract.buildShipTx to produce the registry transaction. The salt gives each strategy a unique hash, so one wallet can hold several. The backend returns the two ERC-20 approvals and the ship() calldata. Flutter sends each one through the wallet and waits for its receipt. The backend then checks the ship receipt. It confirms the call went to the configured Aqua registry and decodes the Aqua events. The app marks a strategy active only after it sees Shipped . Docking works the same way with buildDockTx and the Docked event. For swaps, the backend decodes the shipped strategy, asks SwapVM for an on-chain quote, and prepares router calldata with a minimum-output limit. How the 1inch tools helped: using the official SDK builders meant we never hand-wrote calldata. The same SDK gave us the strategy encoding, the hashing and the SwapVM quote, so the app talks to the real protocol and not a mock. Notable and hacky parts A fork instead of a testnet. The SDK lists no Aqua registry on Base Sepolia, so we forked all of Base mainnet in Ganache and run against Base's real Aqua and SwapVM contracts. Transactions there are local only. The backend fails closed on any chain without an explicitly verified Aqua deployment. Receipts, not wallet responses, are the source of truth. A confirmed transaction isn't enough: if Aqua didn't emit Shipped , the app throws instead of showing the strategy as active. Pending transactions are re-checked when the app restores saved state. Balance snapshots are written on device. A new one is stored when the value changes by at least 0.1% or 15 minutes have passed. projects.project_description_markdown:
IdleCash is a self-custodial control panel for 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer where a maker’s tokens stay in their own wallet while the same balance backs swap strategies.

The problem: Aqua lets liquidity providers keep custody, but managing strategies today means building raw calldata, signing by hand and checking block explorers to see whether anything actually happened. IdleCash gives makers a mobile app for that workflow, so they never have to hand assets to a centralized platform.

What it does:

A Flutter wallet app and a TypeScript backend use the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM SDKs to build a WETH/USDC constant-product strategy and prepare the ERC-20 approvals and the Aqua ship() call.
The maker’s own wallet signs every transaction. The app and backend never hold keys or funds.
After each transaction, the backend checks the receipt and the Aqua event. A strategy only shows as active once its Shipped event is confirmed, and as docked once Docked is confirmed. Anything unverified stays unverified.
One wallet can run several strategies, each with its own hash, status and transaction history.
The app can fetch a SwapVM quote and prepare slippage-limited swap calldata.
The portfolio view shows wallet balances separately from Aqua allocations, so the same tokens aren’t counted twice.

How it was tested: Aqua has no listed testnet deployment, so we ran a local fork of Base mainnet using Base’s real Aqua and SwapVM contracts. The transactions are local, not on Base mainnet.

What it does not do yet: it is an unaudited prototype. It doesn’t claim fee earnings, completed taker swaps, or shared execution across independent makers. The next milestones are a verified taker fill, a small-value run on Base mainnet, and verified fee and execution reporting.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Stack
- Frontend: a Flutter app (Android debug build). It connects to the maker's wallet through Reown, signs transactions in that wallet, and saves the wallet session, strategy records and balance snapshots on the device.
- Backend:a TypeScript/Express API with routes to prepare a deposit, prepare a dock, verify a transaction, and prepare a swap.
- 1inch SDKs: `@1inch/aqua-sdk` and `@1inch/swap-vm-sdk`, using the official Aqua and SwapVM deployments on Base.
- Dev environment:Ganache forked from Base mainnet, plus scripts to start the backend against the fork and fund a development account.

How it fits together
1. The user picks a strategy size in Flutter. The backend builds an `AquaXYCAmmStrategy` with a random salt, wraps it in an SwapVM `Order`, encodes and hashes it, and uses `AquaProtocolContract.buildShipTx` to produce the registry transaction. The salt gives each strategy a unique hash, so one wallet can hold several.
2. The backend returns the two ERC-20 approvals and the `ship()` calldata. Flutter sends each one through the wallet and waits for its receipt.
3. The backend then checks the ship receipt. It confirms the call went to the configured Aqua registry and decodes the Aqua events. The app marks a strategy active only after it sees `Shipped`.
4. Docking works the same way with `buildDockTx` and the `Docked` event.
5. For swaps, the backend decodes the shipped strategy, asks SwapVM for an on-chain quote, and prepares router calldata with a minimum-output limit.

How the 1inch tools helped: using the official SDK builders meant we never hand-wrote calldata. The same SDK gave us the strategy encoding, the hashing and the SwapVM quote, so the app talks to the real protocol and not a mock.

Notable and hacky parts
- A fork instead of a testnet. The SDK lists no Aqua registry on Base Sepolia, so we forked all of Base mainnet in Ganache and run against Base's real Aqua and SwapVM contracts. Transactions there are local only. The backend fails closed on any chain without an explicitly verified Aqua deployment.
- Receipts, not wallet responses, are the source of truth. A confirmed transaction isn't enough: if Aqua didn't emit `Shipped`, the app throws instead of showing the strategy as active. Pending transactions are re-checked when the app restores saved state.
- Balance snapshots are written on device. A new one is stored when the value changes by at least 0.1% or 15 minutes have passed. History keeps up to a year or 2,000 snapshots, and the chart shows a trend only once it has two. We label it balance history, not performance, since deposits and withdrawals change it.
- No double counting:wallet balances and Aqua allocations are shown separately, because one wallet balance can back several strategies.
- Prototype Solidity, not wired in:the repo includes a custom SwapVM opcode (`0x81`, a regime-based dynamic spread) and a `RegimeOracle`, with Foundry tests. They are not deployed and not used by the app. We kept them out of the live flow on purpose and say so in the README.

What's not built yet: completed taker swaps, shared execution across independent makers, and fee tracking.

projects.title: Agent-Mesh
projects.description: AgentMesh is a visual orchestration platform to build and deploy autonomous AI agent workflows.
projects.project_description: AgentMesh is a no-code platform for building and deploying autonomous AI agent workflows. On a visual canvas you drag out an agent, connect tools and actions, and wire them together. You choose an LLM (Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, or Mistral), write a system prompt, and deploy. The agent then runs on its own: it decides which tools to call (up to 15 steps per run) and streams every step into live logs.
projects.how_its_made: The product is two processes. The frontend is a Next.js 16 app (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind 4). The workflow editor is a custom SVG canvas: nodes, ports, and wires are drawn and hit-tested in our own code, including the port math and connection rules. That same app is statically exported and wrapped in Capacitor 8, so the website and the Android app ship from one codebase. Mobile-only screens are gated at runtime. The backend is Go. chi serves the HTTP API, pgx talks to PostgreSQL, and golang-migrate runs SQL migrations embedded in the binary on boot. A workflow is a graph of trigger, agent, tool, and action nodes. On deploy, the server walks every agent node, generates an Algorand Ed25519 keypair with the official Go SDK, encrypts the 25-word mnemonic with AES-GCM, and stores only the ciphertext. On run, the engine topologically sorts the graph and executes each level in parallel goroutines. An agent node is a function-calling loop against Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, or Mistral, capped at 15 iterations. Every log line goes through an in-process pub/sub bus and streams to the browser over server-sent events. Schedules run on cron. The payment path is the unusual part, and it is where Algorand earns its place. An x402 tool has no API key. The runner calls the URL, reads the HTTP 402 for price and recipient, decrypts that agent's mnemonic, signs a plain Algorand payment, submits it, and retries the same request with the transaction id in a header. The API checks the chain and returns the body. A basic transfer is the whole on-chain step. Algorand finality is about 3.5 seconds and fees are about $0.0002, so a synchronous pay-per-call round trip is fast and cheap enough to sit inside an agent loop. The x402 Bazaar mirrors a public catalog and keeps only endpoints payable on Algorand. People fund platform LLM credits on a separate rail: INR through Cashfree, or crypto through NOWPayments. Tendril leases are rented machines; the in-app console is an xterm session authenticated with that lease's own ed25519 key. Two sharp edges are worth naming. Postgres sits behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, which rejects prepared statements, so every query and the migrator are forced onto the simple protocol, including a postgres:// to pgx5:// rewrite just so migrations can run through the pooler. And the x402 sign-and-retry code is hash-pinned in tests. That path moves real funds, so it is frozen on purpose.

projects.title: Agile Wallet
projects.description: This wallet uses crypto agility to keep your funds safe during the quantum / AI age
projects.project_description: Agile Wallet is a Chrome extension wallet for an Ethereum smart account that can require any combination of signature schemes: ECDSA and the post-quantum schemes Falcon-512 and SPHINCS-. Users can update the schemes at any time without changing your address. The wallet also lets you subscribe to public break signals: on-chain flags a cryptographer raises when a scheme has been broken, for example by a quantum computer. When a signal you're subscribed to is raised, your wallet automatically requires an extra signature scheme of your choice, such as "if ECDSA is broken, also require SPHINCS-". Your account stays secure even if you never act on it yourself. The project needed a custom mempool for two reasons. First, verifying a post-quantum signature in the EVM costs far more than the canonical EIP-8141 mempool's 100,000-gas validation limit: about 600k gas for Falcon. Second, the canonical rules don't let validation read other contracts' storage, so a wallet can't check whether a break signal has been raised. The Crypto-Agility Mempool fixes both. Calls to listed signature verifiers are charged at a precompile price (3,000 gas for Falcon, as EIP-8052 proposes) instead of their EVM cost, and validation may read the single storage slot of listed break signals. Neither change is a security risk. Only pure signature verification functions get the extra credit, so it can't be spent on arbitrary computation. A break signal's slot can change only once, so it can never be used to repeatedly invalidate pending transactions, which is how mass invalidation attacks work.
projects.how_its_made:
This project consists of a Chrome extension, 5 Solidity contracts, and modified forks of the ERC-8421 Mempool Sidecar and ethrex. EXTENSION
A Chrome MV3 extension built with React, Vite and TypeScript. Keys: one 24-word BIP-39 seed phrase (noble/scure), encrypted with PBKDF2 and AES-GCM. ECDSA keys are derived via BIP-32, Falcon and SPHINCS- keys via HMAC-SHA512 sub-seeds, so breaking one scheme only exposes that scheme's key. Transactions: built with viem and forshtat's hegota-support as EIP-8141 frame transactions: a deploy frame on the first transaction, a VERIFY frame with one signature per required scheme, and SENDER frames for transfers, scheme changes and safeguard changes. Before signing, the extension reads the account's subscribed break signals from the chain and adds the backup scheme's signature for any raised signal. Signing: Falcon uses ZKNOX's falcon.js. For SPHINCS-, I compiled the Rust signer to WASM. Signing runs in Web Workers, so the popup doesn't freeze during the roughly 5 seconds a SPHINCS- signature takes. CONTRACTS
Built with Foundry and forshtat's hegota-support library. AgileWallet: the EIP-8141 smart account. Each transaction carries the wallet's scheme list and one signature per scheme. The wallet only stores the hash of the list. ECDSA uses the frame transaction's native signature. It also stores the hash of its break-signal subscriptions, and once a signal is raised, its VERIFY frame requires that subscription's backup scheme. AgileWalletFactory: deploys wallets with CREATE2. The address depends only on the owner's ECDSA key. FalconVerifier and SphincsVerifier: adapters behind a common IVerifier interface, around ZKNOX's ETHFALCON and nconsigny's SphincsC13Asm. BreakSignal: a contract with one storage slot that can only be set once. ETHREX
To credit the exact gas a verifier uses, the mempool needs the gas of each call. ethrex's ERC-7562 tracer didn't report it, so I forked ethrex and added gasUsed to every call in the trace. MEMPOOL
I forked the ERC-8421 Mempool Sidecar from the EF alt-mempool workshop and made it implement the Crypto-Agility Mempool, a custom alt-mempool ruleset I specified in docs/CRYPTO_AGILITY.md. The ruleset adds two relaxations to the canonical rules. First, for each call into a listed verifier, the sidecar adds the call's gas minus a precompile price to the transaction's verification budget. Second, validation can read slot 0 of a listed break signal without staking. The mempool's ID and gossip topic is the IPFS hash of the spec.
The devnet doesn't run my patched ethrex yet, so the sidecar has a hack to support unpatched ethrex. When the trace has no per-call gas, it credits a fixed amount, measured on the devnet, to every call into a listed verifier. This doesn't check that the call actually verified anything, so it's only safe on a trusted devnet. I built it with Claude Code. AI_USAGE.md logs what was AI-assisted.

projects.title: ALACTIC
projects.description: Verifiable AI support agents on 0G: private TEE answers with on-chain-verified proof receipts
projects.project_description: Alactic lets any business create an AI customer-support agent from its own knowledge (FAQs, documents, website pages) and deploy it as a public chat page, an embeddable website widget, or on Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack and Discord, all powered by one shared runtime. What makes it different is verifiability. Every customer-facing answer is generated on the 0G Compute Network in "Private" trust mode, meaning the model runs inside a hardware enclave (Intel TDX), and the request never silently falls back to a less private provider. For each answer, Alactic independently verifies the enclave's signature: it looks up the provider's service record on 0G Chain, fetches the signature for that chat, and recovers the signer, which must match the TEE signer registered and acknowledged on-chain. The result is shown as a badge and as a public proof receipt that anyone can re-check, with the model, provider address, TEE signer, cost, latency and an answer fingerprint. We're explicit about what is and isn't proven. Verification shows where and by which model an answer was produced, not that it's correct, so every answer cites the knowledge passages it used and falls back to a business-defined answer when the knowledge doesn't cover a question. Businesses sign in with their wallet (Sign-In with Ethereum). Customers chat with no wallet at all. Each agent has a planned public identity under alactic.eth on ENS. Extra features: knowledge-gap inbox, human handoff, agent test cases, voice notes and screenshots, and a daily owner briefing.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router, Cache Components) + TypeScript, Tailwind + shadcn/ui, wagmi + viem for wallet auth (SIWE with single-use nonces, domain binding and DB-backed sessions), PostgreSQL + pgvector (Supabase) with Drizzle ORM, Inngest for background ingestion, deployed on Vercel. 0G Compute (core): all customer-facing answers go through the 0G Compute Router's OpenAI-compatible API. We always pin the trust mode with the X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode header (default "private" = TeeML providers) and request verify_tee. Embeddings for the knowledge base also run on 0G (qwen3-embedding-0.6b, private mode, 1024-dim vectors), and the default chat model is 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b (TeeML). Model choices are validated against 0G's live model and provider catalog, which also shows real-time provider health per trust mode. Notable hack: in live testing on mainnet, the Router didn't return its documented tee_verified field, so we implemented 0G's verification procedure ourselves (mirroring the official SDK's processResponse): read the provider's Service record from the InferenceServing contract on 0G Chain (chain 16661) with viem, take the acknowledged TEE signer (honouring TargetSeparated), fetch {service.url}/v1/proxy/signature/{chatID} using the ZG-Res-Key header as chatID, and recover the EIP-191 signer. We also found that the signed payload is a hash of the end-to-end-encrypted exchange, so our UI states precisely that the proof covers the exchange, not the displayed words. Other live findings we handled: billing in USD micro-units, thinking models that need chat_template_kwargs to avoid spending tokens on reasoning (and leaked <think> text, which we strip), undocumented model_overloaded and trust_mode_mismatch errors, and a key restricted to private mode as defence in depth. Security: tenant isolation is enforced in the database with composite foreign keys (org, agent) from sources → documents → chunks → conversations → inferences; published agent versions are immutable via a Postgres trigger; prompt-injection-resistant prompts (platform policy first, knowledge escaped as untrusted data, no tools); rate limits per visitor, IP and agent; a widget CSP frame-ancestors allowlist; webhook signature checks for every channel; connector credentials encrypted with AES-256-GCM. 199 automated tests.

Overall Architecture: ESP32 → Wi-Fi → Node.js API → PostgreSQL → React Dashboard Payment and audit workflow: Payment → Backend API → Hedera HCS → Immutable Audit Record → Dashboard Verification 3. Database Architecture We implemented a PostgreSQL architecture with six separate schemas to organize different parts of the application. Database Schema Responsibility Stored Information identity User management Users and sessions property Property management Properties, rooms and tenancies metering Electricity monitoring Meters and sensor readings billing Billing management Tariffs, bills and disputes audit Audit and compliance Events and CRE reports system System configuration Integration states and configurations We also use PostgreSQL JSONB fields for flexible storage of sensor metadata, allowing us to accommodate changing ESP32 payload structures without repeatedly modifying database schemas. 4. Hedera Blockchain Integration We use Hedera Consensus Service as an immutable audit layer rather than using blockchain as our primary database. Component Implementation Network Hedera Testnet Service Hedera Consensus Service HCS Topic 0.0.11169785 Main Purpose Payment verification and audit records Primary Storage PostgreSQL Blockchain Storage Payment events and system audit information Wallet HashPack Payment Workflow: Step Action 1 A renter initiates a bill payment. 2 The backend receives the payment information and transaction ID. 3 The backend submits the relevant payment event to the Hedera HCS topic. 4 Hedera Consensus Service records the event with consensus ordering. 5 The application checks the HCS event for verification. 6 The bill status transitions through pending, verifying and paid. 7 Landlord and renter dashboards synchronize the updated information. This separation allows PostgreSQL to handle fast application queries while Hedera provides an independently verifiable audit trail. 5. Interesting Engineering Challenges and Hacky Solutions Challenge Our Solution Why We Did It Stale frontend data Used cache: 'no-store' and documented hard-refresh requirements. Prevented outdated cached readings from being displayed during development. Incorrect property associations Used PostgreSQL JSONB manipulation and runtime room-access checks. Avoided a time-consuming migration of existing development records. Two storage systems Used PostgreSQL for primary data and HCS for immutable audit events. Allowed us to combine application performance with blockchain verification. Different user permissions Implemented reusable role-based API filtering for landlords and renters. Avoided duplicating API endpoints while restricting access to relevant information. Changing sensor payloads Used JSONB for flexible meter metadata. Made it easier to add or modify sensor fields during hardware development. Live dashboard updates Implemented five-second API polling. Avoided the complexity of WebSocket connection management during the hackathon. 6. Hedera Consensus Service Payment and audit event recording Provides consensus ordering and a permanent audit trail. HashPack Wallet connectivity Enables users to interact with the Hedera ecosystem. viem Blockchain and wallet interaction Provides a structured interface for blockchain operations. PostgreSQL Application database Provides reliable relational storage and flexible JSONB support. ESP32 Electricity monitoring hardware Connects physical electricity consumption with the digital application. 7. Security and Data Validation Feature Implementation Data Validation Zod schemas validate incoming data. User Authentication JWT-based sessions. Role-Based Access Separate landlord and renter permissions. Room Access Control Checks whether users can access particular rooms. Meter Validation Verifies meter-room associations. Reading Status Supports accepted, rejected and quarantined readings. API Protection Express rate limiting. Database Organization Six separate PostgreSQL schemas. 8. Current Implementation and Technical Trade-offs Area Current Implementation Future Improvement Dashboard Updates Five-second polling WebSockets for lower-latency updates HCS Integration Event submission and verification Retry mechanisms, exponential backoff and transactional outbox Hardware Firmware Manual ESP32 flashing OTA firmware updates Authentication JWT sessions Refresh tokens, password recovery and email verification Frontend Caching Manual cache-bypass workaround Proper cache invalidation Data Types Shared Zod schemas Automated type generation across application boundaries 9. What Makes ChargeMesh Technically Interesting? Innovation Explanation Physical-to-Digital Integration Connects electricity monitoring hardware with a full-stack web application. Hybrid Architecture Uses PostgreSQL for application data and Hedera for immutable audit records. Transparent Billing Links electricity consumption with billing and payment workflows. Role-Based System Provides separate experiences and permissions for landlords and renters. Flexible Meter Data Uses JSONB to accommodate changing hardware payloads. Blockchain Auditability Makes payment events independently verifiable through Hedera Consensus Service. 10. Overall Development Summary ChargeMesh combines IoT hardware, full-stack web development and blockchain technology into a shared electricity monitoring and billing platform. The most important architectural decision was not putting everything on the blockchain. We deliberately kept frequently accessed application data in PostgreSQL and used Hedera Consensus Service for payment events and auditability. This hybrid approach allowed us to build a practical application while introducing blockchain only where decentralization and independent verification provide meaningful value. Our development prioritized getting the complete physical-to-digital workflow working, from ESP32 electricity readings to dashboards, billing and blockchain-based payment auditing, while documenting the engineering trade-offs that remain for future production improvements.

# ChargeMesh – Complete Project Technical Documentation

## 1. Project Overview

| Category | Details |
|---|---|
| Project Name | ChargeMesh |
| Event | ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026 |
| Project Type | IoT + Blockchain + Electricity Metering and Billing |
| Core Purpose | Transparent electricity monitoring, billing, and blockchain-verified payments |

| Backend URL | http://localhost:4000 |
| HCS Topic | 0.0.11169785 |

**Project Description:**

ChargeMesh is a comprehensive electricity metering and billing platform that bridges physical ESP32-powered electricity submeters with blockchain-verified transactions. It enables landlords to monitor electricity consumption and manage billing while renters can view their electricity usage, manage bills, submit payments, and access verifiable transaction records through the Hedera network.

---

## 2. Technical Architecture

| Metering | PZEM-004T | Measures electrical parameters |

## 7. Electricity Billing Calculation

ChargeMesh calculates electricity charges using cumulative energy readings.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| startingCumulativeKwh | Starting cumulative electricity reading |
| endingCumulativeKwh | Ending cumulative electricity reading |
| consumptionKwh | Electricity consumed during the billing period |
| rateNprPerKWh | Electricity tariff in NPR per kWh |
| electricityChargeNpr | Final electricity charge |

### Billing Formula

```text
consumptionKwh =
endingCumulativeKwh - startingCumulativeKwh

electricityChargeNpr =
consumptionKwh × rateNprPerKWh

electricityChargeNpr =
round to nearest NPR cent
```

### Example Calculation

|---|---:|
| Starting Reading | 10.000 kWh |
| Ending Reading | 15.000 kWh |
| Consumption | 5.000 kWh |
| Electricity Rate | NPR 12.50/kWh |
| Electricity Charge | NPR 62.50 |
