## 15. Project Mission

ChargeMesh aims to bridge the gap between physical electricity meters and digital blockchain verification.

By combining ESP32-based electricity monitoring, a full-stack billing application, PostgreSQL data management and Hedera Consensus Service, ChargeMesh provides a transparent electricity management platform for small-scale rental properties.

Its primary goals are:

1. Make electricity consumption measurable and transparent.
2. Help landlords manage electricity billing efficiently.
3. Give renters better visibility into their electricity bills.
4. Reduce billing disputes through verifiable consumption and payment records.
5. Use blockchain where immutable verification adds meaningful value.
6. Build a foundation for automated electricity management in shared living environments.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
# ChargeMesh – Technical Implementation & Development Details

## 1. Technology Stack

| Layer | Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | React 19, TypeScript | Interactive landlord and renter dashboards |
| Build Tool | Vite 8 | Fast development and frontend bundling |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS 4 | Responsive user interface |
| Navigation | React Router | Navigation between landlord and renter dashboards |
| Icons | Lucide React | UI icons |
| Backend | Node.js + Express | REST API and business logic |
| Language | TypeScript | Type safety across the application |
| Database | PostgreSQL | Stores users, properties, meter readings, bills and audit records |
| Validation | Zod | Runtime validation and shared data schemas |
| Blockchain | Hedera Hashgraph | Decentralized consensus and immutable audit records |
| Blockchain Service | Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) | Records payment events and audit information |
| Wallet | HashPack | Hedera wallet integration |
| SDK | @hiero-ledger/sdk | Hedera network operations |
| Web3 Library | viem | Wallet and blockchain interaction |
| Hardware | ESP32 | Collects electricity meter readings |
| Communication | Wi-Fi + HTTP | Sends hardware readings to the backend |
| Infrastructure | Docker, Environment Variables | Development and configuration |

## 2. System Architecture and Data Flow

| Step | Component | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ESP32 Hardware | Collects electricity measurements such as voltage, current and power. |
| 2 | Wi-Fi | Transmits meter readings to the backend. |
| 3 | Node.js + Express API | Receives and validates incoming sensor data. |
| 4 | PostgreSQL | Stores meter readings, property information and billing records. |
| 5 | React Dashboard | Displays electricity usage, bills and room information. |
| 6 | Hedera HCS | Records payment events and important audit information. |
| 7 | HashPack Wallet | Enables wallet connectivity and Hedera-based payment workflows. |

**Overall Architecture:**

ESP32 → Wi-Fi → Node.js API → PostgreSQL → React Dashboard

Payment and audit workflow:

Payment → Backend API → Hedera HCS → Immutable Audit Record → Dashboard Verification

## 3. Database Architecture

We implemented a PostgreSQL architecture with six separate schemas to organize different parts of the application.

| Database Schema | Responsibility | Stored Information |
|---|---|---|
| identity | User management | Users and sessions |
| property | Property management | Properties, rooms and tenancies |
| metering | Electricity monitoring | Meters and sensor readings |
| billing | Billing management | Tariffs, bills and disputes |
| audit | Audit and compliance | Events and CRE reports |
| system | System configuration | Integration states and configurations |

We also use PostgreSQL JSONB fields for flexible storage of sensor metadata, allowing us to accommodate changing ESP32 payload structures without repeatedly modifying database schemas.

## 4. Hedera Blockchain Integration

We use Hedera Consensus Service as an immutable audit layer rather than using blockchain as our primary database.

| Component | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Network | Hedera Testnet |
| Service | Hedera Consensus Service |
| HCS Topic | 0.0.11169785 |
| Main Purpose | Payment verification and audit records |
| Primary Storage | PostgreSQL |
| Blockchain Storage | Payment events and system audit information |
| Wallet | HashPack |

**Payment Workflow:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | A renter initiates a bill payment. |
| 2 | The backend receives the payment information and transaction ID. |
| 3 | The backend submits the relevant payment event to the Hedera HCS topic. |
| 4 | Hedera Consensus Service records the event with consensus ordering. |
| 5 | The application checks the HCS event for verification. |
| 6 | The bill status transitions through pending, verifying and paid. |
| 7 | Landlord and renter dashboards synchronize the updated information. |

This separation allows PostgreSQL to handle fast application queries while Hedera provides an independently verifiable audit trail.

## 5. Interesting Engineering Challenges and Hacky Solutions

| Challenge | Our Solution | Why We Did It |
|---|---|---|
| Stale frontend data | Used `cache: 'no-store'` and documented hard-refresh requirements. | Prevented outdated cached readings from being displayed during development. |
| Incorrect property associations | Used PostgreSQL JSONB manipulation and runtime room-access checks. | Avoided a time-consuming migration of existing development records. |
| Two storage systems | Used PostgreSQL for primary data and HCS for immutable audit events. | Allowed us to combine application performance with blockchain verification. |
| Different user permissions | Implemented reusable role-based API filtering for landlords and renters. | Avoided duplicating API endpoints while restricting access to relevant information. |
| Changing sensor payloads | Used JSONB for flexible meter metadata. | Made it easier to add or modify sensor fields during hardware development. |
| Live dashboard updates | Implemented five-second API polling. | Avoided the complexity of WebSocket connection management during the hackathon. |

## 6. Partner Technologies and Their Benefits

| Technology / Partner | How We Used It | Benefit to ChargeMesh |
|---|---|---|
| Hedera Hashgraph | Consensus and audit infrastructure | Provides an immutable and independently verifiable record of payment events. |
| Hedera Consensus Service | Payment and audit event recording | Provides consensus ordering and a permanent audit trail. |
| HashPack | Wallet connectivity | Enables users to interact with the Hedera ecosystem. |
| viem | Blockchain and wallet interaction | Provides a structured interface for blockchain operations. |
| PostgreSQL | Application database | Provides reliable relational storage and flexible JSONB support. |
| ESP32 | Electricity monitoring hardware | Connects physical electricity consumption with the digital application. |

## 7. Security and Data Validation

| Feature | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Data Validation | Zod schemas validate incoming data. |
| User Authentication | JWT-based sessions. |
| Role-Based Access | Separate landlord and renter permissions. |
| Room Access Control | Checks whether users can access particular rooms. |
| Meter Validation | Verifies meter-room associations. |
| Reading Status | Supports accepted, rejected and quarantined readings. |
| API Protection | Express rate limiting. |
| Database Organization | Six separate PostgreSQL schemas. |

## 8. Current Implementation and Technical Trade-offs

| Area | Current Implementation | Future Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Dashboard Updates | Five-second polling | WebSockets for lower-latency updates |
| HCS Integration | Event submission and verification | Retry mechanisms, exponential backoff and transactional outbox |
| Hardware Firmware | Manual ESP32 flashing | OTA firmware updates |
| Authentication | JWT sessions | Refresh tokens, password recovery and email verification |
| Frontend Caching | Manual cache-bypass workaround | Proper cache invalidation |
| Data Types | Shared Zod schemas | Automated type generation across application boundaries |

## 9. What Makes ChargeMesh Technically Interesting?

| Innovation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Physical-to-Digital Integration | Connects electricity monitoring hardware with a full-stack web application. |
| Hybrid Architecture | Uses PostgreSQL for application data and Hedera for immutable audit records. |
| Transparent Billing | Links electricity consumption with billing and payment workflows. |
| Role-Based System | Provides separate experiences and permissions for landlords and renters. |
| Flexible Meter Data | Uses JSONB to accommodate changing hardware payloads. |
| Blockchain Auditability | Makes payment events independently verifiable through Hedera Consensus Service. |

## 10. Overall Development Summary

ChargeMesh combines IoT hardware, full-stack web development and blockchain technology into a shared electricity monitoring and billing platform.

The most important architectural decision was not putting everything on the blockchain. We deliberately kept frequently accessed application data in PostgreSQL and used Hedera Consensus Service for payment events and auditability.

This hybrid approach allowed us to build a practical application while introducing blockchain only where decentralization and independent verification provide meaningful value.

Our development prioritized getting the complete physical-to-digital workflow working, from ESP32 electricity readings to dashboards, billing and blockchain-based payment auditing, while documenting the engineering trade-offs that remain for future production improvements.

projects.title: Smartician
projects.description: Smartician: a 0G AI examiner tests machine operators and issues a licence verifiable on ENS
projects.project_description: Machines like CNC machining centres keep getting more complex, and the people who can safely teach them are scarce and expensive. Training on the real machine is risky: a wrong start-up order can wreck the tool or eject a badly clamped part. And as AI starts to decide who is ready to operate dangerous equipment, the training record sits in one company’s database, so after an accident nobody outside can check whether the record, or the AI’s decision, was real. Smartician is a mixed-reality trainer for both problems. On a Meta Quest 3 in passthrough, a worker stands in their real room in front of a life-size virtual machine and works through the procedure with the controllers, while highlights show which control comes next. We didn’t have access to real industrial machinery, so both machines in the demo are 3D models: a CNC vertical machining centre with a 22-step start-up, set-up and run procedure, and a benchtop drill press with a short checklist of 13 interactions. They are simulated twins of the operating procedure, with interlocks modelled on typical machine behaviour (for example, the door must be closed before a cycle starts), not replicas of any manufacturer’s machine. Motion and interlocks run on the headset; the decisions run on 0G. An AI technician on 0G watches each action and the machine’s state, speaks corrections, and must pass the worker at safety checkpoints. In Test mode there are no hints. Every session becomes a hash-chained episode log on 0G Storage with a 0G request id per decision, anchored on 0G Chain. A worker who passes receives a licence: an expiring, revocable ENS subname (ENSv2 on Sepolia) whose records point to that evidence. Before Test mode unlocks, the worker checks in with World, so one real person sat the test (sandbox identities). Anyone can verify a licence without asking us: the public verify page, or ENS and 0G directly, check the licence, the anchor and the stored session live. Without 0G the company could quietly change the AI’s verdict or rewrite the log. Without ENS the licence stays stuck in one database and revocation isn’t public. Without World someone could sit the test for another person.
projects.how_its_made: Smartician has three parts: a Quest 3 mixed-reality app, a hosted backend and a web dashboard. We had no real machinery, so both machines in the demo (a CNC vertical machining centre and a benchtop drill press are 3D models. Headset app. Unity 6 with the Meta XR SDK (OpenXR), passthrough and controllers. The machine bodies were generated with Meshy and imported as glTF. The interactive parts (door, control panel, buttons, E-stop, lever, workpiece, tool) are built in Unity from primitives and placed on anchor points on the model, so the baked-in spindle and table stay static and axis motion shows on the panel readouts. A click-to-activate controller ray drives every control, and a highlight system outlines the next control. Interlocks (a door that is open blocks cycle start, E-stop, power order) run locally on the headset. Motion stays on the device and 0G makes the decisions at key moments. Backend. Node and TypeScript on Fastify, validated with zod, hosted on Railway. After each action the headset sends the new actions and the machine state, and at checkpoints a frame of the worker's view [keep only if still true]. The backend asks a 0G model to judge, validates the reply against a strict schema and returns a verdict. If 0G can't be reached, the headset shows a red "Do not continue" panel and nothing unlocks. There is no fallback that fakes a decision. 0G. The judge is qwen3.8-flash on the 0G Router, and corrections are spoken with 0G text to speech. Each session is uploaded as a hash-chained bundle to 0G Storage with the 0G SDK, every record carrying its 0G request id. A small Solidity contract, SessionRegistry, anchors the root on 0G Galileo. The backend can download a bundle by root hash and re-verify the chain, which powers the replay player. ENS (ENSv2, Sepolia). We deployed our own UserRegistry through the VerifiableFactory under smartician.eth. A custom CertificateRegistrar lets only the issuer wallet issue and revoke licences. The resolver uses Enhanced Access Control so the issuer can write only specific text keys (mrt.evidence, mrt.verdict, mrt.issuedAt, alias, description, class, mrt.human), and writes to other keys are refused. A licence's mrt.evidence record is 0g:// plus the storage root, so the licence points to its own evidence. The machine has a passport name and the AI technician has an agent identity. World. The worker checks in on a phone first. Our server starts a World device-authorization request and validates the signed ID token itself with the jose library (signature, issuer, audience, expiry, freshness, method). The browser result is never trusted, and Test mode stays locked until the server accepts it. Sandbox identities only. Dashboard. React with Vite and Tailwind: live event stream, proof chain, episode replay, licence records and a public verify page. Venue Wi-Fi stalled new connections to 0G and looked like false outages, so we added short per-attempt timeouts with fresh-connection retries and moved the backend to Railway. The model's replies were being cut off by a token limit, so we raised it and repair a reply that is complete except for its final closing brace. The schema still validates it. qwen3.8-flash rejects JSON mode, so the format is enforced by prompt and schema.

projects.title: AfterKey
projects.description: Release gate for ENS config: Chainlink CRE verifies, owner activates, Uniswap LP vaults enforce.
projects.project_description:
AfterKey is a release gate for shared onchain configuration, built on ENSv2, Chainlink CRE and Uniswap v3 on Sepolia. The problem: Teams and AI agents read operators, treasuries and limits from ENS records. Anyone holding a role can change those records, and nothing checks what depends on them first. Offboarding has the same blind spot. Under ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control, removing a departing operator's text-key permission does not remove a separately granted resolver-wide role. In Uniswap v3, revoking one position's approval leaves portfolio-wide approval active. The team believes access is gone when it isn't. How AfterKey works: Stage: The owner publishes a candidate configuration (operator, treasury, expiry) as an ENSv2 data record. Nothing live changes yet.
Verify: A Chainlink CRE workflow independently re-reads the candidate, the gate and every registered Uniswap v3 LP consumer at one block. It then writes a signed, short-lived report onchain through the CRE forwarder. The gate checks the forwarder, workflow ID, owner, candidate digest, epoch and coverage before accepting it.
Activate: Only the owner can activate, and only the exact digest and epoch CRE checked.
Enforce: Each LP consumer contract holds one Uniswap v3 position NFT. Before every collection it asks the gate whether the operator is authorized for the active version. Operators can collect fees but never withdraw liquidity, and fees can only go to the fixed owner treasury. If the config changes, operations prepared against the old version revert.
Offboarding: AfterKey also ships a fully verified offboarding workflow. It scans both ENS permission scopes, registry roles, and individual and portfolio Uniswap approvals for a departing wallet. It then prepares owner-reviewed revocations, broadest first, and verifies afterward that the team's ENS name, records and LP positions are intact. Proof on Sepolia: Ten ENS receipts and 30 historical-state checks
Complete Uniswap offboarding of positions 234145 and 234146, with 14 checks
Authenticated CRE executions that link a completed GitHub departure case to before/after chain state
Release-gate consumers deployed and holding both NFTs, with the CRE workflow binding signed live in MetaMask
CRE never holds the owner's key. Every change is signed in the owner's own wallet.
projects.how_its_made:
Stack: Most of AfterKey is plain TypeScript. The frontend uses Vite 6 and viem, with no framework, and reads ENSv2 and Uniswap v3 straight from Sepolia RPC. There's no indexer, backend database or subgraph. The two Solidity contracts, ENSReleaseGate and ReleaseLPVault, are compiled with solc 0.8.30 inside a Node script. The CRE workflow is TypeScript on @chainlink/cre-sdk, compiled to WASM with the CRE CLI. The signed relay is one policy module that builds three ways: a local Node server, a Vercel function and a Cloudflare Worker. How the pieces fit: ENSv2 is the source of truth. We follow the live registry hierarchy from manager.eth down to our subnames. We verify the official Verifiable Factory, Permissioned Resolver and User Registry implementations against pinned runtime-code hashes, then read Enhanced Access Control with hasRoles. The candidate configuration is published as an ABI-encoded ENS data record (operator, treasury, manager, expiry) and hashed into a digest.
Chainlink CRE is the independent second reader. A cron trigger, an EVM-log trigger on Uniswap approval events and an owner-signed HTTP trigger all run one workflow. It re-reads the gate, the candidate resolver, every registered LP consumer and NFT custody at a single block, then delivers a signed report through the KeystoneForwarder. The gate only accepts it if the forwarder, workflow ID, workflow owner, chain, digest, epoch, coverage hash and validity window all match.
Uniswap v3 holds the actual money. We use the official Sepolia NonfungiblePositionManager only. Each ReleaseLPVault holds one position NFT, and before every collect call it asks the gate whether the operator is authorized for the active version. The recipient is fixed to the owner treasury when the vault is deployed.
How the partner tech helped: ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control made the core problem concrete and measurable. Key-scoped roles and resolver-wide roles are separate grants, so we could show a real narrow revoke leaving a broad role active. CRE gave us a reader that isn't our own browser, which turns "the UI says it's safe" into a signed, onchain attestation. Uniswap's two separate approval paths (getApproved and isApprovedForAll) reproduced the same trap on real assets. The hacky parts: GitHub issues as an HR system. A departure case is a closed, labeled GitHub issue. CRE fetches it over HTTP, uses consensus to check that the right approver closed it, then joins it with before/after chain state.
Browser-signed CRE triggers without a backend key. The browser has MetaMask sign a five-minute authorization tied to the exact request body. The relay checks the signature, body, expiry and deployed scope before forwarding to the CRE gateway, and it never holds a signing key.
Hitting CRE's read limit. Our first release-verification run was accepted but failed at the contract-read capability limit. We rewrote the reader to batch every ENS and Uniswap read through Multicall3 in one call.
Proof from execution logs. CRE output is emitted as digest-bound log chunks. A collector script pulls authenticated CRE logs and rebuilds the result, and it only accepts it as proof if the digest and scope match.
Resolver surgery mid-hackathon. Our first resolver turned out to lack data-write authority for the release record. We deployed a replacement Permissioned Resolver, pulled both NFTs out of the old consumers, and redeposited them into new ones without losing the original name.
No simulations. Every claim in the README links to a real Sepolia receipt or a historical-state check pinned to a block. Read-only checks are labeled separately from mined transactions.
AI assistance (Codex, then Claude Code) helped with implementation, debugging, tests and docs. It's disclosed in docs/overview/AI_ATTRIBUTION.md. Every privileged transaction was reviewed and signed by the owner.

Proof from execution logs. CRE output is emitted as digest-bound log chunks. A collector script pulls authenticated CRE logs and rebuilds the result, and it only accepts it as proof if the digest and scope match.
Resolver surgery mid-hackathon. Our first resolver turned out to lack data-write authority for the release record. We deployed a replacement Permissioned Resolver, pulled both NFTs out of the old consumers, and redeposited them into new ones without losing the original name.
No simulations. Every claim in the README links to a real Sepolia receipt or a historical-state check pinned to a block. Read-only checks are labeled separately from mined transactions.
AI assistance (Codex, then Claude Code) helped with implementation, debugging, tests and docs. It's disclosed in docs/overview/AI_ATTRIBUTION.md. Every privileged transaction was reviewed and signed by the owner.

projects.title: AUTOMATE
projects.description: AI workflows that move money only after a World ID human says yes: USDC on Arc, proof on 0G
projects.project_description: Automate Trust Layer adds trust to Automate, my live workflow builder (automateplatform.in) that small businesses in India use to run AI agents on WhatsApp, email, Zoho and Shopify. Once an AI agent can take payments or issue refunds, two things still run on trust: who approved the money, and what the workflow actually did. I added six steps to the flow builder's canvas: Human approval (World ID Agent Pass): the run waits until the owner signs in fresh with World ID. Verify human (World ID IDKit): one refund per unique human, whatever number they message from. Collect USDC (Arc): the customer pays into TrustEscrow, a contract built in Arc Studio, and the run continues when the payment lands. Send USDC (Arc): refunds or releases the escrowed order, only right after an approval; one approval allows one payment. Proof on 0G (0G Storage): the run's record is sealed on 0G, and anyone can re-verify it by its root hash. AI step on the 0G Compute Router: answers keep their 0G request id in that record. The demo: a customer orders on WhatsApp, pays USDC into escrow, asks for a refund, proves they are one unique human, the owner approves with World ID, the escrow refunds them, and the run's proof lands on 0G. Denied, expired, repeat-claim and second-refund paths move no money. I also added Sign in with MetaMask (Sign-In with Ethereum), from the browser extension or by QR code on a phone. Testnet only.
projects.how_its_made: Automate is a React Router 8 app on a Node.js engine that walks each flow's node graph. A pending store pauses a run at a trust step and resumes it on the outcome's wire (approved, denied, expired, paid). Every trust page is a public link, checked entirely on the server. World ID: Agent Pass through World's OIDC (auth.world.org) with PKCE, a nonce and max_age=300. The server verifies the id_token against World's JWKS (signature, audience, nonce, sign-in time) and binds the first approver. IDKit v4 (@worldcoin/idkit-core) uses a request signed on the server; proofs are verified with /api/v4/verify against our own action, one nullifier per action. Arc: ethers v6 on Arc testnet, with native USDC. TrustEscrow was written, reviewed, tested (65 Foundry tests) and deployed with Arc Studio. Automate's operator signs keccak256(chainId, escrow, orderId, amount, deadline), so only the exact quoted amount can be paid; a watcher reads the escrow's Paid events with eth_getLogs; only the operator can refund or release, and a payer can reclaim after 14 days. 0G: the run record becomes canonical JSON (sorted keys), is hashed with sha256 and uploaded with @0gfoundation/0g-storage-ts-sdk. Verify downloads it by root hash with the Merkle proof and compares three digests: downloaded, stored and rebuilt. Phone numbers become an HMAC id and no message text is stored. The AI step and the Python knowledge service (ported from my earlier MetaCortex RAG) call the 0G Compute Router's OpenAI-compatible API. The hacky part: MetaMask QR sign-in uses our own relay instead of WalletConnect. The QR deep-links into the MetaMask app's browser, the phone signs an EIP-4361 message bound to that request, and the computer polls with a secret kept in an httpOnly cookie. A security review found the QR could be relayed from someone else's screen (QRLJacking), so the phone now shows a 6-digit code the computer must type. "One approval, one payment" is enforced in the engine, not in a prompt. Tests: 333 offline checks (World ID 71, Arc 81, escrow 23, end-to-end flow 46, MetaMask sign-in 81, Python 31), with every outside call faked.

projects.title: 16signals
projects.description: Trustless proof of professional identity for open-source and other developers.
projects.project_description: 16Signals: Your Work Is Your Identity In the age of AI, anyone can write a convincing CV, generate code, or build an impressive GitHub profile. But none of these necessarily prove real engineering experience or technical understanding. 16Signals is building a portable, verifiable professional identity based on evidence of actual work, not self-reported skills. We use privacy-preserving verification, including TLSNotary, to help developers prove their contributions and technical experience across GitHub and cloud infrastructure such as AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, without exposing sensitive data. This evidence becomes a Developer Passport: a reusable professional identity backed by verifiable credentials that developers can carry across companies, countries, and open-source communities. We don't claim to prove someone is a perfect engineer. We provide independently checkable evidence that helps others evaluate their experience beyond a CV. Our vision is a decentralized meritocracy for global talent, where opportunities are based on demonstrated work rather than credentials, geography, or connections.
projects.how_its_made: 16Signals is built with React, NestJS, PostgreSQL, and Go. We use TLSNotary (Ethereum Foundation) for privacy-preserving verification of developers' technical work across GitHub and now (**hackathon feature) cloud platforms, including AWS and Google Cloud. Our system combines cryptographic proofs with deterministic code analysis and issues signed W3C Verifiable Credentials using did:web and ES256. These credentials form a portable Developer Passport. The key innovation is verifying evidence of real technical experience without exposing private repositories, sensitive infrastructure data, or credentials. In the hackathon we added cloud verifications to deepen our evidence sources beyond Github. With these we can expand checks for dev ops engineers or backend and data engineers - and eventually expand to any service that requires to log in and handle data that direclty relates to professional skills through an online portal. In our current implementation we are doing Zero Knowledge Proofs to sanitize data direclty on the extension, so that employer sensitive detials never even hit our servers. Because of this there is a tradeoff here of speed for privacy that we will optimize further after hackathon. It is for this reason that for demo we have 2 options - the full live verificaiton (which can take up to 10-15 mins) and the "fast-replay" which checks simply account ownership and verifies the previously created proofs (up to 2 mins). The fast-replay is intended for demo puproses when time limit is a constraint. This feature was made open source to ensure trust and resilience as we hope it can be built further and verfieid by anybody in the community.

projects.title: MeshRover
projects.description: Robots that never need the internet, and stop safely when their AI is out of reach.
projects.project_description: MeshRover is a fleet of warehouse rovers that never touch the internet. They talk to their base station only over an encrypted Offline Protocol mesh (MLS-sealed, peer to peer, Bluetooth for phones). Only the base goes online. At every junction a rover sends its camera frame over the mesh, and the base asks a TEE-attested 0G vision model what to do. The problem: field robots in warehouses, farms, construction sites and disaster zones lose their link all the time. When their cloud brain is out of reach, most stacks carry on with a stale plan or fall back to a local guess nobody audited. Their local radio control is usually unauthenticated too, so anyone in range can send "go". MeshRover fixes both: No brain means stop. A rover moves only on a 0G decision that answers its pending sequence number before a 6.5 s deadline. A timeout, an answer that doesn't parse, an action it wasn't offered or a wrong seq all lead to SAFE_STOPPED. There's no local model, no default action and no cached plan. Turn off the base's Wi-Fi and the next rover to reach a junction stops and says why. The operator's phone still sees it over Bluetooth. Turn the Wi-Fi back on and the rover carries on. A human signs off on risky moves. Before a rover enters the restricted zone C, the operator approves with World ID on their phone. The link reaches the phone over the mesh. The approval works once and expires after 10 s. Cancel, and the rover stays put. Only the fleet's keys count. The fleet is an ENSv2 namespace (meshrover-demo.eth) with a subname for each robot, operator and the base. Each has a role, an expiry and its engine's mesh key. Both the base and the rover check every command and approval against this roster, offline too. When a contractor's subname expires, their approval is refused. Every episode is on the record. Every decision (with its 0G request ID and the exact frame the model saw), safe-stop, approval and denial goes into one log file. When the episode ends, the log is uploaded to 0G Storage and its root is anchored on 0G Chain. The public dashboard at meshrover.app lists the anchored episodes, replays each one from 0G Storage and shows the ENS roster. Rover A also has a real safety camera: the laptop's webcam is part of its checkpoint frame, and a hand over the lens makes 0G choose stop. A camera frame that is missing or stale also means stop. The rovers are simulated on a Mac for the demo, but each one already runs its own Offline Protocol engine and talks to the base only through it, never through the simulator. Moving to physical robots changes nothing in the mesh, the protocol or the safety checks: the robot runs the same engine with Bluetooth turned on (a config switch), and the simulator's motion and camera are swapped for the robot's own drivers. Motion runs on the rover at 20 Hz and never waits on the network. 0G decides at checkpoints and keeps the record, and nothing a rover does waits on a blockchain.
projects.how_its_made: Stack: one Node + TypeScript package (run with tsx, tested with node:test) for the base and the rover simulator, a Vite dashboard deployed as a Cloudflare Worker, Foundry for the contracts, and a React Native operator app for iOS and Android. Offline Protocol (mesh): each rover and the base drive their own offline-protocol-service engine through its local JSON-RPC-over-WebSocket API. They share no memory, even though they all run on one Mac over loopback peer streams with no LAN. Rover B peers only with rover A, so its traffic is relayed. The base's engine also runs BLE, so the operator phones (React Native, @offline-protocol/mesh-sdk, Bluetooth only, internet off) join the mesh directly. The base exposes five mesh services: fleet.decide and fleet.approve (requests), and fleet.status, fleet.approvals and fleet.roster (subscriptions). Hacky bit: service bodies are only MLS-sealed once the two engines have a session, so each rover sends the base one direct message at startup to open it. Both sides then treat any unsealed body as doubt, which means a stop. The app shows each phone's hop count and how many frames it has relayed for others. 0G Compute: the base calls the 0G Router in verified trust mode (verify_tee: true, temperature 0, JSON output) with 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, a TEE-attested (TDX) vision model. At startup the base checks that the model is listed, takes images and is TEE-attested, or it refuses to start. My spikes set a 6 s timeout on the base and a 6.5 s deadline on the rover. Turning thinking off cut the model's latency from 13-28 s to 1.6-2.6 s per frame. Every request ID and the response key are logged, so each move traces back to a 0G call. 0G Storage + 0G Chain: when the episode ends, the base uploads the JSONL log, which holds every frame, so the root covers the frames too. It then calls EpisodeAnchor.anchor() on Galileo, retrying every 15 s while offline. It checks rootOf() first, so a rerun can't anchor twice. The dashboard reads the anchor events with eth_getLogs straight from the browser, downloads the file from the storage indexer by its root and replays it frame by frame. World ID: robots have no browser, so the base runs World's OAuth device flow. The link and code travel to the operator's phone over the Bluetooth mesh, the only place an approval can happen. The base validates the ID token itself, maps it to an enrolled fleet name and issues a single-use approval. World sub values are never logged or published. ENSv2 (Sepolia): a Foundry script registers meshrover-demo.eth and a subname for each robot, operator and the base, each with its own PermissionedResolver. Text records hold the role, the member list and the engine's signed mesh invite, using ENSIP-5 keys in the fleet's own namespace plus ENSIP-26 agent-context and agent-endpoint on the robots. The base reads the roster with viem every 60 s, turns each invite into a mesh address through the engine's parse_invite and publishes the roster over the mesh. Rovers cache it, so expiries are enforced offline. authorize() checks expiry, then role, then mesh key, on both the base and the rover. Safety camera: ffmpeg grabs the webcam at 2 fps, writing each frame atomically. A reader outside the motion loop decodes the newest one and composites it into the same 640x240 JPEG as the drawn view. The request format, the episode hash and the replay stay the same, and a frame older than 2s means a safe-stop. Also notable: every safety check (parseDecision, acceptDecision, authorize, acceptApproval) has tests for its reject paths. I found a mesh SDK relay bug (each BLE phone counted as two neighbours and pushed rover B out of the base's relay fanout) and worked around it by raising the fanout on the base. I also built a local mock 0G Router for development, but its episodes are labelled and can never be recorded on chain.

projects.title: AgentCV
projects.description: The on-chain resume for AI agents — profiles backed by real eval runs, not claims.
projects.project_description: Agent directories list what AI agents claim. AgentCV shows what they actually did. A buyer searches the directory, or describes a task and lets a 0G model rank matching agents; the model may only return agents that exist in the directory. The buyer can then run a candidate agent's HTTP endpoint against a fixed, versioned task set. AgentCV records every answer, scores it, shows a 95% range beside the score (10/10 on ten tasks is 72–100%, not "100%"), and can replay the run. Builders publish profiles to Arkiv as schema-defined, wallet-owned entities that expire after 30 days, so stale listings disappear by design. World ID sign-in proves a real human owns a listing, and AgentCV says plainly that this does not certify the agent's skill.
projects.how_its_made: AgentCV is a Node.js 22 backend (built-in http, crypto and test runner, no framework) with a React 18 + Vite 6 frontend served from the same process. 0G: the AI Matchmaker calls the 0G Compute Router's OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API; the prompt treats user text as data, demands JSON, and we keep only agent IDs that exist in the directory (max three), so the model cannot invent agents. Without a key a keyword fallback runs and is labelled "LOCAL DEMO — NOT 0G". Arkiv: profiles are entities defined with the SDK's defineSchema (indexed owner, category and agentId), written with createEntity and a 30-day ExpirationTime on the Rabdi testnet, and read back with select().from(schema).fetch(); expiry means abandoned listings disappear without a cleanup job. World: owner sign-in is World ID OIDC with PKCE, state and nonce; every endpoint comes from World's discovery document, and the ID token is verified against World's JWKS with jose. The evaluation runner POSTs ten versioned tasks to an agent's HTTP endpoint, records each answer, latency, a manifest with a fixture digest and SHA-256 digests, and the UI shows a 95% Wilson range beside every score. Hacky bits: the hosted demo runs the web app and two demo agents in one process, because the runner only calls loopback addresses; and .env loading uses Node's built-in process.loadEnvFile instead of a dependency. A small Solidity 0.8.28 contract (EvalAttestationRegistry.sol) records a hash of a completed evaluation on-chain so a run is tamper-evident; it compiles with solc, is deployed and exercised on an in-process EVM in the test suite, and ships with a viem deploy script for any EVM testnet. It is a natural extension of evidence-over-claims, not a sponsor track.

A small Solidity 0.8.28 contract (EvalAttestationRegistry.sol) records a hash of a completed evaluation on-chain so a run is tamper-evident; it compiles with solc, is deployed and exercised on an in-process EVM in the test suite, and ships with a viem deploy script for any EVM testnet. It is a natural extension of evidence-over-claims, not a sponsor track.

projects.title: SwarmAnon
projects.description: SwarmAnon enables private access to the Swarm decentralized storage through the Nym mixnet.
projects.project_description: SwarmAnon is a privacy-focused gateway that combines Ethereum Swarm's decentralized storage infrastructure with the Nym mixnet to protect users' network IP address and traffic patterns. While Swarm enables decentralized storage and website hosting, users typically access content through HTTP gateways. These gateways can observe users' IP addresses, request timestamps, and other metadata, effectively linking users to the content they access. SwarmAnon addresses this privacy gap by enabling ethersphere/swarm-gateway to operate as a service over the Nym mixnet. Instead of connecting directly to a public Swarm gateway, users route their requests through Nym's privacy-preserving network. Nym uses layered encryption and traffic mixing to obscure the origin of network communications, preventing the Swarm gateway from directly observing users' original IP addresses. SwarmAnon acts as a bridge between the Nym network and existing Swarm infrastructure. It receives requests through Nym, forwards them to the Swarm gateway, which communicates with a Bee node, and returns the requested content to users through the mixnet. This approach protects users' originating IP addresses, reduces exposure of network metadata, and enables more private access to files, websites, and decentralized applications hosted on Swarm. By building on existing Swarm infrastructure without requiring changes to the underlying protocol, SwarmAnon provides a foundation for developers to create privacy-conscious decentralized applications. SwarmAnon focuses on network-level privacy rather than claiming complete anonymity, since application-level identifiers may still reveal information. Our vision is simple: bring privacy to decentralized storage and hosting by combining Swarm's decentralized infrastructure with Nym's network privacy technology. Because decentralization should not come at the cost of privacy.
projects.how_its_made: SwarmAnon is built by integrating ethersphere/swarm-gateway with the Nym mixnet to enable privacy-preserving access to decentralized storage and hosting. The project combines Ethereum Swarm, Bee nodes, and Nym's privacy-preserving network. We built a service layer that connects Nym's messaging infrastructure to the existing Swarm gateway, allowing users to access Swarm-hosted content without connecting directly to the gateway. The architecture works by routing client requests through the Nym mixnet to a service adapter running alongside swarm-gateway. The adapter receives requests, forwards them to the gateway over a local connection, and sends responses back through Nym. The Swarm gateway communicates with a Bee node to retrieve content from the decentralized Swarm network. The main technical challenge was bridging HTTP-based communication with Nym's mixnet transport while preserving compatibility with Swarm's existing APIs and request-response behavior. One notable aspect of the implementation is that we didn't need to modify the underlying Swarm protocol. Instead, we made the existing gateway accessible as a Nym service, separating the privacy layer from the storage infrastructure. Nym provides layered encryption and traffic mixing to help conceal users' originating IP addresses, while Swarm provides decentralized storage, content addressing, and website hosting. By combining these technologies, SwarmAnon demonstrates how existing decentralized infrastructure can be extended with network-level privacy without rebuilding the underlying systems.

projects.title: LORI
projects.description: A self-hosted AI workspace for teams, powered by 0G Compute.
projects.project_description: Lori is an AI workspace that helps companies bring research, document creation, and software development together in one place. Teams can use AI to analyze information, prepare reports, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, and work alongside coding agents on software projects. Lori Enterprise gives organizations a self-hosted control plane for managing their AI workspace. Administrators can manage users and teams, configure AI providers, control access to models and tools, and see usage across the organization. For this hackathon, we are connecting Lori to 0G Compute so teams can use decentralized AI inference as part of their everyday workflows. Our goal is to make 0G accessible through a practical enterprise product, giving organizations more choice in the AI infrastructure behind their work. Lori Work is currently in preview. Teams can explore the workspace at https://workspace.lori.sh/sign-up and learn more at https://lori.sh.
projects.how_its_made: Lori Enterprise is built around a self-hosted control plane that connects an organization’s users, teams, devices, AI providers, and workspace settings. Administrators can configure which models, plugins, and skills are available across the company and manage usage from a central interface. For the 0G track, we connect Lori to 0G Compute through its OpenAI-compatible inference interface. Lori’s configurable provider system makes it possible to connect a 0G endpoint and use its models within the workspace. This gives teams access to decentralized AI infrastructure through a familiar workflow. Lori Work brings AI models together with files and connected tools to support research, analysis, and document creation. Lori Code runs supported coding agents as their own command-line tools in a shared interface. Developers can use separate Git worktrees and branches for tasks, then review the changes produced by each agent. The result is an enterprise workspace that combines team management, AI-powered work, coding agents, and a connection to 0G Compute.

projects.title: BhashaPay
projects.description: Marketplace of Indic-language AI APIs paid per call by a budgeted agent using x402 stablecoins
projects.project_description: BhashaPay is a pay-per-call marketplace for Indic-language AI services such as Marathi and Hindi translation, speech-to-text and document OCR. Each service is an API that answers with an HTTP 402 payment request and only runs after payment settles, so small merchants can charge a few cents per request without card rails or subscriptions. An autonomous agent takes a task and a budget, discovers registered services, compares price and quality, pays on its own and reports what it spent. Spend controls (total budget, per-merchant limit, merchant allowlist, and a human-approval threshold) stop the agent from overspending, and a denied or over-budget payment never triggers the paid action. Payments can settle on Hedera using x402, or gaslessly in USDT on Whitechain through a relayer and settlement contracts, with an audit log on Hedera Consensus Service. A dashboard shows services, agent runs, payments and the audit trail.
projects.how_its_made: BhashaPay is a TypeScript monorepo. The frontend is Next.js with Tailwind (marketplace, agent run form with a live SSE timeline, payments, audit log and an approval modal). The backend is Express with SQLite, storing services, runs, payments, receipts and audit references. Protected endpoints use the x402 "exact" scheme on Hedera testnet (0.01 test USDC) before calling an OpenAI-compatible model for translation, transcription and OCR. The Whitechain rail uses Solidity contracts built with Foundry and OpenZeppelin: a service registry, a settlement contract with stored receipts, one-use request hashes, relayer limits, pausing and refunds, and an onchain spend-policy contract. The payer signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization for the Whitechain USDT contract and a private facilitator relays it, so the payer needs no gas token. The facilitator rate-limits by IP, service and payer, and idempotency keys bind each paid request to its receipt so a retry is never charged twice. Hedera Consensus Service provides a tamper-evident payment audit log, read back through the mirror node. Hedera's x402 support made per-request micropayments simple to add to a normal HTTP API, and Whitechain's USDT with EIP-3009 support is what allowed gasless payments.

projects.title: Selfnode
projects.description: Use Ethereum without telling anyone who you are: a private wallet, explorer and swap app.
projects.project_description: Almost every wallet sends your IP address, every address you look up and every trade you're about to make to an RPC provider, and explorers and swap apps add Etherscan's and Uniswap's servers on top. Selfnode is a wallet, block explorer and swap app where none of them learn who you are. Private mode is the default: every RPC call, including label lookups and every transaction broadcast, goes through Anon-RPC, the Ethereum Foundation's standard, over the Nox anonymity network. If Nox fails, Selfnode switches to Nym (or Tor, if you set a gateway), tells you, and switches back when Nox recovers. It never falls back to a direct connection unless you approve that one request. Verified mode checks answers against Ethereum consensus with the Helios light client; it connects directly, and the app says so. My node mode reads from your own node, and the desktop app for macOS and Windows can download, verify and run a pruned Nethermind + Nimbus node for you. Transactions are still broadcast through Anon-RPC, so your node's peers don't learn your IP. Selfnode includes a wallet (Sepolia, multiple wallets and accounts, keys encrypted on your device, a plain-English preview before every signature), an Etherscan-style explorer (Sepolia and mainnet, read-only: live blocks and transactions, address activity, ENS names) with address labels, scam warnings and decoded function names, and Uniswap v4 swaps quoted on-chain, with no Uniswap API and no API keys. The labels are an open dataset we mirrored into Arkiv, so any wallet or explorer can query it without asking us; a public Data page lets anyone browse it. There's no Selfnode backend: the app is static files, and a copy is also served from Swarm, so it keeps working if our domain disappears. A Privacy page sets out exactly what each third party learns in each mode.
projects.how_its_made: A pnpm monorepo in TypeScript: a shared core (transport router, wallet, explorer, swap and labels), a React + Vite web app served as static files from a Cloudflare Worker with a strict CSP, and an Electron desktop app. No backend. Anon-RPC: the @anon-rpc/browser-harness worker is passed to viem as its fetch. One router serves the whole app and counts every answered request by route; failed or retried attempts are counted separately. In a scripted end-to-end session on the live production site (create a wallet, receive funds, swap both ways), 111 of 115 calls (96.5%) went through Anon-RPC. The other 4 were the disclosed bootstrap reads (2 for Nox, 2 for Nym, which starts in the background as the failover backup), and none went direct. If a network fails, the router switches to the next one (Nox → Nym → Tor): reads retry, broadcasts don't (a signed transaction may already be out), and every switch is shown and counted. It retries with backoff while a network makes its first connection, checks the preferred network again every few minutes and switches back when it recovers. Each network's worker-code hash is pinned, and a change needs the user's approval. Uniswap: v4 swaps on Sepolia with viem only (no SDK, no Trading API). Quotes are eth_calls to the v4 Quoter over Anon-RPC, and Universal Router calldata is hand-encoded, with Permit2 and exact-amount approvals. Along the way we found that the deployed Sepolia Universal Router predates the current source and expects a different swap-struct layout, and that with empty hookData both layouts simulate successfully, so testing can't tell you which is right. We confirmed it by checking the deployed bytecode for error selectors (details in FEEDBACK.md). Arkiv: an idempotent importer mirrors MIT-licensed token lists (2,105), address labels and MyEtherWallet's scam list (796), and function names (444 at first import, ranked by real mainnet usage and covering 68.4% of sampled calls; 462 and 72.6% after the latest refresh) into Arkiv's Rabdi testnet. Every entry records its source, licence and exact source commit, and the full licence texts are stored on Arkiv too. A GitHub Action refreshes it daily. Dataset snapshots and a copy of the web app are stored on Swarm, uploaded through our own Bee light node with our own postage batch, and referenced from Arkiv with SHA-256 hashes. The app reads labels through Anon-RPC and warns before you sign a transaction to a flagged address. Desktop: Electron with a sandboxed, context-isolated window and a validated IPC bridge. The node manager downloads only official, checksum-verified Nethermind and Nimbus releases (Nimbus is checked twice), runs them pruned with RPC bound to 127.0.0.1, includes pre-flight and disk-space checks, and shows each client's real sync stage. We chose two minority clients to support client diversity. Graceful shutdown on Windows sends a real console Ctrl+C, verified in CI.

projects.title: Settle
projects.description: The USDT payment gateway: add it in 20 lines, and customers pay with just an email, no gas.
projects.project_description: Settle is the payment gateway for USDT on Whitechain. Cards take a percentage and settle in days. Crypto payments ask the customer for a wallet and gas. Settle removes both problems: a merchant gets USDT in their own account in seconds, and the customer only needs an email address. There are three ways to get paid. On a website, a store installs our npm package, creates an order and opens Settle Checkout, the same way it would add a card gateway. It takes about 20 lines. With a link, a merchant creates an invoice or a subscription plan and shares it. From AI agents, a store puts a price on one route, and an agent can buy over standard x402 with no account, no API key and no gas. The customer logs in with an email and signs one message. Our relayer sends the transaction and pays the gas, and the contract repays it from the merchant's share in the same transaction. That is about 0.055 USDT on any amount, and Settle adds no fee of its own. On a 1,000 sale, a card gateway at 3% takes about 30. Every payment lands in one dashboard, with refunds, subscriptions, reminders, receipts, webhooks and a CSV export. Invoice details live on Arkiv with customer details encrypted, and PDF invoices are stored encrypted on Swarm. Settle is live on Whitechain Sepolia and Arkiv's Rabdi testnet, using test USDT.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts: three Solidity contracts built with Foundry and deployed on Whitechain Sepolia, with 100% test coverage. InvoiceRegistry handles invoices, gasless payments and refunds. It holds no funds and has no owner. Subscriptions takes recurring payments from one signed allowance, capped by the customer. GaslessTransfer sends USDT with no gas for withdrawals. Gasless payments: USDT on Whitechain supports EIP-3009, so a customer signs one message and anyone can submit it. We use receiveWithAuthorization so only our contract can use the signature, and its nonce is tied to one invoice and one payer. The relayer pays gas in WBT, and the contract repays it in USDT in the same transaction. The relayer can't change an amount or redirect money, because the signature fixes both. App and SDK: Next.js, React and TypeScript on Vercel, with Privy for email login. The app also runs the relayer, an x402 facilitator and checkout.js. The SDK is published on npm as @akhr2405/settle-pay, with API keys, orders, a checkout script, webhooks and payment verification that reads the chain. Chai Point is a separate demo store that installs the package from npm and takes payment in 22 lines. Partner technologies: Whitechain is where all the money moves, and its EIP-3009 USDT is what makes email-only checkout possible. Arkiv holds what the contract doesn't: business names, descriptions, encrypted customer details, webhook settings, delivery logs and agent sales, across six entity types. Every read filters on our writer wallet. Swarm stores PDF invoices, encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload, and Arkiv keeps the swarm_reference that points to each file. The hacky part: an agent has USDT but no WBT, so we run our own x402 facilitator. The store answers 402, the agent signs a standard x402 payment, and the relayer sends one Multicall3 transaction in which the agent pays the store and the store repays the gas. Both happen or neither does. We save each sale to Arkiv before paying, and check the token's record of used signatures, so a retry finds the payment and never charges twice. We tested this by killing the server with the payment already on-chain. Our demo agent is a cafe's restock agent run by Gemini.

projects.title: Huma
projects.description: AI detectors guess. Huma shows: a ZK proof of how you typed, backed by World ID and stored on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Huma lets people prove they wrote something themselves, instead of being judged by AI detectors that guess. The problem: AI detectors look at the words and estimate a probability, and they're often wrong. In one Stanford study, popular detectors flagged 61% of essays by non-native English writers as AI. Students, freelancers and writers get accused with no way to defend themselves, because a detector's guess can't be checked. What Huma does: instead of guessing from the final text, Huma records how the text was written. Write in Huma's editor, in the browser or the Mac app. Huma records the writing process on your device: keystrokes, timing, pauses, edits and pastes. Your keystrokes never leave your device. Check-ins: while you write, short "Still writing?" prompts are approved with a passkey or Touch ID, showing a real person is present. projects.project_description_markdown:
Huma lets people prove they wrote something themselves, instead of being judged by AI detectors that guess.

The problem: AI detectors look at the words and estimate a probability, and they're often wrong. In one Stanford study, popular detectors flagged 61% of essays by non-native English writers as AI. Students, freelancers and writers get accused with no way to defend themselves, because a detector's guess can't be checked.

What Huma does: instead of guessing from the final text, Huma records how the text was written.

1) Write in Huma's editor, in the browser or the Mac app. Huma records the writing process on your device: keystrokes, timing, pauses, edits and pastes. Your keystrokes never leave your device.
2) Check-ins: while you write, short "Still writing?" prompts are approved with a passkey or Touch ID, showing a real person is present.
3) Finish: Huma turns that record into a zero-knowledge proof (Noir circuits, proved with Barretenberg), on your own device. It proves the writing rules were met (typed rather than pasted, natural rhythm and pauses, enough time) without revealing the keystrokes, and gives a Huma Score out of 100.
4) Share: you get a link and a PDF report with the proof attached. Anyone can open it and re-verify the proof in their own browser, with no account and no need to trust Huma's server. There's an optional replay of the writing.

World ID: sign-in is World ID only (IDKit, Proof of Human). Each proof is bound to the device's own publishing key, and our server verifies it with World's API. The account is derived from the World ID's nullifier, so one real human gets one account, the same on every device, without ever revealing who they are. Every page a writer shares shows the same anonymous "Verified human · World ID" fingerprint, so writers can claim their work, and nobody can farm fake accounts to mass-produce "human" content. It works on web and Mac: the Mac app signs in through a World ID page bound to its Secure Enclave key.

Arkiv: Huma's whole storage layer runs on Arkiv. Shared pages, proofs, publication records, account documents, handles and short links are stored as Arkiv entities, encrypted with AES-256-GCM and split into 120 KiB chunks, with typed, queryable attributes. For every shared page, Huma also anchors a public, signed hash record on Arkiv: the text hash, proof hash and writer's signature, never the text itself. The verify page reads that record back from Arkiv and checks it against the page, so anyone can confirm a page's record independently of Huma.

Why it matters: soon most writing online will be AI. Huma gives humans a way to show their words are theirs: anonymous, verifiable by anyone, and based on how the text was written rather than how it sounds.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Huma has three parts: a Mac app in Swift, a browser writer and web server in Node.js, and a proving stack shared by both. World ID handles identity; Arkiv handles storage.

1. RECORDING AND PROVING HOW TEXT WAS TYPED

- The editor: on the web it's built on ProseMirror; on the Mac, in SwiftUI/AppKit. Every keystroke, pause, edit and paste is recorded locally by a Rust recorder (compiled to WebAssembly for the browser). Each session's events are signed by the device's own P-256 key: the Secure Enclave on Mac, WebCrypto in the browser. Mid-session check-ins are approved with a passkey or Touch ID.
- The proof: at Finish, Noir circuits (nargo 1.0.0-beta.25) check the writing rules (typed, not pasted; natural timing; real elapsed time), and Barretenberg (bb 5.2.1, UltraHonk) proves them. Long documents are split into parts that prove in the background while you're still writing, plus one final proof, with text tiers of 1,024, 4,096 or 10,000 characters. Finish only waits for the last bit.
- In the browser: bb.js runs multi-threaded in a web worker. That needs a cross-origin-isolated page (COOP/COEP) to get SharedArrayBuffer; witnesses come from Noir's own solver compiled to WebAssembly.
- On the Mac: the proving engine ships inside the app, fully offline, and runs its JavaScript on macOS's built-in JavaScriptCore instead of bundling Node.js (116 MB saved).
- Checking it: anyone can re-verify a proof in their browser against pinned verification keys. The PDF report carries the proof inside it as a standard PDF attachment.
- Real time, not device time: the server issues a session nonce when writing starts, which becomes part of the proof. That stops scripts faking the writing time with a doctored clock.

2. WORLD ID (IDKit 4.6, Proof of Human)

- Sign-in is World ID only. Our server signs each IDKit request with our signing key, so the key never reaches the browser.
- Proofs can't be reused: each one is bound to the device's own publishing key (signal "huma-account:<device key>"), so a proof can't be replayed for another account. The server checks every proof with World's verify API; the browser's answer is never trusted on its own.
- One person, one account: the account ID is derived from the World ID nullifier, so the same human gets the same account everywhere and can't make a second one. Every page shows the same anonymous fingerprint, which lets writers claim their work without revealing who they are.
- Mac sign-in with zero Swift changes: the app already signed in by opening a web page with a secret code and its Secure Enclave key, then polling for the result. We swapped that page to IDKit, proving World ID for the Mac's own key, so the app didn't need to change.
- Partner benefit: a credential that proves "one unique human" is exactly what turns "this text was typed" into "a unique person typed this". It also gives us sybil resistance against account farms, which a typing proof alone can't.

3. ARKIV (@arkiv-network/sdk, Rabdi testnet)

- One drop-in storage layer: we wrote ArkivObjectStore to the same interface as our local and Cloudflare R2 storage. With one setting, HUMA_STORAGE_BACKEND=arkiv, the whole app (pages, proofs, records, documents, handles, short links) runs on Arkiv without changing any other code.
- Encrypted, in chunks: every object is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with its storage key as authenticated data so a payload can't be moved to another key. It's split into 120 KiB chunks, because we measured Arkiv's transaction limit at about 128 KiB. A read only counts once every chunk of a write is present, so half-finished writes are ignored.
- Queryable: entities carry typed, indexed attributes (key, kind, chunk number, time, owner), so Arkiv's SQL-like queries can list, for example, a writer's pages.
- Changing state: data that changes, like documents and handles, is replaced by compare-and-swap. The old chunks are deleted and the new ones created in one transaction.
- A public record per page: for every shared page, we also anchor an unencrypted, signed hash record (text hash, proof hash, writer's signature). The verify page reads it back from Arkiv and checks it against the page.
- Partner benefit: pages and their records live in a public, queryable data layer that isn't just our server. Readers can look up a page's record on Arkiv themselves.

HACKY BITS WORTH MENTIONING

- Colliding writes from one wallet. Sharing writes the text, proof and replay to Arkiv at the same time, and they collided with "replacement transaction underpriced". We fixed it with viem's nonce manager, so parallel writes each get their own nonce: three writes now take about 8 seconds instead of failing.
- A 7-second wait to start writing. Each Arkiv transaction takes about 7 seconds to confirm, which made Start Recording slow. So short-lived state that changes constantly (session nonces, daily counters) stays on the server's disk, and everything that matters goes to Arkiv. Start went from about 7 seconds to about 6 milliseconds.
- An account ID shaped like a wallet. World ID accounts have no wallet, so we derive a wallet-shaped address from the nullifier. That let World ID accounts reuse the existing device-linking code, which expected a wallet address.
- No URL in JavaScriptCore. The Mac's JavaScriptCore has no URL, which silently broke every Mac proof check. We rewrote that origin check with a strict pattern, and confirmed it gives exactly the same answers as URL on our edge cases.
- The access key in error logs. The Arkiv RPC address contains the access key, so the server's error logs blank it out.

projects.title: Enconomy
projects.description: Zero Knowledge Proof of Proximity. Circuits now formally verified, plus a frame tx recovery demo.
projects.project_description: Enconomy proves two devices are physically next to each other, using sound and zero knowledge. Each device plays a coded sound and records both its own and its partner's. The arrival times give a distance with no synced clocks, and under 60 cm reads NEAR. Hardware keys sign each half, and a ZK proof ties that half to the recording without revealing it. We started this at ETHGlobal Tokyo and presented it as a new primitive. Naturally, it included three use-cases: a Safe that only spends when its owners stand side by side, ENS meeting records, and World ID for two different humans as a proof of presence. We're on the Continuity track, and three things are new in Mumbai. Formal verification. The Noir proximity circuits, the basic server flow and the circuit contract's check now have machine-checked Lean proofs. The work also caught problems: silent audio passes today's circuit with a modified app. A tone through a real speaker failed 0 of 800 tries. The fix is planned for the next version, and this is a prototype nobody should rely on until then. This covers those parts under named assumptions, such as verifier soundness. It doesn't make the whole system verified. Three factor native account recovery/key rotation. Your phone is your wallet, and you lost it. With an EIP-8141 frame transaction you rotate to a new phone on the same account, with no funds moved. Getting back in takes three things: your email through Chrome's Email Verification Protocol, your registered laptop, and a proof that the laptop and new phone are side by side. The old key gets a window to cancel. The proofs are checked in the verify frame, at about 11.5M gas, way past the public 100k limit, so this runs on the alt mempool. WVP, the Wallet Verification Protocol. EVP is smooth, but Google holds the off switch. WVP is the wallet version: sign once, and your browser proves you own alice.eth on any site with no more popups. If your wallet is stolen, repoint one ENS record and browsers the old wallet approved stop working. Identity recovery with CROPS. We ran the full rotation with a laptop and a Pixel 6 through the public alt mempool. The email issuer is a local stand-in. A copied laptop key or a stolen, unlocked laptop still beats recovery.
projects.how_its_made: The app is Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose, targeting Android, iOS and the web through Kotlin/Wasm, so the laptop and phone share the same measurement code. The server is Python. Circuits are Noir, proved with Barretenberg, with a native Rust prover on phones. Contracts are Solidity with Foundry. Formal verification is Lean 4. Partner tech and what it gave us: Ethereum frame transactions (EIP-8141): the account itself decides what counts as valid, so recovery needs no Safe co-signer or bundler. A four-frame transaction runs the check in the verify frame. ENS: we deployed the unmodified ENS v2 contracts on our devnet 1337 chain (frame tx&alt mempool), and sign-in reads them. Moving one record cuts off the old wallet. A cold key owns the name and a hot key is the address. Safe and World ID: from the Tokyo build, now split out into independent examples on a small proximity core. WVP runs as an MV3 Chrome extension built on OpenAC (a modified build) with P-256 SD-JWT credentials. There's also a small Chromium patch that attempted to make WVP as native as EVP. The hacky parts: We run our own mempool sidecar with a 16M gas cap, since the public limit is 100k and we check an 11.5M proof bundle during verification. Low gas shows up as a proof failure rather than out of gas, which took a while to spot. The recovery contract needs the two device keys public, so it's not a very private solution. Chrome's EVP needs the page to set the nonce through setAttribute. AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) did much of the writing and reviewing, including the Lean proofs. Lean itself checks the proofs, but the informal specs had only brief human audit.
