projects.title: OASIS Protocol
projects.description: A network on Arkiv where AI agents discover, book, and pay for consultancy services autonomously.
projects.project_description: OASIS Protocol – Open Autonomous Services & Interoperability Standard Project Overview OASIS Protocol is an open, decentralized availability network and autonomous agent commerce protocol developed from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026. The project aims to establish a common infrastructure through which professional services, service providers, availability schedules, credentials, and pricing can be discovered, evaluated, booked, and purchased across independent applications and autonomous AI agents. The fundamental idea behind OASIS is to eliminate the fragmentation of service discovery and booking systems. Today, platforms such as Calendly, Upwork, and Superpeer operate within their own proprietary ecosystems. Service providers must repeatedly manage their offerings, availability, and professional information across different platforms, while customers and AI agents remain restricted by platform-specific discovery and checkout mechanisms. OASIS introduces a decentralized alternative where providers publish their services and availability onto an open, queryable network. These records can subsequently be accessed by any compatible application or autonomous agent without requiring the provider to recreate their listings on every marketplace. The protocol follows a "Publish Once, Be Discoverable Everywhere" architecture, making service discovery interoperable across applications. The project is designed not merely as another appointment-booking application but as an infrastructure layer connecting service providers, independent marketplaces, and autonomous AI agents. Its long-term vision is to make professional services discoverable and purchasable on the open internet, regardless of whether the buyer is a human, an application, or an autonomous AI agent. Arkiv Network – Core Decentralized Data Infrastructure Arkiv Network is the central component of OASIS and serves as its decentralized, queryable data layer. Instead of maintaining service discovery exclusively through a centralized database controlled by a single marketplace, OASIS leverages Arkiv to store and retrieve structured service information, availability schedules, and reservation records. Arkiv enables providers to publish wallet-owned entities representing their services and availability. These entities contain structured metadata such as service titles, categories, skills, hourly rates, durations, provider wallet addresses, and references to professional credentials stored on decentralized storage. A major advantage of using Arkiv is its ability to perform SQL-like queries over structured decentralized entities. Applications and AI agents can directly filter service listings according to parameters such as category, pricing, skills, and other indexed attributes. For example, an autonomous agent searching for a Python developer under a particular budget can query Arkiv for matching providers rather than depending on a centralized marketplace's proprietary search API. OASIS implements three principal entity schemas within Arkiv: Services: Provider-owned entities containing service descriptions, categories, skills, pricing, durations, wallet information, and associated credential references. Availability: Provider-owned entities representing weekly availability schedules through rolling availability bitmasks and recurring booking intervals. Reservations: Platform-managed entities representing temporary booking claims, payment references, and confirmed reservations. The architecture deliberately separates provider-owned availability from platform-managed reservations. Providers retain ownership of their published service and availability records, and OASIS does not modify or delete these provider-owned entities. Instead, reservation records are created separately and queried alongside availability to determine whether a particular slot is temporarily claimed or already booked. This approach enables multiple independent applications to consume the same availability information while maintaining a consistent, publicly queryable reservation state. OASIS is implemented on the Arkiv Rabdi Testnet using Chain ID 7794095 and the Arkiv SDK. The backend uses native Arkiv JSON-RPC queries, while the frontend interacts with Arkiv through its TypeScript SDK. Decentralized Service Discovery and Interoperability One of the primary problems addressed by OASIS is the fragmentation of professional service discovery across closed platforms. Traditionally, a provider must independently publish and maintain their services on multiple marketplaces. Each platform maintains its own database, availability information, search mechanisms, and booking infrastructure. This creates unnecessary duplication and prevents service information from being universally accessible. OASIS changes this model by allowing providers to publish their offerings directly onto Arkiv. Once published, their service records become discoverable through compatible applications and AI agents that query the same decentralized network. This creates a shared discovery infrastructure rather than another isolated marketplace. An application built on OASIS can discover providers independently of the application through which those providers originally published their offerings. The protocol supports discovery based on structured attributes such as service categories, skills, rates, duration, and availability. Applications can independently implement their own interfaces, recommendation systems, and user experiences while relying on the same decentralized service data. The resulting architecture separates the service discovery infrastructure from the applications that consume it, creating the foundation for interoperability between marketplaces and autonomous agents. Decentralized Credentials and Swarm Integration OASIS integrates Swarm as its decentralized, content-addressed storage layer for professional documents and supporting evidence. While Arkiv stores structured and queryable service metadata, documents such as resumes, professional certifications, licenses, portfolios, and sample work require a different storage mechanism. These documents are stored on Swarm, which provides content-addressed references for retrieving the uploaded data. Each provider can upload supporting documents through the application and obtain a corresponding Swarm reference. This reference is subsequently linked to the provider's service entity on Arkiv through the swarmRef attribute. This architecture separates structured service information from large binary documents while maintaining a verifiable relationship between the two. Autonomous AI agents can retrieve these documents directly from Swarm when evaluating providers. Rather than relying exclusively on descriptions or ratings supplied by a marketplace, agents can examine professional qualifications, certifications, portfolios, and supporting evidence to assess the suitability of different providers. The integration allows Arkiv to function as the searchable index of professional offerings while Swarm provides decentralized storage for the documents associated with those offerings. Autonomous AI Agent for Service Discovery and Booking OASIS incorporates an autonomous AI buyer agent built using LangGraph and Groq-powered language models. The agent enables users to interact with the decentralized service network through natural-language requests rather than manually navigating service listings and booking interfaces. The agent is designed to execute the complete service discovery and booking workflow, including requirement extraction, provider discovery, qualification evaluation, availability checking, reservation coordination, payment execution, and booking confirmation. For example, a user can request: "Find me a Python developer available tomorrow for a one-hour consultation under $20. Choose the cheapest qualified professional and book it." The agent interprets the request and converts it into structured requirements, including service category, budget, duration, and scheduling preferences. It then queries Arkiv for matching service providers and their availability schedules. Once suitable candidates are discovered, the agent retrieves associated professional documents from Swarm and evaluates qualifications, experience, pricing, and suitability. The agent compares the available providers and selects the most appropriate service and time slot according to the user's requirements. Before completing the booking, it creates a temporary reservation claim on Arkiv to coordinate slot availability and reduce the possibility of conflicting bookings. The agent subsequently proceeds through the payment workflow, enforcing the user's spending limits before authorizing a payment transaction. After successful payment settlement, the booking is confirmed, the reservation state is updated on Arkiv, and a verifiable booking receipt is returned to the user. The entire workflow is implemented as a tool-calling LangGraph agent with real-time Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming, allowing users to observe the agent's execution as it discovers providers, evaluates options, and completes transactions. Hedera x402 – Autonomous Agent Payments OASIS integrates Hedera x402 to address one of the fundamental limitations of autonomous AI agents: their inability to independently complete conventional payment workflows that require human-operated checkout interfaces. The x402 protocol enables machine-native payments through HTTP 402 Payment Required responses. Instead of relying on traditional checkout pages, an agent can request a protected resource, receive a structured payment challenge, evaluate the payment requirements, and complete the transaction programmatically. OASIS implements an x402-protected FastAPI endpoint for paid consultations and booking operations. When an agent requests a protected service, the server returns a payment challenge containing the required payment information, including the payment scheme, network, recipient, amount, and fee-payer configuration. The autonomous agent evaluates the requested payment against the user's configured spending limit. If the service exceeds the approved budget, the agent raises a BudgetExceededError and stops execution rather than proceeding with an unauthorized payment. For transactions within the permitted budget, the agent constructs a native Hedera TransferTransaction, signs the transaction using its wallet, and submits it through the Hedera x402 facilitator. The facilitator sponsors the network gas fees and submits the transaction for settlement, allowing the agent to complete payments without requiring the buyer to independently manage gas fees. Following successful settlement, the backend verifies the payment and returns the booking receipt and transaction information. The service can then be unlocked, and the corresponding reservation is confirmed. The implementation supports payments using HBAR and USDC on Hedera Testnet and demonstrates an end-to-end autonomous payment workflow with live transaction settlement. Native Hedera Services – HTS and HCS In addition to x402 payments, OASIS integrates native Hedera services to support token transfers, account operations, and verifiable booking records. The architecture uses Hedera Token Service (HTS) for native HBAR and USDC transfers. These transfers are executed using Hedera SDK transactions rather than custom Solidity smart contracts. OASIS also integrates Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) as its tamper-evident audit logging mechanism. Whenever a booking is completed, the system submits a structured booking audit message to a dedicated HCS topic. projects.project_description_markdown:
OASIS Protocol – Open Autonomous Services & Interoperability Standard

1. Project Overview

OASIS Protocol is an open, decentralized availability network and autonomous agent commerce protocol developed from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026. The project aims to establish a common infrastructure through which professional services, service providers, availability schedules, credentials, and pricing can be discovered, evaluated, booked, and purchased across independent applications and autonomous AI agents.

The fundamental idea behind OASIS is to eliminate the fragmentation of service discovery and booking systems. Today, platforms such as Calendly, Upwork, and Superpeer operate within their own proprietary ecosystems. Service providers must repeatedly manage their offerings, availability, and professional information across different platforms, while customers and AI agents remain restricted by platform-specific discovery and checkout mechanisms.

OASIS introduces a decentralized alternative where providers publish their services and availability onto an open, queryable network. These records can subsequently be accessed by any compatible application or autonomous agent without requiring the provider to recreate their listings on every marketplace. The protocol follows a "Publish Once, Be Discoverable Everywhere" architecture, making service discovery interoperable across applications.

The project is designed not merely as another appointment-booking application but as an infrastructure layer connecting service providers, independent marketplaces, and autonomous AI agents. Its long-term vision is to make professional services discoverable and purchasable on the open internet, regardless of whether the buyer is a human, an application, or an autonomous AI agent.

2. Arkiv Network – Core Decentralized Data Infrastructure

Arkiv Network is the central component of OASIS and serves as its decentralized, queryable data layer. Instead of maintaining service discovery exclusively through a centralized database controlled by a single marketplace, OASIS leverages Arkiv to store and retrieve structured service information, availability schedules, and reservation records.

Arkiv enables providers to publish wallet-owned entities representing their services and availability. These entities contain structured metadata such as service titles, categories, skills, hourly rates, durations, provider wallet addresses, and references to professional credentials stored on decentralized storage.

A major advantage of using Arkiv is its ability to perform SQL-like queries over structured decentralized entities. Applications and AI agents can directly filter service listings according to parameters such as category, pricing, skills, and other indexed attributes. For example, an autonomous agent searching for a Python developer under a particular budget can query Arkiv for matching providers rather than depending on a centralized marketplace's proprietary search API.

OASIS implements three principal entity schemas within Arkiv:

- Services: Provider-owned entities containing service descriptions, categories, skills, pricing, durations, wallet information, and associated credential references.
- Availability: Provider-owned entities representing weekly availability schedules through rolling availability bitmasks and recurring booking intervals.
- Reservations: Platform-managed entities representing temporary booking claims, payment references, and confirmed reservations.

The architecture deliberately separates provider-owned availability from platform-managed reservations. Providers retain ownership of their published service and availability records, and OASIS does not modify or delete these provider-owned entities. Instead, reservation records are created separately and queried alongside availability to determine whether a particular slot is temporarily claimed or already booked.

This approach enables multiple independent applications to consume the same availability information while maintaining a consistent, publicly queryable reservation state.

OASIS is implemented on the Arkiv Rabdi Testnet using Chain ID 7794095 and the Arkiv SDK. The backend uses native Arkiv JSON-RPC queries, while the frontend interacts with Arkiv through its TypeScript SDK.

3. Decentralized Service Discovery and Interoperability

One of the primary problems addressed by OASIS is the fragmentation of professional service discovery across closed platforms.

Traditionally, a provider must independently publish and maintain their services on multiple marketplaces. Each platform maintains its own database, availability information, search mechanisms, and booking infrastructure. This creates unnecessary duplication and prevents service information from being universally accessible.

OASIS changes this model by allowing providers to publish their offerings directly onto Arkiv. Once published, their service records become discoverable through compatible applications and AI agents that query the same decentralized network.

This creates a shared discovery infrastructure rather than another isolated marketplace. An application built on OASIS can discover providers independently of the application through which those providers originally published their offerings.

The protocol supports discovery based on structured attributes such as service categories, skills, rates, duration, and availability. Applications can independently implement their own interfaces, recommendation systems, and user experiences while relying on the same decentralized service data.

The resulting architecture separates the service discovery infrastructure from the applications that consume it, creating the foundation for interoperability between marketplaces and autonomous agents.

4. Decentralized Credentials and Swarm Integration

OASIS integrates Swarm as its decentralized, content-addressed storage layer for professional documents and supporting evidence.

While Arkiv stores structured and queryable service metadata, documents such as resumes, professional certifications, licenses, portfolios, and sample work require a different storage mechanism. These documents are stored on Swarm, which provides content-addressed references for retrieving the uploaded data.

Each provider can upload supporting documents through the application and obtain a corresponding Swarm reference. This reference is subsequently linked to the provider's service entity on Arkiv through the swarmRef attribute.

This architecture separates structured service information from large binary documents while maintaining a verifiable relationship between the two.

Autonomous AI agents can retrieve these documents directly from Swarm when evaluating providers. Rather than relying exclusively on descriptions or ratings supplied by a marketplace, agents can examine professional qualifications, certifications, portfolios, and supporting evidence to assess the suitability of different providers.

The integration allows Arkiv to function as the searchable index of professional offerings while Swarm provides decentralized storage for the documents associated with those offerings.

5. Autonomous AI Agent for Service Discovery and Booking

OASIS incorporates an autonomous AI buyer agent built using LangGraph and Groq-powered language models. The agent enables users to interact with the decentralized service network through natural-language requests rather than manually navigating service listings and booking interfaces.

The agent is designed to execute the complete service discovery and booking workflow, including requirement extraction, provider discovery, qualification evaluation, availability checking, reservation coordination, payment execution, and booking confirmation.

For example, a user can request:

"Find me a Python developer available tomorrow for a one-hour consultation under $20. Choose the cheapest qualified professional and book it."

The agent interprets the request and converts it into structured requirements, including service category, budget, duration, and scheduling preferences.

It then queries Arkiv for matching service providers and their availability schedules. Once suitable candidates are discovered, the agent retrieves associated professional documents from Swarm and evaluates qualifications, experience, pricing, and suitability.

The agent compares the available providers and selects the most appropriate service and time slot according to the user's requirements.

Before completing the booking, it creates a temporary reservation claim on Arkiv to coordinate slot availability and reduce the possibility of conflicting bookings.

The agent subsequently proceeds through the payment workflow, enforcing the user's spending limits before authorizing a payment transaction.

After successful payment settlement, the booking is confirmed, the reservation state is updated on Arkiv, and a verifiable booking receipt is returned to the user.

The entire workflow is implemented as a tool-calling LangGraph agent with real-time Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming, allowing users to observe the agent's execution as it discovers providers, evaluates options, and completes transactions.

6. Hedera x402 – Autonomous Agent Payments

OASIS integrates Hedera x402 to address one of the fundamental limitations of autonomous AI agents: their inability to independently complete conventional payment workflows that require human-operated checkout interfaces.

The x402 protocol enables machine-native payments through HTTP 402 Payment Required responses. Instead of relying on traditional checkout pages, an agent can request a protected resource, receive a structured payment challenge, evaluate the payment requirements, and complete the transaction programmatically.

OASIS implements an x402-protected FastAPI endpoint for paid consultations and booking operations. When an agent requests a protected service, the server returns a payment challenge containing the required payment information, including the payment scheme, network, recipient, amount, and fee-payer configuration.

The autonomous agent evaluates the requested payment against the user's configured spending limit. If the service exceeds the approved budget, the agent raises a BudgetExceededError and stops execution rather than proceeding with an unauthorized payment.

For transactions within the permitted budget, the agent constructs a native Hedera TransferTransaction, signs the transaction using its wallet, and submits it through the Hedera x402 facilitator.

The facilitator sponsors the network gas fees and submits the transaction for settlement, allowing the agent to complete payments without requiring the buyer to independently manage gas fees.

Following successful settlement, the backend verifies the payment and returns the booking receipt and transaction information. The service can then be unlocked, and the corresponding reservation is confirmed.

The implementation supports payments using HBAR and USDC on Hedera Testnet and demonstrates an end-to-end autonomous payment workflow with live transaction settlement.

7. Native Hedera Services – HTS and HCS

In addition to x402 payments, OASIS integrates native Hedera services to support token transfers, account operations, and verifiable booking records.

The architecture uses Hedera Token Service (HTS) for native HBAR and USDC transfers. These transfers are executed using Hedera SDK transactions rather than custom Solidity smart contracts.

OASIS also integrates Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) as its tamper-evident audit logging mechanism. Whenever a booking is completed, the system submits a structured booking audit message to a dedicated HCS topic.

The audit record contains relevant booking information such as the booking reference, service identifier, buyer wallet, payment amount, currency, transaction identifier, and timestamp.

These records provide an independently verifiable history of completed booking transactions. Buyers and providers can inspect the corresponding HCS messages and payment transaction proofs through Hedera's public network infrastructure.

The project deliberately uses native Hedera SDKs instead of Solidity smart contracts. Account operations and token transfers are performed using native Hedera transactions, while booking audit records are published through HCS.

This demonstrates how decentralized applications can leverage native blockchain services for payments and verifiable records without requiring a conventional EVM smart-contract architecture.

8. Booking Coordination and Double-Booking Prevention

Another important challenge addressed by OASIS is coordinating bookings when multiple users or autonomous agents attempt to reserve the same service slot.

Because provider availability is published on a decentralized network and can be accessed by multiple independent applications, simply reading an availability record is insufficient to guarantee that a slot remains unoccupied throughout the booking process.

OASIS introduces temporary reservation claims and confirmed reservation records to coordinate booking operations.

When an autonomous agent selects a time slot, it creates a temporary reservation claim on Arkiv. The claim remains valid for a limited period, allowing the agent to complete the payment workflow without immediately treating the slot as permanently booked.

After successful payment settlement, the reservation is confirmed, and the corresponding reservation state is updated.

The implementation combines publicly queryable reservation entities with backend concurrency controls to prevent conflicting bookings. PostgreSQL is used for operational concurrency management, while Arkiv provides the decentralized reservation state that compatible applications can query.

This design separates decentralized booking visibility from the concurrency mechanisms required to coordinate simultaneous booking requests.

9. Authentication and Embedded Wallet Infrastructure

OASIS integrates Privy to simplify authentication and wallet onboarding.

Users can authenticate using familiar Web2 mechanisms such as Google login and email without needing to independently create or configure a blockchain wallet during onboarding.

Privy provides embedded wallets and chain abstraction, enabling users to interact with the Hedera Testnet through the application's interface.

This reduces the complexity associated with decentralized applications and makes the protocol more accessible to users who are unfamiliar with blockchain infrastructure.

The application combines conventional authentication experiences with decentralized service discovery, wallet-based provider ownership, and blockchain-based payment operations.

10. System Architecture and Technology Stack

OASIS is implemented as a full-stack application consisting of a React frontend, a FastAPI backend, decentralized infrastructure integrations, and an autonomous AI agent.

Frontend:
- React 18
- TanStack Start
- TanStack Router
- Tailwind CSS
- Privy embedded wallet integration
- Arkiv TypeScript SDK
- Hedera JavaScript SDK

Backend:
- Python 3.12
- FastAPI
- Uvicorn
- LangGraph
- Groq API
- Hedera Python SDK (hiero-sdk-python)
- Arkiv native JSON-RPC integration
- PostgreSQL for operational concurrency controls

Decentralized Infrastructure:
- Arkiv Network on Rabdi Testnet for structured service discovery, availability, and reservation entities.
- Swarm for decentralized content-addressed document storage.
- Hedera Testnet for native token transfers and account operations.
- Hedera x402 facilitator for sponsored autonomous payments.
- Hedera Consensus Service for tamper-evident booking audit logs.
- Hedera Mirror Node for account balance queries and transaction verification.
- Privy for authentication and embedded wallet infrastructure.

The application exposes backend APIs for service discovery, availability management, booking operations, protected consultations, payment settlement, and transaction verification. The frontend provides interfaces for providers to publish services and credentials, users to discover offerings, and autonomous agents to execute booking requests.

11. What Makes OASIS Different?

OASIS is fundamentally different from conventional service marketplaces because it does not attempt to own the entire service discovery and booking ecosystem.

Traditional platforms control their own service directories, availability information, discovery mechanisms, and payment flows. Providers remain dependent on those platforms for visibility, while autonomous agents must integrate separately with each platform.

OASIS instead establishes a decentralized infrastructure layer where:

- Providers publish services and availability once and retain ownership of their records.
- Multiple applications can independently discover and consume the same provider information.
- Arkiv enables structured, queryable service discovery without relying exclusively on proprietary marketplace databases.
- Swarm provides decentralized storage for professional credentials and portfolios.
- AI agents can evaluate professional qualifications using supporting documents rather than relying only on descriptions and ratings.
- Reservation claims and confirmed bookings are publicly queryable across compatible applications.
- Hedera x402 enables autonomous agents to execute service payments programmatically.
- Native Hedera services provide token transfers and independently verifiable booking audit records.
- Familiar authentication mechanisms allow users to interact with decentralized infrastructure without requiring extensive blockchain knowledge.

The result is an open service availability and commerce protocol that connects decentralized data infrastructure, professional service providers, independent applications, and autonomous AI agents.

12. Project Outcome and Vision

OASIS demonstrates how decentralized infrastructure and autonomous AI agents can work together to enable real-world service discovery and transactions.

The project combines Arkiv's decentralized queryable data layer with Swarm's content-addressed storage and Hedera's native payment and consensus services to create an interoperable service marketplace infrastructure.

Its autonomous buyer agent demonstrates that AI systems can move beyond recommending services and actually execute structured discovery, evaluate professional qualifications, coordinate bookings, enforce spending limits, complete payments, and produce verifiable transaction receipts.

OASIS ultimately aims to make professional services universally discoverable and purchasable across the open internet, creating an ecosystem where providers, applications, and AI agents can participate in service commerce without depending on a single centralized marketplace.

The project was built from scratch at ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026, with substantial implementation across Arkiv, Swarm, Hedera x402, HTS, HCS, native SDK integrations, and autonomous AI agent infrastructure.

How It's Made

We built OASIS Protocol as a full-stack, autonomous scheduling and payment marketplace connecting AI agents and human specialists.

Technologies Used & How They Piece Together
Frontend: React 18, TanStack Router, TanStack Query, Viem, and Tailwind CSS.
Backend: FastAPI (Python 3.12) with Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time agent execution streaming.
AI Agent: Built with LangGraph and Groq (Llama-3.3-70b-versatile or GPT-OSS-120b). The agent extracts user requirements, queries the network, inspects credentials, claims a slot, and pays autonomously.
Onboarding: Privy handles Google/email login and provisions embedded wallets for seamless Web3 interaction.

Partner Technologies & Benefits

Hedera (x402 & Native SDKs):
Benefit: Zero-gas autonomous payments. When an agent books an appointment, our API returns an HTTP 402 challenge. The agent partially signs a transfer, and the official Hedera facilitator (0.0.9185802) sponsors the gas fee and settles the transaction on-chain.
No Solidity Smart Contracts: Built 100% on native Hedera SDKs (hiero-sdk-python and @hiero-ledger/sdk). We use HTS for HBAR/USDC transfers and Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) (Topic 0.0.11339796) to write tamper-evident JSON audit receipts on HashScan for every booking.

Arkiv Network (Rabdi Testnet 7794095):
Benefit: Decentralized, SQL-like queryable database. Providers publish their services and 7-day availability bitmasks under their own wallet keys. The platform creates temporary 5-minute reservations and burns confirmed slots without altering provider entities.
Swarm (bzz://):
Benefit: Decentralized file storage for credentials, CVs, and audit reports via @ethersphere/bee-js. Storing large files on Swarm and linking their 64-hex hashes in Arkiv (swarmRef) keeps on-chain data lean and allows AI agents to inspect real credentials before hiring.


Notable & Hacky Engineering Solutions
Arkiv Block Height vs. Epoch Timestamp Bug: Arkiv’s on-chain $expiresAt stores block height (e.g. 1,628,420), not Unix epoch time. Standard date parsers treated 1.6M seconds as 18 days past the 1970 epoch, rendering 19 Jan 1970. We wrote a custom threshold resolver that distinguishes block numbers from timestamps and formats them cleanly as Block #1,628,420.
Insecure gRPC Fallback in hiero-sdk-python: The Python SDK’s Client.for_testnet() tries fetching node TLS certs from mirror nodes, which failed with a certificate error behind network firewalls. We used client.set_transport_security(False) to route over plain gRPC while preserving full cryptographic security through local ECDSA private-key transaction signing.
MetaMask RPC Path Cleanup: Wallets crashed on wallet_addEthereumChain because the Arkiv SDK chain carried an API key in the URL path. We dynamically stripped path suffixes during wallet network addition while preserving them on HTTP transports for seamless network switching.

projects.title: Kavach AI
projects.description: Private AI for startups: chat with your company's secrets that no one else can read, not even us.
projects.project_description: Startups share their most sensitive data with AI assistants: customer lists, pricing, contracts, plans. Today the AI company can read all of it, store it, and leak it if it gets hacked. Running a local model avoids that, but means weak models, no team access, and no backup. Kavach AI gives startups the privacy of running AI on their own computer with the convenience of the cloud. Documents are encrypted in the browser before they leave the device, so storage only ever holds unreadable data. When the company asks the AI a question, the documents are processed inside a hardware-sealed environment (TEE) on 0G, so neither we, the storage provider, nor the AI provider can read them. Every answer comes with a proof that it ran inside the sealed environment. Chats are forgotten after each session; anything worth keeping is saved to the encrypted vault with one click. The company's master key is split between co-founders, so any two can recover it if one is lost, and nobody alone (including us) holds it.
projects.how_its_made: Kavach AI is a Next.js and TypeScript web app deployed on Vercel. All encryption happens in the browser using the WebCrypto API (AES-GCM), so plaintext documents never reach our server. Encrypted documents are stored on 0G Storage. AI answers come from open models running in 0G's sealed (TEE) inference, which keeps the data unreadable to the infrastructure operator and returns a verifiable proof for each request. Without 0G, the AI provider could read every startup secret the app handles. The company master key is split with Shamir secret sharing into three co-founder shares, any two of which can recover it. A proof screen shows the raw encrypted data in storage and our server logs, to demonstrate that nothing readable is stored or logged. The project was built solo during the hackathon with heavy use of Claude Code as an AI coding assistant; the product design, privacy architecture and scope decisions were mine.

projects.title: CPay
projects.description: Pay anyone just by looking at them: private and hands-free with smart glasses.
projects.project_description: CPay turns paying someone into as simple an action as looking at them. Instead of fumbling with your phone, opening wallet apps, and scanning QR codes, you just wear smart glasses, look at the person you want to pay, and say "pay 5 USDC". Decentralized AI understands your voice command, while zero-knowledge privacy ensures that neither your wallet address nor your transaction history is ever exposed to the person you are paying. It is fast, hands-free, and truly private.
projects.how_its_made:
CPay bridges custom wearable hardware, decentralized AI, and dual-sided zero-knowledge cryptography into a seamless payment pipeline: Hardware & Edge Interface: • Custom smart-glasses prototype built using an ESP32-CAM board and OLED micro-display running custom firmware. It captures low-latency video frames and streams them to a companion Next.js PWA via an HMAC-
authenticated WebSocket bridge. • The user looks at a payment recipient or QR code and speaks a natural prompt (e.g. "pay 5 USDC"). Decentralized AI & Voice (0G Network): • Voice audio is streamed to 0G Serving, which processes speech-to-text and extracts structured payment intents inside a confidential TEE environment. • 0G Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesizes voice confirmations, giving the user hands-free audio feedback. • All AI interactions log verifiable cryptographic receipts and request IDs to create a tamper-proof audit trail. Identity & Guardrails (World ID & Agent Pass): • Users authenticate with World ID for Sybil resistance. • To prevent an autonomous voice loop from rogue spending, we implemented Agent Pass: biometric passkeys derive Ed25519-signed approval tokens that strictly enforce daily spend caps and single-transaction
limits before any transaction can be assembled. Dual-Sided On-Chain Privacy (Railgun + ERC-5564 Stealth Addresses): • Payer Privacy via Railgun: The user holds funds in Railgun’s canonical pool on Ethereum Sepolia. Using @railgun-community/wallet and SnarkJS, the browser generates Groth16 zk-SNARK unshield proofs locally on the user's device. The private seed/mnemonic never leaves the phone. • Recipient Privacy via Stealth Addresses: Funds unshield into a fresh, ephemeral ERC-5564 stealth address derived via ECDH. Observers on-chain see no link between the payer's deposit and the recipient's identity. • Broadcaster Relayer: The pre-proved transaction payload is dispatched to a server-side Broadcaster that sponsors the Sepolia gas, ensuring the payer's personal EOA address never touches the mempool.

      • The user looks at a payment recipient or QR code and speaks a natural prompt (e.g. "pay 5 USDC").                                                                                                          
  2. Decentralized AI & Voice (0G Network):                                                                                                                                                                        
      • Voice audio is streamed to 0G Serving, which processes speech-to-text and extracts structured payment intents inside a confidential TEE environment.                                                       
      • 0G Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesizes voice confirmations, giving the user hands-free audio feedback.                                                                                                        
      • All AI interactions log verifiable cryptographic receipts and request IDs to create a tamper-proof audit trail.                                                                                            
  3. Identity & Guardrails (World ID & Agent Pass):                                                                                                                                                                
      • Users authenticate with World ID for Sybil resistance.                                                                                                                                                     
      • To prevent an autonomous voice loop from rogue spending, we implemented Agent Pass: biometric passkeys derive Ed25519-signed approval tokens that strictly enforce daily spend caps and single-transaction 
      limits before any transaction can be assembled.                                                                                                                                                              
  4. Dual-Sided On-Chain Privacy (Railgun + ERC-5564 Stealth Addresses):                                                                                                                                           
      • Payer Privacy via Railgun: The user holds funds in Railgun’s canonical pool on Ethereum Sepolia. Using @railgun-community/wallet and SnarkJS, the browser generates Groth16 zk-SNARK unshield proofs       
      locally on the user's device. The private seed/mnemonic never leaves the phone.                                                                                                                              
      • Recipient Privacy via Stealth Addresses: Funds unshield into a fresh, ephemeral ERC-5564 stealth address derived via ECDH. Observers on-chain see no link between the payer's deposit and the recipient's  
      identity.                                                                                                                                                                                                    
      • Broadcaster Relayer: The pre-proved transaction payload is dispatched to a server-side Broadcaster that sponsors the Sepolia gas, ensuring the payer's personal EOA address never touches the mempool.

projects.title: Binonce
projects.description: Binonce: stopping the EIP-7702 "one blind signature" wallet drain with on-chain policy vaults.
projects.project_description: A stolen signature should not cost you everything you hold. Today it does. EIP-7702 quietly changed the rules for every hot wallet in crypto. One authorization, the kind phished or leaked every day, now hands an entire account to an attacker. No second approval, no window to react. The signer who was supposed to move funds becomes the one who loses them. This is the shape of the Binance-class loss, and any exchange, custodian, or treasury running an operator key is standing on the same ground. Binonce closes that gap. Put your funds behind it and a compromised key stops being a catastrophe. A payout only goes through if it is the right actor, the right operation, the right approvers, and inside the limit you set, checked on-chain the instant before money moves. The moment a key is hijacked, the payout simply refuses. Your money stays put while you rotate the key, with nothing drained in between. We prove it with real money under real attack. The same break that empties an unprotected wallet runs straight into Binonce and stops cold. Even a 2-of-3 setup, with two honest owners both signing, holds the line the second one of them is compromised. The promise is one sentence: holding a key is no longer a license to drain the account.
projects.how_its_made:
Built on top of Chainwall. Chainwall is a policy-enforced smart-vault stack: a Registry that holds the catalog (tokens, interactions, policies, membership), an Interact contract that checks an operation and its approvals, and a managed vault (an OKAccount, or a guarded Safe) that executes the approved action by running MiniScript bytecode against that catalog. Nothing moves unless an operation satisfies its approval policy and its interaction script. Our project leans on exactly this: the vault only ever pays out by executing a signed, policy-bound interaction, so an attacker who steals a key still can't make the vault act. Architecture. The frontend drives two Chainwall tenants off a single chain registry (chainConfig(chainId)), one per network, with identical UI and only addresses and RPC differing. Wallet signing runs through Privy over wagmi and viem; viem handles EIP-712 typed data for payouts and the EIP-7702 type-4 transactions the attack uses. The Whitechain path is pure viem against the OKAccount. The Sepolia path adds a 2-of-3 guarded Safe and is driven server-side through the chainwall CLI plus Foundry cast against a keystore, with live run traces streamed to the UI over SSE. Contracts, per chain. Whitechain testnet (1874): Registry 0x7c04a72db4f422fab4d1c94067b6a8cdac6bbb74 Interact 0xE389bE2d72c618290E1AdFF7B8BbEE39eC356e45 OKAccount vault 0x371B4E49A510Ee007d7879783B309128975CC1A1 TestUSDC (6dp) 0x1d9F8351F788278D3E181908cEE14c7F5766157F Attack sweeper 0xb17f589b3dd10a05d4ef4ed1bdbe4cee8ec2da25 Ethereum Sepolia (11155111): Registry 0xb42df5308d6cb6a6351973fcfa06b691c8bc9a05 Interact 0x807630c5ad0e8029eb9CFAF9357093221864b218 OKAccount vault 0x66340dE9fbB1795Ed1C425fdf5d464bd35B2a4FB TestUSDC (6dp) 0x52425F27aD08BcA15008F5CD81Cb244821401164 SafeFactory 0x2C6D2BC01f02aa4b59cF202539e2C19F9f897D57 Guarded Safe (the vault) 0x01A7c4101F0665e7B86e4dDB5b9EFb8Dd21B2e1a Attack sweeper 0x4d018751A9BB3786788132E9fB25d99B007A0e41 Both tenants share the same operation-approval policy id 0x16c6cdf01674895064373cb0d719b21d67853b8f64a24a73d7c419b6e0817772, the transfer interaction id 0xc918a5f1cb2670f14afa8bb1928f6a298e37fe1eb914df1b4ec7da9e9f38222a (Whitechain) / Safe-bound interaction 0x954bd171dd7ddebe33f76700c135a325f9ae50d21564d3ab3e6c0a04983cc44f (Sepolia), and the payout recipient 0xcBAee4793486f3Df37dbb584F5a3610ff581A614. Policy and interaction ids are 32-byte catalog ids, not addresses. How the script interaction works and why it helps. An "interaction" is an on-chain MiniScript program, referenced by id, that defines the one action an operation is allowed to perform. It does two jobs at once: it validates the operation's arguments and it produces the exact calldata the vault will run. So a payout isn't "call transfer with whatever the caller passed," it's "run interaction 0xc918…222a, which is the only shape of transfer this vault will ever execute." Because the action is fixed in the catalog and bound by id, the attack surface collapses to what the script permits. The approval policy (a separate catalog entry, also by id) sits in front of it and bounds who must sign and how much can move, independent of the interaction itself. How the Lambdascript works here. We author the interactions and policies in Lambdascript, a small assertion language where a program is a block of $require(...) predicates that must all hold, with no comment syntax (the files are pure code). We compile each to MiniScript bytecode with the chainwall CLI and set it on-chain; the vault's VM runs it at execute time. The transfer interaction reads: {
$require($subjectVault == 0x371B4E49A510Ee007d7879783B309128975CC1A1),
$require($subjectNativeValue == 0),
$require($subjectArgCount == 2),
$require($arg0 != 0),
$require($arg1 > 0),
$require(@token(demo/usdc).transfer($arg0 :: address, $arg1 :: uint256))
} It asserts the operation targets our vault, sends no native value, carries exactly two arguments (recipient, amount), a non-zero recipient and positive amount, and then the last line is the payload: @token(demo/usdc) resolves the USDC token from the Registry catalog and emits the actual transfer(address,uint256) call. The spending-cap policy is a separate Lambdascript program that binds the operation to a specific policy id, vault, and interaction id, requires zero native value and two args, and clamps the amount with $subjectArg(1) > 0 && $subjectArg(1) <= 1000000000000, which is the 1,000,000 USDC ceiling at 6 decimals. Validation (who/how-much) and execution (what calldata) live in auditable, on-chain scripts rather than in frontend code. The point it proves. Chainwall carries no EIP-7702 or 0xef0100 handling anywhere. When a payout runs through directExecuteFromAccount, SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow notices the operator account now holds code (because it was 7702-delegated by the attacker), routes the check to ERC-1271 on the delegate (the sweeper), which can't validate an operator signature, and the call reverts with InvalidActorSignature. The hijacked key still signs; the vault just refuses. The defense is an emergent property of standard signature checking, not a patch for 7702.

projects.title: Infinite Gambit
projects.description: Simultaneous chess on an infinite onchain board. Stake an army, capture kings, betray your allies.
projects.project_description: Infinite Gambit is chess rebuilt for a persistent, permissionless world. Anyone can stake ETH (or any token) to deploy an army (a king and nineteen pieces) at a spawn point they choose in secret. Every cycle, every army moves up to three of its pieces, committed as a hash and then revealed together, and all moves resolve simultaneously against the board as it was at the start of the cycle. Plain chess cannot survive that: it is sequential, two-player, ends at checkmate and is 8 by 8. So the rules change. A piece that moves away dodges the capture aimed at it. Two pieces that swap squares both complete their moves. Two pieces arriving on one square both die, while a piece that stayed put falls to a single arriver. Checkmate means nothing: you have to actually capture a king, and when you do you take its whole stake, its army vanishes from the board, and the piece that took it becomes a queen. Moving three pieces at once is what stops a lone attacker from chasing a king forever: the king steps away while another of its pieces lands on the square it left, and the attacker dies there with it. To take winnings home you bring your king to an exit square. Miss a reveal and your army freezes forever. Staked two-player chess does not really play well onchain, because engines beat humans and nobody stakes against them. With unbounded players and hidden simultaneous moves, the game becomes social as well as tactical: armies can ally against a third, but nothing forces them to keep the promise, so every cycle is a small prisoner's dilemma. The core technical rule is that the order in which reveals land onchain never decides anything, and most of the design follows from it. The same rules also run fully offline on a chain inside the browser, for hotseat and single-player play.
projects.how_its_made:
The game is based on a template : https://github.com/wighawag/template-commit-reveal that bring Solidity, Hardhat v3, Hardhat-deploy v2 along with a commit-reveal setup that include offline play (using an embedded evm and indexer running in your browser) The main challenge for making the game of chess work on an infinite board with no bound to the number of players was due to the simultaneous nature of commit+reveal scheme, that require order-independent resolution. So it was more a game-design challenge than anything. For example if 2 units move to the same destination, what should happen? (I chose to have them both dead, with special rule for kings).
What about 2 piece swaping space or moving on the way of another. I decided that it goes through to not have to track to many thing onchain (storage is expansive, and each reveal come in a different transaction) What I also did (thanks again to webevm) is to not replicate logic of solidity in typescript, instead when I needed to compute the expected outcome in the client, I executed eth_call right in the browser. One good advantage of it is that it does not reveal what data you are interested to fetch, which you need for your move to remain secret, a crucial element for a game like this. I used AI to help us implement the spec we needed. It was a conversation where AI could see many of the potential issue but was left wondering what to do. And while we could get a version working quite quickly, the game design issue mentioned above became aparent and fix them. We also spent the last hours to polish the visuals. One annoying thing I left for later is the spawning mechanism that let someone technically use multi account to prevent anyone from spawning. I intend to fix with an auction mechanism later

projects.title: Web3MCP
projects.description: Let AI agents use any smart contract by its ENS name. You sign every write in your own wallet.
projects.project_description: Web3MCP lets AI agents use any smart contract just by its ENS name, with no custom integration code. Today an agent can only use a protocol if someone writes and maintains an integration for it. With Web3MCP, the protocol publishes a manifest of agent tools in text records on its own ENS name, such as agentswap.web3mcp.eth. Install one plugin in Claude Code or Codex and ask "swap 0.001 ETH for USDC on agentswap.web3mcp.eth". The agent reads the manifest from ENS, checks the contracts, quotes the swap and prepares the transaction. A local signing page shows each step in plain words and your balances after the swap, simulated, and you sign in your own browser wallet. The agent never holds a key. If you don't name a protocol ("swap my ETH to USDC"), the agent searches an index on Arkiv, where any protocol lists itself with its own wallet. It then verifies the result against ENS before using it. It's an onchain web for AI agents: a contract and its tool manifest are the site, ENS is DNS, Arkiv is the search engine, the MCP server is the browser, and your wallet signs. No company runs a server in the middle, and nobody can remove a protocol's listing. Live on Sepolia: AgentSwap, a demo contract that swaps ETH and USDC on Uniswap v4, quotes through Uniswap's Quoter, and refuses any swap more than 3% below Chainlink's ETH/USD price. It's published at agentswap.web3mcp.eth and owner-verified. The plugin for Claude Code and Codex: a generic MCP server, a skill to use protocols, and a skill (web3mcp-build) that helps developers make their own contracts agent-ready and publish them on ENS. The Arkiv search index, with agentswap.web3mcp.eth listed. Safety: manifests are untrusted input, so they're validated and fail closed. A contract is marked owner-verified only when its ENS primary name points back to the publishing name. Contract code, including proxy implementations, is re-checked before every write, and every write is simulated before you see it.
projects.how_its_made: Everything is TypeScript in one npm monorepo, plus Foundry for the contract. SDK (@web3mcp/evm, on npm): a zod schema for the manifest, plus ENS discovery, reads and writes with viem. It reads the org.web3mcp.manifest text record, checks it against the keccak256 digest in org.web3mcp.digest, then validates it and fails closed. A contract is owner-verified when its ENS primary name is the publishing name or a subname of it. The SDK hashes each contract's code, including EIP-1967 and EIP-1822 proxy implementations, and refuses a write if the code changed since discovery. Writes are built from the manifest's argument bindings, approvals that already exist are skipped, and all steps are simulated together with viem's simulateCalls to get the balance changes. MCP server (@web3mcp/mcp): one generic server on the official MCP SDK, with no protocol-specific code. Its tools are search, discover, read, call, status and wallet. Every write opens a local signing page (plain TypeScript and viem, bundled with esbuild) where the user's own browser wallet signs: one prompt through EIP-5792 wallet_sendCalls when the wallet supports batching, otherwise one transaction at a time. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook confirms every write. There's no private key anywhere. Plugin: the server ships as one bundled file in a plugin for Claude Code and Codex, so it needs only Node 22. The web3mcp-build skill carries its own checker, so any coding agent can write, check and publish a manifest. ENS: manifests live in text records on the protocol's own name. The web3mcp-publish CLI detects whether the resolver is ENSv1 or ENSv2's PermissionedResolver and prints the right setText calldata. With ENSv2, a release key can get a role for only the org.web3mcp.* records. Tool inputs accept ENS names, and primary names prove contract ownership. Arkiv: the search engine. Each search term is an indexed attribute, so a search is one Arkiv query filtered by chainId. The publisher's wallet owns its listing; listings expire after 30 days unless refreshed, and an updated manifest replaces its listing atomically with executeBatch. Hosts keep a listing only while its digest matches ENS, so the index can't send an agent anywhere unexpected. Uniswap v4 and Chainlink: AgentSwap swaps straight through the v4 PoolManager (unlock, swap, settle, take) with native ETH and Circle's USDC, and checks the price against Chainlink's ETH/USD feed. It was deployed with the deterministic CREATE2 deployer. Hacky bit: Uniswap's V4Quoter is non-view because it runs the swap and reverts, so we added a dryRun flag to the manifest that lets a read tool call it, only ever as eth_call. Contract tests fork Sepolia and swap on the real pool. Website and docs: Next.js and Mermaid. We built this with Claude Code as an AI coding assistant, and every AI-assisted commit says so.

MCP server (@web3mcp/mcp): one generic server on the official MCP SDK, with no protocol-specific code. Its tools are search, discover, read, call, status and wallet. Every write opens a local signing page (plain TypeScript and viem, bundled with esbuild) where the user's own browser wallet signs: one prompt through EIP-5792 wallet_sendCalls when the wallet supports batching, otherwise one transaction at a time. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook confirms every write. There's no private key anywhere.

Plugin: the server ships as one bundled file in a plugin for Claude Code and Codex, so it needs only Node 22. The web3mcp-build skill carries its own checker, so any coding agent can write, check and publish a manifest.

ENS: manifests live in text records on the protocol's own name. The web3mcp-publish CLI detects whether the resolver is ENSv1 or ENSv2's PermissionedResolver and prints the right setText calldata. With ENSv2, a release key can get a role for only the org.web3mcp.* records. Tool inputs accept ENS names, and primary names prove contract ownership.

Arkiv: the search engine. Each search term is an indexed attribute, so a search is one Arkiv query filtered by chainId. The publisher's wallet owns its listing; listings expire after 30 days unless refreshed, and an updated manifest replaces its listing atomically with executeBatch. Hosts keep a listing only while its digest matches ENS, so the index can't send an agent anywhere unexpected.

Uniswap v4 and Chainlink: AgentSwap swaps straight through the v4 PoolManager (unlock, swap, settle, take) with native ETH and Circle's USDC, and checks the price against Chainlink's ETH/USD feed. It was deployed with the deterministic CREATE2 deployer. Hacky bit: Uniswap's V4Quoter is non-view because it runs the swap and reverts, so we added a dryRun flag to the manifest that lets a read tool call it, only ever as eth_call. Contract tests fork Sepolia and swap on the real pool.

Website and docs: Next.js and Mermaid.

We built this with Claude Code as an AI coding assistant, and every AI-assisted commit says so.

projects.title: pinky promise
projects.description: A sensor signs the cold chain, and a proven breach freezes the tokenized warehouse receipt
projects.project_description: Pinky Promise lets a buyer check how goods were actually stored before buying a warehouse receipt for them. Today that confidence comes from paperwork and the reputation of whoever issued the receipt. A pocket device travels with the lot (our demo is a pharma pallet with a 2–8 °C limit) and signs every temperature and humidity reading with a key rooted in a secure element. At each custody handoff it records the seal with a photo, an NFC tag and a case switch, gets a co-signature from a second microcontroller at the venue, and signs a checkpoint covering every reading since the last one. A vision model on 0G then answers ACCEPT_CUSTODY, REJECT or ESCALATE, based on the seal photo and the readings. The full episode goes encrypted to 0G Storage, so anyone with the lot's view key can replay it and re-verify its signatures. If 0G can't be reached, the handoff stays PENDING: no decision is made up and the token isn't touched. The public evidence lives on Arkiv as read-only entities. The device's own wallet creates the readings and checkpoints, so the gateway relaying them can't forge them, and a reading it withholds shows up as a gap. Raw temperatures and positions stay private: the public record says only whether a reading was in range, plus a zero-knowledge proof that it was taken inside a venue's boundary. The one exception is a confirmed breach, which discloses the single reading that proves it. Evidence expires when the dispute window closes. Each lot is a security token issued through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio. Units trade only while a venue holds the goods and are locked in transit. They freeze when a REJECT is backed by a device-signed out-of-range reading, which the contract verifies itself, so the party relaying 0G's answer can't freeze a lot alone. Only an inspector can release a frozen lot, and holders redeem after delivery. A buyer page reads Arkiv and Hedera directly and checks every signature and proof in the browser before the buyer commits. Current status: the full journey runs end to end on one machine, with a simulated device and local stand-ins for the networks. The stand-ins run the unmodified Arkiv SDK and the real ATS contract bytecode, and decisions come from a mock model that is labelled as a mock everywhere it appears. The testnet adapters are written but haven't sent a transaction yet, and the firmware is written but hasn't run on a board.
projects.how_its_made: It's a TypeScript pnpm monorepo with Solidity contracts (Foundry), a Noir circuit and ESP32-S3 firmware, all sharing one protocol package. The hardware design is an SHT31 sensor, GPS, a camera, a PN532 NFC reader and an ATECC608B secure element, plus a second ESP32-S3 as the venue anchor. The gateway uses Hono and the buyer page uses React and Vite. Readings are 144-byte fixed-width binary payloads hashed with SHA-256, because the same bytes have to be handled by firmware, Solidity and a Noir circuit. SHA-256 is hardware-accelerated on the ESP32, a precompile on the EVM and affordable in a circuit, while keccak fails on the first and third. How the partner technologies helped: 0G is the decision layer. The gateway calls the Compute Router's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with the seal photo and a summary of the readings, and anything other than a clean JSON decision counts as no decision. There is no fallback model. Encrypted episode logs go to 0G Storage, and their root is recorded on Arkiv and inside the attestation sent to Hedera. Arkiv gave us a verifiable data layer without building an indexer. "All out-of-range readings for this lot from this device" is a single query the browser runs directly, scoped by who created the entity. The device isn't online itself, so we gave the Arkiv SDK a viem account whose signTransaction hands the transaction to the device. The device decodes the calldata and signs only read-only creates of its own readings and checkpoints. Per-entity lifetimes make data expiry part of the write. Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio gave us compliant issuance, an allowlist and KYC. ATS has no warehouse-receipt type, so each lot is an equity token with only the redemption right and zero decimals. Our CustodyOracle contract is the token's ERC-3643 compliance module, so every transfer asks it for the lot's custody state. It holds the freeze role and verifies the breach reading itself using the SHA-256 precompile and ecrecover. Freezing an address in ATS would undo the holder's onboarding, so we freeze each holder's units instead, 50 holders at a time with continuation calls so a large lot can't run out of gas. Noir with UltraHonk proves a device-signed reading was inside a venue's bounding box without revealing the position. Proofs are about 8.8 kB, take about two seconds to generate, and verify in the buyer's browser with bb.js. A proof gives privacy, not authenticity, since a spoofed GPS proves just as well. Authenticity comes from the venue anchor's co-signature, and the page says so. The hacky parts: We wrote a local Arkiv node, with its own lexer and parser for the query language, that emulates the entity precompile closely enough for the unmodified SDK to run on it, and we checked it against real testnet responses. For Hedera, we load an anvil chain with a snapshot of the real ATS contracts from testnet, both bytecode and storage. The firmware is a USB serial bridge rather than a standalone device: the device logic runs on the host, and every part has a simulated twin, so hardware can be connected one piece at a time without code changes. The custody rules exist in both TypeScript and Solidity, so we generate all 384 state combinations from the TypeScript and check them against the contract. The code, tests, firmware and docs were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude), working from our architecture plan and under our direction.

projects.title: Adult Verification
projects.description: Privacy-preserving secure age verification Blockchain-based system
projects.project_description: This application is designed to enable users to provide robust proof of their adult status to SaaS providers. Users first verify their age using a "My Number Card" and store this information on their own smartphones. When a SaaS provider requests proof, the verification process is carried out via a smart contract that leverages government public keys verification protocol.
projects.how_its_made: In this project, we focused on two key characteristics of Ethereum: its high resistance to tampering and its inherent challenges regarding privacy protection. By leveraging public-key cryptography, we developed a system that enables age verification while safeguarding user privacy. We began by defining the core concept, features, and operational workflow of the application. Subsequently, we utilized AI to refine the specifications, create mockups, prepare presentation materials, and develop smart contracts, ultimately culminating in the execution of integrated testing.

projects.title: Aquantis
projects.description: Aquantis lets fee-on-transfer tokens like gold-backed XAUH run trading strategies on 1inch’s Aqua.
projects.project_description: Aquantis makes it possible to use a fee-on-transfer (FoT) token on the Aqua protocol, and here is how we got there. We started with Aquantis – Telegram Mini App (TMA), our Telegram Mini App with a built-in AI agent, which worked with the Aqua protocol and its strategies. The next step felt natural: add [Herculis Gold Coin (XAUH)] (https://xauh.gold/), a gold-backed real-world-asset token, so users could run Aqua strategies on a gold-backed asset. That’s where we hit a wall. XAUH takes a fee on every transfer, so the amount received is lower than the amount sent, and tokens like this are notoriously difficult to integrate into DeFi. Aqua was no exception. So we set out to solve it. Aquantis now enables XAUH, a fee-on-transfer token, to run trading strategies on Aqua. And because we built on top of TMA, you also get a bonus: a convenient, all-in-one Telegram experience for managing your XAUH portfolio, where the agent lets you pick an XAUH trading strategy and routes it through whichever Aqua Strategies offer the best terms. On top of that, we’ve integrated [ID Quantique’s] (https://www.idquantique.com/) quantum random number generator (QRNG), bringing true, physically sourced randomness into the product. The Token Behind Aquantis: XAUH. Herculis Gold Coin is a Swiss gold-backed payment token issued by [Herculis Tokens SA] (https://herculis.ch/herculis-tokens-sa), where each token represents one gram of 999.9-purity [LBMA] (https://www.lbma.org.uk/) gold that is refined, audited, stored, and insured in Swiss vaults. XAUH is already live across four networks – [Ethereum] (https://ethereum.org/), [TON] (https://ton.org/), [TRON] (https://tron.network/), and [Polkadot] (https://polkadot.com/), with [JAMTON] (https://app.jamton.network/) serving as the bridge connecting TON and Polkadot infrastructure. On Ethereum specifically, it's deployed as a verified ERC-20 token tracked on [Etherscan] (https://etherscan.io/token/0xa9b17f572341219703Bc951725Bdb3CA756B1A65), with an active XAUH/USDT liquidity pool on [Uniswap] (https://app.uniswap.org/explore/tokens/ethereum/0xa9b17f572341219703Bc951725Bdb3CA756B1A65). Addressing Aqua’s Fee-on-Transfer Limitation. A key technical limitation of Aqua, 1inch's self-custodial shared-liquidity protocol, is that it does not natively support fee-on-transfer tokens – assets that deduct a percentage on every transfer, so the amount received is less than the amount sent. Because Aqua's core contract and its AquaApps track maker and taker balances based on the amount specified in a swap rather than the amount actually delivered, an unhandled FoT token can desynchronize that internal accounting, breaking pricing logic and putting maker funds at risk; 1inch itself lists "Lack of support for Fee-on-Transfer (FoT) tokens" as out of scope in its bug bounty program, treating it as a known, unaddressed gap rather than a bug to be patched. Solving it matters because Aqua's own stated ambition is to become a venue for real-world-asset trading – letting users swap tokenized gold, equities, and other real-world assets (RWA) directly against each other – and fee-on-transfer mechanics are common in exactly that asset class, so leaving this gap unhandled quietly locks a meaningful share of RWA tokens out of Aqua's strategies. Because XAUH is central to what we’re building, we fixed it at the transfer level: Aquantis adds fee-aware transfer handling on top of Aqua, so XAUH swaps settle accurately.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Fee-on-transfer token support in SwapVM + Aqua

About Aqua.sol

The change: Aqua.push now measures the maker's balanceOf before and after safeTransferFrom and credits the received delta instead of the nominal amount:

    uint256 before = IERC20(token).balanceOf(maker);
    IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, maker, amount);
    uint256 received = IERC20(token).balanceOf(maker) - before;
    balance.store(prevBalance + received, tokensCount);

Why this is the only option. The drift is created in exactly one place: push credits the maker's virtual balance with the nominal amount, but the transfer delivers only amount times (1 minus r) to the maker's wallet (the fee is deducted from the recipient). Because that virtual balance is what SwapVM prices against and what Aqua.pull authorizes against, the mismatch compounds into phantom liquidity - reverse swaps can revert, and the pool prices as if it received more input than it did. There is no router-side fix: the router can only choose the single amount passed to push, and push both credits and transfers that same number, so the credited amount must be the measured receipt.

Fully backwards compatible. For a regular token the delta equals amount, so behavior is unchanged. pull is untouched (the maker sends the nominal amount, so its wallet delta is already amount). No signature change, no new entry point.

About AquaSwapVMRouter.sol

The problem. SwapVM's registers assume transferred equals accounted. For an FOT token that is false: the input leg delivers less than the nominal input (maker overpays), and the output leg delivers less than the quoted output (taker receives less than quoted). The AMM therefore priced the wrong amounts and the quote was dishonest.

FeeOnTransfer instruction makes the VM FOT-aware. Two new opcodes - FeeOnTransferIn (slot 23) and FeeOnTransferOut (slot 24), args [uint32 feeBps, uint8 feeFloor], 1e9 = 100%. FeeOnTransferIn: tokenIn is FOT, price on the net input and keep the gross the taker pays. FeeOnTransferOut: tokenOut is FOT, keep the net the taker receives and gross the pull up in settlement. A feeFloor flag mirrors the token's ceil/floor fee so the computed net matches the token exactly. Because the fee is always deducted from the recipient, the taker absorbs the tax and the registers stay taker-facing - amountIn equals gross, amountOut equals net - so quote() is honest and slippage thresholds are checked in the taker's own units. A single bidirectional strategy branches on direction with the existing jumpIfTokenIn, so one shipped strategy serves both legs.

Two-hop vs one-hop, both covered. One-hop (resolver, useTransferFromAndAquaPush=false) transfers once; two-hop (EOA, =true) transfers taker to router to maker and double-taxes the input. A twoHop flag is derived from the taker's flag; FeeOnTransferIn prices G times (1 minus r) versus G times (1 minus r) squared accordingly, and the two-hop transferIn measures the router's received balance and pushes that net. Result: one strategy, a fair quote, and no maker loss, in both modes.

General-purpose SettlementContext. Context gains SettlementRegisters { amountInDelta, amountOutDelta, twoHop }, expressing settlement amount equals quote amount plus delta. It lives on Context, not SwapRegisters, to keep the IExtruction ABI stable. It is a generic settlement-versus-quote channel, not FOT-specific.

Backwards compatible. New opcodes fill the reserved slots (no renumbering, so existing program bytecode is untouched); regular tokens have zero deltas and the push delta equals amount; the Extruction ABI is preserved; the full unit suite passes. The diff is minimal: one new instruction file plus small edits to VM.sol, AquaOpcodes.sol, and SwapVM.sol.

Not covered currently. Rebasing/reflection tokens are unsupported; push costs two extra balanceOf calls; the Pushed event now emits net; FeeProtocol combined with FOT is untested; the SDK opcode table still needs slots 23/24; and two-hop (EOA) inherently pays two transfer fees.

projects.title: Veil402
projects.description: Private payment and inference rails for AI agents — a VPN for AI inference and payments.
projects.project_description:
Veil402 is a private layer for agentic payments and inference. It lets people and AI agents call models and pay per request, without
trusting the provider with their data, handing over their identity, or exposing their spending on chain. AI inference is missing three things. Verifiable inference: you can't know the right model ran, the bill is accurate, or your data stayed
private, so you have only the provider's word. Private identity: paying means an account, an API key, KYC and a billing history. Private
payments: on-chain x402 removes accounts, but a public chain exposes every payment, revealing an agent's strategy to anyone watching. Veil402 solves all three behind one API key created and managed entirely on your device. A local daemon serves an OpenAI-compatible
endpoint, so tools like Aider, OpenHands and Langflow work with no SDK, wallet or signup. 0G Private Compute provides verifiable inference. Models run inside TEEs, and each response is signed and checked against the provider's
on-chain key. Prompts are HPKE-sealed to our AWS Nitro enclave, which meters usage itself, so neither the provider nor our host can read
them. A shielded pool provides private payments. Funds deposited on Hedera become private notes, and every spend is a zero-knowledge proof, so
nothing links a deposit to a spend and no payment graph builds up. Session-based escrow for x402 works like Lightning-style channels. An agent locks one note as a spending ceiling, makes many calls off chain
with no gas per request, and settles once at the end, with the unused balance returned privately. Each session uses fresh keys, so sessions
can't be linked.
projects.how_its_made:
Veil402 — private payment and inference rails for AI agents
Think of it as a VPN for AI inference and payments. You get one OpenAI-compatible API key, created and managed entirely on your own device. No account at a provider, no API key generated on someone else’s site, no card, no identity. The three things missing today Verifiable inference. When you call a provider you cannot check that the model actually ran, that the model you paid for is the one that answered, that the token count on the bill is real, or that your data stayed confidential. A provider’s word isn’t enough. Private payment. Paying for inference usually means exposing your identity — through an account, an API key tied to it, a payment method, and a billing history. Payment privacy. On-chain 402 payments give you accessibility, but they expose the buyer, the seller, the amount, and the whole transaction history, permanently. The three technologies we bring together 0G private compute — verifiable inference. Inference runs on 0G’s TEE providers, so the seller never reads your prompt and you get attestation that the work happened. We don’t replace that; we depend on it. Shielded pool — private payments. Funds enter the pool as ERC-20 and become notes: commitments whose owner, value and asset are hidden inside a Poseidon hash. Spending a note requires a zero-knowledge proof that you know the preimage, without revealing it on chain. No deposit→spend link, no payment graph, no counterparty history. Session-based escrow for x402 — Lightning-like channels for a session. An envelope is a locked note that funds one inference session. It reserves value from the pool, meters usage call by call off chain, and settles the remainder back when the session ends. Funds move only when work is proven, and the chain sees the open and the settle rather than every call. How it works, end to end Shield the funds. You deposit once. What lands on chain is a commitment — a leaf in a depth-20 Merkle tree. Owner, value and asset are inside the hash.
Create an agent mandate. An OpenAI-compatible API key with its own spending budget and policies, and its own ledger. The key is bound to a budget, not to an identity.
Prompt from any OpenAI-compatible tool. We run against Langflow, Aider and OpenHands with two fields changed — base URL and key. Prompts and answers are HPKE-sealed, so the relay sees ciphertext only. An AWS Nitro enclave runs the session and signs what it billed, so the seller is not the one doing the counting.
Pay another agent privately. Agent B returns a price and a payment address (veil402:pay:v1:…). Agent A pays it as a single shielded transact, broadcast through a relay so no buyer address appears on chain. Agent B discovers the incoming note and can spend it. An observer watching the pool sees two commitments and two nullifiers and learns neither the sender, nor the recipient, nor the amount — while each agent’s console shows exactly what it is owed or has spent. Control and settlement without disclosure.
