  AI inference is missing three things. Verifiable inference: you can't know the right model ran, the bill is accurate, or your data stayed
  private, so you have only the provider's word. Private identity: paying means an account, an API key, KYC and a billing history. Private
  payments: on-chain x402 removes accounts, but a public chain exposes every payment, revealing an agent's strategy to anyone watching.

  Veil402 solves all three behind one API key created and managed entirely on your device. A local daemon serves an OpenAI-compatible
  endpoint, so tools like Aider, OpenHands and Langflow work with no SDK, wallet or signup.

  0G Private Compute provides verifiable inference. Models run inside TEEs, and each response is signed and checked against the provider's
  on-chain key. Prompts are HPKE-sealed to our AWS Nitro enclave, which meters usage itself, so neither the provider nor our host can read
  them.

  A shielded pool provides private payments. Funds deposited on Hedera become private notes, and every spend is a zero-knowledge proof, so
  nothing links a deposit to a spend and no payment graph builds up.

  Session-based escrow for x402 works like Lightning-style channels. An agent locks one note as a spending ceiling, makes many calls off chain
  with no gas per request, and settles once at the end, with the unused balance returned privately. Each session uses fresh keys, so sessions
  can't be linked.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Veil402 — private payment and inference rails for AI agents
 Think of it as a VPN for AI inference and payments. You get one OpenAI-compatible API key, created and managed entirely on your own device. No account at a provider, no API key generated on someone else’s site, no card, no identity.

The three things missing today

Verifiable inference. When you call a provider you cannot check that the model actually ran, that the model you paid for is the one that answered, that the token count on the bill is real, or that your data stayed confidential. A provider’s word isn’t enough.

Private payment. Paying for inference usually means exposing your identity — through an account, an API key tied to it, a payment method, and a billing history.

Payment privacy. On-chain 402 payments give you accessibility, but they expose the buyer, the seller, the amount, and the whole transaction history, permanently.

The three technologies we bring together

0G private compute — verifiable inference. Inference runs on 0G’s TEE providers, so the seller never reads your prompt and you get attestation that the work happened. We don’t replace that; we depend on it.

Shielded pool — private payments. Funds enter the pool as ERC-20 and become notes: commitments whose owner, value and asset are hidden inside a Poseidon hash. Spending a note requires a zero-knowledge proof that you know the preimage, without revealing it on chain. No deposit→spend link, no payment graph, no counterparty history.

Session-based escrow for x402 — Lightning-like channels for a session. An envelope is a locked note that funds one inference session. It reserves value from the pool, meters usage call by call off chain, and settles the remainder back when the session ends. Funds move only when work is proven, and the chain sees the open and the settle rather than every call.

How it works, end to end

Shield the funds. You deposit once. What lands on chain is a commitment — a leaf in a depth-20 Merkle tree. Owner, value and asset are inside the hash.
Create an agent mandate. An OpenAI-compatible API key with its own spending budget and policies, and its own ledger. The key is bound to a budget, not to an identity.
Prompt from any OpenAI-compatible tool. We run against Langflow, Aider and OpenHands with two fields changed — base URL and key. Prompts and answers are HPKE-sealed, so the relay sees ciphertext only. An AWS Nitro enclave runs the session and signs what it billed, so the seller is not the one doing the counting.
Pay another agent privately. Agent B returns a price and a payment address (veil402:pay:v1:…). Agent A pays it as a single shielded transact, broadcast through a relay so no buyer address appears on chain. Agent B discovers the incoming note and can spend it. An observer watching the pool sees two commitments and two nullifiers and learns neither the sender, nor the recipient, nor the amount — while each agent’s console shows exactly what it is owed or has spent. Control and settlement without disclosure.

projects.title: FrameGas
projects.description: Pay gas in any ERC20, natively. EIP-8141 paymaster priced on Uniswap v4, via the alt mempool.
projects.project_description: FrameGas lets an account that only holds an ERC20 (a stablecoin, a governance token, an agent's USDC budget) send any transaction on Ethereum without ever touching ETH. You sign one EIP-8141 frame transaction. The paymaster's validation frame reads the token price from a Uniswap v4 pool and checks your cap, balance and allowance. Its settlement frame pulls the token, swaps it for ETH on the same pool and pays the gas. Your call runs. A last frame refunds whatever token wasn't used. All of it is atomic, so if any frame fails nothing moves. This only works in the alternative mempool. Send the same signed bytes to the canonical mempool and it comes back with StorageReadNonSender, because the paymaster reads pool state during validation. The alt mempool lets it in because the paymaster is staked. What's in the repo: the paymaster with 44 contract tests and a 10,000 run fuzz; a bootstrap mode that handles a user's very first transaction in a single tx with no precompile and no relayer; a per account daily quota enforced in validation; a TypeScript SDK (framegas.send({payToken, maxTokenCost, calls})) that simulates first and sizes every frame; an MCP server so agents can pay their own gas from a token budget; a Skill in the Uniswap AI format; a Chainlink CRE workflow for price sanity bounds; a demo with replay and live modes; and docs/findings.md with what I learned about how the devnet's rules differ from ERC-8421, including a 100k shared validation cap for staked entities, disabled precompiles (filed as forshtat/mempool-workshop#1), the state gas cost of crossing a tick for the first time, and what it costs to grief a paymaster that prices from a pool. Measured on the devnet: a normal transaction costs the user 1.04x the gas fee in tokens with a 1.17x reserve. The first transaction per token costs about 0.56 fgUSD more because of the allowance slot. The paymaster can lose at most 0.002 ETH on any single transaction. Limitations: EIP-8141 ships in Hegotá, so this runs on the EF alt mempool devnet (chain 1337) only. The stake is locked for good. Permit deadlines have to be max uint because TIMESTAMP is banned in validation. Thin pools make a failed settlement cheap to force, so I enforce a minimum liquidity check at admission.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, no upgradeability. FrameGasPaymaster stakes itself from its own constructor because the registry keys on msg.sender. Validation is a single extsload of slot0 through Uniswap's StateLibrary, a balance and allowance read, and some arithmetic. That's 45k gas, and it has to fit inside a 100k cap shared across every validation frame. I measured that cap live: 100,000 was admitted, 100,001 was rejected. NUMBER, TIMESTAMP, BASEFEE and GASPRICE are all banned in validation. So the deviation check compares against a reference tick the paymaster keeps in its own storage and advances during settlement, with a permissionless syncReference() that's rate limited per block so a big market move can't brick it. Gas price comes from the signed transaction itself. Validation also pins the next frame to settle() on this paymaster, with the exact calldata shape, zero value and a minimum gas limit, so every griefing path I found fails at admission instead of after the paymaster has already paid. Settlement swaps on a native ETH v4 pool from my own unlock callback, no router. I went native because mainnet's ETH/USDC pool is about seven orders of magnitude deeper than WETH/USDC. Each tick crossed adds roughly 24.5k gas, and crossing a tick for the first time ever needs around 196k of state gas, so the SDK simulates first, searches for state gas and then execution gas per frame, tightens the limits, and re-simulates the whole thing before signing. Bootstrap mode exists because the devnet sidecar runs with precompiles: [], which means ecrecover gets rejected in validation even though OP-062 and CALLING-040 both allow it. Rather than relay a permit, I let the user's first transaction carry a user frame that validation forces to be exactly approve(paymaster, n >= cap), with settlement running after it. One tx, zero ETH, no precompile. The devnet is ethrex on the eip8141 tracer branch with the sidecar from forshtat/mempool-workshop. Uniswap v4 core, Permit2 and Universal Router were already deployed there; I seeded my own native ETH/fgUSD pool at mainnet's price. The Chainlink CRE workflow runs in simulation and compares the devnet pool against mainnet. The demo is Next.js with a replay mode driven by recorded admission reports and receipts, which turned out to matter because the devnet halted for hours mid hackathon. The hacky bits: the stake can never be withdrawn (there's no owner, on purpose). Permit deadlines are max uint. The minimum liquidity threshold is set low on devnet and labelled as such. The explorer forgets everything when the node restarts, so I screenshot evidence into docs/evidence/. I used AI coding assistants (Claude) for implementation. Architecture, rule analysis, security decisions and all testing were reviewed by me.

projects.title: PreSettle
projects.description: Decentralized infrastructure for OTC and premarket trading with secure on-chain settlement.
projects.project_description: PreSettle is a trustless marketplace for two kinds of crypto deals that today happen in Telegram groups and on centralized desks: OTC trades and pre-launch (premarket) token sales. OTC: a maker locks the tokens they want to sell (or the USDC/EURC they want to buy with) in an escrow contract on Arc, sets a price, a deadline and whether partial fills are allowed. Takers fill all or part of the order and the contract computes the price on-chain, so nobody can underpay. The maker can cancel at any time, and once the deadline passes anyone can expire the order. Our keeper does this automatically, so unfilled tokens always go back to the maker. Premarket: an admin opens a market for a token that hasn't launched yet (symbol, TGE time, delivery window). Sellers lock 100% collateral in USDC or EURC and list an amount and price; buyers pay before TGE. After TGE the real token is set and the seller delivers it to every buyer inside the window. If the seller doesn't deliver, anyone can trigger the default: each buyer gets their payment back plus their share of the seller's collateral. If the token never launches, the offer is voided and everyone is refunded. The order book is open data on Arkiv. Every listing is an entity owned by the trader's wallet, not by us, so we can't edit or hide anyone's price. A listing expires on Arkiv at the same moment its deadline passes, so the book cleans itself. Every fill is written as a read-only record, giving each trader a track record nobody can rewrite. Anyone can query the book directly, without our API. Proceeds, refunds, delivered tokens and fees are credited in the escrow and withdrawn from the dashboard, so one blocked address can never freeze settlement for everyone else.
projects.how_its_made: Two chains, each doing what it is best at: money on Arc Testnet, data on Arkiv (Rabdi testnet). There is no centralized database. Contracts (Solidity 0.8.24, OpenZeppelin, Hardhat): OTCMarket and PreMarket. Every price is computed on-chain with Math.mulDiv and rounded in favour of the escrow, so a taker or buyer can never underpay. State changes happen before transfers, every settlement path can run only once, and payouts are pull-based (credit, then withdraw) because Arc's USDC blocklist makes direct transfers to a blocked address revert, and one blocked address must not freeze settlement for everyone. Gas is Arc's native USDC, so users only ever need USDC. 35 Hardhat tests cover fills, fee splits, cancel/expire, delivery, default, void, reclaim and a solvency check after every path, and we verified that the deployed bytecode is identical to the tested build. Arkiv: five typed schemas (OTC orders, premarket offers, fills, trader profiles, the token list). Users sign Arkiv writes with their own wallet, so they own their listings and we cannot edit or hide them. Expiry matches the business rules: an order expires on Arkiv exactly at its on-chain deadline, a premarket offer after TGE plus the delivery window, a fill is created read-only for 90 days, and a profile is patched and extended in one atomic batch. Only the fields the UI filters on are indexed (side, token, price, partial, symbol). The token list is trusted only via createdBy(admin). Backend (Node, Express, viem, Docker on AWS EC2): it queries Arkiv and verifies every listing against the Arc contract (the Arkiv owner must be the on-chain maker and the order must still be open), so a fake listing that copies our schema name is dropped. Market stats are computed straight from Arkiv entities, and prices come from CoinMarketCap. Notable hacks: Arkiv emits no event at expiry, so our keeper caches each order's deadline while the listing is still live, then calls the permissionless expire() on Arc once it passes, refunding the maker automatically. The Arkiv access key lives only in our read client; wallets get a second Rabdi chain config without the key, so it never leaks into MetaMask. One step list walks users through Arc then Arkiv transactions with explorer links. The app waits until the wallet itself reports the new network before sending, and if the Arc part succeeded but the Arkiv write failed, a "Retry the Arkiv step" button finishes it without paying twice. Pre-launch tokens have no address before TGE, so markets are keyed by symbol and the real token is attached at TGE. Admin transactions are simulated first, so a call that would revert costs no gas; contract errors are shown in plain words. Contract ABIs are exported to the frontend and backend on every compile, so the app always matches the contracts. Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind, wagmi, RainbowKit, TanStack Query. Admin sign-in uses Sign-In with Ethereum, checked by the backend and by the on-chain contract owner. Hosted on Vercel; the backend deploys through GitHub Actions to Docker on AWS with automatic CI/CD.

projects.title: vet402
projects.description: Your agent pays once. When the answer goes missing, the seller's deposit on Arc pays it back.
projects.project_description:
vet402 on Arc turns a paid answer that never arrived into a refund from the seller's own deposit, gas included.
On 2026-09-28, vet402, an AI agent I own, made 50 x402 purchases on Arc mainnet, settled in one batch. 31 delivered. 19 charged it and returned nothing it could use.
A payment that goes right sends 0 transactions to the contract, so x402 keeps settling in one step through Circle Gateway.
Tap "Start a dispute" at https://vet402-mumbai-live.vercel.app and a real claim runs on Arc testnet. On 2026-11-06 at 04:23 UTC the seller's answer came through Arc's Memo contract 2 s after the claim, with the claim id, the Gateway transfer and the Swarm box in its memo ( claim , answer ). On the iPhone in the video at 0:10 the same button reaches Delivered in 3.6 s.
With World ID, only the person who set the budget can release the agent's money. With Arkiv, every Arc ruling becomes a record any buyer can query, and with Swarm, anyone can fetch the sealed box of a dispute. x402 now sits at the Linux Foundation with Visa, Mastercard and Google among its premier members, and its stablecoins settle "with zero chargebacks", as Cloudflare puts it. vet402 adds the way back for a paid answer that never came, and the same contract already ran two disputes on Arc mainnet. Bounties: Arc (Arc Studio Continuity Track: Bring Your Project to Arc, Best Smart Contracts with Advanced Stablecoin Logic, In Arc Studio, Best Mobile Web Consumer Agent Using the Marketplace Discovery API), Arkiv (Build on Arkiv and the Arkiv + Swarm bonus, existing projects), and World ([Cont] Best Use of IDKit). Why it matters x402 made the payment final. vet402 on Arc makes the purchase final: the answer arrives, or the seller's deposit pays the buyer back, gas included. When a line drops after payment, a retry pays again. At the event a plain retry to Seller B left 2 transfers in Circle's record for one request: e9cbd6d5-d3a3-4693-9e6d-f9d33a197b31 and b9d962ef-6276-4f29-a94d-87618539a6fd, 2026-11-05 16:04 UTC. circlefin/arc-nanopayments#43 tracks the same case. With SealedDelivery, vet402 asks for the key with the payment it already made, and one request is charged once. Any x402 seller can add it The README of packages/sealed-delivery shows the whole integration in 4 lines that a test runs as written: an import, 2 lines on the seller (the middleware and the route) and 1 on the buyer (openSealed). The middleware seals each answer, signs the promise, and runs a lookout that answers claims on Arc by itself. How it works vet402 pays once through Gateway. That one EIP-3009 signature later doubles as its evidence, so the buyer signs once. The seller returns the answer locked with a fresh key, plus a signed promise: the hashes of the key, the answer and the ciphertext, bound to this buyer, this payment nonce and this price. vet402 asks for the key. When it comes, the job is done and SealedDelivery stays untouched. On 2026-11-06 at 01:42 UTC Seller A delivered in 2.1 s this way (transfer 8df8ff6d-df86-4aa1-b9fb-840347074510). When the key is missing, vet402 sends one claim with the promise and the payment signature it already made. The seller has 60 s to put the key on Arc. Silence ends in finalize. A key that opens a different answer ends in prove. Either verdict credits the buyer the price plus its gas from the seller's deposit and burns the same amount again, sent to 0x…dEaD where no one can spend it. The seller's answer goes through Arc's Memo contract at the seller's cost. The memoId is the claim id, and the memo names the Gateway transfer and the Swarm reference, so one claim id leads to the payment, the evidence and the verdict. Money a dispute wins back goes into the buyer's Gateway balance through depositFor once 0.05 USDC has come back, so the agent spends it again with Nanopayments. The cost of a dispute falls on the side that broke the promise. A claim used about 0.005 to 0.007 USDC of gas at 20 to 25 gwei on 2026-11-06 and a whole dispute about 0.009 to 0.013 USDC, and the seller's deposit pays all of it, so the most a buyer spends is the 0.001 USDC price. The claim measures its own gas. An answer repays that gas in the same transaction, and a verdict repays the price, the claim's gas and 230,000 gas for the calls after it, counted at the claim's gas price up to 100 gwei. Before paying, vet402 reads coverageFor and buys only from a seller whose deposit covers that verdict (server/tryJobWire.ts). With the claim at or below 100 gwei, the later calls at the claim's gas price and a deposit that covers the verdict, the buyer ends at or above zero in every outcome (contracts/README.md, The economics). Honest sellers get a tool too. The claimGuard option of the seller middleware in packages/sealed-delivery reads a buyer's Claimed and KeyRevealed events on Arc through buyerClaimRecord, and a seller can refuse a buyer whose latest claims keep ending in an answer, or ask it a higher price, before anything settles. Measured on Arc Final contract, Arc testnet, 2026-11-06 01:59 to 02:04 UTC, the run in the video. Price 0.001 USDC, four test sellers with 0.5 USDC deposits: Seller A answered the claim. The buyer got the answer, plus 0.000174 USDC over its claim gas ( claim , answer ). Seller F swapped the answer. Buyer after its own gas: +0.009599 USDC ( claim , answer , prove ). Seller E stayed silent. Buyer after its own gas: +0.001731 USDC ( claim , finalize ). Seller D sent a wrong key, which Arc reverted, then stayed silent. Buyer after its own gas: +0.001863 USDC ( claim , reverted answer , finalize ). "Buyer after its own gas" is everything that came back, less the 0.001 USDC price (except for A, which got its answer), less the buyer's fees for the claim, the verdict and the withdrawal. flushBurn, which sends the burned half on, is open to anyone. In this run vet402's buyer also sent each one, at 0.001174 USDC, and still ended ahead every time. Since 2026-11-06 05:40 UTC it leaves flushBurn to others. Video 1:10 to 1:36, and the events on the verified explorer at 1:36. DEMO.md lists every transaction of the event. Arc mainnet runs the same source at 0xf3e2a77e1a93eeb791ae1016f411e5bb8a05e6d9, Sourcify exact_match. On 2026-11-06 from 02:03 to 02:04 UTC the buyer ended 0.000139 USDC ahead when the seller answered and 0.001355 USDC ahead when it stayed silent ( answer , finalize ). Video 3:30. The idea starts from FairSwap (Dziembowski, Eckey, Faust, CCS 2018, https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740). SealedDelivery holds a seller deposit in place of the payment, because the payment has already settled through Gateway. The consumer agent on Arc Open https://vet402-mumbai-live.vercel.app on a phone and type a job. vet402 reads Circle's Discovery catalog for Arc testnet (134 listings on 2026-11-06, Quicknode nodes and BotPay), scores every listing against the words with BM25 and buys from the live seller it picks. On 2026-11-05 at 22:48 UTC, for Did my last payment go through? , it picked Quicknode's Arc testnet node, showed the 3 it compared, and asked "May I spend up to 0.0001 USDC on this job?". projects.how_its_made: I designed SealedDelivery's mechanism: a seller deposit in place of escrow, the double verdict with a burned half, coverageFor before every payment, and the claim's gas repaid at its own price. Arc Studio and Claude Code wrote the code to that design, and every instruction to Arc Studio is in prompts/. Claude Code drives Arc Studio through the arc-studio CLI. SealedDelivery is Solidity 0.8 on OpenZeppelin's ECDSA and EIP712, tested with Foundry (246 passed in Studio's Terminal). The buyer signature is the EIP-3009 authorization Gateway already receives (domain GatewayWalletBatched), so a claim reuses it. Answers are sealed with keccak in counter mode, so prove can decrypt on chain. The backend is Node and Express on Bun, the screen is Vite and React, payments go through @circle-fin/x402-batching, World ID through IDKit with server-side v4 verification, receipts and rulings through @arkiv-network/sdk on Rabdi in one executeBatch per dispute, dispute boxes through @ethersphere/bee-js on my own Bee light node, pinned, and each seller's answer through Arc's Memo contract.

vet402 on Arc turns a paid answer that never arrived into a refund from the seller's own deposit, gas included.
On 2026-09-28, vet402, an AI agent I own, made 50 x402 purchases on Arc mainnet, settled in one batch. 31 delivered. 19 charged it and returned nothing it could use.
A payment that goes right sends 0 transactions to the contract, so x402 keeps settling in one step through Circle Gateway.
Tap "Start a dispute" at https://vet402-mumbai-live.vercel.app and a real claim runs on Arc testnet. On 2026-11-06 at 04:23 UTC the seller's answer came through Arc's Memo contract 2 s after the claim, with the claim id, the Gateway transfer and the Swarm box in its memo ([claim](https://explorer.testnet.arc.io/tx/0x51cbd0f57a5d312a7924917c981f50b33f250876f1367d56621180cf8f035fbb), [answer](https://explorer.testnet.arc.io/tx/0xbf44990914eed4adfce1dbf6f261da3dd8a79a80cdfaaec04b1c724f4099477e)). On the iPhone in the video at 0:10 the same button reaches Delivered in 3.6 s.
With World ID, only the person who set the budget can release the agent's money. With Arkiv, every Arc ruling becomes a record any buyer can query, and with Swarm, anyone can fetch the sealed box of a dispute.

x402 now sits at the Linux Foundation with Visa, Mastercard and Google among its premier members, and its stablecoins settle "with zero chargebacks", as Cloudflare puts it. vet402 adds the way back for a paid answer that never came, and the same contract already ran two disputes on Arc mainnet.

Bounties: Arc (Arc Studio Continuity Track: Bring Your Project to Arc, Best Smart Contracts with Advanced Stablecoin Logic, In Arc Studio, Best Mobile Web Consumer Agent Using the Marketplace Discovery API), Arkiv (Build on Arkiv and the Arkiv + Swarm bonus, existing projects), and World ([Cont] Best Use of IDKit).

### Why it matters

x402 made the payment final. vet402 on Arc makes the purchase final: the answer arrives, or the seller's deposit pays the buyer back, gas included.

When a line drops after payment, a retry pays again. At the event a plain retry to Seller B left 2 transfers in Circle's record for one request: e9cbd6d5-d3a3-4693-9e6d-f9d33a197b31 and b9d962ef-6276-4f29-a94d-87618539a6fd, 2026-11-05 16:04 UTC. circlefin/arc-nanopayments#43 tracks the same case. With SealedDelivery, vet402 asks for the key with the payment it already made, and one request is charged once.

### Any x402 seller can add it

The README of packages/sealed-delivery shows the whole integration in 4 lines that a test runs as written: an import, 2 lines on the seller (the middleware and the route) and 1 on the buyer (openSealed). The middleware seals each answer, signs the promise, and runs a lookout that answers claims on Arc by itself.

### How it works

1. vet402 pays once through Gateway. That one EIP-3009 signature later doubles as its evidence, so the buyer signs once.
2. The seller returns the answer locked with a fresh key, plus a signed promise: the hashes of the key, the answer and the ciphertext, bound to this buyer, this payment nonce and this price.
3. vet402 asks for the key. When it comes, the job is done and SealedDelivery stays untouched. On 2026-11-06 at 01:42 UTC Seller A delivered in 2.1 s this way (transfer 8df8ff6d-df86-4aa1-b9fb-840347074510).
4. When the key is missing, vet402 sends one claim with the promise and the payment signature it already made. The seller has 60 s to put the key on Arc.
5. Silence ends in finalize. A key that opens a different answer ends in prove. Either verdict credits the buyer the price plus its gas from the seller's deposit and burns the same amount again, sent to 0x…dEaD where no one can spend it.
6. The seller's answer goes through Arc's Memo contract at the seller's cost. The memoId is the claim id, and the memo names the Gateway transfer and the Swarm reference, so one claim id leads to the payment, the evidence and the verdict.
7. Money a dispute wins back goes into the buyer's Gateway balance through depositFor once 0.05 USDC has come back, so the agent spends it again with Nanopayments.

The cost of a dispute falls on the side that broke the promise. A claim used about 0.005 to 0.007 USDC of gas at 20 to 25 gwei on 2026-11-06 and a whole dispute about 0.009 to 0.013 USDC, and the seller's deposit pays all of it, so the most a buyer spends is the 0.001 USDC price. The claim measures its own gas. An answer repays that gas in the same transaction, and a verdict repays the price, the claim's gas and 230,000 gas for the calls after it, counted at the claim's gas price up to 100 gwei. Before paying, vet402 reads coverageFor and buys only from a seller whose deposit covers that verdict (server/tryJobWire.ts). With the claim at or below 100 gwei, the later calls at the claim's gas price and a deposit that covers the verdict, the buyer ends at or above zero in every outcome (contracts/README.md, The economics).

Honest sellers get a tool too. The claimGuard option of the seller middleware in packages/sealed-delivery reads a buyer's Claimed and KeyRevealed events on Arc through buyerClaimRecord, and a seller can refuse a buyer whose latest claims keep ending in an answer, or ask it a higher price, before anything settles.

projects.title: CrossFare
projects.description: Cross-chain swap API for AI agents: no signup, pay per call on Hedera, every quote public on Arkiv
projects.project_description: Crossfare is an open-source cross-chain swap API built for AI agents. Today an agent can plan a trade but can't execute one on its own: swap providers need a person to create an API key in a dashboard, and quotes are private promises nobody can check later. With Crossfare, an agent with only a wallet can swap across chains with no signup. It pays 0.01 testnet USDC per quote over x402 on Hedera. Crossfare asks the SwapKit API (THORChain, Chainflip, NEAR Intents and more, across 30+ chains) and the Uniswap Trading API (same-chain swaps) for routes, and ranks them by guaranteed output. It publishes every route as a public entity on Arkiv, which expires with the quote. Before sending funds, the agent reads its quote back from Arkiv and checks the owner and numbers. After delivery, Crossfare records the amount actually received, so anyone can compare what was promised with what arrived. Crossfare never holds the swapped funds: they go from the user's wallet to the provider and on to the receiver. Every settled payment is logged to a public Hedera Consensus Service topic, giving agent owners an audit trail of their agent's spending. It's live. Through the reference agent, 2 USDC on Ethereum delivered 1.997376 USDC on Base. Through the web UI, with no wallet connected, 5 USDC on Ethereum delivered 0.0022257 ETH on Base. Payment, Arkiv record, deposit and delivery are all linked in the README.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript pnpm monorepo, no Solidity anywhere, 462 tests written test-first. packages/core is the route engine: one adapter per venue (SwapKit API v3 for cross-chain, Uniswap Trading API for same-chain), normalized into one route shape and ranked by guaranteed minimum output. apps/api is a Hono service. Payments use the official x402 libraries (@x402/core and @x402/hedera, exact scheme) against the x402.org facilitator, with USDC as an HTS token on Hedera testnet. Our payment guard claims each payment first so replays fail, verifies it before calling any venue, and settles only when the request succeeds, so a failed quote costs the agent nothing. Settled payments are written to an HCS topic through the Hiero SDK. Each route becomes an Arkiv entity owned by Crossfare's service wallet, with indexed attributes (project, venue, assets, status, timestamps) and a lifetime matching the quote. When the swap finishes, Crossfare writes the status and amount received and extends the record to 7 days. The reference agent (viem) has a per-call cap, a total budget and an allowlist of payTo accounts, and refuses any route it can't verify on Arkiv. The web UI (React, Vite, wagmi) works like FixedFloat: no wallet needed, just a deposit address and QR code. Visitors have no Hedera account, so /demo endpoints pay the x402 fee from a rate-limited testnet account. UI on Vercel, API on AWS EC2. Hacky bits: Arkiv lifetimes must be whole 2-second blocks, so we round up. Transaction hashes overflow Arkiv's 128-byte string limit, so we store them as bytes. SwapKit's status lags, so the API also reads the deposit address on chain every 4 seconds. Quote IDs are public on Arkiv, so executing a quote requires a private swap token that only the payer receives.

projects.title: Assetro
projects.description: Assetro: real-world asset tokenization with investor onboarding and on-chain compliance.
projects.project_description: Assetro is an end-to-end platform for issuing and managing tokenized real-world assets. Issuers can create ERC-3643 tokens, review investor KYC, manage whitelists and transfer restrictions, and track cap tables, vesting, and corporate actions. Investors can register, connect wallets, complete onboarding, explore tokens, make purchases, and monitor holdings. A separate admin console provides approvals and oversight. The project brings these workflows together with identity and compliance smart contracts on EVM testnets.
projects.how_its_made: Assetro is a pnpm and Turborepo monorepo containing investor and issuer portals, an admin console, a unified API, a blockchain service, and smart contracts. The web apps use Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The NestJS API uses PostgreSQL and TypeORM for platform data, plus Redis and BullMQ for background jobs. Solidity and Hardhat power the ERC-3643 token, identity, and compliance contracts. Wagmi, viem, and ethers connect wallets and blockchain transactions; Stripe supports payment flows.

projects.title: OMEN
projects.description: A multiplayer Web3 world with playable lessons, a Mumbai venue and human-verified predictions.
projects.project_description: OMEN turns learning about Web3 into a shared, playable experience. Players begin as a courier in Blockhaven, where a missing payment at Maya’s tea stall introduces a story about wallets, signatures and digital payments. They can explore with friends, run shops, exchange messages, post on a community board and ask Alfred, an AI advisor, for practical guidance. The experience expands into a Mumbai-inspired event venue with a main stage, exhibitor booths and interactive stations. Visitors can ask Alfred questions at the mentor station and look up wallet-owned records at the Arkiv booth. Inside Pavilion Two, Bounty Royale lets World ID-verified players predict finalists and sponsor-bounty winners using a one-time allocation of 1,000 free OMEN points. Predictions, shared pools, activity and leaderboards update live. Moderators enter results with a source. Points cannot be purchased, transferred or redeemed for money. OMEN also includes a ChaiPay tutorial for Whitechain testnet payments and optional receipt storage on Arkiv. Simulated actions are clearly labelled: testnet tokens have no monetary value, and real INR payouts are not integrated.
projects.how_its_made: OMEN uses Three.js, custom shaders and HTML/CSS interfaces to render its browser-based worlds. Python scripts using Blender’s bpy API generate reproducible buildings, props and characters, exported as GLB assets. Vite builds the frontend, while Node.js serves HTTP APIs and Socket.IO connections for multiplayer, chat, merchant notifications and live arena updates. PostgreSQL stores shared application data. Bounty Royale uses dedicated tables for players, markets, predictions, point movements and moderator actions. Database transactions, row locks and unique constraints keep point deductions and predictions consistent. Idempotency keys let clients retry a prediction without charging points twice. World ID proofs are checked server-side, and the action-specific nullifier maps returning participants to the same player and one-time points allocation. The ChaiPay tutorial uses wallet-signed payment intents and a relayer on Whitechain Sepolia. The backend checks the resulting contract event before displaying an on-chain order receipt. Arkiv’s SDK lets players write wallet-owned, read-only records with a 30-day lifetime and query them later. Alfred uses external AI inference when configured, with explicitly labelled offline guidance otherwise. One useful implementation detail is the Mumbai venue’s multiplayer adapter: it converts flat-floor coordinates into the direction-vector format already used by the spherical village, allowing both environments to reuse the networking layer. Bounty Royale remains a separate PostgreSQL-backed points game; its predictions do not require cryptocurrency transfers.

projects.title: Aaj
projects.description: Aaj turns multilingual voice notes into simple, actionable daily plans powered by 0G AI.
projects.project_description: Aaj (आज), meaning "today" in Hindi, is a privacy-conscious, AI-powered daily planner that transforms a 30–60 second voice note into a simple, actionable plan. Instead of asking users to manually organize their thoughts, Aaj lets them speak naturally in their preferred language about everything on their mind. Using 0G AI, the application transcribes their speech and generates exactly three priorities, one potential blocker, one immediate first step, and a short encouragement to get started. Designed as a mobile-first web application, Aaj keeps daily plans and task completion history locally in the browser without requiring accounts or centralized storage of personal planning history. Our goal is to make productivity more accessible, multilingual, and less overwhelming. Speak your day. Leave with a plan.
projects.how_its_made: Aaj is being developed using Next.js, TypeScript, and 0G AI as a mobile-first Progressive Web App. The application is designed to capture short voice recordings through the browser's MediaRecorder API, with file upload as an alternative. Audio is sent through a secure Next.js server endpoint to 0G's whisper-large-v3 model for multilingual speech transcription. The resulting transcript is then processed by a configurable 0G language model to generate a structured daily plan with exactly three priorities, one blocker, one first step, and one encouragement. The backend validates model responses against a strict schema to maintain consistent results, while API credentials remain securely on the server. Plans and completion progress are stored locally in the browser, reducing the need for centralized storage of personal information. The architecture also includes a dedicated 0G provider adapter, error handling, and support for displaying authentic inference request IDs when available. Our main technical challenge is combining multilingual speech recognition, reliable structured AI output, and a privacy-conscious user experience into one simple interaction.

projects.title: Klyro
projects.description: Klyro: Evidence-based smart contract analysis, monitoring and verification for Uniswap v4 hooks.
projects.project_description: Klyro is a Uniswap v4 Hook Investigation and Monitoring Platform designed to make smart contract analysis more transparent and reliable. It provides comprehensive hook permission analysis, ENS address resolution, proxy and implementation inspection, external dependency tracking, deterministic security findings, and visual evidence graphs. With historical snapshot comparisons, verifiable Hook Passports, and continuous monitoring capabilities, Klyro helps users understand contract capabilities, investigate potential risks, track changes, and maintain evidence-backed records of smart contract activity.
projects.how_its_made: Klyro is built using a modern Web3 technology stack. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS to deliver a responsive, interactive dashboard. The backend uses Node.js and Express.js, with SQLite for persistent storage of investigations, snapshots and monitoring records. Ethereum RPC endpoints enable blockchain connectivity and on-chain data retrieval, while ethers.js supports smart contract interactions. MetaMask provides wallet connectivity and transaction signing, and ENS integration enables human-readable Ethereum address resolution. The core analysis engine decodes all 14 Uniswap v4 hook permissions, examines proxy implementations and external dependencies, and generates deterministic, evidence-linked findings. Additional modules provide interactive evidence graphs, snapshot comparisons, hash-based Hook Passports and monitoring workflows.

projects.title: anonfolio
projects.description: Ethereum portfolio tracking with Tor privacy, verified balances, and Uniswap price estimates.
projects.project_description: Anonfolio is an Ethereum portfolio tracker that combines network privacy with cryptographic verification, directly in the browser. Users can follow multiple addresses, give them names, add custom ERC-20 tokens, and see their holdings and estimated values without connecting a wallet, signing messages, or creating an account. The project brings privacy to the everyday act of checking a portfolio. Saved addresses, labels, token settings, and previous results stay in browser storage, with no application backend collecting the portfolio. By default, requests travel through Tor using Anon-RPC, hiding the user's IP address from RPC providers. Each tracked address receives its own isolation key to help separate its requests. Providers still see the addresses they serve, so this protects network privacy without claiming to make public blockchain activity secret. Anonfolio also verifies the information it receives. A Helios light client verifies Ethereum consensus from a trusted checkpoint, checks ETH balances against cryptographic proofs, and calculates ERC-20 balances locally using verified contract code and storage. Each address refresh uses one finalized Ethereum block, with block information and timestamps retained alongside the results. For portfolio valuation, anonfolio calculates 30-minute average price estimates from direct Uniswap v3 pools, using USDC as the default quote token. The underlying pool data is verified through the same local execution process. Assets without a qualifying pool remain unpriced, and incomplete totals are clearly identified. The interface supports individual address refreshes, aggregate holdings, custom token icons, and offline access to saved results. Users can explicitly choose direct HTTPS when needed, with verification still enabled; a Tor connection failure never silently changes the connection mode. Hosted  in IPFS
projects.how_its_made: Anonfolio is a static TypeScript app built with Vite, Bun, and native HTML/CSS. Saved portfolios stay in browser storage, and the app can be hosted over HTTPS or IPFS without an application backend. Anon-RPC and tor-js route requests through Tor, with separate isolation keys for each tracked address. Helios runs as WebAssembly in a Web Worker, verifying Ethereum consensus from a trusted checkpoint. ETH balances use account proofs, while ERC-20 balanceOf calls execute locally against verified contract code and storage. A custom fetch adapter routes Helios’s internal requests through Anon-RPC in Tor mode. Price estimates use 30-minute Uniswap v3 TWAPs from direct token/quote pools, with USDC as the default. Pool data is verified at the same finalized block as balances, and calculations use bigint arithmetic. A service worker enables offline reopening, while Bun and Playwright tests cover verification, privacy routing, pricing, and browser behavior.

Anonfolio also verifies the information it receives. A Helios light client verifies Ethereum consensus from a trusted checkpoint, checks ETH balances against cryptographic proofs, and calculates ERC-20 balances locally using verified contract code and storage. Each address refresh uses one finalized Ethereum block, with block information and timestamps retained alongside the results.

For portfolio valuation, anonfolio calculates 30-minute average price estimates from direct Uniswap v3 pools, using USDC as the default quote token. The underlying pool data is verified through the same local execution process. Assets without a qualifying pool remain unpriced, and incomplete totals are clearly identified.

The interface supports individual address refreshes, aggregate holdings, custom token icons, and offline access to saved results. Users can explicitly choose direct HTTPS when needed, with verification still enabled; a Tor connection failure never silently changes the connection mode.

Hosted  in IPFS
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Anonfolio is a static TypeScript app built with Vite, Bun, and native HTML/CSS. Saved portfolios stay in browser storage, and the app can be hosted over HTTPS or IPFS without an application backend.

Anon-RPC and tor-js route requests through Tor, with separate isolation keys for each tracked address. Helios runs as WebAssembly in a Web Worker, verifying Ethereum consensus from a trusted checkpoint. ETH balances use account proofs, while ERC-20 balanceOf calls execute locally against verified contract code and storage. A custom fetch adapter routes Helios’s internal requests through Anon-RPC in Tor mode.

Price estimates use 30-minute Uniswap v3 TWAPs from direct token/quote pools, with USDC as the default. Pool data is verified at the same finalized block as balances, and calculations use bigint arithmetic. A service worker enables offline reopening, while Bun and Playwright tests cover verification, privacy routing, pricing, and browser behavior.

projects.title: Recall
projects.description: Preserve public webpages and code snapshots with evidence anyone can inspect.
projects.project_description: Recall helps people preserve a version of a public webpage and inspect it after the live page changes or disappears. A student can retain an earlier deadline, a journalist can cite a saved notice, and a developer can keep a snapshot of an open-source repository. The browser extension captures supported public HTTPS responses with a witness. The reader shows saved content, compares captured text versions, and reports separate integrity and signature checks. Evidence can be downloaded and checked locally, including offline with the reader already loaded. Evidence lives on Swarm, while Arkiv makes records discoverable. Anyone can help retain eligible records and storage through keep-alive payments. Verification relies on the witness key the reader trusts; capture times remain witness claims, and storage lasts while it is paid for.
projects.how_its_made: Recall is a TypeScript monorepo with a React/Vite reader and a Chrome extension adapted from TLSNotary’s open-source extension. A Rust witness participates in the MPC-TLS session, checks server identity and the revealed request and response, then signs a statement containing their hashes using EIP-712. The reader checks transcript hashes, HTTP structure, and signatures against its configured trusted witnesses. It does not independently verify a portable TLS proof. We use Arkiv’s SDK on the Rabdi testnet to write and query wallet-owned, expiring capture, confirmation, witness, and repository-attachment entities. New records are created read-only, with permissionless expiry extension, so readers can help retain them. Owners can still delete or transfer records; earlier demo records predate the read-only flag. Swarm stores evidence and repository tarballs. The extension stamps paid uploads locally, while Gnosis contracts handle postage payments and top-ups. The frontend is also hosted on Swarm. The ENS name recallapp.eth points to its Swarm feed manifest, providing a stable address across app updates. For repository captures, the small GitHub branch API response goes through MPC-TLS. We download the code tarball separately, recompute its Git tree, and require it to match the tree named in the checked response. Claude Code helped write end-to-end integration tests covering TLSNotary capture, witness signatures, and submission to Arkiv Rabdi. Codex assisted with frontend implementation, documentation, and submission assets. Upstream TLSNotary code and licences are credited in the repository.

projects.title: AnonScope
projects.description: A live observatory that measures whether Anon-RPC networks actually hide you from RPC providers.
projects.project_description: Every time a wallet shows your balance, it asks an RPC provider, and every request reveals your IP address together with your wallet addresses. Anon-RPC fixes this by routing RPC reads through anonymity networks (tor-js, Nym, Nox). But nobody measures whether those networks actually deliver the privacy they promise. AnonScope is a live observatory for Anon-RPC. It runs the same tests through every Anon-RPC network against an RPC endpoint we control, which logs exactly what a real provider would see: source IP, timing, headers and payloads. Each network is scored on: availability, startup time, latency and overhead real-IP leaks identifying-header leaks wallet linkability, with and without isolation keys (synthetic wallets only) which public RPC providers accept or block the network's traffic Runs happen every hour on their own, and the results are published as a public scores.json, so wallets can choose the healthiest and most private network automatically. Early findings: Nox and Nym hide the user's real IP completely, but no live network separated wallets per isolation key in our runs, and the proposed x-anon-rpc-isolation header reaches the provider through Nox. tor-js's demo gateway was unavailable during the hackathon, and the scoreboard shows that too.
projects.how_its_made: Prober: a React + Vite app that drives @anon-rpc/browser-harness. Every probe read goes through worker.fetch. The unprotected baseline uses the official passthrough worker, and the harness's one-time specifier-contract read is answered from a pin made at build time, so runtime RPC traffic is 100% Anon-RPC. Observer: a Node + Hono server on Fly.io (Singapore) that acts as an RPC provider. It logs source IP, timing and headers for probe traffic only, forwards a small allow-list of read methods to an upstream node, rejects writes so it can't be used as an open proxy, and stores runs in SQLite. Dashboard routes never log visitor IPs. Runner: Playwright drives headless Chromium on a separate Fly machine every hour. It starts per run and stops after a 20-minute hard timeout. Measurement: five synthetic wallets per user poll the way a real wallet does, under four variants (no key, isolationKey, isolation header, isolationKey + jitter). An IP-and-timing adversary scores linkability, and a control user is being added to measure the adversary's real advantage over chance. Cost and safety guardrails: fixed machine sizes, an hourly GitHub Actions watchdog, a daily outgoing-data cap, and a dated kill switch. Built with Claude Code from a written plan.

projects.title: Splash
projects.description: Cross-border Stablecoins payments released by travel-rule proof. No proof, no fee.
projects.project_description: Splash is a B2B stablecoin payment and treasury network for Southeast Asian trade corridors, starting with Malaysia to the Philippines. Before ETHGlobal Mumbai, Splash was a Sui testnet build: business wallets, fees, KYB and audit receipts. Its travel-rule records were built offchain and never proven onchain. This weekend we turned one product rule into code: every payment carries a proof of who sent it, who receives it and under which rule, and Splash charges a fee only when that proof is recorded. We commit each payment’s travel-rule record as a salted 32-byte hash. Only the hash goes onchain, never personal data. The proof then plays three roles. Chainlink CCIP 2.0 carries it. The beneficiary institution acknowledges the travel-rule record from its contract on Ethereum Sepolia, and a CCIP 2.0 message delivers that acknowledgement to Arc. Arc enforces it. A USDC escrow written in Arc Studio releases funds to the recipient, and takes Splash’s fee, only inside _ccipReceive when the acknowledgement matches the commitment. If no proof arrives before expiry, the payer is refunded in full and Splash earns nothing. Whitechain records it. A USDT checkout pays the merchant instantly while Splash’s fee waits for the proof. Customers pay gaslessly with EIP-3009 authorizations, merchants get a ~20-line SDK, refunds and an accountant export, and every Splash proof from both rails lands in one append-only registry. Sui keeps the audit anchor. What’s trusted today: the beneficiary’s key and Chainlink’s committee on Arc, and a Splash attestor on Whitechain. Everything runs on public testnets; MYR and PHP legs are simulated. Splash earns only when compliance is proven. That’s the rule banks and regulators already ask for, now enforced by smart contracts instead of paperwork.
projects.how_its_made:
Splash started this event as an existing Sui testnet product (Move packages for business wallets, fees, KYB and audit receipts, plus a Next.js/TypeScript backend). Everything below was built during ETHGlobal in a separate public repo, with our pre-hackathon baseline commit linked. The core is a travel-rule commitment: we BCS-encode the originator and beneficiary record and hash it with blake2b-256 and a 32-byte salt, using the same scheme as our existing Sui receipts. Only the hash goes onchain. Chainlink CCIP 2.0: a Foundry contract on Ethereum Sepolia lets the beneficiary institution acknowledge a payment’s commitment and sends it to Arc over the Sepolia → Arc 2.0 lane. CCIP gave us a verified counterparty acknowledgement instead of a Splash-run attestor key. Hacky bit: the 2.0 extra-args encoding was thin in the docs, so we pulled the GenericExtraArgsV3 bytes from a known-good message via the CCIP API and fork-tested getFee before sending anything. Arc: Arc Studio wrote and deployed SplashProofEscrow, a CCIPReceiver holding USDC. Release and the fee happen only inside _ccipReceive when the acknowledgement matches the commitment; expired payments refund with zero fee. _ccipReceive reverts only on a bad source chain or sender. Every business-logic failure emits AckRejected instead, so a bad message never strands funds and a refund always works. Arc’s USDC gas and sub-second finality made the escrow cheap and instant to demo. Whitechain: a USDT checkout (Foundry, from Whitechain’s template) pays the merchant instantly while Splash’s fee is held until the proof is recorded. Payers sign EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization, so they never hold WBT. We bind each signature to its invoice by setting the nonce to keccak256(invoiceId, contract), which stops replay and front-running. The token has no eip712Domain(), so we hardcoded and onchain-checked its domain separator. Every proof from both rails lands in an append-only registry on Whitechain: our stand-in for Walrus this weekend. Sui: we reused our existing audit_anchor, with anchor_id set to the CCIP message id and backing_blob pointing at the Whitechain receipt, a field built for Walrus blobs. Things that bit us: Our first plan was CCIP into Sui. The CCIP API showed the Sepolia → Sui lane on v1.6 with no delivery since April, so we moved the CCIP endpoint to Arc mid-hackathon and documented the stalled lane as feedback.
Whitechain Sepolia has two “USDT” tokens, and the bridge delivers the wrong one.
Arc’s native USDC uses 18 decimals while its ERC-20 view uses 6.
CCIP latency is longer than any expiry short enough to demo, so we run two payments: one released, one refunded. AI use: Arc Studio wrote the escrow; prompts and chat history are in the repo.

projects.title: Opaque
projects.description: The post-quantum security layer for Ethereum: hash-based keys for accounts, ENS, Uniswap and admins
projects.project_description: Opaque is the post-quantum security layer for Ethereum. It moves what ECDSA guards today (accounts, payments, ENS names, Uniswap liquidity and protocol admin keys) to hash-based keys, and keeps payments private with cryptography a quantum computer has nothing to attack. It is more than a wallet: Opaque is one way in, and MetaMask users, liquidity providers and protocol teams plug in without switching anything. All of it is live on Sepolia and on Ethereum's EIP-8141 devnet. THE PROBLEM Every Ethereum account that has ever sent a transaction has published its public key. A large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm turns that public key back into the private key. On that day, "Q-Day", whoever runs it can sign as you: drain the account, take over any protocol whose owner or admin role the key holds, transfer ENS names and pull Uniswap positions. Privacy breaks too. Stealth addresses and SNARK privacy pools built on elliptic curves and pairings can be unmasked or forged, and anything encrypted with elliptic-curve key exchange today can be recorded now and decrypted later. Nobody knows the date, but moving Ethereum's users and protocols takes years, and every key that moves has to be moved by the vulnerable key itself, before an attacker gets there. WHAT OPAQUE DOES,TODAY Accounts signed by FORS+C. Every signature that moves value is FORS+C, a few-time hash-based signature over keccak; FORS is the few-time layer inside SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). On Sepolia a key is 32 Merkle trees of height 8, and a signature is 9,251 bytes that the browser makes in about 140 ms. Because it is few-time, PQKeyRegistry counts every use on chain: at most 8 signatures per key, which keeps forgery below 2^-160. Each key commits to its successor in advance, so the wallet rotates before the budget runs out, at the same address. One 12-word phrase derives every key on every chain. On Sepolia the account is an ERC-4337 smart account whose operations are signed by FORS+C. On the EIP-8141 devnet the transaction itself is signed by FORS+C alone: the account's VERIFY frame checks the signature in 76,430 gas, under the public mempool's 100,000-gas cap, and the account pays its own gas, with no bundler and no paymaster. A factory creates accounts with no signature at all. Private payments. A payment is a note leaving a pool. The wallet builds a ZKBoo ring proof in the browser (MPC-in-the-head over AES-128: hashes and a block cipher only, no trusted setup, 2^-128 soundness) showing that the note is one of a ring of 8 deposits, without saying which. The 1 MB proof crosses three relays chosen from six, each layer sealed with ML-KEM-768 and AES-256-GCM, and arrives still sealed at the exit. An attester verifies it and signs with its own FORS+C key, and the pool pays the recipient. The sender's account never appears on chain: on Etherscan, the sender is the pool's settler. Pools hold test USDC and ETH. Leaving without Opaque. Every pool is exitable. With every Opaque server switched off, the wallet still finds its notes on chain through the Ethereum Foundation's anon-rpc (the Nox mixnet), announces an exit, waits the pool's 300-second delay and withdraws through a public bundler, while the pool recomputes the note with AES-128 on chain. Nobody's permission is needed, ours included. anon-rpc also carries every ENS lookup, and a Privacy switch sends all of the wallet's reads and operations through it, so no RPC provider learns who is asking. ENSv2 names held by FORS+C. opaque.eth on ENSv2 is held by PQNameController, the only holder of every role on the name and the only admin of its resolver. It acts only on a FORS+C signature that PQKeyRegistry checks, so the ECDSA key that registered the name can no longer change it. Anyone can claim yourname.opaque.eth from the wallet with one FORS+C signature, and the wallet then shows the account by its name. Post-quantum stealth payments. The same claim publishes the wallet's ML-KEM-768 key in the ERC-6538 registry, under a scheme of its own. Paying a name then pays a fresh one-time address, announced on ERC-5564's Announcer, that only the payee can find with its ML-KEM key. The one-time address is itself a FORS+C account; the wallet finds the payment and sweeps it into its notes, and the payee's own address never receives anything. Uniswap v4 hooks. On Uniswap's own v4 PoolManager on Sepolia, PQAccountPoolHook makes a pool that admits only post-quantum accounts: an ordinary wallet's swap reverts with NotPostQuantum. PQGuardHook adds a FORS+C second factor to any liquidity position: removing liquidity needs a signature from the LP's guard key, and the hook pays the signed recipient itself, so a recovered ECDSA key cannot pull the position. On the devnet we deployed v4 ourselves, and the wallet swaps through the Universal Router with FORS+C signatures only. Keep MetaMask: the Q-Day vault. MetaMask users don't have to switch wallets. They deposit into PQVault from MetaMask and register a FORS+C guard key from 12 words; from then on, only that key can take the funds out, even after the MetaMask key is recovered. Any protocol: PQAdmin. Paste a contract address and the page finds its admin keys from what the chain shows: an Ownable owner, an EIP-1967 proxy admin or beacon, every AccessControl role and an AccessManager's admin role. One flow hands each of them to a PQAdmin contract that executes calls only with a FORS+C signature from the team's guard key, in an order that never locks the team out: roles first, DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE last. Upgrades, pauses and fee changes then need the hash-based key, and the guard key rotates without the admin address changing. The Q-Day simulator. A page that plays the quantum computer on live Sepolia. It sets up a victim with money, a protocol, a vault and stealth payments, then hands an attacker the victim's ECDSA private key. On chain, the attacker takes the plain wallet, the protocol it owned and an elliptic-curve stealth payment. The chain refuses it the Q-Day vault, the protocol behind PQAdmin and opaque.eth, each with the contract's own error (BadSignature, OwnableUnauthorizedAccount), and it cannot link the ML-KEM stealth payment. Then the owner moves everything with the FORS+C key alone. Connect with Opaque. The Opaque extension announces itself as an EIP-6963 wallet, so any dapp can use Opaque beside MetaMask. PROOF Every number above comes from the live chains. 154 Foundry tests cover the contracts and 396 tests cover the backend. Eight Playwright suites drive the real pages against Sepolia and the devnet: deposits, private sends, swaps, name claims, stealth sweeps, the exit with every Opaque server blocked, the Q-Day simulator and the PQAdmin handover. The code is open source under Apache-2.0. WHAT WE CAN'T DO YET Opaque protects what users and protocols hold. It cannot make Ethereum itself post-quantum, and we would rather say exactly where the edges are: Consensus. Validators sign with BLS12-381, which Shor's algorithm also breaks, so a quantum attacker could forge validator signatures. Only a protocol upgrade fixes that, with hash-based consensus signatures like those in Ethereum's lean consensus research. Data availability and SNARKs. Blob commitments use KZG over BLS12-381, and most rollups, bridges and privacy pools verify Groth16 or PLONK proofs over pairing-friendly curves. Our own proofs are hash-based; the ecosystem around us isn't yet. The outer transaction on Sepolia. An ERC-4337 bundler, and our settler for private payments, sign the transaction that carries a FORS+C-signed operation, with ECDSA. A recovered courier key can delay or censor an operation, not forge one. Only EIP-8141 removes the courier, and EIP-8141 is a draft that runs on a devnet, not on mainnet. Keys that haven't moved. Funds left in an ordinary account stay exposed until they move. PQAdmin can only take admin powers that a contract stores as a transferable address: an immutable or hardcoded admin, power granted by an ECDSA signature (EIP-712 permits, signed mints, oracle and bridge signers) and Safe owners stay on ECDSA. Every handover has to be signed before Q-Day. Trust. The attester is trusted to judge whether a spend is valid. One operator runs every relay today, so the relays are not yet an anonymity set of their own, and a payment's anonymity set is its ring of 8. Few-time keys. Each key signs 8 times, then rotates. Grover's algorithm halves the bits, so the forgery bound against a quantum attacker is about 2^-80 rather than 2^-160. Lose the 12 words and the keys are gone: there is no recovery path. Stealth payments. Until the payee sweeps a payment, the payer can also derive the one-time account's key, because hash-based keys can't be tweaked the way elliptic-curve keys can. Cost. A FORS+C signature is 9,251 bytes and about 260k gas to verify on Sepolia, plus calldata. It suits payments, swaps and admin actions, not keepers that act every block. Readiness. Opaque runs on Sepolia and the EIP-8141 devnet only. Nothing is audited yet; mainnet comes after an audit and independent operators.

projects.project_description_markdown:
Opaque is the post-quantum security layer for Ethereum. It moves what ECDSA guards today (accounts, payments, ENS names, Uniswap liquidity and protocol admin keys) to hash-based keys, and keeps payments private with cryptography a quantum computer has nothing to attack. It is more than a wallet: Opaque is one way in, and MetaMask users, liquidity providers and protocol teams plug in without switching anything. All of it is live on Sepolia and on Ethereum's EIP-8141 devnet.

THE PROBLEM

Every Ethereum account that has ever sent a transaction has published its public key. A large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm turns that public key back into the private key. On that day, "Q-Day", whoever runs it can sign as you: drain the account, take over any protocol whose owner or admin role the key holds, transfer ENS names and pull Uniswap positions. Privacy breaks too. Stealth addresses and SNARK privacy pools built on elliptic curves and pairings can be unmasked or forged, and anything encrypted with elliptic-curve key exchange today can be recorded now and decrypted later. Nobody knows the date, but moving Ethereum's users and protocols takes years, and every key that moves has to be moved by the vulnerable key itself, before an attacker gets there.

WHAT OPAQUE DOES,TODAY

1. Accounts signed by FORS+C. Every signature that moves value is FORS+C, a few-time hash-based signature over keccak; FORS is the few-time layer inside SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). On Sepolia a key is 32 Merkle trees of height 8, and a signature is 9,251 bytes that the browser makes in about 140 ms. Because it is few-time, PQKeyRegistry counts every use on chain: at most 8 signatures per key, which keeps forgery below 2^-160. Each key commits to its successor in advance, so the wallet rotates before the budget runs out, at the same address. One 12-word phrase derives every key on every chain. On Sepolia the account is an ERC-4337 smart account whose operations are signed by FORS+C. On the EIP-8141 devnet the transaction itself is signed by FORS+C alone: the account's VERIFY frame checks the signature in 76,430 gas, under the public mempool's 100,000-gas cap, and the account pays its own gas, with no bundler and no paymaster. A factory creates accounts with no signature at all.

2. Private payments. A payment is a note leaving a pool. The wallet builds a ZKBoo ring proof in the browser (MPC-in-the-head over AES-128: hashes and a block cipher only, no trusted setup, 2^-128 soundness) showing that the note is one of a ring of 8 deposits, without saying which. The 1 MB proof crosses three relays chosen from six, each layer sealed with ML-KEM-768 and AES-256-GCM, and arrives still sealed at the exit. An attester verifies it and signs with its own FORS+C key, and the pool pays the recipient. The sender's account never appears on chain: on Etherscan, the sender is the pool's settler. Pools hold test USDC and ETH.

3. Leaving without Opaque. Every pool is exitable. With every Opaque server switched off, the wallet still finds its notes on chain through the Ethereum Foundation's anon-rpc (the Nox mixnet), announces an exit, waits the pool's 300-second delay and withdraws through a public bundler, while the pool recomputes the note with AES-128 on chain. Nobody's permission is needed, ours included. anon-rpc also carries every ENS lookup, and a Privacy switch sends all of the wallet's reads and operations through it, so no RPC provider learns who is asking.

4. ENSv2 names held by FORS+C. opaque.eth on ENSv2 is held by PQNameController, the only holder of every role on the name and the only admin of its resolver. It acts only on a FORS+C signature that PQKeyRegistry checks, so the ECDSA key that registered the name can no longer change it. Anyone can claim yourname.opaque.eth from the wallet with one FORS+C signature, and the wallet then shows the account by its name.

5. Post-quantum stealth payments. The same claim publishes the wallet's ML-KEM-768 key in the ERC-6538 registry, under a scheme of its own. Paying a name then pays a fresh one-time address, announced on ERC-5564's Announcer, that only the payee can find with its ML-KEM key. The one-time address is itself a FORS+C account; the wallet finds the payment and sweeps it into its notes, and the payee's own address never receives anything.

6. Uniswap v4 hooks. On Uniswap's own v4 PoolManager on Sepolia, PQAccountPoolHook makes a pool that admits only post-quantum accounts: an ordinary wallet's swap reverts with NotPostQuantum. PQGuardHook adds a FORS+C second factor to any liquidity position: removing liquidity needs a signature from the LP's guard key, and the hook pays the signed recipient itself, so a recovered ECDSA key cannot pull the position. On the devnet we deployed v4 ourselves, and the wallet swaps through the Universal Router with FORS+C signatures only.

7. Keep MetaMask: the Q-Day vault. MetaMask users don't have to switch wallets. They deposit into PQVault from MetaMask and register a FORS+C guard key from 12 words; from then on, only that key can take the funds out, even after the MetaMask key is recovered.

8. Any protocol: PQAdmin. Paste a contract address and the page finds its admin keys from what the chain shows: an Ownable owner, an EIP-1967 proxy admin or beacon, every AccessControl role and an AccessManager's admin role. One flow hands each of them to a PQAdmin contract that executes calls only with a FORS+C signature from the team's guard key, in an order that never locks the team out: roles first, DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE last. Upgrades, pauses and fee changes then need the hash-based key, and the guard key rotates without the admin address changing.

9. The Q-Day simulator. A page that plays the quantum computer on live Sepolia. It sets up a victim with money, a protocol, a vault and stealth payments, then hands an attacker the victim's ECDSA private key. On chain, the attacker takes the plain wallet, the protocol it owned and an elliptic-curve stealth payment. The chain refuses it the Q-Day vault, the protocol behind PQAdmin and opaque.eth, each with the contract's own error (BadSignature, OwnableUnauthorizedAccount), and it cannot link the ML-KEM stealth payment. Then the owner moves everything with the FORS+C key alone.

10. Connect with Opaque. The Opaque extension announces itself as an EIP-6963 wallet, so any dapp can use Opaque beside MetaMask.

PROOF

Every number above comes from the live chains. 154 Foundry tests cover the contracts and 396 tests cover the backend. Eight Playwright suites drive the real pages against Sepolia and the devnet: deposits, private sends, swaps, name claims, stealth sweeps, the exit with every Opaque server blocked, the Q-Day simulator and the PQAdmin handover. The code is open source under Apache-2.0.

WHAT WE CAN'T DO YET

Opaque protects what users and protocols hold. It cannot make Ethereum itself post-quantum, and we would rather say exactly where the edges are:

- Consensus. Validators sign with BLS12-381, which Shor's algorithm also breaks, so a quantum attacker could forge validator signatures. Only a protocol upgrade fixes that, with hash-based consensus signatures like those in Ethereum's lean consensus research.
- Data availability and SNARKs. Blob commitments use KZG over BLS12-381, and most rollups, bridges and privacy pools verify Groth16 or PLONK proofs over pairing-friendly curves. Our own proofs are hash-based; the ecosystem around us isn't yet.
- The outer transaction on Sepolia. An ERC-4337 bundler, and our settler for private payments, sign the transaction that carries a FORS+C-signed operation, with ECDSA. A recovered courier key can delay or censor an operation, not forge one. Only EIP-8141 removes the courier, and EIP-8141 is a draft that runs on a devnet, not on mainnet.
- Keys that haven't moved. Funds left in an ordinary account stay exposed until they move. PQAdmin can only take admin powers that a contract stores as a transferable address: an immutable or hardcoded admin, power granted by an ECDSA signature (EIP-712 permits, signed mints, oracle and bridge signers) and Safe owners stay on ECDSA. Every handover has to be signed before Q-Day.
- Trust. The attester is trusted to judge whether a spend is valid. One operator runs every relay today, so the relays are not yet an anonymity set of their own, and a payment's anonymity set is its ring of 8.
- Few-time keys. Each key signs 8 times, then rotates. Grover's algorithm halves the bits, so the forgery bound against a quantum attacker is about 2^-80 rather than 2^-160. Lose the 12 words and the keys are gone: there is no recovery path.
- Stealth payments. Until the payee sweeps a payment, the payer can also derive the one-time account's key, because hash-based keys can't be tweaked the way elliptic-curve keys can.
- Cost. A FORS+C signature is 9,251 bytes and about 260k gas to verify on Sepolia, plus calldata. It suits payments, swaps and admin actions, not keepers that act every block.
- Readiness. Opaque runs on Sepolia and the EIP-8141 devnet only. Nothing is audited yet; mainnet comes after an audit and independent operators.

projects.title: pickle
projects.description: A labor market where robots hire humans — and each other — to get unstuck.
projects.project_description: Robots fail constantly in the real world, and every failure is a ticket, a technician, and hours of downtime for a fix that takes seconds. Pickle turns the fix into a bounty the robot posts itself. When a robot hits its limits it needs one of three kinds of intervention, and each is a market: Physical intervention — buying hands. A SenseCAP Watcher loses power. Its screen becomes the job poster: a red - face and a QR code. A passerby scans, proves they're a unique human with World ID, and plugs it in. Power returning is the proof. Remote intervention — buying skill. A Unitree G1 (MuJoCo) has a box on its table it has no policy for. It posts a teleop bounty; a World-verified human takes its arms through Snap Spectacles hand-tracking and sweeps the box off. The box hitting the floor is the proof. Machine intervention — buying services from peers. The same dying Watcher offers its job to a second robot (a T-Deck) instead of a human. The T-Deck's own agent decides on 0G Compute, accepts, claims the bounty with its own wallet, and gets paid when power is restored. No World ID — the worker is a machine. In every case the robot's agent decides on 0G Compute, logs the episode to 0G Storage, escrows the payout on 0G Galileo from the robot's own balance, verifies the fix from the robot's own sensors, and settles on-chain citing the compute request and the storage root. All three were demonstrated live on hardware with real transactions.
projects.how_its_made: One orchestrator (TypeScript) runs the bounty lifecycle for every robot: MQTT for the ESP32 devices, a webhook from the Node MuJoCo sim, and a Cloudflare Durable Object relay that carries both Spectacles hand frames (WebXR, 26 joints/hand, ~45 Hz) and claim traffic. World ID: IDKit 4 with one action per bounty, backend RP signing and verification; the nullifier is hashed and bound to the bounty on-chain so a human can claim each job once. The claim page renders the World App connector as a QR, so a phone can claim a job posted on a robot's screen. 0G: every decision and verdict is a 0G Compute request on 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b in sealed/TEE mode, with the robot's real telemetry in the prompt (the T-Deck sends its battery voltage when deciding whether to help). Episodes go to 0G Storage. PickleEscrow on Galileo does post → claim → settle, and settle records the compute request id and storage root. If 0G is unreachable the robot safe-stops rather than fake a decision. Hardware: Watcher firmware in ESP-IDF, with a QR encoder for the poster and USB VBUS detection as the physical proof.
