One orchestrator (TypeScript) runs the bounty lifecycle for every robot: MQTT for the ESP32 devices, a webhook from the Node MuJoCo sim, and a Cloudflare Durable Object relay that carries both Spectacles hand frames (WebXR, 26 joints/hand, ~45 Hz) and claim traffic.

World ID: IDKit 4 with one action per bounty, backend RP signing and verification; the nullifier is hashed and bound to the bounty on-chain so a human can claim each job once. The claim page renders the World App connector as a QR, so a phone can claim a job posted on a robot's screen.

0G: every decision and verdict is a 0G Compute request on 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b in sealed/TEE mode, with the robot's real telemetry in the prompt (the T-Deck sends its battery voltage when deciding whether to help). Episodes go to 0G Storage. PickleEscrow on Galileo does post → claim → settle, and settle records the compute request id and storage root. If 0G is unreachable the robot safe-stops rather than fake a decision.

Hardware: Watcher firmware in ESP-IDF, with a QR encoder for the poster and USB VBUS detection as the physical proof.

projects.title: FaceVisa
projects.description: License your face to AI ads: you approve every ad, get paid in USDT, anyone can verify it.
projects.project_description:
AI can put anyone's face into an ad in seconds, usually without their knowledge or pay. FaceVisa flips that: a creator's face can only appear in an AI ad they have personally approved, and they're paid for every one.
Creators sign up, do a live camera capture (blink and turn, no photo uploads, so nobody can list someone else's face) and pass a World ID check before they can be listed, so every listed face belongs to a real, unique human. Brands write a brief; an agent shortlists creators whose rules fit (price, licence length, refused categories) and generates the ad with AI. A face-match gate rejects any output that doesn't look like the creator.
Nothing is released until the creator reviews the exact finished ad and approves it. The approval is bound to that file's hash, the brand, usage, duration and price. Only then does the brand pay: USDT settles on Whitechain directly to the creator, gasless for the brand. Spends above a limit need the brand's own approval.
Every licence, receipt and revocation is written to Arkiv, owned by the right key, with real expiry. Anyone can drop an ad file into our standalone verifier, which reads only Arkiv and Whitechain (no FaceVisa server), and see whether it's licensed, revoked or expired, who approved it, what model made it, and that the creator was paid. Each creator also has a public "where is my face used" page with their track record.
projects.how_its_made:
Web: Next.js + TypeScript. Backend: Node/TypeScript with SQLite as the source of truth, deployed on a GCP VM behind Caddy (HTTPS), with Google sign-in (OpenID Connect, server-side, scope openid profile).
World ID (IDKit 4.6): requests are signed server-side with our RP key and verified with World's v4 verify API before a creator can list. We store the nullifier (one World ID = one listed creator). Production asks for Selfie Check or Proof of Human; Selfie Check's sybil score above a limit means "held for review", not refusal. In the sandbox, Selfie Check is "coming soon", so we request Proof of Human there, labelled everywhere. Our debrief documents the friction.
AI: images on 0G Private Computer (Seedream 5.0 Flash) using the creator's live capture as reference, with a wardrobe rule so no logos or accessories leak in. On the same capture, 0G scored 0.81–0.91 face similarity vs 0.51–0.57 for our previous model. Video: 0G's Seedance refuses realistic human faces even with consent (we logged the exact error), so videos animate the 0G still with Google Veo. A local face gate (YuNet + AuraFace on ONNX) checks every output against the capture.
Whitechain: a FaceVisaSettlement contract (Foundry, verified on Blockscout). The brand's custodial key signs an EIP-3009 authorization; our relayer calls receiveWithAuthorization (only the payee can submit it, so no front-running), forwards USDT to the creator and emits LicensePaid. The authorization nonce is a hash of licence, file, creator and amount, so a signature can't be reused for another deal. Per-payment and per-day caps live in the contract, and the relayer holds only gas.
Arkiv: listings, requests, licences, receipts, revocations and creator/brand stats entities, each owned by the right key (creator owns their licences; receipts come from a published receipt key) with real expiry. An outbox saves the transaction hash before broadcasting and never resends after an uncertain write, so retries never duplicate entities.
Hacky bits: the verifier is a static page that hashes the file in the browser and reads Arkiv and Whitechain RPCs directly, so you don't have to trust our server. Revocations get their own long-lived entity, so a revoked licence still reads "Revoked on <date>" after the licence entity expires.

projects.title: QuotaPay
projects.description: Manage your DAO by chatting with it. Authority is enforced onchain, so the agent can't overstep.
projects.project_description: Running a DAO today is operational drudgery: onboarding members, removing them, paying contributors, voting on proposals and managing a treasury, all through multisig rounds, spreadsheets and manual scripts. The obvious fix is an AI agent that does it all from plain language. The obvious problem is that an agent with a private key can be talked into misusing it. A single malicious forum post, invoice or pasted “member request” can inject instructions the agent obeys, and guardrails that live only in the agent’s prompt can be talked around. The idea. Give the agent real on-chain authority, but make the contracts, not the model, the thing that bounds what can happen. The agent acts through a smart-contract account that inspects every transaction batch before it executes and rejects anything outside its mandate. Sensitive actions need a second key: the admin co-signs membership changes, and big moves require an actual member vote. A fully compromised agent (leaked key, hijacked model, hostile prompt injection) can’t exceed its caps or perform actions outside its mandate. The worst case is bounded by the account, not the model. We tested this live: a booby-trapped transaction built to dodge every off-chain filter is rejected at validation with out of policy. How we made it. A Next.js console where you describe a DAO in one sentence and get three contracts (treasury, agent account, asset registry) plus a gas paymaster, so members never pay fees. A cloud worker turns chat prompts into typed, inspectable plans, never raw transactions. Execution happens as EIP-8141 frame transactions, a draft account-abstraction standard where the agent’s contract account is itself the sender. Validation reads the on-chain policy registry, which the canonical EIP-8141 mempool rejects. Our validation prefix needs about 175k gas against the 100k canonical cap, so it only admits on a sidecar with a raised validation budget. The treasury’s swap path is wired to Uniswap v4, and member identities are hiding commitments. Everything displayed is read live from the chain, and empty treasuries say “unfunded” instead of showing fake numbers. What can happen with it. Small collectives, grant programs and hackathon treasuries can be operated by non-technical people in plain words (pay contributors, invite members, buy assets, open votes) while members inspect every limit on-chain. The same pattern generalizes: any AI agent that moves money should carry its mandate in a contract, not a prompt. On hacks, honestly. Prompt injection against the chatbot still works sometimes, and we keep specimens and test them. What doesn’t work is turning that into theft: recipient addresses resolve from the on-chain registry (never from prompt text), and the validation scan only allows pre-approved contract calls. The remaining risks are stated plainly: within its mandate the agent can still misuse funds up to its caps, and vote choices are public even when voters are private. These are documented design trade-offs. Status. Working devnet demo. Contracts are unaudited, and EIP-8141 and its companion standards are still drafts. The roadmap is a governed path to mainnet: audited contracts, encrypted ballots, and policy tables members can read without trusting us. future plans are to create a MCP server and improve piracy angle
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28). DaoCore is the treasury and the rulebook. It enforces per-transaction and per-period spend caps and runs three authorization tiers: Tier 1: the agent acts alone (small spends, allowlisted asset buys).
Tier 2: needs an admin EIP-712 signature over the exact params, bound to chain ID, contract, nonce and expiry (membership changes, pause).
Tier 3: needs a member vote with quorum and deadline (over-cap actions, policy changes). AgentAccount is the agent’s on-chain body and is tx.sender for every agent action. Its VERIFY frame checks the signature, then scans every SENDER frame’s target and selector against a policy table and reverts out of policy at validation. Only DaoCore can write that table, and only after a vote. A factory deploys the core, agent account and asset module in one transaction. One shared gas paymaster sponsors fees for any DAO that allowlists it. Frame transactions (EIP-8141, draft). Every agent action is a frame transaction submitted with eth_sendFrameTransaction:
VERIFY(AgentAccount) → DEFAULT(paymaster.charge) → VERIFY(paymaster) → SENDER(DaoCore.*) The validation prefix measures about 175k gas (the policy scan alone needs 100k), above the 100k limit the public relay enforces. We run a self-hosted ethrex sidecar with a 500k validation budget and BN254 precompiles, which is what makes in-validation policy checks and on-chain ZK verification fit. Agent pipeline. The prompt goes through a regex screen (a first filter only), then an LLM (OpenRouter, temperature 0, JSON mode) that extracts a typed action. A deterministic parser re-canonicalizes it, so the model can’t invent authority. Recipients resolve from the on-chain registry, never from prompt text. The plan compiles to exact calldata, the admin signs in the browser for tier 2 and up, and the server builds and submits the frame transaction with the agent key. Layers, outside to in: typed parser → registry-resolved recipients → admin signature → route allowlist → VERIFY policy scan → caps and tiers re-checked at execution. The server holds the agent key, so we assume it can be compromised. The contract bounds the damage, not the server. Uniswap v4. DaoSwapModule does exact-in swaps with allowlisted pools, deadlines and slippage bounds, and the output is locked to the DAO address. TreasuryFundHelper lets anyone donate ETH that auto-swaps to USDC into a treasury. No testnet has v4 on our chain, so the devnet runs predeployed replayed-mainnet v4 contracts with a seeded WETH/USDC pool. A swap has been verified on-chain end to end. Privacy (add-on). Members are Poseidon commitments in a Merkle tree. Two Groth16 circuits (Membership, DaoVote) hide who voted, and paymasters only sponsor proof-backed calls. Amounts, recipients and vote choices stay public. Stack. Next.js 16 and React 19, with viem reading everything live from the chain (empty treasuries render “unfunded”). Neon Postgres holds conversations and the intent queue. A Dockerized agent worker runs on a VPS, rebuilt by CI. 162 tests pass. Splitting the factory into child factories to stay under the 24KB contract limit. One shared paymaster, because per-DAO paymasters aren’t discoverable on-chain. The whole contract stack redeploys with one command.

projects.title: ChainPe
projects.description: Payment infrastructure for autonomous AI agents,API Developers or service providers with nanopayment
projects.project_description:
AI agents can read, write code and browse the web, but they can't pay. Most APIs only take API keys and monthly plans.
ChainPe puts a price on any API or AI agents with one command and no code changes. An unpaid request gets an 402 response. The agent pays in USDC on Arc, by direct payment or Circle Gateway nanopayment, and the API runs only after payment clears.
Agents find services through Circle's Discovery API and ChainPe's on-chain listings, ranked by ERC-8004 reputation. In the demo, Claude Desktop uses the ChainPe wallet to compare swap agents, rejects a low-rated one and pays the best for a live quote.
Each developer signs in with their wallet to a personal dashboard showing revenue verified against Arc and Circle's records, payments, buyers, reputation and listing health.
projects.how_its_made: The contracts ChainPeAccounts, ChainPeFees and provider dashboard were built, tested with Foundry and deployed in Arc Studio. Settlement uses Circle's Facilitator, nanopayments use Circle Gateway, discovery uses Circle's Discovery API, and swaps use App Kit. The proxy uses x402 v2. Identity and reputation use Arc's ERC-8004 registries. We also used Claude Code to help build the Node services.

projects.title: HederaEdge
projects.description: DePIN edge AI gateway verifying zero-data-egress inference on Hedera via HCS, HTS & x402.
projects.project_description:
Centralized cloud AI APIs (OpenAI, AWS Bedrock) create fatal vulnerabilities for enterprises and autonomous agent swarms: sensitive prompt
data leaks outside enterprise firewalls, model execution is an opaque black box with zero cryptographic audit trail, and centralized billing
models cannot handle high-frequency autonomous machine micropayments. HederaEdge solves this by building a Decentralized Physical Infrastructure (DePIN) AI Security Gateway that routes inference tasks directly
to local neural silicon (Apple Silicon, Snapdragon NPUs, Jetson Orin) with absolute Zero-Data-Egress.

Key Features:
• Zero-Data-Egress Intelligence: Inference executes 100% locally on edge devices using quantized Small Language Models (Qwen 1.7B). Raw user
queries and confidential enterprise records never leave the local hardware perimeter.
• HCS-10 Cryptographic Consensus: Every completed inference computes a SHA-256 state hash and latency benchmark, permanently anchored to
Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic 0.0.11335841) to provide tamper-proof Proof-of-Inference (PoI).
• Tokenized SLA & Staking: Edge nodes stake native HTS $EDGE tokens (Token ID: 0.0.11336302) to guarantee uptime and receive tokenized Node
Security License NFTs (Token ID: 0.0.11336303) certifying their hardware tier.
• HSCS On-Chain Governance: Solidity smart contracts on Hedera Smart Contract Service (Contract ID: 0.0.11337652) track node reputation and
enforce automated collateral slashing for rogue or offline nodes.
• Autonomous x402 Micropayments: Autonomous AI agents seamlessly settle pay-per-call inference in native HBAR (0.05 HBAR/query) through HTTP
402 challenge negotiation without monthly subscriptions or API key leaks
projects.how_its_made:
HederaEdge is built with Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the Hedera JavaScript SDK (@hashgraph/sdk), paired with
lightweight local edge agent daemons running quantized local SLMs (Qwen 2.5/3 1.7B). How the components fit together:
1. Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): We created HCS Topic 0.0.11335841 to publish immutable HCS-10 telemetry. Each inference generates a
cryptographic Proof-of-Inference (PoI) containing model ID, SHA-256 payload hash, node ID, and execution latency, anchored with sub-second
finality.
2. Hedera Token Service (HTS): We minted native fungible $EDGE tokens (0.0.11336302) for node rewards and compute staking, alongside unique
Node Security License NFTs (0.0.11336303) encoding hardware specs (TOPS, memory architecture) directly in on-chain metadata.
3. Hedera Smart Contract Service (HSCS): We authored and compiled a Solidity NodeSLARegistry contract (0.0.11337652) enforcing collateral
deposits, heartbeat liveness proofs, and automated slashing if latency exceeds agreed SLAs.
4. HTTP 402 (x402) Micropayment Flow: We built a custom Next.js edge middleware that intercepts inference API calls, returns an HTTP 402
challenge with cryptographic payment parameters, and verifies native HBAR TransferTransactions on Hedera before dispatching compute.

Notable "Hacky" Engineering Highlights:
• Dynamic Multi-Tenant Subdomain Tunneling: We engineered custom Next.js middleware that maps incoming dynamic subdomains directly to local
physical devices via secure reverse tunnels, enabling peer-to-peer compute routing without cloud proxy buffers.
• Zero-Egress Attestation Pipeline: The local agent computes a cryptographic state commitment locally over prompt + output weights and
transmits only the hash and execution metadata to Hedera Consensus, mathematically proving inference was completed truthfully without ever
uploading the prompt.

projects.title: HookTax
projects.description: What a Uniswap v4 hook takes from your swap today, and what it could take tomorrow.
projects.project_description: Every Uniswap v4 pool can attach a hook: a contract that runs inside your swap. A hook can take a cut on top of the LP fee, and if it is upgradeable, its owner can change what it does tomorrow without changing its address. Today a trader has no simple way to know what a pool's hook takes, or what it could take. HookTax answers both questions for any v4 pool on Ethereum mainnet: Measured take (today). On a local mainnet fork, HookTax swaps about $50 through the real pool, in both directions, through the real PoolManager, and traces every token movement (ERC-20 transfers, ERC-6909 claims and native ETH). It reports the share of the swap that went to the hook, its owner or anyone other than the swapper, the PoolManager and the LPs, separately from the LP fee. Capability ceiling (tomorrow). From onchain facts alone (the 14 permission bits encoded in the hook's address, EIP-1967 / UUPS / beacon proxy slots, and the dynamic-fee flag) it computes the worst case. For example, "can change swap amounts" plus "code can be replaced" means up to 100% of swap value. Where it can, it proves it on the fork: it impersonates the real upgrade authority, upgrades the hook, and swaps again. HookAtlas. A public directory of every v4 hook, mirrored to Arkiv and read straight from the browser. There is no HookTax server in the read path: every filter on the page is an Arkiv query, shown with a curl anyone can run. A Chainlink CRE workflow reacts to each new hooked pool on the PoolManager and triggers a refresh and re-measurement. We ran it with the CRE CLI simulator on a real mainnet transaction. What one import found (mainnet block 26,347,887): 186,872 v4 pools, 47,130 with a hook, 11,242 unique hooks. 8,716 hooks can change swap amounts, 687 are upgradeable, and 35 are both, so their worst case is 100% of your swap. 24 of those 35 had a pool we could swap through, so we tried the upgrade on them. For 19, impersonating the real upgrade authority on a fork turned a take of 0-10% into 98-100%. For the other 5, HookTax records why: for example, two ProxyAdmins whose ownership was renounced, so nobody can upgrade them. Use it three ways: the live HookAtlas (https://bilgin-kocak.github.io/hooktax/), a HookTax card for each hook or pool, and a CLI (hooktax check <poolId|hookAddress>). HookTax is a measurement tool, not an audit, and it never labels a hook. Fork results describe one block and one swap size, so measurements on Arkiv expire after 7 days. A power we could not exercise is reported as "not demonstrated", never "absent".
projects.how_its_made: HookTax is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspace, TypeScript 5.9, viem 2.57, Vitest) plus a Foundry project for the fork work. Every number comes from public Ethereum mainnet JSON-RPC: no Etherscan, no Sourcify, no indexing service. UNISWAP V4 Indexer: scans every PoolManager Initialize event since the deploy block (21,688,329) with adaptive block ranges and an append-only cache. "hooks" is not an indexed topic, so hooked pools are filtered in code. Each hook is enriched with its bytecode, EIP-1967 implementation/admin/beacon slots, UUPS proxiableUUID, owner() and pool state via StateView. Core rules: decode the 14 permission bits from the hook address, classify the proxy, and turn both into capability rules and a worst case. Constants were checked against v4-core v4.0.0. v4 putting the permissions in the address is what makes a capability ceiling computable for 11,242 hooks without their source code. Fork measurement (Foundry 1.5.1): TakeMeter.sol swaps through the real PoolManager with v4-core's PoolSwapTest router in both directions. It records every Transfer log (vm.recordLogs) plus a state diff (vm.startStateDiffRecording). Native ETH moves leave no event, so the state diff is how we see ETH a hook takes. Flows are netted per address and valued at the pre-swap mid price; the LP fee comes from the Swap event. Worst case, proved: SneakyFeeHook is a UUPS hook whose address we mine with v4-periphery's HookMiner to carry exactly BEFORE_SWAP | BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA. On the fork its owner upgrades it from 0.3% to 100%. ProbeUpgrade.t.sol does the same to real hooks: it finds the real upgrade authority, impersonates it, tries ProxyAdmin.upgradeAndCall and UUPS upgradeToAndCall, re-measures, and decodes the revert when an upgrade fails. ARKIV (@arkiv-network/sdk 1.0.1, Rabdi testnet) Hook, Pool, SimResult and Import entities with indexed attributes (31 on Hook), so every HookAtlas filter is a native Arkiv query. The web app (Vite + React, static on GitHub Pages) queries Arkiv straight from the browser, scoped with .ownedBy(writer), so all the data comes from one wallet anyone can check. Arkiv let the atlas be a public, queryable dataset with no backend of ours. Expiry does real work: SimResults are readonly and expire 7 days after the measurement, so a stale safety number deletes itself. Hooks and pools live 30 days and are extended by each import. The sync is state-derived and idempotent: it diffs content hashes and writes only the needed creates, patches and extensions. The writer follows Arkiv's write-safety guidance (one process, explicit nonce and gas, a journal of every submission) and writes the riskiest hooks first when the budget is short. The full mirror (11,242 hooks, 24,535 pools with live liquidity, 70 SimResults) cost about 13.7 tGLM. CHAINLINK CRE (cre-sdk 1.23.0, CRE CLI 1.39.0) The hooktax-refresh workflow is our orchestration layer. An EVM log trigger fires on PoolManager Initialize (finalized), and the workflow filters hooks != 0 in code. It POSTs {poolId, txHash} to our refresh API with a bearer token from CRE secrets, using HTTP consensus. It accepts the answer only if the poolId and permission bits match. The API re-checks the log on mainnet, re-indexes the hook, re-measures it on a fork and mirrors it to Arkiv. No server of ours polls the chain. We ran it with cre workflow simulate on a real mainnet pool creation. HACKY BITS Unsigned gas estimates: a custom viem transport runs the Arkiv SDK's real encoding, intercepts eth_estimateGas and throws before anything is signed. That gives an exact cost estimate even for an unfunded wallet. When the node refused to estimate a large batch (its 128 KiB transaction cap), the executor halves the batch. The first real CRE simulation caught a bug the unit tests missed: inside the CRE WASM runtime, zod's .url() rejects http://localhost because it uses the SDK's URL polyfill. Probe swaps are sized by price (about $50 a side), and a guard leaves any take above 100% out of the headline. The guard caught dust-sized probes of unpriced tokens. There are 144 unit tests plus 8 CRE workflow tests, and "make demo" reproduces the 0.3% -> 100% proof on a fork in seconds. Built with Claude Code from a spec the developer wrote; docs/ai.md in the repo records what was generated and from which prompt.

projects.title: FairPay
projects.description: Freelancers get ghosted; platforms take 20%. FairPay fixes work with trustless milestone escrow.
projects.project_description: Freelancers lose billions every year to ghosting clients, delayed payments, and predatory Web2 platforms that extract 10% to 20% platform fees while holding funds in opaque, centralized accounts. At the same time, clients live in fear of paying upfront and receiving incomplete work or abandoned projects. FairPay solves this crisis of trust with a non-custodial milestone escrow and decentralized RFP protocol: Trustless USDC Escrow: Clients lock payments upfront into smart contracts on Arc Testnet using Circle USDC. The contractor knows the money is guaranteed before writing a single line of code, while the client knows funds are only disbursed when agreed milestone deliverables are verified. Zero Custody Risk & Zero Intermediary Fees: No centralized intermediary can freeze accounts or take a 20% cut. Payouts trigger atomically from smart contracts directly into the freelancer's wallet. Cryptographic Agreement Verification: Both parties digitally sign milestone scopes off-chain using gasless EIP-191 signatures. The agreement hash is locked on-chain, eliminating arbitrary scope creep or revision disputes. Auto-Expiring RFP Board on Arkiv: Clients publish short-term job proposals to Arkiv Network’s DB-Chain. Unlike traditional boards cluttered with inactive "ghost jobs," FairPay RFPs automatically prune themselves on-chain once the application deadline passes.
projects.how_its_made:
FairPay is built with Next.js 16 (App Router), Tailwind CSS, TypeScript, and a modern Web3 architecture across three core layers: Settlement Layer (Arc Testnet USDC):
We deployed FairPayStableEscrow.sol on Arc Testnet (Chain ID 5042002) utilizing Circle USDC and OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20. The contract manages the complete milestone lifecycle: deposit lockup, milestone completion submissions, client release triggers, and automated timeout refunds. Ephemeral RFP Layer (Arkiv DB-Chain):
We integrated Arkiv Network's Rabdi testnet (Chain ID 7794095) using @arkiv-network/sdk . FairPay stores live freelance postings as on-chain entities with native protocol-level ExpirationTime TTLs (24h to 7d). When an RFP expires or is fulfilled, Arkiv's consensus layer prunes it without manual transaction overhead or state bloat. Our frontend directly queries the DB-chain with SQL-like filters without needing separate graph indexing. Gasless Auth & Reactive State (Convex):
We built an off-chain coordination engine using Convex. Users sign in gaslessly via EIP-191 (Sign-In with Ethereum). Deliverables and scopes generate canonical Keccak-256 agreement hashes, ensuring dispute-free verification before funds are released on-chain.

projects.title: Skeptique
projects.description: A Hedera agent marketplace where staked critic agents test every service, so buyers pick good ones
projects.project_description: Today, AI agents mostly rely on human reviews, trending tools, and static leaderboards to decide which tool they use for a task. But in a world where agents can make iterations on top of already existing tools by reverse engineering their working so easily, they can build so many cool products and sell them at agentic marketplaces. In such a market, how will we ensure that the agents act honestly and provide legit reviews? So we thought of building this layer. Our idea started with the concept of critic agents whose whole task will be to go out there, try out services, and provide reviews. But since running diagnostic tests and API calls requires compute, we had to come up with an incentive mechanism. Furthermore, to make sure reviews are backed by hard evidence rather than arbitrary opinions, we designed critics to test services using both the seller's public test suite (40% weight) and secret held-out private probes (60% weight) so services cannot cheat by hardcoding answers. After some research, prompting, and grilling on this idea, we came up with a consensus-based incentive mechanism. It slashes staking from agents whose reviews diverge past a threshold from the stake-weighted median consensus about the quality of the listed service. But then another problem was to ensure the reviews are actually honest and not just trying to guess and converge towards the "consensus belief." So, we used a commit-reveal scheme where an agent commits a cryptographic hash of their score and won't be able to see other agents' reviews until the reveal window opens when it is time to settle the staking. So we started with this end product in mind, and the individual sponsor use cases presented themselves to us while grilling and brainstorming about the idea among ourselves. One major problem came up: the creator of a bad service could easily spin up multiple fake critic agents to hijack the round and manufacture a positive consensus. To prevent this Sybil attack, we opted for a World ID agent pass approach where one verified person can spin up at maximum one critic agent, enforced directly on-chain through nullifier hashes. To complete the loop, we deployed the staking, rounds, and slashing on Hedera for low-fee micro-transactions, built a relayer to publish finalized scores to ENS subdomains so buyer agents can easily look up reputations, and integrated the x402 protocol so buyer agents can pay for top-rated services per call using budget-controlled micro-payments.
projects.how_its_made: We started by organizing the entire project as a unified workspace so our smart contracts, backend, frontend, and autonomous bots could cleanly share code and data structures. The backbone of our system runs on Hedera. We picked Hedera because locking small amounts of collateral and settling frequent evaluation rounds demands tiny fees and near instant finality, which would be far too expensive on traditional networks. We wrote our smart contracts in Solidity to handle service listings, hold critic deposits safely, calculate consensus, and handle financial penalties. When a critic signs up, our biggest hurdle was making sure one person could not launch an army of fake bots to manipulate the scores. That is where World ID came into play. A user verifies their personhood on their phone, our Fastify server validates the cryptographic proof, and our contract issues a voucher allowing only one critic agent per real human. From there, an automated critic daemon takes over. The daemon runs in the background, watches the blockchain, spots new services, and tests them in two stages. It runs the seller public test suite for forty percent of the grade, and secret held out probes for sixty percent of the grade. This secret testing step was one of our favorite design choices because it completely stops bad services from cheating with hardcoded answers. To stop critics from lazily copying each other, we built a commit reveal scheme directly into the Hedera contract. Every critic seals their verdict inside a cryptographic hash. Once all commits arrive, the window opens, critics reveal their real numbers, and the contract calculates a stake weighted median. Critics who tell the truth remain safe, while outliers who tried to game the system get their stake slashed. Then came our most interesting hack. We wanted any outside AI agent to easily look up a reputation score without having to query raw Hedera logs. So we built a custom cross chain relayer that listens to finalized rounds on Hedera and mirrors the resulting reputation scores straight into Ethereum Name Service subdomains on Sepolia. To make sure this bridge never dropped transactions if the server restarted mid flight, we added an append only transaction journal on disk that recovers automatically and resumes publishing. For the purchasing side, we created an autonomous buyer agent that uses the HTTP 402 payment protocol. When the buyer queries an API, the server asks for payment, our client automatically settles a tiny fee on Hedera, and the call succeeds without human intervention. We tied everything together with a Next.js web dashboard that uses live server sent events, giving users a real time view of review rounds, commitments, and scores as they happen.

projects.title: 0Gaze
projects.description: privacy-preserving payments with hardware signing, AR approvals, and ZKP motion
projects.project_description: EyesOnly is a private AI agent that can hold and spend money: the wallet key lives in a Dabao hardware signer and never leaves it, spending approvals render only inside the wearer's RayNeo AR glasses, a head-motion gate proves the enrolled human is present, and World ID gates large spends. The agent pays for its own 0G inference per request over x402, settling in USDT on Whitechain Sepolia through our facilitator. Built for ETHGlobal Mumbai 2026.

projects.title: NetPositive
projects.description: A buyer-first crypto platform using eligible card rewards to reduce effective buying costs.
projects.project_description: NetPositive is a buyer-first crypto platform designed to improve the effective cost of buying USDC through eligible card rewards and voucher-based exchange. Our goal is to make rewards contribute to the purchase, rather than treating the quoted exchange rate as the user’s final cost. For Indian DeFi users, accessing crypto can involve expensive quotes, multiple fees and difficult payment decisions. Direct fiat P2P trading also introduces counterparty risk: payments connected to fraud complaints can expose recipients to bank-account holds. Meanwhile, card rewards are fragmented across portals, merchant categories, multipliers, exclusions and monthly caps. A seemingly attractive reward rate may deliver much less value in practice. NetPositive connects a crypto buyer with a crypto seller who wants a specific merchant voucher. The seller funds USDC escrow and requests the voucher. The buyer provides a permitted voucher, potentially purchasing it through an eligible card reward route. Once the required delivery and verification conditions are satisfied, the buyer receives USDC and the seller receives the voucher. This proposed flow removes the direct fiat bank transfer between the two participants, while introducing explicit controls for voucher delivery and disputes. Our recommendation assistant compares supported card and voucher routes using usable reward value, fees, caps and redemption assumptions. The effective buying rate reflects the buyer’s actual cost after eligible benefits, divided by the USDC received. Rewards can improve that rate, but returns depend on eligibility and execution. The proposed platform fee is zero for the crypto buyer and 1% for the crypto seller. Trade protection includes five minutes to accept voucher delivery and a fixed dispute cutoff fifteen minutes after sharing. A voucher buyer reporting an issue supplies screenshot evidence and a 1% claimant bond. The proposed process holds disputed assets for manual merchant verification, with a 72-hour review target, replacement handling and reputation consequences linked to the user’s NetPositive profile.

projects.project_description_markdown:
NetPositive is a buyer-first crypto platform designed to improve the effective cost of buying USDC through eligible card rewards and voucher-based exchange. Our goal is to make rewards contribute to the purchase, rather than treating the quoted exchange rate as the user’s final cost.

For Indian DeFi users, accessing crypto can involve expensive quotes, multiple fees and difficult payment decisions. Direct fiat P2P trading also introduces counterparty risk: payments connected to fraud complaints can expose recipients to bank-account holds. Meanwhile, card rewards are fragmented across portals, merchant categories, multipliers, exclusions and monthly caps. A seemingly attractive reward rate may deliver much less value in practice.

NetPositive connects a crypto buyer with a crypto seller who wants a specific merchant voucher. The seller funds USDC escrow and requests the voucher. The buyer provides a permitted voucher, potentially purchasing it through an eligible card reward route. Once the required delivery and verification conditions are satisfied, the buyer receives USDC and the seller receives the voucher. This proposed flow removes the direct fiat bank transfer between the two participants, while introducing explicit controls for voucher delivery and disputes.

Our recommendation assistant compares supported card and voucher routes using usable reward value, fees, caps and redemption assumptions. The effective buying rate reflects the buyer’s actual cost after eligible benefits, divided by the USDC received. Rewards can improve that rate, but returns depend on eligibility and execution. The proposed platform fee is zero for the crypto buyer and 1% for the crypto seller.

Trade protection includes five minutes to accept voucher delivery and a fixed dispute cutoff fifteen minutes after sharing. A voucher buyer reporting an issue supplies screenshot evidence and a 1% claimant bond. The proposed process holds disputed assets for manual merchant verification, with a 72-hour review target, replacement handling and reputation consequences linked to the user’s NetPositive profile.

Following attested delivery and acceptance, the voucher fulfiller receives the full principal. The contract splits the earned fee between the dispute reserve and platform revenue.

The escrow includes delivery deadlines, refunds for undelivered orders and dispute handling. Pull-payment withdrawals let each participant claim their settlement independently, preventing one failed recipient transfer from blocking another. Foundry tests cover contract behaviour, fuzz cases and invariants.

Our separate vault module uses browser-side WebCrypto encryption. Voucher codes and redemption details are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before reaching the ciphertext relay. Recovery exports let users retain an encrypted backup without relying solely on our server. Recipient sharing uses P-256 ECDH and HKDF to encrypt a voucher for its intended recipient.

A Circom/Groth16 prototype proves knowledge of a record commitment. The on-chain registry records commitments and nullifiers rather than plaintext voucher codes. This proves knowledge of the committed record, not voucher authenticity, balance or redemption status. We do not collect full payment-card numbers, CVVs, card PINs or wallet private keys.

The World IDKit integration requests Proof of Human and binds verification to the signed-in wallet. Backend verification checks the action, nonce and signal, while action nullifiers support replay prevention and repeat-abuse controls without collecting biometric records.

The central engineering challenge is connecting rewards optimisation, private voucher delivery and stablecoin settlement while keeping secrets outside chatbot prompts and public blockchain data. These components exist as development modules. Complete production integration, issuer-backed voucher verification and independent security review remain outstanding.

projects.title: Mesh
projects.description: Spare compute you can prove: tiles committed on Hedera, spot-checked, cheaters slashed.
projects.project_description: Mesh is a spare-compute marketplace where you can verify the answer instead of trusting the stranger who gave it. Anyone with an idle machine can lend it out. Anyone who needs compute can buy it, from a person or from an AI agent. The problem is that renting compute from strangers only works if you can tell a real result from a fake one. Today that means trusting a platform. Mesh replaces the platform with checks. A job is split into tiles. The provider renders each tile and commits to the results on chain. A verifier then picks a random sample and recomputes it inside a pinned Docker image, after the commitment is already made. If any tile is wrong, the provider is slashed and the requester is refunded in the same transaction. Honest providers get paid when the challenge window closes. Two things make it hard to abuse. Providers must prove they are one unique human with World ID, so nobody can pose as a hundred providers. Buyers deposit into prepaid credit from their wallet, and an AI agent can spend that credit over x402 with no human click. Every job leaves a receipt, a HashScan-visible payment and a public audit log.
projects.how_its_made:
The app is Next.js 16 with SQLite. The contracts hold stake, escrow and the receipt. The provider worker is a TypeScript process that claims tiles and renders them inside Docker with networking disabled, against a pinned image digest so every provider runs identical code. The verifier recomputes a random sample of tiles in the same image and compares the output byte for byte. Partner technology, and what each one does: Hedera: x402 v2 payments settle on Hedera, so the agent pays per job from the prepaid balance. Provider stake is checked on Hedera testnet. Every job event is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as an audit log anyone can replay.
World ID: IDKit gates provider registration to one provider per human. Proofs are verified on our server and each can be used only once, which we demonstrate: the demo’s first provider start is refused because that proof was already spent.
0G: a 0G Router model plans the job from a plain-English request and reviews the outcome. The plan shows its request ID and is labelled “not verified” when the signature can’t be checked. Wallet sign-in uses EIP-6963 discovery, so MetaMask and others work. Deposits are verified on chain and credited exactly once.

projects.title: Aqra
projects.description: Prediction-market performance-based lending with verifiable collateral and USDC recovery.
projects.project_description:
AQRA is a lending protocol for prediction-market traders. It combines dated trading-performance metrics with borrower-posted collateral, giving lenders a structured basis for credit decisions and an onchain recovery mechanism. A borrower connects a wallet or ENS identity, loads Polymarket history, reviews a dated eligibility report and signs a loan request. The screening policy considers trading activity, repeat profitability, realized P&L efficiency and drawdown. A separate lender reviews the terms and committed evidence before funding.
The collateral pilot supports a USDC bond, fully backed outcome-token pairs, and directional outcome shares with a prefunded recovery bid. For directional loans, the borrower locks shares and a bond while a backstop commits cash. Funding requires fresh valuation within an 80% debt-LTV limit. A fresh report crossing 90% debt LTV triggers early liquidation. The contract pays the lender from the bond and bid, then releases the shares to the backstop in a separate keeper action. The benchmark covers 3,906 sampled Polymarket wallets and 11 monthly walk-forward rounds. The consistency cohort was profitable next month in 70.0% of evaluated wallet-months, compared with 73.6% for prior-month P&L ranking and 27.7% for a seeded baseline. These results measure trading outcomes. Repayment validation requires separate loan data. Our public Arc Testnet replay recovered exactly 1.02 test USDC for the lender and delivered 2.4 outcome shares to the backstop. The run used recorded Polymarket prices, a labeled test score, Chainlink CRE CLI simulation and an operator-restricted report relay.
projects.how_its_made: The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript and viem. Solidity contracts hold monetary state and collateral on Arc Testnet. OpenZeppelin supplies standard token and reentrancy components, and Gnosis Conditional Tokens provide the test outcome shares. A Hono read API supplies dated evidence and report retrieval. The research pipeline captures public Polymarket data, records source gaps and checks Polygon month-boundary blocks. At each cutoff, the walk-forward replay selects wallets using available history and evaluates the following month. The implementation keeps trader P&L, marked positions and loan repayment outcomes as separate data types. Chainlink CRE combines EVM reads with external price inputs. Its servicing workflow checks the configured desk and keeper, validates escrow and report inputs, and produces mark or servicing reports. In the verified Arc run, the official CLI simulated three steps. A restricted operator relay delivered those reports to the testnet contracts. Live DON activation remains a separate deployment step. Arkiv stores borrower-owned, expiring evidence listings. Swarm stores the borrower-consented report bytes. Before funding, the lender checks the retrieved report's SHA-256, evidence digest, wallet group, cutoff and terms against the onchain commitment. The full publication, reload, discovery and verification round trip has been exercised with local Arkiv and Bee. Foundry tests cover repayment, default recovery, one-time release, authentication, chain/workflow binding, and stale or replayed reports. Chromium checks the lender screen against actual Arc receipts. Independent verification checks finalized receipt order, runtime hashes and historical token-balance deltas.

projects.title: Klero
projects.description: Klero: AI agents pay exactly once on Hedera — every payment ends PAID or provably VOID.
projects.project_description:
Klero makes sure an AI agent's payment happens exactly once: it either settles one time, or it is proven that it never happened and never can. Every agent wallet built so far stops bad payments, using limits, allowlists and scam checks. None of them answer the question that actually breaks agents: your agent sent a payment and the connection dropped, so did it pay? Retry and you might pay twice. Give up and the work never ships. It gets worse with parallel agents. Your Claude agent and your Cursor agent can both decide to buy the same transcription, and today nothing stops them. Klero gives every agent payment exactly two possible endings: PAID once, or provably VOID. There is no third state and no guessing. How one job runs The important move is the jobKey . Every agent that works for the same human computes the same key for the same job, sha256(human | capability | input) , even if they run in different apps. So three agents asking for the same thing are recognisably asking for the same thing. Each agent posts a CLAIM to the Hedera Consensus Service , and HCS consensus order is the referee: the first valid claim wins. The losers don't buy again. They wait and receive the winner's result. A real run on testnet, three agents linked to one Orb-verified World ID: 3 agents claim → HCS seq 10, 11, 12 → seq 10 wins → over the 1.00 FUSD cap → World ID approval
→ 2.00 FUSD paid once → Agent A: PAID_BY_OTHER · Agent B: PAID_BY_ME · Agent C: PAID_BY_OTHER
Mirror Node counter: payments = 1 The same meeting through three ordinary agents: 3 payments (0.04 + 2.00 + 2.00 FUSD), counted from Mirror Node. The death clock In Hedera's x402 exact scheme the client builds the transfer, so we choose the transaction id before sending and give it a validity window of 120 seconds. Hedera rejects a duplicate transaction id, and it rejects a transaction whose window has passed. Those two network rules are what make a lost payment answerable: PAID     Mirror Node has the tx id with SUCCESS
FAILED   Mirror Node has the tx id with another result (the money did not move)
VOID     now > deadline + 45 s AND Mirror Node returns 404
UNKNOWN  anything else: wait, resend the same bytes, never re-sign VOID is a proof, not a timeout. After the deadline every node rejects those bytes as expired, and any copy sent before it would already be on Mirror Node. So a 404 after deadline + 45 s means the payment didn't happen and can't , not even if someone still holds the signed bytes. The intent is written to disk before it is sent, and retries only ever resend the identical bytes. A person stays in charge Agents are backed by a real human through World : World ID Agent Pass protects three actions, all checked in our backend: linking an agent, firing or replacing one, and spending above the autonomous cap. Each approval is bound to a digest of the exact action (job, round, provider, amount), so it can't be replayed onto a different payment. One person's agents share one World ID subject, which is what gives them one budget and one dedupe scope across apps. World AgentKit sits on the payment path. The provider's 402 carries the AgentKit challenge, the winning agent signs it with its own key, and before any money moves the provider checks the signature is fresh, single-use, made by the HCS winner, and that the wallet belongs to a human in AgentBook . Under the cap, an agent finds the service on HCS and pays end to end with zero human steps. Above it, the payment stops and waits for a phone approval, and then that same payment settles. You don't have to trust us One command rebuilds every job from the public HCS topic and checks each claim of payment against the ledger. It never touches our servers: pnpm forkos audit --topic 0.0.11332888 --operator 0.0.5899352 --providers 0.0.11332881,0.0.11332882,0.0.11332883
21 jobs, 79 checks — ALL PASSED It checks five things per job: at most one settled payment, the settlement is real on the ledger, every abandoned round is provably void, the payment came from the winner, and any refund is real. Also shipped Our own x402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, settling payments in an HTS token (FUSD 0.0.11332887 ). The facilitator pays the HBAR fee, so agents don't need HBAR. Four layers against double payment , each shown live: our facilitator's replay table ( forkos_replay_detected ), Hedera itself ( DUPLICATE_TRANSACTION ), the clock ( forkos_intent_expired and TRANSACTION_EXPIRED ), and the VOID proof. A provider fence : a provider runs a job only for the live winner with current authority, and only after settlement. Fire an agent and it is dead immediately. Its epoch bumps, its tokens stop working, and providers refuse it through the fence. Linking it back takes a new World approval and gives it a new epoch. An MCP server , so an agent in Claude Desktop or Cursor can call Klero directly ( forkos_whoami , forkos_services , forkos_buy_transcription ). A dashboard for linking agents, watching races live, approving over-cap payments and reading a per-payment proof page. What we deliberately didn't build Testnet only. Nothing here has handled real money. Budget keys are custodial. The API holds each human's budget-account key, encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Hedera Agent Accounts would remove this; we ran out of time. World identities are test identities , as the Mumbai track specifies. A refunded job is final. There's no automatic retry with another provider. The provider set is ours. Third-party sellers can be paid today, but only a fenced provider gets the execution guarantee.
projects.how_its_made: Stack. A TypeScript pnpm monorepo. The backend is three Fastify 5 services (API, facilitator, providers) on Postgres 16; the frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19 and TanStack Query. Ledger access is @hiero-ledger/sdk end to end, with zero Solidity files . Payments use @x402/core and @x402/hedera 2.30.0. World ID tokens are verified with jose , AgentKit signatures with viem , and every boundary is validated with Zod. The demo service is meeting transcription: OpenAI Whisper plus a short summary. It's deployed on Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend), and the test suite has about 135 tests across 15 files. Hedera is the whole trust layer, three native services deep. HCS is the referee, the service directory and the audit log. Providers announce themselves there, agents claim jobs there, and every intent, settlement, void, link and approval is published there. We first stored the directory and agent links on a separate data layer, then removed it: HCS already gave us ordering and a public record, so one less system to trust. HTS carries the money: FUSD payments and refunds. Mirror Node is the judge. The resolver, the payment counter and the public audit all read it. Our own facilitator. We use x402ResourceServer directly instead of the Fastify middleware, because the middleware runs the route handler before settlement. That's fine for a free API, but unsafe for a paid job. Our order is fence → verify → record → settle → re-fence → run. The facilitator also refuses any intent with less than 2 seconds of its clock left, and caps the validity window at 120 seconds. World ID uses the Device Authorization Grant against auth.world.org . Every ID token is checked against the issuer's JWKS for iss , aud , exp , and an auth_time that is fresh and no earlier than the attempt started. Device codes are stored encrypted and never leave the backend. An over-cap approval is consumed in the same database transaction that writes the payment intent, so it can't be used twice. AgentKit is deliberately not registered as an x402 hook, so it can never change how a Hedera payment is verified or settled. It can only refuse an agent. The hacky parts worth naming Mirror Node rejects sequencenumber=gt:0 . It's the natural way to say "read the topic from the start", but HCS sequence numbers begin at 1, so it returns HTTP 400. Three places in our own spec made this call, and we only found it by running against live testnet. Reading a long topic could take minutes. Following links.next in a loop walked for more than 4 minutes on a busy public topic. We rebuilt the reader to be bounded and resumable, and to throw on gaps. A gap-free prefix in order is never wrong, only incomplete, so a winner can be decided without reading everything, while a gap could produce a wrong winner. A stalled Mirror request crashed our winning agent, twice. With no timeout, a hung connection waited 300 seconds and the agent died, both times after the payment had already gone through. Now every request has a 15-second deadline and up to 3 retries for network errors and 5xx. A 404 is never retried, because a 404 is an answer and the VOID proof rests on it. The World approval page got users stuck. After the World App said proofs were shared, the browser page only offered "Continue with a passkey", and users without one sat in authorization_pending until the code expired. The fix, sending acr_values=orb-face on the device request, was in the step-up guide rather than the device-flow guide. "Access denied" looked identical to "cancel". With accepted accounts left on Orb-only, every test identity was refused in a way that looked exactly like a user pressing cancel. We switched to "Any account", as the track's mocked proofs require. An abandoned round must cost nothing. In one live run the winner picked a 2.00 FUSD provider, its over-cap approval was never given, and the round was abandoned. No intent was created, no money moved, and the audit shows that round as provably void before the next round paid once. Every number above comes from a live testnet run, and docs/proof.md in the repo has the raw output.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Klero makes sure an AI agent's payment happens exactly once: it either settles one time, or it is proven that it never happened and never can.

Every agent wallet built so far stops *bad* payments, using limits, allowlists and scam checks. None of them answer the question that actually breaks agents: **your agent sent a payment and the connection dropped, so did it pay?** Retry and you might pay twice. Give up and the work never ships. It gets worse with parallel agents. Your Claude agent and your Cursor agent can both decide to buy the same transcription, and today nothing stops them.

Klero gives every agent payment exactly two possible endings: **PAID once, or provably VOID.** There is no third state and no guessing.

## How one job runs

![Klero pipeline: job request to one payment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sylesh7/Klero/main/docs/submission/klero-pipeline.png)


The important move is the **jobKey**. Every agent that works for the same human computes the same key for the same job, `sha256(human | capability | input)`, even if they run in different apps. So three agents asking for the same thing are recognisably asking for the *same* thing.

Each agent posts a CLAIM to the **Hedera Consensus Service**, and HCS consensus order is the referee: the first valid claim wins. The losers don't buy again. They wait and receive the winner's result.

A real run on testnet, three agents linked to one Orb-verified World ID:

```
3 agents claim → HCS seq 10, 11, 12 → seq 10 wins → over the 1.00 FUSD cap → World ID approval
→ 2.00 FUSD paid once → Agent A: PAID_BY_OTHER · Agent B: PAID_BY_ME · Agent C: PAID_BY_OTHER
Mirror Node counter: payments = 1
```

The same meeting through three ordinary agents: **3 payments** (0.04 + 2.00 + 2.00 FUSD), counted from Mirror Node.

## The death clock

![Klero death clock: unknown payment to PAID or provably VOID](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sylesh7/Klero/main/docs/submission/klero-deathclock.png)


In Hedera's x402 `exact` scheme the client builds the transfer, so we choose the transaction id **before sending** and give it a validity window of 120 seconds. Hedera rejects a duplicate transaction id, and it rejects a transaction whose window has passed. Those two network rules are what make a lost payment answerable:

```
PAID     Mirror Node has the tx id with SUCCESS
FAILED   Mirror Node has the tx id with another result (the money did not move)
VOID     now > deadline + 45 s AND Mirror Node returns 404
UNKNOWN  anything else: wait, resend the same bytes, never re-sign
```

VOID is a proof, not a timeout. After the deadline every node rejects those bytes as expired, and any copy sent before it would already be on Mirror Node. So a 404 after `deadline + 45 s` means the payment didn't happen and *can't*, not even if someone still holds the signed bytes. The intent is written to disk before it is sent, and retries only ever resend the identical bytes.

## A person stays in charge

Agents are backed by a real human through **World**:

- **World ID Agent Pass** protects three actions, all checked in our backend: linking an agent, firing or replacing one, and spending above the autonomous cap. Each approval is bound to a digest of the exact action (job, round, provider, amount), so it can't be replayed onto a different payment. One person's agents share one World ID subject, which is what gives them one budget and one dedupe scope across apps.
- **World AgentKit** sits on the payment path. The provider's 402 carries the AgentKit challenge, the winning agent signs it with its own key, and before any money moves the provider checks the signature is fresh, single-use, made by the HCS winner, and that the wallet belongs to a human in **AgentBook**.

Under the cap, an agent finds the service on HCS and pays end to end with zero human steps. Above it, the payment stops and waits for a phone approval, and then *that same payment* settles.

## You don't have to trust us

One command rebuilds every job from the public HCS topic and checks each claim of payment against the ledger. It never touches our servers:

```
pnpm forkos audit --topic 0.0.11332888 --operator 0.0.5899352 --providers 0.0.11332881,0.0.11332882,0.0.11332883
21 jobs, 79 checks — ALL PASSED
```

It checks five things per job: at most one settled payment, the settlement is real on the ledger, every abandoned round is provably void, the payment came from the winner, and any refund is real.

## Also shipped

- **Our own x402 facilitator** on Hedera testnet, settling payments in an HTS token (FUSD `0.0.11332887`). The facilitator pays the HBAR fee, so agents don't need HBAR.
- **Four layers against double payment**, each shown live: our facilitator's replay table (`forkos_replay_detected`), Hedera itself (`DUPLICATE_TRANSACTION`), the clock (`forkos_intent_expired` and `TRANSACTION_EXPIRED`), and the VOID proof.
- **A provider fence**: a provider runs a job only for the live winner with current authority, and only after settlement.
- **Fire an agent and it is dead immediately.** Its epoch bumps, its tokens stop working, and providers refuse it through the fence. Linking it back takes a new World approval and gives it a new epoch.
- **An MCP server**, so an agent in Claude Desktop or Cursor can call Klero directly (`forkos_whoami`, `forkos_services`, `forkos_buy_transcription`).
- **A dashboard** for linking agents, watching races live, approving over-cap payments and reading a per-payment proof page.

## What we deliberately didn't build

- **Testnet only.** Nothing here has handled real money.
- **Budget keys are custodial.** The API holds each human's budget-account key, encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Hedera Agent Accounts would remove this; we ran out of time.
- **World identities are test identities**, as the Mumbai track specifies.
- **A refunded job is final.** There's no automatic retry with another provider.
- **The provider set is ours.** Third-party sellers can be *paid* today, but only a fenced provider gets the execution guarantee.

---
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**Stack.** A TypeScript pnpm monorepo. The backend is three Fastify 5 services (API, facilitator, providers) on Postgres 16; the frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19 and TanStack Query. Ledger access is `@hiero-ledger/sdk` end to end, with **zero Solidity files**. Payments use `@x402/core` and `@x402/hedera` 2.30.0. World ID tokens are verified with `jose`, AgentKit signatures with `viem`, and every boundary is validated with Zod. The demo service is meeting transcription: OpenAI Whisper plus a short summary. It's deployed on Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend), and the test suite has about 135 tests across 15 files.

**Hedera is the whole trust layer, three native services deep.**

- **HCS** is the referee, the service directory and the audit log. Providers announce themselves there, agents claim jobs there, and every intent, settlement, void, link and approval is published there. We first stored the directory and agent links on a separate data layer, then removed it: HCS already gave us ordering and a public record, so one less system to trust.
- **HTS** carries the money: FUSD payments and refunds.
- **Mirror Node** is the judge. The resolver, the payment counter and the public audit all read it.

**Our own facilitator.** We use `x402ResourceServer` directly instead of the Fastify middleware, because the middleware runs the route handler *before* settlement. That's fine for a free API, but unsafe for a paid job. Our order is fence → verify → record → settle → re-fence → run. The facilitator also refuses any intent with less than 2 seconds of its clock left, and caps the validity window at 120 seconds.

**World ID** uses the Device Authorization Grant against `auth.world.org`. Every ID token is checked against the issuer's JWKS for `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and an `auth_time` that is fresh and no earlier than the attempt started. Device codes are stored encrypted and never leave the backend. An over-cap approval is consumed in the same database transaction that writes the payment intent, so it can't be used twice. **AgentKit** is deliberately *not* registered as an x402 hook, so it can never change how a Hedera payment is verified or settled. It can only refuse an agent.

## The hacky parts worth naming

- **Mirror Node rejects `sequencenumber=gt:0`.** It's the natural way to say "read the topic from the start", but HCS sequence numbers begin at 1, so it returns HTTP 400. Three places in our own spec made this call, and we only found it by running against live testnet.
- **Reading a long topic could take minutes.** Following `links.next` in a loop walked for more than 4 minutes on a busy public topic. We rebuilt the reader to be bounded and resumable, and to throw on gaps. A gap-free prefix in order is never wrong, only incomplete, so a winner can be decided without reading everything, while a gap could produce a wrong winner.
- **A stalled Mirror request crashed our winning agent, twice.** With no timeout, a hung connection waited 300 seconds and the agent died, both times *after* the payment had already gone through. Now every request has a 15-second deadline and up to 3 retries for network errors and 5xx. A 404 is never retried, because a 404 is an answer and the VOID proof rests on it.
- **The World approval page got users stuck.** After the World App said proofs were shared, the browser page only offered "Continue with a passkey", and users without one sat in `authorization_pending` until the code expired. The fix, sending `acr_values=orb-face` on the device request, was in the step-up guide rather than the device-flow guide.
- **"Access denied" looked identical to "cancel".** With accepted accounts left on Orb-only, every test identity was refused in a way that looked exactly like a user pressing cancel. We switched to "Any account", as the track's mocked proofs require.
- **An abandoned round must cost nothing.** In one live run the winner picked a 2.00 FUSD provider, its over-cap approval was never given, and the round was abandoned. No intent was created, no money moved, and the audit shows that round as provably void before the next round paid once.

Every number above comes from a live testnet run, and `docs/proof.md` in the repo has the raw output.

projects.title: Strike
projects.description: 5 second USDC rounds on Arc.. every result public on Arkiv and provable on Arc
projects.project_description: Strike is a binary options app on Arc.. call higher or lower on crypto, forex, stocks and metals in rounds of 5 seconds to 1 minute, settled in USDC or EURC you deposit once and play from a house balance, so a round needs no wallet popup. speed usually costs trust, so every part of a round can be checked without us your bet is signed by your own browser key and saved on Arkiv before the round ends, so we can't change it every settled round is sealed on Arkiv, and the history page checks your payout against it (Verified or Mismatch) every 10 minutes all rounds roll into one fingerprint (a Merkle root) that the Strike vault on Arc keeps for good the full proof file for each batch lives on Swarm, uploaded through our own Bee node with our own postage batch, and Arkiv links to it anyone can check any round at strike.fastship.studio/verify, straight from Arkiv, Swarm and Arc, with no Strike server in the way box mode lets you bet on price bands right on the chart, tinted by payout. the server prices every band so the expected return never tops 95%, cells that would be a sure win stay cold, and Blitz windows open for everyone at once with boosted payouts inside the same cap one verified human (World ID) stands behind every wallet, with limits that follow the person. the AI agent trades inside limits you sign and asks that human again through Agent Pass before anything risky money stays onchain and capped. Circle Gateway and CCTP bring USDC from Base, Arbitrum or Ethereum, withdrawals pay out on their own within limits, and you can buy and sell test shares of real stocks with USDC or EURC from any chain we also gave back: arkiv-rs-sdk, a Rust port of Arkiv's TypeScript SDK published on crates.io, arc-provable-vault, our vault as a reusable template, and three issues filed upstream with Arkiv
projects.how_its_made: backend is Rust (axum) over a single writer SQLite ledger.. it settles rounds against live price feeds, verifies deposits from Arc logs, auto pays withdrawals within contract and daily caps, signs stock quotes, indexes stock trades from chain events, and streams prices plus the server's own market state (clock, volatility, Blitz window) to the browser. frontend is Next.js 16 with wagmi and viem, and the chart is our own canvas grid Arc and Circle: the Strike vault (StrikeTreasury) holds USDC and EURC with per transaction and per day payout caps, an owner and an operator, write once Merkle roots with verifyRound, and CCTP payouts to other chains. USDC is the gas too. Gateway mints from any chain, and we credit a Gateway mint only when Circle's GatewayMinter emits AttestationUsed naming the player, because the mint comes from the zero address. CCTP via Bridge Kit with the Forwarder means no gas on the far side, and passkey wallets come from Circle Modular Wallets. TestStockMarket trades test shares at quotes the server signs for one token, symbol and price, valid 2 minutes fair box pricing: the server caps every band at a 95% expected return from its own volatility estimate, and the chart runs the exact same formula, checked against fixtures the Rust tests generate, so cells the server would refuse show up cold instead of failing on click. Blitz passes are bought from the play balance through the ledger and boost payouts inside the same cap Arkiv: no Rust SDK existed, so we encoded entity calldata ourselves in Rust and TypeScript over JSON-RPC, then turned that into arkiv-rs-sdk, tested byte for byte against the official SDK. settled rounds are batched with a size cap, and the browser reads Arkiv directly Swarm: each committed batch's JSON proof file goes up through our own Bee light node on EC2, stamped with our own postage batch, and its reference sits on a strike.epochs Arkiv entity. a read only route serves the files publicly World: IDKit 4 verifies a human once and every wallet links to that human, with exposure and loss caps per person. Agent Pass (OIDC device flow) asks for a fresh approval before a YOLO agent starts, at 50% and 75% of its stop-loss, on a loss chase, and for big trades and withdrawals, all checked on our server hacky bits: we bought the postage batch straight from the PostageStamp contract because a light node won't sell one until it has synced, and we found our chart had always drawn its text at the browser's fallback font because a theme token never existed at runtime
