projects.title: AegisJIT
projects.description: AegisJIT: 3 custom SwapVM opcodes on 1inch Aqua. ZK humans pay less, bots pay surge, whales capped.
projects.project_description: AegisJIT is a self-custodial just-in-time liquidity vault whose pricing logic lives inside the 1inch SwapVM interpreter. A Maker keeps their capital in two ERC-4626 vaults (USDC and WETH) and ships a single Aqua order whose bytecode is executed by AegisSwapVMRouter, a SwapVM router extended with three custom opcodes. Everything a trade pays is decided by that bytecode, so router.asView().quote() and swap() return the same amounts to the wei: every custom opcode is view-safe, with no storage writes on the quote path. The three opcodes: 0x2A ZKIdentityGuard (46-byte args). A taker can attach a zero-knowledge proof of personhood to takerData: a World ID Orb proof (type 1) or an Anon Aadhaar Groth16 proof generated from the Aadhaar Secure QR (type 2). The opcode routes the payload to the matching verifier adapter. The proof is bound to the taker address (signal) and its nullifier stays with the first address that used it, so one person is one trader. In tiered mode nothing ever reverts: a valid proof buys the verified-human tier, no proof means the taker is priced as a bot. A strict mode and an optional jurisdiction check exist for compliance use. After the first proof a 33-byte binding claim replaces the proof for the epoch, which costs about 5k gas instead of 225k (World ID) or 288k (Aadhaar). Aggregators can trade on behalf of a verified user with an EIP-712 authorization. 0x9A JITVaultReserves (86-byte args). Reads the Maker's real ERC-4626 balances by staticcall and exposes only lambda = 25% of them per execution and per 600-second window (a token-bucket budget), with a 2x virtual concentration around the current price. A 500,000 USDC whale reverts with JITExposureCapExceeded; four 25% executions in one block fill once and revert three times. The other 75% never leaves the vault and keeps earning. A hook withdraws the exact slice just in time and re-deposits the proceeds in the same transaction. 0x7A VolatilitySurgeFee (20-byte args). A dynamic LVR and toxic-flow fee: 0.30% base, halved to 0.15% for verified humans, plus a 1.5% marginal surge on flow beyond 1% utilisation of the active reserves. The flow bucket is on a fixed time grid, so splitting an order inside a window buys nothing: five 10k trades pay the same fee as one 50k trade and receive slightly less. Rounding always favours the Maker, which keeps the curve sub-additive and monotonic. Identity stack. World ID runs through IDKit 4.x with relying-party-signed requests; on World Chain Sepolia the adapter verifies proofs through the chain's real World ID Router (proofs come from World App or the World ID Simulator). Locally and on Ethereum Sepolia, Semaphore depth-30 proofs are generated in the browser and checked by World ID's own SemaphoreVerifier. Anon Aadhaar proofs are produced by a local prover from a signed Secure QR after an in-browser RSA-2048 check; the QR never leaves the user's machine. Both passes land on the identical fee tier. What is proven. 128 Hardhat tests with real Groth16 proofs and 19 Foundry property tests cover quote == swap, exact-in/exact-out symmetry within 2 wei, sub-additivity against split orders, monotonicity, tier differentiation and the lambda cap. A judge demo script runs the scenarios end to end with real proofs in about 17 seconds. What is live. Ethereum Sepolia: 15 source-verified contracts and a recorded 10-scenario run. World Chain Sepolia: 13 verified contracts and a 10-scenario run that includes a real World ID proof executed on-chain (582,931 gas against a 335,741 gas bot baseline). A hosted dashboard decodes the live order from Aqua's Shipped event, quotes every profile (human, bot, split attacker, whale), shows the surge bucket and the vault exposure, and lets a judge verify through the World ID Simulator against the real router: https://aegis-jit.niklabh811.workers.dev. Code, byte layouts and the threat model are in the repo: https://github.com/niklabh/aegis-jit-amm. Honest limits. USDC and WETH are mintable mocks on the testnets, the Aadhaar signer is a published test key rather than UIDAI's, the Aadhaar circuit's timestamp and state public signals can still link trades across epochs. The repo was started from template https://github.com/1inch/swap-vm-template.git Thats why it has old commits. The real work started from commit id 29ba759565c54a1fd5cc1d2665dc5d796014e086.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts. AegisSwapVMRouter inherits 1inch's SwapVM (v1.0.1/1.0.2) and AquaOpcodes and overrides _dispatch(ctx, opcode, args): opcodes 0x2A, 0x9A and 0x7A go to three instruction libraries in contracts/instructions/, everything else falls through to the stock interpreter. The libraries work only on SwapVM's Context struct (balanceIn/balanceOut, amountIn/amountOut, isExactIn, maker, taker, takerData via tryChopTakerArgs), use SwapVM's own 1e7-bps fee precision, and never write storage on the quote path, which is what makes router.asView().quote() equal to swap(). AegisJITStrategy builds the order bytecode on-chain, AegisJITVaultHook does the just-in-time ERC-4626 withdraw and re-deposit around Aqua.pull/push, AegisZKForwarder is a reference aggregator that trades for a verified user with an EIP-712 TakerAuthorization. Identity verifiers hide behind one IZKVerifier interface: WorldIDAdapter (calls a World ID router's 6-argument verifyProof) and AnonAadhaarAdapter (vendored snarkjs Groth16 verifier, BN254 ecPairing). The router runtime is 22.6 KB of the 24,576-byte EIP-170 limit, so opcode argument layouts are packed by hand (46, 86 and 20 bytes) and the order bytecode is compiled by a TypeScript ProgramBuilder that mirrors SwapVM's [opcode][len][args] framing. Identity payloads. A takerData payload is a 22-byte takerTraits header plus a typed envelope: type 1 World ID (root, epoch, nullifierHash, proof[8], 320 bytes) or type 2 Anon Aadhaar (timestamp, epoch, pubkeyHash, proof[8], 352 bytes), each optionally followed by the EIP-712 authorization. The header encodes slice offsets that depend on the payload length, so the UI keeps one header per payload type and appends a fresh proof. The proof signal is the taker address; the nullifier is bound to the first address that used it. After the first proof a 33-byte binding claim costs one storage read instead of a pairing (5k gas instead of 225k or 288k). World ID. In the browser the World ID tab generates a Semaphore v3 depth-30 proof with snarkjs over the public PSE artifacts (self-hosted, same verification key as World ID's SemaphoreVerifier) and checks it by eth_call before attaching it. For real World ID, IDKit 4.x (IDKitRequestWidget with the orbLegacy preset, allow_legacy_proofs and signal = taker) talks to World App or the World ID Simulator; IDKit 4 requires every request to be signed with the app's relying-party key, so a small server signs rp_context with @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing. That server is the local prover process in development and a Cloudflare Worker on the hosted dashboard; the key never reaches the browser. On World Chain Sepolia the adapter is wired to the chain's real World ID Router and the recorded run executed a Simulator proof on-chain. Anon Aadhaar. The Aadhaar Secure QR is decoded with zxing-wasm, decompressed with pako, parsed and RSA-2048-verified with Web Crypto in the browser, then proven with the official Anon Aadhaar v2 circuit (artifacts ~620 MB, SHA-256 pinned, about 12 seconds and a few GB of RAM per proof) by a prover on 127.0.0.1 only, so QR data never leaves the machine. Tests and demos use a signed test QR from a published test signer, clearly marked as not UIDAI. Nullifiers rotate per 24-hour epoch with a grace window. Tooling. Hardhat + Mocha (128 tests, real proofs included), Foundry property tests (19) through a SwapVMImport shim and a forge-std sync step, hardhat-dependency-compiler for 1inch's sources, TypeChain, viem in the UI. Vite + React + Tailwind dashboard: a disassembler that decodes the live order from Aqua's Shipped event frame by frame, a quote simulator per taker profile with an independent TypeScript mirror of the opcode math checked against the chain, a split-attack sandbox on evm_snapshot/evm_revert, and a vault exposure panel. Deployment scripts are resumable with checkpoints, verify through Etherscan API V2 (Worldscan is chainid 4801 on the same API), and the public-chain demo runner writes demo.json after every scenario. The dashboard is hosted on Cloudflare Workers as static assets plus the signing Worker; the client switches to same-origin endpoints whenever it is not served from a loopback host. Partner technologies. 1inch Aqua and SwapVM gave us a shared liquidity layer with programmable orders, so the whole protocol is three opcodes and a hook rather than a new AMM. World ID gives Sybil resistance with a nullifier we can bind on-chain; Anon Aadhaar (PSE) gives Indian users a sovereign alternative on the same tier; the USDC side of the Maker's capital sits in an ERC-4626 vault and keeps earning while 75% of it is never exposed. Hacky bits worth knowing. (1) Hardhat executes eth_call at the latest block timestamp while the next block is at least one second later, so any per-second fee decay breaks quote == swap; both the surge bucket and the lambda budget therefore live on a fixed time grid, constant inside a window and leaking one threshold per elapsed window. (2) The hosted World ID Simulator only resolves apps registered in the production Developer Portal; our first app lived in the staging portal and the Simulator reported "App not found", so the first live run injected the app metadata into the Simulator's page store from the browser console, after which we re-registered the app and redeployed the adapter cleanly. (3) Public load-balanced RPC replicas can lag a block, which made one pre-swap quote look wrong; the demo runner now pins every read to the block of its latest receipt. (4) The fee mirror in the UI is a deliberate second implementation of the opcode math, so a mismatch shows up as a red badge instead of a silent wrong number.

In the browser the World ID tab generates a Semaphore v3 depth-30 proof with snarkjs over the public PSE artifacts (self-hosted, same verification key as World ID's SemaphoreVerifier) and checks it by eth_call before attaching it. For real World ID, IDKit 4.x (IDKitRequestWidget with the orbLegacy preset, allow_legacy_proofs and signal = taker) talks to World App or the World ID Simulator; IDKit 4 requires every request to be signed with the app's relying-party key, so a small server signs rp_context with @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing. That server is the local prover process in development and a Cloudflare Worker on the hosted dashboard; the key never reaches the browser. On World Chain Sepolia the adapter is wired to the chain's real World ID Router and the recorded run executed a Simulator proof on-chain.

Anon Aadhaar. The Aadhaar Secure QR is decoded with zxing-wasm, decompressed with pako, parsed and RSA-2048-verified with Web Crypto in the browser, then proven with the official Anon Aadhaar v2 circuit (artifacts ~620 MB, SHA-256 pinned, about 12 seconds and a few GB of RAM per proof) by a prover on 127.0.0.1 only, so QR data never leaves the machine. Tests and demos use a signed test QR from a published test signer, clearly marked as not UIDAI. Nullifiers rotate per 24-hour epoch with a grace window.

Tooling. Hardhat + Mocha (128 tests, real proofs included), Foundry property tests (19) through a SwapVMImport shim and a forge-std sync step, hardhat-dependency-compiler for 1inch's sources, TypeChain, viem in the UI. Vite + React + Tailwind dashboard: a disassembler that decodes the live order from Aqua's Shipped event frame by frame, a quote simulator per taker profile with an independent TypeScript mirror of the opcode math checked against the chain, a split-attack sandbox on evm_snapshot/evm_revert, and a vault exposure panel. Deployment scripts are resumable with checkpoints, verify through Etherscan API V2 (Worldscan is chainid 4801 on the same API), and the public-chain demo runner writes demo.json after every scenario. The dashboard is hosted on Cloudflare Workers as static assets plus the signing Worker; the client switches to same-origin endpoints whenever it is not served from a loopback host.

Partner technologies. 1inch Aqua and SwapVM gave us a shared liquidity layer with programmable orders, so the whole protocol is three opcodes and a hook rather than a new AMM. World ID gives Sybil resistance with a nullifier we can bind on-chain; Anon Aadhaar (PSE) gives Indian users a sovereign alternative on the same tier; the USDC side of the Maker's capital sits in an ERC-4626 vault and keeps earning while 75% of it is never exposed.

Hacky bits worth knowing. (1) Hardhat executes eth_call at the latest block timestamp while the next block is at least one second later, so any per-second fee decay breaks quote == swap; both the surge bucket and the lambda budget therefore live on a fixed time grid, constant inside a window and leaking one threshold per elapsed window. (2) The hosted World ID Simulator only resolves apps registered in the production Developer Portal; our first app lived in the staging portal and the Simulator reported "App not found", so the first live run injected the app metadata into the Simulator's page store from the browser console, after which we re-registered the app and redeployed the adapter cleanly. (3) Public load-balanced RPC replicas can lag a block, which made one pre-swap quote look wrong; the demo runner now pins every read to the block of its latest receipt. (4) The fee mirror in the UI is a deliberate second implementation of the opcode math, so a mismatch shows up as a red badge instead of a silent wrong number.

projects.title: zk-seal
projects.description: Hide faces, keep proof: zkSeal edits, World ID names on ENS, records on Arkiv, pictures on Swarm.
projects.project_description: A photo is easy to fake, and AI makes it easier. Cameras can now sign photos at capture (C2PA), but that signature has two gaps. Any edit breaks it, even covering a stranger's face. And it says nothing about who posted the photo, so one person with fifty accounts can look like fifty witnesses. zkSeal is a working demo of how to close both gaps, with real names on Ethereum mainnet. Seal. You take a photo and mark the faces. zkSeal turns those areas grey and makes a proof that nothing else changed from the signed original. The app draws a mask or mosaic over the grey. Name. You pass World ID once and get a username like alice.users.zk-seal.eth. One World ID, one name. Publish. You scan your event badge and approve the photo with World ID. The picture goes to Swarm, a public read-only record goes to Arkiv, and the photo gets its own ENS name, like image1.ethglobal.events.zk-seal.eth. Check. Open zk-seal.eth.limo. The gallery reads ENS, Arkiv and Swarm from the browser, with no server of ours, and shows each event as folders of names and photos. Anyone can count the distinct names behind an event. Why these partners: ENSv2 puts every person, event and photo in one tree of real names. Arkiv makes the records public, read-only and open to anyone's query. Swarm holds the pictures. World ID answers the one question we need, whether this is one person, with no passport data. What is true in this demo: our test key signs in place of a camera. World IDs are test identities. The sealing service is closed. The cover is drawn by the app and not proved. Our server holds the address keys, acts as the registrar, and takes the seal's hash from the app without checking it.
projects.how_its_made: zkSeal is an existing private product that proves how an edited photo follows from a signed original. It stays closed. Everything below is new at ETHGlobal Mumbai and in the public repo, except closed service around that product. Seal: the app sends each photo to that closed service, which uses zkSeal to turn the marked areas grey and make the proof that nothing else changed. Phone app: Swift for iOS, with World's IDKit Swift package. It covers faces with a mask or mosaic, scans the event badge, and runs the World step for each photo. Tonight it talks to our server over a cable. Web server: Next.js and TypeScript. It checks World proofs on the server and acts as the registrar. A read-only copy runs on Vercel with no keys. ENS: we use ENSv2 on Ethereum mainnet. Under zk-seal.eth we built a tree: users.zk-seal.eth for people and events.zk-seal.eth for events, with each photo as its own name. The photo's contenthash points to its picture on Swarm, and text records name the seal and the user. Each person's address has their username as its primary name. Arkiv: four kinds of read-only record on the Rabdi testnet, written with the Arkiv SDK: users, seals, pictures and names. Every read filters on the wallet that created the row, so a fake row handed to our wallet does not pass. Swarm: pictures go through the public gateway. We own no batch, so nobody promises how long files stay. The gallery itself is also on Swarm. Gallery: one HTML file with no server, opened at zk-seal.eth.limo. It reads Arkiv, ENS and Swarm directly from the browser. Hacky parts: World allows one proof per person and action, so each photo gets its own action, and a session ties it to the username. Arkiv has no unique field, so we keep the earliest row as the real one. We also wrote registrar contracts and tested them on a fork, but they are not wired in: tonight the registrar is our server.

projects.title: Heartbeat
projects.description: Autonomous AI-powered defense that detects DeFi exploits and coordinates on-chain rescue.
projects.project_description:
DeFi protocols operate in an increasingly hostile environment where exploits can drain millions of dollars within minutes. Traditional security mechanisms are largely reactive: they generate alerts, depend on human intervention, and often respond too slowly to prevent catastrophic losses. Heartbeat Protocol is an autonomous, AI-powered security and emergency-response system designed to detect, investigate, and respond to threats targeting decentralized finance protocols. Inspired by the human cardiovascular system, Heartbeat continuously monitors the health of DeFi protocols, identifies abnormal activity, diagnoses potential exploits, and coordinates emergency responses before vulnerabilities escalate into catastrophic financial losses. The system operates through six interconnected stages: Detect — Continuous Threat Monitoring
Heartbeat monitors blockchain transaction activity, smart contract events, and protocol telemetry to identify suspicious behavior, abnormal transaction patterns, and potential exploit indicators. Diagnose — AI-Powered Security Analysis
When suspicious activity is detected, the system uses AI-powered analysis to investigate transaction data, event logs, and relevant contract information. Local AI inference through Ollama enables security analysis without depending entirely on external AI services. Investigate — Protocol-Wide Risk Assessment
Heartbeat extends beyond individual transactions by scanning DAO portfolios and associated protocols to identify shared vulnerabilities, interconnected risks, and potential systemic exposure. Respond — Autonomous Emergency Intervention
When a critical threat is identified, the system coordinates emergency response through its HeartbeatGuardian smart contract. Its rescue mechanism is designed to facilitate emergency fund protection and recovery operations. Record — Immutable Security Audit Trail
VitalRegistry records security events, detected anomalies, and intervention outcomes on-chain, providing a transparent and verifiable history of security operations. Visualize — Real-Time Security Intelligence
A web-based monitoring dashboard brings together protocol health, threat detection, investigation results, and emergency-response activity. The architecture combines smart contract enforcement, autonomous blockchain workflows, and AI-powered threat intelligence to move DeFi security from reactive monitoring toward proactive, automated defense. Heartbeat Protocol aims to give decentralized financial systems something they have historically lacked: an autonomous defense mechanism capable of detecting a threat, understanding its implications, and coordinating an emergency response when every second matters.
projects.how_its_made:
Heartbeat Protocol is built using a combination of Solidity smart contracts, Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE), local AI inference, and a modern Web3 frontend. The architecture is divided into four primary layers: Smart Contract Layer — Solidity & Foundry
The on-chain infrastructure is implemented in Solidity and tested using Foundry. It consists of three core contracts: HeartbeatGuardian.sol: The primary emergency-response contract responsible for coordinating security interventions and emergency fund-rescue operations. VitalRegistry.sol: Maintains an immutable on-chain record of security incidents, anomalies, and intervention events. ArrhythmicVault.sol: Provides the vault infrastructure used in the emergency-response and fund-rescue architecture. These contracts establish the on-chain foundation for security enforcement, response coordination, and auditability. Autonomous Workflow Layer — Chainlink CRE
Chainlink Runtime Environment powers the orchestration layer, connecting blockchain monitoring, off-chain analysis, and on-chain execution. The CRE workflow is organized into specialized modules: exploitDetector.js: Identifies suspicious blockchain activity and potential exploit indicators. aiAnalyzer.js: Coordinates AI-powered investigation and threat analysis. portfolioScanner.js: Examines DAO portfolios and associated protocol exposure. responseExecutor.js: Coordinates the appropriate emergency-response operations. index.ts: Connects the individual components into the overall CRE workflow. Chainlink CRE provides the infrastructure for orchestrating off-chain computation and interacting with on-chain smart contracts. AI Intelligence Layer — Ollama
We integrated Ollama to support locally hosted AI inference. Rather than making every security-analysis operation dependent on third-party AI APIs, the architecture supports local model execution for analyzing suspicious transactions, security telemetry, and potential exploit scenarios. This approach offers greater control over inference, data handling, and model selection while allowing the intelligence layer to operate alongside the blockchain infrastructure. Frontend Layer — Next.js & Web3
The monitoring interface is built using Next.js 14 and Tailwind CSS. Wagmi, Viem, and RainbowKit provide the Web3 integration layer for wallet connectivity and smart contract interactions. The dashboard brings together protocol monitoring, security intelligence, detected threats, and emergency-response activity in a unified interface. What Makes the Architecture Interesting The most interesting engineering challenge is connecting autonomous off-chain intelligence with on-chain emergency execution. AI analysis cannot directly enforce blockchain security. It must operate within a carefully designed execution architecture where smart contracts remain responsible for enforcing permissions and validating critical operations. Heartbeat separates detection, diagnosis, investigation, and execution into distinct components. This modular approach makes it possible to evolve the AI models and detection mechanisms without having to redesign the entire on-chain infrastructure. The result is an integrated security architecture combining AI-driven intelligence, decentralized workflow orchestration, and smart contract-based emergency response.

projects.title: Kall Markets
projects.description: X, Telegram, any chat, phone or laptop: see a call, trade it right there. Trading just got faster.
projects.project_description:
Hawk Tuah’s memecoin fell 91% in under three hours while insider wallets held most of the supply.
https://cointelegraph.com/news/hawk-tuah-memecoin-dumps-90-percent-outrage-token-launch-insider
https://blog.bubblemaps.io/how-hailey-welchs-hawk-token-became-a-500m-disaster/ Argentina’s president posted $LIBRA on X. 86% of buyers lost money, and the post was deleted hours later.
https://www.web3isgoinggreat.com/single/milei-memecoin-promotion Crypto runs on calls, and followers only ever see the wins. When a call fails, the post disappears. Even the contract address can be fake: hacked accounts have pushed fake tokens.
https://bitpinas.com/cryptocurrency/coins-hack-pump-fun-x/ Kall Markets prices every call the minute it’s posted, scores it when its time is up, and writes it to Arkiv, where nobody can edit it. Deleting the tweet doesn’t delete the record. The check and the trade happen in the same place. Copy a call from X or any chat, and Kall shows the caller’s record and blocks fake contracts. Then you trade it on Definitive Flash, with no tab-switching. Where you trade it On X: a Chrome extension puts the caller’s record under the post and flags fake contracts. You sign the trade without leaving X.
In any chat: the Kall keyboard on iPhone and Android. Copy the call in Telegram or WhatsApp, and the keyboard reads it, checks it and trades it there.
Web app: one feed of every caller you follow, with their record next to each post.
https://kallmarkets.vercel.app Behind all three is one server: it reads the call, checks the contract, prices it, trades on Definitive Flash and records everything on Arkiv. Andriod Kall Keyboard apk -
https://kall-markets-downloads-308324916322.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/apps/kall-keyboard.apk
projects.how_its_made:
We started on X: a Chrome extension that puts the caller’s record and a trade button under the post. Then we noticed most calls aren’t on X. They’re in WhatsApp groups, private Telegram groups and paid call channels, and an extension can’t reach them, least of all on a phone. Every chat app has a keyboard, though. So we built Kall Keyboard. It reads a call, checks the caller and trades it, in any app. Android: a fork of the open-source FlorisBoard. It types normally, and one key opens the trading panel. Sign in with X and you get a Privy wallet on Base. You can also hold the mic and say “buy $20 of ETH, take profit 10%”, and ElevenLabs transcribes it.
iPhone: a native SwiftUI keyboard with the same panel: callers you follow, trade, orders, wallet. A small capped demo wallet on our server places the order.
Reading calls: copy a call or a contract, and gpt-4.1-mini works out the coin and whether it’s long or short. Fake contracts are flagged. Under all of it: Definitive Flash: every trade, on Base. TP/SL go in with the order, and approvals are capped to the order size.
Chainlink: price feeds set the entry price at the minute of the post. CRE checks that a coin is the real one and records verdicts on Base Sepolia.
Arkiv: every call, result and trade is a read-only record, and anyone can check a caller.
Swarm: a copy of the post, so deleting the tweet doesn’t delete the proof.
Web app: Next.js on Vercel, with one feed of every caller you follow.

projects.title: CallLedger
projects.description: Tamper-proof track records for crypto callers on X, plus one-signature copy trading
projects.project_description: Crypto "alpha" on X is easy to fake. Callers delete the posts that went wrong, and screenshots prove nothing. CallLedger fixes that. We watch the traders people follow on X, spot the posts that are actual trade calls (entry, take profit, stop loss, long or short), and archive each one on-chain through Arkiv. Once it's there, nobody can edit it or quietly delete it, and anyone can check the record. Users get a web dashboard to discover creators, follow them, and read their archived call history. A Chrome extension adds a CallLedger bar right under posts on X. It highlights the call, shows a chart for the token, and lets you act on it in one click. If you want to copy a call, CallLedger builds a trade draft from the post. You set your size and limits, get a live quote through Definitive Flash, and sign with your own wallet. We never hold your keys or funds. You always decide.
projects.how_its_made: It's a TypeScript monorepo run with Turborepo. The web app is Next.js with Tailwind. We used Lightweight Charts for the token charts and motion for the landing page. The backend is Express 5 with Postgres and Drizzle ORM. A separate worker polls creator sources on a schedule, using database leases so two workers never process the same source. The browser extension is built with React and Vite on Manifest V3. It uses a mutation observer to detect posts as you scroll X, so it can add the CallLedger bar and a hover chart on cash tags. Arkiv is the core of the project. When the worker finds a new post, a keyword-based classifier decides whether it's a real trade call. We don't use an LLM for this, so it's cheap and predictable. If it is, we write an entity to Arkiv on the Rabdi testnet with viem. Only the structured data goes on-chain: handle, post ID, timestamp, assets, and signal fields. A local table keeps a reference to each entity key and transaction hash. Before writing, we check for duplicates both locally and on Arkiv itself. The archive page then reads straight back from Arkiv, so what you see is the on-chain record rather than our database. For execution we wrote a typed client for Definitive Flash. It asks for a quote and gets back EIP-712 typed data. The user signs that with MetaMask, and we submit the order and poll its status until the fill shows a transaction hash. The API key stays server-side only and is never bundled into the extension or frontend. We also never auto-retry order submission. If the network fails, we check the order status first so a trade can't be sent twice. Sign-in is a wallet nonce signature, and creator X tokens are encrypted with AES-256-GCM.

The browser extension is built with React and Vite on Manifest V3. It uses a mutation observer to detect posts as you scroll X, so it can add the CallLedger bar and a hover chart on cash tags.

Arkiv is the core of the project. When the worker finds a new post, a keyword-based classifier decides whether it's a real trade call. We don't use an LLM for this, so it's cheap and predictable. If it is, we write an entity to Arkiv on the Rabdi testnet with viem. Only the structured data goes on-chain: handle, post ID, timestamp, assets, and signal fields. A local table keeps a reference to each entity key and transaction hash. Before writing, we check for duplicates both locally and on Arkiv itself. The archive page then reads straight back from Arkiv, so what you see is the on-chain record rather than our database.

For execution we wrote a typed client for Definitive Flash. It asks for a quote and gets back EIP-712 typed data. The user signs that with MetaMask, and we submit the order and poll its status until the fill shows a transaction hash. The API key stays server-side only and is never bundled into the extension or frontend. We also never auto-retry order submission. If the network fails, we check the order status first so a trade can't be sent twice. Sign-in is a wallet nonce signature, and creator X tokens are encrypted with AES-256-GCM.

projects.title: Private PQ Messaging
projects.description: Post-quantum private messaging on Ethereum: Kyber512 + ZK proofs, sender and recipient hidden.
projects.project_description: pq is post-quantum private messaging for Web3 payments, private coordination and transaction negotiation. Messages are stored publicly on-chain, yet only the two ends of a conversation can read them, and the chain never shows who is talking to whom. The problem: today's encrypted messaging relies on elliptic-curve cryptography (ECDH), which is exposed to "harvest now, decrypt later" quantum attacks. Anything on a public chain is stored forever, so it's harvested by default. How it works: Join: create a passkey. It derives your Sender Key and a Kyber512 (lattice-based, post-quantum) User Key, which your wallet registers. Open a Channel: your browser encrypts a Channel Key to the recipient's Kyber512 key and proves in zero knowledge that the encryption is well formed, without revealing who the recipient is. Send: each message is encrypted with its own Message Key and stored under a Message ID that only the two ends can compute. Read: recipients find Channels opened to them by trial-decryption, then read messages by ID. Bulky post-quantum data (800-byte User Keys, Encrypted Channel Keys) lives on Arkiv, with only keccak256 hashes on Ethereum, cutting gas by 83-88%. A Fixed Sender relays every transaction, so on-chain you only see it calling the contract. Live on Sepolia; an unaudited research prototype.
projects.how_its_made: A Scaffold-ETH 2 monorepo with three packages: Circuits (Go + gnark): Kyber512 CPA-PKE, via our fork of Cloudflare's CIRCL that exposes Kyber's polynomial math, plus a Groth16 circuit on BN254 proving the Encrypted Channel Key is a valid Kyber encryption of a key matching its public hash. The recipient's key is a private input, so the recipient stays hidden. ~49k constraints, 384-byte proof. Every hash is Poseidon2. Browser prover: the same Go code compiled to WASM, so hashing and Kyber have one implementation across native, circuit and browser. Proving takes ~8s on CPU, with gnark's WebGPU runtime taking over where available. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry): PqMsg registers Users, opens Channels after checking the opening proof with the gnark-generated Verifier.sol, and stores messages. Deployed on Sepolia. Storage on Arkiv: post-quantum keys are big, so User Keys and Channels are stored whole as Arkiv entities (Rabdi testnet), and PqMsg keeps only their keccak256 hashes. Readers drop any entity that doesn't match its on-chain hash, so Arkiv needs no trust. This cut register from 3.02M to 0.36M gas (-88%) and openChannel from 5.01M to 0.83M (-83%). Frontend (Next.js, React, TypeScript, wagmi/viem): passkey (WebAuthn PRF) key derivation, the chat UI, and a "Deep dive" mode that explains each crypto step as it runs and links new Arkiv entities. A server-side Fixed Sender submits transactions and writes to Arkiv so users stay unlinkable; the browser reads Arkiv directly and fetches recipient keys over Anon-RPC. Notably hacky: leaving Kyber ciphertext uncompressed so the circuit can check it, packing 768 coefficients into 37 field elements, and a 2^64 domain tag for key separation.

projects.title: Paymesh
projects.description: AI agents that hire each other, pay per use in USDC on Arc, and obey their owner's spending rules.
projects.project_description: PayMesh lets agents buy services from each other in USDC on Arc, with per-request budgets, approval thresholds, and hard caps you set. Your agent hires a Trip Planner, which pays Weather, FX, and Encyclopedia agents from its own wallet. Each hire is an x402 Nanopayment through Circle Gateway, settled only after the work succeeds.
projects.how_its_made: PayMesh is one Next.js 16 process, written in TypeScript with React, that hosts five agents. Each has its own EOA key and paid HTTP endpoint. viem is the only other runtime package. The agents call each other over HTTP, so each hire takes the same path a remote agent would. Payments use x402. A seller answers with a 402, and the buyer signs an EIP-712 authorization and retries. The seller verifies it through Circle Gateway, checks the buyer's balance, does the work, and settles in USDC on Arc Testnet only if the work succeeded. The agents use regex rules, not an LLM, and a small policy function enforces the owner's limits. Data comes from Open-Meteo, Frankfurter, and Wikipedia. Claude Code and Codex wrote all of the code, and I made the product decisions.

projects.title: Chinki
projects.description: Gift USDT without gas. Claim a prepaid local fiat card with a passkey.
projects.project_description: Chinki turns a personal gift into a prepaid dollar card, paid for in USDT. A sender chooses an envelope design, an amount, a private note and a claim window, then signs one gasless authorization. The recipient opens a private link, confirms a passkey and claims one card with a spending budget matching the gift without connecting a wallet. Each gift has its own card and a live budget ledger. Card approvals reserve available value; cleared purchases settle against the gift on Whitechain. Unused value returns to the sender after expiry and reconciliation. The sender can follow funding, claiming, spending and returns through verifiable receipts. Personal notes are encrypted in the browser and opened with the private gift link. The current demo uses official test USDT on Whitechain testnet and genuine Lithic sandbox cards. Card purchases are simulated; no real money moves and USDT is not converted into card funds. Campaign limits are per passkey, not proof of one unique person.
projects.how_its_made: Chinki is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript and PostgreSQL. The sender signs an EIP-712/EIP-3009 USDT authorization. A sponsored relayer calls receiveWithAuthorization through our gift vault on Whitechain testnet, so the sender does not need WBT for gas. Gift terms and a private-link secret hash are committed to the authorization nonce. Recipients authenticate using WebAuthn passkeys. The browser encrypts gift notes with AES-GCM using key material derived from the link secret. After the on-chain claim confirms, a durable worker creates one gift-sized Lithic sandbox virtual card. Sensitive card details are displayed only through short-lived Lithic-hosted frames; our API never serves PAN or CVV. Signed Lithic Auth Stream Access requests use a transactional PostgreSQL ledger to reserve budget synchronously. Provider clearing events are reconciled asynchronously and enqueue idempotent partial vault settlements. Expiry closure waits for outstanding holds and settlements before returning unused value. Ambiguous card issuance is recovered by its persisted reference instead of blindly creating another card. The deployed vault, real testnet receipts, unit/integration tests and browser passkey checks are in the public repository. Whitechain provides the official USDT authorization and settlement rail; Lithic provides card issuance and the sandbox purchase lifecycle.

projects.title: Aegis IDS
projects.description: Real-time network intrusion detection with Scapy, rule-based detectors, and ML anomaly scoring.
projects.project_description: Aegis IDS is a network intrusion detection system with a dashboard for reviewing suspicious traffic patterns. It analyzes packet data for port scans, traffic spikes, unusual DNS activity, ARP changes, new devices, and ICMP floods. An Isolation Forest model adds anomaly detection based on traffic statistics. The dashboard presents alerts, traffic charts, and a device inventory, with filtering and CSV export. The public demo uses fictional sample data and is read-only; it does not display live network traffic.
projects.how_its_made: The detection system is written in Python. Scapy parses network packets, and separate detector modules check traffic against configurable thresholds. Scikit-learn’s Isolation Forest analyzes traffic statistics for anomalies. Flask serves the dashboard and API, while SQLite stores alerts and statistics. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, and Jinja templates. The public review demo is a separate static site with fictional sample data, so it can be accessed without exposing the live monitoring dashboard or network information.

projects.title: PINT PROTOCOLS
projects.description: An SDK for DeFi wallet developers to optimize trades, enforce safeguards, and verify outcomes.
projects.project_description: Northtrail — Intelligent DeFi Execution & Verifiable Transaction Assurance Northtrail is a non-custodial DeFi intelligence and transaction-assurance platform, built around an embeddable SDK that enables wallets and trading applications to integrate quantitative liquidity analysis, execution optimization, transaction safeguards, and cryptographically verifiable decision records. The Problem Decentralized exchanges have made token swaps increasingly accessible, but executing a transaction successfully does not necessarily mean executing it efficiently or making an informed financial decision. Users face fragmented liquidity, varying protocol fees, slippage, price impact, gas costs, market volatility, and complex token approvals. Even after a transaction is confirmed, understanding why a particular execution route was selected—and whether its outcome matched the original expectations—remains challenging. Northtrail addresses this gap by introducing an intelligence and accountability layer between financial decision-making and blockchain execution. Our Solution Northtrail brings together several complementary capabilities through a unified platform: 1. Uniswap Integration & Compass — Trade Intelligence Northtrail integrates with Uniswap's liquidity infrastructure to observe supported swap quotes, evaluate trading costs, and analyze potential execution outcomes. Compass enables users to stress-test price movements and assess financial exposure, while exact integer arithmetic ensures precision in token-denominated calculations. 2. Curve Atlas — Quantitative Liquidity Optimization Curve Atlas analyzes how liquidity depth, fee tiers, gas costs, and price impact influence trading efficiency across different order sizes. By comparing Uniswap pool scenarios against 1inch routing benchmarks, it helps users understand why the most economical liquidity source can change as transaction size increases. 3. Chronos — Risk-Aware Execution Strategy Chronos explores three execution approaches: trading immediately, splitting an order into multiple transactions, or waiting. Its quantitative planning models evaluate execution-cost assumptions, repeated gas expenses, and downside risk using measures such as Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR). These scenarios demonstrate how execution decisions can be evaluated systematically rather than relying solely on quoted prices. 4. 1inch Integration & Aqua Maker Studio — Liquidity Strategy Intelligence Beyond using 1inch Pathfinder as a cross-DEX routing benchmark, Northtrail explores 1inch Aqua's virtual liquidity architecture. Aqua Maker Studio models capital coverage, maker liquidity availability, and strategy lifecycle operations through an interactive simulation, highlighting the relationship between advertised liquidity and actual available capital. 5. Universe Risk Lens & ML Pool Intelligence Northtrail incorporates quantitative research tools for understanding market exposure, including volatility, drawdowns, Value at Risk, and liquidity-stress scenarios. These analytical workspaces make complex financial concepts more accessible and support the development of data-driven execution strategies. 6. Wallet Assurance & World Agent Pass Northtrail maintains a strict non-custodial design philosophy. Its authorization demonstrations examine token approvals, transaction permissions, and spending limits. World Agent Pass additionally explores human-in-the-loop governance for sensitive automated-agent actions, emphasizing that algorithmic recommendations must never independently grant financial authority. 7. Decision Trail & Trade Proof — Verifiable Accountability This is Northtrail's central differentiation. Decision Trail uses RFC 8785 canonical JSON and SHA-256 cryptographic hashing to generate tamper-evident, independently verifiable decision records. It preserves the reasoning and parameters behind a trading decision, including a deliberate decision not to execute. Trade Proof complements this capability through blockchain transaction-receipt observation, exposing evidence such as transaction status and gas expenditure while distinguishing receipt confirmation from complete token-settlement verification. Together, these components establish a foundation for connecting financial decisions with independently inspectable execution evidence. Built for Developers, Not Just End Users The deployed Northtrail interface is a demonstration of a broader infrastructure product. Its core capabilities are organized into a modular TypeScript monorepo using Next.js, Fastify, Zod, PostgreSQL/PGlite, and an embeddable SDK. Rather than requiring users to adopt another standalone trading application, Northtrail is designed to let existing DeFi wallets, treasury platforms, and trading interfaces incorporate its intelligence and assurance capabilities directly into their own products. The current platform demonstrates read-only protocol observations, quantitative research scenarios, cryptographic decision verification, and transaction-receipt inspection. Advanced execution planning, Aqua strategy operations, and agent-governance workflows are clearly distinguished where they operate as simulations rather than live financial execution. Our Vision We're not building another decentralized exchange. We're building the intelligence and accountability infrastructure that existing DeFi applications can build upon. By combining Uniswap liquidity analysis, 1inch routing and strategy research, quantitative financial modeling, non-custodial authorization principles, and verifiable decision evidence, Northtrail establishes a foundation for trading experiences that are more informed, transparent, and accountable. Northtrail — Know the choice. Prove the outcome.
projects.how_its_made: How It's Made — Northtrail We built Northtrail as a modular, non-custodial DeFi intelligence and transaction-assurance infrastructure layer , designed to integrate directly into existing wallets and trading applications through a reusable TypeScript SDK. Our biggest engineering challenge was combining real DeFi protocol data, quantitative financial analysis, and cryptographic decision verification without compromising precision, transparency, or user control. 1. Architecture & Technology Stack Northtrail is built as a TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm , separating financial computation, protocol integrations, persistent evidence, APIs, and user interfaces. Our core technology stack includes: Next.js for the responsive financial analytics and developer demonstration workspace. Fastify and Node.js for the backend REST API, request validation, protocol communication, and rate limiting. TypeScript and Zod for strict data contracts, runtime validation, and consistent API/SDK interfaces. PostgreSQL and PGlite for persistent decision records, database migrations, and append-only evidence lineage. RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme and SHA-256 for deterministic, independently verifiable decision-record fingerprints. Vitest and Playwright for automated testing, integration verification, and browser-level functionality. Vercel and Railway for frontend and backend deployment. The system follows a clear flow: protocol observations → financial analysis → decision evidence → API/SDK → user-facing applications . 2. Uniswap — Our Primary Protocol Integration Uniswap forms the foundation of Northtrail's liquidity intelligence. We implemented server-side Uniswap V3 quote observation to retrieve trading information for supported token pairs, including expected output and slippage constraints. Rather than simply displaying a swap quote, we feed these observations into Compass , our financial scenario engine, to help users understand transaction economics and evaluate alternative decisions. We also developed Curve Atlas , an interactive liquidity-frontier research workspace that illustrates how Uniswap fee tiers, pool depth, price impact, and order size influence trading efficiency. This enables users to explore an important execution insight: the most attractive liquidity pool can change as trade size increases . 3. 1inch — Routing Intelligence & Aqua Strategy Research We integrated 1inch Swap API v6.1 as an additional quote-observation source, providing a cross-DEX routing benchmark alongside Uniswap. This allows Northtrail to examine the economic differences between individual liquidity-pool scenarios and aggregator-based routing alternatives. We extended our 1inch work into Aqua Maker Studio , exploring Aqua's virtual-liquidity architecture and its capital-efficiency implications. One particularly interesting implementation is our capital-coverage inspector , exposed through the SDK. It evaluates available capital against virtual liquidity allocations to highlight potential undercollateralization. The workspace also demonstrates a simulated Ship → Fill → Dock strategy lifecycle, making Aqua's underlying concepts easier to inspect and understand. 4. Quantitative Finance & Execution Intelligence We developed several interconnected research modules: Compass evaluates financial scenarios and trade-cost comparisons using precise token-denominated calculations. Curve Atlas illustrates trade-size-dependent liquidity economics. Chronos compares executing immediately, splitting an order, or waiting, incorporating estimated transaction costs and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR). Universe Risk Lens explores volatility, drawdowns, exponentially weighted volatility, and Value at Risk across selected crypto assets. ML Pool Intelligence provides interactive liquidity-stress and model-based scenarios. These workspaces distinguish illustrative modeling from live execution and validated predictive performance. Their purpose is to make quantitative methods understandable and establish a foundation for more advanced execution research. 5. Cryptographic Decision Trail & Transaction Evidence One of our most distinctive engineering decisions was treating the decision itself as a verifiable artifact . We implemented canonical JSON serialization using RFC 8785, followed by SHA-256 hashing, to generate deterministic decision fingerprints. This means independently implemented clients can verify record integrity without depending entirely on the Northtrail frontend. Our append-only database design also preserves decision revisions instead of silently overwriting previous evidence. An especially useful capability is the ability to record and verify a deliberate decision not to trade . Financial accountability shouldn't begin only when a transaction is broadcast. Alongside this, Trade Proof supports blockchain transaction-receipt observation, exposing transaction status and gas information while explicitly distinguishing receipt confirmation from full token-settlement verification. 6. Non-Custodial Security & World Agent Pass Northtrail's protocol observers never receive financial signing authority. We maintain strict separation between market information, financial recommendations, and wallet authorization. Our wallet-assurance workspace demonstrates approval risks, transaction restrictions, and spending boundaries. We also explored World Agent Pass for human-in-the-loop governance, illustrating how sensitive automated-agent policy exceptions can require additional human verification without treating that verification as permission to spend funds. 7. Notable Engineering Decisions Several implementation details make Northtrail particularly interesting: Exact bigint token arithmetic: Avoids floating-point precision errors in financial calculations. Deterministic cryptographic evidence: Makes decision records independently checkable and resistant to undetected modification. Decoupled protocol adapters: Keeps Uniswap and 1inch market observations separate from spending authorization. Pure financial computation: Allows mathematical logic to be tested without wallets, network requests, or a running frontend. PGlite/PostgreSQL compatibility: Supports lightweight local development alongside persistent database deployments. Independent SDK consumer: Demonstrates that Northtrail's core capabilities can be integrated outside our own web interface. Explicit execution-state boundaries: Distinguishes live observations, illustrative research, simulations, and actual blockchain evidence. The repository also documents 207 automated tests across 13 test suites , alongside type checking, linting, build verification, SDK smoke tests, and browser testing. 8. Deployment & The Bigger Picture We deployed the Next.js frontend on Vercel and the Fastify backend on Railway , creating an accessible demonstration of the platform's research, financial computation, and verification capabilities. However, the web application is only the demonstration interface . Our core product is the embeddable Northtrail SDK, designed to let DeFi wallet developers integrate financial intelligence and decision-assurance functionality without rebuilding the underlying infrastructure. We deliberately preserve the distinction between live quote observations, simulated trading strategies, cryptographic record verification, and actual on-chain settlement. This ensures the platform communicates what its evidence genuinely establishes. Ultimately, we built Northtrail to connect three capabilities that are often fragmented across DeFi: quantitative intelligence, user-controlled financial authorization, and verifiable decision evidence. Northtrail — Know the choice. Prove the outcome.

**4. 1inch Integration & Aqua Maker Studio — Liquidity Strategy Intelligence**

Our biggest engineering challenge was combining real DeFi protocol data, quantitative financial analysis, and cryptographic decision verification without compromising precision, transparency, or user control.

### 1. Architecture & Technology Stack

Northtrail is built as a **TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm**, separating financial computation, protocol integrations, persistent evidence, APIs, and user interfaces.

Our core technology stack includes:

- **Next.js** for the responsive financial analytics and developer demonstration workspace.
- **Fastify and Node.js** for the backend REST API, request validation, protocol communication, and rate limiting.
- **TypeScript and Zod** for strict data contracts, runtime validation, and consistent API/SDK interfaces.
- **PostgreSQL and PGlite** for persistent decision records, database migrations, and append-only evidence lineage.
- **RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme and SHA-256** for deterministic, independently verifiable decision-record fingerprints.
- **Vitest and Playwright** for automated testing, integration verification, and browser-level functionality.
- **Vercel and Railway** for frontend and backend deployment.

The system follows a clear flow: **protocol observations → financial analysis → decision evidence → API/SDK → user-facing applications**.

### 2. Uniswap — Our Primary Protocol Integration

Uniswap forms the foundation of Northtrail's liquidity intelligence.

We implemented server-side Uniswap V3 quote observation to retrieve trading information for supported token pairs, including expected output and slippage constraints.

Rather than simply displaying a swap quote, we feed these observations into **Compass**, our financial scenario engine, to help users understand transaction economics and evaluate alternative decisions.

We also developed **Curve Atlas**, an interactive liquidity-frontier research workspace that illustrates how Uniswap fee tiers, pool depth, price impact, and order size influence trading efficiency.

This enables users to explore an important execution insight: **the most attractive liquidity pool can change as trade size increases**.

### 3. 1inch — Routing Intelligence & Aqua Strategy Research

We integrated **1inch Swap API v6.1** as an additional quote-observation source, providing a cross-DEX routing benchmark alongside Uniswap.

This allows Northtrail to examine the economic differences between individual liquidity-pool scenarios and aggregator-based routing alternatives.

We extended our 1inch work into **Aqua Maker Studio**, exploring Aqua's virtual-liquidity architecture and its capital-efficiency implications.

One particularly interesting implementation is our **capital-coverage inspector**, exposed through the SDK. It evaluates available capital against virtual liquidity allocations to highlight potential undercollateralization.

The workspace also demonstrates a simulated **Ship → Fill → Dock** strategy lifecycle, making Aqua's underlying concepts easier to inspect and understand.

### 4. Quantitative Finance & Execution Intelligence

We developed several interconnected research modules:

**Compass** evaluates financial scenarios and trade-cost comparisons using precise token-denominated calculations.

**Curve Atlas** illustrates trade-size-dependent liquidity economics.

**Chronos** compares executing immediately, splitting an order, or waiting, incorporating estimated transaction costs and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR).

**Universe Risk Lens** explores volatility, drawdowns, exponentially weighted volatility, and Value at Risk across selected crypto assets.

**ML Pool Intelligence** provides interactive liquidity-stress and model-based scenarios.

These workspaces distinguish illustrative modeling from live execution and validated predictive performance. Their purpose is to make quantitative methods understandable and establish a foundation for more advanced execution research.

### 5. Cryptographic Decision Trail & Transaction Evidence

One of our most distinctive engineering decisions was treating **the decision itself as a verifiable artifact**.

We implemented canonical JSON serialization using RFC 8785, followed by SHA-256 hashing, to generate deterministic decision fingerprints.

This means independently implemented clients can verify record integrity without depending entirely on the Northtrail frontend.

Our append-only database design also preserves decision revisions instead of silently overwriting previous evidence.

An especially useful capability is the ability to record and verify a deliberate **decision not to trade**. Financial accountability shouldn't begin only when a transaction is broadcast.

Alongside this, **Trade Proof** supports blockchain transaction-receipt observation, exposing transaction status and gas information while explicitly distinguishing receipt confirmation from full token-settlement verification.

### 6. Non-Custodial Security & World Agent Pass

Northtrail's protocol observers never receive financial signing authority.

We maintain strict separation between market information, financial recommendations, and wallet authorization.

Our wallet-assurance workspace demonstrates approval risks, transaction restrictions, and spending boundaries.

We also explored **World Agent Pass** for human-in-the-loop governance, illustrating how sensitive automated-agent policy exceptions can require additional human verification without treating that verification as permission to spend funds.

### 7. Notable Engineering Decisions

Several implementation details make Northtrail particularly interesting:

- **Exact `bigint` token arithmetic:** Avoids floating-point precision errors in financial calculations.
- **Deterministic cryptographic evidence:** Makes decision records independently checkable and resistant to undetected modification.
- **Decoupled protocol adapters:** Keeps Uniswap and 1inch market observations separate from spending authorization.
- **Pure financial computation:** Allows mathematical logic to be tested without wallets, network requests, or a running frontend.
- **PGlite/PostgreSQL compatibility:** Supports lightweight local development alongside persistent database deployments.
- **Independent SDK consumer:** Demonstrates that Northtrail's core capabilities can be integrated outside our own web interface.
- **Explicit execution-state boundaries:** Distinguishes live observations, illustrative research, simulations, and actual blockchain evidence.

The repository also documents **207 automated tests across 13 test suites**, alongside type checking, linting, build verification, SDK smoke tests, and browser testing.

### 8. Deployment & The Bigger Picture

We deployed the **Next.js frontend on Vercel** and the **Fastify backend on Railway**, creating an accessible demonstration of the platform's research, financial computation, and verification capabilities.

However, **the web application is only the demonstration interface**.

Our core product is the embeddable Northtrail SDK, designed to let DeFi wallet developers integrate financial intelligence and decision-assurance functionality without rebuilding the underlying infrastructure.

We deliberately preserve the distinction between live quote observations, simulated trading strategies, cryptographic record verification, and actual on-chain settlement. This ensures the platform communicates what its evidence genuinely establishes.

**Ultimately, we built Northtrail to connect three capabilities that are often fragmented across DeFi: quantitative intelligence, user-controlled financial authorization, and verifiable decision evidence.**

**Northtrail — Know the choice. Prove the outcome.**

projects.title: Andthen
projects.description: Bridge to Arc and then instantly do anything: pay, hold, lend, leverage or LP.
projects.project_description:
Nobody bridges for fun. You always bridge because you want to do something after: pay someone, get paid, put money in a pool, lend it. Every bridge stops at "funds arrived" and leaves the rest to you.
andthen is one sentence: "Move 10 USDC from Base to Arc, and then pay alex.eth 9 EURC." Every part is a dropdown. You pick the amount, the source chain and what you want to do and our contracts finish the job for you.
What can come after "and then": pay an exact amount in USDC or EURC (we swap through the Uniswap v4 USDC/EURC pool on Arc) convert into EURC or cirBTC add liquidity to the v4 pool, with the position minted to you deposit into a Morpho USDC vault, or loop cirBTC
The main use case is pay links. A merchant asks for 25 EURC on Arc and gets a link. The payer pays from another chain, the merchant gets exactly 25 EURC tagged with the invoice id, and a receipt goes back over CCIP to unlock the invoice on the source chain. Anything left after fees goes back to the payer, and if the action fails everything is refunded.
Everything is on testnet and works end to end: a payment sent from Sepolia settled on Arc in 92 seconds.
projects.how_its_made: CCTP v2 carries both the money and the instruction. The router on Base or Ethereum Sepolia optionally swaps into USDC through Uniswap v4, then burns USDC over CCTP fast transfer with the whole intent packed into the hook data. Once Circle attests, our relayer (or the user’s wallet, if none is running) calls receiveFunds on Arc, and AndThenSettlement mints the USDC and runs the action in that same tx: pay an exact amount in USDC or EURC, swap everything into EURC, LP into the v4 USDC/EURC pool, or deposit into Morpho. It checks the CCTP sender is our router, so only intents our router built can run. Leftovers go back to the payer, and a failed action is refunded. We first had CCIP carry the intent next to the CCTP transfer, and it worked (92 secs end to end from Sepolia), but waiting on two messages slowed the UX. So now CCIP only does what CCTP can’t: it carries the receipt back from Arc so InvoiceBook marks the pay link paid on Base, paid for from the order’s leftover USDC. CCIP fees on Arc can’t be paid with the USDC ERC20, only native value, and native USDC there has 18 decimals. USDC from chains without a CCIP lane to Arc (Arbitrum, Optimism, Avalanche, Unichain and more) and non-USDC assets (EURC, WETH, cirBTC) go through Circle Bridge Kit, and the “and then” runs from the user’s wallet on Arc. Arc’s Memo contract rejects contract callers, so the settlement contract emits its own Settled event with the invoice id. Arc Studio audited the contracts (3 high, 6 medium, 6 low; every high and medium fixed with a regression test). Contracts are Foundry, 34 tests against a real v4 PoolManager. Frontend is Next.js + wagmi + viem, with live numbers from Circle App Kit and Uniswap v4’s Quoter and StateView.

projects.title: Moonglade
projects.description: The 1inch Aqua AMM for Morpho Midnight: lend, borrow, or exit fixed-rate loans in one swap.
projects.project_description: Moonglade makes fixed-rate credit tradable through swaps. Built on 1inch Aqua, SwapVM, and Morpho Midnight, it lets users lend, borrow against collateral, and exit lending positions through the same AMM interface. Morpho Midnight provides fixed-rate, fixed-term loans through an order book. Trading depends on finding an offer at the right size and rate. Lenders may struggle to exit before maturity, borrowers may wait for offers to fill, and makers need infrastructure to keep orders updated. Moonglade adds an AMM alongside that order book, giving users executable quotes from maker-run bond desks. The core asset is mgNOTE, an ERC-20 share of a Midnight market’s net credit. Each market has its own note contract. This turns a credit position into something users can hold, transfer, and trade through standard token interfaces. Users have four main actions: Lend: Swap the market’s loan asset for mgNOTE. The purchase price determines the return available from holding the credit to maturity, assuming repayment. Missing note inventory is created during settlement. Borrow: Supply collateral to your own Midnight position and approve a bounded borrowing allowance. A swap then mints the necessary note shortfall and sells it for the loan asset. The resulting debt belongs to your account, backed by your collateral. Exit early: Sell existing mgNOTE back to a desk while it is trading and has available liquidity. You receive the current market quote, allowing you to exit without waiting for maturity. The exit price can differ from your entry price. Redeem: After maturity, burn mgNOTE for its proportional share of repaid Midnight credit as repayments become available. Makers operate these desks from their own wallets. Aqua lets multiple strategies share the same wallet balances, so idle capital does not need to be deposited into separate liquidity pools. Makers select a pricing curve, set their trading fee, and configure debt and collateral limits. Moonglade’s settlement hooks create inventory only when a trade needs it. When a lender buys notes, the desk can originate Midnight credit to supply them. When notes flow back, the desk can retain them as inventory or burn them to cancel maker debt and release surplus collateral. The default YieldSpace curve prices remaining maturity and inventory imbalance. Trading changes the quoted rate, encouraging offsetting flow between lenders and borrowers. Makers earn fees in both directions, while their exposure depends on the balance of that flow. Wrapping and unwrapping Midnight offers also lets arbitrageurs trade price differences between desks and the order book. The protocol is designed around Midnight markets rather than one specific asset pair. The current Base mainnet deployment demonstrates a USDC desk with WETH collateral. Real lending, borrowing, and early-exit transactions have completed on mainnet; separate fork demonstrations cover maturity redemption and shared liquidity across strategies.
projects.how_its_made: I built Moonglade in Solidity with Foundry, combining Morpho Midnight’s fixed-rate credit markets with 1inch Aqua’s shared wallet liquidity and a custom SwapVM router. The tokenization layer is mgNOTE, an ERC-20 share of a Midnight market’s net credit. A factory deploys one note per market, while a shared ratifier authorizes only the note’s active settlement offer. Notes can also wrap and unwrap Midnight order-book offers, connecting the AMM to the existing credit market. On SwapVM, I added a custom MoongladeSwap opcode (0xd0). It queries a maker-selected pricing contract, snaps the quote to Midnight’s tick grid with directional rounding, and validates the final amounts. The default YieldSpace curve prices remaining maturity and inventory imbalance, with maker-configurable fees embedded in both bid and ask prices. Aqua makes the desk capital-efficient: makers register virtual budgets while idle funds remain in their wallets, available across strategies. The unusual part is inventory creation during settlement. preTransferOut mints missing maker inventory; preTransferIn mints a borrower’s note shortfall under a bounded, expiring approval. Borrowing becomes a note sale that opens a real Midnight loan on the borrower’s own collateral. After incoming notes settle, postTransferIn can burn them to cancel maker debt and release surplus collateral. One practical hack was handling incompatible compiler pins: Midnight requires Solidity 0.8.34, while SwapVM pins 0.8.30. I compiled separate dependency graphs and used vm.getCode with assembly CREATE to deploy their artifacts from one Foundry script. The frontend is client-only React, TypeScript, and Vite, using RainbowKit, wagmi, and viem for wallets, live quotes, simulations, and transactions, hosted on Vercel. The protocol runs on Base against the official Aqua and Midnight deployments. Lending, borrowing, and early exits have executed with real mainnet funds; fork scripts demonstrate the wider lifecycle, including maturity redemption and shared liquidity.
