projects.title: AnonAI
projects.description: Private keystorage, permission, and gas sponsorship for autonomous AI agents via EIP-8141 altmempool
projects.project_description: Ethereum was built around the larger vision of self-sovereignty - we should retain control over our identities, assets, and actions without depending on centralised 'trusted' intermediaries. But as autonomous AI agents begin acting on behalf of users, a new question emerges: Can we delegate our ability to act without also giving up our privacy and sovereignty? Today, an agent acting on Ethereum often acquires a persistent, publicly observable on-chain identity. Its transactions can reveal what it does, which contracts it interacts with, and potentially who operates it. Delegated signing and smart wallets may restrict what an agent can do, but they do not inherently prevent its activities from being traced. Meanwhile, more sophisticated privacy-preserving authorization mechanisms can exceed the validation limits of Ethereum's canonical mempool, pushing developers toward specialized transaction infrastructure. AnonAI enables autonomous AI agents to transact on Ethereum without exposing individual on-chain identities, while allowing their owners to retain cryptographically enforced control over what they can do. AnonAI combines privacy-preserving keystorage and authorization using Semaphore zero-knowledge proofs, anonymous execution through a shared smart account, and programmable gas sponsorship through a paymaster. Built on EIP-8141 frame transactions and the public ERC-8421 alternative mempool, it also integrates Anon-RPC to extend privacy to browser-based blockchain reads. Instead of assigning each agent a publicly identifiable wallet, AnonAI allows multiple agents belonging to different owners to transact through a shared smart account. Each agent proves its authorization anonymously using a Semaphore zero-knowledge proof, while on-chain policies enforce exactly which contracts it can interact with, how much it can spend, and how frequently it can act. Owners can revoke these permissions at any time, without requiring the agent to hold their private keys. Gas is sponsored through shared policy-class budgets, removing the need to fund individual agent wallets with ETH. Transactions are propagated through a public alternative mempool rather than a proprietary private relay, allowing privacy-preserving authorization to coexist with open, permissionless transaction infrastructure. For agents, this means the freedom to act autonomously without a conventional Ethereum signing key, an ETH balance, or a unique on-chain identity that links their actions together. For owners, it means delegating authority without surrendering control or unnecessarily exposing their identity and activity. The current architecture of AnonAI provides anonymous authorization within shared policy groups but that imposes a limitation on accessing privacy for complex and highly customised policies. Our next step is to decouple identity anonymity from policy uniformity, allowing agents with individually programmable permissions to prove compliance in zero knowledge without fragmenting their anonymity sets. We believe autonomous agents should inherit Ethereum's guarantees of self-sovereignty, not become an exception to them. AnonAI is an open-source effort to make privacy-preserving, permissionless agent execution a native part of Ethereum's emerging account abstraction infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made: AnonAI is built on EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool , with Solidity smart contracts, Semaphore v4 zero-knowledge proofs, TypeScript, viem, an MCP integration for Claude, and Anon-RPC. The core engineering challenge was to separate an agent's identity, authorization, execution, and gas payment without losing the ability to enforce permissions on-chain. Three main contracts - Keystore, SharedAccount, and BudgetPaymaster - connected through a four-frame transaction that handles authorization, payment, and execution atomically. -- 1. Keystore: anonymous authorization and revocable permissions On-chain Keystore using Semaphore v4 and Poseidon-based incremental Merkle trees (LeanIMT). Agents are registered under shared policy classes, where each class defines a specific set of permissions: the allowed contract address, function selector, maximum ETH value, and maximum token transfer amount. Each agent has a private Semaphore identity secret, while only its cryptographic commitment is inserted into the Keystore's Merkle tree. Multiple agents belonging to different owners can register under the same policy class. When an agent wants to transact, it generates a Groth16 zero-knowledge membership proof locally. The proof demonstrates that it belongs to an authorized group without revealing which registered member it is. Crucially, the proof is bound to the exact action being requested — including the target contract, calldata, chain ID, shared account, and policy class. This prevents a valid authorization from being reused for an unrelated transaction. Demo currently uses depth-10 Semaphore proofs, supporting up to 1,024 members per policy class. One interesting design decision was how rate limit and replay protection were implemented. Instead of building a separate on-chain nullifier registry, used the Semaphore nullifier directly as an EIP-8250 keyed nonce , with the nonce sequence set to zero. Each committed Keystore root defines an authorization epoch. An agent can act once within that epoch, and the protocol's nonce mechanism prevents the same authorization from being used again. The Keystore also supports revocation. Removing an agent's commitment increments the policy class's generation, invalidating previously committed roots for authorization purposes. Additionally integrated EIP-8272 recent-root references to help the mempool track root freshness. This enables anonymous membership proofs, single-use authorization, rate limiting, and revocation without revealing the agent's identity during execution. -- 2. SharedAccount: executing without individual agent wallets All agents transact through a common SharedAccount smart contract, which acts as the sender of EIP-8141 frame transactions. The account's validation logic supports two authorization modes: Zero-knowledge mode: A Semaphore Groth16 proof establishes anonymous membership in a policy class. The transaction uses EIP-8141's arbitrary signature scheme rather than a conventional Ethereum signing key. One-time-key mode: Each agent uses a registered, single-use secp256k1 key. This is computationally cheaper but sacrifices the anonymity provided by Semaphore membership proofs. The agent registers a batch of one-time key addresses as class members. Each key is derived from the agent secret and used once. In both modes, SharedAccount checks the actual execution frame against the policy: permitted contract, function selector, ETH value, token amount, and the transaction's nonce. Only after these checks succeed does the account approve execution. The important distinction is that authorization is enforced by the smart contract rather than by instructions to the AI model . An agent cannot bypass its spending limits simply by deciding to perform a different action. -- 3. BudgetPaymaster: programmable gas sponsorship Stateful paymaster that sponsors gas from budgets assigned to shared policy classes rather than individual agents or owners. This means the agent doesn't need to maintain an ETH balance, and gas payment doesn't require revealing a unique owner-associated wallet in each transaction. The paymaster reserves the maximum transaction cost from the relevant class budget before approving payment. Solved an interesting issue with frame coordination on the devnet: the expected FRAMEPARAM status inspection was not working, and transient storage wasn't persisting between frames. Workaround was to create a persistent charge receipt keyed by TXPARAM(SIG_HASH) . The paymaster's payment-verification frame checks that the same transaction has already successfully charged its budget before approving payment. Stateful, policy-based gas sponsorship within the frame transaction model. -- 4. EIP-8141: combining everything in one transaction The entire AnonAI execution flow fits into a single four-frame transaction: Frame 0 — Authorization (VERIFY): SharedAccount verifies the Semaphore proof or one-time signature, checks the Keystore and the requested action against its permissions, and approves execution. Frame 1 — Gas reservation (pre_verify): BudgetPaymaster checks the policy-class gas budget, reserves the maximum transaction cost, and records a charge receipt. Frame 2 — Payment approval (VERIFY): BudgetPaymaster verifies the charge receipt and approves gas payment. Frame 3 — Execution (SENDER): The authorized transaction executes from the shared account, such as transferring WETH to a recipient. This is where EIP-8141 becomes particularly useful: authorization, gas sponsorship, and execution can be programmed independently while remaining part of one atomic transaction. The agent never needs to sign a conventional Ethereum transaction from its own wallet or fund an individual address with ETH. -- 5. ERC-8421: why the alternative mempool is essential Zero-knowledge authorization consumes approximately 296,823 validation gas , well above the canonical EIP-8141 mempool's 100,000-gas validation limit. The SharedAccount also needs to read external Keystore and verifier state, while BudgetPaymaster needs to read and update shared budget storage during validation. These patterns are restricted under canonical mempool rules. Integrated with the public ERC-8421 workshop alternative mempool , running through its gateway and miner sidecars and the ethrex execution client. The alternative mempool supports more expressive validation under staking, reputation, and resource-accounting rules designed to protect nodes against denial-of-service attacks. Deployed and staked both SharedAccount and BudgetPaymaster, and built the TypeScript transaction builder around the workshop's @forshtat/hegota-support package. Transactions are submitted using eth_sendFrameTransaction , simulated by the sidecar, evaluated against its admission rules, and propagated for block inclusion. A direct comparison with the canonical mempool is implemented: the same ZK-authorized frame transaction is rejected by the canonical mempool but admitted and mined through the alternative mempool. This is a central demonstrations. ERC-8421 isn't simply an alternative transaction submission endpoint for AnonAI — it enables the computationally expensive cryptographic authorization and stateful paymaster logic that the canonical mempool cannot accommodate. -- 6. Anon-RPC: extending privacy to blockchain reads Anonymous authorization alone doesn't eliminate every source of privacy leakage. RPC providers can still observe which addresses, balances, contracts, and transactions a user is querying. Integrated @anon-rpc/browser-harness into frontend to add a separate privacy layer for blockchain reads. The browser harness uses an isolated, null-origin iframe and Web Worker, with support for Tor, Nym, and passthrough transports. When enabled and ready, dashboard RPC requests are routed through this environment instead of being sent directly from the user's ordinary browser connection. This complements Semaphore's on-chain anonymity by addressing network-level observability during blockchain reads. The current integration covers the browser dashboard; the Node-based MCP server and runner still use direct RPC connections. The browser also falls back to direct requests if the privacy transport is unavailable. -- 7. MCP integration: giving Claude autonomous execution capabilities Local Model Context Protocol server using the TypeScript MCP SDK, allowing Claude to interact with AnonAI directly. The server exposes tools for inspecting the agent's permissions, reading blockchain state, performing authorized WETH transfers, checking transaction status, and comparing canonical versus alternative mempool behavior. When Claude requests a transaction, the local runtime retrieves the agent's authorization credential, constructs the required proof, assembles the four-frame transaction, submits it to the alternative mempool, and returns the on-chain result. The private Semaphore credential stays with the local runtime rather than being passed to the AI model. This provides a working demonstration of an autonomous agent performing blockchain actions under cryptographically enforced permissions without holding a conventional Ethereum signing key or ETH for gas. -- 8. Dashboard, testing, and engineering challenges React/Vite dashboard with a local HTTP and Server-Sent Events runner to visualize the full transaction lifecycle: agent request, authorization, frame construction, mempool admission, mining, and execution. projects.project_description_markdown:
## Ethereum was built around the larger vision of self-sovereignty - we should retain control over our identities, assets, and actions without depending on centralised 'trusted' intermediaries.

But as autonomous AI agents begin acting on behalf of users, a new question emerges: **Can we delegate our ability to act without also giving up our privacy and sovereignty?**

---
---

Today, an agent acting on Ethereum often acquires a persistent, publicly observable on-chain identity. Its transactions can reveal what it does, which contracts it interacts with, and potentially who operates it. Delegated signing and smart wallets may restrict what an agent can do, but they do not inherently prevent its activities from being traced. Meanwhile, more sophisticated privacy-preserving authorization mechanisms can exceed the validation limits of Ethereum's canonical mempool, pushing developers toward specialized transaction infrastructure.

AnonAI enables autonomous AI agents to transact on Ethereum without exposing individual on-chain identities, while allowing their owners to retain cryptographically enforced control over what they can do.

AnonAI combines privacy-preserving keystorage and authorization using Semaphore zero-knowledge proofs, anonymous execution through a shared smart account, and programmable gas sponsorship through a paymaster. Built on EIP-8141 frame transactions and the public ERC-8421 alternative mempool, it also integrates Anon-RPC to extend privacy to browser-based blockchain reads.

Instead of assigning each agent a publicly identifiable wallet, **AnonAI allows multiple agents belonging to different owners to transact through a shared smart account.** Each agent proves its authorization anonymously using a Semaphore zero-knowledge proof, while on-chain policies enforce exactly which contracts it can interact with, how much it can spend, and how frequently it can act. Owners can revoke these permissions at any time, without requiring the agent to hold their private keys.

Gas is sponsored through shared policy-class budgets, removing the need to fund individual agent wallets with ETH. Transactions are propagated through a public alternative mempool rather than a proprietary private relay, allowing privacy-preserving authorization to coexist with open, permissionless transaction infrastructure.

***

**For agents, this means the freedom to act autonomously without a conventional Ethereum signing key, an ETH balance, or a unique on-chain identity that links their actions together. For owners, it means delegating authority without surrendering control or unnecessarily exposing their identity and activity.**

The current architecture of AnonAI provides anonymous authorization within shared policy groups but that imposes a limitation on accessing privacy for complex and highly customised policies. Our next step is to decouple identity anonymity from policy uniformity, allowing agents with individually programmable permissions to prove compliance in zero knowledge without fragmenting their anonymity sets.

**We believe autonomous agents should inherit Ethereum's guarantees of self-sovereignty, not become an exception to them. AnonAI is an open-source effort to make privacy-preserving, permissionless agent execution a native part of Ethereum's emerging account abstraction infrastructure.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
AnonAI is built on **EIP-8141 frame transactions and the ERC-8421 alternative mempool**, with Solidity smart contracts, Semaphore v4 zero-knowledge proofs, TypeScript, viem, an MCP integration for Claude, and Anon-RPC.

The core engineering challenge was to separate an agent's identity, authorization, execution, and gas payment without losing the ability to enforce permissions on-chain. 

Three main contracts - **Keystore, SharedAccount, and BudgetPaymaster** - connected through a four-frame transaction that handles authorization, payment, and execution atomically.


--
--


**1. Keystore: anonymous authorization and revocable permissions**

- On-chain Keystore using Semaphore v4 and Poseidon-based incremental Merkle trees (LeanIMT).

- Agents are registered under shared policy classes, where each class defines a specific set of permissions: the allowed contract address, function selector, maximum ETH value, and maximum token transfer amount.

- Each agent has a private Semaphore identity secret, while only its cryptographic commitment is inserted into the Keystore's Merkle tree. Multiple agents belonging to different owners can register under the same policy class.

- When an agent wants to transact, it generates a Groth16 zero-knowledge membership proof locally. The proof demonstrates that it belongs to an authorized group without revealing which registered member it is.

- Crucially, the proof is bound to the exact action being requested — including the target contract, calldata, chain ID, shared account, and policy class. This prevents a valid authorization from being reused for an unrelated transaction.

- Demo currently uses depth-10 Semaphore proofs, supporting up to 1,024 members per policy class.

- **One interesting design decision was how rate limit and replay protection were implemented.**

- Instead of building a separate on-chain nullifier registry, used the Semaphore nullifier directly as an **EIP-8250 keyed nonce**, with the nonce sequence set to zero.

- Each committed Keystore root defines an authorization epoch. An agent can act once within that epoch, and the protocol's nonce mechanism prevents the same authorization from being used again.

- The Keystore also supports revocation. Removing an agent's commitment increments the policy class's generation, invalidating previously committed roots for authorization purposes. Additionally integrated **EIP-8272 recent-root references** to help the mempool track root freshness.

- This enables anonymous membership proofs, single-use authorization, rate limiting, and revocation without revealing the agent's identity during execution.


--
--

 
**2. SharedAccount: executing without individual agent wallets**

All agents transact through a common `SharedAccount` smart contract, which acts as the sender of EIP-8141 frame transactions.

The account's validation logic supports two authorization modes:

- **Zero-knowledge mode:** A Semaphore Groth16 proof establishes anonymous membership in a policy class. The transaction uses EIP-8141's arbitrary signature scheme rather than a conventional Ethereum signing key.
- **One-time-key mode:** Each agent uses a registered, single-use secp256k1 key. This is computationally cheaper but sacrifices the anonymity provided by Semaphore membership proofs. The agent registers a batch of one-time key addresses as class members. Each key is derived from the agent secret and used once.

In both modes, SharedAccount checks the actual execution frame against the policy: permitted contract, function selector, ETH value, token amount, and the transaction's nonce.

Only after these checks succeed does the account approve execution.

The important distinction is that **authorization is enforced by the smart contract rather than by instructions to the AI model**. An agent cannot bypass its spending limits simply by deciding to perform a different action.

--
--


**3. BudgetPaymaster: programmable gas sponsorship**

- Stateful paymaster that sponsors gas from budgets assigned to shared policy classes rather than individual agents or owners.

- This means the agent doesn't need to maintain an ETH balance, and gas payment doesn't require revealing a unique owner-associated wallet in each transaction.

- The paymaster reserves the maximum transaction cost from the relevant class budget before approving payment.

- Solved an interesting issue with frame coordination on the devnet: the expected `FRAMEPARAM` status inspection was not working, and transient storage wasn't persisting between frames.

- Workaround was to create a persistent charge receipt keyed by `TXPARAM(SIG_HASH)`. The paymaster's payment-verification frame checks that the same transaction has already successfully charged its budget before approving payment.

- Stateful, policy-based gas sponsorship within the frame transaction model.

--
--


**4. EIP-8141: combining everything in one transaction**

The entire AnonAI execution flow fits into a single four-frame transaction:

- **Frame 0 — Authorization (VERIFY):** SharedAccount verifies the Semaphore proof or one-time signature, checks the Keystore and the requested action against its permissions, and approves execution.

- **Frame 1 — Gas reservation (pre_verify):** BudgetPaymaster checks the policy-class gas budget, reserves the maximum transaction cost, and records a charge receipt.

- **Frame 2 — Payment approval (VERIFY):** BudgetPaymaster verifies the charge receipt and approves gas payment.

- **Frame 3 — Execution (SENDER):** The authorized transaction executes from the shared account, such as transferring WETH to a recipient.

This is where EIP-8141 becomes particularly useful: authorization, gas sponsorship, and execution can be programmed independently while remaining part of one atomic transaction.

The agent never needs to sign a conventional Ethereum transaction from its own wallet or fund an individual address with ETH.


--
--


**5. ERC-8421: why the alternative mempool is essential**

Zero-knowledge authorization consumes approximately **296,823 validation gas**, well above the canonical EIP-8141 mempool's 100,000-gas validation limit.

The SharedAccount also needs to read external Keystore and verifier state, while BudgetPaymaster needs to read and update shared budget storage during validation. These patterns are restricted under canonical mempool rules.

Integrated with the public **ERC-8421 workshop alternative mempool**, running through its gateway and miner sidecars and the ethrex execution client.

The alternative mempool supports more expressive validation under staking, reputation, and resource-accounting rules designed to protect nodes against denial-of-service attacks.

Deployed and staked both SharedAccount and BudgetPaymaster, and built the TypeScript transaction builder around the workshop's `@forshtat/hegota-support` package.

Transactions are submitted using `eth_sendFrameTransaction`, simulated by the sidecar, evaluated against its admission rules, and propagated for block inclusion.

A direct comparison with the canonical mempool is implemented: **the same ZK-authorized frame transaction is rejected by the canonical mempool but admitted and mined through the alternative mempool.**

This is a central demonstrations. ERC-8421 isn't simply an alternative transaction submission endpoint for AnonAI — it enables the computationally expensive cryptographic authorization and stateful paymaster logic that the canonical mempool cannot accommodate.


--
--


**6. Anon-RPC: extending privacy to blockchain reads**

- Anonymous authorization alone doesn't eliminate every source of privacy leakage. RPC providers can still observe which addresses, balances, contracts, and transactions a user is querying.

- Integrated **`@anon-rpc/browser-harness`** into frontend to add a separate privacy layer for blockchain reads.

- The browser harness uses an isolated, null-origin iframe and Web Worker, with support for Tor, Nym, and passthrough transports. When enabled and ready, dashboard RPC requests are routed through this environment instead of being sent directly from the user's ordinary browser connection.

- This complements Semaphore's on-chain anonymity by addressing network-level observability during blockchain reads.

- The current integration covers the browser dashboard; the Node-based MCP server and runner still use direct RPC connections. The browser also falls back to direct requests if the privacy transport is unavailable.

--
--


**7. MCP integration: giving Claude autonomous execution capabilities**

- Local **Model Context Protocol server** using the TypeScript MCP SDK, allowing Claude to interact with AnonAI directly.

- The server exposes tools for inspecting the agent's permissions, reading blockchain state, performing authorized WETH transfers, checking transaction status, and comparing canonical versus alternative mempool behavior.

- When Claude requests a transaction, the local runtime retrieves the agent's authorization credential, constructs the required proof, assembles the four-frame transaction, submits it to the alternative mempool, and returns the on-chain result.

- The private Semaphore credential stays with the local runtime rather than being passed to the AI model.

- This provides a working demonstration of an autonomous agent performing blockchain actions under cryptographically enforced permissions without holding a conventional Ethereum signing key or ETH for gas.


--
--


**8. Dashboard, testing, and engineering challenges**

React/Vite dashboard with a local HTTP and Server-Sent Events runner to visualize the full transaction lifecycle: agent request, authorization, frame construction, mempool admission, mining, and execution.

The dashboard also exposes the distinction between public and private information, compares ZK authorization with one-time-key authorization, and demonstrates permission revocation and canonical mempool rejection.

The development process involved several protocol-specific challenges:

- **Real ZK verification:** integrated Semaphore's Groth16 verifier into the SharedAccount's validation frame rather than simulating authorization.
- **Protocol-native replay protection:** mapped Semaphore nullifiers to EIP-8250 keyed nonces, avoiding separate spent-nullifier storage.
- **Cross-frame payment coordination:** implemented transaction-bound charge receipts to work around missing frame-status functionality in the development client.
- **Mempool propagation:** After observing unreliable gossip between gateway and miner sidecars following restarts, we added direct submission of identical transaction bytes to both public sidecars.
- **Gas and validation constraints:** measured approximately 296,823 gas for ZK verification, 53,591 for one-time-key authorization, 42,127 for gas reservation, and 27,437 for payment approval.

**Foundry** + Solidity development and testing, including tests that generate actual Semaphore proofs through FFI. The repository includes 31 Solidity tests, deployed contract artifacts, setup scripts, CLI tools, an MCP server, and the interactive frontend.

The implementation is running on the public ERC-8421 workshop devnet (chain ID 1337), where both authorization modes have been demonstrated end-to-end.


--
--

**Ultimately, AnonAI demonstrates how Ethereum's emerging native account abstraction and alternative mempool infrastructure can support anonymous authorization, programmable keystorage, revocable agent permissions, and gas-sponsored execution without depending on a proprietary private relay.**

projects.title: Dabbawala Protocol
projects.description: Infrastructure for autonomous robot fleets with scoped identities, auditable decisions and payments.
projects.project_description: Dabbawala Protocol is a bounded-authority coordination and operating layer for autonomous delivery agents and robot fleets. Instead of allowing an AI model to directly control a robot or spend funds, it separates identity, decision-making and execution authority. The architecture gives each robot its own ENSv2 identity and permissioned resolver, holding machine-readable mission context such as permitted zones, spending limits, operational status and its latest episode reference. ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control defines who can modify each record: operators manage mission policies, safety officers can update operational status, and each robot can publish only its own episode reference. At mission decision checkpoints, 0G Compute provides a proposed action. A separate Policy Gate evaluates that proposal against the robot's permissions and mission constraints before the action can be applied. The model's output is never treated as authorization. Invalid responses or unavailable inference trigger a safe-stop rather than an unsafe fallback. The prototype is designed to maintain an auditable, replayable trail connecting inference request IDs, model proposals, policy verdicts and simulation events, with 0G Storage supporting episode evidence. The architecture also incorporates Hedera x402 for programmatic payments, allowing approved agent-to-service transactions to follow explicit spending and authorization rules. Dabbawala Protocol explores how autonomous fleets can operate safely in a multi-agent economy: with verifiable identities, narrowly scoped permissions, accountable decisions and controlled payments. The current demonstration is simulation-based and does not claim physical robot execution.
projects.how_its_made: Dabbawala Protocol is built using a combination of blockchain infrastructure, smart contracts, AI inference and backend services. We wanted to make sure that AI agents could make decisions and coordinate missions without giving them unrestricted control over robots or funds. For agent identity and permissions, we're integrating ENSv2. Each robot gets its own ENS identity and Permissioned Resolver, with Enhanced Access Control (EAC) allowing us to scope permissions to specific text records. This means the operator, safety officer and individual robots can have different levels of authority instead of everyone having access to everything. For the AI decision layer, we use 0G Compute to generate proposed actions at mission checkpoints. The important part is that the model never directly executes anything. Its output goes through our Policy Gate, which checks it against the robot's permissions, mission constraints and operational state before allowing the action to proceed. If inference fails or the response is invalid, the system fails closed and triggers a safe-stop. We're also using 0G Storage to maintain mission episode evidence, connecting inference request IDs, proposed actions, policy decisions and simulation events into a replayable trail. Hedera x402 is part of the payment layer, enabling agents to make programmatic payments while keeping spending within predefined limits. The backend is built around modular adapters so that individual infrastructure providers can be integrated without coupling the entire system to one service. We also built a simulation and replay workflow to test scenarios like restricted-zone access, stale telemetry and inference unavailability without needing physical hardware. One of the interesting engineering decisions was separating what an AI model suggests from what the system is actually allowed to execute . We treat AI as a decision proposer, not an authority. ENSv2 handles identity and permissions, 0G handles inference and evidence, and the Policy Gate remains the final enforcement layer. That's essentially the core idea behind Dabbawala Protocol.

projects.title: deWo
projects.description: An agent marketplace where robots earn payments through independently verified work.
projects.project_description:
Dewo is a marketplace where AI agents hire other agents and pay for independently verified work. Its first use case is simulated robot navigation: a Requester posts a Mission and funds a bounty, while Workers submit sealed Bids committed to a specific AI Policy.
The winning Worker receives a hidden Course Seed and pilots a rover toward its goal. Independent Verifiers replay the Episode, check its Decisions, and determine whether the Worker completed the Mission within its Step Budget without collisions. Two matching Verifier signatures authorize settlement. Successful Workers earn payment; failed attempts lose their Bid Stake.
Dewo combines sealed bidding, verifiable execution, and programmable payments to make agent collaboration accountable. Reliability reflects verified Outcomes, while XP and Levels provide a separate leaderboard.
projects.how_its_made:
Dewo’s architecture separates simulation, agent execution, verification, and settlement. The planned simulation layer uses Python and MuJoCo to generate seeded Courses and replay robot Actions deterministically. Worker Policies define the model, prompt, and memory used for each Decision.
The integration design uses 0G Compute for model inference, 0G Storage for Episode Logs and Policies, and an EpisodeRegistry contract on 0G Galileo to record submissions. Arkiv provides the Mission Board, encrypted Bids, Seed Releases, and Verdict history. Verifiers are designed to sell Replay services through x402 payments on Hedera.
The implemented contract module uses Solidity and Foundry. MissionEscrow verifies two distinct EIP-712 signatures for Awards and Verdicts, collects the signed Bid Stake, handles Outcome-specific payouts, and provides deadline-based rescue refunds. EpisodeRegistry preserves the first submission for each Mission and Worker. The local suite contains 46 passing tests covering signatures, payouts, deadlines, rescue, and fund isolation.

projects.title: Invoice Agent
projects.description: Invoice financing paid by an AI agent inside on-chain limits a verified human controls.
projects.project_description:
Invoice Agent is invoice financing where the payer is an AI agent that can only act within rules a human controls. THE PROBLEM
Small suppliers wait 30 to 90 days to be paid. Investors who would fund them cannot tell whether the buyer will pay. And when the buyer is an AI agent spending on someone's behalf, nobody can see what limits it runs under. WHAT IT DOES A supplier lists an unpaid invoice. The buyer agent reviews it and accepts it. An invoice cannot be funded until the buyer's vault accepts it, so nobody can invent a debt for a vault. An investor funds it at a discount and receives a bond token on Hedera. On the due date the agent pays from its vault. The vault enforces a daily limit, a supplier allowlist and an approval threshold. Above the threshold, a World-verified human sponsor must approve. If the sponsor denies, cancels or lets it expire, nothing is paid. The agent has an ENS name that publishes its limits and payment record. Investors, and their own agents, read it before funding. An investor agent pays an x402 fee on Hedera to get a risk score. Every step is written to a Hedera Consensus Service audit log with HashScan links. WHY IT IS DIFFERENT
On-chain invoice projects usually assume a human debtor who clicks approve. We assume the payer is an agent, and we make its rules readable (ENS), enforceable (vault) and overridable only by a verified human (World). This is a testnet prototype, not financial advice.
projects.how_its_made: HEDERA (x402 and Tokenize). Solidity contracts built with Foundry on the Hedera EVM testnet: InvoiceMarket (listing, buyer acceptance, funding at a discount, payment, late and default states) and BuyerVault (daily limit, supplier allowlist, EIP-712 sponsor approvals above a threshold, a sponsor pause switch). Funded invoices are issued as bond tokens with Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio. The investor agent pays an x402-protected risk-score endpoint settled on Hedera, under a budget, a per-merchant cap and an allowlist, with no human approving. A Hedera Consensus Service topic logs each lifecycle event, the due-date payment uses a Scheduled Transaction, and settled transaction IDs link to HashScan. WORLD. The approval service starts a World ID Agent Pass step-up authentication for the sponsor when a payment is above the threshold. The approval is bound to the exact payment (invoice, payee, amount, expiry), single use, and validated on our backend. Denied, expired and cancelled paths are tested and the payment never executes. ENS. Each buyer agent is an ENSv2 name on Sepolia. Its limits, allowlist and payment record are published by a publisher wallet with a scoped role, and the app and the investor agent read them live, with no hard-coded values. AGENTS. A buyer agent and an investor agent built on the Claude API. The model only returns approve, review or reject plus a reason; deterministic guardrails make the final decision, and invoice text is treated as untrusted data. APP. TypeScript backend with Postgres and an indexer, Next.js and Tailwind frontend. TESTING. Foundry unit, fuzz and invariant tests, an attack suite (replayed approvals, wrong payee, over-limit, hostile invoice text), and end-to-end scripts that run the full lifecycle on testnet. A hidden demo-controls page advances time so the due-date payment can be shown in one take.

projects.title: Kanyarasi
projects.description: Non-custodial USDT payments SaaS on Whitechain: payment links, invoices, subscriptions, refunds.
projects.how_its_made:
Contracts: Solidity, built and unit-tested with Hardhat. They cover the core WhitePay contract (payments, subscriptions, refunds and operator limits), an agent contract with spending policies, a metered-billing contract and a payout splitter. 64 contract tests run in memory, because they cover 30-day timers that can’t be waited out on a live chain.
Backend: Node.js with Express and SQLite.
Prices are signed as EIP-712 quotes. Gasless payments use EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization, submitted by a relayer.
An indexer reads contract events into the ledger. A keeper charges due subscriptions. Webhooks are signed with HMAC.
Passwords use scrypt. Sessions are opaque tokens kept in an httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie. Optional TOTP two-factor.
Frontend: Next.js 16 with TypeScript and the App Router. One app serves the marketing site, the business console, the operator console and the customer checkout pages. Browser code never sees a credential: it calls a /bff proxy that attaches the session cookie and checks the request origin. Wallet actions (register, refund, plans) are signed in the browser with ethers and the user’s own wallet.
Whitechain: the contracts are deployed on the testnet. The app uses its RPC and block explorer, and WBT pays for gas.
Testing: about 400 end-to-end checks run against the live testnet. Block finality takes 8–37 minutes there, so the tests use a faster “seen” confirmation policy. They also use short contract timers and throw-away funded wallets. Hacky bits worth mentioning: An off-chain test clock lets the tests fast-forward quote and billing logic that is computed on the server. It is disabled on mainnet.
Email confirmation is off by default for easy hackathon testing. A flag turns it on, and invites return a copy-able link instead of needing email.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Contracts: Solidity, built and unit-tested with Hardhat. They cover the core WhitePay contract (payments, subscriptions, refunds and operator limits), an agent contract with spending policies, a metered-billing contract and a payout splitter. 64 contract tests run in memory, because they cover 30-day timers that can’t be waited out on a live chain.
Backend: Node.js with Express and SQLite.
Prices are signed as EIP-712 quotes. Gasless payments use EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization, submitted by a relayer.
An indexer reads contract events into the ledger. A keeper charges due subscriptions. Webhooks are signed with HMAC.
Passwords use scrypt. Sessions are opaque tokens kept in an httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie. Optional TOTP two-factor.
Frontend: Next.js 16 with TypeScript and the App Router. One app serves the marketing site, the business console, the operator console and the customer checkout pages. Browser code never sees a credential: it calls a /bff proxy that attaches the session cookie and checks the request origin. Wallet actions (register, refund, plans) are signed in the browser with ethers and the user’s own wallet.
Whitechain: the contracts are deployed on the testnet. The app uses its RPC and block explorer, and WBT pays for gas.
Testing: about 400 end-to-end checks run against the live testnet. Block finality takes 8–37 minutes there, so the tests use a faster “seen” confirmation policy. They also use short contract timers and throw-away funded wallets.

projects.title: SupaBrain
projects.description: Stops prompt injection between AI agents: each AI gets ENS rules, every handoff is signed on Arkiv.

Its rules are public ENS text records: where it may write (sb.scope), paths it may never touch (sb.deny), which attack types it may never pass on (sb.guard), a daily write limit, and an on/off switch. Each AI's newest commit is published on ENS (sb.memory.head), like a git branch. Every call is checked. Content that tries to steer the next AI (instruction override, remote code, payment redirect, secret leak, rule tampering, AI-to-AI commands) is stopped: saved as evidence, revoked on Arkiv, and never delivered to another AI. Detection can miss, so the ENS rules are the guarantee: even if the wording slips through, the write outside the AI's scope is still refused. We provisioned 10 brains, each its own ENSv2 UserRegistry under supabrain.eth, with 30 AI names. Roles are fixed at registration: the server's team key may only set text records (no transfer, no re-pointing), each AI's wallet may only set its own sb.memory.head, and the owner key stays offline. Wallets are derived per brain and per AI from one mnemonic, so 30 wallets came from one secret, and we measured write costs from real receipts. projects.title: ASM-Endersift
projects.description: An AI agent that finds data sellers via ENS, pays them on Hedera and analyses the results on 0G.
projects.project_description: Endersift is an autonomous threat-intelligence agent that buys the data it needs from other agents, pays for each request on its own, and keeps a public record of every payment. You give it a task, for example "check OpenSSL and lodash@4.17.21 for known vulnerabilities". The agent then works through these steps: Discover sellers on ENS.Three data providers are registered as ENSv2 subnames of chirag126.eth on Sepolia: kev: the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list cve: NVD CVE records osv: the OSV open-source vulnerability database Each subname's text records publish what the provider sells, its endpoint, its price and its Hedera payout account. The agent reads these from the chain at run time, so nothing is hard-coded. Changing a record changes what the agent finds. Each provider and the agent also have an ERC-8004 identity. Plan with 0G. A model on 0G's mainnet Private Computer reads the task and the discovered catalogs. It decides which data to buy and returns its plan as schema-checked JSON. Every 0G call is capped at a worst-case cost before it is sent, and a ledger compares the agent's records with 0G's own billing. Pass the spending firewall.Before any money moves, a deterministic policy checks each purchase against limits per payment, per run and per day, and against a cap on the number of payments. The AI's output can't override it, and a purchase outside the limits is refused. Pay on Hedera with x402. Providers answer with HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent signs an HBAR payment on Hedera testnet, a facilitator settles it, and the agent checks the settled transaction on the Mirror Node before trusting the data. Every payment is a real transaction you can open on HashScan. Analyse with 0G.The model turns the purchased data into a short security brief: which vulnerabilities matter, whether they are actively exploited, and what to do. Audit on Hedera Consensus Service. Each run's key events (plan, payments, result) are written to an HCS topic. Anyone can check them independently. The web app shows the whole run live: discovery, plan, payments, verification and the final brief. It also has pages for payments, 0G usage, ENS permissions and evidence, a 7-day activity overview, voice input through Whisper on 0G, and three visual themes. The agent runs unattended too, producing a daily brief for a watchlist within a fixed budget. Each track has a distinct role: ENS- is how agents find each other and what they offer. Hedera- is how they pay and prove what happened. 0G-is where the agent's reasoning runs. Remove any one of them and the system can't work. Every claim in the project is backed by on-chain evidence: Hedera transaction IDs, HCS messages, Sepolia transaction hashes and 0G request IDs.
projects.how_its_made: Endersift is a TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm. It runs on Node 22 using Node's built-in TypeScript type stripping, so the server runs its source files directly with no build step. Tests use node:test. Structure: apps/server: the agent. A Hono API, the task orchestrator, the scheduler for daily briefs, a SQLite database, and server-sent events that stream every step of a run to the browser. apps/providers: three x402-protected data sellers (kev, cve, osv) that proxy CISA KEV, NVD and OSV. apps/web: a React + Vite app with three themes, live run timelines and simple bar charts built from plain HTML elements. packages/hedera, packages/ens, packages/zg, packages/policy: one package per integration, so each can be tested on its own. Hedera: We use the official Hiero SDK (@hiero-ledger/sdk) and the x402 packages. A provider answers 402 Payment Required with its price. The agent's x402 client signs an HBAR transfer on Hedera testnet, and the Blocky402 facilitator settles it, with x402.org as a fallback. The agent doesn't trust the facilitator's answer on its own. It looks up the settled transaction on the Hedera Mirror Node and checks the payer, receiver, amount and success status before using the data. Payments go through an explicit state machine (quoted, approved, signed, settled, verified, failed), so a crash halfway never pays twice. Every run also writes plan, payment and result messages to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as a public audit trail. Hedera's fast finality and very low fees are what make per-request micropayments practical. ENS: Providers are ENSv2 subnames of chirag126.eth on Sepolia. Their text records publish the service description, endpoint, price, payout account and an ERC-8004 agent ID. We use viem to discover them: read the registry's logs for subnames, then resolve each record through the Universal Resolver. The resolvers are PermissionedResolvers, and an operator key is allowed to change only specific records. We tested this on-chain: allowed edits succeed and forbidden ones revert. A provisioning script sets everything up, and changing a record really changes what the agent finds on its next run. Discovered endpoints and records are treated as untrusted input and validated before use. 0G: All AI runs on 0G Private Computer mainnet through the 0G Router (OpenAI-compatible). It uses 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, with qwen2.5-vl-72b-instruct as a fallback, plus whisper-large-v3 for voice tasks. The planner and analyser use structured output: we turn zod schemas into JSON Schema with z.toJSONSchema, and any reply that doesn't match is rejected. Before each call we reserve its worst-case cost against per-call and daily caps. An inference ledger then compares our records with 0G's own usage history, so every request ID and its cost can be checked. Running on 0G means the model can't be quietly swapped, and every call has a billed, traceable ID. Safety: The spending firewall in packages/policy is plain deterministic code: per-payment, per-run and daily limits plus a cap on payments per run. The model's output can propose purchases but can never override the firewall. Secrets are only in environment variables, are checked against a spec at startup and are redacted from logs. The ENS admin key and the 0G management key are never deployed. Access to the demo is protected by a code, with signed stateless sessions. Deployment: Both services run on Render's free plan in Singapore. GitHub Actions runs type checks, linting, tests and a secret scan on every change. Hacky bits worth mentioning: Render's free services sleep after 15 minutes. When the agent called a sleeping provider host from the server, it got HTTP 429 and the host never woke. A request from a real browser does wake it. So the web app wakes the provider host from the visitor's browser by calling its /health endpoint, which is allowed through a tightly scoped Content Security Policy. Meanwhile the agent waits up to 3 minutes per host before giving up. The free plan has no disk, so the database is wiped on every restart. Logins survive restarts because sessions are stateless HMAC-signed tokens derived from the access code. The evidence that matters lives on-chain anyway: on Hedera, HCS, Sepolia and in 0G's billing. Alchemy's free tier limits log queries to about 10 blocks. Our discovery uses adaptive log windows, which turned into thousands of requests on Alchemy. We switched to RPC providers that allow wider ranges. Every claim in our evidence files is produced by scripts from real transactions, never written by hand. Tools: We built the project with Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code as a coding agent, working in small reviewed pull requests. The AI usage section of the README describes this in detail.

projects.title: Social Trade w/Flash
projects.description: Flash limit and market orders straight from askRoger’s X-powered token leaderboard.
projects.project_description: askRoger ranks tokens by what is happening on X right now: who is talking about them, how many KOLs, how many smart followers, plus launch risk flags from onchain data. Until this hackathon the only way to act on that was a referral link to GMGN or Photon. You left our app, found the token again, and traded somewhere else. This project closes that gap with Definitive’s Flash API. Every Base and Arbitrum token on the leaderboard and on its token page now has a Trade with Flash button. It opens a drawer where you buy with USDC as a market order, or set a limit order with Matcha style controls (Market, -2%, -5%, -10%, custom) and an expiry. You approve USDC once, sign the order in your wallet, and Flash executes it onchain and pays the gas. Resting limit orders wait with Flash and can be cancelled from the Orders tab or from a new My Flash trades page that lists every order you placed, open and filled, with the fill transaction on BaseScan. The social part: each token page shows how many askRoger traders already acted on it through Flash, with a one click share to X. We charge an integrator fee on every order through Flash, so this is monetised from day one. Continuity track disclosure: askRoger existed before the event (leaderboard, token pages, signals, alerts, a Flask API, no wallet or trading of any kind). Everything related to trading was built during the event, is in the public repo with full commit history, and is live on app.askroger.ai. Verified on Base mainnet with real orders: a market buy filled, limit orders rested and were cancelled.
projects.how_its_made: Two pieces. A Flask blueprint sits between our webapp and Flash. It holds the Flash API key server side, pins our integrator fee on every quote and order, validates chain and order type, strips the quote only fields Flash rejects on submit, and forwards the rest. It records every order in a MySQL table and keeps statuses in sync from Flash’s order list, which also backs the My trades page. Hermetic tests, no network. The frontend is a React module with no new dependencies. Wallet access is raw window.ethereum JSON-RPC: eth_sendTransaction for the one time USDC approval, eth_signTypedData_v4 for the Permit2 and FlashOrder payloads Flash returns, personal_sign for cancels, eth_call for the USDC balance. We read Definitive’s open source flash-mcp client and copied the things that matter: domain.chainId comes back as a string and has to be coerced before signing, and Flash’s /order can create an order and still answer 4xx, so a failed submit is reconciled against the order list before we ever show an error, never retried blindly. Two things bit us. Our API sits behind CloudFront, which cached the order status poll for two minutes, so the first real order filled onchain while the UI still said accepted. Fixed with a cache buster and no-store headers. And Flash returns 404 on the first status read for about a second after accepting an order, so that is tolerated rather than treated as failure. Flash was the right fit because it is non custodial, runs every order type through one endpoint, and pays execution gas, which is exactly what a trade from a social feed needs.

projects.description: Sealed, quantum-safe swaps on EIP 8141 that bots can't touch.
projects.project_description:
Description LeanSeal is a quantum-safe wallet and sealed transaction protocol built on EIP-8141 and ERC-8421, combining post-quantum cryptography, time-locked encryption, and on-chain execution enforcement to make Ethereum transactions private until execution and resistant to sandwich attacks.
Just think that we are removing the 3rd party defi guys who says they can stop our attacks but works on contract orchestrations and we are someone who does that directly using alt-mempools and PQ signatures.
The idea builds on a concept discussed by Vitalik Buterin at Cypherpunk: encrypting a transaction package with the information needed by its intended recipient, locking it for a predetermined number of time steps, and allowing it to be broadcast or revealed only after that time has elapsed. We took this concept further by turning time-locked encryption into an executable transaction lane, where encrypted orders move across a network of nodes and become available for execution only at their designated drand round. Today, every swap on Ethereum exposes its intent before execution. Bots monitor public mempools, buy ahead of transactions, and sell immediately afterward, extracting value from user slippage. We measured this firsthand: a small swap on our chain suffered a 3% loss to a sandwich attack. At the same time, conventional ECDSA wallet keys face a long-term threat from sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Existing MEV protection relies heavily on private relays, builders, or protected RPC endpoints. This replaces public exposure with trust in intermediaries. We wanted to eliminate that dependency by enforcing transaction validity and execution rules at the protocol and EVM levels. We protocolised EIP-8141 and extended the ERC-8421 alternative mempool infrastructure to make this possible. Quantum-Safe Wallets LeanSeal accounts verify NIST SLH-DSA post-quantum signatures directly on-chain inside the transaction's VERIFY frame. Signature verification costs approximately 154k gas, exceeding the public mempool's 100k verification cap. We extended the alternative mempool's staked verification budget and precompile support to admit these transactions. Sealed Transaction Lane Orders are encrypted against future drand rounds and submitted as hash commitments. Our custom ERC-8421 mempool distributes time-locked orders between nodes under publicly published admission rules. Before the designated round, nobody, including the operators, can reveal the order. Once the round arrives, any node can decrypt and submit it for execution. This creates sealed order flow on public infrastructure without private relays or privileged access. On-Chain Fair Execution A custom Uniswap v4 hook enforces batch settlement directly inside the EVM. Orders are revealed and settled together at one clearing price per side. Every unauthorized swap is rejected by the hook, preventing bots from inserting front-runs around the batch. Protection is enforced by the pool itself, not by a trusted third party. Measured Results A swap that suffered a 3% loss in the public mempool experienced 0% loss through LeanSeal. Every attempted bot front-run was rejected, both locally and on the live hackathon devnet. Designed for Individuals and Institutions Individuals can authenticate using Face ID or fingerprint, with quantum-safe keys generated directly inside the browser. Their first transaction deploys the wallet, verifies the post-quantum signature, and completes a sponsored deposit without requiring ETH. Institutions receive a dedicated trading interface for sealed block trades, supporting buy and sell orders, amounts, price limits, vault balances, and withdrawals. Large-order size and direction remain hidden until execution. Why It Matters LeanSeal demonstrates a new transaction architecture for Ethereum. By protocolising EIP-8141, extending ERC-8421, and combining them with drand and Uniswap v4, we bring programmable post-quantum verification, time-locked transaction delivery, and enforceable fair execution together.
projects.how_its_made: LeanSeal is built across six technical layers, connecting post-quantum cryptography, programmable transaction validation, alternative mempool infrastructure, time-locked encryption, and Uniswap v4 execution. Quantum-Safe Wallet Architecture Technologies: Solidity, C, Rust, Yul, EIP-8141. We built an EIP-8141 smart account that reads arbitrary signature data using SIGDATACOPY, validates it against the protocol transaction sighash using TXPARAM 0x08, and authorizes execution through APPROVE. The wallet integrates open-source SPHINCS+ verifiers supporting NIST SLH-DSA-SHA2-128-24 and the research scheme leanSphincs-s, with a dedicated Yul frame module. One major engineering challenge was signature generation. The reference SLH-DSA signer required approximately 354 seconds per signature. We forked and optimized it using 16 threads, ARMv8 SHA-256 instructions, and a 128 MB tree cache, bringing signing time down to approximately 3 seconds. We also implemented EIP-1167 minimal proxy wallets with public keys appended to their bytecode (45 + 104 bytes), eliminating storage writes. This reduced wallet creation from approximately 2.7M to 412k state gas. Protocol-Level Alternative Mempool Technologies: ERC-8421, Bun, TypeScript, libp2p. We extended the Ethereum Foundation's ERC-8421 sidecar to support high-cost post-quantum verification and custom transaction lanes. Our contributions include the staked verification budget supporting up to 1M gas, hash precompile support through CALLING-040, a customMempools plugin extension point, and a dedicated custom_mempool_v1 gossip topic. During integration, we discovered that the live devnet incorrectly rejected the SHA-256 precompile as an undeployed contract, preventing NIST wallet verification. We isolated and reported the issue, which was subsequently fixed. On top of this infrastructure, we implemented our sealed mempool as a custom plugin. It has an IPFS CID-based identifier referencing publicly published admission rules, REV-010 through REV-060, and its own gossip network. Nodes exchange drand-time-locked reveal tickets, while keepers coordinate scheduled reveals and settlements. Uniswap v4 Fair Execution Engine Technologies: Solidity, Uniswap v4, PoolManager. We developed SealedPoolHook to enforce commit, reveal, and settle execution in rounds of four blocks. Users submit encrypted orders, which become available at the designated drand round. During settlement, PoolManager.unlock and flash accounting allow us to net opposing buy and sell orders at the pool price, execute only the remaining imbalance, and provide one clearing price per side. The beforeSwap callback rejects unauthorized swaps, ensuring that trades cannot bypass the batch settlement mechanism. A particularly hacky implementation detail was mining a CREATE2 salt to obtain a hook address with exactly the required beforeSwap permission bit. We also use extsload to read pool pricing data directly from PoolManager storage. Time-Locked Encryption Technologies: drand, tlock-js. Orders are encrypted against future drand rounds. Before the designated round, nobody, including our own operators, can decrypt them. Once the round arrives, anyone can reveal them. We combine this with on-chain hash commitments to ensure that nodes cannot replace or modify orders during the reveal process. This removes the need for a centralized decryption authority and enables publicly verifiable time-locked execution. Passkeys and Browser-Based Cryptography Technologies: WebAuthn PRF, HKDF, Rust, WebAssembly. We wanted quantum-safe wallets to be usable without exposing users to complicated key management. A passkey's PRF output is processed through HKDF to derive a seed for the quantum-safe key. Our Rust leanSphincs-s signer is compiled into a 67 KB WASM module, generating keys inside the browser in approximately 0.3 seconds and signing in approximately 30 milliseconds. Private keys never leave the browser or get stored on our servers. Another unusual engineering solution is our browser-based signing bridge. Server-side scripts use a lightweight signer CLI stand-in that forwards signing requests to the user's active browser tab through Server-Sent Events. The returned signatures are independently verified using the native verifier before being accepted. Infrastructure and Devnet Deployment Technologies: ethrex, Lighthouse, Docker, DigitalOcean, pm2, Caddy. Locally, we run an ethrex EIP-8141 branch alongside Lighthouse through Docker. Our public deployment runs on the hackathon devnet, with two sealed-mempool nodes hosted on DigitalOcean, managed through pm2 and exposed using Caddy with automatic HTTPS. Each public demo visitor receives an isolated session, run queue, and spending limits. RPC access uses

Description

LeanSeal is a quantum-safe wallet and sealed transaction protocol built on EIP-8141 and ERC-8421, combining post-quantum cryptography, time-locked encryption, and on-chain execution enforcement to make Ethereum transactions private until execution and resistant to sandwich attacks.
Just think that we are removing the 3rd party defi guys who says they can stop our attacks but works on contract orchestrations and we are someone who does that directly using alt-mempools and PQ signatures.
The idea builds on a concept discussed by Vitalik Buterin at Cypherpunk: encrypting a transaction package with the information needed by its intended recipient, locking it for a predetermined number of time steps, and allowing it to be broadcast or revealed only after that time has elapsed. We took this concept further by turning time-locked encryption into an executable transaction lane, where encrypted orders move across a network of nodes and become available for execution only at their designated drand round.

Today, every swap on Ethereum exposes its intent before execution. Bots monitor public mempools, buy ahead of transactions, and sell immediately afterward, extracting value from user slippage. We measured this firsthand: a small swap on our chain suffered a 3% loss to a sandwich attack. At the same time, conventional ECDSA wallet keys face a long-term threat from sufficiently powerful quantum computers.

Existing MEV protection relies heavily on private relays, builders, or protected RPC endpoints. This replaces public exposure with trust in intermediaries. We wanted to eliminate that dependency by enforcing transaction validity and execution rules at the protocol and EVM levels.

We protocolised EIP-8141 and extended the ERC-8421 alternative mempool infrastructure to make this possible.

Quantum-Safe Wallets

LeanSeal accounts verify NIST SLH-DSA post-quantum signatures directly on-chain inside the transaction's VERIFY frame. Signature verification costs approximately 154k gas, exceeding the public mempool's 100k verification cap. We extended the alternative mempool's staked verification budget and precompile support to admit these transactions.

Sealed Transaction Lane

Orders are encrypted against future drand rounds and submitted as hash commitments. Our custom ERC-8421 mempool distributes time-locked orders between nodes under publicly published admission rules. Before the designated round, nobody, including the operators, can reveal the order. Once the round arrives, any node can decrypt and submit it for execution. This creates sealed order flow on public infrastructure without private relays or privileged access.

On-Chain Fair Execution

A custom Uniswap v4 hook enforces batch settlement directly inside the EVM. Orders are revealed and settled together at one clearing price per side. Every unauthorized swap is rejected by the hook, preventing bots from inserting front-runs around the batch. Protection is enforced by the pool itself, not by a trusted third party.

Measured Results

A swap that suffered a 3% loss in the public mempool experienced 0% loss through LeanSeal. Every attempted bot front-run was rejected, both locally and on the live hackathon devnet.

Designed for Individuals and Institutions

Individuals can authenticate using Face ID or fingerprint, with quantum-safe keys generated directly inside the browser. Their first transaction deploys the wallet, verifies the post-quantum signature, and completes a sponsored deposit without requiring ETH.

Institutions receive a dedicated trading interface for sealed block trades, supporting buy and sell orders, amounts, price limits, vault balances, and withdrawals. Large-order size and direction remain hidden until execution.


Why It Matters

LeanSeal demonstrates a new transaction architecture for Ethereum. By protocolising EIP-8141, extending ERC-8421, and combining them with drand and Uniswap v4, we bring programmable post-quantum verification, time-locked transaction delivery, and enforceable fair execution together.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
LeanSeal is built across six technical layers, connecting post-quantum cryptography, programmable transaction validation, alternative mempool infrastructure, time-locked encryption, and Uniswap v4 execution.

1. Quantum-Safe Wallet Architecture

Technologies: Solidity, C, Rust, Yul, EIP-8141.

We built an EIP-8141 smart account that reads arbitrary signature data using SIGDATACOPY, validates it against the protocol transaction sighash using TXPARAM 0x08, and authorizes execution through APPROVE.

The wallet integrates open-source SPHINCS+ verifiers supporting NIST SLH-DSA-SHA2-128-24 and the research scheme leanSphincs-s, with a dedicated Yul frame module.

One major engineering challenge was signature generation. The reference SLH-DSA signer required approximately 354 seconds per signature. We forked and optimized it using 16 threads, ARMv8 SHA-256 instructions, and a 128 MB tree cache, bringing signing time down to approximately 3 seconds.

We also implemented EIP-1167 minimal proxy wallets with public keys appended to their bytecode (45 + 104 bytes), eliminating storage writes. This reduced wallet creation from approximately 2.7M to 412k state gas.

2. Protocol-Level Alternative Mempool

Technologies: ERC-8421, Bun, TypeScript, libp2p.

We extended the Ethereum Foundation's ERC-8421 sidecar to support high-cost post-quantum verification and custom transaction lanes.

Our contributions include the staked verification budget supporting up to 1M gas, hash precompile support through CALLING-040, a customMempools plugin extension point, and a dedicated custom_mempool_v1 gossip topic.

During integration, we discovered that the live devnet incorrectly rejected the SHA-256 precompile as an undeployed contract, preventing NIST wallet verification. We isolated and reported the issue, which was subsequently fixed.

On top of this infrastructure, we implemented our sealed mempool as a custom plugin. It has an IPFS CID-based identifier referencing publicly published admission rules, REV-010 through REV-060, and its own gossip network. Nodes exchange drand-time-locked reveal tickets, while keepers coordinate scheduled reveals and settlements.

3. Uniswap v4 Fair Execution Engine

Technologies: Solidity, Uniswap v4, PoolManager.

We developed SealedPoolHook to enforce commit, reveal, and settle execution in rounds of four blocks.

Users submit encrypted orders, which become available at the designated drand round. During settlement, PoolManager.unlock and flash accounting allow us to net opposing buy and sell orders at the pool price, execute only the remaining imbalance, and provide one clearing price per side.

The beforeSwap callback rejects unauthorized swaps, ensuring that trades cannot bypass the batch settlement mechanism.

A particularly hacky implementation detail was mining a CREATE2 salt to obtain a hook address with exactly the required beforeSwap permission bit. We also use extsload to read pool pricing data directly from PoolManager storage.

4. Time-Locked Encryption

Technologies: drand, tlock-js.

Orders are encrypted against future drand rounds. Before the designated round, nobody, including our own operators, can decrypt them. Once the round arrives, anyone can reveal them.

We combine this with on-chain hash commitments to ensure that nodes cannot replace or modify orders during the reveal process.

This removes the need for a centralized decryption authority and enables publicly verifiable time-locked execution.

5. Passkeys and Browser-Based Cryptography

Technologies: WebAuthn PRF, HKDF, Rust, WebAssembly.

We wanted quantum-safe wallets to be usable without exposing users to complicated key management.

A passkey's PRF output is processed through HKDF to derive a seed for the quantum-safe key. Our Rust leanSphincs-s signer is compiled into a 67 KB WASM module, generating keys inside the browser in approximately 0.3 seconds and signing in approximately 30 milliseconds.

Private keys never leave the browser or get stored on our servers.

Another unusual engineering solution is our browser-based signing bridge. Server-side scripts use a lightweight signer CLI stand-in that forwards signing requests to the user's active browser tab through Server-Sent Events. The returned signatures are independently verified using the native verifier before being accepted.

6. Infrastructure and Devnet Deployment

Technologies: ethrex, Lighthouse, Docker, DigitalOcean, pm2, Caddy.

Locally, we run an ethrex EIP-8141 branch alongside Lighthouse through Docker. Our public deployment runs on the hackathon devnet, with two sealed-mempool nodes hosted on DigitalOcean, managed through pm2 and exposed using Caddy with automatic HTTPS.

Each public demo visitor receives an isolated session, run queue, and spending limits. RPC access uses

projects.title: Tracer
projects.description: Tracer catches unverified proxy and diamond upgrades and writes a public record on Arkiv.
projects.project_description: Tracer A public record of contract changes. Tracer watches Ethereum proxies and cross chain diamonds, asks Sourcify whether the new code is verified, and writes the result to Arkiv. A swap to unverified code is the critical signal. The same record sells attested real world data, and a change can reach you in the browser and on Telegram. Build on Arkiv.
projects.how_its_made: Tracer is a Vite and React dashboard on Vercel and one Express process on Render. The browser reads Arkiv directly with wagmi and the Arkiv SDK. Proxy checks, diamond checks, and marketplace listings all go through the API, which is the only process holding the writer key. In development, Vite proxies /api to that process. In production, vercel.json rewrites /api to the Render URL, so the UI stays on one origin. The watcher reads implementation storage directly: EIP-1967 and the legacy OpenZeppelin slot, which is how USDC is included. On a change it asks Sourcify whether the new code is verified, then writes an upgrade.alert owned by the watcher wallet. Alerts expire after 30 days. Each proxy’s upgrade.state row is patched in place and extended so the watcher’s memory stays alive. An unverified implementation is critical, a verified one is a warning, and the first sight of a proxy is info. A diamond has no single implementation. For LI.FI, Tracer calls facets() and owner() on each chain, hashes the deployed bytecode, and diffs that against a pinned manifest. A new unverified facet or a new owner is critical. A facet moved to a new address with the same code hash is ignored. A code change at the same address is a real change. Arkiv is the public record. Indexed attributes let the page filter by severity, verification, proxy, and block. ownedBy(watcher) keeps a forged alert from another wallet out of the feed. Expiry makes the feed a rolling 30-day window with no cleanup job. The same shape sells data: Aethera readings start at NREL, land on Aptos with a transaction as proof, and are reattested on Arkiv as aethera.solar. Listing metadata is public on Arkiv. The gated payload stays in a JSON file on the server, because anything written to Arkiv is readable by anyone. Buyers pay in tGLM on Rabdi. Two rough edges are load-bearing. Telegram is queued in a SQLite outbox the moment a proxy or diamond is classified, before the Arkiv write, and the same implementation is never sent twice. The monitor, the manual check, and the marketplace relayer share one writer, so a mutex keeps their nonces from colliding. Simulations are labeled and do not clear a live finding. Viem errors can contain the Arkiv access key, so the server strips that key before the message reaches the browser, and it will not bind a public host unless an operator token is set.

projects.title: Plan B
projects.description: Plan B turns X trading signals into protected Flash advanced orders signed from your own wallet.
projects.project_description: Plan B is an X-native social trading product that turns trade signals into ready-to-sign, non-custodial Definitive Flash advanced orders. Most tools turn a tweet into a market-buy button. Plan B asks what the post actually means. A “buy on pullback” signal becomes a limit order with protection; a breakout becomes a stop entry; a late call can become a TWAP; and stated stop/target levels become a bracket. Users always choose their own size and sign from their own wallet. The extension only appears on signed Caller Cards or posts with both a token reference and clear trading intent. Groq parses untrusted text into a constrained draft, then the backend validates the exact contract, chain, price levels, safety signals, and order logic before any quote is requested. Plan B also makes social trading accountable. Every signal receives a Signal Passport containing source evidence, contract, Flash capture price, expiry, strategy terms, source availability, and later outcome. Radar, Caller Rankings, Outcomes, and Chrome alerts let followers track strategies and actual Flash execution results without copying a wallet or giving up custody.
projects.how_its_made: Plan B has three connected parts: a Manifest V3 Chrome extension, a Node/Express backend, and a static social-trading dashboard. The extension injects a Plan B action into eligible X posts and renders its order panel in a Shadow DOM so it works cleanly across X’s light and dark themes. A page-context bridge relays wallet requests from MetaMask/Rabby or Solana wallets because content scripts cannot directly access injected wallet providers. The extension also uses Chrome alarms, storage, and native notifications to poll Radar for followed callers and signal swarms. The backend uses Groq structured output to turn a post or voice instruction into a constrained trade draft. It never trusts the model for wallet access, size, or execution permission. Server-side validation resolves the asset, checks contract integrity, compares signal prices with current data, and compiles the result into the appropriate Flash order shape. Definitive Flash is the execution core: Plan B uses Flash search, quotes, orders, updates, cancellation, balances, and the Orders WebSocket. It supports market, limit, TWAP/DCA, stop entry, stop-loss, take-profit, bracket, trailing-stop, and trailing-stop-limit workflows. Flash handles managed onchain execution; the user signs every required action. For safety, Plan B combines exact-contract rules with GoPlus and Honeypot checks. For accountability, PostgreSQL persists Caller Cards, Signal Passports, revisions, subscriptions, follower plans, Flash lifecycle events, and World Proof of Human enrollment records. World ID can gate Caller Card creation to make caller reputation more resistant to Sybil farming, while wallet signatures still bind every strategy to its creator.

projects.title: Wallet labeled tape
projects.description: Live Hyperliquid trade tape that names both wallets on every trade and tags them by 30-day results
projects.project_description: Order flow tools show you what traded. Wallet-Labeled Tape shows you who traded. Hyperliquid publishes both wallet addresses on every trade, so we stream the live BTC, ETH and SOL tape and label each side: Profitable, Unprofitable or Mixed over the last 30 days, Large, Likely automated or Likely market maker, with the sample size and days covered next to every tag. Each trade also shows what it did to that wallet's position: open, add, reduce, close or flip. Filters cut the noise down to profitable wallets opening in size. Click any address for its full record: net PnL after fees, return on volume, profit factor, max drawdown, weeks positive, maker share, open positions and recent trades. A flow panel counts how many profitable wallets raised or cut exposure per coin in the last 15 minutes, counting wallets, not dollars, so one whale cannot fake it. You cannot build this on Binance because its trades are anonymous. Unscored wallets say Pending instead of guessing. Not financial advice.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript end to end, Node 22 and React. The backend opens Hyperliquid's public WebSocket trade stream for BTC, ETH and SOL (every trade carries both user addresses) with reconnect and backoff. Each new address joins a priority queue ranked by trade size and recency. A scorer pulls the wallet's last 30 days of fills from the REST API, rebuilds them into round trips, and computes net PnL after fees (including a builder fee we found while probing the API), drawdown, profit factor and maker share, then assigns tags. Hyperliquid allows 1,200 request weight per minute, so every call goes through our own weight-based token bucket capped at 1,000: the biggest traders get scored first, and wallets that look like bots stop after one page. A position tracker replays each scored wallet's fills so every live trade gets its action (open, add, reduce, close, flip). State lives in Node's built-in SQLite, so a restart reloads every score. One small relay serves the web app, a WebSocket for the tape and a JSON endpoint for the wallet drawer, so the whole product is one process, deployed on Render. The frontend is React and Vite with no UI library. 60 unit tests run in GitHub Actions. Zero cost: no API keys, no paid services. AI use is logged file by file in AI_USAGE.md.
