projects.title: I was here
projects.description: Go there. Prove it. Keep it. Collect World ID-verified stamps for real places around the World
projects.project_description: wrld3 is an Android app that turns real places into collectible stamps. You open a full-screen map, walk to a landmark or an event spot, and once you are inside the capture radius (20 metres at most spots) the stamp unlocks. You see a 3D coin of the place in the camera view. When you keep it, a non-transferable ERC-1155 token is minted to your passport on Sepolia. The token records only your wallet and the spot id, never where you stood. Why this exists Proof-of-attendance badges have a trust problem. POAP, the best known one, wound down in 2026 after more than five years. Its co-founder said the business model could not be made sustainable without undermining what made it meaningful. Our view of the design side is that a badge handed out through a shared link or code proves nothing about who claimed it or whether they were there, so farmers and bots collect everything and the badge loses its value. wrld3 fixes both parts. projects.project_description_markdown:
wrld3 is an Android app that turns real places into collectible stamps. You open a full-screen map, walk to a landmark or an event spot, and once you are inside the capture radius (20 metres at most spots) the stamp unlocks. You see a 3D coin of the place in the camera view. When you keep it, a non-transferable ERC-1155 token is minted to your passport on Sepolia. The token records only your wallet and the spot id, never where you stood.

### Why this exists

Proof-of-attendance badges have a trust problem. POAP, the best known one, wound down in 2026 after more than five years. Its co-founder said the business model could not be made sustainable without undermining what made it meaningful. Our view of the design side is that a badge handed out through a shared link or code proves nothing about who claimed it or whether they were there, so farmers and bots collect everything and the badge loses its value. wrld3 fixes both parts. Every stamp needs a unique human (World ID) who is physically at the place (server-checked location), and the place's own sponsors pay for it, so there is a business model from day one.

### The business idea

A stamp is a place a sponsor can fund. At a conference, sponsors pay to be inside the event. Around a landmark or a tourist spot, the same thing works for the merchants nearby: the cafe beside a monument, the shop near a station, a local tourism board. A merchant funds a stamp and runs an ad campaign for the people who mint it. The ad shows on the stamp screen right after a verified capture, so the merchant pays for real people who were really there, not for impressions that bots can fake. This scales with every landmark, not only with events.

### Stamps that expire

Each spot is an Arkiv entity with an expiry, and the spot's campaign has a start and an end. When an event ends, the stamp becomes unmintable: the Sepolia contract keeps a registry of spots with an open window and refuses to mint outside it, and the organizer can close a spot at any time. The ad campaign ends on its dates too, and its Arkiv entity expires seven days later. Stamps already minted stay as memories. A finished event cannot be farmed afterwards, and the public list does not fill up with stale pins.

### The money design

A merchant's stake or funding on a stamp is split with 10% going to the protocol and the rest going to the people who minted the stamp and still hold it. Holders are the ones who were really there, so the sponsor's money reaches them. This split is designed but not built yet. The payout escrow is future work.

### How a capture is checked

The hard problem for any "go somewhere and get a reward" app is that bots and GPS spoofers farm it, and a payout makes that worse. So we treat every capture as evidence, and the server makes the decision, never the phone. The phone sends its position, its accuracy and a timestamp. The backend then runs these checks in order:

1. It burns the single-use nonce it issued for that spot.
2. It rejects a reading older than 60 seconds or less accurate than 25 metres.
3. It recomputes the haversine distance to the spot itself and refuses if you are outside the radius.
4. It asks World's servers to verify the World ID proof for that spot's own action.
5. It checks that this person's nullifier has not already captured the spot.

Only if every check passes does it sign a mint voucher. Every refusal has a plain reason (too far, poor signal, stale, already captured, not verified), and nothing is minted on a refusal.

### World ID

World ID is what makes a stamp mean "a real, unique person was here", and it is why the payout idea is safe to build. Each spot has its own action, so one person can claim a spot once, and the nullifiers for different spots cannot be linked to each other. We only ask for Proof of Human, because stopping duplicate and bot claims needs a unique human and nothing more.

### Onchain

The stamp contract is deployed on Sepolia at `0x489D88266FF1ED2022B1Abc9F575ca0C9e4f3E19`.

- Minting needs an EIP-712 voucher (recipient, spotId, nonce, deadline) signed by our backend, and each nonce works once.
- One stamp per wallet per spot. All transfers and approvals revert. The holder can burn their own stamp.
- A public registry holds each spot's id, name and open window, with no coordinates.
- A relayer pays the gas, so travelers never need funds.
- A Foundry test loads a voucher signed by the Node backend, to prove the two sides agree.

### Arkiv

The spot list is public on Arkiv. Each spot is an entity written from the organizer wallet `0xf47cB2e4353F5daF04fA7AF0955551ab7DB74b52` on the Rabdi testnet, with coordinates rounded to about 110 m, a 30-day expiry that renews on re-save, and indexed fields for the event, the spot id and the rounded position. Anyone can run one query (`node backend/scripts/arkiv-query.mjs`) and read the spots without our server. Sponsors publish campaigns from their own wallets, so the organizer can decline to show an ad but cannot forge or rewrite it.

### ENS

Each traveler can claim an opt-in passport name on ENSv2 on Sepolia, under `wrld3.eth`. Their stamps are written to a record on that name, with permissions that let our server write that record and nothing else.

### Organizers and events

Organizers use a dashboard to drop a 3D model on the map, set the capture radius and run events that open and close on their own clock. A quest stamp unlocks after you finish a few others. The app is built for ETHGlobal Mumbai, with 19 spots across the city: the venue, the sponsor tracks, landmarks and the Aqua Line stations. Everything runs on testnets, and sign-in currently needs an Orb-verified World ID.

projects.title: GrantScope
projects.description: GrantScope privately scans, analyzes, and revokes risky Web3 token permissions using Anon-RPC.
projects.project_description: GrantScope — Privacy-First Web3 Permission Management GrantScope is a privacy-first Web3 security platform that helps Ethereum users discover, understand, and revoke token-spending permissions while protecting their blockchain query privacy through the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC . The Problem Every time users interact with decentralized exchanges or DeFi applications, they may grant smart contracts permission to spend their tokens. These approvals, sometimes unlimited, can remain active long after the original transaction is completed. If an authorized contract is compromised or malicious, users' funds may be exposed without their private keys being stolen. The problem becomes more complex with Uniswap Permit2 and smart accounts , where permissions can exist across multiple authorization layers. Revoking one permission does not necessarily eliminate every related authorization. Additionally, traditional wallet security scanners send blockchain queries directly to RPC providers, potentially exposing users' IP addresses alongside the wallet addresses they inspect. Our Solution GrantScope combines wallet permission security with privacy-preserving blockchain infrastructure. Key Features: Privacy-First Scanning: Integrates Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC to route blockchain reads through supported anonymizing transports such as Tor or Nym, reducing direct exposure of users' IP addresses to RPC providers. ERC-20 Permission Discovery: Identifies token-spending approvals using blockchain events and smart contract allowance queries. Permit2 Analysis: Inspects supported Uniswap Permit2 permissions and explains the relationship between underlying ERC-20 approvals and individual spender authorizations. Risk Assessment: Highlights unlimited allowances, excessive spending permissions, expired authorizations, and permissions requiring review. Permission Revocation: Enables users to revoke unwanted approvals through wallet-authorized transactions and verify the updated blockchain state. Smart Account Awareness: Supports read-only inspection of smart-account addresses while clearly identifying limitations around account-specific delegations. Privacy Transparency: Provides visibility into RPC routing, anonymized requests, network performance, and disclosed privacy exceptions. How It Works Users enter an Ethereum wallet address without connecting their wallet. GrantScope retrieves supported permission data through Anon-RPC, analyzes active allowances, and presents an understandable security dashboard. Users can inspect which contracts have spending authority, understand their potential exposure, and connect their wallet only when they choose to revoke a permission. After the transaction is confirmed, GrantScope checks the updated allowance to verify the result. What Makes GrantScope Different? Unlike traditional approval dashboards, GrantScope emphasizes both permission security and inspection privacy . It helps users understand layered token authorizations while minimizing unnecessary exposure of their network identity during blockchain reads. GrantScope does not claim to hide public blockchain transactions or support every smart-account permission mechanism. Instead, it provides transparent privacy guarantees, explainable assessments, and user-controlled security actions. Our Vision We believe checking your wallet's security should not require sacrificing your privacy. GrantScope makes Ethereum permissions understandable, revocable, and more private to inspect—empowering users to take control of their Web3 security.
projects.how_its_made: How It's Made — GrantScope GrantScope is built using React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS , with a modular, browser-first architecture designed around privacy, security, and performance. Frontend and Architecture We used React and TypeScript to build a responsive Web3 security dashboard, with Tailwind CSS for styling and reusable UI components. The application separates wallet inspection, permission discovery, risk analysis, transaction execution, and privacy monitoring into independent modules. Instead of relying on a centralized backend to process wallet data, we designed GrantScope to perform blockchain analysis directly in the browser, minimizing unnecessary exposure of wallet information. Ethereum Foundation — Anon-RPC Integration The core integration is the Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC , which enables privacy-preserving blockchain reads through anonymizing transports such as Tor and Nym. We integrated the Anon-RPC browser harness into our Ethereum RPC layer, allowing supported JSON-RPC requests to pass through an anonymizing worker rather than directly contacting a conventional RPC provider. A particularly important engineering challenge was handling anonymous transport initialization, network timeouts, and gateway availability. We designed the transport layer to fail closed , meaning it does not silently switch to a non-anonymous RPC connection when an anonymous transport fails. We also developed a Privacy Lab to report RPC routing, transport status, request latency, and disclosed non-anonymous operations. ERC-20 and Permit2 Permission Analysis We used viem and Ethereum smart contract ABIs to inspect ERC-20 token balances and allowances through functions such as balanceOf() and allowance() . Our permission discovery engine uses Ethereum Approval events and eth_getLogs queries to identify potential token-spender relationships, followed by current-state contract reads to verify active allowances. We also incorporated Uniswap Permit2's AllowanceTransfer model to analyze an additional authorization layer, including spender allowances and expiration times. A key technical design decision was distinguishing underlying ERC-20 approvals from Permit2 permissions so overlapping spending authority is not incorrectly double-counted. Permission Revocation GrantScope integrates wallet-based transaction signing to help users revoke unwanted token permissions. For ERC-20 tokens, revocation uses approve(spender, 0) . Supported Permit2 authorizations can be revoked through the appropriate Permit2 contract functions. After transaction confirmation, the application rechecks the current permission state instead of assuming that submitting a transaction means the permission was successfully removed. For testing, we deployed a custom GrantScope Test Token (GST) on Ethereum Sepolia, minted test tokens, and created a positive token allowance to validate the scanning and revocation workflow. Explainable Security Analysis We built a deterministic permission assessment engine that evaluates allowance size, token balances, expiration, spender information, and available scanning coverage. Rather than labeling unknown contracts as malicious, GrantScope explains which permissions deserve review and why. We also support read-only scanning of smart-account addresses while acknowledging that session keys and account-specific modules require additional integration. What Makes It Technically Interesting? The most distinctive part of GrantScope is combining privacy-preserving RPC infrastructure with practical wallet security operations . The architecture includes: Browser-based blockchain scanning without mandatory wallet connection. Anon-RPC transport integration with explicit failure handling. Event-based ERC-20 permission discovery. Cross-layer ERC-20 and Permit2 authorization analysis. Wallet-authorized revocation with post-transaction verification. A transparent privacy dashboard that distinguishes anonymized requests from exceptions. GrantScope demonstrates how Ethereum security tools can help users inspect and manage onchain permissions while reducing unnecessary exposure of their blockchain query activity.
projects.project_description_markdown:
## GrantScope — Privacy-First Web3 Permission Management

**GrantScope** is a privacy-first Web3 security platform that helps Ethereum users discover, understand, and revoke token-spending permissions while protecting their blockchain query privacy through the Ethereum Foundation's **Anon-RPC**.

### The Problem

Every time users interact with decentralized exchanges or DeFi applications, they may grant smart contracts permission to spend their tokens. These approvals, sometimes unlimited, can remain active long after the original transaction is completed. If an authorized contract is compromised or malicious, users' funds may be exposed without their private keys being stolen.

The problem becomes more complex with **Uniswap Permit2 and smart accounts**, where permissions can exist across multiple authorization layers. Revoking one permission does not necessarily eliminate every related authorization.

Additionally, traditional wallet security scanners send blockchain queries directly to RPC providers, potentially exposing users' IP addresses alongside the wallet addresses they inspect.

### Our Solution

GrantScope combines wallet permission security with privacy-preserving blockchain infrastructure.

**Key Features:**

- **Privacy-First Scanning:** Integrates Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC to route blockchain reads through supported anonymizing transports such as Tor or Nym, reducing direct exposure of users' IP addresses to RPC providers.
- **ERC-20 Permission Discovery:** Identifies token-spending approvals using blockchain events and smart contract allowance queries.
- **Permit2 Analysis:** Inspects supported Uniswap Permit2 permissions and explains the relationship between underlying ERC-20 approvals and individual spender authorizations.
- **Risk Assessment:** Highlights unlimited allowances, excessive spending permissions, expired authorizations, and permissions requiring review.
- **Permission Revocation:** Enables users to revoke unwanted approvals through wallet-authorized transactions and verify the updated blockchain state.
- **Smart Account Awareness:** Supports read-only inspection of smart-account addresses while clearly identifying limitations around account-specific delegations.
- **Privacy Transparency:** Provides visibility into RPC routing, anonymized requests, network performance, and disclosed privacy exceptions.

### How It Works

Users enter an Ethereum wallet address without connecting their wallet. GrantScope retrieves supported permission data through Anon-RPC, analyzes active allowances, and presents an understandable security dashboard.

Users can inspect which contracts have spending authority, understand their potential exposure, and connect their wallet only when they choose to revoke a permission. After the transaction is confirmed, GrantScope checks the updated allowance to verify the result.

### What Makes GrantScope Different?

Unlike traditional approval dashboards, GrantScope emphasizes **both permission security and inspection privacy**. It helps users understand layered token authorizations while minimizing unnecessary exposure of their network identity during blockchain reads.

GrantScope does not claim to hide public blockchain transactions or support every smart-account permission mechanism. Instead, it provides transparent privacy guarantees, explainable assessments, and user-controlled security actions.

### Our Vision

We believe checking your wallet's security should not require sacrificing your privacy.

**GrantScope makes Ethereum permissions understandable, revocable, and more private to inspect—empowering users to take control of their Web3 security.**
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
## How It's Made — GrantScope

GrantScope is built using **React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS**, with a modular, browser-first architecture designed around privacy, security, and performance.

### Frontend and Architecture

We used **React and TypeScript** to build a responsive Web3 security dashboard, with Tailwind CSS for styling and reusable UI components. The application separates wallet inspection, permission discovery, risk analysis, transaction execution, and privacy monitoring into independent modules.

Instead of relying on a centralized backend to process wallet data, we designed GrantScope to perform blockchain analysis directly in the browser, minimizing unnecessary exposure of wallet information.

### Ethereum Foundation — Anon-RPC Integration

The core integration is the **Ethereum Foundation's Anon-RPC**, which enables privacy-preserving blockchain reads through anonymizing transports such as Tor and Nym.

We integrated the Anon-RPC browser harness into our Ethereum RPC layer, allowing supported JSON-RPC requests to pass through an anonymizing worker rather than directly contacting a conventional RPC provider.

A particularly important engineering challenge was handling anonymous transport initialization, network timeouts, and gateway availability. We designed the transport layer to **fail closed**, meaning it does not silently switch to a non-anonymous RPC connection when an anonymous transport fails.

We also developed a Privacy Lab to report RPC routing, transport status, request latency, and disclosed non-anonymous operations.

### ERC-20 and Permit2 Permission Analysis

We used **viem and Ethereum smart contract ABIs** to inspect ERC-20 token balances and allowances through functions such as `balanceOf()` and `allowance()`.

Our permission discovery engine uses Ethereum `Approval` events and `eth_getLogs` queries to identify potential token-spender relationships, followed by current-state contract reads to verify active allowances.

We also incorporated **Uniswap Permit2's AllowanceTransfer model** to analyze an additional authorization layer, including spender allowances and expiration times.

A key technical design decision was distinguishing underlying ERC-20 approvals from Permit2 permissions so overlapping spending authority is not incorrectly double-counted.

### Permission Revocation

GrantScope integrates wallet-based transaction signing to help users revoke unwanted token permissions.

For ERC-20 tokens, revocation uses `approve(spender, 0)`. Supported Permit2 authorizations can be revoked through the appropriate Permit2 contract functions.

After transaction confirmation, the application rechecks the current permission state instead of assuming that submitting a transaction means the permission was successfully removed.

For testing, we deployed a custom **GrantScope Test Token (GST)** on Ethereum Sepolia, minted test tokens, and created a positive token allowance to validate the scanning and revocation workflow.

### Explainable Security Analysis

We built a deterministic permission assessment engine that evaluates allowance size, token balances, expiration, spender information, and available scanning coverage.

Rather than labeling unknown contracts as malicious, GrantScope explains which permissions deserve review and why.

We also support read-only scanning of smart-account addresses while acknowledging that session keys and account-specific modules require additional integration.

### What Makes It Technically Interesting?

The most distinctive part of GrantScope is combining **privacy-preserving RPC infrastructure with practical wallet security operations**.

The architecture includes:

- Browser-based blockchain scanning without mandatory wallet connection.
- Anon-RPC transport integration with explicit failure handling.
- Event-based ERC-20 permission discovery.
- Cross-layer ERC-20 and Permit2 authorization analysis.
- Wallet-authorized revocation with post-transaction verification.
- A transparent privacy dashboard that distinguishes anonymized requests from exceptions.

**GrantScope demonstrates how Ethereum security tools can help users inspect and manage onchain permissions while reducing unnecessary exposure of their blockchain query activity.**

projects.title: Delulu
projects.description: A private AI diary for women that talks with you and helps you move through life.
projects.project_description: Delulu is a private AI diary for women that talks with you and helps you move through life. Women already tell AI the things they would never say out loud: the 2 AM thoughts, the group-chat drama, "should I text him back?". Today those words sit in plain text at an AI company. Delulu is built so they don't. You open it and write, like a diary. No sign-up, no setup questions, no commands. It talks back like a friend who remembers you: your people, your plans, what you decided last week. When you are stuck on a choice, your split personality answers: the sane one, you at 30, and your bestie, side by side. You pick the voice you follow, and a few days later Delulu checks in: "so... how did it go?" Before the salon, you can try a new haircut, hair color or nail look on your own photo, and Delulu writes the brief to show your stylist. Every chat is private. Each answer comes from a sealed AI on 0G Private Computer and shows its request ID. Your memory is encrypted on your own phone, and one sentence, "delete everything", erases it all.
projects.how_its_made: Delulu is a mobile-first web app built with Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript) and Tailwind 4, hosted on Vercel. You open it and write; there is no sign-up and no setup. Partner tech: 0G Private Computer runs every AI call. We call 0G's OpenAI-compatible router with the model 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b and the header "X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private", so only TEE (TeeML) providers can answer. Every reply comes back marked "x-0g-e2ee: sealed", and the app shows each answer's 0G request ID on screen, so anyone can check it. This is why we can say "every chat is private": the model runs sealed, and our server only passes messages in memory and never stores or logs them. projects.title: Headroom
projects.description: Long-context LLM inference on cheap memory, sold per token to AI agents over x402 on Hedera
projects.project_description: Headroom sells long-context LLM inference to AI agents at H100 prices instead of H200 prices, by keeping only the hot KV cache in GPU memory and parking the rest in CPU DRAM and NVMe. The problem: in 2026, memory, not compute, prices GPUs. H200 rentals rose about 160% this year versus about 35% for H100, mostly because of 141 GB of HBM versus 80 GB. At long context, a model's KV cache can take more memory than its weights, and agents are the workload that grows context every turn. The insight: agents are idle most of their wall-clock time, waiting on tool calls between turns. Their KV cache does not need to sit in HBM while they wait. Headroom parks it in DRAM or NVMe and reloads it on the next turn, so one 80 GB GPU carries far more live agent sessions. Agents tolerate the reload latency; chat users do not, so we sell to agents first. How agents use it: Headroom is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. An agent swaps its base URL and pays per request with no account and no human in the loop: Pay as you go (x402 on Hedera): every request is quoted from the exact prompt token count, paid in USDC (HTS) and settled on Hedera testnet before the GPU sees a token. Every paid request is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic as a tamper-evident spend log. Spend controls: per-wallet daily caps, per-request max price and a model allowlist. Over-cap requests are refused before any quote. Tab mode (Arc): builders running a fleet deposit USDC once into a savings-share escrow on Arc testnet. Usage settles in Merkle-batched posts with a dispute window; any record can be challenged with a proof and its signed EIP-712 receipt. Fair pricing: a Chainlink CRE workflow pulls live H100 and H200 rental prices and sets the H200-equivalent baseline. Buyers always pay less than that baseline, and the escrow rejects any batch priced above it on-chain. A public dashboard shows the capacity curve, cost per 1M tokens versus the H200 baseline, KV tier hits and live paid receipts, with every number linked to a benchmark row or an on-chain transaction.
projects.how_its_made: One rented GPU node runs everything Headroom owns. Hedera, Arc and Chainlink are the only outside dependencies. Inference: vLLM with LMCache in one pinned Docker image (lmcache/vllm-openai), serving Llama 3.1 8B Instruct through an OpenAI-compatible API. Hot KV stays in HBM, warm KV is offloaded to CPU DRAM and cold KV and shared prefixes to NVMe. A benchmark harness replays synthetic agent sessions with tool-call gaps across three configs (baseline, FP8 KV, FP8 KV + LMCache offload) and produces the capacity curve, TTFT and KV reuse numbers. We check that greedy outputs are identical with offload on and off. Payments, Hedera (x402 v2): a TypeScript gateway in front of vLLM. A request with no payment is tokenized (vLLM /tokenize, CPU only), checked against the buyer's caps and answered with 402 and a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header: scheme exact, network hedera:testnet, asset USDC via HTS (0.0.429274), amount = exact micro-USDC quote from a published formula. The agent's x402 client signs a partial HTS transfer and retries; the gateway rejects replays, the Blocky402 facilitator verifies and settles on Hedera, and only then does the request reach vLLM. A meter (SQLite ledger) records tokens, cached tokens, tier hits, latency and price, signs an EIP-712 receipt and writes one message per paid request to an HCS topic. "make audit-prices" recomputes every price from the ledger. Tab settlement, Arc: HeadroomEscrow is a Solidity contract built and tested with Foundry (12 tests) and deployed to Arc testnet from the CLI. Deposit, session keys, Merkle batch posts by a TypeScript signer (viem), a 600 s dispute window, challenge with Merkle proof + signed receipt (refund + penalty), release and withdraw. A reconcile script checks released + refunded + remaining = deposited. Price baseline, Chainlink CRE: a CRE workflow on a cron trigger fetches H100 and H200 rental offers from the Vast.ai API on every node, takes the consensus median and writes the H200-equivalent baseline to the escrow on Arc (CRE supports Arc testnet). Each baseline is also published to its own HCS topic so Hedera holds the audit trail of the Chainlink price. Dashboard: Next.js, reading the ledger and benchmark CSVs on the same node, exposed over a Cloudflare tunnel. Demo buyer agent: a budget-aware long-context agent in TypeScript that pays on its own and slows down near its cap. Hacky bits: CRE lists Arc but not Hedera, so the baseline goes to Arc via CRE and is mirrored to Hedera via HCS. In simulation the CRE MockForwarder means the operator relays the consensus values with setBaseline, labelled with the cre_run_id.

projects.title: zeno
projects.description: On-chain index baskets on Arc: deposit USDC, get basket shares at live NAV, redeem any time.
projects.project_description: ZenoIndex lets anyone hold a basket of assets as a single on-chain token. A manager defines a basket: its tokens, target weights, and entry and exit fees. Investors deposit USDC and receive ERC-20 basket shares priced at the live NAV; they redeem shares for USDC whenever they want, or in kind. Every fee is accounted on-chain in a FeeEscrow that splits it between the platform and the basket's manager. We built it for Arc because Arc is USDC-native: gas is paid in USDC too, so investors think in one currency from deposit to redemption, and blocks finalise in well under a second. Investors use the Zeno Android app. They sign in with an email (a wallet is created for them) or connect any WalletConnect wallet, browse baskets, see NAV, AUM, holdings and fees, and invest or redeem with a preview of shares, fees and the network fee before they sign. Manager Mode lets an allowlisted manager create a basket, set weights, seed it and claim fees. Live on Arc testnet: the factory, vault, fee escrow, access control and Uniswap v4 adapter contracts, a demo basket (USDC plus NVDA, TSLA, META, MU and SPCX test tokens), the API, a website with live basket data, and the Android APK. The stock tokens have no Uniswap liquidity on testnet yet, so deposits are currently held and redeemed in USDC; rebalancing swaps go live once pools are seeded. ZenoIndex began on Robinhood Chain before this hackathon. At ETHGlobal we ported it to Arc and shipped it end to end; the public repo keeps the full original git history and its README lists exactly what was built here.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry): a factory deploys one vault per basket as an OpenZeppelin minimal-proxy clone, each with its own ERC-20 share token. Deposits mint shares at NAV and redemptions burn them; an AccessMaster holds roles; a FeeEscrow splits fees between platform and manager. Asset prices come from an admin price table guarded by staleness limits and maximum-change checks. Rebalancing swaps go through our Uniswap v4 adapter: an unlock-callback router that chains multi-hop exact-input swaps and only accepts allowlisted hooks. For Arc we added zero-address and path checks and overflow-safe price math (FullMath); the Arc suite runs 274 Foundry tests. API (TypeScript, Hono, viem, Postgres on Neon): it reads every basket from Arc in batched Multicall3 calls, signs users in with SIWE or a Privy access token, prepares unsigned transactions for the app, and only confirms an order after checking that the mined transaction matches the one it prepared. It is bundled with esbuild into a single Vercel function, with a daily Vercel Cron for NAV snapshots. App (Expo 58 / React Native 0.88): Privy embedded wallets for email sign-in, WalletConnect via Reown's UniversalProvider for external wallets, viem for chain reads, and BigInt decimal maths so money is never a float. Partner tech: Arc and Circle's USDC are the core. Because gas is USDC, the app keeps a fee reserve out of "max" deposits and shows the network fee in USDC. Arc's native USDC is 18 decimals for gas while the USDC ERC-20 baskets use is 6 decimals, which our chain config had to get right. Uniswap v4 powers rebalancing, Privy and WalletConnect handle sign-in, and Vercel with Neon host the API and website. Hacky bits: Arc's public RPC refuses eth_getLogs over 10k blocks, so basket activity walks back from the chain head in 5k-block chunks. The website reads the vault straight from Arc with raw eth_calls if the API is down. We tested the full invest and redeem flow in the iOS simulator by pairing the app with a scripted WalletConnect wallet that signed real Arc transactions.

projects.title: WEB3MADEAZY
projects.description: Learn Ethereum by doing. Verify you're human, master concepts, and earn real onchain rewards.
projects.project_description: Ethereum is changing how the internet works. But before the next billion people can use Web3, they need to understand it. And today, that learning curve is still too steep. That's the problem we're solving with Web3MadEazy. Inspired by the simplicity of platforms like W3Schools, we built an interactive Web3 learning platform, starting with Ethereum, that makes complex blockchain concepts approachable for everyone, from complete beginners to aspiring Web3 developers. Instead of overwhelming learners with technical jargon, Web3MadEazy teaches through familiar real-world analogies, step-by-step explanations, interactive simulations, and hands-on experiments. We want people to experience how blockchain works, not just memorize definitions. The platform offers two learning paths: Everyday Explorer: A beginner-friendly journey that explains Ethereum through simple language, relatable examples, and interactive demonstrations. Developer Path: A deeper technical journey covering Ethereum concepts through guided lessons, practical simulations, and knowledge assessments. But we wanted to go beyond education. What if someone's first experience of Ethereum wasn't just reading about tokens, but actually earning one through learning? That's why we introduced LEARN, our ERC-20 learning reward token on Ethereum Sepolia. Students complete chapter quizzes, demonstrate their understanding through a final Master Challenge, and become eligible to claim real onchain learning rewards. However, this introduced a fundamental challenge: How do we ensure rewards are distributed fairly? Traditional email verification cannot prevent someone from creating multiple accounts. Wallet verification alone isn't enough either, because anyone can generate multiple wallets. This is where World ID becomes essential to our architecture. We integrate World ID to verify unique humans without requiring students to share personal identity documents with our platform. Combined with backend-enforced chapter-specific reward eligibility, this allows us to limit each verified human to one reward-eligible Master Challenge attempt per chapter reward scope, regardless of how many accounts or wallets they create. Our reward system combines server-side assessment verification, MongoDB-based eligibility tracking, wallet ownership verification, and smart contracts on Ethereum Sepolia to distribute LEARN tokens securely while preventing duplicate rewards. World ID isn't just an integration for us. It's what makes our human-first learning reward system possible. Our vision is simple: make Web3 understandable, practical, and rewarding for anyone curious enough to learn. Web3MadEazy — Don't just learn Web3. Experience it.
projects.how_its_made: Web3MadEazy is built using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion for an interactive learning experience with hands-on blockchain simulations. The backend uses Node.js, Express, MongoDB, and Mongoose for authentication, learning progress, server-side quiz validation, and reward eligibility. We integrated World ID (IDKit) for privacy-preserving proof of unique humanity, preventing multiple accounts or wallets from claiming duplicate chapter rewards. For Web3 integration, we use wagmi and viem for wallet connections, ownership verification, and blockchain interactions. Our Solidity smart contracts, built with OpenZeppelin and Foundry, manage LEARN ERC-20 token rewards on Ethereum Sepolia. A dedicated backend reward worker handles transaction processing, confirmation, and recovery to ensure reliable onchain reward distribution.

projects.title: 0xpay
projects.description: A privacy wallet for proof-backed payments and private blockchain reads via Anon-RPC.
projects.project_description: I built 0xPay to address two privacy leaks in a payment. An ordinary transfer can make the path from a funding wallet to a recipient easy to follow. At the same time, a wallet’s RPC provider can connect the addresses it queries with the user’s IP address. In 0xPay, I deposit 0.1 test ETH into a payment pool and keep an encrypted note that I can back up and restore in another browser. When I pay someone, my browser proves I can spend a deposited note without identifying which deposit authorized the payment. A fresh account with zero ETH submits the transaction, while the pool covers gas and deducts the fee shown in the payment review. Supported wallet reads go through Anon-RPC by default. If that route disconnects, the wallet stops those reads instead of silently using a direct RPC connection. There is also a wallet-free private lookup for checking an address or transaction. In our hosted devnet run, a recovered note paid 0.09614 test ETH to a fresh recipient; after reload, the note showed as spent. The privacy boundaries are visible: deposits, recipients, payout amounts and timing remain public. The RPC endpoint still sees the content of a routed query, but does not receive that request directly from the browser’s IP.
projects.how_its_made: I built the interface with React, TypeScript and Vite. For supported blockchain requests, it uses Ethereum Foundation’s Anon-RPC browser harness and the Nox privacy worker. The wallet encrypts payment notes in browser storage and lets users export a separate encrypted backup, so a note can be recovered in a clean browser profile. The payment pool is a Solidity contract using a Poseidon Merkle tree. In the browser, snarkjs generates a Groth16 proof tied to the pool root, note nullifier, recipient and reviewed fee. The contract verifies the proof, prevents a note from being spent twice, sponsors gas and pays the recipient. Payments use EIP-8141 frame transactions submitted by a fresh account with no ETH. The proof check needs more validation work than the ordinary mempool accepts. 0xPay therefore checks the exact signed transaction and sends it through the normal alternative-mempool sidecar. In the recorded devnet payment, the ordinary path rejected the transaction, the alternative mempool admitted it, and the payment was included in block 6078. Anon-RPC protects the request route; the alternative mempool makes that proof-backed payment possible.

projects.title: Taksh
projects.description: Stay active between your prompts, type a vibe and 0G turns it into a game you play with your body
projects.project_description: Taksh turns a typed or spoken game idea into a game you play with your body. Type "box a rival robot on a Mumbai rooftop" and a few seconds later you are dodging and punching in front of your laptop webcam. No controller, no install. There are 21 game templates: boxing, rowing a koli boat, Dahi Handi, rhythm slashing, a goalkeeper and more. Each one uses moves a laptop camera reads well from a few metres back, like side steps, jumps, squats, punches and hands up. The model picks the template, world, art style and tuning, and code checks every choice before the game runs. In Counter Bout and Last Line you face a rival whose every shot is picked by an LLM on 0G while the round is running. After a run, 0G designs your next level from how you actually played. Scores, the daily challenge and shared games live on Arkiv, and a published game gets its own ENSv2 name whose records are the game itself.
projects.how_its_made: Next.js 16 app. MediaPipe's pose landmarker runs in the browser at camera frame rate, and our move detector turns landmarks into moves. It has regression tests on real webcam footage. The games render with three.js. 0G: an idea goes through the 0G Router to glm-5.3 on the private tier, so only TEE providers serve it. Each call's request id and cost are shown on screen. Whisper on 0G handles spoken ideas. The rival asks glm-5.3 for its next shots whenever its plan runs low. If 0G is slow, the rival keeps its guard up and logs a safe stop. It never fakes a shot. Every finished round (seed, inputs and each 0G decision with its request id) is uploaded to 0G Storage, and npm run replay-episode <root> downloads it with a Merkle proof and replays it to the same score. Players can sign in with a 0G account so their own credits pay. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet): scores, shared games and the daily challenge are typed entities with expiry. Scores live 30 days and shared games 182, so a board is always the last month of play. Writes go through a nonce manager so concurrent posts don't collide. ENSv2 on Sepolia: publishing a game creates a name under taksh-games.eth, and its text records hold the game spec, so the name is the game. The rival agent has its own emancipated namespace. The part we like most: the model never writes code. It fills a typed spec against 21 hand-built templates and code checks every range, which is why generated games run the first time.

projects.title: Ghosty
projects.description: Ghosty: market intelligence besides you 24/7. It speaks the news so you never miss a move.
projects.project_description:
Ghosty is a pocket-sized voice pod with a private trading copilot inside. It watches
crypto and world news around the clock (four news wires, Polymarket odds and a Claude
web-search scout), scores every source for credibility with Ethos, and stays quiet
until a headline can actually move your positions: a war, a sanction, an exchange hack. When that happens, Ghosty buys a short "headline intelligence" report from an
independent seller, paying for it itself over x402 on Hedera. It then asks its brain
on 0G Compute what the news means for you, and speaks the answer out loud: "Strikes
near Hormuz. I suggest a small long on gold. Press to confirm." One press within two
minutes opens a capped Hyperliquid perp (gold, oil, stocks or BTC) plus a small
Uniswap swap on Base. No press, no trade. You can also just talk to it. Hold the button and ask "what's moving gold?" and it
answers from live prices and headlines. Ghosty is accountable and private by design. Every decision is written to 0G Storage
as a tamper-evident chain of episodes with its 0G request ID, and every payment and
trade is posted to a public Hedera audit topic. Your memory and trading style are
encrypted with your own key on 0G, not kept in our database. It pays for information
on its own, inside daily caps, but it never moves your money without a press. If its
brain is unreachable it says so and refuses to trade, rather than guessing. There's also a web app with Live, Device and Feed views, and a Simulate mode that
replays real past events (the SEC suing Binance, the Bybit hack, the Israel-Iran
strikes) on historical prices with real 0G decisions and paper trades.
projects.how_its_made:
Hardware. An ESP32-S3 (N16R8) with an INMP441 I2S microphone, a MAX98357A I2S amp and
speaker, one button, and a 3D-printed ghost enclosure (we wrote a small STL generator
for it). Firmware is Arduino core 3.x with the new ESP_I2S driver. Hold-to-talk
records 16 kHz mono PCM into PSRAM, adds a WAV header, and POSTs it. The server streams
back raw 16 kHz PCM, which we write straight to I2S. We deliberately skipped MP3
decoding on the device: the usual library is GPL and grabs its own I2S channel. The
pod talks HTTPS to our Dockerised server on AWS, with the Amazon root CAs pinned in
firmware. Server. Node 22, TypeScript and Fastify, with zod-validated config and server-sent
events for the UI. It has a strict "live" mode with no stand-ins: a provider without
keys returns "not configured" instead of fake data. A provider-health registry and a doctor command probe every integration. 322 tests. Voice and research. Groq whisper-large-v3-turbo for speech-to-text, and ElevenLabs
flash v2.5 asked for pcm_16000, so the bytes go straight to the speaker. Claude
Sonnet 5.5 answers spoken questions from live context, and its web_search tool runs
a news scout. An intent router sends questions to Claude and anything about trading
to 0G. 0G. Compute through the OpenAI-compatible 0G router (glm-4.7, JSON mode,
zod-validated output, one retry). We capture the router's own request ID for every
decision. If 0G is unreachable, a safe-stop engages and nothing trades. Storage
through the 0G TypeScript SDK: Memory is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload. We chose GCM over the SDK's
built-in AES-CTR so a wrong key or a tampered blob fails loudly. Each decision is an "episode" that stores the previous episode's root hash, so
the log is a verifiable chain. All uploads go through one serial queue, so two writers never race on wallet
nonces.
0G is what makes Ghosty accountable: you can hand a judge a root hash and ask "why
did it buy gold at 3 a.m.?" Hedera. x402 with @x402/core, @x402/hedera and @x402/fetch. The "Signal Desk" is a separate merchant service with its own account. It sells
a bundle of Ethos source credibility, how many outlets corroborate the story, and
shock severity. The agent buys it before each 0G decision and the decision uses
it. Payment prefers USDC as an HTS token, with HBAR as fallback. After the facilitator settles, we check the transfer ourselves on the Hedera
mirror node before marking it paid. Payments, decisions and trades go to an HCS topic as small structured JSON, with
a dedicated submit key that holds no funds. Custody is split three ways: a treasury, a capped agent hot wallet, and the
merchant. Per-asset daily caps; an idempotent hedera:setup script.
Hedera's ~3 s finality and sub-cent fees are what make paying per headline practical. Execution. Hyperliquid through @nktkas/hyperliquid, signed by an API (agent) wallet
that can trade but never withdraw. We use HIP-3 builder markets on the xyz dex (gold,
oil, US stocks), computing asset IDs as 100000 + dex × 10000 + index. A leg-fitting
step keeps every order above Hyperliquid's $10 minimum and under our cap. The spot
leg uses the Uniswap Trading API (check_approval, quote, swap) with native ETH on
Base, signed with viem. Web app. React, Vite and TypeScript, built on our own design tokens. An SSE reducer
batches event bursts so the feed never jumps. The Device page doubles as the pod:
browser mic to 16 kHz WAV to the same endpoint the hardware uses. That let us test
the whole loop before the hardware was ready. Simulation. It replays real past events with their real headlines and sources, on a
compressed clock. Every decision is a real 0G call, but trades fill on a paper venue
at historical prices. Replay walks the episode chain back from 0G Storage. Hacky bits worth mentioning. Hyperliquid only keeps hourly candles back to April 2026, so the historical
simulations are priced from Binance's public klines, with PAXG as a proxy for
gold. Our ISP reset connections to the 0G testnet router and to Polymarket. So compute
runs on the 0G mainnet router while storage stays on Galileo testnet, and the
health monitor degrades gracefully instead of failing. The mic and the amp share one I2S port's clocks in full duplex, and the 24-bit
INMP441 samples are shifted into 16-bit audio on the fly. A confirm only executes an alert the wearer has actually heard, and only within
120 seconds. A stray button press can never trade.

projects.title: Navik
projects.description: Vercel-style deployments for fully onchain immutable websites, controlled by ENSv2
projects.project_description: Navik deploys websites to Ethereum the way Vercel deploys them to the cloud. navik deploy stores a site in contract bytecode as an immutable ERC-8244 release and gives it a permanent immutable ENS name, like 3.example.navik.eth . Production is example.navik.eth and can be updated to point at any deployment, so promoting or rolling back is one ENS write. Preview is preview.example.navik.eth and always points to the latest deplyoment. Who may deploy is an ENSv2 permission: a project owner can grant a CI key "publish" but not "promote", scoped to that project and revocable at any time. Nobody, including us, can change or remove a published release. Reads are private by default. The dashboard, itself hosted on Navik though the same mechanism at navik.eth , sends every chain read through anon-rpc over the Nym mixnet, so the RPC provider never sees who is looking at what. The wallet only signs. Every site opens in any browser through eth.limo, with no server of ours, and our fork of Freedom Browser opens them natively with no gateway at all: type navik.eth and the browser resolves ENS and reads the site straight from Ethereum. Anyone can rebuild a site and compare it byte for byte with what its served deployment. Build provenance and reproduction attestations live on Arkiv, and source archives on Swarm. navik.eth itself ships this way: its dashboard's source is on Swarm, and rebuilding from there matches mainnet exactly.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Foundry). A factory stores content-addressed chunks of up to 24,575 bytes as contract bytecode, so identical chunks are shared across all projects. It deploys each release at a CREATE3 address known before upload. Each project gets its own Permissioned Resolver and release registry. Release names have no expiry and no roles. CLI and dashboard (TypeScript, viem, Preact, Vite). The CLI builds a Vite app, packs dist/ into one document and smoke-tests it in a sandboxed Chromium before spending gas. A GitHub Action previews every merge, reproduces the build on a fresh runner, and promotes after approval. Freedom Browser fork (Electron). We added native support for contract websites, on this branch . Bare ENS names and web3:// URLs resolve ERC-6821 contentcontract records and open ERC-8244 sites through the browser's verified chain-data router, and ERC-4804 and ERC-6860 contract calls work too. Sites stay in the browser's sandbox with no network access, and an opt-in, per-document permission lets an app like our dashboard run anon-rpc there. Partner tech. ENSv2 provides the namespace, per-project registries, release names, least-privilege deploy keys and custom domains through aliasing. anon-rpc carries all dashboard reads, with worker hashes pinned at build time, so no un-anonymized bootstrap read is ever made. If the network is down, reads fail closed. Arkiv stores signed, queryable provenance and attestations with no server. A record is trusted only if its creator matches the publisher logged onchain. navik.eth 's mainnet release has both on Rabdi. Swarm holds the git archive of a release's source. navik reproduce navik.eth fetches it, checks its hash and commit, and rebuilds the dashboard exactly. Notably hacky. Compressed sites are a small loader page holding base64 gzip, which decompresses itself with DecompressionStream and replays the page's scripts in order. Fonts and images get chunks of their own, so changing one word in an app costs 3.5M gas instead of 90M. eth.limo serves sites through ERC-8121 contenthash hooks: a contract function returns the whole page as a data: URL. anon-rpc has no usable Node harness, so navik --anon runs the browser harness in headless Chromium and bridges viem's transport to it, with keys staying in Node. Nym's worker drops Content-Type , which Arkiv's node requires, so Arkiv reads take a separate route over Nox. Our Swarm node is Freedom's antd running standalone, which buys postage in plain xDAI, so we never had to acquire xBZZ.

Every site opens in any browser through eth.limo, with no server of ours, and our fork of Freedom Browser opens them natively with no gateway at all: type `navik.eth` and the browser resolves ENS and reads the site straight from Ethereum.

Anyone can rebuild a site and compare it byte for byte with what its served deployment. Build provenance and reproduction attestations live on Arkiv, and source archives on Swarm. `navik.eth` itself ships this way: its dashboard's source is on Swarm, and rebuilding from there matches mainnet exactly.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
**Contracts (Solidity, Foundry).** A factory stores content-addressed chunks of up to 24,575 bytes as contract bytecode, so identical chunks are shared across all projects. It deploys each release at a CREATE3 address known before upload. Each project gets its own Permissioned Resolver and release registry. Release names have no expiry and no roles.

**CLI and dashboard (TypeScript, viem, Preact, Vite).** The CLI builds a Vite app, packs `dist/` into one document and smoke-tests it in a sandboxed Chromium before spending gas. A GitHub Action previews every merge, reproduces the build on a fresh runner, and promotes after approval.

**Freedom Browser fork (Electron).** We added native support for contract websites, on [this branch](https://github.com/0xAkuti/freedom-browser/tree/feat/web3-names-contract-sites). Bare ENS names and `web3://` URLs resolve ERC-6821 `contentcontract` records and open ERC-8244 sites through the browser's verified chain-data router, and ERC-4804 and ERC-6860 contract calls work too. Sites stay in the browser's sandbox with no network access, and an opt-in, per-document permission lets an app like our dashboard run anon-rpc there.

**Partner tech.**
- **ENSv2** provides the namespace, per-project registries, release names, least-privilege deploy keys and custom domains through aliasing.
- **anon-rpc** carries all dashboard reads, with worker hashes pinned at build time, so no un-anonymized bootstrap read is ever made. If the network is down, reads fail closed.
- **Arkiv** stores signed, queryable provenance and attestations with no server. A record is trusted only if its creator matches the publisher logged onchain. `navik.eth`'s mainnet release has both on Rabdi.
- **Swarm** holds the `git archive` of a release's source. `navik reproduce navik.eth` fetches it, checks its hash and commit, and rebuilds the dashboard exactly.

**Notably hacky.**
- Compressed sites are a small loader page holding base64 gzip, which decompresses itself with `DecompressionStream` and replays the page's scripts in order.
- Fonts and images get chunks of their own, so changing one word in an app costs 3.5M gas instead of 90M.
- eth.limo serves sites through ERC-8121 `contenthash` hooks: a contract function returns the whole page as a `data:` URL.
- anon-rpc has no usable Node harness, so `navik --anon` runs the browser harness in headless Chromium and bridges viem's transport to it, with keys staying in Node.
- Nym's worker drops `Content-Type`, which Arkiv's node requires, so Arkiv reads take a separate route over Nox.
- Our Swarm node is Freedom's `antd` running standalone, which buys postage in plain xDAI, so we never had to acquire xBZZ.

projects.title: Semantic Quorum
projects.description: AI agent marketplace with semantic rubric evaluation, revisions, and USDC escrow settlement.
projects.project_description: Semantic Quorum is a verification and settlement layer for AI-agent marketplaces. A buyer selects an agent, defines the work, reviews an AI-generated rubric, chooses independent evaluators, and funds an ERC-8183 job with USDC. Evaluators score every rubric criterion and the overall deliverable. Passing work pays the agent, deficient work receives precise revision feedback, and rejected or timed-out work refunds the buyer. Semantic Quorum is designed as reusable infrastructure for ERC-8183 marketplaces rather than being tied to a specific agent type or evaluator model.
projects.how_its_made: Semantic Quorum uses Arc’s deployed AgenticCommerce ERC-8183 contract for USDC escrow and a custom Solidity SQController for frozen rubric and evaluator commitments, revision limits, evaluator-fee accounting, signed verdicts, and atomic settlement. Worker agents use models accessed through 0G, while Laya and Vela decision models evaluate each rubric criterion and overall quality. JEV is supported as an alternative evaluator. Evaluators produce EIP-712 signed reports. A Chainlink CRE workflow verifies their signatures and evidence bindings, applies deterministic quorum rules, and runs a two-phase decision process. Draft attempts receive PASS, REVISE, or REJECT; only passing work is submitted to ERC-8183. CRE then verifies the final Arc submission and produces the signed ACCEPT or REJECT verdict used by SQController . A coordinator micro-service starts workers, routes attempts to evaluators, collects reports, triggers CRE, and broadcasts signed verdicts to Arc. It never holds buyer escrow and cannot forge evaluator reports or alter CRE decisions. The coordinator and evaluator services use typescript and are deployed separately on Railway. The React, Vite, and wagmi marketplace is deployed through GitHub Pages, with buyers signing all financial transactions from their wallets. One notable integration challenge is that AgenticCommerce exposes the submitted deliverable hash through its JobSubmitted event rather than getJob() . CRE reads the submission receipt and confirms that its hash matches the evaluated version before signing ACCEPT. Contracts are tested with Foundry unit, invariant, and Arc fork tests. The interface also recovers interrupted funding flows and presents attempts, evaluator scorecards, CRE decisions, and Arc transactions as an auditable deal history.

projects.title: DarkTrace
projects.description: Uniswap v4 hooks detect sandwich MEV, Arkiv seals the proof, and Arc pays back native USDC.
projects.project_description: Liquidity providers and swappers lose over $1B annually to MEV sandwich attacks. Most Uniswap v4 MEV defenses try to prevent extraction inside beforeSwap by adding dynamic fee spikes, delays, or swap reverts—which adds gas overhead to every normal trade and breaks aggregator routing when natural volatility looks like an attack. Meanwhile, MEV analytics dashboards visualize historical extraction after the fact but never return a single cent to the victim. DarkTrace decouples MEV attribution from swap execution to provide post-trade forensics and automated USDC restitution: Passive On-Chain Detection (Base Sepolia): Our Uniswap v4 hook (DarkTraceHook v1 & v2) never blocks, delays, or taxes a swap. Instead, it tracks intra-block tick movements and BalanceDelta round-trip profitability across swaps. When a searcher frontruns a victim and backruns in the opposite direction for a positive net token delta within the same block, the hook emits ExtractionDetected. For split-contract sandwiches where the frontrun and backrun use two different contracts signed by the same EOA, our indexer's off-chain linked-origin scanner catches the evasion from PoolManager Swap logs. Counterfactual Slippage Decomposition: Our deterministic simulator reconstructs the pool's pre-attack reserves from PoolManager events and prices the victim's swap twice using the constant-product formula—once against pre-attack reserves and once after the frontrun—isolating normal liquidity slippage (e.g., 90 bps) from injected MEV slippage (e.g., +35 bps, or $3.54 USDC lost). Tamper-Evident Proof Ledger (Arkiv Rabdi): Every ExtractionReceipt, SearcherProfile, and LPClaim is sealed on Arkiv Rabdi (chain 7794095) signed by our verified writer wallet. Every page in the web app queries Arkiv live with zero mock fallbacks. Beneficiary-Gated USDC Restitution (Arc Testnet): Losses are attested in SimulationRegistry on Arc Testnet, and victims claim native 6-decimal USDC rebates from RebateVault. Only the victim wallet (beneficiary) can claim—we proved on-chain in Verified Run #2 that an unauthorized claim reverts with NotBeneficiary before the separate Victim EOA successfully claimed $3.54 USDC.
projects.how_its_made:
DarkTrace is built as a TypeScript/Solidity monorepo (pnpm workspaces, Foundry, Solc 0.8.26 with Cancun EVM, Next.js 14, wagmi v2, viem, and @arkiv-network/sdk) spanning three testnets: Base Sepolia (84532), Arkiv Rabdi (7794095), and Arc Testnet (5042002). Uniswap v4 Hook (Base Sepolia — 0xCeF7…c0c0 & 0xBCC9…80c0):
We mined CREATE2 salts (0x139d for v1, 0x180d for v2) against Foundry's canonical deployer so the hook address bits match BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG | AFTER_SWAP_FLAG (0x00C0). Notable hacky detail #1 (EIP-1153 tstore vs. multi-tx sandwiches): We initially used EIP-1153 transient storage (tstore/tload) for all hook state, then discovered that while a single-bundle sandwich works in tstore, a real 3-transaction sandwich wipes tstore at the end of tx1! In Hook v2, beforeSwap uses pure tstore (since beforeSwap and afterSwap of a single swap share one transaction frame), while cross-swap state in afterSwap uses a packed 2-slot tload-to-sload fallback keyed by uint48(block.number). Sub-threshold clean swaps execute zero sstore operations, cutting hook gas overhead by 53.7% (58,522 -> 27,085 gas). Notable hacky detail #2 (Eliminating false positives & router batching): Hook v2 consumes PoolManager's BalanceDelta in afterSwap to require strictly positive searcher round-trip profit (frontrunAmount0 + backrunAmount0 > 0), and supports opt-in hookData (0x01 || abi.encode(trader)) so shared aggregator routers can attribute end-user victims without tx.origin. Arkiv Rabdi Proof Ledger (Chain 7794095 — Namespace darktrace.v1):
We built a strict fail-loud wrapper around @arkiv-network/sdk defining three schemas: ExtractionReceipt, SearcherProfile, and LPClaim. Every UI route (/dashboard, /receipt/[hash], /pool/[id], /searcher/[address], /lp/[address]) runs live server-side select().where().ownedBy(writerWallet) queries on every request and displays the exact query in a "Live from Arkiv Rabdi" provenance bar. Deliberate TTL engineering: Standard receipts are written with a 30-day TTL, but our indexer uses Arkiv's extendEntity API to extend receipts with open, unclaimed rebates to a 90-day TTL (verified on Rabdi in tx 0x03512e4f…8744 to block #4,172,852) so forensic evidence never expires while a victim can still claim. Arc Testnet & Arc Studio (Chain 5042002 — Native 6-Decimal USDC at 0x3600…0000):
We generated and validated SimulationRegistry.sol and RebateVault.sol in Arc Studio (60/60 unit, fuzz, invariant, and reentrancy tests passing at 0x5279…2983 / 0x6760…c1de). Because Arc Studio's cloud deployer key is non-exportable and cannot call transferOwnership to our live indexer wallet, we deployed our evolved v2 beneficiary-gated settlement contracts (0xd501…61a2 / 0x238d…4d5b) and v2 Escrow + Claim Expiry contracts (0x31d5…0E77 / 0x0897…E104) via Foundry. Advanced stablecoin guardrails: RebateVault v2 enforces beneficiary-only claims (NotBeneficiary), replay nullifiers (AlreadyClaimed), an escrow dispute window (flagDispute / resolveDispute) where challengers can freeze wash-traded or self-sandwiched claims, and on-chain claim expiry recycling (expireUnclaimedRebate) that returns unclaimed USDC liabilities back into active vault reserves.

projects.title: StratPool
projects.description: Connecting aspiring traders with expert strategies - making trading accessible to everyone.
projects.project_description: Getting started in trading can be intimidating, especially for beginners who lack the experience, technical knowledge or confidence to develop their own strategies. Meanwhile experienced traders and strategists have spent years refining strategies that could benefit a much wider audience. Our product StratPool bridges this gap by creating a marketplace where trading expertise become accessible to everyone. Our platform allows traders and strategist to build, publish and monetize their trading strategies while aspiring traders can discover and execute strategies that align with their individual trading goals and risk preferences. We don't expect users to blindly trust a strategy just because an expert created it, every published strategy goes through a verification process powered by historical market data retrieved through The Graph, leveraging indexed Uniswap trading activity. By analyzing historical performance and market conditions, we can backtest strategies and provide data-driven insights into their potential risks and returns, helping users make more informed decisions. To make the experience even more personalized, our platform features an intelligent strategy matching engine that doesn't force beginners to navigate hundreds of complex strategies and users simply describe their trading intent, and our system recommends the most relevant strategies by applying 2 layers of filtering which incudes hard filtering that matches strategies based on explicit parameters like market, protocol, amount intended to invest etc. The 2nd layer of filtering works on backtesting  which as mentioned earlier evaluates remaining strategies and filters based on performance metrics and ranking all these highlights the best match. Once a user finds a strategy they're comfortable with, they can execute the strategy which is parsed from the workflow into Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) compatible workflow code, enabling secure, verifiable, and automated strategy execution. All trades or swaps involved in the strategy execution is carried out using Uniswap's universal router and Swap API initially focusing on UNISWAP_V3 and UNISWAP_V4 protocols. We've also designed this project to be accessible to strategy creators. Our intuitive drag and drop strategy builder allows strategists to visually define asset flows and trading logic without having to build complex execution infrastructure from scratch. And what makes our incentive model different is that strategists earn commissions only when their strategies generate profits for users. If a trade doesn't make a profit, the strategist doesn't receive a commission. This aligns the interests of strategy creators and traders, rewarding strategies that deliver real value rather than simply attracting subscribers. Our vision is simple: to lower the barriers to trading by connecting people who understand the market with people who want to participate in it. With our product, beginners don't have to start from zero, and experienced traders have a new way to turn their expertise into an earning opportunity.
projects.how_its_made: StratPool brings together blockchain infrastructure, historical market data, automated strategy execution, and intelligent strategy matching to create a secure and accessible marketplace for trading strategies. At the core of StratPool are Solidity smart contracts deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and Ethereum Mainnet. These contracts securely manage user assets through dedicated vault contracts, automate on-chain trade execution, handle performance-based commission distribution to strategists, and manage disputes. By enforcing these processes on-chain, we reduce the need for trust between traders and strategy creators while ensuring transparency and accountability. One of StratPool's most important features is its strategy verification system. We use The Graph to fetch real historical trading data from Uniswap liquidity pools through API queries. This data powers our standalone backtesting engine, which simulates how published strategies would have performed under historical market conditions. Rather than relying solely on claims made by strategy creators, we evaluate strategies using measurable performance metrics to support verification, comparison, and ranking. This encourages strategists to publish meaningful, well-designed strategies and creates a competitive marketplace where quality and performance matter. For decentralized trading, we integrated Uniswap's Universal Router to support on-chain token swaps, initially focusing on Uniswap V3 and V4 protocols. This allows strategies to interact with decentralized liquidity pools and execute trades directly on-chain. We also integrated Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) to orchestrate automated strategy workflows. CRE enables strategies to run through recurring evaluation and execution cycles, monitoring predefined market conditions and triggering appropriate on-chain actions when those conditions are met. This allows users to participate in automated trading without constantly monitoring the market or manually executing transactions. On the frontend, we used Next.js to build a modern, responsive, and intuitive interface. Users can explore strategies, evaluate their historical performance, and discover strategies suited to their trading goals. We also developed an interactive drag and drop strategy builder that allows strategists to visually define asset workflows and trading logic without having to deal directly with complex underlying infrastructure. Our backend follows an asynchronous, microservice based architecture built primarily with Node.js. We developed two independent services: a backtesting engine that simulates strategy execution using historical Uniswap market data for evaluation, verification, and ranking, and a strategy matching engine that analyzes a trader's requirements to recommend the the most relevant strategy. To connect these services with our Next.js REST APIs, we use BullMQ, a high-performance job queue and worker framework backed by Redis through ioredis. This architecture allows computationally intensive operations like backtesting and strategy matching to run asynchronously without blocking user-facing requests. It also provides reliable job processing, retries, and scalability as the platform grows. For data persistence, we use PostgreSQL to store published strategies, historical backtesting results, evaluation metrics, and other essential platform information. We designed and managed our database schema using Prisma ORM, which helped us rapidly prototype and iterate during development. Within our asynchronous microservices, we use the lightweight node-postgres (pg) driver for direct database interactions, giving us greater control over queries while avoiding unnecessary ORM overhead during job processing. By combining Solidity, Ethereum, Uniswap, The Graph, Chainlink CRE, Next.js, Node.js, BullMQ, Redis, and PostgreSQL, we built an end-to-end platform where trading strategies can be visually created, evaluated against real historical data, intelligently matched to user requirements, and securely executed on-chain. Our goal with StratPool is to make professional trading expertise more accessible while creating an ecosystem that rewards strategists for delivering real value. By combining transparent performance evaluation with profit-based incentives, we aim to build a marketplace where aspiring traders can participate with greater confidence and experienced strategists can monetize their expertise.

projects.title: “Verbatim”
projects.description: You say what you want, and that's the only thing your money can do.
projects.project_description: Verbatim makes your own words the rule for your money, and no app can skip it. Type what you want in plain English. 0G's sealed AI turns the sentence into checks, and every check quotes the exact words it came from. Your vault runs the transaction, then checks the real result on-chain: at most this much leaves, at least that much arrives, only your saved contacts, only contracts ENS says are real, a fair price from Uniswap's own pools, and nothing else. If a hacked app, a fake contract, a bad hook or a stolen key tries anything else, the whole transaction never happens. Our MetaMask Snap shows the same checks inside MetaMask before you sign. projects.title: Chase Dinosaurs
projects.description: A pixel-art egg-chase party game with live points, verified-human leaderboards and bots on 0G.
projects.project_description: Chase Dinosaurs is a pixel-art party game for phones and PCs. One egg, up to four dinosaurs, two minutes: whoever holds the egg when the timer hits zero wins, so you grab it and then survive being chased. It existed before this event, so this is a Continuity entry. It was first shown at ETHOnline 2026 (https://ethglobal.com/showcase/chase-dinosaurs-wecqx), and everything up to the tag pre-ethglobal-mumbai-2026 (7 Oct 2026) came before. Its ETHOnline Web3 layer (Arc stakes, Privy, World ID, the subgraph, 0G agents) was removed on 24 Sep 2026. At Mumbai we shipped the layer that turns it into something to play on an event floor: Points and a live board: 1 point a second with the egg, 5 per steal, 30 for the win, scored by the server and shown in every match. An all-time leaderboard (longest hold, most steals, wins) where only humans verified with World ID rank, one row per person. An admin-only spectator mode that puts any live match on a big screen, with the camera following the egg. Player names instead of dino names everywhere: rooms, name tags, boards and results. Controller support: an Xbox pad plays the match and now drives every menu too. Settings → Controls for keyboard, controller and phone, which lights up whatever you press, plus a choice of stick side on phones. The bots' trash talk on the 0G Compute Router, with a receipt (the request id) under every end-of-match roast. Play it at https://chasedinosaurs.fun. Everything built at the event is in git log pre-ethglobal-mumbai-2026..main, with a build log entry per push and AI use disclosed file by file in docs/ethglobal-mumbai/
projects.how_its_made: The client is React 18 and Phaser 3.90 (Vite, Tailwind, Zustand), shipped as a PWA and as Capacitor apps. The server is Node with Socket.IO and Express on Render. It's authoritative for the egg, the clock and now the score: a steal only counts if the server agrees on distance, timing and shields, and it broadcasts the live board every second. The all-time board keeps each player's best single match, not a sum, so one great match stays on it. Render's free plan wipes the disk on every restart, so the board lives in Upstash Redis over its REST API, with retries and a merge if a read fails at boot. World ID 4.0 (IDKit 4) gates ranking, not playing. The server signs each request with the RP key and checks that the proof is for our action, environment and credential before forwarding it, unchanged, to World's /api/v4/verify. It then stores the nullifier against the player, so a second profile from the same person is refused. The widget is a 409 KB chunk that loads only when someone taps Verify. The bots' lines go through any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. On the 0G Compute Router every response carries x_0g_trace (request id and provider address), which we keep. The results screen shows it under the roast, and /ai/receipts lists the latest. Each line has a 1.1-second budget before the game falls back to a canned one, so synchronous TEE verification stays off for now. Controllers use the Gamepad API, polled every frame into the same input channel as the touch stick. Menus get spatial navigation: the nearest button in the pressed direction, measured edge to edge, because measuring centre to centre sent Down from Play to a footer link. Names follow one rule set on client and server: letters in any script with their vowel signs, digits, and "Name 2" on a clash. Built with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) as a pair programmer. Every AI-assisted commit carries a co-author trailer, and docs/ethglobal-mumbai/AI_USAGE.md attributes each file and logs every prompt verbatim. We set the features and the scoring rules, reviewed and merged every PR, and tested on the live site.
