projects.title: Zoro
projects.description: A firewall for AI agents: only audited MCP tools run, sealed on Hedera, approved by a real human
projects.project_description: Zoro is a security gateway for AI agents. It sits between an agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or any MCP client) and the MCP servers it uses. It makes sure the agent only ever sees tools that were audited, and only does something dangerous when a real person says yes. The problem: MCP tools are text that agents obey. A server can change a tool's description after you approved it (a "rug pull"), hide instructions in invisible Unicode or Morse code, write one tool's description so it hijacks another tool, or slip an instruction into a tool result. The agent then mails out your .env file, deletes a production database or signs away a wallet, and nobody notices until it is too late. Nothing checks this today. How Zoro works: Seal. Every tool definition is fingerprinted and audited by Sentinel: deterministic rules, a diff against the last sealed version, and an AI review. The signed verdict is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic and written to ENS text records, and a Hedera Token Service NFT badge is minted for that exact version. The agent only sees sealed text. If a server changes a tool, the new version is quarantined until it is re-audited. Guard every call. Before a call runs, Zoro checks for private data heading outside, actions that cannot be undone (delete, drop, wipe, force-push, transfer), transactions (decoded into one plain sentence, e.g. "Gives UNLIMITED USDT spending to an unknown contract 0xab12…"), an agent using a powerful new ability for the first time, risky package installs, and hidden instructions inside tool results. Ask a human. Risky calls are held until a person approves that exact action with a World ID Human Seal (Proof of Human). The agent, a script or malware on the same computer can click an "Approve" button; none of them can produce a World ID proof. Because verdicts live on a public ledger, a revocation is a global kill switch. Every Zoro gateway follows the registry topic through the Hedera Mirror Node and blocks the revoked version within seconds, and its NFT badge is burned. Anyone can check a tool on the Verify page: it recomputes the fingerprint, checks the Auditor's signature and reads ENS and the Hedera Mirror Node from your browser, so you don't have to trust our server. Try it live at https://zoro-mcp-guard.vercel.app (nothing to install): Attack Lab: 13 scenarios run against a real gateway (rug pull, invisible-ink poisoning, tool shadowing, cross-server exfiltration, Morse heist, nine-second wipe, wallet drain and more). Each verdict is published to Hedera testnet with a HashScan link. Console: incidents, approvals, a tamper-evident audit log anchored to Hedera, a panic button, and Ask Zoro, an assistant that answers from Zoro's records and reads the Hedera ledger through the Hedera Agent Kit. Registry and Verify: every sealed tool with its ENS name, Hedera message and NFT badge. Organizations: employees join with World ID (one verified human, one member). The manager sees which MCP servers, packages and AI clients each person uses, never their prompts or files. Claude Code connects to the hosted gateway with one command, or you can run Zoro locally to protect the MCP servers already on your machine.
projects.how_its_made: Zoro is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces) with four packages. GitHub Actions runs typecheck, tests and a production build on every push; the backend runs on Render and the frontend on Vercel. @zoro/core is the shared engine, and it runs in both Node and the browser: canonical JSON and sha256 fingerprints for tool definitions, Sentinel's rules and capability detection, a decoder that unwraps Morse, base64, hex, URL encoding, ROT13, reversed text, leetspeak and invisible Unicode two levels deep, the transaction decoder, the policy engine and keccak Merkle trees. Because the same code ships to the browser, the Verify page computes a fingerprint exactly the way the gateway does. @zoro/daemon is the gateway, built on Hono and the official MCP SDK. It is an MCP server to the agent and an MCP client to every upstream server (stdio and Streamable HTTP), so every tools/list and tools/call passes through it. State lives in node:sqlite (no native builds), the audit log is hash-chained, and ledger writes go through an outbox with retries, so a slow chain never blocks the agent. Sentinel's AI review and Ask Zoro use an OpenAI-compatible API (Groq, gpt-oss-120b). It also ships a Claude Code hook (built-in Bash/Write/Edit get the same checks), a watchdog on AI client config files, and a small bridge for Claude Desktop. @zoro/blockchain holds the Hedera SDK code, the ENS code (viem) and the Auditor key that signs every verdict (EIP-191 over the verdict's keccak256 hash). @zoro/web is the site and Console: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, IDKit 4, with three.js and GSAP on the landing pages. Hedera (no Solidity; only native services through @hashgraph/sdk): Consensus Service: three topics, each with a submit key. The public registry carries signed verdicts, revocations and disputes; the Attack Lab has its own topic; the organization topic carries Merkle roots of audit logs, so an entry can be proven without revealing the log. HCS gives an ordered, timestamped, append-only record with finality in seconds for a fraction of a cent, which is what makes a global kill switch practical. Token Service: the "Zoro Seal Badge" (ZSEAL) NFT. Each sealed tool version gets a serial and revocation burns it, so the supply always equals the number of tool versions currently trusted, visible to anyone on HashScan. Mirror Node REST API: gateways follow the registry topic and recover the Auditor's signature on every message before acting on it, so a revocation published once blocks the tool everywhere and a forged message is ignored. The Verify page reads the Mirror Node straight from the browser. Hedera Agent Kit: Ask Zoro answers questions like "What did Zoro publish today?" or "How much HBAR is left for ledger writes?" through five Agent Kit query tools (topic messages, topic info, token info, HBAR balance, transaction record). It is read-only by construction: only allowlisted tools load, loading fails if any of them is not a query tool, the kit runs in RETURN_BYTES mode, and its client has no operator key. Ledger messages carry third-party text (tool names, revocation reasons), so they reach the model marked as untrusted data, and every ledger citation in an answer becomes a HashScan link. ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): each MCP server gets a namespace under zoro-registry.eth (for example deepwiki.zoro-registry.eth) with its own resolver. Each tool version gets a name derived from its fingerprint, plus current.<tool> for the latest sealed version. The verdict is stored as text records: zoro.fingerprint, zoro.verdict, zoro.risk, zoro.capabilities, zoro.attestation (the Auditor's signature), zoro.ledger (a pointer to the Hedera message) and zoro.status. Any wallet, agent or tool can check a verdict with a plain ENS lookup. A revocation sets zoro.status to revoked, and the gateway re-reads the records and treats any disagreement as a security signal. World ID (IDKit 4, Proof of Human): the daemon signs each request with a key the browser never sees. Each approval gets its own action, and the signal is the digest of the exact call, so one proof approves one call, once. Proofs are checked with World's v4 verify API, and then Zoro checks the credential itself: the verify API does not confirm which credential the app asked for, so a modified page could request a weaker one and still get a valid proof. Zoro refuses anything but Proof of Human (or Orb for World ID 3.0) and opens an incident. Nullifiers count distinct people, so "two approvers" really means two humans. Notable details: The Attack Lab runs real malicious MCP servers in-process against the production gateway code, not a mock-up. Sentinel cannot be talked into a pass: text in a manifest addressed to the auditor ("this tool is pre-approved") is itself a critical finding. npx servers are pinned to the exact version that was verified, so a new publish cannot slip in. Render's free tier wipes the disk on every restart, so Hedera is the source of truth: the gateway rebuilds the public feed from the Mirror Node on boot. HashScan has no page for a single topic message, so Zoro links each message to the transaction at its consensus timestamp.

projects.title: Hundi
projects.description: Pay in USDT with no network. Spend it on, offline. A double-spend costs the sender their deposit.
projects.project_description: Access Now counted 65 internet shutdowns in India in 2025. During a shutdown, wallets and payment apps stop working, and apps that queue a payment give the receiver nothing they can check or spend. For centuries, Indian merchants used the hundi, a paper note that passed from hand to hand and was cashed later. Hundi does the same with USDT. You add USDT and a safety deposit while online. After that, you pay by QR code with no network. The merchant's phone checks the payment on the spot and shows Paid. The merchant can pay their supplier with the same money, still offline. Whoever gets signal first taps Claim and gets the test USDT on chain, with no gas and no seed phrase. Offline, nothing can prevent a double-spend. Hundi proves it afterwards: the contract finds two signatures for the same money, pays both receivers, and takes double from the sender's deposit.
projects.how_its_made: The contract is on Whitechain Sepolia (chain 1874). It holds the USDT and the deposits, and it checks the signature chain on every note when someone claims. Phone keys are P-256 keys made in the browser, and Whitechain's 0x100 precompile verifies them on chain, which is what makes a phone key possible with no seed phrase. The wallet is an installable web app that works offline and passes payments by QR code. A load uses receiveWithAuthorization on the test USDT, so a new user needs no gas. projects.project_description_markdown:
Access Now counted 65 internet shutdowns in India in 2025. During a shutdown, wallets and payment apps stop working, and apps that queue a payment give the receiver nothing they can check or spend.

For centuries, Indian merchants used the hundi, a paper note that passed from hand to hand and was cashed later. Hundi does the same with USDT.

You add USDT and a safety deposit while online. After that, you pay by QR code with no network. The merchant's phone checks the payment on the spot and shows Paid. The merchant can pay their supplier with the same money, still offline. Whoever gets signal first taps Claim and gets the test USDT on chain, with no gas and no seed phrase.

Offline, nothing can prevent a double-spend. Hundi proves it afterwards: the contract finds two signatures for the same money, pays both receivers, and takes double from the sender's deposit.

projects.title: Kredo
projects.description: The unified payment layer for AI apps. One balance. One network. One interface.
projects.project_description:
Every AI app sells its own credits. Users end up with a dozen small balances stuck in apps they no longer use, and every new app has to win a fresh card form before anyone tries it. Kredo is the unified payment layer for the AI ecosystem: one balance, one network, one interface. Users sign in with email, top up once, and spend that balance in any app on the network. No wallet, no seed phrase, no gas. Each app gets a spending limit the user signs, and the vault contract rejects anything above it, even from our own server. Joining the ecosystem takes about 20 lines of code. An app prices its actions in credits and charges with one SDK call. Long jobs like video renders hold credits up front, then capture on success or release on failure. Apps that already sell their own credits can join in light mode and accept Kredo credits as a top-up. Every charge settles on-chain on Whitechain, and apps withdraw their earnings in USDT whenever they like. Every credit is backed 1:1 by USDT in one vault contract. There is no admin mint, and a public reserves page proves the vault covers every balance, live. Useful links Live app and dashboard: https://kredo-omega.vercel.app
Parley, AI chat, paid per message: https://parley-chi-sepia.vercel.app
Lumen, AI images and video paid per use: https://lumen-gamma-rouge.vercel.app
Proof of reserves: https://kredo-omega.vercel.app/reserves
Docs: https://kredo-omega.vercel.app/docs
Server SDK: npm i kredo
React kit: npm i kredo-react
CreditVault (verified): https://explorer.testnet.whitechain.io/address/0xaaA19C7160FDe7532F5f4Fbd698b549A884c664A Try it: buy credits in Lumen, make an image, then open Parley. The same balance is already there. Why this matters 1 balance across every app, instead of one stranded balance per app
0 crypto steps for users: email sign-in, gas paid by the network
~20 lines for any app to join the ecosystem and get paid in USDT
every credit backed by USDT, checked onchain, live
projects.how_its_made: Kredo has three layers: a vault contract on Whitechain, an API with a gas relayer, and a set of hosted pages and SDKs that apps plug into. The vault is CreditVault, a Solidity contract built with Foundry and OpenZeppelin and verified on Whitechain Sepolia. It holds the USDT and tracks every balance, spending limit and hold. Every user action is a signature: deposits use a USDT permit, and connecting, revoking and sending are EIP-712 messages the contract verifies itself. Users never touch crypto. Privy gives each user an email login and an embedded wallet only they can sign with, so we never hold their keys. Users sign, and our relayer submits the transaction and pays the gas in WBT. A charge costs under 0.0005 WBT and settles in about a second. The backend is a TypeScript API on Express and Postgres, talking to the chain through viem. An indexer rebuilds state from vault events and notifies apps through webhooks. The hosted pages run on Next.js 16. Apps plug in with two npm packages: kredo on the server, and kredo-react for a drop-in connect button and live balance. Connecting works like OAuth, so an app only ever sees the user who approved it. Our demo apps join like any outside company, through the public SDK. Parley is a ChatGPT-style chat app, and Lumen is a Higgsfield-style studio for AI images and video. The trickiest part was making a relayer that's safe to run on a single hot key. It simulates every transaction before sending, so a charge that would fail never costs gas. Daily and per-app gas budgets stop one leaked API key from draining the rest. If the relayer runs low, it still lets exits through, so users can always reclaim their credits. And every write carries a unique ref, so a retried request can never charge twice. The demo apps run serverless on Vercel. Parley keeps its session in a signed cookie, and a test key runs every SDK call against fake credits, so apps can build before going live.

projects.title: Upfront
projects.description: Tokenized financing of future receivables: turn a signed contract into USDT funding on Whitechain.
projects.project_description: ABC Builder just won a $100M data centre contract from a global tech company. The client pays when the work is done, but land, materials, machinery and thousands of workers have to be paid for long before that. So ABC goes to the bank, where a loan is slow, needs collateral, and depends on the few lenders who can write a cheque that size. Ordinary investors can't get near a deal like this at all. Big contracts shouldn't wait for big banks, so we built Upfront. It lets ABC sell units of its future payment to investors at a discount and get USDT today. At 10% off, investors put in $90M now and receive $100M at the due date, repaid in USDT on Whitechain. It starts with the signed agreement. ABC uploads it to Upfront, the document stays offchain, and its fingerprint goes onchain so nobody can swap it later. The client confirms the agreement from its own wallet, and investors can see that Verified tag before they buy. ABC then lists the units for sale. An investor joins by proving with World ID that they're one unique human. Their wallet gets the Investor role, they don't share anything else, and if the same person comes back with a second wallet, they're refused, so nobody can get around a deal's investor cap. When they buy, USDT reaches ABC and units reach the investor in the same transaction. Units can move between approved investors, and when ABC settles, one transaction pays 1 USDT per unit to whoever holds them at that moment. The smart contracts hold everyone to the rules: who can take part, how much one investor can hold, where units can move, and when a deal matures. If ABC misses the due date, the deal is marked Defaulted publicly and permanently. Our Admin approves businesses but can never touch anyone's money. All of this is already live on Whitechain Sepolia, with verified contracts and real test USDT. We ran a full deal end to end: two investors paid 9 USDT for a 10 USDT receivable, one resold units to the other, and a single settlement transaction repaid them both. The World ID join works in the live app using World's simulator, including refusing the same person's second wallet. Next, we want World ID to handle compliance too. We set out to block citizens of OFAC-sanctioned countries, such as North Korea, from becoming investors, using World ID's passport credential so that Upfront never sees the passport itself. That selective disclosure is still in preview, so we shipped Proof of Human first. After that come real KYB for businesses, client-paid escrow so repayment doesn't depend on the builder, an insurance pool that repays investors if a seller defaults, and a resale screen in the app. Upfront is on testnet today, and a real launch needs an audit and licensing. Upfront would earn 0.5% of the money raised, paid by the seller when a deal is funded, which is $450,000 on a $90M raise. We only charge when a deal funds, and investors pay nothing extra. That fee is planned and isn't in the contracts yet. Selling receivables is already a big business: global factoring passed 4 trillion euros in 2025, and McKinsey expects $6.7 trillion of data centre investment by 2030. We'd start with data centre builders and their blue-chip clients.
projects.how_its_made: Upfront is three Solidity contracts on Whitechain Sepolia, a React app, and a small NestJS backend. The chain is the source of truth, and the backend never touches money. Each receivable is its own token ID in one ERC-1155 contract, so every deal gets fractional units and all deals share the same rulebook. Every token movement passes through a single check, so nothing can skip the transfer rules. A second contract holds the Seller, Buyer and Investor roles. We're proudest of how the money moves. When an investor buys, USDT goes straight to the seller and units go to the investor in one atomic transaction. At settlement, the contract pays every current holder directly, also in one transaction, so repayment follows the units even after a resale. The contract never holds anyone's USDT. A bank transfer can't swap money for a transfer-restricted token in one step, or pay a list of holders set by a smart contract. USDT on Whitechain can, with fast blocks and low fees, and all three contracts are verified on its explorer. World ID has no verifier on Whitechain, so we connected the two ourselves. IDKit requests Proof of Human with the wallet address as the signal. The backend verifies the proof with World's API and signs a short-lived voucher for that wallet. InvestorGate then checks the voucher, refuses any human it has already seen, and grants the Investor role with no Admin involved. So the proof is checked offchain, and the one-human rule is enforced onchain. The signed PDF stays offchain and its SHA-256 hash goes onchain, so anyone can check a file against the chain. The frontend uses React, Vite, TypeScript, wagmi and viem, and the backend runs on Firebase.

projects.title: Trenches
projects.description: The collaborative social layer for on-chain traders. Turn solo trading into a team sport.
projects.project_description:
Trenches turns solo trading into a team sport.
Found a Trench with people you trust — one tag, one leader, up to fifty traders, open to anyone or invite-only. Enter seasons from your own wallet: internal seasons inside your Trench, global seasons against everyone. Rise up a public ladder nobody can fake: one human per slot, every fill scored on-chain, prizes that pay out on their own.
A season is a trading competition with the assets, the window, the prize pool and the split fixed up front. The pool is escrowed on Hedera when it's funded. Entrants pass one World ID check — one human, one slot, no alt accounts — and trade through Definitive Flash advanced orders (market, DCA, bracket, limit, TWAP) from their own wallet; nothing is custodied, nothing is faked. Fills rank the board on Arkiv in real time, and at the deadline the pool pays the winners while every ranking snapshot and payout is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic.
Your results lift your Trench. Trenches climb a monthly ladder on their members' season results, scored so a crew is ranked on its traders, not its biggest wallet. Every trader carries a handle, XP and a title from Recruit to Warlord across seasons, and appears on every board as  handle · title.
Everything public - Trenches, memberships, seasons, entries, boards, scores, payouts, profiles — lives on Arkiv as wallet-owned entities anyone can query without asking us.
On-chain trading is solitary and unverifiable: a wallet, a chart, a screenshot. Trenches gives traders a crew to climb with and a record nobody can dispute.
projects.how_its_made:
Monorepo: Next.js 15 (App Router) + Tailwind for the mobile-first web app and API routes, a separate Node worker (node-cron) for order polling, board and ladder recompute, XP and settlement, Postgres via Drizzle as a cache/index, and pure TypeScript packages for P&L, Trench score, XP, prize and fee math with 73 unit tests. No Solidity anywhere.
Definitive Flash is the execution rail: quote → order with a platform fee attached → trader signs via Privy (embedded or external wallet) → Flash lands the trade on Base. The worker polls open orders every 15 s and ingests fills with tx hashes; the board uses average-cost P&L with mark prices from Flash quotes.
Arkiv is the public source of truth: trench, membership, season, entry, board, score, payout and profile entities with filterable annotations, wallet ownership and expiry. The ladder, boards, season discovery, Trench pages and profiles read straight from Arkiv queries in server components; Postgres only speeds up joins. Memberships are stored as dated windows, so a trader's fills count only for the Trench they were in at the time, and a leader who leaves hands over to the longest-standing member.
World ID IDKit (Proof of Human, action join-trench, signal = season id) gates entry. Proofs are verified server-side; the nullifier is hashed and unique per season, which gives one human one slot; one handle per nullifier. Success, cancel, invalid and duplicate paths are all handled. Proofs are mocked during the hackathon per World's instructions.
Hedera via the JS SDK, no contracts: one escrow account and one HCS topic per season; prize pool in an HTS token; a TransferTransaction pays winners at settlement; Mirror Node REST shows escrow balance and payout status. Escrow keys are generated per season and stored AES-256-GCM encrypted.
Hacky bits: a DEMO_MODE fast-forward endpoint ends a season and runs settlement on demand so a full season fits in a 3-minute video; Trench scores clamp each member's ROI to ±50% so one whale can't carry a crew; the OG share card is generated per season with @vercel/og so leaders can post the live top 3; and the Trench layer was added in the final three hours behind a feature flag, with the previous build kept deployable as a fallback.

projects.title: PoP
projects.description: PoP brings protected checkout, seller verification and purchase-backed reviews to COD commerce.
projects.project_description:
In India, “Do you offer cash on delivery?” carries a question larger than the payment itself: if I trust you, and something goes wrong, who carries the loss? In most attempts to bridge this gap, one side ends up more protected than the other, when perhaps both should be able to protect each other.
With PoP, we aim to make that possible. A buyer finds a product on Instagram. The conversation moves to WhatsApp. There are photographs, reviews and assurances. Yet at payment, the buyer asks for COD. The seller hesitates too. Packing costs money. Shipping costs money. A refused parcel returns, but those costs do not.
We kept returning to that exchange. Both sides have something worth protecting. Neither should have to build an entire system of trust before making a sale. That trust platform should be automatic and be given to them. PoP: Proof of Purchase, brings protected checkout, merchant operations and portable reputation into one flow. Our ambition is to become a layer of trust for the Indian commerce that already happens across social platforms, especially for small businesses whose credibility has to be earned one conversation at a time.
The buyer pays test USDT into a smart contract on Whitechain Sepolia. The seller’s offer commits to the purchase terms and fulfilment deadlines. At the door, the buyer provides a six-word delivery code, which confirms the handover and starts a short window to report a problem before normal seller settlement. If shipping or delivery deadlines are missed, anyone can trigger the applicable full-refund rule. Disputes have an arbiter and a timeout, so an unresolved case has a defined way forward. For the seller, PoP becomes part of running the business. They open a shop by proving control of their social handle, currently an Instagram handle through a bio code (checked by our team, and auto-approved in demo mode on testnet), and completing a World ID uniqueness check. They receive a payment link and QR code, a dashboard to manage shipping and withdrawals, and a CSV export. Our separate demonstration merchant, Kurta Co., integrates Pay with PoP and receives signed order notifications that it checks against the chain.
We also wanted a completed purchase to leave behind something more useful than a receipt.
A World-verified buyer can leave one review per seller after an eligible completed order. That review becomes a read-only Arkiv entity, transferred to the buyer’s wallet and independently readable by other applications. Kurta Co. already reads those records with its own Arkiv access key. A seller’s earned reputation can reach the next storefront without asking us to open our private database. Reviews live for about 180 days because they describe recent experience. The order history, completed-order counts, lost disputes and bans remain in the Whitechain contracts. There is room for a seller to improve, without rewriting what happened. The current product runs on test networks with test USDT. It demonstrates protected prepayment for a market that often turns to COD for reassurance. Our broader goal is to make that reassurance available across platforms, with evidence that buyers can inspect and credibility that sellers can carry. For us, a brand of trust begins there. A small business with less infrastructure and a large industry should be able to say “you can trust us” and give its customer a way to check regardless, and without worry. In a nutshell, we aim to enable a thought of trust first, just because we will always have the option to.
projects.how_its_made:
We began with a practical question: when something goes wrong with an order, which promises can the software actually enforce?
That question shaped the architecture. PoP is a Next.js application backed by two Solidity contracts, with separate systems for settlement, human verification and published reputation. Each has a specific responsibility in the transaction. PoPCheckout holds the buyer’s USDT and enforces the order lifecycle. It verifies the seller-signed offer, checks the six-word delivery code against its hash, tracks ship-by and deliver-by deadlines, and handles the dispute window and arbitration timeout. When a refund becomes eligible, anyone can submit the transaction that applies the contract’s rule. SellerRegistry maintains seller registrations and bans. We built and tested the contracts with Foundry and OpenZeppelin, using 58 tests invariant testing, then deployed them to Whitechain Sepolia and verified them on Blockscout. The checkout uses the prize-specified test USDT. Whitechain gives the buyer and merchant the same independently inspectable payment record, including what happened after the initial transfer.

projects.project_description_markdown:
In India, “Do you offer cash on delivery?” carries a question larger than the payment itself: if I trust you, and something goes wrong, who carries the loss? In most attempts to bridge this gap, one side ends up more protected than the other, when perhaps both should be able to protect each other.
With PoP, we aim to make that possible.

A buyer finds a product on Instagram. The conversation moves to WhatsApp. There are photographs, reviews and assurances. Yet at payment, the buyer asks for COD. The seller hesitates too. Packing costs money. Shipping costs money. A refused parcel returns, but those costs do not.
We kept returning to that exchange. Both sides have something worth protecting. Neither should have to build an entire system of trust before making a sale. That trust platform should be automatic and be given to them.

PoP: Proof of Purchase, brings protected checkout, merchant operations and portable reputation into one flow. Our ambition is to become a layer of trust for the Indian commerce that already happens across social platforms, especially for small businesses whose credibility has to be earned one conversation at a time.
The buyer pays test USDT into a smart contract on Whitechain Sepolia. The seller’s offer commits to the purchase terms and fulfilment deadlines. At the door, the buyer provides a six-word delivery code, which confirms the handover and starts a short window to report a problem before normal seller settlement. If shipping or delivery deadlines are missed, anyone can trigger the applicable full-refund rule. Disputes have an arbiter and a timeout, so an unresolved case has a defined way forward.

For the seller, PoP becomes part of running the business. They open a shop by proving control of their social handle, currently an Instagram handle through a bio code (checked by our team, and auto-approved in demo mode on testnet), and completing a World ID uniqueness check. They receive a payment link and QR code, a dashboard to manage shipping and withdrawals, and a CSV export. Our separate demonstration merchant, Kurta Co., integrates Pay with PoP and receives signed order notifications that it checks against the chain.
We also wanted a completed purchase to leave behind something more useful than a receipt.
A World-verified buyer can leave one review per seller after an eligible completed order. That review becomes a read-only Arkiv entity, transferred to the buyer’s wallet and independently readable by other applications. Kurta Co. already reads those records with its own Arkiv access key. A seller’s earned reputation can reach the next storefront without asking us to open our private database.

Reviews live for about 180 days because they describe recent experience. The order history, completed-order counts, lost disputes and bans remain in the Whitechain contracts. There is room for a seller to improve, without rewriting what happened.

The current product runs on test networks with test USDT. It demonstrates protected prepayment for a market that often turns to COD for reassurance. Our broader goal is to make that reassurance available across platforms, with evidence that buyers can inspect and credibility that sellers can carry.

For us, a brand of trust begins there. A small business with less infrastructure and a large industry should be able to say “you can trust us” and give its customer a way to check regardless, and without worry.

In a nutshell, we aim to enable a thought of trust first, just because we will always have the option to.

projects.title: QDay
projects.description: Post-quantum hardware wallet for Ethereum: XMSS & ML-DSA signing, EIP-8141 accounts, no ECDSA
projects.project_description: QDay is a quantum-safe hardware wallet for Ethereum. Once an account has signed a transaction its public key is public, and a large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could recover the secp256k1 key from it. So QDay leaves no ECDSA key anywhere in charge of funds. The device is an ESP32-S3 with a 2.8" touch screen and four buttons. It holds two post-quantum signature schemes from one 24-word seed: XMSS over keccak256 (hash-based, 1,024 one-time keys per tree, 2,500-byte signatures) and ML-DSA-44 (NIST FIPS 204, lattice-based, 2,420-byte signatures). You switch schemes on the device. It decodes every transaction itself, shows exactly what it will sign, and signs only after you approve and enter your passcode. Each scheme has its own EIP-8141 smart account. Frame transactions let the account's own code decide what a valid signature is and pay its own gas, so the account checks the post-quantum signature in Solidity in its VERIFY frame (about 120k gas for XMSS, 1.25M for ML-DSA). There is no ECDSA owner, no EOA and no 7702 delegation left behind. EIP-8141 is scheduled for Ethereum's Hegotá upgrade; QDay runs on it today. XMSS keys are one-time, so two independent locks stop reuse: the device advances a flash counter before it signs, and the account refuses any key index below its on-chain nextIndex, even from a cloned device. Private payments: every wallet has a post-quantum stealth address. A payer derives a one-time ML-DSA key from it with X-Wing (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) and pays a shared pool contract. The owner's wallet finds the payment with a view key that can't spend, and the device signs the claim with the one-time key. Finding and spending are both post-quantum, unlike secp256k1 stealth addresses. The web wallet connects to the device over USB with Web Serial: create the account, send ETH and ERC-20 tokens, pay and claim privately, and read every transaction back in a built-in explorer that decodes frame transactions. No device? "Try without a device" opens a demo wallet in the browser on the same chain. It all runs on our own hosted EIP-8141 devnet. Signed on the real board: XMSS transfers at about 192k-197k gas, ML-DSA transfers at 1.31M, and private payments and claims from both schemes. A prototype: not audited, devnet only, the ESP32-S3 isn't a secure element, and the one-time stealth signer is an unreviewed variant.
projects.how_its_made: QDay is Rust end to end, so the device, the browser and the laptop share one codebase: qday-xmss: our keccak256 variant of XMSS, no_std, with a byte-exact spec and test vectors. qday-mldsa: ML-DSA-44 behind a small API (the fips204 crate), plus the one-time keys for private payments. qday-wallet: device logic without hardware: the one-way counter, the key store in flash, passcode, 24-word backup and restore, the USB protocol, the EIP-8141 frame-transaction codec, and stealth payments with X-Wing (the x-wing crate). qday-ui: the screens and five themes. The same code renders them to PNG on a laptop for tests and docs. Firmware: esp-hal, mipidsi and embedded-graphics on a YD-ESP32-S3 with an ILI9341 touch display, its framebuffer in PSRAM. qday-wasm: the frame-transaction codec compiled to WebAssembly, so the web wallet builds exactly the bytes the device signs. Tests compare it with the CLI byte for byte. Contracts (Foundry): an XMSS verifier in Solidity with inline assembly (68k-87k gas per signature); the EIP-8141 account with its VERIFY frame and the nextIndex lock; a CREATE2 factory of EIP-1167 clones, so the address is known before deployment and the account pays for its own creation; the ML-DSA account and factory; and the lattice pool for private payments. The ML-DSA verifier is Fireblocks' evm-ml-dsa-verifier (about 1.23M gas), vendored and patched. Web wallet: React 19, Vite, Tailwind v4, viem and Web Serial. Network: ethrex's EIP-8141 build, Lighthouse, and the ERC-8421 alternative-mempool gateway that carries frame transactions, as one Docker Compose stack on Coolify, with every contract at a fixed CREATE2 address. EIP-8141 is what makes the design possible: without native account abstraction an ECDSA key would still sign somewhere. The hacky parts: Solidity can't emit EIP-8141's new opcodes (APPROVE, TXPARAM, SIGDATACOPY), so the account deploys tiny helper contracts from raw bytecode and calls them. The public mempool caps verification at 100k gas. We patched one line of the gateway's compiled JavaScript to read the budget from an environment variable, and raised it to 10M. The mempool bans the GAS opcode during validation, so we removed 9 profiling GAS opcodes from the ML-DSA verifier and added a test that scans its bytecode for banned opcodes. The pool's verifier takes each one-time key in calldata and reads a shared matrix from a 16 KB data contract, so nothing is deployed per payment. Code costs about 1,555 gas per byte on this chain, so deploying an ML-DSA account costs about 37M gas, most of it the 20,545-byte key. Standard explorers can't read frame transactions, so the wallet has its own. The browser demo signer reads the chain's nextIndex before every signature and saves its counter before it signs, so a cleared browser can't reuse a key the chain has seen. One script runs 654 Rust, 124 contract and 67 web tests; CI runs the Rust and contract ones on every pull request. Built with Claude Code as a coding assistant.

projects.title: Enigma Ai
projects.description: Private AI with self-destructing data. Get answers, plus on-chain proof we forgot
projects.project_description: Enigma AI lets people use AI on sensitive documents and then proves the data is gone. Hospitals, law firms and banks can't paste patient records or contracts into an AI tool. They can't tell where the data ends up or whether it ever gets deleted. A promise from the provider that it was deleted doesn't count as an audit trail. We wanted something you can check instead of trust. Here's how a job works. You pick a file and your browser makes a one-time AES-256-GCM key and encrypts the file before it leaves your machine. The encrypted file goes to 0G Storage. You pay for the job from a prepaid USDT balance on Whitechain. The document text is then sent to a model running inside a TEE on 0G Compute, which returns the analysis along with an attestation. Our backend only passes this along and doesn't store or log it. The browser encrypts the AI's answer with the same key and the backend saves that ciphertext on Arkiv with an expiry timer, anywhere from 5 minutes to 30 days. A receipt goes on-chain on Whitechain with the result hash and the TEE attestation hash. When the timer runs out, the browser wipes the key and Arkiv drops the entity, so whatever is left can never be decrypted. The backend holds no keys and no plaintext at rest. Everything stored is ciphertext it can't read. One honest caveat is that the plaintext does pass through the backend on its way to the TEE. It is never written to disk, but you do have to trust that hop. We list this in docs/SECURITY.md. The demo page shows a split screen. One side is what the user sees and the other is what the system holds, so you can watch the data get encrypted, processed and erased. Built with Next.js, Tailwind, RainbowKit and wagmi on the frontend, client-side PDF, DOCX and XLSX parsing, a Solidity escrow contract tested with Hardhat, and a Node backend. We use 0G for storage and TEE inference, Arkiv for expiring result storage and Whitechain for payments and receipts.
projects.how_its_made: Everything is one Next.js App Router app. The UI and the API live together: the API is route handlers under /api for jobs, infer, history, balance and a cron endpoint. It's styled with Tailwind, with RainbowKit and wagmi for the wallet. A separate Hardhat project holds the Solidity contract. The encryption happens in the browser with the Web Crypto API. Each job gets a fresh AES-256-GCM key that lives in sessionStorage, and the file is encrypted before it goes anywhere. We parse PDF, DOCX and XLSX on the client so the raw document never has to reach our server to be read. The server only ever receives ciphertext and hashes, apart from the one hop to the TEE described below. The contract (EnigmaAI.sol, on Whitechain testnet) is an escrow. A company deposits USDT, createJob locks the 0.50 USDT price, and completeJob releases it. completeJob requires an EIP-712 signature from our oracle key, with the chain ID and contract address in the domain so it can't be replayed on another chain. It stores resultHash, attestationHash and fileHash as the compliance receipt. If a job times out, refundJob returns the money. Whitechain has no real USDT on testnet, so we deployed a mock ERC20. Hardhat tests cover the lifecycle, credits and low-balance edge cases. For inference we call 0G Compute with the 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b model and send the header X-0G-Provider-Trust-Mode: private. That restricts routing to TeeML providers (Intel TDX), and if none is available the request returns a 503 instead of quietly falling back to a non-TEE provider. We hash the returned attestation and put it on-chain. 0G Storage holds the encrypted uploads. There's also a direct mode: if the user's wallet is on the 0G testnet, the browser talks straight to the TEE provider using @0gfoundation/0g-compute-ts-sdk, so the plaintext skips our server completely. Otherwise it falls back to the proxy. Arkiv is what makes the self-destruct real. The browser encrypts the AI result and our server writes it as an Arkiv entity with an expiry matching the job's TTL. When the entity expires the chain drops it, and the browser wipes the key at the same moment. The demo page shows both: the ciphertext query comes back empty and decryption fails. Having the expiry enforced by the protocol, and not by a cron job we run, is what makes the claim believable. Hacky and notable things: Arkiv expiry is a block height, not a timestamp. Our first countdown was wrong because we read it as unix time. We now convert it with the chain's block timing. Arkiv TTLs are whole blocks. We round up to a multiple of the block duration, because rounding down would delete the data early. Our first version rounded to whole days, so a 25-hour request lived for two. Arkiv entities are public, so the design assumes the stored data is ciphertext only. Whitechain's RPC rejects wide eth_getLogs ranges, so the history endpoint scans the job table directly instead of reading events. The server never logs document content. Error messages go through a scrubber (redact.ts) so a failed request can't leak plaintext into logs. One real limit: in proxy mode the plaintext passes through our server's memory on its way to the TEE. It's never written to disk, but that hop is trusted. Direct mode removes it, and docs/SECURITY.md lays out the trust assumptions.

projects.title: Poros
projects.description: Poros turns community trading ideas into AI-assisted strategies you can inspect, test, and improve.
projects.project_description: Poros is a community platform where traders can turn shared ideas into strategies they can inspect, test, sell, and improve together and they can just drag and drop strategies and trade. It connects community discussion, a visual strategy builder, AI interpretation, creator memberships, and trading history in one application. Trading communities often share strategies through screenshots or short messages. These posts can leave out entry conditions, risk limits, or changes made later. A trader can also delete an unsuccessful call, leaving followers with an incomplete picture. Poros addresses this by connecting discussions to wallet-authored strategy versions and their revisions, giving community members more context when deciding whose ideas to follow. Users can discover a strategy in a community and import it into a drag-and-drop canvas. The canvas makes its conditions and actions visible so users can review the rules, change parameters, and backtest with virtual funds. For written strategies, 0G inference helps translate the idea into a structured proposal that passes validation before the user reviews it. projects.title: Inklink
projects.description: Privacy-first printing at local stationary: AI sets up the job, an agent pays it in USDC on Hedera.
projects.project_description: Inklink is a privacy-aware intelligent printing infrastructure that unifies AI assisted document editing and processing, independent print shops, autonomous payments, and physical printing devices into a seamless end-to-end workflow for customers. Instead of manually sending documents over messaging applications and explaining edits to shopkeepers, customers can upload documents and describe modifications using natural language. Inklink's AI processing layer interprets these instructions into structured operations, which are validated and executed by a deterministic document engine. Customers can review and approve the resulting document before proceeding with a quotation and payment. Inklink integrates 0G Private Computer for privacy-aware AI computation and Hedera's x402 ecosystem for autonomous payment coordination. Payment settlement is verified by the backend before the workflow proceeds, rather than trusting a transaction initiation alone. The architecture also connects digital workflows to local printing infrastructure through a shop gateway and ESP32-S3 hardware interface. Blockchain-based verification and document-integrity records form part of the decentralized infrastructure, while sensitive document contents and personal information are kept off-chain. Inklink aims to transform traditional printing shops into intelligent, connected service points through privacy-aware AI, verifiable payments and locally executable infrastructure.
projects.how_its_made: Inklink is built using a combination of AI agent orchestration, privacy-aware computation, blockchain payment infrastructure and embedded hardware. The frontend uses React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, with React Native and Expo for the mobile experience. The backend is built around Python FastAPI, with Firestore for cloud metadata and SQLite for local persistence. Strands Agent SDK orchestrates the intelligent document-processing workflow. One of our key architectural decisions was separating AI reasoning from document execution. Instead of allowing an LLM to directly modify documents, we use AI to interpret natural-language instructions and generate structured operations. These operations are validated and executed by a deterministic Python document engine. This makes document modifications more predictable and controlled. For privacy-aware AI computation, we integrated 0G Private Computer using the GLM-5.3 model, with Standard, Verified and Private processing modes. Sensitive document workflows can use the Private mode. For autonomous payments, Inklink integrates the Hedera x402 ecosystem with the Blocky402 facilitator. The backend handles payment state management and settlement verification, ensuring that a transaction is not considered complete merely because payment was initiated. We also developed an ESP32-S3 hardware interface using an OLED display, physical buttons, LEDs and a buzzer. It communicates with our deployed backend through authenticated HTTPS endpoints, sending device heartbeats and retrieving live job and payment information. Our notable engineering approach is the separation of responsibilities: AI interprets, deterministic code executes, blockchain infrastructure supports verifiability, the payment backend verifies settlement, and local hardware connects the digital workflow to physical printing. The result is an architecture that brings intelligent document processing, privacy-aware computation, autonomous payments and local printing infrastructure into one connected system.

projects.title: Quiet-Pay
projects.description: Gasless USDT payments for shoppers and AI agents, with refunds and verifiable merchant records.
projects.project_description:
QuietPay: Gasless USDT payment toolkit on Whitechain Sepolia. It enables merchants to receive stablecoin payments without the need for customers to hold the network’s gas token or submit transactions themselves. the customer signs a payment authorization A relayer sends it to a smart contract, which atomically transfers the merchant payout and the relay fee. The authorization locks the order, amount, payout address and fee so that the relayer cannot change those payment terms. The project includes an embeddable checkout widget, a TypeScript merchant SDK, a demo storefront, and a merchant dashboard with wallet sign-in. Merchants can track payments and issue partial or full refunds to the original payer. Signed webhooks and persistent receipt storage connect onchain settlement to the merchant’s application. QuietPay also supports machine-to-machine payments through an x402 facilitator and a paid API demo. A budget-controlled agent client can authorize payments for API access while enforcing spending limits.
For reconciliation, an indexer turns blockchain events into merchant ledger records and CSV exports. A separate verifier independently reconstructs those records from chain data to detect missing, duplicated, or altered entries.
QuietPay is a testnet prototype using official Whitechain test USDT. It demonstrates customer checkout, merchant operations, and agent payments through one payment toolkit.
projects.how_its_made: QuietPay is built using TypeScript in a pnpm monorepo, with Solidity smart contracts developed and tested using Foundry. We use React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the storefront and merchant dashboard, while Lit helps us create a checkout component that merchants can easily add to their websites. Fastify powers our backend APIs, viem handles blockchain interactions and signatures, and Zod validates incoming data. For payments, we use the official test USDT on Whitechain Sepolia. Normally, customers would need gas tokens to approve and send a payment themselves. QuietPay simplifies this using EIP-3009 ReceiveWithAuthorization. Customers just sign an EIP-712 payment authorization, and our relayer pays the WBT gas fee to submit the transaction. The PaymentRouter smart contract then sends the merchant's payment and relay fee together, ensuring both happen in a single transaction. To keep payments secure, we include the merchant, order, payout address, amount, and relay fee in the authorization nonce. This means nobody can change the payment details without invalidating the signature. We also support full and partial refunds, where the merchant authorizes funds to be returned directly to the original customer using separate refund nonces. On the backend, SQLite stores orders, payment attempts, webhook deliveries, and refund requests. We also save signed transactions before broadcasting them, so if the blockchain RPC gives an unclear response, we don't accidentally submit the same payment twice. Signed webhooks help merchants automatically update their applications when payments are completed. We also built an x402 facilitator that allows AI agents to pay for API services automatically. Our agent client follows a spending budget, making sure automated payments stay within defined limits. For merchant accounting, an indexer reads blockchain events and converts them into transaction records and CSV reports. A separate verifier checks those records directly against blockchain data, helping identify missing, duplicate, or modified entries without relying only on our database. To test everything, we use Foundry for smart contract tests, Vitest for backend and security-related tests, fast-check for property-based testing, and Playwright for browser testing. GitHub Actions runs our automated checks to help catch issues whenever we push code..

projects.title: Openbox
projects.description: Pay on proof: USDT checkout that pays sellers only when the right box is verified at your door.
projects.project_description: OpenBox is a checkout where the buyer pays upfront, but the seller is paid only when the right box is verified at the buyer's door. The problem: online buyers and sellers don't trust each other. Buyers fear getting a soap bar instead of a phone. Sellers fear fake "it was empty" claims. So many people use cash on delivery: couriers carry cash, refused parcels travel both ways, and sellers wait days for their money. How OpenBox works: The buyer pays in USDT on Whitechain. There's no gas and no wallet popup: the buyer signs once and our relayer pays the fee. The money is held in the DeliveryCheckout contract, not sent to the seller. A courier delivers the box. The courier proves they're the same person at pickup and at the door with World ID (simulated in the hosted demo). The buyer opens the box in front of the doorbell camera. The household's AI agent finds an independent inspector and pays it per check over x402 on Hedera, with no human involved. The inspector checks the serial number and condition, logs the verdict on Hedera and returns a signed result. One settle call on Whitechain then moves the money: Right item: the seller and courier are paid. Wrong item: the buyer is refunded. Damaged: the agent can accept a partial refund only after the household owner approves on their phone with World ID Agent Pass. Get paid early: a seller doesn't have to wait for delivery. They can sell the unpaid order to a lender as a ReceivableNote token on Whitechain and get USDT today. When the delivery is verified, the same settle call repays the lender automatically. Notes can only move between approved lenders, and a small seller bond covers wrong-item or damage losses. What we built: Solidity contracts on Whitechain Sepolia, all verified on the explorer, with 60 Foundry tests. A drop-in checkout SDK: a store adds it in about 15 lines. Separate apps for the merchant, the household (deliveries, doorbell, AI agent spending limits, approvals), the courier and the lender. An x402-paid AI inspection service and a household agent with a spending policy (budget, max price, allowlist). It refuses inspectors that are too expensive and pays the cheapest one. A real World ID Agent Pass approval flow against auth.world.org, with the ID token checked on our server. Business: an example merchant with $400k a month in sales wastes about $8k a month on refused parcels. A 0.75% fee earns $3k per merchant per month and still saves the merchant money. Lending against verified deliveries adds a second revenue line. The same flow scales to factory docks, warehouses and cross-border trade. Everything is live on testnet: real USDT payments, settlements, refunds, a lender repaid at delivery, an x402 payment on Hedera, and a refund approved with a real Orb-verified World ID.

Whitechain: DeliveryCheckout holds each order's official USDT and pays out in one settle call: seller, courier or buyer refund. Gasless checkout: official USDT supports EIP-3009, so the buyer signs once and our relayer pays the gas. The relayer is capped by function allowlist, gas, rate and daily budget. ReceivableNote (ERC-721) turns an unpaid order into an invoice token. A lender pays the seller today and is repaid automatically at delivery. All contracts are verified on the explorer, with 60 tests. Hedera: Inspectors list their URL and price on an HCS topic. The household AI agent reads that list, checks its budget, and pays the cheapest inspector per check over x402 with HTS USDC, with no human involved. Payments and verdicts are logged to HCS. Benefit: inspection becomes a paid service any agent can use, with no API keys or invoices. World ID: Agent Pass: before the agent accepts a partial refund, the household owner approves on their phone via auth.world.org. We verify the signed ID token on our server, including Orb level and the same owner each time. The courier check uses IDKit. It's simulated in the demo because the sandbox app returned feature_unavailable. Hacky bits: Test USDT can't be minted, so we swap testnet WBT for it on Whitechain's Uniswap pool to fund demo buyers. Four Node services didn't fit in Render's free 512 MB, so we run one process per service and a single inspector on the hosted version. World can't bind a message to the approval yet, so we tie each approval to one order on our server. Judges without World App get a clearly labelled "simulated approval" so they can finish the flow.

How OpenBox works:

1. The buyer pays in USDT on Whitechain. There's no gas and no wallet popup: the buyer signs once and our relayer pays the fee.

3. A courier delivers the box. The courier proves they're the same person at pickup and at the door with World ID (simulated in the hosted demo).

5. One settle call on Whitechain then moves the money:
6. Right item: the seller and courier are paid.
7. Wrong item: the buyer is refunded.
8. Damaged: the agent can accept a partial refund only after the household owner approves on their phone with World ID Agent Pass.
9. Get paid early: a seller doesn't have to wait for delivery. They can sell the unpaid order to a lender as a ReceivableNote token on Whitechain and get USDT today. When the delivery is verified, the same settle call repays the lender automatically. Notes can only move between approved lenders, and a small seller bond covers wrong-item or damage losses.

1. Solidity contracts on Whitechain Sepolia, all verified on the explorer, with 60 Foundry tests.
2. A drop-in checkout SDK: a store adds it in about 15 lines.
3. Separate apps for the merchant, the household (deliveries, doorbell, AI agent spending limits, approvals), the courier and the lender.
4. An x402-paid AI inspection service and a household agent with a spending policy (budget, max price, allowlist). It refuses inspectors that are too expensive and pays the cheapest one.
5. A real World ID Agent Pass approval flow against auth.world.org, with the ID token checked on our server.

Monorepo: Solidity contracts (Foundry), a Node/Fastify backend, an AI inspection service, a checkout SDK and Next.js apps.

Whitechain:

1. DeliveryCheckout holds each order's official USDT and pays out in one settle call: seller, courier or buyer refund.
2. Gasless checkout: official USDT supports EIP-3009, so the buyer signs once and our relayer pays the gas. The relayer is capped by function allowlist, gas, rate and daily budget.
3. ReceivableNote (ERC-721) turns an unpaid order into an invoice token. A lender pays the seller today and is repaid automatically at delivery.
4. All contracts are verified on the explorer, with 60 tests.

Hedera:

1. Inspectors list their URL and price on an HCS topic.
2. The household AI agent reads that list, checks its budget, and pays the cheapest inspector per check over x402 with HTS USDC, with no human involved. Payments and verdicts are logged to HCS.
3. Benefit: inspection becomes a paid service any agent can use, with no API keys or invoices.

World ID:

1. Agent Pass: before the agent accepts a partial refund, the household owner approves on their phone via auth.world.org. We verify the signed ID token on our server, including Orb level and the same owner each time.
2. The courier check uses IDKit. It's simulated in the demo because the sandbox app returned feature_unavailable.

Hacky bits:

1. Test USDT can't be minted, so we swap testnet WBT for it on Whitechain's Uniswap pool to fund demo buyers.
2. Four Node services didn't fit in Render's free 512 MB, so we run one process per service and a single inspector on the hosted version.
3. World can't bind a message to the approval yet, so we tie each approval to one order on our server.
4. Judges without World App get a clearly labelled "simulated approval" so they can finish the flow.

projects.title: Supercall
projects.description: Copy-trade crypto callers whose every call, outcome, and payout lives on-chain
projects.project_description: Supercall is a copy-trading platform where callers publish crypto trade calls and followers copy them in one click. What makes it different: every call is an immutable record on Arkiv, burned to a dead address the moment it’s created. Nobody — not the caller, not the platform — can edit a call after the fact. The caller builds a verifiable track record; the follower reads it without trusting anyone’s word. A follower picks a caller, picks a size, and signs. Supercall places a bracket order through Definitive’s Flash API — a market buy with the call’s target as take-profit and stop as stop-loss, attached atomically. When the position closes, the on-chain Hisaab contract on Arc settles the outcome: the caller’s cut, the follower’s return, and the platform fee all move as USDC in one batch transaction. The entire lifecycle — call, copy, status, close, settlement — is written to Arkiv and queryable by anyone without the platform. Users can also bridge any token from Base, Arbitrum, or Ethereum into ARC USDC through a single cross-chain Flash order, so they never need to leave the app to fund their wallet.
projects.how_its_made: The backend is a Hono API on Node, the frontend is Next.js with Tailwind, and the contracts are Solidity deployed with Foundry. Everything lives in a pnpm monorepo with shared packages for the chain config, API schema (zod), fee math, Flash client, and Arkiv client. Trading runs through Definitive’s Flash API. Every copy is a bracket order — market or limit entry with take-profit and stop-loss attached — placed with the follower’s EIP-712 signature and Permit2 approval. The platform fee is collected separately through the Hisaab contract on Arc using a Permit2 witness transfer, not through Flash’s integrator fee. Arc (chain 5042) is the settlement chain. Its native gas token is USDC, so followers never need ETH for gas. The Hisaab contract handles fee collection, call registration, and batch settlement — up to 50 copies per transaction. The worker reads DEX pool events (Aerodrome, Uniswap v3) on Arc to judge whether a call hit its target or stop. Arkiv stores five record types: caller, call, status, close, and settlement. Calls, closes, and settlements are burned (ownership transferred to 0x...dEaD) and marked readonly. Statuses and callers stay mutable for updates. The API snapshots all records once per minute and serves them from memory. Every record carries indexed attributes so anyone can query directly via Arkiv’s SDK or JSON-RPC. Wallet auth is Privy with embedded wallets. Signing uses eth_signTypedData_v4 through Privy’s provider. The deposit bridge switches the wallet to the source chain, signs via Flash’s cross-chain flow, and polls until the USDC arrives on Arc.

The backend is a Hono API on Node, the frontend is Next.js with Tailwind, and the contracts are Solidity deployed with Foundry. Everything lives in a pnpm monorepo with shared packages for the chain config, API schema (zod), fee math, Flash client, and Arkiv client.

Trading runs through Definitive’s Flash API. Every copy is a bracket order — market or limit entry with take-profit and stop-loss attached — placed with the follower’s EIP-712 signature and Permit2 approval. The platform fee is collected separately through the Hisaab contract on Arc using a Permit2 witness transfer, not through Flash’s integrator fee.

Arc (chain 5042) is the settlement chain. Its native gas token is USDC, so followers never need ETH for gas. The Hisaab contract handles fee collection, call registration, and batch settlement — up to 50 copies per transaction. The worker reads DEX pool events (Aerodrome, Uniswap v3) on Arc to judge whether a call hit its target or stop.

Arkiv stores five record types: caller, call, status, close, and settlement. Calls, closes, and settlements are burned (ownership transferred to 0x...dEaD) and marked readonly. Statuses and callers stay mutable for updates. The API snapshots all records once per minute and serves them from memory. Every record carries indexed attributes so anyone can query directly via Arkiv’s SDK or JSON-RPC.

Wallet auth is Privy with embedded wallets. Signing uses eth_signTypedData_v4 through Privy’s provider. The deposit bridge switches the wallet to the source chain, signs via Flash’s cross-chain flow, and polls until the USDC arrives on Arc.

projects.title: OpenBounty
projects.description: Open-source GitHub bounties, AI-reviewed and paid in USDT with no wallet needed
projects.project_description: OpenBounty turns a GitHub issue into a funded agreement with proof. Open-source maintainers fund a bounty from an issue and agree on acceptance criteria. A contributor claims it and opens a pull request. An AI review on 0G Private Computer checks the PR against those criteria, with a request ID on every call so the review can be traced. A maintainer, or an opt-in automatic payout once the PR is merged and the review recommends approval, releases the reward. Payment runs on Whitechain with USDT held in an escrow contract. Nobody needs a wallet app, a seed phrase or gas: users sign in with a passkey, and OpenBounty pays the network fees.
projects.how_its_made:
OpenBounty has three parts: a React client, a Node backend and Solidity contracts on Whitechain Sepolia. Client and backend. The client is React, Vite and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. Sign-in is Firebase with GitHub. The API is Express and Socket.IO on Render, with MongoDB. The Socket.IO server drives live project chat, where members and the AI agent talk. It also fetches GitHub issues and PRs, and receives GitHub webhooks. 0G Private Computer. This is the AI core. Every call goes through the 0G router with the glm-5.2 model: Project Q&A answers questions from a pinned repository snapshot.
Criteria drafting writes acceptance criteria for a task or issue.
PR review checks each pull request criterion by criterion. Every response keeps its 0G request ID and the E2EE header details. These show up in chat, the review screen, the GitHub comment and an activity tab. CI results are kept separate from the AI’s opinion, and the review’s citations are checked against the actual diff. Without 0G there are no criteria, no evidence reports and no automatic payouts. Whitechain. Rewards are USDT held in a BountyEscrow contract (Solidity 0.8.28, OpenZeppelin 5, Hardhat). A payout needs two separate signatures: an EIP-712 approval from a maintainer, or from an opt-in capped payout agent;
a backend attestation that binds the reviewed commit, the merge and the report hash. The recipient is fixed when a claim is accepted. Users have no wallet app. Each gets a passkey smart account (WebAuthn P-256, ERC-1271, created through a CREATE2 factory). OpenBounty’s gas sponsor pays the WBT fees, so users only ever hold USDT. The sponsor can only call allowlisted functions, simulates every transaction first, and has per-user and daily limits. An indexer mirrors escrow events into MongoDB. Both contracts are deployed and verified on the explorer.

projects.title: tocsin
projects.description: Open standard for onchain registry of scam address reports, verified on your device before you sign
projects.project_description: Every wallet decides whether an address is dangerous by asking a company. Some keep their own list; most pull from Etherscan, Blockscout, Blockaid, ScamSniffer, etc. over an API. The user cannot verify the answer, and the company learns every address the user checks. Devcon 8 is full of talks about light clients and anonymous RPCs because access to Ethereum is still centralised. Security is the part nobody solved yet. Tocsin is an append-only log of scam infrastructure that lives in Ethereum state. It has no owner, no pause, no upgrade, and no delete. Anyone appends flags, but only into their own namespace, and the contract hashes every flag into the writer's chain so nothing can be removed or rewritten. The log never says who to believe. A trust list, signed by whoever maintains it and published under an ENS name, says which writers count. A wallet pins the lists it wants. One listed writer warns, two independent writers block, and the user can always override on the device. The wallet reads it without trusting anyone. Helios verifies the state root, one storage proof covers the writers the user's lists name, the entries come from any mirror and are replayed against the proven head, and every address check runs locally. All execution reads go through the EF's Anon-RPC worker, so the RPC can neither lie nor learn what was looked up. In the demo the RPC says "clean"; the wallet catches the chain mismatch, pulls the same entries from a mirror it does not trust either, and blocks anyway. We do not chase throwaway lookalike addresses, which a local prefix check handles better. We remember what attackers reuse for years: the operators that plant dust, the funders behind them, drainer receivers and spenders, malicious delegates, and malicious tokens. A flag costs its writer about half a cent. Readers pay nothing. There is an ERC draft, "Append-Only Threat Flag Log", that specifies the log, the entry format, the trust lists, and the read procedure. The log runs on Sepolia. Trust lists live as ENSv2 subregistries. The wallet does the whole read path through Helios and Anon-RPC. All of it is open source, MIT for the code and CC0 for the ERC.
projects.how_its_made: The contract is Solidity, built with Foundry inside Scaffold-ETH 2. It stores no flags. Each writer gets a head and a count at a fixed storage slot, and an append folds the new leaf hash into the head, so a reader proves a writer's whole history with one storage proof. We deploy with CREATE2 through the deterministic deployment proxy, salt zero, so the address is the same on anvil, Sepolia and mainnet. It is live on Sepolia with 92 seeded leaves under the maintainer key and one under the detector's. The tests cover normative cases 1 to 9 from our ERC draft, the signature and ERC-1271 boundaries, fuzzed batches, a replay invariant and a gas snapshot that puts a flag in a 100-leaf batch at 9,865 gas. We also wrote ERC-7730 clear-signing descriptors for both write functions, append and appendSigned. The wallet side is one TypeScript reader built on viem, copied into both hosts. It proves the heads of the pinned writers against a state root, pulls their entries with eth_getLogs from any source, replays the hash chain from a checkpoint and checks addresses on the device. If the logs don't hash to the proven head it returns unverifiable, never clean. Trust lists are EIP-712 documents signed by a maintainer and published as a text record under an ENS name. The reader finds a record with one eth_call to the Universal Resolver, CCIP-read off, so a host can route it through its light client, and it pins the maintainer on first use. One listed writer warns and two independent writers block. The hub itself is on ENSv2 Sepolia, set up with ensjs 5: tocsin.eth owns an emancipated subregistry, so nobody can revoke a claimed name, and a MirrorRegistrar lets whoever owns label.eth claim label.tocsin.eth in one transaction. A hot key may set only the list record, through ENSv2's text-record roles. Three lists ship by default: our own core.tocsin.eth and two curator lists. Two hosts use the reader. Kohaku, the EF privacy wallet, is the primary one and ships as two patches on a pinned upstream clone, so the repo holds no Kohaku source. A TocsinController in kohaku-commons checks the send recipient, the spenders and EIP-7702 delegates in sign-account-op, the permit spenders in sign-message, and the token contract itself, so a malicious token blocks Send whatever the recipient. A Tocsin page in Settings holds the RPC and the sync. The MetaMask Snap uses transaction and signature insights to check recipients, spenders, Permit2 and EIP-2612 spenders, Uniswap swap recipients and token contracts, and raises MetaMask's critical warning on a match. The Snap reads proofs from a configured RPC. The hacky part is the Anon-RPC wiring in Kohaku. We fetch the Anon-RPC worker through a mainnet Helios, a16z's light client, so it checks the worker's hash against the on-chain specifier before we load it. Then we shim globalThis.fetch so the reads go through the worker over Tor. The RPC never learns which addresses you check. The worker lives in an offscreen document, the service worker relays its fetches over a named port, and the harness's isolation frame is a manifest sandbox page because the extension CSP blocks the inline one. Every Tocsin read goes through the worker, and Kohaku's own balance, gas and bundler reads stay direct on purpose. Kohaku takes the header and proofs from one RPC for now, so a lie about the head is only as detectable as that RPC is honest, while a lie about the entries still fails replay. Nym has a switch and no test yet. For the demo we built a seed script, a relayer, a detector, a lying RPC proxy, a snapshot mirror and a one-button demo board. The detector is an automated writer with its own name, detector.tocsin.eth, and its own list. It flags the operators behind address-poisoning dust, applies the ERC-4337 sender rule, and its live mode found two real sprayers in a 40-block scan of mainnet. Point the wallet at the lying proxy and it says "unverifiable, chain mismatch at sequence N". Pull the same entries from the mirror and the block comes back. All three beats were verified in Kohaku on 6 November with no direct RPC request leaving the service worker, and one script starts the Tor gateway, the static site and the lying proxy. A walkaway test deletes our ENS records, list host and mirror, and the built Snap still blocks the seeded drainer.
