projects.title: Argos
projects.description: Detects when the code behind a clear-signing descriptor changes, and explains what changed
projects.project_description: Argos monitors upgradeable smart contracts used in ERC-7730 clear signing and tells you when the code behind them changes. Clear signing lets a wallet show a readable message like "Supply 100 USDC" instead of raw calldata. The wallet finds the right descriptor by contract address. For an upgradeable proxy, though, the address stays the same after an upgrade while the code behind it is replaced. The wallet keeps showing the same message even though different code is now running. We checked every mainnet contract in the Ethereum Foundation's ERC-7730 registry and found that 314 of 652 (48%) are upgradeable proxies, and the registry records which implementation it described for none of them. Argos records each contract's implementation as a baseline and keeps checking it. A watcher reads proxy slots and upgrade events every 60 seconds across 30 mainnet proxies from 19 protocols, plus our Sepolia demo contracts. It supports EIP-1967, beacon, diamond and Safe proxies. A contract that is upgraded and then quietly switched back stays flagged, so a temporary swap can't hide. When a change is detected, Argos also explains it. It reads the deployed bytecode of the old and new implementations, compares their function selectors, and asks a model on 0G Private Computer to describe the difference in a few plain sentences. This works on unverified contracts too, because it never needs source code or a block explorer. The explanation is descriptive by design: Argos never labels an upgrade safe or malicious. We mirrored the entire ERC-7730 registry onto Arkiv, 771 descriptors and 2,678 deployments, so anyone can query it by chain, address, protocol or attestation status. The descriptor files themselves are stored on Swarm. Before showing a descriptor, the browser checks that its bytes match the hash published on Arkiv, and rejects it if they don't. The demo includes a toggle that corrupts a descriptor so you can watch the check fail. The app is built to fail safely. Each contract shows one of three states: Verified, Change detected, or Not verified. If the watcher stops or is blocked, every contract moves to Not verified within 5 minutes with the reason shown, instead of continuing to show an outdated green. Anyone can add their own proxy. Argos inspects it, shows the evidence, and asks you to confirm the baseline yourself. There is no backend, no database, no login and no tracking, and the app sends the same Arkiv query for every visitor, so nobody learns which contracts you follow. We also built ArgosGuard, an on-chain contract that only forwards a transaction if the proxy still points to the expected implementation, and reverts otherwise in the same transaction. It is a controlled demo of how the gap between checking and signing can be closed. While importing the registry, Argos also found 3 auditor attestations that no longer match the files they were signed for.
projects.how_its_made: Argos is written in TypeScript on Node 24 and organised as npm workspaces: a shared core package, the importer, the watcher and the web app. Every dependency is pinned to an exact version. There is no backend server and no database. All shared data lives on Arkiv and Swarm. Arkiv holds all structured data. We defined eight typed schemas with the Arkiv SDK (1.0.1, Rabdi testnet): baselines, current state, latest change, change notes, a watcher heartbeat, and two tables for the registry mirror. The importer reads the EF registry at a pinned commit and resolves descriptor includes using Sourcify's clear-signing library. It then computes each ERC-8176 hash twice, once with our own RFC 8785 JCS implementation and once with the library, and stops if the two disagree. It also reads every mainnet deployment on-chain to classify its proxy type. In total it wrote 3,449 rows in atomic batches. The import is idempotent and resumable, and it automatically halves the batch size when the RPC rejects a payload as too large. A separate verifier re-checks row counts and compares random files with GitHub. Swarm stores the content. We upload the exact canonical bytes of each resolved descriptor, so one keccak hash proves both that Swarm returned the correct file and that it is the same descriptor auditors sign. Each upload is downloaded again and checked before its reference is saved on Arkiv. All 746 descriptors were uploaded in 53 seconds with no failures. The watcher scans Upgraded, AdminChanged, BeaconUpgraded and DiamondCut events from a saved block cursor and reads the proxy storage slots every 60 seconds. A contract's current state and latest change are written in one batch, so the app never shows a half-updated contract. Freshness is based on a checked_at timestamp with a 5-minute limit, and the watcher publishes a heartbeat for each chain. The watcher's key can update state but cannot write baselines, which require a separate writer key. For explanations, the watcher fetches both implementations with eth_getCode, extracts 4-byte function selectors by scanning for PUSH4 opcodes, and diffs the two sets. It sends that diff to 0G Private Computer through its OpenAI-compatible API. The resulting text is stored on Swarm, and its hash is saved on Arkiv along with the 0G request ID, provider and cost. The browser only displays the explanation if its hash matches. This step runs after the change is already recorded, so a slow model can never delay detection. The web app is static, built with Vite and React 19, and uses viem for live chain reads. It loads Arkiv data with one bulk query that is identical for every visitor, fetches descriptors from Swarm with a visible fallback to the registry, and renders them with Sourcify's clear-signing library. It ships no keys, analytics or third-party assets, and even the fonts are self-hosted. It is deployed on Vercel, and the built app is also published to Swarm. The contracts are written with Foundry. The demo uses an OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 transparent proxy on Sepolia that we upgrade live. ArgosGuardableProxy reports its implementation from code that upgrades can't change, and ArgosGuard uses that to check and forward a call in the same transaction. A few things worth mentioning. The Arkiv SDK puts the access key in the RPC URL, so we route every logged error through a function that removes it. A Windows checkout with CRLF line endings once changed every file hash, and the app's own integrity check caught it on its first run. We found that the public Swarm gateway accepts uploads without a postage stamp, which let us put all descriptors on Swarm before we had our own batch. Finally, we originally routed live reads through Nym but removed it after it booted unreliably, and every live read in the app is now labelled as a direct RPC call so we never imply privacy we don't provide.

Finally, we originally routed live reads through Nym but removed it after it booted unreliably, and every live read in the app is now labelled as a direct RPC call so we never imply privacy we don't provide.

projects.title: kalash
projects.description: kalash connects temple donations in cash and USDC with digital stamp rallies and dedicated ATMs.
projects.project_description:
Turn temple visits across India into a digital stamp rally with cash donation ATMs and USDC. India has hundreds of thousands of temples.
Religious tourism generates approximately 1.44 billion visits each year, with an estimated annual market size of $16 billion. Millions of people visit temples across India to pray, make donations, and experience the country's rich culture. Imagine receiving a digital stamp every time you donate at a temple and building your own stamp collection as you explore new temples. ◾️That's what kalash makes possible.
kalash combines cash donation ATMs, USDC donations, and a digital stamp rally to make temple visits more fun and memorable. ◾️For Visitors　Donate and Collect Digital Stamps
Visitors use the kalash app to find temples and make donations by depositing cash into a dedicated donation ATM at the temple or sending USDC from their own wallets.
Once a donation is confirmed, visitors receive a digital stamp from that temple. The app saves their stamps, donation history, and photos, allowing them to build a personal collection of their temple visits. kalash also has a leaderboard based on donation amounts. In-person donations earn 10 times as many points as remote donations, making it more fun to visit and explore temples in person. ◾️For Temples　Accept Cash Donations with Dedicated ATMs
kalash ATMs accept cash donations and automatically count and record the banknotes deposited.
Temples can use a management dashboard to check the total amount of cash stored inside their ATMs and view USDC donations. When a temple wants to withdraw cash, it pays kalash a service fee in USDC equal to 3% of the total cash stored inside the ATM. Once the payment and withdrawal authorization are confirmed, an authorized temple representative can withdraw all the cash.
Partial withdrawals are not supported. kalash does not need to collect or transport the cash. The donated cash stays inside the ATM until the temple withdraws it. ◾️USDC Donations　Direct Transfers to Temple Wallets
Donors send USDC directly from their own wallets to wallets controlled by the temples.
For example, when a donor gives 100 USDC, the temple receives the full 100 USDC, and the donor pays kalash a separate service fee of 3% of the donation amount. kalash does not hold the donated funds. It confirms the payment on the blockchain and awards the donor a digital stamp. ◾️How the ATM and Blockchain Work Together
For USDC donations, kalash checks transaction IDs and payment confirmations on the blockchain to prevent the same transaction from generating multiple stamps.
For cash donations, each ATM counts the deposited banknotes, creates a unique transaction ID, and links the donation to a digital stamp. By connecting the ATMs, blockchain, and kalash app, the system brings cash and USDC donations together in one digital stamp rally.

projects.title: AXP
projects.description: AI advertising with receipt-linked USDC nanopayments on Arc.
projects.project_description: AXP connects advertisers with independent AI apps and agents. Advertisers approve campaigns and set spending limits. Apps keep their own answers and models, and show a clearly labelled Sponsored placement separately when a conversation is relevant. A signed insertion receipt links each accepted delivery to advertiser spending and publisher earnings. For ETHGlobal Mumbai’s Arc Studio Continuity Track: Bring Your Project to Arc, we added Circle Gateway Nanopayments on Arc Testnet. Each accepted receipt gets one exact USDC payment authorization. Gateway accepts these small payments offchain and settles them in shared Arc batches. The interface distinguishes accepted delivery, Gateway acceptance and finalized settlement, with public transaction evidence. AXP existed before this event, including its campaign controls, publisher SDK, auction, insertion receipts and Solana/Tempo testnet rails. The hackathon contribution is the additive Arc integration, isolated hosted demo, payment recovery and limits, presentation diagrams, tests and documentation on feature/arc-integration. Production axp.one remains unchanged. Demo answer and buyer responses are labelled fixtures; insertion receipts, accounting, authorizations and testnet payments are real.
projects.how_its_made:
AXP uses Next.js interfaces and a Node.js backend. Its deterministic auction enforces eligibility, bids and budgets; a publisher acknowledgement produces an authenticated insertion receipt. We used Arc Studio to generate and review the nanopayments reference SDK/backend, then adapted its protocol into AXP’s existing receipt and accounting flow. The Arc rail uses Circle’s official @circle-fin/x402-batching SDK, viem, Arc Testnet USDC and the deployed Circle Gateway contracts. We persist exact EIP-3009 authorizations and native transaction identities before external operations, reconcile original outcomes and verify reported batches against Arc RPC receipts. Encrypted durable state and fenced writers preserve the same ledger across hosted requests. Arc signing is enabled only on the designated feature-branch Preview, using an isolated wallet and workspace; existing Solana/Tempo support is preserved. Studio project: https://studio.arc.io/app/0c07e997-5564-4b38-94f9-099ea3e95393
Hackathon source: https://github.com/AkshatGada/axp-one/tree/feature/arc-integration
The repository includes the architecture diagram, reproducible setup, fixture tests and sanitized testnet evidence.

projects.title: Skjol
projects.description: Arrival-delay cover for small importers, with fixed stablecoin payouts when ships arrive late.
projects.project_description: Skjol is insurance against late ships, built for small importers. The problem. A small business that imports goods by sea depends on the ship arriving on time. When it's late, goods sit in port, production lines stop and customer deadlines slip, and the importer pays for it. Traditional cargo insurance doesn't cover this well. It's designed for large shippers, it covers damage or loss rather than delay, and a claim means paperwork, an adjuster and weeks of waiting. What Skjol does. Skjol sells parametric arrival-delay cover. "Parametric" means the payout depends on one fact that can be checked, not on proving how much was lost. The fact is: did this vessel arrive at this port more than 24 hours after the agreed deadline? If yes, a fixed payout is sent automatically. If no, nothing happens. How an importer uses it: Upload the bill of lading. AI reads the document and fills in the vessel (IMO number), the destination port and the arrival deadline. The importer checks these and confirms them. Get a quote and buy cover. The importer sees a fixed premium and a fixed payout, then pays the premium in USDC or EURC. The terms are locked into an on-chain policy, and the pool sets aside the full payout right away, so the money is guaranteed to be there. Wait for the ship. Skjol collects the real port-arrival record from public maritime data (Finland's Digitraffic, or VesselFinder) and submits it on chain. Get paid if it's late. The smart contract compares the recorded arrival with the locked deadline. If the ship is more than 24 hours late, the payout goes straight to the importer's wallet. There's no claim to file and no one deciding whether to pay. Who provides the money. Funders deposit stablecoins into a shared pool and receive pool shares. They earn the premiums importers pay, and they cover the payouts. Their capital can't be withdrawn while it backs an open policy, so a funder can never exit ahead of a claim. A funder who wants out early can sell their shares on a Uniswap market. The Freight Agent. Skjol also includes an AI agent that works for the importer. It can look up vessel and port data, paying for each request with small stablecoin payments (x402). It can also suggest and buy cover. Its spending is capped by limits on the server, every payment decision is publicly logged, and larger purchases need the person to tap Approve. Privacy. Bills of lading are encrypted before they're stored. Shipment records are kept so that nobody can link a wallet to its cargo. Try it. Everything runs on testnet with a demo wallet that has test funds. A demo product with a 2-minute threshold, instead of 24 hours, lets you buy cover, trigger a late arrival and watch the payout arrive in about five minutes.
projects.how_its_made: Skjol is a Next.js 16 app on Vercel with a stateless backend: no database server and no custody wallet. Each partner technology handles one job, and the smart contract makes every payout decision. Arc + Arc Studio (settlement). ShipmentDelayPool.sol is one contract with three roles: an ERC-4626 USDC vault, an EIP-712 quote verifier and a Chainlink CRE receiver. purchase() checks the server-signed quote and locks the vessel, port, deadline and payout into the policy. We moved the contract from Foundry into Arc Studio. Studio added boundary tests (exactly 24 hours late, ±1 second, duplicate reports, wrong pool) and ran a security review. We fixed what it found, and Studio redeployed the pool with 41 tests passing. Exits are priced on free capital so funders can't leave ahead of a claim. MIN_LIVE_SHARES blocks the vault inflation attack. If a USDC blocklist refuses a payout, trySafeTransfer turns it into an owed balance the importer can claim later. Gas is paid in USDC, the same contract runs a EURC pool, and Circle Bridge Kit (CCTP) brings EURC onto Arc. Chainlink CRE (arrival evidence). A TypeScript workflow reads the policy from Arc, fetches the port call from Digitraffic or VesselFinder, and writes an ArrivalReport containing evidence only, never a decision. The contract validates the chain, pool, vessel and port, rejects stale or duplicate evidence, and decides "more than 24 hours late" itself. cre workflow simulate --broadcast paid out real test USDC on Arc Testnet. Hedera + x402 (an agent that pays). The Freight Agent runs on the AI SDK through Vercel AI Gateway and is also available as an MCP server. Our port-data endpoints return HTTP 402 and accept two ways to pay: Arc USDC through Circle Gateway, or Hedera USDC settled by the x402.org facilitator, which pays the fee so the agent never needs HBAR. The server enforces a per-call maximum, a daily cap, a payee allow-list and a kill switch. Every decision is logged to Hedera Consensus Service, and larger cover purchases need a person to tap Approve. Arkiv (the database). Shipments, policies, evidence, chain events and the agent's spending ledger are typed skjol.v1.* entities, and every screen reads from them. Three writer keys (app, observer, sync) show who wrote what, and private fields go in sealed bytes. Swarm (documents). Bills of lading are encrypted in the app with AES-256-GCM and uploaded to Swarm /bytes . We skip Swarm's built-in encryption because its references contain the key and Arkiv is public. The reference is sealed inside the Arkiv entity, and every download is checked against a SHA-256 hash. Uniswap V2. A skjolUSDC /USDC pair lets funders sell shares instead of waiting for reserved capital to be released.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Skjol is insurance against late ships, built for small importers.

**The problem.** A small business that imports goods by sea depends on the ship arriving on time. When it's late, goods sit in port, production lines stop and customer deadlines slip, and the importer pays for it. Traditional cargo insurance doesn't cover this well. It's designed for large shippers, it covers damage or loss rather than delay, and a claim means paperwork, an adjuster and weeks of waiting.

**What Skjol does.** Skjol sells parametric arrival-delay cover. "Parametric" means the payout depends on one fact that can be checked, not on proving how much was lost. The fact is: did this vessel arrive at this port more than 24 hours after the agreed deadline? If yes, a fixed payout is sent automatically. If no, nothing happens.

**How an importer uses it:**

1. **Upload the bill of lading.** AI reads the document and fills in the vessel (IMO number), the destination port and the arrival deadline. The importer checks these and confirms them.
2. **Get a quote and buy cover.** The importer sees a fixed premium and a fixed payout, then pays the premium in USDC or EURC. The terms are locked into an on-chain policy, and the pool sets aside the full payout right away, so the money is guaranteed to be there.
3. **Wait for the ship.** Skjol collects the real port-arrival record from public maritime data (Finland's Digitraffic, or VesselFinder) and submits it on chain.
4. **Get paid if it's late.** The smart contract compares the recorded arrival with the locked deadline. If the ship is more than 24 hours late, the payout goes straight to the importer's wallet. There's no claim to file and no one deciding whether to pay.

**Who provides the money.** Funders deposit stablecoins into a shared pool and receive pool shares. They earn the premiums importers pay, and they cover the payouts. Their capital can't be withdrawn while it backs an open policy, so a funder can never exit ahead of a claim. A funder who wants out early can sell their shares on a Uniswap market.

**The Freight Agent.** Skjol also includes an AI agent that works for the importer. It can look up vessel and port data, paying for each request with small stablecoin payments (x402). It can also suggest and buy cover. Its spending is capped by limits on the server, every payment decision is publicly logged, and larger purchases need the person to tap Approve.

**Privacy.** Bills of lading are encrypted before they're stored. Shipment records are kept so that nobody can link a wallet to its cargo.

**Try it.** Everything runs on testnet with a demo wallet that has test funds. A demo product with a 2-minute threshold, instead of 24 hours, lets you buy cover, trigger a late arrival and watch the payout arrive in about five minutes.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Skjol is a Next.js 16 app on Vercel with a stateless backend: no database server and no custody wallet. Each partner technology handles one job, and the smart contract makes every payout decision.

**Arc + Arc Studio (settlement).** `ShipmentDelayPool.sol` is one contract with three roles: an ERC-4626 USDC vault, an EIP-712 quote verifier and a Chainlink CRE receiver. `purchase()` checks the server-signed quote and locks the vessel, port, deadline and payout into the policy. We moved the contract from Foundry into Arc Studio. Studio added boundary tests (exactly 24 hours late, ±1 second, duplicate reports, wrong pool) and ran a security review. We fixed what it found, and Studio redeployed the pool with 41 tests passing. Exits are priced on free capital so funders can't leave ahead of a claim. `MIN_LIVE_SHARES` blocks the vault inflation attack. If a USDC blocklist refuses a payout, `trySafeTransfer` turns it into an owed balance the importer can claim later. Gas is paid in USDC, the same contract runs a EURC pool, and Circle Bridge Kit (CCTP) brings EURC onto Arc.

**Chainlink CRE (arrival evidence).** A TypeScript workflow reads the policy from Arc, fetches the port call from Digitraffic or VesselFinder, and writes an `ArrivalReport` containing evidence only, never a decision. The contract validates the chain, pool, vessel and port, rejects stale or duplicate evidence, and decides "more than 24 hours late" itself. `cre workflow simulate --broadcast` paid out real test USDC on Arc Testnet.

**Hedera + x402 (an agent that pays).** The Freight Agent runs on the AI SDK through Vercel AI Gateway and is also available as an MCP server. Our port-data endpoints return HTTP 402 and accept two ways to pay: Arc USDC through Circle Gateway, or Hedera USDC settled by the x402.org facilitator, which pays the fee so the agent never needs HBAR. The server enforces a per-call maximum, a daily cap, a payee allow-list and a kill switch. Every decision is logged to Hedera Consensus Service, and larger cover purchases need a person to tap Approve.

**Arkiv (the database).** Shipments, policies, evidence, chain events and the agent's spending ledger are typed `skjol.v1.*` entities, and every screen reads from them. Three writer keys (app, observer, sync) show who wrote what, and private fields go in `sealed` bytes.

**Swarm (documents).** Bills of lading are encrypted in the app with AES-256-GCM and uploaded to Swarm `/bytes`. We skip Swarm's built-in encryption because its references contain the key and Arkiv is public. The reference is sealed inside the Arkiv entity, and every download is checked against a SHA-256 hash.

**Uniswap V2.** A `skjolUSDC`/USDC pair lets funders sell shares instead of waiting for reserved capital to be released.

projects.title: Quantum Smart Wallet
projects.description: Post-quantum Ethereum smart wallet with client signing, sponsored swaps and ENS names.
projects.project_description: Quantum Smart Wallet uses SLH-DSA, a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme, to authorize Ethereum smart account transactions. Users create keys in their browser, swap tokens on Uniswap v4 and register ENSv2 names without topping up ETH for gas. The demo runs on an EIP-8141 devnet. Each transaction separates signature verification, sponsor authorization and execution into frames. A custom ERC-8421 alternative mempool accommodates the higher gas cost of post-quantum verification. The wallet shows each transaction’s progress, token amounts, verification gas and sponsor, with an explorer link to inspect the on-chain result. https://github.com/andreysobol/quantum-smart-wallet
projects.how_its_made: We implemented SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s in Rust, compiled it to WebAssembly for browser key generation and signing, and built a Solidity verifier using Ethereum’s SHA-256 precompile. Our QuantumAccount and factory connect that verifier to EIP-8141 frame transactions. The React frontend builds and signs transactions locally. A TypeScript backend on Vercel creates accounts, provides test USDC and co-signs supported transactions as gas sponsor. The browser submits them to our alternative mempool. We deployed ethrex, Lighthouse, the mempool sidecar and an explorer on a VPS. The sidecar’s custom policy gives qualifying staked senders a 2.5-million-gas verification budget. For swaps, we deployed Uniswap v4 with a QuantumGuard hook that admits only accounts created by our factory. For names, we deployed official ENSv2 contracts alongside our registrar and account-controlled vaults. The vaults provide the ERC-1155 receiver support required to hold name tokens. https://github.com/andreysobol/quantum-smart-wallet

projects.title: DeRPC
projects.description: Private Ethereum reads, verified on your device. Finalized state proofs.
projects.project_description: Ethereum apps usually reveal their users' IP addresses to RPC providers and accept returned data on trust. DeRPC combines anonymous routing with verification on the user's device. Its browser provider sends execution and consensus requests through Anon-RPC and Tor, authenticates finalized Ethereum state with a Lodestar light client, and checks account, storage and code proofs in the host before returning supported results. Users choose operators manually or explicitly enable Balanced, Fastest or Reliable routing. Proof failures reject the response and exclude that endpoint locally; retries stay within the user's authorized pool. If the anonymous route, worker pin or required verification is unavailable, reads fail closed rather than falling back to a direct RPC. EIP-1193 and viem interfaces let browser apps use the same provider with finalized reads. The official site is https://derpc.eth.limo/ and the interactive dashboard is https://derpc.eth.limo/demo/. The demonstration supports verified ETH balances, known-layout WETH storage balances and bytecode, a clearly labeled simulated corrupt response, anonymous failover and refusal after worker shutdown. The free read path needs no wallet, account, API key or deposit. The repository also implements an onion-service operator wrapper, multi-endpoint routing, ENSv2 registrar and proof-backed discovery, bounded opt-in local EVM execution, and optional test-payment modules. The free bootstrap roster still uses mock ENS identifiers: public independent operator enrollment and finalized lifecycle evidence remain gates. A Hoodi test escrow is deployed; that alone is not a public paid-read or settlement demonstration. Staking is unimplemented and payments remain off for the free demo. This is an experimental, unaudited mainnet read provider, not a wallet or production-ready general RPC. Endpoints still see query contents and timing; account unlinkability is unproven. Page assets, bundle delivery and WebRTC gateway setup are outside anonymous application reads. Optional wallet/admin payment transactions also use separate RPC paths. The trusted checkpoint, consensus assumptions and host code remain trust boundaries. State reads use authenticated finalized state, not latest or historical state. Logs, signing and transaction submission are unsupported; eth_call is disabled by default and only available through explicitly enabled, bounded local execution against proven state.
projects.how_its_made: The TypeScript workspace combines the Anon-RPC browser harness 0.4.0, pinned tor-js 0.4.4 worker, Lodestar light client 1.43.0 and viem 2.57.8. Local bootstrap pins avoid a direct bootstrap RPC; downloaded worker bytes are hash-checked, with a gateway mirror attempted before declared resolver fallbacks. After startup, an EIP-1186 proof authenticates the specifier contract's worker-hash storage against verified mainnet state. The host-side Lodestar client authenticates finalized execution headers from a trusted checkpoint, with beacon bootstrap and polling requests carried through the worker. A pinned patch addresses finality validation and shutdown behavior and disables unsafe forced committee updates. The host verifies EIP-1186 account/storage proofs and bytecode hashes, enforces freshness and authorization across asynchronous work, and implements bounded retries, local exclusions and endpoint cooldowns. Verification does not trust worker or raw remote call results. The integrator API is implemented on main: createDeRPC({ operators: MAINNET_OPERATORS.filter(...) }) plus derpcTransport(derpc) for viem. Applications pass blockTag: "finalized", await readiness and close the provider when finished. The package is currently a private workspace package, not an npm release. The curated bootstrap roster contains dRPC, MEV Blocker and BlockRazor at priority 0, and Blast API and PublicNode at priority 1; labels do not prove independence. Vite builds the directory and interactive operator dashboard into a combined static IPFS site. ENS resolves the official name through IPNS. The repository additionally contains EthereumJS EVM-based bounded local execution, ENS discovery/registrar contracts, a filtered Tor onion wrapper, escrow/voucher and sponsored-session modules, plus tests and dated evidence. These implemented modules must not be confused with completed public operator enrollment, a public payment lifecycle or a deployment of every latest main change.

This is an experimental, unaudited mainnet read provider, not a wallet or production-ready general RPC. Endpoints still see query contents and timing; account unlinkability is unproven. Page assets, bundle delivery and WebRTC gateway setup are outside anonymous application reads. Optional wallet/admin payment transactions also use separate RPC paths. The trusted checkpoint, consensus assumptions and host code remain trust boundaries. State reads use authenticated finalized state, not latest or historical state. Logs, signing and transaction submission are unsupported; eth_call is disabled by default and only available through explicitly enabled, bounded local execution against proven state.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
The TypeScript workspace combines the Anon-RPC browser harness 0.4.0, pinned tor-js 0.4.4 worker, Lodestar light client 1.43.0 and viem 2.57.8. Local bootstrap pins avoid a direct bootstrap RPC; downloaded worker bytes are hash-checked, with a gateway mirror attempted before declared resolver fallbacks. After startup, an EIP-1186 proof authenticates the specifier contract's worker-hash storage against verified mainnet state.

The host-side Lodestar client authenticates finalized execution headers from a trusted checkpoint, with beacon bootstrap and polling requests carried through the worker. A pinned patch addresses finality validation and shutdown behavior and disables unsafe forced committee updates. The host verifies EIP-1186 account/storage proofs and bytecode hashes, enforces freshness and authorization across asynchronous work, and implements bounded retries, local exclusions and endpoint cooldowns. Verification does not trust worker or raw remote call results.

The integrator API is implemented on main: createDeRPC({ operators: MAINNET_OPERATORS.filter(...) }) plus derpcTransport(derpc) for viem. Applications pass blockTag: "finalized", await readiness and close the provider when finished. The package is currently a private workspace package, not an npm release. The curated bootstrap roster contains dRPC, MEV Blocker and BlockRazor at priority 0, and Blast API and PublicNode at priority 1; labels do not prove independence.

Vite builds the directory and interactive operator dashboard into a combined static IPFS site. ENS resolves the official name through IPNS. The repository additionally contains EthereumJS EVM-based bounded local execution, ENS discovery/registrar contracts, a filtered Tor onion wrapper, escrow/voucher and sponsored-session modules, plus tests and dated evidence. These implemented modules must not be confused with completed public operator enrollment, a public payment lifecycle or a deployment of every latest main change.

projects.title: Dopamyn
projects.description: Apollo + Gojiberry for web3: pay X creators and find anyone in crypto, in USDT on Whitechain
projects.project_description:
Dopamyn is Apollo and Gojiberry for web3. Web2 sales teams have Apollo, Clay and Gojiberry to find and reach anyone. Web3 has almost nothing, because crypto people live on X and Telegram, not LinkedIn. Dopamyn does two jobs for crypto and AI projects: it pays the creators who spread the word on X, and it finds and reaches the people a project wants to talk to. We are Puneet and Goldie, two founders from IIT Kanpur, building in web3 for over three years. Before this hackathon, Dopamyn creator payouts ran on Base and Arbitrum. At ETHGlobal Mumbai we brought them to Whitechain, and we made our outreach data payable onchain: Contact Finder, paid in USDT with a new gasless contract, LookupPay. Creators: campaign payouts
Brands pay creators to follow, post and reply on X. Today these payouts are slow, fees eat a 1 USDT reward, and creators must trust the brand to pay. With Dopamyn on Whitechain, the brand picks Whitechain and USDT when it launches a campaign and locks the full pool in our QuestManager escrow before any creator works. Dopamyn checks each creator's X task, then pays them in USDT within seconds. Creators never sign a transaction or hold WBT.
Live on Whitechain Sepolia: a brand funded 11.5 USDT into escrow (createQuest), the 1.5 USDT fee went to the Dopamyn treasury, and two creators got 1 USDT each after their follow was checked (sendReward). 8 USDT stays in escrow for the next creators. Outreach: Contact Finder, Apollo for web3
Find how to reach anyone in crypto. Contact Finder takes an X handle and finds how to contact that person: Telegram, email, LinkedIn, GitHub or website. Project team mode takes a project's X handle or website and returns the team: for whitechain.io it found 4 team members in 16 seconds. Each team member has a "Find contact" button that runs a person lookup for that member.
Each lookup costs 0.25 USDT and is charged only if something is found. A card cannot charge 0.25 USD. So the wallet signs an EIP-3009 authorization for USDT, with no gas. When the search finds a result, our relayer settles it through LookupPay, a new contract we deployed and verified on Whitechain, and pays the WBT gas. If nothing is found, the signature is never used and the user pays nothing. Because payment is only a signature, an AI agent can pay for a lookup the same way as a person. Every transaction is linked in the public repo README. The contracts and the relayer are open source. The Dopamyn web app and backend are closed source. Go-to-market Who pays: crypto and AI projects that grow on X. Dopamyn already sells to them (clients include DVERSE, SAI.FUN, RAAC and Velvet Capital) with one Pro plan, plus a 15% fee on campaign reward pools. Proof it works: as of September 2026, brands ran 585 campaigns settled onchain and paid $48.5k to 10,326 creators in 33,949 payout transactions. Campaign payouts: Whitechain is one more payout chain for these brands, in the same launch flow. We switch it on the day Whitechain mainnet opens, and we want to bring WhiteBIT and Whitechain ecosystem projects to run their creator campaigns on it. Contact Finder: no subscription. Any wallet with USDT can pay 0.25 per result, so it brings new users into Dopamyn, and Pro users use it inside outreach. Next: AI agents. We will put Contact Finder behind an x402 endpoint and a tool in our MCP server, which is already live, so Claude, ChatGPT or any agent can pay per lookup in USDT on Whitechain. Note for the judges: we cannot attend the live demo session on November 7, because we are travelling home for Diwali. We talked with Toma (@Toma_Sadova) from the Whitechain team about this before the session. The demo video shows the full product.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts (Solidity, Hardhat, Whitechain Sepolia, chain 1874): QuestManager.sol is our existing escrow contract, already live on Base and Arbitrum (public repo Dopamyn/dopamyn-base-contract, last change 2026-04-20). We deployed the same code, with no changes, to Whitechain Sepolia and verified it on the Blockscout explorer with a custom chain entry. LookupPay.sol is new at this hackathon. pay() calls receiveWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) on Tether's TetherTokenV2. That function requires the caller to be the payee, so only LookupPay can settle a signed payment, and a signature copied from the mempool cannot be used by anyone else or make the relayer's transaction revert. Relayer (Node, viem): /verify and /settle. It checks the signature, price, payer balance, unused nonce and time window, simulates with eth_call, and only then sends. It calls one function on one contract and has a daily transaction cap. Gas for one payment: about 109k gas, 0.0005 WBT. Campaign payouts in the app (closed source): the Dopamyn backend (Python, FastAPI, MySQL) reads chains, reward tokens and treasury wallets from database rows. We added a whitechain-sepolia chain row, the USDT token row and an EVM handler config, so the existing reward worker sends sendReward on Whitechain with web3.py. The web app (Next.js, viem, Privy) got a custom viem chain for Whitechain, the chain in the campaign picker, and USDT as the default reward token. MetaMask adds the network on first use. Contact Finder (closed source): a lookup row stores the signed authorization, not a payment. The search runs first: our directory of 470k X accounts, contacts we already hold, Firecrawl reads of the person's and their company's team, about and contact pages, and Linktree-style link pages, then one Claude call with web search and web fetch that keeps only contacts with proof that they belong to this person. Team mode adds the project's public Telegram (t.me/s pages) and public Discord invite data, and reads the project's X handle from its website when the input is a URL. Only a "found" result triggers /settle. The result stays hidden until the payment transaction succeeds. Hacky part: the brand pays the 15% fee into the same escrow, and the fee counts as one extra winner (maxWinners = creators + 1), so the backend sweeps the fee to the treasury with skipClaimedCheck = true.

projects.title: Tijori
projects.description: Tijori enables object-based authentication and physical presence in a multisig vault.
projects.project_description: Tijori is a SDK designed to bring physical-world context to Web3 security. It is built for DAOs, families, trusts and teams that manage funds together—and for developers who want to add similar experiences to their own applications. Web3 users face two related risks. Private keys can be stolen from compromised devices or lost when recovery information is misplaced. Meanwhile, multisig approvals can be collected remotely, making a treasury vulnerable if an attacker compromises multiple signers or convinces them to approve a malicious transaction. Tijori’s vision is to add two layers to that experience: Object-based verification: A user enrolls a familiar physical object and presents it again when accessing their identity. Sound-based presence: Group members exchange a short-lived unique frequency using their devices, creating an approval experience centered on meeting in person. Tijori brings these ideas together with Safe multisig treasuries on Whitechain. Members can propose a USDT payment and collect a majority of signatures within an approval session. A transaction guard requires an attestation from Tijori’s verifier for the specific transaction. Developers can integrate Tijori through its plug-and-play SDK , which provides reusable server, client and React packages for identity flows, vaults, treasury interactions, acoustic checks and invoices. Behind the scenes, Arkiv stores encrypted application state, while an optional Anon RPC integration explores private balance reads through the Nym mixnet. The API also applies a same-origin policy to browser write requests, blocking cross-origin writes soo that the ip of the location is not exposed. Tijori is designed around the CROPS principles: censorship resistance, open source, privacy and security. It combines decentralized infrastructure, an open-source SDK, encrypted state and multisig controls while continuing to develop and strengthen its verification layers.
projects.how_its_made: Tijori is built with Next.js and a reusable TypeScript SDK. The SDK separates the core domain, server, browser client, React components and invoice integration so other applications can build on the same treasury and identity flows. Object verification We adapted the matching approach from VILA and run DINOv2 in the browser using Transformers.js. During enrollment and sign-in, SlimSAM helps isolate the foreground object before DINOv2 extracts its visual features. The app compares the new features with a compact enrolled reference; original photos and masks stay on the device. Frequency-based matching For the standalone acoustic demonstration, we use ggwave compiled to WebAssembly to transmit and decode data through device speakers and an opt-in microphone. The sender broadcasts a fresh, short-lived challenge, and another member’s device listens for it. The app supports audible and approximately 15–19.5 kHz modes; hardware may filter high frequencies, and some people may hear them. A decoded match is recorded with the group’s session in encrypted state. Whitechain and Safe For the treasury prototype, we deploy Safe 1.4.1 multisigs on Whitechain Sepolia with a strict-majority threshold. A payout proposal is fixed to a Safe transaction and nonce for an approval session. Signers provide EIP-712 transaction signatures, and a Tijori verifier signs an attestation for that transaction. Our TichoriPresenceGuard requires a matching attestation before the guarded Safe execution can proceed. A relayer submits the transaction and can receive a USDT gas refund from the vault, so signers do not need to hold the network’s gas token for that flow. We deployed and demonstrated a testnet USDT payout. The current treasury object and presence providers are simulated, and the contract trusts the verifier; the guard cannot independently determine whether people were together. The separate ggwave demonstration is not yet connected to treasury authorization. Arkiv We use the Arkiv SDK on Rabdi to store an encrypted aggregate containing application state such as identities, group metadata, proposals and session records. The server checks the entity’s expected creator and owner, verifies transaction receipts and reads state back after writes. A durable local journal and serialized writer help reconcile uncertain submissions without automatically resending them. Anon RPC We added an optional, read-only Anon RPC diagnostic using the browser harness and Nym mixnet for supported balance queries. Soo it is bringing browser-based visual matching, device-to-device audio, encrypted decentralized storage and a guarded Safe treasury into one workflow while keeping their current boundaries explicit.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Tijori is a SDK designed to bring physical-world context to Web3 security. It is built for DAOs, families, trusts and teams that manage funds together—and for developers who want to add similar experiences to their own applications.

Web3 users face two related risks. Private keys can be stolen from compromised devices or lost when recovery information is misplaced. Meanwhile, multisig approvals can be collected remotely, making a treasury vulnerable if an attacker compromises multiple signers or convinces them to approve a malicious transaction.

Tijori’s vision is to add two layers to that experience:

- **Object-based verification:** A user enrolls a familiar physical object and presents it again when accessing their identity.
- **Sound-based presence:** Group members exchange a short-lived unique frequency using their devices, creating an approval experience centered on meeting in person.

Tijori brings these ideas together with Safe multisig treasuries on Whitechain. Members can propose a USDT payment and collect a majority of signatures within an approval session. A transaction guard requires an attestation from Tijori’s verifier for the specific transaction.

Developers can integrate Tijori through its **plug-and-play SDK**, which provides reusable server, client and React packages for identity flows, vaults, treasury interactions, acoustic checks and invoices.

Behind the scenes, Arkiv stores encrypted application state, while an optional Anon RPC integration explores private balance reads through the Nym mixnet. The API also applies a same-origin policy to browser write requests, blocking cross-origin writes soo that the ip of the location is not exposed.

Tijori is designed around the CROPS principles: censorship resistance, open source, privacy and security. It combines decentralized infrastructure, an open-source SDK, encrypted state and multisig controls while continuing to develop and strengthen its verification layers.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
Tijori is built with Next.js and a reusable TypeScript SDK. The SDK separates the core domain, server, browser client, React components and invoice integration so other applications can build on the same treasury and identity flows.

**Object verification**

We adapted the matching approach from VILA and run DINOv2 in the browser using Transformers.js. During enrollment and sign-in, SlimSAM helps isolate the foreground object before DINOv2 extracts its visual features. The app compares the new features with a compact enrolled reference; original photos and masks stay on the device. 

**Frequency-based matching**

For the standalone acoustic demonstration, we use ggwave compiled to WebAssembly to transmit and decode data through device speakers and an opt-in microphone. The sender broadcasts a fresh, short-lived challenge, and another member’s device listens for it. The app supports audible and approximately 15–19.5 kHz modes; hardware may filter high frequencies, and some people may hear them. A decoded match is recorded with the group’s session in encrypted state. 

**Whitechain and Safe**

For the treasury prototype, we deploy Safe 1.4.1 multisigs on Whitechain Sepolia with a strict-majority threshold. A payout proposal is fixed to a Safe transaction and nonce for an approval session. Signers provide EIP-712 transaction signatures, and a Tijori verifier signs an attestation for that transaction. Our `TichoriPresenceGuard` requires a matching attestation before the guarded Safe execution can proceed.

A relayer submits the transaction and can receive a USDT gas refund from the vault, so signers do not need to hold the network’s gas token for that flow. We deployed and demonstrated a testnet USDT payout. The current treasury object and presence providers are simulated, and the contract trusts the verifier; the guard cannot independently determine whether people were together. The separate ggwave demonstration is not yet connected to treasury authorization.

**Arkiv**

We use the Arkiv SDK on Rabdi to store an encrypted aggregate containing application state such as identities, group metadata, proposals and session records. The server checks the entity’s expected creator and owner, verifies transaction receipts and reads state back after writes. A durable local journal and serialized writer help reconcile uncertain submissions without automatically resending them.

**Anon RPC**

We added an optional, read-only Anon RPC diagnostic using the browser harness and Nym mixnet for supported balance queries. 

Soo it is bringing browser-based visual matching, device-to-device audio, encrypted decentralized storage and a guarded Safe treasury into one workflow while keeping their current boundaries explicit.

projects.title: Sacred Markets
projects.description: Onchain shariah-powered money markets. Earn, Leverage trade, Borrow without interest.
projects.project_description:
Sacred is an onchain shariah-powered neobank, which allows its users to earn up to 7% stablecoin yield, access up to 5x leverage, and borrow against crypto majors. Centered around the principle of murabaha in islamic finance, which involves selling of a commodity-like asset to the buyer at a fixed deferred payment, as opposed to lending it to them for interest. Sacred takes capital from stablecoin depositors and uses it to buy levered assets on behalf of leverage traders and settle it at their will sell it to borrowers
at a fixed markup cost and time interval. This markup goes to stablecoin depositors as yield, and part of it goes to the protocol as revenue. For the first time, allowing muslims onchain to get access to shariah-compliant yield, leverage and credit, in a single product.
projects.how_its_made: Used Arc Studio to author the code of Sacred's smart contracts, frontend and keeper backends, and had it reviewed and tested by my own agents (astra, fable, opus). Contracts are deployed on the Arc testnet. The system uses uniswap v4 pools to execute its spot buys for the leverage traders. I seeded a cirBTC / USDC pool on the arc testnet for this purpose. Also developed a simple keeper that runs as a background worker in Arc Studio's cloud sandbox that settles the leverage + stablecoin positions and executes liquidations, honestly this made things very convenient for me (to not have to run this keeper on a VPS, AWS etc). I developed the system specification with my agents, then directed them to use Arc Studio CLI as their subagent to develop the core system, instead of perma-prompting the arc studio UI and pasting its results to my agents for reviewing it.

projects.title: FrameCap
projects.description: Daily quotas for EIP-8141 Frames — canonical reject, staked alt-mempool admit.
projects.project_description: FrameCap lets users set an onchain daily spending limit for a wallet, bot, or session key. When a Frame transaction is validated, the quota is checked and updated using flexible state access that the canonical public Frame mempool rejects for DoS/safety reasons. The same transaction can be admitted through the staked EIP-8141 alternative mempool. We demonstrate the core reason the alt mempool exists: useful account-abstraction validation patterns that the public mempool will not propagate. The live demo shows canonical rejection, alt-mempool admission after staking, explorer proof, and over-quota rejection.
projects.how_its_made: FrameCap is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and viem on the public Frames/alt-mempool workshop stack. We use @forshtat/hegota-support for profile-correct EIP-8141 Frame encoding and signing against the ethrex-eip8141-tracer profile. Smart contracts inherit HegotaSupport for frame opcodes (approve, frameparam, txparam). A quota registry/paymaster stores daily limits and spent amounts. Validation uses Frame VERIFY/pre_verify patterns that read and update non-trivial state, which canonical ethrex public-mempool rules reject (e.g. foreign storage / flexible validation), while the workshop sidecar alt mempool can admit the transaction when the entity is staked. Submission path: eth_sendRawTransaction for canonical comparison, eth_sendFrameTransaction for alt-mempool admission, then skandha explorer APIs / explorer.altmempool.wtf for admission evidence. The UI shows side-by-side canonical vs alt outcomes and links the admitted transaction. We intentionally reuse protocol-native tooling instead of reimplementing the Frame codec.

projects.title: Shepherd
projects.description: EIP-8141 agent leash: scoped session keys, VERIFY policy, owner co-sign.
projects.project_description: Shepherd — Give AI agents permission, not ownership. AI agents are becoming capable of doing real work, including interacting with wallets and executing blockchain transactions. But giving an agent access to a wallet often means giving it far more control than it actually needs. Shepherd changes that. Shepherd is an account infrastructure that lets people delegate limited onchain permissions to AI agents without handing over ownership of their wallets. The owner keeps control of the main account. Each agent operates with its own scoped session key, limited by rules defined by the owner. Here's how it works: Scoped permissions: Agents can only interact with approved contracts, functions and transaction values. Policy enforcement: Every transaction passes through an onchain verification process before execution. Human approval: High-risk transactions can be escalated to the owner for approval. Instant revocation: Owners can revoke an agent's permissions when they no longer trust it. Delegated sessions: Child agents inherit their parent's restrictions and cannot exceed their permissions. Shepherd uses EIP-8141 Frame Transactions to implement transaction-level verification. Its policy checks rely on external contract state, which introduces a mempool validation constraint. We address this through ERC-8421 staked alternative-mempool admission. This allows Shepherd to demonstrate something important: the same policy-dependent transaction that fails canonical mempool validation can be admitted through the appropriate staked alternative mempool. The result: AI agents can execute useful onchain actions independently, while humans retain control over the decisions that matter. Shepherd isn't about trusting AI with your wallet. It's about deciding exactly how much authority AI should have.
projects.how_its_made: Shepherd is built around account-level transaction verification using Solidity, EIP-8141 Frame Transactions and ERC-8421 alternative-mempool admission. Smart contracts Built with Solidity 0.8.28 and Foundry. ShepherdAccount implements the account and EIP-8141 VERIFY logic. projects.project_description_markdown:
Shepherd — Give AI agents permission, not ownership.

AI agents are becoming capable of doing real work, including interacting with wallets and executing blockchain transactions. But giving an agent access to a wallet often means giving it far more control than it actually needs.

Shepherd changes that.

Shepherd is an account infrastructure that lets people delegate limited onchain permissions to AI agents without handing over ownership of their wallets.

The owner keeps control of the main account. Each agent operates with its own scoped session key, limited by rules defined by the owner.

Here's how it works:

Scoped permissions: Agents can only interact with approved contracts, functions and transaction values.

Policy enforcement: Every transaction passes through an onchain verification process before execution.

Human approval: High-risk transactions can be escalated to the owner for approval.

Instant revocation: Owners can revoke an agent's permissions when they no longer trust it.

Delegated sessions: Child agents inherit their parent's restrictions and cannot exceed their permissions.

Shepherd uses EIP-8141 Frame Transactions to implement transaction-level verification. Its policy checks rely on external contract state, which introduces a mempool validation constraint. We address this through ERC-8421 staked alternative-mempool admission.

This allows Shepherd to demonstrate something important: the same policy-dependent transaction that fails canonical mempool validation can be admitted through the appropriate staked alternative mempool.

The result: AI agents can execute useful onchain actions independently, while humans retain control over the decisions that matter.

Shepherd isn't about trusting AI with your wallet. It's about deciding exactly how much authority AI should have.

projects.title: Floor
projects.description: Live security ratings for bridged DeFi collateral: enforced onchain, verifiable in your browser
projects.project_description: In April 2026 a forged LayerZero message released 116,500 rsETH from Kelp's bridge. The attacked route had been set to a single verifier 12.5 months earlier, and nothing that watches for changes had anything to report, because nothing changed. Lenders kept accepting rsETH as collateral the whole time. Floor grades the security that is actually in force behind a collateral asset: every bridge route that can create or release it, how many independent verifiers must agree once defaults and optional thresholds are resolved, whether the receive library is pinned, and who can change all of that and how fast. It checks the result against Aave's DAO-approved risk framework and publishes a grade (OK / DEGRADED / UNKNOWN / BREACHED) with every onchain read it came from. What runs today: Live market: every Aave V3 market (24) read straight from its chain by your browser every minute: which assets are collateral, how much is supplied, and which are bridged by LayerZero. A scheduler checks every chain for bridge config changes every 15 minutes. rsETH the day before the hack grades BREACHED: 24 of 26 inbound routes had one effective verifier. Kelp replay on a mainnet fork with the attacker's real transactions: with Floor in the path, the borrow reverts and $0 is borrowed on Aave; repay and liquidation still work. Inbound-limit probe of 64 LayerZero adapters behind Aave-listed tokens on 8 chains: 31 have no inbound bound, meaning one message releases the whole escrow or mints with no cap. The full loop on public testnets: a Chainlink CRE workflow writes the grade on Ethereum Sepolia, CCIP carries it to Base Sepolia, and Floor's sentinel cuts a real Morpho Vault V2 cap to 0. Anyone can verify a grade in their browser with no Floor server: rating from Arkiv, evidence from Swarm, all 624 reads replayed over Tor through EF Anon-RPC. VERIFIED, 99.7-99.8% of requests anonymised. Flip one byte and it says MISMATCH. Enforcement is bounded: it only ever reduces new exposure. It never moves funds, never blocks repay, withdraw or liquidation, and turning exposure back on stays with a human. Everything that writes runs on testnets; mainnet is only read.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript monorepo (pnpm) plus Solidity (Foundry). Resolver (viem): reads a LayerZero OApp's effective config at a pinned block and cross-checks it on 3 RPC providers. It resolves what the raw settings hide: 0 means "inherit the endpoint default", 255 means NIL, an optional threshold can turn "3 verifiers" into "any 1 of 3", and the receive library may be unpinned. Each scan becomes a canonical evidence bundle (every eth_call with block, target, calldata and result) that is hashed with keccak256. Rule pack: Aave's Risk Framework encoded as versioned rules. A failed read is UNKNOWN, never a pass. Inbound probe: on a fork, calls each adapter from the real LayerZero endpoint with a well-formed credit from its configured peer, then classifies the revert reason. It refuses to run unless a non-endpoint caller and a wrong peer are both rejected first. Chainlink CRE (TS SDK, compiled to WASM): a cron trigger re-reads the evidence on mainnet at the pinned block on every node and refuses to write if the feed understates risk or the evidence is forged; a log trigger on LayerZero's UlnConfigSet reacts to config changes, tested on Kelp's real April 2025 transaction. We had no deploy access, so it ran with cre workflow simulate --broadcast , which wrote rsETH = BREACHED to our FloorRegistry on Sepolia. Chainlink CCIP 2.0: FloorBroadcaster sends the rating Sepolia -> Base Sepolia; FloorMirror._ccipReceive stores it; FloorSentinel, set as a Morpho Vault V2 sentinel, reads the mirror and decreases the cap. It can only lower caps (fuzz and invariant tests). Fork-tested with chainlink-local on the real lanes. Arkiv (Rabdi testnet, @arkiv-network/sdk): ratings, 52 routes, the 64-adapter dataset and a flight recorder of rsETH's bridge history, all queried with createdBy(writer) so only our writer's entities are trusted. A re-runnable importer, with a no-key gas preflight. Swarm: evidence bundles (the Swarm reference and hash live on the Arkiv entity), and the whole site is republished to Swarm on every deploy. EF Anon-RPC: the browser verifier routes the Arkiv lookup, the Swarm download, the registry check and all chain reads through tor-js (Nym selectable), with a traffic meter that counts every request by route. Hacky bits: Sepolia's Glamsterdam upgrade made state creation about 5x costlier and Forge underestimated gas, so we deploy with a 900% gas multiplier plus a node eth_estimateGas preflight. Nym drops the Content-Type header (Arkiv answers 415), so Arkiv falls back to direct and the meter shows it. Free RPCs fail in creative ways (429s without CORS, non-JSON-RPC errors), so the transport benches failing providers and retries in 5 rounds. Web: React + Vite app, a three.js/Tailwind landing, GitHub Actions for CI, the 15-minute watcher, the hourly probe and deploys to GitHub Pages + Swarm. Tests: 56 Solidity (27 unit incl. fuzz/invariants, 29 fork) plus about 70 TypeScript tests.

projects.title: Nidhi
projects.description: Pay contributors on any chain, only once their work is verified. Uniswap v4 hook, CCIP 2.0, ENSv2
projects.project_description: DAOs hand out a lot of money for work: grants, bounties, milestones. Almost all of it still runs on trust. A multisig signs a transfer, everyone hopes the work was actually done, and if the contributor lives on another chain somebody bridges it by hand afterwards. Nidhi (Sanskrit for "treasury") makes the payment itself enforce the rules. A grant can only leave the treasury if three things hold at the moment of the swap: Two different accounts signed it: an approver who says "pay this" and an auditor who says "the work is real". Who counts as an approver or auditor isn't stored in our contracts. It's read live from the DAO's ENS name (nidhi-dao.eth on ENSv2). Revoke someone in ENS and they're out instantly. The payee is an ENS subname like alice.nidhi-dao.eth, and her address is resolved for the destination chain at payout time. If the name has expired or has no address on that chain, nothing moves. The amount fits under a daily cap and inside a price band quoted with Uniswap's V4Quoter and guarded against manipulation with StateView. When all of that holds, a Uniswap v4 hook swaps the treasury's WETH into the payout token, takes the entire output itself via afterSwapReturnDelta, and hands it straight to Chainlink CCIP 2.0. The tokens never sit in anyone's wallet in between. On the destination chain, a defensive receiver pays the grantee and sends an ACK receipt back, so the source chain marks the grant SETTLED. If the payout or ACK fails on the far side, the funds are held in the contract-never lost—and retried automatically via Chainlink Automation or permissionless calls. Chains with no direct CCIP lane are reached through an on-chain multi-hop relay. For code work we went one step further and built an autonomous milestone pipeline. The DAO posts a task on-chain via NidhiBountyBoard (an ERC-1271 contract signer holding the ENS approver role): title, repo, amount, and required file paths. When a PR tagged with that task ID is merged and CI is green, the agent verifies it against a deterministic rubric, signs as auditor, and triggers the swap payout without needing a human at payout time. Open bounties work too: the first merged PR wins, and the contributor gets their own <github-name>.nidhi-dao.eth subname. It's live on four testnets (Sepolia, Base Sepolia, Arbitrum Sepolia, Unichain Sepolia) with a working app that reads everything straight from chain. With CCIP 2.0 Faster-Than-Finality, grants reach the grantee in about 7 minutes instead of 15 to 25. We measured 6m 36s to Base and 7m 15s to Arbitrum on live testnet grants.
projects.how_its_made: Contracts are written in Solidity 0.8.26 with Foundry. The core is NidhiHook, a Uniswap v4 hook built on OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseHook with exactly three permissions: beforeSwap, afterSwap, and afterSwapReturnDelta. The address flag bits are 0xC4, mined with HookMiner per chain. Because sender inside a Uniswap v4 hook is the router rather than the user, NidhiSwapRouter stores msg.sender in EIP-1153 transient storage (tstore) before calling PoolManager.unlock(), and NidhiHook reads it via msgSender() (tload) to bind execution to mandate.executor. beforeSwap decodes the grant from hookData and enforces 10 sequential checks: an EIP-712 mandate from an approver and an attestation from an auditor (ECDSA first, ERC-1271 fallback so a Safe or NidhiBountyBoard can hold the role); the two signers must be distinct and hold live roles via IGrantAuthority; the grantId has never been used, the deadline hasn't passed, and the swap is exact-input; the payee address matches live ENSv2 subname resolution for the destination chain; the daily spending cap; an optional reference-price guard reading a canonical pool's slot0 through StateView. afterSwap then take()s the full output directly into NidhiDispatcher and returns +output as the hook delta, so the swapper receives zero tokens. The hacky bit: a gated hook normally breaks quoting because V4Quoter simulates the swap without a signed mandate. We pass the chain's V4Quoter into the hook and let it through with a zero delta (the quoter reverts its own swap anyway), so the app quotes every grant with the real V4Quoter. Liquidity is minted as a DAO-owned NFT through PositionManager with Permit2 after we proved in a fork test that liquidity seeded via the v4 test router can be drained by anyone. ENS: ENSv2Authority maps each role (approver, auditor, guardian) to an Enhanced Access Control (EAC) ROLE_SET_TEXT permission on nidhi-dao.eth's PermissionedResolver. resolveGrantee walks registry -> subregistry -> resolver and reads addr using the ENSIP-11 coin type of the destination chain. We tested three subname models: alice (shared resolver), bob (own resolver, DAO control renounced), and carol (expiring grant window). NidhiBountyBoard holds the approver role on-chain, and the agent's identity is auditor.nidhi-dao.eth. CCIP: NidhiDispatcher sends a programmable token transfer (tokens + grant data) and maintains a forward-only ledger (NONE -> DISPATCHED -> HELD / SETTLED). DestinationReceiver decouples the payout and return ACK in separate try/catch blocks so a reverting transfer or depleted fee reserve never reverts ccipReceive. Chainlink Automation (checkUpkeep / performUpkeep, MAX_BATCH=10) automatically retries held payouts and pending ACKs. For chains without a direct lane, NidhiHopRelay forwards the token transfer across an intermediate chain and rewrites the messageId on the return receipt; we settled Base -> Arbitrum -> Unichain live. For CCIP 2.0 Faster-Than-Finality, NidhiDispatcher encodes GenericExtraArgsV3 with a configurable block depth per lane, and DestinationReceiver opts in via getCCVsAndFinalityConfig strictly for its known source dispatcher. Probing the lanes live showed Sepolia -> Base and Sepolia -> Arbitrum require a 32-block depth, cutting settlement to 6m 36s and 7m 15s. Agent & Frontend: The TypeScript/viem agent runs in GitHub Actions on PR merge. A deterministic rubric checks merge status, review count, green CI runs, file globs, and diff bounds, while a multi-LLM jury (Groq, Cerebras, Gemini, Claude) holds advisory veto power only. The React + Vite + wagmi/viem + TanStack Query frontend runs statically on GitHub Pages with a build-time snapshot and incremental log cache for sub-3s loads. Testing & Security: 139 Foundry tests across 16 suites (unit, fuzz, and invariant tests proving zero residual balances, value conservation, and daily cap enforcement), Slither static analysis (38 findings triaged, 0 open High/Medium), live Sepolia fork tests, and mainnet fork rehearsals across 7 chains.

projects.title: Agent Reviews
projects.description: Google Reviews for x402 APIs, where agents share experiences to help other agents save time when
projects.project_description: Agent Reviews is Google Reviews for x402 APIs, written and read by AI agents. Before an agent pays for an API call, it checks what earlier agents experienced with that exact endpoint for the same task. After the call, it leaves a short review backed by its own settled payment and approved by a verified human. Today, agents choose services from listings and advertised capabilities. But what a service promises does not always match what it delivers: an API can claim "every invoice, every line item, any language" and silently drop half the data. Each agent pays to discover that, and the next agent pays to learn the same lesson. Agent Reviews is a CLI, plus an agent skill that teaches Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents to use it, with three commands: check: resolves each endpoint to its ERC-8004 identity on Hedera, reads its reputation for the task, and returns recommended, avoid, or unknown. pay: buys one call over x402, in USDC on Hedera testnet, from the agent's own account and within a spending cap. Above the cap, a person must approve with World ID. submit: a person approves that exact review with World ID, our server confirms the reviewer actually paid the service's owner, and the agent writes the score to the ERC-8004 reputation registry. The detailed review lives offchain, linked and hashed from the onchain record. World ID makes the reviews Sybil-resistant. Every counted review needs a fresh sign-in by a verified human and counts once per person, service and task, no matter how many agents or wallets that person runs. A merchant cannot manufacture reviewers by spinning up more agents. Unapproved reviews stay unverified and do not count. In our demo, two invoice-extraction APIs advertise the same capability, but API A silently drops Hindi line items. Agent A pays it, gets 2 of 4 items, and leaves a failing review. Agent B checks reviews, skips A, pays API B, and gets all 4. Every step is a real Hedera testnet transaction linked on HashScan. One agent's experience becomes evidence for the next buyer.
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript end to end on Node 22, run directly with --experimental-strip-types (no build step), in an npm workspace: the CLI, a Hono server on Railway, shared Hedera and ERC-8004 code, and a Next.js landing page on Vercel. Payments (Hedera + x402): The demo seller APIs sit behind @x402/hono's paywall with @x402/hedera's exact scheme. Payment is USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) on Hedera testnet, verified and settled by the x402.org facilitator, which also pays the network fees. On the buyer side, "reviews pay" runs the x402 steps itself instead of using the wrapped fetch. That lets it read the 402 terms, refuse unknown networks or tokens, enforce the spending cap, time the challenge and the paid call separately, and capture the settlement transaction ID. It then checks the Hedera mirror node to confirm that exactly that amount moved from the agent to the merchant. Identity and reputation (ERC-8004 on Hedera): Both demo APIs are registered in the ERC-8004 identity registry on Hedera testnet (agents 169 and 170). "check" trusts an endpoint only if both directions agree: the domain's /.well-known/agent-registration.json lists the agent, and the agent's onchain URI lists that exact endpoint. Anything less stays "unknown". Reviews are written with giveFeedback from the agent's own key (score, task tag, outcome, document URL and keccak256 hash). Our server serves the full review at its feedbackURI and marks it published only once it finds the matching NewFeedback event onchain. Chain reads and writes use viem over Hedera's JSON-RPC relay. World ID Agent Pass: OpenID Connect against auth.world.org with PKCE and max_age=0, so every approval needs a fresh sign-in. The CLI shows a QR code in the terminal and the person approves on their phone. The server exchanges the code using the client secret and checks the ID token against World's keys (issuer, audience, signature, nonce, a fresh auth_time and the acr). Each approval is bound to one exact action and consumed atomically, so it cannot be replayed. The app-specific World ID subject, stored hashed, enforces one counted review per person, service and task. The review records that a person approved it, never who. Reviews and approvals are stored in Postgres through Drizzle. Notable and hacky bits: Our agents' Hedera accounts come from plain ECDSA keys. Sending testnet HBAR to a key's EVM address auto-creates the account, and we look up its 0.0.x ID on the mirror node. The same key signs Hedera USDC transfers and the EVM-side ERC-8004 calls. ERC-8004 does not check payments, so our reviews server does. It accepts a review only if the reviewer is the account that paid, the payment went to the service's ERC-8004 owner, and the mirror node confirms the transfer. The mirror node lags consensus by a few seconds, so these checks retry. We started on Arc and moved to Hedera mid-hackathon: x402.org settles hedera:testnet payments and pays the fees, and the ERC-8004 registries sit at the same addresses. Our first live World ID approvals stalled inside World App's sign-in. We added "submit --approval <id>" to resume an approval and "--no-wait" to hand the approval link to the user. A scripted demo agent with a Hindi invoice checker runs the whole loop from one command.

projects.how_its_made_markdown:
TypeScript end to end on Node 22, run directly with --experimental-strip-types (no build step), in an npm workspace: the CLI, a Hono server on Railway, shared Hedera and ERC-8004 code, and a Next.js landing page on Vercel.

Payments (Hedera + x402): The demo seller APIs sit behind @x402/hono's paywall with @x402/hedera's exact scheme. Payment is USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) on Hedera testnet, verified and settled by the x402.org facilitator, which also pays the network fees. On the buyer side, "reviews pay" runs the x402 steps itself instead of using the wrapped fetch. That lets it read the 402 terms, refuse unknown networks or tokens, enforce the spending cap, time the challenge and the paid call separately, and capture the settlement transaction ID. It then checks the Hedera mirror node to confirm that exactly that amount moved from the agent to the merchant.

Identity and reputation (ERC-8004 on Hedera): Both demo APIs are registered in the ERC-8004 identity registry on Hedera testnet (agents 169 and 170). "check" trusts an endpoint only if both directions agree: the domain's /.well-known/agent-registration.json lists the agent, and the agent's onchain URI lists that exact endpoint. Anything less stays "unknown". Reviews are written with giveFeedback from the agent's own key (score, task tag, outcome, document URL and keccak256 hash). Our server serves the full review at its feedbackURI and marks it published only once it finds the matching NewFeedback event onchain. Chain reads and writes use viem over Hedera's JSON-RPC relay.

World ID Agent Pass: OpenID Connect against auth.world.org with PKCE and max_age=0, so every approval needs a fresh sign-in. The CLI shows a QR code in the terminal and the person approves on their phone. The server exchanges the code using the client secret and checks the ID token against World's keys (issuer, audience, signature, nonce, a fresh auth_time and the acr). Each approval is bound to one exact action and consumed atomically, so it cannot be replayed. The app-specific World ID subject, stored hashed, enforces one counted review per person, service and task. The review records that a person approved it, never who. Reviews and approvals are stored in Postgres through Drizzle.

Notable and hacky bits:
- Our agents' Hedera accounts come from plain ECDSA keys. Sending testnet HBAR to a key's EVM address auto-creates the account, and we look up its 0.0.x ID on the mirror node. The same key signs Hedera USDC transfers and the EVM-side ERC-8004 calls.
- ERC-8004 does not check payments, so our reviews server does. It accepts a review only if the reviewer is the account that paid, the payment went to the service's ERC-8004 owner, and the mirror node confirms the transfer. The mirror node lags consensus by a few seconds, so these checks retry.
- We started on Arc and moved to Hedera mid-hackathon: x402.org settles hedera:testnet payments and pays the fees, and the ERC-8004 registries sit at the same addresses.
- Our first live World ID approvals stalled inside World App's sign-in. We added "submit --approval <id>" to resume an approval and "--no-wait" to hand the approval link to the user.
- A scripted demo agent with a Hindi invoice checker runs the whole loop from one command.
