projects.title: tomoshibi
projects.description: AI agents use your API keys without ever holding them. The light goes out when the skill changes.
projects.project_description:
Agent skills are starting to ask for our API keys the way apps once asked for passwords: a secret with
no scope, no expiry and no receipt, handed to code we did not read. https://kou-uni.github.io/ethglobal-mumbai/web/flow.html TOMOSHIBI puts one button an AI cannot press in front of the key. You sign a scope on a Ledger device —
which key, which destination, which operation, how many times, until when — and the four lines on the
device screen are built from the same bytes that get signed. The skill never receives the secret. It
asks a broker to act, and anything outside the signed scope is refused before it happens, and recorded
with the skill's own signature on the request. Nothing here answers with a bare "it failed". Four refusals are kept apart, because a different stop
means a different responsibility: DENIED — you drew that line in advance. STOPPED — nobody could decide,
because the sealed model was unreachable, and we would rather do nothing than invent a verdict.
NEEDS_PRESS — this request is irreversible and no human has pressed for it yet. human_denied /
proof_expired — a person refused to vouch, or nobody was there. Stars are not reviews. A star means: I, a verified human, am using this version with my own key. When
the version changes, every star goes out at once. Reviews never expire; a flame does.
projects.how_its_made:
Ledger (hardware).
A custom Ledger app, written in Rust, computes the EIP-712 digest inside the
device from the same four values it displays, so the screen and the signature cannot disagree. No blind signing, and the host never sends a digest. The device/broker boundary is frozen as one JSON contract plus a published test vector, so both halves of the team could build against it in parallel. Broker (Node, viem).
It holds a child token, never the root key, and runs the gate: scope check →
weight → press → proxy execute → append-only trail. 50 tests, including the frozen cross-side signature vector. 0G — in the decision loop, not as a log sink.
Before acting, the broker asks 0G Private Computer how heavy the request is: routine / important / irreversible, using 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b, a TeeML model (tee_attested, Intel TDX, verified by dstack). The body of the request is part of that judgement, and
that is exactly why 0G is here: you cannot grade a request without reading it, and we do not want to read it. The sealed enclave reads it; we never do. The verdict changes the outcome — an irreversible request will not pass on a standing permit, only on a press made for that one request — and every decision carries the 0G request id. Episode logs go to 0G Storage (append-only Log layer, Flow contract
0x22E03a6A89B950F1c82ec5e74F8eCa321a105296 on Galileo, chain id 16602) and the root hash goes in the trail. If 0G cannot be reached, nothing happens: no default, no local rule standing in for the model,
no fabricated verdict. The request stops and the stop is recorded. World — who, once.
Issuing a star is where a person stakes their reputation, so that is where World
ID Agent Pass sits, not on every key use (the Ledger already answers "do I allow this, now"). The broker
is headless, so it uses the OIDC device_code grant: it starts the request, the person finishes on their own phone, and the broker verifies the id_token against the JWKS (iss / aud / exp) in the backend — the client secret never leaves it. The refusal paths are the protocol's own: access_denied (a person said no) and expired_token (nobody was there) are recorded as two different events. One sector-scoped pseudonym can star one version once. Privacy by separation.
The device knows the scope and nothing of the body. World knows only that you
are a human and the same human. 0G reads the body sealed. The public trail carries neither keys nor bodies. MIT licensed, no trackers, no analytics. What is not done, said plainly.
The broker holds key material and is the single trusted point; the
honest next step is to run the broker itself inside 0G Private Computer. Stars live in an append-only
log — the on-chain registry is specified, not deployed.

projects.title: Houseful
projects.description: One human, one ticket, face value only: pick a seat, pay in dollars, hand it back to resell
projects.project_description: Houseful is a ticketing app where every ticket belongs to one verified person and sells only at its face value. Fans browse 49 test listings in 20 cities across 14 countries, pick a seat on a seat map, and pay in dollars. They can pay with a wallet or with Ethereum, which is swapped into the ticket price through Uniswap inside the same transaction. World ID is how a person signs in and how we limit each person to one ticket per show, so bots and bulk buyers cannot hold a room. A ticket cannot be resold for profit. If you cannot go, you hand it back: you get your money back and the seat goes to the next person in a public waitlist at the same price. Entry is a code that changes every 20 seconds and is checked by the door scanner, which keeps working without a network connection after one sync. If a host cancels a show, every fan can pull their own refund from the contract and nobody can block it. Hosts list shows, see sales, and withdraw their proceeds after the show ends. Everything runs on a test network with test money, and the worldwide listings are labelled as test listings with a link to the official seller.
projects.how_its_made: The web app is Next.js 16 with Tailwind, a libSQL database on Turso, and hosting on Vercel. The Houseful contract on Unichain Sepolia holds tickets, seats, a public waitlist whose order is a running hash that any browser can recompute, and two separate money pots, one for sale proceeds and one for refunds, so a host can never withdraw a fan's refund. Everything settles in a test USDT with six decimals. Paying in ETH goes through Uniswap v3 SwapRouter02: one multicall runs exactOutputSingle and then refundETH inside the buy transaction, and the contract checks that its USDT balance rose by exactly the ticket price before it credits the sale. A QuoterV2 quote shows the ETH amount first. We created and seeded a WETH and test USDT pool at the 0.3 percent fee through the NonfungiblePositionManager. World ID: IDKit runs in the browser, our server checks the proof with World's verify API, and then signs a single-use EIP-712 attestation that the contract checks before it admits a buyer. Fans sign in with World ID and hosts sign in with a wallet signature. Door passes are ed25519 credentials plus a code the holder's phone signs every 20 seconds. The scanner verifies them offline, and a hand-back or recovery raises a generation counter that stops the old code at every scanner that has synced since. Tests: 55 Hardhat contract tests including randomized invariant tests, more than 230 unit tests, 83 door pass tests, and a Playwright suite that runs the whole flow on a disposable local chain with World ID stubbed at the network edge, on desktop and on a 375px phone. The worldwide listings come from a research file with official links, and fields an official page does not state show as "Not published" instead of being invented. Known limits: a screenshot of the live code works for 20 to 40 seconds at a scanner that has not seen it, and an offline scanner that has not synced can still admit a ticket that was handed back. The one-ticket rule has a gap we know about and list in docs/threat-model.md: a purchase made signed out uses a per-show World check while a signed-in purchase uses the login identity, so one person can currently end up with two places until the two are joined. The contract trusts one attestation signer key.

projects.title: NIVASA
projects.description: Verifiable RWA lifecycle on Hedera with gated ATS issuance & 0G AI intelligence.
projects.project_description: NIVASA is an India-first prototype that demonstrates a complete lifecycle for a fictional Mumbai commercial property: property documents are submitted for review, investor rights are recorded, and token issuance is gated on approved evidence. The demo uses Hedera Testnet to show restricted issuance, investor eligibility, settlement recovery, and pausing and resuming an offering when evidence changes. A public verification page lets visitors inspect technical records, while 0G Private Computer helps explain changes between property snapshots. The project uses simulated data and is not an investment offering, proof of property ownership or title, or a government-approved service.
projects.how_its_made: NIVASA is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Supabase providing Postgres workflow records, role-based access, row-level security and private storage for uploaded evidence. Its design separates document review, verification decisions and on-chain recordkeeping, so sensitive files stay off-chain while their hashes can be used to check integrity. For the blockchain layer, we use Hedera Testnet and the Asset Tokenization Studio SDK to manage restricted asset issuance and record evidence-manifest and rights hashes. A protected worker processes chain actions through a transactional outbox and reconciles their results, helping settlement recover safely after interruptions. Public verification checks the recorded asset state against Hedera data. AI supports change analysis: deterministic code computes and validates differences between property snapshots, then 0G Private Computer generates an explanation grounded in those inputs. AI output does not make verification decisions or authorize transactions. A key engineering choice is requiring the approved evidence and rights hashes to be read back from the asset before an offering can activate, connecting the reviewed evidence to the on-chain record.

projects.title: ORCA
projects.description: ORCA: A decentralized AI network for collaborative, verifiable marine scientific research.
projects.project_description: ORCA is a platform that enables marine research institutions to collaborate on scientific investigations using independently operated AI agents. Today, oceanographic datasets, scientific models, and research expertise are distributed across different institutions, making it difficult for researchers to access relevant information, combine datasets, coordinate analyses, and independently verify findings. ORCA addresses this by allowing institutions to register their organizations, connect existing datasets and computational tools, and deploy their own specialized research agents without giving up control of their infrastructure or data. When a researcher submits a scientific question, such as investigating unusual sea surface temperature changes in the Arabian Sea, ORCA identifies the required datasets, breaks the investigation into tasks, discovers suitable institutional agents, and coordinates their work. These agents retrieve scientific observations, process differences in measurement units, geographic coordinates, time periods, and data formats, and perform calculations using documented scientific methods. ORCA uses Agent2Agent (A2A) for communication between agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect them with scientific tools and data sources. ENSv2 allows institutions to manage identities for their agents and control who can update their records, while Arkiv provides a shared system where participating agents can publish research tasks, claim assignments, and record references to their results and reviews. Scientific datasets and computations remain off-chain. An important part of ORCA is independent verification: when an agent produces a finding, another institution's agent can reproduce the calculations, examine the underlying evidence, and identify disagreements caused by different datasets, methods, or assumptions. Researchers can follow the entire investigation through a dashboard that displays scientific maps, data visualizations, agent activities, source information, calculation methods, and verification results. The platform also maintains records of which agents contributed to an investigation, what data they used, and how their conclusions were reached. Rather than replacing existing research institutions or scientific tools, ORCA connects their capabilities so researchers can conduct joint investigations, evaluate each other's findings, and produce scientific results that others can examine, reproduce, and challenge.
projects.how_its_made: ORCA is designed as a modular platform that connects independently operated scientific AI agents, institutional datasets, and research tools through a shared investigation workflow. Our technology stack includes Next.js and TypeScript for the research dashboard, Python and FastAPI for backend services and agent orchestration, and scientific libraries such as xarray, NumPy, Pandas, and SciPy for processing oceanographic data. PostgreSQL with PostGIS manages research metadata and geographic information, while object storage is used for scientific datasets, computational outputs, and supporting evidence. The core architecture uses an investigation coordinator that breaks a research question into smaller scientific tasks, identifies agents with the required capabilities, checks their permissions, and coordinates their execution. We use the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol to support communication between independently hosted agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents with existing scientific tools, datasets, and computation services. This allows institutions to participate without replacing their existing infrastructure or transferring all their data to ORCA. We incorporated two Ethereum ecosystem technologies into the architecture. ENSv2 provides institution-controlled identities for scientific agents , allowing organizations to manage agent names, publish discovery information, delegate limited permissions, and revoke access when necessary. Arkiv provides the shared coordination layer , where independent agents can discover research tasks, submit claims, record assignments, and publish references to scientific results and reviews. We connect these systems through signed identity bindings so that an agent's ENS identity can be associated with an authorized Arkiv wallet. The actual scientific computations and large datasets remain off-chain. One of the more interesting engineering challenges is handling scientific data from different providers. Oceanographic datasets can use different temperature units, coordinate conventions, spatial resolutions, time intervals, and measurement definitions. Our processing architecture addresses this through structural validation, scientific quality checks, unit normalization, spatial and temporal alignment, and documented calculation methods. Rather than asking an LLM to calculate scientific results directly, the agents coordinate executable scientific tools and preserve the datasets, methods, and evidence used. Another important design decision is independent verification. Instead of treating an agent's response as automatically correct, ORCA allows a separate scientific agent to reproduce calculations, compare methodologies, identify inconsistencies, and submit a documented challenge. We maintain separate checks for agent identity, artifact integrity, and scientific reproducibility, since a valid blockchain record does not necessarily mean a scientific conclusion is accurate. The goal is to connect existing research infrastructure through open protocols while giving institutions control over their agents and enabling researchers to independently examine how scientific findings were produced.

We maintain separate checks for agent identity, artifact integrity, and scientific reproducibility, since a valid blockchain record does not necessarily mean a scientific conclusion is accurate.

The goal is to connect existing research infrastructure through open protocols while giving institutions control over their agents and enabling researchers to independently examine how scientific findings were produced.

projects.title: Aftercheck
projects.description: Aftercheck checks Uniswap swap outcomes against declared rules - with replayable evidence
projects.project_description: A successful blockchain transaction doesn't necessarily mean it satisfied the user's financial requirements. Aftercheck is a read-only, local-first verification tool that examines completed Uniswap swaps and evaluates their recorded effects against user-declared financial policies. Built around Uniswap v3 on Ethereum Sepolia, Aftercheck validates transaction evidence, identifies the actual router and liquidity pool, reconciles Swap and Transfer events, and checks financial requirements such as maximum spending, minimum received amounts, and expected recipients. Crucially, it separates four things: transaction execution, protocol support, evidence completeness, and financial-policy compliance. The same successful transaction can produce PASS under one policy and VIOLATION under another. If the available evidence cannot establish a requirement - such as the wallet's balance immediately after the transaction - Aftercheck reports UNKNOWN rather than inventing a reassuring answer. The browser interface lets users inspect evidence, adjust retrospective financial requirements, and export complete verification packages. These packages can be independently reproduced through an offline CLI without depending on our website, backend, or live RPC access. We also integrated Chainlink CRE for additional historical Uniswap pool-identity corroboration. An official local CRE CLI simulation successfully demonstrated MATCH, controlled MISMATCH, and UNAVAILABLE outcomes, without changing the core financial verdict. Aftercheck is experimental verification infrastructure, not a wallet, an execution guard, or a guarantee of financial safety.
projects.how_its_made: Aftercheck is built with TypeScript, JavaScript, Node.js 24, native browser APIs, and Ethereum JSON-RPC. The frontend uses lightweight HTML, CSS, and native JavaScript modules rather than a heavyweight web framework. Our Uniswap integration directly supports v3 SwapRouter02 exactInputSingle on Ethereum Sepolia. The read-only evidence collector retrieves historical transaction, receipt, block, and contract observations. It uses EIP-1898 block-hash-bound requests to establish consistent historical protocol context. The verification engine decodes the exact seven-field Router02 calldata, checks the deployed router and factory-selected pool, and reconciles signed Uniswap Swap events with ordered ERC-20 Transfer events. Financial calculations use bigint arithmetic, avoiding floating-point precision errors. Strict validation checks transaction identities, evidence integrity, supported routes, and policy inputs. Missing or conflicting information produces explicit UNKNOWN or unsupported results rather than false PASS verdicts. The same deterministic evaluation logic runs in Node.js and the browser. Users can adjust retrospective policies, inspect individual checks, and download a verification package containing evidence, policy, JSON/Markdown reports, and offline reproduction instructions. Our optional Chainlink CRE integration combines an HTTPS capability retrieving a revision-pinned public evidence manifest with an EVM capability reading the historical Uniswap v3 factory on Sepolia. We successfully executed official CRE CLI simulations for matching, deliberately mismatching, and unavailable evidence, then consumed their outputs as separate corroboration results without changing the original financial verdict. The browser application is deployed as a static site on DigitalOcean. Core verification requires no proprietary backend, database, wallet connection, signing authority, or AI inference. GitHub Actions validates the implementation through automated tests, browser/CLI parity checks, adversarial cases, and reproducible exports.

projects.title: Parable
projects.description: Every trading strategy has a graveyard. Parable is where AI trading bots can't hide theirs.
projects.project_description: Anyone showcasing or selling an AI trading bot today can play a simple survivorship-bias trick: launch twenty bots, quietly delete the seventeen that failed, and advertise the three lucky survivors. Followers never see the graveyard because the bot or its creator controls the logs. Parable removes that trick structurally. On Parable, AI trading bots never hold the money and never write their own history, a shared Sepolia vault contract does both: One human per creator (World ID): Every launch requires human approval via World ID (OIDC + PKCE), with a clearly labeled demo approval path so judges without a phone can still test end-to-end. On-chain, ParableVault binds each verified creator ID 1-to-1 to a single creator wallet, preventing a creator from spinning up a fresh identity to escape old losses. Identity before the first trade (ENSv2): Before a bot can trade once, it receives an expiring, soulbound ENSv2 subname under parable.eth (e.g., bot-5-d0a5.parable.eth) storing its strategy, model brain, loss limit, and code_hash fingerprint. ParableVault checks this badge on every trade via EnsV2BadgeOracle and unregisters the subname when the bot stops. The vault keeps score (Ethereum Sepolia + Chainlink): ParableVault holds practice capital, checks the bot's ENSv2 badge and per-trade cap on every trade, prices ETH swaps using the live Chainlink ETH/USD oracle on Sepolia, tracks high-water-mark drawdown, and stops bots when their lease expires or loss limit is reached. Nothing can be deleted (Arkiv): Every birth, trade, vault refusal, and stop event is written to Arkiv Rabdi as a publicly queryable record. Stopped bots remain permanently in the paginated Public Graveyard, and the dashboard continuously cross-checks Arkiv's public record count against ParableVault's on-chain counter so missing records cannot hide. On the live dashboard (https://parable-demo.centralindia.cloudapp.azure.com), anyone can: Launch a solo bot using a plain-English sentence builder (choosing between Google Gemini/Gemma, Jev Autoloops models, or a deterministic rule baseline). Watch all running bots live and open the slide-down Telemetry drawer for 10-second live charts, per-agent tables, and copy-paste curl / cast verification commands. Dry-run real "Try to cheat" attacks against the Sepolia contract (unregistered wallet trade, 10x over-limit trade, and second-wallet sybil attempt) and see the contract's exact revert reason. Launch an AI Swarm where one supervisor "mind" model audits multiple worker bots every minute under one World ID approval. Connect Claude Code or OpenAI Codex directly to the live server via Parable's 14-tool MCP server.
projects.how_its_made:
Smart Contracts (Solidity 0.8.24 + Foundry, 39 tests):
We built and verified two contracts on Ethereum Sepolia (Sourcify + Etherscan): ParableVault.sol (0x5432bE5713f358225d648eAb2EC9f699B25Ef317): The non-custodial kernel. It registers bots with immutable risk rules (starting balance, max trade size, max drawdown in bps, lease duration), binds creatorId <-> creatorWallet 1-to-1, prices practice ETH trades against Sepolia's Chainlink ETH/USD feed (0x694AA1769357215DE4FAC081bf1f309aDC325306), enforces per-trade caps and high-water-mark loss limits, and exposes permissionless expiry/loss revocation. EnsV2BadgeOracle.sol (0x087077ceBb69d8617b41735aAe24232697Af4EcA): Bridges ENSv2 on-chain state into ParableVault.trade() so the vault verifies in a single atomic call that the caller's ENSv2 subname exists, resolves to the bot's address, and has not expired or been revoked. ENSv2 Integration (Sepolia):
Under our parent name parable.eth (Registry 0x944523b32916F123923920d32aD92877341990f4), we deployed a dedicated PermissionedRegistry subregistry and PermissionedResolver. At bot birth, the engine mints a soulbound subname with roleBitmap = 0 (non-transferable by the bot) and lease-bound expiry, writing strategy, brain, max_loss_bps, and a SHA-256 code_hash fingerprint into resolver text records. On death, the subname is unregistered on-chain. Arkiv Integration (Rabdi Testnet):
Because the experimental Python client hit JSON-RPC parameter mismatches on Rabdi, we built a local, token-authenticated Node.js microservice (arkiv-bridge) around the official @arkiv-network/sdk (v1.0.1). It writes three schemas: parable.bot (TTL matched to lease), parable.event (readonly: true), and parable.death (readonly: true, 180-day retention with permissionlessExtension so anyone can keep graves alive). All queries fail closed by filtering on both our vault address and writer wallet ($owner = addr(0x4Bf4Cf3Ac386A57DBf7C8b5eB93cE942d4504570)). World ID Integration:
Implemented server-side OIDC + Authorization Code with PKCE in Python (world_pass.py), verifying ID tokens against World's JWKS endpoint with single-use state, cryptographic nonce, and max_age=0 so every launch requires a fresh human check. Denied or expired approvals cleanly abort before touching the chain. A rate-limited demo approval mode lets judges without World App test the pipeline while tagging those records separately as "demo". Notable Engineering & "Battle-Tested" Fixes: Shared Nonce-Safe Tx Sender & Gas Discovery: Concurrent bot launches initially clashed on operator nonces, and Sepolia's current fork required >21,000 gas to fund a fresh empty bot EOA (causing silent status=0 gas top-up reverts until we traced receipts and raised the gas limit). We built a per-wallet locked transaction sender with nonce recovery and receipt verification. Outbox + Self-Healing Vault-to-Arkiv Repair: If an Arkiv testnet write lags or drops during a launch spike, an in-process outbox retries writes while a 60-second repair loop scans ParableVault on Sepolia and reconstructs any missing bot or grave entity on Arkiv—keeping vault_count_matches: true across 25+ live Sepolia bots. Engine, AI Brains, MCP & Frontend: Python FastAPI + web3.py backend running Google Gemini/Gemma and Jev (Autoloops) structured-output brains (with automatic deterministic fallback if an LLM times out), a 14-tool FastMCP server, and a custom React + TypeScript + Vite "Public Register" UI with zero-dependency SVG telemetry charts, backed by 215 automated tests (167 Python, 39 Foundry, 9 Vitest) and deployed on Azure behind Caddy HTTPS.

projects.title: tryAspen.ai
projects.description: An MCP that gives AI agents live market commentary from X & YouTube as scored trading signals
projects.project_description: Aspen MCP is a research layer for AI agents that trade or analyse markets. Plug it into Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Codex and your agent can see what traders and analysts are saying right now, already turned into structured, scored trading signals, with a track record behind every source. Aspen follows ~130 sources: X accounts, YouTube channels and websites. When one posts, Aspen reads the post (or the full video transcript), separates observations from actual calls, resolves which markets it is about (crypto, US stocks, indices, commodities, pre-IPO names, all tradable as perps on Hyperliquid) and records the direction, confidence, rationale and the market price at the moment of the call. Every call is then scored against what the price did next, so each source has a measured record per market. The MCP exposes all of this as 10 read-only tools with no sign-in: get_feed, search_feed, get_feed_facets: the live signal feed, filterable by market, side, source, topic and time window, plus semantic search ("rate cuts", "AI capex") list_sources, get_source, get_similar_sources: who Aspen follows, and who posts about the same things get_source_record, get_source_history: hit rate, mean signed move, and whether following or countering a source has paid, per market list_markets: every market on the venue with its max leverage get_positioning: how Aspen's users are positioned with real money, per market So an agent can answer "What are people saying about NVDA this week, who is bearish, and have they been right before?" in one conversation, with every claim linked back to the original post. Endpoint: https://api.tryaspen.ai/mcp (Streamable HTTP, no auth)
projects.how_its_made: TypeScript end to end on Effect. The MCP server is built with Effect's AI module (McpServer + Toolkit) and mounted on the same HTTP router as Aspen's public API. Each tool calls the exact loader its HTTP route uses and answers with the API's own contract schema as its output schema, so the agent and the app can never disagree about the data. The pipeline underneath: the X API and Supadata (YouTube transcripts) for ingestion; OpenAI models for the analysis that turns a post into observations and market-resolved long/short signals; OpenAI embeddings + Qdrant for semantic search and "similar sources"; Postgres for the feed, signals and scoring; Hyperliquid for the market universe, entry prices and price history used to score every call. The notable part is how we tuned it for agents rather than humans. We wrote a 50-question eval (breaking news, asset commentary, "is it priced in?", crowd positioning, source credibility, edge cases) and ran it against production with one Claude agent per section, using only the MCP. The baseline showed answers costing 120 to 340 KB per search call. We then cut responses down for a model's context: page limits on feed and search, post text trimmed to card length with the full post one link away, a summary-by-default track record (per-trade charts only on request), and folding of repeated calls from the same source within 72 hours. We also added the get_positioning tool and last-polled timestamps so an agent can tell a quiet source from a broken one. Transport details: Streamable HTTP supporting four MCP protocol versions including the sessionless 2026-07-28 revision, a bounded session ledger with idle eviction, a 16 KiB request body cap, and search rate-limited per client using the same limiter as the HTTP route. Every tool is annotated read-only and idempotent, and nothing touches a user account.

projects.title: LPFY
projects.description: LPFY lets Uniswap LPs borrow USDC against their LP positions while continuing to earn trading fees.
projects.project_description: LPFY is a lending protocol that allows liquidity providers to use their Uniswap V3 and Uniswap V4 liquidity positions as collateral to borrow stablecoins without selling or unwinding their LP positions. Lenders deposit USDC into ERC-4626 lending vaults and receive vault shares representing their position in the lending pool.Borrowers deposit supported Uniswap V3 or V4 LP positions as collateral and can borrow USDC based on the current value of the collateral and the configured loan-to-value ratio. LPFY derives the value of each liquidity position from its underlying assets and external price feeds. While the LP position remains locked as collateral, the borrower continues to retain the economic benefits of the position, including the ability to claim trading fees generated by that liquidity. Interest accrues on outstanding loans at a fixed borrow rate and is reflected in the ERC-4626 vault’s total assets, allowing lenders to earn yield from borrower interest. If a position becomes undercollateralized and crosses the configured liquidation threshold, it becomes eligible for liquidation. A liquidator can repay the outstanding debt and receive the LP collateral with a predefined liquidation incentive. For the hackathon, LPFY focuses on a minimal but complete lending lifecycle: lender deposits, V3/V4 LP collateralization, collateral valuation, borrowing, interest accrual, fee claiming, repayment, collateral withdrawal, and liquidation. The broader goal of LPFY is to make DEX liquidity more capital-efficient by allowing LPs to unlock borrowing power from their liquidity positions while continuing to participate in liquidity provision.
projects.how_its_made: Solidity Smart Contracts — Core lending, borrowing, repayment, interest, collateral, and liquidation logic. ERC-4626 Lending Vault — Lenders supply USDC and receive vault shares representing their share of the lending pool. Uniswap V3 Adapter — Handles V3 LP position validation, underlying asset calculation, fee collection, and collateral interaction. Uniswap V4 Adapter — Provides a separate integration layer for V4 LP positions without changing the core lending logic. Modular Adapter Architecture — The lending market interacts with Uniswap LP positions through adapters, making it easier to support additional DEXs later. Chainlink Price Feeds — Used to convert the underlying LP assets into USD value for LTV and liquidation calculations. Collateral Valuation Engine — Combines LP position data with oracle prices to determine borrowing power. Factory Contract — Deploys and manages individual lending markets with configurable LTV, liquidation threshold, penalty, and borrow rate. Interest Accounting — Tracks fixed-rate borrower interest and reflects accrued interest in ERC-4626 vault value. LP Fee Claiming — Borrowers can claim trading fees generated by their collateralized Uniswap positions through the protocol. Chainlink CRE Liquidation Engine — Allows unhealthy positions to be liquidated once their debt crosses the configured collateral threshold.

projects.project_description_markdown:
T-REX Capital Market is a self-service platform that enables institutions, asset managers, and businesses to tokenize, issue, manage, and distribute regulated financial assets onchain. Built on ERC-3643, the platform combines investor onboarding, identity verification, compliance, token issuance, stablecoin investments, portfolio management, and redemptions into a single workflow.

**The challenge we're solving**

Tokenizing an asset is only the beginning. Once an institution launches a tokenized financial product, it must continuously manage the asset's valuation, investor subscriptions, redemptions, and compliance requirements.

For assets such as tokenized funds, private credit, or managed portfolios, valuations can change frequently. These changes affect how many tokens investors receive when investing and how much they receive when redeeming.

Previously, T-REX required asset managers to log into the platform, manually enter an updated token price, and sign an onchain transaction. Although this provided control, it introduced unnecessary operational overhead, especially for institutions managing multiple assets or reporting valuations frequently.

**What we built during this hackathon**

We introduced a **Secure Automated Price Reporting Module** that allows issuers and asset managers to update token prices directly from their existing financial systems, without manually signing every price-update transaction.

An asset manager can configure automated reporting for each tokenized asset and obtain a dedicated API endpoint. The integration supports API authentication, IP whitelisting, and cryptographically signed price updates using authorized service wallets.

To make the process safer and more configurable, managers can define price-change thresholds, cumulative limits, minimum and maximum prices, cooldown periods, and reporting frequency.

Once an authorized price update passes the configured checks, it is submitted onchain. The latest reported price is then used by the existing investment and redemption workflows.

**Multi-chain expansion**

T-REX already supported Arc Testnet with USDC-based investment and redemption, ERC-3643 compliance controls, and Circle CCTP for cross-chain USDC transfers.

During this hackathon, we are upgrading our existing Arc contracts and expanding the platform to **Hedera and Whitechain**, bringing automated valuation reporting to the supported networks.

This allows institutions to use the same tokenization infrastructure and reporting experience across multiple blockchain ecosystems.

**Why it matters**

Our goal is to make institutional asset tokenization practical beyond the initial token issuance. By connecting an institution's internal financial systems directly to secure, configurable onchain workflows, we reduce manual operations while retaining issuer control, compliance enforcement, and transparent transaction records.

**Continuity Track Disclosure**

T-REX Capital Market existed before this hackathon and was previously submitted to ETHGlobal. The original platform included the complete regulated tokenization lifecycle and manual price management.

Our new contributions are automated, cryptographically authorized price reporting, configurable reporting safeguards, the Arc contract upgrade, and deployment/integration work for Hedera and Whitechain.

Previous ETHGlobal submission: https://ethglobal.com/showcase/t-rex-capital-market-mssaj
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
T-REX Capital Market combines **React, Node.js, Solidity, ERC-3643, OnchainID, Privy, EIP-712, Arc, Circle USDC/CCTP, Hedera, and Whitechain**.

**Existing Architecture (Before the Hackathon)**

Our existing platform provides separate issuer and investor interfaces through React, with a Node.js backend responsible for authentication, application workflows, token configuration, transaction orchestration, and blockchain integration.

We use ERC-3643/T-REX smart contracts for regulated token issuance. Each token is connected to identity and modular compliance infrastructure, enabling issuers to enforce eligibility requirements such as jurisdiction restrictions, investor balance limits, and maximum investor counts.

OnchainID handles investor identity and verification claims, while Privy provides embedded wallets and email-based authentication, reducing onboarding friction for users unfamiliar with Web3.

The existing `TREXPlatformController.sol` contract coordinates token issuance and redemption with stablecoin settlement. On Arc Testnet, investors subscribe using USDC and receive regulated tokens based on the current reported price. Redemption reverses this process, with tokens burned and USDC returned to investors.

We also integrated Circle CCTP for USDC transfers between Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet.

Before this hackathon, token valuation updates required an asset manager to manually enter a price through the dashboard and authorize the onchain transaction.

**New Architecture (Built During the Hackathon)**

Our primary development is an automated price-reporting infrastructure consisting of four connected components.

**1. Configurable Reporting Dashboard**

We extended the issuer interface so asset managers can enable automated reporting for individual tokenized assets. Managers can obtain API integration details, configure authorized service wallets, manage API credentials and approved IP addresses, and define operational controls.

These controls include minimum and maximum prices, permissible price-change thresholds, cumulative change limits, cooldown periods, and update frequency.

**2. Secure Reporting API**

We introduced backend API workflows through which an institution's existing accounting, NAV, or portfolio management system can submit updated valuations.

Rather than granting the platform unrestricted authority to modify prices, the issuer's system produces a cryptographic signature using its authorized service wallet.

The API validates access restrictions and the submitted signature before allowing the reporting workflow to proceed.

**3. EIP-712 Smart Contract Authorization**

We extended the existing `TREXPlatformController.sol` contract with EIP-712 typed-data signature verification for authorized price updates.

The platform's transaction-submission service can submit an issuer-signed price update onchain, while the smart contract verifies that the authorization comes from the registered issuer service wallet.

This separates transaction submission from authorization: the reporting service can relay transactions, but it cannot legitimately approve arbitrary prices without the issuer's signature.

Configured price restrictions and timing controls provide additional safeguards around automated reporting.

**4. Integration with Investment and Redemption**

Once a valid price update is accepted onchain, the existing token issuance and redemption workflows use the updated valuation to determine the applicable investment or redemption amounts.

We reused the existing asset lifecycle rather than building an independent valuation or tokenization protocol.

**Multi-Chain Development**

We are extending the same architecture across Arc, Hedera, and Whitechain. The original Arc deployment serves as the existing integration, while Hedera and Whitechain are additional network deployments introduced during this hackathon.

We used **Arc Studio** to plan and modify the existing platform controller contract, including the EIP-712 authorization logic.

Arc Studio project: https://studio.arc.io/app/a24fa5b1-e6ae-411d-982f-efdd6cede71f

**What makes the implementation notable**

The new module is not simply a scheduled bot that sends transactions. It provides an issuer-controlled authorization flow that connects traditional financial reporting systems to onchain asset valuation, with configurable security and operational restrictions.

This is particularly relevant for tokenized funds and financial products that require frequent NAV or token price updates without exposing critical smart contract permissions to an external automation service.

**Continuity Disclosure**

All existing issuer/investor onboarding, ERC-3643 tokenization, compliance, wallet integration, and original investment/redemption functionality predate this hackathon. The newly developed work is the automated reporting API, configuration interface, service-wallet authorization, EIP-712 contract extension, reporting safeguards, and multi-chain deployment/integration.

projects.title: Photeon Retina
projects.description: DePIN Oracle using YOLOv8 to audit solar energy and mint verified Carbon Credit RWAs on Whitechain.
projects.project_description: Photeon Retina is a DePIN oracle bridging physical solar infrastructure with Web3 DeFi. Solar farms waste massive energy due to undetected thermal defects. Photeon Retina uses a YOLOv8 computer vision model to scan panels in real-time, detecting anomalies and calculating energy optimizations. Instead of opaque Web2 databases, our off-chain oracle directly triggers a smart contract on the Whitechain network to mint Photeon Carbon Credits (PCC) as Real World Assets (RWA). This creates an immutable, transparent proof of ESG compliance and transforms physical energy savings into liquid on-chain assets.
projects.how_its_made:
Photeon Retina’s architecture bridges Web2 AI and Web3. The off-chain Oracle backend is powered by Python and FastAPI, serving a YOLOv8 model for real-time optical and thermal anomaly detection. We also integrated CodeCarbon to track the AI's own carbon inference footprint.
On the Web3 side, we designed an ERC-20 smart contract (PCC) targeted for Whitechain and EVM-compatible networks. For this hackathon MVP, we built a custom Vanilla JS/HTML/Tailwind frontend (leveraging Gemini as a pair-programming copilot for rapid UI boilerplate). The dashboard integrates directly with MetaMask via the window.ethereum API to simulate the full DePIN loop: the AI scans the video feed, validates the physical asset, triggers the minting process, and allows users to sign cryptographic Web3 transactions to transfer their RWA tokens.

projects.title: Dynaura
projects.description: A smart solar energy distribution and management system, powered by AI and paid on-chain.
projects.project_description:
Distributed solar is growing faster than the systems that manage it. Power is now
generated at thousands of small sites, such as rooftops, housing societies, campuses
and community microgrids, and consumed by many parties at once. Yet distribution,
billing and maintenance still run on estimates, manual meter readings and trust.
Energy goes unused at peak hours, surplus is sold back at the lowest price, and
payments between producers, consumers and service providers are slow and hard to
audit.
Dynaura is a smart solar energy distribution and management system that closes the
loop from generation to payment: measure, decide, settle and record.
Measure. An edge node meters generation and every consumer in real time and signs
each reading at the source, so the data can't be changed later.
Decide. An AI planner on 0G combines the weather forecast with consumption
history to schedule loads into peak generation, route surplus to where it's needed,
price it by scarcity, and detect when a panel is losing output. Every decision can be
verified through its 0G request ID and an audit log on 0G Storage and 0G Chain.
Settle. Payments run in USDC on Arc smart contracts that release funds only against
metered proof. Buyers prepay and are refunded for energy not delivered,
consumption is billed per unit, revenue is shared by measured contribution, and
maintenance is paid from escrow only once output is restored.
Record. Arkiv holds an open ledger of readings, decisions, trades, bills and service
jobs that every participant can check.
We run it end to end on working hardware: A model showcasing 3 flats, Raspberry Pi,
live meters and relays. The same design scales to a housing society, a campus or a
community grid.
projects.how_its_made:
Hardware. A working prototype on one board. A Raspberry Pi 4 reads four INA219
meters over I2C: one on a real solar panel and one for each of three consumers (A, B,
C). A 4-channel relay module switches each consumer between solar and grid, shown
by yellow and blue LEDs, and drives a water pump as a shared load. A power bank
stands in for the grid, a lamp plays the sun, and tracing paper on the panel simulates
dust.
Pi software (Python). A FastAPI service meters everything once a second, signs each
1-minute summary with the device key (eth-account), and streams live state to the
app over SSE. It runs as systemd services, with a SIM mode for development and a
safe stop (all flats on grid, pump off) whenever anything fails.
0G. The planner, dust check and spare-sun trader call the 0G Compute Router
through the OpenAI SDK with verify_tee on. Each decision is saved as a hash
chained episode on 0G Storage (Go storage client) and indexed by an
EpisodeRegistry contract on 0G Galileo. If 0G is unreachable the Pi never fakes a
verdict: it falls back to a labelled no-AI rule and logs the outage.
Arc. Four Solidity contracts written, tested and deployed in Arc Studio:
CleaningEscrow (conditional escrow, meter-proven release, dispute and refund),
ShopTrade (prepay, settle by delivered Wh, refund the rest), SolarBilling (monthly bill
split between solar and grid) and SolarCredits (revenue paid out by each flat's
unused share). The Pi is the oracle and posts with web3.py; residents, the shop and
the cleaner sign from their own wallets with viem.
Arkiv. A Node bridge with @arkiv-network/sdk writes readings, decisions, trades,
bills and cleaning jobs from one building wallet. Expiry does real work: a 2-minute
heartbeat is the offline alarm, shop offers close at sunset, and the planner reads the
last 7 days back from Arkiv into every 0G prompt.
App. React, Vite and Tailwind, mobile-first, with resident, committee, cleaner and
shop roles. It reads Arkiv straight from the browser.
Hacky bit: the panel had no load, so the INA219 read 0 mA. We switched to sensing
the panel's voltage between lamp-off and lamp-on, calibrated live at the venue.

projects.title: Pact Agent
projects.description: Get paid in USDT on Whitechain. Your client signs once. We pay the gas. So do agents.
projects.project_description: A designer sends a $1,000 invoice to a client abroad. If the client pays by card, Stripe takes $54.30 before she sees a cent, and a dispute costs another $15. Right away. USDT should fix that. It doesn't, because now the client needs a wallet, the right chain and gas just to pay one invoice. Pact removes that step. The client signs once. Our relayer sends the transaction and pays the gas. The client's AI agent can pay the same way, over x402, inside spending caps the merchant sets. Getting the first payment through is easy. We spent the weekend on what comes after it: refunds, renewals that can't overcharge, invoices she can sell today instead of waiting 30 days ($1,000 due next month becomes $865 now), and Face ID instead of seed phrases. She pays 0.8%. She signs those terms once, and after that nobody can raise them. Not her client, and not us. Testnet only (Whitechain Sepolia, chain 1874).
projects.how_its_made:
We don't trust our own server. The frontend only collects signatures. The backend only turns them into transactions. Every rule that touches money lives in the contracts, so if our API goes down, the contracts still refuse anything outside the rules. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.26, built and tested with Foundry, targeting Prague because that's what Whitechain runs. All deployed on Whitechain Sepolia on 7 Nov: FeeSchedule holds versioned fee terms. The merchant accepts one version with an EIP-712 signature and stays on it until she signs a newer one, so nobody can raise her fee.
Router checks the signed intent against every rule. When it says no, the reason is emitted onchain, not buried in our logs.
PaymentEscrow does the one-signature charge and takes the fee out of the payment. The payer signs a single USDT authorization, so there's no approval transaction first. Refunds are capped and signed by the merchant herself, and she pays their gas in USDT.
PasskeyAccount verifies WebAuthn signatures onchain through the P256 precompile Whitechain gets from the OP Stack. In the demo, you pay with your laptop's fingerprint.
SubscriptionManagerV2 caps every renewal, and every refused renewal is an event.
X402AgentAccount gives each AI agent a per-call and a daily limit. Permit2 and the standard x402 contracts are already on Whitechain, so an unmodified x402 client can pay a merchant's API.
InvoiceReceivables + InvestorRegistry turn a signed invoice into something an approved investor can buy. Payment and receivable swap in one transaction. It can't be sold twice or moved in the last 24 hours before it's due, and after a 7-day grace anyone can mark it defaulted. The registry is a testnet stand-in for KYC. Gas sponsorship can't lose money. A payment costs about 168k gas. The relayer measures it and refuses any payment whose fee wouldn't cover it, and the fee floor is enforced in the contract. We couldn't subsidize ourselves into a hole even if we tried. Off-chain: the API is Hono on Node with SQLite. It runs the relayer, the indexer, the renewal keeper, signed webhooks and an x402 facilitator built on the x402 packages. The merchant app is Next.js with Privy for sign-in and viem for the chain. There's a TypeScript SDK with React and React Native checkout components, and agent-first docs with an llms.txt.

projects.title: Vyomanaut
projects.description: A distributed storage network powered by the idle disks of everyday Phones and Computers.
projects.project_description:
Vyomanaut: storage on ordinary computers, with a trust layer that doesn’t depend on us The world is generating data faster than ever, and AI is accelerating it. Most of that data still ends up in a few large data centres that are expensive to build, power, cool and maintain. Meanwhile, millions of ordinary phones and PCs sit with spare disk space. Putting that space to work is the idea behind distributed storage, and Vyomanaut is built on it. Files are encrypted on the owner’s device before they leave, split into 5 pieces, and spread across independently run machines. Any 3 of the 5 rebuild the file. When a provider leaves, its pieces are rebuilt elsewhere. The machines only ever hold unreadable noise. The problem is trust, not storage. Distributed storage has been tried before. The hard part is not storing the pieces. It is getting strangers to rely on an operator they cannot see. Providers have to trust the operator to pay them. projects.how_its_made: Vyomanaut is being engineered as a distributed storage system, with Go powering its core infrastructure. Our architecture moves away from relying entirely on a central coordinator and towards a peer-to-peer network built using libp2p. We use distributed peer discovery and the Kademlia Distributed Hash Table (DHT) to help nodes discover and communicate with one another. QUIC provides a modern transport layer for peer communication. On the storage side, we use RocksDB as the persistent local storage engine. Files are processed into smaller chunks before distribution across participating nodes. Our architecture incorporates authenticated encryption, peer identity verification, and storage auditing to address data confidentiality and node reliability. We are also developing automated repair mechanisms to handle node failures and maintain data availability without requiring manual intervention. Erasure coding and distributed verification form important parts of our approach to fault tolerance and storage integrity. The system is being developed primarily in Go, with an emphasis on modularity, concurrency, efficient resource utilisation, and cross-platform deployment. The biggest engineering challenge is not simply distributing files. It is making a network of independently operated, intermittently available devices behave like dependable cloud storage infrastructure.

projects.title: Newton's Lobby
projects.description: Newton's Lobby: Decentralised infrastructure bridging physical locations and the digital economy.
projects.project_description:
Newton’s Lobby (com.example.unilink) is an AI-native, privacy-preserving Campus Operating System and student collaboration network. Powered by World ID 4.0 and World ID Agent Pass (https://auth.world.org/) with App ID app_23a9608a2238c84f5588e72b1e101d93, Newton's Lobby guarantees 100% Sybil-resistant human identity via Orb Proof of Human (Orb Verified 🌐), Selfie Check, and NFC Passport credentials.
The platform integrates 0G Private Computer for zero-knowledge AI video proof analysis across daily campus challenges in the DareDrop Arena (NPC Challenge, Crashed Code Face, $10M Victory Dance, ETHGlobal Meme, Startup Slogan, Developer Networking), automatically awarding UniCoins and verified badges.
Academic notes and research repositories are indexed on-chain using Arkiv Network DB-Chain (@arkiv-network/sdk) with 30-day time-scoped expiration and Swarm AES-256 encrypted decentralized storage.
projects.how_its_made:
Newton’s Lobby is built using native Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and XML layouts targeting Android 15/16 (minSdk 24, compileSdk 35). The app is engineered around a hybrid Web3 decentralized architecture that integrates World ID 4.0, 0G Private Computer, Arkiv Network DB-Chain, Swarm Decentralized Storage, and WebRTC Full HD 1080p. 🌐 World ID 4.0 & World ID Agent Pass Integration:
We integrated the official World ID Agent Pass (https://auth.world.org/ & https://auth.world.org/v1/verify) with App ID app_23a9608a2238c84f5588e72b1e101d93 and Relying Party ID rp_f622b6e137cc091b. Using IDKit v4, the app enforces a Proportional Trust Engine:•
Orb Proof of Human (Credential ID 1) for scarce Day 7 streak rewards (+150 UniCoins & Pro Pass).
•
Selfie Check (Credential ID 11) for liveness gates on hackathon team creation.
•
Passport NFC (Credential ID 9303) for encrypted international scholar verification. SHA-256 nullifier hashes (worldHumanNullifiers) are verified on our Netlify server backend (server/gate.js) and Firestore transactions to prevent duplicate account linking. 🤖 0G Private Computer (CP) ZK AI Inferences:
For the 6 ETHGlobal Mumbai DareDrop challenges (NPC Challenge, Crashed Code Face, $10M Victory Dance, Meme, Startup Slogan, Developer Networking), we connected to 0G Private Computer (0gm-1.0 / qwen-omni). When students upload video or photo proofs, 0G executes zero-knowledge verified AI inference to inspect the content and automatically award +25 UniCoins & Human Verified 🌐 Star Badges. 🗄️ Arkiv Network DB-Chain & Swarm Decentralized Storage:
Campus study notes and project repositories are indexed on-chain using Arkiv Network DB-Chain (@arkiv-network/sdk) with 30-day time-scoped expiration (ExpirationTime.fromDays(30)). Heavy media and PDF files are uploaded to Swarm decentralized blob storage (bzz://...), with raw BZZ references encrypted via AES-256 before being bound to public Arkiv entity fields. 📹 Studio-Grade 1080p SpeedLink & Reels Live Switcher:
Video matching utilizes WebRTC P2P mesh running at 1080p 30 FPS. For campus live streams, we built a vertical Instagram Reels-style gesture switcher (▲ REEL LIVE ▼) to swipe seamlessly between active live streams. 💡 Notable & Clever Hacks:
•
16 KB Page-Size Boundary Alignment: Verified 100% 16 KB page-alignment ((OK)) on all C++ shared libraries (libjingle_peerconnection_so.so, libimage_processing_util_jni.so, libsurface_util_jni.so) with zipalign -c -v 16384 to prevent Android 15/16 kernel page faults.
•
PhotoPicker URI Cache Copy: Temporarily streams Android PhotoPicker content URIs to a local cache file (daredrop_cache/vid_XYZ.mp4) before permission revocation, generating permanent HTTPS Firebase Storage download URLs.
•
30-Minute Midnight Auto-Rotation: Uses modulo arithmetic elapsed since midnight ((now - midnightMs) / (30 * 60 * 1000) % 6) to rotate the 6 competition dares seamlessly across all devices.

projects.title: UltraRentz
projects.description: A rent deposit that earns interest, and a clean-tenancy record that moves with the tenant.
projects.project_description:
UltraRentz is an onchain rent-deposit escrow on Arc. Tenants hand over thousands in deposits that sit idle for the whole tenancy and often come back late, reduced, or not at all, especially for international students who leave the country before a dispute is resolved. UltraRentz holds each deposit in a tenancy-specific USDC vault that earns interest for the tenant. The release rules are agreed upfront and enforced by code: a deduction needs a claim, and if there is no valid claim by the deadline, the deposit returns to the tenant. This is a Continuity Track project. Before ETHGlobal Mumbai we had a working USDC deposit vault on Arc testnet with a two-step release flow, tenancy roles (tenant, landlord, arbiter, agent), simulated yield and a React frontend. At ETHGlobal Mumbai (5 to 7 Nov) we added the Deposit Passport: A clean tenancy is recorded on Arc, and its evidence is stored on Arkiv. The page re-hashes the evidence from Arkiv and compares it with the hash on Arc.
A tenant can move the deposit to a new tenancy with a server-signed approval (EIP-712), after a human check. Two rollovers have run live on Arc testnet.
The human check uses World ID Agent Pass. The real flow is built and tested, but World’s sandbox could not issue a test identity, so the demo uses a clearly labelled mock.
Practice money on testnet; unaudited; no paying customers yet.
projects.how_its_made: Arc: USDC is both the gas token and the deposit asset on Arc testnet. All contract deployment, testing and the live rollovers ran on Arc. Arc Studio: https://studio.arc.io/app/b0ba1b26-562d-42ff-8f5f-336a74d33ced World: a server-side OIDC step-up (World ID Agent Pass) gates the approval. The server signs a one-time EIP-712 approval, and the contract checks the signature before it moves the deposit. The demo uses a labelled mock because the sandbox couldn’t issue a test identity. AI usage: I built this with Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and planning assistant. Claude helped write and test the contract changes, the serverless functions, the React page, the documentation and the slides. I made the product decisions, ran the deployments and transactions, and checked every claim against the live app and the Arc explorer. The mock human check is labelled as a mock in the UI and the video.

projects.title: Kept
projects.description: Crypto calls with a real stop. Pull it, and the group sees it, on Base, Arkiv and ENS.
projects.project_description: The most dangerous thing in a trading group isn't a bad call. It's a caller who can delete the evidence. Telegram channels with tens of thousands of followers post trades with a stop loss attached. Followers buy. When the price turns, the caller quietly cancels the stop, sells into the people who copied them, and deletes the post. Only the winning screenshots stay. Kept makes the stop real. Every call is a market buy on Base through Definitive Flash, with the stop-loss and take-profit attached as one bracket order that rests from the first second. Followers ride the same call from their own wallets: their own size, their own signatures, the same exits. Then Kept watches. Cancel the stop, widen it, or move the tokens out while it is live, and the call reads PULLED. A signed cancel flipped the Telegram card to PULLED 7 seconds later. A sale under a live stop was caught 1 min 53 s after its block, with the exact Base transaction on the call page. Every ending lands where nobody can quietly edit it. @KeptCallsBot posts each call as its own card and edits that card to KEPT or PULLED, so deleting the caller's message hides nothing. Arkiv holds each call and its outcome, extended to a 180-day record window when the call ends. ENS carries the caller's reputation: riya.kept.eth reads kept:2;pulled:4, and every call has its own name, <callId>.riya.kept.eth, with its terms, status, fill and exit. Only Kept's attester can write them, and any app that resolves ENS reads them. All 7 of riya's calls read back from ENS match Kept's own record. Callers can also put money behind a call. KeptBond locks USDC on Base: keep the stop and it comes back, pull it and it pays the riders, weighted by what each of them actually filled. You can delete a post. You cannot delete the trade.
projects.how_its_made: Archiv is the backend with ENS as the social layer. The order engine is a Cloudflare Durable Object with a 30-second alarm. Shared logic lives in one TypeScript core package: the Flash client, the Arkiv store and queries, the exit detector, the ENS client and zod schemas. KeptBond is a Solidity contract built and tested with Foundry, including Base fork tests. Definitive Flash is the execution layer. Every call and every ride is a Flash quote with an attached bracket, signed twice over EIP-712 and posted to the order API; fills settle on Base through Flash's settlement contract. The part we're proudest of: a cancelled stop is a signed message, not a transaction, so it never appears onchain. Only the app that placed the order sees it. Kept holds Flash's org-level Orders WebSocket open and turns fills, stop hits, take-profits, expiries and signed cancels into the public record. Raising a stop is one signature: we rebuild Flash's bracket update message byte for byte, the owner signs it, and PATCH /orders replaces the stop leg while the target stays untouched. Riders get a Match button that copies the raise. The hacky bit is catching a dump without watching every block. Every 30 seconds, one multicall reads every live position's balance. Only a wallet holding less than its fill triggers a newest-first log search for the Transfer or WETH unwrap. The worker waits 45 blocks and reads the Flash stop order before writing, so a bracket's own stop sale is never counted as a dump. Arkiv is the database. Profiles, calls, rides, outcomes, alerts and seals are entities with indexed attributes, and the feed, call pages, leaderboard and live pull radar are all Arkiv queries. One executeBatch ends a call: it patches the status and extends the call and its outcomes to a 180-day record window, so waiting out a short horizon erases nothing. Sealed calls use Arkiv's $creator and $owner split: the caller's wallet creates the terms and hands the entity to Kept's attester in the same batch, so neither side can rewrite them alone. ENS is the reputation layer. Each caller gets a non-transferable <name>.kept.eth with a dedicated resolver. kept.record, kept.history and kept.stats sit on the caller's name, and every call gets its own <callId>.<name>.kept.eth carrying kept.call, kept.status, kept.fill and kept.exit. Only Kept's attester can write them. The worker mints a call's name when it posts and updates it on every outcome, and /ens/<name> reads the whole history back through the Universal Resolver and checks each call against Kept's own record. The Telegram bot runs inside the same worker and edits its own cards with editMessageText, driven by the same events that write Arkiv and ENS. KeptBond settles from a dedicated settler key that refuses to run if it matches the Arkiv or ENS key, and weights each rider by the USDC their Flash entry order actually filled.

KeptBond settles from a dedicated settler key that refuses to run if it matches the Arkiv or ENS key, and weights each rider by the USDC their Flash entry order actually filled.

projects.title: RentAnLLM
projects.description: Rent open LLMs running on people's own machines. AI agents pay per request in USDC.
projects.project_description: RentAnLLM is an inference market for AI agents. Anyone can sell an open model (Llama, FLUX and others) running on their own machine, and agents buy it one request at a time, paying the seller directly in USDC on Hedera over x402. No account, no API key, no subscription. How a request works: A seller runs our node agent next to Ollama and lists a model with a price. An agent calls our OpenAI-compatible endpoint and gets back an HTTP 402 quoting the cheapest online seller. The agent signs a USDC transfer to that seller and sends the request again. The seller's machine answers, the payment settles on Hedera, and the answer comes back with the transaction ID as a receipt. If the seller fails, nothing is charged. You can use it from any OpenAI client, from a fully autonomous CLI agent, or from Claude Desktop / Claude Code / Cursor through our hosted MCP connector, which gives each user their own agent wallet. Why you can trust it: Spending limits (daily budget, max per request, per-seller limits, allowlist, pause) are enforced by the gateway before any money moves. Small payments go through on their own, and anything above a threshold needs the human behind the agent to approve it with World ID. Every payment is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic that anyone can audit. Sellers have an onchain identity and an uptime/latency reputation (ERC-8004 on Hedera) that they can't write themselves. Live offers and receipts are public on Arkiv, and the market reads them from there. Live at rentanllm.xyz. Example settled payment: https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.9185802%401793922799.072231068
projects.how_its_made:
TypeScript monorepo on Bun, with almost all the backend written in Effect. Five apps: Gateway (Docker on a VPS): the x402 market. OpenAI-compatible chat and image endpoints, pricing, verify/settle through the x402.org facilitator, and a WebSocket tunnel to seller machines, so a seller behind home NAT never opens a port. Node agent: runs beside Ollama or stable-diffusion.cpp on the seller's machine. Our demo seller is an RTX 3090 serving llama3.1:8b and FLUX.2. API (Vercel): seller accounts (SIWE), listings, budgets, and a remote MCP server with OAuth 2.1. On first connect it creates a Hedera account for the user and stores the key encrypted. MCP client + autonomous buyer: signs payments with @x402/hedera. Web (Next.js): market, seller console, budgets. Designed in Paper first.
Postgres (Drizzle) and Redis underneath, Grafana/Loki/Tempo for tracing paid requests. How we used each partner: Hedera: HTS USDC for the payments themselves. The facilitator pays the HBAR fee, so agents only ever need USDC, and money goes buyer → seller without us holding it. HCS topic 0.0.11332573 is the spend audit log. ERC-8004 registries on Hedera EVM plus an HCS-14 agent ID give sellers identity, and a separate monitor wallet posts their reputation every 6 hours. The mirror node checks a seller can actually receive USDC before they list. World ID: the OIDC device flow, with the ID token validated on our server. Each approval is tied to one exact amount and payee and works only once. The npm SDK was out of date, so we ported its logic onto oauth4webapi + jose. Arkiv: the gateway writes offers every 3 minutes and one receipt per sale, and the homepage, /v1/models and Claude's list_models all read from Arkiv instead of our db. Hacky bits and things that bit us: Pay only on delivery. Our first version settled before serving, so when our image server ran out of GPU memory the buyer paid for nothing. Now we verify up front and settle the moment the seller starts answering, before any output is sent. A seller failure costs nothing, and a failed settlement returns no output. Images pretend to be text: one image is billed as a million output tokens, so receipts, budgets and Arkiv reuse the chat code untouched. Anyone can write a fake "rentanllm.offer" on Arkiv, so every reader only trusts entities owned by our writer wallet (ownedBy). Circle's faucet silently dropped our first claim because the wallet wasn't associated with USDC yet, and the 2-hour limit blocked a retry. Sellers hit the same trap, so the console now checks and offers one-click association. Paying needs only USDC, but registering as an ERC-8004 seller needs HBAR, so a new seller holding only USDC fails. Still on our list.

projects.title: HIR
projects.description: An ENSv2-powered evidence layer for verifiable  authority, actions, and audit trails.
projects.project_description:
HIR - History · Integrity · Responsibility is an ENSv2-powered evidence layer designed to make authority, records, decisions, and actions independently verifiable. The idea behind HIR starts with a simple problem: a cryptographic signature can tell us which wallet signed something, but it doesn't necessarily tell us whether that wallet was authorized to act on behalf of an organization, what permissions it had at that point in time, or what happened afterward. HIR aims to connect these missing pieces. Organizations can publish identities and delegated authority through ENSv2. Records, requests, decisions, and outcomes can then be linked to that published authority using cryptographic signatures and onchain evidence. This creates a verifiable history that third parties can independently inspect without relying solely on the organization or HIR's application. The objective is to answer three questions:
•	Who was authorized to do what?
•	What was recorded, decided, or reported to have happened?
•	Can someone independently verify the evidence afterward? For the hackathon, we built two working applications of this approach. Invoice Authenticity An organization publishes its authorized invoice signer and approved payment instructions through ENSv2. Each issued invoice has its own resolvable ENS identity and signed evidence.
A recipient can independently verify that the invoice was authorized, its payment details match the organization's policy, its revision is current, and the PDF hasn't been tampered with. This helps address Business Email Compromise (BEC), where attackers impersonate suppliers or alter invoices and payment instructions to redirect funds to fraudulent accounts. HIR allows recipients to verify payment instructions against the organization's published authority before making a payment. AI Agent Authority & Evidence As AI agents become more autonomous and start interacting with other agents, businesses, and external services, an important question arises: How does a third party know what an AI agent is actually authorized to do on behalf of an organization? Without a verifiable source of authority, third parties may have to rely on the agent's own claims, creating risks of unauthorized actions, misuse of permissions, and a lack of accountability. HIR addresses this by allowing organizations to publish AI agents' identities and permissions through ENSv2. When an agent requests an action from another agent, the receiving agent can independently verify its published authority before deciding whether to proceed. Our working demonstration uses two real LLM agents. One requests an analysis service, while the other checks the published 50-credit limit and accepts or rejects the request. HIR preserves evidence of the request, decision, and outcome, including whether the decision complied with the organization's published policy. The goal is to make delegated authority independently verifiable and autonomous agent interactions auditable, rather than relying solely on trust between agents. HIR is not trying to claim that blockchain proves every real-world action. It establishes attributable records, published authority, and tamper-evident evidence that can be independently checked. The distinction between what someone was permitted to do and what they actually claimed or attempted to do is central to the design. Our larger objective is to make verifiable authority and evidence a reusable foundation for interactions between organizations, people, and autonomous systems.
projects.how_its_made:
HIR is built around a common architecture: ENSv2 provides organizational identity and delegated authority, cryptographic signatures bind records and actions to their participants, and smart contracts preserve verifiable evidence. We implemented two independent applications to demonstrate how the same approach works across different use cases. ENSv2 — Identity and Authority HIR uses an organization's existing ENS identity as the foundation for publishing authority.
Using ENSv2's hierarchical namespace and permissioned resolvers, organizations can establish application-specific identities and publish records defining authorized signers, agent identities, permissions, and other policies. These records can be retrieved independently through ENSv2's native resolution infrastructure. ENS is therefore not just a readable name or branding element; it is the source of organizational authority used by HIR's verification mechanisms. Cryptographic Evidence and Smart Contracts We use Solidity smart contracts deployed on Ethereum Sepolia, EIP-712 typed-data signatures, and cryptographic commitments to link records and actions to their authorization context. The contracts serve different purposes depending on the application. The invoice evidence ledger validates authorization before accepting issuance, while the agent evidence contract records authenticated interactions, including decisions that may violate published permissions. Full documents and agent conversations are not stored onchain. Instead, HIR records commitments to evidence that can be retained, downloaded, and independently verified.
Invoice Authenticity Application The invoice application generates PDFs using PDFKit and hashes the exact document bytes.
An EIP-712 signed record binds the invoice identity, issuer, amount, payment destination, token, revision, and PDF fingerprint. A dedicated evidence ledger validates the relevant ENS-published authority and payment instructions before accepting publication. Each invoice also receives an ENSv2-resolvable evidence reference, allowing recipients to independently discover and verify its records without relying on HIR's database. AI Agent Authority Application We built two real LLM agents using the OpenAI Agents SDK, with separate roles and tools.
The requesting agent signs a structured request. The receiving agent independently retrieves the requesting agent's authority from ENSv2, uses deterministic policy assessment, and decides whether to accept or reject the request. The receiving agent performs a real calculation when it accepts an authorized request.
The request, policy checkpoint, decision, and execution outcome are signed and linked together. A separate evidence contract records their commitment onchain. Historical verification checks the permissions that existed at the time of the interaction rather than relying only on the current ENS policy. Our live Sepolia demonstration includes an accepted 40-credit request and a rejected 80-credit request under a published 50-credit permission. Technology and Infrastructure The applications use JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Tailwind CSS, Cloudflare Workers, and SQLite-backed Durable Objects for application state and offchain evidence. Solidity and OpenZeppelin support the smart contracts and signature verification, while Viem handles Ethereum interactions, typed-data encoding, ENS resolution, and transaction verification.
Technical Challenges One of the main challenges was establishing authority at the time an action occurred, even if the organization's policy subsequently changed. We addressed this through historical ENS policy checkpoints and independently verifiable signed evidence. Another challenge was maintaining a clear distinction between published permissions, participant decisions, and execution outcomes. HIR preserves these separately instead of treating an accepted request as proof that the action was completed or authorized.
The completed prototype demonstrates both applications on Sepolia, with actual ENSv2 records, signed evidence, confirmed onchain commitments, and independent verification.
