projects.title: Unseen Shield
projects.description: Check your wallet's risky approvals and balances privately: every read goes through Anon-RPC.
projects.project_description:
When you use a crypto app, you give it an approval to spend your tokens. It lasts forever and is usually unlimited. When one of those contracts is hacked, thieves drain wallets through old approvals: LI.FI users lost about $10M in July 2024, Socket users about $3.3M in January 2024. Approval checkers exist, but checking leaks you. They query servers, indexers and RPC providers that see your wallet address next to your IP. You end up telling a stranger "this wallet is mine, and it might be vulnerable". Security tools shouldn't make you less safe.
Unseen Shield checks a wallet without anyone learning whose it is. Type an address or ENS name and press "Check privately". You get one report: Approvals: which contracts can still spend your tokens. Red for contracts already drained through approvals, orange for unlimited approvals on tokens you hold. A Revoke button sets each one back to zero from your own wallet. Holdings: your coins and major tokens on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon and BNB Chain, priced with Chainlink feeds read on-chain. Privacy receipt: the route the check took through the Nym mixnet, proof that two independent providers gave identical answers, and every request that left the device.
A Compare page runs the same check the normal way, so you can watch a provider log your device and link your wallets, while Unseen Shield's requests reveal nothing.
No accounts, no server database, no trackers. The wallet list stays in your browser, and only if you choose to remember it.
projects.how_its_made:
Unseen Shield is a Next.js + TypeScript app that runs entirely in the browser. All blockchain reads use viem through a custom transport built on the Ethereum Foundation's @anon-rpc/browser-harness. On page
load, the harness reads the network's on-chain specifier contract, downloads the Nym mixnet client, verifies its keccak256 hash and runs it in a sandboxed null-origin iframe. Every RPC request then goes through worker.fetch over Nym (Nox is selectable), so providers see a mixnet exit, never the user's IP. The only direct request is the harness's bootstrap read of the specifier, which contains no wallet data, and we disclose it.
Privacy details: Each wallet gets its own Anon-RPC isolationKey, so a user's wallets can't be linked together, even by the mixnet. We deliberately avoid indexers (they would learn whose wallet it is). Instead, each scan is one Multicall3 bundle of about 160 read-only calls at a fixed block: ERC-20 allowance() for 11 tokens across 12 commonly approved contracts (including the exploited LI.FI Diamond and Socket Gateway), Permit2 allowances for Uniswap's Universal Router, balanceOf(), and 8 Chainlink price feeds (latestRoundData()). One more bundle per chain reads balances on Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon and BNB Chain. Every token and feed address was verified on-chain.
Trust and reliability: Double-check: a second provider on a separate private path answers the same bundle at the same block. Matching answers are shown as double-checked; a mismatch warns the user. Safety guard: if too many approval checks come back unanswered, the app retries with another provider and otherwise shows an error, never a false "safe". Some RPC providers stall on mixnet traffic, so requests rotate across providers. Two failures in a row rebuild the route (a fresh exit) and rescan. Switching networks shuts down the previous worker  immediately.
Revoking sends approve(spender, 0) (or Permit2 approve with amount 0) from the user's own wallet. We have no smart contract and never request any approval.
Hosted on Vercel; the code is MIT-licensed on GitHub and runs locally with npm install && npm run dev. Tor (tor-js) is supported in the code but hidden from the picker because its public demo gateway was  too overloaded to connect reliably during the event.
AI use: we used Claude Code as a coding and research assistant: writing and refactoring code, verifying contract addresses on-chain, browser testing and UI design. We reviewed and can explain every part.

projects.title: Till
projects.description: Get paid by people and AI agents that can't be tricked into overpaying.
projects.project_description: Till is a checkout a small online shop adds in about 20 lines to get paid in USDT by two kinds of customers: people and AI agents. Try it live at till.ishtails.xyz: open the demo shop, sign in with any email, get free test USDT, and buy a $0.10 report. People pay with just an email or a Google login: no wallet app, no seed phrase and no gas. They sign the payment, and Till's relayer submits it on Whitechain and pays the fee. AI agents pay per API call over x402, with no sign-up, API key or monthly bill. They settle in USDT on Whitechain or USDC on Hedera. After the payment, the merchant refunds in one click, in full or in part, and the contract never lets a refund pass what was paid. Agent payments on Whitechain refund the same way. The dashboard exports a CSV for the accountant, and the merchant prepays its customers' gas from a gas tank in USDT, charged at cost plus 10%. Every receipt is saved on Arkiv, so the customer's receipt page, and a list of their purchases from every Till shop, don't depend on the shop's database. The second half is a spending guard for whoever runs the agent: an allowlist, per-call and daily caps, and a daily budget, all checked in the agent's wallet before anything is signed. A payment that breaks a rule is blocked outright; one that's only unusual, above the auto-pay limit, waits for the owner to approve it on their phone. The owner signs the limits, and the agent checks that signature, so even Till can't loosen them. Before the event I tested a poisoned-link attack on three Claude models, and it fooled every one, every time. In the demo, a review page sends the agent to a look-alike API that asks 10 times the price. The guard blocks it, because the payee isn't on its list or the shop's address in Till's registry on Arkiv. Every payment, approval and blocked attempt goes to a public log on Hedera, and the agent's identity is registered on ERC-8004.
projects.how_its_made: A Bun monorepo: a Hono server, a React app (Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui on Base UI, Motion) for the landing page, docs, checkout, receipts, the customer's account, the merchant dashboard and the agent console (each opens only for its own wallet), a separate demo shop that only uses our SDK, and the agent. It runs live on one small server behind Caddy, at till.ishtails.xyz; the live demo has a faucet that sends a new email wallet 0.2 test USDT, gas-free through the same relayer, with per-wallet and daily limits. Whitechain: customers sign in with a Privy email or Google wallet and sign an EIP-3009 ReceiveWithAuthorization for the test USDT. Our relayer submits it to a small Checkout contract (Foundry, verified on Blockscout), which pays the merchant and emits Paid and Refunded events keyed by order ID. Refunds can be partial, and the contract caps their total at the amount paid. A checkout payment costs about 180k gas (~0.0009 WBT). Each merchant has a gas tank: the relayer reads the real fee of every transaction it sends for that shop from the receipt, charges it in USD plus 10%, and stops relaying when the tank is empty; top-ups are USDT transfers the merchant signs. Refunds of agent payments are EIP-3009 transfers back to the agent, signed by the merchant and submitted by the relayer. The relayer only signs three calls, only for real orders from registered merchants, simulates each one first, and has rate limits and daily caps. Agent payments use x402 v2 (@x402/core, /evm, /hedera). The same server is our own x402 facilitator on Whitechain (chain 1874) and on Hedera, where we added an expiry check and a settlement cache on top of the library, with x402.org as the fallback. The agent is Claude, run headless on the claude CLI with only an MCP wallet server as its tools. The spending guard runs in the x402 client's onBeforePaymentCreation hook, inside the wallet, so the model can't talk its way past it. Payments above the auto-pay limit pause there: the agent posts an approval request, the owner approves or denies on the console with a wallet-signed message, and the agent polls for the answer. The limits themselves are signed by the owner on the console, and the agent verifies the signature before using them. Paid, approved and blocked attempts are written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, and after each run the agent's spend report reads them back from the public mirror node. The agent is registered in the ERC-8004 Identity Registry already deployed on Hedera testnet; it puts its ID in each x402 payment's extensions, and the server checks the payer against the registry after settling. Arkiv: after each payment or refund, the server saves a receipt record on Arkiv's Rabdi testnet (SDK 1.0.1) with a typed schema. The receipt page and the customer's account page query Arkiv straight from the browser, filtered to our writer wallet, so they still load with our server stopped. The server also lists each merchant on Arkiv (prices, payout addresses per network); the agent's find_sellers tool queries it, and the guard blocks any payee that doesn't match the seller's record. Hacky bits: the test USDT has no version(), so we recovered its EIP-712 domain from DOMAIN_SEPARATOR. Hedera payments expire 120 s after signing, so our facilitator rejects stale ones at verify instead of failing at settle. Claude Code was the coding assistant and R&D tool; see AI_USAGE.md.
projects.project_description_markdown:
Till is a checkout a small online shop adds in about 20 lines to get paid in USDT by two kinds of customers: people and AI agents.

Try it live at till.ishtails.xyz: open the demo shop, sign in with any email, get free test USDT, and buy a $0.10 report.

People pay with just an email or a Google login: no wallet app, no seed phrase and no gas. They sign the payment, and Till's relayer submits it on Whitechain and pays the fee.

AI agents pay per API call over x402, with no sign-up, API key or monthly bill. They settle in USDT on Whitechain or USDC on Hedera.

After the payment, the merchant refunds in one click, in full or in part, and the contract never lets a refund pass what was paid. Agent payments on Whitechain refund the same way. The dashboard exports a CSV for the accountant, and the merchant prepays its customers' gas from a gas tank in USDT, charged at cost plus 10%. Every receipt is saved on Arkiv, so the customer's receipt page, and a list of their purchases from every Till shop, don't depend on the shop's database.

The second half is a spending guard for whoever runs the agent: an allowlist, per-call and daily caps, and a daily budget, all checked in the agent's wallet before anything is signed. A payment that breaks a rule is blocked outright; one that's only unusual, above the auto-pay limit, waits for the owner to approve it on their phone. The owner signs the limits, and the agent checks that signature, so even Till can't loosen them. Before the event I tested a poisoned-link attack on three Claude models, and it fooled every one, every time. In the demo, a review page sends the agent to a look-alike API that asks 10 times the price. The guard blocks it, because the payee isn't on its list or the shop's address in Till's registry on Arkiv. Every payment, approval and blocked attempt goes to a public log on Hedera, and the agent's identity is registered on ERC-8004.

projects.title: PranaNet
projects.description: Honest air-quality nodes anyone can run: signed, cross-checked, slashable readings you can verify
projects.project_description:
Air-quality readings are easy to fake, and it keeps happening. In 2016, officials in Xi'an stuffed cotton into air monitors; seven were jailed. In Delhi in 2025, officials were accused of spraying water around monitoring stations, and 163 hours of peak Diwali data were reported missing. Whoever is being measured often holds the meter.
PranaNet is a democracy of honest air sensors. Anyone can run a node. Each node generates its own key and signs every reading on the device, so nobody downstream, including us, can change it. Operators prove they're unique humans with World ID (at most three nodes each), so nobody can fake a crowd. Every node gets an ENSv2 name with its location cell. Raw readings are public on Arkiv, so anyone can re-check them. Every epoch, each node is compared with its neighbours and the nearest official monitor; three outliers in a row and it's slashed: its stake goes to the reward pool and its ENS name is revoked. Customers, including AI agents paying over x402 on Hedera, buy the cross-checked data, and that revenue pays honest nodes. Cheaters pay the honest.
We start in Mumbai, where dust monitoring is legally required at 3,166 construction sites and BMC pays auditors to check sensors by hand. Then Delhi NCR, where the idea began, then any city that argues about its air. No token: rewards come from revenue.
projects.how_its_made: Hardware and firmware: two ESP32 DevKit boards with Sharp GP2Y1014 dust sensors (10k/22k divider into an ADC1 pin) and a DHT22. Each board generates its own secp256k1 key on first boot and keeps it in flash. It signs every reading with the mbedTLS library that ships with the ESP32 core (RFC 6979 deterministic signatures, low-s), plus our own Keccak-256 and recovery-id code. The device packs a 264-byte message (device, epoch, PM2.5, PM10, temp, humidity, nonce, chainId, contract address) and signs it EIP-191 style. A serial self-test proves the device's signature is byte-identical to viem's. Each node gets a one-point calibration against the nearest official monitor when installed. Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, 51 tests including fork tests against live ENSv2 on Sepolia): Registry, Readings, Stake, RewardPool and DeviceNamer. Readings rebuilds the message, runs ecrecover and rejects replays. Three consecutive neighbour flags slash a node: its stake moves to the reward pool, it's deactivated and its ENS name is revoked in the same transaction. How each partner helped: ENSv2: every node gets a readable, accountable name like bkc-01.prananet.eth through the ENSv2 UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver, with addr, geohash and status records. Owners can only edit metadata; the network revokes a cheater's name. World ID 4.0: stops one person faking a crowd of sensors. IDKit on the web uses the node's address as the signal; the relayer verifies the proof server-side with the v4 verify API and checks the signal hash; the contract caps each human at 3 nodes. Proof of Human gives uniqueness without revealing identity. Arkiv: every raw reading, device and flag is a public entity on Arkiv (Rabdi testnet), queryable by location cell, node and time, with the signature stored alongside. Readings expire after 3 days, flags after 30, while summaries stay on Sepolia. The website queries Arkiv straight from the visitor's browser and re-verifies signatures there, so nobody has to trust our server. Hedera + x402: AI agents buy the cleaned, cross-checked data per request. The API returns HTTP 402, the agent pays in HBAR through the x402.org facilitator on hedera:testnet, with a hard budget cap and every purchase logged to an HCS topic. A bridge re-checks each payment on the Hedera mirror node, then funds the reward pool on Sepolia, and honest nodes claim from it. Off-chain: a Node/TypeScript relayer (viem) that can't alter data, only deliver it. It checks signatures and nonces, writes to Arkiv, submits to Sepolia and streams a live feed. A verifier compares each node with the median of its neighbours and the nearest OpenAQ reference station and calls flag() on-chain. Relayer, verifier and API run on Render; the Next.js site (folk-art story with interactive "try to cheat" and tamper demos, plus a live map) runs on Vercel. Hacky bits: Sepolia contract creation needed about 7x forge's gas estimate, so the deploy script applies a multiplier. Arkiv string columns cap at 128 bytes, so signatures are stored as bytes. The contract's try/catch around the ENS revoke hid an out-of-gas error, so the verifier now sends flag() with a fixed gas limit. And a node that booted in smoky air set its zero point too high and got slashed while honest, so the firmware's baseline can now only move down.

projects.title: Glyf
projects.description: An AI keyboard for mobile that swaps on Uniswap, places Flash orders and thinks privately on 0G.
projects.project_description: Glyf is an AI keyboard for mobile, on iPhone (TestFlight) and Android. At ETHGlobal Mumbai we taught the iPhone keyboard to trade from the words you already type, in any app: WhatsApp, Messages, X, anywhere. Definitive Flash, for orders that wait. "sell my eth if it drops below 3000", "take profit at 4500", "protect my eth with a 5% trail", "buy $20 of eth every day for a week". The keyboard reads the sentence on the phone (no AI, no server), shows a live Flash quote you can edit, and places stop-losses, take-profits, limits, stop buys, brackets, trailing stops and TWAP, on Base and on Solana. Open orders list with Cancel. Uniswap, for trades now. "swap 0.05 eth to usdc on base" gets a live Uniswap quote inside the keyboard, any token to any token, with token and chain pickers, on Base, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism and Unichain. You keep the keys. Glyf builds every transaction on the phone, then signs with its own wallet (one 24-word phrase makes both its Ethereum and Solana wallets) or hops to MetaMask or Phantom by deeplink and comes straight back. No web page, no WalletConnect relay, and every signature is checked before anything is sent. Trading is social. Share a trade into the chat; a friend taps Copy this trade and the same order opens in their Glyf, waiting for their tap. Private AI on 0G. A keyboard sees everything you type, so its AI has to be private. On this build every AI call (answers, rewrites, and recommendations: type "dca 20$ in eth each month" and a chip offers the Flash plan, filled in) runs on 0G Private Computer inside a TEE, and each answer's 0G request id is listed in the app as a receipt.
projects.how_its_made: Three parts: a native Swift keyboard extension, a Flutter app that holds the wallets and signs, and a Fastify/TypeScript server on Vercel. They talk through an App Group (shared settings) and glyf:// links. Keyboard (Swift). TradeIntent.swift reads trades in plain words with no model: amounts, "$50 of", "all my", prices, percentages, durations, chains, ENS and SNS names. TradeSurface.swift draws the quote, the editable amounts and prices, and the token and chain pickers inside the keyboard, with each chain's real logo parsed from its SVG path data on the phone. One tap hands the trade to the app. Definitive Flash. The server proxies /quote and /order with our integrator key and maps symbols to assets per chain. On EVM the phone signs Flash's evmOrderTypedData, Permit2 and the attached bracket (EIP-712). On Solana, Flash's setup instructions (token accounts, SOL wrap, delegation) become one transaction built on the phone; Phantom signs it and the order message, and each signature is checked with Ed25519 before Flash sees it. Flash's 30-day TWAP limit is why a monthly DCA becomes a plan. Uniswap. The Trading API when keyed; otherwise QuoterV2 over every fee tier in one Multicall3 call, two-pool routes through WETH or USDC, and SwapRouter02 calldata, proven with eth_call balance overrides before we had funds. 0G. One header (X-Glyf-AI: 0g), read through AsyncLocalStorage, sends every existing AI route to 0G's OpenAI-compatible router with Private trust mode and verify_tee: no route changed. 0gm-1.0-35b-a3b-sia streams a rewrite in about 2.2 s for about $0.0002, and each x_0g_trace request id is saved as a receipt. TestFlight builds never send the header and keep their usual models. Hacky bits: trades are understood with zero AI calls; MetaMask's archived iOS SDK deeplink protocol re-implemented in about 150 lines of Dart (connect, sign, a chain switch batched in front, replies on glyf://); stand-ins that answer as MetaMask and Phantom so the whole flow runs in the simulator and in unit tests.

projects.title: WalletCordon
projects.description: WalletCordon gives AI agents wallet access without giving them unrestricted control.
projects.project_description: WalletCordon is a personalized security layer between an AI agent and a user’s wallet. The goal is simple: let AI agents perform useful on-chain actions without giving them unrestricted control over a user’s money. Instead of accessing the wallet directly, the agent must propose the exact transaction to WalletCordon, including the chain, wallet address, contract, calldata, value, nonce, gas, and fees. The transaction then passes through five stages: Propose, Normalize, Check, Simulate, and Decide. First, WalletCordon normalizes the proposal so the transaction being checked is exactly the one that may later reach the wallet. Its deterministic engine then compares it against the user’s policy. Allowed contracts, function selectors, spending limits, token approvals, recipients, gas limits, slippage, expiry, blocked addresses, and other rules. It also checks fresh protocol-state information to determine whether a contract is operational, paused, stale, or potentially compromised. WalletCordon then simulates the complete transaction using independent trace-capable nodes. This analysis goes beyond checking whether the transaction succeeds. It inspects internal contract calls, token transfers, approvals, emitted logs, gas usage, storage changes, and unexpected code changes. The nodes must agree on the result before the transaction can continue. Most importantly, this simulation is personalized. A professional trader may be comfortable allowing a 1,000 USDC swap, while another user may want a maximum limit of 100 USDC. The same transaction could therefore be approved for one user and denied for another. WalletCordon evaluates whether a transaction is safe for that specific user, not just whether it looks generally safe. Users can create these rules in plain language with the Policy AI Maker and review or modify every permission using the visual Block Builder. AI only generates a draft; deterministic code validates and enforces the actual policy. If a rule is broken, a hidden internal call appears, protocol state is unsafe, or simulations disagree, WalletCordon denies the transaction before the wallet is asked to sign.
projects.how_its_made: WalletCordon is built with Node.js, Next.js, React, ethers.js, Solidity, Foundry, and two independent Anvil nodes. A guarded EIP-1193 provider acts as the enforcement boundary. It normalizes the exact transaction envelope, evaluates machine-readable JSON policy rules, verifies threshold-signed Ed25519 protocol-state bundles, and requires full-trace simulation consensus before forwarding eth_sendTransaction. The simulator compares internal calls, logs, gas usage, state writes, code changes, and asset movements across both nodes. Our Solidity demo includes a normal router and a compromised path containing a hidden internal call, proving that valid-looking calldata can still be denied. The Policy Studio uses AI to translate plain-language requirements into constrained draft rules. Deterministic code then resolves addresses, compiles exact limits, and validates the result. The AI never sees a private key and cannot activate a policy. Decisions are stored as hash-chained audit receipts, while the interface displays the complete allow-or-deny evidence.

The AI never sees a private key and cannot activate a policy. Decisions are stored as hash-chained audit receipts, while the interface displays the complete allow-or-deny evidence.

projects.title: Lattice
projects.description: Private solver mesh powered by Js-libp2p. Intents settled before the chain sees them.
projects.project_description: Lattice is a decentralized, private solver mesh where user swap intents are propagated over a js-libp2p GossipSub network, auctioned via a two-phase commit-reveal protocol, and settled on Arbitrum through EIP-712 signed smart contracts — all before touching the public mempool. Solvers compete in a private RFQ auction; the winning bid executes a Uniswap v3 swap onchain. MEV vectors including timing fingerprinting, auction sniping, front-running, and overpromise slashing are explicitly mitigated at both the p2p and contract layers.

Solvers bid via a custom "/defi/rfq/1.0.0" stream protocol with a two-phase commit-reveal auction (0–60ms commit, 60–80ms reveal) to prevent sniping. Smart contracts in Solidity 0.8.34 (Foundry): IntentSettlement.sol calls Uniswap v3 SwapRouter (ExactInput) for execution and QuoterV2 for solver bid estimation; SolverRegistry.sol handles stake, tier gating, slashing, and a Safe multisig treasury. During Hackathon:I deployed MockIntentSettlement to Arbitrum Sepolia for a fully green demo flow, and hardened mainnet contracts with Safe-guarded treasury, CEI + nonReentrant + SafeERC20, ECDSA.tryRecover, and stored settlementActualOutput for slash-proof overpromise detection. (PoW in demo video)

projects.title: Kosha
projects.description: AI agents pay APIs over x402 on Hedera, and Kosha withholds tax in the same transaction.
projects.project_description: Kosha is a tax-native x402 payment gateway on Hedera. AI agents pay APIs in USDC over x402, and Kosha works out the Indian tax on each payment and withholds it in the same Hedera transaction. The problem: under Indian law, USDC is a virtual digital asset. When an agent pays an Indian API in USDC, the API owner is treated as the buyer of that asset, so the owner must deduct 1% TDS (tax deducted at source) once a payer's yearly total passes ₹10,000, or 20% if the payer has no PAN (Indian tax ID). No agent-payment tool handles this when the payment happens. Every API owner selling to agents would have to track yearly totals per payer and withhold the tax by hand, and mistakes cost interest and penalties. How Kosha works: an API owner adds Kosha Gate, a few lines of server middleware, so the endpoint answers HTTP 402 and is paid through Kosha. When an agent calls it, Kosha Core (our x402 facilitator) quotes the payment. It looks up the agent's identity, converts the price to rupees, checks this payer and API pair's yearly total, and runs a tax engine whose rules live in a versioned rule pack, so a chartered accountant can review and change them without touching code. The agent's client, Kosha Pay, checks every leg against its owner's spending policy (per-payment and daily limits, yearly budget, allowlist), then signs. Core settles it as one atomic Hedera TransferTransaction: the API receives exactly its price, and the TDS goes to a reserve account the agent owns jointly with Kosha (a 2-of-2 key). Core then writes the decision to Hedera Consensus Service: the amounts, the rate, the rule-pack hash and the pair's running total. Anyone can recompute the tax from that public log. After the tax is paid to the government each month, the reserve is released through a scheduled transaction that the agent co-signs. Kosha Console is the dashboard for API owners, agent owners and their accountants: live payments, earnings, progress toward the threshold, the TDS ledger, and filing exports. Every 402 response also offers the standard x402 "exact" scheme, so an unmodified x402 client can still pay through Kosha. We've settled such a payment on testnet. Why Hedera: fixed fees of a fraction of a cent make it worth withholding 1% of an ₹8 API call. A native multi-party transfer splits the payment atomically without a smart contract. HCS provides an ordered, append-only evidence log that only Kosha can write to. Scheduled transactions handle the jointly controlled reserve without custody code. Kosha uses no smart contracts, only native HTS, HCS and scheduled transactions. Core pays all Hedera fees, so agents and API owners never need HBAR. Agents get an identity through HCS-14 and HCS-11 profiles.
projects.how_its_made:
Kosha is a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces and Turborepo, Node 24) with four parts that ship and three shared packages. Kosha Core is our own x402 facilitator: a Fastify 5 server with Zod 4 schemas, Postgres through Drizzle ORM, and node-cron jobs. It quotes, verifies and settles payments, runs the tax engine, and is the only component that touches Hedera, as the fee payer. Kosha Gate is middleware an API owner drops into an Express server. Kosha Pay wraps fetch on the agent's side. The Console is Next.js 16 with Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui and TanStack Query. The tax engine is a pure function, decide(), with no I/O, driven by a versioned JSON rule pack. Every wire format is a Zod schema in one shared package, so Core, Gate, Pay and the Console validate against the same contracts. Hedera is the backbone. We use the Hiero SDK and no smart contracts, only native services: HTS: one TransferTransaction sends the price to the API and the tax to the agent's reserve, atomically. A contract-free split like this is what makes 1% of an ₹8 API call worth withholding at a fixed fraction-of-a-cent fee.
HCS: every tax decision is published to a topic whose submit key is Core's, with the amounts, rate, rule-pack hash and the pair's running yearly total, so anyone can recompute it.
Scheduled transactions: each agent's reserve is a 2-of-2 KeyList account (agent plus Kosha). After the monthly tax payment, Core schedules the release and the agent co-signs it, so Kosha never holds an agent's key.
Mirror Node: payer keys, reconciling timed-out receipts, and Gate's reserve proof.
HCS-14 and HCS-11 give each demo agent a UAID and an on-chain profile.
The demo agent runs on Hedera Agent Kit v4 with LangChain. Settlement runs on Circle testnet USDC, plus our own 6-decimal test token for development, because the faucet only gives 20 USDC every two hours.
We follow x402 v2 exactly (PAYMENT-REQUIRED, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, PAYMENT-RESPONSE headers, network hedera:testnet) using @x402/core's codecs. The interesting parts: We had to invent our own x402 scheme. The official Hedera "exact" scheme rejects any credit except one to payTo, so a tax split can't fit in it. Every 402 offers two entries: "kosha-split", our atomic split for Kosha Pay, and the standard "exact" one. Compatibility mode lets a stock x402 client pay a Kosha endpoint unchanged. The client pays the all-in amount to a Kosha settlement account, and a loop in Core forwards the price to the API and the tax to a pooled reserve in a second transaction. We record that transaction's ID before submitting it. If it times out, we ask the Mirror Node what happened instead of resubmitting, so nothing is ever paid twice. We tested this with unmodified @x402/fetch and @x402/hedera. Gate doesn't take Core's word that the tax was reserved. Before serving the response, it reads the settled transaction from the Mirror Node itself and checks the reserve was credited. It imports a fetch-only Mirror Node module, so the Hedera SDK never enters the API owner's bundle. Because Core pays every fee, it is what an attacker would target. Its verifier rejects anything that isn't exactly the quoted transfer: wrong fee payer, memo or nodes, a fee cap that's too high, any HBAR, NFT or allowance transfer, an extra credit, or a tax leg that doesn't go to the payer's own reserve. Each failure has its own error code. Pay runs the mirror-image checks before it signs. To make sure we never under-deduct, a pair's yearly total also counts quotes still open, so two concurrent quotes just under the ₹10,000 threshold can't both skip the tax. Tax is rounded up twice: in rupees, then again in USDC micro-units. Money is always an integer, never a float. HCS writes go through an outbox stored in the same database transaction as the payment, so a slow consensus write never blocks a payment or loses evidence. Privacy: no PAN or counterparty name ever reaches HCS. A payer and receiver pair appears only as an HMAC, and a PAN only as a salted commitment in Postgres. Tests use PGlite, Postgres running in-process, so they need no Docker. The tax engine also has fast-check property tests checking that it never under-deducts and that tax never drops as the amount rises.

projects.title: Ethereum Game Box
projects.description: A tabletop console where friends tap NFC wallet badges to play for prizes on Ethereum.
projects.project_description: Ethereum Game Box is a tabletop console where friends tap NFC wallet badges to play games for an onchain prize pool. Nobody needs a wallet app, ETH for gas, or transaction pop-ups. Each badge holds a private key that never leaves its NFC chip. Players tap to join, claim an ENS name, and stake test USDC. The Box runs the game, signs the result with a hardware P-256 key, and submits it through a relayer that pays the gas. The contract pays the winner on Sepolia. ENS handles Box licenses, player names, and competitive titles. A win can transfer champion.stockduel.gamebox.eth and count toward a cup. Players keep their names across Boxes, and anyone can look up the titles and championship results. The Box includes Quick Draw and Stock Duel. Games from the store use an AI judge running through 0G's private inference. The judge reads the match log and decides the payout. We also built a deliberately rigged game that reports inflated scores to test whether the judge catches cheating. The hardware is a Raspberry Pi 5 with a touchscreen, wireless NFC tap stations, and a USB signing token
projects.how_its_made: The project is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo with Solidity contracts built using Foundry. Each player uses a HaLo NFC wallet badge. ESP32-S3 tap stations read the badges through PN532 readers and send packets over ESP-NOW to a USB receiver on the Pi. We use libhalo to communicate with the chips. Each station has a display, light, and vibration motor for immediate tap feedback. The Box signs operations with a HYP2003 USB token. It generates its P-256 private key internally and never exports it. A Python daemon accesses the token through PKCS#11 and patched OpenSC. Ethereum's P256VERIFY precompile checks the signatures onchain. GameBoxNames registers each Box's public key, so contracts can verify which Box authorized a stake or result. A Cloudflare Worker relays signed requests and pays the gas. A Durable Object submits transactions one at a time. The relayer simulates each request before spending gas. We use ENSv2 on Sepolia for Box licenses, player identities, and expiring championship titles. GBX staking keeps a Box's license active. Signed wins transfer titles and score cups. The public site reads ENS and contract events through viem without a backend or database. For store games, a Cloudflare Worker starts an AI judge in a Cloudflare Container. The judge uses 0G's private inference to compare the game's claims with the Box's match log. Our rigged game deliberately inflates its scores to test this check. The Worker verifies each turn's enclave signature against 0G's serving contract, then submits the verdict to StorePot. Valid verdicts pay the players; failed judging returns their stakes. This flow has judged and settled real matches on Sepolia.

projects.title: Atlas
projects.description: Atlas — Connecting Global Assets. Unlocking Intelligent Liquidity.
projects.project_description: Atlas is a Web3 platform for trading global markets from one wallet. Users sign in with MetaMask, prove they are a unique human with World ID, and can use an ENS name as public identity. Their profiles are stored encrypted on Arkiv. What it does: Global stock markets on-chain: five ERC-1155 market contracts on Sepolia hold 50 synthetic stocks. Prices come in each stock's native currency and are converted through FX into USD and USDT. Trades are funded from a reserve and settled in a demo USDT token. Vault: an ERC-4626 vault where users deposit USDT and earn yield. Strategy marketplace: users build trading strategies in a strategy studio, publish them, browse and clone other people's, and pay creators a fee. Each strategy shows simulated performance. Natural-language intent engine: users describe a strategy in plain English and confirm it before it runs. Paper trading simulator: users can test strategies against seeded or replayed market data without sending any real transactions. Admin console: for listing new stocks, managing roles and updating prices. All assets are synthetic demo assets on testnet and give no legal ownership of real equity.
projects.how_its_made: The Atlas demo maps directly to production, with signed intents, risk checks, liquidity decisions, and state management transitioning to EIP-712 verification, Solidity policy contracts, Go-based risk services and keepers, Uniswap v4 pools and hooks, and an indexer database. Uniswap v4 provides liquidity infrastructure, Chainlink or Pyth supplies price feeds, Safe enables multisig treasury controls, and Permit2 streamlines token approvals. Production readiness will require third-party audits, fork-based testing, pre-trade simulation, MEV protection, resilient keepers, and compliance gating for regulated assets. The prototype already includes 28 tests covering atomic reverts, token conservation, spend limits, and deterministic resets, with exact integer arithmetic for prices and balances.

projects.title: Mergit
projects.description: Mergit pays AI agents only for audited work; we gave each agent a verifiable ENSv2 name on mainnet.
projects.project_description: WHAT MERGIT IS (existing project). Mergit is a trust and settlement layer for autonomous AI agent work. Today, when you hand a task to an agent you pay for the attempt, and nothing measures whether the task was actually done. In Mergit, a requester funds a plan into escrow on Base Sepolia, an agent runs each task in a sandbox, every step is recorded in a signed receipt, and a validator audits the result against a check the requester approved up front. Payment is released only when the check passes, and a failed attempt is refunded and handed to the next agent. Agents stake collateral, are identified by an ERC-8004-style on-chain identity, and earn a record only from audited outcomes. It runs live today: a web app, a Python orchestration layer, a Rust gateway and validator, and the escrow, stake and reputation contracts. WHAT WE BUILT ON TOP FOR ENS (new in this hackathon). Agents had on-chain ids but no human-readable, checkable identity. We gave each agent a public ENSv2 name under mergit.eth on Ethereum mainnet. A name is linked to its agent in both directions: an ENSIP-25 style record on the name points at the agent, and the agent's registration file points back at the name. The web app resolves the names live and shows a Verified badge only when both sides agree, or the exact reason it can't. Each name also carries a description, a public profile page, a mirror of the agent's audited track record, and its current operator. A final ledger of audited outcomes is committed to ENS as a hash plus a URL, and a /ledger page re-checks the file against it. Agents, money and receipts stay on Base Sepolia; only names and records are on mainnet.
projects.how_its_made: EXISTING (before the hackathon): Rust services (receipt builder and verifier, chain gateway, validator and receipt store), a Python FastAPI control plane (planner, task graph, router, sandbox worker), Solidity contracts on Base Sepolia (identity, escrow, stake vault, challenge manager, reputation anchor), and a React web app, deployed with Docker and Caddy. NEW FOR ENS: One ENSv2 PermissionedResolver on mainnet serves every agent subname, so adding an agent means writing records, not minting a token. A one-shot script (TypeScript, viem) deploys the resolver, grants narrow per-key roles (a publisher key may write only mergit.reputation, mergit.operator and mergit.ledger; an editor key only agent-context and agent-endpoint[web]), writes the records in one multicall, copies mergit.eth's own address record, and repoints mergit.eth last, so the name never stops resolving. Testing on a mainnet fork showed that ENS scopes a role to the whole resolver, so operators get no direct role and Mergit's key writes after checking ownership on Base. A publisher folds OutcomeRecorded events from the Base ReputationAnchor into the record (tier 0 only, one count per task, a challenge ruling beats an audit). The React app reads ENS live with viem, renders chain text as plain text, and never lets ENS data steer routing. Hacky bits: every chain write is a dry run unless --execute, and 193 ens tests plus 508 frontend tests run on forks of mainnet and Base Sepolia.

Agents, money and receipts stay on Base Sepolia; only names and records are on mainnet.
projects.how_its_made_markdown:
EXISTING (before the hackathon): Rust services (receipt builder and verifier, chain gateway, validator and receipt store), a Python FastAPI control plane (planner, task graph, router, sandbox worker), Solidity contracts on Base Sepolia (identity, escrow, stake vault, challenge manager, reputation anchor), and a React web app, deployed with Docker and Caddy.

NEW FOR ENS: One ENSv2 PermissionedResolver on mainnet serves every agent subname, so adding an agent means writing records, not minting a token. A one-shot script (TypeScript, viem) deploys the resolver, grants narrow per-key roles (a publisher key may write only mergit.reputation, mergit.operator and mergit.ledger; an editor key only agent-context and agent-endpoint[web]), writes the records in one multicall, copies mergit.eth's own address record, and repoints mergit.eth last, so the name never stops resolving. Testing on a mainnet fork showed that ENS scopes a role to the whole resolver, so operators get no direct role and Mergit's key writes after checking ownership on Base. A publisher folds OutcomeRecorded events from the Base ReputationAnchor into the record (tier 0 only, one count per task, a challenge ruling beats an audit). The React app reads ENS live with viem, renders chain text as plain text, and never lets ENS data steer routing. Hacky bits: every chain write is a dry run unless --execute, and 193 ens tests plus 508 frontend tests run on forks of mainnet and Base Sepolia.

projects.title: Eagle Byte
projects.description: Helping businesses receive international payments with lower-cost crypto transfers.
projects.project_description: Eaglebyte is a digital agency building a portal to make international payments easier for founders and business owners. When a client pays from another country, the business can use the platform to receive payment through supported crypto channels. The goal is to make cross-border payments faster and reduce additional charges, while giving businesses a straightforward way to manage incoming payments.
projects.how_its_made: The portal is designed to connect businesses with supported crypto payment and exchange services. A browser-based interface helps users manage payment flows, while a state-channel hub-and-spoke model coordinates transfers. The project uses Rust for the backend and MobX for the frontend, with integrations planned for Coinbase and Bitfinex APIs.

projects.title: veris
projects.description: Clip-on hardware for phones & cameras that proves a photo is real the instant the shutter fires.
projects.project_description:
Veris is a hardware-to-blockchain authenticity system that proves a photo is real at the exact moment it’s taken. It’s a small device that attaches to the camera you already use: the VERIS Clip for phones and the VERIS Hotshoe for DSLR and mirrorless cameras. Every time you press the shutter, Veris captures its own witness image of the same scene, signs it with a key locked inside its hardware, proves it with a zero-knowledge proof, stores everything on decentralized storage, and mints an on-chain certificate of ownership to the photographer. Anyone can then verify the photo at veris.live in seconds. Authenticity becomes a hardware guarantee, not a software promise. 📌 The Problem
Real photos are losing the ability to be believed. A journalist photographs a politician in a room with someone who shouldn’t be there, posts it, and within minutes people call it AI. A forensic expert photographs a crime scene with the weapon in frame; if that weapon later disappears, there’s no way to prove the photo wasn’t edited. Deepfake detectors only guess after the fact, and the guesses get worse as generators improve. Watermarks and metadata can be stripped or forged. Photographers have no reliable way to prove their work is real, and no clean way to prove ownership or license it. 💡 Solution
Veris proves a photo is real instead of guessing whether it’s fake. Clip it onto your phone or slide it into your camera’s hot shoe and shoot as normal. At the instant of capture, Veris records an independent, hardware-signed image of the scene, checks it matches your main photo, and seals both with cryptographic proof. The photographer gets a certificate of ownership, and the world gets a public, tamper-evident record anyone can check without trusting us. 🛠️ How It Works Capture: You shoot as usual. Veris fires in sync with your shutter and captures its own witness image. Attest: The device signs the image with a private key generated inside its hardware. The key can’t be extracted, copied, or faked. Match: Our models confirm the witness image and your main high-res photo show the same real scene, so your photo inherits the hardware proof. Prove: A zero-knowledge proof confirms the signature, device identity, and image integrity without revealing the photographer, exact GPS, or device serial. Store: The photo, witness image, proof, and metadata are stored on decentralized storage so nothing can be quietly edited or swapped. Certify: An ownership certificate is minted on-chain to the photographer’s wallet. Verify: Anyone uploads a photo at veris.live and sees whether it’s genuine, when and roughly where it was taken, and the full claim record. 🎯 Applications Verified journalism: proof that a real device captured a real moment, especially for conflict and political reporting Forensic evidence: proof of exactly what a scene looked like at capture time, aligned with the electronic evidence certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam in India Insurance claims backed by photos that can’t be staged after the fact Photographer ownership and licensing at under half a cent per photo Privacy-preserving authenticity: prove a photo is real without leaking who took it or exactly where
projects.how_its_made:
🔧 Hardware Layer
Veris is built on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a Camera Module, acting as a self-contained cryptographic witness that sits alongside your main camera. When you shoot, Veris captures its own image of the same moment and handles signing, hashing, and handoff to the Web3 pipeline right on the device. It pairs with the VERIS app over Bluetooth. The full design uses a TPM 2.0 chip to hold the device key and a GPS module to bind location into every capture. We weren’t able to get hold of either in time for this build, so the pipeline is built TPM- and GPS-ready and both slot in without changing anything downstream. 🔐 Hardware Identity Module
Until the TPM 2.0 is in, Veris generates its keypair from silicon entropy inside a Hardware Identity Module. The private key never leaves the device and signs every capture alongside its image hash, giving each photo a non-forgeable device origin. 👁️ Dual-Capture Matching
This is what lets Veris work with cameras people already own. The phone or DSLR shoots a high-res image while Veris shoots its own, and the two differ in lens, resolution, and framing. An RL model maps structure, framing, and capture settings between the two images so they can be aligned and compared.
A 5-layer verification model then confirms both images show the same real scene, outputting forensic SSIM, change type, and a consistency score with visual and content components.
The scene description, tags, and an AI-generation assessment on the witness image are all written into the claim record. 🧠 Zero-Knowledge Proof Pipeline
Signed captures generate a zero-knowledge proof that the image hash matches, the signing key belongs to a genuine Veris device, and the capture is fresh, without exposing raw metadata, location, or identity. The proof is verified on-chain by our VerisVerifier.sol contract on RISC Zero. 📦 Storage Layer (0G + Arkiv)
0G stores the main image, witness image, proof, and metadata JSON. We needed storage that’s decentralized and able to hold full-resolution images, because the whole point is that nothing can be changed after capture.
Arkiv is our database for claim records: device ID, camera ID, image hash, signature, storage IDs, transaction hash, location, AI assessment, and the companion capture block. This is what makes lookups on the verify page fast.
IPFS is an automatic fallback if Arkiv is unavailable, so verification never goes down. 🔗 Smart Contracts & Chains (Arc + Base)
VerisVerifier.sol: verifies the ZK proof and validates image and metadata hashes
VerisERC1155.sol: mints the ownership certificate to the photographer’s wallet Certificates are minted on Arc and Base. Arc’s stablecoin-based fees keep things predictable, which makes per-photo licensing viable. 🌐 Claim & Verify Portal (veris.live)
Each capture gets a unique claim ID and QR code. The photographer scans to claim the certificate to their wallet. Every photo has a public claim page at veris.live/claim/<id>, and anyone can upload an image at veris.live/search to check it against the record. No account and no trust in us required. ⚙️ Hacky Engineering
Using an independently signed witness capture to vouch for a high-res photo, instead of trying to secure the main camera’s sensor
Building the pipeline TPM- and GPS-ready so we could ship without the parts, using a silicon-entropy key in the meantime
An RL model to align two completely different cameras’ views of the same moment
Running capture, signing, hashing, ZK proof requests, and uploads together on a single Raspberry Pi 4 without lagging the capture
Dual-minting on Arc and Base, and Arkiv with automatic IPFS fallback, so one chain or service going down never breaks a photo’s proof

projects.title: GTMmaxing.com
projects.description: OpenRouter for GTM tools, where AI agents pay from their own wallets and stop by ENS name.
projects.project_description: GTMMAXING is OpenRouter for GTM tools. One account and one credit balance give people and AI agents contact enrichment, lead lists, web research and social listening, from the browser, MCP, a CLI or an API. This is a Continuity Track project: GTMMAXING was live before this event. The problem. Agents can now do sales research on their own, but they can't fill in a card form. An agent that ran out of credits simply stopped until a person found a card and bought a plan. And nobody outside the product could see or stop what an agent was allowed to spend. What we added at ETHGlobal Mumbai: Uniswap: agents pay for themselves. A refused call now says where to buy and exactly how many credits are needed. Once its owner switches this on, the agent pays from its own wallet, up to $50 a payment, and repeats the same call. People can buy any plan the same way, with almost any token on eight networks, and we receive USDC on Base. Small payments can go into a Token Jar, which a keeper clears for USDC when that's profitable. ENS: a public off switch. An agent's ENSv2 name holds one text record that decides whether it may start paid work. On a Permissioned Resolver, Enhanced Access Control lets a limited wallet edit only that key, so a teammate can stop an agent without controlling the name. Arc: the simplest checkout. USDC is both money and gas, so one transfer is the whole payment. We built it on our live site and in Arc Studio. It runs on Arc Testnet and never grants credits. Proof, all real transactions: 0.001 ETH from Arbitrum became $2.21 USDC on Base and 147 credits. A full Token Jar round cleared on Base. An agent bought 66 credits from its own wallet. A mainnet ENS record points at a production agent, written by the limited wallet. Test USDC payments confirmed on Arc from both the live site and the Arc Studio app. Not proven yet: a full plan payment hasn't been made, though real quotes cover plan prices. The hourly jar clearing hasn't been seen running. ENS stop and resume were tested on a local build against real mainnet ENS.
projects.how_its_made: Repo notes. This continues a live product whose production code is in a private monorepo, so the entry can't be a fork of it. The public repository holds the Uniswap, ENS and Arc work under MIT. Its first commit holds those files as they stood before the event, and later commits replay our real commits from the private repository, limited to these files. Supplier integrations and server wiring stay private, so it doesn't build into the full app. The README points to the exact lines and transactions. The backend is a Cloudflare Worker (TypeScript, Hono) with a D1 database, and the site is Astro and React. All wallet actions are decided by the server, so the page can't redirect a payment. Uniswap API: /quote, /check_approval, /swap and /plan. CLASSIC, BRIDGE and CHAINED routes all pay a treasury the server sets. Chained routes needed the x-chained-actions-enabled header, which isn't in the integration guide, and permit data needed converting into a shape wallets can sign. Both are in our FEEDBACK.md. Fixed prices were the hard part. Exact-output quotes only worked for us within one chain, so we invert exact-input quotes: price the token, scale the payment until even the guaranteed minimum covers the plan price, then check. Any excess comes back as credits. Credits only come from what the chain shows. The wallet signs for one account, the transaction must match the calldata Uniswap built, plans must be owned by our API key, and unique indexes stop a delivery being used twice. A database trigger adds the credits in the same statement. Token Jar (TJAR): we deployed a jar and releaser through the Factory on Base. We wrote an open-source keeper in TypeScript with viem that prices the jar through the Uniswap API, clears it when profitable, and swaps the proceeds back. It runs from the command line and from an hourly job. ENS: every new agent run reads the text record through the ENS Universal Resolver on mainnet. A confirmed answer stands for 30 seconds, and during a chain outage the last answer stands for an hour, then the run is refused. Enhanced Access Control on the Permissioned Resolver limits the delegate wallet to this key. Arc: the checkout sends one ERC-20 transfer on the USDC contract, and the server confirms the receipt, amount, sender and treasury on chain, using unique transaction hashes. The test path can't reach the credit ledger. A separate version was built and deployed from Arc Studio, and its source is in arc-studio/. We hit RPC rate limits on the official endpoints, so we moved to dRPC.
